(b) The presumption of subdivision (a) is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof and may be rebutted by admissible evidence showing that application of the formula would be unjust or inappropriate in the particular case, consistent with the principles set forth in Section 4053, because one or more of the following factors is found to be applicable by a preponderance of the evidence, and the court states in writing or on the record the information required in subdivision (a) of Section 4056:

clauses.title: The Statewide Guideline Formula
clauses.body: California's guideline formula for calculating child support is codified as an algebraic equation: CS = K[HN - (H%)(TN)]. In the formula, CS is the child support amount; K is the share of both parents' combined income allocated to child support; HN is the higher-earning parent's net monthly disposable income; H% is the approximate percentage of time the higher-earning parent has (or will have) primary physical responsibility for the children, compared to the other parent; and TN is the total net monthly disposable income of both parents combined. The statute further specifies that K itself is not a fixed number — it is calculated from a formula that varies with H% and with the parents' combined net monthly income, using a bracketed schedule set out in the statute. {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} may reference their own net incomes and time-sharing percentages for {{childName}} as informational inputs, without this document performing or certifying a guideline calculation.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that an income-based guideline formula with this specific algebraic structure exists and is codified in exact numeric detail — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter, and not a representation that this formula applies outside California. The formula, its defined variables, and its K-factor schedule are all jurisdiction-specific; most states use an entirely different model (for example, an "income shares" model rather than California's percentage-of-income model), so neither the equation nor its coefficients transfer to another state's guideline. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4055) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4055(a)-(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the formula and its defined variables
citations.quote: The statewide uniform guideline for determining child support orders is as follows: CS = K[HN - (H%)(TN)]. (b) (1) The components of the formula are as follows: (A) CS = child support amount. (B) K = amount of both parents' income to be allocated for child support as set forth in paragraph (3). (C) HN = high earner's net monthly disposable income. (D) H% = approximate percentage of time that the high earner has or will have primary physical responsibility for the children compared to the other parent. In cases in which parents have different time-sharing arrangements for different children, H% equals the average of the approximate percentages of time the high earner parent spends with each child. (E) TN = total net monthly disposable income of both parties.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4055(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the K-factor income-band schedule
citations.quote: K (amount of both parents' income allocated for child support) equals one plus H% (if H% is less than or equal to 50 percent) or two minus H% (if H% is greater than 50 percent) times the following fraction: Total Net Disposable Income Per Month K $0–2,900 0.165 + TN/82,857 $2,901–5,000 0.131 + TN/42,149 $5,001–10,000 0.250 $10,001–15,000 0.10 + 1,499/TN Over $15,000 0.12 + 1,200/TN

clauses.title: Enumerated Principles Behind the Guideline
clauses.body: California's child support statute states that the courts must adhere to a specific, enumerated list of principles when implementing the guideline, including: a parent's first and principal obligation is to support the parent's minor children according to the parent's circumstances and station in life; both parents are mutually responsible for the support of their children; each parent should pay for the support of the children according to the parent's ability; the guideline seeks to place the interests of children as the state's top priority; children should share in the standard of living of both parents, and child support may therefore appropriately improve the standard of living of the custodial household; the financial needs of the children should be met through private financial resources as much as possible; and the guideline is intended to be presumptively correct in all cases, with departures below the guideline formula reserved for special circumstances.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a real, specific, enumerated set of policy principles underlies a guideline child support system — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. Whether any such principles are codified, and what they say, varies by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 4053); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4053 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the enumerated statutory principles
citations.quote: In implementing the statewide uniform guideline, the courts shall adhere to the following principles: (a) A parent's first and principal obligation is to support the parent's minor children according to the parent's circumstances and station in life. (b) Both parents are mutually responsible for the support of their children. (c) The guideline takes into account each parent's actual income and level of responsibility for the children. (d) Each parent should pay for the support of the children according to the parent's ability. (e) The guideline seeks to place the interests of children as the state's top priority. (f) Children should share in the standard of living of both parents. Child support may therefore appropriately improve the standard of living of the custodial household to improve the lives of the children. (g) Child support orders in cases in which both parents have high levels of responsibility for the children should reflect the increased costs of raising the children in two homes and should minimize significant disparities in the children's living standards in the two homes. (h) The financial needs of the children should be met through private financial resources as much as possible. (i) It is presumed that a parent having primary physical responsibility for the children contributes a significant portion of available resources for the support of the children. (j) The guideline seeks to encourage fair and efficient settlements of conflicts between parents and seeks to minimize the need for litigation. (k) The guideline is intended to be presumptively correct in all cases, and only under special circumstances should child support orders fall below the child support mandated by the guideline formula. (l) Child support orders shall ensure that children actually receive fair, timely, and sufficient support reflecting the state's high standard of living and high costs of raising children compared to other states.

clauses.title: Enumerated Grounds for Departing from the Guideline
clauses.body: California's statute lists specific, enumerated factors that can support a departure from the guideline formula amount, including: the parties have stipulated to a different amount under the statute's stipulation provision; sale of the family residence is deferred and the rental value of the residence where the children reside exceeds the mortgage, insurance, and property tax payments; the parent ordered to pay support has an extraordinarily high income and the formula amount would exceed the children's needs; a party is not contributing to the children's needs at a level commensurate with that party's custodial time; a support obligor qualifies for the statute's low-income adjustment and the formula amount (after that adjustment) would still exceed 50 percent of the obligor's net disposable income; and other special circumstances, including different time-sharing arrangements for different children, a large disparity in housing-cost burden between parents with substantially equal timeshare, a child's special medical or other needs, or a child found to have more than two parents.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that departure from a guideline formula is limited to a specific, enumerated list of grounds rather than open-ended negotiation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. This draws on the same statutory section as the presumptive-correctness clause above (§ 4057); no additional independent source was found for the departure list itself. What circumstances (if any) justify departing from a guideline amount is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4057(b)(1)-(6) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the enumerated departure grounds
citations.quote: (1) The parties have stipulated to a different amount of child support under subdivision (a) of Section 4065. (2) The sale of the family residence is deferred pursuant to Chapter 8 (commencing with Section 3800) of Part 1 and the rental value of the family residence where the children reside exceeds the mortgage payments, homeowner's insurance, and property taxes. The amount of any adjustment pursuant to this paragraph shall not be greater than the excess amount. (3) The parent being ordered to pay child support has an extraordinarily high income and the amount determined under the formula would exceed the needs of the children. (4) A party is not contributing to the needs of the children at a level commensurate with that party's custodial time. (5) A support obligor qualifies for the low-income adjustment pursuant to paragraph (7) of subdivision (b) of Section 4055 and the amount of child support established by the formula exceeds 50 percent of the support obligor's net disposable income as defined in Section 4059 after application of the low-income adjustment. The amount of any adjustment pursuant to this paragraph shall not be greater than the amount exceeding 50 percent of the support obligor's net disposable income. (6) Application of the formula would be unjust or inappropriate due to special circumstances in the particular case. These special circumstances include, but are not limited to, the following: (A) Cases in which the parents have different time-sharing arrangements for different children. (B) Cases in which both parents have substantially equal time-sharing of the children and one parent has a much lower or higher percentage of income used for housing than the other parent. (C) Cases in which the children have special medical or other needs that could require child support that would be greater than the formula amount. (D) Cases in which a child is found to have more than two parents.

clauses.title: Conditions for a Stipulated Below-Guideline Amount
clauses.body: California's statute allows parties to stipulate to a child support amount, subject to court approval, but sets specific conditions before a court may approve a stipulated amount that is below the guideline formula amount. The statute requires the parties to declare that: they are fully informed of their rights concerning child support; the order is being agreed to without coercion or duress; the agreement is in the best interests of the children involved; the needs of the children will be adequately met by the stipulated amount; and the right to support has not been assigned to the county and no public assistance application is pending.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a below-guideline agreed amount is conditioned on a specific, enumerated set of declarations rather than free negotiation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter, and not a certification that these conditions have been met here. Whether a jurisdiction permits stipulated below-guideline support at all, and on what conditions, is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 4065(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4065(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the conditions for a stipulated below-guideline amount
citations.quote: Unless prohibited by applicable federal law, the parties may stipulate to a child support amount subject to approval of the court. However, the court shall not approve a stipulated agreement for child support below the guideline formula amount unless the parties declare all of the following: (1) They are fully informed of their rights concerning child support. (2) The order is being agreed to without coercion or duress. (3) The agreement is in the best interests of the children involved. (4) The needs of the children will be adequately met by the stipulated amount. (5) The right to support has not been assigned to the county pursuant to Section 11477 of the Welfare and Institutions Code and no public assistance application is pending.

clauses.title: Low-Income Adjustment
clauses.body: California's guideline statute includes a specific low-income adjustment mechanism. Where the support-paying parent's net disposable monthly income is less than the amount of monthly gross income earned from full-time minimum wage, there is a rebuttable presumption that parent is entitled to a low-income adjustment reducing the guideline amount, calculated by a statutory fraction. That presumption can be rebutted by evidence that applying the lowest permitted support amount would be unjust and inappropriate in the particular case, considering the statute's stated principles and the impact of the adjustment on both parents' net incomes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a guideline formula can include a specific, codified low-income adjustment mechanism, rather than assuming one exists — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. This draws on the same statutory section as the guideline-formula clause above (§ 4055); no additional independent source was found for the low-income adjustment itself. Whether a low-income adjustment exists, and how it is calculated, is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4055(b)(7) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the low-income adjustment presumption
citations.quote: In all cases in which the net disposable income per month of the obligor is less than the amount of monthly gross income earned from full-time minimum wage, established by Section 1182.12 of the Labor Code, at 40 hours per week, 52 weeks per year, there is a rebuttable presumption that the obligor is entitled to a low-income adjustment. The presumption may be rebutted by evidence showing that the application of the lowest amount of child support permitted pursuant to this paragraph would be unjust and inappropriate in the particular case. In determining whether the presumption is rebutted, the court shall consider the principles provided in Section 4053, and the impact of the contemplated adjustment on the respective net incomes of the obligor and the obligee.

clauses.title: Mandatory vs. Discretionary Add-On Expenses
clauses.body: California's statute distinguishes mandatory from discretionary additional child support amounts. It requires courts to order, as additional child support: childcare costs actually incurred that are related to employment or to reasonably necessary education or training for employment skills (unless already included in the guideline calculation), and reasonable uninsured health care costs for the children. Separately, it authorizes but does not require courts to order, as additional child support: costs related to the educational or other special needs of the children, and travel expenses for visitation.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a guideline system can distinguish mandatory from discretionary add-on expense categories, and how one state actually draws that line — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. Which expense categories (if any) are mandatory versus discretionary is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state. This is a single statutory section (§ 4062(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4062(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mandatory/discretionary add-on distinction
citations.quote: (a) The court shall order the following as additional child support: (1) Childcare costs, if those expenses are actually incurred, related to employment or to reasonably necessary education or training for employment skills, as described in Section 4063, unless those costs are specifically included in the guideline calculation itself. (2) The reasonable uninsured health care costs for the children as provided in Section 4063. (b) The court may order the following as additional child support: (1) Costs related to the educational or other special needs of the children. (2) Travel expenses for visitation.

clauses.title: Duration of the Support Obligation
clauses.body: California's statute establishes that the parental duty to support a minor child continues as to an unmarried child who has turned 18, is a full-time high school student, and is not self-supporting, until the child completes the 12th grade or turns 19, whichever occurs first; a child who has a physician-documented medical condition preventing full-time school attendance is excused from the full-time-student requirement without ending the support duty on that basis alone.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a parental child support duty can be tied by statute to a specific age plus a school-enrollment condition, rather than a flat age cutoff — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. The age, school-enrollment condition, and any medical exception are all jurisdiction-specific and vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3900 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the general parental support obligation
citations.quote: Subject to this division, the father and mother of a minor child have an equal responsibility to support their child in the manner suitable to the child's circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3901(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the age-18-plus-high-school-student extension and its medical exception
citations.quote: (1) The duty of support imposed by Section 3900 continues as to an unmarried child who has attained 18 years of age, is a full-time high school student, unless excused pursuant to paragraph (2), and who is not self-supporting, until the time the child completes the 12th grade or attains 19 years of age, whichever occurs first. (2) A child is excused from the requirement to be a full-time high school student for purposes of paragraph (1) if the child has a medical condition documented by a physician that prevents full-time school attendance.

clauses.title: Support Orders Include an Earnings Assignment
clauses.body: California's statute provides that when a court orders a party to pay support, or modifies a support amount, the court's order must include an earnings assignment order directing the paying parent's employer to pay the support obligee directly, in an amount sufficient to cover both the ongoing support amount and any amount ordered toward liquidating arrears. The statute states this earnings assignment order is effective and enforceable even without the employer's name, address, or other identifying information on file at the time it issues.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a court-ordered support obligation can carry an automatic wage/earnings withholding mechanism directed at the paying parent's employer — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific child support matter. Whether an earnings assignment is automatic, optional, or unavailable, and how it is triggered, is jurisdiction-specific and varies by state; this clause also does not describe how withholding would apply to a private agreement that has not been entered as a court order. This is a single statutory section (§ 5230(a)-(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 5230(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mandatory earnings assignment order
citations.quote: (a) When the court orders a party to pay an amount for support or orders a modification of the amount of support to be paid, the court shall include in its order an earnings assignment order for support that orders the employer of the obligor to pay to the obligee that portion of the obligor's earnings due or to become due in the future as will be sufficient to pay an amount to cover both of the following: (1) The amount ordered by the court for support. (2) An amount which shall be ordered by the court to be paid toward the liquidation of any arrearage. (b) An earnings assignment order for support shall be issued, and shall be effective and enforceable pursuant to Section 5231, notwithstanding the absence of the name, address, or other identifying information regarding the obligor's employer.

clauses.title: Declaration of Parents and Support Amount
clauses.body: {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}, as the parents of {{childName}} (date of birth: {{childDOB}}), state that they intend the following child support arrangement: {{payorName}} agreeing to pay {{payeeName}} the amount of ${{monthlySupportAmount}} per month, beginning {{supportStartDate}}, until the arrangement ends or is modified as described in this document.

clauses.title: Add-On Expense Allocation
clauses.body: The parents allocate the following categories of additional expenses for {{childName}} as follows: childcare/employment-related care costs — {{childcareAllocation}}; uninsured health care costs — {{healthcareAllocation}}; educational or special-needs costs — {{educationAllocation}}; travel expenses for visitation — {{travelAllocation}}. This schedule is a blank-fill allocation reference only and states no legal claim about which of these categories any jurisdiction treats as mandatory or discretionary.

clauses.title: Signature Block
Eligibility to Register as Domestic Partners
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, as of {{filingDate}}, each of the following is true: neither is married to another person or a partner in another domestic partnership that has not been terminated, dissolved, or adjudged a nullity; the two are not related by blood in a way that would prevent marriage to each other in California; each is at least 18 years of age; and each is capable of consenting to a domestic partnership.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as real evidence of what "domestic partnership" eligibility can require — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific couple's registration, or that these are the only requirements anywhere. Domestic partnership and civil union status varies enormously by state, and many states have no such status at all now that marriage is available nationally regardless of sex. This is a single statutory section (§ 297); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 297(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the current eligibility requirements
citations.quote: (a) Domestic partners are two adults who have chosen to share one another's lives in an intimate and committed relationship of mutual caring. (b) A domestic partnership shall be established in California when both persons file a Declaration of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State pursuant to this division, and, at the time of filing, all of the following requirements are met: (1) Neither person is married to someone else or is a member of another domestic partnership with someone else that has not been terminated, dissolved, or adjudged a nullity. (2) The two persons are not related by blood in a way that would prevent them from being married to each other in this state. (3) Both persons are at least 18 years of age, except as provided in Section 297.1. (4) Both persons are capable of consenting to the domestic partnership.

clauses.title: How a Domestic Partnership Is Registered
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that a domestic partnership is established by filing a Declaration of Domestic Partnership with the California Secretary of State, and that the Declaration form requires each person to state that they meet the statutory eligibility requirements, provide a mailing address, consent to the jurisdiction of the California Superior Courts for a future dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation proceeding, and sign under penalty of the form's declaration that all statements are true and complete, with the signature notarized. The Secretary of State registers the filed Declaration and returns a Certificate of Registered Domestic Partnership to the partners.
clauses.gap: This is one state's filing mechanism, used as real evidence of how a registration-based partnership status can be created — not a claim about which state's procedure applies to a specific couple, or that every jurisdiction with a similar status uses this same mechanism. Registration procedures, required disclosures, and notarization rules vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 298(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: required Declaration form content
citations.quote: The Declaration of Domestic Partnership shall require each person who wants to become a domestic partner to (1) state that the person meets the requirements of Section 297 at the time the form is signed, (2) provide a mailing address, (3) state that the person consents to the jurisdiction of the Superior Courts of California for the purpose of a proceeding to obtain a judgment of dissolution or nullity of the domestic partnership or for legal separation of partners in the domestic partnership, or for any other proceeding related to the partners' rights and obligations, even if one or both partners ceases to be a resident of, or to maintain a domicile in, this state, (4) sign the form with a declaration that representations made therein are true, correct, and contain no material omissions of fact to the best knowledge and belief of the applicant, and (5) have a notary public acknowledge the signature. Both partners' signatures shall be affixed to one Declaration of Domestic Partnership form, which shall then be transmitted to the Secretary of State according to the instructions provided on the form. Filing an intentionally and materially false Declaration of Domestic Partnership shall be punishable as a misdemeanor.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 298.5(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: filing and registration by the Secretary of State
citations.quote: (a) Two persons desiring to become domestic partners may complete and file a Declaration of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State. (b) The Secretary of State shall register the Declaration of Domestic Partnership in a registry for those partnerships, and shall return a copy of the registered form, a Certificate of Registered Domestic Partnership, and a copy of the brochure ... to the domestic partners at the mailing address provided by the domestic partners.

clauses.title: Statutory Effect of Registration — Same Rights and Duties as Spouses
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, under California law, registered domestic partners have the same rights, protections, and benefits, and are subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties under law — whether arising from statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, or any other source of law — as are granted to and imposed upon spouses, including with respect to any child of either partner.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a domestic partnership can carry marriage-equivalent legal consequences under that state's law — not a claim about the legal effect of a specific domestic partnership in any other state or under federal law generally. Whether a domestic partnership registered in one state produces marriage-equivalent rights in another state, or is recognized at all, is not addressed by this statute. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 297.5(a), (d)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(a), (d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the same-rights-and-duties statute
citations.quote: (a) Registered domestic partners shall have the same rights, protections, and benefits, and shall be subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties under law, whether they derive from statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, or any other provisions or sources of law, as are granted to and imposed upon spouses. ... (d) The rights and obligations of registered domestic partners with respect to a child of either of them shall be the same as those of spouses.

clauses.title: Community Property and Marital Property Statutes Apply
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, for purposes of the community property statutes, mutual responsibility for debts to third parties, spousal-support rights on dissolution, and other property statutes that turn on the date of a marriage, California law treats the date of registration of the domestic partnership as the reference date, in the same way the date of marriage functions for spouses.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subsection (§ 297.5(k)(1)); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a domestic partnership status can be tied to community-property rules by law — not a claim about which state's property regime, if any, applies to a specific couple's property. Community property is itself a minority regime among U.S. states, and a domestic partnership registered elsewhere may carry no property consequences at all.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 297.5(k)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the registration date functions as the marriage-date reference
citations.quote: For purposes of the statutes, administrative regulations, court rules, government policies, common law, and any other provision or source of law governing the rights, protections, and benefits, and the responsibilities, obligations, and duties of registered domestic partners in this state, as effectuated by this section, with respect to community property, mutual responsibility for debts to third parties, the right in particular circumstances of either partner to seek financial support from the other following the dissolution of the partnership, and other rights and duties as between the partners concerning ownership of property, any reference to the date of a marriage shall be deemed to refer to the date of registration of a domestic partnership with the state.

clauses.title: Ending a Domestic Partnership — Administrative Notice vs. Court Dissolution
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that California law provides two distinct paths to end a registered domestic partnership. A simplified administrative path — filing a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State without a court proceeding — is available only if, at the time of filing, both partners sign the Notice; there are no children of the relationship (born, adopted, or on the way) common to the partners; the partnership is not more than five years in duration; neither partner has any interest in real property (with a narrow exception for a short-term residential lease without a purchase option); neither partner has unpaid obligations or community-property assets above the statutory thresholds tied to Family Code § 2400; the partners have executed an agreement dividing their assets and liabilities; both partners waive any right to support from the other; both have read the Secretary of State's brochure on terminating a domestic partnership; and both desire termination. Absent those conditions, ending a partnership requires a dissolution, nullity, or legal-separation proceeding in California Superior Court, following the same procedures and producing the same rights, protections, benefits, responsibilities, obligations, and duties as apply to the dissolution, nullity, or legal separation of a marriage.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a registration-based partnership status can be terminated administratively versus judicially — not a claim about which state's procedure, if any, applies to a specific termination, nor a claim about the current dollar thresholds referenced in Family Code § 2400 (which are indexed and change over time and were not independently verified here). Many states have no simplified administrative termination procedure for any relationship status. This is a single statutory section (§ 299); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 299(a), (d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: administrative termination conditions and court dissolution
citations.quote: (a) A registered domestic partnership may be terminated without filing a proceeding for dissolution of domestic partnership by the filing of a Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership with the Secretary of State pursuant to this section, provided that all of the following conditions exist at the time of the filing: (1) The Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership is signed by both registered domestic partners. (2) There are no children of the relationship of the parties born before or after registration of the domestic partnership or adopted by the parties after registration of the domestic partnership, and neither of the registered domestic partners, to their knowledge, is pregnant. (3) The registered domestic partnership is not more than five years in duration. (4) Neither party has any interest in real property wherever situated, with the exception of the lease of a residence occupied by either party which satisfies the following requirements: (A) The lease does not include an option to purchase. (B) The lease terminates within one year from the date of filing of the Notice of Termination of Domestic Partnership. (5) There are no unpaid obligations in excess of the amount described in paragraph (6) of subdivision (a) of Section 2400, as adjusted by subdivision (b) of Section 2400, incurred by either or both of the parties after registration of the domestic partnership, excluding the amount of any unpaid obligation with respect to an automobile. (6) The total fair market value of community property assets, excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, including any deferred compensation or retirement plan, is less than the amount described in paragraph (7) of subdivision (a) of Section 2400, as adjusted by subdivision (b) of Section 2400, and neither party has separate property assets, excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, in excess of that amount. (7) The parties have executed an agreement setting forth the division of assets and the assumption of liabilities of the community property, and have executed any documents, title certificates, bills of sale, or other evidence of transfer necessary to effectuate the agreement. (8) The parties waive any rights to support by the other domestic partner. (9) The parties have read and understand a brochure prepared by the Secretary of State describing the requirements, nature, and effect of terminating a domestic partnership. (10) Both parties desire that the domestic partnership be terminated. ... (d) The superior courts shall have jurisdiction over all proceedings relating to the dissolution of domestic partnerships, nullity of domestic partnerships, and legal separation of partners in a domestic partnership. The dissolution of a domestic partnership, nullity of a domestic partnership, and legal separation of partners in a domestic partnership shall follow the same procedures, and the partners shall possess the same rights, protections, and benefits, and be subject to the same responsibilities, obligations, and duties, as apply to the dissolution of marriage, nullity of marriage, and legal separation of spouses in a marriage, respectively, except as provided in subdivision (a).

clauses.title: Confidential Domestic Partnership Category
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that California law separately provides for a confidential domestic partnership: two people who have been living together as domestic partners and who meet the substantive eligibility requirements may enter a confidential Declaration of Domestic Partnership, which the Secretary of State maintains as a permanent record not open to public inspection except by court order on a showing of good cause.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 298.7); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a confidential, non-public filing track for a registration-based partnership status can exist alongside the standard public filing — not a claim about whether any other state offers a comparable confidential category, or that this California category applies outside California. Confidential marriage and confidential-partnership categories are not universal among states.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 298.7 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the confidential domestic partnership process
citations.quote: The Secretary of State shall establish a process by which two persons, who have been living together as domestic partners and who meet the requirements of paragraphs (1) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (b) of Section 297, may enter into a confidential domestic partnership. This process shall do all of the following: (a) Maintain each confidential Declaration of Domestic Partnership as a permanent record that is not open to public inspection except upon order of the court issued upon a showing of good cause. (b) Authorize the Secretary of State to charge a reasonable fee to offset costs directly connected with maintaining confidentiality of a Declaration of Domestic Partnership.

clauses.title: Effect of the Same Partners Later Marrying Each Other
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that California law does not treat a subsequent marriage between the same two registered domestic partners as automatically terminating or merging into the domestic partnership; instead, partners who are also married to one another may petition the court to dissolve both the domestic partnership and the marriage together, in a single proceeding.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subsection (§ 299(e)); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction sequences a domestic partnership and a later marriage between the same two people — not a claim about how another state, if different, would treat that sequence. Some states that recognize domestic partnerships or civil unions have adopted automatic-merger or automatic-termination rules instead; this statute does not describe those.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 299(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: combined dissolution petition for a married domestic-partner couple
citations.quote: Parties to a registered domestic partnership who are also married to one another may petition the court to dissolve both their domestic partnership and their marriage in a single proceeding, in a form that shall be prescribed by the Judicial Council.

clauses.title: Recognition of Equivalent Out-of-State Legal Unions
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that California law recognizes, as a valid California domestic partnership, a legal union of two people — other than a marriage — that was validly formed in another jurisdiction and is substantially equivalent to a California domestic partnership, regardless of what name that other jurisdiction gives it.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 299.2); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a state can choose to recognize an out-of-state, non-marital legal union as equivalent to its own domestic partnership status — not a claim about whether any specific out-of-state union meets California's "substantially equivalent" standard, or about how any other state (if different from California) treats an out-of-state civil union or domestic partnership. Recognition rules for non-marital relationship statuses vary widely, and many states have no equivalent status to recognize at all.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 299.2 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: recognition of an equivalent out-of-state union
citations.quote: A legal union of two persons, other than a marriage, that was validly formed in another jurisdiction, and that is substantially equivalent to a domestic partnership as defined in this part, shall be recognized as a valid domestic partnership in this state regardless of whether it bears the name domestic partnership.

clauses.title: Bar on a New Filing or Marriage While a Prior Partnership Is Unresolved
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, under California law, a person who has already filed a Declaration of Domestic Partnership may not file a new one, or enter a civil marriage with someone other than their registered partner, unless the most recent domestic partnership has been terminated or a final judgment of its dissolution or nullity has been entered — except that this bar does not apply if the prior partnership ended because a partner died.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subsection (§ 298.5(c)); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a registration-based partnership status can carry an exclusivity requirement enforced at the point of a later filing — not a claim about whether any other state imposes an equivalent bar.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 298.5(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the exclusivity bar on a new filing or marriage
citations.quote: A person who has filed a Declaration of Domestic Partnership may not file a new Declaration of Domestic Partnership or enter a civil marriage with someone other than their registered domestic partner unless the most recent domestic partnership has been terminated or a final judgment of dissolution or nullity of the most recent domestic partnership has been entered. This prohibition does not apply if the previous domestic partnership ended because one of the partners died.

clauses.title: Declaration of Intent to Register
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} declare that they intend to become registered domestic partners and, on or about {{filingDate}}, intend to complete and file a Declaration of Domestic Partnership with the office of the California Secretary of State, or with the corresponding filing authority of the state in which they register.

clauses.title: Recitals — Parties and Basis
clauses.body: This Domestic Partnership Declaration is made by {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} (together, "the Partners") in connection with their registration, or intended registration, as domestic partners. This document is intended to record facts and statutory citations relevant to that registration; it does not itself constitute the statutory filing, which is made on the form prescribed by the applicable filing authority.

clauses.title: Signatures and Acknowledgment
clauses.body:
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} have executed this Domestic Partnership Declaration on {{filingDate}}.

{{party1Name}}: ☐ _________________________

{{party2Name}}: ☐ _________________________

Notary acknowledgment block, if required by the filing jurisdiction, follows on a separate page.

clauses.title: Legislative Basis and Legal Effect of a Voluntary Declaration
clauses.body: California's Legislature has found a compelling state interest in establishing parentage for all children, treating establishment of parentage as "the first step toward a child support award" and the gateway to benefits including social security, health insurance, survivors' benefits, military benefits, and inheritance rights. California law further provides that a completed voluntary declaration of parentage that complies with statutory requirements and is filed with the state child support agency "is equivalent to a judgment of parentage of the child and confers on the declarant all rights and duties of a parent," subject to the statute's own listed exceptions (void declarations, rescission, later challenge, and minor-signer rules).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a voluntary-parentage-declaration system is structured and what legal weight such a declaration can carry — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parentage declaration, nor a claim that every jurisdiction uses this same mechanism, timeline, or effect. Whether a voluntary declaration is available at all, what form it must take, and what legal effect it carries varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7570(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the legislative findings
citations.quote: There is a compelling state interest in establishing parentage for all children. Establishing parentage is the first step toward a child support award, which, in turn, provides children with equal rights and access to benefits, including, but not limited to, social security, health insurance, survivors' benefits, military benefits, and inheritance rights.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7573(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a completed declaration's judgment-equivalent effect
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 7573.5, 7575, 7576, 7577, and 7580, a completed voluntary declaration of parentage that complies with this chapter and that has been filed with the Department of Child Support Services is equivalent to a judgment of parentage of the child and confers on the declarant all rights and duties of a parent.

clauses.title: Who Signs, and the Witnessing Requirement
clauses.body: Under California's model, a voluntary declaration must be signed by both the woman who gave birth to the child and the other person seeking to establish parentage, and the signatures must be attested by a notary or witnessed. At a hospital birth, hospital staff are the typical witness, and are required to forward the signed declaration to the Department of Child Support Services within 20 days of the date the declaration was signed. Signing is not limited to the hospital — if it is not completed there, it may be completed by the attesting parents, notarized, and mailed to the Department of Child Support Services at any time after the child's birth.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how a voluntary-declaration signing and witnessing process can be structured — not a claim about which state's law governs the signing of any specific declaration. Who must sign, who may serve as a witness, and whether notarization is an alternative to witnessing all vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7571(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: hospital-staff witnessing and the 20-day forwarding requirement
citations.quote: Staff in the hospital shall witness the signatures of parents signing a voluntary declaration of parentage and shall forward the signed declaration to the Department of Child Support Services within 20 days of the date the declaration was signed.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7573(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: who must sign and the attestation requirement
citations.quote: A voluntary declaration of parentage shall be in a record signed by the woman who gave birth to the child and by either the only possible genetic parent other than the woman who gave birth or the intended parent of a child conceived through assisted reproduction, and the signatures shall be attested by a notary or witnessed.

clauses.title: The Rescission Period After Signing
clauses.body: California law gives either signer a defined window to undo an already-signed declaration by filing a rescission form, rather than by going to court: either parent may rescind the voluntary declaration of parentage by filing a rescission form with the Department of Child Support Services within 60 days of the date of execution of the declaration by the attesting parents, whichever signature is later, unless a court order for custody, visitation, or child support has already been entered in an action in which the signatory seeking to rescind was a party.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 7575); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a voluntary-declaration system can include a short, self-service rescission window with a specific triggering condition (a later court order in a case the rescinding signer was a party to) — not a claim about which state's law governs the rescission of any specific declaration. Whether a rescission period exists at all, how long it runs, how it is counted (from signing versus from filing), and what cuts it off differ significantly by state; this is exactly the kind of date-sensitive fact that does not transfer across jurisdictions.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7575(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the 60-day rescission window and its cutoff condition
citations.quote: Either parent may rescind the voluntary declaration of parentage by filing a rescission form with the Department of Child Support Services within 60 days of the date of execution of the declaration by the attesting parents, whichever signature is later, unless a court order for custody, visitation, or child support has been entered in an action in which the signatory seeking to rescind was a party.

clauses.title: Later Challenge by a Signer After Rescission Closes
clauses.body: After the rescission window closes, California law still allows a signer of the declaration to bring a court challenge, but only on narrow grounds and only within a further fixed outer deadline: not later than two years after the declaration's effective date, a signatory may commence a proceeding to challenge it on the basis of fraud, duress, or material mistake of fact. That two-year outer limit does not apply if the declaration was void from the start.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 7576); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a voluntary-declaration system can pair a short rescission window with a longer, narrower, outer challenge deadline for the people who signed — not a claim about which state's law, grounds, or deadline governs any specific challenge. The statutory text of this section names fraud, duress, and material mistake of fact as the grounds for a signer's post-rescission challenge; it does not itself state that genetic testing must accompany that challenge or that a "best interest of the child" standard applies to it — that best-interest standard is expressly written into a different section governing challenges brought by non-signatories, and this clause does not extend that standard to signer challenges without a textual basis for doing so. Grounds, deadlines, and any best-interest overlay for challenging a signed declaration vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7576(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the two-year outer deadline and the fraud/duress/mistake grounds
citations.quote: After the period for rescission provided in Section 7575 expires, but not later than two years after the effective date provided in subdivision (c) of Section 7573 of a voluntary declaration of parentage, a signatory of the voluntary declaration of parentage may commence a proceeding to challenge the declaration on the basis of fraud, duress, or material mistake of fact.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7576(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the exception for a declaration that was void from the start
citations.quote: The limitations period provided in subdivision (a) shall not apply if the voluntary declaration of parentage is void under Section 7573.5.

clauses.title: What the Declaration Establishes — and What It Does Not
clauses.body: A completed, filed declaration is equivalent to a judgment of parentage and confers on the declarant all rights and duties of a parent. Separately, California's statute repeatedly treats custody, visitation, and support as governed by their own court orders rather than by the declaration itself — for example, an order for custody, visitation, or child support remains in effect until a court determines the declaration should be set aside, subject to the court's power to modify the order as otherwise provided by law.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can structure its voluntary-declaration system so that establishing parentage and setting custody, visitation, or support terms are treated as distinct steps — not a claim about how custody, visitation, or support would be established for any specific child, and not a claim that a signed declaration does or does not itself create enforceable custody or support terms. Whether — and how — a parentage declaration interacts with custody, visitation, and support determinations varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7573(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the declaration's judgment-equivalent effect on parentage itself
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 7573.5, 7575, 7576, 7577, and 7580, a completed voluntary declaration of parentage that complies with this chapter and that has been filed with the Department of Child Support Services is equivalent to a judgment of parentage of the child and confers on the declarant all rights and duties of a parent.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7577(j)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: custody/visitation/support orders remain separately governed
citations.quote: An order for custody, visitation, or child support shall remain in effect until the court determines that the voluntary declaration of parentage should be set aside, subject to the court's power to modify the orders as otherwise provided by law.

clauses.title: When a Competing Presumed Parent Already Exists
clauses.body: California's voluntary-declaration statute does not operate independently of the state's marital and other parentage presumptions — it builds in a specific disqualifying condition. A declaration is void from the outset if, at the time of signing, a person other than the woman who gave birth to the child or the person seeking to establish parentage through the declaration is already a presumed parent under the marital presumption or one of the statute's other presumed-parent categories.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subsection (§ 7573.5(a)(1)); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a voluntary-declaration mechanism can be built to yield to an existing marital or other statutory presumption of parentage for a different person rather than override it — not a claim about whether any such competing presumption exists, or how it would be resolved, in any specific case or jurisdiction. Whether a marital or other presumption blocks use of a voluntary declaration, and how that conflict is resolved, varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7573.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: voidness when a competing presumed parent already exists
citations.quote: A voluntary declaration of parentage is void if, at the time of signing, any of the following are true: (1) A person other than the woman who gave birth to the child or a person seeking to establish parentage through a voluntary declaration of parentage is a presumed parent under Section 7540 or subdivision (a), (b), or (c) of Section 7611.

clauses.title: Genetic Testing in a Non-Signer's Challenge
clauses.body: California's statute ties a right to expedited genetic testing to one specific kind of challenge — one brought by someone who did not sign the declaration and who claims standing as an alleged genetic parent. If the court holds a hearing to determine that person's standing, the hearing must be held on an expedited basis, and if the person challenging the declaration is an alleged genetic parent, genetic testing must be ordered on an expedited basis.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subsection (§ 7577(c)); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a voluntary-declaration system can attach an expedited genetic-testing right to a non-signer's standing challenge — not a claim about whether genetic testing is available, required, or excluded in any specific challenge or jurisdiction. This statute's own text does not extend this genetic-testing provision to the separate signer's-challenge mechanism described elsewhere in this document; whether, and on what terms, genetic testing is available in a signer's own post-rescission challenge varies by state and was not confirmed by this research.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7577(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: expedited genetic testing for a non-signatory's standing challenge
citations.quote: If the court holds a hearing to determine standing, the hearing shall be held on an expedited basis. If the person challenging the voluntary declaration of parentage is an alleged genetic parent, genetic testing shall be ordered on an expedited basis.

clauses.title: Timing Rules When a Signer Is a Minor
clauses.body: California's statute delays both the effective date and the rescission clock when a signer is a minor. A voluntary declaration signed by a minor parent does not establish parentage until 60 days after both signatories have reached 18 years of age or are emancipated, whichever first occurs. The rescission right tracks that same delay: a person who signs as a minor may rescind at any time up to 60 days after that signatory reaches 18 or becomes emancipated, whichever first occurs.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subsection (§ 7580); no additional independent source was found for this. It is used as real evidence that a voluntary-declaration system can adjust both the effective date and the rescission timeline when a signer is a minor — not a claim about which state's law governs a declaration signed by a minor, or about the age, emancipation status, or timeline applicable in any specific case. Whether minor-signer rules exist at all, and how they alter timing, varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7580(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: delayed effective date for a minor signer
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (c) of Section 7573, a voluntary declaration of parentage that is signed by a minor parent does not establish parentage until 60 days after both signatories have reached 18 years of age or are emancipated, whichever first occurs.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7580(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the extended rescission right for a minor signer
citations.quote: A person who signs a voluntary declaration of parentage as a minor may rescind the voluntary declaration of parentage at any time up to 60 days after the signatory reaches 18 years of age or becomes emancipated, whichever first occurs.

clauses.title: Declaration of Intent to Establish Parentage
clauses.body: {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} state that {{childName}} is their child, and that they intend by signing this document to voluntarily and jointly establish {{parent2Name}}'s legal parentage of {{childName}}, without a court proceeding, through the process described in this document.

clauses.title: Statement Regarding Other Possible Parents
clauses.body: {{parent1Name}} states that, to {{parent1Name}}'s knowledge, no other person is married to {{parent1Name}} or otherwise legally presumed to be a parent of {{childName}}, and that {{parent2Name}} is the only other person being asked to sign this document as {{childName}}'s parent.

clauses.title: Signature Block
clauses.body:
Signed by {{parent1Name}}: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

Signed by {{parent2Name}}: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

This document is signed in the presence of a witness or notary, consistent with the witnessing or notarization requirement described elsewhere in this document; the identity and role of the witness or notary are recorded separately.

clauses.title: The Written Commission Agreement Requirement
clauses.body: Under California law, whenever an employer enters into a contract of employment with an employee for services to be rendered within California and the contemplated method of paying that employee involves commissions, the contract must be in writing and must set forth the method by which the commissions are to be computed and paid. This document reflects that requirement for the compensation arrangement between {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific written-commission-agreement requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement, and not a claim that other states impose the same written-agreement mandate. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 2751(a)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2751(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the core written commission contract requirement
citations.quote: Whenever an employer enters into a contract of employment with an employee for services to be rendered within this state and the contemplated method of payment of the employee involves commissions, the contract shall be in writing and shall set forth the method by which the commissions shall be computed and paid.

clauses.title: Signed Copy and Signed Receipt
clauses.body: California law requires the employer to give a signed copy of the written commission contract to every employee who is a party to it, and to obtain a signed receipt for the contract from each employee. The signature and receipt-acknowledgment section of this document is designed to satisfy that requirement for {{employeeName}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific written-commission-agreement requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement, and not a claim that other states impose the same written-agreement mandate. Both this clause and this document's clause on continuation after contract expiration derive from the same statutory subsection, § 2751(b); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2751(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the signed-copy and signed-receipt requirement
citations.quote: The employer shall give a signed copy of the contract to every employee who is a party thereto and shall obtain a signed receipt for the contract from each employee.

clauses.title: Continuation After Contract Expiration
clauses.body: If a written commission contract expires and {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}} nevertheless continue to work under its terms, California law presumes the contract's terms remain in full force and effect until the contract is superseded or the employment relationship is terminated by either party.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific written-commission-agreement requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement, and not a claim that other states impose the same written-agreement mandate. This clause and this document's clause on the signed-copy/signed-receipt requirement both derive from the same statutory subsection, § 2751(b); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2751(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the presumed continuation of an expired contract's terms
citations.quote: In the case of a contract that expires and where the parties nevertheless continue to work under the terms of the expired contract, the contract terms are presumed to remain in full force and effect until the contract is superseded or employment is terminated by either party.

clauses.title: What Counts as a "Commission"
clauses.body: California law defines "commission wages" as compensation paid to a person for services rendered in the sale of the employer's property or services, based proportionately on the amount or value of that property or those services — the same definition the written-commission-contract requirement itself cross-references. For purposes of that writing requirement specifically, the term "commission" does not include short-term productivity bonuses such as those paid to retail clerks, temporary variable incentive payments that increase (but do not decrease) payment under the written contract, or bonus and profit-sharing plans — unless the employer has offered to pay a fixed percentage of sales or profits as compensation for work performed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific written-commission-agreement requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement, and not a claim that other states impose the same written-agreement mandate. The borrowed definition sits inside § 204.1, a section whose main operative sentence otherwise sets a payday rule specific to vehicle dealers; the definition and the exclusion list are both expressly scoped ("for purposes of this section only") to the § 2751 writing requirement, not stated as a definition of "commission" for every other purpose in the Labor Code. Section 2752, the section immediately following, was checked directly and returned no codified content — it does not contain a separate exclusion list.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2751(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: what does not count as a commission for the writing requirement
citations.quote: As used in this section, “commissions” has the meaning set forth in Section 204.1. For purposes of this section only, “commission” does not include any of the following: (1) Short-term productivity bonuses such as are paid to retail clerks. (2) Temporary, variable incentive payments that increase, but do not decrease, payment under the written contract. (3) Bonus and profit-sharing plans, unless there has been an offer by the employer to pay a fixed percentage of sales or profits as compensation for work to be performed.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 204.1 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the definition of commission wages
citations.quote: Commission wages are compensation paid to any person for services rendered in the sale of such employer's property or services and based proportionately upon the amount or value thereof.

clauses.title: When Commission Wages Must Be Paid
clauses.body: Outside a narrow vehicle-dealer-specific rule, California's Labor Code does not set a distinct payday schedule for commission wages as such. Commissions earned by {{employeeName}} generally fall under the ordinary rule that wages other than those specifically listed elsewhere in the Labor Code (including vehicle-dealer commissions and wages due on discharge or quitting) are due and payable twice during each calendar month, on regular paydays designated in advance by {{companyName}}. Only for a person employed by a vehicle dealer licensed by the Department of Motor Vehicles does the Labor Code set a distinct commission-specific payday rule: commission wages there are due and payable once during each calendar month, on a day designated in advance by the employer as the regular payday.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific written-commission-agreement requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific commission arrangement, and not a claim that other states impose the same written-agreement mandate. The twice-monthly general payday rule and the once-monthly vehicle-dealer-specific commission payday rule are the only statutory payday-timing rules this research found; there is no separate general "commission wages must be paid within X days of being earned" statute distinct from the ordinary payday rule and the final-pay-on-discharge rule already covered elsewhere in this corpus, which this clause does not re-derive.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 204(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the general twice-monthly payday rule
citations.quote: All wages, other than those mentioned in Section 201, 201.3, 202, 204.1, or 204.2, earned by any person in any employment are due and payable twice during each calendar month, on days designated in advance by the employer as the regular paydays.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 204.1 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the vehicle-dealer-specific once-monthly commission payday rule
citations.quote: Commission wages paid to any person employed by an employer licensed as a vehicle dealer by the Department of Motor Vehicles are due and payable once during each calendar month on a day designated in advance by the employer as the regular payday.

clauses.title: Declaration of Parties
clauses.body: This Commission Agreement is entered into between {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}, effective {{effectiveDate}}, regarding compensation for services {{employeeName}} will render in the position of {{jobTitle}}.

clauses.title: Commission Structure and Rate Schedule
clauses.body: The method by which {{employeeName}}'s commissions are computed and paid is set forth as follows: ☐ {{commissionStructure}}.

clauses.title: Signature and Receipt Acknowledgment
The Personal-Property Small Estate Threshold and 40-Day Wait
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 13100 lets a successor of {{decedentName}} collect money owed to {{decedentName}}, receive {{decedentName}}'s tangible personal property, or have evidence of a debt, security, or similar right transferred, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of a will, when two things are both true: the gross value of {{decedentName}}'s real and personal property located in California — after excluding the property categories listed in Probate Code § 13050 — does not exceed $166,250, and at least 40 days have elapsed since {{dateOfDeath}}. That $166,250 figure is the amount currently written into the statute, as amended effective January 1, 2025; Probate Code § 890 separately directs the Judicial Council to re-adjust it for inflation every three years, so a different dollar amount can be the one actually operative depending on the decedent's exact date of death.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's no-probate small-estate collection mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, and not a statement that any particular estate qualifies. Small-estate thresholds and procedures vary enormously by state; some states have no comparable mechanism at all, and California's own figure is scheduled for further periodic inflation adjustment, so the dollar amount in effect on a particular date of death can differ from the figure quoted here. This is a single statutory section (§ 13100); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13100
citations.cite: California Probate Code, personal-property small estate affidavit threshold and 40-day wait
citations.quote: Excluding the property described in Section 13050 and any property included in a petition filed under Section 13151, if the gross value of the decedent's real and personal property in this state does not exceed one hundred sixty-six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($166,250), as adjusted periodically in accordance with Section 890, and if 40 days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, the successor of the decedent may, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of the will, do any of the following with respect to one or more particular items of property: (a) Collect any particular item of property that is money due the decedent. (b) Receive any particular item of property that is tangible personal property of the decedent. (c) Have any particular item of property that is evidence of a debt, obligation, interest, right, security, or chose in action belonging to the decedent transferred, whether or not secured by a lien on real property.

clauses.title: Property Excluded From the Small-Estate Calculation
clauses.body: Probate Code § 13050 lists what does not count toward the $166,250 ceiling. Excluded: property {{decedentName}} held in joint tenancy, a life estate or other interest that ended at death, property that passed outright to a surviving spouse under § 13500, property in a trust revocable by {{decedentName}} during {{decedentName}}'s lifetime, and a multiple-party (joint or pay-on-death) account, to the extent the funds belong after death to a surviving party or named P.O.D. payee or beneficiary. Also excluded: vehicles registered, or vessels numbered, under the Vehicle Code, and manufactured homes, mobilehomes, commercial coaches, truck campers, and floating homes registered under the Health and Safety Code. Also excluded from the value calculation: any amount owed to {{decedentName}} for Armed Forces service, and up to $16,625 of unpaid salary or other compensation (including unused vacation pay) owed to {{decedentName}} from employment.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what one state excludes from a small-estate calculation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. Other states define — and limit — comparable exclusion lists very differently, and property not listed here (most other financial accounts, most personal belongings, and most vehicles outside the specific Vehicle Code categories quoted) still counts toward the ceiling. This is a single statutory section (§ 13050); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13050
citations.cite: California Probate Code, property excluded from the small-estate calculation
citations.quote: (a) For the purposes of this part: (1) Any property or interest or lien thereon that, at the time of the decedent's death, was held by the decedent as a joint tenant, or in which the decedent had a life or other interest terminable upon the decedent's death, or that was held by the decedent and passed to the decedent's surviving spouse pursuant to Section 13500, shall be excluded in determining the property or estate of the decedent or its value. This excluded property shall include, but not be limited to, property in a trust revocable by the decedent during the decedent's lifetime. (2) A multiple-party account to which the decedent was a party at the time of the decedent's death shall be excluded in determining the property or estate of the decedent or its value, whether or not all or a portion of the sums on deposit are community property, to the extent that the sums on deposit belong after the death of the decedent to a surviving party, P.O.D. payee, or beneficiary. ... (b) For the purposes of this part, all of the following property shall be excluded in determining the property or estate of the decedent or its value: (1) Any vehicle registered under Division 3 (commencing with Section 4000) of the Vehicle Code or titled under Division 16.5 (commencing with Section 38000) of the Vehicle Code. (2) Any vessel numbered under Division 3.5 (commencing with Section 9840) of the Vehicle Code. (3) Any manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home registered under Part 2 (commencing with Section 18000) of Division 13 of the Health and Safety Code. (c) For the purposes of this part, the value of the following property shall be excluded in determining the value of the decedent's property in this state: (1) Any amounts due to the decedent for services in the Armed Forces of the United States. (2) The amount, not exceeding sixteen thousand six hundred twenty-five dollars ($16,625), as adjusted periodically in accordance with Section 890, of salary or other compensation, including compensation for unused vacation, owing to the decedent for personal services from any employment.

clauses.title: What the Affidavit Must State
clauses.body: Probate Code § 13101(a) lists what an affidavit or declaration under this procedure must state: the decedent's name; the date and place of death; that at least 40 days have elapsed since death, as shown by a certified copy of the death certificate attached to the affidavit; either that no California proceeding for administration of the estate is being or has been conducted, or that the personal representative has consented in writing to the transfer; the current gross fair market value of the decedent's California real and personal property (excluding § 13050 property), stated not to exceed the applicable statutory dollar amount; a description of the property sought; the name of the successor entitled to it; a statement that the affiant is that successor, or is authorized under § 13051 to act on the successor's behalf; a statement that no other person has a superior right to the property; a request that the property be paid, delivered, or transferred to the affiant; and a statement, made under penalty of perjury under California law, that the foregoing is true and correct.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what one state's affidavit form must contain — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, or that this exact list satisfies any other state's comparable procedure. This is a single statutory section (§ 13101); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13101(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, required contents of the small estate affidavit
