citations.quote: (a) To collect money, receive tangible personal property, or have evidences of a debt, obligation, interest, right, security, or chose in action transferred under this chapter, an affidavit or a declaration under penalty of perjury under the laws of this state shall be furnished to the holder of the decedent's property stating all of the following: (1) The decedent's name. (2) The date and place of the decedent's death. (3) "At least 40 days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, as shown in a certified copy of the decedent's death certificate attached to this affidavit or declaration." (4) Either of the following, as appropriate: (A) "No proceeding is now being or has been conducted in California for administration of the decedent's estate." (B) "The decedent's personal representative has consented in writing to the payment, transfer, or delivery to the affiant or declarant of the property described in the affidavit or declaration." (5) "The current gross fair market value of the decedent's real and personal property in California, excluding the property described in Section 13050 of the California Probate Code and any property included in a petition filed under Section 13151 of the California Probate Code, does not exceed [Insert dollar amount specified in subdivision (g) of Section 13101 of the California Probate Code]." (6) A description of the property of the decedent that is to be paid, transferred, or delivered to the affiant or declarant. (7) The name of the successor of the decedent, as defined in Section 13006, to the described property. (8) Either of the following, as appropriate: (A) "The affiant or declarant is the successor of the decedent (as defined in Section 13006 of the California Probate Code) to the decedent's interest in the described property." (B) "The affiant or declarant is authorized under Section 13051 of the California Probate Code to act on behalf of the successor of the decedent (as defined in Section 13006 of the California Probate Code) with respect to the decedent's interest in the described property." (9) "No other person has a superior right to the interest of the decedent in the described property." (10) "The affiant or declarant requests that the described property be paid, delivered, or transferred to the affiant or declarant." (11) "The affiant or declarant affirms or declares under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct."

clauses.title: Multiple Successors and the Attached Death Certificate
clauses.body: Where more than one person is entitled to the described property, Probate Code § 13101(b) requires the required statements to be modified to reflect that fact when each such person executes the affidavit or declaration — the statute contemplates joint execution by the interested successors rather than a single successor certifying on the others' behalf. Separately, § 13101(d) requires a certified copy of the decedent's death certificate to be attached to the affidavit or declaration.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's rule for multiple successors and required attachments — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. This is a single statutory section (§ 13101); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13101(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, modification of statements for multiple successors
citations.quote: (b) Where more than one person executes the affidavit or declaration under this section, the statements required by subdivision (a) shall be modified as appropriate to reflect that fact.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13101(d)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, death certificate attachment requirement
citations.quote: (d) A certified copy of the decedent's death certificate shall be attached to the affidavit or declaration.

clauses.title: The Holder's Duty to Honor the Affidavit, and Its Liability Protection
clauses.body: Probate Code § 13106(a) provides that once the requirements of §§ 13100 to 13104 are satisfied, a holder of the decedent's property (such as a bank or transfer agent) who pays, delivers, or transfers property in reliance on the affidavit or declaration is discharged from any further liability with respect to that money or property — the holder may rely in good faith on the statements in the affidavit and has no duty to inquire into the truth of any of them. If a holder instead refuses to pay, deliver, or transfer the property to the successor within a reasonable time, Probate Code § 13105(b) lets the successor bring an action to recover the property or compel the transfer, and directs the court to award reasonable attorney's fees to the successor if it finds the holder acted unreasonably in refusing.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's rule protecting institutions that rely on this kind of affidavit — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, or that a given institution outside California would treat an out-of-state equivalent the same way.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13106(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, holder's discharge from liability
citations.quote: (a) If the requirements of Sections 13100 to 13104, inclusive, are satisfied, receipt by the holder of the decedent's property of the affidavit or declaration constitutes sufficient acquittance for the payment of money, delivery of property, or changing registered ownership of property pursuant to this chapter and discharges the holder from any further liability with respect to the money or property. The holder may rely in good faith on the statements in the affidavit or declaration and has no duty to inquire into the truth of any statement in the affidavit or declaration.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13105(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, successor's remedy for a holder's unreasonable refusal
citations.quote: (b) If the holder of the decedent's property refuses to pay, deliver, or transfer any personal property or evidence thereof to the successor of the decedent within a reasonable time, the successor may recover the property or compel its payment, delivery, or transfer in an action brought for that purpose against the holder of the property. If an action is brought against the holder under this section, the court shall award reasonable attorney's fees to the person or persons bringing the action if the court finds that the holder of the decedent's property acted unreasonably in refusing to pay, deliver, or transfer the property to them as required by subdivision (a).

clauses.title: The Separate Real Property Small-Value Affidavit
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 13200 provides a second, distinct mechanism for small amounts of real property — separate from, and structured differently than, the personal-property affidavit procedure in §§ 13100-13106. No sooner than six months after the decedent's death, a successor may file an affidavit, on a Judicial Council form, in the superior court of the county where the decedent was domiciled (or, if not California-domiciled, where the real property is located), stating a legal description of the property, that funeral expenses, last-illness expenses, and all unsecured debts of the decedent have been paid, and that the property's gross value does not exceed the statutory ceiling for this chapter. Unlike the personal-property procedure — which involves no court filing at all — this affidavit must be accompanied by an inventory and appraisal of the real property made by a probate referee, and, once filed, the court clerk issues a certified copy that is recorded with the county recorder, indexed with the decedent as grantor and the successor as grantee. As last written into the statute's own text (effective January 1, 2020), the dollar ceiling recited in § 13200 is $55,425 for decedents who died before April 1, 2022; for deaths on or after that date, the statute points to the adjusted dollar amount separately published by the Judicial Council under § 890, without itself restating that current adjusted number in the code section's text — unlike § 13100/§ 13101, which were directly re-amended in 2024 to state $166,250.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a second, separate, court-filing-based small-estate mechanism exists for real property alone — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, and not a claim that $55,425 (as opposed to a later Judicial Council-published adjustment) is the number actually controlling on any particular date of death. Real-property small-estate procedures, where they exist at all, vary widely by state, and many states have no equivalent to this six-month, court-filed, real-property-only track. Two of these three citations (§ 13200(a) and § 13200(h)) are subsections of the same statutory section; no additional independent source was found for the dollar-ceiling text itself, though the recording step is separately confirmed at the genuinely independent § 13202.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13200(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, real property small-value affidavit — filing and required contents
citations.quote: (a) No sooner than six months from the death of a decedent, a person or persons claiming as successor of the decedent to a particular item of property that is real property may file in the superior court in the county in which the decedent was domiciled at the time of death, or if the decedent was not domiciled in this state at the time of death, then in any county in which real property of the decedent is located, an affidavit in the form prescribed by the Judicial Council pursuant to Section 1001 stating all of the following: (1) The name of the decedent. (2) The date and place of the decedent's death. (3) A legal description of the real property and the interest of the decedent therein. (4) The name and address of each person serving as guardian or conservator of the estate of the decedent at the time of the decedent's death, so far as known to the affiant. (5) "The gross value of all real property in the decedent's estate located in California, as shown by the inventory and appraisal attached to this affidavit, excluding the real property described in Section 13050 of the California Probate Code, does not exceed [Insert dollar amount specified in subdivision (h)]." (6) "At least six months have elapsed since the death of the decedent as shown in a certified copy of decedent's death certificate attached to this affidavit." (7) Either of the following, as appropriate: (A) "No proceeding is now being or has been conducted in California for administration of the decedent's estate." (B) "The decedent's personal representative has consented in writing to use of the procedure provided by this chapter." (8) "Funeral expenses, expenses of last illness, and all unsecured debts of the decedent have been paid." (9) "The affiant is the successor of the decedent (as defined in Section 13006 of the Probate Code) and to the decedent's interest in the described property, and no other person has a superior right to the interest of the decedent in the described property." (10) "The affiant declares under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct."

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13200(h)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, real property small-value affidavit dollar ceiling
citations.quote: (h) (1) When the decedent dies prior to April 1, 2022, the dollar amount for paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) is fifty-five thousand four hundred twenty-five dollars ($55,425). (2) When the decedent dies on or after April 1, 2022, the dollar amount for paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) is the adjusted dollar amount, published in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 890, in effect on the date of the decedent's death.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13202
citations.cite: California Probate Code, recording the real property small-value affidavit
citations.quote: Upon receipt of the affidavit and the required fee, the court clerk, upon determining that the affidavit is complete and has the required attachments, shall file the affidavit and attachments and shall issue a certified copy of the affidavit without the attachments. The certified copy shall be recorded in the office of the county recorder of the county where the real property is located. The county recorder shall index the certified copy in the index of grantors and grantees. The decedent shall be indexed as the grantor and each person designated as a successor to the property in the certified copy shall be indexed as a grantee.

clauses.title: The Transferee's Ongoing Liability for Debts and Superior Claims
clauses.body: Receiving property under this affidavit procedure does not clear the underlying debts or claims against {{decedentName}}'s estate. Probate Code § 13109 makes a transferee who receives property this way personally liable for {{decedentName}}'s unsecured debts, enforceable against the transferee the same way the debt could have been enforced against {{decedentName}}, though that personal liability cannot exceed the fair market value of the transferred property, less any liens, at the time the affidavit was presented. Separately, Probate Code § 13111 lets a personal representative who later determines someone else has a superior right to the transferred property demand its return to the estate — restitution of the property itself, or, if the transferee no longer has it, its fair market value plus 7 percent annual interest — and, if the transferee obtained the property by fraud, restitution of three times its fair market value.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that one state's affidavit procedure does not itself discharge a recipient's exposure to the decedent's debts or to a person with a better claim — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, or about what liability rules apply outside California.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13109(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, transferee's personal liability for the decedent's unsecured debts
citations.quote: (a) A transferee is personally liable, to the extent provided in this section for the unsecured debts of the decedent. That debt may be enforced against the transferee in the same manner as it could have been enforced against the decedent if the decedent had not died. In any action based upon the debt, the transferee may assert any defense, cross-complaint, or setoff that would have been available to the decedent if the decedent had not died. Nothing in this section permits enforcement of a claim that is barred under Part 4 (commencing with Section 9000) of Division 7. Section 366.2 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies in an action under this section. (b) The personal liability under subdivision (a) shall not exceed the fair market value of the transferred property at the time the affidavit or declaration is presented under this chapter, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances on the transferred property at that time, and less the amount of any payment made pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 13110.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13111(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, restitution when another person has a superior right
citations.quote: (a) If property is paid, delivered, or transferred to a transferee under this chapter, and the decedent's personal representative determines that another person has a superior right to the property by testate or intestate succession from the decedent, the personal representative may request that the transferred property be restored to the estate. Subject to subdivisions (b), (c), (d), (e), and (g) if the personal representative makes that request, the transferee is liable for all of the following: (1) If the transferee still has the transferred property, restitution of the transferred property to the decedent's estate. (2) If the transferee no longer has the transferred property, restitution to the decedent's estate of the fair market value of the transferred property plus interest from the date of disposition at the rate of 7 percent per annum on the fair market value of the transferred property. ... (b) Subject to subdivision (c) and subject to any additional liability the transferee has under Sections 13109 to 13113.5, inclusive, if the transferee fraudulently secured the payment, delivery, or transfer of the decedent's property under this chapter, the transferee is liable under this section for restitution of three times the fair market value of the transferred property.

clauses.title: The 40-Day Waiting Period, Precisely
clauses.body: The personal-property small-estate procedure is unavailable until 40 days have elapsed after {{decedentName}}'s death on {{dateOfDeath}}: Probate Code § 13100 makes the entire procedure conditional on that 40-day elapse, and § 13101(a)(3) separately requires the affidavit or declaration itself to state that at least 40 days have elapsed, as shown by the certified copy of the death certificate attached to it. This 40-day figure applies only to the personal-property affidavit — the separate real-property affidavit under § 13200 instead requires six months to elapse.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one state's specific waiting period for this specific no-court procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, or that 40 days is a period used by any other state's comparable mechanism, where one exists.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13100
citations.cite: California Probate Code, 40-day condition on the procedure's availability
citations.quote: and if 40 days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, the successor of the decedent may, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of the will, do any of the following with respect to one or more particular items of property

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13101(a)(3)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, required affidavit statement of the 40-day elapse
citations.quote: "At least 40 days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, as shown in a certified copy of the decedent's death certificate attached to this affidavit or declaration."

A certified copy of {{decedentName}}'s death certificate is attached to this declaration.

clauses.title: Formation and Partners
clauses.body: {{partnershipName}} is a general partnership carrying on business as coowners for profit. Its partners are {{partner1Name}} and {{partner2Name}}.

clauses.title: Capital Contributions
Acknowledgment
Formation — With or Without a Written Agreement
clauses.body: California's partnership statute treats {{partnershipName}} as formed by law itself, not by this or any other document: the association of two or more persons — here, {{partner1Name}} and {{partner2Name}} — to carry on as coowners a business for profit forms a partnership, whether or not those persons intend to form one. The statute separately defines a "partnership agreement" as the agreement among partners concerning the partnership, which can be written, oral, or implied — meaning a general partnership, unlike the corporations and LLCs this project also documents, can exist under California law with no signed paperwork at all. This document memorializes and supplements whatever partnership already exists (or is being formed) between the parties named above.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how general partnership formation works as a matter of law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. The formation rule quoted above has real, narrower statutory carve-outs beyond the ones quoted here: an association formed under a different statute (Corp. Code § 16202(b)) is not a partnership under this chapter, and separate provisions of the same section state that joint tenancy, tenancy in common, and similar co-ownership arrangements do not by themselves establish a partnership, and that receiving a share of profits as payment of a debt, wages, rent, an annuity, loan interest, or the sale price of business goodwill does not by itself make the recipient a partner (Corp. Code § 16202(c)). Two of these four citations (§ 16101(a)(9) and § 16101(a)(10)) are subsections of the same statutory section; no additional independent source was found for that specific point beyond it.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16101(a)(9)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, statutory definition of 'partnership'
citations.quote: “Partnership” means an association of two or more persons to carry on as coowners a business for profit formed under Section 16202, predecessor law, or comparable law of another jurisdiction, and includes, for all purposes of the laws of this state, a registered limited liability partnership, and excludes any partnership formed under Chapter 4.5 (commencing with Section 15900).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16101(a)(10)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, a 'partnership agreement' can be written, oral, or implied
citations.quote: “Partnership agreement” means the agreement, whether written, oral, or implied, among the partners concerning the partnership, including amendments to the partnership agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16202(a)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, formation by operation of law
citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (b), the association of two or more persons to carry on as coowners a business for profit forms a partnership, whether or not the persons intend to form a partnership.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16202(b)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, exception for associations formed under another statute
citations.quote: (b) An association formed under a statute other than this chapter, a predecessor statute, or a comparable statute of another jurisdiction is not a partnership under this chapter.

clauses.title: Sharing Profits and Losses — The Default Rule
clauses.body: Absent a different rule stated in this agreement, California partnership law entitles each partner of {{partnershipName}} to an equal share of partnership profits, and makes each partner chargeable with a share of partnership losses in proportion to that partner's share of the profits — regardless of how much capital, property, or work each partner actually contributed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, often-surprising default profit-and-loss allocation rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. Nothing about this default is affected by unequal capital contributions: two partners who contributed vastly different amounts of capital still split profits equally under this rule unless their partnership agreement (which, as noted elsewhere in this document, doesn't have to be written) sets a different split. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 16401(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16401(b)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, default equal profit share and proportional loss share
citations.quote: (b) Each partner is entitled to an equal share of the partnership profits and, subject to Sections 16306 and 16957, is chargeable with a share of the partnership losses in proportion to the partner’s share of the profits.

clauses.title: Management Rights — The Default Rule
clauses.body: Absent a different rule stated in this agreement, California partnership law gives each partner of {{partnershipName}} equal rights in the management and conduct of the partnership's business — regardless of each partner's capital contribution, time commitment, or role.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the default management rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. The same statutory section separately defaults ordinary-course business decisions to majority-of-partners approval, and reserves acts outside the ordinary course of business, and any amendment to the partnership agreement, for unanimous consent — defaults this document's own management and voting terms may or may not track. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 16401(f)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16401(f)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, default equal management rights
citations.quote: (f) Each partner has equal rights in the management and conduct of the partnership business.

clauses.title: Partners' Fiduciary Duties to Each Other
clauses.body: Each partner of {{partnershipName}} owes the partnership and the other partners a duty of loyalty and a duty of care. The duty of loyalty requires a partner to account for and hold as trustee any property, profit, or benefit the partner derives from the partnership's business or from using partnership property or information (including taking a partnership opportunity for themselves); to refrain from dealing with the partnership on behalf of someone whose interests are adverse to it; and to refrain from competing with the partnership before it dissolves. The duty of care is narrower than it might sound: it's limited to refraining from grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law — ordinary negligence, by itself, does not breach it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine default fiduciary-duty structure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. Every partner also owes an independent obligation of good faith and fair dealing in exercising rights and discharging duties, and a partner does not violate any of these duties merely by acting in their own self-interest — the statute states both points directly. All three citations below are subsections of a single statutory section (§ 16404); no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16404(a)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the two fiduciary duties a partner owes
citations.quote: (a) The fiduciary duties a partner owes to the partnership and the other partners are the duty of loyalty and the duty of care set forth in subdivisions (b) and (c).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16404(b)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the statutory duty of loyalty
citations.quote: (b) A partner’s duty of loyalty to the partnership and the other partners includes all of the following: (1) To account to the partnership and hold as trustee for it any property, profit, or benefit derived by the partner in the conduct and winding up of the partnership business or derived from a use by the partner of partnership property or information, including the appropriation of a partnership opportunity. (2) To refrain from dealing with the partnership in the conduct or winding up of the partnership business as or on behalf of a party having an interest adverse to the partnership. (3) To refrain from competing with the partnership in the conduct of the partnership business before the dissolution of the partnership.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16404(c)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the statutory duty of care — a low bar, not ordinary negligence
citations.quote: (c) A partner’s duty of care to the partnership and the other partners in the conduct and winding up of the partnership business is limited to refraining from engaging in grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law.

clauses.title: Partnership Property vs. a Partner's Own Property
clauses.body: Whether an asset counts as {{partnershipName}}'s property, or as one partner's own separate property, turns on a specific statutory test rather than on whoever happens to be using it. Property is partnership property if it's acquired in the partnership's own name, or acquired by one or more partners with the instrument transferring title indicating either their capacity as partners or the partnership's existence — and property is presumed to be partnership property if it was purchased with partnership assets, even without such an indication. Conversely, property acquired in a partner's own name, with no indication of partnership capacity or existence and without using partnership assets, is presumed to be that partner's separate property — even if the partnership actually uses it for partnership purposes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory ownership test — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. Both directions of this test are rebuttable presumptions, not absolute rules — the statute itself frames the partnership-assets presumption and the partner's-own-name presumption as presumptions, not conclusive determinations. Both citations below are subsections of a single statutory section (§ 16204); no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16204(a)-(c)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the test for partnership property
citations.quote: (a) Property is partnership property if acquired in the name of either of the following: (1) The partnership. (2) One or more partners with an indication in the instrument transferring title to the property of the person’s capacity as a partner or of the existence of a partnership but without an indication of the name of the partnership. (b) Property is acquired in the name of the partnership by a transfer to either of the following: (1) The partnership in its name. (2) One or more partners in their capacity as partners in the partnership, if the name of the partnership is indicated in the instrument transferring title to the property. (c) Property is presumed to be partnership property if purchased with partnership assets, even if not acquired in the name of the partnership or of one or more partners with an indication in the instrument transferring title to the property of the person’s capacity as a partner or of the existence of a partnership.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16204(d)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, the presumption of separate (non-partnership) property
citations.quote: (d) Property acquired in the name of one or more of the partners, without an indication in the instrument transferring title to the property of the person’s capacity as a partner or of the existence of a partnership and without use of partnership assets, is presumed to be separate property, even if used for partnership purposes.

clauses.title: Each Partner's Personal Liability for Partnership Obligations
clauses.body: California partnership law does not give {{partnershipName}}'s partners the liability shield that the LLCs and corporations covered elsewhere in this project have: all partners are liable jointly and severally for all obligations of the partnership, unless otherwise agreed by the claimant or provided by law. A partner admitted into an already-existing partnership is not personally liable for a partnership obligation that was incurred before that partner was admitted.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a general partnership's default liability structure has no shield comparable to an LLC's or corporation's — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. The statute carves out a distinct, separate liability regime for a "registered limited liability partnership" (Corp. Code § 16306(c)-(h)), a different, specifically-registered entity type that this document does not cover. Both citations below are subsections of a single statutory section (§ 16306); no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16306(a)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, joint and several liability for partnership obligations
citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), all partners are liable jointly and severally for all obligations of the partnership unless otherwise agreed by the claimant or provided by law.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16306(b)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, a newly admitted partner isn't liable for pre-admission obligations
citations.quote: (b) A person admitted as a partner into an existing partnership is not personally liable for any partnership obligation incurred before the person’s admission as a partner.

clauses.title: Dissociation — What Triggers a Partner Leaving the Partnership
clauses.body: A partner of {{partnershipName}} is legally "dissociated" from the partnership — meaning that partner's status as a partner ends — on the occurrence of any of several specific statutory events: the partnership's having notice of that partner's express will to withdraw (or a later withdrawal date the partner specifies); an event the partnership agreement itself designates as causing dissociation; the partner's expulsion under the partnership agreement's own terms, by unanimous vote of the other partners under specific statutory circumstances, or by judicial determination; the partner becoming a debtor in bankruptcy or a similar insolvency event occurring; and, for a partner who is an individual, that partner's death, incapacity, or the appointment of a guardian or conservator for them.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory list of dissociation triggers — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. Dissociation is a distinct legal event from dissolution of the entire partnership; a companion clause in this document addresses when dissociation does, and does not, trigger dissolution. The statute lists additional dissociation events, for partners that are corporate entities, trusts, or estates, that this summary does not itemize. All citations below are subsections of a single statutory section (§ 16601); no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16601(1)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissociation by a partner's express will to withdraw
citations.quote: A partner is dissociated from a partnership upon the occurrence of any of the following events: (1) The partnership’s having notice of the partner’s express will to withdraw as a partner or on a later date specified by the partner.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16601(2)-(3)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissociation by agreed event or agreement-based expulsion
citations.quote: (2) An event agreed to in the partnership agreement as causing the partner’s dissociation. (3) The partner’s expulsion pursuant to the partnership agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16601(6)(A)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissociation on becoming a debtor in bankruptcy
citations.quote: (6) The partner’s act or failure to act in any of the following instances: (A) By becoming a debtor in bankruptcy.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16601(7)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissociation of an individual partner by death or incapacity
citations.quote: (7) In the case of a partner who is an individual, by any of the following: (A) The partner’s death. (B) The appointment of a guardian or general conservator for the partner. (C) A judicial determination that the partner has otherwise become incapable of performing the partner’s duties under the partnership agreement.

clauses.title: Dissolution — A Partner's Departure Doesn't Always End the Partnership
clauses.body: Under California's current partnership statute, a partner's dissociation from {{partnershipName}} does not, by itself, automatically dissolve the partnership. Instead, the partnership dissolves only on the occurrence of specific listed events. If {{partnershipName}} is a partnership at will (the partners haven't agreed to a fixed term or a particular undertaking), dissolution requires the express will to wind up the business from at least half of the partners, including any partners who wrongfully dissociated within the preceding 90 days. If {{partnershipName}} instead has a definite term or a particular undertaking, dissolution can be triggered after certain kinds of partner dissociation (such as death) if a majority in interest of the remaining partners doesn't agree to continue the partnership within 90 days, by the express will of all partners to wind up the business, or by the expiration of the term or completion of the undertaking. Other listed events — an event the partnership agreement itself designates, an uncured illegality, or specific judicial determinations — can also trigger dissolution.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's modern partnership law does not automatically dissolve a partnership every time a partner leaves — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership, and not a claim about how any particular older or other state's partnership statute treats dissociation. This is a genuinely significant change from the 1914 Uniform Partnership Act's default rule, under which most partner departures did dissolve the partnership by operation of law; California adopted the newer Uniform Partnership Act of 1994 (RUPA-based) framework quoted here, which decouples a partner's exit from the partnership's continued existence in most circumstances. All citations below are subsections of a single statutory section (§ 16801); no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16801(1)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissolution trigger for an at-will partnership
citations.quote: A partnership is dissolved, and its business shall be wound up, only upon the occurrence of any of the following events: (1) In a partnership at will, by the express will to dissolve and wind up the partnership business of at least half of the partners, including partners, other than wrongfully dissociating partners, who have dissociated within the preceding 90 days, and for which purpose a dissociation under paragraph (1) of Section 16601 constitutes an expression of that partner’s will to dissolve and wind up the partnership business.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16801(2)(A)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissolution trigger for a term partnership after certain dissociations
citations.quote: (2) In a partnership for a definite term or particular undertaking, when any of the following occurs: (A) After the expiration of 90 days after a partner’s dissociation by death or otherwise under paragraphs (6) to (10), inclusive, of Section 16601, or a partner’s wrongful dissociation under subdivision (b) of Section 16602 unless before that time a majority in interest of the partners, including partners who have rightfully dissociated pursuant to subparagraph (A) of paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 16602, agree to continue the partnership.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16801(2)(B)-(C)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissolution of a term partnership by unanimous will or term expiration
citations.quote: (B) The express will of all of the partners to wind up the partnership business. (C) The expiration of the term or the completion of the undertaking.

clauses.title: Partner's Right to Partnership Books and Records
clauses.body: Partners of {{partnershipName}} have a statutory right to access the partnership's books and records: the partnership must provide partners (and their agents and attorneys) access to inspect and copy its books and records during ordinary business hours, and a former partner retains that same access for the period during which they were a partner. The partnership may charge a reasonable fee, covering the cost of labor and materials, for copies it furnishes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine partner records-access right — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific general partnership. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 16403(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16403(b)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, partner and former-partner access to books and records
citations.quote: (b) A partnership shall provide partners and their agents and attorneys access to its books and records. It shall provide former partners and their agents and attorneys access to books and records pertaining to the period during which they were partners. The right of access provides the opportunity to inspect and copy books and records during ordinary business hours. A partnership may impose a reasonable charge, covering the costs of labor and material, for copies of documents furnished.

clauses.title: Parties and Property
clauses.body: This is a residential purchase agreement between {{sellerName}} ("Seller") and {{buyerName}} ("Buyer") for the property at {{propertyAddress}}, for a purchase price of ${{purchasePrice}}.

clauses.title: Contingencies and Closing Date
clauses.body: This agreement is contingent on the following, to be satisfied or waived in writing by the stated deadlines: {{contingencies}}. Closing (transfer of title) is scheduled to take place on or before {{closingDate}}.

clauses.title: Signatures
Transfer Disclosure Statement Requirement
clauses.body: Except for the specific exemptions below, California law requires the seller of single-family residential property to deliver to a prospective buyer a completed written Transfer Disclosure Statement, for any transfer by sale, exchange, real property sales contract, lease with an option to purchase, other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements. Any waiver of this requirement is void as against public policy. The following transfers are specifically exempted from this requirement: transfers pursuant to court order (including probate-court sales, writ-of-execution sales, foreclosure sales, bankruptcy-trustee transfers, eminent domain, and decree-of-specific-performance sales); sales or transfers by a fiduciary in the administration of a trust, guardianship, conservatorship, or decedent's estate (with an exception to this exemption if the trustee is a natural person who is also a former owner or was a recent occupant of the property); transfers from one co-owner to one or more other co-owners; transfers to a spouse or to a person in the transferor's line of consanguinity; transfers between spouses resulting from a dissolution or legal-separation judgment or an incidental property settlement agreement; and sales, transfers, or exchanges to or from a governmental entity.
clauses.gap: This exemption list is longer and more specific than commonly assumed — the decedent's-estate fiduciary exemption in particular has its own built-in exception that's easy to miss on a first read. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines residential transfer-disclosure exemptions — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential purchase; real estate disclosure requirements vary enormously by state. The statute's scope term is "single-family residential property," which is narrower-sounding than the "one to four dwelling units" language this same body of California disclosure law uses elsewhere (for example, in the liquidated-damages and Megan's Law notice statutes cited elsewhere in this document) — this document does not resolve or equate those two scope terms for any specific transaction. The two citations to § 1102 below are subsections of the same statutory section; the six citations to § 1102.2 are also subsections of the same statutory section as each other, and § 1102.2 is a genuinely separate, independent section from § 1102.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, TDS requirement and scope
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 1102.2, this article applies to any transfer by sale, exchange, real property sales contract as defined in Section 2985, lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements of any single-family residential property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102(c)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, waiver of the TDS requirement is void
citations.quote: Any waiver of the requirements of this article is void as against public policy.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, court-order/foreclosure/bankruptcy exemption
citations.quote: Sales or transfers pursuant to court order, including, but not limited to, sales ordered by a probate court in the administration of an estate, sales pursuant to a writ of execution, sales by any foreclosure sale, transfers by a trustee in bankruptcy, sales by eminent domain, and sales resulting from a decree for specific performance.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(d)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, fiduciary/estate-administration exemption
citations.quote: Sales or transfers by a fiduciary in the course of the administration of a trust, guardianship, conservatorship, or decedent's estate. This exemption shall not apply to a sale if the trustee is a natural person who is a trustee of a revocable trust and is a former owner of the property or was an occupant in possession of the property within the preceding year.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(e)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, co-owner-to-co-owner exemption
citations.quote: Sales or transfers from one coowner to one or more other coowners.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(f)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, spouse/direct-relative exemption
citations.quote: Sales or transfers made to a spouse, or to a person or persons in the line of consanguinity of one or more of the transferors.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(g)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, divorce/legal-separation exemption
citations.quote: Sales or transfers between spouses resulting from a judgment of dissolution of marriage or of legal separation or from a property settlement agreement incidental to that judgment.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.2(j)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, governmental-entity exemption
citations.quote: Sales or transfers or exchanges to or from any governmental entity.

clauses.title: What the Disclosure Statement Must Cover
clauses.body: The Transfer Disclosure Statement is set forth in, and must be made on a copy of, a specific statutory disclosure form. The disclosure requirement covers any fact materially affecting the value and desirability of the property, including the physical conditions of the property and previously received reports of physical inspections. Delivery of the disclosure statement cannot be waived in an "as is" sale. The form has a specific three-part structure: Sections I and II, and — if the seller is represented by an agent in the transaction — also Section III (the agent's own inspection disclosure).
clauses.gap: The exact, current checkbox-by-checkbox wording of the statutory disclosure form itself (Civil Code § 1102.6) could not be confirmed from a fetchable primary source: leginfo's own page for § 1102.6 displays a literal "NOTICE OF INCOMPLETE TEXT" placeholder rather than the form's actual content, pointing instead to a printed page range in the chaptered bill; the underlying 2020 chaptered bill (SB 1371), fetched directly from leginfo, likewise shows a "PRINTER PLEASE NOTE: TIP-IN MATERIAL TO BE INSERTED" placeholder in place of the form text. Because of that, this clause does not quote the form's specific line items (named systems, appliances, or specific defect/environmental/legal categories) as statutory language — doing so would have meant asserting text that could not be independently verified. What's stated above is drawn from statutory language that is genuinely fetchable and confirmed twice. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a residential-purchase disclosure obligation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential purchase. The two quotes credited to § 1102.1(a) below are from a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for that specific point. § 1102.6(a) and § 1102.3 are each separate, independent sections.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.6(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the disclosure must be made on the statutory form
citations.quote: The disclosures required by this article pertaining to the property proposed to be transferred are set forth in, and shall be made on a copy of, the following disclosure form:

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.1(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the material-fact disclosure standard
citations.quote: The Legislature did not intend to affect the existing obligations of the parties to a real estate contract, or their agents, to disclose any fact materially affecting the value and desirability of the property, including, but not limited to, the physical conditions of the property and previously received reports of physical inspections noted on the disclosure form set forth in Section 1102.6 or 1102.6a, and that nothing in this article shall be construed to change the duty of a real estate broker or salesperson pursuant to Section 2079.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.1(a) [as-is sale]
citations.cite: California Civil Code, disclosure can't be waived in an 'as is' sale
citations.quote: It is also the intent of the Legislature that the delivery of a real estate transfer disclosure statement may not be waived in an “as is” sale, as held in Loughrin v. Superior Court (1993) 15 Cal. App. 4th 1188.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.3
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the form's Section I/II/III structure
citations.quote: The period of time the prospective buyer has in which to terminate the offer commences when Sections I and II, and, if the seller is represented by an agent in the transaction, then also Section III, in the form described in Section 1102.6, are completed and delivered to the buyer or buyer's agent.

clauses.title: Disclosure Timing and Buyer's Right to Terminate
clauses.body: In the case of a sale, the seller must deliver the completed Transfer Disclosure Statement to the prospective buyer as soon as practicable before transfer of title. If any disclosure, or a material amendment to a disclosure, is delivered after the buyer's offer to purchase has already been executed, the buyer has three days after delivery in person, five days after delivery by mail, or five days after delivery of an electronic record (where the parties have agreed to conduct the transaction electronically) to terminate the offer, by delivering written notice of termination to the seller or the seller's agent. Noncompliance with this disclosure article does not by itself invalidate the transfer, but a person who willfully or negligently violates or fails to perform any duty under this article is liable to the buyer for the buyer's actual damages.
clauses.gap: This specific termination right applies to a disclosure or material amendment delivered after the buyer's offer was already executed — its own text doesn't establish a freestanding right to cancel at any later time after simply receiving a disclosure that was delivered before the offer was signed. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's disclosure-timing and cure mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential purchase; timing rules and termination windows vary by state. The two citations to § 1102.3 below are subsections of the same statutory section; § 1102.13's non-invalidation/liability rule is a separate, independent section.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.3(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, delivery timing — as soon as practicable
citations.quote: The seller of any single-family real property subject to this article shall deliver to the prospective buyer the completed written statement required by this article, as follows: (a) In the case of a sale, as soon as practicable before transfer of title.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.3 [termination right]
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the 3/5/5-day termination right
citations.quote: If any disclosure, or any material amendment of any disclosure, required to be made by this article, is delivered after the execution of an offer to purchase, the prospective buyer shall have three days after delivery in person, five days after delivery by deposit in the mail, or five days after delivery of an electronic record in transactions where the parties have agreed to conduct the transaction by electronic means, pursuant to provisions of the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (Title 2.5 (commencing with Section 1633.1) of Part 2 of Division 3), to terminate the offer by delivery of a written notice of termination to the seller or the seller's agent.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.13
citations.cite: California Civil Code, noncompliance doesn't invalidate the sale, but creates liability
citations.quote: No transfer subject to this article shall be invalidated solely because of the failure of any person to comply with any provision of this article. However, any person who willfully or negligently violates or fails to perform any duty prescribed by any provision of this article shall be liable in the amount of actual damages suffered by a transferee.

clauses.title: Natural Hazard Disclosure
clauses.body: Separately from the Transfer Disclosure Statement, California law requires a distinct Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement whenever the seller or the seller's agent is required by other law to disclose the property's location within a hazard zone. This statement must disclose, as its own itemized categories: whether the property lies within a special flood hazard area (FEMA Zone "A" or "V"); an area of potential flooding shown on a dam-failure inundation map; a high or very-high fire hazard severity zone (which also carries its own vegetation-maintenance requirement for the owner); a wildland area that may contain substantial forest-fire risks and hazards (which also carries its own maintenance requirement for the owner, and a statement that the state is not responsible for fire protection to structures there absent a specific cooperative agreement); an earthquake fault zone; and a seismic hazard zone (landslide or liquefaction). The statement itself says this information is not a warranty, though prospective buyers may rely on it in deciding whether and on what terms to buy. Any waiver of these natural-hazard disclosure requirements is void as against public policy. Separately, for a home constructed before January 1, 2010 and located in a high or very-high fire hazard severity zone, the seller must provide an additional, specific wildfire-hardening disclosure notice, in statutorily specified language.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines its natural-hazard disclosure categories — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential purchase; hazard-disclosure categories and the underlying hazard-zone maps are jurisdiction- and geography-specific. All citations to § 1103 below are subsections of the same statutory section as each other; all citations to § 1103.2 (the actual disclosure-form text) are subsections of that different, independent section; § 1102.6f (the separate pre-2010 wildfire notice) is a third, independently-authored section. The wildland-area quotation was re-verified on 2026-09-03 and updated to reflect the current statutory text as amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 80 (effective January 1, 2025), which added a sentence on the state's fire-protection responsibility; this correction was identified during independent research for this corpus's separate Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement — Information Sheet document.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the natural hazard disclosure article
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 1103.1, this article applies to a sale, exchange, real property sales contract, as defined in Section 2985, lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements, of any single-family residential real property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103(d)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, waiver of natural hazard disclosure is void
citations.quote: Any waiver of the requirements of this article is void as against public policy.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.2(a) [flood zone]
citations.cite: California Civil Code, special flood hazard area category
citations.quote: A SPECIAL FLOOD HAZARD AREA (Any type Zone “A” or “V”) designated by the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.2(a) [dam inundation]
citations.cite: California Civil Code, dam-failure inundation area category
citations.quote: AN AREA OF POTENTIAL FLOODING shown on a dam failure inundation map pursuant to Section 8589.5 of the Government Code.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.2(a) [fire hazard]
citations.cite: California Civil Code, fire hazard severity zone category
citations.quote: A HIGH or VERY HIGH FIRE HAZARD SEVERITY ZONE (FHSZ) as identified by the Director of Forestry and Fire Protection pursuant to Section 51178 of the Government Code or Article 9 (commencing with Section 4201) of Chapter 1 of Part 2 of Division 4 of the Public Resources Code. The owner of this property is subject to the maintenance requirements of Section 51182 of the Government Code.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.2(a) [wildland area]
citations.cite: California Civil Code, wildland fire area category
citations.quote: A WILDLAND AREA THAT MAY CONTAIN SUBSTANTIAL FOREST FIRE RISKS AND HAZARDS pursuant to Section 4125 of the Public Resources Code. The owner of this property is subject to the maintenance requirements of Section 4291 of the Public Resources Code. Additionally, it is not the state’s responsibility to provide fire protection services to any building or structure located within the wildlands unless the Department of Forestry and Fire Protection has entered into a cooperative agreement with a local agency for those purposes pursuant to Section 4142 of the Public Resources Code.
