clauses.title: Lead-Based Paint Disclosure (Federal Law)
clauses.body: For "target housing" — housing constructed before 1978, with narrow exceptions for housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities and for 0-bedroom dwellings where no child under 6 resides or is expected to reside — before the buyer becomes obligated under any contract to purchase, the seller must: provide the buyer an EPA-prescribed lead hazard information pamphlet; disclose the presence of any known lead-based paint or lead-based paint hazards and provide any available lead hazard evaluation report; and permit the buyer a 10-day period (unless the parties mutually agree to a different period) to conduct a risk assessment or inspection for lead-based paint hazards. Every purchase contract for such housing must contain a statutorily specified Lead Warning Statement, along with a statement signed by the buyer confirming receipt of the pamphlet, the 10-day (or agreed) opportunity, and understanding of the Lead Warning Statement.
clauses.gap: Unlike the other clauses in this document, which cite California's Civil Code as one state's real evidence of how a state structures its residential-purchase disclosure requirements, this clause states federal law. 42 U.S.C. § 4852d and its implementing EPA/HUD regulation (40 C.F.R. § 745.113) apply nationwide to any "target housing" purchase, regardless of which state's law otherwise governs the transaction — this is not a state-specific rule and doesn't vary by which state's law a specific purchase is otherwise governed by. The two quotes from 42 U.S.C. § 4852d below are subsections of the same statutory section; the "target housing" definition (a separate section, § 4851b) and the CFR regulation are independently-authored sources.

citations.cite: Federal law, pamphlet/disclosure/10-day inspection requirements
citations.quote: The regulations shall require that, before the purchaser or lessee is obligated under any contract to purchase or lease the housing, the seller or lessor shall— (A) provide the purchaser or lessee with a lead hazard information pamphlet, as prescribed by the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency under section 406 of the Toxic Substances Control Act [15 U.S.C. 2686]; (B) disclose to the purchaser or lessee the presence of any known lead-based paint, or any known lead-based paint hazards, in such housing and provide to the purchaser or lessee any lead hazard evaluation report available to the seller or lessor; and (C) permit the purchaser a 10-day period (unless the parties mutually agree upon a different period of time) to conduct a risk assessment or inspection for the presence of lead-based paint hazards.

citations.cite: Federal law, the required Lead Warning Statement text
citations.quote: Every purchaser of any interest in residential real property on which a residential dwelling was built prior to 1978 is notified that such property may present exposure to lead from lead-based paint that may place young children at risk of developing lead poisoning. Lead poisoning in young children may produce permanent neurological damage, including learning disabilities, reduced intelligence quotient, behavioral problems, and impaired memory. Lead poisoning also poses a particular risk to pregnant women. The seller of any interest in residential real property is required to provide the buyer with any information on lead-based paint hazards from risk assessments or inspections in the seller's possession and notify the buyer of any known lead-based paint hazards. A risk assessment or inspection for possible lead-based paint hazards is recommended prior to purchase.

citations.cite: Federal law, definition of 'target housing'
citations.quote: The term “target housing” means any housing constructed prior to 1978, except housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities or any 0-bedroom dwelling (unless any child who is less than 6 years of age resides or is expected to reside in such housing).

citations.cite: Federal regulation, the contract attachment requirement
citations.quote: Each contract to sell target housing shall include an attachment containing the following elements, in the language of the contract (e.g., English, Spanish): (1) A Lead Warning Statement consisting of the following language:

clauses.title: Megan's Law Database Notice
clauses.body: Every contract for the sale of residential real property comprised of one to four dwelling units, entered into on or after July 1, 1999, must contain a statutorily specified notice, in not less than 8-point type. For a contract entered into on or after April 1, 2006, the required notice reads: "Notice: Pursuant to Section 290.46 of the Penal Code, information about specified registered sex offenders is made available to the public via an Internet Web site maintained by the Department of Justice at www.meganslaw.ca.gov. Depending on an offender's criminal history, this information will include either the address at which the offender resides or the community of residence and ZIP Code in which the offender resides." Once this notice has been delivered, the seller or broker is not required to provide additional information about the proximity of registered sex offenders, and the notice does not give rise to any cause of action against the disclosing party by a registered sex offender.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's approach to a statewide sex-offender registry notice requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential purchase. Note this statute's scope term — "one to four dwelling units" — differs from the "single-family residential property" scope term used in the main Transfer Disclosure Statement statute cited elsewhere in this document; the two phrases aren't equated here, and a specific transaction's classification under each statute isn't resolved by this document. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2079.10a); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.10a(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the Megan's Law notice requirement
citations.quote: Every lease or rental agreement for single-family residential real property entered into on or after July 1, 1999, any leasehold interest in real property consisting of multiunit residential property with more than four dwelling units entered into after that date, and every contract for the sale of residential real property comprised of one to four dwelling units entered into on or after that date, shall contain, in not less than 8-point type, a notice as specified in paragraph (1), (2), or (3).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.10a(a)(3)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, current required notice text
citations.quote: A contract entered into by the parties on or after April 1, 2006, shall contain the following notice: Notice: Pursuant to Section 290.46 of the Penal Code, information about specified registered sex offenders is made available to the public via an Internet Web site maintained by the Department of Justice at www.meganslaw.ca.gov. Depending on an offender's criminal history, this information will include either the address at which the offender resides or the community of residence and ZIP Code in which the offender resides.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.10a(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, delivering the notice is deemed adequate
citations.quote: Subject to subdivision (c), upon delivery of the notice to the lessee or buyer of the real property, the lessor, seller, or broker is not required to provide information in addition to that contained in the notice regarding the proximity of registered sex offenders.

clauses.title: Good-Faith Deposit as Liquidated Damages
clauses.body: For a purchase contract for "residential property" — a dwelling of no more than four residential units, where at the time the contract is made the buyer intends to occupy the dwelling or one of its units as a residence — a provision stating that all or part of a payment made by the buyer will constitute liquidated damages to the seller if the buyer fails to complete the purchase is valid, to the extent the payment is actually made in cash or check, if it does not exceed 3 percent of the purchase price; above that 3 percent threshold, the provision is presumed invalid unless the party seeking to enforce it proves the amount is reasonable as liquidated damages. Separately, to be valid at all, such a provision must be separately signed or initialed by each party to the contract, and — if included in a printed contract — must be set out in at least 10-point bold type or in contrasting red print of at least 8-point bold type.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a residential-purchase liquidated-damages presumption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential purchase; liquidated-damages caps and formatting requirements vary by state and some states don't have a presumptive-validity statute like this one at all. § 1675 and § 1677 are different, independently-authored sections of the same statutory chapter (Title 4.5, Chapter 2 — Default on Real Property Purchase Contract), not subsections of a single section; the two citations to § 1675 below are subsections of that one section.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1675(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of qualifying 'residential property'
citations.quote: As used in this section, “residential property” means real property primarily consisting of a dwelling that meets both of the following requirements: (1) The dwelling contains not more than four residential units. (2) At the time the contract to purchase and sell the property is made, the buyer intends to occupy the dwelling or one of its units as his or her residence.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1675(c)-(d)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the 3% presumptive-validity cap
citations.quote: If the amount actually paid pursuant to the liquidated damages provision does not exceed 3 percent of the purchase price, the provision is valid to the extent that payment is actually made unless the buyer establishes that the amount is unreasonable as liquidated damages. ... If the amount actually paid pursuant to the liquidated damages provision exceeds 3 percent of the purchase price, the provision is invalid unless the party seeking to uphold the provision establishes that the amount actually paid is reasonable as liquidated damages.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1677
citations.cite: California Civil Code, separate-signature and type-size requirement
citations.quote: A provision in a contract to purchase and sell real property liquidating the damages to the seller if the buyer fails to complete the purchase of the property is invalid unless: (a) The provision is separately signed or initialed by each party to the contract; and (b) If the provision is included in a printed contract, it is set out either in at least 10-point bold type or in contrasting red print in at least eight-point bold type.

clauses.title: The Marvin Doctrine — Enforceability of Express Contracts Between Nonmarital Partners
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, under California case law, a court will enforce an express contract between nonmarital partners concerning the property, earnings, and other financial affairs the partners acquire or manage during their relationship, except to the extent the contract is explicitly founded on the consideration of meretricious sexual services. This rule was announced by the California Supreme Court in Marvin v. Marvin (1976) 18 Cal.3d 660, which held that the property-division provisions that apply to married couples do not govern the distribution of property acquired during a nonmarital relationship, and that such a relationship instead remains subject to distribution under principles the courts themselves develop, including the enforcement of an express contract between the partners.
clauses.gap: This is one state's judicial doctrine — established entirely by the California Supreme Court, not by any statute — used as real evidence of how a court can treat a contract between unmarried cohabitants, not a claim about which state's law, if any, governs a specific couple's cohabitation agreement or that every state enforces this kind of contract the same way. This is one of the most jurisdiction-variable areas of family law: some states enforce express nonmarital cohabitation contracts in essentially the way California does, some require such a contract to satisfy a statutory writing requirement before it is enforceable, some apply significantly more restrictive tests, and some decline to enforce this category of contract at all as a matter of that state's own public policy. This is a single source (the Marvin opinion); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Marvin v. Marvin
citations.quote: We conclude: (1) The provisions of the Family Law Act do not govern the distribution of property acquired during a nonmarital relationship; such a relationship remains subject solely to judicial decision. (2) The courts should enforce express contracts between nonmarital partners except to the extent that the contract is explicitly founded on the consideration of meretricious sexual services. (3) In the absence of an express contract, the courts should inquire into the conduct of the parties to determine whether that conduct demonstrates an implied contract, agreement of partnership or joint venture, or some other tacit understanding between the parties. The courts may also employ the doctrine of quantum meruit, or equitable remedies such as constructive or resulting trusts, when warranted by the facts of the case.

clauses.title: Implied Contracts and Equitable Remedies Absent an Express Agreement
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, under the same California case law, a court is not limited to enforcing an express written or oral contract between nonmarital partners. In the absence of an express agreement, a California court may examine the conduct of the partners to determine whether that conduct demonstrates an implied contract, an implied agreement of partnership or joint venture, or some other tacit understanding between them, and may apply equitable remedies such as a constructive trust or a resulting trust, or allow recovery in quantum meruit for the reasonable value of household services rendered, less the reasonable value of any support received, where a partner rendered those services with the expectation of monetary reward.
clauses.gap: This is the same single source as the Marvin doctrine clause above (a different passage of the same 1976 California Supreme Court opinion); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's judicial doctrine, used as real evidence that a court can extend relief to unmarried cohabitants beyond an express contract — not a claim about which state's law, if any, applies to a specific couple, or that every state recognizes these same implied-contract and equitable remedies for unmarried cohabitants. Recognition of implied contracts, constructive or resulting trusts, and quantum meruit claims between unmarried partners varies by state, and some states limit recovery to an express written contract only.

citations.case: Marvin v. Marvin
citations.quote: We add that in the absence of an express agreement, the courts may look to a variety of other remedies in order to protect the parties' lawful expectations. The courts may inquire into the conduct of the parties to determine whether that conduct demonstrates an implied contract or implied agreement of partnership or joint venture (see Estate of Thornton (1972) 81 Wn.2d 72 [499 P.2d 864]), or some other tacit understanding between the parties. The courts may, when appropriate, employ principles of constructive trust (see Omer v. Omer (1974) 11 Wash.App. 386 [523 P.2d 957]) or resulting trust (see Hyman v. Hyman (Tex.Civ.App. 1954) 275 S.W.2d 149). Finally, a nonmarital partner may recover in quantum meruit for the reasonable value of household services rendered less the reasonable value of support received if he can show that he rendered services with the expectation of monetary reward. (See Hill v. Estate of Westbrook, supra, 39 Cal.2d 458, 462.)

clauses.title: The Meretricious-Consideration Limit and Severability
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, under the same California case law, a contract between nonmarital partners is unenforceable only to the extent it is explicitly and inseparably founded on the consideration of sexual services — that is, only where sexual acts form an inseparable part of the consideration for the agreement, so that the agreement is, in substance, a contract for the performance of sexual services. The mere fact that the partners cohabit, or that they have or had a sexual relationship, does not itself invalidate an agreement between them concerning their earnings, property, or expenses, and such an agreement is not invalid merely because the partners contemplated the creation or continuation of their relationship when they entered into it. Where a contract's consideration includes sexual services but is not inseparably based on them, a court may still enforce any severable portion of the contract that is supported by independent, lawful consideration.
clauses.gap: This is the same single source as the two authority clauses above (two further passages of the same 1976 opinion); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's line-drawing test for when a nonmarital-partner contract is unenforceable, used as real evidence of how narrowly one court has drawn that limit — not a claim about which state's test, if any, applies to a specific couple's agreement, or that every state draws the line the same way. Some states apply a broader unenforceability standard to any contract connected to an unmarried couple's sexual relationship, rather than California's narrower explicitly-and-inseparably-founded-on-sexual-services standard.

citations.case: Marvin v. Marvin
citations.quote: The fact that a man and woman live together without marriage, and engage in a sexual relationship, does not in itself invalidate agreements between them relating to their earnings, property, or expenses. Neither is such an agreement invalid merely because the parties may have contemplated the creation or continuation of a nonmarital relationship when they entered into it. Agreements between nonmarital partners fail only to the extent that they rest upon a consideration of meretricious sexual services.

citations.case: Marvin v. Marvin
citations.quote: The decisions in the Hill and Updeck cases thus demonstrate that a contract between nonmarital partners, even if expressly made in contemplation of a common living arrangement, is invalid only if sexual acts form an inseparable part of the consideration for the agreement. In sum, a court will not enforce a contract for the pooling of property and earnings if it is explicitly and inseparably based upon services as a paramour. The Court of Appeal opinion in Hill, however, indicates that even if sexual services are part of the contractual consideration, any severable portion of the contract supported by independent consideration will still be enforced.

clauses.title: No Automatic Sharing of Property Between Unmarried Cohabitants
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, under California law, the statutory property-division rules that apply to married spouses do not apply automatically to unmarried cohabitants. The California Supreme Court has held that the provisions of the Family Law Act do not govern the distribution of property acquired during a nonmarital relationship, and that unmarried partners may, by agreement, choose to pool their earnings and hold property acquired during the relationship in the manner the law governing community property provides, or may instead agree that each partner's earnings and the property acquired from those earnings remains that partner's separate property — meaning that, absent such an agreement, no automatic sharing of property or income between unmarried cohabitants results merely from their living together.
clauses.gap: This is drawn from the Marvin opinion's own framing (two passages of the same 1976 California Supreme Court opinion already cited above); no additional independent source was found for this despite a search for a later California Court of Appeal restatement. Two candidate later Court of Appeal decisions were checked (Bergen v. Wood (1993) 14 Cal.App.4th 854 and Velez v. Smith (2006) 142 Cal.App.4th 1154); both discuss Marvin but only recite its holding rather than independently confirming this default with separate reasoning, so neither was used as a second source here. It is one state's judicial framework, used as real evidence that a default rule of no automatic property-sharing for unmarried cohabitants exists in that state's case law — not a claim about which state's default rule, if any, applies to a specific couple absent an agreement, or that every state has the same default. Some states' common-law-marriage doctrines, domestic-partnership statutes, or other relationship-status statutes may produce a different default outcome for a long-term unmarried couple than California's default of no automatic sharing.

citations.case: Marvin v. Marvin
citations.quote: The provisions of the Family Law Act do not govern the distribution of property acquired during a nonmarital relationship; such a relationship remains subject solely to judicial decision.

citations.case: Marvin v. Marvin
citations.quote: In summary, we base our opinion on the principle that adults who voluntarily live together and engage in sexual relations are nonetheless as competent as any other persons to contract respecting their earnings and property rights. Of course, they cannot lawfully contract to pay for the performance of sexual services, for such a contract is, in essence, an agreement for prostitution and unlawful for that reason. But they may agree to pool their earnings and to hold all property acquired during the relationship in accord with the law governing community property; conversely they may agree that each partner's earnings and the property acquired from those earnings remains the separate property of the earning partner. So long as the agreement does not rest upon illicit meretricious consideration, the parties may order their economic affairs as they choose, and no policy precludes the courts from enforcing such agreements.

clauses.title: California Has Not Codified the Marvin Doctrine — State Variation Disclosure
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that the Marvin doctrine described above has never been enacted into a California statute. The California Supreme Court itself observed that no language in the Family Law Act addresses the property rights of nonmarital partners and that nothing in that act's legislative history suggests the California Legislature considered the subject, and that the rights of nonmarital partners had, before and after the Family Law Act, been fixed entirely by judicial decision rather than by statute. No provision of the California Family Code or Civil Code was located that codifies the Marvin doctrine or otherwise creates a specific statutory cause of action for an unmarried cohabitant's contract or property claim against a partner; the doctrine remains a product of case law that later California appellate decisions can narrow, extend, or depart from without any accompanying change in a statute.
clauses.gap: This is drawn from the Marvin opinion's own framing (a further passage of the same 1976 opinion already cited above), together with an independent check for a codifying statute that did not locate one; a search failure is not proof that no such statute exists, only that this search did not find one, so no additional independent source is claimed here. It is one state's approach — California's choice to leave nonmarital-cohabitant contract and property rights to case law rather than statute — used as real evidence that at least one state takes this approach, not a claim about which state's law, if any, governs a specific couple's cohabitation agreement. Contract and property rights of unmarried cohabitants are widely understood to be one of the most jurisdiction-variable areas of family law in the United States: some states enforce express cohabitation contracts largely as California does; some impose a statutory writing requirement or other formal prerequisites before such a contract is enforceable; some apply a substantially more restrictive test to any contract connected to an unmarried couple's relationship; and some states' courts have declined to enforce this category of contract at all as against that state's public policy. This document does not identify which, if any, of those approaches would apply to a particular couple or in a particular state.

citations.case: Marvin v. Marvin
citations.quote: No language in the Family Law Act addresses the property rights of nonmarital partners, and nothing in the legislative history of the act suggests that the Legislature considered that subject. The delineation of the rights of nonmarital partners before 1970 had been fixed entirely by judicial decision; we see no reason to believe that the Legislature, by enacting the Family Law Act, intended to change that, state of affairs.

clauses.title: Recitals — Parties and Purpose
clauses.body: This Cohabitation Agreement is made by {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} (together, "the Parties"), who state that they are two unmarried adults sharing a household, dated {{agreementDate}}. The Parties enter into this Agreement to record their mutual understanding regarding the property they own individually and together, the expenses of their shared household, and the financial expectations they hold toward one another during their relationship, separate and apart from any statute or doctrine governing marriage or a registered domestic partnership.

clauses.title: The Meal Period Requirement (First and Second Meal Periods)
clauses.body: California law prohibits {{companyName}} from employing {{employeeName}} for a work period of more than 5 hours per day without providing a meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if {{employeeName}}'s total work period for the day is no more than 6 hours, the meal period may be waived by mutual consent of {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}. If {{employeeName}} works more than 10 hours in a day, {{companyName}} must provide a second 30-minute meal period, except that if the total hours worked is no more than 12, the second meal period may be waived by mutual consent — but only if the first meal period was not waived.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 512(a)), offered as documented evidence of what that provision says — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law imposes no meal-period requirement at all, and most other states either have no meal-break statute or a far less detailed one; California's two-tier, waiver-conditioned structure is unusually specific by national comparison. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 512(a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific text, though its interpretation is separately confirmed by case law cited elsewhere in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 512(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 512, subd. (a)
citations.quote: An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than five hours per day without providing the employee with a meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total work period per day of the employee is no more than six hours, the meal period may be waived by mutual consent of both the employer and employee. An employer shall not employ an employee for a work period of more than 10 hours per day without providing the employee with a second meal period of not less than 30 minutes, except that if the total hours worked is no more than 12 hours, the second meal period may be waived by mutual consent of the employer and the employee only if the first meal period was not waived.

clauses.title: The Rest Period Requirement
clauses.body: Separately from the meal period requirement, California requires {{companyName}} to authorize and permit {{employeeName}} to take rest periods, insofar as practicable in the middle of each work period. The authorized rest time is based on total hours worked daily, at the rate of ten minutes of net rest time per four hours worked or major fraction of four hours — though a rest period need not be authorized if {{employeeName}}'s total daily work time is less than three and one-half hours. Authorized rest period time is counted as hours worked, and no deduction from wages may be made for it.
clauses.gap: This provision does not appear in the California Labor Code at all — it is a regulation adopted by the Industrial Welfare Commission, codified in Wage Order No. 4-2001 ("Professional, Technical, Clerical, Mechanical and Similar Occupations"), the general catch-all order used here because it is not industry-specific; an employer in a covered industry such as manufacturing, mercantile, or the motion picture industry would instead look to that industry's own numbered wage order, which may phrase the same 10-minutes-per-4-hours rule slightly differently. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what it says — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer. Federal law has no rest-break requirement, and most states impose none either. This is a single regulatory subdivision; no additional independent source was found for the rest-period formula itself.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 12(A)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 12(A)
citations.quote: Every employer shall authorize and permit all employees to take rest periods, which insofar as practicable shall be in the middle of each work period. The authorized rest period time shall be based on the total hours worked daily at the rate of ten (10) minutes net rest time per four (4) hours or major fraction thereof. However, a rest period need not be authorized for employees whose total daily work time is less than three and one-half (3½) hours. Authorized rest period time shall be counted as hours worked for which there shall be no deduction from wages.

clauses.title: The Premium Pay Remedy for a Missed Meal or Rest Period
clauses.body: If {{companyName}} fails to provide {{employeeName}} a meal or rest period required by an applicable statute or IWC wage order, California law requires {{companyName}} to pay {{employeeName}} one additional hour of pay at {{employeeName}}'s regular rate of compensation for each workday the meal or rest period is not provided. {{companyName}} may also not require {{employeeName}} to work during a meal, rest, or recovery period mandated by an applicable statute, regulation, or order.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 226.7(b)-(c)) — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship. Federal law has no comparable premium-pay remedy for missed breaks, and most states with meal/rest laws do not attach an automatic one-hour-of-pay remedy the way California does. The statutory text sets one additional hour of pay for each workday a meal, rest, or recovery period is not provided — it does not, in these words, separately cap or itemize a meal-period premium against a rest-period premium as two distinct amounts; the widely applied practitioner reading is that up to two separate one-hour premiums (one for a meal violation, one for a rest violation) can apply on the same workday, but that reading is not itself quoted statutory text and is not asserted here as such. This is a single statutory section (§ 226.7); no additional independent source was found for this specific remedy language. Separately, § 226.7 currently exists in two operative versions enacted by the same 2020 session law: the version quoted here is the one operative now; a different version (expanding the definitions used for heat-illness recovery periods) becomes operative January 1, 2027.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.7(b)-(c)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 226.7, subds. (b)-(c)
citations.quote: (b) An employer shall not require an employee to work during a meal or rest or recovery period mandated pursuant to an applicable statute, or applicable regulation, standard, or order of the Industrial Welfare Commission, the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board, or the Division of Occupational Safety and Health. (c) If an employer fails to provide an employee a meal or rest or recovery period in accordance with a state law, including, but not limited to, an applicable statute or applicable regulation, standard, or order of the Industrial Welfare Commission, the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board, or the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, the employer shall pay the employee one additional hour of pay at the employee's regular rate of compensation for each workday that the meal or rest or recovery period is not provided.

clauses.title: The "Provide, Not Ensure" Standard
clauses.body: The California Supreme Court has held that {{companyName}}'s duty regarding meal breaks is an obligation to provide a meal period, not to ensure no work is performed during it. {{companyName}} satisfies this obligation if it relieves {{employeeName}} of all duty, relinquishes control over {{employeeName}}'s activities, and permits {{employeeName}} a reasonable opportunity to take an uninterrupted 30-minute break, without impeding or discouraging {{employeeName}} from doing so. {{companyName}} is not obligated to police meal breaks to ensure no work is performed afterward — if {{employeeName}} is bona fide relieved of duty and {{companyName}} has relinquished control, work {{employeeName}} chooses to perform during that break does not itself create premium-pay liability for {{companyName}}.
clauses.gap: This is a holding of the California Supreme Court interpreting one state's statute and regulation — Labor Code § 512(a) and a wage order — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer, and not a claim that this standard would apply outside California. No comparable federal standard exists, since federal law imposes no meal-period obligation to interpret. This clause draws on a single opinion (Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court); the timing-rule clause elsewhere in this document also draws on this same opinion — they are not independent sources of one another.

citations.case: Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court
citations.quote: To summarize: An employer's duty with respect to meal breaks under both section 512, subdivision (a) and Wage Order No. 5 is an obligation to provide a meal period to its employees. The employer satisfies this obligation if it relieves its employees of all duty, relinquishes, control over their activities and permits them a reasonable opportunity to take an uninterrupted 30-minute break, and does not impede or discourage them from doing so. ... On the other hand, the employer is not obligated to police meal breaks and ensure no work thereafter is performed. Bona fide relief from duty and the relinquishing of control satisfies the employer's obligations, and work by a relieved employee during a meal break does not thereby place the employer in violation of its obligations and create liability for premium pay under Wage Order No. 5, subdivision 11(B) and Labor Code section 226.7, subdivision (b).

clauses.title: The Meal Period Timing Rule
clauses.body: The California Supreme Court has held that, absent a valid waiver, § 512 requires {{companyName}} to provide {{employeeName}} a first meal period no later than the end of {{employeeName}}'s fifth hour of work, and a second meal period (if applicable) no later than the end of {{employeeName}}'s tenth hour of work.
clauses.gap: This is a holding of the California Supreme Court interpreting Labor Code § 512, one state's statute — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. Federal law sets no such timing requirement, having no meal-period requirement at all. This clause draws on the same opinion as the "provide, not ensure" clause elsewhere in this document (Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court); they are not independent sources of each other.

citations.case: Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court
citations.quote: We conclude that, absent waiver, section 512 requires a first meal period no later than the end of an employee's fifth hour of work, and a second meal period no later than the end of an employee's 10th hour of work.

clauses.title: On-Duty Meal Periods (Narrow Exception)
clauses.body: Unless {{employeeName}} is relieved of all duty during a 30-minute meal period, that period is considered an "on duty" meal period and counted as time worked. California law permits an on-duty meal period only when the nature of {{employeeName}}'s work prevents {{employeeName}} from being relieved of all duty, and only by written agreement between {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}, stating that {{employeeName}} may revoke the agreement in writing at any time. When an employee is employed for five hours, California's meal-period framework requires the employer to choose among: providing an off-duty meal period, obtaining a mutually agreed waiver where one hour or less will end the shift, or obtaining a written on-duty meal period agreement where circumstances permit one.
clauses.gap: This is one state's regulatory text (an IWC wage order provision) and a passage from the California Supreme Court's decision describing that same regulatory structure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. The on-duty-meal-period concept described here does not exist as a matter of federal law, which imposes no meal-period requirement to except from. This clause draws on two genuinely independent sources: a regulation (the wage order) and case law (Brinker) describing it.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 11(A)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 11(A)
citations.quote: Unless the employee is relieved of all duty during a 30 minute meal period, the meal period shall be considered an "on duty" meal period and counted as time worked. An "on duty" meal period shall be permitted only when the nature of the work prevents an employee from being relieved of all duty and when by written agreement between the parties an on-the-job paid meal period is agreed to. The written agreement shall state that the employee may, in writing, revoke the agreement at any time.

citations.case: Brinker Restaurant Corp. v. Superior Court
citations.quote: When someone is suffered or permitted to work—i.e., employed—for five hours, an employer is put to a choice: it must (1) afford an off-duty meal period; (2) consent to a mutually agreed-upon waiver if one hour or less will end the shift; or (3) obtain written agreement to an on-duty meal period if circumstances permit.

clauses.title: Policy Statement
clauses.body: {{companyName}} maintains this Meal and Rest Break Policy to describe the meal and rest periods made available to non-exempt employees, including {{employeeName}}, in the ordinary course of employment. This policy sets out when meal and rest periods are made available, the circumstances under which a meal period may be waived, and the conditions under which a meal period may be designated "on duty." This policy is a statement of {{companyName}}'s practice; it does not itself waive, expand, or limit any right or obligation that may exist under applicable law.

clauses.title: Employee Acknowledgment
clauses.body: {{employeeName}} acknowledges having received and reviewed a copy of this Meal and Rest Break Policy. {{employeeName}} understands that meal and rest periods are made available as described in this policy, that a meal period may be waived only under the specific circumstances described above, and that any on-duty meal period requires a separate written agreement that {{employeeName}} may revoke in writing at any time.

clauses.title: Signature and Receipt
clauses.body:
Employee Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

Employer Representative Signature: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

clauses.title: Property Eligible for a TOD Deed
clauses.body: California's Revocable Transfer on Death Deed statute applies only to real property that is (1) a parcel of land improved with one to four residential dwelling units, or (2) a residential unit (such as a condominium) and its appurtenant common area within a common interest development. A parcel of agricultural land greater than 40 acres does not qualify, regardless of how it is otherwise improved. The property at {{propertyAddress}}, described as {{legalDescription}}, is represented to fall within one of the qualifying categories.
clauses.gap: This is California's own statutory definition, offered as evidence of how one state defines eligible property — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular property or transfer. Transfer-on-death deeds are a relatively recent and unevenly adopted mechanism: not every state authorizes one, and states that do vary in what property qualifies and under what formalities. Separately, California frames the 40-acre limit as an exclusion from an otherwise-qualifying residential parcel, not as an independent "agricultural property with a single-family residence" category — a distinction worth preserving rather than collapsing into shorthand. Finally, this entire statute (Probate Code Part 4, §§ 5600-5698) is presently scheduled to repeal itself on January 1, 2032 unless a later-enacted statute extends or removes that date; it has been amended several times since 2015 but has not been made permanent as of the most recent amendment located (2023, effective 2024). This is a single statutory section (§ 5610); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5610
citations.cite: California Probate Code, Revocable Transfer on Death Deed — definition of "real property"
citations.quote: (a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), “real property” means either of the following: (1) A parcel of land that is improved with one to four residential dwelling units. (2) A residential separate interest and its appurtenant common area in a common interest development, regardless of the number of separate interests in the common interest development. (b) “Real property” does not include a parcel of agricultural land that is greater than 40 acres in size.

clauses.title: Revocability and No Present Transfer During Owner's Lifetime
clauses.body: During {{ownerName}}'s lifetime, executing and recording this deed does not affect {{ownerName}}'s ownership of the property at {{propertyAddress}}. {{ownerName}} may sell, mortgage, lease, or otherwise deal with the property without {{beneficiaryName}}'s consent, and the property remains subject to {{ownerName}}'s creditors as though this deed had not been made. {{beneficiaryName}} holds no legal or equitable interest in the property, and the property is not reachable by {{beneficiaryName}}'s creditors, unless and until the deed operates at {{ownerName}}'s death.
clauses.gap: This describes California's own statutory rule for revocable TOD deeds specifically, not a general statement about how every deed-like instrument works, and not a claim about which state's law applies to a given transfer — TOD-deed statutes are not uniform across the states that have them. This is a single statutory section (§ 5650); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5650
citations.cite: California Probate Code, effect during transferor's life
citations.quote: During the transferor’s life, execution and recordation of a revocable transfer on death deed: (a) Does not affect the ownership rights of the transferor, and the transferor or the transferor’s agent or other fiduciary may convey, assign, contract, encumber, or otherwise deal with the property, and the property is subject to process of the transferor’s creditors, as if no revocable transfer on death deed were executed or recorded. (b) Does not create any legal or equitable right in the beneficiary, and the property is not subject to process of the beneficiary’s creditors. (c) Does not transfer or convey any right, title, or interest in the property.

clauses.title: Statutory Form and Execution Formalities
clauses.body: This deed must be substantially in the statutory form, signed and dated by {{ownerName}}, signed by two witnesses present together who either watch {{ownerName}} sign or hear {{ownerName}} acknowledge the signature, and acknowledged before a notary public. It is not effective unless it is also recorded in the county where the property is located on or before 60 days after the date it is notarized.
clauses.gap: This describes California's specific formalities (two witnesses plus notarization, and a 60-day recording deadline). These requirements are not uniform even among the small number of states that authorize a transfer-on-death or beneficiary deed — some require only notarization and no witnesses, some impose no recording deadline at all, and this is not a claim about which state's formalities apply to a particular deed.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5624
citations.cite: California Probate Code, conditions for effectiveness — signing, witnesses, notarization
citations.quote: A revocable transfer on death deed is not effective unless all of the following conditions are satisfied: (a) The deed is signed by the transferor and dated. (b) The deed is signed by two witnesses who were present at the same time and who witnessed either the signing of the deed or the transferor’s acknowledgment that the transferor had signed the deed. (c) The deed is acknowledged before a notary public.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5626
citations.cite: California Probate Code, recording deadline
citations.quote: (a) A revocable transfer on death deed is not effective unless the deed is recorded on or before 60 days after the date it was acknowledged before a notary.

clauses.title: How a TOD Deed Is Revoked
clauses.body: {{ownerName}} may revoke this deed at any time before death, without {{beneficiaryName}}'s joinder, consent, or agreement, and without giving {{beneficiaryName}} notice. Under California's statute, a recorded TOD deed can be revoked in any of three ways: recording a new TOD deed for the same property (the later-recorded deed controls and revokes the earlier one), recording a separate instrument of revocation executed and recorded with the same formalities as a TOD deed, or selling, giving away, or otherwise transferring the property to someone else before death and recording that transfer.
clauses.gap: This is California's specific set of revocation mechanisms, offered as evidence for one state's statute rather than a general or universal description of how transfer-on-death instruments are revoked elsewhere.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5628
citations.cite: California Probate Code, later-recorded deed revokes earlier deed
citations.quote: (a) If a revocable transfer on death deed is recorded for the same property for which another revocable transfer on death deed is recorded, the later executed deed is the operative instrument and its recordation revokes the earlier executed deed.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5630
citations.cite: California Probate Code, revocation at any time
citations.quote: A transferor who has the capacity to contract may revoke a revocable transfer on death deed at any time.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5632
citations.cite: California Probate Code, instrument of revocation; no beneficiary consent required
citations.quote: (a) An instrument revoking a revocable transfer on death deed shall be executed and recorded in the same manner as execution and recordation of a revocable transfer on death deed. (b) Joinder, consent, or agreement of, or notice to, the beneficiary is not required for revocation of a revocable transfer on death deed.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5642(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, statutory form — sale or transfer as revocation
citations.quote: There are three ways to revoke a recorded TOD deed: (1) Complete, have witnessed and notarized, and RECORD a revocation form. (2) Create, have witnessed and notarized, and RECORD a new TOD deed. (3) Sell or give away the property, or transfer it to a trust, before your death and RECORD the deed. A TOD deed can only affect property that you own when you die.

clauses.title: Priority Between a TOD Deed and a Will or Other Instrument
clauses.body: If this deed and another instrument (such as a will) both purport to dispose of the same property, and the other instrument makes a revocable disposition of it, whichever of the two was executed later controls. If the other instrument instead makes an irrevocable disposition of the property, that instrument controls regardless of which was executed later. California's statutory TOD deed form itself states that a TOD deed cannot be revoked by a will.
clauses.gap: California's operative priority rule (Probate Code § 5660) refers generically to "another instrument" that makes a "revocable" or "irrevocable" disposition — it does not use the word "will" in its own text. A will is generally a revocable disposition under California law, which is why the general later-executed-controls rule is described here as applying to wills, but that characterization is an inference from the general nature of wills, not a direct quotation of § 5660 itself. Separately, the statute's own mandated form language does state directly, in its own words, that a TOD deed cannot be revoked by a will. This is California's rule; other states' TOD/beneficiary-deed statutes may resolve a deed-versus-will conflict differently, or may not address it at all.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5660
citations.cite: California Probate Code, conflicting instruments
citations.quote: (a) If a revocable transfer on death deed recorded on or before 60 days after the date it was acknowledged before a notary public and another instrument both purport to dispose of the same property: (1) If the other instrument makes a revocable disposition of the property, the later executed of the revocable transfer on death deed or the other instrument is the operative instrument. (2) If the other instrument makes an irrevocable disposition of the property, the other instrument and not the revocable transfer on death deed is the operative instrument.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5642(b) [will]
citations.cite: California Probate Code, statutory form — TOD deed not revocable by will
citations.quote: A TOD deed cannot be revoked by will, or by purporting to leave the subject property to anyone via will.

clauses.title: Joint Tenancy and Community Property Interaction
clauses.body: If, at {{ownerName}}'s death, title to the property at {{propertyAddress}} is held in joint tenancy or as community property with right of survivorship, this deed is void, and the property instead passes according to the right of survivorship. If {{ownerName}} holds the property as community property with a spouse, additional statutory requirements governing spousal consent, revocation of consent, or modification of a community-property TOD deed also apply, and are ineffective unless recorded within the time otherwise required for that consent, revocation, or modification.
clauses.gap: This is California's specific statutory treatment; it was verified directly from the statute's text rather than assumed. The deed is void under this rule only if the survivorship co-ownership is still in place at the owner's death — for example, if the owner is the first joint tenant or spouse to die. Other states with a TOD/beneficiary deed statute may treat co-owned property differently, and this is not a claim about which state's rule applies to a given property.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5664
citations.cite: California Probate Code, deed void if held in joint tenancy or community property with right of survivorship
citations.quote: If, at the time of the transferor’s death, title to the property described in the revocable transfer on death deed is held in joint tenancy or as community property with right of survivorship, the revocable transfer on death deed is void. The transferor’s interest in the property is governed by the right of survivorship and not by the revocable transfer on death deed.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5666
citations.cite: California Probate Code, community property consent and timing requirements
citations.quote: (a) Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 5010) of Part 1 applies to a revocable transfer on death deed of community property. (b) For the purpose of application of Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 5010) of Part 1 to a revocable transfer on death deed of community property, written consent to the deed, revocation of written consent to the deed, or modification of the deed, is ineffective unless recorded within the time required by that chapter for execution or service of the written consent, revocation, or modification.

clauses.title: Beneficiary Predeceasing the Owner
clauses.body: {{beneficiaryName}}'s interest under this deed is contingent on surviving {{ownerName}}. If {{beneficiaryName}} does not survive {{ownerName}}, that interest lapses. If more than one beneficiary is named, the named beneficiaries take the property as tenants in common in equal shares, and a lapsed beneficiary's share is redistributed among the surviving named beneficiaries in equal shares. If every named beneficiary fails to survive {{ownerName}}, the deed has no effect and the property does not pass under it.
clauses.gap: California's statute expressly disapplies its own general anti-lapse rule (Probate Code § 21110, which for wills and certain other instruments can substitute a deceased beneficiary's issue) to a TOD deed — the lapse here is unconditional, with no automatic substitution of the deceased beneficiary's descendants. This is a real, checkable difference from how a lapsed gift under a will is often handled in California, and it is specific to this deed mechanism. The "if every beneficiary fails to survive, the deed has no effect" consequence is drawn from the statute's own mandated explanatory form text rather than from the numbered operative subsections alone. This is California's rule; other states' TOD-deed statutes are not assumed to handle predeceased beneficiaries the same way.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5652(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, survivorship condition; lapse; tenants in common; redistribution
citations.quote: (2) The interest of a beneficiary is contingent on the beneficiary surviving the transferor. Notwithstanding Section 21110, the interest of a beneficiary that fails to survive the transferor lapses. (3) Except as provided in paragraph (4), if there is more than one beneficiary, they take the property as tenants in common, in equal shares. (4) If there is more than one beneficiary, the share of a beneficiary that lapses or fails for any reason is transferred to the others in equal shares.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5642(b) [predecease]
citations.cite: California Probate Code, statutory form — effect if all beneficiaries predecease
citations.quote: If all beneficiaries die before you, the TOD deed has no effect. If a beneficiary dies before you, but other beneficiaries survive you, the share of the deceased beneficiary will be divided equally between the surviving beneficiaries.

clauses.title: Creditor Claims and Medi-Cal Recovery Exposure
clauses.body: Passing outside probate does not shield the property from claims against {{ownerName}}'s estate. For purposes of Medi-Cal eligibility, executing and recording this deed is not treated as a lifetime transfer of the property, and the property remains subject to claims by the California Department of Health Care Services to the extent otherwise authorized by law. More generally, {{beneficiaryName}} may be personally liable — capped at the fair market value of the property received, minus any liens and encumbrances on it — for {{ownerName}}'s unsecured debts, and a creditor holding a lien on the property recorded at {{ownerName}}'s death has priority over that property superior to any of {{beneficiaryName}}'s own creditors.
clauses.gap: The Medi-Cal-specific provision confirms that recording this deed does not remove the property from Department of Health Care Services claims, but it does so by cross-reference ("to the extent authorized by law") rather than by spelling out the mechanics of Medi-Cal estate recovery itself — those mechanics live in the Welfare and Institutions Code, outside this Probate Code part, and were not independently traced in this research; that narrower point is disclosed honestly rather than guessed at. The general creditor-liability provisions (personal liability capped at property value received, and lien-holder priority) are separately and directly codified. This is California's statutory scheme specifically; whether transferred property remains reachable by creditors or a state Medicaid-recovery program after a similar deed varies by state and is not assumed to be uniform.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5654
citations.cite: California Probate Code, Medi-Cal eligibility and Department of Health Care Services claims
citations.quote: (a) For the purpose of determination of eligibility for health care under Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 14000) or Chapter 8 (commencing with Section 14200) of Part 3 of Division 9 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, execution and recordation of a revocable transfer on death deed is not a lifetime transfer of the property. (b) Property transferred by a revocable transfer on death deed is subject to claims of the State Department of Health Care Services to the extent authorized by law.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5670
citations.cite: California Probate Code, lien-holder priority over property
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other statute governing priorities among creditors, a creditor of the transferor whose right is evidenced at the time of the transferor’s death by an encumbrance or lien of record on property transferred by a revocable transfer on death deed has priority against the property over a creditor of the beneficiary, regardless of whether the beneficiary’s obligation was created before or after the transferor’s death and regardless of whether the obligation is secured or unsecured, voluntary or involuntary, recorded or unrecorded.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5672
citations.cite: California Probate Code, beneficiary personal liability for transferor's unsecured debts
citations.quote: Each beneficiary is personally liable to the extent provided in Section 5674 for the unsecured debts of the transferor. Any such debt may be enforced against the beneficiary in the same manner as it could have been enforced against the transferor if the transferor had not died.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5674(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, cap on beneficiary's liability
citations.quote: (b) The personal liability of a beneficiary under Section 5672 shall not exceed the fair market value at the time of the transferor’s death of the property received by the beneficiary pursuant to the revocable transfer on death deed, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances on the property at that time.

clauses.title: Owner, Beneficiary, and Property Declaration
clauses.body: {{ownerName}}, being the owner of the real property located at {{propertyAddress}}, legally described as {{legalDescription}}, creates this Revocable Transfer on Death Deed. {{ownerName}} transfers all of {{ownerName}}'s interest in the described property to {{beneficiaryName}} on {{ownerName}}'s death. {{ownerName}} retains the right to revoke this deed at any time before then, and this deed conveys no present interest in the property to {{beneficiaryName}}. This deed transfers only {{ownerName}}'s own share of the property; it does not transfer the share of any co-owner of the property.

clauses.title: Multiple-Beneficiary Designation
clauses.body: {{ownerName}} may name more than one beneficiary. If {{additionalBeneficiaryName}} is named as an additional beneficiary alongside {{beneficiaryName}}, the named beneficiaries take title to the property as tenants in common in equal shares on {{ownerName}}'s death. California's transfer-on-death deed statute does not provide a separate "contingent" or fallback beneficiary who stands in only if the primary beneficiary predeceases the owner; instead, if a named beneficiary does not survive {{ownerName}}, that beneficiary's share is redistributed among the other named beneficiaries who do survive. If no named beneficiary survives {{ownerName}}, this deed has no effect, and the property does not pass under it.

clauses.title: Signature, Witnesses, and Notarial Acknowledgment
clauses.body:
SIGNATURE AND DATE: {{ownerName}} signs and dates this deed below; the name should exactly match the name shown on the property's title documents.

Signature of {{ownerName}}: ☐ _________________________ Date: _______________

WITNESSES: This deed is signed by two witnesses, present together at the same time, who witness {{ownerName}}'s signing of this deed or {{ownerName}}'s acknowledgment that it is {{ownerName}}'s deed. Witness signatures do not need to be notarized.
