citations.quote: It shall be unlawful for any employer to collect or receive from an employee any part of wages theretofore paid by said employer to said employee.

citations.case: Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC
citations.quote: In referring to “wages” paid, section 221 prohibits an employer only from collecting or receiving wages that have already been earned by performance of agreed-upon requirements.

clauses.title: Statement of the Earned Commission and Signature
This Petition Information Sheet Describes a Court Proceeding, Not a Private Designation
clauses.body: A conservatorship over {{proposedConserveeName}}, an adult, under California law is established only through an actual court proceeding under Probate Code Division 4, Part 3 — a filed petition, notice, an investigation, and a hearing that ends in a court order — not by a private agreement, family consensus, or the mere signing of this document. This is a genuinely different process from a power of attorney or advance health care directive, both of which are private, voluntary designations an adult makes for themself, in advance, while still able to do so; a conservatorship is instead a court-supervised proceeding brought about someone else, over their objection if necessary. California Probate Code § 1820(a) lists who may file the petition that starts that proceeding: the proposed conservatee themself, the proposed conservatee's spouse or domestic partner, a relative of the proposed conservatee, an interested state or local public entity, officer, or employee, or any other interested person or friend of the proposed conservatee.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that an adult conservatorship is created only through an actual court proceeding, and of who may file the petition that starts it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This document is informational: it describes the statutory conservatorship petition process and does not itself establish a conservatorship, appoint anyone as conservator, or determine that the proposed conservatee lacks capacity for any purpose; only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, investigation, and hearing process can do that. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1820(a)); no additional independent source was found for the list of persons who may petition. Section 1820(b) and (c), addressing petitions filed during a proposed conservatee's minority and a bar on most creditor-filed petitions, are not covered by this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1820(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1820(a)
citations.quote: A petition for the appointment of a conservator may be filed by any of the following: (1) The proposed conservatee. (2) The spouse or domestic partner of the proposed conservatee. (3) A relative of the proposed conservatee. (4) Any interested state or local entity or agency of this state or any interested public officer or employee of this state or of a local public entity of this state. (5) Any other interested person or friend of the proposed conservatee.

clauses.title: Conservator of the Person, Conservator of the Estate — Two Distinct, Severable Kinds of Conservatorship
clauses.body: California law recognizes two distinct kinds of adult conservatorship, and a petition may seek either or both for {{proposedConserveeName}}. A conservator of the person may be appointed for a person who is "unable to provide properly for his or her personal needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter" — authority over day-to-day care and living arrangements. A conservator of the estate may be appointed for a person who "is substantially unable to manage his or her own financial resources or resist fraud or undue influence," with the added statutory caution that "[s]ubstantial inability may not be proved solely by isolated incidents of negligence or improvidence" — authority over money and property instead of personal care. A conservator of the person and estate may be appointed where both descriptions apply, but the two are legally severable: a court petition, and a resulting court order, may establish one without the other. Whichever type is sought, the standard of proof for the appointment is clear and convincing evidence.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the two distinct, severable types of adult conservatorship recognized under California law and the standard of proof that applies to each — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites four subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1801(a), (b), (c), and (e)); no additional independent source beyond § 1801 itself was found for the two-types distinction, the severability of the two types, or the clear-and-convincing standard of proof. Subdivision (d) of the same section — the limited conservatorship for a developmentally disabled adult — is deliberately not quoted in this clause; it is addressed on its own in this document's companion clause because it is a narrower, separately governed category that this document does not treat as interchangeable with a general conservatorship of the person or estate.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1801(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1801(a)
citations.quote: A conservator of the person may be appointed for a person who is unable to provide properly for his or her personal needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter, except as provided for the person as described in subdivision (b) or (c) of Section 1828.5.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1801(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1801(b)
citations.quote: A conservator of the estate may be appointed for a person who is substantially unable to manage his or her own financial resources or resist fraud or undue influence, except as provided for that person as described in subdivision (b) or (c) of Section 1828.5. Substantial inability may not be proved solely by isolated incidents of negligence or improvidence.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1801(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1801(c)
citations.quote: A conservator of the person and estate may be appointed for a person described in subdivisions (a) and (b).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1801(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1801(e)
citations.quote: The standard of proof for the appointment of a conservator pursuant to this section shall be clear and convincing evidence.

clauses.title: What the Petition Must Say — Including Alternatives Considered and Who Must Be Named
clauses.body: The petition to appoint a conservator for {{proposedConserveeName}} must request appointment for the person, the estate, or both; specify the proposed conservator's and proposed conservatee's names, addresses, and telephone numbers; and state the reasons a conservatorship is necessary. Unless the petitioner or proposed conservator is a bank or trust company, supplemental information must also address, among other categories, the proposed conservatee's inability to provide for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter; the nature of the proposed conservatee's residence; alternatives to conservatorship that were considered and why they were not suitable — expressly including supported decision-making agreements, powers of attorney, advance health care directives, and health care surrogate designations; health or social services provided in the preceding year; and the proposed conservatee's substantial inability to manage financial resources or resist fraud or undue influence. So far as known to the petitioner or proposed conservator, the petition must also set forth the names and addresses of the proposed conservatee's spouse or domestic partner and relatives within the second degree.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the required contents of a California conservatorship petition — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1821(a)(1) and § 1821(b)); no additional independent source beyond § 1821 itself was found for these requirements. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: on the actual statutory text, § 1821 does not require the petition to include a capacity declaration from a licensed physician or other qualified professional, and no such physician-declaration requirement was located anywhere in § 1821. The petition-stage requirement that exists instead is the supplemental-information showing quoted above. The actual mechanism that brings a treating physician's or other health care provider's input into the case is a separate one, described in this document's companion clause on the court investigator: under § 1826(a)(9), it is the court investigator — not the petitioner — who is required to gather and review the proposed conservatee's relevant medical reports as part of the mandatory investigation, after the petition is filed.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1821(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The petition shall request that a conservator be appointed for the person or estate, or both, shall specify the name, address, and telephone number of the proposed conservator and the name, address, and telephone number of the proposed conservatee, and state the reasons why a conservatorship is necessary. Unless the petitioner or proposed conservator is a bank or other entity authorized to conduct the business of a trust company, the petitioner or proposed conservator shall also file supplemental information as to why the appointment of a conservator is required. The supplemental information to be submitted shall include a brief statement of facts addressed to each of the following categories: (A) The inability of the proposed conservatee to properly provide for their own needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter. (B) The location and nature of the proposed conservatee's residence and the ability of the proposed conservatee to live in the residence while under conservatorship. (C) Alternatives to conservatorship considered by the petitioner or proposed conservator and reasons why those alternatives are not suitable... Those alternatives include, but are not limited to, all of the following: (i) Supported decisionmaking agreements, as defined in Section 21001 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. (ii) Powers of Attorney set forth in Division 4.5 (commencing with Section 4000). (iii) Advanced Health Care Directives set forth in Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 4670) of Part 2 of Division 4.7. (iv) Designations of a health care surrogate as set forth in Section 4711. (D) Health or social services provided to the proposed conservatee during the year immediately preceding the filing of the petition, when the petitioner or proposed conservator has information as to those services. (E) The substantial inability of the proposed conservatee to manage their own financial resources, or to resist fraud or undue influence.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1821(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1821(b)
citations.quote: The petition shall set forth, so far as they are known to the petitioner or proposed conservator, the names and addresses of the spouse or domestic partner, and of the relatives of the proposed conservatee within the second degree.

clauses.title: The Court Investigator's Mandatory Independent Investigation and Interview
clauses.body: Regardless of whether {{proposedConserveeName}} attends the hearing, a court investigator must personally interview {{proposedConserveeName}}, along with all petitioners, all proposed conservators who are not petitioners, and {{proposedConserveeName}}'s spouse or registered domestic partner and close relatives. As part of that same investigation, the court investigator must inform {{proposedConserveeName}} of the contents of the petition, of the nature, purpose, and effect of the proceeding, and of the right to oppose the petition, to attend the hearing, to have the matter tried by jury, to be represented by legal counsel, and to have legal counsel appointed by the court if not otherwise represented. The investigator must also gather and review relevant medical reports regarding the proposed conservatee from the proposed conservatee's primary care physician and other relevant mental and physical health care providers, and must report the findings to the court in writing at least five days before the hearing.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, independent, pre-appointment investigation and interview requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1826(a)(1)-(2) and § 1826(a)(9)-(10)); no additional independent source beyond § 1826 itself was found for these requirements. This investigation requirement does not apply, under § 1826(d), to a proposed conservatee who has personally executed the petition or who has nominated their own conservator, if that proposed conservatee attends the hearing — an exception this clause does not otherwise describe.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1826(a)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Regardless of whether the proposed conservatee attends the hearing, the court investigator shall do all of the following: (1) Conduct the following interviews: (A) The proposed conservatee personally. (B) All petitioners and all proposed conservators who are not petitioners. (C) The proposed conservatee's spouse or registered domestic partner and relatives within the first degree... (2) Inform the proposed conservatee of the contents of the petition and citation, of the nature, purpose, and effect of the proceeding, and of the right of the proposed conservatee to oppose the petition, to attend the hearing on the petition, to have the matter of the establishment of the conservatorship tried by jury, to be represented by legal counsel, and to have legal counsel appointed by the court if not otherwise represented by legal counsel.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1826(a)(9)-(10) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (9) Gather and review relevant medical reports regarding the proposed conservatee from the proposed conservatee's primary care physician and other relevant mental and physical health care providers. (10) Report to the court in writing, at least five days before the hearing, concerning all of the foregoing...

clauses.title: The Proposed Conservatee's Rights at the Hearing
clauses.body: Before a conservatorship over {{proposedConserveeName}} may be established, the court must inform {{proposedConserveeName}} that the establishment of a conservatorship is a legal adjudication of an inability to properly provide for personal needs or to manage financial resources, or both, and of its effect on {{proposedConserveeName}}'s basic rights. The court must also inform {{proposedConserveeName}} of the right to oppose the proceeding, to have the matter tried by jury, to be represented by legal counsel of {{proposedConserveeName}}'s own choosing, and to have legal counsel appointed by the court if not otherwise represented by legal counsel. Separately, the court is required to hear and determine the matter of establishing the conservatorship according to the law and procedure that governs the trial of civil actions, including trial by jury if demanded by the proposed conservatee.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific rights a proposed conservatee has before and at the hearing on a conservatorship petition — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. These citations are two different code sections (§ 1828(a)(6) and § 1827); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. Section 1828 also requires the court to inform the proposed conservatee of several other matters not covered by this clause, including the identity of the proposed conservator and, for an allegedly developmentally disabled adult, the specific effects of each limitation requested; and § 1828(c) excuses this requirement altogether where the proposed conservatee is absent from, and not required to attend, the hearing under § 1825.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1828(a)(6) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The proposed conservatee has the right to oppose the proceeding, to have the matter of the establishment of the conservatorship tried by jury, to be represented by legal counsel if the proposed conservatee so chooses, and to have legal counsel appointed by the court if not otherwise represented by legal counsel.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1827 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1827
citations.quote: The court shall hear and determine the matter of the establishment of the conservatorship according to the law and procedure relating to the trial of civil actions, including trial by jury if demanded by the proposed conservatee.

clauses.title: Limited Conservatorship for a Developmentally Disabled Adult Is a Different, Narrower Category
clauses.body: California law separately provides for a limited conservatorship of the person or estate, or both, for a developmentally disabled adult — a genuinely different and narrower category from the general conservatorship described in the rest of this document, not an interchangeable label for the same thing. A limited conservatorship "may be utilized only as necessary to promote and protect the well-being of the individual, shall be designed to encourage the development of maximum self-reliance and independence of the individual, and shall be ordered only to the extent necessitated by the individual's proven mental and adaptive limitations," and the limited conservatee "shall not be presumed to be incompetent and shall retain all legal and civil rights except those which by court order have been designated as legal disabilities and have been specifically granted to the limited conservator." Consistent with that narrower scope, a limited conservator's default authority over the limited conservatee's person is confined to care, custody, control, and securing appropriate habilitation, treatment, training, education, and social or vocational services — the broader powers a general conservator of the person can hold are, for a limited conservator, available only if specifically requested in the petition and granted by the court's order.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a limited conservatorship for a developmentally disabled adult is a distinct, narrower statutory category from a general conservatorship — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. These citations are two different code sections (§ 1801(d) and § 2351.5(a)); no single section is cited more than once in this clause. This document addresses only the general conservatorship of the person and of the estate described in its other clauses; it does not describe, and should not be read as a stand-in for, the limited conservatorship petition process itself, which carries its own additional procedural requirements not covered here — including a regional center assessment and report under § 1827.5, and the court's specific findings on adaptive functioning and capacity under § 1828.5 — that this document does not address.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1801(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1801(d)
citations.quote: A limited conservator of the person or of the estate, or both, may be appointed for a developmentally disabled adult. A limited conservatorship may be utilized only as necessary to promote and protect the well-being of the individual, shall be designed to encourage the development of maximum self-reliance and independence of the individual, and shall be ordered only to the extent necessitated by the individual's proven mental and adaptive limitations. The conservatee of the limited conservator shall not be presumed to be incompetent and shall retain all legal and civil rights except those which by court order have been designated as legal disabilities and have been specifically granted to the limited conservator.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2351.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (1) The limited conservator has the care, custody, and control of the limited conservatee. (2) The limited conservator shall secure for the limited conservatee those habilitation or treatment, training, education, medical and psychological services, and social and vocational opportunity as appropriate and as will assist the limited conservatee in the development of maximum self-reliance and independence.

clauses.title: Proposed Conservator — Information and Declaration in Support of Petition
clauses.body: I, {{proposedConservatorName}}, am the person proposed to serve as conservator of {{proposedConserveeName}}, an adult. I state that my relationship to {{proposedConserveeName}} is: {{relationshipToConservatee}}. The conservatorship sought is: {{conservatorshipTypeSought}} (for example, conservator of the person, conservator of the estate, or conservator of the person and estate). This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for appointment of a conservator, to be filed in the California probate court under Probate Code Division 4, Part 3. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not appoint, authorize, or confirm {{proposedConservatorName}} — or anyone else — as {{proposedConserveeName}}'s conservator, and it does not itself adjudicate {{proposedConserveeName}}'s capacity for any purpose. Only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, investigation, and hearing process described in this document can actually establish a conservatorship or appoint a conservator.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Conservatorship Petition Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{proposedConservatorName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual conservatorship petition filed with the California probate court. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not establish a conservatorship or appoint a conservator; only a court order does that.]

clauses.title: Cal-COBRA Eligibility — Small-Employer Scope and Qualified Beneficiary Definition
clauses.body: California's Cal-COBRA statute defines who counts as an "employer" and who counts as a "qualified beneficiary" for purposes of this state continuation-coverage scheme. An "employer" is one that meets the Knox-Keene Act's definition of a "small employer" and that employed 2 to 19 eligible employees on at least half its working days during the preceding calendar year (or calendar quarter, for an employer not in business the full preceding year), that has contracted for coverage through a group health care service plan, and that is not itself subject to federal COBRA. A "qualified beneficiary" is any individual who, on the day before the qualifying event, was enrolled in that group benefit plan and who has a qualifying event as the statute defines that term. {{employeeName}} and, where applicable, {{employeeName}}'s covered spouse and dependents who were enrolled in {{planName}} immediately before the qualifying event fall within this statutory "qualified beneficiary" definition if {{companyName}} meets the statutory "employer" definition described above.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Cal-COBRA scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or plan. It is federal and California law together in the sense that the statutory "employer" definition below cross-references (and excludes employers subject to) 29 U.S.C. § 1161 et seq. (federal COBRA), but no federal statutory text is quoted in this clause. This clause quotes two different subdivisions of the same statutory section, Health and Safety Code § 1366.21 — subdivision (e) (the "employer" definition) and subdivision (c)(1) (the "qualified beneficiary" definition) — which are disclosed together here rather than as separate authorities. This clause states the general statutory definitions; it does not determine whether this particular company actually meets the 2-to-19-employee threshold, whether its plan is a Knox-Keene group benefit plan rather than a self-funded or federally-covered plan, or whether this particular individual was in fact enrolled immediately before the event described.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1366.21(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code, Cal-COBRA "employer" definition
citations.quote: “Employer” means any employer that meets the definition of “small employer” as set forth in Section 1357 and (1) employed 2 to 19 eligible employees on at least 50 percent of its working days during the preceding calendar year, or, if the employer was not in business during any part of the preceding calendar year, employed 2 to 19 eligible employees on at least 50 percent of its working days during the preceding calendar quarter, (2) has contracted for health care coverage through a group benefit plan offered by a health care service plan, and (3) is not subject to Section 4980B of the United States Internal Revenue Code or Chapter 18 of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, 29 U.S.C. Section 1161 et seq.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1366.21(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code, Cal-COBRA "qualified beneficiary" definition
citations.quote: “Qualified beneficiary” means any individual who, on the day before the qualifying event, is an enrollee in a group benefit plan offered by a health care service plan pursuant to Article 3.1 (commencing with Section 1357) and has a qualifying event, as defined in subdivision (d).

clauses.title: Cal-COBRA Qualifying Events
clauses.body: California's Cal-COBRA statute lists five events that can be a "qualifying event" for a qualified beneficiary: (1) the death of the covered employee; (2) the termination of employment or a reduction in hours of the covered employee's employment, except that termination for gross misconduct does not qualify; (3) the divorce or legal separation of the covered employee from the covered employee's spouse; (4) the loss of dependent status by a dependent enrolled in the group benefit plan; and (5), with respect to a covered dependent only, the covered employee's entitlement to Medicare benefits under Title XVIII of the Social Security Act. On {{qualifyingEventDate}}, the event identified for {{employeeName}} was: {{qualifyingEventType}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Cal-COBRA scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or plan. This clause cites a single subdivision of a single statutory section (Health and Safety Code § 1366.21(d)); no additional independent source was found for this. Whether the event identified above was, in fact, a "termination of employment" rather than a termination "for gross misconduct" (the one carve-out named in the statute for category (2)) is a fact-specific determination this clause does not make.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1366.21(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code, Cal-COBRA qualifying events
citations.quote: “Qualifying event” means any of the following events that, but for the election of continuation coverage under this article, would result in a loss of coverage under the group benefit plan to a qualified beneficiary: (1) The death of the covered employee. (2) The termination of employment or reduction in hours of the covered employee’s employment, except that termination for gross misconduct does not constitute a qualifying event. (3) The divorce or legal separation of the covered employee from the covered employee’s spouse. (4) The loss of dependent status by a dependent enrolled in the group benefit plan. (5) With respect to a covered dependent only, the covered employee’s entitlement to benefits under Title XVIII of the United States Social Security Act (Medicare).

clauses.title: Cal-COBRA Notice Obligations Run Through the Health Plan, Not Necessarily the Employer
clauses.body: Cal-COBRA's notice chain is structured differently from federal COBRA's. Under Cal-COBRA, the group contract between the health care service plan and the employer must require the employer to notify the health care service plan, in writing, of an employee's termination-of-employment or reduction-of-hours qualifying event within 30 days of that event. The health care service plan itself is then the party the statute directs to act next: the plan (or an employer or administrator that has separately contracted with the plan to perform these notice and administrative services) must, within 14 days of receiving notice of the qualifying event, send the qualified beneficiary the benefits information, premium information, enrollment forms, and disclosures needed to elect continuation coverage. Separately, for qualifying events the employer may not independently know about — divorce or legal separation, a dependent losing dependent status, or a covered dependent's Medicare entitlement — the qualified beneficiary is instead responsible for notifying the health care service plan (or the employer, if the employer has contracted to perform that administrative function) within 60 days of the qualifying event.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Cal-COBRA scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or plan. This clause quotes two different subdivisions of the same statutory section, Health and Safety Code § 1366.25 — subdivision (a) (employer-to-plan notice) and subdivision (e) (plan-to-beneficiary notice) — which are disclosed together here rather than as separate authorities; it also draws, without a separate quoted citation, on the beneficiary's own 60-day notice duty stated in Health and Safety Code § 1366.24(b). This clause states the general statutory notice structure; it does not identify who has actually performed which notice step for this particular company's plan, nor whether this employer's plan documents in fact allocate the health care service plan's administrative duties to the employer or a third-party administrator, which the statute allows by contract.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1366.25(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code, Cal-COBRA employer notice to health care service plan
citations.quote: Every group contract between a health care service plan and an employer subject to this article that is issued, amended, or renewed on or after July 1, 1998, shall require the employer to notify the plan, in writing, of any employee who has had a qualifying event, as defined in paragraph (2) of subdivision (d) of Section 1366.21, within 30 days of the qualifying event.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1366.25(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code, Cal-COBRA health care service plan notice to qualified beneficiary
citations.quote: Every health care service plan, or employer or administrator that contracts to perform the notice and administrative services pursuant to this section, shall, within 14 days of receiving a notice of a qualifying event, provide to the qualified beneficiary the necessary benefits information, premium information, enrollment forms, and disclosures consistent with the notice requirements contained in subdivisions (b) and (c) of Section 1366.24 to allow the qualified beneficiary to formally elect continuation coverage.

clauses.title: Cal-COBRA Premium Cap — Up to 110% of Applicable Rate
clauses.body: California's Cal-COBRA statute caps what a health care service plan may charge a qualified beneficiary for continuation coverage at not more than 110% of the applicable rate charged for a covered employee, or, for dependent coverage, not more than 110% of the applicable rate charged to a similarly situated individual under the group benefit plan being continued. A higher cap of up to 150% of the group rate applies only to a qualified beneficiary determined to be disabled under Title II or Title XVI of the Social Security Act, and only after the first 18 months of continuation coverage. The estimated monthly premium under this article for {{employeeName}}'s continuation coverage is {{monthlyPremiumAmount}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Cal-COBRA premium ceiling — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or plan, and not a claim about what this particular health care service plan actually charges or what this particular qualified beneficiary will actually be billed. This clause cites a single statutory section (Health and Safety Code § 1366.26); no additional independent source was found for this. Cal-COBRA's 110% cap is higher than federal COBRA's 102% cap; this clause states California's own figure and does not restate the separate federal figure.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1366.26 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code, Cal-COBRA premium cap
citations.quote: A qualified beneficiary electing continuation coverage shall pay to the health care service plan, on or before the due date of each payment but not more frequently than on a monthly basis, not more than 110 percent of the applicable rate charged for a covered employee or, in the case of dependent coverage, not more than 110 percent of the applicable rate charged to a similarly situated individual under the group benefit plan being continued under the group contract. In the case of a qualified beneficiary who is determined to be disabled pursuant to Title II or Title XVI of the United States Social Security Act, the qualified beneficiary shall be required to pay to the health care service plan an amount no greater than 150 percent of the group rate after the first 18 months of continuation coverage provided pursuant to this section.

clauses.title: Cal-COBRA Maximum Coverage Duration — 36 Months
clauses.body: Unlike federal COBRA's tiered 18-month/36-month structure, California's Cal-COBRA statute sets a single maximum coverage period of 36 months after the date the qualified beneficiary's benefits would otherwise have terminated because of the qualifying event, regardless of which of the statute's qualifying-event categories applies. This 36-month outer limit applies both to a qualifying event that is a termination of employment or reduction of hours and to the other qualifying-event categories (death, divorce or legal separation, loss of dependent status, or a dependent's Medicare entitlement), subject to earlier termination on the other grounds the statute separately lists (for example, nonpayment of premium, the employer ceasing to offer any group benefit plan, or the qualified beneficiary moving out of the plan's service area). Continuation coverage elected in connection with the qualifying event identified for {{employeeName}} may last for up to {{maxCoverageMonths}} months under this statutory maximum, subject to those other statutory termination grounds.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Cal-COBRA scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or plan. This clause quotes two different paragraphs of the same subdivision of the same statutory section, Health and Safety Code § 1366.27(a)(1) and § 1366.27(a)(3), which are disclosed together here rather than as separate authorities. This clause states the general 36-month maximum; it does not restate every one of the statute's other termination grounds in full, and it does not determine whether any of those other grounds has actually occurred for this particular qualified beneficiary.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1366.27(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code, Cal-COBRA 36-month maximum for termination/reduced-hours events
citations.quote: In the case of a qualified beneficiary who is eligible for continuation coverage pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (d) of Section 1366.21, the date 36 months after the date the qualified beneficiary’s benefits under the contract would otherwise have terminated because of a qualifying event.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1366.27(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code, Cal-COBRA 36-month maximum for other qualifying events
citations.quote: In the case of a qualified beneficiary who is eligible for continuation coverage pursuant to paragraph (1), (3), (4), or (5) of subdivision (d) of Section 1366.21, the date 36 months after the date the qualified beneficiary’s benefits under the contract would otherwise have terminated by reason of a qualifying event.

clauses.title: Cal-COBRA Extension for People Who Exhaust Federal COBRA
clauses.body: California law provides a further, separate right for someone who has exhausted federal COBRA continuation coverage and who was entitled to less than 36 months of it under COBRA. Under the Knox-Keene Act, a health care service plan must offer such an enrollee the opportunity to continue coverage for up to 36 months total, measured from the date the enrollee's COBRA continuation coverage began, on the same rate terms Cal-COBRA otherwise applies. A parallel provision in the Insurance Code imposes the same obligation on a health insurer providing coverage through an insured (rather than Knox-Keene-regulated) group health plan. Notification of this extension right must be included in the notice of pending COBRA termination that is otherwise required to be sent to COBRA beneficiaries.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Cal-COBRA scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or plan. This clause cites two parallel provisions in two different California codes, Health and Safety Code § 1366.29(a) (health care service plans) and Insurance Code § 10128.59(a) (health insurers); each governs a different plan structure and neither restates the other. The 36-month period this extension describes runs from the date the enrollee's federal COBRA continuation coverage began, not from the date of the original qualifying event, and not from the date federal COBRA is exhausted; those dates will often be close together but are not stated by the statute to be identical. This clause does not determine which of the two provisions, if either, applies to a particular plan, or whether a particular person was in fact entitled to less than 36 months of coverage under federal COBRA.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 1366.29(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code, Cal-COBRA extension after exhausting federal COBRA
citations.quote: A health care service plan shall offer an enrollee who has exhausted continuation coverage under COBRA the opportunity to continue coverage for up to 36 months from the date the enrollee’s continuation coverage began, if the enrollee is entitled to less than 36 months of continuation coverage under COBRA. The health care service plan shall offer coverage pursuant to the terms of this article, including the rate limitations contained in Section 1366.26.

citations.case: Cal. Insurance Code § 10128.59(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Insurance Code, parallel Cal-COBRA extension for insured group plans
citations.quote: A health insurer that provides coverage under a group benefit plan to an employer shall offer an insured who has exhausted continuation coverage under COBRA the opportunity to continue coverage for up to 36 months from the date the insured’s continuation coverage began if the insured is entitled to less than 36 months of continuation coverage under COBRA. The health insurer shall offer coverage pursuant to terms of this article, including the rate limitations contained in Section 10128.56.

clauses.title: Cal-COBRA Election Notice Letter
clauses.body:
CAL-COBRA CONTINUATION COVERAGE ELECTION NOTICE

Date: {{noticeDate}}

To: {{employeeName}}

From: {{companyName}}, in connection with {{planName}}

Re: Your Right to Elect Continuation Coverage Under California's Cal-COBRA Law

This notice is to inform you of rights that may be available to you under California's Cal-COBRA statute (Health and Safety Code § 1366.20 et seq.), a state law separate from federal COBRA that applies to certain group health plans offered by small employers.

1. Qualifying Event. On {{qualifyingEventDate}}, the following qualifying event was identified: {{qualifyingEventType}}. This event resulted, or will result, in a loss of coverage under {{planName}}.

2. Who May Elect Coverage. You, and any covered spouse or dependent children who were enrolled under the plan immediately before the qualifying event, are each a "qualified beneficiary" under Cal-COBRA and may independently elect continuation coverage.

3. Notice and Election Timing. California law requires an employer to notify the health care service plan of a termination or reduced-hours qualifying event within 30 days of that event, and requires the health care service plan (or an employer or administrator under contract to perform this function) to send you the information needed to elect continuation coverage within 14 days after that notice is received. You then have 60 days from the later of (a) the date your coverage under the plan would otherwise end, or (b) the date this notice is sent to you, to elect continuation coverage.

4. Cost of Coverage. If you elect continuation coverage, California law permits the health care service plan to charge up to 110% of the applicable rate. The estimated monthly premium is {{monthlyPremiumAmount}}. Your first premium payment is not due until 45 days after the date you provide written notice of your election.

5. Duration of Coverage. Continuation coverage elected in connection with this qualifying event may last for up to {{maxCoverageMonths}} months under California's Cal-COBRA statute, subject to the statutory grounds for earlier termination (for example, nonpayment of premium, the employer ceasing to offer any group benefit plan, or moving outside the plan's service area).

6. How to Elect. To elect continuation coverage, complete and return the attached election form, by first-class mail or other reliable means of delivery, to {{planAdministratorName}} at {{planAdministratorAddress}} by {{electionDeadline}}.

This notice summarizes rights that may be available under California's Cal-COBRA statute. It is not a complete description of the statute or of the plan, and it does not modify the plan's actual terms.

clauses.title: Required Elements of an Effective Takedown Notification
clauses.body: Federal copyright law specifies what a notification of claimed infringement must contain to be treated as effective under the notice-and-takedown procedure of 17 U.S.C. § 512(c) — the provision that lets an online service provider qualify for a safe harbor from monetary liability for infringing material its users store on its system. To be effective, a notification must be a written communication, provided to the service provider's designated agent, that includes substantially: a physical or electronic signature of a person authorized to act on behalf of the owner of the exclusive right claimed to be infringed; identification of the copyrighted work claimed to have been infringed (or a representative list, if a single notification covers multiple works at one online site); identification of the material claimed to be infringing, along with information reasonably sufficient to permit the service provider to locate it; information reasonably sufficient to permit the service provider to contact the complaining party; a statement that the complaining party has a good faith belief that the use complained of is not authorized by the copyright owner, its agent, or the law; and a statement, made under penalty of perjury, that the information in the notification is accurate and that the complaining party is authorized to act on behalf of the owner of the exclusive right claimed to be infringed. A notification that fails to comply substantially with these elements generally is not counted, under the statute, toward whether a service provider had the knowledge that triggers its duty to remove or disable access to material.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of what 17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(3)(A) requires a takedown notification to contain — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a particular website, a particular hosting arrangement, or a particular piece of content, or that any individual online service provider's own submission form asks for exactly this list and nothing more (a platform's internal process can require additional information beyond the statutory floor). The consequence of only partial compliance is addressed in the adjoining subsection, 17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(3)(B), which is not cited separately here as an independent source — it is a continuation of the same statutory provision, not corroborating evidence from elsewhere.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, elements of an effective notification of claimed infringement
citations.quote: To be effective under this subsection, a notification of claimed infringement must be a written communication provided to the designated agent of a service provider that includes substantially the following: (i) A physical or electronic signature of a person authorized to act on behalf of the owner of an exclusive right that is allegedly infringed. (ii) Identification of the copyrighted work claimed to have been infringed, or, if multiple copyrighted works at a single online site are covered by a single notification, a representative list of such works at that site. (iii) Identification of the material that is claimed to be infringing or to be the subject of infringing activity and that is to be removed or access to which is to be disabled, and information reasonably sufficient to permit the service provider to locate the material. (iv) Information reasonably sufficient to permit the service provider to contact the complaining party, such as an address, telephone number, and, if available, an electronic mail address at which the complaining party may be contacted. (v) A statement that the complaining party has a good faith belief that use of the material in the manner complained of is not authorized by the copyright owner, its agent, or the law. (vi) A statement that the information in the notification is accurate, and under penalty of perjury, that the complaining party is authorized to act on behalf of the owner of an exclusive right that is allegedly infringed.

clauses.title: Effective Notice Must Reach the Service Provider's Designated Agent
clauses.body: Federal copyright law ties the safe harbor described elsewhere in this document to whether a service provider has designated an agent to receive notifications of claimed infringement, and to whether a notification is delivered to that agent. A service provider qualifies for the safe harbor in the first place only if it has designated such an agent — by making the agent's name, address, phone number, and email address available through its service (including on its website) and by providing that information to the Copyright Office, which maintains a public directory of designated agents. A notification directed somewhere other than the designated agent (for example, a general customer-support inbox or a form unrelated to copyright) does not necessarily trigger the notice-and-takedown mechanism described in this document.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that the designated-agent mechanism exists and is a precondition to the safe harbor under 17 U.S.C. § 512(c) — not a claim about whether any particular website has designated an agent, what that agent's current contact information is, or whether a specific service provider's public-facing abuse or copyright-report channel qualifies as its designated agent for a given piece of content. The Copyright Office's public directory of designated agents is a separate, non-statutory resource this clause does not independently verify.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 512(c)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, designated agent requirement for the service-provider safe harbor
citations.quote: The limitations on liability established in this subsection apply to a service provider only if the service provider has designated an agent to receive notifications of claimed infringement described in paragraph (3), by making available through its service, including on its website in a location accessible to the public, and by providing to the Copyright Office, substantially the following information: (A) the name, address, phone number, and electronic mail address of the agent.

clauses.title: Notification of Claimed Infringement — Identification
clauses.body:

2. The copyrighted work claimed to have been infringed is described as follows: {{copyrightedWorkDescription}}.

clauses.title: Notice Signature Block
Liability for Knowingly Misrepresenting Infringement
clauses.body: Federal copyright law imposes liability on a person who knowingly materially misrepresents, in a submission under this notice-and-takedown mechanism, that material or activity is infringing. A person found to have made such a misrepresentation is liable for any damages — including costs and attorney's fees — incurred by the party injured by the misrepresentation (which can include the person whose material was removed, the copyright owner, or the service provider) as a result of the service provider relying on the misrepresentation to remove or disable access to material, or to restore it. The same liability applies to a knowing material misrepresentation that material was removed or disabled by mistake or misidentification, made in a counter-notification.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that 17 U.S.C. § 512(f) creates a damages remedy for a knowing material misrepresentation in a takedown notice or counter-notification — not a claim about whether any particular notice or counter-notification meets that standard, which turns on facts (including the sender's actual, subjective state of mind, not merely whether they were mistaken) that this clause doesn't resolve. A well-known Ninth Circuit decision, Lenz v. Universal Music Corp., 815 F.3d 1145 (9th Cir. 2016), addressed whether a copyright owner must consider fair use before sending a takedown notice and what "knowingly materially misrepresents" means under this subsection. That case could not be independently verified for this clause: the CourtListener research tool returned a daily rate-limit error (125 requests/day, next available in roughly 16 hours) on every attempt, and direct or automated fetches of the case from other sources (courtlistener.com, the Ninth Circuit's own courts.gov opinion PDF, and a legal-research aggregator) were each blocked by this environment's network egress controls. Rather than quote the case from memory, it is omitted from the citations below; only the directly fetched and verified statutory text of § 512(f) is cited. Anyone relying on this clause should treat the Lenz case as a genuine, disclosed research gap, not as verified content.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 512(f) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, misrepresentations in a takedown notice or counter-notification
citations.quote: Any person who knowingly materially misrepresents under this section— (1) that material or activity is infringing, or (2) that material or activity was removed or disabled by mistake or misidentification, shall be liable for any damages, including costs and attorneys' fees, incurred by the alleged infringer, by any copyright owner or copyright owner's authorized licensee, or by a service provider, who is injured by such misrepresentation, as the result of the service provider relying upon such misrepresentation in removing or disabling access to the material or activity claimed to be infringing, or in replacing the removed material or ceasing to disable access to it.

clauses.title: The Counter-Notification Process and Put-Back Timeline
clauses.body: Federal copyright law gives the person whose material was removed or disabled in response to a takedown notification a way to seek its restoration. That person (the statute calls them a "subscriber") may submit a written counter notification to the service provider's designated agent, which must include substantially: a physical or electronic signature of the subscriber; identification of the removed material and its location before removal; a statement, under penalty of perjury, that the subscriber has a good faith belief the material was removed or disabled as a result of mistake or misidentification; and the subscriber's name, address, and telephone number, together with a statement consenting to the jurisdiction of the applicable federal district court and agreeing to accept service of process from the person who sent the original notification. Once the service provider receives a valid counter notification, it must promptly provide a copy to the person who sent the original takedown notice and tell that person it will restore the material in 10 business days. The service provider must then restore the material not less than 10, and not more than 14, business days after receiving the counter notification — unless its designated agent first receives notice that the original complaining party has filed a lawsuit seeking a court order restraining the subscriber's allegedly infringing activity.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the counter-notification content requirements and the 10-to-14-business-day put-back window under 17 U.S.C. § 512(g) — not a claim about whether any particular service provider actually follows this process (the safe harbor described in this subsection is optional protection for the service provider, not a legal duty automatically owed to any given subscriber), or about how a service provider's own terms of service handle counter-notifications and restoration. These citations are both to subsections of the same statutory section, 17 U.S.C. § 512(g); they are not independent sources corroborating each other.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(2)(B)-(C) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, notice to the complaining party and the put-back timeline
citations.quote: upon receipt of a counter notification described in paragraph (3), promptly provides the person who provided the notification under subsection (c)(1)(C) with a copy of the counter notification, and informs that person that it will replace the removed material or cease disabling access to it in 10 business days; and (C) replaces the removed material and ceases disabling access to it not less than 10, nor more than 14, business days following receipt of the counter notice, unless its designated agent first receives notice from the person who submitted the notification under subsection (c)(1)(C) that such person has filed an action seeking a court order to restrain the subscriber from engaging in infringing activity relating to the material on the service provider's system or network.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, required contents of a counter notification
citations.quote: To be effective under this subsection, a counter notification must be a written communication provided to the service provider's designated agent that includes substantially the following: (A) A physical or electronic signature of the subscriber. (B) Identification of the material that has been removed or to which access has been disabled and the location at which the material appeared before it was removed or access to it was disabled. (C) A statement under penalty of perjury that the subscriber has a good faith belief that the material was removed or disabled as a result of mistake or misidentification of the material to be removed or disabled. (D) The subscriber's name, address, and telephone number, and a statement that the subscriber consents to the jurisdiction of Federal District Court for the judicial district in which the address is located...

clauses.title: A Takedown Notice Is a Different Mechanism Than a Copyright Infringement Lawsuit
clauses.body: The notice-and-takedown procedure described in this document is a mechanism aimed at online service providers: it lets a service provider qualify for a safe harbor from certain monetary liability by responding to a notification and, separately, gives the service provider its own protection from claims when it takes down material in good faith. By its own terms, the statute does not affect any other defense a service provider may have, and nothing in the notice-and-takedown provisions creates a claim against the person who posted the allegedly infringing material — a copyright owner's claim against an infringer, if any, arises separately, under the general infringement provisions of Title 17, which allow the legal or beneficial owner of an exclusive right to bring a civil infringement action against an infringer. Sending a takedown notice under 17 U.S.C. § 512(c) also does not require that the copyrighted work be registered with the U.S. Copyright Office — registration is not listed among the required elements of an effective notification. Filing a civil infringement lawsuit is different: with narrow exceptions, federal law generally bars a civil action for infringement of a U.S. work until the work has been registered, or preregistered, with the Copyright Office.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that 17 U.S.C. § 512 is a liability-limitation and takedown mechanism directed at service providers rather than a source of a direct legal claim against an infringer, and that copyright registration is a precondition to filing an infringement lawsuit under 17 U.S.C. § 411(a) but is not listed among the required elements of a takedown notification under § 512(c)(3)(A) — not a claim about whether registration would be strategically useful before sending any particular notice, whether a specific work has in fact been registered, or how the narrow exceptions to the registration requirement in § 411 (such as for a refused application, or for certain works not originating in the United States) apply to any particular situation. The citations below are to three different statutory sections (§ 512(l), § 501(b), and § 411(a)), not different subsections of one section.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 512(l) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, other defenses not affected by the safe harbor
citations.quote: The failure of a service provider's conduct to qualify for limitation of liability under this section shall not bear adversely upon the consideration of a defense by the service provider that the service provider's conduct is not infringing under this title or any other defense.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 501(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, who may institute a civil action for copyright infringement
citations.quote: The legal or beneficial owner of an exclusive right under a copyright is entitled, subject to the requirements of section 411, to institute an action for any infringement of that particular right committed while he or she is the owner of it.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 411(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, registration as a precondition to a civil infringement action
citations.quote: no civil action for infringement of the copyright in any United States work shall be instituted until preregistration or registration of the copyright claim has been made in accordance with this title.

clauses.title: Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Petition for Dissolution of Marriage — Information Sheet concerns the marriage of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, who were married on {{marriageDate}}. It is prepared for use alongside an actual petition for dissolution of marriage that would be filed in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. This information sheet describes California's statutory dissolution process — the filing and residency requirements, the legal grounds, and the waiting period before a judgment becomes final — as background for that filing. It is not itself a court filing, and completing it does not dissolve, terminate, or otherwise change the marital status of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. Only a court judgment of dissolution can do that.

clauses.title: Dissolution, Legal Separation, and Nullity Are Three Distinct Proceedings
clauses.body: California law addresses the end or alteration of a marriage's legal status through three legally distinct types of proceeding, grouped within the same division of the Family Code but governed by different statutory parts: dissolution of marriage, legal separation of the parties, and nullity of marriage. A proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties is commenced by filing a petition that must itself state which of the two is sought. Nullity — a judicial determination that a marriage was void or voidable from the start — is governed by an entirely separate part of the same division, with its own distinct grounds (for example, that a party was under 18 at the time of the marriage without the statutory exception applying) that are unrelated to the no-fault dissolution grounds described elsewhere in this document. This document addresses only the dissolution and legal-separation process; it does not address nullity, and does not itself determine which of the three proceedings applies to any specific marriage.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's dissolution-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or divorce. This document is informational: it does not itself dissolve a marriage, establish residency, or determine grounds for any specific case; only a court judgment does that. These two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 2330 and § 2210), not subsections of the same section. This document does not describe nullity's substantive grounds in full, or the separate 'void marriage' category (incestuous and bigamous marriages, addressed in a different chapter this document's research did not independently re-verify with a second fetch); it cites § 2210's voidable-marriage grounds only as evidence that nullity is governed by a distinct statutory framework from dissolution, not as a complete statement of nullity law.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2330(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a dissolution/legal-separation petition must state which is sought
citations.quote: A proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties is commenced by filing a petition or joint petition entitled “In re the marriage of ____ and ____,” which shall state whether it is a petition for dissolution of the marriage or for legal separation of the parties.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2210 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: nullity's distinct, separately codified grounds
citations.quote: A marriage is voidable and may be adjudged a nullity if any of the following conditions existed at the time of the marriage: (a) The party who commences the proceeding or on whose behalf the proceeding is commenced was under 18 years of age, unless the party entered into the marriage pursuant to Section 302 or 303.

clauses.title: Legal Grounds for Dissolution: A No-Fault Standard
clauses.body: Dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties in California may be based on only two grounds, pleaded generally rather than by reciting the underlying facts: irreconcilable differences that have caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage, or permanent legal incapacity to make decisions. Irreconcilable differences are grounds the court determines to be substantial reasons for not continuing the marriage and that make it appear the marriage should be dissolved. A marriage may be dissolved on the ground of permanent legal incapacity to make decisions only upon proof, including competent medical or psychiatric testimony, that the spouse was, at the time the petition was filed, and remains, permanently lacking the legal capacity to make decisions.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's dissolution-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or divorce. This document is informational: it does not itself dissolve a marriage, establish residency, or determine grounds for any specific case; only a court judgment does that. This clause verifies that California Family Code § 2310 lists exactly two grounds and requires that they be "pleaded generally"; the statement that California's dissolution statute contains no fault-based ground (such as adultery or cruelty) is drawn from the absence of any such ground in § 2310's text, not from a separate statute that affirmatively abolishes fault grounds — no such separate abolition statute was located or is cited here. Many other states retain fault-based grounds for divorce alongside or instead of no-fault grounds; that comparison is not independently verified here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2310(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the two exclusive, generally-pleaded grounds for dissolution
citations.quote: Dissolution of the marriage or legal separation of the parties may be based on either of the following grounds, which shall be pleaded generally: (a) Irreconcilable differences, which have caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage. (b) Permanent legal incapacity to make decisions.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2311 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory definition of irreconcilable differences
citations.quote: Irreconcilable differences are those grounds which are determined by the court to be substantial reasons for not continuing the marriage and which make it appear that the marriage should be dissolved.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2312 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the proof standard for permanent legal incapacity
citations.quote: A marriage may be dissolved on the grounds of permanent legal incapacity to make decisions only upon proof, including competent medical or psychiatric testimony, that the spouse was at the time the petition was filed, and remains, permanently lacking the legal capacity to make decisions.

clauses.title: Residency Requirement for Filing (and the Same-Sex Marriage Exception)
clauses.body: Except as provided by a specific statutory exception, a judgment of dissolution of marriage may not be entered in California unless one of the parties has been a resident of California for six months and a resident of the county in which the proceeding is filed for three months, both periods measured immediately preceding the filing of the petition. A distinct statutory exception allows a judgment of dissolution, nullity, or legal separation of a marriage between persons of the same sex to be entered even if neither spouse is a California resident or domiciliary at the time of filing, if the marriage was entered into in California and neither party resides in a jurisdiction that will dissolve the marriage — with a rebuttable presumption that a jurisdiction not recognizing the marriage will not dissolve it. In that circumstance, the superior court in the California county where the marriage was entered is the proper court for the proceeding, and the case is adjudicated under California law.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's dissolution-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or divorce. This document is informational: it does not itself dissolve a marriage, establish residency, or determine grounds for any specific case; only a court judgment does that. Two of this clause's citations — § 2320(a) and § 2320(b)(1)-(2) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2320); both are quoted because they state two distinct rules (the general six-month/three-month residency requirement and a specific exception to it for same-sex marriages entered in California), not because a second independent source was located for either. Nothing in this clause states, or is evidence of, whether either party to a specific marriage actually satisfies the general residency requirement or the same-sex-marriage exception, or whether any particular county is one where filing would be proper for a specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2320(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the six-month state / three-month county residency requirement
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), a judgment of dissolution of marriage may not be entered unless one of the parties to the marriage has been a resident of this state for six months and of the county in which the proceeding is filed for three months next preceding the filing of the petition.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2320(b)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the same-sex-marriage exception to the residency requirement
citations.quote: (b) (1) A judgment for dissolution, nullity, or legal separation of a marriage between persons of the same sex may be entered, even if neither spouse is a resident of, or maintains a domicile in, this state at the time the proceedings are filed, if the following apply: (A) The marriage was entered in California. (B) Neither party to the marriage resides in a jurisdiction that will dissolve the marriage. If the jurisdiction does not recognize the marriage, there shall be a rebuttable presumption that the jurisdiction will not dissolve the marriage. (2) For the purposes of this subdivision, the superior court in the county where the marriage was entered shall be the proper court for the proceeding. The dissolution, nullity, or legal separation shall be adjudicated in accordance with California law.

clauses.title: The Six-Month Waiting Period Before a Judgment Becomes Final
clauses.body: Subject to a small set of statutory exceptions, no judgment of dissolution becomes final for the purpose of terminating the marriage relationship of the parties until six months have expired, measured from the date of service of a copy of the summons and petition, or the date of the respondent's appearance, whichever occurs first. A court may extend that six-month period for good cause shown.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's dissolution-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or divorce. This document is informational: it does not itself dissolve a marriage, establish residency, or determine grounds for any specific case; only a court judgment does that. This is a single statutory section (§ 2339, subdivisions (a) and (b)); no additional independent source was found for this. Subdivision (a) itself cross-references a further set of exceptions (Sections 2340 to 2344) that this document's research did not independently fetch or verify, and which are not described here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2339(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the six-month waiting period and its trigger event
citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivision (b) and to Sections 2340 to 2344, inclusive, no judgment of dissolution is final for the purpose of terminating the marriage relationship of the parties until six months have expired from the date of service of a copy of summons and petition or the date of appearance of the respondent, whichever occurs first. (b) The court may extend the six-month period described in subdivision (a) for good cause shown.

clauses.title: Property Division Absent a Settlement Agreement — the Community-Property Default
clauses.body: Absent {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}'s written agreement, their oral stipulation in open court, or another statutory exception, a court in a dissolution or legal separation proceeding is required to divide the community estate of the parties equally. Where the parties instead reach and document their own agreement on how to divide property, that agreement — not this default rule — controls the division; the terms such an agreement would contain are addressed by this document's companion Marital Settlement Agreement document and are not restated here.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's dissolution-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or divorce. This document is informational: it does not itself dissolve a marriage, establish residency, or determine grounds for any specific case; only a court judgment does that. This is a single statutory section (§ 2550); no additional independent source was found for this. This same section is independently cited in this corpus's Marital Settlement Agreement document (clause msa_equal_division_default) for the settlement-terms context; it is cited again here, independently re-verified against the statute's live text, only to state the default a court applies when no settlement exists — this clause does not restate that document's fuller treatment of community versus separate property, the date-of-separation test, or the written-agreement exception's mechanics.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2550 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the equal-division default rule and its written-agreement exception
citations.quote: Except upon the written agreement of the parties, or on oral stipulation of the parties in open court, or as otherwise provided in this division, in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, the court shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally.

clauses.title: Information Referenced When a Dissolution Petition Is Filed
clauses.body: A proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation is commenced by filing a petition captioned "In re the Marriage of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}," which states whether it seeks dissolution or legal separation and sets out, among other matters, the date of marriage and the date of separation. For reference: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} were married on {{marriageDate}} and identify {{separationDate}} as their date of separation, for a proceeding contemplated in {{countyOfFiling}}. This information sheet gathers that background information; it is not the petition itself and does not commence a court proceeding.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment — Not a Court Filing
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{party1Name}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual petition for dissolution of marriage filed with the California superior court. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not dissolve a marriage, establish residency, or determine grounds for any specific case; only a court judgment of dissolution can dissolve a marriage.]

clauses.title: Statement of Information — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This Statement of Information relates to {{companyName}}, a California {{entityType}}. Filing articles of incorporation or articles of organization with the California Secretary of State creates a business entity, but it does not end that entity's reporting obligations to the state. California law separately requires the entity to periodically file a Statement of Information with the Secretary of State after formation, reporting current information such as the entity's officers, directors, managers, or members; its agent for service of process; and its principal business address, so the state's public record stays current. This is a California state filing made with the Secretary of State. It is separate from, and unrelated to, any federal reporting obligation that may apply to a business entity — including, for some entities, federal beneficial ownership reporting under the Corporate Transparency Act. This document's research addressed only the California statutes governing this state filing; it did not research or verify the current status, scope, or requirements of any federal reporting regime, which has been the subject of significant federal litigation and rulemaking changes in recent years. Any reference to a federal regime here is unverified background context, not this document's authority, and not a substitute for checking that federal requirement directly.

clauses.title: Current Information for the Next Filing
clauses.body: The information below reflects {{companyName}}'s current records for use in preparing its next Statement of Information filing with the California Secretary of State. Principal office address: {{principalOfficeAddress}}. Agent for service of process: {{agentName}}, at {{agentAddress}}. Current officers and directors (if {{companyName}} is a corporation) or managers and members (if {{companyName}} is an LLC): {{keyPersonnelNames}}. General type of business that constitutes {{companyName}}'s principal business activity: {{businessActivityDescription}}. This worksheet organizes the entity's current information for reference. It is not itself the Secretary of State's official statement form, which must be completed and filed in the format the Secretary of State prescribes.

clauses.title: Initial and Recurring Filing Deadlines
clauses.body: California sets separate statutory deadlines for a corporation's Statement of Information and an LLC's Statement of Information, and the two schedules are not the same. A California corporation must file an initial statement within 90 days after its articles of incorporation are filed, and then again every year during its assigned filing period.
