clauses.title: Recitals — Corporate Dissolution and Winding Up
clauses.body: {{companyName}} elected to voluntarily wind up and dissolve effective {{dissolutionDate}}, based on {{dissolutionReason}}. This document records the winding up of {{companyName}}'s affairs and the certificate of dissolution that formally ends {{companyName}}'s corporate powers, rights, and privileges with the California Secretary of State. It addresses the statutory winding-up and dissolution process itself — a separate matter from whatever dissolution triggers or approval procedures appear in {{companyName}}'s own bylaws or shareholder agreements, which govern only when and how the decision to dissolve is made internally, not how the corporation's existence is actually wound up and ended with the state.

clauses.title: Grounds for Voluntary Dissolution
clauses.body: California law lets a corporation elect to voluntarily wind up and dissolve in two distinct ways. First, any corporation may make that election by the vote of shareholders holding shares representing 50 percent or more of the voting power — a single, fixed threshold. Second, a narrower election path is available to the board alone, without any shareholder vote, but only for a corporation that falls into one of three specific categories: one as to which a federal bankruptcy court has entered an order for relief under Chapter 7; one that has disposed of all its assets and has not conducted any business for the five years immediately preceding the board's resolution to dissolve; or one that has issued no shares at all.
clauses.gap: This corrects an assumption this research started with: Corporations Code section 1900 sets a fixed 50-percent-or-more shareholder-vote threshold for the general voluntary-dissolution election, and its text includes no 'or as otherwise specified in the articles' qualifier letting the articles of incorporation raise, lower, or otherwise vary that threshold — unlike some other California entity-dissolution statutes (including the LLC dissolution statutes addressed in a separate document in this project), section 1900 does not defer to the corporation's own governing documents on this point. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; other states impose different dissolution procedures, including different vote thresholds. Both quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 1900, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1900(a)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, voluntary dissolution by shareholder vote
citations.quote: Any corporation may elect voluntarily to wind up and dissolve by the vote of shareholders holding shares representing 50 percent or more of the voting power.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1900(b)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, the narrower board-only election path
citations.quote: Any corporation which comes within one of the following descriptions may elect by approval by the board to wind up and dissolve:(1) A corporation as to which an order for relief has been entered under Chapter 7 of the federal bankruptcy law.(2) A corporation which has disposed of all of its assets and has not conducted any business for a period of five years immediately preceding the adoption of the resolution electing to dissolve the corporation.(3) A corporation which has issued no shares.

clauses.title: The Certificate of Election and the Certificate of Dissolution
clauses.body: Formally dissolving a California corporation generally involves a certificate evidencing the election to wind up and dissolve, filed once that election is made, and a separate certificate of dissolution filed later, once winding up is complete. The certificate of election must be an officers' certificate, or be signed and verified by a majority of the sitting directors, or by shareholders authorized to sign it by holders of 50 percent or more of the voting power, and it must state that the corporation elected to dissolve along with details of how that election was made. If the election was made by the vote of all the outstanding shares — not merely 50 percent or more — and the later certificate of dissolution itself states that the election was made by all outstanding shares, the separate certificate of election does not need to be filed at all. The certificate of dissolution itself, once winding up is complete, is signed and verified by a majority of the sitting directors and states that the corporation has been completely wound up, how its known debts and liabilities were handled, that its known assets have been distributed (or that none were acquired), that the corporation is dissolved, and that a final franchise tax return has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board. Filing that certificate of dissolution is what causes the corporation's corporate powers, rights, and privileges to cease.
clauses.gap: This clause corrects a naming trap this research started with: for a California corporation, 'certificate of dissolution' does not refer to the first-filed document the way an analogous name does under the separate LLC dissolution scheme addressed in a different document in this project. For a corporation, the certificate of election under Cal. Corp. Code § 1901 is the (often-skippable) first filing, and the certificate of dissolution under Cal. Corp. Code § 1905 is the filing that actually terminates the corporation's powers, rights, and privileges — the reverse of the LLC scheme, where a certificate of dissolution is filed first and a later certificate of cancellation is what actually ends the LLC's existence. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; other states impose different dissolution procedures, including different filing sequences and document names. The two citations below are to two different statutory sections (§ 1901 and § 1905), not subsections of a single section.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1901
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, the certificate of election to wind up and dissolve
citations.quote: (a) Whenever a corporation has elected to wind up and dissolve a certificate evidencing such election shall forthwith be filed. (b) The certificate shall be an officers’ certificate or shall be signed and verified by at least a majority of the directors then in office or by one or more shareholders authorized to do so by shareholders holding shares representing 50 percent or more of the voting power and shall set forth: (1) That the corporation has elected to wind up and dissolve. (2) If the election was made by the vote of shareholders, the number of shares voting for the election and that the election was made by shareholders representing at least 50 percent of the voting power. (3) If the certificate is executed by a shareholder or shareholders, that the subscribing shareholder or shareholders were authorized to execute the certificate by shareholders holding shares representing at least 50 percent of the voting power. (4) If the election was made by the board pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 1900, the certificate shall also set forth the circumstances showing the corporation to be within one of the categories described in said subdivision. (c) If an election to dissolve made pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 1900 is made by the vote of all the outstanding shares and a statement to that effect is added to the certificate of dissolution pursuant to Section 1905, the separate filing of the certificate of election pursuant to this section is not required.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1905
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, the certificate of dissolution and its effect
citations.quote: (a) When a corporation has been completely wound up without court proceedings therefor, a majority of the directors then in office shall sign and verify a certificate of dissolution stating:(1) That the corporation has been completely wound up.(2) That its known debts and liabilities have been actually paid, or adequately provided for, or paid or adequately provided for as far as its assets permitted, or that it has incurred no known debts or liabilities, as the case may be. If there are known debts or liabilities for payment of which adequate provision has been made, the certificate shall state what provision has been made, setting forth the name and address of the corporation, person or governmental agency that has assumed or guaranteed the payment, or the name and address of the depositary with which deposit has been made or any other information that may be necessary to enable the creditor or other person to whom payment is to be made to appear and claim payment of the debt or liability.(3) That its known assets have been distributed to the persons entitled thereto or that it acquired no known assets, as the case may be.(4) That the corporation is dissolved.(5) If no certificate of election is to be filed pursuant to subdivision (c) of Section 1901, that the election to dissolve was made by the vote of all the outstanding shares.(6) That a final franchise tax return, as described by Section 23332 of the Revenue and Taxation Code, has been or will be filed with the Franchise Tax Board, as required under Part 10.2 (commencing with Section 18401) of Division 2 of the Revenue and Taxation Code.(b) The certificate of dissolution shall be filed with the Secretary of State and thereupon the corporate powers, rights, and privileges of the corporation shall cease. The Secretary of State shall notify the Franchise Tax Board of the dissolution.

clauses.title: Commencement of Winding Up and the Board's Powers
clauses.body: Voluntary winding-up proceedings for a corporation commence upon the adoption of the shareholders' or directors' resolution electing to wind up and dissolve, or upon the filing with the corporation of a written consent of shareholders to that effect. Once that happens, the corporation must stop carrying on business except so far as necessary to wind up beneficially, or during whatever period the board considers necessary to preserve the corporation's goodwill or going-concern value pending a sale of its business or assets. The board must give written notice by mail of the start of the winding-up proceeding to all shareholders — except shareholders who voted in favor of the dissolution — and to all known creditors and claimants whose addresses appear on the corporation's own records. The board continues to act as the board throughout, both before and after the certificate of dissolution is filed, and state law gives the directors and officers a specific, non-exclusive list of powers to exercise in the corporation's name for winding up: electing officers and employing agents and attorneys to liquidate the corporation's affairs; continuing the business only so far as necessary for its disposal or winding up; carrying out contracts and collecting, paying, compromising, and settling debts and claims for or against the corporation; defending suits brought against the corporation; suing in the corporation's name for amounts owed to it or to recover its property; collecting unpaid share subscriptions or recovering unlawful distributions; selling, exchanging, conveying, or otherwise disposing of corporate assets on terms the board deems reasonable; and, generally, making contracts and doing anything in the corporation's name that is proper or convenient for winding up, settling, and liquidating its affairs.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; other states impose different dissolution procedures, including different winding-up mechanics and director powers. This clause also corrects an assumption this research started with: the concrete list of winding-up activities (collecting assets, disposing of property not to be distributed in kind, discharging or providing for liabilities, and so on) is not found in Cal. Corp. Code § 1903, which instead addresses only when winding up commences, when the corporation must stop ordinary business, and what notice the board must give; the actual statutory list of the directors' and officers' winding-up powers and activities is codified separately, at Cal. Corp. Code § 2001. The two citations below are to two different statutory sections (§ 1903 and § 2001), not subsections of a single section.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1903
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, commencement of voluntary winding up and notice to shareholders and creditors
citations.quote: (a) Voluntary proceedings for winding up the corporation commence upon the adoption of the resolution of shareholders or directors of the corporation electing to wind up and dissolve, or upon the filing with the corporation of a written consent of shareholders thereto.(b) When a voluntary proceeding for winding up has commenced, the board shall continue to act as a board and shall have full powers to wind up and settle its affairs, both before and after the filing of the certificate of dissolution.(c) When a voluntary proceeding for winding up has commenced, the corporation shall cease to carry on business except to the extent necessary for the beneficial winding up thereof and except during such period as the board may deem necessary to preserve the corporation’s goodwill or going-concern value pending a sale of its business or assets, or both, in whole or in part. The board shall cause written notice of the commencement of the proceeding for voluntary winding up to be given by mail to all shareholders (except no notice need be given to the shareholders who voted in favor of winding up and dissolving the corporation) and to all known creditors and claimants whose addresses appear on the records of the corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2001
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, the directors' and officers' powers during winding up
citations.quote: The powers and duties of the directors (or other persons appointed by the court pursuant to Section 1805) and officers after commencement of a dissolution proceeding include, but are not limited to, the following acts in the name and on behalf of the corporation:(a) To elect officers and to employ agents and attorneys to liquidate or wind up its affairs.(b) To continue the conduct of the business insofar as necessary for the disposal or winding up thereof.(c) To carry out contracts and collect, pay, compromise and settle debts and claims for or against the corporation.(d) To defend suits brought against the corporation.(e) To sue, in the name of the corporation, for all sums due or owing to the corporation or to recover any of its property.(f) To collect any amounts remaining unpaid on subscriptions to shares or to recover unlawful distributions.(g) To sell at public or private sale, exchange, convey or otherwise dispose of all or any part of the assets of the corporation for cash in an amount deemed reasonable by the board without compliance with the provisions of Section 1001 (except subdivision (d) thereof), or (subject to compliance with the provisions of Sections 1001, 1200 and 1201, but Chapter 13 (commencing with Section 1300) shall not be applicable thereto) upon such other terms and conditions and for such other considerations as the board deems reasonable or expedient; and to execute bills of sale and deeds of conveyance in the name of the corporation.(h) In general, to make contracts and to do any and all things in the name of the corporation which may be proper or convenient for the purposes of winding up, settling and liquidating the affairs of the corporation.

clauses.title: Distribution Priority for Remaining Corporate Assets
clauses.body: After determining that a corporation's known debts and liabilities have all been paid or adequately provided for, state law requires the board to distribute the corporation's remaining assets among the shareholders according to their respective rights and preferences — a formulation that folds in whatever liquidation preferences a corporation's own articles of incorporation may have created among different classes or series of stock — or, if the corporation has no shareholders, to whoever else is entitled to them. If the winding up is happening through a court proceeding, or is subject to court supervision, the distribution cannot be made until after any court-ordered period for creditors to present claims has expired.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; other states impose different dissolution procedures, including different asset-distribution rules. This distribution rule expressly turns on shareholders' 'respective rights and preferences,' which can differ across classes or series of stock under a corporation's own articles of incorporation; this document does not state what those rights and preferences are for any particular corporation, since that is a matter of the corporation's own articles, not something this statute defines on its own. This is a single statutory section (Cal. Corp. Code § 2004); no additional independent source was found for this specific distribution-priority rule.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2004
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, distribution of remaining assets on winding up
citations.quote: After determining that all the known debts and liabilities of a corporation in the process of winding up have been paid or adequately provided for, the board shall distribute all the remaining corporate assets among the shareholders according to their respective rights and preferences or, if there are no shareholders, to the persons entitled thereto. If the winding up is by court proceeding or subject to court supervision, the distribution shall not be made until after the expiration of any period for the presentation of claims which has been prescribed by order of the court.

clauses.title: Continued Existence and Surviving Claims After Dissolution
clauses.body: Filing the certificate of dissolution does not erase a corporation out of existence for every purpose, and it does not cut off claims against the corporation or its former shareholders. State law lets a dissolved corporation continue to exist afterward, but only for a narrow set of purposes: winding up its affairs, prosecuting or defending lawsuits by or against it in order to collect and discharge what it owes, disposing of and conveying its property, and collecting and dividing its remaining assets — the corporation may not continue conducting business beyond what winding up actually requires. No lawsuit involving the corporation is dismissed just because dissolution happened or because winding-up proceedings are underway, and any asset inadvertently missed during winding up stays with the dissolved corporation for whoever is entitled to it. Separately, state law lets a cause of action against a dissolved corporation — whether it arose before or after the dissolution — be enforced against the dissolved corporation itself, up to its undistributed assets, and, if assets were already distributed to shareholders, against those shareholders individually, up to the lesser of their pro-rata share of the claim or what they actually received on dissolution. A claim against a shareholder on this basis is extinguished unless the claimant sues before the earlier of the ordinary statute of limitations applicable to that claim or four years after the corporation's dissolution became effective.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; other states impose different dissolution procedures, including different post-dissolution survival periods, and some impose none at all. The first two quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 2010, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones; the third quote is a different section, Cal. Corp. Code § 2011, addressed separately. This document states only the general rule under section 2011(a)(1)-(2) — enforcement against the corporation's undistributed assets or against shareholders individually, and the four-year/statute-of-limitations cutoff; it does not address the separate quiet-title-action survival rule in section 2011(c) (which the statute states has no time limit), the procedural rule allowing suit against shareholders in the corporation's own name under section 2011(a)(3), or the corporation's or creditors' separate rights under Corporations Code section 2009 or the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, which section 2011(a)(3) expressly preserves without this document independently verifying their content.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2010(a)-(b)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, continued existence for winding-up purposes after dissolution
citations.quote: (a) A corporation which is dissolved nevertheless continues to exist for the purpose of winding up its affairs, prosecuting and defending actions by or against it and enabling it to collect and discharge obligations, dispose of and convey its property and collect and divide its assets, but not for the purpose of continuing business except so far as necessary for the winding up thereof.(b) No action or proceeding to which a corporation is a party abates by the dissolution of the corporation or by reason of proceedings for winding up and dissolution thereof.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2010(c)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, assets omitted from winding up
citations.quote: Any assets inadvertently or otherwise omitted from the winding up continue in the dissolved corporation for the benefit of the persons entitled thereto upon dissolution of the corporation and on realization shall be distributed accordingly.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2011(a)(1)-(2)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, causes of action against a dissolved corporation and its shareholders, and the four-year cutoff
citations.quote: (1) Causes of action against a dissolved corporation, whether arising before or after the dissolution of the corporation, may be enforced against any of the following:(A) Against the dissolved corporation, to the extent of its undistributed assets, including, without limitation, any insurance assets held by the corporation that may be available to satisfy claims.(B) If any of the assets of the dissolved corporation have been distributed to shareholders, against shareholders of the dissolved corporation to the extent of their pro rata share of the claim or to the extent of the corporate assets distributed to them upon dissolution of the corporation, whichever is less.A shareholder’s total liability under this section may not exceed the total amount of assets of the dissolved corporation distributed to the shareholder upon dissolution of the corporation.(2) Except as set forth in subdivision (c), all causes of action against a shareholder of a dissolved corporation arising under this section are extinguished unless the claimant commences a proceeding to enforce the cause of action against that shareholder of a dissolved corporation prior to the earlier of the following:(A) The expiration of the statute of limitations applicable to the cause of action.(B) Four years after the effective date of the dissolution of the corporation.

clauses.title: Franchise Tax Board Clearance and the Minimum Franchise Tax
clauses.body: Filing a certificate of dissolution does not, by itself, stop the corporation's minimum franchise tax. Under California's Revenue and Taxation Code, a corporation owes no further minimum franchise tax for a given taxable year only if it does all of the following: files a timely final franchise tax return with the Franchise Tax Board for that taxable year; does no further business in California after that taxable year ends; and files a certificate of dissolution with the Secretary of State within 12 months of the date that final return was filed.
clauses.gap: This confirms, with a correction, the research assumption that a distinct Franchise Tax Board tax-clearance mechanism applies to corporations. Verified directly, that mechanism is Rev. & Tax. Code § 23332(c), not Corp. Code § 1905 itself: section 1905(a)(6), addressed elsewhere in this document, only requires the corporation's own certificate of dissolution to represent that a final franchise tax return has been or will be filed — it is section 23332(c), a separate statute, that actually ties minimum-franchise-tax relief to that representation being true and to the certificate of dissolution being filed within 12 months of the final return. This mechanism mirrors, but is not the same statute as, the analogous LLC mechanism verified elsewhere in this project's LLC Dissolution and Cancellation document: corporations look to Rev. & Tax. Code § 23332, while LLCs look to a different section, Rev. & Tax. Code § 17947. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's corporate dissolution process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not tax advice about any particular corporation's own filings or filing deadlines. This document does not independently verify Rev. & Tax. Code § 18601 (defining a 'final franchise tax return') or the several other entity-specific dissolution and surrender statutes that section 23332(c)(1)(C) cross-references by number (Corp. Code §§ 1809, 2112, 6615, 8615, and 12635, and Fin. Code § 3126) beyond the fact that section 23332 itself names them; their own text was not independently fetched and verified as part of this research. This is a single statutory section (Rev. & Tax. Code § 23332(c)); no additional independent source was found for this specific tax-clearance mechanism.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope — Informational Only
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, California's statutory process for a nonjudicial ("power of sale") foreclosure of a deed of trust under California Civil Code §§ 2924 et seq. — the process used for the large majority of California residential mortgage foreclosures. It concerns a loan affecting the real property commonly known as {{propertyAddress}}, secured by a deed of trust naming {{trustorName}} as trustor (borrower) and {{beneficiaryName}} as beneficiary (lender). This sheet is informational only. It does not itself record, rescind, or otherwise affect any notice of default or notice of sale; it does not initiate, accelerate, halt, postpone, or complete any foreclosure of this or any other property; and it does not determine whether any actual default, notice, recording, posting, publication, or sale relating to this loan has complied — or failed to comply — with the statutory requirements it describes. Only the party or parties actually entitled to exercise the power of sale, acting through the statutory notice-and-waiting process described here, can begin or carry a nonjudicial foreclosure forward; only an actual reinstatement payment, payoff, or court order can stop one already begun.

clauses.title: Power-of-Sale (Nonjudicial) Foreclosure Distinguished From Judicial Foreclosure
clauses.body: A deed of trust encumbering {{propertyAddress}} may contain a "power of sale" clause — a private contractual grant of authority, running from {{trustorName}} to a trustee, to sell the property after a default without first suing in court. California Civil Code § 2924(a) itself frames the power-of-sale mechanism this way: once "a power of sale is conferred upon the mortgagee, trustee, or any other person, to be exercised after a breach of the obligation for which that mortgage or transfer is a security," the statutory notice-and-waiting sequence described in this document is what governs how that power may actually be exercised. This is a fundamentally different mechanism from a judicial foreclosure, in which a lender files a lawsuit and a court enters a judgment or decree of foreclosure and orders the property sold — Section 2924(a) itself carves out, as a separate category, a transfer "made pursuant to an order, judgment, or decree of a court of record." A nonjudicial, power-of-sale foreclosure under a deed of trust involves no lawsuit and no judge; it proceeds entirely through the recorded notices and statutory waiting periods described in this document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nonjudicial foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property or loan; foreclosure procedures vary significantly by state, and many states require judicial foreclosure instead. This clause quotes a single passage from Civil Code § 2924(a) that itself frames the power-of-sale mechanism and, in the same sentence, distinguishes it from a transfer made pursuant to a court order, judgment, or decree — that definitional contrast is drawn directly from the statute's own text and independently verified. Separately, the widely repeated practitioner claim that most California residential mortgage lenders specifically choose a deed of trust with a power-of-sale clause, rather than a mortgage without one, because it enables this faster nonjudicial process, was not independently verified against a primary source to the same standard as the statutory quotes in this document — it is not stated as fact in this clause, and no such claim is made or relied on here beyond the statute's own text.

clauses.title: Notice of Default — Statutory Trigger and Required Content
clauses.body: Before a trustee's sale of {{propertyAddress}} can occur under a power of sale, California Civil Code § 2924(a)(1) requires that "The trustee, mortgagee, or beneficiary, or any of their authorized agents shall first file for record, in the office of the recorder of each county wherein the mortgaged or trust property or some part or parcel thereof is situated, a notice of default." If a Notice of Default affecting {{propertyAddress}} has been recorded, its recording date is stated as: {{noticeOfDefaultRecordingDate}}. By statute, that recorded notice of default must include: (A) "A statement identifying the mortgage or deed of trust by stating the name or names of the trustor or trustors and giving the book and page, or instrument number, if applicable, where the mortgage or deed of trust is recorded or a description of the mortgaged or trust property"; (B) "A statement that a breach of the obligation for which the mortgage or transfer in trust is security has occurred"; (C) "A statement setting forth the nature of each breach actually known to the beneficiary and of the beneficiary’s election to sell or cause to be sold the property to satisfy that obligation and any other obligation secured by the deed of trust or mortgage that is in default"; and (D), where the default is curable, a statement of the borrower's reinstatement rights under Section 2924c. If an amount has been stated as in default for this loan, it is stated as: {{defaultAmount}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nonjudicial foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property or loan; foreclosure procedures vary significantly by state, and many states require judicial foreclosure instead. All five quoted passages in this clause are drawn from a single statutory paragraph, Civil Code § 2924(a)(1), and its four lettered subparagraphs (A) through (D) — they are quoted together, rather than in separate clauses, because they jointly define the single statutory content requirement for one document (the notice of default), not because they are unrelated provisions being combined.

clauses.title: Who May Record a Notice of Default
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2924(a)(1) identifies who may record a notice of default: "The trustee, mortgagee, or beneficiary, or any of their authorized agents" — meaning the loan's beneficiary, the trustee under the deed of trust, or an authorized agent of either. Section 2924(a)(6) narrows that further: "An entity shall not record or cause a notice of default to be recorded or otherwise initiate the foreclosure process unless it is the holder of the beneficial interest under the mortgage or deed of trust, the original trustee or the substituted trustee under the deed of trust, or the designated agent of the holder of the beneficial interest." For the loan encumbering {{propertyAddress}}, the beneficiary named is {{beneficiaryName}}, and the trustee named, if known, is {{trusteeName}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nonjudicial foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property or loan; foreclosure procedures vary significantly by state, and many states require judicial foreclosure instead. This clause cites two different subsections of the same statutory section — Civil Code § 2924(a)(1) (who may generally file a notice of default) and § 2924(a)(6) (the narrower restriction on who may actually record one or otherwise initiate foreclosure) — quoted together because the second subsection qualifies and narrows the first.

clauses.title: Minimum Waiting Period Between Notice of Default and Notice of Sale
clauses.body: After a notice of default affecting {{propertyAddress}} is recorded, California Civil Code § 2924(a)(2) requires that "Not less than three months shall elapse from the filing of the notice of default" before a notice of sale may be given. Section 2924(a)(3) then ties the next statutory step to that waiting period: "after the lapse of the three months described in paragraph (2), the mortgagee, trustee, or other person authorized to take the sale shall give notice of sale, stating the time and place thereof, in the manner and for a time not less than that set forth in Section 2924f." A limited exception in Section 2924(a)(4) permits a notice of sale to be recorded up to five days before the three-month period lapses, provided the sale date itself is set no earlier than three months and 20 days after the notice of default was recorded.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nonjudicial foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property or loan; foreclosure procedures vary significantly by state, and many states require judicial foreclosure instead. This clause cites two different subsections of the same statutory section — Civil Code § 2924(a)(2) (the three-month minimum waiting period itself) and § 2924(a)(3) (which ties the notice-of-sale step to that period) — quoted together because the second subsection is the operative consequence of the first.

clauses.title: Notice of Sale — Minimum Timing, Posting, and Publication Requirements
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2924f governs the notice of sale that follows a notice of default. Before a trustee's sale of {{propertyAddress}} can occur, "notice of the sale thereof shall be given by posting a written notice of the time of sale and of the street address and the specific place at the street address where the sale will be held, and describing the property to be sold, at least 20 days before the date of sale in one public place in the city where the property is to be sold, if the property is to be sold in a city, or, if not, then in one public place in the county seat of the county where the property is to be sold, and publishing a copy once a week for three consecutive calendar weeks." The statute further requires that "[t]he first publication [be] at least 20 days before the date of sale, in a newspaper of general circulation published in the public notice district in which the property or some part thereof is situated"; that "A copy of the notice of sale shall also be posted in a conspicuous place on the property to be sold at least 20 days before the date of sale, where possible and where not restricted for any reason"; and that the notice of sale "be recorded with the county recorder of the county in which the property or some part thereof is situated at least 20 days prior to the date of sale."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nonjudicial foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property or loan; foreclosure procedures vary significantly by state, and many states require judicial foreclosure instead. This clause cites four different paragraphs of the same statutory subdivision — Civil Code § 2924f(b)(1) through (b)(4) — each addressing a distinct minimum-20-day requirement (posting in a public place, first newspaper publication, posting on the property itself, and recording with the county recorder), quoted together because they are the four components of one statutory notice-of-sale requirement. Separately, Civil Code § 2924f exists on the California Legislative Information site in two chaptered versions for 2025 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 200, Secs. 7 and 8); the version quoted here is the one that the site's own amendment history marks as currently operative (effective January 1, 2026, and, by its own terms, remaining in effect only until January 1, 2031), confirmed by direct comparison of two independently fetched copies of the compiled article text. This document does not address subdivisions (c) through (f) of Section 2924f, which cover narrower topics such as owner-occupied single-family residences purchased under installment sales contracts, tenant purchase-agreement postponement rights, and minimum-bid fair market value requirements.

clauses.title: Right to Reinstate the Loan by Curing the Default
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2924c gives the trustor and certain other interested parties a statutory right to cure a default and reinstate the loan secured by {{propertyAddress}} — without paying the full loan balance. The trustor or mortgagor, their successor in interest, or certain subordinate lienholders "may pay to the beneficiary or the mortgagee or their successors in interest, respectively, the entire amount due, at the time payment is tendered, with respect to (A) all amounts of principal, interest, taxes, assessments, insurance premiums, or advances actually known by the beneficiary to be, and that are, in default and shown in the notice of default, under the terms of the deed of trust or mortgage and the obligation secured thereby, (B) all amounts in default on recurring obligations not shown in the notice of default, and (C) all reasonable costs and expenses, subject to subdivision (c), that are actually incurred, or will be incurred as a direct result of the payment being tendered, in enforcing the terms of the obligation, deed of trust, or mortgage, and trustee's or attorney's fees, subject to subdivision (d), other than the portion of principal as would not then be due had no default occurred, and thereby cure the default theretofore existing, and thereupon, all proceedings theretofore had or instituted shall be dismissed or discontinued and the obligation and deed of trust or mortgage shall be reinstated and shall be and remain in force and effect, the same as if the acceleration had not occurred." As to timing, Section 2924c(e) provides that "[r]einstatement of a monetary default under the terms of an obligation secured by a deed of trust, or mortgage may be made at any time within the period commencing with the date of recordation of the notice of default until five business days prior to the date of sale set forth in the initial recorded notice of sale. In the event the sale does not take place on the date set forth in the initial recorded notice of sale or a subsequent recorded notice of sale is required to be given, the right of reinstatement shall be revived as of the date of recordation of the subsequent notice of sale."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nonjudicial foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property or loan; foreclosure procedures vary significantly by state, and many states require judicial foreclosure instead. This clause cites two different subsections of the same statutory section — Civil Code § 2924c(a)(1) (the reinstatement right and the cure-amount, rather than full-payoff, measure of what must be paid) and § 2924c(e) (the reinstatement right's timing deadline and its revival if a scheduled sale does not go forward) — quoted together because the timing subsection defines when the right described in the first subsection may be exercised.

clauses.title: Anti-Deficiency Protection After a Nonjudicial (Power-of-Sale) Foreclosure Sale
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure § 580d provides a distinct consumer-protection rule specific to nonjudicial, power-of-sale foreclosure sales: "Except as provided in subdivision (b), no deficiency shall be owed or collected, and no deficiency judgment shall be rendered for a deficiency on a note secured by a deed of trust or mortgage on real property or an estate for years therein executed in any case in which the real property or estate for years therein has been sold by the mortgagee or trustee under power of sale contained in the mortgage or deed of trust." In other words, if {{propertyAddress}} is sold at a nonjudicial trustee's sale for less than the amount owed on the loan, {{beneficiaryName}} may not obtain a court judgment against {{trustorName}} for that shortfall on the note secured by the deed of trust. The statute carves out one express limit on that protection: "[t]he fact that no deficiency shall be owed or collected under the circumstances set forth in subdivision (a) does not affect the liability that a guarantor, pledgor, or other surety might otherwise have with respect to the deficiency, or that might otherwise be satisfied in whole or in part from other collateral pledged to secure the obligation that is the subject of the deficiency."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nonjudicial foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property or loan; foreclosure procedures vary significantly by state, and many states require judicial foreclosure instead. This clause cites two different subsections of the same statutory section — Code of Civil Procedure § 580d(a) (the core anti-deficiency rule for nonjudicial foreclosure sales) and § 580d(b) (its express carve-out for guarantors, pledgors, other sureties, and other pledged collateral) — quoted together because the second subsection is an express, statutorily stated limit on the first. This anti-deficiency rule under § 580d applies specifically to nonjudicial, power-of-sale foreclosure sales; California law treats deficiency liability differently after a judicial foreclosure sale, a topic this document does not address.
