clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Privacy Notice
clauses.body: This Website/App Privacy Policy and Notice at Collection ("Notice") describes how {{businessName}} collects, uses, and discloses personal information about consumers who visit or use {{businessName}}'s website or application, and describes the rights California consumers have with respect to that personal information under the California Consumer Privacy Act, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (California Civil Code § 1798.100 et seq.). Consumers with questions about this Notice, or who wish to exercise a right described in it, may contact {{businessName}} as follows: {{contactMethod}}. This Notice is directed to consumers and does not itself set out the contract terms between {{businessName}} and any vendor or service provider that processes personal information on {{businessName}}'s behalf; those terms are addressed in a separate document.

clauses.title: The Notice-at-Collection Requirement
clauses.body: California law requires that a business that controls the collection of a consumer's personal information inform consumers, at or before the point of collection, of the categories of personal information to be collected and the purposes for which those categories of personal information are collected or used, and whether that information is sold or shared. If the business collects sensitive personal information, the same at-or-before-collection notice must separately identify the categories of sensitive personal information to be collected and the purposes for which they are collected or used, and whether that information is sold or shared. The same notice must also state the length of time the business intends to retain each category of personal information, or, if that is not possible, the criteria used to determine that retention period. A business may not collect additional categories of personal information, or use personal information for additional purposes, that are incompatible with the disclosed purpose, without providing a further notice consistent with this requirement. Separately, the statute allows a business that, acting as a third party, controls the collection of personal information about a consumer to satisfy this notice obligation by providing the required information prominently and conspicuously on the homepage of its internet website, and imposes an at-the-location notice duty on a third party that collects personal information on its own premises.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.100 — subdivision (a) (the point-of-collection notice content requirement, including its three numbered paragraphs) and subdivision (b) (the alternative homepage-posting method available to a business that, acting as a third party, controls the collection, and the related premises-notice duty) — because both come from the same statutory section describing a business's general notice duties and are necessary to state the notice-at-collection requirement completely. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA consumer-facing disclosure requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states now have their own, differently-structured privacy statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. This clause does not determine whether a specific business meets the CCPA's revenue or volume thresholds to qualify as a "business" subject to this title in the first place, whether a specific business is acting as a first party or a third party with respect to a specific collection, or whether the homepage-posting alternative in subdivision (b) is available for a specific collection — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, point-of-collection notice content requirement
citations.quote: (a) A business that controls the collection of a consumer’s personal information shall, at or before the point of collection, inform consumers of the following: (1) The categories of personal information to be collected and the purposes for which the categories of personal information are collected or used and whether that information is sold or shared. A business shall not collect additional categories of personal information or use personal information collected for additional purposes that are incompatible with the disclosed purpose for which the personal information was collected without providing the consumer with notice consistent with this section. (2) If the business collects sensitive personal information, the categories of sensitive personal information to be collected and the purposes for which the categories of sensitive personal information are collected or used, and whether that information is sold or shared. A business shall not collect additional categories of sensitive personal information or use sensitive personal information collected for additional purposes that are incompatible with the disclosed purpose for which the sensitive personal information was collected without providing the consumer with notice consistent with this section. (3) The length of time the business intends to retain each category of personal information, including sensitive personal information, or if that is not possible, the criteria used to determine that period provided that a business shall not retain a consumer’s personal information or sensitive personal information for each disclosed purpose for which the personal information was collected for longer than is reasonably necessary for that disclosed purpose.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.100(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, homepage-posting alternative for a third party controlling collection
citations.quote: (b) A business that, acting as a third party, controls the collection of personal information about a consumer may satisfy its obligation under subdivision (a) by providing the required information prominently and conspicuously on the homepage of its internet website. In addition, if a business acting as a third party controls the collection of personal information about a consumer on its premises, including in a vehicle, then the business shall, at or before the point of collection, inform consumers as to the categories of personal information to be collected and the purposes for which the categories of personal information are used, and whether that personal information is sold, in a clear and conspicuous manner at the location.

clauses.title: Categories of Personal Information Collected and Purposes of Use
clauses.body: At or before the point {{businessName}} collects personal information from a consumer through its website or application, {{businessName}} discloses the following categories of personal information collected: {{categoriesCollected}}. {{businessName}} collects and uses those categories of personal information for the following purposes: {{purposesOfUse}}. {{businessName}} does not collect additional categories of personal information, or use personal information collected for additional purposes, that are incompatible with the purposes disclosed above without providing consumers a further notice. Whether any category of personal information identified above is sold or shared with third parties, and the length of time {{businessName}} intends to retain each category, are addressed elsewhere in this Notice.

clauses.title: Consumer Rights to Delete, Correct, and Know What Personal Information Is Collected, Sold, or Shared
clauses.body: California law gives consumers four related rights concerning personal information a business has collected about them. First, a consumer has the right to request that a business delete personal information the business has collected from the consumer. Second, a consumer has the right to request that a business that maintains inaccurate personal information about the consumer correct that inaccurate personal information, taking into account the nature of the personal information and the purposes of processing it. Third, a consumer has the right to request that a business that collects personal information about the consumer disclose the categories of personal information it has collected about that consumer, the categories of sources from which that information is collected, the business or commercial purpose for collecting, selling, or sharing it, the categories of third parties to whom the business discloses it, and the specific pieces of personal information the business has collected about that consumer. Fourth, a consumer has the right to request that a business that sells or shares the consumer's personal information, or discloses it for a business purpose, disclose the categories of personal information sold, shared, or disclosed for a business purpose, and the categories of third parties or persons to whom it was sold, shared, or disclosed.
clauses.gap: This clause cites four separate statutory sections — Civil Code §§ 1798.105(a), 1798.106(a), 1798.110(a), and 1798.115(a) — each of which independently creates one of the four rights described in this clause; because each citation is to a different section rather than to different subsections of one section, no additional cross-subsection disclosure is required here beyond noting that all four sections are part of the same California Consumer Privacy Act title. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA consumer-facing disclosure requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states now have their own, differently-structured privacy statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. This clause does not restate the statutory exceptions to the deletion right (Civil Code § 1798.105(d)), which permit a business to decline a deletion request for reasons such as completing a transaction, security, debugging, free speech, legal compliance, and certain research uses — those exceptions exist in the statute's text but were not independently quoted or verified for this clause, and this document does not represent that they do or do not apply to any specific deletion request. No case law was checked on any of these four provisions; each statute's own text is unambiguous, so the statutes stand as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.105(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, consumer's right to delete personal information
citations.quote: (a) A consumer shall have the right to request that a business delete any personal information about the consumer which the business has collected from the consumer.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.106(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, consumer's right to correct inaccurate personal information
citations.quote: (a) A consumer shall have the right to request a business that maintains inaccurate personal information about the consumer to correct that inaccurate personal information, taking into account the nature of the personal information and the purposes of the processing of the personal information.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.110(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, consumer's right to know what personal information is collected and to access it
citations.quote: (a) A consumer shall have the right to request that a business that collects personal information about the consumer disclose to the consumer the following: (1) The categories of personal information it has collected about that consumer. (2) The categories of sources from which the personal information is collected. (3) The business or commercial purpose for collecting, selling, or sharing personal information. (4) The categories of third parties to whom the business discloses personal information. (5) The specific pieces of personal information it has collected about that consumer.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.115(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, consumer's right to know what personal information is sold or shared and to whom
citations.quote: (a) A consumer shall have the right to request that a business that sells or shares the consumer’s personal information, or that discloses it for a business purpose, disclose to that consumer: (1) The categories of personal information that the business collected about the consumer. (2) The categories of personal information that the business sold or shared about the consumer and the categories of third parties to whom the personal information was sold or shared, by category or categories of personal information for each category of third parties to whom the personal information was sold or shared. (3) The categories of personal information that the business disclosed about the consumer for a business purpose and the categories of persons to whom it was disclosed for a business purpose.

clauses.title: Statement of Consumer Rights and How to Exercise Them
clauses.body: Consumers whose personal information {{businessName}} collects have the right to: request deletion of personal information {{businessName}} has collected from the consumer; request correction of inaccurate personal information {{businessName}} maintains about the consumer; request disclosure of the categories and specific pieces of personal information {{businessName}} has collected about the consumer; request disclosure of the categories of personal information {{businessName}} has sold, shared, or disclosed for a business purpose, and the categories of third parties or persons to whom it was sold, shared, or disclosed; direct {{businessName}} not to sell or share the consumer's personal information; and direct {{businessName}} to limit its use of the consumer's sensitive personal information, to the extent {{businessName}} uses sensitive personal information for purposes beyond those necessary to provide the goods or services requested. A consumer, or a person authorized by the consumer to act on the consumer's behalf, may submit a request to exercise any of these rights as follows: {{contactMethod}}.

clauses.title: Consumer Rights to Opt Out of Sale or Sharing and to Limit Use of Sensitive Personal Information
clauses.body: California law gives a consumer the right, at any time, to direct a business that sells or shares the consumer's personal information to third parties not to sell or share it — a right the statute calls the right to opt out of sale or sharing. Separately, California law gives a consumer the right, at any time, to direct a business that collects sensitive personal information about the consumer to limit its use of that sensitive personal information to the use necessary to perform the goods or services reasonably expected by an average consumer requesting them, along with certain other statutorily authorized uses; a business that uses or discloses a consumer's sensitive personal information for purposes beyond those specified must provide notice of that use and of the consumer's right to limit it.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two separate statutory sections — Civil Code §§ 1798.120(a)(1) and 1798.121(a) — each of which independently creates one of the two rights described in this clause; because each citation is to a different section rather than to different subsections of one section, no additional cross-subsection disclosure is required here beyond noting that both sections are part of the same California Consumer Privacy Act title. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA consumer-facing disclosure requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states now have their own, differently-structured privacy statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. This clause does not restate the separate age-based restriction on selling or sharing a minor consumer's personal information (Civil Code § 1798.120(c)), which was not independently quoted or verified for this clause and is outside its scope. No case law was checked on either provision; each statute's own text is unambiguous, so the statutes stand as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.120(a)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, consumer's right to opt out of sale or sharing
citations.quote: (a) (1) A consumer shall have the right, at any time, to direct a business that sells or shares personal information about the consumer to third parties not to sell or share the consumer’s personal information. This right may be referred to as the right to opt out of sale or sharing.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.121(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, consumer's right to limit use of sensitive personal information
citations.quote: (a) A consumer shall have the right, at any time, to direct a business that collects sensitive personal information about the consumer to limit its use of the consumer’s sensitive personal information to that use which is necessary to perform the services or provide the goods reasonably expected by an average consumer who requests those goods or services, to perform the services set forth in paragraphs (2), (4), (5), and (8) of subdivision (e) of Section 1798.140, and as authorized by regulations adopted pursuant to subparagraph (C) of paragraph (18) of subdivision (a) of Section 1798.185. A business that uses or discloses a consumer’s sensitive personal information for purposes other than those specified in this subdivision shall provide notice to consumers, pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 1798.135, that this information may be used, or disclosed to a service provider or contractor, for additional, specified purposes and that consumers have the right to limit the use or disclosure of their sensitive personal information.

clauses.title: The "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information" Link, and the Opt-Out Preference Signal Alternative
clauses.body: A business that sells or shares consumers' personal information, or that uses or discloses sensitive personal information for purposes beyond those the statute authorizes without a consumer's separate direction, must provide a clear and conspicuous link on the business's internet homepages, titled "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information," to a web page that lets a consumer opt out of the sale or sharing of the consumer's personal information; a second, separately titled link, "Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information"; or, at the business's discretion, a single combined link in place of the first two. As an alternative to posting these links, the statute provides that a business is not required to comply with the link-posting requirement if the business instead allows consumers to opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal information, and to limit the use of their sensitive personal information, through an "opt-out preference signal" — a signal sent, with the consumer's consent, by a platform, technology, or mechanism meeting technical specifications set out in regulations, indicating the consumer's intent to opt out or to limit use.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.135 — subdivision (a), paragraphs (1) through (3) (the homepage link requirements and the single-combined-link option), and subdivision (b), paragraph (1) (the opt-out-preference-signal alternative to posting links) — because both come from the same statutory section describing a business's methods of honoring the opt-out and limit-use rights and are necessary to state the requirement and its alternative together. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA consumer-facing disclosure requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states now have their own, differently-structured privacy statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. Correction to a working assumption in the research brief that prompted this clause: the statute's own text does not name any specific opt-out signal, such as the Global Privacy Control, by name — it refers generically to an "opt-out preference signal" sent by a platform, technology, or mechanism meeting technical specifications the California Privacy Protection Agency adopts by regulation. The Global Privacy Control is a commonly cited example of such a signal in secondary sources and regulatory guidance, but that identification was not independently verified against the Agency's regulations for this clause, and this clause does not represent that the Global Privacy Control is the only, or a statutorily named, qualifying signal. This clause also does not address the separate provision allowing a business with a dedicated California-consumer homepage to post the required links there instead of on its general public homepage (Civil Code § 1798.135(d)), which was not independently quoted or verified for this clause. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.135(a)(1)-(3) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information" homepage link requirements
citations.quote: (1) Provide a clear and conspicuous link on the business’ internet homepages, titled “Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information,” to an internet web page that enables a consumer, or a person authorized by the consumer, to opt out of the sale or sharing of the consumer’s personal information. (2) Provide a clear and conspicuous link on the business’ internet homepages, titled “Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information,” that enables a consumer, or a person authorized by the consumer, to limit the use or disclosure of the consumer’s sensitive personal information to those uses authorized by subdivision (a) of Section 1798.121. (3) At the business’ discretion, utilize a single, clearly labeled link on the business’ internet homepages, in lieu of complying with paragraphs (1) and (2), if that link easily allows a consumer to opt out of the sale or sharing of the consumer’s personal information and to limit the use or disclosure of the consumer’s sensitive personal information.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.135(b)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, opt-out preference signal as an alternative to posting links
citations.quote: (b) (1) A business shall not be required to comply with subdivision (a) if the business allows consumers to opt out of the sale or sharing of their personal information and to limit the use of their sensitive personal information through an opt-out preference signal sent with the consumer’s consent by a platform, technology, or mechanism, based on technical specifications set forth in regulations adopted pursuant to paragraph (19) of subdivision (a) of Section 1798.185, to the business indicating the consumer’s intent to opt out of the business’ sale or sharing of the consumer’s personal information or to limit the use or disclosure of the consumer’s sensitive personal information, or both.

clauses.title: Required Content of a Business's Online Privacy Policy
clauses.body: California law requires a business to disclose specific information in its online privacy policy or policies, or, if it has none, on its internet website, and to update that information at least once every 12 months. The required content includes: a description of the consumer's rights to know, delete, correct, access, and opt out described elsewhere in this Notice, together with two or more designated methods for submitting requests to exercise them (subject to a narrower, email-only alternative for a business that operates exclusively online and has a direct relationship with the consumer); a list of the categories of personal information the business has collected about consumers in the preceding 12 months, the categories of sources of that information, the business or commercial purpose for collecting, selling, or sharing it, and the categories of third parties to whom the business discloses it; a separate list of the categories of personal information the business has sold or shared about consumers in the preceding 12 months (or, if none, a statement to that effect); and a separate list of the categories of personal information the business has disclosed about consumers for a business purpose in the preceding 12 months (or, if none, a statement to that effect).
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Civil Code § 1798.130(a)(5) in full, including its subparagraphs (A) through (C), as a single integrated statutory list describing everything a business's privacy policy must contain; because the entire quotation comes from one paragraph, no cross-subsection disclosure beyond that is required. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA consumer-facing disclosure requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states now have their own, differently-structured privacy statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. Honest gap: this clause's summary references the "two or more designated methods" requirement and its narrower online-only exception because paragraph (5)(A)'s own text cross-references "subparagraph (A) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (a)" for that exception, but this clause does not separately quote or independently verify the text of § 1798.130(a)(1)(A) itself; a reader relying on the precise contours of that exception should check § 1798.130(a)(1)(A) directly rather than this clause's paraphrase. This document's own drafting clauses for consumer contact information use a single templated contact-method field and do not themselves guarantee that two or more designated methods (or the narrower online-only exception) are satisfied; that is a fact-specific question about how a specific business actually implements that field which this document does not resolve. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.130(a)(5) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, required content of a business's online privacy policy
citations.quote: (5) Disclose the following information in its online privacy policy or policies if the business has an online privacy policy or policies and in any California-specific description of consumers’ privacy rights, or if the business does not maintain those policies, on its internet website, and update that information at least once every 12 months: (A) A description of a consumer’s rights pursuant to Sections 1798.100, 1798.105, 1798.106, 1798.110, 1798.115, and 1798.125 and two or more designated methods for submitting requests, except as provided in subparagraph (A) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (a). (B) For purposes of subdivision (c) of Section 1798.110: (i) A list of the categories of personal information it has collected about consumers in the preceding 12 months by reference to the enumerated category or categories in subdivision (c) that most closely describe the personal information collected. (ii) The categories of sources from which consumers’ personal information is collected. (iii) The business or commercial purpose for collecting, selling, or sharing consumers’ personal information. (iv) The categories of third parties to whom the business discloses consumers’ personal information. (C) For purposes of paragraphs (1) and (2) of subdivision (c) of Section 1798.115, two separate lists: (i) A list of the categories of personal information it has sold or shared about consumers in the preceding 12 months by reference to the enumerated category or categories in subdivision (c) that most closely describe the personal information sold or shared, or if the business has not sold or shared consumers’ personal information in the preceding 12 months, the business shall prominently disclose that fact in its privacy policy. (ii) A list of the categories of personal information it has disclosed about consumers for a business purpose in the preceding 12 months by reference to the enumerated category in subdivision (c) that most closely describes the personal information disclosed, or if the business has not disclosed consumers’ personal information for a business purpose in the preceding 12 months, the business shall disclose that fact.

clauses.title: Non-Discrimination for Exercising CCPA Rights, and the Financial Incentive Exception
clauses.body: California law prohibits a business from discriminating against a consumer because the consumer exercised any right the CCPA/CPRA gives consumers, including by denying goods or services to the consumer, charging the consumer different prices or rates for goods or services (including through discounts, other benefits, or penalties), providing a different level or quality of goods or services to the consumer, or suggesting that the consumer will receive any of those different treatments. Separately, and as a limited exception to that general prohibition, the statute permits a business to offer financial incentives — including payments to consumers as compensation — for the collection, sale, sharing, or retention of personal information, and permits a business to offer a different price, rate, level, or quality of goods or services if that difference is reasonably related to the value the consumer's data provides to the business. A business offering such a financial incentive program must notify consumers of the incentive, may enter a consumer into the program only with the consumer's prior opt-in consent that clearly describes the program's material terms, and must allow the consumer to revoke that consent at any time; if a consumer refuses to provide opt-in consent, the business must wait at least 12 months before asking the consumer to provide it again.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.125 — subdivision (a), paragraph (1) (the general non-discrimination prohibition and its listed examples) and subdivision (b), paragraphs (1) through (3) (the financial incentive program exception and its conditions) — because both come from the same statutory section and the exception cannot be stated accurately without the general prohibition it qualifies. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA consumer-facing disclosure requirements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business; other states now have their own, differently-structured privacy statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. The quoted text of § 1798.125(a)(1) includes a subparagraph (E) prohibiting retaliation against an employee, applicant for employment, or independent contractor for exercising rights under the title; that subparagraph is included because it is part of the single integrated list the statute enacts, but it addresses an employment-context right distinct from the consumer-facing disclosures this document otherwise covers, and this document does not separately address employee or applicant privacy rights under Civil Code § 1798.145(m). This clause also does not restate § 1798.125(a)(2)'s clarification that a business may charge a different price or provide a different quality of service where the difference is reasonably related to the value of the consumer's data, or § 1798.125(a)(3)'s statement that loyalty, rewards, premium-feature, discount, or club-card programs are not themselves prohibited; both ideas are folded into this clause's summary of subdivision (b) rather than independently quoted. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.125(a)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, prohibition on discriminating against a consumer for exercising CCPA rights
citations.quote: (a) (1) A business shall not discriminate against a consumer because the consumer exercised any of the consumer’s rights under this title, including, but not limited to, by: (A) Denying goods or services to the consumer. (B) Charging different prices or rates for goods or services, including through the use of discounts or other benefits or imposing penalties. (C) Providing a different level or quality of goods or services to the consumer. (D) Suggesting that the consumer will receive a different price or rate for goods or services or a different level or quality of goods or services. (E) Retaliating against an employee, applicant for employment, or independent contractor, as defined in subparagraph (A) of paragraph (2) of subdivision (m) of Section 1798.145, for exercising their rights under this title.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1798.125(b)(1)-(3) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, financial incentive program exception
citations.quote: (b) (1) A business may offer financial incentives, including payments to consumers as compensation, for the collection of personal information, the sale or sharing of personal information, or the retention of personal information. A business may also offer a different price, rate, level, or quality of goods or services to the consumer if that price or difference is reasonably related to the value provided to the business by the consumer’s data. (2) A business that offers any financial incentives pursuant to this subdivision, shall notify consumers of the financial incentives pursuant to Section 1798.130. (3) A business may enter a consumer into a financial incentive program only if the consumer gives the business prior opt-in consent pursuant to Section 1798.130 that clearly describes the material terms of the financial incentive program, and which may be revoked by the consumer at any time. If a consumer refuses to provide opt-in consent, then the business shall wait for at least 12 months before next requesting that the consumer provide opt-in consent, or as prescribed by regulations adopted pursuant to Section 1798.185.

clauses.title: Declaration of Purpose — Petition for Change of Name Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Petition for Change of Name — Information Sheet concerns a proposed change from {{currentName}}'s present legal name to the proposed name {{proposedName}}. It is prepared for use alongside an actual petition for change of name that would be filed by {{petitionerName}} in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. This information sheet describes California's statutory change-of-name petition process — who may file, what the petition must state, the order to show cause and publication requirements, and the standard a court applies in deciding whether to grant or deny the petition — as background for that filing. It is not itself a court filing, and completing it does not change {{currentName}}'s legal name in any respect. Only a court order (a decree granting the petition) can actually change a person's legal name through this process.

clauses.title: Where and How a Change-of-Name Petition Is Filed
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure § 1275 provides that applications for change of names must be determined by the Superior Courts. Under § 1276(a)(1), an application for change of name is made to the superior court of the county where the person whose name is proposed to be changed resides, and is filed either by petition signed by that person or, if the person is under 18 years of age, by one of the person's parents, by any guardian of the person, or, if both parents are deceased and there is no guardian, by a near relative or friend of the person. Under § 1276(a)(2), the petition must specify the place of birth and residence of the person, the person's present name, the name proposed, and the reason for the change of name. A narrower, separately added venue rule in § 1276(g)(1) allows a person who does not reside in California to file in the county tied to a California birth certificate or California marriage license the person is seeking to change; that limited nonresident route is not the general filing rule this clause otherwise describes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's name-change petition process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific name change. This document is informational: it does not itself change any person's legal name; only a court order (decree) granting the petition can do that. Three of these citations — § 1276(a)(1), § 1276(a)(2), and § 1276(g)(1) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1276); the fourth, § 1275, is a separate, one-sentence section establishing only that superior courts (rather than some other tribunal) decide these applications. This clause corrects an assumption in the original research brief, which asked to verify § 1277 as 'the actual statutory basis for filing a petition for change of name in superior court': on the verified statutory text, § 1276(a)(1) — not § 1277 — is the section that actually authorizes filing and states the superior-court, county-of-residence venue rule; § 1277 instead governs the order to show cause, hearing, and publication process that follows a filing, covered in this document's companion clauses. Section 1276(a)(1)(B)'s cross-reference to Family Code § 7638 — a name-change route available within a Uniform Parentage Act proceeding — is not detailed further here; that separate route is addressed by this corpus's Paternity Action (Petition to Establish Parental Relationship) Information Sheet document.

clauses.title: A Minor's Name Change: Petition Contents and Notice to the Other Parent
clauses.body: When the person whose name is proposed to be changed is under 18 years of age, several minor-specific requirements apply. Under § 1276(c), if a petition for a minor's name change is signed by only one parent, the petition must specify the other parent's address, if known and if that parent is living. Separately, under § 1277(a)(4), if a petition has been filed for a minor by one parent and the other parent, if living, does not join in consenting to it, the petitioner must cause notice of the hearing — or a copy of the order to show cause — to be served on the other parent at least 30 days before the hearing, in the manner used for service of a summons (or, where that cannot reasonably be accomplished, in a manner the court determines is reasonably calculated to give actual notice, which may include publication). Where a guardian, rather than a parent, files the petition on behalf of a minor ward, § 1277(f) separately requires the guardian to serve notice of the hearing on any living parent of the minor by personal service at least 30 days before the hearing, or, if a parent is deceased or cannot be located, to serve notice instead on the child's grandparents, if living.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's name-change petition process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific name change. This document is informational: it does not itself change any person's legal name; only a court order (decree) granting the petition can do that. Two of these citations — § 1277(a)(4) and § 1277(f) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1277); § 1276(c) is a separate, independently cited section. This clause does not identify, and the statute does not itself provide, any minor-specific standard for resolving a notified parent's actual objection to a proposed name change of the parties' minor child: an objection instead triggers the same general objection-and-hearing process, and the same 'good cause' standard, described in this document's companion clause on the hearing standard, which applies without regard to whether the objecting party is a parent. Separately, § 1276(e) — not independently verified in full detail here — directs that petitions for a minor's name change filed by a guardian appointed by the juvenile or probate court, or by certain court-appointed attorneys for a minor in the juvenile-dependency or delinquency system, be made in the court already exercising jurisdiction over the minor, rather than under the general filing rule described in this document's companion clause; that narrower jurisdictional carve-out is not detailed further here.

clauses.title: The Order to Show Cause and the Publication Requirement
clauses.body: Once a petition for change of name is filed, § 1277(a)(1) requires the court to make an order reciting the filing of the petition and directing all interested persons to appear at a hearing set not less than 6 weeks nor more than 12 weeks from the date of the order (unless the court sets a different time), to show cause why the petition should not be granted; the order also directs that any written objection, stating the reasons for it, be filed with the court at least two court days before the hearing, and states that if no written objection is timely filed, the court may grant the petition without a hearing. Under § 1277(a)(2)(A), a copy of that order to show cause must be published, under Government Code § 6064, in a newspaper of general circulation designated in the order and published in the county (or, if none exists, posted by the clerk of the court in three of the most public places in the county). Under § 1277(a)(3), four weekly publications are sufficient to satisfy this requirement — specifically, publication once a week for four successive weeks is sufficient if the order is published in a daily newspaper.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's name-change petition process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific name change. This document is informational: it does not itself change any person's legal name; only a court order (decree) granting the petition can do that. All three citations in this clause — § 1277(a)(1), § 1277(a)(2)(A), and § 1277(a)(3) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1277); no additional independent source was located or is cited for these requirements. This confirms, rather than merely assumes, the once-a-week-for-four-successive-weeks publication frequency referenced in the original research brief. This clause does not detail § 1277(a)(2)(B), a separate 2023-added publication-venue rule for nonresident petitioners filing under § 1276(g), or the posting-in-lieu-of-publication alternative beyond the single sentence quoted above.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The order shall direct all persons interested in the matter to appear before the court at a time and place specified, which shall be not less than 6 weeks nor more than 12 weeks from the time of making the order, unless the court orders a different time, to show cause why the application for change of name should not be granted. The order shall direct all persons interested in the matter to make known any objection that they may have to the granting of the petition for change of name by filing a written objection, which includes the reasons for the objection, with the court at least two court days before the matter is scheduled to be heard and by appearing in court at the hearing to show cause why the petition for change of name should not be granted. The order shall state that, if no written objection is timely filed, the court may grant the petition without a hearing.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A copy of the order to show cause shall be published pursuant to Section 6064 of the Government Code in a newspaper of general circulation to be designated in the order published in the county.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Four weekly publications shall be sufficient publication of the order to show cause. If the order is published in a daily newspaper, publication once a week for four successive weeks shall be sufficient.

clauses.title: The Confidential and Sealed-Record Exception to Publication
clauses.body: California's name-change statute includes a distinct mechanism allowing certain petitioners to avoid the general publication requirement and to keep the current and proposed names confidential. Under § 1277(b)(1), if a petition alleges a reason described in paragraph (2) and the petitioner has established that the petitioner is an active participant in the state's address confidentiality program and that the name the petitioner is seeking to acquire is on file with the Secretary of State, the petition is exempt from the § 1277(a) publication requirement, and the petition and the court's order indicate only that the proposed name is confidential and on file with the Secretary of State, rather than reciting it. Under § 1277(b)(2), that procedure applies to petitions alleging any of four specific reasons: to avoid domestic violence, to avoid stalking, to avoid sexual assault, or to avoid human trafficking, each as defined by a cross-referenced statute. Under § 1277(b)(3), the petitioner's current legal name is likewise kept confidential by the court in that circumstance, and is not published or posted in the court's public calendars, indexes, or register of actions. Separately, under § 1277(b)(5), any petitioner may ask the court to file the petition and related papers under seal, which the court may grant only on findings that include that an overriding interest exists that overcomes the public's right of access to the record and that the interest supports sealing it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's name-change petition process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific name change. This document is informational: it does not itself change any person's legal name; only a court order (decree) granting the petition can do that. All four citations in this clause — § 1277(b)(1), § 1277(b)(2), § 1277(b)(3), and § 1277(b)(5) — are subsections of the same statutory subdivision (§ 1277(b)); no additional independent source was located or is cited for this confidential/sealed-record mechanism. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief, which asked to verify a confidential/sealed name-change mechanism 'under Code Civ. Proc. § 1276': on the verified statutory text, that mechanism is codified in § 1277(b) — part of the order-to-show-cause and publication section — not in § 1276, which instead governs who may file a petition and what it must contain (covered in this document's companion clause). This clause does not independently detail the separate Address Confidentiality Program statute itself (Government Code § 6205 et seq.), the definitions of domestic violence, stalking, sexual assault, or human trafficking that § 1277(b)(2) cross-references, or § 1277(b)(4)'s narrower exception allowing the court to disclose the petitioner's name and new name together at the petitioner's own request.

citations.quote: If the petition for a change of name alleges a reason or circumstance described in paragraph (2), and the petitioner has established that the petitioner is an active participant in the address confidentiality program created pursuant to Chapter 3.1 (commencing with Section 6205) of Division 7 of Title 1 of the Government Code, and that the name the petitioner is seeking to acquire is on file with the Secretary of State, the action for a change of name is exempt from the requirement for publication of the order to show cause under subdivision (a), and the petition and the order of the court shall, in lieu of reciting the proposed name, indicate that the proposed name is confidential and is on file with the Secretary of State pursuant to the provisions of the address confidentiality program.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1277(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)

(B) To avoid stalking, as defined in Section 646.9 of the Penal Code. (C) To avoid sexual assault, as defined in Section 1036.2 of the Evidence Code. (D) To avoid human trafficking, as defined in Section 236.1 of the Penal Code.

citations.quote: A petitioner may request that the court file the petition and any other papers associated with the proceeding under seal. The court may consider the request at the same time as the petition for name change, and may grant the request in any case in which the court finds that all of the following factors apply: (A) There exists an overriding interest that overcomes the right of public access to the record.

clauses.title: The Hearing Standard and the Court's Limited Grounds to Deny the Petition
clauses.body: If a written objection is timely filed, § 1278(a)(1) provides that the petition is heard only if the objection can show the court "good cause against the change of name"; at that hearing, the court may examine on oath any petitioner, objector, or other person concerning the petition, and may make an order granting the change of name or dismissing the petition, as the court deems right and proper. Under § 1278(a)(2), if no objection is filed at least two court days before the scheduled hearing, the court may grant the petition without a hearing. Where the confidentiality provisions of § 1277(b) apply, § 1278(b) separately requires that the court not disclose the proposed name unless the court finds, by clear and convincing evidence, that the petition's allegations of domestic violence, stalking, or sexual assault are false. Where a guardian, rather than a parent, files the petition on behalf of a minor ward, § 1278(d) requires the court first to find that the ward is likely to remain in the guardian's care until reaching the age of majority and is not likely to be returned to a parent's custody, and allows the court to grant the petition, upon making those findings, only if it also finds the proposed name change is in the child's best interest. Separately, under § 1279.5(e), a court must deny a name-change petition filed by a person required to register as a sex offender under Penal Code § 290, unless the court determines that granting it is in the best interest of justice and will not adversely affect public safety.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's name-change petition process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific name change. This document is informational: it does not itself change any person's legal name; only a court order (decree) granting the petition can do that. Four of these citations — § 1278(a)(1), § 1278(a)(2), § 1278(b), and § 1278(d) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1278); § 1279.5(e) is a separate, independently cited section. This clause corrects an assumption in the original research brief, which asked to confirm that § 1278 states a 'proper and reasonable causes' standard and lists specific denial grounds such as 'an intent to defraud or evade creditors': on the verified statutory text of § 1278 (and of § 1279.5), no such phrase or enumerated list appears. The statute instead frames the matter as an objector's burden to show 'good cause against the change of name' before a hearing is even held, coupled with the court's general discretion at that hearing, and it separately imposes one specific, mandatory denial rule — the sex-offender-registrant bar in § 1279.5(e) — and one specific, mandatory grant condition for guardian-filed minor petitions in § 1278(d). A 'proper and reasonable cause' formulation, and examples like an intent to defraud creditors, are commonly associated with California name-change practice in secondary legal sources and in case law construing this statute's predecessors, but this research did not independently verify a specific, quotable judicial opinion stating that standard — an attempted case-law search was blocked by a research-tool rate limit — so that formulation is not included in this clause's body and should not be assumed to appear in the statute's text itself.

At the hearing, the court may examine on oath any of the petitioners, remonstrants, or other persons touching the petition or application, and may make an order changing the name, or dismissing the petition or application, as the court may deem right and proper.

Upon making those findings, the court shall consider the petition and may grant the petition only if it finds that the proposed name change is in the best interest of the child.

clauses.title: A Name Change Tied to Marriage or Domestic Partnership Uses a Separate, Non-Court Process
clauses.body: A separate, simplified name-change mechanic exists for a name adopted in connection with marriage, and it does not involve filing a change-of-name petition under the court process described elsewhere in this document. Family Code § 306.5(a) provides that parties to a marriage are not required to have the same name, that neither party is required to change their name, and that a person's name does not change upon marriage unless that person elects to change it under subdivision (b). Under § 306.5(b)(1), a party may elect to change the middle or last name, or both, by which that party wishes to be known after the marriage, by entering the new name in the spaces provided on the marriage license application itself, without intent to defraud — a mechanism built into the marriage-license process rather than a separate court filing or hearing. A comparable no-court-petition mechanic applies to a name selected upon registration of a domestic partnership: Family Code § 298.5(e) provides that the Certificate of Registered Domestic Partnership issued by the Secretary of State includes both the name used by each party before registration and the new name, if any, selected by each party upon registration of the domestic partnership.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's name-change petition process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific name change. This document is informational: it does not itself change any person's legal name; only a court order (decree) granting the petition, or, for a marriage- or partnership-related name, the marriage license or partnership registration process described in this clause, actually changes it. Two of these citations — § 306.5(a) and § 306.5(b)(1) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 306.5); § 298.5(e) is a separate, independently cited section. This document addresses only the separate court-petition process under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 1275–1279.6 described in this document's other clauses; it does not further detail the marriage-license or domestic-partnership-registration name-change mechanic beyond confirming, with the citations above, that a distinct and simpler process exists for those circumstances and generally does not require a court petition.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 306.5(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: One party or both parties to a marriage may elect to change the middle or last names, or both, by which that party wishes to be known after solemnization of the marriage by entering the new name in the spaces provided on the marriage license application without intent to defraud.

The person's stated place of birth is {{placeOfBirth}}, and the stated reason for the proposed change of name is: {{reasonForChange}}. clauses.title: HOA Assessment Lien and Foreclosure — Introduction and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, the statutory lien and foreclosure process available to a homeowners association under California's Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act, Civil Code §§ 5650–5740, for unpaid assessments owed by an owner of a separate interest. It concerns the separate interest commonly known as {{propertyAddress}}, owned of record by {{ownerName}}, and assessments and related charges owed to {{hoaName}}. This process is distinct from a seller's document-disclosure obligations to a buyer under the Davis-Stirling Act's disclosure article (Civil Code § 4525 et seq.), and distinct from a mortgage lender's nonjudicial foreclosure of a deed of trust under Civil Code §§ 2924 et seq. Here, the creditor is the association itself, collecting a debt for unpaid regular or special assessments — not a mortgage lender collecting a loan secured by a deed of trust. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien; it does not initiate, accelerate, halt, postpone, or complete any collection or foreclosure action; and it does not determine whether any specific assessment, fine, fee, or other charge is validly owed by {{ownerName}}, or whether any actual notice, recording, board vote, or sale relating to this property has complied — or failed to comply — with the statutory requirements it describes.

clauses.title: The Assessment Debt and When It Becomes Delinquent
clauses.body: Under California Civil Code § 5650(a), "[a] regular or special assessment and any late charges, reasonable fees and costs of collection, reasonable attorney’s fees, if any, and interest, if any, as determined in accordance with subdivision (b), shall be a debt of the owner of the separate interest at the time the assessment or other sums are levied." Section 5650(b) fixes when that debt becomes delinquent and what may then be added to it: regular and special assessments are "delinquent 15 days after they become due, unless the declaration provides a longer time period," and once delinquent the association may recover reasonable costs of collection (including reasonable attorney's fees), "a late charge not exceeding 10 percent of the delinquent assessment or ten dollars ($10), whichever is greater" (unless the declaration sets a smaller amount), and interest "at an annual interest rate not to exceed 12 percent, commencing 30 days after the assessment becomes due" (unless the declaration sets a lower rate). If a dollar figure has been stated as delinquent on {{ownerName}}'s account with {{hoaName}}, it is stated as: {{amountDelinquent}}, as of {{delinquencyDate}}.
clauses.gap: Civil Code § 5650 creates the underlying personal debt owed by the owner and fixes the 15-day delinquency trigger and the statutory caps on late charges (10% or $10, whichever is greater) and interest (12% per annum); it does not itself create a recorded lien on the owner's separate interest — that additional step is governed by a separate statute, Civil Code § 5675, addressed in another clause of this document. The two citations in this clause are to subsections (a) and (b) of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 5650; they are not independent sections corroborating each other. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.

citations.quote: A regular or special assessment and any late charges, reasonable fees and costs of collection, reasonable attorney’s fees, if any, and interest, if any, as determined in accordance with subdivision (b), shall be a debt of the owner of the separate interest at the time the assessment or other sums are levied.

citations.quote: Regular and special assessments levied pursuant to the governing documents are delinquent 15 days after they become due, unless the declaration provides a longer time period, in which case the longer time period shall apply.

clauses.title: Pre-Lien Notice — 30 Days' Written Notice Before Recording a Lien
clauses.body: Before recording a lien for delinquent assessments against {{propertyAddress}} to collect a debt owed by {{ownerName}}, California law requires the association to give written notice and certain rights. Civil Code § 5660 provides: "At least 30 days prior to recording a lien upon the separate interest of the owner of record to collect a debt that is past due under Section 5650, the association shall notify the owner of record in writing by certified mail" of a specified list of items. Under § 5660(a), those items include "a general description of the collection and lien enforcement procedures of the association," the owner's right to inspect association records, and a required notice in 14-point boldface type or capital letters: "IMPORTANT NOTICE: IF YOUR SEPARATE INTEREST IS PLACED IN FORECLOSURE BECAUSE YOU ARE BEHIND IN YOUR ASSESSMENTS, IT MAY BE SOLD WITHOUT COURT ACTION." Under § 5660(b), the notice must include "an itemized statement of the charges owed by the owner," broken out among delinquent assessments, fees and costs of collection, attorney's fees, late charges, and interest. Under § 5660(e), the owner has "the right to dispute the assessment debt by submitting a written request for dispute resolution to the association pursuant to the association's ‘meet and confer’ program," and under § 5660(f), "the right to request alternative dispute resolution with a neutral third party ... before the association may initiate foreclosure against the owner's separate interest, except that binding arbitration shall not be available if the association intends to initiate a judicial foreclosure." Separately, Civil Code § 5670 restates the dispute-resolution offer in more general terms: "Prior to recording a lien for delinquent assessments, an association shall offer the owner and, if so requested by the owner, participate in dispute resolution pursuant to the association's ‘meet and confer’ program."
clauses.gap: The citations to § 5660(a), (b), (e), and (f) are to four subsections of the same statutory section; they are quoted together because they are the components of a single 30-day pre-lien notice requirement. The citation to § 5670 is to a separate, shorter statutory restatement of the meet-and-confer offer described in § 5660(e) — the redundancy exists in the statute's own text and is not this document combining unrelated provisions. This clause does not reproduce § 5660(c) and (d) in full (a statement that the owner is not liable if the assessment was in fact paid on time, and the right to request a payment-plan meeting with the board under Section 5665). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.

citations.quote: At least 30 days prior to recording a lien upon the separate interest of the owner of record to collect a debt that is past due under Section 5650, the association shall notify the owner of record in writing by certified mail

clauses.title: How the Lien Is Actually Created and Its Priority
clauses.body: The debt described in Civil Code § 5650 becomes an actual, recorded lien on an owner's separate interest only when the association takes an additional statutory step. Civil Code § 5675(a) provides: "The amount of the assessment, plus any costs of collection, late charges, and interest assessed in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 5650, shall be a lien on the owner's separate interest in the common interest development from and after the time the association causes to be recorded with the county recorder of the county in which the separate interest is located, a notice of delinquent assessment, which shall state the amount of the assessment and other sums imposed in accordance with subdivision (b) of Section 5650, a legal description of the owner's separate interest in the common interest development against which the assessment and other sums are levied, and the name of the record owner of the separate interest in the common interest development against which the lien is imposed." If the lien is to be enforced by nonjudicial foreclosure, Section 5675(c) further requires that "the notice of delinquent assessment shall state the name and address of the trustee authorized by the association to enforce the lien by sale." Once recorded, Civil Code § 5680 provides that the resulting lien "shall be prior to all other liens recorded subsequent to the notice of delinquent assessment, except that the declaration may provide for the subordination thereof to any other liens and encumbrances." If a notice of delinquent assessment affecting {{propertyAddress}} has been recorded, its recording date is stated as: {{lienRecordingDate}}.
clauses.gap: Civil Code § 5650 creates the underlying personal debt; it is Civil Code § 5675 — not § 5650 itself — that actually creates and perfects the recorded lien on the owner's separate interest, and only as of the recording of a notice of delinquent assessment meeting § 5675(a)'s content requirements. Two of the three citations in this clause, to § 5675(a) and § 5675(c), are to subsections of the same statutory section; they are quoted together because (c) states an additional content requirement that applies only when the lien is to be enforced nonjudicially. The third citation, to § 5680, is to a separate section addressing lien priority once recorded. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.

clauses.title: Fines and Penalties Cannot Be Enforced Through the Assessment Lien
clauses.body: California law limits an association's ability to use its lien and foreclosure remedies to collect fines and penalties, as distinct from assessments themselves. This limitation applies to any assessment lien {{hoaName}} may record or seek to foreclose against {{propertyAddress}}. Civil Code § 5725(a) permits one narrow exception: "A monetary charge imposed by the association as a means of reimbursing the association for costs incurred by the association in the repair of damage to common area and facilities caused by a member or the member's guest or tenant may become a lien against the member's separate interest enforceable by the sale of the interest under Sections 2924, 2924b, and 2924c, provided the authority to impose a lien is set forth in the governing documents." Outside that exception, Civil Code § 5725(b) is explicit: "A monetary penalty imposed by the association as a disciplinary measure for failure of a member to comply with the governing documents, except for the late payments, may not be characterized nor treated in the governing documents as an assessment that may become a lien against the member's separate interest enforceable by the sale of the interest under Sections 2924, 2924b, and 2924c." The statutory notice required in an association's annual policy statement, Civil Code § 5730, restates the same limitation for owners: "The association may not use nonjudicial foreclosure to collect fines or penalties, except for costs to repair common area damaged by a member or a member's guests, if the governing documents provide for this."
clauses.gap: The citations to § 5725(a) and § 5725(b) are to two subsections of the same statutory section, quoted together because (a) states the narrow common-area-damage-repair exception to the general rule stated in (b). The additional citation to § 5730 is to a separate section — the required content of an association's annual policy statement — that restates the same § 5725 limitation in summary form for owners. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.

clauses.title: Minimum Dollar Amount and Delinquency Period Before Foreclosure
clauses.body: California law sets a minimum dollar amount and, alternatively, a minimum delinquency period before an association may use judicial or nonjudicial foreclosure to collect delinquent assessments. Civil Code § 5720(b) provides that an association seeking to collect "delinquent regular or special assessments of an amount less than one thousand eight hundred dollars ($1,800), not including any accelerated assessments, late charges, fees and costs of collection, attorney's fees, or interest, may not collect that debt through judicial or nonjudicial foreclosure," though it may still pursue small claims court, or record a lien it may not yet foreclose. Section 5720(b)(2) provides that an association that records a lien in this situation "may not foreclose until the amount of the delinquent assessments secured by the lien ... equals or exceeds one thousand eight hundred dollars ($1,800) or the assessments secured by the lien are more than 12 months delinquent." Section 5720(c) confirms that "[t]he limitation on foreclosure of assessment liens for amounts under the stated minimum in this section does not apply to" assessments "more than 12 months delinquent," assessments on time-share estates, or assessments owed by the developer. If a total delinquent-assessment amount for {{ownerName}}'s account with {{hoaName}} has been stated, it is stated as: {{amountDelinquent}}.
clauses.gap: The citations to § 5720(b), § 5720(b)(2), and § 5720(c) are to subsections of the same statutory section; they are quoted together because they define one threshold rule (the $1,800 floor) and its express exceptions (delinquency exceeding 12 months, time-share assessments, and developer-owed assessments). This document does not restate the procedural details of the small-claims-court alternative described in § 5720(b)(1). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.

clauses.title: Board Votes Required to Record a Lien and to Initiate Foreclosure
clauses.body: California law requires the association's board itself — not staff or an outside collection agent — to make two separate decisions in this process, each by a specified vote recorded in the board's minutes, and requires a further dispute-resolution offer before the second decision. These requirements apply to any decision by {{hoaName}}'s board to record a lien against, or foreclose upon, {{propertyAddress}}. First, before a lien for delinquent assessments is recorded, Civil Code § 5673 provides: "For liens recorded on or after January 1, 2006, the decision to record a lien for delinquent assessments shall be made only by the board and may not be delegated to an agent of the association. The board shall approve the decision by a majority vote of the directors in an open meeting. The board shall record the vote in the minutes of that meeting." Second, before the association initiates foreclosure of a lien that has already been validly recorded, Civil Code § 5705(b) requires the association to first offer dispute resolution: "the association shall offer the owner and, if so requested by the owner, participate in dispute resolution pursuant to the association's ‘meet and confer’ program ... or alternative dispute resolution ... The decision to pursue dispute resolution or a particular type of alternative dispute resolution shall be the choice of the owner, except that binding arbitration shall not be available if the association intends to initiate a judicial foreclosure." The decision to actually initiate foreclosure is then governed by § 5705(c): "The decision to initiate foreclosure of a lien for delinquent assessments that has been validly recorded shall be made only by the board and may not be delegated to an agent of the association. The board shall approve the decision by a majority vote of the directors in an executive session. The board shall record the vote in the minutes of the next meeting of the board open to all members. The board shall maintain the confidentiality of the owner or owners of the separate interest by identifying the matter in the minutes by the parcel number of the property, rather than the name of the owner or owners. A board vote to approve foreclosure of a lien shall take place at least 30 days prior to any public sale."
clauses.gap: This document's own research corrected an initial assumption that a single Civil Code section (variously anticipated as § 5673 or § 5710) governs the board-vote requirement for a decision to foreclose. As fetched, § 5673 governs a different, earlier decision — the vote to record the lien in the first place, taken by majority vote in an open meeting; the vote to initiate foreclosure of an already-recorded lien is instead governed by § 5705(c), taken by majority vote in an executive session, at least 30 days before any public sale. Civil Code § 5710, by contrast, governs how a trustee's sale is conducted once foreclosure has been decided (addressed in another clause of this document), not the board-vote requirement itself. The citations to § 5705(b) and § 5705(c) are to two subsections of the same statutory section, quoted together because (b) is a precondition to the board's exercise of the vote described in (c); the citation to § 5673 is to a separate section governing an earlier, different board decision. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.

clauses.title: Waiting Period, Trustee's Sale Mechanics, and the Right of Redemption
clauses.body: Once a lien has been recorded and the association has completed the steps described above, California law sets further mechanics and timing for an actual sale of {{propertyAddress}}. Civil Code § 5700(a) provides that, subject to other provisions of the article, "after the expiration of 30 days following the recording of a lien created pursuant to Section 5675, the lien may be enforced in any manner permitted by law, including sale by the court, sale by the trustee designated in the notice of delinquent assessment, or sale by a trustee substituted pursuant to Section 2934a." If a trustee's sale is used, Civil Code § 5710(a) requires that it "be conducted in accordance with Sections 2924, 2924b, and 2924c applicable to the exercise of powers of sale in mortgages and deeds of trust" — the same statutory notice-of-default and notice-of-sale framework used for mortgage foreclosures. Section 5710(b) adds an association-specific requirement on top of that framework: "the association shall serve a notice of default on the person named as the owner of the separate interest in the association's records or, if that person has designated a legal representative ..., on that legal representative," served "in accordance with the manner of service of summons" under the Code of Civil Procedure. Unlike a mortgage lender's nonjudicial foreclosure sale, a completed HOA assessment-lien foreclosure sale carries a statutory right of redemption: Civil Code § 5715(b) provides that "[a] nonjudicial foreclosure by an association to collect upon a debt for delinquent assessments shall be subject to a right of redemption[, and t]he redemption period within which the separate interest may be redeemed from a foreclosure sale under this paragraph ends 90 days after the sale."
clauses.gap: The citations to § 5710(a) and § 5710(b) are to two subsections of the same statutory section, quoted together because (b) is an association-specific service requirement layered on top of the general mortgage-foreclosure sale framework incorporated by (a). The citations to § 5700(a) and § 5715(b) are to separate sections addressing, respectively, the 30-day wait after a lien is recorded and the post-sale right of redemption. The 90-day right of redemption under § 5715(b) is a feature specific to an association's foreclosure of an assessment lien; it does not describe redemption rights, if any, following a mortgage lender's nonjudicial foreclosure of a deed of trust, a separate topic addressed in a different document in this corpus. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's HOA assessment lien and foreclosure process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific HOA or property; other states impose different or no comparable HOA lien/foreclosure limits. This document is informational: it does not itself create, record, or foreclose any lien, and does not determine whether a specific assessment or fine is validly owed.
