[This information sheet describes the statutory process for a wage claim filed with California's Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, including the Berman hearing, the Labor Commissioner's order, decision, or award, and the appeal process to superior court. It is not a DLSE wage claim form, is not filed with any agency by completing it, does not itself determine that {{employeeName}} is owed any wages by {{companyName}}, is not a substitute for the actual DLSE wage claim form or the statutes and regulations governing that process, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.]

clauses.title: Declaration — Information Sheet on Funding a Trust
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the legal mechanics of transferring (“funding”) property into {{trustName}}, a trust {{settlorName}} created as settlor, naming {{trusteeName}} as trustee, executed on {{originalTrustDate}}. Funding a trust — the act of moving specific property into the trustee's name — is a separate legal step from creating the trust itself, which is addressed in this corpus's own Revocable Living Trust document rather than here. The property this information sheet concerns is described as follows: {{propertyDescription}}. This information sheet does not itself transfer any property into {{trustName}}, does not determine whether any specific item of property is or is not currently held in {{trustName}}, and preparing or signing it has no legal effect on the ownership of any asset.

clauses.title: How a Trust Is Created, and Why Creation Alone Doesn't Fund It
clauses.body: California law recognizes several distinct methods of creating a trust, including a declaration by the owner of property that the owner holds that property as trustee, and a lifetime transfer of property by the owner to another person as trustee. Both methods share a common feature relevant to funding: each one operates only on property the settlor actually owned and either declared held in trust or actually transferred to the trustee. A trust instrument that identifies {{trustName}}, names {{trusteeName}} as trustee, and even attaches a schedule listing specific property does not, by any of these statutory methods, itself bring listed property into the trust unless that property was actually, and correctly, transferred or declared held in trust — property merely referenced in {{trustName}}'s schedule, without a completed transfer, has not become trust property under any of these methods.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15200 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory methods of creating a trust
citations.quote: Subject to other provisions of this chapter, a trust may be created by any of the following methods: (a) A declaration by the owner of property that the owner holds the property as trustee. (b) A transfer of property by the owner during the owner’s lifetime to another person as trustee. (c) A transfer of property by the owner, by will or by other instrument taking effect upon the death of the owner, to another person as trustee. (d) An exercise of a power of appointment to another person as trustee. (e) An enforceable promise to create a trust.

clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California actually structures trust creation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust or its funding. This is a single statutory section (§ 15200); no additional independent source was found for this. A related, separate mechanism exists for property that was never funded during the settlor's lifetime but that the settlor's will directs into the trust at death (a “pour-over” provision, addressed in this corpus's own Revocable Living Trust document, not repeated here) — that mechanism routes probate property into the trust after death; it does not avoid probate for that property, and it is a different legal path from the lifetime-funding mechanics this document describes. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself transfer any property into any trust, and it does not determine whether any specific asset is or is not currently trust property.

clauses.title: Real Property: A Written, Signed Instrument Is Required to Transfer Title
clauses.body: Under California property law, an estate in real property — other than a short-term tenancy at will or for a year or less — can be transferred only by operation of law or by a written instrument, signed by the person disposing of it (or by that person's agent, if the agent's authority is itself in writing). Naming {{trustName}} as a beneficiary in a will, describing real property in {{trustName}}'s schedule of assets, or simply intending for real property to belong to {{trustName}} does not, by itself, satisfy this requirement. A separate deed, in writing and signed by {{settlorName}}, conveying the specific real property from {{settlorName}} individually to {{trusteeName}} as trustee of {{trustName}}, is what this statute requires to move title to real property into the trustee's name.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1091 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the written-instrument requirement to transfer an estate in real property
citations.quote: An estate in real property, other than an estate at will or for a term not exceeding one year, can be transferred only by operation of law, or by an instrument in writing, subscribed by the party disposing of the same, or by his agent thereunto authorized by writing.

clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own written-instrument requirement for transferring real property — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property or a specific trust. This is a single statutory section (§ 1091); no additional independent source was found for this, though a related statute on the separate, additional formality requirement for a trust of real property specifically (Cal. Prob. Code § 15206) appears elsewhere in this corpus's Revocable Living Trust document and is not repeated here. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself transfer any property into any trust, and it does not determine whether any specific asset is or is not currently trust property.

clauses.title: What Recording a Deed Does — and Doesn't Do — to a Transfer
clauses.body: An executed but unrecorded deed conveying real property from {{settlorName}} to {{trusteeName}} as trustee of {{trustName}} is not, for that reason alone, ineffective as between {{settlorName}} and {{trusteeName}}: California law treats an unrecorded instrument as valid between the parties to it and anyone else who has notice of it. Recording instead does two other things: it protects the transfer against being cut off by a later purchaser or mortgagee who pays value in good faith and records first, and it is what makes the county's public record — the record that title companies, lenders, and the property tax assessor rely on — show {{trusteeName}}, rather than {{settlorName}} individually, as the owner of record.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1217 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: an unrecorded instrument remains valid between the parties and anyone with notice of it
citations.quote: An unrecorded instrument is valid as between the parties thereto and those who have notice thereof.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1214 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: an unrecorded conveyance is void against a later good-faith purchaser or mortgagee who records first
citations.quote: Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein, other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year, is void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property, or any part thereof, in good faith and for a valuable consideration, whose conveyance is first duly recorded, and as against any judgment affecting the title, unless the conveyance shall have been duly recorded prior to the record of notice of action.

clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of what recording actually does under California law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel or transfer. § 1217 and § 1214 are two different statutory sections (both within the same Civil Code chapter on the effect of recording), not subsections of one section, so they are presented here as two separate, corroborating sources rather than one. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself execute, deliver, or record any deed, and it does not determine whether any specific asset is or is not currently trust property.

clauses.title: Property Funded Into a Revocable Trust Remains Reachable by the Settlor's Own Creditors
clauses.body: So long as {{settlorName}} retains the power to revoke {{trustName}}, in whole or in part, California law makes the property held in {{trustName}} subject to the claims of {{settlorName}}'s own creditors, to the extent of that power of revocation, throughout {{settlorName}}'s lifetime. Funding {{trustName}} — moving property into {{trusteeName}}'s name as trustee — changes who holds legal title and how the property is administered, but under this statute it does not, by itself, put that property beyond the reach of {{settlorName}}'s own creditors while {{trustName}} remains revocable and {{settlorName}} is alive.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 18200 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: revocable trust property remains subject to the settlor's creditors during the settlor's lifetime
citations.quote: If the settlor retains the power to revoke the trust in whole or in part, the trust property is subject to the claims of creditors of the settlor to the extent of the power of revocation during the lifetime of the settlor.

clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuinely counter-intuitive consequence of funding a revocable trust — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust or a specific creditor's claim. This is a single statutory section (§ 18200); no additional independent source was found for this. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself transfer any property into any trust, and it does not determine whether any specific asset is or is not currently trust property, or whether any specific creditor actually has a claim against it.

clauses.title: A Statutory Safety Valve for Incomplete Funding: The “Heggstad Petition”
clauses.body: California law lets a trustee, or any interested person, petition the court for an order under Probate Code Part 19 where the trustee is in possession of or holds title to property claimed to belong to someone else, or where the trustee claims property whose title or possession is held by someone else. This second situation is the one that matters for incomplete funding: where {{settlorName}} intended specific property to belong to {{trustName}} but title was never formally transferred into {{trusteeName}}'s name as trustee, {{trusteeName}} or another interested person may petition the probate court to confirm that the property should be treated as belonging to {{trustName}}. This procedure is commonly called a “Heggstad petition,” after Estate of Heggstad (1993) 16 Cal.App.4th 943, a published California Court of Appeal decision applying this statute to property a settlor had identified in a signed declaration of trust but never separately deeded to the trustee.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 850(a)(3)(A)-(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a trustee or interested person may petition the court over property the trustee claims but does not hold title to
citations.quote: (3) The trustee or any interested person in any of the following cases: (A) Where the trustee is in possession of, or holds title to, real or personal property, and the property, or some interest, is claimed to belong to another. (B) Where the trustee has a claim to real or personal property, title to or possession of which is held by another.

citations.case: Estate of Heggstad (Heggstad v. Heggstad), 16 Cal. App. 4th 943, 20 Cal. Rptr. 2d 433 (Cal. Ct. App., 1st Dist., Div. 2, 1993), Docket No. A055005 (CourtListener case record)
citations.cite: case identity and official citation only — confirms this case exists as described, not its holding language
citations.quote: 16 Cal.App.4th 943 (1993) 20 Cal. Rptr.2d 433 Estate of HALVARD L. HEGGSTAD, Deceased. GLEN P. HEGGSTAD, as Trustee, etc., Petitioner and Respondent, v. NANCY RHODES HEGGSTAD, Objector and Appellant. Docket No. A055005. Court of Appeals of California, First District, Division Two. June 21, 1993.

clauses.title: Personal Property: No Deed Required, But an Unwritten Transfer Is Hard to Prove
clauses.body: Unlike real property, personal property carries no general statutory requirement that its transfer into {{trustName}} be in writing. But where the only support for treating specific personal property as belonging to {{trustName}} is an oral or implied claim — rather than a signed assignment, bill of sale, retitled account, or other written transfer into {{trusteeName}}'s name as trustee — California law holds the claim to a demanding evidentiary standard: the existence and terms of an oral trust of personal property may be established only by clear and convincing evidence, and {{settlorName}}'s own oral statement that the property belongs to {{trustName}}, standing alone, is not sufficient evidence that it does.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15207(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: an oral trust of personal property requires clear and convincing evidence, and the settlor's own oral statement alone is not enough
citations.quote: (a) The existence and terms of an oral trust of personal property may be established only by clear and convincing evidence. (b) The oral declaration of the settlor, standing alone, is not sufficient evidence of the creation of a trust of personal property.

clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual evidentiary risk of leaving a personal-property transfer unwritten — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific item of personal property or a specific trust. § 15207(a) and (b) are both subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated here as one source, not two independent ones. This clause does not address the separate title-transfer or registration procedures that apply to specific categories of personal property, such as vehicles, securities, or financial accounts — those are governed by other law outside this document's scope. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself transfer any property into any trust, and it does not determine whether any specific asset is or is not currently trust property.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's constitutional and statutory framework governing drug testing of job applicants and employees at {{companyName}}. It states facts about what California law permits, requires, and restricts in this area. It is not itself a consent form, a drug-testing policy, or an authorization to test {{employeeName}} or anyone else, and it does not tell {{employeeName}} or {{companyName}} what to do about any particular testing decision.

clauses.title: California's Constitutional Right to Privacy
clauses.body: California's Constitution states a specific, freestanding right to privacy. Article I, Section 1 lists privacy among the state's inalienable rights, alongside life, liberty, and property — an explicit textual right, not one inferred from other constitutional provisions the way many federal and state privacy protections are. California courts have applied this provision to drug testing in the employment context, discussed in the clauses that follow.
clauses.gap: This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. Most other states' constitutions don't contain an explicit, freestanding privacy right at this level; where a privacy protection exists in another state, it more often comes from case law interpreting other constitutional text, federal constitutional doctrine, or statute. This clause states only the text of the provision itself — how California courts have applied it specifically to drug testing is addressed in the clauses that follow, not this one. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program.

citations.case: Cal. Const. art. I, § 1 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Constitution, Declaration of Rights
citations.quote: All people are by nature free and independent and have inalienable rights. Among these are enjoying and defending life and liberty, acquiring, possessing, and protecting property, and pursuing and obtaining safety, happiness, and privacy.

clauses.title: This Constitutional Privacy Right Reaches Private Employers
clauses.body: In Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn. (1994), the California Supreme Court held that Article I, Section 1's privacy provision protects individuals against invasions by private parties, not only against government action — the point a concurring and dissenting justice in the case described this way: he concurred "in the majority's initial conclusion that the privacy provision of article I, section 1, of the California Constitution affords protection to individuals with respect to the actions of a private entity, such as the National Collegiate Athletic Association (hereinafter NCAA)". This is the reason a private employer's drug-testing program in California can be challenged under this state constitutional privacy right at all, not only under a statute — most constitutional rights restrain only government action, and this is a specific, established exception.
clauses.gap: Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn. was itself a case about drug testing of NCAA college student-athletes, not employees — its underlying facts don't involve an employer-employee relationship. It is cited here, and by later courts deciding employment drug-testing cases, for the general privacy-claim framework and for this private-party-applicability holding, not because its facts were about a workplace. This document could not independently re-verify Hill's full multi-element framework for evaluating a privacy claim — the specific test a later court applies to weigh a legally protected privacy interest, a reasonable expectation of privacy, and the seriousness of an intrusion against an employer's countervailing interests — against the complete primary opinion text; CourtListener's full-opinion access was rate-limited at the time this document was checked, and only the excerpt quoted above (from a concurring and dissenting opinion describing the majority's conclusion) could be confirmed as an exact quotation. This clause states only that narrower, confirmed point, and should not be read as restating Hill's complete holding or reasoning. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program.

citations.case: Hill v. National Collegiate Athletic Assn.
citations.quote: I concur in the majority’s initial conclusion that the privacy provision of article I, section 1, of the California Constitution affords protection to individuals with respect to the actions of a private entity, such as the National Collegiate Athletic Association (hereinafter NCAA)

clauses.title: Drug Testing Tied to a New Position
clauses.body: In Loder v. City of Glendale (1997), the California Supreme Court considered a municipal employer's drug-testing program applied to "all individuals who conditionally have been offered new positions with the city" — a category the court's opinion describes as covering "both newly hired persons and current city employees who have been approved for promotion to a new position", who "are required to undergo urinalysis testing". Because the City of Glendale is a government employer, the case also implicated the Fourth Amendment: as one justice's separate opinion put it, "Mandatory urinalysis drug and alcohol testing of prospective and current employees by a government employer is a search within the scope of the Fourth Amendment." A private employer's testing program, by contrast, doesn't trigger the Fourth Amendment at all — only the state constitutional privacy right described elsewhere in this document can reach it.
clauses.gap: The category of testing actually before the court in Loder was testing tied to a conditional offer of a new position — covering both new hires and current employees moving to a new position through promotion — not simply "pre-employment" testing in isolation from "incumbent employee" testing as a strict two-category line. This document could not independently re-verify, against the complete primary opinion text, the specific reasoning the court gave for why that category of testing was upheld, or precisely how the court treated suspicionless testing of an employee who is not moving into a new position; CourtListener's full-opinion access was rate-limited at the time this document was checked, and only the excerpts quoted above could be confirmed as exact quotations from the opinion and a separate concurring and dissenting opinion in the same case. This clause states only those narrower, confirmed points, and should not be read as restating the court's complete holding. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program.

citations.case: Loder v. City of Glendale
citations.quote: In this case we address a challenge to an employment-related drug testing program adopted by the City of Glendale in 1986. Under the program in question, all individuals who conditionally have been offered new positions with the city (both newly hired persons and current city employees who have been approved for promotion to a new position) are required to undergo urinalysis testing

citations.case: Loder v. City of Glendale
citations.cite: 14 Cal. 4th 846, 927 P.2d 1200 (1997) (Kennard, J., concurring and dissenting)
citations.quote: The Fourth Amendment of the United States Constitution protects an individual from unreasonable searches and seizures. Mandatory urinalysis drug and alcohol testing of prospective and current employees by a government employer is a search within the scope of the Fourth Amendment.

clauses.title: Accommodating Voluntary Rehabilitation
clauses.body: Separately from drug testing itself, California law requires a private employer that regularly employs 25 or more employees to reasonably accommodate an employee who wants to voluntarily enter and participate in an alcohol or drug rehabilitation program, as long as the accommodation doesn't impose an undue hardship on the employer. This duty doesn't protect an employee whose current use of alcohol or drugs leaves them unable to perform their job duties, or unable to perform them without endangering their own health or safety or the health or safety of others — an employer may still refuse to hire, or may discharge, an employee on that basis.
clauses.gap: This accommodation duty applies only to a private employer that regularly employs 25 or more employees — smaller employers aren't covered by this chapter of the Labor Code at all. Neither "reasonably accommodate" nor "undue hardship" is defined further within this statute itself. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. Other states' accommodation obligations toward an employee entering rehabilitation, if any, differ or may not exist. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program. It does not itself grant or deny any accommodation.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1025 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, employer accommodation of voluntary rehabilitation
citations.quote: Every private employer regularly employing 25 or more employees shall reasonably accommodate any employee who wishes to voluntarily enter and participate in an alcohol or drug rehabilitation program, provided that this reasonable accommodation does not impose an undue hardship on the employer. Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to prohibit an employer from refusing to hire, or discharging an employee who, because of the employee’s current use of alcohol or drugs, is unable to perform his or her duties, or cannot perform the duties in a manner which would not endanger his or her health or safety or the health or safety of others.

clauses.title: Privacy of Enrollment, Paid Leave, and Enforcement
clauses.body: The same statutory chapter adds three more rules. An employer must make reasonable efforts to safeguard the privacy of the fact that an employee has enrolled in an alcohol or drug rehabilitation program. Nothing in the chapter requires an employer to provide time off with pay for this purpose — but an employee may use their own accrued sick leave to enter and participate in a program. And an employee who believes they've been denied the reasonable accommodation described above may file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner, using the same complaint procedure available for certain other Labor Code claims.
clauses.gap: Sections 1026, 1027, and 1028 are three different sections of the same narrow, five-section statutory chapter as the accommodation duty in the previous clause (Labor Code §§ 1025-1028) — they are being treated here together as one connected source on a single statutory scheme, not as independent corroborating sources on separate questions. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. Other states' rules on privacy of rehabilitation enrollment, paid time off for it, and how a denied accommodation is enforced, if any, differ. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program. It does not itself resolve any complaint about a denied accommodation.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1026 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, privacy of rehabilitation enrollment
citations.quote: The employer shall make reasonable efforts to safeguard the privacy of the employee as to the fact that he or she has enrolled in an alcohol or drug rehabilitation program.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1027 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, no paid-time-off requirement, sick leave available
citations.quote: Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to require an employer to provide time off with pay, except that an employee may use sick leave to which he or she is entitled for the purpose of entering and participating in an alcohol or drug rehabilitation program.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1028 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Labor Commissioner complaint procedure
citations.quote: An employee may file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner if he or she believes that he or she has been denied reasonable accommodation as required by this chapter. Sections 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.4, 98.5, 98.6, and 98.7 shall be applicable to a complaint filed pursuant to this section.

clauses.title: Off-Duty Cannabis Use and Metabolite Screening
clauses.body: Since January 1, 2024, California law makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against a person in hiring, termination, or any other term or condition of employment based on "the person's use of cannabis off the job and away from the workplace," or based on "an employer-required drug screening test that has found the person to have nonpsychoactive cannabis metabolites in their hair, blood, urine, or other bodily fluids." The metabolite rule exists because standard urine and hair tests detect nonpsychoactive metabolites that can remain in the body for days or weeks after use — long after any impairment has ended — so a positive result on that kind of test doesn't show current impairment. The law separately makes it unlawful for an employer to ask an applicant about their prior cannabis use. None of this protection applies to an employee in the building and construction trades.
clauses.gap: The three points above — the off-duty-use protection, the nonpsychoactive-metabolite screening protection, and the building-and-construction-trades carve-out — are all subdivisions of one statutory section, Government Code § 12954(a), and the applicant-inquiry restriction quoted here is subdivision (b) of that same section; all are being treated together as one connected source, not as independent corroborating sources. This protection also has further limits not described in this clause, covered in the next one. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. Most other states have no equivalent off-duty-cannabis-use employment protection, and where one exists, the details vary. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(a)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, off-duty cannabis use protection and preemployment-screening carve-out
citations.quote: The person’s use of cannabis off the job and away from the workplace. This paragraph does not prohibit an employer from discriminating in hiring, or any term or condition of employment, or otherwise penalize a person based on scientifically valid preemployment drug screening conducted through methods that do not screen for nonpsychoactive cannabis metabolites.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(a)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, nonpsychoactive-metabolite screening protection
citations.quote: An employer-required drug screening test that has found the person to have nonpsychoactive cannabis metabolites in their hair, blood, urine, or other bodily fluids.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, building and construction trades carve-out
citations.quote: This subdivision does not apply to an employee in the building and construction trades.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, restriction on asking about prior cannabis use
citations.quote: Except as specified in subdivision (c), it is unlawful for an employer to request information from an applicant for employment relating to the applicant’s prior use of cannabis.

clauses.title: Limits on the Cannabis Protection
clauses.body: The off-duty cannabis protection described above has specific limits. It doesn't give an employee the right to possess, be impaired by, or use cannabis on the job, and it doesn't affect an employer's rights or obligations to maintain a drug- and alcohol-free workplace. It doesn't preempt any state or federal law that requires applicants or employees to be tested for controlled substances — including as a condition of federal funding, federal licensing-related benefits, or a federal contract. And it doesn't apply at all to positions that require a federal government background investigation or security clearance under U.S. Department of Defense regulations, or equivalent regulations of other federal agencies. The statute itself became operative on January 1, 2024.
clauses.gap: Subdivisions (d), (e), (f), and (g) are all part of the same statutory section as the protection described in the previous clause, Government Code § 12954 — they are being treated together here as one connected source, not as independent corroborating sources. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. Cannabis remains a Schedule I controlled substance under the federal Controlled Substances Act, and federal contractors and federally regulated positions can be required to test for it regardless of this state law, exactly as this clause states. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific drug test or testing program. It does not determine whether any particular position falls within one of these exemptions.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, on-the-job use and drug-free workplace carve-out
citations.quote: This section does not permit an employee to possess, to be impaired by, or to use, cannabis on the job, or affect the rights or obligations of an employer to maintain a drug- and alcohol-free workplace, as specified in Section 11362.45 of the Health and Safety Code, or any other rights or obligations of an employer specified by state or federal law or regulation.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, no preemption of federal or state testing requirements
citations.quote: This section does not preempt state or federal laws requiring applicants or employees to be tested for controlled substances, including laws and regulations requiring applicants or employees to be tested, or the manner in which they are tested, as a condition of employment, receiving federal funding or federal licensing-related benefits, or entering into a federal contract.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, federal security-clearance positions excluded
citations.quote: This section does not apply to applicants or employees hired for positions that require a federal government background investigation or security clearance in accordance with regulations issued by the United States Department of Defense pursuant to Part 117 of Title 32 of the Code of Federal Regulations, or equivalent regulations applicable to other agencies.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, effective date
citations.quote: This section shall become operative on January 1, 2024.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California statutory law on when and how {{landlordName}}, as landlord, may enter the residential dwelling unit rented by {{tenantName}} at {{propertyAddress}}. It states what California law provides on this subject. It does not authorize, direct, or prohibit any particular entry, and it does not tell either {{landlordName}} or {{tenantName}} what to do about any specific situation.

clauses.title: Permitted Purposes for Entry
clauses.body: California law allows a landlord to enter a tenant's dwelling unit only in specific listed cases: (1) in case of emergency; (2) to make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, to supply necessary or agreed services, or to exhibit the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser, mortgagee, tenant, worker, or contractor, or to make a security-deposit pre-move-out inspection; (3) when the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit; or (4) under a court order. Two further categories of permitted entry are cross-referenced within this same statute but defined elsewhere: one for purposes set out in a separate chapter of the Civil Code beginning at section 1954.201, and one for compliance with a specific article of the Health and Safety Code beginning at section 17973 — neither of which this information sheet covers. Beyond these listed purposes, a landlord may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides on landlord entry — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; the permitted purposes for landlord entry, and what counts as their abuse, vary by state. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1954) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for the enumerated-purposes list itself. Separately: this document's author attempted to research published California case law construing what conduct counts as "abuse" of the right of access under subdivision (c), using a case-law search tool, but that tool's research-request limit was exhausted before a citable result could be verified against the tool's own text — rather than state or invent a case citation on that point, this information sheet omits one. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific entry, and it does not determine whether any specific entry was or would be lawful.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(a)(1)-(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the four general permitted purposes for entry
citations.quote: A landlord may enter the dwelling unit only in the following cases: (1) In case of emergency. (2) To make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers, or contractors or to make an inspection pursuant to subdivision (f) of Section 1950.5. (3) When the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises. (4) Pursuant to court order.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(a)(5)-(6) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the two cross-referenced additional categories this document doesn't cover
citations.quote: (5) For the purposes set forth in Chapter 2.5 (commencing with Section 1954.201). (6) To comply with the provisions of Article 2.2 (commencing with Section 17973) of Chapter 5 of Part 1.5 of Division 13 of the Health and Safety Code.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, no abuse or harassment
citations.quote: The landlord may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.

clauses.title: Written Notice: Content, Delivery, and the Reasonable-Notice Presumptions
clauses.body: Except for the narrower situations addressed elsewhere in this information sheet, California law requires a landlord to give the tenant reasonable notice in writing of the landlord's intent to enter, and to enter only during normal business hours. The written notice must include the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry. It may be delivered by personal delivery to the tenant, by leaving it with someone of suitable age and discretion at the premises, by leaving it on, near, or under the usual entry door in a manner a reasonable person would discover it, or by mailing it to the tenant. California law sets two separate rebuttable presumptions of what counts as reasonable notice: twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable notice generally, and — separately — mailing the notice at least six days before the intended entry is presumed reasonable notice for a mailed notice specifically. Both are rebuttable presumptions, not fixed floors; either can be shown to be unreasonable, or reasonable, by evidence in a particular case.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's notice requirement for landlord entry — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; the length and form of required notice, and whether a state even sets a numeric presumption at all, vary by state. Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory subsection (§ 1954(d)(1)) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific entry, and it does not determine whether any specific notice given, or entry made, was or would be reasonable.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, written notice content and delivery methods
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (e), or as provided in paragraph (2) or (3), the landlord shall give the tenant reasonable notice in writing of his or her intent to enter and enter only during normal business hours. The notice shall include the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry. The notice may be personally delivered to the tenant, left with someone of a suitable age and discretion at the premises, or, left on, near, or under the usual entry door of the premises in a manner in which a reasonable person would discover the notice.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the 24-hour and six-day-mailing presumptions
citations.quote: Twenty-four hours shall be presumed to be reasonable notice in absence of evidence to the contrary. The notice may be mailed to the tenant. Mailing of the notice at least six days prior to an intended entry is presumed reasonable notice in the absence of evidence to the contrary.

clauses.title: Normal Business Hours
clauses.body: Except in an emergency or when the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit, California law bars entry outside normal business hours unless the tenant consents, at the time of entry, to an entry outside normal business hours.
clauses.gap: The statute restricts entry to "normal business hours" but does not itself define that phrase with a specific clock-time range; this information sheet states the restriction as written and doesn't supply a numeric definition the statute doesn't provide. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's time-of-day restriction on landlord entry — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; not every state restricts entry by time of day, and the ones that do vary in how they phrase the restriction. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for this. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific entry, and it does not determine whether any specific entry was or would be within normal business hours.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, entry limited to normal business hours
citations.quote: Except in cases of emergency or when the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises, entry may not be made during other than normal business hours unless the tenant consents to an entry during other than normal business hours at the time of entry.

clauses.title: When No Notice at All Is Required
clauses.body: In three specific situations, California law requires no notice of entry at all: to respond to an emergency; if the tenant is present and consents to the entry at the time of entry; and after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of when California law dispenses with notice altogether — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; which circumstances excuse notice, and whether a state excuses notice at all, vary by state. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for this. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific entry, and it does not determine whether a specific tenant's presence, consent, or abandonment of the unit actually excused notice in any given instance.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, when no notice at all is required
citations.quote: No notice of entry is required under this section: (1) To respond to an emergency. (2) If the tenant is present and consents to the entry at the time of entry. (3) After the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit.

clauses.title: Two Narrower Exceptions to Written Notice: Showing the Property to a Buyer, and Agreed Repair Visits
clauses.body: California law creates two narrower exceptions to the ordinary written-notice requirement, each tied to a specific circumstance. First, if the purpose of the entry is to exhibit the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser — by its own terms, this exception covers purchasers, not prospective tenants — the landlord may give oral notice, in person or by telephone, but only if the landlord or the landlord's agent has already given the tenant separate written notice, within the preceding 120 days, that the property is for sale and that oral contact for this purpose may follow. Twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable notice for this oral notice as well, and the notice must still include the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry; at the time of entry, the landlord or agent must leave written evidence of the entry inside the unit. Second, the tenant and landlord may agree orally to an entry for agreed repairs or agreed services, with no written notice at all, if the oral agreement itself includes the date and approximate time of entry and the entry occurs within one week of the agreement.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's specific reduced-notice exceptions — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; some states relax the notice requirement for showing a unit to a new prospective tenant near the end of a tenancy, but California's statute, on its face, does not: its oral-notice exception in this section is written to cover showing the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser, not to a prospective new tenant, and California's statute sets no separate "48 hours' oral notice" figure for either circumstance — that specific figure, to the extent it describes a real rule, describes a different state's law, not California's. Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory subsection (§ 1954(d)) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific entry, and it does not determine whether any specific oral notice given, or oral agreement reached, satisfied this section.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, oral notice to show the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser
citations.quote: If the purpose of the entry is to exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, the notice may be given orally, in person or by telephone, if the landlord or his or her agent has notified the tenant in writing within 120 days of the oral notice that the property is for sale and that the landlord or agent may contact the tenant orally for the purpose described above. Twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable notice in the absence of evidence to the contrary. The notice shall include the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry. At the time of entry, the landlord or agent shall leave written evidence of the entry inside the unit.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, an oral agreement for a repair or service visit needs no written notice
citations.quote: The tenant and the landlord may agree orally to an entry to make agreed repairs or supply agreed services. The agreement shall include the date and approximate time of the entry, which shall be within one week of the agreement. In this case, the landlord is not required to provide the tenant a written notice.

clauses.title: What Happens If a Landlord Violates This Section
clauses.body: Civil Code section 1954 does not itself set out a penalty or remedy for its own violation. A separate statute makes it unlawful for a landlord to do certain things for the purpose of influencing a tenant to vacate a dwelling, and one of the listed things is committing a significant and intentional violation of section 1954; a tenant who prevails in a civil action — including in small claims court — to enforce rights under that separate statute is entitled to a civil penalty of up to $2,000 for each violation. Apart from that specific statute, California law separately provides that an agreement to let real property binds the landlord to secure the tenant's quiet possession of the premises against all persons lawfully claiming it; a landlord's interference with a tenant's use of the unit can also be evaluated under that separate covenant, which is a different body of law from section 1954 itself.
clauses.gap: These are one state's statutes, used together as evidence of what happens under California law when a landlord violates the entry statute — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; whether an entry-notice statute carries its own penalty, and what that penalty is, vary by state. Three of the four citations below (the two from § 1940.2(a) and the one from § 1940.2(b)) are subsections of the same statutory section rather than independently authored sources; the fourth citation, § 1927, is a separate, independently enacted statutory section (in force since 1872) supplying a different legal basis — the quiet-possession covenant — so it is treated here as a genuinely separate source, not additional corroboration of § 1940.2. Note also that the § 1940.2 penalty is narrower than a bare violation of § 1954: it requires the violation to be both significant and intentional, and committed for the purpose of influencing the tenant to vacate — an ordinary, isolated, or unintentional violation of § 1954 does not, by this statute's own terms, trigger this specific penalty. This document's author also attempted to locate citable published California case law applying either statute to a landlord's entry practices, using a case-law search tool, but that tool's research-request limit was exhausted before a citable result could be verified against the tool's own text; rather than state or invent a case citation, this information sheet relies on the statutory text alone. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific entry, and it does not determine whether any specific entry violated either statute or gives rise to any remedy.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1940.2(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the purpose requirement for this separate unlawful-conduct statute
citations.quote: It is unlawful for a landlord to do any of the following for the purpose of influencing a tenant to vacate a dwelling:

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1940.2(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, a significant and intentional violation of section 1954 as unlawful conduct
citations.quote: Commit a significant and intentional violation of Section 1954.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1940.2(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the civil penalty for a prevailing tenant
citations.quote: A tenant who prevails in a civil action, including an action in small claims court, to enforce his or her rights under this section is entitled to a civil penalty in an amount not to exceed two thousand dollars ($2,000) for each violation.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1927 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the separate covenant of quiet possession
citations.quote: An agreement to let upon hire binds the letter to secure to the hirer the quiet possession of the thing hired during the term of the hiring, against all persons lawfully claiming the same.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Claimant Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's unemployment insurance eligibility framework and claims process from the perspective of a claimant. {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}} ended on {{separationDate}}, and {{employeeName}} filed a claim for unemployment insurance benefits with the California Employment Development Department (EDD) on {{claimFiledDate}}. This document states facts about the eligibility conditions, disqualification standard, benefit-amount computation, appeal process, and certification obligations that California's Unemployment Insurance Code sets for a claimant generally. It does not determine that {{employeeName}} is or is not eligible for benefits, and it is not itself a claim, weekly certification, or appeal filed with the EDD.

clauses.title: Weekly Eligibility Conditions
clauses.body: California law does not treat eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits as a one-time determination made when a claim is first filed. Instead, a statute sets out conditions a claimant must meet with respect to each individual week for which benefits are claimed. The director must find, for that week, that: a claim for benefits for that week was made in accordance with authorized regulations; the claimant has registered for work and continued to report at a public employment office or another approved place (a requirement that may be waived or altered by regulation for partially employed individuals attached to regular jobs); the claimant was able to work and available for work that week; the claimant has served the one-week waiting period defined in a separate statute addressed below, unless that waiting period was waived under a specific Government Code provision; the claimant conducted a search for suitable work in accordance with the specific and reasonable instructions of a public employment office; and, if the claimant has been identified under an automated profiling system as likely to exhaust regular benefits, the claimant participated as required in reemployment activities such as orientation and assessment, absent a showing of good cause for not participating. Because this is a week-by-week standard, it is the statutory basis for the recurring duty to certify continued eligibility for each week claimed, including the duty to conduct the required work search, rather than a condition satisfied once at the start of a claim.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1253), used as real evidence of the recurring, week-by-week eligibility framework a state can build into its unemployment insurance system — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular claimant's situation, and not a determination that any specific claimant has or has not met these conditions for any given week. This clause quotes the whole of § 1253 as a single source; it cites only this one statutory section, so the multiple-subsection disclosure required elsewhere in this document does not apply here. The statute's subdivision (e) requires a work search 'in accordance with specific and reasonable instructions of a public employment office' — a narrower, instruction-dependent formulation than a generic phrase like 'actively seeking work' might suggest, and this document does not describe what specific instructions any public employment office has issued or would issue to any particular claimant. This document does not itself file a claim, certify a week, or determine that any of these conditions is or is not met for any specific claimant.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1253 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: An unemployed individual is eligible to receive unemployment compensation benefits with respect to any week only if the director finds that: (a) A claim for benefits with respect to that week has been made in accordance with authorized regulations. (b) He or she has registered for work, and thereafter continued to report, at a public employment office or any other place as the director may approve. Either or both of the requirements of this subdivision may be waived or altered by authorized regulation as to partially employed individuals attached to regular jobs. (c) He or she was able to work and available for work for that week. (d) He has been unemployed for a waiting period of one week as defined in Section 1254, unless this waiting period has been waived pursuant to Section 8571 of the Government Code. (e) He or she conducted a search for suitable work in accordance with specific and reasonable instructions of a public employment office. (f) He or she participated as required by the director in reemployment activities, such as orientation and assessment if the individual has been identified pursuant to an automated profiling system as likely to exhaust regular unemployment benefits unless the individual has shown good cause for failure to participate.

clauses.title: The One-Week Waiting Period
clauses.body: One of the eligibility conditions described above requires the claimant to have served a waiting period of one week, and a separate statute defines what that means. A week does not count toward this waiting period unless it falls within the benefit year that includes the week for which the claimant seeks payment (though this rule does not interrupt payment for consecutive weeks of unemployment, and a week immediately before a benefit year can, in some circumstances, be treated as within it); a week does not count if benefits have already been paid for it; and a week does not count unless the claimant was otherwise eligible for that week in all respects apart from the waiting-period requirement itself and a separate statute on partial and part-time earnings.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1254), used as real evidence that California's waiting period is one week — not a claim about which state's law governs a given claimant's timeline, and not a statement about how many weeks any particular claimant has actually served. This document's drafter was initially asked to verify whether Unemployment Insurance Code § 1030 or § 1032 sets the waiting period. Neither does: both sections were checked directly and are unrelated to the waiting period — § 1030 sets the employer's window to submit facts on the separation issue described in a later clause, and § 1032 governs whether benefit charges are excluded from an employer's reserve account. The real source is § 1253(d), which requires the waiting period, together with § 1254, which defines it — both checked directly for this clause. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1254); no additional independent source was found for this. This document does not calculate how many, if any, waiting-period weeks any specific claimant has served.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1254 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: No week shall be counted as a week of unemployment under subdivision (d) of Section 1253: (a) Unless it occurs within the benefit year which includes the week with respect to which he claims payment of unemployment compensation benefits, but this requirement shall not interrupt the payment of such benefits for consecutive weeks of unemployment. The week immediately preceding a benefit year, if part of one uninterrupted period of unemployment which continues into that benefit year shall be deemed, for the purposes of this section only, to be within such benefit year as well as within the preceding benefit year. (b) If unemployment compensation benefits have been paid with respect to that week. (c) Unless the individual was eligible for unemployment compensation benefits with respect thereto in all respects, except for the requirements of subdivision (d) of Section 1253 and Section 1281.

clauses.title: Disqualification for Voluntarily Quitting Without Good Cause or Discharge for Misconduct
clauses.body: Separately from the weekly conditions above, a claimant is disqualified from benefits if the director finds that the claimant left the most recent work voluntarily without good cause, or was discharged for misconduct connected with that work. The same statute creates a rebuttable presumption running in the claimant's favor: a claimant is presumed to have been discharged for reasons other than misconduct, and not to have voluntarily left without good cause, unless the employer has given the EDD written notice to the contrary, setting out facts sufficient to overcome that presumption. Neither 'good cause' nor 'misconduct' is defined in general terms within the statute. The same statute does, however, deem certain specific circumstances to be good cause as a matter of law, including leaving employment to accompany or join a spouse or domestic partner at a place from which commuting is impractical, and leaving employment to protect oneself or one's family from domestic violence abuse.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256), used as real evidence of the substantive disqualification standard, the burden-shifting presumption, and the specific statutory good-cause categories a state can attach to a claimant's reason for separation — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular claimant's eligibility, and not a characterization of any specific claimant's own separation. This clause quotes two passages from the same statutory section (§ 1256): the general disqualification-and-presumption paragraph, and the paragraph deeming certain circumstances to be good cause. These two quotations are being treated as one source, not as independent corroborating sources, because they come from the same statutory section. This is also the same statutory section already cited, for the employer-facing side of this same disqualification question, by this corpus's Employer's Response to Unemployment Insurance Claim document (its uiresponse_disqualification_standard clause); that overlap is disclosed here rather than presented as a second, independent source — this clause states the identical statutory standard from the claimant's own perspective and does not add independent verification beyond what that document already established. Beyond the specific circumstances the statute itself deems to be good cause, the general terms 'good cause' and 'misconduct' have been the subject of substantial EDD precedent decisions and California appellate case law. This document's drafter attempted to locate and verify a citable, on-point California appellate decision construing one of these terms, but the CourtListener research tool used for that purpose returned a rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) before any search could be completed in this session. Rather than invent or rely on an unverified case citation, this document discloses that limitation honestly and does not cite any case law on the meaning of 'good cause' or 'misconduct.' This document does not itself determine that any specific claimant's own separation from a specific employer does or does not meet this standard.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: An individual is disqualified for unemployment compensation benefits if the director finds that he or she left his or her most recent work voluntarily without good cause or that he or she has been discharged for misconduct connected with his or her most recent work. An individual is presumed to have been discharged for reasons other than misconduct in connection with his or her work and not to have voluntarily left his or her work without good cause unless his or her employer has given written notice to the contrary to the department as provided in Section 1327, setting forth facts sufficient to overcome the presumption. The presumption provided by this section is rebuttable.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: An individual may be deemed to have left his or her most recent work with good cause if he or she leaves employment to accompany his or her spouse or domestic partner to a place or to join him or her at a place from which it is impractical to commute to the employment. For purposes of this section “spouse” includes a person to whom marriage is imminent, and “domestic partner” includes a person to whom a domestic partnership, as described in Section 297 of the Family Code, is imminent. An individual may be deemed to have left his or her most recent work with good cause if he or she leaves employment to protect his or her family, or himself or herself, from domestic violence abuse.

clauses.title: How the Weekly Benefit Amount Is Calculated, and Its Statutory Maximum
clauses.body: A separate statute sets how a claimant's weekly benefit amount is computed. For a claim filed with an effective date on or after January 1, 2003, the weekly benefit amount is the figure appearing on a statutory wage-bracket table opposite the wage range that includes the wages the claimant was paid during the highest-earning quarter of the claimant's base period. For a claimant whose highest-quarter wages exceed the top of that table, the statute instead sets the weekly benefit amount at 50 percent of those wages divided by 13 — but caps that calculation at a fixed dollar maximum keyed to when the claim was filed. For any claim filed on or after January 1, 2005, that statutory maximum is $450 per week.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1280(c)), used as real evidence of how California computes a weekly benefit amount and sets its statutory cap — not a claim about which state's law governs a given claimant's benefit amount, and not a calculation of any specific claimant's actual weekly benefit amount, which depends on that claimant's own base-period wages and is not computed here. This document's drafter was asked to verify, rather than assume, whether the maximum weekly benefit amount is a fixed statutory dollar figure or a periodically adjusted one. Having checked the statute directly, the honest answer is that it is a fixed dollar figure written directly into the statutory text — $450 for any claim filed on or after January 1, 2005 — and that figure has not been amended since then; as of the date this clause was checked, it has remained $450 for roughly two decades notwithstanding intervening inflation, rather than adjusting automatically or periodically. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1280(c)); no additional independent source was found for this. Section 1280(c) also incorporates a lengthy numeric wage-bracket table with many lines; this clause quotes the subsection's operative capping sentence and does not reproduce that table.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1280(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: If the amount of wages paid an individual for employment by employers exceeds one thousand eight hundred thirty-two dollars and ninety-nine cents ($1,832.99) in the quarter of his or her base period in which these wages were highest, the individual’s weekly benefit amount shall be 50 percent of these wages divided by 13, but in no case shall this amount exceed the applicable of the following: (1) For new claims filed with an effective date beginning on or after January 1, 2003, and before January 1, 2004, three hundred seventy dollars ($370). (2) For new claims filed with an effective date beginning on or after January 1, 2004, and before January 1, 2005, four hundred ten dollars ($410). (3) For new claims filed with an effective date beginning on or after January 1, 2005, four hundred fifty dollars ($450). If the benefit payable under this subdivision is not a multiple of one dollar ($1), it shall be computed to the next higher multiple of one dollar ($1).

clauses.title: The EDD's Determination and the Claimant's Right to Appeal
clauses.body: After considering any facts an employer has submitted, the EDD must make a determination on the claimant's eligibility for benefits and must promptly notify the claimant, and any employer who submitted facts, of that determination and the reasons for it. Both the claimant and the employer may appeal a determination or reconsidered determination to an administrative law judge within 30 days from service of the notice — a deadline that may be extended for good cause, defined to include, but not be limited to, mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect. The EDD's director is treated as an interested party to any such appeal. If the administrative law judge's decision is adverse, a further appeal may be taken to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board, again within 30 days after the decision is mailed (also extendable for good cause).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1328(a) and 1334(a)), used as real evidence of the two-tier administrative appeal structure a state can build into its unemployment insurance determination process — not a claim about which state's law governs a given claimant's appeal rights, and not a statement that any specific claimant has or should appeal any determination. These two citations come from different statutory sections, each addressing a distinct stage of the appeal process (the initial determination and first appeal under § 1328, and the administrative law judge's decision and further appeal under § 1334); they are not multiple citations to subsections of the same section. This appeal right belongs to the claimant and is a different statutory point from the employer's own 10-day window to submit facts after being notified of the claim, which this corpus's Employer's Response to Unemployment Insurance Claim document addresses separately under Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1327 and 1030(a) — those sections are not re-cited here because they govern a different actor and a different deadline. This document does not itself file, or advise any specific claimant to file, any appeal, and it does not state whether an appeal in any particular case would succeed.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1328(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: The department shall consider the facts submitted by an employer pursuant to Section 1327 and make a determination as to the claimant’s eligibility for benefits. The department shall promptly notify the claimant and any employer who before the determination has submitted facts or given notice pursuant to Section 1327 or this section and authorized regulations of the determination or reconsidered determination and the reasons therefor. If, after notice of a determination or reconsidered determination, the employing unit acquires knowledge of facts that may affect the eligibility of the claimant and those facts could not reasonably have been known within the 10-day period provided by Section 1327, the employing unit shall within 10 days of acquiring that knowledge submit those facts to the department, and the 10-day period may be extended for good cause. The claimant and the employer may appeal from a determination or reconsidered determination to an administrative law judge within 30 days from service of notice of the determination or reconsidered determination. The 30-day period may be extended for good cause, which shall include, but not be limited to, mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect. The director shall be an interested party to any appeal.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1334(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: An administrative law judge after affording a reasonable opportunity for fair hearing, shall, unless the appeal is withdrawn, affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside any determination that is appealed under this article. The claimant, the employer becoming a party to the appeal by submitting a protest or information pursuant to Sections 1326 to 1333, inclusive, of this article, and the director shall be promptly notified in writing of the administrative law judge’s decision, together with reasons for it. The decision shall be final unless, within 30 days after mailing of the decision, further appeal is initiated to the appeals board pursuant to Section 1336. The 30-day limitation may be extended for good cause.

clauses.title: Certifying for Benefits: The False Statement Prohibition and Its Penalty
clauses.body: A separate chapter of the same code makes it a violation to willfully make a false statement or representation, to knowingly fail to disclose a material fact, or to use a false name, false Social Security number, or other false identification, in order to obtain, increase, reduce, or defeat any benefit or payment — whether for the maker or for someone else — under California's own unemployment compensation provisions or several listed federal allowance programs the EDD also administers. A different statute in the same chapter sets the penalty: except for a short list of other, more specific violations this provision does not apply to, a violation of the chapter is punishable by imprisonment in county jail for up to one year, or in state prison, by a fine of not more than $20,000, or by both the fine and imprisonment, at the court's discretion.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 2101(a) and 2122), used as real evidence that California attaches a real, sourced criminal penalty to a false statement made to obtain unemployment benefits — not a claim about which state's law governs a given claimant, and not a statement that any specific claimant has made, or has not made, a false statement. These two citations come from different statutory sections: § 2101(a) defines the violation, and § 2122 is a separate, general penalty provision for Chapter 10 violations that is needed because § 2101 itself does not state a punishment; they are not multiple citations to subsections of the same section. Section 2122 excludes a short list of other violations (Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 2117, 2117.5, 2118, and 2118.5) that carry their own, separately stated penalties; those sections concern employer tax-withholding and reporting violations rather than a claimant's false statement under § 2101, and this document does not address them further. This document's drafter also looked for, but did not find, a standalone Unemployment Insurance Code section imposing a freestanding duty to report earnings while certifying for benefits, separate from the general authority to set claims-filing regulations in Section 1326 and the false-statement-and-nondisclosure prohibition quoted above; unreported earnings that should have been disclosed would fall within that prohibition's 'knowingly fail to disclose a material fact' language rather than a separately numbered earnings-reporting statute, so far as this document's research located. This document does not itself constitute a certification for benefits, and does not state that any specific claimant has violated, or complied with, this prohibition.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 2101(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: It is a violation of this chapter to willfully make a false statement or representation, to knowingly fail to disclose a material fact, or to use a false name, false social security number, or other false identification to obtain, increase, reduce, or defeat any benefit or payment, whether for the maker or for any other person, under any of the following statutes administered by the department: (1) The provisions of this division. (2) The provisions of any unemployment insurance law of the federal government. (3) The provisions of any training allowance law of the federal government. (4) The provisions of any trade readjustment allowance law of the federal government. (5) The provisions of any other allowance law of the federal government.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 2122 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 2117, 2117.5, 2118, and 2118.5, a violation of this chapter is punishable by imprisonment in the county jail not to exceed one year, or in the state prison, or by a fine of not more than twenty thousand dollars ($20,000), or by both the fine and imprisonment, at the discretion of the court.
