clauses.title: Seller's Permit Information Sheet — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet relates to {{businessName}}, a {{entityType}}, with a California place of business at {{principalOfficeAddress}}, engaged in selling {{businessActivityDescription}}. It describes California's statutory requirement, set out in the Sales and Use Tax Law (Revenue and Taxation Code Division 2, Part 1), that a person desiring to engage in business as a seller of tangible personal property in California register with the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA) and hold a seller's permit for each place of business, along with the statutory definitions that determine who that requirement reaches, how a permit is issued and may be suspended or revoked, the criminal penalty for engaging in business as a seller without one, and CDTFA's statutory authority to require a security deposit. This document is not this project's LLC Articles of Organization, Articles of Incorporation, Statement of Information, Fictitious Business Name (DBA) Statement, or Foreign LLC/Corporation Qualification document. Those documents concern filings with the California Secretary of State: creating a corporation or LLC, that entity's periodic reporting after formation, county-level registration of a name other than a registrant's true legal name, or an out-of-state entity's registration to transact business in California. This document instead concerns a separate statutory scheme administered by a separate state agency — CDTFA's registration of retail sellers under the Sales and Use Tax Law — which applies regardless of how, or whether, the seller's business is formed or named, and applies independently of any Secretary of State filing. A business can complete every Business Formation filing in this project and still separately need to register with CDTFA, and a person can need to register with CDTFA without forming any entity at all. This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself register {{businessName}}, or any other person, with CDTFA; it does not determine whether {{businessName}}'s specific activities constitute engaging in business as a seller within the meaning of California law; and it does not obtain a seller's permit for {{businessName}} or any other person.

clauses.title: Requirement to File an Application for a Seller's Permit
clauses.body: California's Sales and Use Tax Law states that every person desiring to engage in or conduct business as a seller within California shall file an application for a permit for each place of business. The application must be made on a form the agency prescribes, must state the name under which the applicant transacts or intends to transact business and the location of the applicant's place or places of business, must state that the applicant will actively engage in or conduct business as a seller of tangible personal property, and may be filed using electronic media. The statute itself directs this filing to "the board," a reference to the former State Board of Equalization's sales and use tax function. Since July 1, 2017, California's Government Code states that the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA) is the successor to, and is vested with, all of the duties, powers, and responsibilities the board held under sales and use tax statutes such as this one; CDTFA is accordingly the agency that now administers the seller's-permit application requirement described here, even though the codified text of Section 6066 has not been amended to replace the word "board" with "department."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own seller's-permit filing requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific person's obligations, and not a claim that other states impose an identical registration requirement for retail sellers. This clause cites a single subsection of one Revenue and Taxation Code section, Section 6066(a), together with a section of a different code, Government Code Section 15570.22, for the separate point that CDTFA succeeded to the former State Board of Equalization's sales-tax duties; these are two independent sources on two different points, not multiple subsections of the same section presented as corroborating each other. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file an application for a seller's permit with CDTFA on behalf of the business named in this document or any other person, and it does not determine whether any specific person is required to hold one.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6066(a)
citations.cite: California Sales and Use Tax Law, Article 2 (Permits), application requirement
citations.quote: Every person desiring to engage in or conduct business as a seller within this state shall file with the board an application for a permit for each place of business. Every application for a permit shall be made upon a form prescribed by the board and shall set forth the name under which the applicant transacts or intends to transact business, the location of his place or places of business, and such other information as the board may require.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 15570.22
citations.cite: Government Code, transfer of the State Board of Equalization's sales and use tax duties to CDTFA
citations.quote: the department is the successor to, and is vested with, all of the duties, powers, and responsibilities of the board.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions of "Seller" and "Retailer"
clauses.body: The seller's-permit filing requirement applies to a person engaging in business "as a seller," a term the Sales and Use Tax Law defines separately from "retailer." "Seller" includes every person engaged in the business of selling tangible personal property of a kind whose gross receipts from a retail sale are required to be included in the measure of the sales tax, whether or not that particular property is ever actually sold at retail. "Retailer" is defined separately and more narrowly, and includes every seller who makes any retail sale of tangible personal property, every person engaged in the business of making retail sales at auction of tangible personal property owned by that person or others, and every person engaged in the business of making sales for storage, use, or other consumption. The statute also lets the state tax agency treat certain salespersons, representatives, peddlers, or canvassers as agents of the dealers, distributors, or employers they sell for, and separately provides that a newspaper carrier is not a retailer.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines "seller" and "retailer" for its own sales and use tax law — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific person's activities, and not a claim that other states define these terms identically. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6014 defines "seller," and Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6015(a)(1) defines "retailer," in separately worded provisions; these are treated as two independent sources on two related but distinct terms, not as one term's definition standing in for the other. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether the business named in this document or any other specific person is a "seller" or "retailer" within the meaning of California law.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6014
citations.cite: California Sales and Use Tax Law, Chapter 1 (General Provisions and Definitions), definition of "seller"
citations.quote: “Seller” includes every person engaged in the business of selling tangible personal property of a kind the gross receipts from the retail sale of which are required to be included in the measure of the sales tax.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6015(a)(1)
citations.cite: California Sales and Use Tax Law, Chapter 1 (General Provisions and Definitions), definition of "retailer"
citations.quote: “Retailer” includes: (1) Every seller who makes any retail sale or sales of tangible personal property, and every person engaged in the business of making retail sales at auction of tangible personal property owned by the person or others.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions of "Sale" and "Retail Sale"
clauses.body: The permit requirement is further keyed to what counts as a "sale" and a "retail sale." As currently operative, "sale" means and includes any transfer of title or possession, exchange, or barter, conditional or otherwise, in any manner or by any means whatsoever, of tangible personal property for a consideration, among several other enumerated transactions (including certain fabrication and processing work, and most leases of tangible personal property) that the same section separately treats as sales. A "retail sale" or "sale at retail" is defined separately, in a different section, as a sale for a purpose other than resale in the regular course of business, in the form of tangible personal property, with a further provision extending that definition to a sale by a convicted counterfeiter regardless of resale purpose.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines "sale" and "retail sale" for its own sales and use tax law — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific transaction, and not a claim that other states define these terms identically. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6006 defines "sale," and Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6007(a)(1) defines "retail sale"/"sale at retail," in separately worded provisions, treated as two independent sources on two related but distinct terms. Section 6006 has already been amended by Statutes 2026, Chapter 23 to add digital-product provisions and to rename the administering agency in its text from "the board" to "the department," but that amendment does not become operative until January 1, 2027; the text quoted here is the version that was operative on the checkedDate above, and this clause does not describe the version taking effect January 1, 2027. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific transaction of the business named in this document or any other person is a "sale" or "retail sale" within the meaning of California law.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6006
citations.cite: California Sales and Use Tax Law, Chapter 1 (General Provisions and Definitions), definition of "sale" (version operative through December 31, 2026)
citations.quote: “Sale” means and includes: (a) Any transfer of title or possession, exchange, or barter, conditional or otherwise, in any manner or by any means whatsoever, of tangible personal property for a consideration.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6007(a)(1)
citations.cite: California Sales and Use Tax Law, Chapter 1 (General Provisions and Definitions), definition of "retail sale"/"sale at retail"
citations.quote: A “retail sale” or “sale at retail” means a sale for a purpose other than resale in the regular course of business in the form of tangible personal property.

clauses.title: Issuance of the Permit and Its Non-Assignability
clauses.body: Once an applicant has complied with the application requirement of Section 6066 and, where applicable, the security requirement of Section 6701, and after the applicant has been given the notice Section 6066.5 requires, California's Sales and Use Tax Law directs the state tax agency to grant and issue to each applicant a separate permit for each place of business within the state. The statute states that a permit is not assignable and is valid only for the person in whose name it is issued and for the transaction of business at the place designated in it, and that it must at all times be conspicuously displayed at the place for which it was issued.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own rule that a seller's permit is non-assignable and place- and person-specific — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific permit, and not a claim that other states' analogous licenses are non-transferable in the same way. This clause quotes a single statutory section, Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6067, so no same-section multiple-subsection issue arises here. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself issue a seller's permit to the business named in this document or any other person, and it does not determine whether any specific person or place of business qualifies for one.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6067
citations.cite: California Sales and Use Tax Law, Article 2 (Permits), issuance and non-assignability
citations.quote: the board shall grant and issue to each applicant a separate permit for each place of business within the state. A permit is not assignable and is valid only for the person in whose name it is issued and for the transaction of business at the place designated therein. It shall at all times be conspicuously displayed at the place for which issued.

clauses.title: Suspension or Revocation of a Seller's Permit
clauses.body: None of the seller's-permit statutes reviewed for this document set a fixed expiration date or a recurring renewal period for a permit once issued. California's Sales and Use Tax Law instead addresses how a permit may end before its holder ends the underlying business: whenever a person fails to comply with any Sales Tax Law provision or related regulation, the state tax agency, after giving the person 10 days' written notice of a hearing and requiring the person to show cause why the permit or permits should not be revoked, may revoke or suspend any one or more of that person's permits following the hearing. The agency must give the permit holder written notice of any suspension or revocation, and the statute separately restricts reissuance: the agency may not issue a new permit after a revocation unless it is satisfied the former holder will comply with the Sales Tax Law and its regulations going forward.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own suspension-and-revocation procedure for seller's permits — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific permit, and not a claim that other states use an identical hearing procedure or notice period. This clause quotes a single statutory section, Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6070, so no same-section multiple-subsection issue arises here. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific person's permit has been or should be suspended or revoked, and it does not itself provide the notice, conduct the hearing, or take any action this statute describes.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6070
citations.cite: California Sales and Use Tax Law, Article 2 (Permits), suspension and revocation procedure
citations.quote: Whenever any person fails to comply with any provision of this part relating to the sales tax or any rule or regulation of the board relating to the sales tax prescribed and adopted under this part, the board upon hearing, after giving the person 10 days’ notice in writing specifying the time and place of hearing and requiring him to show cause why his permit or permits should not be revoked, may revoke or suspend any one or more of the permits held by the person.

clauses.title: Criminal Penalty for Engaging in Business as a Seller Without a Permit
clauses.body: California's Sales and Use Tax Law makes it a misdemeanor for a person to engage in business as a seller in California without a permit or permits, or to continue doing so after a permit has been suspended or revoked; the statute extends this to each officer of a corporation that engages in business as a seller without a permit. Rather than stating its own fine amount, Section 6071 cross-references Section 7153, the Sales and Use Tax Law's general misdemeanor-penalty provision. Section 7153 states that a violation of the Sales and Use Tax Law, except as otherwise provided, is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not less than $1,000 and not more than $5,000, or by imprisonment not exceeding one year in county jail, or by both the fine and imprisonment, in the court's discretion.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own criminal penalty for unlicensed selling — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific person's conduct, and not a claim that other states attach the same penalty, or any penalty, to comparable conduct. This clause cites two different statutory sections, not subsections of one section: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6071 defines the misdemeanor and states that its punishment is as provided in a separate section, and Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 7153 is that separate section, supplying the actual fine range and imprisonment term; these are treated as two sources on two connected points — the offense and its punishment — not as independent corroboration of the same fact. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific person has engaged in business as a seller without a permit, or what penalty, if any, would apply to any specific person's conduct.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6071
citations.cite: California Sales and Use Tax Law, Article 2 (Permits), misdemeanor for unlicensed selling
citations.quote: A person who engages in business as a seller in this state without a permit or permits or after a permit has been suspended or revoked, and each officer of any corporation which so engages in business, is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable as provided in Section 7153.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 7153
citations.cite: California Sales and Use Tax Law, Chapter 10 (Violations), general misdemeanor penalty
citations.quote: Any violation of this part by any person, except as otherwise provided, is a misdemeanor. Each offense shall be punished by a fine of not less than one thousand dollars ($1,000) and not more than five thousand dollars ($5,000), or imprisonment not exceeding one year in the county jail, or both the fine and imprisonment in the discretion of the court.

clauses.title: CDTFA's Authority to Require a Security Deposit
clauses.body: Separately from the permit itself, California's Sales and Use Tax Law gives the state tax agency authority to require a security deposit from a person subject to the law, whenever the agency deems it necessary to ensure compliance; this statute already refers to "the department" by name. Security may be posted as cash, government bonds, or insured bank or savings-and-loan deposits, and is held in trust to be used only as the statute provides. The amount is capped: ordinarily it may not exceed twice a quarterly filer's, or three times a monthly filer's, estimated average tax liability, or $50,000, whichever is less, though a higher cap (three or five times, respectively, or $50,000, whichever is less) applies to a person who has been given notice of a hearing to show cause why a permit should not be revoked, or whose permit has already been revoked or suspended. Security held by the department is released after a three-year period in which the person has filed all returns and paid all required tax on time, and the department may sell posted security at public auction to recover unpaid tax, with any surplus returned to the person who posted it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of CDTFA's own security-deposit authority under California's sales and use tax law — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific person's obligations, and not a claim that other states condition an analogous permit or license on a security deposit in the same way or amount. This clause cites a single statutory section, Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6701, so no same-section multiple-subsection issue arises here. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether the business named in this document or any other specific person would be required to post security, in what amount, or as a condition of what specific permit.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 6701
citations.cite: California Sales and Use Tax Law, Article 1 (Security for Tax), CDTFA's authority to require security
citations.quote: The department, whenever it deems it necessary to ensure compliance with this part, may require any person subject thereto, to place with it any security that the department may determine.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature Block — Seller's Permit Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet regarding {{businessName}}'s potential registration with the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration was prepared by {{authorizedSignerName}}.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{authorizedSignerName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California's statutory requirement that a person engaging in business as a seller of tangible personal property register with CDTFA and hold a seller's permit for each place of business, the statutory definitions that determine who that requirement reaches, how a permit is issued, suspended, or revoked, the criminal penalty for engaging in business as a seller without one, and CDTFA's authority to require a security deposit. It is not CDTFA's official seller's permit application or any other CDTFA form, does not itself register {{businessName}} or any other person with CDTFA, does not obtain a seller's permit for {{businessName}} or any other person, does not constitute legal advice, and does not determine whether {{businessName}}'s specific activities require a seller's permit. The current official application and instructions are published by the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration.]

clauses.title: Proposed Guardian of the Estate — Information and Declaration in Support of Petition
clauses.body: I, {{proposedGuardianName}}, am the person proposed to serve as guardian of the ESTATE of {{childName}}, a minor born {{childDOB}}. I state that my relationship to {{childName}} is: {{relationshipToChild}}. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for appointment of a guardian of the estate, to be filed in the California probate court under Probate Code Division 4, Part 2. A guardianship of the estate concerns management of {{childName}}'s money and property; it is a legally distinct appointment from a guardianship of {{childName}}'s person, which concerns {{childName}}'s custody and day-to-day care, and the two appointments may be requested together in a single petition or sought separately. This declaration is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not appoint, authorize, or confirm {{proposedGuardianName}} — or anyone else — as guardian of {{childName}}'s estate. {{childName}}'s parent(s) of record, so far as known, are {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}, where applicable. Only a court order issued after the statutory petition, notice, investigation, and hearing process can actually appoint a guardian of {{childName}}'s estate.

clauses.title: Estate Information Summary
clauses.body: This information sheet summarizes the property proposed to be placed under a guardianship of the estate for {{childName}}. Estimated value of {{childName}}'s total estate, including money and other property, as of the date below: {{estimatedEstateValue}}. General description of the money or property involved: {{estateDescription}}. If a petition for guardianship of the estate is filed, it would be filed in the Superior Court of California, County of {{countyOfFiling}}. This information sheet does not itself determine whether a full guardianship of the estate, a smaller-estate alternative, or some other statutory mechanism applies to any particular amount or item of property; California's statutory framework for guardianships of the estate, and the narrower alternatives to it, are described in the accompanying authority clauses of this document.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Guardianship of the Estate Petition Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{proposedGuardianName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual guardianship-of-the-estate petition filed with the California probate court. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not appoint a guardian; only a court order does that.]

clauses.title: Guardianship of the Estate Is a Legally Distinct Appointment From Guardianship of the Person
clauses.body: A guardianship of the estate of {{childName}} is a separate court appointment from a guardianship of {{childName}}'s person: a guardian of the estate manages {{childName}}'s money and property, while a guardian of the person has {{childName}}'s custody and day-to-day care. California Probate Code § 1510(b) allows a single petition to request either appointment, or both, providing that the petition "shall request that a guardian of the person or estate of the minor, or both, be appointed." Where a guardianship of the estate is sought, § 1510(c) adds an estate-specific item to the petition's required contents that is not required for a guardianship of the person alone: so far as known to the petitioner, the petition must set forth "the spouse of the proposed ward" in the case of a guardianship of the estate. Once appointed, California Probate Code § 2400 defines the "estate" that a guardian of the estate administers, for purposes of the chapter governing a guardian's powers and duties, as "all of the . . . ward's personal property, wherever located, and real property located in this state," and in that same chapter defines "guardian" to mean "the guardian of the estate." Nothing in these sections requires that a guardian of {{childName}}'s estate also serve as guardian of {{childName}}'s person, or the reverse; the two appointments may be sought together or separately.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that guardianship of the estate and guardianship of the person are distinct California court appointments, sought through the same petition mechanism but covering different subject matter — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites two subsections of one statutory section (§ 1510(b) and § 1510(c)) as one source, not two independent ones, and separately cites two subsections of a second section (§ 2400(b) and § 2400(c)) as a second single source; no additional independent source was found for either provision. This document is informational: it describes the statutory distinction between the two guardianship appointments and does not itself establish, appoint, or determine that either guardianship should be granted for the minor named in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1510(b)
citations.quote: The petition shall request that a guardian of the person or estate of the minor, or both, be appointed, shall specify the name and address of the proposed guardian and the name and date of birth of the proposed ward, and shall state that the appointment is necessary or convenient.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1510(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1510(c)
citations.quote: The petition shall set forth, so far as is known to the petitioner, the names and addresses of all of the following: (1) The parents of the proposed ward. (2) The person having legal custody of the proposed ward and, if that person does not have the care of the proposed ward, the person having the care of the proposed ward. (3) The relatives of the proposed ward within the second degree. (4) In the case of a guardianship of the estate, the spouse of the proposed ward.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2400(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2400(b)
citations.quote: “Estate” means all of the conservatee’s or ward’s personal property, wherever located, and real property located in this state.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2400(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2400(c)
citations.quote: “Guardian” means the guardian of the estate.

clauses.title: Who May Be Appointed Guardian of the Estate, and the Standard the Court Applies
clauses.body: In deciding whether, and whom, to appoint as guardian of {{childName}}'s estate, California Probate Code § 1514 sets out a standard specific to estate guardianships, distinct from the child-custody standard the same section applies to a guardian of the person. Under § 1514(a), "[u]pon hearing of the petition, if it appears necessary or convenient, the court may appoint a guardian of the person or estate of the proposed ward or both." If a parent nominated a guardian of the estate for {{childName}} under Probate Code § 1500 before this proceeding, § 1514(c) directs that "the court shall appoint a guardian nominated under Section 1500 insofar as the nomination relates to the guardianship of the estate unless the court determines that the nominee is unsuitable." Subject to that nomination priority, § 1514(e) directs the court, in appointing a guardian of the estate, to be guided by the proposed ward's best interest — including the proposed guardian's ability to manage and preserve the estate and the proposed guardian's concern for and interest in the ward's welfare — and, if the proposed ward is of sufficient age to form an intelligent preference, to give consideration to that preference. Unlike a guardian of the person — whom § 1514(b)(2) bars from being the minor's own parent, except in the limited circumstances described in Probate Code § 1510.1 or § 2105 — § 1514 states no comparable general bar on a parent serving as guardian of a minor's estate. This document states that statutory difference as a fact about California's guardianship framework; it does not assert that any particular parent is, or is not, a suitable guardian of {{childName}}'s estate.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the appointment standard, nomination priority, and parent-eligibility rules for a guardian of a minor's estate — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petition. This clause cites four subsections of a single statutory section (§ 1514(a), § 1514(b)(2), § 1514(c), and § 1514(e)); these are treated as one source, not four independent ones, and no additional independent source was found for this material. This document is informational: it describes the statutory standard and eligibility rules a court applies in deciding whom to appoint, and does not itself determine that any specific person — parent or otherwise — should or should not be appointed guardian of any specific minor's estate, and it does not find or assert that any parent is unfit or unable to manage a child's property.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1514(a)
citations.quote: Upon hearing of the petition, if it appears necessary or convenient, the court may appoint a guardian of the person or estate of the proposed ward or both.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 1510.1 or 2105, a minor’s parent may not be appointed as a guardian of the person of the minor.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1514(c)
citations.quote: The court shall appoint a guardian nominated under Section 1500 insofar as the nomination relates to the guardianship of the estate unless the court determines that the nominee is unsuitable.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1514(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1514(e)
citations.quote: (1) The court is to be guided by what appears to be in the best interest of the proposed ward, taking into account the proposed guardian’s ability to manage and to preserve the estate as well as the proposed guardian’s concern for and interest in the welfare of the proposed ward. (2) If the proposed ward is of sufficient age to form an intelligent preference as to the person to be appointed as guardian, the court shall give consideration to that preference in determining the person to be so appointed.

clauses.title: The Bonding Requirement for a Guardian of the Estate
clauses.body: Before letters of guardianship issue, California Probate Code § 2320(a) requires that, "[e]xcept as otherwise provided by statute, every person appointed as guardian or conservator shall, before letters are issued, give a bond approved by the court." Under § 2320(b), that bond runs "for the benefit of the ward or conservatee and all persons interested in the guardianship or conservatorship estate" and is conditioned on the guardian's faithful performance of the office's duties according to law. Except as otherwise provided by statute, § 2320(c) sets the default bond amount, when the bond is given by an admitted surety insurer, as the sum of listed components, including "the value of the personal property of the estate" and "the probable annual gross income of all of the property of the estate," plus additional components tied to the ward's public benefit payments and to the cost of recovering on the bond, which this clause does not itemize. A separate subsection not quoted here, § 2320(d), doubles that amount when the bond is instead given by personal sureties rather than an admitted surety insurer.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California requires a bond of a court-appointed guardian of a minor's estate, and of how the default bond amount is calculated — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship. This clause cites three subsections of a single statutory section (§ 2320(a), § 2320(b), and § 2320(c)); these are treated as one source, not three independent ones, and no additional independent source was found for this material. This clause does not analyze the circumstances in which a bond may be waived or reduced under § 2320(a)'s "[e]xcept as otherwise provided by statute" language, nor the full list of components in § 2320(c)(3)-(4) or the personal-sureties rule in § 2320(d), which this document does not otherwise describe. This document is informational: it does not itself set, waive, or determine a bond amount for any actual guardian of a minor's estate; only a court order can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2320(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2320(a)
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by statute, every person appointed as guardian or conservator shall, before letters are issued, give a bond approved by the court.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2320(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2320(b)
citations.quote: The bond shall be for the benefit of the ward or conservatee and all persons interested in the guardianship or conservatorship estate and shall be conditioned upon the faithful execution of the duties of the office, according to law, by the guardian or conservator.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2320(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2320(c)
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by statute, unless the court increases or decreases the amount upon a showing of good cause, the amount of a bond given by an admitted surety insurer shall be the sum of all of the following: (1) The value of the personal property of the estate. (2) The probable annual gross income of all of the property of the estate.

clauses.title: The Guardian's Duty to File an Inventory and Appraisal, and Periodic Accountings
clauses.body: Once appointed, a guardian of {{childName}}'s estate has statutory reporting duties to the probate court. California Probate Code § 2610(a) requires that, "[w]ithin 90 days after appointment, or within any further time as the court for reasonable cause upon ex parte petition of the guardian or conservator may allow," the guardian file with the court clerk "an inventory and appraisal of the estate, made as of the date of the appointment." Under § 2610(b), the guardian must "take and subscribe to an oath that the inventory contains a true statement of all of the estate of the ward . . . of which the guardian . . . has possession or knowledge." Beyond that initial inventory, § 2620(a) requires that, "[a]t the expiration of one year from the time of appointment and thereafter not less frequently than biennially, unless otherwise ordered by the court to be more frequent," the guardian present an accounting of the estate's assets to the court for settlement and allowance. A narrower exception exists for smaller estates: under § 2628(a), the court may order that the guardian need not present those periodic accounts if, among other conditions listed in that subsection, the estate's value (excluding the ward's residence) stays under $15,000 and the estate's monthly income (excluding public benefits) stays under $2,000 throughout the accounting period.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real inventory-and-appraisal deadline and a real periodic-accounting requirement for a guardian of a minor's estate — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship. This clause cites two subsections of a single statutory section (§ 2610(a) and § 2610(b)) as one source, not two independent ones, and separately cites one subsection each of two further sections in the same statutory chapter (§ 2620(a) and § 2628(a)); no additional independent source was found for any of this material. This clause does not describe every condition in § 2628(a) for the small-estate accounting exception (only two of its three listed conditions are quoted), nor the supplemental-inventory duty in a separate, uncited section (§ 2613) that applies when after-discovered property surfaces. This document is informational: it does not itself file any inventory or accounting, and no filing occurs unless and until an actual court-appointed guardian submits one to the court.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2610(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2610(a)
citations.quote: Within 90 days after appointment, or within any further time as the court for reasonable cause upon ex parte petition of the guardian or conservator may allow, the guardian or conservator shall file with the clerk of the court and deliver pursuant to Section 1215 to the conservatee and to the attorneys of record for the ward or conservatee, along with notice of how to file an objection, an inventory and appraisal of the estate, made as of the date of the appointment of the guardian or conservator.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2610(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2610(b)
citations.quote: The guardian or conservator shall take and subscribe to an oath that the inventory contains a true statement of all of the estate of the ward or conservatee of which the guardian or conservator has possession or knowledge.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2620(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2620(a)
citations.quote: At the expiration of one year from the time of appointment and thereafter not less frequently than biennially, unless otherwise ordered by the court to be more frequent, the guardian or conservator shall present the accounting of the assets of the estate of the ward or conservatee to the court for settlement and allowance in the manner provided in Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 1060) of Part 1 of Division 3.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2628(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2628(a)
citations.quote: The court may make an order that the guardian or conservator need not present the accounts otherwise required by this chapter so long as all of the following conditions are satisfied: (1) The estate at the beginning and end of the accounting period for which an account is otherwise required consisted of property, exclusive of the residence of the ward or conservatee, of a total net value of less than fifteen thousand dollars ($15,000). (2) The income of the estate for each month of the accounting period, exclusive of public benefit payments, was less than two thousand dollars ($2,000).

clauses.title: Court Approval Before Selling or Encumbering Significant Estate Property
clauses.body: Selling significant property of {{childName}}'s estate is not left to a guardian's unilateral decision by default. California Probate Code § 2540(a) provides that, with exceptions this clause does not itemize, "sales of real or personal property of the estate under this article are subject to authorization, confirmation, or direction of the court, as provided in this article." California law also lets the court remove that case-by-case approval requirement in advance for certain transactions: under § 2590(a), the court may, in its discretion, grant the guardian "any one or more or all of the powers specified in Section 2591" where the court determines doing so would be to the estate's advantage, benefit, and best interest — a list that includes, for example under § 2591(c)(1), "the power to sell at public or private sale real or personal property of the estate without confirmation of the court of the sale." Absent such an order, § 2590(b) states that "the guardian or conservator does not have a power specified in Section 2591 without authorization by a court under this article or other express provisions of this code."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that court approval is the default rule for a guardian's sale of estate property, and that a court may instead grant a guardian defined powers to act independently — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship. This clause cites two subsections of a single statutory section (§ 2590(a) and § 2590(b)) as one source, not two independent ones, and separately cites one subsection each of two further sections (§ 2540(a) and § 2591(c)(1)); no additional independent source was found for any of this material. This clause does not analyze the exceptions referenced in § 2540(a) itself (Sections 2544 and 2545, and the separate rule in § 2540(b) for selling a conservatee's personal residence, which by its terms concerns a conservatee rather than a minor ward), nor the full list of 28 powers a court may grant under § 2591, of which only one example is quoted here. This document is informational: it does not authorize, confirm, or restrict any sale or encumbrance of the minor's property; only a court order in an actual guardianship proceeding can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2540(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2540(a)
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in Sections 2544 and 2545, and except for the sale of a conservatee’s present or former personal residence as set forth in subdivision (b), sales of real or personal property of the estate under this article are subject to authorization, confirmation, or direction of the court, as provided in this article.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2590(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2590(a)
citations.quote: The court may, in its discretion, make an order granting the guardian or conservator any one or more or all of the powers specified in Section 2591 if the court determines that, under the circumstances of the particular guardianship or conservatorship, it would be to the advantage, benefit, and best interest of the estate to do so.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2590(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2590(b)
citations.quote: The guardian or conservator does not have a power specified in Section 2591 without authorization by a court under this article or other express provisions of this code.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2591(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The power to sell at public or private sale real or personal property of the estate without confirmation of the court of the sale, other than the personal residence of a conservatee.

clauses.title: Simpler Alternatives to a Full Guardianship of the Estate for Smaller Amounts
clauses.body: California law does not require a court-supervised guardianship of the estate for every amount of money or property belonging to a minor. A minor's "total estate" is defined by California Probate Code § 3400(a) to include "both the money and other property belonging to the minor and the money and other property belonging to the guardianship estate, if any, of the minor." Where that total estate does not exceed $5,000 in value, § 3401(a) allows the money or property to instead "be paid or delivered to a parent of the minor entitled to the custody of the minor to be held in trust for the minor until the minor reaches majority," subject to the written-assurance and other conditions in § 3401(c), including that "[t]he total estate of the minor, including the money and other property to be paid or delivered to the parent, does not exceed five thousand dollars ($5,000) in value." Separately, § 3400(b)(1) confirms that "[c]ustodial property" held under the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act, Probate Code Part 9 (commencing with Section 3900), is deducted from that $5,000 calculation — meaning a custodianship under that Act is treated by the statute as a distinct mechanism from a guardianship of the estate, governed by that Act's own separate rules, which this document does not otherwise describe.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California recognizes a $5,000 total-estate threshold below which a full guardianship of the estate is not required, and a separately recognized custodianship mechanism under the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific minor's property, and dollar thresholds and available mechanisms vary by state. This clause cites two subsections of one statutory section (§ 3400(a) and § 3400(b)(1)) as one source, and separately cites two subsections of a second section (§ 3401(a) and § 3401(c)) as a second single source; no additional independent source was found for either provision, and the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act's own creation, custodian-duty, and termination rules (Probate Code Part 9, commencing with Section 3900) are not analyzed in this document beyond the cross-reference in § 3400(b)(1) itself. This document is informational: it does not itself determine which mechanism, if any, applies to any particular minor's property, and it does not pay, deliver, transfer, or place any money or property under any of these mechanisms.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3400(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 3400(a)
citations.quote: As used in this article, “total estate of the minor” includes both the money and other property belonging to the minor and the money and other property belonging to the guardianship estate, if any, of the minor.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3400(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Custodial property” held pursuant to the California Uniform Transfers to Minors Act, Part 9 (commencing with Section 3900).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3401(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 3401(a)
citations.quote: Where a minor does not have a guardian of the estate, money or other property belonging to the minor may be paid or delivered to a parent of the minor entitled to the custody of the minor to be held in trust for the minor until the minor reaches majority if the requirements of subdivision (c) are satisfied.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 3401(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The total estate of the minor, including the money and other property to be paid or delivered to the parent, does not exceed five thousand dollars ($5,000) in value.

clauses.title: When a Guardianship of the Estate Ends
clauses.body: A guardianship of {{childName}}'s estate does not continue indefinitely. California Probate Code § 1600(a) provides that "[a] guardianship of the person or estate or both terminates when the ward attains majority," subject to a narrower extension mechanism under § 1510.1 that, by its own terms, applies only to a guardianship of the person, not the estate. Section 1600(c) adds a separate termination trigger for the estate specifically: "a guardianship of the estate terminates upon the death of the ward, except as provided by Section 2467 and Article 4 (commencing with Section 2630) of Chapter 7 of Part 4, and except as otherwise provided by law." Before majority, § 1601 lets "the guardian, a parent, the minor ward, or, in the case of an Indian child custody proceeding, an Indian custodian or the ward’s tribe" petition the court to terminate the guardianship early if termination would be in the ward's best interest, and requires the court to terminate the guardianship on the petition of a ward who has already turned 18. Termination does not end the guardian's accounting obligations: California Probate Code § 2630 states that termination of the guardian-ward relationship, however it occurs, "does not cause the court to lose jurisdiction of the proceeding for the purpose of settling the accounts of the guardian or conservator or for any other purpose incident to the enforcement of the judgments and orders of the court upon such accounts."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of when and how a guardianship of a minor's estate ends under California law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific guardianship. This clause cites two subsections of a single statutory section (§ 1600(a) and § 1600(c)) as one source, not two independent ones, and separately cites two further, distinct sections (§ 1601 and § 2630); no additional independent source was found for any of this material. This clause does not describe the extension mechanism in § 1510.1, which by its terms applies only to guardianship of the person, or the post-death estate-custody duty in § 2467, both of which are cross-referenced but not analyzed here. This document is informational: it does not itself terminate, extend, or continue any guardianship of a minor's estate; only a court order, or the statutory triggers described above, can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1600(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1600(a)
citations.quote: A guardianship of the person or estate or both terminates when the ward attains majority unless, pursuant to Section 1510.1, the ward requests the extension of, or consents to the extension of, the guardianship of the person until the ward attains 21 years of age.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1600(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1600(c)
citations.quote: A guardianship of the estate terminates upon the death of the ward, except as provided by Section 2467 and Article 4 (commencing with Section 2630) of Chapter 7 of Part 4, and except as otherwise provided by law.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1601 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 1601
citations.quote: Upon petition of the guardian, a parent, the minor ward, or, in the case of an Indian child custody proceeding, an Indian custodian or the ward’s tribe, the court may make an order terminating the guardianship if the court determines that it is in the ward’s best interest to terminate the guardianship. Upon petition of a ward who is 18 years of age or older, the court shall make an order terminating the guardianship.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 2630 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 2630
citations.quote: The termination of the relationship of guardian and ward or conservator and conservatee by the death of either, by the ward attaining majority, by the determination of the court that the guardianship or conservatorship is no longer necessary, by the removal or resignation of the guardian or conservator, or for any other reason, does not cause the court to lose jurisdiction of the proceeding for the purpose of settling the accounts of the guardian or conservator or for any other purpose incident to the enforcement of the judgments and orders of the court upon such accounts or upon the termination of the relationship.

clauses.title: Local Business License / Business Tax Certificate Information Sheet — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet relates to {{businessName}}, a {{entityType}}, with a place of business at {{principalOfficeAddress}} in the City of {{cityOfOperation}}, County of {{countyOfOperation}}, California, engaged in {{businessActivityDescription}}. It describes California's constitutional and statutory framework authorizing California cities and counties to require a local business license or business tax certificate as a condition of operating a business within their jurisdiction — a framework that grants and bounds a city's or county's own licensing power, but that leaves the actual license or certificate, its name, its fee, its renewal cycle, and its application procedure to be enacted, defined, and administered independently by each city and county, rather than by a single state agency or a single statewide statute. This document is not this project's Seller's Permit (California Department of Tax and Fee Administration Registration) Information Sheet, Fictitious Business Name (DBA) Statement, or Foreign LLC/Corporation Qualification document. Those documents concern, respectively: registration with the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (CDTFA) as a seller of tangible personal property under the state Sales and Use Tax Law; a county-level filing required when a business uses a name other than its true legal name; and an out-of-state entity's registration with the California Secretary of State to transact business in California. A local business license or business tax certificate is a further and separate requirement that a city or county may impose under its own ordinance. A business can complete every one of those other filings and still separately be required, under the ordinance of the specific city or county in which it operates, to hold a local business license or business tax certificate, and a business can be required to hold a local business license or business tax certificate regardless of whether it has made any of those other filings at all. Unlike the seller's permit, California does not have one statewide statute that itself creates a business license requirement, names it, sets its fee, or defines its application procedure; state law instead grants cities and counties broad authority to adopt their own licensing and business-tax ordinances under that authority, and the specific license or certificate name, the businesses and activities it reaches, its fee or tax amount, its renewal cycle, and its application procedure are set locally and vary enormously from one city or county to the next, including among cities and counties within California. This information sheet is informational only. It does not itself obtain a local business license or business tax certificate for {{businessName}} or any other person; it does not determine whether {{businessName}}'s specific business or specific location is required to hold one; and it does not state what the City of {{cityOfOperation}}, the County of {{countyOfOperation}}, or any other specific city or county actually requires.

clauses.title: Constitutional Source of Local Licensing and Regulatory Authority
clauses.body: The ultimate source of a California city's or county's authority to require a local business license or business tax certificate traces to the California Constitution's grant of local "police power." Article XI, Section 7 of the California Constitution states that a county or city may make and enforce, within its own limits, all local, police, sanitary, and other ordinances and regulations that are not in conflict with general laws. This provision does not itself create a business license or business tax requirement, set a fee, or name any specific license; it is the broader constitutional grant of local regulatory and police-power authority on which a city's or county's own business licensing and business-tax ordinances are built, together with the more specific statutory grants described in the other authority clauses of this document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's constitution, used as real evidence of the ultimate source of a California city's or county's local police power — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific person's or business's obligations, and not a claim that other states' constitutions grant local governments an identical or even similar police power. This clause quotes a single constitutional section, Cal. Const. art. XI, § 7, so no same-section multiple-subsection issue arises here. Article XI, Section 7 is a general grant of local police power, not itself a business license or business tax statute; the actual license or certificate requirements, fees, and procedures that a specific city or county adopts under this and the related statutory grants described elsewhere in this document are set locally and vary by city and county, and this document does not and cannot state what any specific city or county requires. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself obtain a local business license or business tax certificate for the business named in this document or any other person, and it does not determine whether any specific business or jurisdiction requires one.

citations.case: Cal. Const. art. XI, § 7
citations.cite: California Constitution, Article XI (Local Government), local police power
citations.quote: A county or city may make and enforce within its limits all local, police, sanitary, and other ordinances and regulations not in conflict with general laws.

clauses.title: Statutory Authority for a City to License Business for Revenue and Regulation
clauses.body: Two separate California statutes, in two different codes, expressly authorize a city's legislative body to license business activity within its jurisdiction and to set the license fee or tax. Government Code Section 37101(a), part of the Government Code's general provisions on the government of cities, states that a city's legislative body may license, for revenue and regulation, and fix the license tax upon, every kind of lawful business transacted in the city, including shows, exhibitions, and games, and may provide for collecting that license tax by suit or otherwise. Separately, Business and Professions Code Section 16000(a), part of a different code's general business regulations, states that the legislative body of an incorporated city may, in the exercise of its police power and for the purpose of regulation, license any kind of business not prohibited by law that is transacted and carried on within the limits of its jurisdiction, including shows, exhibitions, and lawful games, and may fix the rates of the license fee and provide for its collection by suit or otherwise. These are two independent, overlapping statutory grants of essentially the same core authority — one framed around a city's revenue and regulation power, the other around a city's police power — rather than a single unified statute, and this document does not treat them as the same enactment.
clauses.gap: These are two of this state's statutes, used as real evidence of California cities' own statutory authority to license business — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific business's obligations, and not a claim that other states grant their cities an identical or even similar licensing power. This clause cites two different statutory sections in two different codes, Cal. Gov. Code § 37101(a) and Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(a), each independently verified; they are treated as two separate, overlapping sources of city licensing authority, not as subsections of one section or as one source restated. Neither statute itself names a specific city's license or certificate, sets its fee, or defines its application procedure; the specific license or tax that any given city actually imposes under this authority is set by that city's own ordinance and varies by city, and this document does not and cannot state what any specific city requires. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself obtain a local business license or business tax certificate for the business named in this document or any other person, and it does not determine whether any specific business or city requires one.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 37101(a)
citations.cite: Government Code, Title 4 (Government of Cities), Chapter 3 (General Powers), business license for revenue and regulation
citations.quote: The legislative body may license, for revenue and regulation, and fix the license tax upon, every kind of lawful business transacted in the city, including shows, exhibitions, and games.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(a)
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code, Division 7 (General Business Regulations), Chapter 1 (Licensing by Cities), police-power license for regulation
citations.quote: The legislative body of an incorporated city may, in the exercise of its police power, and for the purpose of regulation, as herein provided, and not otherwise, license any kind of business not prohibited by law transacted and carried on within the limits of its jurisdiction, including all shows, exhibitions and lawful games, and may fix the rates of the license fee and provide for its collection by suit or otherwise.

clauses.title: Statutory Authority for a County to License Business for Revenue and Regulation
clauses.body: A California county's authority to license business is set out in a separate statute from the city authority described elsewhere in this document. Revenue and Taxation Code Section 7284(a) states that the board of supervisors of any county may license, for revenue and regulation, and fix the license tax upon, every kind of lawful business transacted in the unincorporated area of the county, including shows, exhibitions, and games, and that the board may provide for collecting that license tax by suit or otherwise. By its own terms, this statute reaches business activity in a county's unincorporated area; it does not itself extend a county's licensing power to activity within an incorporated city located inside that county, which is instead addressed by the city licensing statutes described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California counties' own statutory authority to license business in unincorporated areas — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific business's obligations, and not a claim that other states grant their counties an identical or even similar licensing power. This clause quotes a single statutory section, Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 7284(a), so no same-section multiple-subsection issue arises here. This statute does not itself name a specific county's license or certificate, set its fee, or define its application procedure; the specific license or tax that any given county actually imposes under this authority is set by that county's own ordinance and varies by county, and this document does not and cannot state what any specific county requires. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself obtain a local business license or business tax certificate for the business named in this document or any other person, and it does not determine whether any specific business or county requires one.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 7284(a)
citations.cite: Revenue and Taxation Code, Part 1.7 (Additional Local Taxes), Chapter 1.5 (Local Agency Levy Powers and Limitations), county license for revenue and regulation
citations.quote: The board of supervisors of any county may license, for revenue and regulation, and fix the license tax upon, every kind of lawful business transacted in the unincorporated area of the county, including shows, exhibitions, and games.

clauses.title: Multi-Jurisdiction Apportionment and the Nonprofit/Clergy Exemption from an Income- or Gross-Receipts-Measured License Tax
clauses.body: The same statute that grants a city's licensing authority also limits how that authority may be exercised. Government Code Section 37101(b) states that any legislative body, including the legislative body of a charter city, that levies a license tax on a business operating both within and outside its taxing jurisdiction must levy the tax so that the measure of the tax fairly reflects the proportion of the taxed activity actually carried on within that jurisdiction. Government Code Section 37101(c) separately states that no license tax that is measured by a licensee's income or gross receipts, whether levied by a charter or general law city, may apply to a nonprofit organization exempted from taxes under the specified state and federal nonprofit-exemption provisions, or to a minister, clergyperson, Christian Science practitioner, rabbi, or priest of a religious organization granted a federal income tax exemption under Internal Revenue Code Section 501(c)(3) or a successor provision. Business and Professions Code Section 16000(b), the parallel provision tied to the separate police-power licensing statute described elsewhere in this document, states essentially the same nonprofit and clergy exemption from a license fee measured by income or gross receipts.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutory framework, used as real evidence of California's own apportionment rule and its nonprofit/clergy exemption from an income- or gross-receipts-measured local license tax or fee — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific business's or organization's obligations, and not a claim that other states impose the same apportionment rule or grant the same exemption. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Gov. Code § 37101(b) and § 37101(c); these two subsections are treated as one source on two related points within a single enactment, not as independent corroborating sources. The clause additionally cites a separate section of a different code, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(b), as an independently verified, parallel provision on the nonprofit/clergy exemption tied to that other statute's own police-power licensing authority. Neither statute exempts a nonprofit organization or clergy member from every local business license or business tax certificate requirement — the exemption described here reaches only a license tax or fee measured by income or gross receipts — and any exemption an organization or individual actually receives, and any apportionment a specific city applies, depends on that city's own ordinance, which this document does not and cannot state. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether the business or organization named in this document, or any other specific person or entity, qualifies for this exemption or any local apportionment rule.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 37101(b)
citations.cite: Government Code, Title 4 (Government of Cities), Chapter 3 (General Powers), apportionment for multi-jurisdiction business
citations.quote: Any legislative body, including the legislative body of a charter city, that levies a license tax pursuant to subdivision (a) upon a business operating both within and outside the legislative body’s taxing jurisdiction, shall levy the tax so that the measure of tax fairly reflects that proportion of the taxed activity actually carried on within the taxing jurisdiction.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 37101(c)
citations.cite: Government Code, Title 4 (Government of Cities), Chapter 3 (General Powers), nonprofit and clergy exemption from an income/gross-receipts-measured license tax
citations.quote: No license tax levied pursuant to subdivision (a) that is measured by the licensee’s income or gross receipts, whether levied by a charter or general law city, shall apply to any nonprofit organization that is exempted from taxes by Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 23701) of Part 11 of Division 2 of the Revenue and Taxation Code or Subchapter F (commencing with Section 501) of Chapter 1 of Subtitle A of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, or the successor of either, or to any minister, clergyperson, Christian Science practitioner, rabbi, or priest of any religious organization that has been granted an exemption from federal income tax by the United States Commissioner of Internal Revenue as an organization described in Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code or a successor to that section.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(b)
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code, Division 7 (General Business Regulations), Chapter 1 (Licensing by Cities), parallel nonprofit and clergy exemption
citations.quote: No license fee levied pursuant to subdivision (a) that is measured by the licensee’s income or gross receipts, whether levied by a charter or general law city, shall apply to any nonprofit organization that is exempted from taxes by Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 23701) of Part 11 of Division 2 of the Revenue and Taxation Code or Subchapter F (commencing with Section 501) of Chapter 1 of Subtitle A of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, or the successor of either, or to any minister, clergyman, Christian Science practitioner, rabbi, or priest of any religious organization that has been granted an exemption from federal income tax by the United States Commissioner of Internal Revenue as an organization described in Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code or a successor to that section.

clauses.title: Contractor License Verification Before Issuance, and the Disabled-Veteran Peddler Exemption
clauses.body: Two further, unrelated provisions of the same Business and Professions Code chapter that authorizes city business licensing also constrain or exempt from that authority. Business and Professions Code Section 16000(c) states that before a city, including a charter city, issues a business license to a person to conduct business as a contractor, as defined in Business and Professions Code Section 7026, the city must verify that the person is licensed by the Contractors' State License Board. Business and Professions Code Section 16001 separately states that every honorably discharged or honorably relieved soldier, sailor, or marine who served in an enumerated list of wars, who is physically unable to obtain a livelihood by manual labor, and who is a voter of California, may distribute circulars and hawk, peddle, and vend goods, wares, or merchandise the person owns — other than intoxicating liquor — without paying any license tax or fee, whether municipal, county, or state, and that the legislative body must issue that person a license for it without cost.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutory framework, used as real evidence of two specific California constraints on local business licensing power — a contractor-license verification step and a disabled-veteran peddler exemption — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific business's or individual's obligations, and not a claim that other states impose an identical verification step or grant an identical exemption. This clause cites two different sections of the same code, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(c) and § 16001, addressing two distinct and unrelated topics; they are treated as two independent points, not as corroborating each other or as one combined rule. Section 16001's enumerated list of wars (through World War II) reflects the statute's text as currently codified and verified on the checkedDate above; this document does not opine on whether, or how, that list has been or should be judicially or administratively applied to a currently living veteran. Neither provision states what license, if any, a specific city actually requires, or how a specific city implements the contractor-verification step or processes a veteran's exemption claim; those specifics are set by each city's own ordinance and procedure. This information sheet is informational only: it does not verify any contractor's license, does not determine whether any specific person qualifies for the exemption described in Section 16001, and does not itself obtain a local business license or business tax certificate, or an exemption from one, for the business or person named in this document or any other person.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(c)
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code, Division 7 (General Business Regulations), Chapter 1 (Licensing by Cities), contractor license verification before issuance
citations.quote: Before a city, including a charter city, issues a business license to a person to conduct business as a contractor, as defined in Section 7026, the city shall verify that the person is licensed by the Contractors’ State License Board.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16001
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code, Division 7 (General Business Regulations), Chapter 1 (Licensing by Cities), disabled-veteran peddler exemption
citations.quote: Every honorably discharged or honorably relieved soldier, sailor, or marine of the United States or Confederate States who served in the Civil War, any Indian war, the Spanish-American War, any Philippine insurrection, the Chinese Relief Expedition, the World War of 1914 and years following, or World War II, who is physically unable to obtain a livelihood by manual labor, and who is a voter of this state, may distribute circulars, and hawk, peddle, and vend any goods, wares or merchandise owned by him, except spirituous, malt, vinous, or other intoxicating liquor, without payment of any license tax or fee whatsoever, whether municipal, county or state, and the legislative body shall issue to such soldier, sailor or marine, without cost, a license therefor.

clauses.title: No Statewide Fee Cap Found; Voter-Approval Requirement for Local Tax Increases Under Article XIII C
clauses.body: None of the constitutional or statutory provisions reviewed for this document set a statewide dollar cap, statewide rate ceiling, or statewide uniformity standard on the amount a city or county may charge for a local business license or business tax certificate; on the contrary, Government Code Section 37101(a) and Business and Professions Code Section 16000(a), described elsewhere in this document, each state that a city's legislative body "may fix" the license tax or license fee, and Revenue and Taxation Code Section 7284(a) uses the same "may fix" language for a county's board of supervisors. What state law does impose is a procedural constraint on increasing certain local taxes, not a fee ceiling. Article XIII C, Section 2 of the California Constitution, added by a 1996 voter initiative, states that no local government may impose, extend, or increase any general tax unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a majority vote, and separately states that no local government may impose, extend, or increase any special tax unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote. Where a city's or county's business license charge is structured as a tax within the meaning of this constitutional article, rather than as a regulatory fee, this voter-approval requirement can apply to a new levy or a rate increase; the article does not, however, set a numeric ceiling on what a voter-approved local business license tax or business tax certificate fee may be.
clauses.gap: This is one state's constitution and statutes, used as real evidence that California imposes no statewide dollar cap or uniformity standard on a local business license fee or tax, and that a distinct constitutional voter-approval procedure instead applies to certain local tax increases — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific city's or county's charge, and not a claim that other states cap local business license fees or require voter approval to raise them. This clause cites two subsections of the same constitutional section, Cal. Const. art. XIII C, § 2(b) and § 2(d); these two subsections are treated as one source on two related points (general-tax and special-tax voter approval) within a single enactment, not as independent corroborating sources. This clause also references, without re-quoting, the "may fix" language of Cal. Gov. Code § 37101(a), Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16000(a), and Cal. Rev. & Tax Code § 7284(a), each of which is separately cited and quoted in full in its own clause elsewhere in this document; those references are not offered here as additional independent citations for this clause. Whether a specific city's or county's business license charge is a "general tax," a "special tax," or a regulatory fee outside Article XIII C's voter-approval requirement, and what fee or tax amount a specific city or county actually charges, are determined by that city's or county's own ordinance and enactment history, which this document does not and cannot state. This information sheet is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific local business license charge is subject to Article XIII C's voter-approval requirement, has received the voter approval that requirement demands, or is instead a fee outside that requirement.

citations.case: Cal. Const. art. XIII C, § 2(b)
citations.cite: California Constitution, Article XIII C (Voter Approval for Local Tax Levies), voter approval for a general tax
citations.quote: No local government may impose, extend, or increase any general tax unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a majority vote.

citations.case: Cal. Const. art. XIII C, § 2(d)
citations.cite: California Constitution, Article XIII C (Voter Approval for Local Tax Levies), voter approval for a special tax
citations.quote: No local government may impose, extend, or increase any special tax unless and until that tax is submitted to the electorate and approved by a two-thirds vote.
