clauses.title: Confirming the Actual Agency Relationship, in Writing
clauses.body: Separate from the general disclosure form describing the possible kinds of agency relationship, California statutory law requires the agent's actual relationship in a specific transaction to be confirmed in writing. As soon as practicable, the buyer's agent must disclose to both the buyer and the seller whether that agent is acting as the buyer's agent or as a dual agent representing both; this relationship must then be confirmed in the purchase-and-sale contract itself, or in a separate writing executed or acknowledged by the seller, the buyer, and the buyer's agent, prior to or coincident with execution of that contract by the buyer and seller. As soon as practicable, the seller's agent must likewise disclose to the seller whether that agent is acting as the seller's agent or as a dual agent, confirmed in the contract or a separate writing executed or acknowledged by the seller and the seller's agent, prior to or coincident with the seller's execution of the contract. The statute prescribes a specific checkbox form for this confirmation, under which each named agent's brokerage and license number is identified as representing the seller, the buyer, or both as a dual agent. This confirmation requirement is in addition to — not a substitute for — the general disclosure form described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's confirmation requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific transaction. The four citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2079.17) and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself confirm, execute, or acknowledge any agent's actual role in this or any other transaction, and it does not satisfy the written confirmation that this statute requires — that confirmation must appear in the actual purchase contract or a separate signed writing meeting the statutory form, not in this information sheet.

clauses.title: Required Content of Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Articles
clauses.body: California's Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law contains its own required-content statute for a mutual benefit corporation's articles of incorporation, separate from the required-content statute that governs a nonprofit public benefit corporation and separate again from the one that governs an ordinary for-profit corporation. The mutual benefit statute requires the filed articles to state: the corporation's name; a specific, statutorily prescribed statement that the corporation "is a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation organized under the Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law" and that its purpose "is to engage in any lawful act or activity, other than credit union business, for which a corporation may be organized under such law" (two narrow exceptions substitute other prescribed purpose language for a corporation formed under the California Credit Union Law or as a statutorily defined public bank, and the articles may, but need not, add a further definition of the corporation's purposes); the name and California street address of the corporation's initial agent for service of process; the corporation's initial street address; and its initial mailing address, if that differs from the street address. Unlike the required content for a nonprofit public benefit corporation's articles, the mutual benefit statute's fixed statement does not ask the incorporator to elect "public" or "charitable" purposes, and does not make any further purpose description mandatory — a further description is optional in every case for a mutual benefit corporation, where it is mandatory for a public benefit corporation electing "public" purposes. As with a nonprofit public benefit corporation, nothing in this list calls for a statement of authorized shares — a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation has no shareholders and issues no stock; it has members instead.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what one state's required formation-document content for this specific type of nonprofit corporation looks like — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's formation, and required content for a nonprofit corporation's founding filing varies by state. The two citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 7130, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, file anything with the California Secretary of State, or determine whether any corporation qualifies for federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate determination made by the Internal Revenue Service under federal law, not by this document or by the California statute it describes.

(b) (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2) or (3), the following statement: “This corporation is a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation organized under the Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law. The purpose of this corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity, other than credit union business, for which a corporation may be organized under such law.”

clauses.title: Mutual Benefit Purpose Distinguished From Public Benefit Purpose
clauses.body: California's Nonprofit Corporation Law separates its three nonprofit corporation types by statute, not merely by convention, and a mutual benefit corporation's authorizing statute states the dividing line in its own text. A corporation may be formed under the Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law "for any lawful purpose," but the same statute affirmatively bars from that part any corporation whose assets are irrevocably dedicated to charitable, religious, or public purposes and which, by law or by its own articles or bylaws, must distribute its assets on dissolution to a person carrying on a charitable, religious, or public purpose — that kind of corporation belongs instead under the Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law or the Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law. The mutual benefit naming statute reinforces the same line from the other direction: the Secretary of State will not file mutual benefit articles setting forth a name that "may create the impression that the purpose of the corporation is public, charitable, or religious or that it is a charitable foundation." Read together, these are the statutory basis for describing a mutual benefit corporation's purpose as something other than a public or charitable one — an organization such as a trade association, homeowners association, business league, or social club, formed for a lawful purpose that does not carry the irrevocable public/charitable asset dedication a public benefit or religious corporation carries, and whose formation filing and name may not represent that it does.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of how that one state's Corporations Code itself draws the line between a mutual benefit and a public benefit purpose — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and the mutual/public benefit distinction, and the vocabulary used to describe it, vary by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 7111 and Cal. Corp. Code § 7122, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation and does not determine which nonprofit category best fits a specific organization's activities or a specific corporation's federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate IRS determination this document does not make.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 7111
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, the "any lawful purpose" authorization and its charitable/religious/public-purpose exclusion
citations.quote: Subject to any other provision of law of this state applying to the particular class of corporation or line of activity, a corporation may be formed under this part for any lawful purpose; provided that a corporation all of the assets of which are irrevocably dedicated to charitable, religious, or public purposes and which as a matter of law or according to its articles or bylaws must, upon dissolution, distribute its assets to a person or persons carrying on a charitable, religious, or public purpose or purposes may not be formed under this part.

clauses.title: Federal Tax-Exempt Status Is a Separate Federal Question the State Statute Does Not Answer
clauses.body: Nothing in California's Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law — including the required purpose statement discussed above — addresses federal tax-exempt status; the state formation statute governs only what must appear in the articles filed with the California Secretary of State, and is silent on the separate question of federal tax treatment. Federal tax-exempt recognition is governed entirely by the Internal Revenue Code and administered by the IRS, under provisions distinct from the 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) charitable-organization status commonly associated with public benefit corporations. Because a mutual benefit corporation's own statutory purpose is not limited to charitable, religious, or public purposes, a mutual benefit corporation is not the kind of organization § 501(c)(3) describes; organizations of the kind California law calls "mutual benefit" — for example trade associations, business leagues, or civic and social welfare organizations — more commonly correspond to other Internal Revenue Code categories, such as § 501(c)(4), covering "civic leagues or organizations not organized for profit but operated exclusively for the promotion of social welfare," or § 501(c)(6), covering "business leagues, chambers of commerce, real-estate boards, boards of trade" and similar organizations not organized for profit. Each of those federal categories has its own separate eligibility requirements under federal law, and qualifying for one is a distinct, later step from forming the corporation under California's mutual benefit statute; the state statute does not require, guarantee, or evaluate eligibility for any of them.
clauses.gap: The Internal Revenue Code is federal law, not California law; it is cited here as evidence of a separate, nationwide requirement layered on top of state law for any organization, in any state, that wants federal tax-exempt recognition — not as evidence of what California itself requires. The two federal citations below are subsections of the same Internal Revenue Code section, 26 U.S.C. § 501(c), so they are treated as one source illustrating a category of federal provisions, not two independent corroborating sources, and they are not exhaustive of every federal exemption category a mutual benefit-type organization might potentially fit. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation and does not determine federal tax-exempt status for any organization under any Internal Revenue Code provision — that determination is made by the IRS, not by this document or by the California statute it describes.

citations.quote: (4)(A) Civic leagues or organizations not organized for profit but operated exclusively for the promotion of social welfare, or local associations of employees, the membership of which is limited to the employees of a designated person or persons in a particular municipality, and the net earnings of which are devoted exclusively to charitable, educational, or recreational purposes.

citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, business leagues and similar organizations exemption category
citations.quote: (6) Business leagues, chambers of commerce, real-estate boards, boards of trade, or professional football leagues (whether or not administering a pension fund for football players), not organized for profit and no part of the net earnings of which inures to the benefit of any private shareholder or individual.

clauses.title: Distributions to Members Restricted Outside of Dissolution
clauses.body: California's Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law contains its own distributions chapter, and its central rule reads, on its face, almost the same as the flat no-distributions rule that applies to a nonprofit public benefit corporation: "no corporation shall make any distribution except upon dissolution," subject only to a narrow carve-out letting a corporation purchase or redeem memberships, itself conditioned on meeting further statutory requirements found elsewhere in the same chapter. That provision, by its own terms, does not apply to the winding-up and dissolution process itself — dissolution-stage asset distribution is instead governed by a separate set of statutes. Put together, these two sections mean that while a mutual benefit corporation is an ongoing, operating entity, it is barred from distributing its earnings or assets to its members in the way a business corporation pays dividends to shareholders, aside from the narrow membership purchase-or-redemption exception; the statutory feature that actually distinguishes a mutual benefit corporation from a public benefit corporation is not a general license to pay profits to members while operating, but rather what happens to remaining assets specifically at dissolution, addressed in a separate clause below.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of a distinct, statute-based restriction and its scope in that one state — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and whether a state restricts distributions by a mutual-benefit-type nonprofit corporation, and how, varies by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 7410 and Cal. Corp. Code § 7411, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation and does not determine federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate IRS determination this document does not make.

citations.quote: This chapter does not apply to any proceeding for winding up and dissolution of corporations under Chapters 15 (commencing with Section 8510), 16 (commencing with Section 8610), and 17 (commencing with Section 8710).

clauses.title: Dissolution: Remaining Assets May Be Distributed to Members
clauses.body: California's dissolution statutes for a nonprofit mutual benefit corporation state a genuinely different rule for what happens to remaining assets than the rule that applies to a nonprofit public benefit corporation. After a mutual benefit corporation's board determines that known debts and liabilities have been paid or adequately provided for, the board distributes the remaining corporate assets under a specific statutory sequence. That sequence provides that if the articles or bylaws state how remaining assets are to be disposed of, they are disposed of that way; but if the articles and bylaws do not provide a manner of disposition, the statute itself supplies a default rule: the assets "shall be distributed among the members in accordance with their respective rights therein." A nonprofit public benefit corporation's remaining assets, by contrast, are disposed of in conformity with its own articles or bylaws too, but subject to any charitable trust under which the assets are held and ordinarily only by a superior court decree in a proceeding to which the California Attorney General is a party — and a related federal tax regulation treats an organization's assets as failing the federal tax-exemption "organizational test" if dissolution assets could go to the organization's own members. A mutual benefit corporation's default dissolution rule runs the other way: absent a contrary articles or bylaws provision, distribution to members is exactly what the statute itself directs.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of that state's own dissolution-distribution rule for this specific type of nonprofit corporation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's dissolution, and default asset-distribution rules on a nonprofit's dissolution vary by state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 8713 and Cal. Corp. Code § 8717, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only: it does not itself form, dissolve, or wind up any corporation, and it does not determine federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate IRS determination this document does not make — an organization that has obtained federal tax-exempt recognition under a category with its own asset-dedication requirements may face federal constraints on member distributions that this state-law default rule, by itself, does not address.

citations.cite: California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, the board's duty to distribute remaining assets after paying debts
citations.quote: After determining that all the known debts and liabilities of a corporation in the process of winding up have been paid or adequately provided for, the board shall distribute all the remaining corporate assets in the manner provided in Sections 8715 to 8717, inclusive.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 8717(a)-(b)

citations.quote: After complying with the provisions of Section 8713 and except as otherwise provided in Sections 8715 and 8716, assets held by a corporation shall be disposed of on dissolution as follows: (a) If the articles or bylaws provide the manner of disposition, the assets shall be disposed of in that manner. (b) If the articles or bylaws do not provide the manner of disposition, the assets shall be distributed among the members in accordance with their respective rights therein.

clauses.title: Member Approval Required for Sale of Substantially All Assets and for Mergers
clauses.body: California's Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law requires member approval, not board approval alone, for certain major transactions. A mutual benefit corporation may sell, lease, convey, exchange, transfer, or otherwise dispose of all or substantially all of its assets only when the principal terms are approved by the board, and — unless the transaction is in the corporation's usual and regular course of activities — also approved by the members, whose approval may come either before or after the board's approval and either before or after the transaction itself. A comparable member-approval requirement applies to mergers: the principal terms of a merger must be approved by the members of each class of each constituent corporation, in addition to whatever other approvals the articles independently require, and that member approval may likewise be given before or after the board's approval. In both cases, the statute gives members of a mutual benefit corporation a direct statutory voice in a transaction that could fundamentally change or end the corporation, beyond whatever role the board plays.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of specific transactions that this state's mutual benefit corporation law requires members to approve — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation's transactions, not a complete inventory of every transaction requiring member approval under this law, and not a claim about member-approval requirements in any other state. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 7911 and Cal. Corp. Code § 8012, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, does not itself effect any sale of assets or merger, and does not determine federal tax-exempt status, which is a separate IRS determination this document does not make.

clauses.title: California's Statutory Right of Publicity: The Knowing-Use Standard and Statutory Remedies for Living Persons
clauses.body: California's principal right-of-publicity statute creates civil liability for any person who knowingly uses another's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, in any manner, on or in products, merchandise, or goods, or for purposes of advertising or selling, or soliciting purchases of, products, merchandise, goods, or services, without that person's prior consent (or, for a minor, the prior consent of a parent or legal guardian). The statute's own text requires a "knowing" use — it is not a strict-liability standard that reaches an innocent or unaware use. Where liability is established, the statute sets the injured party's recovery at the greater of $750 or the person's actual damages, and separately allows recovery of any profits from the unauthorized use that are not already counted in that actual-damages figure — meaning the statutory floor and the disgorgement-of-profits remedy are cumulative with each other, not alternatives a plaintiff must choose between. The statute places the burden of proving gross revenue attributable to the use on the injured party, and the burden of proving deductible expenses on the person who violated the statute. Punitive damages may also be awarded. Separately, the statute makes the prevailing party in any action under this section entitled to attorney's fees and costs — a mandatory, prevailing-party fee-shifting rule that is not limited to a prevailing plaintiff and does not depend on a discretionary "exceptional case" finding of the kind this tool's Trademark Infringement Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet describes for federal trademark claims.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Civil Code section 3344, specifically subdivision (a)(1)), used as real evidence of California's statutory right-of-publicity standard for living persons — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's actual situation, and not a claim that the conduct described on this sheet meets the knowing-use standard, satisfies any element, or would result in any particular damages award, all of which this clause does not resolve. Both citations below are to the same statutory subdivision, Section 3344(a)(1); they are quoted as two separate passages because they address two distinct topics within that one subdivision — the conduct the statute prohibits, and the remedies available for it — not because they are independent corroborating sources. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness violates Section 3344 or any other right, and completing or sending this information sheet does not itself send any cease-and-desist letter.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, right of publicity — knowing-use standard for living persons
citations.quote: Any person who knowingly uses another’s name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, in any manner, on or in products, merchandise, or goods, or for purposes of advertising or selling, or soliciting purchases of, products, merchandise, goods, or services, without that person’s prior consent, or, in the case of a minor, the prior consent of their parent or legal guardian, shall be liable for any damages sustained by the person or persons injured as a result thereof.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3344(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, statutory damages, profits, punitive damages, and prevailing-party attorney's fees
citations.quote: the person who violated the section shall be liable to the injured party or parties in an amount equal to the greater of seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) or the actual damages suffered by them as a result of the unauthorized use, and any profits from the unauthorized use that are attributable to the use and are not taken into account in computing the actual damages. In establishing these profits, the injured party or parties are required to present proof only of the gross revenue attributable to the unauthorized use, and the person who violated this section is required to prove their deductible expenses. Punitive damages may also be awarded to the injured party or parties. The prevailing party in any action under this section shall also be entitled to attorney’s fees and costs.

clauses.title: A 2025 Amendment: Injunctions, Temporary Restraining Orders, and a Two-Business-Day Compliance Window
clauses.body: In addition to the damages, profits, punitive-damages, and attorney's-fee remedies described elsewhere in this document, California's statute separately allows a party to seek an injunction or temporary restraining order under Code of Civil Procedure section 527. The statute further provides that if a court grants an order under Code of Civil Procedure section 527(c) requiring the respondent to remove, recall, or otherwise cease the publication or distribution of the petitioner's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, the respondent must complete that removal, recall, or cessation within two business days of being served with the order, unless the order itself states otherwise. This injunctive-relief provision was added to the statute by a 2025 amendment effective January 1, 2026, and is current law as of the date this clause was checked.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Civil Code section 3344, subdivision (a)(2)), used as real evidence that this injunctive-relief mechanism and compliance deadline exist in current California law — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any court would grant, or that any party is entitled to, an injunction or temporary restraining order with respect to any specific use described on this sheet. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision; no additional independent source was needed for it. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness violates Section 3344 or any other right, and completing or sending this information sheet does not itself send any cease-and-desist letter or seek any injunction or restraining order from any court.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3344(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)

citations.quote: In addition to the remedies available in paragraph (1), a party may seek an injunction or temporary restraining order pursuant to Section 527 of the Code of Civil Procedure. If the court grants the applicant an order under subdivision (c) of Section 527 of the Code of Civil Procedure that requires the respondent to remove, recall, or otherwise cease the publication or distribution of the petitioner’s name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, the respondent shall complete the removal or recall, or cease the publication or distribution, within two business days from the day the order is served, unless otherwise required by the order.

clauses.title: Statutory Exceptions: News and Political Use, Commercial-Medium Sponsorship, and the Innocent-Publisher Exemption
clauses.body: California's living-person right-of-publicity statute contains three distinct, narrow carve-outs, rather than one general exemption. First, a use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness in connection with any news, public affairs, or sports broadcast or account, or any political campaign, is not a use for which consent is required. Second, use in a commercial medium is not automatically exempt merely because the material containing the use is commercially sponsored or contains paid advertising — the statute makes this a question of fact, turning on whether the use was so directly connected with the commercial sponsorship or paid advertising as to itself require consent. Third, the statute exempts the owners or employees of an advertising medium (the statute's own examples include newspapers, magazines, radio and television networks and stations, cable television systems, billboards, and transit ads) who publish or disseminate someone else's violating advertisement or solicitation, unless it is established that those owners or employees had knowledge of the unauthorized use — an innocent-publisher defense that runs to the medium, not to the person who created the unauthorized use. None of these three provisions is the same as the "single and original work of fine art" language that appears in California's separate posthumous right-of-publicity statute, addressed in another clause of this document; the living-person statute does not contain that specific phrase.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own statutory carve-outs for living persons — not a claim that any specific use described on this sheet falls within, or outside, any of these exceptions, which depends on facts this clause does not resolve, and not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. This clause cites three subdivisions of the same statutory section, Cal. Civ. Code § 3344 — subdivisions (d), (e), and (f) — and they are not independent sources; all three are grouped together here because they together describe the statute's own exceptions to the consent requirement, not because they corroborate one another. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness violates Section 3344 or any other right, and completing or sending this information sheet does not itself send any cease-and-desist letter.

clauses.title: The Posthumous Right of Publicity Under Section 3344.1: The Same Remedies, But No 'Knowing Use' Requirement in the Statutory Text
clauses.body: California has a separate statute addressing the right of publicity of a deceased personality. Its liability standard tracks the living-person statute in most respects — a person who uses a deceased personality's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, in any manner, on or in products, merchandise, or goods, or for purposes of advertising or selling, or soliciting purchases of, products, merchandise, goods, or services, without prior consent from the statutorily specified person or persons, is liable, with the same remedy structure: the greater of $750 or actual damages, plus profits not already counted in actual damages, potential punitive damages, and prevailing-party attorney's fees and costs. But comparing the two sections' actual text side by side reveals a real difference: the living-person statute's operative sentence begins "Any person who knowingly uses...," while the posthumous statute's operative sentence begins "a person who uses a deceased personality's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness... without prior consent... shall be liable" — with no "knowingly" or other knowledge qualifier appearing in that sentence. On the statutory text alone, the posthumous claim is not conditioned on the same knowing-use language that the living-person claim's own text requires.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's posthumous right-of-publicity standard and of a specific textual difference between it and the living-person statute — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific use described on this sheet meets either statute's standard. This clause cites one subdivision of Cal. Civ. Code § 3344.1 (subdivision (a)(1)(A)) together with, for direct textual comparison only, the same subdivision of the separate statutory section, Cal. Civ. Code § 3344(a)(1), that is independently cited and quoted in this document's "California's Statutory Right of Publicity" clause; these are two different statutory sections presented side by side for comparison, not corroborating citations to the same source. This document was not able to independently verify, through a citable, primary-source case, whether California's common-law right of publicity (which this document does not otherwise source, as disclosed in its introductory clause) also requires proof of knowledge, or instead reaches an unaware use the way the posthumous statute's text appears to: a CourtListener case-law search for Eastwood v. Superior Court and for the elements of California's common-law right-of-publicity claim was attempted for this document but returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, daily limit reported as exhausted) before any case could be retrieved and independently verified, so no case citation on that point is included here. clauses.title: The Posthumous Right's 70-Year Duration, Statutory Successors, and the Secretary of State Registration Requirement
clauses.body: California's posthumous right-of-publicity statute is time-limited: an action may not be brought under the statute by reason of any use of a deceased personality's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness occurring after the expiration of 70 years after the death of the deceased personality. The statute vests these rights, after death, in specified persons and allows the right to be exercised, on behalf of and for the benefit of all of them, by those who together hold more than a one-half interest — the statute's own formula then allocates that interest among a surviving spouse, surviving children and grandchildren, or surviving parents, depending on who survives the deceased personality. The statute also conditions a successor-in-interest's or licensee's ability to recover damages on registration: a successor in interest or licensee may not recover damages for a use that occurs before that person registers a claim of rights with the California Secretary of State, on a prescribed, verified form that must include the deceased personality's name and date of death, the claimant's name and address, the basis of the claim, and the rights claimed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's posthumous right's duration, the statutory scheme for who may hold and exercise it, and the Secretary of State registration precondition to recovering damages — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific person is or is not a statutory successor in interest to any deceased personality's rights, which depends on facts (survivorship, testamentary instruments, and registration status) this clause does not resolve. This clause cites four provisions of the same statutory section, Cal. Civ. Code § 3344.1 — subdivision (d) (who holds the rights after death), subdivision (f)(1) and (f)(2) (the registration precondition and process), and subdivision (g) (the 70-year duration limit) — and they are not independent sources; all four are grouped together here because they together describe one statutory scheme governing the posthumous right's holders, its registration precondition, and its duration, not because they corroborate one another. clauses.title: The Posthumous Statute's Entertainment-Work and Single-and-Original-Work-of-Art Exemption
clauses.body: California's posthumous right-of-publicity statute contains an exemption with no identically worded counterpart in the living-person statute described elsewhere in this document. A play, book, magazine, newspaper, musical composition, audiovisual work, radio or television program, single and original work of art, work of political or newsworthy value, or an advertisement or commercial announcement for any of these works, is not considered a "product, article of merchandise, good, or service" under the statute if it is fictional or nonfictional entertainment, or a dramatic, literary, or musical work — meaning a deceased personality's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness used within such a work generally falls outside the conduct the statute otherwise reaches. The statute narrows that exemption, however, for a use within such a work that functions as advertising: if the work includes a use connected with a product, article of merchandise, good, or service, that specific use is not exempt if the claimant proves it is so directly connected with the product, article of merchandise, good, or service as to constitute an act of advertising, selling, or soliciting purchases of it by the deceased personality without the required consent. In other words, the exemption protects the work itself but does not extend to a merchandising or advertising use embedded within an otherwise-exempt work.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own posthumous-statute exemption for entertainment and fine-art works, and of its carve-back for advertising uses embedded in such works — not a claim that any specific work or use described on this sheet falls within, or outside, this exemption, which depends on facts this clause does not resolve, and not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. This clause cites two clauses within a single statutory subparagraph of Cal. Civ. Code § 3344.1 — subparagraph (a)(1)(B)'s clause (i) (the exemption) and clause (ii) (the advertising carve-back) — and they are not independent sources; both are quoted together because clause (ii) is the express limit on the exemption clause (i) creates, not a separate corroborating provision. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness violates Section 3344.1 or any other right, and completing or sending this information sheet does not itself send any cease-and-desist letter.

clauses.title: A 2024 Amendment: The Digital Replica Provision for AI-Generated Voice or Likeness of a Deceased Personality
clauses.body: A 2024 amendment to California's posthumous right-of-publicity statute, effective January 1, 2025, added a separate liability provision aimed at AI-generated "digital replicas." A person who produces, distributes, or makes available the digital replica of a deceased personality's voice or likeness in an expressive audiovisual work or sound recording, without prior consent from the statutorily specified person or persons, is liable to the injured party in an amount equal to the greater of $10,000 or actual damages — a statutory minimum substantially higher than the $750 minimum that applies under the statute's general provision described elsewhere in this document. The statute defines "digital replica" as a computer-generated, highly realistic electronic representation, readily identifiable as an individual's voice or visual likeness, embodied in a sound recording, image, audiovisual work, or transmission, where the individual either did not actually perform or appear, or did perform or appear but the fundamental character of that performance or appearance has been materially altered; the definition expressly excludes ordinary electronic reproduction, sampling, remixing, mastering, or digital remastering that the copyright holder has authorized. The statute also lists specific circumstances in which a digital replica may be used without consent, including use connected with news, public affairs, or sports broadcasts; use for comment, criticism, scholarship, satire, or parody; a documentary or historical or biographical representation of the individual as themselves (unless intended to, and actually does, create the false impression of an authentic recording); and fleeting or incidental use.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, recently enacted digital-replica liability provision and its own definitions and use-without-consent list — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific content described on this sheet is or is not a "digital replica" within this definition, or falls within any listed use-without-consent circumstance, all of which this clause does not resolve. This clause cites three provisions within a single paragraph of the same statutory section, Cal. Civ. Code § 3344.1(a)(2) — the liability standard in clause (A)(i), the use-without-consent list in clause (A)(ii), and the "digital replica" definition in clause (B)(ii)(I) — and they are not independent sources; all three are grouped together here because they together describe one statutory digital-replica framework, not because they corroborate one another. Because this provision took effect January 1, 2025, it is comparatively recent, and this clause does not represent that any court has yet interpreted its terms. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific content violates Section 3344.1 or any other right, and completing or sending this information sheet does not itself send any cease-and-desist letter.

clauses.title: About This California Paid Sick Leave Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This California Paid Sick Leave — Information Sheet describes California's statewide paid sick leave law, the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act of 2014 (Labor Code §§ 245-249), as it relates to the working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}. It summarizes selected requirements of that law: who accrues paid sick leave and how, the alternative ways an employer may satisfy the accrual requirement, the statute's own permitted reasons for using paid sick leave, its definition of "family member" for that purpose, its anti-retaliation protection, its workplace-posting and recordkeeping duties, and the categories of workers the statute's own definitions exclude from coverage.

This document goes further into the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act than the brief references to paid sick leave already found elsewhere in this project's forms. The Vacation/PTO Payout at Termination document's sick-leave-distinction clause cites a single subsection of the Act — § 246(g)(1) — for the narrow point that accrued sick leave, unlike vacation, need not be paid out at termination; this document does not re-argue that point, but builds on it with the statute's own rehire-reinstatement exception, which that existing clause identifies as outside its own scope. The Wage Theft Prevention Act Notice to Employee document lists "paid sick leave rights" as one of several categories of information a hiring-time notice under a different statute (Labor Code § 2810.5) must contain; it does not describe the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act's own, separate workplace-posting requirement, which this document addresses directly as a distinct statutory duty from that hiring-time notice.

This information sheet is not itself the poster Labor Code § 247 requires an employer to display, does not itself compute or verify any specific amount of accrued or available paid sick leave for {{employeeName}}, and does not determine that any particular policy of {{companyName}}'s is or is not compliant with California law.

clauses.title: The Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act and Its Relationship to Other Rights
clauses.body: California's statewide paid sick leave statute is codified at Labor Code §§ 245 through 249 and states, in its own text, that it "shall be known and may be cited as the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act of 2014." The statute also states, in its own text, that its provisions are in addition to and independent of any other legal rights, remedies, or procedures available under any other law, and that the Act does not diminish, alter, or negate those other rights, remedies, or procedures.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's paid-sick-leave law and its own stated relationship to other legal rights — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation; a majority of states have no equivalent statewide paid-sick-leave mandate at all. Both citations below are to subdivisions (a) and (b) of a single statutory section, Section 245; they are treated here as one source describing the Act's title and its own non-exclusivity clause, not as independent corroborating sources. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself grant, calculate, or deny any specific amount of paid sick leave for any reader, and does not determine that any specific employer's policy is or is not compliant with the Act.

clauses.title: Accrual Rate, the Alternative Accrual and Upfront-Grant Methods, and the Accrual and Usage Caps
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 246, an employee who works for the same employer in California for 30 or more days within a year of the start of employment is entitled to paid sick days as the statute specifies. Absent a different method, an employee accrues paid sick days at a rate of not less than one hour for every 30 hours worked. The statute permits an employer to use a different accrual method instead, provided the accrual happens regularly enough that the employee has no less than 24 hours or 3 days of accrued sick leave (or paid time off usable for the same purposes) by the 120th calendar day of employment, or of each calendar year or 12-month period, and no less than 40 hours or 5 days by the 200th calendar day. Separately, an employer may satisfy the accrual requirement entirely by instead providing the statute's "full amount of leave" — defined as five days or 40 hours — up front, at the beginning of each year of employment, calendar year, or 12-month period, rather than through incremental accrual; where an employer does this, the statute does not require accrual or carryover. Where accrual instead applies, the statute lets an employer limit how much accrued paid sick leave an employee may use in a given year, calendar year, or 12-month period to 40 hours or five days, and separately lets an employer cap an employee's total banked accrual at no more than 80 hours or 10 days, so long as the employee's accrual and use rights are not otherwise limited beyond what the statute allows.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's accrual mechanics — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about what any specific employer's own written policy actually provides. All five citations below are to subdivisions (a)(1), (b)(1), (b)(4), (d), and (j) of a single statutory section, Section 246; they are treated here as one source describing one accrual framework, not as independent corroborating sources. The 40-hours-or-5-days upfront-grant and annual-use figures quoted below are the statute's current, amended figures, effective January 1, 2024 under Stats. 2023, Ch. 309 (SB 616) — the statute's own text, as fetched this session, states the earlier 24-hours-or-3-days upfront figure only as a historical accrual-method threshold tied to an employee's 120th day, not as the current annual full-grant amount; this clause's drafter confirms the quoted text below is the section's present, operative language rather than a superseded, pre-2024 version. This clause does not address subdivision (a)(2)'s separate eligibility rule for in-home supportive services and waiver personal-care-services providers, subdivision (b)(2)'s rule for certain overtime-exempt employees, subdivision (b)(3)'s general alternative-accrual-method rule, subdivision (c)'s 90-day waiting period before newly accrued leave may be used, subdivision (e)'s separate in-home-supportive-services "full amount of leave" phase-in schedule, or subdivision (f)'s rules for employers with a pre-existing paid-leave policy — an honest gap, disclosed rather than covered, because this clause focuses only on the general accrual, alternative-method, upfront-grant, and cap figures. clauses.title: Permitted Reasons for Using Paid Sick Leave
clauses.body: Labor Code § 246.5 requires an employer, upon an employee's oral or written request, to provide paid sick days for specified purposes. The first is diagnosis, care, or treatment of an existing health condition of, or preventive care for, the employee or the employee's family member. The second is use for a purpose described in other, separately cross-referenced statutes addressing leave connected to crime victimization and violence; as currently in effect, that cross-reference points to specified paragraphs of Government Code § 12945.8. The third, added for agricultural employees, permits use to avoid smoke, heat, or flooding conditions created by a proclaimed local or state emergency, including when the employee's worksite is closed because of those conditions. Government Code § 12945.8 in turn defines "qualifying act of violence," for these cross-referenced purposes, as including domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, and, more broadly, any act or pattern of conduct causing bodily injury or death, involving the exhibition or use of a firearm or other dangerous weapon, or involving an actual or threatened use of force to cause physical injury or death.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's own list of permitted paid-sick-leave uses — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The first three citations below are to paragraphs (1), (2), and (3) of subdivision (a) of a single statutory section, Labor Code § 246.5; they are treated here as one source describing one list of permitted uses, not as independent corroborating sources. The fourth citation, to Government Code § 12945.8(j)(5), is to a separate, independently cross-referenced statute, not a further subdivision of § 246.5 itself, and is not treated as corroborating the § 246.5 citations — it is cited because § 246.5(a)(2) itself points to Section 12945.8 for the specific content of this permitted use, and this clause verifies that pointer's current target directly rather than assuming what it says. § 246.5(a)(2)'s text also states a now-superseded, time-limited cross-reference to former Labor Code § 230(c) and § 230.1(a), applicable only to leave taken or requested on or before December 31, 2024; this clause does not independently verify the text of those two former sections, because they are no longer the operative cross-reference for leave requested after that date. Government Code § 12945.8 is a lengthy statute with many subdivisions (definitions, notice duties, accommodation duties, certification procedures, and leave-length limits among them) that this clause does not summarize beyond the single "qualifying act of violence" definition quoted; an honest gap, disclosed rather than covered. clauses.title: The Statute's Definition of "Family Member"
clauses.body: For purposes of using paid sick leave to care for someone other than the employee, Labor Code § 245.5 defines "family member" to mean a child (a biological, adopted, or foster child, a stepchild, a legal ward, or a child to whom the employee stands in loco parentis, regardless of the child's age or dependency status); a biological, adoptive, or foster parent, stepparent, or legal guardian of the employee or of the employee's spouse or registered domestic partner, or a person who stood in loco parentis when the employee was a minor child; a spouse; a registered domestic partner; a grandparent; a grandchild; a sibling; and a "designated person," defined as a person the employee identifies at the time the employee requests paid sick days, which an employer may limit to one designated person per 12-month period.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's paid-sick-leave law itself defines "family member" — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about who any specific reader's own family member is. This clause quotes subdivision (c) of a single statutory section, § 245.5, as one continuous quotation rather than as separately numbered citations, so the multiple-citations-from-one-section disclosure required elsewhere in this document does not apply here in the same way; it remains one statutory source for one definition. The "designated person" category is a comparatively recent addition to this definition, added by Stats. 2023, Ch. 309 (SB 616), effective January 1, 2024, alongside the accrual-figure changes described in this document's accrual clause; a reader relying on an older summary of this statute could reasonably not know that category exists. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific individual is or is not a particular employee's "family member" under this definition, and does not grant, calculate, or deny any specific amount of paid sick leave.

citations.quote: “Family member” means any of the following: (1) A child, which for purposes of this article means a biological, adopted, or foster child, stepchild, legal ward, or a child to whom the employee stands in loco parentis. This definition of a child is applicable regardless of age or dependency status. (2) A biological, adoptive, or foster parent, stepparent, or legal guardian of an employee or the employee’s spouse or registered domestic partner, or a person who stood in loco parentis when the employee was a minor child. (3) A spouse. (4) A registered domestic partner. (5) A grandparent. (6) A grandchild. (7) A sibling. (8) A designated person, which, for purposes of this article, means a person identified by the employee at the time the employee requests paid sick days. An employer may limit an employee to one designated person per 12-month period for paid sick days.

clauses.title: No Payout of Accrued Sick Leave at Termination, With a Rehire-Reinstatement Exception
clauses.body: California's paid-sick-leave statute states directly that, except as specified in a rehire-reinstatement rule, an employer is not required to compensate an employee for accrued, unused paid sick days upon termination, resignation, retirement, or other separation from employment. The statute pairs that no-payout rule with the reinstatement rule itself: if an employee separates from an employer and is rehired by that same employer within one year of the date of separation, the employee's previously accrued and unused paid sick days must be reinstated, and the employee may use those reinstated days and continue accruing more, subject to the statute's usual use-and-accrual limits. The statute also states that an employer is not required to reinstate paid time off that was already paid out to the employee at the time of the earlier termination, resignation, or separation.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own no-payout and rehire-reinstatement rules for accrued paid sick leave — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. Both citations below are to paragraphs (1) and (2) of subdivision (g) of a single statutory section, Labor Code § 246; they are treated here as one source describing one rule and its reinstatement exception, not as independent corroborating sources. This project's existing Vacation/PTO Payout at Termination document already contains a clause, § 246(g)(1)-sourced, distinguishing vacation payout from sick-leave payout; that existing clause expressly states it does not address subdivision (g)(2)'s rehire-reinstatement rule. This clause independently verifies § 246(g)(1) directly this session rather than relying on that existing clause's citation, and adds § 246(g)(2) to cover the gap that clause disclosed; it does not, in turn, repeat that document's discussion of the vacation-versus-combined-PTO distinction, which remains addressed there. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any accrued paid sick leave a particular employee held at a particular employer was or was not paid out, was or was not properly withheld from payout, or is or is not subject to reinstatement, and does not determine that any particular employer's own practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 246.

The employee shall be entitled to use those previously accrued and unused paid sick days and to accrue additional paid sick days upon rehiring, subject to the use and accrual limitations set forth in this section.

clauses.title: Anti-Retaliation Protection for Using or Requesting Paid Sick Leave
clauses.body: Labor Code § 246.5(c) prohibits an employer from denying an employee the right to use accrued sick days, or from discharging, threatening to discharge, demoting, suspending, or otherwise discriminating against an employee, for using accrued sick days, attempting to exercise the right to use them, filing a complaint alleging a violation of the statute, cooperating in an investigation or prosecution of an alleged violation, or opposing a policy, practice, or act the statute prohibits. The statute also creates a rebuttable presumption of unlawful retaliation where an employer denies the right to use accrued sick days, or discharges, threatens to discharge, demotes, suspends, or otherwise discriminates against an employee, within 30 days of that employee filing a complaint with the Labor Commissioner, cooperating with an investigation or prosecution of an alleged violation, or opposing a prohibited policy, practice, or act.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own anti-retaliation protection for paid sick leave — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific adverse action taken against any specific employee was or was not retaliatory. Both citations below are to paragraphs (1) and (2) of subdivision (c) of a single statutory section, Labor Code § 246.5; they are treated here as one source describing the prohibition and its accompanying presumption, not as independent corroborating sources. This anti-retaliation protection is codified at § 246.5(c), not at § 247.5: this document's drafter checked § 247.5's own text directly and found it addresses a different subject entirely — the employer's duty to keep sick-leave records for at least three years, the presumption that applies when records are inadequate, and a statement that the employer need not inquire into or record why leave was used (addressed in a separate clause of this document); § 247.5 contains no retaliation language. citations.quote: An employer shall not deny an employee the right to use accrued sick days, discharge, threaten to discharge, demote, suspend, or in any manner discriminate against an employee for using accrued sick days, attempting to exercise the right to use accrued sick days, filing a complaint with the department or alleging a violation of this article, cooperating in an investigation or prosecution of an alleged violation of this article, or opposing any policy or practice or act that is prohibited by this article.

(B) The cooperation of an employee with an investigation or prosecution of an alleged violation of this article. clauses.title: The Workplace-Posting and Recordkeeping Duties This Act Imposes
clauses.body: Labor Code § 247 requires an employer to display, in a conspicuous place in each of its workplaces, a poster stating that an employee is entitled to accrue, request, and use paid sick days; the amount of sick days the Act provides; the terms of use of paid sick days; and that retaliation or discrimination against an employee who requests or uses paid sick days is prohibited, along with the employee's right to file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner. The statute directs the Labor Commissioner to create such a poster and make it available to employers, and states that an employer who willfully violates this posting requirement is subject to a civil penalty of not more than $100 per offense. Separately, Labor Code § 247.5 requires an employer to keep, for at least three years, records documenting the hours worked and the paid sick days accrued and used by an employee, to allow the Labor Commissioner access to those records, and to make them available to the employee in the same manner as other wage-statement-related records; if an employer does not maintain adequate records, the statute presumes the employee is entitled to the maximum number of accruable hours under the Act, unless the employer rebuts that presumption with clear and convincing evidence. Section 247.5 also states that, notwithstanding any other provision of the Act, an employer is not obligated to inquire into or record the specific purpose for which an employee uses paid leave or paid time off.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's own posting and recordkeeping duties under this Act — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The first three citations below are to subdivisions (a) through (c) of a single statutory section, Labor Code § 247, and are treated as one source describing the posting duty; the last two citations are to subdivisions (a) and (b) of a different statutory section, Labor Code § 247.5, and are treated as a second, independent source describing the recordkeeping duty — the two sections are not treated as corroborating one another, since they impose two distinct obligations. This posting duty is a separate requirement from the hiring-time written notice this project's Wage Theft Prevention Act Notice to Employee document already addresses under a different statute, Labor Code § 2810.5: that statute requires an individualized written notice to a new employee at hiring, listing paid sick leave rights as one of several required content categories, while § 247 requires a conspicuously displayed workplace poster covering paid sick leave specifically; this clause does not restate that other document's content and instead addresses only this Act's own posting and recordkeeping duties. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it is not itself the poster Section 247 requires, does not itself constitute the records Section 247.5 requires an employer to keep, and does not determine that any particular employer's own posting or recordkeeping practices are compliant or noncompliant with either section.

clauses.title: Categories of Workers the Statute's Own Definitions Exclude
clauses.body: Labor Code § 245.5's definition of "employee," for purposes of this Act, excludes five categories of workers. The first is an employee covered by a valid collective bargaining agreement that expressly provides for wages, hours, and working conditions; expressly provides paid sick days (or a paid leave or paid time off policy permitting sick-day use) and final and binding arbitration of disputes over those provisions; and provides premium overtime rates and a regular hourly rate at least 30 percent above the state minimum wage — except that this exclusion does not reach the specific victim-of-violence-related permitted use described elsewhere in this Act. The second is a construction-industry employee covered by a qualifying collective bargaining agreement meeting similar wage and overtime conditions, where the agreement either predates January 1, 2015, or expressly and unambiguously waives this Act's requirements. The third is an air carrier flight deck or cabin crew member covered by Title II of the federal Railway Labor Act, so long as the individual receives compensated time off equal to or exceeding this Act's own default accrual amount. The fourth is a state or local public retiree drawing a retirement allowance who returns to work without reinstatement into the applicable public retirement system. The fifth is an employee as defined in a specified provision of the federal Railway Labor Act, 45 U.S.C. § 351(d).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of which categories of workers this particular paid-sick-leave statute's own definition excludes — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific collective bargaining agreement or any specific worker's role meets the detailed conditions the statute sets out for these exclusions. All five citations below are to paragraphs (1) through (5) of subdivision (a) of a single statutory section, Labor Code § 245.5; they are treated here as one source describing one exclusion list, not as independent corroborating sources. The first and second exclusions are narrower than a blanket exemption for any collective-bargaining-covered employee: each requires the agreement itself to meet specific content conditions (arbitration, premium overtime, a minimum hourly-rate floor, and, for the second, either a pre-2015 date or an express waiver) that this clause does not determine any particular agreement satisfies. clauses.title: The Federal New-Hire Reporting Framework (PRWORA)
clauses.body: Federal law requires each state to establish an automated "State Directory of New Hires" containing information that employers report on each newly hired employee. Correspondingly, federal law requires each employer to furnish a report — containing the employee's name, address, and Social Security number, the date the employee first performed services for pay, and the employer's name, address, and federal identifying number — to the state directory for the state in which the employee works. This federal requirement, enacted as part of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996, is the underlying framework beneath state new-hire reporting programs such as California's; it exists mainly to support child-support enforcement, by letting states and the federal government locate a parent's new employer quickly.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as evidence of what the federal government requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file a new-hire report with the California Employment Development Department or any other agency, and it does not itself fulfill any employer's reporting duty. Both citations below are to different paragraphs of the same statutory section, 42 U.S.C. § 653a — subsection (a)(1)(A) (the state's duty to establish a directory) and subsection (b)(1)(A) (the employer's duty to report into it) — and are treated as one source, not independent; this clause draws no conclusion from that shared section other than that they are two halves of a single directory-and-reporting structure. Separately, this clause describes only the general reporting rule; § 653a itself carves out exceptions (a multistate-employer election in (b)(1)(B), a federal-government-employer routing rule in (b)(1)(C), and a narrow intelligence/counterintelligence employee exclusion in (a)(2)(A)(ii)) that are not summarized here. Federal law leaves each state to set its own reporting deadline and civil penalty within federal outer limits; California's own choices on those points are addressed in separate clauses of this information sheet, not this one.

clauses.title: California's New Hire Reporting Duty and Deadline
clauses.body: California implements the federal new-hire reporting framework through Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5, which since July 1, 1998 has required every employer to file specified information on new employees with the Employment Development Department ("EDD"), in addition to the routine wage reports already required under § 1088. An employer must submit the required report within 20 days of hiring an employee it is required to report. An employer that transmits its reports magnetically or electronically is not held to that same report-by-report 20-day clock; instead, it may submit its reports in two monthly transmissions, spaced not less than 12 days and not more than 16 days apart — an alternative batched-reporting schedule, not simply a shorter or longer version of the 20-day deadline.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file a new-hire report with the California Employment Development Department or any other agency, and it does not itself fulfill any employer's reporting duty. All three citations below are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section, Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5 — subdivision (a) (the general filing duty), and subdivision (d), paragraphs (1) (the 20-day deadline) and (2) (the electronic-filer alternative) — and are treated as one source, not independent. This clause corrects a framing worth stating directly: the electronic-filer rule in (d)(2) is not a categorically "shorter" deadline than 20 days; it replaces the per-hire 20-day clock with a twice-monthly transmission schedule, which can in practice fall before or after 20 days from any given hire depending on when in the cycle the hire occurs. Section 1088.5(c) also exempts United States government employers, and limits reporting by state agencies for employees performing intelligence or counterintelligence functions in specified circumstances; those exemptions are not elaborated here.

clauses.title: What Counts as a Reportable "New Employee" or "Rehire"
clauses.body: For California new-hire reporting purposes, an employer must report the hiring of any employee who works in the state and to whom the employer anticipates paying wages. Separately, an employer must also report the hiring of any employee who previously worked for that same employer but had been separated from that prior employment for at least 60 consecutive days — a rehire. A employee's return after a break in service shorter than 60 consecutive days does not, on the statute's own terms, trigger this separate rehire-reporting duty. California's 60-consecutive-day rehire threshold matches the floor set by the federal statute underlying this program, which defines a "newly hired employee" the same way for federal new-hire-reporting purposes.
clauses.gap: This is California and federal law, used as evidence of what California and the federal government requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself file a new-hire report with the California Employment Development Department or any other agency, and it does not itself fulfill any employer's reporting duty. The two citations below are to genuinely independent, separately numbered sources — California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(b) and federal 42 U.S.C. § 653a(a)(2)(C) — not subsections of a single section, so no same-source caveat applies; this clause notes only that the two definitions happen to converge on the same 60-day figure, not that either is derived from the other. Neither statute defines a minimum hours, wage amount, or duration-of-employment threshold for when a first-time hire itself becomes reportable; on the text reviewed, the reporting duty for a first-time hire turns only on working in the state and an anticipated wage payment, not on any minimum length of the job.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, the new-employee and rehire definitions
citations.quote: Each employer shall report the hiring of any employee who works in this state and to whom the employer anticipates paying wages, and also shall report the hiring of any employee who previously worked for the employer but had been separated from that prior employment for at least 60 consecutive days.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 653a(a)(2)(C) (Cornell LII text)
