clauses.title: Federal Labor Law: Section 7 Rights and Severance Non-Disparagement Clauses
clauses.body: Separately from California law, federal law gives most private-sector employees — unionized or not — the right to engage in concerted activity for mutual aid or protection, including discussing wages, working conditions, and workplace disputes with coworkers, a union, government agencies, or others. It's a federal unfair labor practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in exercising that right. Applying these provisions, the National Labor Relations Board held in McLaren Macomb (372 NLRB No. 58, Feb. 21, 2023) that an employer commits an unfair labor practice merely by offering — not just by enforcing — a severance agreement to a covered employee that contains an overly broad non-disparagement or confidentiality provision, where that provision could reasonably be read to restrict the employee's ability to discuss workplace conditions or disputes with coworkers, a union, the Board, another government agency, the media, or others, as part of protected concerted activity. Under this reasoning, the proffer itself can be unlawful even if the employee never signs the agreement and the clause is never invoked.
clauses.gap: Sourcing honesty note: the McLaren Macomb decision itself was not independently read or quote-verified against primary NLRB text in this research session. CourtListener's case-law search was already rate-limited (125 requests/day, exhausted) before this clause could be checked there, and every attempted direct fetch of nlrb.gov (where NLRB decisions are published) was blocked by this environment's network egress controls. The case's citation, date, and holding as described above are drawn from secondary reporting collected through web search (law-firm client alerts from Holland & Knight, White & Case, Littler, Mintz, and others describing the decision), not from an independently read primary opinion — for that reason, no quotation from the McLaren Macomb opinion itself appears in the citations below; only the two directly fetched and byte-identical-confirmed federal statutory sections are quoted. The same secondary reporting indicates McLaren Macomb remains Board precedent as of mid-2026 (reporting describes an NLRB administrative law judge applying it in a May 2026 case, Detrex Corporation) even though the NLRB General Counsel's own explanatory guidance on it (Memorandum GC 23-05) was rescinded by an Acting General Counsel in February 2025 — a General Counsel memo is prosecutorial guidance, not binding Board law, so its rescission doesn't by itself overrule the underlying decision, but this document's account of that rescission and its practical significance also rests on the same secondary sourcing, not on an independently read primary NLRB document. Both statutory citations below are drawn from separate, independently numbered sections (29 U.S.C. §§ 157 and 158), not subsections of one section. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the employer or employee is in — unlike the California statutes elsewhere in this document — but whether it protects a specific person's specific statement still turns on facts this document doesn't resolve. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is lawful or enforceable in a specific case.

clauses.title: Who Section 7 Doesn't Cover: The Supervisor Exclusion
clauses.body: The federal protection above is not universal. The National Labor Relations Act's own definition of "employee" — the term Section 7's rights are written around — expressly excludes several categories of workers, including any individual employed as a supervisor, along with independent contractors, agricultural laborers, domestic workers in a private home, and certain railway-industry employees. Because Section 7 protection, and the reasoning applied in McLaren Macomb, run to "employees" as the Act defines that term, someone who meets the Act's own definition of "supervisor" generally falls outside that protection.
clauses.gap: "Supervisor" is itself a separately defined term under the same statute (29 U.S.C. § 152(11), not independently fetched or quoted for this clause), generally turning on whether a person has authority to hire, fire, discipline, or responsibly direct other employees using independent judgment — not simply on having a manager-sounding job title. Whether a specific employee meets that definition is a fact-specific question this document doesn't resolve. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 152(3)); no additional independent source was found for this beyond that subsection. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the employer or employee is in — unlike the California statutes elsewhere in this document — but whether it protects a specific person's specific statement still turns on facts this document doesn't resolve. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is lawful or enforceable in a specific case.

clauses.title: Non-Disparagement Clauses as Ordinary Contract Terms
clauses.body: Outside the specific statutory contexts above, California has no single statute that bans non-disparagement clauses generally — unlike, for example, its broad statutory restriction on employee noncompete agreements. A non-disparagement clause outside those specific contexts is ordinarily treated as just another contract term, subject to the same general rules that apply to any contract provision under California law: a term is not lawful if it is contrary to an express provision of law, contrary to the policy of the law even without an express prohibition, or otherwise contrary to good morals, and a contract term that tries to exempt someone from responsibility for their own fraud, willful injury to another, or violation of law is against the policy of the law. Within that framework, a non-disparagement clause that doesn't run into one of the specific statutory bans described elsewhere in this document is generally enforced like any other bargained-for contract restriction.
clauses.gap: § 1667 and § 1668 are two separate, independently numbered statutory sections, not subsections of one section. These are old, general-purpose statutes (both enacted in 1872) applied here to a modern contract type; no case law applying them specifically to a non-disparagement clause was checked in this research, so this clause states the general statutory backdrop rather than a case-tested application of it to this particular kind of provision. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific non-disparagement clause is enforceable in a specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1667 (Leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, general definition of an unlawful contract term
citations.quote: That is not lawful which is: 1. Contrary to an express provision of law; 2. Contrary to the policy of express law, though not expressly prohibited; or, 3. Otherwise contrary to good morals.

citations.quote: All contracts which have for their object, directly or indirectly, to exempt any one from responsibility for his own fraud, or willful injury to the person or property of another, or violation of law, whether willful or negligent, are against the policy of the law.

clauses.title: Non-Disparagement vs. Confidentiality, and Whether Truth Is a Defense
clauses.body: A non-disparagement clause and a confidentiality (nondisclosure) clause are often drafted together in a single paragraph and colloquially treated as interchangeable, but they restrict different things. A confidentiality clause restricts disclosing information at all, regardless of whether the information is flattering, neutral, or damaging. A non-disparagement clause instead restricts making negative or critical statements — it doesn't stop someone from disclosing information so much as from characterizing it unfavorably. California's own statute in this area draws that same distinction in its own text, separately regulating a provision that "prevents or restricts the disclosure of factual information" and a provision precluding disclosure of a settlement amount, rather than treating all restrictions on speech about a claim as one undifferentiated category. Whether a truthful statement can still count as "disparaging" for purposes of a contract's own non-disparagement clause is a genuinely open question as a matter of ordinary contract interpretation: a non-disparagement clause's own wording may or may not include a truth-based defense, and courts interpreting a given clause look to what that specific clause's language actually says, not to a single fixed legal rule that truth is always, or never, an excuse.
clauses.gap: The first citation below is the same statutory section as nondisparagement_ccp_1001_scope and nondisparagement_ccp_1001_carveouts (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001) — it is not independent corroboration of those clauses, and is used here only as evidence that the fact/opinion distinction described above has a real textual hook in California statute, not as a general rule that all non-disparagement clauses everywhere draw that same line. The point about truthful statements possibly still being "disparaging" is stated honestly as an open, unresolved question rather than settled either way — no single California or federal statute was found in this research that resolves it as a general matter, and this document does not resolve it either. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific non-disparagement clause is enforceable in a specific case.

citations.quote: a provision within a settlement agreement that prevents or restricts the disclosure of factual information related to a claim filed in a civil action or a complaint filed in an administrative action

clauses.title: Mutual Non-Disparagement
clauses.body: {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}} mutually agree not to make any statement, written or oral, that disparages the other, including (for {{employeeName}}) {{companyName}}'s officers, directors, and management-level employees acting in that capacity, and (for {{companyName}}) {{employeeName}}. This does not restrict either party from: providing truthful information in response to a subpoena, court order, or valid request from a government agency; filing a charge or complaint with, or participating in an investigation or proceeding conducted by, a government agency; discussing or disclosing information about unlawful acts in the workplace, including harassment, discrimination, or any other conduct either party has reason to believe is unlawful; or making truthful statements in a legal proceeding between the parties. Nothing in this clause limits any right either party has under federal labor law to discuss wages, hours, or other terms and conditions of employment.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
The Core Requirement: Rest, Recovery, and Nonproductive Time Paid Separately
clauses.body: California law governing piece-rate compensation applies to {{employeeName}} for any pay period in which {{employeeName}} is compensated on a piece-rate basis, and it does not limit or alter minimum wage or overtime requirements, or {{companyName}}'s obligation to compensate {{employeeName}} for all hours worked under any other statute or local ordinance. This law defines "applicable minimum wage" as the highest of the federal, state, or local minimum wage applicable to the employment, and defines "other nonproductive time" as time under {{companyName}}'s control, excluding rest and recovery periods, that is not directly related to the piece-rate activity. For any pay period in which {{employeeName}} is compensated on a piece-rate basis, California law requires that {{employeeName}} be compensated for rest and recovery periods and other nonproductive time separately from any piece-rate compensation.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute — used as evidence of California's specific piece-rate compensation requirements, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Piece-rate pay itself is lawful everywhere; California's requirement that rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time be compensated separately, on top of piece-rate earnings, is a distinctly California rule, and most states impose no comparable separate-compensation requirement for piece-rate workers. The statute itself defines "applicable minimum wage" and "other nonproductive time," but it does not define "rest and recovery periods" anywhere within its own text — that phrase is used, not defined, in this section; this clause does not assert that some other statute (such as the general rest-period requirement in Labor Code § 226.7 or an Industrial Welfare Commission wage order) supplies that definition, only that § 226.2 itself does not. The two quoted passages below (the definitions preamble and paragraph (a)(1)) both come from the same statutory section, § 226.2 — treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources for one another. This clause states the general separate-compensation rule only; the required minimum rate of pay for that time, the wage-statement itemization it triggers, and the now-expired transitional safe harbor for past noncompliance are addressed in separate clauses in this set.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.2 (preamble)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2 (unnumbered introductory paragraph)
citations.quote: This section shall apply for employees who are compensated on a piece-rate basis for any work performed during a pay period. This section shall not be construed to limit or alter minimum wage or overtime compensation requirements, or the obligation to compensate employees for all hours worked under any other statute or local ordinance. For the purposes of this section, “applicable minimum wage” means the highest of the federal, state, or local minimum wage that is applicable to the employment, and “other nonproductive time” means time under the employer’s control, exclusive of rest and recovery periods, that is not directly related to the activity being compensated on a piece-rate basis.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(1)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(1)
citations.quote: (a) For employees compensated on a piece-rate basis during a pay period, the following shall apply for that pay period:(1) Employees shall be compensated for rest and recovery periods and other nonproductive time separate from any piece-rate compensation.

clauses.title: The Minimum Rate for Rest and Recovery Period Pay
clauses.body: California law sets a floor for how {{employeeName}}'s rest and recovery periods must be paid: {{employeeName}} must be compensated for rest and recovery periods at a regular hourly rate no less than the higher of (i) an average hourly rate, calculated by dividing {{employeeName}}'s total compensation for the workweek — excluding compensation for rest and recovery periods and any overtime premium — by {{employeeName}}'s total hours worked during the workweek, excluding rest and recovery periods; or (ii) the applicable minimum wage. For a semimonthly payroll, California law permits {{companyName}} to pay {{employeeName}} at least the applicable minimum wage rate for rest and recovery periods together with other wages for the payroll period in which they occurred, with any additional amount owed under the average-hourly-rate calculation payable no later than the payday for the next regular payroll period.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute — used as evidence of California's specific piece-rate compensation requirements, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Piece-rate pay itself is lawful everywhere; California's requirement that rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time be compensated separately, on top of piece-rate earnings, is a distinctly California rule, and most states impose no comparable separate-compensation requirement for piece-rate workers. Both quoted passages come from the same statutory paragraph, § 226.2(a)(3) — subparagraphs (A) and (B) — treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources for one another. The "higher of" comparison in subparagraph (A) is calculated per workweek even where wages are paid semimonthly; subparagraph (B) is a payroll-timing accommodation for semimonthly payers, not a different rate floor — it lets the true-up land on the following payday rather than requiring same-period computation. This clause does not calculate any particular employee's actual average hourly rate for any actual workweek; that arithmetic depends on real pay and hours data this clause does not have.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(3)(A)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(3)(A)
citations.quote: (3) (A) Employees shall be compensated for rest and recovery periods at a regular hourly rate that is no less than the higher of:(i) An average hourly rate determined by dividing the total compensation for the workweek, exclusive of compensation for rest and recovery periods and any premium compensation for overtime, by the total hours worked during the workweek, exclusive of rest and recovery periods.(ii) The applicable minimum wage.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(3)(B)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(3)(B)
citations.quote: (B) For employers who pay on a semimonthly basis, employees shall be compensated at least at the applicable minimum wage rate for the rest and recovery periods together with other wages for the payroll period during which the rest and recovery periods occurred. Any additional compensation required for those employees pursuant to clause (i) of subparagraph (A) is payable no later than the payday for the next regular payroll period.

clauses.title: The Minimum Rate for Other Nonproductive Time, and How the Hours Are Counted
clauses.body: California law requires that {{employeeName}} be compensated for other nonproductive time at an hourly rate no less than the applicable minimum wage. {{companyName}} may determine the amount of {{employeeName}}'s other nonproductive time either through actual records or through {{companyName}}'s reasonable estimates, whether for a group of employees or for {{employeeName}} individually. Separately, an employer who pays an hourly rate of at least the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked, in addition to any piece-rate compensation, is deemed in compliance with the other-nonproductive-time pay requirement without a separate hourly nonproductive-time calculation.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute — used as evidence of California's specific piece-rate compensation requirements, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Piece-rate pay itself is lawful everywhere; California's requirement that rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time be compensated separately, on top of piece-rate earnings, is a distinctly California rule, and most states impose no comparable separate-compensation requirement for piece-rate workers. The three quoted passages below all come from the same statutory subdivision, § 226.2(a) — paragraphs (4), (5), and (7) — treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources for one another. This clause does not restate paragraph (6) of the same subdivision, which limits — but does not eliminate — an employer's exposure to statutory civil penalties (though not the underlying wage liability itself) for a good-faith error in estimating other-nonproductive-time hours, provided the employer met the wage-statement and payment conditions that paragraph separately specifies; that narrower point is not asserted here. This clause does not determine, for any actual employee or pay period, what qualifies as "other nonproductive time" versus time directly related to the piece-rate activity — that is a fact-specific characterization the statute leaves to be applied to particular circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(4)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(4)
citations.quote: (4) Employees shall be compensated for other nonproductive time at an hourly rate that is no less than the applicable minimum wage.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(5)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(5)
citations.quote: (5) The amount of other nonproductive time may be determined either through actual records or the employer’s reasonable estimates, whether for a group of employees or for a particular employee, of other nonproductive time worked during the pay period.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(7)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(7)
citations.quote: (7) An employer who, in addition to paying any piece-rate compensation, pays an hourly rate of at least the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked, shall be deemed in compliance with paragraph (4).

clauses.title: The Piece-Rate-Specific Addition to the Itemized Wage Statement
clauses.body: On top of the itemized-wage-statement categories California law requires of every employer, California law requires that {{employeeName}}'s itemized wage statement, for any pay period in which {{employeeName}} is compensated on a piece-rate basis, separately state: the total hours of {{employeeName}}'s compensable rest and recovery periods, the rate of compensation for that time, and the gross wages paid for those periods during the pay period; and, unless {{companyName}} instead pays {{employeeName}} an hourly rate of at least the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked, the total hours of {{employeeName}}'s other nonproductive time, the rate of compensation for that time, and the gross wages paid for that time during the pay period.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute — used as evidence of California's specific piece-rate compensation requirements, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Piece-rate pay itself is lawful everywhere; California's requirement that rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time be compensated separately, on top of piece-rate earnings, is a distinctly California rule, and most states impose no comparable separate-compensation requirement for piece-rate workers. This clause is deliberately narrow: it covers only the two piece-rate-specific categories § 226.2(a)(2) adds to an itemized wage statement — rest-and-recovery-period totals and other-nonproductive-time totals, each broken into hours, rate, and gross wages. It does not restate the nine general items every itemized wage statement must show under Labor Code § 226(a) (gross wages, total hours, deductions, and so on), which are covered in a separate clause in this document set (the "nine required itemized statement items" clause) and are not duplicated here; § 226.2(a)(2) itself states that these piece-rate additions come "in addition to the other items specified in" § 226(a)'s subdivision, and that the general remedies and enforcement provisions of § 226 also apply to these added items. This clause does not restate the separate exception in § 226.2(a)(2)(B) for employers who instead pay an hourly rate of at least the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked (covered in a separate clause in this set) beyond noting that the exception exists.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.2(a)(2)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2, subd. (a)(2)
citations.quote: (2) The itemized statement required by subdivision (a) of Section 226 shall, in addition to the other items specified in that subdivision, separately state the following, to which the provisions of Section 226 shall also be applicable:(A) The total hours of compensable rest and recovery periods, the rate of compensation, and the gross wages paid for those periods during the pay period.(B) Except for employers paying compensation for other nonproductive time in accordance with paragraph (7), the total hours of other nonproductive time, as determined under paragraph (5), the rate of compensation, and the gross wages paid for that time during the pay period.

clauses.title: The Now-Expired Transitional Safe Harbor for Past Noncompliance
clauses.body: When California first enacted Labor Code § 226.2 (operative January 1, 2016 through December 31, 2020), that original version of the statute included a transitional affirmative defense: an employer had a defense to claims for recovery of wages, damages, liquidated damages, or statutory or civil penalties based solely on a failure to timely pay compensation due for rest and recovery periods and other nonproductive time for time periods before and including December 31, 2015, if the employer met a set of conditions by specific deadlines. Those conditions included making back payments to current and former employees for previously uncompensated or undercompensated rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time from July 1, 2012 through December 31, 2015, calculated either as the actual sums owed with interest, or as a flat 4% of the employee's gross piece-rate-period earnings during that window (reduced, up to a 1% cap, by amounts already separately paid for that time); filing a written election notice with the Department of Industrial Relations no later than July 1, 2016; and completing payments to each employee (or, for employees who could not be located, to the Labor Commissioner) no later than December 15, 2016. This transitional safe harbor is no longer operative: the statute that created it stated its own effective end date, and it was repealed as of January 1, 2021. The current version of § 226.2 contains no equivalent cure or affirmative-defense mechanism.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute — used as evidence of California's specific piece-rate compensation requirements, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Piece-rate pay itself is lawful everywhere; California's requirement that rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time be compensated separately, on top of piece-rate earnings, is a distinctly California rule, and most states impose no comparable separate-compensation requirement for piece-rate workers. This clause is presented for historical and informational context only — it describes a mechanism that no longer exists in current law, not a currently available option. All five quoted passages below come from the same enactment: the original (2016-2020) version of § 226.2, added by Section 4 of 2015 Cal. Stats., ch. 754 (Assembly Bill 1513) — treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources for one another. This clause summarizes only the payment-formula and deadline mechanics; it does not restate every condition and exclusion the original statute attached to the defense (for example, the separate accurate-statement requirement accompanying each payment, the narrower good-faith-error cure window, the tolling of the statute of limitations during the election period, or the several categories of pre-existing claims the statute carved out of the defense's reach entirely), and it takes no position on whether any particular employer actually made a timely, compliant election and payment during the window that existed. Because the deadlines this mechanism depended on (July 1, 2016 and December 15, 2016) and the mechanism's own repeal date (January 1, 2021) have all passed, this clause is included to explain why the safe harbor is no longer available, not to describe a present cure path for current noncompliance.

clauses.title: What "Piece-Rate Compensation" Means: No Dedicated Statutory Definition
clauses.body: California's piece-rate compensation statute does not itself define the term "piece-rate compensation" or "piece-rate basis"; the statute defines only "applicable minimum wage" and "other nonproductive time," and otherwise uses the phrase "compensated on a piece-rate basis" without further elaboration. The closest general statutory anchor is California's broad definition of "wages," which lists "piece" as one of several methods by which the amount of labor compensation may be fixed or ascertained, alongside time, task, and commission basis. Beyond that general listing, California statute leaves "piece-rate compensation" to its ordinary usage: compensation calculated by reference to a completed unit of production, or a fixed amount per task, rather than by the hour.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute — used as evidence of California's specific piece-rate compensation requirements, not as a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. Piece-rate pay itself is lawful everywhere; California's requirement that rest, recovery, and other nonproductive time be compensated separately, on top of piece-rate earnings, is a distinctly California rule, and most states impose no comparable separate-compensation requirement for piece-rate workers. This clause reports an absence, not a finding: no statutory definition of "piece-rate compensation" or "piece-rate basis" was located within § 226.2 or within the general wage definitions in § 200 of the same code; this clause does not assert that no such definition exists anywhere in California law, regulation, or agency guidance (for example, in Division of Labor Standards Enforcement guidance or Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders), only that this clause's own search of these two primary statutory sources did not find one. The two quoted passages below come from two different statutory sections (§ 226.2 and § 200) and are independent of each other in that sense, though both are used only to show what the statutory text does and does not define, not to establish any operative rule beyond that.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226.2 (defined terms)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 226.2 (unnumbered introductory paragraph)
citations.quote: For the purposes of this section, “applicable minimum wage” means the highest of the federal, state, or local minimum wage that is applicable to the employment, and “other nonproductive time” means time under the employer’s control, exclusive of rest and recovery periods, that is not directly related to the activity being compensated on a piece-rate basis.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 200, subd. (a)
citations.quote: “Wages” includes all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment
Authorization and Termination
clauses.body: California law authorizes a trust created for the care of {{animalDescription}}, treating it as a trust for a lawful noncharitable purpose, subject to the requirements of Probate Code section 15212. Unless {{trustName}} expressly provides otherwise, it terminates when no animal who was living on the date of {{settlorName}}'s death remains alive — the operative cutoff is death, not merely the passage of time or a change in circumstances. A court construing {{trustName}} is directed to do so liberally to bring it within this statute, to presume against reading it as a merely precatory or unenforceable honorary gesture, and to carry out {{settlorName}}'s general intent; extrinsic evidence is admissible to determine that intent.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's pet trust statute actually authorizes and when it terminates — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 15212(a)); no additional independent source was found for this. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the core authorization for a trust for the care of an animal, its termination trigger, and its rule of construction
citations.quote: Subject to the requirements of this section, a trust for the care of an animal is a trust for a lawful noncharitable purpose. Unless expressly provided in the trust, the trust terminates when no animal living on the date of the settlor’s death remains alive. The governing instrument of the animal trust shall be liberally construed to bring the trust within this section, to presume against the merely precatory or honorary nature of the disposition, and to carry out the general intent of the settlor. Extrinsic evidence is admissible in determining the settlor’s intent.

clauses.title: What "Animal" Means, and What This Statute Does Not Reach
clauses.body: The statute defines "animal," for its own purposes, narrowly: a domestic or pet animal for the benefit of which a trust has been established. And its termination rule is tied to a specific point in time — an animal has to be living on the date of the settlor's death for the trust to continue past that date, since the trust terminates once no animal living on that date remains alive. Neither of those two rules is framed around whether an animal was alive at some earlier point during the settlor's lifetime; an animal that predeceased the settlor is not "living on the date of the settlor's death," and the statute's own text does not extend this authorization to an animal that did not yet exist as of the settlor's death, such as a future or unborn animal, or to a wild or non-domestic animal outside its definition of "animal."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual scope limits California's pet trust statute states in its own text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. § 15212(a) and § 15212(i) are both subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated here as one source, not two independent ones. The conclusion that a not-yet-existing or predeceased animal falls outside this authorization is this document's own reading of what the statute's stated termination trigger and definition imply, offered as a factual inference from the quoted text rather than as a separate express statutory statement — the statute does not contain a sentence that says so in those words, and no case law was sought to confirm or narrow that reading. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the death-of-settlor cutoff for which animals the trust covers
citations.quote: the trust terminates when no animal living on the date of the settlor’s death remains alive

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory definition of "animal"
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, “animal” means a domestic or pet animal for the benefit of which a trust has been established.

clauses.title: Use Restriction and Distribution on Termination
clauses.body: Unless {{trustName}} expressly provides otherwise, the principal or income of a trust for the care of an animal cannot be converted to the trustee's own use or to any use other than for the benefit of the animal. When the trust terminates, the trustee distributes whatever trust property is left over, in a fixed order: first as {{trustName}} itself directs; if it doesn't direct a distribution and the trust was created in a nonresiduary clause of a will or codicil, then under that will's residuary clause; and if neither of those results in a distribution, to the settlor's heirs under Probate Code section 21114.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual use restriction and the actual order in which leftover trust property is distributed on termination — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. § 15212(b)(1) and § 15212(b)(2) are both subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated here as one source, not two independent ones. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: the statute contains no mechanism allowing a court to reduce the amount of property transferred into the trust on the ground that it substantially exceeds the amount needed for the animal's care — that provision does not appear anywhere in the current text of § 15212. What the statute does address is only what happens to property left over once the trust terminates (the order above), which is a different question from whether an oversized initial transfer can be cut down while the trust is ongoing. No such reduction mechanism was found and none is asserted here. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the restriction limiting trust property to the animal's benefit
citations.quote: Except as expressly provided otherwise in the trust instrument, the principal or income shall not be converted to the use of the trustee or to any use other than for the benefit of the animal.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory order for distributing unexpended trust property on termination
citations.quote: Upon termination of the trust, the trustee shall distribute the unexpended trust property in the following order: (A) As directed in the trust instrument. (B) If the trust was created in a nonresiduary clause in the settlor’s will or in a codicil to the settlor’s will, under the residuary clause in the settlor’s will. (C) If the application of subparagraph (A) or (B) does not result in distribution of unexpended trust property, to the settlor’s heirs under Section 21114.

clauses.title: Who Can Enforce the Trust
clauses.body: The intended use of the trust's principal or income may be enforced by a person the trust instrument itself designates for that purpose or, if none is designated, by a person a court appoints. Standing to raise the trust with a court is not limited to that enforcer: any person interested in the animal's welfare, or any nonprofit charitable organization whose principal activity is the care of animals, may also petition the court about the trust, in addition to the persons Probate Code section 17200(a) already identifies as able to petition regarding a trust generally.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual enforcement mechanism and who has standing to invoke it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 15212(c)); no additional independent source was found for this. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: this enforcement and standing mechanism is set out in subdivision (c) of § 15212, not subdivision (b) — subdivision (b) instead sets the use restriction and termination-distribution order addressed in a separate clause of this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: who may enforce the trust and who has standing to petition the court about it
citations.quote: The intended use of the principal or income may be enforced by a person designated for that purpose in the trust instrument or, if none is designated, by a person appointed by a court. In addition to a person identified in subdivision (a) of Section 17200, any person interested in the welfare of the animal or any nonprofit charitable organization that has as its principal activity the care of animals may petition the court regarding the trust as provided in Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 17200) of Part 5.

clauses.title: Trustee Vacancy and the Court's Supervisory Authority
clauses.body: If no trustee is designated for a trust for the care of an animal, or a designated or successor trustee is unwilling or unable to serve, a court will name one. A court may also order trust property transferred to a court-appointed trustee where that's required to carry out the trust's intended use and no willing, able successor trustee is designated, and may make any other orders or determinations it considers advisable to carry out the settlor's intent and the statute's purpose.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory fallback for a vacant trusteeship and the actual scope of a court's supervisory authority over this kind of trust — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 15212(d)); no additional independent source was found for this. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: court authority to name a trustee and make other orders carrying out the trust's purpose
citations.quote: If a trustee is not designated or no designated or successor trustee is willing or able to serve, a court shall name a trustee. A court may order the transfer of the trust property to a court-appointed trustee, if it is required to ensure that the intended use is carried out and if a successor trustee is not designated in the trust instrument or if no designated successor trustee agrees to serve or is able to serve. A court may also make all other orders and determinations as it shall deem advisable to carry out the intent of the settlor and the purpose of this section.

clauses.title: Accounting Duty, the $40,000 Threshold, and Inspection Rights
clauses.body: A trustee of a pet trust does owe an accounting duty, but a limited one: the accountings Probate Code section 16062 requires go to the beneficiaries who would be entitled to a distribution if the animal were then deceased, and to any nonprofit charitable corporation whose principal activity is the care of animals if it has requested them in writing. That duty largely disappears for a smaller trust, though — if the trust's assets don't exceed $40,000, no filing, report, registration, periodic accounting, separate fund maintenance, appointment, or fee is required by reason of the trustee's fiduciary relationship, unless a court orders it or the trust instrument itself requires it. Separately, any beneficiary, any person the trust instrument or a court designates to enforce the trust, or any qualifying nonprofit charitable organization may, on reasonable request, inspect the animal, the premises where it's kept, or the trust's books and records.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual accounting duty this statute imposes, its $40,000 threshold, and the actual inspection rights it creates — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. § 15212(e) and § 15212(f) are both subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated here as one source, not two independent ones. This corrects an assumption in the original research brief: the statute is not silent on accounting or court supervision — it affirmatively imposes an accounting duty (cross-referencing the general accounting statute, § 16062, not quoted here) while also affirmatively cutting most of the ordinary fiduciary formalities away for a trust holding $40,000 or less, unless a court or the trust instrument requires them anyway. This document does not independently quote or verify the content of § 16062's general accounting requirements; only § 15212's own text specifying who receives those accountings and the dollar threshold is quoted here. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the accounting duty and its $40,000 small-trust exception
citations.quote: The accountings required by Section 16062 shall be provided to the beneficiaries who would be entitled to distribution if the animal were then deceased and to any nonprofit charitable corporation that has as its principal activity the care of animals and that has requested these accountings in writing. However, if the value of the assets in the trust does not exceed forty thousand dollars ($40,000), no filing, report, registration, periodic accounting, separate maintenance of funds, appointment, or fee is required by reason of the existence of the fiduciary relationship of the trustee, unless ordered by the court or required by the trust instrument.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the inspection right
citations.quote: Any beneficiary, any person designated by the trust instrument or the court to enforce the trust, or any nonprofit charitable corporation that has as its principal activity the care of animals may, upon reasonable request, inspect the animal, the premises where the animal is maintained, or the books and records of the trust.

clauses.title: How This Differs from an Outright Gift "for the Care of" a Pet
clauses.body: California's general statute governing a trust for a noncharitable purpose caps how long a trustee may perform it at 21 years, regardless of whether any beneficiary can seek its enforcement or termination, and regardless of what the trust's own terms contemplate — the kind of limited, hard-to-enforce arrangement historically called an "honorary trust." Probate Code section 15212 expressly takes a trust for the care of an animal outside that general rule: that 21-year statute does not apply to a trust governed by section 15212. A pet trust created under section 15212 is also carved out of the separate rule letting a trustee unilaterally terminate a trust whose principal is worth $100,000 or less because its value has become too low relative to administration costs — that rule does not apply to a trust governed by section 15212 either.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's pet trust statute is structured relative to its own general noncharitable-purpose-trust and low-value-termination rules — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a claim about the common-law history of "honorary trusts" as a doctrine beyond what this statutory text itself shows. § 15212(g) and § 15212(h) are both subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated here as one source, not independent of each other; the citation to § 15211 is to a separate statutory section, cited independently of that pair. This document did not fetch or rely on California Law Revision Commission commentary or any other legislative history to reach this conclusion — the operative text of § 15212(h), expressly exempting a trust governed by section 15212 from section 15211, is itself sufficient, direct, primary-source evidence that the Legislature treated a statutory pet trust as a distinct, better-secured arrangement than a bare noncharitable-purpose or honorary trust, without resort to secondary sources this document did not independently verify. No case law was sought on this point. This document is informational only: it does not itself create any trust or resolve any dispute about one.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(h) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the express exemption of a pet trust from the general noncharitable-purpose-trust statute
citations.quote: Section 15211 does not apply to a trust governed by this section.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15212(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the express exemption of a pet trust from unilateral low-value termination
citations.quote: A trust governed by this section is not subject to termination pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 15408.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15211 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the general noncharitable-purpose-trust statute (the "honorary trust" rule) a pet trust is exempt from
citations.quote: A trust for a noncharitable corporation or unincorporated society or for a lawful noncharitable purpose may be performed by the trustee for only 21 years, whether or not there is a beneficiary who can seek enforcement or termination of the trust and whether or not the terms of the trust contemplate a longer duration.

clauses.title: Adopting an Alternative Workweek Schedule: The Two-Thirds Secret-Ballot Vote
clauses.body: California law lets the employees within a readily identifiable work unit adopt a regularly scheduled alternative workweek — for example, four 10-hour days — authorizing work of up to 10 hours a day within a 40-hour workweek without triggering the daily overtime that would otherwise apply to hours beyond eight in a day. A proposed alternative workweek schedule takes effect only if it is approved, before any work is performed under it, by at least two-thirds of the affected employees in the work unit, voting in a secret ballot election.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation; most states have no equivalent alternative-workweek election mechanism at all, and the federal Fair Labor Standards Act has no comparable provision. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself adopt, disclose, conduct, certify, or repeal any alternative workweek schedule, and it does not determine that any specific work unit, proposed schedule, disclosure, election, or repeal petition described using this document actually satisfies Labor Code section 511 or the applicable IWC Wage Order. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed almost entirely by statutory and regulatory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session. The two citations below are independent sources corroborating the same rule: Labor Code section 511(a) is the statute, and IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C)(2), is the Industrial Welfare Commission's regulatory election-procedure text implementing it — a different, independently promulgated source, not a subsection of the same document. Wage Order 4-2001 was fetched as the representative order for this research; Labor Code section 511(f) identifies Wage Order Numbers 1, 4, 5, 7, and 9 as the orders under which alternative workweek schedules can be adopted, and this clause does not independently verify that the other four orders phrase the election-procedure text identically to Wage Order 4, though the statute itself (section 511(a)-(b)) states the core two-thirds vote and overtime rule directly and is not order-specific.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 511(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, alternative workweek schedule adoption and vote threshold
citations.quote: A proposal to adopt an alternative workweek schedule shall be deemed adopted only if it receives approval in a secret ballot election by at least two-thirds of affected employees in a readily identifiable work unit.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(2)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(2)
citations.quote: In order to be valid, the proposed alternative workweek schedule must be adopted in a secret ballot election, before the performance of work, by at least a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the affected employees in the work unit. The election shall be held during regular working hours at the employees’ work site.

clauses.title: What an Adopted Alternative Workweek Schedule Changes About Overtime
clauses.body: Adopting an alternative workweek schedule does not eliminate overtime; it changes when daily overtime starts. Within the regularly scheduled hours the alternative workweek agreement sets for a scheduled workday — up to 10 hours — those hours are not paid as daily overtime. Hours worked beyond the regularly scheduled hours on a scheduled day, up to 12 hours in that day, and any hours worked beyond 40 in the workweek, are paid at one and one-half times the regular rate. Hours worked beyond 12 in a day, and any hours worked on a day the alternative workweek schedule did not schedule the employee to work at all, are paid at double the regular rate.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation; most states have no equivalent alternative-workweek election mechanism at all, and the federal Fair Labor Standards Act has no comparable provision. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself adopt, disclose, conduct, certify, or repeal any alternative workweek schedule, and it does not determine that any specific work unit, proposed schedule, disclosure, election, or repeal petition described using this document actually satisfies Labor Code section 511 or the applicable IWC Wage Order. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed almost entirely by statutory and regulatory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session. The first two citations below (Labor Code section 511, subdivisions (a) and (b)) are two subdivisions of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not independent corroboration of each other. The third citation, IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(B)(1), is an independent source — a separately promulgated regulation — and is the specific textual basis for the double-time-for-unscheduled-day-work rule stated in the last sentence above, which is present in the wage order's text in materially the same terms as the statute's own subdivision (b) but is quoted from the wage order here because its unscheduled-day framing is clearer there.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 511(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, the 10-hour alternative workweek cap
citations.quote: the employees of an employer may adopt a regularly scheduled alternative workweek that authorizes work by the affected employees for no longer than 10 hours per day within a 40-hour workweek without the payment to the affected employees of an overtime rate of compensation pursuant to this section.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 511(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, overtime for hours beyond the scheduled alternative workweek day
citations.quote: An affected employee working longer than eight hours but not more than 12 hours in a day pursuant to an alternative workweek schedule adopted pursuant to this section shall be paid an overtime rate of compensation of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay of the employee for any work in excess of the regularly scheduled hours established by the alternative workweek agreement and for any work in excess of 40 hours per week.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(B)(1)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(B)(1)
citations.quote: All work performed in excess of 12 hours per day and any work in excess of eight (8) hours on those days worked beyond the regularly scheduled number of workdays established by the alternative workweek agreement shall be paid at double the employee’s regular rate of pay.

clauses.title: What Counts as a "Work Unit"
clauses.body: The vote to adopt or repeal an alternative workweek schedule is taken separately within each readily identifiable work unit, not on a company-wide basis. A work unit can be a division, a department, a job classification, a shift, a separate physical location, or a recognized subdivision of any of those — and, as long as the criteria for an identifiable work unit are otherwise met, a work unit can consist of a single employee.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation; most states have no equivalent alternative-workweek election mechanism at all, and the federal Fair Labor Standards Act has no comparable provision. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself adopt, disclose, conduct, certify, or repeal any alternative workweek schedule, and it does not determine that any specific work unit, proposed schedule, disclosure, election, or repeal petition described using this document actually satisfies Labor Code section 511 or the applicable IWC Wage Order. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed almost entirely by statutory and regulatory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session. The two citations below are independent sources: Labor Code section 511(i) is the statutory definition, and IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C)(2), is the Industrial Welfare Commission's separately promulgated election-procedure text, which states the same list of examples in near-identical wording. Neither source gives a general test for when a proposed work unit is "readily identifiable" beyond the listed examples, and this clause does not resolve whether any particular grouping of employees would qualify.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 511(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "work unit"
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, “work unit” includes a division, a department, a job classification, a shift, a separate physical location, or a recognized subdivision thereof. A work unit may consist of an individual employee as long as the criteria for an identifiable work unit in this section is met.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(2)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(2)
citations.quote: “affected employees in the work unit” may include all employees in a readily identifiable work unit, such as a division, a department, a job classification, a shift, a separate physical location, or a recognized subdivision of any such work unit. A work unit may consist of an individual employee as long as the criteria for an identifiable work unit in this subsection are met.

clauses.title: Required Pre-Election Disclosure and How the Vote Must Be Conducted
clauses.body: Before any secret ballot vote on a proposed alternative workweek schedule, the employer must give affected employees a written disclosure describing the proposed schedule's effects on their wages, hours, and benefits, including at least one duly noticed meeting — held at least 14 days before the vote — for the purpose of discussing those effects. An employer that does not comply with this disclosure requirement forfeits the election: it is null and void. The vote itself, and any later vote to repeal the schedule, must be held at the affected employees' work site during regular working hours, at the employer's expense.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation; most states have no equivalent alternative-workweek election mechanism at all, and the federal Fair Labor Standards Act has no comparable provision. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself adopt, disclose, conduct, certify, or repeal any alternative workweek schedule, and it does not determine that any specific work unit, proposed schedule, disclosure, election, or repeal petition described using this document actually satisfies Labor Code section 511 or the applicable IWC Wage Order. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed almost entirely by statutory and regulatory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session. All three citations below are to paragraphs (3) and (4) of the same wage-order subsection, IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C) — they are treated as one source describing a single election-procedure scheme, not as independent corroboration of each other. Labor Code section 511 itself does not state these disclosure, notice-timing, or worksite/cost requirements; they exist only in the wage order text, which is why no independent statutory citation is offered alongside them. The wage order also requires the written disclosure to be provided in a non-English language when at least five percent of affected employees primarily speak that language, and requires mailing the disclosure to employees who do not attend the meeting; those details are not quoted here but are part of the same disclosure requirement.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(3)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(3)
citations.quote: Prior to the secret ballot vote, any employer who proposed to institute an alternative workweek schedule shall have made a disclosure in writing to the affected employees, including the effects of the proposed arrangement on the employees’ wages, hours, and benefits. Such a disclosure shall include meeting(s), duly noticed, held at least 14 days prior to voting, for the specific purpose of discussing the effects of the alternative workweek schedule.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(3)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(3)
citations.quote: Failure to comply with this paragraph shall make the election null and void.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(4)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(4)
citations.quote: Any election to establish or repeal an alternative workweek schedule shall be held at the work site of the affected employees. The employer shall bear the costs of conducting any election held pursuant to this section.

clauses.title: Reporting Election Results: A Real Discrepancy Between the Statute and the Wage Order
clauses.body: The results of an alternative workweek schedule election must be reported by the employer within 30 days after the results are final. Labor Code section 511 identifies the recipient as the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement. The applicable IWC Wage Order identifies the recipient as the Office of the Director – Research, Department of Industrial Relations, and requires that the report include the final vote tally, the size of the unit, and the nature of the employer's business, as a public document.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation; most states have no equivalent alternative-workweek election mechanism at all, and the federal Fair Labor Standards Act has no comparable provision. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself adopt, disclose, conduct, certify, or repeal any alternative workweek schedule, and it does not determine that any specific work unit, proposed schedule, disclosure, election, or repeal petition described using this document actually satisfies Labor Code section 511 or the applicable IWC Wage Order. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed almost entirely by statutory and regulatory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session. This is a genuine, unresolved discrepancy in the primary sources rather than a drafting error on this clause's part: the statute (Labor Code section 511(e)) and the wage order (IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C)(6)) name two different recipient offices for the same 30-day report. Both are independent sources — a statute and a separately promulgated regulation — and both were independently fetched and verified this session; neither text was altered or reconciled to make them agree, and this clause does not resolve which office actually receives reports in current practice. Note for the reader of this research: the recipient named in the wage order, the "Office of the Director – Research," is the current name for what other guidance sometimes calls the Division of Labor Statistics and Research ("DLSR") — neither name refers to the Employment Development Department ("EDD"), which is a different state agency (it administers unemployment insurance and separate new-hire reporting) with no role in this specific reporting requirement.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 511(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, reporting to the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement
citations.quote: The results of any election conducted pursuant to this section shall be reported by an employer to the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement within 30 days after the results are final.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(6)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(6)
citations.quote: The results of any election conducted pursuant to this section shall be reported by the employer to the Office of the Director – Research, Department of Industrial Relations within 30 days after the results are final, and the report of election results shall be a public document.

clauses.title: Repeal: A One-Third Petition Forces a New Vote
clauses.body: An adopted alternative workweek schedule is not permanent. Affected employees can force a new secret ballot election to repeal it by a petition signed by at least one-third of the affected employees in the work unit; reversing the schedule then requires the same two-thirds vote used to adopt it. The repeal election must be held within 30 days after the petition is submitted, except that a work unit that already voted — to adopt or to repeal — must generally wait at least 12 months before voting on the schedule again. Separately, an employer may not use the adoption, repeal, or nullification of an alternative workweek schedule as an occasion to reduce an employee's regular hourly pay rate.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation; most states have no equivalent alternative-workweek election mechanism at all, and the federal Fair Labor Standards Act has no comparable provision. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself adopt, disclose, conduct, certify, or repeal any alternative workweek schedule, and it does not determine that any specific work unit, proposed schedule, disclosure, election, or repeal petition described using this document actually satisfies Labor Code section 511 or the applicable IWC Wage Order. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed almost entirely by statutory and regulatory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session. The repeal mechanics quoted below (petition threshold, election timing, and the 12-month interval) come from a single source, IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C)(5); Labor Code section 511 itself does not spell out the one-third-petition mechanism in its own text, though section 511(f) separately addresses which pre-2000 alternative workweek schedules survived as a historical matter, a different question this clause does not restate. The wage-reduction protection quoted below, Labor Code section 511(c), is an independent source — the statute, not the wage order — and corroborates that both the statute and the wage order contemplate repeal as a real, live possibility rather than describing the schedule as effectively permanent once adopted. The wage order's text also contains a now-historical exception, for schedules adopted between October 1, 1999 and October 1, 2000, to the 12-month interval; that exception is not restated above because it concerns elections from that specific historical window and is not general-purpose guidance.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(5)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(5)
citations.quote: Any type of alternative workweek schedule that is authorized by the Labor Code may be repealed by the affected employees. Upon a petition of one-third (1/3) of the affected employees, a new secret ballot election shall be held and a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the affected employees shall be required to reverse the alternative workweek schedule. The election to repeal the alternative workweek schedule shall be held not more than 30 days after the petition is submitted to the employer, except that the election shall be held not less than 12 months after the date that the same group of employees voted in an election held to adopt or repeal an alternative workweek schedule.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 511(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, no pay-rate reduction on adoption, repeal, or nullification
citations.quote: An employer shall not reduce an employee’s regular rate of hourly pay as a result of the adoption, repeal, or nullification of an alternative workweek schedule.

clauses.title: Anti-Coercion and Anti-Retaliation Protection for the Vote
clauses.body: Employers may not intimidate or coerce employees to vote for or against a proposed alternative workweek schedule, and may not discharge or otherwise discriminate against an employee for expressing an opinion about the proposal or for supporting or opposing its adoption or repeal. An employer remains free to state its own position on the proposal to affected employees; the restriction is on coercion and retaliation against employees, not on the employer speaking.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation; most states have no equivalent alternative-workweek election mechanism at all, and the federal Fair Labor Standards Act has no comparable provision. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself adopt, disclose, conduct, certify, or repeal any alternative workweek schedule, and it does not determine that any specific work unit, proposed schedule, disclosure, election, or repeal petition described using this document actually satisfies Labor Code section 511 or the applicable IWC Wage Order. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed almost entirely by statutory and regulatory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session. This protection was checked directly against Labor Code section 511 and against a section 511.5, on the possibility that the anti-coercion rule might be separately codified there as framed in the research request for this clause: no Labor Code section 511.5 exists (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov returns no section by that number), and section 511 itself contains no anti-coercion or anti-retaliation language. The protection quoted below exists only in the wage order, IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C)(8) — a single source, not independently corroborated by statutory text — which also states that a violation is "subject to Labor Code Section 98 et seq.," the Labor Commissioner's general wage-claim enforcement procedure; that cross-reference is not independently traced or quoted here.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(8)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(8)
citations.quote: Employers shall not intimidate or coerce employees to vote either in support of or in opposition to a proposed alternative workweek. No employees shall be discharged or discriminated against for expressing opinions concerning the alternative workweek election or for opposing or supporting its adoption or repeal.

clauses.title: This Is Not the Same as an Individual Flex-Time Arrangement
clauses.body: An alternative workweek schedule adopted through this process is a formal, group-level change to a work unit's regularly scheduled workweek, and it changes when daily overtime is legally owed only if it is established through the statutory two-thirds secret-ballot election described above. An informal arrangement between an employer and a single employee to work a compressed or flexible schedule, reached outside a section 511 election, is a different thing: it does not, by itself, change the point at which daily overtime is owed under California law.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific employer's situation; most states have no equivalent alternative-workweek election mechanism at all, and the federal Fair Labor Standards Act has no comparable provision. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself adopt, disclose, conduct, certify, or repeal any alternative workweek schedule, and it does not determine that any specific work unit, proposed schedule, disclosure, election, or repeal petition described using this document actually satisfies Labor Code section 511 or the applicable IWC Wage Order. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed almost entirely by statutory and regulatory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session. This clause reuses, rather than newly re-quotes, the same two citations already verified in this document's clause on the two-thirds vote requirement (Labor Code section 511(a) and IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 3(C)(2)) as the direct textual evidence that the statutory mechanism is a group vote within a defined work unit, not an individual agreement; the same source-independence description given there applies here. This clause does not address whether some other, separate legal basis (for example, an individual exempt-employee classification, or a different statutory schedule such as a 4/10 schedule under a collective bargaining agreement negotiated under different rules) might also change when overtime is owed — it addresses only the contrast between a section 511 election and an informal, unvoted flex-time arrangement.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 511(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, alternative workweek schedule adoption and vote threshold
citations.quote: A proposal to adopt an alternative workweek schedule shall be deemed adopted only if it receives approval in a secret ballot election by at least two-thirds of affected employees in a readily identifiable work unit.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 3(C)(2)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 3(C)(2)
citations.quote: In order to be valid, the proposed alternative workweek schedule must be adopted in a secret ballot election, before the performance of work, by at least a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the affected employees in the work unit. The election shall be held during regular working hours at the employees’ work site.
