Assignment Must Carry the Goodwill of the Business Connected With the Mark
clauses.body: Federal trademark law does not treat a mark as a piece of property that can be sold on its own, detached from the business it identifies. The statute states that a registered mark, or a mark for which an application has been filed, is assignable only with the goodwill of the business in which the mark is used, or with that part of the goodwill of the business connected with the use of and symbolized by the mark. This is why an assignment like this one for {{trademarkDescription}} is written to expressly transfer the goodwill of the business connected with the mark's use, alongside the mark itself, rather than transferring the mark by itself.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the statutory condition on assignability — not a claim that the goodwill actually being transferred by the assignor to the assignee under this particular agreement is sufficient in fact or in law, which depends on the underlying business and transaction and is not resolved by this clause. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(1), first sentence); the companion clause below on intent-to-use applications quotes a second sentence of that same subsection (a)(1), and is not an independent source from this one. This is federal law that applies nationwide; it does not address any state's separate law on assignment of a state-registered or common-law mark, which is addressed in a separate clause below. This document is informational only and does not itself determine whether any specific transfer of the mark described on this sheet complies with this statute.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, assignment of marks — goodwill requirement
citations.quote: A registered mark or a mark for which an application to register has been filed shall be assignable with the good will of the business in which the mark is used, or with that part of the good will of the business connected with the use of and symbolized by the mark.

clauses.title: An Intent-to-Use Application Generally Cannot Be Assigned Before Use Is Shown
clauses.body: The general goodwill-assignability rule has a specific statutory carve-out for an application filed on an intent-to-use basis. The statute states that no application to register a mark filed under the intent-to-use provision is assignable before the applicant either files an amendment converting the application to a use-based filing, or files the verified statement of use required to complete registration — except for an assignment to a successor to the business of the applicant, or the portion of that business to which the mark pertains, if that business is ongoing and existing. In other words, until use in commerce has actually been shown (or the application amended to reflect it), an intent-to-use application generally cannot be assigned to just any buyer; the only assignee the statute permits at that stage is a successor to the applicant's own ongoing business. If {{trademarkDescription}} is the subject of a pending intent-to-use application rather than an issued registration or a use-based application, this restriction, not the general rule above, controls whether this assignment from {{assignorName}} to {{assigneeName}} is one the statute permits at this time.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a statutory restriction distinct from, and narrower than, the general goodwill-assignability rule in the companion clause above; both quotes come from the same statutory subsection, 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(1) (the first and second sentences of that subsection), and are not independent sources of each other. This clause does not determine whether the named assignee in fact qualifies as a successor to the assignor's ongoing business, which is a factual question outside this document's scope, nor does it resolve whether the particular filing being assigned is registered, use-based, or intent-to-use — that characterization depends on the actual USPTO filing. This is federal law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, assignment of marks — restriction on assigning an intent-to-use application before use is shown
citations.quote: Notwithstanding the preceding sentence, no application to register a mark under section 1051(b) of this title shall be assignable prior to the filing of an amendment under section 1051(c) of this title to bring the application into conformity with section 1051(a) of this title or the filing of the verified statement of use under section 1051(d) of this title, except for an assignment to a successor to the business of the applicant, or portion thereof, to which the mark pertains, if that business is ongoing and existing.

clauses.title: "Assignment in Gross" — the Consequence of Assigning a Mark Without the Goodwill It Symbolizes
clauses.body: The goodwill requirement described above is not just a drafting formality. When a mark is transferred without the goodwill of the business connected with its use — sometimes called an "assignment in gross" — the transfer falls outside what the statute makes assignable, and courts applying the Lanham Act have treated such a transfer as legally deficient: an assignment in gross can be held invalid, and the assignee can be denied the ability to claim the priority of the assignor's earlier registration date or earlier date of first use, meaning the assignee may be treated as if its own rights in the mark began only with its own, later use rather than stepping into the assignor's shoes. This is the reason this agreement expressly states, in the declaration below, that the goodwill of the business connected with the use of {{trademarkDescription}} is included in what {{assignorName}} is transferring to {{assigneeName}} — that statement is directed at avoiding exactly this doctrine.
clauses.gap: This clause describes a judicial doctrine construing the statutory goodwill requirement quoted in the first clause above (15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(1)); it is not independent of that citation, and no additional statutory citation is given here. This session was not able to independently verify a specific court decision applying the assignment-in-gross doctrine with a checked quotation: CourtListener's case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, "125/day" quota already exhausted, with the quota not resetting until later than this research session) when queried for this doctrine, and the secondary legal-research and treatise sites this session attempted to reach for a description of the doctrine (including USPTO.gov, Wikipedia, and other commentary sites) were unreachable through this environment's network egress policy. Rather than fabricate a case citation or quote, this clause describes the doctrine's substance — that it is a widely recognized construction of the statutory goodwill requirement, consistent with that requirement's own text — without citing a specific case for it, and that description should be understood as this document's own characterization of a body of case law that was not independently checked source-by-source in this session. This is federal law that applies nationwide; it does not resolve whether the specific transfer described in this agreement in fact includes goodwill sufficient to avoid this doctrine, which depends on the underlying business and transaction.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, assignment of marks — goodwill requirement (statutory basis for the assignment-in-gross doctrine)
citations.quote: A registered mark or a mark for which an application to register has been filed shall be assignable with the good will of the business in which the mark is used, or with that part of the good will of the business connected with the use of and symbolized by the mark.

clauses.title: A Trademark Assignment Must Be in Writing
clauses.body: Unlike a trademark license, which the Lanham Act does not require to be in writing, an assignment of a registered mark or a pending application must be by an instrument in writing, duly executed. This is part of why a signed, written document like this one — rather than a verbal understanding — is what is needed to actually transfer {{assignorName}}'s ownership of {{trademarkDescription}} to {{assigneeName}}.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the writing requirement — not a claim about what specific form of signature (handwritten, scanned, or fully electronic under the federal E-SIGN Act or a state UETA-equivalent statute) satisfies "instrument in writing" in every circumstance, which this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(3)); the companion recording clause below quotes a second sentence of that same subsection together with a separate subsection, (a)(4), and neither is an independent source from this one. This is federal law that applies nationwide; California's own state trademark statute imposes a parallel writing requirement for assignment of a state-registered mark, addressed in a separate clause below.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, assignment of marks — writing requirement
citations.quote: Assignments shall be by instruments in writing duly executed.

clauses.title: Recording a Trademark Assignment With the USPTO
clauses.body: Federal law permits, but does not itself require, an assignment like this one to be recorded with the United States Patent and Trademark Office. Recording matters because of a specific consequence for not doing so: an assignment is void against a later, good-faith purchaser who pays valuable consideration for the same mark without notice of this assignment, unless this assignment is recorded with the USPTO within three months of its date, or before the date of that later purchase. Separately, the statute describes what recording itself establishes: an acknowledged assignment is prima facie evidence that it was executed, and when the assignment is recorded with the USPTO, that record is likewise made prima facie evidence of execution — evidence, in other words, that the document was signed, not a USPTO determination that the underlying transfer is legally valid, that it includes the goodwill the statute requires, or that {{assigneeName}}'s resulting title is free of competing claims. Recording this assignment of {{trademarkDescription}} from {{assignorName}} to {{assigneeName}} is a step the parties can take with the USPTO; this document does not itself record anything.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes two sentences of the same statutory subsection area, 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a) — the third sentence of paragraph (a)(3) and paragraph (a)(4) — and treats them as one source, not independent of each other. The statement that recording is evidence of execution rather than an examination of the assignment's underlying validity is drawn directly from the statute's own limited description of what recording establishes ("prima facie evidence of execution"); this session did not locate, and this clause does not cite, a separate case or USPTO manual addressing the scope of USPTO's examination of a recorded assignment beyond what this statutory text itself says, because USPTO.gov and other secondary sources were unreachable through this environment's network egress policy during this research session (see the companion assignment-in-gross clause above for the same limitation). This is federal law that applies nationwide; it does not resolve whether recording occurs for any particular signed copy of this agreement, which is a step the parties would need to take themselves and which this document does not track.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, assignment of marks — recording as prima facie evidence of execution
citations.quote: when the prescribed information reporting the assignment is recorded in the United States Patent and Trademark Office, the record shall be prima facie evidence of execution

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1060(a)(4) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, assignment of marks — three-month recording window against a subsequent purchaser
citations.quote: An assignment shall be void against any subsequent purchaser for valuable consideration without notice, unless the prescribed information reporting the assignment is recorded in the United States Patent and Trademark Office within 3 months after the date of the assignment or prior to the subsequent purchase.

clauses.title: California Has Its Own, Parallel Assignment Statute for State-Registered Marks
clauses.body: Separate from the federal Lanham Act, California's own trademark statute — the Model State Trademark Law — addresses assignment of a mark registered with the California Secretary of State. It uses the same basic structure as the federal statute: a mark and its state registration are assignable with the goodwill of the business in which the mark is used, or with that part of the goodwill of the business connected with the use of and symbolized by the mark; the assignment must be by a written, duly executed instrument; and an assignment is void against a subsequent purchaser for valuable consideration without notice unless it is recorded with the Secretary of State within three months of the assignment's date or before that later purchase. This state statute is a separate, independent legal source from the federal recording and goodwill rules described above, and applies on its own terms to a mark registered under California's state trademark statute, distinct from a federal USPTO registration or application.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own, separately codified assignment rule for a state-registered mark — not a claim that the mark described on this sheet is in fact registered with the California Secretary of State, or about which jurisdiction's law governs this assignment, either of which depends on facts this clause does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory section, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14220; no additional independent state-law source was needed. This provision addresses assignment specifically; it is a different section of the same Model State Trademark Law chapter as Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14259, which this project's existing Trademark Infringement — Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet document cites for a different point (the statute's preservation of common-law trademark rights), and this clause does not restate that separate point. This state statute does not apply to, and this clause does not address, a purely federal registration or application that has no separate California state registration.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14220(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Model State Trademark Law, assignment of a state-registered mark
citations.quote: Any mark and its registration hereunder shall be assignable with the good will of the business in which the mark is used, or with that part of the good will of the business connected with the use of and symbolized by the mark. Assignment shall be by instrument in writing duly executed and may be recorded with the secretary upon the payment of the recording fee payable to the secretary as set forth in subdivision (b) of Section 12193 of the Government Code, who, upon recording of the assignment, shall issue in the name of the assignee a new certificate for the remainder of the term of the registration or of the last renewal thereof. An assignment of any registration under this chapter shall be void as against any subsequent purchaser for valuable consideration without notice, unless it is recorded with the secretary within three months after the date thereof or prior to the subsequent purchase.

clauses.title: Core Nonrecognition Rule for Real Property Exchanges
clauses.body: Federal tax law states that no gain or loss is recognized for federal income tax purposes on the exchange of real property held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment, if that real property is exchanged solely for real property of like kind that is likewise to be held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment. This rule is codified at 26 U.S.C. § 1031(a)(1) and applies only to real property. Before 2018, an equivalent nonrecognition rule also reached exchanges of certain personal property. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 amended § 1031 to limit nonrecognition treatment to real property, substituting "real property" for "property" throughout subsection (a)(1); that amendment applies to exchanges completed after December 31, 2017, subject to a transition rule preserving prior law for an exchange where the property given up was disposed of on or before that date, or the exchange was underway pursuant to a written agreement entered into on or before that date.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as evidence of what § 1031 provides generally about real property exchanges — not tax advice about whether any specific taxpayer's exchange qualifies for nonrecognition treatment. Both citations below are drawn from the same law.cornell.edu page for 26 U.S.C. § 1031: the first quotes the codified text of subsection (a)(1) itself, and the second quotes the reproduced text of the uncodified effective-date provision of Pub. L. 115-97, § 13303(c) (the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act), which appears on that same page as an editorial note rather than as codified Code text. They are treated here as one source, not independent corroboration, since both come from the single fetched page for this section. No case law was researched for this clause; the topic is resolved directly by unambiguous statutory text, and this research is primarily statutory/regulatory in nature.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 1031(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)

citations.quote: No gain or loss shall be recognized on the exchange of real property held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment if such real property is exchanged solely for real property of like kind which is to be held either for productive use in a trade or business or for investment.

clauses.title: The "Like Kind" Standard for Real Property
clauses.body: Treasury regulations interpreting § 1031 state that the words "like kind," as used in the statute, refer to the nature or character of property, not to its grade or quality. Applying that standard, the regulations state that whether real estate is improved or unimproved is not material, because that fact relates only to grade or quality, not to kind or class — so real property is broadly treated as like kind to other real property regardless of grade or quality. The regulations illustrate this with examples of qualifying like-kind exchanges: a taxpayer who is not a real estate dealer exchanging city real estate for a ranch or farm, and an exchange of improved real estate for unimproved real estate. This broad like-kind standard for real property comes from Treasury regulations, not from the text of § 1031 itself — the statute does not define "like kind" or state this grade-or-quality distinction.
clauses.gap: This is a federal Treasury regulation, used as evidence of how "like kind" is defined for real property under § 1031 — not tax advice about whether any specific two parcels of real property are like kind to one another in a given exchange. Both citations below are subsections — (b) and (c) — of the same regulation section, 26 C.F.R. § 1.1031(a)-1, and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. This regulation's general definition and examples predate the 2017 real-property-only limitation and were written when § 1031 covered personal as well as real property, but a separate paragraph of the same regulation section, § 1.1031(a)-1(a)(3), cross-references this definition as continuing to apply to exchanges of real property after 2017. No case law was researched for this clause, consistent with this research being primarily statutory/regulatory rather than case-law-driven.

clauses.title: Identification and Exchange-Completion Deadlines
clauses.body: Federal tax law fixes deadlines, measured from the transfer of the relinquished property, for identifying and receiving replacement property in a § 1031 exchange. Under 26 U.S.C. § 1031(a)(3), property received by the taxpayer is treated as property that is not like-kind property — and so falls outside nonrecognition treatment — unless it is identified as replacement property on or before the day that is 45 days after the date the taxpayer transfers the relinquished property, and it is received by the earlier of the day that is 180 days after that transfer date, or the due date (taking extensions into account) of the taxpayer's tax return for the year in which the transfer of the relinquished property occurs.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as evidence of the identification and completion deadlines § 1031 imposes generally — not tax advice about whether any specific taxpayer's exchange met these deadlines. Both citations below are subparagraphs — (A) and (B) — of the same statutory paragraph, § 1031(a)(3), and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. The statute's own mechanism is narrower than an outright disqualification of the whole exchange: property received outside these deadlines is treated as not like-kind, which triggers the boot-recognition and basis rules described elsewhere in this document rather than necessarily voiding nonrecognition treatment for property that was properly identified and received. No case law was researched for this clause; the deadlines are stated in unambiguous statutory text.

citations.quote: such property is not identified as property to be received in the exchange on or before the day which is 45 days after the date on which the taxpayer transfers the property relinquished in the exchange

clauses.title: What This Nonrecognition Rule Does Not Cover
clauses.body: Federal tax law places two real property exchanges outside § 1031's nonrecognition rule, on two different legal grounds. First, § 1031(a)(2) states that the nonrecognition rule does not apply to any exchange of real property held primarily for sale — property a dealer holds as inventory, rather than for productive use in a trade or business or for investment. Second, a separate provision, § 1031(h), states that real property located in the United States and real property located outside the United States are not property of a like kind to one another; an exchange of domestic for foreign real property therefore falls outside § 1031 because it fails the like-kind requirement itself, on different statutory grounds than the dealer-property exclusion in (a)(2), even though both are commonly described together as exclusions from the exchange rule.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as evidence of what § 1031 excludes generally — not tax advice about whether any specific property is dealer inventory or about where any specific replacement property is located. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, § 1031 — (a)(2) and (h) — and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. Correction to a common assumption: the foreign-real-property rule has never been housed within (a)(2)'s exclusion list; it has always been a separate provision (subsection (h), added in 1989) framed as a like-kind definition rather than an exclusion, and this structure predates the 2017 amendment. Before 2017, (a)(2) additionally excluded stocks, bonds, partnership interests, and several other categories of personal property from the exchange rule; those categories became moot for (a)(2) once the 2017 amendment limited § 1031 to real property generally, described in this document's clause on the core nonrecognition rule. No case law was researched for this clause.

clauses.title: Boot and Basis Carryover
clauses.body: If a taxpayer receives money or other non-like-kind property — commonly called "boot" — along with like-kind real property in a § 1031 exchange, 26 U.S.C. § 1031(b) states that any gain on the exchange is recognized, but only up to the amount of that money plus the fair market value of that other property; § 1031(c) states the parallel rule that a loss on the exchange is not recognized where boot is received. Separately, 26 U.S.C. § 1031(d) states that the taxpayer's basis in property acquired in the exchange is the same as the basis of the property given up, decreased by any money the taxpayer received and increased or decreased by any gain or loss recognized on the exchange; where the property received is partly like-kind replacement property and partly other property, that carried-over basis is allocated between them based on their relative fair market value at the date of the exchange.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as evidence of how § 1031 treats boot and basis generally — not tax advice computing the recognized gain or resulting basis for any specific taxpayer's exchange. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, § 1031 — (b) and (d) — and are treated here as one source, not as independent corroborating sources. As the task instructions anticipated, this clause states the boot-recognition principle and the fact that basis carries over with adjustment at a factual level; it does not work through the basis-allocation formula in full technical detail. No case law was researched for this clause.

citations.quote: then the gain, if any, to the recipient shall be recognized, but in an amount not in excess of the sum of such money and the fair market value of such other property.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, basis of property received in the exchange
citations.quote: the basis shall be the same as that of the property exchanged, decreased in the amount of any money received by the taxpayer and increased in the amount of gain or decreased in the amount of loss to the taxpayer that was recognized on such exchange.

clauses.title: California's Information-Return Requirement for Out-of-State Replacement Property
clauses.body: California imposes its own tracking requirement on a taxpayer who defers California-source gain through a § 1031 exchange. Under California Revenue and Taxation Code § 18032 (personal income tax) and the parallel § 24953 (corporation tax), if gain or loss from an exchange of California real property is not recognized because of § 1031 of the Internal Revenue Code, and the replacement property acquired in that exchange is located outside California, the taxpayer must file an information return with the California Franchise Tax Board for the taxable year of the exchange and for each later taxable year in which that gain or loss remains unrecognized, in the form and manner the Franchise Tax Board prescribes. This is a reporting obligation, not a withholding tax collected out of the exchange proceeds: neither section requires money to be withheld under this particular provision. If a taxpayer fails to file this information return and also fails to file the income tax return otherwise required for that year, the Franchise Tax Board may estimate the taxpayer's net income from available information — including the deferred gain — and propose an assessment of tax, interest, and penalties. This filing requirement applies to exchanges occurring in taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2014.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own tracking requirement for California real property exchanged into an out-of-state replacement property — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific taxpayer's exchange, and not tax advice about whether any specific taxpayer must file this return. Correction to a common assumption: the mechanism the task described as "withholding" is, on the statutory text, an information-return filing requirement, not a withholding tax; California does have a separate, more general real-estate withholding statute (Rev. & Tax. Code § 18662) for certain California real property sales, but that provision is not part of this § 1031-specific tracking mechanism and was not researched for this document. Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code §§ 18032 and 24953 are separately codified sections — one under the Personal Income Tax Law, one under the Corporation Tax Law — rather than subsections of a single section, but they are near-identical mirror provisions enacted together by the same 2013 bill (Stats. 2013, Ch. 26 (AB 92)); they are cited together as confirmation that the same requirement reaches both individual and corporate taxpayers, not as fully independent corroboration of the underlying rule. The Franchise Tax Board's own form for this filing is commonly referred to as FTB Form 3840, "California Like-Kind Exchanges" — that form name and number come from the Franchise Tax Board's published guidance, not from the statutory text quoted below, and could not be independently verified against a primary ftb.ca.gov source in this research session because outbound access to ftb.ca.gov is blocked in this environment; it is stated here for reader orientation only, not as a verified citation. No case law was researched for this clause.

clauses.title: Signature and Certification
Professional Corporation Defined; Moscone-Knox as a General Regulatory Framework
clauses.body: California's Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act (Cal. Corp. Code § 13400 et seq.) is the statute requiring a corporation that renders certain licensed services to organize as a "professional corporation" rather than as an ordinary business corporation. Its structure is a general framework, not a fixed list of named professions written into the Act itself. The Act defines "professional services" generically, by cross-reference to licensure: any service "lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certification, or registration authorized by the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, or the Osteopathic Act." A "professional corporation" is, in turn, a corporation organized under the General Corporation Law that renders professional services in a single profession pursuant to a currently effective "certificate of registration issued by the governmental agency regulating the profession." That certificate-of-registration mechanism is itself not universal within the Act: the same subsection carves out a specific list of licensing boards — including the Medical Board of California, the Podiatric Medical Board, the Osteopathic Medical Board, the Dental Board, the Dental Hygiene Board, the State Board of Pharmacy, the Veterinary Medical Board, the California Architects Board, the Court Reporters Board, the Board of Behavioral Sciences, the Speech-Language Pathology and Audiology and Hearing Aid Dispensers Board, the Board of Registered Nursing, the State Board of Optometry, and the California Board of Occupational Therapy — whose licensees are not required to obtain a Moscone-Knox certificate of registration at all, because those professions are instead governed by their own separate profession-specific corporation provisions elsewhere in the Business and Professions Code. Professions not on that carve-out list, such as law and public accountancy, do go through the Moscone-Knox certificate-of-registration process, administered by their own regulating agency (for example, the State Bar for a law corporation). Either way, the profession-specific acts layer additional, profession-specific requirements on top of — they do not replace — the Moscone-Knox framework itself.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 13401, so they are treated as one source, not two independent ones. This description of the certificate-of-registration carve-out is limited to the licensing boards Section 13401(b) itself names as of the version fetched here; it is not a claim that this list is exhaustive of every California licensed profession or that it will remain unchanged. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's corporation, and professional-corporation requirements (including which professions must use one, ownership rules, naming rules, and licensing-board oversight) vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, does not itself obtain any certificate of registration or licensing-board approval, and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's or group's plan to incorporate.

clauses.title: Share Ownership Restricted to Licensed Persons, With a Narrow Minority Exception
clauses.body: California's general rule for a professional corporation's shares is an ownership restriction, not merely a management restriction: shares of capital stock "may be issued only to a licensed person or to a person who is licensed to render the same professional services" in the jurisdiction where that person practices, and "any shares issued in violation of this restriction shall be void." A separate section, Cal. Corp. Code § 13401.5, then supplies a narrow, list-based exception to that rule: for a specifically designated set of professional corporation types — mostly health-care professions, such as a medical corporation, podiatric medical corporation, psychological corporation, nursing corporation, dental corporation, and a number of others enumerated by subdivision (a) through (s) of that section — certain other licensed persons who are not licensed in the corporation's own profession may nonetheless be shareholders, officers, directors, or professional employees, subject to two caps: the shares those other licensed persons collectively hold cannot exceed 49 percent of the total shares, and the number of such shareholders cannot exceed the number of shareholders licensed in the corporation's own profession. This exception is not universal — it applies only to the professional corporation types Section 13401.5 itself designates, and, notably, does not extend to a law corporation or an accountancy corporation, neither of which appears among the designated types.

clauses.title: Professional Corporation Naming Governed by Profession-Specific Law, Not Ordinary Corporate Naming Rules
clauses.body: A professional corporation's permitted name is not fixed by the Moscone-Knox Act's own text the way an ordinary corporation's name is fixed by the General Corporation Law. Instead, Cal. Corp. Code § 13409(a) hands the naming question to whatever law or regulation governs the specific profession: a professional corporation "may adopt any name permitted by a law expressly applicable to the profession in which the corporation is engaged or by a rule or regulation of the governmental agency regulating that profession," and the Secretary of State may require an affidavit establishing that the chosen name complies with that profession-specific law. This means the actual naming rule a given professional corporation must follow — for example, whether it must include a shareholder's surname, the words "Professional Corporation" or an abbreviation such as "P.C." or "Prof. Corp.," or a term describing the type of practice — is set by that profession's own governing law or its regulating board's rules, not by Moscone-Knox itself. Section 13409(a) is also expressly "[s]ubject to Section 201," so a professional corporation's name remains bound by the General Corporation Law's baseline naming rules even after satisfying the profession-specific requirement: the Secretary of State will not accept a name it determines is "likely to mislead the public," and the name must be "distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State" from other registered and reserved corporate names.

Code § 201, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. The specific naming requirement for any one profession (for example, whether a surname or a particular abbreviation is required) is set by that profession's own governing law or regulating board's rules, which this clause does not individually verify for every profession — it verifies only the Moscone-Knox and General Corporation Law framework that hands that question to profession-specific law in the first place. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's corporation, and professional-corporation requirements (including which professions must use one, ownership rules, naming rules, and licensing-board oversight) vary by state. clauses.title: Incorporation Does Not Shield a Professional From Liability for Their Own Malpractice
clauses.body: Neither the Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act nor the profession-specific acts layered on top of it contain an express provision stating that a licensed professional's own liability for their own professional negligence disappears when they incorporate. Forming a professional corporation is understood, under general California corporate and agency principles, to shield a shareholder-professional from personal liability for the corporation's ordinary business debts and, in most circumstances, from liability for the malpractice of other shareholders or employees — but it does not extend that shield to a professional's liability for their own individually negligent or wrongful acts in rendering professional services, which remains a matter of personal responsibility regardless of the corporate form through which the services were rendered. Two profession-specific statutes in the Business and Professions Code supply indirect but real statutory evidence that this liability exposure persists notwithstanding incorporation: both the law corporation article and the accountancy corporation article condition the corporation's certificate of registration on the corporation maintaining insurance or other security for client claims arising out of the rendering of professional services — a mandatory-insurance condition that would serve no purpose if incorporating eliminated the underlying liability the insurance is meant to cover.
clauses.gap: This clause differs from the others in this document in kind, not just in citation: unlike Sections 13401, 13401.5, 13406, 13409, 13403, 13404, and 13410, no provision of the Moscone-Knox Act itself was found, in the text verified here, to state in so many words that a professional corporation does not shield a professional from liability for their own malpractice. The rule as stated in the body above rests substantially on general California common-law and agency principles (that an individual remains personally liable for their own tortious conduct regardless of the corporate form through which they act) rather than on a single operative Moscone-Knox statute, and no case law citation establishing this specific rule for professional corporations is included here — case law research for this point was not completed as part of this verification pass, consistent with this document's statutory focus. The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted profession-specific statutes, Bus. & Prof. Code § 6171 (law corporations) and Bus. & Prof. Code § 5157 (accountancy corporations), and are used here only as indirect evidence — a mandatory-insurance requirement consistent with continuing personal liability exposure — not as a direct statutory statement of the liability rule itself; they are treated as two independent sources. The mandatory-insurance requirement they state applies, by its own terms, only to law corporations and accountancy corporations specifically, not to every professional corporation type; other professions' corporation acts were not individually checked for an equivalent insurance requirement here. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's corporation, and professional-corporation requirements (including which professions must use one, ownership rules, naming rules, and licensing-board oversight) vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, does not itself obtain any certificate of registration or licensing-board approval, and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's or group's plan to incorporate.

clauses.title: General Corporation Law Applies Except Where Moscone-Knox Conflicts
clauses.body: A professional corporation is not governed by an entirely separate corporate-law regime. Cal. Corp. Code § 13403 states the relationship directly: "[t]he provisions of the General Corporation Law shall apply to professional corporations, except where such provisions are in conflict with or inconsistent with the provisions of this part." Consistent with that structure, Cal. Corp. Code § 13404 confirms that a professional corporation is formed the same way an ordinary corporation is formed — "under the General Corporation Law" — for the added purpose of qualifying as a professional corporation, with the one required deviation that its articles of incorporation "shall contain a specific statement that the corporation is a professional corporation within the meaning of this part." So a professional corporation exists on the same General Corporation Law chassis as an ordinary for-profit corporation, modified by the Moscone-Knox Act's own rules only where the two conflict — for example, Section 13403 itself goes on to supply special reduced-director rules for a professional corporation with only one or two shareholders, displacing what the General Corporation Law would otherwise require.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 13403 and Cal. Corp. Code § 13404, and are treated as two independent sources, not subsections of one section. This clause describes the general relationship Moscone-Knox itself states between it and the General Corporation Law; it does not catalog every specific point of conflict or modification between the two bodies of law. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's corporation, and professional-corporation requirements (including which professions must use one, ownership rules, naming rules, and licensing-board oversight) vary by state. The articles of incorporation of a professional corporation shall contain a specific statement that the corporation is a professional corporation within the meaning of this part.

clauses.title: Separate Licensing Board Registration Required in Addition to Filing Articles
clauses.body: Filing articles of incorporation with the California Secretary of State is not, by itself, enough to let a professional corporation render professional services. Cal. Corp. Code § 13410(a) subjects a professional corporation to the applicable rules, regulations, and disciplinary provisions of "the governmental agency regulating the profession in which such corporation is engaged" — the same licensing board that regulates individual practitioners of that profession, layered onto the corporation itself. A concrete, verified example of the two-step process this creates is the law corporation: Bus. & Prof. Code § 6160 defines a "law corporation" as one that "is registered with the State Bar of California and has a currently effective certificate of registration from the State Bar pursuant to the Professional Corporation Act ... and this article," and identifies the State Bar as "the governmental agency" Moscone-Knox itself refers to for a law corporation. Filing articles with the Secretary of State creates the corporation as a legal entity; obtaining and maintaining the certificate of registration from the profession's own regulating agency is what actually authorizes that corporation to render the licensed professional services in question, and the two steps are governed by different statutes and different state offices.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections in two different codes, Cal. Corp. The State Bar / law corporation example is used here as one verified, concrete illustration of the general Moscone-Knox rule; the specific registering agency, application process, and fee differ for each profession and were not individually verified for every profession this document might apply to. As noted in the definitional clause above, some professions' licensing boards are exempted from the Moscone-Knox certificate-of-registration requirement itself because a separate profession-specific act governs their registration instead — that carve-out does not mean no licensing-board-level step exists for those professions, only that it is not the Moscone-Knox certificate specifically. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's corporation, and professional-corporation requirements (including which professions must use one, ownership rules, naming rules, and licensing-board oversight) vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any corporation, does not itself obtain any certificate of registration or licensing-board approval, and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's or group's plan to incorporate.

Purpose of This Appeal Information Sheet and Appeal Request Declaration
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's process for appealing a determination the Employment Development Department (EDD) has made on an unemployment insurance claim to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board (CUIAB). {{appealingParty}} appeals from the EDD's determination dated {{determinationDate}}, EDD case number {{eddCaseNumber}}, concerning the unemployment insurance claim between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}. The grounds for this appeal are: {{groundsForAppeal}}. This document states facts about the deadline to appeal, who may appeal, what a hearing before an administrative law judge involves, the further appeal available to the CUIAB itself, the judicial review available after that, and whether benefits continue while an appeal is pending — facts that California's Unemployment Insurance Code and Code of Civil Procedure set generally for this administrative process. It does not itself constitute an appeal filed with the EDD, an administrative law judge, or the CUIAB, and it does not determine that this or any appeal will succeed.

clauses.title: The Right to Appeal a Determination to an Administrative Law Judge, and the 30-Day Deadline
clauses.body: After the EDD considers whatever facts an employer has submitted and makes a determination on a claimant's eligibility for benefits, a statute gives both the claimant and the employer — not the claimant alone — the right to appeal that determination, or a reconsidered determination, to an administrative law judge. The event that starts the clock on this appeal is service of notice of the determination, not the date printed on the determination itself: the deadline is 30 days from that service. The same statute lets this 30-day period be extended for good cause, a term the statute itself defines to include, but not limit to, mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect, and it makes the EDD's own director an interested party to any appeal.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1328(a)), used as real evidence of California's own two-party appeal right and 30-day deadline running from service of the determination — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular claimant's or employer's appeal rights, and not a statement that any specific appeal, if filed, would succeed. This clause cites a single statutory subsection (§ 1328(a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific right-and-deadline claim. This corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Benefits — Claimant Information Sheet document already cites this same subsection, in its own uiclaimant_determination_and_appeal clause, for substantially the same right-and-deadline fact stated from the claimant's own perspective; that overlap is disclosed here rather than presented as new independent corroboration of § 1328(a) itself — this clause restates the identical statutory text as the entry point to a fuller, appeal-focused document, and the hearing-process, further-appeal, judicial-review, and continued-benefits clauses that follow are this document's genuinely new research, not previously cited anywhere in this corpus. This document does not itself file, or advise any specific claimant or employer to file, any appeal, and it does not calculate the actual 30-day deadline applicable to any specific determination.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1328(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: The claimant and the employer may appeal from a determination or reconsidered determination to an administrative law judge within 30 days from service of notice of the determination or reconsidered determination. The 30-day period may be extended for good cause, which shall include, but not be limited to, mistake, inadvertence, surprise, or excusable neglect. The director shall be an interested party to any appeal.

clauses.title: The Administrative Law Judge Hearing: In Person or by Telephone, Relaxed Evidence Rules, and Subpoena Power
clauses.body: California's Unemployment Insurance Code devotes a separate chapter, titled "Hearing Procedure," to what a hearing before an administrative law judge actually involves. The manner in which appeals are presented and hearings are conducted is set by rules the appeals board itself prescribes, and the appeals board must permit a party or representative to participate in a hearing by telephone if that party or representative requests it and shows good cause, under regulations the board has adopted — meaning a hearing is not confined only to an in-person format, though telephone participation is available on request rather than being the unconditional default. The administrative law judge and the appeals board's own representatives are not bound by common-law or statutory rules of evidence, or by technical or formal rules of procedure, though they must conduct the hearing so as to ascertain the parties' substantial rights; a full and complete record is kept of the proceeding, and testimony is recorded. Separately, any member of the appeals board, an administrative law judge, or an authorized employee the appeals board designates may administer oaths, take depositions, and issue subpoenas to compel a witness's attendance and the production of documents — so witnesses and documentary evidence are a real, statutorily contemplated part of this process, not merely informal fact-gathering.
clauses.gap: This is one state's set of statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 1951, 1952, and 1953, all within the same "Hearing Procedure" chapter), used as real evidence of what a California unemployment insurance administrative hearing actually involves — not a claim about which state's law governs a given hearing, and not a description of how any specific claimant's or employer's own hearing will actually be run, which remains subject to the appeals board's own prescribed rules and the presiding administrative law judge's own conduct of that particular proceeding. These three citations come from three separate statutory sections within the same chapter, each addressing a genuinely distinct procedural point — the manner of proceeding and telephone-participation right under § 1951, the relaxed evidence standard and recordkeeping duty under § 1952, and the oath/subpoena power under § 1953 — so they are not being presented as multiple citations to subsections of a single section. This document's drafter was asked to verify the actual citation for hearing procedures, including whether it appears in Title 22 of the California Code of Regulations. Title 22 of the CCR does contain the appeals board's own implementing hearing regulations, adopted under the rulemaking authority Unemployment Insurance Code § 411 gives the board, but this document's drafter could not independently verify any specific Title 22 CCR section's text against a primary source in this session: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, the primary source this project otherwise relies on for California statutes, does not host the California Code of Regulations, and a direct fetch of the regulations' official host returned a server error rather than section text. Rather than cite or quote a CCR section that could not be verified this way, this clause relies solely on the Unemployment Insurance Code's own Chapter 8 hearing-procedure sections quoted above, which independently and directly establish the facts this clause states. This document does not itself conduct, or determine the outcome of, any specific hearing.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1951 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: The appeals board shall permit a party or representative to participate in a hearing by telephone upon the party’s or representative’s request and showing a good cause, in accordance with regulations adopted by the board.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1952 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: The appeals board and its representatives and administrative law judges are not bound by common law or statutory rules of evidence or by technical or formal rules of procedure but may conduct the hearings and appeals in such manner as to ascertain the substantial rights of the parties. A full and complete record shall be kept of all proceedings in connection with disputed claims. All testimony at any hearing held in this state upon a disputed claim arising under this division shall be recorded and, when feasible, by a reporter in shorthand or by machine writing.

clauses.title: Further Appeal From the Administrative Law Judge's Decision to the CUIAB Itself
clauses.body: An administrative law judge's decision is not necessarily the last word inside the administrative process. The same statute that creates the first-level appeal right provides that the administrative law judge's decision, together with the reasons for it, must be sent in writing to the claimant, to the employer who became a party to the appeal, and to the director — and that the decision becomes final only if no further appeal is initiated within 30 days after the decision is mailed, the same 30-day period as the first-level appeal, likewise extendable for good cause. A separate statute defines what that further appeal actually allows: the director, or any party to the administrative law judge's decision, may appeal to the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board (CUIAB) — the same body named elsewhere in this document — and the appeals board itself may order that additional evidence be taken, and may affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside the administrative law judge's decision.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1334(a), for the 30-day further-appeal deadline, and § 1336, for the scope of the appeals board's own review), used as real evidence of California's second administrative appeal level — not a claim about which state's law governs a given appeal, and not a statement that a further appeal in any specific case has been, or should be, filed. These two citations come from different statutory sections; they are not multiple citations to subsections of a single section. This corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Benefits — Claimant Information Sheet document already cites § 1334(a) in its own uiclaimant_determination_and_appeal clause, for a shorter, claimant-facing statement of this same 30-day further-appeal deadline; that overlap is disclosed here rather than presented as new independent corroboration of § 1334(a) itself. Section 1336 — the source for the appeals board's actual scope of review on a further appeal — was checked directly against this corpus and does not appear to have been cited by any existing clause; it is genuinely new to this document's research. This document does not itself initiate, or advise any specific claimant or employer to initiate, a further appeal to the appeals board, and it does not state whether any such further appeal would succeed.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1334(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: An administrative law judge after affording a reasonable opportunity for fair hearing, shall, unless the appeal is withdrawn, affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside any determination that is appealed under this article. The claimant, the employer becoming a party to the appeal by submitting a protest or information pursuant to Sections 1326 to 1333, inclusive, of this article, and the director shall be promptly notified in writing of the administrative law judge’s decision, together with reasons for it. The decision shall be final unless, within 30 days after mailing of the decision, further appeal is initiated to the appeals board pursuant to Section 1336. The 30-day limitation may be extended for good cause.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1336 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: The director or any party to a decision by an administrative law judge may appeal to the appeals board from the decision. The appeals board may order the taking of additional evidence and may affirm, reverse, modify, or set aside the decision of the administrative law judge.

clauses.title: Judicial Review After the CUIAB's Decision, and the Six-Month Deadline
clauses.body: A CUIAB decision is not the absolute final word either. A statute makes a decision of the appeals board final "except for such action as may be taken by a judicial tribunal as permitted or required by law," and gives the director — and, with narrow statutory exceptions, any other party — the right to seek judicial review of an appeals board decision. That right must be exercised not later than six months after the date of the appeals board's decision (or, if the decision is designated as a precedent decision, six months from that designation date, if later) — a considerably longer deadline than the 30-day windows that apply to the two administrative appeal stages described above. Separately, California's general statute governing a writ of administrative mandate applies by its own terms to "any final administrative order or decision made as the result of a proceeding in which by law a hearing is required to be given, evidence is required to be taken, and discretion in the determination of facts is vested in" the deciding body — a description that, on its face, matches the evidentiary, discretion-involving hearing process this document describes above.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 410, for the right to seek judicial review of a CUIAB decision and its six-month deadline, and Code of Civil Procedure § 1094.5, for the state's general writ-of-administrative-mandate procedure), used as real evidence that California provides judicial review after the administrative appeal process is exhausted, and of the actual deadline for seeking it — not a claim about which state's law governs a given case, and not a statement that judicial review in any specific matter has been, or should be, sought. These are two independent statutes from two different codes, not subsections of a single section. This document's drafter was asked to verify whether judicial review proceeds specifically by a petition for writ of administrative mandate under Code of Civil Procedure § 1094.5. Section 410 itself does not name § 1094.5 or any other specific procedural vehicle; it only describes a general right to "such action as may be taken by a judicial tribunal as permitted or required by law." This clause connects that general right to § 1094.5 based on this document's own reading of § 1094.5's own text — a CUIAB decision is a final administrative order issued after a hearing at which evidence is taken and the deciding body exercises discretion in finding facts, which is exactly what § 1094.5 describes — rather than on a verified judicial decision holding that CUIAB review specifically proceeds under § 1094.5 (as opposed to, for example, ordinary mandate under a different Code of Civil Procedure section). The CourtListener case-law research tool used to search for such a confirming decision returned a rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) before any search could be completed in this session; rather than invent or assume a case citation, this document discloses that limitation honestly instead of citing one. This document does not itself seek, or advise any specific claimant or employer to seek, judicial review of any decision, and it does not state whether such review in any specific case would succeed.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 410 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: A decision of the appeals board is final, except for such action as may be taken by a judicial tribunal as permitted or required by law. A decision of the appeals board is binding on the director with respect to the parties involved in the particular appeal. The director shall have the right to seek judicial review from an appeals board decision irrespective of whether or not he or she appeared or participated in the appeal to the administrative law judge or to the appeals board. Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the right of the director, or of any other party except as provided by Sections 1241, 1243, and 5313, to seek judicial review from an appeals board decision shall be exercised not later than six months after the date of the decision of the appeals board or the date on which the decision is designated as a precedent decision, whichever is later.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1094.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.quote: Where the writ is issued for the purpose of inquiring into the validity of any final administrative order or decision made as the result of a proceeding in which by law a hearing is required to be given, evidence is required to be taken, and discretion in the determination of facts is vested in the inferior tribunal, corporation, board, or officer, the case shall be heard by the court sitting without a jury.

clauses.title: Whether Benefits Continue While an Appeal Is Pending
clauses.body: California's general claims-payment statute ties benefit payment directly to the EDD's own determination: except as otherwise provided, the EDD must promptly pay benefits if it finds a claimant eligible, and must promptly deny benefits if it finds the claimant ineligible. Nothing in that statute creates a separate, freestanding right for a claimant to keep receiving payments during the pendency of an appeal from a determination that already found the claimant ineligible or disqualified — the determination under appeal, not the filing of the appeal itself, is what the statute ties payment to. The practical direction can run the other way: where a determination has found a claimant eligible and benefits have been paid, and that determination is later reversed on an employer's appeal or on further appeal, a separate statute makes the recipient of an overpayment liable for the amount overpaid, subject to a statutory waiver where the overpayment was not due to fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure, was received without fault on the recipient's part, and recovering it would be against equity and good conscience.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1326, for the pay-if-eligible/deny-if-ineligible rule, and § 1375(a), for overpayment liability and its non-fault, equity-based waiver), used as real evidence of how California ties benefit payment to its own determination, and of what happens when a payment later turns out to have been based on a determination that did not hold up — not a claim about which state's law governs a given claim, and not a statement about whether any specific claimant is currently receiving, or should currently be receiving, payments during any specific pending appeal. These are two independent statutory sections, not subsections of a single section. This document's drafter was specifically asked not to assume a continued-benefits-pending-appeal rule exists, and direct review of the statute confirms that caution was warranted: no Unemployment Insurance Code section found in this research creates a general entitlement for a claimant, once found ineligible or disqualified, to keep receiving payments merely because an appeal from that determination has been timely filed. This document does not itself determine that any specific claimant is or is not entitled to payment during any specific appeal, and it does not state whether any specific overpayment would qualify for the statutory waiver described above.

citations.quote: Claims for unemployment compensation benefits shall be made in accordance with authorized regulations of the director. Except as otherwise provided in this article, the department shall promptly pay benefits if it finds the claimant is eligible or shall promptly deny benefits if it finds the claimant is ineligible.
