clauses.title: The FLSA's Default Rule for Interns
clauses.body: The Fair Labor Standards Act requires that covered employers pay at least the federal minimum wage to each of their "employees," and pay overtime of at least one and one-half times the regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a workweek. An intern who is legally an "employee" under the Act is covered by both requirements in exactly the same way as any other employee — the label "intern," "trainee," or "volunteer" attached to a position does not itself change whether the Act's minimum-wage and overtime requirements apply. Being unpaid is therefore not the default status of an internship at a for-profit employer; it is an exception that exists only where the specific legal test described elsewhere in this document is actually met.
clauses.gap: This describes the federal floor only. It does not by itself determine whether any particular internship qualifies as unpaid — that question is addressed by the separate clauses below, and this clause states only what follows once (or unless) an intern is found to be an "employee." Some states set a higher minimum wage or additional overtime requirements than federal law requires; this document does not catalog those. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific internship is, or is not, an employment relationship covered by the FLSA, and does not determine that any particular employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with the Act.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 206(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Fair Labor Standards Act, minimum wage
citations.quote: Every employer shall pay to each of his employees who in any workweek is engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce , or is employed in an enterprise engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce , wages at the following rates:

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 207(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Fair Labor Standards Act, overtime
citations.quote: no employer shall employ any of his employees who in any workweek is engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce , or is employed in an enterprise engaged in commerce or in the production of goods for commerce , for a workweek longer than forty hours unless such employee receives compensation for his employment in excess of the hours above specified at a rate not less than one and one-half times the regular rate at which he is employed.

clauses.title: Why an Intern's Status Requires a Legal Test, Not Just a Label
clauses.body: The Fair Labor Standards Act does not define "intern" or "trainee" at all, and its definition of "employee" is notoriously circular and broad: the statute defines "employee" as any individual employed by an employer, and separately defines "employ" to include "to suffer or permit to work." Because the statute's own text supplies no separate standard for distinguishing a genuine trainee or student from a worker who happens to be unpaid, courts and the Department of Labor have had to develop their own tests — described in the following clauses — to decide when an unpaid intern is, in substance, an "employee" the Act was written to protect.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are to different subsections of the same statutory section, 29 U.S.C. § 203; they are treated as one source, not independent. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular intern is, or is not, an "employee" within the meaning of the Act.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 203(e)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Fair Labor Standards Act, definitions
citations.quote: the term “ employee ” means any individual employed by an employer .

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 203(g) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Fair Labor Standards Act, definitions
citations.quote: “ Employ ” includes to suffer or permit to work.

clauses.title: The 'Primary Beneficiary' Test
clauses.body: The test federal courts and the U.S. Department of Labor currently use to decide whether an intern at a for-profit employer is an "employee" under the FLSA is commonly called the "primary beneficiary" test. It asks, in substance, whether the economic reality of the internship shows that the intern is the primary beneficiary of the relationship (in which case an unpaid arrangement can be lawful) or that the employer is the primary beneficiary (in which case the intern is an employee entitled to minimum wage and overtime). This flexible, no-single-factor-controlling approach traces back to the Supreme Court's 1947 decision holding that railroad brakeman trainees were not "employees" where the employer received no immediate advantage from their work — a case still cited as the doctrinal starting point for the modern test.
clauses.gap: This clause's account of the primary-beneficiary test's current form and adoption rests on more than one tier of sourcing, and that mix is disclosed here rather than papered over. What is independently verified below is the older, foundational case — Walling v. Portland Terminal Co., 330 U.S. 148 (1947) — fetched and quoted directly from a primary-source text. What is NOT independently verified in this session is the specific case usually credited with articulating the "primary beneficiary" test by that name, Glatt v. Fox Searchlight Pictures, Inc. (2d Cir., decided 2015 and amended 2016), or its later adoption by other circuits (including, per this research session's own case-law search results, the Ninth Circuit's Benjamin v. B & H Education) and by the U.S. Department of Labor. This session's attempts to verify Glatt against primary opinion text failed on every channel tried: the CourtListener API tool returned a daily rate-limit error (125 requests/day); a direct fetch of the individual CourtListener opinion page was blocked by CourtListener's own bot-challenge system (an AWS WAF JavaScript challenge, distinct from any rate limit); and the WebFetch tool reported that courtlistener.com is blocked by this environment's network egress policy. A CourtListener case-law search (a lighter, non-rate-limited endpoint) did confirm that opinions captioned "Glatt v. Fox Searchlight Pictures, Inc." exist in the database, dated 2015 and 2016 from the Second Circuit, and that a case captioned "Jacqueline Benjamin v. B & H Education" also exists — consistent with, but not a substitute for, independently reading either opinion's actual text. The description of the test and its case-law lineage in this clause's body is accordingly based on this document's general legal knowledge, not on primary-source text examined in this session, and is a materially weaker sourcing tier than the Walling citation below. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular internship's economic reality favors the intern or the employer.

citations.case: Walling v. Portland Terminal Co.
citations.cite: 330 U.S. 148 (1947) (Cornell LII text)
citations.quote: Accepting the unchallenged findings here that the railroads receive no 'immediate advantage' from any work done by the trainees, we hold that they are not employees within the Act's meaning.

clauses.title: Factors Bearing on Which Party Is the Primary Beneficiary
clauses.body: Rather than a rigid checklist where every element must be satisfied, the primary-beneficiary analysis is commonly described as weighing a non-exhaustive set of factors, with no single factor controlling and the answer depending on the totality of the circumstances of a given internship. Current U.S. Department of Labor guidance (Wage and Hour Division Fact Sheet #71, in the version issued in January 2018) is understood to describe seven such factors: (1) the extent to which the intern and the employer clearly understand there is no expectation of compensation; (2) the extent to which the internship provides training similar to that given in an educational environment; (3) the extent to which the internship is tied to the intern's formal education program, through integrated coursework or the receipt of academic credit; (4) the extent to which the internship accommodates the intern's academic commitments by corresponding to the academic calendar; (5) the extent to which the internship's duration is limited to the period in which it provides the intern with beneficial learning; (6) the extent to which the intern's work complements, rather than displaces, the work of paid employees while providing significant educational benefits to the intern; and (7) the extent to which the intern and the employer understand that the internship is conducted without entitlement to a paid job at its conclusion.
clauses.gap: This clause's seven-factor list carries a materially weaker sourcing tier than the rest of this document, and that is disclosed plainly rather than dressed up as verified. Every attempt to fetch DOL's own text of Fact Sheet #71 (or the related Field Assistance Bulletin No. 2018-2 describing the same seven factors) failed in this session: a direct fetch of dol.gov returned an HTTP 403 "Access Denied" response, and the WebFetch tool separately reported that www.dol.gov is blocked by this environment's network egress policy. This document's own general legal knowledge is the source of the specific seven-factor list stated above; an automated web search run in this session returned law-firm and industry-blog summaries that corroborate the existence, general framing, and roughly the first three factors of the same list, but those summary snippets were not independently fetched and checked against DOL's own primary text, so they do not upgrade this to a verified citation. No factor listed above was invented for this document, but none of the seven should be treated as independently confirmed against DOL's own current text in the way the citation below is. What IS independently verified is the older Supreme Court case establishing that this kind of question is decided by weighing the whole relationship rather than any one circumstance in isolation. This document is informational only: it does not itself weigh these factors for any particular internship or reach a conclusion about any specific intern's status.

citations.case: Walling v. Portland Terminal Co.
citations.cite: 330 U.S. 148 (1947) (Cornell LII text)
citations.quote: The Fair Labor Standards Act was not intended to penalize railroads for providing, free of charge, the same kind of instruction at a place and in a manner which would most greatly benefit the trainees.

clauses.title: A Separate Rule for Volunteers at Public Agencies
clauses.body: A different, narrower regulatory framework — not the primary-beneficiary test — governs unpaid volunteers at public agencies, meaning state and local government employers. Federal regulations provide that an individual who performs services for a public agency for civic, charitable, or humanitarian reasons, without promise, expectation, or receipt of compensation, is a volunteer for the time so spent, and is not subject to the Act's minimum-wage, overtime, and recordkeeping provisions for that time, subject to further conditions in the same regulations — including that the services be offered freely and without coercion, and that the individual not be otherwise employed by the same public agency to perform the same type of services.
clauses.gap: This regulation applies specifically to public agencies — government employers — and does not by its own terms extend to for-profit employers, which is the primary subject of the rest of this document, or automatically to private nonprofit organizations, which are addressed separately in this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular public-agency arrangement meets every condition this regulation requires.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 553.101(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, definition of "volunteer"
citations.quote: An individual who performs hours of service for a public agency for civic, charitable, or humanitarian reasons, without promise, expectation or receipt of compensation for services rendered, is considered to be a volunteer during such hours.

clauses.title: Nonprofit Employers Are Not Categorically Exempt
clauses.body: Calling an unpaid worker at a nonprofit organization a "volunteer" or an "associate," rather than an intern, does not by itself remove that person from the FLSA's coverage. The Supreme Court has held that unpaid workers at a nonprofit religious organization were "employees" under the Act because they worked in contemplation of compensation — there, compensation in the form of food, clothing, shelter, and other in-kind benefits, which the Court treated as wages in another form — applying the same "economic reality" test used generally to determine employee status, rather than any special nonprofit exemption.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are to the same Supreme Court decision; they are treated as one source, not independent. This is a single, older (1985) case addressing a specific fact pattern — in-kind compensation at a residential religious foundation — not a general holding about internship programs at nonprofits, and this document does not independently verify how, or whether, the specific primary-beneficiary test described elsewhere in this document (developed in later case law addressing for-profit employers by its own terms) has been extended by courts or by the Department of Labor to nonprofit-employer internships specifically; any such extension was not checked against primary source text in this session. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular nonprofit's unpaid workers are, or are not, "employees" under the Act.

clauses.title: California's DLSE Applies Its Own Federal-Derived Test — Not the Primary-Beneficiary Test
clauses.body: California has no state statute or regulation of its own that expressly exempts interns from the state's wage-and-hour laws. California's Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (DLSE), in its own currently published Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, states that it evaluates unpaid intern and trainee arrangements using a six-factor test the federal Department of Labor derived from the Supreme Court's Walling v. Portland Terminal Co. decision — not the newer, more flexible "primary beneficiary" test described elsewhere in this document. As of this manual's currently posted text, DLSE adopted this six-factor federal test, in preference to an older and stricter eleven-factor test it had previously applied, in a 2010 opinion letter.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are to the same source — section 46.6.4 of DLSE's Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual — and are treated as one source, not independent. The specific pages of the manual quoted here carry a "JULY, 2017" revision date printed in that section's own page footer, even though the manual's cover page is dated August 2019 and other sections carry later revision dates (some as recent as December 2020); this document fetched the manual live from California's Department of Industrial Relations website on the date shown above and quotes the section as currently published there, but cannot rule out that DLSE has since updated its position on interns specifically in a way not reflected in this publicly posted edition, and this document did not separately search for a more recent DLSE opinion letter on point. Note also that this section predates the U.S. Department of Labor's January 2018 adoption of the primary-beneficiary test described elsewhere in this document; whether DLSE's internal practice has since converged with the federal primary-beneficiary approach, notwithstanding what its own published manual currently states, was not independently verified. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine which test would actually be applied to any specific California internship, or by whom.

clauses.title: DLSE's Earlier, Stricter Eleven-Factor Test (Historical, Superseded)
clauses.body: Before 2010, DLSE opinion letters applied a stricter eleven-factor test, drawn from a legal treatise rather than from a statute or regulation, under which an unpaid arrangement was lawful only if every one of the eleven listed criteria was satisfied — not merely a majority of them. As reflected in a 1998 DLSE opinion letter applying that test to a newspaper's unpaid editorial interns, the agency treated the test's own first prong, requiring training similar to that given in a vocational school, as capable by itself of disqualifying an internship where the intern's duties strayed into ordinary clerical or business work.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are to the same source — a single 1998 DLSE opinion letter — and are treated as one source, not independent. This eleven-factor test is historical background, not the currently operative DLSE standard: the separate clause in this document on DLSE's current position states that DLSE replaced this eleven-factor test with a six-factor federal test in a 2010 opinion letter, on the reasoning that the five additional factors this older test required would have made no difference to the outcome. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular internship would, or would not, have satisfied this now-superseded test.

clauses.title: If an Unpaid Internship Is Later Found Not to Qualify
clauses.body: If an internship treated as unpaid is later determined to have been, in substance, an employment relationship covered by the FLSA, the statute makes the employer liable to the affected intern for the amount of unpaid minimum wages or unpaid overtime compensation, as applicable, plus an additional equal amount as liquidated damages — in effect, double the wages that should have been paid. This liability attaches to the work actually performed; it is not avoided by the fact that the arrangement was labeled, or intended by both sides, to be unpaid.
clauses.gap: This describes the federal remedy only; it does not state the FLSA's own statute of limitations for bringing such a claim, which this document does not independently verify. This document also does not restate California's separate wage-claim enforcement process and remedies — including the DLSE's Berman hearing process, its order-decision-award mechanism, and California-specific penalties — which are addressed in a separate information sheet elsewhere in this corpus (its DLSE Wage Claim Information Sheet) rather than duplicated here; an intern's or employer's actual exposure in California may include state-law remedies in addition to, and calculated differently from, the federal liquidated-damages remedy described in this clause. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular internship was misclassified, and does not calculate any specific amount owed.

clauses.title: Required Elements of an Effective Counter-Notification
clauses.body: Federal copyright law specifies what a subscriber's counter notification must contain to be effective under 17 U.S.C. § 512(g) — the provision that lets a person whose material was removed in response to a takedown notification seek its restoration. To be effective, a counter notification must be a written communication, provided to the service provider's designated agent, that includes substantially four elements, in this order: first, a physical or electronic signature of the subscriber; second, identification of the material that has been removed or to which access has been disabled, and the location at which the material appeared before it was removed or disabled; third, a statement, made under penalty of perjury, that the subscriber has a good faith belief that the material was removed or disabled as a result of mistake or misidentification of the material to be removed or disabled; and fourth, the subscriber's name, address, and telephone number, together with a statement that the subscriber consents to the jurisdiction of the federal district court for the judicial district where that address is located (or, if the address is outside the United States, any judicial district where the service provider may be found), and that the subscriber will accept service of process from the person who sent the original takedown notification or that person's agent. The statute places the signature requirement first and the sworn good-faith statement third, ahead of the contact-and-consent information, which comes last.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of what 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(3) requires a counter notification to contain — not a claim about whether any particular service provider's own counter-notification submission form asks for exactly this list and nothing more, or about how a specific platform processes a counter notification that is missing one of these elements. The companion DMCA Takedown Notice document in this corpus already quotes this same subsection, in the course of describing the put-back process generally, as part of a clause covering both the elements and the restoration timeline together; this clause is not an independent corroborating source from a different provision — it is the same statutory text, restated here as the primary subject of a document devoted to the counter-notification side of the process in more depth.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, required contents of a counter notification
citations.quote: To be effective under this subsection, a counter notification must be a written communication provided to the service provider’s designated agent that includes substantially the following: (A) A physical or electronic signature of the subscriber. (B) Identification of the material that has been removed or to which access has been disabled and the location at which the material appeared before it was removed or access to it was disabled. (C) A statement under penalty of perjury that the subscriber has a good faith belief that the material was removed or disabled as a result of mistake or misidentification of the material to be removed or disabled. (D) The subscriber’s name, address, and telephone number, and a statement that the subscriber consents to the jurisdiction of Federal District Court for the judicial district in which the address is located, or if the subscriber’s address is outside of the United States, for any judicial district in which the service provider may be found, and that the subscriber will accept service of process from the person who provided notification under subsection (c)(1)(C) or an agent of such person.

clauses.title: The Put-Back Sequence: Notice to the Subscriber, Forwarding, and the 10-to-14-Business-Day Restoration Window
clauses.body: Federal copyright law ties a service provider's protection from liability to the subscriber — for taking down material in the first place — to the provider following a specific three-step sequence once it removes or disables material in response to a takedown notification. First, the provider must take reasonable steps promptly to notify the subscriber that it has removed or disabled access to the material. Second, if the subscriber then submits a valid counter notification, the provider must promptly provide a copy of it to the person who sent the original takedown notification, and inform that person that the provider will restore the material in 10 business days. Third, the provider must actually restore the material — replacing it or ceasing to disable access to it — not less than 10, nor more than 14, business days after receiving the counter notification, unless its designated agent first receives notice that the person who sent the original notification has filed an action seeking a court order to restrain the subscriber from the allegedly infringing activity. That exception is narrow: it requires the complaining party to have actually filed a lawsuit seeking that specific kind of court order, not merely to have objected, sent a follow-up letter, or threatened legal action. The statute measures the window in business days, not calendar days, and does not itself define what counts as a business day.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the sequence and timing 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(2) sets for restoring removed material — not a claim about whether any particular service provider actually follows this sequence in a given case, about how a specific platform's internal restoration process works, or about what counts as a 'business day' for a particular provider, which the statute does not define. Compliance with this sequence is what preserves the provider's own liability protection under this subsection (addressed in a companion clause in this document), not a duty a subscriber can necessarily compel a court to enforce on its own; this clause does not claim otherwise. Both citations below are to subsections of the same statutory section, 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(2); they are treated as one source, not independent, corroborating sources. The companion DMCA Takedown Notice document in this corpus already quotes § 512(g)(2)(B)-(C); this clause adds the preceding step, § 512(g)(2)(A), which a document focused on sending a takedown notice does not need to dwell on.

citations.quote: unless the service provider— (A) takes reasonable steps promptly to notify the subscriber that it has removed or disabled access to the material;

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(2)(B)-(C) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, forwarding the counter notification and the restoration window
citations.quote: upon receipt of a counter notification described in paragraph (3), promptly provides the person who provided the notification under subsection (c)(1)(C) with a copy of the counter notification, and informs that person that it will replace the removed material or cease disabling access to it in 10 business days; and (C) replaces the removed material and ceases disabling access to it not less than 10, nor more than 14, business days following receipt of the counter notice, unless its designated agent first receives notice from the person who submitted the notification under subsection (c)(1)(C) that such person has filed an action seeking a court order to restrain the subscriber from engaging in infringing activity relating to the material on the service provider’s system or network.

clauses.title: Misrepresentation Liability Applies to a False Counter-Notification, Not Just a False Takedown Notice
clauses.body: Federal copyright law's misrepresentation-liability provision applies in both directions. A person who knowingly materially misrepresents, in a submission made under the notice-and-takedown provisions, either that material or activity is infringing (the takedown-notice direction) or that material or activity was removed or disabled by mistake or misidentification (the counter-notification direction) is liable for any damages — including costs and attorney's fees — incurred by whoever is injured by the misrepresentation, as a result of the service provider relying on it. For a false counter notification specifically, the person typically exposed to this liability is the subscriber who submitted it, and the party typically injured is the copyright owner or its authorized licensee whose material was restored, or ceased being disabled, based on the subscriber's sworn but knowingly false statement that removal was a mistake or misidentification. The statute lists the same set of potentially injured parties — the alleged infringer, a copyright owner or its authorized licensee, or a service provider — for either direction of misrepresentation, because whichever way the misrepresentation runs, any of those parties could end up being the one harmed by the service provider's reliance on it.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that 17 U.S.C. § 512(f) creates a damages remedy for a knowing material misrepresentation made in either a takedown notice or a counter notification — not a claim about whether any particular counter notification meets that standard, which turns on facts (including the subscriber's actual, subjective state of mind in swearing to a mistake-or-misidentification belief, not merely whether the subscriber turned out to be wrong) that this clause doesn't resolve. This is the same statutory subsection already quoted in the companion DMCA Takedown Notice document's dmca_misrepresentation_liability clause in this corpus, which addresses both directions in a single sentence; this clause restates the same text to focus specifically on the counter-notification direction, which that document treats only briefly. A well-known Ninth Circuit decision, Lenz v. Universal Music Corp., addressed what 'knowingly materially misrepresents' means under this subsection (in the takedown-notice direction); it could not be independently verified for this clause because the CourtListener research tool returned a daily rate-limit error (125 requests/day, next available in roughly 10 hours) on the attempt made while researching this document, so it is omitted from the citations below rather than quoted from memory. This topic is primarily statutory, and case law is not required to support the clause.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 512(f) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, misrepresentations in a takedown notice or counter-notification
citations.quote: Any person who knowingly materially misrepresents under this section— (1) that material or activity is infringing, or (2) that material or activity was removed or disabled by mistake or misidentification, shall be liable for any damages, including costs and attorneys’ fees, incurred by the alleged infringer, by any copyright owner or copyright owner’s authorized licensee, or by a service provider, who is injured by such misrepresentation, as the result of the service provider relying upon such misrepresentation in removing or disabling access to the material or activity claimed to be infringing, or in replacing the removed material or ceasing to disable access to it.

clauses.title: Only the Subscriber May File a Counter-Notification, and Doing So Forwards the Subscriber's Real Identity
clauses.body: Federal copyright law's counter-notification mechanism belongs to the 'subscriber' — the statute's term for the person at whose direction the removed material resided on the service provider's system or network before it was taken down. Section 512 does not separately define 'subscriber' anywhere, including in the subsection that defines other terms used throughout the section (which defines only 'service provider' and 'monetary relief'); the word is used in its ordinary sense, referring to the person whose account or posting held the material. Filing an effective counter notification requires disclosing that subscriber's real name, address, and telephone number, together with a statement consenting to the jurisdiction of the applicable federal district court and agreeing to accept service of process — and the statute requires the service provider, on receiving a valid counter notification, to promptly provide a copy of it (which necessarily includes that identifying and jurisdictional information) to the person who sent the original takedown notification. An anonymous or pseudonymous poster who wants the counter-notification process to work as the statute describes faces a practical consequence built into this design: using it means the poster's real identity and address reach the party who complained about the material, as a direct result of the forwarding step the statute itself requires.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence that 17 U.S.C. § 512 uses the term 'subscriber' without separately defining it, that an effective counter notification must include the subscriber's real name, address, and telephone number under § 512(g)(3)(D), and that § 512(g)(2)(B) requires the service provider to forward the counter notification to the original complaining party — not a claim about how any particular service provider actually handles or redacts that forwarded information in practice, about whether a specific platform allows a counter notification to be filed with real contact information withheld from public view while still being forwarded privately to the complaining party (the statutory forwarding obligation runs to that party regardless of what is or isn't made public), or about safety, immigration, or other consequences that might follow from a particular person's identity being disclosed to a particular complaining party. All citations below are to subsections of the single statutory section 17 U.S.C. § 512 (subsections (g) and (k)), fetched from the same primary-source page; they are listed separately for precision but are treated as one source, not independent, corroborating sources.

clauses.title: Why a Service Provider Has an Incentive to Follow This Process: Its Own Safe Harbor Depends On It
clauses.body: Federal copyright law gives a service provider its own reason, independent of any duty it owes to a particular subscriber, to follow the counter-notification and put-back procedure correctly. As a general matter, a service provider is not liable to any person for a claim based on its good-faith removal of material believed to be infringing, regardless of whether the material turns out to be infringing. But that protection does not apply to a claim by the subscriber whose material was removed unless the service provider also does three things: promptly notifies the subscriber of the removal, promptly forwards a valid counter notification to the original complaining party while telling that party it will restore the material in 10 business days, and then actually restores the material within the 10-to-14-business-day window described elsewhere in this document (or continues withholding it, without losing this protection, if the complaining party has filed suit seeking a restraining court order in that window). A service provider that skips or botches these steps loses this particular liability shield with respect to the subscriber whose material it removed — which is a reason built into the statute's own incentive structure for a service provider to follow the process, not a promise this document makes about what any specific platform will actually do in a given case.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the incentive structure 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(1)-(2) creates for a service provider — not a claim about whether any particular service provider follows this process correctly, promptly, or at all in a given case, or about what remedy (if any) a subscriber has against a provider that does not. The protection described in this clause is a liability shield running to the service provider, not an independent legal duty a court will necessarily order the provider to perform on a subscriber's demand. This clause also quotes § 512(g)(4), which describes a related but separate protection — a service provider's compliance with the paragraph (2) sequence does not expose it to copyright-infringement liability toward the original complaining party for restoring the material. Both citations below are to subsections of the same statutory section, 17 U.S.C. § 512(g); they are treated as one source, not independent, corroborating sources.

(2) Exception.—Paragraph (1) shall not apply with respect to material residing at the direction of a subscriber of the service provider on a system or network controlled or operated by or for the service provider that is removed, or to which access is disabled by the service provider, pursuant to a notice provided under subsection (c)(1)(C), unless the service provider—

clauses.title: The Sworn Statement Is Narrow: Mistake or Misidentification of the Material, Not Disagreement or Fair Use
clauses.body: Federal copyright law limits what a counter notification's sworn statement may say. The statute requires a statement, made under penalty of perjury, that the subscriber has a good faith belief that the material was removed or disabled as a result of mistake or misidentification of the material to be removed or disabled — a statement about whether the takedown targeted the wrong material, or was the product of some other error in identifying it, not a statement that the subscriber simply disagrees with the copyright owner's infringement claim on the merits. The provision does not ask the subscriber to swear that the use was authorized, that it qualifies as fair use, that the underlying copyright claim is invalid, or that the copyright owner is wrong about infringement generally — it asks only whether the takedown targeted the wrong material, or resulted from some other identification error. A subscriber whose actual objection is that their use was fair use, or that the copyright owner has no valid claim, is being asked by this specific sworn statement to address something narrower than either of those positions.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the specific, narrow content 17 U.S.C. § 512(g)(3)(C) requires the counter notification's sworn statement to have — not legal advice about whether a particular removal was, in fact, a mistake or misidentification, whether a particular subscriber's belief is held in good faith, or how a court would treat a counter notification framed around a fair-use or non-infringement argument instead of the statutory mistake-or-misidentification language, which is a question of statutory interpretation this clause does not resolve. This is the same subsection quoted in the companion DMCA Takedown Notice document's dmca_counternotice_putback clause in this corpus, as part of that document's summary of the full counter-notification-elements list; this clause is not an independent corroborating source from elsewhere — it restates the same statutory text to focus specifically on interpreting what the sworn statement is, and is not, permitted to say.

clauses.title: Counter-Notification Signature Block
The General Power to Amend Articles of Incorporation
clauses.body: California's amendment-of-articles chapter gives every corporation a broad, standing statutory power to change its own articles after formation: by following that chapter's procedures, a corporation may amend its articles from time to time, in any and as many respects as desired, so long as the articles as amended contain only provisions that would be lawful to insert in original articles filed at the time of the amendment. The Legislature intended this power to reach the fullest extent of the state's reserved authority over corporations, and the power applies even if a provision in the amendment would not have been permissible when the corporation was originally incorporated. That broad power has one narrow carve-out: a corporation cannot use an amendment to add or alter the original articles' historical statements of its initial street and mailing address, the names and addresses of its first directors, or the name and address of its initial agent for service of process -- except to correct an error in one of those statements, or to delete that information entirely once the corporation has since filed a statement of information under a separate statute.
clauses.gap: A premise treating Cal. Corp. Code section 900 or section 902 as interchangeable candidates for the source of the general power to amend is worth resolving precisely: section 900 is the section that actually grants the general power to amend articles; section 902 (the next clause) instead governs only the board-and-shareholder approval mechanics for exercising that power, not the power's existence. The two quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code section 900, and are treated as one source, not independent ones. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This document is informational only and does not itself amend any corporation's articles.

clauses.title: Board and Shareholder Approval of an Amendment
clauses.body: Once a corporation has issued any shares, California's amendment statute requires two separate approvals for an ordinary amendment of the articles, in either order: approval by the board, and approval by the outstanding shares entitled to vote under the statute's general shareholder-approval definition. Beyond that baseline majority-of-outstanding-shares rule, the statute also locks in place any higher voting threshold the articles themselves already specify: whenever the articles require a larger proportion of shares of a class or series, or a larger proportion of directors, than the statute otherwise demands, that heightened requirement cannot itself be altered, amended, or repealed except by that same heightened vote, unless the articles provide otherwise. The statute separately allows a narrow set of specific, post-issuance amendments to be adopted by board approval alone, without any shareholder vote: extending or making perpetual the existence of a corporation organized before August 14, 1929; a stock split (including a proportionate increase in authorized shares) for a corporation with only one class of shares outstanding; and deleting the same categories of original-articles historical information described in the general-power clause above.
clauses.gap: This corrects a specific assumption about where a pre-issuance, board-only amendment mechanism lives: that mechanism is a distinct, separate statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code section 901 (described in the next clause), not part of section 902. Section 902's own board-alone exceptions -- subdivisions (b), (c), and (d) -- instead apply after shares have already been issued, and only to a narrow, specifically enumerated set of amendments, not as a general "minor or technical amendment" carve-out. The two quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code section 902, and are treated as one source, not independent ones. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This document is informational only and does not itself amend any corporation's articles.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 902(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, board and shareholder approval required
citations.quote: After any shares have been issued, amendments may be adopted if approved by the board and approved by the outstanding shares (Section 152), either before or after the approval by the board.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 902(e)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, articles-based supermajority requirements are locked in
citations.quote: Whenever the articles require for corporate action the vote of a larger proportion or of all of the shares of any class or series, or of a larger proportion or of all of the directors, than is otherwise required by this division, the provision in the articles requiring such greater vote shall not be altered, amended or repealed except by such greater vote unless otherwise provided in the articles.

clauses.title: Amendment Before Any Shares Have Been Issued
clauses.body: California's amendment statute treats a corporation that has not yet issued any shares differently from one that has. Before any shares have been issued, an amendment of the articles may be adopted simply by a signed writing, and the statute specifies who must sign it: a majority of the incorporators, if the corporation never named or elected directors, or a majority of the directors, if directors were named in the original articles or have since been elected. To make that pre-issuance amendment effective, the corporation must also file a certificate of amendment signed and verified by that same majority of incorporators or directors, stating that the signers constitute at least a majority of the incorporators or of the board, that the corporation has issued no shares, and that they adopt the amendment set out in the certificate; if the amendment was adopted by incorporators rather than directors, the certificate must also state that directors were never named in the original articles and have not been elected.
clauses.gap: This corrects the assumption that a pre-issuance, no-shareholder-vote amendment mechanism lives inside Cal. Corp. Code section 902: it is in fact its own separate statutory section, section 901. It is also not accurately described as "board alone" in every case: section 901 authorizes either a majority of the incorporators or a majority of the directors to sign, depending on whether directors have been named or elected -- not the board specifically as a fixed rule. The two citations below are to two different statutory sections, section 901 and section 906, not subsections of one section, so each is treated as an independent source. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. This document is informational only and does not itself amend any corporation's articles.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 901
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, amendment before shares are issued
citations.quote: Before any shares have been issued, any amendment of the articles may be adopted by a writing signed by a majority of the incorporators, if directors were not named in the original articles and have not been elected, or, if directors were named in the original articles or have been elected, by a majority of the directors.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 906
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the pre-issuance certificate of amendment
citations.quote: In the case of amendments adopted by the incorporators or the board under Section 901, the corporation shall file a certificate of amendment signed and verified by a majority of the incorporators or of the board, as the case may be, which shall state that the signers thereof constitute at least a majority of the incorporators or of the board, that the corporation has issued no shares and that they adopt the amendment or amendments therein set forth.

clauses.title: Required Content of the Certificate of Amendment
clauses.body: For an amendment adopted after a corporation has issued any shares, California's statute requires the corporation to file a certificate of amendment consisting of an "officers' certificate" -- a specific, defined term meaning a certificate signed and verified by one officer from one group (the chairperson of the board, the president, or any vice president) and one officer from a second group (the secretary, the chief financial officer, the treasurer, or any assistant secretary or assistant treasurer). That officers' certificate must state: the wording of the amendment or amended articles, established according to the statute's separate wording-mechanics rule; that the amendment has been approved by the board; if approval by the outstanding shares was required, that the amendment was approved by the required shareholder vote, the total number of outstanding shares of each class entitled to vote, and that the shares voting in favor equaled or exceeded the vote required, specifying the required percentage for each class; and, if the amendment was one the board could adopt alone, the facts entitling the board to do so without a shareholder vote. Separately, the statute's wording-mechanics rule requires the certificate to establish the text of the amendment in one of three ways: stating that the articles are amended to read as set forth in full, identifying an existing provision (by its designation or its wording) that is being struck or amended to read as stated, or stating that new provisions are being added.
clauses.gap: This corrects the assumption that the required content of the certificate of amendment is set out in Cal. Corp. Code section 906: for a corporation that has already issued shares, that content is instead governed by section 905 (what the certificate must state) together with section 907 (how the amendment's wording must be established); section 906 governs the different, pre-issuance certificate described in the clause above. The three citations below draw from three independently enacted sections -- section 905, section 907, and section 173 -- none of which is a subsection of another, so each is treated as an independent source. This is one state's list of required certificate content, not a claim about what any other state's equivalent filing must contain. This document is informational only and does not itself amend any corporation's articles.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 905
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, required content of the post-issuance certificate of amendment
citations.quote: In the case of amendments adopted after the corporation has issued any shares, the corporation shall file a certificate of amendment, which shall consist of an officers’ certificate stating: (a) The wording of the amendment or amended articles in accordance with Section 907; (b) That the amendment has been approved by the board; (c) If the amendment is one for which the approval of the outstanding shares (Section 152) is required, that the amendment was approved by the required vote of shareholders in accordance with Section 902, 903 or 904; the total number of outstanding shares of each class entitled to vote with respect to the amendment; and that the number of shares of each class voting in favor of the amendment equaled or exceeded the vote required, specifying the percentage vote required of each class entitled to vote; and (d) If the amendment is one which may be adopted with approval by the board alone, a statement of the facts entitling the board alone to adopt the amendment.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 907(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, how the amendment's wording must be stated
citations.quote: The certificate of amendment shall establish the wording of the amendment or amended articles by one or more of the following means: (1) By stating that the articles shall be amended to read as therein set forth in full. (2) By stating that any provision of the articles, which shall be identified by the numerical or other designation given it in the articles or by stating the wording thereof, shall be stricken from the articles or shall be amended to read as set forth in the certificate. (3) By stating that the provisions set forth therein shall be added to the articles.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 173
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, definition of "officers' certificate"
citations.quote: “Officers’ certificate” means a certificate signed and verified by the chairperson of the board, the president or any vice president and by the secretary, the chief financial officer, the treasurer or any assistant secretary or assistant treasurer.

clauses.title: Amendments Requiring a Separate Class Vote
clauses.body: California's amendment statute requires a proposed amendment to be separately approved by the outstanding shares of a particular class -- whether or not the articles otherwise give that class any vote at all -- whenever the amendment would: increase or decrease that class's aggregate authorized shares (subject to two specific statutory exceptions); effect an exchange, reclassification, or cancellation of all or part of that class's shares (a reverse stock split counts, an ordinary stock split does not); effect or create a right to exchange another class's shares into that class; change that class's rights, preferences, privileges, or restrictions; create a new class, or increase the rights, preferences, privileges, or authorized shares of an existing class, ranking ahead of that class; in the case of preferred shares, divide the class into series with different rights (or authorize the board to do so); or cancel or otherwise affect dividends that have accrued on that class but remain unpaid. Different series within the same class do not count as different classes for this class-voting purpose, unless a particular series is adversely affected by the amendment differently than other shares of the same class. This class-level approval requirement is in addition to, not instead of, the amendment's separate approval by the outstanding voting shares as a whole.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; whether and when a class vote is required on a charter amendment varies by state. The two quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code section 903, and are treated as one source, not independent ones. This document is informational only and does not itself amend any corporation's articles.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 903(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, amendments requiring a separate class vote
citations.quote: A proposed amendment must be approved by the outstanding shares (Section 152) of a class, whether or not such class is entitled to vote thereon by the provisions of the articles, if the amendment would: (1) Increase or decrease the aggregate number of authorized shares of such class, other than an increase as provided in either subdivision (b) of Section 405 or subdivision (c) of Section 902. (2) Effect an exchange, reclassification, or cancellation of all or part of the shares of such class, including a reverse stock split but excluding a stock split. (3) Effect an exchange, or create a right of exchange, of all or part of the shares of another class into the shares of such class. (4) Change the rights, preferences, privileges or restrictions of the shares of such class. (5) Create a new class of shares having rights, preferences or privileges prior to the shares of such class, or increase the rights, preferences or privileges or the number of authorized shares of any class having rights, preferences or privileges prior to the shares of such class. (6) In the case of preferred shares, divide the shares of any class into series having different rights, preferences, privileges or restrictions or authorize the board to do so. (7) Cancel or otherwise affect dividends on the shares of such class which have accrued but have not been paid.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 903(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, class approval is in addition to overall shareholder approval
citations.quote: In addition to approval by a class as provided in subdivision (a), a proposed amendment must also be approved by the outstanding voting shares (Section 152).

clauses.title: When an Amendment Becomes Effective
clauses.body: Filing the certificate of amendment with the Secretary of State is what actually changes the articles: upon that filing, the articles are amended in accordance with the certificate, any stock split, reverse split, reclassification, cancellation, exchange, or other change to shares takes effect, and a Secretary-of-State-certified copy of the certificate becomes prima facie evidence that the conditions for adopting the amendment were satisfied. California's general corporate-filing statute separately allows a filed instrument to specify a delayed effective date up to 90 days after its filing date -- and unlike original articles of incorporation (which that delayed-effective-date mechanism expressly excludes), a certificate of amendment is exactly the kind of "instrument filed with respect to a corporation" the delayed-effective-date option is written to cover. If a delayed effective date is specified, the amendment can still be stopped before it takes effect by filing a revocation certificate, executed the same way as the original instrument, before the specified date.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; when a filed amendment becomes effective, and whether a delayed effective date is available, vary by state. The two citations below are to two independently enacted statutory sections, Cal. Corp. Code section 908 and section 110, not subsections of one section, so each is treated as an independent source; section 110 is the same general filing-mechanics statute already used elsewhere in this corpus for the original Articles of Incorporation document's delayed-filing-date clause, and was independently re-verified here for this document. This document is informational only and does not itself amend any corporation's articles.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 908
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, effect of filing the certificate of amendment
citations.quote: Upon the filing of the certificate of amendment, the articles shall be amended in accordance with the certificate and any stock split, reverse stock split, reclassification, cancellation, exchange or other change in shares shall be effected, and a copy of the certificate, certified by the Secretary of State, is prima facie evidence of the performance of the conditions necessary to the adoption of the amendment.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 110(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the delayed-effective-date option for filed instruments
citations.quote: Any instrument filed with respect to a corporation, other than original articles or instruments filed pursuant to Section 119, may provide that it is to become effective not more than 90 days subsequent to its filing date. In case such a delayed effective date is specified, the instrument may be prevented from becoming effective by a certificate stating that by appropriate corporate action it has been revoked and is null and void, executed in the same manner as the original instrument and filed before the specified effective date.

clauses.title: Restated Articles as an Alternative to a Standalone Certificate of Amendment
clauses.body: California law gives a corporation a second, separate filing option distinct from a standalone certificate of amendment: it may consolidate its entire articles as amended into one integrated document by filing a certificate -- signed either as an officers' certificate or, in the narrower circumstances where incorporators or the board may amend the articles under the pre-issuance provisions described above, by a majority of the incorporators or the board -- titled "Restated Articles of Incorporation," setting out the articles as amended to the date of filing. That restatement can also itself amend the articles further, in which case the certificate must independently satisfy the ordinary certificate-of-amendment content and wording rules. Once filed, restated articles supersede the original articles and every amendment and certificate of determination filed before them, for all purposes -- replacing the patchwork of the original articles plus each separate amendment with one current, self-contained document, rather than adding one more standalone amendment on top of that patchwork.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation; whether a restated-articles mechanism exists, and its practical effect, vary by state. The two quotes below are subsections of the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code section 910, and are treated as one source, not independent ones. This document is informational only and does not itself amend, restate, or supersede any corporation's articles.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 910(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, filing restated articles of incorporation
citations.quote: A corporation may restate in a single certificate the entire text of its articles as amended by filing an officers’ certificate or, in circumstances where incorporators or the board may amend a corporation’s articles pursuant to Sections 901 and 906, a certificate signed and verified by a majority of the incorporators or the board, as applicable, entitled Restated Articles of Incorporation, which shall set forth the articles as amended to the date of the filing of the certificate

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 910(d)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, restated articles supersede the original articles and prior amendments
citations.quote: Restated articles of incorporation filed pursuant to this section shall supersede for all purposes the original articles and all amendments and certificates of determination filed prior thereto.

The following amendment to the articles of incorporation of {{companyName}} has been adopted: {{amendedArticleText}} This amendment has been approved by the board of directors of {{companyName}} and, to the extent approval by the outstanding shares is required by law, has also been approved by the required vote of the outstanding shares of {{companyName}} entitled to vote on it.

clauses.title: Declaration of Parties, Marriage Date, and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Nullity of Marriage (Annulment) — Petition Information Sheet concerns the marriage of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, who were married on {{marriageDate}}. It is prepared for use alongside an actual petition for nullity of marriage that would be filed in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. The ground on which nullity is sought is: {{nullityGround}}. The factual basis asserted for that ground is: {{nullityFactualBasis}}. This information sheet describes California's statutory framework for a judgment of nullity — the distinct grounds for a void marriage and for a voidable marriage, who may sue and by when, and the property, support, and custody consequences of such a judgment — as background for that filing. It is not itself a court filing, and completing it does not annul, void, or otherwise change the marital status of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. Only a court judgment of nullity can do that, and — for a marriage that is void rather than voidable — the marriage may already be void by operation of law whether or not any judgment is ever obtained.

clauses.title: Void Marriage: Incestuous and Bigamous or Polygamous Marriages
clauses.body: California law recognizes a category of marriage that is void — automatically invalid by operation of law — as distinct from a merely voidable marriage. Two relationship-based grounds make a marriage void: incest and bigamy/polygamy. An incestuous marriage — between parents and children, ancestors and descendants of any degree, siblings of the half or whole blood, or uncles or aunts and nieces or nephews — is void from the beginning, regardless of whether the family relationship itself is legitimate or illegitimate. A bigamous or polygamous marriage — a subsequent marriage contracted by a person while a former spouse from an undissolved prior marriage is still living, with someone other than that former spouse — is illegal and void, unless one of two statutory exceptions applies: the former marriage was already dissolved or adjudged a nullity before the subsequent marriage, or the absent former spouse was not known to be living for the five years immediately preceding the subsequent marriage (or was generally reputed or believed dead when it was contracted). When one of those two bigamy exceptions applies, the subsequent marriage is not void at all — it falls instead into the voidable category addressed elsewhere in this document, with different legal consequences.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nullity-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself declare a marriage void, adjudicate nullity, or determine which ground (if any) applies to a specific marriage; only a court judgment does that, and for a void marriage, only operation of law does that regardless of any judgment. These two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 2200 and § 2201), not subsections of the same section, so they are independent sources. This clause does not address the voidable-marriage grounds (Cal. Fam. Code § 2210), standing and time limits to sue (§ 2211), the putative spouse doctrine (§ 2251), or the property/support/custody consequences of a nullity judgment (§§ 2251-2254) — those are addressed in separate clauses of this document. No case law was independently verified for this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

clauses.title: Void From the Outset Versus Voidable Until Annulled — and the Bigamy Exception That Crosses Between Them
clauses.body: California's nullity statute treats void and voidable marriages very differently in legal effect, even though a judgment of nullity can be sought for either kind under the same part of the Family Code. A void marriage (incestuous, or bigamous/polygamous absent an exception) is invalid from its inception by operation of law; it needs no court judgment to be void, though one may still be obtained to establish that fact for the record. A voidable marriage, by contrast, is valid and has full legal effect unless and until a court adjudges it a nullity — the statute's own language is that such a marriage 'is voidable and may be adjudged a nullity,' not that it already is a nullity. The clearest illustration of this distinction sits inside the bigamy statute itself: when a person remarries reasonably believing an absent or presumed-dead former spouse is no longer living, the resulting marriage is not void bigamy at all — the statute expressly provides that this subsequent marriage 'is valid until its nullity is adjudged' under the voidable-marriage ground for an undissolved prior marriage. The same underlying fact pattern (an existing prior marriage) can therefore fall on either side of the void/voidable line depending on what the remarrying party knew or believed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nullity-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself determine whether a specific marriage is void or voidable, or which exception (if any) applies; only a court can make that determination, and a void marriage is void regardless of whether any court ever rules on it. These two citations are to two different Family Code sections (§ 2210 and § 2201), not subsections of the same section, so they are independent sources. This clause's statement that 'one may still be obtained' to establish a void marriage's status is drawn from the structure of Part 2 of the Family Code, captioned 'Judicial Determination of Void or Voidable Marriage,' which applies its judgment-effect provision (Cal. Fam. Code § 2212, addressed in a separate clause) to both void and voidable marriages without distinction — it is not drawn from a single statute that says so in as many words. No case law was independently verified for this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

citations.quote: A marriage is voidable and may be adjudged a nullity if any of the following conditions existed at the time of the marriage:

citations.cite: a good-faith remarriage under the bigamy exception is voidable, not void
citations.quote: In either of the cases described in paragraph (2) of subdivision (a), the subsequent marriage is valid until its nullity is adjudged pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 2210.

clauses.title: Six Statutory Grounds for a Voidable Marriage
clauses.body: California Family Code § 2210 lists exactly six conditions, existing at the time of the marriage, on which a marriage is voidable and may be adjudged a nullity, in this statutory order: (a) the party seeking nullity (or on whose behalf it is sought) was under 18 at the time of marriage, unless the marriage was entered under the statutory exception for a minor who obtained a court order or parental/guardian consent permitting the marriage; (b) the other spouse from an undissolved prior marriage was living and that prior marriage was still in force, and that spouse either had been absent and not known to be living for the five years immediately preceding the later marriage, or was generally reputed or believed dead when the later marriage was contracted (this is the voidable-marriage counterpart to the bigamy ground addressed elsewhere in this document); (c) either party was of unsound mind, unless that party later freely cohabited with the other after coming to reason; (d) either party's consent was obtained by fraud, unless that party later freely cohabited with the other with full knowledge of the facts constituting the fraud; (e) either party's consent was obtained by force, unless that party later freely cohabited with the other; or (f) either party was, at the time of marriage, physically incapable of entering into the marriage state, with that incapacity continuing and appearing incurable. Grounds (c), (d), and (e) are each subject to a statutory ratification exception (freely continuing to cohabit with knowledge or after the incapacity ends) that can extinguish the ground even though it once existed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nullity-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself determine whether any of these six conditions existed in a specific marriage, or whether a ratification exception applies; only a court can make that determination. Both citations are to subsections of the same Family Code section (§ 2210(a) and § 2210(f)) and are treated as one source, not independent. This clause covers only the substantive grounds; who may sue on each ground and by when is addressed in a separate clause on Cal. Fam. Code § 2211, and the statutory exception for underage marriage referenced in subdivision (a) (Cal. Fam. Code §§ 302-303) was not independently re-verified with a second fetch in this research. No case law was independently verified for this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

citations.quote: The party who commences the proceeding or on whose behalf the proceeding is commenced was under 18 years of age, unless the party entered into the marriage pursuant to Section 302 or 303.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2210(f) (California Legislative Information text)

citations.quote: Either party was, at the time of marriage, physically incapable of entering into the marriage state, and that incapacity continues, and appears to be incurable.

clauses.title: Who May Sue for Nullity of a Voidable Marriage, and by When
clauses.body: California Family Code § 2211 separately allocates standing and a time limit for each of the six voidable-marriage grounds in § 2210, rather than applying one uniform rule. For the underage-at-marriage ground, either the party who was married under the age of legal consent may sue, within four years after reaching that age, or a parent, guardian, conservator, or other person having charge of the minor may sue at any time before the minor reaches the age of legal consent — so the minor's own window opens only after majority, while a guardian's window closes at that same point. For the undissolved-prior-marriage ground, either party to the later marriage may sue during the life of the other, or the former spouse from the earlier marriage may sue; no separate discovery-based limitations period is stated for this ground. For the unsound-mind ground, the party injured, or a relative or conservator of the party of unsound mind, may sue at any time before the death of either party. For the fraud ground, only the party whose consent was obtained by fraud may sue, within four years after discovering the facts constituting the fraud — a discovery rule, unlike the other grounds. For the force ground, only the party whose consent was obtained by force may sue, within four years after the marriage itself (not after discovery). For the physical-incapacity ground, only the injured party may sue, within four years after the marriage. This is the version of § 2211 in effect from January 1, 2026; a further 2025 amendment to the same statute becomes operative January 1, 2027 and will add a good-cause exception allowing a court to permit a late-filed petition on the force ground, while otherwise restating the same standing-and-time-limit framework.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's nullity-of-marriage process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage. This document is informational: it does not itself determine whether a specific petition is timely or who has standing to bring it; only a court can make that determination. Both citations are to subsections of the same Family Code section (§ 2211(a) and § 2211(d)) and are treated as one source, not independent. California Family Code § 2211 was enacted in two versions by the same 2025 chapter (AB 1134): one operative from January 1, 2026 through December 31, 2026 (quoted here, and current as of this document's research date), and a second, textually similar version operative starting January 1, 2027 that adds a good-cause exception for a late-filed force-ground petition — a reader using this document after that date should confirm which version is then in force. No case law was independently verified for this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

citations.quote: The party to the marriage who was married under the age of legal consent, within four years after arriving at the age of consent.
