clauses.title: What a P.O.D. Account Is
clauses.body: California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law (Probate Code Part 2 of Division 5, commencing with § 5100) defines a "P.O.D. account" as an account payable on request to one person during that person's lifetime and, on that person's death, to one or more P.O.D. payees, or an account payable on request to two or more people during their lifetimes and, on the death of all of them, to one or more P.O.D. payees. A "P.O.D. payee" is the person designated on the account as the one to whom it becomes payable after the death of the party or parties who owned it. "P.O.D." is the statute's own abbreviation for "payable on death." California's statute treats a "Totten trust account" as a separate, distinctly defined type of account — one titled in the name of one or more parties "as trustee for" one or more named beneficiaries, rather than as a P.O.D. account naming P.O.D. payees. A P.O.D. account and a Totten trust account are often used interchangeably in everyday conversation because both let a bank or financial account pass to a named person at death without probate, but they are two separately defined account forms with different titling conventions under California law, alongside a third, unrelated category (a joint account). This information sheet addresses a P.O.D. account specifically, as designated on {{accountDescription}} held at {{financialInstitutionName}}.
clauses.gap: This is California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law specifically. Other states that authorize a P.O.D. (payable-on-death) or Totten-trust bank account — many adapted from the Uniform Probate Code or the older Uniform TOD Security Registration Act rather than California's own multiple-party-account statute — are not assumed to define, create, or govern these accounts the same way, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular account or financial institution's own paperwork. Separately, this statutory definition covers only what makes an account a "P.O.D. account" as a matter of California law once it exists; it does not itself address the mechanics of how such an account is opened or titled with a financial institution, which is covered in a separate clause of this document. § 5140, § 5142, § 80, and § 5132 are four separate statutory sections, each independently retrieved and independently verified.

clauses.title: How a P.O.D. Designation Is Created
clauses.body: A P.O.D. designation is not created by a will, a trust document, or any separate estate-planning instrument. It is created by the terms of the account itself — the signature card, passbook, contract, or other instrument establishing {{accountDescription}} with {{financialInstitutionName}}. California's statute supplies model language for this purpose: for a P.O.D. account with a single party, "This account or certificate is owned by the named party. Upon the death of that party, ownership passes to the named pay-on-death payee(s)." For a P.O.D. account with more than one party (for example, two co-owners), the model language instead has ownership pass to the surviving party or parties first, and only on the death of all of them does ownership pass to the named P.O.D. payee(s). Using this exact model language is not legally required — an account is governed by California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law as long as the deposit agreement creates substantially the same relationship, whether or not the statute's own words are used verbatim.

(payable-on-death) or Totten-trust bank account — many adapted from the Uniform Probate Code or the older Uniform TOD Security Registration Act rather than California's own multiple-party-account statute — are not assumed to define, create, or govern these accounts the same way, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular account or financial institution's own paperwork. clauses.title: Rights During the Original Party's Lifetime
clauses.body: During {{accountHolderName}}'s lifetime, a P.O.D. designation gives {{beneficiaryName}} no present right to the funds on deposit in {{accountDescription}}. As between {{accountHolderName}} and {{beneficiaryName}}, the account belongs to {{accountHolderName}}; {{beneficiaryName}}'s status as P.O.D. payee carries no current ownership interest and no right to withdraw, and {{financialInstitutionName}} owes {{beneficiaryName}} no duties regarding the account until {{accountHolderName}}'s death. This is a default rule, not an absolute one — it can be overcome by clear and convincing evidence of a different intent. It is also a rule about beneficial ownership among the parties and payee, not about who has power to withdraw from the account day to day; that power is set independently by the account contract with {{financialInstitutionName}}.

(payable-on-death) or Totten-trust bank account — many adapted from the Uniform Probate Code or the older Uniform TOD Security Registration Act rather than California's own multiple-party-account statute — are not assumed to define, create, or govern these accounts the same way, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular account or financial institution's own paperwork. The "clear and convincing evidence of a different intent" qualifier is part of the statute's own text, not an inference — this default is rebuttable, and this sheet does not attempt to describe what would count as sufficient evidence of a different intent in a given case. § 5301 and § 5201 are two separate statutory sections, each independently retrieved.

clauses.title: Effect at Death — No Probate Required
clauses.body: On the death of the sole party to {{accountDescription}}, or on the death of the last survivor if it has more than one party, any sums remaining on deposit belong to {{beneficiaryName}}, if surviving, without a probate proceeding. This transfer takes effect by reason of the account contract with {{financialInstitutionName}} and the operation of California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law itself. The statute expressly states that a transfer of this kind is not to be treated as testamentary, and that {{beneficiaryName}}'s right to the funds is not denied, limited, or affected merely because it was not created by a writing that meets the formalities California otherwise requires for a valid will.

(payable-on-death) or Totten-trust bank account — many adapted from the Uniform Probate Code or the older Uniform TOD Security Registration Act rather than California's own multiple-party-account statute — are not assumed to define, create, or govern these accounts the same way, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular account or financial institution's own paperwork. "No probate" describes only the mechanics of transferring this particular account to the P.O.D. payee; it is not a statement that the funds are shielded from the original party's creditors, from a surviving spouse's community property rights, or from other legal claims against the party's estate — those questions are addressed, to the extent the statute addresses them at all, in a separate clause of this document. Section 5302 also opens by making its rules "[s]ubject to Section 5040," California's rule that automatically revokes certain nonprobate transfers to a former spouse after divorce; that rule is discussed in the revocability clause of this document. § 5302 and § 5304 are two separate statutory sections, each independently retrieved.

clauses.title: Multiple P.O.D. Payees and Survivorship
clauses.body: {{accountHolderName}} may name more than one P.O.D. payee on {{accountDescription}} — for example, both {{beneficiaryName}} and {{additionalBeneficiaryName}}. If two or more named P.O.D. payees survive {{accountHolderName}}, California's default rule is that they take the sums on deposit in equal and undivided shares; the parties can displace this default only by express terms in the account or deposit agreement providing for different shares. If a named P.O.D. payee does not survive {{accountHolderName}}, the sums pass to the P.O.D. payee or payees who do survive, not to the deceased payee's own estate or heirs. Once two or more P.O.D. payees have both survived {{accountHolderName}} and taken their respective shares, there is no further right of survivorship between them if one of them dies afterward — each payee's share becomes that payee's own separate property — unless the account or deposit agreement expressly provides for survivorship between the payees themselves.
clauses.gap: This is California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law specifically. Other states that authorize a P.O.D. (payable-on-death) or Totten-trust bank account — many adapted from the Uniform Probate Code or the older Uniform TOD Security Registration Act rather than California's own multiple-party-account statute — are not assumed to define, create, or govern these accounts the same way, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular account or financial institution's own paperwork. This default — equal and undivided shares, with a surviving payee's share not passing back into a right of survivorship among the payees — is what the statute supplies when the account or deposit agreement is silent; it does not resolve disputes over what specific account or deposit-agreement language would count as "expressly providing" for different shares or for survivorship between payees. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 5302(b)(2)(B)-(C)); no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5302(b)(2)(B)-(C)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, multiple P.O.D. payees take in equal shares; no further survivorship among payees
citations.quote: if two or more P.O.D. payees survive, any sums remaining on deposit belong to them in equal and undivided shares unless the terms of the account or deposit agreement expressly provide for different shares, and (C) if two or more P.O.D. payees survive, there is no right of survivorship in the event of death of a P.O.D. payee thereafter unless the terms of the account or deposit agreement  expressly provide for survivorship between them.

clauses.title: Revocability, Community Property, and Creditor Exposure After Death
clauses.body: A P.O.D. designation is not an irrevocable trust and does not bind {{accountHolderName}} the way a completed, irrevocable gift would. During {{accountHolderName}}'s lifetime, {{accountHolderName}} may change or eliminate the P.O.D. designation on {{accountDescription}} only by closing the account and reopening it under different terms, by presenting {{financialInstitutionName}} with a signed modification agreement, or by following whatever modification procedure the deposit agreement itself provides; withdrawing funds also reduces {{beneficiaryName}}'s eventual interest by the amount withdrawn. California's statute does not treat a later will as a way to change a P.O.D. designation — a right of survivorship arising from a P.O.D. payee designation cannot be changed by will, so revoking or changing the designation requires acting on the account itself through {{financialInstitutionName}}, not through {{accountHolderName}}'s other estate-planning documents. Separately, if a P.O.D. designation naming a former spouse as {{beneficiaryName}} was made before or during a marriage that later ends in divorce or annulment, California's statute generally causes that designation to fail as to the former spouse, subject to statutory exceptions. If {{accountHolderName}} is married and {{accountDescription}} was funded with community property, titling the account as a P.O.D. account does not by itself eliminate that community property character — the net contribution is presumed to remain community property, subject to a surviving spouse's community property rights, unless that presumption is rebutted in one of the specific ways the statute allows. California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law does not set out a scheme — comparable to the one it provides for a Transfer-on-Death Deed on real property — spelling out a P.O.D. payee's personal liability to {{accountHolderName}}'s creditors after death, or a creditor's priority against the account; whether and how a deceased account holder's creditors can reach P.O.D. funds after death is not resolved by this statute.
clauses.gap: This is California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law specifically. Other states that authorize a P.O.D. (payable-on-death) or Totten-trust bank account — many adapted from the Uniform Probate Code or the older Uniform TOD Security Registration Act rather than California's own multiple-party-account statute — are not assumed to define, create, or govern these accounts the same way, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular account or financial institution's own paperwork. The two § 5303 citations below (subdivisions (b) and (c)) are drawn from the same statutory section and are treated as one source, not independent; § 5302(e), § 5305, and § 5040 are three further, separate statutory sections, each independently retrieved and verified. The statute never uses the word "revocable" to describe a P.O.D. account the way it does for a Transfer-on-Death Deed — revocability here is this sheet's own accurate description of what the modification mechanics in § 5303 actually permit, not a quotation of a labeled "revocability" provision. On creditor exposure specifically: this sheet discloses honestly that no comparable statutory scheme was located within the Multiple-Party Accounts Law itself; the absence of such a provision is not the same as an affirmative statutory statement that P.O.D. funds are immune from creditor claims, and a reader should not assume either outcome from this silence.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, methods of changing the terms of a multiple-party account
citations.quote: Once established, the terms of a multiple-party account can be changed only by any of the following methods:(1) Closing the account and reopening it under different terms.(2) Presenting to the financial institution a modification agreement that is signed by all parties with a present right of withdrawal. If the financial institution has a form for this purpose, it may require use of the form.(3) If the provisions of the terms of the account or deposit agreement provide a method of modification of the terms of the account, complying with those provisions.

citations.quote: Withdrawal of funds from the account by a party also eliminates rights of survivorship with respect to the funds withdrawn to the extent of the withdrawing party’s net contribution to the account.

clauses.title: Account Holder and P.O.D. Beneficiary Declaration
clauses.body: {{accountHolderName}} is the owner of the account described as {{accountDescription}} at {{financialInstitutionName}}. {{accountHolderName}} intends this account to be designated as a P.O.D. (payable-on-death) account under California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law, naming {{beneficiaryName}} as P.O.D. payee. If {{additionalBeneficiaryName}} is also named, {{beneficiaryName}} and {{additionalBeneficiaryName}} are both named as P.O.D. payees, to take the sums on deposit in equal and undivided shares if both survive {{accountHolderName}}, unless {{accountHolderName}} instead directs {{financialInstitutionName}} in writing to use different shares. This declaration records {{accountHolderName}}'s intended designation for {{accountHolderName}}'s own planning purposes; it does not, by itself, create a legally effective P.O.D. designation. A P.O.D. designation becomes legally effective only when it is reflected in the signature card, beneficiary form, or other account agreement that {{financialInstitutionName}} itself uses to open or modify the account.

clauses.title: The Statutory Quiet Title Action: Scope of the Action
clauses.body: California's Code of Civil Procedure sets out a specific statutory chapter, titled "Quiet Title," governing an action to establish title against adverse claims. That statute states that an action may be brought under this chapter to establish title against adverse claims to real or personal property or any interest therein — a quiet title action is therefore not limited to real property, and is not limited to resolving an uncertain boundary line between adjoining parcels. This is a court proceeding: a lawsuit filed with, and decided by, a court, in contrast to a boundary line agreement (addressed in a separate document in this library), which is a private, out-of-court instrument by which adjoining owners record their own agreement fixing a previously uncertain boundary line without any court's involvement. A quiet title action can be used to resolve a boundary dispute, but it can equally be used to resolve any other adverse claim to title — for example, a dispute over a deed's validity, a lien, an easement's existence or scope, or a claim of adverse possession, which the quiet title statute itself contemplates a plaintiff may rely on as the basis of the title asserted in the action. This clause states only that this statutory cause of action exists and what claims it may address in general terms; it does not evaluate whether a quiet title action is an available or appropriate procedure on the facts of any specific title dispute.
clauses.gap: This clause cites only subdivision (a) of Cal. Code Civ. Proc. section 760.020. The same section's subdivisions (b) and (c), not quoted or relied on in this clause, address a narrow, separate topic (actions to confirm, or challenge, agreements entered into under Public Resources Code sections 6307 or 6357) that has no bearing on the general quiet title action described here and is not addressed anywhere in this document. This clause does not address every procedural prerequisite to filing a quiet title action, such as parties who must be joined, which are addressed, to the extent this document addresses them at all, in other clauses of this same document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's law on the availability and scope of a quiet title action — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of property or a specific title dispute; other states' procedures for quieting title, if any, may differ from California's statutory chapter described here.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 760.020(a)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Quiet Title chapter, the action's scope
citations.quote: (a) An action may be brought under this chapter to establish title against adverse claims to real or personal property or any interest therein.

clauses.title: Required Content of a Quiet Title Complaint, and the Verified-Pleading Requirement
clauses.body: California's quiet title statute states specific, mandatory requirements for what a complaint commencing a quiet title action must contain. The complaint must be verified, and must include: (a) a description of the property that is the subject of the action, which, in the case of real property, must include both its legal description and its street address or common designation, if any; (b) the title of the plaintiff as to which a determination is sought and the basis of that title, and, if the title is based on adverse possession, the specific facts constituting the adverse possession; (c) the adverse claims to the plaintiff's title against which a determination is sought; (d) the date as of which the determination is sought, together with a statement of reasons if that date is not the date the complaint is filed; and (e) a prayer for the determination of the plaintiff's title against the adverse claims. The verification requirement is a distinct, and easy to overlook, procedural feature of a quiet title complaint: unlike an ordinary civil complaint, which in most California actions need not be verified, a quiet title complaint must be verified as a matter of this same statute's own text.
clauses.gap: All five content requirements ((a) through (e)) and the verification requirement are stated in a single sentence of a single statutory section, Cal. Code Civ. Proc. section 761.020; they are treated here as one source, not as independent sources. This clause does not address the separate, general statutes governing how a pleading is verified (the form of the affidavit or declaration, and who may make it), which are addressed, to the extent this document addresses them, in a separate clause of this same document. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific complaint's description of the property, statement of title, or statement of adverse claims in fact satisfies this statute, and does not evaluate whether a specific claimant's title is in fact based on adverse possession or any other basis. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's pleading requirements for a quiet title action — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of property or a specific complaint; other states' pleading requirements for an action to quiet title, if any, may differ from the requirements described here, including on whether verification is required.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 761.020
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Quiet Title chapter, required complaint content and verification
citations.quote: The complaint shall be verified and shall include all of the following: (a) A description of the property that is the subject of the action. In the case of tangible personal property, the description shall include its usual location. In the case of real property, the description shall include both its legal description and its street address or common designation, if any. (b) The title of the plaintiff as to which a determination under this chapter is sought and the basis of the title. If the title is based upon adverse possession, the complaint shall allege the specific facts constituting the adverse possession. (c) The adverse claims to the title of the plaintiff against which a determination is sought. (d) The date as of which the determination is sought. If the determination is sought as of a date other than the date the complaint is filed, the complaint shall include a statement of the reasons why a determination as of that date is sought. (e) A prayer for the determination of the title of the plaintiff against the adverse claims.

clauses.title: Commencing the Action and the Lis Pendens Recording Requirement
clauses.body: California's quiet title statute states that an action under this chapter is commenced by filing a complaint with the court, and that immediately upon commencement of the action, the plaintiff must file a notice of the pendency of the action — commonly called a "lis pendens" — in the office of the county recorder of each county in which any real property described in the complaint is located. This recording requirement is a mandatory step tied to the action's commencement, not an optional or later-stage filing. A recorded lis pendens functions as a public record: it gives constructive notice to third parties, such as a prospective purchaser or lender, that title to the described real property is the subject of a pending court action, before that action is resolved.
clauses.gap: Subdivisions (a) and (b) of Cal. Code Civ. Proc. section 761.010 are subsections of a single statutory section, treated here as one source, not as independent sources. This clause states the fact that a notice of pendency must be filed, and describes its general constructive-notice function as a public recording; it does not independently research or restate the separate statutory provisions elsewhere in California law that define what a lis pendens must contain, when a claim is a "real property claim" eligible to support one, or how a lis pendens may be expunged, none of which are addressed in this document. This clause does not evaluate whether a lis pendens was in fact properly or timely recorded in any specific action. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's procedure for commencing a quiet title action and its constructive-notice mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of property or a specific action; other states' procedures for commencing a title action, and their notice-of-pendency mechanisms, if any, may differ from California's.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 761.010(a)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Quiet Title chapter, commencement of the action
citations.quote: (a) An action under this chapter is commenced by filing a complaint with the court.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 761.010(b)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, treated as one source with § 761.010(a) above, not an independent source; the lis pendens recording requirement
citations.quote: (b) Immediately upon commencement of the action, the plaintiff shall file a notice of the pendency of the action in the office of the county recorder of each county in which any real property described in the complaint is located.

clauses.title: The Judgment: No Default Without Evidence of Title, and Its Binding Effect
clauses.body: California's quiet title statute departs from the ordinary rule that a defendant's failure to answer a complaint entitles the plaintiff to a default judgment. In a quiet title action, the court must examine into and determine the plaintiff's title against the claims of all the defendants, must not enter judgment by default, and must in all cases require evidence of the plaintiff's title, hearing such evidence as may be offered respecting the claims of any defendant, other than claims whose validity the plaintiff has admitted in the complaint; the court then renders judgment in accordance with the evidence and the law. In other words, a defendant's silence or non-appearance does not by itself establish the plaintiff's title — the statute requires the court to independently examine evidence of title even where no defendant contests the action. Once entered, the statute separately states that the judgment is binding and conclusive, regardless of any legal disability, on all persons known and unknown who were parties to the action and who have any claim to the property, and, subject to a further statutory exception not addressed in this clause, on persons who were not parties to the action but whose claim to the property was not of record at the time the lis pendens (or, if none was filed, the judgment) was recorded.
clauses.gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. sections 764.010 and 764.030 are genuinely separate statutory sections within the same Article (Article 5, Judgment), treated here as two independent sources. This clause's description of the judgment's binding effect is qualified by an exception stated in section 764.045, which this clause does not independently quote or fully describe, and by section 764.060's separate protection for a purchaser or encumbrancer who relied on the judgment in good faith; a reader should not assume this clause's summary of binding effect is complete without those provisions. This clause states these as general facts about how a California court must proceed and what effect its judgment has; it does not evaluate what evidence would in fact be sufficient to establish any particular plaintiff's title, and does not evaluate the binding effect of any specific judgment on any specific person. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's quiet title judgment procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific title dispute; other states' rules on default judgments and the binding effect of a title judgment, if any, may differ from California's.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 764.010
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Quiet Title chapter, no default judgment without evidence of title
citations.quote: The court shall examine into and determine the plaintiff’s title against the claims of all the defendants. The court shall not enter judgment by default but shall in all cases require evidence of plaintiff’s title and hear such evidence as may be offered respecting the claims of any of the defendants, other than claims the validity of which is admitted by the plaintiff in the complaint. The court shall render judgment in accordance with the evidence and the law.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 764.030
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Quiet Title chapter, binding and conclusive effect of the judgment
citations.quote: The judgment in the action is binding and conclusive on all of the following persons, regardless of any legal disability: (a) All persons known and unknown who were parties to the action and who have any claim to the property, whether present or future, vested or contingent, legal or equitable, several or undivided. (b) Except as provided in Section 764.045, all persons who were not parties to the action and who have any claim to the property which was not of record at the time the lis pendens was filed or, if none was filed, at the time the judgment was recorded.

clauses.title: No Single Statute of Limitations for a Quiet Title Action; It Depends on the Underlying Title Theory
clauses.body: California's quiet title chapter (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 760.010 through 765.060) does not itself state a specific limitations period for filing a quiet title action. Independently of that chapter, California's general statute governing actions to recover real property states that no action for the recovery of real property, or its possession, can be maintained unless the plaintiff, or the plaintiff's ancestor, predecessor, or grantor, was seized or possessed of the property within five years before the action is commenced, and a parallel section applies the same five-year period to a cause of action, or defense, arising out of title to real property. Separately, where a plaintiff's claimed title rests on adverse possession — which the quiet title statute itself recognizes as one available basis for a plaintiff's title — California's adverse possession statute requires that the land have been occupied and claimed continuously for five years, with timely payment of taxes levied on the land during that period, before adverse possession is established. Which of these (or other) time periods applies to a given quiet title action depends on the specific legal theory underlying the plaintiff's claimed title and the nature of the adverse claim being challenged, not on a single, uniform statute of limitations that applies to every quiet title action as such.
clauses.gap: This clause independently verifies three genuinely separate statutory sections — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 318, 319, and 325(b) — as evidence that California's real-property recovery statutes state a general five-year period and that its adverse possession statute separately requires five years of continuous occupation; these are treated as three independent sources. This clause does not identify a single quiet title-specific limitations statute because independent research in this session, limited to primary statutory sources, did not locate one; whether, and how, a court applies these or other limitations periods (or equitable doctrines such as laches) to a quiet title action asserting a particular theory of title is a question of case law and statutory construction that this clause does not resolve, and a CourtListener search attempted in this research session for case law addressing a quiet title action's limitations period returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (125 requests/day already exhausted, with the next availability reported roughly 9.4 hours out), so no case law is cited or relied on for this clause's statement that no single limitations statute governs every quiet title action. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific quiet title action, or any specific claimed basis of title, is or is not time-barred. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's separate limitations periods for real property and adverse possession claims — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of property or a specific claim; other states' limitations periods for an action to quiet title, or for adverse possession, if any, differ from California's.

citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, five-year limitations period for an action to recover real property
citations.quote: No action for the recovery of real property, or for the recovery of the possession thereof, can be maintained, unless it appear that the plaintiff, his ancestor, predecessor, or grantor, was seized or possessed of the property in question, within five years before the commencement of the action.

clauses.title: How a Pleading Is Verified: Subscription, Affidavit Content, and the Declaration-Under-Penalty-of-Perjury Alternative
clauses.body: Separately from the quiet title statute's own requirement that a quiet title complaint be verified, California's general pleading statutes state what verifying a pleading requires. Every pleading must be subscribed by the party or the party's attorney, and where a pleading is verified, the affidavit of the party must state that its contents are true of the party's own knowledge, except as to matters stated on information or belief, which the party must state a belief to be true. A separate, general California statute allows an unsworn written statement, declaration, or verification to be used in place of a sworn affidavit for any purpose — including verifying a pleading — if it recites that it is certified or declared to be true under penalty of perjury, is signed, and states the date (and, if executed within California, the place) of execution; that statute sets out suggested language for this purpose, including, for a declaration executed within California, a certification that "the foregoing is true and correct," made under penalty of perjury.
clauses.gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 446(a) and Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 2015.5 are genuinely separate statutory sections in different titles of the same code, treated here as two independent sources. This clause addresses the general mechanics of pleading verification and the statutory alternative of an unsworn declaration under penalty of perjury; it does not independently verify, through case law, whether a declaration in this form has in every circumstance been accepted as satisfying the quiet title statute's own verification requirement (addressed in a separate clause of this document), and does not evaluate the sufficiency of any specific verification. This is one state's general pleading-verification statutes, used as real evidence of how a California pleading may be verified — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific pleading; other states' pleading-verification rules, if any, differ from California's.

clauses.title: Key Statutory Terms — "Gestational Carrier," "Intended Parent," and "Assisted Reproduction"
clauses.body: California's gestational-surrogacy statute does not actually use the phrase "gestational carrier agreement" as a defined term — the operative contract is defined and referred to throughout Family Code §§ 7960-7962 as an "assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers," built on the more general "assisted reproduction agreement" defined in Family Code § 7606(b) as "a written contract that includes a person who intends to be the legal parent of a child or children born through assisted reproduction and that defines the terms of the relationship between the parties to the contract." "Assisted reproduction" itself means "conception by any means other than sexual intercourse" (§ 7606(a)). Family Code § 7960(c) defines "intended parent" as "an individual, married or unmarried, who manifests the intent to be legally bound as the parent of a child resulting from assisted reproduction" — a definition that is not limited to a married couple, a genetically related person, or any fixed number of intended parents. Section 7960(f) defines "surrogate" as an umbrella term covering two distinct, separately defined categories: a "gestational carrier," meaning "a woman who is not an intended parent and who agrees to gestate a genetically unrelated embryo pursuant to an assisted reproduction agreement," and a "traditional surrogate," meaning a woman who is herself the source of the egg used.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California defines the parties and agreement type in its gestational-surrogacy framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor that every state uses this same terminology or draws its definitions the same way. Whether a jurisdiction recognizes gestational surrogacy agreements at all, and how it defines "intended parent," "gestational carrier," or the agreement itself, varies by state. This clause cites Family Code § 7960(c) and § 7960(f), both subsections of the same statutory section, as well as § 7606(a) and § 7606(b), both subsections of a different statutory section — the two § 7960 citations are treated as one source, not independent, and the two § 7606 citations are likewise treated as one source, not independent, though § 7606 as a whole is an independent source from § 7960. No case law was researched for this clause; the definitions are stated directly from statutory text.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7606(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definitions of "assisted reproduction" and "assisted reproduction agreement"
citations.quote: “Assisted reproduction” means conception by any means other than sexual intercourse. (b) “Assisted reproduction agreement” means a written contract that includes a person who intends to be the legal parent of a child or children born through assisted reproduction and that defines the terms of the relationship between the parties to the contract.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7960(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definition of "intended parent"
citations.quote: “Intended parent” means an individual, married or unmarried, who manifests the intent to be legally bound as the parent of a child resulting from assisted reproduction.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7960(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definitions of "surrogate," "traditional surrogate," and "gestational carrier"
citations.quote: “Surrogate” means a woman who bears and carries a child for another through medically assisted reproduction and pursuant to a written agreement, as set forth in Sections 7606 and 7962. Within the definition of surrogate are two different and distinct types: (1) “Traditional surrogate” means a woman who agrees to gestate an embryo, in which the woman is the gamete donor and the embryo was created using the sperm of the intended father or a donor arranged by the intended parent or parents. (2) “Gestational carrier” means a woman who is not an intended parent and who agrees to gestate a genetically unrelated embryo pursuant to an assisted reproduction agreement.

clauses.title: The Statutory Requirements for a Valid Assisted Reproduction Agreement for Gestational Carriers
clauses.body: Family Code § 7962 sets out specific, mandatory requirements for the written agreement between a gestational carrier and the intended parent or parents. The agreement must contain, at minimum: the date it was executed; the source of the gametes used (or, if donor gametes were used, whether the donated material was eggs, sperm, or embryos, without necessarily naming the donor); the identity of the intended parent or parents; and disclosure of how the intended parents will cover the medical expenses of the gestational carrier and the newborn or newborns, including — if insurance is used — a review of the policy's coverage for surrogate pregnancy (§ 7962(a)). Before the agreement is executed, the gestational carrier and the intended parent or parents must each be represented by separate, independent, licensed attorneys of their own choosing (§ 7962(b)). The agreement must then be executed by the parties, with signatures notarized or witnessed by an equivalent method as required in the jurisdiction of execution (§ 7962(c)). Critically, the parties may not undergo an embryo transfer procedure, or even begin injectable medication to prepare for one, until the agreement has been fully executed under both the independent-counsel and notarization/witnessing requirements (§ 7962(d)).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California requires for its own gestational-surrogacy agreements to carry the effects described elsewhere in this framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific agreement, nor that every state imposes these same requirements or in this same combination. Whether a gestational carrier agreement is enforceable at all, and what formalities it must satisfy, varies by state. This clause cites four subsections of the same statutory section, Family Code § 7962 — subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (d) — which are treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; the requirements are stated directly from statutory text. This clause corrects and completes a research-request assumption: the statute's required contents (§ 7962(a)) do not include a psychological evaluation as a stand-alone statutory requirement — that item does not appear in the § 7962 text found here — and this clause does not represent the four items listed as the complete universe of what a well-drafted agreement might address, only the specific minimum content and formalities that § 7962 itself requires by name.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: required contents of the agreement
citations.quote: An assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers shall contain, but shall not be limited to, all of the following information: (1) The date on which the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers was executed. (2) The persons from which the gametes originated, unless donated gametes were used, in which case the assisted reproduction agreement does not need to specify the name of the donor but shall specify whether the donated gamete or gametes were eggs, sperm, or embryos, or all. (3) The identity of the intended parent or parents. (4) Disclosure of how the intended parents will cover the medical expenses of the gestational carrier and of the newborn or newborns.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: independent-counsel requirement
citations.quote: Prior to executing the written assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers, a surrogate and the intended parent or intended parents shall be represented by separate independent licensed attorneys of their choosing.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: notarization or witnessing requirement
citations.quote: The assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers shall be executed by the parties and the signatures on the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers shall be notarized or witnessed by an equivalent method of affirmation as required in the jurisdiction where the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers is executed.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no embryo transfer or injectable medication before full execution
citations.quote: The parties to an assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers shall not undergo an embryo transfer procedure, or commence injectable medication in preparation for an embryo transfer for assisted reproduction purposes, until the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers has been fully executed as required by subdivisions (b) and (c) of this section.

clauses.title: How Parentage Is Established — Before Birth, and Without the Carrier Being a Legal Parent
clauses.body: A properly executed assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers has two distinct legal effects on parentage under Family Code § 7962(f). First, a notarized agreement signed by all parties, with the attorneys' declarations attached and lodged with the superior court, rebuts the marital and other parentage presumptions that might otherwise apply to the gestational carrier or the carrier's spouse or partner (§ 7962(f)(1)). Second, upon petition of any party to a properly executed agreement, the court "shall" issue a judgment or order establishing the intended parent or parents as the legal parent(s) and establishing that the gestational carrier — and the carrier's spouse or partner, if any — is not a parent and has no parental rights or duties with respect to the child (§ 7962(f)(2)). That judgment or order may be issued either before or after the child's birth, and, absent a good-faith, reasonable belief by the court or a party that the agreement or attorney declarations were not properly executed, it issues "forthwith and without further hearing or evidence" (§ 7962(f)(2)) — this is the mechanism sometimes referred to informally as a pre-birth (or pre- or post-birth) parentage judgment. A pre-birth judgment or order is expressly permitted under the general provision governing parentage actions, Family Code § 7633, which allows an action, order, or judgment to be entered before the child's birth, but requires that enforcement of that order or judgment be stayed until the child is actually born.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's framework ties a court judgment to a properly executed gestational carrier agreement, including permitting that judgment before birth — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor that every state offers a comparable pre-birth mechanism or ties it to the same agreement requirements. Whether, and how, a jurisdiction allows parentage to be established before a child's birth through a gestational carrier agreement varies by state. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Family Code § 7962(f)(1) and § 7962(f)(2), which are treated as one source, not independent; § 7633 is an independent source from a different part of the Family Code (the general Uniform Parentage Act determination-of-parentage chapter, rather than Part 7's gestational-carrier-specific provisions). No case law was researched for this clause; the mechanism is stated directly from statutory text.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: agreement rebuts marital and other parentage presumptions as to the carrier
citations.quote: A notarized assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers signed by all the parties, with the attached declarations of independent attorneys, and lodged with the superior court in accordance with this section, shall rebut any presumptions contained within Part 2 (commencing with Section 7540), subdivision (a) of Section 7610, and Sections 7611 and 7613, as to the gestational carrier surrogate, or the gestational carrier surrogate’s spouse or partner, being a parent of the child or children.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(f)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: court-ordered judgment establishing intended parents, before or after birth
citations.quote: the judgment or order shall establish the parent and child relationship of the intended parent or intended parents identified in the surrogacy agreement and shall establish that the surrogate, and the surrogate’s spouse or partner, is not a parent of, and has no parental rights or duties with respect to, the child or children. The judgment or order shall be issued forthwith and without further hearing or evidence, unless the court or a party to the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers has a good faith, reasonable belief that the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers or attorney declarations were not executed in accordance with this section.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7633 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: pre-birth order permitted, enforcement stayed until birth
citations.quote: An action under this chapter may be brought, an order or judgment may be entered before the birth of the child, and enforcement of that order or judgment shall be stayed until the birth of the child.

clauses.title: What Happens if the Agreement Does Not Meet the Statutory Requirements
clauses.body: An assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers that is executed in accordance with Family Code § 7962 is "presumptively valid and shall not be rescinded or revoked without a court order" — but that presumption of validity is itself rebuttable: "any failure to comply with the requirements of this section shall rebut the presumption of the validity" of the agreement (§ 7962(i)). Noncompliance does not, however, automatically defeat the intended parents' claim to parentage. The statute expressly states that it "does not prevent a court from finding and declaring that the intended parent is, or intended parents are, the parent or parents of the child where compliance with this section has not been met"; in that situation the statute requires only that "the court shall require sufficient proof entitling the parties to the relief sought" (§ 7962(f)(2)). In other words, a noncompliant agreement loses the streamlined, forthwith, presumption-rebutting mechanism described elsewhere in this framework, but the statute does not foreclose a court from still finding the intended parent or parents to be the legal parent(s) through ordinary proof.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California treats a noncompliant gestational carrier agreement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific agreement, nor that every state's framework offers a comparable fallback path to parentage where its own formal requirements are not met. Whether, and how, a jurisdiction treats a noncompliant surrogacy agreement varies by state; some states may treat such an agreement as void or unenforceable without any fallback. This clause corrects a research-request assumption: the statutory text found here does not itself say that a noncompliant agreement is admitted as evidence of the parties' intent in a parentage determination — that specific evidentiary framing does not appear in § 7962's text; what the statute actually says is narrower — that noncompliance is not an automatic bar to a court finding intended-parent status, subject to "sufficient proof." This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Family Code § 7962(f)(2) and § 7962(i), which are treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; the treatment is stated directly from statutory text.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: presumptive validity, rebutted by noncompliance
citations.quote: An assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers executed in accordance with this section is presumptively valid and shall not be rescinded or revoked without a court order. For purposes of this part, any failure to comply with the requirements of this section shall rebut the presumption of the validity of the assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(f)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: court not barred from finding parentage despite noncompliance, subject to proof
citations.quote: This section does not prevent a court from finding and declaring that the intended parent is, or intended parents are, the parent or parents of the child where compliance with this section has not been met; however, the court shall require sufficient proof entitling the parties to the relief sought.

clauses.title: Compensation — Not Prohibited, and Fee Handling Is Regulated Where a Facilitator Is Involved
clauses.body: California's statutory text does not prohibit paying a gestational carrier for her role, and the statute's own structure assumes money changes hands: Family Code § 7962(a)(4) requires the agreement to disclose how the intended parents will cover the gestational carrier's and the newborn's medical expenses, including a review of insurance coverage for surrogate pregnancy where applicable. Separately, where a "surrogacy or donor facilitator" is involved, Family Code § 7960(b) defines a "fund management agreement" as the agreement between the intended parents and the facilitator covering "the fee or other valuable consideration for services rendered" by the facilitator, and Family Code § 7961 requires that facilitator to direct client funds into either a bonded, independent escrow account or an attorney trust account, disbursed "only ... as set forth in the assisted reproduction agreement and fund management agreement." Nothing in the text of §§ 7960-7962 sets a required dollar amount, cap, or specific structure for what a gestational carrier herself may be paid beyond the medical-expense disclosure requirement described above.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California does not statutorily bar payment to a gestational carrier and regulates how compensation-related funds are handled where a paid facilitator is used — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor that every state permits compensated gestational surrogacy on the same terms (or at all). Whether compensated gestational surrogacy is permitted, and how any payment must be structured or disclosed, varies significantly by state. This clause draws on three different statutory sections — Family Code § 7962(a)(4), § 7960(b), and § 7961 — each an independent source from the others. No case law was researched for this clause; the absence of a statutory dollar-amount rule and the escrow/fund-management framework are stated directly from statutory text. This clause corrects a research-request framing: the statutory text found here does not itself contain an affirmative sentence declaring compensated gestational surrogacy lawful or not against public policy; the conclusion that compensation is not prohibited rests on the absence of any prohibition in §§ 7960-7962 combined with the statute's own assumption, in the provisions quoted above, that fees and medical costs are paid.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7962(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: medical expense disclosure requirement
citations.quote: Disclosure of how the intended parents will cover the medical expenses of the gestational carrier and of the newborn or newborns.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7960(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definition of "fund management agreement"
citations.quote: “Fund management agreement” means the agreement between the intended parents and the surrogacy or donor facilitator relating to the fee or other valuable consideration for services rendered or that will be rendered by the surrogacy or donor facilitator.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7961(a), (c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: escrow/trust handling of client funds by a facilitator
citations.quote: A nonattorney surrogacy or donor facilitator shall direct the client to deposit all client funds into either of the following: (1) An independent, bonded escrow depository maintained by a licensed, independent, bonded escrow company. (2) A trust account maintained by an attorney.

clauses.title: This Framework Covers Gestational Surrogacy, Not Traditional (Genetic) Surrogacy
clauses.body: California's definitions statute expressly distinguishes two categories of surrogate, and the operative agreement statute is written for only one of them. Family Code § 7960(f) defines "surrogate" as an umbrella term with "two different and distinct types": a "traditional surrogate," who is herself "the gamete donor" for the embryo she carries, and a "gestational carrier," who is defined as "a woman who is not an intended parent and who agrees to gestate a genetically unrelated embryo." The requirements and effects set out in Family Code § 7962 — independent counsel, notarization or witnessing, the bar on embryo transfer before full execution, the rebuttal of parentage presumptions, and the forthwith court judgment establishing the intended parent or parents — are all written to apply specifically to "an assisted reproduction agreement for gestational carriers" (§ 7962(a)), tracking the Part 7 heading itself: "ASSISTED REPRODUCTION AGREEMENTS FOR GESTATIONAL CARRIERS." Nothing in the text of §§ 7960-7962 extends that same mechanism, by its own terms, to an agreement with a traditional surrogate.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's own text defines these as two distinct categories and writes its formal agreement mechanism for only the gestational-carrier category — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific arrangement, nor a comprehensive statement of what law (if any) governs traditional surrogacy agreements in California. This clause does not resolve, and readers should not assume it resolves, what legal framework — if any — applies to a traditional (genetic) surrogacy arrangement in California; that question is outside the scope of what §§ 7960-7962 addresses, and this clause deliberately does not speculate about it. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Family Code § 7960(f) and § 7962(a) — different subsections of different sections (7960 and 7962) and so treated as independent of each other, while the two definitional sub-parts within § 7960(f) itself are treated as one source, not independent. No case law was researched for this clause; the distinction is stated directly from statutory text.

(2) “Gestational carrier” means a woman who is not an intended parent and who agrees to gestate a genetically unrelated embryo pursuant to an assisted reproduction agreement.

clauses.title: General Statutory Authorization for Business Entity Conversion
clauses.body: California law lets one type of business entity convert into a different type of business entity while continuing as the same legal entity, without a separate merger or dissolution and re-formation. This authorization is not contained in one single, entity-neutral statute. Instead, California has enacted parallel, entity-specific conversion statutes, each located within that entity type's own governing law: for a corporation, Chapter 11.5 of the General Corporation Law (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 1150-1159) authorizes a corporation to convert into a different kind of entity, and authorizes a different kind of entity to convert into a corporation; for a limited liability company, Article 10 of the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 17710.01-17710.19) does the same for LLCs, on both the outbound and inbound side. Each of these statutes independently authorizes the type of entity it governs to convert out to a different entity type, and to receive an inbound conversion from a different entity type, subject to two conditions that appear in both schemes: the law governing the entity type being converted into must itself permit formation by conversion, and the converting entity must comply with any other law applicable to converting into that particular kind of entity.
clauses.gap: This corrects the framing this research started with. The general conversion authorization is not found in Cal. Corp. Code § 1150 alone (that section is only the chapter's definitions section) and it is not located in "Title 1, Division 3" of the Corporations Code. Verified directly, the corporation-side conversion chapter, Chapter 11.5 (§§ 1150-1159), sits in Title 1, Division 1 (the General Corporation Law), not Division 3. There is also no single chapter that governs conversions for every business entity type at once; a separate, self-contained chapter exists in each entity type's own governing law (this document verifies the corporation and LLC versions; a general partnership or limited partnership converting under California law would look to conversion provisions in its own separate governing statute -- the Uniform Partnership Act or the Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act -- which were not independently verified for this document). The two citations below are to two different statutory schemes (Cal. Corp. Code § 1151, in the General Corporation Law, and Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.02, in the LLC Act), not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides -- not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific entity's conversion, and not a claim that other states' conversion statutes (where they exist at all) work the same way. This document is informational only; it does not itself convert any entity and does not determine whether a specific conversion is available, permitted, or advisable for any specific entity.

citations.quote: A corporation may be converted into a domestic other business entity, foreign other business entity, or foreign corporation pursuant to this chapter

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.02(a)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, Article 10 (Merger and Conversion), authorization for an LLC to convert into a different business entity
citations.quote: A limited liability company may be converted into an other business entity or a foreign other business entity or a foreign limited liability company pursuant to this article

clauses.title: Continuity of the Same Entity Through Conversion
clauses.body: The core legal feature that distinguishes a statutory conversion from dissolving one entity and forming a new one is continuity: California's conversion statutes treat the converted entity as a continuation of the converting entity, not as a newly created entity receiving a transfer from the old one. Upon a conversion taking effect, all of the converting entity's rights and property -- real, personal, or mixed -- vest automatically in the converted entity; all of the converting entity's debts, liabilities, and obligations continue as debts, liabilities, and obligations of the converted entity; creditors' rights and liens on the converting entity's property remain preserved and enforceable against the converted entity to the same extent as if the conversion had never happened; and any lawsuit pending by or against the converting entity may simply continue against the converted entity, as if the conversion had not occurred. This means the property and debts do not need to be separately assigned, deeded, or assumed as part of the conversion -- the statute itself vests and continues them.
clauses.gap: This continuity principle is stated in nearly identical terms in both of the entity-specific conversion statutes this document addresses: Cal. Corp. Code § 1158(b) (corporation as converting or converted party) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.09(b) (LLC as converting or converted party). The two citations below are to those two different statutory schemes, not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for these two entity types specifically -- not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific entity's conversion, and not a claim that a general partnership's or limited partnership's conversion under its own separate governing statute works identically (those provisions were not independently verified for this document). A closely related point -- that this continuity is also carved out of, and does not automatically extend to, certain provisions of California's own tax code -- is addressed separately in this document. This document is informational only; it does not itself convert any entity, vest any property, or determine the debts, liabilities, or pending litigation exposure of any specific entity.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1158(b)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, effect of conversion: vesting of rights and property, continuation of debts and liabilities, preservation of creditors' rights, and continuation of pending actions
citations.quote: All the rights and property, whether real, personal, or mixed, of the converting entity or converting corporation are vested in the converted entity or converted corporation. (2) All debts, liabilities, and obligations of the converting entity or converting corporation continue as debts, liabilities, and obligations of the converted entity or converted corporation. (3) All rights of creditors and liens upon the property of the converting entity or converting corporation shall be preserved unimpaired and remain enforceable against the converted entity or converted corporation to the same extent as against the converting entity or converting corporation as if the conversion had not occurred. (4) Any action or proceeding pending by or against the converting entity or converting corporation may be continued against the converted entity or converted corporation as if the conversion had not occurred.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.09(b)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, effect of conversion: vesting of rights and property, continuation of debts and liabilities, preservation of creditors' rights, and continuation of pending actions
citations.quote: All the rights and property, whether real, personal, or mixed, of the converting entity or converting limited liability company are vested in the converted entity or converted limited liability company. (2) All debts, liabilities, and obligations of the converting entity or converting limited liability company continue as debts, liabilities, and obligations of the converted entity or converted limited liability company. (3) All rights of creditors and liens upon the property of the converting entity or converting limited liability company shall be preserved unimpaired and remain enforceable against the converted entity or converted limited liability company to the same extent as against the converting entity or converting limited liability company as if the conversion had not occurred. (4) Any action or proceeding pending by or against the converting entity or converting limited liability company may be continued against the converted entity or converted limited liability company as if the conversion had not occurred.

clauses.title: Approval Requirements Depend on the Converting Entity's Own Governing Law
clauses.body: The approval a conversion requires from the converting entity's owners is set by that entity's own conversion statute, and it differs by entity type. For a corporation converting out, the plan of conversion must be approved by the board and by the outstanding shares of each class; if the converting corporation is a close corporation, at least two-thirds of each class of outstanding shares must approve (though the articles may set a lower threshold, not below a bare majority). For an LLC converting out, the plan of conversion must be approved by all managers and a majority of the members of each class of membership interest (or, if the LLC has no managers, a majority of the members of each class), unless the operating agreement requires a greater approval -- except that if the conversion would make members personally liable for obligations of the converted entity, approval by all of the members is required, unless the plan of conversion instead gives every member dissenters' rights. When an entity of one type converts into an entity of a different type, the receiving entity's own statute separately confirms that the converting entity's approval is governed by the law under which the converting entity is organized, not by the receiving entity's own approval rules.
clauses.gap: This corrects the framing this research started with. There is no single, uniform vote threshold that applies to a conversion regardless of entity type, and the approval requirement is not a direct statutory cross-reference to that entity's separate merger-approval statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 1201 for corporate reorganizations, or Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.12 for LLC mergers). Rather, each entity type's conversion chapter states its own, self-contained conversion-approval rule, which happens to track the general shape of that entity type's merger-approval rule (board-plus-shareholder-vote for a corporation; manager-plus-member-vote for an LLC) without formally incorporating it by reference. The two citations below are to two different statutory schemes (Cal. Corp. Code § 1152, the corporation conversion chapter, and Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.03, the LLC conversion article), not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for these two entity types specifically -- not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific entity's conversion, and not a claim that a general partnership's or limited partnership's approval requirements under its own separate governing statute work identically (those provisions were not independently verified for this document). This document is informational only; it does not itself approve any conversion and does not determine what approval a specific entity's specific conversion requires -- that depends on the converting entity's specific entity type, its governing documents, and (for an LLC facing potential personal liability on conversion) the specific terms of the conversion.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1152(b)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, board and shareholder approval of a corporation's plan of conversion
citations.quote: The plan of conversion shall be approved by the board of the converting corporation (Section 151), and the principal terms of the plan of the conversion shall be approved by the outstanding shares (Section 152) of each class of the converting corporation. The approval of the outstanding shares may be given before or after approval by the board. Notwithstanding the foregoing, if a converting corporation is a close corporation, the conversion shall be approved by the affirmative vote of at least two-thirds of each class, or a greater vote if required in the articles, of outstanding shares (Section 152) of that converting corporation; provided, however, that the articles may provide for a lesser vote, but not less than a majority of the outstanding shares of each class.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.03(b)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, manager and member approval of an LLC's plan of conversion
citations.quote: (1) The plan of conversion shall be approved by all managers and a majority of the members of each class of membership interest or if there are no managers, a majority of the members of each class of membership of the converting limited liability company, unless a greater approval is required by the operating agreement of the converting limited liability company. (2) However, if the members of the limited liability company would become personally liable for any obligations of the converted entity as a result of the conversion, the plan of conversion shall be approved by all of the members of the converting limited liability company, unless the plan of conversion provides that all members will have dissenters’ rights as provided in Article 11 (commencing with Section 17711.01).

clauses.title: Required Secretary of State Filing to Effect a Conversion
clauses.body: A conversion is effected with the California Secretary of State through a single, combined filing, not two separate documents. When the converted entity is a corporation, the conversion becomes effective upon filing the converted corporation's own articles of incorporation, containing a "statement of conversion" that sets forth the name, form, and jurisdiction of organization of the converting entity and, if the converting entity has a Secretary of State file number, that file number (foreign converting entities must include additional statements about their own authorization and approval to convert). This same combined-filing structure runs the other direction as well: when a limited liability company converts into a domestic corporation, the LLC statute confirms that the statement of conversion is completed on -- and filed as part of -- the converted corporation's articles of incorporation, rather than as a separate certificate.
clauses.gap: This confirms, with a correction, the framing this research started with. There is a specific required filing, and it is combined with the converted entity's new organizational document as the assumption suggested -- but the required content is a "statement of conversion" embedded in that new document, not a separate certificate confirming the required approval was obtained (the statute requires stating that approval was obtained only for a foreign converting entity's statement of conversion, not for a domestic one). The two citations below verify the same combined-filing mechanic from both directions: Cal. Corp. Code § 1157(d)-(e) (from the receiving corporation's own conversion chapter) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.06(a)(3) (from the converting LLC's own conversion article) are two different statutory schemes, not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources. This document verifies only the specific case of an LLC converting into a domestic corporation; the required filing content differs for other entity-type combinations (for example, converting into a limited partnership or a domestic partnership, per Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.06(a)(1)-(2), which were not independently verified for this document). This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides -- not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific entity's conversion. This document is informational only; it does not itself file anything with the California Secretary of State and is not a substitute for the Secretary of State's current official forms and instructions.

clauses.title: Effect of Conversion on Shares and Membership Interests
clauses.body: California's conversion statutes address what happens to the converting entity's outstanding ownership interests. An LLC's plan of conversion must state the manner of converting each member's membership interest into shares of, securities of, or other interests in the converted entity -- so the members' economic and governance interests in the old LLC become their interests in the new entity, on the terms the plan sets, rather than being cashed out or left unaddressed by operation of law. A corporation's conversion statute imposes an equal-treatment floor on the same process running the other direction: unless all shareholders of a class or series consent, each share of that same class or series must be treated equally with respect to any cash, rights, securities, or other property received in the conversion, and nonredeemable common shares of the converting corporation may be converted only into nonredeemable equity securities of the converted entity, unless all shareholders of that class consent otherwise.
clauses.gap: This confirms the framing this research started with -- membership interests and shares do convert into the equivalent ownership interests of the converted entity according to the conversion's terms -- while identifying the specific statutory basis for each direction: Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.03(a)(3) requires the LLC's plan of conversion to state the manner of converting membership interests into interests in the converted entity, and Cal. Corp. Code § 1151(a)(1)-(2) imposes equal-treatment and nonredeemable-conversion protections on a corporation's outstanding shares when a corporation is the entity converting out. The two citations below are to two different statutory schemes, not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources. Because this document's worked example is an LLC converting into a corporation, § 17710.03(a)(3) is the provision that governs that specific direction; § 1151(a) is cited to show the parallel, reciprocal protection that applies when a corporation is the converting entity rather than the converted one, not because it independently governs an LLC-to-corporation conversion. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for these two entity types specifically -- not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific entity's conversion, and not a claim that a general partnership's or limited partnership's own governing statute imposes identical terms (those provisions were not independently verified for this document). This document is informational only; it does not itself convert any interests and does not state the specific terms on which any specific entity's conversion will treat its owners' interests -- those terms are set by the plan of conversion the converting entity's owners approve.
