clauses.title: Tax Consequences Are a Separate Consideration Outside the Conversion Statute
clauses.body: California's conversion statutes themselves flag that a conversion's continuity for state-law purposes does not automatically carry over into every area of tax law. Both the corporation and LLC conversion statutes state that a converted entity is treated as the same entity that existed before the conversion "for all purposes" -- except specifically for the purposes of the California Personal Income Tax Law, the Administration of Franchise and Income Tax provisions, and the Corporation Tax Law. The LLC statute adds that the conversion "shall not be deemed a transfer of property" for state-law purposes generally. Beyond what these two statutes themselves carve out, converting an entity from one type to another -- for example, an LLC taxed as a partnership converting into a corporation -- can carry significant, entity-type-specific and situation-specific federal and state tax consequences (including potential gain recognition), separate from anything California's conversion statute itself resolves. This document does not analyze federal tax law, the tax classification rules that apply to any specific entity, or how a specific conversion would be taxed.
clauses.gap: This is a factual flag, not a tax analysis, and this document does not attempt to resolve it: the specific federal and state tax treatment of any particular conversion depends on the entities and elections involved (for example, an LLC's federal tax classification going into the conversion, and the mechanics of the specific transaction) and was not independently researched here. The two citations below verify only that California's own conversion statutes expressly except certain Revenue and Taxation Code purposes from the general continuity-of-entity rule -- they are not a statement of what tax result actually follows. Cal. Corp. Code § 1158(a) (the corporation conversion chapter) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17710.09(a) (the LLC conversion article) are two different statutory schemes, not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources; note that the two statutes describe the same excepted Revenue and Taxation Code part with slightly different part numbers ("Part 10.20" in § 1158(a) versus "Part 10.2" in § 17710.09(a)), quoted here exactly as each statute states it, without attempting to resolve or reconcile that discrepancy. This document does not independently verify the substance of federal tax law (including the Internal Revenue Code's treatment of entity conversions and elections) or of the excepted Revenue and Taxation Code parts themselves. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California's own conversion statutes provide -- not a claim about which state's or country's tax law would apply to a specific entity's conversion, and not tax advice about any particular entity's own tax situation or filings.

clauses.title: The Statutory Consent Element Under Section 3344(a) — No Written-Form Requirement in the Statute's Text
clauses.body: California's living-person right-of-publicity statute makes the absence of "prior consent" part of what a plaintiff must show: liability attaches to a knowing use of another's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness "without that person's prior consent," or, for a minor, without "the prior consent of their parent or legal guardian." The statute's own text does not say that this consent must be written, signed, or take any other particular form in order to prevent liability from attaching — the operative word in the statute is "consent," unqualified by any form requirement, not "written consent." This is a fact about the statute's text as enacted; it is not a statement that an unwritten or informal consent is, as a practical or evidentiary matter, as easy to establish after the fact as a signed document, or that written consent is unnecessary or unhelpful.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Civil Code section 3344, subdivision (a)(1)), used as real evidence of what that statute's own liability-creating sentence does and does not say about the form consent must take — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any particular unwritten consent did or did not occur, or would or would not be believed, in any specific dispute. This is a single statutory subdivision; no additional independent source was needed to confirm what its own text does, and does not, say. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific consent, release, or use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness is valid, sufficient, or binding under Section 3344, Section 3344.1, or any other law, and completing or signing this information sheet's accompanying consent declaration does not itself resolve any of those questions or constitute legal advice about any reader's specific situation.

citations.quote: without that person’s prior consent, or, in the case of a minor, the prior consent of their parent or legal guardian

clauses.title: Consent Has Limits: General Contract-Interpretation Rules, and a California Supreme Court Case Illustrating a Dispute Over a Different, Later Use
clauses.body: A consent or release is itself a contract, and California's general rules for interpreting contracts apply to it as they do to any other contract. Under those rules, however broad a contract's terms may be, it extends only to the things the parties actually intended to contract about, and any uncertainty left over after applying the other rules of interpretation is resolved against the party who caused that uncertainty to exist — ordinarily the party who drafted the document. Applied to a consent or release describing a specific use, these general rules mean that consent given for one described use is a factually and legally distinct question from whether consent was given for some other, different use that the document does not describe. The California Supreme Court's decision in Christoff v. Nestle USA, Inc. illustrates this distinction on real facts: a professional model was paid to pose for a photograph intended for one specific use — a label used in Canada — and the same photograph was later used, without his knowledge, in a different market and format for years afterward; the later use was treated as raising its own, separate question of consent rather than being automatically covered by whatever arrangement existed for the earlier, different use.
clauses.gap: The two Civil Code sections cited here — section 1648 and section 1654 — are separate, distinct statutory provisions within California's general law of contract interpretation, not subsections of one section; each independently states a different interpretive rule. The Christoff citation is limited to that opinion's own recitation of undisputed background facts, not its legal holding or reasoning: this document's connection to CourtListener's full case-search tool had exhausted its daily request limit (a 429 rate-limit response reporting the daily cap already used) before a search for on-point right-of-publicity or model-release case law could be run through it, and a direct, unauthenticated fetch of the full opinion page was itself blocked by the court-records site's own bot-detection challenge; only a short, separately-fetched and independently-verified text excerpt from the case's own search index was available, and only that verified excerpt is quoted below. This is one state's case and two of its general contract-interpretation statutes, used as real evidence that a consent or release's scope is not unlimited and that a described use does not automatically cover a different, undescribed use — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about how any specific release's own language would be interpreted, which depends on that document's actual wording and the facts surrounding it. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific consent, release, or use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness is valid, sufficient, or binding under Section 3344, Section 3344.1, or any other law, and completing or signing this information sheet's accompanying consent declaration does not itself resolve any of those questions or constitute legal advice about any reader's specific situation.

clauses.title: Revocability: A Validly Formed Contract May Generally Be Undone Only on Statutorily Specified Grounds, Not by a Later Change of Mind
clauses.body: Under California's general law of contracts, a contract requires parties capable of contracting, their consent, a lawful object, and a sufficient cause or consideration. Once a contract meeting these requirements has been validly formed, California statute lists the circumstances in which a party may rescind it: all parties can rescind by mutual agreement, or a party may rescind unilaterally where the statute allows it — for example, where that party's own consent was obtained by mistake, duress, menace, fraud, or undue influence, or where the consideration for that party's obligation fails, becomes void, or was never received. A later, unexplained change of mind by the party who gave consent is not one of the grounds this statute lists. This is a general statement about how California law treats a validly formed, consideration-supported contract; it does not itself determine whether any particular consent or release was validly formed in the first place, or whether any of the statute's listed grounds for rescission apply to any specific document or set of facts.
clauses.gap: These citations are to two separate California contract-formation statutes — Civil Code section 1550 (the elements of a contract) and section 1689 (the statutory grounds for rescinding one) — not subsections of a single section. This document does not independently cite a case addressing the more specific, and more genuinely case-law-dependent, question of how California courts have characterized a signed, compensated publicity or model release itself — for example, whether courts treat it as an irrevocable grant once signed and paid for, as opposed to how they might treat a bare, uncompensated permission with no independent contractual basis: this document's connection to CourtListener's case-search tool had already exhausted its daily request limit (a 429 rate-limit response reporting the daily cap already used and reporting the specific reset time remaining) after the search performed for the scope-of-consent clause elsewhere in this document, before a search on this narrower revocability question could be run, so this clause is grounded in California's general contract-formation and rescission statutes rather than in a case specifically about publicity or model releases. This is one state's general contract law, used as real evidence of how it treats a validly formed contract generally — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific consent or release was validly formed, supported by consideration, or free of any statutory ground for rescission. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific consent, release, or use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness is valid, sufficient, or binding under Section 3344, Section 3344.1, or any other law, and completing or signing this information sheet's accompanying consent declaration does not itself resolve any of those questions or constitute legal advice about any reader's specific situation.

citations.quote: It is essential to the existence of a contract that there should be: 1. Parties capable of contracting; 2. Their consent; 3. A lawful object; and, 4. A sufficient cause or consideration.

clauses.title: A Minor's Own Signature: the Publicity Statute's Own Parent-or-Guardian Language, and the General Rule That a Minor's Contract May Be Disaffirmed
clauses.body: Two separate bodies of California law bear on a minor's own capacity to consent to use of the minor's own name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness. First, Section 3344 itself does not treat a minor's own consent, standing alone, as the relevant consent for purposes of that statute: its text specifies that where the person is a minor, it is "the prior consent of their parent or legal guardian" that the statute addresses. Second, and separately, as a matter of California's general law governing minors' contracts, a contract entered into by a minor may be disaffirmed by the minor before reaching majority, or within a reasonable time afterward, or, if the minor dies within that period, by the minor's heirs or personal representative — a rule that applies to a minor's contracts generally, except where some other statute provides otherwise for a particular kind of contract. Taken together, these are two independent, factual reasons why a document recording a minor's own consent to use of the minor's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness sits differently, as a matter of California law, than the same document signed by an adult.
clauses.gap: These citations are to two different California codes — Civil Code section 3344(a)(1) and Family Code section 6710 — not subsections of a single section, and each independently establishes the point made about it above. Family Code section 6710 is itself qualified by the phrase "except as otherwise provided by statute": this document does not independently research or resolve whether some other, more specific California statute displaces the general disaffirmance rule for any particular category of contract a minor might sign, which is a real limitation on how far this clause's general statement reaches. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of how California's publicity statute and general minors'-contract law each separately address a minor's own consent — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific minor's consent was or was not effective, or that any specific contract was or was not disaffirmed, which depends on facts this clause does not resolve. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific consent, release, or use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness is valid, sufficient, or binding under Section 3344, Section 3344.1, or any other law, and completing or signing this information sheet's accompanying consent declaration does not itself resolve any of those questions or constitute legal advice about any reader's specific situation.

clauses.title: How a Lifetime Consent Interacts With the Separate Posthumous Right Under Section 3344.1
clauses.body: California's posthumous right of publicity, addressed at length in this corpus's companion Right of Publicity Demand Letter document, is a legally separate statute from Section 3344, with its own rules about who may give or withhold consent after a person's death. Section 3344.1's own text specifies that the consent it requires is exercisable, after a person's death, by whoever the right of consent was transferred to under a lifetime contract, and only if no such transfer occurred does the right instead pass to the statutory successors the posthumous statute separately describes. The posthumous statute goes on to state expressly that nothing in it renders invalid or unenforceable a contract a person entered into during their own lifetime by which that person assigned, in whole or in part, the rights to use their own name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness — regardless of when that contract was signed. Read together, these provisions mean that a lifetime consent or release does not automatically bind a person's statutory successors for uses occurring after that person's death simply because the person consented to something during their lifetime; whether it does depends, under the statute's own text, on whether that lifetime document operated as an assignment of the underlying rights the posthumous statute recognizes, as opposed to a narrower permission limited to a specific use during the person's lifetime — itself a scope question of the kind addressed elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are to the same statutory section, Cal. Civ. Code § 3344.1 — subdivisions (b) and (c) — and are treated as one source, not as independently corroborating sources; they are quoted together because subdivision (c) states who may exercise the posthumous consent right and subdivision (b) is what makes a lifetime assignment contract the thing subdivision (c) looks to first. This document does not independently verify, through a citable case, whether a particular kind of lifetime document — for example, a release describing only a specific, limited use rather than an outright assignment of rights — would be treated by a court as the kind of "assignment" subdivision (b) describes; that line-drawing question is not resolved by the statute's text alone, and no case addressing it was independently verified for this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how its own text relates a lifetime consent or assignment to the separate posthumous right — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about how any specific document, lifetime or otherwise, would be characterized under this statute. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific consent, release, or use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness is valid, sufficient, or binding under Section 3344, Section 3344.1, or any other law, and completing or signing this information sheet's accompanying consent declaration does not itself resolve any of those questions or constitute legal advice about any reader's specific situation.

clauses.title: Consideration Under California's General Contract Law, and Why This Document Does Not Rely on This Corpus's Other No-Consideration Statutes
clauses.body: California statute lists a sufficient cause or consideration among the elements essential to the existence of a contract generally, alongside capable parties, their consent, and a lawful object. The same body of law defines what counts as good consideration for a promise: a benefit conferred, or agreed to be conferred, on the promisor by someone not otherwise entitled to confer it, or a prejudice suffered, or agreed to be suffered, by that other person as an inducement to the promisor. A consent or release agreement, as an ordinary bilateral contract, is subject to this general consideration requirement unless some other, specific doctrine dispenses with it. This corpus's own trust and premarital-agreement documents separately note statutes that do dispense with the need for consideration for those particular kinds of instruments; those are express, narrow statutory exceptions to the general rule stated here, applicable to the specific instruments those statutes name, and they are not evidence that consideration is unnecessary for an ordinary consent or release agreement of the kind this document addresses.
clauses.gap: These citations are to two separate California contract-formation statutes — Civil Code section 1550 and section 1605 — not subsections of a single section. The cross-referenced no-consideration statutes are Prob. Code § 15208 (trusts) and Fam. Code §§ 1611 and 1614 (premarital agreements), each already cited and quoted in this corpus's own trust and premarital-agreement documents; they are described here only to explain why they do not apply to this document, not re-quoted, so as not to duplicate sourcing this corpus has already independently verified elsewhere. This is one state's general contract law, used as real evidence of California's own default consideration requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific consent or release was, or was not, supported by sufficient consideration, which depends on facts this clause does not resolve. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific consent, release, or use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness is valid, sufficient, or binding under Section 3344, Section 3344.1, or any other law, and completing or signing this information sheet's accompanying consent declaration does not itself resolve any of those questions or constitute legal advice about any reader's specific situation.

Reporting Time Pay — The Core Rule
clauses.body: California law requires {{companyName}} to pay {{employeeName}} for each workday that {{employeeName}} is required to report for work and does report, but is not put to work or is furnished less than half of {{employeeName}}'s usual or scheduled day's work. The required payment is half of {{employeeName}}'s usual or scheduled day's work, but in no event less than two hours nor more than four hours, at {{employeeName}}'s regular rate of pay, which may not be less than the applicable minimum wage.
clauses.gap: This provision does not appear in the California Labor Code — it is a regulation adopted by the Industrial Welfare Commission, codified in IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 ("Professional, Technical, Clerical, Mechanical and Similar Occupations"), the general catch-all order used elsewhere in this corpus (see the rest-period and meal-period clauses) because it applies broadly rather than to one industry. Other numbered wage orders (for example, Wage Order 5 for public housekeeping or Wage Order 7 for mercantile employees) contain reporting-time-pay language in the same numbered section with materially the same formula, but those other orders were not independently fetched or checked in this session — this clause verifies Wage Order 4-2001 only. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law (the Fair Labor Standards Act) has no reporting-time-pay requirement at all, and most states impose none either; California's rule is unusually protective by national comparison. This is a single regulatory subdivision (§ 5(A)); no additional independent source was located for this specific formula. This clause states a fact about what the law requires — it does not instruct any specific employer or employee on how that formula applies to a particular workday, schedule, or pay period.

citations.quote: Each workday an employee is required to report for work and does report, but is not put to work or is furnished less than half said employee’s usual or scheduled day’s work, the employee shall be paid for half the usual or scheduled day’s work, but in no event for less than two (2) hours nor more than four (4) hours, at the employee’s regular rate of pay, which shall not be less than the minimum wage.

clauses.title: Reporting Time Pay for a Second Reporting in the Same Workday
clauses.body: Separately from the core reporting-time-pay rule, if {{employeeName}} is required to report for work a second time in the same workday and is furnished less than two hours of work on that second reporting, California law requires {{companyName}} to pay {{employeeName}} for two hours at {{employeeName}}'s regular rate of pay, which may not be less than the applicable minimum wage.
clauses.gap: This is a separate, second-reporting rule within the same regulatory section as the core reporting-time-pay rule (§ 5(A)) — both are subdivisions of IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5, so this clause and the core-rule clause elsewhere in this document draw on the same source, not independent corroboration of each other. Unlike the first-reporting formula in § 5(A), which pays half the scheduled day (bounded between two and four hours), this second-reporting rule sets a flat two-hour minimum with no formula tied to the scheduled day's length and no four-hour cap stated in this subdivision. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law has no comparable requirement, and most states impose none either. This clause states a fact about what the law requires; it does not instruct any specific employer or employee on how it applies to a particular workday.

citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 5(B)
citations.quote: If an employee is required to report for work a second time in any one workday and is furnished less than two (2) hours of work on the second reporting, said employee shall be paid for two (2) hours at the employee’s regular rate of pay, which shall not be less than the minimum wage.

clauses.title: Exceptions to Reporting Time Pay
clauses.body: California's reporting-time-pay requirements do not apply when operations cannot commence or continue because of a threat to employees or property, or because civil authorities recommend that work not begin; when public utilities fail to supply electricity, water, or gas, or there is a failure in the public utilities or sewer system; or when the interruption of work is caused by an act of God or another cause outside {{companyName}}'s control. Separately, the reporting-time-pay requirements do not apply to {{employeeName}} while on paid standby status who is called in to perform assigned work at a time other than {{employeeName}}'s scheduled reporting time.
clauses.gap: The two citations below, IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(C) and § 5(D), are both subdivisions of the same regulatory section (§ 5) as the core reporting-time-pay rule and the second-reporting rule cited elsewhere in this document — they are treated as one source, not independent corroboration of each other. Subdivision (C) lists three circumstances under which the reporting-time-pay obligations described elsewhere in this document do not apply; subdivision (D) is a separate, narrower carve-out limited to employees on paid standby status who are called in outside their scheduled reporting time — the wage order's own text does not list it as a fourth item within subdivision (C)'s list, though it has the same practical effect of taking a situation outside the reporting-time-pay requirement. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law has no comparable requirement or exceptions to it. This clause states facts about what the law provides; it does not determine whether any specific employer's operational shutdown, utility failure, or standby arrangement actually satisfies these provisions.

citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 5(C)(1)-(3)
citations.quote: The foregoing reporting time pay provisions are not applicable when: (1) Operations cannot commence or continue due to threats to employees or property; or when recommended by civil authorities; or (2) Public utilities fail to supply electricity, water, or gas, or there is a failure in the public utilities, or sewer system; or (3) The interruption of work is caused by an Act of God or other cause not within the employer’s control.

clauses.title: Reporting Time Pay Requires Actual Reporting
clauses.body: California's reporting-time-pay rule, by its own terms, applies when an employee 'is required to report for work and does report.' The wage order's text does not address, in these words, what happens when {{companyName}} notifies {{employeeName}} that a shift is cancelled before {{employeeName}} reports for that shift — whether reporting-time pay is owed in that circumstance is a fact-specific question this text alone does not resolve.
clauses.gap: This clause's citation is the same wage order subdivision quoted in the core-rule clause elsewhere in this document (IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(A)) — not an independent source, but the same text examined for a different interpretive point: the rule is triggered only when the employee 'is required to report for work and does report.' The wage order's text does not, in these words, address what happens when an employer cancels or changes a shift before the employee reports — for example, by notifying the employee the night before that a shift is cancelled. This clause does not assert a definitive answer to that scenario; it states only what the quoted text itself says (that actual reporting is a stated element of the rule) and flags the pre-report-cancellation question as genuinely unresolved by the text quoted here. Practitioner or agency guidance addressing advance-notice cancellations was not independently verified in this session and is not relied on. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee. This clause states a fact about what the text says and does not say; it does not instruct any specific employer or employee on how to handle a particular scheduling change.

clauses.title: Reporting Time Pay Is Separate From Overtime and Meal/Rest Premium Pay
clauses.body: Reporting time pay is a separate wage requirement from California's overtime rules and from the premium pay owed for a missed meal or rest period. Nothing in the reporting-time-pay provisions reduces, replaces, or is satisfied by wages {{companyName}} owes {{employeeName}} under those other requirements, and nothing in those other requirements reduces or satisfies the reporting-time-pay obligation described in this document.
clauses.gap: This clause cites the same wage order subdivision as the core-rule clause elsewhere in this document (IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 5(A)) — not an independent source for this specific point, but the operative text establishing that reporting time pay is itself a wage payment computed under its own formula. The wage order does not, in these words, state expressly that reporting time pay is "in addition to" or "not an offset against" other wage requirements; that conclusion is drawn here from the fact that overtime (governed by this same wage order's Section 3, not independently re-verified in this session) and meal/rest period premium pay (governed by California Labor Code § 226.7, already verified in this corpus's meal-and-rest-break-policy document as the clause mealrest_premium_pay) are stated in separate, independently numbered provisions with their own triggering conditions and formulas, none of which cross-references or reduces the Section 5 reporting-time-pay obligation. This document does not restate the overtime or meal/rest premium rules; readers are directed to this corpus's existing overtime and meal-and-rest-break-policy clauses for those requirements. This is one state's regulatory framework, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee. This clause states a fact about how these requirements relate structurally; it does not instruct any specific employer or employee on how to calculate total wages owed for a particular pay period.

clauses.title: The Split Shift Premium (A Related, Separate Requirement)
clauses.body: Related to, but distinct from, reporting time pay, California law requires {{companyName}} to pay {{employeeName}} one additional hour of pay at the minimum wage for any workday {{employeeName}} works a split shift — a schedule interrupted by an unpaid, non-working period other than a bona fide meal or rest period — except when {{employeeName}} resides at the place of employment.
clauses.gap: This is a related but conceptually distinct wage requirement, found in the same wage order's minimum-wage section rather than its reporting-time-pay section: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 4(C). A split shift triggers its own one-hour premium at minimum wage, separate from, and calculated differently than, the reporting-time-pay formulas described elsewhere in this document — the split-shift premium does not depend on whether the employee was sent home early or given a second reporting event, and the reporting-time-pay rules do not depend on whether the day's schedule was split. This clause was verified from the same primary-source PDF fetched for the reporting-time-pay clauses in this document, but § 4(C) is a single regulatory subdivision; no additional independent source was located for the split-shift premium formula. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee. Federal law has no comparable split-shift premium. This clause states a fact about what the law requires; it does not instruct any specific employer or employee on how it applies to a particular schedule.

clauses.title: The At-Will Default and How a Specified Term Displaces It
clauses.body: California's default employment rule is that an employment with no specified term may be ended by either the employer or the employee at will, on notice to the other. A "specified term" is what takes an employment relationship out of that default, and the same statute defines the phrase directly: employment for a specified term means employment for a period greater than one month. A fixed-term employment contract — one stating a defined period, such as one year, or running until a specified event — is, by this statutory definition, employment for a specified term, and the at-will default does not govern it for the duration of that term.
clauses.gap: This is California's own statutory definition (Cal. Labor Code § 2922), used here as the statutory trigger that takes an employment relationship out of the at-will default — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific employment relationship, and not a claim that any specific document or arrangement actually creates a valid specified term (that depends on the actual contract language, which this document does not evaluate). The statute defines "specified term" only by minimum duration (more than one month); it does not itself require that the term be stated as a calendar date rather than a described event, and this document does not resolve how a court would treat a term defined by an event (e.g., "until completion of Project X") rather than a date, which was not separately researched. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself create, interpret, or enforce any fixed-term employment contract, and it does not determine that any specific reader's employment is, or is not, for a specified term.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2922
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employment, having no specified term, may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other. Employment for a specified term means an employment for a period greater than one month.

clauses.title: Early Termination During a Specified Term — What the Statute Treats as Sufficient Cause
clauses.body: A fixed-term employment contract can still be ended before the term expires without giving rise to the compensation described elsewhere in this document, if there is sufficient cause. California's statute governing employment for a specified term identifies specific grounds on which the employer may end it early: a willful breach of duty by the employee in the course of the employment, the employee's habitual neglect of duty, or the employee's continued incapacity to perform it. A parallel statute gives the employee a mirror right to end the employment early for any willful or permanent breach by the employer of its obligations as an employer. Ending a specified-term employment on one of these statutory grounds is not the kind of premature termination that triggers a damages remedy for the other party.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two different statutory sections (Cal. Labor Code §§ 2924 and 2925), not subsections of a single section, so they are independent sources on this point. Neither statute uses the phrase "sufficient cause" itself, and neither statute defines that phrase in the abstract; the enumerated grounds quoted here (willful breach of duty, habitual neglect of duty, continued incapacity to perform) are the closest statutory anchor this research found for what counts as adequate cause to end a specified-term employment early, on the employer's side, without triggering the premature-termination remedy described elsewhere in this document. Beyond these enumerated categories, whether specific conduct amounts to a willful breach, habitual neglect, or continued incapacity is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve, and a particular contract's own terms may define "cause" more specifically than the statute does. This research session's CourtListener case-law lookups returned a daily rate-limit error (125/day) on every attempt, so no case law interpreting these statutory grounds is cited here; that is disclosed as an honest gap rather than filled with an unverified citation. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific termination was, or was not, supported by sufficient cause.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2924
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employment for a specified term may be terminated at any time by the employer in case of any willful breach of duty by the employee in the course of his employment, or in case of his habitual neglect of his duty or continued incapacity to perform it.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2925
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employment for a specified term may be terminated by the employee at any time in case of any wilful or permanent breach of the obligations of his employer to him as an employee.

clauses.title: Compensation for Ending a Specified Term Early Without Sufficient Cause
clauses.body: California's employment-termination statutes do not themselves state a specific damages formula for dismissing a specified-term employee before the term expires without sufficient cause. Instead, the state's general rule for breach of any contract supplies the measure: for breach of a contractual obligation, the measure of damages is the amount that will compensate the aggrieved party for all detriment proximately caused by the breach, or that would, in the ordinary course of things, be likely to result from it — limited to damages that are clearly ascertainable in both their nature and origin. This general contract-damages measure is what applies when a specified-term employment contract is broken by an early termination without sufficient cause, because no more specific statute displaces it. This stands in contrast to an employee with no specified term (an at-will employee) who is dismissed: California's employment statutes limit that employee's entitlement to compensation for services already rendered up to the time of dismissal, not to compensation for the detriment of losing the remainder of an expected term — because an at-will employee has no specified term to lose.
clauses.gap: This clause cites three different statutory sections — Cal. Civil Code § 3300, Cal. Civil Code § 3301 (a different section from § 3300, not a subsection of it, so independently cited), and Cal. Labor Code § 2926 — each independently verified. None of these sections is written specifically for employment contracts; §§3300 and 3301 are the state's general contract-damages provisions, and this document applies them to a specified-term employment contract by inference from the statutory text (Labor Code §§2920–2929, the chapter specifically addressing termination of employment, contains no separate damages-measure provision of its own). This research session's CourtListener case-law lookups returned a daily rate-limit error (125/day) on every attempt, so this document does not cite any case applying § 3300's general measure to a specific fixed-term employment dispute, or describing how a court calculates that measure in practice (for example, whether and how amounts the employee could have earned elsewhere during the remaining term are subtracted); that is disclosed as an honest gap. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself calculate or award any measure of damages, and it does not determine that any specific early termination was, or was not, for sufficient cause, or that any specific dollar amount is owed as a result.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 3300
citations.cite: California Civil Code
citations.quote: For the breach of an obligation arising from contract, the measure of damages, except where otherwise expressly provided by this Code, is the amount which will compensate the party aggrieved for all the detriment proximately caused thereby, or which, in the ordinary course of things, would be likely to result therefrom.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 3301
citations.cite: California Civil Code
citations.quote: No damages can be recovered for a breach of contract which are not clearly ascertainable in both their nature and origin.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2926
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employee who is not employed for a specified term and who is dismissed by his employer is entitled to compensation for services rendered up to the time of such dismissal.

clauses.title: Continuing to Work After the Specified Term Ends
clauses.body: Current California employment law contains no statute stating that an employee who keeps working after a specified term ends, without a new agreement, is presumed to be renewed on the original terms for a further period such as one month. The chapter of the Labor Code that specifically addresses termination of employment lists expiration of the appointed term as one way an employment ends, but it does not separately address what happens if work continues after that. A differently worded holdover-renewal presumption does exist in California law, but it is written for real property leases, not employment: it applies by its own terms to "a lessee of real property" who remains in possession after a lease expires and whose landlord accepts rent, and presumes the parties renewed the lease on the same terms for a further period — not exceeding one month if rent was paid monthly, and never more than one year. That real-property rule does not, by its text, extend to an employment relationship. Absent a specific agreement addressing what happens after the term ends, the statutory default that applies to employment is the one described elsewhere in this document: an employment relationship with no specified term is at-will — so an employee who keeps working past a fixed term's end date, without the parties reaching a new specified-term agreement, would fall back within that no-specified-term default rather than continuing to have a specified term.
clauses.gap: This clause corrects a common assumption: no Cal. Labor Code section — including § 2920, which lists expiration of the appointed term as a way employment ends — states a holdover-renewal presumption for employment. The one-month renewal presumption a reader may be thinking of (Cal. Civil Code § 1945) is real, verified, and quoted here, but it governs leases of real property, a different subject; this document cites it only to show what it actually covers and why it does not transfer to employment, not as authority for any employment rule. The final sentence's conclusion — that continued work after a specified term ends, without a new specified-term agreement, defaults back to at-will status under Cal. Labor Code § 2922 — is this document's own textual inference from § 2922's definition of "specified term," not a holding this research verified in any court decision; this research session's CourtListener case-law lookups returned a daily rate-limit error (125/day) on every attempt, so no case law confirming or rejecting that inference is cited here. A specific contract may itself address renewal or holdover on different terms, which would displace this default; this document does not evaluate any specific contract's language. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself determine what terms, if any, govern any specific reader's continued employment after a stated term ends.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2920
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Every employment is terminated by any of the following: (a) Expiration of its appointed term. (b) Extinction of its subject. (c) Death of the employee. (d) The employee’s legal incapacity to act as such.

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1945
citations.cite: California Civil Code
citations.quote: If a lessee of real property remains in possession thereof after the expiration of the hiring, and the lessor accepts rent from him, the parties are presumed to have renewed the hiring on the same terms and for the same time, not exceeding one month when the rent is payable monthly, nor in any case one year.

clauses.title: How a Fixed Term Differs From an At-Will Offer, Including One With a Probationary Period
clauses.body: A fixed-term employment contract removes California's at-will default for the duration of its stated term, because that default applies only where the employment has no specified term. An at-will offer letter does not do this, even where it mentions an anticipated duration, a target end date, or an initial "probationary period," unless the contract's language goes further and actually establishes a specified term as California's statute defines it. Mentioning an expected duration, or labeling an early period of employment "probationary," is not by itself the same as agreeing to a specified term.
clauses.gap: The statutory half of this clause — that the at-will default applies only to employment with "no specified term" — is Cal. Labor Code § 2922, the same statute cited and quoted in this document's clause on the at-will default and specified-term trigger; it is not re-quoted here to avoid duplicating that clause, and is cross-referenced rather than independently re-verified as a second source in this clause. The narrower claim that a probationary period, by itself, does not create a specified term is not directly codified: no statute in the chapter governing termination of employment (Cal. Labor Code §§2920–2929) mentions probationary periods at all. That narrower claim reflects a general pattern in how California courts have approached implied-contract and at-will disputes — treating features like a stated probationary period, an anticipated review date, or a described initial term as relevant evidence of the parties' expectations, without treating any one of them as conclusively creating a fixed term absent clearer contractual language to that effect. This research session's CourtListener case-law lookups returned a daily rate-limit error (125/day) on every attempt, and this document did not have access to it at any point in this research session; as a result, no case is cited for this proposition, and it is disclosed here as an interpretive pattern drawn from general legal understanding of this area rather than a holding this document has independently verified against primary case-law text. This information sheet is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific offer letter, probationary-period provision, or other document actually creates a specified term, or whether any specific reader's employment is at-will or for a specified term.

clauses.title: Signature
Age Discrimination Can Be Proven Without Proof of Intent
clauses.body: Federal law does not only forbid an employer from intentionally targeting older workers in a layoff. The Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) separately makes it unlawful for an employer "to limit, segregate, or classify" employees in a way that would deprive or tend to deprive an individual of employment opportunities, or otherwise adversely affect their status as an employee, because of age — language that does not require proof of intent, and that courts and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have read to permit a "disparate impact" theory of age discrimination: a claim that a facially neutral, uniformly applied selection method (for example, a layoff process built around a criterion that is not itself age) had a disproportionate adverse effect on older workers as a group, regardless of the employer's intent.
clauses.gap: This clause's description of disparate-impact theory under the ADEA rests on well-known, publicly reported background about Smith v. City of Jackson, 544 U.S. 228 (2005), in which the U.S. Supreme Court held that the ADEA authorizes disparate-impact claims. That description could not be independently verified against the Court's own opinion text in this research session: CourtListener, the primary-source case-law tool this corpus otherwise uses, returned a rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) when queried for this case, and no quote from the opinion is offered here as a result — consistent with this document's practice of not presenting an unverified citation as verified. The statutory text quoted above (29 U.S.C. § 623(a)(2)) was independently verified by two separate fetches of the U.S. Code from law.cornell.edu, made with distinct User-Agent headers (Chrome/Windows and Safari/Mac) on 2026-09-02, and confirmed textually identical both times. Separately, and importantly: recognizing that a disparate-impact theory exists under the ADEA is not the same as saying such a claim is easy to win. As described in the next clause of this document, the ADEA gives an employer a defense — that the differentiation was based on reasonable factors other than age — that has no identical counterpart under Title VII's disparate-impact framework, and the scope of that defense is a central, separate legal question this clause does not resolve. This document is informational only. It does not determine whether any specific selection method a specific employer used or is considering would, if challenged, be found to have an unlawful disparate impact, and it does not itself state a rule of any state law.

citations.quote: to limit, segregate, or classify his employees in any way which would deprive or tend to deprive any individual of employment opportunities or otherwise adversely affect his status as an employee, because of such individual’s age

clauses.title: The "Reasonable Factors Other Than Age" Defense
clauses.body: The ADEA itself states a defense specific to age-based claims: it is not unlawful for an employer to take an action otherwise prohibited by the statute "where the differentiation is based on reasonable factors other than age." This "RFOA" defense sits alongside, but is textually and legally distinct from, Title VII's business-necessity defense to a race or sex disparate-impact claim — the two statutes use different words for the standard an employer's justification must meet.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subsection (29 U.S.C. § 623(f)(1)); no additional independent source is cited for this specific point beyond it. The regulatory content of what "reasonable" requires under this defense — the factors the EEOC looks to in deciding whether a differentiation was based on reasonable factors other than age — is addressed in the next clause of this document, sourced from the EEOC's regulation at 29 C.F.R. § 1625.7, not from the statute quoted here. This document does not determine whether a reasonable-factors-other-than-age defense would succeed for any specific employer's specific layoff selection method; whether it succeeds turns on the particular facts and circumstances of that layoff, which this document does not evaluate. This document is informational only.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 623(f)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Age Discrimination in Employment Act, reasonable-factors-other-than-age defense
citations.quote: or where the differentiation is based on reasonable factors other than age

clauses.title: What "Reasonable" Means Under the RFOA Defense
clauses.body: The EEOC's regulation interpreting the reasonable-factors-other-than-age defense defines a reasonable factor other than age as "a non-age factor that is objectively reasonable when viewed from the position of a prudent employer mindful of its responsibilities under the ADEA under like circumstances," decided on the particular facts of each situation. To establish the defense, the regulation states that an employer must show the practice was both reasonably designed to further a legitimate business purpose and administered in a way that reasonably achieves that purpose given what the employer knew or should have known. The regulation lists several considerations relevant to that inquiry, including but not limited to: the extent to which the factor relates to the employer's stated business purpose; the extent to which the employer defined and applied the factor accurately and fairly, including whether managers were trained to apply it and avoid discrimination; the extent to which the employer limited supervisors' discretion to assess employees subjectively, particularly where the criteria involved are known to be subject to negative age-based stereotypes; the extent to which the employer assessed the adverse impact of the practice on older workers; and the degree of harm to the affected age group, including whether the employer took steps to reduce that harm.
clauses.gap: The two quotations below are both drawn from the same regulatory subsection, 29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e) — its opening definitional paragraph, (e)(1), and its non-exhaustive list of considerations, (e)(2) — and are treated as one source, not independent corroboration of each other. The regulation itself states that no single consideration is required to be present, and that the presence of one does not automatically establish the defense — this document does not weigh those considerations against one another for any specific employer's specific layoff. Both quotations were independently verified by two separate fetches of this regulation from law.cornell.edu, made with distinct User-Agent headers (Chrome/Windows and Safari/Mac) on 2026-09-02, and confirmed textually identical both times. This document is informational only. It does not determine whether any specific factor a specific employer used to select employees for layoff is, in fact, reasonable, and it does not itself perform the fact-specific weighing the regulation calls for.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(1) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, definition of a reasonable factor other than age
citations.quote: A reasonable factor other than age is a non-age factor that is objectively reasonable when viewed from the position of a prudent employer mindful of its responsibilities under the ADEA under like circumstances.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(1) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, standard for establishing the RFOA defense
citations.quote: To establish the RFOA defense, an employer must show that the employment practice was both reasonably designed to further or achieve a legitimate business purpose and administered in a way that reasonably achieves that purpose in light of the particular facts and circumstances that were known, or should have been known, to the employer.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(2) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, non-exhaustive list of relevant considerations
citations.quote: (i) The extent to which the factor is related to the employer's stated business purpose; (ii) The extent to which the employer defined the factor accurately and applied the factor fairly and accurately, including the extent to which managers and supervisors were given guidance or training about how to apply the factor and avoid discrimination; (iii) The extent to which the employer limited supervisors' discretion to assess employees subjectively, particularly where the criteria that the supervisors were asked to evaluate are known to be subject to negative age-based stereotypes; (iv) The extent to which the employer assessed the adverse impact of its employment practice on older workers; and (v) The degree of the harm to individuals within the protected age group, in terms of both the extent of injury and the numbers of persons adversely affected, and the extent to which the employer took steps to reduce the harm, in light of the burden of undertaking such steps.

clauses.title: California's Parallel Rule for Age-Based Layoffs
clauses.body: California's own employment discrimination statute, the Fair Employment and Housing Act, does not stop at forbidding intentional age discrimination. By statute, the California Legislature has expressly declared "its intent that the use of salary as the basis for differentiating between employees when terminating employment may be found to constitute age discrimination if use of that criterion adversely impacts older workers as a group," and further declared its intent "that the disparate impact theory of proof may be used in claims of age discrimination" — language enacted specifically to address layoff-type terminations built around a criterion, such as salary, that is not itself age but that can correlate with it.
clauses.gap: This statute has a specific origin worth stating plainly, because it corrects a framing this document's research brief left open: this provision (Gov. Code § 12941) was enacted for the specific purpose of legislatively overriding a California Court of Appeal decision, Marks v. Loral Corp. (1997) 57 Cal.App.4th 30, which had held disparate-impact theory unavailable for age claims under California law; the statute's own text states the Legislature's "rejection" of that opinion. This document was not able to independently verify the Marks opinion's own reasoning against a primary source — the same CourtListener rate-limit that affected this document's federal case research (see the ADEA disparate-impact clause above) applies equally to California case law, and no quotation from Marks is offered as a result. Beyond the Legislature's own statement of intent quoted above, this document did not independently verify any specific California appellate decision applying disparate-impact theory to a group layoff's age composition; if such case law exists and would apply to a specific employer's specific layoff, this document does not identify or evaluate it. This statute is one state's law, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer's specific layoff, and not a claim that every state recognizes the same theory under its own anti-discrimination statute. This document is informational only.

citations.quote: The Legislature declares its intent that the use of salary as the basis for differentiating between employees when terminating employment may be found to constitute age discrimination if use of that criterion adversely impacts older workers as a group, and further declares its intent that the disparate impact theory of proof may be used in claims of age discrimination.

clauses.title: Statistical Analysis of a Proposed Layoff List
clauses.body: Because the RFOA defense described earlier in this document turns partly on "the extent to which the employer assessed the adverse impact of its employment practice on older workers," employers conducting a group layoff commonly compare the age composition (and sometimes the composition by other protected characteristics) of the group of employees selected for layoff against the group retained, before the layoff list is finalized — a statistical check against the specific legal risk described in the clauses above, not a step required by any single, universally applicable numeric formula.
clauses.gap: This clause draws its statistical-analysis framing from one specific EEOC consideration under the ADEA's own regulation, quoted above (29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(2)(iv)) — it does not restate the full reasonableness-factors clause and should be read alongside it, not as an independent regulatory source. A correction to a common assumption worth stating directly: the EEOC's separate, frequently cited "four-fifths rule" for measuring adverse impact statistically — a selection rate for one group that is less than four-fifths of the rate for the group with the highest rate is generally regarded as evidence of adverse impact — comes from a different regulation, the Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures at 29 C.F.R. § 1607.4(D), and that regulation's own text defines the rule by reference to "race, sex, or ethnic group," not age. This document did not find, within 29 C.F.R. part 1625 (the ADEA-specific regulations), an EEOC adoption of the four-fifths rule as the specific numeric test for an age-based disparate-impact claim; the four-fifths figure is cited here only as background on a widely used general statistical benchmark, not as a rule this document confirms applies, by its own terms, to age. This document does not perform, or instruct the reader to perform, any statistical analysis of any specific layoff list, and does not state what result such an analysis would need to show to avoid liability in a specific case. This document is informational only.

citations.quote: The extent to which the employer assessed the adverse impact of its employment practice on older workers

citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures, the "four-fifths rule"
citations.quote: A selection rate for any race, sex, or ethnic group which is less than four-fifths ( 4/5 ) (or eighty percent) of the rate for the group with the highest rate will generally be regarded by the Federal enforcement agencies as evidence of adverse impact

clauses.title: Subjective Versus Objective Selection Criteria
clauses.body: The EEOC's own regulation interpreting the reasonable-factors-other-than-age defense singles out, as one consideration relevant to whether a layoff-selection factor was reasonable, "the extent to which the employer limited supervisors' discretion to assess employees subjectively, particularly where the criteria that the supervisors were asked to evaluate are known to be subject to negative age-based stereotypes." More broadly, and consistent with that regulatory focus, subjective or discretionary selection criteria for a layoff (such as an individual supervisor's unstructured judgment about who is a stronger performer) are generally described by courts and the EEOC as carrying higher discrimination-claim risk than objective, uniformly applied criteria (such as seniority or a documented performance-rating system applied consistently across the workforce) — because subjective criteria are harder to defend against a claim that they were a pretext for a discriminatory reason, and easier for a claimant to second-guess after the fact.
clauses.gap: This document verified the quoted regulatory language directly (29 C.F.R. § 1625.7(e)(2)(iii)); the broader statement that courts and the EEOC generally draw this subjective/objective distinction reflects a widely reported pattern in employment-discrimination law, not a single additional primary source independently fetched and quoted in this research session — this corpus's CourtListener case-law tool was rate-limited (125 requests/day exhausted) at the time of this research, so no case citation is offered for that broader pattern beyond the one regulation quoted. Describing subjective criteria as carrying comparatively higher risk is not a statement that subjective criteria are unlawful, or that objective criteria are automatically lawful — an objective criterion, including a facially neutral one like seniority or salary, can itself produce an unlawful disparate impact, as described elsewhere in this document. This document does not recommend which selection criteria a specific employer should use for a specific layoff, and does not evaluate whether any specific criteria a specific employer has used or is considering would withstand a discrimination challenge. This document is informational only.

citations.quote: The extent to which the employer limited supervisors' discretion to assess employees subjectively, particularly where the criteria that the supervisors were asked to evaluate are known to be subject to negative age-based stereotypes

clauses.title: Connection to the Group-Termination Release Disclosure Rule
clauses.body: The selection-criteria risk described throughout this document connects directly to a separate federal disclosure duty that arises only if a release of claims is used in connection with a group layoff: under the Older Workers Benefit Protection Act, if a release of age-discrimination claims is requested in connection with an exit-incentive or other employment-termination program offered to a group or class of employees, the employer must inform each individual in writing, at the start of the consideration period, of the job titles and ages of everyone eligible or selected for the program, and the ages of everyone in the same job classification or organizational unit who was not eligible or selected. In practice, that disclosure obligation puts the very same age composition of the selected-versus-not-selected group described earlier in this document directly in front of the employees being asked to sign a release.
clauses.gap: This is the same federal statutory provision, 29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1)(H), already covered in full — along with the OWBPA's other release requirements, its 21-day/45-day and 7-day timing rules, and its EEOC-participation carve-out — by this corpus's Severance Agreement document, in the clause titled "Age Discrimination Release Requirements" (clause id sev_owbpa). This clause does not re-derive that requirement; it exists only to connect this document's layoff-selection-criteria topic to that separately covered disclosure duty, for a reader using both documents together. The quotation below was independently re-verified for this document by two separate fetches of 29 U.S.C. § 626 from law.cornell.edu, made with distinct User-Agent headers (Chrome/Windows and Safari/Mac) on 2026-09-02, and confirmed textually identical both times, rather than simply copied forward from the earlier document's research. This disclosure duty applies only when a release of claims is being requested in connection with a group program — it does not apply to a layoff where no release is used, and this document does not determine whether any specific layoff involves the kind of "exit incentive or other employment termination program offered to a group or class of employees" that triggers it. This document is informational only.

citations.quote: if a waiver is requested in connection with an exit incentive or other employment termination program offered to a group or class of employees, the employer (at the commencement of the period specified in subparagraph (F)) informs the individual in writing in a manner calculated to be understood by the average individual eligible to participate, as to— (i) any class, unit, or group of individuals covered by such program, any eligibility factors for such program, and any time limits applicable to such program; and (ii) the job titles and ages of all individuals eligible or selected for the program, and the ages of all individuals in the same job classification or organizational unit who are not eligible or selected for the program.

clauses.title: Selection-Criteria Documentation
