clauses.title: Duty to Notify Employer of Injury
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 5400 — not § 5401 — is the section that states the employee's notice duty: except as provided by §§ 5402 and 5403, no claim to recover workers' compensation may be maintained unless, within thirty days after the injury occurs, written notice signed by the injured person (or, if the person has died, by a dependent) is served on the employer. Section 5401 is a different duty running the other way — it requires the employer, not the employee, to hand over a claim form once the employer has notice or knowledge of the injury, and is addressed in a separate clause of this document. Section 5403 qualifies § 5400's thirty-day rule: a failure to give notice, or a defect or inaccuracy in the notice that was given, is not a bar to recovery if it is found as a fact that the employer was not in fact misled or prejudiced by the failure or defect.
clauses.gap: Correcting the framing in the research request: § 5400 itself is the source of the thirty-day notice duty, and it is § 5400 — not § 5401 — that states it; § 5401 imposes a distinct, employer-side duty (the claim-form and notice-of-eligibility duty), addressed in a separate clause. Section 5403's exception is also narrower than a general "good cause for late notice" standard: it does not ask whether the employee had a good excuse for being late, but only whether the employer was in fact misled or prejudiced by the missing or defective notice — an employer who was not misled or prejudiced cannot defeat the claim on notice grounds even without any excuse for the delay, and an employer who was misled or prejudiced might still defeat it even if the employee had a good excuse. A third, related exception — that an employer's own actual knowledge of the injury from any source is equivalent to notice under § 5400 — is stated in § 5402(a) and is addressed in a separate clause of this document rather than repeated here; §§ 5400, 5402, and 5403 are three separate sections of the same statutory chapter (Chapter 2, Limitations of Proceedings), not independent sources from one another, and this disclosure is repeated in each clause that draws on that chapter. This clause is one state's statute, stating a fact about California's notice requirement — not a claim about what any specific reader with a specific injury should do about giving or not giving notice.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 5400 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 5400
citations.quote: no claim to recover compensation under this division shall be maintained unless within thirty days after the occurrence of the injury which is claimed to have caused the disability or death, there is served upon the employer notice in writing, signed by the person injured or someone in his behalf

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 5403 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 5403
citations.quote: The failure to give notice under section 5400, or any defect or inaccuracy in a notice is not a bar to recovery under this division if it is found as a fact in the proceedings for the collection of the claim that the employer was not in fact misled or prejudiced by such failure.

clauses.title: Employer's Actual Knowledge as Equivalent to Notice
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 5402(a) states that knowledge of an injury, obtained from any source, on the part of the employer, the employer's managing agent, superintendent, foreman, or other person in authority — or knowledge that a claim of injury is being asserted, sufficient to give the employer an opportunity to investigate — is equivalent to the written notice that § 5400 otherwise requires the employee to serve on the employer.
clauses.gap: This is a fact about what satisfies the notice requirement, not a claim about whether any specific employer in fact had the relevant knowledge in any given case — that is a factual question this document does not resolve. Section 5402 also contains, in separate subdivisions (b) and (c), the claim-response and treatment-authorization rules addressed in a different clause of this document ("Time Limit to Reject the Claim; Presumption of Compensability"); this clause and that one draw on different subdivisions of the same statutory section, so they are not independent sources of each other, and this disclosure is repeated in the other clause.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 5402(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 5402, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Knowledge of an injury, obtained from any source, on the part of an employer, the employer’s managing agent, superintendent, foreman, or other person in authority, or knowledge of the assertion of a claim of injury sufficient to afford opportunity to the employer to make an investigation into the facts, is equivalent to service under Section 5400.

clauses.title: Employer's Duty to Provide the Claim Form
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 5401(a) requires the employer, within one working day of receiving notice or knowledge of an injury that causes lost time beyond the employee's work shift or requires medical treatment beyond first aid, to provide the injured employee (or, in case of death, the dependents) a claim form and a notice of potential eligibility for benefits, personally or by first-class mail. The claim form itself must request the employee's name and address, social security number, the time and address where the injury occurred, and the nature of and body part affected by the injury. Section 5401(b) further requires that the notice of potential eligibility, insofar as practicable combined with the claim form into a single document, be easily understandable, available in English and Spanish, and cover specified topics — including the claims procedure, the types of benefits available, how to obtain medical care while the claim is pending, and the employee's right to consult an attorney.
clauses.gap: The claim form § 5401 describes is commonly referred to in practice as form "DWC-1," but that name and number do not themselves appear anywhere in the text of § 5401 — the statute only calls it "a claim form." This document did not independently fetch or verify the regulation that assigns that form its title and number, so no citation or quote is offered for the "DWC-1" label itself; it is stated here only as commonly-used shorthand for the form § 5401 describes, not as a verified statutory fact. This clause is one state's statute, stating a fact about what California requires an employer to provide and when — not a claim about whether any specific employer has done so in any given case.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 5401(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 5401, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Within one working day of receiving notice or knowledge of injury under Section 5400 or 5402, which injury results in lost time beyond the employee’s work shift at the time of injury or which results in medical treatment beyond first aid, the employer shall provide, personally or by first-class mail, a claim form and a notice of potential eligibility for benefits under this division to the injured employee

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 5401(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 5401, subd. (a)
citations.quote: The claim form shall request the injured employee’s name and address, social security number, the time and address where the injury occurred, and the nature of and part of the body affected by the injury.

clauses.title: Time Limit to Reject the Claim; Presumption of Compensability
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 5402(b)(1) states that if liability is not rejected within 90 days after the date the claim form is filed under § 5401, the injury is presumed compensable — a presumption rebuttable only by evidence discovered after that 90-day period. (§ 5402(b)(2) sets a shorter 75-day version of that same presumption for certain injuries or illnesses defined elsewhere in the Labor Code, at §§ 3212 through 3212.85 and 3212.9 through 3213.2.) Separately, § 5402(c) requires the employer, within one working day after the employee files the claim form, to authorize treatment for the alleged injury and continue providing it until liability is accepted or rejected — with the employer's liability for that pre-decision treatment capped at $10,000 while the claim remains undecided.
clauses.gap: Correcting the framing in the research request: the statutory text of § 5402 does not itself contain, describe, or use the term "delay letter" anywhere in its current form. A "delay letter" is a term used in workers' compensation administrative practice for correspondence a claims administrator sends to extend its investigation, but no provision of § 5402 was found stating a right or procedure by that name, and this document does not independently verify against the applicable regulations (outside the Labor Code itself) whether or how such a letter affects the 90-day or 75-day period stated here. That specific mechanism is therefore omitted from this clause rather than asserted without a verified source. The 75-day presumption for the injury categories cross-referenced in § 5402(b)(2) is stated here only by cross-reference; this document does not independently identify or verify what those injury categories are. This clause is one state's statute, used as evidence of the actual statutory timing — not a claim about whether any specific claim was or was not timely rejected.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 5402(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 5402, subd. (b)(1)
citations.quote: If liability is not rejected within 90 days after the date the claim form is filed under Section 5401, the injury shall be presumed compensable under this division. The presumption of this subdivision is rebuttable only by evidence discovered subsequent to the 90-day period.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 5402(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 5402, subd. (c)
citations.quote: Within one working day after an employee files a claim form under Section 5401, the employer shall authorize the provision of all treatment, consistent with Section 5307.27, for the alleged injury and shall continue to provide the treatment until the date that liability for the claim is accepted or rejected. Until the date the claim is accepted or rejected, liability for medical treatment shall be limited to ten thousand dollars ($10,000).

clauses.title: Time Limit to File a Workers' Compensation Claim
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 5405 sets a one-year period to commence proceedings to collect medical-treatment benefits or disability-payment benefits, running from any of three alternative dates: the date of injury; the expiration of any period covered by disability payments; or the last date on which medical benefits were furnished — whichever produces the latest date is, as a practical matter, the one that governs, since the statute states these as three independent starting points rather than requiring all three. Separately, § 5401(d) provides that once a claim form is filed with the employer, that filing tolls (pauses) the running of this time limit — for injuries occurring on or after January 1, 1994 — until the claim is either denied by the employer or becomes presumptively compensable under § 5402.
clauses.gap: Correcting the framing in the research request: § 5405's one-year period does not run from the date of injury alone — the statute states three independent alternative trigger dates, and the last-furnished-benefits or last-payment dates can extend the effective deadline well past one year from the injury itself where treatment or disability payments continued. This document does not resolve, for any specific case, which of the three dates produces the applicable deadline, nor does it independently verify what benefits were or were not furnished in a specific case. The tolling rule in § 5401(d) is stated by its own terms to apply to injuries occurring on or after January 1, 1994; this document does not evaluate whether that date restriction is a live limitation for any specific injury. Sections 5401 and 5405 are two separate sections of the same statutory chapter, not independent sources from each other.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 5405 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 5405
citations.quote: The period within which proceedings may be commenced for the collection of the benefits provided by Article 2 (commencing with Section 4600) or Article 3 (commencing with Section 4650), or both, of Chapter 2 of Part 2 is one year from any of the following: (a) The date of injury. (b) The expiration of any period covered by payment under Article 3 (commencing with Section 4650) of Chapter 2 of Part 2. (c) The last date on which any benefits provided for in Article 2 (commencing with Section 4600) of Chapter 2 of Part 2 were furnished.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 5401(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 5401, subd. (d)
citations.quote: Filing of the claim form with the employer shall toll, for injuries occurring on or after January 1, 1994, the time limitations set forth in Sections 5405 and 5406 until the claim is denied by the employer or the injury becomes presumptively compensable pursuant to Section 5402.

clauses.title: Workers' Compensation as the Exclusive Remedy
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 3600(a) makes an employer liable for workers' compensation, without regard to negligence, whenever specified conditions concur — including that the injury arose out of and in the course of employment. Labor Code § 3602(a) then states the exclusivity consequence: where § 3600's conditions of compensation concur, the right to recover workers' compensation is, except as specifically provided in § 3602 itself and in §§ 3706 and 4558, the sole and exclusive remedy of the employee (or dependents) against the employer — meaning a separate civil lawsuit against the employer for the same injury is generally unavailable. Section 3602(a) also states that an employer's occupying some other or "dual" capacity besides employer does not, by itself, open the door to a civil damages action.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general rule only; the named, specific exceptions to it — including the ones § 3602(a) itself cross-references — are addressed in a separate clause of this document rather than repeated here, so this clause should not be read in isolation as stating an absolute bar. Sections 3600 and 3602 are two separate sections of the same statutory chapter (Chapter 3, Conditions of Compensation Liability), not independent sources from each other. Two further cross-referenced exceptions — Labor Code § 3706 (concerning uninsured employers) and § 4558 (concerning power-press injuries) — are named in both § 3600(a) and § 3602(a) but were not independently fetched or verified in this session, so this document does not state or quote what either of those sections provides; a reader would need to separately check those two sections' actual text, which this document does not do. This clause is one state's statute, stating a fact about the general scope of California's exclusive-remedy rule — not a claim about whether workers' compensation is in fact the exclusive remedy for any specific injury or any specific reader's situation.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3600(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3600, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Liability for the compensation provided by this division, in lieu of any other liability whatsoever to any person except as otherwise specifically provided in Sections 3602, 3706, and 4558, shall, without regard to negligence, exist against an employer for any injury sustained by his or her employees arising out of and in the course of the employment and for the death of any employee if the injury proximately causes death

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3602(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3602, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Where the conditions of compensation set forth in Section 3600 concur, the right to recover compensation is, except as specifically provided in this section and Sections 3706 and 4558, the sole and exclusive remedy of the employee or his or her dependents against the employer.

clauses.title: Statutory Exceptions to the Exclusive Remedy Rule
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 3602(b) names specific, narrow instances in which an employee (or dependents, if the employee dies) may bring a civil damages action against the employer despite § 3602(a)'s general exclusivity rule: (1) where the injury or death is proximately caused by a willful physical assault by the employer; (2) where the injury is aggravated by the employer's fraudulent concealment of the existence of the injury and its connection to the employment — in which case the employer's civil liability is limited to the damages proximately caused by that aggravation, and the employer bears the burden of proving how much of the harm to apportion away from it; and (3) where the injury or death is proximately caused by a defective product the employer manufactured and then sold, leased, or otherwise transferred for value to an independent third person, who in turn provided it for the employee's use.
clauses.gap: Correcting the framing in the research request: California's statutory exceptions to exclusivity are not a general "intentional torts" carve-out — § 3602(b) names three specific, narrowly worded instances (willful physical assault by the employer; fraudulent concealment of an existing injury; and a defective-product chain involving a third party), not intentional wrongdoing by the employer generally. Whether a given intentional act by an employer falls within the willful-physical-assault exception specifically, as opposed to being barred by exclusivity like other workplace torts, is a fact-specific application question this document does not resolve, and this document does not independently research case law construing the scope of that exception's terms. This clause quotes § 3602(b)(1) and (b)(2); § 3602(b)(3) (the defective-product exception) is described but not separately quoted here. Section 3602 is the same section already quoted (subdivision (a)) in a separate clause of this document addressing the general exclusivity rule; that clause and this one draw on the same statutory section, not independent sources of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3602(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3602, subd. (b)(1)
citations.quote: An employee, or his or her dependents in the event of his or her death, may bring an action at law for damages against the employer, as if this division did not apply, in the following instances: (1) Where the employee’s injury or death is proximately caused by a willful physical assault by the employer.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3602(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3602, subd. (b)(2)
citations.quote: Where the employee’s injury is aggravated by the employer’s fraudulent concealment of the existence of the injury and its connection with the employment, in which case the employer’s liability shall be limited to those damages proximately caused by the aggravation.

clauses.title: Injury and Claim Information Declaration
clauses.body:

The injury is described here as: {{injuryDescription}}, occurring on {{injuryDate}}. Written notice of the injury was given to {{companyName}} on {{employerNoticeDate}}.

This information sheet describes California's statutory framework governing an employee's duty to notify an employer of a work injury, an employer's duty to provide a claim form, the timing for the claim to be accepted or rejected, the deadline to file a workers' compensation claim, and the general rule that workers' compensation is an employee's exclusive remedy against the employer, subject to specific statutory exceptions.

This information sheet is not a workers' compensation claim form, is not itself filed with any employer, insurer, or agency by completing it, and does not initiate a workers' compensation claim. Completing it does not determine that {{employeeName}}'s injury is compensable, and does not determine the outcome of any claim. clauses.title: Home State Jurisdiction: The Primary Basis for an Initial Custody Determination
clauses.body: California's Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (UCCJEA), Family Code sections 3400-3465, defines “home state” as the state in which a child lived with a parent or a person acting as a parent for at least six consecutive months immediately before the commencement of a child custody proceeding; for a child under six months old, the term instead means the state in which the child has lived from birth with any of those persons; and a period of temporary absence by the child or a listed adult counts as part of that period rather than interrupting it. Home-state status is the primary jurisdictional basis for an initial child custody determination: except when temporary emergency jurisdiction applies (addressed separately in this document), a California court has jurisdiction to make an initial custody determination if California is the child's home state on the date the proceeding commences, or was the child's home state within the six months before commencement and the child is now absent from California but a parent or a person acting as a parent continues to live here. The UCCJEA lists this home-state basis first among the statutory grounds for initial jurisdiction; the alternative bases available when no state qualifies as the home state are addressed in a separate clause.
clauses.gap: California's UCCJEA is codified at Family Code Division 8, Part 3, sections 3400 through 3465 -- confirmed directly by fetching leginfo.legislature.ca.gov's own part-heading text ("PART 3. UNIFORM CHILD CUSTODY JURISDICTION AND ENFORCEMENT ACT [3400 - 3465]"), so the section range given in this document's framing is correct as stated, not merely assumed. This clause cites two separately numbered statutory sections -- Family Code section 3402(g) (definitions, Chapter 1) and section 3421(a)(1) (initial jurisdiction, Chapter 2) -- both within the same 1999 enactment (Stats. 1999, Ch. 867) that created this part, so they are independent in the sense of being separately numbered provisions but not in the sense of separately-enacted law. Both sections were fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and each quote was confirmed programmatically as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of the fetched section text. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's enactment of the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act actually defines and applies the home-state concept -- not a claim about which state's courts have jurisdiction over any specific child or family, and not a claim that every other state's UCCJEA enactment uses identical section numbers or wording (nearly all U.S. states have enacted some version of the UCCJEA, but California's specific codification, cited here, is what this document describes). This document is informational only: it does not itself determine which state is a specific child's home state or that a California court has jurisdiction over any specific custody matter -- only a court, applying section 3421 to the facts of a filed case, can make that determination. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by clear statutory definitions rather than by contested judicial interpretation, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3402(g)
citations.cite: the statutory definition of "home state"
citations.quote: “Home state” means the state in which a child lived with a parent or a person acting as a parent for at least six consecutive months immediately before the commencement of a child custody proceeding. In the case of a child less than six months of age, the term means the state in which the child lived from birth with any of the persons mentioned. A period of temporary absence of any of the mentioned persons is part of the period.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3421(a)(1)
citations.cite: home state as the primary basis for jurisdiction to make an initial custody determination
citations.quote: This state is the home state of the child on the date of the commencement of the proceeding, or was the home state of the child within six months before the commencement of the proceeding and the child is absent from this state but a parent or person acting as a parent continues to live in this state.

clauses.title: Alternative Jurisdictional Bases When No State Qualifies as the Home State
clauses.body: When no state -- including California -- qualifies as the child's home state under the definition addressed in a separate clause, or the home-state court has declined jurisdiction in favor of a more appropriate forum, Family Code section 3421(a)(2) permits a California court to make an initial custody determination on a "significant connection" basis, but only if two conditions are both true: the child and the child's parents (or the child and at least one parent or person acting as a parent) have a significant connection with California other than mere physical presence, and substantial evidence is available in California concerning the child's care, protection, training, and personal relationships. If every court with jurisdiction under the home-state or significant-connection bases has declined to exercise it on the ground that California is the more appropriate forum, section 3421(a)(3) supplies a further basis (not separately quoted here). And if no other state would have jurisdiction under any of the first three bases, section 3421(a)(4) makes California's jurisdiction available by elimination. Section 3421(b) then states that this list -- home state, significant connection, forum-declination, and no-other-state-has-jurisdiction -- is the exclusive jurisdictional basis for an initial custody determination by a California court: physical presence of the child in California, or personal jurisdiction over a parent, is by itself neither necessary nor sufficient.
clauses.gap: This clause cites Family Code section 3421(a)(2) and section 3421(a)(4)-(b), both subsections of the single statutory section already cited (in a different subsection, (a)(1)) in this document's home-state clause, and is treated as the same source, not an independent one, for source-independence purposes. Both quoted excerpts were fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and each quote was confirmed programmatically as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of the fetched section text. Correction/verification of the user's framing: the "significant connection" test does have two conjunctive prongs, as the user's framing anticipated, but this clause states them as actually written in the statute (a significant connection with the state other than mere physical presence, plus the availability of substantial evidence in the state concerning the child's care, protection, training, and personal relationships) rather than assuming their content in advance; California's UCCJEA also states a third and fourth basis (forum-declination and no-other-state-would-have-jurisdiction) not always emphasized in general summaries of the "significant connection" test, and this clause includes them. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's enactment of the UCCJEA structures its jurisdictional list -- not a claim about which state's courts have jurisdiction over any specific child, and not a claim that every other state's UCCJEA enactment states these bases in identical language. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any of these bases is satisfied for a specific child or family -- only a court can make that determination on the facts before it. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by clear statutory text, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3421(a)(2)
citations.cite: the significant-connection basis for initial jurisdiction when no state is the home state
citations.quote: A court of another state does not have jurisdiction under paragraph (1), or a court of the home state of the child has declined to exercise jurisdiction on the grounds that this state is the more appropriate forum under Section 3427 or 3428, and both of the following are true: (A) The child and the child’s parents, or the child and at least one parent or a person acting as a parent, have a significant connection with this state other than mere physical presence. (B) Substantial evidence is available in this state concerning the child’s care, protection, training, and personal relationships.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3421(a)(4)-(b)
citations.cite: the default basis when no other state would have jurisdiction, and the exclusivity of this list of bases
citations.quote: No court of any other state would have jurisdiction under the criteria specified in paragraph (1), (2), or (3). (b) Subdivision (a) is the exclusive jurisdictional basis for making a child custody determination by a court of this state.

clauses.title: Exclusive, Continuing Jurisdiction to Modify a Custody Determination
clauses.body: Once a California court has made a child custody determination consistent with the initial-jurisdiction rules addressed elsewhere in this document, Family Code section 3422(a) gives that court "exclusive, continuing jurisdiction" over the determination -- meaning California, and no other state, generally retains the power to modify it -- until one of two things happens: a California court itself determines that neither the child, nor the child and one parent, nor the child and a person acting as a parent, any longer has a significant connection with California and that substantial evidence concerning the child's care, protection, training, and personal relationships is no longer available here; or a California court or a court of another state determines that the child, the child's parents, and any person acting as a parent no longer presently reside in California. This is structurally similar to, but a genuinely separate statute from, UIFSA's continuing-exclusive-jurisdiction concept for child and spousal support (addressed in this corpus's separate UIFSA Registration Information Sheet document): the UCCJEA's version turns on significant connection and evidence availability, or on where the child, the parents, and any person acting as a parent currently reside, not on where an individual "obligor" or "obligee" resides, and it has no party-consent mechanism paralleling UIFSA's. Correspondingly, Family Code section 3423 states that another state's court generally may not modify a California custody determination unless that other state would itself have jurisdiction to make an initial determination and either California determines it no longer has exclusive, continuing jurisdiction (or that the other state is a more convenient forum), or a court determines that the child, the child's parents, and any person acting as a parent no longer reside in California.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two separately numbered statutory sections -- Family Code section 3422(a) and section 3423 -- both within the same 1999 enactment that created this part, so they are independent in the sense of separately numbered provisions but not in the sense of separately-enacted law. Both were fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and each quote was confirmed programmatically as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of the fetched section text. Correction of the user's framing: this rule is structurally similar to UIFSA's continuing-exclusive-jurisdiction concept for support, as the framing anticipated, but is not identical in its substantive trigger -- the UCCJEA's version does not use UIFSA's residency-of-the-obligor-or-obligee-or-child framing at all; it instead turns on "significant connection" and evidence availability, or on where the child, the child's parents, and any person acting as a parent currently reside, and section 3422 has no analog to UIFSA's party-consent-to-continued-jurisdiction provision. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's enactment of the UCCJEA structures continuing jurisdiction over its own custody determinations -- not a claim about which state's courts retain jurisdiction over any specific determination, and not a claim that every other state's UCCJEA enactment states this rule in identical language. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether a specific California custody determination retains exclusive, continuing jurisdiction, or whether another state may modify it -- only a court can make that determination on the facts before it. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by clear statutory text, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3422(a)
citations.cite: the conditions under which California retains exclusive, continuing jurisdiction to modify a custody determination it made
citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided in Section 3424, a court of this state that has made a child custody determination consistent with Section 3421 or 3423 has exclusive, continuing jurisdiction over the determination until either of the following occurs: (1) A court of this state determines that neither the child, nor the child and one parent, nor the child and a person acting as a parent have a significant connection with this state and that substantial evidence is no longer available in this state concerning the child’s care, protection, training, and personal relationships. (2) A court of this state or a court of another state determines that the child, the child’s parents, and any person acting as a parent do not presently reside in this state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3423
citations.cite: when another state's court may modify a California custody determination
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in Section 3424, a court of this state may not modify a child custody determination made by a court of another state unless a court of this state has jurisdiction to make an initial determination under paragraph (1) or (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3421 and either of the following determinations is made: (a) The court of the other state determines it no longer has exclusive, continuing jurisdiction under Section 3422 or that a court of this state would be a more convenient forum under Section 3427. (b) A court of this state or a court of the other state determines that the child, the child’s parents, and any person acting as a parent do not presently reside in the other state.

clauses.title: Temporary Emergency Jurisdiction: A Separate, Time-Limited Basis Distinct From the Ex Parte Order Procedure
clauses.body: The UCCJEA contains its own, separate jurisdictional basis -- distinct from home-state, significant-connection, and exclusive-continuing jurisdiction, all addressed elsewhere in this document -- for a California court to act even when it otherwise lacks jurisdiction under those rules. Family Code section 3424(a) gives a California court "temporary emergency jurisdiction" if the child is physically present in California and either the child has been abandoned, or it is necessary in an emergency to protect the child because the child (or a sibling or parent of the child) is subjected to, or threatened with, mistreatment or abuse, or because the child has been unable to obtain gender-affirming health care or gender-affirming mental health care as statutorily defined. This jurisdictional basis is genuinely distinct from this corpus's separate Emergency (Ex Parte) Custody Order Information Sheet document, which addresses the procedural mechanism -- California Rules of Court, rule 5.151, and Family Code section 3064's immediate-harm standard -- for requesting an emergency order without advance notice to the other parent in a case where a California court already has jurisdiction; section 3424 instead addresses whether a California court has jurisdiction to act on an emergency basis at all, including in a case where no other jurisdictional basis under this document is available. An order made under section 3424 is expressly temporary: if no other state's court with jurisdiction under the ordinary rules has yet acted, section 3424(b) states that the California emergency order remains in effect only until an order is obtained from a court of a state having jurisdiction under those ordinary rules, unless no such proceeding is commenced and California itself becomes the child's home state, in which case the order can become a final determination. Section 3424(d), not quoted here, additionally requires a California court exercising this emergency jurisdiction to immediately communicate with the court of any state that already has, or is exercising, jurisdiction under the ordinary rules.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two subsections of the single statutory section, Family Code section 3424(a) and section 3424(b), and treats them as one source, not independent. Both were fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and each quote was confirmed programmatically as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of the fetched section text. This clause states the factual distinction between section 3424's emergency-jurisdiction basis and this corpus's separate ex parte order document's procedural mechanism (Cal. Rules of Court, rule 5.151, and Family Code section 3064) as a description of that other document's already-published content, not as a new citation independently re-verified in this session; this document does not restate or re-verify rule 5.151's or section 3064's text, and nothing here duplicates that document's content. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's enactment of the UCCJEA structures its emergency-jurisdiction basis -- not a claim about which state's courts have emergency jurisdiction over any specific child, and not a claim that every other state's UCCJEA enactment defines "emergency" in identical language (states vary somewhat in the specific triggering conditions they have enacted, though the underlying home-state and significant-connection concepts are common to all UCCJEA-adopting states). This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that a specific set of facts satisfies section 3424's emergency standard, or that a California court will exercise this jurisdiction -- only a court can make that determination.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3424(a)
citations.cite: the grounds for temporary emergency jurisdiction
citations.quote: (a) A court of this state has temporary emergency jurisdiction if the child is present in this state and the child has been abandoned or it is necessary in an emergency to protect the child because the child, or a sibling or parent of the child, is subjected to, or threatened with, mistreatment or abuse, or because the child has been unable to obtain gender-affirming health care or gender-affirming mental health care, as defined by Section 16010.2 of the Welfare and Institutions Code.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3424(b)
citations.cite: the temporary, time-limited duration of an order made under emergency jurisdiction
citations.quote: If there is no previous child custody determination that is entitled to be enforced under this part and a child custody proceeding has not been commenced in a court of a state having jurisdiction under Sections 3421 to 3423, inclusive, a child custody determination made under this section remains in effect until an order is obtained from a court of a state having jurisdiction under Sections 3421 to 3423, inclusive.

clauses.title: Registering an Out-of-State Custody Determination for Enforcement Under the UCCJEA
clauses.body: Distinct from UIFSA's own registration mechanism for enforcing an out-of-state support order (addressed in this corpus's separate UIFSA Registration Information Sheet document), the UCCJEA has its own, separate registration mechanism -- a different statute -- for enforcing another state's custody determination in California. Family Code section 3445(a) allows a child custody determination issued by a court of another state to be registered in California, with or without a simultaneous request for enforcement, by sending to the appropriate California court: a letter or other document requesting registration; two copies (one certified) of the determination, together with a statement under penalty of perjury that, to the best of the requester's knowledge, the order has not been modified; and (except as otherwise provided elsewhere in the UCCJEA for certain safety-sensitive cases) the name and address of the person seeking registration and of any parent or person acting as a parent who was awarded custody or visitation in the determination. Once registered, section 3446 states the registered determination's effect: a California court may grant any relief normally available under California law to enforce it, and shall recognize and enforce -- but, except in accordance with the jurisdiction chapter addressed elsewhere in this document, may not modify -- a registered custody determination of another state's court. Registration also triggers a contest procedure: section 3445(c) requires the notice served on the other parties to state that a hearing to contest the registration's validity must be requested within 20 days of service, and that failing to timely contest results in the determination being confirmed by operation of law and precludes later contesting any matter that could have been raised at registration.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two separately numbered statutory sections -- Family Code section 3445 and section 3446 -- both within the same 1999 enactment that created this part, so they are independent in the sense of separately numbered provisions but not in the sense of separately-enacted law; the contest-procedure description also draws on section 3445(c), a further subsection of the same section already cited for the registration mechanism in (a), and is treated as the same source, not independent of it. All three quoted excerpts were fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and each quote was confirmed programmatically as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of the fetched section text. This clause does not restate section 3445(d)'s full list of enumerated defenses available to a person contesting registration (lack of jurisdiction in the issuing court, vacatur/stay/modification by a court with jurisdiction to do so, or inadequate notice in the issuing proceeding), which a fuller treatment of contesting a registered custody determination would need to cover; this clause states only that a contest right and a 20-day deadline exist. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's enactment of the UCCJEA structures registration and enforcement of another state's custody determination -- not a claim about which state's courts have jurisdiction over any specific determination, and not a claim that every other state's UCCJEA enactment uses identical procedures or deadlines. This document is informational only: it does not itself register, enforce, confirm, or contest any custody determination. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by clear statutory text, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3445(a)
citations.cite: the records that must be sent to register another state's custody determination in California
citations.quote: (a) A child custody determination issued by a court of another state may be registered in this state, with or without a simultaneous request for enforcement, by sending all of the following to the appropriate court in this state: (1) A letter or other document requesting registration. (2) Two copies, including one certified copy, of the determination sought to be registered, and a statement under penalty of perjury that to the best of the knowledge and belief of the person seeking registration the order has not been modified. (3) Except as otherwise provided in Section 3429, the name and address of the person seeking registration and any parent or person acting as a parent who has been awarded custody or visitation in the child custody determination sought to be registered.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3445(c)
citations.cite: the required notice of the 20-day deadline to contest registration, and confirmation by operation of law if uncontested
citations.quote: (c) The notice required by paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) shall state all of the following: (1) That a registered determination is enforceable as of the date of the registration in the same manner as a determination issued by a court of this state. (2) That a hearing to contest the validity of the registered determination must be requested within 20 days after service of the notice. (3) That failure to contest the registration will result in confirmation of the child custody determination and preclude further contest of that determination with respect to any matter that could have been asserted.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3446(a)-(b)

citations.quote: (a) A court of this state may grant any relief normally available under the law of this state to enforce a registered child custody determination made by a court of another state. (b) A court of this state shall recognize and enforce, but may not modify, except in accordance with Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 3421), a registered child custody determination of a court of another state.

clauses.title: Simultaneous Proceedings in Two States: Deference and Required Communication
clauses.body: The UCCJEA directly addresses what happens if custody proceedings concerning the same child are filed in two different states at roughly the same time. Family Code section 3426(a) states that, except when temporary emergency jurisdiction applies, a California court may not exercise jurisdiction over a custody proceeding if, at the time the California proceeding commences, a proceeding concerning the same child's custody has already been commenced in another state whose court has jurisdiction substantially in conformity with the UCCJEA -- unless that other proceeding has been terminated, or the other state's court has stayed its own proceeding because it has determined California is the more convenient forum. Section 3426(b), not separately quoted here, makes this a mandatory, not merely discretionary, screening step: before hearing a custody proceeding, a California court must examine the court documents and other information the parties have supplied and, if it determines a qualifying proceeding is already pending in another state, must stay its own proceeding and communicate with that state's court; if the other court does not determine that California is the more appropriate forum, the California court must dismiss its proceeding. This deference-and-communication structure depends on the general authority California courts have, under Family Code section 3410(a), to communicate directly with a court of another state concerning a proceeding arising under the UCCJEA -- a distinct, more general communication provision (in the UCCJEA's general-provisions chapter) than section 3426's specific simultaneous-proceedings rule.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two separately numbered statutory sections from different chapters of the same 1999 enactment -- Family Code section 3426 (Chapter 2, Jurisdiction) and section 3410 (Chapter 1, General Provisions) -- so they are independent in the sense of separately numbered provisions in different chapters, though not in the sense of separately-enacted law. Both were fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and each quote was confirmed programmatically as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of the fetched section text. This clause quotes only section 3426(a) directly and describes, without a separate quoted citation, section 3426(b)'s mandatory stay-and-communicate procedure and section 3426(c)'s separate rule for simultaneous enforcement/modification proceedings (a related but distinct scenario from two competing proceedings both seeking an initial or modified determination, not covered by this clause's quoted text). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's enactment of the UCCJEA structures deference between simultaneous proceedings -- not a claim about which state's courts should hear a specific two-state dispute, and not a claim that every other state's UCCJEA enactment states this rule in identical language. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine which of two simultaneously filed proceedings should be stayed or dismissed -- only the courts involved, communicating as section 3410 and section 3426 direct, can make that determination. No case law is cited in this clause; this topic is governed by clear statutory text, and CourtListener was not queried for it this session.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3426(a)

citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided in Section 3424, a court of this state may not exercise its jurisdiction under this chapter if, at the time of the commencement of the proceeding, a proceeding concerning the custody of the child has been commenced in a court of another state having jurisdiction substantially in conformity with this part, unless the proceeding has been terminated or is stayed by the court of the other state because a court of this state is a more convenient forum under Section 3427.

citations.quote: (a) A court of this state may communicate with a court in another state concerning a proceeding arising under this part.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the two-step notice process the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) requires before an employer takes an adverse employment action based on a consumer report, together with the individualized-assessment and notice process California's Fair Chance Act requires when an employer bases a decision on an applicant's or employee's conviction history. It states facts about what federal and California law require of {{companyName}} in that situation. It is not itself a pre-adverse-action notice, an individualized assessment, a final adverse-action notice, or a decision, and it does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} what to do about any particular applicant, employee, or background-check result.

clauses.title: The Federal Two-Step Process, Step One: The Pre-Adverse-Action Notice
clauses.body: Before {{companyName}} takes an adverse employment action against {{employeeName}} based in whole or in part on a consumer report, federal law requires two things to happen first: {{employeeName}} must receive a copy of the report itself, and a written description of consumer rights under the Fair Credit Reporting Act — both provided before the adverse action is taken, not after. This step is commonly called the pre-adverse-action notice.
clauses.gap: The statute doesn't set a minimum number of days that must pass between providing this pre-adverse-action notice and taking the final adverse action — it requires only that the report copy and rights description be provided before the adverse action is taken, without specifying how long after that a final decision may follow. A narrower exception, not addressed in this document, lets certain transportation-industry applicants who apply by mail, phone, computer, or similar means receive a different, after-the-fact notice instead.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, pre-adverse-action requirement
citations.quote: Except as provided in subparagraph (B), in using a consumer report for employment purposes, before taking any adverse action based in whole or in part on the report, the person intending to take such adverse action shall provide to the consumer to whom the report relates— (i) a copy of the report; and (ii) a description in writing of the rights of the consumer under this subchapter, as prescribed by the Bureau under section 1681g(c)(3)

clauses.title: The Federal Two-Step Process, Step Two: The Final Adverse-Action Notice
clauses.body: Once {{companyName}} actually takes an adverse action against {{employeeName}} based in whole or in part on information in a consumer report, a second, separate notice requirement applies under a different part of the same federal law. {{companyName}} must provide notice of the adverse action itself, the name, address, and telephone number of the consumer reporting agency that furnished the report, a statement that the agency did not make the decision and cannot explain the specific reasons for it, and notice of {{employeeName}}'s right to obtain a free copy of the report and to dispute its accuracy or completeness with that agency.
clauses.gap: This final notice may be given orally, in writing, or electronically — the statute doesn't require any particular format or a stand-alone document the way the earlier disclosure step does. Federal law also specifically forecloses states from adding their own separate requirements on these particular duties (see the relationship clause below), so this description states the federal floor without layering any state-law content on top of it here.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, final adverse-action notice
citations.quote: (a) Duties of users taking adverse actions on basis of information contained in consumer reports If any person takes any adverse action with respect to any consumer that is based in whole or in part on any information contained in a consumer report, the person shall— (1) provide oral, written, or electronic notice of the adverse action to the consumer;

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a)(3)-(4) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, final adverse-action notice content
citations.quote: (3) provide to the consumer orally, in writing, or electronically— (A) the name, address, and telephone number of the consumer reporting agency (including a toll-free telephone number established by the agency if the agency compiles and maintains files on consumers on a nationwide basis) that furnished the report to the person; and (B) a statement that the consumer reporting agency did not make the decision to take the adverse action and is unable to provide the consumer the specific reasons why the adverse action was taken; and (4) provide to the consumer an oral, written, or electronic notice of the consumer’s right— (A) to obtain, under section 1681j of this title, a free copy of a consumer report on the consumer from the consumer reporting agency referred to in paragraph (3), which notice shall include an indication of the 60-day period under that section for obtaining such a copy; and (B) to dispute, under section 1681i of this title, with a consumer reporting agency the accuracy or completeness of any information in a consumer report furnished by the agency.

clauses.title: California's Fair Chance Act: Individualized Assessment and Preliminary Notice
clauses.body: Separately, if {{companyName}} is considering denying {{employeeName}} a position solely or in part because of conviction history, California's Fair Chance Act requires an individualized assessment before any such denial — whether that conviction history has a direct and adverse relationship with the specific duties of the job, considering the nature and gravity of the offense or conduct, the time that has passed since the offense or conduct and completion of sentence, and the nature of the job held or sought. If {{companyName}} reaches a preliminary decision to disqualify {{employeeName}} on that basis, California law requires written notice of that preliminary decision before it becomes final — identifying the disqualifying conviction(s), including a copy of the conviction history report if any, and explaining {{employeeName}}'s right to respond and the deadline for doing so.
clauses.gap: This requirement applies to employers with five or more employees, subject to statutory exceptions (for example, certain positions where a background check is otherwise legally required) that this document doesn't catalog. This provision was previously codified at Labor Code § 432.9; the current text of the California codes, as published by the California Legislative Information website, places it at Government Code § 12952 — the Labor Code section itself is currently blank on that site.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, individualized-assessment requirement
citations.quote: An employer that intends to deny an applicant a position of employment solely or in part because of the applicant’s conviction history shall make an individualized assessment of whether the applicant’s conviction history has a direct and adverse relationship with the specific duties of the job that justify denying the applicant the position. In making the assessment described in this paragraph, the employer shall consider all of the following: (i) The nature and gravity of the offense or conduct. (ii) The time that has passed since the offense or conduct and completion of the sentence. (iii) The nature of the job held or sought. (B) An employer may, but is not required to, commit the results of this individualized assessment to writing. (2) If the employer makes a preliminary decision that the applicant’s conviction history disqualifies the applicant from employment, the employer shall notify the applicant of this preliminary decision in writing. That notification may, but is not required to, justify or explain the employer’s reasoning for making the preliminary decision. The notification shall contain all of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, required content of the preliminary notice
citations.quote: (A) Notice of the disqualifying conviction or convictions that are the basis for the preliminary decision to rescind the offer. (B) A copy of the conviction history report, if any. (C) An explanation of the applicant’s right to respond to the notice of the employer’s preliminary decision before that decision becomes final and the deadline by which to respond. The explanation shall inform the applicant that the response may include submission of evidence challenging the accuracy of the conviction history report that is the basis for rescinding the offer, evidence of rehabilitation or mitigating circumstances, or both.

clauses.title: California's Fair Chance Act: Response Window and Final Notice
clauses.body: After receiving the preliminary notice described above, {{employeeName}} has at least five business days to respond before {{companyName}} may make a final decision. If, within those five business days, {{employeeName}} notifies {{companyName}} in writing of a dispute about the accuracy of the conviction history report and states that specific steps are being taken to obtain supporting evidence, {{employeeName}} gets five additional business days — ten business days in total — to respond. If {{companyName}} then makes a final decision to deny employment solely or in part because of conviction history, California law requires written notice of that final denial, any existing procedure {{companyName}} has for {{employeeName}} to challenge the decision or request reconsideration, and notice of the right to file a complaint with California's Civil Rights Department.
clauses.gap: Neither the preliminary nor the final notice is required to explain the employer's reasoning, though either may. This clause states the business-day figures set by the statute itself; it doesn't address separate notice-timing and mail-service presumptions (for example, how many days after mailing a notice counts as received) that appear in the Fair Chance Act's implementing regulations rather than in the statute, which this document did not independently verify against the regulatory text.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, response window
citations.quote: The applicant shall have at least five business days to respond to the notice provided to the applicant under paragraph (2) before the employer may make a final decision. If, within the five business days, the applicant notifies the employer in writing that the applicant disputes the accuracy of the conviction history report that was the basis for the preliminary decision to rescind the offer and that the applicant is taking specific steps to obtain evidence supporting that assertion, then the applicant shall have five additional business days to respond to the notice.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(c)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, required content of the final notice
citations.quote: If an employer makes a final decision to deny an application solely or in part because of the applicant’s conviction history, the employer shall notify the applicant in writing of all the following: (A) The final denial or disqualification. The employer may, but is not required to, justify or explain the employer’s reasoning for making the final denial or disqualification. (B) Any existing procedure the employer has for the applicant to challenge the decision or request reconsideration. (C) The right to file a complaint with the department.

clauses.title: How the Federal and California Processes Relate
clauses.body: When {{companyName}} uses a third-party consumer reporting agency to run a criminal-history background check on {{employeeName}}, the federal process and the California process described above are separate legal requirements that can both apply to the same background check. Federal law's general rule is that it does not override state law on the collection, distribution, or use of consumer information, except to the extent a state law actually conflicts with a specific federal provision. California's Fair Chance Act separately states that its own remedies are in addition to, and not a substitute for, whatever other rights and remedies an applicant has under other law.
clauses.gap: Federal law does carve out one specific, narrower exception to that general rule: no state may impose its own separate requirement or prohibition specifically regulating "the duties of a person who takes any adverse action" under Section 1681m(a)-(b) of the federal law — the final-notice step described above. Whether, or to what extent, that narrower federal carve-out affects any part of California's Fair Chance Act process is a question this document does not resolve; answering it would require a preemption analysis, which is a legal conclusion, not a fact this document states. This document did not locate, and could not check for, a published court decision analyzing that specific interaction — CourtListener returned a rate-limit error when queried for this document, so no case law is cited on this point.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1681t(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, general state-law savings clause
citations.quote: (a) In general Except as provided in subsections (b) and (c), this subchapter does not annul, alter, affect, or exempt any person subject to the provisions of this subchapter from complying with the laws of any State with respect to the collection, distribution, or use of any information on consumers, or for the prevention or mitigation of identity theft, except to the extent that those laws are inconsistent with any provision of this subchapter, and then only to the extent of the inconsistency.

citations.case: 15 U.S.C. § 1681t(b)(1)(C) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, specific preemption of state adverse-action-duty requirements
citations.quote: (C) subsections (a) and (b) of section 1681m of this title, relating to the duties of a person who takes any adverse action with respect to a consumer;

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12952(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Chance Act, cumulative-remedies clause
citations.quote: (e) The remedies under this section shall be in addition to and not in derogation of all other rights and remedies that an applicant may have under any other law, including any local ordinance.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Overpayment and Fraud Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's statutory framework for unemployment insurance benefit overpayments — what happens after the Employment Development Department (EDD) determines that {{employeeName}} was paid more in unemployment compensation benefits than the law allowed. {{employeeName}} received an overpayment determination from the EDD dated {{determinationDate}}, EDD case number {{eddCaseNumber}}, concerning benefits previously paid on a claim related to {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}}, in the amount of {{overpaymentAmount}}. This document states facts about the statutory distinction between a non-fraud and a fraudulent overpayment, the conditions under which repayment of a non-fraud overpayment may be waived, the specific penalties a fraud finding carries, the notice and appeal rights that attach to an overpayment determination, and the methods California law gives the EDD to recover an overpayment. It does not itself constitute an appeal filed with the EDD, an administrative law judge, or the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board (CUIAB); it does not determine that {{employeeName}}'s overpayment is or is not due to fraud; and it does not determine that any waiver applies to {{employeeName}}'s specific overpayment.

clauses.title: The Statutory Distinction Between a Non-Fraud and a Fraudulent Overpayment
clauses.body: California's Unemployment Insurance Code treats an overpayment of benefits as a single general category — any person overpaid any amount of benefits is liable for the amount overpaid unless a statutory exception applies — but a separate statute carves fraud out as a distinct, more narrowly defined category within that whole. A fraudulent overpayment exists only where the director finds that the individual was overpaid because he or she willfully, for the purpose of obtaining unemployment compensation benefits, either made a false statement or representation with actual knowledge of its falsity, or withheld a material fact. Everything else — an overpayment that was not due to fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure on the recipient's part — falls instead into the non-fraud category that the general liability statute expressly distinguishes from fraud, misrepresentation, and willful nondisclosure. The consequences that follow this classification are not symmetric: a non-fraud overpayment can, as described in the clause below, be waived entirely under specific conditions, while a finding of fraud triggers a mandatory monetary penalty, a distinct disqualification period, and, potentially, criminal exposure, described in the clauses that follow.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375, for the general liability rule and its non-fraud language, and § 1375.1, for the specific fraud-finding standard), used as real evidence that California's overpayment scheme is built around a binary fraud/non-fraud classification with different statutory consequences on each side — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular overpayment, and not a determination that any specific claimant's own overpayment is, or is not, due to fraud. These are two independent statutory sections, not subsections of a single section. The quoted language from § 1375 is the identical opening-sentence-and-subdivision-(a) text this corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Appeal — Information Sheet document already cites, in its own uiappeal_continued_benefits clause, for the related but distinct point that an overpaid claimant is liable for the overpayment subject to a waiver; that overlap is disclosed here rather than presented as new independent corroboration of § 1375(a) itself. The specific waiver conditions that attach to a non-fraud finding, and the specific penalty, disqualification, and recovery consequences that attach to a fraud finding, are new research not previously cited anywhere in this corpus, and are addressed in the clauses that follow. This document does not itself find, or advise any specific claimant regarding, whether any specific overpayment is due to fraud.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: Any person who is overpaid any amount of benefits under this part is liable for the amount overpaid unless any of the following is applicable: (a) (1) The overpayment was not due to fraud, misrepresentation or willful nondisclosure on the part of the recipient, and (2) the overpayment was received without fault on the part of the recipient, and its recovery would be against equity and good conscience.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375.1 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: If the director finds that an individual has been overpaid unemployment compensation benefits because he or she willfully, for the purpose of obtaining unemployment compensation benefits, either made a false statement or representation, with actual knowledge of the falsity thereof, or withheld a material fact

clauses.title: Waiver of Repayment for a Non-Fraud Overpayment
clauses.body: The same statute that makes an overpaid claimant generally liable for the amount overpaid sets out three separate, independent grounds on which that liability can be waived. The first, described in the clause above, applies where the overpayment was not due to fraud, misrepresentation, or willful nondisclosure, was received without fault on the recipient's part, and recovering it would be against equity and good conscience — a three-part, conjunctive standard, so all three elements must be met, not merely one. The statute provides two further, independent grounds beyond that equity-and-good-conscience standard. The second applies where the person who received the overpayment cooperates with the department in an investigation that results in the assessment of a penalty against someone else — specifically, a penalty against an employer under a statute addressing employer-induced fraudulent claims, or a prosecution or other penalty action under the general false-statement penalty statute. The third applies where the department itself determines that waiving all or part of the liability is in the interest of justice because the overpayment was a direct result of inducement, solicitation, or coercion by the employer, rather than by the claimant's own conduct.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375, subdivisions (b) and (c)), used as real evidence that California's non-fraud waiver standard is not limited to the equity-and-good-conscience test alone, but includes two additional, independently sufficient waiver grounds — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular overpayment, and not a determination that any specific claimant's own overpayment satisfies any of these three grounds. These two quoted passages, subdivisions (b) and (c), come from the same statutory section as each other and as the equity-and-good-conscience ground quoted in the clause above; they are being treated as one source together with that ground, not as independent corroborating sources on separate points, though each subdivision states a substantively distinct, independently sufficient basis for waiver. Subdivision (b)'s cross-references — to a penalty statute addressing employer-induced fraudulent claims, and to a general false-statement penalty-action provision — were checked directly against the statutory text quoted here rather than assumed; this document does not independently verify or restate those cross-referenced provisions' own substance beyond confirming their citation numbers appear correctly in the quoted text. This document does not itself apply for a waiver, and does not determine that any specific overpayment does, or does not, meet any of these three grounds.

clauses.title: The Penalty, Disqualification, and Criminal Exposure a Fraud Finding Carries
clauses.body: A fraud finding under the statute described above carries consequences beyond the underlying repayment obligation itself. First, a mandatory monetary penalty: once the director finds a fraudulent overpayment, the statute requires the director to assess against the individual an amount equal to 30 percent of the overpayment amount — a fixed, non-discretionary percentage added on top of the overpaid benefits themselves, not an alternative to repaying them. Second, a period of disqualification from future benefits: a related statute independently disqualifies an individual who willfully made a false statement or representation, or withheld a material fact, in order to obtain unemployment compensation benefits, and a further statute sets the length of that disqualification at two weeks (running from the week the disqualification determination is served) plus up to 13 further weeks, within a three-year window, for an individual who was not actually paid benefits as a result of the false statement. Third, potential criminal exposure: this corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Benefits — Claimant Information Sheet document already establishes, and this document does not re-verify independently here, that a willful false statement or material nondisclosure made to obtain benefits is separately punishable under the same code's general false-statement penalty chapter by up to one year in county jail, imprisonment in state prison, a fine of up to $20,000, or both.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1375.1, for the 30-percent monetary penalty; § 1257(a), for the disqualification standard; and § 1260(c), for the length of disqualification where no benefits were actually paid), used as real evidence of the specific, sourced consequences California attaches to a fraud finding beyond the underlying repayment obligation — not a claim about which state's law governs a given overpayment, and not a statement that any specific claimant has been found, or should be found, to have committed fraud. The § 1375.1 quote here is a different passage — the section's penalty-assessment clause — from the definitional passage already quoted in the distinction clause above; the two quotes are non-overlapping substrings of the same section, not independent sources. Section 1257(a) and Section 1260 are different sections from each other and from § 1375.1, not subsections of a single section. This document's drafter confirmed directly that § 1260 also sets a longer, five-week-plus-up-to-10-further-week disqualification, within the same three-year window, for an individual who was actually paid benefits as a result of the false statement (§ 1260(d)); that longer alternative is not separately quoted here to avoid duplicating an already-lengthy citation, but its existence is disclosed so this clause is not read as stating the only possible disqualification length. Section 1260(c) also states that its disqualification 'shall not apply to an individual convicted under Section 2101' — meaning this administrative disqualification and a criminal conviction are not simply cumulative in every case, a nuance this document discloses rather than resolves. The criminal-penalty statement here relies on, and does not independently re-verify beyond, this corpus's own prior verification of Unemployment Insurance Code §§ 2101(a) and 2122 in the existing uiclaimant_false_statement_penalty clause; that reliance is disclosed rather than presented as new independent verification of those two sections. This document does not itself impose any penalty, disqualification, or criminal charge, and does not determine that any of these consequences applies to any specific claimant's overpayment.
