clauses.title: Background on the Contested Move-Away Standard and Joint-Custody Cases
clauses.body: Beyond the statutory right described elsewhere in this document, California's move-away rules are substantially shaped by case law that this document does not independently verify against the primary court opinions and therefore does not cite as legal authority. Family-law commentary and secondary sources widely report that where one parent has sole or primary physical custody, the parent opposing a proposed move bears the burden of showing the move would cause detriment to {{childName}}, at which point a court weighs the child's best interest using a multi-factor inquiry -- commonly summarized as including the child's need for stability and continuity, the distance of the move, the child's age, the child's relationship with each parent, the parents' ability to communicate and cooperate, the child's own wishes if the child is mature enough, the reasons given for the move, and the extent to which custody is currently shared -- and that this framework, and the presumption that precedes it, is reported to apply differently, or not to apply in the same form, where the parents instead share joint physical custody rather than one parent holding sole or primary physical custody. Because this document has not independently confirmed this description against the text of the underlying court opinions, {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} should not rely on the summary above as a citation-quality statement of the law, and should instead consult the actual case law -- or an attorney -- for {{childName}}'s specific situation, particularly to confirm which presumption, if any, applies to their own custody arrangement.

clauses.title: Where Final Wages Must Be Delivered: The Statutory Place-of-Payment Rule
clauses.body: Separately from when final wages are due, California law also addresses where a discharged or quitting employee's final wages must be delivered. The statute distinguishes the two situations: an employee who is discharged must be paid at the place of discharge, while an employee who quits must be paid at the office or agency of the employer in the county where the employee has been performing labor. This letter treats {{terminationDate}} as the date {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}} ended, based on a separation described here as: {{separationType}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the place-of-payment rule for a discharged versus a quitting employee — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular separation, and not a claim about where this particular final paycheck was, or should have been, delivered. The statute also states that '[a]ll payments shall be made in the manner provided by law,' a cross-reference to the article's other payment-method provisions (including the mailing and direct-deposit rules addressed in separate clauses) rather than an independent, self-contained rule in its own right. This is a single statutory section (§ 208); no additional independent source was found for this specific point.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 208
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 208
citations.quote: Every employee who is discharged shall be paid at the place of discharge, and every employee who quits shall be paid at the office or agency of the employer in the county where the employee has been performing labor. All payments shall be made in the manner provided by law.

clauses.title: The Mailing Option for Final Wages and Its Effect on the Payment Date
clauses.body: California law gives some, but not all, separating employees a statutory right to have final wages mailed rather than delivered in person. An employee who quits without giving the employer at least 72 hours' notice is entitled to receive payment by mail if the employee requests it and designates a mailing address, and the date of mailing is treated as the date of payment for purposes of the 72-hour payment deadline that applies to that kind of quit. A comparable statutory right to demand mailed payment exists for a discharged employee only in one narrow category: an employer laying off a group of employees due to the end of seasonal employment in curing, canning, or drying perishable fruit, fish, or vegetables must make payment by mail to any employee in that group who requests it and designates a mailing address.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of when a mailed-payment option is expressly available and how the mailing date interacts with a payment deadline — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular separation, and not a claim that a mailed-payment right exists for every kind of discharge or quit. Outside the two situations quoted below (a no-notice quit, and a seasonal perishable-food-industry group layoff), this research did not locate express statutory text giving a general right to demand mailed final-wage payment for an ordinary discharge or for a quit preceded by 72 hours' notice; that gap is disclosed here rather than assumed away, since silence in a statute is not the same as a prohibition and is not treated as one by this clause. The two citations below come from two separate statutory sections (§§ 201(a) and 202(a)) and are independent sources of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 202(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 202, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other law, an employee who quits without providing a 72-hour notice shall be entitled to receive payment by mail if he or she so requests and designates a mailing address. The date of the mailing shall constitute the date of payment for purposes of the requirement to provide payment within 72 hours of the notice of quitting.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 201(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 201, subd. (a)
citations.quote: provided, however, that the reasonable time shall not exceed 72 hours, and further provided that payment shall be made by mail to any employee who so requests and designates a mailing address therefor.

clauses.title: Direct Deposit and Final Wages
clauses.body: California's general wage-payment-method statute permits an employer to pay wages by direct deposit into an account of the employee's choice, with the employee's voluntary authorization, and separately addresses using direct deposit for a final paycheck: where an employee is discharged or quits, the employer may pay the wages earned and unpaid at that time by direct deposit, provided the employer complies with the same statutory provisions that otherwise govern payment of wages upon termination or quitting. The statute does not, in its own text, spell out additional mechanics — such as a shortened bank-processing window or a requirement that deposited funds be immediately available to the employee — beyond that cross-reference back to the termination and quitting payment rules.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's direct-deposit statute actually says about final wages — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular payment, and not a claim that California imposes a special, self-contained direct-deposit rule of the kind some other states have adopted for final paychecks (for example, requiring funds to be available on the regular payday regardless of the bank's normal processing time). No such additional, freestanding rule was located in this section or elsewhere in this research session; that absence is disclosed here rather than papered over with a citation that does not actually say it. What the statute does establish is narrower and procedural: direct deposit of final wages is conditioned on the employer otherwise complying with the applicable termination-or-quitting payment provisions, which is what determines the deadline by which those wages are due regardless of the payment method chosen. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 213(d)); no additional independent source was found for this specific point.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 213(d)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 213, subd. (d)
citations.quote: If an employer discharges an employee or the employee quits, the employer may pay the wages earned and unpaid at the time the employee is discharged or quits by making a deposit authorized pursuant to this subdivision, provided that the employer complies with the provisions of this article relating to the payment of wages upon termination or quitting of employment.

clauses.title: The Itemized Wage Statement Requirement Still Applies to a Final Paycheck
clauses.body: California's itemized-wage-statement requirement is not excused because a particular paycheck happens to be an employee's last one: the statute requires an employer to furnish an itemized statement semimonthly or at the time of each payment of wages, without carving out a final payment. This document set already contains a dedicated, separately verified clause covering that requirement in full — including its specific nine-item list, its penalty structure, and its own disclosed limits — and does not re-derive that content here; this clause exists only to confirm that a final paycheck does not fall outside it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that the itemized-wage-statement requirement applies to a final wage payment on the same terms as any other — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular payment, and not a claim about the statement's full content, which the corpus's dedicated wage-statement clauses address separately rather than duplicating here. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 226(a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific point.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 226(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 226, subd. (a)
citations.quote: An employer, semimonthly or at the time of each payment of wages, shall furnish to their employee, either as a detachable part of the check, draft, or voucher paying the employee’s wages, or separately if wages are paid by personal check or cash, an accurate itemized statement in writing showing

clauses.title: Purpose of This Job Applicant Record Retention Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's statutory record-retention requirements for job application materials, resumes, and related hiring records -- for applicants {{companyName}} hires and applicants {{companyName}} does not hire alike -- together with the shorter federal baseline those requirements exceed. It reflects {{companyName}}'s record-retention policy for this category of records as of {{effectiveDate}}. It states facts about what California and federal law require; it does not itself determine that any specific record must be retained or destroyed on any particular date, and it does not tell {{companyName}} what to do about any specific record, applicant, employee, subpoena, litigation hold, or pending charge, complaint, or lawsuit -- circumstances like those can extend the time before which a record covered by this document may be destroyed, beyond the general periods described here.

clauses.title: California's Four-Year Retention Requirement for Applicant and Employment Records
clauses.body: Government Code § 12946(a), part of the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), makes it an unlawful practice for an employer, labor organization, or employment agency subject to FEHA -- including {{companyName}} -- to fail to maintain and preserve applications, personnel, membership, or employment referral records and files for a minimum of four years after the records and files are initially created or received, and separately makes it unlawful for an employer to fail to retain personnel files of applicants or terminated employees for a minimum of four years after the date of the employment action taken. That reaches both a hired applicant's personnel file and a rejected applicant's application materials. This four-year duration took effect January 1, 2022. Before that date the statute required only two years; the current four-year period was enacted by 2021 legislation, Stats. 2021, ch. 278 (SB 807), whose Legislative Counsel's Digest describes the change as increasing "the above-described records and files retention requirement from 2 years to 4 years."
clauses.gap: This is California's own statute, used as evidence of California's own requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. The Legislative Counsel's Digest is part of the same 2021 enactment as the statute itself (the bill that produced the current text of § 12946), so it is disclosed here as part of the same source rather than as a fully independent second authority; it is quoted because it is the clearest primary-source statement of the prior (2-year) duration and the reason the period changed, a fact the current statutory text alone does not state. The statute's four-year clock runs from two different starting points depending on the record type -- from creation or receipt of the record for the general category, or from the date of the employment action for personnel files of applicants or terminated employees -- and this clause does not resolve which starting point applies to any specific record.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12946(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful practice for employers, labor organizations, and employment agencies subject to the provisions of this part to fail to maintain and preserve any and all applications, personnel, membership, or employment referral records and files for a minimum period of four years after the records and files are initially created or received, or for employers to fail to retain personnel files of applicants or terminated employees for a minimum period of four years after the date of the employment action taken.

clauses.title: What Records Are Covered: Applications, Personnel Files, and Employment Referral Records
clauses.body: The same statutory text that sets the four-year duration also defines what it reaches. Government Code § 12946(a) names the covered categories by name: applications, personnel records, membership records, and employment referral records and files -- for any employer, labor organization, or employment agency subject to FEHA -- and separately names personnel files of applicants or terminated employees. For a job applicant specifically, this covers the application itself, resume and any submitted supporting materials, and records generated during {{companyName}}'s hiring process concerning that applicant, whether {{companyName}} ultimately hired the applicant or not.
clauses.gap: This is California's own statute, used as evidence of California's own requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. This clause quotes the same subdivision, § 12946(a), already quoted in this document's duration clause -- it is the same source used a second time to address a distinct question (scope, not duration), not a second independent authority for the point. The statute does not itself define terms like "personnel records" or "employment referral records" beyond naming them; whether a specific document -- for example, an interviewer's informal notes, or a message exchanged with a staffing agency -- falls within one of these named categories is a characterization this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12946(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful practice for employers, labor organizations, and employment agencies subject to the provisions of this part to fail to maintain and preserve any and all applications, personnel, membership, or employment referral records and files for a minimum period of four years after the records and files are initially created or received, or for employers to fail to retain personnel files of applicants or terminated employees for a minimum period of four years after the date of the employment action taken.

clauses.title: A Filed Complaint Extends the Retention Period Until Final Disposition
clauses.body: The four-year period is a floor, not a fixed endpoint. Government Code § 12946(b) provides that once an employer, labor organization, or employment agency has notice that a verified complaint has been filed against it under FEHA, it must maintain and preserve all records and files -- not only those relating to the specific complainant -- until the later of two dates: the first date after the time for filing a civil action has expired, or the first date after the complaint has been fully and finally disposed of and all administrative proceedings, civil actions, appeals, or related proceedings have terminated. For {{companyName}}, notice of a verified complaint under FEHA extends the applicable retention obligation past the routine four-year period for as long as that complaint, and any resulting proceedings, remain unresolved.
clauses.gap: This is California's own statute, used as evidence of California's own requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, § 12946(b); no additional independent source was sought for this point. The subdivision's text extends the duty to "any and all records and files" once notice of a verified complaint is received, without limiting that duty to records connected to the specific complaint -- this clause states that scope as written, without resolving how it interacts in practice with unrelated records the employer may routinely destroy on other schedules. The statute also does not address what happens if a verified complaint is filed after records that predate it, and that would otherwise have fallen due for destruction, have already been lawfully destroyed under the routine four-year rule -- that scenario is not addressed in this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12946(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: Upon notice that a verified complaint against it has been filed under this part, any such employer, labor organization, or employment agency shall maintain and preserve any and all records and files until the later of the following: (1) The first date after the period of time for filing a civil action has expired. (2) The first date after the complaint has been fully and finally disposed of and all administrative proceedings, civil actions, appeals, or related proceedings have terminated.

clauses.title: The Federal Baseline Is Shorter: One Year Under EEOC Regulations, Two for Most Federal Contractors
clauses.body: Federal law imposes its own, separate recordkeeping duty on employers covered by Title VII, and it is shorter than California's. An EEOC regulation, 29 C.F.R. § 1602.14, requires that any personnel or employment record made or kept by a covered employer -- including application forms submitted by applicants and other records having to do with hiring -- be preserved for one year from the date the record is made or the personnel action occurs, whichever is later; for an involuntary termination, the terminated employee's personnel records must be kept for one year from the date of termination. That same federal regulation contains its own complaint-filing extension, parallel to California's: where a charge of discrimination has been filed, or an action brought by the EEOC or the Attorney General, against the employer under Title VII, the ADA, or GINA, the employer must preserve all personnel records relevant to the charge or action until its final disposition. A separate federal regulation applies a longer period to certain federal contractors: 41 C.F.R. § 60-1.12(a) requires a covered contractor to preserve personnel or employment records -- expressly including applications and resumes -- for not less than two years, or one year if the contractor has fewer than 150 employees or does not hold a government contract of at least $150,000.
clauses.gap: These are two independent federal regulations issued by two different agencies for two different purposes -- 29 C.F.R. § 1602.14 (EEOC, applying to employers generally covered by Title VII, the ADA, and GINA) and 41 C.F.R. § 60-1.12(a) (OFCCP, applying specifically to covered federal contractors and subcontractors) -- not two subsections of the same regulation. This clause does not address every other record-retention rule that could separately apply to a given employer's hiring records -- for example, the federal Form I-9 retention rule, which this project's separate documents already cover -- nor does it determine whether a given employer meets the size or contract-value thresholds that would make the federal contractor regulation, rather than the general EEOC regulation, apply to it.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1602.14 (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.quote: Any personnel or employment record made or kept by an employer (including but not necessarily limited to requests for reasonable accommodation, application forms submitted by applicants and other records having to do with hiring, promotion, demotion, transfer, lay-off or termination, rates of pay or other terms of compensation, and selection for training or apprenticeship) shall be preserved by the employer for a period of one year from the date of the making of the record or the personnel action involved, whichever occurs later.

citations.case: 41 C.F.R. § 60-1.12(a) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.quote: Any personnel or employment record made or kept by the contractor shall be preserved by the contractor for a period of not less than two years from the date of the making of the record or the personnel action involved, whichever occurs later. However, if the contractor has fewer than 150 employees or does not have a Government contract of at least $150,000, the minimum record retention period shall be one year from the date of the making of the record or the personnel action involved, whichever occurs later.

clauses.title: California's Longer Period Controls for a California Employer -- a Floor, Not a Ceiling
clauses.body: Where California's four-year retention period and the shorter one-year (or, for some federal contractors, two-year) federal period both apply to the same employer, the two periods are not alternatives that let an employer choose the shorter one -- they function as a floor and ceiling, with the longer period actually controlling. Title VII contains its own savings clause on this point: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-7 provides that nothing in Title VII "shall be deemed to exempt or relieve any person from any liability, duty, penalty, or punishment provided by any present or future law of any State," except a state law that purports to require or permit conduct that Title VII itself makes an unlawful employment practice. California's longer retention requirement does not require or permit anything Title VII forbids -- it requires more retention, not less -- so satisfying only the shorter federal period does not relieve {{companyName}} of the separate, longer duty California law imposes.
clauses.gap: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-7 is a general non-preemption (savings) provision addressing Title VII's relationship to state law broadly; it is not a court decision or agency guidance applying that provision specifically to the two record-retention regulations described elsewhere in this document, and no such case law or agency guidance was independently verified this session. This clause states the general floor/ceiling principle those texts support; it does not address whether some other, more specific federal statute -- outside Title VII -- could expressly preempt a state recordkeeping duty in a way this general savings clause would not reach, a question this document does not attempt to resolve.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-7 (Cornell LII text)
citations.quote: Nothing in this subchapter shall be deemed to exempt or relieve any person from any liability, duty, penalty, or punishment provided by any present or future law of any State or political subdivision of a State, other than any such law which purports to require or permit the doing of any act which would be an unlawful employment practice under this subchapter.

clauses.title: Enforcement: Gov. Code § 12946 Authorizes Judicial Relief, Not a Stated Recordkeeping Penalty
clauses.body: Government Code § 12946 itself does not state a specific dollar penalty for an employer's failure to retain the records it covers. What the statute provides instead, in subdivisions (c) and (d), is rulemaking and enforcement authority: the (now Civil Rights) council is directed to adopt suitable rules, regulations, and standards to carry out the purposes of the section, and, where necessary, the department may, under its separate powers, seek temporary or preliminary judicial relief to enforce the section.
clauses.gap: This is California's own statute, used as evidence of California's own enforcement mechanism -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. This clause is drawn from a single statutory section's remaining subdivisions, § 12946(c) and (d); no additional independent source was sought for this point. Unlike some other California recordkeeping statutes -- for example, Labor Code § 1198.5, covered in this project's separate personnel-records-request document, which states a specific $750 penalty for noncompliance -- § 12946 does not itself state a comparable penalty for a retention failure. Disclosed honestly: this document does not assert that a missing record produces any particular evidentiary consequence, such as an adverse inference, in a later discrimination proceeding -- no case law or regulation establishing such a rule specific to this statute was fetched and confirmed against a primary source this session, so no such claim is made here.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Policy
The Statutory Fair Use Defense and Its Illustrative List of Purposes
clauses.body: Federal copyright law creates a fair use defense in a single statutory provision. Under 17 U.S.C. § 107, "[n]otwithstanding the provisions of sections 106 and 106A, the fair use of a copyrighted work, including such use by reproduction in copies or phonorecords or by any other means specified by that section, for purposes such as criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching (including multiple copies for classroom use), scholarship, or research, is not an infringement of copyright." The specific purposes named in that sentence -- criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, and research -- are introduced with the words "such as," and the Copyright Act's own definitions section states that "[t]he terms 'including' and 'such as' are illustrative and not limitative." 17 U.S.C. § 101. A use is accordingly not disqualified from fair use merely because it serves some purpose other than the six purposes § 107 happens to name, and a use is not automatically fair use merely because it does match one of them; the named purposes are examples of the kind of use fair use can cover, not a closed list. The work identified in this document, {{copyrightedWorkDescription}}, and the use described as {{useDescription}}, are addressed by the remaining clauses in this document, which describe the four-factor analysis § 107 requires in every case.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of § 107's own introductory language and of § 101's definition of "including" and "such as" as illustrative rather than exhaustive terms -- not a claim that the use described in this document, or any other use, actually falls within fair use, which turns on the four-factor analysis addressed in the following clauses and is not resolved by this clause alone. This clause cites two different sections of the same statute (§ 107 and § 101); they are treated here as two provisions of one integrated statutory scheme, not as fully independent corroborating sources, though each was independently fetched and confirmed. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that the use described in this document, or any other use, is or is not a fair use, and does not resolve any dispute between the person completing this document and any copyright owner.

clauses.title: The Four Statutory Factors
clauses.body: The fair use statute does not leave the analysis to open-ended judicial discretion; it names four factors that a court must consider. Under 17 U.S.C. § 107, "[i]n determining whether the use made of a work in any particular case is a fair use the factors to be considered shall include -- (1) the purpose and character of the use, including whether such use is of a commercial nature or is for nonprofit educational purposes; (2) the nature of the copyrighted work; (3) the amount and substantiality of the portion used in relation to the copyrighted work as a whole; and (4) the effect of the use upon the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work." The statute also adds a rule specific to unpublished works: "[t]he fact that a work is unpublished shall not itself bar a finding of fair use if such finding is made upon consideration of all the above factors." As with the illustrative list of purposes in this provision's opening sentence, the phrase "shall include" before the four factors is not read as a closed list -- 17 U.S.C. § 101 states that "the terms 'including' and 'such as' are illustrative and not limitative" -- so a court may weigh considerations beyond the four named factors, though the four are the ones the statute specifically requires to be considered in every case.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the exact text of § 107's four factors and its unpublished-work rule -- not a claim about how any of the four factors applies to the specific use described in this document, which is a fact-intensive question this clause does not resolve. This document is informational only: it does not itself weigh the four factors as applied to any specific work or use, and does not determine that the use described in this document is or is not a fair use.

clauses.title: "Transformative Use" Is a Judicial Gloss on Factor One, Not Statutory Text
clauses.body: The word "transformative" does not appear anywhere in 17 U.S.C. § 107. It is a term courts use when applying the statute's first factor -- the purpose and character of the use -- and its leading source is the Supreme Court's 1994 decision in Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569 (1994), a case about whether a commercial rap-music parody of a rock ballad could be a fair use. Explaining what the first factor asks, the Court wrote that a court must consider whether the new work "adds something new, with a further purpose or different character, altering the first with new expression, meaning, or message; it asks, in other words, whether and to what extent the new work is 'transformative.'" The Court also made clear that this judge-made concept is not a mandatory checkbox: "[a]lthough such transformative use is not absolutely necessary for a finding of fair use," the Court explained, a more transformative use makes the other statutory factors, including commercial character, matter less to the outcome. A use can accordingly be evaluated for how transformative it is under the first statutory factor, but "transformative use" itself is case law's label for part of that factor's analysis, not separate statutory language, and satisfying or failing it does not by itself decide fair use.

clauses.title: No Fixed Percentage, Word Count, or Bright-Line Rule
clauses.body: Neither the fair use statute nor the case law applying it sets a specific percentage, word count, or other numeric threshold that automatically makes a use fair or unfair. The statute's third factor asks about "the amount and substantiality of the portion used in relation to the copyrighted work as a whole," 17 U.S.C. § 107(3), without specifying any number, proportion, or length. Interpreting that factor and the fair use inquiry generally, the Supreme Court in Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569 (1994), wrote that "[t]he task is not to be simplified with bright-line rules, for the statute, like the doctrine it recognizes, calls for case-by-case analysis." On the amount-used factor specifically, the Court explained that "the extent of permissible copying varies with the purpose and character of the use" -- meaning the same amount of copying can be reasonable for one purpose and excessive for another, so no fixed quantity is inherently safe or inherently disqualifying.

Acuff-Rose Music, Inc. was verified two ways: by directly fetching the Supreme Court's slip opinion as archived by Cornell's Legal Information Institute (law.cornell.edu/supct/html/92-1292.ZO.html), and, independently, through the CourtListener case-law database (opinion text for cluster 112936), which was initially rate-limited (HTTP 429) during this research session but became reachable again. The two sources' wording differs in one respect: Cornell's slip-opinion archive renders the phrases as "bright line rules" and "case by case analysis" (unhyphenated), while CourtListener's opinion text -- which carries official U.S. Reports pagination -- renders them hyphenated ("bright-line rules," "case-by-case analysis"). Cornell's own page notes the slip opinion "is subject to formal revision before publication in the preliminary print of the United States Reports," so the hyphenated, paginated CourtListener text is used as the quoted wording below, and both readings were confirmed consistent in substance. This clause states that no fixed numeric rule exists; it does not supply, and no such rule exists to supply, any specific percentage, word count, or other quantity that would make the use described in this document fair or unfair. clauses.title: Fair Use as an Affirmative Defense, and Who Carries the Burden
clauses.body: Section 107 itself does not say who has the burden of proving fair use -- it states that a qualifying use "is not an infringement of copyright" and lists the factors a court considers, without allocating a burden of proof to either side. The Supreme Court has described where that burden falls when fair use is litigated. In Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569 (1994), addressing a party's failure to offer evidence on the fourth statutory factor (market effect), the Court wrote: "Since fair use is an affirmative defense, its proponent would have difficulty carrying the burden of demonstrating fair use without favorable evidence about relevant markets." That statement treats fair use as an affirmative defense whose proponent -- the party relying on it, not the copyright owner -- bears the burden of demonstrating it, at least as to the market-effect factor at issue in that passage. Consistent with that description, fair use is examined by weighing all four statutory factors together in light of the facts of a particular use, rather than by treating any single factor, or any use that happens to resemble one of § 107's listed purposes, as automatically establishing or defeating the defense.

Acuff-Rose Music, Inc. was verified two ways: by directly fetching the Supreme Court's slip opinion as archived by Cornell's Legal Information Institute (law.cornell.edu/supct/html/92-1292.ZO.html), and, independently, through the CourtListener case-law database (opinion text for cluster 112936), which was initially rate-limited (HTTP 429, "125/day" quota) during this research session but became reachable again and returned matching text, including the official U.S. Reports pagination (page 590) cited below. clauses.title: The Elements of a Prescriptive Easement and Its Borrowed Five-Year Period
clauses.body: California has no statute that separately names and defines a "prescriptive easement" the way Code of Civil Procedure §§ 322 and 324 name and define adverse possession under color of title or under a bare claim of right (addressed in this corpus's separate Adverse Possession — Information Sheet document). Instead, California's courts have developed the doctrine as case law. California's Supreme Court has stated its elements directly: "The elements necessary to establish a prescriptive easement are well settled. The party claiming such an easement must show use of the property which has been open, notorious, continuous and adverse for an uninterrupted period of five years." Five years is also the period Code of Civil Procedure § 321 states for adverse possession generally, within the same statutory chapter governing the time for commencing an action to recover real property. A prescriptive easement claimed over the Servient Property at {{servientPropertyAddress}} for the benefit of Claimant's Property at {{dominantPropertyAddress}} differs from adverse possession in what it can produce even when proven: adverse possession, if established, can transfer fee title to the possessor; a prescriptive easement, even if established, transfers only a right to use another's land for a stated purpose — the kind of right this corpus's Easement Agreement document addresses when it is created by grant rather than by this doctrine. Establishing a prescriptive easement does not make Claimant the owner of the Servient Property.
clauses.gap: This clause's elements quotation is drawn from a single case, Warsaw v. Chicago Metallic Ceilings, Inc. (1984) 35 Cal.3d 564, 570. That opinion in turn attributes the elements test to an earlier Court of Appeal decision, Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. Crockett Land & Cattle Co. (1924) 70 Cal.App. 283, 290; this research session verified Warsaw's own text directly but did not separately pull and verify the 1924 opinion it cites, so no citation to that earlier case appears here. This clause states that the five-year figure in the prescriptive-easement elements test is the same figure Code Civ. Proc. § 321 fixes for adverse possession; that is a comparison of the numeral each verified source states, not a claim that Warsaw's own opinion, in the text checked this session, expressly cites § 321 as the source of that number — secondary sources commonly describe the prescriptive-easement period as borrowed from the adverse possession statute by analogy, and this clause does not independently confirm that specific textual lineage through a case that states it. This clause does not restate the separate statutory elements that apply only to adverse possession and not to a prescriptive easement — the property-tax-payment requirement and the requirement that possession be exclusive — addressed, to the extent this document addresses them and only if independently verified, in a separate clause. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific claimant's use in fact satisfies these elements on the facts of a particular dispute. This is case law and a statute of one state, used as real evidence of California's prescriptive-easement doctrine — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property; other states' doctrines and periods may differ.

citations.quote: In every action for the recovery of real property, or the possession thereof, the person establishing a legal title to the property is presumed to have been possessed thereof within the time required by law, and the occupation of the property by any other person is deemed to have been under and in subordination to the legal title, unless it appear that the property has been held and possessed adversely to such legal title, for five years before the commencement of the action.

clauses.title: How a Prescriptive Easement or Easement by Necessity Can Be Extinguished
clauses.body: California's Civil Code, in the same chapter that defines what counts as an easement (addressed in this corpus's Easement Agreement document), separately states how a servitude — the Code's general term covering an easement however it was created — is extinguished. The statute lists four ways: by the vesting of the right to the servitude and the right to the servient tenement in the same person; by the destruction of the servient tenement; by the performance of any act upon either tenement, by the owner of the servitude or with the owner's assent, that is incompatible with the servitude's nature or exercise; or, where the servitude was acquired by enjoyment (as a prescriptive easement is), by disuse of it by the owner of the servitude for the period prescribed for acquiring title by enjoyment. For a prescriptive easement, that last rule means a period of disuse matching the same five-year period that created the easement can extinguish it. An act by Claimant that is incompatible with continuing to use the easement claimed over the Servient Property at {{servientPropertyAddress}} — the third statutory ground — can extinguish it regardless of how long any period of disuse has run. An easement by necessity has an additional, doctrine-specific termination rule tied to the necessity itself, stated in California case law: "although a strict necessity at the time of conveyance can create an easement by way of necessity, it does not preserve it for all time" — "an easement by necessity will exist only so long as the necessity exists." An easement by necessity claimed over the Servient Property at {{servientPropertyAddress}} for the benefit of Claimant's Property at {{dominantPropertyAddress}} therefore ends when the necessity that created it ends — for example, if Claimant's Property later gains its own legally adequate access to a public road — regardless of whether any of § 811's four grounds has also occurred.
clauses.gap: This clause rests on two sources. Cal. Civ. Code § 811 is a single statutory section, within Civil Code Chapter 3 (Servitudes [801-813]) — the same chapter as §§ 801, 802, and 806, addressed in this corpus's Easement Agreement document. § 811 states its four extinguishment rules for "a servitude" generally, without separately addressing how the servitude was created (by express grant, by prescription, or by necessity); this clause applies § 811 to a prescriptive easement or an easement by necessity on the same basis this corpus's existing easement_statutory_servitudes_basis clause applies §§ 801-802 to any right of way regardless of how it arose — because it is the same substantive right, a servitude, whatever its origin — rather than because § 811 itself names either doctrine; this research session located no case applying § 811's numbered grounds specifically to a prescriptive easement or an easement by necessity, so that application is this clause's own reading of the statute's general terms, not an independently verified judicial holding construing § 811 in that specific context. The necessity-specific termination rule is quoted from Kellogg v. Garcia (2002) 102 Cal.App.4th 796, 810, which in turn attributes the same principle to Lichty v. Sickels (1983) 149 Cal.App.3d 696, 699, Daywalt v. Walker (1963) 217 Cal.App.2d 669, 676-677, and Moores v. Walsh (1995) 38 Cal.App.4th 1046, 1051; this research session verified Kellogg's own text directly but did not independently fetch and verify those three earlier decisions, so none is separately cited here. Kellogg also states that the party arguing that a necessity has ended bears the burden of proving that a new, adequate right of way in fact became available — a burden-of-proof point this clause does not separately restate. This is one state's statute and case law, used as real evidence of California's law on extinguishing a servitude — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property.

clauses.title: No Exclusivity and No Tax-Payment Requirement: How a Prescriptive Easement Differs From Adverse Possession
clauses.body: California case law directly distinguishes a prescriptive easement from adverse possession on two points commonly, and correctly, described as required for adverse possession but not for a prescriptive easement: exclusivity of use, and payment of property taxes. A California Court of Appeal has explained the two doctrines side by side: "Adverse possession is a means to acquire ownership of land. In adverse possession, the claimant must prove open and notorious use, hostile to the true owner, for a period of five years, and he must also show that he has paid taxes on the parcel of land. By comparison, an easement is merely a right to use the land of another." California's adverse possession statute independently confirms the tax-payment half of that comparison — it requires a claimant to have "timely paid all state, county, or municipal taxes" levied on the land for the full statutory period before adverse possession is established under any section of the Code of Civil Procedure, a requirement addressed in this corpus's Adverse Possession — Information Sheet document. The case law above states a narrow exception on the easement side of that same comparison: "if taxes are separately assessed against an easement, the claimant must pay these" — a circumstance the same court described as unusual. On exclusivity, the same court held it was error to award a claimant an easement that, as a practical matter, completely excluded the record owner from the area, reasoning that "[a]n easement, after all, is merely the right to use the land of another for a specific purpose" and "is not an ownership interest," so that treating a claimant's use as exclusive "perverts the classical distinction in real property law between ownership and use." This document's use-history declaration accordingly describes Claimant's use of the Servient Property at {{servientPropertyAddress}} as a use, not as an exclusion of {{recordOwnerName}} or any other person from the same area, and does not state that Claimant has paid property taxes assessed against the Servient Property unless the easement area has been separately assessed for tax purposes.
clauses.gap: This clause's two case-law quotations are both drawn from a single case, Silacci v. Abramson (1996) 45 Cal.App.4th 558, 562, 564 — a Sixth Appellate District decision, not a California Supreme Court decision. Silacci itself favorably discusses two other Court of Appeal decisions reaching consistent results on similar facts (Raab v. Casper (1975) 51 Cal.App.3d 866 and, on the exclusivity point specifically, distinguishes rather than rejects Otay Water Dist. v. Beckwith (1991) 1 Cal.App.4th 1041, which upheld an exclusive prescriptive easement on different facts involving a public water utility's reservoir); this research session verified Silacci's own text describing those two decisions but did not independently fetch and verify either decision's own opinion text, so neither is cited here as an independent source. Silacci's exclusivity holding is fact-specific — it reverses a finding of an "exclusive" prescriptive easement on the facts of an enclosed residential backyard use and remands to let the claimant instead pursue adverse possession — and, as Silacci's own discussion of Otay Water Dist. v. Beckwith shows, this clause does not state that a prescriptive easement can never be found exclusive under any circumstance. This clause's statutory citation, Code Civ. Proc. § 325(b), states the adverse-possession-side tax rule directly; it does not itself state that a prescriptive easement lacks an equivalent requirement, which rests on Silacci's own reasoning rather than on separate statutory text, because — as a companion clause of this document explains — no statute separately defines a prescriptive easement's elements at all. This clause does not evaluate whether Claimant's own use in fact meets, or fails to meet, these elements on the facts of a particular dispute. This is case law and a statute of one state, used as real evidence of California's law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property.

clauses.title: Easement by Necessity: Common Ownership at Severance and Strict Necessity
clauses.body: California has no Civil Code provision that separately creates or names an "easement by necessity" the way Civil Code § 1104 creates a different implied easement out of a transferred property's own prior, obvious, and permanent use (addressed in this corpus's Easement Agreement document). The necessity doctrine is instead stated by California's courts as case law, with two elements: "An easement by way of necessity arises by operation of law when it is established that (1) there is a strict necessity for the right-of-way, as when the claimant's property is landlocked and (2) the dominant and servient tenements were under the same ownership at the time of the conveyance giving rise to the necessity." California case law also states what "strict necessity" requires, as distinct from mere convenience: "The right of way from necessity must be in fact what the term naturally imports and cannot exist except in cases of strict necessity. It will not exist when a man can get to his property over his own land. That the way over his own land is too steep or too narrow or that other and like difficulties exist, does not alter the case, and it is only when there is no way through his own land that a grantee can claim a right over that of his grantor. It must also appear that the grantee has no other way." For an easement by necessity claimed over the Servient Property at {{servientPropertyAddress}} for the benefit of Claimant's Property at {{dominantPropertyAddress}}, both elements must be shown: that {{priorCommonOwnerName}} owned both properties as a single parcel until the severance on {{severanceDate}} that created them as separate parcels, and that Claimant's Property was, at that time, and remains, landlocked in the strict sense this case law describes — not merely less convenient to reach than Claimant might prefer.
clauses.gap: This clause's two citations are both drawn from a single case, Kellogg v. Garcia (2002) 102 Cal.App.4th 796 — a Third Appellate District decision. Both quoted passages are themselves Kellogg's own block quotations of earlier authority: the two-element test quotes Moores v. Walsh (1995) 38 Cal.App.4th 1046, 1049, and the strict-necessity passage quotes Bully Hill Copper Mining & Smelting Co. v. Bruson (1906) 4 Cal.App. 180, 183. This research session verified Kellogg's own text directly, including that it presents both passages as quotations of those earlier decisions, but did not independently fetch and verify either earlier opinion's own text, so neither is cited here as an independent source. This is a case-law doctrine: this research session located no Civil Code or Code of Civil Procedure section that separately names or defines an "easement by necessity" as such. Kellogg's own facts hold that common ownership by the federal government can satisfy the common-ownership element just as common ownership by a private party can; this clause does not restate that specific extension, since it may not apply to Claimant's own severance history. This clause does not evaluate whether Claimant's Property in fact meets either element on the facts of a particular severance history. This is case law of one state, used as real evidence of California's easement-by-necessity doctrine — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of real property; other states' necessity-easement doctrines, and whether they are codified, may differ.

clauses.title: Policy Declaration and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: {{companyName}} maintains this Personnel and Payroll Record Retention Duration Information Sheet to describe, as a matter of California and federal law, how long {{companyName}} is required to keep the personnel records and payroll records it maintains relating to {{employeeName}} and other employees, and where those records must be kept. This information sheet is about the employer's underlying duty to retain records for a set period — it does not describe, and should not be confused with, the separate statutory right of a current or former employee to inspect or receive a copy of those records, which is addressed in this project's separate Employee's Request to Inspect Personnel and Payroll Records document. This is a statement of general legal requirements; it does not state what {{companyName}} should do about any particular record, and it is not a substitute for {{companyName}}'s own document-retention schedule or legal advice.

clauses.title: Personnel Records: At Least Three Years After Termination of Employment, Under § 1198.5(c)(1)
clauses.body: Separately from the inspection right described elsewhere in this project's documents, Labor Code § 1198.5(c) imposes an affirmative duty on {{companyName}} to keep personnel records for a minimum period, regardless of whether any employee ever asks to inspect them. With regard to all employees, § 1198.5(c)(1) requires {{companyName}} to maintain a copy of each employee's personnel records for a period of not less than three years after termination of employment. The statute's trigger for this duration is termination of employment, not the date a given record was created — so a personnel record created early in a long employment relationship must still be kept for at least three years measured from when that employment relationship ends, not three years from when the record itself was made.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's personnel-records retention duty — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee, and not a claim about how long any particular document should actually be kept in a specific case (a longer period may be prudent, or required by some other law not addressed here). This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, § 1198.5(c)(1); no additional independent source was sought for this specific duration figure. This clause does not restate § 1198.5(c)(2)-(3), the same subdivision's separate rules on where and how a current or former employee's records must be made available once a request is made — those rules govern the inspection process, addressed in this project's separate personnel-records-request document, not the retention duration itself.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1198.5(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: With regard to all employees, maintain a copy of each employee’s personnel records for a period of not less than three years after termination of employment.

clauses.title: Payroll Records: At Least Three Years on File, at the Workplace or a Central California Location, Under § 226(a)
clauses.body: Labor Code § 226(a) requires {{companyName}} to furnish an itemized wage statement to {{employeeName}} and other employees with each payment of wages, and it separately requires {{companyName}} to keep records of the deductions made. The deductions made from payment of wages must be recorded in ink or other indelible form, properly dated, showing the month, day, and year, and a copy of the wage statement together with the record of the deductions must be kept on file by {{companyName}} for at least three years, at the place of employment or at a central location within the State of California. Unlike the personnel-records duration described elsewhere in this document, § 226(a) does not state termination of employment as the event that starts this three-year period running; by its terms, the requirement is that the copy and deduction record be "kept on file" for at least three years, without conditioning that duration on when (or whether) the employment relationship ends.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's payroll-records retention duty — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, § 226(a); no additional independent source was sought for this specific duration and location figure. This same statutory language is also the subject of this project's separate Wage Statement Itemization Policy document, which addresses the nine required content items of an itemized wage statement in full; this clause addresses only the retention-duration and location requirement within that same subdivision, not the content requirements themselves. This clause does not resolve, for a specific record created mid-employment, exactly which date within the employment relationship the three-year period is measured from (for example, the date of the pay period, the date the statement was furnished, or some other date) — the statutory text quoted here states only that the copy and deduction record must be kept on file for the stated minimum duration, without further specifying the precise starting date for that calculation.

citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: a copy of the statement and the record of the deductions shall be kept on file by the employer for at least three years at the place of employment or at a central location within the State of California.

clauses.title: Two Different Three-Year Periods, Not One: Comparing the § 1198.5(c)(1) and § 226(a) Retention Durations
clauses.body: It is easy to assume that because both the personnel-records retention duty and the payroll-records retention duty are commonly described as "three years," they describe the same three-year period. They do not. Labor Code § 1198.5(c)(1) requires {{companyName}} to maintain a copy of each employee's personnel records for a period of not less than three years after termination of employment — a duration expressly triggered by the end of the employment relationship. Labor Code § 226(a), by contrast, requires that a copy of the wage statement and the record of deductions be kept on file by the employer for at least three years at the place of employment or at a central location within the State of California — language that states a minimum period the records must remain on file, without tying the start of that period to termination of employment at all. Because the two statutes name different triggers, a payroll record and a personnel record created on the same day, for the same still-employed worker, are not necessarily required to be destroyed or retained on the same schedule: the payroll-records duty under § 226(a) is, by its terms, already running while the employee remains employed, while the personnel-records duty under § 1198.5(c)(1) does not even begin to run until that employment ends. The two statutes also differ in a second respect: § 226(a) specifies where the payroll records must be kept (the place of employment or a central location within California), while the text of § 1198.5(c)(1) quoted here states no comparable location requirement for personnel records.
clauses.gap: This is one state's two statutes, used as real evidence that California's personnel-records and payroll-records retention durations are textually distinct rather than a single unified rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee. The two citations below are to two different California statutes (Labor Code §§ 1198.5(c)(1) and 226(a)), not two subsections of the same statute, so no same-section duplication is being treated as two independent sources; the same two subdivisions are also each cited and quoted independently, for their own separate points, in the two clauses of this document that precede this one. This clause does not address whether some other law not examined here (for example, a wage order, an industry-specific regulation, or a different Labor Code section) might impose a longer retention period for either category of record in a specific case; it compares only the text of these two statutes.

clauses.title: What the Statutes Actually Say About Failing to Retain, as Opposed to Failing to Permit Inspection
clauses.body: The two statutes described in this document treat the consequence of a retention failure differently, and neither one states a penalty that is worded as applying specifically and only to a failure to retain. Labor Code § 1198.5(k) states a $750 penalty, recoverable by the current or former employee or the Labor Commissioner, where an employer "fails to permit a current or former employee, or their representative, to inspect or copy personnel records within the times specified in this section" — a penalty keyed to a failure to permit timely inspection or copying once a request is made, not to a failure to retain records for the three-year period standing alone. If {{companyName}} did not retain a given personnel record for the required period and, as a result, could not produce it in response to a timely request, that would likely trigger the § 1198.5(k) inspection-failure penalty in practice — but the statutory text of § 1198.5(k) itself is written around the failure to permit inspection, not around the retention duty in § 1198.5(c)(1) directly. Labor Code § 226 is structured differently: the retention-duration sentence itself is written into the same subdivision, § 226(a), that also states the wage-statement content requirements, and § 226(e)(1) provides that an employee suffering injury as a result of a knowing and intentional failure by an employer to comply with subdivision (a) is entitled to recover the greater of all actual damages or fifty dollars ($50) for the initial pay period in which a violation occurs and one hundred dollars ($100) per employee for each violation in a subsequent pay period, not to exceed an aggregate penalty of four thousand dollars ($4,000), and is entitled to an award of costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Because the retention sentence sits inside subdivision (a) itself, a failure to comply with that retention sentence falls within the literal scope of what § 226(e)(1) calls "a failure by an employer to comply with subdivision (a)" — though § 226(e)(1) also requires that the failure be knowing and intentional and that the employee suffer injury as a result, elements this document does not resolve for any specific case.
clauses.gap: This is two of California's statutes, used as real evidence of what each one's text actually says (and does not say) about a retention failure specifically — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee, and not a claim that a court has actually applied § 226(e)(1)'s penalty to a pure retention failure (as opposed to a wage-statement content defect) in a reported decision; no case law on that specific application was located or relied on here, only the statutory text itself. The § 1198.5(k) citation below is the same subdivision already quoted, independently, in this project's separate personnel-records-request document; it is not a new source, and it is quoted here for the different, narrower point that its penalty is worded around inspection failure rather than retention failure as such. The § 226(e)(1) citation is a different subdivision of § 226 than the § 226(a) retention text quoted elsewhere in this document, so the two are not the same textual passage, though they are subsections of the same statutory section and are not being counted as independent sources from one another. This clause does not identify any additional, free-standing statutory penalty — beyond the two described here — that applies specifically to a bare failure to retain personnel or payroll records where no inspection request was ever made and no wage-statement defect occurred; if such a penalty exists elsewhere in California law, it was not located in this session's research and is not asserted here.

clauses.title: A Third, Federally Distinct Duration for Form I-9: the Later of Three Years After Hire or One Year After Termination
clauses.body: Form I-9 sits outside the two California retention durations described in this document, because it is governed by a separate federal statute rather than by Labor Code §§ 1198.5 or 226. Under 8 U.S.C. § 1324a(b)(3), after completion of Form I-9, {{companyName}} must retain a paper, microfiche, microfilm, or electronic version of the form and make it available for inspection by specified federal officials, during a period beginning on the date of hiring and, in the case of the hiring of an individual, ending three years after the date of such hiring, or one year after the date the individual's employment is terminated, whichever is later. This is a third, distinct duration formula: unlike the flat three-years-after-termination period for personnel records under § 1198.5(c)(1), and unlike the flat at-least-three-years-on-file period for payroll records under § 226(a), the I-9 duration under § 1324a(b)(3) is the later of two alternative measurements, one running from hire and one running from termination.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of a third retention-duration formula for a specific document (Form I-9) that is distinct from the two California retention durations otherwise addressed in this information sheet — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation. This project's separate I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification Information Sheet already addresses this same statutory retention rule in more depth (including the officials named in the statute who may inspect the retained form); this clause states it briefly for comparison purposes only, and was independently re-verified against the same primary source (Cornell Legal Information Institute's text of 8 U.S.C. § 1324a) in this session rather than copied without a fresh check. This clause does not address whether some other federal or state law imposes a different retention period for any other specific hiring-related document; it addresses only the Form I-9 duration under § 1324a(b)(3).

clauses.title: Acknowledgment and Signature
The Core Kin Care Right and Its Six-Month Calculation Mechanic
clauses.body: California's "kin care" statute, Labor Code § 233(a), requires that any employer who provides sick leave for employees must permit an employee to use, in any calendar year, the employee's accrued and available sick leave entitlement in an amount not less than the sick leave that would be accrued during six months at the employee's then-current rate of entitlement, for the reasons specified in Labor Code § 246.5(a) (which include, among other things, caring for a family member's existing health condition or providing a family member preventive care). The statute itself puts the choice with the employee: the designation of sick leave taken for these reasons is made at the employee's sole discretion, not the employer's. The statute also expressly states what it does not do: it does not extend the maximum period of leave available under the California Family Rights Act (Government Code § 12945.2) or the federal Family and Medical Leave Act, regardless of whether the employee receives sick leave compensation during that separate leave.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own kin care law and its own stated calculation mechanic — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a calculation of any specific amount of sick leave available to any specific reader. This clause quotes subdivision (a) of a single statutory section, Labor Code § 233, as one continuous quotation, not as separately numbered citations; it is one statutory source for the core right described here, not independently corroborated by a second source within this clause. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. As the California Supreme Court held in McCarther v. Pacific Telesis Group — addressed in a separate clause of this document rather than repeated here — this six-month calculation mechanic does not apply to every form of employer-provided compensated time off for illness; it applies only where the employer's sick leave program is an accrual-based, measurable, banked benefit, not an uncapped sickness-absence policy. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself calculate, grant, or deny any specific amount of kin care leave for any reader, and does not determine that any particular employer's own policy is or is not compliant with Labor Code § 233.

citations.quote: Any employer who provides sick leave for employees shall permit an employee to use in any calendar year the employee’s accrued and available sick leave entitlement, in an amount not less than the sick leave that would be accrued during six months at the employee’s then current rate of entitlement, for the reasons specified in subdivision (a) of Section 246.5. The designation of sick leave taken for these reasons shall be made at the sole discretion of the employee. This section does not extend the maximum period of leave to which an employee is entitled under Section 12945.2 of the Government Code or under the federal Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 (29 U.S.C. Sec. 2601 et seq.), regardless of whether the employee receives sick leave compensation during that leave.

clauses.title: Kin Care's Cross-Reference to the Paid Sick Leave Family Member Definition
clauses.body: Labor Code § 233 does not define "family member" on its own terms. Instead, § 233(b)(2) states that, for purposes of the kin care statute, "family member" has the same meaning given to that term by Labor Code § 245.5 — the definitional section of the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act. Section 245.5(c) defines "family member" to include a child (a biological, adopted, or foster child, a stepchild, a legal ward, or a child to whom the employee stands in loco parentis, regardless of the child's age or dependency status); a biological, adoptive, or foster parent, stepparent, or legal guardian of the employee or of the employee's spouse or registered domestic partner, or a person who stood in loco parentis when the employee was a minor child; a spouse; a registered domestic partner; a grandparent; a grandchild; a sibling; and a "designated person" identified by the employee at the time the employee requests paid sick days, whom an employer may limit to one per 12-month period.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of how California's kin care law itself defines "family member" — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about who any specific reader's own family member is. The two citations below are not independent corroborating sources of the same fact: § 233(b)(2) is the cross-reference itself, and § 245.5(c) is the definition that cross-reference points to; together they are treated as one chain of authority for a single definition, not as two independently corroborating sources. Both statutory texts quoted below were fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific individual is or is not a particular employee's "family member" under this definition, and does not grant, calculate, or deny any specific amount of kin care leave.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, kin care's cross-reference to the paid sick leave family member definition
citations.quote: “Family member” has the same meaning as defined in Section 245.5.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 245.5(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "family member"
citations.quote: “Family member” means any of the following: (1) A child, which for purposes of this article means a biological, adopted, or foster child, stepchild, legal ward, or a child to whom the employee stands in loco parentis. This definition of a child is applicable regardless of age or dependency status. (2) A biological, adoptive, or foster parent, stepparent, or legal guardian of an employee or the employee’s spouse or registered domestic partner, or a person who stood in loco parentis when the employee was a minor child. (3) A spouse. (4) A registered domestic partner. (5) A grandparent. (6) A grandchild. (7) A sibling. (8) A designated person, which, for purposes of this article, means a person identified by the employee at the time the employee requests paid sick days. An employer may limit an employee to one designated person per 12-month period for paid sick days.

clauses.title: How Kin Care Relates to the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act
clauses.body: Labor Code § 233 is not a stand-alone right to additional sick leave, and its reasons for use are not a separate list from the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act's own list. Section 233(b)(3)(A) defines "sick leave," for kin care purposes, as accrued increments of compensated leave provided by an employer for use during an absence "for any of the reasons specified in subdivision (a) of Section 246.5" — the same reasons list the general paid sick leave statute itself uses, which includes diagnosis, care, or treatment of an existing health condition of, or preventive care for, an employee or an employee's family member. Section 233 therefore functions as a usage-volume floor layered onto whatever sick leave benefit an employer already provides (commonly, today, a Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act policy): it guarantees that at least the amount that would accrue in six months of that same benefit remains available in a calendar year for the § 246.5(a) reasons, rather than creating an independent, differently defined right. The California Supreme Court has confirmed that this floor does not reach every form of employer-provided paid time off for illness. In McCarther v. Pacific Telesis Group, the court held that "Labor Code section 233 does not apply to paid sick leave policies that provide for an uncapped number of compensated days off," reasoning that the statute's six-month calculation requirement means "the reach of the statute is limited to employers that provide a measurable, banked amount of sick leave."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes and one state supreme court's construction of them, used as real evidence of California's own kin care law and its relationship to its general paid-sick-leave statute — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any specific employer's own sick leave program is or is not an "accrual-based" or "uncapped" one. The two statutory citations below are to genuinely separate Labor Code sections — § 233(b)(3)(A) and § 246.5(a)(1) — not subdivisions of the same section, and are treated as two source statutes describing one shared reasons list, not as independent corroboration of separate facts. The case citation is to a third, genuinely independent source (a California Supreme Court opinion construing § 233), not a restatement of the statutory text. Both statutory texts quoted below were fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times; the case quotations were confirmed this session as exact, literal matches against the opinion's text on CourtListener. McCarther construed a 2010-era version of § 233's operative sentence, which at that time listed specific family relationships directly in the statute rather than cross-referencing § 246.5(a); this document relies on McCarther only for its reasoning about the "accrued," "measurable," and "banked" character of covered sick leave programs — a holding the 2020 amendment did not disturb — not for the since-superseded relationship language the opinion happens to quote. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer's sick leave program is or is not subject to Labor Code § 233, and does not grant, calculate, or deny any specific amount of kin care leave.

clauses.title: The Prohibition on Counting Kin Care Leave Against a No-Fault Attendance Policy
clauses.body: Labor Code § 233 itself does not say that an employer may impose the same notice or documentation conditions on kin care use that apply to an employee's own sick leave use; the current text of § 233 is silent on notice and documentation procedure, leaving that to whatever procedure already governs the underlying sick leave benefit (commonly, the oral-or-written-request procedure of Labor Code § 246.5(a) itself). What Labor Code § 234 does address is a specific kind of employer condition: it provides that an employer absence-control policy that counts sick leave taken under § 233 as an absence that may lead to or result in discipline, discharge, demotion, or suspension is a per se violation of § 233, and that an employee working under such a policy is entitled to appropriate legal and equitable relief under § 233. The California Supreme Court has read § 233 and § 234 together as working in tandem: in McCarther v. Pacific Telesis Group, the court explained that where § 233 requires an employer to permit an employee to use a portion of its compensated leave for kin care, "section 234, by its terms, would prohibit defendants from using its attendance management policy to limit the amount of kin care that an employee could claim."
clauses.gap: This is a correction to, not a confirmation of, the assumption that Labor Code § 233 itself authorizes an employer to impose the same notice or documentation conditions on kin care leave as on the employee's own sick leave use; this research found no such conditions in § 233's current text, and discloses that gap here rather than inventing one. What this clause verifies instead is a related, but distinct, statutory limitation on employer conditions: the no-fault absence-control-policy prohibition of a separate Labor Code section, § 234. This is one state's statutes and one state supreme court's construction of them, used as real evidence of California's own law — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any specific employer's own attendance policy does or does not violate § 234. The § 234 citation is to a Labor Code section genuinely independent of § 233 (added by a later, separate enactment, Stats. 2002, Ch. 1107), not a subdivision of the section addressed in this document's other clauses; the case citation is to the same McCarther v. Pacific Telesis Group opinion cited in this document's relationship clause, not an independent case source. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times; the case quotation was confirmed this session as an exact, literal match against the opinion's text on CourtListener. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer's attendance or discipline policy is or is not a per se violation of Labor Code § 234, and does not grant, calculate, or deny any specific amount of kin care leave.

An employee working under this policy is entitled to appropriate legal and equitable relief pursuant to Section 233.
