clauses.title: Adoption of Election Operating Rules
clauses.body: California law requires an association to adopt its own written election operating rules, through a specified rulemaking procedure, and requires those rules to address a defined list of subjects. Civil Code § 5105(a) provides: "An association shall adopt operating rules in accordance with the procedures prescribed by Article 5 (commencing with Section 4340) of Chapter 3, that do all of the following:" Among the items that follow, § 5105(a)(3) requires the rules to "[s]pecify the qualifications for candidates for the board and any other elected position, subject to subdivision (b), and procedures for the nomination of candidates, consistent with the governing documents," adding that "[a] nomination or election procedure shall not be deemed reasonable if it disallows any member from nominating themself for election to the board." Section 5105(a)(5) requires the rules to "[s]pecify a method of selecting one or three independent third parties as inspector or inspectors of elections," by board appointment, member election, "[or] any other method for selecting the inspector or inspectors." The rules must also, among other things, ensure equal access to association media and to common-area meeting space for candidates and members campaigning on either side of an issue (§ 5105(a)(1)-(2)); specify voting power, proxy rules, and the voting period (§ 5105(a)(4)); and require retention of a candidate registration list and a voter list as association election materials, with a process for members to verify and correct their own listed information (§ 5105(a)(6)-(7)). Section 5105(h)(4) further requires the rules to obligate the inspector of elections to "deliver, or cause to be delivered, at least 30 days before an election, to each member both of the following documents: (A) The ballot or ballots. (B) A copy of the election operating rules," and provides that rules adopted under this section "shall not be amended less than 90 days prior to an election." These requirements concern any election operating rules {{hoaName}} adopts; this clause does not itself adopt, amend, or interpret any specific association's rules.
clauses.gap: All quoted material in this clause comes from subsections and paragraphs of a single statutory section, Civil Code § 5105; it is one source, not independent corroborating sources. The full list of required subjects in § 5105(a) runs to seven enumerated paragraphs, and § 5105 as a whole runs considerably longer than reproduced here, including a separate framework in subdivisions (b) through (g) governing when and how an association may disqualify a nominee (for example, for not being current on regular or special assessments, subject to statutory exceptions) and a separate optional framework in subdivision (i) for electronic secret ballots; a generic assumption that the statute's list is limited to "candidate qualifications, campaigning, ballot procedures" understates its breadth (it also covers proxies, quorum-related voting-period rules, the method of selecting the inspector of elections, and record retention) without being wrong about those three examples themselves. This clause also does not quote or verify the separate rulemaking procedure incorporated by reference, Article 5 (commencing with Section 4340) of Chapter 3, or the disqualification framework in § 5105(b)-(g); those were not independently fetched and verified for this document. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's HOA board-election framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific association; other states impose different or no comparable requirement that an association adopt election operating rules.

clauses.title: The Independent Third Party Who Conducts the Election
clauses.body: California law requires that an association's election be conducted by an independent third party, and defines both who qualifies and who is disqualified from serving in that role. Civil Code § 5110(a) provides: "The association shall select an independent third party or parties as an inspector of elections. The number of inspectors of elections shall be one or three." Section 5110(b) explains who may — and may not — serve: "an independent third party includes, but is not limited to, a volunteer poll worker with the county registrar of voters, a licensee of the California Board of Accountancy, or a notary public. An independent third party may be a member, but may not be a director or a candidate for director or be related to a director or to a candidate for director. An independent third party may not be a person, business entity, or subdivision of a business entity who is currently employed or under contract to the association for any compensable services other than serving as an inspector of elections." Section 5110(c) lists the inspector's duties, including determining the number of memberships entitled to vote, determining the validity of proxies, receiving ballots, hearing and determining challenges to the right to vote, counting and tabulating votes, determining when polls close, and determining the tabulated results. Section 5110(d) requires the inspector or inspectors to "perform all duties impartially, in good faith, to the best of the inspector or inspectors of elections' ability, as expeditiously as is practical, and in a manner that protects the interest of all members of the association," and provides that where there are three inspectors, "the decision or act of a majority shall be effective in all respects as the decision or act of all." This description concerns the inspector-of-elections requirement generally; it does not identify, evaluate, or disqualify any specific person as an inspector of elections for {{hoaName}}.
clauses.gap: The quoted material in this clause comes from subsections (a), (b), and (d) of a single statutory section, Civil Code § 5110; it is one source, not independent corroborating sources. This clause summarizes rather than quotes the inspector's list of duties in § 5110(c) and the electronic-secret-ballot compliance duties cross-referenced in § 5110(c)(4); those paragraphs were fetched as part of the same section but are not separately block-quoted here. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's HOA board-election framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific association; other states impose different or no comparable independent-third-party requirement.

clauses.title: Notice Timing and the Double-Envelope Secret-Ballot Procedure
clauses.body: California law sets specific notice-timing requirements for a director election and a specific double-envelope mechanism for preserving ballot secrecy. Civil Code § 5115(a) provides, for elections of directors and recall elections: "An association shall provide general notice of the procedure and deadline for submitting a nomination at least 30 days before any deadline for submitting a nomination." Section 5115(b) separately requires the association to give general notice of the ballot-return date, time, and address, of the meeting at which a quorum will be determined and ballots counted, and of the list of candidates' names, "at least 30 days before the ballots are distributed." Section 5115(c) then requires that "[b]allots and two preaddressed envelopes with instructions on how to return ballots shall be mailed by first-class mail or delivered by the association to every member not less than 30 days prior to the deadline for voting," and describes the resulting double-envelope mechanism: "The ballot itself is not signed by the voter, but is inserted into an envelope that is sealed. This envelope is inserted into a second envelope that is sealed. In the upper left-hand corner of the second envelope, the voter shall sign the voter's name, indicate the voter's name, and indicate the address or separate interest identifier that entitles the voter to vote." That second, signed envelope is then addressed to the inspector or inspectors of elections for tabulation. Section 5115(d) addresses a separate topic, quorum: if the governing documents require a quorum for a director election and it is not met, the association may adjourn to a reconvened meeting at least 20 days later, at which a 20 percent quorum (voting in person, by proxy, or by secret ballot) applies unless the governing documents set a lower figure. These notice-timing and ballot-secrecy requirements apply generally to a director election conducted by {{hoaName}}; this clause does not itself calculate any specific deadline or verify that any particular notice or mailing by {{hoaName}} met these requirements.
clauses.gap: The quoted material in this clause comes from subsections (a), (b), (c), and (d) of a single statutory section, Civil Code § 5115; it is one source, not independent corroborating sources. The recurring '30 days' figure across subsections (a), (b), and (c) is the same statutory period restated for three distinct notice-and-mailing steps (nomination-deadline notice, pre-distribution ballot-logistics notice, and the ballot-and-envelope mailing itself), not three independently-confirmed different figures; a generic assumption of a single undifferentiated notice period would obscure that these are three separate 30-day deadlines tied to three different triggering events, and the reconvened-meeting quorum period in subdivision (d) is a distinct 20-day figure for a different purpose. As fetched, this section (Civil Code § 5115) was last amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67 (AB 1170), effective January 1, 2026 — the current calendar year as of this document's verification date — so a description of this article's ballot-notice mechanics naming an older, superseded section number or an outdated timing figure would not reflect the currently operative text. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's HOA board-election framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific association; other states impose different or no comparable double-envelope secret-ballot procedure.

clauses.title: How Ballots Are Counted, Tabulated, and Reported
clauses.body: California law requires that ballots be counted in public, restricts who may handle ballots before the count, and sets a deadline for reporting results. Civil Code § 5120(a) provides: "All votes shall be counted and tabulated by the inspector or inspectors of elections, or the designee of the inspector or inspectors of elections, in public at a properly noticed open meeting of the board or members. Any candidate or other member of the association may witness the counting and tabulation of the votes. A person, including a member of the association or an employee of the management company, shall not open or otherwise review any ballot before the time and place at which the ballots are counted and tabulated." The same subdivision allows the inspector to "verify the member's information and signature on the outer envelope prior to the meeting at which ballots are tabulated," and provides that "[o]nce a secret ballot is received by the inspector or inspectors of elections, it shall be irrevocable." Section 5120(b) then sets a reporting deadline: "The tabulated results of the election shall be promptly reported to the board and shall be recorded in the minutes of the next meeting of the board and shall be available for review by members of the association. Within 15 days of the election, the board shall give general notice pursuant to Section 4045 of the tabulated results of the election." Section 5120(c) extends the same before-the-count restriction to electronic ballots: a person "shall not open or otherwise review any tally sheet of votes cast by electronic secret ballots before the time and place at which the ballots are counted and tabulated." These counting, reporting, and confidentiality requirements apply generally to an election conducted by {{hoaName}}; this clause does not itself count, tabulate, or report the results of any specific election.

This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's HOA board-election framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific association; other states impose different or no comparable public-counting or 15-day results-notice requirement.

clauses.title: Background Information — Trust Decanting
clauses.body: I, {{trusteeName}}, am serving, or have been asked to serve, as trustee of {{trustName}}, executed {{originalTrustDate}} (referred to in this information sheet as the "first trust"). This information sheet describes California's statutory trust decanting framework, the Uniform Trust Decanting Act (Probate Code § 19501 et seq.), as background in connection with a potential distribution of principal from {{trustName}} to a proposed second trust, {{secondTrustName}}. This information sheet is not itself an exercise of the decanting power described in this document, is not the signed writing that Probate Code § 19510 requires to exercise that power, and is not the notice that Probate Code § 19507 requires before that power is exercised. Preparing, reviewing, or signing this information sheet does not distribute any property out of {{trustName}}, does not modify {{trustName}}'s terms, and does not satisfy {{trusteeName}}'s notice obligation, if any, in connection with {{trustName}} or any other trust. Only an actual signed writing that satisfies § 19510, preceded (or accompanied, as § 19507 allows in limited circumstances) by notice that satisfies § 19507 or a signed waiver of that notice period, does that.

clauses.title: What 'Decanting' Means Under California's Uniform Trust Decanting Act
clauses.body: California's Uniform Trust Decanting Act, enacted in 2018 and codified at Probate Code §§ 19501-19530, defines the 'decanting power' as the power of an authorized fiduciary to distribute property of a 'first trust' to one or more 'second trusts,' or to modify the terms of the first trust. A 'first trust' is a trust over which an authorized fiduciary may exercise the decanting power -- potentially {{trustName}} -- and a 'second trust' is either the first trust itself after modification under the Act, or a separate trust to which a distribution of property from the first trust is or may be made, such as a proposed {{secondTrustName}}. Decanting under this Act is therefore a mechanism a trustee (or certain other fiduciaries) can use, not one a settlor uses directly; it operates by the fiduciary distributing or redirecting trust principal, or reshaping the first trust's own terms, rather than by the settlor amending or restating the instrument.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's decanting framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust; other states that have adopted the Uniform Trust Decanting Act, or that use their own decanting statutes, can differ from California's version in scope and detail, and this document addresses California's enactment only. This clause cites three different subdivisions of the same statutory section, Probate Code § 19502 (subdivisions (j), (l), and (v)); no single subdivision is quoted more than once in this clause, and all three subdivisions come from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times. This document does not determine whether any specific trust is, in fact, a 'first trust' over which any specific person may exercise the decanting power, or whether a specific proposed new trust would qualify as a 'second trust' under the Act -- addressed further, as to threshold eligibility, in a separate clause of this document.

citations.quote: “Decanting power” or “the decanting power” means the power of an authorized fiduciary under this part to distribute property of a first trust to one or more second trusts or to modify the terms of the first trust.

clauses.title: Who May Exercise the Decanting Power, and What Kind of Trust the Act Applies To
clauses.body: The Act's threshold requirement is built into its definition of who counts as an 'authorized fiduciary' able to exercise the decanting power at all: principally, a trustee or other fiduciary, other than a settlor, that already has discretion to distribute or direct a trustee to distribute part or all of the principal of the first trust to one or more current beneficiaries. Without that pre-existing discretion to distribute principal, a trustee is not an 'authorized fiduciary' under this Act, and the decanting power described in this document is not available to that trustee on that basis. Separately, the Act's own scope provision limits which trusts it reaches in the first place: except in limited circumstances, it applies to an express trust that is irrevocable, or that is revocable by the settlor only with the consent of the trustee or a person holding an adverse interest. A trust the settlor alone can still revoke or amend outright is accordingly outside the scope of this Act as described here.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's decanting framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document does not determine whether any specific trustee actually holds the principal-distribution discretion the Act requires to qualify as an 'authorized fiduciary' of a specific trust, or whether a specific trust is, in fact, irrevocable or revocable only with the trustee's or an adverse party's consent -- those are fact- and instrument-specific questions this document does not resolve. This clause cites two different statutory sections, § 19502(c)(1) and § 19503(a); both come from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times. Separately, this corpus's own Trust Amendment document addresses a different statutory mechanism -- a settlor's own power under Probate Code § 15402 to modify a trust that is still revocable by that settlor -- which is why § 19503(a)'s scope language matters here: the Act described in this document is generally the mechanism available once a trust is no longer one the settlor alone can simply amend, not an alternative to that simpler amendment power for a trust that still is.

citations.quote: “Authorized fiduciary” means any of the following:(1) A trustee or other fiduciary, other than a settlor, that has discretion to distribute or direct a trustee to distribute part or all of the principal of the first trust to one or more current beneficiaries.

clauses.title: 'Expanded' Versus 'Limited' Distributive Discretion, and Why the Difference Matters
clauses.body: California's Act draws a distinction between two kinds of principal-distribution discretion a trustee may hold, and ties different decanting rules to each. 'Expanded distributive discretion' means a discretionary power of distribution that is not limited to an ascertainable standard or a reasonably definite standard -- broadly, discretion beyond a fixed standard such as a beneficiary's health, education, support, or maintenance. An authorized fiduciary with expanded distributive discretion over a first trust's principal may exercise the decanting power over that principal, subject to specific limits described elsewhere in this document. 'Limited distributive discretion,' by contrast, means a discretionary power of distribution that is limited to an ascertainable standard or a reasonably definite standard. A fiduciary with only limited distributive discretion may still exercise the decanting power over the first trust's principal, but under a different and more restrictive rule: the second trust or trusts, taken together, must grant each beneficiary of the first trust beneficial interests that are 'substantially similar' to that beneficiary's beneficial interests in the first trust, meaning no material change in those interests except as the statute itself allows.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's Act specifically draws this distinction -- not an assumption that California's version matches every other state's decanting statute, or the model Uniform Trust Decanting Act, on this point; the presence and precise scope of an expanded/limited-discretion distinction can vary by state, and this document addresses California's current text only. This clause cites four different statutory sections -- § 19502(k) (defining 'expanded distributive discretion'), § 19511(b) (the expanded-discretion authority to decant), § 19512(a) (defining 'limited distributive discretion' for purposes of that section), and § 19512(c) (the substantially-similar requirement) -- fetched as part of the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers, with identical text returned both times. This clause does not itself catalog every specific change a second trust may or may not make under either form of discretion -- that is addressed, for the expanded-discretion case, in a separate clause of this document; this document does not separately catalog every specific change (beyond the substantially-similar standard) available or unavailable under limited distributive discretion.

For purposes of this subdivision, “substantially similar” means that there is no material change in a beneficiary’s beneficial interests, except as provided in subdivision (d).

clauses.title: Notice Before Decanting, the Right to Object, and Why Court Approval Is Not Automatically Required
clauses.body: An authorized fiduciary may exercise the decanting power without the consent of any person and without court approval, so long as the fiduciary complies with the Act's own requirements -- chiefly, advance notice. Except in limited circumstances, the fiduciary must give notice of the intended exercise of the decanting power not later than 60 days before the exercise to each settlor of the first trust then living or in existence, each qualified beneficiary of the first trust, each holder of a presently exercisable power of appointment over any part of the first trust, each person who currently has the right to remove or replace the authorized fiduciary, each other fiduciary of the first trust, each fiduciary of the second trust, and the Attorney General if the first trust holds certain charitable interests. Separately, the Act defines a 'notice period' for this purpose as beginning on the day notice is given and ending 59 days after that day, and requires the notice itself to include a specific warning, in boldface type, that a recipient who does not bring a court action to contest the proposed decanting within 59 days of the notice will lose the right to contest it. Receiving notice does not prevent a person from later applying to court: on application by an authorized fiduciary, a person entitled to notice, a beneficiary, or (as to a charitable interest) the Attorney General, a court may provide instructions on whether a proposed exercise is permitted, appoint a special fiduciary, approve an exercise of the decanting power, or grant other relief the Act separately describes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's decanting notice framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust; notice periods and required contents vary across states that have adopted versions of the Uniform Trust Decanting Act. This document is informational: it does not itself constitute or serve the notice this section describes, and preparing it does not start, toll, or satisfy the 60-day notice deadline for any specific trust -- only an actual, compliant notice does that. This corrects a natural but imprecise assumption: the statute does not set a single symmetrical '60-day notice period.' The required advance notice must be given at least 60 days before the exercise, but the defined 'notice period' itself runs only 59 days from the day notice is given, and the required contest warning likewise refers to 59 days, not 60 -- so the advance-notice figure and the contest-window figure described in this clause are not the same number. This clause cites five different subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 19507 (subdivisions (a), (b), (c), and (g)(5)), plus a separate section, § 19509(a); all come from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers, with identical text returned both times. Section 19507 shows a 2023 amendment (effective January 1, 2024) in the fetched text, confirming this is the current, operative version rather than the statute's original 2019 text. This document does not address several related, narrower rules this research did not fully develop into their own clauses -- among them, that certain other actions under the Act (such as increasing an authorized fiduciary's own compensation, or modifying who may remove or replace the fiduciary) require either beneficiary consent or court approval even though the general decanting exercise described in this clause does not.

clauses.title: What an Authorized Fiduciary With Expanded Discretion Cannot Do to a Beneficiary's Interest
clauses.body: Even where an authorized fiduciary holds expanded distributive discretion sufficient to exercise the decanting power, the Act places specific limits on what the resulting second trust may do. In an exercise of the decanting power under this expanded-discretion authority, a second trust may not include as a current beneficiary a person who is not already a current beneficiary of the first trust (except as the statute separately allows), may not include as a presumptive remainder or successor beneficiary a person who does not already hold one of those categories of interest in the first trust (subject to the same exception), and may not reduce or eliminate a 'vested interest' -- a term the Act itself defines to include, among other things, a current and noncontingent right to a mandatory distribution of income or a set dollar amount or percentage, and a presently exercisable general power of appointment. This is a narrower, more specific protection than a generic rule against reducing 'a beneficiary's interest' in the abstract: it turns on whether the particular interest at stake qualifies as a current beneficiary interest, a presumptive remainder or successor interest, or a statutorily defined vested interest, and it operates differently from the separate 'substantially similar' protection that applies instead when a fiduciary is decanting under limited, rather than expanded, distributive discretion.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's specific beneficiary protections under this Act -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, or about how any specific first trust's beneficiaries or interests should be categorized under this statute. This corrects a natural but imprecise assumption from a generic description of decanting statutes: California's statute does not flatly bar 'adding a new beneficiary' in every sense, and it does not use a single undifferentiated concept of 'a beneficiary's fixed income interest.' The restriction in subdivision (c) is limited to adding a person as a current beneficiary, or as a presumptive remainder or successor beneficiary, who does not already hold an equivalent category of interest in the first trust (itself subject to an exception in subdivision (d), which this document does not independently quote or address, for new or modified powers of appointment in favor of existing beneficiaries), and the protection against reduction turns on the statute's own defined term 'vested interest' -- a term this document does not exhaustively quote in full -- rather than on every fixed or scheduled payment a beneficiary might expect. This clause cites a single statutory section, § 19511(c); no additional independent source was sought for this, and it was fetched as part of the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) described in this document's other clauses, twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers, with identical text returned both times.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 19511(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the restrictions on adding beneficiaries and reducing or eliminating a vested interest, under expanded distributive discretion
citations.quote: (c) Subject to Section 19513, in an exercise of the decanting power under this section, a second trust may not do any of the following:(1) Include as a current beneficiary a person that is not a current beneficiary of the first trust, except as otherwise provided in subdivision (d).(2) Include as a presumptive remainder beneficiary or successor beneficiary a person that is not a current beneficiary, presumptive remainder beneficiary, or successor beneficiary of the first trust, except as otherwise provided in subdivision (d).(3) Reduce or eliminate a vested interest.

clauses.title: Protections for Tax-Sensitive Provisions and Charitable Interests
clauses.body: The Act separately restricts decanting where a first trust holds a charitable interest or property whose tax treatment depends on specific terms. If a first trust contains a charitable interest, the second trust or trusts may not diminish that charitable interest, may not diminish the interest of an identified charitable organization that holds it, may not alter any charitable purpose stated in the first trust instrument, and may not alter any condition or restriction related to that charitable interest. Independently, a set of tax-qualification protections applies across a list of specific tax provisions the statute itself enumerates -- for example, if a first trust contains property that qualified, or would have qualified, for a marital deduction for gift or estate tax purposes, the second trust instrument may not include or omit a term that would have prevented that qualification, or reduced the deduction, under the same provision that let the original transfer qualify. The statute applies a parallel rule to several other tax-sensitive attributes it separately lists, including charitable-deduction qualification, the gift-tax annual exclusion, S-corporation shareholder eligibility, generation-skipping-transfer zero-inclusion-ratio status, and minimum-distribution treatment of retirement-plan property; the statute also gives a settlor, specifically, the right to object in a signed writing during the notice period where decanting would change whether the settlor retains the power to cause a trust to cease being a 'grantor trust' for income tax purposes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's decanting protections for charitable interests and tax-sensitive provisions -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a determination that any specific trust actually holds a charitable interest or actually qualified for any specific tax benefit. This document quotes only two of the statute's tax-sensitive protections directly -- the charitable-interest restrictions in § 19514(c), and the marital-deduction protection in § 19519(b)(1) -- as representative examples of a considerably longer enumerated list in § 19519(b) that this document does not quote in full; the settlor's grantor-trust objection right described in this clause's body is drawn from § 19519(b)(10)(A), quoted below, which is one specific condition among the several that subdivision addresses, not the whole of it. This clause cites three different statutory sections -- § 19514(c), § 19519(b)(1), and § 19519(b)(10) -- all fetched as part of the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) described in this document's other clauses, twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers, with identical text returned both times. This document does not independently verify the underlying federal tax rules (marital deduction, grantor trust status, or otherwise) that these state-law protections are designed to preserve; it addresses only what California's decanting statute itself requires or forbids in a second trust instrument.

citations.quote: (c) If a first trust contains a charitable interest, the second trust or trusts may not do any of the following:(1) Diminish the charitable interest.(2) Diminish the interest of an identified charitable organization that holds the charitable interest.(3) Alter any charitable purpose stated in the first trust instrument.(4) Alter any condition or restriction related to the charitable interest.

clauses.title: Transfer and Claim Declaration
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's property tax reassessment exclusion for a transfer of real property located at {{propertyAddress}}, Assessor's Parcel Number {{parcelNumber}}, between {{transferorName}} ("Transferor") and {{transfereeName}} ("Transferee"), who is Transferor's {{relationshipToTransferor}}. This exclusion is set out in California Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2, enacted to implement Article XIII A, Section 2.1 of the California Constitution (added by Proposition 19, approved by California voters on November 3, 2020), for transfers occurring on or after February 16, 2021.

This declaration is a factual record of the parties, relationship, and property involved. It is not itself the claim for exclusion that Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(b) requires to be filed with the county assessor on the form the State Board of Equalization prescribes, and completing it does not determine that this transfer in fact qualifies for exclusion from reassessment, does not determine whether the property has become or will become {{transfereeName}}'s principal residence, and does not determine whether the property qualifies as a family farm.

clauses.title: Signature and Certification
Effective Date and Transition from the Former Parent-Child Exclusion
clauses.body: The California property tax reassessment exclusion for transfers between parents and children, and between grandparents and grandchildren, changed substantially as a result of Proposition 19, a constitutional amendment California voters approved on November 3, 2020. Before that measure, Article XIII A, Section 2(h) of the California Constitution excluded from "change in ownership" a principal-residence transfer between parents and children, along with the first $1,000,000 of full cash value of other real property transferred between them, without requiring the transferee to use the property as a principal residence. A new constitutional provision added by Proposition 19, Article XIII A, Section 2.1(d), makes that former provision, Section 2(h), inoperative for any purchase or transfer occurring on or after February 16, 2021, while continuing to apply Section 2(h) to any purchase or transfer that occurred on or before February 15, 2021. Consistent with that constitutional transition, the statute enacted to implement the new rule, Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2, states that its exclusion applies beginning on and after that same date, February 16, 2021. The older implementing statute, Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.1 — which does not itself state a principal-residence-use requirement for the transferee, as described in this document's clause on that requirement — continues, by its own terms, to apply to transfers of real property completed on or after November 6, 1986, but its practical effect for transfers after February 15, 2021 depends on the fact that its constitutional authorization was made inoperative by Section 2.1(d), rather than on any cutoff date written into Section 63.1's own statutory text.
clauses.gap: This draws on two separately enacted sources treated here as independent: Article XIII A, Section 2.1(d) of the California Constitution (added by the Proposition 19 ballot initiative) and Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a) (implementing legislation, since amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 539 (SB 293)). Correction to a natural assumption: a reader consulting only the current text of Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.1 will not find any statement there that it stopped applying to transfers on or after February 16, 2021 — that limit is not written into Section 63.1 itself. It arises instead because Section 63.1 implements the constitutional exclusion in the former Article XIII A, Section 2(h), and Section 2.1(d) separately makes Section 2(h) inoperative for later transfers. This clause does not itself apply either statute to any specific reader's transfer, and does not determine which statute's exclusion mechanism governs any particular transaction.

clauses.title: Requirement That the Property Become the Transferee's Principal Residence
clauses.body: Under the current parent-child and grandparent-grandchild exclusion, a transfer of a family home qualifies only if the property was the transferor's principal residence and becomes the transferee's principal residence within one year of the transfer. Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(1)(A)-(C) states that the transferee must also file for the homeowners' exemption or the disabled veterans' exemption within a year of the transfer, and that the exclusion is removed — with the property's base year value re-enrolled as it would otherwise have stood, adjusted for inflation and new construction — as of the lien date immediately following the date the transferee (or a later eligible transferee who timely filed for the exemption) stops being eligible for either exemption. Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(5) of the California Constitution states the same exemption-filing mechanism: the transferee must claim the homeowners' or disabled veterans' exemption at the time of the transfer to receive the benefit immediately, but a transferee who misses that timing may still claim the benefit by filing for the exemption within one year of the transfer, in which case the transferee is entitled to a refund of taxes paid between the transfer date and the date the exemption is claimed. This is a change from the exclusion that applied before February 16, 2021: the former constitutional exclusion, Article XIII A, Section 2(h)(1), excluded a transfer of "the principal residence of the transferor" between parents and children without requiring that the property become the transferee's principal residence at all, and without any homeowners'- or disabled-veterans'-exemption filing condition.
clauses.gap: Two independent sources state today's rule — Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(1) (statute) and Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(5) (constitution) — and a third, separately enacted and now-superseded constitutional provision, Article XIII A, Section 2(h)(1), is cited only to state precisely what the pre-February-16-2021 rule required, for contrast; it does not describe current law. This clause addresses the family-home version of the requirement; Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(d) extends the identical mechanism to a family farm, addressed in this document's clause on the family farm and non-residence-property rules. This clause does not determine whether any specific property has become, or will become, any specific transferee's principal residence, or whether any specific transferee has timely filed for either exemption.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 63.2(a)(1)(A)-(C)
citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, principal-residence and homeowners'/disabled veterans' exemption-filing requirements
citations.quote: The transfer is required to be of a principal residence of the transferor, and become the principal residence of the transferee within one year of the transfer.(B) The transferee shall file for the homeowners’ or disabled veterans’ exemption within a year of the transfer, and the exclusion shall be removed on the date an eligible transferee, or a subsequent eligible transferee who files for the homeowners’ or disabled veterans’ exemption within one year, is no longer eligible for either the homeowners’ or disabled veterans’ exemption.(C) If applicable, as of the lien date immediately following the date the eligible transferee or subsequent eligible transferee no longer qualifies for the exclusion provided by this section, the base year value established as of the change in ownership date to which the exclusion applied, adjusted annually in accordance with paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 51, shall be enrolled.

citations.case: Cal. Const. art. XIII A, § 2.1(c)(5)

citations.quote: in order to receive the property tax benefit provided by this section for the purchase or transfer of a family home, the transferee shall claim the homeowner’s exemption or disabled veteran’s exemption at the time of the purchase or transfer of the family home.(B) A transferee who fails to claim the homeowner’s exemption or disabled veteran’s exemption at the time of the purchase or transfer of the family home may receive the property tax benefit provided by this section by claiming the homeowner’s exemption or disabled veteran’s exemption within one year of the purchase or transfer of the family home and shall be entitled to a refund of taxes previously owed or paid between the date of the transfer and the date the transferee claims the homeowner's exemption or disabled veteran’s exemption.

clauses.title: The Current Taxable-Value Formula for an Excluded Family Home or Family Farm
clauses.body: Rather than excluding a family home or family farm from reassessment outright, the current rule caps how much of any increase in value is added to the transferred property's taxable value. Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(d) states that the new taxable value of an excluded family home or family farm is the sum of (1) the taxable value the property already carried immediately before the transfer, and (2) an additional amount that depends on a comparison: if the property's fair market value upon transfer is less than that existing taxable value plus $1,000,000, the additional amount is zero; if that fair market value is equal to or more than the existing taxable value plus $1,000,000, the additional amount equals the fair market value minus the sum of the existing taxable value and $1,000,000. In effect, only the amount by which fair market value exceeds the prior taxable value plus $1,000,000 is added to the property's new taxable value; the transferred property does not receive a full reassessment to current fair market value. Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(1)(B) of the California Constitution states the same two-branch formula for a family home, describing the comparison value as the property's "assessed value" rather than, as the statute does, its "fair market value."
clauses.gap: Two independently enacted sources state this formula in materially the same terms — Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(d) (statute) and Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(1) (constitution) — and are treated here as independent. This clause notes, without resolving it, a terminology difference between the two texts: the statute frames the comparison using the property's "fair market value... as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 110," while the constitutional provision uses "assessed value" for the same comparison; this document does not determine whether that difference in wording produces any difference in outcome. This clause states the formula in general terms; it does not compute the resulting taxable value for the property described in this document, which depends on that property's own prior taxable value and its fair market value on the date of transfer.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 63.2(d)
citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, new taxable value formula for an excluded family home or family farm
citations.quote: The new taxable value of the family home or family farm shall be the sum of both of the following:(1) The taxable value of the family home or family farm as determined in accordance with Section 110.1, with the adjustments permitted by subdivision (b) of Section 2 of Article XIII A of the California Constitution and subdivision (f) of Section 110.1, determined as of the date immediately prior to the date the principal residence or family farm is purchased or transferred to the transferee.(2) The applicable of the following amounts:(A) If the fair market value, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 110, of the family home or family farm upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee is less than the sum of the taxable value described in paragraph (1) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), then zero dollars ($0).(B) If the fair market value, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 110, of the family home or family farm upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee is equal to or more than the sum of the taxable value described in paragraph (1) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), an amount equal to the fair market value of the family home upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee, minus the sum of the taxable value described in paragraph (1) and one million dollars ($1,000,000).

citations.case: Cal. Const. art. XIII A, § 2.1(c)(1)(B)
citations.cite: California Constitution, parallel taxable-value formula for a family home
citations.quote: (B) The applicable of the following amounts:(i) If the assessed value of the family home upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee is less than the sum of the taxable value described in subparagraph (A) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), then zero dollars ($0).(ii) If the assessed value of the family home upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee is equal to or more than the sum of the taxable value described in subparagraph (A) plus one million dollars ($1,000,000), an amount equal to the assessed value of the family home upon purchase by, or transfer to, the transferee, minus the sum of the taxable value described in subparagraph (A) and one million dollars ($1,000,000).

clauses.title: Biennial Inflation Adjustment of the $1,000,000 Figure
clauses.body: The $1,000,000 figure used in the current taxable-value formula is not fixed permanently at that dollar amount. Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(4) of the California Constitution states that, beginning on February 16, 2023, and every other February 16 after that, the State Board of Equalization must adjust the $1,000,000 amount for inflation, to reflect the percentage change in the House Price Index for California for the preceding calendar year, as determined by the Federal Housing Finance Agency, and that the State Board of Equalization calculates and publishes the resulting adjustment.
clauses.gap: This inflation-adjustment mechanism is stated only in Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(4) of the California Constitution; the implementing statute, Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(d), states the taxable-value formula using a flat "one million dollars ($1,000,000)" figure and does not itself repeat or cross-reference the adjustment mechanism in its own text. This clause is therefore based on a single verified source, not independently corroborated by the statute's own wording, and that gap between the statute's flat figure and the constitution's adjustment instruction is stated here as a fact about the text of each provision, not resolved as a claim about which figure a county assessor applies to any particular transfer in any given year. This clause does not state the currently adjusted dollar figure for any specific year, which was not independently verified in this research.

citations.case: Cal. Const. art. XIII A, § 2.1(c)(4)
citations.cite: California Constitution, biennial inflation adjustment of the $1,000,000 exclusion amount
citations.quote: Beginning on February 16, 2023, and every other February 16 thereafter, the State Board of Equalization shall adjust the one million dollar ($1,000,000) amount described in paragraph (1) for inflation to reflect the percentage change in the House Price Index for California for the prior calendar year, as determined by the Federal Housing Finance Agency.

clauses.title: Family Farms and the End of the General Exclusion for Non-Residence Property
clauses.body: The current exclusion reaches only two categories of property: a family home that meets the principal-residence conditions described elsewhere in this document, and a family farm. Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(2) extends the same exclusion mechanism to "a family farm of an eligible transferor," applying it separately to each legal parcel making up the farm, except that a parcel containing a family home is instead evaluated under the family-home rule. This differs from the exclusion that applied to transfers before February 16, 2021, which — as described in this document's clause on the pre-2021 rule — also excluded up to $1,000,000 of full cash value of "other real property" between parents and children generally, with no requirement that the property be a farm or that the transferee use it as a residence. The current statute contains no comparable general exclusion for other real property that is neither a principal residence nor a family farm. Article XIII A, Section 2.1(a)(2) of the California Constitution states the Legislature's and voters' stated purpose in adopting this narrower scope: to protect the ability of parents and grandparents to pass on a family home for continued use as a primary residence, while ending the exclusion as applied to vacation homes, income properties, and other non-residence real property.
clauses.gap: This states two independent sources: Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(2) (the statutory family-farm provision) and Article XIII A, Section 2.1(a)(2) (a constitutional statement of purpose accompanying the same measure). The statement-of-purpose language is cited to confirm the general direction of the change — narrowing the exclusion to residence and farm property — not as an operative rule with independent legal force apart from the operative text of Section 63.2(a) itself, which by its own structure lists only a principal residence (paragraph (1)) and a family farm (paragraph (2)) as excluded categories. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific parcel is, in fact, a family farm within the statutory definition, which depends on the property's actual use.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 63.2(a)(2)
citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, family farm exclusion
citations.quote: The purchase or transfer is of a family farm of an eligible transferor in the case of a purchase or transfer between parents and their children or between grandparents and their grandchildren, if all of the parents, other than stepparents, of that grandchild or those grandchildren, who qualify as the children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of purchase or transfer.

citations.case: Cal. Const. art. XIII A, § 2.1(a)(2)
citations.cite: California Constitution, stated purpose narrowing the exclusion to residence and farm property
citations.quote: Limit property tax increases on family homes used as a primary residence by protecting the right of parents and grandparents to pass on their family home to their children and grandchildren for continued use as a primary residence, while eliminating unfair tax loopholes used by East Coast investors, celebrities, wealthy non-California residents, and trust fund heirs to avoid paying a fair share of property taxes on vacation homes, income properties, and beachfront rentals they own in California.

clauses.title: The Grandparent-Grandchild Transfer's Own Eligibility Condition
clauses.body: A transfer between a grandparent and a grandchild qualifies for the same exclusion as a parent-child transfer only if an additional condition is met. Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(1) extends the family-home exclusion to a transfer "between grandparents and their grandchildren" only "if all of the parents, other than stepparents, of that grandchild or those grandchildren, who qualify as the children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of purchase or transfer," and the same statute applies an identical condition to the family-farm exclusion in § 63.2(a)(2). Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(2) of the California Constitution states the same condition for a family-home transfer between grandparents and grandchildren: it applies "if all of the parents of those grandchildren, who qualify as children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of the purchase or transfer." In substance, the grandparent-grandchild exclusion is unavailable while a grandchild's parent — a child of the grandparent — is still living, unless that living parent is only a stepparent to the grandchild.
clauses.gap: This states two independent sources: Revenue and Taxation Code § 63.2(a)(1) (statute) and Article XIII A, Section 2.1(c)(2) (constitution). A precise nuance worth flagging: the statutory text expressly carves out stepparents ("other than stepparents") from the deceased-parent condition, while the constitutional text quoted here states the condition without that express stepparent carve-out appearing in this particular passage. This clause does not resolve that wording difference or determine how it would apply to any specific grandchild's family circumstances; it states what each text says. This clause addresses only the deceased-parents eligibility condition; it does not restate the principal-residence and homeowners'/disabled-veterans'-exemption requirements described elsewhere in this document, which apply to a qualifying grandparent-grandchild transfer in the same way they apply to a parent-child transfer.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, deceased-parents condition for a grandparent-grandchild transfer
citations.quote: The purchase or transfer of real property that is the principal residence of an eligible transferor in the case of a purchase or transfer between parents and their children or between grandparents and their grandchildren, if all of the parents, other than stepparents, of that grandchild or those grandchildren, who qualify as the children of the grandparents, are deceased as of the date of purchase or transfer.

clauses.title: Who May Disclaim, and the Basic Right to Disclaim
clauses.body: Under California Probate Code § 262, a “beneficiary” is the person entitled, but for a disclaimer, to take an interest — the person who would otherwise receive property, whether from {{decedentName}}'s estate or some other source covered by this part. Section 264 uses a separate term, “disclaimant,” for whoever actually executes the disclaimer: that can be the beneficiary personally, or someone else acting on the beneficiary's behalf, such as a guardian, conservator, or personal representative acting for a minor, a conservatee, or a deceased beneficiary (Prob. Code §§ 276–277 separately require a court order before that kind of representative's disclaimer on another person's behalf becomes effective). Section 275 then states the core right in a single sentence: a beneficiary may disclaim any interest, in whole or in part, by filing a disclaimer as provided in this part.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes three separate sections of California Probate Code Division 2, Part 8 — §§ 262, 264, and 275 — each independently fetched twice (two separate requests using distinct User-Agent strings against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) with identical results both times; they are three distinct sections of the same statutory part, not three unrelated sources. The parenthetical reference to the guardian/conservator/personal-representative court-order requirement in Prob. Code §§ 276–277 is drawn from the same verified fetch of those two sections but is not independently quoted in this clause; a reader concerned with disclaiming on behalf of a minor, conservatee, or decedent should consult those sections' full text directly.

citations.quote: “Beneficiary” means the person entitled, but for the person’s disclaimer, to take an interest.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 264
citations.cite: California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — definition of “disclaimant”
citations.quote: “Disclaimant” means a beneficiary who executes a disclaimer on his or her own behalf or a person who executes a disclaimer on behalf of a beneficiary.

clauses.title: What Counts as a Disclaimable “Interest”
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 267 defines “interest” broadly for purposes of the disclaimer statute. Subdivision (a) covers the whole of any property, real or personal, legal or equitable, any fractional part or share of it, any estate in it, any power to appoint, consume, apply, or expend property, and any other right, power, privilege, or immunity relating to property. Subdivision (b) then lists fifteen specific ways an interest can be created that fall within this definition, and states that the list is illustrative rather than exhaustive (“includes, but is not limited to”). The listed categories reach well beyond a probate-estate inheritance: they include an interest created by intestate succession or under a will, but also an interest under a trust, an interest created by succession to a previously disclaimed interest, an interest arising from an election to take against a will, a power of appointment (whether its creation, or its exercise or nonexercise), an inter vivos gift outright or in trust, an interest arising from surviving the death of a depositor of a Totten trust account or P.O.D. account, an interest under an insurance or annuity contract, an interest arising from surviving the death of another joint tenant, an interest under an employee benefit plan, an interest under an individual retirement account, annuity, or bond, an interest under a transfer-on-death beneficiary designation in a deed or other instrument, and a final catch-all for “any other interest created by a testamentary or inter vivos instrument or by operation of law.”
clauses.gap: This quotes the entirety of a single statutory section, Prob. Code § 267 (both subdivisions (a) and (b), including the full fifteen-item list), fetched twice independently (two separate requests using distinct User-Agent strings against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) with identical results. Several terms this list uses — for example, “employee benefit plan” (defined at Prob. Code § 266) and “creator of the interest” (defined at Prob. Code § 263, quoted in this document's disclaimer_effect clause) — are themselves defined elsewhere in the same Part 8 definitions chapter; this clause does not separately restate every cross-referenced definition.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 267
citations.cite: California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — definition of “interest” and its statutory scope
citations.quote: (a) “Interest” includes the whole of any property, real or personal, legal or equitable, or any fractional part, share, or particular portion or specific assets thereof, or any estate in any such property, or any power to appoint, consume, apply, or expend property, or any other right, power, privilege, or immunity relating to property. (b) “Interest” includes, but is not limited to, an interest created in any of the following manners: (1) By intestate succession. (2) Under a will. (3) Under a trust. (4) By succession to a disclaimed interest. (5) By virtue of an election to take against a will. (6) By creation of a power of appointment. (7) By exercise or nonexercise of a power of appointment. (8) By an inter vivos gift, whether outright or in trust. (9) By surviving the death of a depositor of a Totten trust account or P.O.D. account. (10) Under an insurance or annuity contract. (11) By surviving the death of another joint tenant. (12) Under an employee benefit plan. (13) Under an individual retirement account, annuity, or bond. (14) Under a transfer on death beneficiary designation in a deed or other instrument. (15) Any other interest created by a testamentary or inter vivos instrument or by operation of law.

clauses.title: Formal Requirements for a Valid Disclaimer
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 278 sets out three formal requirements a disclaimer must meet: it must be in writing, it must be signed by the disclaimant, and it must identify the creator of the interest, describe the interest to be disclaimed, and state the disclaimer and its extent — meaning whether the disclaimant is disclaiming the whole interest or only part of it. Beyond signing and content, Prob. Code § 280(a) separately requires that the written disclaimer be filed — with the superior court in the county administering the decedent's estate (or, if there is no administration, any county where administration would be proper), with the trustee, personal representative, other fiduciary, or person responsible for distributing the interest, with any other person having custody, possession, or legal title to the interest, or with the creator of the interest itself. A disclaimer that affects real property or an obligation secured by real property may also be acknowledged and recorded like a grant of real property, under Prob. Code § 280(b), though that subdivision states that failing to record it does not, by itself, affect the validity of a transaction with respect to the property.
clauses.gap: This draws on two sections of the same Probate Code Part 8 — § 278 (writing, signature, and content, quoted in full) and § 280(a) (where a disclaimer must be filed, quoted through the end of its four-item list) — plus an unquoted, paraphrased reference to § 280(b)'s real-property recording option; both quoted sections were independently fetched twice, using distinct User-Agent strings, with identical results. This clause does not address the guardian/conservator/personal-representative court-petition process under §§ 276–277, which imposes additional content and notice requirements beyond § 278 when someone other than the beneficiary personally is disclaiming on the beneficiary's behalf.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 278
citations.cite: California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — writing, signature, and content requirements
citations.quote: The disclaimer shall be in writing, shall be signed by the disclaimant, and shall: (a) Identify the creator of the interest. (b) Describe the interest to be disclaimed. (c) State the disclaimer and the extent of the disclaimer.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 280(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — where a disclaimer must be filed
citations.quote: (a) A disclaimer shall be filed with any of the following: (1) The superior court in the county in which the estate of the decedent is administered or, if there is no administration of the decedent’s estate, the superior court in any county in which administration of the estate of the decedent would be proper. (2) The trustee, personal representative, other fiduciary, or person responsible for distributing the interest to the beneficiary. (3) Any other person having custody or possession of or legal title to the interest. (4) The creator of the interest.

clauses.title: Timing: No Fixed Deadline, a Nine-Month Safe Harbor, and a Separate Federal Rule
clauses.body: California's own disclaimer statute does not set a single fixed deadline. Prob. Code § 279(a) instead requires only that a disclaimer be filed within a reasonable time after the person able to disclaim acquires knowledge of the interest — an open-ended standard. Subdivision (b) then creates a safe harbor for most of the interest categories this part covers (an interest created under a will, by intestate succession, by exercise or nonexercise of a testamentary power of appointment, by surviving the death of a Totten-trust or P.O.D. depositor, under a life insurance or annuity contract, by surviving the death of a joint tenant, under an employee benefit plan, under an individual retirement account, annuity, or bond, or under a transfer-on-death beneficiary designation): a disclaimer filed within nine months after the creator of the interest's death, or nine months after the interest becomes indefeasibly vested, whichever is later, is conclusively presumed to have been filed within a reasonable time. Subdivisions (c), (d), and (e) of the same section set parallel nine-month presumption windows, measured from different triggering events, for a living-trust interest, a presently exercisable power of appointment, an inter vivos gift, a future estate, and other interests not otherwise listed; and subdivision (f) makes clear that missing these nine-month windows does not automatically invalidate a disclaimer — it only shifts the burden onto the disclaimant to show the filing was still within a reasonable time. This state-law nine-month presumption should not be confused with the separate nine-month deadline federal tax law imposes for a disclaimer to qualify for certain federal estate- and gift-tax treatment (commonly discussed as a “qualified disclaimer” under federal law) — a federal statute this document does not independently verify or address. California's own statute connects to federal law in one specific way, at Prob. Code § 295: if a disclaimer or transfer is treated under federal law (Title 26 of the United States Code and its regulations) as though the disclaimed interest had never been transferred to the beneficiary, then that disclaimer or transfer is also effective as a disclaimer under this California statute, regardless of any other provision of this part.
clauses.gap: This draws on § 279 (subdivision (a), quoted in full, and subdivision (b), quoted only through its introductory clause rather than its full nine-item list of covered interests) and on § 295 in Chapter 3 of the same Part 8 (quoted in full); both were independently fetched twice, using distinct User-Agent strings, with identical results, but they are sections of the same statutory part, not unrelated sources. This clause references, but has not itself fetched or verified, the text of the federal statute it distinguishes California's rule from (the federal “qualified disclaimer” provision, 26 U.S.C. § 2518) — a reader should not rely on this clause for that federal provision's own requirements. This clause also does not separately quote § 279's subdivisions (c), (d), or (e), each of which sets a similarly structured nine-month presumption window keyed to different triggering events.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — the reasonable-time filing standard
citations.quote: (a) A disclaimer to be effective shall be filed within a reasonable time after the person able to disclaim acquires knowledge of the interest.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — nine-month conclusive presumption of timeliness
citations.quote: (b) In the case of any of the following interests, a disclaimer is conclusively presumed to have been filed within a reasonable time if it is filed within nine months after the death of the creator of the interest or within nine months after the interest becomes indefeasibly vested, whichever occurs later:

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 295
citations.cite: California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — disclaimers effective under federal law
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of this part, if as a result of a disclaimer or transfer the disclaimed or transferred interest is treated pursuant to the provisions of Title 26 of the United States Code, as now or hereafter amended, or any successor statute thereto, and the regulations promulgated thereunder, as never having been transferred to the beneficiary, then the disclaimer or transfer is effective as a disclaimer under this part.

clauses.title: Legal Effect of a Valid Disclaimer
clauses.body: Once effective, a disclaimer under this part has two main statutory consequences. First, under Prob. Code § 281, it is irrevocable and binding upon the beneficiary and all persons claiming by, through, or under the beneficiary, including creditors of the beneficiary — a disclaimant cannot later change their mind about property connected to {{decedentName}} or anyone else. Second, Prob. Code § 282(a) sets the default rule for where a disclaimed interest goes: unless the creator of the interest has provided for a specific disposition in the event of a disclaimer, the disclaimed interest passes as if the disclaimant had predeceased the creator of the interest (for a present interest) or as if the disclaimant had died before the interest's taker became finally ascertained and indefeasibly vested (for a future interest), and the disclaimer relates back to the date of the creator's death or the determinative event for all purposes. Because the statute directs the property to descend under this predecease fiction — or under whatever alternative disposition the creator of the interest itself specified — rather than to wherever the disclaimant might prefer, this section does not give a disclaimant the power to redirect a disclaimed interest to a person of the disclaimant's own choosing. Subdivision (b) adds two further, narrower qualifications for a disclaimer filed on or after January 1, 1985: the disclaiming beneficiary is not treated as having predeceased the decedent for purposes of determining which generation an estate divides at under Part 6 (commencing with Section 240) or under a will, trust, or other instrument's own generation-based provisions, and is likewise not treated as having predeceased the decedent when applying Prob. Code § 6409(d) or § 6410(b).
clauses.gap: This quotes § 281 in full and the whole of § 282 (both subdivisions (a) and (b)) in full, each independently fetched twice, using distinct User-Agent strings, with identical results; they are two separate sections of the same Part 8. This clause's statement that § 282(a) does not give a disclaimant a power to redirect the property to a chosen third person is this document's own reading of what the quoted text does and does not say — the statute nowhere grants such a power, and directs disposition only to the alternative the creator of the interest specified or, failing that, under the predecease fiction — rather than a separate statutory sentence stating a redirection ban in so many words. This clause does not separately research or quote the anti-lapse provisions in Part 6 (commencing with Section 240) or Prob. Code §§ 6409–6410 that subdivision (b) cross-references; a reader wanting those provisions' own text should consult them directly.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 281
citations.cite: California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — irrevocability of an effective disclaimer
citations.quote: A disclaimer, when effective, is irrevocable and binding upon the beneficiary and all persons claiming by, through, or under the beneficiary, including creditors of the beneficiary.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 282
citations.cite: California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — the predecease mechanism governing where a disclaimed interest passes
citations.quote: (a) Unless the creator of the interest provides for a specific disposition of the interest in the event of a disclaimer, the interest disclaimed shall descend, go, be distributed, or continue to be held (1) as to a present interest, as if the disclaimant had predeceased the creator of the interest or (2) as to a future interest, as if the disclaimant had died before the event determining that the taker of the interest had become finally ascertained and the taker’s interest indefeasibly vested. A disclaimer relates back for all purposes to the date of the death of the creator of the disclaimed interest or the determinative event, as the case may be. (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), where the disclaimer is filed on or after January 1, 1985: (1) The beneficiary is not treated as having predeceased the decedent for the purpose of determining the generation at which the division of the estate is to be made under Part 6 (commencing with Section 240) or other provision of a will, trust, or other instrument. (2) The beneficiary of a disclaimed interest is not treated as having predeceased the decedent for the purpose of applying subdivision (d) of Section 6409 or subdivision (b) of Section 6410.

clauses.title: Partial Disclaimers and Bars to Disclaiming
clauses.body: Section 275 — already quoted in this document's disclaimer_who_may_disclaim clause — states the partial-disclaimer rule in the same sentence as the core right: a beneficiary may disclaim any interest in whole or in part. A disclaimant is not required to give up an entire interest in order to disclaim at all. Prob. Code § 285 then sets the principal bar: subdivision (a) states that a disclaimer may not be made after the beneficiary has accepted the interest sought to be disclaimed, and subdivision (b) defines what counts as acceptance — a voluntary assignment, conveyance, encumbrance, pledge, or transfer of the interest, or a contract to do so; executing a written waiver of the right to disclaim under § 284; accepting the interest or a benefit under it; or having the interest sold at a judicial sale — while carving out an exception for a beneficiary who makes a gratuitous conveyance of their entire interest to whoever would have received it under an otherwise qualified disclaimer. Subdivision (c) further allows a beneficiary who already accepted one interest to still disclaim a second, later interest that came to the beneficiary only because someone else disclaimed first, so long as the beneficiary had no knowledge of that second interest at the time of the original acceptance; and subdivision (d) clarifies that a joint tenant's acceptance of the original joint-tenancy interest is not, by itself, an acceptance of the separate interest the joint tenant later receives by surviving another joint tenant. Separately, Prob. Code § 286 states that the right to disclaim exists regardless of any limitation imposed on the interest of a beneficiary in the nature of an expressed or implied spendthrift provision or similar restriction — a spendthrift clause in a trust does not, by itself, block a beneficiary from disclaiming.
clauses.gap: The partial-disclaimer point restates Prob. Code § 275, already independently fetched and quoted in this document's disclaimer_who_may_disclaim clause — it is not an independent source for that specific point here. Section 285 (its full text, subdivisions (a) through (d)) and § 286 (in full) were each independently fetched twice, using distinct User-Agent strings, with identical results; they are separate sections within the same Part 8. This clause describes § 285(b)(2)'s cross-reference to the § 284 written-waiver alternative and § 285(c)'s exception for succession to a previously disclaimed interest without separately quoting § 284 in full, and does not address this corpus's separate slayer-statute predecease mechanism (Prob. Code §§ 250–254) covered in the Slayer Statute Information Sheet.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 275
citations.cite: California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — the right to disclaim in whole or in part
citations.quote: A beneficiary may disclaim any interest, in whole or in part, by filing a disclaimer as provided in this part.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 285
citations.cite: California Probate Code, disclaimer-of-interest statute — bar to disclaiming after acceptance of the interest
citations.quote: (a) A disclaimer may not be made after the beneficiary has accepted the interest sought to be disclaimed. (b) For the purpose of this section, a beneficiary has accepted an interest if any of the following occurs before a disclaimer is filed with respect to that interest: (1) The beneficiary, or someone acting on behalf of the beneficiary, makes a voluntary assignment, conveyance, encumbrance, pledge, or transfer of the interest or part thereof, or contracts to do so; provided, however, that a beneficiary will not have accepted an interest if the beneficiary makes a gratuitous conveyance or transfer of the beneficiary’s entire interest in property to the person or persons who would have received the property had the beneficiary made an otherwise qualified disclaimer pursuant to this part. (2) The beneficiary, or someone acting on behalf of the beneficiary, executes a written waiver under Section 284 of the right to disclaim the interest. (3) The beneficiary, or someone acting on behalf of the beneficiary, accepts the interest or part thereof or benefit thereunder. (4) The interest or part thereof is sold at a judicial sale. (c) An acceptance does not preclude a beneficiary from thereafter disclaiming all or part of an interest if both of the following requirements are met: (1) The beneficiary became entitled to the interest because another person disclaimed an interest. (2) The beneficiary or other person acting on behalf of the beneficiary at the time of the acceptance had no knowledge of the interest to which the beneficiary so became entitled. (d) The acceptance by a joint tenant of the joint tenancy interest created when the joint tenancy is created is not an acceptance by the joint tenant of the interest created when the joint tenant survives the death of another joint tenant.
