citations.cite: California Civil Code, disclosure limited to seller/agent/buyer, not usable by other parties
citations.quote: The disclosure required by this article is only a disclosure between the seller, the seller’s agent, and the prospective buyer, and shall not be used by any other party, including, but not limited to, insurance companies, lenders, or governmental agencies, for any purpose.

clauses.title: Good Faith and the Third-Party Report Safe Harbor
clauses.body: The statute provides that neither the seller nor any seller's or buyer's agent is liable for an error, inaccuracy, or omission in information delivered under the natural-hazard disclosure article if the error, inaccuracy, or omission was outside that person's personal knowledge, was based on information timely provided by a public agency or by another qualifying person, and ordinary care was exercised in obtaining and transmitting it. As one way of qualifying for that protection, the statute states that delivery, in response to a request, of a report or opinion prepared by a licensed engineer, land surveyor, geologist, or other expert in natural hazard discovery, addressing matters within that professional's license or expertise, is sufficient compliance for this exemption. The statutory disclosure form itself contains a checkbox by which the seller and agent may instead acknowledge that they exercised good faith in selecting a third-party report provider and that the form's representations rest on that provider's report as a substituted disclosure, rather than on the seller's or agent's own independent verification. Separately, the article states a general good-faith standard applicable to every disclosure and act performed under it, and defines "good faith," for these purposes, as honesty in fact in the conduct of the transaction.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures its good-faith and third-party-report safe harbor for natural-hazard disclosure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer. The first two citations below, to Civil Code section 1103.4(a) and (c), are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source; the third citation, to Civil Code section 1103.7, is a separate, independently enacted section defining the "good faith" standard used elsewhere in this article, including on the statutory form's own third-party-report checkbox referenced in the body above.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.4(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, liability shield for errors outside personal knowledge
citations.quote: Neither the seller nor any seller’s agent or buyer’s agent shall be liable for any error, inaccuracy, or omission of any information delivered pursuant to this article if the error, inaccuracy, or omission was not within the personal knowledge of the seller or the seller’s agent or buyer’s agent and was based on information timely provided by public agencies or by other persons providing information as specified in subdivision (c) that is required to be disclosed pursuant to this article, and ordinary care was exercised in obtaining and transmitting the information.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.4(c)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, third-party expert report as sufficient compliance
citations.quote: The delivery of a report or opinion prepared by a licensed engineer, land surveyor, geologist, or expert in natural hazard discovery dealing with matters within the scope of the professional’s license or expertise shall be sufficient compliance for application of the exemption provided by subdivision (a) if the information is provided to the prospective buyer pursuant to a request therefor, whether written or oral.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.7
citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of "good faith" for this article
citations.quote: Each disclosure required by this article and each act that may be performed in making the disclosure shall be made in good faith. For purposes of this article, “good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct of the transaction.

clauses.title: No Ongoing Duty to Update After Compliance
clauses.body: The statute provides that once a seller and the seller's agent comply with the disclosure-form requirement, they are relieved of further duty under the article with respect to the items they disclosed, and are not required to notify the prospective buyer if that information later becomes inaccurate because of governmental action, a map revision, changed information, or another subsequent act or occurrence — unless the seller or agent has actual knowledge that the information has become inaccurate. Correspondingly, the statute states that if previously disclosed information is later rendered inaccurate by such a subsequent governmental action, map revision, changed information, or other occurrence, that resulting inaccuracy does not itself constitute a violation of the article.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction limits the duration of its natural-hazard disclosure duty — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code section 1103.5, and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.5(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, no duty to notify of later inaccuracy absent actual knowledge
citations.quote: After a seller and his or her agent comply with Section 1103.2, they shall be relieved of further duty under this article with respect to those items of information. The seller and the seller’s agent shall not be required to provide notice to the prospective buyer if the information provided subsequently becomes inaccurate as a result of any governmental action, map revision, changed information, or other act or occurrence, unless the seller or agent has actual knowledge that the information has become inaccurate.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1103.5(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, later inaccuracy from subsequent events is not a violation
citations.quote: If information disclosed in accordance with this article is subsequently rendered inaccurate as a result of any governmental action, map revision, changed information, or other act or occurrence subsequent to the delivery of the required disclosures, the inaccuracy resulting therefrom does not constitute a violation of this article.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Receipt and Review
Proposed Petitioner — Information and Declaration in Support of a Family Allowance Petition
clauses.body: I, {{petitionerName}}, am the person seeking a family allowance from the estate of {{decedentName}}, who died on {{dateOfDeath}}. My relationship to {{decedentName}} is: {{relationshipToDecedent}}. This declaration relates to a proceeding in the estate of {{decedentName}}, to be filed in the Superior Court of California, County of {{countyOfFiling}}, under Probate Code §§ 6540-6545. The monthly family allowance amount I am requesting is: {{requestedAllowanceAmount}}. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual petition for family allowance. It is not itself a court filing, and signing it does not grant, modify, or set the amount of any family allowance for {{petitionerName}} or anyone else — only a court order, issued after the statutory petition and (where required) notice process described in this document, can do that.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Family Allowance Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityOfExecution}}, California.

Signature of {{petitionerName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual petition for family allowance filed with the California superior court in the administration of {{decedentName}}'s estate. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not grant, modify, terminate, or set the amount of any family allowance; only a court order does that.]

clauses.title: Who May Receive a Family Allowance, and the Standard the Court Applies
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6540(a) entitles three categories of people to a reasonable family allowance out of {{decedentName}}'s estate — an amount necessary for their maintenance according to their circumstances during administration of the estate: the surviving spouse of {{decedentName}}; {{decedentName}}'s minor children; and {{decedentName}}'s adult children who are physically or mentally incapacitated from earning a living and were actually dependent in whole or in part on {{decedentName}} for support. § 6540(b) separately allows the court, in its discretion, to give a reasonable family allowance to two further categories on the same maintenance-according-to-circumstances standard: other adult children of {{decedentName}} who were actually dependent in whole or in part on {{decedentName}} for support, and a parent of {{decedentName}} who was actually dependent in whole or in part on {{decedentName}} for support. § 6540(c) limits both categories: if a person otherwise eligible for a family allowance has reasonable maintenance from other sources and there are one or more other persons entitled to a family allowance, the allowance is granted only to those who do not have reasonable maintenance from other sources.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's family allowance procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or about whether any specific person qualifies under it. This clause quotes three parts of a single statutory section (§ 6540(a), (b), and (c)); no independent second section was found addressing eligibility itself, so this clause relies on one section only. § 6540 states the maintenance-according-to-circumstances standard as the basis for both the entitled and discretionary categories, but this statute does not itself list the specific factors a court weighs in fixing a dollar amount (for example, the estate's size or the claimant's other income) beyond that general standard; this clause does not attempt to supply factors the statute's text does not state. This document is informational: it does not itself grant a family allowance, determine any specific person's eligibility, or set any dollar amount — only a court order can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6540(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 6540(a)
citations.quote: The following are entitled to such reasonable family allowance out of the estate as is necessary for their maintenance according to their circumstances during administration of the estate: (1) The surviving spouse of the decedent. (2) Minor children of the decedent. (3) Adult children of the decedent who are physically or mentally incapacitated from earning a living and were actually dependent in whole or in part upon the decedent for support.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6540(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 6540(b)
citations.quote: The following may be given such reasonable family allowance out of the estate as the court in its discretion determines is necessary for their maintenance according to their circumstances during administration of the estate: (1) Other adult children of the decedent who were actually dependent in whole or in part upon the decedent for support. (2) A parent of the decedent who was actually dependent in whole or in part upon the decedent for support.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6540(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 6540(c)
citations.quote: If a person otherwise eligible for family allowance has a reasonable maintenance from other sources and there are one or more other persons entitled to a family allowance, the family allowance shall be granted only to those who do not have a reasonable maintenance from other sources.

clauses.title: Who May Petition, and the Ex Parte Option Before the Inventory Is Filed
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6541(a) lets the court grant or modify a family allowance for {{decedentName}}'s estate on petition of any interested person — not only the person who would receive the allowance. § 6541(b) then ties the procedure to timing relative to the inventory: before the inventory is filed, an order for the § 6540(a)-entitled allowance may be made or modified either ex parte or after notice of the hearing has been given as provided in Probate Code § 1220; after the inventory is filed, such an order may be made or modified only after that § 1220 notice has been given. § 6541(c) requires that a § 6540(b)-discretionary allowance be ordered only after § 1220 notice has been given to each person listed in § 1220, each known heir whose interest in the estate would be affected by the petition, and each known devisee whose interest in the estate would be affected by the petition.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's family allowance procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This clause quotes three subdivisions of a single statutory section (§ 6541(a), (b), and (c)); no independent second section was found addressing the petition-and-notice procedure itself. § 6541(b)(1)(A)'s ex parte option — available only before the inventory is filed, and only for the § 6540(a) categories — is the statute's mechanism for obtaining an allowance before a noticed hearing can be held; this clause does not independently verify the content of the § 1220 notice requirements themselves, referencing § 1220 only as the notice provision § 6541 points to. This document is informational: it does not itself petition for, grant, or modify any family allowance, or give any specific notice — only an actual petition, followed by a court order (and, where required, notice under § 1220), can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6541(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 6541(a)
citations.quote: The court may grant or modify a family allowance on petition of any interested person.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6541(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 6541(b)
citations.quote: With respect to an order for the family allowance provided for in subdivision (a) of Section 6540: (1) Before the inventory is filed, the order may be made or modified either (A) ex parte or (B) after notice of the hearing on the petition has been given as provided in Section 1220. (2) After the inventory is filed, the order may be made or modified only after notice of the hearing on the petition has been given as provided in Section 1220.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6541(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 6541(c)
citations.quote: An order for the family allowance provided in subdivision (b) of Section 6540 may be made only after notice of the hearing on the petition has been given as provided in Section 1220 to all of the following persons: (1) Each person listed in Section 1220. (2) Each known heir whose interest in the estate would be affected by the petition. (3) Each known devisee whose interest in the estate would be affected by the petition.

clauses.title: When a Family Allowance Begins, and How Far Back It May Reach
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6542 lets a family allowance for {{decedentName}}'s estate commence on the date of the court's order, or on such other date as the court's order provides, whether that date is before or after the date of the order, as the court in its discretion determines. The one fixed limit is that the allowance may not be made retroactive to a date earlier than {{decedentName}}'s date of death.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's family allowance procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or about what commencement date any specific court would set. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 6542); no independent second section was found addressing the commencement date itself. Read together with the companion clause on § 6541, the earliest a family allowance can practically start flowing is set by when a petition (potentially ex parte, before the inventory is filed) is granted, while the earliest date the order itself may reach back to is the decedent's date of death; this clause does not resolve, for any specific estate, how a court would exercise its discretion between those two points. This document is informational: it does not itself set any commencement date or grant any family allowance — only a court order does that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6542 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 6542
citations.quote: A family allowance commences on the date of the court’s order or such other time as may be provided in the court’s order, whether before or after the date of the order, as the court in its discretion determines, but the allowance may not be made retroactive to a date earlier than the date of the decedent’s death.

clauses.title: How Long a Family Allowance Continues
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6543(a) fixes an outer limit on a family allowance for {{decedentName}}'s estate: it must terminate no later than the entry of the order for final distribution of the estate, or, if the estate is insolvent, no later than one year after the granting of letters. Within that limit, § 6543(b) provides that the allowance continues until modified or terminated by the court, or until such time as the court's order itself provides.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's family allowance procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or about how long any specific allowance would run. This clause quotes two subdivisions of a single statutory section (§ 6543(a) and (b)); no independent second section was found addressing duration itself. This clause does not independently verify the statutory definition of estate insolvency used in § 6543(a), or the point at which letters are considered granted for purposes of that one-year outer limit. This document is informational: it does not itself continue, modify, or terminate any family allowance — only a court order (or the passage of the statutory outer limit) does that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6543(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 6543(a)
citations.quote: A family allowance shall terminate no later than the entry of the order for final distribution of the estate or, if the estate is insolvent, no later than one year after the granting of letters.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6543(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 6543(b)
citations.quote: Subject to subdivision (a), a family allowance shall continue until modified or terminated by the court or until such time as the court may provide in its order.

clauses.title: The Estate, Not the Petitioner Personally, Bears the Costs of a Family Allowance Proceeding
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6544 provides that the costs of proceedings under the family allowance chapter — the chapter under which a petition for {{decedentName}}'s estate would be brought — are paid by the estate as expenses of administration.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's family allowance procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or about what specific costs any specific petition would generate. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 6544); no independent second section was found addressing costs of the proceeding itself. This clause does not address attorney's fees separately from costs, and does not independently verify how 'expenses of administration' is defined elsewhere in the Probate Code for purposes of this section. This document is informational: it does not itself allocate any specific cost to any specific estate — only a court order does that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6544 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 6544
citations.quote: The costs of proceedings under this chapter shall be paid by the estate as expenses of administration.

clauses.title: Where a Family Allowance Ranks Among the Estate's Other Debts
clauses.body: Probate Code § 11420(a) sets a fixed order of priority in which {{decedentName}}'s estate's debts are paid, apart from debts owed to the United States or California that have their own statutory preference: (1) expenses of administration; (2) obligations secured by a mortgage, deed of trust, or other lien, so far as payable from the proceeds of the property securing them; (3) funeral expenses; (4) expenses of last illness; (5) family allowance; (6) wage claims; and (7) general debts, including unsecured judgments and all other debts not included in a prior class. A family allowance therefore ranks below expenses of administration, secured obligations, funeral expenses, and expenses of last illness, but ahead of wage claims and general debts. § 11420(b) provides that debts within the same class are paid without preference over one another, that no debt of any class may be paid until all debts of prior classes are paid in full, and that if estate property is insufficient to pay a class in full, each debt in that class is paid a proportionate share.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's debt-payment priority scheme — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or about whether any specific estate's assets are sufficient to reach the family-allowance class. This clause quotes two subdivisions of a single statutory section (§ 11420(a) and (b)); no independent second section was found addressing this priority order itself. This clause condenses § 11420(a)'s seven-class list and omits the full text of class (2) (the treatment of secured obligations and any shortfall reclassified as a general debt) beyond the summary given here; the full text is available at the cited source. This document is informational: it does not itself pay any debt, allowance, or class of claims, or determine solvency for any specific estate — only the personal representative's administration of the estate, under court supervision where required, does that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 11420(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Debts shall be paid in the following order of priority among classes of debts, except that debts owed to the United States or to this state that have preference under the laws of the United States or of this state shall be given the preference required by such laws: (1) Expenses of administration.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 11420(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (3) Funeral expenses. (4) Expenses of last illness. (5) Family allowance. (6) Wage claims. (7) General debts, including judgments not secured by a lien and all other debts not included in a prior class.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 11420(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by statute, the debts of each class are without preference or priority one over another. No debt of any class may be paid until all those of prior classes are paid in full. If property in the estate is insufficient to pay all debts of any class in full, each debt in that class shall be paid a proportionate share.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: {{preparerName}}, whose relationship to {{decedentName}} is {{relationshipToDecedent}}, is reviewing this information sheet in connection with the estate of {{decedentName}}. This sheet explains, on a general informational basis only, California's statutory protections for a spouse who married {{decedentName}}, or a child born to or adopted by {{decedentName}}, after {{decedentName}} signed a will or created a revocable trust that later became irrevocable — protections that come into play when an estate plan is never updated to add that spouse or child. These are commonly called "omitted spouse" and "omitted (pretermitted) heir" statutes. This sheet states general facts about how those statutes work, including the exceptions that can defeat them. It does not identify whether any specific spouse or child actually qualifies as "omitted" under {{decedentName}}'s actual estate plan, and it does not advise {{preparerName}} or anyone else on what to do about any actual situation.

clauses.title: Which Instruments These Protections Reach
clauses.body: These omitted-spouse and omitted-child protections are not limited to a will. They apply to property passing by will through a decedent's estate, and separately to property passing under a trust — but only a trust that became irrevocable solely because the settlor died, not a trust that was already irrevocable for some other reason during the settlor's lifetime. A trust that remained revocable by {{decedentName}} until death, then locked into place at death, is treated the same way a will is treated for this purpose.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute defining which instruments these omitted-heir protections reach — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate plan. The statute cross-references the Probate Code's general definition of "trust" in Section 82; that separate definitional section is not independently quoted here, only the irrevocability distinction actually stated in Section 21600.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21600 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the instruments these protections reach
citations.quote: This part shall apply to property passing by will through a decedent’s estate or by a trust, as defined in Section 82, that becomes irrevocable only on the death of the settlor.

clauses.title: The Omitted Spouse's Default Share
clauses.body: If {{decedentName}} married someone after signing all of {{decedentName}}'s testamentary instruments — a term that includes both a will and a qualifying trust of the kind described above — and the estate plan was never updated to provide for that spouse, California law entitles the omitted spouse, unless one of the exceptions described in the next clause applies, to a default share of the estate: one-half of the community property belonging to {{decedentName}}, one-half of the quasi-community property belonging to {{decedentName}}, and a share of {{decedentName}}'s separate property equal in value to what the spouse would have received had {{decedentName}} died with no will or trust at all — capped at one-half of the separate property in the estate.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, automatic default — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate plan. This share is calculated differently from the omitted child's share described further below: the spouse's default share draws on California's community-property framework (half of community and quasi-community property, plus a capped intestate-equivalent share of separate property), while the child's default share is simply the child's full intestate share, with no comparable cap.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21610 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the omitted spouse's default share
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 21611, if a decedent fails to provide in a testamentary instrument for the decedent’s surviving spouse who married the decedent after the execution of all of the decedent’s testamentary instruments, the omitted spouse shall receive a share in the decedent’s estate, consisting of the following property in said estate: (a) The one-half of the community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 100. (b) The one-half of the quasi-community property that belongs to the decedent under Section 101. (c) A share of the separate property of the decedent equal in value to that which the spouse would have received if the decedent had died without having executed a testamentary instrument, but in no event is the share to be more than one-half the value of the separate property in the estate.

clauses.title: When the Omitted Spouse's Share Doesn't Apply
clauses.body: The omitted spouse's default share does not apply if any of several things is established: that {{decedentName}}'s failure to provide for the spouse was intentional and that intention appears from the testamentary instruments; that {{decedentName}} provided for the spouse through a transfer outside the estate plan, with intent that the transfer replace a provision in it; that the spouse signed a valid agreement waiving the right to share in the estate; or — a narrower anti-abuse rule — that the spouse was a paid "care custodian" who provided health or social services to {{decedentName}} as a legally defined "dependent adult" (broadly, someone 65 or older unable to properly provide for their own physical needs or with certain cognitive deficits, or someone 18 or older with substantial difficulty managing finances or resisting fraud or undue influence because of a cognitive deficit), where the marriage began while that care was being provided or within 90 days after it ended, and {{decedentName}} died less than six months after the marriage began — unless the spouse proves by clear and convincing evidence that the marriage was not the product of fraud or undue influence. A person who had an unpaid, personal relationship with the dependent adult predating certain statutory time thresholds is excluded from the definition of "care custodian" altogether.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific, real limits on the omitted spouse's default share — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate plan. Two of these exceptions (an intentional omission shown in the instrument itself, and an outside transfer meant to replace a provision in it) have direct counterparts among the omitted-child exceptions described further below; the waiver-agreement exception and the care-custodian anti-abuse rule do not — the statute contains no equivalent "valid agreement" or care-custodian carve-out on the omitted-child side. The "care custodian" and "dependent adult" definitions quoted here are incorporated by cross-reference from a different part of the Probate Code (the presumption-of-fraud-or-undue-influence statutes, §§ 21360–21392) rather than defined within the omitted-spouse chapter itself.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21611 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, when the omitted-spouse share doesn't apply
citations.quote: The spouse shall not receive a share of the estate under Section 21610 if any of the following is established: (a) The decedent’s failure to provide for the spouse in the decedent’s testamentary instruments was intentional and that intention appears from the testamentary instruments. (b) The decedent provided for the spouse by transfer outside of the estate passing by the decedent’s testamentary instruments and the intention that the transfer be in lieu of a provision in said instruments is shown by statements of the decedent or from the amount of the transfer or by other evidence. (c) The spouse made a valid agreement waiving the right to share in the decedent’s estate. (d) (1) If both of the following apply: (A) The spouse was a care custodian, as that term is defined in Section 21362, of the decedent who was a dependent adult, as that term is defined in Section 21366, and the marriage commenced while the care custodian provided services to the decedent, or within 90 days after those services were last provided to the decedent. (B) The decedent died less than six months after the marriage commenced. (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), a spouse described by this subdivision shall be entitled to receive a share of the estate pursuant to Section 21610 if the spouse proves by clear and convincing evidence that the marriage between the spouse and the decedent was not the product of fraud or undue influence.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21362 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the definition of "care custodian"
citations.quote: “Care custodian” means a person who provides health or social services to a dependent adult, except that “care custodian” does not include a person who provided services without remuneration if the person had a personal relationship with the dependent adult (1) at least 90 days before providing those services, (2) at least six months before the dependent adult’s death, and (3) before the dependant adult was admitted to hospice care, if the dependent adult was admitted to hospice care.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21366 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the definition of "dependent adult" used by the care-custodian carve-out
citations.quote: “Dependent adult” means a person who, at the time of executing the instrument at issue under this part, was a person described in either of the following: (a) The person was 65 years of age or older and satisfied one or both of the following criteria: (1) The person was unable to provide properly for his or her personal needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter. (2) Due to one or more deficits in the mental functions listed in paragraphs (1) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (a) of Section 811, the person had difficulty managing his or her own financial resources or resisting fraud or undue influence. (b) The person was 18 years of age or older and satisfied one or both of the following criteria: (1) The person was unable to provide properly for his or her personal needs for physical health, food, clothing, or shelter. (2) Due to one or more deficits in the mental functions listed in paragraphs (1) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (a) of Section 811, the person had substantial difficulty managing his or her own financial resources or resisting fraud or undue influence.

clauses.title: The Omitted Child's Default Share
clauses.body: A child of {{decedentName}} who is born or adopted after {{decedentName}} signed all of {{decedentName}}'s testamentary instruments, and who isn't provided for in them, is entitled by default — unless an exception described in the next clause applies — to a share of the estate equal in value to what that child would have received had {{decedentName}} died with no will or qualifying trust at all. The same default share reaches a child who was already alive when the instruments were signed but was left out solely because {{decedentName}} believed the child was dead or did not know the child had been born.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, automatic protection for an after-born, after-adopted, or unknown-and-presumed-dead child — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate plan. Unlike the omitted spouse's share described above, which is calculated using the community-property framework and capped at half the separate property, the omitted child's share is simply the child's full intestate share, with no comparable cap. A child already provided for elsewhere in the estate plan, or left out for a reason other than these two specific circumstances, is not an "omitted child" under this statute at all. The two citations below are separate, independently numbered sections of the same statutory chapter rather than independently authored sources.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21620 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the omitted after-born or after-adopted child's default share
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 21621, if a decedent fails to provide in a testamentary instrument for a child of decedent born or adopted after the execution of all of the decedent’s testamentary instruments, the omitted child shall receive a share in the decedent’s estate equal in value to that which the child would have received if the decedent had died without having executed any testamentary instrument.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21622 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, a child the decedent believed dead or didn't know about
citations.quote: If, at the time of the execution of all of decedent’s testamentary instruments effective at the time of decedent’s death, the decedent failed to provide for a living child solely because the decedent believed the child to be dead or was unaware of the birth of the child, the child shall receive a share in the estate equal in value to that which the child would have received if the decedent had died without having executed any testamentary instruments.

clauses.title: When the Omitted Child's Share Doesn't Apply
clauses.body: The omitted child's default share does not apply if any of the following is established: that {{decedentName}}'s failure to provide for the child was intentional and that intention appears from the testamentary instruments; that {{decedentName}} had one or more children and left substantially all of the estate to the omitted child's other parent; or that {{decedentName}} provided for the child through a transfer outside the estate plan, with intent that the transfer replace a provision in it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific, real limits on the omitted child's default share — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate plan. This section was amended effective January 1, 2025 (Stats. 2024, Ch. 80, Sec. 108.5); the quote below reflects that current, in-force text, independently re-verified rather than assumed unchanged. The "other parent" exception has no counterpart among the omitted-spouse exceptions described above, and the omitted-spouse chapter's care-custodian anti-abuse rule and waiver-agreement exception have no counterpart here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21621 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, when the omitted-child share doesn't apply
citations.quote: A child shall not receive a share of the estate under Section 21620 if any of the following is established: (a) The decedent’s failure to provide for the child in the decedent’s testamentary instruments was intentional and that intention appears from the testamentary instruments. (b) The decedent had one or more children and devised or otherwise directed the disposition of substantially all the estate to the other parent of the omitted child. (c) The decedent provided for the child by transfer outside of the estate passing by the decedent’s testamentary instruments and the intention that the transfer be in lieu of a provision in said instruments is shown by statements of the decedent or from the amount of the transfer or by other evidence.

clauses.title: How an Omitted Share Is Actually Paid
clauses.body: Once an omitted spouse's or omitted child's share is established, the law sets a specific order for satisfying it: the share is drawn first from any part of {{decedentName}}'s estate that isn't disposed of by the will or trust, and only if that isn't enough is the remainder taken proportionally from everyone who takes under {{decedentName}}'s testamentary instruments, based on the value each would otherwise receive, measured as of the date of death. If applying that proportional reduction would defeat the obvious intent behind some specific gift or provision, that gift or provision can be exempted from the reduction and a different apportionment, more consistent with the intent behind it, adopted instead.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how an omitted spouse's or omitted child's share is actually satisfied once established — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate plan. This apportionment mechanism applies identically to both the omitted-spouse share (addressed in the chapter governing Sections 21610–21612) and the omitted-child share (addressed in the chapter governing Sections 21620–21623); the statute treats the two the same at this satisfaction stage, even though it treats them differently at the entitlement and exceptions stages described in the clauses above.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21623 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, how an omitted share is satisfied
citations.quote: (a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), in satisfying a share provided by this chapter: (1) The share will first be taken from the decedent’s estate not disposed of by will or trust, if any. (2) If that is not sufficient, so much as may be necessary to satisfy the share shall be taken from all beneficiaries of decedent’s testamentary instruments in proportion to the value they may respectively receive. The proportion of each beneficiary’s share that may be taken pursuant to this subdivision shall be determined based on values as of the date of the decedent’s death. (b) If the obvious intention of the decedent in relation to some specific gift or devise or other provision of a testamentary instrument would be defeated by the application of subdivision (a), the specific devise or gift or provision of a testamentary instrument may be exempted from the apportionment under subdivision (a), and a different apportionment, consistent with the intention of the decedent, may be adopted.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Toxic Mold Protection Act of 2001 (Health & Safety Code §§ 26100-26157) as it may apply to the property at {{propertyAddress}}, as between {{sellerLandlordName}} and {{buyerTenantName}}. It states what California law provides on this subject, including the ways the Act's own disclosure duties are conditioned on regulatory action that this document reports has not, as of the date below, been shown to have occurred. It does not authorize, direct, or prohibit any particular disclosure, and it does not tell either {{sellerLandlordName}} or {{buyerTenantName}} what to do about any specific condition at the property.

clauses.title: The Toxic Mold Protection Act and the Department's Role
clauses.body: California's Health and Safety Code chapter on toxic mold is officially titled the Toxic Mold Protection Act of 2001. The Act designates the department -- defined in the statute as the State Department of Health Services -- as the lead agency for adopting permissible exposure limits to mold in indoor environments, mold identification and remediation efforts, and guidelines for what constitutes mold infestation. In a later, separate statutory reorganization, the State Department of Public Health was made the successor to, and vested with, the duties and functions of the former State Department of Health Services as they relate to public health. Before the department is required to adopt permissible exposure limits, the statute first directs it to consider whether doing so is feasible.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides on toxic mold regulation -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's property. The two citations to Health & Safety Code § 26101 and § 26102 are subsections/sections within the same chapter of the same code and are not independent sources of each other; the citation to § 131050 is a separate, independently enacted statutory section addressing the 2007 state health-agency reorganization, offered as a genuinely independent source for the successor-agency point (not as corroboration of §§ 26101-26102). This document does not independently verify the department's current internal organization, name, or any regulations it may have adopted outside the statutory text itself -- only the statutory text was checked.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26100 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health and Safety Code, short title of the Act
citations.quote: This chapter shall be known, and may be cited, as the Toxic Mold Protection Act of 2001.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26101(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health and Safety Code, definition of "department" as lead agency
citations.quote: “Department” means the State Department of Health Services, designated as the lead agency in the adoption of permissible exposure limits to mold in indoor environments, mold identification and remediation efforts, and the development of guidelines for the determination of what constitutes mold infestation.

citations.quote: the State Department of Public Health shall succeed to and be vested with all the duties, powers, purposes, functions, responsibilities, and jurisdiction of the former State Department of Health Services as they relate to public health

citations.quote: The department shall consider the feasibility of adopting permissible exposure limits to mold in indoor environments.

clauses.title: The Act's Standards, Guidelines, and Funding-Contingent Structure
clauses.body: The Act's substantive framework -- permissible exposure limits, health-threat assessment standards, and identification and remediation guidelines -- is not self-executing. By the statute's own terms, the department is only required to adopt permissible exposure limits "if the department finds that adopting permissible exposure limits to mold in indoor environments is feasible." Several of the Act's own disclosure provisions, including the residential landlord disclosure duty, then state that their own requirements "shall not apply until the first January 1 or July 1 that occurs at least six months after the department adopts standards pursuant to Sections 26103 and 26105 and develops guidelines pursuant to Section 26130" -- meaning those specific disclosure duties are, by the statute's own text, contingent on the department having first adopted those standards and guidelines. Separately, the Act's implementation article states that the entire chapter "shall be implemented only to the extent that the department determines that funds are available for the implementation of this chapter."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's property. The four citations below are to four different, independently enacted statutory sections within the same chapter (§§ 26102, 26103, 26147, 26156), not different subdivisions of one section, and are treated here as separate sources; note, however, that the quoted "shall not apply until..." triggering sentence in § 26147(e) recurs, in essentially identical wording, in several other sections of the same Article 4 (including §§ 26140(d), 26141(e), 26142(b), 26143(b), 26145(b), and 26146(d)) -- this document cites only the § 26147 instance as representative rather than treating each repetition as an independently corroborating source. This document reports what the statutory text itself says about the conditions under which the department's standards, guidelines, and the resulting disclosure duties take effect; it does not independently verify -- from the department's own current regulations, website, or any other source outside this statutory text -- whether the department has in fact adopted permissible exposure limits, assessment standards, or guidelines as of the checked date. A reader who needs to know the department's current regulatory status should consult the department directly or its current regulations, not this document.

clauses.title: Residential Landlord Disclosure of Known Mold
clauses.body: Subject to the conditions described elsewhere in this information sheet, California law requires a residential landlord to provide written disclosure to prospective and current tenants of an affected unit when the landlord "knows, or has reasonable cause to believe," that mold -- visible or hidden -- is present that affects the unit or building and either exceeds the permissible exposure limits established under Section 26103 or poses a health threat under the department's guidelines developed under Section 26105. A residential landlord is not required to conduct air or surface testing to determine whether mold exceeds those exposure limits. Where the duty applies, written disclosure must be provided to prospective tenants before they enter into the rental or lease agreement, and to current tenants of an affected unit as soon as reasonably practical. A residential landlord is exempt from the disclosure duty to prospective tenants if the mold was remediated according to the department's mold remediation guidelines developed under Section 26130.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a residential landlord's mold disclosure duty -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy. All four citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (§ 26147) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was sought for the elements of this specific duty. As described in this document's other clauses, § 26147(e) itself states that these requirements do not apply until at least six months after the department has adopted standards under Sections 26103 and 26105 and developed guidelines under Section 26130 -- a condition this document does not independently verify has been satisfied. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine whether any specific landlord knew or had reasonable cause to believe mold was present, or whether any specific disclosure was required or adequate.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26147(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health and Safety Code, the core residential landlord disclosure duty
citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivisions (b), (d), and (e), residential landlords shall provide written disclosure to prospective and current tenants of the affected units as specified in subdivision (b) when the residential landlord knows, or has reasonable cause to believe, that mold, both visible and invisible or hidden, is present that affects the unit or the building and the mold either exceeds the permissible exposure limits to molds established by subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) of Section 26103 or poses a health threat according to the department’s guidelines as developed pursuant to Section 26105.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 26147(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health and Safety Code, no air or surface testing required
citations.quote: (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), a residential landlord shall not be required to conduct air or surface tests of units or buildings to determine whether the presence of molds exceeds the permissible exposure limits to molds established by subdivisions (a) and (b) of Section 26103.

citations.cite: Health and Safety Code, timing of the written disclosure
citations.quote: (c) The written disclosure required by subdivision (a) shall be provided: (1) To prospective tenants prior to entering into the rental or lease agreement. (2) To current tenants in affected units as soon as is reasonably practical.

citations.quote: (d) A residential landlord shall be exempt from providing written disclosure to prospective tenants pursuant to this section if the presence of mold was remediated according to the mold remediation guidelines developed by the department pursuant to Section 26130.

clauses.title: Residential Landlord Consumer Booklet Disclosure
clauses.body: Separately from the disclosure duty described elsewhere in this information sheet, California law also directs residential landlords to provide prospective tenants with written disclosure of the potential health risks and health impact that may result from mold exposure, by distributing a consumer-oriented booklet developed and disseminated by the department, before the tenant enters into the rental or lease agreement. This booklet-distribution duty, like the disclosure duty described elsewhere in this information sheet, does not apply until at least six months after the department approves the consumer-oriented booklet.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a residential landlord's booklet-disclosure duty -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy. The two citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (§ 26148) rather than independently authored sources. This document does not independently verify whether the department has in fact approved a consumer-oriented booklet as of the checked date -- only the statutory text conditioning the duty on that approval was checked. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine whether any specific landlord's booklet-distribution duty has taken effect.

citations.cite: Health and Safety Code, residential landlord consumer-booklet disclosure duty
citations.quote: (a) Residential landlords shall provide written disclosure to prospective tenants of the potential health risks and the health impact that may result from exposure to mold by distributing a consumer-oriented booklet developed and disseminated by the department.

citations.cite: Health and Safety Code, booklet duty delayed until department approves the booklet
citations.quote: (c) The requirements of this section shall not apply until the first January 1 or July 1 that occurs at least six months after the department approves the consumer-oriented booklet, as described in subdivision (a).

clauses.title: Scope: The Act's Sale-Related Disclosure Duty Covers Commercial and Industrial Property, Not Residential Sales
clauses.body: The Act's specific disclosure duty tied to a property sale applies to a "seller or transferor of commercial or industrial real property," who must disclose known mold meeting the same exceeds-limits-or-health-threat standard described elsewhere in this information sheet to prospective buyers as soon as practicable before transfer of title. The Act does not contain a parallel, mold-specific disclosure section addressed to the seller of residential real property. The Act separately states that nothing in its disclosure article relieves any seller, transferor, lessor, agent, landlord, or tenant of other existing legal obligations, including specified Civil Code duties and any other duties under common law, and that nothing in the article affects the existing obligation of parties to a real estate contract, or their agents, to disclose facts materially affecting the value and desirability of the property.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's transaction. The three citations below are to three different, independently enacted statutory sections within the same Article 4 (§§ 26140, 26149, 26150), not subdivisions of one section, and are treated here as separate sources. This document reports only that the Act's own mold-specific sale-disclosure section names commercial and industrial property, and that the Act separately preserves other, non-Act disclosure obligations without describing what those other obligations are; it does not independently verify the content, scope, or applicability of any other disclosure statute (including the Civil Code sections referenced in §§ 26149-26150) to a residential sale, and does not address whether or how a residential seller's general disclosure duties might reach a known mold condition. This document is informational only and does not determine any party's disclosure obligations in a specific transaction.

citations.quote: (a) Nothing in this article shall relieve a seller, transferor, lessor, agent, landlord, or tenant from any responsibility for compliance with other obligations, laws, ordinances, codes, or regulations, including but not limited to the duties outlined in Sections 1941 and 1941.1 of the Civil Code and any other duties provided for under common law.

citations.quote: Nothing in this article shall affect the existing obligations of the parties or transferor to a real estate contract, or their agents, to disclose any facts materially affecting the value and desirability of the property, including, but not limited to, the physical conditions of the property and previously received reports of physical inspections noted on the disclosure form set forth in Section 1102.6 or 1102.6a of the Civil Code.

clauses.title: Liability Limitation and Enforcement
clauses.body: California law limits liability for an error, inaccuracy, or omission in information delivered under the Act's disclosure article: neither the transferor nor any listing or selling agent is liable for such an error if it was not within their personal knowledge, or was based on information timely provided by public agencies or by other persons delivering a report or opinion within the scope of their professional license or expertise, provided ordinary care was exercised in obtaining and transmitting the information. On enforcement, designated public health officers, code enforcement officers, environmental health officers, city attorneys, and other appropriate government entities may respond to complaints about mold and enforce the disclosure requirements described elsewhere in this information sheet. No penalty may be assessed against an owner for failure to disclose under the residential landlord disclosure section if the owner provides disclosure to tenants in a form that substantially conforms to the disclosure form the department develops.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides on liability limitation and enforcement for mold disclosures -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's property. The two citations below are to two different, independently enacted statutory sections (§§ 26153 and 26154), not subdivisions of one section, and are treated here as separate sources. This document does not independently verify whether the department has adopted the disclosure form or the "disclosure enforcement guidelines" that § 26154 itself makes a precondition to local enforcement authority, nor does it address any liability theory outside this specific statutory liability limitation (such as common-law negligence, fraud, or habitability claims, or liability under the Civil Code duties preserved by §§ 26149-26150). This document is informational only; it does not itself determine whether any specific error, omission, or disclosure was made with ordinary care, or whether any specific disclosure substantially conforms to a department-developed form.

clauses.title: About This Heat Illness Prevention Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Heat Illness Prevention — Information Sheet describes California's Cal/OSHA heat illness prevention standards for outdoor places of employment, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395, and for indoor places of employment, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396, as those requirements relate to the working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.

It summarizes selected requirements of those two regulations: which outdoor and indoor workplaces they cover and at what temperatures, the requirement to provide access to drinking water, the requirement to provide access to shade (outdoors) or a cool-down area (indoors), the additional procedures required at higher temperature thresholds, the requirement to closely observe newly assigned and heat-wave-exposed employees during an acclimatization period, the training that must be given to employees and supervisors, and the requirement to maintain a written Heat Illness Prevention Plan.

This topic is distinct from this corpus's Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) — Information Sheet, which describes California's general written workplace-safety-program requirement under Labor Code § 6401.7 and 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, and from this corpus's Workplace Violence Prevention Plan — Information Sheet, which describes a different specific workplace hazard under Labor Code § 6401.9. Both the outdoor and indoor heat illness standards state that their required measures may instead be integrated into an employer's IIPP.

{{companyName}} has identified {{programAdministratorName}} as the person responsible for heat illness prevention matters described in this information sheet.

This information sheet is not itself {{companyName}}'s written Heat Illness Prevention Plan, does not itself satisfy 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395's or § 3396's written-plan requirement, and does not determine that any particular practice of {{companyName}}'s is or is not compliant with California law.

clauses.title: Which Outdoor and Indoor Workplaces Are Covered
clauses.body:
California has two separate Cal/OSHA heat illness prevention regulations, one for outdoor places of employment and one for indoor places of employment. The outdoor standard, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(a)(1), states that it 'shall apply to all outdoor places of employment.' Within that broad outdoor coverage, § 3395(a)(2) lists a narrower set of industries that must also comply with the standard's high-heat procedures (addressed in a companion clause of this information sheet): agriculture, construction, landscaping, oil and gas extraction, and the transportation or delivery of agricultural products, construction materials, or other heavy materials. An employer in an industry not on that list is not required to comply with the high-heat-procedures subsection, per the exception stated directly under § 3395(a)(1).

The indoor standard, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396(a)(1), applies on its own terms to 'all indoor work areas where the temperature equals or exceeds 82 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present.' A narrower set of conditions then triggers full coverage under the indoor standard, including its assessment-and-control-measures subsection: § 3396(a)(2)(A) provides that full coverage applies where 'the temperature equals or exceeds 87 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present,' and the same subsection separately triggers full coverage where the heat index reaches 87 degrees Fahrenheit, where employees wear clothing that restricts heat removal and the temperature reaches 82 degrees Fahrenheit, or where employees work in a high radiant heat area at 82 degrees Fahrenheit. The indoor standard also states exceptions for teleworking from a location not under the employer's control, for certain brief incidental heat exposures, for emergency operations, and for specified state and local confinement facilities.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two formally independent Cal/OSHA regulations — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395 (outdoor) and § 3396 (indoor) — codified and adopted separately, not two subdivisions of one section; each section's own quotations in this clause, however, are drawn from subdivisions of that same section (§ 3395(a)(1) and (a)(2) are both part of § 3395; § 3396(a)(1) and (a)(2)(A) are both part of § 3396), so within each regulation the citations are not independent corroborating sources of each other. This document did not independently quote the indoor standard's teleworking, incidental-exposure, emergency-operations, or confinement-facility exceptions, or its 'Order to Take Special Action' provision in § 3396(a)(3); they are described here only in summary based on the fetched text, and their precise conditions and exact wording are not reproduced as citations. This is a description of what these regulations require in general, not a determination of whether any specific workplace of the employer's is or is not covered.

clauses.title: Access to Drinking Water
clauses.body: Both the outdoor and indoor standards impose the same core drinking-water access requirement in nearly identical language. The outdoor standard, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(c), requires that 'Employees shall have access to potable drinking water meeting the requirements of Sections 1524, 3363, and 3457, as applicable, including but not limited to the requirements that it be fresh, pure, suitably cool, and provided to employees free of charge.' The indoor standard, § 3396(c), states the same requirement using the same cross-referenced sections. Both standards further require that where drinking water is not plumbed or otherwise continuously supplied, it 'shall be provided in sufficient quantity at the beginning of the work shift to provide one quart per employee per hour for drinking for the entire shift,' quoting § 3395(c); § 3396(c) states the identical one-quart-per-employee-per-hour quantity requirement, and both allow an employer to begin a shift with a smaller quantity if it has effective procedures to replenish water during the shift as needed.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes both § 3395(c) and § 3396(c) because they are formally independent regulations, each separately adopted, even though their water-access language is nearly identical to one another; within each regulation, the quotations are drawn from a single subdivision, (c), not from separate independent parts of that regulation. This clause does not quote or independently verify the specific technical water-quality requirements of the cross-referenced sections — 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 1524, 3363, and 3457 — which were not separately fetched for this document; it states only that the heat illness standards themselves cross-reference those sections. This is a description of a general regulatory requirement, not a determination of whether water has actually been made available at any particular worksite.

clauses.title: Access to Shade (Outdoors) and Cool-Down Areas (Indoors)
clauses.body:
The outdoor standard ties the shade requirement to a specific temperature threshold. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(d)(1) states: 'Shade shall be present when the temperature exceeds 80 degrees Fahrenheit.' Once that threshold is crossed, the employer must maintain one or more shaded areas at all times employees are present, and the amount of shade present 'shall be at least enough to accommodate the number of employees on recovery or rest periods, so that they can sit in a normal posture fully in the shade without having to be in physical contact with each other,' per the same subdivision. Below 80 degrees Fahrenheit, § 3395(d)(2) requires the employer either to provide shade on the same terms or to provide timely access to shade upon an employee's request. Employees must be allowed and encouraged to take a preventative cool-down rest in the shade whenever they feel the need to do so, per § 3395(d)(3).

The indoor standard uses the term 'cool-down area' rather than shade, and adds a temperature ceiling for that area. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396(d)(1) requires the employer to have and maintain one or more cool-down areas at all times employees are present, sized on the same normal-posture, no-physical-contact standard as the outdoor shade requirement, and states that 'the temperature in indoor cool-down areas shall be maintained at less than 82 degrees Fahrenheit, unless the employer demonstrates it is infeasible.'
clauses.gap: This clause quotes both § 3395(d) and § 3396(d) because they are formally independent regulations; within § 3395, the two quoted passages are both drawn from subdivision (d)(1), not from independent parts of that regulation. The outdoor standard's shade-adequacy definition (what counts as sufficient blockage of sunlight, found in § 3395(b)'s definition of 'Shade') and the indoor standard's parallel 'cool-down area' definition in § 3396(b)(4) were reviewed in the course of this research but are not separately quoted or summarized in this clause; readers should not assume this clause states every detail of either definition. This is a description of a general regulatory requirement, not a determination of whether shade or a cool-down area has actually been provided at any particular worksite.

citations.quote: Shade shall be present when the temperature exceeds 80 degrees Fahrenheit.

clauses.title: Additional Requirements at Higher Temperatures
clauses.body:
Both standards impose additional obligations once the temperature crosses a second, higher threshold, beyond the water and shade/cool-down requirements described elsewhere in this information sheet. Under the outdoor standard, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(e) provides: 'The employer shall implement high-heat procedures when the temperature equals or exceeds 95 degrees Fahrenheit,' and those procedures — required only of the specific industries listed in § 3395(a)(2) — include maintaining effective communication with employees, observing employees for signs of heat illness, designating employees authorized to call for emergency medical services, reminding employees to drink water, and holding pre-shift meetings. For employees in agriculture specifically, § 3395(e)(6) requires that 'the employer shall ensure that the employee takes a minimum ten minute net preventative cool-down rest period every two hours' once temperatures reach 95 degrees or above.

The indoor standard instead requires the employer to measure temperature and heat index and apply control measures once a work area meets one of the § 3396(a)(2) conditions described in a companion clause of this information sheet. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396(e)(2)(A) requires that 'Engineering controls shall be used to reduce and maintain both the temperature and heat index to below 87 degrees Fahrenheit when employees are present, or to reduce the temperature to below 82 degrees Fahrenheit where employees wear clothing that restricts heat removal or work in high radiant heat areas, except to the extent that the employer demonstrates such controls are infeasible.' Where feasible engineering controls are not sufficient to reach those thresholds, the same subdivision requires the use of administrative controls and, where still insufficient, personal heat-protective equipment.
clauses.gap: This clause describes two distinct regulatory mechanisms that both key off elevated temperature but are not the same requirement: the outdoor standard's 'high-heat procedures' at 95 degrees Fahrenheit (a fixed, industry-limited list of procedural obligations), and the indoor standard's tiered engineering-control, administrative-control, and personal-protective-equipment hierarchy aimed at keeping the workplace below 87 (or 82) degrees Fahrenheit. This clause does not independently quote or summarize every high-heat procedure listed in § 3395(e)(1) through (e)(5), or the indoor standard's administrative-control and personal-heat-protective-equipment provisions in § 3396(e)(2)(B) and (e)(2)(C) beyond noting that they apply when engineering controls are insufficient; those provisions were reviewed but are not reproduced as citations here. Both quoted § 3395 passages come from the same regulatory section (subdivisions (e) and (e)(6)) and are not independent of one another; the § 3396 quotation is drawn from the separate, independent regulation, § 3396(e)(2)(A). This is a description of a general regulatory requirement, not a determination of whether any particular workplace of the employer's has reached these thresholds or has implemented these measures.

clauses.title: Acclimatization and Training Requirements
clauses.body:
Both standards define 'Acclimatization' the same way and require close observation of employees during an acclimatization period. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(b) defines it as temporary adaptation of the body to work in the heat, and states: 'Acclimatization peaks in most people within four to fourteen days of regular work for at least two hours per day in the heat.' Consistent with that timeframe, § 3395(g)(2) requires that 'An employee who has been newly assigned to a high heat area shall be closely observed by a supervisor or designee for the first 14 days of the employee's employment,' and § 3395(g)(1) separately requires close observation of all employees during a defined 'heat wave.' The indoor standard imposes a parallel 14-day observation requirement in § 3396(g)(2): 'An employee who has been newly assigned to any of the following shall be closely observed by a supervisor or designee for the first 14 days of employment,' tied to the same temperature and work-condition triggers described in a companion clause of this information sheet.

Both standards also require employee and supervisor training before work that should reasonably be anticipated to expose the employee to the risk of heat illness. 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(h)(1) requires that 'Effective training in the following topics shall be provided to each supervisory and non-supervisory employee before the employee begins work that should reasonably be anticipated to result in exposure to the risk of heat illness,' covering environmental and personal risk factors, the employer's water/shade/cool-down/first-aid procedures, the importance of frequent water consumption, and, per § 3395(h)(1)(D), 'The concept, importance, and methods of acclimatization pursuant to the employer's procedures.' Both standards require separate supervisor training on those same topics plus supervisor-specific procedures, and § 3396 further requires training on the additional control measures the indoor standard adds.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two formally independent regulations, § 3395 (outdoor) and § 3396 (indoor); the 14-day observation quotations from each section are drawn from a single subdivision within that section, (g)(2), and are not independent of the other quotations from the same section used elsewhere in this clause. This clause does not independently quote every training topic listed in § 3395(h)(1)(A) through (I) or § 3396(h)(1)(A) through (I) — only the risk-factor, acclimatization, and general training-trigger language is quoted; the remaining listed topics (signs and symptoms of heat illness, reporting procedures, emergency-response and emergency-medical-services procedures) are described only in summary based on the fetched text. This clause also does not independently quote the supervisor-training subdivisions, § 3395(h)(2) and § 3396(h)(2), beyond stating that they exist and require training on the same and supervisor-specific topics. This is a description of a general regulatory requirement, not a determination of whether any particular employee or supervisor of the employer's has received this training or has been observed as the regulations describe.

clauses.title: The Written Heat Illness Prevention Plan Requirement
clauses.body:
Both standards require a written plan, and both allow that plan to be folded into an employer's existing Injury and Illness Prevention Program. For outdoor workplaces, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3395(i) states: 'The employer shall establish, implement, and maintain, an effective heat illness prevention plan,' and separately requires: 'The plan shall be in writing in both English and the language understood by the majority of the employees and shall be made available at the worksite to employees and to representatives of the Division upon request.' The same subdivision states that this Heat Illness Prevention Plan 'may be included as part of the employer's Illness and Injury Prevention Program required by section 3203,' and must at minimum contain procedures for water and shade, the high-heat procedures, emergency response procedures, and acclimatization methods.

For indoor workplaces, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3396(i) imposes the same core written-plan duty: 'The employer shall establish, implement, and maintain an effective Heat Illness Prevention Plan.' It likewise permits that plan to be included as part of the employer's IIPP under § 3203 or its outdoor Heat Illness Prevention Plan under § 3395, and requires the plan to contain, at minimum, procedures for water, cool-down areas, the temperature/heat-index measurement and control measures described in a companion clause of this information sheet, emergency response procedures, and acclimatization procedures.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes both § 3395(i) and § 3396(i) because they are formally independent regulations, each imposing its own written-plan duty, even though a single written document may in practice satisfy both where an employer's operations are subject to both standards; the two § 3395(i) quotations in this clause are both drawn from that same subdivision of that same regulation and are not independent of one another. This clause does not independently quote every item on either standard's minimum-content list beyond the general summary given here (procedures for water/shade or water/cool-down, the temperature-triggered procedures, emergency response, and acclimatization); readers should not assume this clause states the full text of either list. This is a description of a general regulatory requirement, not a representation that the employer has or has not adopted a written Heat Illness Prevention Plan, and this information sheet is not itself that plan.

clauses.title: Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act — Transition Record
Who and What the Act Covers
clauses.body: California's Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act applies only within a specific set of defined terms. A "contractor" for purposes of the chapter is limited to a person that employs 25 or more individuals and that enters into a service contract with an "awarding authority" (the person awarding janitorial or building-maintenance service contracts, including subcontracts). Not every worker at a covered site is a covered "employee": the definition is limited to a service employee who works at least 15 hours per week, whose primary place of employment is in California, working under a contract to provide janitorial or building-maintenance services — and it expressly excludes managerial, supervisory, or confidential employees, including anyone who would be classified that way under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act. The obligations described in the clauses below apply only when a "successor service contract" exists: a service contract to perform essentially the same services previously performed under a different service contract at the same facility that terminated within the previous 30 days. A contract entered into more than 30 days after the predecessor contract terminated is still treated as a "successor service contract" if its execution was delayed for the purpose of avoiding the chapter.
clauses.gap: All three quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1060) rather than independently authored sources. This clause does not address the separate defined terms in § 1060 for "person," "service contract," or "subcontractor," which are more mechanical in nature and are used, where relevant, in the other clauses of this document.
