citations.cite: California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, "contractor" definition
citations.quote: “Contractor” means any person that employs 25 or more individuals and that enters into a service contract with the awarding authority.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1060(c) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, "employee" definition and exclusions
citations.quote: “Employee” means any person employed as a service employee of a contractor or subcontractor who works at least 15 hours per week and whose primary place of employment is in the State of California under a contract to provide janitorial or building maintenance services. “Employee” does not include a person who is a managerial, supervisory, or confidential employee, including those employees who would be so defined under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act.

A service contract entered into more than 30 days after the termination of a predecessor service contract shall be considered a “successor service contract” if its execution was delayed for the purpose of avoiding application of this chapter.

clauses.title: What Happens When a Covered Contract Is Terminated
clauses.body: The chain of obligations under the Act begins when an awarding authority notifies a contractor that a covered service contract has been or will be terminated. At that point the awarding authority must state, in that same notification, whether a successor service contract has been or will be awarded, and if so, must identify the successor contractor by name and address. The terminated contractor then has a short, fixed window — three working days after receiving that notification — to provide the identified successor contractor with the name, date of hire, and job classification of each employee working at the site(s) covered by the terminated contract at the time of termination. If the terminated contractor does not yet know who the successor contractor is, that same employee information instead goes to the awarding authority, which becomes responsible for passing it along once a successor has been selected. These notice and information-transfer duties apply equally to subcontractors of a terminated contractor, not just to the prime contractor.
clauses.gap: Both quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1061(a)) rather than independently authored sources. The retention obligation itself — what the successor contractor must then do with that employee information — is addressed in a separate clause of this document, sourced to § 1061(b).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1061(a)(1) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, termination notice and employee-information transfer
citations.quote: If an awarding authority notifies a contractor that the service contract between the awarding authority and the contractor has been terminated or will be terminated, the awarding authority shall indicate in that notification whether a successor service contract has been or will be awarded in its place and, if so, shall identify the name and address of the successor contractor. The terminated contractor shall, within three working days after receiving that notification, provide to the successor contractor identified by the awarding authority, the name, date of hire, and job classification of each employee employed at the site or sites covered by the terminated service contract at the time of the contract termination.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1061(a)(3) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, application to subcontractors
citations.quote: The requirements of this section shall be equally applicable to all subcontractors of a terminated contractor.

clauses.title: The 60-Day Retention Obligation and Its Cause Exception
clauses.body: The core obligation the Act imposes is a retention requirement, not a general job-security guarantee: a successor contractor or successor subcontractor must retain, for a 60-day transition employment period, each employee who was employed by the terminated contractor or its subcontractors for the preceding four months or longer at the site(s) now covered by the successor service contract. The one statutory exception is narrow — the successor need not hire a particular employee if it has "reasonable and substantiated cause," and that cause must be based on the employee's own performance or conduct while working under the terminated contract, not on cost, headcount reduction as such, or any other unrelated ground. The statute also requires that this retention requirement be disclosed in advance: awarding authorities must state it in all initial bid packages governed by the chapter, so that anyone bidding on a covered contract knows the retention obligation will apply if awarded.
clauses.gap: The quote below is a single subdivision (Labor Code § 1061(b)(1)) of the statutory section covering retention. Note for anyone researching a physical notice-posting requirement: this section does not impose one. The disclosure mechanism the statute actually specifies is inclusion of the retention requirement in awarding authorities' initial bid packages — not a workplace posting. No posting requirement appears anywhere in Labor Code §§ 1060-1065 as verified for this document; if a posting requirement exists for building-service transitions, it would have to come from a source outside this chapter (for example, a local ordinance under § 1064, discussed in a separate clause of this document), which was not researched here.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1061(b)(1) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, 60-day retention requirement and cause exception
citations.quote: A successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall retain, for a 60-day transition employment period, employees who have been employed by the terminated contractor or its subcontractors, if any, for the preceding four months or longer at the site or sites covered by the successor service contract unless the successor contractor or successor subcontractor has reasonable and substantiated cause not to hire a particular employee based on that employee’s performance or conduct while working under the terminated contract. This requirement shall be stated by awarding authorities in all initial bid packages that are governed by this chapter.

clauses.title: Written Offer Terms and Seniority When Fewer Employees Are Needed
clauses.body: Where the retention obligation applies, the Act specifies how the offer itself must be made, not just that it must be made. The successor contractor or successor subcontractor must give each covered employee a written offer of employment in that employee's primary language, or another language the employee is literate in, and the offer must state a deadline to accept that is no shorter than 10 days. Notably, the statute does not require wage or benefit matching: nothing in the chapter obligates the successor to pay the same wages or offer the same benefits the terminated contractor or subcontractor provided. If the successor determines it needs fewer employees than the terminated contractor used at the same site(s), it cannot pick and choose freely among the otherwise-eligible employees — it must retain by seniority within each job classification.
clauses.gap: Both quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1061(b)(2)-(3)) as the retention obligation covered in a separate clause of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1061(b)(2) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, written offer requirements
citations.quote: The successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall make a written offer of employment to each employee, as required by this section, in the employee’s primary language or another language in which the employee is literate. That offer shall state the time within which the employee must accept that offer, but in no case may that time be less than 10 days. Nothing in this section requires the successor contractor or successor subcontractor to pay the same wages or offer the same benefits as were provided by the prior contractor or prior subcontractor.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1061(b)(3) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, seniority-based retention when fewer employees are needed
citations.quote: If at any time the successor contractor or successor subcontractor determines that fewer employees are needed to perform services under the successor service contract or successor subcontract than were required by the terminated contractor under the terminated contract or terminated subcontract, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall retain employees by seniority within the job classification.

clauses.title: Employee Lists and the Preferential Hiring List
clauses.body: The Act builds in reporting obligations meant to make retention decisions checkable. Once the successor contractor or successor subcontractor begins service under the successor contract, it must give the awarding authority a list of its own employees and its subcontractors' employees working at the covered site(s), indicating which of them were previously employed there by the terminated contractor or subcontractor. It must also provide a separate list identifying any of the terminated contractor's employees who were not retained, together with the stated reason each was not retained. During the 60-day transition period itself, the successor must maintain a preferential hiring list of eligible covered employees it did not initially retain, and must hire additional employees from that list until every one of the terminated contractor's or subcontractor's employees has been offered employment with the successor.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, employee-list disclosure to the awarding authority
citations.quote: The successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall also provide a list of any of the terminated contractor’s employees who were not retained either by the successor contractor or successor subcontractor, stating the reason these employees were not retained.

clauses.title: Protection Against Discharge Without Cause, and What Happens After 60 Days
clauses.body: Retention under the Act carries a corresponding job-security floor during the transition period itself: for the initial 60-day transition employment period, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor may not discharge a retained employee without cause, and cause has to rest only on that particular employee's own performance or conduct. At the end of the 60-day period, the statute requires a written performance evaluation for each retained employee. If that employee's performance during the 60 days was satisfactory, the successor must offer continued employment. The Act's protections are time-limited, however: employment after the 60-day transition period converts to ordinary at-will employment, under which the employee may then be terminated without cause.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act, no discharge without cause during the transition period
citations.quote: During the initial 60-day transition employment period, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall not discharge without cause an employee retained pursuant to this chapter. Cause shall be based only on the performance or conduct of the particular employee.

citations.quote: At the end of the 60-day transition employment period, a successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall provide a written performance evaluation to each employee retained pursuant to this chapter. If the employee’s performance during that 60-day period is satisfactory, the successor contractor or successor subcontractor shall offer the employee continued employment. Any employment after the 60-day transition employment period shall be at-will employment under which the employee may be terminated without cause.

clauses.title: Effective Date and What the Act Does Not Change
clauses.body: The Act's obligations are not open-ended in time or in reach. By its own terms, the chapter applies only to contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2002. And apart from the notice and retention obligations specifically described in Labor Code § 1061(a) and (b), the chapter does not otherwise change or expand the legal relationship or duties between a property owner or awarding authority (or their agents) and contractors, subcontractors, or their employees. The Act also does not restrict a property owner's or awarding authority's underlying business decisions: nothing in the chapter limits the right to terminate a service contract, to replace one contractor with another, or to bring building maintenance in-house using the property owner's or awarding authority's own employees — the retention obligation applies to whichever party ends up as the successor employer of the covered work, not to the decision of whether to make that change at all.
clauses.gap: All three quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1063). This document does not separately research or verify whether any particular local government ordinance imposes greater standards than this chapter, though § 1064 (not quoted in this document) expressly permits local agencies to enact such ordinances.

clauses.title: How the Act Is Enforced
clauses.body: The Act is enforced through a private right of action, not a state agency complaint process. An employee who was not offered employment in violation of the chapter, or who was discharged in violation of it, or an agent of that employee, may sue the successor contractor or successor subcontractor in California superior court. On a finding of violation, the court must award backpay (including the value of benefits) for each day the violation has occurred and continues, calculated as whichever is greater of two measures: the employee's average regular rate of pay over the last three years in the same occupational classification, multiplied by average hours worked over that same three-year period, or the employee's final regular rate of pay at the time the predecessor contract terminated, multiplied by the employee's usual hours. Courts may also order a preliminary or permanent injunction against continued violation, and a prevailing employee is entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs. One limit built into the enforcement scheme: absent an underlying claim that the employee was terminated in violation of the chapter, an employee cannot sue solely because the employer failed to provide the end-of-period written performance evaluation described elsewhere in this document.

clauses.title: Certification
Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This CCPA Employee and Job Applicant Data — Information Sheet describes how the California Consumer Privacy Act, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (California Civil Code § 1798.100 et seq.), applies to personal information {{businessName}} collects and maintains about its own personnel — job applicants, current and former employees, and other personnel described in this information sheet — as distinct from personal information {{businessName}} collects from its customers or website visitors. A job applicant, employee, or other personnel with questions about this information sheet, or who wishes to exercise a right described in it, may contact {{businessName}} as follows: {{contactMethod}}. This information sheet does not itself set out the consumer-facing privacy notice {{businessName}} provides to its customers or website visitors, or the contract terms between {{businessName}} and any vendor or service provider that processes personal information on {{businessName}}'s behalf; those are addressed in separate documents.

clauses.title: The Former, Temporary Employee/HR Data Exemption Has Expired
clauses.body: When California's Consumer Privacy Act was first enacted, it included two temporary, limited exemptions — codified as subdivisions (m) and (n) of Civil Code § 1798.145 — under which personal information a business collected about its own job applicants, employees, owners, directors, officers, medical staff members, or independent contractors, solely within the context of that role, was not subject to most of the Act's obligations, and a similar, narrower exemption applied to personal information reflecting a business-to-business communication or transaction with a natural person acting on behalf of another company, partnership, sole proprietorship, nonprofit, or government agency. Both of these exemptions were, by their own statutory terms, temporary: each subdivision states that it became inoperative on January 1, 2023. That expiration is not merely a historical footnote — it is recorded in the official history note appended to the current, in-force version of § 1798.145 (as most recently amended effective January 1, 2024), which states plainly that 'Subdivisions (m) and (n) inoperative January 1, 2023, by their own provisions.' The text of subdivisions (m) and (n) still appears in the printed statute, but neither has had any legal effect since January 1, 2023. As a result, and subject to the Act's other, non-employment-specific exemptions and exceptions, personal information a business collects about its own job applicants, employees, and other personnel has been fully subject to the CCPA/CPRA's general framework — the same framework that applies to a business's customers — since that date.

clauses.title: A Business's Own Personnel Can Be “Consumers” Under the Act's General Definition
clauses.body: The CCPA/CPRA defines “consumer,” for purposes of the entire title, broadly: a natural person who is a California resident, however identified, including by any unique identifier. Nothing in that general definition turns on whether the natural person is a customer, a website visitor, or instead a job applicant, employee, or other person who performs services for the business. Before January 1, 2023, a job applicant's, employee's, or other personnel's status as such was addressed separately, through the now-inoperative exemption described elsewhere in this information sheet. With that exemption no longer in effect, a business's own personnel who are California residents fall within the Act's general “consumer” definition on the same terms as anyone else, so that personal information a business collects and maintains about them is, subject to the Act's other, non-employment-specific exemptions and exceptions, personal information about a consumer for purposes of the title.
clauses.gap: This clause cites a single statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.140(i), the Act's definition of “consumer.” This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer; other states now have their own, differently structured privacy and employment statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. This clause does not itself determine whether any specific job applicant, employee, or other individual is in fact a California resident within the meaning of the cross-referenced regulation, which is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause also does not restate the Act's other, non-employment-specific exemptions and exceptions (for example, the deidentified/aggregate information exemption or the evidentiary-privilege limitation in § 1798.145), which continue to apply to personal information about personnel on the same terms they apply to any other consumer's personal information and were not independently verified for this clause. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

clauses.title: Which Employers Are Subject to These Obligations
clauses.body: The obligations described in this information sheet apply only to an entity that meets the CCPA/CPRA's own definition of a “business.” Among other structural requirements — including that the entity is organized or operated for the profit or financial benefit of its shareholders or other owners, collects consumers' personal information (or has it collected on the entity's behalf), determines the purposes and means of processing that personal information, and does business in California — the statute requires that the entity satisfy at least one of three numerical thresholds: annual gross revenue in excess of $25,000,000 in the preceding calendar year; annually buying, selling, or sharing the personal information of 100,000 or more consumers or households, alone or in combination; or deriving 50 percent or more of its annual revenue from selling or sharing consumers' personal information. An entity that does not meet the statutory definition of a “business” is not, on that basis, subject to the obligations this information sheet describes with respect to personal information about its own personnel, regardless of whether the now-inoperative employee/personnel exemption discussed elsewhere in this information sheet would otherwise have applied.
clauses.gap: This clause cites a single statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.140(d)(1), and quotes it in full together with its three numerical thresholds. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer; other states now have their own, differently structured privacy and employment statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. This clause does not restate § 1798.140(d)(2) through (4), which extend the “business” definition to certain affiliated entities sharing common branding, certain joint ventures and partnerships, and entities that voluntarily certify compliance with the title; those provisions were reviewed as part of the same fetched section but are not separately quoted or detailed here because they are narrower extensions of, rather than substitutes for, the general threshold test quoted in this clause. This clause does not determine whether any specific employer in fact meets one of these thresholds, which is a fact-specific financial and operational question this document does not resolve. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.quote: (d) “Business” means:(1) A sole proprietorship, partnership, limited liability company, corporation, association, or other legal entity that is organized or operated for the profit or financial benefit of its shareholders or other owners, that collects consumers’ personal information, or on the behalf of which such information is collected and that alone, or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of consumers’ personal information, that does business in the State of California, and that satisfies one or more of the following thresholds:(A) As of January 1 of the calendar year, had annual gross revenues in excess of twenty-five million dollars ($25,000,000) in the preceding calendar year, as adjusted pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 1798.199.95.(B) Alone or in combination, annually buys, sells, or shares the personal information of 100,000 or more consumers or households.(C) Derives 50 percent or more of its annual revenues from selling or sharing consumers’ personal information.

clauses.title: The Notice-at-Collection Requirement Applies to Personal Information Collected From Personnel
clauses.body: California law requires that a business that controls the collection of a consumer's personal information inform consumers, at or before the point of collection, of the categories of personal information to be collected and the purposes for which those categories are collected or used, and whether that information is sold or shared; a business may not then collect additional categories of personal information, or use personal information for additional purposes, that are incompatible with the disclosed purpose, without providing a further notice consistent with this requirement. Because a business's own job applicants, employees, and other personnel who are California residents are “consumers” under the Act's general definition, and because the former exemption that once excused a business from most CCPA obligations toward personal information collected in that context is now inoperative, this notice-at-collection requirement applies to personal information a business collects from its personnel in the same way it applies to personal information the business collects from its customers. The statute imposes parallel content requirements — addressed elsewhere in the same section — for sensitive personal information and for disclosing the length of time, or the criteria for determining the length of time, a business intends to retain each category of personal information.
clauses.gap: This clause cites Civil Code § 1798.100(a)(1) of the CCPA/CPRA's notice-at-collection statute. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer; other states now have their own, differently structured privacy and employment statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. This clause quotes only paragraph (1) of subdivision (a); it does not separately quote paragraphs (2) (the parallel sensitive-personal-information notice content) and (3) (the retention-period disclosure) of the same subdivision, or subdivision (b) (the alternative homepage-posting method available to a third party that controls collection, which is unlikely to be the applicable method for personnel-directed notices and was not evaluated for that context) — the full text of subdivision (a) and (b) is independently verified and quoted in this corpus's existing CCPA consumer-facing privacy policy document, which addresses the same statutory section from the customer-facing side. This clause does not determine, for any specific business, the actual categories of personal information collected from personnel, the purposes of that collection, or the retention period the business intends — those are fact-specific determinations left to the drafting portion of this information sheet. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.cite: California Consumer Privacy Act, point-of-collection notice content requirement
citations.quote: (a) A business that controls the collection of a consumer’s personal information shall, at or before the point of collection, inform consumers of the following:(1) The categories of personal information to be collected and the purposes for which the categories of personal information are collected or used and whether that information is sold or shared. A business shall not collect additional categories of personal information or use personal information collected for additional purposes that are incompatible with the disclosed purpose for which the personal information was collected without providing the consumer with notice consistent with this section.

clauses.title: The Rights to Know, Delete, and Correct Personal Information Now Apply to Personnel Data
clauses.body: California law gives a consumer the right to request that a business delete personal information the business has collected from the consumer; the right to request that a business that maintains inaccurate personal information about the consumer correct that inaccurate personal information, taking into account the nature of the personal information and the purposes of processing it; and the right to request that a business that collects personal information about the consumer disclose the categories of personal information it has collected, the categories of sources, the business or commercial purpose for collecting it, the categories of third parties to whom it is disclosed, and the specific pieces of personal information collected about that consumer. Because the former exemption for personal information collected in the job-applicant, employee, or other personnel context is now inoperative, these three rights apply, on the same terms described in this section, to personal information a business maintains about a current or former job applicant, employee, or other personnel described in this information sheet — for example, information in a personnel file, application materials, or performance or compensation records — to the extent that information is personal information about a California-resident natural person within the meaning of the Act. The Act's other consumer rights (including the rights to know what personal information is sold or shared and to whom, to opt out of sale or sharing, and to limit use of sensitive personal information) and its non-discrimination provision likewise apply to personnel on the same general terms they apply to any other consumer, though this clause addresses only the right to know, delete, and correct.
clauses.gap: This clause cites three separate statutory sections — Civil Code §§ 1798.105(a), 1798.106(a), and 1798.110(a) — each of which independently creates one of the three rights described in this clause; because each citation is to a different section rather than to different subdivisions of one section, no additional cross-subsection disclosure is required beyond noting that all three sections are part of the same California Consumer Privacy Act title. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's CCPA/CPRA framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer; other states now have their own, differently structured privacy and employment statutes, and this document addresses California's CCPA/CPRA only. This clause does not restate the statutory exceptions to the deletion right (Civil Code § 1798.105(d)), which permit a business to decline a deletion request for reasons such as completing a transaction, security, debugging, legal compliance, and certain other statutory grounds, and which apply to a request from personnel on the same terms they apply to a request from any other consumer; those exceptions were not independently quoted or verified for this clause. This clause's closing sentence, noting that the Act's other consumer rights and non-discrimination provision likewise now apply to personnel, restates the logical consequence of this document's clause on the expired exemption rather than independently quoting or verifying the text of those other provisions (§§ 1798.115, 1798.120, 1798.121, and 1798.125) for this document; a reader wanting the verified text of those provisions should consult this corpus's existing CCPA consumer-facing privacy policy document, which quotes them directly. No case law was checked on any of these three provisions; each statute's own text is unambiguous, so the statutes stand as the source here without a corroborating case.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's work-permit requirement for minors employed in California — the statutory process by which {{minorName}}, a minor considered for or holding the position of {{jobTitle}} with {{companyName}}, and {{minorName}}'s parent or legal guardian, {{parentGuardianName}}, obtain the work permit that {{minorName}}'s school, {{educationalInstitution}}, is authorized to issue, and the obligations that fall on {{companyName}} once {{minorName}} is employed. It states facts about what the Education Code's Permits to Work article and the related Labor Code provisions require. This corpus separately includes an I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification — Information Sheet, which addresses a different, federal requirement — verifying that a new hire of any age is authorized to work in the United States. The work-permit requirement described here is a distinct, California-specific, age-based requirement that applies in addition to, not instead of, federal I-9 verification. This document is not itself a work permit, a permit application, or a certificate of age, and it does not tell {{companyName}}, {{minorName}}, or {{parentGuardianName}} what to do about any particular hire, application, or permit.

clauses.title: Who Counts as a "Minor" Under This Framework
clauses.body: For purposes of the Labor Code chapter governing the occupational privileges and restrictions of minors, "minor" is a defined term. It includes any person under the age of 18 who is required to attend school under the Education Code's compulsory-attendance provisions, and, separately, any person under the age of six, regardless of school-attendance status.
clauses.gap: This document quotes only Labor Code § 1286(c)'s definition of "minor" for purposes of Labor Code Chapter 2 (Occupational Privileges and Restrictions). It did not independently fetch or verify the compulsory-attendance provisions that definition cross-references (Education Code §§ 48200 and 48400 et seq.), and it does not address the separate sentence in § 1286(c) covering a minor under 18 who is not required to attend California schools solely because of nonresident status.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1286(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Chapter 2 (Occupational Privileges and Restrictions), definition of “minor”
citations.quote: “Minor” means any person under the age of 18 years who is required to attend school under Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 48200) and Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 48400) of Part 27 of Division 4 of Title 2 of the Education Code and any person under the age of six years.

clauses.title: Who May Issue a Work Permit, and How the Process Starts
clauses.body: California channels the work-permit process through the minor's school rather than through the employer. A work permit may be issued by the superintendent of the school district where the minor resides; the chief executive officer (or equivalent) of a charter school the minor attends; a school employee holding a pupil personnel services credential, or a certificated work-experience-education teacher or coordinator, authorized in writing by that superintendent or chief executive officer; the county superintendent of schools, for a minor outside any district's jurisdiction; or, subject to further statutory conditions, the principal of the public or private school the minor attends. The process does not begin with the employer: a work permit cannot be issued at all until a written request for it — from the minor's parent, guardian, foster parent, caregiver with whom the minor resides, or a residential-shelter-services provider — has been filed with whichever official is acting as the issuing authority.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are subdivisions of the same statute, Education Code § 49110 — subdivision (b) (who may issue a permit) and subdivision (c) (the written-request prerequisite) — not two independent sources. This document does not quote § 49110(a) (a legislative-intent statement about issuer training), (d), (e), or (f) (backup-issuer authority and how school-calendar-based hour limits apply to a permit), nor subparagraphs (A) through (C) under paragraph (b)(5), which impose self-certification, superintendent-revocation, and no-issuing-to-one's-own-child conditions specifically on a principal who issues permits.

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 49110(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Education Code, Permits to Work article, individuals authorized to issue a work permit
citations.quote: (b) Any of the following individuals may issue a work permit to a minor subject to the requirements and conditions of this chapter: (1) The superintendent of a school district in which the minor resides. (2) The chief executive officer, or the equivalent position, of a charter school that the minor attends. (3) A person holding a services credential with a specialization in pupil personnel services authorized by the superintendent of the school district or chief executive officer in writing, or a certificated work experience education teacher or coordinator authorized by the superintendent of the school district or chief executive officer in writing. (4) If the minor resides in a portion of a county not under the jurisdiction of the superintendent of a school district and does not attend a charter school, the county superintendent of schools, a person holding a services credential with a specialization in pupil personnel services authorized by the county superintendent of schools in writing, or a certificated work experience education teacher or coordinator authorized by the county superintendent of schools in writing may issue a work permit. (5) Subject to the requirements and conditions in subparagraphs (A) to (C), inclusive, the principal of a public or private school may issue, or designate another administrator in the school to issue, work permits to pupils who attend the school.

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 49110(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Education Code, Permits to Work article, written-request prerequisite
citations.quote: (c) A work permit shall not be issued until the written request for the permit from the parent, guardian, foster parent, caregiver with whom the minor resides, or residential shelter services provider, has been filed with the issuing authority.

clauses.title: The Permit to Employ, Employer Recordkeeping, and Expiration
clauses.body: The permit system has an employer-facing side as well. The same official authorized to issue permits to work or to employ may issue a certificate of age to a minor who appears with a parent, guardian, or other person in control of the minor and presents the required evidence of age; that certificate of age itself serves as the permit to employ a minor who is not legally required to attend school but who is otherwise required to hold a permit to work. Once a minor is employed, the employer — directly or through anyone acting on the employer's behalf — must keep on file all such permits and certificates, whether to work or to employ, issued under the Labor Code chapter or under the Education Code's minors-employment provisions, and must keep those files open at all times to inspection by school attendance and probation officers, the State Board of Education, and the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement. A permit to work issued during the school year does not last indefinitely: it expires five days after the opening of the next school year.
clauses.gap: This clause combines three separate statutes — Education Code § 49114 (certificate of age / permit to employ), Labor Code § 1299 (employer recordkeeping), and Education Code § 49118 (expiration) — because together they describe the employer-facing half of the same permit system; none of the three is a subdivision of either of the other two. This document did not verify what specific "evidence of age" § 49114 requires beyond its own general cross-reference, and it did not verify whether or how a permit to work issued outside the school year (for example, under Education Code § 49111, for vacation-period employment) expires, since § 49118 by its own terms addresses only permits "issued during the school year."

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 49114 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Education Code, certificate of age serving as a permit to employ
citations.quote: The person authorized to issue permits to work or to employ may issue to any minor a certificate of age when the minor accompanied by his parent, guardian, or other person in control or charge of the minor, presents to the authority, the evidence of age specified in this chapter. The certificate of age shall serve as a permit to employ a minor who is not by law required to attend school, and who is otherwise required to hold a permit to work.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1299 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, employer recordkeeping and inspection of minor-employment permits
citations.quote: Every person, or agent or officer thereof, employing minors, either directly or indirectly through third persons, shall keep on file all permits and certificates, either to work or to employ, issued under this chapter or Part 27 (commencing with Section 48000) of the Education Code. The files shall be open at all times to the inspection of the school attendance and probation officers, the State Board of Education, and the officers of the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement.

citations.cite: California Education Code, expiration of a school-year work permit
citations.quote: Permits to work issued during the school year shall expire five days after the opening of the next succeeding school year.

clauses.title: Hour and Time-of-Day Limits, and Revocation for Impairment
clauses.body: Separate from the permit-issuance process, the Labor Code directly limits when and how long a minor may work, keyed to age and to whether school is in session. A minor 15 or younger may not be employed more than eight hours in a day or 40 hours in a week, or before 7 a.m. or after 7 p.m. (extended to 9 p.m. from June 1 through Labor Day); while school is in session, that drops to no more than three hours on a schoolday or 18 hours in a week, never during school hours, with an exception for a minor enrolled in a school-supervised work-experience and career-exploration program (up to 23 hours). A minor 16 or 17 may not be employed more than eight hours in a day or 48 hours in a week, or before 5 a.m. or after 10 p.m. on a night before a schoolday (extended to 12:30 a.m. before a nonschoolday); while school is in session, that drops to no more than four hours on a schoolday, subject to listed exceptions including personal-attendant occupations, school-approved work experience, cooperative vocational education, and a minor who has been issued a permit to work under Education Code § 49112(c). "Schoolday" for these limits means any day the minor is required to attend school for 240 minutes or more. Separately, the authority that issued a minor's permit to work may revoke it if shown, to that authority's satisfaction, that the minor's schoolwork or health is being impaired by the employment.
clauses.gap: The hour limits quoted here come from Labor Code § 1391. Education Code § 49116(a)-(b) states hour limits for 14-15 and 16-17 year-olds that closely track Labor Code § 1391(a)(2) and (a)(4); to avoid presenting the same restriction as if it came from two independent sources, this document cites only Labor Code § 1391 for the hour limits themselves and cites Education Code § 49116 only for its distinct subdivision (c), the impairment-based revocation rule that § 1391 does not itself contain. This document does not address the separate, generally different hour and time limits that apply to minors in the entertainment industry under Labor Code § 1308.7, which § 1391(a) expressly carves out of its own coverage, or the misdemeanor penalties § 1391(c) attaches to a violation.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1391(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, age-based hour and time-of-day limits on employing a minor
citations.quote: (a) Except as provided in Sections 1297, 1298, and 1308.7: (1) An employer shall not employ a minor 15 years of age or younger for more than eight hours in one day of 24 hours, or more than 40 hours in one week, or before 7 a.m. or after 7 p.m., except that from June 1 through Labor Day, a minor 15 years of age or younger may be employed for the hours authorized by this section until 9 p.m. in the evening. (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), while school is in session, an employer shall not employ a minor 14 or 15 years of age for more than three hours in any schoolday, nor more than 18 hours in any week, nor during school hours, except that a minor enrolled in and employed pursuant to a school-supervised and school-administered work experience and career exploration program may be employed for no more than 23 hours, any portion of which may be during school hours. (3) An employer shall not employ a minor 16 or 17 years of age for more than eight hours in one day of 24 hours or more than 48 hours in one week, or before 5 a.m., or after 10 p.m. on any day preceding a schoolday. However, a minor 16 or 17 years of age may be employed for the hours authorized by this section during any evening preceding a nonschoolday until 12:30 a.m. of the nonschoolday. (4) Notwithstanding paragraph (3), while school is in session, an employer shall not employ a minor 16 or 17 years of age for more than four hours in any schoolday, except as follows: (A) The minor is employed in personal attendant occupations, as defined in the Industrial Welfare Commission Minimum Wage Order No. 15 (8 Cal. Code Regs. Sec. 11150), school-approved work experience, or cooperative vocational education programs. (B) The minor has been issued a permit to work pursuant to subdivision (c) of Section 49112 of the Education Code and is employed in accordance with the provisions of that permit. (b) For purposes of this section, “schoolday” means any day in which a minor is required to attend school for 240 minutes or more.

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 49116(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Education Code, revocation of a work permit for impairment of schoolwork or health
citations.quote: (c) If evidence is shown, to the satisfaction of the authority issuing the permit to work, that the schoolwork or the health of the minor is being impaired by the employment, that authority may revoke the permit.

clauses.title: Exemption for Minors Who Have Already Graduated High School (or Its Equivalent)
clauses.body: The entire Education Code chapter governing the employment of minors — and, by extension, the work-permit mechanics described above — does not apply to a minor who has already graduated from a four-year high school course above the eighth grade, who has had an equivalent amount of education in a private school or by private tuition, or who has been awarded a certificate of proficiency under Education Code § 48412.
clauses.gap: This document examined the Education Code sections in Part 27, Chapter 7 (the work-permit chapter) but did not find, and so does not assert, a separate express statutory exemption specifically naming emancipated minors within the sections it reviewed; it also did not independently fetch or verify Education Code § 48412 (the certificate-of-proficiency provision this exemption cross-references), or Education Code § 49102 through § 49104, section numbers that returned no content when queried directly and that this document therefore treats as not currently in force rather than as a source of any additional exemption. A reader whose situation may involve emancipation, home schooling, or a certificate of proficiency should not assume any of those is or is not covered based on this document alone.

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 49101 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Education Code, exemption for a minor who has graduated high school or its equivalent
citations.quote: The provisions of this chapter shall not apply to any minor who has been graduated from a high school maintaining a four-year course above the eighth grade of elementary schools, or who has had an equal amount of education in a private school or by private tuition, or who has been awarded a certificate of proficiency pursuant to Section 48412 of the Education Code.

clauses.title: Signature and Certification
Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California Corporations Code section 309 — the statutory standard of care that governs how a director of a California corporation performs the duties of a director, the statutory right of a director to rely on information and reports from certain other sources in performing those duties, and the statutory consequence for a director who performs duties consistently with that standard and that reliance right. It is prepared with reference to {{directorName}}'s service as a director of {{companyName}}. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing what section 309 provides; it does not evaluate, and is not evidence of, whether any specific decision, vote, or other conduct by {{directorName}} as a director of {{companyName}} satisfied the standard of care described here, whether {{directorName}} was in fact entitled to rely on any specific information or report, or whether the liability protection described here would apply to any specific act or omission. Those are fact-specific questions this Information Sheet does not answer. This document treats section 309 as it applies to a California corporation's directors specifically, in more depth than this project's existing Founders' Agreement document, which addresses fiduciary duties only briefly and only as one comparison point among the different duties owed by partners, corporate directors, and LLC members or managers depending on which entity form founders have chosen.

clauses.title: The Statutory Standard of Care for a Director's Performance of Duties
clauses.body: California law sets a single statutory standard for how a director of a California corporation must perform the duties of a director, including duties performed as a member of a board committee. The statute requires a director to act (1) in good faith; (2) in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders; and (3) with the care, including reasonable inquiry, that an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances. This is the standard against which {{directorName}}'s performance of duties as a director of {{companyName}} is measured under California corporate law; this clause states the standard itself and does not evaluate whether any specific decision by {{directorName}} met it.
clauses.gap: This is one California statute (Corporations Code section 309, subdivision (a)) and is offered as evidence of what that subdivision provides, not as a claim about which state's law governs any specific company or as a determination that any specific company is in fact organized as a California corporation. This clause does not address how California courts have applied or weighted the standard's three elements in a specific dispute, nor does it address a director's right to rely on others in satisfying this standard, which is covered in the following clauses quoting subdivision (b) of this same statutory section — the citations across this document's clauses are different subdivisions of the single statute, Corporations Code section 309, not independent sources corroborating one another.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 309(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, standard of care for a director's performance of duties
citations.quote: A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner such director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances.

clauses.title: The Statutory Right to Rely on Officers, Experts, and Board Committees
clauses.body: In performing the duties described in the preceding clause, California law entitles a director to rely on information, opinions, reports, or statements — including financial statements and other financial data — that are prepared or presented by any of three categories of sources: (1) one or more officers or employees of the corporation whom the director believes to be reliable and competent in the matters presented; (2) counsel, independent accountants, or other persons as to matters the director believes to be within that person's professional or expert competence; or (3) a board committee on which the director does not serve, as to matters within that committee's designated authority, if the director believes the committee merits confidence. The statute attaches conditions to this reliance right, addressed in the following clause. This clause states which categories of sources {{directorName}} may rely on under the statute as a director of {{companyName}}; it does not determine whether any specific officer, employee, professional, or committee that {{directorName}} in fact relied on falls within one of these categories.
clauses.gap: This is the same California statute as the preceding and following clauses in this document (Corporations Code section 309), quoting subdivision (b) in full, including its concluding conditions clause — it is not an independent source corroborating the standard-of-care clause or the liability-protection clause; all three quote different subdivisions of one statutory section. The statute lists three categories of permissible reliance and does not state whether that list is illustrative or exhaustive; this clause does not address whether reliance on a source outside these three categories could be supported under some legal theory outside section 309 itself.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 309(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, sources a director may rely on and the conditions attached
citations.quote: In performing the duties of a director, a director shall be entitled to rely on information, opinions, reports or statements, including financial statements and other financial data, in each case prepared or presented by any of the following: (1) One or more officers or employees of the corporation whom the director believes to be reliable and competent in the matters presented. (2) Counsel, independent accountants or other persons as to matters which the director believes to be within such person’s professional or expert competence. (3) A committee of the board upon which the director does not serve, as to matters within its designated authority, which committee the director believes to merit confidence, so long as, in any such case, the director acts in good faith, after reasonable inquiry when the need therefor is indicated by the circumstances and without knowledge that would cause such reliance to be unwarranted.

clauses.title: Conditions on the Reliance Right, and What It Does Not Excuse
clauses.body: The statutory right to rely on officers, experts, and board committees described in the preceding clause is not unconditional. California law makes reliance on any of the three categories of sources available only if the director acts in good faith, after reasonable inquiry when the circumstances indicate a need for it, and without knowledge that would make the reliance unwarranted. This means the reliance right does not excuse a director who reviews the information, opinion, report, or statement in question but who knows something that would make reliance on it unreasonable, and it does not excuse a director who fails to make a reasonable inquiry when the circumstances call for one. This clause states the statutory conditions themselves; it does not evaluate whether {{directorName}}, as a director of {{companyName}}, in fact acted in good faith, made a reasonable inquiry, or possessed knowledge that would make a specific instance of reliance unwarranted — those are fact-specific determinations this clause does not make.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the concluding conditions sentence of Corporations Code section 309, subdivision (b) — the same subdivision (b) quoted in full, including this identical sentence, in the preceding clause. It is isolated here only to highlight the conditions specifically; it is not an independent additional source, and the two clauses' citations should not be read as corroborating one another rather than being the same statutory text. The statute does not define "reasonable inquiry" or specify what circumstances "indicate" a need for it, and this clause does not supply those definitions.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 309(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, conditions attached to a director's statutory reliance right
citations.quote: so long as, in any such case, the director acts in good faith, after reasonable inquiry when the need therefor is indicated by the circumstances and without knowledge that would cause such reliance to be unwarranted.

clauses.title: The Liability Protection for a Director Who Meets the Standard
clauses.body: California law provides that a person who performs the duties of a director consistently with the standard of care and the reliance right described in the preceding clauses has no liability based on any alleged failure to discharge that person's obligations as a director. This is the statutory codification of what is commonly referred to as business judgment rule protection for a California corporate director: a director who satisfies the good-faith, best-interests, and ordinarily-prudent-person standard (and, where applicable, the conditions on reliance) is not liable merely because a decision, in hindsight, turned out badly for the corporation. The statute separately notes that a corporation's liability for monetary damages against a director may also be eliminated or limited in the corporation's articles, to the extent a different statute (Corporations Code section 204, subdivision (a), paragraph (10)) permits — a distinct, additional protection this clause does not itself describe in detail. This clause states the statutory liability protection itself; it does not determine whether {{directorName}}'s conduct as a director of {{companyName}} in fact met the standard described in the preceding clauses, or whether {{companyName}}'s articles of incorporation contain any exculpatory provision of the kind referenced here.
clauses.gap: This is the same California statute as the two preceding authority clauses (Corporations Code section 309), quoting subdivision (c) — not an independent source corroborating them. This clause references, but does not independently fetch, quote, or verify, Corporations Code section 204, subdivision (a), paragraph (10) (the separate statute governing exculpatory provisions in a corporation's articles); that cross-reference is stated only because it appears within the verified text of section 309(c) itself, and readers should consult section 204 directly rather than relying on this clause for its substance. This clause also does not address the separate, non-statutory common-law business judgment rule as California courts have applied it in specific disputes (for example, the deference given to a board's decision absent fraud, illegality, or a conflict of interest) — no case law is cited or verified anywhere in this document; this document is limited to the verified statutory text of section 309.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 309(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, liability protection for a director who meets the standard of subdivisions (a) and (b)
citations.quote: A person who performs the duties of a director in accordance with subdivisions (a) and (b) shall have no liability based upon any alleged failure to discharge the person’s obligations as a director. In addition, the liability of a director for monetary damages may be eliminated or limited in a corporation’s articles to the extent provided in paragraph (10) of subdivision (a) of Section 204.

clauses.title: Certification
clauses.body:
I certify that the description of California Corporations Code section 309 in this Information Sheet reflects the statutory text as in effect on the date below, and that this Information Sheet is a general informational reference regarding {{directorName}}'s service as a director of {{companyName}}, not legal advice about, or a determination of, whether any specific act or omission by {{directorName}} satisfied the standard of care, qualified for the statutory reliance right, or is protected from liability under the statute described above.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

clauses.title: Recitals — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This Confidential Marriage — Information Sheet is prepared in connection with {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}'s interest in California's confidential marriage license, a distinct license track from the standard public marriage license issued under Family Code Part 2 (commencing with Section 350). This document is informational only. It records facts and statutory citations about the confidential-marriage track generally; it does not itself apply for or issue a marriage license, does not solemnize a marriage, and states no conclusion about whether a confidential marriage license is available to, or the better choice for, {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} specifically.

clauses.title: Eligibility — Living Together as Spouses
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, under California law, the confidential-marriage track is available only where two unmarried people, neither of whom is a minor, have been living together as spouses; a couple who meets that condition may be married under the confidential-marriage chapter by a person authorized to solemnize a marriage under the same statute (Family Code Part 3, Chapter 1, commencing with Section 400) that authorizes solemnization of a standard public marriage.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (Family Code § 500); no additional independent source was found for this. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the substantive eligibility condition for California's confidential-marriage track specifically — not a claim about which state's law, if any, governs a specific couple's situation, about whether any other state offers a comparable confidential license, or about how "living together as spouses" is defined or proven for this purpose (the statute itself does not define the phrase).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 500 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the confidential-marriage eligibility condition
citations.quote: When two unmarried people, not minors, have been living together as spouses, they may be married pursuant to this chapter by a person authorized to solemnize a marriage under Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 400) of Part 3.

clauses.title: How a Confidential Marriage License Is Issued — County Clerk or an Approved Notary Public
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, except in a limited physical-inability circumstance addressed elsewhere in the statute, a confidential marriage license is issued by the county clerk upon the personal appearance together of both parties and payment of the required statutory fees. California law separately allows the county clerk to issue a confidential marriage license at the request of a notary public whom the county clerk has approved to issue confidential marriage licenses, upon that notary public's payment of the same statutory fees; the parties then reimburse the notary public for the fee amount.
clauses.gap: This draws on two different statutory sections within the same statutory Part (Family Code §§ 501(a) and 503); each was independently verified against the leginfo text. Both are one state's statutes, used as real evidence that a confidential-marriage license can be issued either directly by a county official or through a specially approved private notary public — a two-track issuance mechanism this project has not found stated for California's standard public marriage license. Not a claim about how any other state, if it has a comparable confidential-license category, structures issuance, nor about the physical-inability exception in § 502, which is not quoted here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 501(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: issuance by the county clerk on personal appearance
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 502, a confidential marriage license shall be issued by the county clerk upon the personal appearance together of the parties to be married and their payment of the fees required by Sections 26840.1 and 26840.8 of the Government Code and any fee imposed pursuant to the authorization of Section 26840.3 of the Government Code.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 503 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: issuance through an approved notary public
citations.quote: The county clerk shall issue a confidential marriage license upon the request of a notary public approved by the county clerk to issue confidential marriage licenses pursuant to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 530) and upon payment by the notary public of the fees specified in Sections 26840.1 and 26840.8 of the Government Code. The parties shall reimburse a notary public who issues a confidential marriage license for the amount of the fees.

clauses.title: Approval and Training Required Before a Notary Public May Issue Confidential Marriage Licenses
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that a notary public may not issue a confidential marriage license unless first approved to do so by the county clerk, that approval requires the notary public to complete a county-clerk-conducted course of instruction on issuing confidential marriage licenses not exceeding six hours in duration, and that an approval, once granted, is valid for one year and must be renewed to continue issuing confidential marriage licenses.
clauses.gap: This draws on three different statutory sections within the same statutory Part (Family Code §§ 530(a), 532, and 533); each was independently verified against the leginfo text. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a licensing and training regime for a private official (a notary public) issuing a category of marriage license can exist under state law — not a claim that any other state authorizes a notary public to issue any category of marriage license, or a statement of the renewal fee or the misdemeanor penalty for an unapproved notary's issuance, which this clause does not quote.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 530(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the approval requirement
citations.quote: No notary public shall issue a confidential marriage license pursuant to this part unless the notary public is approved by the county clerk to issue confidential marriage licenses pursuant to this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 532 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the required course of instruction
citations.quote: No approval, or renewal of the approval, shall be granted pursuant to this chapter unless the notary public shows evidence of successful completion of a course of instruction concerning the issuance of confidential marriage licenses that was conducted by the county clerk in the county of registration. The course of instruction shall not exceed six hours in duration.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 533 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the one-year validity of an approval
citations.quote: An approval to issue confidential marriage licenses pursuant to this chapter is valid for one year.

clauses.title: No Witness-Signature Requirement Stated for the Confidential-Marriage Ceremony
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, for a standard public marriage license, California law requires the person solemnizing the marriage to enter on the license the printed name, signature, and mailing address of at least one, and no more than two, witnesses to the ceremony. The parallel statute governing a confidential marriage license after the ceremony — requiring only that the license be presented to the person solemnizing the marriage, that the solemnization section be completed, and that the license be returned to the county clerk within 10 days — states no witness-signature requirement.
clauses.gap: This compares two different statutory sections in two different Parts of the Family Code (§ 359, governing the standard public marriage license, and § 506, governing a confidential marriage license after the ceremony); each was independently verified against the leginfo text. The absence of a witness-signature requirement in § 506 is drawn from that section's silence on the point, set against § 359(d)'s explicit requirement — this project found no Family Code provision in the confidential-marriage chapter (§§ 500-511) that affirmatively states witnesses are not required, so this clause is limited to the textual contrast actually verified rather than that broader affirmative claim.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 359(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the witness-signature requirement for a standard marriage license
citations.quote: (d) The person solemnizing the marriage shall complete the solemnization sections on the marriage license, and shall cause to be entered on the marriage license the printed name, signature, and mailing address of at least one, and no more than two, witnesses to the marriage ceremony.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 506 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: completion and return of a confidential marriage license, with no witness-signature requirement stated
citations.quote: (a) The confidential marriage license shall be presented to the person solemnizing the marriage.(b) Upon performance of the ceremony, the solemnization section on the confidential marriage license shall be completed by the person solemnizing the marriage.(c) The confidential marriage license shall be returned by the person solemnizing the marriage to the office of the county clerk in the county in which the license was issued within 10 days after the ceremony.

clauses.title: The Confidential Marriage Record Is Not Open to Public Inspection
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that, under California law, the county clerk maintains a confidential marriage certificate as a permanent record that is not open to public inspection except upon a court order issued on a showing of good cause, and that a confidential marriage license itself is a confidential record not open to public inspection without a court order. The county clerk may search for a confidential marriage certificate to confirm that a marriage exists, but the date of the marriage and any other information in the certificate may not be disclosed except upon court order.
clauses.gap: Both quotes below are subdivisions (a) and (c) of the same statutory section, Family Code § 511; this is a single statutory section, and no additional independent source was found for it. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a confidential, non-public records track for a marriage license and certificate can exist alongside a standard, more publicly accessible marriage record — not a claim about how any other state, if it offers a comparable confidential-marriage category, handles public access to those records, and not a claim about what "good cause" means or how a court order under this section is obtained.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 511(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the confidential, not-publicly-inspectable record
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), the county clerk shall maintain confidential marriage certificates filed pursuant to Section 506 as permanent records which shall not be open to public inspection except upon order of the court issued upon a showing of good cause. The confidential marriage license is a confidential record and not open to public inspection without an order from the court.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 511(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the limited existence-confirmation search
citations.quote: The county clerk may conduct a search for a confidential marriage certificate for the purpose of confirming the existence of a marriage, but the date of the marriage and any other information contained in the certificate shall not be disclosed except upon order of the court.

clauses.title: Who May Obtain a Certified Copy of the Confidential Marriage Certificate
clauses.body: {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} state that California law allows a party to a confidential marriage to obtain a certified copy of the confidential marriage certificate from the county clerk of the county where the certificate is filed, by submitting an application meeting the requirements set for certified copies of vital records under the Health and Safety Code, and upon payment of the fee equivalent to that charged for copies of a standard marriage certificate. The statute describes this certified-copy path as available to the parties to the marriage.
clauses.gap: Both quotes below are subdivisions (a) and (b) of the same statutory section, Family Code § 509; this is a single statutory section, and no additional independent source was found for it. It is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a confidential-marriage record system can still make a certified copy available to the married parties themselves despite the record's general non-public status — not a claim about the exact Health and Safety Code application requirements referenced in § 509(a) (Chapter 14, commencing with § 103525), which were not independently verified here, nor a claim about whether anyone other than a party to the marriage may obtain a certified copy through this specific provision.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 509(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a party's right to obtain a certified copy
citations.quote: A party to a confidential marriage may obtain a certified copy of the confidential marriage certificate from the county clerk of the county in which the certificate is filed by submitting an application that satisfies the requirements of Chapter 14 (commencing with Section 103525) of Part 1 of Division 102 of the Health and Safety Code.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 509(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the fee for a certified copy
citations.quote: Copies of a confidential marriage certificate may be issued to the parties to the marriage upon payment of the fee equivalent to that charged for copies of a marriage certificate.

clauses.title: Signatures and Acknowledgment
clauses.body:
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} acknowledge review of this Confidential Marriage — Information Sheet on {{dateSigned}}, prepared with reference to the confidential-marriage provisions of the {{countyOfFiling}} county clerk's office and the California Family Code sections cited above.
