clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}}, states what California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.01 et seq.) provides about a limited liability company's ability to render licensed "professional services" in California — a question that comes up for a licensed professional (for example, in law, medicine, accountancy, architecture, or another licensed field) who is considering the limited liability company as a business form. Where a specific profession or a specific proposed business name is named below, those are {{professionType}} and {{companyName}}; this sheet can also be read on its own, without either filled in, as a general reference to what the statute says. This sheet is a companion to this project's separate Professional Corporation — Formation Information Sheet, which addresses the professional corporation form that many licensed professions use instead. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any particular profession, business plan, or proposed entity is or is not permitted to use the limited liability company form, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: General Lawful Purpose, and a Conditional Licensed-Services Carve-Out
clauses.body: California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act states, as a general matter, that a limited liability company "may have any lawful purpose, regardless of whether for profit," subject to three named exclusions: the banking business, the business of issuing policies of insurance and assuming insurance risks, and the trust company business. The same subdivision then addresses licensed services directly: a domestic or foreign limited liability company "may render services that may be lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certificate, or registration authorized by the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, the Osteopathic Act, or the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act" — but only "if the applicable provisions" of that same body of law "authorize a limited liability company or foreign limited liability company to hold that license, certificate, or registration." Read on its own, this is a conditional permission, not an automatic one: whether an LLC may render a given licensed service depends on what the specific licensing statute for that service itself says about an LLC holding the license — this subdivision does not, by itself, supply that authorization.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the general conditional structure Section 17701.04(b) itself sets out; it does not survey which, if any, specific licenses, certificates, or registrations under the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, the Osteopathic Act, or the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act currently authorize a limited liability company to hold them — that determination depends on each profession's own governing statute, which was not individually checked here. The next clause in this document addresses a separate, more narrowly defined category of services, to which subdivision (e) of this same section applies a different, unconditional rule. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's choice of business form, and limited-liability-company requirements vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any entity and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's plan to organize a business.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.04(b)
citations.cite: Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, general lawful-purpose provision and conditional licensed-services carve-out
citations.quote: A limited liability company may have any lawful purpose, regardless of whether for profit, except the banking business, the business of issuing policies of insurance and assuming insurance risks, or the trust company business. A domestic or foreign limited liability company may render services that may be lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certificate, or registration authorized by the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, the Osteopathic Act, or the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act, if the applicable provisions of the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, the Osteopathic Act, or the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act authorize a limited liability company or foreign limited liability company to hold that license, certificate, or registration.

clauses.title: Unconditional Bar on Rendering "Professional Services" as Defined for This Purpose
clauses.body: A separate subdivision of the same section states a different and unconditional rule for a specifically cross-referenced category of services: "[n]othing in this title shall be construed to permit a domestic or foreign limited liability company to render professional services, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 13401 and in Section 13401.3, in this state." Unlike subdivision (b)'s conditional carve-out — which turns on what a particular profession's own governing statute separately says about an LLC holding a license — subdivision (e) does not leave that possibility open for the specific category of services it defines by cross-reference as "professional services." It states directly that nothing in the Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act ("this title") should be read as itself supplying, or as inviting an inference of, authorization for an LLC to render professional services in that defined sense. Which occupations actually fall within that defined category is addressed in the next clause of this document.
clauses.gap: Subdivisions (b) and (e) of Section 17701.04 are treated in this document as one primary source (both are part of the same statutory section, fetched and confirmed together), not as two independent sources — the description above of how they relate is this document's own reading of that one section's text, not a claim drawn from a second, independent authority. Section 17701.04 does not itself state, in so many words, that subdivision (e) "overrides" or otherwise interacts with subdivision (b) in any particular way for professional services as defined by Section 13401(a) and Section 13401.3; that description is a plain-text reading of the two subdivisions, not a conclusion drawn from any judicial or administrative interpretation, and no case law construing this specific relationship was located or reviewed as part of this verification pass. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's choice of business form, and limited-liability-company requirements vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any entity and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's plan to organize a business.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.04(e)
citations.cite: Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, bar on rendering "professional services" as cross-referenced
citations.quote: Nothing in this title shall be construed to permit a domestic or foreign limited liability company to render professional services, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 13401 and in Section 13401.3, in this state.

clauses.title: "Professional Services" Defined for This Purpose, by Cross-Reference
clauses.body: The "professional services" that subdivision (e) places off-limits to a limited liability company are defined by cross-reference to two other statutes, not restated within Section 17701.04 itself. Cal. Corp. Code § 13401(a) — part of the Moscone-Knox Professional Corporation Act — defines "[p]rofessional services" to mean "any type of professional services that may be lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certification, or registration authorized by the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, or the Osteopathic Act." Cal. Corp. Code § 13401.3 then adds one further category to that same definition, "[a]s used in this part": professional services "that may be lawfully rendered only pursuant to a license, certification, or registration authorized by the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act." Together, these two sections supply the entire defined universe Section 17701.04(e) points to: a domestic or foreign LLC may not render any service that may lawfully be rendered only pursuant to a license, certification, or registration under the Business and Professions Code, the Chiropractic Act, the Osteopathic Act, or the Yacht and Ship Brokers Act. Because the Business and Professions Code separately licenses a very wide range of occupations, this defined category is broad by cross-reference, not limited to a short, fixed list of named professions written into Section 17701.04, Section 13401, or Section 13401.3 themselves.

This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's choice of business form, and limited-liability-company requirements vary by state. clauses.title: One Narrow, Named Exception: A Health Care Service Plan Subsidiary
clauses.body: Section 17701.04 itself supplies one specifically named exception to its general framework, though by its own terms it is framed as an exception to subdivision (b)'s lawful-purpose provision rather than as an exception to subdivision (e)'s professional-services bar. Subdivision (d) states that, "[n]otwithstanding subdivision (b) and as specifically provided in this subdivision, a limited liability company may operate as a health care service plan licensed pursuant to Chapter 2.2 (commencing with Section 1340) of Division 2 of the Health and Safety Code if the limited liability company is a subsidiary of a health care service plan licensed pursuant to those provisions and the limited liability company is established to serve an existing line of business of the parent health care service plan." The same subdivision adds a liability-specific rule for this narrow case: the tort or contract liability of such an LLC and its members "is not limited or restricted in any manner because of the limited liability company status of the health care service plan." This exception is narrow and specifically conditioned — it applies only to a health care service plan LLC that is a subsidiary of an already-licensed parent health care service plan and that serves an existing line of that parent's business — not to health care service plans generally, and not to an individual licensed professional organizing their own practice as an LLC.

Code § 17701.04, and is treated as part of that same primary source, not as an independent citation. Subdivision (d) is framed by its own text as an exception to subdivision (b) ("[n]otwithstanding subdivision (b)"), not expressly to subdivision (e)'s professional-services bar; whether or how a health care service plan might separately fall within the "professional services" defined by Section 13401(a) and Section 13401.3 was not independently researched here, and this clause does not draw that conclusion either way. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's choice of business form, and limited-liability-company requirements vary by state. clauses.title: Contrast: The Registered Limited Liability Partnership Form Is Available, but Only to a Narrower, Named Set of Professions
clauses.body: California law makes a different kind of limited-liability entity available to a specific, named set of licensed professions: the registered limited liability partnership. Cal. Corp. Code § 16951 states that "[f]or purposes of this chapter, the only types of limited liability partnerships that shall be recognized are a registered limited liability partnership and a foreign limited liability partnership, as defined in Section 16101," and adds directly that "[n]o registered limited liability partnership or foreign limited liability partnership may render professional limited liability partnership services in this state except through licensed persons." Cal. Corp. Code § 16101 in turn defines a "[r]egistered limited liability partnership," in relevant part, as a partnership formed under Article 10 and registered under Section 16953 that is either composed of partners individually licensed to provide professional limited liability partnership services, related to a qualifying partnership under specific conditions, or — the branch most relevant here — one that "is licensed under the laws of the state to engage in the practice of architecture, the practice of public accountancy, the practice of engineering, the practice of land surveying, or the practice of law." Unlike the limited liability company, which subdivision (e) of Section 17701.04 bars from rendering the broadly cross-referenced set of "professional services" defined by Section 13401(a) and Section 13401.3, the registered limited liability partnership form is affirmatively available under Section 16101 — but only to this specific, shorter, named list of professions, and even then only through the partnership's own licensed persons.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are drawn from two independently enacted sections, Cal. Corp. Code § 16951 and Cal. Corp. Code § 16101, and are treated as two independent sources. As of this verification, the California Legislative Information website listed two different 2024-amended versions of Section 16101 on file (one reflecting Stats. 2024, Ch. 361, Sec. 9, and a separate one reflecting Stats. 2024, Ch. 361, Sec. 10, each itself building on a 2019 amendment); the quoted text above is drawn from, and independently double-fetched and confirmed against, the Sec. 9 version specifically, and the Sec. 10 version was not independently checked to confirm whether it states the quoted definition identically — a reader should not assume the two versions are necessarily identical in every respect. This clause states what these two statutes provide about the registered limited liability partnership form; it does not evaluate whether any specific person's or group's practice qualifies for that form, and does not address every other business-entity alternative (such as the professional corporation form, addressed in this project's separate Professional Corporation — Formation Information Sheet) that may be available to a given licensed profession. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific kind of entity — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific licensed professional's choice of business form, and these requirements vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself form any entity and does not determine which state's law, or which profession-specific rules, apply to any specific person's plan to organize a business.

clauses.title: Signature and Certification
De Facto Parent Status Request — Information and Declaration
clauses.body: I, {{petitionerName}}, am not {{childName}}'s legal or biological parent. My relationship to {{childName}}, a minor born {{childDOB}}, is: {{relationshipToChild}}. This information sheet provides background information about California's de facto parent doctrine -- a status a juvenile court may recognize, on a sufficient showing, for a person who has assumed a day-to-day parental role in a child's life -- for use alongside an actual application for de facto parent status in a pending Welfare and Institutions Code section 300 juvenile dependency proceeding concerning {{childName}}, in the {{countyOfFiling}} Superior Court (juvenile division) or other court of competent jurisdiction. This information sheet is not itself an application for de facto parent status, and it is not a court filing; signing it does not grant {{petitionerName}} de facto parent status, custody, or visitation of {{childName}}. {{childName}}'s legal parent(s) of record, so far as known, are {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}, where applicable. Only a court's own finding, on a sufficient showing, that {{petitionerName}} has assumed the day-to-day role of parent to {{childName}} can grant de facto parent status, and, as this document's other clauses describe, that status itself does not make {{petitionerName}} {{childName}}'s legal parent or guardian and does not itself grant custody or visitation.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — De Facto Parent Status Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{petitionerName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual application for de facto parent status in a pending Welfare and Institutions Code section 300 juvenile dependency proceeding concerning {{childName}}, in the {{countyOfFiling}} Superior Court (juvenile division) or other court of competent jurisdiction. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that application, and it does not itself grant de facto parent status, standing, custody, or visitation; only a court's own finding on a sufficient showing does that.]

clauses.title: What "De Facto Parent" Status Means, and the Juvenile-Dependency Context in Which the Term Is Defined — California Rules of Court, Rule 5.502(10)
clauses.body: California Rules of Court, rule 5.502(10) defines the term for use throughout the state's juvenile court rules: "'De facto parent' means a person who has been found by the court to have assumed, on a day-to-day basis, the role of parent, fulfilling both the child's physical and psychological needs for care and affection, and who has assumed that role for a substantial period." This is a status a court finds to exist on a sufficient showing -- it does not arise automatically merely from providing care, and, as this document's other clauses describe, it is not the same as being {{childName}}'s legal parent. Rule 5.502's own preamble lists the statutory provisions its definitions serve, and every one of them is a Welfare and Institutions Code section (for example, sections 300, 303, 319, 361, and 361.5(a)(3)) or a related federal statute -- none is a Family Code section. That confirms that "de facto parent," as this rule defines and uses it, is a term of art within California's juvenile dependency court system, not within the general Family Code custody and visitation framework addressed in this corpus's separate Third-Party (Nonparent) Custody and Visitation document.
clauses.gap: This is a California Rule of Court, fetched directly from courts.ca.gov and independently re-fetched with a distinct User-Agent string; both fetches were confirmed byte-identical after whitespace normalization. This clause cites two parts of the same rule -- the definitions preamble and subdivision (10) -- so this is not independent corroboration from two separate sources, only two parts of one source; that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent confirmation. This corrects an assumption in the research request that prompted this document: California Family Code sections 3040 and 7601 were independently fetched and re-fetched (courts.ca.gov and leginfo.legislature.ca.gov are treated separately for this purpose) and, as of the dates checked, neither section's text uses the phrase "de facto parent" anywhere -- the corpus's existing Third-Party (Nonparent) Custody and Visitation document's coverage of Family Code section 3040(a)(3)'s "any other person" custody-preference language and section 3100(a)'s "any other person having an interest in the welfare of the child" visitation language remains accurate on its own terms, but neither provision is, on its face, the statutory home of the de facto parent doctrine. This clause does not resolve whether a party to a Family Code custody or visitation proceeding could, as a factual matter, also independently qualify for the very different Family Code pathways described in that companion document; it addresses only the Rules of Court' own definition and its juvenile-dependency statutory anchoring.

clauses.title: The Standing and the Three Specific Rights De Facto Parent Status Confers — California Rules of Court, Rule 5.534(a)
clauses.body: California Rules of Court, rule 5.534(a) states what recognition as a de facto parent actually does for a person in a dependency case: "On a sufficient showing, the court may recognize the child's present or previous custodian as a de facto parent and grant him or her standing to participate as a party in the dispositional hearing and any hearing thereafter at which the status of the dependent child is at issue." The rule then lists exactly what that standing includes: "The de facto parent may: (1) Be present at the hearing; (2) Be represented by retained counsel or, at the discretion of the court, by appointed counsel; and (3) Present evidence." Recognition is discretionary ("the court may recognize"), conditioned on "a sufficient showing," and, by the rule's own terms, tied to the dispositional hearing and later hearings concerning {{childName}}'s status as a dependent -- not to every stage of a case.
clauses.gap: This is a California Rule of Court, fetched directly from courts.ca.gov and independently re-fetched with a distinct User-Agent string; both fetches were confirmed byte-identical after whitespace normalization. This clause quotes a single subdivision, rule 5.534(a); the rule's separate subdivision (b), which gives a relative of the child a narrower right (to be present and address the court, without the retained- or appointed-counsel right this subdivision gives a de facto parent), was not independently quoted here. The rule does not itself define "a sufficient showing" -- this document's companion clause on In re B.G. (1974) 11 Cal.3d 679 addresses the standard California's courts have used for that showing, but this clause does not resolve how that standard applies to any specific applicant's facts. This clause also does not address whether, or how, a person recognized as a de facto parent may participate at the separate jurisdictional hearing (the hearing at which the truth of the allegations that brought the case into dependency court is decided, as distinct from the dispositional hearing this rule's text names) -- that question was not independently researched for this document. Nothing in this rule's text grants a de facto parent custody, visitation, reunification services, or any right beyond the three this subdivision lists.

The de facto parent may: (1) Be present at the hearing; (2) Be represented by retained counsel or, at the discretion of the court, by appointed counsel; and (3) Present evidence.

clauses.title: Origin of the Doctrine and the Standard for Determining Who Qualifies — In re B.G. (1974) 11 Cal.3d 679
clauses.body: California's de facto parent doctrine originated in the California Supreme Court's 1974 decision In re B.G., which coined the term: "We use the term 'de facto parent' to refer to that person who, on a day-to-day basis, assumes the role of parent, seeking to fulfill both the child's physical needs and his psychological need for affection and care." The court held that a person meeting that description "should be permitted to appear as parties in juvenile court proceedings," not merely as a friend of the court: "Their standing should not depend upon the filing of a petition for guardianship, although the filing of such petition may aid in attesting to their interest in the custody of the child; nor should their participation be restricted to the limited role of an amicus curiae; they should be permitted to appear as parties to assert and protect their own interest in the companionship, care, custody and management of the child." On the standard for qualifying, the court did not set out a rigid checklist: "We anticipate that juvenile courts will experience little difficulty in determining whether a person is a de facto parent for purposes of standing to appear in a juvenile court custody proceeding. The simple fact that a person cares enough to seek and undertake to participate goes far to suggest that the court would profit by hearing his views as to the child's best interests; if the participant lacks a close relationship with the child, that fact will undoubtedly emerge during the proceedings."
clauses.gap: This case was read from two independently formatted CourtListener source records for the same opinion -- one captioned "In re B.G." (opinion id 1163726) and one captioned "Vlasta Z. v. San Bernardino County Welfare Department" (opinion id 5451963) -- both carrying the identical official citation, 11 Cal.3d 679, 523 P.2d 244, 114 Cal.Rptr. 444; the quoted passages were confirmed to match across both records (differing only in cosmetic formatting, such as straight versus curly quotation marks). This 1974 decision predates the current numbering of the California Rules of Court; this document's companion clauses cite the doctrine's present codification at rule 5.502(10) and rule 5.534(a), but this document does not independently trace the renumbering history between 1974 and today. This clause states the general qualifying standard the opinion articulated; it does not resolve whether any specific applicant meets that standard on particular facts, and it does not address later decisions -- including this document's companion clause on In re Kieshia E. -- that have narrowed the doctrine's application in particular circumstances.

Their standing should not depend upon the filing of a petition for guardianship, although the filing of such petition may aid in attesting to their interest in the custody of the child; nor should their participation be restricted to the limited role of an amicus curiae; they should be permitted to appear as parties to assert and protect their own interest in the companionship, care, custody and management of the child.

The simple fact that a person cares enough to seek and undertake to participate goes far to suggest that the court would profit by hearing his views as to the child's best interests; if the participant lacks a close relationship with the child, that fact will undoubtedly emerge during the proceedings.

clauses.title: De Facto Parent Status Is Not Legal Parentage or Guardianship, and Does Not Carry All of a Legal Parent's Rights — In re B.G., fn. 21, and In re Kieshia E.
clauses.body: In re B.G. itself limited what the de facto parent status it created actually means: "We do not hold that a de facto parent is a 'parent' or 'guardian' as those terms are used in the Juvenile Court Law, nor do we express a position whether constitutional principles of due process or equal protection may require that a de facto parent, in some instances, receive rights of notice, hearing, or counsel afforded natural parents or guardians under that law." Nearly twenty years later, the California Supreme Court in In re Kieshia E. restated that limit and confirmed it remained the law: "In re B.G., supra, expressly declined to hold that nonparents who assume a parental role thereby become 'parents' or 'guardians,' with all the rights such a status implies." The Kieshia E. court added that Courts of Appeal had likewise held that de facto parents "are not equated with ... parents or guardians for purposes of dependency proceedings and standing to participate does not give them all of the rights and preferences accorded [parents or guardians]." In practical terms, and read together with this document's companion clause on rule 5.534(a): de facto parent status gives {{petitionerName}} the right to be present, to be represented by counsel, and to present evidence at the specified hearings concerning {{childName}} -- it does not, by itself, make {{petitionerName}} {{childName}}'s legal parent or guardian, and it does not itself grant custody, visitation, or the reunification services or other statutory entitlements the Juvenile Court Law affords a legal parent or guardian.
clauses.gap: The Kieshia E. quotations were read from two independently formatted CourtListener source records for the same opinion -- one captioned "In re Kieshia E." (opinion id 2613175) and one captioned "San Diego County Department of Social Services v. Williams" (opinion id 5452096), both carrying the identical official citation, 6 Cal.4th 68, 859 P.2d 1290, 23 Cal.Rptr.2d 775 -- and the quoted passages were confirmed to match across both records. That said, this clause's two case-law citations are not fully independent of each other in substance: Kieshia E.'s own quoted passage is expressly restating and quoting In re B.G.'s footnote 21, and, in turn, quoting a Court of Appeal decision, In re Rachael C. (1991) 235 Cal.App.3d 1445, 1452, that this document does not independently verify -- so this clause offers one line of authority (B.G., reaffirmed and extended by Kieshia E.), not two unrelated ones. Separately, Kieshia E.'s actual holding was narrower and more fact-specific than the general limitation quoted here: the court held that an adult who committed the sexual or other serious physical abuse that caused a child to become a juvenile court dependent cannot attain or retain de facto parent status as to that child. That specific holding is noted here for context but is not itself summarized or relied on as this clause's point; this clause's point is only the general, unqualified proposition -- true independent of Kieshia E.'s facts -- that de facto parent status is not legal parentage or guardianship and does not carry all of a legal parent's rights. This clause does not address, and this document does not independently research, how a legal parent's rights and entitlements under the Juvenile Court Law compare item-by-item to a de facto parent's.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's statutory prohibition on polygraph and lie detector testing of job applicants and employees, codified at California Labor Code § 432.2, as it relates to {{companyName}}. It states facts about what California law prohibits, permits, and requires in this area. It is not itself a testing policy, a consent form, or a determination that any particular test, request, or examination involving {{employeeName}} does or does not comply with this law, and it does not tell {{employeeName}} or {{companyName}} what to do about any particular hiring or employment decision.

clauses.title: Core Prohibition on Polygraph and Lie Detector Tests
clauses.body: California law prohibits an employer from demanding or requiring an applicant for employment or prospective employment, or an employee, to submit to or take a polygraph, lie detector, or similar test or examination as a condition of employment or continued employment. The statute applies to both stages of the employment relationship it names: the hiring stage ("applicant for employment or prospective employment") and ongoing employment ("employee"). The prohibition is stated as a blanket rule tied to any test used "as a condition of employment or continued employment" — the statute's own text does not limit it to any particular industry, job type, or reason the employer might want the test administered.
clauses.gap: This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. A separate federal statute, the Employee Polygraph Protection Act, imposes an overlapping but not identical prohibition on many employers nationwide, addressed in a later clause of this document. This clause states the general rule; a following clause addresses a specific, textual exception within this same statutory section for government employers, and another addresses a separate written-notice obligation the same section imposes when a test is requested rather than demanded or required. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific test, request, or examination.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 432.2, subd. (a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, prohibition on polygraph and lie detector tests as a condition of employment
citations.quote: No employer shall demand or require any applicant for employment or prospective employment or any employee to submit to or take a polygraph, lie detector or similar test or examination as a condition of employment or continued employment.

clauses.title: Exception for Federal, State, and Local Government Employers
clauses.body: The same statutory sentence that states the prohibition also states its own express exception: the prohibition does not apply to the federal government or any of its agencies, or to state government or any of its agencies or local subdivisions, including counties, cities and counties, cities, districts, authorities, and agencies. In other words, on the text of this section, government employers at every level named — federal, state, and local — are excluded from this particular prohibition; a private employer is not.
clauses.gap: This exception is part of the same sentence and the same subdivision (a) of Labor Code § 432.2 as the core prohibition in the previous clause — it is not an independent source, but the second half of the same statutory text already quoted there. This is a genuine, textual carve-out worth flagging on its own: a reader assuming this statute reaches every employer in California without exception would be assuming something the statute's own text does not say. This document does not address whether some other statute, regulation, or constitutional provision might separately restrict polygraph or lie detector testing by a government employer; it addresses only the specific exception written into this section. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation, and not a claim about how any other state treats government employers. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any particular employer falls within this exception.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 432.2, subd. (a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, government-employer exception
citations.quote: The prohibition of this section does not apply to the federal government or any agency thereof or the state government or any agency or local subdivision thereof, including, but not limited to, counties, cities and counties, cities, districts, authorities, and agencies.

clauses.title: Written Notice of Rights Before a Requested Test
clauses.body: A separate subdivision of the same statute addresses a situation distinct from demanding or requiring a test: an employer requesting that a person take such a test, or administering one. In that situation, the statute prohibits the employer from requesting or administering the test without first advising the person, in writing, at the time the test is to be administered, of the rights the statute guarantees. On the statute's own structure, subdivision (a)'s prohibition on demanding or requiring a test as a condition of employment is an absolute bar with only the government-employer exception described elsewhere in this document; subdivision (b)'s written-notice obligation is a separate, narrower rule addressing a request for, or administration of, a test that is not being demanded or required as a condition of employment.
clauses.gap: This clause states subdivision (b) of the same Labor Code § 432.2 already quoted in the two preceding clauses — all three clauses draw on the same single statutory section, not independent corroborating sources. The statute's text does not itself define what "advising the person in writing... of the rights guaranteed by this section" must specifically say beyond referencing those statutory rights, and this document does not attempt to supply model notice language. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. This document is informational only: it does not itself constitute the written notice this subdivision describes, and does not determine whether any particular request for, or administration of, a test complies with it.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, written notice of statutory rights before a requested or administered test
citations.quote: No employer shall request any person to take such a test, or administer such a test, without first advising the person in writing at the time the test is to be administered of the rights guaranteed by this section.

clauses.title: Misdemeanor Penalty for Violation
clauses.body: A separately numbered section of the same statutory article — the article covering contracts and applications for employment, which includes the polygraph and lie detector prohibition described elsewhere in this document — makes a violation of any provision of that article a misdemeanor. On its text, this penalty provision is not limited to the polygraph and lie detector section specifically; it applies to "this article" as a whole, meaning it also covers violations of the other, separately numbered sections within the same article on contracts and applications for employment.
clauses.gap: This is a genuinely separate, independently numbered statutory section (Labor Code § 433) from Labor Code § 432.2 cited in the preceding clauses, appearing in the same statutory article rather than as a subdivision of the same section — it is treated here as an independently verified source, not as a restatement of § 432.2's own text. Because § 433 penalizes violation of the entire article (Labor Code §§ 430–435), it is not specific to polygraph testing by its own terms; this document does not independently verify or describe what other conduct that article covers beyond the polygraph and lie detector provisions already addressed. This document did not locate, and does not describe, any separate civil penalty, administrative remedy, or private right of action specific to § 432.2 within this same article; only this criminal misdemeanor provision was found and confirmed. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation, and not a claim about how any other state penalizes similar conduct. clauses.title: Comparison to the Federal Employee Polygraph Protection Act
clauses.body: Separately from California law, a federal statute — the Employee Polygraph Protection Act — also restricts lie detector testing in employment. Subject to two statutory exceptions found elsewhere in that same federal law, it is unlawful for a covered employer to require, request, suggest, or cause an employee or prospective employee to take or submit to a lie detector test; to use, accept, refer to, or inquire about the results of such a test; or to discharge, discipline, discriminate against, deny employment or promotion to, or threaten any such action against a person who refuses to take the test, based on its results, or for exercising rights under the federal law. This federal prohibition applies to "any employer engaged in or affecting commerce or in the production of goods for commerce," a jurisdictional test grounded in federal commerce-power coverage, rather than the government-employer exception found in the California statute described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This is a separate, independently confirmed federal source (29 U.S.C. § 2002) — not a subdivision of the California Labor Code sections cited elsewhere in this document — genuinely corroborating that a comparable, broader-reaching prohibition also exists at the federal level. The quoted provision itself states that it applies "except as provided in sections 2006 and 2007" of the same federal title; this document did not independently fetch or verify the text of those two referenced exception sections, so their specific scope (which is understood to include certain government employers, security-service and pharmaceutical-manufacturing businesses under ongoing investigations, and related situations) is not confirmed here and should not be assumed to mirror California's own, narrower, government-employer exception. This federal law and the California statute are separate legal regimes that can overlap in their coverage of the same employer; this document does not state which one, if either, would govern any particular reader's situation, and does not attempt to reconcile every difference between them beyond the specific points stated in this clause.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Information and Background — Alleged Retaliation for a Wage Claim or Related Activity
clauses.body:
I, {{employeeName}}, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment with {{companyName}}. The wage claim, Labor Commissioner-related activity, or other conduct I believe may be connected to an adverse action against me is described here as: {{allegedProtectedActivity}}. The adverse action I believe may be connected to that activity is described here as: {{allegedAdverseAction}}, which I understand to have occurred on {{adverseActionDate}}.

This information sheet describes California Labor Code section 98.6 — a statute that separately prohibits an employer from discharging, discriminating, or retaliating against an employee or applicant because of certain wage-claim, Labor Commissioner-related, and other statutorily listed conduct — along with the related administrative complaint process under Labor Code section 98.7. It is not a Labor Commissioner complaint, is not a civil complaint or any other court filing, is not filed with the Labor Commissioner, the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, any court, or any other agency by completing it, and does not initiate any proceeding. Completing it does not establish that {{employeeName}} engaged in any conduct protected under Labor Code section 98.6, that {{companyName}} took any adverse action because of that conduct, or that any specific fact stated here is true. Only a court, or the Labor Commissioner acting under Labor Code section 98.7, can determine whether a violation of Labor Code section 98.6 occurred.

clauses.title: The Core Prohibition and the Statute's Own List of Protected Conduct
clauses.body: California law prohibits an employer from discharging an employee, or in any manner discriminating, retaliating, or taking any adverse action against an employee or applicant for employment, because that person engaged in conduct this statute and a related chapter of the Labor Code delineate as protected. The statute's own text lists several distinct categories of protected conduct rather than a single one: engaging in conduct described elsewhere in the same statutory chapter, including whistleblower-type conduct addressed in a separate Labor Code provision; filing a bona fide complaint or claim, or instituting or causing to be instituted any proceeding, relating to rights under the Labor Commissioner's jurisdiction; making a written or oral complaint that the person is owed unpaid wages; initiating an action or notice, or testifying or being about to testify, in a proceeding under the Labor Code's Private Attorneys General Act provision; and the exercise, on behalf of the employee or others, of any rights the statute affords.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (a) of Labor Code § 98.6. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) across two independent fetches performed in this research session using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard Chrome browser string and a distinct research-tool string) on 2026-09-03; the quote below was confirmed as an exact substring of that fetched text. This clause covers only subdivision (a) — the statute's own remedies, its rebuttable-presumption and civil-penalty provisions, its applicant- and family-member-specific protections, and the related administrative complaint deadline under a separate Labor Code section are addressed in other clauses of this document, each disclosing its own subdivision or section relationships rather than treating all quoted text as one undifferentiated source. This document independently re-verifies this statute's text rather than relying on a passing description of it that already exists elsewhere in this corpus's separate Wrongful Termination in Violation of Public Policy information sheet; that existing description is limited to a single clause covering only subdivision (a)'s core prohibition together with subdivisions (b)(1) and (b)(3), and does not address subdivision (b)(2)'s separate misdemeanor provision, subdivision (c)'s applicant-specific protections, subdivision (e)'s family-member protection, or the administrative complaint process and deadline under Labor Code § 98.7, all of which this document covers in other clauses. No claim is made about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship, or that any specific complaint, activity, or exercise of rights actually falls within this statute's coverage. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that any specific adverse action was taken because of protected conduct, or that a violation of Labor Code § 98.6 occurred in this or any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 98.6(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: A person shall not discharge an employee or in any manner discriminate, retaliate, or take any adverse action against any employee or applicant for employment because the employee or applicant engaged in any conduct delineated in this chapter, including the conduct described in subdivision (k) of Section 96, and Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 1101) of Part 3 of Division 2, or because the employee or applicant for employment has filed a bona fide complaint or claim or instituted or caused to be instituted any proceeding under or relating to their rights that are under the jurisdiction of the Labor Commissioner, made a written or oral complaint that they are owed unpaid wages, or because the employee has initiated any action or notice pursuant to Section 2699, or has testified or is about to testify in a proceeding pursuant to that section, or because of the exercise by the employee or applicant for employment on behalf of themselves or others of any rights afforded them.

clauses.title: The Remedies This Statute Itself Provides
clauses.body: For an employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, retaliated against, subjected to an adverse action, or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment because of the statute's listed protected conduct, the statute itself entitles that employee to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts. Separately, an employer who willfully refuses to hire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee or former employee already determined eligible for rehiring or promotion through a grievance procedure, arbitration, or legally authorized hearing is guilty of a misdemeanor. In addition to other available remedies, an employer who violates this statute is also liable for a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per employee for each violation, to be awarded to the employee or employees who suffered the violation.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes three separate provisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 98.6(b)(1) (the reinstatement-and-reimbursement portion of that paragraph, quoted separately from its rebuttable-presumption sentence, which is addressed in a different clause of this document), (b)(2), and (b)(3) — which is disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources from one another. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) across two independent fetches in this research session using distinct User-Agent strings on 2026-09-03; each quote below was confirmed as an exact substring of that fetched text. This document does not assume the (b)(2) misdemeanor-for-willful-refusal-to-rehire provision carries the reinstatement/reimbursement or civil-penalty remedies described in (b)(1) and (b)(3) — the statute's own text states (b)(2) as a standalone misdemeanor, without cross-referencing either of those remedy provisions, and this document states it that way rather than assuming the remedy structures are interchangeable. This document is informational: it does not itself award, calculate, or determine entitlement to reinstatement, reimbursement, or any civil penalty amount in this or any specific case.

clauses.title: The 90-Day Rebuttable Presumption and the Separate One-Year Administrative Complaint Deadline
clauses.body: If an employer takes an action this statute prohibits within 90 days of the employee's protected activity, California law creates a rebuttable presumption in the employee's favor — meaning the burden shifts to the employer to offer a non-retaliatory explanation for its action, not that retaliation is conclusively established. Separately, a different Labor Code section gives a person who believes they were discharged or otherwise discriminated against in violation of any law under the Labor Commissioner's jurisdiction — which includes this statute — the option of filing an administrative complaint with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement within one year after the violation, a period the Labor Commissioner may extend for good cause. Filing that administrative complaint is not required before pursuing other rights and remedies under the law; the statute governing that administrative process states there is no exhaustion-of-administrative-remedies requirement.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two independent statutory sections and discloses that distinction rather than treating them as one source: (1) Labor Code § 98.6(b)(1)'s rebuttable-presumption sentence, and (2) Labor Code § 98.7(a)(1) and (g), a separate section governing the Labor Commissioner's administrative discrimination-complaint process generally (not limited to § 98.6 violations). Both were fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and each confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) across two independent fetches in this research session using distinct User-Agent strings on 2026-09-03; each quote below was confirmed as an exact substring of its respective fetched text. The 90-day presumption is rebuttable, not conclusive, and this document does not treat it as establishing that any specific adverse action was retaliatory. The one-year period in § 98.7(a)(1) governs the administrative complaint filed with the Division, not a civil lawsuit; this research session did not identify, and does not state, a specific statute of limitations that applies to a private civil action brought directly under Labor Code § 98.6 itself — that is disclosed here as an honest gap rather than filled in with an assumed or unverified deadline. § 98.7(a)(1) also separately notes a 30-day period, applicable specifically to complainants alleging a violation of Labor Code §§ 6310 or 6311 (workplace safety retaliation, not the wage-claim and Labor Commissioner-jurisdiction conduct this document addresses), to file a separate concurrent complaint with the United States Department of Labor; that 30-day period is not the one-year period described in this clause's body and is not applicable to the conduct this document covers, so it is not otherwise repeated here. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that any presumption applies to a specific case, that a specific complaint would be timely, or that a violation of Labor Code § 98.6 occurred in this or any specific case.

clauses.title: Beyond the Employee Discharged: Applicant and Family-Member Protections
clauses.body: The statute's protections are not limited to an employee who is already discharged. A job applicant who is refused employment, not selected for a training program leading to employment, or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of an employment offer, because of the same categories of protected conduct addressed elsewhere in this document, is separately entitled to employment and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the prospective employer. The statute also separately prohibits an employer, or a person acting on the employer's behalf, from retaliating against an employee because that employee is a family member of a person who has, or is perceived to have, engaged in protected conduct under this statute.

This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) across two independent fetches in this research session using distinct User-Agent strings on 2026-09-03; each quote below was confirmed as an exact substring of that fetched text. The statute's text also states, in a subdivision not quoted in this document, that the family-member protection in (e) does not apply to certain lawful off-duty-conduct claims addressed elsewhere in the same chapter unless that conduct itself involves the exercise of rights covered by subdivision (a); that narrower qualification is noted here for completeness but is not independently analyzed in this document. These applicant- and family-member-specific protections are not addressed in this corpus's existing Wrongful Termination in Violation of Public Policy information sheet, whose own treatment of this statute is limited to the discharge-focused core prohibition and the reinstatement, presumption, and civil-penalty provisions. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that any specific applicant or family member was denied employment or retaliated against because of protected conduct, or that a violation of Labor Code § 98.6 occurred in this or any specific case.

clauses.title: How This Statute Differs From Labor Code § 132a's Workers'-Compensation-Specific Scheme
clauses.body: Labor Code § 98.6, addressed throughout this document, is enforceable through a private civil action, and separately through an optional administrative complaint filed with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement under Labor Code § 98.7 — filing that administrative complaint is not a prerequisite to pursuing other remedies. This is a structurally different enforcement path from this corpus's separate Workers' Compensation Retaliation (Labor Code § 132a) information sheet, which covers a statute that is instead enforced exclusively through a petition filed with, and adjudicated by, the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board, subject to a one-year deadline running from the discriminatory act or date of termination, with the appeals board having no jurisdiction over any misdemeanor charge under that statute. The two statutes also protect different conduct: Labor Code § 98.6 protects wage-claim and Labor Commissioner-related activity, together with certain other Labor Code rights, while Labor Code § 132a protects the filing of, or testimony concerning, a workers' compensation claim.
clauses.gap: This clause compares Labor Code § 98.6 (independently re-verified in this research session, as documented in other clauses of this document) against Labor Code § 132a's closing paragraph, describing the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board's exclusive petition procedure and one-year deadline; that closing paragraph was independently fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov in this research session and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings on 2026-09-03, rather than copied without re-verification from this corpus's existing Workers' Compensation Retaliation (Labor Code § 132a) information sheet, which separately verified the same statutory text in an earlier research session. clauses.title: Declaration
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the federal statutory termination right created by 17 U.S.C. § 203, and, where a grant predates the current copyright statute, the related pathway in 17 U.S.C. § 304(c) and (d) — the right that lets an individual author, or certain statutorily defined successors, terminate a copyright transfer or license decades after it was made, regardless of what the transfer agreement itself says. It is prepared with reference to a grant by {{creatorName}} to {{granteeName}} covering {{workTitle}}, executed on or about {{grantExecutionDate}}, for use as background information about how the federal termination-of-transfer provisions generally operate. This sheet does not itself terminate any grant, does not constitute or substitute for an advance notice of termination under 17 U.S.C. § 203 or § 304, and does not determine whether {{creatorName}}, {{granteeName}}, or any grant between them is in fact eligible for termination — eligibility depends on facts (including who executed the grant, when, and whether the underlying work was made for hire) that this sheet does not resolve. Copyright is exclusively a matter of federal law; this sheet describes no California-specific rule.

clauses.title: The Termination Right and Its Override of Contrary Agreements
clauses.body: Federal copyright law lets an author terminate a grant — an exclusive or nonexclusive transfer or license of copyright, or of any right under a copyright — that the author executed on or after January 1, 1978, other than by will. This termination right exists notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, including an agreement to make a will or to make a future grant, so a waiver of the termination right written into the original transfer agreement does not by itself prevent termination. This is a rule of federal law only; copyright is exclusively federal, and this termination right is not a feature of California law.
clauses.gap: The statute's override language is quoted from 17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(5); the identical override rule also appears, independently, in 17 U.S.C. § 304(c)(5), which governs a related but separate termination pathway for grants executed before 1978 (addressed elsewhere in this document). This clause states the general contours of the right — who specifically may exercise it, exactly when, and how — without addressing eligibility for a particular grant, which depends on facts such as who executed the grant, when, and whether the work is a work made for hire.

clauses.title: The Work-Made-for-Hire Exception
clauses.body: The termination right does not apply to a work made for hire. This exception is written directly into the statute's own conditions for termination, both for grants executed on or after January 1, 1978 and, separately, for the related pre-1978 termination pathway for renewal-term grants. A work made for hire is, by definition elsewhere in the Copyright Act, typically either work created by an employee within the scope of employment, or one of several specifically enumerated categories of specially ordered or commissioned work for which the parties have signed a written work-for-hire agreement — a status this sheet does not itself determine for any particular work.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are drawn from two independent statutory sections — 17 U.S.C. § 203 (grants executed on or after January 1, 1978) and § 304(c) (pre-1978 renewal-term grants) — each of which independently excludes a work made for hire from its own termination right. Neither citation itself defines "work made for hire"; that definition appears in 17 U.S.C. § 101 and is addressed separately by this project's Copyright Assignment Agreement document, not reproduced or re-verified here.

clauses.title: Who May Exercise the Right — Author and Statutory Heirs
clauses.body: Where a single author executed the grant, that author may effect termination, or, if the author has died, termination may be effected by whoever under the statute's ownership rules owns and is entitled to exercise more than one-half of that author's termination interest. Where an author has died, the statute distributes that author's termination interest among specific classes of survivors in a fixed order: the surviving spouse owns the entire interest unless the author also left surviving children or grandchildren, in which case the spouse owns one-half and the children (or, per stirpes, the surviving children of a deceased child) own the balance. This ownership scheme is not a general default for who inherits a decedent's property generally — it is a termination-interest allocation rule specific to this statute.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory provision, 17 U.S.C. § 203(a) (clauses (1) and (2)); they are not independent sources of each other. Independent confirmation instead comes from a separate section: 17 U.S.C. § 304(c)(2)(A), governing the different pre-1978 termination pathway, uses identical operative language for the same spousal-share rule, which corroborates that this is the general statutory ownership formula rather than an artifact particular to § 203. This clause does not address the further per-stirpes subdivision among grandchildren, the rule for when no spouse, children, or grandchildren survive, or the joint-work rule requiring majority action among multiple living co-authors, all of which the statute also addresses in more granular detail than reproduced here.

clauses.title: The Termination Window — Post-1978 Grants and the Separate Pre-1978 Pathway
clauses.body: For a grant executed on or after January 1, 1978, termination may be effected at any time during a five-year window that begins at the end of thirty-five years from the date the grant was executed — or, if the grant covers the right of publication, the window instead begins at the earlier of thirty-five years from the date of publication under the grant or forty years from the date of execution. A separate, older pathway applies to a grant of renewal-term rights executed before January 1, 1978: there, the five-year termination window begins at the end of fifty-six years from the date copyright was originally secured (or January 1, 1978, whichever is later). Because a 1998 statutory amendment lengthened copyright's term, the statute also created a second, later five-year window — beginning at the end of seventy-five years from the date copyright was originally secured — for cases where the fifty-six-year-based termination right had already expired unused by the time that 1998 amendment took effect.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two independent statutory sections: 17 U.S.C. § 203 (grants executed on or after January 1, 1978) and § 304(c)/(d) (grants executed before January 1, 1978, covering renewal-term rights). Within § 304, subsection (c)(3) and subsection (d)(2) are subdivisions of the same section and are not independent of each other; § 304(d)'s later window is available only where no termination was made under § 304(c) and only for copyrights originally secured in a specific historical date range, a further condition this clause does not restate in full. This clause states timing rules only; it does not address the separate two-to-ten-year advance notice requirement (addressed in another clause of this document) or resolve, for any specific grant, which of these windows (if any) applies.

clauses.title: Notice Timing, Content, and Recordation
clauses.body: To exercise the termination right, an advance written notice must be served on the grantee or the grantee's successor in title, stating an effective termination date that falls within the applicable five-year window; the notice itself must be served not less than two nor more than ten years before that stated effective date. A copy of the notice must be recorded with the U.S. Copyright Office before the effective date of termination as a condition to the termination actually taking effect. The statute delegates the notice's required form, content, and manner of service to regulations the Register of Copyrights is directed to prescribe. The Copyright Office's own regulation implementing that delegation confirms it covers notices under both termination pathways — 17 U.S.C. § 203 and § 304(c)/(d) — states that the Office does not provide a printed form for this purpose, and requires that a notice under § 203 clearly identify, among other things, a statement that the termination is made under § 203, the grantee's name and address for service, the date of execution of the grant (and, if applicable, date of publication), the work's title and the author's name, a statement identifying the grant being terminated, and the stated effective date of termination.
clauses.gap: The statutory citation (17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(4)(B)) and the regulatory citation (37 C.F.R. § 201.10) are independent sources of each other — one is enacted statute, the other is the U.S. Copyright Office's own implementing regulation issued under the statute's delegation of rulemaking authority. This clause summarizes only the § 203-specific content list in 37 C.F.R. § 201.10(b)(2); the regulation's content requirements for a § 304(c)/(d) notice differ somewhat and are not restated here, nor is the regulation's separate treatment of permitted service methods, harmless-error rules, or the mechanics of Copyright Office recordation once a notice has been served.

clauses.title: Effect of a Completed Termination
clauses.body: Once termination takes effect, all rights under the Copyright Act that were covered by the terminated grant revert to the author, authors, or other persons who owned termination interests — including anyone who did not personally join in signing the notice of termination but was entitled to. Reversion is not absolute, however: a derivative work already prepared under the grant's authority before termination may continue to be used under the terms of the original grant even after termination, though this carve-out does not extend to preparing any new derivative works after termination. Separately, once rights revert, the statute restricts who may make a further grant of those same rights and generally requires that any further grant be made only after termination's effective date, subject to a narrow first-refusal-style exception for the original grantee.
clauses.gap: The reversion rule (17 U.S.C. § 203(b)) and the specific derivative-work carve-out (§ 203(b)(1)) are drawn from the same statutory subsection and are not independent of each other. Independent confirmation of the derivative-work carve-out specifically comes from a separate section, § 304(c)(6)(A), governing the different pre-1978 termination pathway, which uses identical operative language. This clause does not restate the further-grant restrictions of § 203(b)(3)-(4) in full, including their own numerosity and timing requirements.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet is provided by {{companyName}} to {{employeeName}} to explain, on a general informational basis only, California's job-protected leave and anti-retaliation protections for an employee who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or certain other crimes -- or who has a family member who is such a victim -- when taking time off from work for reasons connected to that victimization, such as obtaining a restraining order, seeking medical or psychological treatment, attending related court proceedings, or engaging in safety planning. It states general facts about how California law in this area works, including how that law has changed over time and where it is presently codified. It does not describe {{employeeName}}'s own situation, does not determine whether {{employeeName}} or any other person qualifies as a victim or a family member of a victim under any statute, and does not advise {{employeeName}} or {{companyName}} on what to do about any actual circumstance.

clauses.title: Where This Protection Is Codified Today
clauses.body: California Labor Code §§ 230 and 230.1 were, for many years, the primary statutes protecting an employee who is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or certain other crimes -- including the additional leave purposes those sections made available to employees of larger employers. Both sections remain on the books, but by their own current terms each now applies only to alleged actions or inactions occurring on or before December 31, 2024, and each is scheduled for repeal on January 1, 2035. Effective January 1, 2025, this same body of protection was relocated into the Fair Employment and Housing Act, and is presently codified at Government Code § 12945.8, most recently amended by AB 406 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 148), effective October 1, 2025. This information sheet accordingly describes the substance of the former Labor Code §§ 230 and 230.1 protections, and separately identifies where that same protection is now found and how its scope has changed.
clauses.gap: This section's independent verification of Labor Code § 230.1's current transitional status is a genuine extension beyond this corpus's existing Jury Duty and Witness Leave Information Sheet, which addressed only the jury-duty and witness-leave portions of former Labor Code § 230 and expressly declined to make any claim about § 230.1's current status. This document does not address whether any particular employee's leave, taken before or after any of these transition dates, is governed by the former or the current statute, and it does not independently verify secondary commentary about the legislative history of AB 2499 or AB 406 -- only the current statutory text of Labor Code §§ 230 and 230.1 and Government Code § 12945.8 was verified. The Labor Code § 230 citation and the Labor Code § 230.1 citation below are each drawn from a single subsection of their respective, separately-numbered sections, so the two Labor Code citations are independent of each other; the Government Code citation is from a third, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both.

clauses.title: Core Victim Leave Protection and Job Protection
clauses.body: Under former Labor Code § 230(c) -- and, for present-day conduct, under Government Code § 12945.8(a)(3) -- an employer may not discharge an employee, or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee, who is a victim for taking time off from work to obtain or attempt to obtain relief such as a temporary restraining order, restraining order, or other injunctive relief intended to help ensure the health, safety, or welfare of the victim or the victim's child. Government Code § 12945.8(a)(4) separately prohibits, commencing January 1, 2026, discharge or discrimination or retaliation against an employee who is a victim or a family member of a victim for taking time off to attend judicial proceedings related to the crime, including a delinquency proceeding, a postarrest release decision, a plea, a sentencing, a postconviction release decision, or any proceeding in which a right of that person is at issue.
clauses.gap: This clause does not restate the separate witness-leave protection already covered by this corpus's existing Jury Duty and Witness Leave Information Sheet (Government Code § 12945.8(a)(2), extended to but not limited to victims). It also does not resolve who qualifies as a 'victim' or 'family member' for these purposes -- those are defined terms addressed only in general terms elsewhere in this document -- nor does it address the January 1, 2026 commencement date of subdivision (a)(4) in relation to any particular set of facts. The Government Code § 12945.8(a)(3) and § 12945.8(a)(4) citations below are two paragraphs of the same subdivision of the same section and are not independent of each other; the Labor Code § 230(c) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8(a)(3), victim relief leave protection
citations.quote: (3) Discharge or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee who is a victim for taking time off from work to obtain or attempt to obtain any relief. Relief includes, but is not limited to, a temporary restraining order, restraining order, or other injunctive relief, to help ensure the health, safety, or welfare of the victim or their child.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)

citations.quote: (c) An employer shall not discharge or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee who is a victim for taking time off from work to obtain or attempt to obtain any relief. Relief includes, but is not limited to, a temporary restraining order, restraining order, or other injunctive relief, to help ensure the health, safety, or welfare of the victim or their child.

clauses.title: Additional Leave Purposes for Employers With 25 or More Employees
clauses.body: Former Labor Code § 230.1(a), and now Government Code § 12945.8(b), each impose an additional, broader set of job-protection duties that apply only to an employer with 25 or more employees. Under the current Government Code § 12945.8(b), such an employer may not discharge, discriminate, or retaliate against an employee who is a victim, or who has a family member who is a victim, for taking time off from work for any of ten enumerated purposes, including seeking relief for a family member, seeking or assisting a family member to seek medical attention, domestic-violence-shelter or victim services, or psychological counseling, participating in safety planning, relocating, providing care to a recovering family member, seeking legal services, attending legal proceedings, or arranging childcare or dependent care made necessary by the qualifying act of violence. The former Labor Code § 230.1(a) covered a narrower set of four purposes for the same 25-or-more-employee threshold: seeking medical attention, obtaining domestic-violence-shelter or victim services, obtaining psychological counseling, and safety planning or relocation. Government Code § 12945.8(i) also allows an employer to cap total leave taken for these subdivision (b) purposes at 12 weeks, and to impose a shorter 5-day or 10-day cap in certain circumstances where the leave is taken because of a family member's (rather than the employee's own) victimization.
clauses.gap: This clause states the 25-or-more-employee threshold and the numbers and general subject matter of the enumerated purposes as they appear in the statutory text; it does not attempt to state which specific facts satisfy any one of those purposes, and it does not address how an employer's total employee count is measured or on what date it is measured, none of which the text of either section specifies. It also does not restate the corpus's existing citation to Government Code § 12945.8(b)'s chapeau language, but independently re-verifies it here. The two Government Code § 12945.8 citations below (the subdivision (b) chapeau and the leave-cap subdivision (i)) are from the same section and are not independent of each other; the Labor Code § 230.1(a) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both -- it is this independent Labor Code source that establishes the historical, narrower four-purpose list, in contrast to the current ten-purpose list.

citations.quote: (b) An employer with 25 or more employees shall not discharge or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against an employee who is a victim or who has a family member who is a victim for taking time off from work for any of the following purposes:

citations.quote: (1) An employer may limit total leave time taken pursuant to subdivision (b) to 12 weeks. (2) If an employee’s family member is a victim who is not deceased as a result of a crime, and the employee is not a victim, and the employee takes leave pursuant to paragraph (6) of subdivision (b), the employer may limit the leave taken for that reason to five days. (3) If any employee’s family member is a victim who is not deceased as a result of crime, and the employee is not a victim, the employer may limit the total leave taken pursuant to subdivision (b) to 10 days.

(2) To obtain services from a domestic violence shelter, program, rape crisis center, or victim services organization or agency as a result of the crime or abuse. (3) To obtain psychological counseling or mental health services related to an experience of crime or abuse. (4) To participate in safety planning and take other actions to increase safety from future crime or abuse, including temporary or permanent relocation.

clauses.title: Advance Notice and Certification
clauses.body: As a condition of taking time off for the relief-leave, family-relief, or 25-or-more-employee purposes described above, Government Code § 12945.8(c)(1) states that the employee shall give the employer reasonable advance notice of the employee's intention to take time off, unless advance notice is not feasible. When an unscheduled absence occurs instead, § 12945.8(c)(2) provides that the employer shall not take action against the employee if the employee, within a reasonable time after the absence, provides a certification -- which the statute treats as sufficient in several listed forms, including a police report, a qualifying court order or other court or prosecutorial evidence of a court appearance, documentation from a licensed medical professional, domestic violence counselor, sexual assault counselor, victim advocate, or other health care provider or counselor, or another form of documentation that reasonably verifies the qualifying act of violence occurred. Former Labor Code § 230(d)(2) contained a substantively similar certification list.
clauses.gap: This clause does not attempt to define how much advance notice is 'reasonable' or when advance notice is 'not feasible,' terms the statute does not itself define. It also does not restate the full text of every certification category, only the general structure and some examples, and it does not address the reasonable-accommodation-specific certification and recertification provisions found elsewhere in § 12945.8(e)(7), which this document treats separately. The two Government Code § 12945.8 citations below (subdivisions (c)(1) and (c)(2)) are from the same section and are not independent of each other; the Labor Code § 230(d)(2) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both.
