citations.quote: (c) (1) As a condition of taking time off for a purpose set forth in paragraph (1), (3), or (4) of subdivision (a), or subdivision (b), the employee shall give the employer reasonable advance notice of the employee’s intention to take time off, unless the advance notice is not feasible.

citations.quote: (2) When an unscheduled absence occurs, the employer shall not take any action against the employee if the employee, within a reasonable time after the absence, provides a certification to the employer upon request by the employer. Certification shall be sufficient in the form of any of the following: (A) A police report indicating that the employee or a family member of the employee was a victim.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230(d)(2), the historical version of the same certification provision
citations.quote: (2) When an unscheduled absence occurs, the employer shall not take any action against the employee if the employee, within a reasonable time after the absence, provides a certification to the employer. Certification shall be sufficient in the form of any of the following: (A) A police report indicating that the employee was a victim.

clauses.title: Confidentiality of Leave and Accommodation Records
clauses.body: Government Code § 12945.8(c)(3) states that, to the extent allowed by law, an employer shall maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting leave under the relief-leave, judicial-proceeding, or 25-or-more-employee provisions, and that furnishing evidence or a certification does not waive any confidentiality or privilege that may otherwise exist between the employee or the employee's family member and a third party. A parallel confidentiality duty applies to reasonable-accommodation documentation under § 12945.8(e)(7)(D): any verbal or written statement, police or court record, or other documentation identifying an employee or the employee's family member as a victim must be maintained as confidential by the employer and not disclosed except as required by federal or state law or as necessary to protect the employee's safety in the workplace, and the employee must be given notice before any authorized disclosure. Former Labor Code § 230(d)(3) contained the same confidentiality duty for relief-leave requests.
clauses.gap: This clause does not attempt to define the outer limits of 'to the extent allowed by law,' a qualifier the statute leaves undefined, and it does not address what remedy, if any, is available to an employee for a breach of this confidentiality duty -- that is not stated in the confidentiality subdivisions themselves. It also does not independently verify whether any other statute (for example, general personnel-file or privacy statutes) supplies additional confidentiality protection. The Government Code § 12945.8(c)(3) and § 12945.8(e)(7)(D) citations below are from the same section and are not independent of each other; the Labor Code § 230(d)(3) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of both.

citations.quote: (3) To the extent allowed by law and consistent with subparagraph (D) of paragraph (7) of subdivision (e), the employer shall maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting leave under paragraph (3) or (4) of subdivision (a), or subdivision (b). Furnishing evidence or providing a certification under this subdivision shall not waive any confidentiality or privilege that may exist between the employee or employee’s family member and a third party.

The employee shall be given notice before any authorized disclosure.

clauses.title: Reasonable Accommodation for Workplace Safety
clauses.body: Separately from the leave provisions above, Government Code § 12945.8(e)(1) requires an employer to provide reasonable accommodations for an employee who is a victim, or whose family member is a victim, of a qualifying act of violence, when the employee requests an accommodation for the employee's safety while at work. Unlike the additional leave purposes discussed above, this accommodation duty is not limited to employers with 25 or more employees. Section 12945.8(e)(2) gives examples of reasonable accommodations, including a transfer, reassignment, modified schedule, changed work telephone or permission to carry a telephone at work, changed work station, installed lock, assistance documenting an incident, an implemented safety procedure, another adjustment to a job structure, workplace facility, or work requirement, or referral to a victim assistance organization. Section 12945.8(f) separately makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or attempt to exercise, any right provided under the section. Former Labor Code § 230(f)(1) contained a substantively similar reasonable-accommodation duty.
clauses.gap: This clause does not attempt to define 'undue hardship,' a limit on the accommodation duty that the statute defines by cross-reference to Government Code § 12926 and Labor Code § 6400, both of which this document did not independently fetch or verify. It also does not restate the accommodation-specific certification and six-month recertification provisions found in § 12945.8(e)(7), addressing only the confidentiality portion of that paragraph in a separate clause. The Government Code § 12945.8(e)(1), § 12945.8(e)(2), and § 12945.8(f) citations below are all from the same section and are not independent of one another; the Labor Code § 230(f)(1) citation is from a separate, independently-numbered section and so is independent of all three.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the substantive grounds California law recognizes for challenging the validity of a will or trust made by {{decedentName}}, who died on {{dateOfDeath}}, and the basic procedural rules -- standing and time limits -- for raising such a challenge in {{countyOfFiling}} County, California. It states facts about California law generally. It does not determine whether any ground for a challenge exists on these particular facts, and it does not advise on whether to bring, join, or forgo a challenge.

clauses.title: Ground: Lack of Testamentary Capacity
clauses.body: One recognized ground for contesting the validity of {{decedentName}}'s will is that {{decedentName}} lacked testamentary capacity when it was signed. Under California law, an individual lacks the mental competency required to make a will if, at the time of making it, the individual either did not have sufficient mental capacity to understand the nature of the act of making a will, to understand and recall the nature and extent of the individual's own property, and to remember and understand the individual's relationships with living descendants, spouse, and parents and others affected by the will -- or if the individual suffered from a mental health disorder involving delusions or hallucinations that actually caused a specific distribution the individual would not otherwise have made.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Prob. Code section 6100.5(a)), used as real evidence of the actual legal test a capacity-based contest must satisfy -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. This same statutory subsection is already stated elsewhere in this corpus, in a different clause (the Last Will and Testament document's testamentary-capacity clause), framed there as a drafting-time requirement for the will to be valid rather than as a ground a contestant can raise; this clause independently re-verified the identical primary source (fetched and cross-checked again for this document) and restates it framed around a contest instead. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was located for the capacity test itself. This clause does not address the separate, narrower rule that a conservator may make a will for a conservatee only with prior court authorization, and does not state how a capacity-based contest must be pleaded or proven at trial.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6100.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the two-part testamentary capacity test
citations.quote: An individual is not mentally competent to make a will if, at the time of making the will, either of the following is true: (1) The individual does not have sufficient mental capacity to be able to do any of the following: (A) Understand the nature of the testamentary act. (B) Understand and recollect the nature and situation of the individual’s property. (C) Remember and understand the individual’s relations to living descendants, spouse, and parents, and those whose interests are affected by the will. (2) The individual suffers from a mental health disorder with symptoms including delusions or hallucinations, which delusions or hallucinations result in the individual’s devising property in a way that, except for the existence of the delusions or hallucinations, the individual would not have done.

clauses.title: Grounds: Duress, Menace, Fraud, and Undue Influence
clauses.body: California law separately recognizes four other grounds for treating a will (or part of one) -- and, under the same statutory language, a revocation of a will -- as invalid: the execution or revocation is ineffective to the extent it was procured by duress, menace, fraud, or undue influence. Unlike the capacity ground, these four grounds go to how {{decedentName}}'s will, or its revocation, actually came about, rather than to whether {{decedentName}} had the mental capacity to make it at all, and by the statute's own wording each ground is effective only to the extent it actually procured the execution or revocation at issue.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Prob. Code section 6104), used as real evidence of the four procurement-based invalidity grounds -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will. This is the entire operative text of a single statutory section; there is no subsection breakdown to disclose, and no additional independent source was located for this specific list of four grounds. The statute does not itself define 'duress,' 'menace,' or 'fraud'; this sheet's separate clause on Probate Code section 86 addresses how 'undue influence' is defined for these purposes, but this clause does not independently verify statutory definitions for the other three terms, which are left to case law.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6104 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, procurement-based grounds for invalidity
citations.quote: The execution or revocation of a will or a part of a will is ineffective to the extent the execution or revocation was procured by duress, menace, fraud, or undue influence.

clauses.title: How "Undue Influence" Is Defined for a Will or Trust Contest
clauses.body: California Probate Code section 86 answers the definitional question left open by the previous clause: for purposes of the Probate Code, "undue influence" has the same meaning given to that term in Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.70. The Legislature's own statement of intent is that this cross-reference supplements the pre-existing common-law meaning of undue influence, rather than replacing or overriding it. So a contest raising undue influence as a ground can draw on both that statutory definition and the body of case law that predates and coexists with it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Prob. Code section 86), used as real evidence that the Probate Code defines 'undue influence' by cross-reference to Welfare and Institutions Code section 15610.70, rather than leaving the term wholly undefined in this context -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will or trust, and not a restatement of section 15610.70's own definition. That definition, and its four evidentiary factors, is already stated in this corpus's separate elder-financial-abuse clause citing Welf. & Inst. Code section 15610.70 directly; this clause does not requote that text, to avoid duplicating it, and instead independently verifies only the cross-reference and the Legislature's supplement-not-supersede statement that appear in section 86 itself. This is a single statutory section; no additional independent source was located for the existence of this cross-reference. Whether a court applying section 6104 in a specific will or trust contest actually applies the section 15610.70 factors, as opposed to relying purely on common-law undue-influence doctrine, is a question of case law this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 86 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, definition of "undue influence" by cross-reference
citations.quote: “Undue influence” has the same meaning as defined in Section 15610.70 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. It is the intent of the Legislature that this section supplement the common law meaning of undue influence without superseding or interfering with the operation of that law.

clauses.title: Who May Object, and How a Pre-Probate Contest Proceeds
clauses.body: Standing to raise most of these grounds turns on being an "interested person" -- a term California law defines to include an heir, devisee, child, spouse, creditor, beneficiary, or anyone else with a property right in or claim against the estate that the proceeding may affect, as well as anyone with priority for appointment as personal representative, or a fiduciary representing an interested person; the statute adds that exactly who qualifies can vary with the specific proceeding and purpose involved. Where a will is contested before it is admitted to probate, the contestant files a written objection to probate with the court in {{countyOfFiling}} County, a summons then issues and is served together with a copy of that objection, and the summons must direct the persons served to file a written response within 30 days of service.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the standing concept and the pre-admission contest procedure -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will, and not a claim that every ground described in this document requires "interested person" status in every proceeding type. The "interested person" definition (Cal. Prob. Code section 48) and the pre-admission contest procedure (Cal. Prob. Code section 8250(a)) are two independently-numbered sections in different divisions of the Probate Code, not subsections of one; each was independently verified. This clause does not state the separate rule for contesting the appointment of a personal representative (section 8004(a)), and does not cover the rule that a person named as executor has no duty to defend a contest until appointed (section 8250(b)).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 48 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, definition of "interested person"
citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivision (b), “interested person” includes any of the following: (1) An heir, devisee, child, spouse, creditor, beneficiary, and any other person having a property right in or claim against a trust estate or the estate of a decedent which may be affected by the proceeding. (2) Any person having priority for appointment as personal representative. (3) A fiduciary representing an interested person.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8250(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, pre-admission will contest procedure
citations.quote: (a) When a will is contested under Section 8004, the contestant shall file with the court an objection to probate of the will. Thereafter, a summons shall be issued and served, with a copy of the objection, on the persons required by Section 8110 to be served with notice of hearing of a petition for administration of the decedent’s estate. The summons shall be issued and served as provided in Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 412.10) and Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 413.10) of Title 5 of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The summons shall contain a direction that the persons summoned file with the court a written pleading in response to the contest within 30 days after service of the summons.

clauses.title: Deadline to Contest After a Will Has Already Been Admitted
clauses.body: Once a will has already been admitted to probate, a separate deadline applies to raising these grounds: an interested person may petition to revoke that probate within 120 days after the will was admitted, unless that person was already a party to a will contest or had actual notice of one in time to have joined it. California law carves out one exception to that 120-day deadline: a person who was a minor, or who was incompetent and had no guardian or conservator, when the will was admitted to probate may petition to revoke the probate at any time before the court enters an order for final distribution.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Prob. Code section 8270), used as real evidence of the actual post-admission deadline and its minor/incompetent exception -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific will, and not a claim about when any particular estate's final distribution will occur. Both the 120-day deadline (section 8270(a)) and the minor/incompetent exception (section 8270(b)) are subsections of the same statutory section, disclosed here as the same source rather than as independent corroboration of each other. This clause's own citation is independent, however, of the pre-admission standing-and-procedure clause elsewhere in this document, which draws on separately-numbered sections 48 and 8250.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8270 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, 120-day deadline to petition to revoke probate
citations.quote: (a) Within 120 days after a will is admitted to probate, any interested person, other than a party to a will contest and other than a person who had actual notice of a will contest in time to have joined in the contest, may petition the court to revoke the probate of the will. The petition shall include objections setting forth written grounds of opposition. (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), a person who was a minor or who was incompetent and had no guardian or conservator at the time a will was admitted to probate may petition the court to revoke the probate of the will at any time before entry of an order for final distribution.

clauses.title: A Trust Contest Runs on a Different Clock
clauses.body: A trust contest does not automatically follow the same procedural timeline as a will contest. Where a revocable trust, or part of one, becomes irrevocable because a settlor died, California law requires the trustee to serve a formal notification on each beneficiary of the now-irrevocable trust and on each heir of the deceased settlor. Once that notification has been served, the recipient may not bring an action to contest the trust more than 120 days after the notification was served, or, if a copy of the trust's terms is later delivered during that 120-day window, more than 60 days after that delivery -- whichever of the two deadlines is later.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a trust contest runs on its own notice-triggered deadline rather than automatically sharing the will-contest deadlines described elsewhere in this document -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a claim that every trust contest is subject to this deadline (a trust that never becomes irrevocable by a settlor's death, or for which no notification is ever served, is not addressed by this clause, nor is standing to bring a trust contest). The 120/60-day deadline itself comes from Cal. Prob. Code section 16061.8; the trustee's duty to serve the notification that starts that clock comes from a separate section, section 16061.7(a)(1) -- these are two independently-numbered sections, not subsections of one, though they are substantively linked (one creates the triggering notice, the other states the deadline it triggers), which is disclosed here rather than presented as two unrelated confirmations of the identical fact. This clause does not assume that the "interested person" / procedural concepts used elsewhere in this document for will contests apply identically to a trust contest.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.8 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, 120/60-day trust contest deadline
citations.quote: A person upon whom the notification by the trustee is served pursuant to paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 16061.7, whether the notice is served on the person within or after the time period set forth in subdivision (f) of Section 16061.7, shall not bring an action to contest the trust more than 120 days from the date the notification by the trustee is served upon the person, or 60 days from the date on which a copy of the terms of the trust is delivered pursuant to Section 1215 to the person during that 120-day period, whichever is later.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16061.7(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, trustee's duty to serve the triggering notification
citations.quote: (a) A trustee shall serve a notification by the trustee as described in this section in the following events: (1) When a revocable trust or any portion thereof becomes irrevocable because of the death of one or more of the settlors of the trust, or because, by the express terms of the trust, the trust becomes irrevocable within one year of the death of a settlor because of a contingency related to the death of one or more of the settlors of the trust.

clauses.title: Certification of Understanding
Purpose and Scope — Informational Only
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, borrower-protection provisions of California's Homeowner Bill of Rights that constrain how a mortgage servicer may pursue foreclosure of certain residential loans, codified principally at California Civil Code §§ 2923.5, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.11, 2924.12, 2924.15, and 2924.18. It concerns a loan secured by the real property commonly known as {{propertyAddress}}, on which {{trustorName}} is identified as borrower and {{beneficiaryName}} as beneficiary (lender); the loan is currently serviced by {{mortgageServicerName}}, loan number {{loanNumber}}. This sheet summarizes, at a general level: the pre-foreclosure borrower-contact requirement that must be satisfied before a notice of default may be recorded; the prohibition on recording a notice of default or notice of sale, or conducting a trustee's sale, while a complete first-lien loan-modification application is pending (sometimes called "dual tracking"); the requirement that a servicer establish a single point of contact once a borrower requests a foreclosure prevention alternative; the statutory scope limits and small-servicer exemption that determine which loans and which servicers these provisions reach; and the statutory remedies available for a material violation. It is a companion to — and does not duplicate or replace — an information sheet describing California's general nonjudicial foreclosure process under Civil Code § 2924 et seq. (the notice of default's statutory content, the waiting period before a notice of sale, the right of reinstatement, and the antideficiency rule); the protections summarized in this sheet operate as additional requirements layered on top of, not in substitution for, that general process. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself contact any borrower, evaluate or approve any loan modification or other foreclosure prevention alternative, establish or designate any single point of contact, record or rescind any notice, or determine whether any mortgage servicer's actual conduct toward this or any other loan has complied — or failed to comply — with any statute described here.

clauses.title: Statutory Scope — Owner-Occupied Loans Secured by a First Lien
clauses.body: The Homeowner Bill of Rights provisions summarized in this sheet do not apply to every residential mortgage loan. California Civil Code § 2924.15(a) provides: "Unless otherwise provided, paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) of Section 2924 and Sections 2923.5, 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, and 2924.18 shall apply only to a first lien mortgage or deed of trust that is secured by owner-occupied residential real property containing no more than four dwelling units." "Owner-occupied" carries a defined meaning for this purpose: Section 2924.15(b) provides that "[f]or purposes of this section, 'owner-occupied' means that the property is the principal residence of the borrower and is security for a loan made for personal, family, or household purposes." As applied to the loan secured by {{propertyAddress}}, whether that property is the principal residence of {{trustorName}} and whether the loan identified as {{loanNumber}} is a first-lien loan made for personal, family, or household purposes determines whether the pre-foreclosure contact, dual-tracking, single-point-of-contact, and related requirements described in this sheet apply to that loan at all.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory law, used as real evidence of that state's Homeowner Bill of Rights scope limits — not a determination of which state's law governs any specific loan, nor a determination that the property and loan identified on this sheet in fact meet the owner-occupied, first-lien, four-or-fewer-unit definition this section requires. Both quoted passages are drawn from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 2924.15, subdivisions (a) and (b) — they are quoted together, rather than as independent sources, because subdivision (b) directly defines a term used in subdivision (a).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2924.15(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Unless otherwise provided, paragraph (5) of subdivision (a) of Section 2924 and Sections 2923.5, 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, and 2924.18 shall apply only to a first lien mortgage or deed of trust that is secured by owner-occupied residential real property containing no more than four dwelling units.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2924.15(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, “owner-occupied” means that the property is the principal residence of the borrower and is security for a loan made for personal, family, or household purposes.

clauses.title: Pre-Foreclosure Borrower Contact Required Before a Notice of Default
clauses.body: Before a notice of default may be recorded against a covered loan such as the one secured by {{propertyAddress}}, California Civil Code § 2923.5(a)(1) requires that a mortgage servicer first make contact, or satisfy a due-diligence standard for attempting contact, with the borrower. As enacted, subdivision (a)(1)(A) requires "[e]ither 30 days after initial contact is made as required by paragraph (2) or 30 days after satisfying the due diligence requirements as described in subdivision (e)" before a notice of default pursuant to Section 2924 may be recorded. The required contact itself is described in subdivision (a)(2)(A): "A mortgage servicer shall contact the borrower in person or by telephone in order to assess the borrower's financial situation and explore options for the borrower to avoid foreclosure." During that contact, the mortgage servicer must advise the borrower of the right to request a follow-up meeting (to be scheduled within 14 days) and must provide the toll-free HUD housing-counseling referral number. A recorded notice of default must include a declaration that the mortgage servicer has contacted the borrower, tried with due diligence to do so, or that no contact was required. Whether {{mortgageServicerName}} has made or attempted the contact this section describes with respect to {{trustorName}} concerning the loan secured by {{propertyAddress}} is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory law, presented as real evidence of one state's pre-foreclosure contact requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific loan; other states impose different or no comparable pre-foreclosure contact requirements. Both quoted passages are drawn from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 2923.5, subdivisions (a)(1)(A) and (a)(2)(A) — they are quoted together, rather than as independent sources, because they describe the timing rule and the substantive contact requirement it is measured from within one integrated provision. This section applies only to the class of loans described in Civil Code § 2924.15 (see the scope clause of this sheet) and only to entities described in subdivision (b) of Civil Code § 2924.18 (see the scope/exemption clause of this sheet); it does not apply universally to every residential mortgage servicer or loan.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2923.5(a)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Either 30 days after initial contact is made as required by paragraph (2) or 30 days after satisfying the due diligence requirements as described in subdivision (e).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2923.5(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A mortgage servicer shall contact the borrower in person or by telephone in order to assess the borrower’s financial situation and explore options for the borrower to avoid foreclosure.

clauses.title: Prohibition on Pursuing Foreclosure While a Complete Loan Modification Application Is Pending ("Dual Tracking")
clauses.body: Two separate, independently numbered Civil Code sections restrict a mortgage servicer from pursuing foreclosure of a covered loan while a complete first-lien loan-modification application submitted by the borrower is pending — a practice sometimes referred to as "dual tracking." Civil Code § 2923.6(c) provides: "If a borrower submits a complete application for a first lien loan modification offered by, or through, the borrower's mortgage servicer at least five business days before a scheduled foreclosure sale, a mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall not record a notice of default or notice of sale, or conduct a trustee's sale, while the complete first lien loan modification application is pending." A separately numbered section, Civil Code § 2924.18(a)(1), independently imposes an overlapping prohibition: "If a borrower submits a complete application for a first lien loan modification offered by, or through, the borrower's mortgage servicer at least five business days before a scheduled foreclosure sale, a mortgage servicer, trustee, mortgagee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall not record a notice of default, notice of sale, or conduct a trustee's sale while the complete first lien loan modification application is pending, and until the borrower has been provided with a written determination by the mortgage servicer regarding that borrower's eligibility for the requested loan modification." Section 2923.6 also sets out a longer sequence of follow-on protections not quoted here — including a borrower's right to appeal a denial and specific content requirements for a denial notice — that apply only where Section 2923.6 itself applies (see the scope/exemption clause of this sheet); Section 2924.18(a)'s dual-tracking prohibition applies more broadly and is not subject to that same carve-out.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory law, used as real evidence of California's dual-tracking prohibition — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific loan; dual-tracking restrictions vary by state and many states impose none. The two quoted passages are drawn from two separate, independently numbered Civil Code sections — § 2923.6(c) and § 2924.18(a)(1) — and are genuinely independent of each other, not subdivisions of a single section; they are quoted together because they impose substantially overlapping dual-tracking prohibitions that apply to a different scope of servicers (see the small-servicer exemption clause of this sheet, under which § 2923.6(c)-(h) does not apply to small servicers described in § 2924.18(b), while § 2924.18(a) itself is not subject to that same carve-out). Both sections apply only to the class of loans described in Civil Code § 2924.15 (see the scope clause of this sheet).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2923.6(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If a borrower submits a complete application for a first lien loan modification offered by, or through, the borrower’s mortgage servicer at least five business days before a scheduled foreclosure sale, a mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall not record a notice of default or notice of sale, or conduct a trustee’s sale, while the complete first lien loan modification application is pending.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2924.18(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If a borrower submits a complete application for a first lien loan modification offered by, or through, the borrower’s mortgage servicer at least five business days before a scheduled foreclosure sale, a mortgage servicer, trustee, mortgagee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall not record a notice of default, notice of sale, or conduct a trustee’s sale while the complete first lien loan modification application is pending, and until the borrower has been provided with a written determination by the mortgage servicer regarding that borrower’s eligibility for the requested loan modification.

clauses.title: Single Point of Contact Once a Foreclosure Prevention Alternative Is Requested
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2923.7(a) requires: "When a borrower requests a foreclosure prevention alternative, the mortgage servicer shall promptly establish a single point of contact and provide to the borrower one or more direct means of communication with the single point of contact." The single point of contact is a defined role with specific statutory duties, not merely a named individual: it must, among other things, communicate the application process and deadlines, coordinate receipt of application documents, stay informed of the current status of the borrower's foreclosure prevention alternative, ensure the borrower is considered for all alternatives the servicer offers, and — as Section 2923.7(b)(5) specifically provides — have "access to individuals with the ability and authority to stop foreclosure proceedings when necessary." The single point of contact must remain assigned to the borrower's account until the servicer determines that all loss mitigation options have been exhausted or the account becomes current, and the servicer must ensure the single point of contact refers the borrower to a supervisor on request, if the single point of contact has one. Whether {{mortgageServicerName}} has established a single point of contact for {{trustorName}} in connection with the loan secured by {{propertyAddress}} is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory law, used as real evidence of one state's single-point-of-contact requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific loan; single-point-of-contact requirements vary by state and many states impose none. Both quoted passages are drawn from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 2923.7, subdivisions (a) and (b)(5) — they are quoted together, rather than as independent sources, because subdivision (b) defines the duties of the single point of contact that subdivision (a) requires the servicer to establish. This section applies only to the class of loans described in Civil Code § 2924.15 and does not apply to certain small servicers (see the scope/exemption clause of this sheet).

citations.quote: When a borrower requests a foreclosure prevention alternative, the mortgage servicer shall promptly establish a single point of contact and provide to the borrower one or more direct means of communication with the single point of contact.

citations.quote: (5) Having access to individuals with the ability and authority to stop foreclosure proceedings when necessary.

clauses.title: Small-Servicer Exemption from Certain Homeowner Bill of Rights Provisions
clauses.body: Not every mortgage servicer is subject to every Homeowner Bill of Rights provision described in this sheet. Civil Code § 2924.18(b) defines two categories of smaller-volume servicers to which certain sections apply on different terms. The first category, under paragraph (1), is: "A depository institution chartered under state or federal law, a person licensed pursuant to Division 9 (commencing with Section 22000) or Division 20 (commencing with Section 50000) of the Financial Code, or a person licensed pursuant to Part 1 (commencing with Section 10000) of Division 4 of the Business and Professions Code, that, during its immediately preceding annual reporting period, as established with its primary regulator, foreclosed on 175 or fewer residential real properties, containing no more than four dwelling units, that are located in California." The second category, under paragraph (2), is: "A person or entity that services seven or fewer loans encumbering residential real property located in California in a calendar year." A separately numbered section, Civil Code § 2923.6(i), then carves entities meeting that definition out of the dual-tracking and appeal provisions described elsewhere in this sheet: "Subdivisions (c) to (h), inclusive, shall not apply to entities described in subdivision (b) of Section 2924.18." California Civil Code § 2924.18(c) further provides that if a small servicer within the meaning of paragraph (1) later exceeds the 175-foreclosure threshold, it must notify its primary regulator and any delinquent borrower of the date — the first day of the sixth month after the close of the relevant reporting period — on which it becomes subject to Sections 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, and 2924.12. Whether {{mortgageServicerName}} falls within either category described in Section 2924.18(b), and therefore whether the dual-tracking, single-point-of-contact, and related provisions described in this sheet reach the servicing of the loan secured by {{propertyAddress}}, is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory law, used as real evidence of one state's small-servicer exemption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific servicer, nor a determination that the servicer identified on this sheet does or does not meet either statutory category. The three quoted passages are drawn from two separate, independently numbered Civil Code sections — § 2924.18(b) (its two paragraphs, (1) and (2), quoted separately but not independent of each other since both are subdivisions of the same statutory sentence) and § 2923.6(i), which is independent of § 2924.18(b) — they are quoted together because § 2924.18(b) supplies the definition that § 2923.6(i) applies. This exemption, by its own terms, reaches only the specific sections it lists (§§ 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, and 2924.12) — it does not, on this sheet's reading of the statutory text, exempt a small servicer from the pre-foreclosure contact requirement of § 2923.5 or from § 2924.18's own dual-tracking prohibition, both of which are discussed in separate clauses of this sheet.

clauses.title: Statutory Remedies for a Material Violation
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2924.12 creates a private right of action for a material violation of certain Homeowner Bill of Rights provisions, and the remedy available differs depending on whether a trustee's sale has already occurred. Before a sale, Section 2924.12(a)(1) provides: "If a trustee's deed upon sale has not been recorded, a borrower may bring an action for injunctive relief to enjoin a material violation of Section 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, or 2924.17." Any such injunction remains in place until the violation is corrected and remedied. After a trustee's deed upon sale has been recorded, Section 2924.12(b) instead provides a damages remedy: "a mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall be liable to a borrower for actual economic damages pursuant to Section 3281, resulting from a material violation of Section 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, or 2924.17 by that mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent where the violation was not corrected and remedied prior to the recordation of the trustee's deed upon sale. If the court finds that the material violation was intentional or reckless, or resulted from willful misconduct by a mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent, the court may award the borrower the greater of treble actual damages or statutory damages of fifty thousand dollars ($50,000)." A prevailing borrower may also recover reasonable attorney's fees and costs, and a violation of the listed sections by certain state-licensed persons is separately deemed a violation of that person's licensing law.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory law, used as real evidence of one state's remedy for Homeowner Bill of Rights violations — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific loan, and not a determination that any violation has in fact occurred with respect to the loan or servicer identified on this sheet. Both quoted passages are drawn from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 2924.12, subdivisions (a)(1) and (b) — they are quoted together, rather than as independent sources, because they describe the pre-sale and post-sale phases of a single remedy scheme. As this sheet reads the statutory text, Section 2924.12's private right of action is expressly limited to material violations of the sections it lists by number — §§ 2923.55, 2923.6, 2923.7, 2924.9, 2924.10, 2924.11, and 2924.17 — which does not, on its face, include a violation of the pre-foreclosure contact requirement of § 2923.5 or of § 2924.18's own dual-tracking prohibition; this sheet does not resolve what remedy, if any, exists for a violation of those two sections specifically, and that question is not addressed further here. Civil Code § 2924.12(i) further provides that this remedy section does not apply to entities described in subdivision (b) of Section 2924.18 (see the small-servicer exemption clause of this sheet), and Section 2924.12(e) provides that no violation affects the validity of a sale to a bona fide purchaser for value without notice.

If the court finds that the material violation was intentional or reckless, or resulted from willful misconduct by a mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent, the court may award the borrower the greater of treble actual damages or statutory damages of fifty thousand dollars ($50,000).

clauses.title: Acknowledgment — Informational Sheet Only
clauses.body:

clauses.title: Purpose of This Ellis Act Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's Ellis Act (Government Code sections 7060 through 7060.7), a state statute that prohibits a public entity from compelling the owner of residential real property to offer, or to continue to offer, all of the residential rental units at a property for rent or lease -- in effect permitting a landlord to go out of the residential rental business by withdrawing all of the units from the rental market, subject to notice, tenancy-extension, and re-offering provisions described in this document. It concerns the property commonly known as {{propertyAddress}}, the landlord {{landlordName}}, and the tenancy of {{tenantName}}.

This document is distinct from an information sheet describing California's statewide Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482), which addresses a different statutory scheme -- a cap on rent increases and a just-cause requirement before ending a tenancy (Civil Code sections 1946.2 and 1947.12). An Ellis Act withdrawal from the rental business is a separate statutory mechanism from that just-cause framework, not a category of just cause defined by it. This document is also distinct from any specific notice of intent to withdraw accommodations that a landlord may deliver to a public entity or to a tenant, and from any specific termination notice, and it describes instead the broader statutory framework within which such notices operate. This information sheet does not itself determine whether any specific structure or unit qualifies as "accommodations" under this chapter, whether the public entity with jurisdiction over {{propertyAddress}} has adopted an implementing ordinance or regulation under this chapter, or whether any specific withdrawal, notice, tenancy extension, or re-offering complies with this chapter or with any local ordinance adopted under it.

clauses.title: The Statewide Right to Withdraw All Rental Units From the Market
clauses.body: Government Code section 7060(a) prohibits a public entity from using its statutory, ordinance, regulatory, or administrative power to compel the owner of residential real property to offer, or to continue to offer, "accommodations" in the property for rent or lease, subject to a narrow exception for certain long-standing residential hotels in large cities. Section 7060(b)(1) defines "accommodations" broadly enough to reach an entire property rather than a single unit: for a detached structure with four or more residential rental units, it means the residential rental units in that structure; for a structure with three or fewer residential rental units, it means the residential rental units in that structure and in any other structure on the same parcel of land. Section 7060.7 states that the Legislature's intent in enacting this chapter was to supersede any conflicting holding in Nash v. City of Santa Monica, a California Supreme Court decision, "so as to permit landlords to go out of business." Taken together, these provisions establish the Act's central right: a residential landlord's statutory ability to exit the rental business entirely by withdrawing all of the accommodations at a property from the rental market, notwithstanding a public entity's otherwise-applicable rent-control or eviction-control authority.
clauses.gap: The citations to Government Code section 7060(a) and section 7060(b)(1) are to subdivisions of the same statutory section; they are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. The citation to section 7060.7 is to a separate, independently numbered section of the same chapter and is offered as independent corroboration of the Legislature's stated purpose. This clause does not reproduce the narrow residential-hotel exception in section 7060(a)(1)-(3) in full, and does not address the *Nash v. City of Santa Monica* decision itself, which this document does not independently verify. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Ellis Act framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific property; a landlord's ability to withdraw rental units from the market, and the conditions on doing so, vary significantly by state. This document addresses California's statewide Ellis Act statute (Government Code sections 7060-7060.7) only. Many California cities and counties with local rent-control or price-control programs -- including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Santa Monica, and West Hollywood, among others -- have adopted their own Ellis Act implementing ordinances or regulations under this chapter, and those local ordinances commonly set their own notice periods, relocation-payment dollar amounts, filing procedures, and re-offering restrictions that go beyond, or fill in gaps left open by, the bare statutory text. This document does not catalog any specific local ordinance, and it does not determine whether any particular public entity has adopted an implementing ordinance or regulation under this chapter. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific structure or unit is "accommodations" within the meaning of this chapter, whether any specific public entity has adopted an implementing statute, ordinance, or regulation under this chapter, whether any specific notice of intent to withdraw complies with this chapter or any local ordinance adopted under it, or whether any specific withdrawal, tenancy extension, or re-offering is lawful.

citations.quote: No public entity, as defined in Section 811.2, shall, by statute, ordinance, or regulation, or by administrative action implementing any statute, ordinance or regulation, compel the owner of any residential real property to offer, or to continue to offer, accommodations in the property for rent or lease, except for guestrooms or efficiency units within a residential hotel, as defined in Section 50519 of the Health and Safety Code, if the residential hotel meets all of the following conditions:

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 7060(b)(1)(A)-(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (1) “Accommodations” means either of the following: (A) The residential rental units in any detached physical structure containing four or more residential rental units. (B) With respect to a detached physical structure containing three or fewer residential rental units, the residential rental units in that structure and in any other structure located on the same parcel of land, including any detached physical structure specified in subparagraph (A).

citations.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature in enacting this chapter to supersede any holding or portion of any holding in Nash v. City of Santa Monica, 37 Cal.3d 97 to the extent that the holding, or portion of the holding, conflicts with this chapter, so as to permit landlords to go out of business.

clauses.title: Withdrawal Must Cover All Units, With Limited Owner-Occupancy Exceptions
clauses.body: Government Code section 7060.7 lists things the Ellis Act is "not otherwise intended" to permit, in addition to superseding Nash v. City of Santa Monica. Subdivision (d) states that the Act does not permit an owner to withdraw from rent or lease less than all of the accommodations at a property, as "accommodations" is defined in section 7060(b) -- meaning a landlord's statutory right under this chapter is to withdraw the entire property (or, for a small structure, the entire parcel) from the rental market, not to selectively withdraw only some units while continuing to rent others. Subdivision (d) also states that the Act does not permit an owner to decline to make a written re-rental offer, in the manner and timeframe set out in section 7060.2, to a tenant who occupied a unit when the owner gave notice of intent to withdraw -- except that this re-rental-offer requirement does not apply to a unit that was, and continues to be, the principal residence of the owner or an owner's family member, or to a unit that becomes the owner's own principal residence when the accommodations return to the rental market (subject to a 30-day re-offer obligation if the owner later vacates that unit within 10 years of the withdrawal).
clauses.gap: All three citations below are to subdivision (d) of Government Code section 7060.7, a single statutory section; they are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. The all-units requirement and the owner-occupancy exceptions are stated by the statute as things the Act is "not otherwise intended" to permit an owner to do, rather than as freestanding affirmative commands; this clause paraphrases that structure in its body without reproducing every word of the statute's own framing. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Ellis Act framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific property; a landlord's ability to withdraw rental units from the market, and the conditions on doing so, vary significantly by state. This document addresses California's statewide Ellis Act statute (Government Code sections 7060-7060.7) only. citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.7 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: However, this act is not otherwise intended to do any of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.7(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (d) Permit an owner to do any of the following: (1) Withdraw from rent or lease less than all of the accommodations, as defined by paragraph (1) or (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 7060.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.7(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (2) Decline to make a written rerental offer to any tenant or lessee who occupied a unit at the time when the owner gave the public entity notice of its intent to withdraw the accommodations, in the manner and within the timeframe specified in paragraph (3) of subdivision (b), or in subdivision (c), of Section 7060.2. But the requirements of this paragraph shall not apply to: (A) A unit that was the principal place of residence of any owner or owner’s family member at the time of withdrawal, provided that it continues to be that person’s or those persons’ principal place of residence when accommodations are returned to the rental market as provided in this section. (B) A unit that is the principal place of residence of an owner when the accommodations are returned to the rental market, if it is the owners’ principal place of residence, at the time of return to the rental market, as provided in this section. If the owner vacates the unit within 10 years from the date of withdrawal, the owner shall, within 30 days, offer to rerent if required under this paragraph.

clauses.title: Notice to the Public Entity and the Statutory "Date of Withdrawal"
clauses.body: Government Code section 7060.4(a) provides that a public entity that already has some form of price control over rents in effect (adopted as a valid exercise of its police power) may require, by statute, ordinance, or a regulation adopted under section 7060.5, that a landlord file a notice of intent to withdraw accommodations with that entity, and may require that the notice contain sworn statements about the number of units, their address, the tenants' names, and the applicable rents (which the statute treats as confidential information). Section 7060.4(b) provides that, where the public entity's statute, ordinance, or regulation requires the owner to record a summarizing memorandum with the county recorder and to certify that steps to terminate existing tenancies have begun, the statutory "date of withdrawal" of the accommodations -- the trigger date for other deadlines described elsewhere in this chapter -- is 120 days after that notice is delivered to the public entity, in person or by first-class mail. Section 7060.5, a separate section, confirms that a public entity may adopt this notice-and-recording framework either by ordinance or, where its governing body is directly elected, by a form of regulation subject to voter referendum.
clauses.gap: This framework is triggered only where a public entity has both (1) some form of existing rent- or price-control system and (2) has itself adopted a statute, ordinance, or regulation under section 7060.4 requiring the notice-and-recording procedure described in subdivision (b) -- the statute's own text ties the 120-day "date of withdrawal" rule to that situation ("[i]n that situation"). This document does not determine whether the public entity with jurisdiction over any specific property has adopted such a requirement; where none has been adopted, this particular 120-day date-of-withdrawal mechanism, as such, may not have a directly applicable counterpart under this chapter for that property, and the timing and process for any withdrawal there would instead depend on whatever notice period applies to ending the tenancy generally, and on any applicable local ordinance, neither of which this document addresses. The citations to section 7060.4(a) and 7060.4(b) are to subdivisions of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source. The citation to section 7060.5 is to a separate, independently numbered section and is offered as independent corroboration that this notice-and-recording framework is a local-ordinance-or-regulation mechanism rather than a directly self-executing statewide notice requirement. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Ellis Act framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific property; a landlord's ability to withdraw rental units from the market, and the conditions on doing so, vary significantly by state. This document does not catalog any specific local ordinance, and it does not determine whether any particular public entity has adopted an implementing ordinance or regulation under this chapter. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific structure or unit is "accommodations" within the meaning of this chapter, whether any specific public entity has adopted an implementing statute, ordinance, or regulation under this chapter, whether any specific notice of intent to withdraw complies with this chapter or any local ordinance adopted under it, or whether any specific withdrawal, tenancy extension, or re-offering is lawful.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.4(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) Any public entity which, by a valid exercise of its police power, has in effect any control or system of control on the price at which accommodations are offered for rent or lease, may require by statute or ordinance, or by regulation as specified in Section 7060.5, that the owner notify the entity of an intention to withdraw those accommodations from rent or lease and may require that the notice contain statements, under penalty of perjury, providing information on the number of accommodations, the address or location of those accommodations, the name or names of the tenants or lessees of the accommodations, and the rent applicable to each residential rental unit.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.4(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (b) The statute, ordinance, or regulation of the public entity may require that the owner record with the county recorder a memorandum summarizing the provisions, other than the confidential provisions, of the notice in a form which shall be prescribed by the statute, ordinance, or regulation, and require a certification with that notice that actions have been initiated as required by law to terminate any existing tenancies. In that situation, the date on which the accommodations are withdrawn from rent or lease for purposes of this chapter is 120 days from the delivery in person or by first-class mail of that notice to the public entity.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The actions authorized by Sections 7060.2 and 7060.4 may be taken by regulation adopted after public notice and hearing by a public body of a public entity, if the members of the body have been elected by the voters of the public entity.

clauses.title: One-Year Extension for a Qualifying Elderly or Disabled Tenant
clauses.body: Within the notice-and-recording framework described elsewhere in this document, Government Code section 7060.4(b) provides an extended timeline for certain tenants: if a tenant or lessee is at least 62 years of age or disabled, and has lived in their unit for at least one year before the date the notice of intent to withdraw was delivered to the public entity, that tenant's own date of withdrawal is extended to one year after that delivery date -- provided the tenant gives the owner written notice of the tenant's entitlement to the extension within 60 days of the notice's delivery to the public entity. During that extended period, the statute requires the tenancy to continue on the same terms and conditions that existed on the date the notice was delivered to the public entity (subject to adjustments otherwise available under the local price-control system), and states that no party is relieved of any obligation under the lease or rental agreement. Section 7060(b)(2), a separate section, defines "disabled" for purposes of this chapter by cross-reference to the definition of disability in Government Code section 12955.3.
clauses.gap: Like the underlying 120-day date-of-withdrawal mechanism it modifies, this one-year extension for a qualifying tenant applies within the notice-and-recording framework described in section 7060.4(b), which itself depends on the public entity having adopted an implementing statute, ordinance, or regulation under that section; this document does not determine whether that has occurred for any specific property, and does not determine whether any specific tenant meets the age, disability, residency, or 60-day-notice conditions the statute sets out. The citations to section 7060.4(b) (the extension rule and its two -numbered paragraphs) are to the same statutory section and are treated here as one source; the citation to section 7060(b)(2) is to a separate section (defining "disabled") and is offered as independent corroboration of that term. This clause does not reproduce every detail of section 7060.4(b)'s paragraphs (3) through (6), which address an owner's option to extend other units, the owner's own notice deadlines to the public entity, and how the "date of withdrawal" is calculated for the accommodations as a whole when one or more tenancies are extended. citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 7060.4(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: However, if the tenant or lessee is at least 62 years of age or disabled, and has lived in their accommodations or unit within the accommodations for at least one year prior to the date of delivery to the public entity of the notice of intent to withdraw pursuant to subdivision (a), then the date of withdrawal of the accommodations of that tenant or lessee shall be extended to one year after the date of delivery of that notice to the public entity, provided that the tenant or lessee gives written notice of their entitlement to an extension to the owner within 60 days of the date of delivery to the public entity of the notice of intent to withdraw.

clauses.title: Restrictions on Re-Offering Withdrawn Units, and the Absence of a State-Set Relocation Payment
clauses.body: Government Code section 7060.2 allows a public entity that already has a rent- or price-control system in effect to provide, by statute, ordinance, or regulation, that units withdrawn under this chapter remain subject to restrictions if they return to the rental market. Under subdivision (b)(3), an owner who offers a unit for rent again must first offer it back to the tenant or lessee displaced from that unit, if that person advised the owner in writing within 30 days of displacement of a desire to be considered for renewal and supplied an address for that purpose; subdivision (b)(1)-(2) separately makes the owner liable to a displaced tenant for actual and exemplary damages, and exposes the owner to a public entity's own suit for exemplary damages, if the unit is re-offered within two years of withdrawal (each within a three-year limitations period). Under subdivision (c), a public entity may extend this first-offer obligation to a period of up to 10 years from withdrawal, with an owner who fails to comply liable for punitive damages up to six months' contract rent. Section 7060.7(d)(2), a separate section, confirms that the Act does not permit an owner to decline to make this written re-rental offer in the manner and timeframe set out in section 7060.2. None of the text of Government Code sections 7060 through 7060.7 sets a specific dollar amount, or a formula for one, that a landlord must pay a displaced tenant as relocation assistance for an Ellis Act withdrawal itself.
clauses.gap: The citations to section 7060.2's introductory sentence, subdivision (b)(3), and subdivision (c) are to the same statutory section and are treated here as one source; the citation to section 7060.7(d)(2) is to a separate, independently numbered section and is offered as independent corroboration that the re-rental-offer obligation is not optional for an owner once it applies. This clause does not reproduce subdivision (a)'s separate five-year rent-level-freeze provision, subdivision (d)'s rule for demolished-and-rebuilt accommodations, or the full three-year limitations language in subdivision (b), in exact quoted form beyond what appears above. As with the notice framework addressed elsewhere in this document, all of section 7060.2's restrictions apply only where a public entity with an existing price-control system has chosen, by statute, ordinance, or regulation, to impose them; this document does not determine whether that has occurred for any specific property. Separately and importantly: this document did not locate any state-law-set dollar figure for relocation assistance tied to an Ellis Act withdrawal anywhere in this chapter -- unlike, for example, the one-month's-rent relocation-assistance-or-rent-waiver figure that Civil Code section 1946.2 sets for certain no-fault terminations under the Tenant Protection Act. Some California cities with their own Ellis Act implementing ordinances (for example, San Francisco and Los Angeles) do set specific relocation-payment dollar amounts by local ordinance, but this document does not catalog any of them, and a reader should not assume any particular dollar figure applies as a matter of state law. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Ellis Act framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific property; a landlord's ability to withdraw rental units from the market, and the conditions on doing so, vary significantly by state. citations.quote: If a public entity, by valid exercise of its police power, has in effect any control or system of control on the price at which accommodations may be offered for rent or lease, that entity may, notwithstanding any provision of this chapter, provide by statute or ordinance, or by regulation as specified in Section 7060.5, that any accommodations which have been offered for rent or lease and which were subject to that control or system of control at the time the accommodations were withdrawn from rent or lease, shall be subject to the following:

The owner of the accommodations shall be liable to any tenant or lessee who was displaced by that action for failure to comply with this paragraph, for punitive damages in an amount which does not exceed the contract rent for six months, and the payment of which shall not be construed to extinguish the owner’s obligation to comply with this subdivision.

clauses.title: What the Act Does Not Preempt, and a Tenant's Defense in an Unlawful Detainer Action
clauses.body: Government Code section 7060.1 lists things this chapter does not do, notwithstanding the withdrawal right described in section 7060. Among them, the chapter does not diminish or enhance a public entity's land-use, planning, zoning, or subdivision-map-approval power (except as specifically provided in section 7060.2), and does not diminish or enhance a public entity's power to mitigate the impact of displacement on persons displaced by a withdrawal. Section 7060.1(d) states that the chapter does not supersede several other named bodies of law, including the state relocation-assistance law (Government Code Chapter 16, commencing with section 7260), the Fair Employment and Housing Act (commencing with section 12900), the Unfair Competition Law (Business and Professions Code, commencing with section 17200), a body of Civil Code provisions commencing at section 43, the Mobilehome Residency Law (Civil Code, commencing with section 1925), the state's unlawful detainer procedure (Code of Civil Procedure, commencing with section 1159), and the Community Redevelopment Law (Health and Safety Code, commencing with section 33000). Section 7060.1(e) states that the chapter does not relieve any party to a lease or rental agreement of the duty to perform any obligation under it. Separately, section 7060.6, an independently numbered section, gives a tenant facing an unlawful detainer action arising from an Ellis Act withdrawal the right to appear and answer or demur, and to assert as a defense that the owner has not complied with this chapter or with an implementing statute, ordinance, or regulation adopted under it.
clauses.gap: The citations to section 7060.1's lead-in sentence, subdivision (d), and subdivision (e) are to the same statutory section and are treated here as one source. The citation to section 7060.6 is to a separate, independently numbered section and is offered as independent corroboration that this chapter's requirements are judicially enforceable as a defense, not merely aspirational. This clause summarizes, rather than independently verifies the substance of, each of the other statutory schemes that section 7060.1(d) lists as not superseded by this chapter; it does not describe what those other laws themselves require. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Ellis Act framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific property; a landlord's ability to withdraw rental units from the market, and the conditions on doing so, vary significantly by state.
