clauses.title: Spousal or Domestic Partner Property Petition — Information and Background
clauses.body: This information sheet discusses the California superior court petition procedure of Probate Code §§ 13650-13660, sometimes called a spousal or domestic partner property petition, in connection with the estate of {{decedentName}}, who died on {{dateOfDeath}}. {{survivingSpouseName}} is the surviving spouse or registered domestic partner of {{decedentName}}. The property discussed is: {{propertyDescription}}. Under this procedure, a petition may be filed in the superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}, California, requesting an order that administration of some or all of {{decedentName}}'s estate is unnecessary because the property described passes to {{survivingSpouseName}}, and/or an order confirming that property already belongs to {{survivingSpouseName}} under Probate Code §§ 100 or 101. This document is background information only. It is not the petition itself, is not filed with any court, and does not by itself request, obtain, or constitute any court order. Only a petition actually filed with the superior court, followed by notice, and a hearing resulting in a signed court order, can determine that administration is unnecessary or confirm ownership of any property.

clauses.title: Two Distinct Requests the Statute Allows in One Petition
clauses.body: Probate Code § 13650(a) authorizes a petition to request either or both of two distinct things: first, an order that administration of all or part of the deceased spouse's estate is not necessary because that property is 'property passing to the surviving spouse' (for example, by intestate succession or by the decedent's will); and second, an order confirming the ownership of property that already belongs to the surviving spouse under § 100 (the surviving spouse's own one-half of the community property) or § 101 (the surviving spouse's own one-half of the quasi-community property) — property that was never the decedent's to begin with. Probate Code § 13656 confirms the statute treats these as separate determinations: subdivision (a) directs the court, when it finds the estate is property passing to the surviving spouse, to issue an order 'determining that the property is property passing to the surviving spouse, and determining that no administration is necessary,' while subdivision (c) separately directs the court, on the confirmation branch, to issue an order 'confirming the ownership of the surviving spouse' where the petition described the survivor's own § 100 or § 101 interest and the court so finds. Subdivision (b) further allows a mixed outcome, with the court finding that part of the estate is not property passing to the surviving spouse (and is therefore subject to administration) while the remaining part is.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs any specific decedent's estate or about which type of order, if any, is appropriate for a specific case. § 13650 and § 13656 are separately numbered sections within the same statutory chapter, independently verified; they are not subsections of one section. This clause's quotes from § 13656(a) and § 13656(c) are subdivisions of the same section and are not independent confirmations of each other. This document is informational only; it does not itself request or obtain any court order.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13650(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the two requests a spousal or domestic partner property petition may make
citations.quote: A surviving spouse or the personal representative, guardian of the estate, or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse may file a petition in the superior court of the county in which the estate of the deceased spouse may be administered requesting an order that administration of all or part of the estate is not necessary for the reason that all or part of the estate is property passing to the surviving spouse. The petition may also request an order confirming the ownership of the surviving spouse of property belonging to the surviving spouse under Section 100 or 101.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13656(a)-(c)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the court's orders corresponding to each type of request
citations.quote: (a) If the court finds that all of the estate of the deceased spouse is property passing to the surviving spouse, the court shall issue an order describing the property, determining that the property is property passing to the surviving spouse, and determining that no administration is necessary. The court may issue any further orders which may be necessary to cause delivery of the property or its proceeds to the surviving spouse. (b) If the court finds that all or part of the estate of the deceased spouse is not property passing to the surviving spouse, the court shall issue an order (1) describing any property which is not property passing to the surviving spouse, determining that that property does not pass to the surviving spouse and determining that that property is subject to administration under this code and (2) describing the property, if any, which is property passing to the surviving spouse, determining that that property passes to the surviving spouse, and determining that no administration of that property is necessary. If the court determines that property passes to the surviving spouse, the court may issue any further orders which may be necessary to cause delivery of that property or its proceeds to the surviving spouse. (c) If the petition filed under this chapter includes a description of the interest of the surviving spouse in the community or quasi-community property, or both, which belongs to the surviving spouse pursuant to Section 100 or 101 and the court finds that the interest belongs to the surviving spouse, the court shall issue an order describing the property and confirming the ownership of the surviving spouse and may issue any further orders which may be necessary to cause ownership of the property to be confirmed in the surviving spouse.

clauses.title: Who May File, and in Which Court
clauses.body: Probate Code § 13650(a) limits who may file this petition to the surviving spouse, or the personal representative, guardian of the estate, or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse, and fixes venue in the superior court of the county in which the deceased spouse's estate may be administered. Section 13650(c) separately dispenses with any need for a guardian or conservator to obtain authorization from the guardianship or conservatorship court before filing. Two further, separately numbered sections fix which proceeding the petition goes into: Probate Code § 13652 requires that if a proceeding for administration of the deceased spouse's estate is already pending, the petition must be filed in that same proceeding, without payment of an additional filing fee; Probate Code § 13653 provides that if no such proceeding is pending, the petition may, but need not, be filed together with a petition for probate of the will or for administration of the estate.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate or about who, if anyone, has standing to file a petition for a specific decedent. The quoted text of § 13650(a) also appears in this document's companion clause on the two types of relief a petition may request, since both clauses draw on the same verified source; § 13650(a) and § 13650(c), quoted here as two separate citation entries, are subdivisions of one section and are not independent of each other. § 13652 and § 13653 are separately numbered sections, independently verified, and independent of § 13650 and of each other. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine who may file a petition for any specific estate.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13650(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, standing to file and venue for a spousal or domestic partner property petition
citations.quote: A surviving spouse or the personal representative, guardian of the estate, or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse may file a petition in the superior court of the county in which the estate of the deceased spouse may be administered requesting an order that administration of all or part of the estate is not necessary for the reason that all or part of the estate is property passing to the surviving spouse. The petition may also request an order confirming the ownership of the surviving spouse of property belonging to the surviving spouse under Section 100 or 101.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13650(c)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, no separate court authorization needed for a guardian or conservator to file
citations.quote: A guardian or conservator may file a petition under this section without authorization or approval of the court in which the guardianship or conservatorship proceeding is pending.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13652
citations.cite: California Probate Code, filing within a pending estate proceeding, no additional fee
citations.quote: If proceedings for the administration of the estate of the deceased spouse are pending, a petition under this chapter shall be filed in those proceedings without the payment of an additional fee.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13653
citations.cite: California Probate Code, filing when no estate proceeding is pending
citations.quote: If proceedings for the administration of the estate of the deceased spouse are not pending, a petition under this chapter may, but need not, be filed with a petition for probate of the will of the deceased spouse or for administration of the estate of the deceased spouse.

clauses.title: What the Petition Must Allege and Attach
clauses.body: Probate Code § 13651(a) requires the petition to allege that administration is unnecessary and to set out: if no estate proceeding is pending, the facts needed to determine the proper county of filing; a description of the property alleged to be passing to the surviving spouse, including the trade or business name of any unincorporated business involved; the facts supporting that allegation; a description of any separate community or quasi-community property interest the petitioner asks the court to confirm as already belonging to the surviving spouse under § 100 or § 101; and the name, age, address, and relation to the decedent of each heir and devisee, plus the names and addresses of any named executors and any appointed personal representatives, so far as known — along with disclosure of any written non-pro-rata division agreement between the spouses, or an affirmative statement that none exists. Section 13651(b) requires a copy of the decedent's will to be attached if the petitioner's allegation rests on the will, and § 13651(c) requires a copy of any written non-pro-rata division agreement to be attached if the petitioner's property description rests on one.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides, not a claim about what a specific petition must contain in a specific case. All of the citations in this clause are subdivisions of the same section, § 13651, and are not independent confirmations of each other; no other, separately numbered section is cited in this clause. This document is informational only; it does not itself constitute a petition or satisfy any of these requirements.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13651(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, required contents of a spousal or domestic partner property petition
citations.quote: A petition filed pursuant to Section 13650 shall allege that administration of all or a part of the estate of the deceased spouse is not necessary for the reason that all or a part of the estate is property passing to the surviving spouse, and shall set forth all of the following information: (1) If proceedings for the administration of the estate are not pending, the facts necessary to determine the county in which the estate of the deceased spouse may be administered. (2) A description of the property of the deceased spouse which the petitioner alleges is property passing to the surviving spouse, including the trade or business name of any property passing to the surviving spouse that consists of an unincorporated business or an interest in an unincorporated business which the deceased spouse was operating or managing at the time of death, subject to any written agreement between the deceased spouse and the surviving spouse providing for a non pro rata division of the aggregate value of the community property assets or quasi-community assets, or both. (3) The facts upon which the petitioner bases the allegation that all or a part of the estate of the deceased spouse is property passing to the surviving spouse. (4) A description of any interest in the community property or quasi-community property, or both, which the petitioner requests the court to confirm to the surviving spouse as belonging to the surviving spouse pursuant to Section 100 or 101, subject to any written agreement between the deceased spouse and the surviving spouse providing for a non pro rata division of the aggregate value of the community property assets or quasi-community assets, or both. (5) The name, age, address, and relation to the deceased spouse of each heir and devisee of the deceased spouse, the names and addresses of all persons named as executors of the will of the deceased spouse, and the names and addresses of all persons appointed as personal representatives of the deceased spouse, which are known to the petitioner. Disclosure of any written agreement between the deceased spouse and the surviving spouse providing for a non pro rata division of the aggregate value of the community property assets or quasi-community property assets, or both, or the affirmative statement that this agreement does not exist.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13651(b)-(c)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, required attachments — the will, and any non-pro-rata division agreement
citations.quote: (b) If the petitioner bases the allegation that all or part of the estate of the deceased spouse is property passing to the surviving spouse upon the will of the deceased spouse, a copy of the will shall be attached to the petition. (c) If the petitioner bases the description of the property of the deceased spouse passing to the surviving spouse or the property to be confirmed to the surviving spouse, or both, upon a written agreement between the deceased spouse and the surviving spouse providing for a non pro rata division of the aggregate value of the community property assets or quasi-community assets, or both, a copy of the agreement shall be attached to the petition.

clauses.title: Notice of the Hearing
clauses.body: Probate Code § 13655(a) requires notice of the hearing on the petition — given as provided in Probate Code § 1220 — to each person listed in § 1220, each person named as executor in any will of the deceased spouse, and all devisees and known heirs of the deceased spouse (and, where the petitioner is a trustee of a devisee trust, all persons interested in that trust), whenever an estate proceeding is already pending, or whenever no estate proceeding is pending and the petition is filed on its own rather than together with a petition for probate or administration. Section 13655(b) separately requires that same notice to be delivered to the California Attorney General, addressed to the Attorney General's office in Sacramento, if the petitioner's allegation that property is passing to the surviving spouse rests on the decedent's will and that will involves or may involve a testamentary charitable trust without a resident designated trustee, or a charitable devise without an identified devisee or beneficiary.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides, not a claim about what notice is required in a specific case. Both quotes in this clause are subdivisions of the same section, § 13655, and are not independent confirmations of each other. This clause references, but does not itself independently fetch, quote, or verify, the separate manner-of-service requirements of Probate Code § 1220, which § 13655 incorporates by reference; that section's text is not confirmed in this document. This document is informational only; it does not itself give notice of any hearing.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13655(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, who must receive notice of the petition hearing
citations.quote: If proceedings for the administration of the estate of the deceased spouse are pending at the time a petition is filed under this chapter, or if the proceedings are not pending and if the petition filed under this chapter is not filed with a petition for probate of the deceased spouse’s will or for administration of the estate of the deceased spouse, notice of the hearing on the petition filed under this chapter shall be given as provided in Section 1220 to all of the following persons: (1) Each person listed in Section 1220 and each person named as executor in any will of the deceased spouse. (2) All devisees and known heirs of the deceased spouse and, if the petitioner is the trustee of a trust that is a devisee under the will of the decedent, all persons interested in the trust, as determined in cases of future interests pursuant to paragraph (1), (2), or (3) of subdivision (a) of Section 15804.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13655(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, notice to the Attorney General for petitions involving a charitable interest
citations.quote: The notice specified in subdivision (a) shall also be delivered as provided in subdivision (a) to the Attorney General, addressed to the office of the Attorney General at Sacramento, if the petitioner bases the allegation that all or part of the estate of the deceased spouse is property passing to the surviving spouse upon the will of the deceased spouse and the will involves or may involve either of the following: (1) A testamentary trust of property for charitable purposes other than a charitable trust with a designated trustee, resident in this state. (2) A devise for a charitable purpose without an identified devisee or beneficiary.

clauses.title: Finality of the Order, and Protection for Business Creditors
clauses.body: Probate Code § 13657 provides that once an order under § 13656 becomes final — whether it determines that property is passing to the surviving spouse or confirms the surviving spouse's ownership of property already belonging to them under § 100 or § 101 — that order 'shall be conclusive on all persons, whether or not they are in being.' Separately, Probate Code § 13658 addresses one specific category of property: if the court determines that property passing to the surviving spouse includes an unincorporated business, or an interest in one, that the decedent was operating or managing at death, the court must require the surviving spouse to file a list of the business's known creditors and the amounts owed to each, and the court may issue any order necessary to protect those creditors' interests, including requiring an undertaking or an inventory and appraisal.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides, not a claim about the finality or effect of any order in a specific case. § 13657 and § 13658 are separately numbered sections within the same chapter, independently verified, and independent of each other. This document is informational only; it does not itself constitute or obtain a final court order.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13657
citations.cite: California Probate Code, conclusiveness of a final order under this chapter
citations.quote: Upon becoming final, an order under Section 13656 (1) determining that property is property passing to the surviving spouse or (2) confirming the ownership of the surviving spouse of property belonging to the surviving spouse under Section 100 or 101 shall be conclusive on all persons, whether or not they are in being.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13658
citations.cite: California Probate Code, protection for creditors of an unincorporated business passing to the surviving spouse
citations.quote: If the court determines that all or a part of the property passing to the surviving spouse consists of an unincorporated business or an interest in an unincorporated business which the deceased spouse was operating or managing at the time of death, the court shall require the surviving spouse to file a list of all of the known creditors of the business and the amounts owing to each of them. The court may issue any order necessary to protect the interests of the creditors of the business, including, but not limited to, the filing of (1) an undertaking and (2) an inventory and appraisal in the form provided in Section 8802 and made as provided in Part 3 (commencing with Section 8800) of Division 7.

clauses.title: How This Petition Differs From the Small Estate Affidavit and From a Petition for Probate
clauses.body: This court petition procedure is structurally different from both of this corpus's other estate-administration documents. Unlike the small estate affidavit — a sworn declaration a successor presents directly to a property holder, with no court filing or hearing at all — this petition is filed in superior court, requires notice under Probate Code § 13655, and results in a court order under § 13656 that (per § 13657) becomes conclusive on all persons once final; it produces a recordable judicial determination rather than a private declaration. Unlike a petition for probate, which seeks appointment of a personal representative and, once Letters issue, ongoing court-supervised authority over the whole estate, this petition seeks a one-time determination that administration of specific property is unnecessary or a confirmation of the surviving spouse's existing ownership share — it does not appoint anyone or issue Letters. The procedure is also lighter administratively: Probate Code § 13659 dispenses with the inventory and appraisal that a full probate administration ordinarily requires, except for the unincorporated-business protections of § 13658, and, as already reflected in this corpus's Community Property Agreement — Information Sheet, Probate Code § 13660 lets attorney's fees for this petition be set by private agreement rather than by court approval, with court involvement available only if attorney and client later dispute the fee or its meaning.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides, not a claim about which procedure, if any, is appropriate for a specific estate. § 13659 and § 13660 are separately numbered sections within the same chapter, independently verified in this document, and independent of each other. This clause's description of the small estate affidavit and petition-for-probate procedures is a structural comparison drawing on this corpus's separately verified Small Estate Affidavit and Petition for Probate — Information Sheet documents; it does not re-quote or independently re-verify those documents' own citations (e.g., the § 13100 dollar ceiling or the § 8002 petition contents) in this session, and readers should treat that comparison as a summary rather than as newly verified statutory text. This document is informational only; it does not itself select or complete any procedure for any specific estate.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13659
citations.cite: California Probate Code, no inventory and appraisal ordinarily required for this petition
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 13658, no inventory and appraisal of the estate of the deceased spouse is required in a proceeding under this chapter. However, within three months after the filing of a petition under this chapter, or within such further time as the court or judge for reasonable cause may allow, the petitioner may file with the clerk of the court an inventory and appraisal made as provided in Part 3 (commencing with Section 8800) of Division 7.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13660
citations.cite: California Probate Code, attorney's fees for this petition set by private agreement
citations.quote: The attorney’s fees for services performed in connection with the filing of a petition and obtaining of a court order under this chapter shall be determined by private agreement between the attorney and the client and are not subject to approval by the court. If there is no agreement between the attorney and the client concerning the attorney’s fees for services performed in connection with the filing of a petition and obtaining of a court order under this chapter and there is a dispute concerning the reasonableness of the attorney’s fees for those services, a petition may be filed with the court in the same proceeding requesting that the court determine the reasonableness of the attorney’s fees for those services.

clauses.title: Purpose
clauses.body: {{companyName}} provides this information sheet to {{employeeName}} to describe the California statutory right to a day of rest set out in Labor Code sections 550 through 558.1, including the core one-day-rest-in-seven provisions, the statutory exceptions to those provisions, and how California's courts have construed them. This information sheet states general rules of California law. It is not a statement of {{companyName}}'s scheduling practices, and it does not describe what any particular schedule for {{employeeName}} does or should look like.

clauses.title: Entitlement to One Day's Rest in Seven
clauses.body: California law entitles every person employed in any occupation of labor to one day's rest in seven. This entitlement is stated as a right belonging to the employee, distinct from the separate statutory prohibition on an employer causing an employee to work more than six days in seven.
clauses.gap: This is California law. Section 551 states the entitlement in the passive voice, from the employee's perspective ("is entitled to"), without itself defining "one day's rest," specifying how the seven-day period is measured, or prescribing a remedy for its own violation; the companion clause in this information sheet describing the California Supreme Court's construction in Mendoza v. Nordstrom addresses how the seven-day period is measured. Section 551 does not by its own terms distinguish exempt from non-exempt employees; the separate exceptions described in this information sheet (Labor Code §§ 554, 556) apply to both section 551 and section 552 alike.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 551 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Division 2, Part 2, Chapter 1 (General), day of rest entitlement
citations.quote: Every person employed in any occupation of labor is entitled to one day's rest therefrom in seven.

clauses.title: Prohibition on Causing More Than Six Days' Work in Seven
clauses.body: California law separately prohibits an employer from causing its employees to work more than six days in seven. This provision is framed as a duty on the employer, addressed to what the employer causes, rather than solely as a right the employee may waive or decline to exercise. A companion clause in this information sheet describes how the California Supreme Court has construed what it means for an employer to "cause" an employee to go without a day of rest.
clauses.gap: This is California law. Section 552, standing alone, does not define the word "cause"; the companion Mendoza v. Nordstrom clause in this information sheet addresses that construction question, drawn from a different, independent source (a California Supreme Court opinion) rather than from the statutory text itself. Section 552 and section 551 are both part of the same statutory chapter (Labor Code §§ 550-558.1) and are not independent sources of each other, though they are independently numbered sections addressing distinct legal questions (an employee entitlement versus an employer prohibition).

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 552 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Division 2, Part 2, Chapter 1 (General), prohibition on employer causing excess work
citations.quote: No employer of labor shall cause his employees to work more than six days in seven.

clauses.title: Exception for Short Total Weekly or Daily Hours
clauses.body: Sections 551 and 552 do not apply to any employer or employee when the total hours of employment do not exceed 30 hours in any week or six hours in any one day of that week. A companion clause in this information sheet describes the California Supreme Court's construction of how this exception applies across the days of a single week.
clauses.gap: This is California law. Section 556 is written as an exception to sections 551 and 552 specifically, and its own text does not state whether the six-hours-in-any-one-day language means no single day may exceed six hours, or whether at least one qualifying day is enough; the companion Mendoza v. Nordstrom clause addresses that construction question using a separate, independent source (a California Supreme Court opinion), not the statutory text of section 556 itself. Section 556 does not state a total combined weekly-hours-and-daily-hours test beyond the "30 hours in any week or six hours in any one day" language quoted here.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 556 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Division 2, Part 2, Chapter 1 (General), exception for short total hours
citations.quote: Sections 551 and 552 shall not apply to any employer or employee when the total hours of employment do not exceed 30 hours in any week or six hours in any one day thereof.

clauses.title: Emergency, Accumulation, and Collective-Bargaining Exceptions
clauses.body: California law provides further exceptions to sections 551 and 552 beyond the short-total-hours exception. Sections 551 and 552 do not apply to cases of emergency, to work performed in the protection of life or property from loss or destruction, or to any common carrier engaged in or connected with the movement of trains. Separately, the statute permits an accumulation of days of rest when the nature of the employment reasonably requires that an employee work seven or more consecutive days, provided the employee receives, within each calendar month, days of rest equivalent to one day's rest in seven; where a valid collective bargaining agreement addresses hours of work, the equivalent-one-day-in-seven requirement applies notwithstanding other provisions of this chapter relating to such agreements, unless the agreement expressly provides otherwise. The Chief of the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement may also exempt an employer or employees from sections 551 and 552 upon a judgment that hardship will result.
clauses.gap: This is California law, drawn from Labor Code section 554, a separate and independently numbered section from sections 551, 552, and 556 discussed in this information sheet's other authority clauses, though it is part of the same statutory chapter and cross-references sections 551 and 552 directly rather than standing wholly apart from them. Section 554 does not itself define "emergency," "case of emergency," or what makes a hardship determination proper; it commits the hardship-exemption judgment to the Chief of the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement without stating a further standard in the statutory text quoted here. This clause does not address whether any particular employer or employee circumstance falls within these exceptions.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 554(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Division 2, Part 2, Chapter 1 (General), emergency and accumulation exceptions
citations.quote: Sections 551 and 552 do not apply to cases of emergency or to work performed in the protection of life or property from loss or destruction, or to any common carrier engaged in or connected with the movement of trains. Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to prevent an accumulation of days of rest when the nature of the employment reasonably requires that the employee work seven or more consecutive days, if in each calendar month the employee receives days of rest equivalent to one day's rest in seven.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 554(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Division 2, Part 2, Chapter 1 (General), hardship exemption authority
citations.quote: In addition to the exceptions specified in subdivision (a), the Chief of the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement may, when in his or her judgment hardship will result, exempt any employer or employees from the provisions of Sections 551 and 552.

clauses.title: Mendoza v. Nordstrom: How the Right Is Measured
clauses.body: The California Supreme Court, answering questions certified to it by the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, construed the day-of-rest statutes in three respects. First, the one-day's-rest-in-seven guarantee is measured by the workweek, not by any rolling period of seven consecutive days; a period of more than six consecutive days of work that stretches across more than one workweek is not automatically prohibited on that basis alone. Second, the section 556 exception for short daily hours applies only to an employee who never exceeds six hours of work on any day of the workweek; if an employee works more than six hours on even one day of the week, a day of rest must be provided during that workweek, subject to whatever other exceptions might otherwise apply. Third, an employer "causes" an employee to go without a day of rest, within the meaning of section 552, when it induces the employee to forgo rest to which the employee is entitled; an employer is not forbidden from permitting or allowing an employee, fully apprised of the entitlement to rest, to independently choose not to take a day of rest.
clauses.gap: This is a California Supreme Court decision construing California statutes discussed elsewhere in this information sheet (Labor Code §§ 551, 552, 556); it is a different kind of source from those statutes (case law rather than enacted text) and is independent of them, though it directly interprets their wording rather than addressing a separate legal question. The case arose on certified questions from a federal appellate case (a Private Attorneys General Act action against a specific retail employer), and the summary above states the court's own numbered answers to the certified questions as the court wrote them; it does not address every fact-specific application the opinion discusses, such as how the "cause" standard applies to any particular scheduling practice.

citations.case: Mendoza v. Nordstrom, Inc. (2017) 2 Cal.5th 1074
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, construing Labor Code §§ 551, 552, and 556
citations.quote: 1. A day of rest is guaranteed for each workweek. Periods of more than six consecutive days of work that stretch across more than one workweek are not per se prohibited. 2. The exemption for employees working shifts of six hours or less applies only to those who never exceed six hours of work on any day of the workweek. If on any one day an employee works more than six hours, a day of rest must be provided during that workweek, subject to whatever other exceptions might apply. 3. An employer causes its employee to go without a day of rest when it induces the employee to forgo rest to which he or she is entitled. An employer is not, however, forbidden from permitting or allowing an employee, fully apprised of the entitlement to rest, independently to choose not to take a day of rest.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This California Fair Pay Act Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes selected requirements of California Labor Code section 1197.5, sometimes referred to as California's Fair Pay Act or Equal Pay Act, as it may relate to compensation paid by {{companyName}} to {{employeeName}} in connection with the position of {{jobTitle}}. Section 1197.5 addresses pay comparisons based on sex and, separately, on race or ethnicity, the specific factors an employer may rely on to justify a pay differential, protections against retaliation for invoking or assisting in the enforcement of the section, and a wage-and-job-classification recordkeeping duty. This document is California-specific: it describes only what this one California statute says. It is not a determination that any wage rate paid or not paid by {{companyName}} to {{employeeName}}, or to any other employee, complies or fails to comply with section 1197.5, and it does not itself satisfy any recordkeeping, notice, or reporting duty the statute may impose.

clauses.title: The Core Prohibition: Sex-Based and Race/Ethnicity-Based Pay Differentials for Substantially Similar Work
clauses.body: California Labor Code section 1197.5 states its core prohibition in two separate, parallel subdivisions rather than a single unified provision. Subdivision (a) prohibits an employer from paying any of its employees at wage rates less than the rates paid to employees of another sex for substantially similar work, when viewed as a composite of skill, effort, and responsibility, and performed under similar working conditions, unless the employer demonstrates specified factors. Subdivision (b), using materially identical wording, separately prohibits paying any of its employees at wage rates less than the rates paid to employees of another race or ethnicity for substantially similar work, viewed and performed under the same composite standard, unless the employer demonstrates the same kind of factors. The comparison standard in both subdivisions is "substantially similar work," assessed as a composite of skill, effort, and responsibility performed under similar working conditions — not a requirement that the compared jobs be identical.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1197.5(a) and (b)), used as real evidence of the statute's core prohibition and its comparison standard — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The two citations below are to subdivisions (a) and (b) of a single statutory section; they are not independent sources of each other, since subdivision (b) was evidently drafted as a parallel to subdivision (a) and both were confirmed from the same two fetches of the same section. This section was last amended effective January 1, 2026 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 468 (SB 642)); this clause reflects the section's currently codified text as fetched on the date below, not any prior or superseded version. Section 1197.5's own text does not define "substantially similar work" beyond the composite-factors language quoted here, and this clause does not determine whether any two specific positions, or the work actually performed in them, are or are not substantially similar within the meaning of the statute.

clauses.title: The Affirmative Defense: Enumerated Bona Fide Factors, and the Limit on Prior Salary
clauses.body: Section 1197.5 does not prohibit every pay differential between employees of different sexes, races, or ethnicities doing substantially similar work; it makes the prohibition subject to an affirmative defense the employer bears the burden of demonstrating. Under subdivision (a) (and, in parallel, subdivision (b) for race and ethnicity), the wage differential must be based upon one or more of a specific, enumerated list of factors: a seniority system; a merit system; a system that measures earnings by quantity or quality of production; or a bona fide factor other than sex (or, under subdivision (b), other than race or ethnicity), such as education, training, or experience. That last, catch-all factor is itself conditioned: it applies only if the employer demonstrates the factor is not based on or derived from a sex-based (or race- or ethnicity-based) differential in compensation, is job related to the position in question, and is consistent with a "business necessity," which the statute defines as an overriding legitimate business purpose that the factor effectively fulfills; even then, the catch-all defense does not apply if the employee demonstrates an alternative business practice exists that would serve the same business purpose without producing the wage differential. Beyond identifying a qualifying factor, the statute imposes two further requirements: each factor relied upon must be applied reasonably, and the factor or factors relied upon must account for the entire wage differential, not merely part of it. Separately, the statute states that prior salary shall not justify any disparity in compensation, while clarifying that this does not prevent an employer from basing a compensation decision on a current employee's existing salary, so long as any resulting wage differential is itself justified by one or more of the enumerated factors.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1197.5(a)(1) through (a)(4), and the parallel language in (b)(1) through (b)(4)), used as real evidence of the statute's affirmative-defense structure — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any specific pay differential is or is not justified. The citations below are all to subparagraphs of subdivision (a) of a single statutory section; subdivision (b) restates the same structure with "race or ethnicity" substituted for "sex" and is not cited separately as an independent source, since it is textually parallel rather than independently corroborating. This clause does not resolve, and the statute's text does not itself specify, how much of a wage differential must be "accounted for" before a factor is treated as covering the "entire" differential in a case involving more than one factor, nor does it identify any particular alternative-business-practice showing that would or would not defeat the catch-all factor in a specific case; this clause does not identify any reported court decision applying these factors to particular facts, an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption.

clauses.title: Remedies for a Violation and the Statute of Limitations
clauses.body: Section 1197.5 states that an employer who violates the sex-based prohibition in subdivision (a) or the race/ethnicity-based prohibition in subdivision (b) is liable to the affected employee for the amount of wages and interest of which the employee was deprived, plus an additional equal amount as liquidated damages. Consistent with this, an employee receiving less than the wage to which the employee is entitled may recover the balance of the wages, including interest, an equal amount as liquidated damages, and the costs of suit and reasonable attorney's fees, in a civil action, and this remedy applies notwithstanding any agreement to work for a lesser wage. The statute sets its own limitations period for this kind of civil action: a civil action to recover wages under subdivision (a) or (b) must be commenced no later than three years after the last date the cause of action occurs, while the employee's entitlement to relief for a continuing violation can reach back for the entire period the violation existed, up to a maximum of six years.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1197.5(c), (h), (i)(1), and (i)(2)), used as real evidence of the statute's remedies and limitations period — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular employee is entitled to any particular recovery. The four citations below are all to subdivisions of a single statutory section and are treated as one source describing one connected remedial scheme, not as independent corroborating sources. This clause does not restate subdivision (i)(3)'s definitions of when a cause of action "occurs," subdivision (i)(4)'s preservation of the continuing-violation and discovery-rule doctrines, subdivision (d)'s administrative enforcement track through the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, subdivision (g)'s provision for a civil action brought by the department or division itself, or subdivision (j)'s offset against a related federal Equal Pay Act recovery; a reader consulting the statute's full text will find additional remedial and procedural detail beyond what this clause summarizes. This clause does not identify any reported court decision applying these remedies or this limitations period to particular facts, an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption.

clauses.title: Recordkeeping Duty and Administrative Enforcement by the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement
clauses.body: Section 1197.5 requires every employer to maintain records of the wages and wage rates, job classifications, and other terms and conditions of employment of the persons it employs, and requires those records to be kept on file for a period of three years. The statute assigns administrative responsibility for the section to the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, which the statute directs to administer and enforce the section, including by investigating an employee's complaint that wages paid are less than the wages to which the employee is entitled, or that the employer has violated the anti-retaliation subdivision. In connection with a complaint alleging a violation of the sex-based prohibition, the race/ethnicity-based prohibition, or the anti-retaliation provision, the statute directs the Division to keep confidential the name of the complaining employee until the Division establishes the validity of the complaint, unless confidentiality must be abridged to investigate, and states that the name remains confidential if the complaint is withdrawn before that point.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1197.5(d), (e), and (f)), used as real evidence of the recordkeeping duty and the administrative enforcement and confidentiality framework — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The three citations below are to subdivisions of a single statutory section and are treated as one source describing one connected recordkeeping-and-enforcement scheme, not as independent corroborating sources; this recordkeeping duty and its three-year retention period are also cited, from the same subdivision (e), in a separate clause of a different information sheet in this corpus addressing Labor Code section 432.3, disclosed here rather than presented as a newly discovered source. This clause does not restate the full text of subdivision (f)'s complaint-investigation cross-reference to Labor Code section 98.7(b), and does not determine that any particular employer has or has not maintained the required records for any particular employee, or that the Division has or would find any particular complaint valid. clauses.title: Anti-Retaliation Provision and the Protected Right to Discuss Wages
clauses.body: Section 1197.5 includes its own anti-retaliation provision, separate from the general prohibition on unequal pay. It states that an employer shall not discharge, or in any manner discriminate or retaliate against, an employee by reason of any action the employee takes to invoke or assist in enforcing the section, and that if an employer takes a prohibited action within 90 days of the employee's protected activity, a rebuttable presumption arises in favor of the employee's claim. Within this same provision, the statute separately protects pay-transparency-related conduct: an employer shall not prohibit an employee from disclosing the employee's own wages, discussing the wages of others, inquiring about another employee's wages, or aiding or encouraging another employee to exercise rights under the section, though the statute is explicit that this does not itself create any obligation to disclose wages. An employee who has been discharged, discriminated, or retaliated against in violation of this provision may recover, in a civil action, reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits, including interest, as well as appropriate equitable relief; such an action must be commenced no later than one year after the cause of action occurs.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1197.5(k)(1) through (k)(3)), used as real evidence of the section's anti-retaliation and wage-discussion provisions — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The citations below are all to paragraphs of a single statutory subdivision, (k), and are treated as one source, not as independent corroborating sources; the 90-day rebuttable-presumption language and the wage-discussion protection are both drawn from the same paragraph, (k)(1), and are not independent of each other either. This clause does not determine that any particular employer action taken toward any particular employee was or was not "by reason of" protected activity within the meaning of subdivision (k)(1), does not determine that any particular 90-day window applies to any particular set of facts, and does not identify any reported court decision applying this provision to particular facts, an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This No-Rehire Clause Restriction in Settlement Agreements — Information Sheet is prepared for use alongside a settlement agreement resolving an employment dispute between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}, dated {{dateSigned}}. It describes what California Code of Civil Procedure section 1002.5 says about no-rehire provisions in agreements settling employment disputes — provisions that would prohibit, prevent, or otherwise restrict {{employeeName}} from obtaining future employment with {{companyName}} or its parent company, subsidiary, division, affiliate, or contractor. This information sheet is not itself a settlement agreement, and it does not itself determine whether any specific provision in any specific agreement between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}} is void, valid, or enforceable.

clauses.title: No-Rehire Provisions Void in Employment-Dispute Settlement Agreements
clauses.body: California law provides that an agreement settling an employment dispute may not contain a provision that prohibits, prevents, or otherwise restricts a settling party who is an “aggrieved person” from obtaining future employment with the employer against which that person filed a claim, or with any parent company, subsidiary, division, affiliate, or contractor of that employer. A provision in an agreement entered into on or after January 1, 2020, that violates this rule is void as a matter of law and against public policy.
clauses.gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5 is a distinct statute from Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1001, which separately restricts non-disparagement and confidentiality provisions covering the factual information underlying certain harassment, discrimination, and retaliation claims (that statute is covered in this corpus's Non-Disparagement Agreement — Information Sheet document). Section 1002.5 addresses a narrower and different subject: whether a settling employee can be barred from future employment with the employer or its corporate family. The voiding rule applies only to a provision in an agreement “entered into on or after January 1, 2020” — the statute's own text ties the void-as-a-matter-of-law consequence to that date, which is verified from the statute's own text rather than assumed; this indicates the rule is prospective rather than retroactive, though the statute's text does not itself state what result follows for an otherwise-identical provision in an agreement entered into before that date. The statute does not further define “parent company,” “subsidiary,” “division,” “affiliate,” or “contractor” within this section. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific no-rehire provision is void in a specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5(a) (Leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Agreements Settling Employment Disputes, no-rehire provision ban
citations.quote: (a) An agreement to settle an employment dispute shall not contain a provision prohibiting, preventing, or otherwise restricting a settling party that is an aggrieved person from obtaining future employment with the employer against which the aggrieved person has filed a claim, or any parent company, subsidiary, division, affiliate, or contractor of the employer. A provision in an agreement entered into on or after January 1, 2020, that violates this section is void as a matter of law and against public policy.

clauses.title: Who Is Protected: Definition of “Aggrieved Person”
clauses.body: The no-rehire voiding rule protects only a settling party who qualifies as an “aggrieved person.” The statute defines that term as a person who, in good faith, has filed a claim against the person's employer in court, before an administrative agency, in an alternative dispute resolution forum, or through the employer's internal complaint process.
clauses.gap: This citation is to a subsection of the same statutory section as the other clauses in this document (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5) — it is treated as one source with them, not independent corroboration of each other or of it. Because the voiding rule by its terms applies only to an “aggrieved person,” the statute's own text indicates it protects a settling party who has filed a claim through one of the listed channels in good faith; the statute's text does not itself extend the voiding rule to a settling party who has not filed such a claim. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5(c)(1) (Leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Agreements Settling Employment Disputes, definition of “aggrieved person”
citations.quote: “Aggrieved person” means a person who, in good faith, has filed a claim against the person’s employer in court, before an administrative agency, in an alternative dispute resolution forum, or through the employer’s internal complaint process.

clauses.title: Exceptions: Ending Current Employment and a Pre-Claim Good-Faith Determination
clauses.body: The voiding rule does not preclude an employer and an aggrieved person from agreeing to end a current employment relationship. Separately, it also does not preclude them from agreeing to prohibit or otherwise restrict the settling aggrieved person's future employment with the settling employer where the employer made and documented a good-faith determination, before the aggrieved person filed the claim, that the aggrieved person engaged in sexual harassment, sexual assault, or any criminal conduct.
clauses.gap: This citation is to a subsection of the same statutory section as the other clauses in this document (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5) — it is treated as one source with them, not independent corroboration. This exception, by the statute's own text, has three specific conditions: the good-faith determination must (i) be made and documented, (ii) occur before the aggrieved person filed the claim, and (iii) concern sexual harassment, sexual assault, or criminal conduct specifically — it is not a general “any legitimate reason” exception. A separate, broader exception for a “legitimate non-discriminatory or non-retaliatory reason” appears elsewhere in this same subdivision and is addressed in the next clause; the two exceptions have different scopes and different timing/documentation requirements and are not interchangeable, as verified by comparing the statute's own text for each. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5(b)(1) (Leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Agreements Settling Employment Disputes, end-of-employment and pre-claim good-faith determination exceptions
citations.quote: (1) Preclude the employer and aggrieved person from making an agreement to do either of the following: (A) End a current employment relationship. (B) Prohibit or otherwise restrict the settling aggrieved person from obtaining future employment with the settling employer, if the employer has made and documented a good faith determination, before the aggrieved person filed the claim that the aggrieved person engaged in sexual harassment, sexual assault, or any criminal conduct.

clauses.title: Exception: Legitimate Non-Discriminatory or Non-Retaliatory Reason
clauses.body: Separately, the voiding rule does not require an employer to continue to employ or rehire a person if there is a legitimate non-discriminatory or non-retaliatory reason for terminating the employment relationship or refusing to rehire the person.
clauses.gap: This citation is to a subsection of the same statutory section as the other clauses in this document (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5) — it is treated as one source with them, not independent corroboration. Unlike the sexual-harassment/sexual-assault/criminal-conduct exception in subdivision (b)(1)(B), the statute's text for this exception does not include an express “made and documented” or “before the aggrieved person filed the claim” requirement, and it is not limited to any particular category of misconduct — this is a difference drawn directly from comparing the statute's own text for the two exceptions, not an inference beyond it. The statute's text does not itself define what qualifies as a “legitimate non-discriminatory or non-retaliatory reason.” This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only.

citations.quote: (2) Require an employer to continue to employ or rehire a person if there is a legitimate non-discriminatory or non-retaliatory reason for terminating the employment relationship or refusing to rehire the person.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions and Legislative History
clauses.body: For purposes of the good-faith-determination exception, the statute defines “sexual assault” as conduct that would constitute a crime under specified Penal Code sections (243.3, 261, 262, 264.1, 286, 287, or 289), assault with the intent to commit any of those crimes, or an attempt to commit any of those crimes. It defines “sexual harassment” as having the same meaning given in Government Code section 12940(j). The chapter containing this section was added by legislation enacted in 2019, and the section was later amended, with the amendment effective January 1, 2021.
clauses.gap: These citations are all to the same statutory section as the other clauses in this document (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1002.5) and to that section's own official history note — they are treated as one source with the rest of this document, not independent corroboration of each other. The cross-referenced definitions in Penal Code §§ 243.3, 261, 262, 264.1, 286, 287, and 289, and in Government Code § 12940(j), were not separately fetched or independently verified in this research — only § 1002.5's own text, which names them, was fetched and confirmed. The “void as a matter of law” consequence in subdivision (a) is tied to an agreement “entered into on or after January 1, 2020,” matching the chapter's original 2020 effective date; the source page's official history note also shows a later amendment effective January 1, 2021, but the statute's own text does not indicate that amendment changed the January 1, 2020 operative date attached to the void-as-a-matter-of-law rule. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's current rule on this point — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific person's situation. This document is informational only.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Trade Secret Preemption Doctrine Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's trade secret preemption doctrine under Civil Code section 3426.7, part of the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act (CUTSA) — the statutory provision that addresses which other civil claims may, and may not, be brought alongside or instead of a trade secret misappropriation claim when those claims rest on the same underlying facts. It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning a situation involving {{companyName}} and {{adversePartyName}}. The other claims or remedies under consideration, beyond a trade secret misappropriation claim itself, are described as follows: {{otherClaimsDescription}}. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference describing what section 3426.7 says and how published California case law has construed it. It does not itself determine whether any specific claim described above is, or is not, based on the same nucleus of facts as a trade secret misappropriation claim, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is also distinct from, and is meant as a companion to, this project's existing Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter document: that document addresses the definition of misappropriation and the remedies available for it, while this one addresses a separate question — what happens to other, non-trade-secret civil claims arising from the same facts.

clauses.title: What CUTSA Does Not Supersede: Other Trade-Secret-Specific Statutes
clauses.body: California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act is not, by its own terms, a complete replacement for every other California statute that touches trade secrets. Civil Code section 3426.7, subdivision (a), states that unless a statute expressly provides otherwise, CUTSA does not supersede any other statute relating to trade secret misappropriation or any statute otherwise regulating trade secrets. This subdivision addresses CUTSA's relationship to other trade-secret-specific statutes; it is a separate question from subdivision (b) of the same section, addressed in a companion clause of this document, which addresses CUTSA's relationship to non-statutory common-law claims and other civil, contractual, and criminal remedies.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of CUTSA's own stated relationship to other trade-secret-specific statutes — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not an exhaustive list of which other California statutes "relat[e] to misappropriation of a trade secret" or "otherwise regulat[e] trade secrets" for purposes of this subdivision; no such statute is identified or discussed here. This clause quotes subdivision (a) of Cal. Civ. Code section 3426.7; a companion clause in this document quotes subdivision (b) and another quotes subdivision (c) of that same section — all three are subdivisions of one statutory section, not independent sources of each other, and are disclosed as such throughout this document. The full text of section 3426.7 was retrieved twice directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov — the official California Legislative Information website — as two separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical text for the whole section (after whitespace normalization), so this is one primary source checked twice for consistency, not two independent sources. No case law construing subdivision (a) specifically was checked in this research; the subdivision's own text is unambiguous on its face, so the statute stands as the source here without a corroborating case. This is California-specific: CUTSA preemption doctrine, including this non-supersession rule, is a creature of California statute, and many other states have adopted their own versions of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act with their own (not necessarily identical) provisions on this same question, which this document does not address.

clauses.title: What CUTSA Does Not Affect: Contractual, Criminal, and Non-Trade-Secret Civil Remedies
clauses.body: Civil Code section 3426.7, subdivision (b), expressly preserves three categories of remedy from CUTSA's displacing effect: (1) contractual remedies, whether or not they are also based on trade secret misappropriation; (2) other civil remedies that are not based on trade secret misappropriation; and (3) criminal remedies, whether or not they are also based on trade secret misappropriation. This is the core statutory text underlying what courts and litigants commonly call "CUTSA preemption" — a claim falling within one of these three preserved categories is not displaced by CUTSA merely because the same underlying facts could also support a trade secret misappropriation claim. Notably, the statutory text of section 3426.7 does not itself use the word "preempt" or "preemption" anywhere; that terminology comes from courts construing this subdivision, not from the statute's own language, as described in a companion clause of this document.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of what CUTSA expressly preserves — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that any specific claim described in this Information Sheet falls into one of these three preserved categories; that is a fact-specific characterization this document does not make. This clause quotes subdivision (b) of Cal. Civ. Code section 3426.7; companion clauses in this document quote subdivisions (a) and (c) of that same section — all three are subdivisions of one statutory section, not independent sources of each other. The full text of section 3426.7 was retrieved twice directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as two separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical text for the whole section (after whitespace normalization), so this is one primary source checked twice for consistency, not two independent sources. This document's own text-search of both retrieved copies of section 3426.7 confirmed that neither the word "preempt" nor "preemption" (nor any variant) appears anywhere in the statute's text; the statute instead uses "supersede" (in subdivision (a)) and "does not affect" (in subdivision (b) and (c)). This is California-specific: many other states have adopted their own versions of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act, several with their own preemption or displacement provisions that are not necessarily worded or construed identically to California's, and this document does not address them.

clauses.title: A Separate Carve-Out: The California Public Records Act
clauses.body: Civil Code section 3426.7, subdivision (c), sets out a further, narrower carve-out specific to public records: CUTSA does not affect the disclosure of a record by a state or local agency under the California Public Records Act. The statute directs that whether disclosure of a record under the Public Records Act would constitute a trade secret misappropriation, and what rights and remedies would apply, is instead governed by the law that was in effect before CUTSA's own operative date. This is a distinct, narrower preservation than the general categories described in subdivision (b) — it addresses only agency records-disclosure questions, not the broader universe of contractual, criminal, and non-trade-secret civil claims.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, additional carve-out in CUTSA's displacement provision — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not an explanation of what "the law in effect before the operative date of this title" actually required; that pre-CUTSA law is not researched or described anywhere in this document. This clause quotes subdivision (c) of Cal. Civ. Code section 3426.7; companion clauses in this document quote subdivisions (a) and (b) of that same section — all three are subdivisions of one statutory section, not independent sources of each other. No case law construing subdivision (c) specifically was checked in this research. This is California-specific: the California Public Records Act itself, and this carve-out's interaction with it, are matters of California law only, and this document does not address how any other state's public-records or trade-secret statute would treat the same question.

clauses.title: Case Law: The "Same Nucleus of Facts" Test for CUTSA Preemption
clauses.body: Although section 3426.7's own text never uses the word "preempt" or "preemption," published California case law construing that section does use that terminology, and has developed a specific test for applying it. In K.C. Multimedia, Inc. v. Bank of America Technology & Operations, Inc., the California Court of Appeal held that section 3426.7, subdivision (b), preempts common-law claims that are based on the same nucleus of facts as a trade secret misappropriation claim — adopting, as California law, a test the court found in earlier federal decisions applying California law. Under this test, whether a particular non-trade-secret civil claim survives alongside a trade secret misappropriation claim can turn on whether that claim rests on facts distinct from the misappropriation, or instead restates the same underlying factual allegations under a different legal label.
clauses.gap: K.C. Multimedia, Inc. v. Bank of America Technology & Operations, Inc., 171 Cal.App.4th 939 (Cal. Ct. App., 6th Dist. 2009), is a published opinion of the California Court of Appeal, confirmed as "Published" status via the CourtListener database. Its text was retrieved via CourtListener's document-read function (returning the opinion's full html-with-citations text) and the exact quoted sentence was independently re-confirmed as an exact match via a separate CourtListener full-text search query for that phrase — both checks queried the same underlying CourtListener database rather than two independently published sources, so this is one primary source (the published opinion) checked two different ways, not two independent sources, and is disclosed on that basis. The same phrase, and citation to this case, also appeared in results from other, later opinions in that same search (for example, a 2014 federal district court decision applying California law), which were not independently read or verified in this research and are not cited here; they are mentioned only to note that this test has been repeated elsewhere, not as an independently verified additional source. This is a single California Court of Appeal decision from one appellate district (the Sixth Appellate District); it is not a California Supreme Court decision, and this document does not represent that every California appellate district has adopted identical language for this test, or that no California case has stated the test differently. This is California-specific case law construing a California statute; it says nothing about how any other state's version of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act treats the same question.

citations.case: K.C. Multimedia, Inc. v. Bank of America Technology & Operations, Inc., 171 Cal. App. 4th 939 (Cal. Ct. App., 6th Dist., Mar. 3, 2009)
citations.cite: California Court of Appeal, Sixth Appellate District, adopting the "same nucleus of facts" test for CUTSA preemption
citations.quote: In sum, we agree with the federal cases applying California law, which hold that section 3426.7, subdivision (b), preempts common law claims that are “based on the same nucleus of facts as the misappropriation of trade secrets claim for relief.”

clauses.title: Case Law: How the Test Was Applied to Specific Common-Law Claims
clauses.body: In the same decision, the California Court of Appeal applied the "same nucleus of facts" test to the specific claims pleaded in that case and affirmed the trial court's conclusion that the plaintiff's claims for breach of confidence, interference with contract, and statutory unfair competition were all preempted by CUTSA, because each rested on the same factual allegations as the plaintiff's trade secret misappropriation claim. This illustrates that the same test can reach claims styled under a range of different common-law and statutory labels — the label a claim is given does not by itself determine whether it survives; the test instead looks to whether the claim's factual basis is the same as, or distinct from, the trade secret misappropriation claim's factual basis.
clauses.gap: This is the same K.C. Multimedia, Inc. v. Bank of America Technology & Operations, Inc., 171 Cal.App.4th 939 (Cal. Ct. App., 6th Dist. 2009) opinion quoted in the companion case-law clause of this document — not an independent source from it, and disclosed as such. This clause quotes a different passage of that same opinion (the court's application of the test to the specific claims before it, near the end of its preemption discussion), rather than the passage stating the test itself; the two passages are treated here as one source, not independently corroborating ones. This clause describes what claims were found preempted on the specific pleading before that court; it does not state that breach of confidence, interference with contract, or unfair competition claims are always, or even usually, preempted — the same test applied to a differently pleaded claim, resting on facts distinct from the misappropriation itself, can reach the opposite result, and this document does not evaluate that question for any specific claim. This is a single published California Court of Appeal decision from one appellate district; it is not a California Supreme Court decision. This is California-specific case law construing a California statute; it says nothing about how any other state's version of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act, or that state's own preemption case law, would treat the same or similarly labeled claims.
