Applying that construction to the operative pleading here, we agree with the trial court’s conclusion that appellant’s claims for breach of confidence, interference with contract, and statutory unfair competition are all preempted by CUTSA.

clauses.title: Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Marital Summary Dissolution — Information Sheet concerns the marriage of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, who were married on {{marriageDate}} and identify {{separationDate}} as their date of separation. It is prepared for background use in connection with the possible filing of a joint petition for summary dissolution of marriage under Family Code §§ 2400-2406 in the Superior Court of California, County of {{countyOfFiling}}, or, if the eligibility conditions described in this document are not met, an ordinary petition for dissolution of marriage in the same court. This information sheet describes California's summary dissolution procedure — its narrow eligibility conditions, the joint-petition process, the right to revoke before judgment, and the effect and limited set-aside grounds of the eventual judgment — as background for that filing. It is not itself a joint petition or any other court filing, and completing it does not dissolve, terminate, or otherwise change the marital status of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. Only a court judgment of dissolution can do that.

clauses.title: Eligibility Conditions for Summary Dissolution
clauses.body: California law allows a marriage to be dissolved through the summary dissolution procedure only if all of the following conditions exist at the time the proceeding is commenced: either party independently meets the same jurisdictional (residency) requirements that apply to an ordinary dissolution of marriage; irreconcilable differences have caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage and it should be dissolved; there are no children of the relationship born before or during the marriage or adopted by the parties during the marriage, and neither party, to that party's knowledge, is pregnant; the marriage is not more than five years in duration as of the date of separation; neither party has any interest in real property wherever located, apart from a narrow lease exception — a residential lease occupied by either party that includes no purchase option and terminates within one year of the date the petition is filed; unpaid obligations incurred by either or both parties after the date of marriage, excluding any obligation relating to an automobile, do not exceed the statutory dollar threshold, stated in the statute's current codified text as four thousand dollars ($4,000); the total fair market value of community property assets — excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, but including any deferred compensation or retirement plan — is less than the statutory dollar threshold, stated in the statute's current codified text as twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), and neither party's separate property assets (subject to the same exclusions) exceed that same $25,000 figure; the parties have executed an agreement dividing their community assets and liabilities, along with any documents, title certificates, bills of sale, or other transfer paperwork needed to carry it out; the parties waive any right to spousal support from each other; the parties irrevocably waive their respective rights to appeal and to move for a new trial upon entry of the judgment; the parties have read and understand the summary dissolution brochure that the statute requires each superior court to make available; and the parties desire that the court dissolve the marriage. The $4,000 and $25,000 figures printed in the statute's own text are not fixed permanently: the statute separately directs that the unpaid-obligations figure be adjusted for changes in the value of the dollar on January 1 of every odd-numbered year beginning in 1985, and that the community/separate-property figure be adjusted the same way beginning in 1993, with the adjustments computed and published by the Judicial Council rather than written into the statute's text itself.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for summary dissolution of a marriage — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific marriage. This document is informational only: it does not itself dissolve any marriage or determine eligibility, grounds, or property/debt values for any specific case; only a court judgment does that. This clause cites a single statutory section with two subsections (§ 2400(a) and § 2400(b)); both are quoted because they state distinct rules (the twelve eligibility conditions, and the mechanism for periodically adjusting two of the dollar figures those conditions use) — this is not two independent sources. The $4,000 and $25,000 figures quoted here are the amounts printed in the statute's own currently codified text (last amended effective January 1, 2015); because subdivision (b) requires the Judicial Council to compute and publish inflation-adjusted current versions of those two figures outside the statute's own text, the actually-applicable current dollar thresholds may differ from $4,000 and $25,000, and this document's research did not independently locate or verify any Judicial Council publication stating the present adjusted amounts.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2400(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the twelve conditions for summary dissolution and the mechanism for periodically adjusting the dollar thresholds
citations.quote: (a) A marriage may be dissolved by the summary dissolution procedure provided in this chapter if all of the following conditions exist at the time the proceeding is commenced: (1) Either party has met the jurisdictional requirements of Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 2320) with regard to dissolution of marriage. (2) Irreconcilable differences have caused the irremediable breakdown of the marriage and the marriage should be dissolved. (3) There are no children of the relationship of the parties born before or during the marriage or adopted by the parties during the marriage, and neither party, to that party’s knowledge, is pregnant. (4) The marriage is not more than five years in duration as of the date of separation of the parties. (5) Neither party has any interest in real property wherever situated, with the exception of the lease of a residence occupied by either party which satisfies the following requirements: (A) The lease does not include an option to purchase. (B) The lease terminates within one year from the date of the filing of the petition. (6) There are no unpaid obligations in excess of four thousand dollars ($4,000) incurred by either or both of the parties after the date of their marriage, excluding the amount of any unpaid obligation with respect to an automobile. (7) The total fair market value of community property assets, excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, including any deferred compensation or retirement plan, is less than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), and neither party has separate property assets, excluding all encumbrances and automobiles, in excess of twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000). (8) The parties have executed an agreement setting forth the division of assets and the assumption of liabilities of the community, and have executed any documents, title certificates, bills of sale, or other evidence of transfer necessary to effectuate the agreement. (9) The parties waive any rights to spousal support. (10) The parties, upon entry of the judgment of dissolution of marriage pursuant to Section 2403, irrevocably waive their respective rights to appeal and their rights to move for a new trial. (11) The parties have read and understand the summary dissolution brochure provided for in Section 2406. (12) The parties desire that the court dissolve the marriage. (b) On January 1, 1985, and on January 1 of each odd-numbered year thereafter, the amounts in paragraph (6) of subdivision (a) shall be adjusted to reflect any change in the value of the dollar. On January 1, 1993, and on January 1 of each odd-numbered year thereafter, the amounts in paragraph (7) of subdivision (a) shall be adjusted to reflect any change in the value of the dollar. The adjustments shall be made by multiplying the base amounts by the percentage change in the California Consumer Price Index as compiled by the Department of Industrial Relations, with the result rounded to the nearest thousand dollars. The Judicial Council shall compute and publish the amounts.

clauses.title: Commencing the Proceeding: The Joint Petition
clauses.body: A summary dissolution proceeding is commenced by filing a joint petition for summary dissolution, in the form prescribed by the Judicial Council. The petition must be signed under oath by both spouses, and must include a statement that, as of the date the joint petition is filed, all of the eligibility conditions described elsewhere in this document have been met; the mailing address of each spouse; and a statement of whether either spouse elects to have a former name restored and, if so, what name. Unlike an ordinary dissolution proceeding, which one spouse alone may commence by petition, the summary dissolution procedure requires both spouses to jointly sign and file the same petition from the outset.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for summary dissolution of a marriage — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific marriage. This document is informational only: it does not itself commence any proceeding or dissolve any marriage. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 2401); no additional independent source was located for it.

citations.quote: (a) A proceeding for summary dissolution of the marriage shall be commenced by filing a joint petition for summary dissolution in the form prescribed by the Judicial Council. (b) The petition shall be signed under oath by both spouses and shall include all of the following: (1) A statement that as of the date of the filing of the joint petition all of the conditions set forth in Section 2400 have been met. (2) The mailing address of each spouse. (3) A statement whether a spouse elects to have their former name restored and, if so, the name to be restored.

clauses.title: Right to Revoke the Joint Petition Before Judgment
clauses.body: At any time before an application for judgment is filed, either party to the marriage may revoke the joint petition for summary dissolution — acting alone, without the other party's agreement — which terminates the summary dissolution proceeding. Revocation is accomplished by filing a notice of revocation, in the form prescribed by the Judicial Council, with the clerk of the court where the proceeding was commenced. The revoking party must send a copy of the notice of revocation to the other party by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to that party's last known address.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for summary dissolution of a marriage — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific marriage. This document is informational only: it does not itself revoke any petition or affect any pending proceeding. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 2402); no additional independent source was located for it.

citations.quote: (a) At any time before the filing of application for judgment pursuant to Section 2403, either party to the marriage may revoke the joint petition for summary dissolution and thereby terminate the summary dissolution proceeding filed pursuant to this chapter. (b) The revocation shall be effected by filing with the clerk of the court where the proceeding was commenced a notice of revocation in a form and content as shall be prescribed by the Judicial Council. (c) The revoking party shall send a copy of the notice of revocation to the other party by first-class mail, postage prepaid, at the other party’s last known address.

clauses.title: Six-Month Wait and Entry of Judgment
clauses.body: Once six months have expired from the date the joint petition for summary dissolution was filed, the court is required to enter a judgment dissolving the marriage, unless a revocation has been filed before then. Entry of the judgment restores both parties to the status of single persons, and either party may marry after the judgment is entered. The court clerk is required to send a notice of entry of judgment to each party at that party's last known address.

This document is informational only: it does not itself enter any judgment or dissolve any marriage; only a court judgment does that. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 2403); no additional independent source was located for it.

citations.quote: When six months have expired from the date of the filing of the joint petition for summary dissolution, the court shall, unless a revocation has been filed pursuant to Section 2402, enter the judgment dissolving the marriage. The judgment restores to the parties the status of single persons, and either party may marry after the entry of the judgment. The clerk shall send a notice of entry of judgment to each of the parties at the party’s last known address.

clauses.title: Effect of the Judgment and the Statutory Right to Seek to Set It Aside
clauses.body: Entry of the judgment operates as a final adjudication of the parties' rights and obligations regarding both the status of the marriage and their property rights, and it constitutes a waiver of each party's rights to spousal support, to appeal, and to move for a new trial. That finality is not absolute: the statute separately preserves the right of either party to bring an action to set the judgment aside for fraud, duress, accident, mistake, or another ground recognized at law or in equity, or to bring a motion under Code of Civil Procedure § 473. If either party proves that the parties did not actually meet the eligibility conditions at the time the petition was filed, the court is required to set the judgment aside as to every matter except the dissolved status of the marriage itself — meaning the marital status the judgment established remains intact even where the judgment is otherwise set aside on that ground.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California), used as evidence of what that state's law provides for summary dissolution of a marriage — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific marriage. This document is informational only: it does not itself adjudicate any rights, waive any right on behalf of any party, or set aside any judgment. This clause cites two separately and independently numbered statutory sections (§ 2404 and § 2405) that address distinct subjects — the effect of the judgment, and the statutory grounds and scope for setting it aside — so, unlike the other authority clauses in this document, this one rests on two genuinely independent sections rather than subsections of a single section.

(b) A waiver of their respective rights to spousal support, rights to appeal, and rights to move for a new trial.

citations.quote: (a) Entry of the judgment pursuant to Section 2403 does not prejudice nor bar the rights of either of the parties to institute an action to set aside the judgment for fraud, duress, accident, mistake, or other grounds recognized at law or in equity or to make a motion pursuant to Section 473 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (b) The court shall set aside a judgment entered pursuant to Section 2403 regarding all matters except the status of the marriage, upon proof that the parties did not meet the requirements of Section 2400 at the time the petition was filed.

clauses.title: How This Differs From the Corpus's Domestic Partnership Administrative Termination
clauses.body: The summary dissolution procedure addressed in this document is available only to married spouses, and only through a court proceeding: eligibility depends on a party independently meeting the same jurisdictional (residency) requirements that apply to an ordinary marital dissolution, and the proceeding is commenced by filing a joint petition with the superior court, which itself enters the eventual judgment. That is a different mechanism from the one described in this corpus's Domestic Partnership Dissolution — Information Sheet, under which a registered domestic partnership meeting a separately defined set of statutory conditions can be terminated without any court proceeding at all, simply by filing a Notice of Termination directly with the Secretary of State. The two mechanisms share a family resemblance in their numeric eligibility conditions — both use a duration cap on the relationship, dollar thresholds tied to Family Code § 2400 for debts and property, and a similar real-property/lease exception — but they are codified in different parts of the Family Code, apply to a different legal status (marriage, as opposed to a registered domestic partnership), and are decided by different government actors: a superior court judgment for summary dissolution of a marriage, as opposed to the Secretary of State's administrative processing of a Notice of Termination for a domestic partnership.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope — Involuntary Dissolution of a Corporation Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a {{entityType}} organized under the laws of California, and describes Cal. Corp. Code §§ 1800 through 1806, and § 2000 — the General Corporation Law's involuntary-dissolution statute, which sets out the specific grounds on which a court may dissolve a corporation, which categories of directors or shareholders may petition a court for that relief, the procedure a court follows once such a petition is filed, and a statutory alternative that can avoid dissolution altogether. It is prepared with reference to {{petitionerName}}'s relationship to {{companyName}}. Statutory ground or grounds this information sheet may relate to, if known: {{groundsForProceeding}}.

This information sheet describes the general involuntary-dissolution rule that applies to a California corporation that has not elected close-corporation status under Cal. Corp. Code § 158. This project's existing Close Corporation — Formation Information Sheet document already describes, in its clause on deadlock and dissolution, how close-corporation status expands who may petition for dissolution beyond the general rule; this information sheet instead sets out that general rule itself — the six statutory grounds, the standing categories that apply regardless of close-corporation status, the court procedure, and the buyout alternative to dissolution — in depth that document does not.

This information sheet is educational only. It is not a verified complaint, does not itself commence any court proceeding, and does not determine whether any ground described below applies to {{companyName}}'s circumstances, whether {{petitionerName}} meets any standing category described below, or whether a court would order dissolution, an alternative remedy, or no relief at all in any specific case.

clauses.title: Statutory Grounds for Involuntary Dissolution
clauses.body: California's involuntary-dissolution statute, Cal. Corp. Code § 1800, states the grounds on which a court may order a corporation's involuntary dissolution as a list introduced by the phrase “The grounds for involuntary dissolution are that:” — six grounds in total. The first ground is that the corporation has abandoned its business for more than one year. The second is a specific form of board deadlock: an even number of directors equally divided and unable to agree on management, combined with a shareholder body itself so factionalized that it cannot elect a board with an uneven number of directors. The third ground covers internal shareholder-level dissension: two or more shareholder factions so deadlocked that the corporation's business can no longer be conducted to the shareholders' advantage, or a failure at two consecutive annual meetings to elect successor directors. The fourth ground reaches misconduct by those in control of the corporation — persistent and pervasive fraud, mismanagement, or abuse of authority, persistent unfairness toward any shareholders, or misapplication or waste of corporate property by directors or officers. The fifth ground is available only to a corporation with 35 or fewer shareholders (determined under Cal. Corp. Code § 605) and asks only whether liquidation is reasonably necessary to protect the complaining shareholder's or shareholders' rights or interests, without requiring proof of fraud, mismanagement, or deadlock. The sixth ground applies when the period for which the corporation was formed has terminated without extension. A separate subdivision of the same section excludes certain regulated corporations — those subject to California's Banking Law, Public Utilities Act, Savings Association Law, or a specified article of the Insurance Code — from the entire section.
clauses.gap: Single-source disclosure: all six grounds are subdivisions of one statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 1800, and are not independent of each other or of the standing categories described in this document's companion clause on standing, which are also drawn from § 1800. This clause describes only the grounds the general involuntary-dissolution statute itself enumerates; it does not describe the separate ground on which the Attorney General may sue to dissolve a corporation under Cal. Corp. Code § 1801, which rests on different conduct (offenses against the corporations statutes, fraudulent abuse of corporate privileges, and similar) and is not a shareholder- or director-initiated proceeding, and this document does not otherwise address § 1801. Nothing in this clause determines whether any specific corporation's circumstances satisfy any of these grounds.

citations.quote: (1) The corporation has abandoned its business for more than one year.

citations.quote: (2) The corporation has an even number of directors who are equally divided and cannot agree as to the management of its affairs, so that its business can no longer be conducted to advantage or so that there is danger that its property and business will be impaired or lost, and the holders of the voting shares of the corporation are so divided into factions that they cannot elect a board consisting of an uneven number.

citations.quote: (3) There is internal dissension and two or more factions of shareholders in the corporation are so deadlocked that its business can no longer be conducted with advantage to its shareholders or the shareholders have failed at two consecutive annual meetings at which all voting power was exercised, to elect successors to directors whose terms have expired or would have expired upon election of their successors.

clauses.title: Standing to Petition for Involuntary Dissolution — the General Rule
clauses.body: Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a) identifies the persons who may file a verified complaint for a corporation's involuntary dissolution on one or more of the statute's enumerated grounds, and where that complaint must be filed: the superior court of the proper county. Four categories of petitioner are listed. The first is one-half or more of the directors then in office. The second is a shareholder or shareholders together holding shares representing not less than 33 1/3 percent of the corporation's outstanding shares (counting convertible preferred shares as converted), or of its outstanding common shares, or of its equity — excluding, in each of those three measures, shares held by anyone who personally participated in the fraud, mismanagement, or abuse-of-authority conduct described in the statute's fourth ground, and excluding any shareholder or shareholders of a close corporation, for whom the same subdivision separately grants standing without regard to percentage. The third category is any shareholder at all, without regard to the size of that shareholder's holding, but only where the asserted ground is the sixth ground: that the corporation's stated term has expired without extension. The fourth category is any other person the corporation's own articles of incorporation expressly authorize to bring the action. A separate subdivision of the same section extends the statute's use of the word “shareholder” to include a beneficial owner of shares who has entered into an agreement under Cal. Corp. Code § 300 or § 706.
clauses.gap: Single-source disclosure: all four standing categories, and the beneficial-owner definition, are subdivisions of one statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 1800, and are not independent of each other or of the grounds described in this document's companion clause on grounds, which are also drawn from § 1800. This clause describes only the general standing rule that applies whether or not a corporation has elected close-corporation status; it deliberately omits the close-corporation-specific expansion of the second category (to any close-corporation shareholder regardless of percentage) and the parallel close-corporation expansion of standing to petition for court supervision of a voluntary winding up under § 1904, both of which this project's existing Close Corporation — Formation Information Sheet document already covers (clause closecorp_deadlock_dissolution) and which are not repeated here. This clause also does not describe the Attorney General's separate standing to sue under § 1801, a different, non-shareholder proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(1)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for involuntary dissolution: directors
citations.quote: (1) One-half or more of the directors in office.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(2)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for involuntary dissolution: shareholders holding 33 1/3 percent
citations.quote: (2) A shareholder or shareholders who hold shares representing not less than 33 1 / 3 percent of (i) the total number of outstanding shares (assuming conversion of any preferred shares convertible into common shares) or (ii) the outstanding common shares or (iii) the equity of the corporation, exclusive in each case of shares owned by persons who have personally participated in any of the transactions enumerated in paragraph (4) of subdivision (b), or any shareholder or shareholders of a close corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(3)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for involuntary dissolution: any shareholder on the term-expiration ground
citations.quote: (3) Any shareholder if the ground for dissolution is that the period for which the corporation was formed has terminated without extension thereof.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)(4)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, standing to petition for involuntary dissolution: persons authorized in the articles
citations.quote: (4) Any other person expressly authorized to do so in the articles.

citations.quote: (e) For the purposes of this section, “shareholder” includes a beneficial owner of shares who has entered into an agreement under Section 300 or 706.

clauses.title: Filing, Intervention, Receivership, and the Court's Decree
clauses.body: The involuntary-dissolution action begins with a verified complaint filed in the superior court of the proper county, as Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a) itself specifies. Once the action is pending, § 1800(c) gives any shareholder or creditor of the corporation — not only the original petitioner — the right to intervene in the action at any time before trial. If, at the time the complaint is filed or at any later point, the court has reasonable grounds to believe the corporation's and its shareholders' interests will suffer before the complaint can be heard and decided unless a receiver is appointed, Cal. Corp. Code § 1803 authorizes the court, on the plaintiff's application, after a noticed hearing, and upon the plaintiff's giving of security under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 566 and 567, to appoint a receiver to take over and manage the corporation's business and affairs and preserve its property pending that hearing and determination. After the hearing on the merits, Cal. Corp. Code § 1804 gives the court two distinct paths: it may decree a winding up and dissolution of the corporation if cause for that relief is shown, or — with or without ordering winding up and dissolution — it may instead make whatever orders, decrees, and injunctions in the case that justice and equity require. The statute's text does not limit that second path to any particular list of alternative orders.
clauses.gap: Source-independence disclosure: the quotations from § 1800(a) and § 1800(c) are subdivisions of the same statutory section as the grounds and standing categories described in this document's other clauses and are not independent of them. The quotations from § 1803 and § 1804 are each drawn from independently numbered sections of the same chapter (Chapter 18, Involuntary Dissolution) and are independent of § 1800 and of each other for source-diversity purposes, though all three sections were adopted together as part of one 1975 enactment (Stats. 1975, Ch. 682), which is disclosed here rather than presented as unrelated corroboration. This clause does not catalog every procedural detail Chapter 18 addresses — for example, § 1801's Attorney General dissolution action, and §§ 1807 through 1809's creditor-claims-bar, final-decree, and Secretary of State filing provisions, which govern the later and more granular mechanics of a completed dissolution — and is not exhaustive of the chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, filing venue for an involuntary dissolution complaint
citations.quote: (a) A verified complaint for involuntary dissolution of a corporation on any one or more of the grounds specified in subdivision (b) may be filed in the superior court of the proper county by any of the following persons:

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, right of a shareholder or creditor to intervene
citations.quote: (c) At any time prior to the trial of the action any shareholder or creditor may intervene therein.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1803
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, pendente lite receiver in an involuntary dissolution action
citations.quote: 1803. If, at the time of the filing of a complaint for involuntary dissolution or at any time thereafter, the court has reasonable grounds to believe that unless a receiver of the corporation is appointed the interests of the corporation and its shareholders will suffer pending the hearing and determination of the complaint, upon the application of the plaintiff, and after a hearing upon such notice to the corporation as the court may direct and upon the giving of security pursuant to Sections 566 and 567 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court may appoint a receiver to take over and manage the business and affairs of the corporation and to preserve its property pending the hearing and determination of the complaint for dissolution. (Added by Stats. 1975, Ch. 682.)

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1804
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the court's post-hearing decree power
citations.quote: 1804. After hearing the court may decree a winding up and dissolution of the corporation if cause therefor is shown or, with or without winding up and dissolution, may make such orders and decrees and issue such injunctions in the case as justice and equity require. (Added by Stats. 1975, Ch. 682.)

clauses.title: Provisional Director as an Interim Remedy for Board Deadlock
clauses.body: Where the asserted ground for an involuntary-dissolution complaint is board deadlock — the ground Cal. Corp. Code § 1800(b)(2) defines as an evenly divided board that cannot agree on management, coupled with a shareholder body too factionalized to elect an uneven-numbered board — Cal. Corp. Code § 1802 gives the court a specific interim option: rather than proceeding only toward dissolution, the court may appoint a provisional director. Section 1802 does not create its own separate standard for that appointment; it incorporates by reference the provisional-director procedure of Cal. Corp. Code § 308(c), which governs the powers, term, and other conditions of a provisional director once appointed. This option exists specifically inside the involuntary-dissolution proceeding, for the deadlock ground — the statute's text ties it only to § 1800(b)(2), not to the statute's other five grounds for dissolution.
clauses.gap: Independent-source disclosure: § 1802 is an independently numbered section of Chapter 18, separate from § 1800, § 1803, and § 1804 cited elsewhere in this document. This clause quotes and describes only § 1802's incorporation of § 308(c) by cross-reference; it does not itself quote or independently re-verify the text of § 308, which this project's existing Close Corporation — Formation Information Sheet document already quotes and verifies (as § 308(a)) for a different, narrower point — that the provisional-director remedy generally is not limited to close corporations. This clause's point is different and additional: that within an involuntary-dissolution action specifically, § 1802 makes a provisional director an available alternative to full dissolution when the ground is board deadlock. This clause does not evaluate whether appointing a provisional director, rather than proceeding toward dissolution, would be appropriate in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1802
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, provisional director as an alternative to dissolution for board deadlock
citations.quote: 1802. If the ground for the complaint for involuntary dissolution of the corporation is a deadlock in the board as set forth in subdivision (b)(2) of Section 1800, the court may appoint a provisional director. The provisions of subdivision (c) of Section 308 apply to any such provisional director so appointed. (Amended by Stats. 1977, Ch. 235.)

clauses.title: Court Supervision of the Winding-Up Process
clauses.body: When a court orders a corporation's involuntary winding up under Cal. Corp. Code § 1804, that order itself marks the start of the winding-up proceeding, as § 1805(a) states. From that point, § 1805(b) puts the board itself in charge of conducting the winding up, but only subject to the supervision of the court, unless the court instead appoints other persons, on a showing of good cause, to conduct it; either the board or any court-appointed substitute may exercise their powers through the corporation's executive officers without needing a separate court order for each act. Under § 1805(c), once winding up has commenced the corporation must stop carrying on business except to the extent winding up itself requires, or as needed to preserve goodwill or going-concern value pending a sale of the business or its assets, and the directors must mail written notice of the winding-up proceeding to all shareholders and to all known creditors and claimants whose addresses appear on the corporation's records. Cal. Corp. Code § 1806 then defines what the court's ongoing jurisdiction over that winding up covers, including the presentation and barring of creditors' claims, the determination of shareholders' rights to the corporation's assets, the settling of the accounts of the persons conducting the winding up, the filling of board vacancies, staying other suits against the corporation, and — as one specific example — removing a director for dishonesty, misconduct, neglect, or abuse of trust in conducting the winding up, with the further power either to enjoin that director's re-election or to appoint a replacement director directly rather than ordering a new election.
clauses.gap: Independent-source disclosure: § 1805 and § 1806 are each independently numbered sections of Chapter 18, separate from § 1800, § 1802, § 1803, and § 1804 cited elsewhere in this document, and from each other, though all were enacted as part of the same 1975 chapter (Stats. 1975, Ch. 682). Within this clause, § 1805(a), (b), and (c) are subdivisions of one section and are not independent of each other; the § 1806 introductory clause and § 1806(g) quoted below are similarly subdivisions of one section and not independent of each other. This clause covers only the subdivisions of § 1805 and § 1806 that describe the general shape of court-supervised winding up; it summarizes rather than quotes § 1806's remaining specific jurisdictional grants (subdivisions (a) through (f) and (h) through (l)) for length, and omits §§ 1807 through 1809, which separately govern the creditor-claims-bar notice procedure, the final decree of dissolution, and the requirement to file that decree with the Secretary of State. This clause does not evaluate whether court-supervised winding up, rather than some other outcome, would apply to any specific proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1805(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, commencement of an involuntary winding-up proceeding
citations.quote: (a) Involuntary proceedings for winding up a corporation commence when the order for winding up is entered under Section 1804.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1805(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the board conducts winding up subject to court supervision
citations.quote: (b) When an involuntary proceeding for winding up has commenced, the board shall conduct the winding up of the affairs of the corporation, subject to the supervision of the court, unless other persons are appointed by the court, on good cause shown, to conduct the winding up. The directors or such other persons may, subject to any restrictions imposed by the court, exercise all their powers through the executive officers without any order of court.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1805(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, restriction on carrying on business and notice to shareholders and creditors during winding up
citations.quote: (c) When an involuntary proceeding for winding up has commenced, the corporation shall cease to carry on business except to the extent necessary for the beneficial winding up thereof and except during such period as the board may deem necessary to preserve the corporation’s goodwill or going-concern value pending a sale of its business or assets, or both, in whole or in part. The directors shall cause written notice of the commencement of the proceeding for involuntary winding up to be given by mail to all shareholders and to all known creditors and claimants whose addresses appear on the records of the corporation, unless the order for winding up has been stayed by appeal therefrom or otherwise or the proceeding or the execution of the order has been enjoined.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1806
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the scope of the court's jurisdiction during involuntary winding up
citations.quote: 1806. When an involuntary proceeding for winding up has been commenced, the jurisdiction of the court includes:

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1806(g)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the court's power to remove a director during winding up
citations.quote: (g) The removal of any director if it appears that the director has been guilty of dishonesty, misconduct, neglect or abuse of trust in conducting the winding up or if the director is unable to act. The court may order an election to fill the vacancy so caused, and may enjoin, for such time as it considers proper, the reelection of the director so removed; or the court, in lieu of ordering an election, may appoint a director to fill the vacancy caused by such removal. Any director so appointed by the court shall serve until the next annual meeting of shareholders or until a successor is elected or appointed.

clauses.title: Buyout Alternative to Dissolution
clauses.body: A separate statute, outside Chapter 18, gives the corporation itself — or, if the corporation does not act, its own majority shareholders — a way to stop an involuntary-dissolution action without a dissolution ever being decreed. Cal. Corp. Code § 2000(a) provides that, subject to any contrary provision in the articles, in any suit for involuntary dissolution the corporation or, if it does not elect to purchase, the holders of 50 percent or more of the corporation's voting power (the statute's defined “purchasing parties”) may avoid the corporation's dissolution and the appointment of any receiver by purchasing for cash, at fair value, the shares owned by the plaintiffs in the dissolution action (the statute's defined “moving parties”). Fair value under § 2000(a) is measured on a liquidation-value basis as of the valuation date, but taking into account the possibility of selling the entire business as a going concern rather than piecemeal. Any damages the moving parties owe the purchasing parties for breaching an agreement by initiating the dissolution suit may be deducted from what the purchasing parties owe for the shares — except where the dissolution ground is § 1800(b)(4)'s fraud, mismanagement, or abuse-of-authority ground, in which case § 2000(a) does not allow that deduction. If the purchasing parties elect to buy the shares but cannot agree with the moving parties on fair value, § 2000(b) requires them to post a bond covering the moving parties' reasonably estimated litigation expenses, after which the court stays the dissolution proceeding and itself proceeds to fix fair value. Under § 2000(c), that valuation is made by three court-appointed disinterested appraisers, whose award, once confirmed by the court, is final and conclusive on all parties, subject to appeal, and the court's resulting decree provides for winding up and dissolution to proceed unless the purchasing parties pay for the shares within the time the decree specifies. Section 2000(f) fixes the valuation date, for an involuntary-dissolution suit under § 1800, as the date that suit was commenced, subject to the court's power to designate a different date for good cause.
clauses.gap: Independent-source disclosure: § 2000 is codified in a different chapter of the General Corporation Law (Chapter 20, General Provisions Relating to Dissolution, §§ 2000–2011) than § 1800 and the other Chapter 18 sections cited elsewhere in this document (Chapter 18, Involuntary Dissolution, §§ 1800–1809), and is independent of them for source-diversity purposes, though it cross-references § 1800 directly and both chapters were enacted in the same 1975 legislation (Stats. 1975, Ch. 682). Within this clause, § 2000(a), (b), (c), and (f) are subdivisions of one section and are not independent of each other. This clause does not describe § 2000(d) (payment mechanics once value is fixed) or § 2000(e) (the beneficial-owner definition, which parallels § 1800(e)) in the same depth, and does not evaluate whether this buyout alternative would be available, elected, or advantageous in any specific dissolution proceeding — that depends on the corporation's articles, the specific ground alleged, and facts about value that this clause does not address.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2000(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the buyout alternative to dissolution
citations.quote: (a) Subject to any contrary provision in the articles, which may include a reference to a separate written agreement between two or more shareholders pertaining to the purchase of shares: In any suit for involuntary dissolution, or in any proceeding for voluntary dissolution initiated by the vote of shareholders representing only 50 percent of the voting power, the corporation or, if it does not elect to purchase, the holders of 50 percent or more of the voting power of the corporation (the “purchasing parties”) may avoid the dissolution of the corporation and the appointment of any receiver by purchasing for cash the shares owned by the plaintiffs or by the shareholders so initiating the proceeding (the “moving parties”) at their fair value. The fair value shall be determined on the basis of the liquidation value as of the valuation date but taking into account the possibility, if any, of sale of the entire business as a going concern in a liquidation. In fixing the value, the amount of any damages resulting if the initiation of the dissolution is a breach by any moving party or parties of an agreement with the purchasing party or parties may be deducted from the amount payable to the moving party or parties, unless the ground for dissolution is that specified in paragraph (4) of subdivision (b) of Section 1800. The election of the corporation to purchase may be made by the approval of the outstanding shares (Section 152) excluding shares held by the moving parties.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2000(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, bond and stay procedure when the parties cannot agree on fair value
citations.quote: (b) If the purchasing parties (1) elect to purchase the shares owned by the moving parties, and (2) are unable to agree with the moving parties upon the fair value of those shares, and (3) give bond with sufficient security to pay the estimated reasonable expenses (including attorneys’ fees) of the moving parties if those expenses are recoverable under subdivision (c), the court upon application of the purchasing parties, either in the pending action or in a proceeding initiated in the superior court of the proper county by the purchasing parties in the case of a voluntary election to wind up and dissolve, shall stay the winding up and dissolution proceeding and shall proceed to ascertain and fix the fair value of the shares owned by the moving parties.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2000(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, court-appointed appraisers and the resulting decree
citations.quote: (c) The court shall appoint three disinterested appraisers to appraise the fair value of the shares owned by the moving parties, and shall make an order referring the matter to the appraisers so appointed for the purpose of ascertaining the value. The order shall prescribe the time and manner of producing evidence, if evidence is required. The award of the appraisers or of a majority of them, when confirmed by the court, shall be final and conclusive upon all parties. The court shall enter a decree, which shall provide in the alternative for winding up and dissolution of the corporation unless payment is made for the shares within the time specified by the decree. If the purchasing parties do not make payment for the shares within the time specified, judgment shall be entered against them and the surety or sureties on the bond for the amount of the expenses (including attorneys’ fees) of the moving parties. Any shareholder aggrieved by the action of the court may appeal the court’s decision.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2000(f)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the valuation date for a Section 1800 involuntary dissolution suit
citations.quote: (f) For the purposes of this section, the valuation date shall be (1) in the case of a suit for involuntary dissolution under Section 1800, the date upon which that action was commenced, or (2) in the case of a proceeding for voluntary dissolution initiated by the vote of shareholders representing only 50 percent of the voting power, the date upon which that proceeding was initiated. However, in either case the court may, upon the hearing of a motion by any party, and for good cause shown, designate some other date as the valuation date.

clauses.title: Declaration of Purpose — Independent Adoption Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Independent Adoption — Information Sheet describes California's statutory process for {{petitionerName}} to adopt {{childName}} (born {{childDOB}}), a child whom {{birthParentName}}, the child's birth parent, proposes to place for adoption directly with {{petitionerName}} rather than through a licensed adoption agency, under California Family Code Division 13, Part 2, Chapter 3 (Independent Adoptions, §§ 8800–8823). It is prepared for use alongside an actual independent adoption request contemplated for filing in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}.

An independent adoption is its own distinct statutory track — separate from an agency adoption, in which the State Department of Social Services, a county adoption agency, or a licensed adoption agency is a party to or joins in the adoption petition, and separate from a stepparent adoption under Family Code Chapter 5 (§§ 9000–9007), which applies only where the person adopting is the spouse or domestic partner of the child's existing legal parent. In an independent adoption, {{birthParentName}} personally selects {{petitionerName}} as the prospective adoptive parent, and a state or county agency investigates the proposed adoption and reports to the court, but is not itself a party filing or joining in the adoption petition.

This information sheet is not itself a court filing. Completing it does not adopt {{childName}}, does not terminate any parent's rights, does not accept or record any consent to adoption, and does not determine that any specific adoption should or will be granted. Only a final court decree of adoption, entered after the statutory adoption request, consent, investigation, and hearing process described in this document's companion clauses, can actually do that.

clauses.title: What Makes an Adoption "Independent," as Distinct From an Agency Adoption
clauses.body: California's adoption statutes define two structurally different tracks by reference to who is a party to the adoption petition, not by reference to who investigates it. Family Code § 8524 defines "independent adoption" to mean "the adoption of a child in which neither the department, county adoption agency, nor agency licensed by the department is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition." By contrast, Family Code § 8506 defines "agency adoption" to mean "the adoption of a minor, other than an intercountry adoption, in which the department, county adoption agency, or licensed adoption agency is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition." The distinction these two definitions draw is precise: in both an independent adoption and an agency adoption, a state or county agency has a statutory role — an independent adoption is not an unsupervised private arrangement — but only in an agency adoption is that agency itself a party to, or joiner in, the petition asking the court to grant the adoption. "The department," as referenced in both definitions, is defined by Family Code § 8518 to mean the State Department of Social Services.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California law itself distinguishes an independent adoption from an agency adoption — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific adoption, and not a claim that the adoption described in this document has been, or will be, classified by any court as an independent adoption. Family Code § 8524 and § 8506 are separate, independently numbered sections within the same Part 1 definitions chapter, and are treated here as two independent sources; § 8518's definition of "the department" is referenced for context but is not independently load-bearing for the independent/agency distinction itself, so it is not counted as a third independent source for that specific point. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that the child or the prospective adoptive parent named in this document's companion clauses is, or is not, the subject of an independent adoption within the meaning of § 8524, and it does not file, join in, or accept any adoption petition.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 8524 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Independent adoption” means the adoption of a child in which neither the department, county adoption agency, nor agency licensed by the department is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 8506 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Agency adoption” means the adoption of a minor, other than an intercountry adoption, in which the department, county adoption agency, or licensed adoption agency is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition.

clauses.title: Birth-Parent Selection of the Prospective Adoptive Parent, and Who May File the Adoption Request
clauses.body: Two separate statutory rules together give an independent adoption its defining, agency-free character at the front end. First, Family Code § 8801(a) requires that "the selection of a prospective adoptive parent or parents shall be personally made by the child's birth parent or parents and may not be delegated to an agent," and that this selection "shall be based upon personal knowledge of the prospective adoptive parent or parents" — meaning {{birthParentName}}, not an agency, is the one who chooses {{petitionerName}} as the prospective adoptive parent. Second, once a prospective adoptive parent has been so selected, Family Code § 8802(a) identifies which adult persons may then file the adoption request with the court, "in a county authorized by Section 8609.5," including, among other listed categories, "a person with whom a child has been placed for adoption," a case in which "a copy of the independent adoption placement agreement shall be attached to the petition."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who selects the prospective adoptive parent and who may file the adoption request in a California independent adoption — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific adoption, and not a claim that the birth parent named in this document's companion clauses has made, or the petitioner named there is eligible to make, any specific selection or filing described in this clause. Family Code § 8801 and § 8802 are separate, independently numbered sections, cited here as two independent sources; only subdivision (a) of each is quoted, and this clause does not detail § 8801(b)'s further definition of "personal knowledge," the five other filing categories listed in § 8802(a)(1)–(2) and (4)–(6), or § 8802(b)–(g)'s separate procedural requirements for the adoption request's contents and the court clerk's notice to the department. This document is informational only: it does not itself select any prospective adoptive parent, does not file any adoption request, and does not determine that the adoption described in this document's companion clauses meets these statutory requirements in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 8801(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The selection of a prospective adoptive parent or parents shall be personally made by the child’s birth parent or parents and may not be delegated to an agent. The act of selection by the birth parent or parents shall be based upon personal knowledge of the prospective adoptive parent or parents.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 8802(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Any of the following adult persons who desire to adopt a child may, for that purpose, file an adoption request in a county authorized by Section 8609.5: ... (3) A person with whom a child has been placed for adoption, in which case a copy of the independent adoption placement agreement shall be attached to the petition.

clauses.title: The Required Investigation and Report Before the Court Rules on the Petition
clauses.body: Even though no agency is a party to the petition in an independent adoption, a state or county agency must still investigate the proposed adoption and report to the court before the adoption can be finalized. Family Code § 8806 directs that "the department or delegated county adoption agency shall accept the consent of the birth parents to the adoption of the child by the petitioners and, before filing its report with the court, shall ascertain whether the child is a proper subject for adoption and whether the proposed home is suitable for the child." Family Code § 8807(a) sets a deadline for that investigation: "[e]xcept as provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), within 180 days after receiving 50 percent of the fee, the department or delegated county adoption agency shall investigate the proposed independent adoption and, after the remaining balance of the fee is paid, submit to the court a full report of the facts disclosed by its inquiry with a recommendation regarding the granting of the petition."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the pre-decision investigation and reporting duty imposed on the department or a delegated county adoption agency in a California independent adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, or about what investigation, if any, another state's process requires. Family Code § 8806 and § 8807 are separate, independently numbered sections, cited here as two independent sources; § 8807 is itself subdivided, and this clause quotes only subdivision (a) — it does not detail § 8807(b)'s rule requiring immediate filing where the investigation finds a serious question about suitability, care, or consent, § 8807(c)'s allowance for a court-granted extension of the 180-day period, or § 8807(d)'s separate rule for a petitioner residing outside California. This document does not detail the separate investigation fee structure set by Family Code § 8810, referenced in § 8807(a) but not independently verified for this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself investigate, report on, or determine the suitability of the petitioner or the home described in this document's companion clauses, and it does not determine whether, or by when, any such investigation and report will occur in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 8806 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The department or delegated county adoption agency shall accept the consent of the birth parents to the adoption of the child by the petitioners and, before filing its report with the court, shall ascertain whether the child is a proper subject for adoption and whether the proposed home is suitable for the child.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 8807(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), within 180 days after receiving 50 percent of the fee, the department or delegated county adoption agency shall investigate the proposed independent adoption and, after the remaining balance of the fee is paid, submit to the court a full report of the facts disclosed by its inquiry with a recommendation regarding the granting of the petition.

clauses.title: How and Before Whom Consent to an Independent Adoption Is Signed
clauses.body: California law requires a birth parent's consent to an independent adoption to be signed under agency supervision, not merely in a private agreement between the birth parent and the prospective adoptive parent. Family Code § 8814(a) provides that, except in a narrow circumstance described in Family Code § 7662, "the consent of the birth parent or parents who did not place the child for adoption, as described in Section 8801.3, to the adoption shall be signed in the presence of an agent of the department or of a delegated county adoption agency on a form prescribed by the department," and that "[t]he consent shall be filed with the clerk of the appropriate superior court."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the procedure California law requires for signing consent to an independent adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, or about what consent procedure, if any, another state's process requires, and not a claim that the birth parent named in this document's companion clauses has signed, or is required to sign, consent in any specific manner in any specific case. Family Code § 8814 is not subdivided into independent sources for purposes of this clause: only subdivision (a) is quoted, and no additional, separately numbered statutory section was located and independently confirmed for this specific procedural point, so this clause rests on a single statutory section. This clause does not detail § 8814(b)'s rule on the evidentiary effect of a consent reciting sole custody, § 8814(c)'s separate procedure for a birth parent located outside California, § 8814(d)'s rule preserving a minor birth parent's right to consent, or the cross-referenced exception in Family Code § 7662, none of which were independently verified for this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself take, witness, or file any consent to adoption, and it does not determine that any signature described in this document's companion clauses satisfies this statutory procedure.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 8814(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 7662, the consent of the birth parent or parents who did not place the child for adoption, as described in Section 8801.3, to the adoption shall be signed in the presence of an agent of the department or of a delegated county adoption agency on a form prescribed by the department. The consent shall be filed with the clerk of the appropriate superior court.

clauses.title: The 30-Day Right to Revoke Consent, and When Consent Becomes Permanent
clauses.body: California law gives a birth parent who has signed consent to an independent adoption a specific, time-limited window to change that decision before it becomes final. Family Code § 8814.5(a) provides that "[a]fter a consent to the adoption is signed by the birth parent or parents pursuant to Section 8801.3 or 8814, the birth parent or parents signing the consent shall have 30 days to take one of the following actions," including, under paragraph (a)(1), to "[s]ign and deliver to the department or delegated county adoption agency a written statement revoking the consent and requesting the child to be returned to the birth parent or parents." Absent an earlier signed waiver of the right to revoke, paragraph (a)(3) provides that the birth parent may instead "[a]llow the consent to become a permanent consent on the 31st day after signing," and subdivision (b) confirms that "[t]he consent may not be revoked after a waiver of the right to revoke consent has been signed or after 30 days, beginning on the date the consent was signed ... whichever occurs first." A separate section describes the practical consequence of this timing: Family Code § 8815(a) provides that "[o]nce the revocable consent to adoption has become permanent as provided in Section 8814.5, the consent to the adoption by the prospective adoptive parents may not be withdrawn," while § 8815(b) provides that "[b]efore the time when the revocable consent becomes permanent as provided in Section 8814.5, the birth parent or parents may request return of the child," in which case "the child shall immediately be returned to the requesting birth parent or parents, unless a court orders otherwise."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific 30-day consent-revocation window and permanence rule California law applies to an independent adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, or about what revocation period, if any, another state's process allows, and not a claim that any consent described in this document's companion clauses has been, will be, revoked, waived, or made permanent in any specific case. Within Family Code § 8814.5, subdivisions (a)(1), (a)(3), and (b) are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as separate independent sources for one another; Family Code § 8815 is a separate, independently numbered section, and its subdivisions (a) and (b) are likewise treated as one source internal to that section. Taken together, § 8814.5 and § 8815 are counted here as two independent statutory sources for the revocability rule generally, though neither corroborates the other's specific 30-day figure, which appears only in § 8814.5. This clause does not detail § 8814.5(a)(2)'s separate procedure for signing an earlier waiver of the right to revoke, which can shorten this window, or § 8815(c)'s separate provision on reporting fitness concerns to a child welfare agency, neither of which is independently verified here beyond the text quoted. This document is informational only: it does not itself calculate whether any specific 30-day period has run, does not revoke, waive, or accept any consent, and does not determine whether any child described in this document's companion clauses must be returned to, or may be retained by, any party in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 8814.5(a), (a)(1), (a)(3) & (b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: After a consent to the adoption is signed by the birth parent or parents pursuant to Section 8801.3 or 8814, the birth parent or parents signing the consent shall have 30 days to take one of the following actions: (1) Sign and deliver to the department or delegated county adoption agency a written statement revoking the consent and requesting the child to be returned to the birth parent or parents. ... (3) Allow the consent to become a permanent consent on the 31st day after signing. (b) The consent may not be revoked after a waiver of the right to revoke consent has been signed or after 30 days, beginning on the date the consent was signed or as provided in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a), whichever occurs first.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 8815(a) & (b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) Once the revocable consent to adoption has become permanent as provided in Section 8814.5, the consent to the adoption by the prospective adoptive parents may not be withdrawn. (b) Before the time when the revocable consent becomes permanent as provided in Section 8814.5, the birth parent or parents may request return of the child. In that case the child shall immediately be returned to the requesting birth parent or parents, unless a court orders otherwise.

clauses.title: How an Independent Adoption Differs, Structurally, From a Stepparent Adoption
clauses.body: California law places independent adoptions and stepparent adoptions in separate chapters of the same statutory part, built around a different eligibility premise. Family Code § 8524 defines "independent adoption" as "the adoption of a child in which neither the department, county adoption agency, nor agency licensed by the department is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition" — a definition that says nothing about the adopting person's relationship to the child's existing legal parent, because none is required. By contrast, Family Code § 9000(a), in the separate Chapter 5 governing stepparent adoptions, authorizes only "[a] stepparent desiring to adopt a child of the stepparent's spouse" to "file a petition in any county authorized by Section 8609.5" (with § 9000(b) extending the same right to a domestic partner adopting the other partner's child). An independent adoption under Chapter 3 (§§ 8800–8823) is available to a wider, differently defined set of prospective adoptive parents identified in Family Code § 8802(a) — including certain relatives, a person named in a deceased parent's will, a person with whom the child has already been placed for adoption, and certain long-term legal guardians — none of which requires the petitioner to be the spouse or domestic partner of the child's existing legal parent, and none of which is satisfied merely because the petitioner is a stepparent.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California places independent adoptions and stepparent adoptions in separate statutory chapters with different eligibility premises — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific adoption, and not a claim that the adoption described in this document's companion clauses is, or is not, eligible for either track; that depends on the specific relationship between the prospective adoptive parent and the child's existing legal parent, among other facts. Family Code § 8524 and § 9000(a) are separate, independently numbered sections in different chapters, cited here as two independent sources; § 8802(a) is referenced for the breadth of the independent-adoption filing categories but is the same section already cited and detailed in this document's companion clause on birth-parent selection and filing, so it is not counted as an additional independent source here. This clause does not restate every eligibility category listed in § 8802(a) or § 9000(a)–(g)'s further procedural rules, and it does not address the possibility that a specific individual could, on different facts, qualify under either chapter (for example, as both a relative and a stepparent) — which chapter in fact governs a specific petition is a determination for the filing court, not this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine which statutory chapter governs the adoption described in this document's companion clauses, and it does not file, join in, or grant any adoption petition.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 8524 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Independent adoption” means the adoption of a child in which neither the department, county adoption agency, nor agency licensed by the department is a party to, or joins in, the adoption petition.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 9000(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A stepparent desiring to adopt a child of the stepparent’s spouse may for that purpose file a petition in any county authorized by Section 8609.5.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope — Dissenters' Rights Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a {{entityType}} organized under the laws of California, and to {{shareholderName}}'s status as a shareholder of {{companyName}} holding {{numberOfSharesHeld}}, in connection with the following corporate transaction: {{reorganizationDescription}}. It describes the dissenters' rights (sometimes called appraisal rights) that Cal. Corp. Code §§ 1300-1313 -- Chapter 13 of the General Corporation Law, titled "Dissenters' Rights" -- give a shareholder of a California corporation who dissents from certain reorganizations requiring outstanding-share approval under Section 1201, from a short-form merger, or from a conversion treated as a reorganization under Section 1313, to require the corporation to purchase the shareholder's dissenting shares for cash at fair market value rather than accept whatever consideration the transaction otherwise provides.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute a written demand on {{companyName}} under Section 1301, does not determine whether {{shareholderName}}'s shares meet the statutory definition of "dissenting shares" in Section 1300(b) for {{reorganizationDescription}}, does not determine whether the "market-out" exception described below removes or preserves dissenters' rights for any specific shares, and does not calculate the fair market value of any specific shares.

clauses.title: What Dissenters' Rights Are, and the Transactions That Trigger Them
clauses.body: California's General Corporation Law gives a shareholder of a corporation a statutory right to "dissent" from certain reorganizations and demand cash instead of whatever the reorganization otherwise provides. Specifically, if outstanding-share approval of a corporation is required for a reorganization under particular subdivisions of Section 1201, each shareholder of that corporation entitled to vote on the transaction -- and each shareholder of a subsidiary corporation in a short-form merger -- may, by complying with the dissenters'-rights chapter's procedure, require the corporation in which the shareholder holds shares to purchase for cash, at fair market value, the shares owned by the shareholder that qualify as "dissenting shares." This right is not limited to mergers and asset-reorganization transactions structured as corporate reorganizations in the first instance: a conversion of a corporation into a different business-entity type is itself deemed to constitute a reorganization for purposes of this same chapter, so a shareholder facing a conversion can likewise have dissenters' rights, to the extent the conversion statute provides.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, defined shareholder right -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction's appraisal-rights statute works the same way. The two citations below (Cal. Corp. Code § 1300(a) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1313) are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections of the dissenters'-rights chapter, so they are treated as independent sources of that chapter's own scope. Section 1300(a) itself cross-references "subdivisions (a) and (b) or subdivision (e) or (f) of Section 1201" as the specific reorganizations that trigger the right, and separately cross-references the short-form merger procedure; this document quotes that cross-reference as it appears in Section 1300's own text, but Section 1201's substantive definitions of those reorganization subdivisions were not independently fetched and confirmed twice for this document, so this document does not itself catalog which specific transaction structures fall within subdivisions (a), (b), (e), or (f) of Section 1201. This document also does not determine whether a specific proposed transaction is a reorganization requiring outstanding-share approval, whether a specific shareholder is "entitled to vote on the transaction," or whether a specific conversion triggers dissenters' rights under Section 1313's cross-reference to Section 1159 (which was likewise not independently verified here).
