citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, Chapter 13 ("Dissenters' Rights"), the right to demand cash purchase of dissenting shares
citations.quote: If the approval of the outstanding shares (Section 152) of a corporation is required for a reorganization under subdivisions (a) and (b) or subdivision (e) or (f) of Section 1201, each shareholder of the corporation entitled to vote on the transaction and each shareholder of a subsidiary corporation in a short-form merger may, by complying with this chapter, require the corporation in which the shareholder holds shares to purchase for cash at their fair market value the shares owned by the shareholder which are dissenting shares as defined in subdivision (b).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1313
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, dissenters'-rights chapter extended to certain entity conversions
citations.quote: A conversion pursuant to Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 1150) shall be deemed to constitute a reorganization for purposes of applying the provisions of this chapter, in accordance with and to the extent provided in Section 1159.

clauses.title: The "Market-Out" Exception for Listed Shares, and Its Carve-Backs
clauses.body: California's dissenters'-rights statute does not give every shareholder of a corporation involved in a qualifying reorganization the right to demand a cash purchase; a share loses eligibility as a "dissenting share" if, immediately before the reorganization or short-form merger, it was listed on a national securities exchange certified by the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation under Section 25100(o), and the notice of the shareholders' meeting summarized the dissenters'-rights statutes -- this is the "market-out" exception. That exception is narrower than a blanket rule against dissenters' rights for all listed shares, in two distinct ways. First, it does not apply at all to shares subject to any restriction on transfer imposed by the corporation or by any law or regulation, regardless of listing status. Second, and independently, it does not apply to any shares whose holder is required by the terms of the reorganization or short-form merger to accept anything other than (A) shares of another corporation that are themselves listed on a certified national exchange when the transaction becomes effective, (B) cash in lieu of fractional shares of that listed stock, or (C) a combination of (A) and (B) -- meaning a listed shareholder who will be cashed out, or paid in unlisted securities or debt, keeps dissenters' rights even though the shareholder's own stock was listed. A separate and textually distinct exclusion, resting on the share's own contractual terms rather than its trading market, removes an entire class of shares from most of the dissenters'-rights chapter (though not from the chapter's provision limiting other remedies) when that class's own terms and provisions specifically state what its holders are to be paid in a reorganization or merger.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual, narrower scope of this exception -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction's market-out rule has the same carve-backs. It is worth stating precisely because it corrects a natural assumption: the market-out exception is not a blanket denial of dissenters' rights whenever a shareholder's stock happens to be exchange-listed. It applies only when the reorganization's notice of meeting summarized the dissenters'-rights statutes, and even then it is defeated (i.e., dissenters' rights survive) if there is any transfer restriction on the shares, or if the consideration the shareholder must accept is anything other than listed stock of the acquirer (plus cash only for fractional shares). This document does not independently confirm which specific exchanges are currently certified by the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation under Section 25100(o), and does not determine whether a specific corporation's shares were listed on such an exchange immediately before a specific transaction, or whether a specific transaction's notice of meeting in fact summarized the required statutes. The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1300(b)(1) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1311); within Section 1300(b)(1) itself, no second independent source was located or used to further corroborate that specific subdivision's text beyond the two independent fetches of Section 1300 described in this document's overall verification record. Section 1311's contractual-terms exclusion described here is a separate exception from the market-out rule -- it turns on a share class's own stated redemption or payment terms, not on whether the shares are exchange-listed -- and this document does not address how the two exceptions interact if both could apply to the same shares.

citations.quote: This chapter, except Section 1312, does not apply to classes of shares whose terms and provisions specifically set forth the amount to be paid in respect to such shares in the event of a reorganization or merger.

clauses.title: Procedural Steps and Deadlines to Demand Purchase
clauses.body: A shareholder who wants the corporation to purchase the shareholder's shares for cash must make a written demand on the corporation for the purchase and for payment of their fair market value in cash. That demand is not effective for any purpose unless the corporation or its transfer agent receives it by a statutory deadline: not later than the date of the shareholders' meeting to vote on the reorganization, for shares described in Section 1300(b); or, in any other case, within 30 days after the date the corporation mailed the shareholder its notice of the outstanding-share approval, or the notice required under Section 1110(h). The written demand itself must state the number and class of shares of record the shareholder demands that the corporation purchase, and must state what the shareholder claims to be the shares' fair market value -- which itself operates as an offer by the shareholder to sell at that stated price. Separately from making that demand, and within the same 30-day window measured from the mailed notice, the shareholder must also submit the shares for endorsement: for certificated shares, submitting the certificates to the corporation or its transfer agent to be stamped or endorsed as dissenting shares (or exchanged for correspondingly stamped or endorsed certificates); for uncertificated shares, submitting written notice of the number of shares the shareholder demands the corporation purchase.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual procedural steps and deadlines -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction's appraisal procedure works the same way. The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1301(b)-(c) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1302). This document quotes, but does not resolve, an ambiguity in Section 1301(b)(1)'s own text: it ties the meeting-date deadline to "shares described in subdivision (b) of Section 1300," which is the same subdivision that defines dissenting shares generally (including, in its own text, a proviso about written-consent approval versus a shareholders' meeting) -- this document does not independently determine exactly which demands fall under the meeting-date track versus the 30-day-after-mailed-notice track beyond what each section's own text states, and a specific shareholder's applicable deadline depends on the specific transaction's approval method and notice. This document also does not calculate or confirm any specific deadline date for a specific transaction, and does not itself constitute the written demand or submission for endorsement that Sections 1301 and 1302 describe.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1301(b)-(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, written demand for purchase of dissenting shares and its statutory deadline
citations.quote: Any shareholder who has a right to require the corporation to purchase the shareholder’s shares for cash under Section 1300, subject to compliance with paragraphs (3) and (4) of subdivision (b) thereof, and who desires the corporation to purchase shares shall make written demand upon the corporation for the purchase of those shares and payment to the shareholder in cash of their fair market value. The demand is not effective for any purpose unless it is received by the corporation or any transfer agent thereof (1) in the case of shares described in subdivision (b) of Section 1300, not later than the date of the shareholders’ meeting to vote upon the reorganization, or (2) in any other case, within 30 days after the date on which the notice of the approval by the outstanding shares pursuant to subdivision (a) or the notice pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1110 was mailed to the shareholder.

citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, deadline and method for submitting dissenting shares for endorsement
citations.quote: Within 30 days after the date on which notice of the approval by the outstanding shares or the notice pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1110 was mailed to the shareholder, the shareholder shall submit to the corporation at its principal office or at the office of any transfer agent thereof, (a) if the shares are certificated securities, the shareholder’s certificates representing any shares which the shareholder demands that the corporation purchase, to be stamped or endorsed with a statement that the shares are dissenting shares or to be exchanged for certificates of appropriate denomination so stamped or endorsed or (b) if the shares are uncertificated securities, written notice of the number of shares which the shareholder demands that the corporation purchase.

clauses.title: How Fair Market Value Is Determined, and When Payment Is Due
clauses.body: The statute fixes both the valuation date and the valuation method for dissenting shares: fair market value is determined as of the day of, and immediately prior to, the first announcement of the terms of the proposed reorganization or short-form merger, excluding any appreciation or depreciation that results from the proposed transaction itself, and as adjusted for any stock split, reverse stock split, or share dividend that becomes effective after that date. If the corporation and the shareholder agree that the shares are dissenting shares and agree on a price, the shareholder is entitled to that agreed price plus interest at the legal rate on judgments running from the date of the agreement, and the agreement fixing fair market value must be filed with the corporation's secretary. Once fair market value is set (by agreement, or otherwise as described elsewhere in this chapter), payment is due within 30 days after the amount is agreed, or within 30 days after any statutory or contractual conditions to the reorganization are satisfied, whichever is later, and -- for certificated shares -- payment is subject to surrender of the certificates unless the parties agree otherwise.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual valuation date, valuation method, and payment timing -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction's appraisal statute fixes the same valuation date or measures value the same way. The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1300(a) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1303(a)-(b)). This document does not describe the separate mechanism (Section 1306, not independently verified for this document) under which unpaid fair market value can become a subordinated debt of the corporation if a distributions-restriction statute prevents payment, and it does not calculate the fair market value, the applicable legal rate of interest, or any specific payment date for any specific shares or transaction.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1300(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, valuation date and method for dissenting shares' fair market value
citations.quote: The fair market value shall be determined as of the day of, and immediately prior to, the first announcement of the terms of the proposed reorganization or short-form merger, excluding any appreciation or depreciation in consequence of the proposed reorganization or short-form merger, as adjusted for any stock split, reverse stock split, or share dividend that becomes effective thereafter.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1303(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, agreed price and timing of payment for dissenting shares
citations.quote: If the corporation and the shareholder agree that the shares are dissenting shares and agree upon the price of the shares, the dissenting shareholder is entitled to the agreed price with interest thereon at the legal rate on judgments from the date of the agreement. Any agreements fixing the fair market value of any dissenting shares as between the corporation and the holders thereof shall be filed with the secretary of the corporation. (b) Subject to the provisions of Section 1306, payment of the fair market value of dissenting shares shall be made within 30 days after the amount thereof has been agreed or within 30 days after any statutory or contractual conditions to the reorganization are satisfied, whichever is later, and in the case of certificated securities, subject to surrender of the certificates therefor, unless provided otherwise by agreement.

clauses.title: Court Action to Resolve Disputed Status or Value, and How Costs Are Allocated
clauses.body: If the corporation denies that particular shares are dissenting shares, or if the corporation and the shareholder cannot agree on fair market value, the shareholder demanding purchase (or any interested corporation) may file a complaint in the superior court of the proper county asking the court to determine whether the shares are dissenting shares, the shares' fair market value, or both -- or may intervene in a pending action raising the same questions. That complaint must be filed within six months after the date the corporation mailed its notice of outstanding-share approval, or the Section 1110(h) notice, to the shareholder; the statute states this deadline applies "but not thereafter." On the resulting trial, the court decides any disputed status issue first, and then determines fair market value itself or appoints one or more impartial appraisers to do so. Costs of that action, including reasonable compensation for court-appointed appraisers, are generally allocated as the court finds equitable; but if the appraised value exceeds the price the corporation had offered, the corporation must pay the costs, and the court has discretion to include attorneys' fees, expert-witness fees, and interest at the legal rate running from the date the shareholder complied with the demand-and-endorsement statutes, if the value the court awards for the shares turns out to be more than 125 percent of the price the corporation had offered.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual court-enforcement mechanism and cost-shifting rule -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction's appraisal statute allocates litigation costs the same way. The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1304(a) and Cal. Corp. Code § 1305(e)). This document does not describe the separate rules in Section 1304(b)-(c) (joinder and consolidation of multiple dissenting shareholders' claims) or Section 1305(a)-(d) (the appraisers' reporting procedure and the form of judgment) in full, and does not determine whether a specific corporation's denial of dissenting-share status, or a specific valuation dispute, would in fact be litigated in a specific county's superior court, nor does it calculate any specific award, cost allocation, or the 125 percent threshold for any specific transaction.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1304(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, action to determine dissenting-share status or fair market value, and its filing deadline
citations.quote: If the corporation denies that the shares are dissenting shares, or the corporation and the shareholder fail to agree upon the fair market value of the shares, then the shareholder demanding purchase of such shares as dissenting shares or any interested corporation, within six months after the date on which notice of the approval by the outstanding shares (Section 152) or notice pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1110 was mailed to the shareholder, but not thereafter, may file a complaint in the superior court of the proper county praying the court to determine whether the shares are dissenting shares or the fair market value of the dissenting shares or both or may intervene in any action pending on such a complaint.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1305(e)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, allocation of litigation costs and fee-shifting when the court's appraisal exceeds the corporation's offer
citations.quote: The costs of the action, including reasonable compensation to the appraisers to be fixed by the court, shall be assessed or apportioned as the court considers equitable, but, if the appraisal exceeds the price offered by the corporation, the corporation shall pay the costs (including in the discretion of the court attorneys’ fees, fees of expert witnesses and interest at the legal rate on judgments from the date of compliance with Sections 1300, 1301 and 1302 if the value awarded by the court for the shares is more than 125 percent of the price offered by the corporation under subdivision (a) of Section 1301).

clauses.title: Losing Dissenting-Share Status, and the Statute's Limits on Attacking the Transaction Itself
clauses.body: Shares can lose their status as dissenting shares -- and their holder can cease to be entitled to require the corporation to purchase them -- in any of several ways the statute lists: if the corporation abandons the reorganization (in which case the corporation must instead pay, on demand, the good-faith dissenting shareholder's necessary expenses and reasonable attorneys' fees incurred pursuing the dissenters'-rights process); if the shares are transferred before being submitted for endorsement, or are surrendered for conversion into another class under the articles; if the shareholder and corporation fail to agree on the shares' status or price and neither side files (or intervenes in) a court action within six months after the relevant notice was mailed; or if the shareholder withdraws the demand for purchase with the corporation's consent. Separately, the dissenters'-rights chapter limits what other remedies a shareholder who holds this cash-purchase right can pursue over the underlying transaction: a shareholder with a right under this chapter to demand cash for their shares generally has no right, at law or in equity, to attack the validity of the reorganization or short-form merger, or to have it set aside or rescinded -- except in an action testing whether the required vote to authorize or approve the transaction was legally obtained. That said, a holder of a share class whose own terms specifically set out what is to be paid on a reorganization is entitled to payment under those terms.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of both the actual triggers for losing dissenting-share status and the actual limits this chapter places on other remedies -- not a claim about which state's law would apply to a specific corporation, and not a claim that dissenters' rights are always a shareholder's exclusive remedy in every jurisdiction. The two citations below are drawn from two separately, independently numbered sections (Cal. Corp. Code § 1309 and Cal. Corp. Code § 1312(a)). This document does not restate Section 1312(b)-(c) in full (the separate rule, and burden of proof, that applies when one party to the reorganization directly or indirectly controls another party to it), and it does not determine whether a specific shareholder's shares have in fact lost dissenting-share status, or whether a specific challenge to a specific transaction falls within the narrow vote-legality exception this section preserves.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1309
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, events that cause shares to lose their status as dissenting shares
citations.quote: Dissenting shares lose their status as dissenting shares and the holders thereof cease to be dissenting shareholders and cease to be entitled to require the corporation to purchase their shares upon the happening of any of the following: (a) The corporation abandons the reorganization. Upon abandonment of the reorganization, the corporation shall pay on demand to any dissenting shareholder who has initiated proceedings in good faith under this chapter all necessary expenses incurred in such proceedings and reasonable attorneys’ fees.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1312(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, dissenters' rights as the shareholder's limited remedy against the reorganization itself
citations.quote: No shareholder of a corporation who has a right under this chapter to demand payment of cash for the shares held by the shareholder shall have any right at law or in equity to attack the validity of the reorganization or short-form merger, or to have the reorganization or short-form merger set aside or rescinded, except in an action to test whether the number of shares required to authorize or approve the reorganization have been legally voted in favor thereof; but any holder of shares of a class whose terms and provisions specifically set forth the amount to be paid in respect to them in the event of a reorganization or short-form merger is entitled to payment in accordance with those terms and provisions or, if the principal terms of the reorganization are approved pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 1202, is entitled to payment in accordance with the terms and provisions of the approved reorganization.

Code §§ 1300-1313, including the transactions that trigger the right, the "market-out" exception and its carve-backs, the procedural steps and deadlines for demanding purchase, how fair market value is determined and when payment is due, the court process for resolving disputes, and the ways dissenting-share status can be lost. It is not a completed written demand under Section 1301, does not itself preserve, waive, or exercise any dissenters' rights with respect to {{companyName}}, and does not constitute legal advice. The current statutory text is published by the California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov).]

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: {{companyName}} provides this Information Sheet to describe, in general terms, California's regulations governing the use of automated decisionmaking technology ("ADMT") to make significant employment-related decisions, including decisions about hiring, work allocation and compensation, promotion, demotion, suspension, and termination. This Information Sheet explains what the law requires; it is educational in nature, does not constitute legal advice, and does not itself determine whether or how {{companyName}} uses ADMT with respect to any particular applicant or employee.

clauses.title: What Counts as Automated Decisionmaking Technology (ADMT)
clauses.body: California regulations define "automated decisionmaking technology" or "ADMT" as any technology that processes personal information and uses computation to replace human decisionmaking or substantially replace human decisionmaking. Technology substantially replaces human decisionmaking when its output is used to make a decision without human involvement — meaning a human reviewer who knows how to interpret and use the output, reviews and analyzes the output and other relevant information, and has the authority to make or change the decision based on that analysis. ADMT includes profiling that replaces or substantially replaces human decisionmaking. It does not include tools such as web hosting, firewalls, spam filtering, spellcheckers, calculators, databases, and spreadsheets, provided those tools do not replace human decisionmaking.
clauses.gap: California-specific: this describes only the California Privacy Protection Agency's regulations under the CCPA/CPRA (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11), not any other state's or federal automated-decision-technology rule. All three citations below are subdivisions of the single definition in section 7001, subsection (e), of the same regulatory text adopted in one rulemaking action — they are not independent sources of each other, only independent excerpts of one provision. This is a newly operative area (the regulations took effect January 1, 2026) with no judicial or CPPA enforcement decisions yet interpreting how "substantially replace human decisionmaking" applies to specific employment tools; the wording above tracks the adopted regulatory text itself, not any interpretation of it.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7001(e) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, ADMT defined
citations.quote: “Automated decisionmaking technology” or “ADMT” means any technology that processes personal information and uses computation to replace human decisionmaking or substantially replace human decisionmaking.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7001(e)(1) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, the human-involvement test
citations.quote: (A) Know how to interpret and use the technology’s output to make the decision; (B) Review and analyze the output of the technology, and any other information that is relevant to make or change the decision; and (C) Have the authority to make or change the decision based on their analysis in subsection (B).

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7001(e)(3) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, tools excluded from ADMT
citations.quote: ADMT does not include web hosting, domain registration, networking, caching, website-loading, data storage, firewalls, anti-virus, anti-malware, spam- and robocall-filtering, spellchecking, calculators, databases, and spreadsheets, provided that they do not replace human decisionmaking.

clauses.title: "Significant Decision" in Employment
clauses.body: California regulations define a "significant decision" as a decision that results in the provision or denial of specified categories of opportunities or services, including "employment or independent contracting opportunities or compensation." For employment, the regulations specify that this category covers: hiring; the allocation or assignment of work for employees, and salary, hourly or per-assignment compensation, incentive compensation such as a bonus, or another benefit; promotion; and demotion, suspension, and termination. A decision that consists only of advertising to a consumer does not qualify as a significant decision.
clauses.gap: California-specific: describes only the CPPA's own regulatory definition (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7001(ddd)), not any other state's or the federal government's definition of a covered employment decision. All three citations below are subdivisions of the same section 7001(ddd) definition, adopted in the same single rulemaking action as the other admt_ clauses in this set — they confirm the wording of one definition, not independent legal propositions. The definition does not itself say which specific tools (e.g., resume-screening software, video-interview scoring, productivity-monitoring software) qualify as ADMT for a given significant decision; that turns on the separate ADMT definition in section 7001(e) (see the companion clause) applied to the facts of a particular tool.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7001(ddd) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, "significant decision" defined
citations.quote: “Significant decision” means a decision that results in the provision or denial of financial or lending services, housing, education enrollment or opportunities, employment or independent contracting opportunities or compensation, or healthcare services.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7001(ddd)(4) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, employment decisions covered
citations.quote: “Employment or independent contracting opportunities or compensation” means: (A) Hiring; (B) Allocation or assignment of work for employees; or salary, hourly or per-assignment compensation, incentive compensation such as a bonus, or another benefit (“allocation/assignment of work and compensation”); (C) Promotion; and (D) Demotion, suspension, and termination.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7001(ddd)(6) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, advertising excluded
citations.quote: Significant decision does not include advertising to a consumer.

clauses.title: When the ADMT Requirements Apply
clauses.body: Under California regulations effective January 1, 2026, {{companyName}}'s use of ADMT to make a significant decision concerning a consumer — including an applicant or employee — is subject to the pre-use notice, opt-out, and access requirements described in this Information Sheet. The regulations set a phased compliance timeline distinct from that general effective date: for ADMT already in use for a significant decision before January 1, 2027, compliance with these requirements is required no later than January 1, 2027. For ADMT first used for a significant decision on or after January 1, 2027, compliance is required at the time of that use, with no phase-in period.
clauses.gap: California-specific: applies only to the CPPA's own regulations (Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7200). The two citations below are subdivisions (a) and (b) of that same section, adopted together in one rulemaking action, so they are not independent of each other. This provision's phased timeline is easy to state imprecisely: January 1, 2026 is the regulations' general effective date, but January 1, 2027 is a separate, later compliance deadline that applies specifically to ADMT already in use before that date for a significant decision — not a delay of the regulations' effectiveness generally. This distinction was confirmed directly against the regulatory text of section 7200 itself, and separately against the CPPA's own summary of the rulemaking ("Effective Date: January 1, 2026") on its regulations status page, fetched independently of the regulation-text PDF.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7200(a) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, general applicability of the ADMT article
citations.quote: A business that uses ADMT to make a significant decision concerning a consumer must comply with the requirements of this Article.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7200(b) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, phased compliance deadline
citations.quote: A business that uses ADMT for a significant decision prior to January 1, 2027, must be in compliance with the requirements of this Article no later than January 1, 2027. A business that uses ADMT on or after January 1, 2027, must be in compliance with the requirements of this Article any time it is using ADMT for a significant decision.

clauses.title: Pre-Use Notice Requirement
clauses.body: Before processing an applicant's or employee's personal information using ADMT for a significant decision, California regulations require {{companyName}} to provide a Pre-use Notice, presented prominently and conspicuously and in the manner {{companyName}} primarily uses to interact with the individual. The notice must include a specific, non-generic explanation of the purpose for which the ADMT will be used — the regulations expressly identify describing the purpose only as "to make a significant decision" as insufficient — together with a description of the right to opt out of the ADMT, or, where an exception to the opt-out right applies, the right to appeal the decision to a human reviewer and how to submit that appeal, a description of the right to access information about the ADMT, and a statement that retaliation for exercising CCPA rights is prohibited.
clauses.gap: California-specific: describes only the pre-use notice required by Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7220. All three citations are subdivisions of that same section, adopted in one rulemaking action, and are not independent of each other. Section 7220 also permits a consolidated Pre-use Notice covering multiple ADMT uses or purposes, and allows the notice to be folded into an existing Notice at Collection if that notice meets the same content requirements; those permitted formats are not restated in the body above. This clause does not address the additional, more detailed "how the ADMT works" disclosure that section 7220(c)(5) separately requires.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7220(a) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, Pre-use Notice requirement
citations.quote: A business that uses ADMT as set forth in section 7200, subsection (a), must provide consumers with a Pre-use Notice. The Pre-use Notice must inform consumers about the business’s use of ADMT and consumers’ rights to opt-out of ADMT and to access ADMT, as set forth in this section.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7220(c)(1) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, purpose explanation cannot be generic
citations.quote: A plain language explanation of the specific purpose for which the business plans to use the ADMT. The business must not describe the purpose in generic terms, such as “to make a significant decision” without further information, because this does not describe to the consumer the specific decision for which the business plans to use ADMT with respect to them.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7220(c)(4) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, no-retaliation statement required
citations.quote: That the business is prohibited from retaliating against consumers for exercising their CCPA rights.

clauses.title: Right to Opt Out of ADMT and Its Employment Exceptions
clauses.body: California regulations give consumers — including applicants and employees — the right to opt out of {{companyName}}'s use of ADMT to make a significant decision, except where a specific exception applies. One exception applies where {{companyName}} instead provides a method to appeal the decision to a human reviewer who has the authority to overturn it. A separate exception applies to certain employment decisions: for admission, acceptance, or hiring decisions, where the ADMT is used solely to assess the individual's ability to perform the job and works for that purpose without unlawfully discriminating based on protected characteristics; and, on the same conditions, for decisions allocating or assigning work or compensation. Where {{companyName}} relies on the human-appeal exception rather than offering an opt-out, the Pre-use Notice must instead describe how to submit an appeal.
clauses.gap: California-specific: describes only the opt-out right and exceptions created by Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7221. All three citations are subdivisions of that same section, adopted in one rulemaking action, and are not independent of each other. Section 7221 also imposes detailed process requirements once an opt-out is exercised (e.g., two or more submission methods, no account-creation requirement, an at-least-12-month waiting period before re-soliciting consent, and timelines for stopping processing) that are not restated here. Whether a particular hiring or work-allocation tool actually "works for the business's purpose and does not unlawfully discriminate" so as to qualify for the two employment-specific exceptions is a fact-specific determination the regulatory text does not resolve in the abstract, and no case law yet construes that standard.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7221(a) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, general opt-out right
citations.quote: A business must provide consumers with the ability to opt-out of the use of ADMT to make a significant decision concerning the consumer, except as set forth in subsection (b).

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7221(b)(1) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, human-appeal exception
citations.quote: The business provides the consumer with a method to appeal the decision to a human reviewer who has the authority to overturn the decision.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7221(b)(2) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, hiring-decision exception
citations.quote: (A) The business uses the ADMT solely for the business’s assessment of the consumer’s ability to perform at work or in an educational program to determine whether to admit, accept, or hire them; and (B) The ADMT works for the business’s purpose and does not unlawfully discriminate based upon protected characteristics.

clauses.title: Right to Access Information About ADMT
clauses.body: California regulations give consumers — including applicants and employees — the right to request access to information about {{companyName}}'s use of ADMT to make a significant decision concerning them. In response to such a request, {{companyName}} must provide plain-language explanations of the specific, non-generic purpose for which it used the ADMT, information about the logic of the ADMT sufficient for the consumer to understand how it processed their personal information to generate an output, and the outcome of the decisionmaking process, including whether the output was the sole factor in the decision or, if not, what other factors were involved.
clauses.gap: California-specific: describes only the access right created by Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7222. All three citations are subdivisions of that same section, adopted in one rulemaking action, and are not independent of each other. Section 7222 also allows a business to withhold trade secrets and certain security-related information from an access response, requires identity verification under the CCPA's general verification rules, and permits a secure self-service portal as a compliance method; those details are not restated here. This right is separate from, and additional to, the general CCPA right to know what personal information a business holds.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7222(a) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, right to access ADMT information
citations.quote: A business that uses ADMT to make a significant decision must provide a consumer with information about this use when responding to a consumer’s request to access ADMT.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7222(b)(1) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, purpose disclosure cannot be generic
citations.quote: The specific purpose for which the business used ADMT with respect to the consumer. The business must not describe the purpose in generic terms, such as “to improve our services.”

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 11, § 7222(b)(2) (CPPA Approved Regulation Text, filed with the Secretary of State Sept. 22, 2025)
citations.cite: California Code of Regulations, logic disclosure required
citations.quote: Information about the logic of the ADMT. Such information must enable a consumer to understand how the ADMT processed their personal information to generate an output with respect to them

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Receipt
About This Injury and Illness Recording Requirements Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Cal/OSHA Injury and Illness Recording Requirements — Information Sheet describes California's workplace injury and illness recordkeeping regulations, set out at 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 14300–14300.48, and the separate serious-injury-and-illness reporting regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 342, as those requirements relate to the working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.

It summarizes selected requirements of those regulations: what makes a workplace injury or illness “recordable” and the basic duty to record it on the Cal/OSHA Form 300 log, the partial exemption from routine recordkeeping available to some smaller employers and some lower-hazard industries, how long recorded records must be kept, the annual summary that must be created, certified, and posted each year, and the separate, more time-sensitive duty to report a serious injury, illness, or death to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health directly.

This topic is distinct from this corpus's Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) — Information Sheet, which describes California's general written workplace-safety-program requirement under Labor Code § 6401.7 and 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203 — a forward-looking duty to identify, evaluate, and correct workplace hazards — rather than the after-the-fact duty addressed here to record, and for serious cases report, a workplace injury or illness that has already occurred.

{{companyName}} has identified {{programAdministratorName}} as the person responsible for injury and illness recordkeeping matters described in this information sheet.

This information sheet is not itself {{companyName}}'s Cal/OSHA Form 300 log or Cal/OSHA Form 300A annual summary, does not itself satisfy 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 14300–14300.48's or § 342's requirements, and does not determine that any particular practice of {{companyName}}'s is or is not compliant with California law.

clauses.title: The Basic Duty to Record and What Makes an Injury or Illness Recordable
clauses.body: The purpose section of California's Cal/OSHA recordkeeping regulation states directly that its purpose is to require employers to record work-related fatalities, injuries, and illnesses, and that recording a case does not by itself mean the employer or employee was at fault, that a Cal/OSHA regulation was violated, or that the employee is eligible for workers' compensation or other benefits. The regulation's general recording criteria section then states the operative test: an injury or illness must be considered recordable if it results in death, one or more days away from work, restricted work or transfer to another job, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness. Separately, a case must also be considered recordable — even without any of those five outcomes — if it involves a significant injury or illness diagnosed by a physician or other licensed health care professional; the regulation names cancer, a chronic irreversible disease, a fractured or cracked bone, and a punctured eardrum as examples that must always be recorded at the time of diagnosis on that basis.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are drawn from the same regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 14300 and 14300.7, which are consecutively numbered sections of the same article (Article 2, Chapter 7) adopted together in the same 2002 rulemaking — they are not independent sources from one another. This clause does not independently verify the regulation's more detailed, category-specific recording criteria for particular injury types — for example, its separate provisions on needlestick and sharps injuries (§ 14300.8), work-related musculoskeletal disorders (§ 14300.12), or hearing loss, tuberculosis, or medical removal cases — or its definitions of “medical treatment” and “first aid” found later in § 14300.7(b)(5); those are not summarized here and no citation is offered for their specific terms. This is a description of what the regulation requires in general, not a determination that any particular injury or illness is or is not recordable.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300
citations.quote: The purpose of this rule (Article 2) is to require employers to record work-related fatalities, injuries and illnesses.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.7 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.7, subd. (a)
citations.quote: You must consider an injury or illness to meet the general recording criteria, and therefore to be recordable, if it results in any of the following as detailed in subsections (b)(2) through (b)(6) of this section: death, days away from work, restricted work or transfer to another job, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.7 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.7, subd. (b)(7)
citations.quote: Work-related cases involving cancer, chronic irreversible disease, a fractured or cracked bone, or a punctured eardrum must always be recorded under the general criteria at the time of diagnosis by a physician or other licensed health care professional.

clauses.title: The Partial Exemption From Routine Recordkeeping for Small Employers and Certain Industries
clauses.body: The recordkeeping regulation states two separate partial exemptions from the duty to keep the Cal/OSHA Form 300 log. The first is based on company size: if a company had ten (10) or fewer employees at all times during the last calendar year, it does not need to keep Cal/OSHA injury and illness records unless OSHA or the Bureau of Labor Statistics informs it in writing that records must be kept under specified government-request provisions. The regulation's own implementation guidance states that this size-based exemption is measured by the number of employees in the entire company — based on the company's peak employment during the last calendar year — not by the number of employees at any single establishment. The second exemption is based on industry classification: an employer whose business establishment is classified in one of the specific industry groups listed in a table of North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes does not need to keep Cal/OSHA injury and illness records for that establishment, again unless the government makes a written request for records under the same government-request provisions. Unlike the size-based exemption, the industry-based exemption applies establishment by establishment: a company with several establishments in different lines of business may have some establishments that must keep records and others that are exempt. Both provisions state, in the same sentence granting the exemption, that the exemption does not affect the separate duty to report a serious injury, illness, or death directly to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, addressed in a companion clause of this information sheet.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are drawn from two separate, consecutively numbered sections of the same article, 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 14300.1 and 14300.2 — both adopted in the same 2002 rulemaking under the same statutory authority (Labor Code § 6410) — and are not independent sources from one another. This clause does not independently reproduce the industry table itself (Table 1 in Appendix A to § 14300.2), which the fetched text confirms exists and lists specific NAICS codes and industry names (for example, several retail, information, real estate, and professional-services categories), but which is too long to quote here in full; no representation is made about whether any particular NAICS code is or is not on that list beyond what is quoted below. This clause also does not independently verify the government-request provisions, 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 14300.41 and 14300.42, that can override either exemption; they are named here only as topics the regulation itself cross-references, not as verified content.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.1 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.1, subd. (a)(1)
citations.quote: If your company had ten (10) or fewer employees at all times during the last calendar year, you do not need to keep Cal/OSHA injury and illness records unless OSHA or the BLS informs you in writing that you must keep records under the provisions of Section 14300.41 or Section 14300.42. However, all employers must continue to file reports of occupational injuries and illnesses with the Division of Labor Statistics and Research as required by Article 1 of this subchapter, and to immediately report to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health any workplace incident that results in serious injury or illness, or death, as required by Title 8 Section 342.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.1 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.1, subd. (b)(1)
citations.quote: The partial exemption for size is based on the number of employees in the entire company.

citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 14300.2, subd. (a)(1)

clauses.title: How Long Recorded Injury and Illness Records Must Be Kept
clauses.body: For an employer that is not exempt from routine recordkeeping, the regulation requires the Cal/OSHA Form 300 log, the privacy case list (if one exists), the Cal/OSHA Form 300A annual summary, and the Cal/OSHA Form 301 Incident Reports to be saved for five years following the end of the calendar year the records cover. During that five-year storage period, the regulation requires the stored Form 300 log itself to be updated to include newly discovered recordable injuries or illnesses and to reflect any change in the classification of a previously recorded case, but it does not require the stored annual summary (Form 300A) or the stored incident reports (Form 301) to be updated, though an employer may choose to do so.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are drawn from the same regulatory section, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.33, subdivisions (a) and (b)(1) — not independent sources from one another. This five-year retention period is a different figure from, and should not be confused with, the one-year retention period this corpus's Injury and Illness Prevention Program (IIPP) — Information Sheet describes for a written IIPP's inspection and training records under the separate regulation 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203(b); the two regulations impose distinct retention duties for distinct categories of records. This clause does not independently verify § 14300.33(b)(2) or (b)(3), which state that updating the Form 300A and Form 301 is optional; those provisions are described in this clause's body based on the fetched text but are not separately quoted or cited.

clauses.title: The Annual Summary: Creation, Certification, and Posting
clauses.body: At the end of each calendar year, the regulation requires a covered employer to review the Cal/OSHA Form 300 log for completeness and accuracy, create an annual summary of the recorded cases using the Cal/OSHA Form 300A, certify that summary, and post it. The certification must be made by a “company executive” as the regulation defines that term, who must certify having examined the Form 300 and reasonably believing, based on knowledge of how the information was recorded, that the annual summary is correct and complete. The completed, certified summary must then be posted in each establishment in a conspicuous place or places where notices to employees are customarily posted, without alteration, defacement, or being covered by other material, and the regulation fixes the posting window itself: no later than February 1 of the year following the year the records cover, with the posting kept in place until April 30.

Code Regs. § 14300.32, subdivisions (a), (b)(3), (b)(5), and (b)(6) — not independent sources from one another. This clause does not independently quote § 14300.32(b)(4), which lists the four categories of person who may qualify as the “company executive” permitted to certify the summary (an owner, a corporate officer, the highest-ranking company official at the establishment, or that official's immediate supervisor); it is described in this clause's body based on the fetched text but not separately cited. This clause also does not address § 14300.32(b)(7)'s separate requirement to present or mail the summary to employees who do not normally report to a posting location, or § 14300.32(b)(8)'s treatment of closed establishments; those provisions are not summarized here. This clause describes the general annual-summary duty for a non-exempt employer, not whether any specific employer's summary was in fact prepared, certified, or posted as required.

clauses.title: The Separate Duty to Report a Serious Injury, Illness, or Death Directly to Cal/OSHA
clauses.body: Apart from the routine Form 300 recordkeeping duty addressed in the other clauses of this information sheet, a separate Cal/OSHA regulation — 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 342, found in a different chapter of Title 8 that governs Cal/OSHA's own reporting and enforcement procedures rather than in the recordkeeping article — requires every employer to report immediately to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health any serious injury or illness, or death, of an employee occurring in a place of employment or in connection with any employment, by telephone or through a specified online mechanism the Division has established for that purpose. The regulation defines “immediately” with a specific outer limit: as soon as practically possible, but not longer than 8 hours after the employer knows, or with diligent inquiry would have known, of the death or serious injury or illness — extended to not longer than 24 hours after the incident only if the employer can demonstrate that exigent circumstances exist. This duty applies without regard to whether the employer is otherwise partially exempt from routine Form 300 recordkeeping under the size-based or industry-based exemptions addressed in a companion clause of this information sheet; the recordkeeping regulation's own cross-reference restates the same reporting duty in shorthand, requiring a report “within eight (8) hours,” as required by § 342. “Serious injury or illness” is itself a defined term, found in a companion section of the same reporting-procedure chapter: an injury or illness occurring in a place of employment or in connection with any employment that requires inpatient hospitalization for other than medical observation or diagnostic testing, or in which an employee suffers an amputation, the loss of an eye, or any serious degree of permanent disfigurement — excluding, with one exception, an injury, illness, or death caused by an accident on a public street or highway, the exception being an accident that occurred in a construction zone.
clauses.gap: The citations to 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 342 and § 330 are independent of the citations to the § 14300 series elsewhere in this information sheet in the sense that §§ 342 and 330 sit in a different chapter of Title 8 (Chapter 3.2, the Cal/OSHA regulations governing the Division of Occupational Safety and Health's own procedures) from the recordkeeping regulation's Chapter 7, Article 2, and were adopted separately (§ 342 originally in 1974, § 330(h) most recently amended in 2020); they are not, however, independent of each other, since both are sections of the same Article 3 (§ 342) and Article 1 (§ 330) of that same chapter, and the § 342 citations (the two paragraphs of subdivision (a)) are two sentences of the same subdivision. The quotation from 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 14300.7(b)(2) is drawn from the same regulation cited in this information sheet's recording-criteria clause and is not an independent source. The regulation's own text of § 330(h), as currently in force, does not state a minimum duration of inpatient hospitalization (such as a 24-hour minimum stay) as a condition of the definition; this document did not fetch or verify the parallel federal OSHA serious-injury-and-illness reporting regulation, 29 C.F.R. § 1904.39, so no comparison is made here between California's definition or 8-hour/24-hour reporting timeline and any federal counterpart, and the two should not be assumed identical. This clause does not independently verify § 342(c)'s list of information a report should include, or § 342(b)'s separate notification duty for responding fire or police agencies; those are not summarized here.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Idea Submission Doctrine Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's common-law idea submission doctrine, originating in the California Supreme Court's 1956 decision in Desny v. Wilder — the body of law that addresses when a person who discloses an idea to another (for example, a business, a studio, or a company) may be entitled to payment for that idea's use, apart from and independent of any copyright or trade secret protection. It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning an idea described as follows: {{ideaDescription}}. That idea was submitted to {{recipientName}} on or around {{submissionDate}}. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference describing what the Desny v. Wilder opinion, and later published California case law applying it, actually say about this doctrine. It does not itself determine whether the disclosure described above did, or did not, give rise to an implied-in-fact contract, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This is a California common-law doctrine; other states have developed their own idea-submission rules, which are not necessarily identical to California's and which this Information Sheet does not address. This document is also distinct from, and does not replace, this project's existing Non-Disclosure Agreement, Mutual Non-Disclosure Agreement, and Invention Assignment & Confidentiality Agreement documents, each of which concerns an express, signed, written contract rather than the implied-in-fact contract theory this Information Sheet describes.

clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Signature of {{preparerName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This Information Sheet is a general reference describing California's idea submission doctrine as stated in Desny v. Wilder (1956) 46 Cal.2d 715 and later published California case law applying it. It is not a contract, a demand letter, a court filing, or legal advice about whether any specific submission described in this Information Sheet gave rise to an enforceable obligation to pay, and completing or signing this Information Sheet does not itself create, establish, or waive any such obligation.]

clauses.title: Why This Doctrine Exists: An Idea, by Itself, Is Not Protected Property
clauses.body: Under California law, an abstract idea is not treated as property that its originator can exclusively own, and it is not protected by copyright, which extends only to the expression of an idea and never to the idea itself. In Desny v. Wilder, the California Supreme Court confirmed that general rule, and went on to explain that a claim for the use of someone's story synopsis or composition does not depend on that material qualifying for copyright protection at all — the claim can instead rest entirely on ordinary contract law, separate from and unconcerned with copyright's requirements. Because neither general property law nor copyright law protects a bare idea, and because an idea disclosed without any confidentiality restriction placed on the recipient may not, without more, qualify as a trade secret either, California courts developed a separate, contract-based doctrine — described in the remaining clauses of this Information Sheet — to address whether, and on what basis, a person who submits an idea to another can recover for its use.
clauses.gap: Both quotations cited below come from the same source — the California Supreme Court's 1956 opinion in Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal.2d 715 — so this is one primary source, not two independent ones. That repetition recurs across several clauses of this Information Sheet because Desny is the single foundational case for this entire doctrine; each clause's own gap notes this explicitly. The opinion's text was retrieved and its quoted sentences confirmed via two distinct retrieval methods within the CourtListener database: (1) CourtListener's document-read/search-document tools, which serve the opinion's `html_with_citations` text, and (2) a direct call to CourtListener's underlying `opinions` REST API endpoint requesting the raw `xml_harvard` field (the Harvard Caselaw Access Project digitization CourtListener has ingested for this particular opinion) — both paths returned character-for-character identical text for the quoted sentences. Because both paths ultimately query the same CourtListener-hosted database, and for this particular opinion draw on the same underlying Harvard-sourced digitization (no separate Lawbox or Columbia text layer was available for this 1956 opinion, unlike for the 1979 opinion cited elsewhere in this Information Sheet), this is disclosed honestly as one primary source checked two ways, not two independently hosted sources. The sentence in this clause's body about trade secret protection describes a general principle of California trade secret law (that a claimed trade secret must be the subject of reasonable efforts to maintain its secrecy) without a separate statutory citation in this clause — no fresh, independent confirmation of that statutory text was performed in this research session, since the relevant California statute is hosted only at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, which this session's network access could not reach. Readers may also consult this project's existing Non-Disclosure Agreement clauses, which independently cite and quote California's statutory trade secret definition (Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1(d)). This is California common-law doctrine; other states have their own idea-submission rules, not necessarily identical to California's, which this document does not address.

citations.quote: it is clear that California does not now accord individual property type protection to abstract ideas.

citations.quote: It is not essential to recovery that plaintiff’s story or synopsis possess the elements of copyright protectibility if the fact of consensual contract be found.

clauses.title: The Implied-in-Fact Contract Theory Desny v. Wilder Articulated
clauses.body: Desny v. Wilder addressed a person who submits an idea to another party without ever obtaining a signed agreement, and held that such a person can still recover for the idea's use — but only under contract principles, never because of any property interest in the idea itself. The California Supreme Court explained that an idea's originator cannot prevail unless there is either an express promise to pay, made before or after disclosure, or circumstances showing a contract described as "implied-in-fact" — meaning a genuine, if unwritten and unspoken, meeting of the minds that is inferred from conduct rather than from words. The court was explicit that this implied promise cannot simply be assumed because an idea turned out to be valuable or was later used; it must instead be grounded in circumstances the recipient actually knew, and conduct by which the recipient voluntarily accepted the idea's disclosure, before the idea itself was revealed.
clauses.gap: Both quotations cited below come from the same source — the California Supreme Court's 1956 opinion in Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal.2d 715 — so this is one primary source, not two independent ones, as explained more fully in this Information Sheet's first authority clause. The opinion's text and these specific sentences were confirmed via the same two distinct retrieval methods described there: CourtListener's document-read/search-document tools (serving `html_with_citations`) and a direct CourtListener REST API call to the `opinions` endpoint requesting the raw `xml_harvard` field, which returned identical text. This describes the general contract theory Desny recognizes; it does not by itself describe every limit the opinion places on that theory — those limits are addressed in the following clauses of this Information Sheet.

citations.case: Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal. 2d 715, 738–739 (Cal., Jun. 28, 1956)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court's statement of the two ways an idea's originator may recover: an express promise, or a promise implied-in-fact
citations.quote: the idea purveyor cannot prevail in an action to recover compensation for an abstract idea unless (a) before or after disclosure he has obtained an express promise to pay, or (b) the circumstances preceding and attending disclosure, together with the conduct of the offeree acting with knowledge of the circumstances, show a promise of the type usually referred to as "implied” or "implied-in-fact.”

citations.case: Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal. 2d 715, 739 (Cal., Jun. 28, 1956)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court's requirement that an implied-in-fact promise be grounded in circumstances known to, and voluntary conduct by, the recipient before disclosure
citations.quote: Such inferred or implied promise, if it is to be found at all, must be based on circumstances which were known to the producer at and preceding the time of disclosure of the idea to him and he must voluntarily accept the disclosure, knowing the conditions on which it is tendered.

clauses.title: Desny's Limits: An Unconditioned Disclosure Does Not, by Itself, Create an Obligation to Pay
clauses.body: Desny v. Wilder places a significant limit on the implied-in-fact contract theory it recognizes: an obligation to pay does not arise merely because a valuable idea was disclosed, was later used, and produced a profit for the recipient, or merely because the person disclosing it hoped or expected to be paid. The California Supreme Court held that a person who discloses an idea without first securing some condition on that disclosure — a condition communicated to, and accepted by, the recipient before the idea itself is revealed — cannot later have that condition read into the transaction by a court. The opinion frames this as a matter of bargaining position: it is the timing and communication of the condition, not the discloser's private hopes or subsequent demands, that the law examines.
clauses.gap: This quotation comes from the same source cited throughout this Information Sheet — the California Supreme Court's 1956 opinion in Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal.2d 715 — confirmed via the same two retrieval methods described in this Information Sheet's first authority clause (CourtListener's document-read tool serving `html_with_citations`, and a direct CourtListener REST API call to the `opinions` endpoint's raw `xml_harvard` field), which returned identical text. The quotation below reproduces two consecutive sentences from a single paragraph of the opinion as one continuous, exact excerpt.

citations.case: Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal. 2d 715, 739 (Cal., Jun. 28, 1956)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court holding that an unconditioned disclosure of an idea does not give rise to an implied promise to pay, even if the idea is later used for profit
citations.quote: The idea man who blurts out his idea without having first made his bargain has no one but himself to blame for the loss of his bargaining power. The law will not in any event, from demands stated subsequent to the unconditioned disclosure of an abstract idea, imply a promise to pay for the idea, for its use, or for its previous disclosure. The law will not imply a promise to pay for an idea from the mere facts that the idea has been conveyed, is valuable, and has been used for profit; this is true even though the conveyance has been made with the hope or expectation that some obligation will ensue.

clauses.title: A Later California Court of Appeal's Four-Part Synthesis of the Desny Test (Faris v. Enberg)
clauses.body: In 1979, the California Court of Appeal in Faris v. Enberg distilled Desny v. Wilder's implied-in-fact contract theory — applied there to an idea for a televised sports quiz show — into a four-part statement of what a person asserting this theory must show: that they prepared the work; that they disclosed the work to the offeree for sale; that, under all the circumstances attending disclosure, the offeree can be found to have voluntarily accepted the disclosure while knowing the conditions on which it was offered (necessarily meaning the offeree had an opportunity to reject the disclosure on those terms); and the reasonable value of the work. Applying that framework to the record before it, the Court of Appeal affirmed summary judgment against the plaintiff, because the evidence showed no indication the plaintiff had ever communicated an expectation of payment, or that the recipient had reason to believe the submission was conditioned on one.
clauses.gap: Faris v. Enberg, 97 Cal.App.3d 309 (Cal. Ct. App., 2d Dist. 1979), is a published opinion of the California Court of Appeal, confirmed as a distinct, later California appellate decision via CourtListener search results. Its text, and the quoted sentence specifically, were confirmed via two distinct retrieval methods: (1) CourtListener's document-read/search-document tools, serving the opinion's `html_with_citations` text, and (2) a direct call to CourtListener's `opinions` REST API endpoint requesting three separately-digitized raw text fields the platform has ingested for this opinion — `html_lawbox`, `html_columbia`, and `xml_harvard`, corresponding to three historically distinct digitization projects (Public.Resource.Org/Lawbox, Columbia Law School's caselaw archive, and the Harvard Caselaw Access Project). Two of the three fields (`html_lawbox` and `html_columbia`) contained the quoted sentence character-for-character identically; the third (`xml_harvard`) contained the same sentence with two minor OCR-type artifacts not reproduced in this document's quote — "conditions On which" (capitalized "On") in place of "conditions on which," and "and- the reasonable value" (an inserted hyphen) in place of "and the reasonable value" — which this document treats as digitization noise rather than as a genuine textual variant, given that two independently-produced sources agree on the clean reading. Because all three fields are ultimately served through the same CourtListener-hosted database, this is disclosed honestly as one platform queried multiple ways rather than genuinely separate hosting infrastructure; the agreement of two of the three independently-produced source digitizations, with the third differing only by evident OCR noise, still provides meaningfully stronger confirmation of the quoted language than a single source alone would. This is one Court of Appeal decision from one appellate district (the Second Appellate District); it is not a California Supreme Court decision, and this document does not represent that every California appellate district has adopted identical language for this four-part synthesis, or that no California case has stated the elements differently.
