citations.quote: for an implied-in-fact contract one must show: that he or she prepared the work; that he or she disclosed the work to the offeree for sale; under all circumstances attending disclosure it can be concluded that the offeree voluntarily accepted the disclosure knowing the conditions on which it was tendered (i.e., the offeree must have the opportunity to reject the attempted disclosure if the conditions were unacceptable); and the reasonable value of the work.

clauses.title: One Commonly-Assumed Element the Desny Opinion Does Not Impose on This Theory: Novelty
clauses.body: Secondary summaries of the idea submission doctrine sometimes describe novelty — meaning that the idea must be new, and not already widely known — as a required element of a Desny claim. The Desny v. Wilder opinion itself does not impose that requirement on the implied-in-fact contract theory it recognizes. Quoting language it expressly adopted as the law of California, the California Supreme Court stated that even an idea that is widely known and generally understood may still be protected by an express contract providing that it will be paid for regardless of its lack of novelty. The court distinguished this contract-based theory from a separate literary-property theory (concerning whether a written composition itself, as opposed to the bare idea it embodies, qualifies as protectible property), under which the concepts of originality and novelty carry their own, different significance — a distinct question from whether a promise to pay for an idea's use can be inferred from conduct.
clauses.gap: This quotation comes from Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal.2d 715, 733, in which the California Supreme Court described itself as adopting, as the law of California, language originating in Justice Traynor's dissenting opinion in Stanley v. Columbia Broadcasting System (1950) 35 Cal.2d 653, 674, and stated that this language had already been accepted as California law in Weitzenkorn v. Lesser (1953) 40 Cal.2d 778, 791–792 — meaning the quoted sentence did not originate with the Desny opinion itself, although this document quotes it exactly as it appears within, and as adopted and applied by, the Desny opinion (neither Stanley's dissent nor Weitzenkorn was independently retrieved or verified in this research). Independently of that history, this same sentence was also confirmed, in this research, to appear — quoted approvingly and for the identical proposition — within a separate, later opinion: Faris v. Enberg (1979) 97 Cal.App.3d 309, 314, a California Court of Appeal decision issued 23 years after Desny. Both opinions' texts were independently retrieved via CourtListener using the two retrieval methods described in this Information Sheet's other clauses. This document treats that as confirmation that the quoted sentence is accurately reproduced (since it is found, verbatim, in two separately-retrieved published California opinions), not as confirmation that Faris v. Enberg is itself an independent source for the underlying legal proposition — Faris is simply quoting Desny on this point, as this document's own body text explains. This document does not independently address whether novelty may carry different significance for other legal theories besides this implied-in-fact contract theory (for example, a common law copyright theory, or a breach-of-confidence theory) — published California case law encountered in this research, including within Faris v. Enberg's own discussion of other authorities, suggested such theories may impose different requirements, but those theories and that case law were not independently read or verified here and are outside the scope of this document.

citations.case: Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal. 2d 715, 733 (Cal., Jun. 28, 1956)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court holding that an idea's lack of novelty does not bar its protection by contract
citations.quote: Even though the idea disclosed may be ‘widely known and generally understood’ [citation], it may be protected by an express contract providing that it will be paid for regardless of its lack of novelty.

clauses.title: How This Doctrine Differs from a Written NDA or Invention Assignment Agreement
clauses.body: The Desny v. Wilder doctrine addresses a contract the law infers from conduct and surrounding circumstance — what the opinion calls a contract "implied-in-fact" — rather than a contract the parties put in writing and signed. The California Supreme Court described this as one of two distinct ways a recipient can become bound to pay for a disclosed idea: either the recipient makes an express promise to pay, or the surrounding circumstances and the recipient's own conduct, undertaken with knowledge of the condition on which the idea was offered, show the functional equivalent of an agreement even though nothing was ever spoken or written down. This project's existing Non-Disclosure Agreement, Mutual Non-Disclosure Agreement, and Invention Assignment & Confidentiality Agreement documents all operate on the first of these two tracks: each is an express, signed, written contract whose confidentiality and assignment obligations do not depend on a court inferring them from conduct after the fact. The doctrine described in this Information Sheet instead addresses what happens — and what a person disclosing an idea, or a person receiving one, may be exposed to — when no such signed agreement exists.
clauses.gap: This quotation comes from the same source cited throughout this Information Sheet — the California Supreme Court's 1956 opinion in Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal.2d 715 — confirmed via the same two retrieval methods described in this Information Sheet's first authority clause. This clause references, but does not reproduce or duplicate, the substantive terms of this project's existing Non-Disclosure Agreement, Mutual Non-Disclosure Agreement, or Invention Assignment & Confidentiality Agreement documents; readers consulting this clause for a contrast with those documents should read this clause alongside those documents' own clauses, not as a substitute for them.

citations.case: Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal. 2d 715, 738 (Cal., Jun. 28, 1956)
citations.cite: California Supreme Court's description of how a condition on disclosure, if clearly communicated and knowingly accepted, produces either an express or an implied-in-fact contract
citations.quote: if the idea purveyor has clearly conditioned his offer to convey the idea upon an obligation to pay for it if it is used by the offeree and the offeree, knowing the condition before he knows the idea, voluntarily accepts its disclosure (necessarily on the specified basis) and finds it valuable and uses it, the law will either apply the objective test (discussed, supra, pp. 801-802) and hold that the parties have made an express (sometimes called implied-in-fact) contract, or under those circumstances, as some writers view it, the law itself, to prevent fraud and unjust enrichment, will imply a promise to compensate.

clauses.title: Information and Background — Alleged Constructive Discharge
clauses.body: I, {{employeeName}}, am completing this information sheet in connection with the ending of my employment with {{companyName}}. I resigned from that employment, and this document treats my resignation as having occurred on {{resignationDate}}. The working conditions I believe may have been so intolerable that a reasonable employee in my position would have felt compelled to resign are described here as: {{allegedIntolerableConditions}}. The separate legal claim to which this constructive-discharge analysis would be relevant, if any, is described here as: {{underlyingClaimDescription}}. This information sheet provides background on California's constructive discharge doctrine for someone evaluating whether a resignation may be treated in law as an employer-initiated termination for purposes of that separate claim. It is not a court filing, a demand letter, an employer policy, or a legal determination of any kind, and completing it does not establish, prove, or determine that {{employeeName}}'s resignation from {{companyName}} was a constructive discharge, or that any underlying claim described above is valid. Only a court, or another body with legal authority to decide the question, can determine whether a specific resignation amounted to a constructive discharge.

clauses.title: The Doctrine: A Resignation Treated in Law as a Firing
clauses.body: California recognizes a judicially created doctrine, established primarily by the California Supreme Court's 1994 decision in Turner v. Anheuser-Busch, Inc., under which an employee's resignation can be treated in law as an employer-initiated termination rather than as a voluntary quit. Under this doctrine, when an employer's conduct effectively forces an employee to resign, the employment relationship is regarded as having been severed involuntarily by the employer's own acts and against the employee's will, even though the employee is the one who says the words "I quit." As a result, a resignation that qualifies under this doctrine is legally regarded as a firing rather than a resignation.
clauses.gap: Both citations in this clause quote the same opinion, Turner v. Anheuser-Busch, Inc. (1994) 7 Cal.4th 1238 — that is disclosed here rather than presented as independent sources. Verification path: the opinion's full text (the html-with-citations version) was read directly from the CourtListener case-law database (opinion cluster ID 1258971) via the CourtListener MCP tool. A second, genuinely distinct retrieval path was used to cross-check the same passages: a web search (not a CourtListener query) returned indexed snippet text of this opinion reproduced by multiple independently hosted secondary sources discussing the case (including a law review case comment and case-summary/commentary sites unaffiliated with CourtListener), which reproduced the identical language quoted here without contradiction. Several other domains that host primary case text (including Justia, a Stanford California courts archive, Leagle, and CourtListener's own website) could not be fetched directly in this research session because this environment's network egress controls blocked those domains; the CourtListener MCP tool itself was not blocked and is the source of the exact quotations here. This document addresses California law only. Other jurisdictions apply their own constructive-discharge doctrines, which are not necessarily identical to California's; the Turner opinion itself notes, for example, that the federal Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals has required proof of an employer's express intent to force a resignation, a requirement California's courts have declined to adopt (addressed further below). This document does not itself determine that any specific resignation was a constructive discharge, and does not determine which state's law governs any specific employment relationship.

clauses.title: A Doctrine That Supports Another Claim — Not a Standalone Claim Itself
clauses.body: Constructive discharge is not itself a separate, standalone legal claim. The doctrine responds to a specific problem: in an attempt to avoid the liability that would come with an actual firing, an employer may avoid directly discharging an employee and instead engage in conduct designed or allowed to cause the employee to quit on their own. California's constructive discharge doctrine addresses this kind of employer-attempted "end run" around wrongful discharge and other legal claims that require an employer-initiated termination of employment as one of their elements. Put differently, establishing a constructive discharge does not by itself win any claim; it supplies the fact of an employer-initiated "termination," which is then evaluated under whatever separate underlying claim actually requires that kind of termination — for example, a claim for wrongful termination in violation of public policy, or an employment discrimination claim.

clauses.title: Intolerable Conditions Judged by an Objective, Reasonable-Employee Standard
clauses.body: Whether a resignation qualifies as a constructive discharge is measured by an objective standard, not by a particular employee's own subjective reaction to their job. The question is whether a reasonable person, faced with the working conditions actually experienced, would have had no reasonable alternative except to quit. This means the inquiry does not turn solely on how upsetting, unfair, or stressful a particular employee personally found their situation to be; it turns on whether those same conditions would have been intolerable to a hypothetical reasonable employee in the same position.

The quoted language is itself the Turner court's own restatement, in its own voice, of a formulation it discusses as having originated in a Court of Appeal decision (Rochlis v. This document addresses California law only, and does not determine which state's law governs any specific employment relationship, or that any specific working conditions were or were not intolerable under this standard.

clauses.title: A High Threshold — Aggravated Conditions or a Continuous Pattern, Not Isolated Incidents
clauses.body: California's constructive discharge doctrine sets a demanding threshold for what counts as "intolerable." Working conditions generally must be unusually aggravated, or must amount to a continuous pattern, before they will be deemed intolerable for purposes of this doctrine. A single, trivial, or isolated act is generally not enough by itself to establish a constructive discharge — including ordinary supervisory actions such as a single negative performance review, instance of criticism, or demotion, since reviewing, criticizing, demoting, transferring, and disciplining employees are activities every employer engages in from time to time in the ordinary course of managing a business.

Both citations in this clause quote the same opinion. This document addresses California law only. This document does not determine that any specific set of working conditions was, or was not, sufficiently aggravated or a sufficiently continuous pattern to meet this threshold in any particular case.

clauses.title: The Employer Must Have Created or Knowingly Permitted the Conditions
clauses.body: Beyond the intolerable-conditions element, California's constructive discharge doctrine requires a showing tied to the employer's own conduct or knowledge. A claim does not succeed merely because an employer should have known, or could have discovered through reasonable diligence, that conditions were intolerable — that kind of after-the-fact, constructive knowledge alone is not enough under California's doctrine. Instead, the employer, or someone acting on the employer's behalf, must have either deliberately created the intolerable conditions, or actually known about them and failed to remedy the situation, in order for the resulting resignation to be treated as a discharge. California's courts do not require proof that the employer's express purpose was to force the employee to quit; an employer's actual knowledge of intolerable conditions, combined with a failure to fix them, can itself support treating the resignation as employer-caused.

Elixir Industries) that had allowed a claim based on the employer's mere constructive knowledge of the conditions; the Turner court expressly declined to follow that broader constructive-knowledge approach. clauses.title: Background Information — Uniform Prudent Investor Act
clauses.body: I, {{trusteeName}}, am serving, or have been asked to serve, as trustee of {{trustName}}, executed {{originalTrustDate}}. This information sheet describes California's Uniform Prudent Investor Act (Probate Code §§ 16045-16054), the statutory standard of care that governs how a trustee invests and manages trust assets, including the requirement that individual investment and management decisions be evaluated in the context of the trust portfolio as a whole rather than in isolation. This information sheet is educational only. It does not evaluate, approve, or ratify any specific investment, investment strategy, or asset allocation decision made or proposed for {{trustName}}; does not determine whether {{trusteeName}} has satisfied the prudent investor rule or any other fiduciary duty in connection with {{trustName}}; and is not investment advice or legal advice. Preparing, reviewing, or signing this information sheet does not itself satisfy, waive, or discharge any duty {{trusteeName}} owes as trustee of {{trustName}}.

clauses.title: The Prudent Investor Standard and the Portfolio-as-a-Whole Rule
clauses.body: California has adopted the Uniform Prudent Investor Act as Probate Code §§ 16045-16054. Under this article, except where the trust instrument itself provides otherwise, a trustee who invests and manages trust assets owes a duty to the trust's beneficiaries to comply with the prudent investor rule. The statute defines that rule to require a trustee to invest and manage trust assets as a prudent investor would, by considering the purposes, terms, distribution requirements, and other circumstances of the trust, and to exercise reasonable care, skill, and caution in doing so. Critically, the statute does not permit an individual investment or course of action to be judged on its own: it expressly requires that a trustee's investment and management decisions respecting individual assets and courses of action be evaluated not in isolation, but in the context of the trust portfolio as a whole and as a part of an overall investment strategy having risk and return objectives reasonably suited to the trust. The statute also states directly that a trustee may invest in any kind of property or type of investment, or engage in any course of action or investment strategy, consistent with these standards -- the rule is not a list of approved or forbidden asset classes, but a standard for how investment and management decisions are made and evaluated.
clauses.gap: This is California's own codification of a model uniform act; other states that have enacted versions of the Uniform Prudent Investor Act may have adopted different or modified text, and this document does not address any other state's version. This document does not determine whether any specific trustee's specific investment or management decisions for a specific trust satisfy the prudent investor rule, whether any specific trust portfolio's risk and return objectives are reasonably suited to that trust, or how a court would evaluate any specific decision in the context of a specific portfolio -- those are fact-specific determinations this document does not resolve. This clause cites Probate Code § 16046(a) and § 16047(a) and (b). The subdivisions of § 16047 -- (a) and (b) -- are not independent of each other, since they come from the same statutory section; § 16046 is a separate section from § 16047. Each section was fetched twice independently from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text (after whitespace normalization) returned both times for both sections.

In satisfying this standard, the trustee shall exercise reasonable care, skill, and caution. clauses.title: Factors a Trustee Must Consider Under the Prudent Investor Rule
clauses.body: The statute enumerates a specific, non-exclusive list of circumstances that are appropriate to consider in investing and managing trust assets, to the extent relevant to the trust or its beneficiaries: general economic conditions; the possible effect of inflation or deflation; the expected tax consequences of investment decisions or strategies; the role that each investment or course of action plays within the overall trust portfolio; the expected total return from income and the appreciation of capital; other resources of the beneficiaries known to the trustee as determined from information provided by the beneficiaries; needs for liquidity, regularity of income, and preservation or appreciation of capital; and an asset's special relationship or special value, if any, to the purposes of the trust or to one or more of the beneficiaries. The statute separately requires a trustee to make a reasonable effort to ascertain facts relevant to the investment and management of trust assets.
clauses.gap: This clause cites Probate Code § 16047(c) and (d); this is the same statutory section cited in the companion authority clause on the core prudent investor standard (§ 16047(a)-(b)), so these citations are not independent of that clause's citation, only of the citations to different sections such as § 16046 and § 16048. Each subdivision was fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers, with identical text returned both times. The statutory list is introduced as circumstances that are appropriate to consider 'to the extent relevant to the trust or its beneficiaries' and is not stated as an exhaustive list -- this document does not determine which of these factors are, in fact, relevant to any specific trust, or how a trustee should weigh them against one another for any specific trust or investment decision.

clauses.title: Duty to Diversify, and Its Prudent-Under-the-Circumstances Exception
clauses.body: In making and implementing investment decisions, the statute imposes on a trustee a duty to diversify the investments of the trust -- but this duty is not absolute. The same sentence that states the duty also states its exception: the duty to diversify does not apply where, under the circumstances, it is prudent not to diversify. The statute does not itself enumerate what circumstances make non-diversification prudent; it leaves that determination to be made in light of the facts and circumstances of the particular trust and investment decision, informed by the same considerations set out elsewhere in this article (such as the trust's purposes, distribution requirements, and the beneficiaries' other resources).
clauses.gap: This clause is based on a single sentence within a single statutory section, § 16048; there is no second section to cross-reference for independence, so its independence rests solely on the two separately-conducted fetches of that one section (distinct User-Agent headers, identical text returned both times). This is California's own codification of the Uniform Prudent Investor Act; other states' versions of the uniform act may state the diversification duty or its exception differently, or not at all. This document does not determine whether diversifying, or not diversifying, is in fact prudent for any specific trust's assets under any specific set of circumstances -- the statute commits that determination to case-by-case application, not to a fixed rule this document can state in advance.

clauses.title: The Trust Instrument's Power to Expand or Restrict the Standard
clauses.body: The prudent investor rule described in this article is a default rule, not one that necessarily applies unaltered to every trust. The statute expressly permits a trust's settlor to expand or restrict the prudent investor rule by express provisions in the trust instrument, and separately provides that a trustee is not liable to a beneficiary for the trustee's good faith reliance on those express provisions. This means the specific standard of care that applies to investment and management decisions for a given trust can only be determined by reading that trust's own instrument together with this default statutory rule, since the instrument may have broadened, narrowed, or otherwise modified what the statute would otherwise require.

The statute's own text says a settlor may 'expand or restrict' the rule by express trust provisions; it does not use the word 'eliminate,' and this document does not take a position on whether or to what degree a restriction could reduce the rule's practical application to a specific trust, or on what express language would be required to accomplish any particular expansion or restriction -- those are drafting and interpretation questions specific to the trust instrument in question, not resolved by this document. This document also does not determine whether any specific trust instrument in fact contains such express provisions, or what those provisions say.

clauses.title: Timing of the Prudent Investor Determination: No Hindsight
clauses.body: The statute fixes the vantage point from which compliance with the prudent investor rule is measured: compliance is determined in light of the facts and circumstances existing at the time of a trustee's decision or action, and not by hindsight. Under this rule, a later, unfavorable outcome for a particular investment or course of action does not, by itself, establish that the decision failed to meet the prudent investor standard when it was made.

This is California's own codification of the Uniform Prudent Investor Act; other states' versions may state this timing rule differently or not include it. clauses.title: California Solar Rights Act — Introduction and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, the California Solar Rights Act provisions found at Civil Code § 714 and § 714.1, in connection with the property located at {{propertyAddress}} and, where applicable, the common interest development association {{hoaName}}. Civil Code § 714 makes void and unenforceable any covenant, restriction, or condition in a deed, contract, security instrument, or other transfer instrument, and any provision of a common interest development governing document, that effectively prohibits or restricts the installation or use of a solar energy system — subject to a statutory exception for restrictions that are genuinely "reasonable" as the statute defines that term. It covers the general voiding rule; the line the statute draws between a permissible reasonable restriction and a prohibited effective ban, including the different numeric cost and efficiency thresholds the statute sets for solar water-heating and pool-heating systems versus photovoltaic systems; the health, safety, and technical standards a solar energy system may still be required to meet; the timeline within which an association or other approving entity must act on an application, including the 45-day deemed-approved rule; the specific restrictions Civil Code § 714.1 permits (and forbids) a common interest development association to impose; and the damages, civil penalty, and attorney's-fee remedies the statute provides for a willful violation. This topic is distinct from a seller's document-disclosure obligations to a buyer under the Davis-Stirling Act (addressed in this corpus's HOA/CC&R Disclosure document) and from an association's assessment lien and foreclosure remedy for unpaid assessments (addressed in this corpus's HOA Assessment Lien and Foreclosure — Information Sheet). This sheet is informational only. It does not itself approve, deny, install, modify, or evaluate any solar energy system; it does not interpret, amend, or apply any specific deed, CC&R, or governing document affecting {{propertyAddress}}; and it does not determine whether any actual covenant, restriction, condition, association action, or application-review decision relating to {{propertyAddress}} or {{hoaName}} complies — or fails to comply — with the statutory requirements it describes.

clauses.title: Covenants and Restrictions That Effectively Prohibit Solar Are Void
clauses.body: California's Solar Rights Act states a general rule voiding private restrictions on solar energy systems. Civil Code § 714(a) provides: "Any covenant, restriction, or condition contained in any deed, contract, security instrument, or other instrument affecting the transfer or sale of, or any interest in, real property, and any provision of a governing document, as defined in Section 4150 or 6552, that effectively prohibits or restricts the installation or use of a solar energy system is void and unenforceable." By its terms, this rule reaches restrictions in deeds, contracts, and security instruments affecting real property generally, and separately reaches any provision of a common interest development "governing document" (a term the statute cross-references to Civil Code § 4150 or § 6552). The statute's use of the phrase "effectively prohibits or restricts" means the voiding rule can reach a restriction that does not use the word "solar" or "prohibit" at all, if its practical effect is to prohibit or restrict solar installation or use. This general rule is qualified by a statutory exception for reasonable restrictions, addressed elsewhere in this corpus. This description concerns the statutory rule generally; it does not determine whether any specific covenant, restriction, or condition affecting {{propertyAddress}} is void or unenforceable under it.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single subdivision, Civil Code § 714(a); it is one source, not independently corroborated by a second source. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's Solar Rights Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property; other states impose different or no comparable solar-restriction voiding rule. This clause does not address the reasonable-restrictions exception referenced in § 714(a)'s companion subdivision (b), which is covered in a separate clause in this corpus, nor does it resolve what the cross-referenced governing-document definitions in Civil Code § 4150 or § 6552 provide, since those sections were not independently fetched or verified for this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 714(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Any covenant, restriction, or condition contained in any deed, contract, security instrument, or other instrument affecting the transfer or sale of, or any interest in, real property, and any provision of a governing document, as defined in Section 4150 or 6552, that effectively prohibits or restricts the installation or use of a solar energy system is void and unenforceable.

clauses.title: The Line Between a Permissible "Reasonable Restriction" and a Prohibited Effective Ban
clauses.body: Civil Code § 714 does not void every restriction that touches a solar energy system — it carves out restrictions the statute itself defines as "reasonable." Section 714(b) provides: "This section does not apply to provisions that impose reasonable restrictions on solar energy systems. However, it is the policy of the state to promote and encourage the use of solar energy systems and to remove obstacles thereto. Accordingly, reasonable restrictions on a solar energy system are those restrictions that do not significantly increase the cost of the system or significantly decrease its efficiency or specified performance, or that allow for an alternative system of comparable cost, efficiency, and energy conservation benefits." The statute then gives "significantly" a precise, quantified meaning that differs by category of system. Section 714(d)(1)(A) provides that "[f]or solar domestic water heating systems or solar swimming pool heating systems that comply with state and federal law, ‘significantly’ means an amount exceeding 10 percent of the cost of the system, but in no case more than one thousand dollars ($1,000), or decreasing the efficiency of the solar energy system by an amount exceeding 10 percent, as originally specified and proposed." Section 714(d)(1)(B) sets a different formula for a different category of system: "For photovoltaic systems that comply with state and federal law, ‘significantly’ means an amount not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) over the system cost as originally specified and proposed, or a decrease in system efficiency of an amount exceeding 10 percent as originally specified and proposed." In practical terms, for a solar water-heating or pool-heating system the statutory cost threshold is whichever is smaller of 10% of the system's cost or $1,000, while for a photovoltaic system the statutory cost threshold is a flat $1,000 over the originally specified and proposed cost; both categories share the same 10%-efficiency-decrease threshold. This description concerns the statutory reasonable-restriction standard generally; it does not calculate or determine whether any specific restriction, cost impact, or efficiency impact affecting {{propertyAddress}} falls within or outside that standard.
clauses.gap: The citations to § 714(b) and § 714(d)(1)(A)-(B) are to subdivisions of the same statutory section and are not independent of each other. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's Solar Rights Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property; other states impose different or no comparable reasonable-restriction test. The statute defines "significantly" only for cost and efficiency impacts; it does not, in the text quoted here, separately define a numeric threshold for the "specified performance" language used in § 714(b), and this clause does not speculate about what a performance-based (as opposed to cost- or efficiency-based) restriction would require. This clause also does not address § 714.1's separate, HOA-specific list of restrictions an association may or may not impose, which is covered in a different clause in this corpus.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 714(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: This section does not apply to provisions that impose reasonable restrictions on solar energy systems. However, it is the policy of the state to promote and encourage the use of solar energy systems and to remove obstacles thereto. Accordingly, reasonable restrictions on a solar energy system are those restrictions that do not significantly increase the cost of the system or significantly decrease its efficiency or specified performance, or that allow for an alternative system of comparable cost, efficiency, and energy conservation benefits.

clauses.title: Health, Safety, and Technical Standards a Solar Energy System May Still Be Required to Meet
clauses.body: Civil Code § 714's voiding rule does not exempt a solar energy system from otherwise-applicable health, safety, and technical standards. Section 714(c)(1) provides: "A solar energy system shall meet applicable health and safety standards and requirements imposed by state and local permitting authorities, consistent with Section 65850.5 of the Government Code." Two more specific technical requirements follow, again distinguishing solar water-heating systems from photovoltaic systems. Section 714(c)(2) provides: "Solar energy systems used for heating water in single family residences and solar collectors used for heating water in commercial or swimming pool applications shall be certified by an accredited listing agency as defined in the Plumbing and Mechanical Codes." Section 714(c)(3) provides: "A solar energy system for producing electricity shall also meet all applicable safety and performance standards established by the California Electrical Code, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, and accredited testing laboratories such as Underwriters Laboratories and, where applicable, rules of the Public Utilities Commission regarding safety and reliability." These technical-compliance requirements exist independently of, and are not themselves voided by, the reasonable-restriction standard described elsewhere in this corpus. This description concerns the statutory technical-standards requirements generally; it does not determine whether any specific solar energy system proposed or installed at {{propertyAddress}} meets them.

This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's Solar Rights Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property or system; other jurisdictions impose different technical and certification standards. This clause does not independently verify the content of the cross-referenced Government Code § 65850.5, the Plumbing and Mechanical Codes, the California Electrical Code, or the standards of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, Underwriters Laboratories, or the Public Utilities Commission, none of which were fetched for this clause.

clauses.title: Processing a Solar Energy System Application: The 45-Day Deemed-Approved Rule
clauses.body: Civil Code § 714 regulates not only the substance of solar restrictions but also the process an approving entity — including a homeowners association — must follow when a solar energy system application requires approval. Section 714(e)(1) provides: "Whenever approval is required for the installation or use of a solar energy system, the application for approval shall be processed and approved by the appropriate approving entity in the same manner as an application for approval of an architectural modification to the property, and shall not be willfully avoided or delayed." For an association that is not a public entity, the statute adds two further requirements and a firm deadline. Section 714(e)(2)(A) provides: "The approval or denial of an application shall be in writing." Section 714(e)(2)(B) provides: "If an application is not denied in writing within 45 days from the date of receipt of the application, the application shall be deemed approved, unless that delay is the result of a reasonable request for additional information." This description concerns the statutory application-processing timeline generally; it does not determine whether any specific application submitted to {{hoaName}} concerning {{propertyAddress}} was timely processed, denied in writing, delayed by a reasonable request for additional information, or deemed approved under this rule.

This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's application-processing requirement for a solar energy system — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific association or property; other jurisdictions impose different, or no comparable, deemed-approved deadlines. The 45-day deemed-approved rule quoted here applies, by its terms, to an approving entity that is "an association, as defined in Section 4080 or 6528, and that is not a public entity"; this clause does not independently verify the content of those cross-referenced association definitions, which were not fetched for this clause.

clauses.title: Restrictions an Association May Impose Under § 714.1, and Actions It May Not Take
clauses.body: A separate section of the Solar Rights Act, Civil Code § 714.1, addresses common interest development associations specifically, listing restrictions an association may impose alongside actions it may not take. Section 714.1(a) provides: "Notwithstanding Section 714, an association may impose reasonable provisions that:" restrict solar installations in common areas to association-approved systems, require an owner to obtain association approval before installing a solar energy system in a separate interest owned by someone else, provide for roof and building-component maintenance, repair, or replacement, and require installers to indemnify or reimburse the association or its members for loss or damage the installation, maintenance, or use of the system causes. The statute quotes those four categories as follows: "(1) Restrict the installation of solar energy systems in common areas to those systems approved by the association. (2) Require the owner of a separate interest to obtain the approval of the association for the installation of a solar energy system in a separate interest owned by another. (3) Provide for the maintenance, repair, or replacement of roofs or other building components. (4) Require installers of solar energy systems to indemnify or reimburse the association or its members for loss or damage caused by the installation, maintenance, or use of the solar energy system." Section 714.1(b) then draws a specific line an association may not cross for household rooftop solar: an association "shall not" "[e]stablish a general policy prohibiting the installation or use of a rooftop solar energy system for household purposes on the roof of the building in which the owner resides, or a garage or carport adjacent to the building that has been assigned to the owner for exclusive use," nor "[r]equire approval by a vote of members owning separate interests in the common interest development, including that specified by Section 4600, for installation of a solar energy system for household purposes on the roof of the building in which the owner resides, or a garage or carport adjacent to the building that has been assigned to the owner for exclusive use." The statute makes the consequence explicit: "An action by an association that contravenes paragraph (1) or (2) shall be void and unenforceable." This description concerns the statutory framework generally; it does not determine whether any specific provision, policy, vote requirement, or association action affecting {{hoaName}} or {{propertyAddress}} complies — or fails to comply — with § 714.1.

Section 714.1 is textually related to, but a distinct code section from, § 714 — it opens "Notwithstanding Section 714" — so it supplements rather than duplicates the general reasonable-restriction standard described in a separate clause in this corpus. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's HOA-specific solar-restriction framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific association; other states impose different or no comparable rules. This clause does not independently verify the cross-referenced Civil Code § 4600 (governing certain membership votes) or the association, common area, and separate interest definitions in § 714.1(c), none of which were fetched or block-quoted for this clause.

clauses.title: Remedies for a Willful Violation: Damages, Civil Penalty, and Attorney's Fees
clauses.body: Civil Code § 714 provides specific remedies tied to noncompliance with the section. Section 714(f) provides: "Any entity, other than a public entity, that willfully violates this section shall be liable to the applicant or other party for actual damages occasioned thereby, and shall pay a civil penalty to the applicant or other party in an amount not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000)." That damages-and-penalty remedy is limited by its own terms to a violation the statute characterizes as "willful" and to a non-public-entity violator. Section 714(g) states a separate, broader fee-shifting rule: "In any action to enforce compliance with this section, the prevailing party shall be awarded reasonable attorney's fees." On its face, § 714(g)'s prevailing-party attorney's-fee rule is not limited to willful violations and is not framed as available only to the applicant; it applies to "any action to enforce compliance with this section." This description concerns the statutory remedies generally; it does not determine whether any specific violation, damages amount, civil penalty, or attorney's-fee award applies to any actual dispute concerning {{propertyAddress}} or {{hoaName}}.
clauses.gap: The citations to § 714(f) and § 714(g) are to subdivisions of the same statutory section and are not independent of each other. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's Solar Rights Act remedies — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific dispute; other states provide different or no comparable statutory damages, penalty, or fee-shifting remedies for a solar-restriction violation. This clause does not address § 714(h)'s separate public-entity grant-and-loan-eligibility consequence, which applies only to public entities and was not selected for a dedicated clause in this corpus because it does not bear on a private party's rights or remedies.

clauses.title: Right to Repair Act — Purpose and Background Declaration
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Right to Repair Act (Civil Code §§ 895–945.5, enacted by Senate Bill 800 in 2002), which sets detailed construction-defect performance standards for new residential construction and establishes a mandatory prelitigation notice-and-opportunity-to-repair process a homeowner generally must follow before suing a builder for an alleged construction defect. It concerns the residence located at {{propertyAddress}}, as between {{homeownerName}} and {{builderName}}, described here as the builder of that residence. This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute, serve, or complete the written notice of claim the Act requires; it does not determine that any specific condition at {{propertyAddress}} violates any standard set forth in the Act; and it does not initiate, waive, toll, extend, or complete any statutory deadline, inspection, repair offer, or legal action described in the Act. Only the notice, inspection, and repair process the Act itself describes — and, ultimately, a court or other body with authority to decide the question — can determine whether a specific condition violates the Act, or what remedy, if any, is available with respect to {{propertyAddress}}.

clauses.title: What the Right to Repair Act Covers, and How Its Performance Standards Are Structured
clauses.body: California's Right to Repair Act is codified at Civil Code §§ 895 through 945.5, under Title 7 of the Civil Code, titled "Requirements for Actions for Construction Defects." Its actionable-defects chapter, Civil Code § 896, states that in an action seeking recovery of damages "arising out of, or related to deficiencies in, the residential construction, design, specifications, surveying, planning, supervision, testing, or observation of construction," a builder — and, to the extent set out in the Act's prelitigation chapter (Chapter 4, commencing with § 910), a general contractor, subcontractor, material supplier, individual product manufacturer, or design professional — is liable for, and the claimant's claims are generally limited to, violation of the specific standards § 896 lists. Section 896 further states that "[t]his title applies to original construction intended to be sold as an individual dwelling unit," and separately that "[a]s to condominium conversions, this title does not apply to or does not supersede any other statutory or common law." Rather than relying on a general negligence or implied-warranty standard, § 896 sets out a long, itemized list of specific performance standards organized by subject matter: subdivision (a) addresses water issues (for example, doors, windows, roofs, decks, and foundations), (b) structural issues, (c) soil issues, (d) fire protection issues, (e) plumbing and sewer issues, (f) electrical system issues, and (g) a further set of standards addressing other areas of construction, including exterior pathways, paint and stains, dryer ducts, and landscaping.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's actual construction-defect performance-standards scheme for new residential construction — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular project, and not a claim that other states have a comparable statutory scheme (most do not). Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 896 (its unnumbered introductory paragraph), rather than from independently authored sources, so they corroborate one internally consistent provision rather than two separate ones. This clause does not attempt to reproduce § 896's very long, detailed list of specific numbered performance standards; a companion clause quotes a small, genuinely verified sample of them rather than summarizing the list exhaustively. This clause also does not state whether a particular structure is "original construction intended to be sold as an individual dwelling unit" as the statute uses that phrase, whether a particular transaction is a "condominium conversion," or whether the Act — as opposed to ordinary negligence, contract, or warranty law — governs a particular claim.

citations.quote: In any action seeking recovery of damages arising out of, or related to deficiencies in, the residential construction, design, specifications, surveying, planning, supervision, testing, or observation of construction, a builder, and to the extent set forth in Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 910), a general contractor, subcontractor, material supplier, individual product manufacturer, or design professional, shall, except as specifically set forth in this title, be liable for, and the claimant's claims or causes of action shall be limited to violation of, the following standards, except as specifically set forth in this title.

clauses.title: Examples of § 896's Actionable Performance Standards, Including Their Embedded Time Limits
clauses.body: Civil Code § 896's list of actionable standards is extensive — it covers dozens of specific defect categories across water intrusion, structural, soil, fire protection, plumbing, electrical, and other systems — and this clause does not attempt to summarize it exhaustively. Instead, a few individually verified examples illustrate both the specificity of the standards and a feature that runs through several of them: some standards carry their own embedded time limit, stated within the same numbered standard, on when an action may be brought for a violation of that particular standard. A structural example, from subdivision (b)(1), carries no such stated limit in its own text: "Foundations, load bearing components, and slabs, shall not contain significant cracks or significant vertical displacement." By contrast, the plumbing-and-sewer standard in subdivision (e) states both the performance requirement and its own four-year limit: "Plumbing and sewer systems shall be installed to operate properly and shall not materially impair the use of the structure by its inhabitants. However, no action may be brought for a violation of this subdivision more than four years after close of escrow." The electrical-system standard in subdivision (f) uses parallel four-year language. Other standards in subdivision (g) carry shorter embedded limits: the interunit noise-transmission standard in (g)(6) states that "no action shall be brought pursuant to this paragraph more than one year from the original occupancy of the adjacent unit," while the paint-and-stains standard in (g)(10) states a five-year limit running from close of escrow. These standard-specific time limits operate alongside, and independently of, the Act's outer 10-year limitations period discussed in a separate clause of this document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific, verified examples drawn from California's actionable construction-defect standards — not a claim that these four examples represent the full scope, severity, or relative importance of § 896's standards, and not a claim about which state's law governs a particular defect. All four citations below are numbered standards within the same statutory section, Civil Code § 896, rather than independently authored sources, so they corroborate one internally consistent list rather than four separate ones. This clause deliberately does not attempt to reproduce § 896's full list of standards (which runs to dozens of numbered items across subdivisions (a) through (g)), and it does not state whether a particular observed condition meets the technical elements of any specific standard, when a particular standard's clock (such as "close of escrow" or "original occupancy") actually started running on particular facts, or what standard (if any) applies to a defect not resembling these four examples.

clauses.title: The Mandatory Prelitigation Notice of Claim
clauses.body: Before filing an action against any party alleged to have contributed to a violation of the § 896 standards, Civil Code § 910 requires a claimant to initiate a prelitigation procedure, beginning with written notice. Section 910(a) requires the claimant or the claimant's legal representative to "provide written notice via certified mail, overnight mail, or personal delivery to the builder" of the claimant's claim that the residence's construction violates one or more of the § 896 standards, and specifies what the notice must contain: it "shall provide the claimant's name, address, and preferred method of contact, and shall state that the claimant alleges a violation pursuant to this part against the builder, and shall describe the claim in reasonable detail sufficient to determine the nature and location, to the extent known, of the claimed violation." For a group of homeowners or an association, the notice may identify claimants solely by address or another description sufficient to apprise the builder of the affected residences. The statute treats this written notice as formally significant — "[t]hat document shall have the same force and effect as a notice of commencement of a legal proceeding" — and it is distinct from, and not satisfied by, a request made instead through a builder's own contractual, warranty, or customer-service process. Once notice is served, Civil Code § 913 requires the builder or the builder's representative to "acknowledge, in writing, receipt of the notice of the claim within 14 days after receipt of the notice of the claim," and, if the claimant is represented by an attorney, to include that attorney in subsequent substantive communications.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's actual prelitigation notice requirement for a construction-defect claim under the Right to Repair Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular claim, and not a claim that other states impose a comparable prelitigation notice-and-repair requirement. The two citations below are to different code sections (§ 910 and § 913) within the same statutory chapter (Chapter 4 of Title 7, added by the same 2002 enacting bill, SB 800), rather than to independently authored sources outside that single legislative scheme; they are treated here as corroborating one internally consistent prelitigation process rather than as independent confirmations from unrelated sources. This clause does not state what level of factual detail satisfies "reasonable detail sufficient to determine the nature and location" of a claimed violation on particular facts, whether a particular notice was properly served under § 910's specified delivery methods, or what happens under this title when the underlying claim is not the kind the Act's prelitigation chapter reaches at all (for example, claims outside § 896's scope).

citations.quote: The claimant or his or her legal representative shall provide written notice via certified mail, overnight mail, or personal delivery to the builder, in the manner prescribed in this section, of the claimant's claim that the construction of his or her residence violates any of the standards set forth in Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 896). That notice shall provide the claimant's name, address, and preferred method of contact, and shall state that the claimant alleges a violation pursuant to this part against the builder, and shall describe the claim in reasonable detail sufficient to determine the nature and location, to the extent known, of the claimed violation. ... That document shall have the same force and effect as a notice of commencement of a legal proceeding.

clauses.title: The Builder's Inspection and Repair-Offer Process, and the Homeowner's Response
clauses.body: If a builder elects to inspect the claimed unmet standards, Civil Code § 916(a) requires the builder to "complete the initial inspection and testing within 14 days after acknowledgment of receipt of the notice of the claim, at a mutually convenient date and time," with all inspection and testing costs borne by the builder. Within 30 days of that inspection (or a second inspection, if the builder reasonably requests one), Civil Code § 917 allows the builder to "offer in writing to repair the violation," and requires that offer to compensate the homeowner for applicable damages recoverable under § 944, and to include "a detailed, specific, step-by-step statement identifying the particular violation that is being repaired, explaining the nature, scope, and location of the repair, and setting a reasonable completion date for the repair," along with the names, license numbers, and contact information of the contractors the builder intends to use. Once the homeowner receives that offer, Civil Code § 918 gives the homeowner 30 days to authorize the builder to proceed, or, at the homeowner's option, to instead request "the names, addresses, telephone numbers, and license numbers for up to three alternative contractors who are not owned or financially controlled by the builder and who regularly conduct business in the county where the structure is located" — after which the statute sets further deadlines (a 20-day additional inspection window if the homeowner so elects, 35 days for the builder to present a choice of contractors, and 20 more days for the homeowner to authorize a repair).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's actual builder-inspection and repair-offer timeline under the Right to Repair Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular claim, and not a claim that other states impose a comparable process. The three citations below (§§ 916, 917, and 918) are separate code sections within the same statutory chapter (Chapter 4 of Title 7, added by the same 2002 enacting bill, SB 800) rather than independently authored sources outside that single legislative scheme, and are treated here as corroborating one internally consistent process rather than as independent confirmations. This clause does not reproduce every procedural detail of §§ 916 through 918 (for example, the second-inspection process under § 916(c), or the consequences under § 916(d) if a builder fails to inspect at all, which a separate clause of this document does not independently verify), and it does not state what happens on particular facts if a deadline described here is missed, disputed, or extended by agreement.

Any such offer shall be accompanied by a detailed, specific, step-by-step statement identifying the particular violation that is being repaired, explaining the nature, scope, and location of the repair, and setting a reasonable completion date for the repair.

The homeowner may alternatively request, at the homeowner's sole option and discretion, that the builder provide the names, addresses, telephone numbers, and license numbers for up to three alternative contractors who are not owned or financially controlled by the builder and who regularly conduct business in the county where the structure is located.

clauses.title: The Act's Outer Limitations Period, and Tolling During the Prelitigation Process
clauses.body: Apart from the shorter, standard-specific time limits embedded within particular § 896 standards, the Right to Repair Act sets a general outer boundary on when an action may be brought at all. Civil Code § 941(a) provides: "Except as specifically set forth in this title, no action may be brought to recover under this title more than 10 years after substantial completion of the improvement but not later than the date of recordation of a valid notice of completion." Separately, Civil Code § 927 addresses what happens to an otherwise-running limitations period while the prelitigation notice-and-repair process is underway: "If the applicable statute of limitations has otherwise run during this process, the time period for filing a complaint or other legal remedies for violation of any provision of this title, or for a claim of inadequate repair, is extended from the time of the original claim by the claimant to 100 days after the repair is completed, whether or not the particular violation is the one being repaired." Section 927 also addresses the builder's non-participation: if the builder fails to timely acknowledge the claim, elects not to proceed under the statutory process, or fails to timely request an inspection, the filing period is instead extended "to 45 days after the time for responding to the notice of claim has expired."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's actual outer limitations period and prelitigation-tolling rule under the Right to Repair Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular claim's timing, and not a claim that other states impose a comparable 10-year outer period or tolling rule. The two citations below (§ 941(a) and § 927) are separate code sections within the same statutory title (Title 7, added by the same 2002 enacting bill, SB 800) rather than independently authored sources outside that single legislative scheme. This clause does not state how the 10-year period under § 941(a) interacts, on particular facts, with the shorter standard-specific periods embedded in individual § 896 standards described in a companion clause, does not address § 941's separate rules on tolling doctrine generally or on indemnity actions, and does not state when a particular improvement reached "substantial completion" or when a particular "notice of completion" was validly recorded.

clauses.title: Recoverable Damages and the Act's Statutory Affirmative Defenses
clauses.body: Civil Code § 944 limits what a homeowner may recover in a damages claim under the Right to Repair Act: "the homeowner is only entitled to damages for the reasonable value of repairing any violation of the standards set forth in this title, the reasonable cost of repairing any damages caused by the repair efforts, the reasonable cost of repairing and rectifying any damages resulting from the failure of the home to meet the standards, the reasonable cost of removing and replacing any improper repair by the builder, reasonable relocation and storage expenses, lost business income if the home was used as a principal place of a business licensed to be operated from the home, reasonable investigative costs for each established violation, and all other costs or fees recoverable by contract or statute." Separately, Civil Code § 945.5 gives a builder (and, correspondingly, a general contractor, subcontractor, material supplier, individual product manufacturer, or design professional) a defined set of affirmative defenses, available "under the principles of comparative fault," that can excuse liability in whole or in part — including, among others, an "unforeseen act of nature" exceeding the applicable design criteria (§ 945.5(a)), a homeowner's "unreasonable failure to minimize or prevent" damages, including failing to allow reasonable and timely access for inspection and repair or failing to give timely notice after discovering a violation (§ 945.5(b)), and a homeowner's failure to follow the builder's or manufacturer's written maintenance recommendations, where the builder shows those recommendations were reasonably communicated and reasonable when issued (§ 945.5(c)).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's actual damages measure and statutory affirmative defenses under the Right to Repair Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular claim's damages or defenses, and not a claim that other states provide a comparable statutory defense list. The two citations below (§ 944 and § 945.5) are separate code sections within the same statutory chapter (Chapter 5 of Title 7, added or amended by the same 2002/2003 enacting legislation) rather than independently authored sources outside that single legislative scheme. This clause does not reproduce all of § 945.5's defenses (it also lists, among others, a homeowner's alterations or misuse, a builder's successful repair of the particular violation, and the running of the applicable time limitation, in § 945.5(d) through (g), not independently quoted here), and it does not state whether a particular defense would actually succeed, in whole or in part, on any specific set of facts — that determination belongs to a court or other body with authority to decide the question.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: {{preparerName}} is reviewing this information sheet in connection with {{trustName}}, created by {{settlorName}} as settlor, naming {{trusteeName}} as trustee. This information sheet describes, on a general informational basis only, California's statutory Rule Against Perpetuities, Probate Code §§ 21200–21231 (the Uniform Statutory Rule Against Perpetuities as adopted and modified in California), which limits how long a nonvested property interest or an unexercised power of appointment created under an instrument such as {{trustName}} may remain contingent before it must vest, terminate, or otherwise resolve. It describes the statutory two-alternative validity test, the parallel rule for powers of appointment, the judicial reformation remedy available for an interest that would otherwise violate the rule, and certain exclusions the statute itself states. This information sheet does not identify, evaluate, or reach any conclusion about whether any specific provision of {{trustName}}, or of any other instrument, actually satisfies or violates this rule; whether a particular nonvested property interest or power of appointment is valid under Probate Code §§ 21200–21231 depends on the precise terms of the instrument creating it and is a legal determination this information sheet does not make.

clauses.title: Statutory Citation, Supersession of the Common Law Rule, and Scope
clauses.body: The statutory scheme now governing how long a nonvested property interest — a property interest that has not yet vested, such as many contingent trust interests — and an unexercised power of appointment may remain contingent in California is Probate Code Part 2 (§§ 21200–21231), formally cited as the Uniform Statutory Rule Against Perpetuities. This statutory scheme supersedes California's earlier common-law rule against perpetuities (the traditional rule requiring that an interest be certain to vest, if at all, within "lives in being plus 21 years") rather than operating alongside it. Except for a property interest or power of appointment whose validity has already been determined in a judicial proceeding or by a settlement among interested persons, the statutory scheme applies to nonvested property interests and unexercised powers of appointment regardless of whether they were created before, on, or after January 1, 1992.
clauses.gap: This clause cites three separate California Probate Code sections — § 21200, § 21201, and § 21202 — that together form Article 1 (General Provisions) of the same statutory part; they are independent code sections but not independent legal sources of each other, since all three were enacted together as part of the same 1991 adoption of the Uniform Statutory Rule Against Perpetuities. Each section was fetched twice independently from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (two distinct browser User-Agent strings) and returned byte-identical text (after whitespace normalization) both times. California's version is a modified adoption of the Uniform Statutory Rule Against Perpetuities and may not be identical in every respect to the original Uniform Act or to another state's version of it; this clause describes only California's enacted text and does not independently compare it to the Uniform Act or to any other state's statute. Neither this clause nor the cited sections define "nonvested property interest"; no separate statutory definitions section for that term was located within Probate Code §§ 21200–21231, and the description of the term here reflects how the statute uses it rather than a quoted statutory definition. This is California-specific law; it does not describe the rule against perpetuities of any other state.

(b) This part does not apply to any property interest or power of appointment the validity of which has been determined in a judicial proceeding or by a settlement among interested persons.

clauses.title: The Two-Alternative Validity Test for a Nonvested Property Interest
clauses.body: California's statutory Rule Against Perpetuities does not use a single test for whether a nonvested property interest is valid. Under Probate Code § 21205, a nonvested property interest is invalid unless it satisfies at least one of two separate alternatives. The first is the traditional alternative: when the interest is created, it is certain to vest or terminate no later than 21 years after the death of an individual then alive. The second is the independent 90-year "wait-and-see" alternative: the interest actually vests or terminates within 90 years after its creation, whether or not it was certain to do so when it was created. An interest that cannot satisfy the first alternative when created is not automatically invalid — it can still be validated later by actually vesting or terminating within the 90-year period, and an interest is likewise valid if it meets the first alternative even though the 90-year period would also have been satisfied. The statute treats these as two independent routes to validity, not as a single combined test, and an interest is invalid only if it fails both.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section, Cal. Prob. Code § 21205; subdivisions (a) and (b) quoted together here are two subdivisions of that one section, not independent sources of each other, and are quoted together because the section states a single two-alternative test that cannot accurately be described from only one subdivision. The section was fetched twice independently from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (two distinct browser User-Agent strings) and returned byte-identical text (after whitespace normalization) both times. California's version is a modified adoption of the Uniform Statutory Rule Against Perpetuities and may not be identical in every respect to the original Uniform Act or to another state's version of it; no independent comparison to the Uniform Act or other states' statutes was performed. This clause does not address the parallel, separately codified rule for powers of appointment (Probate Code §§ 21206–21207) or the judicial reformation remedy (§ 21220), each addressed in other clauses of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21205 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the two-alternative statutory rule against perpetuities for a nonvested property interest
citations.quote: A nonvested property interest is invalid unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) When the interest is created, it is certain to vest or terminate no later than 21 years after the death of an individual then alive. (b) The interest either vests or terminates within 90 years after its creation.

clauses.title: Parallel Rule for Powers of Appointment
clauses.body: California's statutory Rule Against Perpetuities applies its two-alternative validity structure not only to nonvested property interests but, separately, to powers of appointment. Probate Code § 21206 addresses a general power of appointment that is not presently exercisable because of a condition precedent: the power is invalid unless, when created, the condition precedent is certain to be satisfied or become impossible to satisfy no later than 21 years after the death of an individual then alive, or the condition precedent actually is satisfied or becomes impossible to satisfy within 90 years after the power's creation. Probate Code § 21207 applies the same two-alternative structure to a nongeneral power of appointment or a general testamentary power of appointment: the power is invalid unless, when created, it is certain to be irrevocably exercised or otherwise to terminate no later than 21 years after the death of an individual then alive, or it actually is irrevocably exercised or otherwise terminates within 90 years after its creation.
clauses.gap: § 21206 and § 21207 are two separate California Probate Code sections, each independently fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (two distinct browser User-Agent strings) with byte-identical text (after whitespace normalization) returned both times for each. They are independent code sections from each other and from § 21205 (the nonvested-property-interest rule addressed in a separate clause of this document), but all three sit within the same Article 2 of the same 1991 statutory scheme and apply the identical 21-years/90-years structure to different subject matter (a condition precedent to exercise, in § 21206, versus irrevocable exercise or termination, in § 21207) rather than confirming the same fact through independent means. This clause does not address every provision of Article 2 (§§ 21205–21209); a related provision, § 21231, separately addresses how an individual described only as the spouse of a living person is treated for purposes of measuring the 21-years-after-death alternative, and is not covered here.

citations.quote: A general power of appointment not presently exercisable because of a condition precedent is invalid unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) When the power is created, the condition precedent is certain to be satisfied or become impossible to satisfy no later than 21 years after the death of an individual then alive. (b) The condition precedent either is satisfied or becomes impossible to satisfy within 90 years after its creation.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21207 (California Legislative Information text)
