citations.quote: A nongeneral power of appointment or a general testamentary power of appointment is invalid unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) When the power is created, it is certain to be irrevocably exercised or otherwise to terminate no later than 21 years after the death of an individual then alive. (b) The power is irrevocably exercised or otherwise terminates within 90 years after its creation.

clauses.title: Judicial Reformation Remedy for an Interest That Would Otherwise Violate the Rule
clauses.body: California's statutory scheme provides a judicial reformation remedy rather than leaving every interest that would otherwise fail the rule permanently void. Under Probate Code § 21220, on the petition of an interested person, a court shall reform a disposition in the manner that most closely approximates the transferor's manifested plan of distribution, and the reformed disposition must itself stay within the 90 years allowed by the applicable provision in Article 2 (§§ 21205–21209). This remedy is available if any one of three conditions is satisfied: a nonvested property interest or a power of appointment has already become invalid under the statutory rule; a class gift is not yet invalid but might become invalid, and the time has arrived when the share of any class member is to take effect in possession or enjoyment; or a nonvested property interest that is not validated by the traditional 21-years-after-death alternative of § 21205(a) can vest, but not within 90 years after its creation. The reformation is framed as mandatory ("a court shall reform") once a petition is filed and one of the three triggering conditions is established, and it uses the transferor's own manifested plan of distribution — approximated as closely as possible within the 90-year outer limit — as its guiding standard, rather than simply voiding the interest or substituting a court's own preferred disposition.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section, Cal. Prob. Code § 21220, fetched twice independently from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (two distinct browser User-Agent strings) with byte-identical text (after whitespace normalization) returned both times. The section's own cross-references to § 21205 (repeated in the introductory clause and in subdivisions (a), (b), and (c)) are quotations of that same statutory language already addressed in this document's clause on the two-alternative test, not an independent source. § 21220 does not itself define "interested person" or specify the procedural mechanics of a reformation petition (for example, which court, what showing beyond the three listed conditions, or how competing petitions are resolved); this clause does not go beyond what § 21220 states to fill in those gaps. Whether a court will actually reform a given disposition, and what reformed terms it will adopt, depends on the specific facts and the transferor's actual manifested plan of distribution in each case — something this clause does not evaluate for any particular instrument.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21220 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the judicial reformation remedy for an interest that would otherwise violate the statutory rule against perpetuities
citations.quote: On petition of an interested person, a court shall reform a disposition in the manner that most closely approximates the transferor’s manifested plan of distribution and is within the 90 years allowed by the applicable provision in Article 2 (commencing with Section 21205), if any of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) A nonvested property interest or a power of appointment becomes invalid under the statutory rule against perpetuities provided in Article 2 (commencing with Section 21205). (b) A class gift is not but might become invalid under the statutory rule against perpetuities provided in Article 2 (commencing with Section 21205), and the time has arrived when the share of any class member is to take effect in possession or enjoyment. (c) A nonvested property interest that is not validated by subdivision (a) of Section 21205 can vest but not within 90 years after its creation.

clauses.title: Statutory Exclusions From the Rule
clauses.body: The statutory rule of § 21205 does not apply to every nonvested property interest or power of appointment; Probate Code § 21225 lists categories the rule does not reach. Most broadly, the rule does not apply to a nonvested property interest or power of appointment arising out of a nondonative transfer — except that eight specifically listed categories of nondonative transfer remain subject to the rule despite arising from a bargained-for exchange rather than a gift: a premarital or postmarital agreement, a separation or divorce settlement, a spouse's election, a similar arrangement arising out of a marital relationship, a contract to make or not to revoke a will or trust, a contract to exercise or not to exercise a power of appointment, a transfer in satisfaction of a duty of support, or a reciprocal transfer. Separately excluded, without any carve-back, are: a fiduciary's power relating to the administration or management of assets, including the power to sell, lease, or mortgage property and the power to determine principal and income; a power to appoint a fiduciary; a trustee's discretionary power to distribute principal to a beneficiary who already holds an indefeasibly vested interest in the trust's income and principal, before the trust terminates; a nonvested property interest held by a charity, government, or governmental agency or subdivision, where that interest is preceded by an interest held by another charity, government, or governmental agency or subdivision; a nonvested property interest or power of appointment in a pension, profit-sharing, stock bonus, health, disability, death benefit, income deferral, or similar employee benefit plan, except one created by an election of a participant, beneficiary, or spouse; a property interest, power of appointment, or arrangement that was not subject to the common law rule against perpetuities or that is excluded by another California statute; and a trust created to provide benefits under hospital service contracts, group life insurance, group disability insurance, group annuities, or a combination of those, as defined in the Insurance Code.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section, Cal. Prob. Code § 21225; its eight subdivisions, (a) through (h), are quoted together as one continuous exact substring and are not independent of each other. The section was fetched twice independently from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (two distinct browser User-Agent strings) with byte-identical text (after whitespace normalization) returned both times; the retrieved text shows the section was last amended in 1996 (effective January 1, 1997), not merely as originally added in 1991. Subdivision (a)'s structure is a double exclusion — the rule generally does not apply to nondonative transfers, but the eight listed categories are carved back out of that exclusion and so remain subject to the rule — and this clause's description preserves that structure rather than simplifying it into a single list. This clause does not independently verify how § 21225(f)'s cross-referenced federal or state employee-benefit-plan concepts (for example, what qualifies as a "pension" or "profit-sharing" plan for this purpose) are defined elsewhere; it states only what § 21225 itself says.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21225 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, statutory exclusions from the rule against perpetuities
citations.quote: Article 2 (commencing with Section 21205) does not apply to any of the following: (a) A nonvested property interest or a power of appointment arising out of a nondonative transfer, except a nonvested property interest or a power of appointment arising out of (1) a premarital or postmarital agreement, (2) a separation or divorce settlement, (3) a spouse’s election, (4) or a similar arrangement arising out of a prospective, existing, or previous marital relationship between the parties, (5) a contract to make or not to revoke a will or trust, (6) a contract to exercise or not to exercise a power of appointment, (7) a transfer in satisfaction of a duty of support, or (8) a reciprocal transfer. (b) A fiduciary’s power relating to the administration or management of assets, including the power of a fiduciary to sell, lease, or mortgage property, and the power of a fiduciary to determine principal and income. (c) A power to appoint a fiduciary. (d) A discretionary power of a trustee to distribute principal before termination of a trust to a beneficiary having an indefeasibly vested interest in the income and principal. (e) A nonvested property interest held by a charity, government, or governmental agency or subdivision, if the nonvested property interest is preceded by an interest held by another charity, government, or governmental agency or subdivision. (f) A nonvested property interest in or a power of appointment with respect to a trust or other property arrangement forming part of a pension, profit-sharing, stock bonus, health, disability, death benefit, income deferral, or other current or deferred benefit plan for one or more employees, independent contractors, or their beneficiaries or spouses, to which contributions are made for the purpose of distributing to or for the benefit of the participants or their beneficiaries or spouses the property, income, or principal in the trust or other property arrangement, except a nonvested property interest or a power of appointment that is created by an election of a participant or a beneficiary or spouse. (g) A property interest, power of appointment, or arrangement that was not subject to the common law rule against perpetuities or is excluded by another statute of this state. (h) A trust created for the purpose of providing for its beneficiaries under hospital service contracts, group life insurance, group disability insurance, group annuities, or any combination of such insurance, as defined in the Insurance Code.

clauses.title: About This Right-to-a-Copy-of-Signed-Documents Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes a California statutory right that can arise in connection with {{companyName}}'s hiring and employment of {{employeeName}} for the position of {{jobTitle}}: the right of an employee or applicant who signs an instrument relating to obtaining or holding employment to receive a copy of that instrument. It summarizes selected requirements of California Labor Code section 432. It is not a determination that any specific instrument signed by {{employeeName}}, any specific request made to {{companyName}}, or any specific copy furnished or withheld by {{companyName}} in connection with the {{jobTitle}} position complies or fails to comply with Section 432, and it does not itself make or satisfy a request, furnish a copy, or create any recordkeeping duty.

clauses.title: The Core Right: Any Signed Instrument Relating to Obtaining or Holding Employment
clauses.body: California law gives an employee or applicant who signs an instrument relating to obtaining or holding employment a right to receive a copy of that instrument. By its own text, the statute is not limited to a named category of document, such as an offer letter, an arbitration agreement, or a policy acknowledgment; it extends, on its face, to any instrument that an employee or applicant signs relating to the obtaining or holding of employment. The right belongs to "an employee or applicant" alike, so its text does not, on its face, distinguish between someone already on the payroll and someone who has not yet been hired.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432), used as real evidence of California's copy-of-signed-instrument right — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The section is a single, undivided sentence with no lettered or numbered subdivisions, so this citation and the citations in this information sheet's other authority clauses on Section 432 are drawn from that same one sentence; they are not independent corroborating sources of one another. The statute does not itself define "instrument" or state what makes a document "relating to the obtaining or holding of employment," and this clause does not resolve where that line falls for any particular document a particular employer uses. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific document used by any particular employer is or is not an "instrument" within the meaning of Section 432, and does not determine that any particular employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with it.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, right to a copy of a signed employment-related instrument
citations.quote: If an employee or applicant signs any instrument relating to the obtaining or holding of employment, he shall be given a copy of the instrument upon request.

clauses.title: Compliance Is Triggered by a Request, Not Made Automatic at the Time of Signing
clauses.body: By its own text, Section 432 conditions the duty to furnish a copy on a request: the statute provides that a signer "shall be given a copy of the instrument upon request." The statute's text does not state that a copy must be furnished automatically, without any request, at the time of signing. Its text also does not itself specify a deadline within which a copy must be furnished after a request is made, the form a request must take, whether it must be written or may be oral, or the person or office within an employer's organization to whom a request must be directed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432), the same single, undivided sentence relied on in this information sheet's other authority clauses addressing Section 432; it is not an independent corroborating source. The reading that the duty is request-triggered rather than automatic rests on the plain "upon request" language quoted in this clause's citation; the statute does not separately use words like "automatically" or "at signing" in either direction, and this clause does not resolve how promptly "upon request" must be honored once a request is made. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific request made or not made, or any specific copy furnished or withheld, by any particular employer toward any particular applicant or employee complied or failed to comply with Section 432.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432 (California Legislative Information text)

clauses.title: What Section 432's Text Does Not Specify — Deadline, Method, and Remedy
clauses.body: Section 432, in its own current text, does not specify a time limit within which an employer must furnish a requested copy, does not specify a required method or format for furnishing it, and does not itself state a penalty, civil remedy, or enforcement procedure for a failure to furnish a copy upon request. The section is a single, undivided provision, unlike some neighboring Labor Code sections on related hiring-document subjects that are broken into lettered or numbered subdivisions.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 432), used to document what its own text does and does not say — not a claim that no other law anywhere addresses timing, format, or remedy for a request of this kind, and not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. This finding of statutory silence was reached by reading the section's complete current codified text, which is short enough to read in full, rather than a partial excerpt; the current codified version verified for this clause carries the annotation "(Amended by Stats. 1969, Ch. 714.)," confirming this is the section's current, unrepealed form as of the checked date, last amended in 1969. This clause does not identify any regulation, opinion letter, or reported court decision that fills these silences — an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. A separate California statute, Labor Code section 1198.5, gives an employee or former employee a distinct right to inspect and receive copies of the employee's own personnel records and, unlike Section 432, does specify a response timeframe; this clause does not state that Section 432's copy-of-signed-instrument right and Section 1198.5's personnel-file-inspection right are the same right, that they share a timeframe, or that Section 432 incorporates Section 1198.5's timeframe by reference — nothing in Section 432's own text cross-references Section 1198.5. This clause is informational only and does not determine that any particular employer's practices are compliant or noncompliant with Section 432.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, full operative text confirming the absence of a deadline, method, or remedy provision
citations.quote: If an employee or applicant signs any instrument relating to the obtaining or holding of employment, he shall be given a copy of the instrument upon request.

clauses.title: Statutory Placement Among the Labor Code's Hiring-Document Provisions
clauses.body: Section 432 appears in Article 3, "Contracts and Applications for Employment," a group of Labor Code sections numbered 430 through 435 addressing contracts and applications for employment. Other sections within that same numeric range address different subjects: Section 432.2 addresses polygraph, lie detector, and similar examinations required as a condition of employment; Section 432.5 addresses requiring an employee or applicant to agree in writing to a term or condition known to be prohibited by law; and Section 432.7 addresses inquiries into certain arrest, detention, and pretrial or posttrial diversion program history. None of those neighboring sections, in their own text, address an employee's or applicant's right to receive a copy of an instrument that employee or applicant has signed; within this article, that specific right appears in Section 432 alone.

clauses.title: Information and Background — Refusal to Perform Work Believed Hazardous
clauses.body:
I, {{employeeName}}, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment with {{companyName}}, where my job title is {{jobTitle}}. The work I am describing here is: {{workDescription}}. I believed that performing this work, under the circumstances I describe here, would violate an occupational safety or health standard, a safety order, or a provision of the Labor Code, in a way that would create a real and apparent hazard. I describe that hazard here as: {{incidentDescription}}. This work was to be performed at {{incidentLocation}}, and the date on which I refused to perform it is {{incidentDate}}. The supervisor or other representative of {{companyName}} I discussed this with, if any, is {{supervisorName}}.

This information sheet describes California Labor Code sections 6310, 6311, and 6312 — statutes addressing an employee's refusal to perform work that would violate an occupational safety or health standard, order, or the Labor Code itself where doing so would create a real and apparent hazard, and a related, broader protection for certain workplace safety complaints and other specified safety-related conduct. This California law applies to employment within California; it does not describe the law of any other state. Completing this sheet is not a complaint or petition. It does not file anything with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, the United States Department of Labor, or any court, and does not itself establish that performing the work described above would in fact have violated any safety standard, order, or Labor Code provision, that a real and apparent hazard in fact existed, or that any adverse action taken by {{companyName}} was connected to the refusal described here. Only the Labor Commissioner, a court, or another body with jurisdiction over a specific complaint can determine whether a violation of these statutes occurred.

clauses.title: The Core Right — Refusing Work That Would Violate a Safety Standard, Order, or the Labor Code Itself
clauses.body: California law provides that no employee shall be laid off or discharged for refusing to perform work in the performance of which the Labor Code (including Labor Code section 6400), any occupational safety or health standard, or any safety order of the Division of Occupational Safety and Health or the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Board will be violated, where the violation would create a real and apparent hazard to the employee or the employee's fellow employees. The statute's own text states two conditions, both of which must be present: first, that performing the work would violate the Labor Code itself, an occupational safety or health standard, or a safety order of the division or the standards board; and second, that the violation would create a hazard that is both real and apparent to the employee or a fellow employee. This is a California statute; it does not describe the law of any other state.

The quote below was confirmed as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of that fetched text. The statute's own text does not itself define the phrase 'real and apparent hazard,' and this research session did not independently verify any published California appellate decision construing that phrase, so this clause states only what the statute's own text says and does not supply a definition beyond it — that is disclosed here as an honest gap rather than filled in with an assumed standard. This document does not itself determine that any specific work would in fact have violated a safety standard, order, or Labor Code provision, or that a real and apparent hazard in fact existed in any specific case.

clauses.title: What the Statute's Own Text Does — and Does Not — Condition the Right On
clauses.body: Labor Code section 6311's own text conditions the right described elsewhere in this document only on the two elements stated in that same text: that performing the work would violate the Labor Code, an occupational safety or health standard, or a safety order of the division or standards board, and that the violation would create a real and apparent hazard to the employee or a fellow employee. The statute's own text does not itself state, as a separate express precondition to that right, that the employee must first have notified the employer of the hazard, asked that it be corrected, or waited any specific period of time before refusing to perform the work.

A general web search conducted in this research session located secondary, non-statutory sources — including practitioner and legal-aid summaries — describing a practice of first notifying a supervisor of the hazard and asking that it be corrected, and describing conditions resembling the standard for refusing hazardous work under the separate federal Occupational Safety and Health Act framework (29 C.F.R. § 1977.12(b)(2)), which asks whether a reasonable person would conclude there is a real danger of death or serious injury and there is insufficient time to eliminate the danger through resort to regular statutory enforcement channels. This document accordingly does not state a prior-notice precondition, a waiting period, or the federal reasonable-person/imminent-danger standard as if it were part of Labor Code section 6311's own text, and discloses this as an honest, deliberate gap rather than filling it in with an assumed or borrowed standard. clauses.title: The Remedy the Statute Itself Provides — A Right of Action for Wages, Not Automatic Continued Pay
clauses.body: The same statute provides that an employee who is laid off or discharged in violation of section 6311, or who is otherwise not paid because the employee refused to perform work under the circumstances described elsewhere in this document, has a right of action for wages for the time the employee is without work as a result of the layoff or discharge. This is a right of action — a basis to pursue a legal remedy for the wages lost during that time — rather than a guarantee that an employee who refuses work under this statute automatically continues to receive pay while the refusal is ongoing. Section 6311's protection also extends to a domestic work employee, with a specific exception for a person who performs household domestic service that is publicly funded.

The statute's own text does not itself state a filing deadline for this right of action; a separate clause of this document addresses the one-year deadline (extendable for good cause) that applies to a Labor Commissioner complaint filed under Labor Code sections 6312 and 98.7, but this document does not assume that the same deadline necessarily governs a right of action for wages framed as a direct civil claim under section 6311 itself, as distinct from that administrative complaint route — this research session did not independently verify a specific limitations period for such a direct claim, and that is disclosed here as an honest gap. clauses.title: Enforcement Procedure — A Labor Commissioner Complaint Under Sections 6312 and 98.7, With Deadlines Distinct From Other Retaliation Claims
clauses.body: A separate statute provides that an employee who believes they have been discharged or otherwise discriminated against in violation of Labor Code section 6310 or 6311 may file a complaint with the Labor Commissioner. The statute governing that complaint procedure generally allows a complaint to be filed within one year after the occurrence of the violation, a period that may be extended for good cause, and it requires the Labor Commissioner to inform a complainant charging a violation of section 6310 or 6311, at the time of initial contact, of the complainant's right to file a separate, concurrent complaint with the United States Department of Labor within 30 days after the occurrence of the violation. That same procedural statute also provides an appeal path to the Director of Industrial Relations, available specifically for cases arising under sections 6310 and 6311, from a Labor Commissioner determination that would otherwise be final for other categories of claims within the Labor Commissioner's jurisdiction.

Both were fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and each confirmed textually identical (after whitespace normalization) across two independent fetches in this research session using distinct User-Agent strings on 2026-09-04; each quote below was confirmed as an exact substring of its respective fetched text. The one-year period described here governs the administrative complaint filed with the Division under sections 6312 and 98.7; as disclosed in a separate clause of this document, this research session did not independently verify whether the same one-year period governs the distinct right of action for wages that section 6311 itself provides. clauses.title: A Genuinely Broader, Separate Protection — Section 6310's Complaint-Based Prohibition
clauses.body: A separate statute, Labor Code section 6310, prohibits an employer from discharging or in any manner discriminating against an employee because the employee made an oral or written complaint about employee safety or health to the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, another responsible government agency, the employer, or the employer's representative; instituted or participated in a related proceeding; participated in an employer-employee occupational health and safety committee; or reported a work-related fatality, injury, or illness, requested certain injury or illness records, or exercised other rights protected by the federal Occupational Safety and Health Act. This protection is genuinely broader than, and distinct from, the refusal-to-perform-work right described elsewhere in this document: it protects making a safety-related complaint or engaging in the other listed conduct, generally, whether or not the employee ever refused to perform any specific work. An employee who prevails on this protection is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts, and an employer who willfully refuses to rehire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee determined eligible for that relief through a grievance procedure, arbitration, or hearing authorized by law is guilty of a misdemeanor. The same statute separately prohibits retaliation against an employee because the employee is a family member of a person who has, or is perceived to have, engaged in conduct this statute protects. This statute's own text expressly excludes from its coverage a case in which the employee alleges retaliation for having filed or made known an intention to file a workers' compensation claim under Labor Code section 132a, which it states is instead under the exclusive jurisdiction of the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board.

Before drafting this document, the corpus's existing Workers' Compensation Retaliation (Labor Code Section 132a) information sheet was read in full to confirm no duplication: that document covers Labor Code section 132a's separate prohibition on retaliation for filing, or making known an intention to file, a workers' compensation claim, adjudicated before the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board rather than through the Labor Commissioner complaint procedure addressed in this document; section 6310's own text, quoted in this clause, expressly carves that category of claim out of its own coverage and confirms it is committed to the appeals board's exclusive jurisdiction, so this document does not restate or duplicate that separate document's coverage. clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes a qualified legal immunity that California Civil Code § 47(c) can provide for a job-reference communication from {{companyName}} about {{employeeName}}'s job performance or qualifications. It is a companion resource to, and is distinct from, this project's Neutral Reference / Employment Verification Policy document: that document sets out an employer's internal reference-handling policy choices, while this document explains only the underlying statutory immunity itself -- what § 47(c) covers, what published California case law says "without malice" requires, the specific rehire-related protections the statute adds, and where the statute's own text says the privilege does not reach. This document states California law as background information. It does not tell {{companyName}} what to communicate to {{inquiringPartyName}} about {{employeeName}}, and it does not determine whether any particular past or future communication about {{employeeName}} was, or will be, privileged.

clauses.title: The Underlying Privilege — Civil Code § 47(c)
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 47(c) makes certain communications "privileged" -- meaning they cannot support a defamation claim under California law -- when made without malice to a person interested in the communication, under any one of three circumstances the statute lists in the disjunctive: the communication is made (1) by someone who is also interested in the subject, (2) by someone who stands in a relation to the interested person that affords a reasonable ground for supposing the communication's motive to be innocent, or (3) by someone the interested person has requested to give the information. This is the general common-interest privilege framework; a more specific set of rules within the same subdivision, addressed in this document's companion clauses, governs communications about an applicant's job performance or qualifications specifically.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a qualified reference privilege of this kind exists in California -- not a claim about which state's law governs a particular communication. This clause quotes the general chapeau language of § 47(c) that precedes its employment-specific sentences; this document's other authority clauses quote and address those employment-specific sentences separately. All of this document's statutory citations are to subdivisions and sentences within the single subsection Civil Code § 47(c) -- they are not independent of one another, and that lack of independence is disclosed here rather than presented as multiple separate sources. The statutory text was confirmed by fetching Cal. Civ. Code § 47 directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov twice, using two different User-Agent strings and request headers, on 2026-09-04; both fetches produced byte-identical section text once whitespace was normalized.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 47(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code
citations.quote: In a communication, without malice, to a person interested therein, (1) by one who is also interested, or (2) by one who stands in such a relation to the person interested as to afford a reasonable ground for supposing the motive for the communication to be innocent, or (3) who is requested by the person interested to give the information.

clauses.title: The Employment-Reference Sentence and "Credible Evidence"
clauses.body: Within § 47(c), a sentence added by a 1994 amendment applies the privilege specifically to a communication concerning an applicant's job performance or qualifications: it covers a communication based upon credible evidence, made without malice, by a current or former employer to, and upon request of, one the employer reasonably believes is a prospective employer of the applicant. Published California case law construing this exact sentence has held that the phrase "based on credible evidence" does not lower the applicable standard to ordinary negligence. A California Court of Appeal, addressing a former employer's statement to a background-check company (a prospective employer's agent) about a former employee, held that the Legislature did not intend, by adding that phrase, to make the privilege inapplicable in the employment-reference context merely because an employer's statement turned out to be negligently mistaken -- malice, not negligence, remains the standard a plaintiff must meet to defeat the privilege.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and one state's published appellate case construing it -- not a claim about which state's law governs a particular reference. The statutory citation here is to a sentence within the same Civil Code § 47(c) subsection cited in this document's other authority clauses, so it is not an independent statutory source. The case citation (Noel v. River Hills Wilsons, Inc.) was located and read via the CourtListener MCP server; its text was retrieved through two separate CourtListener tool calls (a full-document read and a chunked read of the same opinion), and its citation and published status were independently cross-checked against CourtListener's separate case-cluster metadata endpoint, which returned the same reporter citation (113 Cal.App.4th 1363) and "Published" status. Attempts to verify the opinion text against a source outside CourtListener's own database -- Justia (HTTP 403), CourtListener's own public website (blocked by an automated-traffic check, HTTP 202 with no body), and Google Scholar (blocked by this environment's outbound network policy) -- were made but did not succeed from this research environment; that limitation on source independence is disclosed honestly rather than concealed. The underlying facts of Noel involved a mistaken statement about the wrong former employee (a factual error in a background check, not a rehire question specifically); this document's own account above is limited to the legal standard the case actually announced, not an extension of its facts to every kind of employment-reference error.

citations.cite: California Civil Code
citations.quote: This subdivision applies to and includes a communication concerning the job performance or qualifications of an applicant for employment, based upon credible evidence, made without malice, by a current or former employer of the applicant to, and upon request of, one whom the employer reasonably believes is a prospective employer of the applicant.

citations.case: Noel v. River Hills Wilsons, Inc.
citations.quote: we hold that in including the “based on credible evidence” language in the 1994 amendment to section 47, subdivision (c), the Legislature did not intend to make the common-interest privilege inapplicable in the employment reference context on a showing of the defendant’s mere negligence.

clauses.title: What "Without Malice" Requires — Published Case Law
clauses.body: Because § 47(c)'s privilege applies only "without malice," a communication made with malice falls outside it. A California Court of Appeal decision addressing this exact statutory language in the employment-reference context described the malice needed to defeat the privilege as "actual malice," established in either of two ways: a showing that the communication was motivated by hatred or ill will toward the person discussed, or a showing that the person making the communication lacked reasonable grounds for believing it true and therefore acted in reckless disregard of the other person's rights. The same body of California case law draws a further distinction: an honest mistake is not malice. Mere negligence -- an oversight, an unintentional error, or a careless mix-up -- is not by itself enough to establish malice; only negligence that rises to a reckless or wanton disregard for the truth, amounting to a willful disregard of or avoidance of accuracy, satisfies the standard.
clauses.gap: This is California case law construing a California statute -- not a claim about which state's law governs a particular communication, and not a claim about how any specific California court would resolve a specific dispute. This clause closes a gap left open in this project's earlier, briefer treatment of § 47(c) (the Neutral Reference / Employment Verification Policy document's reference_qualified_privilege clause), whose own gap field disclosed that independent case law on what defeats this privilege had not been verified because CourtListener research was rate-limited during that document's drafting and was not pursued further. That research was repeated here: Noel v. River Hills Wilsons, Inc. (2003) 113 Cal.App.4th 1363 was located via the CourtListener MCP server's search tool, read via two separate CourtListener tool calls, and cross-checked against CourtListener's separate case-cluster metadata endpoint for its citation and published status; independent verification outside CourtListener's own database was attempted (Justia returned HTTP 403; CourtListener's public website returned an empty HTTP 202 behind an automated-traffic check; Google Scholar was blocked by this environment's outbound network policy) but did not succeed, so this remains, honestly, a single-database confirmation rather than two fully independent ones. Whether any particular communication was made with malice, or with only negligence, is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve for any individual's situation.

citations.quote: The malice necessary to defeat a qualified privilege is “actual malice” which is established by a showing that the publication was motivated by hatred or ill will towards the plaintiff or by a showing that the defendant lacked reasonable grounds for belief in the truth of the publication and therefore acted in reckless disregard of the plaintiff’s rights

citations.quote: mere negligence ... in the sense of oversight or unintentional error, is not alone enough to constitute malice. It is only when the negligence amounts to a reckless or wanton disregard for the truth, so as to reasonably imply a wilful disregard for or avoidance of accuracy, that malice is shown.

clauses.title: Rehire Questions and Sexual-Harassment-Related Communications
clauses.body: The same statutory sentence adds two further, more specific protections. First, it lets a current or former employer, or the employer's agent, state -- without malice -- whether or not the employer would rehire a current or former employee, and whether a decision not to rehire is based on the employer's determination that the former employee engaged in sexual harassment. Second, and separately, the subdivision extends to a complaint of sexual harassment by an employee to an employer based upon credible evidence, and to communications between the employer and interested persons regarding such a complaint -- in both cases, only if made without malice. This second sentence is not limited to communications with a prospective employer; by its own terms it covers internal communications about a harassment complaint among the employer and other interested persons.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what these specific sentences within § 47(c) do and do not protect -- not a claim about which state's law governs a particular disclosure. Both quoted sentences come from the same Civil Code § 47(c) subsection quoted in this document's other authority clauses, so they are not independent statutory sources of each other; this corrects and substantially expands on an earlier, briefer description of the rehire-related language in this project's Neutral Reference / Employment Verification Policy document, which quoted only the rehire sentence and did not separately address the harassment-complaint sentence quoted here. No published California case law specifically construing either of these two sentences (as opposed to the general job-performance-and-qualifications sentence addressed in this document's other clauses) was located or verified for this clause; the malice standard described in this document's companion clause on that subject was developed in a case addressing the job-performance-and-qualifications language, and this document does not claim that standard has been judicially applied to these two more specific sentences, even though both sentences use the same "without malice" language.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 47(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code
citations.quote: This subdivision authorizes a current or former employer, or the employer’s agent, to answer, without malice, whether or not the employer would rehire a current or former employee and whether the decision to not rehire is based upon the employer’s determination that the former employee engaged in sexual harassment.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 47(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code
citations.quote: This subdivision applies to and includes a complaint of sexual harassment by an employee, without malice, to an employer based upon credible evidence and communications between the employer and interested persons, without malice, regarding a complaint of sexual harassment.

clauses.title: A Statutory Limit — Constitutionally Protected Speech or Activities
clauses.body: The same subdivision also states an express limit on its own reach: it does not apply to a communication concerning the speech or activities of an applicant for employment if that speech or activity is constitutionally protected, or is otherwise protected by Code of Civil Procedure § 527.3 (California's statute concerning labor-related peaceful picketing and speech) or any other provision of law. This carve-out means the employment-reference privilege described in this document's other clauses is not unlimited by its own terms -- it does not extend to every communication about a job applicant's job performance or qualifications, but excludes, at minimum, communications concerning constitutionally protected speech or activity.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of an express textual limit on California's employment-reference privilege -- not a claim about which state's law governs a particular communication, and not a claim about the outer boundary of what counts as "constitutionally protected" speech or activity in this context, which the statute does not itself define. This quoted sentence comes from the same Civil Code § 47(c) subsection quoted in this document's other authority clauses, so it is not an independent statutory source. No published California case law specifically applying this carve-out in the employment-reference context was located or verified during this research; that absence is reported honestly rather than filled with an unverified case citation, consistent with the discipline this document otherwise applies to the malice case law addressed in its companion clauses.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 47(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code
citations.quote: This subdivision does not apply to a communication concerning the speech or activities of an applicant for employment if the speech or activities are constitutionally protected, or otherwise protected by Section 527.3 of the Code of Civil Procedure or any other provision of law.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Grant of Patent License
clauses.body:
{{licensorName}} ("Licensor") owns or controls all right, title, and interest in and to {{patentDescription}} (the "Licensed Patent"). Subject to {{licenseeName}}'s ("Licensee") compliance with this agreement, Licensor grants Licensee a license under the Licensed Patent to make, use, offer for sale, sell, and/or import the invention it claims, within the territory, field of use, and other scope described in this agreement. This is a license, not an assignment or sale of the Licensed Patent: Licensor retains all right, title, and interest in and to the Licensed Patent, including record ownership of it, except for the specific rights expressly granted to Licensee under this agreement. No rights in the Licensed Patent are granted to Licensee by implication, estoppel, or otherwise, other than as expressly stated here.

___ This license is exclusive: Licensor will not itself practice the Licensed Patent, and will not grant any other license under it, within the scope described above.

___ This license is non-exclusive: Licensor may itself continue to practice the Licensed Patent, and may grant other licenses under it, including to others who compete with Licensee.

clauses.title: Term and Termination
clauses.body: This license begins on the date this agreement is signed and continues, unless terminated earlier as described below, until the natural expiration of the Licensed Patent's term (or, if {{patentDescription}} covers more than one patent or a pending application, until the natural expiration of the last of them to expire). Either party may terminate this agreement upon written notice if the other party materially breaches this agreement and does not cure that breach within 30 days after receiving notice describing it. Upon termination or expiration, all rights granted to Licensee under this agreement end, and Licensee must stop making, using, offering for sale, selling, or importing the invention claimed by the Licensed Patent, except to the extent this agreement expressly states otherwise.
