clauses.body:
Please sign below to indicate agreement to the terms above.

Licensor: {{licensorName}} _______________________ Date: _______________

Licensee: {{licenseeName}} _______________________ Date: _______________

clauses.title: License vs. Assignment: Different Legal Effects Under Patent Law
clauses.body: A patent license and a patent assignment do different legal work, even though both involve one party's rights under a patent moving toward another party's benefit. An assignment transfers ownership itself -- title to the whole patent, an undivided share of it, or the exclusive right to the whole patent within a specified part of the United States -- and this project's separate Patent Assignment Agreement document covers that kind of transaction. A license does something narrower: it permits {{licenseeName}} to do what would otherwise infringe {{licensorName}}'s rights in {{patentDescription}}, without transferring {{licensorName}}'s ownership of the patent itself. The U.S. Supreme Court has held that whether a particular transfer counts, legally, as an assignment or merely a license does not depend on what the parties call it, but on the actual legal effect of what was transferred: only a transfer of the whole patent, an undivided share of it, or the exclusive right to the whole patent within a specified part of the United States is an assignment; anything short of that is, in the law's eyes, a mere license, conveying no ownership interest or title in the patent itself -- regardless of how the document transferring it is titled or worded.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two passages from the same 1891 U.S. Supreme Court decision, Waterman v. Mackenzie, rather than two independent sources -- both illustrate the same holding rather than corroborating it independently. This is federal law, binding nationwide; patents are exclusively a creature of federal statute, with no state-by-state variation on the assignment/license distinction. Waterman interpreted the then-governing statute, Revised Statutes section 4898; that statute's operative language -- an assignment being limited to the whole patent, an undivided share of it, or an exclusive right within a specified part of the United States -- persists essentially unchanged in the current codification, 35 U.S.C. § 261, independently verified against the current U.S. Code text in this document's other clauses. This clause doesn't resolve every possible hybrid arrangement against Waterman's three categories -- for instance, an exclusive license limited to a particular field of use or product line rather than a geographic part of the United States, which Waterman's own opinion treats as still being a 'mere license' on facts resembling that pattern, but a comprehensive survey of later case law on every field-of-use fact pattern was not undertaken here. Both quotations below were independently confirmed by retrieving the opinion's text through two different methods against CourtListener's database and verifying the passages were identical both times.

citations.case: Waterman v. Mackenzie
citations.quote: Whether a transfer of a particular right or interest under a patent is an assignment or a license does not depend upon the name by which it calls itself, but upon the legal effect of its provisions.

citations.case: Waterman v. Mackenzie
citations.quote: Any assignment or transfer, short of one of these, is a mere license, giving the licensee no title in the patent, and no right to sue at law in his own name for an infringement.

clauses.title: The Patent Statute Never Defines "License"
clauses.body: Title 35 of the United States Code -- the federal Patent Act -- never actually defines the word "license," even though the concept is central to countless real transactions like this one. The statute governing ownership and transfer, 35 U.S.C. § 261, speaks in terms of what is "assignable" by "instrument in writing," and separately authorizes a patent owner to "grant and convey an exclusive right" limited to "the whole or any specified part of the United States" -- but nowhere in that section, or elsewhere in the Patent Act's core ownership provisions, does Congress define what a "license" is or spell out its required terms or form. What that means in practice is that a patent license -- including this one -- is fundamentally a creature of ordinary contract law layered on top of the patent statute's property-law framework for ownership, rather than a transaction with its own detailed statutory template the way a patent assignment's writing requirement is spelled out in that same section.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are drawn from the same federal statutory section, 35 U.S.C. § 261, rather than two independent sources -- they corroborate a single provision's actual wording rather than two separately authored ones. This clause was verified by fetching the current U.S. Code text at Cornell's Legal Information Institute twice, using different request headers (a browser-style User-Agent and a plain command-line one), and confirming the returned text was byte-identical both times. This is federal law, uniform nationwide; patent law does not vary state to state. This clause states an absence -- the word "license" does not appear in § 261's operative text -- rather than affirmatively characterizing every source of patent licensing law; other Patent Act provisions elsewhere in Title 35 (for example, the patent-misuse safe harbor addressed in a separate clause of this document) do use the word "license" in narrower contexts, and this clause doesn't survey the entire Title. It also doesn't mean licensing is unregulated by anything beyond the parties' own contract -- ordinary state contract law, and in some circumstances federal antitrust and patent-misuse law, still bears on a specific license's terms and enforceability, and those bodies of law are not what this clause addresses.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 261 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, ownership; assignment of patents and applications
citations.quote: Applications for patent, patents, or any interest therein, shall be assignable in law by an instrument in writing.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 261 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, ownership; assignment of patents and applications
citations.quote: The applicant, patentee, or his assigns or legal representatives may in like manner grant and convey an exclusive right under his application for patent, or patents, to the whole or any specified part of the United States.

clauses.title: Recording With the USPTO: Assignments and Exclusive Territorial Grants, Not Necessarily a Bare License
clauses.body: Federal law requires a patent assignment, grant, or conveyance to be recorded with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office within three months of its date -- or before a later purchaser or mortgagee buys the same rights in good faith and for value -- or else it becomes void against that later, unaware purchaser. This project's separate Patent Assignment Agreement document addresses that recording rule for an outright assignment. Whether the same recording rule reaches a license like this one turns on what kind of transfer it actually is: under the U.S. Supreme Court's own framework for what counts as an assignment, grant, or conveyance in the first place, an exclusive right limited to a specified geographic part of the United States is treated as an assignment for these purposes -- but a mere license, granting {{licenseeName}} something short of that (for instance, a non-exclusive right, or an exclusive right limited to a particular field of use or product rather than a defined part of the United States), doesn't obviously fall within what the recording statute calls an "assignment, grant or conveyance." This document doesn't resolve that question for every possible license structure, and recording an agreement like this one with the USPTO, even where not clearly required, remains something the parties may choose to do.
clauses.gap: This clause combines one statutory citation (35 U.S.C. § 261) with one case-law citation (Waterman v. Mackenzie, also cited in a separate clause of this document on a different passage of the same opinion, so the two clauses are not fully independent of each other where they both rely on Waterman). The statutory text was verified by fetching the current U.S. Code text at Cornell's Legal Information Institute twice with different request headers and confirming byte-identical results; the case-law passage was independently confirmed by retrieving the opinion's text through two different methods against CourtListener's database and verifying it was identical both times. This is federal law, uniform nationwide. This clause states the recording statute's text and the general shape of Waterman's assignment/license line-drawing; it does not resolve how a court would categorize every specific exclusivity arrangement (particularly a field-of-use or product-line exclusivity that isn't tied to a geographic part of the United States), and it is not a comprehensive account of USPTO recording practice for licenses, which in practice are sometimes recorded voluntarily regardless of whether the recording statute's priority-against-subsequent-purchasers consequence technically applies to them.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 261 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, ownership; assignment of patents and applications
citations.quote: An interest that constitutes an assignment, grant or conveyance shall be void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee for a valuable consideration, without notice, unless it is recorded in the Patent and Trademark Office within three months from its date or prior to the date of such subsequent purchase or mortgage.

citations.case: Waterman v. Mackenzie
citations.quote: For instance, a grant of an exclusive right to make, use and vend two patented machines within a certain district, is an assignment, and gives the grantee the right to sue in his own name for an infringement within the district, because the right, although limited to making, using and vending two machines, excludes all other persons, even the patentee, from making, using or vending like machines within the district.

clauses.title: What a Patent Actually Grants: A Right to Exclude, Not a Right to Practice
clauses.body: A common misconception is that owning a patent gives the owner an affirmative legal right to make, use, or sell the patented invention. What federal law actually grants a patent owner is narrower, and in a sense the opposite: the right to exclude other people from making, using, offering for sale, or selling the invention -- not a guarantee that the patent owner is itself free to do those things, which can separately depend on other patents, regulations, or rights that exist independently of {{licensorName}}'s own patent. Understanding a patent as a right to exclude, rather than a right to practice, clarifies what a license under it actually does: it is fundamentally {{licensorName}}'s promise not to exercise that exclusionary right against {{licenseeName}} within the scope this agreement describes, permitting {{licenseeName}} to do what would otherwise infringe -- rather than some independently existing permission that {{licensorName}} is handing over.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, uniform nationwide. This clause cites a single statutory section, 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(1), verified by fetching the current U.S. Code text at Cornell's Legal Information Institute twice, using different request headers, and confirming the returned text was byte-identical both times; no second, independent source was located or needed for this specific textual point, since the "right to exclude" framing is the statute's own express language rather than a contested characterization requiring case-law corroboration. This clause doesn't address the separate, genuinely contested question of exactly how broadly a particular patent's right to exclude extends against a specific accused product or process -- that depends on the scope of the patent's claims as construed by a court, which this document doesn't and can't evaluate for the patent described in this agreement.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, contents and term of patent; provisional rights
citations.quote: Every patent shall contain a short title of the invention and a grant to the patentee, his heirs or assigns, of the right to exclude others from making, using, offering for sale, or selling the invention throughout the United States or importing the invention into the United States

clauses.title: Standing to Sue Infringers: A Statutory Blank Filled In by Case Law for Exclusive Licensees
clauses.body: Federal law gives the civil remedy for patent infringement to "a patentee" -- and the Patent Act's own definitions section says that word "includes not only the patentee to whom the patent was issued but also the successors in title to the patentee," meaning an assignee. Read on its own, that statutory language doesn't obviously extend the right to sue an infringer to a mere licensee, and under the U.S. Supreme Court's own long-standing rule (addressed in a separate clause of this document), a licensee holding less than an assignment generally cannot sue an infringer in its own name at all -- any such suit has to be brought by, or in the name of, the patent owner. Case law has, however, filled in real relief for a narrower category: an exclusive licensee, meaning one granted the sole right to make, use, or sell the invention -- excluding even the patent owner -- within the scope of the license. The U.S. Supreme Court has held that a patent owner who grants that kind of exclusive right holds title to the patent in trust for the exclusive licensee to that extent, and can be required -- even against the patent owner's own wishes, and even joined involuntarily as a co-plaintiff -- to let its name be used so the exclusive licensee can pursue an infringer. This is a judge-made gap-filler layered on top of the statute's bare text, not something the statute spells out for licensees itself.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on three sources: two different sections of the same federal statute (35 U.S.C. §§ 281 and 100(d)), which are not independent of each other in the sense that both are non-case-law text from the same Act rather than separately authored sources, and one U.S. Supreme Court decision, Independent Wireless Telegraph Co. v. Radio Corp. of America. The statutory sections were each verified by fetching the current U.S. Code text at Cornell's Legal Information Institute twice with different request headers and confirming byte-identical results. The case-law passage was independently verified by retrieving the opinion's text through two different methods against CourtListener's database and confirming the quoted passage was identical both times; one intermediate retrieval of the same underlying opinion, through a different stored text field of the same database record, showed what appears to be a single stray scanning artifact in that field only (rendering one word as "by'" rather than "by"), and the quote used here reflects the reading confirmed identically by the two other, independently retrieved renderings of the same passage. This is federal law, uniform nationwide, since patent standing to sue is exclusively a matter of the federal Patent Act and federal case law construing it. This clause states a 1926 Supreme Court framework, not a full modern account of patent-standing doctrine -- the Federal Circuit (the federal appellate court with exclusive jurisdiction over patent appeals) has developed further, more granular doctrine since then on exactly how much of the bundle of exclusive rights a licensee must hold to sue entirely on its own without even joining the patent owner, and that more recent doctrine was not independently verified in this research session, so this clause does not state a position on it.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 281 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, remedy for infringement of patent
citations.quote: A patentee shall have remedy by civil action for infringement of his patent.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 100(d) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, definitions -- "patentee"
citations.quote: The word “patentee” includes not only the patentee to whom the patent was issued but also the successors in title to the patentee.

citations.case: Independent Wireless Telegraph Co. v. Radio Corp. of America
citations.quote: It seems clear then on principle and authority that the owner of a patent who grants to another the exclusive right to make, use or vend the invention, which does not constitute a statutory assignment, holds the title to the patent in trust for such a licensee, to the extent that he must allow the use of his name as plaintiff in any action brought at the instance of the licensee in law or in equity to obtain damages for the injury to his exclusive right by an infringer or to enjoin infringement of it.

clauses.title: A Patent Owner's Right to License -- or Refuse to License -- and the Limits of Patent Misuse
clauses.body: Federal law expressly protects a patent owner's freedom to decide who gets a license and on what terms. The same statute that defines patent infringement also lists specific things a patent owner can do without being denied relief for infringement or found guilty of "misuse" of the patent -- including refusing to license the patent to anyone at all, and licensing it to some parties but not others. That protection has a limit: conditioning a license under {{patentDescription}} on the licensee also taking a license to a separate patent, or buying a separate product, can still cross into patent misuse if -- but only if -- {{licensorName}} has market power in the relevant market for the patent or product the license or sale is conditioned on. Outside that specific tying scenario, and outside other doctrines not addressed here, the statute does not require {{licensorName}} to license {{patentDescription}} to any particular party, or on any particular terms, and granting a license -- exclusive or not -- to {{licenseeName}} does not by itself expose the underlying patent to a misuse defense.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, uniform nationwide; patent misuse is a doctrine created and limited by the federal Patent Act, without state-by-state variation. This clause cites a single statutory subsection, 35 U.S.C. § 271(d)(4)-(5), verified by fetching the current U.S. Code text at Cornell's Legal Information Institute twice, using different request headers, and confirming the returned text was byte-identical both times; no independent case-law source was added for this specific textual point, since the safe harbor and its tying-based limit are the statute's own express terms. This clause doesn't define "market power" in the relevant market, doesn't address the separate common-law patent misuse doctrine as it existed before this 1988 statutory safe harbor was enacted, and doesn't address antitrust law, which can impose its own, separately sourced constraints on licensing terms beyond what the patent misuse doctrine covers.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 271(d) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, infringement of patent -- patent misuse safe harbor
citations.quote: (4) refused to license or use any rights to the patent; or (5) conditioned the license of any rights to the patent or the sale of the patented product on the acquisition of a license to rights in another patent or purchase of a separate product, unless, in view of the circumstances, the patent owner has market power in the relevant market for the patent or patented product on which the license or sale is conditioned.

clauses.title: Name Availability and Reservation Information Sheet — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet addresses California's requirement that a proposed corporate or limited liability company name be distinguishable on the records of the California Secretary of State before an entity can be formed under that name, and the procedure by which a proposed name can be reserved with the Secretary of State in advance of filing formation documents. It relates to the proposed name "{{proposedName}}" under consideration for a {{entityType}} to be formed in California. This document is not this project's LLC Articles of Organization or Articles of Incorporation document — those documents state the name that is ultimately included in the formation filing itself. This document instead addresses a distinct, often earlier step: whether a proposed name is legally available for use, what categories of words in a proposed name can require separate regulatory approval, how a proposed name can be reserved for a period of time before the formation documents are filed, and what happens if an entity is nonetheless formed under a name that turns out not to have been distinguishable. This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself reserve "{{proposedName}}," or any other name, with the California Secretary of State, and it does not determine whether "{{proposedName}}" is in fact distinguishable from any name already on file or under reservation.

clauses.title: The Distinguishable-Name Standard
clauses.body: California law imposes the same two-part naming standard on both corporations and limited liability companies, stated in parallel language in two separate statutes. For a corporation, the name "shall not be a name that the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public" and must be "distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State" from the names of other corporations, from foreign corporations authorized to transact business in California, and from names currently under reservation. The California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act imposes the identical two-part standard on an LLC's name — not likely to mislead the public, and distinguishable in the Secretary of State's records from other LLC names, from foreign LLCs authorized to transact intrastate business here, and from names currently reserved under the LLC reservation statute.
clauses.gap: Cal. Corp. Code § 201 (corporations) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.08 (limited liability companies) are separate, independently enacted statutory sections in different titles of the Corporations Code — not subsections of a single section — so the two citations below are independent sources corroborating a parallel rule, not two views of one provision. This document's research covered only corporations and limited liability companies; it did not research the naming rules that apply to general partnerships, limited partnerships, limited liability partnerships, or nonprofit corporations, which may differ. Neither statute quoted here states the specific comparison methodology the Secretary of State uses to decide whether two names are "distinguishable" (for example, how differences in punctuation, spacing, capitalization, or required entity designators like "LLC" or "Inc." are treated) — that operational detail, to the extent it exists, is Secretary of State administrative practice rather than statutory text, and this document does not state it because it was not verified against a primary legal source.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 201(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the distinguishable-name standard for corporations
citations.quote: The name of a corporation shall not be a name that the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public and shall be distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State from all of the following: (1) The name of any corporation. (2) The name of any foreign corporation authorized to transact intrastate business in this state.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.08(b)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the distinguishable-name standard for LLCs
citations.quote: The name of a limited liability company shall not be a name that the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public and shall be distinguishable in the records of the Secretary of State from all of the following: (1) The name of any limited liability company. (2) The name of any foreign limited liability company authorized to transact intrastate business in this state.

clauses.title: Name Reservation Procedure and Duration
clauses.body: California law lets a person apply to the Secretary of State, and pay the prescribed fee, to reserve the exclusive use of a proposed corporate or LLC name before filing formation documents. For a corporation, upon payment of the fee, an applicant "may... obtain from the Secretary of State a certificate of reservation of any name not prohibited by subdivision (b) [the distinguishable-name standard], and upon the issuance of the certificate the name stated therein shall be reserved for a period of 60 days." For a limited liability company, if the Secretary of State finds that the applied-for name is available, the statute directs that "it shall reserve the name for the applicant's exclusive use for up to 60 days and issue a certificate of reservation." Neither statute permits back-to-back reservations of the same name: the Secretary of State will not issue certificates reserving the same name for two or more consecutive 60-day periods to the same applicant or for the same person's benefit, nor consecutive reservations of a name so similar to another name that it would fail the distinguishable-name standard. For an LLC name reservation specifically, the statute also allows the reservation's owner to transfer it to another person by delivering a signed notice of the transfer to the Secretary of State.
clauses.gap: Cal. Corp. Code § 201(e) (corporations) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.09 (limited liability companies) are separate, independently enacted sections and are treated as independent sources here. Both statutes reference a filing fee set elsewhere, in Government Code Article 3 (commencing with Section 12180) of Chapter 3, Part 2, Division 3, Title 2 — this document's research did not extend to that separate Government Code fee schedule, so no specific dollar amount is stated; the current fee is published by the Secretary of State. This document verified the reservation-transfer provision only for LLC name reservations (§ 17701.09(b)); the corporation naming statute (§ 201) as verified here does not contain a comparable transfer provision, and this document does not state that corporations can or cannot transfer a name reservation because that was not independently verified.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 201(e)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, corporate name reservation procedure and 60-day duration
citations.quote: Any applicant may, upon payment of the fee prescribed therefor in Article 3 (commencing with Section 12180) of Chapter 3 of Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code, obtain from the Secretary of State a certificate of reservation of any name not prohibited by subdivision (b), and upon the issuance of the certificate the name stated therein shall be reserved for a period of 60 days.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.09(a)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, LLC name reservation procedure and 60-day duration
citations.quote: a person may apply to reserve the exclusive use of the name of a limited liability company or foreign limited liability company, including an alternative name for a foreign limited liability company whose name is not available. If the Secretary of State finds that the name applied for is available, it shall reserve the name for the applicant’s exclusive use for up to 60 days and issue a certificate of reservation.

clauses.title: Restricted Words Requiring Separate Regulatory Approval
clauses.body: Beyond the general distinguishable-name standard, California law separately restricts specific categories of words in a corporation's or LLC's name. For a corporation, the Secretary of State "shall not file articles setting forth a name in which 'bank,' 'trust,' 'trustee,' or related words appear, unless the certificate of approval of the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation is attached" to the articles — meaning those words are not banned outright for a corporation, but are conditioned on a named regulator's prior approval. A separate corporate-naming statute imposes the same kind of approval condition where the corporation's business is to be an insurer: the Secretary of State "shall not file articles in which the business is to be an insurer unless the certificate of the Insurance Commissioner approving the corporate name is attached." The LLC-naming statute takes a different approach to some of the same words: rather than an approval pathway, it flatly bars an LLC's name from including "'bank,' 'trust,' 'trustee,' 'incorporated,' 'inc.,' 'corporation,' or 'corp.'" and from including "'insurer' or 'insurance company' or any other words suggesting that it is in the business of issuing policies of insurance and assuming insurance risks" — there is no statutory mechanism, as verified here, for an LLC to obtain approval to use those words the way a corporation can for the banking- and insurance-related terms.
clauses.gap: Cal. Corp. Code § 201(a), § 201.5, and § 17701.08(e) are three separate, independently enacted statutory provisions (§ 201.5 was added by a different, later-dated bill than § 201, and § 17701.08 sits in an entirely different title of the code governing LLCs rather than corporations), so the citations below are independent sources, not subsections of one section presented as several. This document verified only the banking/trust/trustee and insurer-related restricted-word rules. It did not find, and does not claim to have verified, any statutory restriction in the Corporations Code tying other words — such as words suggesting affiliation with a specific licensed profession (e.g., "attorney," "CPA," "engineer") — to a name-approval requirement; if such rules exist, they were not located during this research and are not addressed here. This document also does not state the current fee or application procedure for obtaining the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation's or the Insurance Commissioner's approval, since that operational detail was not verified.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 201(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, bank/trust/trustee name approval requirement for corporations
citations.quote: The Secretary of State shall not file articles setting forth a name in which “bank,” “ trust,” “trustee,” or related words appear, unless the certificate of approval of the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation is attached thereto.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 201.5
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, insurer-name approval requirement for corporations
citations.quote: The Secretary of State shall not file articles in which the business is to be an insurer unless the certificate of the Insurance Commissioner approving the corporate name is attached thereto.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.08(e)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, outright bank/trust/insurer word restriction for LLCs
citations.quote: The name shall not include the words “bank,” “trust,” “trustee,” “incorporated,” “inc.,” “corporation,” or “corp.” and shall not include the words “insurer” or “insurance company” or any other words suggesting that it is in the business of issuing policies of insurance and assuming insurance risks.

clauses.title: Consequence of Filing Under a Name That Is Not Actually Distinguishable
clauses.body: California's naming statutes do not provide that a corporation's or LLC's existence is automatically dissolved, or that its articles are automatically void, if the entity's name turns out not to have been distinguishable at the time of filing. Instead, both statutes provide a narrower, forward-looking remedy: for a corporation, "the use... of a name in violation of this section may be enjoined notwithstanding the filing of its articles by the Secretary of State," and the identical rule applies to an LLC — "the use by a limited liability company of a name in violation of this section may be enjoined notwithstanding the filing of its articles by the Secretary of State." In other words, the statutory consequence for continuing to use a name that violates the distinguishable-name standard is that a court may enjoin (order a stop to) that use, even though the Secretary of State already accepted the filing — the filing itself is not automatically undone.
clauses.gap: Cal. Corp. Code § 201(d) (corporations) and Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.08(c) (limited liability companies) are separate, independently enacted sections and are treated as independent sources here. Neither statute, as verified, states who may bring an action to enjoin the use of a noncompliant name, what showing is required, or any other procedural detail of that remedy — this document does not state those details because they were not verified against primary text. This document also did not verify, and does not describe, any Secretary of State administrative practice of screening or rejecting a proposed name for distinguishability at the time of filing (as opposed to at the time of a separate name-reservation request) — to the extent such an intake screening practice exists, it is an administrative practice rather than something stated in the statutory text quoted above, and it is disclosed here as an honest gap rather than assumed.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 201(d)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, injunction remedy for a noncompliant corporate name
citations.quote: The use by a corporation of a name in violation of this section may be enjoined notwithstanding the filing of its articles by the Secretary of State.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.08(c)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, injunction remedy for a noncompliant LLC name
citations.quote: The use by a limited liability company of a name in violation of this section may be enjoined notwithstanding the filing of its articles by the Secretary of State.

clauses.title: Closing and Name Reservation Request Record
clauses.body:
Name availability and reservation information sheet relating to the proposed {{entityType}} name "{{proposedName}}," prepared by {{applicantName}}.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{applicantName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California's statutory distinguishable-name standard for corporations and limited liability companies, the procedure and duration for reserving a proposed name with the Secretary of State, restricted words that require separate regulatory approval or are barred outright, and the statutory consequence of filing under a name that later turns out not to have been distinguishable. It is not the Secretary of State's official Name Reservation Request form, does not itself reserve "{{proposedName}}" or any other name with the California Secretary of State, does not constitute legal advice, and does not determine whether "{{proposedName}}" is in fact available or distinguishable. The current official form, instructions, and fee amounts are published by the California Secretary of State.]

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope — Stock Certificates and Uncertificated Shares Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a corporation organized under the laws of {{stateOfFormation}}. It describes the rules the California Corporations Code sets for how a California corporation may evidence a shareholder's ownership of shares — whether by issuing a physical, signed stock certificate or by using an uncertificated (book-entry) system instead — along with what a certificate or its uncertificated equivalent must state when shares are classified, and how a corporation may replace a certificate that is lost, stolen, or destroyed.

This information sheet is educational only. It states the applicable statutes as written; it does not recommend whether {{companyName}} should issue certificated or uncertificated shares, does not draft or format any specific certificate or shareholder notice, and does not determine which state's law governs {{companyName}} if {{companyName}} was not organized in California or does not otherwise have California as its internal-affairs state. This document is not this project's Corporate Bylaws or Close Corporation documents, which govern a corporation's internal affairs and (for an electing close corporation) its own additional certificate-legend requirement; this document instead focuses specifically on the general certificate-mechanics statutes in Chapter 4 of the General Corporation Law.

clauses.title: Every Shareholder's Default Entitlement to a Certificate, and Who May Sign It
clauses.body: Under California law, every holder of shares in a corporation is entitled to have a certificate issued in the corporation's name, certifying the number of shares and the class or series of shares that shareholder owns. The certificate must be signed by two categories of officer acting together: (1) the chairperson or vice chairperson of the board, or the president or a vice president; and (2) the chief financial officer or an assistant treasurer, or the secretary or any assistant secretary. Any or all of these required signatures may be a facsimile signature rather than an original. A certificate signed, or facsimile-signed, by someone who held the required office (or was the transfer agent or registrar) at the time of signing remains valid even if that person has since left that position by the time the certificate is actually issued.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 416(a)), used as evidence of the actual statutory floor for a shareholder's default entitlement to a certificate and the officers who must sign it — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction's certificate-signature rule is the same. Both quotes below are drawn from the same subdivision, § 416(a), and are not independent of one another; they are presented as one source describing two related rules within that subdivision (the signature requirement, and the former-officer validity rule). This default entitlement yields to Cal. Corp. Code § 416(b), under which a corporation may instead adopt an uncertificated system in place of issuing any certificates at all — that alternative is covered in a separate clause of this document rather than here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 416(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, entitlement to a signed certificate and required officer signatures
citations.quote: Every holder of shares in a corporation shall be entitled to have a certificate signed in the name of the corporation by the chairperson or vice chairperson of the board or the president or a vice president and by the chief financial officer or an assistant treasurer or the secretary or any assistant secretary, certifying the number of shares and the class or series of shares owned by the shareholder. Any or all of the signatures on the certificate may be facsimile.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 416(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, a certificate signed by a since-departed officer remains valid
citations.quote: In case any officer, transfer agent or registrar who has signed or whose facsimile signature has been placed upon a certificate has ceased to be such officer, transfer agent or registrar before such certificate is issued, it may be issued by the corporation with the same effect as if such person were an officer, transfer agent or registrar at the date of issue.

clauses.title: California Does Not Require Physical Certificates — Uncertificated (Book-Entry) Shares Are Permitted
clauses.body: California law does not require a corporation to issue physical share certificates for every shareholder. Notwithstanding a shareholder's default entitlement to a signed certificate, a corporation may instead adopt a system for issuing, recording, and transferring its shares by electronic or other means that does not involve issuing any certificates at all — commonly described as uncertificated or book-entry shares. Such a system must include provisions for giving purchasers written notice in substitution for the information that would otherwise appear on a certificate under the statutes governing certificate content and dissenting-share endorsement, and it must also satisfy at least one of three conditions: approval by the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, authorization under a federal statute, or compliance with Division 8 of the California Commercial Code. If a corporation has already issued physical certificates for its outstanding shares, a newly adopted uncertificated system does not take effect as to those already-certificated shares until the certificates for them have been surrendered to the corporation.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 416(b)), used as evidence that certificated shares are not mandatory in California and that a corporation may instead use an uncertificated system — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not a claim that every jurisdiction permits uncertificated shares on the same terms. The two quotes below are both drawn from the single subdivision § 416(b) and are not independent of one another; they are one source describing two parts of the same rule (the conditions for adopting an uncertificated system, and the surrender requirement for shares that were already certificated). This document does not independently verify the separate California Commercial Code Division 8 (Investment Securities) requirements that would apply to an uncertificated system relying on that route, and does not verify what the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation currently requires in administering the Corporate Securities Law of 1968 — both are referenced by name in the statute's text but were not independently confirmed against their own primary sources here; an attempted direct fetch of California Commercial Code § 8408 did not return usable statutory text and that specific point is omitted rather than guessed at.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 416(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, a corporation may adopt an uncertificated (electronic) share system
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (a), a corporation may adopt a system of issuance, recordation and transfer of its shares by electronic or other means not involving any issuance of certificates, including provisions for notice to purchasers in substitution for the required statements on certificates under Sections 417, 418, and 1302, and as may be required by the commissioner in administering the Corporate Securities Law of 1968, which system (1) has been approved by the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, (2) is authorized in any statute of the United States, or (3) is in accordance with Division 8 (commencing with Section 8101) of the Commercial Code.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 416(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, an uncertificated system is not effective against already-issued certificates until surrender
citations.quote: Any system so adopted shall not become effective as to issued and outstanding certificated securities until the certificates therefor have been surrendered to the corporation.

clauses.title: What a Certificate (or Its Uncertificated Equivalent) Must State When Shares Are Classified
clauses.body: If a corporation's shares are classified into different classes, or if any class of shares has two or more series, the certificate — or, for uncertificated shares, the initial transaction statement and written statements the corporation sends the shareholder in its place — must contain one of three things: a full statement of the rights, preferences, privileges, and restrictions granted to or imposed on each class or series and its holders; a summary of those rights, preferences, privileges, and restrictions that references the specific provisions of the articles of incorporation and any certificate of determination establishing them; or a statement identifying the corporate office or agency from which a shareholder may obtain a copy of the full statement, on request and without charge.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 417), used as evidence of the actual required content for a corporation with more than one class or series of shares — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation, and not a claim that a single-class corporation with no series has any obligation under this particular section. This clause does not address the separate, additional statutory content requirements under Cal. Corp. Code § 418(a)-(b) for share-transfer restrictions, redemption rights, voting agreements, irrevocable proxies, or assessability and partly-paid status — this project's Buy-Sell Agreement document separately covers the § 418(a)(1) transfer-restriction-disclosure point for its own purpose, and that ground is not duplicated here. This clause also does not address the separate, stricter close-corporation certificate legend under Cal. Corp. Code § 418(c)-(d), which this project's Close Corporation document covers.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 417
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, required disclosure of class and series rights on the certificate or its uncertificated equivalent
citations.quote: If the shares of the corporation are classified or if any class of shares has two or more series, there shall appear on the certificate or, in the case of uncertificated securities, the initial transaction statement and written statements, one of the following: (a) A statement of the rights, preferences, privileges and restrictions granted to or imposed upon each class or series of shares authorized to be issued and upon the holders thereof. (b) A summary of such rights, preferences, privileges and restrictions with reference to the provisions of the articles and any certificates of determination establishing the same. (c) A statement setting forth the office or agency of the corporation from which shareholders may obtain, upon request and without charge, a copy of the statement referred to in subdivision (a).

clauses.title: Replacing a Lost, Stolen, or Destroyed Certificate
clauses.body: California law lets a corporation issue a new share certificate to replace one that was lost, stolen, or destroyed. Before doing so, the corporation may require the certificate's owner — or the owner's legal representative — to give the corporation a bond or other adequate security, sufficient to indemnify the corporation against any claim, including any expense or liability, arising from the alleged loss, theft, or destruction of the original certificate or from issuing the new one. If a corporation refuses to issue a replacement certificate, the owner or the owner's legal representative may bring an action in superior court for an order requiring the corporation to issue one.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 419(a)-(b)), used as evidence of the actual replacement procedure and the corporation's ability to require indemnification security before reissuing a certificate — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. The two quotes below, from § 419(a) and § 419(b), are subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another; they are treated as one source describing two branches of the same procedure — the corporation issuing a replacement voluntarily under subdivision (a), or a shareholder seeking a court order under subdivision (b) if the corporation refuses. This document does not describe subdivision (c)'s further detail on what a court must find before ordering reissuance or the bond it may direct the plaintiff to post, and does not address whether or how an equivalent replacement procedure applies to a lost or misappropriated written notice for uncertificated shares — Section 419's text refers only to a "certificate," and that gap is not resolved here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 419(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, a corporation may issue a replacement certificate and require indemnification security
citations.quote: A domestic or foreign corporation may issue a new share certificate or a new certificate for any other security in the place of any certificate theretofore issued by it, alleged to have been lost, stolen or destroyed, and the corporation may require the owner of the lost, stolen or destroyed certificate or the owner’s legal representative to give the corporation a bond (or other adequate security) sufficient to indemnify it against any claim that may be made against it (including any expense or liability) on account of the alleged loss, theft or destruction of any such certificate or the issuance of such new certificate.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 419(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, a court may order reissuance if the corporation refuses
citations.quote: If a corporation refuses to issue a new share certificate or other certificate in place of one theretofore issued by it, or by any corporation of which it is the lawful successor, alleged to have been lost, stolen or destroyed, the owner of the lost, stolen or destroyed certificate or the owner’s legal representative may bring an action in the superior court of the proper county for an order requiring the corporation to issue a new certificate in place of the one lost, stolen or destroyed.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature Block — Stock Certificates and Uncertificated Shares Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet regarding {{companyName}} was prepared in connection with {{shareholderName}}'s status as the holder of record of {{numberOfSharesHeld}}.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{shareholderName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes the California Corporations Code statutes governing stock certificates and uncertificated shares — the default entitlement to a signed certificate, the permitted alternative of an uncertificated system, the required content when shares are classified, and the procedure for replacing a lost, stolen, or destroyed certificate. It does not itself constitute a stock certificate, an initial transaction statement, or a written notice under any of the statutes it describes, does not determine what {{companyName}}'s own articles, bylaws, or share records currently provide, and does not constitute legal advice. The current statutory text is published by the California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov).]

clauses.title: Purpose and Identification of Retirement Interest
clauses.body: This document addresses the division of a retirement plan interest between {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, who married on {{marriageDate}} and separated on {{separationDate}}, arising from the dissolution of their marriage. It concerns the retirement plan or account known as {{planName}}. It states legal background on how retirement benefits are treated in a dissolution and on the federal mechanism — a qualified domestic relations order, or QDRO — used to divide certain retirement plans. This document is not itself a qualified domestic relations order, is not a court order, and does not by itself direct any retirement plan or plan administrator to pay any amount to any person; it does not state whether {{party1Name}} or {{party2Name}} needs a QDRO or any other specific order for {{planName}}, or how any specific benefit should be divided.

clauses.title: California's Rule: Full Community-Property Share of Retirement Benefits
clauses.body: Except in limited circumstances, a court is directed to make whatever orders are necessary or appropriate to ensure that each party receives that party's full community property share in any retirement plan, whether public or private, including all survivor and death benefits. The statute lists several non-exclusive mechanisms a court may use to accomplish this, including ordering the disposition of retirement benefits payable on death consistent with the equal-division statute, ordering a party to elect a survivor benefit annuity for the other party's benefit, and ordering a retirement plan to make payments directly to the nonmember party of that party's community property interest in the retirement benefits. Any division of a retirement plan interest of {{party1Name}} or {{party2Name}} under this document draws on this statutory framework.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one community-property jurisdiction directs courts to divide retirement benefits — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or retirement plan. Both citations in this clause come from the same statutory subdivision, Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(a), and this clause, qdro_ca_public_plan_specific_statutes, and qdro_ca_retirement_division_limits all come from the same statutory section (§ 2610), so none of them is an independent source of authority from the others; they are presented together only because California is a single, real jurisdiction being used as an illustrative example. This clause does not state how a court values or apportions a benefit that was earned partly before marriage and partly during it (sometimes called a "time rule" or similar apportionment approach) — attempts to verify a citable primary source (statute or case) for that specific formula were not completed with confidence in the time available, so that topic is omitted here rather than described.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's authority and mechanisms for dividing retirement plan benefits
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), the court shall make whatever orders are necessary or appropriate to ensure that each party receives the party's full community property share in any retirement plan, whether public or private, including all survivor and death benefits, including, but not limited to, any of the following: (1) Order the disposition of retirement benefits payable upon or after the death of either party in a manner consistent with Section 2550. (2) Order a party to elect a survivor benefit annuity or other similar election for the benefit of the other party, as specified by the court, when a retirement plan provides for that election, provided that no court shall order a retirement plan to provide increased benefits determined on the basis of actuarial value.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the direct-payment-to-nonmember-party mechanism
citations.quote: Order a retirement plan to make payments directly to a nonmember party of the nonmember party's community property interest in retirement benefits.

clauses.title: Public Retirement Systems: A Separate Statutory Mechanism
clauses.body: California's general retirement-division statute expressly cross-references separate statutes that govern the division of specific public (governmental) retirement systems, rather than treating public-plan division as governed by the same mechanism as a private plan. It provides that, upon the agreement of the nonemployee spouse, a court may order division of accumulated community property contributions and service credit "as provided in the following or similar enactments," naming provisions of the Government Code and Education Code that govern named categories of state and local public retirement systems (including a state employees' retirement system, a state teachers' retirement system, county retirement systems, and a judges' retirement system). This confirms that a public, governmental retirement plan is not divided through the same federal mechanism described elsewhere in this document, but through a separate, system-specific statutory process.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes and confirms only what Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(a)(3) itself says — that separate enactments exist and cross-references their Government Code and Education Code locations. It has not independently fetched or verified the text of those cross-referenced sections (e.g., Gov. Code § 21290 et seq. or Ed. Code § 22650 et seq.) or the operational procedures of any specific public system (such as CalPERS or CalSTRS) for processing a domestic relations order; this document does not describe those procedures because they were not independently verified against primary sources. This clause and qdro_ca_retirement_division_authority both derive from Cal. Fam. Code § 2610, so they are not independent of one another as sources.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the cross-reference to separate public-retirement-system division statutes
citations.quote: Upon the agreement of the nonemployee spouse, order the division of accumulated community property contributions and service credit as provided in the following or similar enactments: (A) Article 2 (commencing with Section 21290) of Chapter 9 of Part 3 of Division 5 of Title 2 of the Government Code. (B) Chapter 12 (commencing with Section 22650) of Part 13 of Division 1 of Title 1 of the Education Code. (C) Article 8.4 (commencing with Section 31685) of Chapter 3 of Part 3 of Division 4 of Title 3 of the Government Code. (D) Article 2.5 (commencing with Section 75050) of Chapter 11 of Title 8 of the Government Code.

clauses.title: Limits on a Court's Retirement-Division Orders
clauses.body: A court's authority to divide retirement plan benefits is not unlimited. A court is not permitted to make an order that requires a retirement plan to make payments in a manner that increases the amount of benefits the plan provides, and, apart from the public-plan mechanism described elsewhere in this document, a court may not require a retirement plan to pay benefits to a party at any time before the member retires unless the plan itself provides for that.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a court's retirement-division authority is bounded — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific plan. This clause and qdro_ca_retirement_division_authority both derive from Cal. Fam. Code § 2610 (the same statutory section, different subdivisions), so they are not independent of one another as sources.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2610(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: limits on a court's retirement-division orders
citations.quote: A court shall not make an order that requires a retirement plan to do either of the following: (1) Make payments in a manner that will result in an increase in the amount of benefits provided by the plan. (2) Make the payment of benefits to a party at any time before the member retires, except as provided in paragraph (3) of subdivision (a), unless the plan so provides.

clauses.title: Federal Law: The Anti-Assignment Rule and Its QDRO Exception
clauses.body: Under federal law governing private-sector employee pension plans, each pension plan is required to provide that benefits under the plan may not be assigned or alienated. That general rule is subject to an exception: it does not apply to the creation, assignment, or recognition of a right to a benefit payable to a participant pursuant to a domestic relations order, where that order is determined to be a "qualified domestic relations order" (a QDRO). Where an order qualifies, each pension plan is required to pay benefits in accordance with the order's applicable requirements.
clauses.gap: This is a federal statute (ERISA), used as real evidence of the general rule and its domestic-relations-order exception for pension plans covered by this federal law. This clause combines two subparagraphs of the same statutory paragraph, 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1) and § 1056(d)(3)(A), so they are not independent sources from one another, though both are independent of the California statutes cited elsewhere in this document (different sovereign, different statute). This clause does not address plans excluded from this federal scheme, which is addressed separately in this document.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(1) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.cite: the general anti-assignment/anti-alienation rule for pension plans
citations.quote: Each pension plan shall provide that benefits provided under the plan may not be assigned or alienated.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(A) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.cite: the qualified-domestic-relations-order exception to that rule
citations.quote: Paragraph (1) shall apply to the creation, assignment, or recognition of a right to any benefit payable with respect to a participant pursuant to a domestic relations order, except that paragraph (1) shall not apply if the order is determined to be a qualified domestic relations order. Each pension plan shall provide for the payment of benefits in accordance with the applicable requirements of any qualified domestic relations order.

clauses.title: What a Domestic Relations Order Must Contain to Qualify
clauses.body: Federal law defines a "qualified domestic relations order" as a domestic relations order that creates or recognizes an alternate payee's right to receive all or a portion of a participant's benefits under a plan, and that meets certain content requirements. To meet those content requirements, an order must clearly specify: the name and last known mailing address of the participant and of each alternate payee covered by the order; the amount or percentage of the participant's benefits to be paid to each alternate payee, or the manner in which that amount or percentage is to be determined; the number of payments or the period to which the order applies; and each plan to which the order applies. A domestic relations order that requires a plan to provide a type or form of benefit not otherwise available under the plan, or that requires increased benefits (measured by actuarial value), does not meet these requirements.
clauses.gap: This is a federal statute (ERISA), used as real evidence of the specific content requirements a domestic relations order must satisfy to be treated as a QDRO. This clause combines subparagraphs (B) and (C) of the same statutory paragraph, 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3), so they are not independent sources from one another. This clause states the statutory definition and content requirements only; it does not state whether any particular order concerning any specific plan would qualify, which is a determination made by the plan administrator (addressed elsewhere in this document) and, ultimately, is fact- and plan-specific.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(B)(i) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.cite: the definition of qualified domestic relations order
citations.quote: the term "qualified domestic relations order" means a domestic relations order— (I) which creates or recognizes the existence of an alternate payee's right to, or assigns to an alternate payee the right to, receive all or a portion of the benefits payable with respect to a participant under a plan, and (II) with respect to which the requirements of subparagraphs (C) and (D) are met

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(C) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.cite: the required contents of a qualifying order
citations.quote: A domestic relations order meets the requirements of this subparagraph only if such order clearly specifies— (i) the name and the last known mailing address (if any) of the participant and the name and mailing address of each alternate payee covered by the order, (ii) the amount or percentage of the participant's benefits to be paid by the plan to each such alternate payee, or the manner in which such amount or percentage is to be determined, (iii) the number of payments or period to which such order applies, and (iv) each plan to which such order applies.

clauses.title: Federal Law Does Not Reach Governmental Retirement Plans
clauses.body: The federal statutory scheme described elsewhere in this document — including its anti-assignment rule and the qualified-domestic-relations-order exception to it — does not apply to a governmental plan. Federal law expressly excludes a governmental plan, along with certain other categories of plans, from the subchapter of federal law in which the QDRO mechanism appears. This is separate confirmation, from the federal side, of the same distinction reflected in California's cross-reference to separate public-retirement-system statutes: a public employer's retirement plan is not governed by the private-sector federal mechanism described in this document.
clauses.gap: This is a federal statute, used as real evidence that governmental plans are excluded from this part of ERISA — it is genuinely independent of the California statute cited elsewhere in this document (different sovereign, different law), even though both point toward the same real-world distinction. This clause does not itself define which retirement systems qualify as a "governmental plan" for this purpose (that definition appears in a separate cross-referenced section, 29 U.S.C. § 1002(32), which was not independently fetched and verified here) and does not state that any specific plan is or is not a governmental plan.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1003(b)(1) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.cite: the governmental-plan exclusion from ERISA's Title I subchapter
citations.quote: The provisions of this subchapter shall not apply to any employee benefit plan if— (1) such plan is a governmental plan (as defined in section 1002(32) of this title)

clauses.title: A QDRO Is a Separate Order Requiring the Plan Administrator's Own Determination
clauses.body: Federal law does not treat a domestic relations order as automatically qualified once a court signs it. When a plan receives a domestic relations order, the plan administrator is required to promptly notify the participant and each alternate payee that the order was received and to describe the plan's procedures for determining whether the order is qualified, and, within a reasonable period after receipt, the plan administrator is required to determine whether the order is a qualified domestic relations order and to notify the participant and each alternate payee of that determination. This is a separate process, involving the plan administrator's own review, from the entry of a marital settlement agreement or dissolution judgment.
clauses.gap: This is a federal statute, used as real evidence that a domestic relations order goes through the plan administrator's own separate qualification process. It does not state how long that process typically takes in practice, what any specific plan's internal procedures require, or whether any specific order will be found qualified — those are plan-specific and fact-specific questions this clause does not address.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1056(d)(3)(G)(i) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.cite: the plan administrator's notice and determination obligations
citations.quote: the plan administrator shall promptly notify the participant and each alternate payee of the receipt of such order and the plan's procedures for determining the qualified status of domestic relations orders, and (II) within a reasonable period after receipt of such order, the plan administrator shall determine whether such order is a qualified domestic relations order and notify the participant and each alternate payee of such determination.

clauses.title: Retirement Benefit Information and Signatures
Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet addresses one specific issue that can arise in a divorce, dissolution, annulment, or legal separation involving a current or former member of the uniformed services: {{memberName}}, who has served in the {{serviceBranch}}, and {{spouseName}}, {{memberName}}'s spouse or former spouse. It explains, as a matter of federal law, how a state court's authority to divide military retired pay in a divorce is affected by a federal statute, the Uniformed Services Former Spouses' Protection Act (10 U.S.C. § 1408), and how a separate mechanism under that same statute governs direct payment of a share of that retired pay from the Defense Finance and Accounting Service (DFAS) to a former spouse. The parties were married on {{marriageDate}}. This sheet states what the federal statute says. It does not state whether military retired pay in this particular case will be divided, in what amount, or whether direct payment from DFAS will be available -- those are outcomes that depend on the facts of the case, the terms of the state court's order, and DFAS's own application of the statute to that order.

clauses.title: USFSPA: State Courts May Treat Disposable Retired Pay as Divisible Property
clauses.body: Before 1981, whether a state court could divide a service member's military retired pay as marital or community property upon divorce was itself contested. In McCarty v. McCarty, the U.S. Supreme Court took up 'the question ... whether, upon the dissolution of a marriage, federal law precludes a state court from dividing military nondisability retired pay pursuant to state community property laws,' and reversed a California Court of Appeal judgment that had divided such pay as community property, holding that federal law did preclude the state-law division. Congress responded the same year by enacting the Uniformed Services Former Spouses' Protection Act (USFSPA), codified at 10 U.S.C. § 1408, which authorizes -- but does not require -- state courts to treat military retired pay as divisible property. The statute's operative authorization states: 'Subject to the limitations of this section, a court may treat disposable retired pay payable to a member for pay periods beginning after June 25, 1981, either as property solely of the member or as property of the member and his spouse in accordance with the law of the jurisdiction of such court.' The statute goes on to bar a court from treating retired pay as divisible property in a proceeding involving a final divorce, dissolution, annulment, or legal separation decree that was issued before June 25, 1981, and that did not treat or reserve jurisdiction to treat any retired pay as property of the member and spouse. Whether, and how, disposable retired pay is actually divided in a given case is governed by the law of the state whose court has jurisdiction -- USFSPA authorizes state-law property division of this pay; it does not itself impose a particular division formula or outcome.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two genuinely independent, different-type sources: the current statutory text of 10 U.S.C. § 1408(c)(1) (fetched from Cornell Legal Information Institute, law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/10/1408, and independently re-fetched with a second, distinct User-Agent string and request configuration -- the two fetches returned byte-identical text) and the U.S. Supreme Court's opinion in McCarty v. McCarty, 453 U.S. 210 (1981) (fetched via the CourtListener case-law database, a different source and source type entirely -- primary case law rather than the U.S. Code). One precise detail worth flagging rather than glossing over: the statute's retroactivity cutoff is pay periods beginning after June 25, 1981 -- one day before the McCarty decision issued (June 26, 1981) -- not the date of the decision itself; this clause states the statutory date exactly as codified rather than approximating it to the decision date. Note also that the commonly cited case-reporter citation for McCarty is sometimes miswritten as 452 U.S. 210; the citation actually returned by CourtListener's official reporter data is 453 U.S. 210, which is the citation used here. This clause does not address the separate, further requirements for direct payment from DFAS (a different question from divisibility, covered in a separate clause), nor the statutory definition of 'disposable retired pay' itself (also covered separately).

citations.quote: Subject to the limitations of this section, a court may treat disposable retired pay payable to a member for pay periods beginning after June 25, 1981, either as property solely of the member or as property of the member and his spouse in accordance with the law of the jurisdiction of such court.

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of "Disposable Retired Pay"
clauses.body: USFSPA's authorization to treat retired pay as divisible property applies specifically to "disposable retired pay," a defined term -- not necessarily a member's full gross retired pay. The statute defines it as follows: 'The term "disposable retired pay" means the total monthly retired pay to which a member is entitled less amounts which-- (i) are owed by that member to the United States for previous overpayments of retired pay and for recoupments required by law resulting from entitlement to retired pay; (ii) are deducted from the retired pay of such member as a result of forfeitures of retired pay ordered by a court-martial or as a result of a waiver of retired pay required by law in order to receive compensation under title 5 or title 38; (iii) in the case of a member entitled to retired pay under chapter 61 of this title, are equal to the amount of retired pay of the member under that chapter computed using the percentage of the member's disability on the date when the member was retired (or the date on which the member's name was placed on the temporary disability retired list); or (iv) are deducted because of an election under chapter 73 of this title to provide an annuity to a spouse or former spouse to whom payment of a portion of such member's retired pay is being made pursuant to a court order under this section.' In plain terms, the statute's own text excludes from the divisible amount: prior overpayment recoupments owed to the United States; court-martial forfeitures and certain waivers required to receive VA or federal civil-service compensation; the disability-percentage-computed portion of pay for a member retired under the statute's disability-retirement chapter (chapter 61); and amounts deducted for a Survivor Benefit Plan annuity election benefiting the spouse or former spouse who is already receiving a court-ordered share.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 10 U.S.C. § 1408(a)(4)(A), fetched from Cornell Legal Information Institute and independently re-fetched with a second, distinct User-Agent string and request configuration; both fetches returned byte-identical text. This is the same statutory section as the surrounding clauses in this document (10 U.S.C. § 1408) -- not an independent source from those clauses, only a different subsection of the same section. The statute contains an additional subparagraph, § 1408(a)(4)(B), setting out special rules for computing a member's hypothetical retired pay when a property-division decree becomes final before the member actually retires; that computation-heavy provision is not quoted here. This clause states only the statutory exclusions themselves; it does not state, and should not be read to suggest, what any particular service member's disposable retired pay amount is or would be.
