clauses.title: The "10/10 Rule" Governs Direct DFAS Payment, Not Whether Retired Pay Can Be Divided
clauses.body: A frequently repeated shorthand -- the "10/10 rule" -- is often described as though it decides whether military retired pay can be divided as property at all. The statutory text does not support that description. The 10-year overlap requirement appears only in the part of USFSPA that governs direct payment by DFAS to a former spouse, not in the part that authorizes courts to treat retired pay as divisible property (addressed in a separate clause, which contains no marriage-length or service-length threshold). The direct-payment provision states: 'If the spouse or former spouse to whom payments are to be made under this section was not married to the member for a period of 10 years or more during which the member performed at least 10 years of service creditable in determining the member's eligibility for retired pay, payments may not be made under this section to the extent that they include an amount resulting from the treatment by the court under subsection (c) of disposable retired pay of the member as property of the member or property of the member and his spouse.' In plain terms: if the marriage and the member's creditable military service did not overlap for at least 10 years, DFAS will not make direct payments to the former spouse of the property-division portion of a court order under this statute -- but this provision, by its own terms, only limits payments 'under this section' (i.e., direct payment by DFAS); it does not purport to limit a court's separate authority under subsection (c) to treat the retired pay as divisible property in the first place. A court order dividing retired pay issued in a marriage that does not meet the 10/10 overlap can still be enforced -- just not through DFAS's direct-payment mechanism.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 10 U.S.C. § 1408(d)(2), fetched from Cornell Legal Information Institute and independently re-fetched with a second, distinct User-Agent string and request configuration; both fetches returned byte-identical text. This is the same statutory section as the surrounding clauses in this document (10 U.S.C. § 1408) -- not an independent source from those clauses, only a different subsection of the same section. This clause states what the statutory text itself says about the scope of the 10/10 rule (a direct-payment limitation) versus the divisibility authorization in subsection (c); it does not address how a former spouse who does not meet the 10/10 overlap might otherwise seek to collect an awarded share directly from the member, which is a matter of state enforcement law outside this federal statute and not covered here.

citations.quote: If the spouse or former spouse to whom payments are to be made under this section was not married to the member for a period of 10 years or more during which the member performed at least 10 years of service creditable in determining the member’s eligibility for retired pay, payments may not be made under this section to the extent that they include an amount resulting from the treatment by the court under subsection (c) of disposable retired pay of the member as property of the member or property of the member and his spouse.

clauses.title: Statutory Caps on the Percentage Payable Through DFAS
clauses.body: USFSPA caps how much of a member's disposable retired pay DFAS may pay out through its direct-payment mechanism, and the statute sets more than one cap depending on what is being paid. For property-division orders specifically, the statute provides: 'The total amount of the disposable retired pay of a member payable under all court orders pursuant to subsection (c) may not exceed 50 percent of such disposable retired pay.' A separate, broader cap applies when property-division payments are combined with other legal process against the same pay (for example, wage-garnishment-type process for child support or alimony under the Social Security Act): 'the total amount of the disposable retired pay of a member payable by the Secretary concerned under all court orders pursuant to this section and all legal processes pursuant to section 459 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 659) with respect to a member may not exceed 65 percent of the amount of the retired pay payable to such member that is considered under section 462 of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 662) to be remuneration for employment that is payable by the United States.' In plain terms, the statute sets a 50 percent ceiling on the disposable retired pay DFAS will pay out under property-division court orders alone, and a separate, higher 65 percent ceiling that applies when property-division payments are combined with other garnishment-type legal process against the same member's pay.

These two subsections are not independent of one another, or of the other clauses in this document -- all are the same statutory section, 10 U.S.C. § 1408. This clause does not attempt to compute what percentage would apply in any particular case, does not address the separate 25 percent cap the statute sets for child-abuse garnishment orders under a different subsection, and does not address how these caps interact with a member's own separate wage garnishment or allotment obligations outside this statute.

clauses.title: A Separate Federal Mechanism -- Not an ERISA Plan or QDRO
clauses.body: Military retired pay is not divided through the same legal mechanism used for a typical private-employer pension or 401(k). Division of private-sector retirement plans generally proceeds under Title I of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), using an order commonly called a Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO). ERISA's own text says that Title I 'shall not apply to any employee benefit plan if ... such plan is a governmental plan (as defined in section 1002(32) of this title),' and separately defines that term: 'The term "governmental plan" means a plan established or maintained for its employees by the Government of the United States, by the government of any State or political subdivision thereof, or by any agency or instrumentality of any of the foregoing.' Military retired pay is a benefit established and maintained by the United States government for its own uniformed-service personnel. Division of military retired pay upon divorce is instead governed entirely by the separate federal statute discussed throughout this document, 10 U.S.C. § 1408, which sets its own definitions, its own state-court authorization, and its own direct-payment mechanism through DFAS.
clauses.gap: This clause's ERISA quotations -- 29 U.S.C. § 1003(b)(1) and 29 U.S.C. § 1002(32) -- were fetched from Cornell Legal Information Institute and independently re-fetched with a second, distinct User-Agent string and request configuration; both fetches returned byte-identical text. Those two ERISA sections are not independent of one another (both are provisions of the same statute, ERISA), though as a pair they are an independent source from the 10 U.S.C. § 1408 material quoted in this document's other clauses -- a genuinely different federal statute. This clause was deliberately kept narrow: it verifies only that ERISA Title I's own governmental-plan exclusion covers a benefit plan of the United States government (which military retired pay is), and that the QDRO mechanism is a creature of that same excluded Title I. It does not assert that court orders dividing military retired pay are called "military pension division orders" or any other specific term of art -- no primary source located in this research used that phrase in describing 10 U.S.C. § 1408, so that terminology is not used here. It also does not address California's CalPERS or CalSTRS public-employee pension systems, which are governed by their own state statutes; no primary citation for those systems' treatment on divorce was verified in this research, so that comparison is omitted rather than asserted.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act of 2008 (GINA), a federal employment-discrimination statute, as it relates to {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}. It states facts about what GINA prohibits with respect to genetic information in employment, the specific statutory exceptions that let an employer request or acquire genetic information in limited circumstances, and the confidentiality requirement that applies to genetic information an employer lawfully holds. Genetic information is a category of information distinct from the disability-related medical information addressed by the Americans with Disabilities Act; this document does not restate ADA obligations and is not itself a medical inquiry, a consent form, or an authorization for any specific request. It does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} whether any particular request, inquiry, or record involves genetic information under GINA, or what to do about any specific situation.

clauses.title: Discrimination Because of Genetic Information Is an Unlawful Employment Practice
clauses.body: Federal law makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to fail or refuse to hire, to discharge, or otherwise to discriminate against an employee with respect to compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of genetic information with respect to that employee. It is separately an unlawful employment practice for an employer to limit, segregate, or classify its employees in a way that would deprive or tend to deprive an employee of employment opportunities, or that would otherwise adversely affect the employee's status as an employee, because of genetic information with respect to that employee. Under the statute's own definitions, this protection extends to applicants as well as current employees.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory subsection, 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-1(a), quoted in full below; it is not corroborated by a second, independent statutory source. The point that the statute's protection extends to applicants comes from GINA's own definitions section, 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff(2)(A)(i), which defines 'employee' by cross-reference to a Title VII definition that itself includes an applicant; that cross-reference was reviewed in this research but is not separately quoted as a citation here, and is stated in the body as a summarized fact rather than a directly verified quote. This clause states only that the described conduct is an unlawful employment practice under the statute; it does not determine whether any specific employer's treatment of any specific individual was because of genetic information, and it does not address the separate, narrower restriction on requesting or acquiring genetic information in the first place, which is covered in a later clause.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-1(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act, Title II, employer practices — discrimination based on genetic information
citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer — (1) to fail or refuse to hire, or to discharge, any employee , or otherwise to discriminate against any employee with respect to the compensation, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment of the employee , because of genetic information with respect to the employee; or (2) to limit, segregate, or classify the employees of the employer in any way that would deprive or tend to deprive any employee of employment opportunities or otherwise adversely affect the status of the employee as an employee, because of genetic information with respect to the employee.

clauses.title: What Counts as "Genetic Information" Under GINA
clauses.body: GINA defines "genetic information," with respect to an individual, as information about: the individual's own genetic tests; the genetic tests of the individual's family members; and the manifestation of a disease or disorder in the individual's family members. This third category is commonly described as family medical history, and the statute's definition reaches it directly — GINA's protection is not limited to genetic tests alone. The definition also includes, for any individual, a request for or receipt of genetic services, or participation in clinical research that includes genetic services, by that individual or a family member. The statute separately defines "genetic test" as an analysis of human DNA, RNA, chromosomes, proteins, or metabolites that detects genotypes, mutations, or chromosomal changes, and it expressly excludes an analysis of proteins or metabolites that does not detect genotypes, mutations, or chromosomal changes. The definition of "genetic information" expressly excludes information about an individual's sex or age.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory section, 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff(4) (with the 'genetic test' definition drawn from paragraph (7) of that same section); these paragraphs are subsections of one section and are not independent sources of one another. The statute's definition of 'family member' (42 U.S.C. § 2000ff(3)) — which reaches first-, second-, third-, and fourth-degree relatives of the individual, plus certain dependents — was reviewed as part of this research but is not separately quoted or made a citation in this clause; a reader should not assume 'family member' is limited to immediate family for GINA purposes. This clause states the statutory definition only; it does not determine whether any particular piece of information about any specific individual meets that definition.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff(4) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: GINA, Title II, definitions — "genetic information"
citations.quote: The term “ genetic information ” means, with respect to any individual, information about— (i) such individual’s genetic tests , (ii) the genetic tests of family members of such individual, and (iii) the manifestation of a disease or disorder in family members of such individual. (B) Inclusion of genetic services and participation in genetic research Such term includes, with respect to any individual, any request for, or receipt of, genetic services , or participation in clinical research which includes genetic services , by such individual or any family member of such individual. (C) Exclusions The term “ genetic information ” shall not include information about the sex or age of any individual.

clauses.title: Restriction on Requesting, Requiring, or Purchasing Genetic Information
clauses.body: Separately from the discrimination prohibition described above, federal law makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to request, require, or purchase genetic information with respect to an employee or a family member of the employee, subject to six specific statutory exceptions. Those exceptions apply where: (1) the employer inadvertently requests or requires family medical history; (2) the employer offers health or genetic services, including as part of a wellness program, the employee has given prior, knowing, voluntary, written authorization, and specific statutory limits are met on who may receive individually identifiable results and how the employer may receive them; (3) the employer requests or requires family medical history from the employee to comply with the certification provisions of the federal Family and Medical Leave Act or a comparable state family and medical leave law; (4) the employer purchases documents that are commercially and publicly available — such as newspapers, magazines, periodicals, and books, but not including medical databases or court records — that happen to include family medical history; (5) the information is used for genetic monitoring of the biological effects of toxic substances in the workplace, subject to written-notice, authorization-or-legal-mandate, individual-results, regulatory-compliance, and aggregate-reporting conditions specified in the statute; or (6) the employer conducts DNA analysis for law enforcement purposes as a forensic laboratory or for human remains identification, limited to using the results for quality-control analysis of DNA identification markers to detect sample contamination.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory subsection, 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-1(b), quoted here in full; it is not corroborated by a second, independent source. Each of the six exceptions carries additional statutory conditions beyond the short description in this clause's body — for example, the genetic-monitoring exception (5) has five separate lettered sub-conditions, and the wellness-program exception (2) has four lettered sub-conditions — all of which appear in the quoted text below but are only summarized, not individually restated, in the body above. This clause does not determine whether any specific employer's request, requirement, or purchase of information about any specific individual falls within or outside any of these exceptions.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-1(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: GINA, Title II, employer practices — acquisition of genetic information and statutory exceptions
citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to request, require, or purchase genetic information with respect to an employee or a family member of the employee except— (1) where an employer inadvertently requests or requires family medical history of the employee or family member of the employee; (2) where— (A) health or genetic services are offered by the employer, including such services offered as part of a wellness program; (B) the employee provides prior, knowing, voluntary, and written authorization; (C) only the employee (or family member if the family member is receiving genetic services ) and the licensed health care professional or board certified genetic counselor involved in providing such services receive individually identifiable information concerning the results of such services; and (D) any individually identifiable genetic information provided under subparagraph (C) in connection with the services provided under subparagraph (A) is only available for purposes of such services and shall not be disclosed to the employer except in aggregate terms that do not disclose the identity of specific employees; (3) where an employer requests or requires family medical history from the employee to comply with the certification provisions of section 2613 of title 29 or such requirements under State family and medical leave laws; (4) where an employer purchases documents that are commercially and publicly available (including newspapers, magazines, periodicals, and books, but not including medical databases or court records) that include family medical history; (5) where the information involved is to be used for genetic monitoring of the biological effects of toxic substances in the workplace, but only if— (A) the employer provides written notice of the genetic monitoring to the employee; (B) (i) the employee provides prior, knowing, voluntary, and written authorization; or (ii) the genetic monitoring is required by Federal or State law; (C) the employee is informed of individual monitoring results; (D) the monitoring is in compliance with— (i) any Federal genetic monitoring regulations, including any such regulations that may be promulgated by the Secretary of Labor pursuant to the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 ( 29 U.S.C. 651 et seq.), the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 ( 30 U.S.C. 801 et seq.), or the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 ( 42 U.S.C. 2011 et seq.); or (ii) State genetic monitoring regulations, in the case of a State that is implementing genetic monitoring regulations under the authority of the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 ( 29 U.S.C. 651 et seq.); and (E) the employer , excluding any licensed health care professional or board certified genetic counselor that is involved in the genetic monitoring program, receives the results of the monitoring only in aggregate terms that do not disclose the identity of specific employees; or (6) where the employer conducts DNA analysis for law enforcement purposes as a forensic laboratory or for purposes of human remains identification, and requests or requires genetic information of such employer’ s employees, but only to the extent that such genetic information is used for analysis of DNA identification markers for quality control to detect sample contamination.

clauses.title: Confidentiality of Genetic Information the Employer Lawfully Holds
clauses.body: If an employer possesses genetic information about an employee, federal law requires that information to be maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files, and treated as a confidential medical record of the employee. The statute itself provides a specific route to compliance: an employer is considered to be in compliance with this requirement if the genetic information is maintained with, and treated as, a confidential medical record under the Americans with Disabilities Act's own post-offer medical-examination confidentiality provision, 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(3)(B). Federal law also limits disclosure of genetic information the employer holds to a specific, enumerated list of circumstances, including disclosure to the employee at the employee's own written request, in response to a court order (limited to the information the order expressly authorizes), to government officials investigating compliance, in connection with an employee's compliance with family-and-medical-leave certification requirements, and to certain researchers and public health agencies under conditions specified in the statute.
clauses.gap: The confidentiality requirement (42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-5(a)) and the disclosure-limitation list (42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-5(b)) are both part of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another; they are treated here as one connected source, and the disclosure-limitation list is summarized rather than separately quoted. The statute's own text ties GINA confidentiality directly to the ADA's confidentiality provision, 42 U.S.C. § 12112(d)(3)(B) — it states that an employer maintaining genetic information in compliance with that ADA provision is considered to be in compliance with GINA's own separate-forms/separate-files requirement — but that ADA provision's text was not independently re-fetched and re-verified in this research session; the fact that GINA cross-references it is verified below, but the ADA text itself is not separately confirmed here. A reader should not assume the two confidentiality regimes are identical in every respect, only that the statute makes compliance with one a recognized route to compliance with the other. This clause does not itemize every sub-condition of the disclosure exceptions listed in the statute, and it does not determine whether any specific disclosure by any specific employer is permitted.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff-5(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: GINA, Title II — confidentiality of genetic information, treatment as part of confidential medical record
citations.quote: If an employer , employment agency , labor organization , or joint labor-management committee possesses genetic information about an employee or member, such information shall be maintained on separate forms and in separate medical files and be treated as a confidential medical record of the employee or member. An employer, employment agency, labor organization, or joint labor-management committee shall be considered to be in compliance with the maintenance of information requirements of this subsection with respect to genetic information subject to this subsection that is maintained with and treated as a confidential medical record under section 12112(d)(3)(B) of this title .

clauses.title: Which Employers Are Covered: The Fifteen-Employee Threshold
clauses.body: GINA's employment provisions apply only to an "employer" as the statute defines that term. GINA's own definitions section defines "employer" for the ordinary private-sector case by cross-reference to the definition used in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b) (GINA's definitions section also cross-references several narrower categories covering certain federal, state, and congressional employers, not addressed here). Title VII's definition, which GINA borrows in this way, defines "employer" as a person engaged in an industry affecting commerce who has fifteen or more employees for each working day in each of twenty or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year, subject to specific statutory exclusions, including the United States, corporations wholly owned by the United States government, Indian tribes, and certain bona fide private membership clubs exempt from taxation.
clauses.gap: These two citations are not independent corroboration of the same point: 42 U.S.C. § 2000ff(2)(B)(i) is GINA's own definitions section, and it establishes the fifteen-employee threshold only by cross-referencing 42 U.S.C. § 2000e(b), a separate section of Title VII that GINA's text incorporates rather than restates; the two are genuinely distinct, independently numbered sections of the U.S. Code, but one supplies the actual numeric threshold that the other merely borrows by reference, so they are presented together as a citation chain rather than as two independent sources reaching the same conclusion. This clause does not address the several other, narrower employer categories GINA's definition also cross-references (state employees, congressional employees, and certain other federal employees under Title 2 and Title 3 of the U.S. Code), and it does not determine whether any specific entity meets the fifteen-or-more-employees threshold in any given year.

Purpose
clauses.body: {{companyName}} maintains this California Suitable Seating Information Sheet to describe the suitable-seating requirement that applies to working employees, including {{employeeName}}, under the applicable California IWC Wage Order, and to summarize how California courts have construed that requirement. This information sheet states facts about California law; it does not determine whether any particular job, task, or workspace at {{companyName}} does or does not require a seat, and it is not a statement that {{companyName}} has or has not provided suitable seating for any specific position.

clauses.title: The Wage Order Seating Requirement
clauses.body: California's Industrial Welfare Commission (IWC) Wage Orders require that "[a]ll working employees shall be provided with suitable seats when the nature of the work reasonably permits the use of seats." Separately, when an employee is not engaged in the active duties of employment and the nature of the work requires standing, the same wage order requires that "an adequate number of suitable seats shall be placed in reasonable proximity to the work area" and that employees be permitted to use those seats when doing so does not interfere with the performance of their duties.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 14 (the general, catch-all wage order for professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations, used elsewhere in this corpus for the same reason). It was fetched directly from the California Department of Industrial Relations (dir.ca.gov) using two separate curl requests with different User-Agent strings, both returning byte-identical PDF content (HTTP 200); the extracted text was then confirmed as an exact, whitespace-normalized substring of that fetched text. WebFetch was not used for this domain in this session (it is expected to be blocked in this environment for dir.ca.gov, based on prior sessions' notes), so the curl-with-two-User-Agents method served as the verification substitute. The identical section 14(A) and 14(B) language was independently confirmed to also appear, word for word, in IWC Wage Order No. 7-2001 (Mercantile Industry), fetched the same way. This is not, however, proof that every one of the 17 other IWC wage orders phrases section 14 identically — only Wage Orders 4-2001 and 7-2001 were fetched and checked this session. The two subdivisions quoted, section 14(A) and section 14(B), are two paragraphs of the same wage-order section and are not independent sources of each other; they describe two different circumstances (actively working, versus not engaged in active duties) rather than corroborating the same rule twice. This is California regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific employer or employee; the federal Fair Labor Standards Act contains no comparable seating requirement, and most states impose none. This clause states what the wage order requires; it does not state whether any particular job or task "reasonably permits the use of seats," which is addressed in the case-law clauses below.

clauses.title: “Nature of the Work” — The Kilby Test
clauses.body: In Kilby v. CVS Pharmacy, Inc. (2016) 63 Cal.4th 1, the California Supreme Court construed what the wage order's "nature of the work" language means. The Court held that "[t]he 'nature of the work' refers to an employee's tasks performed at a given location for which a right to a suitable seat is claimed, rather than a 'holistic' consideration of the entire range of an employee's duties anywhere on the jobsite during a complete shift." The Court further held that whether the nature of the work reasonably permits sitting "is a question to be determined objectively based on the totality of the circumstances," and that "[a]n employer's business judgment and the physical layout of the workplace are relevant but not dispositive factors," with the inquiry focused on the nature of the work rather than on an individual employee's characteristics.

The opinion text was read directly from CourtListener (opinion id 3191160, cluster id 3191248) and both quoted passages were confirmed as exact, whitespace-normalized substrings of that fetched opinion text. This clause states the legal test the Court adopted; it does not apply that test to any specific job, task, or workplace, and Kilby itself did not resolve whether either of the underlying employees (a CVS customer service representative or Chase bank tellers) was entitled to a seat — it returned the certified-question answers to the Ninth Circuit for further proceedings in each case.

clauses.title: Burden of Proof on Seat Availability
clauses.body: The California Supreme Court in Kilby v. CVS Pharmacy, Inc. also addressed who bears the burden of proof on whether a suitable seat is available. The Court held that "[a]n employer seeking to be excused from the requirement bears the burden of showing compliance is infeasible because no suitable seating exists." The Court reasoned that the wage order's text "unambiguously states employees 'shall be provided with suitable seats'" once the nature of the work reasonably permits seated work, and that there is no language requiring an employee to additionally prove that a particular type of seat would satisfy that requirement.

The opinion text was read directly from CourtListener (opinion id 3191160) and the quoted passage was confirmed as an exact, whitespace-normalized substring of that fetched opinion text. This clause states which party bears the burden of proof on the question of seat availability as a matter of law; it does not state whether a suitable seat is or is not available for any specific job or workplace, and it does not address burdens of proof on any other element of a seating claim (such as whether the nature of the work reasonably permits sitting in the first place, which is addressed by the totality-of-the-circumstances test in the preceding clause).

clauses.title: How the Seating Requirement Is Enforced
clauses.body: The suitable-seating requirement is a "condition[] of labor" fixed by an IWC wage order. California Labor Code section 1198 provides that "[t]he maximum hours of work and the standard conditions of labor fixed by the commission shall be the maximum hours of work and the standard conditions of labor for employees," and that employment "under conditions of labor prohibited by the order is unlawful." Separately, the Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA) provides that, for Labor Code provisions that do not otherwise specify a civil penalty, "there is established a civil penalty for a violation of these provisions," which an "aggrieved employee" may recover through a civil action "as an alternative" to enforcement by the Labor and Workforce Development Agency.
clauses.gap: Neither the wage order text nor Kilby v. CVS Pharmacy specifies a penalty amount for a suitable-seating violation, and this clause does not identify a case applying a specific dollar penalty to a seating violation. The mechanism described here is inferred from two Labor Code provisions read together: section 1198 (which makes employment under conditions prohibited by a wage order "unlawful" but does not itself set a penalty) and section 2699, subdivisions (a) and (f) (the PAGA default civil penalty and private-right-of-action provisions, which apply to Labor Code provisions — like section 1198 — that lack their own specified civil penalty). Section 2699(a) and section 2699(f) are two subdivisions of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another; together they are one source, independent of the section 1198 citation and of the wage-order and case-law citations in the other clauses of this document. This clause also does not address Labor Code section 1199, which separately makes a violation of wage order conditions of labor a criminal misdemeanor (fine of not less than $100 or imprisonment of not less than 30 days, or both) — a different, non-civil enforcement track this document does not describe further. clauses.title: Declaration and Purpose
clauses.body:
This information sheet concerns a work described as {{workDescription}}, titled {{workTitle}}, created by {{artistName}} (the "work"). {{ownerName}} is identified here as the work's current owner or possessor, for reference only. This sheet summarizes provisions of the federal Visual Artists Rights Act, 17 U.S.C. § 106A, which gives the author of a narrowly defined category of "work of visual art" (17 U.S.C. § 101) personal rights of attribution and integrity that exist separately from copyright ownership itself. It also summarizes the federal preemption provision, 17 U.S.C. § 301(f), which addresses how § 106A relates to state-law moral-rights statutes, including California's Art Preservation Act, Cal. Civ. Code § 987, which is covered in a separate document in this corpus.

This sheet is an informational record only. It does not determine whether {{workDescription}} meets § 106A's or § 101's own definition of a "work of visual art," does not determine whether any state-law right in {{workDescription}} is or is not preempted by 17 U.S.C. § 301(f), and does not itself assert, waive, reserve, or enforce any right under these statutes or any other law. It is not legal advice and is not a substitute for reading the statutes directly.

clauses.title: The Two Core Rights: Attribution and Integrity
clauses.body:
Separately from copyright ownership, the federal Visual Artists Rights Act, 17 U.S.C. § 106A, gives the author of a "work of visual art" two personal rights, independent of the exclusive rights that copyright itself provides under 17 U.S.C. § 106. Subsection (a) states: "Subject to section 107 and independent of the exclusive rights provided in section 106, the author of a work of visual art — (1) shall have the right— (A) to claim authorship of that work, and (B) to prevent the use of his or her name as the author of any work of visual art which he or she did not create; (2) shall have the right to prevent the use of his or her name as the author of the work of visual art in the event of a distortion, mutilation, or other modification of the work which would be prejudicial to his or her honor or reputation; and (3) subject to the limitations set forth in section 113(d), shall have the right— (A) to prevent any intentional distortion, mutilation, or other modification of that work which would be prejudicial to his or her honor or reputation, and any intentional distortion, mutilation, or modification of that work is a violation of that right, and (B) to prevent any destruction of a work of recognized stature, and any intentional or grossly negligent destruction of that work is a violation of that right."

Paragraphs (1) and (2) together make up what is commonly called the right of attribution; paragraph (3) is commonly called the right of integrity. Both belong only to the individual human author of the work, whether or not the author is also the work's copyright owner. Subsection (b) states: "Only the author of a work of visual art has the rights conferred by subsection (a) in that work, whether or not the author is the copyright owner." Whether any specific modification of {{workDescription}} would be "prejudicial to [{{artistName}}'s] honor or reputation," or whether {{workDescription}} is a work "of recognized stature" for purposes of the destruction right, are determinations the statute leaves to be made under its own terms; this sheet does not make either determination.

Subsection (c), which this clause does not quote, states two exceptions this sheet has not incorporated into its own body text: a modification resulting from "the passage of time or the inherent nature of the materials" is not a distortion, mutilation, or other modification described in the integrity right, and a modification resulting from conservation or from the public presentation of the work (including lighting and placement) is likewise not covered unless it is caused by gross negligence. clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of "Work of Visual Art"
clauses.body:
The rights described elsewhere in this document apply only to a work meeting the definition of "work of visual art" in 17 U.S.C. § 101. That definition states: "A 'work of visual art' is— (1) a painting, drawing, print, or sculpture, existing in a single copy, in a limited edition of 200 copies or fewer that are signed and consecutively numbered by the author, or, in the case of a sculpture, in multiple cast, carved, or fabricated sculptures of 200 or fewer that are consecutively numbered by the author and bear the signature or other identifying mark of the author; or (2) a still photographic image produced for exhibition purposes only, existing in a single copy that is signed by the author, or in a limited edition of 200 copies or fewer that are signed and consecutively numbered by the author."

The same definition then expressly excludes several categories from that coverage: "A work of visual art does not include— (A)(i) any poster, map, globe, chart, technical drawing, diagram, model, applied art, motion picture or other audiovisual work, book, magazine, newspaper, periodical, data base, electronic information service, electronic publication, or similar publication; (ii) any merchandising item or advertising, promotional, descriptive, covering, or packaging material or container; (iii) any portion or part of any item described in clause (i) or (ii); (B) any work made for hire; or (C) any work not subject to copyright protection under this title." Whether {{workDescription}} falls within the included categories and outside all of the excluded ones is a determination the statute leaves to be made under its own terms; this sheet does not make that determination.

clauses.title: How Long the Rights Last
clauses.body:
17 U.S.C. § 106A(d) fixes how long the attribution and integrity rights last, and the rule differs depending on when the work was created relative to the Visual Artists Rights Act's effective date. Section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, a session-law note that is not itself codified in Title 17 but is referenced directly by § 106A(d), states that the Act's provisions "take effect 6 months after the date of the enactment of this Act [Dec. 1, 1990]" — that is, on June 1, 1991.

For a work created on or after that effective date, § 106A(d)(1) states: "With respect to works of visual art created on or after the effective date set forth in section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, the rights conferred by subsection (a) shall endure for a term consisting of the life of the author." For a work created before that effective date but not yet transferred out of the author's hands as of that date, a different rule applies. Section 106A(d)(2) states: "With respect to works of visual art created before the effective date set forth in section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, but title to which has not, as of such effective date, been transferred from the author, the rights conferred by subsection (a) shall be coextensive with, and shall expire at the same time as, the rights conferred by section 106."

clauses.title: How the Rights Can Be Waived
clauses.body:
17 U.S.C. § 106A(e) states its own rule for giving up the attribution and integrity rights, distinct from the waiver rule under any state moral-rights statute. Subsection (e)(1) states: "The rights conferred by subsection (a) may not be transferred, but those rights may be waived if the author expressly agrees to such waiver in a written instrument signed by the author. Such instrument shall specifically identify the work, and uses of that work, to which the waiver applies, and the waiver shall apply only to the work and uses so identified. In the case of a joint work prepared by two or more authors, a waiver of rights under this paragraph made by one such author waives such rights for all such authors."

The statute also separates a waiver of these rights from a transfer of the work itself or of the copyright in it. Subsection (e)(2) states: "Ownership of the rights conferred by subsection (a) with respect to a work of visual art is distinct from ownership of any copy of that work, or of a copyright or any exclusive right under a copyright in that work. Transfer of ownership of any copy of a work of visual art, or of a copyright or any exclusive right under a copyright, shall not constitute a waiver of the rights conferred by subsection (a). Except as may otherwise be agreed by the author in a written instrument signed by the author, a waiver of the rights conferred by subsection (a) with respect to a work of visual art shall not constitute a transfer of ownership of any copy of that work, or of ownership of a copyright or of any exclusive right under a copyright in that work."

clauses.title: How VARA Relates to State Moral-Rights Statutes
clauses.body:
The Copyright Act's general preemption section, 17 U.S.C. § 301, contains a subsection addressing specifically how the Visual Artists Rights Act relates to state-law moral rights. Subsection (f)(1) states: "On or after the effective date set forth in section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990, all legal or equitable rights that are equivalent to any of the rights conferred by section 106A with respect to works of visual art to which the rights conferred by section 106A apply are governed exclusively by section 106A and section 113(d) and the provisions of this title relating to such sections. Thereafter, no person is entitled to any such right or equivalent right in any work of visual art under the common law or statutes of any State."

That rule is narrower than a blanket preemption of state moral-rights law. By its own terms it reaches only rights that are "equivalent" to the § 106A rights, and only "with respect to works of visual art to which the rights conferred by section 106A apply" — that is, works meeting § 106A's and § 101's own definition described elsewhere in this document. The same subsection then expressly preserves certain state-law rights and remedies. Subsection (f)(2) states: "Nothing in paragraph (1) annuls or limits any rights or remedies under the common law or statutes of any State with respect to— (A) any cause of action from undertakings commenced before the effective date set forth in section 610(a) of the Visual Artists Rights Act of 1990; (B) activities violating legal or equitable rights that are not equivalent to any of the rights conferred by section 106A with respect to works of visual art; or (C) activities violating legal or equitable rights which extend beyond the life of the author."

Read together, § 301(f) states that state-law rights equivalent to § 106A's, in a work meeting § 106A's own "work of visual art" definition, are governed exclusively by § 106A as to conduct on or after VARA's effective date — but state law is expressly left in place, by the statute's own terms, for a cause of action from conduct that began before that effective date, for a state-law right that is not equivalent to a § 106A right, for a state-law right in a work falling outside § 106A's own "work of visual art" definition (since paragraph (f)(1) does not reach such a work at all), and for a state-law right that by its own terms extends beyond the life of the author.

Code § 987(g)(1) states that the state statute's rights and duties exist "until the 50th anniversary of the death of the artist," while 17 U.S.C. § 106A(d)(1) states that, for a work created on or after VARA's effective date, the federal rights last only "for a term consisting of the life of the author" — a state-law right that, by its own terms, extends beyond the author's death falls within the express carve-out in § 301(f)(2)(C) for "activities violating legal or equitable rights which extend beyond the life of the author," and this document does not find that such a right is preempted. This document does not reach any conclusion about the preemption status of any other specific state-law right, and no other conclusion should be inferred from it.

Thereafter, no person is entitled to any such right or equivalent right in any work of visual art under the common law or statutes of any State.

clauses.title: Record and Signature
Group Life Insurance Conversion Notice
Right to Convert to an Individual Policy Without Evidence of Insurability
clauses.body: California law requires that a group life insurance policy contain a provision allowing an employee whose employment terminates, for any reason, to obtain an individual life insurance policy. To do so, {{employeeName}} must apply to {{insurerName}} within 31 days after the termination of employment and pay the premium applicable to the class of risk {{employeeName}} belongs to and to the form and amount of the policy at {{employeeName}}'s then-attained age. If application and payment are made within that 31-day period, the statute entitles the applicant to issuance of the individual policy without producing evidence of insurability. The individual policy must be one of the forms the insurer customarily issues, other than term insurance.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory law (Cal. Insurance Code Section 10209(a)(2)), used as real evidence of the conversion right the statute creates for group life policies delivered in California — not a claim that any particular group life plan is in fact a policy "delivered in this state" and therefore governed by this section, or that a particular employee's own termination and application will in fact satisfy the statute's conditions. This clause and the other California-law clauses in this document (the face-amount clause, the death-during-the-conversion-period clause, and the notice/extension clause) all cite different subdivisions of this same statutory section, Insurance Code Section 10209; they are not independent of one another as sources. The statute's own text refers to two exceptions, Sections 10203.5 and 10203.8, that this document does not independently verify or restate.

citations.case: Cal. Insurance Code Section 10209(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Insurance Code, group life policy conversion right
citations.quote: A provision that if the employment terminates for any reason whatsoever and the employee applies to the insurer within 31 days after the termination, paying the premium applicable to the class of risk to which he or she belongs and to the form and amount of the policy at his or her then attained age, he or she is entitled, without producing evidence of insurability, to the issue by the insurer of any individual life policy in any one of the forms, other than term insurance, customarily issued by the insurer.

clauses.title: Amount of the Converted Individual Policy
clauses.body: California law states that the individual policy issued in lieu of group insurance must be in an amount equal to the amount of the employee's protection under the group insurance at the time of the termination. The statute does not authorize the insurer to issue a converted policy for a lesser face amount, and does not itself state a separate cap distinct from the group coverage amount in force at termination -- here, {{groupCoverageFaceAmount}} under {{planName}}.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory law (Cal. Insurance Code Section 10209(a)(3)), used as real evidence of the statutory face-amount rule -- not a claim about what a particular employee's group coverage amount actually was at termination, which depends on the group policy's own terms (for example, coverage amounts can themselves depend on salary or a scheduled benefit that may already have changed before termination). This clause cites the same statutory section as the conversion-right, death-during-window, and notice/extension clauses in this document (Insurance Code Section 10209); they are not independent of one another as sources.

citations.case: Cal. Insurance Code Section 10209(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Insurance Code, amount of converted individual policy
citations.quote: A statement that the policy in lieu of group insurance will be in an amount equal to the amount of his or her protection under the group insurance at the time of the termination.

clauses.title: Death During the 31-Day Conversion Period
clauses.body: California law provides that if the employee dies during the 31-day period within which the employee is entitled to have an individual policy issued, and before the individual policy has become effective, the amount of life insurance the employee was entitled to have issued under the individual policy is payable as a claim under the group policy. This is true whether or not the employee had applied for the individual policy or paid the first premium for it before death.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory law (Cal. Insurance Code Section 10209(a)(4)), used as real evidence of this statutory death-during-conversion rule -- not a claim about any particular person's cause or date of death, or about who the beneficiary of any resulting claim would be, which depends on the group policy's own beneficiary-designation terms and is not addressed by this clause. This clause cites the same statutory section as the conversion-right, face-amount, and notice/extension clauses in this document (Insurance Code Section 10209); they are not independent of one another as sources.

citations.case: Cal. Insurance Code Section 10209(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Insurance Code, death during the conversion period
citations.quote: A provision that if the employee dies during the 31-day period within which he or she is entitled to have an individual policy issued to him or her in accordance with this section and before the policy shall have become effective, the amount of life insurance that the employee is entitled to have issued to him or her under the individual policy shall be payable as a claim under the group policy, whether or not application for the individual policy or the payment of the first premium therefor has been made.

clauses.title: Notice of the Conversion Right and the Extension When Notice Is Late
clauses.body: California law provides that if an employee entitled to convert group life coverage without evidence of insurability is not given notice of the existence of that right at least 15 days before the conversion period would otherwise expire, the employee has an additional period to exercise the right. That additional period expires 25 days after the employee is given the notice, but in no event does it extend beyond 60 days after the expiration date the policy otherwise provided. Written notice presented to the employee, or mailed by the policyholder or the insurer to the employee's last-known address, satisfies this notice requirement. This rule does not, by itself, extend any insurance coverage beyond the period the policy provides.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory law (Cal. Insurance Code Section 10209(b)), used as real evidence of the statutory notice-and-extension rule -- not a claim about whether a particular employee has, or has not, already been given the notice this rule describes, or about the date any such notice was given, which are facts this clause does not establish. Section 10209 itself does not specify who -- the employer, the plan administrator, or the insurer -- bears the obligation to give this notice in the first instance; it states only the consequence (an extended period) if notice of the right is not given at least 15 days before the period would otherwise expire. This clause cites the same statutory section as the conversion-right, face-amount, and death-during-window clauses in this document (Insurance Code Section 10209); they are not independent of one another as sources. This document did not locate a separate, independently-numbered statutory section imposing an affirmative notice-timing deadline on the employer or insurer specific to Section 10209 conversions; that is a gap in this document's research, not an assertion that no such obligation could exist under some other source (for example, a plan's own summary plan description or ERISA disclosure obligations, which were not researched for this document).

citations.case: Cal. Insurance Code Section 10209(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Insurance Code, extension when notice of the conversion right is late
citations.quote: If any employee insured under a group life insurance policy delivered in this state becomes entitled under the terms of the policy to have an individual policy of life insurance issued to him or her without evidence of insurability, subject to making of application and payment of the first premium within the period specified in the policy, and if the employee is not given notice of the existence of the right at least 15 days prior to the expiration date of the period, the employee shall have an additional period within which to exercise the right, but nothing in this section shall be construed to continue any insurance beyond the period provided in the policy. This additional period shall expire 25 days next after the employee is given the notice but in no event shall the additional period extend beyond 60 days next after the expiration date of the period provided in the policy.

clauses.title: This Right Is Separate From, and Unaffected By, COBRA and Cal-COBRA
clauses.body: The federal COBRA statute requires the plan sponsor of a "group health plan" to provide qualified beneficiaries the opportunity to elect continuation coverage. "Group health plan" is itself defined, for this purpose, as an employee welfare benefit plan providing medical care to participants or beneficiaries. Group life insurance is not medical care and is not a "group health plan" within this federal definition, so the federal COBRA continuation-coverage scheme -- and California's parallel Cal-COBRA scheme, which extends a similar right for small employers not covered by federal COBRA -- do not apply to group life insurance coverage. The conversion right described in this document arises instead from California's Insurance Code provisions on group life policies, an entirely separate body of law, and operates independently of whatever rights {{employeeName}} may separately have regarding continuation of group health coverage.
clauses.gap: This clause combines two independent, separately-numbered federal statutory sections -- 29 U.S.C. Section 1161(a) (the COBRA continuation-coverage obligation itself) and 29 U.S.C. Section 1167(1) (COBRA's definition of "group health plan") -- which is a genuinely independent verification, not two subdivisions of one section. It is offered as real evidence of federal law's own textual scope (medical care plans), used to support the general proposition that life insurance is not a COBRA-covered benefit -- not a claim that any particular group life plan has been individually confirmed to fall outside COBRA's scope, and not a restatement of California's Cal-COBRA statute, which this document does not independently quote here (see this corpus's separate Cal-COBRA Election Notice document, whose own clauses describe Cal-COBRA's scope as extending continuation rights for group health coverage specifically). This clause does not address whether some other law -- for example, a state law mandating conversion rights for other insurance types, or an employer's own severance-plan terms -- might separately touch group life insurance; none was researched for this document.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. Section 1161(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, COBRA continuation-coverage obligation runs to group health plans
citations.quote: The plan sponsor of each group health plan shall provide, in accordance with this part, that each qualified beneficiary who would lose coverage under the plan as a result of a qualifying event is entitled, under the plan, to elect, within the election period, continuation coverage under the plan.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. Section 1167(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, COBRA's definition of "group health plan"
citations.quote: The term “group health plan” means an employee welfare benefit plan providing medical care (as defined in section 213(d) of title 26) to participants or beneficiaries directly or through insurance, reimbursement, or otherwise.

clauses.title: Record of Conversion Application
Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet addresses what happens to a landlord's claim for unpaid rent and other damages under California Civil Code § 1951.2 if {{tenantName}} breaches the lease and abandons the property at {{propertyAddress}} before {{leaseEndDate}} — the end of the lease term that began {{leaseStartDate}} — or if {{landlordName}} instead terminates {{tenantName}}'s right to possession because of a breach of the lease. It is a companion to the underlying lease between {{landlordName}} and {{tenantName}} for that property, at a monthly rent of ${{monthlyRent}}, and addresses only what happens to a landlord's damages claim after an abandonment or breach-based termination — not the lease terms themselves. This document states California statutory law and reported case law as of the date signed below. It does not determine that any breach, abandonment, or termination has occurred in this or any specific case, does not determine that any particular reletting effort was or was not reasonable, and does not calculate any landlord's actual recoverable damages.

clauses.title: When a Landlord's § 1951.2 Damages Claim Arises
clauses.body: Under California Civil Code § 1951.2, if a tenant breaches the lease and abandons the property before the end of the lease term — or if the tenant's right to possession is instead terminated by the landlord because of a breach of the lease — the lease terminates by operation of this statute. Upon that termination, the statute lets the landlord recover from the tenant the categories of damages the statute itself defines, described in the next clause of this document. This rule is stated as the general rule; a separate statute, Civil Code § 1951.4, provides an alternative remedy that a landlord may use instead in some circumstances, addressed later in this document.
clauses.gap: This clause and the next several clauses in this document all draw on subdivisions of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1951.2 — they are not independent of one another. Section 1951.2 does not itself define "abandons" or "abandonment," and this document does not supply a definition beyond the statute's own text; whether a tenant has abandoned a specific property in a specific case is a factual question this document does not resolve. This is one state's statute; the remedies and mitigation rules that apply when a tenant abandons leased property vary by state, and this document addresses only California law.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the triggering events and general termination rule
citations.quote: if a lessee of real property breaches the lease and abandons the property before the end of the term or if his right to possession is terminated by the lessor because of a breach of the lease, the lease terminates.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the section's own cross-reference to the alternative remedy in § 1951.4
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in Section 1951.4

clauses.title: The Four Categories of Recoverable Damages
clauses.body: Once a tenancy terminates under Civil Code § 1951.2, the statute lets the landlord recover, from the tenant, up to four categories of amounts: (1) the worth at the time of award of unpaid rent already earned before termination; (2) the worth at the time of award of unpaid rent that would have been earned between termination and the time of award, minus the amount of that rental loss the tenant proves could have been reasonably avoided; (3) — subject to a further condition addressed in a separate clause of this document — the worth at the time of award of unpaid rent for the remainder of the lease term after the time of award, minus the amount of that rental loss the tenant proves could be reasonably avoided; and (4) any other amount necessary to compensate the landlord for detriment proximately caused by the tenant's failure to perform the tenant's obligations under the lease, or that would likely result from that failure in the ordinary course of things. The statute also defines how "worth at the time of award" is computed: for categories (1) and (2), by allowing interest at the rate stated in the lease, or the legal rate if the lease states none; for category (3), by discounting the amount at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco's discount rate at the time of award, plus one percent.
clauses.gap: All five citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1951.2 (subdivisions (a) and (b)) — not independent sources of one another. "Worth at the time of award" is a defined term of art under this statute, not an everyday-language damages figure; a specific landlord's actual recoverable amount in a specific case depends on proof (of unpaid rent, of the discount or interest rate that applies, and of any offset described in the following clauses) that this document does not supply or calculate.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, damages category 1 — rent already earned
citations.quote: The worth at the time of award of the unpaid rent which had been earned at the time of termination

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, damages category 2 — rent between termination and award, minus avoidable loss
citations.quote: The worth at the time of award of the amount by which the unpaid rent which would have been earned after termination until the time of award exceeds the amount of such rental loss that the lessee proves could have been reasonably avoided

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, damages category 3 — rent for the balance of the term, minus avoidable loss
citations.quote: Subject to subdivision (c), the worth at the time of award of the amount by which the unpaid rent for the balance of the term after the time of award exceeds the amount of such rental loss that the lessee proves could be reasonably avoided

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, damages category 4 — other proximately caused detriment
citations.quote: Any other amount necessary to compensate the lessor for all the detriment proximately caused by the lessee’s failure to perform his obligations under the lease or which in the ordinary course of things would be likely to result therefrom.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, how "worth at the time of award" is computed
citations.quote: The “worth at the time of award” of the amounts referred to in paragraphs (1) and (2) of subdivision (a) is computed by allowing interest at such lawful rate as may be specified in the lease or, if no such rate is specified in the lease, at the legal rate. The worth at the time of award of the amount referred to in paragraph (3) of subdivision (a) is computed by discounting such amount at the discount rate of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco at the time of award plus 1 percent.

clauses.title: The Mitigation Offset Within the Rent-Damages Calculation
clauses.body: California's statute frames the landlord's duty to mitigate as a subtraction built into the rent-damages calculation itself, rather than as a separate, all-or-nothing bar on recovery. For damages categories (2) and (3) described in the preceding clause — unpaid rent between termination and the time of award, and unpaid rent for the remainder of the lease term — the statute allows the landlord to recover only the unpaid rent for the relevant period minus whatever amount of that rental loss could reasonably have been avoided. The statute places the burden of proving that a loss could have been reasonably avoided on the tenant, not the landlord, for both of those categories. Separately, the statute states that a landlord's own efforts to mitigate damages by attempting to relet the property do not waive the landlord's right to recover damages under this statute.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on the same statutory section as the two clauses before it, Civil Code § 1951.2 (subdivisions (a) and (d)) — not independent of them. The mitigation offset described here applies only to damages categories (2) and (3); the statute's text states no equivalent offset for category (1), the rent already earned before termination. The statute's own text does not define what makes a rental loss one that "could have been reasonably avoided," and no such definition was found in § 1951.2 itself; a further condition on recovering category (3) damages specifically, and a court's discussion of the practical difficulty this burden allocation creates for tenants, are addressed in the next clause.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, tenant's burden on the interim-period offset
citations.quote: the amount of such rental loss that the lessee proves could have been reasonably avoided

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, tenant's burden on the remaining-term offset
citations.quote: the amount of such rental loss that the lessee proves could be reasonably avoided

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, mitigation efforts do not waive the landlord's recovery
citations.quote: Efforts by the lessor to mitigate the damages caused by the lessee’s breach of the lease do not waive the lessor’s right to recover damages under this section.

clauses.title: Recovering Future-Term Rent: The Reletting Precondition and Burden of Proof
clauses.body: The statute puts an additional condition on damages category (3) — unpaid rent for the balance of the lease term after the time of award. The landlord may recover that category of damages only if either: the lease itself provides for recovering it, using language about the amount by which unpaid rent for the balance of the term exceeds rental loss the tenant proves could be reasonably avoided; or the landlord relet the property before the time of award and proves that, in reletting it, the landlord acted reasonably and in a good-faith effort to mitigate the damages — in which case recovery under this category remains subject to any limitations stated in the lease. A California Court of Appeal, interpreting this statute, has observed that it places the tenant at a considerable procedural disadvantage on the mitigation issue: the burden is on the tenant to prove the landlord's reletting conduct was less than reasonable, even though exclusive possession and control of the property, and exclusive knowledge of what reletting efforts were or were not made, belong to the landlord.
clauses.gap: The two Civil Code citations below are both subdivision (c) of the same section, § 1951.2, quoted at length elsewhere in this document — not independent of those other citations. The Desert Plaza Partnership v. Waddell citation is an independently authored source, a published California Court of Appeal opinion rather than another subsection of the statute, but the quoted passage was offered by the court, in its own words, "although not at issue in this case" — it is the court's discussion of how the statute's burden allocation operates in practice, not the holding the court actually decided (the case turned on whether the parties had agreed to cancel the lease, a different question). Neither § 1951.2's text nor this case defines, with any checklist or numeric standard, what reletting efforts are "reasonable" or made in "good faith" — for example, neither source states that a landlord must use the same leasing efforts used for other units, advertise at a specific rent, or act within a specific number of days; no such statutory or judicial standard was found, and this document does not supply one.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, recovering category-3 damages by the lease's own terms
citations.quote: The lease provides that the damages he may recover include the worth at the time of award of the amount by which the unpaid rent for the balance of the term after the time of award, or for any shorter period of time specified in the lease, exceeds the amount of such rental loss for the same period that the lessee proves could be reasonably avoided

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.2(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, recovering category-3 damages by actually reletting and proving reasonable, good-faith efforts
citations.quote: The lessor relet the property prior to the time of award and proves that in reletting the property he acted reasonably and in a good-faith effort to mitigate the damages, but the recovery of damages under this paragraph is subject to any limitations specified in the lease.

citations.case: Desert Plaza Partnership v. Waddell, 180 Cal. App. 3d 805, 813–814 (1986)
citations.cite: California Court of Appeal, Fourth District, on the tenant's procedural disadvantage under § 1951.2's mitigation burden
citations.quote: section 1951.2 puts the lessee at a considerable procedural disadvantage in respect to the issue of mitigation of damages. The burden is placed on the lessee to prove the lessor’s conduct in attempting to relet was less than reasonable. However, exclusive possession and control of the premises and exclusive control over reletting efforts, including the knowledge of what efforts have or have not been made, are given exclusively to the lessor.

clauses.title: The Alternative Remedy: Continuing the Lease Instead of Terminating It
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1951.2 states it applies "except as otherwise provided in Section 1951.4" — a separate statute giving landlords an alternative remedy. Under § 1951.4, even after a tenant has breached the lease and abandoned the property, the lease continues in effect for as long as the landlord does not terminate the tenant's right to possession, and the landlord may enforce the landlord's rights and remedies under the lease — including recovering rent as it becomes due — rather than pursuing the accelerated damages calculation under § 1951.2. This alternative remedy is available only if the lease itself provides for it, and, under the statute, only if the lease also permits the tenant to sublet the property or assign the tenant's interest in it. The statute further identifies specific landlord conduct that does not, by itself, count as terminating the tenant's right to possession for these purposes: maintaining or preserving the property, efforts to relet it, having a receiver appointed to protect the landlord's interest, and withholding or terminating consent to a subletting or assignment consistent with the tenant's rights under the statute.
clauses.gap: Civil Code §§ 1951.4(a), (b), and (c) are subdivisions of the same statutory section — not independent of one another, and the § 1951.2 cross-reference quoted here, while textually located in a different Civil Code section, is the same section 1951.2 quoted at length elsewhere in this document. Section 1951.4(b) sets out three distinct ways a lease's sublet/assignment terms can qualify a landlord for this remedy, including a presumption (which the statute itself calls one "affecting the burden of proof") that a lease's own standards for consent to subletting are reasonable; this document states only the general condition — that the lease must permit subletting or assignment in some qualifying way — and omits that more granular sub-rule rather than state it imprecisely. This document does not determine whether any specific lease qualifies for this alternative remedy, and does not address which remedy — this one or the § 1951.2 damages remedy described elsewhere in this document — a landlord has elected in a specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.4(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, this remedy requires the lease to provide for it
citations.quote: The remedy described in this section is available only if the lease provides for this remedy.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.4(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the lease continues in effect and rent may be recovered as it becomes due
citations.quote: Even though a lessee of real property has breached the lease and abandoned the property, the lease continues in effect for so long as the lessor does not terminate the lessee’s right to possession, and the lessor may enforce all the lessor’s rights and remedies under the lease, including the right to recover the rent as it becomes due under the lease, if any of the following conditions is satisfied

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.4(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, conduct that does not itself terminate the tenant's right to possession
citations.quote: For the purposes of subdivision (b), the following do not constitute a termination of the lessee’s right to possession: (1) Acts of maintenance or preservation or efforts to relet the property. (2) The appointment of a receiver upon initiative of the lessor to protect the lessor’s interest under the lease. (3) Withholding consent to a subletting or assignment, or terminating a subletting or assignment, if the withholding or termination does not violate the rights of the lessee specified in subdivision (b).
