clauses.title: About This Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLST) Form
clauses.body: This document concerns a Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment (POLST) form for {{patientName}}, prepared under Part 4 (commencing with Section 4780) of Division 4.7 of the California Probate Code. A POLST form is a category of "request regarding resuscitative measures" under that Part. It is a set of medical orders — not an advance health care directive — completed by a health care provider and signed by both {{patientName}} (or {{patientName}}'s legally recognized health care decisionmaker, {{agentName}}) and a physician, or a nurse practitioner or physician assistant acting under a physician's supervision. This document states facts about what California's Probate Code says a POLST form is and how it operates; it does not recommend whether {{patientName}} should complete one, what medical treatments to choose, or how to fill out its clinical order sections. A POLST form itself, as approved by the Emergency Medical Services Authority, is a separate clinical form completed with a health care provider — this document does not replace it.

clauses.title: What the Statute Defines a POLST Form to Be
clauses.body: Under the Probate Code, a “request regarding resuscitative measures” is defined as a written document, signed by (A) an individual with capacity, or a legally recognized health care decisionmaker, and (B) the individual’s physician, that directs a health care provider regarding resuscitative measures. That defined category includes both a prehospital “do not resuscitate” form and a Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment (POLST) form approved by the Emergency Medical Services Authority. The statute separately defines a “Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form” as a request regarding resuscitative measures that directs a health care provider regarding resuscitative and life-sustaining measures — meaning a POLST form is the broader category's version that covers life-sustaining measures generally, not only resuscitation.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4780(a)), not independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this specific definitional structure. This clause states only what the statute defines the form to be — it does not describe the separate EMSA-approved clinical form itself, which is not part of the codified text.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definition of “request regarding resuscitative measures” and that it is not an advance health care directive
citations.quote: “Request regarding resuscitative measures” means a written document, signed by (A) an individual with capacity, or a legally recognized health care decisionmaker, and (B) the individual’s physician, that directs a health care provider regarding resuscitative measures. A request regarding resuscitative measures is not an advance health care directive.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(a)(2)-(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the POLST form as one form of request regarding resuscitative measures, and its separate definition
citations.quote: (A) A prehospital “do not resuscitate” form as developed by the Emergency Medical Services Authority or other substantially similar form. (B) A Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form, as approved by the Emergency Medical Services Authority.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own Distinction Between a POLST Form and an Advance Health Care Directive
clauses.body: The Probate Code states directly, in the same sentence that defines the category, that “a request regarding resuscitative measures is not an advance health care directive” — and a POLST form is one form of request regarding resuscitative measures. The statute also directs that, while a health care provider completes the POLST form, the provider “should inform the patient about the difference between an advance health care directive and the Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form.” Beyond stating that a POLST is not an advance health care directive and that the difference should be explained, the codified text of this Part does not itself spell out every legal distinction between the two documents (for example, it does not codify a general rule for which document controls if their terms diverge).
clauses.gap: Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory section (§ 4780, subdivisions (a) and (c)), not independently authored sources. The statute's own text supports that a POLST is legally distinct from an advance directive and that providers should explain the difference, but beyond those two textual points, further characterization of exactly how the two differ in legal effect is a matter of general medical/legal practice guidance, not codified statutory text, and is not asserted here as codified law.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a request regarding resuscitative measures (which includes a POLST form) is not an advance health care directive
citations.quote: A request regarding resuscitative measures is not an advance health care directive.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the provider's duty to explain the difference between the two documents
citations.quote: The health care provider, during the process of completing the Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form, should inform the patient about the difference between an advance health care directive and the Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form.

clauses.title: Who Must Sign a POLST Form, and Who May Execute It on a Patient's Behalf
clauses.body: By statute, a legally recognized health care decisionmaker — such as {{agentName}}, if acting in that role for {{patientName}} — may execute a POLST form only if {{patientName}} lacks capacity, or {{patientName}} has designated that the decisionmaker's authority is effective under Probate Code § 4682. As to the form itself, the statute requires that a health care provider explain the POLST form and the medical interventions and procedures it offers, that the provider complete the form based on patient preferences and medical indications, and that the form be signed by a physician (or a nurse practitioner or physician assistant acting under the physician's supervision and within their scope of practice) and by {{patientName}} or {{patientName}}'s legally recognized health care decisionmaker — here, {{physicianName}} as the signing physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 4780(b) and (c)), not independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for these specific execution mechanics. The statute cross-references § 4682 (regarding when a decisionmaker's authority becomes effective) without this document independently verifying the text of § 4682 itself.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: when a legally recognized health care decisionmaker may execute the form
citations.quote: A legally recognized health care decisionmaker may execute the Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form only if the individual lacks capacity, or the individual has designated that the decisionmaker’s authority is effective pursuant to Section 4682.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: who must complete, explain, and sign the form
citations.quote: The Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form and medical intervention and procedures offered by the form shall be explained by a health care provider, as defined in Section 4621. The form shall be completed by a health care provider based on patient preferences and medical indications, and signed by a physician, or a nurse practitioner or a physician assistant acting under the supervision of the physician and within the scope of practice authorized by law, and the patient or his or her legally recognized health care decisionmaker.

clauses.title: How a POLST Form Can Be Revoked
clauses.body: An individual with capacity — {{patientName}}, while having capacity — may revoke a POLST form at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke, consistent with Probate Code § 4695 (the same revocation standard the statute applies to most parts of an advance health care directive other than an agent designation).
clauses.gap: This clause rests on a single statutory subsection (§ 4780(d)); no additional independent source was located for this specific revocation rule for POLST forms. The statute cross-references § 4695 by number rather than restating its text within this Part; this document does not separately re-verify § 4695's text here (a companion Advance Health Care Directive document in this corpus verifies § 4695 directly). The statute does not, in this Part, address revocation by an individual who lacks capacity, or how a health care decisionmaker's own revocation authority for a POLST form is exercised once decisionmaker authority is in effect.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4780(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: revocation standard for a POLST form
citations.quote: An individual having capacity may revoke a Physician Orders for Life Sustaining Treatment form at any time and in any manner that communicates an intent to revoke, consistent with Section 4695.

clauses.title: Health Care Providers Covered, Reliance on the Form, and What the Statute Does Not Say
clauses.body: The statute defines “health care provider” for purposes of this Part to include, without limitation, persons described in Probate Code § 4621 (health care professionals and institutions), as well as emergency response employees — including firefighters, law enforcement officers, EMT-I and EMT-II personnel, and paramedics — trained under Emergency Medical Services Authority standards. A health care provider who honors a request regarding resuscitative measures, including a POLST form, is not subject to criminal prosecution, civil liability, professional discipline, administrative sanction, or any other sanction as a result of that reliance, provided the provider believes in good faith the action is consistent with this Part and has no knowledge the action would be inconsistent with a decision the individual would have made personally. Separately, in the absence of knowledge to the contrary, a health care provider may presume a request regarding resuscitative measures — including a POLST form — is valid and unrevoked.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on three independently numbered statutory sections (§§ 4781, 4782, and 4784), which are genuinely independent of one another rather than subsections of a single section. A notable gap: unlike the advance health care directive statute, this Part does not contain an explicit provision stating that a health care provider or EMS/first responder “must” honor a POLST form, nor does it state a rule for resolving a conflict between a POLST form and a later-expressed wish or a health care agent's decision. The statutory text instead (a) broadly defines who counts as a covered health care provider, (b) immunizes providers who honor the form in good faith, and (c) lets providers presume the form valid and unrevoked absent contrary knowledge — which functions as a practical incentive toward compliance without amounting to a codified duty to comply. Any rule about which document controls in a conflict is a matter of medical practice guidance outside the codified text reviewed here, and is not asserted as statutory law.

citations.quote: “health care provider” includes, but is not limited to, the following: (a) Persons described in Section 4621. (b) Emergency response employees, including, but not limited to, firefighters, law enforcement officers, emergency medical technicians I and II, paramedics, and employees and volunteer members of legally organized and recognized volunteer organizations, who are trained in accordance with standards adopted as regulations by the Emergency Medical Services Authority

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4782 (California Legislative Information text)

citations.quote: A health care provider who honors a request regarding resuscitative measures is not subject to criminal prosecution, civil liability, discipline for unprofessional conduct, administrative sanction, or any other sanction, as a result of his or her reliance on the request, if the health care provider (a) believes in good faith that the action or decision is consistent with this part, and (b) has no knowledge that the action or decision would be inconsistent with a health care decision that the individual signing the request would have made on his or her own behalf under like circumstances.

citations.quote: In the absence of knowledge to the contrary, a health care provider may presume that a request regarding resuscitative measures is valid and unrevoked.

clauses.title: This Part Does Not Displace Other Health Care Decisionmaking Law
clauses.body: The Probate Code states that this Part on requests regarding resuscitative measures, including POLST forms, “does not repeal or narrow laws relating to health care decisionmaking.” It also states that the Part applies whether the individual executing a request regarding resuscitative measures is inside or outside a hospital or other health care institution.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two independently numbered statutory sections (§§ 4785 and 4786) within the same Part; while both are part of Part 4 of Division 4.7, they are separately numbered, independently worded sections rather than subsections of one section. No portability or interstate-reciprocity provision was located anywhere in Probate Code §§ 4780–4786 for POLST forms; that topic is therefore omitted from this document rather than asserted without a verified citation.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment and Signatures
Purpose of This Homestead Exemption Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's automatic homestead exemption for a judgment debtor's principal residence, codified at California Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.710-704.850 (Enforcement of Judgments, Division 2, Chapter 4, Article 4, “Homestead Exemption”). It covers the statutory definitions of “dwelling” and “homestead,” how the exempt dollar amount is calculated, how this automatic exemption differs from California's separate “declared homestead” recording procedure under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.910-704.995 (Article 5), the court-supervised procedure a judgment creditor must use to force a sale of a homestead dwelling, and how sale proceeds are distributed. It concerns the dwelling located at {{propertyAddress}}, {{county}}, California, and is prepared by {{homeownerName}}. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing California statutes; it is not a court filing, a recorded instrument, a claim of exemption, an application for a homestead declaration, or legal advice about whether the exemption, any specific dollar amount, or any specific outcome applies to {{homeownerName}}'s dwelling or circumstances.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions of "Dwelling" and "Homestead"
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure § 704.710 defines the terms used throughout the homestead exemption statutes. Under § 704.710(a), a “dwelling” means a place where a person resides, and the statute lists examples including a house with its outbuildings and land, a mobilehome, a boat or other waterborne vessel, a condominium, a planned development, a stock cooperative, and a community apartment project. Under § 704.710(c), a “homestead” means the principal dwelling in which the judgment debtor or the judgment debtor's spouse resided on the date the judgment creditor's lien attached to the dwelling, and in which the judgment debtor or spouse resided continuously after that date until a court determines that the dwelling is a homestead. Only a person's principal dwelling can qualify as a homestead under this definition — the statute does not extend the exemption to a second home or investment property that is not the person's principal residence.
clauses.gap: California Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.710(a) and 704.710(c) are both subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another as sources. Section 704.710 also defines “family unit” (§ 704.710(b)) and “spouse” (§ 704.710(d)) for purposes of this article; those definitions are not described in this Information Sheet. This document states California's statutory definitions; it does not determine whether any specific property is a person's principal dwelling or otherwise qualifies as a homestead.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.710(a)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, definition of “dwelling” for the homestead exemption article
citations.quote: “Dwelling” means a place where a person resides and may include but is not limited to the following:(1) A house together with the outbuildings and the land upon which they are situated.(2) A mobilehome together with the outbuildings and the land upon which they are situated.(3) A boat or other waterborne vessel.(4) A condominium, as defined in Section 783 of the Civil Code.(5) A planned development, as defined in Section 11003 of the Business and Professions Code.(6) A stock cooperative, as defined in Section 11003.2 of the Business and Professions Code.(7) A community apartment project, as defined in Section 11004 of the Business and Professions Code.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.710(c)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, definition of “homestead” for the homestead exemption article
citations.quote: “Homestead” means the principal dwelling (1) in which the judgment debtor or the judgment debtor’s spouse resided on the date the judgment creditor’s lien attached to the dwelling, and (2) in which the judgment debtor or the judgment debtor’s spouse resided continuously thereafter until the date of the court determination that the dwelling is a homestead.

clauses.title: The Amount of the Homestead Exemption
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure § 704.730(a) sets the amount of the homestead exemption as the greater of two figures: (1) the countywide median sale price for a single-family home in the calendar year before the year the judgment debtor claims the exemption, capped at $600,000; or (2) $300,000 flat. Section 704.730(b) provides that both the $600,000 cap and the $300,000 floor adjust annually for inflation, beginning January 1, 2022, based on the change in the California Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers published by the Department of Industrial Relations, with each adjusted figure rounded to the nearest $25. This formula — a floor tied to a flat dollar amount and a ceiling tied to countywide median home prices — replaced the flat, status-based dollar amounts (previously keyed to marital status, head-of-household status, or age or disability) that applied under this section before it was amended effective January 1, 2021.
clauses.gap: California Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.730(a) and 704.730(b) are both subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another as sources. The $300,000 and $600,000 figures quoted here are the statutory floor and ceiling as codified in the text fetched for this Information Sheet (the section was last amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 80, Sec. 24 (SB 1525), effective January 1, 2025); § 704.730(b)'s annual inflation adjustment means the dollar figures a court actually applies as of any given date may be higher than $300,000/$600,000, and those adjusted figures are published administratively rather than restated in the statutory text itself. This Information Sheet states only the statutory floor, ceiling, and adjustment mechanism — it does not state a current-year adjusted dollar figure. Determining the countywide median sale price for a particular county and year, and therefore the precise exemption amount that would apply to any specific dwelling, requires consulting county-specific data not addressed here.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.730(a)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, formula for the homestead exemption amount (floor and ceiling)
citations.quote: (a) The amount of the homestead exemption is the greater of the following:(1) The countywide median sale price for a single-family home in the calendar year prior to the calendar year in which the judgment debtor claims the exemption, not to exceed six hundred thousand dollars ($600,000).(2) Three hundred thousand dollars ($300,000).

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.730(b)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, annual inflation adjustment of the homestead exemption amounts
citations.quote: The amounts specified in this section shall adjust annually for inflation, beginning on January 1, 2022, based on the change in the annual California Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, published by the Department of Industrial Relations, for the most recent one-year period ending on December 31 preceding the adjustment, with each adjusted amount rounded to the nearest twenty-five dollars ($25).

clauses.title: This Automatic Exemption Is Distinct From a Recorded "Declared Homestead"
clauses.body: The homestead exemption described in this Information Sheet, under California Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.710-704.850 (Article 4), applies without any recorded declaration: Code of Civil Procedure § 704.720(a) states that a homestead is exempt from a forced sale to the extent provided elsewhere in that article, and § 704.740(a) requires a judgment creditor seeking to sell a debtor's dwelling to obtain a court order for sale, with the dwelling exemption “determined under this article” — that is, in the court proceeding itself, at the time enforcement is sought, rather than through any prior recorded filing. California law separately provides an optional “declared homestead” procedure under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.910-704.995 (Article 5). Under § 704.920, a dwelling becomes a “declared homestead” only by recording a homestead declaration with the county recorder of the county where the dwelling is located, and only “from and after the time of recording.” The declared homestead is a separate statutory mechanism, defined and governed by its own set of Article 5 sections, and this Information Sheet does not describe what additional or different protections a declared homestead provides.
clauses.gap: Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.720 and 704.740 (Article 4) and § 704.920 (Article 5) are separately numbered, independently enacted sections in different articles of the Enforcement of Judgments Law, not subsections of one section, so they are independent sources. Neither § 704.720(a) nor § 704.740(a) contains the words “automatic” or “no recording required”; the statement that the Article 4 exemption requires no recorded declaration is drawn from the structure of Article 4 itself — it conditions the exemption on a court determination made in an enforcement proceeding, not on any recorded document — contrasted with Article 5's express recording requirement in § 704.920. This Information Sheet does not describe the declared homestead's specific requirements, effects, or any protections it provides beyond what Article 4 already provides; a reader whose questions concern a declared homestead specifically should look to §§ 704.910-704.995 directly, which are outside this document's scope.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.720(a)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, existence of the homestead exemption from forced sale
citations.quote: A homestead is exempt from sale under this division to the extent provided in Section 704.800.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.740(a)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, requirement of a court order for sale and article-based exemption determination
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), the interest of a natural person in a dwelling may not be sold under this division to enforce a money judgment except pursuant to a court order for sale obtained under this article and the dwelling exemption shall be determined under this article.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.920
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, recording requirement to create a declared homestead (Article 5)
citations.quote: A dwelling in which an owner or spouse of an owner resides may be selected as a declared homestead pursuant to this article by recording a homestead declaration in the office of the county recorder of the county where the dwelling is located. From and after the time of recording, the dwelling is a declared homestead for the purposes of this article.

clauses.title: How a Forced Sale of a Homestead Dwelling Works
clauses.body: Before a judgment creditor can force the sale of a debtor's homestead dwelling, California Code of Civil Procedure § 704.750(a) requires the levying officer, promptly after levying on the dwelling, to notify the judgment creditor that the property will be released unless the creditor acts; the judgment creditor then has 20 days after that notice to apply to the court for an order for sale of the dwelling and to file a copy of the application with the levying officer, or the levying officer must release the dwelling. If a sale does go forward under a resulting court order, § 704.800(a) provides that if no bid at the sale exceeds the amount of the homestead exemption plus any additional amount necessary to satisfy all liens and encumbrances on the property — including but not limited to any attachment or judgment lien — the homestead is not sold; it is released, and the same judgment creditor cannot bring a new application for a court order for sale of that homestead for a period of one year.
clauses.gap: Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.750 and 704.800 are separately numbered, independently enacted sections and are independent sources. Section 704.800(a)'s own text names “liens and encumbrances on the property” broadly and gives “attachment or judgment lien” only as non-exclusive examples; in the text fetched, it does not separately itemize a mortgage or deed of trust, a mechanic's lien, or a property tax lien by name. A consensual lien such as a mortgage or deed of trust recorded against the dwelling is commonly understood to be an “encumbrance on the property” within this provision's plain language, but this Information Sheet has not independently verified statutory carve-outs specific to mechanic's liens or property tax liens against a primary source, and does not state whether those particular lien types are treated any differently — that determination is outside what §§ 704.750 and 704.800 were verified to say. This Information Sheet also does not describe the court hearing procedure by which the exemption amount is determined and the order for sale is granted or denied, only the notice/application timeline and the minimum-bid rule described above.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.750(a)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, notice after levy and the judgment creditor's 20-day deadline to apply for a court order for sale
citations.quote: Promptly after a dwelling is levied upon (other than a dwelling described in subdivision (b) of Section 704.740), the levying officer shall serve notice on the judgment creditor that the levy has been made and that the property will be released unless the judgment creditor complies with the requirements of this section. Service shall be made personally or by mail. Within 20 days after service of the notice, the judgment creditor shall apply to the court for an order for sale of the dwelling and shall file a copy of the application with the levying officer. If the judgment creditor does not file the copy of the application for an order for sale of the dwelling within the allowed time, the levying officer shall release the dwelling.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.800(a)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, minimum-bid rule requiring a bid to exceed the exemption plus liens and encumbrances
citations.quote: If no bid is received at a sale of a homestead pursuant to a court order for sale that exceeds the amount of the homestead exemption plus any additional amount necessary to satisfy all liens and encumbrances on the property, including but not limited to any attachment or judgment lien, the homestead shall not be sold and shall be released and is not thereafter subject to a court order for sale upon subsequent application by the same judgment creditor for a period of one year.

clauses.title: Distribution of Sale Proceeds When a Homestead Is Sold
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure § 704.850(a) sets out the order in which a levying officer must distribute the proceeds of a homestead sale: first, to the discharge of all liens and encumbrances on the property; second, to the judgment debtor in the amount of the applicable homestead exemption; third, to the levying officer for unreimbursed costs; fourth, to the judgment creditor, first for costs and interest accruing after the writ issued and then for the amount due on the judgment; and fifth, any amount remaining to the judgment debtor. Under this priority order, existing liens and encumbrances on the property are paid before the judgment debtor receives the exempt amount, and the judgment debtor receives the exempt amount before the judgment creditor is paid anything toward satisfying the judgment.
clauses.gap: This Information Sheet relies on a single statutory section, California Code of Civil Procedure § 704.850(a); no second, independent source is cited for this specific distribution order. Section 704.850(b) also makes Code of Civil Procedure §§ 701.820 and 701.830 applicable to distribution of these proceeds; this Information Sheet does not describe what those two additional, cross-referenced sections provide.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.850(a)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, order of distribution of homestead sale proceeds
citations.quote: The levying officer shall distribute the proceeds of sale of a homestead in the following order:(1) To the discharge of all liens and encumbrances, if any, on the property. (2) To the judgment debtor in the amount of any applicable exemption of proceeds pursuant to Section 704.720.(3) To the levying officer for the reimbursement of the levying officer’s costs for which an advance has not been made.(4) To the judgment creditor to satisfy the following:(A) First, costs and interest accruing after issuance of the writ pursuant to which the sale is conducted.(B) Second, the amount due on the judgment with costs and interest, as entered on the writ.(5) To the judgment debtor in the amount remaining.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment — Homestead Exemption Information Sheet
Purpose and Scope — Informational Only
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, California's constitutional and statutory framework governing eminent domain and inverse condemnation. It is prepared in connection with the real property located at {{propertyAddress}}, of record in the name of {{ownerName}}, and the public project or action described as: {{projectDescription}}, involving {{publicEntityName}}. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself commence, oppose, settle, or resolve any eminent domain proceeding or inverse condemnation claim; it does not determine whether any specific act, plan, project, or occurrence involving {{publicEntityName}} constitutes a "taking" or a "damaging" of the property described above, whether any resolution of necessity has been validly adopted, or whether any particular compensation figure is accurate or adequate. It states only what the California Constitution and California's Eminent Domain Law generally provide.

clauses.title: State Constitutional Foundation — Taking or Damaging for Public Use
clauses.body: Article I, section 19, subdivision (a) of the California Constitution provides that private property may be taken or damaged for a public use, and only when just compensation — ascertained by a jury unless waived — has first been paid to, or into court for, the owner. This text protects against both a "taking" of private property and a "damaging" of it, and by its own terms it reaches property that is merely damaged for a public use, not only property that is physically taken. This is broader than the wording of the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which by its text addresses property that is "taken," without a corresponding reference to property that is "damaged." Article I, section 19(a) also authorizes the Legislature to allow a condemning entity to take possession of the property after commencing an eminent domain proceeding, upon depositing in court, and promptly releasing to the owner, the amount the court determines to be the probable just compensation. Separate subdivisions of the same section — (b) through (e) — restrict the use of eminent domain to acquire an owner-occupied residence for the purpose of conveying it to a private person, subject to listed exceptions for protecting public health and safety, preventing serious repeated criminal activity, responding to an emergency, remedying environmental contamination, and acquiring property for a public work or improvement.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes and describes subdivision (a) of Article I, section 19, which is the operative taking/damaging and just-compensation text. It also summarizes, without separately quoting, subdivisions (b) through (e) of the same section (the owner-occupied-residence restriction and its exceptions and definitions) — those subdivisions are part of the same constitutional section already cited, not an independent source. The comparison to the U.S. Constitution's Fifth Amendment states the well-established textual difference between the two provisions' wording but is not itself supported by a citation to federal constitutional text fetched in this research.

citations.case: California Constitution
citations.cite: Cal. Const., art. I, § 19, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Private property may be taken or damaged for a public use and only when just compensation, ascertained by a jury unless waived, has first been paid to, or into court for, the owner.

clauses.title: The Eminent Domain Law — Public Use and Necessity Findings
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure sections 1230.010 through 1273.050 are known and may be cited as the "Eminent Domain Law," and, except as otherwise specifically provided by another statute, this is the framework under which the power of eminent domain may be exercised in California. Under this law, the power of eminent domain may be exercised to acquire property only for a public use; where the Legislature has provided by statute that a given use, purpose, object, or function is one for which eminent domain may be exercised, that statutory designation is itself treated as a declaration that the use is a public use. Before property may be acquired for a proposed project, the statute requires that all of the following be established: that the public interest and necessity require the project; that the project is planned or located in the manner that will be most compatible with the greatest public good and the least private injury; and that the property sought to be acquired is necessary for the project.
clauses.gap: The four citations below are separate sections within the same statutory title — Code of Civil Procedure, Title 7, the Eminent Domain Law (§§ 1230.010–1273.050) — rather than independently enacted, unrelated statutes; they should be read together as one integrated legislative scheme, not as separately corroborating sources. This clause states only the general public-use and necessity-findings requirement. It does not describe the procedural steps of an eminent domain action itself (service of the complaint, deposit and possession, trial on compensation, entry of judgment, and so on), which are addressed by other sections of the same title not covered here.

citations.case: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1230.010
citations.quote: This title shall be known and may be cited as the Eminent Domain Law.

citations.case: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1230.020
citations.quote: Except as otherwise specifically provided by statute, the power of eminent domain may be exercised only as provided in this title.

citations.case: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1240.010
citations.quote: The power of eminent domain may be exercised to acquire property only for a public use.

citations.case: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1240.030
citations.quote: The power of eminent domain may be exercised to acquire property for a proposed project only if all of the following are established:

clauses.title: Resolution of Necessity — Prerequisite to Filing
clauses.body: Before a public entity may exercise the power of eminent domain, the Eminent Domain Law requires that its governing body first adopt a resolution of necessity meeting statutory requirements; a public entity may not commence an eminent domain proceeding until it has done so. Among other things, the resolution must contain a general statement of the public use for which the property is to be taken and a reference to the statute authorizing the acquisition; a description of the property's general location and extent, with sufficient detail for reasonable identification; and the governing body's declaration that it has found and determined that the public interest and necessity require the project, that the project is planned or located in the manner most compatible with the greatest public good and least private injury, and that the property is necessary for the project. Unless a greater vote is required by statute, charter, or ordinance, the resolution must be adopted by a vote of two-thirds of all members of the entity's governing body. Except as otherwise provided by statute, a resolution of necessity adopted in this manner conclusively establishes the matters it addresses (the public-interest, compatible-location, and necessity findings).
clauses.gap: The citations below are all provisions of the same statutory article — Code of Civil Procedure, Chapter 4, Article 2 (Resolution of Necessity, §§ 1245.210–1245.270) — plus one cross-referenced section from the same title's general provisions (§ 1240.040); they are not independent sources of one another and should be read as one integrated procedural scheme. This clause omits the statute's carve-outs from the conclusive-presumption rule (§ 1245.250, subds. (b)–(d)), under which a resolution creates only a rebuttable presumption, rather than a conclusive one, for certain takings of local public-utility property or property not located entirely within the acquiring entity's boundaries — those exceptions were reviewed in the same fetch but are not restated here in full. It also does not describe the separate statutory requirement that the public entity make a precondemnation offer to the property owner before adopting the resolution (Gov. Code § 7267.2, referenced but not independently verified here) or the emergency-project exception to that offer requirement.

clauses.title: Just Compensation Standard — Fair Market Value
clauses.body: The Eminent Domain Law's own compensation provisions describe how "just compensation" for property taken is measured. Compensation is awarded for the property taken, and the measure of that compensation is the property's fair market value. The statute defines fair market value as the highest price, on the date of valuation, that would be agreed to by a seller who is willing to sell but under no particular or urgent necessity to do so and not obliged to sell, and a buyer who is ready, willing, and able to buy but under no particular necessity to do so, with each party dealing with the other with full knowledge of all the uses and purposes for which the property is reasonably adaptable and available. Where there is no relevant, comparable market for the property taken, the statute instead defines fair market value as the property's value on the date of valuation as determined by any method of valuation that is just and equitable.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are adjacent sections of the same statutory article — Code of Civil Procedure, Chapter 9, Article 4 (Measure of Compensation for Property Taken, §§ 1263.310–1263.330) — and are not independent of one another. This clause addresses only the measure of compensation for property actually taken. It does not describe the statute's separate rules for severance damage to a remainder parcel, for benefits offset against severance damage, or for loss of business goodwill, all of which are addressed elsewhere in the same chapter and are not covered here.

citations.case: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1263.310
citations.quote: Compensation shall be awarded for the property taken. The measure of this compensation is the fair market value of the property taken.

citations.case: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1263.320
citations.quote: The fair market value of the property taken is the highest price on the date of valuation that would be agreed to by a seller, being willing to sell but under no particular or urgent necessity for so doing, nor obliged to sell, and a buyer, being ready, willing, and able to buy but under no particular necessity for so doing, each dealing with the other with full knowledge of all the uses and purposes for which the property is reasonably adaptable and available.

clauses.title: Inverse Condemnation — A Property Owner's Reverse Action
clauses.body: California recognizes a cause of action called "inverse condemnation," by which a property owner — rather than the public entity — brings an action against a public entity for having taken or damaged private property for a public use without the entity having exercised the formal eminent domain procedure. Unlike eminent domain, in which the public entity commences the proceeding, an inverse condemnation action is initiated by the affected property owner. California's statutes governing litigation costs refer to and presuppose the existence of an "inverse condemnation proceeding" as an established type of action, but they do not themselves define when a taking or damaging has occurred; based on the sources reviewed for this document, the cause of action itself derives directly from the state constitutional "taken or damaged" language, as interpreted by California courts, rather than from a separate statute defining its elements. In Albers v. County of Los Angeles (1965) 62 Cal.2d 250 — a case arising from a major landslide that destroyed and damaged homes near a county road project — the California Supreme Court held that liability for inverse condemnation under this constitutional provision does not depend on a showing that the public entity acted negligently: the court concluded that, with certain stated exceptions, any actual physical injury to real property proximately caused by a public improvement as deliberately designed and constructed is compensable under the constitutional provision, whether or not the injury was foreseeable.
clauses.gap: The constitutional citation in this clause is the same provision — Cal. Const., art. I, § 19, subd. (a) — already quoted in this document's constitutional-foundation clause; it is not an independent source of that clause's citation, though it is being applied here to a different point (the inverse-condemnation cause of action rather than the general taking/damaging and just-compensation rule). The Code of Civil Procedure section and the Albers opinion are independent, differently-typed sources (a statute and a judicial opinion) that corroborate the existence and general contours of the doctrine. This clause describes one landmark, and long-standing, California Supreme Court case on the no-fault character of inverse condemnation liability; it does not catalog the large body of subsequent case law refining causation, design-immunity, and comparative-fault questions in inverse condemnation, none of which is addressed here. It also does not identify any statute that comprehensively defines the elements of an inverse condemnation cause of action, because none was found in this research — if such a statute exists for a particular context (for example, certain flood-control or public-utility contexts), it was not verified here and is not described.

citations.case: California Constitution
citations.cite: Cal. Const., art. I, § 19, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Private property may be taken or damaged for a public use and only when just compensation, ascertained by a jury unless waived, has first been paid to, or into court for, the owner.

citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1036
citations.quote: In any inverse condemnation proceeding, the court rendering judgment for the plaintiff by awarding compensation, or the attorney representing the public entity who effects a settlement of that proceeding, shall determine and award or allow to the plaintiff, as a part of that judgment or settlement, a sum that will, in the opinion of the court, reimburse the plaintiff’s reasonable costs, disbursements, and expenses

clauses.title: Litigation Expenses in Eminent Domain and Inverse Condemnation Proceedings
clauses.body: California statutes address a property owner's recovery of litigation expenses differently in eminent domain proceedings and in inverse condemnation proceedings. In an eminent domain proceeding, the plaintiff public entity must file and serve its final offer of compensation, and the defendant property owner must file and serve a final demand, at least 20 days before trial on compensation issues; if, on the defendant's motion made within 30 days after entry of judgment, the court finds that the public entity's offer was unreasonable and the property owner's demand was reasonable in light of the evidence and the compensation awarded, the property owner's recoverable costs must include the owner's "litigation expenses" — defined by the statute as the party's reasonable attorney's fees and costs, including reasonable expert witness and appraiser fees. In an inverse condemnation proceeding, a different statute requires the court rendering judgment for the plaintiff, or the public entity's attorney in effecting a settlement, to award the plaintiff a sum reimbursing the plaintiff's reasonable costs, disbursements, and expenses — including reasonable attorney, appraisal, and engineering fees — actually incurred because of the proceeding, whether in the trial court or on any appeal on which the plaintiff prevails on any issue.
clauses.gap: The two statutes cited are independent of one another — they are codified in different titles of the Code of Civil Procedure (one within the Eminent Domain Law itself; the other within the general costs provisions applicable to civil actions) and govern different proceeding types. The eminent domain fee-shifting rule is conditional and requires a specific comparison of the entity's offer, the owner's demand, and the compensation ultimately awarded; the inverse condemnation costs statute does not use that same offer/demand comparison and instead turns on the plaintiff obtaining a judgment or settlement in its favor. This clause states the general operation of each provision; it does not describe every procedural detail (for example, the role of a deposit under a separate chapter, or the treatment of offers made under the precondemnation-offer statute) that a court may consider in applying either rule.

citations.case: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1250.410
citations.quote: If the court, on motion of the defendant made within 30 days after entry of judgment, finds that the offer of the plaintiff was unreasonable and that the demand of the defendant was reasonable viewed in the light of the evidence admitted and the compensation awarded in the proceeding, the costs allowed pursuant to Section 1268.710 shall include the defendant’s litigation expenses.

citations.case: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1036
citations.quote: In any inverse condemnation proceeding, the court rendering judgment for the plaintiff by awarding compensation, or the attorney representing the public entity who effects a settlement of that proceeding, shall determine and award or allow to the plaintiff, as a part of that judgment or settlement, a sum that will, in the opinion of the court, reimburse the plaintiff’s reasonable costs, disbursements, and expenses, including reasonable attorney, appraisal, and engineering fees, actually incurred because of that proceeding in the trial court or in any appellate proceeding in which the plaintiff prevails on any issue in that proceeding.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) requirement that an employer reasonably accommodate an employee's or applicant's religious belief or observance, Government Code section 12940(l), as it relates to {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}. It states facts about what the statute requires, the statutory definitions of "religious dress practice" and "religious grooming practice," the statute's own definition of "undue hardship," and the statute's specific rule that segregating an employee is not a reasonable accommodation. Religious accommodation is a category of FEHA coverage distinct from the physical- and mental-disability accommodation requirement in Government Code section 12940(m) and from the genetic-information provisions of the federal Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act; this document does not restate those other bodies of law and is not itself a request for accommodation, a determination that any accommodation is or is not required, or an interactive-process record. It does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} whether any specific request, practice, or belief qualifies for accommodation under the statute, whether providing or denying any specific accommodation would create undue hardship, or what to do about any specific situation.

clauses.title: Failure to Reasonably Accommodate Religious Belief or Observance Is an Unlawful Employment Practice
clauses.body: California's Fair Employment and Housing Act makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer or other entity covered by the Act to refuse to hire or employ a person, to refuse to select a person for a training program leading to employment, to bar or discharge a person from employment or a training program, or to discriminate against a person in compensation or in the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of a conflict between the person's religious belief or observance and an employment requirement. This prohibition applies unless the employer or other covered entity demonstrates that it has explored any available reasonable alternative means of accommodating the religious belief or observance -- including the possibility of excusing the person from the conflicting duties or permitting those duties to be performed at another time or by another person -- but is unable to reasonably accommodate the religious belief or observance without undue hardship on the conduct of its business. By its own terms, the statute applies to apprenticeship training programs, unpaid internships, and other unpaid workplace experience programs, not only to paid employment.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory paragraph, Government Code section 12940(l)(1), quoted in full below; it is not corroborated by a second, independent statutory source. The statute cross-references its own definition of "undue hardship" (Government Code section 12926(u)) and its own definitions of "religious dress practice" and "religious grooming practice" (Government Code section 12926(q)); those definitions are quoted and discussed in separate clauses below rather than repeated here. This clause states only that the described conduct is an unlawful employment practice under the statute; it does not determine whether any specific employer's treatment of any specific individual was because of a religious belief or observance, and it does not determine whether any specific accommodation was reasonably available or would have caused undue hardship.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(l)(1)
citations.cite: California Fair Employment and Housing Act, unlawful employment practices -- failure to reasonably accommodate religious belief or observance
citations.quote: (l) (1) For an employer or other entity covered by this part to refuse to hire or employ a person or to refuse to select a person for a training program leading to employment or to bar or to discharge a person from employment or from a training program leading to employment, or to discriminate against a person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment because of a conflict between the person’s religious belief or observance and any employment requirement, unless the employer or other entity covered by this part demonstrates that it has explored any available reasonable alternative means of accommodating the religious belief or observance, including the possibilities of excusing the person from those duties that conflict with the person’s religious belief or observance or permitting those duties to be performed at another time or by another person, but is unable to reasonably accommodate the religious belief or observance without undue hardship, as defined in subdivision (u) of Section 12926, on the conduct of the business of the employer or other entity covered by this part.

clauses.title: "Religious Dress Practice" and "Religious Grooming Practice" Are Specifically Defined
clauses.body: The FEHA religious-accommodation requirement expressly states that "religious belief or observance," as used in the accommodation section, includes but is not limited to observance of a Sabbath or other religious holy day or days, reasonable time necessary for travel before and after a religious observance, and religious dress practice and religious grooming practice as those terms are described in a separate FEHA definitions section, Government Code section 12926(q). That definitions section states that "religious creed," "religion," "religious observance," "religious belief," and "creed" include all aspects of religious belief, observance, and practice, including religious dress and grooming practices, and it defines "religious dress practice" and "religious grooming practice" as terms to be construed broadly. "Religious dress practice" is defined to include the wearing or carrying of religious clothing, head or face coverings, jewelry, artifacts, and any other item that is part of an individual observing a religious creed. "Religious grooming practice" is defined to include all forms of head, facial, and body hair that are part of an individual observing a religious creed.
clauses.gap: This clause combines two citations that are not independent corroboration of each other: Government Code section 12940(l)(1) is the accommodation requirement itself, and it establishes that religious dress and grooming practices are covered only by cross-referencing Government Code section 12926(q), a separate definitions section within the same FEHA definitions statute that supplies the actual defined terms. The 12940(l)(1) language quoted here is the same paragraph already quoted in the preceding clause on the core prohibition, so this clause is also not independent of that one. This clause states the statutory definitions only; it does not determine whether any specific item of clothing, head or face covering, jewelry, artifact, or form of hair in any specific case is part of an individual observing a religious creed within the meaning of the statute.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(l)(1)
citations.cite: FEHA, unlawful employment practices -- religious belief or observance includes religious dress and grooming practice
citations.quote: Religious belief or observance, as used in this section, includes, but is not limited to, observance of a Sabbath or other religious holy day or days, reasonable time necessary for travel prior and subsequent to a religious observance, and religious dress practice and religious grooming practice as described in subdivision (q) of Section 12926. This subdivision shall also apply to an apprenticeship training program, an unpaid internship, and any other program to provide unpaid experience for a person in the workplace or industry.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(q)
citations.cite: FEHA definitions -- "religious dress practice" and "religious grooming practice"
citations.quote: “Religious creed,” “religion,” “religious observance,” “religious belief,” and “creed” include all aspects of religious belief, observance, and practice, including religious dress and grooming practices. “Religious dress practice” shall be construed broadly to include the wearing or carrying of religious clothing, head or face coverings, jewelry, artifacts, and any other item that is part of an individual observing a religious creed. “Religious grooming practice” shall be construed broadly to include all forms of head, facial, and body hair that are part of an individual observing a religious creed.

clauses.title: FEHA's Own "Undue Hardship" Standard
clauses.body: The religious-accommodation requirement does not define "undue hardship" in its own text; it cross-refers to a general definition set out elsewhere in FEHA, Government Code section 12926(u), that applies to undue-hardship determinations throughout the Act, not only to religious accommodation. That definition states that "undue hardship" means an action requiring significant difficulty or expense, considered in light of five listed factors: the nature and cost of the accommodation needed; the overall financial resources of the facility or facilities involved and the effect of the accommodation on the facility's expenses, resources, or operations; the overall financial resources of the covered entity, including its overall size and the number, type, and location of its facilities; the type of operations of the entity, including the composition, structure, and functions of its workforce; and the geographic separateness or administrative or fiscal relationship of the facility or facilities. This is a multi-factor balancing test defined directly in the statute's text, not left to case law to define from scratch.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, Government Code section 12926(u), which is a different, independently numbered section of the Government Code from section 12940 (the accommodation requirement itself); it is used here because section 12940(l)(1) cross-refers to it by name, and that cross-reference is quoted in the core-prohibition clause above rather than repeated here. Federal Title VII also imposes a duty to accommodate religious practice, and its "undue hardship" standard was addressed by the U.S. Supreme Court in Groff v. DeJoy, 600 U.S. 447 (2023); this document does not independently verify the text of the federal statute or the Groff opinion, does not restate the federal standard, and does not state whether the state and federal standards would produce the same result in any given case -- a reader should not assume FEHA's defined standard is identical to the federal one. This clause states the statutory factors only; it does not determine whether any specific accommodation would require significant difficulty or expense in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(u)
citations.cite: FEHA definitions -- "undue hardship"
citations.quote: “Undue hardship” means an action requiring significant difficulty or expense, when considered in light of the following factors: (1) The nature and cost of the accommodation needed. (2) The overall financial resources of the facilities involved in the provision of the reasonable accommodations, the number of persons employed at the facility, and the effect on expenses and resources or the impact otherwise of these accommodations upon the operation of the facility. (3) The overall financial resources of the covered entity, the overall size of the business of a covered entity with respect to the number of employees, and the number, type, and location of its facilities. (4) The type of operations, including the composition, structure, and functions of the workforce of the entity. (5) The geographic separateness or administrative or fiscal relationship of the facility or facilities.

clauses.title: Segregating an Employee Is Not a Reasonable Accommodation of Religious Dress or Grooming
clauses.body: The statute states directly that an accommodation of an individual's religious dress practice or religious grooming practice is not reasonable if the accommodation requires segregation of the individual from other employees or from the public. This is a specific rule stated in the text of the statute itself, not a general inference from the reasonable-accommodation requirement.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from Government Code section 12940(l)(2), a different paragraph of the same subdivision (l) as the core prohibition quoted above; it is not an independent statutory source from that clause, though it states a distinct, specific rule within that subdivision. This clause states the statutory rule only; it does not describe what would or would not constitute "segregation" in any specific workplace arrangement, and it does not address accommodations of religious belief or observance generally (as opposed to religious dress or grooming practice specifically), which the statute's text ties this particular rule to.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(l)(2)
citations.cite: FEHA, unlawful employment practices -- segregation is not a reasonable accommodation of religious dress or grooming practice
citations.quote: (2) An accommodation of an individual’s religious dress practice or religious grooming practice is not reasonable if the accommodation requires segregation of the individual from other employees or the public.

clauses.title: An Accommodation Is Not Required If It Would Itself Violate the Law
clauses.body: The statute states that an accommodation is not required under the religious-accommodation subdivision if it would result in a violation of the Fair Employment and Housing Act itself or of any other law prohibiting discrimination or protecting civil rights, including the Unruh Civil Rights Act's prohibition on business-establishment discrimination (Civil Code section 51(b)) and the state's general prohibition on discrimination in state-funded and state-conducted programs and activities (Government Code section 11135).
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from Government Code section 12940(l)(3), a different paragraph of the same subdivision (l) as the core prohibition and segregation clauses above; it is not an independent statutory source from those clauses. This clause identifies the two other statutes the text cross-references by name; it does not restate or quote the text of Civil Code section 51(b) or Government Code section 11135 themselves, and it does not determine whether any specific accommodation would in fact violate either of those laws or any other antidiscrimination law in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(l)(3)
citations.cite: FEHA, unlawful employment practices -- accommodation not required if it would violate antidiscrimination law
citations.quote: (3) An accommodation is not required under this subdivision if it would result in a violation of this part or any other law prohibiting discrimination or protecting civil rights, including subdivision (b) of Section 51 of the Civil Code and Section 11135 of this code.

clauses.title: Requesting a Religious Accommodation Is a Protected Act, Regardless of Outcome
clauses.body: The statute separately makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer or other covered entity to retaliate or otherwise discriminate against a person for requesting a religious accommodation, regardless of whether the request was granted. The statute states this protection is in addition to the general retaliation protections that apply to opposing practices forbidden under FEHA or filing a complaint, testifying, or assisting in any proceeding under the Act.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from Government Code section 12940(l)(4), a different paragraph of the same subdivision (l) as the clauses above; it is not an independent statutory source from those clauses. This clause does not restate or quote the general retaliation-protection subdivision, section 12940(h), that this paragraph cross-references; it states only that the religious-accommodation retaliation protection applies regardless of whether the underlying request was granted, and it does not determine whether any specific adverse treatment of any specific individual was retaliation for requesting an accommodation.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(l)(4)
citations.cite: FEHA, unlawful employment practices -- retaliation for requesting religious accommodation
citations.quote: (4) For an employer or other entity covered by this part to, in addition to the employee protections provided pursuant to subdivision (h), retaliate or otherwise discriminate against a person for requesting accommodation under this subdivision, regardless of whether the request was granted.

clauses.title: Which Employers Are Covered: The Five-Employee Threshold
clauses.body: FEHA's employment provisions, including the religious-accommodation requirement, apply to an "employer" as FEHA's own definitions section defines that term. That definition states that "employer" includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, subject to stated exceptions. The definition further states that "employer" does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from Government Code section 12926(d), which is a different, independently numbered section of the Government Code from section 12940 (the accommodation requirement itself), but it is a different subdivision of the same section 12926 already relied on in the dress/grooming-definitions and undue-hardship clauses above, so it is not independent corroboration of those clauses' points -- all three (subdivisions (d), (q), and (u) of section 12926) are drawn from the same definitions statute. The religious-accommodation subdivision, section 12940(l), applies by its own terms to "an employer or other entity covered by this part," a broader phrase than "employer" alone; this clause addresses only the numerical threshold for "employer" and does not verify what threshold, if any, applies to the other categories of covered entity (such as labor organizations or employment agencies) that the broader phrase may also reach. This clause states the statutory definition only; it does not determine whether any specific entity regularly employs five or more persons in any given period, and it does not address the religious-association-or-nonprofit exclusion's scope beyond quoting it.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(d)
citations.cite: FEHA definitions -- "employer," five-or-more-employees threshold
citations.quote: “Employer” includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, except as follows: “Employer” does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet explains the statutory duty of {{companyName}} to reimburse {{employeeName}} for necessary business expenses under California Labor Code § 2802. It is meant to inform {{employeeName}} about the legal framework that applies to work-related expenses. It does not itself request, approve, or certify any specific expense — a separate Business Expense Reimbursement Form is used for that purpose.

clauses.title: The Statutory Duty to Reimburse
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 2802(a) requires an employer to indemnify its employee for all necessary expenditures or losses the employee incurs in direct consequence of discharging the employee's duties, or of obeying the employer's directions — including a direction later found unlawful, unless the employee believed at the time that it was unlawful. This duty is a general one; the statute itself applies to {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}} to the extent {{employeeName}} incurs expenditures or losses of the kind the statute describes.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general statutory duty; it does not determine whether any particular expense reported by the employee qualifies as a 'necessary expenditure or loss' — that depends on the facts of each expenditure. The interest clause and the definition/fee-shifting clause elsewhere in this document quote different subsections ((b) and (c)) of this same Labor Code § 2802; they are not independent statutory sources from this clause, only different parts of the same section, and are disclosed here as such rather than presented as separate corroboration.

citations.case: California Labor Code
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2802(a)
citations.quote: An employer shall indemnify his or her employee for all necessary expenditures or losses incurred by the employee in direct consequence of the discharge of his or her duties, or of his or her obedience to the directions of the employer, even though unlawful, unless the employee, at the time of obeying the directions, believed them to be unlawful.

clauses.title: Interest on Unpaid Reimbursement
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 2802(b), any award made by a court, or by the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, to reimburse necessary expenditures under this section carries interest at the same rate as a civil judgment. That interest accrues from the date the employee incurred the expenditure or loss, not from the date of any later award or demand.
clauses.gap: This clause describes only how interest is calculated once an award is made under the statute; it does not state whether the employee is owed reimbursement for any particular expense, and it does not address the procedure for obtaining such an award. It quotes subsection (b) of the same Labor Code § 2802 discussed in the statutory-duty clause elsewhere in this document — the two clauses are not independent sources, only different subsections of one statute.

citations.case: California Labor Code
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2802(b)
citations.quote: All awards made by a court or by the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement for reimbursement of necessary expenditures under this section shall carry interest at the same rate as judgments in civil actions. Interest shall accrue from the date on which the employee incurred the necessary expenditure or loss.

clauses.title: Definition of "Necessary Expenditures or Losses" and Attorney's Fees
clauses.body: Labor Code § 2802(c) defines the term "necessary expenditures or losses," as used throughout the statute, to include all reasonable costs — expressly including, but not limited to, attorney's fees — that an employee incurs in enforcing the reimbursement right created by this section. A fee award for an employee who enforces the statute is therefore written into the statute's own text, not left solely to a court's general discretion.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subsection (c)'s definition and fee-inclusion language; it does not address the legal standard a court applies to determine whether an employee has succeeded in enforcing the statute, or how a reasonable fee amount is calculated in a given case. It quotes the same Labor Code § 2802 discussed in the statutory-duty and interest clauses elsewhere in this document — these are different subsections of one statute, not independent sources.

citations.case: California Labor Code
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2802(c)
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, the term “necessary expenditures or losses” shall include all reasonable costs, including, but not limited to, attorney’s fees incurred by the employee enforcing the rights granted by this section.

clauses.title: The Right Cannot Be Waived by Private Agreement
clauses.body: Labor Code § 2804 — a separately numbered section within the same article of the Labor Code as § 2802 — provides that any contract or agreement, express or implied, by which an employee purports to waive the benefits of that article (which includes § 2802) is null and void. The same section states that the article does not deprive an employee of any right or remedy otherwise available under California law.
clauses.gap: Section 2804 is an independently numbered Labor Code section, not merely a different subsection of § 2802, so it is presented here as a genuinely separate statutory source rather than a restatement of it. This clause states only that a private, prospective waiver of the article's benefits is void; it does not address distinct legal doctrines — such as the settlement or release of an already-existing, disputed claim — that can operate differently from a prospective waiver and are outside the scope of this document.

citations.case: California Labor Code
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 2804
citations.quote: Any contract or agreement, express or implied, made by any employee to waive the benefits of this article or any part thereof, is null and void, and this article shall not deprive any employee or his personal representative of any right or remedy to which he is entitled under the laws of this State.

clauses.title: Application to Personal Cell Phones and Remote Work
clauses.body: In Cochran v. Schwan's Home Service, Inc. (2014) 228 Cal.App.4th 1137, a California Court of Appeal held that when an employer requires employees to use their personal cell phones for work-related calls, § 2802 requires the employer to reimburse a reasonable percentage of the employee's cell phone bill. The court held that this obligation applies whether the employee's cell phone plan has unlimited minutes or limited minutes, and that it does not matter whether the phone bill is paid by the employee personally or by someone else. The court left the calculation of the specific reasonable percentage owed in any given case to the trial court and the parties.
clauses.gap: Cochran addressed personal cell phone expenses in the context of a class-certification appeal; the Court of Appeal expressly left the calculation of any specific percentage or dollar figure to the trial court and the parties in each case, and this document does not state what percentage of any specific employee's phone bill is owed. Cochran's reasoning was stated in terms of personal cell phone use specifically; this document has not independently verified that the same reasoning has been extended by a published California decision to other remote-work expenses such as home internet, home office equipment, or utilities, and readers should not assume that extension has been confirmed here. Cochran is a Court of Appeal decision; the California Supreme Court denied the losing party's petition for review (S221319, denied November 25, 2014) without issuing its own published opinion on the question. This is a genuinely independent source from Labor Code §§ 2802 and 2804 cited elsewhere in this document — it is case law construing the statute, not another subsection or cross-referenced provision of the statutory text itself.
