clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
Prohibition on Conditioning Wage Payment on a Release
clauses.body: California Labor Code section 206.5(a) states that an employer shall not require the execution of a release of a claim or right on account of wages due, or to become due, or made as an advance on wages to be earned, unless payment of those wages has actually been made. The statute further states that a release required or executed in violation of this section is null and void as between the employer and the employee, and that violation of the section by an employer is a misdemeanor.
clauses.gap: This clause covers only wages the statute treats as ‘due’ — that is, wages the employer does not genuinely dispute owing. A separate clause in this document describes how a California appellate court has distinguished a release of wages already due from a release given to settle a good-faith dispute over whether wages are owed at all; this document does not determine which category any particular wage claim falls into. Section 206.5 also does not itself define ‘wages’ — see the companion clause on that point. This document does not determine whether any specific release, in any specific situation, complies with or violates this statute.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 206.5(a)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 206.5, subd. (a)
citations.quote: An employer shall not require the execution of a release of a claim or right on account of wages due, or to become due, or made as an advance on wages to be earned, unless payment of those wages has been made. A release required or executed in violation of the provisions of this section shall be null and void as between the employer and the employee. Violation of this section by the employer is a misdemeanor.

clauses.title: What Counts as “Execution of a Release” Under the Statute
clauses.body: The same statutory section defines the term further. For purposes of section 206.5, California law states that “execution of a release” also includes requiring an employee, as a condition of being paid, to execute a statement of the hours worked during a pay period that the employer knows to be false.
clauses.gap: This citation is to subdivision (b) of the same section 206.5 quoted in the prior clause, not to an independent statutory source — the two are not independent of one another. This anti-evasion provision reaches only a false hours statement the employer knows to be false; the statute's text does not describe any other specific method of extracting a release as covered by this same definition, and this document does not determine whether any particular employer practice falls within it.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 206.5(b)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 206.5, subd. (b)
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, “execution of a release” includes requiring an employee, as a condition of being paid, to execute a statement of the hours he or she worked during a pay period which the employer knows to be false.

clauses.title: How “Wages” Is Defined Elsewhere in the Same Article
clauses.body: Section 206.5 does not itself define the term “wages.” California Labor Code section 200(a) — a separately numbered section of the Labor Code, within the same article as section 206.5 (Article 1, General Occupations, sections 200 through 244) — states that “wages” includes all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation.
clauses.gap: Section 206.5's own text contains no express cross-reference to section 200 or to any other definitional section — the full current text of section 206.5 was read for this document and nowhere mentions section 200. The connection described here rests on the two sections' shared placement within the same statutory article (section 200 begins ‘As used in this article’), not on any language inside section 206.5 pointing to section 200. Because section 200 and section 206.5 are separately numbered sections rather than subdivisions of the same section, this citation is genuinely independent of the section 206.5 citations in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 200(a)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 200, subd. (a)
citations.quote: “Wages” includes all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation.

clauses.title: A Settlement of a Genuinely Disputed Wage Claim Is Treated Differently
clauses.body: A California Court of Appeal has held that section 206.5's prohibition reaches wages that are due — meaning wages the employer does not dispute owing — and does not reach a release given to settle a bona fide (genuine, good-faith) dispute over whether wages are owed at all. In Chindarah v. Pick Up Stix, Inc., the court held that “there is no statute providing that an employee cannot release his claim to past overtime wages as part of a settlement of a bona fide dispute over those wages,” and that “this public policy is not violated by a settlement of a bona fide dispute over wages already earned.”
clauses.gap: This is the clearest published authority found on how section 206.5 relates to a broader settlement-style release, but it involved a class and collective wage-and-hour settlement, not a severance agreement specifically, and the court did not need to decide how section 206.5 treats a release exchanged for consideration beyond the wages themselves (as in a severance agreement) where the wages in question are not genuinely disputed at all. No case addressing that exact scenario was located, so this document does not resolve it, and this document does not determine whether any specific wage claim is genuinely disputed or whether any specific release fits within the distinction described here.

citations.case: Chindarah v. Pick Up Stix, Inc.
citations.quote: there is no statute providing that an employee cannot release his claim to past overtime wages as part of a settlement of a bona fide dispute over those wages

citations.case: Chindarah v. Pick Up Stix, Inc.
citations.quote: This public policy is not violated by a settlement of a bona fide dispute over wages already earned.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Letter
Statutory Prohibited Acts Under Penal Code Section 502(c)
clauses.body: California Penal Code section 502(c) lists specific acts that, when committed knowingly, are a public offense. Among the acts listed: knowingly accessing and, without permission, altering, damaging, deleting, destroying, or otherwise using data, a computer, a computer system, or a computer network in order to devise or execute a scheme to defraud, deceive, or extort, or to wrongfully control or obtain money, property, or data; knowingly accessing and, without permission, taking, copying, or making use of data from a computer, computer system, or computer network, or taking or copying supporting documentation; and knowingly and without permission using or causing to be used computer services. Subdivision (c) lists additional prohibited acts beyond these three, including adding or altering data, disrupting computer services, providing a means of unauthorized access, introducing a computer contaminant, and provisions specific to government and public-safety-infrastructure computer systems.
clauses.gap: Cal. Penal Code § 502(c) lists fourteen numbered prohibited acts, (1) through (14); this clause quotes only the introductory clause and paragraphs (1) through (3), the acts most commonly at issue in a private unauthorized-access dispute. It does not quote paragraphs (4) through (14), the felony/misdemeanor/infraction punishment schedule in subdivision (d), the forfeiture provision in subdivision (g), or the lawful-employment exemption in subdivision (h) -- all of which affect how subdivision (c) applies and are not otherwise addressed by this document. This clause does not state that any specific access was or was not authorized, or that any specific conduct falls within one of these paragraphs.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 502(c) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act, prohibited acts
citations.quote: (c) Except as provided in subdivision (h), any person who commits any of the following acts is guilty of a public offense: (1) Knowingly accesses and without permission alters, damages, deletes, destroys, or otherwise uses any data, computer, computer system, or computer network in order to either (A) devise or execute any scheme or artifice to defraud, deceive, or extort, or (B) wrongfully control or obtain money, property, or data. (2) Knowingly accesses and without permission takes, copies, or makes use of any data from a computer, computer system, or computer network, or takes or copies any supporting documentation, whether existing or residing internal or external to a computer, computer system, or computer network. (3) Knowingly and without permission uses or causes to be used computer services.

clauses.title: Civil Cause of Action for Unauthorized Computer Access
clauses.body: California law gives the owner or lessee of a computer, computer system, computer network, computer program, or data a private civil cause of action against a person who violates Penal Code section 502(c), where the owner or lessee suffers damage or loss by reason of that violation. This civil action is available in addition to any other civil remedy that may exist. A court may award compensatory damages and injunctive relief or other equitable relief; compensatory damages include any expenditure reasonably and necessarily incurred by the owner or lessee to verify whether a computer system, computer network, computer program, or data was or was not altered, damaged, or deleted by the access.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory law, quoted from Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(1), used as evidence of the existence and scope of the civil cause of action -- not a claim that any specific access violated subdivision (c), and not a claim that any specific person suffered damage or loss. Subdivision (e)(1) also imputes an unemancipated minor's conduct to a parent or legal guardian under Civil Code section 1714.1 for purposes of this civil action; that imputation provision is mentioned in the statute but not separately quoted or analyzed here.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act, private civil action
citations.quote: (e) (1) In addition to any other civil remedy available, the owner or lessee of the computer, computer system, computer network, computer program, or data who suffers damage or loss by reason of a violation of any of the provisions of subdivision (c) may bring a civil action against the violator for compensatory damages and injunctive relief or other equitable relief. Compensatory damages shall include any expenditure reasonably and necessarily incurred by the owner or lessee to verify that a computer system, computer network, computer program, or data was or was not altered, damaged, or deleted by the access.

clauses.title: Attorney's Fees and Punitive Damages Available Under Section 502
clauses.body: In an action brought under Penal Code section 502(e), the statute allows a court to award reasonable attorney's fees. Separately, where a violation of subdivision (c) was willful, and it is proved by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant acted with oppression, fraud, or malice as those terms are defined in Civil Code section 3294(c), the statute allows a court to additionally award punitive or exemplary damages.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes two paragraphs of the same statutory subdivision, Cal. Penal Code § 502(e) -- paragraph (2) (attorney's fees) and paragraph (4) (punitive damages) -- so these two citations are not independent of one another; both come from the same subdivision of the same section. Unlike some other fee-shifting statutes, subdivision (e)(2)'s text does not itself condition the fee award on which party prevails or on a bad-faith finding -- it states only that the court may award such fees in an action brought under the subdivision; this clause does not interpret how a court would exercise that discretion in practice. The punitive-damages standard in paragraph (4) incorporates by reference the definitions of oppression, fraud, and malice in Civil Code section 3294(c), which are not themselves quoted or independently verified here.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(2) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act, attorney's fees
citations.quote: (2) In any action brought pursuant to this subdivision the court may award reasonable attorney’s fees.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(4) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act, punitive damages
citations.quote: (4) In any action brought pursuant to this subdivision for a willful violation of the provisions of subdivision (c), where it is proved by clear and convincing evidence that a defendant has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 3294 of the Civil Code, the court may additionally award punitive or exemplary damages.

clauses.title: Three-Year Period to Bring a Civil Action
clauses.body: A civil action under Penal Code section 502(e) may not be brought unless it is initiated within three years of the date of the act complained of, or the date of the discovery of the damage, whichever is later.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory law, quoted from Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(5) -- not a claim about when any specific act occurred or was discovered, and not a claim about whether any tolling doctrine might extend or suspend this three-year period in a specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 502(e)(5) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act, limitations period
citations.quote: (5) No action may be brought pursuant to this subdivision unless it is initiated within three years of the date of the act complained of, or the date of the discovery of the damage, whichever is later.

clauses.title: Case Law Addressing the Scope of "Without Permission"
clauses.body: Penal Code section 502 does not itself define the phrase "without permission," even though that phrase appears throughout the prohibited acts listed in subdivision (c); subdivision (b) separately defines fifteen other terms used in the section, and "without permission" is not among them. In Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc., the Ninth Circuit addressed how permission that was initially given can later be revoked for purposes of section 502: where a computer owner had impliedly authorized certain access and then expressly revoked that authorization -- there, through a cease-and-desist letter -- the court held that continued access after the party received that revocation was "without permission" within the meaning of section 502(c)(2).
clauses.gap: Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc., 844 F.3d 1058 (9th Cir. 2016), is a Ninth Circuit decision applying California law, not a decision of a California state court, so it is persuasive rather than binding authority on how a California state court would apply section 502. Its holding is tied to its facts -- an express, individualized cease-and-desist letter revoking previously implied permission -- and does not establish a general rule for every situation in which permission might be contested. The observation that subdivision (b)'s fifteen defined terms do not include "without permission" is this researcher's own count of the definitions listed in the fetched statutory text (the same text quoted in the prohibited-acts authority clause in this document); it is not a holding of any case, and no case specifically addressing the absence of that statutory definition was located.

citations.case: Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc.
citations.quote: But when Facebook sent the cease and desist letter, Power, as it conceded, knew that it no longer had permission to access Facebook’s computers at all. Power, therefore, knowingly accessed and without permission took, copied, and made use of Facebook’s data. Accordingly, we affirm in part the district court’s holding, that Power violated section 502.

clauses.title: How Section 502 Differs From the Federal Computer Fraud and Abuse Act
clauses.body: California's Penal Code section 502 and the federal Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA), 18 U.S.C. section 1030, are separate statutes, and conduct can potentially be examined under either or both. The Ninth Circuit has held that section 502 "is different" from the CFAA because, unlike the CFAA's requirement of unauthorized access, section 502 "does not require unauthorized access" and "merely requires knowing access" -- with the separate requirement, described in the prohibited-acts clause above, that the access be "without permission."
clauses.gap: This quote comes from the same case used in the preceding authority clause on the scope of "without permission" -- Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc., 844 F.3d 1058 (9th Cir. 2016) -- so these two clauses are not independent sources of case law from each other, even though each addresses a different point. The Ninth Circuit was itself quoting its own earlier decision, United States v. Christensen, 801 F.3d 970, 994 (9th Cir. 2015), which is not independently fetched or verified here. Like the previous clause, this is a federal court of appeals interpretation of California law, not a decision of a California state court. This clause addresses only the specific "knowing access" versus "unauthorized access" distinction the court identified; it does not compare every element of the two statutes, and it does not address the CFAA's own jurisdictional requirements, damage thresholds, or remedies, none of which were independently verified for this document.

citations.case: Facebook, Inc. v. Power Ventures, Inc.
citations.cite: 844 F.3d 1058, 1069 (9th Cir. 2016), quoting United States v. Christensen, 801 F.3d 970, 994 (9th Cir. 2015)
citations.quote: This statute, we have held, is “different” than the CFAA. United States v. Christensen, 801 F.3d 970, 994 (2015). “[T]he California statute does not require unauthorized access. It merely requires knowing access.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California Corporations Code section 312 — the statutory provisions governing which officers a California corporation must have, how those officers are chosen, and the board of directors' statutory authority over an officer's continued service in office. It is prepared with reference to {{officerName}}'s service as {{officerTitle}} of {{companyName}}. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing what section 312 provides; it does not evaluate, and is not evidence of, whether removing {{officerName}} from the office of {{officerTitle}} would be proper under any specific circumstances, whether such a removal would breach any contract of employment, or what {{companyName}}'s board of directors should do. Those are fact-specific questions this Information Sheet does not answer. This document is a companion to, and does not duplicate, this project's existing Corporate Bylaws document, whose officers clause states only a general default (that officers are chosen by the board and serve at the board's discretion) without quoting the statutory text or addressing the statute's rules on required offices, dual office-holding, resignation, or the officer's contract rights that this document addresses in depth.

clauses.title: The Officers a California Corporation Must Have
clauses.body: California law requires every California corporation to have certain officers: (1) a chairperson of the board — who may instead, or in addition, be given the title of president — (2) a secretary, and (3) a chief financial officer, along with any other officers with titles and duties stated in the bylaws or determined by the board that are necessary to enable the corporation to sign instruments and share certificates. Unless the articles or bylaws provide otherwise, the president (or, if there is no president, the chairperson of the board) is by default the corporation's general manager and chief executive officer. This clause states which offices the statute requires and who functions as chief executive officer by default; it does not state which of {{companyName}}'s existing offices satisfy each statutory category, and it does not evaluate whether {{companyName}}'s articles or bylaws have departed from these statutory defaults.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes two sentences from a single subdivision (subdivision (a)) of Corporations Code section 312; the two quotations are not independent sources of one another. It does not address subdivision (b) of the same section, which governs how officers are chosen and removed and an officer's right to resign — covered in separate clauses of this document using the same statute. This clause does not identify which title, if any, an officer's stated office corresponds to under the statute's own categories.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 312(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, required corporate officers
citations.quote: A corporation shall have (1) a chairperson of the board, who may be given the title of chair of the board, chairperson of the board, chairperson, or a president or both, (2) a secretary, (3) a chief financial officer, and (4) such other officers with such titles and duties as shall be stated in the bylaws or determined by the board and as may be necessary to enable it to sign instruments and share certificates.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 312(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, default chief executive officer
citations.quote: The president, or if there is no president the chairperson of the board, is the general manager and chief executive officer of the corporation, unless otherwise provided in the articles or bylaws.

clauses.title: Holding More Than One Office
clauses.body: California law permits any number of corporate offices to be held by the same person, unless a corporation's articles of incorporation or bylaws provide otherwise. This clause states the default statutory rule; it does not determine whether {{companyName}}'s own articles or bylaws restrict {{officerName}} or any other individual from holding more than one office at the same time.
clauses.gap: This is the same subdivision of Corporations Code section 312 (subdivision (a)) quoted in the preceding clause of this document — not an independent source corroborating it. The statute does not state whether the corporation's minimum required officer positions (described in the preceding clause) may all be satisfied by a single office-holder in every circumstance; this clause states only the general dual-office-holding default.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 312(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, one person holding multiple offices
citations.quote: Any number of offices may be held by the same person unless the articles or bylaws provide otherwise.

clauses.title: How Officers Are Chosen and the Board's Authority Over Their Continued Service
clauses.body: Under California law, unless a corporation's articles or bylaws provide otherwise, a corporation's officers are chosen by the board of directors, and an officer serves at the pleasure of the board. This means the board holds the statutory power to end an officer's service in that office, and the statute does not condition that power on the board having any particular reason for doing so. The statute expressly makes this board authority subject to "the rights, if any, of an officer under any contract of employment" — meaning the statute itself preserves whatever separate contractual rights an officer may have, without stating what those rights are or whether any specific contract creates them. This clause states the statutory default itself; it does not state whether {{companyName}}'s articles or bylaws have altered this default, whether {{officerName}} has an employment contract, or what rights any such contract might create.
clauses.gap: This is subdivision (b) of Corporations Code section 312, the same statutory subdivision quoted in the following clause of this document (which addresses an officer's own right to resign) — not an independent source corroborating it. The statute uses the phrase "serve at the pleasure of the board"; the quoted text does not itself contain the phrase "with or without cause," and this clause does not represent that it does. The statute states that this board authority is subject to an officer's contract rights, if any, but does not itself define what a contract of employment must contain to create such rights, and does not state whether removing a specific officer without cause would constitute a breach of any specific contract — those are fact-specific and contract-specific questions this clause does not answer.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 312(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, selection of officers and the board's authority over an officer's continued service
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by the articles or bylaws, officers shall be chosen by the board and serve at the pleasure of the board, subject to the rights, if any, of an officer under any contract of employment.

clauses.title: An Officer's Right to Resign
clauses.body: California law also gives an officer the separate, reciprocal right to resign from office at any time, on written notice to the corporation. The statute states that a resignation is without prejudice to any rights the corporation may separately have under a contract to which the resigning officer is a party. This clause states the statutory resignation right and the statute's preservation of the corporation's own contract rights; it does not state whether {{companyName}} has a contract with {{officerName}} or what rights, if any, that contract would preserve.
clauses.gap: This is the same subdivision of Corporations Code section 312 (subdivision (b)) quoted in the preceding clause of this document — not an independent source. The statute does not specify a notice period, form, or delivery method for an officer's resignation beyond stating that notice must be in writing and given to the corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 312(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, an officer's right to resign
citations.quote: Any officer may resign at any time upon written notice to the corporation without prejudice to the rights, if any, of the corporation under any contract to which the officer is a party.

clauses.title: How This Differs From At-Will Employee Status
clauses.body: Corporations Code section 312 and its "serve at the pleasure of the board" rule govern the corporate-law validity of removing a person from a corporate office — a title and role created by the corporation's own governance structure. That is a separate body of law from the common default rule for a rank-and-file employee's job, found in Labor Code section 2922, which provides that an employment relationship with no specified term may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other. An individual can simultaneously hold a corporate office covered by section 312 and be an employee of the corporation covered by section 2922 (or by a separate employment contract); the two statutes address two different legal relationships — the office, and the employment — and removal from one does not by itself state what happens to the other. This clause states that these are separate statutes governing separate relationships; it does not state whether {{officerName}}'s relationship with {{companyName}} includes an employment relationship distinct from the office of {{officerTitle}}, or what would happen to any such employment relationship if {{officerName}} were removed from office.
clauses.gap: Corporations Code section 312 and Labor Code section 2922 are independently numbered statutes in different codes, not subsections of the same section — genuinely independent sources, unlike the other citation pairs in this document. This clause states only that these are distinct legal relationships governed by distinct statutes; it does not describe the statutory and common-law exceptions to at-will employment under California law (such as express or implied contract terms, or public-policy limits), which this project's other documents cover separately, and it does not state whether any specific facts would place a given officer's situation within such an exception.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 312(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the board's authority over a corporate office
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by the articles or bylaws, officers shall be chosen by the board and serve at the pleasure of the board, subject to the rights, if any, of an officer under any contract of employment.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2922 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, default at-will rule for an employment relationship
citations.quote: An employment, having no specified term, may be terminated at the will of either party on notice to the other.

clauses.title: Declaration Regarding Domestic Violence Custody Presumption Information
clauses.body: This information sheet concerns a child custody proceeding involving {{childName}}, filed or to be filed in {{countyOfFiling}} County, California, between {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. It is prepared to explain California Family Code section 3044 -- the statute that creates a rebuttable presumption against awarding sole or joint custody to a parent whom a court has found to have perpetrated domestic violence within a specified look-back period, and that lists the factors a court considers in deciding whether that presumption has been overcome. This information sheet is a companion to, and distinct from, this corpus's Domestic Violence Restraining Order Information Sheet: that document explains the process for obtaining a protective order under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Family Code section 6200 et seq.); this document explains a separate, later-stage legal consequence -- how a court finding of domestic violence affects a subsequent custody determination under Family Code section 3044. This information sheet does not itself assert that either party has perpetrated domestic violence, does not assert that the presumption applies to this matter, and does not make or substitute for any finding a court is required to make under Family Code section 3044 -- only the court, applying section 3044 to the evidence and facts of the case before it, can make that determination.

clauses.title: The Core Rebuttable Presumption -- Family Code Section 3044(a)
clauses.body: Family Code section 3044(a) provides that upon a finding by the court that a party seeking custody of a child has perpetrated domestic violence within the previous five years against the other party seeking custody of the child, or against the child or the child's siblings, or against a person described in Family Code section 3011(a)(2)(A) with whom the party has a relationship, there is a rebuttable presumption that an award of sole or joint physical or legal custody of a child to a person who has perpetrated domestic violence is detrimental to the best interest of the child. The persons described in Family Code section 3011(a)(2)(A) are: a child to whom the parent or person seeking custody is related by blood or affinity or with whom that parent or person has had a caretaking relationship, no matter how temporary; the other parent; and a parent, current spouse, or cohabitant of the parent or person seeking custody, or a person with whom that parent or person has a dating or engagement relationship. The statute states that this presumption may only be rebutted by a preponderance of the evidence.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes two different, independently numbered Family Code sections -- section 3044(a) and section 3011(a)(2)(A), which section 3044(a) itself cross-references by citation -- rather than two subsections of the same section, so this is not a case requiring the single-section-independence disclosure; however, because section 3044(a) incorporates section 3011(a)(2)(A) by direct cross-reference rather than restating it, the two quotes together describe one integrated statutory rule, not two separately corroborating sources on the same point. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own custody-presumption rule -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific custody matter, and not a claim that an equivalent presumption exists in every state (domestic-violence-related custody presumptions vary significantly by state, including whether one exists at all, the look-back period, and what conduct or relationships trigger it). The version of section 3044 quoted throughout this document was added by Stats. 2024, Ch. 544 (SB 899) and became operative January 1, 2026; this research fetched and confirmed that current, operative text directly (twice, from independent requests) rather than relying on a summary or an earlier version of the section. Whether a specific party's conduct meets the threshold for a court "finding" that domestic violence was "perpetrated," and whether a specific relationship falls within section 3011(a)(2)(A), are determinations the court makes on the evidence before it -- this clause states only the statutory text, not how it applies to any individual's facts.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(a)
citations.cite: the core rebuttable presumption
citations.quote: Upon a finding by the court that a party seeking custody of a child has perpetrated domestic violence within the previous five years against the other party seeking custody of the child, or against the child or the child’s siblings, or against a person in subparagraph (A) of paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3011 with whom the party has a relationship, there is a rebuttable presumption that an award of sole or joint physical or legal custody of a child to a person who has perpetrated domestic violence is detrimental to the best interest of the child, pursuant to Sections 3011 and 3020. This presumption may only be rebutted by a preponderance of the evidence.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3011(a)(2)(A)
citations.cite: the persons protected by the presumption, as cross-referenced by section 3044(a)
citations.quote: (2) (A) A history of abuse by one parent or any other person seeking custody against any of the following: (i) A child to whom the parent or person seeking custody is related by blood or affinity or with whom the parent or person seeking custody has had a caretaking relationship, no matter how temporary. (ii) The other parent. (iii) A parent, current spouse, or cohabitant, of the parent or person seeking custody, or a person with whom the parent or person seeking custody has a dating or engagement relationship.

clauses.title: Overcoming the Presumption -- The Statutory Factors Under Section 3044(b)
clauses.body: Family Code section 3044(b) states that to overcome the presumption in subdivision (a), the court shall find that paragraph (1) is satisfied and shall find that the factors in paragraph (2), on balance, support the legislative findings in Family Code section 3020. Paragraph (1) requires that the perpetrator of domestic violence has demonstrated that giving sole or joint physical or legal custody of a child to the perpetrator is in the best interest of the child under Family Code sections 3011 and 3020, and specifies that in making that determination, the preference for frequent and continuing contact with both parents (Family Code section 3020(b)) or with the noncustodial parent (Family Code section 3040(a)(1)) may not be used to rebut the presumption, in whole or in part. Paragraph (2) lists these additional factors: (A) whether the perpetrator has successfully completed a batterer's treatment program meeting the criteria in Penal Code section 1203.097(c); (B) whether the perpetrator has successfully completed a program of alcohol or drug abuse counseling, if the court determines counseling is appropriate; (C) whether the perpetrator has successfully completed a parenting class, if the court determines the class is appropriate; (D) whether the perpetrator is on probation or parole, and has or has not complied with its terms and conditions; (E) whether the perpetrator is restrained by a protective order or restraining order, and has or has not complied with its terms and conditions; (F) whether the perpetrator has committed further acts of domestic violence; and (G) whether the court has determined, under Family Code section 6322.5, that the perpetrator is a restrained person in possession or control of a firearm or ammunition in violation of Family Code section 6389, Code of Civil Procedure section 527.9, or Penal Code section 18120.
clauses.gap: Family Code section 3044(b), including its paragraph (1) and the seven lettered factors of paragraph (2), are all provisions of a single statutory section (§ 3044); no additional, independently-numbered statutory source exists for this specific factor list, so this clause relies on a single section for its core content, though the cross-referenced provisions it names (sections 3020, 3040, 1203.097 of the Penal Code, 6322.5, 6389, and Code of Civil Procedure section 527.9) are each independently enacted and are quoted as section 3044(b) itself frames them, not independently re-verified against their own full text in this research pass. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific factor list California's presumption directs a court to weigh -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific custody matter, and other states' domestic-violence custody presumptions, where they exist, commonly use different rebuttal factors. This clause states the statutory list only; it does not state whether any specific party has satisfied any of these factors, and does not state how a court weighs the factors relative to one another beyond the statute's own "on balance" language.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(b)(1)
citations.cite: the best-interest showing required, and the bar on using the frequent-contact preference to rebut
citations.quote: The perpetrator of domestic violence has demonstrated that giving sole or joint physical or legal custody of a child to the perpetrator is in the best interest of the child pursuant to Sections 3011 and 3020. In determining the best interest of the child, the preference for frequent and continuing contact with both parents, as set forth in subdivision (b) of Section 3020, or with the noncustodial parent, as set forth in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3040, may not be used to rebut the presumption, in whole or in part.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(b)(2)(A)-(G)
citations.cite: the seven additional rebuttal factors
citations.quote: (A) The perpetrator has successfully completed a batterer’s treatment program that meets the criteria outlined in subdivision (c) of Section 1203.097 of the Penal Code. (B) The perpetrator has successfully completed a program of alcohol or drug abuse counseling, if the court determines that counseling is appropriate. (C) The perpetrator has successfully completed a parenting class, if the court determines the class to be appropriate. (D) The perpetrator is on probation or parole, and has or has not complied with the terms and conditions of probation or parole. (E) The perpetrator is restrained by a protective order or restraining order, and has or has not complied with its terms and conditions. (F) The perpetrator of domestic violence has committed further acts of domestic violence. (G) The court has determined, pursuant to Section 6322.5, that the perpetrator is a restrained person in possession or control of a firearm or ammunition in violation of Section 6389, Section 527.9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or Section 18120 of the Penal Code.

clauses.title: How "Perpetrated Domestic Violence" Is Established for This Section
clauses.body: Family Code section 3044(c) provides its own, self-contained definition of when a person has "perpetrated domestic violence" for purposes of this section: when the person is found by the court to have intentionally or recklessly caused or attempted to cause bodily injury, or sexual assault, or to have placed a person in reasonable apprehension of imminent serious bodily injury to that person or to another, or to have engaged in behavior involving, but not limited to, threatening, striking, harassing, destroying personal property, or disturbing the peace of another, for which a court may issue an ex parte order under Family Code section 6320. Separately, Family Code section 3044(d)(1) states that the required court finding may also be satisfied by evidence that a party has been convicted, within the previous five years, after a trial or a plea of guilty or no contest, of a crime against the other party that comes within the definition of domestic violence contained in Family Code section 6211 and of abuse contained in Family Code section 6203. Section 3044(d)(2) states that the finding requirement is also satisfied if any court -- whether or not it is hearing the custody proceeding -- has made a finding under subdivision (a) based on conduct occurring within the previous five years.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on subdivisions (c) and (d) of the same statutory section (§ 3044); the cross-referenced sections 6211 and 6203 are independently-numbered Family Code sections, but this research did not independently re-fetch and quote their full current text in this document (section 6211's current text was separately spot-checked, without a formal two-fetch confirmation, and found consistent with the definition already verified and cited in this corpus's DVRO Petition Information document, but is not independently cited here). The important, easily-missed nuance this clause is built around: section 3044 does not simply cross-reference the DVPA's "domestic violence" definition (§ 6211) or "abuse" definition (§ 6203) as the general test for whether this section's presumption applies -- subdivision (c) sets out its own definition of "perpetrated domestic violence," which overlaps substantially with, but is not textually identical to, section 6203's abuse definition (both include causing or attempting bodily injury, sexual assault, and placing a person in reasonable apprehension of imminent serious bodily injury; the DVPA cross-reference to sections 6211 and 6203 appears only in subdivision (d)(1), as one specific way -- a prior criminal conviction -- of satisfying the finding requirement, not as the operative definition for a contested finding made directly under subdivision (a). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California structures this specific definitional question -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that other states structure an analogous presumption's triggering definition the same way.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(c)
citations.cite: the self-contained definition of "perpetrated domestic violence" for this section
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, a person has “perpetrated domestic violence” when the person is found by the court to have intentionally or recklessly caused or attempted to cause bodily injury, or sexual assault, or to have placed a person in reasonable apprehension of imminent serious bodily injury to that person or to another, or to have engaged in behavior involving, but not limited to, threatening, striking, harassing, destroying personal property, or disturbing the peace of another, for which a court may issue an ex parte order pursuant to Section 6320 to protect the other party seeking custody of the child or to protect the child and the child’s siblings.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(d)(1)
citations.cite: how the required court finding may be established by prior conviction referencing sections 6211 and 6203
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, the requirement of a finding by the court shall be satisfied by, among other things, and not limited to, evidence that a party seeking custody has been convicted within the previous five years, after a trial or a plea of guilty or no contest, of a crime against the other party that comes within the definition of domestic violence contained in Section 6211 and of abuse contained in Section 6203, including, but not limited to, a crime described in subdivision (e) of Section 243 of, or Section 261, 273.5, 422, or 646.9 of, or former Section 262 of, the Penal Code.

clauses.title: When and How the Finding Is Made -- Interaction With the General Custody Process
clauses.body: Family Code section 3044(g) states that in an evidentiary hearing or trial in which custody orders are sought and where there has been an allegation of domestic violence, the court shall determine whether this section applies before issuing a custody order, unless the court finds a continuance necessary to make that determination -- in which case the court may issue a temporary custody order for a reasonable period, provided the order complies with Family Code sections 3011 and 3020. Section 3044(e) states that when a court makes a finding that a party has perpetrated domestic violence, the court may not base that finding solely on conclusions reached by a child custody evaluator or on the recommendation of Family Court Services staff, but shall consider any relevant, admissible evidence submitted by the parties. Section 3044(f)(1) states that it is the intent of the Legislature that subdivision (f) be interpreted consistently with Jaime G. v. H.L. (2018) 25 Cal.App.5th 794, which requires the court, in determining that the presumption has been overcome, to make specific findings on each of the factors in subdivision (b); section 3044(f)(2) requires the court, if it determines the presumption has been overcome, to state its reasons in writing or on the record for why subdivision (b)'s paragraph (1) is satisfied and why the paragraph (2) factors, on balance, support the legislative findings in section 3020. Section 3044(h) separately requires that in a custody or restraining order proceeding where a party has alleged the other party perpetrated domestic violence under this section, the court shall inform the parties of the existence of this section and give them a copy of it before custody mediation in the case.
clauses.gap: Subdivisions (e), (f), (g), and (h) are all provisions of a single statutory section (§ 3044); this clause does not draw on a second, independent statutory source, though it does cite one case, Jaime G. v. H.L. (2018) 25 Cal.App.5th 794, only because the statute's own text names that decision and directs that subdivision (f) be interpreted consistently with it -- this clause states what the statute says about that case, not an independent reading of the opinion itself, which was not separately retrieved or reviewed for this clause. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own procedural sequencing and evidentiary rules for this specific presumption -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proceeding. This clause does not restate Family Code section 3011's full best-interest factor list or Family Code section 3020's legislative findings referenced throughout section 3044(b) and (g); those are separate statutory provisions this document does not independently verify or reproduce.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3044(g)
citations.cite: the requirement to determine applicability before a custody order issues, and the temporary-order exception
citations.quote: In an evidentiary hearing or trial in which custody orders are sought and where there has been an allegation of domestic violence, the court shall make a determination as to whether this section applies prior to issuing a custody order, unless the court finds that a continuance is necessary to determine whether this section applies, in which case the court may issue a temporary custody order for a reasonable period of time, provided the order complies with Sections 3011 and 3020.

citations.cite: the Jaime G. v. H.L. specific-findings requirement
citations.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature that this subdivision be interpreted consistently with the decision in Jaime G. v. H.L. (2018) 25 Cal.App.5th 794, which requires that the court, in determining that the presumption in subdivision (a) has been overcome, make specific findings on each of the factors in subdivision (b).

citations.quote: If the court determines that the presumption in subdivision (a) has been overcome, the court shall state its reasons in writing or on the record as to why paragraph (1) of subdivision (b) is satisfied and why the factors in paragraph (2) of subdivision (b), on balance, support the legislative findings in Section 3020.

clauses.title: Required Notice to the Parties Before Custody Mediation
clauses.body: Family Code section 3044(h) provides that in a custody or restraining order proceeding in which a party has alleged that the other party has perpetrated domestic violence in accordance with the terms of this section, the court shall inform the parties of the existence of this section and shall give them a copy of this section before custody mediation in the case.
clauses.gap: This is a single provision of Family Code section 3044 (subdivision (h)); no independent second source was sought for this specific procedural requirement, which is stated plainly and only once in the statute. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, checkable procedural step California's own courts must take -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proceeding, and not a claim that an equivalent notice-before-mediation requirement exists in every state's custody mediation process. This clause states only that the statute requires this notice; it does not describe California's broader custody mediation process itself, which this document does not otherwise cover.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope — Restrictions on Distributions to Shareholders
clauses.body:
This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a {{entityType}} organized under the laws of California, and to the statutory restrictions on {{companyName}}'s ability to make a distribution to its shareholders. It was prepared by {{preparerName}}, {{officerTitle}} of {{companyName}}, in connection with the following distribution under consideration: {{proposedDistributionDescription}}.

It describes the restrictions that Chapter 5 of the California General Corporation Law (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 500-511), titled "Dividends and Reacquisitions of Shares," places on when a California corporation or its subsidiaries may make a distribution to shareholders -- including the statutory definition of "distribution to its shareholders," the alternative balance-sheet-based tests in Section 500, the separate ability-to-pay-debts test in Section 501, and the statutory consequences under Sections 316 and 506 for directors and shareholders when a distribution violates these provisions.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not calculate whether {{proposedDistributionDescription}} satisfies any test described below, does not determine whether {{companyName}}'s board of directors has made or can make the good-faith determination Section 500 requires, and does not constitute legal, financial, or accounting advice regarding {{companyName}} or any specific distribution.

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of "Distribution to Its Shareholders"
clauses.body:
The restrictions described in this information sheet apply to a defined statutory term. California's General Corporation Law defines "distribution to its shareholders" as the transfer of cash or property by a corporation to its shareholders without consideration, whether by way of dividend or otherwise, except a dividend in shares of the corporation, or the purchase or redemption of its shares for cash or property -- and this includes a transfer, purchase, or redemption made by a subsidiary of the corporation, not only by the corporation itself. The statute also fixes when a distribution is deemed to occur: a distribution by way of dividend is timed to the date of declaration, and a distribution by purchase or redemption of shares is timed to the date cash or property is transferred, regardless of whether that transfer occurs under an earlier contract.

The definition excludes three narrow categories from the term "distribution to its shareholders": satisfaction of a final court judgment ordering rescission of a share issuance; a board-determined rescission of a share issuance, subject to specific board findings; and a repurchase of shares issued under Section 408, also subject to specific board findings. Each of the latter two exclusions requires the board to determine, among other things, that the corporation is likely to be able to meet its liabilities (except those otherwise adequately provided for) as they mature.
clauses.gap: Both citations are drawn from the same statutory section (Section 166) and are not independent of one another. This clause states the statutory definition only; it does not state the separate tests in Sections 500 and 501 that govern when a transfer meeting this definition is permitted (see other clauses in this information sheet), and it does not address the sinking-fund timing rule or the debt-exchange timing rule that Section 166 also contains.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 166
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, definition of "distribution to its shareholders"
citations.quote: “Distribution to its shareholders” means the transfer of cash or property by a corporation to its shareholders without consideration, whether by way of dividend or otherwise, except a dividend in shares of the corporation, or the purchase or redemption of its shares for cash or property, including the transfer, purchase, or redemption by a subsidiary of the corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 166
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, exclusions from the definition of "distribution to its shareholders"
citations.quote: “Distribution to its shareholders” shall not include (a) satisfaction of a final judgment of a court or tribunal of appropriate jurisdiction ordering the rescission of the issuance of shares, (b) the rescission by a corporation of the issuance of it shares, if the board determines (with any director who is, or would be, a party to the transaction not being entitled to vote) that (1) it is reasonably likely that the holder or holders of the shares in question could legally enforce a claim for the rescission, (2) that the rescission is in the best interests of the corporation, and (3) the corporation is likely to be able to meet its liabilities (except those for which payment is otherwise adequately provided) as they mature, or (c) the repurchase by a corporation of its shares issued by it pursuant to Section 408, if the board determines (with any director who is, or would be, a party to the transaction not being entitled to vote) that (1) the repurchase is in the best interests of the corporation and that (2) the corporation is likely to be able to meet its liabilities (except those for which payment is otherwise adequately provided) as they mature.

clauses.title: Section 500's Alternative Balance-Sheet Tests
clauses.body:
Section 500 of the California General Corporation Law restricts when a corporation, or any of its subsidiaries, may make a distribution to the corporation's shareholders. The statute does not use a single fixed test; it prohibits a distribution unless the corporation's board of directors has determined in good faith that at least one of two alternative conditions is satisfied. The first alternative is a retained-earnings test: that the corporation's retained earnings immediately before the distribution equal or exceed the sum of the proposed distribution plus the "preferential dividends arrears amount" (the amount of any cumulative, unpaid dividends owed on shares senior to the shares receiving the distribution, which the articles of incorporation can reduce to zero). The second alternative is an asset-versus-liabilities test: that immediately after the distribution, the value of the corporation's assets would equal or exceed the sum of its total liabilities plus the "preferential rights amount" (the amount that would be needed, if the corporation dissolved at the time of the distribution, to satisfy dissolution-preference rights senior to the shares receiving the distribution, which the articles can likewise reduce to zero).

As currently written, the statute does not specify a fixed numeric cushion or ratio (such as a 1.25-to-1 asset-to-liability ratio) for either alternative -- the second alternative requires assets to equal or exceed liabilities plus the preferential rights amount, without a stated multiplier. The board may base its good-faith determination under either alternative on financial statements prepared under accounting practices reasonable under the circumstances, a fair valuation, or any other method reasonable under the circumstances, and the effect of the distribution is measured as of the date it is authorized if payment occurs within 120 days of that authorization.
clauses.gap: All of the quoted material comes from a single statutory section (Section 500, subdivisions (a), (b), and (d)) and is not independent of one another as a source. This clause does not describe Section 500's separate rules on indebtedness issued as a distribution (subdivision (e)) or its exclusion for certain licensed broker-dealers (subdivision (f)), and it does not describe the distinct ability-to-pay-debts test in Section 501, which is covered in a separate clause. The statutory text quoted was current as of the check date above (reflecting amendments effective January 1, 2023); a reader should confirm no later amendment has changed it.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 500(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, the two alternative tests for a permitted distribution
citations.quote: (a) Neither a corporation nor any of its subsidiaries shall make any distribution to the corporation’s shareholders (Section 166) unless the board of directors has determined in good faith either of the following: (1) The amount of retained earnings of the corporation immediately prior to the distribution equals or exceeds the sum of (A) the amount of the proposed distribution plus (B) the preferential dividends arrears amount. (2) Immediately after the distribution, the value of the corporation’s assets would equal or exceed the sum of its total liabilities plus the preferential rights amount.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 500(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, definition of "preferential rights amount" used in the asset-versus-liabilities test
citations.quote: “preferential rights amount” means the amount that would be needed if the corporation were to be dissolved at the time of the distribution to satisfy the preferential rights, including accrued but unpaid dividends, of other shareholders upon dissolution that are superior to the rights of the shareholders receiving the distribution

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 500(d)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, timing rule for measuring a distribution's effect
citations.quote: (d) The effect of a distribution under paragraph (1) or (2) of subdivision (a) is measured as of the date the distribution is authorized if the payment occurs within 120 days after the date of authorization.

clauses.title: Section 501's Separate Ability-to-Pay-Debts Test
clauses.body: In addition to the two balance-sheet-based tests in Section 500, California's General Corporation Law imposes a separate, independently stated restriction in Section 501: neither a corporation nor any of its subsidiaries may make a distribution to the corporation's shareholders if the corporation or the subsidiary making the distribution is, or as a result of the distribution would be, likely to be unable to meet its liabilities as they mature, except liabilities whose payment is otherwise adequately provided for. This is an equitable-insolvency-style, ability-to-pay-debts test, distinct from the retained-earnings and asset-versus-liabilities tests in Section 500 -- a distribution can satisfy one or both of Section 500's balance-sheet tests and still be restricted separately by Section 501 if it would leave the corporation or subsidiary unable to meet maturing liabilities.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses Section 501 alone, a section separately numbered from and independent of Section 500 and Section 166. It does not restate the balance-sheet tests of Section 500 (covered in a separate clause) and does not describe what accounting method or evidentiary standard a corporation must use to assess its ability to meet maturing liabilities, a point Section 501's text does not itself specify.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 501
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, restriction on distributions that would leave a corporation unable to meet maturing liabilities
citations.quote: Neither a corporation nor any of its subsidiaries shall make any distribution to the corporation’s shareholders (Section 166) if the corporation or the subsidiary making the distribution is, or as a result thereof would be, likely to be unable to meet its liabilities (except those whose payment is otherwise adequately provided for) as they mature.

clauses.title: Section 316's Liability of Directors Who Approve an Unlawful Distribution
clauses.body:
California's General Corporation Law imposes a specific statutory consequence on directors who approve a distribution that violates Sections 500 through 503. Under Section 316, directors of a corporation who approve a distribution to shareholders that is contrary to Sections 500 to 503 are jointly and severally liable to the corporation, for the benefit of creditors or shareholders entitled to sue, up to the amount of the illegal distribution (or, for a distribution of property, its fair market value at the time of the distribution), plus interest at the legal rate on judgments from the date of the distribution, plus reasonably incurred appraisal or valuation costs -- capped at the liabilities owed to nonconsenting creditors at the time of the violation and the injury suffered by nonconsenting shareholders. A director who is present at the board (or committee) meeting where the distribution is approved and abstains from voting is treated as having approved it. A director held liable under Section 316 may compel contribution from other liable directors, and is subrogated to the corporation's rights against the shareholders who received the unlawful distribution.

Section 316's liability is expressly made "subject to the provisions of Section 309." Section 309 states the general standard of director conduct: that a director must perform the director's duties in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders, and with the care -- including reasonable inquiry -- that an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances, and that a director may rely in specified circumstances on information and reports prepared by officers, employees, counsel, accountants, or board committees. Section 309 further states that a director who performs the director's duties in accordance with that standard has no liability based on an alleged failure to discharge the director's obligations as a director.
clauses.gap: The two statutory sections cited (Section 316 and Section 309) are genuinely distinct, independently numbered General Corporation Law sections, not merely subsections of the same section -- Section 316's own text cross-references Section 309, and this clause relies on the text of both. This clause does not determine how Section 309's good-faith/reasonable-care standard applies to any specific director's conduct or any specific distribution, and does not address Section 316's separate liability provisions for post-dissolution asset distributions or unlawful loans/guaranties (subdivision (a)(2) and (3)), which concern different corporate actions than an ordinary distribution to shareholders.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 316(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, director liability for a distribution contrary to Sections 500-503
citations.quote: 316. (a) Subject to the provisions of Section 309, directors of a corporation who approve any of the following corporate actions shall be jointly and severally liable to the corporation for the benefit of all of the creditors or shareholders entitled to institute an action under subdivision (c): (1) The making of any distribution to its shareholders to the extent that it is contrary to the provisions of Sections 500 to 503, inclusive.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 316(d)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, measure of damages recoverable from a liable director
citations.quote: The damages recoverable from a director under this section shall be the amount of the illegal distribution (or if the illegal distribution consists of property, the fair market value of that property at the time of the illegal distribution) plus interest thereon from the date of the distribution at the legal rate on judgments until paid

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 309(a), (c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, general standard of director conduct and its liability shield
citations.quote: (a) A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner such director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances.

clauses.title: Section 506's Liability of a Shareholder Who Receives an Unlawful Distribution
clauses.body: California's General Corporation Law also creates a specific statutory consequence for a shareholder, not only for directors. Under Section 506, a shareholder who receives a distribution prohibited by Chapter 5 (which includes distributions that violate Section 500 or Section 501) with knowledge of facts indicating the impropriety of the distribution is liable to the corporation, for the benefit of creditors or shareholders entitled to sue, for the amount received (or, for noncash property, its fair market value at the time of the illegal distribution, plus appraisal or valuation costs), with interest at the legal rate on judgments -- capped, as with director liability, at the liabilities owed to nonconsenting creditors at the time of the violation and the injury suffered by nonconsenting shareholders. A shareholder sued under Section 506 may implead other liable shareholders and compel contribution. A cause of action to recover a distribution under Section 506 is extinguished unless brought within four years of the date the distribution was made.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses Section 506 alone, a section separately numbered from and independent of Sections 500, 501, and 316, though it operates as part of the same statutory scheme (violations of Sections 500 or 501 trigger the liability). Section 506 conditions shareholder liability on the shareholder having received the distribution "with knowledge of facts indicating the impropriety thereof" -- this clause does not determine whether any specific shareholder had such knowledge with respect to any specific distribution, and does not describe Section 506(d)'s cross-reference to fraudulent-transfer liability under the Civil Code, which this clause has not separately verified.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 506(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, liability of a shareholder who knowingly receives a prohibited distribution
