clauses.title: Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This document concerns the marriage of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, married on {{marriageDate}}, in connection with a proceeding for dissolution of marriage contemplated in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes California's statutory procedure under Family Code § 2337 for requesting an early and separate trial on the sole issue of the dissolution of marital status — sometimes called "bifurcation" — apart from the remaining issues in a dissolution case, such as property division, support, and attorney's fees. It is a companion to this project's Petition for Dissolution of Marriage — Information Sheet, which describes the overall dissolution process; this document instead goes into the specific procedural mechanism for severing and trying the marital-status issue early, before the rest of the case is resolved. It is not itself a noticed motion, does not itself request or grant bifurcation, and does not dissolve, terminate, or otherwise change the marital status of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. Only a court order granting bifurcation, followed by a judgment on the status issue, can do that.

clauses.title: The Bifurcation Mechanism: An Early, Separate Trial on Marital Status
clauses.body: California Family Code § 2337 addresses a specific procedural mechanism available in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage: upon a noticed motion, the court may sever the issue of the dissolution of the marital status of the parties and grant an early and separate trial on that issue alone, apart from the other issues in the case. The statute's own language is permissive — the court "may" sever the status issue — meaning the decision whether to grant a request for bifurcation is committed to the court's discretion rather than being automatic upon a party's request. By its own terms, § 2337 is framed as applying in "a proceeding for dissolution of marriage." A judgment of legal separation does not itself terminate marital status (the parties remain married after a legal separation judgment), so this early-severance-of-status mechanism is specific to the dissolution process rather than to the separate legal-separation process described in this project's Petition for Legal Separation — Information Sheet.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific California procedural mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or dissolution, and not a claim about whether a court would grant bifurcation in any particular case. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 2337(a)); no additional independent source was located for the core grant of authority itself (the practical-effect clause elsewhere in this document separately verifies related points using two independent California Court of Appeal decisions). The observation that a proceeding for legal separation does not terminate marital status is drawn from this corpus's own prior research on the legal-separation and dissolution statutes generally (reflected in this project's existing Family Law documents), not from a fresh, independently re-fetched quote captured specifically for this clause; it is offered here only to explain why § 2337 is described as a dissolution-specific mechanism, not as a full restatement of legal-separation law.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the discretionary noticed-motion mechanism for an early, separate trial on marital status
citations.quote: In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, the court, upon noticed motion, may sever and grant an early and separate trial on the issue of the dissolution of the status of the marriage apart from other issues.

clauses.title: Preliminary Declaration of Disclosure Must Accompany the Motion
clauses.body: When a party files the noticed motion for bifurcation of marital status described elsewhere in this document, California law requires that a preliminary declaration of disclosure — together with a completed schedule of assets and debts — be served on the nonmoving party along with that motion. This requirement has two statutory exceptions: it does not apply if the preliminary declaration of disclosure has already been served previously, and it does not apply if the parties have stipulated in writing to defer service of the preliminary declaration of disclosure until a later time. This ties the bifurcation motion procedurally to California's general financial-disclosure framework in dissolution proceedings, rather than allowing the marital-status issue to be severed and tried before the parties have exchanged at least preliminary financial information (unless they have agreed in writing to defer it).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific California procedural requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or dissolution, and not a claim about whether any specific document filed in a specific case satisfies this requirement. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 2337(b)); no additional independent source was located for it. This clause does not describe the broader preliminary-declaration-of-disclosure requirements that apply to dissolution proceedings generally (what the schedule of assets and debts must contain, the separate final declaration of disclosure, or the consequences of nondisclosure) — it addresses only the specific timing rule tying that disclosure to a § 2337 bifurcation motion, not the general disclosure statutes themselves, which were not independently re-verified for this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the preliminary declaration of disclosure requirement and its two exceptions
citations.quote: A preliminary declaration of disclosure with a completed schedule of assets and debts shall be served on the nonmoving party with the noticed motion unless it has been served previously, or unless the parties stipulate in writing to defer service of the preliminary declaration of disclosure until a later time.

clauses.title: Conditions a Court May Impose: Indemnification for Insurance, Tax, and Retirement/Survivor Benefit Consequences
clauses.body: In granting a severance of the marital-status issue, California Family Code § 2337(c) authorizes — but does not require — the court to impose on the moving party any of a specific list of statutory conditions, and provides that an order imposing any of these conditions continues to bind that party's estate if the party dies. Among the conditions the statute lists: a party may be required to indemnify and hold the other party harmless for taxes, reassessments, interest, and penalties that would not have been payable had the parties still been married when the community estate was divided; to maintain the other party's and any minor children's existing health and medical insurance coverage (or provide comparable substitute coverage, or otherwise demonstrate the ability to pay for care that coverage would have covered) until judgment has been entered on all remaining issues and has become final; to indemnify the other party against loss of retirement, survivor, or deferred-compensation benefits — or associated elections or options — that the other party would have been entitled to as the spouse or surviving spouse of the party; and to indemnify the other party against loss of social security survivor benefits or elections the other party would have been entitled to as the surviving spouse of the party. Separately, § 2337(g) provides that if the party dies after entry of the judgment granting dissolution of marital status, any obligation imposed under this section remains enforceable against any asset — including its proceeds — against which the obligation would have been enforceable before the party's death.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific California procedural mechanism — not a claim about whether a court would impose any of these conditions in a specific case. All five citations in this clause are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2337(c) and (g)), not independent sources of one another; they are quoted together because they state five distinct rules within one integrated conditions-and-enforcement scheme. Family Code § 2337(c) lists ten numbered categories of conditions in total; this clause describes only the indemnification-style conditions in paragraphs (1), (2), (5), and (6) (tax consequences, health insurance, retirement/survivor/deferred-compensation benefits, and social security benefits). It does not describe paragraph (3) (probate homestead rights), paragraph (4) (probate family allowance rights), paragraph (7) (beneficiary-designation orders for certain nonprobate transfers under the Probate Code), or paragraph (8) (orders concerning IRA distribution deferral) — those paragraphs were fetched as part of the same primary-source text but are not restated or quoted here. The security-interest and bond-related conditions in paragraph (9), and the general catchall in paragraph (10), are addressed in a separate clause of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's discretionary authority to impose conditions, binding on the party's estate
citations.quote: The court may impose upon a party any of the following conditions on granting a severance of the issue of the dissolution of the status of the marriage, and in case of that party’s death, an order of any of the following conditions continues to be binding upon that party’s estate:

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the tax-consequence indemnification condition
citations.quote: The party shall indemnify and hold the other party harmless from any taxes, reassessments, interest, and penalties payable by the other party in connection with the division of the community estate that would not have been payable if the parties were still married at the time the division was made.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the health and medical insurance coverage condition
citations.quote: Until judgment has been entered on all remaining issues and has become final, the party shall maintain all existing health and medical insurance coverage for the other party and any minor children as named dependents, so long as the party is eligible to do so.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the retirement, survivor, and deferred-compensation benefits indemnification condition
citations.quote: Until judgment has been entered on all remaining issues and has become final, the party shall indemnify and hold the other party harmless from any adverse consequences to the other party if the bifurcation results in the loss of the other party’s rights with respect to any retirement, survivor, or deferred compensation benefits under any plan, fund, or arrangement, or to any elections or options associated therewith, to the extent that the other party would have been entitled to those benefits or elections as the spouse or surviving spouse of the party.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: post-death enforceability of conditions imposed under this section
citations.quote: If the party dies after the entry of judgment granting a dissolution of marriage, any obligation imposed by this section shall be enforceable against any asset, including the proceeds thereof, against which these obligations would have been enforceable prior to the person’s death.

clauses.title: Conditions a Court May Impose: Security Interests, Bonds, and Other Undertakings
clauses.body: Beyond the indemnification obligations described elsewhere in this document, California Family Code § 2337(c)(9) separately authorizes the court, upon a showing that circumstances exist that would place a substantial burden on enforcing either party's community property rights — or would eliminate the surviving party's ability to enforce those rights if the other party died before the community property was divided, distributed, or paid as ordered — to order a specific security interest designed to reduce or eliminate the likelihood that a postmortem enforcement proceeding would be ineffective or unduly burdensome to the surviving party. The statute lists, among the forms such an order may take, an order that the party provide an undertaking (a bond), and an order to provide a security interest by Qualified Domestic Relations Order from that party's share of a retirement plan or plans. Separately, § 2337(c)(10) allows the court to impose, as a condition of severance, any other condition the court determines is just and equitable — a catchall beyond the specifically enumerated conditions in the rest of the subdivision.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific California procedural mechanism — not a claim about whether a court would order a bond or other security interest in a specific case. All four citations in this clause are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2337(c)(9)-(10)), not independent sources of one another. Paragraph (9) itself lists several additional forms of order this document does not separately quote (for example, an order for the creation of a trust, or other reasonably necessary arrangements), and cross-references its own exceptions for certain nonprobate transfers not created by either party, irrevocable trusts, and similar circumstances (§ 2337(c)(9)(B)) that this clause does not restate.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(9) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the showing required, and the court's authority to order a specific security interest
citations.quote: Upon a showing that circumstances exist that would place a substantial burden of enforcement upon either party’s community property rights or would eliminate the ability of the surviving party to enforce his or her community property rights if the other party died before the division and distribution or compliance with any court-ordered payment of any community property interest therein, including, but not limited to, a situation in which preemption under federal law applies to an asset of a party, or purchase by a bona fide purchaser has occurred, the court may order a specific security interest designed to reduce or eliminate the likelihood that a postmortem enforcement proceeding would be ineffective or unduly burdensome to the surviving party.

citations.cite: an order that the party provide an undertaking (a bond)
citations.quote: An order that the party provide an undertaking.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(9)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a security interest by Qualified Domestic Relations Order
citations.quote: An order to provide a security interest by Qualified Domestic Relations Order from that party’s share of a retirement plan or plans.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(c)(10) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the general catchall condition
citations.quote: Any other condition the court determines is just and equitable.

clauses.title: Mandatory Pre-Judgment Steps for Retirement Plans
clauses.body: Unlike the discretionary conditions described elsewhere in this document, California Family Code § 2337(d) imposes mandatory steps tied specifically to retirement and pension plans that must occur prior to, or simultaneously with, entry of judgment granting dissolution of the status of the marriage. First, the party's retirement or pension plan must be joined as a party to the dissolution proceeding, unless joinder is precluded or made unnecessary by Title 1 of the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) or other applicable law. Second, to preserve each spouse's claims in all retirement plan benefits, the court must enter — for each retirement plan in which either party is a participant, in connection with the status judgment — one of three things: an order under Family Code § 2610 disposing of each party's interest in the retirement plan benefits, including survivor and death benefits; an interim order preserving the nonemployee party's right to those benefits, including survivor and death benefits, pending entry of judgment on the remaining issues; or a specified statutory attachment to the status judgment that provisionally awards each party a one-half interest in benefits accrued during the marriage and continues the parties' treatment as married for survivor-benefit purposes to that extent, pending further order. Family Code § 2337(e) further requires the moving party to promptly serve a copy of any such order, interim order, or attachment, together with a copy of the status judgment, on the retirement or pension plan administrator.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific California procedural mechanism — not a claim about whether any specific retirement plan would in fact be joined, or which of the three protective mechanisms a court would select, in a specific case. All citations in this clause are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2337(d)-(e)), not independent sources of one another. This clause does not independently verify the substantive content of the cross-referenced Family Code § 2610 (governing orders dividing retirement plan benefits) — it is cited here only as the first of three named options under § 2337(d)(2), not re-verified in its own right. The statutory attachment language quoted in part is a fixed, capitalized form of words the statute itself prescribes for use in the judgment; this clause paraphrases its general effect rather than reproducing it in full.

citations.cite: the timing requirement for retirement-plan-related steps
citations.quote: Prior to, or simultaneously with, entry of judgment granting dissolution of the status of the marriage, all of the following shall occur:

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: mandatory joinder of the retirement or pension plan
citations.quote: The party’s retirement or pension plan shall be joined as a party to the proceeding for dissolution, unless joinder is precluded or made unnecessary by Title 1 of the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (29 U.S.C. Sec. 1001 et seq.), as amended (ERISA), or any other applicable law.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the requirement to enter one of three protective orders for each retirement plan
citations.quote: To preserve the claims of each spouse in all retirement plan benefits upon entry of judgment granting a dissolution of the status of the marriage, the court shall enter one of the following in connection with the judgment for each retirement plan in which either party is a participant:

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(d)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the interim-order option preserving retirement plan benefits
citations.quote: An interim order preserving the nonemployee party’s right to retirement plan benefits, including survivor and death benefits, pending entry of judgment on all remaining issues.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the moving party's obligation to serve the retirement plan administrator
citations.quote: The moving party shall promptly serve a copy of any order, interim order, or attachment entered pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (d), and a copy of the judgment granting a dissolution of the status of the marriage, on the retirement or pension plan administrator.

clauses.title: Effect on Marital Status: Reserved Jurisdiction and the End of the Marriage
clauses.body: California Family Code § 2337(f) requires that a judgment granting dissolution of the status of the marriage expressly reserve jurisdiction for later determination of all other pending issues in the case — meaning a status judgment under this section does not itself resolve property division, support, attorney's fees, or other remaining issues; those continue to be litigated in the same proceeding after the status judgment is entered. California appellate decisions describe the practical effect of such a judgment on the parties themselves. In In re Marriage of Turfe (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 1118, the Court of Appeal described a husband's status-only dissolution judgment as one that terminated his marriage to his wife and reserved jurisdiction over all other issues, and separately noted that a "status only" dissolution judgment is immediately appealable as a final judgment on the issue of dissolution of marital status, citing Family Code § 2337(a). And in In re Marriage of Fink (1976) 54 Cal.App.3d 357 — the decision that established the bifurcated-trial procedure the Legislature later codified in § 2337 — the Court of Appeal observed that, because the wife's appeal of a status-only judgment remained pending, the husband had been unable to secure his final decree and freedom to remarry, reflecting that once such a judgment becomes final, the party regains the freedom to remarry notwithstanding that the remaining issues in the case are still being litigated.
clauses.gap: These are two genuinely independent California Court of Appeal decisions (Turfe, decided in 2018 by California's Second Appellate District, and Fink, decided in 1976 by California's Second Appellate District in an earlier era of that same court, applying the predecessor Family Law Act) — not two subsections of the same statute — so they are independent of one another and of the statutory citation in this clause. Fink predates the 1994 recodification that created the current Family Code and today's § 2337; it was decided under the former Civil Code framework and used the term "final decree" rather than today's "judgment," but the current Turfe opinion cites Fink for the closely related proposition that a status-only judgment is immediately appealable under current § 2337(a), which is why it is treated here as continuing, on-point authority. Neither case, and no statutory text located in this document's research, states as an abstract, generally applicable rule that marital status is restored, or that a party becomes free to remarry, at any specific, universally applicable moment (for example, immediately upon the trial court's ruling versus only once that ruling becomes final and unappealable); Fink's "freedom to remarry" statement arises from the specific procedural posture of that case — a pending appeal delaying finality — rather than from a freestanding statutory holding, and Family Code § 2337 itself never uses the word "remarry." This clause's statutory citation (§ 2337(f)) concerns only the reserved-jurisdiction requirement; the remarriage point rests on these two cases rather than on statutory text.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2337(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the requirement that a status judgment expressly reserve jurisdiction over remaining issues
citations.quote: A judgment granting a dissolution of the status of the marriage shall expressly reserve jurisdiction for later determination of all other pending issues.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Turfe (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 1118 (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: the practical effect of a status-only dissolution judgment on the parties
citations.quote: Robert Turfe (husband) appeals a judgment of dissolution of marriage as to status only. The judgment terminated his marriage to Summer Turfe (wife) and reserved jurisdiction over all other issues.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Turfe (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 1118, footnote 1 (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: confirming a status-only judgment is immediately appealable under Family Code § 2337(a)
citations.quote: A "status only" dissolution judgment is immediately appealable as a final judgment on the issue of dissolution of marital status. (Fam. Code, § 2337, subd. (a) [early and separate trial on dissolution of marital status]

citations.case: In re Marriage of Fink (1976) 54 Cal.App.3d 357, 367 (opinion text via CourtListener)
citations.cite: freedom to remarry following a final status judgment
citations.quote: In the case at bench, due to wife’s appeal, husband has been unable to secure his final decree and freedom to remarry.

clauses.title: Purpose
clauses.body: {{companyName}} maintains this California Workplace Smoking Prohibition Information Sheet to describe the general prohibition on smoking of tobacco products in enclosed places of employment under California Labor Code section 6404.5, the statute's own defined terms, its listed exceptions, and its enforcement mechanism, for the information of employees including {{employeeName}}. This information sheet states facts about California law; it does not determine whether any particular space, area, or situation at {{companyName}} is or is not covered by section 6404.5, and it is not a statement that {{companyName}}'s current smoking policy does or does not comply with the statute.

clauses.title: The General Prohibition
clauses.body: California Labor Code section 6404.5, subdivision (c) provides that "[a]n employer or owner-operator of an owner-operated business shall not knowingly or intentionally permit, and a person shall not engage in, the smoking of tobacco products at a place of employment or in an enclosed space." The Legislature's stated intent in enacting the statute was "to prohibit the smoking of tobacco products in all (100 percent of) enclosed places of employment in this state, as covered by this section, thereby eliminating the need of local governments to enact workplace smoking restrictions within their respective jurisdictions."
clauses.gap: Both quotations come from Cal. Labor Code section 6404.5 -- the subdivision (a) legislative-intent quote and the subdivision (c) operative prohibition quote are two subdivisions of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another. The statutory text was fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two separate curl requests with different User-Agent strings, both returning HTTP 200 with byte-identical (whitespace-normalized) content; each quoted passage was confirmed programmatically as an exact, whitespace-normalized substring of that fetched text. This clause states the general rule; it does not state what counts as an "enclosed space" or a "place of employment" (addressed in the following clauses), nor whether any specific location is covered.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 6404.5, subd. (a)
citations.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature in enacting this section to prohibit the smoking of tobacco products in all (100 percent of) enclosed places of employment in this state, as covered by this section, thereby eliminating the need of local governments to enact workplace smoking restrictions within their respective jurisdictions.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 6404.5(c)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 6404.5, subd. (c)
citations.quote: An employer or owner-operator of an owner-operated business shall not knowingly or intentionally permit, and a person shall not engage in, the smoking of tobacco products at a place of employment or in an enclosed space.

clauses.title: "Enclosed Space" and "Owner-Operated Business" Defined
clauses.body: Labor Code section 6404.5, subdivision (b) provides that "'[e]nclosed space' includes covered parking lots, lobbies, lounges, waiting areas, elevators, stairwells, and restrooms that are a structural part of the building and not specifically defined in subdivision (e)." The same subdivision defines an "owner-operated business" as "a business having no employees, independent contractors, or volunteers, in which the owner-operator of the business is the only worker."
clauses.gap: Both defined terms are quoted from the same subdivision, section 6404.5(b), and are not independent of one another as sources, though they define two distinct terms used elsewhere in the statute. The statutory text was fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two separate curl requests with different User-Agent strings, both returning HTTP 200 with byte-identical (whitespace-normalized) content; the quoted passages were confirmed programmatically as exact, whitespace-normalized substrings of that fetched text. The statute's definition of "enclosed space" is an inclusive, non-exhaustive list (it uses "includes") rather than a closed, exhaustive definition, and it expressly excludes areas "specifically defined in subdivision (e)" -- the statute's list of places that do not count as a "place of employment" at all, covered in a separate clause below. This clause does not state whether any particular room, area, or structure at any specific workplace meets this definition.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 6404.5, subd. (b)
citations.quote: “Enclosed space” includes covered parking lots, lobbies, lounges, waiting areas, elevators, stairwells, and restrooms that are a structural part of the building and not specifically defined in subdivision (e).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 6404.5(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 6404.5, subd. (b)

clauses.title: Statutory Exceptions -- What Is Not a "Place of Employment"
clauses.body: Labor Code section 6404.5, subdivision (e) provides that "[f]or purposes of this section, 'place of employment' does not include any of the following:" (1) "Retail or wholesale tobacco shops and private smokers' lounges"; (2) "Cabs of motortrucks, as defined in Section 410 of the Vehicle Code, or truck tractors, as defined in Section 655 of the Vehicle Code, if nonsmoking employees are not present"; (3) "Theatrical production sites, if smoking is an integral part of the story in the theatrical production"; (4) "Medical research or treatment sites, if smoking is integral to the research and treatment being conducted"; (5) "Private residences, except for private residences licensed as family day care homes where smoking is prohibited pursuant to Section 1596.795 of the Health and Safety Code"; and (6) "Patient smoking areas in long-term health care facilities, as defined in Section 1418 of the Health and Safety Code."
clauses.gap: All six quoted items are paragraphs of the same subdivision, section 6404.5(e), and are not independent of one another as sources, though each defines a separately numbered, distinct exclusion. The statutory text was fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two separate curl requests with different User-Agent strings, both returning HTTP 200 with byte-identical (whitespace-normalized) content; each quoted item was confirmed programmatically as an exact, whitespace-normalized substring of that fetched text. This is the CURRENT list under the statute as last amended (Stats. 2023, Ch. 182, Sec. 3, effective January 1, 2024, per the statute's own end-of-section history note); it does not include exemptions that may have existed under earlier, superseded versions of this section, and this clause does not attempt to summarize the statute's amendment history beyond noting the current effective date. This clause states what the statute itself excludes from the definition of "place of employment"; it does not state whether any specific business, room, or vehicle at any specific workplace falls within one of these exclusions -- for example, none of the retail-tobacco-shop, private-residence, hotel, or small-business exclusions found in earlier versions of this law necessarily still exist in the current text quoted above, and this clause does not represent that any exclusion beyond the six quoted here currently exists.

clauses.title: Employer Steps Regarding Nonemployee Smokers
clauses.body: Labor Code section 6404.5, subdivision (d) provides that an employer or owner-operator "who permits any nonemployee access to their place of employment or owner-operated business on a regular basis has not acted knowingly or intentionally in violation of this section if the employer or owner-operator has taken the following reasonable steps to prevent smoking by a nonemployee": posting signs -- where smoking is prohibited throughout the building, "a sign stating 'No smoking' shall be posted at each entrance," and where smoking is permitted in designated areas, "a sign stating 'Smoking is prohibited except in designated areas' shall be posted at each entrance" -- and having "requested, when appropriate, that a nonemployee who is smoking refrain from smoking in the enclosed workplace or owner-operated business."
clauses.gap: All quoted language comes from the same subdivision, section 6404.5(d), and is not independent of one another as a source. The statutory text was fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two separate curl requests with different User-Agent strings, both returning HTTP 200 with byte-identical (whitespace-normalized) content; the quoted passages were confirmed programmatically as exact, whitespace-normalized substrings of that fetched text. Subdivision (d) describes what the statute treats as "reasonable steps" for purposes of a safe harbor against a knowing-or-intentional violation involving a nonemployee's smoking -- it does not itself impose a freestanding, independent posting requirement outside that context, and this clause does not state that any specific set of signage or requests does or does not satisfy the statute for any particular workplace. The subdivision also states that "reasonable steps" does not include physically ejecting a nonemployee or requiring a request under circumstances risking physical harm to the employer, an employee, or the owner-operator; this clause summarizes but does not separately quote that limiting language.

(B) Where smoking is permitted in designated areas of the building or structure, a sign stating “Smoking is prohibited except in designated areas” shall be posted at each entrance to the building or structure.

clauses.title: Penalty and Enforcement
clauses.body: Labor Code section 6404.5, subdivision (i) provides that "[a] violation of the prohibition set forth in subdivision (c) is an infraction, punishable by a fine not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100) for a first violation, two hundred dollars ($200) for a second violation within one year, and five hundred dollars ($500) for a third and for each subsequent violation within one year," and that this "subdivision shall be enforced by local law enforcement agencies, including, but not limited to, local health departments, as determined by the local governing body." Subdivision (j) separately provides that, "[n]otwithstanding Section 6309, the division is not required to respond to any complaint regarding the smoking of tobacco products in an enclosed space at a place of employment, unless the employer has been found guilty pursuant to subdivision (i) of a third violation of subdivision (c) within the previous year."
clauses.gap: Both quoted subdivisions, (i) and (j), come from the same statutory section, section 6404.5, and are not independent of one another as sources, though they address two distinct points: the penalty amount and enforcing body, and a separate limit on the Division of Occupational Safety and Health's ("the division"'s) own duty to respond to complaints. The statutory text was fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two separate curl requests with different User-Agent strings, both returning HTTP 200 with byte-identical (whitespace-normalized) content; the quoted passages were confirmed programmatically as exact, whitespace-normalized substrings of that fetched text. This clause does not independently verify the cross-referenced Labor Code section 6309 (defining "the division"'s general complaint-response duty) -- that section was not separately fetched this session -- and states only what section 6404.5 itself says about the exception to it. This clause does not state that any particular local agency will or will not act on any specific report.

This subdivision shall be enforced by local law enforcement agencies, including, but not limited to, local health departments, as determined by the local governing body.

clauses.title: Electronic Smoking Devices and Vaping
clauses.body: Labor Code section 6404.5 does not define "smoking" or "tobacco product" on its own terms; instead, subdivision (l) provides that, "[f]or purposes of this section, 'smoking' has the same meaning as in subdivision (c) of Section 22950.5 of the Business and Professions Code," and subdivision (m) provides that "'tobacco product' means a product or device as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 22950.5" of that code. Business and Professions Code section 22950.5, subdivision (c) defines "smoking" to mean "inhaling, exhaling, burning, or carrying any lighted or heated cigar, cigarette, or pipe, or any other lighted or heated tobacco or plant product intended for inhalation, whether natural or synthetic, in any manner or in any form," and further provides that "'[s]moking' includes the use of an electronic smoking device that creates an aerosol or vapor, in any manner or in any form, or the use of any oral smoking device for the purpose of circumventing the prohibition of smoking." Subdivision (d) of that same section defines "tobacco product" to include "[a]n electronic device that delivers nicotine or other vaporized liquids to the person inhaling from the device, including, but not limited to, an electronic cigarette, cigar, pipe, or hookah."
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two genuinely distinct, independently numbered code sections: Labor Code section 6404.5 (subdivisions (l) and (m), which are two subdivisions of the same section and not independent of each other) and Business and Professions Code section 22950.5 (subdivisions (c) and (d), likewise two subdivisions of the same section and not independent of each other). The Labor Code and Business and Professions Code sections are independent of one another as sources. All statutory text was fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two separate curl requests with different User-Agent strings for each code section, all four returning HTTP 200 with byte-identical (whitespace-normalized) content; every quoted passage was confirmed programmatically as an exact, whitespace-normalized substring of the fetched text. Business and Professions Code section 22950.5 is itself part of a different statutory scheme (the Stop Tobacco Access to Kids Enforcement Act) that Labor Code section 6404.5 incorporates only by cross-reference for the meaning of these two specific terms; this clause does not address any other part of that Act. The section 22950.5 text fetched carries its own amendment history note (Stats. 2016, 2nd Ex. Sess., Ch. 7, Sec. 1, effective June 9, 2016), consistent with California's 2016 expansion of its smoking laws to cover electronic cigarettes.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Data Broker Registration Act Information Sheet describes California's Data Broker Registration Act, Civil Code § 1798.99.80 et seq., as amended by the Delete Act (Stats. 2023, Ch. 709 (SB 362)) and by Stats. 2025, Ch. 466 (SB 361). It is prepared in connection with {{businessName}}'s data practices and is intended as background alongside, not a substitute for, {{businessName}}'s separate California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA/CPRA) materials. The Data Broker Registration Act is a distinct, additional statutory scheme from the CCPA: the CCPA generally governs a covered business's collection, use, and sale of personal information regardless of the business's relationship to the consumer, while the Data Broker Registration Act imposes separate annual registration, fee, and deletion-platform obligations that apply specifically to a "data broker" as that term is defined in Civil Code § 1798.99.80(c) — a category of business defined, in part, by the absence of a direct relationship with the consumer whose information it collects and sells. A business can be subject to the CCPA without meeting the Data Broker Registration Act's narrower "data broker" definition, and a business that does meet that definition is subject to both statutory schemes at once. Questions about {{businessName}}'s data collection and disclosure practices may be directed as follows: {{contactMethod}}.

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of "Data Broker," and Its Exemptions
clauses.body: California's Data Broker Registration Act defines "data broker" to mean a business that knowingly collects and sells to third parties the personal information of a consumer with whom the business does not have a direct relationship. The absence of a direct relationship between the business and the consumer is the element that separates a "data broker" under this Act from a business more generally subject to the CCPA, which is not limited to businesses lacking a direct consumer relationship. The statute defines "data broker" to exclude four categories of entities, each only to the extent the entity is actually covered by the referenced other law: (1) an entity to the extent it is covered by the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act; (2) an entity to the extent it is covered by the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and its implementing regulations; (3) an entity to the extent it is covered by California's Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act; and (4) an entity, or a business associate of a covered entity, to the extent its processing of personal information is exempt under Civil Code § 1798.146 (the CCPA's own exemption for entities and information governed by the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act or HIPAA).
clauses.gap: Both citations below are from the same statutory subsection, Civil Code § 1798.99.80(c) — the definition's opening sentence and its four-item exclusion list — so they are not independent of one another; both are quoted because the exclusions cannot be stated accurately without the definition they qualify. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Data Broker Registration Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business. This clause states the statutory definition and exemption categories; it does not determine whether any specific business (i) knowingly collects and sells personal information, (ii) has or lacks a "direct relationship" with the consumers whose information it sells, or (iii) actually falls within one of the four exemption categories for its own operations — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make. Civil Code § 1798.99.80(a) also incorporates the CCPA's own definitions from Section 1798.140 (for terms such as "business," "sell," "personal information," and "consumer") except where this title specifies otherwise; those incorporated CCPA definitions were not independently re-quoted here and are addressed in this corpus's separate CCPA documents. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.cite: Data Broker Registration Act, definition of "data broker"
citations.quote: (c) “Data broker” means a business that knowingly collects and sells to third parties the personal information of a consumer with whom the business does not have a direct relationship. “Data broker” does not include any of the following:

(2) An entity to the extent that it is covered by the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (Public Law 106-102) and implementing regulations. (3) An entity to the extent that it is covered by the Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act (Article 6.6 (commencing with Section 791) of Chapter 1 of Part 2 of Division 1 of the Insurance Code). (4) An entity, or a business associate of a covered entity, to the extent their processing of personal information is exempt under Section 1798.146. For purposes of this paragraph, “business associate” and “covered entity” have the same meanings as defined in Section 1798.146.

clauses.title: Annual Registration with the California Privacy Protection Agency, and the Registration Fee
clauses.body: Under the current text of the Data Broker Registration Act, a business that meets the statutory definition of "data broker" for a given year must register with the California Privacy Protection Agency ("CPPA") on or before January 31 of the following year. The CPPA, not the California Attorney General, is the agency currently named in the statute as the registering authority; the CPPA also administers the "Data Brokers' Registry Fund" created in the State Treasury, into which registration fees, penalties, and other amounts collected under this title are deposited. As part of registering, a data broker must pay a registration fee, in an amount the CPPA determines, that may not exceed the reasonable costs of establishing and maintaining the CPPA's public data-broker informational website and the reasonable costs of establishing, maintaining, and providing access to the accessible deletion mechanism described elsewhere in this title.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.99.82 — subdivision (a) (the registration deadline and the CPPA as registering authority) and subdivision (b), paragraph (1) (the fee requirement) — so they are not independent of one another; both are quoted because the fee obligation cannot be stated accurately apart from the registration duty it attaches to. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Data Broker Registration Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business. The currently codified text names the California Privacy Protection Agency, not the Attorney General, as the registering and fee-setting authority; this document did not independently verify or trace the legislative history of that change from the statute's original 2019 enactment (which predates the Agency's creation) through the Delete Act's 2023 amendments — a reader interested in that history should consult the amendment notes on the statute's own text or the bill history for SB 362, which are outside the scope of what this clause verifies. This clause does not state the specific dollar amount of any registration fee the CPPA has actually set, since the statute leaves that amount to the Agency's own determination rather than fixing it in the statutory text itself, and this document did not independently verify a current fee schedule. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

citations.quote: (a) On or before January 31 following each year in which a business meets the definition of data broker as provided in this title, the business shall register with the California Privacy Protection Agency pursuant to the requirements of this section.

Registration fees shall be deposited in the Data Brokers’ Registry Fund, created within the State Treasury pursuant to Section 1798.99.81, and used for the purposes outlined in this paragraph.

clauses.title: Information a Data Broker's Registration Must Include
clauses.body: Beyond paying the registration fee, the Data Broker Registration Act requires a registering data broker to provide the CPPA with specific information as part of registration, including: the data broker's name and its primary physical, email, and internet website addresses; metrics the data broker separately compiles about consumer requests it receives and how it responds to them; whether it collects personal information of minors; whether it collects specific categories of sensitive information such as government-issued identification numbers, biometric data, precise geolocation, citizenship or immigration status, union membership, sexual orientation, gender identity, or reproductive health care data; whether it has shared or sold consumer data to a foreign actor, the federal government, other state governments, law enforcement, or a developer of a generative artificial intelligence system or model in the past year; a link to a webpage, free of dark patterns, describing how consumers may exercise their existing CCPA rights to delete, correct, know, opt out of sale or sharing, and limit use of sensitive personal information; and whether and to what extent the data broker or its subsidiaries are also regulated under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, California's Insurance Information and Privacy Protection Act, or federal/state medical-information confidentiality laws (HIPAA and the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act).
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the entirety of Civil Code § 1798.99.82(b)(2), a single statutory paragraph with subparagraphs (A) through (X), as one integrated list; because the entire quotation comes from one paragraph, no cross-subsection independence disclosure beyond that is required for this clause's single citation. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Data Broker Registration Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business. This clause does not determine what information a specific data broker must actually disclose in its own registration, nor does it verify how the CPPA's public-facing registry website in fact displays or withholds any of this information (Section 1798.99.84 separately withholds subparagraphs (D), (G), and (T) from public display, which this document's registration-content clause does not itself restate). No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

(B) The metrics compiled pursuant to paragraphs (1) and (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 1798.99.85. (C) Whether the data broker collects the personal information of minors. (F) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ drivers’ license number, California identification card number, tax identification number, social security number, passport number, military identification number, or other unique identification number issued on a government document commonly used to verify the identity of a specific individual. (G) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ mobile advertising identification numbers, connected television identification numbers, or vehicle identification numbers (VIN). (H) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ citizenship data, including immigration status. (I) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ union membership status. (J) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ sexual orientation status. (K) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ gender identity and gender expression data. (L) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ biometric data. (M) Whether the data broker collects consumers’ precise geolocation. clauses.title: The Delete Request and Opt-out Platform ("DROP"), and Its Phased Compliance Deadlines
clauses.body: The Delete Act's central new mechanism, commonly referred to as "DROP" (the Delete Request and Opt-out Platform), is an accessible deletion mechanism the statute directs the CPPA to establish. The statute set January 1, 2026, as the deadline for the CPPA to establish this mechanism. As designed, the mechanism must let a consumer submit a single, verifiable request that every registered data broker holding that consumer's personal information delete it, while also allowing the consumer to selectively exclude specific data brokers from that single request, and to request an alteration of a prior request after at least 45 days have passed. Separately, the statute sets August 1, 2026, as the date beginning which a registered data broker must access the mechanism at least once every 45 days and, within 45 days of receiving a deletion request through it, process and complete the deletion of the requesting consumer's personal information (subject to statutory exceptions the mechanism itself administers). As of the September 4, 2026 date of this information sheet's preparation, both the January 1, 2026 platform-establishment deadline and the August 1, 2026 data-broker compliance-start deadline set out in the current statutory text have already passed.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.99.86 — subdivision (a) (the CPPA's platform-establishment deadline and the single-request/selective-exclusion design requirements) and subdivision (c), paragraph (1) (the data broker's own compliance-start deadline and 45-day processing duty) — so they are not independent of one another; both are quoted because a data broker's compliance deadline cannot be stated accurately apart from the platform-establishment deadline it follows. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Delete Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business, and not a claim about whether DROP was actually operational, on schedule, or accepting requests by either statutory date; this document verifies only the text of the legal deadlines the statute currently sets, not the CPPA's or any data broker's actual, on-the-ground implementation status as of any date, which is a factual question outside what a statutory-text check can confirm. This clause does not restate the statute's separate, later-phased third-party audit requirement for data brokers, which the statute's text (§ 1798.99.86(e)(1)) sets beginning January 1, 2028, and every three years thereafter — that requirement was independently fetched and confirmed in the same section but is not detailed further in this clause's body. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

clauses.title: Administrative Fines for Failing to Register or Failing to Comply with DROP
clauses.body: The Data Broker Registration Act's current text provides two separate administrative fine schemes, both enforced by the California Privacy Protection Agency through an administrative action. First, a data broker that fails to register as the statute requires is liable for an administrative fine of $200 for each day it fails to register, plus an amount equal to the registration fees that were due during the period of nonregistration, plus the CPPA's reasonable investigation and administration expenses. Second, and separately, a data broker required to register that fails to comply with the DROP-related deletion requirements of Civil Code § 1798.99.86 is liable for an administrative fine of $200 for each deletion request, for each day the data broker fails to delete the information as that section requires, plus the CPPA's reasonable investigation and administration expenses. All penalties, fines, fees, and expenses recovered under either scheme are deposited into the Data Brokers' Registry Fund.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.99.82 — subdivision (c) (the failure-to-register fine) and subdivision (d) (the failure-to-comply-with-DROP fine) — so they are not independent of one another; both are quoted together because they are the statute's two parallel administrative-fine schemes under the same enforcement section. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Data Broker Registration Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business, and not a claim that any specific business has, or has not, incurred any fine described here. This clause does not address any other enforcement mechanism that might separately apply to conduct also covered by the general CCPA (such as CCPA-specific Attorney General or CPPA enforcement actions), which this document's companion CCPA documents address separately, nor does it verify whether the CPPA has actually brought any administrative action of the kind described. No case law was checked on this provision; the statute's own text is unambiguous, so it stands as the source here without a corroborating case.

[This information sheet is prepared as background concerning California's Data Broker Registration Act, Civil Code § 1798.99.80 et seq. It does not itself register {{businessName}} with the California Privacy Protection Agency, does not determine whether {{businessName}} meets the statutory definition of "data broker," and does not itself satisfy any deadline, deletion, or compliance obligation the statute describes; only an actual registration filed with, and deletion requests actually processed through the mechanism established by, the California Privacy Protection Agency can do that.]

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California Labor Code § 1024.5, a statute that restricts whether {{companyName}} may use a consumer credit report to make an employment decision about {{employeeName}} regarding the position of {{jobTitle}} — a different, and more specific, restriction than California's Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act (ICRAA), Civil Code §§ 1786 et seq., addressed elsewhere in this corpus. ICRAA governs the disclosure, authorization, agency-certification, and adverse-action mechanics an employer must follow when it seeks to obtain an investigative consumer report — a report on a person's character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living. Labor Code § 1024.5 addresses a different, threshold question that does not turn on any of ICRAA's disclosure steps: whether an employer may use an ordinary credit-based consumer credit report — a report concerning a person's credit worthiness, credit standing, or credit capacity — to make most employment decisions at all, regardless of what disclosure or authorization the employer has obtained, unless the position at issue falls within one of a specific statutory list of exceptions. This document states facts about what § 1024.5 says: its core prohibition, its statutory list of exempted positions, its own definitions, an exclusion it states for certain financial institutions, and how the statute is enforced. It does not determine, and does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}}, whether the position of {{jobTitle}} falls within any exception, whether {{companyName}}'s use of a consumer credit report for that position is lawful, or what either party should do about any particular use of a consumer credit report.

clauses.title: The Core Prohibition: Consumer Credit Reports Restricted to Listed Positions
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 1024.5(a) states that an employer or prospective employer shall not use a consumer credit report for employment purposes unless the position of the person for whom the report is sought falls within one of the categories the statute itself lists. By its own terms, the prohibition is written as a default rule against using a consumer credit report for employment purposes, with the statute's list of categories operating as its own stated exceptions — the statute introduces that list with the phrase "is any of the following," rather than offering the list as illustrative examples.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the statute's opening prohibition; the list of exempted categories the prohibition refers to is addressed in a separate clause below rather than repeated here. The statute does not itself define the word "use," and this document does not address whether obtaining, requesting, or merely possessing a consumer credit report — as distinct from using one to make an employment decision — falls within the prohibition. Only one source is cited for this clause, since it states a single provision's opening sentence rather than combining multiple sources.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1024.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Chapter 3.6 (Employer Use of Consumer Credit Reports), core prohibition
citations.quote: An employer or prospective employer shall not use a consumer credit report for employment purposes unless the position of the person for whom the report is sought is any of the following:

clauses.title: The Statutory List of Exempted Positions
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1024.5(a) lists eight categories of position for which an employer may use a consumer credit report for employment purposes: (1) a managerial position (a term the statute separately defines); (2) a position in the state Department of Justice; (3) that of a sworn peace officer or other law enforcement position; (4) a position for which the information contained in the report is required by law to be disclosed or obtained; (5) a position that involves regular access — for any purpose other than the routine solicitation and processing of credit card applications in a retail establishment — to all three of a single person's bank or credit card account information, Social Security number, and date of birth; (6) a position in which the person is, or would be, a named signatory on the employer's bank or credit card account, authorized to transfer money on the employer's behalf, or authorized to enter into financial contracts on the employer's behalf; (7) a position that involves access to confidential or proprietary information — including a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, process, or trade secret — meeting the statute's own two-part description of independent economic value from secrecy and a reasonable effort to maintain that secrecy; and (8) a position that involves regular access to cash totaling ten thousand dollars ($10,000) or more of the employer, a customer, or client, during the workday.
clauses.gap: This clause states the statutory list as written; it does not determine whether the duties of the position at issue fall within any category, and does not address how a court or agency would apply an undefined term the statute uses — such as "regular access" in categories (5) and (8), or the scope of "confidential or proprietary information" in category (7) beyond the statute's own two-part description. The definition of "managerial position" referenced in category (1) is addressed in a separate clause below rather than repeated here. Only one source is cited, since the entire list comes from a single subdivision of a single statutory section.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1024.5(a)(1)-(8) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Chapter 3.6 (Employer Use of Consumer Credit Reports), list of exempted positions
citations.quote: (1) A managerial position. (2) A position in the state Department of Justice. (3) That of a sworn peace officer or other law enforcement position. (4) A position for which the information contained in the report is required by law to be disclosed or obtained. (5) A position that involves regular access, for any purpose other than the routine solicitation and processing of credit card applications in a retail establishment, to all of the following types of information of any one person: (A) Bank or credit card account information. (B) Social security number. (C) Date of birth. (6) A position in which the person is, or would be, any of the following: (A) A named signatory on the bank or credit card account of the employer. (B) Authorized to transfer money on behalf of the employer. (C) Authorized to enter into financial contracts on behalf of the employer. (7) A position that involves access to confidential or proprietary information, including a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, process or trade secret that (i) derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to, and not being readily ascertainable by proper means by, other persons who may obtain economic value from the disclosure or use of the information, and (ii) is the subject of an effort that is reasonable under the circumstances to maintain secrecy of the information. (8) A position that involves regular access to cash totaling ten thousand dollars ($10,000) or more of the employer, a customer, or client, during the workday.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: "Consumer Credit Report" and "Managerial Position"
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1024.5(c) defines two terms the statute uses. First, "consumer credit report" is defined to have the same meaning given in Civil Code § 1785.3(c) — a definition from California's separate Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act (CCRAA) — except that § 1024.5's own definition excludes a report that both verifies income or employment and does not include credit-related information, such as credit history, credit score, or credit record. Civil Code § 1785.3(c) itself defines "consumer credit report" broadly: any written, oral, or other communication of information by a consumer credit reporting agency bearing on a person's credit worthiness, credit standing, or credit capacity, used or expected to be used (among other listed purposes) as a factor in establishing a person's eligibility for employment purposes. Second, § 1024.5(c) defines "managerial position" — the first category on the exempted-positions list — as an employee covered by the executive exemption set forth in Wage Order 4 of the Industrial Welfare Commission, codified at 8 California Code of Regulations § 11040.
clauses.gap: The Civil Code § 1785.3(c) citation below is not independent corroboration of the Labor Code § 1024.5(c)(1) citation — § 1024.5(c)(1) expressly adopts the Civil Code definition by cross-reference, so the two citations describe the same defined term at its point of origin (Civil Code § 1785.3(c)) and at the statute that adopts it by reference (Labor Code § 1024.5(c)(1)), not two independently corroborating sources. The two Labor Code citations below, § 1024.5(c)(1) and § 1024.5(c)(2), are likewise subdivisions of the same statutory section, not independent sources. This document did not independently fetch or verify the text of Wage Order 4 of the Industrial Welfare Commission or 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 11040 themselves, which § 1024.5(c)(2) cross-references for the "executive exemption" that in turn defines "managerial position" — that regulatory text is not quoted or restated here. Civil Code § 1785.3(c) also lists several categories of report its own text excludes from the CCRAA's "consumer credit report" definition (for example, certain internal-organization communications, and reports based on personal interviews about character, general reputation, personal characteristics, or mode of living) that are not restated in this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1024.5(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Chapter 3.6 (Employer Use of Consumer Credit Reports), definition of "consumer credit report"
citations.quote: (1) “Consumer credit report” has the same meaning as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1785.3 of the Civil Code, but does not include a report that (A) verifies income or employment, and (B) does not include credit-related information, such as credit history, credit score, or credit record.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1024.5(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Chapter 3.6 (Employer Use of Consumer Credit Reports), definition of "managerial position"
citations.quote: (2) “Managerial position” means an employee covered by the executive exemption set forth in subparagraph (1) of paragraph (A) of Section 1 of Wage Order 4 of the Industrial Welfare Commission (8 Cal. Code Regs. 11040).

citations.case: Cal. Civil Code § 1785.3(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act, definition of "consumer credit report"
citations.quote: “Consumer credit report” means any written, oral, or other communication of any information by a consumer credit reporting agency bearing on a consumer’s credit worthiness, credit standing, or credit capacity, which is used or is expected to be used, or collected in whole or in part, for the purpose of serving as a factor in establishing the consumer’s eligibility for: (1) credit to be used primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, or (2) employment purposes, or (3) hiring of a dwelling unit, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1940, or (4) other purposes authorized in Section 1785.11.

clauses.title: Exclusion for Certain Financial Institutions Subject to Federal Privacy Law
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1024.5(b) states that the section does not apply to a person or business subject to 15 U.S.C. §§ 6801-6809 — provisions of the federal Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act — and to state and federal statutes or regulations implementing those sections, if that person or business is subject to compliance oversight by a state or federal regulatory agency with respect to those laws.
clauses.gap: This document did not independently fetch or verify the text of 15 U.S.C. §§ 6801-6809 themselves, nor did it identify which state or federal regulatory agencies exercise the "compliance oversight" the statute refers to, or which categories of person or business are, in fact, subject to that oversight. Only Labor Code § 1024.5(b) itself is cited below; this clause does not identify, and does not determine, whether the employer at issue is a person or business within this exclusion's scope.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1024.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Chapter 3.6 (Employer Use of Consumer Credit Reports), financial-institution exclusion
citations.quote: (b) This section does not apply to a person or business subject to Sections 6801 to 6809, inclusive, of Title 15 of the United States Code and state and federal statutes or regulations implementing those sections if the person or business is subject to compliance oversight by a state or federal regulatory agency with respect to those laws.

clauses.title: Enforcement: No Section-Specific Remedy Stated; General PAGA Mechanism
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1024.5 does not itself state a private right of action, a specific civil penalty, or any other enforcement mechanism for a violation of its terms — unlike, for example, ICRAA's own civil-liability provision addressed in this corpus's ICRAA document. Separately, the Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act of 2004 (PAGA), Labor Code §§ 2698-2699.8, states that any provision of the Labor Code that provides for a civil penalty to be assessed and collected by the state Labor and Workforce Development Agency may, as an alternative, be recovered through a civil action brought by an aggrieved employee on behalf of themselves and other current or former employees, following the procedures the statute specifies. For a Labor Code provision that does not itself specify a civil penalty, Labor Code § 2699(f) establishes a default civil penalty structure: five hundred dollars for a violation where the person does not, at the time of the alleged violation, employ one or more employees, or, where the person does employ one or more employees, one hundred dollars for each aggrieved employee per pay period, subject to exceptions the statute states for certain other, unrelated Labor Code provisions not addressed in this document.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general PAGA enforcement framework as its own text describes it; it does not determine that a court would in fact apply PAGA's default civil penalty to a Labor Code § 1024.5 violation specifically, and no source located in this research discusses PAGA's application to § 1024.5 by name. This document does not address PAGA's separate requirement that an aggrieved employee give notice to the Labor and Workforce Development Agency before filing a civil action (Labor Code § 2699.3), which was not independently fetched or verified here, and it does not address whether a remedy for a § 1024.5 violation might also be available under some other law, such as California's Unfair Competition Law — this document did not research that possibility. The two citations below, Labor Code § 2699(a) and § 2699(f), are both subdivisions of the same statutory section, so they corroborate PAGA's own internal structure rather than serving as two independent sources; neither is independent of Labor Code § 1024.5 either, since § 1024.5's own text says nothing about PAGA — this clause connects the two based on the plain terms of § 2699(f) ("[f]or all provisions of this code except those for which a civil penalty is specifically provided"), not on any source that discusses § 1024.5's enforcement specifically.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2699(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Private Attorneys General Act of 2004, civil-action alternative to agency-collected civil penalties
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, any provision of this code that provides for a civil penalty to be assessed and collected by the Labor and Workforce Development Agency or any of its departments, divisions, commissions, boards, agencies, or employees, for a violation of this code, may, as an alternative, be recovered through a civil action brought by an aggrieved employee on behalf of the employee and other current or former employees against whom a violation of the same provision was committed pursuant to the procedures specified in Section 2699.3.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2699(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Private Attorneys General Act of 2004, default civil penalty for provisions without a specified penalty
citations.quote: For all provisions of this code except those for which a civil penalty is specifically provided, there is established a civil penalty for a violation of these provisions, as follows: (1) If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person does not employ one or more employees, the civil penalty is five hundred dollars ($500). (2) If, at the time of the alleged violation, the person employs one or more employees, the civil penalty is as follows: (A) One hundred dollars ($100) for each aggrieved employee per pay period, except that:
