clauses.title: Purpose of This Unclaimed Final Wages Information Sheet
clauses.body:
Re: Unclaimed Final Wages — {{employeeName}}

This information sheet describes California's Unclaimed Property Law (Code of Civil Procedure § 1500 et seq.) as it applies to final wages that {{companyName}} owes to {{employeeName}} but has been unable to deliver because {{employeeName}} cannot be located or has not claimed them. {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}} ended on {{terminationDate}}. It is a companion to, and does not repeat, this document set's separate Final Paycheck Delivery Method and Location information sheet, which addresses how and where a final paycheck must be delivered when the employer knows where to send it; this document instead addresses what the statute says happens when that delivery cannot be completed because the wages go unclaimed. It states facts about what the statute requires of a holder of unpaid wages; it does not determine that these particular wages are, or are not, subject to escheat, and it does not tell {{companyName}} what to do about this specific unpaid amount.

clauses.title: The One-Year Dormancy Period for Unclaimed Wages
clauses.body: California's Unclaimed Property Law sets a general three-year dormancy period for most kinds of unclaimed personal property held in the ordinary course of a holder's business, but wages and salaries are carved out and given a shorter, specific period of their own: any wages or salaries that have remained unclaimed by the owner for more than one year after they become payable escheat to the state. This one-year wage rule sits within the same statutory section that lists other categories of property (chiefly bank and financial-organization deposits and accounts) escheating on their own separate terms, and it applies to wages or salaries held or owing by a "business association" -- a term the statute defines broadly to include private corporations, business trusts, partnerships, and other business associations of two or more people, whether or not organized for profit. Unpaid wages currently identified for {{employeeName}} as of {{terminationDate}} total {{unpaidWagesAmount}}, according to {{companyName}}'s records.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that wages are treated as their own category of unclaimed property with a one-year dormancy period distinct from the three-year general rule -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount, and not a claim that these specific wages have, in fact, gone unclaimed for the necessary period. The one-year wage provision and the statutory definition of "business association" both come from the Unclaimed Property Law but are, respectively, a single statutory paragraph (§ 1513, subd. (a)(7)) and a single statutory subdivision of a different, definitional section (§ 1501, subd. (c)); the two citations below are not independent of one another within each grouping, though the definitional citation is a genuinely separate section from the dormancy-period citation. This document does not address how an employer's holder status might differ for a sole proprietor or other holder that does not meet the statutory definition of "business association," which this research did not investigate further.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1513, subd. (a)(7)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1513, subd. (a)(7)
citations.quote: Any wages or salaries that have remained unclaimed by the owner for more than one year after the wages or salaries become payable.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1513, subd. (a)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1513, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Subject to Sections 1510 and 1511, the following property held or owing by a business association escheats to this state:

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1501, subd. (c)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1501, subd. (c)
citations.quote: “Business association” means any private corporation, joint stock company, business trust, partnership, or any association for business purposes of two or more individuals, whether or not for profit, including, but not by way of limitation, a banking organization, financial organization, life insurance corporation, and utility.

clauses.title: The Pre-Report Notice Requirement and Its Dollar Threshold
clauses.body: Before unclaimed property becomes reportable to the State Controller, the Unclaimed Property Law requires a holder that has an apparent owner's address on file -- and whose records do not show that address to be inaccurate -- to make reasonable efforts to notify the owner by mail (or electronically, if the owner has consented to electronic notice) that the property will escheat to the state, but only where the property is valued at fifty dollars ($50) or more. That notice must be mailed not less than six nor more than twelve months before the property becomes reportable to the Controller, and the statute prescribes specific required content for it, including a heading stating that California law requires notification that the property may be transferred to the state.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a $50 pre-report notice threshold and a 6-to-12-month notice window within the Unclaimed Property Law -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount. The quoted notice requirement appears in Code of Civil Procedure § 1520, subdivision (b), a section whose subdivision (a) sets the general three-year dormancy period and, by its own terms, excludes wage property covered by § 1513 from that three-year rule. Subdivision (b)'s notice duty is worded more broadly, applying to property that "will escheat to the state pursuant to this chapter" (not just property escheating under subdivision (a) of the same section), and it lists specific exceptions for property already covered by other sections' own notice rules -- Section 1513.5 (bank and financial-organization deposits), Section 1514, Section 1516, and Section 1516.5 -- without listing wages under Section 1513 among those exceptions. This document reads that structure as meaning the general $50/6-to-12-month notice duty in § 1520(b) is the one that applies to unclaimed wages under § 1513(a)(7), since no other section in this chapter was located that sets out a separate, wage-specific pre-report notice rule. That reading is not stated in so many words anywhere in the statutory text, so it is disclosed here as an inference from the section's structure and cross-references rather than as an explicit statutory statement naming wages.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1520, subd. (b)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1520, subd. (b)
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (a) of Section 1513.5, subdivision (b) of Section 1514, subdivision (d) of Section 1516, and subdivisions (b) and (c) of Section 1516.5, if the holder has in its records an address for the apparent owner of property valued at fifty dollars ($50) or more, which the holder’s records do not disclose to be inaccurate, the holder shall make reasonable efforts to notify the owner by mail or, if the owner has consented to electronic notice, electronically, that the owner’s property will escheat to the state pursuant to this chapter. The notice shall be mailed not less than 6 nor more than 12 months before the time when the owner’s property held by the business becomes reportable to the Controller in accordance with this chapter.

clauses.title: The Annual Report to the State Controller
clauses.body: The Unclaimed Property Law requires every person holding property that has escheated to the state under this chapter -- a category that includes unclaimed wages -- to report that property to the State Controller. For most holders, that report must be filed before November 1 of each year, covering property status as of the preceding June 30 (or the holder's fiscal year end).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the general reporting duty and its annual November 1 filing deadline -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount, and not a claim that November 1 is the deadline for every category of holder (the statute sets an earlier May 1 deadline for life insurance corporations and certain demutualization proceeds, which this document does not address because it is outside the wage scenario this document covers). Both citations below come from the same statutory section (§ 1530, subds. (a) and (d)) and are not independent of one another.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1530, subd. (a)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1530, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Every person holding funds or other property escheated to this state under this chapter shall report to the Controller as provided in this section.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1530, subd. (d)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1530, subd. (d)
citations.quote: The report shall be filed before November 1 of each year as of June 30 or fiscal yearend next preceding

clauses.title: The Deadline for Delivering Unclaimed Wages to the Controller
clauses.body: Filing the annual report is not, by itself, the end of the process: the Unclaimed Property Law separately requires every person who filed that report to actually pay or deliver the escheated property to the Controller within a specific window measured from the report's filing deadline -- no sooner than seven months, and no later than seven months and fifteen days, after the final date for filing the report. The Controller may postpone this payment-or-delivery date, and the report deadline, on the Controller's own motion or on written request from the holder.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific remittance window that follows the annual report -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount, and not a claim about whether a postponement has been sought or granted in any specific case. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 1532, subd. (a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific point.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1532, subd. (a)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1532, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Every person filing a report as provided by Section 1530 shall, no sooner than seven months and no later than seven months and 15 days after the final date for filing the report, pay or deliver to the Controller all escheated property specified in the report.

clauses.title: Discharge of the Holder's Liability, and How a Former Employee Later Claims the Wages
clauses.body: Once escheated property is paid or delivered to the Controller, the state assumes custody of it, and a holder who made that payment or delivery -- having made reasonable efforts to notify the owner in substantial compliance with the statute's notice provisions, where the holder had an address on file that its records did not show to be inaccurate -- is relieved of all liability, to the extent of the value of the property delivered, for any claim on that property that then exists or that might later arise. A former employee (or, after their death, their heirs or estate representative) can later recover wages that were escheated to the state by filing a verified claim with the Controller on a Controller-prescribed form; the Controller must consider the claim, and may hold a hearing and take evidence, within 180 days of filing, but no interest is payable on a claim paid under this chapter.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the discharge-from-liability rule and the claims process available afterward -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount, and not a claim that any specific delivery to the Controller has occurred here or that this discharge rule has already been triggered for these wages. The discharge provision (§ 1560, subd. (a)) conditions relief from liability on notice given "in substantial compliance with Sections 1513.5, 1514, 1516, and 1520" -- a list that does not name Section 1513 (the wage provision) by number. Read together with the pre-report notice clause elsewhere in this document, which explains why this document treats Section 1520's general notice duty as the one that applies to wages, this document treats that Section 1520 reference in the discharge provision as covering wage holders as well; that reading is an inference from cross-referenced statutory structure, not an explicit statement in the discharge provision itself naming wages. The two citations below come from two separate, independently numbered sections (§§ 1560 and 1540) and are independent sources of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1560, subd. (a)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1560, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Upon the payment or delivery of escheated property to the Controller, the state shall assume custody and shall be responsible for the safekeeping of the property. Any person who pays or delivers escheated property to the Controller under this chapter and who, prior to escheat, if the person’s records contain an address for the apparent owner that the holder’s records do not disclose to be inaccurate, has made reasonable efforts to notify the owner by mail or, if the owner has consented to electronic notice, electronically, in substantial compliance with Sections 1513.5, 1514, 1516, and 1520, that the owner’s property, deposit, account, shares, or other interest will escheat to the state, is relieved of all liability to the extent of the value of the property so paid or delivered for any claim that then exists or that thereafter may arise or be made in respect to the property.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1540, subds. (a)-(c)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1540, subds. (a)-(c)
citations.quote: Any person, excluding another state, who claims to have been the owner, as defined in subdivision (d), of property paid or delivered to the Controller under this chapter may file a claim to the property or to the net proceeds from its sale.

clauses.title: Interest for Failure to Report, Pay, or Deliver Unclaimed Property on Time
clauses.body: The Unclaimed Property Law attaches a specific consequence to a holder's failure to meet its reporting or remittance deadlines: unless the failure is due to reasonable cause, a holder who fails to report, pay, or deliver unclaimed property within the time the statute prescribes must pay the Controller interest at the rate of 12 percent per year on that property (or its value), running from the date the property should have been reported, paid, or delivered. This interest is owed to the Controller, not to the former employee, and is separate from any damages, penalties, or fines the holder may face under other laws.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific interest rate and trigger for late reporting or remittance -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount, and not a claim that any specific deadline in this case has, in fact, been missed. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 1577, subd. (a)); no additional independent source was found for this specific point. The same section caps interest at $10,000 in one narrow circumstance (a report that is filed and paid on time but not in substantial compliance with the reporting-content requirements) and allows the Controller to waive the interest for reasonable cause or full participation in a voluntary compliance program; this document does not address those provisions in further detail.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1577, subd. (a)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1577, subd. (a)
citations.quote: In addition to any damages, penalties, or fines for which a person may be liable under other provisions of law, any person who fails to report, pay, or deliver unclaimed property within the time prescribed by this chapter, unless that failure is due to reasonable cause, shall pay to the Controller interest at the rate of 12 percent per annum on that property or value thereof from the date the property should have been reported, paid, or delivered.

clauses.title: Unclaimed Final Wages — Recordkeeping Worksheet
Megan's Law Database Notice
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2079.10a requires that every lease or rental agreement for single-family residential real property, and every leasehold interest in multiunit residential property with more than four dwelling units, entered into on or after July 1, 1999, contain a statutorily specified notice, in not less than 8-point type. For a lease or rental agreement entered into on or after April 1, 2006, the required notice reads: "Notice: Pursuant to Section 290.46 of the Penal Code, information about specified registered sex offenders is made available to the public via an Internet Web site maintained by the Department of Justice at www.meganslaw.ca.gov. Depending on an offender's criminal history, this information will include either the address at which the offender resides or the community of residence and ZIP Code in which the offender resides." Once this notice has been delivered, the lessor or broker is not required to provide additional information about the proximity of registered sex offenders, and the notice does not give rise to any cause of action against the disclosing party by a registered sex offender.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's approach to a statewide sex-offender registry notice requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific lease. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2079.10a); no additional independent source was found for this. This clause states the same statutory notice already verified elsewhere in this corpus for a residential purchase agreement, adapted to lease-specific language, since § 2079.10a's own scope provision expressly covers both leases and sales.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the Megan's Law notice requirement
citations.quote: Every lease or rental agreement for single-family residential real property entered into on or after July 1, 1999, any leasehold interest in real property consisting of multiunit residential property with more than four dwelling units entered into after that date, and every contract for the sale of residential real property comprised of one to four dwelling units entered into on or after that date, shall contain, in not less than 8-point type, a notice as specified in paragraph (1), (2), or (3).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.10a(a)(3)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, current required notice text
citations.quote: A contract entered into by the parties on or after April 1, 2006, shall contain the following notice: Notice: Pursuant to Section 290.46 of the Penal Code, information about specified registered sex offenders is made available to the public via an Internet Web site maintained by the Department of Justice at www.meganslaw.ca.gov. Depending on an offender's criminal history, this information will include either the address at which the offender resides or the community of residence and ZIP Code in which the offender resides.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2079.10a(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, delivering the notice is deemed adequate
citations.quote: Subject to subdivision (c), upon delivery of the notice to the lessee or buyer of the real property, the lessor, seller, or broker is not required to provide information in addition to that contained in the notice regarding the proximity of registered sex offenders.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Probate Homestead Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's probate homestead set-aside, codified at Probate Code §§ 6520-6528 (Division 6, Part 3, Chapter 3, "Setting Aside Probate Homestead"). It concerns a probate court's discretionary power, exercised during the court-supervised administration of a decedent's estate, to select and set apart a homestead for the use of a surviving spouse and/or minor children. This is a distinct statutory mechanism from an automatic homestead exemption or a recorded declared homestead that protects a living person's equity from creditors during that person's lifetime; the probate homestead set-aside described here can arise only after a person's death and only through a probate court proceeding, under the Probate Code rather than the Code of Civil Procedure. This Information Sheet concerns the estate of {{decedentName}}, who died on {{dateOfDeath}}, with respect to property that may include the property located at {{propertyAddress}}, and is prepared in connection with a potential petition by {{petitionerName}}. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing California statutes; it is not a court filing, a petition, an order, or legal advice about whether a probate homestead will be set aside, what property or terms a court would select, or any other outcome specific to {{decedentName}}'s estate or {{petitionerName}}'s circumstances.

clauses.title: Who May Petition, and For Whose Use a Probate Homestead May Be Set Apart
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6520 gives a probate court discretion, upon the filing of the inventory or at any later time during administration of the estate, to select and set apart one probate homestead on petition, in the manner the chapter provides. Probate Code § 6521 states that the probate homestead is set apart for the use of one or more of two categories of persons: (a) the surviving spouse, and (b) the minor children of the decedent. Probate Code § 6525(a) states who may file the petition that starts this process: "any interested person," not only the surviving spouse or a minor child (or someone acting for a minor child).
clauses.gap: Probate Code §§ 6520, 6521, and 6525 are separately numbered, independently enacted sections of the same chapter, so they are independent sources of one another. This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of § 6525; subdivision (a) also cross-references notice requirements under Probate Code § 1220, and § 6525(b) separately lists three categories of persons entitled to notice of the hearing — those notice provisions were fetched as part of the same primary-source text but are not restated or quoted in this clause. This clause states who the statute allows to petition and for whose use the homestead may be set apart; it does not state whether a probate court would grant a set-aside on the facts of any particular case, which is a matter left to the court's discretion under other sections of this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6520
citations.cite: California Probate Code, existence and timing of the court's discretionary power to set apart a probate homestead
citations.quote: Upon the filing of the inventory or at any subsequent time during the administration of the estate, the court in its discretion may on petition therefor select and set apart one probate homestead in the manner provided in this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6521
citations.cite: California Probate Code, persons for whose use a probate homestead is set apart
citations.quote: The probate homestead shall be set apart for the use of one or more of the following persons: (a) The surviving spouse. (b) The minor children of the decedent.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6525(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, who may file a petition to select and set apart a probate homestead
citations.quote: A petition to select and set apart a probate homestead may be filed by any interested person.

clauses.title: Property Eligible to Be Selected as a Probate Homestead
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6522(a) sets an order of preference for what property a probate homestead may be selected from, giving first preference to community and quasi-community property, or property owned in common by the decedent and the person entitled to have the homestead set apart. If the homestead is for the surviving spouse, or the surviving spouse and minor children, it is drawn from community or quasi-community property; if for the surviving spouse, or minor children, or both, it may also be drawn from property owned in common by the decedent and the persons entitled to the homestead, from the decedent's separate property, or, if the decedent was unmarried at death, from property the decedent owned. Section 6522(b) limits this further: the probate homestead cannot be selected out of property in which the right to possession is vested in a third person unless that third person consents, where a "third person" is someone whose right to possession existed at, or arose upon, the decedent's death and was not created by testate or intestate succession from the decedent.
clauses.gap: Probate Code §§ 6522(a) and 6522(b) are both subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another as sources. This clause states the property-selection rules on their face; it does not determine what property is community property, quasi-community property, separate property, or property owned in common as to any specific decedent's estate, and it does not determine whether any specific person qualifies as a "third person" under § 6522(b).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6522(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, order of preference for property from which a probate homestead may be selected
citations.quote: The probate homestead shall be selected out of the following property, giving first preference to the community and quasi-community property of, or property owned in common by, the decedent and the person entitled to have the homestead set apart: (1) If the homestead is set apart for the use of the surviving spouse or for the use of the surviving spouse and minor children, out of community property or quasi-community property. (2) If the homestead is set apart for the use of the surviving spouse or for the use of the minor children or for the use of the surviving spouse and minor children, out of property owned in common by the decedent and the persons entitled to have the homestead set apart, or out of the separate property of the decedent or, if the decedent was not married at the time of death, out of property owned by the decedent.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6522(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, limit on selecting property in which a third person's right of possession is vested
citations.quote: The probate homestead shall not be selected out of property the right to possession of which is vested in a third person unless the third person consents thereto. As used in this subdivision, “third person” means a person whose right to possession of the property (1) existed at the time of the death of the decedent or came into existence upon the death of the decedent and (2) was not created by testate or intestate succession from the decedent.

clauses.title: The Court's Discretion: Factors Considered and Terms of the Set-Aside
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6523(a) lists the factors a court must consider in selecting and setting apart a probate homestead: the needs of the surviving spouse and minor children; liens and encumbrances on the property; the claims of creditors; the needs of the decedent's heirs or devisees; and the decedent's intent regarding the property and the decedent's estate plan, as shown by inter vivos and testamentary transfers or other means. Section 6523(b) then directs the court, in light of those factors and other relevant considerations within its discretion, to (1) select the most appropriate available property suitable for use as a homestead, including adjoining property beyond the dwelling itself where reasonable, and (2) set the homestead apart for a term and upon conditions the court considers proper, which may include conditions such as the homestead recipient assigning other property to the decedent's heirs or devisees. The statutory text does not itself state a fixed dollar value limit or a fixed duration for a probate homestead; instead, it commits both the term and the conditions of the set-aside to the court's discretion, applied to the factors listed in subdivision (a).
clauses.gap: Probate Code §§ 6523(a) and 6523(b) are both subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another as sources. This clause states that the fetched statutory text does not itself impose a fixed dollar-value cap or a fixed term of years; it does not independently verify the absence of any such limit elsewhere in the Probate Code or in case law construing this chapter, and it does not describe how a court would weigh the listed factors against one another in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6523(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, factors the court must consider in selecting and setting apart a probate homestead
citations.quote: In selecting and setting apart the probate homestead, the court shall consider the needs of the surviving spouse and minor children, the liens and encumbrances on the property, the claims of creditors, the needs of the heirs or devisees of the decedent, and the intent of the decedent with respect to the property in the estate and the estate plan of the decedent as expressed in inter vivos and testamentary transfers or by other means.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6523(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the court's discretion to select property and set the term and conditions of the homestead
citations.quote: The court, in light of subdivision (a) and other relevant considerations as determined by the court in its discretion, shall: (1) Select as a probate homestead the most appropriate property available that is suitable for that use, including in addition to the dwelling itself such adjoining property as appears reasonable. (2) Set the probate homestead so selected apart for such a term and upon such conditions (including, but not limited to, assignment by the homestead recipient of other property to the heirs or devisees of the property set apart as a homestead) as appear proper.

clauses.title: Duration of the Set-Aside and Its Effect on Estate Administration
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6524 caps how long a probate homestead may last: it may be set apart only for a limited period designated in the court's order, and in no case beyond the surviving spouse's lifetime or, as to a child, beyond that child's minority. The same section states that the decedent's property remains subject to administration, including testate and intestate succession, subject to the probate homestead right — meaning the set-aside does not remove the property from the estate or from the succession process, but instead creates a right that the ongoing administration and succession are subject to for the designated period. Section 6524 further provides that, to the extent applicable, the parties' rights during the period the probate homestead is set apart are governed by the Legal Estates Principal and Income Law, Chapter 2.6 (commencing with Section 731) of Title 2 of Part 1 of Division 2 of the Civil Code.
clauses.gap: This clause relies on a single statutory section, Probate Code § 6524; no second, independent source is cited for these specific duration and administration-effect rules. Section 6524 cross-references the Legal Estates Principal and Income Law (Civil Code §§ 731 et seq.) for the parties' rights during the set-aside period; that cross-referenced law was not independently fetched or verified for this clause, so this clause does not describe what those provisions say. This clause also does not describe the separate circumstances under which a court may modify or terminate a probate homestead right before the outer limits stated here are reached, which this Information Sheet does not address.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6524
citations.cite: California Probate Code, outer time limits on a probate homestead and its relationship to ongoing estate administration
citations.quote: The property set apart as a probate homestead shall be set apart only for a limited period, to be designated in the order, and in no case beyond the lifetime of the surviving spouse, or, as to a child, beyond its minority. Subject to the probate homestead right, the property of the decedent remains subject to administration including testate and intestate succession. The rights of the parties during the period for which the probate homestead is set apart are governed, to the extent applicable, by the Legal Estates Principal and Income Law, Chapter 2.6 (commencing with Section 731) of Title 2 of Part 1 of Division 2 of the Civil Code.

clauses.title: Priority of the Probate Homestead Right Relative to Creditors' Claims
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6526 states three rules about how the probate homestead right relates to claims against the estate. Under § 6526(a), property set apart as a probate homestead remains liable for claims against the decedent's estate, subject to the probate homestead right itself; the probate homestead right in that property is liable for claims secured by liens and encumbrances that existed on the property at the time of the decedent's death, but is exempt, to the extent of the homestead exemption, from any claim that would have been subject to a homestead exemption at the time of death under Code of Civil Procedure Article 4 (commencing with § 704.710) of Chapter 4, Division 2, Title 9, Part 2. Under § 6526(b), the probate homestead right is not liable for claims against the person for whose use the homestead is set apart. Under § 6526(c), property set apart as a probate homestead remains liable, after administration, for claims against the decedent's testate or intestate successors or other successors to the property, again subject to the probate homestead right.
clauses.gap: Probate Code §§ 6526(a), 6526(b), and 6526(c) are all subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another as sources. Section 6526(a) cross-references the Code of Civil Procedure's homestead-exemption Article 4 (commencing with § 704.710) to define the scope of its own exemption from lien-secured claims; this clause does not restate or re-verify the current dollar-amount formula under that cross-referenced Code of Civil Procedure article, which is addressed in this corpus's separate homestead exemption information sheet and was not re-fetched for this clause. This clause states the statutory liability and exemption rules as written; it does not determine how those rules would apply to any specific claim, lien, or encumbrance against a specific decedent's estate.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6526(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, liability of a probate homestead for lien-secured claims and its exemption to the extent of the homestead exemption
citations.quote: Property of the decedent set apart as a probate homestead is liable for claims against the estate of the decedent, subject to the probate homestead right. The probate homestead right in property of the decedent is liable for claims that are secured by liens and encumbrances on the property at the time of the decedent’s death but is exempt to the extent of the homestead exemption as to any claim that would have been subject to a homestead exemption at the time of the decedent’s death under Article 4 (commencing with Section 704.710) of Chapter 4 of Division 2 of Title 9 of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6526(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, non-liability of the probate homestead right for claims against the homestead recipient personally
citations.quote: The probate homestead right in the property of the decedent is not liable for claims against the person for whose use the probate homestead is set apart.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6526(c)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, continued liability of the property for claims against successors after administration
citations.quote: Property of the decedent set apart as a probate homestead is liable for claims against the testate or intestate successors of the decedent or other successors to the property after administration, subject to the probate homestead right.

clauses.title: This Chapter Does Not Affect a Separate Declaration of Homestead
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6528 expressly states that nothing in this chapter terminates or otherwise affects a declaration of homestead by, or for the benefit of, a surviving spouse or minor child of the decedent with respect to the community, quasi-community, or common interest of the surviving spouse or minor child in property in the decedent's estate; the statute adds that this section is declaratory of, and does not constitute a change in, existing law. On its face, this confirms that the probate homestead set-aside described in this Information Sheet is a distinct right from a declaration of homestead, and that a probate court's action (or inaction) under this chapter does not by itself terminate or otherwise affect any such separate declaration.
clauses.gap: This clause relies on a single statutory section, Probate Code § 6528; no second, independent source is cited for this specific point. Section 6528 refers to "a declaration of homestead" without itself defining that term or citing the Code of Civil Procedure provisions that create declared homesteads or the automatic homestead exemption; this clause does not describe what protections a declaration of homestead provides, which is addressed in this corpus's separate homestead exemption information sheet (covering Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.710-704.995) and was not re-verified here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6528
citations.cite: California Probate Code, this chapter does not terminate or affect a separate declaration of homestead
citations.quote: Nothing in this chapter terminates or otherwise affects a declaration of homestead by, or for the benefit of, a surviving spouse or minor child of the decedent with respect to the community, quasi-community, or common interest of the surviving spouse or minor child in property in the decedent’s estate. This section is declaratory of, and does not constitute a change in, existing law.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment — Probate Homestead Information Sheet
Purpose of This Reference — Statutory Compensation of the Personal Representative
clauses.body: This document describes, as general information, the statutory framework that California's Probate Code uses to set compensation for a personal representative — an executor named in a will or an administrator appointed without one — for ordinary services performed in administering the estate of {{decedentName}}. {{executorName}} is identified here as the personal representative (or proposed personal representative) whose statutory compensation this reference describes. This document does not calculate, request, approve, or pay any specific dollar amount of compensation for {{executorName}} or for any other person, and it does not itself authorize any payment from {{decedentName}}'s estate. Under California law, a personal representative's compensation for ordinary services is ultimately allowed by the probate court as part of the estate administration, typically on a petition presented with an accounting; this document is background information for that process, not a substitute for it, and not a computation of what any specific estate's fee would be.

clauses.title: The Statutory Percentage Fee Schedule for the Personal Representative's Ordinary Services
clauses.body: Probate Code § 10800(a) sets a tiered statutory percentage schedule for a personal representative's compensation for ordinary services in administering an estate such as {{decedentName}}'s: four percent on the first $100,000 of the value of the estate accounted for; three percent on the next $100,000; two percent on the next $800,000; one percent on the next $9,000,000; one-half of one percent on the next $15,000,000; and, for all amounts above $25,000,000, a reasonable amount to be determined by the court. Section 10800(b) defines "the value of the estate accounted for by the personal representative," for purposes of this schedule, as the total amount of the appraisal value of property in the inventory, plus gains over the appraisal value on sales, plus receipts, less losses from the appraisal value on sales, without reference to encumbrances or other obligations on estate property — meaning the percentages are applied to that defined figure, not directly to the estate's gross fair market value or to its net value after debts.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's statutory personal-representative compensation scheme — not a computation of any dollar amount for any specific decedent's estate or personal representative, and not a claim about which state's law governs any particular estate. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 10800(a) and § 10800(b); they are not independent of one another. Honest gap: this clause does not address how the court treats jointly held, non-probate, or otherwise non-inventoried property for purposes of this percentage schedule, and it does not address the separate, similarly tiered statutory schedule for compensation of the attorney for the personal representative under Probate Code §§ 10810-10811, which this document does not cover.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10800(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) Subject to the provisions of this part, for ordinary services the personal representative shall receive compensation based on the value of the estate accounted for by the personal representative, as follows: (1) Four percent on the first one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000). (2) Three percent on the next one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000). (3) Two percent on the next eight hundred thousand dollars ($800,000). (4) One percent on the next nine million dollars ($9,000,000). (5) One-half of one percent on the next fifteen million dollars ($15,000,000). (6) For all amounts above twenty-five million dollars ($25,000,000), a reasonable amount to be determined by the court.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10800(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (b) For the purposes of this section, the value of the estate accounted for by the personal representative is the total amount of the appraisal value of property in the inventory, plus gains over the appraisal value on sales, plus receipts, less losses from the appraisal value on sales, without reference to encumbrances or other obligations on estate property.

clauses.title: Extraordinary Services Are Compensated Separately, at the Court's Discretion — Not by a Fixed Percentage
clauses.body: Probate Code § 10801(a) allows the probate court, in addition to the ordinary-services compensation set by § 10800, to allow additional compensation to the personal representative for extraordinary services, in an amount the court determines is just and reasonable. Unlike the ordinary-services schedule, § 10801(a) does not itself specify a percentage, formula, or fixed rate for extraordinary-services compensation; the statute leaves that amount to the court's determination of what is just and reasonable in the circumstances.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's statutory personal-representative compensation scheme — not a claim about whether any specific service performed in any particular decedent's estate would qualify as "extraordinary," and not an estimate of what amount a court would find just and reasonable. This clause cites a single statutory subsection, § 10801(a); no additional independent source was found for this. Honest gap: § 10801(a), on its own text, does not define "extraordinary services" or list examples of what qualifies; that determination is left to the court.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10801(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) Subject to the provisions of this part, in addition to the compensation provided by Section 10800, the court may allow additional compensation for extraordinary services by the personal representative in an amount the court determines is just and reasonable.

clauses.title: A Will's Own Compensation Provision Displaces the Statutory Schedule, and No Side Agreement Can Provide More Than the Statute Allows
clauses.body: Probate Code § 10802(a) provides that, except as otherwise provided in that section, if a decedent's will makes provision for the compensation of the personal representative, the compensation provided by the will — not the § 10800 statutory percentage schedule — is the full and only compensation for the personal representative's services. Section 10802(b) allows the personal representative to petition the court to be relieved from such a will provision, which the statute's later subsections tie to a noticed hearing and a court finding that relief is to the estate's advantage. Separately, Probate Code § 10803 provides that an agreement between the personal representative and an heir or devisee for compensation higher than that provided by this part is void — meaning that outside of a court-approved will provision or a court order, the personal representative and the estate's heirs or devisees cannot privately agree to pay more than the statutory or will-based amount.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's statutory personal-representative compensation scheme — not a claim about whether any specific decedent's will contains a compensation provision, or about what any court would do with a petition for relief from one. This clause cites two separate, independently numbered statutory sections, § 10802(a)-(b) and § 10803; § 10802(a) and § 10802(b) are themselves subsections of the same section and are not independent of one another. Honest gap: this clause does not quote § 10802's remaining subsections, which set out the notice and best-interest-of-the-estate findings required before a court will relieve a personal representative from a will's compensation provision; it also does not address how § 10802 or § 10803 interact with a separate agreement for extraordinary-services compensation under § 10801.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10802(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided in this section, if the decedent’s will makes provision for the compensation of the personal representative, the compensation provided by the will shall be the full and only compensation for the services of the personal representative.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10802(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (b) The personal representative may petition the court to be relieved from a provision of the will that provides for the compensation of the personal representative.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10803 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: An agreement between the personal representative and an heir or devisee for higher compensation than that provided by this part is void.

clauses.title: A Personal Representative Who Is Also an Attorney Keeps the Personal Representative's Own Statutory Fee
clauses.body: Probate Code § 10804 provides that, notwithstanding any provision in the decedent's will, a personal representative who is an attorney is entitled to receive the personal representative's own compensation as provided in this part, but is not entitled to also receive compensation for services as the attorney for the personal representative unless the court specifically approves that right to compensation in advance and finds that the arrangement is to the advantage, benefit, and best interests of the estate.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's statutory personal-representative compensation scheme — not a claim about whether any specific personal representative is an attorney or about how any court would rule on an advance-approval request in any particular estate. This clause cites a single statutory section, § 10804; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10804 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any provision in the decedent’s will, a personal representative who is an attorney shall be entitled to receive the personal representative’s compensation as provided in this part, but shall not receive compensation for services as the attorney for the personal representative unless the court specifically approves the right to the compensation in advance and finds that the arrangement is to the advantage, benefit, and best interests of the decedent’s estate.

clauses.title: Two or More Personal Representatives Divide One Statutory Fee — Each Does Not Receive a Full Fee
clauses.body: Probate Code § 10805 provides that if there are two or more personal representatives, the personal representative's compensation is apportioned among them by the court according to the services actually rendered by each, or as agreed to by the personal representatives. Under this section, the statutory percentage amount produced by the § 10800 schedule is a single amount to be divided among co-personal-representatives — not a separate full statutory fee for each of them.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's statutory personal-representative compensation scheme — not a claim about whether any specific decedent's estate has, or will have, more than one personal representative, or about how a court would apportion compensation among them. This clause cites a single statutory section, § 10805; no additional independent source was found for this.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10805 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If there are two or more personal representatives, the personal representative’s compensation shall be apportioned among the personal representatives by the court according to the services actually rendered by each personal representative or as agreed to by the personal representatives.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment — Statutory Compensation of the Personal Representative Reference
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that I have reviewed the foregoing statutory compensation information in connection with the estate of {{decedentName}}.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

It does not itself calculate, request, approve, or authorize payment of any specific dollar amount of compensation, and it is not a substitute for the petition, accounting, and court order process by which a personal representative's compensation is actually allowed and paid from an estate.]

clauses.title: Declaration of Co-Ownership Interest and Contemplated Partition Relief
clauses.body:
{{plaintiffName}} states the following regarding real property located at {{propertyAddress}}, described as {{legalDescription}} (the "Property"), also identified by Assessor's Parcel Number {{parcelNumber}}, provided for identification only and not as part of the Property's legal description.

{{plaintiffName}} holds an interest in the Property as a co-owner, together with {{otherCoOwnersNames}}, under a form of concurrent ownership described as {{coOwnershipType}}.

{{plaintiffName}} is considering, or intends to pursue, a partition action under California Code of Civil Procedure Title 10.5 (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 872.010-874.323), seeking {{requestedPartitionType}} of the Property.

This declaration states {{plaintiffName}}'s own description of the Property, the co-ownership at issue, and the type of partition relief being considered; it does not itself divide, sell, or transfer any interest in the Property, and does not determine any co-owner's rights in the Property, which are decided by a court in a partition action, not by this document.

clauses.title: Who May Bring a Partition Action, and the Property Interests It Covers
clauses.body: California's partition statute states specifically who may commence and maintain a partition action: a coowner of personal property, or an owner of an estate of inheritance, an estate for life, or an estate for years in real property where that property or estate is owned by several persons concurrently or in successive estates. The statute's own text does not use the phrases "tenants in common" or "joint tenants"; it instead describes the covered ownership generally, as real property or an estate in real property owned by several persons concurrently (or in successive estates). Concurrent ownership of an estate in real property by several persons is the general category that both tenancy in common and joint tenancy fall within, but this clause does not evaluate whether a specific form of co-ownership, or a specific person's interest, in fact qualifies. Separately, the statute's governing title states that it governs actions for partition of real property and, except to the extent not applicable, actions for partition of personal property as well — a partition action is therefore not limited to real estate. The statute also contains an express carve-out: notwithstanding the persons and interests just described, an action between spouses or putative spouses for partition of their community or quasi-community property, or their quasi-marital interest in property, may not be commenced or maintained under this title.
clauses.gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 872.210, subdivisions (a) and (b), are subsections of a single statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as independent sources; Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 872.020 is a genuinely separate, independently numbered section and is treated as an independent source from § 872.210. This clause does not evaluate whether spouses or putative spouses seeking to divide community or quasi-community real property have an alternative remedy, such as under the Family Code, which this document does not address. This clause states only who is statutorily entitled to bring the action and what property interests are covered in general terms; it does not evaluate the sufficiency of any specific person's claimed interest, the classification of any specific property as separate or community property, or whether a specific co-ownership arrangement is a tenancy in common, a joint tenancy, or some other form of concurrent ownership. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's law on who may bring a partition action and what it covers — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of property or a specific co-ownership dispute; other states' partition statutes, if any, may define eligible parties and covered property differently.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 872.210(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Partition of Real and Personal Property, persons who may bring a partition action and the spousal community property carve-out
citations.quote: (a) A partition action may be commenced and maintained by any of the following persons: (1) A coowner of personal property. (2) An owner of an estate of inheritance, an estate for life, or an estate for years in real property where such property or estate therein is owned by several persons concurrently or in successive estates. (b) Notwithstanding subdivision (a), an action between spouses or putative spouses for partition of their community or quasi-community property or their quasi-marital interest in property may not be commenced or maintained under this title.

clauses.title: The Court's Equitable Power to Order Accounting and Contribution Among Co-Owners
clauses.body: California's partition statute gives the court a general equitable power, applicable to every partition action, to address financial imbalances among co-owners: "The court may, in all cases, order allowance, accounting, contribution, or other compensatory adjustment among the parties according to the principles of equity." This is the statutory hook that allows a partition court to take into account, as part of resolving the action, that one co-owner may have paid more than a proportionate share of expenses associated with the property, or received more than a proportionate share of its benefits, while the property was jointly owned. The statute's own text is general: it does not itself list or define specific categories of expense (such as property taxes, mortgage payments, or the cost of necessary repairs) or benefit (such as rental income or exclusive use) that qualify for an accounting or contribution award. It instead commits that determination, category by category and case by case, to the court's application of "the principles of equity."
clauses.gap: This clause is based on a single statutory section, Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 872.140. It states only that this general equitable power exists; it does not itself enumerate which categories of expense or benefit a court has treated as subject to contribution or accounting under this section, does not research or cite the case law that has applied "the principles of equity" to specific categories of expense in a partition action, and does not evaluate whether an accounting, contribution, or other compensatory adjustment would be available, or in what amount, on the facts of any specific co-ownership dispute. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a California partition court holds this general equitable power — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property dispute; other states' partition statutes, if any, may state this power differently or not at all.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 872.140
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Partition of Real and Personal Property, court's equitable power over accounting, contribution, and compensatory adjustment
citations.quote: The court may, in all cases, order allowance, accounting, contribution, or other compensatory adjustment among the parties according to the principles of equity.

clauses.title: Costs of Partition, Including Attorney's Fees, and How They Are Apportioned
clauses.body: California's partition statute states its own, specific rule for attorney's fees in a partition action, distinct from the general default rule (sometimes called the "American Rule") under which each party bears its own attorney's fees absent a statute or contract providing otherwise. The partition statute defines a category called "costs of partition," which by its own terms includes "[r]easonable attorney's fees incurred or paid by a party for the common benefit," along with other listed items such as a referee's fee and the cost of a title report. Having defined that category, the statute then states the default rule for dividing it among the parties: "Except as otherwise provided in this article, the court shall apportion the costs of partition among the parties in proportion to their interests or make such other apportionment as may be equitable." Where the action is governed by California's Partition of Real Property Act (addressed in a separate clause of this document), an added, more specific limitation applies to that apportionment: the court "may apportion the costs of partition, including an appraisal fee," under this same proportion-or-equity standard, "except that the court shall not apportion the costs of partition to any party that opposes the partition unless doing so is equitable and consistent with the purposes of this chapter."
clauses.gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 874.010 and 874.040 are both provisions of Article 1 of Chapter 8 (Costs of Partition) of the same governing title, and are treated here as related, not independent, sources. Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 874.321.5 is a genuinely separate, independently numbered section in a different chapter (Chapter 10, added in 2021 and amended in 2022) that by its own text cross-references and narrows § 874.040's apportionment standard; it is treated as an independent source from §§ 874.010 and 874.040, though the three provisions operate together. This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of § 874.010's list of items included in "costs of partition"; the remaining items in that same subdivision, and the entire remainder of Chapter 8, are not independently quoted or fully described here. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific attorney's fees were in fact incurred "for the common benefit," does not evaluate what apportionment would be equitable on the facts of any specific action, and does not evaluate whether § 874.321.5's added limitation applies to any specific party or action. This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of California's cost-and-fee-allocation rule for a partition action — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific dispute; other states' partition statutes, if any, may allocate attorney's fees and costs differently, including by following the general American Rule with no partition-specific exception.

clauses.title: Partition in Kind vs. Partition by Sale: The Statutory Preference and the "Great Prejudice" Standard
clauses.body: Under California's Partition of Real Property Act (addressed in a separate clause of this document as to when it applies), the statute states an explicit preference for one of the two basic forms of partition relief. Once a determination of value has been made and any statutory buyout process has concluded, "the court shall order partition in kind unless the court, after consideration of the factors listed in Section 874.319, finds that partition in kind will result in great prejudice to the cotenants as a group." Partition in kind — physical division of the property into separately titled parcels — is therefore the statute's default outcome; partition by sale is available only if the court affirmatively finds, after weighing the statutory factors, that dividing the property in kind would cause great prejudice to the cotenants as a group. Those factors include, among others, "[w]hether the property practicably can be divided among the cotenants," and "[w]hether partition in kind would apportion the property in such a way that the aggregate fair market value of the parcels resulting from the division would be materially less than the value of the property if it were sold as a whole, taking into account the condition under which a court-ordered sale likely would occur." The statute also directs the court to consider "[t]he degree to which the cotenants have contributed their pro rata share of the property taxes, insurance, and other expenses associated with maintaining ownership of the property or have contributed to the physical improvement, maintenance, or upkeep of the property." Finally, the statute states that no single factor controls this determination on its own: "The court shall not consider any one factor in subdivision (a) to be dispositive without weighing the totality of all relevant factors and circumstances."
clauses.gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 874.318, subdivisions (a) and (b), are subsections of a single statutory section and are treated here as one source, not independent of each other. Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 874.319 is a genuinely separate, independently numbered section, treated as an independent source from § 874.318, even though the two sections work together as a single standard (§ 874.318 states the preference and the ultimate legal question; § 874.319 lists the factors bearing on that question). This clause quotes only two of the seven listed factors in § 874.319(a) and the closing no-single-factor-is-dispositive rule in § 874.319(b); the remaining factors are not independently quoted here, and a reader should not assume this clause is a complete statement of every factor a court must consider. This preference for partition in kind, and the great-prejudice standard described here, apply only where the Partition of Real Property Act applies to the action in the first place, as addressed in a separate clause of this document; this clause does not address what standard governs the choice between partition in kind and partition by sale in a partition action to which that Act does not apply, and does not independently verify or quote any other provision of Title 10.5 that might state a different standard for such an action. This clause does not evaluate whether partition in kind or partition by sale would in fact result in great prejudice on the facts of any specific property or dispute. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's preference between the two forms of partition relief and the standard for choosing between them — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property dispute; other states' partition statutes, if any, may state a different preference or standard.

clauses.title: The Partition of Real Property Act: When Its Procedures Apply by Default, and Their Limit to Tenancy in Common
clauses.body: In 2021 and 2022, California enacted and then substantially amended Chapter 10 of its partition title, Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 874.311-874.323, titled the "Partition of Real Property Act" — California's version of a uniform act commonly associated with protecting "heirs property." The statute's own scope provision, however, is not limited by its terms to inherited property or to family heirs: it "applies to real property held in tenancy in common where there is no agreement in a record binding all the cotenants which governs the partition of the property," and it "applies to actions for partition of real property filed on or after January 1, 2023." The statute then makes this chapter's procedures — including the appraisal, buyout right, and partition-in-kind preference described elsewhere in this document — the default rule, not merely an optional or narrow add-on: "In an action to partition real property, the property shall be partitioned under this chapter unless all of the cotenants otherwise agree in a record," and, where this chapter governs, it "shall control over any provisions of this title that are inconsistent with this chapter." In other words, for a real property partition action among tenants in common filed on or after January 1, 2023, this chapter's procedures apply by default unless every cotenant has agreed, in a record, to a different partition arrangement.
clauses.gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. §§ 874.311 and 874.313 are genuinely separate, independently numbered statutory sections, treated here as two independent sources. This clause quotes only subdivisions (b) and (c) of § 874.311; subdivision (a), stating the act's short title, is not quoted. By its own text, § 874.311(b) applies this chapter to real property "held in tenancy in common" — the statutory text verified for this clause does not extend this chapter's default procedures to real property held in joint tenancy or another form of concurrent ownership, and this document does not independently research or verify whether, or how, any of this chapter's procedures apply to a joint tenancy partition action; a reader whose co-ownership is a joint tenancy should not assume that the appraisal, buyout, or partition-in-kind procedures described elsewhere in this document apply to their situation without further research. This clause does not evaluate whether a specific action was in fact filed on or after January 1, 2023, whether a specific instrument is an "agreement in a record" that would take an action outside this chapter, or whether a specific co-ownership is in fact a tenancy in common. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's default partition procedure for tenancy-in-common real property — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel of property or a specific co-ownership dispute; other states' adoptions of a uniform partition-of-heirs-property act, if any, may define their scope differently, including by limiting it to inherited property specifically.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 874.311(b)-(c)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure, Partition of Real Property Act, scope: tenancy in common with no governing agreement, actions filed on or after January 1, 2023
citations.quote: This act applies to real property held in tenancy in common where there is no agreement in a record binding all the cotenants which governs the partition of the property. (c) This act applies to actions for partition of real property filed on or after January 1, 2023.

citations.quote: In an action to partition real property, the property shall be partitioned under this chapter unless all of the cotenants otherwise agree in a record. (b) This chapter supplements the other provisions of this title and, if an action is governed by this chapter, this chapter shall control over any provisions of this title that are inconsistent with this chapter.

clauses.title: Under the Partition of Real Property Act: Court-Ordered Appraisal, and a Co-Owner's Right to Buy Out Cotenants Who Requested Sale
clauses.body: Where California's Partition of Real Property Act applies (addressed in a separate clause of this document), the statute builds in a valuation step and a buyout opportunity before the court decides between partition in kind and partition by sale. On valuation: "Except as otherwise provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), the court shall determine the fair market value of the property by ordering an appraisal," and where an appraisal is ordered, "the court shall appoint a disinterested real estate appraiser licensed in the State of California to determine the fair market value of the property assuming sole ownership of the fee simple estate." Once that value has been determined, and if any cotenant has requested partition by sale, the statute gives every other cotenant — meaning a cotenant who did not request sale — a statutory opportunity to buy out the interests of the cotenants who did request sale, before any forced sale occurs: "the court shall... send notice to the parties that any cotenant except a cotenant that requested partition by sale may buy all the interests of the cotenants that requested partition by sale," and "[n]ot later than 45 days after the notice is sent... any cotenant except a cotenant that requested partition by sale may give notice to the court that it elects to buy all the interests of the cotenants that requested partition by sale." The statute elsewhere sets the buyout price at the court-determined value multiplied by the electing cotenant's fractional ownership, and provides further rules for what happens when more than one cotenant elects to buy, or when an electing cotenant fails to pay.
clauses.gap: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 874.316, subdivisions (a) and (d), are subsections of a single statutory section, treated here as one source, not independent of each other. Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 874.317, subdivisions (a) and (b), are subsections of a different, genuinely separate statutory section, treated here as a second independent source; the two sections operate sequentially as one appraisal-then-buyout procedure. This clause does not independently quote § 874.316's subdivisions (b) and (c), addressing when the parties' own agreed valuation is adopted instead of a court-ordered appraisal, or when the court may forgo an appraisal because its cost outweighs its evidentiary value; it does not independently quote § 874.317's remaining subdivisions (c) through (h), which set the buyout price formula, the payment deadlines, and the procedure when multiple cotenants elect to buy or an electing cotenant fails to pay; and it does not address the separate, related sections governing the partition-by-sale procedure itself (§ 874.320) or the broker's reporting duties (§ 874.321). A reader should not assume this clause is a complete statement of the valuation or buyout procedure. This clause does not evaluate whether a buyout right would in fact be available, or advantageous, on the facts of any specific co-ownership dispute, and does not evaluate the fair market value of any specific property. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's appraisal-and-buyout procedure under this Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property dispute; other states' adoptions of a uniform partition-of-heirs-property act, if any, may state a different, or no, buyout procedure.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment
Smoke Alarm and Carbon Monoxide Device Compliance Disclosure
clauses.body: This disclosure concerns the property at {{propertyAddress}}, being transferred from {{sellerName}} ("Transferor") to {{buyerName}} ("Transferee"). It addresses California's separate statutory requirements for smoke alarms and carbon monoxide devices in residential dwellings, and the transferor's compliance statement obligation tied to this transfer.

clauses.title: Smoke Alarm Requirement and Transferor's Written Compliance Statement
clauses.body: California law requires that every single-family dwelling and factory-built housing which is sold have an operable smoke alarm. At the time of installation, the alarm must be approved and listed by the State Fire Marshal and installed in accordance with the State Fire Marshal's regulations; unless prohibited by local rules, regulations, or ordinances, a battery-operated smoke alarm that met the smoke-alarm standards in effect at the time of installation satisfies this requirement. Separately, the transferor of real property containing such a single-family dwelling — whether the transfer is by sale, exchange, or real property sales contract — must deliver to the transferee a written statement indicating that the transferor is in compliance with this requirement. This disclosure statement may be included in the deposit receipt for the transaction, an addendum attached to it, or a separate document. The transferor must deliver the statement as soon as practicable before transfer of title in the case of a sale or exchange, or before execution of the contract where the transfer is by a real property sales contract.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction ties a life-safety device standard to a transfer disclosure obligation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer; smoke alarm and disclosure requirements vary by state. The statute's scope term is 'single-family dwelling,' which the statute itself defines to include a one- or two-unit dwelling but to exclude a manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial coach — a narrower and differently-drawn category than the 'single-family residential property' language used in the Transfer Disclosure Statement statute. The citations below to subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) are all subsections of the same statutory section (Health & Safety Code § 13113.8) and are not independent of one another.

citations.cite: Health & Safety Code § 13113.8(a)
citations.quote: On and after January 1, 1986, every single-family dwelling and factory-built housing, as defined in Section 19971, which is sold shall have an operable smoke alarm. At the time of installation, the alarm shall be approved and listed by the State Fire Marshal and installed in accordance with the State Fire Marshal’s regulations. Unless prohibited by local rules, regulations, or ordinances, a battery-operated smoke alarm that met the standards adopted pursuant to Section 13114 for smoke alarms at the time of installation shall be deemed to satisfy the requirements of this section.

The disclosure statement shall be either included in the receipt for deposit in a real estate transaction, an addendum attached thereto, or a separate document.

clauses.body: The smoke alarm compliance statement requirement does not apply to: transfers required to be preceded by a public report under Business and Professions Code § 11018.1; transfers pursuant to court order, including probate-court sales, writ-of-execution sales, bankruptcy-trustee transfers, eminent domain, or a decree for specific performance; transfers to a mortgagee by a defaulting mortgagor, to a beneficiary of a deed of trust by a defaulting trustor, or by any foreclosure sale or trustee's sale after default; transfers by a fiduciary in the administration of a decedent's estate, guardianship, conservatorship, or trust; transfers from one co-owner to one or more other co-owners; transfers to a spouse or to a person in the lineal line of consanguinity of a transferor; transfers between spouses resulting from a dissolution or legal-separation decree or an incidental property settlement; transfers by the Controller administering the Unclaimed Property Law; and transfers under the Revenue and Taxation Code provisions governing tax-defaulted property sales.
clauses.gap: This exemption list overlaps with, but is not identical to, the exemption list this corpus documents for the general Transfer Disclosure Statement requirement: this statute additionally exempts public-report transfers and Unclaimed Property Law and tax-default sale transfers, categories not listed among the TDS exemptions documented elsewhere in this corpus, and each list should be checked on its own terms rather than assumed to mirror the other. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's exemption structure for a device-specific transfer disclosure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Health & Safety Code § 13113.8) and are not independent of one another.

(2) Transfers pursuant to court order, including, but not limited to, transfers ordered by a probate court in the administration of an estate, transfers pursuant to a writ of execution, transfers by a trustee in bankruptcy, transfers by eminent domain, or transfers resulting from a decree for specific performance.
