(4) Transfers by a fiduciary in the course of the administration of a decedent’s estate, guardianship, conservatorship, or trust. (5) Transfers from one coowner to one or more coowners. (6) Transfers made to a spouse, or to a person or persons in the lineal line of consanguinity of one or more of the transferors. (7) Transfers between spouses resulting from a decree of dissolution of a marriage, from a decree of legal separation, or from a property settlement agreement incidental to either of those decrees. (8) Transfers by the Controller in the course of administering the Unclaimed Property Law provided for in Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 1500) of Title 10 of Part 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (9) Transfers under the provisions of Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 3691) or Chapter 8 (commencing with Section 3771) of Part 6 of Division 1 of the Revenue and Taxation Code.

clauses.title: Smoke Alarm Statement: Agent Liability and Transfer Remedy
clauses.body: No liability arises against, and no action may be brought or maintained against, any agent of any party to a transfer of title, including a person or entity acting as escrow, for an error, inaccuracy, or omission relating to the smoke alarm compliance statement a transferor must make — except that this protection does not extend to a real estate licensee who participates in making the disclosure with actual knowledge that it is false. This requirement does not create or imply a duty on a licensee or on any agent of a party to the transfer, including an escrow, to monitor or ensure compliance with the smoke alarm requirement. No transfer of title is invalidated for a failure to comply with the smoke alarm requirement; the exclusive remedy for noncompliance is an award of actual damages not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100), exclusive of court costs and attorney's fees.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction caps the remedy for noncompliance with a device-specific transfer disclosure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer, or about what remedies (if any) another jurisdiction's law would allow. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Health & Safety Code § 13113.8) and are not independent of one another.

clauses.title: Carbon Monoxide Device Installation Requirement
clauses.body: Under the Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Prevention Act of 2010, an owner of a dwelling unit intended for human occupancy must install a carbon monoxide device, approved and listed by the State Fire Marshal, in each existing dwelling unit that has a fossil-fuel-burning heater or appliance, a fireplace, or an attached garage. The installation deadline depended on the type of dwelling: on or before July 1, 2011 for existing single-family dwelling units; on or before January 1, 2013 for other existing dwelling units; and on or before January 1, 2017 for existing hotel and motel dwelling units — deadlines that have all now passed, so the installation requirement applies to all covered existing dwelling units as of the date of this disclosure. As to the number and placement of the devices, the owner must install them consistent with the building standards that apply to new construction for the relevant type of occupancy, or with the manufacturer's instructions, where technically feasible.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a device-installation requirement tied to dwelling occupancy — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific dwelling. Unlike the smoke alarm statute, this statute's installation duty is not framed as sale-triggered; it is framed as an ongoing owner obligation tied to occupancy of a dwelling unit having the listed fuel-burning or garage features, and it does not itself state a duty to deliver a written compliance statement to a transferee at the time of a sale comparable to the smoke alarm statute's separate written-statement requirement. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Health & Safety Code § 17926) and are not independent of one another; a separately numbered section, § 17926.1, imposes a related but distinct carbon-monoxide-device maintenance duty on an owner or owner's agent who rents or leases a dwelling unit to a tenant, which is not a transfer-of-title disclosure duty and is not relied on here.

citations.case: Health & Safety Code, carbon monoxide device installation trigger and deadlines
citations.cite: Health & Safety Code § 17926(a)
citations.quote: An owner of a dwelling unit intended for human occupancy shall install a carbon monoxide device, approved and listed by the State Fire Marshal pursuant to Section 13263, in each existing dwelling unit having a fossil fuel burning heater or appliance, fireplace, or an attached garage, within the earliest applicable time period as follows: (1) For all existing single-family dwelling units intended for human occupancy on or before July 1, 2011. (2) For all existing hotel and motel dwelling units intended for human occupancy on or before January 1, 2017. (3) For all other existing dwelling units intended for human occupancy on or before January 1, 2013.

citations.case: Health & Safety Code, number/placement standard
citations.cite: Health & Safety Code § 17926(b)
citations.quote: With respect to the number and placement of carbon monoxide devices, an owner shall install the devices in a manner consistent with building standards applicable to new construction for the relevant type of occupancy or with the manufacturer’s instructions, if it is technically feasible to do so.

clauses.title: Carbon Monoxide Device: Violation Penalty and Transfer Remedy
clauses.body: A violation of the carbon monoxide device installation requirement is an infraction punishable by a maximum fine of two hundred dollars ($200) per offense, but a property owner must first receive a 30-day notice to correct, and the fine may be assessed only if the owner fails to correct within that period. Separately, no transfer of title is invalidated for a failure to comply with the carbon monoxide device requirement; the exclusive remedy for noncompliance is an award of actual damages not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100), exclusive of court costs and attorney's fees, and this limit does not affect any other duties, rights, or remedies otherwise available at law.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures both a code-enforcement penalty and a separate, capped transfer-related remedy for the same device requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific dwelling or transfer. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Health & Safety Code § 17926) and are not independent of one another; they are also not independent of the installation-requirement citations in the preceding clause, which cite different subsections of this same section.

citations.cite: Health & Safety Code § 17926(c)
citations.quote: a violation of this section is an infraction punishable by a maximum fine of two hundred dollars ($200) for each offense. (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), a property owner shall receive a 30-day notice to correct. If an owner receiving notice fails to correct within that time period, the owner may be assessed the fine pursuant to paragraph (2).

This subdivision is not intended to affect any duties, rights, or remedies otherwise available at law.

clauses.title: Purpose
clauses.body: This document describes what California Labor Code § 980 says about an employer's ability to require or request access to an employee's or applicant's personal social media. It is provided for information about {{employeeName}}'s and {{companyName}}'s rights and obligations under that statute; it does not itself instruct either party on what to do in any specific situation.

clauses.title: What an Employer May Not Require or Request
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 980 defines "social media," for purposes of the chapter, broadly — as an electronic service or account, or electronic content, including but not limited to videos, still photographs, blogs, video blogs, podcasts, instant and text messages, email, online services or accounts, or internet website profiles or locations. Using that definition, the statute states that an employer shall not require or request an employee or an applicant for employment to do any of three things: (1) disclose a username or password for the purpose of accessing personal social media; (2) access personal social media in the employer's presence; or (3) divulge any personal social media, except as provided in the statute's own investigation exception. The statute does not distinguish, within this prohibition, between social media content shared publicly and content shared only with a limited audience — the prohibition as written does not turn on that distinction.
clauses.gap: Both quotations below come from the same single statutory section, Labor Code § 980 — subdivision (a)'s definition and subdivision (b)'s prohibition list — so they are not independent of one another; no second, independently-numbered source was located or used to corroborate this point. This clause describes only what § 980 itself says on its face; it does not address how any court has since construed "personal social media," the presence requirement, or any other term in the statute, and no case law applying § 980 was located or verified in this research. The statute applies by its terms to "an employee or applicant for employment" — this clause does not narrow that to describe obligations toward one and not the other.

citations.case: California Labor Code § 980(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 980(a)
citations.quote: As used in this chapter, “social media” means an electronic service or account, or electronic content, including, but not limited to, videos, still photographs, blogs, video blogs, podcasts, instant and text messages, email, online services or accounts, or Internet Web site profiles or locations.

citations.case: California Labor Code § 980(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 980(b)
citations.quote: An employer shall not require or request an employee or applicant for employment to do any of the following: (1) Disclose a username or password for the purpose of accessing personal social media. (2) Access personal social media in the presence of the employer. (3) Divulge any personal social media, except as provided in subdivision (c).

clauses.title: Exception: Misconduct or Legal-Violation Investigations
clauses.body: Labor Code § 980 states one exception to its own prohibition. It does not affect an employer's existing rights and obligations to request that an employee divulge personal social media reasonably believed to be relevant to an investigation of allegations of employee misconduct or of an employee's violation of applicable laws and regulations — provided that the social media disclosed is used solely for the purposes of that investigation or a related proceeding. By its own terms, this exception is tied to an investigation of misconduct or a legal violation, and it conditions use of whatever is divulged to that investigation or a related proceeding; the statute does not state a broader, general-purpose exception beyond that.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single subsection, § 980(c), of the same statutory section already cited in the companion clause on the core prohibition — it is not an independent source. The statute states that this exception does not affect the employer's "existing rights and obligations"; it does not itself create a separate, freestanding right to demand social media disclosure — what rights or obligations already exist for a given investigation is a question this clause does not resolve, and no case law construing this exception was located or verified in this research.

citations.case: California Labor Code § 980(c)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 980(c)
citations.quote: Nothing in this section shall affect an employer’s existing rights and obligations to request an employee to divulge personal social media reasonably believed to be relevant to an investigation of allegations of employee misconduct or employee violation of applicable laws and regulations, provided that the social media is used solely for purposes of that investigation or a related proceeding.

clauses.title: Exception: Employer-Issued Devices
clauses.body: Labor Code § 980 states a second exception: nothing in the section precludes an employer from requiring or requesting that an employee disclose a username, password, or other method for the purpose of accessing an employer-issued electronic device. On its face, this exception is limited to accessing the device itself — it addresses employer-issued equipment, not personal social media accessed on that equipment.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single subsection, § 980(d), of the same statutory section already cited in the companion clauses in this document — it is not an independent source. The statute does not itself define "employer-issued electronic device," and this clause does not attempt to draw the line between that device-access exception and the personal-social-media prohibition in subdivision (b) for a case where personal social media happens to be reachable from employer-issued equipment; no case law on that question was located or verified in this research.

citations.case: California Labor Code § 980(d)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 980(d)
citations.quote: Nothing in this section precludes an employer from requiring or requesting an employee to disclose a username, password, or other method for the purpose of accessing an employer-issued electronic device.

clauses.title: Retaliation Protection
clauses.body: Labor Code § 980 states that an employer shall not discharge, discipline, threaten to discharge or discipline, or otherwise retaliate against an employee or applicant for not complying with a request or demand by the employer that violates this section. The same sentence states a limit on that protection: the statute does not prohibit an employer from terminating or otherwise taking an adverse action against an employee or applicant if otherwise permitted by law. The statute's own text does not spell out a separate enforcement mechanism, private right of action, or remedy for a violation of this section beyond stating the retaliation prohibition itself.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single subsection, § 980(e), of the same statutory section already cited in the companion clauses in this document — it is not an independent source. This research did not locate, within the text of § 980 itself, any provision naming a specific enforcement mechanism, agency, private right of action, or damages/penalty remedy for a violation — that omission is disclosed here rather than filled in with an assumed remedy (for example, an assumption that Labor Code § 98.6, the general retaliation-remedy statute, or the Private Attorneys General Act necessarily applies to a § 980 violation was not checked or verified in this research and is not asserted). What "otherwise permitted by law" means, and how it interacts with the retaliation prohibition in a specific case, is also not resolved by this clause or by any case law verified in this research.

citations.case: California Labor Code § 980(e)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 980(e)
citations.quote: An employer shall not discharge, discipline, threaten to discharge or discipline, or otherwise retaliate against an employee or applicant for not complying with a request or demand by the employer that violates this section. However, this section does not prohibit an employer from terminating or otherwise taking an adverse action against an employee or applicant if otherwise permitted by law.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's statutory framework governing an employer's duty to secure workers' compensation insurance coverage, as set out in California Labor Code sections 3700 through 3710.1. It is prepared in connection with {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}.

This information sheet describes the acceptable ways an employer may secure the payment of workers' compensation, the criminal penalties the Labor Code attaches to an employer's failure to do so, the Director of Industrial Relations' stop-order authority over an employer found out of compliance, and the civil-action rights the Labor Code gives an injured employee against an employer who has failed to secure coverage.

This information sheet does not determine whether {{companyName}} has in fact secured workers' compensation coverage, does not determine whether any specific workplace injury is compensable, and is not a substitute for the actual text of the statutes it describes.

clauses.title: The Mandatory Duty to Secure Workers' Compensation Coverage
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 3700 requires every employer except the state to secure the payment of workers' compensation in one or more of the ways the statute itself lists. Two of those ways are: (a) by being insured against liability to pay compensation by one or more insurers duly authorized to write compensation insurance in California; or (b) by securing from the Director of Industrial Relations a certificate of consent to self-insure, either as an individual employer or as one employer in a group of employers, issued upon proof satisfactory to the Director of ability to self-insure and to pay any compensation that may become due to the employer's employees. A separate provision of the same section, § 3700(c), sets out a further self-insurance certification pathway specifically for counties, cities, and other public entities. Nothing in the text of § 3700 conditions this duty on the employer's number of employees.
clauses.gap: Section 3700 excepts "the state" itself from this particular coverage-securing duty and, in the same sentence, defines "state" for purposes of the section to include the superior courts of California; this document does not research or state what alternative mechanism, if any, covers state employees, since that would require researching statutes outside the sections fetched for this document. Subdivision (c) (the public-entity self-insurance pathway) was read but is only summarized, not quoted, here, since it is not the general private-employer rule this clause centers on. This document did not find the statutory text of § 3700 to name the State Compensation Insurance Fund specifically as one of the listed ways to secure coverage; whatever the popular understanding, the two ways quoted here are the private-insurance and self-insurance-certificate mechanisms the statute's own text sets out, and this document does not assume additional mechanisms the fetched text does not state. This is one state's statute, stating a fact about what California law requires of employers generally — not a claim about whether any specific employer has in fact secured coverage.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3700 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3700
citations.quote: Every employer except the state shall secure the payment of compensation in one or more of the following ways:

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3700, subd. (a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3700, subds. (a)-(b)
citations.quote: (a) By being insured against liability to pay compensation by one or more insurers duly authorized to write compensation insurance in this state. (b) By securing from the Director of Industrial Relations a certificate of consent to self-insure either as an individual employer, or as one employer in a group of employers, which may be given upon furnishing proof satisfactory to the Director of Industrial Relations of ability to self-insure and to pay any compensation that may become due to his or her employees.

clauses.title: Criminal Penalty for Failing to Secure Coverage
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 3700.5 makes it a misdemeanor for an employer who knew, or who because of the employer's knowledge or experience should reasonably have been expected to know, of the obligation to secure the payment of workers' compensation, to fail to secure it. A first conviction is punishable by up to one year in county jail, or by a fine of up to double the premium amount that would otherwise have been due to secure coverage during the uninsured period (but not less than $10,000), or by both. A second or subsequent conviction is punishable by up to one year in county jail, a fine of triple that premium amount (but not less than $50,000), or both. The statute also allows the court, in its discretion, to charge a first-time offender the costs of investigation, and requires that a repeat offender be charged those costs — payable only after any owed employee benefits, director reimbursement, and other penalty assessments are paid.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes § 3700.5, subdivisions (a) and (b); subdivision (c) (governing costs of investigation and their payment priority) is summarized but not separately quoted. This is one state's criminal statute, stating a fact about the penalty California law attaches to a knowing failure to secure coverage — not a claim about whether any specific employer's conduct meets the statute's knowledge requirement, which only a court can determine.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3700.5, subd. (a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3700.5, subd. (a)
citations.quote: The failure to secure the payment of compensation as required by this article by one who knew, or because of his or her knowledge or experience should be reasonably expected to have known, of the obligation to secure the payment of compensation, is a misdemeanor punishable by imprisonment in the county jail for up to one year, or by a fine of up to double the amount of premium, as determined by the court, that would otherwise have been due to secure the payment of compensation during the time compensation was not secured, but not less than ten thousand dollars ($10,000), or by both that imprisonment and fine.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3700.5, subd. (b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3700.5, subd. (b)
citations.quote: A second or subsequent conviction shall be punished by imprisonment in the county jail for a period not to exceed one year, by a fine of triple the amount of premium, or by both that imprisonment and fine, as determined by the court, that would otherwise have been due to secure the payment of compensation during the time payment was not secured, but not less than fifty thousand dollars ($50,000).

clauses.title: The Director's Authority to Issue a Stop Order
clauses.body: Separately from the criminal penalty in § 3700.5, California Labor Code § 3710.1 authorizes the Director of Industrial Relations, upon finding that an employer has failed to secure the payment of compensation as § 3700 requires, to issue and serve on that employer a stop order prohibiting the use of employee labor until the employer comes into compliance with § 3700; the stop order takes effect immediately upon service. Employees affected by the resulting work stoppage must be paid by the employer for time lost, up to 10 days, while compliance is pending. An employer may protest the stop order by filing a written request for a hearing with the director within 20 days of service; the statute requires the hearing to be held within 5 days of that filing, requires the director to mail a written notice of findings within 24 hours after the hearing concludes, and allows the employer to seek a writ of mandate from the findings in superior court within 45 days after the notice is mailed.
clauses.gap: Section 3710.1 gives this stop-order authority to "the director," i.e., the Director of Industrial Relations — the same official named in § 3700(b) as issuing self-insurance certificates — not to the Labor Commissioner, a separate DIR official whose office administers different Labor Code enforcement functions this document does not address. This clause quotes most, but not all, of § 3710.1's procedural sequence; the exact wording governing the content and mailing of the director's post-hearing findings was read but is only summarized, not quoted, here. This is one state's statute, stating a fact about the director's enforcement authority in general — not a claim that any specific employer has been found out of compliance or is subject to a stop order.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3710.1 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3710.1
citations.quote: Where an employer has failed to secure the payment of compensation as required by Section 3700, the director shall issue and serve on such employer a stop order prohibiting the use of employee labor by such employer until the employer’s compliance with the provisions of Section 3700.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3710.1 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3710.1
citations.quote: Any employee so affected by such work stoppage shall be paid by the employer for such time lost, not exceeding 10 days, pending compliance by the employer. Such employer may protest the stop order by making and filing with the director a written request for a hearing within 20 days after service of such stop order.

clauses.title: An Injured Employee's Civil Action Against an Uninsured Employer
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 3706 states that if an employer fails to secure the payment of compensation, an injured employee (or the employee's dependents) may bring a civil action at law against that employer for damages, as if the workers' compensation division of the Labor Code did not apply — meaning the ordinary exclusive-remedy bar on suing an employer directly does not apply where the employer has failed to secure coverage. Labor Code § 3707 further allows the employee or dependents to attach the employer's property, at any time on or after the action is filed, in an amount fixed by the court, to secure payment of an eventual judgment. Labor Code § 3708 then shifts the burden of proof in that civil action: it is presumed the injury directly resulted from and grew out of the employer's negligence, and the employer bears the burden of rebutting that presumption; the statute also removes the defenses of contributory negligence, assumption of risk, and the fellow-servant rule for the employer in that action, and states that no contract or regulation may restore any of those defenses to the employer.
clauses.gap: Sections 3706, 3707, and 3708 are three separate, independently numbered sections of the same statutory chapter (Chapter 4, Compensation Insurance and Security), so while each was independently fetched and verified, they are not independent in the sense of being separately enacted bodies of law — they operate together as one linked remedy scheme. Section 3708's presumption-and-lost-defenses rule contains a further cross-reference: the statute states it does not apply to an employer of an employee as defined in Labor Code § 3351(d), with respect to that employee, but does apply to employers of employees described in § 3715(b), with respect to those employees. Neither § 3351(d) nor § 3715(b) was independently fetched or verified in this session, so this document does not state what categories of employer or employee those cross-referenced provisions describe; a reader would need to separately check those two sections to know whether this exception applies to a particular employment relationship. This is one state's statute, stating a fact about the civil remedy and evidentiary consequences California law attaches to an employer's failure to secure coverage generally — not a claim about whether any specific employer failed to secure coverage or that any specific employee's action would succeed.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3706 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3706
citations.quote: If any employer fails to secure the payment of compensation, any injured employee or his dependents may bring an action at law against such employer for damages, as if this division did not apply.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3707 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3707
citations.quote: The injured employee or his dependents may in such action attach the property of the employer, at any time upon or after the institution of such action, in an amount fixed by the court, to secure the payment of any judgment which is ultimately obtained.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3708 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3708
citations.quote: In such action it is presumed that the injury to the employee was a direct result and grew out of the negligence of the employer, and the burden of proof is upon the employer, to rebut the presumption of negligence.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 3708 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3708
citations.quote: It is not a defense to the employer that the employee was guilty of contributory negligence, or assumed the risk of the hazard complained of, or that the injury was caused by the negligence of a fellow servant. No contract or regulation shall restore to the employer any of the foregoing defenses.

It is not a workers' compensation claim form, is not filed with any employer, insurer, or agency by completing it, does not itself determine whether {{companyName}} has secured coverage or whether any statutory penalty or remedy applies to any specific set of facts, is not a substitute for the actual statutes and regulations it describes, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.]

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body:
Re: Payment of a Deceased Employee's Wages Without Full Probate — {{decedentName}}

This information sheet describes California Probate Code §§ 13600-13606, a statutory procedure that allows {{companyName}}, as an employer, to pay salary or other compensation owed to {{decedentName}}, a deceased employee, directly to {{survivingSpouseName}} -- as {{decedentName}}'s surviving spouse, or the guardian or conservator of the surviving spouse's estate -- without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of {{decedentName}}'s will. {{decedentName}} died on {{dateOfDeath}}. This document is a companion to, and does not repeat, this document set's separate Unclaimed Final Wages information sheet, which addresses the different scenario where final wages cannot be delivered and eventually escheat to the state under the Unclaimed Property Law; this document instead addresses the affirmative scenario where the employer has been notified of the employee's death and a person entitled under Probate Code §§ 13600-13606 presents a declaration to collect the wages directly. This information sheet states facts about what the statute requires and permits; it does not determine that {{survivingSpouseName}} is, in fact, entitled to collect these particular wages, and it does not tell {{companyName}} what to do about this specific unpaid amount.

clauses.title: The Core Authorization: Collecting a Deceased Spouse's Compensation Without Probate
clauses.body: Probate Code Chapter 4 of the statutes governing passage of property to a surviving spouse without administration -- titled "Collection by Affidavit of Compensation Owed to Deceased Spouse" -- authorizes the surviving spouse of a deceased employee, or the guardian or conservator of that surviving spouse's estate, to collect salary or other compensation an employer owes for the deceased spouse's personal services, including compensation for unused vacation, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of the will. This may be done "at any time after a spouse dies" -- the statute states no waiting period comparable to the 40-day wait that applies to some other small-estate procedures. The amount collectible this way is capped, net, and the statute's own dollar figure is periodically adjusted under a separate Probate Code provision (§ 890) every three years, each April 1, based on a Consumer Price Index formula; the Judicial Council publishes the current adjusted figure. As adjusted, the cap under §§ 13600 and 13601 is $16,625 for a decedent who died before April 1, 2022; $18,450 for a death on or after April 1, 2022 and before April 1, 2025; and $20,875 for a death on or after April 1, 2025, with the next scheduled adjustment on April 1, 2028. Currently identified unpaid compensation for {{decedentName}}, according to {{companyName}}'s records, is {{unpaidWagesAmount}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the procedure's scope, its lack of a stated waiting period, and its dollar cap mechanism -- not a claim about which state's law governs this particular unpaid amount, and not a claim that the surviving spouse at issue qualifies as the statutory surviving spouse or that this specific amount falls within the current cap. This chapter, by its own text and the title of the Part it sits within ("Passage of Property to Surviving Spouse Without Administration"), is limited to a surviving spouse (or that spouse's guardian or conservator) collecting a deceased spouse's own compensation -- it does not name, and this document does not extend it to, other successors or an order of priority among multiple claimants, unlike the separate small-estate personal-property affidavit procedure elsewhere in the Probate Code (§ 13100 et seq.), which does list an order of priority among successors generally. The two citations below come from genuinely independent sources: the statutory text itself (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) and a Judicial Council publication (courts.ca.gov) reporting the currently adjusted dollar figures under the separate CPI-adjustment mechanism in § 890; they were fetched independently and are not subsections of the same document. This document did not independently verify whether registered domestic partners are treated as a "surviving spouse" for purposes of this chapter and does not address that question.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13600, subd. (a)
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 13600, subd. (a)
citations.quote: At any time after a spouse dies, the surviving spouse or the guardian or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse may, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of the will, collect salary or other compensation owed by an employer for personal services of the deceased spouse, including compensation for unused vacation, not in excess of sixteen thousand six hundred twenty-five dollars ($16,625), as adjusted periodically in accordance with Section 890, net.

citations.case: Judicial Council of California, Maximum Amounts for Determining Eligibility for Summary Succession Procedures
citations.cite: Judicial Council of California, Maximum Amounts for Determining Eligibility for Summary Succession Procedures (adjusted amounts under Prob. Code § 890)

clauses.title: What the Declaration Must State
clauses.body: To collect compensation under this chapter, the statute requires that an affidavit or a declaration under penalty of perjury be furnished to the employer stating specified content, including: the decedent's name; the date and place of the decedent's death; a statement identifying the affiant or declarant as either the surviving spouse or the guardian or conservator of the surviving spouse's estate; a statement that the surviving spouse is entitled to the decedent's earnings under the decedent's will or by intestate succession and that no one else has a superior right to them; and a statement that no proceeding is being or has been conducted in California for administration of the decedent's estate. The declaration must also state the statutory dollar cap and any amount already collected from other employers, and must close with a declaration that the statements are true and correct under penalty of perjury under the laws of California. The employer must also be given reasonable proof of the identity of the surviving spouse (and, where applicable, reasonable proof of a guardian's or conservator's appointment).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the declaration's required statutory content -- not a claim that any particular declaration submitted to the employer does, or does not, satisfy these requirements. Both citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (§ 13601) and are not independent of one another. This document quotes the required identity-proof and appointment-proof language only in summary form and does not separately verify the cross-referenced identity-proof standard in § 13104, which this research did not investigate further.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13601, subd. (a)
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 13601, subd. (a)
citations.quote: an affidavit or a declaration under penalty of perjury under the laws of this state shall be furnished to the employer of the deceased spouse stating all of the following: (1) The name of the decedent. (2) The date and place of the decedent’s death. (3) Either of the following, as appropriate: (A) “The affiant or declarant is the surviving spouse of the decedent.” (B) “The affiant or declarant is the guardian or conservator of the estate of the surviving spouse of the decedent.” (4) “The surviving spouse of the decedent is entitled to the earnings of the decedent under the decedent’s will or by intestate succession and no one else has a superior right to the earnings.” (5) “No proceeding is now being or has been conducted in California for administration of the decedent’s estate.”

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13601, subd. (a)(10)
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 13601, subd. (a)(10)
citations.quote: “The affiant or declarant affirms or declares under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.”

clauses.title: The Employer's Duty to Pay Promptly Once the Declaration Is Presented
clauses.body: If the statutory requirements are satisfied, the employer to whom the affidavit or declaration is presented must promptly pay the decedent's earnings, including compensation for unused vacation, up to the applicable statutory cap, to the person who presented it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the employer's payment duty once a conforming declaration is presented -- not a claim that any specific declaration presented to the employer does, in fact, satisfy the statutory requirements referenced in it. This is a single statutory section (§ 13602); no additional independent source was located for this specific point.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13602
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 13602
citations.quote: If the requirements of Section 13600 are satisfied, the employer to whom the affidavit or declaration is presented shall promptly pay the earnings of the decedent, including compensation for unused vacation, as provided in Section 13600, to the person presenting the affidavit or declaration.

clauses.title: The Employer's Discharge From Liability for Good-Faith Reliance
clauses.body: The statute gives the employer a specific protection: if the requirements for the declaration are satisfied, the employer's receipt of the affidavit or declaration is sufficient acquittance for the compensation paid and discharges the employer from any further liability with respect to that payment. The employer may rely in good faith on the statements in the affidavit or declaration and has no duty to inquire into the truth of any statement in it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the discharge-from-liability rule that applies to an employer paying in good-faith reliance on a conforming declaration -- not a claim that this discharge has, in fact, been triggered for any specific payment the employer has made or is considering. This is a single statutory section (§ 13603); no additional independent source was located for this specific point.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13603
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 13603
citations.quote: If the requirements of Section 13601 are satisfied, receipt by the employer of the affidavit or declaration constitutes sufficient acquittance for the compensation paid pursuant to this chapter and discharges the employer from any further liability with respect to the compensation paid. The employer may rely in good faith on the statements in the affidavit or declaration and has no duty to inquire into the truth of any statement in the affidavit or declaration.

clauses.title: Consequences If the Employer Refuses to Pay
clauses.body: The statute also addresses the other side of the transaction: if the employer refuses to pay as the chapter requires, the surviving spouse may bring an action against the employer to recover the amount the surviving spouse is entitled to receive under the chapter, and the court must award reasonable attorney's fees to the surviving spouse if it finds the employer acted unreasonably in refusing to pay.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the remedy and fee-shifting rule that apply to an employer's refusal to pay under this chapter -- not a claim about whether any refusal by the employer would be found reasonable or unreasonable, and not a claim that any such refusal has occurred. This is a single statutory section (§ 13604, subds. (a)-(b)); no additional independent source was located for this specific point.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13604, subds. (a)-(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 13604, subds. (a)-(b)
citations.quote: (a) If the employer refuses to pay as required by this chapter, the surviving spouse may recover the amount the surviving spouse is entitled to receive under this chapter in an action brought for that purpose against the employer. (b) If an action is brought against the employer under this section, the court shall award reasonable attorney’s fees to the surviving spouse if the court finds that the employer acted unreasonably in refusing to pay as required by this chapter.

clauses.title: This Procedure Does Not Preclude Probate, and the Recipient Remains Accountable
clauses.body: The statute limits what this procedure accomplishes in two ways. First, nothing in the chapter limits the rights of the deceased spouse's heirs or devisees, and payment under the chapter does not preclude later proceedings for administration of the decedent's estate -- collecting compensation this way does not close off probate. Second, the person to whom payment is made remains answerable and accountable for it to the decedent's personal representative and is liable for the amount to any other person with a superior right to it; a person who fraudulently secures payment under the chapter is liable for three times the amount to a person with a superior right. Separately, the statute states that this affidavit/declaration procedure is cumulative: it is in addition to, and not in place of, any other method of collecting compensation owed to a decedent.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that the procedure is non-exclusive and that a recipient remains accountable to the estate and to persons with superior rights -- not a claim about whether the surviving spouse at issue has, or lacks, a superior right to any specific payment. The two citations below come from two separate, independently numbered sections (§§ 13605 and 13606) and are independent of one another; the two subdivisions cited within § 13605, subds. (a) and (b), are not independent of one another.

citations.quote: Nothing in this chapter limits the rights of the heirs or devisees of the deceased spouse. Payment of a decedent’s compensation pursuant to this chapter does not preclude later proceedings for administration of the decedent’s estate.

citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 13606
citations.quote: The procedure provided in this chapter is in addition to, and not in lieu of, any other method of collecting compensation owed to a decedent.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Paid Family Leave (PFL) program, a wage-replacement insurance benefit funded through State Disability Insurance (SDI) payroll deductions and administered by the Employment Development Department (EDD). PFL is a benefit program under the Unemployment Insurance Code, not a leave-granting law, and it operates separately from job-protected leave statutes such as the California Family Rights Act (CFRA) and the federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA). {{employeeName}} may be eligible to draw on PFL benefits during time away from work at {{companyName}} for a qualifying reason, whether or not that time away is separately protected under CFRA, FMLA, or another leave law.

clauses.title: What Paid Family Leave Is
clauses.body: California's Paid Family Leave program — formally called Family Temporary Disability Insurance — is a wage-replacement benefit that is a component of the state's unemployment compensation disability insurance program. It is funded through employee contributions (State Disability Insurance, or SDI, payroll deductions) and is administered in accordance with the policies of that disability insurance program. The Unemployment Insurance Code separately establishes the Employment Development Department (EDD), within the Labor and Workforce Development Agency, as the state agency administering the state's unemployment and disability compensation programs, of which Paid Family Leave is a part.
clauses.gap: The citations to Section 3300(b) and 3300(g) are subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another. Section 301 is a separate, independently numbered section, but it establishes the Employment Development Department generally for the whole Unemployment Insurance Code and doesn't itself mention Paid Family Leave by name — this document infers that 'the department' referenced throughout the Paid Family Leave chapter (for example, in its claim-filing deadline provisions) refers to the EDD established by Section 301, since Paid Family Leave sits within the same code division EDD administers. This document doesn't cover the specific procedure or website for filing a PFL claim with EDD.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 3300(b) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Paid Family Leave chapter, legislative findings
citations.quote: Family Temporary Disability Insurance shall be known as Paid Family Leave.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 3300(g) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Paid Family Leave chapter, legislative findings
citations.quote: The family temporary disability insurance program shall be a component of the state’s unemployment compensation disability insurance program, shall be funded through employee contributions, and shall be administered in accordance with the policies of the state disability insurance program created pursuant to this part.

citations.quote: There is in the Labor and Workforce Development Agency the Employment Development Department, which is vested with the duties, purposes, responsibilities, and jurisdiction heretofore exercised by the State Department of Benefit Payments or the California Health and Human Services Agency with respect to job creation activities.

clauses.title: What Paid Family Leave Benefits Are For
clauses.body: Paid Family Leave provides wage-replacement benefits to workers who take time off work for one of three statutory reasons: to care for a seriously ill child, spouse, parent, grandparent, grandchild, sibling, or domestic partner; to bond with a minor child within one year of the child's birth or placement in connection with foster care or adoption; or to participate in a qualifying exigency related to the covered active duty, or call to covered active duty, of the worker's spouse, domestic partner, child, or parent in the Armed Forces of the United States.
clauses.gap: This is the currently operative text of Section 3301, in effect from January 1, 2026 under Stats. 2025, Ch. 772, Sec. 1 (SB 590) until a conditional repeal on or before July 1, 2028. A later version of this same section, added by Sec. 2 of that same 2025 statute, becomes operative July 1, 2028 and adds a fourth family-care-recipient category, a self-identified 'designated person,' to the list quoted here — this document reflects only the text currently in force, not that future version.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 3301(a)(1) (leginfo text, version operative Jan. 1, 2026)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Paid Family Leave chapter, program purpose and qualifying reasons
citations.quote: Family temporary disability insurance shall provide up to eight weeks of wage replacement benefits to workers who take time off work to care for a seriously ill child, spouse, parent, grandparent, grandchild, sibling, or domestic partner, to bond with a minor child within one year of the birth or placement of the child in connection with foster care or adoption, or to participate in a qualifying exigency related to the covered active duty or call to covered active duty of the individual’s spouse, domestic partner, child, or parent in the Armed Forces of the United States.

clauses.title: Benefit Duration
clauses.body: Family Temporary Disability Insurance (Paid Family Leave) benefits are capped at eight weeks: no more than eight weeks of benefits may be paid within any 12-month period. The maximum amount payable during any disability benefit period is eight times the worker's weekly benefit amount, though in no case can total benefits exceed the total wages the worker was paid during the disability base period.
clauses.gap: Both citations are subsections of the same statutory section, Section 3301, and are not independent of one another. This reflects the currently operative version of Section 3301 (effective January 1, 2026 under Stats. 2025, Ch. 772, Sec. 1); a later version of this same section, not yet operative, is scheduled to take effect July 1, 2028 and retains the identical eight-week duration language as fetched. This document doesn't track how the eight-week figure has changed by amendment in years prior to this currently operative text.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 3301(d) (leginfo text, version operative Jan. 1, 2026)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Paid Family Leave chapter, 12-month duration cap
citations.quote: No more than eight weeks of family temporary disability insurance benefits shall be paid within any 12-month period.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 3301(c) (leginfo text, version operative Jan. 1, 2026)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Paid Family Leave chapter, maximum benefit amount
citations.quote: The maximum amount payable to an individual during any disability benefit period for family temporary disability insurance shall be eight times the individual’s “weekly benefit amount,” but in no case shall the total amount of benefits payable be more than the total wages paid to the individual during the individual’s disability base period.

clauses.title: Wage-Replacement Formula
clauses.body: For periods of disability commencing on or after January 1, 2025, a worker's weekly benefit amount is calculated from the wages paid during the highest-earning quarter of the worker's disability base period. If those quarterly wages are less than $722.50, the weekly benefit amount is a flat $50. If those quarterly wages are $722.50 or more but no more than 70 percent of the state average quarterly wage, the weekly benefit amount equals 90 percent of those quarterly wages divided by 13, capped at the maximum workers' compensation temporary disability indemnity weekly benefit amount set by the Department of Industrial Relations. If those quarterly wages exceed 70 percent of the state average quarterly wage, the weekly benefit amount equals the greater of 70 percent of those quarterly wages divided by 13 (capped the same way) or 63 percent of the state average weekly wage.
clauses.gap: All three citations are subsections of the same statutory section, Section 3301(b)(2), and are not independent of one another. This tiered formula took effect for periods of disability commencing on or after January 1, 2025, replacing a different, lower formula that applied to earlier periods (referenced in this same subdivision as 'the amount provided in Section 2655'), which this document doesn't independently verify or state. This document also doesn't state the current dollar value of the 'state average quarterly wage,' the 'state average weekly wage,' or the Department of Industrial Relations' maximum temporary disability indemnity rate under Labor Code Section 4453 — those figures are set and periodically adjusted outside Section 3301 itself and weren't independently fetched and verified here.

citations.quote: When the amount of wages paid to the individual for employment by employers during the quarter of the individual’s disability base period in which these wages were highest is less than seven hundred twenty-two dollars and fifty cents ($722.50), then fifty dollars ($50).

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 3301(b)(2)(C) (leginfo text, version operative Jan. 1, 2026)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Paid Family Leave chapter, weekly benefit amount, middle tier (90 percent)
citations.quote: When the amount of wages paid to the individual for employment by employers during the quarter of the individual’s disability base period in which these wages were highest is seven hundred twenty-two dollars and fifty cents ($722.50) or more, but 70 percent or less than the state average quarterly wage, then the weekly benefit amount shall be equal to 90 percent of the wages paid to an individual for employment by employers during the quarter of the individual’s disability base period in which these wages were highest, divided by 13, but not exceeding the maximum workers’ compensation temporary disability indemnity weekly benefit amount established by the Department of Industrial Relations pursuant to Section 4453 of the Labor Code.

citations.quote: When the amount of wages paid to the individual for employment by employers during the quarter of the individual’s disability base period in which these wages were highest is more than 70 percent of the state average quarterly wage, the weekly benefit amount shall be equal to the greater of 70 percent of the wages paid to an individual for employment by employers during the quarter of the individual’s disability base period in which these wages were highest, divided by 13, but not exceeding the maximum workers’ compensation temporary disability indemnity weekly benefit amount established by the Department of Industrial Relations pursuant to Section 4453 of the Labor Code, or 63 percent of the state average weekly wage.

clauses.title: How Paid Family Leave Relates to Job-Protected Leave
clauses.body: Paid Family Leave is a wage-replacement benefit, not a job-protection law. The Legislature's own findings draw this distinction: the federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) and CFRA entitle eligible employees working for covered employers to take unpaid, job-protected leave for up to 12 workweeks in a 12-month period, while state disability insurance benefits — of which Paid Family Leave is a part — provide wage replacement for time off but historically did not cover leave to care for a sick or injured family member or leave to bond with a new child. Nothing in the Paid Family Leave chapter is to be construed to abridge the rights and responsibilities conveyed under CFRA or under California's pregnancy disability leave law: Paid Family Leave and job-protected leave run on separate statutory tracks, and a worker may draw PFL wage-replacement benefits whether or not the underlying time away from work is separately job-protected.
clauses.gap: The citations to Section 3300(d) and 3300(e) are subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another; the citation to Section 3301(a)(2) is to a separate, independently numbered section. Section 3300(e)'s description of what state disability insurance benefits 'do not cover' is a legislative finding explaining why the Paid Family Leave program was created, not a statement of Paid Family Leave's own current operative rules — the qualifying reasons Paid Family Leave itself covers are stated separately in Section 3301(a)(1). This document doesn't independently verify whether any CFRA- or FMLA-specific job-protection right attaches to a particular period of time an employee takes while drawing Paid Family Leave benefits; that depends on whether the underlying absence is separately CFRA- or FMLA-qualifying, which is a question for those statutes (addressed in this corpus's separate CFRA document), not for the Paid Family Leave statute itself.

citations.quote: State disability insurance benefits currently provide wage replacement for workers who need time off due to their own nonwork-related injuries, illnesses, or conditions, including pregnancy, that prevent them from working, but do not cover leave to care for a sick or injured child, spouse, parent, grandparent, grandchild, sibling, or domestic partner, or leave to bond with a new child.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Family Code Section 2640 Reimbursement Information Sheet concerns {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, whose marital dissolution or legal separation proceeding is pending, or may be filed, in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes what California Family Code section 2640 says about a right, applied at the time the community estate is divided, to reimbursement for separate-property funds a party traces to the acquisition of property of the community estate — for example, a down payment on a residence acquired during the marriage. This information sheet states what the Family Code says about this reimbursement right in general terms. It does not determine, calculate, or assert that the right applies to {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}'s specific property or contributions, whether any contribution has been adequately traced to a separate property source, or whether any waiver has occurred; those are matters for the court to decide based on the specific facts, or for {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} to resolve by their own written agreement.

clauses.title: What Counts as a "Contribution to the Acquisition of Property" Under Section 2640
clauses.body: Family Code section 2640 defines "contributions to the acquisition of property," as the term is used in that section, to include down payments, payments for improvements, and payments that reduce the principal of a loan used to finance the purchase or improvement of the property. The statute's definition expressly excludes two categories of payment: payments of interest on the loan, and payments made for maintenance, insurance, or taxation of the property. Only a payment falling within the statute's own included categories is a "contribution to the acquisition of property" for purposes of the reimbursement right described in this document's companion clauses.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2640(a), the Legislature's own definitional subdivision, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. This citation is to the same statutory section, 2640, cited by this document's other authority clauses (which quote subdivisions (b) and (c)) — they are not independent of one another; all are different subdivisions of one enacted section. This document does not address how a court or party establishes that a particular payment falls within one category rather than another (for example, distinguishing a payment that reduces loan principal from a blended payment that also includes interest), which the statute's text does not itself resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2640(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statute's own definition of "contributions to the acquisition of property," including its express exclusions
citations.quote: “Contributions to the acquisition of property,” as used in this section, include downpayments, payments for improvements, and payments that reduce the principal of a loan used to finance the purchase or improvement of the property but do not include payments of interest on the loan or payments made for maintenance, insurance, or taxation of the property.

clauses.title: The Right to Reimbursement and the Written-Waiver Requirement
clauses.body: Family Code section 2640 provides that, in the division of the community estate, a party shall be reimbursed for that party's contributions to the acquisition of property of the community property estate to the extent the party traces the contributions to a separate property source. This right does not apply where the party has made a written waiver of the right to reimbursement, or has signed a writing that has the effect of a waiver. Subject to that written-waiver exception, the statute states the reimbursement right in mandatory terms — the reimbursed party "shall be reimbursed" once separate-source contributions to the community acquisition are traced.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2640(b)'s first sentence, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. This citation is to the same statutory section, 2640, cited by this document's companion clauses on the statute's definition (subdivision (a)) and the dollar limit on reimbursement (subdivision (b)'s second sentence, quoted separately) — they are not independent of one another; all are different parts of one enacted section. The statute's own text does not specify what particular language or form a waiver, or a writing that has "the effect of a waiver," must take beyond being written and, where not itself a waiver, signed; this document does not address that question further, nor does it address how a party establishes tracing of a contribution to a separate property source, which the statute's text does not itself define.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2640(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the reimbursement right for traced separate-property contributions to community property, and the written-waiver exception
citations.quote: In the division of the community estate under this division, unless a party has made a written waiver of the right to reimbursement or has signed a writing that has the effect of a waiver, the party shall be reimbursed for the party’s contributions to the acquisition of property of the community property estate to the extent the party traces the contributions to a separate property source.

clauses.title: The Amount of Reimbursement Is Limited to the Contribution Itself
clauses.body: Family Code section 2640 fixes the amount of reimbursement in specific terms: the amount reimbursed shall be without interest or adjustment for change in monetary values, and may not exceed the net value of the property at the time of the division. By its own text, the statute reimburses only the dollar amount of the traced contribution itself, capped at the community property's net value at the time of division — it does not provide for interest on that amount, and it does not adjust the reimbursed amount upward or downward to reflect how the property's value has changed since the contribution was made.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2640(b)'s second sentence, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. This citation is to the same statutory section, 2640, cited by this document's companion clauses on the statute's definition (subdivision (a)) and the reimbursement right and waiver exception (subdivision (b)'s first sentence) — they are not independent of one another; all are different parts of one enacted section. This same without-interest, no-adjustment, net-value-cap sentence also appears verbatim in subdivision (c), addressed in this document's companion clause on contributions to the other spouse's separate property; it is quoted here from subdivision (b) because that is the subdivision governing contributions to community property. This document does not compare this fixed-dollar reimbursement formula to any pro-rata appreciation-sharing formula used in a different doctrinal context, and takes no position on how any such other formula works; it states only what section 2640's own text provides. The statute's text states that reimbursement occurs "in the division of the community estate" but does not itself spell out a sequential mechanics (for example, a required order of operations before other division steps); this document does not characterize the mechanism beyond that statutory phrase.

citations.cite: the statutory limit: reimbursement without interest or adjustment for change in monetary values, capped at the property's net value at the time of division
citations.quote: The amount reimbursed shall be without interest or adjustment for change in monetary values and may not exceed the net value of the property at the time of the division.

clauses.title: A Related but Distinct Rule: Contributions to the Other Spouse's Separate Property
clauses.body: The same statutory section that creates the reimbursement right described in this document's other clauses also addresses a related but distinct situation: a party's separate property contributions to the acquisition of property of the OTHER spouse's separate property estate, made during the marriage. Family Code section 2640 provides that a party shall be reimbursed for such contributions unless there has been a transmutation in writing under the statute governing transmutations, or a written waiver of the right to reimbursement. This document's other clauses concern contributions to the ACQUISITION OF COMMUNITY property; this clause is included only to mark that boundary, so that a contribution to the other spouse's separate estate is not conflated with the community-property reimbursement right this document otherwise describes.

This citation is to the same statutory section, 2640, cited by this document's other authority clauses (subdivisions (a) and (b)) — they are not independent of one another; all are different subdivisions of one enacted section. This document does not address the separate transmutation-in-writing rules that subdivision (c) cross-references (Family Code section 850 and following), which govern a different question — whether property has changed character between separate and community — and are outside this document's scope.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope — Director's Inspection Rights Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a California corporation, and to {{directorName}}'s status as a director of {{companyName}}. It describes the statutory right a California corporation's director has to inspect and copy the corporation's books, records, and documents, and to inspect its physical properties -- a right that belongs to a director personally, arising from the director's own oversight role on the board, and that is distinct from the shareholder's inspection right described in this project's separate Shareholder and Member Inspection Rights information sheet.

This information sheet is educational only. It does not itself constitute a demand on {{companyName}}, and it does not resolve any dispute about whether {{directorName}} is a currently serving director of {{companyName}} at the time inspection is sought. This document is not this project's Corporate Bylaws document, which governs {{companyName}}'s internal affairs generally; this document instead focuses specifically on the director-inspection statute.

clauses.title: Director's Absolute Right to Inspect Books, Records, Documents, and Physical Properties
clauses.body: California's General Corporation Law gives every director an "absolute right" -- that is the statute's own wording, not a court's characterization of it -- at any reasonable time, to inspect and copy all books, records, and documents of every kind, and to inspect the physical properties, of the corporation of which the person is a director, and also of its subsidiary corporations, whether domestic or foreign. On its face, this right is broader in category than a shareholder's separate books-and-records right described elsewhere in this document (which reaches accounting books, records, and minutes of proceedings): the director's right reaches all books, records, and documents of every kind, plus the corporation's physical properties, without that narrower accounting-and-minutes framing. The statute's text does not condition this right on the director stating any purpose at all, unlike the shareholder's right, which the statute expressly limits to a "purpose reasonably related to" the shareholder's interest -- § 1602 contains no comparable qualifying language. Inspection by a director may be made in person or through an agent or attorney, and the right of inspection includes the right to copy and make extracts; the statute does not state any express limit on that agent-or-attorney method. Finally, the statute expressly extends to a director of a foreign corporation that has its principal office in California or that customarily holds its board meetings in California.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine, distinctly-worded director right -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation or about how a court would resolve a dispute over what is "reasonable" timing for a particular inspection. Unlike the shareholder inspection statutes described elsewhere in this document (Corp. Code §§ 1600(d), 1601(b)), which each expressly state that the right "may not be limited by the articles or bylaws," § 1602 contains no equivalent non-waivability sentence of its own; this document does not claim, and did not find support for, a rule that a corporation's articles or bylaws cannot limit a director's own inspection right -- that question is left open rather than assumed either way. This document also does not resolve what counts as a "reasonable time" for a given inspection, or what happens to this right once a person's board service ends, both of which the statute leaves undefined. Section 1602 is a single, undivided statutory paragraph with no lettered subsections, so only one citation is offered below; there is no second subsection of this section to disclose as non-independent of it.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1602 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, director's right to inspect books, records, documents, and physical properties
citations.quote: Every director shall have the absolute right at any reasonable time to inspect and copy all books, records and documents of every kind and to inspect the physical properties of the corporation of which such person is a director and also of its subsidiary corporations, domestic or foreign. Such inspection by a director may be made in person or by agent or attorney and the right of inspection includes the right to copy and make extracts. This section applies to a director of any foreign corporation having its principal office in California or customarily holding meetings of its board in California.

clauses.title: Court Remedy for a Refused Inspection Demand, Read Against a Refused Director Demand
clauses.body: California's inspection chapter gives a court a remedy phrased generally around "a lawful demand for inspection," not phrased around a shareholder's demand specifically: upon refusal of a lawful demand for inspection, the superior court of the proper county may enforce the right of inspection on just and proper conditions, or, for good cause shown, appoint one or more competent inspectors or accountants to audit the corporation's books and records and investigate its property, funds, and affairs (including those of its subsidiaries), and report to the court. This remedy provision is codified in the same chapter of the Corporations Code -- captioned "Rights of Inspection" and spanning sections 1600 through 1605 -- as the director's own inspection right, and its own wording does not single out shareholder demands, so its enforcement mechanism reads as available for a refused director demand as well as a refused shareholder demand.
clauses.gap: Section 1602 does not itself state a remedy or cross-reference the remedy section by number, and the remedy section does not name directors or cite section 1602 specifically -- its "lawful demand for inspection" language is chapter-general wording rather than an explicit statutory cross-reference naming the director's right. This clause's application of that remedy to a refused director demand is therefore a structural reading, based on the statute's placement within the same inspection chapter and the remedy provision's own unqualified wording, not an express statutory statement that the remedy section covers a section 1602 refusal; no court decision confirming this reading was located and verified for this document, so this document does not claim one exists. This corpus's existing Shareholder and Member Inspection Rights information sheet already documents this same remedy section's fuller mechanics as applied to a refused shareholder demand -- the officers'-and-agents' duty to produce records to a court-appointed inspector on penalty of contempt, and the default rule that the person who sought the audit bears its expense unless the court shifts that cost to the corporation -- and this document does not restate those additional subsections separately. The chapter-heading citation below is pulled from the same California Legislative Information display page as section 1602 itself, offered only as evidence of the Corporations Code's own chapter organization, not as an independent source from the statutory text it appears alongside.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1603(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, court enforcement of a refused inspection demand
citations.quote: Upon refusal of a lawful demand for inspection, the superior court of the proper county, may enforce the right of inspection with just and proper conditions or may, for good cause shown, appoint one or more competent inspectors or accountants to audit the books and records kept in this state and investigate the property, funds and affairs of any domestic corporation or any foreign corporation keeping records in this state and of any subsidiary corporation thereof, domestic or foreign, keeping records in this state and to report thereon in such manner as the court may direct.

Corp. Code § 1602), and the related court remedy for a refused demand. It is not a completed demand, does not itself compel {{companyName}} to permit any inspection, and does not constitute legal advice.
