clauses.title: Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Preliminary and Final Declarations of Disclosure — Information Sheet concerns the marriage of {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, who were married on {{marriageDate}}, in connection with a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, legal separation, or nullity contemplated in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes California's statutory financial-disclosure framework under Family Code sections 2100 through 2113 — the Legislature's stated purpose for requiring disclosure, what a preliminary declaration of disclosure and a final declaration of disclosure must each contain and when each must be served, the limited circumstances in which the parties may mutually waive the final declaration, and the consequences the statute states for noncompliance. It is not itself a preliminary or final declaration of disclosure, does not itself satisfy either party's disclosure obligations, and does not determine what disclosure is legally required in any specific case; only the actual Judicial Council forms, completed, executed under penalty of perjury, and served, can do that.

clauses.title: The Legislature's Stated Purpose: Full Disclosure and a Continuing Duty to Update
clauses.body: California's Family Code sets out the Legislature's own findings and declared purpose for the mandatory financial-disclosure framework that applies in dissolution, legal-separation, and nullity proceedings. The Legislature states that it is the policy of the State of California to marshal, preserve, and protect community and quasi-community assets and liabilities that exist at the date of separation so as to avoid dissipation of the community estate before distribution; to ensure fair and sufficient child and spousal support awards; and to achieve a proper division of community and quasi-community assets and liabilities on dissolution or nullity of marriage or legal separation of the parties. The Legislature further states that sound public policy favors reducing the adversarial nature of marital dissolution and its attendant costs by fostering full disclosure and cooperative discovery, and that, to promote this policy, a full and accurate disclosure of all assets and liabilities in which one or both parties have or may have an interest — together with a disclosure of all income and expenses — must be made in the early stages of a dissolution or legal-separation proceeding, regardless of whether an asset or liability is characterized as community or separate. The statute expressly states that each party has a continuing duty to immediately, fully, and accurately update and augment that disclosure to the extent there have been any material changes, so that by the time the parties reach an agreement resolving these issues, or by the time of trial on these issues, each party has full and complete knowledge of the relevant underlying facts.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's stated legislative purpose for its financial-disclosure framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage, dissolution, or legal separation, and not a claim about what disclosure is legally required in any specific case. This clause quotes subdivisions (a) through (c) of a single statutory section (Family Code section 2100); no additional independent source was located for it, and the three subdivisions are not independent of one another. This clause states the statute's own findings and its continuing-duty language; it does not itself describe the mechanics of the preliminary or final declaration of disclosure, which are addressed in other clauses of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2100(a)-(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the Legislature's findings and stated purpose for requiring disclosure, and each party's continuing duty to update
citations.quote: (a) It is the policy of the State of California (1) to marshal, preserve, and protect community and quasi-community assets and liabilities that exist at the date of separation so as to avoid dissipation of the community estate before distribution, (2) to ensure fair and sufficient child and spousal support awards, and (3) to achieve a division of community and quasi-community assets and liabilities on the dissolution or nullity of marriage or legal separation of the parties as provided under California law. (b) Sound public policy further favors the reduction of the adversarial nature of marital dissolution and the attendant costs by fostering full disclosure and cooperative discovery. (c) In order to promote this public policy, a full and accurate disclosure of all assets and liabilities in which one or both parties have or may have an interest must be made in the early stages of a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties, regardless of the characterization as community or separate, together with a disclosure of all income and expenses of the parties. Moreover, each party has a continuing duty to immediately, fully, and accurately update and augment that disclosure to the extent there have been any material changes so that at the time the parties enter into an agreement for the resolution of any of these issues, or at the time of trial on these issues, each party will have a full and complete knowledge of the relevant underlying facts.

clauses.title: Two Separate, Sequential Disclosures Are Required: Preliminary and Final
clauses.body: California law requires each party to a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation to serve on the other party two separate statutory disclosures: a preliminary declaration of disclosure, and — unless waived or not required under a statutory exception — a final declaration of disclosure. Each party must also file proof of service of each declaration with the court. The preliminary declaration and the final declaration are governed by distinct statutory sections, each with its own content requirements, timing, and (for the final declaration only) a mutual-waiver mechanism, addressed in other clauses of this document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific California procedural requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific marriage or dissolution, and not a claim about whether a specific document filed in a specific case satisfies this requirement. This is a single statutory section (section 2103); no additional independent source was located for it. This clause references, but does not independently describe, the statutory exceptions this section itself cross-references for waiving service of the preliminary declaration (section 2107, addressed in a separate clause of this document) and for when service is not required at all (section 2110, governing default judgments) — section 2110's default-judgment-specific procedure was not independently re-verified for this document and is not described here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2103 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the requirement to serve both a preliminary and a final declaration of disclosure, and to file proof of service of each
citations.quote: In order to provide full and accurate disclosure of all assets and liabilities in which one or both parties may have an interest, each party to a proceeding for dissolution of the marriage or legal separation of the parties shall serve on the other party a preliminary declaration of disclosure under Section 2104, unless service of the preliminary declaration of disclosure is waived as provided in Section 2107 or is not required pursuant to Section 2110, and a final declaration of disclosure under Section 2105, unless service of the final declaration of disclosure is waived pursuant to Section 2105, 2107, or 2110, and shall file proof of service of each with the court.

clauses.title: The Preliminary Declaration of Disclosure: Required Content and Service Deadlines
clauses.body: The preliminary declaration of disclosure must be executed under penalty of perjury on a form prescribed by the Judicial Council, and must include all tax returns filed by the declarant within the two years preceding the date the party served the declaration. The statute states that the commission of perjury on the preliminary declaration of disclosure may be grounds for setting aside the judgment, in addition to any other civil or criminal remedies otherwise available for perjury. The preliminary declaration must set forth, with enough particularity that a person of reasonable and ordinary intelligence can ascertain it: the identity of all assets in which the declarant has or may have an interest and all liabilities for which the declarant is or may be liable, regardless of whether the asset or liability is characterized as community, quasi-community, or separate property; and, where property is not solely owned by one or both parties, the declarant's percentage of ownership in each asset and percentage of obligation for each liability (the declarant may also, but is not required to, state a characterization of each asset or liability). On timing: the petitioner must serve the preliminary declaration of disclosure either concurrently with the petition for dissolution or legal separation, or within 60 days of filing the petition (or, where the summons and petition were served by publication or posting and the respondent files a response before a default judgment is entered, within 30 days of that response being filed); the respondent must serve it either concurrently with the response to the petition, or within 60 days of filing the response. These time periods may be extended by the parties' written agreement or by court order.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific California content and timing requirements — not a claim about what a specific party's disclosure must contain, or about whether any specific service was timely, in any actual case. This clause quotes three subdivisions of a single statutory section (section 2104(a), (c), and (f)); they are not independent of one another, though each states a distinct rule (the perjury/tax-return content requirement, the particularity-of-content standard, and the service deadlines). This clause does not describe section 2104(b) (the rule against filing the preliminary declaration with the court absent a court order) or section 2104(d)-(e) (the right to amend without leave of court, and the accompanying income and expense declaration requirement) — those subdivisions were fetched as part of the same primary-source text but are not restated or quoted here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2104(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the perjury execution requirement, the two-year tax return content requirement, and the perjury-based ground for setting aside a judgment
citations.quote: Except by court order for good cause, as provided in Section 2107, or when service of the preliminary declaration of disclosure is not required pursuant to Section 2110, in the time period set forth in subdivision (f), each party shall serve on the other party a preliminary declaration of disclosure, executed under penalty of perjury on a form prescribed by the Judicial Council. The commission of perjury on the preliminary declaration of disclosure may be grounds for setting aside the judgment, or any part or parts thereof, pursuant to Chapter 10 (commencing with Section 2120), in addition to any and all other remedies, civil or criminal, that otherwise are available under law for the commission of perjury. The preliminary declaration of disclosure shall include all tax returns filed by the declarant within the two years prior to the date that the party served the declaration.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2104(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the particularity standard for identifying assets, liabilities, and ownership/obligation percentages
citations.quote: The preliminary declaration of disclosure shall set forth with sufficient particularity, that a person of reasonable and ordinary intelligence can ascertain, all of the following: (1) The identity of all assets in which the declarant has or may have an interest and all liabilities for which the declarant is or may be liable, regardless of the characterization of the asset or liability as community, quasi-community, or separate. (2) The declarant’s percentage of ownership in each asset and percentage of obligation for each liability when property is not solely owned by one or both of the parties. The preliminary declaration may also set forth the declarant’s characterization of each asset or liability.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2104(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the service deadlines for the petitioner and respondent, and the extension mechanism
citations.quote: The petitioner shall serve the other party with the preliminary declaration of disclosure either concurrently with the petition for dissolution or legal separation, or within 60 days of filing the petition. When a petitioner serves the summons and petition by publication or posting pursuant to court order and the respondent files a response prior to a default judgment being entered, the petitioner shall serve the other party with the preliminary declaration of disclosure within 30 days of the response being filed. The respondent shall serve the other party with the preliminary declaration of disclosure either concurrently with the response to the petition, or within 60 days of filing the response. The time periods specified in this subdivision may be extended by written agreement of the parties or by court order.

clauses.title: The Final Declaration of Disclosure: Required Content, Timing, and the Mutual Waiver
clauses.body: Unless the parties mutually waive it, each party (or that party's attorney) must serve on the other party a final declaration of disclosure and a current income and expense declaration, executed under penalty of perjury on a form prescribed by the Judicial Council. The statute ties the service deadline to whichever of two events occurs: absent a court order for good cause, service must occur before or at the time the parties enter into an agreement resolving property or support issues other than pendente lite support, or, if the case goes to trial, no later than 45 days before the first assigned trial date. As with the preliminary declaration, the statute states that the commission of perjury on the final declaration of disclosure may be grounds for setting aside the judgment, in addition to any other civil or criminal remedies otherwise available for perjury. The final declaration must include all material facts and information regarding: the characterization of all assets and liabilities; the valuation of all assets contended to be community property or in which the community is contended to have an interest; the amounts of all obligations contended to be community obligations or for which the community is contended to have liability; and the earnings, accumulations, and expenses of each party as set forth in the income and expense declaration. California law does allow the parties to waive the final declaration of disclosure, but only by mutual stipulation, executed under penalty of perjury, entered in open court or by separate stipulation — and only where that waiver includes specific representations: that both parties have complied with the preliminary-declaration statute and have completed and exchanged their preliminary declarations; that both parties have completed and exchanged a current income and expense declaration covering all material facts about that party's earnings, accumulations, and expenses; that both parties have fully complied with the parties' ongoing disclosure obligations under Family Code section 2102 and have fully augmented their preliminary declarations with all material facts on characterization, valuation, and the amount of obligations; that the waiver is knowing, intelligent, and voluntary; and that each party understands the waiver does not limit the parties' underlying legal disclosure obligations — it is only a sworn statement that those obligations have already been fulfilled — and that noncompliance with those obligations will still result in the court setting aside the judgment.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific California content, timing, and waiver requirements — not a claim about what a specific party's final declaration must contain, whether any specific waiver would be valid, or whether any specific service was timely, in any actual case. This clause quotes three subdivisions of a single statutory section (section 2105(a), (b), and (d)); they are not independent of one another, though each states a distinct rule (the service obligation, deadline, and perjury consequence; the required content; and the mutual-waiver mechanism with its required representations). This clause does not restate section 2105(c) (the court's authority, in setting aside a judgment for noncompliance with this section, to limit the set-aside to the portions of the judgment materially affected by the nondisclosure) — that subdivision was fetched as part of the same primary-source text but is addressed only in this document's separate noncompliance-consequences clause. The waiver's own required representation of compliance with Family Code section 2102 is stated here because it is one of the waiver's five representations; section 2102 itself is not independently quoted or verified as a citation in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2105(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the service obligation, the two triggering deadlines, and the perjury-based ground for setting aside a judgment
citations.quote: Except by court order for good cause, before or at the time the parties enter into an agreement for the resolution of property or support issues other than pendente lite support, or, if the case goes to trial, no later than 45 days before the first assigned trial date, each party, or the attorney for the party in this matter, shall serve on the other party a final declaration of disclosure and a current income and expense declaration, executed under penalty of perjury on a form prescribed by the Judicial Council, unless the parties mutually waive the final declaration of disclosure. The commission of perjury on the final declaration of disclosure by a party may be grounds for setting aside the judgment, or any part or parts thereof, pursuant to Chapter 10 (commencing with Section 2120), in addition to any and all other remedies, civil or criminal, that otherwise are available under law for the commission of perjury.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2105(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the required content of the final declaration of disclosure
citations.quote: The final declaration of disclosure shall include all of the following information: (1) All material facts and information regarding the characterization of all assets and liabilities. (2) All material facts and information regarding the valuation of all assets that are contended to be community property or in which it is contended the community has an interest. (3) All material facts and information regarding the amounts of all obligations that are contended to be community obligations or for which it is contended the community has liability. (4) All material facts and information regarding the earnings, accumulations, and expenses of each party that have been set forth in the income and expense declaration.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2105(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mutual-waiver mechanism and its five required representations
citations.quote: The parties may stipulate to a mutual waiver of the requirements of subdivision (a) concerning the final declaration of disclosure, by execution of a waiver under penalty of perjury entered into in open court or by separate stipulation. The waiver shall include all of the following representations: (1) Both parties have complied with Section 2104 and the preliminary declarations of disclosure have been completed and exchanged. (2) Both parties have completed and exchanged a current income and expense declaration, that includes all material facts and information regarding that party’s earnings, accumulations, and expenses. (3) Both parties have fully complied with Section 2102 and have fully augmented the preliminary declarations of disclosure, including disclosure of all material facts and information regarding the characterization of all assets and liabilities, the valuation of all assets that are contended to be community property or in which it is contended the community has an interest, and the amounts of all obligations that are contended to be community obligations or for which it is contended the community has liability. (4) The waiver is knowingly, intelligently, and voluntarily entered into by each of the parties. (5) Each party understands that this waiver does not limit the legal disclosure obligations of the parties, but rather is a statement under penalty of perjury that those obligations have been fulfilled. Each party further understands that noncompliance with those obligations will result in the court setting aside the judgment.

clauses.title: Consequences of Noncompliance: Mandatory Monetary Sanctions and Setting Aside the Judgment
clauses.body: California's disclosure statute states specific consequences for a party's noncompliance, separate from the perjury-based grounds for setting aside a judgment described elsewhere in this document. First, sanctions: if a party fails to comply with any provision of the disclosure chapter, the statute states that the court shall, in addition to any other remedy provided by law, impose money sanctions against the noncomplying party, in an amount sufficient to deter repetition of the conduct, and that the sanction shall include reasonable attorney's fees, costs incurred, or both, unless the court finds the noncomplying party acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the sanction unjust. Second, setting aside the judgment: except as otherwise provided, if a court enters a judgment when the parties have failed to comply with all of the chapter's disclosure requirements, the statute states that the court shall set aside the judgment, and that the failure to comply does not constitute harmless error. A narrower rule applies where the complying party has already obtained a court-granted voluntary waiver of receiving the noncomplying party's preliminary declaration: in that circumstance, the court sets aside the judgment only at the complying party's request, unless the motion to set aside is instead based on actual fraud that kept the defrauded party ignorant of, or fraudulently prevented from fully participating in, the proceeding, or on perjury (as defined in Penal Code section 118) in the preliminary or final declaration, in the waiver of the final declaration, or in the current income and expense statement.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific California consequences for noncompliance with the disclosure requirements — not a claim about whether any specific party's disclosure was or was not compliant, or about what remedy a court would actually order in any specific case. This clause quotes two subdivisions of a single statutory section (section 2107(c) and (d)); they are not independent of one another. This clause does not describe section 2107(a)-(b) (the complying party's procedural options — requesting further particularity, then moving to compel a further response, to preclude evidence, or to obtain a voluntary waiver of the noncomplying party's declaration — that precede the sanctions and set-aside consequences in subdivisions (c)-(d)) or section 2107(e) (the court's authority, on a motion to set aside, to order production of the exchanged declarations, which are otherwise returned to the parties rather than filed with the court) — those subdivisions were fetched as part of the same primary-source text but are not restated or quoted here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2107(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mandatory money-sanctions remedy for noncompliance with any provision of the disclosure chapter
citations.quote: If a party fails to comply with any provision of this chapter, the court shall, in addition to any other remedy provided by law, impose money sanctions against the noncomplying party. Sanctions shall be in an amount sufficient to deter repetition of the conduct or comparable conduct, and shall include reasonable attorney’s fees, costs incurred, or both, unless the court finds that the noncomplying party acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2107(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mandatory set-aside-the-judgment consequence for a failure to comply with the disclosure requirements, and its exceptions
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this subdivision, if a court enters a judgment when the parties have failed to comply with all disclosure requirements of this chapter, the court shall set aside the judgment. The failure to comply with the disclosure requirements does not constitute harmless error. If the court granted the complying party’s voluntary waiver of receipt of the noncomplying party’s preliminary declaration of disclosure pursuant to paragraph (3) of subdivision (b), the court shall set aside the judgment only at the request of the complying party, unless the motion to set aside the judgment is based on one of the following: (1) Actual fraud if the defrauded party was kept in ignorance or in some other manner was fraudulently prevented from fully participating in the proceeding. (2) Perjury, as defined in Section 118 of the Penal Code, in the preliminary or final declaration of disclosure, in the waiver of the final declaration of disclosure, or in the current income and expense statement.

clauses.body:

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This document states California's statutory default rules on member dissociation for {{companyName}}, a limited liability company formed under the laws of {{stateOfFormation}}: the events that cause a member of {{companyName}} to be legally dissociated, the default legal effect of dissociation on that person's voting, management, and economic rights, and whether {{companyName}} continues in existence afterward. It is a statement of the applicable statute's own default rules, not advice about how any particular member's dissociation should be handled. The members of {{companyName}} remain free to adopt different rules in a written operating agreement to the extent the statute allows.

clauses.title: Statutory Dissociation Triggers
clauses.body: Under California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a member of an LLC is legally "dissociated" — meaning that person's status as a member ends — on the occurrence of any of a specific list of statutory events. These include: the LLC's having notice of the member's express will to withdraw (or a later withdrawal date the member specifies); an event the operating agreement itself designates as causing dissociation; the member's expulsion under the operating agreement's own terms, by unanimous consent of the other members under specified circumstances (including an unlawful continuation with that member, a full transfer of the member's transferable interest other than for security or an unforeclosed charging order, or certain dissolution-related events for a corporate or entity member), or by judicial order on specified grounds (wrongful conduct materially affecting the LLC, persistent material breach, or conduct making it impracticable to carry on with the member); for an individual member, death or, in a member-managed LLC, the appointment of a guardian or conservator or a judicial finding of incapacity; in a member-managed LLC, the member becoming a debtor in bankruptcy; for a member that is a trust or an estate, distribution of that trust's or estate's entire interest (other than by a mere trustee or representative substitution); for any other non-individual member, the member's own termination; the LLC's participation in certain mergers where the member ceases to be a member; and the LLC's own termination.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory list of events that dissociate a member from a California LLC — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This is a distinct statute from the one governing dissociation of a partner from a California general partnership (the Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, cited elsewhere in this library under a different set of section numbers); LLC and general-partnership dissociation are separate statutory schemes in California, even though several of the underlying trigger events sound similar. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (Section 17706.02); they are not independent of one another.

citations.case: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, dissociation by express will to withdraw, agreed event, or agreement-based expulsion
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.02(a)-(c)
citations.quote: A person is dissociated as a member from a limited liability company when any of the following occur: (a) The limited liability company has notice of the person’s express will to withdraw as a member, but, if the person specified a withdrawal date later than the date the limited liability company had notice, on that later date. (b) An event stated in the operating agreement as causing the person’s dissociation to occur. (c) The person is expelled as a member pursuant to the operating agreement.

citations.case: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, dissociation of an individual member by death and, in a member-managed LLC, by bankruptcy
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.02(f)-(g)
citations.quote: (f) In the case of a person who is an individual, if either of the following applies: (1) The person dies. (2) In a member-managed limited liability company if either of the following applies: (A) A guardian or general conservator for the person is appointed. (B) There is a judicial order that the person has otherwise become incapable of performing the person’s duties as a member under this title or the operating agreement. (g) In a member-managed limited liability company, the person becomes a debtor in bankruptcy.

clauses.title: Power to Dissociate and Wrongful Dissociation
clauses.body: Under California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a member always has the power to dissociate by express withdrawal, even if doing so is wrongful. Dissociation is wrongful only in specific circumstances the statute defines — chiefly, when it breaches an express provision of the operating agreement, or when it occurs before the LLC terminates and results from the member's own express withdrawal, judicial expulsion, becoming a debtor in bankruptcy, or (for an entity member) dissolving or terminating. A member who wrongfully dissociates is liable to the LLC and to the other members for any damages the dissociation causes, on top of any other debt, obligation, or liability the member already owes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's actual default rule distinguishing a member's power to dissociate (which always exists) from the right to do so without liability (which is narrower) — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. The statute's definition of "wrongful" dissociation lists several specific circumstances beyond the ones summarized here. All citations below are subsections of a single statutory section (Section 17706.01); no additional independent source was found for this specific point beyond it.

citations.case: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, a member's power to dissociate
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.01(a)
citations.quote: A person has the power to dissociate as a member at any time, rightfully or wrongfully, by withdrawing as a member by express will pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 17706.02.

citations.case: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, liability for wrongful dissociation
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.01(c)
citations.quote: A person that wrongfully dissociates as a member is liable to the limited liability company and to the other members for any damages caused by the dissociation.

clauses.title: Effect of Dissociation on a Member's Rights
clauses.body: Under California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, when a member is dissociated, three things happen by default: the person's right to vote or otherwise participate in managing the LLC ends; if the LLC is member-managed, that person's fiduciary duties as a member end going forward (though not for matters or events that arose before dissociation); and any transferable interest the person held as a member is thereafter held solely as a transferee — an economic-interest holder with a right to distributions, but without a member's voting or management rights. Dissociation does not, by itself, discharge the person from any debt, obligation, or other liability to the LLC or the other members that the person already incurred while a member.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default status of a dissociated LLC member under California law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (Section 17706.03); they are not independent of one another.

citations.case: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, loss of voting/management rights and transferee-only status on dissociation
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.03(a)
citations.quote: When a person is dissociated as a member of a limited liability company all of the following apply: (1) The person’s right to vote or participate as a member in the management and conduct of the limited liability company’s activities terminates. (2) If the limited liability company is member-managed, the person’ s fiduciary duties as a member end with regard to matters arising and events occurring after the person’s dissociation. (3) Subject to Section 17705.04 and Article 10 (commencing with Section 17710.01), any transferable interest owned by the person immediately before dissociation in the person’s capacity as a member is owned by the person solely as a transferee.

citations.case: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, dissociation does not discharge pre-existing debts or liabilities
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17706.03(b)
citations.quote: A person’s dissociation as a member of a limited liability company does not of itself discharge the person from any debt, obligation, or other liability to the limited liability company or the other members that the person incurred while a member.

clauses.title: Dissociation Does Not Itself Dissolve the LLC
clauses.body: Under California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, an LLC dissolves only on the occurrence of one of a specific, exhaustive list of statutory events: an event the operating agreement or articles of organization designate; a vote of members holding 50% or more of the voting interests (or a higher threshold the governing documents set); 90 consecutive days with no members at all; or a court's decree of judicial dissolution. An individual member's dissociation — by withdrawal, expulsion, death, bankruptcy, or any of the other triggers listed above — is not itself one of those listed events, so a member's dissociation does not by itself dissolve the LLC. The LLC continues by default with its remaining members unless the dissociation happens to coincide with one of the statute's actual dissolution triggers (for example, the departing member was the sole member) or the operating agreement designates that particular dissociation as a dissolution event.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's LLC act keeps a member's exit legally separate from the company's continued existence — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC. This citation is to a different, independently numbered section (Section 17707.01) than the dissociation-trigger and dissociation-effect sections cited above (Sections 17706.01-17706.03), so it is an independent source for this specific point.

citations.case: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, exhaustive list of statutory dissolution triggers
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17707.01
citations.quote: A limited liability company is dissolved, and its activities shall be wound up, upon the happening of the first to occur of the following: (a) On the happening of an event set forth in a written operating agreement or the articles of organization.

clauses.title: No General Statutory Buyout on Ordinary Dissociation
clauses.body: California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act does not give an ordinarily dissociated member — one who withdraws, is expelled, dies, or is otherwise dissociated under the statute's dissociation-trigger list — a default statutory right to force the LLC or its remaining members to buy out that person's interest. The statute's own stated consequence of ordinary dissociation is that the person's interest continues to be held solely as a transferee, entitled only to distributions the LLC actually makes, with no built-in cash-out mechanism. The one buyout mechanism the statute does provide is narrower and different in kind: in a lawsuit for judicial dissolution, the other members may avoid dissolution by purchasing the suing member's interest for cash at its fair market value, with a court-supervised appraisal process if the parties cannot agree on that value. That mechanism is triggered only by a member's own lawsuit seeking judicial dissolution on specific statutory grounds — it is not a general buyout right that arises whenever a member dissociates.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's current LLC act does not adopt a general default buyout right for a dissociated member's interest the way some other business-entity statutes (including California's own modern partnership statute, cited elsewhere in this library) provide fuller default buyout mechanisms for departing owners — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific LLC, and not a claim that no other state's LLC statute provides a broader default buyout. The two citations below are to different, independently numbered sections (Section 17706.03 and Section 17707.03) and are independent sources for this point; note that the second citation describes a buyout tied specifically to a judicial-dissolution lawsuit, not to dissociation generally, and this document does not claim the statute provides any dissociation-triggered buyout beyond what these sections actually state.

(2) If the limited liability company is member-managed, the person’ s fiduciary duties as a member end with regard to matters arising and events occurring after the person’s dissociation. (3) Subject to Section 17705.04 and Article 10 (commencing with Section 17710.01), any transferable interest owned by the person immediately before dissociation in the person’s capacity as a member is owned by the person solely as a transferee.

clauses.title: Purpose and Overview
clauses.body: This document states what California's Invasion of Privacy Act, Penal Code §§ 630-638.55 ("the Act"), provides regarding the recording, interception, and disclosure of communications. The Act is a distinct body of law from the workplace-monitoring principles addressed elsewhere in this corpus, which concern an employer's own computer, email, and network systems; the Act instead governs the recording, wiretapping, and interception of communications more broadly -- including telephone calls and in-person conversations -- regardless of whether an employment relationship is involved, and it carries both criminal penalties and a private civil right of action. This document states the Act's text and structure; it does not identify what law governs any particular recording, call, or conversation, and it does not state whether any specific practice of {{companyName}} complies with the Act.

clauses.title: Wiretapping and Unauthorized Connection to Communication Lines
clauses.body: Penal Code § 631(a) separately prohibits two kinds of conduct. First, it prohibits intentionally tapping, or making any unauthorized connection -- whether physical, electrical, acoustic, inductive, or otherwise -- with any telegraph or telephone wire, line, cable, or instrument, including the wire, line, cable, or instrument of an internal telephonic communication system. Second, and separately, it prohibits willfully and without the consent of all parties to the communication, or in any other unauthorized manner, reading or attempting to read, or learning the contents or meaning of, a message, report, or communication while it is in transit or while it is being sent from, or received at, a place within California. Section 631(a) further prohibits using, or attempting to use, information obtained through either of those acts, and prohibits aiding, agreeing with, employing, or conspiring with another person to do any act the section describes. A violation is punishable by a fine not exceeding $2,500, by imprisonment in county jail not exceeding one year, by imprisonment under Penal Code § 1170(h), or by both a fine and imprisonment; a person previously convicted of violating § 631 or §§ 632, 632.5, 632.6, 632.7, or 636 faces an enhanced fine not exceeding $10,000, within the same range of imprisonment. Section 631(b) exempts public utilities and telephone companies (and their officers, employees, and agents) acting for the construction, maintenance, or operation of communications services and facilities, the use of equipment furnished under a public utility's tariffs, and telephonic communication systems used exclusively within a state or local correctional facility.
clauses.gap: The two prohibited-conduct quotes and the penalty quote below are all drawn from a single subdivision, § 631(a), of a single statutory section; they are not independent of one another. This clause does not restate § 631(b)'s exemptions in the statute's own full defined-term detail (e.g., its cross-reference to the "telephone company" definition in § 638(c)(3)), and it does not address how § 631 has been applied to non-telephonic technologies such as VoIP, text messaging, or internet-based communications -- that was not researched here.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 631(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 631(a)
citations.quote: intentionally taps, or makes any unauthorized connection, whether physically, electrically, acoustically, inductively, or otherwise, with any telegraph or telephone wire, line, cable, or instrument

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 631(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 631(a)
citations.quote: willfully and without the consent of all parties to the communication, or in any unauthorized manner, reads, or attempts to read, or to learn the contents or meaning of any message, report, or communication while the same is in transit

citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 631(a)

clauses.title: Recording or Eavesdropping on a Confidential Communication -- Consent of All Parties
clauses.body: Penal Code § 632(a) prohibits a person from intentionally, and without the consent of all parties to a confidential communication, using an electronic amplifying or recording device to eavesdrop upon or record that confidential communication -- whether the communication is carried on in the parties' presence or by telegraph, telephone, or other device, with an exception for radio. This is the source of what is commonly called California's "all-party" or "two-party" consent rule: § 632(a)'s own text conditions the prohibition on the consent of all parties to the confidential communication, not merely one of them, which is a stricter consent requirement than the one-party-consent standard used under federal wiretap law and in a number of other states. A first violation is punishable by a fine not exceeding $2,500 per violation, by imprisonment in county jail not exceeding one year or in state prison, or by both; a person previously convicted of violating § 632 or §§ 631, 632.5, 632.6, 632.7, or 636 faces an enhanced fine not exceeding $10,000 per violation, within the same range of imprisonment. Section 632(e) exempts public utilities (and their officers, employees, and agents) acting for the construction, maintenance, or operation of communications services and facilities, the use of equipment furnished under a public utility's tariffs, and telephonic communication systems used exclusively within a state or local correctional facility; § 632(f) separately exempts the use of hearing aids and similar devices by persons with impaired hearing.
clauses.gap: The core-prohibition quote and the repeat-offender penalty quote below are both drawn from a single subdivision, § 632(a), of a single statutory section; they are not independent of one another. This clause states § 632(a)'s all-party consent requirement as the statute's own text frames it; it does not address how courts have applied that requirement to specific recording methods or technologies (e.g., automated call-recording announcements, single-party recording apps, or out-of-state calls into California), which was not researched here.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 632(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 632(a)
citations.quote: A person who, intentionally and without the consent of all parties to a confidential communication, uses an electronic amplifying or recording device to eavesdrop upon or record the confidential communication, whether the communication is carried on among the parties in the presence of one another or by means of a telegraph, telephone, or other device, except a radio, shall be punished by a fine not exceeding two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500) per violation, or imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or in the state prison, or by both that fine and imprisonment.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 632(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 632(a)
citations.quote: If the person has previously been convicted of a violation of this section or Section 631, 632.5, 632.6, 632.7, or 636, the person shall be punished by a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000) per violation, by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or in the state prison, or by both that fine and imprisonment.

clauses.title: "Confidential Communication" and "Person" Defined
clauses.body: Penal Code § 632(c) defines "confidential communication," for purposes of § 632, as any communication carried on in circumstances that may reasonably indicate that a party to it desires the communication to be confined to the parties to it. The definition expressly excludes a communication made in a public gathering, a communication made in any legislative, judicial, executive, or administrative proceeding open to the public, and any other circumstance in which the parties to the communication may reasonably expect that it may be overheard or recorded. Section 632(b) defines "person," for purposes of § 632, broadly to include an individual, business association, partnership, corporation, limited liability company, or other legal entity, and an individual acting or purporting to act for or on behalf of a federal, state, or local government or subdivision of one -- but excludes an individual who is known by all parties to a confidential communication to be overhearing or recording it.
clauses.gap: The "confidential communication" definition and the "person" definition quoted below are both drawn from subdivisions of a single statutory section, § 632(b)-(c); they are not independent of one another. This clause states only § 632's own definitions; it does not restate case law applying those definitions to particular fact patterns (for example, what circumstances make an expectation of being overheard "reasonable"), which was not researched here.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 632(c)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 632(c)
citations.quote: “confidential communication” means any communication carried on in circumstances as may reasonably indicate that any party to the communication desires it to be confined to the parties thereto, but excludes a communication made in a public gathering or in any legislative, judicial, executive, or administrative proceeding open to the public, or in any other circumstance in which the parties to the communication may reasonably expect that the communication may be overheard or recorded.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 632(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 632(b)
citations.quote: excludes an individual known by all parties to a confidential communication to be overhearing or recording the communication.

clauses.title: Exclusion of Unlawfully Obtained Evidence
clauses.body: Both § 631 and § 632 state their own evidentiary exclusion rule. Penal Code § 631(d) provides that, except as proof in an action or prosecution for violation of § 631 itself, no evidence obtained in violation of § 631 is admissible in any judicial, administrative, legislative, or other proceeding. Penal Code § 632(d) states a parallel rule for § 632: except as proof in an action or prosecution for violation of § 632, evidence obtained as a result of eavesdropping upon or recording a confidential communication in violation of § 632 is not admissible in any judicial, administrative, legislative, or other proceeding.
clauses.gap: Penal Code §§ 631 and 632 are separate, independently-numbered statutory sections, each stating its own exclusionary rule in its own subdivision (d); the two citations below are therefore independent of one another, not two subsections of a single section. This clause states only the Act's own admissibility rule; it does not address inadmissibility doctrines arising from other bodies of law -- such as the Evidence Code, or state or federal constitutional exclusionary rules -- which were not researched here.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 631(d)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 631(d)
citations.quote: Except as proof in an action or prosecution for violation of this section, no evidence obtained in violation of this section shall be admissible in any judicial, administrative, legislative, or other proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 632(d)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 632(d)
citations.quote: Except as proof in an action or prosecution for violation of this section, evidence obtained as a result of eavesdropping upon or recording a confidential communication in violation of this section is not admissible in any judicial, administrative, legislative, or other proceeding.

clauses.title: Private Right of Action, Statutory Damages, and Injunctive Relief
clauses.body: Penal Code § 637.2(a) creates a private civil right of action: any person injured by a violation of "this chapter" -- Penal Code Chapter 1.5, Invasion of Privacy, §§ 630-638.55, which includes §§ 631 and 632 among its other sections -- may bring an action against the person who committed the violation for the greater of two amounts: $5,000 per violation, or three times the plaintiff's actual damages, if any. Section 637.2(b) separately authorizes an action, brought in accordance with the injunction provisions commencing at Code of Civil Procedure § 525, to enjoin and restrain a violation of the chapter, and allows a plaintiff to seek that injunctive relief and the damages described in § 637.2(a) in the same action. Section 637.2(c) states that suffering, or being threatened with, actual damages is not a necessary prerequisite to bringing an action under § 637.2.
clauses.gap: The three quotes below are all drawn from subdivisions (a) through (c) of a single statutory section, § 637.2; they are not independent of one another. Section 637.2(a)'s right of action reaches a violation of "this chapter" as a whole -- the full Invasion of Privacy chapter, §§ 630-638.55 -- not only violations of §§ 631 or 632 specifically; this clause does not restate every other section within that chapter. This clause does not address the statute of limitations applicable to a § 637.2 action, nor § 637.2(d)'s cross-reference preserving Civil Code trade-secret provisions, neither of which was independently verified here.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(a)
citations.quote: Any person who has been injured by a violation of this chapter may bring an action against the person who committed the violation for the greater of the following amounts: (1) Five thousand dollars ($5,000) per violation. (2) Three times the amount of actual damages, if any, sustained by the plaintiff.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(b)
citations.quote: Any person may, in accordance with Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 525) of Title 7 of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, bring an action to enjoin and restrain any violation of this chapter, and may in the same action seek damages as provided by subdivision (a).

citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(c)

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose
clauses.body: {{companyName}} provides this information sheet to {{employeeName}} to describe the California statutory protections for employees' political activities and affiliations set out in Labor Code sections 1101 through 1106, including the core prohibition on employer rules or policies restricting political activity, the separate prohibition on coercing employees through threat of discharge, how California courts have construed the scope of "political activity" under these statutes, and the penalties and remedies the statute itself provides. This information sheet states general rules of California law. It is not a statement of {{companyName}}'s policies or practices, and it does not describe whether any particular conduct by {{employeeName}} or {{companyName}} does or does not fall within these statutes.

clauses.title: The Core Prohibition on Employer Rules Restricting Political Activity
clauses.body: California Labor Code section 1101 prohibits an employer from making, adopting, or enforcing any rule, regulation, or policy that either (a) forbids or prevents employees from engaging or participating in politics or from becoming candidates for public office, or (b) controls or directs, or tends to control or direct, the political activities or affiliations of employees.
clauses.gap: Section 1101 does not itself define "political activity" or "political activities or affiliations"; how California courts have construed those terms is addressed in a separate clause of this document. This clause states the statute's own text; it does not determine whether any particular rule, regulation, policy, or practice of the employer does or does not fall within section 1101's prohibition, which is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1101 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Chapter 5 (Political Affiliations), Part 3, Division 2
citations.quote: No employer shall make, adopt, or enforce any rule, regulation, or policy: (a) Forbidding or preventing employees from engaging or participating in politics or from becoming candidates for public office. (b) Controlling or directing, or tending to control or direct the political activities or affiliations of employees.

clauses.title: A Separate Prohibition on Coercing Employees' Political Choices
clauses.body: California Labor Code section 1102 separately prohibits an employer from coercing or influencing, or attempting to coerce or influence, employees, through or by means of threat of discharge or loss of employment, to adopt or follow, or refrain from adopting or following, any particular course or line of political action or political activity. This is a distinct prohibition from the one stated in section 1101: section 1101 addresses employer rules, regulations, or policies restricting political activity generally, while section 1102 addresses the specific mechanism of coercing or influencing employees through the threat of discharge or loss of employment.
clauses.gap: This clause cites section 1102 alone; the comparison it draws to section 1101 is addressed with its own citation in a separate clause of this document, so the two are not combined here as though verified by a single source. This clause states the statute's own text; it does not determine whether any particular statement or action by the employer does or does not amount to coercion or influence within the meaning of section 1102, which is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Chapter 5 (Political Affiliations), Part 3, Division 2
citations.quote: No employer shall coerce or influence or attempt to coerce or influence his employees through or by means of threat of discharge or loss of employment to adopt or follow or refrain from adopting or following any particular course or line of political action or political activity.

clauses.title: How the California Supreme Court Has Construed "Political Activity" Under These Statutes
clauses.body: Neither section 1101 nor section 1102 defines "political activity." The California Supreme Court has held that sections 1101 and 1102 serve to protect "the fundamental right of employees in general to engage in political activity without interference by employers," and that these statutes "cannot be narrowly confined to partisan activity" such as voting or campaign work. The Supreme Court approved a description of "political activity" as connoting "the espousal of a candidate or a cause, and some degree of action to promote the acceptance thereof by other persons." Applying that description, the Supreme Court held that a complaint alleging an employer discriminated against employees who identified themselves as members of an advocacy movement and worked to advance its cause stated a claim under sections 1101 and 1102.
clauses.gap: Both quotations in this clause are drawn from the same single opinion, Gay Law Students Assn. v. Pacific Tel. & Tel. Co. (1979) 24 Cal.3d 458 -- the "fundamental right" and "not narrowly confined to partisan activity" language, and the "espousal of a candidate or a cause" description (which that opinion in turn quotes from an earlier Court of Appeal decision, Mallard v. Boring (1960) 182 Cal.App.2d 390) -- so they are not independent of one another; only one source was independently fetched and verified for this clause. This is a single, on-point California Supreme Court construction of these statutes, not an exhaustive catalogue of every activity that has been or could be held to qualify as "political activity," and it does not determine whether any specific activity by the employee does or does not qualify for this statutory protection in a particular case.

citations.case: Gay Law Students Assn. v. Pacific Tel. & Tel. Co.
citations.quote: These sections serve to protect “the fundamental right of employees in general to engage in political activity without interference by employers.”

citations.case: Gay Law Students Assn. v. Pacific Tel. & Tel. Co.
citations.quote: These statutes cannot be narrowly confined to partisan activity.

citations.case: Gay Law Students Assn. v. Pacific Tel. & Tel. Co., quoting Mallard v. Boring (1960) 182 Cal.App.2d 390, 395
citations.quote: The term ‘political activity’ connotes the espousal of a candidate or a cause, and some degree of action to promote the acceptance thereof by other persons.

clauses.title: The Penalties and Civil Remedy This Chapter Itself Provides
clauses.body: This chapter of the Labor Code states its own penalty and remedy. On the criminal side, an employer, or any other person or entity, that violates the chapter is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable -- in the case of an individual -- by imprisonment in the county jail not to exceed one year, a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars, or both, and -- in the case of a corporation -- by a fine not to exceed five thousand dollars. On the civil side, the chapter states that nothing in it prevents an injured employee from recovering damages from the employer for injury suffered through a violation of the chapter. Consistent with that text, the California Supreme Court has recognized that an employee discriminated against in violation of sections 1101 or 1102 may maintain a civil cause of action against the employer to recover damages sustained from the employer's unlawful conduct.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two genuinely separate, independently-numbered sections of the same chapter -- section 1103 (the criminal misdemeanor penalty) and section 1105 (the statement preserving an injured employee's ability to recover civil damages) -- together with California Supreme Court case law (Gay Law Students Assn. v. Pacific Tel. & Tel. Co. (1979) 24 Cal.3d 458, 488-89) recognizing a civil damages action consistent with section 1105's text; that Supreme Court discussion in turn cites, but this clause does not independently verify, an earlier decision, Lockheed Aircraft Corp. v. Superior Court (1946) 28 Cal.2d 481. This document does not state that any misdemeanor charge would in fact be brought, or that any particular employer conduct would in fact expose it to criminal or civil liability under this chapter -- those are fact-specific and prosecutorial-discretion questions this document does not resolve. Section 1104 (employer responsibility, in a prosecution under this chapter, for the acts of its managers, officers, agents, and employees) and section 1106 (which extends the chapter's "employee" definition to certain public-sector workers, but only for purposes of sections 1102.5, 1102.6, 1102.7, 1102.8, 1104, and 1105 -- not for purposes of sections 1101, 1102, or 1103 themselves) were also verified but are not restated in the body of this clause.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, Chapter 5 (Political Affiliations), Part 3, Division 2
citations.quote: An employer or any other person or entity that violates this chapter is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable, in the case of an individual, by imprisonment in the county jail not to exceed one year or a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) or both that fine and imprisonment, or, in the case of a corporation, by a fine not to exceed five thousand dollars ($5,000).

citations.cite: California Labor Code, Chapter 5 (Political Affiliations), Part 3, Division 2
citations.quote: Nothing in this chapter shall prevent the injured employee from recovering damages from his employer for injury suffered through a violation of this chapter.
