citations.quote: our court established the principle that an employee who has been discriminated against in violation of sections 1101 or 1102 may maintain a cause of action against his employer to recover damages sustained as a result of the employer’s unlawful conduct.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Notice
clauses.body: This notice describes what California Labor Code Section 432.6 says about requiring arbitration as a condition of employment, and the current, court-ordered limits on enforcing that statute. It is provided by {{companyName}} to {{employeeName}} for informational purposes and does not itself waive, modify, expand, or create any right, agreement, or obligation between {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}.

clauses.title: California's Restriction on Requiring Arbitration
clauses.body: California Labor Code Section 432.6 states that a person may not, as a condition of employment, continued employment, or the receipt of any employment-related benefit, require an applicant for employment or an employee to waive any right, forum, or procedure for a violation of the California Fair Employment and Housing Act or the Labor Code — including the right to file a civil action or a complaint with a government agency. The statute separately bars threatening, retaliating against, or terminating an applicant or employee because they refused to consent to that kind of waiver, and it treats an agreement that requires someone to affirmatively opt out of a waiver, rather than opt in, as itself a "condition of employment" covered by the same prohibition.
clauses.gap: Fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov on 2026-09-04 using two distinct User-Agent strings; the two fetches of the statutory text were byte-identical after whitespace normalization. This clause quotes only subdivisions (a) through (c) of the section; the next clause quotes subdivision (f) of the same section, so the two are not independent of one another as sources — both come from Labor Code Section 432.6 itself.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 432.6(a)-(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code § 432.6, subdivisions (a) through (c)
citations.quote: 432.6. (a) A person shall not, as a condition of employment, continued employment, or the receipt of any employment-related benefit, require any applicant for employment or any employee to waive any right, forum, or procedure for a violation of any provision of the California Fair Employment and Housing Act (Part 2.8 (commencing with Section 12900) of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code) or this code, including the right to file and pursue a civil action or a complaint with, or otherwise notify, any state agency, other public prosecutor, law enforcement agency, or any court or other governmental entity of any alleged violation. (b) An employer shall not threaten, retaliate or discriminate against, or terminate any applicant for employment or any employee because of the refusal to consent to the waiver of any right, forum, or procedure for a violation of the California Fair Employment and Housing Act or this code, including the right to file and pursue a civil action or a complaint with, or otherwise notify, any state agency, other public prosecutor, law enforcement agency, or any court or other governmental entity of any alleged violation. (c) For purposes of this section, an agreement that requires an employee to opt out of a waiver or take any affirmative action in order to preserve their rights is deemed a condition of employment.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own Carve-Out for FAA-Enforceable Agreements
clauses.body: Section 432.6 says, in its own text, that nothing in the section is intended to invalidate a written arbitration agreement that is otherwise enforceable under the Federal Arbitration Act. The section also doesn't apply to postdispute settlement agreements or negotiated severance agreements, or to a person covered by a securities self-regulatory organization's own arbitration rules, and by its terms it applies only to employment contracts entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2020.
clauses.gap: Fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov on 2026-09-04 using two distinct User-Agent strings; the two fetches were byte-identical after whitespace normalization. This clause and the one above quote different subdivisions of the same Labor Code section, so they are not independent of one another as sources. Subdivision (f)'s savings clause matters beyond its own terms: as the next clause describes, the Ninth Circuit pointed to this exact language as evidence that the statute targets the formation of arbitration agreements rather than their enforceability — which is what drove the court's preemption analysis.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 432.6(e)-(h) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code § 432.6, subdivisions (e) through (h)
citations.quote: (e) This section does not apply to a person registered with a self-regulatory organization as defined by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (15 U.S.C. Sec. 78c) or regulations adopted under that act pertaining to any requirement of a self-regulatory organization that a person arbitrate disputes that arise between the person and their employer or any other person as specified by the rules of the self-regulatory organization. (f) Nothing in this section is intended to invalidate a written arbitration agreement that is otherwise enforceable under the Federal Arbitration Act (9 U.S.C. Sec. 1 et seq.). (g) This section does not apply to postdispute settlement agreements or negotiated severance agreements. (h) This section applies to contracts for employment entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2020.

clauses.title: The Ninth Circuit Held the FAA Preempts This Statute
clauses.body: In Chamber of Commerce of the United States v. Bonta, a divided panel of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals held that the Federal Arbitration Act preempts Section 432.6 to the extent it applies to arbitration agreements, and affirmed a district court order preliminarily enjoining California officials from enforcing it. The majority reasoned that Section 432.6 discriminates against the formation of arbitration agreements — pointing to subdivision (f)'s own admission that an arbitration agreement formed in violation of the statute remains enforceable — and held that a state rule burdening arbitration agreements at the formation stage is preempted for the same reasons the U.S. Supreme Court has struck down state rules that single out arbitration agreements for different treatment than other contracts.
clauses.gap: Read via CourtListener (opinion id 9371215, cluster id 9375739) on 2026-09-04. This was a 2-1 panel decision (Judges Ikuta and W. Fletcher in the majority, Judge Lucero dissenting), not an en banc ruling. The docket shows an earlier version of this opinion (13 F.4th 766, filed Sept. 15, 2021) drew a petition for rehearing en banc; the panel then sua sponte granted panel rehearing, withdrew that opinion, and the en banc petition was denied as moot when the panel reissued this opinion on Feb. 15, 2023. No further en banc or Ninth Circuit petition followed this opinion — the appellate docket (No. 20-15291) shows the mandate issued March 9, 2023, and the case then returned to the district court, whose final disposition is the subject of the next clause. Whether the dissent's narrower reading of FAA preemption is correct was not resolved by any higher court; the litigation ended by stipulated judgment rather than further appellate review, so this holding was never tested by the U.S. Supreme Court or an en banc Ninth Circuit panel.

citations.case: Chamber of Commerce of the United States of America v. Bonta
citations.quote: Because all provisions of AB 51 work together to burden the formation of arbitration agreements, we conclude that the FAA preempts AB 51 as a whole to the extent it applies to arbitration agreements. ... Because AB 51 is preempted by the FAA, the district court correctly held that the Chamber of Commerce is likely to succeed on the merits of its claim for declaratory and injunctive relief. And because California does not challenge the district court's holding that the remaining factors also weigh in favor of the Chamber of Commerce, we hold that the district court did not abuse its discretion when it granted the Chamber of Commerce's motion for a preliminary injunction. AFFIRMED.

clauses.title: Current Enforcement Status
clauses.body: After the Ninth Circuit's decision, the parties to that lawsuit stipulated to a final judgment. On January 1, 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California entered a permanent injunction barring California's Attorney General, Labor Commissioner, the Secretary of the Labor and Workforce Development Agency, and the Director of the Department of Fair Employment and Housing — and each of their successors — from enforcing Labor Code Section 432.6, subdivisions (a), (b), or (c), or the related civil-penalty provision in Government Code Section 12953, wherever the alleged "waiver" consists of entering into an arbitration agreement covered by the Federal Arbitration Act. The court dismissed the underlying case with prejudice, retained jurisdiction to enforce that injunction, and closed the case.
clauses.gap: Read directly from the docket and the filed order (E.D. Cal. Case No. 2:19-cv-02456-KJM-DB, ECF No. 87, "Order Regarding Permanent Injunction," entered Jan. 2, 2024) via CourtListener on 2026-09-04. This is a district court order, not an appellate opinion, so it is independent of the Ninth Circuit opinion above as a source, even though it implements that decision. Nothing in the docket entries retrieved here (95 entries total, the last dated Jan. 2, 2024) shows the injunction being modified, appealed further, or reopened since it was entered — but this research did not turn up, and cannot rule out, developments outside that docket. The injunction is also limited to its own terms: it runs against these named California officials specifically, and only bars enforcing Section 432.6(a)-(c) and Government Code Section 12953 where the alleged waiver takes the form of entering into an FAA-covered arbitration agreement. The statute's text remains on the books, unrepealed, and this record does not establish what — if anything — of Section 432.6 still has force where a waiver doesn't take the form of an FAA-covered arbitration agreement, or whether Section 432.6(d)'s reference to a "prevailing plaintiff" reflects some private right of action distinct from the enjoined state officials' own enforcement.

citations.case: Chamber of Commerce of the United States of America v. Bonta, Order Regarding Permanent Injunction
citations.cite: No. 2:19-cv-02456-KJM-DB, ECF No. 87 (E.D. Cal. entered Jan. 2, 2024)
citations.quote: It is hereby ORDERED that Defendants Rob Bonta, in his official capacity as the Attorney General of the State of California; Lilia Garcia Brower, in her official capacity as the Labor Commissioner of the State of California; Stewart Knox, in his official capacity as the Secretary of the California Labor and Workforce Development Agency; and Kevin Kish, in his official capacity as Director of the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing; and each of their successors, are: 1. Enjoined from enforcing sections 432.6(a), (b), and (c) of the California Labor Code where the alleged "waiver of any right, forum, or procedure" is the entry into an arbitration agreement that is covered by the Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. §§ 1-16 ("FAA"); and 2. Enjoined from enforcing section 12953 of the California Government Code where the alleged violation of "Section 432.6 of the Labor Code" is the entry into an arbitration agreement that is covered by the FAA. ... It is further ORDERED that this action is dismissed with prejudice; It is further ORDERED that this Court shall retain jurisdiction over this action for purposes of implementing and enforcing the final judgment.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Receipt
Declaration — Wage-and-Hour Claim Filing Deadlines Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I, {{employeeName}}, am completing this information sheet in connection with wages I believe {{companyName}} owes me from my employment, which is described here, where applicable, as having ended on {{terminationDate}}.

This information sheet describes California's general civil filing deadlines — statutes of limitations — for the different ways a wage-and-hour claim can be legally characterized once employment has ended: as a claim on a liability created by statute, as a claim founded on a written contract, and as a claim for the waiting-time penalty under Labor Code section 203. It is not a substitute for the DLSE wage claim process or a civil complaint, does not calculate any specific filing deadline for any specific claim, and does not determine that any wages described here are in fact owed. Only the Labor Commissioner, or a court, can determine whether a specific claim was filed within the applicable deadline.

clauses.title: The Three-Year Deadline for a Claim on a Liability Created by Statute
clauses.body: California's general civil statutes of limitations set a three-year deadline for "[a]n action upon a liability created by statute, other than a penalty or forfeiture." California's highest court has applied this three-year period to an action to recover final wages not paid as required by the Labor Code, and has separately held that the extra pay a statute requires for a missed meal or rest period is itself a "wage or premium pay" governed by this same three-year period, rather than a "penalty" governed by a shorter period — because the obligation to pay it is created by statute rather than sounding purely in penalty.
clauses.gap: This is one state's general civil statute of limitations and two California Supreme Court decisions applying it — used as real evidence of how long a statutory wage claim generally has to be filed, not a claim about which state's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim about exactly how many years remain for any specific claim, since accrual dates, tolling, and the specific type of claim asserted can all affect the actual deadline. The two case-law citations below both confirm the three-year period applies to different categories of unpaid compensation (final wages, and meal/rest period premium pay) rather than repeating the same holding, and neither case addresses every Labor Code wage claim by name; this document does not independently verify, claim by claim, that every possible wage-and-hour claim (for example, every minimum-wage or overtime scenario) is treated the same way.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 338(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.quote: Within three years: (a) An action upon a liability created by statute, other than a penalty or forfeiture.

citations.case: Murphy v. Kenneth Cole Productions, Inc.
citations.quote: This case presents two issues: first, whether the “one additional hour of pay” provided for in Labor Code section 226.7 constitutes a wage or premium pay subject to a three-year statute of limitations (Code Civ. Proc., § 338) or a penalty subject to a one-year statute of limitations (Code Civ. Proc., § 340) . . . We conclude that the remedy provided in Labor Code section 226.7 constitutes a wage or premium pay and is governed by a three-year statute of limitations.

clauses.title: The Four-Year Deadline for a Claim Founded on a Written Contract
clauses.body: California's general civil statutes of limitations separately set a four-year deadline for "[a]n action upon any contract, obligation or liability founded upon an instrument in writing" (subject to statutory exceptions not addressed here). This is a longer period than the three-year deadline that generally applies to a claim on a liability created by statute.
clauses.gap: This is one state's general civil statute of limitations, used as real evidence that a longer, four-year filing deadline exists in California law for a claim founded on a written instrument — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that this longer period applies to any particular wage claim. This document did not locate, and does not cite, California case law specifically confirming when a claim to recover wages is treated by a court as "founded upon" a written employment contract for purposes of this four-year period, as opposed to being treated as a claim on a liability created by statute under the three-year period described elsewhere in this document, even where a written employment agreement exists. That characterization can depend on how the specific claim is pled and on the terms of the particular written agreement, and is not resolved by the text of this statute alone; this gap is disclosed rather than filled with an assumed answer.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.quote: Within four years: (a) An action upon any contract, obligation or liability founded upon an instrument in writing, except as provided in Section 336a; provided, that the time within which any action for a money judgment for the balance due upon an obligation for the payment of which a deed of trust or mortgage with power of sale upon real property or any interest therein was given as security, following the exercise of the power of sale in such deed of trust or mortgage, may be brought shall not extend beyond three months after the time of sale under such deed of trust or mortgage.

clauses.title: Why the Waiting-Time Penalty's Filing Deadline Follows the Underlying Wage Claim, Not the General One-Year Penalty Period
clauses.body: California's general civil statutes of limitations set a one-year deadline for "[a]n action upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture," unless the statute imposing the penalty prescribes a different limitation. The waiting-time-penalty statute, Labor Code section 203, itself prescribes a different limitation: it states that suit for these penalties may be filed "at any time before the expiration of the statute of limitations on an action for the wages from which the penalties arise." The California Supreme Court has confirmed that this cross-reference means a claim for section 203 penalties is not governed by the general one-year penalty deadline; instead, it is governed by whatever deadline would apply to a claim for the underlying unpaid final wages, and the Court held this is true even when an employee sues to recover the waiting-time penalty alone, without also suing to recover unpaid wages (because, for example, the wages were eventually paid before suit was filed).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes and one California Supreme Court decision construing them, used as real evidence of how the waiting-time-penalty filing deadline is structured — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim about exactly how many years remain for any specific claim. The three citations below are to two separate statutes (Code of Civil Procedure section 340 and Labor Code section 203, in different codes) and one case construing both, so they are independent of one another rather than restating the same source. This clause does not itself identify which specific deadline (three years, four years, or another period) governs any particular underlying wage claim; that threshold question is addressed by the other authority clauses in this document rather than repeated here.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 340(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Code of Civil Procedure
citations.quote: Within one year: (a) An action upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture, if the action is given to an individual, or to an individual and the state, except if the statute imposing it prescribes a different limitation.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 203(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Suit may be filed for these penalties at any time before the expiration of the statute of limitations on an action for the wages from which the penalties arise.

citations.case: Pineda v. Bank of America, N.A.
citations.quote: Code of Civil Procedure section 340, subdivision (a) provides that a one-year statute of limitations applies to “[a]n action upon a statute for a penalty or forfeiture . . . .” Thus, if section 203(a) comprised the entire statute, a suit to recover its provided-for penalties would undoubtedly have to be filed within one year of the accrual of the cause of action. However, Code of Civil Procedure section 312 acknowledges the Legislature can, if it so chooses, prescribe a different statute of limitations to govern specific civil actions. To that end, section 203(b) provides, “Suit may be filed for these penalties at any time before the expiration of the statute of limitations on an action for the wages from which the penalties arise.” Actions for final wages not paid as required by sections 201 and 202 are governed by Code of Civil Procedure section 338, subdivision (a), which provides that a three-year statute of limitations applies . . . Section 203(b) sets forth a single limitations period governing all actions to recover section 203 penalties regardless of whether an employee seeks both unpaid wages and penalties or penalties alone.

clauses.title: No Separate Filing-Deadline Text for a DLSE Administrative Wage Claim
clauses.body: The Labor Code statute authorizing the Labor Commissioner to investigate wage complaints and hold a hearing on them does not itself state a separate filing deadline — shorter or longer than the general civil deadlines described elsewhere in this document — for a wage claim brought through that administrative process rather than through a civil lawsuit.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, reviewed for the presence or absence of specific language — used as real evidence that the particular statutory text granting the Labor Commissioner hearing authority does not itself set a separate administrative filing deadline, not as a comprehensive claim that no provision anywhere in the Labor Code or in Division of Labor Standards Enforcement policy could ever impose a different timing rule for some other purpose. This document reviewed only the text of Labor Code section 98 for this point; it does not independently verify the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's internal Policies and Procedures manual, or every other Labor Code section referencing the Labor Commissioner's hearing process, so an administrative-specific timing rule located elsewhere cannot be ruled out from what was verified here. That absence is disclosed rather than treated as a complete negative confirmation.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 98(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The Labor Commissioner is authorized to investigate employee complaints. The Labor Commissioner may provide for a hearing in any action to recover wages, penalties, and other demands for compensation, including liquidated damages if the complaint alleges payment of a wage less than the minimum wage fixed by an order of the Industrial Welfare Commission or by statute, properly before the division or the Labor Commissioner, including orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission, and shall determine all matters arising under his or her jurisdiction.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature Block — Wage-and-Hour Claim Filing Deadlines Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{employeeName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California's general civil filing deadlines for wage-and-hour claims after employment ends, including the three-year period for a statutory wage claim, the four-year period for a claim founded on a written contract, and how the waiting-time-penalty deadline under Labor Code section 203 is tied to the underlying wage claim's own deadline. It is not a DLSE wage claim form or civil complaint, is not filed with any court or agency by completing it, does not itself determine that {{employeeName}} is owed any wages by {{companyName}} or that any specific filing deadline has or has not passed, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.]

clauses.title: Water-Conserving Plumbing Fixture Compliance Disclosure
clauses.body: This disclosure concerns the property at {{propertyAddress}}, being transferred from {{sellerName}} ("Transferor") to {{buyerName}} ("Transferee"). It addresses California's statutory requirement that certain older residential and commercial real property be equipped with water-conserving plumbing fixtures, Civil Code §§ 1101.1-1101.9, and the transferor's written disclosure obligation tied to a sale or transfer of such property.

clauses.title: Applicability and the Statute's Defined Terms
clauses.body: Except for the exemptions the statute itself states, this statutory article applies to residential and commercial real property built and available for use on or before January 1, 1994. The statute defines "noncompliant plumbing fixture" to mean any toilet manufactured to use more than 1.6 gallons of water per flush, any urinal manufactured to use more than one gallon of water per flush, any showerhead manufactured to have a flow capacity of more than 2.5 gallons of water per minute, or any interior faucet that emits more than 2.2 gallons of water per minute. It defines a "water-conserving plumbing fixture" as any fixture that complies with the current building standards applicable to newly constructed real property of the same type. It further defines "single-family residential real property" as real property improved with a building containing not more than one unit intended for human habitation, "multifamily residential real property" as real property improved with a building containing more than one such unit (or a mixed residential-commercial building intended for human habitation, including residential hotels but not non-residential hotels and motels), and "commercial real property" as real property improved with a building intended for commercial use, including hotels and motels, that is not single-family or multifamily residential real property. "Sale or transfer" is defined to mean the sale or transfer of an entire real property estate or the fee interest in it, and does not include the sale or transfer of a partial interest, including a leasehold.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines a water-conservation plumbing standard and ties it to property age and type — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property or transfer, or about whether a given fixture meets or fails the statute's numeric thresholds. The citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1101.3, together with the applicability rule at § 1101.2) and are not independent of one another.

citations.case: Civil Code, article applicability by construction date
citations.cite: Civil Code § 1101.2
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 1101.7, this article shall apply to residential and commercial real property built and available for use on or before January 1, 1994.

citations.case: Civil Code, definition of "noncompliant plumbing fixture"
citations.cite: Civil Code § 1101.3(c)
citations.quote: “Noncompliant plumbing fixture” means any of the following: (1) Any toilet manufactured to use more than 1.6 gallons of water per flush. (2) Any urinal manufactured to use more than one gallon of water per flush. (3) Any showerhead manufactured to have a flow capacity of more than 2.5 gallons of water per minute. (4) Any interior faucet that emits more than 2.2 gallons of water per minute.

citations.case: Civil Code, definition of "water-conserving plumbing fixture"
citations.cite: Civil Code § 1101.3(e)
citations.quote: “Water-conserving plumbing fixture” means any fixture that is in compliance with current building standards applicable to a newly constructed real property of the same type.

citations.case: Civil Code, definition of "sale or transfer"
citations.cite: Civil Code § 1101.3(f)
citations.quote: “Sale or transfer” means the sale or transfer of an entire real property estate or the fee interest in that real property estate and does not include the sale or transfer of a partial interest, including a leasehold.

clauses.title: Single-Family Residential Property: Retrofit Deadline and Seller's Disclosure Duty
clauses.body: For single-family residential real property built and available for use on or before January 1, 1994 (absent an applicable exemption), the statute states two independent retrofit triggers: on or before January 1, 2017, the property owner must replace all noncompliant plumbing fixtures with water-conserving plumbing fixtures; and, separately, for any building alteration or improvement to such property, replacing all noncompliant plumbing fixtures with water-conserving fixtures is a condition the local building department attaches to issuing a certificate of final completion and occupancy or final permit approval. The statute also imposes a disclosure duty tied to a sale or transfer: a seller or transferor of single-family residential real property must disclose in writing to the prospective purchaser or transferee both the January 1, 2017 replacement requirement and whether the real property includes any noncompliant plumbing fixtures.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction ties a plumbing-fixture retrofit duty to a permitted-alteration trigger and to a fixed calendar deadline, and separately requires a seller's written disclosure of fixture status at sale — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property, sale, or renovation. The citations below to subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) are all subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1101.4) and are not independent of one another.

citations.case: Civil Code, permit-conditioned retrofit for alterations or improvements
citations.cite: Civil Code § 1101.4(a)
citations.quote: For all building alterations or improvements to single-family residential real property, as a condition for issuance of a certificate of final completion and occupancy or final permit approval by the local building department, the permit applicant shall replace all noncompliant plumbing fixtures with water-conserving plumbing fixtures.

citations.case: Civil Code, January 1, 2017 owner retrofit deadline
citations.cite: Civil Code § 1101.4(b)
citations.quote: On or before January 1, 2017, noncompliant plumbing fixtures in any single-family residential real property shall be replaced by the property owner with water-conserving plumbing fixtures.

citations.case: Civil Code, seller's written disclosure duty
citations.cite: Civil Code § 1101.4(c)
citations.quote: A seller or transferor of single-family residential real property shall disclose in writing to the prospective purchaser or transferee the requirements of subdivision (b) and whether the real property includes any noncompliant plumbing fixtures.

clauses.title: Multifamily and Commercial Property: Retrofit Deadlines and Seller's Disclosure Duty
clauses.body: For multifamily residential real property and commercial real property built and available for use on or before January 1, 1994 (absent an applicable exemption), the statute states an on-or-before January 1, 2019 deadline for the property owner to replace all noncompliant plumbing fixtures with water-conserving plumbing fixtures. The statute separately requires that, on and after January 1, 2019, a seller or transferor of multifamily residential real property or commercial real property disclose in writing to the prospective purchaser or transferee both this replacement requirement and whether the property includes any noncompliant plumbing fixtures; the statute states that this disclosure may be included in other transactional documents.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction sets a later calendar deadline and a parallel written-disclosure duty for multifamily and commercial property, as distinct from the single-family retrofit and disclosure rule addressed in a separate clause of this document — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property or transfer. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1101.5) and are not independent of one another; that section also contains additional retrofit triggers tied to building additions and to alteration-cost thresholds (§ 1101.5(d)) that are not quoted or relied on here.

citations.case: Civil Code, January 1, 2019 owner retrofit deadline for multifamily/commercial property
citations.cite: Civil Code § 1101.5(a)
citations.quote: On or before January 1, 2019, all noncompliant plumbing fixtures in any multifamily residential real property and in any commercial real property shall be replaced with water-conserving plumbing fixtures.

citations.case: Civil Code, seller's written disclosure duty for multifamily/commercial property
citations.cite: Civil Code § 1101.5(e)
citations.quote: On and after January 1, 2019, a seller or transferor of multifamily residential real property or of commercial real property shall disclose to the prospective purchaser or transferee, in writing, the requirements of subdivision (a) and whether the property includes any noncompliant plumbing fixtures. This disclosure may be included in other transactional documents.

clauses.title: Properties Exempt from This Article
clauses.body: The statute states that this article does not apply to registered historical sites; to real property for which a licensed plumber certifies that, due to the age or configuration of the property or its plumbing, installation of water-conserving plumbing fixtures is not technically feasible; or to a building for which water service is permanently disconnected.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's exemption list for a plumbing-fixture retrofit requirement — a narrower and differently-drawn list than the exemption lists this corpus documents for other California transfer-disclosure statutes (for example, the smoke alarm compliance statute's exemption list), and it should not be assumed to mirror those other lists. It is not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property.

citations.case: Civil Code, statutory exemptions
citations.cite: Civil Code § 1101.7
citations.quote: This article shall not apply to any of the following: (a) Registered historical sites. (b) Real property for which a licensed plumber certifies that, due to the age or configuration of the property or its plumbing, installation of water-conserving plumbing fixtures is not technically feasible. (c) A building for which water service is permanently disconnected.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet explains California's real property recording system: the statutes that let a person put the county's public record on notice of an interest in real property, and the rule those statutes use to decide which of two competing claims to the same real property has priority when both cannot be honored in full. It is prepared in connection with real property located at {{propertyAddress}}, more particularly described as {{legalDescription}}, Assessor's Parcel Number {{parcelNumber}}, in {{recordingCounty}}. It is prepared for {{requestingPartyName}}, in connection with an interest in that property also claimed by {{adverseClaimantNames}}. This sheet describes California's recording statutes and how California courts have construed them. It does not determine who holds superior title to this specific property, does not itself record, correct, or clear any instrument affecting title, and is not a substitute for a professional title search, a policy of title insurance, or a quiet title action.

clauses.title: The Core Priority Rule: Civil Code Section 1214
clauses.body: California Civil Code section 1214 supplies the statutory rule that decides priority between competing claims to the same real property, such as an interest in {{propertyAddress}}. Under that section, a conveyance of real property is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee of the same property who takes in good faith, pays valuable consideration, and is the first of the two to duly record — even if that later purchaser's own interest was actually created after the earlier, unrecorded (or later-recorded) one. California courts have described this as a "race-notice" framework: a subsequent purchaser obtains priority only by combining three things — good-faith, paid-for status without notice of the earlier interest; the fact that the earlier interest was in place before the subsequent purchaser acquired its own interest; and being the first of the two to duly record.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own recording-priority rule for real property — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel or transfer, and not a determination of whether the person this sheet is prepared for, or the other claimant it names, in fact qualifies as the protected "subsequent purchaser or mortgagee" or holds the earlier interest on the facts of any specific dispute. The statutory quote and the case-law quote are independent sources — one is the Legislature's text, the other is a Court of Appeal's construction of it in a specific dispute over lien priority between two lenders — but the case does not carry the force of a statute and could in principle be narrowed or distinguished by a later decision. This clause states the general rule and its three-part structure only; it does not address what counts as "good faith" or "notice" for these purposes (addressed in a separate clause of this sheet) or how the rule applies when two conveyances are recorded at literally the same moment.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1214 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the race-notice recording-priority rule for real property
citations.quote: Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein, other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year, is void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property, or any part thereof, in good faith and for a valuable consideration, whose conveyance is first duly recorded, and as against any judgment affecting the title, unless the conveyance shall have been duly recorded prior to the record of notice of action.

citations.case: First Bank v. East West Bank
citations.quote: Under these "race-notice" rules, a subsequent purchaser obtains priority for a real property interest by (1) acquiring the interest as a bona fide purchaser for valuable consideration with neither actual knowledge nor constructive notice of (2) a previously created interest and (3) "first duly record[ing]" the interest, i.e., recording before the previously created interest is recorded.

clauses.title: What Recording Does: Constructive Notice Under Civil Code Section 1213
clauses.body: Civil Code section 1213 states what recording accomplishes: once a conveyance of real property is acknowledged (or proved), certified, and recorded as prescribed by law, it becomes constructive notice of its contents to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees, from the time it is filed with the county recorder for record. "Constructive notice" in this context is a legal presumption, not a factual finding about who actually read the county's records — the law treats a later purchaser or mortgagee as bound by a properly recorded document's contents whether or not that person actually saw it. California courts have also construed the phrase "recorded as prescribed by law" to require more than the physical act of depositing a document with the recorder: the document must also be indexed, since it is the indexing — not the recording alone — that makes a document findable through a search of the public record and that triggers constructive notice.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute plus one Court of Appeal's construction of it — genuinely independent sources, since one is legislative text and the other is a judicial gloss reached in an unrelated dispute over the priority of two lenders' recorded trust deeds. This clause does not address the mechanics of how a particular county recorder's office indexes documents, how quickly indexing typically follows recording, or what happens if an indexing error occurs; those questions were not independently verified here. It also does not resolve whether the recording of any specific instrument affecting the property this sheet identifies was in fact properly acknowledged, certified, and indexed as section 1213 requires — that is a factual question about the specific instrument and county record, not something this sheet determines.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1213 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: recording as constructive notice to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees
citations.quote: Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein acknowledged or proved and certified and recorded as prescribed by law from the time it is filed with the recorder for record is constructive notice of the contents thereof to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees; and a certified copy of such a recorded conveyance may be recorded in any other county and when so recorded the record thereof shall have the same force and effect as though it was of the original conveyance and where the original conveyance has been recorded in any county wherein the property therein mentioned is not situated a certified copy of the recorded conveyance may be recorded in the county where such property is situated with the same force and effect as if the original conveyance had been recorded in that county.

citations.case: First Bank v. East West Bank
citations.quote: The recording of a document does not impart constructive notice; "[t]he operative event [for purposes of constructive notice] is actually the indexing of the document . . . ."

clauses.title: An Unrecorded Instrument's Effect: Civil Code Section 1217
clauses.body: Civil Code section 1217 states the flip side of the recording system: an unrecorded instrument affecting real property is not void or ineffective just because it was never recorded. It remains valid as between the original parties to it, and as against anyone else who has notice of it. What an unrecorded instrument cannot do is defeat the specific, protected category of later claimant described elsewhere in this sheet — a subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property who takes in good faith, for valuable consideration, and records first. Read together, sections 1214 and 1217 describe the same underlying rule from two directions: section 1214 states when an earlier conveyance is cut off, and section 1217 confirms that outside that specific situation, an unrecorded instrument keeps its full effect.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what an unrecorded instrument does and does not do under California law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific parcel or instrument. Section 1217 is presented here on its own as a single statutory section; this sheet's companion clause on section 1214 is not offered as a second independent source for the point made in this clause specifically, since section 1217's function is largely to restate, from the opposite direction, the same priority rule section 1214 states directly — the two sections are not independent of one another on that shared point, even though each is separately numbered and separately quoted. This same section is also cited, for narrower purposes tied to a specific type of transfer, in other documents in this collection (a deed conveying property into a trust, for example); this sheet cites it instead for the general recording-system rule itself. This clause does not address what counts as "notice" sufficient to bind someone other than the original parties — that is addressed in a separate clause of this sheet.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1217 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: an unrecorded instrument remains valid between the parties and anyone with notice of it
citations.quote: An unrecorded instrument is valid as between the parties thereto and those who have notice thereof.

clauses.title: What "Good Faith" and "Notice" Mean: How California Courts Have Construed These Terms
clauses.body: Neither section 1214 nor section 1213 defines "good faith" or "notice" in detail; California courts have filled in those terms. A California Court of Appeal has described the elements a subsequent purchaser or mortgagee must show to qualify for section 1214's protection as payment of value, good faith, and the absence of actual or constructive notice of the earlier claimant's rights — the absence of notice being treated as an essential requirement, not merely one relevant factor among others. Separately, another Court of Appeal has explained that notice under these statutes can be actual (express information of a fact) or constructive (notice the law imputes regardless of what a person actually knew), and that a person generally has "notice" of a particular fact if that person has knowledge of circumstances which, upon reasonable inquiry, would lead to that particular fact.
clauses.gap: This clause rests on two separately decided California Courts of Appeal opinions — First Bank v. East West Bank (2011) and Gregg v. Cloney (2001) — genuinely independent of one another, though both apply the same statutory scheme (Civil Code §§ 1213-1214) and neither is a decision of the California Supreme Court, so neither is binding on every California trial or appellate court and either could in principle be distinguished or narrowed by a later decision. First Bank v. East West Bank is also cited elsewhere in this sheet, for two different, more specific propositions (the overall race-notice framework, and the indexing requirement for constructive notice); it is not counted as a second independent source within those other clauses. This clause does not resolve what "reasonable inquiry" requires on any particular set of facts, does not address whether knowledge held by a purchaser's agent (such as an escrow officer or title company) can be imputed to the purchaser, and does not determine whether either party this sheet identifies in fact had, or lacked, notice of the other's competing claim to the property — those are fact-specific questions this sheet does not resolve.

citations.case: First Bank v. East West Bank
citations.cite: 199 Cal. App. 4th 1309, 1314 (2011), quoting Gates Rubber Co. v. Ulman, 214 Cal. App. 3d 356, 364 (1989)
citations.quote: The elements of bona fide purchase are payment of value, in good faith, and without actual or constructive notice of another's rights.

citations.case: Gregg v. Cloney
citations.quote: By statute, notice may be actual or constructive. Actual notice is defined as "express information of a fact," while constructive notice is that "which is imputed by law." ... A person generally has "notice" of a particular fact if that person has knowledge of circumstances which, upon reasonable inquiry, would lead to that particular fact.

clauses.title: Declarant Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Reference — Notice of Proposed Action Procedure
clauses.body: This document describes, as general information, the notice-of-proposed-action procedure set out in Probate Code §§ 10580-10592 — the mechanism that lets a personal representative who has Independent Administration of Estates Act (IAEA) authority take many actions in administering the estate of {{decedentName}} by giving written notice to interested persons, rather than by filing a separate court petition for each action. {{executorName}} is identified here as the personal representative (or proposed personal representative) of {{decedentName}}'s estate to whom this reference applies. This document does not itself propose, describe, or give notice of any specific action regarding {{decedentName}}'s estate; it does not draft, serve, or file any actual Notice of Proposed Action, objection, waiver, consent, or restraining order; and it does not determine whether any particular action available to {{executorName}} requires this procedure, is exempt from it, or has already been waived or consented to by a given interested person. This document is background information for that separate process, not a substitute for it, and not itself a notice, objection, waiver, or consent with legal effect.

clauses.title: When a Personal Representative Must Give Notice of Proposed Action, and When Giving It Is Optional
clauses.body: The notice-of-proposed-action procedure does not apply to every action a personal representative with IAEA authority might take regarding {{decedentName}}'s estate. Probate Code § 10580(a) requires a personal representative who has IAEA authority to give notice of proposed action under this chapter before taking a proposed action without court supervision only if the specific provision of Chapter 3 (Probate Code §§ 10500 et seq.) that grants the power to take that action itself requires notice to be given; § 10580(a) also makes clear that this chapter does not by itself authorize a personal representative to take any action the personal representative does not otherwise have power to take under Part 6. Separately, § 10580(b) permits a personal representative to give notice of proposed action voluntarily even for an action that Chapter 3 permits to be taken without notice — but doing so for one action does not create a notice obligation for other actions where § 10580(a) does not require it, and does not expand the personal representative's underlying authority.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes both subdivision (a) and subdivision (b) of the same statutory section, Probate Code § 10580, as a single continuous quotation — they are not independent sources of one another. Whether a given action requires notice under this chapter depends on the specific Chapter 3 provision (§§ 10500 et seq.) granting the power to take it; this document does not enumerate those individual provisions or state which of them require notice, which permit it optionally, and which require neither. Within the sections fetched and verified for this document (§§ 10580-10592 and Probate Code § 1215), no separate expedited, shortened, or emergency-notice procedure for urgent matters was found; this document does not represent that no such procedure exists anywhere else in the Probate Code, only that none appears in the sections checked here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10580 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: 10580. (a) A personal representative who has been granted authority to administer the estate under this part shall give notice of proposed action as provided in this chapter prior to the taking of the proposed action without court supervision if the provision of Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 10500) giving the personal representative the power to take the action so requires. Nothing in this subdivision authorizes a personal representative to take an action under this part if the personal representative does not have the power to take the action under this part. (b) A personal representative who has been granted authority to administer the estate under this part may give notice of proposed action as provided in this chapter even if the provision of Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 10500) giving the personal representative the power to take the action permits the personal representative to take the action without giving notice of proposed action.

clauses.title: Who Must Be Given Notice, and How Written Consent or a Written Waiver Eliminates That Requirement
clauses.body: Probate Code § 10581 identifies who must be given notice of a proposed action regarding {{decedentName}}'s estate: each known devisee and each known heir whose interest in the estate would be affected by the proposed action, each person who has filed a request for special notice of petitions in the proceeding, and the Attorney General (at the Attorney General's Sacramento office) if any part of the estate would escheat to the state and the state's interest would be affected. Two statutes let that notice obligation be eliminated for a particular person. Probate Code § 10582 provides that notice need not be given to a person who consents in writing to the proposed action, and that consent may be signed before or after the action is taken. Probate Code § 10583(a) provides that notice need not be given to a person who, in writing, waives the right to notice of proposed action for that particular proposed action — a waiver that may likewise be signed before or after the action is taken, may describe the particular action, and may waive only particular aspects of notice (such as the delivery, mailing, or time requirements) or the giving of notice for that action in its entirety; § 10583(b) also recognizes a Judicial-Council-form Statutory Waiver that can be either a general waiver of notice or a waiver as to an entire category of transactions. Probate Code § 10584 governs revoking a waiver or consent already given: revocation must be in writing and is effective only when the personal representative actually receives it; a copy may be, but need not be, filed with the court for the revocation to be effective.
clauses.gap: This clause cites four separately numbered statutory sections — §§ 10581, 10582, 10583, and 10584 — each quoted once; none of the four citations is a subsection of another cited section, so they are independent of one another. Section 10583(b)'s reference to the Judicial Council's prescribed Statutory Waiver of Notice of Proposed Action form is described here only as the statute itself describes it; this document does not reproduce or link to that form.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10581 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 10582 and 10583, notice of proposed action shall be given to all of the following: (a) Each known devisee whose interest in the estate would be affected by the proposed action. (b) Each known heir whose interest in the estate would be affected by the proposed action. (c) Each person who has filed a request under Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 1250) of Part 2, of Division 3 for special notice of petitions filed in the administration proceeding. (d) The Attorney General, at the office of the Attorney General in Sacramento, if any portion of the estate is to escheat to the state and its interest in the estate would be affected by the proposed action.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10582 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Notice of proposed action need not be given to any person who consents in writing to the proposed action. The consent may be executed at any time before or after the proposed action is taken.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10583(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) Notice of proposed action need not be given to any person who, in writing, waives the right to notice of proposed action with respect to the particular proposed action. The waiver may be executed at any time before or after the proposed action is taken.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10584 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) A waiver or consent may be revoked only in writing and is effective only when the writing is received by the personal representative. (b) A copy of the revocation may be filed with the court, but the effectiveness of the revocation is not dependent upon a copy being filed with the court.

clauses.title: What the Notice Must Say, and How and When It Must Be Delivered
clauses.body: Probate Code § 10585(a) requires a notice of proposed action to state: the personal representative's name, mailing address, and electronic address; the name, telephone number, and electronic address of a person who can be contacted for more information; the proposed action itself, described in reasonably specific terms (with additional required detail — the material transaction terms, including sale price and any commission or compensation arrangement — if the action involves the sale or exchange of real property or granting an option to purchase real property); and the date on or after which the action is to be taken. The notice may use the current Judicial Council form, or a substantially similar form that contains the § 10585(a) statements and an objection form substantially like the Judicial Council's. Probate Code § 10586 requires the notice to be delivered, under Probate Code § 1215, to each person entitled to it not less than 15 days before the date stated in the notice as the date on or after which the action will be taken, and requires that a mailed notice be addressed to the person's last known address. Section 1215 itself sets out three delivery methods available for this notice (absent a different rule specific to the notice): delivery by mail (first-class mail within the United States, international mail otherwise), which is complete when deposited in the mail; personal delivery, complete when the notice is handed to the recipient; and electronic delivery, available only where the recipient has expressly consented on the appropriate Judicial Council form and supplied an electronic address for that purpose, complete when the notice is sent. Section 1215 states expressly that, for both mailed and electronic delivery, the period of notice is not extended — the 15-day period under § 10586 runs the same way regardless of which of these delivery methods is used.
clauses.gap: This clause cites three separately numbered, independently sourced statutes: Probate Code §§ 10585 and 10586 (Division 7, Part 6, Chapter 4 — the notice-of-proposed-action chapter itself) and Probate Code § 1215 (Division 3, Part 2, Chapter 2 — the Probate Code's general mailing-and-delivery statute, in an entirely different division of the code). None is a subsection of another cited section here, so all three are independent of one another. Section 1215(a)(3) also cross-references Probate Code § 1212 regarding the address to which a mailed notice must be sent; this document does not independently verify or quote § 1212. This clause does not reproduce the Judicial Council's prescribed Notice of Proposed Action form referenced in § 10585(b)-(c).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10585 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) The notice of proposed action shall state all of the following: (1) The name, mailing address, and electronic address of the personal representative. (2) The name, telephone number, and electronic address of a person who may be contacted for additional information. (3) The action proposed to be taken, with a reasonably specific description of the action. If the proposed action involves the sale or exchange of real property, or the granting of an option to purchase real property, the notice of proposed action shall state the material terms of the transaction, including, if applicable, the sale price and the amount of, or method of calculating, any commission or compensation paid or to be paid to an agent or broker in connection with the transaction. (4) The date on or after which the proposed action is to be taken.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10586 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The notice of proposed action shall be delivered pursuant to Section 1215 to each person required to be given notice of proposed action not less than 15 days before the date specified in the notice of proposed action on or after which the proposed action is to be taken. If mailed, the notice of proposed action shall be addressed to the person at the person’s last known address.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1215 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) Delivery by mail. (1) A notice or other paper shall be delivered by mail as follows: (A) By first-class mail if the person’s address is within the United States. First-class mail includes certified, registered, and express mail. (B) By international mail if the person’s address is not within the United States. International mail includes first-class mail international, priority mail international, priority mail express international, and global express guaranteed. (2) The notice or other paper shall be deposited for collection in the United States mail, in a sealed envelope, with postage paid, addressed to the person to whom it is mailed. (3) Subject to Section 1212, the notice or other paper shall be addressed to the person at the person’s place of business or place of residence. (4) Delivery by mail is complete when the notice or other paper is deposited in the mail. The period of notice is not extended. (b) Personal delivery. (1) A notice or other paper may be delivered personally to that person. (2) Personal delivery is complete when the notice or other paper is delivered personally to the person who is to receive it. (c) Electronic delivery. (1) A notice or other paper shall not be delivered by electronic means unless the person to receive notice has expressly consented on the appropriate Judicial Council form to receive electronic delivery in the proceeding before the court and has provided an electronic address for that express purpose. (2) Electronic delivery is complete when the notice or other paper is sent. The period of notice is not extended.

clauses.title: How a Person Objects to a Proposed Action, and the Restraining-Order Alternative
clauses.body: Probate Code § 10587(a) gives any person entitled to notice of a proposed action under § 10581 the right to object to it. Under § 10587(b), the objection is made by delivering — under Probate Code § 1215 — a written objection to the personal representative at the address stated in the notice, either using the Judicial Council form or any other writing that identifies the proposed action with reasonable certainty and states that the person objects to it. Section 10587(c) provides that the personal representative is deemed to have notice of the objection if it is delivered or received at that address before whichever is later: the date stated in the notice as the date on or after which the action is to be taken, or the date the action is actually taken. Separately, Probate Code § 10588(a) lets any person entitled to notice apply to the court for an order restraining the personal representative from taking the proposed action without court supervision, and requires the court to grant that order without notice to the personal representative and without the applicant having to show cause.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two separately numbered sections, §§ 10587 and 10588, each quoted once; neither citation is a subsection of the other. Probate Code § 10588(b), which addresses how and when a personal representative is deemed to have notice of a restraining order (including a cross-reference to Code of Civil Procedure §§ 415.10 and 415.30 for the manner of service), was reviewed but is not quoted or independently verified against those Code of Civil Procedure sections here, so this clause omits its specific terms rather than characterize them without that verification.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10587 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) Any person entitled to notice of proposed action under Section 10581 may object to the proposed action as provided in this section. (b) The objection to the proposed action is made by delivering pursuant to Section 1215 a written objection to the proposed action to the personal representative at the address stated in the notice of proposed action. The person objecting to the proposed action either may use the Judicial Council form or may make the objection in any other writing that identifies the proposed action with reasonable certainty and indicates that the person objects to the taking of the proposed action. (c) The personal representative is deemed to have notice of the objection to the proposed action if it is delivered or received at the address stated in the notice of proposed action before whichever of the following times is the later: (1) The date specified in the notice of proposed action on or after which the proposed action is to be taken. (2) The date the proposed action is actually taken.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10588(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) Any person who is entitled to notice of proposed action for a proposed action described in subdivision (a) of Section 10580, or any person who is given notice of a proposed action described in subdivision (b) of Section 10580, may apply to the court having jurisdiction over the proceeding for an order restraining the personal representative from taking the proposed action without court supervision. The court shall grant the requested order without requiring notice to the personal representative and without cause being shown for the order.

clauses.title: What Happens After a Timely Objection — and What Happens If No One Objects
clauses.body: Probate Code § 10589 states what a personal representative must do once notified of a timely objection or restraining order. Under § 10589(a), if the proposed action is one that would have required court supervision had the personal representative not held IAEA authority, and the personal representative has notice of a written objection under § 10587 or a restraining order under § 10588, the personal representative may take that action — if still desired — only under the Probate Code's ordinary court-supervision provisions for that kind of action; the notice-of-proposed-action procedure itself does not authorize taking it. Under § 10589(b), if the proposed action is one that would not have required court supervision even without IAEA authority, but the personal representative chose to give notice anyway and then received a timely objection or restraining order, the personal representative must request instructions from the court and may take the action only under whatever order the court enters. On the other side, Probate Code § 10590(a) addresses what happens when no one objects: except in narrow circumstances described elsewhere in that section, a person described in § 10581 who has been given notice under §§ 10580 through 10586 and does not object within the time and manner § 10587 provides waives the right to have a court review the action, or to object to it, after it has been taken; the same waiver applies to a person who has consented to or waived notice of the action under §§ 10582 through 10584.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Probate Code § 10589 (subdivisions (a) and (b), as one continuous quotation — not independent of one another) and Probate Code § 10590, subdivision (a) only, as a second, independent citation. Section 10590 contains further subdivisions — (b) and (c) — that create narrow exceptions to the waiver described here (for a person who establishes actual non-receipt of the notice before the objection period ran, and for an heir or devisee who lacked capacity or was a minor at the time notice was given, under further conditions involving that person's guardian, conservator, or other legal representative) and a subdivision (d) defining how an objection is made for purposes of that section; this clause does not quote or independently verify those additional subdivisions and does not purport to state them.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10589 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) If the proposed action is one that would require court supervision if the personal representative had not been granted authority to administer the estate under this part and the personal representative has notice of a written objection made under Section 10587 to the proposed action or a restraining order issued under Section 10588, the personal representative shall, if the personal representative desires to take the proposed action, take the proposed action under the provisions of this code dealing with court supervision of that kind of action. (b) If the proposed action is one that would not require court supervision even if the personal representative had not been granted authority to administer the estate under this part but the personal representative has given notice of the proposed action and has notice of a written objection made under Section 10587 to the proposed action or a restraining order issued under Section 10588, the personal representative shall, if he or she desires to take the proposed action, request instructions from the court concerning the proposed action. The personal representative may take the proposed action only under such order as may be entered by the court.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10590(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) Except as provided in subdivision (c), only a person described in Section 10581 has a right to have the court review the proposed action after it has been taken or otherwise to object to the proposed action after it has been taken. Except as provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), a person described in Section 10581 waives the right to have the court review the proposed action after it has been taken, or otherwise to object to the proposed action after it has been taken, if either of the following circumstances exists: (1) The person has been given notice of a proposed action, as provided in Sections 10580 to 10586, inclusive, and fails to object as provided in subdivision (d). (2) The person has waived notice of or consented to the proposed action as provided in Sections 10582 to 10584, inclusive.

clauses.title: Consequences If the Personal Representative Does Not Follow the Notice Procedure
clauses.body: Two statutes address what follows if a personal representative fails to comply with the notice-of-proposed-action procedure. Probate Code § 10591(a) provides that the personal representative's failure to comply with § 10580(a) and with §§ 10581, 10585, 10586, and 10589 — and taking the action without that compliance — does not itself affect the validity of the action taken, or the title of a bona fide purchaser to property conveyed or transferred, or the rights of a third person who dealt in good faith with the personal representative and changed position in reliance on the action without actual notice of the noncompliance; § 10591(b) adds that a person dealing with the personal representative has no duty to inquire or investigate whether the personal representative complied with those provisions. Separately, Probate Code § 10592 addresses the personal representative's own exposure for noncompliance: under § 10592(a), where notice of proposed action is required by this chapter, the court has discretion to remove the personal representative from office unless the personal representative gives the required notice, obtains a waiver of it, or obtains consent to the action, as the chapter provides; under § 10592(b), the court also has discretion to remove the personal representative for taking a proposed action in violation of § 10589 — that is, proceeding despite a timely objection or restraining order without the court supervision or instructions § 10589 requires.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two separately numbered sections, §§ 10591 and 10592, each quoted once in full; neither citation is a subsection of the other. Both provisions describe removal or protection as matters within the court's discretion ("may") rather than automatic consequences, and this clause does not characterize either outcome as guaranteed to occur in any particular case.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10591 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) The failure of the personal representative to comply with subdivision (a) of Section 10580 and with Sections 10581, 10585, 10586, and 10589, and the taking of the action by the personal representative without such compliance, does not affect the validity of the action so taken or the title to any property conveyed or transferred to bona fide purchasers or the rights of third persons who, dealing in good faith with the personal representative, changed their position in reliance upon the action, conveyance, or transfer without actual notice of the failure of the personal representative to comply with those provisions. (b) No person dealing with the personal representative has any duty to inquire or investigate whether or not the personal representative has complied with the provisions listed in subdivision (a).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 10592 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) In a case where notice of proposed action is required by this chapter, the court in its discretion may remove the personal representative from office unless the personal representative does one of the following: (1) Gives notice of proposed action as provided in this chapter. (2) Obtains a waiver of notice of proposed action as provided in this chapter. (3) Obtains a consent to the proposed action as provided in this chapter. (b) The court in its discretion may remove the personal representative from office if the personal representative takes a proposed action in violation of Section 10589.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment — Notice of Proposed Action Procedure Reference
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that I have reviewed the foregoing information about the notice-of-proposed-action procedure in connection with the estate of {{decedentName}}.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{executorName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This reference describes California's statutory notice-of-proposed-action procedure under Probate Code §§ 10580-10592. It does not itself give, waive, consent to, or object to notice of any proposed action, and it is not a substitute for an actual Notice of Proposed Action, written consent, written waiver, written objection, or court filing prepared and delivered in accordance with that procedure.]

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes two related California statutory doctrines that can determine what a beneficiary of {{decedentName}}'s estate actually receives: ademption (Probate Code §§ 21133-21140), which governs what happens to a specific gift in a will or trust when the specifically-given property is no longer part of the estate at death, and abatement (Probate Code §§ 21400-21406), which governs the order in which gifts are reduced or eliminated when the estate's assets are insufficient to pay all debts, expenses, and gifts in full. It states facts about California law generally. It does not determine how these doctrines apply to any specific gift in {{decedentName}}'s estate, and it does not advise on what to do about a particular gift or asset.

clauses.title: Ademption by Extinction: The Statutory Right to Substitutes
clauses.body: California's specific-gift statute gives the recipient of a specific gift a right to the gifted property only to the extent the property is still owned by the transferor when the gift takes effect. If the specifically-gifted property is no longer part of the estate, the statute nonetheless gives the recipient a right to several enumerated substitutes in its place: any unpaid balance of the purchase price from a sale of the property, any unpaid eminent domain award for a taking of the property, any unpaid insurance proceeds or other recovery for injury to the property, and property the transferor acquired through foreclosure (or in lieu of foreclosure) of a security interest connected to the specifically-given obligation.
clauses.gap: This section identifies four categories of substitute rights tied to how the property left the estate (sale, condemnation, casualty, or foreclosure). It does not itself address every circumstance in which specifically-gifted property might be missing from the estate, and Probate Code § 21139 states that the statute's ademption rules generally are not exhaustive.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21133
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 21133
citations.quote: A recipient of an at-death transfer of a specific gift has a right to the property specifically given, to the extent the property is owned by the transferor at the time the gift takes effect in possession or enjoyment, and all of the following: (a) Any balance of the purchase price (together with any security agreement) owing from a purchaser to the transferor at the time the gift takes effect in possession or enjoyment by reason of sale of the property. (b) Any amount of an eminent domain award for the taking of the property unpaid at the time the gift takes effect in possession or enjoyment. (c) Any proceeds unpaid at the time the gift takes effect in possession or enjoyment on fire or casualty insurance on or other recovery for injury to the property. (d) Property owned by the transferor at the time the gift takes effect in possession or enjoyment and acquired as a result of foreclosure, or obtained in lieu of foreclosure, of the security interest for a specifically given obligation.

clauses.title: Ademption Exception: Sales or Encumbrances by a Conservator, Agent, or Trustee for an Incapacitated Person
clauses.body: A separate statute displaces the ordinary ademption result when specifically-given property is sold or encumbered, after the instrument of gift is executed, by a conservator, by an agent acting under a durable power of attorney for an incapacitated principal, or by a trustee acting for an incapacitated settlor of a revocable trust. In that circumstance, the recipient of the specific gift instead has a right to a general pecuniary gift equal to the net sale price (or the amount of the encumbrance), unreduced by payoff of the encumbrance, as well as to the property itself. The statute presumes that acts of an agent under a durable power of attorney are for an incapacitated principal, with no adjudication of incapacity required before death, but it applies no comparable presumption to a trustee's acts. The statute also carves out conservatorships: this substitute-gift rule does not apply if the conservatorship later terminates and the transferor survives that termination by one year.
clauses.gap: The quoted subdivisions (a) and (c) are both parts of the same statutory section, Probate Code § 21134, and are not independent of one another. Subdivision (b) of that same section (not quoted here) states a parallel rule for eminent domain awards and insurance proceeds paid to a conservator, agent, or trustee.
