This exception applies specifically to sales, encumbrances, or their proceeds handled by a conservator, an agent under a durable power of attorney, or a trustee for an incapacitated person — not to sales the transferor made personally, which are addressed by the ordinary ademption rule.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21134(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 21134(a)
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this section, if, after the execution of the instrument of gift, specifically given property is sold, or encumbered by a deed of trust, mortgage, or other instrument, by a conservator, by an agent acting within the authority of a durable power of attorney for an incapacitated principal, or by a trustee acting for an incapacitated settlor of a trust established by the settlor as a revocable trust, the transferee of the specific gift has the right to a general pecuniary gift equal to the net sale price of the property unreduced by the payoff of any such encumbrance, or the amount of the unpaid encumbrance on the property as well as the property itself.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21134(c)
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 21134(c)
citations.quote: For the purpose of the references in this section to a conservator, this section does not apply if, after the sale, mortgage, condemnation, fire, or casualty, or recovery, the conservatorship is terminated and the transferor survives the termination by one year.

clauses.title: Ademption by Satisfaction: Lifetime Gifts Credited Against a Testamentary Gift
clauses.body: California's statute treats ademption by extinction (addressed above) and "satisfaction" as governed by separate rules. A lifetime gift from the transferor to a beneficiary is treated as satisfying (reducing or eliminating) that beneficiary's at-death gift only if one of four conditions is met: the instrument itself provides for deducting the lifetime gift from the at-death gift; the transferor declares in a writing made at the time of the gift that it is meant to satisfy, or be deducted from, the at-death gift; the beneficiary acknowledges in writing that the gift is meant to satisfy, or be deducted from, the at-death gift; or the lifetime gift is of the same property that is the subject of a specific gift to that person. A separate statute states that these ademption and satisfaction rules are not exhaustive, and that nothing in them is intended to increase the incidence of ademption under California law.
clauses.gap: Subdivisions (b) through (d) of § 21135 (governing how a lifetime gift is valued for partial satisfaction, and what happens if the recipient of the lifetime gift predeceases the transferor) are not quoted here. Section 21139 is a separate, independently numbered section from § 21135; because it states that the rules in §§ 21133-21135 are not exhaustive, other circumstances affecting a specific gift may be governed by rules outside those three sections.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21135(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 21135(a)
citations.quote: (a) Property given by a transferor during his or her lifetime to a person is treated as a satisfaction of an at-death transfer to that person in whole or in part only if one of the following conditions is satisfied: (1) The instrument provides for deduction of the lifetime gift from the at-death transfer. (2) The transferor declares in a contemporaneous writing that the gift is in satisfaction of the at-death transfer or that its value is to be deducted from the value of the at-death transfer. (3) The transferee acknowledges in writing that the gift is in satisfaction of the at-death transfer or that its value is to be deducted from the value of the at-death transfer. (4) The property given is the same property that is the subject of a specific gift to that person.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21139
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 21139
citations.quote: The rules stated in Sections 21133 to 21135, inclusive, are not exhaustive, and nothing in those sections is intended to increase the incidence of ademption under the law of this state.

clauses.title: Abatement: The Statutory Order in Which Gifts Are Reduced
clauses.body: When an estate's assets are insufficient to pay all debts, expenses, and gifts in full, California's abatement statute sets out the order in which categories of gifts are reduced. Shares of beneficiaries abate in this order: (1) property not disposed of by the instrument; (2) residuary gifts; (3) general gifts to persons other than the transferor's relatives; (4) general gifts to the transferor's relatives; (5) specific gifts to persons other than the transferor's relatives; (6) specific gifts to the transferor's relatives. For this purpose, a "relative" of the transferor is defined by reference to California's intestate succession statutes — a person to whom property would pass from the transferor under Probate Code § 6401 or § 6402 if the transferor had died intestate with no other person having priority.
clauses.gap: The quoted subdivisions (a) and (b) are both parts of the same statutory section, Probate Code § 21402, and are not independent of one another. How shares abate within each of these six classes (pro rata, with an exception for annuities and demonstrative gifts) is addressed in a separate clause.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21402(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 21402(a)
citations.quote: (a) Shares of beneficiaries abate in the following order: (1) Property not disposed of by the instrument. (2) Residuary gifts. (3) General gifts to persons other than the transferor’s relatives. (4) General gifts to the transferor’s relatives. (5) Specific gifts to persons other than the transferor’s relatives. (6) Specific gifts to the transferor’s relatives.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21402(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 21402(b)
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, a “relative” of the transferor is a person to whom property would pass from the transferor under Section 6401 or 6402 (intestate succession) if the transferor died intestate and there were no other person having priority.

clauses.title: Abatement's Scope, and a Testator's Power to Override the Statutory Order
clauses.body: The statutory abatement order is a default, not a mandatory rule. California's statute provides that if the instrument itself provides for abatement, or if the transferor's plan or the purpose of the transfer would otherwise be defeated by the statutory abatement order, shares instead abate as necessary to effectuate the instrument, plan, or purpose. Absent such an override, the statutory order applies broadly: it governs abatement for all purposes, including payment of the estate's debts, expenses, and administration charges, satisfaction of gifts, and payment of expenses on specifically devised property, and it applies without any priority as between real and personal property.
clauses.gap: Section 21401 also carves out shares of an omitted spouse (Probate Code § 21612) or an omitted child (Probate Code § 21623), and tax proration under Probate Code Division 10 (commencing with § 20100), from the general abatement order described above; those carve-outs are separate statutory schemes not detailed further in this sheet. Sections 21400 and 21401 are separately numbered sections and are cited independently of one another.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21400
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 21400
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of this part, if the instrument provides for abatement, or if the transferor’s plan or if the purpose of the transfer would be defeated by abatement as provided in this part, the shares of beneficiaries abate as is necessary to effectuate the instrument, plan, or purpose.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21401
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 21401
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 21612 (omitted spouse) and 21623 (omitted children) and in Division 10 (commencing with Section 20100) (proration of taxes), shares of beneficiaries abate as provided in this part for all purposes, including payment of the debts, expenses, and charges specified in Section 11420, satisfaction of gifts, and payment of expenses on specifically devised property pursuant to Section 12002, and without any priority as between real and personal property.

clauses.title: Within Each Class: Pro Rata Reduction, Demonstrative Gifts, and Exoneration
clauses.body: Within each of the six classes described above, California's statute reduces shares pro rata -- proportionally -- rather than by any other method, subject to one exception: gifts of annuities and "demonstrative" gifts (gifts payable from a particular fund or source but not limited to it) are treated as specific gifts to the extent satisfied from the fund or property named in the gift, and as general gifts to the extent satisfied from other property. Separately, if an instrument requires that property subject to a specific gift be exonerated from a mortgage, deed of trust, or other lien, a specific gift of other property does not abate to pay for exonerating that encumbered property.
clauses.gap: The quoted subdivisions (a) and (b) of Probate Code § 21403 are both parts of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another. Section 21404 is a separate, independently numbered section addressed to instruments that require exoneration of a specific gift from an encumbrance, and is cited independently of § 21403.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21403(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 21403(a)
citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivision (b), shares of beneficiaries abate pro rata within each class specified in Section 21402.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21403(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 21403(b)
citations.quote: (b) Gifts of annuities and demonstrative gifts are treated as specific gifts to the extent they are satisfied out of the fund or property specified in the gift and as general gifts to the extent they are satisfied out of property other than the fund or property specified in the gift.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21404
citations.cite: Cal. Prob. Code § 21404
citations.quote: If an instrument requires property that is the subject of a specific gift to be exonerated from a mortgage, deed of trust, or other lien, a specific gift of other property does not abate for the purpose of exonerating the encumbered property.

clauses.title: Certification of Understanding
Purpose and Declaration
clauses.body: This document sets out information about California's Domestic Worker Bill of Rights, Labor Code sections 1450 through 1455, prepared in connection with domestic work performed for {{companyName}} by {{employeeName}} in the position of {{jobTitle}}, beginning on or about {{startDate}}. This document describes what the statute itself provides. It is not legal advice about how the statute applies to any particular person's specific work arrangement, hours, or duties.

clauses.title: Statutory Title and Coverage
clauses.body: Labor Code Part 4.5, sections 1450 through 1455, is titled and may be cited as the Domestic Worker Bill of Rights. It applies to "domestic work," which the statute defines as services related to the care of persons in private households or the maintenance of private households or their premises, including occupations such as childcare providers, caregivers of people with disabilities or of sick, convalescing, or elderly persons, house cleaners, housekeepers, and maids.
clauses.gap: Section 1451(a)(2) also states that domestic work does not include care of persons in facilities providing board or lodging in addition to medical, nursing, convalescent, aged, or child care, including residential care facilities for the elderly; that facility-based exclusion is not separately quoted here and this document does not independently verify how it applies to any specific facility. This document also does not address Labor Code section 1452 (a Governor's advisory committee provision) or section 1455 (a Division of Labor Standards Enforcement outreach and education program), which this document confirmed exist in the same Part but which do not themselves create worker entitlements.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1450 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: This part shall be known and may be cited as the Domestic Worker Bill of Rights.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1451(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: “Domestic work” means services related to the care of persons in private households or maintenance of private households or their premises. Domestic work occupations include childcare providers, caregivers of people with disabilities, sick, convalescing, or elderly persons, house cleaners, housekeepers, maids, and other household occupations.

clauses.title: Definition of Personal Attendant
clauses.body: Within the domestic work category, the statute separately defines "personal attendant." A personal attendant is any person employed by a private householder, or by a third-party employer recognized in the health care industry to work in a private household, to supervise, feed, or dress a child, or a person who by reason of advanced age, physical disability, or mental deficiency needs supervision. The statute states that personal attendant status applies only when no significant amount of other work is required, and it defines "no significant amount of work" as work other than supervising, feeding, or dressing that does not exceed 20 percent of the total weekly hours worked.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on a single statutory subsection, section 1451(d), so it is not a claim independently confirmed by more than one source. This document does not address how the 20-percent threshold is calculated or documented in practice, or how disputes over whether it is met would be resolved.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1451(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: “Personal attendant” means any person employed by a private householder or by any third-party employer recognized in the health care industry to work in a private household, to supervise, feed, or dress a child, or a person who by reason of advanced age, physical disability, or mental deficiency needs supervision. The status of personal attendant shall apply when no significant amount of work other than the foregoing is required. For purposes of this subdivision, “no significant amount of work” means work other than the foregoing did not exceed 20 percent of the total weekly hours worked.

clauses.title: Domestic Work Employee Status and Statutory Exclusions
clauses.body: The statute defines a "domestic work employee" as an individual who performs domestic work, a category that includes both live-in domestic work employees and personal attendants. The statute then excludes several categories of people from that definition, including any person who performs services through the In-Home Supportive Services program under specified Welfare and Institutions Code provisions, and any person who is the parent, grandparent, spouse, sibling, child, or legally adopted child of the domestic work employer.
clauses.gap: The two Labor Code citations in this clause -- section 1451(b)(1) and section 1451(b)(2)(A) and (B) -- are subsections of the same statutory section, 1451, and are not independent of one another as separate sources. The statute lists additional exclusion categories in section 1451(b)(2)(C) through (G) -- including certain minors employed as babysitters, casual babysitters, employees of licensed health facilities, certain regional-center-funded caregivers, and certain exempt child care providers -- that this document confirmed exist but does not separately quote or summarize here. This document does not independently verify how any of these exclusions applies to a specific working relationship.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1451(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: “Domestic work employee” means an individual who performs domestic work and includes live-in domestic work employees and personal attendants.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1451(b)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Any person who is the parent, grandparent, spouse, sibling, child, or legally adopted child of the domestic work employer.

clauses.title: Overtime Formula for Personal Attendants
clauses.body: The statute sets a distinct overtime formula for personal attendants that differs from California's general overtime thresholds. A domestic work employee who is a personal attendant is entitled to one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay for hours worked over nine in a workday and for hours worked over 45 in a workweek. This differs from the general California standard, under which the regular workday and workweek are eight hours and 40 hours, with overtime due for hours worked beyond those thresholds.
clauses.gap: This document does not address how "regular rate of pay" is calculated for a personal attendant, how the nine-hour/45-hour thresholds interact with double-time rules that apply under the general overtime statute, or whether any other wage order provisions modify these thresholds for particular personal attendants. This document also confirmed that the statute creating this Part, Labor Code sections 1450 through 1455, does not itself contain meal-break or rest-break provisions for personal attendants or other domestic work employees; meal and rest break requirements are governed by other California wage-and-hour law outside this Part, which this document does not address.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1454 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: A domestic work employee who is a personal attendant shall not be employed more than nine hours in any workday or more than 45 hours in any workweek unless the employee receives one and one-half times the employee’s regular rate of pay for all hours worked over nine hours in any workday and for all hours worked more than 45 hours in the workweek.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 510(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Eight hours of labor constitutes a day’s work. Any work in excess of eight hours in one workday and any work in excess of 40 hours in any one workweek and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in any one workweek shall be compensated at the rate of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay for an employee.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment
How California Courts Define "Misconduct": Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd.
clauses.body: Because Section 1256 does not itself define "misconduct," California courts have supplied the definition. The leading California Supreme Court decision construing the term, Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984) 35 Cal.3d 671, adopted and applied a definition originating in the Court of Appeal's decision in Maywood Glass Co. v. Stewart (1959) 170 Cal.App.2d 719: disqualifying misconduct is conduct evincing willful or wanton disregard of the employer's interests, shown in deliberate violation of standards of behavior the employer has the right to expect, or in carelessness or negligence of a degree or recurrence manifesting equal culpability, wrongful intent, or evil design, or an intentional and substantial disregard of the employer's interests or the employee's duties. On the other side of that line, the same definition states that mere inefficiency, unsatisfactory conduct, failure in good performance due to inability or incapacity, isolated inadvertencies or ordinary negligence, or good-faith errors in judgment or discretion are not "misconduct" within the meaning of the statute. The Amador court also traced this distinction to the code's own stated policy of providing benefits to "persons unemployed through no fault of their own," describing fault as the basic element in interpreting and applying the misconduct disqualification. Applying this standard to the facts before it, the Amador court held that a hospital employee who was discharged for willfully refusing to perform a procedure she reasonably and in good faith believed would jeopardize patient health had not committed "misconduct" within the meaning of Section 1256.
clauses.gap: This document's drafter located Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984) 35 Cal.3d 671 via CourtListener, confirmed its citation (35 Cal.3d 671, 677 P.2d 224, 200 Cal.Rptr. 298), and read the opinion's full text (CourtListener opinion id 9571860) before treating any holding or quotation from it as verified. Only Amador's own opinion was read and independently confirmed. The Maywood Glass Co. v. Stewart definition, and the code-policy "fault" language, are both block-quoted inside the Amador opinion rather than independently pulled from Maywood Glass Co.'s own opinion or from the Rowe v. Hansen decision Amador cites for the "fault" point; this document attributes those quotations to Amador (which itself quotes them) rather than implying independent verification of Maywood Glass Co. or Rowe. This document does not apply this standard to, or draw any conclusion about, any specific claimant's own conduct or separation.

citations.case: Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984)
citations.quote: The term “misconduct,” as used in the code, is limited to “ ‘conduct evincing such wilful or wanton disregard of an employer’s interests as is found in deliberate violations or disregard of standards of behavior which the employer has the right to expect of his employee, or in carelessness or negligence of such degree or recurrence as to manifest equal culpability, wrongful intent or evil design, or to show an intentional and substantial disregard of the employer’s interests or of the employee’s duties and obligations to his employer. On the other hand mere inefficiency, unsatisfactory conduct, failure in good performance as the result of inability or incapacity, inadvertencies or ordinary negligence in isolated instances, or good faith errors in judgment or discretion are not to be deemed “misconduct” within the meaning of the statute.’ ”

citations.case: Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984)
citations.quote: The policy of the code is to provide benefits to “persons unemployed through no fault of their own.” (§ 100.) “Accordingly, fault is the basic element to be considered in interpreting and applying the code sections on unemployment compensation.” ... [T]his court holds that a worker who has been discharged for wilfully refusing to perform work which she reasonably and in good faith believed would jeopardize the health of others has not committed “misconduct” within the meaning of section 1256.

clauses.title: How "Good Cause" Case Law Relates to the Misconduct Standard
clauses.body: Although Section 1256 states voluntary quit without good cause and discharge for misconduct as separate disqualifying grounds, Amador observed that case law on one informs the other: if a claimant's reasons for refusing a work directive would constitute good cause sufficient to justify resigning outright, those same reasons should also justify the less drastic step of refusing that particular work assignment, so that a discharge for such a refusal is not "misconduct." On the general meaning of "good cause" itself, Amador reiterated that the concept cannot be arbitrarily limited, and that it must account for real circumstances, substantial reasons, objective conditions, adequate excuses that will bear the test of reason, just grounds for action, and always the element of good faith. Amador also noted, as a general principle limiting misconduct disqualifications, that a claimant may not be denied benefits solely on the basis of a good-faith error in judgment.
clauses.gap: As with the preceding clause, this document's drafter read and independently confirmed Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984) 35 Cal.3d 671 via CourtListener (opinion id 9571860) before treating any quotation from it as verified; this clause is not an independent source from the preceding clause, since both quote the same opinion. The good-cause formulation quoted here is itself a passage Amador quotes from Gibson v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1973) 9 Cal.3d 494, which in turn quotes California Portland Cement Co. v. California Unemployment Ins. Appeals Board (1960) 178 Cal.App.2d 263; and the good-faith-error-in-judgment principle is a passage Amador quotes from Delgado v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1974) 41 Cal.App.3d 788. This document's drafter did not independently pull and verify the Gibson, California Portland Cement, or Delgado opinions themselves via CourtListener, and so does not cite them as independently verified sources; both quotations here are attributed to Amador, the opinion actually read, rather than to the cases Amador is quoting. This document does not apply this standard to, or draw any conclusion about, any specific claimant's own reasons for leaving or refusing work.

citations.case: Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984)
citations.quote: Although this case involves a discharge for “misconduct,” the law concerning voluntary terminations for “good cause” is also relevant. If a claimant’s reasons for refusing work constitute “good cause” sufficient to justify resignation, it follows that they should also justify the less drastic step of refusing a work assignment.

citations.case: Amador v. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd. (1984)
citations.quote: the concept of ‘good cause’ cannot be arbitrarily limited; the board must take account of ‘ “real circumstances, substantial reasons, objective conditions, palpable forces that operate to produce correlative results, adequate excuses that will bear the test of reason, just grounds for action, and always the element of good faith.” ’ ... A claimant may not be denied benefits solely on the basis of a “good faith error in judgment.”

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Genetic Information Privacy Act, Civil Code section 56.18 et seq. (Chapter 2.6 of the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act) — a state consumer-privacy statute governing direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies' collection, use, and disclosure of consumers' genetic data. It states facts about who the statute regulates, the express-consent categories it requires, the security and consumer-rights mechanisms it imposes, and its enforcement structure, as those may relate to {{businessName}}. This document is distinct from the federal Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (GINA), an employment-discrimination statute covered elsewhere in this collection: the statute described here regulates a company's data practices toward consumers, not an employer's treatment of employees or applicants. This information sheet does not itself constitute a privacy notice, does not obtain any consumer's consent, and does not tell {{businessName}} whether it is a "direct-to-consumer genetic testing company" under this statute or what to do about any specific product, practice, or consumer request.

clauses.title: Who the Statute Regulates: "Direct-to-Consumer Genetic Testing Company" and "Express Consent"
clauses.body: The Genetic Information Privacy Act applies to a defined category of entity. Civil Code § 56.18(b)(5) defines a "direct-to-consumer genetic testing company" as an entity that does any of three things: sells, markets, interprets, or otherwise offers consumer-initiated genetic testing products or services directly to consumers; analyzes genetic data obtained from a consumer, except to the extent the analysis is performed by a person licensed in the healing arts for diagnosis or treatment of a medical condition; or collects, uses, maintains, or discloses genetic data collected or derived from a direct-to-consumer genetic testing product or service, or directly provided by a consumer. The statute also defines the consent it requires in a specific way: under § 56.18(b)(6), "express consent" means a consumer's affirmative authorization given in response to a clear, meaningful, and prominent notice about a specific collection, use, maintenance, or disclosure of genetic data. The statute states that express consent cannot be inferred from inaction, and that agreement obtained through use of a "dark pattern" does not constitute consent.
clauses.gap: Both quotes are subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 56.18 — they are not independent of one another. This clause states the statute's own definitional scope; it does not determine whether any particular entity meets this definition. The statute's own text limits the analysis prong of the definition to entities other than a person licensed in the healing arts acting for diagnosis or treatment, and this clause does not address the statute's separate definitions of "genetic data," "biological sample," "consumer," or "service provider" (also in § 56.18(b) but not quoted here), nor the statute's scope exemptions for certain HIPAA- and Confidentiality of Medical Information Act-covered entities, research institutions, and other categories, which appear in a different section not covered in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.18(b)(5) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, definitions — "direct-to-consumer genetic testing company"
citations.quote: “Direct-to-consumer genetic testing company” means an entity that does any of the following: (A) Sells, markets, interprets, or otherwise offers consumer-initiated genetic testing products or services directly to consumers. (B) Analyzes genetic data obtained from a consumer, except to the extent that the analysis is performed by a person licensed in the healing arts for diagnosis or treatment of a medical condition. (C) Collects, uses, maintains, or discloses genetic data collected or derived from a direct-to-consumer genetic testing product or service, or is directly provided by a consumer.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.18(b)(6) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, definitions — "express consent"
citations.quote: “Express consent” means a consumer’s affirmative authorization to grant permission in response to a clear, meaningful, and prominent notice regarding the collection, use, maintenance, or disclosure of genetic data for a specific purpose. The nature of the data collection, use, maintenance, or disclosure shall be conveyed in clear and prominent terms in such a manner that an ordinary consumer would notice and understand it. Express consent cannot be inferred from inaction. Agreement obtained through use of dark patterns does not constitute consent.

clauses.title: Required Privacy Practices Summary and Privacy Notice
clauses.body: Before it may rely on the consents described below, the statute requires a direct-to-consumer genetic testing company to make specific disclosures available to a consumer. Civil Code § 56.181(a)(1) requires the company to provide clear and complete information about its data policies and procedures by making available to the consumer a summary of its privacy practices, written in plain language, and a prominent and easily accessible privacy notice containing, at a minimum, complete information about the company's data collection, consent, use, access, disclosure, maintenance, transfer, security, and retention and deletion practices, along with information that clearly describes how to file a complaint alleging a violation of the statute.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subsection, § 56.181(a)(1); no additional independent source was located for it. This clause states the notice-content requirement; it does not address the separate, additional consent requirement of § 56.181(a)(2), covered in a companion clause in this document, does not restate the statute's separate required notice concerning sharing of deidentified data for research purposes, and does not specify the format, length, or delivery method a notice must use beyond what the statute's own text requires.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(a)(1) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, privacy practices summary and privacy notice requirement
citations.quote: Provide clear and complete information regarding the company’s policies and procedures for the collection, use, maintenance, and disclosure, as applicable, of genetic data by making available to a consumer all of the following: (A) A summary of its privacy practices, written in plain language, that includes information about the company’s collection, use, maintenance, and disclosure, as applicable, of genetic data. (B) A prominent and easily accessible privacy notice that includes, at a minimum, complete information about the company’s data collection, consent, use, access, disclosure, maintenance, transfer, security, and retention and deletion practices, and information that clearly describes how to file a complaint alleging a violation of this chapter, pursuant to subdivision (c) of Section 56.182.

clauses.title: Express Consent Is a Menu of Separate Consents, Not One Blanket Consent
clauses.body: The statute does not treat a single consent as covering every use of a consumer's genetic data. Civil Code § 56.181(a)(2) requires a direct-to-consumer genetic testing company to obtain a consumer's express consent for the collection, use, and disclosure of the consumer's genetic data, and states that this includes, at a minimum, separate and express consent for each of several distinct categories: the use of the genetic data collected through the genetic testing product or service itself, including who has access to it, how it may be shared, and the specific purposes for which it will be collected, used, and disclosed; the storage of a consumer's biological sample after the initial testing requested by the consumer has been fulfilled; any use of genetic data or the biological sample beyond the primary purpose of the genetic testing or service and its inherent contextual uses; any transfer or disclosure of the consumer's genetic data or biological sample to a third party other than a service provider, including the name of that third party; and the marketing or facilitation of marketing to a consumer based on the consumer's genetic data, or by a third party based on the consumer having ordered, purchased, received, or used a genetic testing product or service.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subsection, § 56.181(a)(2); no additional independent source was located for it. The statute's marketing-consent category carries its own further conditions and a narrow same-company advertising exception, at § 56.181(a)(2)(E)(ii)-(iii), that are not restated in full here. This clause states which categories require separate consent under the statute's own text; it does not state what form a compliant consent must take beyond the statute's separate "express consent" definition covered in a companion clause, and does not address the revocation mechanism the statute requires once consent is given, also covered in a companion clause.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(a)(2) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, menu of separate express consents
citations.quote: Obtain a consumer’s express consent for collection, use, and disclosure of the consumer’s genetic data, including, at a minimum, separate and express consent for each of the following: (A) The use of the genetic data collected through the genetic testing product or service offered to the consumer, including who has access to genetic data, and how genetic data may be shared, and the specific purposes for which it will be collected, used, and disclosed. (B) The storage of a consumer’s biological sample after the initial testing requested by the consumer has been fulfilled. (C) Each use of genetic data or the biological sample beyond the primary purpose of the genetic testing or service and inherent contextual uses. (D) Each transfer or disclosure of the consumer’s genetic data or biological sample to a third party other than to a service provider, including the name of the third party to which the consumer’s genetic data or biological sample will be transferred or disclosed. (E) (i) The marketing or facilitation of marketing to a consumer based on the consumer’s genetic data or the marketing or facilitation of marketing by a third party based upon the consumer having ordered, purchased, received, or used a genetic testing product or service.

clauses.title: Revocation, Sample Destruction, Data Security, and Consumer Access/Deletion Rights
clauses.body: Once a company has obtained the consents described above, the statute imposes several follow-on obligations. Civil Code § 56.181(b) requires the company to provide effective mechanisms, without unnecessary steps, for a consumer to revoke consent after giving it, with at least one such mechanism using the company's primary medium of communication with consumers. Under § 56.181(c), the company must honor a revocation as soon as practicable and no later than 30 days after the consumer revokes consent, and must destroy the consumer's biological sample within 30 days of receiving a revocation of consent to store the sample. Separately, § 56.181(d) requires the company to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices to protect a consumer's genetic data against unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure, and to develop procedures and practices enabling a consumer to easily access the consumer's genetic data, delete the consumer's account and genetic data (except data the company must retain to comply with applicable legal and regulatory requirements), and have the consumer's biological sample destroyed.
clauses.gap: All three citations are subsections of a single statutory section, § 56.181 — they are not independent of one another. This clause states the revocation, sample-destruction, security, and access/deletion mechanisms the statute's own text requires; it does not state what "reasonable security procedures and practices" specifically requires beyond that general statutory language, and it does not address the separate consent-menu requirement of § 56.181(a)(2) or the nondiscrimination and insurer/employer disclosure restrictions of § 56.181(e)-(f), each covered in a companion clause.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, mechanism to revoke consent
citations.quote: A company that is subject to the requirements described in paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) shall provide effective mechanisms, without any unnecessary steps, for a consumer to revoke their consent after it is given, at least one of which utilizes the primary medium through which the company communicates with consumers.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, revocation deadline and sample destruction
citations.quote: If a consumer revokes the consent that they provided pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (a), the company shall honor the consumer’s consent revocation as soon as practicable, but not later than 30 days after the individual revokes consent, in accordance with both of the following: (1) Revocation of consent under this section shall comply with Part 46 of Title 45 of the Code of Federal Regulations. (2) The company shall destroy a consumer’s biological sample within 30 days of receipt of revocation of consent to store the sample.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.181(d) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, data security duty and consumer access/deletion rights
citations.quote: The direct-to-consumer genetic testing company shall do both of the following: (1) Implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices to protect a consumer’s genetic data against unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure. (2) Develop procedures and practices to enable a consumer to easily do any of the following: (A) Access the consumer’s genetic data. (B) Delete the consumer’s account and genetic data, except for genetic data that is required to be retained by the company to comply with applicable legal and regulatory requirements. (C) Have the consumer’s biological sample destroyed.

clauses.title: Nondiscrimination for Exercising Rights, and Restriction on Disclosure to Insurers and Employers
clauses.body: The statute also restricts what a company may do in response to a consumer's exercise of rights, and to whom it may disclose genetic data. Civil Code § 56.181(e) provides that a person or public entity shall not discriminate against a consumer because the consumer exercised rights under the statute, including by denying goods, services, or benefits, charging different prices or rates (including through discounts, incentives, or penalties), providing a different level or quality of goods, services, or benefits, suggesting the consumer would receive different treatment, or treating the exercise of rights as a basis for suspicion of criminal wrongdoing. Separately, § 56.181(f)(1) provides that, subject to a stated exception, a direct-to-consumer genetic testing company shall not disclose a consumer's genetic data to any entity responsible for administering or making decisions regarding health insurance, life insurance, long-term care insurance, disability insurance, or employment, or to any entity that provides advice to such an entity.
clauses.gap: Both citations are subsections of a single statutory section, § 56.181 — they are not independent of one another. This clause states the statute's nondiscrimination rule and its restriction on disclosure to insurance- and employment-decision entities; it does not restate the statute's own exception to that disclosure restriction, set out in § 56.181(f)(2), for an entity not primarily engaged in those functions whose relevant agents or divisions are walled off from the data, and it does not address the separate consent, revocation, security, or notice obligations covered in companion clauses.

citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, nondiscrimination for exercising statutory rights
citations.quote: A person or public entity shall not discriminate against a consumer because the consumer exercised any of the consumer’s rights under this chapter by doing any of the following, including, but not limited to: (1) Denying goods, services, or benefits to the customer. (2) Charging different prices or rates for goods or services, including through the use of discounts or other incentives or imposing penalties.

citations.cite: Genetic Information Privacy Act, restriction on disclosure to insurance and employment decisionmakers
citations.quote: a direct-to-consumer genetic testing company shall not disclose a consumer’s genetic data to any entity that is responsible for administering or making decisions regarding health insurance, life insurance, long-term care insurance, disability insurance, or employment or to any entity that provides advice to an entity that is responsible for performing those functions.

clauses.title: Enforcement: Civil Penalties Prosecuted by Public Officials
clauses.body: The statute states its own civil penalty amounts and names who may bring an enforcement action. Civil Code § 56.182(a) provides that a person who negligently violates the statute shall be assessed a civil penalty of up to one thousand dollars ($1,000) plus court costs. Section 56.182(b) provides that a person who willfully violates the statute shall be assessed a civil penalty of not less than one thousand dollars ($1,000) and not more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) plus court costs. Under § 56.182(c), actions for relief under the statute must be prosecuted exclusively in a court of competent jurisdiction by the Attorney General, a district attorney, an authorized county counsel, or specified city attorneys or city prosecutors, in the name of the People of the State of California, brought upon their own complaint, upon the complaint of a board, officer, person, corporation, or association, or upon the complaint of a person who has suffered injury in fact and lost money or property as a result of the violation. Section 56.182(d) provides that penalties recovered under the statute are paid to the individual to whom the genetic data at issue pertains.
clauses.gap: All four citations are subsections of a single statutory section, § 56.182 — they are not independent of one another. The statute's own text places prosecution of a violation exclusively in the hands of the named public officials; on this text, it does not give a consumer a standalone civil claim to file and litigate directly the way some other California privacy statutes do — a consumer's own complaint of injury in fact is instead one stated basis on which a public official may choose to bring an action, and a consumer to whom the genetic data pertains is the one to whom any penalty ultimately recovered is paid. Whether some other statute (for example, the state's Unfair Competition Law) supplies a separate, independent avenue was not researched for this clause and is not addressed here.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Declaration and Purpose
clauses.body:
This information sheet concerns the working relationship between {{artistName}} (the "artist") and {{talentRepresentativeName}}, who is identified here as the artist's representative for entertainment-industry business matters, for reference only. This sheet summarizes provisions of California's Talent Agencies Act, Labor Code section 1700 et seq., which regulates who may lawfully engage in the occupation of procuring, offering, promising, or attempting to procure employment or engagements for an artist, requires that person or corporation to first obtain a license from the California Labor Commissioner, and gives the Labor Commissioner a role in hearing controversies arising under the Act.

This sheet is an informational record only. It does not determine whether {{talentRepresentativeName}}'s activities on behalf of {{artistName}} do or do not fall within the Act's definition of "talent agency," does not determine whether any particular engagement of {{talentRepresentativeName}} by {{artistName}} is governed by the Act, and does not itself create, terminate, license, or otherwise affect any legal relationship between them. It is not legal advice and is not a substitute for reading the statute, and the case law construing it, directly.

clauses.title: Who Is a "Talent Agency": Statutory Definition and the Recording-Contract Exception
clauses.body:
California's Talent Agencies Act defines who is regulated as a "talent agency." Labor Code section 1700.4(a) states: "'Talent agency' means a person or corporation who engages in the occupation of procuring, offering, promising, or attempting to procure employment or engagements for an artist or artists, except that the activities of procuring, offering, or promising to procure recording contracts for an artist or artists shall not of itself subject a person or corporation to regulation and licensing under this chapter. Talent agencies may, in addition, counsel or direct artists in the development of their professional careers."

Section 1700.4(b) defines "artists" broadly: "'Artists' means actors and actresses rendering services on the legitimate stage and in the production of motion pictures, radio artists, musical artists, musical organizations, directors of legitimate stage, motion picture and radio productions, musical directors, writers, cinematographers, composers, lyricists, arrangers, models, and other artists and persons rendering professional services in motion picture, theatrical, radio, television and other entertainment enterprises."

The statute's own text draws the regulatory line at the activity of procuring, offering, promising, or attempting to procure employment or engagements for an artist — not at a job title such as "agent" or "manager." It expressly carves the activity of procuring, offering, or promising to procure a recording contract, standing alone, out of what triggers licensure, and it expressly permits a talent agency to also counsel or direct an artist's career. Whether {{talentRepresentativeName}}'s specific activities on behalf of {{artistName}} do or do not fall within this definition is a determination this sheet does not make.

This is one primary source checked twice for consistency, not two independent sources. This clause quotes subsections (a) and (b) of that same section; they are not independent of one another. Neither subsection states where the line falls between a person who occasionally helps arrange a single engagement and a person who is "engaged in the occupation" of procuring engagements — California case law addressing that line, and the related question of whether a "personal manager" can fall within this definition, is covered in a separate clause in this document rather than restated here.

Talent agencies may, in addition, counsel or direct artists in the development of their professional careers.

clauses.title: Licensing Requirement
clauses.body:
The Act requires a license before anyone engages in the occupation of a talent agency. Labor Code section 1700.5 states: "No person shall engage in or carry on the occupation of a talent agency without first procuring a license therefor from the Labor Commissioner." The same section also requires that the license be posted in a conspicuous place in the licensee's office and that the license number be referred to in any advertisement soliciting talent for the agency.

This licensing requirement attaches to the occupation described in Labor Code section 1700.4 — procuring, offering, promising, or attempting to procure employment or engagements for an artist — rather than to any particular business title. Whether {{talentRepresentativeName}} holds, or is required to hold, a license under this section is a fact this sheet does not state.

This clause relies on a single statutory section, so no source-independence disclosure beyond that dual-fetch consistency check applies here.

clauses.title: Required Contract Approval and Disclosure
clauses.body:
The Act requires a licensed talent agency to use a form of contract approved in advance by the Labor Commissioner and to disclose its license status on the contract itself. Labor Code section 1700.23 states: "Every talent agency shall submit to the Labor Commissioner a form or forms of contract to be utilized by such talent agency in entering into written contracts with artists for the employment of the services of such talent agency by such artists, and secure the approval of the Labor Commissioner thereof. Such approval shall not be withheld as to any proposed form of contract unless such proposed form of contract is unfair, unjust and oppressive to the artist. Each such form of contract, except under the conditions specified in Section 1700.45, shall contain an agreement by the talent agency to refer any controversy between the artist and the talent agency relating to the terms of the contract to the Labor Commissioner for adjustment. There shall be printed on the face of the contract in prominent type the following: 'This talent agency is licensed by the Labor Commissioner of the State of California.'"

This sheet does not state whether any contract between {{artistName}} and {{talentRepresentativeName}} has been submitted to or approved by the Labor Commissioner under this section, or whether it carries the disclosure language this section describes.

clauses.title: Labor Commissioner's Role in Controversies Under the Act
clauses.body:
The Act channels disputes arising under it to the Labor Commissioner in the first instance. Labor Code section 1700.44(a) states: "In cases of controversy arising under this chapter, the parties involved shall refer the matters in dispute to the Labor Commissioner, who shall hear and determine the same, subject to an appeal within 10 days after determination, to the superior court where the same shall be heard de novo." The same subsection describes a bonding requirement to stay any money award pending appeal, and a procedure for the Labor Commissioner to certify, without a hearing, that no controversy exists when there is no dispute over the fee owed.

Section 1700.44(b) separately addresses what does not happen when a person fails to hold a required license: "Notwithstanding any other provision of law to the contrary, failure of any person to obtain a license from the Labor Commissioner pursuant to this chapter shall not be considered a criminal act under any law of this state." Section 1700.44(c) imposes a time limit: "No action or proceeding shall be brought pursuant to this chapter with respect to any violation which is alleged to have occurred more than one year prior to commencement of the action or proceeding."

This sheet does not state whether any dispute between {{artistName}} and {{talentRepresentativeName}} is a "controversy arising under this chapter" for purposes of this section, and does not calculate any one-year period that might apply to a specific dispute.

This clause quotes subsections (a), (b), and (c) of that same section; they are not independent of one another. The statute's own text does not use the phrase "exclusive original jurisdiction"; California case law construing the scope and effect of this referral requirement is covered in a separate clause in this document rather than restated here. Subsection (d) of this section, which this clause does not quote, states that it is not unlawful for an unlicensed person or corporation to act in conjunction with, and at the request of, a licensed talent agency in negotiating an employment contract; this sheet notes that exception exists but does not characterize its scope further.

clauses.title: California Case Law: Personal Managers and the Act
clauses.body:
The California Supreme Court has addressed how the Act applies to a "personal manager" — a role the Act itself does not define — when that manager's activities include procuring employment. In Marathon Entertainment, Inc. v. Blasi (2008) 42 Cal.4th 974, the court observed: "The line dividing the functions of agents, who must be licensed, and of managers, who need not be, is often blurred and sometimes crossed." The court held that the Act's licensing requirement applies to a personal manager who procures employment for an artist, not only to someone who holds themselves out as an agent: "the strictures of the Talent Agencies Act (Lab. Code, § 1700 et seq.) (Act) apply to managers as well as agents."

The court also held that when a manager procures employment without a license, the Labor Commissioner is not required to void the entire management contract. The Labor Commissioner has authority to void the contract from its inception for that violation, but also has discretion, under the doctrine of severability, to enforce the lawful parts of the contract separately from the unlawful ones: "while the Labor Commissioner has the authority to void manager-talent contracts ab initio for unlawful procurement, she also has discretion to apply the doctrine of severability to partially enforce these contracts." This sheet does not state whether {{talentRepresentativeName}}'s activities on behalf of {{artistName}} involve procuring employment, and does not state how any severability analysis would apply to their arrangement.

It is genuinely independent of the Labor Code sections cited elsewhere in this document, since it is case law construing the statute rather than a subsection of the same statutory text. This clause does not address every holding in the opinion (for example, its discussion of the constitutional challenges Marathon raised, which the court did not reach on the merits before remanding on the severability question) and does not describe any later case applying or limiting this decision.

clauses.title: Record and Signature
Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet explains what California law does — and does not — require regarding severance pay when {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}} ends. It addresses severance pay specifically: additional compensation not tied to work already performed. It does not address, and is separate from, final wages — compensation {{employeeName}} has already earned by working, which California law separately requires {{companyName}} to pay by its own deadlines regardless of whether any severance is ever paid.

clauses.title: No General Right to Severance Pay
clauses.body: California law does not give {{employeeName}} a general, default right to severance pay simply because {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}} ends. Unlike final wages — which state law requires to be paid by fixed deadlines regardless of the circumstances of separation — severance pay is additional money not tied to work already performed, and no California statute or common-law rule entitles an employee to it by default. The California Supreme Court has approached severance pay as a matter of ordinary contract law rather than a right the law supplies automatically: whether an employer's severance-related policy binds the employer is treated as a question of contract formation — whether the employer made a promise and the employee accepted it — not as the application of a standing legal entitlement that exists independent of any such promise.
clauses.gap: This clause's conclusion rests on two things verified this session: (1) published California Supreme Court case law that analyzes severance-pay policies exclusively through contract-formation doctrine (offer, acceptance, and unilateral-contract principles), reasoning that would be unnecessary if the law already guaranteed severance pay by default; and (2) this corpus's own separate, already-verified documents addressing money owed at the end of employment (final wages, the waiting-time penalty, and unclaimed final wages), none of which identify any general severance-pay mandate. This session's network access to primary California government sources — California Legislative Information's Labor Code text and the Department of Industrial Relations' published guidance — was blocked by this environment's network controls, so this clause does not rest on an exhaustive, line-by-line canvass of the Labor Code affirmatively ruling out every possible severance provision, and no source was found or verified this session stating the negative proposition — "California has no general severance-pay statute" — in so many words. The citation below comes from a wrongful-termination/implied-contract case rather than a case or agency source addressing severance pay's absence head-on.

citations.case: Scott v. Pacific Gas & Electric Co.
citations.quote: Conceptually, there is no rational reason why an employer’s policy that its employees will not be demoted except for good cause, like a policy restricting termination or providing for severance pay, cannot become an implied term of an employment contract. In each of these instances, an employer promises to confer a significant benefit on the employee, and it is a question of fact whether that promise was reasonably understood by the employee to create a contractual obligation.

clauses.title: An Employer's Own Promise of Severance Can Become Binding
clauses.body: While California law does not require {{companyName}} to offer severance in the first place, a severance policy or promise {{companyName}} does choose to adopt — in an employee handbook, an individual agreement, or an established practice — can become a binding legal obligation once made. California courts have recognized that an employer's promise to pay severance benefits can form an enforceable "unilateral contract": an offer that becomes binding once an employee accepts it, typically simply by continuing to work for the employer after the policy is adopted. That is the legal mechanism that separates an unenforceable gratuity from a binding commitment — not any default statutory entitlement, but the ordinary contract-law consequence of a promise, once made and accepted.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are drawn from the same opinion (Asmus v. Pacific Bell), so they are not independent of one another. The first is that opinion's own bracketed characterization of a separate, older Court of Appeal decision, Chinn v. China National Aviation Corp. (1955) 138 Cal.App.2d 98, 99-100 — Chinn itself was not independently read or verified for this document. Asmus's broader holding (not restated in this clause) concerned a different question: once such a policy has become a binding unilateral contract through employee acceptance, on what terms an employer may later modify or terminate it prospectively; this clause only draws on Asmus for the antecedent point that such a policy can become binding in the first place, which the parties in that case did not dispute.

citations.quote: [employer's agreement to pay severance benefits becomes enforceable unilateral contract if employee accepts benefit offer by continuing employment]

citations.case: Asmus v. Pacific Bell
citations.quote: In a unilateral contract, there is only one promisor, who is under an enforceable legal duty.

clauses.title: How This Differs from the California WARN Act
clauses.body: One specific, narrow rule operates alongside the general absence of a severance requirement described above: the California WARN Act (Cal/WARN, Labor Code § 1400 et seq., covered fully in this project's California WARN Act (Cal/WARN) Information Sheet) does not create a right to severance pay either, but it does impose its own separate monetary liability on a covered employer that orders a qualifying mass layoff, relocation, or termination without first giving the 60 days' written notice California law requires. An employer who violates that notice requirement is liable to each affected employee for back pay and the value of lost benefits, capped at 60 days of liability (or half the employee's total time worked, if smaller). In practice, that liability can resemble severance pay — money paid to a terminated employee beyond wages already earned — but legally it is a penalty tied specifically to the employer's failure to give the required notice, not a severance entitlement in its own right: an employer that gives timely, complete notice owes nothing further under this law, and an event or employer that does not meet Cal/WARN's own coverage thresholds and triggering conditions is not reached by it at all.
clauses.gap: This clause's description of the Cal/WARN liability formula restates — rather than independently re-verifies — the primary-source Labor Code § 1402 quotations already fetched and verified for this project's existing California WARN Act (Cal/WARN) Information Sheet document (clause id calwarn_liability, checked 2026-09-02); this session's access to leginfo.legislature.ca.gov was blocked by this environment's network controls, so the statute could not be independently re-fetched for this document. The two citations below are both subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 1402) and so are not independent of one another. Readers should treat the existing California WARN Act (Cal/WARN) Information Sheet document, not this one, as the authoritative source for Cal/WARN's coverage thresholds, triggering events, notice content, exceptions, and enforcement mechanics — including the coverage threshold (a facility employing 75 or more people) and the definition of a qualifying mass layoff, relocation, or termination, neither of which is restated here.

(2) The value of the cost of any benefits to which the employee would have been entitled had his or her employment not been lost, including the cost of any medical expenses incurred by the employee that would have been covered under an employee benefit plan.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Family Code Section 2641 Reimbursement Information Sheet concerns {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, whose marital dissolution or legal separation proceeding is pending, or may be filed, in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes what California Family Code section 2641 says about the community's right, upon dissolution of marriage or legal separation, to reimbursement for community or quasi-community property spent on the education or training of one party where that education or training substantially enhanced that party's earning capacity. Section 2641 addresses a different reimbursement mechanism than Family Code section 2640, which is the subject of a separate information sheet in this set: section 2640 concerns a spouse's SEPARATE property contributions to the ACQUISITION of COMMUNITY property (for example, a down payment on a house), while section 2641 concerns COMMUNITY contributions to one party's EDUCATION OR TRAINING. This information sheet states what the Family Code says about the section 2641 reimbursement right in general terms. It does not determine, calculate, or assert that the right applies to {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}'s specific payments, education, or training, whether any statutory ground for reduction or presumption applies to their specific facts, or whether an express written agreement to the contrary exists between them; those are matters for the court to decide based on the specific facts, or for {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} to resolve by their own written agreement.

clauses.title: What Counts as "Community Contributions to Education or Training" Under Section 2641
clauses.body: Family Code section 2641 defines "community contributions to education or training," as the term is used in that section, to mean payments made with community or quasi-community property for education or training, or for the repayment of a loan incurred for education or training. By the statute's own terms, this definition applies whether the payments were made while the parties were resident in California or resident outside California. This definition is distinct from, and should not be confused with, Family Code section 2640's separate definition of "contributions to the acquisition of property" (down payments, improvements, and loan-principal payments toward acquiring community property), which is addressed in this corpus's companion Section 2640 Reimbursement Information Sheet and is not restated here.

This citation is to the same statutory section, 2641, cited by this document's other authority clauses (which quote subdivisions (b), (c), (d), and (e)) — they are not independent of one another; all are different subdivisions of one enacted section. The statute's own text does not define "quasi-community property" within section 2641 itself (that term is defined elsewhere in the Family Code), and this document does not address that separate definition. This document also does not address how a party establishes, as an evidentiary matter, that a particular historical payment was made with community or quasi-community property rather than separate property, which the statute's text does not itself resolve.

clauses.title: The Community's Right to Reimbursement With Interest, and the Assignment of Related Loans
clauses.body: Family Code section 2641 provides that, upon dissolution of marriage or legal separation, subject to the limitations stated elsewhere in the statute, the community shall be reimbursed for community contributions to education or training of a party that substantially enhances the earning capacity of that party. This reimbursement is with interest: the statute specifies that the amount reimbursed shall be with interest at the legal rate, accruing from the end of the calendar year in which the contributions were made. Separately, the statute addresses a loan incurred during the marriage for a party's education or training: such a loan is not included among the community's liabilities for purposes of dividing the community estate, but is instead assigned for payment by the party whose education or training the loan financed.

This citation is to the same statutory section, 2641, cited by this document's other authority clauses (subdivisions (a), (c), (d), and (e)) — they are not independent of one another; all are different subdivisions of one enacted section. This section 2641(b) reimbursement (with interest at the legal rate) is a materially different formula than Family Code section 2640(b)'s reimbursement (without interest or adjustment for value change, capped at net value at division), which is addressed in this corpus's companion Section 2640 Reimbursement Information Sheet; this document does not restate that separate formula and takes no position on how the two compare beyond noting they are different statutory mechanisms. The statute's own text does not define "the legal rate" numerically within section 2641, nor does it define "substantially enhances the earning capacity," and this document does not address either further. clauses.title: Reduction for Unjust Circumstances and the Ten-Year Rebuttable Presumption
clauses.body: Family Code section 2641 states that the reimbursement and assignment the statute otherwise requires shall be reduced or modified to the extent circumstances render that disposition unjust, and lists specific circumstances — stated by the statute to be a non-exhaustive list — that can support such a reduction. One listed circumstance is that the community has substantially benefited from the education, training, or loan incurred for the education or training of the party. The statute attaches a rebuttable presumption, affecting the burden of proof, to the timing of the community's contributions relative to when the dissolution or legal separation proceeding commenced, and the presumption runs in different directions depending on that timing: contributions made LESS than 10 years before commencement of the proceeding are presumed NOT to have substantially benefited the community, while contributions made MORE than 10 years before commencement of the proceeding are presumed TO HAVE substantially benefited the community. Because the statute states this is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof, rather than a conclusive rule, its own text does not make either directional presumption automatically decide whether reimbursement is reduced in a given case.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2641(c) and its first listed circumstance, subdivision (c)(1), fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. This citation is to the same statutory section, 2641, cited by this document's other authority clauses (subdivisions (a), (b), (d), and (e)) — they are not independent of one another; all are different subdivisions of one enacted section. The introductory sentence quoted here ("The reimbursement and assignment required by this section shall be reduced or modified to the extent circumstances render such a disposition unjust, including, but not limited to, any of the following:") also governs the two additional statutory grounds addressed in this document's companion clause on other reduction grounds, subdivisions (c)(2) and (c)(3) — that companion clause is likewise not independent of this one; both quote language from the same subdivision (c). The statute's own text does not specify what evidence or procedure rebuts either directional presumption, nor does it define "commencement of the proceeding" within section 2641 itself, and this document does not address either further. This clause states only the statute's substantial-benefit ground and its associated ten-year presumption; it does not state whether or how that presumption has been applied to any particular set of facts, which is a matter for the court.

citations.cite: the reduce-or-modify-if-unjust standard and its non-exhaustive list, and the ten-year rebuttable presumption on whether the community has substantially benefited
citations.quote: The reimbursement and assignment required by this section shall be reduced or modified to the extent circumstances render such a disposition unjust, including, but not limited to, any of the following: (1) The community has substantially benefited from the education, training, or loan incurred for the education or training of the party. There is a rebuttable presumption, affecting the burden of proof, that the community has not substantially benefited from community contributions to the education or training made less than 10 years before the commencement of the proceeding, and that the community has substantially benefited from community contributions to the education or training made more than 10 years before the commencement of the proceeding.

clauses.title: Other Statutory Grounds for Reducing or Modifying Reimbursement
clauses.body: In addition to the community's substantial benefit from the education or training addressed in this document's companion clause, Family Code section 2641 lists two further circumstances that can support reducing or modifying the reimbursement and assignment the statute otherwise requires. First, the statute lists as a ground for reduction that the education or training received by the party is offset by the education or training received by the other party for which community contributions have been made. Second, the statute lists as a ground for reduction that the education or training enables the party who received it to engage in gainful employment that substantially reduces the need of that party for support that would otherwise be required. As with the substantial-benefit ground, the statute's own text states its list of circumstances is not exhaustive.

The statute's own text does not define "offset," "gainful employment," or how "substantially reduces the need" is measured, and this document does not address any of those terms further. clauses.title: Exclusive Remedy, Relationship to Spousal Support, and Waiver by Written Agreement
clauses.body: Family Code section 2641 states that reimbursement for community contributions and assignment of loans under this section is the exclusive remedy of the community or a party for the education or training and any resulting enhancement of the earning capacity of a party — meaning the statute does not provide the community, or either party, with a separate or additional remedy for that same education, training, or earning-capacity enhancement outside of this reimbursement and assignment mechanism. The statute's own text qualifies that exclusivity in one respect: it states that nothing in that subdivision limits consideration of the effect of the education, training, or enhancement, or the amount reimbursed under section 2641, on the circumstances of the parties for purposes of a spousal support order under Family Code section 4320 — a separate statute governing spousal support factors, addressed in this corpus's Marital Settlement Agreement document and not restated here. Finally, section 2641 states that the entire section is subject to an express written agreement of the parties to the contrary.

clauses.title: Declaration of Purpose — Interstate Compact on Placement of Children Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Interstate Compact on Placement of Children (ICPC) Information Sheet describes California's adoption, by California Family Code § 7900, of the multistate compact set out in full at Family Code § 7901, which governs the interstate placement of a child — here, {{childName}}, born {{childDOB}} — for foster care or as a preliminary to a possible adoption, where the placement involves California and {{otherState}}. {{placingPartyName}} is identified, for reference, as the person or agency proposing or arranging {{childName}}'s placement.

The ICPC is not itself a permit, license, or court order, and this information sheet does not itself place {{childName}} anywhere, does not obtain or record any state's approval of a proposed placement, and does not determine whether the compact applies to, excludes, or otherwise governs any specific proposed movement of {{childName}} across state lines. This document's companion clauses describe the compact's own stated purpose, its definition of a covered "placement" and a statutory exclusion from that definition, its pre-placement notice requirement, its continuing-jurisdiction rule, and California's own statutory designation of the state agency that administers compact notices on California's behalf.

clauses.title: The Compact's Own Statement of Purpose and Policy
clauses.body: Article 1 of the compact text enacted at California Family Code § 7901 states its own purpose and policy in the compact's own words: "It is the purpose and policy of the party states to cooperate with each other in the interstate placement of children to the end that:" a receiving state's authorities may fully evaluate a proposed placement, a sending state's authorities may obtain complete information before making it, and appropriate jurisdictional arrangements for the child's care are promoted. As Article 1(b) states it, the purpose extends to ensuring "the appropriate authorities in a state where a child is to be placed may have full opportunity to ascertain the circumstances of the proposed placement, thereby promoting full compliance with applicable requirements for the protection of the child." Article 1(d) further states that "appropriate jurisdictional arrangements for the care of children will be promoted."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the compact's own stated purpose as enacted into California law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proposed placement, and not a claim that any specific placement of the child named in this document's companion clauses furthers, or fails to further, that purpose. All three citations in this clause are quotations from Article 1 of the single compact text codified at Family Code § 7901, and are not independent of one another. This clause does not quote Article 1(a) or 1(c), which state two further purposes — maximizing a placed child's opportunity for a suitable environment, and letting the sending state's authorities gather complete information before placement — not independently verified beyond the text of Article 1 itself, of which they are also a part. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific placement of the child named in this document's companion clauses is, or is not, consistent with the compact's stated purpose.
