clauses.title: What Counts as a Covered "Placement," and a Statutory Exclusion for Certain Relatives
clauses.body: The compact does not apply to every movement of a child across state lines; it applies only to what the compact itself defines as a "placement," and it then expressly excludes certain placements even within that definition. Article 2(d) of the compact text enacted at Family Code § 7901 defines "placement" to mean "the arrangement for the care of a child in a family free or boarding home or in a child-caring agency or institution, but does not include any institution caring for persons with developmental disabilities or mental health disorders or any institution primarily educational in character, and any hospital or other medical facility." Separately, Article 8 of that same compact text states that "this compact shall not apply to: (a) The sending or bringing of a child into a receiving state by the child's parent, stepparent, grandparent, adult brother or sister, adult uncle or aunt, or the child's guardian and leaving the child with any such relative or nonagency guardian in the receiving state."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the compact's own definition of a covered "placement" and of a statutory exclusion for certain relative placements — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proposed movement of a child across state lines, and not a claim that the movement of the child named in this document's companion clauses is, or is not, excluded under Article 8. Both citations in this clause are Articles of the single compact text codified at Family Code § 7901, and are not independent of one another. Article 8 also excludes, at Article 8(b), a placement made pursuant to a different interstate compact or agreement between the same two states that has the force of law; that separate exclusion is not detailed or quoted in this clause. This clause does not detail Article 2's other three definitions — "child," "sending agency," and "receiving state" — beyond what this document's companion clauses separately quote. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether the compact's placement definition, or the Article 8 relative exclusion, applies to any specific proposed movement of the child named in this document's companion clauses; that determination depends on the specific facts, including the identity and relationship of the person sending or bringing the child.

clauses.title: The Pre-Placement Notice Requirement Before a Child May Be Sent Into Another State
clauses.body: Before a covered placement can lawfully proceed, the sending agency must give the receiving state written notice and may not act until that state responds. Article 3(a) of the compact text enacted at Family Code § 7901 provides that "a sending agency shall not send, bring, or cause to be sent or brought into any other party state any child for placement in foster care or as a preliminary to a possible adoption unless the sending agency complies with each and every requirement set forth in this article and with the applicable laws of the receiving state governing the placement of children therein." Article 3(b) requires that, before doing so, the sending agency "shall furnish the appropriate public authorities in the receiving state written notice of the intention to send, bring, or place the child in the receiving state," containing the child's name, date, and place of birth; the identity and address of the parents or legal guardian; the identity of the person, agency, or institution to whom the child is to be sent; and a statement of the reasons for the proposed placement and the authority for it. Article 3(d) then makes the receiving state's approval a precondition to the placement itself: "the child shall not be sent, brought, or caused to be sent or brought into the receiving state until the appropriate public authorities in the receiving state notify the sending agency, in writing, to the effect that the proposed placement does not appear to be contrary to the interest of the child."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the compact's own pre-placement notice-and-approval requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proposed placement, and not a claim that any specific notice regarding the child named in this document's companion clauses has been given, or that any specific receiving state has approved or will approve a proposed placement. All three citations in this clause are Articles of the single compact text codified at Family Code § 7901, and are not independent of one another. This clause does not detail Article 3(c)'s separate provision letting the receiving state request additional supporting information from the sending agency, and it does not detail the penalty Article 4 imposes for a placement made in violation of Article 3, which this document does not otherwise cover. A separate California statute, Family Code § 7903, designates the specific California agency that receives and acts on Article 3 notices on this state's behalf; that designation is addressed in this document's companion clause and is not restated here. This document is informational only: it does not itself furnish, receive, or act on any Article 3 notice, and it does not determine that any specific proposed placement of the child named in this document's companion clauses does, or does not, appear contrary to that child's interest.

clauses.title: The Sending Agency's Continuing Jurisdiction Over a Child Placed Out of State
clauses.body: Placing a child in another state under the compact does not transfer legal jurisdiction over that child to the receiving state. Article 5(a) of the compact text enacted at Family Code § 7901 provides that "the sending agency shall retain jurisdiction over the child sufficient to determine all matters in relation to the custody, supervision, care, treatment, and disposition of the child that it would have had if the child had remained in the sending agency's state, until the child is adopted, reaches majority, becomes self-supporting, or is discharged with the concurrence of the appropriate authority in the receiving state." That retained jurisdiction "shall also include the power to effect or cause the return of the child or the child's transfer to another location and custody pursuant to law," and the sending agency "shall continue to have financial responsibility for support and maintenance of the child during the period of the placement." Article 5(a) also preserves the receiving state's own separate authority over conduct occurring there: "nothing contained herein shall defeat a claim of jurisdiction by a receiving state sufficient to deal with an act of delinquency or crime committed therein."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the compact's continuing-jurisdiction rule for a sending agency — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific placement, and not a claim that any sending agency described in this document's companion clauses retains, or has been relieved of, jurisdiction over the child named there in any specific case. This clause quotes only Article 5(a) of the single compact text codified at Family Code § 7901; it does not detail Article 5(b), which lets a public sending agency contract with a receiving-state agency to perform services as the sending agency's agent, or Article 5(c), which addresses a private charitable agency's role in the receiving state, neither of which is independently verified beyond the text of Article 5 itself. A separate California statute, Family Code § 7902, addresses how financial responsibility questions under Article 5 are resolved when a placement partially or completely defaults; that statute is not detailed in this clause. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine, retain, or relieve any jurisdiction over the child named in this document's companion clauses, and it does not determine when that child has been adopted, reached majority, become self-supporting, or been discharged for purposes of Article 5.

clauses.title: The California Agency Designated to Receive and Act on Compact Notices
clauses.body: Separate from the compact text itself, California has enacted its own statute identifying which California agency the compact's Article 3 notice provisions refer to. Family Code § 7903 provides in full: "The phrase ‘appropriate public authorities’ as used in Article 3 of the Interstate Compact on the Placement of Children means, with reference to this state, the State Department of Social Services, and that department shall receive and act with reference to notices required by Article 3 of the compact." A companion statute, Family Code § 7904, makes the same designation for a related compact term: "The phrase ‘appropriate authority in receiving state’ as used in paragraph (a) of Article 5 of the Interstate Compact on the Placement of Children, with reference to this state, means the State Department of Social Services."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of which California agency the compact's Article 3 and Article 5(a) terms refer to as enacted into California law — not a claim about which agency, if any, administers the compact in a different party state, and not a claim about how the State Department of Social Services in fact carries out that role in practice, day to day, beyond what these two statutes themselves state. Family Code § 7903 and § 7904 are two separate, independently numbered statutory sections, cited here as two independent sources; neither is a subsection of the other or of Family Code § 7901, the section codifying the compact text itself. This clause does not detail Family Code § 7905, which separately empowers California officers and agencies to enter into Article 5(b) service agreements with other party states, subject to Controller or local fiscal officer approval for any agreement carrying a financial commitment, or Family Code § 7902's rule on resolving financial-responsibility defaults; neither is independently verified beyond what this clause states. This document is informational only: it does not itself constitute, request, or record any notice, application, or approval addressed to the State Department of Social Services, and it does not determine that department's disposition of any specific proposed placement of the child named in this document's companion clauses.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}}, states what California's Revenue and Taxation Code provides about the separate LLC fee imposed by Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17942 — a state fee, based on a limited liability company's total income, that is distinct from the flat $800 annual minimum franchise tax imposed by Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17941. Where a specific business name is named below, that is {{companyName}}; this sheet can also be read on its own, without it filled in, as a general reference to what the statute says. This sheet states the law; it does not calculate, estimate, or evaluate what any particular limited liability company owes, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal or tax advice.

clauses.title: Who the LLC Fee Applies To
clauses.body: The § 17942 fee is imposed on "every limited liability company subject to tax under Section 17941" — and § 17941 itself defines "limited liability company," for its own purposes, to exclude an organization "that is not taxable as a corporation for California tax purposes." An organization formed as an LLC under state law but that has elected, or is otherwise taxable, as a corporation for California tax purposes falls outside that definition, and so outside the tax and fee imposed by this chapter.
clauses.gap: This is the statute's own definitional language, not a restatement of federal "check-the-box" terminology; the statute does not use the words "partnership" or "disregarded entity" in this definition. This document does not independently verify how the Franchise Tax Board applies this exclusion to every possible LLC tax election scenario, and it does not address any particular company's own tax classification, which is addressed by this project's separate Operating Agreement documents. Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code §§ 17941 and 17942 are two separate, independently numbered sections; the two citations below are independent of one another.

citations.cite: Tax and Fees on Limited Liability Companies, imposition of the LLC fee
citations.quote: In addition to the tax imposed under Section 17941, every limited liability company subject to tax under Section 17941 shall pay annually to this state a fee equal to:

citations.quote: For purposes of this section, “limited liability company” means an organization, other than a limited liability company that is exempt from the tax and fees imposed under this chapter pursuant to Section 23701h or Section 23701x, that is formed by one or more persons under the law of this state, any other country, or any other state, as a “limited liability company” and that is not taxable as a corporation for California tax purposes.

clauses.title: The LLC Fee Is Owed In Addition to the $800 Minimum Tax
clauses.body: The § 17942 LLC fee does not replace or offset the flat annual tax imposed by § 17941 (currently $800, per the amount set by Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(d)(1) and cross-referenced by § 17941(a)) — the statute's own text imposes the fee "[i]n addition to" that tax. A limited liability company within the fee's income brackets owes both amounts: the flat annual tax under § 17941, and the separate, income-tiered fee under § 17942.
clauses.gap: This document does not restate every detail of the § 17941 annual tax itself, including its due date, its continuing obligation until dissolution, or recent statutory amendments to it — those are addressed by this project's LLC Articles of Organization document. Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code §§ 17941 and 17942 are two separate, independently numbered sections; the two citations below are independent of one another.

citations.quote: In addition to the tax imposed under Section 17941, every limited liability company subject to tax under Section 17941 shall pay annually to this state a fee equal to:

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17941(a)
citations.cite: Tax and Fees on Limited Liability Companies, the annual tax for doing business in the state
citations.quote: for each taxable year beginning on or after January 1, 1997, a limited liability company doing business in this state (as defined in Section 23101) shall pay annually to this state a tax for the privilege of doing business in this state in an amount equal to the applicable amount specified in subdivision (d) of Section 23153 for the taxable year.

clauses.title: The Fee Schedule
clauses.body: The LLC fee is set on a tiered schedule keyed to total income: $900 at total income of $250,000 or more (but less than $500,000); $2,500 at $500,000 or more (but less than $1,000,000); $6,000 at $1,000,000 or more (but less than $5,000,000); and $11,790 at $5,000,000 or more. An LLC with total income below $250,000 owes no fee under this section (though it may still owe the separate $800 minimum tax addressed elsewhere in this project).
clauses.gap: This is the fee schedule as codified in Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17942(a)(1)–(4) as of this verification date; it does not reflect any inflation adjustment or amendment enacted after that date. This document does not calculate any particular company's total income or which bracket it falls into.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17942(a)(1)–(4)
citations.cite: Tax and Fees on Limited Liability Companies, the tiered LLC fee schedule
citations.quote: (1) Nine hundred dollars ($900), if the total income from all sources derived from or attributable to this state for the taxable year is two hundred fifty thousand dollars ($250,000) or more, but less than five hundred thousand dollars ($500,000). (2) Two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500), if the total income from all sources derived from or attributable to this state for the taxable year is five hundred thousand dollars ($500,000) or more, but less than one million dollars ($1,000,000). (3) Six thousand dollars ($6,000), if the total income from all sources derived from or attributable to this state for the taxable year is one million dollars ($1,000,000) or more, but less than five million dollars ($5,000,000). (4) Eleven thousand seven hundred ninety dollars ($11,790), if the total income from all sources derived from or attributable to this state for the taxable year is five million dollars ($5,000,000) or more.

clauses.title: "Total Income" Means Gross Income, Not Net Profit
clauses.body: "Total income from all sources" is not net profit. The statute defines it as gross income — as gross income is defined for California corporation tax purposes, which itself adopts the federal Internal Revenue Code's definition of gross income — plus the cost of goods sold paid or incurred in the taxpayer's trade or business. Business expenses, deductions, and losses that would reduce net profit generally do not reduce this figure; a company can owe a substantial LLC fee for a year in which it had little or no net profit, if its gross income was high enough.
clauses.gap: This document quotes the statute's cross-reference to "gross income, as defined in Section 24271" and Section 24271's own text, which in turn adopts Internal Revenue Code § 61's definition of gross income; this document does not independently trace or quote 26 U.S.C. § 61 itself. Section 17942(b)(1)(A) also excludes certain LLC-to-LLC allocations from this figure and, in 17942(b)(1)(B), ties the sourcing rules to Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code §§ 25135–25137 — provisions on assigning sales to California that this document does not independently restate. Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code §§ 17942 and 24271 are two separate, independently numbered sections; the two citations below are independent of one another.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17942(b)(1)(A)
citations.cite: Tax and Fees on Limited Liability Companies, definition of "total income from all sources"
citations.quote: “total income from all sources derived from or attributable to this state” means gross income, as defined in Section 24271, plus the cost of goods sold that are paid or incurred in connection with the trade or business of the taxpayer.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 24271(a)
citations.cite: Gross Income, adoption of the federal Internal Revenue Code definition
citations.quote: Section 61 of the Internal Revenue Code, relating to gross income defined, shall apply, except as otherwise provided.

clauses.title: The Fee Is Paid By Estimate, Mid-Year
clauses.body: The LLC fee is not paid after the year closes, the way the underlying return is filed — the statute requires it to be estimated and paid on or before the 15th day of the sixth month of the current taxable year (for a calendar-year LLC, June 15), based on the LLC's estimate of its own total income for that year. A 10% penalty applies to any underpayment of that estimate, unless the amount paid by that date is at least equal to the LLC's total fee for the preceding taxable year.
clauses.gap: This document does not independently trace Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 18633.5 (the return-filing provision cross-referenced for the fee's ultimate due date and for identifying which LLCs must file that return) or the FTB's own form instructions for the estimate payment (commonly made using FTB Form 3536); it states only what §§ 17942(c) and (d) themselves say about timing. Subdivisions (c) and (d) quoted below are both part of the same section, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17942, and are not independent of one another.

citations.cite: Tax and Fees on Limited Liability Companies, when the fee is due
citations.quote: The fee assessed under this section shall be due and payable on the date the return of the limited liability company is required to be filed under Section 18633.5, shall be collected and refunded in the same manner as the taxes imposed by this part, and shall be subject to interest and applicable penalties.

citations.cite: Tax and Fees on Limited Liability Companies, the mid-year estimate requirement
citations.quote: The fee imposed by this section shall be estimated and paid on or before the 15th day of the sixth month of the current taxable year.

clauses.title: Series LLC Information Sheet Declaration
clauses.body: This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a series limited liability company formed under the law of {{stateOfFormation}}. It describes California's treatment of a series LLC that has not been formed as a California entity: the absence of any domestic series-LLC formation mechanism in California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, the foreign-registration framework that instead applies when such an entity transacts business in California, and the California Franchise Tax Board's treatment of each series within a series LLC as a separate limited liability company for annual tax and fee purposes. This document does not itself register {{companyName}} or any series of it with the California Secretary of State, does not determine whether {{companyName}}'s specific activities in California constitute transacting intrastate business, and does not constitute legal advice.

clauses.title: No California Series-LLC Formation Mechanism
clauses.body: California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (Corp. Code §§ 17701.01-17713.13) sets out, in a single subdivision, the complete list of what a limited liability company's articles of organization must state to form a California LLC: a lawful-purpose statement, the LLC's name, its principal office address, its agent for service of process, and, only if applicable, a statement that it will be manager-managed or managed by a single manager. That list contains no option to designate the LLC, or any part of it, as a "series" with its own separately shielded assets, members, or liabilities. The Act's only membership-tiering mechanism, its Class Provisions article, lets an LLC's articles of organization or operating agreement create classes of members with different relative rights, powers, and duties -- including rights senior to other classes -- but says nothing about partitioning the LLC's own assets or liabilities among those classes, which is the defining feature of a series LLC under the series statutes some other states have adopted. No provision of the Act authorizes forming a "series LLC," under that name or any other, as a California entity.
clauses.gap: This finding rests on a direct, described search of the Act's actual text, not just an inability to find a provision: this document reviewed the complete table of articles for Title 2.6 (all 13 articles, §§17701.01-17713.13, as listed on the Legislature's own table of contents for the title) and separately fetched and full-text-searched the complete text of every one of those 13 articles for the word "series," finding zero occurrences anywhere in the Act's operative text. It separately confirmed that the Act's formation statute (§17702.01(b)) exhaustively lists the articles of organization's required content with no series option, and that the Act's Class Provisions section (§17712.01) -- the only membership-tiering mechanism anywhere in the Act -- creates classes of members, not asset-partitioned series. Sections 17702.01 and 17712.01 are independently numbered sections of the Act, not subsections of the same section, so these two citations are independent of one another. This document does not review any other state's series-LLC statute and makes no claim about how any other jurisdiction's law does or does not compare to California's; it also does not claim California's law could never change to add a domestic series mechanism -- only that the currently codified Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act does not contain one.

citations.case: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, articles-of-organization required content
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17702.01(b)
citations.quote: The articles of organization shall state all of the following: (1) A statement that the purpose of the limited liability company is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a limited liability company may be organized under this title. (2) The name of the limited liability company, which shall comply with Section 17701.08. (3) The street address of the initial principal office and the mailing address of the limited liability company if different from the street address of the initial principal office. (4) The name and street address of the initial agent for service of process of the limited liability company who meets the qualifications specified in subdivision (c) of Section 17701.13. If a corporate agent is designated, only the name of the agent shall be set forth. (5) If the limited liability company is to be manager-managed, the articles of organization shall contain a statement to that effect. (6) If the limited liability company is to be managed by only one manager, the articles of organization shall contain a statement to that effect.

citations.case: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, Class Provisions article
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17712.01
citations.quote: The articles of organization or the operating agreement may provide for the creation of classes of members having those relative rights, powers, and duties as the articles of organization or operating agreement may provide, including rights, powers, and duties senior to other classes of members.

clauses.title: Foreign Series LLC Registers Like Any Other Foreign LLC
clauses.body: A series LLC formed under another state's law does not register to transact business in California through any series-specific procedure. It instead falls under California's ordinary foreign-limited-liability-company registration statute, the same statute that governs any other out-of-state LLC applying for a certificate of registration to transact intrastate business here. That statute's application-content requirements -- the company's name, the state or jurisdiction of its formation, its principal office address, its agent for service of process in California, and a certificate of good standing from its home jurisdiction -- contain no field or provision addressing a series, and the statute describes no separate application procedure for registering an individual series of a series LLC. California's own Franchise Tax Board separately states that a series LLC cannot be formed in California and that one formed in another state must register with the California Secretary of State before doing business here, using this same foreign-qualification framework.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 17708.02) describing the application content required of any foreign LLC, series or not; the absence of series-specific content is a finding about what this statute's text does and does not say, not the result of a separate targeted search of the Secretary of State's own forms or filing instructions, which this document did not independently review. The Franchise Tax Board webpage cited here is administrative guidance describing the Secretary of State's registration requirement in general terms; it is not itself the registration statute, and it is an independent source from the statutory citation -- a separate agency publication, not a subsection of the same section.

citations.case: California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, foreign LLC application for certificate of registration
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17708.02(a)
citations.quote: A foreign limited liability company may apply for a certificate of registration to transact business in this state by delivering an application to the Secretary of State for filing on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State.

citations.case: Series LLC (business type), California Franchise Tax Board
citations.cite: FTB.ca.gov, "Series LLC" business-type page
citations.quote: A SLLC cannot be formed in California. A SLLC is formed in another state must register with the California Secretary of State (SOS) before they start doing business in California.

clauses.title: Each Series Treated as a Separate LLC for the $800 Tax and Fee
clauses.body: For a series LLC formed under a state law that both limits each series' redemption, liquidation, and income rights to that series' own assets and confines each series' expenses, charges, and liabilities to that series' own assets -- conditions the Franchise Tax Board's own instructions illustrate using a Delaware series LLC as the example -- the Franchise Tax Board's published instructions for the LLC annual return direct that each series be treated as a separate LLC for California tax purposes: each series must file its own Form 568 and pay its own separate $800 annual tax and separate LLC fee, if that series is registered or doing business in California. Practically, an out-of-state series LLC with several series each registered or doing business in California can owe that $800 minimum tax, and a separate LLC fee, once for every qualifying series -- not once for the series LLC as a whole. On the filing mechanics, the first series to pay tax or file a return uses the Secretary of State file number as its identifying number, while every other series leaves its identification number blank on its first payment voucher and is assigned its own separate identification number by the Franchise Tax Board.
clauses.gap: This per-series tax treatment is stated in the Franchise Tax Board's own published instructions for the LLC annual return (its Form 568 tax booklet) and on the Franchise Tax Board's own "Series LLC" informational webpage -- both official Franchise Tax Board publications this document directly fetched and read in full -- rather than in the text of the Revenue and Taxation Code itself: the annual-tax statute (Rev. & Tax. Code § 17941) was directly checked and contains no series-specific language, so this per-series treatment rests on the Franchise Tax Board's own administrative interpretation and filing instructions, not on a codified statutory rule. This document searched for, but did not locate, a numbered Franchise Tax Board Legal Ruling or Chief Counsel Ruling addressing series LLCs specifically; two candidate numbers were checked directly and ruled out as unrelated (Legal Ruling 2014-01 addresses multiple-member LLC members' "doing business" filing obligations, and Legal Ruling 2015-01 addresses tribal-member reservation residency for personal income tax), so no such ruling is cited here, and this document does not claim the per-series rule has been embodied in a formal legal ruling at all. The two sources cited are independent Franchise Tax Board publications -- one a tax-return instruction booklet, the other a separate informational webpage -- not subsections of the same document.

citations.case: 2025 Limited Liability Company Tax Booklet, Form 568 instructions, "Series LLCs"
citations.cite: Cal. Franchise Tax Board, 2025 Form 568 Booklet
citations.quote: If the laws of the state where the LLC is formed provide for the designation of series of interests (for example, a Delaware Series LLC) and: (1) the holders of the interests in each series are limited to the assets of that series upon redemption, liquidation, or termination, and may share in the income only of that series, and (2) under home state law, the payment of the expenses, charges, and liabilities of each series is limited to the assets of that series, then each series in a series LLC is considered a separate LLC and must file its own Form 568 and pay its own separate LLC annual tax and fee, if it is registered or doing business in California.

citations.case: Series LLC (business type), California Franchise Tax Board
citations.cite: FTB.ca.gov, "Series LLC" business-type page
citations.quote: If the series LLC is registered in California, the first LLC in the series uses the SOS number as the identification number on its initial payment voucher. All other LLCs in the series must leave the identification numbers blank on their first payment vouchers.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's "Coogan Law" trust-account requirement, Family Code §§ 6750-6753, as it may relate to a contract between {{minorName}}, a minor, and {{companyName}} for artistic, creative, or other services within the scope of that chapter. It states facts about when that chapter requires a portion of a minor's earnings under such a contract to be set aside in trust, and about the trust account itself. This corpus separately includes a California Talent Agencies Act information sheet, which addresses who may lawfully procure entertainment employment for an artist, and a Minor Work Permits information sheet, which addresses the school-issued work-permit requirement for minors employed generally. Neither of those sheets addresses the trust-account requirement described here, and this sheet does not address theirs. This document does not state whether any particular contract involving {{minorName}} is of a type covered by Family Code §§ 6750-6753, does not calculate the amount required to be set aside under any specific contract, and does not tell {{companyName}}, {{minorName}}, or {{parentGuardianName}} what to do about any particular contract, earnings, or trust account.

clauses.title: What Contracts This Chapter Covers, and Whether Court Approval Is Required to Trigger It
clauses.body:
Family Code Chapter 3 of Part 3 of Division 11 applies to specific categories of contract between an unemancipated minor and a third party entered into on or after January 1, 2000, including a contract under which a minor is employed or agrees to render artistic or creative services (defined to include acting, dancing, music, comedy, singing, stunt work, voice-over work, content creation, and other performing or entertainment roles, among others), a contract disposing of literary, musical, or dramatic properties or of rights in a person's likeness, voice, performance, or life story for entertainment-industry use, and a contract under which a minor is employed or agrees to render services as a sports participant or player.

A separate section of the same chapter, Family Code § 6751, allows a party to petition the superior court to approve such a contract, which then cannot later be disaffirmed on the ground that it was entered into during minority. But court approval of the contract is not what triggers the trust obligation described in this document. Family Code § 6752 imposes the trust requirement in both situations: where a court approves the contract, and, separately, where the contract is not submitted for court approval at all, or where the court denies approval.
clauses.gap: Family Code §§ 6750-6753 were fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent strings; after stripping the surrounding page markup and normalizing whitespace, the statutory text returned was byte-identical on both fetches for every section quoted in this document. This clause cites Family Code § 6750(a) (the definition of covered contracts) together with § 6752(b)(1) and § 6752(c)(1) (the two circumstances that trigger the set-aside requirement); § 6750 is an independent section from § 6752, but § 6752(b) and § 6752(c) are both subdivisions of the same section and are not independent of one another. This clause does not quote § 6750's full list of covered contract types (including its provisions on loan-out companies, casting agencies, and content creators) or its separate rules for who counts as the minor's "employer" in each scenario; a reader whose situation may involve a loan-out company, casting agency, or online content platform should not assume coverage or non-coverage based on this summary alone. This document does not address Family Code § 6751 beyond noting that court approval exists as an option and is not the trigger for the trust requirement.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6750(a)
citations.cite: Family Code § 6750(a) (contracts covered by this chapter)
citations.quote: This chapter applies to the following types of contracts entered into between an unemancipated minor and a third party on or after January 1, 2000: (1) A contract pursuant to which a minor is employed or agrees to render artistic or creative services, either directly or through a third party, including, but not limited to, a personal services corporation (loan-out company), or through a casting agency.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6752(b)(1)
citations.cite: Family Code § 6752(b)(1) (trust required when a court approves the contract)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other statute, in an order approving a minor’s contract of a type described in Section 6750, the court shall require that 15 percent of the minor’s gross earnings pursuant to the contract be set aside by the minor’s employer, except an employer of a minor for services as an extra, background performer, or in a similar capacity, as described in paragraph (3) of subdivision (b) of Section 6750.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6752(c)(1)
citations.cite: Family Code § 6752(c)(1) (trust also required when the contract is not submitted for approval, or approval is denied)
citations.quote: for any minor’s contract of a type described in Section 6750 that is not being submitted for approval by the court pursuant to Section 6751, or for which the court has issued a final order denying approval, 15 percent of the minor’s gross earnings pursuant to the contract shall be set aside by the minor’s employer

clauses.title: The 15% Set-Aside and the Meaning of "Gross Earnings"
clauses.body: For a contract covered by this chapter, Family Code § 6752 sets the required set-aside at 15 percent of the minor's gross earnings under the contract, to be set aside by the minor's employer and held in trust for the minor's benefit — with an express exception for an employer of a minor working as an extra, background performer, or in a similar capacity. Family Code § 6750(d)(1) defines "gross earnings," for purposes of this chapter, as the total compensation payable to the minor under the contract or, where the minor's services are rendered through a third-party individual or loan-out company, the total compensation payable to that third party for the minor's services. A separate, narrower definition applies specifically to a minor employed as a musician, singer, songwriter, musical producer, or arranger, which this document does not restate here.
clauses.gap: Family Code §§ 6750 and 6752 were fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent strings; the statutory text returned was byte-identical on both fetches after normalizing whitespace. This clause cites Family Code § 6750(d)(1) and § 6752(b)(1), which are independent sections of the same chapter, not subdivisions of one section. It does not restate the alternative "gross earnings" definition in § 6750(d)(2) for musicians, singers, songwriters, musical producers, and arrangers, which excludes deductions to offset advances or other employer expenses; a reader whose situation involves that category of work should not assume the general definition quoted here applies to them. It also does not restate the extra/background-performer carve-out's cross-reference to § 6750(b)(3) in any further detail.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6752(b)(1)
citations.cite: Family Code § 6752(b)(1) (15 percent set-aside requirement)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other statute, in an order approving a minor’s contract of a type described in Section 6750, the court shall require that 15 percent of the minor’s gross earnings pursuant to the contract be set aside by the minor’s employer, except an employer of a minor for services as an extra, background performer, or in a similar capacity, as described in paragraph (3) of subdivision (b) of Section 6750.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6750(d)(1)
citations.cite: Family Code § 6750(d)(1) (definition of "gross earnings")
citations.quote: For purposes of this chapter, the minor’s “gross earnings” means the total compensation payable to the minor under the contract or, if the minor’s services are being rendered through a third-party individual or personal services corporation (loan-out company), the total compensation payable to that third party for the services of the minor.

clauses.title: The Coogan Trust Account: Where It Must Be Held and When the Minor Can Access It
clauses.body:
Family Code § 6753 requires the trustee to establish the required trust account — which the statute itself names a "Coogan Trust Account" — at a bank, savings and loan institution, credit union, brokerage firm, or company registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940, located in California (unless a similar trust has already been established), within seven business days after the minor's contract is signed. The account must be held at a financial institution that remains insured by the FDIC, SIPC, or NCUSIF (or their successors), or with a company that remains registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940.

The account is blocked in the sense that, before the beneficiary turns 18 or a declaration of the minor's emancipation issues, no withdrawal may be made by the beneficiary or anyone else without a written order of the superior court. Once the beneficiary turns 18, the funds may be withdrawn only after the beneficiary provides the financial institution with a certified copy of their birth certificate.
clauses.gap: Family Code § 6753 was fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent strings; the statutory text returned was byte-identical on both fetches after normalizing whitespace. This clause quotes subsections (a), (b), and (d) of the same section, § 6753, so these citations are not independent of one another. This document does not restate subsection (c)'s detail on the trustee's written statement, or subsection (e)'s provisions permitting the financial institution to transfer funds or invest them in specified index funds, government securities, or similar instruments; a reader with questions about how funds already in a Coogan Trust Account may be moved or invested should not rely on this summary alone.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6753(a)
citations.cite: Family Code § 6753(a) (establishing the Coogan Trust Account)
citations.quote: The trustee or trustees shall establish a trust account, that shall be known as a Coogan Trust Account, pursuant to this section at a bank, savings and loan institution, credit union, brokerage firm, or company registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940, that is located in the State of California, unless a similar trust has been previously established

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6753(b)
citations.cite: Family Code § 6753(b) (blocked until age 18 or emancipation)
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this section, prior to the date on which the beneficiary of the trust attains the age of 18 years or the issuance of a declaration of emancipation of the minor under Section 7122, no withdrawal by the beneficiary or any other individual, individuals, entity, or entities may be made of funds on deposit in trust without written order of the superior court

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6753(d)
citations.cite: Family Code § 6753(d) (financial institution insurance/registration requirements)
citations.quote: The trust shall be established in California either with a financial institution that is and remains insured at all times by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC), or the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund (NCUSIF) or their respective successors, or with a company that is and remains registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940.

clauses.title: What Happens If No Trustee's Statement Is Provided: Transfer to The Actors' Fund of America
clauses.body: Family Code § 6752 states a specific consequence when the trust account is not set up and documented in time: if a parent, guardian, or trustee fails to give the minor's employer a true and accurate photocopy of the trustee's statement (the document identifying the account and financial institution, described in § 6753(c)) within 180 days after the minor's employment begins, the employer must forward the 15 percent set-aside, along with identifying information about the minor, to The Actors' Fund of America, which then becomes trustee of those funds. The statute does not describe this outcome as an escheat to the state; instead, it directs the funds to this specific charitable organization, and separately exempts funds received by The Actors' Fund of America under this chapter from the state's Unclaimed Property Law.
clauses.gap: Family Code § 6752 was fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent strings; the statutory text returned was byte-identical on both fetches after normalizing whitespace. This clause cites § 6752(b)(9)(A) and § 6752(h), both subdivisions of the same section, so they are not independent of one another. This document quotes only the 180-day, court-approved-contract version of this consequence in § 6752(b)(9)(A); a materially parallel 180-day rule appears in § 6752(c)(7)(A) for contracts not submitted for court approval, which this document does not separately quote because the two provisions largely track each other. This document does not describe § 6752(e) and (f), governing how The Actors' Fund of America must then manage, account for, and pay interest on funds it holds as trustee, or the further transfer and disbursement mechanics in § 6752(e)(3); a reader whose funds have been forwarded to The Actors' Fund of America should not assume this summary states everything that governs those funds.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6752(b)(9)(A)
citations.cite: Family Code § 6752(b)(9)(A) (forwarding to The Actors' Fund of America after 180 days)
citations.quote: If a parent, guardian, or trustee fails to provide the minor’s employer with a true and accurate photocopy of the trustee’s statement pursuant to Section 6753 within 180 days after the commencement of employment, the employer shall forward to The Actors’ Fund of America 15 percent of the minor’s gross earnings pursuant to the contract

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6752(h)
citations.cite: Family Code § 6752(h) (exemption from the Unclaimed Property Law)
citations.quote: All funds received by The Actors’ Fund of America pursuant to this section shall be exempt from the application of the Unclaimed Property Law (Title 10 (commencing with Section 1300) of Part 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure), including, but not limited to, Section 1510 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment and Signature
Grocery Worker Retention Law — Transition Record
Who and What the Law Covers
clauses.body: California's grocery worker retention law applies only within a specific set of defined terms found in Labor Code § 2502. A “grocery establishment” is limited to a retail store located in California that is over 15,000 square feet in size and that sells primarily household foodstuffs for offsite consumption — including fresh produce, meats, poultry, fish, deli products, dairy products, canned and dry foods, beverages, and baked or prepared foods — with any other merchandise being secondary to that primary food-sales purpose; a store that has ceased operating for 12 months or more falls outside the definition, while a distribution center a grocery establishment owns and operates mainly to supply its own stores counts as a grocery establishment regardless of its square footage. The triggering event is a “change in control”: a sale, purchase, assignment, acquisition, transfer, contribution, or other disposition of all or substantially all of the assets, cash on hand, or a controlling interest of the incumbent grocery employer, including through a merger, consolidation, or reorganization — not simply any change in day-to-day management or personnel. The employer that owned, controlled, or operated the grocery establishment before that event is the law's “incumbent grocery employer”; the one that owns, controls, or operates it afterward is the “successor grocery employer,” which the statute notes may in fact be the same entity as the incumbent employer when a change in control occurs without a change in the employer of record. Only certain workers qualify for the law's protections: an “eligible grocery worker” is an individual whose primary place of employment is the covered establishment and who worked for the incumbent grocery employer for at least six months before the transfer document was executed, and the definition expressly excludes managerial, supervisory, or confidential employees.
clauses.gap: All four quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 2502) rather than independently authored sources. This clause does not separately quote § 2502's definitions of “employment commencement date,” “job classification,” “person,” or “transfer document,” which are more mechanical and are used, where relevant, elsewhere in this document. This law (Lab. Code §§ 2500-2522) is a wholly separate statute from the Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act (Lab. Code §§ 1060-1065) covered elsewhere in this corpus: the janitor law is triggered by a change in an awarding authority's janitorial-services contract, while this law is triggered by a change in ownership or control of the grocery establishment itself, and the two statutes use different size thresholds, different retention periods (60 days under the janitor law versus 90 days here), and different defined terms.

Other household supplies or other products shall be secondary to the primary purpose of food sales. A distribution center owned and operated by a grocery establishment and used primarily to distribute goods to or from its owned stores shall be considered a grocery establishment, regardless of its square footage. A grocery establishment does not include a retail store that has ceased operations for 12 months or more.

A successor grocery employer may be the same entity as an incumbent employer when a change in control occurs but the covered employer remains the same.

clauses.title: Information Transfer and Posted Public Notice After a Change in Control
clauses.body: Once a covered change in control occurs, the law imposes information-sharing and posting duties that run separately from the retention obligation itself. Within 15 days after the transfer document is executed, the incumbent grocery employer must give the successor grocery employer and any collective bargaining representative the name, address, date of hire, and job classification of each eligible grocery worker, along with that worker's cellular telephone number and email address if known; if the incumbent grocery employer misses that 15-day deadline, the successor grocery employer may instead obtain the same information from a collective bargaining representative. Separately, the incumbent grocery employer must post public notice of the change in control at the affected grocery establishment within five business days after the transfer document is executed, and the notice must remain posted through any closure of the establishment and until it reopens as fully operational under the successor grocery employer. That posted notice must state the incumbent grocery employer's name and contact information, the successor grocery employer's name and contact information, and the effective date of the change in control, and it must be placed somewhere conspicuous where eligible grocery workers, other employees, customers, and the public can readily see it.
clauses.gap: The two § 2504(a) quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 2504) and are not independent of one another; the two § 2508 quotes are likewise subdivisions of a single, separate section (Labor Code § 2508) and are not independent of one another, though § 2504 and § 2508 are independently numbered sections relative to each other. This clause does not address § 2504(b)'s preferential-hiring-list requirement or § 2504(c)'s written-offer record-retention requirement, which are covered in a separate clause of this document.

citations.quote: The incumbent grocery employer shall, within 15 days after the execution of the transfer document, provide to the successor grocery employer and any collective bargaining representative the name, address, date of hire, employment occupation classification, and, if known, the cellular telephone number and email address of each eligible grocery worker.

Notice shall remain posted during any closure of the grocery establishment and until the grocery establishment is fully operational and open to the public under the successor grocery employer.

(c) Notice shall be posted in a conspicuous place at the grocery establishment in a manner to be readily viewed by eligible grocery workers and other employees, customers, and members of the public.

clauses.title: The Preferential Hiring List and the 90-Day Retention Obligation
clauses.body: The law's central protection is a retention requirement built around a preferential hiring list. The successor grocery employer must maintain a preferential hiring list made up of the eligible grocery workers identified through the notice process, and must hire from that list for a period beginning when the transfer document is executed and continuing for 90 days after the grocery establishment reopens as fully operational under the successor grocery employer. Each eligible grocery worker the successor grocery employer hires under the law must then be retained for at least 90 days measured from that worker's own “employment commencement date” (the date the worker actually starts working for the successor grocery employer), during which the worker is employed on the terms and conditions the successor grocery employer sets, subject to any applicable collective bargaining agreement. If, during that hiring-list period, the successor grocery employer determines it needs fewer eligible grocery workers than the incumbent grocery employer required, it cannot pick and choose among them freely: workers within a job classification must be retained by seniority to the extent comparable classifications exist (or under the terms of a relevant collective bargaining agreement), and workers who are not classified must be retained by seniority and experience, or under the terms of a relevant collective bargaining agreement.
clauses.gap: The § 2506(a) and § 2506(b) quotes below are both subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 2506) and are not independent of one another. The § 2504(b) quote is drawn from a separate, independently numbered section (Labor Code § 2504); § 2506(b) cross-references the hiring-list period defined in § 2504(b) by its own subdivision letter, so the two sections operate together even though they are not subdivisions of the same section.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2504(b) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, preferential hiring list requirement
citations.quote: The successor grocery employer shall maintain a preferential hiring list of eligible grocery workers identified by the incumbent grocery employer or collective bargaining representative pursuant to subdivision (a) and shall hire from that list for a period beginning upon the execution of the transfer document and continuing for 90 days after the grocery establishment is fully operational and open to the public under the successor grocery employer.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2506(a) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, 90-day retention requirement
citations.quote: A successor grocery employer shall retain each eligible grocery worker hired pursuant to this part for at least 90 days after the eligible grocery worker’s employment commencement date. During this 90-day transition employment period, eligible grocery workers shall be employed under the terms and conditions established by the successor grocery employer and pursuant to the terms of a relevant collective bargaining agreement, if any.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2506(b) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Grocery Workers law, seniority-based retention when fewer workers are needed
citations.quote: If, within the period established in subdivision (b) of Section 2504, the successor grocery employer determines that it requires fewer eligible grocery workers than were required by the incumbent grocery employer, the successor grocery employer shall retain eligible grocery workers by seniority within each job classification to the extent that comparable job classifications exist or pursuant to the terms of a relevant collective bargaining agreement, if any. Nonclassified eligible grocery workers shall be retained by seniority and according to experience or pursuant to the terms of a relevant collective bargaining agreement, if any.

clauses.title: Discharge Protection, the End-of-Period Evaluation, and Anti-Retaliation
clauses.body: Retention under the law carries a job-security floor for as long as it lasts, plus a separate check-in point when it ends. During the 90-day transition employment period itself, the successor grocery employer may not discharge a retained eligible grocery worker without cause. At the end of that 90-day period, the successor grocery employer must give each retained eligible grocery worker a written performance evaluation and keep a copy of it for at least three years; if the worker's performance during the 90 days was satisfactory, the successor grocery employer must consider offering the worker continued employment on the terms and conditions the successor grocery employer sets and as otherwise required by law. Separately from the retention and evaluation mechanics, the law includes its own anti-retaliation provision: an employer may not refuse to employ, terminate, reduce the pay of, or otherwise take adverse action against an employee for seeking to enforce rights under the law, including by participating in a proceeding, opposing a practice the law prohibits, or otherwise asserting rights under it — and that protection extends to an employee who mistakenly, but in good faith, alleges the law was not followed.
clauses.gap: The § 2506(c) and § 2506(d) quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 2506) and are not independent of one another. The § 2509 quote is drawn from a separate, independently numbered section (Labor Code § 2509). Note for anyone comparing this to the Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act covered elsewhere in this corpus: that statute expressly states that employment after its transition period becomes ordinary at-will employment (Lab. Code § 1061(f)). This grocery worker law does not contain equivalent language — § 2506(d) requires only that the successor grocery employer “consider offering” continued employment after a satisfactory 90-day evaluation, and this document did not locate, and does not assume, any provision in §§ 2500-2522 that independently classifies the legal status of employment after the 90-day period ends.

citations.quote: During the 90-day transition employment period, the successor grocery employer shall not discharge without cause an eligible grocery worker retained pursuant to this part.

This section applies to an employee who mistakenly, but in good faith, alleges noncompliance with this part.

clauses.title: Small-Employer Exemption, Bargaining Out, and How the Law Is Enforced
clauses.body: The law's reach has specific limits, and its enforcement runs through both a private right of action and the Labor Commissioner. It does not apply to a change in control where the incumbent and successor grocery employers' combined nationwide grocery-worker headcounts, counted immediately before the change in control, total fewer than 300 — a small-employer exemption that reuses the statute's own “grocery establishment” definition but expands it to include out-of-state stores for purposes of that headcount. Parties covered by the law may also bargain out of some or all of its requirements: a collective bargaining agreement can supersede the law's requirements, but only if the agreement says so explicitly, in clear and unambiguous terms identifying which requirements it replaces. As for enforcement, an aggrieved employee or an employee representative (such as a union or a nonprofit corporation) may sue in superior court for violations and may recover hiring and reinstatement rights, front or back pay, and the value of lost benefits — but only after first giving the employer written notice identifying the alleged violation and its supporting facts, and then waiting 33 days from that notice for the employer to cure the violation before filing suit. The Labor Commissioner has independent authority to investigate, order temporary relief, issue citations, and sue over violations, and a violation exposes an employer to a $100 civil penalty per affected employee, plus liquidated damages of $100 per employee for each day a violation continues uncured, capped at $1,000 per employee.
clauses.gap: The § 2510(a) and § 2510(b) quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code § 2510) and are not independent of one another. The § 2517 and § 2512 quotes come from separate, independently numbered sections and are independent both of § 2510 and of each other. This clause does not separately quote or otherwise address every scope-limiting provision in the chapter: § 2516 (not quoted here) exempts certain grocery establishments located in long-standing former food deserts, § 2518 (not quoted here) preserves an eligible grocery worker's separate right to sue for wrongful termination, and § 2520 (not quoted here) states that the law does not preempt a local ordinance that offers equal or greater protection — their existence is noted here only so a reader knows to look further if a store's location or a wrongful-termination claim may be relevant. This clause also does not quote § 2510(c)-(d) (the Labor Commissioner's parallel administrative remedies) or § 2510(f)-(j) (citation procedure, injunctive relief, interest, and cumulative-remedies provisions).

(2) The number of grocery workers employed, immediately prior to the change in control, by the successor grocery employer across that employer’s grocery establishments nationwide.

clauses.title: Certification
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes a specific requirement of California's Industrial Welfare Commission (IWC) Wage Orders: the duty of an employer to provide and maintain a uniform it requires an employee to wear, and the Wage Orders' own definition of what counts as a "uniform" for that purpose. It states facts about that requirement as it applies to {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}}. It is separate from, and does not restate, this project's existing information sheet on the general duty under Labor Code § 2802 to reimburse necessary business expenses — the Wage Order uniform requirement described here has its own statutory definition of "uniform" and its own provide-and-maintain mechanism, independent of that statute.

clauses.title: The Wage Order's Provide-and-Maintain Duty
clauses.body: California's Industrial Welfare Commission (IWC) Wage Orders provide that "When uniforms are required by the employer to be worn by the employee as a condition of employment, such uniforms shall be provided and maintained by the employer." This duty applies to {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}} to the extent {{companyName}} requires {{employeeName}} to wear a uniform, as that term is defined in the following clause.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 9(A) (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040) — the general, catch-all wage order for professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations, used elsewhere in this corpus for the same reason. It was fetched directly from the California Department of Industrial Relations (dir.ca.gov) using two separate curl requests with different User-Agent strings, both returning byte-identical PDF content (HTTP 200); the extracted text was then confirmed as an exact, whitespace-normalized substring of that fetched text. WebFetch was not used for this domain in this session (it is expected to be blocked in this environment for dir.ca.gov), so the curl-with-two-User-Agents method served as the verification substitute. The identical sentence was independently confirmed to also appear, word for word, in IWC Wage Order No. 7-2001 (Mercantile Industry, Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11070), fetched and verified the same way, and separately in a California Court of Appeal's own footnote quoting that same Wage Order No. 7-2001 provision — the second citation below, which is a genuinely independent source (a judicial opinion, not another wage order) even though the quoted sentence happens to be word for word identical. A near-identical but not word-for-word version of the requirement also appears at section 8(A) of IWC Wage Order No. 16-2001 (Certain On-Site Occupations in the Construction, Drilling, Logging and Mining Industries, Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11160), also fetched and verified this session, which reorders the sentence to read "When the employer requires uniforms to be worn by the employee..." rather than "When uniforms are required by the employer..." and numbers the provision as its own section 8 rather than section 9. This confirms the requirement recurs across at least these three of California's 17 industry/occupation wage orders, but is not proof that its exact wording or section number is identical in every one of them — only these three were fetched and checked this session. Neither the wage order text nor the case law fetched this session specifies a dollar formula, percentage, or other fixed method for calculating the cost of "maintaining" a uniform (for example, a specific reimbursement rate for an employee who launders a required uniform at home); this clause states that a maintenance duty exists, not how its cost is to be calculated in a specific case. Separately, this clause does not restate the general necessary-expense reimbursement duty under Labor Code § 2802 (covered in this project's other information sheet on that subject); a California Court of Appeal has recognized that a uniform-cost claim can implicate both that statute and the Wage Order's own uniform provision, but this document addresses only the Wage Order rule.

clauses.title: What Counts as a "Uniform": Distinctive Design or Color, Not Ordinary Wardrobe
clauses.body: The Wage Order defines the term "uniform," for purposes of this requirement, so that it "includes wearing apparel and accessories of distinctive design or color." California's Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (DLSE) — the agency that enforces the Wage Orders — has stated that this definition "is sufficiently flexible to allow the employer to specify basic wardrobe items which are usual and generally usable in the occupation, such as white shirts, dark pants and black shoes and belts, all of unspecified design," without the employer having to furnish those items. DLSE's stated position is that "If a required black or white uniform or accessory does not meet the test of being generally usable in the occupation the employee may not be required to pay for it."
clauses.gap: This clause's first citation quotes IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 9(A) (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040), fetched and verified using the same two-User-Agent curl method described in the preceding clause, and confirmed as an exact, whitespace-normalized substring of that fetched text; the identical definition sentence also appears, word for word, in Wage Order No. 7-2001 and Wage Order No. 16-2001, both also fetched this session. Separately, the two quoted sentences describing "basic wardrobe items" are drawn from a single source, section 45.5.5 of the DLSE's own Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual (fetched from dir.ca.gov using the same two-User-Agent method, byte-identical both times), and are two consecutive sentences of that same subsection — not independent of one another. That Manual passage itself states that this "basic wardrobe" language originated in the IWC's own Statement as to the Basis for the wage orders beginning in 1980, and that despite later amendments to the wage orders, "the basis for the language remains valid." This document did not independently fetch or verify the text of that original 1980 Statement of Basis — only the DLSE Manual's own reproduction and adoption of it as current enforcement policy, which is a genuinely different, independent source from the Wage Order's own operative regulatory text quoted in the first citation, but is agency interpretive guidance rather than the Wage Order's own codified language. The DLSE Manual and a published Court of Appeal decision (Dep't of Indus. Relations v. UI Video Stores, Inc. (1997) 55 Cal.App.4th 1084) both reference further examples of what has been found to be, or not be, a qualifying "uniform" — for instance, a distinctively colored "tropical shirt" per a DLSE opinion letter the Manual cites, and a required blue shirt and tan or khaki pants (the dress code at issue in UI Video Stores itself) — but this session did not independently fetch and verify the text of that underlying DLSE opinion letter, and this clause does not itself determine whether any specific garment an employer may require an employee to wear meets or fails the distinctive-design-or-color test; that remains a fact-specific determination that the Wage Order's own text and this agency guidance leave to be applied case by case. Separately, the source PDF for Wage Order No. 4-2001 renders the nested quotation marks immediately around the single word "uniform" in this same sentence ("The term 'uniform' includes...") as two non-standard characters instead of ordinary curly quotation marks — confirmed to be a rendering artifact of that specific PDF's embedded font by visually inspecting a rendering of the PDF page itself, and resolved here by quoting only the portion of the sentence after that word, which extracts cleanly and identically from all three wage orders' PDFs.

clauses.title: Which Employees and Industries This Requirement Covers
clauses.body: This uniform requirement is not confined to a single industry: it appears, in substantively identical form, at section 9(A) of Wage Order No. 4-2001 (professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations) and Wage Order No. 7-2001 (Mercantile Industry), and — reworded and renumbered as section 8(A) — in Wage Order No. 16-2001 (certain on-site construction, drilling, logging, and mining occupations). Separately, most of a Wage Order's substantive requirements, including this one, do not apply to an employee who meets the Wage Order's own administrative, executive, or professional exemption: "Provisions of Sections 3 through 12 shall not apply to persons employed in administrative, executive, or professional capacities." And except for a short list of provisions that does not include the uniform requirement, a Wage Order's provisions do not apply to an employee directly employed by the State or a political subdivision such as a city, county, or special district: "Except as provided in Sections 1, 2, 4, 10, and 20, the provisions of this order shall not apply to any employees directly employed by the State or any political subdivision thereof, including any city, county, or special district."
clauses.gap: This clause's two citations, section 1(A) and section 1(B), are both subsections of the same "Applicability of Order" section of Wage Order No. 4-2001 — not independent of one another. Both were fetched and verified using the same two-User-Agent curl method described in the preceding clauses. Wage Order No. 7-2001's section 1(B) was independently confirmed to state the identical political-subdivision exclusion, word for word (Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11070, subd. 1(B)), also fetched and verified this session. Wage Order No. 16-2001's equivalent applicability section states a materially different, shorter list of provisions that continue to apply to public employees — "Sections 1, Applicability; 2, Definitions; 4, Minimum Wages; 9, Meals and Lodging; and 18, Penalties" rather than "Sections 1, 2, 4, 10, and 20" — and its own uniform requirement (numbered section 8, not section 9, in that order) is likewise absent from that shorter list; this document does not claim the excepted-sections list, or the uniform provision's own section number, is identical across all 17 of California's industry/occupation wage orders, only that the uniform requirement was confirmed absent from the public-employee carve-out in each of the three wage orders actually fetched this session (Nos. 4-2001, 7-2001, and 16-2001) — no claim is made about the other 14. Separately, a published Court of Appeal decision has held that Labor Code § 2802's indemnification duty does not require several categories of public entity employers (the State, a Regents-governed university system, and general-law and charter counties and cities) to pay for uniform purchase and maintenance, reasoning from those entities' own constitutional and statutory wage-setting authority rather than from the Wage Orders themselves (In re Work Uniform Cases (2005) 133 Cal.App.4th 328, read directly from CourtListener this session but not formally cited here with a verified quote); it is noted only as further, independent confirmation that public-sector coverage of a uniform-cost duty is a genuinely separate question from the private-sector Wage Order rule this document describes, not as an extension of that holding to any specific public employer. This clause does not determine whether a specific job qualifies for the administrative, executive, or professional exemption, or whether a specific employer is "the State or a political subdivision" for this purpose — both are fact-specific determinations outside its scope.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, Civil Code § 1798.99.28 et seq. (added in 2022 by AB 2273) — a state statute directed at businesses whose online services, products, or features are likely to be accessed by children under 18, requiring, among other things, a Data Protection Impact Assessment, default privacy settings favoring a high level of privacy, an age estimation practice, and restrictions on certain uses of a child's personal information. It also describes the ongoing federal court litigation, NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta, which has enjoined enforcement of some of the Act's provisions on First Amendment and vagueness grounds while leaving others in effect, as those facts may relate to {{businessName}}'s online service, product, or feature located at {{websiteURL}}. This information sheet does not itself determine whether {{businessName}}'s online service, product, or feature is “likely to be accessed by children” within the meaning of the Act, does not constitute a Data Protection Impact Assessment or a privacy notice, and does not tell {{businessName}} what to do about any specific product, design feature, or practice.

clauses.title: Coverage Trigger: the Statute's Own “Likely to Be Accessed by Children” Test
clauses.body: The Age-Appropriate Design Code Act does not apply to every online service, product, or feature that a child could theoretically visit. Civil Code § 1798.99.30(b)(4) defines “likely to be accessed by children” to mean that, based on six separately enumerated indicators, it is reasonable to expect that the online service, product, or feature would be accessed by children: whether it is directed to children under the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act; whether it is determined, based on competent and reliable evidence regarding audience composition, to be routinely accessed by a significant number of children; whether it carries advertisements marketed to children; whether it is substantially similar to a service, product, or feature routinely accessed by a significant number of children; whether it has design elements known to be of interest to children, such as games, cartoons, music, or celebrities who appeal to children; and whether a significant amount of its audience is determined, based on internal company research, to be children. Separately, § 1798.99.30(b)(1) defines “child” or “children,” unless otherwise specified in the title, to mean a consumer or consumers who are under 18 years of age.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.99.30 — subdivision (b)(4) (the six-indicator coverage test) and subdivision (b)(1) (the definition of “child”) — they are not independent of one another. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business. The statute's own text does not state that all six indicators must be present, or that any particular combination is required; a Ninth Circuit panel has since read the provision, on the record before it, as meaning that satisfying any single indicator is sufficient, a case-law gloss addressed in a companion clause of this document rather than restated here. This clause does not quote § 1798.99.30(a), which separately incorporates the California Consumer Privacy Act's definitions (including its definition of covered “business” and that definition's revenue and volume thresholds) except where the Act specifies otherwise; a reader wanting the verified text of that CCPA “business” threshold should consult this corpus's existing CCPA documents, which quote it directly. This clause does not determine whether any specific online service, product, or feature in fact satisfies any of the six indicators, which is a fact-specific evidentiary question this document does not resolve. As of the most recent Ninth Circuit ruling reviewed for this document, no injunction is currently in effect against enforcement of this coverage definition itself; that litigation history is addressed in a companion clause.
