Sec. 6501 et seq.).(B) The online service, product, or feature is determined, based on competent and reliable evidence regarding audience composition, to be routinely accessed by a significant number of children.(C) An online service, product, or feature with advertisements marketed to children.(D) An online service, product, or feature that is substantially similar or the same as an online service, product, or feature subject to subparagraph (B).(E) An online service, product, or feature that has design elements that are known to be of interest to children, including, but not limited to, games, cartoons, music, and celebrities who appeal to children.(F) A significant amount of the audience of the online service, product, or feature is determined, based on internal company research, to be children.

clauses.title: Core Affirmative Duties as Codified: Data Protection Impact Assessment, Age Estimation, and Default Privacy Settings
clauses.body: As codified, Civil Code § 1798.99.31(a) requires a business that provides an online service, product, or feature likely to be accessed by children to take several affirmative actions. Before offering a new online service, product, or feature to the public, the business must complete a Data Protection Impact Assessment for any online service, product, or feature likely to be accessed by children and maintain documentation of that assessment for as long as it is likely to be accessed by children, biennially reviewing all such assessments. The business must estimate the age of child users with a reasonable level of certainty appropriate to the risks that arise from its data management practices, or, as an alternative the statute itself provides, apply the privacy and data protections afforded to children to all consumers instead of estimating age. The business must also configure all default privacy settings provided to children to settings that offer a high level of privacy, unless it can demonstrate a compelling reason that a different setting is in the best interests of children.
clauses.gap: This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.99.31(a) — paragraph (1)(A) (the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement), paragraph (5) (age estimation), and paragraph (6) (default privacy settings) — they are not independent of one another. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business. This clause quotes only the opening sentence of the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement in paragraph (1)(A); it does not separately quote the detailed list of factors that paragraph (1)(B) requires such an assessment to address (including whether a product's design, algorithms, or targeted advertising could harm children, and whether it collects sensitive personal information of children) — that list of factors is the specific statutory text a Ninth Circuit panel held likely facially violates the First Amendment, addressed in a companion clause of this document rather than restated here. As of the most recent Ninth Circuit rulings reviewed for this document, the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement described in this clause is currently under a preliminary injunction and is not being enforced, while the age estimation requirement described in this clause is not currently enjoined; the default privacy settings duty described in this clause was not separately addressed in the Ninth Circuit rulings reviewed for this document, and this document does not represent that it has or has not been the subject of any injunction. That litigation history is addressed in companion clauses. This clause does not determine what specific default settings, age-estimation method, or assessment content would satisfy the statute for any specific business's specific service.

clauses.title: Prohibited Actions as Codified: Data Use Restrictions and the Dark Patterns Restriction
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1798.99.31(b) also lists actions a business that provides an online service, product, or feature likely to be accessed by children shall not take. Among them, the business shall not use the personal information of any child in a way that the business knows, or has reason to know, is materially detrimental to the physical health, mental health, or well-being of a child; the statute lists several related restrictions on profiling children by default, collecting or retaining personal information beyond what is necessary, and using personal information for purposes other than those for which it was collected, each subject to exceptions the business bears the burden of demonstrating. Separately, the statute prohibits a business from using dark patterns to lead or encourage children to provide personal information beyond what is reasonably expected to provide the online service, product, or feature, to forego privacy protections, or to take any action the business knows, or has reason to know, is materially detrimental to the child's physical health, mental health, or well-being.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.99.31(b) — paragraph (1) (the general materially-detrimental-use restriction, quoted in full) and paragraph (7) (the dark patterns restriction, quoted in full) — they are not independent of one another. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business. This clause paraphrases, rather than quotes, paragraphs (2) through (4) (profiling, collection/retention, and purpose-limitation restrictions) and does not quote paragraphs (5), (6), or (8) (precise geolocation restrictions and the age-estimation-data-retention limit) at all; a reader wanting those provisions' exact text should consult the statute directly. As of the most recent Ninth Circuit ruling reviewed for this document, a panel affirmed a preliminary injunction against enforcement of both provisions quoted in this clause — paragraphs (1) through (4) and paragraph (7) — on the ground that their reliance on the undefined terms “material detriment,” “best interests,” and “well-being” renders them unconstitutionally vague, a due process holding independent of the First Amendment content-based-speech theory addressed in a companion clause; that litigation history, including the currently enjoined status of these specific provisions, is addressed in a companion clause rather than restated here. This clause does not determine whether any specific use of a specific child's personal information would in fact be materially detrimental, which the litigation history noted above indicates is itself a live, contested legal question.

clauses.title: Enforcement: Exclusive Attorney General Authority, Civil Penalties, and No Private Right of Action
clauses.body: The statute states its own enforcement mechanism and confirms who may bring an action under it. Civil Code § 1798.99.35(a) provides that a business that violates the title is subject to an injunction and liable for a civil penalty of not more than $2,500 per affected child for each negligent violation, or not more than $7,500 per affected child for each intentional violation, assessed and recovered only in a civil action brought in the name of the People of the State of California by the Attorney General. Separately, § 1798.99.35(d) states that nothing in the title serves as the basis for a private right of action under the title or any other law — the statute's own text confirms there is no private right of action for a consumer to sue directly under it. The statute also included a notice-and-cure mechanism: if a business is in substantial compliance with the Data Protection Impact Assessment provisions, the Attorney General must give written notice before initiating an action, and the business avoids civil penalty for any violation it cures within 90 days of that notice and confirms in writing to the Attorney General.
clauses.gap: This clause cites three subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code § 1798.99.35 — subdivisions (a) (penalties and Attorney General-only enforcement), (d) (no private right of action), and (c)(2) (the notice-and-cure mechanism) — they are not independent of one another. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific business. As of the most recent Ninth Circuit rulings reviewed for this document, the notice-and-cure provision quoted in this clause, § 1798.99.35(c)(2), is currently under a preliminary injunction and is not being enforced, while the general Attorney General-exclusivity, penalty, and no-private-right-of-action provisions quoted alongside it have not themselves been enjoined in the litigation this document reviewed; that litigation history, including why the notice-and-cure provision was enjoined, is addressed in a companion clause rather than restated here. This clause does not address whether some other statute, such as California's Unfair Competition Law, might supply a separate enforcement avenue; that question was not researched for this clause. This clause also does not quote § 1798.99.35(b) (deposit of recovered penalties into the Consumer Privacy Fund) or § 1798.99.35(e) (the Attorney General's regulatory authority), which were reviewed as part of the same fetched section but are not separately detailed here.

clauses.title: NetChoice v. Bonta: The Data Protection Impact Assessment Requirement and the Notice-and-Cure Provision Are Enjoined
clauses.body: The Age-Appropriate Design Code Act has been under continuous federal court challenge since before it took effect. In 2022, NetChoice, LLC, a trade association of online businesses, sued California's Attorney General in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, arguing the Act violates the First Amendment; the district court preliminarily enjoined the Act in its entirety in 2023. On the State's appeal, the Ninth Circuit, in NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta (“NetChoice I”), 113 F.4th 1101 (9th Cir. 2024), vacated most of that injunction and remanded for further proceedings, but affirmed it as to one specific provision: the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement. The panel held that NetChoice was likely to succeed in showing that provision facially violates the First Amendment because the statutory factors such an assessment must address — including whether a product's design, algorithms, or content could harm children — require a business to consider content or proxies for content, triggering First Amendment review. The panel also affirmed the district court's holding that the Act's notice-and-cure provision was not grammatically severable from the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement, so it too remained enjoined. A subsequent Ninth Circuit panel, ruling on a later appeal in the same case, confirmed that this specific holding continues to control, stating that the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement “remains enjoined and is not at issue in this appeal.”
clauses.gap: Both citations in this clause concern the same underlying litigation, NetChoice, LLC v. Bonta — the first is to the Ninth Circuit's 2024 opinion itself (NetChoice I), and the second is to a later Ninth Circuit opinion in the same case that quotes and confirms NetChoice I's holding; they are sequential rulings in one ongoing case rather than fully independent corroborating sources, though each is drawn from a separately published, official Ninth Circuit opinion fetched directly for this clause. This document could not independently re-fetch and read the full text of the 2024 NetChoice I opinion beyond its official case summary (itself fetched directly) because of a research-session rate limit on the legal database used; the quoted language describing NetChoice I's DPIA and notice-and-cure holdings is drawn from that official case summary and from the later panel's own direct quotation of NetChoice I in its 2026 opinion, both fetched and read in full for this clause, rather than from an independent read of NetChoice I's full opinion text. This is a preliminary injunction, not a final judgment: the underlying case remains pending in the district court, and this clause states the litigation's posture as of the most recent, most complete decision this document's research located, not a final resolution. This clause does not restate the statutory text of the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement or the notice-and-cure provision, which are quoted in companion clauses of this document; it also does not address the current status of the coverage definition, age estimation requirement, or data use and dark patterns restrictions, addressed in a companion clause.

The panel therefore affirmed the district court’s decision to enjoin the enforcement of that requirement, and the other provisions that were not grammatically severable from it.

clauses.title: Current Status: Coverage Definition and Age Estimation Not Enjoined; Data Use and Dark Patterns Restrictions Remain Enjoined for Vagueness; Case Still Pending
clauses.body: On remand from NetChoice I, NetChoice sought, and the district court granted, a second preliminary injunction against the entire Act on a new theory: that the coverage definition itself is content based and triggers strict scrutiny for the whole statute. The State appealed again. In a March 12, 2026 opinion, a Ninth Circuit panel (the same panel that decided NetChoice I) rejected that theory and vacated the injunction as to the coverage definition, holding that NetChoice had not carried its burden, on the record developed below, to show that a substantial number of the coverage definition's applications are unconstitutional. The panel likewise vacated the injunction as to the age estimation requirement, holding it could not determine on that record whether the requirement facially violates the First Amendment. However, the panel affirmed the injunction as to the data use restrictions and the dark patterns restriction — not on First Amendment grounds, but because their reliance on the undefined terms “material detriment,” “best interests,” and “well-being” renders them unconstitutionally vague under the Due Process Clause. Finally, the panel vacated the district court's ruling that the Act's remaining valid provisions are not severable from the still-enjoined notice-and-cure provision, holding the record did not yet permit that determination, and remanded the entire case to the district court for further proceedings. As of this document's most recent check, the litigation remains in a preliminary injunction posture with no final judgment on the merits, and the district court proceedings on remand had not yet been located or reviewed for this document.
clauses.gap: Both citations in this clause are drawn from the same March 12, 2026 Ninth Circuit opinion (different passages of that one document), not independent corroborating sources, though each passage was independently located and verified as an exact quotation of the fetched opinion text. This is one specific, dated appellate ruling in a case that the opinion itself remands for further district court proceedings; it is not a final judgment, and the enforceability picture it describes could change again as the case continues. This clause does not resolve the current injunction status of the Act's separate “policy enforcement requirement,” Civil Code § 1798.99.31(a)(9), which the district court had enjoined but which the March 2026 opinion's own footnote states was “not at issue in this appeal” — a genuine, disclosed gap in this document's research rather than an implied statement that the provision is or is not currently enforceable. This clause also does not independently restate the statutory text of the coverage definition, the age estimation requirement, or the data use and dark patterns restrictions, each quoted in companion clauses of this document, or the First Amendment holding regarding the Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement, addressed in a companion clause.

citations.quote: The panel held that NetChoice is not likely to succeed on the merits of its facial challenge to the CAADCA’s coverage definition, which consists of six separately enumerated indicators enabling online businesses to determine whether they are subject to the CAADCA.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Introduction and Scope
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act (Civil Code section 1954.50 et seq.), a 1995 California statute that limits the authority of local governments (cities and counties) to apply residential rent control to certain categories of housing, and that separately addresses the rent a landlord may charge a new tenant after a prior tenancy ends. It concerns the property commonly known as {{propertyAddress}}, the tenancy of {{tenantName}}, and the landlord {{landlordName}}. If a current monthly rent figure is relevant, it is stated here as: {{monthlyRent}}.

Costa-Hawkins is a different, older statute from California's statewide Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482, Civil Code sections 1946.2 and 1947.12), which is addressed in a separate information sheet in this collection. AB 1482 is itself a statewide substantive floor -- a rent-increase cap and a just-cause-for-termination requirement -- that applies directly to a tenancy. Costa-Hawkins works differently: rather than regulating a tenancy directly, it constrains what a city or county's own local rent-control ordinance is allowed to regulate, and it is the source of what is commonly called "vacancy decontrol." This document does not restate AB 1482's rent-cap or just-cause content, and it does not itself determine whether this or any other specific tenancy, unit, or local ordinance is covered by, or exempt from, Costa-Hawkins, AB 1482, or any local rent-control ordinance.

clauses.title: What Costa-Hawkins Does: A Preemption Statute, Not a Rent-Control Law
clauses.body: The Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act does not itself impose rent control; it constrains the residential rent control that a "public entity" -- a term with the same meaning given to it in Government Code section 811.2, which includes a city, a county, and other local governmental bodies -- may otherwise establish, continue, or enforce. Its central operative provisions are framed as overriding contrary local law: an owner "may establish the initial and all subsequent rental rates" for certain categories of housing, and separately "may establish the initial rental rate" when a tenancy turns over, in each case "notwithstanding any other provision of law" -- language that displaces a conflicting local rent-control ordinance rather than creating a new substantive rent-control scheme of its own. The statute's own terms confirm that its target is local law: one of its new-construction categories turns on whether a unit "has already been exempt from the residential rent control ordinance of a public entity" before a specified date.
clauses.gap: This clause establishes only the statute's own framing of what it does -- constrain local ("public entity") rent control -- not a comprehensive description of every California city or county's rent-control ordinance, which vary widely and are not catalogued here. The citations to Civil Code section 1954.52(a) (the preemption clause) and section 1954.52(a)(2) (the public-entity cross-reference) are both to the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources; the citations to section 1954.50 (short title) and section 1954.51(d) (definition of "public entity") are to separate, independently numbered sections. This document addresses Costa-Hawkins only; it is a different, older statute from the statewide Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (AB 1482), which is addressed in a separate information sheet and is not restated here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rent-control-preemption framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific tenancy; landlord-tenant rules vary significantly by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific local ordinance, unit, or tenancy is covered by, or exempt from, this chapter.

clauses.title: The Single-Family Home / Condominium ("Alienable Title") Exemption
clauses.body: Civil Code section 1954.52(a)(3) exempts from local rent control a dwelling or unit that "is alienable separate from the title to any other dwelling unit" -- a category that commonly includes single-family homes and condominium units that can be sold on their own, separate from a larger building -- or that is a subdivided interest in a subdivision as specified in the cross-referenced Business and Professions Code provision. That exemption does not apply, however, in either of two situations: where the preceding tenancy was terminated by the owner using a notice under Civil Code section 1946.1, or was ended by an owner-noticed change in the terms of the tenancy under Civil Code section 827; or, for a condominium specifically, where the unit has not yet been sold separately by the subdivider to a bona fide purchaser for value.
clauses.gap: This exemption is a Costa-Hawkins-specific provision, distinct from the differently worded and differently conditioned alienable-title exemption found in the statewide Tenant Protection Act of 2019 (Civil Code sections 1947.12(d)(5) and 1946.2(e)(8)), which is addressed in a separate information sheet in this collection; this clause does not restate that statute's ownership-type conditions (excluding REITs, corporations, and certain LLCs) or its required tenant-notice language, because Civil Code section 1954.52(a)(3) does not itself contain either of those conditions. The two citations below (subparagraphs (A) and (B)) are both from subdivision (a)(3) of the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1954.52) and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rent-control-preemption framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific tenancy; landlord-tenant rules vary significantly by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific dwelling or unit qualifies for, or has lost, this exemption.

(ii) A condominium dwelling or unit that has not been sold separately by the subdivider to a bona fide purchaser for value.

clauses.title: The New-Construction Exemption
clauses.body: Civil Code section 1954.52(a) exempts new construction from local rent control in two alternative ways, not one single statewide cutoff date. The first is a fixed statewide date: a dwelling or unit with a certificate of occupancy issued after February 1, 1995 qualifies. The second is tied instead to a specific local ordinance's own terms: a dwelling or unit that had already been exempted from a public entity's residential rent control ordinance on or before February 1, 1995, under that ordinance's own preexisting local exemption for newly constructed units, also qualifies -- regardless of when the unit's certificate of occupancy actually issued. Because this second pathway depends on whether, and as of when, a given city or county's own ordinance already exempted new construction, the practical effect of the new-construction exemption is not identical from one local rent-control jurisdiction to the next.
clauses.gap: This clause states the statutory mechanism only; it does not determine the certificate-of-occupancy issuance date for any specific unit, and it does not catalog which California cities' or counties' rent-control ordinances had a newly-constructed-units exemption in effect on or before February 1, 1995, or what that local exemption's own terms were -- both are fact-specific inquiries this document does not undertake. The two citations below (paragraphs (1) and (2)) are both from subdivision (a) of the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1954.52) and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rent-control-preemption framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific tenancy; landlord-tenant rules vary significantly by state. citations.quote: (2) It has already been exempt from the residential rent control ordinance of a public entity on or before February 1, 1995, pursuant to a local exemption for newly constructed units.

clauses.title: Vacancy Decontrol: Resetting Rent Between Tenancies
clauses.body: Civil Code section 1954.53(a) allows an owner to establish the initial rental rate for a dwelling or unit when a tenancy ends -- "notwithstanding any other provision of law," meaning notwithstanding a contrary local rent-control ordinance -- except where the owner itself ended the preceding tenancy by a notice under Civil Code section 1946.1 or changed its terms by a notice under Civil Code section 827. Because that exception covers an owner-initiated no-fault termination, the practical effect is that an owner may reset the rent to a new figure of the owner's choosing where the prior tenant vacated voluntarily or was evicted for cause, but not where the owner itself forced the vacancy through a no-fault termination notice. Once set, that new rate applies for the entire tenancy that follows, including any renewal by the same tenant. The statute also addresses a partial change in occupancy: if the original occupants no longer permanently reside in the unit, the owner may raise the rent for a new sublessee or assignee who did not live there before January 1, 1996 -- but this increase does not apply where one or more of the original occupants remains in lawful possession of the unit, or where a sublessee or assignee who already resided there before January 1, 1996 remains in possession.
clauses.gap: This clause does not reproduce every condition in Civil Code section 1954.53 -- for example, its separate provisions addressing units affected by prior governmental rent-limitation contracts, physically-disabled tenants' right to move within a property, security-deposit handling, or units cited for uncorrected serious health, safety, fire, or building code violations. The four citations below (subdivisions (a), (b), and (d)(2)-(3)) are all from the same statutory section (Civil Code section 1954.53) and are treated here as one source, not as independently corroborating sources. This document uses the commonly used term "vacancy decontrol" as a description of this mechanism; that phrase does not itself appear in the statutory text quoted here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rent-control-preemption framework -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific tenancy; landlord-tenant rules vary significantly by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether this or any other specific rent reset, or any specific unit or tenancy, complies with, or is covered by, this section.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.53(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) Notwithstanding any other provision of law, an owner of residential real property may establish the initial rental rate for a dwelling or unit, except where any of the following applies: (1) The previous tenancy has been terminated by the owner by notice pursuant to Section 1946.1 or has been terminated upon a change in the terms of the tenancy noticed pursuant to Section 827, except a change permitted by law in the amount of rent or fees.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.53(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (b) Subdivision (a) applies to, and includes, renewal of the initial hiring by the same tenant, lessee, authorized subtenant, or authorized sublessee for the entire period of their occupancy at the rental rate established for the initial hiring.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.53(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (2) If the original occupant or occupants who took possession of the dwelling or unit pursuant to the rental agreement with the owner no longer permanently reside there, an owner may increase the rent by any amount allowed by this section to a lawful sublessee or assignee who did not reside at the dwelling or unit prior to January 1, 1996.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.53(d)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (3) This subdivision does not apply to partial changes in occupancy of a dwelling or unit where one or more of the occupants of the premises, pursuant to the agreement with the owner provided for above, remains an occupant in lawful possession of the dwelling or unit, or where a lawful sublessee or assignee who resided at the dwelling or unit prior to January 1, 1996, remains in possession of the dwelling or unit.

clauses.title: Purpose and Parties: The Good Neighbor Fence Act
clauses.body:
{{party1Name}}, the owner of the real property located at {{party1PropertyAddress}} ("Party One"), and {{party2Name}}, the owner of the real property located at {{party2PropertyAddress}} ("Party Two"), are owners of adjoining parcels of real property in California. This document concerns the fence described as: {{fenceLocationDescription}}.

This document describes California Civil Code Section 841, commonly referred to as the Good Neighbor Fence Act, which addresses the sharing of responsibility between adjoining landowners for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of a boundary fence, and the written notice procedure that statute sets out for a landowner who intends to incur those costs and share them with an adjoining landowner. This document states facts about that statute; it does not tell Party One or Party Two what to do about any specific fence, cost, or disagreement between them. Completing the notice section of this document does not, by itself, guarantee that the notice satisfies every requirement of Section 841 in every circumstance; it is a tool for organizing the content that statute's own text requires a notice to include, described in the following sections.

clauses.title: The Statutory Presumption of Equal Responsibility for Fence Costs
clauses.body: California's Civil Code states that adjoining landowners share equally in the responsibility for maintaining the boundaries and monuments between their properties. For a fence specifically, the statute states a further, related presumption: adjoining landowners are presumed to share an equal benefit from any fence dividing their properties, and, unless otherwise agreed to by the parties in a written agreement, are presumed to be equally responsible for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence. This presumption applies by its own terms, without requiring the adjoining landowners to first enter into any agreement; it can be displaced only by the landowners' own written agreement stating otherwise, or by rebutting it in the manner described elsewhere in this document. The statute is commonly referred to as the Good Neighbor Fence Act, referencing the bill that enacted its current text, effective January 1, 2014; that popular name does not itself appear in the statute's own text.
clauses.gap: Cal. Civ. Code § 841(a) and § 841(b)(1) are both subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code Section 841, and are treated here as two citations from one source, not as independent sources, not independent of one another. Section 841's own text defines "landowner" and "adjoining" (quoted in a companion clause of this document) but does not itself define the word "fence," and the phrase "good neighbor fence" does not appear anywhere in the fetched statutory text of Section 841. This document, like common secondary usage, refers to Section 841 as the "Good Neighbor Fence Act"; that popular name was not independently verified against a specific secondary source in this research session and does not appear in the statute's own fetched text, though the statute's own legislative-history line does confirm its current text was "Repealed and added by Stats. 2013, Ch. 86, Sec. 3. (AB 1404) Effective January 1, 2014." This clause does not evaluate whether the presumption in fact applies, or has been displaced by a written agreement, on the facts of any specific fence or dispute.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 841(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, adjoining landowners' equal responsibility for maintaining boundaries and monuments
citations.quote: Adjoining landowners shall share equally in the responsibility for maintaining the boundaries and monuments between them.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 841(b)(1)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, presumption of equal benefit and equal responsibility for reasonable fence costs, treated as one source with § 841(a) above, not an independent source
citations.quote: Adjoining landowners are presumed to share an equal benefit from any fence dividing their properties and, unless otherwise agreed to by the parties in a written agreement, shall be presumed to be equally responsible for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence.

clauses.title: Required Content of the 30-Day Pre-Construction Notice
clauses.body: Where a landowner intends to incur costs for a fence subject to the presumption described elsewhere in this document, California's Civil Code requires that landowner to give 30 days' prior written notice to each affected adjoining landowner before incurring those costs. The statute specifies what that notice must include: notification of the presumption of equal responsibility for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence; a description of the nature of the problem facing the shared fence; the proposed solution for addressing the problem; the estimated construction or maintenance costs involved in addressing the problem; the proposed cost-sharing approach; and the proposed timeline for getting the problem addressed. The statute states these as required content of the notice itself; it does not separately prescribe a particular method of delivery (such as personal service or mail) for giving that notice.
clauses.gap: This clause's closing sentence, that the statute does not separately prescribe a particular method of delivery for the notice, describes the absence of such text in Section 841(b)(2) as fetched and reviewed in full; it is not a citation to a specific provision, since there is no text to quote for an absence. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific written notice in fact satisfies Section 841(b)(2)'s content requirements on the facts of a specific fence dispute.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 841(b)(2)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, 30-day prior written notice and its required content
citations.quote: Where a landowner intends to incur costs for a fence described in paragraph (1), the landowner shall give 30 days’ prior written notice to each affected adjoining landowner. The notice shall include notification of the presumption of equal responsibility for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence. The notice shall include a description of the nature of the problem facing the shared fence, the proposed solution for addressing the problem, the estimated construction or maintenance costs involved to address the problem, the proposed cost sharing approach, and the proposed timeline for getting the problem addressed.

clauses.title: Rebutting the Presumption: Statutory Factors a Court May Consider
clauses.body: The presumption of equal responsibility described elsewhere in this document is not absolute. California's Civil Code states that the presumption may be overcome by a preponderance of the evidence demonstrating that imposing equal responsibility for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence would be unjust. In determining whether equal responsibility would be unjust, the statute directs a court to consider all of the following: whether the financial burden to one landowner is substantially disproportionate to the benefit conferred upon that landowner by the fence in question; whether the cost of the fence would exceed the difference in the value of the real property before and after its installation; whether the financial burden to one landowner would impose an undue financial hardship given that party's financial circumstances, as demonstrated by reasonable proof; the reasonableness of the particular construction or maintenance project, including the extent to which its costs appear unnecessary or excessive, and the extent to which its costs appear to be the result of a landowner's personal aesthetic, architectural, or other preferences; and any other equitable factors appropriate under the circumstances. This clause lists the statute's own factors; it does not evaluate whether any of them would in fact be found to apply, or would in fact overcome the presumption, on the facts of a specific fence dispute.
clauses.gap: This clause does not evaluate whether any of the listed factors would in fact apply to, or overcome the presumption on, the facts of a specific fence dispute; that determination is committed by the statute's own text to a court applying a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard to the facts before it, not to any generalized fact stated in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 841(b)(3)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, standard and factors for overcoming the equal-responsibility presumption
citations.quote: The presumption in paragraph (1) may be overcome by a preponderance of the evidence demonstrating that imposing equal responsibility for the reasonable costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence would be unjust. In determining whether equal responsibility for the reasonable costs would be unjust, the court shall consider all of the following: (A) Whether the financial burden to one landowner is substantially disproportionate to the benefit conferred upon that landowner by the fence in question. (B) Whether the cost of the fence would exceed the difference in the value of the real property before and after its installation. (C) Whether the financial burden to one landowner would impose an undue financial hardship given that party’s financial circumstances as demonstrated by reasonable proof. (D) The reasonableness of a particular construction or maintenance project, including all of the following: (i) The extent to which the costs of the project appear to be unnecessary or excessive. (ii) The extent to which the costs of the project appear to be the result of the landowner’s personal aesthetic, architectural, or other preferences. (E) Any other equitable factors appropriate under the circumstances.

clauses.title: What the Statute Provides, and Does Not Provide, if the Landowners Disagree
clauses.body: California's Civil Code addresses what happens once a party rebuts the presumption of equal responsibility: where a party rebuts the presumption by a preponderance of the evidence, the statute directs the court, in its discretion and consistent with that party's circumstances, to order either a contribution of less than an equal share of the costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence, or to order no contribution. This is the only outcome Section 841's own text specifies for a disagreement over the presumption. The statute's text, as fetched and reviewed in full for this document, does not itself state what happens if an adjoining landowner simply does not respond to a 30-day notice, does not itself specify a particular court (such as small claims court or superior court) in which a dispute is to be brought, and does not itself describe any required mediation, arbitration, or other pre-litigation step. This is a civil, private-dispute statute concerning cost-sharing between adjoining landowners; its own text does not state that a failure to give notice, to respond to notice, or to share costs as the statute presumes, is a crime or a basis for code enforcement action.
clauses.gap: This clause's statements about what Section 841's text does not address (a non-responding landowner, a specific court such as small claims or superior court, or a required pre-litigation step) describe the absence of such text in the statute as fetched and reviewed in full; they are not citations to specific provisions, since there is no text to quote for an absence, and they should not be read as a claim that no such recourse in fact exists under other statutes (for example, California's small claims court has its own general jurisdictional statutes, which were not researched or cited in this clause) — only that Section 841 itself does not specify one. This clause does not evaluate what remedy, if any, would in fact be available on the facts of a specific dispute.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 841(b)(4)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, court's discretionary order when the presumption is rebutted
citations.quote: Where a party rebuts the presumption in paragraph (1) by a preponderance of the evidence, the court shall, in its discretion, consistent with the party’s circumstances, order either a contribution of less than an equal share for the costs of construction, maintenance, or necessary replacement of the fence, or order no contribution.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: "Landowner" and "Adjoining"
clauses.body: For purposes of the presumption, notice, and rebuttal framework described elsewhere in this document, California's Civil Code defines two terms. "Landowner" means a private person or entity that lawfully holds any possessory interest in real property, and does not include a city, county, city and county, district, public corporation, or other political subdivision, public body, or public agency — so a public entity that owns adjoining land is not itself a "landowner" for purposes of this presumption. "Adjoining" means contiguous to or in contact with. The statute does not define the word "fence" itself, and does not use the phrase "good neighbor fence" anywhere in its own text.
clauses.gap: Cal. Civ. Code § 841(c)(1) and § 841(c)(2) are both subsections of the same statutory section, Civil Code Section 841, and are treated here as two citations from one source, not as independent sources, not independent of one another. The statement that the statute does not define "fence" or use the phrase "good neighbor fence" describes the absence of such text in Section 841 as fetched and reviewed in full; it is not a citation to a specific provision, since there is no text to quote for an absence. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific entity or relationship in fact meets these definitions on the facts of a specific dispute.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 841(c)(1)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of "landowner"
citations.quote: “Landowner” means a private person or entity that lawfully holds any possessory interest in real property, and does not include a city, county, city and county, district, public corporation, or other political subdivision, public body, or public agency.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 841(c)(2)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of "adjoining", treated as one source with § 841(c)(1) above, not an independent source
citations.quote: “Adjoining” means contiguous to or in contact with.

clauses.title: 30-Day Written Notice and Signature
Purpose of This Special Administrator Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the special administrator of a decedent's estate under California law — a person a probate court may appoint on a temporary, emergency basis to protect and manage a decedent's estate before a general personal representative (executor or administrator) is appointed and issued Letters. It is prepared in connection with {{decedentName}}'s estate, who died on {{dateOfDeath}}, based on the following circumstances said to require immediate protection of the estate before a general personal representative can be appointed: {{emergencyCircumstances}}. {{petitionerName}} is the person proposed for appointment as special administrator, and this information sheet is intended for use with a petition to be filed in the Superior Court of California, County of {{countyOfFiling}}. This information sheet is not itself a petition, and preparing or signing it does not appoint {{petitionerName}} — or anyone else — special administrator of {{decedentName}}'s estate, does not itself preserve or protect any estate property, and does not itself give {{petitionerName}} any authority to act for the estate. Only a court order, followed by issuance of letters, does that. This document addresses only the special administrator's temporary, emergency role under Probate Code Division 7, Part 2, Chapter 4, Article 8 (§§ 8540-8547); it does not address the separate process for appointing a general personal representative described in this project's Petition for Probate — Information Sheet.

clauses.title: When a Court May Appoint a Special Administrator, and How the Appointment Order Is Structured
clauses.body: Probate Code § 8540(a) provides that if the circumstances of {{decedentName}}'s estate require the immediate appointment of a personal representative, the court may appoint a special administrator to exercise any powers that may be appropriate under the circumstances for the preservation of the estate. § 8540(b) separately provides that the appointment may be for a specified term, to perform particular acts, or on any other terms specified in the court order — meaning the scope and duration of a special administrator's role is set by the individual court order appointing that person, not by a single fixed statutory role that looks the same in every case.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes both subsections of a single statutory section (§ 8540(a) and § 8540(b)) as one citation; they are not independent of one another. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's special administrator process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, and not a claim that any particular estate's circumstances meet this statute's 'immediate appointment' trigger. Special Administrators appear in Probate Code Division 7, Part 2, Chapter 4, Article 8 (§§ 8540-8547) — confirmed directly from the Probate Code's own table of contents at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, which places this article after Article 7 (Changes in Administration, §§ 8520-8525) and before Article 9 (Nonresident Personal Representative, §§ 8570-8577), within the same Part 2 chapter that governs appointment of the general personal representative. This document does not separately address the bond a court may require of a special administrator (§§ 8480-8488, 8543) or the letters-and-oath issuance mechanics for a special administrator (§ 8542). This document is informational: it does not itself appoint any special administrator or determine that immediate appointment is warranted for any specific estate — only a court order does that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8540 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8540
citations.quote: (a) If the circumstances of the estate require the immediate appointment of a personal representative, the court may appoint a special administrator to exercise any powers that may be appropriate under the circumstances for the preservation of the estate. (b) The appointment may be for a specified term, to perform particular acts, or on any other terms specified in the court order.

clauses.title: Notice Is Not Required for Appointment, and the Court's Preference Among Candidates
clauses.body: Probate Code § 8541(a) provides that appointment of a special administrator may be made at any time without notice, or on such notice to interested persons as the court deems reasonable — unlike the notice-and-hearing process this project's companion Petition for Probate — Information Sheet describes for appointment of a general personal representative, the statute leaves whether to require notice, and how much, to the court's own discretion rather than mandating notice in every case. § 8541(b) directs that in making the appointment, the court shall ordinarily give preference to the person entitled to appointment as personal representative, and that the court may instead appoint the public administrator. § 8541(c) allows a request for approval of a particular act to be included in the petition for appointment when the appointment is for a particular act, decided on the same notice and at the same time as the appointment itself. § 8541(d) allows the court to act, if necessary, to remedy errors made in the appointment.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes all four subsections of a single statutory section (§ 8541(a)-(d)) as one citation; they are not independent of one another. The statute's own text uses the phrase 'without notice,' not 'ex parte'; this clause uses the statute's own language. This clause describes the court's statutory authority to dispense with or limit notice — it is not a claim that any particular petition for appointment of a special administrator will, or should, be granted without notice; that remains within the court's discretion on the facts before it. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's special administrator process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This document is informational: it does not itself appoint any special administrator — only a court order does that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8541 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8541
citations.quote: (a) Appointment of a special administrator may be made at any time without notice or on such notice to interested persons as the court deems reasonable. (b) In making the appointment, the court shall ordinarily give preference to the person entitled to appointment as personal representative. The court may appoint the public administrator. (c) In the case of an appointment to perform a particular act, request for approval of the act may be included in the petition for appointment, and approval may be made on the same notice and at the same time as the appointment. (d) The court may act, if necessary, to remedy any errors made in the appointment.

clauses.title: A Special Administrator's Powers Are Limited by Default — Not the Same as a General Personal Representative's Unless the Court Grants More
clauses.body: A special administrator's powers over {{decedentName}}'s estate are narrower than a general personal representative's by default, and are defined largely by the court's own order rather than by statute alone. Probate Code § 8544(a) provides that except to the extent the order appointing a special administrator prescribes terms, the special administrator has the power to do the following without further order of the court: take possession of the estate's real and personal property and preserve it from damage, waste, and injury; collect claims, rents, and other income belonging to the estate; commence and maintain or defend suits and other legal proceedings; and sell perishable property. § 8544(b) separately lists further powers — including borrowing money or leasing, mortgaging, or executing a deed of trust on real property, and paying interest or other amounts on an obligation secured by a mortgage, lien, or deed of trust on estate property under specified circumstances — that a special administrator has only on order of the court, not automatically. § 8544(c) provides that except where the powers, duties, and obligations of a general personal representative are granted under § 8545, the special administrator is not a proper party to an action on a claim against {{decedentName}}. Probate Code § 8545(a) allows the court to grant a special administrator the same powers, duties, and obligations as a general personal representative where to do so appears proper, but requires that grant — where letters have not previously been issued to a general personal representative — to be made on the same notice required under § 8003 for appointment of a personal representative, unless made at a hearing on a petition for appointment of a general personal representative for which that § 8003 notice has already been given.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two different, independently-numbered statutory sections (§ 8544 and § 8545). The central, easily overclaimed point this clause is written to avoid: a special administrator does not automatically have all the powers of a general personal representative; by default under § 8544(a)-(c), those powers are limited to the specific enumerated actions listed above (plus whatever the court's own appointment order additionally prescribes), and the broader powers, duties, and obligations of a general personal representative are available only if the court affirmatively grants them under § 8545, on the notice that section requires. This clause does not quote § 8544(d) (which provides that a special administrator appointed to perform a particular act has no duty to take any other action to protect the estate) or § 8545(b)-(c) (governing an additional bond the court may require as a condition of an § 8545 grant, and the requirement that letters recite the grant); both are honestly disclosed here rather than described. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's special administrator process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This document is informational: it does not itself grant any powers to any special administrator — only a court order does that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8544 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8544
citations.quote: (a) Except to the extent the order appointing a special administrator prescribes terms, the special administrator has the power to do all of the following without further order of the court: (1) Take possession of all of the real and personal property of the estate of the decedent and preserve it from damage, waste, and injury. (2) Collect all claims, rents, and other income belonging to the estate. (3) Commence and maintain or defend suits and other legal proceedings. (4) Sell perishable property. (b) Except to the extent the order prescribes terms, the special administrator has the power to do all of the following on order of the court: (1) Borrow money, or lease, mortgage, or execute a deed of trust on real property, in the same manner as an administrator. (2) Pay the interest due or all or any part of an obligation secured by a mortgage, lien, or deed of trust on property in the estate, where there is danger that the holder of the security may enforce or foreclose on the obligation and the property exceeds in value the amount of the obligation. This power may be ordered only on petition of the special administrator or any interested person, with any notice that the court deems proper, and shall remain in effect until appointment of a successor personal representative. The order may also direct that interest not yet accrued be paid as it becomes due, and the order shall remain in effect and cover the future interest unless and until for good cause set aside or modified by the court in the same manner as for the original order. (3) Exercise other powers that are conferred by order of the court. (c) Except where the powers, duties, and obligations of a general personal representative are granted under Section 8545, the special administrator is not a proper party to an action on a claim against the decedent.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8545(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8545(a)
citations.quote: (a) Notwithstanding Section 8544, the court may grant a special administrator the same powers, duties, and obligations as a general personal representative where to do so appears proper. Notwithstanding Section 8541, if letters have not previously been issued to a general personal representative, the grant shall be on the same notice required under Section 8003 for appointment of a personal representative, unless the appointment is made at a hearing on a petition for appointment of a general personal representative and the notice of that petition required under Section 8003 has been given.

clauses.title: When a Special Administrator's Authority Ends, and the Duty to Deliver Property and Account
clauses.body: Probate Code § 8546(a) provides that the powers of a special administrator cease on issuance of letters to a general personal representative, or as otherwise directed by the court. § 8546(b) then requires the special administrator to promptly deliver to the general personal representative all estate property in the special administrator's possession (subject to the court's authority to let the special administrator complete a pending sale or other transaction), and a list of all creditor claims known to the special administrator — showing each creditor's name and address, the claim amount, and what action has been taken on the claim — with a copy of that list filed with the court. § 8546(c) requires the special administrator to account in the same manner as a general personal representative is required to account, and allows that account to be combined with the general personal representative's first account when the same person has held both roles.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes all three subsections of a single statutory section (§ 8546(a)-(c)) as one citation; they are not independent of one another. § 8546(a) allows termination 'as otherwise directed by the court' in addition to termination on issuance of general letters; this clause does not attempt to catalog every circumstance in which a court might end a special administrator's authority early, since the statute itself leaves that to the court's order in each case. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's special administrator process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate. This document is informational: it does not itself terminate any special administrator's authority or determine what any particular special administrator must deliver or account for — only a court order, and the special administrator's actual compliance with it, does that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8546 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8546
citations.quote: (a) The powers of a special administrator cease on issuance of letters to a general personal representative or as otherwise directed by the court. (b) The special administrator shall promptly deliver to the general personal representative: (1) All property of the estate in the possession of the special administrator. The court may authorize the special administrator to complete a sale or other transaction affecting property in the possession of the special administrator. (2) A list of all creditor claims of which the special administrator has knowledge. The list shall show the name and address of each creditor, the amount of the claim, and what action has been taken with respect to the claim. A copy of the list shall be filed in the court. (c) The special administrator shall account in the same manner as a general personal representative is required to account. If the same person acts as both special administrator and general personal representative, the account of the special administrator may be combined with the first account of the general personal representative.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Special Administrator Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.
