It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not appoint any special administrator, grant any powers, or issue letters; only a court order, followed by issuance of letters, does that. A special administrator's authority under any resulting order is temporary and ends, at the latest, on issuance of letters to a general personal representative for {{decedentName}}'s estate.]

clauses.title: Purpose of This Creditor's Claim Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet states general facts about the formal, statutory procedure set out at Probate Code § 9000 et seq. by which a creditor of {{decedentName}} may file a claim against {{decedentName}}'s probate estate, now pending before {{courtName}} in {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes the claim-filing deadline, what a claim must contain, how and where a claim is filed, and what happens after a claim is filed or rejected. It does not itself file a claim on behalf of any creditor, does not extend, shorten, or waive any deadline this procedure imposes, and does not advise any specific creditor what to do about a specific debt.

clauses.title: What Counts as a "Claim," and the Consequence of Not Filing One
clauses.body: Probate Code § 9000 defines a "claim" broadly to mean a demand for payment of a liability of {{decedentName}} arising in contract, tort, or otherwise; a liability for taxes {{decedentName}} incurred before death (other than property taxes and real-property-lien assessments); or a liability of the estate for {{decedentName}}'s funeral expenses — regardless of whether the demand is due, not due, accrued, not accrued, contingent, liquidated, or unliquidated. The same section defines a "creditor" simply as a person who may have a claim against estate property. Except as otherwise provided by statute, Probate Code § 9002 requires that all such claims be filed in the manner and within the time this part of the Probate Code provides, and states plainly that a claim not filed as this part provides is barred.
clauses.gap: The two § 9000 citations below (the definitions of "claim" and of "creditor") are both drawn from the same statutory section and are not independent of one another; the § 9002 citation is a separate, independently numbered section. This is California's own statutory definition and bar rule, used as real evidence of California's creditor-claims procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. Section 9000(b), not quoted here, separately clarifies that a "claim" does not include a dispute over title to specific property alleged to belong to the estate; that distinct carve-out is not addressed by this clause. This document is informational: it does not itself determine whether any specific demand qualifies as a "claim" or is barred — only a court, or the operation of the statute on a specific creditor's own facts, can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 9000(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 9000(a)
citations.quote: “Claim” means a demand for payment for any of the following, whether due, not due, accrued or not accrued, or contingent, and whether liquidated or unliquidated: (1) Liability of the decedent, whether arising in contract, tort, or otherwise. (2) Liability for taxes incurred before the decedent’s death, whether assessed before or after the decedent’s death, other than property taxes and assessments secured by real property liens. (3) Liability of the estate for funeral expenses of the decedent.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 9000(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 9000(c)
citations.quote: “Creditor” means a person who may have a claim against estate property.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 9002(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 9002
citations.quote: (a) All claims shall be filed in the manner and within the time provided in this part. (b) A claim that is not filed as provided in this part is barred.

clauses.title: The Claim-Filing Deadline: the Later of Two Dates
clauses.body: Probate Code § 9100(a) requires a creditor to file a claim against {{decedentName}}'s estate before the later of two dates: four months after the date letters are first issued to a general personal representative, or 60 days after the date notice of administration is mailed or personally delivered to that particular creditor — whichever of the two comes later. The statute itself is explicit that this creditor-claim deadline does not extend the time provided by Code of Civil Procedure § 366.2, a separate, generally applicable one-year limitations period on actions against a decedent.
clauses.gap: This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 9100(a)); the two numbered deadlines within it are two ends of the same "later of" test, not independent provisions. Probate Code § 9103 separately allows a court, on petition, to permit a late claim in limited circumstances (for example, where the personal representative failed to give proper notice) — that late-claim petition procedure is a real exception to the deadline stated here but is not itself detailed in this clause. This clause does not independently verify the text or scope of Code of Civil Procedure § 366.2 itself, which lies outside the Probate Code part researched for this document; it is mentioned only because § 9100(a) itself cross-references it. This is California's own statutory deadline, used as real evidence of California's creditor-claims procedure — not a claim about which state's law, or which deadline, governs a specific creditor's specific claim.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 9100(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 9100(a)
citations.quote: (a) A creditor shall file a claim before expiration of the later of the following times: (1) Four months after the date letters are first issued to a general personal representative. (2) Sixty days after the date notice of administration is mailed or personally delivered to the creditor. Nothing in this paragraph extends the time provided in Section 366.2 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

clauses.title: What a Claim Must Contain, and How and Where It Is Filed
clauses.body: Probate Code § 9150 requires that a claim against {{decedentName}}'s estate be filed with the court — {{courtName}} in {{countyOfFiling}}, for a claim in this proceeding — and that a copy of the claim be served on {{personalRepresentativeName}} as personal representative, or on whoever is later appointed and qualifies as personal representative; a creditor who files with the court but never serves a copy on the personal representative (or vice versa) has an invalid claim. Probate Code § 9151(a) further requires that the claim be supported by an affidavit of the creditor, or of a person acting on the creditor's behalf, stating that the claim is a just claim, together with — if the claim is currently due — the facts supporting it, its amount, and confirmation that all payments and offsets have been credited, or — if the claim is not yet due, is contingent, or its amount is not yet ascertainable — the facts supporting it.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two different, independently numbered statutory sections (§ 9150 and § 9151); neither is cited more than once in this clause. Probate Code § 9152, not addressed here, separately requires that a claim based on a written instrument attach the original or a copy of it, and § 9153 separately requires the Judicial Council claim form to include a proof-of-delivery section for the copy served on the personal representative. This clause does not address the additional service-timing rule in § 9150(c) (service on the personal representative generally due within the later of 30 days of filing or four months after letters issue) beyond what its quoted text below already shows. This is California's own statutory filing procedure, used as real evidence of California's creditor-claims process — not a claim about which state's law, or which court's local rules, governs a specific claim's filing.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 9150(a)-(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 9150
citations.quote: (a) A claim may be filed by the creditor or a person acting on behalf of the creditor. (b) A claim shall be filed with the court and a copy shall be served on the personal representative, or on a person who is later appointed and qualified as personal representative. (c) Service of the claim on the personal representative shall be made within the later of 30 days of the filing of the claim or four months after letters issue to a personal representative with general powers. Service shall not be required after the claim has been allowed or rejected. (d) If the creditor does not file the claim with the court and serve the claim on the personal representative as provided in this section, the claim shall be invalid.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 9151(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 9151(a)
citations.quote: (a) A claim shall be supported by the affidavit of the creditor or the person acting on behalf of the creditor stating: (1) The claim is a just claim. (2) If the claim is due, the facts supporting the claim, the amount of the claim, and that all payments on and offsets to the claim have been credited. (3) If the claim is not due or contingent, or the amount is not yet ascertainable, the facts supporting the claim. (4) If the affidavit is made by a person other than the creditor, the reason it is not made by the creditor.

clauses.title: The Personal Representative's Options After a Claim Is Filed
clauses.body: Once a claim is filed, Probate Code § 9250(a) requires {{personalRepresentativeName}}, as personal representative, to allow or reject the claim, in whole or in part; that allowance or rejection must be in writing, filed with the court clerk, and served on the creditor with a copy, and by statute must state (among other things) that the creditor has 90 days in which to act on a rejected claim. Probate Code § 9256 separately supplies a default rule for silence: if, within 30 days after a claim is filed, neither the personal representative nor the court has acted on it, the creditor may, at the creditor's own option, treat that inaction as equivalent to a notice of rejection given on the 30th day.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two different, independently numbered statutory sections (§ 9250 and § 9256); neither is cited more than once in this clause. It does not address the separate procedure that applies when the personal representative is not authorized to act under the Independent Administration of Estates Act (§ 9251, court or judge review of the allowance) or when the personal representative or their attorney is personally the creditor (§ 9252). It also does not address § 9255's separate rule for a partial allowance the creditor refuses to accept. This is California's own statutory claims-response procedure, used as real evidence of California's creditor-claims process — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate's claims administration.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 9250(a)-(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 9250
citations.quote: (a) When a claim is filed, the personal representative shall allow or reject the claim in whole or in part. (b) The allowance or rejection shall be in writing. The personal representative shall file the allowance or rejection with the court clerk and give notice to the creditor as provided in Part 2 (commencing with Section 1200) of Division 3, together with a copy of the allowance or rejection. (c) The allowance or rejection shall contain the following information: (1) The name of the creditor. (2) The total amount of the claim. (3) The date of issuance of letters. (4) The date of the decedent’s death. (5) The estimated value of the decedent’s estate. (6) The amount allowed or rejected by the personal representative. (7) Whether the personal representative is authorized to act under the Independent Administration of Estates Act (Part 6 (commencing with Section 10400)). (8) A statement that the creditor has 90 days in which to act on a rejected claim.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 9256 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 9256
citations.quote: If within 30 days after a claim is filed the personal representative or the court or judge has refused or neglected to act on the claim, the refusal or neglect may, at the option of the creditor, be deemed equivalent to giving a notice of rejection on the 30th day.

clauses.title: The Creditor's Deadline to Sue on a Rejected Claim
clauses.body: Probate Code § 9351 bars a creditor from suing {{personalRepresentativeName}}, as {{decedentName}}'s personal representative, on a cause of action against {{decedentName}} unless a claim was first filed as this part of the Probate Code provides, and that claim was rejected, in whole or in part. Once a claim is rejected, Probate Code § 9353(a) bars the rejected part of the claim unless the creditor commences an action on it — or has the matter referred to a referee or to arbitration — within 90 days after the notice of rejection is given, if the claim was already due when rejected, or within 90 days after the claim becomes due, if it was not yet due when rejected. This 90-day claim-rejection deadline is a distinct, statute-specific time limit; it exists separately from, and operates in addition to, whatever generally applicable civil statute of limitations would otherwise apply to the underlying debt.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two different, independently numbered statutory sections (§ 9351 and § 9353); neither is cited more than once in this clause. It does not address § 9352, which separately tolls the otherwise-applicable statute of limitations on the claim from the time the claim (or a late-claim petition under § 9103) is filed through allowance, approval, or rejection, nor § 9353(b)'s separate rule excluding any period during which the personal representative's office is vacant. It also does not address the different procedure in Article 2 of this chapter (commencing with § 9370) that applies when an action or proceeding against the decedent was already pending at the time of death, rather than the no-pending-action situation addressed here. This is California's own statutory procedure and its own deadline, used as real evidence of California's creditor-claims process — not a claim about which state's law, or which limitations period, governs a specific creditor's specific claim.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 9351 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 9351
citations.quote: An action may not be commenced against a decedent’s personal representative on a cause of action against the decedent unless a claim is first filed as provided in this part and the claim is rejected in whole or in part.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 9353(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 9353(a)
citations.quote: (a) Regardless of whether the statute of limitations otherwise applicable to a claim will expire before or after the following times, a claim rejected in whole or in part is barred as to the part rejected unless, within the following times, the creditor commences an action on the claim or the matter is referred to a referee or to arbitration: (1) If the claim is due at the time the notice of rejection is given, 90 days after the notice is given. (2) If the claim is not due at the time the notice of rejection is given, 90 days after the claim becomes due.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
clauses.body: This information sheet was reviewed on {{dateSigned}}, in {{cityState}}. It states general facts about California's statutory creditor's-claim procedure in the administration of {{decedentName}}'s estate. It is not legal advice about any specific claim or debt, does not itself file, preserve, allow, or reject any claim, and does not extend, shorten, or waive any deadline this procedure imposes.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's own statutory worker-classification test — commonly called the "ABC test" — codified at Labor Code §§ 2775-2776, which was enacted to codify the California Supreme Court's decision in Dynamex Operations West, Inc. v. Superior Court (2018) 4 Cal.5th 903. It is prepared in connection with a working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.

California's ABC test is a separate and different legal test from the federal common-law control test addressed elsewhere in this corpus's own Independent Contractor Agreement document. The two tests ask different questions and weigh different things, and they can produce different answers for the very same working relationship between the very same two parties — satisfying one does not by itself show that the other is satisfied. California's ABC test is generally understood to be stricter and more protective of employee status than the federal common-law test.

This information sheet does not itself determine that {{employeeName}} is or is not an employee or an independent contractor of {{companyName}} under California law, does not apply this test to any specific facts, does not investigate or make any finding about any specific working relationship, and does not file anything with any agency or court.

clauses.title: The Statutory Presumption of Employee Status and Who Bears the Burden
clauses.body: California law starts from a presumption that runs against independent-contractor status. Under Labor Code § 2775(b)(1), a person providing labor or services for remuneration is considered an employee rather than an independent contractor unless the hiring entity demonstrates that all of the ABC test's conditions are satisfied. As the statute's own text frames it, the default is employee status, and the burden of proving otherwise falls on the hiring entity — {{companyName}}, in a relationship with {{employeeName}} — not on the worker.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the presumption it states and where the burden of proof falls — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific worker is or is not an employee of any specific hiring entity. This clause states the presumption and burden only; the three specific conditions the hiring entity must satisfy to rebut the presumption are stated in a separate clause of this document. This document does not address how a hiring entity or a court applies this presumption procedurally in an actual dispute (for example, in litigation or before an agency), because that was not researched for this document.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2775(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: a person providing labor or services for remuneration shall be considered an employee rather than an independent contractor unless the hiring entity demonstrates that all of the following conditions are satisfied

clauses.title: The Three ABC Test Factors — All Three Are Required
clauses.body:
To rebut the presumption of employee status, Labor Code § 2775(b)(1) requires the hiring entity to establish all three of the following conditions:

(A) The person is free from the control and direction of the hiring entity in connection with the performance of the work, both under the contract for the performance of the work and in fact.

(B) The person performs work that is outside the usual course of the hiring entity's business.

(C) The person is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, or business of the same nature as that involved in the work performed.

The statute's own structure requires all three conditions, not a majority of them and not simply the most significant one. If the hiring entity fails to establish even one of the three — A, B, or C — the person is an employee rather than an independent contractor for the purposes this test governs, regardless of how the other two conditions come out.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the three conditions it codifies and their all-three structure — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not an application of these factors to any specific worker's or hiring entity's actual working relationship. All three citations below are to the same statutory subdivision, Labor Code § 2775(b)(1), factors (A), (B), and (C) — they are not independent of one another, and are disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not survey the substantial body of California case law interpreting what "free from control," "usual course of business," or "customarily engaged in an independently established" trade mean on specific facts; that research was not conducted for this document.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2775(b)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The person is free from the control and direction of the hiring entity in connection with the performance of the work, both under the contract for the performance of the work and in fact.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2775(b)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The person performs work that is outside the usual course of the hiring entity’s business.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2775(b)(1)(C) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The person is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, or business of the same nature as that involved in the work performed.

clauses.title: What This Test Governs, and the Fallback to the Older Borello Test
clauses.body:
California's ABC test does not present itself as the universal answer to every legal question about a worker's status. By its own terms, Labor Code § 2775(b)(1) states that the test applies "for purposes of this code and the Unemployment Insurance Code, and for the purposes of wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission" — that is, for California Labor Code purposes, unemployment insurance purposes, and the wage orders issued by the Industrial Welfare Commission. It does not, by this text alone, purport to govern every other body of law that might ask whether someone is an employee.

The statute also states its own fallback. If a court of law rules that the three-part test cannot be applied to a particular context on grounds other than an express exception to employment status, the determination of employee or independent-contractor status in that context is instead governed by the older, multi-factor test from S. G. Borello & Sons, Inc. v. Department of Industrial Relations (1989) 48 Cal.3d 341 — the decision the statute itself labels "Borello."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the scope it states for itself and the fallback it provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not an exhaustive account of every California statute, wage order, or other context in which the ABC test or the Borello test actually applies. Both citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 2775, subdivisions (b)(1) and (b)(3) — they are not independent of one another, and are disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document does not independently verify the Borello multi-factor test's own content, having not fetched or quoted S. G. Borello & Sons, Inc. v. Department of Industrial Relations directly; it reports only what § 2775's own text says about when that decision governs instead. This document also does not survey case law on when a court has actually found the three-part test "cannot be applied," and does not address the statute's separate carve-out preserving express statutory or wage-order exceptions to "employee" status (§ 2775(b)(2)), which was not researched for this document.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2775(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: For purposes of this code and the Unemployment Insurance Code, and for the purposes of wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission,

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2775(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: the determination of employee or independent contractor status in that context shall instead be governed by the California Supreme Court’s decision in S. G. Borello & Sons, Inc. v. Department of Industrial Relations (1989) 48 Cal.3d 341 (Borello).

clauses.title: The Business-to-Business Exemption (Labor Code § 2776)
clauses.body:
A separate statute, Labor Code § 2776, states that § 2775's ABC test and the Dynamex holding do not apply to a bona fide business-to-business contracting relationship, as the statute defines it, if the contracting business demonstrates that a list of specific conditions is satisfied. Where that showing is made, the older Borello multi-factor test governs the classification question instead of the ABC test.

The statute lists twelve such conditions. Among them: the business service provider must be free from the contracting business's control and direction over how the work is performed, both under the contract and in fact; and the contract with the business service provider must be in writing and must specify the payment amount, including any applicable rate of pay, and the due date of payment for the services. This information sheet does not restate all twelve conditions here; see the gap note below for which ones are omitted.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the business-to-business exemption it creates and two of its specific conditions — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific relationship between a hiring entity and a worker does or does not qualify for this exemption. All three citations below are to the same statutory section, Labor Code § 2776, its introductory clause and subdivisions (a)(1) and (a)(3) — they are not independent of one another, and are disclosed here rather than presented as independent corroborating sources. This document quotes only 2 of the statute's 12 listed conditions in subdivision (a) — condition (1) (freedom from control) and condition (3) (written contract terms) — and does not restate conditions (2), (4), (5), (6), (7), (8), (9), (10), (11), or (12), which address matters including business licensing, a separate business location, the ability to contract with other businesses and advertise to the public, ownership of tools and equipment, rate-setting, control over hours and location of work, and a carve-out for work requiring a Contractors State License Board license; a reader relying on this exemption should review the statute's full text rather than this summary. This document also does not address subdivision (b) (governing an individual worker's status within a qualifying business-to-business relationship) or subdivision (c) (preserving rights under Labor Code § 2810.3) beyond noting their existence, and does not independently verify the Borello test's own content. This document does not determine that any specific relationship qualifies for this exemption and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Section 2775 and the holding in Dynamex do not apply to a bona fide business-to-business contracting relationship, as defined below, under the following conditions:

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2776(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The business service provider is free from the control and direction of the contracting business entity in connection with the performance of the work, both under the contract for the performance of the work and in fact.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2776(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The contract with the business service provider is in writing and specifies the payment amount, including any applicable rate of pay, for services to be performed, as well as the due date of payment for such services.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's "Eraser Law," Business and Professions Code sections 22580 through 22582 (the "Privacy Rights for California Minors in the Digital World Act") — a state statute requiring an operator of an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application directed to minors, or that has actual knowledge a minor is using it, to permit a minor who is a registered user to remove, or request and obtain removal of, content or information the minor themselves posted. It states facts about who the statute covers, the removal right's precise scope, the notice the statute requires, and the statute's own exceptions and safe harbor, as those may relate to {{businessName}}'s online service, product, or feature located at {{websiteURL}}. This information sheet does not itself determine whether {{businessName}}'s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application is "directed to minors" or whether {{businessName}} has "actual knowledge" a minor is using it, does not constitute the notice or instructions the statute requires an operator to provide, and does not tell {{businessName}} what to do about any specific removal request, design feature, or practice.

clauses.title: Coverage Trigger: "Directed to Minors" or "Actual Knowledge," and the Statute's Own Definitions
clauses.body: The Eraser Law's removal-right duties apply to an operator under either of two independent triggers, joined by "or": an operator whose Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application is directed to minors, or an operator that has actual knowledge that a minor is using its Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application — the duty is not limited to sites built for minors, and reaches an operator of a general-audience site once it has actual knowledge a minor is a user. The statute defines "directed to minors," for this chapter, itself: an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application, or a portion of one, created for the purpose of reaching an audience predominately comprised of minors and not intended for a more general adult audience. Separately, this chapter defines "minor" to mean a natural person under 18 years of age who resides in California, and defines "operator" to mean any person or entity that owns the Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application — expressly excluding a third party that merely operates, hosts, or manages it, or processes information, on the owner's behalf.
clauses.gap: The first citation below is to Business and Professions Code section 22581(a), the operative removal-right section; the remaining three citations are to section 22580(d), (e), and (f) — three subsections of the same statutory section as one another — they are not independent of one another. Section 22580 is a genuinely separate, independently numbered section from section 22581, so the first citation is independent of the other three. Section 22581 does not itself restate these definitions; this clause treats section 22580's definitions of "directed to minors," "minor," and "operator" as governing section 22581 because both sections appear in the same chapter (Chapter 22.1, sections 22580 through 22582) and section 22581 uses the identical defined terms without supplying its own definitions — that is an ordinary statutory-construction reading, not text quoted from section 22581 itself, and no case law was checked confirming that a court has applied section 22580's definitions to section 22581 specifically. On the statute's own text quoted below, the "directed to minors" definition is self-contained and does not cross-reference the federal Children's Online Privacy Protection Act or any other statute's definition — this is a real difference from California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, whose separate "likely to be accessed by children" coverage test (documented elsewhere in this corpus) does cross-reference COPPA as one of several indicators. This clause does not determine whether any specific Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application is in fact "directed to minors" or whether a specific operator in fact has "actual knowledge" a minor is using it — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make.

citations.cite: Eraser Law, dual coverage trigger: directed to minors, or actual knowledge a minor is a user
citations.quote: An operator of an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application directed to minors or an operator of an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application that has actual knowledge that a minor is using its Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application shall do all of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22580(e) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Eraser Law chapter, definition of "directed to minors" (self-contained, no COPPA cross-reference)
citations.quote: “Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application directed to minors” mean an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application, or a portion thereof, that is created for the purpose of reaching an audience that is predominately comprised of minors, and is not intended for a more general audience comprised of adults.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22580(d) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Eraser Law chapter, definition of "minor"
citations.quote: “Minor” means a natural person under 18 years of age who resides in this state.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22580(f) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Eraser Law chapter, definition of "operator"
citations.quote: “Operator” means any person or entity that owns an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application. It does not include any third party that operates, hosts, or manages, but does not own, an Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application on the owner’s behalf or processes information on the owner’s behalf.

clauses.title: The Core Removal Right Is Limited to Content the Minor Registered User Posted Themselves
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code section 22581(a)(1) requires a covered operator to permit a minor who is a registered user to remove, or, if the operator prefers instead, to request and obtain removal of, content or information posted on the operator's Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by that same user. The statute gives the operator a choice of mechanism — direct self-service removal, or a request-and-obtain-removal process — but either way the right runs only to content or information the registered minor user posted. This is not a general right for a minor, or anyone on the minor's behalf, to have all content about the minor taken down: section 22581(b)(2) expressly carves out of the removal duty any content or information that was stored on or posted to the operator's service by a third party other than the minor registered user, including content the minor posted that a third party then stored, republished, or reposted. "Posted," as the statute itself defines the term, means content or information that can be accessed by a user in addition to the minor who posted it, whether that other user is a registered user of the service or not.
clauses.gap: All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Business and Professions Code § 22581 — subdivision (a)(1) (the removal right itself), subdivision (b)(2) (the third-party-posted-content exception), and subdivision (f) (the definition of "posted") — they are not independent of one another. This clause does not address the notice and instructions the operator must separately provide about this right, covered in a companion clause, or the statute's remaining exceptions and its "deemed compliant" safe harbor for making content invisible rather than deleting it, also covered in a companion clause. This clause does not determine, for any specific piece of content, whether it was in fact posted by the minor registered user themselves or by a third party — that is a fact-specific determination this document does not make.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(a)(1) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Eraser Law, core removal right for a minor registered user's own posted content
citations.quote: Permit a minor who is a registered user of the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application to remove or, if the operator prefers, to request and obtain removal of, content or information posted on the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by the user.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(b)(2) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Eraser Law, exception for content posted by a third party rather than the minor registered user
citations.quote: The content or information was stored on or posted to the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by a third party other than the minor, who is a registered user, including any content or information posted by the registered user that was stored, republished, or reposted by the third party.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(f) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Eraser Law, definition of "posted"
citations.quote: “Posted” means content or information that can be accessed by a user in addition to the minor who posted the content or information, whether the user is a registered user or not, of the Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application where the content or information is posted.

clauses.title: Notice and Instructions the Operator Must Provide to a Minor Registered User
clauses.body: Beyond the removal right itself, Business and Professions Code section 22581(a) requires a covered operator to take three further, related actions. The operator must provide notice to a minor registered user that the minor may remove, or, if the operator prefers, request and obtain removal of, content or information the minor posted. The operator must also provide clear instructions to the minor registered user on how to do so. Finally, the operator must provide notice to the minor registered user that this removal does not ensure complete or comprehensive removal of the posted content or information — the statute itself requires the operator to disclose the limits of what removal will accomplish, rather than allowing the notice to imply the content will be permanently or completely gone.
clauses.gap: All three citations below are paragraphs of the same subdivision of the same statutory section, Business and Professions Code § 22581(a) — paragraphs (2), (3), and (4) — they are not independent of one another, and are also not independent of paragraph (1) (the removal right itself), quoted in a companion clause of this document. This clause does not address the statute's exceptions to the underlying removal duty or its "deemed compliant" safe harbor, both covered in a companion clause; a notice given under this clause's requirements can be accurate about the limits of removal precisely because those exceptions and the safe harbor exist. This clause does not specify the notice's required format, placement, or delivery method beyond what the statute's own text requires, and does not determine whether any specific operator's actual notice or instructions in fact satisfy this standard — that is a fact-specific determination this document does not make.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(a)(2) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Eraser Law, duty to notify a minor registered user of the removal right
citations.quote: Provide notice to a minor who is a registered user of the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application that the minor may remove or, if the operator prefers, request and obtain removal of, content or information posted on the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by the registered user.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(a)(3) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Eraser Law, duty to provide clear instructions on how to remove or request removal
citations.quote: Provide clear instructions to a minor who is a registered user of the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application on how the user may remove or, if the operator prefers, request and obtain the removal of content or information posted on the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(a)(4) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Eraser Law, duty to disclose that removal does not ensure complete or comprehensive removal
citations.quote: Provide notice to a minor who is a registered user of the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application that the removal described under paragraph (1) does not ensure complete or comprehensive removal of the content or information posted on the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by the registered user.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own Exceptions, and Its "Deemed Compliant" Safe Harbor: Invisibility, Not Guaranteed Deletion
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code section 22581(b) lists five circumstances in which an operator or a third party is not required to erase or otherwise eliminate, or to enable erasure or elimination of, content or information: where another provision of federal or state law requires the operator or third party to maintain it; where the content was stored or posted by a third party other than the minor registered user (including the minor's own content that a third party stored, republished, or reposted); where the operator anonymizes the content so the minor registered user cannot be individually identified; where the minor fails to follow the removal instructions the operator provided; and where the minor received compensation or other consideration for providing the content. Separately, section 22581(d) states what an operator must actually do to satisfy this section: an operator is deemed compliant if it renders the minor user's posted content or information no longer visible to other users of the service and to the public, even if the content or information remains on the operator's servers in some form — the statute requires inaccessibility to others, not guaranteed deletion from the operator's systems. The same subdivision further provides that an operator remains deemed compliant even if the content stays visible because a third party copied or reposted it, so long as the operator made the minor's original posting invisible.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section, Business and Professions Code § 22581 — subdivision (b) and subdivision (d) — they are not independent of one another, and neither is independent of the removal right, notice duties, or "posted"/third-party-content provisions of the same section quoted in companion clauses of this document. This clause does not quote section 22581(c), which states that this section is not to be construed to limit a law enforcement agency's authority to obtain content or information from an operator as otherwise authorized by law or court order, or section 22581(e), which, like the coverage-trigger provisions addressed in a companion clause, states that the section does not require an operator to collect age information about users — both were reviewed in the same fetched section but are not separately quoted here. This clause states the statute's own text defining what counts as compliance; it does not determine, for any specific operator's specific technical implementation, whether content has in fact been rendered no longer visible to other users and the public, or whether a specific circumstance in fact falls within one of the five listed exceptions — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Eraser Law, the statute's own five exceptions to the removal duty
citations.quote: An operator or a third party is not required to erase or otherwise eliminate, or to enable erasure or elimination of, content or information in any of the following circumstances: (1) Any other provision of federal or state law requires the operator or third party to maintain the content or information. (2) The content or information was stored on or posted to the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by a third party other than the minor, who is a registered user, including any content or information posted by the registered user that was stored, republished, or reposted by the third party. (3) The operator anonymizes the content or information posted by the minor who is a registered user, so that the minor who is a registered user cannot be individually identified. (4) The minor does not follow the instructions provided to the minor pursuant to paragraph (3) of subdivision (a) on how the registered user may request and obtain the removal of content or information posted on the operator’s Internet Web site, online service, online application, or mobile application by the registered user. (5) The minor has received compensation or other consideration for providing the content.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 22581(d) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: Eraser Law, "deemed compliant" safe harbor: invisibility to others, not guaranteed deletion
citations.quote: An operator shall be deemed compliant with this section if: (1) It renders the content or information posted by the minor user no longer visible to other users of the service and the public even if the content or information remains on the operator’s servers in some form. (2) Despite making the original posting by the minor user invisible, it remains visible because a third party has copied the posting or reposted the content or information posted by the minor.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's warehouse quota law, Labor Code §§ 2100–2112 (Part 8.6 of Division 2 of the Labor Code, added by Stats. 2021, Ch. 197 (AB 701), effective January 1, 2022), as it may relate to {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}}. It explains how the statute defines a covered "warehouse distribution center employer" and a "quota," the written quota disclosure the statute requires of a covered employer, the statute's limits on a quota that prevents compliance with meal or rest periods or bathroom use, and the statute's employee data-request and retaliation-presumption provisions. This document does not itself determine whether {{companyName}} meets the statute's coverage threshold, and it does not constitute or substitute for the written quota disclosure a covered employer is required to provide.

clauses.title: Coverage: Which Employers and Quotas the Statute Reaches
clauses.body: California's warehouse quota law defines a "quota" as a work standard under which an employee is assigned or required to perform at a specified productivity speed, to perform a quantified number of tasks, or to handle or produce a quantified amount of material, within a defined time period, where the employee may suffer an adverse employment action for failing to meet the standard. The statute applies only to an "employer" that employs or exercises control over the wages, hours, or working conditions of 100 or more employees at a single warehouse distribution center, or 1,000 or more employees at one or more warehouse distribution centers in the state — counting all employees of the employer's commonly controlled group toward that threshold. A "warehouse distribution center" is defined by specific North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) codes covering general warehousing and storage, and durable- and nondurable-goods merchant wholesalers, and electronic shopping and mail-order houses; the statute expressly excludes the NAICS code for farm product warehousing and storage. Whether {{companyName}}'s workplace meets this employee-count and NAICS-code threshold is a fact-specific determination this document does not make.
clauses.gap: The three citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2100) rather than independently authored sources — not independent of one another. This statute does not apply to every employer that uses a quota system; it applies only to a "warehouse distribution center employer" that both falls within one of the statute's four listed NAICS codes (and is not the excluded farm-product-warehousing code) and meets the 100-employee/single-center or 1,000-employee/statewide threshold, aggregating the employer's commonly controlled group as defined by Revenue and Taxation Code § 25105. The statute separately defines "employee" (§ 2100(d)) as a nonexempt employee who works at a warehouse distribution center — a definition this clause paraphrases but does not quote.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2100(f)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "employer"
citations.quote: “Employer” means a person who directly or indirectly, or through an agent or any other person, including through the services of a third-party employer, temporary service, or staffing agency or similar entity, employs or exercises control over the wages, hours, or working conditions of 100 or more employees at a single warehouse distribution center or 1,000 or more employees at one or more warehouse distribution centers in the state.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2100(h)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "quota"
citations.quote: “Quota” means a work standard under which an employee is assigned or required to perform at a specified productivity speed, or perform a quantified number of tasks, or to handle or produce a quantified amount of material, within a defined time period and under which the employee may suffer an adverse employment action if they fail to complete the performance standard.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2100(i)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "warehouse distribution center"
citations.quote: “Warehouse distribution center” means an establishment as defined by any of the following North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) Codes, however that establishment is denominated: (A) 493110 for General Warehousing and Storage. (B) 423 for Merchant Wholesalers, Durable Goods. (C) 424 for Merchant Wholesalers, Nondurable Goods. (D) 454110 for Electronic Shopping and Mail-Order Houses.

clauses.title: The Written Quota Disclosure Requirement
clauses.body: California law requires a covered warehouse distribution center employer to provide each employee, upon hire or within 30 days of the statute's effective date, a written description of each quota to which the employee is subject. That written description must include the quantified number of tasks to be performed, or materials to be produced or handled, within the defined time period, and any potential adverse employment action that could result from failing to meet the quota.
clauses.gap: This disclosure requirement applies only to an employer that meets the "warehouse distribution center employer" threshold described elsewhere in this document; the statute does not specify a particular form or format for the written description beyond requiring these three categories of content. This clause does not itself constitute or satisfy that written disclosure for any quota the employer applies to the employee.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2101
citations.cite: California Labor Code, the written quota disclosure requirement
citations.quote: Each employer shall provide to each employee, upon hire, or within 30 days of the effective date of this part, a written description of each quota to which the employee is subject, including the quantified number of tasks to be performed or materials to be produced or handled, within the defined time period, and any potential adverse employment action that could result from failure to meet the quota.

clauses.title: Limits: A Quota May Not Prevent Meal/Rest Compliance or Bathroom Use
clauses.body: California law prohibits requiring an employee to meet a quota that prevents compliance with meal or rest periods, use of bathroom facilities — including reasonable travel time to and from bathroom facilities — or occupational health and safety laws in the Labor Code or Division of Occupational Safety and Health standards. An employer may not take adverse employment action against an employee for failing to meet a quota that does not allow the employee to comply with meal and rest periods or those occupational health and safety laws, or for failing to meet a quota that was not disclosed to the employee as required by § 2101. Separately, time an employee spends complying with occupational health and safety laws counts as time on task and productive time for purposes of any quota or monitoring system, though meal and rest breaks themselves are not counted as productive time unless the employee is required to remain on call.
clauses.gap: This part of the statute cross-references, rather than restates, California's separate meal- and rest-period requirements and occupational health and safety standards; it does not itself define what makes a particular meal or rest period or bathroom break compliant. The § 2103 citation below addresses a separately numbered section of this same statutory part and is independent of the § 2102 citation — not two subsections of one section.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2102
citations.cite: California Labor Code, quota limits on meal/rest periods and bathroom use
citations.quote: An employee shall not be required to meet a quota that prevents compliance with meal or rest periods, use of bathroom facilities, including reasonable travel time to and from bathroom facilities, or occupational health and safety laws in the Labor Code or division standards. An employer shall not take adverse employment action against an employee for failure to meet a quota that does not allow a worker to comply with meal and rest periods, or occupational health and safety laws in the Labor Code or division standards, or for failure to meet a quota that has not been disclosed to the employee pursuant to Section 2101.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2103(b)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, meal/rest breaks not counted as productive time
citations.quote: meal and rest breaks are not considered productive time unless the employee is required to remain on call.

clauses.title: Employee's Right to Request Quota and Personal Work Speed Data
clauses.body: If a current or former employee believes that meeting a quota caused a violation of the employee's right to a meal or rest period, or required the employee to violate an occupational health and safety law in the Labor Code or a Division of Occupational Safety and Health standard, California law gives the employee the right to request — and requires the employer to provide — a written description of each quota to which the employee is subject and a copy of the most recent 90 days of the employee's own personal work speed data. A former employee who makes this request receives 90 days of quota and work speed data measured back from the employee's date of separation, and is limited to one such request. An employer that receives a written or oral request under this right must comply as soon as practicable, and no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request. The statute does not require an employer to use quotas or monitor work speed data in the first place, and an employer that does not monitor this data has no obligation to produce it.
clauses.gap: All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2104) rather than independently authored sources — not independent of one another. This is a conditional right, not a general right to request quota data at any time: it is triggered specifically by the employee's belief that meeting a quota caused a meal- or rest-period violation or required violating an occupational health and safety law, and the statute's own text does not describe a broader, unconditional right to the same information.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2104(a)(1)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, the employee data request right
citations.quote: If a current or former employee believes that meeting a quota caused a violation of their right to a meal or rest period or required them to violate any occupational health and safety laws in the Labor Code or division standards, they have the right to request, and the employer shall provide, a written description of each quota to which the employee is subject and a copy of the most recent 90 days of the employee’s own personal work speed data.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2104(b)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, the employer's 21-day response deadline
citations.quote: An employer that receives a written or oral request for information pursuant to subdivision (a) shall comply with the request as soon as practicable, but no later than 21 calendar days from the date of the request.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2104(c)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, no obligation to monitor or use quotas
citations.quote: Nothing in this section requires an employer to use quotas or monitor work speed data. An employer that does not monitor this data has no obligation to provide it.

clauses.title: The Rebuttable Presumption of Retaliation
clauses.body: California law creates a rebuttable presumption of unlawful retaliation if an employer in any manner discriminates, retaliates, or takes any adverse action against an employee within 90 days of the employee initiating the employee's first request in a calendar year for quota or personal work speed data information, or of the employee making a complaint related to a quota that alleges a violation of §§ 2101 through 2104 to the Labor Commissioner, the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, another local or state governmental agency, or the employer itself.
clauses.gap: This is a rebuttable presumption, not a conclusive one — the statute's own text does not itself define what evidence rebuts it. The presumption applies only within the 90-day window described above and only to the two triggering acts identified in § 2105(a) and § 2105(b) (a first-in-calendar-year information request, or a complaint alleging a violation of §§ 2101–2104); adverse action taken outside that window, or unconnected to those triggering acts, is not addressed by this presumption.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 2105
citations.cite: California Labor Code, the retaliation presumption
citations.quote: there shall be a rebuttable presumption of unlawful retaliation if an employer in any manner discriminates, retaliates, or takes any adverse action against any employee within 90 days of the employee doing either of the following:
