clauses.title: Purpose of This Notice
clauses.body: This notice describes what the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Viking River Cruises, Inc. v. Moriana and the California Supreme Court's decision in Adolph v. Uber Technologies, Inc. say about whether an employment arbitration agreement can compel arbitration of an individual claim under California's Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA) while the employee pursues the representative portion of that claim in court. It is provided by {{companyName}} to {{employeeName}} for informational purposes and does not itself waive, modify, expand, or create any right, agreement, or obligation between {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}.

clauses.title: Viking River Cruises: The FAA Preempts California's Rule Against Splitting PAGA Claims
clauses.body: In Iskanian v. CLS Transportation Los Angeles, LLC, the California Supreme Court held that a PAGA action could not be divided by agreement into an arbitrable “individual” claim (based on Labor Code violations the plaintiff personally sustained) and a non-arbitrable “representative” claim (based on violations sustained by other employees). In Viking River Cruises, Inc. v. Moriana, the U.S. Supreme Court held that the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) preempts that anti-splitting rule, meaning an employer can rely on an arbitration agreement's severability clause to compel arbitration of the individual portion of a PAGA claim even though Iskanian would otherwise have kept the whole action in court.
clauses.gap: This is a single U.S. Supreme Court opinion (596 U.S. 639 (2022)), read directly from the official slip opinion published at supremecourt.gov on 2026-09-04. CourtListener's API was not used to independently cross-check this opinion because this research exhausted CourtListener's daily rate limit (125 requests/day) before reaching this case; the official Supreme Court slip opinion was used as the primary source instead. The slip opinion's line breaks required dehyphenating words split across lines (e.g., “in-\nsofar” to “insofar”) and removing running page headers (“Cite as: 596 U.S. ____ (2022)” / “Opinion of the Court”) that the PDF-to-text extraction inserted mid-sentence; genuine compound hyphens (e.g., “non-individual”) were preserved. Viking River left a different part of Iskanian intact: its separate rule that a predispute agreement cannot categorically waive the right to bring a PAGA claim at all remains valid and is not addressed in this clause. The next clause addresses a further, more consequential part of the same opinion — what the Court said should happen to the non-individual claims once the individual claim is sent to arbitration — which is the part of Viking River that a later California Supreme Court decision treats differently.

citations.case: Viking River Cruises, Inc. v. Moriana
citations.quote: We hold that the FAA preempts the rule of Iskanian insofar as it precludes division of PAGA actions into individual and non-individual claims through an agreement to arbitrate.

clauses.title: What Viking River Itself Said Should Happen to the Non-Individual Claims
clauses.body: Having held that Viking could compel arbitration of Moriana's individual PAGA claim, the Court in Viking River Cruises went on to address what should happen to her remaining, non-individual claims. The Court reasoned that PAGA's own standing requirement lets a plaintiff maintain non-individual claims in an action only by also maintaining an individual claim in that same action, so that once the individual claim is pared away into a separate arbitration proceeding, the plaintiff stands in no different position than an uninvolved member of the public. On that reasoning, the Court concluded that the plaintiff loses statutory standing to continue litigating the non-individual claims in court, and that the correct course is to dismiss them.
clauses.gap: All three citations below are drawn from the same U.S. Supreme Court opinion cited in the clause above (596 U.S. 639 (2022)) — not independent sources of one another — and are three separate, non-adjacent passages of that opinion (intervening case-citation text, e.g. a cross-reference to Cal. Lab. Code §§2699(a), (c) and a citation to Kim v. Reins International California, Inc., falls between them in the original); each is quoted here as its own exact, contiguous excerpt rather than joined with an ellipsis, consistent with this corpus's practice of never combining non-adjacent text into a single quote. The sourcing and text-extraction caveats disclosed in the clause above apply here as well. This part of Viking River's reasoning was the Court's own interpretation of what a California statute (PAGA) requires — a question of state law on which the U.S. Supreme Court does not have the final word. As the next clause describes, the California Supreme Court read PAGA's standing requirement differently just over a year later in Adolph v. Uber Technologies; this exact passage is the part of Viking River whose practical effect no longer reflects the operative rule on PAGA standing.

citations.case: Viking River Cruises, Inc. v. Moriana
citations.quote: But as we see it, PAGA provides no mechanism to enable a court to adjudicate nonindividual PAGA claims once an individual claim has been committed to a separate proceeding. Under PAGA’s standing requirement, a plaintiff can maintain non-individual PAGA claims in an action only by virtue of also maintaining an individual claim in that action.

citations.case: Viking River Cruises, Inc. v. Moriana
citations.quote: When an employee’s own dispute is pared away from a PAGA action, the employee is no different from a member of the general public, and PAGA does not allow such persons to maintain suit.

citations.case: Viking River Cruises, Inc. v. Moriana
citations.quote: As a result, Moriana lacks statutory standing to continue to maintain her non-individual claims in court, and the correct course is to dismiss her remaining claims.

clauses.title: Adolph v. Uber: Compelled Arbitration of the Individual Claim Doesn't End Standing
clauses.body: In Adolph v. Uber Technologies, Inc., the California Supreme Court took up the same standing question Viking River Cruises had addressed and reached the opposite conclusion as a matter of California law. The court held that where a plaintiff has brought a PAGA action made up of both an individual claim and non-individual claims, an order compelling arbitration of the individual claim does not strip the plaintiff of standing to litigate the non-individual claims in court, so long as the plaintiff remains an “aggrieved employee.” The court reasoned that arbitrating the individual claim doesn't nullify the fact of the underlying violation or extinguish the plaintiff's status as an aggrieved employee.
clauses.gap: All three citations below are drawn from the same California Supreme Court opinion (14 Cal.5th 1104 (2023)), so they are not independent of one another as sources; the first two are the opinion's summary holding (with substantial intervening text about the statutory 'aggrieved employee' standard omitted between them, so each is quoted as its own exact contiguous excerpt rather than joined with an ellipsis), and the third is a separate passage from the analysis section. Read directly from the official slip opinion published at courts.ca.gov on 2026-09-04; as with Viking River, CourtListener's API was unavailable due to an exhausted daily rate limit, so the official court website was used as the primary source instead, and the same dehyphenation/header-removal text-cleanup caveats described in the Viking River preemption clause's gap apply here. Adolph also explains that a trial court has discretion to stay the non-individual claims in court pending the outcome of the arbitration under Code of Civil Procedure section 1281.4, and that if the arbitrator determines the plaintiff is not in fact an aggrieved employee, and a court confirms that determination, the plaintiff could still lose the ability to prosecute the non-individual claims for lack of standing — so this holding does not make PAGA standing invulnerable to what happens in the arbitration, only immune to being cut off automatically by the mere fact that the individual claim was sent to arbitration.

citations.case: Adolph v. Uber Technologies, Inc.
citations.quote: We hold that the answer is yes.

citations.case: Adolph v. Uber Technologies, Inc.
citations.quote: Where a plaintiff has brought a PAGA action comprising individual and non-individual claims, an order compelling arbitration of the individual claims does not strip the plaintiff of standing as an aggrieved employee to litigate claims on behalf of other employees under PAGA.

citations.case: Adolph v. Uber Technologies, Inc.
citations.quote: Standing under PAGA is not affected by enforcement of an agreement to adjudicate a plaintiff’s individual claim in another forum. Arbitrating a PAGA plaintiff’s individual claim does not nullify the fact of the violation or extinguish the plaintiff’s status as an aggrieved employee

clauses.title: The Combined Current Picture: Arbitrate the Individual Claim, Litigate the Rest
clauses.body: Taken together, Viking River Cruises and Adolph currently mean that an employer with an FAA-covered arbitration agreement can rely on that agreement to compel arbitration of the individual portion of an employee's PAGA claim — the portion based on Labor Code violations the employee personally sustained — but compelling that arbitration does not, by itself, end the employee's standing to pursue the non-individual, representative portion of the PAGA claim in court on behalf of other current or former employees, so long as the employee remains an aggrieved employee.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are independent of one another: one is the U.S. Supreme Court's holding in Viking River Cruises, 596 U.S. 639 (2022), on FAA preemption of the anti-splitting rule; the other is the California Supreme Court's holding in Adolph v. Uber Technologies, 14 Cal.5th 1104 (2023), on standing. Separately, California's 2024 PAGA reform (AB 2288 and SB 92, as further amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67 (AB 1170)) tightened the general statutory definition of “aggrieved employee” to require personally suffering each violation alleged — a change already addressed in this project's PAGA Pre-Suit Notice Letter document (see its paga_aggrieved_employee_standing clause) rather than restated here. This research did not find, and does not represent having found, any 2024 reform provision, or any U.S. Supreme Court or California Supreme Court decision issued after Adolph, that revisits the specific arbitration-splitting question addressed in this document. Whether lower courts have applied Adolph consistently in every context, and whether Adolph's discretionary-stay approach (described in the clause above) has itself generated further litigation since 2023, was not independently reviewed for this document — that is disclosed here as a gap rather than represented as settled.

citations.case: Viking River Cruises, Inc. v. Moriana
citations.quote: Based on this clause, Viking was entitled to enforce the agreement insofar as it mandated arbitration of Moriana’s individual PAGA claim.

citations.case: Adolph v. Uber Technologies, Inc.
citations.quote: Under the statute, a plaintiff who files a PAGA action with individual and non-individual claims does not lose standing to litigate the non-individual claims in court simply because the individual claims have been ordered to arbitration.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Receipt
UCC-1 Financing Statement — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body:
UCC-1 FINANCING STATEMENT — INFORMATION AND FILING WORKSHEET
(California Commercial Code Division 9, Secured Transactions)

This worksheet relates to a proposed or existing financing statement naming {{debtorName}} as debtor and {{securedPartyName}} as secured party, covering the following collateral: {{collateralDescription}}.

A UCC-1 financing statement is the document California Commercial Code Division 9 authorizes a secured party to file with the California Secretary of State to give public notice of a security interest in a debtor's personal property. Filing a financing statement is the step that perfects a security interest (establishes its priority against most third parties) — it is a separate legal event from the security interest attaching (becoming enforceable between the debtor and the secured party in the first place), and separate from whichever set of facts caused attachment to occur. This worksheet does not determine whether a security interest described here has attached, whether it is properly perfected, whether this particular collateral description is legally sufficient, or what priority this security interest holds against any other creditor's claim to the same collateral — those are determinations that depend on the full facts of a transaction and, where disputed, on a court's application of Division 9 to those facts.

clauses.title: What a Financing Statement Must Contain to Be Sufficient
clauses.body: California law states that a financing statement is sufficient only if it satisfies three conditions: it provides the name of the debtor, it provides the name of the secured party (or a representative of the secured party), and it indicates the collateral covered by the financing statement. Additional content requirements apply only to specific categories of collateral not addressed by this worksheet (as-extracted collateral, timber to be cut, or a fixture filing). Separately, the statute confirms that a financing statement may be filed before a security agreement is made or a security interest otherwise attaches — filing is not conditioned on attachment having already occurred.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own content requirements for a sufficient financing statement — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular debtor, collateral, or filing. The two quotations below are both drawn from the same statutory section (§ 9502), specifically its subdivision (a) and subdivision (d): they are not independent of one another. This clause does not state whether a specific financing statement's debtor name, secured-party name, or collateral description actually satisfies these requirements on the facts of any particular transaction — for example, whether a given collateral description is sufficiently specific, or whether a given debtor name matches the standard the statute or the Secretary of State applies to that type of debtor — those questions require applying subsequent sections of Division 9 (and Secretary of State filing rules) that this worksheet does not independently verify or cover.

citations.case: California Commercial Code § 9502(a) — sufficiency of a financing statement
citations.cite: Cal. Com. Code § 9502(a)
citations.quote: a financing statement is sufficient only if it satisfies all of the following conditions: (1) It provides the name of the debtor. (2) It provides the name of the secured party or a representative of the secured party. (3) It indicates the collateral covered by the financing statement.

citations.case: California Commercial Code § 9502(d) — a financing statement may be filed before attachment
citations.cite: Cal. Com. Code § 9502(d)
citations.quote: A financing statement may be filed before a security agreement is made or a security interest otherwise attaches.

clauses.title: Attachment and Perfection Are Two Separate Legal Events
clauses.body: California's secured transactions statute treats attachment and perfection as two distinct legal events, each governed by its own statutory chapter. Attachment is the point at which a security interest becomes enforceable against the debtor with respect to the collateral (subject to the parties' ability to expressly postpone that time by agreement); a separate chapter of the statute sets out the further conditions — including that value has been given and the debtor has rights in the collateral — that must be satisfied before a security interest is enforceable at all. Perfection is a different, later-focused concept: a security interest is perfected once it has attached and all of the applicable statutory requirements for perfection (which include filing a financing statement, among other methods addressed elsewhere in the statute) have been satisfied. A security interest cannot be perfected before it has attached — perfection presupposes attachment — but attachment alone does not perfect a security interest against third parties; that additional step is what a properly filed financing statement is generally for.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, distinct two-step attachment/perfection structure in California's own text — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular transaction. The two citations below are from separate, independently numbered statutory sections (§ 9203 and § 9308), not subsections of the same section. This clause states only the general attachment and perfection rules quoted; it does not restate the full list of alternative conditions under § 9203(b)(3) that can satisfy the 'value given plus rights in collateral' requirement (only the signed-security-agreement path is described above), does not address the specific perfection methods listed in §§ 9310 through 9316 that § 9308(a) cross-references, and does not determine whether attachment or perfection has actually occurred for any specific security interest.

citations.case: California Commercial Code § 9203(a) — when a security interest attaches
citations.cite: Cal. Com. Code § 9203(a)
citations.quote: A security interest attaches to collateral when it becomes enforceable against the debtor with respect to the collateral, unless an agreement expressly postpones the time of attachment.

citations.case: California Commercial Code § 9308(a) — when a security interest is perfected
citations.cite: Cal. Com. Code § 9308(a)
citations.quote: a security interest is perfected if it has attached and all of the applicable requirements for perfection in Sections 9310 to 9316, inclusive, have been satisfied.

clauses.title: Who Must Authorize the Filing of a Financing Statement
clauses.body: California law generally allows a person to file an initial financing statement (or an amendment adding collateral or adding a debtor) only if the debtor authorizes the filing in a signed record, or authorizes it in one of two specific ways the statute itself treats as authorization. One of those statutory paths is directly relevant here: by signing (or otherwise becoming bound as debtor by) a security agreement, a debtor automatically authorizes the filing of an initial financing statement — and later amendments — covering the collateral described in that security agreement. A debtor's signed security agreement therefore does double duty under this statute: it is also the debtor's authorization for the secured party to file a financing statement describing that same collateral, without a further, separate signed authorization document.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own filing-authorization rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular filing. The two quotations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 9509) — specifically subdivisions (a) and (b) — and are not independent of one another. This clause describes only the security-agreement path to authorization; it does not restate the alternative agricultural-lien path in § 9509(a)(2), the after-acquired-collateral authorization in § 9509(c), or the separate rules in § 9509(d)-(e) governing who may authorize filing amendments other than those adding collateral or a debtor (including termination statements) — none of which this worksheet addresses. It also does not determine whether any specific debtor named in this worksheet has, in fact, signed a security agreement or otherwise become bound as debtor.

citations.case: California Commercial Code § 9509(a) — debtor authorization required to file
citations.cite: Cal. Com. Code § 9509(a)
citations.quote: A person may file an initial financing statement, an amendment that adds collateral covered by a financing statement, or an amendment that adds a debtor to a financing statement only if either of the following conditions is satisfied: (1) The debtor authorizes the filing in a signed record or pursuant to subdivision (b) or (c).

citations.case: California Commercial Code § 9509(b) — signing a security agreement authorizes the filing
citations.cite: Cal. Com. Code § 9509(b)
citations.quote: By signing or becoming bound as debtor by a security agreement, a debtor or new debtor authorizes the filing of an initial financing statement, and an amendment, covering both of the following: (1) The collateral described in the security agreement.

clauses.title: Duration of a Financing Statement, and Lapse
clauses.body: California law generally makes a filed financing statement effective for a period of five years after the date of filing (a longer, 30-year period applies only to a financing statement filed in connection with a public finance transaction or a manufactured home transaction, which this worksheet does not address). If that period expires without a timely continuation statement, the financing statement lapses: it ceases to be effective, and any security interest that was perfected by that financing statement becomes unperfected (unless perfected by some other method) — and, as against a purchaser of the collateral for value, is treated as if it had never been perfected at all. A continuation statement can prevent lapse, but only if filed within a narrow statutory window: no earlier than six months before the five-year period (or the 30-year period, if applicable) expires.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own duration and lapse rules for a financing statement — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular filing's effective period. The three quotations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (§ 9515) — specifically subdivisions (a), (c), and (d) — and are not independent of one another. This clause does not restate the separate 30-year rule's own text (subdivision (b)), the rule for a continuation statement's own effect once timely filed (subdivision (e)), or the special rules for a transmitting utility's financing statement or a mortgage recorded as a fixture filing (subdivisions (f)-(g)); none of those are addressed here. It does not determine whether any specific financing statement referenced in this worksheet has lapsed or been timely continued.

citations.case: California Commercial Code § 9515(a) — five-year effective period
citations.cite: Cal. Com. Code § 9515(a)
citations.quote: a filed financing statement is effective for a period of five years after the date of filing.

citations.case: California Commercial Code § 9515(c) — effect of lapse
citations.cite: Cal. Com. Code § 9515(c)
citations.quote: The effectiveness of a filed financing statement lapses on the expiration of the period of its effectiveness unless before the lapse a continuation statement is filed pursuant to subdivision (d). Upon lapse, a financing statement ceases to be effective and any security interest or agricultural lien that was perfected by the financing statement becomes unperfected, unless the security interest is perfected otherwise.

citations.case: California Commercial Code § 9515(d) — window to file a continuation statement
citations.cite: Cal. Com. Code § 9515(d)
citations.quote: A continuation statement may be filed only within six months before the expiration of the five-year period specified in subdivision (a) or the 30-year period specified in subdivision (b), whichever is applicable.

clauses.title: The Basic Priority Rule a Financing Statement Filing Accomplishes
clauses.body: California law's general priority rule for conflicting security interests in the same collateral is a first-in-time rule, but the statute states it with specific mechanics rather than a simple 'first in time' generality: conflicting perfected security interests rank according to priority in time of filing or perfection, and that priority dates from the earlier of when a filing covering the collateral is first made or when the security interest is first perfected — provided there is no later gap when the collateral was covered by neither a filing nor a perfected interest. Separate from that ranking-among-perfected-interests rule, the statute also states directly that a perfected security interest has priority over a conflicting unperfected security interest. Both rules are expressly made subject to exceptions stated elsewhere in the same statutory section and cross-referenced sections — this is not an unqualified 'first to file always wins' rule.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own default priority rule and its own express first-in-time mechanics — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular priority dispute. Both quotations below are drawn from the same statutory subdivision, § 9322(a) — specifically its paragraphs (1) and (2) — and are not independent of one another. This clause does not restate paragraph (3) (the rule for two unperfected, conflicting interests), the further mechanics in subdivisions (b) through (g) (including special rules for proceeds, supporting obligations, certain collateral types perfected by a method other than filing, and specific numbered-section exceptions such as purchase-money priority under other sections this statute cross-references), or the agricultural-lien priority exception in subdivision (g). It does not determine the actual priority of any specific security interest described in this worksheet.

citations.case: California Commercial Code § 9322(a)(1) — priority among perfected interests dates from first filing or perfection
citations.cite: Cal. Com. Code § 9322(a)(1)
citations.quote: priority among conflicting security interests and agricultural liens in the same collateral is determined according to the following rules: (1) Conflicting perfected security interests and agricultural liens rank according to priority in time of filing or perfection. Priority dates from the earlier of the time a filing covering the collateral is first made or the security interest or agricultural lien is first perfected, if there is no period thereafter when there is neither filing nor perfection.

citations.case: California Commercial Code § 9322(a)(2) — a perfected interest has priority over an unperfected one
citations.cite: Cal. Com. Code § 9322(a)(2)
citations.quote: A perfected security interest or agricultural lien has priority over a conflicting unperfected security interest or agricultural lien.

clauses.title: UCC-1 Financing Statement — Filing Worksheet and Acknowledgment
Recitals — Statutory Merger of Constituent Corporations
clauses.body: {{constituentCorporationNames}} (each a constituent corporation) intend to merge into a single corporation under California's General Corporation Law, Chapter 11 (Merger), Cal. Corp. Code §§ 1100-1113. Upon the merger becoming effective, {{survivingCorporationName}} will be the surviving corporation, and the separate existence of each other constituent corporation will cease. This document records the agreement of merger between the constituent corporations and the corporate approvals obtained for it. It addresses the statutory merger procedure itself — a separate matter from whatever merger-approval, first-refusal, or transfer-restriction provisions may already appear in a constituent corporation's own bylaws, shareholder agreements, or buy-sell agreement, which govern only how that corporation's own internal decision to merge is made, not the statutory mechanics of the merger itself.

clauses.title: Required Contents of the Agreement of Merger
clauses.body: California law requires a merger of two or more corporations to proceed by a written agreement of merger, and it specifies what that agreement must contain. The agreement must state the terms and conditions of the merger; the name and place of incorporation of each constituent corporation and which of them is the surviving corporation; and the manner of converting the shares of each constituent corporation into shares or other securities of the surviving corporation — or, where shares are not converted solely into shares or securities of the surviving corporation, the cash, rights, securities, or other property the shareholders are instead to receive, whether in addition to or in lieu of surviving-corporation shares, or a statement that the shares are simply canceled without consideration. The statute also authorizes the agreement to include other terms and provisions the parties want, subject to a separate statutory equal-treatment rule for shares of the same class.
clauses.gap: This document verifies only the general, multi-corporation merger procedure of Chapter 11 (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 1100-1113) for corporations that are themselves the constituent parties. It does not address the separate short-form procedure for a parent corporation merging with a subsidiary it wholly or 90-percent owns, mergers where a foreign corporation or an "other business entity" (e.g., an LLC) is a constituent party, or mergers involving a social purpose corporation — each of which Chapter 11 itself carves out to separate provisions not independently verified here. The three citations below are all to the same statutory section, Cal. Corp. Code § 1101(a) (its introductory sentence and paragraphs (1), (3), and (4)), so they are not independent of one another — they are pieces of one section's list of required contents, not separate corroborating sources. This document also does not restate the equal-treatment rule for shares of the same class and series, which the statute states separately in the remainder of the same subdivision. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific corporation's merger, and not a claim about what terms any specific merger agreement should or must contain beyond this minimum required content. This document is informational only; it does not itself merge any corporations and does not draft or approve a specific agreement of merger.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1101(a)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, introductory requirement that the agreement of merger state all of the required terms
citations.quote: The agreement shall state all of the following: (1) The terms and conditions of the merger.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1101(a)(3)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, agreement of merger must identify each constituent corporation and the surviving corporation
citations.quote: (3) The name and place of incorporation of each constituent corporation and which of the constituent corporations is the surviving corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1101(a)(4)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, agreement of merger must state the manner of converting shares
citations.quote: (4) The manner of converting the shares of each of the constituent corporations into shares or other securities of the surviving corporation and, if any shares of any of the constituent corporations are not to be converted solely into shares or other securities of the surviving corporation, the cash, rights, securities, or other property which the holders of those shares are to receive in exchange for the shares, which cash, rights, securities, or other property may be in addition to or in lieu of shares or other securities of the surviving corporation, or that the shares are canceled without consideration.

clauses.title: Board and Shareholder Approval of the Merger
clauses.body: A merger requires two layers of approval from each constituent corporation. First, the board of each corporation that desires to merge must approve the agreement of merger. Second, unless a narrower statutory exception applies, the principal terms of the merger must separately be approved by "the outstanding shares" of each class of each corporation whose board approval is required. Under California's own statutory definition of that phrase, approval by the outstanding shares means the affirmative vote of a majority of the outstanding shares entitled to vote, and it also includes the affirmative vote of a majority of the outstanding shares of each class or series separately entitled to vote as a class on the matter, plus any greater proportion — up to and including all shares of a class — that the corporation's own articles of incorporation require.
clauses.gap: This states the general two-layer approval requirement; it does not catalog every statutory exception and variation. In particular, this document does not address: the narrower board-only approval available for certain parent-subsidiary short-form mergers under a separate provision of this chapter; the exception (Cal. Corp. Code § 1201(b)) that removes the outstanding-shares-approval requirement for a corporation whose own shareholders will hold more than five-sixths of the resulting voting power; the heightened two-thirds vote that applies to a close corporation's shareholders in some circumstances; or the rule that all shareholders of a class must approve, unless given dissenters' rights, if the merger would make them personally liable for a constituent corporation's obligations. That dissenters'-rights safeguard is itself the subject of a separate document in this collection (California's statutory dissenters'/appraisal rights procedure), which this document does not restate. The three citations below are to three different, independently numbered statutory provisions — Cal. Corp. Code § 1101(a) (board approval), § 1201(a) (the outstanding-shares approval requirement for a merger reorganization), and § 152 (the statutory definition of "approved by the outstanding shares") — so they are independent sources, not subsections of a single section. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific corporation's merger, and not a claim about what approval any specific merger actually requires, which depends on the specific corporations, their articles of incorporation, and which of the statutory exceptions, if any, apply. This document is informational only and does not itself approve any merger.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1101(a)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, board approval of the agreement of merger
citations.quote: The board of each corporation that desires to merge shall approve an agreement of merger.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1201(a)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, shareholder approval of the principal terms of a merger reorganization
citations.quote: The principal terms of a reorganization shall be approved by the outstanding shares (Section 152) of each class of each corporation the approval of whose board is required under Section 1200

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 152
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, statutory definition of "approved by the outstanding shares"
citations.quote: Such approval shall include the affirmative vote of a majority of the outstanding shares of each class or series entitled, by any provision of the articles or of this division, to vote as a class or series on the subject matter being voted upon and shall also include the affirmative vote of such greater proportion (including all) of the outstanding shares of any class or series if such greater proportion is required by the articles or this division.

clauses.title: Effect of Merger: Succession to Rights, Property, and Liabilities
clauses.body: Once a merger under this chapter is effective, the statute specifies exactly what happens to each constituent corporation. The separate existence of each disappearing corporation ceases, and the surviving corporation succeeds — without any separate transfer being needed — to all of the rights and property of each disappearing corporation. At the same time, the surviving corporation becomes subject to all of the debts and liabilities of each disappearing corporation, in the same manner as if the surviving corporation had itself incurred those debts and liabilities. In other words, a merger does not let the surviving corporation pick up a disappearing corporation's assets while leaving its liabilities behind.
clauses.gap: This states the core successor-liability rule of Cal. Corp. Code § 1107(a) precisely as written; it does not overclaim beyond it. This document does not address the related provisions elsewhere in the same section — preservation of creditors' rights and liens on a disappearing corporation's property, continuation of pending litigation against the surviving corporation, or the separate local-agency-license-transfer and tax-return-assumption rules found in the rest of section 1107 and in section 1107.5 — which were not independently quoted here. This is a single statutory section (Cal. Corp. Code § 1107(a)); no additional independent source was sought for this specific rule. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific merger, and not a claim about the actual debts, liabilities, or property of any specific corporation. This document is informational only and does not itself effect any merger or transfer any right, property, debt, or liability.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1107(a)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, effect of merger: cessation of the disappearing corporation and succession to rights, property, and liabilities
citations.quote: Upon merger pursuant to this chapter the separate existence of the disappearing corporations ceases and the surviving corporation shall succeed, without other transfer, to all the rights and property of each of the disappearing corporations and shall be subject to all the debts and liabilities of each in the same manner as if the surviving corporation had itself incurred them.

clauses.title: Filing the Agreement of Merger and Its Effective Date
clauses.body: After the board and any required shareholder approval, the surviving corporation must file a copy of the agreement of merger with the California Secretary of State, along with an officers' certificate from each constituent corporation. That officers' certificate must state the total number of outstanding shares of each class entitled to vote on the merger and either that the required shareholder vote was obtained for the class or classes entitled to vote, or that the merger was instead entitled to be, and was, approved by the board alone under the statute's narrower board-only exception. The merger, and any amendment to the surviving corporation's articles set out in the agreement, becomes effective upon that filing — except that any instrument filed with the Secretary of State with respect to a corporation, including an agreement of merger, may instead specify a delayed effective date of up to 90 days after its filing date, and if no timely revocation certificate is filed to stop it, the instrument becomes effective on that later, specified date rather than on the filing date itself.
clauses.gap: The two citations to Cal. Corp. Code § 1103 (the filing and officers'-certificate requirement, and the statement that the merger becomes effective "thereupon" subject to Section 110(c)) are both drawn from the same statutory section and so are not independent of one another. The citation to Cal. Corp. Code § 110(c) is to a separate, independently numbered section (California's general instrument-filing statute, not specific to mergers) and is an independent source. This document does not address the separate filing mechanics that apply when a foreign corporation is a constituent party (Cal. Corp. Code § 1108, cross-referenced in section 1103 itself) or the short-form parent-subsidiary certificate-of-ownership procedure, neither of which was independently verified here. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific merger's filing, and not a substitute for the Secretary of State's own current official forms, fees, and filing instructions. This document is informational only and does not itself file anything with the California Secretary of State.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1103
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, filing the agreement of merger with an officers' certificate from each constituent corporation
citations.quote: After approval of a merger by the board and any approval of the outstanding shares (Section 152) required by Chapter 12 (commencing with Section 1200), the surviving corporation shall file a copy of the agreement of merger with an officers' certificate of each constituent corporation attached stating the total number of outstanding shares of each class entitled to vote on the merger, that the principal terms of the agreement in the form attached were approved by that corporation by a vote of a number of shares of each class which equaled or exceeded the vote required, specifying each class entitled to vote and the percentage vote required of each class, or that the merger agreement was entitled to be and was approved by the board alone under the provisions of Section 1201.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 1103
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, the merger becomes effective upon that filing, subject to Section 110(c)
citations.quote: The merger and any amendment of the articles of the surviving corporation contained in the merger agreement shall thereupon be effective (subject to subdivision (c) of Section 110 and subject to the provisions of Section 1108) and the several parties thereto shall be one corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 110(c)
citations.cite: General Corporation Law, an instrument filed with the Secretary of State (including a merger agreement) may specify a delayed effective date of up to 90 days
citations.quote: Any instrument filed with respect to a corporation, other than original articles or instruments filed pursuant to Section 119, may provide that it is to become effective not more than 90 days subsequent to its filing date.

clauses.title: Officers' Certification and Signatures
clauses.body:
The undersigned officer(s) of each constituent corporation certify, for filing with the agreement of merger, that: the total number of outstanding shares of each class of {{constituentCorporationNames}} entitled to vote on the merger, and the vote obtained, were as follows: {{outstandingSharesVoteStatement}}; and that this vote equaled or exceeded the vote required for approval, or that the merger was instead entitled to be, and was, approved by the board alone under California's applicable statutory exception.

On behalf of the board of each constituent corporation, the undersigned further certify that the board approved the agreement of merger on {{boardApprovalDate}}, and, if shareholder approval was separately required, that the outstanding shares approved the agreement's principal terms on {{shareholderApprovalDate}}.

clauses.title: Identification of the Out-of-State Protection Order
clauses.body: I, {{protectedPersonName}}, am the protected person under a protection order issued against {{respondentName}} by {{issuingCourtName}}, in {{issuingState}}, case/docket number {{issuingCaseNumber}}, dated {{orderIssuanceDate}} (including any later modification of that order). This document describes how California treats an order of this kind under California's Uniform Interstate Enforcement of Domestic Violence Protection Orders Act (Family Code section 6400 et seq.) and the related federal full faith and credit requirement (18 U.S.C. section 2265). It is informational only: it does not itself register, confirm, or enforce this order, and it does not determine whether this specific order in fact meets the statutory requirements described below -- that determination is made, case by case, by the California court or law enforcement officer asked to enforce it.

clauses.title: The Full Faith and Credit Rule for Protective Orders
clauses.body: Federal law requires every state, Indian tribe, and U.S. territory to give full faith and credit to a protection order issued by another state, tribe, or territory that is consistent with the standard in 18 U.S.C. section 2265(b), and to enforce it as though it were the enforcing jurisdiction's own order. California implements that mandate through its own statute, the Uniform Interstate Enforcement of Domestic Violence Protection Orders Act: a person authorized under California law to enforce a protection order may seek enforcement of a valid foreign protection order in a California tribunal, and the tribunal must enforce its terms -- including relief a California tribunal would otherwise lack power to grant -- following California's own procedures for enforcing protection orders. For purposes of this California statute, a qualifying "protection order" is an injunction or other order issued under the domestic violence, family violence, or antistalking laws of the issuing state to prevent violent or threatening acts, harassment, contact, or physical proximity.
clauses.gap: This clause rests on two independent, separately enacted sources of law -- the federal full faith and credit statute, 18 U.S.C. section 2265(a), enacted as part of the Violence Against Women Act, and California's own Family Code section 6402(a), part of California's Uniform Interstate Enforcement of Domestic Violence Protection Orders Act -- so they corroborate rather than merely restate one another. The third citation, Family Code section 6401(5), is a different, independently numbered section from section 6402, so it is likewise not dependent on the section 6402 citation. This clause states that California's implementing statute reaches orders issued under the domestic violence, family violence, or antistalking laws of the issuing state; it does not resolve, for any specific out-of-state order, whether the issuing state actually classified that order under one of those bodies of law. The federal statute's own scope is broader on its face -- 18 U.S.C. section 2265(b) does not repeat the domestic-violence/family-violence/antistalking limitation found in the California statute's definitions -- and this clause does not attempt to reconcile that difference in scope between the two statutes; it states what each says.

citations.cite: the federal full faith and credit mandate
citations.quote: Any protection order issued that is consistent with subsection (b) of this section by the court of one State, Indian tribe, or territory (the issuing State, Indian tribe, or territory) shall be accorded full faith and credit by the court of another State, Indian tribe, or territory (the enforcing State, Indian tribe, or territory) and enforced by the court and law enforcement personnel of the other State, Indian tribal government or Territory

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6402(a)
citations.cite: California's own enforcement mandate for a valid foreign protection order
citations.quote: A person authorized by the law of this state to seek enforcement of a protection order may seek enforcement of a valid foreign protection order in a tribunal of this state. The tribunal shall enforce the terms of the order, including terms that provide relief that a tribunal of this state would lack power to provide but for this section. The tribunal shall enforce the order, whether the order was obtained by independent action or in another proceeding, if it is an order issued in response to a complaint, petition, or motion filed by or on behalf of an individual seeking protection. In a proceeding to enforce a foreign protection order, the tribunal shall follow the procedures of this state for the enforcement of protection orders.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6401(5)
citations.cite: the statutory definition of a qualifying "protection order"
citations.quote: “Protection order” means an injunction or other order, issued by a tribunal under the domestic violence, family violence, or antistalking laws of the issuing state, to prevent an individual from engaging in violent or threatening acts against, harassment of, contact or communication with, or physical proximity to, another individual.

clauses.title: Conditions a Foreign Order Must Meet: Jurisdiction and Notice
clauses.body: Full faith and credit is not unconditional. Under the federal statute, a protection order is entitled to full faith and credit only if the issuing court had jurisdiction over the parties and the matter, and the respondent was given reasonable notice and an opportunity to be heard sufficient to protect due process -- for an ex parte order, that notice and opportunity to be heard must come within the time required by the issuing jurisdiction's law, and in any event within a reasonable time after the order issued. California's own statute states essentially the same two conditions as part of its definition of a "valid" foreign protection order: the order must identify the protected individual and the respondent, be currently in effect, have been issued by a tribunal with jurisdiction over the parties and subject matter, and have been issued after the respondent received reasonable notice and an opportunity to be heard (or, for an ex parte order, notice and an opportunity to be heard within a reasonable time afterward). An order lacking any of these elements is not a "valid foreign protection order" for purposes of California's mandatory-enforcement statute.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two independent, separately enacted sources -- the federal statute, 18 U.S.C. section 2265(b), and California's own Family Code section 6402(d) -- rather than subsections of a single section, so no single-section disclosure applies. This clause states the statutory standard for validity; it does not, and cannot, determine whether any specific out-of-state order in fact satisfies these jurisdiction and notice requirements -- that is a fact-specific determination made by the enforcing court or officer, and (per the companion clause on this document) an order valid on its face is treated as prima facie evidence of its validity rather than as automatically, conclusively valid.

citations.cite: the federal jurisdiction-and-notice standard for a qualifying protection order
citations.quote: A protection order issued by a State, tribal, or territorial court is consistent with this subsection if— (1) such court has jurisdiction over the parties and matter under the law of such State, Indian tribe, or territory; and (2) reasonable notice and opportunity to be heard is given to the person against whom the order is sought sufficient to protect that person’s right to due process. In the case of ex parte orders, notice and opportunity to be heard must be provided within the time required by State, tribal, or territorial law, and in any event within a reasonable time after the order is issued, sufficient to protect the respondent’s due process rights.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6402(d)
citations.cite: California's own criteria for a "valid" foreign protection order
citations.quote: A foreign protection order is valid if it meets all of the following criteria: (1) Identifies the protected individual and the respondent. (2) Is currently in effect. (3) Was issued by a tribunal that had jurisdiction over the parties and subject matter under the law of the issuing state. (4) Was issued after the respondent was given reasonable notice and had an opportunity to be heard before the tribunal issued the order or, in the case of an order ex parte, the respondent was given notice and has had or will have an opportunity to be heard within a reasonable time after the order was issued, in a manner consistent with the rights of the respondent to due process.

clauses.title: Registration Is Not Required Before California Must Enforce the Order
clauses.body: Neither federal nor California law makes registering an out-of-state protection order in California a precondition to its enforcement here. The federal statute states directly that a qualifying order must be accorded full faith and credit notwithstanding a failure to comply with any requirement that it be registered or filed in the enforcing jurisdiction. California's own statute states the same rule for its enforcement mechanism: registration or filing of an order in California is not required for enforcement of a valid foreign protection order. A protected person does not need to register an out-of-state order with a California court before a California court or law enforcement officer is required to enforce it.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two independent, separately enacted sources -- the federal statute, 18 U.S.C. section 2265(d)(2), and California's own Family Code section 6403(d) -- rather than subsections of a single section, so no single-section disclosure applies. This is likely the single most commonly misunderstood point in this area: many people assume an out-of-state order must first be registered in California before it can be enforced here, and that assumption is incorrect under both statutes quoted above. This clause does not address a separate, optional registration mechanism California provides for a protected person's own convenience, which is covered in a separate clause in this document and does not change the rule stated here.

citations.cite: no prior registration or filing required as a prerequisite for federal full faith and credit
citations.quote: Any protection order that is otherwise consistent with this section shall be accorded full faith and credit, notwithstanding failure to comply with any requirement that the order be registered or filed in the enforcing State, tribal, or territorial jurisdiction.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6403(d)
citations.cite: California's own statement that registration is not required for enforcement
citations.quote: Registration or filing of an order in this state is not required for the enforcement of a valid foreign protection order pursuant to this part.

clauses.title: A California Peace Officer's Duty to Enforce a Facially Valid Order
clauses.body: California's statute gives a California law enforcement officer a specific, checkable standard for enforcing an out-of-state protection order in the field. Once an officer determines there is probable cause to believe a valid foreign protection order exists and has been violated, the officer must enforce it as if it were a California order. Presenting an order that identifies both the protected individual and the respondent and appears, on its face, to be currently in effect is, by itself, enough to establish that probable cause -- an order stored electronically qualifies if it is retrievable in perceivable form, and a certified copy is not required. Separately, if an officer determines that an otherwise valid order cannot yet be enforced because the respondent has not been notified or served, the officer must inform the respondent of the order, make a reasonable effort to serve it, and give the respondent a reasonable opportunity to comply before enforcing it -- verbal notice of the order's terms is sufficient for this purpose.
clauses.gap: Family Code section 6403, subdivisions (a) and (c), quoted here, are both provisions of a single California statutory section -- not independent of one another. This clause does not restate subdivision (b), which separately allows an officer to consider other information toward probable cause when no order is presented, or the officer's civil immunity for a good-faith arrest under a facially regular order, which is addressed by a different, independently numbered section (Family Code section 6405) not covered in this document. This is one state's statute, describing how California specifically implements the federal full faith and credit mandate for its own peace officers; it is not a claim about how any other state's officers are instructed to handle an out-of-state protection order.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6403(a)
citations.cite: the probable-cause standard for enforcement and what constitutes probable cause
citations.quote: A law enforcement officer of this state, upon determining that there is probable cause to believe that a valid foreign protection order exists and that the order has been violated, shall enforce the order as if it were the order of a tribunal of this state. Presentation of a protection order that identifies both the protected individual and the respondent and, on its face, is currently in effect constitutes, in and of itself, probable cause to believe that a valid foreign protection order exists. For the purposes of this section, the protection order may be inscribed on a tangible medium or may have been stored in an electronic or other medium if it is retrievable in perceivable form. Presentation of a certified copy of a protection order is not required for enforcement.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6403(c)
citations.cite: the notice-and-opportunity-to-comply procedure when the respondent has not yet been served
citations.quote: If a law enforcement officer of this state determines that an otherwise valid foreign protection order cannot be enforced because the respondent has not been notified or served with the order, the officer shall inform the respondent of the order, make a reasonable effort to serve the order upon the respondent, and allow the respondent a reasonable opportunity to comply with the order before enforcing the order. Verbal notice of the terms of the order is sufficient notice for the purposes of this section.

clauses.title: An Optional Registration Mechanism, for the Protected Person's Convenience
clauses.body: Separately from the no-registration-required enforcement rule described elsewhere in this document, California's statute gives a protected person the option to register an out-of-state protection order with a California court so that it is entered into the California Restraining and Protective Order System. Registration under this mechanism is initiated upon the request of the person in possession of the order -- the statute's implementing rules describe this as a process by which that person "may voluntarily register" the order. A registered order's record is sealed, with access limited to law enforcement, the person who registered it (upon written request with proof of identification), the defense after arraignment on a criminal charge involving an alleged violation, or by further court order. No fee may be charged for this registration, and the court clerk must provide the required Judicial Council forms free of charge.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (Family Code section 6404, subdivisions (a)-(b), quoted here as one contiguous passage); no additional independent source was found for this specific optional mechanism. This clause should not be read to imply that registration is required for enforcement -- the immediately preceding point in this document (Family Code section 6403(d) and 18 U.S.C. section 2265(d)(2)) states the opposite: enforcement does not depend on registration. This mechanism exists for a protected person's own convenience -- for example, so that the order appears in a statewide law enforcement system -- not as a gatekeeping step. This clause does not describe the Judicial Council rules of court adopted to implement this section in further procedural detail beyond what the statute itself states.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6404(a)-(b)
citations.cite: the optional, voluntary registration mechanism and its sealing and no-fee provisions
citations.quote: A foreign protection order shall, upon request of the person in possession of the order, be registered with a court of this state in order to be entered in the California Restraining and Protective Order System established under Section 6380. The Judicial Council shall adopt rules of court to do the following: (1) Set forth the process whereby a person in possession of a foreign protection order may voluntarily register the order with a court of this state for entry into the California Restraining and Protective Order System. (2) Require the sealing of foreign protection orders and provide access only to law enforcement, the person who registered the order upon written request with proof of identification, the defense after arraignment on criminal charges involving an alleged violation of the order, or upon further order of the court. (b) A fee shall not be charged for the registration of a foreign protection order. The court clerk shall provide all Judicial Council forms required by this part to a person in possession of a foreign protection order free of charge.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment and Signature
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct to the best of my knowledge. Executed on {{signatureDate}}, at {{signatureCity}}, California.

☐ _________________________ {{protectedPersonName}}, signature

This document is informational only. It does not itself register, confirm, or enforce any protection order. Whether a specific out-of-state order meets the statutory requirements described above, and how a specific California court or law enforcement officer will treat it, are determinations made case by case, not by this document.

clauses.title: Consequence of Declining a Court-Ordered Genetic Test
clauses.body: California law attaches a specific consequence to refusing a court-ordered genetic test. Family Code § 7554(a) sets out a framework under which, if the woman who gave birth to {{childName}} is the only other person who is a parent or has a claim to parentage of {{childName}} under this division, the court shall find the alleged father or alleged genetic parent to be a parent if that person meets any of several listed conditions — among them, § 7554(a)(3): if the person "[d]eclines to submit to genetic testing ordered by the court or a local child support agency," the court may find that person to be a parent of the child "even if the person denies a genetic relationship with the child."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can attach a specific adverse consequence to declining a court-ordered genetic test — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what any specific court would find regarding, any specific person's refusal. This clause cites two parts of the same statutory subsection (§ 7554(a)'s introductory clause and § 7554(a)(3)); they are not independent of one another — the introductory clause's own condition (that the woman who gave birth is the only other person who is a parent or has a claim to parentage) applies to the refusal consequence quoted here. Section 7554(a) lists four other bases (identification under § 7555 that is not successfully challenged, an admission accepted by the court, default, and other evidence) on which a court may likewise find a person to be a parent; this clause addresses only the refusal basis and does not restate those other bases. Whether, and under what conditions, a refusal to submit to testing carries this consequence varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7554(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: introductory clause and condition of the § 7554(a) framework
citations.quote: If the woman who gave birth to the child is the only other person who is a parent or has a claim to parentage of the child under this division, the court shall find the person who is the alleged father or genetic parent who is not a donor under Section 7613 to be a parent of the child if the person meets any of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7554(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: consequence of declining court-ordered genetic testing
citations.quote: Declines to submit to genetic testing ordered by the court or a local child support agency, in which case, the court may find that the person is a parent of the child even if the person denies a genetic relationship with the child.

clauses.title: How Genetic Testing Must Be Performed: Laboratory Accreditation and Specimen Types
clauses.body: California law does not leave the reliability of court-ordered genetic testing undefined. Family Code § 7552(a) requires that testing "be of a type reasonably relied on by experts in the field of genetic testing and performed in a testing laboratory accredited by" either the AABB (formerly the American Association of Blood Banks) or a successor organization, or an accrediting body designated by the Secretary of the United States Department of Health and Human Services. Section 7552(b) separately specifies what may be tested: a specimen "may consist of a sample or a combination of samples of blood, buccal cells, bone, hair, or other body tissue or fluid," and the specimen type need not be the same for each person tested.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can condition the reliability of genetic-parentage testing on a specific accreditation standard and a defined, but non-exclusive, list of acceptable specimen types — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what standard would apply to, any specific test. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7552(a) and § 7552(b)); they are not independent of one another. Section 7552 also addresses, in subdivisions (c) and (d) (not quoted here), how a testing laboratory selects the ethnic or racial database used to calculate a relationship index, a process a party or local child support agency may object to and ask the court to revisit; this clause does not cover that separate procedure. Whether, and by what standard, genetic parentage testing must be accredited or performed varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7552(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the expert-reliability and laboratory-accreditation standard
citations.quote: Genetic testing shall be of a type reasonably relied on by experts in the field of genetic testing and performed in a testing laboratory accredited by either of the following: (1) The AABB, formerly known as the American Association of Blood Banks, or a successor organization. (2) An accrediting body designated by the Secretary of the United States Department of Health and Human Services.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7552(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: permissible specimen types
citations.quote: A specimen used in genetic testing may consist of a sample or a combination of samples of blood, buccal cells, bone, hair, or other body tissue or fluid. The specimen used in the testing need not be of the same kind for each person undergoing genetic testing.

clauses.title: Challenging a Genetic-Parent Identification
clauses.body: A person identified as a genetic parent under the statistical threshold described in this document's companion clause on genetic testing does not have unlimited grounds to dispute that identification. Family Code § 7555(b) provides that such a person "may challenge the genetic testing results only by other genetic testing satisfying the requirements of this chapter that either excludes the person as a genetic parent of the child or identifies another person as a possible genetic parent of the child" other than the woman who gave birth or the person challenging parentage. If that further testing itself identifies more than one possible genetic parent other than the woman who gave birth, § 7555(c) provides that "the court shall order each person to submit to further genetic testing to identify a genetic parent."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can limit how a genetic-parent identification may be rebutted — to further qualifying genetic testing only — and can provide a specific mechanism for resolving a further test that identifies multiple possible parents, not a claim about which state's law governs, or how any specific identification would be challenged or resolved. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7555(b) and § 7555(c)); they are not independent of one another, and both are subject to the same section's subdivision (a) identification standard, which is addressed in this document's companion clause on genetic testing and not restated here. Whether, and how, a genetic-parent identification can be challenged varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7555(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the exclusive rebuttal mechanism — further qualifying genetic testing
citations.quote: A person identified pursuant to subdivision (a) as a genetic parent of the child may challenge the genetic testing results only by other genetic testing satisfying the requirements of this chapter that either excludes the person as a genetic parent of the child or identifies another person as a possible genetic parent of the child other than the woman who gave birth to the child or the person challenging parentage.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7555(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: further testing where the rebuttal identifies multiple possible parents
citations.quote: If more than one person, other than the woman who gave birth to the child, is identified by genetic testing as a possible genetic parent of the child, the court shall order each person to submit to further genetic testing to identify a genetic parent.

clauses.title: How the Cost of a Court-Appointed Testing Expert Is Fixed and Allocated
clauses.body: The cost of genetic testing ordered under a court-appointed expert is not left unaddressed. Family Code § 7553(a) provides that the compensation of each court-appointed expert witness "shall be fixed at a reasonable amount" and paid as the court orders; except as provided in § 7553(b), the court may order it paid by the parties in proportions and at times the court sets, may order a party's proportion paid by the county, and may then tax all, part, or none of that amount as costs in the action. Section 7553(b) draws a distinct line for an expert appointed on the court's own motion rather than at a party's request: "If the expert witness is appointed for the court's needs, the compensation shall be paid by the court."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a jurisdiction can both give a court discretion to allocate a testing expert's cost among the parties or the county (and to tax it as costs) and separately require the court itself to bear the cost of an expert it appoints for its own needs — not a claim about which state's law governs, or how any specific testing expert's cost would be allocated in any specific case. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section (§ 7553(a) and § 7553(b)); they are not independent of one another — subdivision (a) is itself expressly qualified by subdivision (b). Whether, and how, the cost of court-ordered genetic testing is allocated varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7553(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: fixing and allocating a party-requested expert's compensation
citations.quote: The compensation of each expert witness appointed by the court shall be fixed at a reasonable amount. It shall be paid as the court shall order. Except as provided in subdivision (b), the court may order that it be paid by the parties in the proportions and at the times the court prescribes, or that the proportion of any party be paid by the county, and that, after payment by the parties or the county or both, all or part or none of it be taxed as costs in the action or proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7553(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court pays for an expert appointed for its own needs
citations.quote: If the expert witness is appointed for the court’s needs, the compensation shall be paid by the court.

clauses.title: Cal-ICWA Information Sheet — Purpose and Declaration
clauses.body: I, {{petitionerName}}, am providing this information sheet in connection with a California proceeding involving {{childName}}, a minor born {{childDOB}}, in which there is an indication that {{childName}} is or may be an “Indian child” as defined by the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. § 1901 et seq.) and California's own implementing statutes, Family Code § 177 and Welfare and Institutions Code §§ 224–224.6. {{childName}}'s possible tribal affiliation, if known, is: {{possibleTribeName}}. My relationship to {{childName}}, if any, is: {{relationshipToChild}}. This information sheet explains, using the statutes' own text, California's Cal-ICWA inquiry, notice, active-efforts, and placement-preference requirements. It does not itself determine whether {{childName}} is in fact an Indian child, does not satisfy any court's, social worker's, or party's inquiry or notice obligation under these statutes, and does not substitute for a determination by the child's tribe, advice from a qualified attorney, or the court's own ruling. Only the court, following the statutory inquiry and notice process, can determine whether Cal-ICWA's heightened protections apply to {{childName}}'s case.

clauses.title: Which Proceedings Trigger Cal-ICWA's Protections — Family Code § 177(a)-(c) and the “Indian Child Custody Proceeding” Definition in Family Code § 170(c)
clauses.body: California Family Code § 177(a) provides: “In an Indian child custody proceeding, the court shall apply Sections 224.2 to 224.6, inclusive, and Sections 305.5, 361.31, and 361.7 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, and the following rules from the California Rules of Court, as they read on January 1, 2007: (1) Paragraph (7) of subdivision (b) of Rule 5.530. (2) Subdivision (i) of Rule 5.534.” Section 177(b) explains how these cross-referenced Welfare and Institutions Code provisions operate inside a Family Code case: “In the provisions cited in subdivision (a), references to social workers, probation officers, county welfare department, or probation department shall be construed as meaning the party seeking a foster care placement, guardianship, or adoption under this code.” Section 177(c) limits the whole rule to Indian-child cases: “This section shall only apply to proceedings involving an Indian child.” Family Code § 170(c) defines the triggering term itself: ““Indian child custody proceeding” means a “child custody proceeding” within the meaning of Section 1903 of the Indian Child Welfare Act, including a voluntary or involuntary proceeding that may result in an Indian child’s temporary or long-term foster care or guardianship placement if the parent or Indian custodian cannot have the child returned upon demand, termination of parental rights, or adoptive placement. An “Indian child custody proceeding” does not include a proceeding under this code commenced by the parent of an Indian child to determine the custodial rights of the child’s parents, unless the proceeding involves a petition to declare an Indian child free from the custody or control of a parent or involves a grant of custody to a person or persons other than a parent, over the objection of a parent.” Regarding {{childName}}, these Cal-ICWA protections accordingly apply only where the proceeding fits this statutory definition — not to every Family Code matter that happens to involve {{childName}}.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of which proceedings trigger Cal-ICWA's heightened protections — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that every Family Code proceeding involving a family member who is an American Indian or Alaska Native triggers these protections. Three of these citations — Fam. Code § 177(a), § 177(b), and § 177(c) — are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 177); no additional independent source beyond § 177 itself was found for that group, so they are not independent of one another. The fourth citation, Fam. Code § 170(c), is a separate, independently numbered section and is independent of the § 177 group. Section 170(c)'s own definition cross-references 25 U.S.C. § 1903 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act for the baseline “child custody proceeding” concept, and Family Code § 170(a) separately cross-references the same federal section for the definition of “Indian child” itself; this document does not independently verify or quote 25 U.S.C. § 1903's own text and relies only on the California statute's cross-reference to it. Family Code § 177(a) also directs application of Welfare and Institutions Code § 305.5, which this document does not address or verify. An ordinary custody dispute between two parents remains outside this definition unless it involves a petition to free the child from a parent's custody and control, or an award of custody to a nonparent over a parent's objection.

(2) Subdivision (i) of Rule 5.534.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 177(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: In the provisions cited in subdivision (a), references to social workers, probation officers, county welfare department, or probation department shall be construed as meaning the party seeking a foster care placement, guardianship, or adoption under this code.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 177(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: This section shall only apply to proceedings involving an Indian child.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 170(c) (California Legislative Information text)
