An “Indian child custody proceeding” does not include a proceeding under this code commenced by the parent of an Indian child to determine the custodial rights of the child’s parents, unless the proceeding involves a petition to declare an Indian child free from the custody or control of a parent or involves a grant of custody to a person or persons other than a parent, over the objection of a parent.

clauses.title: The Affirmative, Continuing Duty to Inquire Whether a Child Is or May Be an Indian Child — Welf. & Inst. Code § 224.2(a), (c)
clauses.body: Welfare and Institutions Code § 224.2(a) provides: “The court, county welfare department, and the probation department have an affirmative and continuing duty to inquire whether a child for whom a petition under Section 300, 601, or 602 may be or has been filed, is or may be an Indian child.” Section 224.2(c) extends that duty into the courtroom itself: “For a court presiding over any juvenile proceeding that could result in placement of an Indian child with someone other than a parent or Indian custodian, including proceedings where the parents or Indian custodian have voluntarily consented to placement of the child, the duty to inquire begins at the first hearing on a petition. At the commencement of the hearing, the court shall ask each party to the proceeding and all other interested persons present whether the child is, or may be, an Indian child, whether they know or have reason to know that the child is an Indian child, and where the child, the parents, or Indian custodian are domiciled, as defined in Section 224.1. Inquiry shall also be made at the first appearance in court of each party or interested person who was not present at the first hearing on the petition. The inquiry and responses shall occur on the record. The court shall instruct the parties and persons present to inform the court if they subsequently receive information that provides reason to know the child is, or may be, an Indian child.” By its own terms, § 224.2(a) attaches this duty to a juvenile-court petition filed under Welfare and Institutions Code § 300 (dependency), § 601, or § 602 (delinquency). When these same Welfare and Institutions Code sections are instead applied within a Family Code proceeding under Family Code § 177, § 177(b) — quoted in this document's companion scope clause — separately construes their references to social workers, probation officers, or county departments as meaning the party seeking a foster care placement, guardianship, or adoption; in that setting, the practical burden of inquiry falls on that party rather than on a county department.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the affirmative, continuing inquiry duty — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 224.2(a) and § 224.2(c); no additional independent source beyond § 224.2 itself was found for this pairing, so they are not independent of one another. Subdivision (a)'s duty is stated as attaching to a petition filed under Welfare and Institutions Code § 300, § 601, or § 602; this clause does not independently verify the text of those three cross-referenced sections. This clause's description of how the same duty operates inside a Family Code proceeding relies on Family Code § 177(b), quoted and cited in this document's companion scope clause rather than re-quoted here, since that document already discloses § 177(b) as part of the § 177 group. This clause does not address § 224.2(b), which describes when a county's own inquiry duty first begins, or § 224.2(e) through (k), covering further inquiry after a lower “reason to believe” showing, the conclusive effect of a tribe's own membership determination, and a tribe's right to participate remotely, none of which was independently verified for inclusion as a quoted citation in this document.

citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 224.2(a)
citations.quote: The court, county welfare department, and the probation department have an affirmative and continuing duty to inquire whether a child for whom a petition under Section 300, 601, or 602 may be or has been filed, is or may be an Indian child.

citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 224.2(c)
citations.quote: For a court presiding over any juvenile proceeding that could result in placement of an Indian child with someone other than a parent or Indian custodian, including proceedings where the parents or Indian custodian have voluntarily consented to placement of the child, the duty to inquire begins at the first hearing on a petition. At the commencement of the hearing, the court shall ask each party to the proceeding and all other interested persons present whether the child is, or may be, an Indian child, whether they know or have reason to know that the child is an Indian child, and where the child, the parents, or Indian custodian are domiciled, as defined in Section 224.1. Inquiry shall also be made at the first appearance in court of each party or interested person who was not present at the first hearing on the petition. The inquiry and responses shall occur on the record. The court shall instruct the parties and persons present to inform the court if they subsequently receive information that provides reason to know the child is, or may be, an Indian child.

clauses.title: “Reason to Know” an Indian Child Is Involved — the Statute's Own Six Triggering Circumstances, and the Resulting Notice Duty — Welf. & Inst. Code § 224.2(d), (f)
clauses.body: Welfare and Institutions Code § 224.2(d) does not leave “reason to know” to unconfirmed suspicion; it lists specific triggering circumstances: “There is reason to know a child involved in a proceeding is an Indian child under any of the following circumstances: (1) A person having an interest in the child, including the child, an officer of the court, a tribe, an Indian organization, a public or private agency, or a member of the child’s extended family informs the court that the child is an Indian child. (2) The residence or domicile of the child, the child’s parents, or Indian custodian is on a reservation or in an Alaska Native village, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1602 of Title 43 of the United State Code. (3) Any participant in the proceeding, officer of the court, Indian tribe, Indian organization, or agency informs the court that it has discovered information indicating that the child is an Indian child. (4) The child who is the subject of the proceeding gives the court reason to know that the child is an Indian child. (5) The court is informed that the child is or has been a ward of a tribal court. (6) The court is informed that either parent or the child possess an identification card indicating membership or citizenship in an Indian tribe.” Once any of these six circumstances exists, § 224.2(f) ties the inquiry to the notice duty: “If there is reason to know, as set forth in subdivision (d), that the child is an Indian child, the party seeking foster care placement with someone other than a parent or Indian custodian shall provide notice in accordance with Section 224.3.” Regarding {{childName}}, only one of these six specific, statutorily defined circumstances — not a general impression or unconfirmed guess — triggers the notice duty described in this document's companion clause on notice requirements.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific circumstances that trigger “reason to know” an Indian child is involved, and of the resulting notice duty — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that this list forecloses the court's, social worker's, or probation officer's separate duty of further inquiry on a lower “reason to believe” showing under § 224.2(e), which this clause does not quote and which does not by itself trigger the notice duty addressed here. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 224.2(d) and § 224.2(f); no additional independent source beyond § 224.2 itself was found for this pairing, so they are not independent of one another. Section 224.2(f)'s own text places the notice-sending duty specifically on “the party seeking foster care placement with someone other than a parent or Indian custodian,” not on the court itself; this clause does not resolve who that party is on any specific family's facts. This clause does not address § 224.2(g) through (k), covering the record the court must make when reason to know exists but membership is unconfirmed, the conclusive effect of a tribe's own determination, and a tribe's right to participate remotely, none of which was independently verified for inclusion as a quoted citation in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 224.2(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 224.2(d)
citations.quote: There is reason to know a child involved in a proceeding is an Indian child under any of the following circumstances: (1) A person having an interest in the child, including the child, an officer of the court, a tribe, an Indian organization, a public or private agency, or a member of the child’s extended family informs the court that the child is an Indian child. (2) The residence or domicile of the child, the child’s parents, or Indian custodian is on a reservation or in an Alaska Native village, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 1602 of Title 43 of the United State Code. (3) Any participant in the proceeding, officer of the court, Indian tribe, Indian organization, or agency informs the court that it has discovered information indicating that the child is an Indian child. (4) The child who is the subject of the proceeding gives the court reason to know that the child is an Indian child. (5) The court is informed that the child is or has been a ward of a tribal court. (6) The court is informed that either parent or the child possess an identification card indicating membership or citizenship in an Indian tribe.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 224.2(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 224.2(f)
citations.quote: If there is reason to know, as set forth in subdivision (d), that the child is an Indian child, the party seeking foster care placement with someone other than a parent or Indian custodian shall provide notice in accordance with Section 224.3.

clauses.title: What the Required Notice Must Say and How It Must Be Sent — Welf. & Inst. Code § 224.3(a)
clauses.body: Once notice is required, Welfare and Institutions Code § 224.3(a) states its own trigger, scope, and recipients: “If the court, a social worker, or probation officer knows or has reason to know, as described in subdivision (d) of Section 224.2, that an Indian child is involved, notice pursuant to Section 1912 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 1901 et seq.) shall be provided for hearings that may culminate in an order for foster care placement, termination of parental rights, preadoptive placement, or adoptive placement, as described in paragraph (1) of subdivision (d) of Section 224.1. The notice shall be sent to the minor’s parents or legal guardian, Indian custodian, if any, and the child’s tribe. Copies of all notices sent shall be served on all parties to the dependency proceeding and their attorneys.” The same section also fixes the required delivery method: “Notice shall be sent by registered or certified mail with return receipt requested. Additional notice by first-class mail is recommended, but not required.”
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the required notice's trigger, scope, recipients, and delivery method — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites two provisions from the same statutory section, § 224.3(a)'s opening paragraph and § 224.3(a)(1); no additional independent source beyond § 224.3 itself was found for this pairing, so they are not independent of one another. This clause does not restate § 224.3(a)(2) through (5), covering the tribal-chairperson service rule, the Secretary of the Interior notice requirement, and the detailed list of information the notice itself must contain (the child's name and birth information, known ancestor names, and a statement of the parents', Indian custodians', and tribe's rights to intervene, to petition for transfer to tribal court, and to appointed counsel, among other items), none of which was independently verified for inclusion as a quoted citation in this document. This clause also does not address § 224.3(b) through the section's remaining subdivisions, covering timing before the hearing and related procedural requirements.

citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 224.3(a)
citations.quote: If the court, a social worker, or probation officer knows or has reason to know, as described in subdivision (d) of Section 224.2, that an Indian child is involved, notice pursuant to Section 1912 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 1901 et seq.) shall be provided for hearings that may culminate in an order for foster care placement, termination of parental rights, preadoptive placement, or adoptive placement, as described in paragraph (1) of subdivision (d) of Section 224.1. The notice shall be sent to the minor’s parents or legal guardian, Indian custodian, if any, and the child’s tribe. Copies of all notices sent shall be served on all parties to the dependency proceeding and their attorneys.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 224.3(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 224.3(a)(1)
citations.quote: Notice shall be sent by registered or certified mail with return receipt requested. Additional notice by first-class mail is recommended, but not required.

clauses.title: The Heightened “Active Efforts” Standard for Foster Care Placement and Termination of Parental Rights — Welf. & Inst. Code § 361.7(a), (b)
clauses.body: Welfare and Institutions Code § 361.7(a) requires more than California's otherwise-applicable reasonable-efforts standard once an Indian child is involved: “Notwithstanding Section 361.5, a party seeking an involuntary foster care placement of, or termination of parental rights over, an Indian child shall provide evidence to the court that active efforts have been made to provide remedial services and rehabilitative programs designed to prevent the breakup of the Indian family and that these efforts have proved unsuccessful. The active efforts shall be documented in detail in the record.” Section 361.7(b) describes what “active efforts” requires, rather than leaving the term undefined: “What constitutes active efforts shall be assessed on a case-by-case basis. The active efforts shall be made in a manner that takes into account the prevailing social and cultural values, conditions, and way of life of the Indian child’s tribe. Active efforts shall utilize the available resources of the Indian child’s extended family, tribe, tribal and other Indian social service agencies, and individual Indian caregiver service providers.”
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the heightened active-efforts standard and the statute's own description of what that standard requires — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a claim that “active efforts” and the otherwise-applicable “reasonable efforts” standard under Welfare and Institutions Code § 361.5 are the same thing; § 361.7(a)'s own opening phrase, “Notwithstanding Section 361.5,” signals that active efforts is a distinct, higher standard, but this document does not independently verify or quote § 361.5's own text for comparison. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 361.7(a) and § 361.7(b); no additional independent source beyond § 361.7 itself was found for this pairing, so they are not independent of one another. This clause does not address § 361.7(c), which separately requires a qualified-expert-witness determination, supported by clear and convincing evidence, before a foster care placement or guardianship may be ordered for an Indian child; the qualified-expert-witness definition itself appears in Welfare and Institutions Code § 224.6, which this document does not independently verify or quote.

citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 361.7(a)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding Section 361.5, a party seeking an involuntary foster care placement of, or termination of parental rights over, an Indian child shall provide evidence to the court that active efforts have been made to provide remedial services and rehabilitative programs designed to prevent the breakup of the Indian family and that these efforts have proved unsuccessful. The active efforts shall be documented in detail in the record.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 361.7(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 361.7(b)
citations.quote: What constitutes active efforts shall be assessed on a case-by-case basis. The active efforts shall be made in a manner that takes into account the prevailing social and cultural values, conditions, and way of life of the Indian child’s tribe. Active efforts shall utilize the available resources of the Indian child’s extended family, tribe, tribal and other Indian social service agencies, and individual Indian caregiver service providers.

clauses.title: The Statutory Placement-Preference Hierarchy for Foster Care/Guardianship and Adoptive Placements — Welf. & Inst. Code § 361.31(b), (c)
clauses.body: For a foster care or guardianship placement of an Indian child, Welfare and Institutions Code § 361.31(b) sets a descending order of preference: “Preference shall be given to the child’s placement with one of the following, in descending priority order: (1) A member of the child’s extended family, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 224.1 and Section 1903 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 1901 et seq.). (2) A foster home licensed, approved, or specified by the child’s Indian tribe. (3) An Indian foster home licensed or approved by an authorized non-Indian licensing authority. (4) An institution for children approved by an Indian tribe or operated by an Indian organization that has a program suitable to meet the Indian child’s needs.” For an adoptive placement, § 361.31(c) sets a separate, shorter order: “In any adoptive placement of an Indian child, preference shall be given to a placement with one of the following, in descending priority order: (1) A member of the child’s extended family, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 224.1 and Section 1903 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 1901 et seq.). (2) Other members or citizens of the child’s Indian tribe. (3) Another Indian family.”
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the statutory placement-preference hierarchy for foster care/guardianship placements and for adoptive placements of an Indian child — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 361.31(b) and § 361.31(c); no additional independent source beyond § 361.31 itself was found for this pairing, so they are not independent of one another. This preference order is not absolute: § 361.31(d) lets a different order established by the child's own tribe take precedence, subject to full faith and credit; and § 361.31(h) through (j) let a party depart from the preference order on a showing of “good cause,” proven by clear and convincing evidence, based on specific considerations the statute lists (among them a parent's own informed request, the child's own request, a sibling attachment that can be maintained only through a particular placement, the child's extraordinary needs, or the unavailability of a suitable preferred placement after a diligent search). None of those subdivisions was independently verified for inclusion as a quoted citation in this document, and this clause does not resolve whether good cause exists on any specific family's facts.

citations.quote: Preference shall be given to the child’s placement with one of the following, in descending priority order: (1) A member of the child’s extended family, as defined in subdivision (c) of Section 224.1 and Section 1903 of the federal Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978 (25 U.S.C. Sec. 1901 et seq.). (2) A foster home licensed, approved, or specified by the child’s Indian tribe. (3) An Indian foster home licensed or approved by an authorized non-Indian licensing authority. (4) An institution for children approved by an Indian tribe or operated by an Indian organization that has a program suitable to meet the Indian child’s needs.

Sec. 1901 et seq.). (2) Other members or citizens of the child’s Indian tribe. (3) Another Indian family.

clauses.title: The Employer Must Pay the Undisputed Portion of Wages Despite a Dispute Over the Rest
clauses.body: When an employer and a discharged or resigning employee disagree about the amount of wages owed, California law requires the employer to pay — without condition, and within the deadline that otherwise applies to final wages — whatever amount of wages, or part of the wages, the employer itself concedes is due. This rule means an employer does not get to withhold an entire final paycheck merely because part of the amount claimed is disputed: the conceded portion must be paid regardless of the ongoing dispute over the balance, and paying it does not resolve, waive, or limit the employee's remedies as to the disputed remainder, which the employee remains free to pursue.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the pay-the-undisputed-portion rule — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular dispute, and not a claim that any particular amount here is actually conceded, disputed, or owed. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 206(a)); a separate clause in this document quotes subdivision (b) of the same section, so that citation is not independent of this one. The statute does not define what makes a dispute a genuine, good-faith one as opposed to a pretextual withholding, and this clause does not attempt to draw that line; a California Court of Appeal decision addressing a related distinction between wages conceded to be due and a bona fide dispute over wages — discussed in this project's separate Prohibition on Requiring a Release as a Condition of Wage Payment information sheet in the context of Labor Code section 206.5 — is not restated here, since that document already covers it and this clause does not duplicate it. This clause also does not work through how the deadline cross-referenced here ("within the time set by this article") interacts with the specific discharge-and-quit deadlines of Labor Code sections 201 and 202, which this project's separate documents address.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 206(a)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 206, subd. (a)
citations.quote: In case of a dispute over wages, the employer shall pay, without condition and within the time set by this article, all wages, or parts thereof, conceded by him to be due, leaving to the employee all remedies he might otherwise be entitled to as to any balance claimed.

clauses.title: One Remedy for the Disputed Balance: A Labor Commissioner Determination
clauses.body: Section 206 also describes one specific remedy available for the disputed balance the employee remains free to pursue: if, after an investigation and hearing, the Labor Commissioner determines the validity of the employee's wage claim, the amount determined to be due becomes due and payable within 10 days after the employer receives notice of that determination. An employer that has the ability to pay and willfully fails to pay within that 10-day window is liable, in addition to any other applicable penalty, for treble the amount of any damages the employee suffers as a direct and foreseeable consequence of that failure to pay.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of this specific remedy pathway — not a claim about which state's law governs this particular claim, and not a claim that any particular claim here has been, or will be, investigated or determined by the Labor Commissioner. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 206(b)); the prior clause in this document quotes subdivision (a) of the same section, so that citation is not independent of this one. This clause describes only this administrative-determination-and-treble-damages remedy; it is one of "all remedies" an employee is left free to pursue under subdivision (a), not the only one — an employee may instead, or also, have other remedies (such as a civil action) that this clause does not describe. This clause does not describe the Labor Commissioner's investigation-and-hearing procedure itself, does not determine whether any particular employer has the ability to pay or has acted willfully within the meaning of this subdivision, and does not address how "damages" here relates to the waiting-time penalty under a separate statute, which this project's separate Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document addresses.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 206(b)
citations.cite: Lab. Code § 206, subd. (b)
citations.quote: If, after an investigation and hearing, the Labor Commissioner has determined the validity of any employee’s claim for wages, the claim is due and payable within 10 days after receipt of notice by the employer that such wages are due. Any employer having the ability to pay who willfully fails to pay such wages within 10 days shall, in addition to any other applicable penalty, pay treble the amount of any damages accruing to the employee as a direct and foreseeable consequence of such failure to pay.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}} on behalf of {{businessName}}, states what California's Business and Professions Code §§ 17940–17943 provide about disclosing that an online communication or interaction is generated by a bot rather than a person. These sections were added to the Business and Professions Code as Chapter 6, captioned "Bots," by Senate Bill 1001 (2018); the statute's own text does not assign the chapter any other short title, though it is sometimes referred to informally, outside the statute itself, as the "B.O.T. Act" or "Bolstering Online Transparency Act." This sheet states what that chapter's own text says; it does not evaluate whether any particular account, message, or business practice complies with it, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: Certification
clauses.body:
I, {{preparerName}}, certify that I prepared this information sheet as a summary of Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17940–17943, for informational reference only regarding {{businessName}}. This information sheet does not evaluate whether any particular account, communication, or practice of {{businessName}} complies with this chapter, and is not a substitute for consulting a person licensed to practice law in the relevant jurisdiction.

Executed on {{signatureDate}}.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: "Bot," "Online," and "Person"
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 17940 defines the terms used throughout this chapter. A "bot" means an automated online account where all or substantially all of the actions or posts of that account are not the result of a person — that is, the statute defines the term by reference to an account's degree of automation, not by reference to any particular software architecture or technology. "Online" means appearing on any public-facing Internet Web site, Web application, or digital application, including a social network or publication. "Person," for purposes of this chapter, is defined broadly to include not only a natural person but also a corporation, limited liability company, partnership, joint venture, association, estate, trust, government, governmental subdivision or agency, or other legal entity, or any combination of those.
clauses.gap: These three definitions are drawn from subsections (a), (b), and (d) of the same statutory section, Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17940, and are not independent of one another or of the separate "online platform" definition in that same section's subsection (c), which is quoted in a separate clause below because it is used only in the service-provider exemption at § 17942(c), not in the definitions of "bot," "online," or "person" themselves. This sheet does not address how these definitions apply to any specific automated account, technology, or business, and it does not address whether any particular account is or is not "substantially" automated within the meaning of the "bot" definition.

citations.cite: Bots (Chapter 6), Definitions
citations.quote: “Bot” means an automated online account where all or substantially all of the actions or posts of that account are not the result of a person.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17940(b)
citations.cite: Bots (Chapter 6), Definitions
citations.quote: “Online” means appearing on any public-facing Internet Web site, Web application, or digital application, including a social network or publication.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17940(d)
citations.cite: Bots (Chapter 6), Definitions
citations.quote: “Person” means a natural person, corporation, limited liability company, partnership, joint venture, association, estate, trust, government, governmental subdivision or agency, or other legal entity or any combination thereof.

clauses.title: The Core Prohibition: Bot Use With Intent to Mislead About Artificial Identity
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 17941(a) makes it unlawful for any person to use a bot to communicate or interact with another person in California online, with the intent to mislead the other person about its artificial identity, for the purpose of knowingly deceiving the person about the content of the communication, in order to incentivize a purchase or sale of goods or services in a commercial transaction or to influence a vote in an election. The statute frames this as two layered mental-state elements — an intent to mislead about the bot's artificial identity, coupled with a purpose of knowingly deceiving about the content of the communication — directed at one of two specific ends: a commercial purchase-or-sale transaction, or an election vote. It is not, by its own terms, a general prohibition on all undisclosed bot activity online. The same subsection also states that a person using a bot is not liable under this section if the person discloses that it is a bot.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what § 17941(a) itself says about the prohibition and its disclosure-based exception; it does not state what counts as an adequate disclosure, which is addressed by § 17941(b) in a separate clause below — subsections (a) and (b) are part of the same statutory section and are not independent sources of authority from one another. This sheet does not address how the "intent to mislead" or "knowingly deceiving" elements would be proven or evaluated in any particular case, does not restate § 17942(a)'s statement that the chapter's duties are cumulative with other law, and does not address whether any particular automated account or communication falls within the prohibition.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17941(a)
citations.cite: Bots (Chapter 6), Unlawful Use of an Undisclosed Bot
citations.quote: (a) It shall be unlawful for any person to use a bot to communicate or interact with another person in California online, with the intent to mislead the other person about its artificial identity for the purpose of knowingly deceiving the person about the content of the communication in order to incentivize a purchase or sale of goods or services in a commercial transaction or to influence a vote in an election. A person using a bot shall not be liable under this section if the person discloses that it is a bot.

clauses.title: What the Statute Requires of an Adequate Disclosure
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 17941(b) states the standard for the disclosure that removes liability under subsection (a): the disclosure must be clear, conspicuous, and reasonably designed to inform persons with whom the bot communicates or interacts that it is a bot. The statute states this standard in general terms; its own text does not further define "clear," "conspicuous," or "reasonably designed," does not specify any particular wording, placement, format, or timing for the disclosure, and does not describe any specific disclosure method as automatically sufficient.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the general standard in § 17941(b)'s own text. This chapter does not itself define what disclosure content or format satisfies "clear, conspicuous, and reasonably designed"; this sheet does not identify any implementing regulations, administrative guidance, or case law construing that standard, and this research did not locate a codified safe harbor in this chapter. Subsection (b) is part of the same statutory section as the core prohibition in subsection (a), addressed in a separate clause above, and the two are not independent sources of authority from one another.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17941(b)
citations.cite: Bots (Chapter 6), Disclosure Standard
citations.quote: (b) The disclosure required by this section shall be clear, conspicuous, and reasonably designed to inform persons with whom the bot communicates or interacts that it is a bot.

clauses.title: Exemption for Service Providers of Online Platforms
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 17942(c) states that this chapter does not impose a duty on service providers of online platforms, including, but not limited to, web hosting and Internet service providers. The chapter separately defines "online platform," in § 17940(c), as any public-facing Internet website, web application, or digital application, including a social network or publication, that has 10,000,000 or more unique monthly United States visitors or users for a majority of months during the preceding 12 months.
clauses.gap: Because "online platform" is a defined term carrying the 10,000,000-monthly-visitor threshold quoted above, § 17942(c)'s exemption for service providers of "online platforms," read together with that definition, is narrower than an exemption for service providers of any website or app regardless of size — this sheet does not resolve whether or how that threshold would be applied to a given service provider or platform. Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17940 and 17942 are two separate, independently numbered sections; the two citations below are independent of one another. This sheet does not otherwise address what "service providers" of an online platform means, and this research did not locate any other exemption stated in this chapter's own text besides this one.

citations.cite: Bots (Chapter 6), Service Provider Exemption
citations.quote: (c) This chapter does not impose a duty on service providers of online platforms, including, but not limited to, Web hosting and Internet service providers.

clauses.title: Declaration and Purpose
clauses.body: This information sheet concerns a fee-charging employment agency relationship involving {{jobseekerName}} (the "jobseeker") and {{employmentAgencyName}}, identified here as an employment agency for reference only. This sheet summarizes provisions of California's Employment Agency, Employment Counseling, and Job Listing Services Act, Civil Code section 1812.500 et seq., which regulates businesses that charge a jobseeker -- rather than only an employer -- a fee to help the jobseeker find work. It is a distinct statute from California's Talent Agencies Act, Labor Code section 1700 et seq., which governs procuring engagements for artists in the entertainment industry.

clauses.title: Record and Signature
Who Is a Fee-Charging "Employment Agency": Statutory Definition
clauses.body:
California's Employment Agency, Employment Counseling, and Job Listing Services Act defines who is regulated as an "employment agency" under Civil Code section 1812.503 et seq. Civil Code section 1812.501(a)(1)(A) defines an "employment agency" or "agency" to include any person who, for a fee or other valuable consideration paid directly or indirectly by a jobseeker, procures, offers, promises, or attempts to procure employment for others, registers persons seeking employment, gives information about where employment may be procured, or provides employment. Section 1812.501(e) separately defines "jobseeker" to mean a person seeking employment.

The statute distinguishes an "employment agency" from two related, separately regulated categories that Civil Code section 1812.501(a)(2) expressly excludes from the "employment agency" definition: an "employment counseling service" (career counseling, résumé preparation, and similar services, defined in section 1812.501(b)) and a "job listing service" (defined in section 1812.501(c)). Whether {{employmentAgencyName}}'s services fall within the "employment agency" definition, the "employment counseling service" definition, the "job listing service" definition, or none of them is a fact this sheet does not state.

This clause relies on a single statutory section for both quoted definitions, so no source-independence disclosure beyond that dual-fetch consistency check applies. This clause states only the statutory definitions; it does not determine which category, if any, a given business falls into, and it does not address section 1812.501(d)'s separate treatment of a "nurses' registry" as an employment agency governed by a different chapter (Chapter 7, commencing with section 1812.524) rather than the Chapter 2 provisions (bonding, fee limits, prohibited practices) this document otherwise summarizes.

citations.quote: Any person who, for a fee or other valuable consideration to be paid, directly or indirectly by a jobseeker, performs, offers to perform, or represents it can or will perform any of the following services:

clauses.title: Surety Bond Requirement
clauses.body:
California does not require a fee-charging employment agency to hold a Labor-Commissioner-issued license comparable to the Talent Agencies Act's license. Instead, Civil Code section 1812.503(a) requires every employment agency subject to the Act to maintain a surety bond, in a principal sum of $3,000, issued by a surety company admitted to do business in California, with a copy filed with the Secretary of State. Section 1812.503(b) states that the bond is payable to the people of the State of California and exists for the benefit of any person damaged by a violation of the Act or by the agency's fraud, dishonesty, misrepresentation, or failure to provide the contracted services.

Section 1812.503(c)(1) states that no employment agency may conduct business without a current bond on file. The statute also permits a cash deposit filed with the Secretary of State in lieu of a bond, under a claims procedure the same section describes.

clauses.title: Jobseeker Fee Schedule, Disclosure, and Limits
clauses.body:
California law imposes disclosure and dollar limits on what a fee-charging employment agency may charge a jobseeker. Civil Code section 1812.505(a)(1) requires an employment agency to provide a copy of its jobseeker fee schedule and payment terms to any jobseeker from whom a fee or deposit is to be received, before the jobseeker is interviewed by a counselor, and requires the fee schedule to indicate the percentage of projected earnings the fee represents. Section 1812.505(a)(3) further requires the current fee schedule to be posted in a conspicuous place in the agency's office.

Section 1812.505(b) states that no fee charged or collected may exceed the fee as scheduled, and section 1812.505(c) separately prohibits an employment agency from accepting a registration fee of any kind. The same section also caps a jobseeker's total fee exposure: under section 1812.505(f)(3), in no case where the accepted employment is later terminated may the fee charged to the jobseeker exceed the jobseeker's total gross earnings from that employment.
clauses.gap: Civil Code section 1812.505 was fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as separate HTTP requests using two distinct User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical text for the full section after whitespace normalization. All three quotations below come from this single section, so this clause is not corroborated by an independent source. This clause states the fee-schedule disclosure requirement and the two flat prohibitions (no above-schedule fee, no registration fee) it quotes directly; it summarizes rather than quotes section 1812.505(f)(3)'s gross-earnings cap and the section's further provisions on temporary-employment fee proration, commission-based fee computation, and interagency fee disputes, which this clause does not otherwise cover. It does not state what fee schedule, if any, any particular employment agency has posted or provided.

clauses.title: Refund Where the Jobseeker Does Not Accept Employment
clauses.body:
California law addresses what happens to a fee or deposit a jobseeker has paid, or become obligated to pay, if the jobseeker does not accept the employment the agency arranged. Civil Code section 1812.506(a) states that in that circumstance, the employment agency must, upon the jobseeker's request, repay the deposit or fee, and if the repayment is not made within 48 hours of the request, the agency must additionally pay the jobseeker a sum equal to the amount of the deposit.

Section 1812.506(c)(1) separately requires that, except as otherwise addressed in subdivision (a), any refund due must be made within 10 working days of the jobseeker's request, or the agency must notify the jobseeker in writing of the specific reasons a refund is not being made.

This clause relies on a single statutory section, so it is not corroborated by an independent source. It quotes only subdivision (a) and summarizes subdivision (c)(1) rather than quoting it; it does not cover subdivision (b)'s separate rules distinguishing a refund or fee reduction for a jobseeker who leaves or is discharged from accepted employment within 90 days, including that subdivision's lists of what counts as "just cause" or "discharge for reasons other than misconduct" versus "misconduct." It does not state whether any refund is currently due between any particular jobseeker and employment agency.

citations.cite: Civil Code § 1812.506(a) (refund if employment not accepted)
citations.quote: If a jobseeker paying or becoming obligated to pay a fee, or making a deposit on a fee for placement fails to accept employment, the employment agency shall, upon request by the jobseeker, repay the amount of the deposit or fee to the jobseeker. Unless the deposit is returned within 48 hours after request, the employment agency shall pay to the jobseeker an additional sum equal to the amount of the deposit.

clauses.title: Prohibited Practices: Nonexistent Jobs and False Representations
clauses.body:
California law specifically prohibits an employment agency from referring a jobseeker to work on the basis of a job order the agency has reason to know does not check out. Civil Code section 1812.507(c) states that an employment agency may not refer a jobseeker to a job knowing or having reason to know that the job does not exist or the jobseeker is not qualified for it, or that the job has been described or advertised by or on behalf of the agency in a false, misleading, or deceptive manner.

A related, more general prohibition reaches advertising and representations to jobseekers as a whole. Civil Code section 1812.508(a) states that an employment agency may not make, or cause to be made, any false, misleading, or deceptive advertisements or representations concerning the services the agency will provide to jobseekers, and section 1812.508(b)(4) separately prohibits an employment agency from giving false information or making false promises or representations concerning an engagement or employment to any jobseeker who registers or applies for one.
clauses.gap: Civil Code sections 1812.507 and 1812.508 were each fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as separate HTTP requests using two distinct User-Agent headers; all four retrievals returned byte-identical text for their respective full sections after whitespace normalization. Sections 1812.507 and 1812.508 independently prohibit overlapping conduct (misrepresenting a job's existence or description), which corroborates that this is a settled feature of the statute rather than an artifact of a single section's drafting; beyond that, this clause is not corroborated by case law or a source outside the statute itself. It quotes only the specific job-order and advertising prohibitions above; it does not cover section 1812.508's separate, detailed rules on "FEE"/"NO FEE" advertisement labeling, salary-advertisement formatting, or the home-health-agency representation restriction, and it does not state whether any specific job referral, advertisement, or statement by any particular employment agency complied with these provisions.

citations.cite: Civil Code § 1812.507(c) (no referral to a job known to be nonexistent or falsely described)
citations.quote: No employment agency shall refer a jobseeker to a job knowing or having reason to know that: (1) The job does not exist or the jobseeker is not qualified for the job. (2) The job has been described or advertised by or on behalf of the agency in a false, misleading, or deceptive manner.

citations.quote: No employment agency shall make, or cause to be made, any false, misleading, or deceptive advertisements or representations concerning the services that the agency will provide to jobseekers.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes additional facts about California's split shift premium pay requirement under the Industrial Welfare Commission (IWC) Wage Orders, beyond the core one-hour premium formula and the live-in-employee exception already described in this project's Reporting Time Pay Information Sheet: the Wage Order's own formal definition of a "split shift," the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's (DLSE) stated position on how long an unpaid interruption must last before it is treated as a split shift rather than a bona fide meal or rest period, and the Wage Order's separate recordkeeping duty for split shift intervals. It states facts about how these requirements apply to {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}}. It does not restate the one-hour premium formula, the offset of wages paid above minimum wage, or the live-in-employee exception, all of which are addressed elsewhere in this project rather than repeated here.

clauses.title: The Wage Order's Definition of a "Split Shift"
clauses.body: The applicable IWC Wage Order defines a "split shift," for purposes of the split-shift premium requirement, as a work schedule that is interrupted by a non-paid, non-working period established by {{companyName}}, other than a bona fide rest or meal period. Under this definition, an interruption that qualifies as a bona fide rest or meal period does not, by itself, turn a day's schedule into a split shift.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 2(R) (the order's "Definitions" section), Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(R) — fetched directly from the California Department of Industrial Relations (dir.ca.gov) using two separate curl requests with different User-Agent strings, both returning byte-identical PDF content (HTTP 200), with the quoted text confirmed as an exact, whitespace-normalized substring of that fetched text (the source PDF line-wraps the sentence between "employer," and "other than," which this clause's quote collapses to a single space). This is the same wage order already cited elsewhere in this corpus for the split-shift premium formula itself (IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 4(C), quoted in this project's Reporting Time Pay Information Sheet) — the definition quoted here is a different, independently numbered subdivision of that same regulatory instrument, not an independent second source confirming the same fact from elsewhere. This clause states the Wage Order's own definitional text; it does not determine whether any specific interruption in a specific work schedule qualifies as a bona fide rest or meal period rather than a split-shift-triggering interruption — that threshold question is addressed, to the extent DLSE guidance was located and verified, in a separate clause of this document. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee.

citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(R)
citations.quote: a work schedule, which is interrupted by non-paid non-working periods established by the employer, other than bona fide rest or meal periods.

clauses.title: DLSE's Position on How Long an Interruption May Last Before It Becomes a Split Shift
clauses.body: California's Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (DLSE), the agency that enforces the Wage Orders, has stated its historical position that a "bona fide" meal period, for purposes of the split-shift definition, is one that does not exceed one hour (60 minutes) in length, and that an unpaid interruption exceeding one hour will give rise to a "split shift" situation.
clauses.gap: Both quotations in this clause's citations are drawn from a single source — a December 11, 2002 DLSE opinion letter (No. 2002.12.11, "Hours Worked — Split Shift") — and are two passages from the same short letter, not independent of one another. That letter was fetched directly from the California Department of Industrial Relations (dir.ca.gov) using two separate curl requests with different User-Agent strings, both returning byte-identical PDF content (HTTP 200); both quotations were confirmed as exact, whitespace-normalized substrings of that fetched text (the source PDF line-wraps each quoted passage mid-sentence, which this clause's quotes collapse to single spaces). The letter itself was written in response to an inquiry about IWC Wage Order No. 9-2001 (Transportation Industry), not Wage Order No. 4-2001, though the letter states that the same split-shift definition "provides, inter alia, at Section 4" — with materially the same operative language — "as with all of the orders," and this project independently confirmed the identical split-shift definition text in Wage Order No. 4-2001, section 2(R) (quoted in the preceding clause of this document). A DLSE opinion letter is agency interpretive guidance stating the Labor Commissioner's enforcement position; it is not itself the Wage Order's own codified regulatory text, and this clause does not determine whether it would be given controlling weight in a specific dispute. This is one state's regulatory and enforcement guidance, offered as documented evidence of what California requires — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employer or employee.
