clauses.title: Mello-Roos / Special Tax Notice Delivery
clauses.body: If {{propertyAddress}} is subject to a special tax lien of the kind described in the Mello-Roos disclosure provisions below, Seller shall deliver to Buyer any Notice of Special Tax or other disclosure notice required by those provisions before Buyer signs a contract to purchase or a deposit receipt for the property, separately from the Transfer Disclosure Statement and Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement referenced elsewhere in this agreement.

clauses.title: Notice of Special Tax — New-Subdivision Sales
clauses.body: Where a lot, parcel, or unit of a subdivision is subject to a special tax levied under the Mello-Roos Community Facilities Act of 1982, California law bars the subdivider, or the subdivider's agent or representative, from selling the lot, parcel, or unit, or leasing it for more than five years, or permitting a prospective purchaser to sign a contract of purchase or a deposit receipt, until that purchaser has been furnished with, and has signed, a written notice in a statutorily specified form. The notice must carry the heading "NOTICE OF SPECIAL TAX" in type no smaller than 8-point type, and the statutory form itself states that the property is subject to a special tax in addition to regular property taxes and other charges, that the tax is imposed because the property is part of a new development, and that if the tax is not paid when due each year the property may be foreclosed upon and sold. "Subdivision" for this purpose means improved or unimproved land divided, or proposed to be divided, into two or more lots, parcels, or units for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing, and by statutory definition includes a condominium project, a community apartment project, a stock cooperative, and a limited-equity housing cooperative.
clauses.gap: This statute's own operative language is keyed to a "subdivider" selling a "subdivision" as that term is defined in subdivision (b) — its most direct textual application is a sale by the entity that created or is marketing a new multi-lot development, not necessarily every later resale between private owners of an existing home. A separate, independently-authored statute — Civil Code Section 1102.6b, addressed in the next clause — supplies the disclosure mechanism for a sale that is subject to California's general residential Transfer Disclosure Statement article and where a notice is not otherwise required under this section; this document does not resolve, for any specific transaction, which of the two provisions applies or whether a given resale qualifies as a sale of a "subdivision" lot under this section's definition. Within this clause, the quotations of the core prohibition, the 8-point heading requirement, and the statutory notice-form's own warning language are all drawn from the same subsection, (a); only the "subdivision" definition is a separate, independent subsection, (b) — these are not independent corroborating sources of each other. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a special-tax notice obligation tied to a new-subdivision sale — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential purchase.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 53341.5(a)
citations.cite: California Government Code, the subdivider's core notice obligation
citations.quote: If a lot, parcel, or unit of a subdivision is subject to a special tax levied pursuant to this chapter, the subdivider, his or her agent, or representative, shall not sell, or lease for a term exceeding five years, or permit a prospective purchaser or lessor to sign a contract of purchase or a deposit receipt or any substantially equivalent document in the event of a lease with respect to the lot, parcel, or unit, or cause it to be sold or leased for a term exceeding five years, until the prospective purchaser or lessee of the lot, parcel, or unit has been furnished with and has signed a written notice as provided in this section.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 53341.5(a) [form heading]
citations.cite: California Government Code, the 8-point 'NOTICE OF SPECIAL TAX' heading requirement
citations.quote: The notice shall contain the heading “NOTICE OF SPECIAL TAX” in type no smaller than 8-point type, and shall be in substantially the following form.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 53341.5(a) [statutory form text]
citations.cite: California Government Code, the statutory notice form's own tax/foreclosure warning
citations.quote: This property is subject to a special tax, that is in addition to the regular property taxes and any other charges, fees, special taxes, and benefit assessments on the parcel. It is imposed on this property because it is a new development, and is not necessarily imposed generally upon property outside of this new development. If you fail to pay this tax when due each year, the property may be foreclosed upon and sold. The tax is used to provide public facilities or services that are likely to particularly benefit the property.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 53341.5(b)
citations.cite: California Government Code, statutory definition of 'subdivision'
citations.quote: “Subdivision,” as used in subdivision (a), means improved or unimproved land that is divided or proposed to be divided for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing, whether immediate or future, into two or more lots, parcels, or units and includes a condominium project, as defined by Section 4125 or 6542 of the Civil Code, a community apartment project, a stock cooperative, and a limited-equity housing cooperative, as defined in Sections 11004, 11003.2, and 11003.4, respectively, of the Business and Professions Code.

clauses.title: Special Tax Disclosure — General Residential Resales
clauses.body: Separately from the subdivider's notice obligation described above, a distinct provision of California's residential Transfer Disclosure Statement article applies to a sale of real property that is subject to that article generally, where the property is subject to a continuing lien securing a special tax levied under the Mello-Roos Community Facilities Act of 1982 (among other listed lien types), and where a notice is not otherwise required under the subdivider-notice statute above. In that situation, in addition to any other disclosure required by the Transfer Disclosure Statement article, the seller must make a good faith effort to obtain a disclosure notice concerning the special tax from each local agency that levies it, and must deliver that notice, or those notices, to the prospective buyer, as long as the local agency makes the notice available.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction supplies a second, resale-context Mello-Roos disclosure mechanism alongside the new-subdivision notice statute in the prior clause — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential purchase. The three quotations below — the section's applicability trigger, its description of the Mello-Roos lien, and its cross-reference to the subdivider-notice statute — are all drawn from the same subsection, (a), and are not independent of each other; only the good-faith-effort obligation, quoted from subsection (b), is a separate, independent subsection. The subsection (b) quotation, in the source statute's own text, also covers two other lien types (1915 Act assessment bonds and contractual assessment programs) that are outside this document's Mello-Roos scope; the quotation is reproduced in full because the statute states the seller's obligation toward all three lien types in one sentence, and this clause's body text above addresses only its application to a Mello-Roos special tax lien.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.6b(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, this section's applicability trigger
citations.quote: This section applies to all sales of real property for which all of the following apply:

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.6b(a)(2)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the Mello-Roos continuing-lien trigger
citations.quote: The property being sold is subject to a continuing lien securing the levy of special taxes pursuant to the Mello-Roos Community Facilities Act (Chapter 2.5 (commencing with Section 53311) of Part 1 of Division 2 of Title 5 of the Government Code), to a fixed lien assessment collected in installments to secure bonds issued pursuant to the Improvement Bond Act of 1915 (Division 10 (commencing with Section 8500) of the Streets and Highways Code), or to a contractual assessment program authorized pursuant to Chapter 29 (commencing with Section 5898.10) of Part 3 of Division 7 of the Streets and Highway Code.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.6b(a)(3)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, cross-reference to the subdivider-notice statute
citations.quote: A notice is not required pursuant to Section 53341.5 of the Government Code.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.6b(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the seller's good-faith-effort disclosure obligation
citations.quote: In addition to any other disclosure required pursuant to this article, the seller of any real property subject to this section shall make a good faith effort to obtain a disclosure notice concerning the special tax as provided for in Section 53340.2 of the Government Code, or a disclosure notice concerning an assessment installment as provided in Section 53754 of the Government Code, from each local agency that levies a special tax pursuant to the Mello-Roos Community Facilities Act, or that collects assessment installments to secure bonds issued pursuant to the Improvement Bond Act of 1915 (Division 10 (commencing with Section 8500) of the Streets and Highways Code), or a disclosure notice concerning the contractual assessment as provided in Section 5898.24 of the Streets and Highways Code, on the property being sold, and shall deliver that notice or those notices to the prospective buyer, as long as the notices are made available by the local agency.

clauses.title: Notice Timing and Buyer's Termination Right — Subdivision Sales
clauses.body: The subdivider's Notice of Special Tax must be furnished before the prospective purchaser enters into a contract to purchase the property, and the statutory form itself states that the seller is required to give the buyer the notice and to obtain a copy signed by the buyer acknowledging receipt. After receiving the notice, the buyer has three days after personal delivery, or five days after delivery by deposit in the mail, to terminate the purchase agreement or deposit receipt, by delivering written notice of that termination to the owner, subdivider, or agent.
clauses.gap: This timing and termination mechanism is specific to the subdivider's Notice of Special Tax under Government Code Section 53341.5, addressed in an earlier clause of this document; it is a separate, independently-authored statute from the Transfer Disclosure Statement article's own three/five/five-day disclosure-timing and termination mechanism cited elsewhere in this document, and this section's termination window does not include that other statute's five-day option for delivery of an electronic record. The two quotations below are drawn from different subsections of Section 53341.5 — the pre-signing framing is part of the statutory notice form's own text within subsection (a) (the same subsection already quoted for other purposes in the prior clause of this document, so it is not independent of those quotations), while the three/five-day termination window is quoted from the separate, independent subsection (c). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's approach to disclosure timing and a buyer's termination right in this specific context — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential purchase.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 53341.5(a) [pre-signing statement]
citations.cite: California Government Code, the notice form's own pre-signing timing statement
citations.quote: THIS IS A NOTIFICATION TO YOU PRIOR TO YOUR ENTERING INTO A CONTRACT TO PURCHASE THIS PROPERTY. THE SELLER IS REQUIRED TO GIVE YOU THIS NOTICE AND TO OBTAIN A COPY SIGNED BY YOU TO INDICATE THAT YOU HAVE RECEIVED AND READ A COPY OF THIS NOTICE.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 53341.5(c)
citations.cite: California Government Code, the buyer's three/five-day termination right
citations.quote: The buyer shall have three days after delivery in person or five days after delivery by deposit in the mail of any notice required by this section, to terminate his or her agreement by delivery of written notice of that termination to the owner, subdivider, or agent.

clauses.title: Consequence of Noncompliance — Subdivision Sales
clauses.body: A failure to furnish the Notice of Special Tax, or a buyer's failure to sign it, does not by itself invalidate the sale, lease, or other conveyance. Separately, a person or entity who willfully violates this notice requirement is liable to the purchaser for the purchaser's actual damages and, in addition, is guilty of a public offense punishable by a fine of up to five hundred dollars; the prevailing party in an action to enforce that liability or fine is entitled to reasonable attorney's fees.
clauses.gap: This remedy provision is specific to the subdivider's Notice of Special Tax under Government Code Section 53341.5, addressed in earlier clauses of this document; the general resale disclosure mechanism under Civil Code Section 1102.6b, also addressed in this document, does not itself state a comparable remedy provision — this clause does not assert that the same remedy applies to a failure under that other section. The two quotations below are drawn from separate, independent subsections of the same statutory section, (d) and (e). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's noncompliance consequence for this specific notice requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential purchase, and not a claim that the fine amount or damages standard stated here is current beyond this section's own text as fetched.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 53341.5(d)
citations.cite: California Government Code, failure to furnish/sign does not invalidate the transfer
citations.quote: The failure to furnish the notice to the buyer or lessee, and failure of the buyer or lessee to sign the notice of a special tax, shall not invalidate any grant, conveyance, lease, or encumbrance.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 53341.5(e)
citations.cite: California Government Code, liability, public-offense fine, and attorney's fees for a willful violation
citations.quote: Any person or entity who willfully violates the provisions of this section shall be liable to the purchaser of a lot or unit that is subject to the provisions of this section, for actual damages, and in addition thereto, shall be guilty of a public offense punishable by a fine in an amount not to exceed five hundred dollars ($500). In an action to enforce a liability or fine, the prevailing party shall be awarded reasonable attorney’s fees.

clauses.title: Scope Limits of the Resale Disclosure Obligation
clauses.body: Under the general residential resale disclosure mechanism described above, once a qualifying disclosure has been delivered to the buyer, the seller or the seller's agent is not required to provide additional information on the subject, and the delivered disclosure is deemed to satisfy the seller's or agent's responsibility to inform the buyer about the special tax or assessment installments and the levying district. That same provision also states that nothing in it imposes a duty to discover a special tax, an assessment installment, or the existence of a levying district that is not actually known to the seller's or agent's agents.
clauses.gap: This scope-limiting language is part of the same statutory section as the resale disclosure mechanism addressed in an earlier clause of this document, Civil Code Section 1102.6b, but is drawn from a separate, independent subsection, (e); it is not an independent corroborating source for the disclosure obligation itself. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction bounds a seller's resale disclosure duty in this specific context — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential purchase, and not a statement about what duty, if any, exists under a different disclosure statute (including the subdivider-notice statute addressed elsewhere in this document, which contains no comparable 'not actually known' limitation in its own text as fetched).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.6b(e)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the disclosure's sufficiency and the no-duty-to-discover limitation
citations.quote: If a disclosure received pursuant to subdivision (b), (c), or (d) has been delivered to the buyer, a seller or his or her agent is not required to provide additional information concerning, and information in the disclosure shall be deemed to satisfy the responsibility of the seller or his or her agent to inform the buyer regarding the special tax or assessment installments and the district. Notwithstanding subdivision (b), (c), or (d), nothing in this section imposes a duty to discover a special tax or assessment installments or the existence of any levying district not actually known to the agents.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's structural pest control inspection report requirements (Business and Professions Code §§ 8516-8519, and the related delivery requirement in Civil Code § 1099) as they may apply to the property at {{propertyAddress}}, as between {{sellerName}} and {{buyerName}}. It states what California law provides on this subject. It does not authorize, direct, or prepare any inspection report, certification, or notice, and it does not resolve whether an inspection report or certification is a condition of any specific contract or financing arrangement.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
clauses.body:
This information sheet regarding structural pest control inspection reports under California's Business and Professions Code, concerning the property at {{propertyAddress}} as between {{sellerName}} and {{buyerName}}, states California law as of the date below. It does not constitute legal advice about, and does not resolve, any specific inspection, infestation, or disclosure question.

Prepared: _______________________ Date: _______________

clauses.title: When a Structural Pest Control Inspection Report Must Be Delivered to a Buyer
clauses.body: Separately from Business and Professions Code §§ 8516-8519 (which govern how a structural pest control inspection report and certification must be prepared once one exists), California's Civil Code states a distinct delivery-to-buyer rule keyed to whether the report was called for in the first place. As soon as practical before transfer of title of real property (or execution of a real property sales contract), a transferor or the transferor's agent must deliver to the transferee a copy of a structural pest control inspection report, upon which a certification may be made, provided that certification or preparation of a report is a condition of the contract effecting the transfer, or is a requirement imposed as a condition of financing the transfer. If a notice of work completed, or a certification, is received by the transferor or the transferor's agent before transfer of title, it must likewise be furnished to the transferee as soon as practical before transfer of title. Noncompliance does not by itself invalidate the transfer, unless the noncompliance is separately a valid ground for rescission.
clauses.gap: This statute's delivery duty is conditional, not universal: its own text ties the duty to certification or preparation of a report being a condition of the contract effecting the transfer, or a requirement imposed as a condition of financing the transfer -- this document does not determine, for any specific transaction, whether a report or certification is in fact such a condition (for example, because a purchase contract requires one, or because a lender requires one for the loan). Where no report or certification is a condition of the contract or of financing, this specific delivery duty, by its own terms, does not apply -- this document takes no position on whether some other disclosure duty might separately require disclosing a known infestation. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a report-delivery duty tied to a real estate transfer -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transaction. The two citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1099) rather than independently authored sources.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1099(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, delivery of a structural pest control inspection report conditioned on it being a contract or financing condition
citations.quote: As soon as practical before transfer of title of any real property or the execution of a real property sales contract as defined in Section 2985, the transferor, fee owner, or his or her agent, shall deliver to the transferee a copy of a structural pest control inspection report prepared pursuant to Section 8516 of the Business and Professions Code upon which any certification in accordance with Section 8519 of the Business and Professions Code may be made, provided that certification or preparation of a report is a condition of the contract effecting that transfer, or is a requirement imposed as a condition of financing such transfer.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1099(d)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, noncompliance doesn't by itself invalidate the transfer
citations.quote: No transfer of title of real property shall be invalidated solely because of the failure of any person to comply with the provisions of this section unless such failure is an act or omission which would be a valid ground for rescission of such transfer in the absence of this section.

clauses.title: Who Must Perform the Inspection, and When the Report Must Be Delivered
clauses.body: California's Structural Pest Control Act, within the Business and Professions Code, applies these requirements only to "wood destroying pests or organisms." A registered structural pest control company or licensee may not commence work on a contract, or sign, issue, or deliver any document expressing an opinion or statement about the absence or presence of wood destroying pests or organisms, until an inspection has been made by a licensed Branch 3 field representative or operator employed by a registered company (subject to a narrow statutory exception). A written inspection report conforming to the statute, on a board-approved form, must then be prepared and delivered to the person who requested the inspection and to the property owner (or the owner's designated agent) within 10 business days from the start of the inspection -- except that a report prepared for use by an attorney for litigation purposes need not be delivered to the board or the property owner. The report must be delivered before work is commenced on the property.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what Business and Professions Code § 8516(b) itself requires once an inspection and report are undertaken; it does not state whether a specific transaction requires an inspection to be ordered in the first place (see the separate clause on the Civil Code § 1099 delivery trigger), nor does it list every item the statute requires the report itself to contain (subdivision (b) goes on to list thirteen specific content requirements, including a foundation diagram, roof-inspection statement, and a mandatory notice about the right to a second opinion, which are not quoted here). This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction licenses and times a structural pest inspection report -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transaction. The two citations below are both from subdivision (b) of the same statutory section (Business and Professions Code § 8516) rather than independently authored sources. Business and Professions Code § 8520, sometimes assumed to be part of this inspection-report framework, is not: it is a separate, independent section (opening a different article of the same chapter) that establishes the existence of the Structural Pest Control Board and is subject to its own sunset/repeal date, and it is not cited here as authority for any inspection-report requirement.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8516(b)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, inspection must be made by a licensed Branch 3 field representative or operator of a registered company
citations.quote: A registered company or licensee shall not commence work on a contract, or sign, issue, or deliver any documents expressing an opinion or statement relating to the absence or presence of wood destroying pests or organisms until an inspection has been made by a licensed Branch 3 field representative or operator employed by a registered company, except as provided in Section 8519.5.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8516(b) [report delivery timing]
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, written report must be delivered within 10 business days
citations.quote: A written inspection report conforming to this section and a form approved by the board shall be prepared and delivered to the person requesting the inspection and the property owner, or to the property owner’s designated agent, within 10 business days from the start of the inspection, except that an inspection report prepared for use by an attorney for litigation purposes is not required to be reported to the board or the property owner.

clauses.title: The Report's Distinction Between Evident Infestation and Conditions Likely to Lead to Infestation
clauses.body: California's structural pest control inspection statute distinguishes, in its own text, between two categories of finding. On request at the time a report is ordered, a registered company or licensee must separately identify, for each recommendation for corrective measures: (1) the infestation or infection that is evident, and (2) the conditions that are present that are deemed likely to lead to infestation or infection. The board-prescribed inspection report form itself is required to separately identify these same two categories. The statute states that, in no event may a condition deemed likely to lead to infestation or infection be characterized as an actual "defect" or an actual "active" infestation or infection, or as needing correction as a precondition to issuing a certification.
clauses.gap: This clause states the statute's own two-category distinction; it does not itself label these categories as "Section 1" and "Section 2" (a naming convention used on the board-prescribed inspection report form and in general industry usage) -- that form's exact current wording could not be independently verified from a fetchable primary source within this research, so this clause states the statutory text underlying the distinction rather than the form's own labels. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction's inspection-report statute distinguishes evident infestation from conditions likely to lead to infestation -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transaction or property. The two citations below are both from Business and Professions Code § 8516, one from subdivision (c) and one from subdivision (e) of that same section, rather than independently authored sources.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8516(c)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, the two categories a requested separate report must identify
citations.quote: (1) The infestation or infection that is evident. (2) The conditions that are present that are deemed likely to lead to infestation or infection.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8516(e)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, a likely-to-lead condition may not be characterized as an actual defect or active infestation
citations.quote: In no event, however, shall conditions deemed likely to lead to infestation or infection be characterized as actual “defects” or as actual “active” infestations or infections or in need of correction as a precondition to issuing a certification pursuant to Section 8519.

clauses.title: The Optional Certification of No Active Infestation
clauses.body: Separately from the inspection report itself, California law provides for an optional "certification." A registered company that makes an inspection report must, if requested by the person who ordered the report, prepare and deliver to that person (or a designated agent) a certification. Where the inspection report disclosed no infestation or infection, the statute specifies the certification's text: "This is to certify that the above property was inspected on ____ (date(s)) in accordance with the Structural Pest Control Act and rules and regulations adopted pursuant thereto, and that no evidence of active infestation or infection was found in the visible and accessible areas." The statute specifies different required text for a certification issued after disclosed infestation or infection has been corrected, or corrected only in part, and for a certification following a limited inspection report.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the certification text for the "no infestation disclosed" scenario; the statute specifies three additional certification texts (for completed correction, partial correction, and a limited-inspection-report scenario) that are not separately quoted here. Certification is requested, not automatic -- this clause does not state that a certification is issued in every transaction where an inspection report exists. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a post-inspection certification -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transaction. The two citations below are both from Business and Professions Code § 8519 rather than independently authored sources.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8519
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, certification must be prepared and delivered if requested
citations.quote: Any registered company which makes an inspection report pursuant to Section 8516, shall, if requested by the person ordering the inspection report, prepare and deliver to that person or his or her designated agent, a certification, to provide:

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8519(a)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, statutory certification text where no infestation or infection was disclosed
citations.quote: This is to certify that the above property was inspected on ____ (date(s)) in accordance with the Structural Pest Control Act and rules and regulations adopted pursuant thereto, and that no evidence of active infestation or infection was found in the visible and accessible areas.

clauses.title: Later Correspondence Must Reference the Report, and Completed Work Must Be Noticed
clauses.body: California law extends the inspection-report requirement to later documents. Any work contract, billing, agreement, letter of work completed, or other correspondence or document expressing an opinion or making a statement about the presence or absence of wood destroying pests or organisms must refer to the inspection report, and must specifically indicate whether all of the report's recommended work was completed or, if not, which recommendations were not completed. Separately, when a registered company completes work under a contract, it must prepare, on a board-prescribed form, a notice of work completed and not completed, and furnish that notice to the property owner (or the owner's agent) within 10 business days after completing the work; the notice must state the cost of the completed work and the estimated cost of work not completed.
clauses.gap: This clause does not state whether any particular correspondence or billing document falls within the described category, or whether any particular work has in fact been completed. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction ties later correspondence and work-completion notices back to the original inspection report -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transaction. The two citations below are from two separate, independently authored sections of the same statutory chapter (Business and Professions Code §§ 8517 and 8518), not subsections of a single section.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8517
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, later documents must refer to the inspection report and completion status
citations.quote: Any work contract, billing, agreement, letter of work completed, or other correspondence or document expressing an opinion or making a statement relating to the presence or absence of wood destroying pests or organisms, shall refer to the inspection report required by Section 8516. These documents shall indicate specifically whether all of the recommended work as set forth in the inspection report was completed, or, if not, the document shall indicate specifically which recommendations were not completed.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 8518(a)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, notice of work completed and not completed
citations.quote: When a registered company completes work under a contract, it shall prepare, on a form prescribed by the board, a notice of work completed and not completed, and shall furnish that notice to the owner of the property or the owner’s agent within 10 business days after completing the work. The notice shall include a statement of the cost of the completed work and estimated cost of work not completed.

clauses.title: Background Information — Trust Director / ‘Trust Protector’ Role
clauses.body: I, {{settlorName}}, am the settlor of {{trustName}}, and {{trusteeName}} is serving, or is proposed to serve, as trustee. This information sheet describes California's statutory framework governing a person who holds authority over some aspect of a trust's administration without serving as trustee — a role a trust instrument itself might label a "trust protector," "trust advisor," "special trustee," or "trust director," and which California's own statute calls a "trust director" holding a "power of direction," under the California Uniform Directed Trust Act, Probate Code §§ 16600-16632. This information sheet is background only: it is not itself a grant of a power of direction to {{trustDirectorName}} or anyone else, does not appoint {{trustDirectorName}} to any role, and does not modify {{trustName}}'s terms. Only {{trustName}}'s own instrument — or a document that amends it using whatever method that instrument or California law makes available — actually grants a power of direction or appoints a trust director.

clauses.title: Signature and Record Block — Trust Director Background Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{settlorName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared as background regarding California's California Uniform Directed Trust Act, Probate Code §§ 16600-16632. It does not itself grant a power of direction, appoint {{trustDirectorName}} as a trust director, or modify {{trustName}}'s terms; only {{trustName}}'s own instrument, drafted and executed in the manner California law requires for a trust amendment or restatement, does that.]

clauses.title: ‘Trust Director’ Is California's Statutory Term — the Statute Itself Does Not Use ‘Trust Protector’
clauses.body: California codified this role in 2023, effective January 1, 2024, as part of the California Uniform Directed Trust Act, Probate Code §§ 16600-16632. The statute's own text uses the terms "trust director," "power of direction," "directed trust," and "directed trustee" — it does not use the phrase "trust protector" anywhere in its operative sections or in the bill that enacted it. Under the statute, a "trust director" is a person granted a power of direction by the terms of a trust, to the extent that power is exercisable while the person is not serving as trustee, and a person is a trust director under this definition regardless of what label the trust instrument itself gives the role — so a role a specific trust instrument calls a "trust protector" can still be a "trust director" for purposes of this statute, and the statute's default rules described elsewhere in this document can still apply to it, depending on how that instrument actually defines the role's powers.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual statutory term California uses for this role and how broadly that term reaches — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a determination that any specific trust instrument's own "trust protector," "trust advisor," or similarly labeled role in fact grants a "power of direction" as the statute defines it. This document does not independently verify that no other operative California statute anywhere uses the phrase "trust protector"; it reports that a search of this specific chapter's text and of the text of the bill that enacted it (2023 Senate Bill 801) did not turn up that phrase. This clause cites two different statutory provisions — § 16600(b) and § 16602(g) — both from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16600(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the Legislature's own description of the arrangement this chapter governs (Probate Code § 16600(b))
citations.quote: This chapter governs an arrangement commonly known as a directed trust. (2) In a directed trust, the terms of the trust grant a person other than a trustee a power over some aspect of the trust’s administration. (3) Under this chapter, this power is called a power of direction, the person that holds the power is called a trust director, a trustee that is subject to the power is called a directed trustee, and the trust is a directed trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16602(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory definition of 'trust director' (Probate Code § 16602(g))
citations.quote: “Trust director” means a person that is granted a power of direction by the terms of a trust, to the extent the power is exercisable while the person is not serving as a trustee. The person is a trust director whether or not the terms of the trust refer to the person as a trust director and whether or not the person is a beneficiary or settlor of the trust.

clauses.title: The Scope of a ‘Power of Direction’ — and What the Statute Excludes From It
clauses.body: A trust instrument may grant a "power of direction" to a trust director, and unless the instrument provides otherwise, a trust director may also exercise any further power appropriate to exercising or not exercising that granted power; where more than one trust director holds a power jointly, the default rule is majority decision, again unless the trust instrument provides otherwise. The statute defines "power of direction" broadly to include a power over the investment, management, or distribution of trust property, or other matters of trust administration — but that definition is not unlimited. The statute expressly excludes several specific powers from its own coverage: a power of appointment; the power to appoint or remove a trustee or trust director; a settlor's own power to revoke the trust; a beneficiary's power over the beneficiary's own beneficial interest; and a power that the trust instrument itself requires to be held in a nonfiduciary capacity to achieve the settlor's federal tax objectives. Because the power to appoint or remove a trustee is expressly excluded, a role that a trust instrument gives only that power — without also granting a power over investment, management, distribution, or some other matter of trust administration — falls outside this statute's own definition of a "power of direction," and the default rules on fiduciary status, trustee compliance, and procedure described elsewhere in this document, which this statute supplies, do not by the statute's own terms reach that power.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual scope and exclusions California's statute states — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a determination that any specific power granted by any specific trust instrument does or does not fall within this statute's definition of a 'power of direction.' This corrects a natural but imprecise assumption: a role commonly described in general estate-planning practice as including the power to remove or appoint a trustee is not, as to that particular power, governed by this chapter's own fiduciary-status and compliance rules — some other body of California trust law may or may not separately govern the exercise of a power to remove or appoint a trustee held by someone other than the trustee, and this document does not independently research or address what that other law provides. This clause cites two different statutory provisions — § 16608 and § 16602(d), together with the exclusions listed in § 16606(a) — all from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16602(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory definition of 'power of direction,' including its cross-reference to the exclusions (Probate Code § 16602(d))
citations.quote: “Power of direction” means a power over a trust granted to a person by the terms of the trust to the extent the power is exercisable while the person is not serving as a trustee. Power of direction includes a power over the investment, management, or distribution of trust property or other matters of trust administration. The term excludes the powers described in subdivision (a) of Section 16606.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16608 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the grant of a power of direction, further powers, and the default majority rule for joint trust directors (Probate Code § 16608)
citations.quote: (a) Subject to Section 16610, the terms of a trust may grant a power of direction to a trust director. (b) Unless the terms of a trust provide otherwise, a trust director may exercise any further power appropriate to the exercise or nonexercise of a power of direction granted to the trust director pursuant to subdivision (a). (c) Unless the terms of a trust provide otherwise, trust directors with joint powers shall act by majority decision.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16606(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the specific powers the statute excludes from its own coverage, including the power to appoint or remove a trustee (Probate Code § 16606(a))
citations.quote: (a) This chapter does not apply to any of the following: (1) A power of appointment. (2) The power to appoint or remove a trustee or trust director. (3) The power of a settlor over a trust, to the extent the settlor has a power to revoke the trust. (4) The power of a beneficiary over a trust, to the extent the exercise or nonexercise of the power affects the beneficial interest of the beneficiary. (5) The power over a trust if both of the following apply: (A) The terms of the trust provide that the power is held in a nonfiduciary capacity. (B) The power is required to be held in a nonfiduciary capacity to achieve the settlor’s tax objectives under the United States Internal Revenue Code of 1986 and regulations issued thereunder.

clauses.title: The Trust Director's Default Fiduciary Status and Standard of Care
clauses.body: Unless a trust instrument provides otherwise, a trust director has — in exercising or not exercising a power of direction, or a further power appropriate to it — the same fiduciary duty and liability that a trustee would have in a like position and under similar circumstances: the same standard as a sole trustee if the trust director holds the power individually, or the same standard as a cotrustee if the power is held jointly with a trustee or another trust director. The trust instrument may vary that duty or liability to the same extent it could vary a trustee's duty or liability in a like position — meaning the statute's default fiduciary standard, like much of trustee law generally, is one the trust instrument itself can adjust, not an immovable floor. A separate default carve-out applies to a trust director who is licensed, certified, or otherwise authorized to provide health care in the ordinary course of that person's business or profession: unless the trust instrument provides otherwise, that person has no duty or liability under this statute to the extent they are acting in that health-care capacity.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default fiduciary standard California's statute states for a trust director — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a determination of any specific trust director's actual liability in any specific circumstance. The statute's default standard is expressly variable by the trust instrument in both directions — it can be raised, lowered, or otherwise reshaped to the same extent a trustee's own duty or liability could be — so this clause states only the default that applies absent a contrary instrument provision, not what a specific instrument's own terms actually provide. This clause cites three different subdivisions of the same statutory section, Probate Code § 16612 (subdivisions (a)(1), (a)(2), and (b)), all from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16612(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the default fiduciary duty and liability standard for a trust director (Probate Code § 16612(a)(1))
citations.quote: A trust director has the same fiduciary duty and liability in the exercise or nonexercise of the power, if the power is held individually, as a sole trustee in a like position and under similar circumstances or, if the power is held jointly with a trustee or another trust director, as a cotrustee in a like position and under similar circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16612(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trust instrument's ability to vary that duty or liability (Probate Code § 16612(a)(2))
citations.quote: The terms of the trust may vary the trust director’s duty or liability to the same extent the terms of the trust could vary the duty or liability of a trustee in a like position and under similar circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16612(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the default carve-out for a trust director acting in a licensed health-care capacity (Probate Code § 16612(b))
citations.quote: Unless the terms of a trust provide otherwise, if a trust director is licensed, certified, or otherwise authorized or permitted by law other than this chapter to provide health care in the ordinary course of the trust director’s business or practice of a profession, to the extent the trust director acts in that capacity, the trust director has no duty or liability under this chapter.

clauses.title: How a Trust Director's Power Relates to the Trustee's Own Duties
clauses.body: Where a trust instrument grants a power of direction to a trust director, the statute also addresses how the trustee — called a "directed trustee" once subject to that power — must respond to it. Subject to one specific exception, a directed trustee must take reasonable action to comply with a trust director's exercise or nonexercise of a power of direction, and, by default, is not liable for taking that action. The exception: a directed trustee must not comply with a trust director's exercise or nonexercise of a power of direction to the extent that complying would itself amount to willful misconduct by the trustee. Separately, the statute imposes a default, reciprocal information-sharing duty: a trustee must provide a trust director, and a trust director must provide a trustee or another trust director, with information that is reasonably related both to that person's own powers or duties and to the recipient's powers or duties.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's statute addresses the relationship between a trust director's power and a directed trustee's own duties — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a determination of any specific trustee's or trust director's actual compliance obligations in any specific circumstance. This document does not address several related default rules in the same chapter that this research did not develop into their own clauses, including the default rule that neither a trustee nor a trust director has a duty to monitor the other or to volunteer advice about how the other might have acted differently (§ 16618), the parallel rule allowing similar relief between cotrustees outside the directed-trust context (§ 16620), the limitation period and available defenses for a breach-of-trust action against a trust director (§§ 16622, 16624), or personal jurisdiction over a trust director who accepts appointment (§ 16626). This clause cites two different statutory sections — § 16614 (subdivisions (a) and (b)) and § 16616 (subdivisions (a) and (b)) — both from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16614(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the default rule that a directed trustee must comply, and is not liable for complying (Probate Code § 16614(a))
citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivision (b), a directed trustee shall take reasonable action to comply with a trust director’s exercise or nonexercise of a power of direction or further power under subdivision (b) of Section 16608, and the trustee is not liable for the action.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16614(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the exception where compliance would itself be willful misconduct (Probate Code § 16614(b))
citations.quote: (b) A directed trustee shall not comply with a trust director’s exercise or nonexercise of a power of direction or further power under subdivision (b) of Section 16608 to the extent that, by complying, the trustee would engage in willful misconduct.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16616(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the reciprocal default duty to share information reasonably related to both persons' powers or duties (Probate Code § 16616(a)-(b))
citations.quote: (a) Subject to Section 16618, a trustee shall provide information to a trust director to the extent the information is reasonably related both to the powers or duties of the trustee and the powers or duties of the trust director. (b) Subject to Section 16618, a trust director shall provide information to a trustee or another trust director to the extent the information is reasonably related both to the powers or duties of the trust director and the powers or duties of the trustee or other trust director.

clauses.title: Default Procedural Rules — Acceptance, Bond, Compensation, Resignation, Vacancy, and When the Statute Applies
clauses.body: Unless a trust instrument provides otherwise, the same statutory rules that apply to a trustee's acceptance of office, the giving of a bond to secure performance, reasonable compensation, resignation or removal, and filling a vacancy in office also apply by default to a trust director. This means a trust instrument that appoints a trust director without separately addressing these mechanics can, by default, fall back on the same statutory framework California's Probate Code already supplies for a trustee in each of those areas. Separately, the statute itself states when it applies at all: it reaches a trust, whenever created, that has its principal place of administration in California, and for a trust created before January 1, 2024, the statute applies only to a decision or action occurring on or after that date — meaning a trust created earlier is not retroactively subject to this statute's rules for decisions or actions that occurred before its effective date.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual default procedural rules and applicability date California's statute states for a trust director — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a determination of whether a specific trust's principal place of administration is, in fact, California. This document does not independently quote or address the individual trustee-focused statutory sections that § 16628 cross-references (Probate Code §§ 15600, 15601, 15602, 15681, and the resignation, removal, and vacancy provisions beginning at § 15640 and at § 15660) — some of those same provisions are addressed in a different clause elsewhere in this corpus, in the context of a trustee rather than a trust director, and are not re-quoted here. This clause cites two different statutory sections — § 16628 and § 16604(a) — both from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16628 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the default rules that apply to a trust director by cross-reference to trustee rules on acceptance, bond, compensation, resignation, and vacancy (Probate Code § 16628)
citations.quote: Unless the terms of a trust provide otherwise, the rules applicable to a trustee apply to a trust director regarding all of the following matters: (a) Acceptance under Sections 15600 and 15601. (b) Giving of a bond to secure performance under Section 15602. (c) Reasonable compensation under Section 15681. (d) Resignation or removal under Article 3 (commencing with Section 15640) of Chapter 1. (e) Vacancy and appointment of a successor under Section 15660.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16604(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: when the statute applies, including its non-retroactive effect for a trust created before January 1, 2024 (Probate Code § 16604(a))
citations.quote: (a) This chapter applies to a trust, whenever created, that has its principal place of administration in this state, subject to all of the following rules: (1) If the trust was created before January 1, 2024, this chapter applies only to a decision or action occurring on or after that date. (2) If the principal place of administration of the trust is changed to this state on or after January 1, 2024, this chapter applies only to a decision or action occurring on or after the date of the change.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: California's Uniform Simultaneous Death Act — Probate Code Part 5 (§§ 220-234), Chapter 1, General Provisions (§§ 220-226) — sets the general default rule for how property passes when two or more people die at the same time, or when it cannot be established which of them died first. This information sheet explains that general statutory framework and its application to intestate succession, gifts conditioned on survivorship generally, joint tenancy, and community property. Two more specific default rules addressed elsewhere in this corpus are not repeated here: the 120-hour survival rule for a will beneficiary, covered in this corpus's Last Will and Testament document, and the simultaneous-death rule for a named life insurance beneficiary, covered in this corpus's Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation document.

clauses.title: The General Default Rule When Priority of Death Can't Be Established
clauses.body: California's Uniform Simultaneous Death Act sets a general default rule under Prob. Code § 220: except as otherwise provided elsewhere in the same chapter, if title to property or its devolution depends on which of two people died first, and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that one of them survived the other, each person's property is administered or distributed as if that person had survived the other. This baseline rule turns on a clear-and-convincing-evidence standard about who survived whom — it does not itself set a fixed 120-hour, or any other numeric, survival period. A specific survival-period requirement, where one applies, comes from a more specific statute outside or within this chapter, not from § 220 itself.
clauses.gap: This is California's own general default provision, used as evidence of what the statute itself provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reader's property, and not a statement about how a court would resolve any actual case's evidence of who died first. Section 220 opens with the phrase "Except as otherwise provided in this chapter," meaning the more specific default rules addressed elsewhere in this clause set (gifts conditioned on survivorship generally, joint tenancy) and in this corpus's other documents (a will beneficiary's 120-hour rule, a life insurance beneficiary's rule) can and do displace this general rule for their particular subject matter — § 220 is the residual baseline, not necessarily the rule that ultimately controls a given asset. This is a single statutory section; no additional independent source was found for this citation.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 220
citations.cite: California Probate Code, general default rule when priority of death cannot be established
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this chapter, if the title to property or the devolution of property depends upon priority of death and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that one of the persons survived the other, the property of each person shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, as if that person had survived the other.

clauses.title: How More Specific Default Rules Relate to This General Rule
clauses.body: This chapter's general default rule does not operate in isolation. Under Prob. Code § 221(a), the chapter containing §§ 220-226 does not apply at all in any case where Prob. Code § 103 (community or quasi-community property between spouses), § 6211 (a California statutory will), or § 6403 (intestate succession) applies — each of those is a separate statute with its own default rule, not simply a restatement of § 220. Section 6403's 120-hour survival requirement for intestate succession is one such distinct, separately triggered rule; it is not an application of § 220 itself, and the two are not interchangeable. Separately, under Prob. Code § 221(b), this chapter also does not apply where a trust, deed, insurance contract, or other governing document makes its own explicit provision for simultaneous death, a common-disaster clause, or a stated survival period different from this chapter's own default.
clauses.gap: This is California's own statute describing how its general default rule relates to more specific default rules found elsewhere in the Probate Code — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reader's situation, and not a determination of which particular statute (§ 103, § 6211, or § 6403) applies to any actual asset or instrument. Only § 221(a) is quoted as a citation here; § 221(b) is deliberately not re-quoted because this corpus's Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation document (clause: Simultaneous Death of the Insured and a Beneficiary) already quotes it in full — this clause cross-references that existing quote rather than duplicating it. This clause likewise does not restate or re-verify the 120-hour text of § 6403(a), already quoted and verified in this corpus's Last Will and Testament document (clause: If a Beneficiary Dies at Nearly the Same Time); § 6403 is described here only to disclose, as § 221(a) itself confirms, that it is a genuinely distinct, separately triggered provision rather than an application of § 220 — this clause does not treat the two as the same rule. Prob. Code § 6211 (a California statutory will's own 120-hour provision) is named by § 221(a) but was not independently fetched or verified for this clause set, and this clause does not assume it is identical in scope to § 6403's intestate-succession rule; that specific question is left to this corpus's will-specific material rather than resolved here. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for the § 221(a) citation itself.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 221(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, general chapter inapplicable where a more specific statute governs
citations.quote: This chapter does not apply in any case where Section 103, 6211, or 6403 applies.

clauses.title: Gifts Conditioned on Survivorship, Generally
clauses.body: Beyond the baseline rule in § 220, Prob. Code § 222 sets a more specific default for a disposition of property that makes a beneficiary's right to it conditional on surviving another person. If it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that the beneficiary survived that other person, the beneficiary is deemed not to have survived them. Where two or more beneficiaries would each have taken the entire property only by surviving the others, and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that any one of them survived the rest, the property is instead divided into as many equal portions as there are beneficiaries, and each portion is administered or distributed as if that beneficiary had survived the others.
clauses.gap: This is California's own statute governing conditional survivorship gifts generally — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific reader's trust, deed, or other instrument, and not a statement about how to word a survivorship condition. Prob. Code § 222(a) and (b) are two subsections of the same statutory section, not independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. This clause does not address the joint-tenancy-specific version of this same kind of rule, which Prob. Code § 223 states separately and which is addressed in a separate clause in this set rather than here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 222(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, a beneficiary deemed not to have survived where conditional survivorship can't be established
citations.quote: If property is so disposed of that the right of a beneficiary to succeed to any interest in the property is conditional upon surviving another person and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that the beneficiary survived the other person, the beneficiary is deemed not to have survived the other person.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 222(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, equal-portion division among mutually-conditioned beneficiaries
citations.quote: If property is so disposed of that one of two or more beneficiaries would have been entitled to the property if he or she had survived the others, and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that any beneficiary survived any other beneficiary, the property shall be divided into as many equal portions as there are beneficiaries and the portion of each beneficiary shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, as if that beneficiary had survived the other beneficiaries.

clauses.title: Joint Tenancy: Division Into Equal Shares at Simultaneous Death
clauses.body: California has a default rule specifically for property held in joint tenancy when the joint tenants die simultaneously, or when it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence which of them survived. Under Prob. Code § 223, "joint tenants" for this purpose includes anyone who owns property under circumstances entitling one or more of them to the whole of it on the others' death — a broader, functional definition rather than a formal-title-only one. If two joint tenants have died and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that one survived the other, the property is administered or distributed one-half as if one joint tenant had survived and one-half as if the other had survived — dividing what would otherwise have passed entirely to a survivor into two separate halves. If more than two joint tenants have died and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that any of them survived the others, the property is instead divided into as many equal portions as there are joint tenants, with each portion administered or distributed as if that joint tenant had survived the rest.
clauses.gap: This is California's own statute, used as evidence of what the law provides for jointly held property specifically — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reader's property, and not a statement about how title to any actual jointly held asset should be recorded or transferred. Prob. Code § 223(a), (b), and (c) are three subsections of the same statutory section, not independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. This rule is distinct from, and stated separately from, this chapter's general rule for conditional survivorship gifts (§ 222) and its default rule for community or quasi-community property (§ 103), each addressed in a separate clause in this set.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 223(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, definition of joint tenants for the simultaneous-death chapter
citations.quote: As used in this section, “joint tenants” includes owners of property held under circumstances that entitled one or more to the whole of the property on the death of the other or others.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 223(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, division into two equal halves between two joint tenants
citations.quote: If property is held by two joint tenants and both of them have died and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that one survived the other, the property held in joint tenancy shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, one-half as if one joint tenant had survived and one-half as if the other joint tenant had survived.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 223(c)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, equal-portion division among more than two joint tenants
citations.quote: If property is held by more than two joint tenants and all of them have died and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that any of them survived the others, the property held in joint tenancy shall be divided into as many portions as there are joint tenants and the share of each joint tenant shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, as if that joint tenant had survived the other joint tenants.

clauses.title: Community and Quasi-Community Property at Simultaneous Death
clauses.body: California has a separate default rule specifically for community and quasi-community property when spouses die simultaneously. Under Prob. Code § 103, except as provided by § 224 (this corpus's separate clause on life insurance that is itself community property), if spouses die leaving community or quasi-community property and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that one spouse survived the other: one-half of the community property and one-half of the quasi-community property is administered or distributed as if one spouse had survived, and belonged to that spouse; and the other one-half is administered or distributed as if the other spouse had survived, and belonged to that spouse. The effect parallels the joint-tenancy division described elsewhere in this clause set — an equal, one-half-and-one-half split — rather than the whole passing to either spouse's estate alone.
clauses.gap: This is California's own statute, used as evidence of what the law provides for community and quasi-community property specifically — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reader's marital property, and not a statement about which particular assets are, in fact, community, quasi-community, or separate property, which this clause does not determine. Prob. Code § 103(a) and (b) are two subsections of the same statutory section, not independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. Notably, § 103 is codified in Probate Code Part 1 (§§ 100-105), not in Part 5's simultaneous-death chapter (§§ 220-234) that contains §§ 220-223 addressed elsewhere in this clause set — it is a separate statute that Prob. Code § 221(a) cross-references as displacing that chapter for community property, and it carries its own internal carve-out to § 224 rather than to anything in §§ 220-223. This clause does not restate § 224's life-insurance-specific community-property provision, already addressed in this corpus's Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation document (clause: Simultaneous Death of the Insured and a Beneficiary).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 103(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, community property default rule and the first equal half
citations.quote: Except as provided by Section 224, if spouses die leaving community or quasi-community property and it cannot be established by clear and convincing evidence that one spouse survived the other: (a) One-half of the community property and one-half of the quasi-community property shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, as if one spouse had survived and as if that one-half belonged to that spouse.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 103(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, community property default rule's other equal half
citations.quote: The other one-half of the community property and the other one-half of the quasi-community property shall be administered or distributed, or otherwise dealt with, as if the other spouse had survived and as if that one-half belonged to that spouse.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}}, summarizes California Labor Code sections 970 through 972 — the statutory scheme, found in the chapter titled "Solicitation of Employees by Misrepresentation," that prohibits inducing a person to move in order to accept work through knowingly false representations about the work, and that gives the affected person a separate civil remedy. Where a specific inducing party and jobseeker are named below, those names are {{companyName}} and {{jobseekerName}}; this sheet can also be used and read on its own, without any specific party named, as a general reference to what this statute says. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any particular advertisement, offer, or communication complies with it, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: Certification
clauses.body:

This information sheet does not constitute legal advice, does not evaluate the lawfulness of any specific advertisement, offer, or communication, and is not a substitute for consulting a person licensed to practice law in the relevant jurisdiction.
