clauses.title: Core Prohibition — Inducing Relocation by Knowingly False Representations
clauses.body: California Labor Code section 970 prohibits any person, or an agent or officer of that person, directly or indirectly, from influencing, persuading, or engaging any person to change residence — within the state, into the state from outside, or out of the state — for the purpose of working in any branch of labor, where that influence, persuasion, or engagement is accomplished through or by means of knowingly false representations. The statute names four specific subjects on which a knowingly false representation triggers the prohibition: (a) the kind, character, or existence of the work; (b) the length of time the work will last, or the compensation for it; (c) the sanitary or housing conditions relating to or surrounding the work; and (d) the existence or nonexistence of a strike, lockout, or other labor dispute pending between the proposed employer and the persons then or last performing the work. A false representation on some other subject, not covered by any of the four listed categories, is outside what this specific statutory section reaches. The representation may be spoken, written, or advertised in printed form.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a prohibition of this kind exists in at least one jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular recruiting or relocation situation. The statute requires the false representation to be "knowingly" false and to be the means by which the person was influenced, persuaded, or engaged to change residence for work; whether a specific statement was knowingly false, and whether it was actually the means of inducing a specific move, are fact-specific questions this document does not resolve. This clause quotes the operative text of a single statutory section (§ 970); the quoted text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page, retrieved with two different User-Agent strings, before being treated as verified. This clause does not address the neighboring sections of the same chapter (Labor Code §§ 973, 974, 976, 977) that impose separate, related disclosure obligations on advertisements for work during a labor dispute or on advertisements for sales/broker/agent compensation — those are different statutory provisions with their own text and are not covered here.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 970 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: No person, or agent or officer thereof, directly or indirectly, shall influence, persuade, or engage any person to change from one place to another in this State or from any place outside to any place within the State, or from any place within the State to any place outside, for the purpose of working in any branch of labor, through or by means of knowingly false representations, whether spoken, written, or advertised in printed form, concerning either: (a) The kind, character, or existence of such work; (b) The length of time such work will last, or the compensation therefor; (c) The sanitary or housing conditions relating to or surrounding the work; (d) The existence or nonexistence of any strike, lockout, or other labor dispute affecting it and pending between the proposed employer and the persons then or last engaged in the performance of the labor for which the employee is sought.

clauses.title: Criminal Penalty for Violating Section 970
clauses.body: Labor Code section 971 makes a violation of section 970 a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not less than fifty dollars ($50) nor more than one thousand dollars ($1,000), or by imprisonment for not more than six months, or by both the fine and imprisonment.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a criminal penalty of this kind exists in at least one jurisdiction for a violation of section 970 — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular situation, and not a statement that any specific conduct has been or would be prosecuted. Criminal enforcement of this section is a matter for public prosecutors; this document does not describe how or whether such enforcement occurs in practice. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 971); the quoted text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page, retrieved with two different User-Agent strings, before being treated as verified. This clause is not fully independent of the core-prohibition clause in this sheet, since section 971's penalty applies only to a violation of section 970, which that other clause covers — that dependency is disclosed here rather than presented as an unrelated confirmation.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 971 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Any person, or agent or officer thereof, who violates Section 970 is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not less than fifty dollars ($50) nor more than one thousand dollars ($1,000) or imprisonment for not more than six months or both.

clauses.title: Separate Civil Remedy — Double Damages
clauses.body: Beyond the misdemeanor criminal exposure described in section 971, Labor Code section 972 gives the aggrieved party a separate civil remedy: any person, or agent or officer of that person, who violates any provision of section 970 is liable to the party aggrieved, in a civil action, for double damages resulting from the misrepresentations. That civil action may be brought by the aggrieved person or that person's assigns or successors in interest, and it may be brought without first establishing any criminal liability.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a private double-damages remedy of this kind exists in at least one jurisdiction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular dispute, and not a calculation of what damages, if any, would be available in a specific case. The statutory text sets the multiplier at double (not treble or another multiple) and describes the measure only in the general terms "double damages resulting from such misrepresentations" — it does not itemize the specific categories of loss that qualify (for example, it does not use the words "moving expenses" anywhere in its text). Whether a particular cost, including the cost of moving to or away from a work location, counts as damages "resulting from" the misrepresentation in a given case is a question this document does not resolve, since answering it would require researching how courts have construed that phrase — case-law research that is outside the scope of this statute-text-only sheet. This clause quotes a single statutory section (§ 972); the quoted text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page, retrieved with two different User-Agent strings, before being treated as verified. Source-independence disclosure: this civil remedy sits in the same chapter as, and by its own text depends on, a violation of section 970 (covered in a separate clause in this sheet) — that dependency is disclosed here rather than presented as an unrelated confirmation.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 972 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: In addition to such criminal penalty, any person, or agent or officer thereof who violates any provision of Section 970 is liable to the party aggrieved, in a civil action, for double damages resulting from such misrepresentations. Such civil action may be brought by an aggrieved person or his assigns or successors in interest, without first establishing any criminal liability.

clauses.title: Purpose and Declaration
clauses.body: This document sets out information about California's Phase-In Overtime for Agricultural Workers Act of 2016, Labor Code sections 857 through 864, prepared in connection with work performed for {{companyName}} by {{employeeName}} in the position of {{jobTitle}}, beginning on or about {{startDate}}. This document describes what the statute itself provides, including a graduated phase-in schedule that has now fully taken effect under the statute's own terms. It is not legal advice about how the statute applies to any particular person's specific work arrangement, hours, or duties.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment
Statutory Title and Legislative Findings
clauses.body: Labor Code Chapter 6, sections 857 through 864, located within the Division 2 working-hours provisions, is titled and may be cited as the Phase-In Overtime for Agricultural Workers Act of 2016. It was added by Assembly Bill 1066 (Statutes 2016, Chapter 313), effective January 1, 2017. In enacting the chapter, the Legislature found that agricultural workers had historically been excluded from wage and overtime protections under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, and it declared its intent to give persons employed in an agricultural occupation in California an opportunity to earn overtime compensation under the same standards as other Californians.
clauses.gap: This clause summarizes the chapter's title provision (section 857) and its legislative findings and declaration of intent (section 858); it does not restate every finding listed in section 858, only the findings quoted below. These findings are legislative background statements, not independently operative rules, and by themselves they do not establish an overtime entitlement; the operative overtime and double-time rules are set out in sections 860 through 862, addressed in separate clauses in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 857 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: This chapter shall be known and may be cited as the Phase-In Overtime for Agricultural Workers Act of 2016.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 858(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: In 1938, the United States Congress enacted the federal Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (29 U.S.C. Sec. 201 et seq.), which excluded agricultural workers from wage protections and overtime compensation requirements.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 858(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature to enact the Phase-In Overtime for Agricultural Workers Act of 2016 to provide any person employed in an agricultural occupation in California, as defined in Order No. 14-2001 of the Industrial Welfare Commission (revised 07-2014) with an opportunity to earn overtime compensation under the same standards as millions of other Californians.

clauses.title: Definition of "Agricultural Occupation"
clauses.body: Chapter 6 applies to a person "employed in an agricultural occupation." The chapter does not itself define that phrase. Instead, section 859 provides that "employed in an agricultural occupation" has the same meaning given to it in Wage Order No. 14-2001 of California's Industrial Welfare Commission, as revised effective July 2014. Section 858 refers to the same source when describing the chapter's intended coverage.
clauses.gap: This document quotes only Chapter 6's own cross-reference to Wage Order No. 14-2001; it does not independently fetch, quote, or verify the text of Wage Order No. 14-2001 itself, which is a separate Industrial Welfare Commission order rather than a Labor Code section, and was not checked against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as part of this research. Determining whether a specific job duty falls within "agricultural occupation" as the Wage Order defines it would require consulting that Wage Order directly, which this document does not do.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 859 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: For purposes of this chapter, “employed in an agricultural occupation” has the same meaning as in Order No.14-2001 of the Industrial Welfare Commission (revised 07-2014).

clauses.title: The Section 860 Phase-In Schedule and Its Current, Fully-Effective Status
clauses.body: Labor Code section 860 set out a graduated schedule under which persons employed in an agricultural occupation became entitled to daily and weekly overtime pay on a step-down basis, moving toward the general 8-hour-per-day/40-hour-per-week overtime threshold that already applied to most other California nonexempt employees. For most agricultural employers, the daily/weekly threshold stepped down in four stages: 9.5 hours per day or 55 hours per week beginning January 1, 2019; 9 hours per day or 50 hours per week beginning January 1, 2020; 8.5 hours per day or 45 hours per week beginning January 1, 2021; and 8 hours per day or 40 hours per week beginning January 1, 2022. The statute set the same four-stage schedule, delayed by three years at each stage, for an employer that employs 25 or fewer employees, with that group's final 8-hour/40-hour stage beginning January 1, 2025. Because January 1, 2025 has passed, section 860's phase-in schedule has now run its full course for both employer-size groups under the statute's own terms, and the 8-hour-workday/40-hour-workweek threshold is the daily/weekly overtime threshold that section 860 currently states for agricultural occupations covered by this chapter, without regard to employer size.
clauses.gap: This clause summarizes all four stages of section 860's schedule for both employer-size categories from a single statutory section; it is not corroborated by an independent second source. Section 863 gave the Governor limited authority, under specified conditions tied to a minimum-wage-increase suspension mechanism, to delay this schedule by up to one year at a time; this document did not research whether the Governor ever exercised that authority for this chapter, so this clause describes the schedule as enacted rather than independently confirming that no delay in fact occurred. This document does not address how "employs 25 or fewer employees" is counted (for example, over what period, or across what related entities), because Chapter 6 does not itself define that counting method.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 860(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Commencing January 1, 2019, except as provided in paragraph (2), any person employed in an agricultural occupation shall not be employed more than nine and one-half hours in any one workday or work in excess of 55 hours in any one workweek, unless the employee receives one and one-half times that employee’s regular rate of pay for all hours worked over nine and one-half hours in any workday or over 55 hours in any workweek.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 860(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Commencing January 1, 2022, except as provided in paragraph (2), any person employed in an agricultural occupation shall not be employed more than eight hours in any one workday or work in excess of 40 hours in any one workweek, unless the employee receives one and one-half times that employee’s regular rate of pay for all hours worked over eight hours in any workday or over 40 hours in any workweek.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 860(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: This subdivision shall apply to an employer who employs 25 or fewer employees commencing January 1, 2025.

clauses.title: Extension of General Overtime Rules and the 12-Hour Double-Time Threshold
clauses.body: Labor Code section 861 provides that, except for the daily/weekly thresholds set out in section 860 and the 12-hour daily double-time threshold set out in section 862(a), all other provisions of California's general overtime statute (Labor Code Chapter 1, commencing with section 500) governing compensation for overtime work apply to workers in an agricultural occupation, effective January 1, 2017. Separately, section 862(a) sets a 12-hour-per-day double-time threshold for agricultural occupations, stated as "consistent with Section 510," California's general double-time statute: work beyond 12 hours in one day is compensated at no less than twice the employee's regular rate of pay. Section 862 phased this 12-hour double-time threshold in on the same two-track, employer-size-based schedule used in section 860: it began applying January 1, 2022 for other employers, and, for an employer that employs 25 or fewer employees, beginning January 1, 2025. Because January 1, 2025 has passed, the 12-hour daily double-time threshold in section 862(a) is now the double-time threshold that section 862 currently states for agricultural occupations covered by this chapter, without regard to employer size.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on sections 861 and 862(a) and (c), which are provisions of the same statutory chapter and are not independent sources of one another. This document does not independently trace how the general seventh-consecutive-workday double-time rule in Labor Code section 510(a) (extended to agricultural occupations by section 861's reference to "other provisions" of the general overtime chapter) interacts with section 862's 12-hour daily double-time rule for this specific worker category; that interaction is not addressed here.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 861 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Except as set forth in Section 860 and subdivision (a) of Section 862, all other provisions of Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 500) regarding compensation for overtime work shall apply to workers in an agricultural occupation commencing January 1, 2017.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 862(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Beginning January 1, 2022, except as provided in subdivision (c), and consistent with Section 510, any work performed by a person, employed in an agricultural occupation, in excess of 12 hours in one day shall be compensated at the rate of no less than twice the employee’s regular rate of pay.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 862(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Subdivision (a) shall apply to an employer who employs 25 or fewer employees commencing January 1, 2025.

clauses.title: The Governor's Now-Lapsed Authority to Delay the Phase-In
clauses.body: Labor Code section 863 gave the Governor limited, conditional authority to temporarily suspend the scheduled phase-in of the overtime and double-time requirements in sections 860 and 862(a), but only if the Governor also suspended a scheduled minimum-wage increase under a specified, cross-referenced provision of Labor Code section 1182.12. Any such suspension could postpone the schedule by at most one additional year at a time, and section 863 fixed an outer limit on how long this suspension authority could exist: it stated that the authority would end once the final phase-in steps described in section 860(d) and section 862(c) took effect, or on January 1, 2025, whichever came first.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from section 863 alone. This document did not research, and does not state, whether the Governor ever exercised this suspension authority during the phase-in period; it addresses only the authority as fixed in the statutory text and the fact that the statute's own end-date for that authority, January 1, 2025, has now passed. This document does not describe the separate minimum-wage-suspension mechanism under Labor Code section 1182.12 that section 863 cross-references, beyond noting that it exists as a precondition to the Governor's authority under section 863.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 863(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code

clauses.title: Temporary Services Employer Final-Wage Timing — Applicability Note
clauses.body: California Labor Code section 201.3 sets final-wage timing rules that apply specifically to an employee of a "temporary services employer" (a staffing agency) — a different, more specific set of deadlines from the general final-paycheck timing rules in Labor Code sections 201 and 202 that apply to most other employees. This concerns {{employeeName}}'s assignment, through {{companyName}}, to perform work for {{clientCompanyName}}, an assignment recorded here as ending on {{assignmentEndDate}}. Section 201.3's specialized schedules turn on the statute's own functional definition of "temporary services employer" and on how a given assignment or the underlying employment relationship ended, both described in the information that follows. Naming {{companyName}} and {{clientCompanyName}} here does not itself determine that {{companyName}} meets the statutory definition of a "temporary services employer," and does not determine which of the statute's several payment schedules applies to this particular assignment.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Temporary Services Employer" for This Section
clauses.body: Labor Code section 201.3 defines "temporary services employer," for purposes of that section's own timing rules, as an employing unit that contracts with clients or customers to supply workers and that performs a specific set of functions with respect to those workers: negotiating with clients over matters such as timing, work type, working conditions, and price; determining worker assignments or reassignments (even if a worker may refuse a specific assignment); retaining authority to reassign a worker a client finds unacceptable; assigning or reassigning workers; setting workers' rate of pay; paying workers from its own account; and retaining the right to hire and terminate workers. The statute excludes three categories from that definition even if they otherwise supply workers to clients: a bona fide nonprofit organization, a farm labor contractor as separately defined in the Labor Code, and a garment manufacturing employer as separately defined in the Labor Code. The statute also defines "client" and "customer," for this section's purposes, as the person with whom the temporary services employer has a contractual relationship to provide the services of one or more of its employees, and it borrows the Unemployment Insurance Code's definition of "employing unit" as a component of its own definition.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivision (a)), used as real evidence of how this specific section defines "temporary services employer" for purposes of the final-wage timing rules addressed in the other clauses here — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not itself a determination that any particular staffing arrangement meets or fails this definition. The seven functional criteria in paragraph (a)(1), subparts (A) through (G), are paraphrased in the body above rather than quoted in full; only that paragraph's introductory sentence is quoted below as an exact, contiguous excerpt, along with the full text of the exclusions in paragraph (a)(2) and the "client"/"customer" definition in paragraph (a)(4). This definition cross-references other statutes this clause did not independently fetch or verify: the definition of "employing unit" in Unemployment Insurance Code section 135, the farm-labor-contractor definition in Labor Code section 1682(b), and the garment-manufacturing "contractor" definition in Labor Code section 2671(d) — an honest gap, disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. All three citations below come from the same statutory subdivision, Section 201.3(a); they are treated as one source describing related definitional provisions, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, temporary services employer definition
citations.quote: “Temporary services employer” means an employing unit that contracts with clients or customers to supply workers to perform services for the clients or customers and that performs all of the following functions:

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, temporary services employer exclusions
citations.quote: “Temporary services employer” does not include any of the following: (A) A bona fide nonprofit organization that provides temporary service employees to clients. (B) A farm labor contractor, as defined in subdivision (b) of Section 1682. (C) A garment manufacturing employer, which, for purposes of this section, has the same meaning as “contractor,” as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 2671.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, client/customer definition
citations.quote: “Client” and “customer” mean the person with whom a temporary services employer has a contractual relationship to provide the services of one or more individuals employed by the temporary services employer.

clauses.title: The General Rule: Weekly Payment Tied to Payroll Weeks, Not to When the Assignment Ends
clauses.body: Subject to several exceptions stated elsewhere in the same section, Labor Code section 201.3 provides that when an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client, that employee's wages are due and payable no less frequently than weekly — regardless of when the specific assignment ends — with wages for a given calendar week due by the regular payday of the following calendar week. The statute states that a temporary services employer who pays on that weekly schedule is deemed to have timely paid the employee's wages upon completion of the assignment, meaning the assignment's end date, standing alone, does not accelerate the payment deadline the way the general discharge and quit rules can. A parallel, narrower provision applies to a security guard employed by a temporary services employer in the security services industry who is registered under a specified Business and Professions Code licensing chapter and employed by a licensed private patrol operator: for that category of worker, the statute uses a "workweek" as defined elsewhere in the Labor Code, rather than a calendar week, as the measuring period, with wages due by the regular payday of the following workweek. The same section states that a temporary services employer who violates this section is subject to the civil penalties provided in Labor Code section 203, and to any other penalties available at law.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (b)(1)(A), (b)(1)(B), and (c)), used as real evidence of the default weekly-payment schedule this section sets for temporary services employees and of the penalty the section itself invokes for a violation — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that this default schedule applies without exception. The statute expressly makes this rule subject to paragraphs (2) through (5) of the same subdivision (the day-to-day, trade-dispute, discharge, and quit provisions addressed in this corpus's other Section 201.3 clauses) and, separately, to the 90-consecutive-day provision in paragraph (6); none of those exceptions are restated here. This clause does not independently verify that the security-guard sub-rule's licensing prerequisites — registration under Business and Professions Code Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 7580) and employment by a private patrol operator licensed under that chapter — are met in any particular case. Nor does this clause restate what a "regular payday" is for a given employer, or the substantive mechanics of the Section 203 waiting-time penalty (its accrual rate and 30-day cap), which this corpus addresses in a separate, dedicated Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document rather than duplicating here. The three citations below come from the same statutory section, Section 201.3; they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, general weekly final-wage timing rule for temporary services employees
citations.quote: Except as provided in paragraphs (2) to (5), inclusive, if an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client, that employee’s wages are due and payable no less frequently than weekly, regardless of when the assignment ends, and wages for work performed during any calendar week shall be due and payable not later than the regular payday of the following calendar week. A temporary services employer shall be deemed to have timely paid wages upon completion of an assignment if wages are paid in compliance with this subdivision.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, security-guard sub-rule using a workweek measuring period
citations.quote: Except as provided in paragraphs (2) to (5), inclusive, if an employee of a temporary services employer in the security services industry is a security guard who is registered pursuant to Chapter 11.5 (commencing with Section 7580) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code, is employed by a private patrol operator licensed pursuant to that chapter, and is assigned to work for a client, that employee’s wages are due and payable no less frequently than weekly, regardless of when the assignment ends, and wages for work performed during any workweek, as defined under Section 500, shall be due and payable not later than the regular payday of the following workweek.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, civil penalty for a violation of this section
citations.quote: A temporary services employer who violates this section is subject to the civil penalties provided for in Section 203 and to any other penalties available at law.

clauses.title: Two Exceptions Requiring Daily Payment Instead of Weekly
clauses.body: Labor Code section 201.3 sets two situations in which a temporary services employee's wages are due and payable at the end of each day, rather than on the section's general weekly schedule, regardless of when the assignment itself ends. The first applies to an employee assigned to work for a client on a day-to-day basis, but only if three conditions are all met: the employee reports to or assembles at the temporary services employer's office (or another specified location); the employee is dispatched to a client's worksite each day and returns to or reports to that office or location upon completing the day's assignment; and the employee's work does not fall within the executive, administrative, or professional classifications defined in the wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission, and is not clerical work. The second applies without those three conditions: an employee assigned to work for a client that is engaged in a trade dispute is paid daily.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (b)(2) and (b)(3)), used as real evidence that these two situations trigger daily rather than weekly payment — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular assignment is or is not a day-to-day assignment or a trade-dispute assignment within the meaning of this statute. The day-to-day exception's three conditions are quoted in full below as one contiguous excerpt from paragraph (b)(2); whether a given assignment in fact satisfies all three — particularly whether specific job duties are "executive, administrative, or professional" or "clerical" — depends on the separate body of Industrial Welfare Commission wage-order classification law, which this clause does not reproduce or apply here. The statute does not itself define "trade dispute" within Section 201.3; this clause does not supply that definition from elsewhere. The two citations below come from the same statutory subdivision, Section 201.3(b); they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, daily payment for a day-to-day assignment
citations.quote: If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client on a day-to-day basis, that employee’s wages are due and payable at the end of each day, regardless of when the assignment ends, if each of the following occurs: (A) The employee reports to or assembles at the office of the temporary services employer or other location. (B) The employee is dispatched to a client’s worksite each day and returns to or reports to the office of the temporary services employer or other location upon completion of the assignment. (C) The employee’s work is not executive, administrative, or professional, as defined in the wage orders of the Industrial Welfare Commission, and is not clerical.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, daily payment for a client engaged in a trade dispute
citations.quote: If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client engaged in a trade dispute, that employee’s wages are due and payable at the end of each day, regardless of when the assignment ends.

clauses.title: When the Temp Employee's Own Employment Ends: Reversion to the General Discharge and Quit Rules
clauses.body: Labor Code section 201.3 distinguishes between an assignment ending (addressed by the section's own weekly or daily schedules described elsewhere in this material) and the temporary services employee's employment with the temporary services employer itself ending. Where an employee assigned to work for a client is discharged by the temporary services employer (the statute's text also refers to a "leasing employer" in this same provision, without separately defining that term), the statute directs that wages are due and payable as provided in Labor Code section 201 — the general immediate-payment-on-discharge rule — rather than under Section 201.3's own weekly or daily schedules. Where such an employee instead quits their employment with the temporary services employer, the statute directs that wages are due and payable as provided in Labor Code section 202 — the general quitting-employee rule, including its 72-hour and notice-based timing.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (b)(4) and (b)(5)), used as real evidence that a discharge or a quit of the underlying employment relationship — as opposed to the mere ending of one client assignment — reverts the applicable timing rule to the general Section 201 or Section 202 standard, not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular separation was in fact a discharge, a quit, or merely the end of one assignment within a continuing employment relationship. This clause does not restate the substantive content of Section 201 or Section 202 themselves (their own payment deadlines and mailing options), which this corpus addresses in its dedicated Final Paycheck Delivery Method and Location document rather than duplicating here. The statutory text as fetched uses the phrase "leasing employer" in paragraph (b)(4) without defining it elsewhere within Section 201.3; that term is quoted as the statute states it, and this clause does not resolve what distinguishes a "leasing employer" from a "temporary services employer" for this purpose — an honest gap, disclosed rather than guessed at. The two citations below come from the same statutory subdivision, Section 201.3(b); they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, discharge reverts to Section 201 timing
citations.quote: If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client and is discharged by the temporary services employer or leasing employer, wages are due and payable as provided in Section 201.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, quitting reverts to Section 202 timing
citations.quote: If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client and quits his or her employment with the temporary services employer, wages are due and payable as provided in Section 202.

clauses.title: A 90-Consecutive-Day Assignment Limit, and This Section's Own Non-Limitation Clause
clauses.body: Labor Code section 201.3 places an outer time limit on its own weekly-payment default: if an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for the same client for more than 90 consecutive calendar days, the section stops applying to that assignment unless the temporary services employer is already paying the employee weekly in compliance with the section's own general rule. The same section also includes its own savings clause, stating that nothing in Section 201.3 is to be interpreted to limit any rights or remedies otherwise available to an employee under state or federal law.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.3, subdivisions (b)(6) and (d)), used as real evidence that a 90-consecutive-day assignment can take a temporary services employee outside this section's coverage, and that the section does not purport to cut off other legal rights or remedies — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular assignment has or has not reached 90 consecutive calendar days with a given client. The statute's own text, as fetched, does not state what timing rule governs a temporary services employee's wages once this section stops applying under paragraph (b)(6) and the employer was not already paying weekly; this clause does not resolve that gap by assuming which other Labor Code provision would then control. The statute also does not define "consecutive calendar days" for this purpose — for example, whether or how a gap in the assignment interrupts consecutiveness — and this clause does not supply that definition from elsewhere. The two citations below come from the same statutory section, Section 201.3; they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(b)(6) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, 90-consecutive-day limit on this section's applicability
citations.quote: If an employee of a temporary services employer is assigned to work for a client for over 90 consecutive calendar days, this section does not apply unless the temporary services employer pays the employee weekly in compliance with paragraph (1) of subdivision (b).

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.3(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, non-limitation of other rights or remedies
citations.quote: This section shall not be interpreted to limit any rights or remedies otherwise available under state or federal law.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Uniform Electronic Transactions Act Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (UETA), Civil Code sections 1633.1 through 1633.17 — the general California statute addressing when an electronic record or an electronic signature satisfies a legal requirement that something be in writing or be signed, when the parties to a transaction are treated as having agreed to conduct that transaction by electronic means, and how an electronic signature's attribution to a particular person and legal effect are determined. It is prepared by {{preparerName}}. Transaction or record this Information Sheet may relate to, if applicable: {{transactionDescription}}. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference describing what UETA's own text says. It does not identify which other law — a specific writing or signature requirement found elsewhere in this project's documents, or in another statute — applies to any particular record, and it does not determine whether the parties to any specific transaction have in fact agreed, by their conduct or otherwise, to conduct that transaction electronically, which UETA itself treats as a fact-specific question to be answered from the context and surrounding circumstances. UETA is a California state statute; other states have enacted their own, not-necessarily-identical versions of the model Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, and Congress has separately enacted the federal Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act (E-SIGN Act), neither of which this Information Sheet addresses.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Uniform Electronic Transactions Act Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{preparerName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This Information Sheet is a general reference describing California's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, Civil Code §§ 1633.1-1633.17, and the text of the specific sections quoted above. It is not a contract, a consent to conduct any transaction electronically, or legal advice about whether UETA applies to, or is satisfied by, any specific record, signature, or transaction described in this Information Sheet, and completing or signing this Information Sheet does not itself create, satisfy, or waive any requirement under UETA or any other law.]

clauses.title: The Core Rule: Electronic Form Alone Does Not Defeat Legal Effect
clauses.body: UETA's central rule states that a record or a signature may not be denied legal effect or enforceability solely because it is in electronic form, and that a contract may not be denied legal effect or enforceability solely because an electronic record was used in its formation. Building on that rule, the statute further states that if a law requires a record to be in writing, an electronic record satisfies that law, and that if a law requires a signature, an electronic signature satisfies that law. These four rules do not, by their own terms, address whether any other specific legal requirement is in fact satisfied by a particular electronic record or signature in a given case — they establish only that electronic form is not, by itself, a basis for denying legal effect.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes all four subdivisions of a single statutory section, Civil Code § 1633.7(a) through (d), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) and confirmed identical across two fetches made with two different User-Agent request headers. It states UETA's own general validity rule; it does not resolve whether the particular writing or signature requirement applicable to any specific document or transaction is, in fact, one UETA reaches — that depends on whether the transaction falls within UETA's scope (see the companion clause on the agreement requirement and the companion clause on scope exclusions below) and on the terms of the other law imposing the specific requirement, neither of which this clause independently verifies for any given case.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1633.7(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, UETA's core non-discrimination-against-electronic-form rule
citations.quote: (a) A record or signature may not be denied legal effect or enforceability solely because it is in electronic form. (b) A contract may not be denied legal effect or enforceability solely because an electronic record was used in its formation.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1633.7(c)-(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, electronic records and signatures satisfy writing/signature requirements
citations.quote: (c) If a law requires a record to be in writing, an electronic record satisfies the law. (d) If a law requires a signature, an electronic signature satisfies the law.

clauses.title: UETA Applies Only Where the Parties Have Agreed to Transact Electronically
clauses.body: UETA does not require that any record or signature be created, sent, received, or otherwise handled electronically — nothing in the statute forces a transaction into electronic form. Rather, UETA applies only to a transaction between parties who have each agreed to conduct that transaction by electronic means, and whether such an agreement exists is determined from the context and the surrounding circumstances, including the parties' conduct, not from any single required form of consent. The statute places specific limits on how that agreement can arise: except for a separate, optional agreement whose primary purpose is to authorize electronic transacting, an agreement to conduct a transaction electronically may not be contained in a standard form contract that is not itself an electronic record, and an agreement in such a standard form contract may not be conditioned on agreeing to transact electronically. The statute also states that an agreement to conduct a transaction electronically may not be inferred solely from the fact that a party used electronic means to pay an account or register a purchase or warranty. A party who has agreed to conduct one transaction electronically may still refuse to conduct other transactions electronically, and where a seller sells goods or services by both electronic and nonelectronic means, a buyer who transacted electronically may refuse to conduct further transactions regarding those goods or services electronically.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (a) through (c) of Civil Code § 1633.5, fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and confirmed identical across two fetches with different User-Agent headers. It states UETA's own threshold applicability rule; it does not determine, for any specific transaction, whether the parties' actual context and conduct in fact show the agreement UETA requires — that remains a fact-specific determination the statute itself commits to the context and circumstances of each transaction, which this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1633.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, UETA does not compel electronic form
citations.quote: (a) This title does not require a record or signature to be created, generated, sent, communicated, received, stored, or otherwise processed or used by electronic means or in electronic form.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1633.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, UETA applies only where the parties agreed to transact electronically
citations.quote: (b) This title applies only to a transaction between parties each of which has agreed to conduct the transaction by electronic means. Whether the parties agree to conduct a transaction by electronic means is determined from the context and surrounding circumstances, including the parties’ conduct.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1633.5(b) [limits on how consent may be shown] (California Legislative Information text)

An agreement in such a standard form contract may not be conditioned upon an agreement to conduct transactions by electronic means. An agreement to conduct a transaction by electronic means may not be inferred solely from the fact that a party has used electronic means to pay an account or register a purchase or warranty.

citations.quote: (c) A party that agrees to conduct a transaction by electronic means may refuse to conduct other transactions by electronic means. If a seller sells goods or services by both electronic and nonelectronic means and a buyer purchases the goods or services by conducting the transaction by electronic means, the buyer may refuse to conduct further transactions regarding the goods or services by electronic means.

clauses.title: How UETA Defines "Electronic Record" and "Electronic Signature"
clauses.body: UETA defines an "electronic record" as a record created, generated, sent, communicated, received, or stored by electronic means. It defines an "electronic signature" as an electronic sound, symbol, or process attached to or logically associated with an electronic record and executed or adopted by a person with the intent to sign the electronic record. The statute further states that a "digital signature" as defined in Government Code § 16.5(d) — a term that refers to a specific cryptographic technology — is one type of electronic signature under UETA, meaning UETA's own definition of "electronic signature" is broader than, and not limited to, that particular technology; a typed name, a click-to-sign action, or another electronic mark or process can also qualify if executed or adopted with the intent to sign.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (g) and (h) of Civil Code § 1633.2, fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and confirmed identical across two fetches with different User-Agent headers. It states UETA's own statutory definitions; it does not determine whether any specific act (for example, typing a name into a form field, clicking an "I agree" button, or applying a scanned signature image) was, in a particular case, executed or adopted "with the intent to sign" — that remains a fact-specific inquiry the statute leaves open, which this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1633.2(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of "electronic record"
citations.quote: “Electronic record” means a record created, generated, sent, communicated, received, or stored by electronic means.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1633.2(h) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of "electronic signature"
citations.quote: “Electronic signature” means an electronic sound, symbol, or process attached to or logically associated with an electronic record and executed or adopted by a person with the intent to sign the electronic record. For purposes of this title, a “digital signature” as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 16.5 of the Government Code is a type of electronic signature.

clauses.title: Attribution: When an Electronic Signature Is "the Act of" a Particular Person
clauses.body: UETA states that an electronic record or an electronic signature is attributable to a person if it was the act of that person, and that this fact — whose act it was — may be shown in any manner, including by showing the efficacy of any security procedure applied to determine whose act it was. The statute does not limit attribution to any single method of proof, such as a password, a click-through log, or a particular authentication technology; it allows attribution to be established by any means that shows the record or signature was in fact that person's act. Separately, the legal effect of an electronic record or signature once attributed to a person is itself determined from the context and surrounding circumstances at the time of its creation, execution, or adoption, including any agreement of the parties, and otherwise as provided by other law.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (a) and (b) of Civil Code § 1633.9, fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and confirmed identical across two fetches with different User-Agent headers. It states UETA's own attribution rule; it does not determine, for any specific electronic record or signature, whose act it in fact was, nor what evidentiary showing would establish that in a particular case — those remain fact-specific questions the statute commits to proof "in any manner," which this clause does not resolve.

citations.quote: (a) An electronic record or electronic signature is attributable to a person if it was the act of the person. The act of the person may be shown in any manner, including a showing of the efficacy of any security procedure applied to determine the person to which the electronic record or electronic signature was attributable.

citations.quote: (b) The effect of an electronic record or electronic signature attributed to a person under subdivision (a) is determined from the context and surrounding circumstances at the time of its creation, execution, or adoption, including the parties’ agreement, if any, and otherwise as provided by law.

clauses.title: Transactions UETA's Own Text Excludes From Its Scope
clauses.body: UETA does not apply to every transaction. Its own text states that the statute does not apply to transactions subject to certain other bodies of law, including a law governing the creation and execution of wills, codicils, or testamentary trusts, and most of the Uniform Commercial Code's provisions on negotiable instruments, documents of title, investment securities, and secured transactions (with narrow carve-outs for a small number of Division 1 UCC sections). The statute also excludes a law that requires specifically identifiable text or disclosures in a record to be separately signed or initialed apart from the rest of the record, subject to its own narrow exceptions, and it separately lists a substantial number of specific California consumer-protection, real estate, insurance, and vehicle-related statutes to which it does not apply. Where a transaction is excluded from UETA's scope under these provisions, the statute states that this exclusion does not itself prohibit the transaction from being conducted electronically if some other applicable law permits that — it only means UETA's own general rules are not what makes electronic form effective for that particular transaction.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (a) and (b)(1)-(2) of Civil Code § 1633.3, and separately subdivision (f), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and confirmed identical across two fetches with different User-Agent headers. Subdivision (c)'s extensive list of additional excluded California statutes (spanning provisions of the Business and Professions, Civil, Code of Civil Procedure, Financial, Health and Safety, Insurance, Public Utilities, and Vehicle Codes) is described here only in general summary, not quoted verbatim, and a transaction potentially covered by one of those specific cross-referenced statutes would need that list's current text checked directly rather than relying on this summary. This clause states what UETA's own scope-exclusion provisions say; it does not determine whether any particular transaction in fact falls within one of these exclusions, which depends on matching the transaction's specific legal character against the statute's own cross-references.

(2) Division 1 (commencing with Section 1101) of the Uniform Commercial Code, except Sections 1206 and 1306.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}}, states what California's Uniform Partnership Act of 1994 provides about two specific questions: (1) the procedure a partnership follows to register with the California Secretary of State as a registered limited liability partnership, under Cal. Corp. Code § 16953, and (2) the extent — and the express statutory limits — of the liability shield that registration creates for a partner, under Cal. Corp. Code § 16306. Where a specific partnership is named below, it is {{partnershipName}}; this sheet can also be read on its own, without that field filled in, as a general reference to what these two statutes provide. This sheet does not address which professions may lawfully use the registered limited liability partnership form in the first place; that separate eligibility question is addressed in this project's Professional LLC Prohibition in California — Information Sheet, in its clause on the registered limited liability partnership's narrower list of eligible professions, and is not restated here. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any particular partnership's registration is complete or correctly filed, whether a particular partner's conduct falls inside or outside the shield, or what a specific partnership or partner should do about either question, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: Registration Procedure: What Must Be Filed with the Secretary of State
clauses.body: California's Uniform Partnership Act of 1994 states, in Cal. Corp. Code § 16953(a), what a partnership must file with the Secretary of State to become a registered limited liability partnership: "a registration, executed by one or more partners authorized to execute a registration," stating the partnership's name; the street address of its principal office; the mailing address of its principal office, if different from the street address; the name and street address of the agent for service of process on the partnership in California; "a brief statement of the business in which the partnership engages"; any other matters the partnership determines to include; and a statement that the partnership is registering as a registered limited liability partnership. Subdivision (b) states that "[t]he registration shall be accompanied by a fee as set forth in subdivision (a) of Section 12189 of the Government Code," and subdivision (c) states the corresponding duty on the Secretary of State's side: the Secretary of State "shall register as a registered limited liability partnership any partnership that submits a completed registration with the required fee." Read together, subdivisions (a) through (c) describe registration as a filing-based act: a partnership becomes registered by submitting these stated items and the fee, and the statute's own text does not add, as part of this filing step, any separate substantive eligibility screening by the Secretary of State beyond completeness of the registration and payment of the fee.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what Cal. Corp. Code § 16953(a)-(c) itself requires to be filed and what it states the Secretary of State does upon a completed filing; it does not address separate content that the same section addresses elsewhere, including the profession-specific state-board or agency filing and registration requirements referenced in § 16953(h), or the Secretary of State's fee-cancellation process in § 16953(d) — those are outside this clause's scope. This clause also does not address which professions are eligible to register as a registered limited liability partnership in the first place; that question is addressed by this project's separate Professional LLC Prohibition in California — Information Sheet, in its clause on the registered limited liability partnership's narrower list of eligible professions (citing Cal. Corp. Code §§ 16951 and 16101), which this clause cross-references rather than restates. All three quoted subdivisions below are drawn from the single statutory section Cal. Corp. Code § 16953 and are treated as one primary source, not as independent citations of separate sections. As of this verification, the California Legislative Information website listed a single current version of Section 16953 on file, last amended by Stats. 2022, Ch. 617, Sec. 111 (effective January 1, 2023), with no competing amended version found for the same statutory year. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific registration procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific partnership's registration, and registration procedures vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself register any partnership and does not determine whether a specific partnership's filing is complete or properly executed.

clauses.title: When Registration Takes Effect, How Long It Continues, and the Statute's Own 'Optional Security Requirement' Language
clauses.body: Cal. Corp. Code § 16953(e) states when registration takes effect and how long it lasts: "[a] partnership becomes a registered limited liability partnership at the time of the filing of the initial registration with the Secretary of State or at any later date or time specified in the registration and the payment of the fee required by subdivision (b)," and it "continues as a registered limited liability partnership until a notice that it is no longer a registered limited liability partnership has been filed pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 16954 or, if applicable, until it has been dissolved and finally wound up." Section 16953's own text does not state, within this subdivision, any separate requirement to periodically re-register or renew the registration itself in order for it to continue — continuation instead runs until an affirmative notice of withdrawal is filed or the partnership dissolves and winds up. Separately, subdivision (g) states that the Secretary of State's registration form "shall include the form for confirming compliance with the optional security requirement pursuant to subdivision (c) of Section 16956" — language that, on its own terms, characterizes that particular requirement as "optional" rather than as a universal precondition stated within Section 16953 itself. The same subdivision also states that the instructional materials accompanying the registration form must include a notice "that filing the registration will obligate the limited liability partnership to pay an annual tax for that taxable year to the Franchise Tax Board pursuant to Section 17948 of the Revenue and Taxation Code," and that this notice must be updated annually to state the current dollar amount.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what Cal. Corp. Code § 16953(e) and (g) themselves say; it does not independently examine the separate statute those subdivisions cross-reference — Section 16956(c), which defines the substance of the "optional security requirement," and Section 16954(b), which governs the notice that a partnership is no longer registered — neither of which was independently fetched or verified as part of this pass, so this clause does not state what either of those two cross-referenced sections themselves require. The annual obligation described in subdivision (g) is a tax-filing consequence of registering (an obligation to the Franchise Tax Board under Revenue and Taxation Code § 17948), not a re-registration or renewal-of-registration requirement under Section 16953 itself; this clause does not address the Revenue and Taxation Code provision beyond what Section 16953(g) itself states about it. Both quoted subdivisions below are drawn from the single statutory section Cal. Corp. Code § 16953 and are treated as one primary source. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific registration procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific partnership's registration, and registration procedures vary by state. This document is informational only: it does not itself register or maintain the registration of any partnership.

A partnership continues as a registered limited liability partnership until a notice that it is no longer a registered limited liability partnership has been filed pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 16954 or, if applicable, until it has been dissolved and finally wound up.

That notice shall be updated annually to specify the dollar amount of the tax.

clauses.title: The Liability Shield: What a Registered Limited Liability Partnership Partner Is Not Liable For, Solely as a Partner
clauses.body: Cal. Corp. Code § 16306(c) states the core liability rule for a registered limited liability partnership. "Notwithstanding any other section of this chapter, and subject to subdivisions (d), (e), (f), and (h), a partner in a registered limited liability partnership is not liable or accountable, directly or indirectly, including by way of indemnification, contribution, assessment, or otherwise, for debts, obligations, or liabilities of or chargeable to the partnership or another partner in the partnership, whether arising in tort, contract, or otherwise, that are incurred, created, or assumed by the partnership while the partnership is a registered limited liability partnership, by reason of being a partner or acting in the conduct of the business or activities of the partnership." This is a shield against liability that would otherwise attach to a person merely by reason of being a partner, or by reason of acting in the conduct of the partnership's business or activities — that is, against vicarious liability for the partnership's debts and for the acts of other partners and the partnership itself. The subdivision states this rule as applying "[n]otwithstanding any other section of this chapter," but expressly makes it "subject to subdivisions (d), (e), (f), and (h)" of the same section, meaning the statute's own text builds named exceptions and qualifications into the shield rather than stating it as absolute.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what Cal. Corp. Code § 16306(c) itself says; the express limits it cross-references in subdivisions (d), (e), (f), and (h) are addressed only in part, by the separate clause of this document on the shield's limits (covering subdivisions (e) and (f)) — subdivisions (d) (a partner's ability to agree in writing to assume specified liabilities) and (h) (a partner's separate ability to act as guarantor or surety) are not covered by either clause and were not independently verified here. This clause is one subsection of the single statutory section Cal. Corp. Code § 16306; this document's separate General Partnership Agreement document already cites subdivisions (a) and (b) of the same section for the different, contrasting point that a general partnership's default rule is joint and several liability with no comparable shield, and flags subdivisions (c) through (h) as a distinct regime it does not cover — this clause is offered specifically to fill that gap for the registered limited liability partnership form, without restating that other document's content. As of this verification, the California Legislative Information website listed a single version of Section 16306 on file, dated as added by Stats. 1996, Ch. 1003, Sec. 2 (effective January 1, 1997), with no amendment or competing version found since. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific partnership is currently a registered limited liability partnership or whether a specific partner's conduct falls inside or outside this shield. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides for this specific entity form — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific partnership, and liability-shield rules vary by state. This document is informational only.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16306(c)
citations.cite: Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, core liability shield for a partner in a registered limited liability partnership
citations.quote: (c) Notwithstanding any other section of this chapter, and subject to subdivisions (d), (e), (f), and (h), a partner in a registered limited liability partnership is not liable or accountable, directly or indirectly, including by way of indemnification, contribution, assessment, or otherwise, for debts, obligations, or liabilities of or chargeable to the partnership or another partner in the partnership, whether arising in tort, contract, or otherwise, that are incurred, created, or assumed by the partnership while the partnership is a registered limited liability partnership, by reason of being a partner or acting in the conduct of the business or activities of the partnership.

clauses.title: The Shield's Limits: A Partner's Own Tortious Conduct, and a Separate Limit for Legal Services
clauses.body: The registered limited liability partnership shield described in Cal. Corp. Code § 16306(c) is not absolute; the same section states named limits on it. Subdivision (e) states: "[n]othing in subdivision (c) shall be construed to affect the liability of a partner of a registered limited liability partnership to third parties for that partner's tortious conduct." By its own terms, subdivision (c)'s shield reaches liability that would otherwise attach to a partner "by reason of being a partner or acting in the conduct of the business or activities of the partnership" — that is, liability arising from the partnership relationship itself — while subdivision (e) states that this shield does not extend to a partner's own tortious conduct toward a third party. Subdivision (f) states a separate, additionally specific limit for the practice of law: "[t]he limitation of liability in subdivision (c) shall not apply to claims based upon acts, errors, or omissions arising out of the rendering of professional limited liability partnership services of a registered limited liability partnership providing legal services unless that partnership has a currently effective certificate of registration issued by the State Bar." Read together, these two subdivisions state that the shield in subdivision (c) coexists with, rather than displaces, a partner's own liability for their own tortious conduct, and that for a law-practice registered limited liability partnership specifically, the shield itself does not apply to professional-service claims at all unless the partnership holds a currently effective State Bar certificate of registration.
clauses.gap: The text of Cal. Corp. Code § 16306(e), as fetched and verified for this clause, states the limit in terms of "that partner's tortious conduct" toward third parties; it does not, in this subdivision or elsewhere in the section as fetched, use language expressly limiting a partner's own conduct to that partner's personal negligence, wrongful acts, or misconduct, or the negligence, wrongful acts, or misconduct of a person under that partner's direct supervision or control — no phrase resembling "direct supervision" or "control" over another person's conduct appears anywhere in the fetched text of Section 16306. A reader should not assume Section 16306 contains that more specific supervision-based formulation found in some other jurisdictions' limited liability partnership statutes; this clause states only the broader "tortious conduct" formulation that California's current text actually uses. This clause also does not address subdivision (d) (a partner's ability to agree in writing to be liable for specified debts) or subdivision (h) (a partner's separate ability to act as guarantor or surety), which are outside its scope. Both quoted subdivisions are drawn from the single statutory section Cal. Corp. Code § 16306 and are treated as one primary source, alongside the separate clause of this document quoting subdivision (c) of the same section. As of this verification, the California Legislative Information website listed a single version of Section 16306 on file, dated as added by Stats. 1996, Ch. 1003, Sec. 2, with no amendment or competing version found since. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific partner's conduct is or is not "tortious conduct" within the meaning of subdivision (e), and does not address professions other than the practice of law under subdivision (f). This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what that state's law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific partner's conduct, and these rules vary by state. This document is informational only.

clauses.title: Formation by Filing a Certificate of Limited Partnership
clauses.body: California's Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008 requires a specific act to bring a limited partnership into existence: a certificate of limited partnership must be filed with, and on a form prescribed by, the Secretary of State, and the statute pinpoints the moment of formation as the moment the Secretary of State files that certificate — not some earlier date on which the partners may have reached their own agreement. The statute separately requires that the partners have entered into a partnership agreement, either before or after that certificate is filed. The certificate itself must state five specific items: the limited partnership's name (which must comply with the statute's own naming requirement); the street address of its initial principal office; the name and street address of its initial agent for service of process; the name and address of each general partner; and, if different from the principal office address, the limited partnership's mailing address.
clauses.gap: This describes only the formation mechanic and required certificate content stated in Cal. Corp. Code § 15902.01(a) and (c); it does not address that section's other subdivisions — the effect of an inconsistency between the certificate and the partnership agreement (subd. (d)), optional county recording (subd. (e)), cancellation for a dishonored filing-fee payment (subd. (f)), or the annual-tax notice requirement (subd. (g)) — none of which were independently researched for this clause. It also does not state current Secretary of State filing fees, the specific form to use, or where or how to file, none of which are statutory text; that is Secretary of State administrative practice, not verified here. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a domestic limited partnership formed under the 2008 Act — not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific limited partnership, and not a claim that a foreign limited partnership's California registration (Article 9, §§ 15909.01 et seq.) works identically; that article was not independently verified for this document. This clause is informational only: it does not itself file, or determine the contents of, any specific limited partnership's certificate.

clauses.title: Naming Requirement for a Limited Partnership
clauses.body: California's limited partnership statute imposes a specific naming requirement: the name of a limited partnership formed under the Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008 must contain the phrase "limited partnership," or the abbreviation "L.P." or "LP," at the end of its name. The statute separately authorizes, without requiring, a limited partnership's name to include the name of any partner.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.08(a) and (b). It does not address the statute's separate distinguishability requirement — that the name not be one the Secretary of State determines is likely to mislead the public, and that it be distinguishable in the Secretary of State's records from other limited partnership and reserved names (subd. (d)) — nor the different designator the statute requires of a foreign limited liability limited partnership registering in California, "limited liability limited partnership" or "LLLP"/"L.L.L.P." (subd. (c)), neither of which is independently detailed here. It does not state the Secretary of State's own methodology for comparing names, which is administrative practice rather than statutory text. This clause is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific proposed name complies with this requirement.

clauses.title: General Partners and Limited Partners — A Structural Distinction
clauses.body: California's limited partnership statute builds a basic structural distinction between a limited partnership's two kinds of partners directly into the statutory text. A general partner is, by statute, an agent of the limited partnership for purposes of its activities, and a general partner's act for apparently carrying on the limited partnership's activities in the ordinary course binds the limited partnership, subject to a stated exception for a counterparty who knew or had notice the general partner lacked authority. A limited partner, by contrast, does not have the right or the power, as a limited partner, to act for or bind the limited partnership.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code §§ 15904.02(a) and 15903.02 — the agency/binding-authority rule for each type of partner. It does not address how a person becomes a general partner or a limited partner in the first place (§§ 15903.01, 15904.01), each type's management rights or fiduciary duties, or the statutory exception under which a limited partner who participates in the control of the business can be held liable as if a general partner (addressed separately in this project's limited-partner liability-shield clause). A partnership agreement can shape a specific limited partnership's internal arrangements within the statute's terms; this clause states the statute's own default agency rule, not a description of any specific limited partnership's governing documents or of which role any specific person holds.

citations.quote: Each general partner is an agent of the limited partnership for the purposes of its activities. An act of a general partner, including the signing of a record in the partnership’s name, for apparently carrying on in the ordinary course the limited partnership’s activities or activities of the kind carried on by the limited partnership binds the limited partnership, unless the general partner did not have authority to act for the limited partnership in the particular matter and the person with which the general partner was dealing knew, had received a notification, or had notice under subdivision (d) of Section 15901.03 that the general partner lacked authority.
