clauses.title: The Limited Partner Liability Shield
clauses.body: California's limited partnership statute states its liability shield for limited partners directly: a limited partner is not liable for an obligation of the limited partnership solely by reason of being a limited partner. The same sentence sets out the shield's own exceptions — it does not protect a person named as a general partner in the certificate, and it does not protect a limited partner who, beyond exercising the rights and powers of a limited partner, participates in the control of the business (a term the statute separately defines through an extensive list of activities that, on their own, do not count as "control"). The statute also states expressly that nothing in the chapter affects a limited partner's own liability to third parties for the limited partner's own tortious conduct.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(a). It does not itemize the statute's extensive safe-harbor list, in subdivision (b), of activities that do not by themselves amount to "participat[ing] in the control of the business" (for example, consulting with a general partner, voting on partnership matters, or serving on a partnership committee); a limited partner's specific conduct and whether it crosses into "control" is a fact-specific question this clause does not answer. It also does not address the narrower liability a limited partner who does participate in control can face under the same subdivision (limited to persons who transacted business with actual knowledge of that participation and a reasonable belief the partner was a general partner), the separate good-faith-investor provision of § 15903.06, or the parallel rules for a foreign limited partnership or a limited liability limited partnership, none of which were independently researched for this clause. This clause is informational only: it does not state whether any specific person's own conduct falls inside or outside this shield.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, limited partner not liable for LP obligations
citations.quote: A limited partner is not liable for any obligation of a limited partnership unless named as a general partner in the certificate or, in addition to exercising the rights and powers of a limited partner, the limited partner participates in the control of the business.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(a) (California Legislative Information text)

citations.quote: Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to affect the liability of a limited partner to third parties for the limited partner’s participation in tortious conduct.

clauses.title: A General Partner's Own Liability for Partnership Obligations
clauses.body: California's limited partnership statute states the converse rule for general partners directly: unless a statutory exception applies, all general partners of a limited partnership are liable jointly and severally for all of the limited partnership's obligations. The statute's own stated exception to that joint-and-several rule is an agreement otherwise reached by the claimant, or a different rule provided elsewhere by law. Separately, a person who becomes a general partner of an already-existing limited partnership is not personally liable for an obligation the limited partnership incurred before that person became a general partner.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.04(a) and (b). It does not address the further collection mechanics of § 15904.05 — including the statute's rule that a judgment against the limited partnership is not by itself a judgment against a general partner, and the specific circumstances (such as an unsatisfied writ of execution against the partnership, or a court's equitable finding) under which a judgment creditor may reach a general partner's own assets — none of which were independently researched for this clause. Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.04 is a separate, independently enacted statutory provision from the general-partnership partner-liability rule this project's General Partnership Agreement document describes elsewhere (Cal. Corp. Code § 16306, in the Uniform Partnership Act of 1994) — the two statutes state a similar joint-and-several rule for their respective entity types, but this clause verifies only the limited-partnership version. This clause is informational only: it does not state whether any specific general partner has personally agreed to different terms with a specific claimant.

citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, general partners jointly and severally liable
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (b), all general partners are liable jointly and severally for all obligations of the limited partnership unless otherwise agreed by the claimant or provided by law.

clauses.title: Declaration of Purpose — Confidential Intermediary Search Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Confidential Intermediary Search — Information Sheet describes the statutory mechanism under California Family Code Division 13, Part 2, Chapter 7 (Disclosure of Information, §§ 9200–9209) by which {{petitionerName}}, as an adoptee or the sibling of an adoptee, may petition the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}} to appoint a confidential intermediary to attempt to locate and, without disclosing the underlying sealed adoption records, seek the consent of {{siblingSoughtName}} to contact or an exchange of identifying information. It is prepared for use alongside an actual petition contemplated for filing in that court.

As codified in Family Code § 9205, California's confidential-intermediary petition mechanism applies specifically to a search between an adoptee and that adoptee's biological, half-, or step-sibling. It is a narrower, court-supervised alternative that operates only where no mutual waiver is already on file; where an adoptee and a sibling, or an adult adoptee and a birth parent, have both already filed written consent with the California Department of Social Services or a licensed adoption agency, disclosure or contact between them may instead proceed directly under Family Code §§ 9203–9204 without any court petition or confidential intermediary. This information sheet is not itself a court filing and does not itself locate, contact, or obtain the consent of any person.

clauses.title: Who May Petition for a Confidential Intermediary
clauses.body: California's confidential-intermediary petition mechanism is codified within Family Code § 9205, a section otherwise governing the release of sibling identifying information upon mutual waiver. Family Code § 9205(g) provides that, "[n]otwithstanding subdivisions (a) and (e), an adoptee or sibling who seeks contact with the other for whom no waiver is on file may petition the court to appoint a confidential intermediary." The statute defines "sibling," for these purposes, in § 9205(h): "For purposes of this section, 'sibling' means a biological sibling, half-sibling, or step-sibling of the adoptee." Once such a petition is filed, § 9205(g) further provides that "[t]he court shall grant the petition unless it finds that it would be detrimental to the adoptee or sibling with whom contact is sought."
clauses.gap: This clause states only what Family Code § 9205 itself provides about who may petition for a confidential intermediary; it does not address any other California statute, does not describe the separate, non-petition, mutual-consent disclosure procedures for an adult adoptee and a birth parent found in Family Code §§ 9203–9204 (addressed in a separate clause of this document), and does not determine that any specific petitioner named in this document's companion clauses is eligible to petition under § 9205(g) or that any petition would be granted. Both quoted passages are drawn from the same subdivision, § 9205(g), of a single statutory section, together with the definition in § 9205(h) of the same section; they are treated here as one statutory source, not multiple independent sources. This document is informational only and does not itself file any petition.

clauses.title: Who Serves as the Confidential Intermediary
clauses.body: Family Code § 9205(g) does not leave the identity of the confidential intermediary to the petitioner's choice; it assigns the role by statute according to who is sought. Where the person being sought is the adoptee, the statute provides that "the intermediary shall be the department, county adoption agency, or licensed adoption agency that provided adoption services as described in Section 8521 or 8533." Where the agency that conducted the adoption cannot serve, § 9205(g) provides a fallback: "[i]f the court finds that the agency that conducted the adoptee's adoption is unable, due to economic hardship, to serve as the intermediary, then the agency shall provide all records related to the adoptee or the sibling to the court and the court shall appoint an alternate confidential intermediary."
clauses.gap: This clause states only what Family Code § 9205(g) itself provides about who serves as confidential intermediary; it does not restate the separate rule in the same subdivision for a sought sibling who was formerly under juvenile court jurisdiction but is not an adoptee, and it does not identify who would in fact be appointed in any specific case. Both quoted passages are drawn from the same subdivision, § 9205(g), of a single statutory section and are treated here as one statutory source, not multiple independent sources. This document is informational only and does not itself appoint, or predict the appointment of, any confidential intermediary.

clauses.title: What a Confidential Intermediary Does — Search, Access, and the Consent Requirement
clauses.body: Once appointed under Family Code § 9205(g), a confidential intermediary is given statutory access to otherwise-sealed material for the specific purpose of locating the sought person and asking whether that person consents to disclosure or contact — access the petitioner does not receive directly. The statute provides: "The intermediary shall have access to all records of the adoptee or the sibling and shall make all reasonable efforts to locate and attempt to obtain the consent of the adoptee, sibling, or adoptive or birth parent, as required to make the disclosure authorized by this section." The statute also requires the intermediary to make clear, once the sought person is located, that responding is voluntary: "The confidential intermediary shall notify any located adoptee, sibling, or adoptive or birth parent that consent is optional, not required by law, and does not affect the status of the adoption. If that individual denies the request for consent, the confidential intermediary shall not make any further attempts to obtain consent."
clauses.gap: This clause states only what Family Code § 9205(g) itself provides about the confidential intermediary's search-and-consent function; it does not restate the section's separate provisions addressing a sought person under 18 years of age, a sought person under juvenile court jurisdiction, or a foreign-born adoptee subject to an intercountry adoption, each of which carries its own statutory rule within the same subdivision. Both quoted passages are drawn from the same subdivision, § 9205(g), of a single statutory section and are treated here as one statutory source, not multiple independent sources. This document is informational only and does not itself conduct, or report the outcome of, any search.

If that individual denies the request for consent, the confidential intermediary shall not make any further attempts to obtain consent.

clauses.title: The Confidentiality Protection — What Stays Sealed and the Limits on the Intermediary's Own Use of Records
clauses.body: California's adoption records are, as a baseline, closed to the parties themselves: Family Code § 9200(a) provides that the petition, consent, agreement, court order, and investigating agency's report filed in an adoption proceeding are "not open to inspection by any person other than the parties to the proceeding and their attorneys and the department, except upon the written authority of the judge of the superior court." The confidential-intermediary mechanism in § 9205(g) does not repeal that baseline for the petitioner; it instead gives the appointed intermediary — not the petitioner — access to the records, and separately restricts what the intermediary may do with what is found: "The confidential intermediary shall use information found in the records of the adoptee or the sibling for authorized purposes only, and may not disclose that information without authorization." If the sought person is located but does not consent, the statute requires the search to stop rather than the records to be released: "the confidential intermediary shall not make any further attempts to obtain consent."
clauses.gap: This clause states only what Family Code §§ 9200(a) and 9205(g) themselves provide about record confidentiality and the intermediary's own duty of nondisclosure; it does not address every exception to § 9200's general sealing rule (for example, the certificate-of-adoption provision in § 9200(c)), and it does not state what, if any, information a court might independently order disclosed under § 9200(a)'s "good cause approaching the necessitous" standard. The § 9200(a) and § 9205(g) quotations are from two separate, independently numbered statutory sections and are treated as two independent sources; the two § 9205(g) quotations are from the same subdivision and are treated as one source, not two. This document is informational only and does not itself disclose any sealed adoption record.

clauses.title: Distinction From the Separate Mutual-Consent Disclosure Procedure for Adult Adoptees and Birth Parents
clauses.body: California law places the court-petition confidential-intermediary mechanism of Family Code § 9205(g) alongside a structurally different, non-petition mechanism in the same chapter for an adult adoptee and a birth parent. Family Code § 9203(a)(1) provides that the department or a licensed adoption agency shall, "[u]pon the request of a person who has been adopted pursuant to this part and who has attained 21 years of age, disclose the identity of the person's birth parent or parents and their most current address shown in the records of the department or licensed adoption agency, if the birth parent or parents have indicated consent to the disclosure in writing." Family Code § 9204(a) similarly provides that, "[n]otwithstanding any other law, if an adult adoptee and the adult adoptee's birth parents have each filed a written consent with the department or licensed adoption agency, the department or licensed adoption agency may arrange for contact between those persons. Neither the department nor a licensed adoption agency may solicit, directly or indirectly, the execution of a written consent." Unlike § 9205(g)'s confidential-intermediary petition, neither § 9203 nor § 9204 involves a court petition, a court-appointed intermediary, or an intermediary's search of sealed records for a person who has not already come forward; both instead operate only after each side has independently filed a written consent or waiver with the department or agency.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what Family Code §§ 9203(a)(1) and 9204(a) themselves provide about the mutual-consent disclosure and contact procedure, as a point of statutory contrast with the § 9205(g) confidential-intermediary petition described in this document's companion clauses; it does not restate § 9203's remaining subdivisions (including the separate procedure for an adoptive parent's request under § 9203(a)(3), fee provisions, or the January 1, 1984 applicability date in § 9203(g)), and it does not address adoptions to which § 9203 does not apply. The § 9203(a)(1) and § 9204(a) quotations are from two separate, independently numbered statutory sections and are treated as two independent sources. This document is informational only and does not itself file any consent, waiver, or request with the department or any adoption agency.

clauses.title: Notice to an Alleged Father in an Adoption Proceeding — Facts Declaration
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's statutory process, under California Family Code Division 12, Part 3, Chapter 5 (§§ 7660–7671), for identifying and giving notice to a man alleged to be the biological father of {{childName}} (born {{childDOB}}) — identified in this document as {{allegedParentName}} — in connection with an adoption of {{childName}} that {{birthParentName}}, the child's birth parent, has relinquished for, consented to, or proposes to relinquish for or consent to, or in connection with which {{childName}} otherwise becomes the subject of an adoption proceeding contemplated for filing in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}.

California does not maintain a centralized "putative father registry" of the kind found in a number of other states — a state database in which a man who believes he may have fathered a child affirmatively registers his own identifying information in advance, before any specific adoption is filed, to preserve a right to later notice. The California mechanism described in this document's companion clauses instead works in the other direction: it places an affirmative duty on the court and a state or county adoption agency to search for and identify an alleged father in connection with a specific, already-pending adoption matter, and then to give that identified alleged father actual notice of that specific proceeding, with a statutory window in which to respond.

This information sheet is not itself a court filing. Completing it does not itself identify, locate, notify, or terminate the parental rights of any alleged father, and does not determine that any specific adoption should or will be granted. Only the statutory inquiry, notice, and (where applicable) court petition process described in this document's companion clauses, followed by a court order, can actually do that.

clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for background use alongside an actual adoption proceeding, or a petition to terminate the parental rights of an alleged father under Family Code § 7662, filed with the California superior court. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete any such filing, does not conduct the inquiry described in this document's companion clauses, does not give or receive notice on behalf of any party, and does not waive, terminate, or preserve any person's parental rights; only the statutory process described in those clauses, and a final court order, can do that.]

clauses.title: California Has No Centralized "Putative Father Registry" — the Statute Instead Imposes a Search-and-Notice Duty
clauses.body: Unlike a number of other states, California's Family Code does not establish a centralized, state-maintained registry in which a man who believes he may have fathered a child affirmatively enrolls his own identifying information, in advance of any specific adoption, to preserve a right to later notice. The California statutory chapter addressing this subject carries its own official heading, "CHAPTER 5. Termination of Parental Rights in Adoption Proceedings [7660 - 7671]" — a search-and-notice framework, not a registry. Rather than requiring an alleged father to register himself, Family Code § 7663(a) places the burden on the court: "In an effort to identify all alleged fathers and presumed parents, the court shall cause inquiry to be made of the mother and any other appropriate person by one of the following:" — and among the bodies the court may direct to carry out that inquiry, § 7663(a)(1) names "The State Department of Social Services."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's own text structures this subject — not a claim about which state's law would govern a specific adoption, nor a claim that every state, or even most states, structures this the same way; a number of other states do maintain a proactive, self-registration putative-father registry, and this document takes no position on how any of those states' registries operate. This clause corrects a premise the underlying research request began with: California is not among the states that maintain such a registry, and no Department of Justice- or California Health and Human Services Agency-administered father-registration database was located in the current Family Code; the state office named in the statute's own text for conducting or assigning the identification inquiry is the State Department of Social Services (Family Code § 7663(a)(1)), not the Department of Justice or the Health and Human Services Agency. This clause cites the Chapter 5 heading itself (part of the same fetched page as § 7660) and two provisions of § 7663(a) (its introductory clause and paragraph (1)); the chapter heading and § 7663 are treated as two independent sources, though the two quoted parts of § 7663(a) are not independent of each other. This document does not describe every state or county agency listed in § 7663(a)(2)-(4) as alternative bodies that may conduct the inquiry in place of the department; that is addressed only in part in this document's companion clause on the inquiry itself. This document is informational only: it does not itself identify, register, or track any specific alleged father, and does not determine that the framework described in this document applies in the same way to every adoption.

clauses.title: What the Court-Directed Inquiry Must Cover in Attempting to Identify an Alleged Father
clauses.body: The identification inquiry described in this document's companion clause is not open-ended; Family Code § 7663(b) lists specific topics it must cover: "The inquiry shall include all of the following:" and, among the five listed topics, paragraph (5) directs inquiry into "The names and whereabouts, if known, of every person presumed or alleged to be the parent of the child, and the efforts made to give notice of the proposed adoption to each person identified." Once that inquiry is complete, § 7663(c) requires that "The agency that completes the inquiry shall file a written report of the findings with the court."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific topics California's own inquiry-and-report duty covers — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what inquiry, if any, another state's process requires regarding a specific child. This clause cites three parts of the same statutory section — § 7663(b)'s introductory clause, § 7663(b)(5), and § 7663(c) — and treats them as one source, not three independent ones. This clause does not restate inquiry topics (b)(1) through (4) — whether the mother was married or cohabiting with a man at the relevant times, whether she received support payments or promises of support, and whether any person has formally or informally acknowledged possible parentage — which this document's companion clause on the no-registry framework references only in passing. This document is informational only: it does not itself conduct any inquiry, does not identify or locate any specific alleged father, and does not determine what an inquiry into the facts of the child named in this document's companion clauses would find.

clauses.title: Notice to an Identified Alleged Father, and the 30-Day Deadline to Respond
clauses.body: Once an alleged father is identified through the inquiry described in this document's companion clause, Family Code § 7666(a) requires that he actually be served with notice of the proceeding: "Except as provided in subdivision (b), notice of the proceeding shall be given to every person identified as the biological father or a possible biological father in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure for the service of process in a civil action in this state at least 10 days before the date of the proceeding, except that publication or posting of the notice of the proceeding is not required, and service on the parent or guardian of a biological father or possible biological father who is a minor is not required unless the minor has previously provided written authorization to serve the minor’s parent or guardian. Proof of giving the notice shall be filed with the court before the petition is heard." That notice starts a fixed statutory clock: under § 7666(b)(4), a man who "has been served with written notice of alleged parentage and the proposed adoption, and has failed to bring an action pursuant to subdivision (c) of Section 7630 within 30 days of service of the notice or the birth of the child, whichever is later," is, on that basis, no longer entitled to notice. A materially similar 30-day, notice-and-no-response condition appears, in almost the same words, as one of the statutory bases under § 7662(a)(2) on which a petition to terminate an alleged father's parental rights may proceed without his consent.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own notice mechanics and the specific 30-day response deadline that attaches once notice is actually served — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what notice or deadline, if any, another state's process applies to a specific child. This clause cites three provisions across two statutory sections: § 7666(a) and § 7666(b)(4) are subsections of the same section and are treated as one source; § 7662(a)(2) is a separate, independently numbered section restating a materially similar 30-day condition in a different procedural context (a petition to terminate parental rights, rather than an order dispensing with notice), and is treated as a second, independent source. This clause does not detail the separate general parentage action described in Family Code § 7630(c) itself — the action a timely response under this 30-day window would take the form of — which is addressed in this corpus's separate Paternity Action (Petition to Establish Parental Relationship) Information Sheet and its companion clauses, not restated here. This document is informational only: it does not itself serve notice on any specific alleged father, does not calculate whether any specific 30-day period has run, and does not determine that the alleged father named in this document's companion clauses has, or has not, brought a timely action.

clauses.title: The Alleged Father's Own Written Waiver or Denial of Parentage
clauses.body: Separate from the consequence of failing to respond to notice within the statutory window, California law also gives an alleged father a direct, voluntary way to waive his own right to further notice. Family Code § 7662(a)(3) lists, among the circumstances under which a petition to terminate an alleged father's parental rights may proceed, that "The alleged father has executed a written form developed by the department to waive notice, to deny parentage, relinquish the child for adoption, or consent to the adoption of the child." Section 7662(b) describes the effect of that signed form directly: "The alleged father may validly execute a waiver or denial of parentage before or after the birth of the child, and, once signed, no notice of, relinquishment for, or consent to adoption of the child shall be required from the alleged father for the adoption to proceed." A materially similar waiver-or-denial mechanism also appears among the separate grounds on which a court may dispense with notice altogether under § 7666(b)(2).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California law provides a direct, voluntary mechanism by which an alleged father may himself waive notice or deny parentage — not a claim about which state's law governs, or whether any specific alleged father has executed, or would execute, such a waiver. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 7662(a)(3) and § 7662(b); they are treated as one source, not independent of each other. The cross-referenced, similarly worded mechanism in § 7666(b)(2) is noted for context but not independently re-quoted here, since it restates rather than adds to this same point. This document does not describe the department-developed form itself, its specific content, or where it may be obtained. This document is informational only: it does not itself waive, deny, relinquish, or consent to anything on behalf of the alleged father named in this document's companion clauses, and does not determine whether any specific waiver or denial is, or would be, validly executed.

clauses.title: When No Alleged Father Can Be Identified, and the Statutory Hearing Deadline
clauses.body: California's statutory scheme also addresses the situation in which the inquiry described in this document's companion clauses cannot identify any alleged father at all. Family Code § 7665 provides that, "If, after the inquiry, the court is unable to identify the biological father or any possible biological father and no person has appeared claiming to be the biological father and claiming custodial rights, the court shall enter an order terminating the unknown biological father’s parental rights with reference to the child." Where an alleged father has been identified, a separate timing rule applies to the petition itself: § 7667(a) provides that "Notwithstanding any other law, an action to terminate the parental rights of an alleged father of a child as specified in this part shall be set for hearing not more than 45 days after filing of the petition, except as provided in subdivision (c)." That exception, in § 7667(c), lets the court dispense with a hearing altogether in specific circumstances, including under § 7667(c)(1) where "The identity or whereabouts of the alleged father are unknown."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's own text handles an alleged father who cannot be identified at all, and of the deadline and ex parte exception that apply to the termination petition itself — not a claim about which state's law governs, or what happens, if any, under another state's process when a specific alleged father cannot be identified or located. This clause cites three statutory provisions: § 7665 is a single, independently numbered section, cited as one source; § 7667(a) and § 7667(c)(1) are subsections of a second, separate section and are treated together as a second source. This clause does not restate § 7667(c)(2)-(3)'s other two ex parte grounds — a validly executed waiver, addressed in this document's companion clause on the alleged father's own waiver, and the 30-day non-response condition, addressed in this document's companion clause on notice and the response deadline — to avoid re-quoting citations already independently verified elsewhere in this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any alleged father named, or not named, in this document's companion clauses is unidentifiable, and does not schedule, waive, or dispense with any hearing.

clauses.title: Notice That Noncompete Clause Is Void
Delivery
clauses.body: This notice is being delivered in writing to {{employeeName}}'s last known address, {{employeeAddress}}, and to {{employeeName}}'s email address, {{employeeEmail}}.

clauses.title: Signature
Duty to Notify Employees the Clause Is Void
clauses.body: Separate from the general prohibition on noncompete clauses, California Business and Professions Code Section 16600.1(b)(1) imposes an affirmative notice duty on the employer. For a current employee, and for a former employee who was employed after January 1, 2022, whose contract includes a noncompete clause -- or who was required to enter a noncompete agreement -- that does not satisfy an exception under this chapter, the statute required the employer to notify that employee, by February 14, 2024, that the noncompete clause or noncompete agreement is void. The statute's own text does not prescribe a particular script beyond that content: it requires that the employee be told the clause or agreement is void, not any specific phrasing beyond that.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the notice duty in Section 16600.1(b)(1) only; it does not restate the general prohibition in Section 16600.1(a) or Section 16600, which this document's other clauses on noncompete clauses cover separately -- see this document's clause on enforceability for that text. February 14, 2024 was a fixed, one-time statutory deadline that has already passed as of when this clause was checked; this clause states that historical fact and does not address what follows for an employer that missed it, or whether any obligation continues for employees hired afterward. The statute's own text does not define 'employer' for purposes of this subdivision, and this clause does not resolve whether or how the notice duty applies to any particular employment relationship. Whether a given noncompete clause 'does not satisfy an exception in this chapter' is a separate legal question this clause does not answer.

citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: For current employees, and for former employees who were employed after January 1, 2022, whose contracts include a noncompete clause, or who were required to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception to this chapter, the employer shall, by February 14, 2024, notify the employee that the noncompete clause or noncompete agreement is void.

clauses.title: Required Form and Delivery of the Notice
clauses.body: California Business and Professions Code Section 16600.1(b)(2) specifies the form the required notice must take: a written, individualized communication to the employee or former employee -- not a general announcement or a posted policy update. The statute's own text further specifies that this notice must be delivered to two channels: the employee's or former employee's last known address, and their email address.
clauses.gap: The statute's text joins the two delivery channels with 'and,' which on its face calls for delivery to both the last known address and the email address, not either one. This clause does not resolve what the statute requires when one of those channels -- most often a former employee's current email address -- is not known to the employer, or what would satisfy the requirement in that circumstance; the statute's own text does not address it, and no case law resolving that gap has been verified here. This clause covers Section 16600.1(b)(2) only.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600.1(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: Notice made under this subdivision shall be in the form of a written individualized communication to the employee or former employee, and shall be delivered to the last known address and the email address of the employee or former employee.

clauses.title: Consequence of Not Giving the Required Notice
clauses.body: California Business and Professions Code Section 16600.1(c) states its own enforcement consequence: a violation of Section 16600.1 -- which includes the notice duty in subdivision (b), not only the underlying noncompete prohibition in subdivision (a) -- is, by the statute's own terms, an act of unfair competition within the meaning of Chapter 5 of the Business and Professions Code, commencing with Section 17200.
clauses.gap: This clause confirms only that Section 16600.1 itself makes a violation an act of unfair competition under Chapter 5 (Section 17200 et seq.); it does not summarize what remedies, penalties, or procedures Chapter 5 itself provides for an act of unfair competition, including whether a private right of action, restitution, or civil penalties are available on these facts -- that is a separate body of law this clause does not cover. It also does not address whether subdivision (c) applies to a violation of subdivision (a) alone, subdivision (b) alone, or both, beyond what the statute's plain text states.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600.1(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: A violation of this section constitutes an act of unfair competition within the meaning of Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200).

clauses.title: Motion Picture / Broadcasting Industry Final-Wage Timing — Applicability Note
clauses.body: California Labor Code section 201.5 sets a distinct final-wage timing rule for "an employee engaged in the production or broadcasting of motion pictures," as that statute itself defines the term — a different rule from the general immediate-on-discharge and 72-hour-on-quit deadlines in Labor Code sections 201 and 202 that apply to most other employees. This concerns {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}}, recorded here as ending on {{terminationDate}}. Section 201.5's own timing rule and its own definitions, both described in the information that follows, turn on whether the work {{employeeName}} performed for {{companyName}} falls within the statute's specific definition of covered work. Naming {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}} here does not itself determine that {{employeeName}}'s job duties meet that statutory definition, and does not determine which final-wage timing rule applies to this particular employment relationship.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of Who This Section Covers
clauses.body: Labor Code section 201.5 defines "an employee engaged in the production or broadcasting of motion pictures," for purposes of that section's own timing rule, as an employee who meets two conditions at once: the employee's job duties relate to or support the production or broadcasting of motion pictures, or the facilities or equipment used in that production or broadcasting; and the employee is hired for a period of limited duration to render services relating to or supporting a particular motion picture production or broadcasting project, or is hired on the basis of one or more daily or weekly calls. The statute separately defines "daily or weekly call" as an employment that, by its own terms, will expire at the conclusion of one day or one week unless renewed. The statute also defines "production or broadcasting of motion pictures" broadly, covering the development, creation, presentation, or broadcasting of theatrical or televised motion pictures, television programs, commercial advertisements, music videos, or other moving images, made for entertainment, commercial, religious, or educational purposes, and presented by film, tape, live broadcast, cable, satellite transmission, webcast, or any other technology now in use or later adopted.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.5, subdivisions (a)(1), (a)(2), and (a)(4)), used as real evidence of how this specific section defines the category of employee and the category of industry activity it covers — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not itself a determination that any particular job duties or hiring arrangement meet this definition. The statute's definition has two conjunctive requirements (job duties tied to production/broadcasting, and limited-duration or call-based hiring); this clause does not resolve whether any specific role satisfies either requirement. The statute does not separately define a corresponding "motion picture industry employer" or "motion picture payroll services company" category within this section — this clause does not supply such a definition because the fetched text of Section 201.5 does not state one. The three citations below come from the same statutory subdivision, Section 201.5(a); they are treated as related definitional provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, motion picture/broadcasting employee definition
citations.quote: “An employee engaged in the production or broadcasting of motion pictures” means an employee to whom both of the following apply: (A) The employee’s job duties relate to or support the production or broadcasting of motion pictures or the facilities or equipment used in the production or broadcasting of motion pictures. (B) The employee is hired for a period of limited duration to render services relating to or supporting a particular motion picture production or broadcasting project, or is hired on the basis of one or more daily or weekly calls.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, "daily or weekly call" definition
citations.quote: “Daily or weekly call” means an employment that, by its terms, will expire at the conclusion of one day or one week, unless renewed.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, "production or broadcasting of motion pictures" definition
citations.quote: “Production or broadcasting of motion pictures” means the development, creation, presentation, or broadcasting of theatrical or televised motion pictures, television programs, commercial advertisements, music videos, or any other moving images, including, but not limited to, productions made for entertainment, commercial, religious, or educational purposes, whether these productions are presented by means of film, tape, live broadcast, cable, satellite transmission, Web cast, or any other technology that is now in use or may be adopted in the future.

clauses.title: The Core Rule: Wages Due by the Next Regular Payday, Not Immediately
clauses.body: Labor Code section 201.5 states that a covered motion picture or broadcasting employee whose employment terminates is entitled to receive payment of wages earned and unpaid at the time of termination by the "next regular payday" — a distinct trigger from the general rule of immediate payment on discharge under Section 201 and the general 72-hour rule for an employee who quits without notice under Section 202. The statute defines "next regular payday," for purposes of this section, as the day designated by the employer, pursuant to Labor Code section 204, for payment of wages earned during the payroll period in which the termination occurs.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.5, subdivisions (a)(3) and (b)), used as real evidence of this section's own final-wage due date and how the statute itself defines that due date — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination of what any particular employer's "regular payday" is or was for a given payroll period. Section 201.5's own definition of "next regular payday" cross-references Labor Code section 204, which sets the general rules for designating regular paydays; this clause does not independently quote or verify the text of Section 204 (it was reviewed only for context, not fetched and confirmed twice under this corpus's verification discipline), so this clause does not restate Section 204's own content and does not resolve how a specific payroll period's payday is determined. The two citations below come from the same statutory subdivisions, Section 201.5(a)(3) and (b); they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, motion picture/broadcasting final-wage due date
citations.quote: An employee engaged in the production or broadcasting of motion pictures whose employment terminates is entitled to receive payment of the wages earned and unpaid at the time of the termination by the next regular payday.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, "next regular payday" definition
citations.quote: “Next regular payday” means the day designated by the employer, pursuant to Section 204, for payment of wages earned during the payroll period in which the termination occurs.

clauses.title: Mailing Option and the Statute's Broad Definition of "Terminates"
clauses.body: Labor Code section 201.5 permits an employer to pay a covered employee's final wages either by mailing payment to the employee or by making it available at a location the employer specifies in the county where the employee was hired or performed labor; the statute deems payment made on the earlier of the date the wages are mailed or the date they are made available at that specified location. The statute also defines "terminates," for purposes of this section, broadly: an employment terminates when the employment relationship ends, whether by discharge, layoff, resignation, completion of employment for a specified term, or otherwise — meaning the next-regular-payday rule described elsewhere in this material is not limited to a discharge or a layoff, but also applies to a resignation or the natural expiration of a specified-term or call-based engagement.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.5, subdivisions (c) and (d)), used as real evidence of this section's own mailing option and its own definition of what counts as a covered termination — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular mailing or on-site availability in fact complies with the statute, or that any particular separation falls within the statute's definition of "terminates." This clause does not restate the substantive mechanics of the Section 203 waiting-time penalty (its accrual rate and 30-day cap), which this corpus addresses in its dedicated Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document rather than duplicating here. The two citations below come from the same statutory section, Section 201.5; they are treated as related provisions of one source, not as independent corroborating sources of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, motion picture/broadcasting final-wage mailing option
citations.quote: The payment of wages to employees covered by this section may be mailed to the employee or made available to the employee at a location specified by the employer in the county where the employee was hired or performed labor. The payment shall be deemed to have been made on the date that the employee’s wages are mailed to the employee or made available to the employee at the location specified by the employer, whichever is earlier.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, "terminates" definition
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, an employment terminates when the employment relationship ends, whether by discharge, lay off, resignation, completion of employment for a specified term, or otherwise.

clauses.title: Collective Bargaining Agreement Carve-Out
clauses.body: Labor Code section 201.5 states that nothing in the section prohibits the parties to a valid collective bargaining agreement from establishing alternative provisions for the final payment of wages to employees covered by this section, so long as those alternative provisions do not exceed the time limitation established in Labor Code section 204.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.5, subdivision (e)), used as real evidence that this section's next-regular-payday rule can be varied by a valid collective bargaining agreement within a stated outer limit — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular collective bargaining agreement is valid, applicable to a given employee, or compliant with the Section 204 time limitation the statute references. This clause does not independently fetch or quote Section 204's own time limitation; it states only that Section 201.5 cross-references that limitation, an honest gap disclosed rather than resolved by assumption. This clause also does not determine whether any particular employee is covered by a collective bargaining agreement at all.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.5(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, collective bargaining agreement carve-out
citations.quote: Nothing in this section prohibits the parties to a valid collective bargaining agreement from establishing alternative provisions for final payment of wages to employees covered by this section if those provisions do not exceed the time limitation established in Section 204.

clauses.title: Section 203 Waiting-Time Penalty Applies to a Violation of This Section
clauses.body: Labor Code section 201.5 does not state its own separate penalty for late payment. Instead, Labor Code section 203 expressly lists Section 201.5 among the final-wage statutes an employer's willful, unabated failure to comply with triggers the general waiting-time penalty: continuation of the employee's wages, as a penalty, from the due date at the same rate the employee was earning until paid or until an action is commenced, capped at 30 days, with an exception where the employee avoids or refuses tender of payment.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 203, subdivision (a)), used as real evidence that Section 201.5 is one of the statutes listed as triggering the general Section 203 waiting-time penalty — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any particular late payment was "willful" within the meaning of Section 203, which is a separate legal standard this clause does not analyze here. This clause does not restate the full mechanics or the 30-day-cap arithmetic of the Section 203 penalty in detail, or its statute-of-limitations provision in subdivision (b); this corpus's dedicated Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document addresses those mechanics generally rather than this clause duplicating them. The single citation below is the operative text of Section 203(a) as currently in force; it is not corroborated by a second, independent source.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 203(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, waiting-time penalty cross-reference
citations.quote: If an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, any wages of an employee who is discharged or who quits, the wages of the employee shall continue as a penalty from the due date thereof at the same rate until paid or until an action therefor is commenced; but the wages shall not continue for more than 30 days.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California Labor Code § 432.7 and § 432.8 — the state statutes restricting when {{companyName}} may ask about, seek, or use information concerning an arrest that did not result in conviction, a referral to or participation in a pretrial or posttrial diversion program, or a conviction that has been judicially dismissed or ordered sealed, in connection with {{employeeName}}'s application for or employment in the position of {{jobTitle}}, together with Section 432.8's separate rule for certain marijuana-related convictions more than two years old. This corpus separately includes a California Fair Chance Act ('Ban the Box') — Information Sheet, which describes the related but distinct restriction on inquiring into conviction history before a conditional offer of employment, and which cross-references Section 432.7 for certain definitions and for one of its own narrow exceptions without independently quoting Section 432.7's own text. This document focuses instead on Section 432.7 and Section 432.8 themselves — what those statutes state an employer may not ask, seek, use, or disclose; the exceptions the statutes state; and the remedies the statutes describe. It states facts about what these statutes require. It is not itself a job application, a background-check report, or any notice, and it does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} what to do about any particular arrest record, conviction, application, or employment decision.

clauses.title: The Core Prohibition: Arrest Not Resulting in Conviction, Diversion Programs, and Dismissed or Sealed Convictions
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 432.7 states that an employer — a public agency, private individual, or corporation — may not ask an applicant for employment to disclose, in writing or verbally, information concerning an arrest or detention that did not result in a conviction, a referral to or participation in a pretrial or posttrial diversion program, or a conviction that has been judicially dismissed or ordered sealed pursuant to law. The statute separately states that an employer may not seek that same category of information from any other source, or utilize it as a factor in determining hiring, promotion, termination, or admission to an apprenticeship or other training program leading to employment. The statute's own text carves out one item from this prohibition: it states that the section does not prevent an employer from asking an applicant or employee about an arrest for which that person is out on bail or on their own recognizance pending trial.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general ask/seek/utilize prohibition in Labor Code § 432.7(a)(1) and its own bail/own-recognizance carve-out. It does not address the statute's separate juvenile-court-record prohibition in subdivision (a)(2), which covers arrest, detention, and court-disposition information arising from juvenile-court proceedings. This clause independently fetched and verified this text directly from the California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) on two separate fetches using different browser identifications, both returning byte-identical section text; it does not rely on the cross-references to this section stated, without independent verification, in this corpus's other documents.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, restriction on employer inquiries into arrest, diversion, and dismissed or sealed conviction records
citations.quote: An employer, whether a public agency or private individual or corporation, shall not ask an applicant for employment to disclose, through any written form or verbally, information concerning an arrest or detention that did not result in conviction, or information concerning a referral to, and participation in, any pretrial or posttrial diversion program, or concerning a conviction that has been judicially dismissed or ordered sealed pursuant to law, including, but not limited to, Sections 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.425, 1203.45, and 1210.1 of the Penal Code.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, restriction on employer seeking or using the same information from any other source
citations.quote: An employer also shall not seek from any source whatsoever, or utilize, as a factor in determining any condition of employment including hiring, promotion, termination, or any apprenticeship training program or any other training program leading to employment, any record of arrest or detention that did not result in conviction, or any record regarding a referral to, and participation in, any pretrial or posttrial diversion program, or concerning a conviction that has been judicially dismissed or ordered sealed pursuant to law, including, but not limited to, Sections 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.425, 1203.45, and 1210.1 of the Penal Code.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, statutory carve-out for arrests while out on bail or own recognizance pending trial
citations.quote: This section shall not prevent an employer from asking an employee or applicant for employment about an arrest for which the employee or applicant is out on bail or on their own recognizance pending trial.

clauses.title: How the Statute Defines "Conviction"
clauses.body: For purposes of Labor Code § 432.7, the statute defines "conviction" to include a plea, verdict, or finding of guilt, regardless of whether the court imposed a sentence. The statute separately states that "conviction," for this purpose, does not include, and is not to be construed to include, any adjudication by a juvenile court or any other court order or action taken with respect to a person who is under the process and jurisdiction of the juvenile court.
clauses.gap: This clause independently verifies the definition of "conviction" in Labor Code § 432.7(a)(3) itself — the definition that this corpus's California Fair Chance Act — Information Sheet document cross-references, through Government Code § 12952(f)(1), without independently quoting Section 432.7's own text. This clause does not address Section 432.7's separate juvenile-record inquiry prohibition in subdivision (a)(2), which restricts inquiry into juvenile-court arrest, detention, and disposition information regardless of whether that proceeding resulted in what this subdivision defines as a "conviction."

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(a)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "conviction"
citations.quote: “Conviction” includes a plea, verdict, or finding of guilt, regardless of whether a sentence is imposed by the court.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(a)(3)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, exclusion of juvenile-court adjudications from the definition of "conviction"
citations.quote: “Conviction” does not include, and shall not be construed to include, any adjudication by a juvenile court or any other court order or action taken with respect to a person who is under the process and jurisdiction of the juvenile court.

clauses.title: Exceptions the Statute States
clauses.body: Labor Code § 432.7 states several exceptions to its own restrictions. Subdivision (e) states that persons seeking employment or already employed as peace officers, and persons seeking employment with the Department of Justice or another criminal justice agency as defined in Penal Code § 13101, are not covered by the section at all. Subdivision (m) states that the prohibition on asking about or seeking information regarding a conviction does not prohibit an employer from asking an applicant about, or seeking, a "particular conviction" of the applicant — regardless of whether that conviction has been expunged, judicially ordered sealed, statutorily eradicated, or judicially dismissed following probation — in any of several circumstances stated by the statute: where a federal or state law requires the employer to obtain that information; where the position sought would require the applicant to possess or use a firearm; where a law prohibits a person with that conviction from holding the position sought; or where a law prohibits the employer from hiring an applicant who has that conviction. The statute defines a "particular conviction," for purposes of this exception, as a conviction for specific criminal conduct or a category of criminal offenses that a federal or state law expressly bases requirements or exclusions on. Separately, subdivision (n) states that the section does not prohibit an employer that is required by state, federal, or local law to conduct criminal background checks, or to restrict employment based on criminal history, from complying with those requirements, and does not prohibit the employer from seeking or receiving a criminal history report obtained under procedures otherwise provided by federal, state, or local law.
clauses.gap: This clause independently verifies the peace-officer/criminal-justice-agency exclusion in subdivision (e)(1), the "particular conviction" exceptions in subdivision (m), and the legally-required-background-check exception in subdivision (n). It does not address subdivision (e)(2)'s narrower rule for nonsworn criminal-justice-agency employees, subdivision (f)'s exception for certain health-facility employer inquiries (referenced, but not independently quoted, in this corpus's Fair Chance Act — Information Sheet document, and not independently verified by this clause either), or subdivisions (g) through (l), which address law-enforcement recordkeeping restrictions and public-agency concessionaire screening — subjects distinct from a private employer's own hiring inquiry. This clause does not determine whether any specific position, employer, or conviction falls within any of these statutory exceptions.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(e)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, exclusion of peace-officer and criminal-justice-agency positions from the section's coverage
citations.quote: Persons seeking employment or persons already employed as peace officers, or persons seeking employment in positions in the Department of Justice or other criminal justice agencies as defined in Section 13101 of the Penal Code are not covered by this section.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(m)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, "particular conviction" exception, introductory clause
citations.quote: Paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) does not prohibit an employer, whether a public agency or private individual or corporation, from asking an applicant about, or seeking from any source information regarding, a particular conviction of the applicant if, pursuant to Section 1829 of Title 12 of the United States Code or any other federal law, federal regulation, or state law, any of the following apply:

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(m)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, "particular conviction" exception where the employer is legally required to obtain the information
citations.quote: The employer is required by law to obtain information regarding the particular conviction of the applicant, regardless of whether that conviction has been expunged, judicially ordered sealed, statutorily eradicated, or judicially dismissed following probation.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(m)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, "particular conviction" exception for positions requiring possession or use of a firearm
citations.quote: The applicant would be required to possess or use a firearm in the course of their employment.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(m)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "particular conviction" for purposes of the subdivision (m) exceptions
citations.quote: For purposes of this subdivision, “particular conviction” means a conviction for specific criminal conduct or a category of criminal offenses prescribed by any federal law, federal regulation, or state law that contains requirements, exclusions, or both, expressly based on that specific criminal conduct or category of criminal offenses.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(n) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, exception for employers legally required to conduct criminal background checks
citations.quote: This section does not prohibit an employer, whether a public agency or private individual or corporation, required by state, federal, or local law to conduct criminal background checks for employment purposes or to restrict employment based on criminal history from complying with those requirements, or to prohibit the employer from seeking or receiving an applicant’s criminal history report that has been obtained pursuant to procedures otherwise provided for under federal, state, or local law.

clauses.title: Separate Treatment of Certain Old Marijuana-Related Convictions
clauses.body: A separate Labor Code section, § 432.8, extends the limitations on employers and the penalties stated in § 432.7 to a conviction for violating specific marijuana-related provisions of the Health and Safety Code — subdivision (b) or (c) of § 11357 (or a statutory predecessor), subdivision (c) of § 11360, or §§ 11364, 11365, or 11550 as those sections related to marijuana before January 1, 1976 (or a statutory predecessor) — once two years have passed from the date of that conviction. As currently published on the California Legislative Information website, Section 432.8 was added to the Labor Code in 1976 and has not been further amended since.
clauses.gap: This clause independently fetched and verified Labor Code § 432.8 directly as its own statutory section — it is a separate section from § 432.7, not a subdivision within it, though it operates by cross-reference to Section 432.7's limitations and penalties. Section 432.8's rule is narrower than a blanket "any marijuana conviction over two years old" rule: it applies only to convictions under the specific Health and Safety Code provisions the statute lists (or their statutory predecessors), not to every marijuana-related offense. This clause does not determine whether any particular conviction falls within one of those listed provisions or their statutory predecessors, which is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve, and it does not address how other, more recent California cannabis-legalization and record-relief statutes may separately affect older marijuana convictions.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.8 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, extension of Section 432.7's limitations and penalties to certain marijuana-related convictions after two years
citations.quote: The limitations on employers and the penalties provided for in Section 432.7 shall apply to a conviction for violation of subdivision (b) or (c) of Section 11357 of the Health and Safety Code or a statutory predecessor thereof, or subdivision (c) of Section 11360 of the Health and Safety Code, or Section 11364, 11365, or 11550 of the Health and Safety Code as they related to marijuana prior to January 1, 1976, or a statutory predecessor thereof, two years from the date of such a conviction.

clauses.title: Remedies the Statute States
clauses.body: Labor Code § 432.7 states its own civil and criminal remedies for a violation. If a person violates the section, or the separate Penal Code provisions on dissemination of criminal history information beginning at Penal Code § 11140, the statute states that the applicant may bring an action to recover actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees. For an intentional violation, the statute states that the applicant may recover treble actual damages or $500, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and that an intentional violation is also a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $500. The statute states that these remedies are in addition to, and not in place of, any other rights and remedies an applicant may have under other law.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the remedies and penalties that Labor Code § 432.7(c)-(d) itself describes. It does not address remedies or requirements that may separately arise under the Fair Chance Act (Government Code § 12952) or the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, both covered independently elsewhere in this corpus, and it does not address how a court would apply these remedy provisions to any particular set of facts, which is a legal conclusion this document does not draw.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, civil damages and misdemeanor penalty for a violation
citations.quote: If a person violates this section, or Article 6 (commencing with Section 11140) of Chapter 1 of Title 1 of Part 4 of the Penal Code, the applicant may bring an action to recover from that person actual damages or two hundred dollars ($200), whichever is greater, plus costs, and reasonable attorney’s fees. An intentional violation of this section shall entitle the applicant to treble actual damages, or five hundred dollars ($500), whichever is greater, plus costs, and reasonable attorney’s fees. An intentional violation of this section is a misdemeanor punishable by a fine not to exceed five hundred dollars ($500).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 432.7(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, remedies stated as cumulative with other law
citations.quote: The remedies under this section shall be in addition to and not in derogation of all other rights and remedies that an applicant may have under any other law.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's pregnancy disability leave law, Government Code Section 12945, part of the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). Section 12945 is a separate statute from the California Family Rights Act (CFRA), Government Code Section 12945.2, and from the federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) — it addresses leave for an employee disabled by pregnancy, childbirth, or a related medical condition, on its own track from CFRA/FMLA family-care and bonding leave. Where a specific employer and employee are named below, those names are {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}; this sheet can also be read on its own, without any specific employer or employee named, as a general reference to what this statute says. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate any particular leave request or employer policy, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: Leave Request
clauses.body:
