Requested start date: _______________
Estimated duration of leave: _______________
Expected return-to-work date: _______________
Accrued vacation leave to be used during this period, if any: _______________________________________________

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
The Core Leave Entitlement
clauses.body: Government Code Section 12945 makes it an unlawful employment practice for a covered employer to refuse to allow an employee disabled by pregnancy, childbirth, or a related medical condition to take a leave for a reasonable period of time not to exceed four months, and thereafter to refuse to allow the employee to return to work, as set forth in the applicable regulations. 'Reasonable period of time' is defined by the statute as the period during which the employee is actually disabled on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or a related medical condition — not a fixed calendar entitlement that every employee receives regardless of their own disability duration. During that leave, the employee is entitled to utilize any accrued vacation leave. An employer may require an employee who plans to take this leave to give the employer reasonable notice of the date the leave will commence and its estimated duration.
clauses.gap: The four-month figure is a statutory cap on the outer length of leave tied to actual disability, not a guaranteed four months regardless of medical need — an employee disabled for a shorter period is entitled to leave for that shorter period, and the statute does not entitle an employee to leave beyond four months under this section. The statute delegates the specific mechanics of what 'thereafter return to work' requires — including whether an employee returns to the same or a comparable position — to regulations adopted by the responsible council; this document quotes only the statute's own text from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and does not independently verify the content of those regulations. This clause also does not cover Section 12945(a)(3), a separate reasonable-accommodation and temporary-transfer right for pregnancy-related conditions embedded in the same statute, which this document doesn't address.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945(a)(1) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, pregnancy disability leave, core entitlement and duration
citations.quote: For an employer to refuse to allow an employee disabled by pregnancy, childbirth, or a related medical condition to take a leave for a reasonable period of time not to exceed four months and thereafter return to work, as set forth in the council’s regulations.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945(a)(1) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, pregnancy disability leave, 'reasonable period of time' defined
citations.quote: Reasonable period of time means that period during which the employee is disabled on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or a related medical condition.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945(a)(1) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, pregnancy disability leave, use of accrued vacation
citations.quote: The employee shall be entitled to utilize any accrued vacation leave during this period of time.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945(a)(1) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, pregnancy disability leave, employer notice requirement
citations.quote: An employer may require an employee who plans to take a leave pursuant to this subdivision to give the employer reasonable notice of the date the leave shall commence and the estimated duration of the leave.

clauses.title: Covered Employers
clauses.body: Section 12945 does not state its own employee-count threshold; instead, its opening subdivision places it 'in addition to' the provisions governing pregnancy, childbirth, or a related medical condition found elsewhere in this part, including Section 12926 — the definitions section for the part of the Government Code that includes Section 12945. Section 12926 defines 'employer,' for these purposes, as any person regularly employing five or more persons, or acting as an agent of such an employer, and separately as the state and any political or civil subdivision of the state and cities, but excludes a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit.
clauses.gap: Section 12945 itself is silent on employer size; this clause's coverage conclusion rests on Section 12926's general 'employer' definition, which Section 12945(a) expressly cross-references as one of the provisions it supplements. This document doesn't independently verify how 'regularly employing five or more persons' is counted for a business with multiple related entities, franchises, or a staffing-agency arrangement, and doesn't address the separate religious-nonprofit exclusion beyond quoting it.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945(a) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, pregnancy disability leave, cross-reference to definitions
citations.quote: In addition to the provisions that govern pregnancy, childbirth, or a related medical condition in Sections 12926 and 12940, each of the following shall be an unlawful employment practice, unless based upon a bona fide occupational qualification:

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(d) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, FEHA definitions, 'employer' definition
citations.quote: “Employer” includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, except as follows:

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(d) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, FEHA definitions, religious-nonprofit exclusion
citations.quote: “Employer” does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit.

clauses.title: Group Health Plan Coverage During Leave
clauses.body: It is also an unlawful employment practice for a covered employer to refuse to maintain and pay for group health plan coverage for an eligible employee who takes leave under Section 12945, for the duration of the leave, not to exceed four months over the course of a 12-month period commencing on the date the leave begins, at the level and under the conditions that would have applied had the employee continued working. An employer is not barred from voluntarily maintaining and paying for that coverage beyond four months.
clauses.gap: The statute separately allows an employer to recover the premiums it paid to maintain coverage if the employee fails to return from leave after the leave period has expired, for a reason other than taking further leave under the California Family Rights Act or a continuing, recurring, or new qualifying health condition or other circumstance beyond the employee's control — this document does not restate that recovery mechanism's full text or the separate rule for state-agency employers governed by collective bargaining agreements.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945(a)(2)(A) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, pregnancy disability leave, group health plan coverage during leave
citations.quote: For an employer to refuse to maintain and pay for coverage for an eligible employee who takes leave pursuant to paragraph (1) under a group health plan, as defined in Section 5000(b)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, for the duration of the leave, not to exceed four months over the course of a 12-month period, commencing on the date the leave taken under paragraph (1) begins, at the level and under the conditions that coverage would have been provided if the employee had continued in employment continuously for the duration of the leave.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945(a)(2)(A) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, pregnancy disability leave, coverage beyond four months permitted
citations.quote: Nothing in this paragraph shall preclude an employer from maintaining and paying for coverage under a group health plan beyond four months.

clauses.title: How This Leave Relates to CFRA and FMLA
clauses.body: The California Family Rights Act (CFRA) statute, Government Code Section 12945.2, states that it 'shall be construed as separate and distinct from Section 12945' — the pregnancy disability leave law described in this sheet. CFRA's own list of qualifying reasons separately excludes leave for 'disability on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions' from the employee's-own-serious-health-condition category that would otherwise trigger CFRA leave. Consistent with that separation, Section 12945.2 states that an employee is entitled to take, in addition to the leave provided under CFRA and the federal FMLA, the leave provided for in Section 12945, if the employee is otherwise qualified for that leave.
clauses.gap: This document does not independently verify the FMLA's own statutory or regulatory text on how federal FMLA leave interacts with California's Section 12945 leave; it states only what the California statutes say about the relationship. This document also does not resolve, for any individual's specific circumstances, whether or how much of a given absence would be treated as Section 12945 leave, CFRA leave, or FMLA leave in combination — that determination depends on facts and application of these several statutes together. The CFRA document in this corpus (Government Code Section 12945.2) covers CFRA's own eligibility, family-care and medical-leave categories, restoration rights, and its own relationship to FMLA in more detail, and is not duplicated here.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(n) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, separateness from pregnancy disability leave law
citations.quote: This section shall be construed as separate and distinct from Section 12945.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(b)(5)(C) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, pregnancy-disability exclusion from CFRA's own-condition category
citations.quote: Leave because of an employee’s own serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform the functions of the position of that employee, except for leave taken for disability on account of pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.2(p) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, California Family Rights Act, additive entitlement to Section 12945 leave
citations.quote: An employee is entitled to take, in addition to the leave provided for under this section and the FMLA, the leave provided for in Section 12945, if the employee is otherwise qualified for that leave.

clauses.title: No Interference, and Relationship to Other Pregnancy-Discrimination Protections
clauses.body: It is also an unlawful employment practice for a covered employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under Section 12945. Section 12945 itself states that it is not to be construed to affect any other provision of law relating to sex discrimination or pregnancy, or to diminish the coverage of pregnancy, childbirth, or a related medical condition under any other provision of the same part, including Section 12940(a).
clauses.gap: This document does not independently verify what Section 12940(a) or other provisions of this part separately provide beyond quoting Section 12945's own reference to them. All citations for this clause are subdivisions of the same statute, Government Code Section 12945 — different parts of one section, not independent sources confirming each other.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945(a)(4) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, pregnancy disability leave, prohibited interference
citations.quote: For an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of, or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under this section.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945(b) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, pregnancy disability leave, non-diminishment of other pregnancy-discrimination coverage
citations.quote: This section shall not be construed to affect any other provision of law relating to sex discrimination or pregnancy, or in any way to diminish the coverage of pregnancy, childbirth, or a medical condition related to pregnancy or childbirth under any other provision of this part, including subdivision (a) of Section 12940.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California Civil Code Section 1710.2, the statute addressing whether an owner of real property or an agent must disclose to a prospective transferee that an occupant died on the property, the manner of that death, or that an occupant had HIV/AIDS, as it may apply to the property at {{propertyAddress}}, as between {{sellerLandlordName}} and {{buyerTenantName}}. It states what the statute's own text provides, including the conditions under which it says no disclosure duty exists. It does not authorize, direct, or prohibit any particular disclosure, and it does not tell either {{sellerLandlordName}} or {{buyerTenantName}} what to do about any specific death or health-status fact concerning the property.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
clauses.body:
This information sheet regarding death-on-property and HIV/AIDS-status disclosure under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, concerning the property at {{propertyAddress}} as between {{sellerLandlordName}} and {{buyerTenantName}}, states California law as of the date below. It does not constitute legal advice about, and does not resolve, any specific disclosure question concerning this property.

Prepared: _______________________ Date: _______________

clauses.title: No Duty to Disclose a Death or Its Manner After Three Years
clauses.body: Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, subject to a stated exception for intentional misrepresentation, an owner of real property or the owner's agent, and any agent of a transferee, is not required to disclose to the transferee the occurrence of an occupant's death upon the property, or the manner of that death, where the death occurred more than three years before the date the transferee offers to purchase, lease, or rent the property; the statute states that this is because such a fact is not a material fact requiring disclosure. The statute further states that no cause of action arises against an owner, the owner's agent, or a transferee's agent for not disclosing this fact. The statute's own definition of "transferee" for this purpose includes a purchaser, a lessee, and a renter of real property.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text states the non-disclosure rule using the single, undifferentiated phrase "the manner of death" — it does not itself break "manner of death" into categories such as natural, accidental, suicide, or homicide, and it does not state a different rule for any one category; this document does not add a categorization the statute's own text does not contain. The three-year period runs from "the date the transferee offers to purchase, lease, or rent the real property," a specific triggering event stated in the statute itself — this document does not calculate or apply that date to any specific transaction. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines a death-on-property disclosure duty — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property transfer; other states' stigmatized-property rules, including any lookback period, vary and some states impose no such statute at all. The no-cause-of-action language is part of the same statutory subdivision (a) as the core disclosure rule and is not an independent corroborating source for it.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(a)(1)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the no-duty-to-disclose rule
citations.quote: (a) (1) Subject to subdivision (d), an owner of real property or his or her agent, or any agent of a transferee of real property, is not required to disclose either of the following to the transferee, as these are not material facts that require disclosure:

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(a)(1)(A)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the death/manner-of-death rule and three-year period
citations.quote: (A) The occurrence of an occupant’s death upon the real property or the manner of death where the death has occurred more than three years prior to the date the transferee offers to purchase, lease, or rent the real property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(a)(3)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, no cause of action for not disclosing
citations.quote: (3) No cause of action shall arise against an owner or his or her agent or any agent of a transferee for not disclosing facts pursuant to paragraph (1).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(a)(2)(B)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, statutory definition of "transferee"
citations.quote: (B) “Transferee” includes a purchaser, lessee, or renter of real property.

clauses.title: No Duty to Disclose an Occupant's HIV/AIDS Status
clauses.body: Separately from the death-and-manner-of-death rule, Civil Code Section 1710.2 states that an owner of real property or the owner's agent, and any agent of a transferee, is not required to disclose to the transferee that an occupant of the property was living with HIV or died from AIDS-related complications; the statute states this is because that fact, too, is not a material fact requiring disclosure. Unlike the death/manner-of-death rule, the statute's own text attaches no three-year (or other) time limit to this HIV/AIDS-status rule. The statute also states that it is the intent of the California Legislature to occupy the field of regulation of disclosure concerning the HIV-positive status of a prior occupant in situations affecting the transfer of real property or any estate or interest in real property.
clauses.gap: "Occupy the field" is the statute's own characterization of its relationship to other disclosure regulation on this specific subject; this document does not interpret what that phrase does or does not preempt for any particular local ordinance, regulation, or common-law claim, and does not resolve whether or how it interacts with disclosure duties arising under a different statute. The statute's own text pairs this occupy-the-field statement with deaths occurring upon real property as well, in the same subdivision (b); this clause focuses on the HIV/AIDS-status half of that statement, and the death-related half is addressed in a separate clause of this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction treats disclosure of a prior occupant's HIV/AIDS status — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property transfer.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(a)(1)(B)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the HIV/AIDS-status no-duty rule
citations.quote: (B) That an occupant of that property was living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or died from AIDS-related complications.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, legislative intent to occupy the field
citations.quote: (b) It is the intent of the Legislature to occupy the field of regulation of disclosure related to either of the following: (1) Deaths occurring upon real property. (2) The HIV-positive status of a prior occupant in situations affecting the transfer of real property or any estate or interest in real property.

clauses.title: What the No-Duty Rules Do Not Change
clauses.body: Civil Code Section 1710.2 states two express limits on its own no-duty rules. First, the statute states that it does not alter the law relating to disclosure of any other physical or mental condition or disease, and does not relieve an owner or agent of any obligation to disclose the physical condition of the premises. Second, the statute states that it does not immunize an owner or the owner's agent from making an intentional misrepresentation in response to a direct inquiry from a transferee, or a prospective transferee, concerning deaths on the property; the statute's core no-duty rule is itself stated as subject to this misrepresentation limitation. The statute defines "agent," for purposes of the entire section, to include any person licensed under the California real estate licensing law referenced in the statute's own text.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text addresses only an "intentional misrepresentation in response to a direct inquiry" — it does not, in this text, define what qualifies as an intentional misrepresentation or a direct inquiry, and this document does not resolve either question for any specific exchange. The "other physical or mental condition or disease" limitation and the intentional-misrepresentation limitation are each stated in a separate subdivision of the same statutory section — subdivisions (c) and (d) respectively — and are not corroborating sources for one another. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction bounds its own stigmatized-property disclosure exemption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific property transfer.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(c)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, no effect on other physical-condition disclosure duties
citations.quote: (c) This section shall not be construed to alter the law relating to disclosure pertaining to any other physical or mental condition or disease, and this section shall not relieve any owner or agent of any obligation to disclose the physical condition of the premises.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(d)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, intentional-misrepresentation carve-out
citations.quote: (d) This section shall not be construed to immunize an owner or his or her agent from making an intentional misrepresentation in response to a direct inquiry from a transferee or a prospective transferee of real property, concerning deaths on the real property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1710.2(a)(2)(A)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, statutory definition of "agent"
citations.quote: (A) “Agent” includes any person licensed pursuant to Part 1 (commencing with Section 10000) of Division 4 of the Business and Professions Code.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: {{preparerName}} is reviewing this information sheet in connection with the estate of {{decedentName}}. This sheet explains, on a general informational basis only, California's default statutory scheme for dividing a decedent's property when all or part of the decedent's estate is not effectively disposed of by a valid will — Probate Code §§ 6400–6402 — including the surviving spouse's or registered domestic partner's statutory share and the order in which other relatives inherit when there is no surviving spouse or registered domestic partner, or for whatever part of the estate does not pass to one. This sheet states general facts about how California's intestate succession statutes are written. It does not determine {{decedentName}}'s heirs, does not characterize any specific item of {{decedentName}}'s property as community, quasi-community, or separate property, and does not advise {{preparerName}} or anyone else on what to do about any actual estate.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block — Intestate Succession Distribution Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{preparerName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California's intestate succession statutes on a general basis. It does not itself determine any decedent's heirs, distribute any property, or open a probate proceeding; only a court's order in an actual probate proceeding, following the statutory petition, notice, and hearing process, does that.]

clauses.title: When California's Intestate Succession Rules Apply
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 6400 provides that any part of a decedent's estate not effectively disposed of by a valid will passes to the decedent's heirs as prescribed in Probate Code Division 6, Part 2 (§§ 6400–6455) — the intestate succession statutes. Whether {{decedentName}}'s estate is governed in whole or in part by these statutes depends on whether {{decedentName}} left a valid will and, if so, whether that will disposed of all of {{decedentName}}'s property; property a will fails to reach — because the will is invalid, silent as to that particular asset, or covers only part of the estate — passes under this same intestate framework even where a will governs the rest of the estate. This information sheet describes the statutory shares set out in Probate Code §§ 6401 and 6402: the surviving spouse's or registered domestic partner's intestate share, and the shares of other relatives when there is no surviving spouse or registered domestic partner, or for whatever portion of separate property does not pass to one.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, Prob. Code § 6400, used as evidence of the basic trigger for California's intestate succession framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. This is a single statutory section; no other independent source is cited in this clause. Neither § 6400 nor this clause addresses how a court or personal representative determines whether a particular document is a valid will or resolves a dispute over whether a will effectively disposes of specific property — those are separate questions this document does not cover.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6400 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 6400
citations.quote: Any part of the estate of a decedent not effectively disposed of by will passes to the decedent’s heirs as prescribed in this part.

clauses.title: The Surviving Spouse's or Domestic Partner's Share of Separate Property
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6401(c) sets the surviving spouse's or registered domestic partner's intestate share of a decedent's separate property — property that is neither community nor quasi-community property — on a sliding scale that depends on which other relatives survive the decedent. The surviving spouse or domestic partner takes the entire intestate estate if the decedent leaves no surviving issue (children, grandchildren, and other descendants), parent, sibling, or issue of a deceased sibling. The share drops to one-half of the intestate estate if the decedent leaves only one child, or the issue of one deceased child, or if the decedent leaves no issue but leaves a parent or parents (or their issue). The share drops further, to one-third of the intestate estate, if the decedent leaves more than one child, one child together with the issue of one or more other deceased children, or the issue of two or more deceased children. This separate-property scale is distinct from the surviving spouse's or domestic partner's share of community and quasi-community property, which — as documented elsewhere in this corpus — is simply the one-half of that property that already belonged to the decedent under Probate Code §§ 100 and 101, confirmed as the surviving spouse's or domestic partner's intestate share of that property by § 6401(a)-(b).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate or which state's law determines whether specific property is separate property. This clause quotes only subdivision (c) of § 6401; subdivisions (a) and (b), addressing the surviving spouse's or domestic partner's share of community and quasi-community property, are independently quoted and verified elsewhere in this corpus (at the commprop_no_administration_rule clause) and are not re-quoted here so as not to duplicate that existing citation, though this clause's body describes what they provide. Section 6401's own text uses the term "surviving spouse" without separately restating "registered domestic partner" within this particular section; the extension of spousal intestate-succession treatment to a registered domestic partner rests on other Probate Code provisions (including §§ 37, 100, and 101 — the latter two independently verified elsewhere in this corpus) that this clause does not itself re-verify. This clause does not address § 6402.5's special rule for property attributable to a predeceased spouse or domestic partner, which this document does not cover.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6401(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 6401(c)
citations.quote: (c) As to separate property, the intestate share of the surviving spouse is as follows: (1) The entire intestate estate if the decedent did not leave any surviving issue, parent, brother, sister, or issue of a deceased brother or sister. (2) One-half of the intestate estate in the following cases: (A) Where the decedent leaves only one child or the issue of one deceased child. (B) Where the decedent leaves no issue, but leaves a parent or parents or their issue or the issue of either of them. (3) One-third of the intestate estate in the following cases: (A) Where the decedent leaves more than one child. (B) Where the decedent leaves one child and the issue of one or more deceased children. (C) Where the decedent leaves issue of two or more deceased children.

clauses.title: Distribution to Descendants, or to Parents, When There Is No Surviving Spouse or Partner
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6402 governs the part of a decedent's intestate estate that does not pass to a surviving spouse or registered domestic partner under § 6401 — and, where there is no surviving spouse or domestic partner at all, the entire intestate estate. Except as provided in a separate statute this document does not cover (§ 6402.5, addressing property attributable to a predeceased spouse or domestic partner), § 6402 first sends that property to the decedent's issue — children, and more remote descendants such as grandchildren — with issue of the same degree of kinship to the decedent taking equal shares, and issue of a more remote degree taking their shares "by representation" under a separate statute, Probate Code § 240, that this document does not independently cover. Only if the decedent leaves no surviving issue does § 6402(b) send that property to the decedent's parent or parents, in equal shares between them if both survive.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, Prob. Code § 6402, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. This clause quotes the section's introductory sentence together with subdivisions (a) and (b); subdivisions (c) through (g), addressing more remote relatives, are quoted in the two clauses that follow this one in this document rather than repeated here, so that no subdivision of § 6402 is quoted more than once across this document. Probate Code § 240's "by representation" method of dividing shares among descendants of unequal degree, and § 6402.5's special rule for property attributable to a predeceased spouse or domestic partner, are both cross-referenced by name in this clause's body but are not independently fetched, quoted, or verified by this document; a reader concerned with either provision should consult it directly.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6402, introductory clause and subdivisions (a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 6402.5, the part of the intestate estate not passing to the surviving spouse, under Section 6401, or the entire intestate estate if there is no surviving spouse, passes as follows: (a) To the issue of the decedent, the issue taking equally if they are all of the same degree of kinship to the decedent, but if of unequal degree those of more remote degree take in the manner provided in Section 240. (b) If there is no surviving issue, to the decedent’s parent or parents equally.

clauses.title: Next in Line: Siblings' Issue, Then Grandparents and Their Issue
clauses.body: If a decedent who dies intestate (or partly intestate, as to the part of the estate not passing to a surviving spouse or registered domestic partner) leaves no surviving issue and no surviving parent, Probate Code § 6402(c) sends that property to the issue of the decedent's parents — that is, the decedent's siblings, or the descendants of a deceased sibling — with those of the same degree of kinship to the decedent taking equal shares and those of a more remote degree taking their shares by representation under § 240. Only if there is no surviving issue, parent, or issue of a parent does § 6402(d) reach the decedent's grandparents: the property passes to the decedent's surviving grandparent or grandparents equally, or, if no grandparent survives, to the issue of the grandparents, again dividing equally among those of the same degree of kinship and by representation among those of a more remote degree.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. This clause quotes subdivisions (c) and (d) of § 6402, the same statutory section already quoted for its introductory sentence and subdivisions (a)-(b) in the intestateshares_no_spouse_or_remainder_to_descendants_parents clause elsewhere in this document; that introductory "passes as follows" language, which subdivisions (c) and (d) both continue from, is not repeated in this clause's quote so that no subdivision of § 6402 is quoted more than once across this document. Subdivisions (e) through (g), reached only after grandparents and their issue are also exhausted, are quoted in the clause that follows this one rather than here. This clause does not independently verify Probate Code § 240's "by representation" method, referenced here only as a cross-reference.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6402(c)-(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (c) If there is no surviving issue or parent, to the issue of the parents or either of them, the issue taking equally if they are all of the same degree of kinship to the decedent, but if of unequal degree those of more remote degree take in the manner provided in Section 240. (d) If there is no surviving issue, parent or issue of a parent, but the decedent is survived by one or more grandparents or issue of grandparents, to the grandparent or grandparents equally, or to the issue of those grandparents if there is no surviving grandparent, the issue taking equally if they are all of the same degree of kinship to the decedent, but if of unequal degree those of more remote degree take in the manner provided in Section 240.

clauses.title: The Final Categories: Issue of a Predeceased Spouse, Next of Kin Generally, and In-Laws
clauses.body: Probate Code § 6402(e) through (g) sets out the last categories in California's intestate order, reached only if every closer category — issue, parent, issue of a parent, grandparent, and issue of a grandparent — is empty. If the decedent is survived by issue of a predeceased spouse or registered domestic partner, § 6402(e) sends the property to that issue, dividing it the same way as the earlier categories: equally among issue of the same degree of kinship to the predeceased spouse, by representation among those of a more remote degree. If there is no surviving issue of a predeceased spouse either, § 6402(f) reaches the decedent's next of kin generally, in equal degree, with a tie-breaking rule for collateral relatives of equal degree who trace through different ancestors: those claiming through the nearest common ancestor are preferred over those claiming through a more remote one. Finally, if there is no surviving next of kin and no surviving issue of a predeceased spouse, § 6402(g) reaches the parents of a predeceased spouse or registered domestic partner, or the issue of those parents.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate. This clause quotes subdivisions (e) through (g) of the same § 6402 already quoted, in two other clauses elsewhere in this document, for its introductory sentence and subdivisions (a) through (d); no subdivision of § 6402 is quoted more than once across this document's clauses. Beyond subdivision (g), if no relative in any of these categories survives, the decedent's property escheats to the State of California under separate statutes this document does not cover. This document deliberately does not attempt to verify or restate every statutory nuance of these final, more rarely applicable categories — including the full mechanics of degree-of-kinship counting — beyond what § 6402's own text states.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6402(e)-(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (e) If there is no surviving issue, parent or issue of a parent, grandparent or issue of a grandparent, but the decedent is survived by the issue of a predeceased spouse, to that issue, the issue taking equally if they are all of the same degree of kinship to the predeceased spouse, but if of unequal degree those of more remote degree take in the manner provided in Section 240. (f) If there is no surviving issue, parent or issue of a parent, grandparent or issue of a grandparent, or issue of a predeceased spouse, but the decedent is survived by next of kin, to the next of kin in equal degree, but where there are two or more collateral kindred in equal degree who claim through different ancestors, those who claim through the nearest ancestor are preferred to those claiming through an ancestor more remote. (g) If there is no surviving next of kin of the decedent and no surviving issue of a predeceased spouse of the decedent, but the decedent is survived by the parents of a predeceased spouse or the issue of those parents, to the parent or parents equally, or to the issue of those parents if both are deceased, the issue taking equally if they are all of the same degree of kinship to the predeceased spouse, but if of unequal degree those of more remote degree take in the manner provided in Section 240.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet on Transfers to a "Disqualified Person"
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's statutory presumption, set out in Probate Code sections 21380 through 21392, that a donative transfer made by a will, trust, or other instrument to certain categories of "disqualified persons" — including the person who drafted the instrument, a fiduciary who transcribed it, and a care custodian of a dependent-adult transferor — is presumed to be the product of fraud or undue influence unless that presumption is rebutted or a statutory exception applies. It is prepared by {{preparerName}}, whose relationship to {{transferorName}} is: {{relationshipToTransferor}}. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference only. It does not itself determine that any specific instrument makes a donative transfer to a disqualified person, that any specific transfer is or is not presumed to be the product of fraud or undue influence, that any such presumption has or has not been rebutted, or that any statutory exception applies to any specific transfer involving {{transferorName}}.

clauses.title: The Core Presumption and What "Affecting the Burden of Proof" Means
clauses.body: Probate Code section 21380(a) provides that a provision of an instrument making a donative transfer to any of several specified categories of persons is presumed to be the product of fraud or undue influence. Section 21380(b) identifies exactly what kind of presumption this is and how it operates: it is "a presumption affecting the burden of proof," and it "may be rebutted by proving, by clear and convincing evidence, that the donative transfer was not the product of fraud or undue influence." So where this presumption applies and is rebuttable, it is not enough for the party defending the transfer to show, by an ordinary preponderance of the evidence, that fraud or undue influence did not produce it — the statute itself sets a higher, clear-and-convincing standard for that showing. California's general Evidence Code provision on this category of presumption, section 606, states what a "presumption affecting the burden of proof" does as a general matter across California law, independent of section 21380 itself: it "impose[s] upon the party against whom it operates the burden of proof as to the nonexistence of the presumed fact" — here, the burden of proving that the transfer was not the product of fraud or undue influence.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence of the specific presumption Probate Code section 21380 creates and of the generic legal meaning of "presumption affecting the burden of proof" under Evidence Code section 606 — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific instrument or transfer. Two sources are cited: Probate Code section 21380(a)-(b) (two subsections of one section, treated as one source) and Evidence Code section 606 (an independent source, cited because section 21380 itself invokes that term of art without redefining it). This clause does not itself list the categories of "disqualified person" the presumption reaches (a separate clause in this document covers that), does not cover the narrower circumstance in which section 21380 makes the presumption conclusive rather than rebuttable (also covered separately), and does not itself determine that any specific transfer is, or is not, subject to the presumption, or that any specific defense has, or has not, met the clear-and-convincing standard.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21380(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) A provision of an instrument making a donative transfer to any of the following persons is presumed to be the product of fraud or undue influence:

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21380(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (b) The presumption created by this section is a presumption affecting the burden of proof. The presumption may be rebutted by proving, by clear and convincing evidence, that the donative transfer was not the product of fraud or undue influence.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 606 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Evid. C. § 606
citations.quote: The effect of a presumption affecting the burden of proof is to impose upon the party against whom it operates the burden of proof as to the nonexistence of the presumed fact.

clauses.title: The Statutory Categories of "Disqualified Person"
clauses.body: Probate Code section 21380(a) attaches the presumption described in the preceding clause only where a donative transfer runs to one of seven specified categories of persons: (1) the person who drafted the instrument; (2) a person who transcribed the instrument, or caused it to be transcribed, and who was in a fiduciary relationship with the transferor when it was transcribed; (3) a care custodian of a transferor who is a dependent adult, but only if the instrument was executed during the period the care custodian provided services to the transferor, or within 90 days before or after that period; (4) a care custodian who married, or began cohabiting or a domestic partnership with, a dependent-adult transferor while providing services, or within 90 days after those services were last provided, if the transfer occurred or the instrument was executed less than six months after that marriage, cohabitation, or partnership began; (5) a person related by blood or affinity, within the third degree, to a person described in categories (1) through (3); (6) a cohabitant or employee of a person described in categories (1) through (3); and (7) a partner, shareholder, or employee of a law firm in which a person described in category (1) or (2) holds an ownership interest. The terms "care custodian" and "dependent adult," used in categories (3) and (4), carry the specific statutory definitions given in Probate Code sections 21362 and 21366 within this same statutory part, rather than their everyday meanings.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the seven specific categories that trigger the section 21380 presumption — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer, and not a claim that any specific person actually falls into any of these categories on any specific facts. This clause quotes a single statutory subsection, (a), with its seven paragraphs; they are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. The "care custodian" and "dependent adult" definitions (Probate Code §§ 21362 and 21366) are not requoted in this clause: this corpus already independently verifies and quotes both definitions in full, word-for-word identical to the text refetched for this project, in the existing Omitted Spouse and Omitted Child (Pretermitted Heir) Information Sheet's clause on the omitted-spouse care-custodian exception — this clause cross-references rather than duplicates that verified text. This clause does not cover the narrower rule making the presumption conclusive, rather than rebuttable, for certain of these categories, which a separate clause in this document addresses.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21380(a)(1)-(7) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) A provision of an instrument making a donative transfer to any of the following persons is presumed to be the product of fraud or undue influence: (1) The person who drafted the instrument. (2) A person who transcribed the instrument or caused it to be transcribed and who was in a fiduciary relationship with the transferor when the instrument was transcribed. (3) A care custodian of a transferor who is a dependent adult, but only if the instrument was executed during the period in which the care custodian provided services to the transferor, or within 90 days before or after that period. (4) A care custodian who commenced a marriage, cohabitation, or domestic partnership with a transferor who is a dependent adult while providing services to that dependent adult, or within 90 days after those services were last provided to the dependent adult, if the donative transfer occurred, or the instrument was executed, less than six months after the marriage, cohabitation, or domestic partnership commenced. (5) A person who is related by blood or affinity, within the third degree, to any person described in paragraphs (1) to (3), inclusive. (6) A cohabitant or employee of any person described in paragraphs (1) to (3), inclusive. (7) A partner, shareholder, or employee of a law firm in which a person described in paragraph (1) or (2) has an ownership interest.

clauses.title: When the Presumption Cannot Be Rebutted, and Who Pays If Rebuttal Fails
clauses.body: Probate Code section 21380(c) narrows the ordinary rebuttable rule stated in subdivision (b) for a specific subset of transfers: "Notwithstanding subdivision (b), with respect to a donative transfer to the person who drafted the donative instrument, or to a person who is related to, or associated with, the drafter as described in paragraph (5), (6), or (7) of subdivision (a), the presumption created by this section is conclusive." By its own terms, this conclusive-presumption rule reaches only a transfer to the drafter personally, or to a blood or affinity relative, cohabitant, employee, or law-firm partner, shareholder, or employee of the drafter as described in paragraphs (5) through (7) of subdivision (a) — a transfer to a fiduciary who merely transcribed the instrument, or to a care custodian described in paragraph (3) or (4), remains subject only to the ordinary rebuttable presumption described in an earlier clause of this document, not this conclusive one. Separately, section 21380(d) attaches a cost-shifting consequence where a rebuttal is attempted and fails: "If a beneficiary is unsuccessful in rebutting the presumption, the beneficiary shall bear all costs of the proceeding, including reasonable attorney's fees."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific, narrower set of transfers to which section 21380 attaches a conclusive rather than rebuttable presumption, and of the cost-shifting consequence that attaches when a rebuttal attempt fails — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer. Both subdivisions (c) and (d) are quoted from the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not independent corroborating sources. The statute's own text does not address, and this clause does not resolve, whether subdivision (d)'s cost-shifting rule has any application to a transfer subject to subdivision (c)'s conclusive presumption, where no rebuttal attempt is legally possible in the first place; that is a gap in the statutory text itself, not a gap this clause fills. This clause does not itself determine that any specific transfer falls within the conclusive-presumption category, or that any specific rebuttal attempt has succeeded or failed.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21380(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (c) Notwithstanding subdivision (b), with respect to a donative transfer to the person who drafted the donative instrument, or to a person who is related to, or associated with, the drafter as described in paragraph (5), (6), or (7) of subdivision (a), the presumption created by this section is conclusive.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21380(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (d) If a beneficiary is unsuccessful in rebutting the presumption, the beneficiary shall bear all costs of the proceeding, including reasonable attorney’s fees.

clauses.title: Statutory Exceptions That Remove a Transfer From Section 21380 Entirely
clauses.body: Probate Code section 21382 lists six categories of instruments or transfers to which the section 21380 presumption does not apply at all: (a) except as provided for the care-custodian-marriage category in section 21380(a)(4), a donative transfer to a person related by blood or affinity, within the fourth degree, to the transferor, or who is the transferor's cohabitant; (b) an instrument drafted or transcribed by such a fourth-degree relative or cohabitant; (c) an instrument approved under a specified court-order procedure, after full disclosure of the relationships of the persons involved; (d) a donative transfer to a federal, state, or local public entity, to an entity that qualifies for a federal tax exemption under Internal Revenue Code section 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(19), or to a trust holding transferred property for such an entity; (e) a donative transfer of property valued at $5,000 or less, where the transferor's total estate equals or exceeds the amount stated in a separate Probate Code section governing small estates; and (f) an instrument executed outside California by a transferor who was not a California resident when the instrument was executed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific categories of instruments and transfers section 21382 places outside the reach of section 21380 entirely — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer, and not a claim that any specific transfer actually qualifies for any of these six exceptions. This clause quotes the whole of a single statutory section, with its six lettered subdivisions, as one contiguous source rather than as independent corroborating sources. Note a scope point stated on the face of the statute itself, not this clause's own interpretation: the blood-or-affinity relationship that removes a transfer from section 21380 under subdivisions (a) and (b) here is measured within the fourth degree, a wider relationship than the third-degree relationship that can trigger the presumption in the first place under section 21380(a)(5) — the statute does not use the same degree of relationship on both sides of the presumption. This clause does not independently verify the cross-referenced court-order procedure in subdivision (c) or the small-estate dollar threshold cross-referenced in subdivision (e); it states only what section 21382 itself says about them.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21382 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Section 21380 does not apply to any of the following instruments or transfers: (a) Except as provided in paragraph (4) of subdivision (a) of Section 21380, a donative transfer to a person who is related by blood or affinity, within the fourth degree, to the transferor or is the cohabitant of the transferor. (b) An instrument that is drafted or transcribed by a person who is related by blood or affinity, within the fourth degree, to the transferor or is the cohabitant of the transferor. (c) An instrument that is approved pursuant to an order under Article 10 (commencing with Section 2580) of Chapter 6 of Part 4 of Division 4, after full disclosure of the relationships of the persons involved. (d) A donative transfer to a federal, state, or local public entity, an entity that qualifies for an exemption from taxation under Section 501(c)(3) or 501(c)(19) of the Internal Revenue Code, or a trust holding the transferred property for the entity. (e) A donative transfer of property valued at five thousand dollars ($5,000) or less, if the total value of the transferor’s estate equals or exceeds the amount stated in Section 13100. (f) An instrument executed outside of California by a transferor who was not a resident of California when the instrument was executed.

clauses.title: A Separate Route Around the Presumption: An Independent Attorney's Certificate of Review
clauses.body: Separate from the exceptions in section 21382, Probate Code section 21384 provides an additional route by which a donative transfer can fall outside the section 21380 presumption: the statute provides that a donative transfer "is not subject to Section 21380 if the instrument is reviewed by an independent attorney" who counsels the transferor, outside the presence of any heir or proposed beneficiary, about the nature and consequences of the intended transfer, attempts to determine whether it is the result of fraud or undue influence, and signs and delivers to the transferor a certificate in a specific form the statute itself sets out — a "Certificate of Independent Review." Section 21384 also restricts who may serve in that reviewing role: under section 21384(c), an attorney who drafted the instrument may review and certify that same instrument only where the disqualified person at issue is a care custodian; in every other circumstance, the statute states that the drafting attorney "may not review and certify the instrument."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that this certificate-of-independent-review route exists and of its central operative requirement and drafting-attorney restriction — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific transfer, and not an exhaustive account of section 21384. Consistent with this research project's intended scope, this clause deliberately does not quote or independently verify the certificate's full required language (the balance of subdivision (a)), the cross-referenced definition of "independent attorney" in Probate Code section 21370, the client-representation limit in subdivision (b), or the delivery-to-the-drafting-attorney requirement in subdivision (d); none of that text is described or relied on here. The two subdivisions quoted, (a) and (c), are drawn from the same statutory section and are treated as one source, not independent corroborating sources. This clause does not itself determine that any specific attorney review or certificate meets section 21384's requirements for any specific instrument.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21384(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) A donative transfer is not subject to Section 21380 if the instrument is reviewed by an independent attorney who counsels the transferor, out of the presence of any heir or proposed beneficiary, about the nature and consequences of the intended transfer, including the effect of the intended transfer on the transferor’s heirs and on any beneficiary of a prior donative instrument, attempts to determine if the intended transfer is the result of fraud or undue influence, and signs and delivers to the transferor an original certificate in substantially the following form:

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21384(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (c) An attorney who drafts an instrument can review and certify the same instrument pursuant to this section, but only as to a donative transfer to a care custodian. In all other circumstances, an attorney who drafts an instrument may not review and certify the instrument.

clauses.title: Accessory Dwelling Unit Application — Project Identification
Ministerial Approval Requirement and the Statutory Timeline
clauses.body: California law requires a local agency's permitting agency to consider and approve a qualifying accessory dwelling unit (ADU) application ministerially -- without discretionary review or a public hearing -- notwithstanding certain other statutes governing variances or special use permits and notwithstanding any local ordinance regulating the issuance of variances or special use permits. The permitting agency must determine whether an application is complete, and give the applicant written notice of that determination, within 15 business days of receiving the application; if it is incomplete, the agency must identify what is missing so the applicant can cure it, and a resubmission is subject to the same 15-business-day completeness-determination timeline. Once an application is complete, the permitting agency must approve or deny it within 60 days if the lot already has an existing single-family or multifamily dwelling; if the ADU application is submitted together with an application to build a new primary dwelling on the same lot, the agency may delay acting on the ADU application until it acts on the new-dwelling application (or, if the applicant requests a delay, the 60-day period is tolled), but the ADU application must still be considered without discretionary review or a hearing. If the local agency does not approve or deny a completed application within the applicable 60-day period, the application is deemed approved by operation of law. If the agency denies an application, it must return a full set of written comments, within the same time period, listing the application's specific defects or deficiencies and how they can be remedied. No local ordinance, policy, or regulation other than an ADU ordinance consistent with this article of the statute may serve as the basis for delaying or denying an ADU building or use permit under this ministerial process. A denied or incomplete-determination decision may be appealed in writing to the agency's governing body (or, for a city or county, at the applicant's option, to the planning commission as well), and the agency must issue a final written determination on that appeal within 60 business days of receiving it.
clauses.gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 66317 as currently in effect. This statute was substantially recodified, effective March 25, 2024 (Stats. 2024, ch. 7 (SB 477)), out of former Government Code section 65852.2 -- a former section number that a reader may encounter in older summaries, articles, or even older versions of this project's own content, and that no longer contains this law. Section 66317 was itself amended again in 2025 (Stats. 2025, ch. 520 (SB 543)), effective January 1, 2026. Because this area of law changes frequently, a reader should confirm, at the time of use, that no further amendment has taken effect. This clause covers only the core ministerial-review mandate and the completeness/approval/appeal timelines in section 66317; it does not cover every procedural detail in that section (for example, the local agency's authority to charge an implementation-cost fee), and it does not address the separate, distinct approval pathways and conditions found elsewhere in this chapter (including the specific unit types described in Government Code section 66323, addressed only in a separate clause of this document). It does not determine whether a particular application is in fact complete, whether a particular local agency's actions complied with these timelines, or whether a particular denial was lawful.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66317(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A permit application for an accessory dwelling unit shall be considered and approved ministerially without discretionary review or a hearing, notwithstanding Section 65901 or 65906 or any local ordinance regulating the issuance of variances or special use permits.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66317(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The permitting agency shall either approve or deny the application to create or serve an accessory dwelling unit within 60 days from the date the permitting agency receives a completed application if there is an existing single-family or multifamily dwelling on the lot.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66317(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If the local agency has not approved or denied the completed application within 60 days, the application shall be deemed approved.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66317(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66317(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: No local ordinance, policy, or regulation, other than an accessory dwelling unit ordinance consistent with this article shall be the basis for the delay or denial of a building permit or a use permit under this section.

clauses.title: Statutory Limits on a Local ADU Ordinance's Lot-Size, Unit-Size, and Height Standards
clauses.body: A local agency's own ADU ordinance may impose objective standards -- including parking, height, setback, landscaping, architectural review, and maximum unit size -- but the statute expressly forbids one of those categories outright: an ordinance may not include any minimum-lot-size requirement for an ADU. On unit size, a local agency may set both minimum and maximum size limits, but a maximum may not be set below 850 square feet of interior livable space (or below 1,000 square feet of interior livable space for a unit with more than one bedroom), and a minimum size requirement may not be set so as to prohibit an efficiency unit. Separately, the statute caps the size of a detached ADU created under a local ordinance at 1,200 square feet of total floor area, and caps an attached ADU at 50% of the existing primary dwelling's total floor area. On height, a local ordinance's height limitation may not be set below specific statutory floors that vary by circumstance: at least 16 feet for a detached ADU on a lot with an existing or proposed single-family or multifamily dwelling; at least 18 feet (plus an additional two feet to accommodate a roof pitch aligned with the primary dwelling's) for a detached ADU within one-half mile walking distance of a major transit stop or high-quality transit corridor, or for a detached ADU on a lot with an existing or proposed multifamily, multistory dwelling; and, for an ADU attached to a primary dwelling, at least 25 feet or the height limit that otherwise applies to the primary dwelling under the local zoning ordinance, whichever is lower (without a local agency being required to allow more than two stories).
clauses.gap: This clause is based on Government Code sections 66314 and 66321 as currently in effect, both part of the March 2024 recodification (Stats. 2024, ch. 7 (SB 477)) of former Government Code section 65852.2, and both since amended in 2025 (section 66314 by Stats. 2025, ch. 67 (AB 1170); section 66321 by Stats. 2025, ch. 520 (SB 543)), effective January 1, 2026. A reader should confirm no further amendment has taken effect. This clause addresses only the lot-size, unit-size, and height limits found in these two sections; it does not cover every objective standard a local ordinance may otherwise impose (for example, architectural review or landscaping standards), does not cover the separate ministerial size allowances that apply notwithstanding a local ordinance under a different statute (addressed in a separate clause of this document), and does not determine whether a specific local agency's ordinance in fact complies with these statutory floors and ceilings.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66314(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Impose objective standards on accessory dwelling units that include, but are not limited to, parking, height, setback, landscape, architectural review, maximum size of a unit, and standards that prevent adverse impacts on any real property that is listed in the California Register of Historical Resources. These standards shall not include requirements on minimum lot size.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66321(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A maximum square footage requirement for either an attached or detached accessory dwelling unit that is less than either of the following: (A) Eight hundred fifty square feet of interior livable space. (B) One thousand square feet of interior livable space for an accessory dwelling unit that provides more than one bedroom.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66314(d)(4)-(d)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If there is an existing primary dwelling, the total floor area of an attached accessory dwelling unit shall not exceed 50 percent of the existing primary dwelling. (5) The total floor area for a detached accessory dwelling unit shall not exceed 1,200 square feet.

citations.quote: Any height limitation that does not allow at least the following, as applicable: (A) A height of 16 feet for a detached accessory dwelling unit on a lot with an existing or proposed single family or multifamily dwelling unit.

clauses.title: Statutory Limits on Local Parking Requirements for ADUs
clauses.body: California law bars a local agency, whether or not it has adopted its own ADU ordinance, from imposing any parking requirement for an ADU in a defined set of circumstances -- among them, when the ADU is within one-half mile walking distance of public transit, when it is within an architecturally and historically significant historic district, when it is part of the existing or proposed primary residence or an accessory structure, when required on-street parking permits are not offered to the ADU's occupant, or when a car-share vehicle is located within one block of the ADU. Separately, when a local agency's ordinance does impose a parking requirement outside those circumstances, the statute caps it at one parking space per ADU or per bedroom, whichever is less, and that space may be provided as tandem parking on a driveway; off-street parking must be permitted in setback areas or as tandem parking unless the agency makes specific findings that doing so is not feasible based on site-specific or regional topographical, fire, or life-safety conditions. When an existing garage, carport, covered parking structure, or uncovered parking space is demolished or converted to create an ADU, the local agency may not require those parking spaces to be replaced.
clauses.gap: This clause is based on Government Code sections 66322 and 66314(b)(2) and (d)(10)-(11), as currently in effect, both part of the March 2024 recodification (Stats. 2024, ch. 7 (SB 477)) of former Government Code section 65852.2; section 66314 was further amended in 2025 (Stats. 2025, ch. 67 (AB 1170)), effective January 1, 2026. A reader should confirm no further amendment has taken effect. This clause covers only the parking-specific limits in these provisions; it does not catalog every listed exemption in section 66322(a) verbatim (for example, the exemption for an ADU submitted together with a new-dwelling application on the same lot is only summarized here, not quoted), and it does not determine whether a specific property in fact falls within any exemption (for instance, whether a specific location is within one-half mile of public transit as the statute defines that term).

citations.quote: A local agency shall not impose any parking standards for an accessory dwelling unit in any of the following instances: (1) Where the accessory dwelling unit is located within one-half of one mile walking distance of public transit.
