clauses.title: No Owner-Occupancy Requirement May Be Imposed on an ADU
clauses.body: For an accessory dwelling unit created under a local agency's ADU ordinance, current California law states that the size, setback, parking, height, and other standards a local agency's ordinance may impose are the maximum standards the agency may use, and that no additional standard -- expressly including an owner-occupancy requirement -- may be imposed. The one exception the statute itself carves out is that a local agency may still require that the property be used only for rentals of terms of 30 days or longer. This is a distinct rule from the one that applies to a junior accessory dwelling unit, which (as described in a separate clause of this document) does carry a conditional owner-occupancy requirement in some circumstances.
clauses.gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 66315, added in the March 2024 recodification (Stats. 2024, ch. 7 (SB 477)) of former Government Code section 65852.2, and unamended since. This is a narrow, single-sentence statute, and this clause states it in full; it does not address the minimum-30-day-rental-term condition in any further depth, does not address whether a property owner's other obligations (for example, under any applicable short-term-rental ordinance) might independently affect how the unit can be used, and does not address the different, conditional owner-occupancy rule that applies to a junior accessory dwelling unit rather than an accessory dwelling unit as such.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66315 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Section 66314 establishes the maximum standards that a local agency shall use to evaluate a proposed accessory dwelling unit on a lot that includes a proposed or existing single-family dwelling. No additional standards, other than those provided in Section 66314, shall be used or imposed, including an owner-occupant requirement, except that a local agency may require that the property may be used for rentals of terms 30 days or longer.

clauses.title: Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit: Statutory Size Cap and Shared Sanitation Facilities
clauses.body: California law defines a junior accessory dwelling unit (JADU) -- a category distinct from an accessory dwelling unit -- as a unit of no more than 500 square feet of interior livable space, contained entirely within a single-family residence (enclosed space such as an attached garage counts as part of the residence for this purpose). A JADU may include its own separate sanitation facilities, or it may instead share sanitation facilities with the rest of the existing structure. A local agency's JADU ordinance must also require a permitted JADU to include a separate entrance from the main entrance of the single-family residence, and to include an efficiency kitchen with a cooking facility with appliances and a food preparation counter and storage cabinets of reasonable size for the unit.
clauses.gap: This clause is based on Government Code sections 66313(d) and 66333, both part of the March 2024 recodification (Stats. 2024, ch. 7 (SB 477)) of former Government Code section 65852.22; section 66313 was further amended in 2025 (Stats. 2025, ch. 520 (SB 543)) and section 66333 in 2025 (Stats. 2025, ch. 507 (AB 1154)), both effective January 1, 2026. A reader should confirm no further amendment has taken effect. This clause covers only the JADU size definition and the shared-sanitation and entrance/kitchen features; the JADU's separate, conditional owner-occupancy rule is addressed in a separate clause of this document, and this clause does not address the required deed restriction, the one-JADU-per-lot limit, or every other condition a JADU ordinance must include under section 66333.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66313(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Junior accessory dwelling unit” means a unit that is no more than 500 square feet of interior livable space in size and contained entirely within a single-family residence. A junior accessory dwelling unit may include separate sanitation facilities, or may share sanitation facilities with the existing structure.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66333(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Require the permitted junior accessory dwelling unit to include an efficiency kitchen, which shall include all of the following: (1) A cooking facility with appliances. (2) A food preparation counter and storage cabinets that are of reasonable size in relation to the size of the junior accessory dwelling unit.

clauses.title: Junior Accessory Dwelling Unit: Owner-Occupancy Requirement Depends on Shared Sanitation
clauses.body: Unlike an accessory dwelling unit -- for which, as described in a separate clause of this document, no owner-occupancy requirement may be imposed at all -- a junior accessory dwelling unit (JADU) is subject to a conditional owner-occupancy rule under current California law. If a local agency's JADU ordinance permits a JADU to share sanitation facilities with the existing structure, that ordinance must require owner-occupancy of the single-family residence in which the JADU is located; the statute specifies that the owner may satisfy this by living in either the remaining portion of the structure or the newly created JADU itself. Owner-occupancy is not required, however, if the JADU instead has its own separate sanitation facilities, or if the owner is a governmental agency, land trust, or housing organization rather than an individual. A local agency's JADU ordinance must also require recordation of a running-with-the-land deed restriction addressing both a prohibition on selling the JADU separately from the single-family residence and a restriction on the JADU's size and attributes, and must require that any rental of a JADU be for a term longer than 30 days.
clauses.gap: This clause is based on Government Code section 66333, part of the March 2024 recodification (Stats. 2024, ch. 7 (SB 477)) of former Government Code section 65852.22, and further amended in 2025 (Stats. 2025, ch. 507 (AB 1154)), effective January 1, 2026. A reader should confirm no further amendment has taken effect. This clause covers only the conditional owner-occupancy rule and the deed-restriction and minimum-rental-term requirements in section 66333; it does not address the one-JADU-per-lot limit, the requirement that a JADU be built within the walls of the residence, the separate-entrance requirement, or the efficiency-kitchen requirement, all addressed only in part (or not at all) elsewhere in this document, and it does not determine whether a specific JADU's sanitation facilities in fact qualify as "shared" or "separate" under the statute, or whether a specific owner in fact qualifies for the governmental-agency, land-trust, or housing-organization exception.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66333(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If the junior accessory dwelling unit has shared sanitation facilities with the existing structure, require owner-occupancy in the single family residence in which the junior accessory dwelling unit will be permitted. The owner may reside in either the remaining portion of the structure or the newly created junior accessory dwelling unit.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66333(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Owner-occupancy shall not be required if the junior accessory dwelling unit has separate sanitation facilities, or if the owner is another governmental agency, land trust, or housing organization.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 66333(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Require the recordation of a deed restriction, which shall run with the land, shall be filed with the permitting agency, and shall include both of the following: (1) A prohibition on the sale of the junior accessory dwelling unit separate from the sale of the single-family residence, including a statement that the deed restriction may be enforced against future purchasers.

clauses.title: Protected Disclosures: What Counts, and to Whom
clauses.body: California law prohibits an employer, or anyone acting on the employer's behalf, from making, adopting, or enforcing any rule, regulation, or policy that would prevent an employee from disclosing information to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee, or to another employee with authority to investigate, discover, or correct a violation, or from providing information to or testifying before any public body conducting an investigation, hearing, or inquiry. This protection applies whenever the employee has reasonable cause to believe the information discloses a violation of a state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation — regardless of whether making that kind of disclosure is part of the employee's own job duties. A report a government-agency employee makes to their own employer counts as a disclosure to a government or law enforcement agency for these same purposes.
clauses.gap: Both citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(a) and § 1102.5(e) — disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. The 'reasonable cause to believe' standard quoted here is drawn directly from this statutory text; this clause does not add independent case law interpreting how courts apply that standard to particular facts, and no such corroborating authority was verified in this research pass. This clause does not itself determine that any specific disclosure, or its actual recipient, falls within this statute's protection in a specific case, and does not address California's separate, narrower securities-fraud-specific whistleblower statutes or the distinct federal Sarbanes-Oxley/Dodd-Frank protections addressed elsewhere in this corpus.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not make, adopt, or enforce any rule, regulation, or policy preventing an employee from disclosing information to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee, or to another employee who has authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance, or from providing information to, or testifying before, any public body conducting an investigation, hearing, or inquiry, if the employee has reasonable cause to believe that the information discloses a violation of state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation, regardless of whether disclosing the information is part of the employee’s job duties.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: A report made by an employee of a government agency to their employer is a disclosure of information to a government or law enforcement agency pursuant to subdivisions (a) and (b).

clauses.title: The Anti-Retaliation Rule Itself
clauses.body: Separately from prohibiting rules or policies that would block a protected disclosure, this same statute independently prohibits an employer, or anyone acting on the employer's behalf, from retaliating against an employee for making a protected disclosure — or because the employer believes the employee disclosed or may disclose that kind of information — to any of the same recipients: a government or law enforcement agency, a person with authority over the employee, or another employee with authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance, or in providing information to or testifying before an investigating public body. The same reasonable-cause-to-believe standard, and the same rule that this protection applies regardless of the employee's job duties, govern this anti-retaliation prohibition.
clauses.gap: This clause's citation is to a single statutory subdivision, Labor Code § 1102.5(b) — the anti-retaliation prohibition itself, distinct from the rule-and-policy prohibition of subdivision (a) addressed in a separate clause of this document. Separately, on verification: this section, as currently codified and as most recently amended by Stats. 2023, Ch. 612 (SB 497), effective January 1, 2024, does not itself contain a rebuttable presumption of retaliation for adverse action taken within a set number of days of the protected activity. Fetching and comparing the current statutory text confirmed this directly, and the bill's own Legislative Counsel's Digest confirms it as well: the 90-day rebuttable presumption created by SB 497 was enacted into a companion statute, Labor Code § 98.6 (and, per that same digest, into Labor Code § 1197.5), while SB 497's amendment to § 1102.5 itself changed only the civil-penalty structure addressed in a separate clause of this document. This document does not state, and does not cite, a 90-day presumption as part of § 1102.5, because none exists in the fetched text of this section; a reader whose situation might involve a wage claim or a complaint within the Labor Commissioner's jurisdiction may find that presumption addressed under Labor Code § 98.6 in this corpus's separate Wrongful Termination in Violation of Public Policy information sheet.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee for disclosing information, or because the employer believes that the employee disclosed or may disclose information, to a government or law enforcement agency, to a person with authority over the employee or another employee who has the authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance, or for providing information to, or testifying before, any public body conducting an investigation, hearing, or inquiry, if the employee has reasonable cause to believe that the information discloses a violation of state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation, regardless of whether disclosing the information is part of the employee’s job duties.

clauses.title: Refusing to Break the Law, and Protection Carried From a Former Job
clauses.body: The same statute also prohibits an employer from retaliating against an employee for refusing to participate in an activity that would violate a state or federal statute, or that would violate or fail to comply with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation. It separately prohibits retaliation against an employee for having exercised these same protections while working for a previous employer, not only the current one.
clauses.gap: Both citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(c) and § 1102.5(d) — disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. This clause does not itself determine that any specific refusal, or any specific prior-employment activity, actually falls within this statute's coverage in a particular case.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee for refusing to participate in an activity that would result in a violation of state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employer, or any person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee for having exercised their rights under subdivision (a), (b), or (c) in any former employment.

clauses.title: What This Statute Does Not Reach, and Who Counts As an "Employer"
clauses.body: This statute does not apply to rules, regulations, or policies implementing — or to employer action against an employee who violates — the lawyer-client privilege, the physician-patient privilege, or the confidentiality of trade secret information. Separately, this statute prohibits retaliation against an employee because that employee is a family member of someone who has engaged in, or is perceived to have engaged in, activity this statute protects. And for purposes of this statute, "employer" is defined broadly enough to include a client employer in certain labor-contracting relationships, and certain employers as defined for workplace safety purposes, not only an employee's own direct employer.
clauses.gap: All three citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(g), (h), and (i) — disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. Subdivision (i)'s definition of covered "employer" cross-references Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(1) (the client-employer definition) and § 6400(b); this document quotes only § 1102.5(i)'s own text making that cross-reference and does not independently fetch or verify the text of § 2810.3 or § 6400 themselves. This clause does not determine that any specific privilege, trade-secret, family-relationship, or multi-employer fact pattern actually falls within or outside this statute's scope in a particular case.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: This section does not apply to rules, regulations, or policies that implement, or to actions by employers against employees who violate, the confidentiality of the lawyer-client privilege of Article 3 (commencing with Section 950) of, or the physician-patient privilege of Article 6 (commencing with Section 990) of, Chapter 4 of Division 8 of the Evidence Code, or trade secret information.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(h) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: An employer, or a person acting on behalf of the employer, shall not retaliate against an employee because the employee is a family member of a person who has, or is perceived to have, engaged in any acts protected by this section.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, “employer” or “a person acting on behalf of the employer” includes, but is not limited to, a client employer as defined in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 2810.3 and an employer listed in subdivision (b) of Section 6400.

clauses.title: Civil Penalty and Attorney's Fees Under This Statute
clauses.body: In addition to any other available remedy, California law makes an employer who violates this statute liable for a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per employee for each violation, awarded to the employee who was retaliated against. In assessing the amount of that penalty, the Labor Commissioner considers the nature and seriousness of the violation based on the evidence obtained during the investigation, including the type of violation, the economic or mental harm suffered, and the chilling effect on the exercise of employment rights in the workplace. Separately, a court may award reasonable attorney's fees to a plaintiff who brings a successful action for a violation of this statute.
clauses.gap: All three citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 1102.5(f)(1), (f)(2), and (j) — disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. The $10,000 figure is a per-employee, per-violation cap the Labor Commissioner may assess after considering the listed factors; it is not an amount awarded automatically or in every case. This same statutory text is also cited, for the same civil-penalty and fee-shifting mechanics, in this corpus's separate Wrongful Termination in Violation of Public Policy information sheet, which addresses this statute in the context of an already-ended employment relationship; this clause states the identical statutory mechanics for a reader who is still employed. This clause does not itself determine that any specific violation occurred, or that any specific penalty or fee award would result, in a particular case.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: In addition to other remedies available, an employer is liable for a civil penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000) per employee for each violation of this section to be awarded to the employee who was retaliated against.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(f)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: In assessing this penalty, the Labor Commissioner shall consider the nature and seriousness of the violation based on the evidence obtained during the course of the investigation. The Labor Commissioner’s consideration of the nature and seriousness of the violation shall include, but is not limited to, the type of violation, the economic or mental harm suffered, and the chilling effect on the exercise of employment rights in the workplace, and shall be considered to the extent evidence obtained during the investigation concerned any of these or other relevant factors.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1102.5(j) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The court is authorized to award reasonable attorney’s fees to a plaintiff who brings a successful action for a violation of these provisions.

clauses.title: Internal Reporting Channel
clauses.body: {{companyName}} provides the following channel(s) for {{employeeName}} to report information the employee has reasonable cause to believe discloses a violation of a state or federal statute, or a violation of or noncompliance with a local, state, or federal rule or regulation: _______________________________________________. Using an internal channel is not required by the statute addressed in this document, which independently protects a report made instead — or also — to a government or law enforcement agency, or to another person or employee with authority to investigate, discover, or correct the violation or noncompliance.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose and Coverage
clauses.body: {{hiringPartyName}} ("Hiring Party") is engaging {{contractorName}} ("Freelance Worker") to provide the following professional services in exchange for {{contractPrice}}: {{workDescription}}. This agreement is intended to satisfy the written-contract requirements of California's Freelance Worker Protection Act, Business and Professions Code § 18100 et seq.

clauses.title: Who and What This Law Covers
clauses.body: California's Freelance Worker Protection Act (Business and Professions Code § 18100 et seq., added by SB 988 and effective January 1, 2025) applies to a contract between a "hiring party" and a "freelance worker" for "professional services" worth $250 or more. A "freelance worker" is a person, or an organization made up of no more than one person, hired as a bona fide independent contractor to provide professional services for an amount that reaches $250 either in a single contract or when several contracts between the same hiring party and worker are added together over the immediately preceding 120 days. A "hiring party" is any person or organization in California that retains a freelance worker for professional services, except the United States government, the State of California or its subdivisions, a foreign government, or an individual hiring services for the personal benefit of themselves, their family members, or their homestead. "Professional services" is defined by cross-reference to a separate Labor Code statute, which lists specific categories of work — including marketing, graphic design, freelance writing, editing, and still photography, among others — several of which carry their own additional conditions. The Act applies only to contracts entered into or renewed on or after January 1, 2025.
clauses.gap: The three citations to Bus. & Prof. Code § 18101 (subdivisions (a), (b), and (c)) are subdivisions of the same statutory section and are not independent corroborating sources for one another. The citation to Labor Code § 2778(b)(2) is an independent section that § 18101(c) incorporates by cross-reference for the definition of "professional services"; that Labor Code definition was itself amended by AB 1514 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 305, Sec. 1), effective January 1, 2026, and the quote here reflects the current, post-amendment text as verified on 2026-09-04. This clause does not reproduce the full list of occupation-specific categories in Labor Code § 2778(b)(2), nor the further conditions attached to several of them (e.g., photographers, translators, licensed estheticians); whether a specific engagement falls within that list is not determined here. The citation to Bus. & Prof. Code § 18107 is an independent section confirming the January 1, 2025 applicability date; it does not address retroactive application to contracts predating that date.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18101(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: “Freelance worker” means a person or organization composed of no more than one person, whether or not incorporated or employing a trade name, that is hired or retained as a bona fide independent contractor by a hiring party to provide professional services in exchange for an amount equal to or greater than two hundred and fifty dollars ($250), either by itself or when aggregated with all contracts for services between the same hiring party and independent contractor during the immediately preceding 120 days.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18101(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: “Hiring party” means a person or organization in the State of California that retains a freelance worker to provide professional services, except any of the following: (1) The United States government. (2) The State of California or any subdivision thereof. (3) A foreign government. (4) An individual hiring services for the personal benefit of themselves, their family members, or their homestead.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18101(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: “Professional services” has the same meaning as paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 2778 of the Labor Code.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2778(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: “Professional services” means services that meet any of the following: (A) Marketing, provided that the contracted work is original and creative in character and the result of which depends primarily on the invention, imagination, or talent of the individual or work that is an essential part of or necessarily incident to any of the contracted work.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18107 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: This part applies only to contracts entered into or renewed on or after January 1, 2025.

clauses.title: Written-Contract Requirement
clauses.body: Whenever a hiring party retains a freelance worker under California's Freelance Worker Protection Act, the contract between them must be in writing. The hiring party must furnish the freelance worker a signed copy of that written contract, either physically or electronically, and must retain the contract for at least four years. A hiring party's refusal to provide a written contract does not by itself defeat a freelance worker's other legal remedies: the law states that a freelance worker may still enforce an oral contract or recover under the doctrine of promissory estoppel, and specific facts — a rate representation by the hiring party, a written summary of the rate and work the freelance worker provided before starting, or the freelance worker's performance of the work as understood — may serve as evidence that a contract was formed.
clauses.gap: Both citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Bus. & Prof. Code § 18103 (subdivisions (a) and (c)), and are not independent sources for one another. This clause does not cover subdivision (b)'s list of required contract contents, addressed in a separate clause, nor the statutory damages that attach to a hiring party's refusal to provide a written contract, addressed in the enforcement clause. It also does not resolve, for a specific dispute, whether an oral agreement or the listed forms of evidence would in fact establish that a contract was formed — that determination is fact-specific and not made here.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18103(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: Whenever a hiring party retains the services of a freelance worker, the contract between the hiring party and the freelance worker shall be in writing. The hiring party shall furnish a signed copy of the written contract, either physically or electronically, to the freelance worker. The hiring party shall retain the contract for no less than four years.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18103(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: This section does not limit existing contract law, including, but not limited to, that it does not prevent a freelance worker from enforcing an oral contract or recovering under the doctrine of promissory estoppel. Notwithstanding a refusal by the hiring party to provide a written contract as required by subdivision (a), the following may be evidence that a contract was formed between the parties: (1) The hiring party made representations to the freelance worker regarding the rate for services to be performed. (2) The freelance worker provided in writing any document to the hiring party, including email, text message, or other electronic communication, a summary of the rate and work to be performed prior to performing the work. (3) The freelance worker performed the work that the freelance worker understood was to be performed.

clauses.title: Minimum Contract Contents
clauses.body: The written contract required by California's Freelance Worker Protection Act must include, at minimum, four items: the name and mailing address of each party; an itemized list of all services to be provided by the freelance worker, including the value of those services and the rate and method of compensation; the date on which the hiring party will pay the contracted compensation, or the mechanism by which that date will be determined; and the date by which the freelance worker must submit a list of services rendered, to meet the hiring party's internal processing deadlines for timely payment.
clauses.gap: This citation is a single subdivision, Bus. & Prof. Code § 18103(b), of the same section covered in the written-contract-requirement clause (subdivisions (a) and (c)) — it is not an independent corroborating source. This clause states only the four statutory minimums; it does not address what additional terms a contract may contain beyond these required items, nor how specific or detailed the required itemization must be to satisfy the statute, which the text does not further define.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18103(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: The contract shall include, at minimum, all of the following information: (1) The name and mailing address of each party. (2) An itemized list of all services to be provided by the freelance worker, including the value of those services and the rate and method of compensation. (3) The date on which the hiring party shall pay the contracted compensation or the mechanism by which the date shall be determined. (4) The date by which a freelance worker shall submit a list of services rendered under the contract to the hiring party to meet the hiring party’s internal processing deadlines for purposes of timely payment of compensation.

clauses.title: Timely-Payment Rule
clauses.body: Under California's Freelance Worker Protection Act, a hiring party must pay a freelance worker the compensation specified in their contract on or before the date the contract specifies as due; if the contract does not specify a due date, payment is due no later than 30 days after the freelance worker completes the contracted services. Once a freelance worker has begun performing services under a contract, the hiring party may not condition timely payment on the freelance worker accepting less compensation than the contract specifies, or on the freelance worker providing more goods or services, or granting more intellectual property rights, than the contract calls for.
clauses.gap: Both citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Bus. & Prof. Code § 18102 (subdivisions (a) and (b)), and are not independent sources for one another. This clause states the payment-timing default and the anti-lowball protection; it does not cover the remedies for a late or refused payment, which are addressed in the enforcement clause, and it does not address the separate written-contract or contract-contents requirements covered in other clauses.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18102(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by law, a hiring party shall pay a freelance worker the compensation specified by a contract for professional services: (1) On or before the date compensation is due pursuant to the contract. (2) If the contract does not specify when the hiring party shall pay, no later than 30 days after the completion of the freelance worker’s services under the contract.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18102(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: Once a freelance worker has commenced performance of services under a contract, a hiring party shall not require as a condition of timely payment that the freelance worker do either of the following: (1) Accept less compensation than the amount of compensation specified by the contract. (2) Provide more goods or services or grant more intellectual property rights than agreed to in the contract.

clauses.title: Anti-Retaliation Protection and Non-Waivability
clauses.body: California's Freelance Worker Protection Act prohibits a hiring party from discriminating against, or taking any adverse action against, a freelance worker that penalizes the freelance worker for, or is reasonably likely to deter the freelance worker from: opposing a practice the Act prohibits; participating in a proceeding to enforce the Act; seeking to enforce rights the Act provides; or otherwise asserting or attempting to assert those rights. The Act separately states that any waiver of its protections is contrary to public policy and is void and unenforceable.
clauses.gap: Bus. & Prof. Code § 18105 and § 18104 are independent sections of the Act, not subdivisions of a single section — each addresses a different protection (anti-retaliation and non-waivability, respectively) rather than corroborating the other. This clause does not further define what specifically counts as an "adverse action" beyond the statute's own list of protected activities, which the Act does not itself elaborate on, nor does it address the civil remedies available for a retaliation violation, which are addressed generally in the enforcement clause.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18105 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: A hiring party shall not discriminate or take any adverse action against a freelance worker that penalizes a freelance worker for, or is reasonably likely to deter a freelance worker from, taking any of the following actions: (a) Opposing any practice prohibited by this part. (b) Participating in proceedings related to the enforcement of this part. (c) Seeking to enforce rights provided by this part. (d) Otherwise asserting or attempting to assert rights provided by this part.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18104 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: A waiver of any provision in this part shall be deemed contrary to public policy and is void and unenforceable.

clauses.title: Enforcement and Remedies
clauses.body: An aggrieved freelance worker, or a public prosecutor, may bring a civil action to enforce California's Freelance Worker Protection Act. A prevailing plaintiff is entitled to reasonable attorney's fees and costs, injunctive relief, and any other remedies the court deems appropriate. The statute sets three specific damages measures: if a freelance worker requested a written contract before starting work and the hiring party refused to provide one, the freelance worker is entitled to an additional $1,000; if the hiring party failed to pay by the time the Act requires, the freelance worker is entitled to damages of up to twice the amount that remained unpaid when payment was due; and for any other violation of the Act, the freelance worker may be awarded damages equal to the value of the contract or of the work performed, whichever is greater.
clauses.gap: Both citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Bus. & Prof. Code § 18106 (subdivisions (a) and (b)), and are not independent sources for one another. Note: the enacted, codified text of § 18106(b)(1) reads "requested a written contact" (not "contract") while the parallel phrase in § 18106(b)(2) reads "requested a written contract" — this inconsistency was verified as present in the official statutory text itself (confirmed identical across two independent fetches with different browser user-agent strings) and is not a transcription error introduced here. This clause does not cover who qualifies as a "public prosecutor" (defined in Bus. & Prof. Code § 18101(d) by cross-reference to Labor Code § 180, not independently verified for this clause set) or the procedural mechanics of bringing such an action.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18106(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: An aggrieved freelance worker or a public prosecutor may bring a civil action to enforce this part.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 18106(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: A prevailing plaintiff in an action alleging a violation of this part is entitled to reasonable attorney’s fees and costs, injunctive relief, and any other remedies deemed appropriate by the court. Damages shall be awarded to an aggrieved freelance worker as follows: (1) If the freelance worker requested a written contact prior to commencing work under the contract and the hiring party refused in violation of Section 18103, the freelance worker shall be awarded an additional one thousand dollars ($1,000). (2) If the hiring party failed to pay the freelance worker the contracted compensation by the time required under Section 18102, the freelance worker shall be awarded damages up to twice the amount that remained unpaid at the time payment was due. If the freelance worker requested a written contract prior to commencing work under the contract and the hiring party refused in violation of Section 18103, the amount unpaid shall be determined by the rate the freelance worker reasonably understood to apply to the work. (3) If the hiring party violates any other provision of this part, the freelance worker may be awarded damages equal to the value of the contract or the work performed, whichever is greater.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Class, Eligibility, and Time-Limit Disclosure for Group Waivers
clauses.body: When {{companyName}} requests a waiver of age-discrimination claims from {{employeeName}} in connection with an exit-incentive program or other employment-termination program offered to a group or class of employees, federal law imposes a disclosure duty on top of the individual waiver's own requirements. At the start of the consideration period, {{companyName}} must inform {{employeeName}} in writing, in a manner calculated to be understood by the average individual eligible to participate, of any class, unit, or group of individuals covered by the program, any eligibility factors for the program, and any time limits applicable to the program. The required information must be given to each individual in the decisional unit who is asked to sign a waiver, and its stated purpose is to give that individual enough information to make an informed choice about signing.
clauses.gap: The statutory quote below (29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1)(H)(i)) is independently verified primary law. The two 29 C.F.R. § 1625.22(f) quotes are EEOC's own regulation interpreting that same statutory disclosure duty — they elaborate the rule rather than corroborate it from a second, independent source, and are treated that way here. This clause is meant to be used together with this corpus's Severance Agreement document: the individual-waiver requirements this group-disclosure duty sits on top of — the 21-day/45-day consideration period, 7-day revocation period, plain-language and attorney-consultation requirements, and the EEOC-participation carve-out — are covered there, in the clause titled "Age Discrimination Release Requirements" (clause id sev_owbpa), not here. This clause does not itself determine whether a specific severance or exit program in fact qualifies as an "exit incentive or other employment termination program offered to a group or class of employees" for purposes of triggering this disclosure duty, and does not define a specific employer's "decisional unit" — the regulation itself treats both as case-by-case, fact-dependent determinations.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1)(H)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Older Workers Benefit Protection Act, group-program class/eligibility/time-limit disclosure
citations.quote: if a waiver is requested in connection with an exit incentive or other employment termination program offered to a group or class of employees, the employer (at the commencement of the period specified in subparagraph (F)) informs the individual in writing in a manner calculated to be understood by the average individual eligible to participate, as to— (i) any class, unit, or group of individuals covered by such program, any eligibility factors for such program, and any time limits applicable to such program;

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1625.22(f)(2) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, who must receive the disclosure
citations.quote: The required information must be given to each person in the decisional unit who is asked to sign a waiver agreement.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1625.22(f)(1)(iv) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, stated purpose of the disclosure
citations.quote: The purpose of the informational requirements is to provide an employee with enough information regarding the program to allow the employee to make an informed choice whether or not to sign a waiver agreement.

clauses.title: Job-Titles-and-Ages Disclosure for Those Selected and Not Selected
clauses.body: The same group-program disclosure duty also requires {{companyName}} to inform {{employeeName}}, in the same writing, of the job titles and ages of all individuals eligible or selected for the program, and the ages of all individuals in the same job classification or organizational unit who are not eligible or selected for the program. EEOC regulations implementing this requirement direct that ages be broken down individually — an age band such as "age 20-30" does not satisfy the requirement — and that if the individuals actually being terminated are only a subset of a larger decisional unit, the disclosure must still cover the entire decisional unit, not only the subset selected.
clauses.gap: The statutory quote below (29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1)(H)(ii)) is independently verified primary law. The two 29 C.F.R. § 1625.22(f)(4) quotes are EEOC's own regulation elaborating that same statutory requirement, not an independent second source, and are treated that way here. This clause is meant to be used together with this corpus's Severance Agreement document, in particular the clause titled "Age Discrimination Release Requirements" (clause id sev_owbpa), which covers the individual 21/45-day consideration period and 7-day revocation period this group disclosure does not restate. This clause does not reproduce every subpart of 29 C.F.R. § 1625.22(f)(4) — for example, its rules on breaking down grades or subcategories within a job title, on combined voluntary/involuntary terminations, and on successive-increment terminations are not covered here. This clause does not itself calculate any specific employer's ages, job titles, or decisional-unit population, and does not determine whether a specific disclosure an employer actually gave satisfied this requirement.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1)(H)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Older Workers Benefit Protection Act, group-program job-title-and-age disclosure
citations.quote: the job titles and ages of all individuals eligible or selected for the program, and the ages of all individuals in the same job classification or organizational unit who are not eligible or selected for the program.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1625.22(f)(4)(ii) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, ages must be disclosed individually, not in bands
citations.quote: Information regarding ages should be broken down according to the age of each person eligible or selected for the program and each person not eligible or selected for the program. The use of age bands broader than one year (such as “age 20-30”) does not satisfy this requirement.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1625.22(f)(4)(v) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, disclosure must cover the whole decisional unit even if only a subset is terminated
citations.quote: If the terminees are selected from a subset of a decisional unit, the employer must still disclose information for the entire population of the decisional unit.

clauses.title: Decisional Unit and What Counts as a Covered Program
clauses.body: EEOC regulations interpreting this disclosure duty explain that "class," "unit," "group," "job classification," and "organizational unit" are examples of categories of employees, and that regardless of which term applies, their scope in a given case is worked out by identifying the employer's "decisional unit" for the program at issue. The same regulations describe two types of programs the disclosure duty can attach to: an exit-incentive program, usually a voluntary program under which employees are offered additional consideration in exchange for resigning and signing a waiver, and another employment-termination program, usually one under which employees are involuntarily terminated and offered additional consideration for signing a waiver.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same regulatory section, 29 C.F.R. § 1625.22(f)(1)(iii) — they are treated as one source elaborating the statutory group-disclosure requirement in 29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1)(H), not as independent corroboration of each other or of the statute. This clause is meant to be used together with this corpus's Severance Agreement document (clause id sev_owbpa), which covers the individual 21/45-day and 7-day requirements this group-disclosure duty does not restate. This clause does not determine whether a specific employer's specific program is in fact an "exit incentive or other employment termination program offered to a group or class of employees" that triggers the disclosure duty, and does not define a specific employer's decisional unit — the regulation itself says both are decided case-by-case on the specific facts, including the employer's own corporate structure.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1625.22(f)(1)(iii)(C) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, scope of covered terms tied to the decisional unit
citations.quote: Regardless of the type of program, the scope of the terms “class,” “unit,” “group,” “job classification,” and “organizational unit” is determined by examining the “decisional unit” at issue.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1625.22(f)(1)(iii)(A) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, exit-incentive programs versus other employment-termination programs
citations.quote: Usually an “exit incentive program” is a voluntary program offered to a group or class of employees where such employees are offered consideration in addition to anything of value to which the individuals are already entitled (hereinafter in this section, “additional consideration”) in exchange for their decision to resign voluntarily and sign a waiver. Usually “other employment termination program” refers to a group or class of employees who were involuntarily terminated and who are offered additional consideration in return for their decision to sign a waiver.

clauses.title: Scope of the Disclosure Requirement Itself
clauses.body: The EEOC regulation implementing this disclosure duty states that its own reach is confined to what the disclosure statute requires: it is limited to the requirements of 29 U.S.C. § 626(f)(1)(H) and is not intended to affect the scope of discovery, or of substantive proceedings, in the processing or litigation of an age-discrimination charge.
clauses.gap: This citation is to 29 C.F.R. § 1625.22(f)(3)(vii) alone — the EEOC's own limiting statement about the reach of its regulation — and is not paired with an independent statutory quote, since the statute itself does not address discovery or litigation scope. Making this disclosure, or complying with it, does not by itself resolve, settle, or waive any age-discrimination claim, and this clause does not state that it does; it states only that the regulation's disclosure rule does not expand or contract discovery or litigation scope beyond what the statute requires. This clause is meant to be used together with this corpus's Severance Agreement document (clause id sev_owbpa) for the individual waiver requirements — the 21/45-day consideration period, 7-day revocation period, and EEOC-participation carve-out — that this clause does not cover. This clause does not determine whether a specific disclosure a specific employer gave was adequate under the statute or regulation.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1625.22(f)(3)(vii) (Cornell LII e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, EEOC interpretive regulation, the disclosure rule's own limited scope
citations.quote: This regulatory section is limited to the requirements of section 7(f)(1)(H) and is not intended to affect the scope of discovery or of substantive proceedings in the processing of charges of violation of the ADEA or in litigation involving such charges.

clauses.title: Group/Class Disclosure Notice
Job Titles and Ages Disclosure
No "Narrow-Restraint" Exception Under Section 16600
clauses.body: Section 16600 directs that it be read broadly, with no carve-out for a restriction that limits only a small or "narrow" slice of someone's business, trade, or profession. California's Court of Appeal has explained that this reflects the state Supreme Court's own refusal, in Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP, to adopt a judicially created "narrow-restraint" exception that a federal appeals court had recognized for a restraint covering only a small or limited part of a person's business, trade, or profession. Applying that rule, the same Court of Appeal held a contractual non-solicitation restriction void under Section 16600 even though the restriction could be characterized as narrow or limited in scope.
clauses.gap: Source independence: the statutory quote below was independently fetched from California Legislative Information (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches with two different User-Agent strings. The case-law quotes below were independently fetched from the official, certified-for-publication opinion PDF hosted on the California Courts website (courts.ca.gov/opinions/documents/D071924.PDF) -- a primary court source, not a mirror -- and likewise confirmed byte-identical across two fetches with two different User-Agent strings; this is the same opinion the corpus already cites elsewhere as 'AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc.' Real limitation on sourcing: the two quotations attributed to Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP itself were not independently fetched from Edwards's own opinion text. CourtListener's API was rate-limited (125 requests/day, already exhausted) and its opinion pages return an AWS WAF bot challenge rather than content; Justia and FindLaw mirror pages returned a Cloudflare bot-challenge page rather than the opinion; the California Courts website's own opinion archive does not retain a 2008 opinion (its D071924 PDF above is retained, but an equivalent S147190 URL for Edwards returns 404). Those two Edwards quotations are therefore reproduced only as block-quoted within AMN Healthcare's verified opinion text, not confirmed against Edwards's own opinion independently -- a meaningfully weaker form of verification than the AMN Healthcare and statutory quotes, which is why the case field for those two citations names the chain explicitly rather than citing Edwards alone. What this clause does not cover: AMN Healthcare's own facts and its own application of this no-narrow-restraint rule concerned a clause barring former employees from soliciting the company's other employees (travel nurses) -- the clause discussed in this document's clause on that split of authority -- not a clause barring solicitation of the company's customers. The customer-solicitation-specific rule (that a court will not directly enforce such a clause, though it may still restrain trade-secret misuse) traces to a different, earlier case, The Retirement Group v. Galante (2009), which AMN Healthcare quotes approvingly elsewhere in the same opinion -- see this document's clause distinguishing customer non-solicitation -- but which this clause does not independently verify by name against a fetched copy of Galante's own opinion; the California Courts archive did not have a retrievable PDF for that 2009 case either. This clause states the broader, general anti-narrow-restraint principle that both the employee-solicitation and customer-solicitation lines of authority are built on; it doesn't independently confirm that Galante's own reasoning used the term "narrow restraint," only that AMN Healthcare's use of that term arose in the employee-solicitation context. Left open: whether this rule applies identically where the person bound is an independent contractor rather than an employee, and whether it applies identically to soliciting prospective customers as opposed to existing ones -- neither question is addressed in the sources fetched for this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: This section shall be read broadly, in accordance with Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937, to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context, or any noncompete clause in an employment contract, no matter how narrowly tailored, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter.

citations.case: AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc.
citations.cite: 28 Cal. App. 5th 923 (2018), certified-for-publication opinion, official court PDF
citations.quote: Our conclusion is further buttressed by the Edwards court's refusal to adopt the "limited or 'narrow-restraint' exception to section 16600" created by the Ninth Circuit in Campbell v. Trustees of Leland Stanford Jr. Univ. (9th Cir. 1987) 817 F.2d 499 (Campbell)

citations.case: Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP, as quoted in AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc. (see gap field on sourcing)
citations.quote: California courts have not embraced the Ninth Circuit's narrow-restraint exception

citations.case: AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc.
citations.cite: 28 Cal. App. 5th 923 (2018), certified-for-publication opinion, official court PDF
citations.quote: If enforced, section 3.2 thus restrained individual defendants from engaging in their chosen profession, even in a "narrow" manner or a "limited" way.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California Labor Code Section 925, which restricts certain forum-selection and choice-of-law provisions that {{companyName}} may require of {{employeeName}} as a condition of employment. It states the statute's own terms. It does not evaluate whether any specific provision in any specific agreement between {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}} is subject to, or violates, Section 925, and it does not determine whether any such provision is void, whether an exception applies, or what either party should do about any particular agreement.

clauses.title: Core Prohibition: Out-of-State Adjudication and Loss of California-Law Protection
clauses.body: California Labor Code Section 925(a) prohibits an employer from requiring an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of two things: (1) require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California, or (2) deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California. Section 925(d) defines "adjudication" for purposes of this section to include both litigation and arbitration, so the prohibition is not limited to court-forum clauses -- it also reaches a clause requiring arbitration outside California, or an arbitration clause that would apply another state's substantive law to a controversy arising in California.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Labor Code Section 925(a) and 925(d)), not independent corroborating sources. This clause covers only the prohibition itself and the statute's own definition of "adjudication"; it does not cover the voidability consequence, the individually-negotiated-with-counsel exception, the attorney's-fee provision, or the applicability date, each addressed in this document's other clauses. The statute's own text does not define "primarily resides and works in California" or "a claim arising in California" beyond that phrasing, and this clause does not determine whether a specific employee or a specific claim meets either description. No case law is cited in this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 925(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 925, subd. (a)
citations.quote: (a) An employer shall not require an employee who primarily resides and works in California, as a condition of employment, to agree to a provision that would do either of the following: (1) Require the employee to adjudicate outside of California a claim arising in California. (2) Deprive the employee of the substantive protection of California law with respect to a controversy arising in California.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 925(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 925, subd. (d)
citations.quote: (d) For purposes of this section, adjudication includes litigation and arbitration.

clauses.title: Voidability and the Governing-Law Consequence of Voiding
clauses.body: California Labor Code Section 925(b) states that a contract provision violating subdivision (a) is voidable by the employee, not automatically void. If the employee requests that such a provision be voided and it is rendered void at that request, the statute's own text further provides that the matter shall then be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute.
clauses.gap: This clause covers Section 925(b) only. Because the statute makes a violating provision voidable rather than void, the statute's own text does not itself describe how or in what forum an employee exercises the option to void a provision (for example, by objection in a pending proceeding, by a separate action, or otherwise); that procedural mechanism is not addressed by this clause. This clause does not address what happens to any part of a contract or provision the employee does not seek to void, or to the remainder of the agreement generally. No case law is cited in this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 925(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 925, subd. (b)
citations.quote: (b) Any provision of a contract that violates subdivision (a) is voidable by the employee, and if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute.

clauses.title: Court's Authority: Injunctive Relief and Attorney's Fees
clauses.body: California Labor Code Section 925(c) states that, in addition to injunctive relief and any other remedies available, a court may award an employee who is enforcing their rights under this section reasonable attorney's fees.
clauses.gap: This clause covers Section 925(c) only. The statute's own text uses the word "may," so a fee award under this subdivision is discretionary with the court, not automatic upon a successful enforcement action. The statute's own text authorizes an award of the employee's reasonable attorney's fees; it does not, in this subdivision, use or define the phrase "actual costs," and this clause does not state that costs (as distinct from attorney's fees) are separately authorized by this subdivision. The phrase "any other remedies available" is not itself defined or enumerated in this subdivision, and this clause does not identify what those other remedies are. This subdivision does not address a fee award running the other direction, to an employer, and this clause does not state that one is or is not available. No case law is cited in this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 925(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 925, subd. (c)
citations.quote: (c) In addition to injunctive relief and any other remedies available, a court may award an employee who is enforcing his or her rights under this section reasonable attorney’s fees.

clauses.title: Exception for a Contract Individually Negotiated With the Employee Represented by Counsel
clauses.body: California Labor Code Section 925(e) states that the section does not apply to a contract with an employee who is in fact individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum in which a controversy arising from the employment contract may be adjudicated, or the choice of law to be applied.
clauses.gap: This clause covers Section 925(e) only. The statute's own text conditions the exception on the employee being "in fact individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating the terms" of the venue, forum, or choice-of-law provision specifically; this clause does not define what representation or negotiation is sufficient to satisfy that standard, and whether a particular employee's representation meets it is a fact-specific question this clause does not resolve. This subdivision, by its own terms, removes the protection of the entire section for a qualifying contract; this clause does not address whether the exception can apply to only part of an agreement. No case law is cited in this clause; it rests on the statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 925(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 925, subd. (e)
citations.quote: (e) This section shall not apply to a contract with an employee who is in fact individually represented by legal counsel in negotiating the terms of an agreement to designate either the venue or forum in which a controversy arising from the employment contract may be adjudicated or the choice of law to be applied.

clauses.title: Applicability Date
clauses.body: California Labor Code Section 925(f) states that the section applies to a contract entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017. The statute's own enactment note on the California Legislative Information website confirms that Section 925 was added by Statutes 2016, Chapter 632, Section 1 (SB 1241), effective January 1, 2017.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are drawn from the same statutory section as published on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov -- subdivision (f)'s applicability text and the page's own enactment/history note for the section -- not from two independent sources. This clause states only the applicability trigger and the enactment date; it does not determine, for any specific contract, whether that contract was entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017, and it does not address how a contract's modification or extension is identified for this purpose, which the statute's own text does not define. No case law is cited in this clause; it rests on the statutory text and the source page's own history note.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 925, subd. (f)
citations.quote: (f) This section shall apply to a contract entered into, modified, or extended on or after January 1, 2017.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 925, history note
citations.quote: (Added by Stats. 2016, Ch. 632, Sec. 1. (SB 1241) Effective January 1, 2017.)

clauses.title: Signature
A Separate Statute: Termination Based on Off-Duty Cannabis Use or Metabolite Testing
clauses.body: Since January 1, 2024, a separate California statute — part of the Fair Employment and Housing Act — independently makes it unlawful for an employer to discriminate against a person in termination, or any other term or condition of employment, based on "the person's use of cannabis off the job and away from the workplace," or based on "an employer-required drug screening test that has found the person to have nonpsychoactive cannabis metabolites in their hair, blood, urine, or other bodily fluids." The metabolite point exists because standard urine and hair tests detect nonpsychoactive metabolites that can remain in the body for days or weeks after use, long after any impairment has ended, so a positive result on that kind of test doesn't by itself show current impairment. This is a distinct statutory protection from the disclosure- and wage-retaliation statutes described elsewhere in this document: it turns on the stated reason for the termination itself, not on whether the employee made a report or complaint.
clauses.gap: The introductory language of subdivision (a)(1) and paragraph (A) within it are part of the same sentence of the same statutory subdivision, Government Code § 12954(a)(1); the metabolite-testing point in paragraph (B) is a separate paragraph of that same subdivision. All are being treated together as one connected source, not as independent corroborating sources. This same statutory section, including its exemptions, is independently described in more detail in this corpus's separate Hiring-category document, the Pre-Employment and Workplace Drug Testing Information Sheet — this clause does not repeat that document's full citation set, and the next clause in this document covers only the exemptions most relevant to a termination that has already occurred. This document does not describe the Civil Rights Department's administrative complaint and right-to-sue process that generally applies to a claim brought directly under this statute, as distinct from the direct-to-court statutes described elsewhere in this document; that procedural framework was not independently verified in this research session and is not addressed here. This is one state's law, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific termination was, or was not, based on off-duty cannabis use or a metabolite test result. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

citations.cite: California Government Code, Fair Employment and Housing Act, off-duty cannabis use protection applied to termination
citations.quote: it is unlawful for an employer to discriminate against a person in hiring, termination, or any term or condition of employment, or otherwise penalizing a person, if the discrimination is based upon any of the following: (A) The person’s use of cannabis off the job and away from the workplace.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12954(a)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, nonpsychoactive-metabolite screening protection
citations.quote: An employer-required drug screening test that has found the person to have nonpsychoactive cannabis metabolites in their hair, blood, urine, or other bodily fluids.

clauses.title: Limits and Exceptions to That Protection
clauses.body: That protection has specific limits relevant to evaluating a termination. It does not apply at all to an employee in the building and construction trades. It does not give an employee the right to possess, be impaired by, or use cannabis on the job, and it does not affect an employer's rights or obligations to maintain a drug- and alcohol-free workplace. It does not preempt any state or federal law requiring applicants or employees to be tested for controlled substances — including as a condition of federal funding, federal licensing-related benefits, or a federal contract. And it does not apply at all to positions that require a federal government background investigation or security clearance under U.S. Department of Defense regulations, or equivalent regulations of other federal agencies.
clauses.gap: All four citations in this clause are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section as the previous clause, Government Code § 12954 — subdivisions (a)(2), (d), (e), and (f) — treated together here as one connected source, not as independent corroborating sources. The same exemptions are independently described in this corpus's separate Hiring-category document, the Pre-Employment and Workplace Drug Testing Information Sheet; this clause restates them only because they bear directly on whether a termination falls within the protection described in the previous clause, not as an independent verification effort. Cannabis remains a Schedule I controlled substance under the federal Controlled Substances Act, so a federal contractor or a federally regulated position can still require testing for it regardless of this state law, exactly as this clause states. This clause does not determine whether any particular employee, position, or employer falls within one of these exemptions, and it does not determine that any specific termination was, or was not, lawful. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that a termination violated public policy or that a wrongful termination occurred in this or any specific case.

citations.quote: This subdivision does not apply to an employee in the building and construction trades.

clauses.title: Employer's Duty to Establish Confidentiality Procedures
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 56.20(a) requires {{companyName}}, as an employer that receives medical information about {{employeeName}}, to establish appropriate procedures to ensure the confidentiality and protection of that information from unauthorized use and disclosure.
clauses.gap: This is a single subdivision of one statutory section, Civil Code § 56.20(a). The statute names two non-exclusive examples of what such procedures 'may include' — instructing employees and agents who handle files on confidentiality, and security systems restricting access to files containing medical information — but does not mandate either specific measure, and its text does not itself require that medical information be kept on separate forms or in a file separate from the employee's regular personnel file (contrast the ADA confidentiality duty covered elsewhere in this corpus, which does require separate forms and files, and is a different, federal statute). This clause states the employer-specific duty in the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act's own employer chapter (Civil Code §§ 56.20-56.245); it does not restate a health care provider's, health care service plan's, or contractor's separate disclosure obligations under Civil Code § 56.10, which is a different audience addressed elsewhere in this corpus.
