citations.cite: Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — employer confidentiality-procedures duty
citations.quote: Each employer who receives medical information shall establish appropriate procedures to ensure the confidentiality and protection from unauthorized use and disclosure of that information.

clauses.title: Restriction on an Employer's Use or Disclosure of Medical Information
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 56.20(c) provides that {{companyName}} may not use, disclose, or knowingly permit its employees or agents to use or disclose medical information that {{companyName}} possesses pertaining to {{employeeName}}, without {{employeeName}} first having signed an authorization under Civil Code § 56.11 or § 56.21 permitting that use or disclosure, except as specifically listed in the statute.
clauses.gap: This is the introductory sentence of Civil Code § 56.20(c). The statute goes on to list four specific exceptions to this authorization requirement in paragraphs (1) through (4); one of them, the benefits-administration exception, is stated as its own clause elsewhere in this document (Civil Code § 56.20(c)(3) — a subdivision of this same statutory section, not an independent corroborating source). This document does not restate the other three listed exceptions (disclosure compelled by judicial or administrative process or other law; information relevant to a lawsuit, arbitration, or grievance between the employer and employee; and disclosure to a health care provider or professional to aid diagnosis or treatment when the patient cannot authorize it). As fetched, this provision's text applies to medical information the employer possesses 'pertaining to its employees'; it does not use the word 'applicant,' and this document does not independently verify that this specific provision, as opposed to some other part of the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act, extends to a job applicant who is not yet an employee. This is California law only; it does not describe any other state's employer medical-information rules.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.20(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — employer disclosure restriction
citations.quote: No employer shall use, disclose, or knowingly permit its employees or agents to use or disclose medical information which the employer possesses pertaining to its employees without the patient having first signed an authorization under Section 56.11 or Section 56.21 permitting such use or disclosure, except as follows:

clauses.title: Permitted Use for Administering Employee Benefit Plans
clauses.body: One statutory exception to that authorization requirement is for benefits administration: Civil Code § 56.20(c)(3) provides that medical information pertaining to {{employeeName}} may be used by {{companyName}} without an authorization only for the purpose of administering and maintaining employee benefit plans, including health care plans and plans providing short-term and long-term disability income, workers' compensation, and for determining eligibility for paid and unpaid leave from work for medical reasons.
clauses.gap: This is paragraph (3) of the same subdivision addressed in another clause of this document, Civil Code § 56.20(c) — it is one of four listed exceptions within that subdivision, not an independent statutory section. This document does not restate the other three exceptions in § 56.20(c)(1), (2), and (4). Separately, Civil Code § 56.20(d), not quoted here, allows an employer to voluntarily narrow its own use or disclosure of medical information below what subdivision (c) otherwise permits, by a written agreement with an employee or a written company policy; that voluntary narrowing is not addressed by this clause. This clause states only that this use is permitted without an authorization for this stated purpose — it does not state that every other use or disclosure by an employer is prohibited, since the statute lists further exceptions this document does not repeat here.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.20(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — benefits-administration exception
citations.quote: The information may be used only for the purpose of administering and maintaining employee benefit plans, including health care plans and plans providing short-term and long-term disability income, workers’ compensation and for determining eligibility for paid and unpaid leave from work for medical reasons.

clauses.title: No Discrimination for Refusing to Sign an Authorization
clauses.body: Civil Code § 56.20(b) provides that {{employeeName}} may not be discriminated against in the terms or conditions of employment with {{companyName}} because {{employeeName}} refused to sign an authorization under this part of the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act, although the statute does not prohibit {{companyName}} from taking action that is necessary in the absence of medical information caused by that refusal.
clauses.gap: This is subdivision (b) of the same statutory section as the confidentiality-procedures duty and the disclosure restriction addressed in other clauses of this document, Civil Code § 56.20 — these are components of one section, not independent corroborating sources. This is a narrow anti-retaliation rule limited to the specific circumstance of an employee declining to sign an authorization under this part of the Act; it does not address retaliation for any other protected activity, and the statute does not itself define what employer action is 'necessary in the absence of medical information,' a phrase this document does not further interpret.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.20(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — no discrimination for refusing to authorize
citations.quote: No employee shall be discriminated against in terms or conditions of employment due to that employee’s refusal to sign an authorization

clauses.title: Civil Penalties and a Private Right of Action for Violations
clauses.body: Civil Code § 56.36 gives an individual a private right of action against a person or entity — which can include an employer — that negligently releases confidential medical information or records in violation of the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act, for nominal damages of $1,000 (without needing to prove actual or threatened damages) and for any actual damages sustained. The same section separately makes a person or entity that negligently discloses medical information in violation of the Act liable for an administrative fine or civil penalty of up to $2,500 per violation, and makes a person or entity, other than a licensed health care professional, that knowingly and willfully obtains, discloses, or uses medical information in violation of the Act liable for an administrative fine or civil penalty of up to $25,000 per violation.
clauses.gap: Civil Code § 56.36 is a general remedies section that applies to a violation of 'this part' — meaning any provision within the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act, Civil Code §§ 56-56.37 — and is not written as an employer-specific penalty provision; it reaches a violation of the employer-specific rules addressed elsewhere in this document, Civil Code § 56.20, only because § 56.20 sits within that same part. The four citations in this clause are all subdivisions of one statutory section, § 56.36: (b)(1) and (b)(2) together define the private civil action described in (b)'s introductory sentence (not separately quoted here), and (c)(1) and (c)(2)(A) are two separate, escalating civil-penalty tiers within the same subdivision (c) — none are independent sections corroborating each other. Section 56.36 contains substantial additional detail this clause does not restate: higher penalty tiers (up to $250,000 per violation) for knowing-and-willful violations done for financial gain, a list of factors used in assessing an administrative fine or civil penalty, an affirmative defense available to a covered entity or business associate that meets specified HIPAA-related conditions, and provisions on who may bring a civil-penalty action and how a recovered penalty is allocated between the state and local governments. This document does not evaluate whether any specific use or disclosure by an employer would actually violate the Act.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.36(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — private right of action, nominal damages
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (e), nominal damages of one thousand dollars ($1,000). In order to recover under this paragraph, it is not necessary that the plaintiff suffered or was threatened with actual damages.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.36(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — civil penalty for negligent disclosure
citations.quote: In addition, a person or entity that negligently discloses medical information in violation of the provisions of this part shall also be liable, irrespective of the amount of damages suffered by the patient as a result of that violation, for an administrative fine or civil penalty not to exceed two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500) per violation.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 56.36(c)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — civil penalty for knowing and willful violation
citations.quote: A person or entity, other than a licensed health care professional, who knowingly and willfully obtains, discloses, or uses medical information in violation of this part shall be liable for an administrative fine or civil penalty not to exceed twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000) per violation.

clauses.title: Signature Block
Information and Background — FEHA Administrative Complaint
clauses.body: I, {{employeeName}}, am completing this information sheet in connection with a possible administrative complaint against {{companyName}} under California's Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), filed with California's Civil Rights Department (CRD). The practice I believe may have been unlawful is described here as: {{allegedPracticeDescription}}. The date on which I believe the alleged unlawful practice occurred is stated here as {{allegedUnlawfulPracticeDate}}. If a complaint has already been filed with the Civil Rights Department, the date it was filed is stated here as {{crdComplaintFiledDate}}; if a right-to-sue notice has already been issued, the date of that notice is stated here as {{rightToSueNoticeDate}}. This information sheet describes, using the statutes' own text, how the CRD administrative complaint process works — the filing deadline, what a complaint must contain, how CRD's investigation process relates to the option of requesting an immediate right-to-sue notice, and the legal effect and filing deadline that follow once a right-to-sue notice issues. It is not a CRD intake form, not a verified complaint, not a right-to-sue notice, not a court filing, and not a legal determination of any kind. Completing this information sheet does not file a complaint with the Civil Rights Department, does not request or obtain a right-to-sue notice, and does not determine that any specific practice by {{companyName}} was unlawful, that any specific complaint would be timely, or that any specific claim is valid. Only the Civil Rights Department, a court, or another body with legal authority to decide the question can make those determinations.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature Block — FEHA Administrative Complaint Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{employeeName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes the statutory framework governing FEHA administrative complaints filed with California's Civil Rights Department. It does not itself determine that {{employeeName}} has, or does not have, a timely or valid FEHA claim against {{companyName}}, is not a CRD intake form or verified complaint, is not a right-to-sue request, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting the actual statutes, the Civil Rights Department's own current filing procedures, or a licensed attorney.]

clauses.title: The Three-Year Deadline to File a FEHA Complaint with the Civil Rights Department
clauses.body: California law sets a specific deadline for filing an administrative complaint alleging a FEHA employment-discrimination, harassment, or retaliation violation with the Civil Rights Department: three years from the date the alleged unlawful practice occurred. This three-year period applies to complaints alleging a violation of the FEHA employment-practices article (the article beginning with Government Code section 12940) — the article that contains FEHA's core discrimination, harassment, and retaliation prohibitions. The statute sets other, different deadlines for complaints alleging violations of certain other, non-FEHA-employment statutes administered by the same department, which this clause does not address.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single subdivision, Government Code section 12960(e)(5), current as most recently amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 321 (SB 477), effective January 1, 2026. The same subdivision (e) of section 12960 also sets different filing deadlines for complaints alleging violations of several other statutes (Civil Code sections 51, 51.5, 51.7, 51.9, 52.5, 54, 54.1, and 54.2, Labor Code section 1197.5, and the state's own nondiscrimination-in-programs statute) — this clause does not restate those other deadlines, which are not FEHA employment claims. Section 12960(e)(6), also not quoted here, lists several categories of extension to the filing periods (a 90-day discovery-based extension, an extension tied to correcting a misidentified employer, an extension tied to discovering a defendant's identity in a Civil Code section 51.7 case, and an extension tied to reaching the age of majority) — this document does not address whether any such extension applies to a specific complaint. Section 12960(f), also not quoted here, separately tolls the time to file a civil action (as distinct from the time to file the administrative complaint itself) while an administrative complaint remains pending with the department, and states that this tolling applies retroactively but does not revive an already-lapsed claim; this document does not address civil-action-deadline tolling for claims other than the one-year deadline following a right-to-sue notice, addressed in a separate clause of this document. This document does not determine whether any specific complaint was, or would be, filed within the applicable deadline, or whether any extension or tolling provision applies to any specific set of facts.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 12960(e)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: A complaint alleging a violation of Section 51.9 of the Civil Code or any other violation of Article 1 (commencing with Section 12940) of Chapter 6 shall not be filed after the expiration of three years from the date upon which the unlawful practice or refusal to cooperate occurred.

clauses.title: How a FEHA Complaint Is Filed and What It Must Contain
clauses.body: Under the statute governing this process, filing a complaint with the Civil Rights Department means filing an intake form with the department; the operative filing date of the resulting verified complaint relates back to the date the intake form was filed. Any person claiming to be aggrieved by an alleged unlawful practice may file with the department a verified complaint, in writing, that states the name and address of the person, employer, labor organization, or employment agency alleged to have committed the unlawful practice, sets forth the particulars of the alleged practice, and contains any other information the department may require. The department's own director, or the director's authorized representative, may separately make, sign, and file a complaint on that person's behalf.
clauses.gap: This clause combines two citations that are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Government Code section 12960(b) and section 12960(c), rather than two independent sources -- disclosed here explicitly. This document does not describe the department's current online intake form itself, its specific fields, or any non-statutory administrative filing procedure the department may use to implement this statutory framework; it states what the statute itself requires and permits. This document does not determine that a specific written submission satisfies the verified-complaint requirement, or that a specific intake filing date has been correctly established.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 12960(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, filing a complaint means filing an intake form with the department and the operative date of the verified complaint relates back to the filing of the intake form.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 12960(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: Any person claiming to be aggrieved by an alleged unlawful practice may file with the department a verified complaint, in writing, that shall state the name and address of the person, employer, labor organization, or employment agency alleged to have committed the unlawful practice complained of, and that shall set forth the particulars thereof and contain other information as may be required by the department.

clauses.title: The Civil Rights Department's Investigation, Conciliation, and Mandatory Dispute Resolution
clauses.body: Once a complaint is filed, the statute contemplates that the Civil Rights Department will first attempt to eliminate an alleged unlawful practice through conference, conciliation, mediation, or persuasion; only if that effort fails -- or, in the director's discretion, in advance of it if circumstances warrant -- may the department's director bring a civil action in the department's own name, acting in the public interest, on behalf of the person claiming to be aggrieved. Before the department may file that kind of civil action, the statute separately requires all parties to participate in mandatory dispute resolution within the department's own internal dispute resolution division, free of charge to the parties, in an effort to resolve the dispute without litigation.
clauses.gap: This clause combines two citations that are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Government Code section 12965(a)(1) and section 12965(a)(2), rather than two independent sources -- disclosed here explicitly. This clause describes only the department-initiated civil-action pathway and the mandatory dispute-resolution step that precedes it; it does not describe the department's internal investigative methods or timeline in the detail the department's own regulations may provide, and it does not describe the separate right of the person claiming to be aggrieved to request a right-to-sue notice instead of waiting on this process, which is addressed in a separate clause of this document. This document does not determine whether the department will investigate, conciliate, or bring a civil action on any specific complaint, or how long any specific investigation will take.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 12965(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: In the case of failure to eliminate an unlawful practice under this part through conference, conciliation, mediation, or persuasion, or in advance thereof if circumstances warrant, the director in the director’s discretion may bring a civil action in the name of the department, acting in the public interest, on behalf of the person claiming to be aggrieved.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 12965(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: Prior to filing a civil action, the department shall require all parties to participate in mandatory dispute resolution in the department’s internal dispute resolution division free of charge to the parties in an effort to resolve the dispute without litigation.

clauses.title: Requesting a Right-to-Sue Notice Instead of Waiting for the Department to Act
clauses.body: The statute gives the person claiming to be aggrieved an alternative to waiting for the department's own investigation or civil action to run its course. If a civil action is not brought by the department within 150 days after the complaint is filed, or if the department earlier determines that no civil action will be brought, the statute requires the department to notify that person in writing that the department will issue a right-to-sue notice on request. If the person does not request a right-to-sue notice, the department instead issues it upon completing its investigation, and no later than one year after the complaint was filed.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single statutory subdivision, Government Code section 12965(c)(1)(A). This document uses the phrase "immediate right-to-sue" as this project's own description of the practical effect of requesting a right-to-sue notice on request rather than waiting for the department's investigation to complete; that exact phrase does not appear in the quoted statutory text itself, and this document does not describe the department's current online or administrative procedure for making that request, which may differ in detail from what the statute itself states. This document does not determine whether requesting an immediate right-to-sue notice, or instead allowing the department's investigation to proceed, would be more advantageous in any specific case, and does not itself request a right-to-sue notice or file anything with the department.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 12965(c)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: if a civil action is not brought by the department pursuant to subdivision (a) within 150 days after the filing of a complaint, or if the department earlier determines that no civil action will be brought pursuant to subdivision (a), the department shall promptly notify, in writing, the person claiming to be aggrieved that the department shall issue, on request, the right-to-sue notice.

clauses.title: The Right-to-Sue Notice's Legal Effect and the One-Year Deadline to Sue
clauses.body: A right-to-sue notice issued under this statute must indicate that the person claiming to be aggrieved may bring a civil action against the person, employer, labor organization, or employment agency named in the verified complaint -- and that the civil action must be brought within one year from the date of that notice. The statute gives California's superior courts jurisdiction over these civil actions, and states that the aggrieved person may file directly in those courts.
clauses.gap: This clause combines two citations that are subdivisions of the same statutory section but different subdivisions -- Government Code section 12965(c)(1)(D) and section 12965(c)(3) -- disclosed here explicitly rather than presented as independent sources. Section 12965(c)(1)(E), not separately quoted here, states that this one-year notice-and-deadline paragraph applies only to complaints alleging unlawful employment practices under the FEHA employment-practices article (the article beginning with Government Code section 12940) -- the category of claim this document addresses. Section 12965(c)(1)(F), and separately section 12965(e) and (f), each not quoted here, set out specific tolling rules that can extend this one-year deadline (including tolling during the department's own dispute-resolution proceedings, tolling under a written agreement between the department and a respondent, and tolling tied to a concurrently filed federal EEOC charge that the department defers) -- this document does not determine whether any such tolling rule applies to any specific right-to-sue notice or claim. This document does not itself constitute a right-to-sue notice, does not determine that any right-to-sue notice has actually issued in any specific case, and does not calculate or confirm any specific one-year deadline.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 12965(c)(1)(D) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: The notices specified in subparagraphs (A), (B), and (C) shall indicate that the person claiming to be aggrieved may bring a civil action under this part against the person, employer, labor organization, or employment agency named in the verified complaint within one year from the date of that notice.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 12965(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: The superior courts of the State of California shall have jurisdiction of actions brought pursuant to this section, and the aggrieved person may file in these courts.

clauses.title: Declaration of Association and Purpose
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California statutory law under the Common Interest Development Open Meeting Act (Civil Code §§ 4900-4955, part of the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act) as it applies to meetings of the board of directors of {{hoaName}}. It states facts about when board meetings must be open to members, what notice the association must give, what limited topics may be discussed in a closed executive session, members' rights to attend and speak, and the requirement that board action generally be taken at a properly noticed open meeting. It does not evaluate whether any particular past or planned meeting, notice, or board action of {{hoaName}} complied with these requirements.

clauses.title: General Rule: Board Action Must Occur at a Board Meeting
clauses.body: The Davis-Stirling Act's Common Interest Development Open Meeting Act, Civil Code § 4900, states: "This article shall be known and may be cited as the Common Interest Development Open Meeting Act." Its central rule appears in Civil Code § 4910(a): "The board shall not take action on any item of business outside of a board meeting." California law also restricts using a series of electronic transmissions (such as email) as a substitute for a meeting for this purpose, except in a narrow emergency circumstance addressed in a separate clause of this document. This rule applies to the board of {{hoaName}}.
clauses.gap: The citations to § 4900 and § 4910(a) are independent, separately-numbered sections of the same article (Article 2, "Board Meeting," of Civil Code §§ 4900-4955); § 4900 is the article's short-title provision and § 4910(a) states the operative no-action-outside-a-meeting rule. This clause does not quote § 4910(b), which separately restricts (with a narrow emergency exception) using a series of electronic transmissions, such as email, as a substitute for a meeting; that restriction is described narratively above but not quoted. This clause does not define what qualifies as a validly convened "board meeting" in every circumstance (for example, ad hoc or informal gatherings of directors), a line California's published guidance and case law address in more granular, fact-specific ways than the statutory text alone. This document does not determine whether any specific decision, communication, or gathering involving the association's board did or did not constitute "action" taken "outside of a board meeting."

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4900 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: This article shall be known and may be cited as the Common Interest Development Open Meeting Act.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4910(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The board shall not take action on any item of business outside of a board meeting.

clauses.title: Notice of Board Meetings: Timing, Delivery, and Required Content
clauses.body: California law sets minimum notice requirements before a board meeting of a common interest development association. Civil Code § 4920(a) provides the general timing rule: "Except as provided in subdivision (b), the association shall give notice of the time and place of a board meeting at least four days before the meeting." A shorter, two-day minimum applies to a nonemergency meeting held solely in executive session: Civil Code § 4920(b)(2) provides, "If a nonemergency board meeting is held solely in executive session, the association shall give notice of the time and place of the meeting at least two days prior to the meeting." A different, notice-free exception applies to a true emergency meeting: Civil Code § 4923 provides, "An emergency board meeting may be called by the president of the association, or by any two directors other than the president, if there are circumstances that could not have been reasonably foreseen which require immediate attention and possible action by the board, and which of necessity make it impracticable to provide notice as required by Section 4920." As to how notice must be delivered, Civil Code § 4920(c) provides: "Notice of a board meeting shall be given by general delivery pursuant to Section 4045," and as to what notice must contain, Civil Code § 4920(d) provides: "Notice of a board meeting shall contain the agenda for the meeting." These timing, delivery, and content requirements apply to board meetings of {{hoaName}}.
clauses.gap: The citations to § 4920(a), § 4920(b)(2), § 4920(c), and § 4920(d) are all subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 4920, and are treated together because they define one integrated notice regime (default timing, the executive-session-only exception, delivery method, and required content). The citation to § 4923 is to a separate, independently-numbered section defining what qualifies as an emergency meeting exempt from advance notice altogether, cross-referenced from § 4920(b)(1) (not independently quoted here). This clause does not quote or verify Civil Code § 4045, the general-delivery mechanics section cross-referenced by § 4920(c), nor does it quote § 4920(b)(3), which allows an association's own governing documents to require a longer notice period than the statutory minimum if the governing documents specifically say so. This document does not state what notice period, if any, the association's own governing documents require, and does not determine whether any specific notice given by the association's board complied with these timing, delivery, or content requirements.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4920(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), the association shall give notice of the time and place of a board meeting at least four days before the meeting.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4920(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If a nonemergency board meeting is held solely in executive session, the association shall give notice of the time and place of the meeting at least two days prior to the meeting.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4923 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: An emergency board meeting may be called by the president of the association, or by any two directors other than the president, if there are circumstances that could not have been reasonably foreseen which require immediate attention and possible action by the board, and which of necessity make it impracticable to provide notice as required by Section 4920.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4920(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Notice of a board meeting shall be given by general delivery pursuant to Section 4045.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4920(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Notice of a board meeting shall contain the agenda for the meeting.

clauses.title: Executive Session: Permitted Topics and Minute-Notation Requirement
clauses.body: California law limits the topics a board may discuss in a closed "executive session" to a specific, enumerated list rather than allowing the board to close a meeting for any reason. Civil Code § 4935(a) provides: "The board may adjourn to, or meet solely in, executive session to consider litigation, matters relating to the formation of contracts with third parties, member discipline, personnel matters, or to meet with a member, upon the member's request, regarding the member's payment of assessments, as specified in Section 5665." Even though executive session excludes the general membership, California law requires that what happened there not disappear from the record entirely: Civil Code § 4935(e) provides, "Any matter discussed in executive session shall be generally noted in the minutes of the immediately following meeting that is open to the entire membership." These executive-session limits and the minute-notation requirement apply to the board of {{hoaName}}.
clauses.gap: The citations to § 4935(a) and § 4935(e) are subdivisions of the same statutory section. This clause does not separately quote § 4935(b), (c), or (d), which respectively make executive session mandatory (rather than merely permitted) to discuss member discipline if the affected member requests it, to discuss an assessment payment plan under Section 5665, and to decide whether to foreclose a lien under subdivision (b) of Section 5705 -- each identifies additional specific circumstances triggering, or narrowing, the executive-session mechanism beyond the general list in subdivision (a). This document does not determine whether any specific topic actually discussed by the association's board in a closed session fell within this statutory list.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4935(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The board may adjourn to, or meet solely in, executive session to consider litigation, matters relating to the formation of contracts with third parties, member discipline, personnel matters, or to meet with a member, upon the member’s request, regarding the member’s payment of assessments, as specified in Section 5665.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4935(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Any matter discussed in executive session shall be generally noted in the minutes of the immediately following meeting that is open to the entire membership.

clauses.title: Members' Right to Attend Open Meetings and to Speak
clauses.body: California law gives every member of a common interest development association a right to attend the association's board meetings, subject to the executive-session exception described elsewhere in this document. Civil Code § 4925(a) provides, in relevant part: "Any member may attend board meetings, except when the board adjourns to, or meets solely in, executive session." A related but distinct right lets members speak, not merely attend: Civil Code § 4925(b) provides, "The board shall permit any member to speak at any meeting of the association or the board, except for meetings of the board held in executive session. A reasonable time limit for all members of the association to speak to the board or before a meeting of the association shall be established by the board." These attendance and speaking rights apply to members of {{hoaName}}.
clauses.gap: The citations to § 4925(a) and § 4925(b) are subdivisions of the same statutory section. This clause quotes only the first sentence of § 4925(a); the remainder of that subdivision (not quoted here) separately addresses a member's right to attend, and have audible to them, the open portion of a teleconference board meeting. This clause does not state what a "reasonable" time limit on member speaking is in any specific case -- § 4925(b) leaves that determination to the board itself, subject to the reasonableness standard the statute states. This document does not determine whether any specific time limit or attendance practice of the association's board complies with this standard.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4925(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Any member may attend board meetings, except when the board adjourns to, or meets solely in, executive session.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4925(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The board shall permit any member to speak at any meeting of the association or the board, except for meetings of the board held in executive session. A reasonable time limit for all members of the association to speak to the board or before a meeting of the association shall be established by the board.

clauses.title: Board Action Generally Limited to Agenda Items Noticed in Advance
clauses.body: Beyond requiring that action be taken at a meeting at all, California law further restricts a nonemergency meeting to discussing or acting on items that were actually placed on the agenda distributed with the meeting notice. Civil Code § 4930(a) provides: "Except as described in subdivisions (b) to (e), inclusive, the board may not discuss or take action on any item at a nonemergency meeting unless the item was placed on the agenda included in the notice that was distributed pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 4920. This subdivision does not prohibit a member or resident who is not a director from speaking on issues not on the agenda." This agenda-based limit on board discussion and action applies to nonemergency meetings of {{hoaName}}'s board.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of § 4930. It does not quote subdivisions (b) through (e) of that same section, which set out specific, narrow exceptions allowing brief staff or director responses to speakers, referrals for information, and -- under defined emergency or supermajority-vote conditions, or where an item carried over from a recent prior meeting -- board action on an item not on the distributed agenda; those exceptions are real and not covered by this clause's single quoted subdivision. This document does not determine whether any specific item discussed or acted on by the association's board was or was not properly on that meeting's noticed agenda, or whether any of the subdivision (b) through (e) exceptions applied to a specific instance.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4930(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Except as described in subdivisions (b) to (e), inclusive, the board may not discuss or take action on any item at a nonemergency meeting unless the item was placed on the agenda included in the notice that was distributed pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 4920. This subdivision does not prohibit a member or resident who is not a director from speaking on issues not on the agenda.

clauses.title: Availability of Meeting Minutes and Members' Right to Enforce This Article
clauses.body: California law requires that minutes of an open board meeting be made available to members, and separately gives members a civil remedy for violations of these open-meeting requirements. Civil Code § 4950(a) provides, in relevant part: "The minutes, minutes proposed for adoption that are marked to indicate draft status, or a summary of the minutes, of any board meeting, other than an executive session, shall be available to members within 30 days of the meeting." If these requirements are violated, Civil Code § 4955(a) provides: "A member of an association may bring a civil action for declaratory or equitable relief for a violation of this article by the association, including, but not limited to, injunctive relief, restitution, or a combination thereof, within one year of the date the cause of action accrues." Civil Code § 4955(b) adds a fee-shifting and penalty rule: "A member who prevails in a civil action to enforce the member's rights pursuant to this article shall be entitled to reasonable attorney's fees and court costs, and the court may impose a civil penalty of up to five hundred dollars ($500) for each violation, except that each identical violation shall be subject to only one penalty if the violation affects each member equally." These minute-availability and enforcement provisions apply to {{hoaName}}.
clauses.gap: The citation to § 4950(a) is to a section separate from § 4955; § 4950(a) and § 4955(a)-(b) are cited together in this clause because they form a related pair (a recordkeeping/transparency duty and the civil remedy for violating the open-meeting requirements generally, including that duty), not because they are subdivisions of one section -- § 4955(a) and § 4955(b) are, by contrast, subdivisions of the same section as each other. This clause does not quote the remainder of § 4950(a) (the distribution-upon-request-and-reimbursement sentence) or § 4950(b) (the annual policy statement's obligation to inform members how to obtain minutes). This clause does not quote the remainder of § 4955(b) addressing a prevailing association's inability to recover costs absent a frivolousness finding. This document does not determine whether a violation of this article has occurred with respect to the association, whether any specific minutes were timely made available, or whether any member would prevail in, or is well-advised to bring, a civil action under § 4955.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4950(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The minutes, minutes proposed for adoption that are marked to indicate draft status, or a summary of the minutes, of any board meeting, other than an executive session, shall be available to members within 30 days of the meeting.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4955(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A member of an association may bring a civil action for declaratory or equitable relief for a violation of this article by the association, including, but not limited to, injunctive relief, restitution, or a combination thereof, within one year of the date the cause of action accrues.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 4955(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A member who prevails in a civil action to enforce the member’s rights pursuant to this article shall be entitled to reasonable attorney’s fees and court costs, and the court may impose a civil penalty of up to five hundred dollars ($500) for each violation, except that each identical violation shall be subject to only one penalty if the violation affects each member equally.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Review
Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}}, states what California law provides about two related but distinct statutory schemes governing franchises in California: the pre-sale disclosure and registration requirements of the Franchise Investment Law (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 31000 et seq.), which apply to the offer or sale of a franchise, and the termination and non-renewal protections of the California Franchise Relations Act (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 20000-20043), which apply to an existing franchise relationship. Where a specific business name is named below, that is {{companyName}}; this sheet can also be read on its own, without it filled in, as a general reference to what these statutes say. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any particular arrangement is a "franchise," whether any particular offer or sale complied with the Franchise Investment Law, or whether any particular termination or non-renewal was lawful, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: Definition of a "Franchise" Under California Law
clauses.body: California law defines "franchise" in materially the same three-part terms in two separately codified places. Under the Franchise Investment Law, a "franchise" is a contract or agreement, express or implied, oral or written, between two or more persons, by which a franchisee is granted the right to engage in the business of offering, selling, or distributing goods or services under a marketing plan or system prescribed in substantial part by a franchisor; the franchisee's business under that plan or system is substantially associated with the franchisor's trademark, service mark, trade name, or other commercial symbol; and the franchisee is required to pay, directly or indirectly, a franchise fee. The California Franchise Relations Act defines "franchise," for its own separate purposes, in the same three-part terms.
clauses.gap: Cal. Corp. Code § 31005(a) and Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 20001(a)-(c) are two independently numbered sections in two different codes, not subdivisions of the same section — the two citations below are independent of one another, though the operative language is nearly identical. This clause does not restate Corp. Code § 31005(b), which extends "franchise" to certain petroleum-marketing arrangements, or § 31005(c), which excludes certain nonprofit cooperative wholesaling organizations; it does not restate Bus. & Prof. Code § 20001(d), which excludes Petroleum Marketing Practices Act franchises, certain incidental retail lease departments and concessions (under 10% of an establishment's sales), and the same category of nonprofit cooperatives. It also does not address the separate statutory extensions of "franchise" to "area franchise" and "subfranchise" arrangements (Corp. Code § 31010; Bus. & Prof. Code § 20006), or the "franchise fee" definition and its own carve-outs (Corp. Code § 31011; Bus. & Prof. Code § 20007). This clause does not evaluate whether any particular business arrangement meets this definition.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 31005(a)
citations.cite: Franchise Investment Law, definition of "franchise"
citations.quote: “Franchise” means a contract or agreement, either expressed or implied, whether oral or written, between two or more persons by which: (1) A franchisee is granted the right to engage in the business of offering, selling or distributing goods or services under a marketing plan or system prescribed in substantial part by a franchisor; and (2) The operation of the franchisee’s business pursuant to such plan or system is substantially associated with the franchisor’s trademark, service mark, trade name, logotype, advertising or other commercial symbol designating the franchisor or its affiliate; and (3) The franchisee is required to pay, directly or indirectly, a franchise fee.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 20001(a)-(c)
citations.cite: California Franchise Relations Act, definition of "franchise"
citations.quote: “franchise” means a contract or agreement, either expressed or implied, whether oral or written, between two or more persons by which: (a) A franchisee is granted the right to engage in the business of offering, selling or distributing goods or services under a marketing plan or system prescribed in substantial part by a franchisor; and (b) The operation of the franchisee’s business pursuant to that plan or system is substantially associated with the franchisor’s trademark, service mark, trade name, logotype, advertising, or other commercial symbol designating the franchisor or its affiliate; and (c) The franchisee is required to pay, directly or indirectly, a franchise fee.

clauses.title: Pre-Sale Registration Requirement
clauses.body: It is unlawful for any person to offer or sell a franchise in California unless the offer of the franchise has been registered with the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation under the Franchise Investment Law, or is exempted under the law's own exemption provisions.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only Corp. Code § 31110, the operative registration requirement; it does not enumerate the exemptions found in Chapter 1 (Corp. Code §§ 31100-31109.1), which that section itself cross-references, and it does not restate the registration application, escrow, or stop-order process (Corp. Code §§ 31111-31118) or the one-year duration and renewal of an effective registration (Corp. Code §§ 31120-31121). It does not evaluate whether any particular offering is registered, exempt, or otherwise compliant.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 31110
citations.cite: Franchise Investment Law, registration requirement for the offer or sale of a franchise
citations.quote: On and after April 15, 1971, it shall be unlawful for any person to offer or sell any franchise in this state unless the offer of the franchise has been registered under this part or exempted under Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 31100) of this part.

clauses.title: The 14-Day Franchise Disclosure Document Delivery Requirement
clauses.body: Separately from the registration requirement, where a franchise is subject to registration, California law makes it unlawful to sell that franchise without first giving the prospective franchisee a copy of the franchise disclosure document, together with copies of all proposed agreements relating to the sale, at least 14 days before whichever comes first: the prospective franchisee's execution of any binding franchise or other agreement, or the franchisor's receipt of any consideration.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only Corp. Code § 31119(a); it does not restate § 31119(b), which addresses electronic delivery of the disclosure document, or the separate requirements governing the disclosure document's required contents (Corp. Code § 31114) and the registration's effective date (Corp. Code § 31116). It does not evaluate whether any particular disclosure document was timely delivered or complete.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 31119(a)
citations.cite: Franchise Investment Law, the 14-day pre-sale disclosure document requirement
citations.quote: It is unlawful to sell any franchise in this state that is subject to registration under this law without first providing to the prospective franchisee, at least 14 days prior to the execution by the prospective franchisee of any binding franchise or other agreement, or at least 14 days prior to the receipt of any consideration, whichever occurs first, a copy of the franchise disclosure document, together with a copy of all proposed agreements relating to the sale of the franchise.

clauses.title: Good Cause Requirement and the Notice-and-Cure Period for Termination
clauses.body: Except as otherwise provided by the California Franchise Relations Act, a franchisor may not terminate a franchise before the end of its stated term except for good cause. Except for the circumstances the Act treats separately as warranting immediate termination, "good cause" is limited to the franchisee's failure to substantially comply with the lawful requirements the franchise agreement imposes on the franchisee — and only after the franchisor has given the franchisee at least 60 days' advance notice of the termination and a reasonable cure opportunity of no less than 60 days from the date of that notice. The cure period the franchisor must allow is not required to exceed 75 days, unless the franchisor and franchisee separately agree to extend it.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 20020 in full; it is a single section, not a composite of independent sections. It does not restate the separate list, in Bus. & Prof. Code § 20021, of circumstances (such as bankruptcy, abandonment of the business, felony conviction, or repeated noncompliance) under which the Act itself deems immediate termination without a cure opportunity reasonable — those circumstances are an exception to, not a restatement of, the general rule quoted here. It also does not restate the franchisor's post-termination repurchase obligations under Bus. & Prof. Code § 20022. It does not evaluate whether good cause existed, or whether required notice was given, in any particular termination.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 20020
citations.cite: California Franchise Relations Act, good cause requirement and notice-and-cure period for termination
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by this chapter, no franchisor may terminate a franchise prior to the expiration of its term, except for good cause. Except as provided in Section 20021, good cause shall be limited to the failure of the franchisee to substantially comply with the lawful requirements imposed upon the franchisee by the franchise agreement after being given notice at least 60 days in advance of the termination and a reasonable opportunity, which in no event shall be less than 60 days from the date of the notice of noncompliance, to cure the failure. The period to exercise the right to cure shall not exceed 75 days unless there is a separate agreement between the franchisor and franchisee to extend the time.

clauses.title: The 180-Day Notice Requirement for Non-Renewal
clauses.body: As a general rule, a franchisor may not fail to renew a franchise unless the franchisor gives the franchisee at least 180 days' prior written notice of its intention not to renew. California's Franchise Relations Act then attaches that general 180-day notice rule to a further set of conditions that vary depending on the circumstances of the non-renewal.
clauses.gap: The quoted text is the opening clause of Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 20025, which continues into six lettered conditions, (a) through (f) — covering a franchisee's opportunity to sell the business, non-competition covenants, non-renewals that would otherwise qualify as terminations for good cause under §§ 20020-20021, mutual agreement, franchisor withdrawal from a market, and failure to agree on renewal terms — that this clause does not restate. It also does not address § 20026, which permits a franchisor to offer a limited term extension to satisfy the 180-day notice period. This clause does not evaluate whether required notice was given, or which of § 20025's conditions applied, in any particular non-renewal.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 20025
citations.cite: California Franchise Relations Act, the 180-day prior written notice requirement for non-renewal
citations.quote: No franchisor may fail to renew a franchise unless such franchisor provides the franchisee at least 180 days prior written notice of its intention not to renew;

clauses.title: Form and Content of a Notice of Termination or Non-Renewal
clauses.body: Every notice of termination or non-renewal that the California Franchise Relations Act requires must be in writing; must be sent by registered mail, certified mail, other receipted mail, or telegram, or personally delivered, to the franchisee; and must state the franchisor's intent to terminate or not renew the franchise, together with the reasons for it and the effective date of the termination, non-renewal, or expiration.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 20030 in full; it is a single section. The statute does not itself specify how compliance with its delivery methods is proven, and this clause does not address that. It does not evaluate whether any particular notice satisfied these form and content requirements.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 20030
citations.cite: California Franchise Relations Act, form and content requirements for notices of termination or non-renewal
citations.quote: All notices of termination or nonrenewal required by this chapter: (a) Shall be in writing; (b) Shall be posted by registered, certified or other receipted mail, delivered by telegram or personally delivered to the franchisee; and (c) Shall contain a statement of intent to terminate or not renew the franchise: (1) Together with the reasons therefor, and (2) The effective date of such termination or nonrenewal or expiration.

clauses.title: Signature and Certification
clauses.body:
I, {{preparerName}}, certify that I prepared this information sheet as a summary of the Franchise Investment Law (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 31000 et seq.) and the California Franchise Relations Act (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 20000-20043), for informational reference only. This information sheet does not evaluate whether {{companyName}} is a party to a "franchise" as these statutes define it, whether any offer, sale, termination, or non-renewal involving {{companyName}} complied with these statutes, and is not a substitute for consulting a person licensed to practice law in the relevant jurisdiction.

clauses.title: Findings the Court Must Make When Fees Are Requested
clauses.body: Family Code § 2030 states that when a request for attorney's fees and costs is made in a proceeding for dissolution, nullity, or legal separation (or a related proceeding after judgment), the court must make findings on whether an award under that section is appropriate, whether there is a disparity between {{petitionerName}} and {{respondentName}} in access to funds to retain counsel, and whether one of them is able to pay for legal representation of both. If those findings show a disparity in access and in ability to pay, the statute directs the court to make an order awarding attorney's fees and costs. The statute also states that a party who lacks the financial ability to hire an attorney may request, without an attorney, that the court order the other party — if that other party has the financial ability — to pay a reasonable amount so the unrepresented party can retain counsel in a timely manner before the matter proceeds.
clauses.gap: This clause covers Family Code § 2030(a)(2) only — the mandatory-findings requirement and the self-represented-litigant request provision, drawn from two passages within that same paragraph. It does not restate § 2030(a)(1)'s underlying statement of the court's duty to ensure access to legal representation and the income-and-needs standard for ordering fees; that provision is already covered by a separate clause elsewhere in this corpus (in the marital settlement agreement document), and is not re-quoted here to avoid duplicating an existing citation. It does not cover the standard for setting the amount of any award (Family Code § 2032) or the procedural mechanism for requesting a fee order during the pendency of the proceeding (Family Code § 2031); both are addressed in separate clauses. The statute does not itself define 'disparity' numerically, and how a court weighs these findings on any particular record is not stated here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2030(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's mandatory findings when a fee request is made
citations.quote: (2) When a request for attorney’s fees and costs is made, the court shall make findings on whether an award of attorney’s fees and costs under this section is appropriate, whether there is a disparity in access to funds to retain counsel, and whether one party is able to pay for legal representation of both parties. If the findings demonstrate disparity in access and ability to pay, the court shall make an order awarding attorney’s fees and costs.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2030(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a self-represented party's request that the other party fund retaining counsel
citations.quote: A party who lacks the financial ability to hire an attorney may request, as an in pro per litigant, that the court order the other party, if that other party has the financial ability, to pay a reasonable amount to allow the unrepresented party to retain an attorney in a timely manner before proceedings in the matter go forward.

clauses.title: Fees May Predate the Case and Be Modified as It Proceeds
clauses.body: Family Code § 2030(b) states that attorney's fees and costs within that section may be awarded for legal services rendered or costs incurred before or after the proceeding commenced. Family Code § 2030(c) states that the court shall augment or modify an original award of attorney's fees and costs as may be reasonably necessary for the prosecution or defense of the proceeding, or any related proceeding, including after any appeal has concluded.
clauses.gap: This clause covers Family Code § 2030(b) and (c), two adjacent subdivisions of the same statutory section addressed by the mandatory-findings clause above (§ 2030(a)(2)) and, separately elsewhere in this corpus, by a clause covering § 2030(a)(1); none of the three restates another's quoted text. This clause does not state a cap on how many times an award may be augmented, a deadline for seeking augmentation, or the procedural mechanism for requesting an initial or augmented award — the general motion/order-to-show-cause procedure for a pendency-of-proceeding request is addressed in a separate clause covering Family Code § 2031, which by its own terms governs temporary orders during the pendency of the action rather than the post-appeal augmentation authority described here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2030(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: fees may cover services or costs before or after the proceeding commenced
citations.quote: (b) Attorney’s fees and costs within this section may be awarded for legal services rendered or costs incurred before or after the commencement of the proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2030(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's duty to augment or modify an award as the proceeding continues
citations.quote: (c) The court shall augment or modify the original award for attorney’s fees and costs as may be reasonably necessary for the prosecution or defense of the proceeding, or any proceeding related thereto, including after any appeal has been concluded.

clauses.title: The "Just and Reasonable" Standard for Setting a Fee Award
clauses.body: Family Code § 2032(a) states that the court may make an award of attorney's fees and costs under Family Code § 2030 or § 2031 where the making of the award, and the amount of the award, are just and reasonable under the relative circumstances of the respective parties.
clauses.gap: This clause covers Family Code § 2032(a) alone, one subdivision of a section that is independent of, but cross-referenced to, § 2030 and § 2031 (each addressed in separate clauses in this set). It states that the 'just and reasonable' standard governs both whether to award fees and how much to award, but it does not itself list what the 'relative circumstances' are — those factors are stated in § 2032(b), covered in a separate clause. It does not state a formula, percentage, or dollar range for a 'just and reasonable' award, and no case law construing that standard is cited here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2032(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the just-and-reasonable standard for both the award and its amount
citations.quote: (a) The court may make an award of attorney’s fees and costs under Section 2030 or 2031 where the making of the award, and the amount of the award, are just and reasonable under the relative circumstances of the respective parties.

clauses.title: Factors in the "Relative Circumstances" Analysis
clauses.body: Family Code § 2032(b) states that in determining what is just and reasonable under the relative circumstances, the court considers the need for the award to enable each party, to the extent practical, to have sufficient financial resources to present the party's case adequately, taking into consideration, to the extent relevant, the circumstances of the respective parties described in Family Code § 4320. The statute further states that a requesting party's own resources to pay their own attorney's fees and costs are not themselves a bar to an order that the other party pay part or all of the fees and costs requested, and that financial resources are only one factor for the court to consider in apportioning the overall cost of the litigation equitably between the parties under their relative circumstances.
clauses.gap: This clause covers two passages within a single subdivision, Family Code § 2032(b). It cross-references Family Code § 4320 for the circumstances the court considers 'to the extent relevant,' but does not itself quote § 4320's list of factors — § 4320 is a spousal-support statute, and no independent verification of its text was performed for this clause; a reader relying on this clause alone will not see that list. It does not state how much weight any single factor carries relative to the others, or how a court resolves conflicting factors on a particular record.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2032(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the relative-circumstances factors, cross-referencing § 4320
citations.quote: (b) In determining what is just and reasonable under the relative circumstances, the court shall take into consideration the need for the award to enable each party, to the extent practical, to have sufficient financial resources to present the party’s case adequately, taking into consideration, to the extent relevant, the circumstances of the respective parties described in Section 4320.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2032(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a requesting party's own resources are not themselves a bar to an award
citations.quote: The fact that the party requesting an award of attorney’s fees and costs has resources from which the party could pay the party’s own attorney’s fees and costs is not itself a bar to an order that the other party pay part or all of the fees and costs requested. Financial resources are only one factor for the court to consider in determining how to apportion the overall cost of the litigation equitably between the parties under their relative circumstances.

clauses.title: Requesting a Fee Order During the Proceeding: Motion or Order to Show Cause
clauses.body: Family Code § 2031(a)(1) states that, except as provided in § 2031(b), during the pendency of a proceeding for dissolution, nullity, or legal separation (or a related proceeding after judgment), an application for a temporary order making, augmenting, or modifying an award of attorney's fees — including a reasonable retainer to hire an attorney — or costs, or both, is made by motion on notice or by an order to show cause. Family Code § 2031(a)(2) states that the court shall rule on such an application within 15 days of the hearing on the motion or order to show cause. Family Code § 2031(b) states that such an order may instead be made without notice, by an oral motion in open court, at the time of the hearing of the cause on the merits, or at any time before entry of a default judgment under Code of Civil Procedure § 585 or § 586, with the court required to rule on a motion made this way within 15 days and before entry of judgment.
clauses.gap: This clause covers Family Code § 2031(a)(1), (a)(2), and (b) — three subdivisions/paragraphs of the same statutory section, independent of the fee-standard sections addressed in the other clauses in this set (§ 2030 and § 2032). It states the statutory pathways and ruling deadlines for a temporary fee order sought during the proceeding; it does not state what Judicial Council form or local court procedure is used in practice (commonly a Request for Order), does not address a request for fees made otherwise than during the pendency of the action (e.g., at judgment or on appeal, addressed by § 2030(c) in a separate clause), and does not address the cross-referenced Code of Civil Procedure default-judgment provisions beyond citing their section numbers.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2031(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a temporary fee order is sought by noticed motion or order to show cause
citations.quote: (a) (1) Except as provided in subdivision (b), during the pendency of a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, for nullity of marriage, for legal separation of the parties, or any proceeding subsequent to entry of a related judgment, an application for a temporary order making, augmenting, or modifying an award of attorney’s fees, including a reasonable retainer to hire an attorney, or costs or both shall be made by motion on notice or by an order to show cause.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2031(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the 15-day ruling deadline for a noticed motion or order to show cause
citations.quote: (2) The court shall rule on an application within 15 days of the hearing on the motion or order to show cause.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2031(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the without-notice, oral-motion exception and its ruling deadline
citations.quote: (b) An order described in subdivision (a) may be made without notice by an oral motion in open court at either of the following times: (1) At the time of the hearing of the cause on the merits. (2) At any time before entry of judgment against a party whose default has been entered pursuant to Section 585 or 586 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The court shall rule on any motion made pursuant to this subdivision within 15 days and prior to the entry of any judgment.

It is offered under California Probate Code Section 18100.5 to establish the existence of the trust and {{trusteeName}}'s authority to act as trustee, without disclosing the trust's dispositive provisions or other terms not called for by this certification.
