clauses.title: What a Certification of Trust Is — Presented in Lieu of the Trust Instrument
clauses.body: California law gives a trustee a specific alternative to handing over the complete trust instrument when a third party — such as a bank, title company, or escrow — needs to confirm a trust exists and that the trustee has authority to act for it: the trustee may present a certification of trust to any person in lieu of providing a copy of the trust instrument. A certification of trust can be executed on the trustee's own initiative or because the person the trustee is dealing with asked for one, and its function is to establish the existence or terms of the trust without disclosing the trust instrument itself.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory section, Probate Code § 18100.5, subdivision (a). It states only that a certification of trust may be presented in lieu of the trust instrument and how it comes to be executed; it does not itself describe what the certification may or must contain (covered in a separate clause), any protection for a person relying on it, any right to demand excerpts, or any liability provision — those are separate subdivisions of this same section, addressed in other clauses in this document. No case law or secondary authority was consulted; this is the statutory text only.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 18100.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a certification of trust may be presented in lieu of the trust instrument
citations.quote: The trustee may present a certification of trust to any person in lieu of providing a copy of the trust instrument to establish the existence or terms of the trust. A certification of trust may be executed by the trustee voluntarily or at the request of the person with whom the trustee is dealing.

clauses.title: What a Certification of Trust May Contain and What It Must State
clauses.body: The statute lists what a certification of trust may confirm or contain: the existence of the trust and date of execution of the trust instrument; the identity of the settlor or settlors and the currently acting trustee or trustees; the powers of the trustee; the revocability or irrevocability of the trust and the identity of any person holding a power to revoke it; where there are multiple trustees, the signature authority of the trustees — that is, whether all or fewer than all currently acting trustees must sign to exercise various powers; the trust's identification number, whether a Social Security number or an employer identification number; the manner in which title to trust assets should be taken; and the legal description of any interest in real property held in the trust. Beyond that list of optional contents, the statute imposes two things the certification must state: that the trust has not been revoked, modified, or amended in a way that would make the certification's representations incorrect, and that it is being signed by all of the currently acting trustees. The certification must be in the form of an acknowledged declaration signed by all currently acting trustees, and a certification signed by the currently acting trustee may be recorded with the county recorder in the county where all or part of any described real property is located.
clauses.gap: Both citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Probate Code § 18100.5 — subdivision (b) (the eight-item list of permissible contents) and subdivision (c) (the two required statements and execution formalities) — not independent sources. This clause does not cover subdivision (d), which addresses whether excerpts from the trust documents may be attached (covered in a separate clause), nor subdivisions (e) through (i). No case law or secondary authority was consulted; this is the statutory text only. The statute's list in subdivision (b) is phrased as what the certification 'may' confirm or contain, not as a mandatory checklist — only the two statements in subdivision (c) are stated as required.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 18100.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the eight facts or items of information a certification may confirm or contain
citations.quote: The certification of trust may confirm the following facts or contain the following information: (1) The existence of the trust and date of execution of the trust instrument. (2) The identity of the settlor or settlors and the currently acting trustee or trustees of the trust. (3) The powers of the trustee. (4) The revocability or irrevocability of the trust and the identity of any person holding any power to revoke the trust. (5) When there are multiple trustees, the signature authority of the trustees, indicating whether all, or less than all, of the currently acting trustees are required to sign in order to exercise various powers of the trustee. (6) The trust identification number, whether a social security number or an employer identification number. (7) The manner in which title to trust assets should be taken. (8) The legal description of any interest in real property held in the trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 18100.5(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the required statements and the acknowledged-declaration/signature formalities
citations.quote: The certification shall contain a statement that the trust has not been revoked, modified, or amended in any manner which would cause the representations contained in the certification of trust to be incorrect and shall contain a statement that it is being signed by all of the currently acting trustees of the trust. The certification shall be in the form of an acknowledged declaration signed by all currently acting trustees of the trust. The certification signed by the currently acting trustee may be recorded in the office of the county recorder in the county where all or a portion of the real property is located.

clauses.title: Excerpts Are Optional for the Trustee to Include, But a Third Party May Require Them
clauses.body: The statute gives the trustee discretion, not an obligation, to attach source material: a certification of trust may, but is not required to, include excerpts from the original trust documents, any amendments, and any other documents evidencing or pertaining to the succession of successor trustees, and the certification is not required to contain the trust's dispositive provisions — the terms setting out how the trust estate is distributed. That trustee-side discretion is paired with a third-party-side right: a person whose interest is or may be affected by the certification may require the trustee offering or recording it to provide copies of excerpts from the original trust documents, any amendments, and any other documents that designate, evidence, or pertain to the succession of the trustee, or that confer on the trustee the power to act in the pending transaction, or both. The statute is explicit that neither the trustee's discretion nor the third party's right to require excerpts is intended to require or imply an obligation to disclose the trust's dispositive provisions or the entire trust and its amendments.
clauses.gap: Both citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Probate Code § 18100.5 — subdivision (d) (excerpts optional for the trustee, dispositive provisions not required) and subdivision (e) (a person whose interest may be affected may require excerpts evidencing succession or authority) — not independent sources. This clause does not describe what happens if a trustee refuses a proper demand for excerpts under subdivision (e), or how subdivision (e)'s excerpt right interacts with the liability provision in subdivision (h), beyond subdivision (h)'s own text (covered in a separate clause, which quotes subdivision (h)'s express cross-reference to subdivision (e)). No case law or secondary authority was consulted; this is the statutory text only.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 18100.5(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: excerpts are optional for the trustee to include, dispositive provisions are not required
citations.quote: The certification of trust may, but is not required to, include excerpts from the original trust documents, any amendments thereto, and any other documents evidencing or pertaining to the succession of successor trustees. The certification of trust shall not be required to contain the dispositive provisions of the trust which set forth the distribution of the trust estate.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 18100.5(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a person whose interest is or may be affected may require excerpts evidencing succession or authority to act
citations.quote: A person whose interest is, or may be, affected by the certification of trust may require that the trustee offering or recording the certification of trust provide copies of those excerpts from the original trust documents, any amendments thereto, and any other documents which designate, evidence, or pertain to the succession of the trustee or confer upon the trustee the power to act in the pending transaction, or both. Nothing in this section is intended to require or imply an obligation to provide the dispositive provisions of the trust or the entire trust and amendments thereto.

clauses.title: Protection for a Third Party Who Relies on a Certification in Good Faith
clauses.body: The statute protects a person who relies on a certification of trust without knowing better: a person who acts in reliance upon a certification of trust without actual knowledge that the representations contained in it are incorrect is not liable to any person for so acting, and a person without actual knowledge that the certification's facts are incorrect may assume without inquiry that those facts exist — actual knowledge is not inferred merely because the relying person happens to hold a copy of all or part of the trust instrument. That protection extends to the transaction itself: any transaction, and any lien it creates, entered into by the trustee and a person relying on a certification of trust is enforceable against the trust assets, except that if the person has actual knowledge the trustee is acting outside the scope of the trust, the transaction is not enforceable against the trust assets. The statute also preserves a separate channel of accountability: nothing in this reliance protection limits the rights of the trust's beneficiaries against the trustee.
clauses.gap: Both citations are drawn from the same subdivision, Probate Code § 18100.5(f), split into two citation objects because the quoted sentences are not contiguous with each other in this clause's structure — the source text is a single subdivision, not independent statutory sections. This clause does not cover subdivision (g), which states that failing to demand a certification does not itself affect a person's separate protection under Probate Code § 18100 or create a negative inference about good faith — that cross-referenced statute, § 18100, was not independently fetched or verified for this document, so no claim is made here about its content beyond what § 18100.5(g) itself says about it. No case law or secondary authority was consulted; this is the statutory text only.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 18100.5(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no liability for reliance without actual knowledge of incorrect representations; no duty of inquiry
citations.quote: A person who acts in reliance upon a certification of trust without actual knowledge that the representations contained therein are incorrect is not liable to any person for so acting. A person who does not have actual knowledge that the facts contained in the certification of trust are incorrect may assume without inquiry the existence of the facts contained in the certification of trust. Actual knowledge shall not be inferred solely from the fact that a copy of all or part of the trust instrument is held by the person relying upon the trust certification.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 18100.5(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a transaction entered into in reliance on the certification is enforceable against trust assets, absent actual knowledge the trustee exceeded the trust's scope
citations.quote: Any transaction, and any lien created thereby, entered into by the trustee and a person acting in reliance upon a certification of trust shall be enforceable against the trust assets. However, if the person has actual knowledge that the trustee is acting outside the scope of the trust, then the transaction is not enforceable against the trust assets.

clauses.title: Liability for Refusing a Certification and Demanding the Complete Trust Documents in Bad Faith
clauses.body: The statute pairs a non-inference rule with a liability provision aimed at refusals to accept a certification. First, a person's failure to demand a certification of trust does not affect the protection provided to that person under a separate statute, Probate Code § 18100, and no inference about that person's good faith may be drawn from the failure to demand one. Second, and distinctly, the statute creates exposure for a person who insists on more than the certification: except when the demand is made by a beneficiary or arises in litigation concerning the trust, and subject to the third party's excerpt right described elsewhere in this section, a person who demands the trust documents in addition to a certification of trust — to prove facts the certification already sets out to that party's satisfaction — is liable for damages, including attorney's fees, incurred as a result of refusing to accept the certification in lieu of the requested documents, if a court determines that person acted in bad faith in requesting the trust documents.
clauses.gap: Both citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Probate Code § 18100.5 — subdivision (g) (the no-inference rule tied to a separately numbered statute, § 18100, which was not independently fetched or verified here) and subdivision (h) (the bad-faith liability provision) — not independent sources. Liability under subdivision (h) requires a court finding of bad faith in requesting the trust documents; the statute does not define bad faith for this purpose, and this clause does not attempt to supply that definition. Subdivision (h)'s liability provision does not apply when a beneficiary makes the demand, when the demand arises in litigation concerning the trust, or to the extent a person is exercising the excerpt right described in subdivision (e). This document does not separately cover subdivision (i), which addresses recording a certification of trust with the county recorder for real property purposes and the recorder's fee — that subdivision was fetched and verified along with the rest of the section but is not the subject of any clause in this document because it falls outside the topics requested. No case law or secondary authority was consulted; this is the statutory text only.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 18100.5(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: failing to demand a certification does not affect a person's protection under Section 18100, and creates no negative inference about good faith
citations.quote: A person’s failure to demand a certification of trust does not affect the protection provided that person by Section 18100, and no inference as to whether that person has acted in good faith may be drawn from the failure to demand a certification of trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 18100.5(h) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: liability for damages and attorney's fees for a bad-faith demand for the trust documents beyond the certification
citations.quote: Except when requested by a beneficiary or in the context of litigation concerning a trust and subject to the provisions of subdivision (e), any person making a demand for the trust documents in addition to a certification of trust to prove facts set forth in the certification of trust acceptable to the third party shall be liable for damages, including attorney’s fees, incurred as a result of the refusal to accept the certification of trust in lieu of the requested documents if the court determines that the person acted in bad faith in requesting the trust documents.

clauses.title: About This Time Off to Vote Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Time Off to Vote — Information Sheet describes the paid-time-off-to-vote rights created by California Elections Code §§ 14000–14002, part of the "Privileges of Voters" chapter of the Elections Code, as it relates to the working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}. It summarizes selected requirements of that law: the condition under which a voter is entitled to take paid time off work to vote, the two-hour cap and default timing on that paid time, the advance notice an employee must give the employer, and the employer's own duty to post notice of these rights before each statewide election.

Elections Code §§ 14000 through 14002 are not the whole of the "Privileges of Voters" chapter. Section 14003, in the same chapter, addresses a voter's exemption from militia duty on election day — an unrelated subject this document does not cover. Section 14004, added to the same chapter effective January 1, 2020, separately bars an employer from requiring or requesting that an employee bring a vote-by-mail ballot to work or vote it at work; that is a distinct right from the paid-time-off right described here, and this document does not address it.

This information sheet is not itself the notice Elections Code § 14001 requires an employer to post, does not itself determine whether {{employeeName}} has sufficient time to vote outside working hours on any particular election day, and does not determine that any particular policy of {{companyName}}'s is or is not compliant with California law.

clauses.title: Sample Workplace Notice — Time Off to Vote
clauses.body:
The following sample notice is offered to help {{companyName}} satisfy the content Elections Code § 14001 requires — a posted notice "setting forth the provisions of Section 14000" — and is not itself an official state-issued poster:

NOTICE TO EMPLOYEES — TIME OFF TO VOTE

If you do not have sufficient time outside of your working hours to vote at a statewide election, you may, without loss of pay, take off enough working time that, when added to the voting time available outside of working hours, will enable you to vote.

No more than two hours of the time taken off for voting will be without loss of pay. The time off for voting will be only at the beginning or end of your regular working shift, whichever allows the most free time for voting and the least time off from your regular working shift, unless you and {{companyName}} otherwise mutually agree.

If you know or have reason to believe, on the third working day before the election, that you will need time off to vote, you must give {{companyName}} at least two working days' notice that you desire time off for voting.

{{companyName}} will keep this notice posted conspicuously at the place of work, or elsewhere where it can be seen as employees come or go from work, not less than 10 days before every statewide election.

clauses.title: Entitlement to Paid Time Off to Vote
clauses.body: Under California law, if a voter does not have sufficient time outside of working hours to vote at a statewide election, the voter may, without loss of pay, take off enough working time that, when added to the voting time available outside working hours, will enable the voter to vote.
clauses.gap: This is subdivision (a) of Elections Code § 14000. The amount-and-timing clause and the advance-notice clause in this set cite subdivisions (b) and (c) of this SAME section § 14000, not independent statutes; the posting clause cites the genuinely separate § 14001, and the applicability clause cites the genuinely separate § 14002. This clause states only the entitlement condition itself — it does not state the amount of paid time allowed, when it must be taken, or the notice an employee must give, all of which are covered in the other clauses of this set. The statute does not define "sufficient time" or "statewide election"; whether a given employee's schedule leaves sufficient time to vote, and whether a given election is a "statewide election," are questions of fact this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Elec. Code § 14000(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov official text)
citations.cite: California Elections Code, time off to vote — entitlement condition
citations.quote: If a voter does not have sufficient time outside of working hours to vote at a statewide election, the voter may, without loss of pay, take off enough working time that, when added to the voting time available outside of working hours, will enable the voter to vote.

clauses.title: Amount of Paid Voting Time and When It Is Taken
clauses.body: No more than two hours of the time taken off to vote is without loss of pay. That paid time off is taken only at the beginning or end of the regular working shift — whichever allows the most free time for voting and the least time off from the shift — unless the employee and employer otherwise mutually agree.
clauses.gap: This is subdivision (b) of the same Elections Code § 14000 addressed in the entitlement clause and the advance-notice clause in this set, not an independent section. The default timing (start or end of shift) applies only "unless otherwise mutually agreed"; this clause does not state what governs if the employee and employer do not reach such an agreement, and does not say whether time beyond two hours may be taken unpaid. It does not restate the entitlement condition in subdivision (a) or the notice duty in subdivision (c), both addressed in separate clauses.

citations.case: Cal. Elec. Code § 14000(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov official text)
citations.cite: California Elections Code, time off to vote — two-hour paid cap and default timing
citations.quote: No more than two hours of the time taken off for voting shall be without loss of pay. The time off for voting shall be only at the beginning or end of the regular working shift, whichever allows the most free time for voting and the least time off from the regular working shift, unless otherwise mutually agreed.

clauses.title: Advance Notice Required From the Employee
clauses.body: If, on the third working day before election day, the employee knows or has reason to believe that time off will be necessary to be able to vote, the employee must give the employer at least two working days' notice that time off for voting is desired.
clauses.gap: This is subdivision (c) of the same Elections Code § 14000 addressed in the entitlement clause and the amount-and-timing clause in this set, not an independent section. The statute frames the trigger for this duty as the employee's knowledge or reason to believe — as of the third working day before the election — that time off will be necessary, rather than a simple flat two-day-before deadline; this clause does not restate that distinction beyond quoting the statutory language. It does not specify a required form (written or otherwise) for the notice, which the statute does not itself prescribe, and does not state the amount of paid time available (subdivision (b)) or the entitlement condition (subdivision (a)), both addressed in separate clauses.

citations.case: Cal. Elec. Code § 14000(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov official text)
citations.cite: California Elections Code, time off to vote — employee's advance-notice duty
citations.quote: If the employee on the third working day prior to the day of election, knows or has reason to believe that time off will be necessary to be able to vote on election day, the employee shall give the employer at least two working days’ notice that time off for voting is desired, in accordance with this section.

clauses.title: Employer's Workplace Posting Duty
clauses.body: Not less than 10 days before every statewide election, every employer must keep posted conspicuously at the place of work — or, if that is not practicable, elsewhere where it can be seen as employees come or go to their place of work — a notice setting forth the time-off-to-vote provisions described above.
clauses.gap: Elections Code § 14001 is an independent section from § 14000, addressed in the entitlement, amount-and-timing, and advance-notice clauses above; this posting clause does not restate those other clauses' content beyond referencing it collectively. The statute requires the notice to be posted "not less than 10 days before every statewide election" and to "set forth the provisions of Section 14000," but does not prescribe the notice's specific wording, format, or size — a separate drafting clause in this set (the sample workplace notice) offers text intended to satisfy that content requirement, not an official state-issued poster. This clause does not address § 14002's extension of the posting duty to public employers, or § 14004's separate vote-by-mail-ballot provision, both left out of the authority clauses in this set (see the applicability clause below and the purpose clause's discussion of § 14004).

citations.case: Cal. Elec. Code § 14001 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov official text)
citations.cite: California Elections Code, time off to vote — employer's workplace-posting duty
citations.quote: Not less than 10 days before every statewide election, every employer shall keep posted conspicuously at the place of work, if practicable, or elsewhere where it can be seen as employees come or go to their place of work, a notice setting forth the provisions of Section 14000.

clauses.title: Applies to Both Public and Private Employers
clauses.body: The paid-time-off-to-vote entitlement, the advance-notice duty, and the employer's workplace-posting duty apply to all public agencies and their employees, as well as to employers and employees in private industry.
clauses.gap: Elections Code § 14002 is an independent section from § 14000 and § 14001, addressed in no other clause in this set. As amended effective January 1, 2020 (Stats. 2019, Ch. 223 (AB 17)), it extends §§ 14000, 14001, AND 14004 to public agencies and their employees as well as private employers; that same 2019 act added § 14004 to the chapter. This clause does not draft any public-agency-specific variation of these duties, and does not cover § 14004's separate substantive right — which bars an employer from requiring or requesting that an employee bring a vote-by-mail ballot to work or vote it at work — a related but genuinely distinct provision from the time-off-to-vote right covered by this clause set, omitted here rather than folded into this citation.

citations.case: Cal. Elec. Code § 14002 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov official text, as amended by Stats. 2019, Ch. 223 (AB 17), eff. Jan. 1, 2020)
citations.cite: California Elections Code, time off to vote — applies to public and private employers alike
citations.quote: Sections 14000, 14001, and 14004 shall apply to all public agencies and the employees thereof, as well as to employers and employees in private industry.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Live Scan / Department of Justice (DOJ) fingerprint-based criminal history clearance system — a state-administered process distinct from the private consumer-reporting-agency background checks addressed elsewhere in this corpus (federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, California's Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, and California's Fair Chance Act pre-offer inquiry restrictions). Live Scan clearance is required, not merely permitted, for certain licensed or regulated positions, and it is run through the state Department of Justice and, for some requests, the federal Bureau of Investigation, rather than through a private consumer reporting agency. This document states facts about the general statutory framework authorizing fingerprint-based DOJ background checks (Penal Code § 11105.3) and two sector-specific mandates independently verified for this document — childcare facility licensing (Health & Safety Code § 1596.871) and intermediate care facilities for the developmentally disabled (Health & Safety Code § 1265.5) — regarding {{employeeName}}'s prospective role with {{companyName}}. It does not identify every occupation or sector subject to a Live Scan requirement, and it does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} whether Live Scan clearance applies to this particular position or what to do about any particular clearance result.

clauses.title: What Live Scan Is
clauses.body: "Live Scan" refers to the electronic fingerprint-capture technology the California Department of Justice uses to process criminal history background checks, as opposed to older ink-and-paper fingerprint cards. State law describes the Legislature's support for "the use of the fingerprint live-scan technology... for fully automating the processing of fingerprints and other data," a system also referred to as the California Crime Information Intelligence System (CAL-CII). Once live-scan technology is operational for a given licensing program, an individual is required to obtain either a criminal record clearance from the Department of Justice or a criminal record exemption from the relevant state department before that individual's initial presence in the regulated facility or role.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Health & Safety Code § 1522.04(a), which describes live-scan technology in the specific statutory context of community care facility licensing (Health & Safety Code Chapter 3 and related chapters). It does not independently verify that identical live-scan technology or terminology governs every sector that uses DOJ fingerprint-based clearance (for example, licensing under the Business and Professions Code), though "Live Scan" is used as a general term across California licensing programs. It does not describe the fingerprinting hardware, vendor network (e.g., approved Live Scan operator locations), or processing-time standards in any further detail.

citations.case: Health & Safety Code § 1522.04(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1522.04(a)
citations.quote: the Legislature supports the use of the fingerprint live-scan technology, as identified in the long-range plan of the Department of Justice, for fully automating the processing of fingerprints and other data by the year 1999, otherwise known as the California Crime Information Intelligence System (CAL-CII) to be used for applicant fingerprints. Therefore, when live-scan technology is operational, individuals shall be required to obtain either a criminal record clearance from the Department of Justice or a criminal record exemption from the State Department of Social Services, before their initial presence in a community care facility.

clauses.title: General Framework — Penal Code § 11105.3
clauses.body: Penal Code § 11105.3 authorizes a "human resource agency or employer" to request criminal history records from the California Department of Justice for a person who applies for a license, employment, or a volunteer position in which that person would have supervisory or disciplinary power over a minor or any other person under their care. The request covers records of convictions and any arrest pending adjudication involving offenses specified in Welfare & Institutions Code § 15660(a). The Department of Justice furnishes the resulting information to the requesting employer and separately sends a copy of the same information to the applicant.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Penal Code § 11105.3(a) only. Subdivision (a) is narrower than a fully general licensing/employment background-check statute: by its own terms it applies to positions involving supervisory or disciplinary power over a minor or a person under the applicant's care, not to every regulated occupation. Subdivision (d) of the same section states that § 11105.3 does not supersede sector-specific mandatory statutes and lists several — including the childcare and community-care-facility statutes in Health & Safety Code Divisions covered partly by this document's other clauses, and Family Code and Welfare & Institutions Code provisions this document does not independently verify. This clause does not address the definitions in subdivision (f) (e.g., "human resource agency," "employer") in full, the notification-to-parents provisions in subdivision (c), or the confidentiality provisions in subdivision (g).

citations.case: Penal Code § 11105.3(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 11105.3(a)
citations.quote: a human resource agency or an employer may request from the Department of Justice records of all convictions or any arrest pending adjudication involving the offenses specified in subdivision (a) of Section 15660 of the Welfare and Institutions Code of a person who applies for a license, employment, or volunteer position, in which they would have supervisory or disciplinary power over a minor or any person under their care. The department shall furnish the information to the requesting employer and shall also send a copy of the information to the applicant.

clauses.title: The State DOJ Role Versus the Federal FBI Role
clauses.body: A Live Scan request under Penal Code § 11105.3 must include the applicant's fingerprints, which may be taken by the requester itself, along with any other data the Department of Justice specifies. The California Department of Justice is the entity that receives and processes the request. Separately, when a request seeks federal-level criminal history information, the Department of Justice forwards that portion of the request to the Federal Bureau of Investigation to be searched for any record of arrests or convictions. In other sector-specific statutes, this same two-tier structure recurs: fingerprint images and related information are submitted to the Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, through the Department of Justice, for a combined state and federal level criminal offender record information search.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two non-adjacent sentences within the same subdivision, Penal Code § 11105.3(b)(1) — the fingerprint-submission requirement and the federal-forwarding provision — separated in the statutory text by intervening sentences about the request form, fee, and a nonprofit fee exemption (not independently quoted here). The final sentence of this clause's body describing the state-and-federal submission structure in "other sector-specific statutes" paraphrases language independently verified in Health & Safety Code § 1596.871(a)(3)(E) and (c)(1)(A), which this document's childcare-sector clause addresses separately; it is not itself a verified quotation in this clause. This clause does not describe the FBI's own processing timeline, its separate legal authority to maintain records, or federal law (e.g., the FBI's rap-back or Compact Council authorities) governing its recordkeeping.

citations.case: Penal Code § 11105.3(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 11105.3(b)(1)
citations.quote: A request for records under subdivision (a) shall include the applicant’s fingerprints, which may be taken by the requester, and any other data specified by the department.

citations.case: Penal Code § 11105.3(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 11105.3(b)(1)
citations.quote: Requests received by the department for federal level criminal offender record information shall be forwarded to the Federal Bureau of Investigation by the department to be searched for any record of arrests or convictions.

clauses.title: The Applicant's Right to a Copy and to Challenge the Report
clauses.body: Under Penal Code § 11105.3, the human resource agency or employer that receives a Live Scan background screening report must notify the applicant in writing of three specific rights: the right to obtain a copy of the background screening report, including any criminal history records it contains; the right to challenge the accuracy and completeness of any information the report contains; and the right to obtain a determination as to the validity of that challenge before the human resource agency or employer makes a final decision based on the criminal history information.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single sentence, Penal Code § 11105.3(b)(2)(F). It does not describe the procedural mechanics of how a challenge is submitted, to whom, on what timeline, or how "a determination as to the validity of such challenge" is made or by whom — the statutory text quoted here does not specify a process for that determination. It also does not address the separate right, stated in some sector-specific statutes such as Health & Safety Code § 1596.871(i) and § 1265.5(k), for an individual to request a copy of the underlying state or federal criminal offender record information search response directly from the licensing department after a denial; those provisions are independent of § 11105.3(b)(2)(F) and are not quoted in this clause.

citations.case: Penal Code § 11105.3(b)(2)(F) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 11105.3(b)(2)(F)
citations.quote: The human resource agency or employer shall notify the person in writing of their right to obtain a copy of any background screening report, including the criminal history records, if any, contained in the report, to challenge the accuracy and completeness of any information contained in any such report, and to obtain a determination as to the validity of such challenge before a final determination regarding the person is made by the human resource agency or employer reviewing the criminal history information.

clauses.title: Sector Example — Childcare Licensing (Health & Safety Code § 1596.871)
clauses.body: California's Child Day Care Act requires positive fingerprint identification of applicants as a condition of issuing licenses, permits, or certificates of approval to operate or provide direct care services in a childcare center or family childcare home. The statute states the Legislature's intent to require fingerprints of individuals whose contact with child day care facility clients may pose a risk to children's health and safety, and requires an individual to obtain either a criminal record clearance or a criminal record exemption from the State Department of Social Services before that individual's initial presence in a child day care facility. The statute extends this requirement beyond the license applicant to other specified persons — including staff, volunteers, and employees who have contact with the children, subject to certain stated exemptions (for example, for time-limited volunteers directly supervised and not left alone with children).
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the introductory paragraph of Health & Safety Code § 1596.871. Section 1596.871 is lengthy (subdivisions (a) through (j)); this clause does not independently verify the specific disqualifying-conviction list in subdivision (a)(1), the exemption criteria and procedure in subdivision (f), the civil-penalty amounts and timelines in subdivision (c), or the fingerprint-clearance transfer provisions in subdivision (h). Health & Safety Code § 1596.871 is one of several statutes Penal Code § 11105.3(d) cross-references as a mandatory statute that § 11105.3 does not supersede; this document treats § 1596.871 as an independent, sector-specific example rather than as a subdivision of § 11105.3.

citations.case: Health & Safety Code § 1596.871 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1596.871
citations.quote: The Legislature recognizes the need to generate timely and accurate positive fingerprint identification of applicants as a condition of issuing licenses, permits, or certificates of approval for persons to operate or provide direct care services in a childcare center or family childcare home. It is the intent of the Legislature in enacting this section to require the fingerprints of those individuals whose contact with child day care facility clients may pose a risk to the children’s health and safety. An individual shall be required to obtain either a criminal record clearance or a criminal record exemption from the State Department of Social Services before the individual’s initial presence in a child day care facility.

clauses.title: Sector Example — Intermediate Care Facilities for the Developmentally Disabled (Health & Safety Code § 1265.5)
clauses.body: Health & Safety Code § 1265.5 requires a Department of Justice fingerprint-based criminal record clearance before licensure, renewal, or hiring of direct care staff at an intermediate care facility for the developmentally disabled (several license subtypes, including habilitative, nursing, and continuous-nursing facilities). Before initial licensure or renewal of such a facility, or upon hiring of its direct care staff, the licensing department must secure Department of Justice criminal offender record information to determine whether the applicant, facility administrator or manager, any direct care staff, or any other adult living in the same location has ever been convicted of a crime other than a minor traffic violation.
clauses.gap: Section 1265.5's title places it in the Health Facilities chapter of the Health & Safety Code's licensing division, but its actual scope, as verified from the fetched text, is narrower than "healthcare facilities" generally: by its own terms it applies specifically to intermediate care facilities for the developmentally disabled (the ICF/DD license subtypes listed in subdivision (a)(1)), not to hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, or other health facility types licensed under the same chapter. This document does not verify whether a separate, differently-numbered statute imposes an equivalent Live Scan mandate on hospitals or other general acute care facilities, and it should not be read as a general statement about all healthcare licensure. This clause also does not address the specific disqualifying-conviction list in subdivision (b), the good-character/rehabilitation factors in subdivision (c), or the AFL (All Facilities Letter) processing-standard mechanism in subdivision (a)(3).

citations.case: Health & Safety Code § 1265.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1265.5(a)(1)
citations.quote: the department shall secure from the Department of Justice criminal offender record information to determine whether the applicant, facility administrator or manager, any direct care staff, or any other adult living in the same location, has ever been convicted of a crime other than a minor traffic violation.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) Employer Pull Notice (EPN) Program, a driving-record monitoring system established under Vehicle Code section 1808.1, in connection with {{companyName}}'s employment of {{employeeName}} in the position of {{jobTitle}} with a start date of {{startDate}}. It summarizes selected requirements of that statute. It is not a substitute for {{companyName}}'s own enrollment paperwork with the DMV's Pull Notice Program, and it does not state whether {{employeeName}}'s particular position in fact falls within the statute's scope, which depends on the vehicle and license class or certificate the position requires.

clauses.title: What the Pull-Notice System Is
clauses.body: California law defines a "pull-notice system" as a process for providing an enrolled employer with a report showing a covered driver's current public driving record as recorded by the department, plus any subsequent convictions, failures to appear, accidents, driver's license suspensions, driver's license revocations, or other actions taken against the driving privilege or certificate that are added to the driver's record while the employer's notification request remains active — without the employer having to separately request a new record each time. Participation means the employer obtains a requester code from the department and enrolls its covered drivers under that code.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (b) of Vehicle Code section 1808.1 only. The pre-hire report duty (subdivision (a)) and the periodic-report duty (subdivision (c)) are separate obligations within the same section, covered in other clauses in this set rather than here. This clause does not cover the enrollment fee the department may charge (subdivision (h)), or the department's own procedures for issuing a requester code, which the statute does not itself spell out. Separately: the statute's text, as fetched and reviewed for this clause set, does not state that the employer must obtain the employee's consent, or give the employee notice, before enrolling them in the pull-notice system or before obtaining the driving-record reports described in this and the related clauses below. That absence is reported as a research finding about the text of this one statute, not as a conclusion that no consent or notice obligation exists anywhere in California or federal law (for example, under general privacy statutes) — that broader question was not researched for this clause set.

citations.case: Cal. Veh. Code § 1808.1(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Vehicle Code, pull-notice system defined
citations.quote: The employer of a driver who drives a vehicle specified in subdivision (k) shall participate in a pull-notice system, which is a process for the purpose of providing the employer with a report showing the driver’s current public record as recorded by the department, and any subsequent convictions, failures to appear, accidents, driver’s license suspensions, driver’s license revocations, or any other actions taken against the driving privilege or certificate, added to the driver’s record while the employer’s notification request remains valid and uncanceled. As used in this section, participation in the pull-notice system means obtaining a requester code and enrolling all employed drivers who drive a vehicle specified in subdivision (k) under that requester code.

clauses.title: Which Vehicles Trigger the Participation Requirement
clauses.body: The pull-notice participation duty applies only to the employer of a driver who operates a vehicle for which the driver is required to hold a class A or class B driver's license, a class C license with certain endorsements, or one of several specified certificates, or who drives certain small passenger vehicles operated for compensation under a charter-party or passenger-stage authority or as a permitted taxicab. An employer whose employees do not drive a vehicle within this defined scope is not brought within the pull-notice requirement by this statute.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (k) of Vehicle Code section 1808.1 only, which defines scope by cross-referencing several other Vehicle Code license and certificate provisions (Sections 15278, 12814.7, 12517, 12519, 12520, 12523, 12523.5, 12527, and 53075.5 of the Government Code); those cross-referenced sections were not independently fetched or verified for this clause set, so this clause states the scope in the general terms subdivision (k) itself uses rather than reciting the detail of each cross-referenced license or certificate type. It also does not cover subdivision (j)'s narrower rule for a "casual driver" (one employed less than 30 days in the preceding six months), or subdivision (m)'s extension of the same obligations to a motor carrier that contracts with a person to drive a covered vehicle it owns or leases. Genuine correction to this brief's premise: Vehicle Code section 12804.6 was fetched and reviewed, and it does connect to the pull-notice system — it provides that a transit busdriver's certificate status becomes part of the pull-notice and periodic reports issued under this section — but it does not itself impose a separate employer mandatory-enrollment duty; it is not cited here because it does not independently expand who must enroll. Vehicle Code section 13369 was also fetched and reviewed, and it is not an enrollment-trigger statute at all: it sets the department's own criteria for refusing, suspending, or revoking specified driver certificates and endorsements (passenger transportation, hazardous materials, schoolbus, and similar categories) based on a driving record; it does not impose or expand any employer pull-notice enrollment obligation, so it is omitted from this clause set as not actually on point.

citations.case: Cal. Veh. Code § 1808.1(k) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Vehicle Code, vehicles and license classes within scope
citations.quote: This section applies to a vehicle for the operation of which the driver is required to have a class A or class B driver’s license, a class C license with any endorsement issued pursuant to Section 15278, a class C license issued pursuant to Section 12814.7, or a certificate issued pursuant to Section 12517, 12519, 12520, 12523, 12523.5, or 12527, a passenger vehicle having a seating capacity of not more than 10 persons, including the driver, operated for compensation by a charter-party carrier of passengers or passenger stage corporation pursuant to a certificate of public convenience and necessity or a permit issued by the Public Utilities Commission, or a permitted taxicab company as described in Section 53075.5 of the Government Code.

clauses.title: Pre-Hire Driving Record Report
clauses.body: Before employing a driver to operate a vehicle within the program's scope, a prospective employer must obtain a report showing that driver's current public driving record as recorded by the department. A report is treated as current only if it was issued less than 30 days before the date the employer employs the driver.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (a) of Vehicle Code section 1808.1 only. It does not cover that same subdivision's further requirements that the report be reviewed, signed, and dated by the employer, maintained at the employer's place of business until the pull-notice report described elsewhere in the section is received, and presented on request to an authorized California Highway Patrol representative — those requirements exist in the statute but are not quoted here. It also does not cover the different, longer six-month currency period that subdivision (j) sets for a "casual driver."

citations.case: Cal. Veh. Code § 1808.1(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Vehicle Code, pre-hire driving record report
citations.quote: The prospective employer of a driver who drives a vehicle specified in subdivision (k) shall obtain a report showing the driver’s current public record as recorded by the department. For purposes of this subdivision, a report is current if it was issued less than 30 days before the date the employer employs the driver.

clauses.title: Periodic Driving Record Report
clauses.body: Beyond the pre-hire report, an employer of a driver who operates a vehicle within the program's scope must obtain a periodic report from the department at least every 12 months, and must use it to verify that the employee's driver's license has not been suspended or revoked, the employee's traffic-violation point count, and whether the employee has been convicted of a violation of Vehicle Code section 23152 or 23153 (driving under the influence).
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (c) of Vehicle Code section 1808.1 only. It does not cover that same subdivision's further requirements that the report be signed and dated by the employer, maintained at the employer's principal place of business, and presented on demand to an authorized California Highway Patrol representative. It also does not cover subdivision (i), under which the department may, when feasible, establish an automatic mail or electronic delivery procedure for these periodic reports without the employer making individual requests.

citations.case: Cal. Veh. Code § 1808.1(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Vehicle Code, periodic driving record report
citations.quote: The employer of a driver of a vehicle specified in subdivision (k) shall, additionally, obtain a periodic report from the department at least every 12 months. The employer shall verify that each employee’s driver’s license has not been suspended or revoked, the employee’s traffic violation point count, and whether the employee has been convicted of a violation of Section 23152 or 23153.

clauses.title: Discontinuing Enrollment When Employment Ends
clauses.body: When a driver's employment ends, the employer must notify the department to discontinue that driver's enrollment in the pull-notice system.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (d) of Vehicle Code section 1808.1 only, a single sentence that is the entirety of that subdivision. It does not address whether or how enrollment must be adjusted for reasons other than termination of employment altogether (for example, a driver's reassignment to a role that no longer involves operating a covered vehicle), which this subdivision does not itself speak to. It also does not describe the department's own procedure for processing a discontinuation notice, which the statute does not specify.

citations.case: Cal. Veh. Code § 1808.1(d) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Vehicle Code, discontinuing pull-notice enrollment
citations.quote: Upon the termination of a driver’s employment, the employer shall notify the department to discontinue the driver’s enrollment in the pull-notice system.

clauses.title: Who This Leave Applies To
clauses.body: California's organ and bone marrow donor leave law, codified at Labor Code §§ 1508-1513 and titled the Michelle Maykin Memorial Donation Protection Act, applies to an "employer," defined for purposes of this part as "any person, partnership, corporation, association, or other business entity that employs 15 or more employees." "Employee" and "employee benefits" carry the same meanings given those terms in Labor Code § 1501, a different statute in this same code that this clause does not independently analyze.
clauses.gap: This is one state statute, used as evidence of California's own organ and bone marrow donor leave coverage threshold — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific workplace, and not a comparison to any other leave law's own coverage threshold (this corpus's separate FMLA and CFRA documents describe those laws' own, different thresholds). Both citations here are subdivisions of a single statutory section, § 1509 (subdivisions (a) and (b)) — not two independent sources. This clause does not itself state or cross-reference the definitions actually found at Labor Code § 1501; it reports only that § 1509 borrows them by reference. This document is informational: it does not determine whether any specific employer meets or falls short of the 15-employee threshold.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1509(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Employer” means any person, partnership, corporation, association, or other business entity that employs 15 or more employees.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1509(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Employee” and “employee benefits” have the same meanings set forth in Section 1501.

clauses.title: The Leave Entitlement
clauses.body: Subject to a written-verification requirement described elsewhere in this statute, a covered employer must grant a covered employee two distinct paid leaves. The first: "A leave of absence, not exceeding 30 business days in a one-year period, to an employee who is an organ donor, for the purpose of donating the employee’s organ to another person." The second: "A leave of absence, not exceeding five business days in a one-year period, to an employee who is a bone marrow donor, for the purpose of donating the employee’s bone marrow to another person." Beyond that paid organ-donation leave, the statute separately requires the employer to grant an additional unpaid leave of absence, not exceeding 30 business days in a one-year period, to an employee who is an organ donor, for the purpose of donating the employee’s organ to another person. In each instance, the one-year period is measured from the date the employee’s leave begins and consists of 12 consecutive months.
clauses.gap: This is one state statute, used as evidence of the specific day-amounts and paid/unpaid character of California's organ and bone marrow donor leave — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific leave, and not a claim that a particular employee currently qualifies. All three citations here are subdivisions of one statutory section, § 1510 (subdivisions (a)(1), (a)(2), and (b)) — not three independent sources. This clause does not address the separate written-verification/medical-necessity condition on receiving this leave, the separate rule against running this leave concurrently with FMLA or CFRA leave, or the separate rule letting an employer require use of accrued sick leave, vacation, or paid time off as a condition of the leave's initial receipt — each addressed in other clauses. Nor does it address whether or how the 30-business-day paid organ leave and the additional 30-business-day unpaid organ leave interact with each other in practice; the statute states them as two distinct grants without further elaboration in the text quoted here.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1510(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A leave of absence, not exceeding 30 business days in a one-year period, to an employee who is an organ donor, for the purpose of donating the employee’s organ to another person.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1510(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A leave of absence, not exceeding five business days in a one-year period, to an employee who is a bone marrow donor, for the purpose of donating the employee’s bone marrow to another person.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1510(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: an employer shall grant an additional unpaid leave of absence, not exceeding 30 business days in a one-year period, to an employee who is an organ donor, for the purpose of donating the employee’s organ to another person.

clauses.title: Verification and Use of Accrued Leave
clauses.body: To receive either the paid organ or bone marrow donation leave, or the additional unpaid organ donation leave, described in this statute, an employee "shall provide written verification to the employer that the employee is an organ or bone marrow donor and that there is a medical necessity for the donation of the organ or bone marrow." Separately, the statute allows an employer to require, as a condition of an employee's initial receipt of bone marrow or organ donation leave, that the employee first use a stated amount of earned but unused paid leave: "up to five days of earned but unused sick leave, vacation, or paid time off for bone marrow donation and up to two weeks of earned but unused sick leave, vacation, or paid time off for organ donation, unless doing so would violate the provisions of any applicable collective bargaining agreement."
clauses.gap: This is one state statute, used as evidence of California's own written-verification condition and its own accrued-leave-use option for this specific leave — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific request, and not a description of any particular employer's actual verification form or practice. Both citations here are subdivisions of a single statutory section, § 1510 (subdivisions (c) and (g)) — not two independent sources. The statute's own text does not specify who must supply the written verification (the employee's own statement, a treating or transplant physician, or some other source) or what "medical necessity" documentation must contain beyond the quoted language; this clause does not fill that gap. This clause also does not address whether an employer that requires use of accrued leave under subdivision (g) must still separately pay the statutory 30-business-day organ or five-business-day bone marrow leave described elsewhere once accrued leave is exhausted; the statute states both provisions without describing how they offset against each other beyond the caps quoted here.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1510(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: In order to receive a leave of absence pursuant to subdivision (a) or (b) an employee shall provide written verification to the employer that the employee is an organ or bone marrow donor and that there is a medical necessity for the donation of the organ or bone marrow.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1510(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: An employer may require, as a condition of an employee’s initial receipt of bone marrow or organ donation leave, that an employee take up to five days of earned but unused sick leave, vacation, or paid time off for bone marrow donation and up to two weeks of earned but unused sick leave, vacation, or paid time off for organ donation, unless doing so would violate the provisions of any applicable collective bargaining agreement.

clauses.title: Relationship to FMLA and CFRA Leave
clauses.body: This statute states its own, separate rule for how organ and bone marrow donation leave relates to leave taken under the federal Family and Medical Leave Act or California's own family-leave statute: "Notwithstanding existing law, bone marrow and organ donation leave shall not be taken concurrently with any leave taken pursuant to the federal Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 (29 U.S.C. Sec. 2601 et seq.) or the Moore-Brown-Roberti Family Rights Act (Sections 12945.2 and 19702.3 of the Government Code)." The statute names the California Family Rights Act by its formal statutory title, the Moore-Brown-Roberti Family Rights Act, and cites it as Government Code §§ 12945.2 and 19702.3.
clauses.gap: This is one state statute, used as evidence of California's own no-concurrent-running rule for this specific leave — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a restatement of the separate rule (found in a different statute) describing how FMLA and CFRA leave run together with each other. This corpus's own, separate CFRA document describes that different concurrency rule between FMLA and CFRA; this clause addresses only organ/bone marrow donation leave's relationship to those two other leaves, not their relationship to each other. This clause quotes a single subdivision of a single statutory section, § 1510(h); no additional independent source was found for this specific rule. The statute's own text does not further explain the mechanical consequence of "shall not be taken concurrently" — for example, whether it means the leaves must be taken in sequence, or only that time on one leave is not counted against the days available under the other; this clause reports the statute's own words without resolving that question.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1510(h) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding existing law, bone marrow and organ donation leave shall not be taken concurrently with any leave taken pursuant to the federal Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 (29 U.S.C. Sec. 2601 et seq.) or the Moore-Brown-Roberti Family Rights Act (Sections 12945.2 and 19702.3 of the Government Code).

clauses.title: Reinstatement After Leave
clauses.body: On the expiration of leave taken under this statute, the employer's reinstatement obligation is stated as follows: "An employer shall, upon expiration of a leave authorized by this part, restore an employee to the position held by him or her when the leave began or to a position with equivalent seniority status, employee benefits, pay, and other terms and conditions of employment." That obligation has a stated limit: "An employer may decline to restore an employee as required in this section because of conditions unrelated to the exercise of rights under this part by the employee."
clauses.gap: This is one state statute, used as evidence of California's own reinstatement rule for this specific leave — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reinstatement decision, and not a claim that any particular employer's stated reason for declining to restore an employee is, or is not, "unrelated to the exercise of rights under this part." This clause quotes the two sentences of a single statutory section, § 1511, in full; no additional independent source was found for this rule. The statute does not define "conditions unrelated to the exercise of rights under this part" beyond that phrase itself, and this clause does not attempt to define it further. Separately, Labor Code § 1510(d) — not quoted in this clause — addresses continuity of service and, during paid organ-donation leave, continued group health plan coverage; this clause does not restate that provision.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1511 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: An employer shall, upon expiration of a leave authorized by this part, restore an employee to the position held by him or her when the leave began or to a position with equivalent seniority status, employee benefits, pay, and other terms and conditions of employment.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1511 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: An employer may decline to restore an employee as required in this section because of conditions unrelated to the exercise of rights under this part by the employee.

clauses.title: Protection Against Interference and Retaliation
clauses.body: This statute states its own, separate prohibitions on interference and retaliation. On interference: "An employer shall not interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise or the attempt to exercise a right established by this part." On retaliation: "An employer shall not discharge, fine, suspend, expel, discipline, or in any other manner discriminate against an employee who does either of the following: (1) Exercises a right provided under this part. (2) Opposes a practice made unlawful by this part."
clauses.gap: This is one state statute, used as evidence of California's own interference and anti-retaliation rules for this specific leave — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific dispute, and not a claim that any specific employer action against any specific employee did or did not violate this statute. Both citations here are subdivisions of a single statutory section, § 1512 (subdivisions (a) and (b)) — not two independent sources. This clause does not describe the separate enforcement mechanism the same statutory part provides — Labor Code § 1513, not quoted here, allows an employee to bring a civil action in superior court and lets the court order equitable relief — nor any deadline, damages, or procedure that might apply to such an action.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Declaration and Scope of This Golden Parachute Excise Tax Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Golden Parachute Excise Tax Information Sheet is prepared with respect to compensation paid or payable to {{employeeName}} by {{companyName}} in connection with a change in ownership or control of {{companyName}} occurring on or about {{changeInControlDate}}. It describes what federal tax law, at 26 U.S.C. §§ 280G and 4999, calls a "parachute payment": compensation contingent on a change in control that, in the aggregate, equals or exceeds three times an individual's base amount. It states the two separate federal tax consequences the statute attaches once that threshold is crossed — loss of {{companyName}}'s federal income tax deduction for the excess portion, and a 20% federal excise tax owed by {{employeeName}} on that same excess portion, in addition to regular federal income tax — and the shareholder-approval exception available to certain corporations whose stock is not publicly traded. This document states facts about how federal tax law defines and treats parachute payments in general; it does not calculate {{employeeName}}'s base amount, determine whether any specific payment is or is not a parachute payment, or state what {{employeeName}} or {{companyName}} should do about their situation.

clauses.title: "Parachute Payment" Defined: Compensation Contingent on a Change in Control
clauses.body: Federal tax law defines a “parachute payment,” for purposes of the golden parachute excise tax rules, as any payment in the nature of compensation to or for the benefit of a “disqualified individual” that meets two conditions: the payment must be contingent on a change in the ownership or effective control of the corporation, or in the ownership of a substantial portion of the corporation's assets, and the aggregate present value of all such contingent payments to that individual must equal or exceed a threshold tied to the individual's base amount. A separate provision of the same statute also treats certain payments made pursuant to an agreement entered into within one year before the change in control as presumptively contingent on that change, unless the contrary is established by clear and convincing evidence.
clauses.gap: This clause and the goldenparachute_three_times_base_amount_threshold clause both cite subdivisions of the same statutory section, 26 U.S.C. § 280G(b)(2) — they are not independent sources of each other. This clause states only the general definitional test in § 280G(b)(2)(A); it does not cover the separate statutory inclusion for payments made in violation of securities laws (§ 280G(b)(2)(B)), the one-year-agreement presumption's exact operation (§ 280G(b)(2)(C)), or the exemptions for reasonable compensation, small business corporations, or qualified retirement plans (§ 280G(b)(4)-(6)), each of which can remove a payment from “parachute payment” treatment even where this general test is met. It does not determine whether any specific payment to the individual named in this document meets this definition.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 280G(b)(2)(A) (Golden parachute payments — parachute payment defined)
citations.quote: The term “ parachute payment ” means any payment in the nature of compensation to (or for the benefit of) a disqualified individual if—

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 280G(b)(2)(A)(i) (Golden parachute payments — change in control condition)
citations.quote: such payment is contingent on a change— (I) in the ownership or effective control of the corporation, or (II) in the ownership of a substantial portion of the assets of the corporation, and

clauses.title: "Disqualified Individual" Defined
clauses.body: The golden parachute excise tax rules apply only to payments to a “disqualified individual.” Federal tax law defines that term as an employee, independent contractor, or other person specified in regulations who performs personal services for a corporation, and who is an officer, a shareholder, or a “highly-compensated individual” of that corporation. The statute further limits “highly-compensated individual” to a person who is (or would be, if an employee) among the highest-paid 1 percent of the corporation's employees, or the highest-paid 250 employees if that number is smaller.
clauses.gap: This clause covers only the general definition in 26 U.S.C. § 280G(c); it does not address the statute's separate treatment of personal service corporations as individuals, or of members of an affiliated group as a single corporation for these purposes (§ 280G(d)(5)), and it does not determine whether the individual named in this document in fact qualifies as an officer, shareholder, or highly-compensated individual of the corporation named in this document.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 280G(c) (Golden parachute payments — disqualified individuals)
citations.quote: an employee, independent contractor, or other person specified in regulations by the Secretary who performs personal services for any corporation, and

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 280G(c)(2) (Golden parachute payments — disqualified individual, officer/shareholder/highly-compensated)
citations.quote: is an officer, shareholder, or highly-compensated individual

clauses.title: The 3-Times-Base-Amount Threshold
clauses.body: A payment is treated as a parachute payment only if the aggregate present value of all payments in the nature of compensation to the disqualified individual that are contingent on the change in control equals or exceeds an amount equal to three times the individual's “base amount.” Federal tax law defines “base amount” as the individual's annualized includible compensation for the base period, which the statute separately defines as the individual's average annual compensation includible in gross income over the most recent five taxable years ending before the change in control (or the portion of that period during which the individual performed services for the corporation).
clauses.gap: This clause and the goldenparachute_parachute_payment_defined clause both cite subdivisions of the same statutory section, 26 U.S.C. § 280G(b) — they are not independent sources of each other. This clause states the 3-times-base-amount threshold and the base-amount definition itself; it does not cover the statute's present-value discount-rate rule (§ 280G(b)(4), applying a rate equal to 120 percent of the applicable federal rate), the rules for allocating base amount across multiple payments (§ 280G(b)(3)(B)), or the base period's own special rules (§ 280G(d)(1)-(2)). It does not calculate the base amount of the individual named in this document, or state whether any payment amount stated in this document in fact equals or exceeds three times it.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 280G(b)(2)(A)(ii) (Golden parachute payments — 3-times-base-amount threshold)
citations.quote: the aggregate present value of the payments in the nature of compensation to (or for the benefit of) such individual which are contingent on such change equals or exceeds an amount equal to 3 times the base amount

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 280G(b)(3)(A) (Golden parachute payments — base amount defined)
citations.quote: The term “ base amount ” means the individual’s annualized includible compensation for the base period .

clauses.title: The Two Consequences: No Employer Deduction, and a 20% Employee Excise Tax
clauses.body: Once a payment is an “excess parachute payment” — generally, the portion of a parachute payment above the share of the base amount allocated to it — federal tax law imposes two separate consequences. First, the paying corporation may not deduct the excess parachute payment as a business expense: no deduction is allowed under the relevant chapter of the Internal Revenue Code for any excess parachute payment. Second, and independently, the individual who receives the excess parachute payment owes a federal excise tax equal to 20 percent of the amount of that payment, imposed in addition to the individual's regular federal income tax on the same amount. The statute defines “excess parachute payment,” for purposes of this 20 percent excise tax, by cross-reference to the deduction-denial section's own definition of that term.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two genuinely independent sections of the Internal Revenue Code: 26 U.S.C. § 280G(a), which denies the employer's deduction, and 26 U.S.C. § 4999(a) and (b), which impose the employee's excise tax and define its base by cross-reference to § 280G(b). It does not restate § 280G(b)'s own definition of “excess parachute payment” (covered in the goldenparachute_three_times_base_amount_threshold clause) and does not cover § 4999(c)'s separate withholding rule for excess parachute payments that are wages, or how the 20 percent excise tax interacts with any other federal or state tax owed on the same income. It does not state whether any payment amount stated in this document is in fact an excess parachute payment.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 280G(a) (Golden parachute payments — general rule, no deduction)
citations.quote: No deduction shall be allowed under this chapter for any excess parachute payment .

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 4999(a) (Golden parachute payments — imposition of 20% excise tax)
citations.quote: There is hereby imposed on any person who receives an excess parachute payment a tax equal to 20 percent of the amount of such payment.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 4999(b) (Golden parachute payments — excess parachute payment defined by cross-reference)
citations.quote: the term “ excess parachute payment ” has the meaning given to such term by section 280G(b).

clauses.title: Shareholder-Approval Exception for Certain Closely-Held Corporations
clauses.body: Federal tax law excludes certain payments from “parachute payment” treatment altogether for corporations whose stock is not publicly traded. Where, immediately before the change in control, no stock in the corporation was readily tradeable on an established securities market or otherwise, a payment to a disqualified individual falls outside the parachute-payment rules if the corporation's shareholders approve it under the statute's shareholder approval requirements. Those requirements are met if the payment was approved by a vote of the persons who owned, immediately before the change in control, more than 75 percent of the voting power of all outstanding stock of the corporation, and if there was adequate disclosure to shareholders of all material facts concerning all payments that would, but for this exception, be parachute payments to that disqualified individual.
clauses.gap: This clause cites subdivisions of the same statutory section as the other clauses in this document, 26 U.S.C. § 280G(b)(5) — it is not an independent source of them. It covers only the closely-held-corporation branch of the exception in § 280G(b)(5)(A)(ii)-(B); it does not cover the separate, unconditional exemption for small business corporations under § 280G(b)(5)(A)(i) (corporations meeting the S corporation ownership-and-structure requirements of § 1361(b)), the Treasury regulatory authority referenced in § 280G(b)(5)(A) to disregard certain indirect public tradeability, or the qualified-plan exemption in § 280G(b)(6). It does not determine whether the corporation named in this document's stock was, in fact, readily tradeable on an established securities market immediately before the change in control described in this document, or whether any shareholder vote meeting these requirements actually occurred.
