Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}} on behalf of {{businessName}}, states what California's Business and Professions Code §§ 22757–22757.6 (the California AI Transparency Act, enacted as Senate Bill 942 and substantially amended by Assembly Bill 853) and California's Civil Code §§ 3110–3111 (the Artificial Intelligence Training Data Transparency Act, enacted as Assembly Bill 2013) provide about disclosing that image, video, or audio content was created or altered by generative artificial intelligence, making an AI-detection tool available, and publicly posting documentation about training data. These are two separate statutes in two separate codes. This sheet states what each statute's own text says; it does not evaluate whether any particular product, system, or business practice of {{businessName}} complies with either statute, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: The AI Transparency Act: Who Is a "Covered Provider," and What Is a "GenAI System"
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 22757 states that Chapter 25 of Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code — which the statute's own text calls the California AI Transparency Act — became operative on August 2, 2026. Section 22757.1(d) defines a "covered provider," the category of business subject to the Act's detection-tool and disclosure duties, as a person that creates, codes, or otherwise produces a generative artificial intelligence system that has over 1,000,000 monthly visitors or users and is publicly accessible within California's geographic boundaries. Section 22757.1(f) defines the "generative artificial intelligence system" or "GenAI system" a covered provider must produce as an artificial intelligence that can generate derived synthetic content — including text, images, video, and audio — that emulates the structure and characteristics of the system's training data.
clauses.gap: § 22757 is an independently numbered section from § 22757.1; the two subdivisions of § 22757.1 quoted here — (d) and (f) — are part of the same statutory section and are not independent sources of authority from one another, and that section also separately defines "large online platform" (a different, 2,000,000-unique-monthly-user category, per § 22757.1(h), that carries its own obligations this sheet does not address), "capture device manufacturer," "manifest," "latent," and "provenance data," none of which is restated here beyond what the later clauses below use. This is very recently operative law — the chapter was added in 2024 (SB 942) and substantially amended in 2025 by AB 853, which is what moved its operative date to August 2, 2026 — and may see further amendment; this sheet does not track amendments after the checked date above. This sheet does not determine whether any particular product or business meets the 1,000,000-monthly-visitor threshold.

clauses.title: The AI Transparency Act: Required AI Detection Tool
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 22757.2(a) requires a covered provider to make available an AI detection tool, at no cost to the user, that allows a user to assess whether image, video, or audio content — or content that is any combination of those — was created or altered by the covered provider's GenAI system. The same subdivision's paragraphs (2) and (3) state what the tool's output must and must not contain: the tool outputs any system provenance data detected in the content, but the tool does not output any personal provenance data detected in the content. The statute's own text separately requires the tool to be publicly accessible (subject to reasonable security-related access limitations), to accept an uploaded file or a URL, and to support an API that allows use without visiting the covered provider's website.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory subdivision, § 22757.2(a), and are not independent of one another; this clause does not restate every one of paragraphs (1) through (6), including the API and public-accessibility requirements described in this clause's body without a citation. This sheet does not separately address § 22757.2(b)'s user-feedback-collection duty or § 22757.2(c)'s limits on the covered provider's own collection and retention of personal information and content submitted to the tool, both of which are part of the same section. This is very recently operative law that may see further amendment.

citations.quote: A covered provider shall make available an AI detection tool at no cost to the user that meets all of the following criteria: (1) The tool allows a user to assess whether image, video, or audio content, or content that is any combination thereof, was created or altered by the covered provider’s GenAI system.

clauses.title: The AI Transparency Act: Manifest and Latent Content Disclosures
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 22757.3(a) requires a covered provider to offer the user the option to include a manifest disclosure — one that identifies content as AI-generated content — in image, video, or audio content that the covered provider's GenAI system created or altered, and states that this disclosure must be clear, conspicuous, appropriate for the medium, understandable to a reasonable person, and permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove to the extent technically feasible. Section 22757.3(b) separately requires the covered provider to include a latent disclosure — one embedded in the content or its metadata rather than visible to a viewer — in AI-generated image, video, or audio content the system created, detectable by the covered provider's own AI detection tool and consistent with widely accepted industry standards.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory section, § 22757.3, subdivisions (a) and (b), and are not independent of one another. This clause does not restate every listed item the latent disclosure must convey under § 22757.3(b)(1) — the covered provider's name, the GenAI system's name and version number, the time and date of creation or alteration, and a unique identifier — nor § 22757.3(c)'s separate contractual and license-revocation duties that apply when a covered provider licenses its GenAI system to a third party. This is very recently operative law that may see further amendment.

clauses.title: The AI Transparency Act: Civil Penalties, an Exemption, and the Operative Date
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 22757.4(a)(1) makes a violator of the chapter liable for a civil penalty of five thousand dollars ($5,000) per violation, collected in a civil action filed by the Attorney General, a city attorney, or a county counsel; § 22757.4(b) states that each day a covered provider, large online platform, or capture device manufacturer is in violation is deemed a discrete violation. Section 22757.5 states that the chapter does not apply to any product, service, internet website, or application that provides exclusively non-user-generated video game, television, streaming, movie, or interactive experiences. Section 22757.6 states that the chapter became operative on August 2, 2026 — later than the Act's original January 1, 2026 effective date, because AB 853 (2025) both amended the chapter's substantive requirements and pushed back when the chapter actually took operative effect.
clauses.gap: §§ 22757.4, 22757.5, and 22757.6 are three independently numbered sections; within § 22757.4, subdivisions (a)(1) and (b) are part of the same section and not independent of one another. This clause does not restate § 22757.4(a)(2)'s prevailing-plaintiff attorney's-fees provision or § 22757.4(c)'s separate injunctive-relief and fee-shifting remedy for a third-party licensee's violation of § 22757.3(c)(3). This sheet does not identify any implementing regulations or enforcement actions under this very recently operative chapter, which may see further amendment.

clauses.title: The Related, Distinct AI Training Data Transparency Law
clauses.body: A separate statute, Civil Code §§ 3110–3111 (Title 15.2, "Artificial Intelligence Training Data Transparency," enacted as Assembly Bill 2013), imposes a different duty on a different category of business than the AI Transparency Act above: it requires the "developer" of a generative artificial intelligence system or service to publicly post documentation about the data used to train it, rather than requiring a detection tool or content disclosures. Civil Code § 3111 requires that, on or before January 1, 2026, and before each later time a generative AI system or service (or a substantial modification to one released on or after January 1, 2022) is made publicly available to Californians, the developer post on its own website documentation about the training data, including the dataset sources, whether the data include copyrighted material or personal information, and the time period the data were collected. Civil Code § 3110(c) defines "generative artificial intelligence," for purposes of this separate title, as artificial intelligence that can generate derived synthetic content, such as text, images, video, and audio, that emulates the structure and characteristics of the artificial intelligence's training data.
clauses.gap: This is a distinct statute, in a distinct code (Civil Code, not Business and Professions Code), from the AI Transparency Act addressed in the clauses above; it is not codified in the Health and Safety Code. Civil Code § 3110 (definitions) and § 3111 (the posting duty) are two separate, independently numbered sections within the same title, and the two citations below are independent of one another. This clause does not restate § 3111(a)'s full twelve-item list of what the posted documentation must include beyond the examples given above, nor § 3111(b)'s exemptions for security-and-integrity-only systems, aircraft-operation systems, and systems developed exclusively for federal national-security, military, or defense use available only to a federal entity. This sheet does not address who qualifies as a "developer" under § 3110(b) in any particular case, and does not address this title's relationship to the separate AI Transparency Act's "covered provider" definition, which uses different terms and a different threshold. This is very recently effective law — § 3111 was itself amended in 2025 by AB 1170 — that may see further amendment.

clauses.title: What a Deed of Trust Is and Its Three-Party Structure
clauses.body: California's Civil Code defines a mortgage as a contract by which specific property is hypothecated for the performance of an act, without a change of possession: "A mortgage is a contract by which specific property, including an estate for years in real property, is hypothecated for the performance of an act, without the necessity of a change of possession." A deed of trust is a distinct instrument the same chapter of the Civil Code expressly treats as something other than a mortgage: the statute defining a security device with a power of sale for purposes of the nonjudicial foreclosure statutes reaches "any security device or instrument, other than a deed of trust, that confers a power of sale affecting real property or an estate for years therein, to be exercised after breach of the obligation so secured" — naming a deed of trust as its own category rather than folding it into "mortgage." Consistent with that distinction, a deed of trust is structured as a three-party transaction, not a two-party one like an ordinary mortgage: {{trustorName}}, as Trustor (the borrower granting the security interest), transfers bare legal title to {{trusteeName}}, as Trustee, to be held in trust for {{beneficiaryName}}, as Beneficiary (the lender), until the secured obligation is paid or the Trustee's power of sale is exercised after a default. California law reflects the Trustee's limited, largely mechanical role by giving Beneficiary a statutory right to replace the Trustee without the Trustee's consent: a trustee under a trust deed "conferring no other duties upon the trustee than those which are incidental to the exercise of the power of sale therein conferred, may be substituted by the recording in the county in which the property is located of a substitution executed and acknowledged by" the beneficiaries under the deed of trust or their successors in interest.
clauses.gap: Civ. Code §§ 2920 and 2934a are genuinely separate statutory sections; the two quotations from § 2920 are subdivisions (a) and (b) of that same section, quoted separately because they make two different points (the general definition of a mortgage, and the express carve-out of a deed of trust from that definition). This clause states California's statutory and structural framework for a deed of trust as a security device; the label "three-party" for a deed of trust's trustor/trustee/beneficiary structure is this document's own description of what these statutes establish through that terminology, not a phrase any single quoted provision uses on its own. This clause does not describe what happens after Trustor defaults — the notice of default, notice of sale, reinstatement right, and anti-deficiency protection that follow are addressed in this corpus's separate Notice of Default / Nonjudicial Foreclosure Process — Information Sheet and California Homeowner Bill of Rights — Information Sheet, and are not restated here. Nor does it address a mortgage — the alternative security instrument these same statutes also govern — as distinct from a deed of trust.

clauses.title: Recording a Deed of Trust: Permissive Recordation and Its Effect on Priority and Enforcement
clauses.body: California law does not require a deed of trust to be recorded for it to be valid and binding as between {{trustorName}}, {{trusteeName}}, and {{beneficiaryName}}; recording is authorized, not mandated, as a general matter for instruments affecting title to real property: "Any instrument or judgment affecting the title to or possession of real property may be recorded pursuant to this chapter." What recording changes is a deed of trust's effect on people outside the transaction: once a conveyance affecting real property is acknowledged, certified, and recorded as prescribed by law, from the time it is filed with the recorder it becomes "constructive notice of the contents thereof to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees" — giving a recorded lien against {{propertyAddress}} priority protection against later purchasers or lenders who take an interest in the Property without actual notice of it. Recording also has a specific, separate significance for the power of sale a deed of trust confers: if {{beneficiaryName}}'s interest is later assigned to someone else, the assignee may exercise the power of sale "only if the assignment is duly acknowledged and recorded."
clauses.gap: This clause states California's own permissive-recording and constructive-notice framework as it bears on a deed of trust; it is not a claim about which state's recording law governs a particular loan or property. Gov. Code § 27280 and Civ. Code §§ 1213 and 2932.5 are three genuinely independent statutory sections, addressed together here because each speaks to a different consequence of recording (authorization to record, priority against later claimants, and an assignee's ability to invoke the power of sale) rather than because they duplicate one another; the quotation from § 2932.5 is that section's second sentence — its first sentence, on the assignability of the power of sale itself, is quoted in this document's separate clause on the power-of-sale mechanism's statutory basis, not repeated here. This clause does not restate California's full "race-notice" priority rule among competing recorded and unrecorded conveyances of title, which this corpus's grant deed and quitclaim deed documents address in the context of an outright transfer rather than a security instrument; nor does it address county-specific recording formatting requirements, transfer tax, or Preliminary Change of Ownership Report obligations that may apply when a deed of trust or the property it encumbers changes hands.

clauses.title: The Power-of-Sale Mechanism's Statutory Basis
clauses.body: A deed of trust's power of sale — the mechanism that lets {{beneficiaryName}} or {{trusteeName}} sell {{propertyAddress}} without going to court after a default — exists only because California statute authorizes it, not automatically as an incident of every security instrument: "A power of sale may be conferred by a mortgage upon the mortgagee or any other person, to be exercised after a breach of the obligation for which the mortgage is a security." That same statutory power of sale can arise "or in any transfer in trust made after July 27, 1917, of a like estate to secure the performance of an obligation," under which "a power of sale is conferred upon the mortgagee, trustee, or any other person, to be exercised after a breach of the obligation for which that mortgage or transfer is a security." The power of sale is also assignable along with the debt it secures: "the power is part of the security and vests in any person who by assignment becomes entitled to payment of the money secured by the instrument."
clauses.gap: The two quotations drawn from Civ. Code § 2924(a) are different clauses of the same sentence within that subdivision, quoted separately from the § 2932 and § 2932.5 quotations, which are genuinely independent sections; the § 2932.5 quotation here is that section's first sentence, on assignability, while its second sentence, on the recording an assignee needs before exercising the power, is quoted in this document's separate recording clause rather than repeated here. § 2924 is the same section this corpus's existing Notice of Default / Nonjudicial Foreclosure Process — Information Sheet already cites, but that document quotes a different part of § 2924(a)(1) — the notice-of-default filing and content requirements — while this clause quotes different language, earlier in subdivision (a), about how the power of sale is created in the first place. This clause states only that the power exists and how it is created and assigned; it does not describe how the power is exercised once a default occurs — the notice of default, the required waiting period, the notice of sale, the right to reinstate, and the anti-deficiency rule that follow a default are covered in that Notice of Default / Nonjudicial Foreclosure Process — Information Sheet and in the companion California Homeowner Bill of Rights — Information Sheet, and are not restated here.

clauses.title: The Reconveyance Obligation Once the Secured Debt Is Paid Off
clauses.body: A deed of trust does not simply disappear once {{trustorName}} pays off the debt it secures; California statute imposes an affirmative, time-limited duty on the lender's side to clear the lien from title: "Within 30 calendar days after the obligation secured by any deed of trust has been satisfied, the beneficiary or the assignee of the beneficiary shall execute and deliver to the trustee the original note, deed of trust, request for a full reconveyance, and other documents as may be necessary to reconvey, or cause to be reconveyed, the deed of trust." The Trustee then has its own statutory deadline to act: "The trustee shall execute the full reconveyance and shall record or cause it to be recorded in the office of the county recorder in which the deed of trust is recorded within 21 calendar days after receipt by the trustee of the original note, deed of trust, request for a full reconveyance, the fee that may be charged pursuant to subdivision (e), recorder's fees, and other documents as may be necessary to reconvey, or cause to be reconveyed, the deed of trust." Recording this reconveyance is what removes the deed of trust as a recorded encumbrance against {{propertyAddress}}.
clauses.gap: Both quotations are drawn from Civ. Code § 2941, and are subdivisions of the same section — § 2941(b)(1) and § 2941(b)(1)(A) — quoted separately because the first states the beneficiary's deadline to hand the paperwork to the trustee and the second states the trustee's separate, later deadline to record the reconveyance itself. § 2941 also has its own parallel provision for an ordinary mortgage (as opposed to a deed of trust) in subdivision (a), which this clause does not quote or address. This clause states only that the reconveyance obligation exists and its statutory timing; it does not address the fee a trustee may charge for a reconveyance under § 2941(e), the electronic-note procedure under later paragraphs of § 2941(b), or any statutory remedy or penalty for a beneficiary's or trustee's failure to meet these deadlines. It also does not address what happens if the debt is instead unpaid and in default — that is the subject of this corpus's separate Notice of Default / Nonjudicial Foreclosure Process — Information Sheet, not of this clause.

clauses.title: Who Must Register: Entities Holding Property for Charitable Purposes
clauses.body: California's Registry of Charitable Trusts, administered by the Attorney General under the Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act, applies broadly to entities that hold or solicit property for charitable purposes, not only to incorporated nonprofits. By statute, the article governing the Registry "applies to all charitable corporations, unincorporated associations, trustees, and other legal entities holding property for charitable purposes, commercial fundraisers for charitable purposes, fundraising counsel for charitable purposes, commercial coventurers, charitable fundraising platforms, and platform charities over which the state or the Attorney General has enforcement or supervisory powers." A separate statutory definition extends "trustee" status — and with it registration coverage — beyond formal trust arrangements: it reaches (among others) “any individual, group of individuals, corporation, unincorporated association, or other legal entity holding property in trust pursuant to any charitable trust,” “any corporation or unincorporated association which has accepted property to be used for a particular charitable purpose as distinguished from the general purposes of the corporation or unincorporated association,” and “a corporation or unincorporated association formed for the administration of a charitable trust, pursuant to the directions of the settlor or at the instance of the trustee." Coverage is not universal, however: a separate statute exempts several categories outright from the article's filing, registration, and reporting provisions, stating that those provisions "do not apply to the United States, any state, territory, or possession of the United States, the District of Columbia, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or to any of their agencies or governmental subdivisions, to any religious corporation sole or other religious corporation or organization that holds property for religious purposes," and separately exempting "a charitable corporation or unincorporated association organized and operated primarily as a religious organization, educational institution, hospital, or a health care service plan licensed pursuant to Section 1349 of the Health and Safety Code."
clauses.gap: This clause draws on three independently enacted sections of the same statutory article — Cal. Gov. Code §§ 12581, 12582, and 12583 — treated as three independent sources. The two citations below drawn from § 12583 are two non-adjacent excerpts of that same single section (separated by unquoted statutory text addressing cemetery corporations and certain campaign-finance committees) and are treated together as one source, not as two independent corroborating ones. Section 12581's current text was added by a 2021 amendment (Stats. 2021, Ch. 616 (AB 488)), effective January 1, 2022 and operative January 1, 2023, which repealed and replaced an earlier version of the section; the text quoted here is the current, operative text, and it is broader than older descriptions of this article might suggest — it now expressly reaches "charitable fundraising platforms" and "platform charities," categories the pre-2023 statute did not name. This clause does not cover the further, narrower exemption for "corporate trustees which are subject to the jurisdiction of the Commissioner of Financial Institutions... or to the Comptroller of the Currency," which appears in a different section (Cal. Gov. Code § 12586(a)) addressed in this document's annual-reporting clause rather than here. The religious-corporation exemption quoted here is the same statutory text already cited, from a different angle (the narrower, separate limit on the Attorney General's regulatory powers over religious corporations specifically), in this project's Nonprofit Religious Corporation document; citing it again here, in the context of who must register with the Registry generally, states an independent point and is not a repetition of that document's distinct one. This clause states which categories of entity the statute names as covered or exempt; it does not evaluate whether any specific organization falls into a covered or exempt category, and it does not address federal 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status, which is a separate federal question this clause does not reach.

clauses.title: Initial Registration and Its 30-Day Deadline
clauses.body: Registration with the Attorney General's Registry of Charitable Trusts is a distinct, ongoing filing obligation separate from formation with the California Secretary of State, and by statute it is triggered by receipt of property, not by the act of incorporating. The statute provides that "every charitable corporation, unincorporated association, and trustee subject to this article shall file with the Attorney General an initial registration form, under oath, setting forth information and attaching documents prescribed in accordance with rules and regulations of the Attorney General, within 30 days after the corporation, unincorporated association, or trustee initially receives property. A trustee is not required to register as long as the charitable interest in a trust is a future interest, but shall do so within 30 days after any charitable interest in a trust becomes a present interest." The Attorney General's own public guidance on this filing states the same 30-day rule in plain terms: "Charitable organizations are required to register with the Registry of Charities and Fundraisers within 30 days of the initial receipt of assets." To administer this and related filings, the Attorney General is separately directed by statute to "establish and maintain a register of charitable corporations, unincorporated associations, and trustees subject to this article and of the particular trust or other relationship under which they hold property for charitable purposes."
clauses.gap: Cal. Gov. Code § 12585 and Cal. Gov. Code § 12584 are independently enacted sections of the same statutory article and are treated as two independent sources; the Attorney General's initial-registration webpage is cited separately as a third, non-statutory source that restates the same 30-day rule in the agency's own words — it corroborates, but is not itself, the statutory text, and this document independently fetched and verified its wording (retrieved twice with different User-Agent strings, byte-identical after whitespace normalization). This clause states only the timing trigger and its statutory deadline; it does not describe the contents required on the initial registration form itself (the statute delegates that content to Attorney General regulations, which this clause does not independently fetch or quote), and it does not address what counts, in any specific factual situation, as the corporation, association, or trustee having "initially received property." It also does not address the separate registration and bonding obligations this same article imposes on commercial fundraisers, fundraising counsel, commercial coventurers, charitable fundraising platforms, and platform charities, which are governed by other provisions of the article not covered by this clause.

A trustee is not required to register as long as the charitable interest in a trust is a future interest, but shall do so within 30 days after any charitable interest in a trust becomes a present interest.

clauses.title: Annual Reporting: Form RRF-1 and Financial Disclosures
clauses.body: Once registered, a charitable corporation, unincorporated association, or trustee subject to the Registry is subject to a recurring, not merely one-time, reporting duty. The statute requires that, with certain exceptions, "every charitable corporation, unincorporated association, and trustee subject to this article shall, in addition to filing copies of the instruments previously required, file with the Attorney General periodic written reports, under oath, setting forth information as to the nature of the assets held for charitable purposes and the administration thereof by the corporation, unincorporated association, or trustee, in accordance with rules and regulations of the Attorney General." The statute itself fixes the deadline for the first such report: "The first periodic written report, unless the filing thereof is suspended as herein provided, shall be filed not later than four months and 15 days following the close of the first calendar or fiscal year in which property is initially received" — the same four-months-and-15-days period that governs each subsequent annual report. The Attorney General's Registry implements this statutory duty through a specific numbered form: its own guidance states that "the Form RRF-1 is a form to renew an existing registration to report on the charity's activities during the prior fiscal year," and separately identifies what must accompany it: "Form RRF-1 along with either: Copy of IRS Form 990, 990-EZ, or 990-PF as filed with the IRS except: Schedule B is not requested or required by the Registry." A separate statutory subdivision layers additional financial-disclosure obligations onto larger organizations: an entity that "receives or accrues in any fiscal year gross revenue of two million dollars ($2,000,000) or more, exclusive of grants from, and contracts for services with, governmental entities for which the governmental entity requires an accounting of the funds received," must, among other things, "[p]repare annual financial statements using generally accepted accounting principles that are audited by an independent certified public accountant in conformity with generally accepted auditing standards." The same statute ties public disclosure of those audited statements to existing federal practice: "A charity shall make its annual audited financial statements available to the public in the same manner that is prescribed for IRS Form 990 by the latest revision of Section 6104(d) of the Internal Revenue Code and associated regulations."
clauses.gap: The four Government Code quotations in this clause are drawn from subdivisions (a), (d), and (e) of the same statutory section, Cal. Gov. Code § 12586, and are treated as one statutory source describing different parts of a single reporting scheme, not as independent corroborating sources; the two Attorney General Registry webpage quotations (from the Registry's initial-registration and renewals pages) are cited separately as non-statutory sources for the specific form name and its accompanying documents, which the statutory text itself does not name, and this document independently fetched and verified the wording of both pages (each retrieved twice with different User-Agent strings, byte-identical after whitespace normalization). This clause does not cover the smaller-organization alternative to IRS Form 990 that the Registry's renewals page also references (a form the Registry calls Form CT-TR-1, not independently quoted here), the $2,000,000 revenue threshold's audit-committee composition requirements, or the officer-compensation-review requirement that the same statutory section separately imposes — none of which this clause's citations quote or this clause describes. It also does not cover the exception in § 12586(a) for certain corporate trustees regulated by state or federal banking authorities.

clauses.title: Attorney General Enforcement and Statutory Penalties
clauses.body: Failure to comply with the Registry's filing and reporting requirements exposes a covered entity, and in some circumstances a person acting for it, to statutory enforcement mechanisms distinct from any private lawsuit. The statute gives the Attorney General general authority to sue for compliance: "The Attorney General may institute appropriate proceedings to secure compliance with this article and to invoke the jurisdiction of the court." A separate statute creates a specific civil penalty for intentional violations: "Any person who violates any provision of this article with intent to deceive or defraud any charity or individual is liable for a civil penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000)." That same statute also authorizes a distinct, accruing penalty not limited to intentional conduct: "The Attorney General may impose a penalty on any person or entity, not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000) per act or omission, for each act or omission that constitutes a violation of this article or Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 300) of Division 1 of Title 11 of the California Code of Regulations," and, following required notice, "Penalties shall accrue, commencing on the fifth day after notice is given, at a rate of one hundred dollars ($100) per day for each day until that person or entity corrects that violation." Separately from these penalties, the statute also authorizes an additional monthly late fee when a covered entity does any of several listed things, including if it "(a) Exists and operates in California without being registered [or] (b) Solicits contributions in California without being registered or, if applicable, bonded."
clauses.gap: Cal. Gov. Code § 12591 is one independently enacted section; the two quotations drawn from Cal. Gov. Code § 12591.1 are both from subsection (c) of that section (except the civil-penalty quotation, which is subsection (a)) and, together with the subsection (a) quotation, are treated as one statutory source — non-adjacent parts of the same section — not as independent corroborating sources; Cal. Gov. Code § 12586.1 is a fourth, independently enacted section. This clause does not cover every remedy available to the Attorney General under § 12591.1 — that section separately authorizes cease-and-desist orders, suspension of registration, a hearing-and-review procedure, and injunctive relief including a receiver, restitution, or accounting, none of which are quoted here, though registration suspension is addressed from a different angle in this document's delinquency clause. It also does not evaluate whether any specific conduct would meet the "intent to deceive or defraud" standard for the $10,000 civil penalty, or whether any specific conduct falls within § 12586.1's list of late-fee triggers beyond the two quoted here — both are factual determinations this clause does not make.

clauses.title: Delinquency, Loss of Good Standing, and Related Consequences
clauses.body: Beyond the civil penalties a statute authorizes directly, the Attorney General's Registry also tracks each registrant's compliance status, and that status carries its own consequences once an entity falls behind on required filings. The Registry's own guidance describes the practical effect of delinquency in these terms: "A charitable organization that is not in good standing with the Registry because of delinquency, suspension, or revocation may not operate or solicit donations in California," a rule the Registry's guidance attributes to a specific California regulation, Cal. Code Regs., tit. 11, section 312. The Registry's guidance on the annual renewal filing separately describes a range of consequences that can follow from failing to renew registration on time: "The failure to renew registration may result in late fees, penalties, a delinquent registration status, suspended registration status, revoked registration status, or other legal action, and the loss of tax-exempt status with the California Franchise Tax Board."
clauses.gap: Both quotations in this clause are drawn from Attorney General Registry of Charities and Fundraisers webpages (the Registry's Delinquency page and its Renewals page), not from the Government Code text itself, and are treated as two independent administrative sources describing the Registry's own compliance practices; this document independently fetched and verified the wording of these two webpages (each retrieved twice, with different User-Agent strings, and found byte-identical after whitespace normalization), but it did not independently fetch or verify the text of the regulation the Delinquency page cites, Cal. Code Regs., tit. 11, section 312 — that regulation's own wording is not quoted here, and only the Registry's own description of its effect is, consistent with this document's discipline of omitting rather than fabricating a quotation from a source it did not itself retrieve. Separately, the specific mechanics and legal basis of the loss of California Franchise Tax Board tax-exempt status mentioned on the Renewals page are governed by California Revenue and Taxation Code provisions this document does not cite or independently verify here. This clause does not state that any specific organization is delinquent, suspended, revoked, or has lost tax-exempt status; it describes only the consequences the Registry's own published guidance associates with those statuses generally.

clauses.title: Declaration and Scope of This Section 409A Payment-Timing Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Section 409A Payment-Timing Information Sheet is prepared with respect to {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}}, which ended on {{separationDate}}. It addresses federal tax law under Internal Revenue Code section 409A as it applies to separation pay and other nonqualified deferred compensation payable upon termination of employment, described in this document as arising under: {{planName}}. It states what section 409A's own text, and the Treasury regulations issued under it, say about which events may trigger payment of such compensation, the additional delay that applies to certain employees of publicly traded corporations, two regulatory exemptions from section 409A's deferred-compensation timing rules, and the tax consequences of a violation. This document states facts about how federal tax law treats nonqualified deferred compensation in general; it does not determine whether any specific payment described in this document is or is not subject to section 409A, does not calculate any tax, and does not state what {{employeeName}} or {{companyName}} should do about their situation.

clauses.title: "Nonqualified Deferred Compensation Plan" Defined
clauses.body: Internal Revenue Code section 409A applies to a "nonqualified deferred compensation plan," a term the statute defines broadly, by exclusion, rather than by a positive list of arrangements it covers. The statute defines the term to mean any plan that provides for the deferral of compensation, other than a "qualified employer plan" (a category that includes tax-qualified retirement plans, certain eligible governmental deferred compensation plans, and certain excess benefit plans, each separately defined elsewhere in the same subsection) and other than any bona fide vacation leave, sick leave, compensatory time, disability pay, or death benefit plan. The statute further provides that the term "plan" includes any agreement or arrangement, including an agreement or arrangement that includes only one person -- meaning an individually negotiated severance or separation agreement can itself be a "plan" for these purposes, not only a formal, multi-participant benefit program.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two subdivisions of the same statutory section, 26 U.S.C. § 409A(d)(1) and § 409A(d)(3) -- they are not independent sources of each other, and both are part of the single, much longer section 409A addressed throughout this document. This clause states only the general definition and the breadth of the term "plan"; it does not restate the statute's own further definition of "qualified employer plan" (§ 409A(d)(2), cross-referencing sections 219(g)(5), 457(b), and 415(m)), and it does not determine whether any specific arrangement described in this document -- including the arrangement identified above -- is or is not a "nonqualified deferred compensation plan" within this definition. This is federal tax law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule; it has no state-law analog. The statutory text was fetched twice this session, directly from law.cornell.edu, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times.

clauses.title: Separation From Service as a Permitted Payment-Triggering Event
clauses.body: Section 409A does not allow a nonqualified deferred compensation plan to distribute deferred compensation whenever the plan or the parties later choose. The statute instead requires that the plan itself provide that compensation deferred under it may not be distributed earlier than one of six specific events or times the statute lists: separation from service (as determined by the Secretary of the Treasury); the date the participant becomes disabled, within a further statutory meaning; death; a specified time, or a schedule fixed under the plan at the time the compensation was deferred; to the extent provided by the Secretary, a change in the ownership or effective control of the corporation, or in the ownership of a substantial portion of its assets; or the occurrence of an unforeseeable emergency. "Separation from service" is listed first among these six permitted triggers, and is the event most directly relevant to separation pay -- compensation a plan makes payable because employment with {{companyName}} ended.
clauses.gap: This clause cites a single statutory subsection, 26 U.S.C. § 409A(a)(2)(A), listing all six clauses (i) through (vi) of that subsection together as the full list of permitted timing events -- they are subdivisions of one subsection, not independent sources. This clause does not restate the statute's own further definitions of "disabled" (§ 409A(a)(2)(C)) or "unforeseeable emergency" (§ 409A(a)(2)(B)(ii)), and it does not address section 409A(a)(3)'s separate rule against accelerating the time or schedule of a payment once fixed, or section 409A(a)(4)'s rules on when a deferral election may first be made or later changed -- both addressed, if at all, only by omission from this document. Nor does this clause address how "separation from service" itself is defined; the statute leaves that term to be "determined by the Secretary," meaning its operative definition is found in Treasury regulations, which this clause does not independently address. This clause does not determine whether any specific payment described in this document is in fact triggered only by one of these six permitted events. This is federal tax law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule; it has no state-law analog. The statutory text was fetched twice this session, directly from law.cornell.edu, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times.

clauses.title: The Six-Month Delay for a "Specified Employee" of a Publicly Traded Corporation
clauses.body: Section 409A imposes an additional timing restriction on separation pay owed to a "specified employee." For any specified employee, the statute provides that the separation-from-service permitted-timing rule described above is met only if the plan does not permit distribution before the date that is six months after the date of separation from service, or, if earlier, the date of the employee's death. The statute defines a "specified employee," for this purpose, as a key employee -- as defined in a cross-referenced statute, without regard to one of that statute's own paragraphs -- of a corporation any stock in which is publicly traded on an established securities market or otherwise. This delay therefore applies only where two conditions are both met: the individual is a key employee within that cross-referenced definition, and the paying corporation's stock is publicly traded; the statute states no comparable six-month delay for a specified employee of a privately held corporation, because a privately held corporation's stock is not publicly traded on an established securities market or otherwise.
clauses.gap: This clause cites 26 U.S.C. § 409A(a)(2)(B)(i), a single statutory subdivision that is itself a special rule qualifying the separation-from-service trigger described in the section409a_separation_from_service_permitted_timing clause of this document, not an independent source from it. This clause does not restate the full definition of "key employee" found in the cross-referenced statute, 26 U.S.C. § 416(i), which this clause does not independently quote or verify this session; it states only that section 409A borrows that definition, with one of that other statute's own paragraphs disregarded. This clause does not address how "publicly traded" is determined for a corporation whose stock trades only indirectly (for example, through a parent or affiliate), a question the statute leaves to "the Secretary" and does not resolve in this subdivision's own text. This clause does not determine whether the individual named in this document is in fact a specified employee, or whether the corporation named in this document's stock is in fact publicly traded. This is federal tax law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule; it has no state-law analog. The statutory text was fetched twice this session, directly from law.cornell.edu, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times.

For purposes of the preceding sentence, a specified employee is a key employee (as defined in section 416(i) without regard to paragraph (5) thereof) of a corporation any stock in which is publicly traded on an established securities market or otherwise.

clauses.title: Two Regulatory Exemptions: the "Short-Term Deferral" Rule and the "Separation Pay Plan" Exception
clauses.body: Section 409A's own statutory text does not define a "short-term deferral" exemption or a "separation pay plan" exemption; both are found instead in Treasury regulations issued under the statute's grant of regulatory authority. The short-term deferral regulation provides that a deferral of compensation does not occur under a plan with respect to a payment that is not a "deferred payment," provided that the service provider actually or constructively receives the payment on or before the last day of a specific window measured from when the compensation is no longer subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture -- a window the regulation defines as the period ending on the later of the 15th day of the third month following the end of the service provider's first taxable year in which the right to the payment is no longer subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture, or the 15th day of the third month following the end of the service recipient's (employer's) corresponding taxable year. Separately, the separation pay plan regulation provides that a separation pay plan that is not collectively bargained, and that provides separation pay only upon an involuntary separation from service or under a window program, does not provide for a deferral of compensation subject to section 409A to the extent the separation pay meets two conditions stated in the regulation: the amount does not exceed two times the lesser of the employee's annualized compensation for the preceding taxable year or the compensation limit applicable to qualified plans under a further cross-referenced statute for the year of separation, and the plan provides that the payment must be made no later than the last day of the second taxable year following the taxable year in which the separation from service occurs.
clauses.gap: These two exemptions come from a single Treasury regulation, 26 CFR § 1.409A-1(b) -- the short-term deferral rule at § 1.409A-1(b)(4)(i) and (b)(4)(i)(A), and the separation pay plan exception at § 1.409A-1(b)(9)(iii)(A) and (B), are subdivisions of that one regulatory section, not independent sources of each other, and neither is itself part of the Internal Revenue Code text addressed in this document's other clauses. This clause states only the general short-term deferral rule and only the involuntary-separation/window-program branch of the separation pay plan exception; it does not address the regulation's separate provisions for collectively bargained separation pay plans (§ 1.409A-1(b)(9)(ii)), foreign separation pay plans (§ 1.409A-1(b)(9)(iv)), reimbursements and medical benefits (§ 1.409A-1(b)(9)(v)), the limited-dollar-amount exception (§ 1.409A-1(b)(9)(v)(D)), the regulation's own definitions of "separation pay plan," "involuntary separation from service," and "window program" (§ 1.409A-1(m), (n), (b)(9)(vi)), or the short-term deferral rule's own exceptions for certain delayed payments (§ 1.409A-1(b)(4)(ii)). It does not determine whether any payment described in this document in fact qualifies for either exemption. This regulatory text was fetched twice this session, directly from law.cornell.edu's CFR text (a Cornell LII mirror of the Code of Federal Regulations, distinct from its U.S. Code text used elsewhere in this document), using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This is a federal Treasury regulation, not a statute, and not California state law; it has no state-law analog and could in principle be amended by the Treasury Department without a corresponding statutory change.

clauses.title: The Consequence of a Section 409A Violation: Income Inclusion, a 20% Additional Tax, and Interest
clauses.body: Section 409A attaches severe consequences where a nonqualified deferred compensation plan fails to meet, or is not operated in accordance with, its distribution-timing, no-acceleration, and election-timing requirements. The statute provides that if at any time during a taxable year the plan fails or is not operated in compliance, all compensation deferred under the plan for that taxable year and all preceding taxable years is includible in the affected participants' gross income for that taxable year, to the extent not already subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture and not previously included in gross income -- not merely the specific payment that was mistimed. Beyond this accelerated income inclusion, the statute imposes two further, separately calculated amounts on top of the participant's regular income tax on that amount: interest, computed at the underpayment rate plus one percentage point, calculated as if the deferred compensation had been included in income when it was first deferred (or, if later, when it first became free of a substantial risk of forfeiture); and an additional tax equal to 20 percent of the compensation required to be included in gross income under this rule.
clauses.gap: This clause cites subdivisions of a single statutory subsection, 26 U.S.C. § 409A(a)(1) -- the income-inclusion rule at § 409A(a)(1)(A)(i), and the interest-and-20%-tax rule at § 409A(a)(1)(B)(i) and (ii), are part of that one subsection and are not independent sources of each other. This clause does not restate § 409A(a)(1)(A)(ii), which limits this consequence to participants "with respect to whom the failure relates" rather than every participant in the plan, and it does not address the separate funding-related consequences under § 409A(b) for offshore trusts or restricted-fund arrangements, which involve different triggering conduct (funding mechanics rather than distribution timing) and a different consequence provision this document does not cover. It does not determine whether any specific plan or payment described in this document has in fact violated section 409A, and it does not calculate the amount of any tax, interest, or income inclusion that would result. This is federal tax law that applies nationwide, not a California-specific rule; it has no state-law analog and operates independently of any separate consequence state law may impose on the same payment. clauses.title: Statement of Separation Pay Facts and Signature
When a Guardian Ad Litem Must or May Be Appointed
clauses.body: Under California Code of Civil Procedure § 372(a)(1), when {{minorOrIncapacitatedPersonName}} is a minor, a person who lacks legal capacity to make decisions, or a person for whom a conservator has been appointed and is a party to a civil action or proceeding, {{minorOrIncapacitatedPersonName}} must appear either through a guardian or conservator of the estate or through a guardian ad litem appointed by the court in which the action or proceeding is pending, or by a judge of that court. Separately, § 372(a)(2)(A) lets a court appoint a guardian ad litem in any case whenever the court deems it expedient to do so, even if {{minorOrIncapacitatedPersonName}} already has a guardian or conservator of the estate who has already appeared on {{minorOrIncapacitatedPersonName}}'s behalf.
clauses.gap: Both citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Code Civ. Proc. § 372 — § 372(a)(1) and § 372(a)(2)(A) — not independently sourced provisions. Section 372(a)(1) states the mandatory rule (such a person "shall appear" only through one of these representatives); § 372(a)(2)(A) states the separate, discretionary "expedient" standard a court may use to appoint a guardian ad litem even over an existing guardian or conservator of the estate. The statute does not define "expedient"; that judgment is left to the court. This clause does not cover the additional showing the statute requires when a guardian or conservator of the estate already exists (covered in a separate clause) or the exceptions letting certain minors appear without a guardian ad litem in specific proceeding types (also covered separately).

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(1)
citations.quote: When a minor, a person who lacks legal capacity to make decisions, or a person for whom a conservator has been appointed is a party, that person shall appear either by a guardian or conservator of the estate or by a guardian ad litem appointed by the court in which the action or proceeding is pending, or by a judge thereof, in each case.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(2)(A)

clauses.title: Who May Be Appointed, and Why This Differs From an Existing Guardian or Conservator of the Estate
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure § 372(a)(1) recognizes two distinct kinds of representative who may appear for {{minorOrIncapacitatedPersonName}} in litigation: an existing guardian or conservator of the estate, or a guardian ad litem appointed by the court specifically for that action or proceeding. When {{minorOrIncapacitatedPersonName}} already has a guardian or conservator of the estate and an application is instead made to appoint a guardian ad litem, § 372(a)(2)(B) permits the court to grant that application only if the applicant gives the existing guardian or conservator of the estate notice and a copy of the application upon filing, the application discloses that guardian or conservator of the estate's existence, and the application states the reasons why that guardian or conservator of the estate is inadequate to represent {{minorOrIncapacitatedPersonName}}'s interests in the action. Under § 372(a)(2)(C), the existing guardian or conservator of the estate then has five court days from receiving that notice to file any opposition.
clauses.gap: Three citations here are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Code Civ. Proc. § 372 — § 372(a)(1), § 372(a)(2)(B), and § 372(a)(2)(C) — not independently sourced provisions. The notice-and-adequacy showing in § 372(a)(2)(B) applies only when the proposed ward already has a guardian or conservator of the estate; the statute does not state a comparable showing for a first appointment where no such guardian or conservator exists. This clause does not address how a court evaluates whether an existing guardian or conservator of the estate is "inadequate" — the statute does not define that term — or the procedure for the existing guardian or conservator of the estate's opposition beyond the five-court-day filing window.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(1)
citations.quote: When a minor, a person who lacks legal capacity to make decisions, or a person for whom a conservator has been appointed is a party, that person shall appear either by a guardian or conservator of the estate or by a guardian ad litem appointed by the court in which the action or proceeding is pending, or by a judge thereof, in each case.

(ii) The application discloses the existence of a guardian or conservator of the estate. (iii) The application sets forth the reasons why the guardian or conservator of the estate is inadequate to represent the interests of the proposed ward in the action.

clauses.title: Who May Apply, and the Pre-Appointment Disclosure Requirement
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure § 373 sets out who may apply for appointment of a guardian ad litem and when, depending on the proposed ward's role in the case. If the minor is the plaintiff, the appointment must be made before the summons is issued, on the minor's own application if the minor is 14 years of age or older, or, if the minor is younger, on the application of a relative or friend of the minor. If the minor is the defendant, appointment is made on the minor's own application if 14 or older and the minor applies within 10 days after service of the summons; if the minor is younger than 14, or neglects to apply, appointment is instead made on the application of a relative or friend of the minor, of any other party to the action, or by the court on its own motion. If the person needing a guardian ad litem is someone who lacks legal competence to make decisions rather than a minor, § 373(c) allows the application to be made by a relative or friend of that person, by any other party to the action or proceeding, or by the court on its own motion. Separately, before the court appoints a guardian ad litem under this chapter, § 372(d) requires the proposed guardian ad litem to disclose to the court and all parties any known actual or potential conflict of interest that would or might arise from the appointment, and any familial or affiliate relationship the proposed guardian ad litem has with any of the parties; § 372(e) requires the guardian ad litem to promptly disclose to the court any new conflict, or any potential conflict that becomes an actual conflict, discovered after appointment.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on five subdivisions from two statutory sections. Three — § 373(a), § 373(b), and § 373(c) — are subdivisions of the same section, Code Civ. Proc. § 373, governing who may apply and by when; two others — § 372(d) and § 372(e) — are subdivisions of the separate section, Code Civ. Proc. § 372, governing conflict-of-interest disclosure. No additional independent source beyond each of those two sections was found for the points drawn from it. This clause does not cover the form the application must take, what it must state beyond the applicant's identity and timing, or the consequence of a proposed guardian ad litem's failure to disclose a conflict once discovered.

citations.cite: Code Civ. Proc. § 373(a)
citations.quote: If the minor is the plaintiff the appointment must be made before the summons is issued, upon the application of the minor, if the minor is 14 years of age or older, or, if under that age, upon the application of a relative or friend of the minor.

(2) Any familial or affiliate relationship the proposed guardian ad litem has with any of the parties.

clauses.title: Scope of a Guardian Ad Litem's Authority in the Litigation
clauses.body: Under California Code of Civil Procedure § 372(a)(3), a guardian or conservator of the estate or guardian ad litem appearing for {{minorOrIncapacitatedPersonName}} has the power, with the approval of the court in which the action or proceeding is pending, to compromise the action, to agree to the order or judgment to be entered for or against {{minorOrIncapacitatedPersonName}}, and to satisfy any judgment or order in {{minorOrIncapacitatedPersonName}}'s favor or to release or discharge {{minorOrIncapacitatedPersonName}}'s claim under that compromise. This authority is expressly tied to the pending action or proceeding and to court approval of the specific litigation decision — it is a narrower, case-bound role than the ongoing management of a person's care or property carried out by a general guardian of the person or a general guardian or conservator of the estate appointed in a separate probate guardianship or conservatorship proceeding, which is why § 372(a)(1) and § 372(a)(2) (addressed in separate clauses of this document) treat a guardian ad litem and an existing guardian or conservator of the estate as two distinct kinds of representative for the same person.
clauses.gap: The quoted text is a single subdivision, Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(3); no additional independent source beyond § 372 itself was found describing the guardian ad litem's litigation powers. This clause describes only the powers § 372(a)(3) itself lists — compromising the action, agreeing to the judgment or order, and satisfying or releasing the resulting claim, all subject to court approval — and the statement that this is narrower than a general guardian's or conservator's ongoing authority is this document's characterization of how § 372(a)(1)-(2) structure the two roles, not itself a quoted statutory definition of "guardian of the person" or "guardian of the estate." This clause does not cover how money or property payable to the minor or incapacitated person under the compromise must be handled, which the statute states is governed by a separate Probate Code provision outside the scope of this document's verification.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code Civ. Proc. § 372(a)(3)
citations.quote: The guardian or conservator of the estate or guardian ad litem so appearing for any minor, person who lacks legal capacity to make decisions, or person for whom a conservator has been appointed shall have power, with the approval of the court in which the action or proceeding is pending, to compromise the same, to agree to the order or judgment to be entered therein for or against the ward or conservatee, and to satisfy any judgment or order in favor of the ward or conservatee or release or discharge any claim of the ward or conservatee pursuant to that compromise.

clauses.title: Exceptions: When a Minor May Appear Without a Guardian Ad Litem in Family-Law and Protective-Order Proceedings
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure § 372 itself carves out proceedings where a minor may appear without a guardian ad litem, notwithstanding the general rule. Under § 372(b)(1), a minor 12 years of age or older may appear in court without a guardian, counsel, or guardian ad litem to request or oppose specified protective orders, including a harassment injunction or restraining order under Code of Civil Procedure § 527.6, a workplace violence injunction or restraining order under Code of Civil Procedure § 527.8, a domestic violence protective order under Family Code Division 10 (commencing with § 6200), or a protective order under Family Code §§ 7710 and 7720; the court may still appoint a guardian ad litem to assist the minor in that proceeding if it does not delay the order. Under § 372(c)(1), a minor who is a parent of the child at issue may also appear without a guardian ad litem in family court proceedings under Family Code Part 3 (commencing with § 7600), in dependency proceedings, in guardianship proceedings for a minor child under the Probate Code, and in other child custody, visitation, or support proceedings — but § 372(c)(2) requires the court to appoint a guardian ad litem for that minor parent if the court finds the minor parent unable to understand the nature of the proceedings or to assist counsel in preparing the case.
clauses.gap: Three citations here — § 372(b)(1), § 372(c)(1), and § 372(c)(2) — are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Code Civ. Proc. § 372, not independently sourced provisions; they were not separately verified against the cross-referenced Family Code sections (§§ 6200, 7710, 7720, and Part 3 commencing with § 7600) or the cross-referenced Welfare and Institutions Code juvenile dependency provisions, which this clause names only as the statute itself names them. This clause does not state what those cross-referenced Family Code or Welfare and Institutions Code proceedings themselves require; it states only that § 372 exempts a minor in the described role from needing a guardian ad litem in them, subject to the court's discretion to appoint one under § 372(b)(1) or its obligation to appoint one under § 372(c)(2). No separate, freestanding Family Code provision governing the guardian ad litem appointment mechanism itself — as distinct from these appearance exceptions — was located in the sections verified for this document.

citations.cite: Code Civ. Proc. § 372(b)(1)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (a), a minor 12 years of age or older may appear in court without a guardian, counsel, or guardian ad litem, for the purpose of requesting or opposing a request for any of the following: (A) An injunction or temporary restraining order or both to prohibit harassment pursuant to Section 527.6. (B) An injunction or temporary restraining order or both against violence or a credible threat of violence in the workplace pursuant to Section 527.8. (C) A protective order pursuant to Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code. (D) A protective order pursuant to Sections 7710 and 7720 of the Family Code.

(B) Dependency proceedings pursuant to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 200) of Part 1 of Division 2 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. (C) Guardianship proceedings for a minor child pursuant to Part 2 (commencing with Section 1500) of Division 4 of the Probate Code. (D) Any other proceedings concerning child custody, visitation, or support.
