clauses.title: Declaration -- Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet addresses the mediation of custody and visitation disputes concerning {{childName}} under California Family Code Chapter 11 (Mediation of Custody and Visitation Issues, commencing with Section 3160), in a matter involving {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} pending in {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes the circumstances under which this mediation is required, the purposes the mediation statute itself states, the confidentiality of communications made in mediation, the mediator's availability, qualifications, and duties, the statutory distinction between a mediator who may submit a custody or visitation recommendation to the court and the separate, narrower confidential mediation program under which a mediator may not, and a domestic-violence-specific mediation procedure that is separate from the pre-mediation notice California law requires under Family Code section 3044(h).

clauses.title: When Mediation Is Required, and Its Timing
clauses.body: Under California law, if it appears on the face of a petition, application, or other pleading to obtain or modify a temporary or permanent custody or visitation order that custody, visitation, or both are contested, the court is required to set the contested issues for mediation. Where a matter is set for mediation under this chapter, the statute requires that the mediation be set before or concurrent with the setting of the matter for hearing.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two independent sections of the same statutory chapter (Family Code Chapter 11, Mediation of Custody and Visitation Issues, Sections 3160-3188): section 3170(a), in Article 2 (Availability of Mediation, Sections 3170-3173), and section 3175, in Article 3 (Mediation Proceedings, Sections 3175-3188). It does not restate section 3170(b)'s separate domestic-violence-protocol provision (addressed in a separate clause of this document), section 3171's parallel mediation trigger for stepparent or grandparent visitation petitions, section 3172's rule that mediation may not be denied because paternity is contested, or section 3173's separate procedure for mediating a dispute over an existing custody or visitation order. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, mandatory pre-hearing (or concurrent-with-hearing) mediation mechanism -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific custody or visitation matter; whether, when, and on what trigger mediation is required varies by state.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3170(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mandatory mediation trigger
citations.quote: (a) If it appears on the face of a petition, application, or other pleading to obtain or modify a temporary or permanent custody or visitation order that custody, visitation, or both are contested, the court shall set the contested issues for mediation.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3175 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the requirement that mediation be set before or concurrent with the hearing
citations.quote: If a matter is set for mediation pursuant to this chapter, the mediation shall be set before or concurrent with the setting of the matter for hearing.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own Statement of Mediation's Purpose
clauses.body: California's mediation-of-custody-and-visitation statute states its own purposes: to reduce acrimony that may exist between the parties; to develop an agreement assuring the child close and continuing contact with both parents that is in the child's best interest, consistent with the statute's general custody provisions; and to effect a settlement of visitation rights that is in the child's best interest.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 3161), quoted in full as one contiguous provision covering its three lettered purposes; no additional independent source was found for this. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's own mediation statute says its purposes are -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific matter, and not a claim about how effectively mediation achieves these stated purposes in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3161 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statute's own statement of mediation's purposes
citations.quote: The purposes of a mediation proceeding are as follows: (a) To reduce acrimony that may exist between the parties. (b) To develop an agreement assuring the child close and continuing contact with both parents that is in the best interest of the child, consistent with Sections 3011 and 3020. (c) To effect a settlement of the issue of visitation rights of all parties that is in the best interest of the child.

clauses.title: Confidentiality of Mediation Communications
clauses.body: Under California law, mediation proceedings held under this chapter must be held in private and are confidential; communications from the parties to the mediator made in the proceeding, whether verbal or written, are official information within the meaning of Evidence Code section 1040. Where notice of mediation is given for the confidential mediation program under section 3188, that notice must itself state that all communications involving the mediator will be kept confidential between the mediator and the disputing parties.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two provisions of the same statutory chapter: section 3177 (the general confidentiality rule for mediation communications) and section 3176(c) (a notice-content requirement tied specifically to section 3188's confidential mediation program, addressed in a separate clause of this document). It does not independently analyze Evidence Code section 1040's 'official information' privilege itself, including any exceptions to that privilege, which is a separate code section this document does not verify. It also does not address how this statutory confidentiality interacts with a mediator's separate statutory authority to report an agreement, a recommendation, or unresolved issues to the court under sections 3183 through 3186, addressed in part in other clauses of this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific confidentiality rule -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific mediation.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3177 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the general confidentiality rule for mediation communications
citations.quote: Mediation proceedings pursuant to this chapter shall be held in private and shall be confidential. All communications, verbal or written, from the parties to the mediator made in the proceeding are official information within the meaning of Section 1040 of the Evidence Code.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3176(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the requirement that notice under the section 3188 confidential mediation program disclose confidentiality
citations.quote: Notice of mediation pursuant to Section 3188 shall state that all communications involving the mediator shall be kept confidential between the mediator and the disputing parties.

clauses.title: The Mediator's Availability, Qualifications, and Duties
clauses.body: Under California law, each superior court must make a mediator available for these proceedings, and is not required to institute a family conciliation court to do so. The mediator may be a member of the professional staff of a family conciliation court, probation department, or mental health services agency, or any other person or agency the court designates, and must meet the minimum qualifications required of a counselor of conciliation. In the mediation proceeding itself, the mediator has the duty to assess the needs and interests of the child involved and is entitled to interview the child when the mediator considers the interview appropriate or necessary, and the mediator is required to use their best efforts to effect a settlement of the custody or visitation dispute that is in the child's best interest.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on three independent sections of the same statutory chapter: section 3160 (availability of a mediator), section 3164 (who may serve as mediator, and minimum qualifications), and section 3180 (the mediator's duty to assess the child and best-efforts standard). It does not address a mediator's authority to exclude counsel or a domestic violence support person from the proceeding (§ 3182), or the separate uniform standards of practice the Judicial Council is required to adopt for mediators (§ 3162), which this document does not independently cover or restate. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific, checkable rules about who mediates these disputes and what the mediator is required to do -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific mediation, and not a description of any individual mediator's actual practice in a specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3160 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the requirement that each superior court make a mediator available
citations.quote: Each superior court shall make a mediator available. The court is not required to institute a family conciliation court in order to provide mediation services.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3164 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: who may serve as mediator, and the minimum qualifications required
citations.quote: (a) The mediator may be a member of the professional staff of a family conciliation court, probation department, or mental health services agency, or may be any other person or agency designated by the court. (b) The mediator shall meet the minimum qualifications required of a counselor of conciliation as provided in Section 1815.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3180 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mediator's duty to assess the child and the best-efforts settlement standard
citations.quote: (a) In mediation proceedings pursuant to this chapter, the mediator has the duty to assess the needs and interests of the child involved in the controversy, and is entitled to interview the child when the mediator considers the interview appropriate or necessary. (b) The mediator shall use their best efforts to effect a settlement of the custody or visitation dispute that is in the best interest of the child, as provided in Section 3011.

clauses.title: Recommending Mediation and the Separate Confidential Mediation Program
clauses.body: Under California law, except as provided in section 3188, a mediator may -- consistent with local court rules -- submit a recommendation to the court on custody or visitation, provided the mediator has first given the parties and their attorneys the recommendation in writing before the hearing; where a mediator is authorized to do this, the statute refers to the process as 'child custody recommending counseling' and to the mediator as a 'child custody recommending counselor.' Separately, a court selected by the Judicial Council may voluntarily adopt a confidential mediation program under which the mediator may not make a recommendation as to custody or visitation to anyone other than the disputing parties, except as the statute otherwise provides. That confidential-mediation-program section does not become operative until the Legislature appropriates funds sufficient to implement it, and by its own terms applies only in four or more superior courts the Judicial Council selects that already allow custody recommendations and have more than 1,000 family law case filings per year, though the Judicial Council may extend it to additional, smaller courts.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two independent sections of the same statutory chapter: section 3183(a) (the default, recommending model, whose availability the statute itself ties to 'local court rules') and section 3188 (the alternative confidential, non-recommending program). The statute itself does not use the shorthand terms 'recommending county' or 'non-recommending county' that California family-law practice commonly uses to describe this distinction -- those are practitioner and court-administration terms, not statutory language -- but sections 3183(a) and 3188 are the statutory provisions that produce the underlying distinction. Section 3188 is narrow on its own terms: it is conditioned on a legislative funding appropriation, and by its text applies only to a limited set of Judicial-Council-selected courts; this document does not verify whether that funding condition has been met, which courts (if any) currently operate under section 3188, or what any individual county's local court rule under section 3183(a) actually provides, since none of that is stated in the statutory text itself and was not independently researched here. This clause also does not restate section 3183(b) and (c) (a mediator's related authority to recommend a further investigation or a temporary restraining order) or section 3184 (a mediator's authority to recommend appointment of counsel for the child), which this document does not otherwise cover.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3183(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the recommending mediation model, tied to local court rules
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 3188, the mediator may, consistent with local court rules, submit a recommendation to the court as to the custody of or visitation with the child, if the mediator has first provided the parties and their attorneys, including counsel for any minor children, with the recommendations in writing in advance of the hearing.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3188(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the alternative confidential mediation program in which the mediator may not recommend to the court
citations.quote: (a)Any court selected by the Judicial Council under subdivision (c) may voluntarily adopt a confidential mediation program that provides for all of the following: (1) The mediator may not make a recommendation as to custody or visitation to anyone other than the disputing parties, except as otherwise provided in this section.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3188(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the funding-appropriation condition and the narrow scope of courts to which section 3188 applies
citations.quote: (b) This section shall become operative upon the appropriation of funds in the annual Budget Act sufficient to implement this section. (c) This section shall apply only in four or more superior courts selected by the Judicial Council that currently allow a mediator to make custody recommendations to the court and have more than 1,000 family law case filings per year. The Judicial Council may also make this section applicable to additional superior courts that have fewer than 1,000 family law case filings per year.

clauses.title: A Domestic-Violence-Specific Mediation Procedure, Separate From the Section 3044(h) Notice Requirement
clauses.body: Where mediation is required under this chapter and there has been a history of domestic violence between the parties, or a protective order is in effect, California law requires the mediator -- at the request of the party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury, or the party protected by the order -- to meet with the parties separately and at separate times; any intake form the family court services agency requires parties to complete before mediation begins must state that this separate-meeting option is available on request. Separately, domestic violence cases are required to be handled by Family Court Services under a written protocol the Judicial Council approves, and the Judicial Council is required to adopt guidelines for services -- other than mediation itself -- that courts or counties may offer parents who have been unable to resolve their disputes.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two independent sections of the same statutory chapter: section 3181 (the separate-meeting procedure and related intake-form disclosure) and section 3170(b) (the separate written protocol and services-guidelines requirement). It is deliberately distinct from, and does not restate, this project's Domestic Violence Custody Presumption document's clause on Family Code section 3044(h), which requires a court to inform the parties of section 3044 itself and give them a copy of it before custody mediation where a party has alleged the other perpetrated domestic violence within the meaning of that section -- a different statutory section, addressed to a different notice (of the section 3044 presumption, not of a right to be interviewed separately), and located outside this mediation chapter. This document does not verify the content of the separate written protocol section 3170(b) requires the Judicial Council to approve, or the guidelines it requires the Judicial Council to adopt, since neither is specified in the statutory text itself. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of specific, mediation-chapter-internal domestic-violence procedures -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific proceeding, and not a claim that these are the only domestic-violence-related safeguards that could apply to a specific mediation.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3181 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mediator's duty to meet with the parties separately and at separate times on request, and the related intake-form disclosure
citations.quote: (a) In a proceeding in which mediation is required pursuant to this chapter, where there has been a history of domestic violence between the parties or where a protective order as defined in Section 6218 is in effect, at the request of the party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury or protected by the order, the mediator appointed pursuant to this chapter shall meet with the parties separately and at separate times. (b) Any intake form that an agency charged with providing family court services requires the parties to complete before the commencement of mediation shall state that, if a party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury or a party protected by a protective order so requests, the mediator will meet with the parties separately and at separate times.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3170(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the separate written domestic-violence protocol and services-guidelines requirement
citations.quote: Domestic violence cases shall be handled by Family Court Services in accordance with a separate written protocol approved by the Judicial Council. The Judicial Council shall adopt guidelines for services, other than services provided under this chapter, that courts or counties may offer to parents who have been unable to resolve their disputes. These services may include, but are not limited to, parent education programs, booklets, video recordings, or referrals to additional community resources.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}} ended on {{separationDate}}. This information sheet describes, as a matter of California law, how severance pay, dismissal pay, wage-continuation payments, and payments made "in lieu of notice" can affect eligibility for California unemployment insurance benefits. This is a separate legal question from whether a claimant is disqualified under Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256 for voluntarily leaving work without good cause or being discharged for misconduct, which is addressed in a separate document in this set. A payment covered by this document can affect the weeks for which a claimant is eligible to receive benefits even where no § 1256 disqualification applies at all, and § 1256's disqualification can apply even where no severance or similar payment was ever made. This document does not determine that any payment {{employeeName}} received or will receive from {{companyName}} does or does not affect {{employeeName}}'s own eligibility for benefits, and it is not itself a claim, weekly certification, or appeal filed with the EDD.

clauses.title: The Statutory Test: 'Unemployed' and 'Wages Payable With Respect To' a Week
clauses.body: California does not determine unemployment insurance eligibility for severance-type payments through a single dedicated allocation formula tied to the claimant's normal weekly wage. Instead, benefits are payable only to individuals who are "unemployed" and otherwise eligible under the code's general eligibility part, and a separate statute defines when an individual is "unemployed": among other conditions, any week during which the individual performs no services and with respect to which no wages are payable to the individual. For this definitional purpose only, the same statute defines "wages" broadly, as any and all compensation for personal services, whether performed as an employee, an independent contractor, a juror, or a witness (with a narrow carve-out for certain military duty pay not relevant here). Because a post-employment payment can be "payable with respect to" a given week even though no work is performed that week, whether a severance-type payment defeats eligibility for a particular week turns on whether that payment counts as "wages" under this definition and is payable with respect to that week — not on any statutory formula that spreads a lump sum across weeks based on the employee's ordinary weekly pay rate.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text — Unemployment Insurance Code § 1251 and § 1252, both directly fetched and verified twice from the California Legislative Information website using two different User-Agent strings, with byte-identical results after whitespace normalization — used as real evidence of the general statutory mechanism that determines whether a post-employment payment can affect a claimant's eligibility for a specific week. It is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular claimant's situation, and it does not determine that any specific payment received by any specific claimant is or is not payable 'with respect to' any specific week. Two of the three citations below (the § 1252(a)(1) and § 1252(c) quotations) are subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 1252, and are treated as one source rather than independent corroboration; the § 1251 citation is to a separate, independent section. Section 1252 contains additional eligibility tests not quoted here — a reduced-hours/partial-earnings test, a jury-duty/witness-service test, and an implementing-regulations provision — none of which concern severance-type payments and none of which this document addresses. How this general 'wages payable with respect to a week' test has actually been applied to severance pay, dismissal pay, wage-continuation pay, and pay in lieu of notice specifically is addressed in separate clauses below; this clause states only the general statutory test itself.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1251 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: Unemployment compensation benefits are payable from the Unemployment Fund to unemployed individuals who are eligible under this part.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1252(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: Any week during which he or she performs no services and with respect to which no wages are payable to him or her.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1252(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: For the purpose of this section only “wages” includes any and all compensation for personal services whether performed as an employee or as an independent contractor or as a juror or as a witness, but does not include any payment received by a member of the National Guard or reserve component of the armed forces for inactive duty training, annual training, or emergency state active duty.

clauses.title: What Unemployment Insurance Code § 1255.3 Actually Governs: The Pension Offset, Not Severance Pay
clauses.body: Unemployment Insurance Code § 1255.3, as currently in force, does not govern severance pay, dismissal pay, wage-continuation pay, or pay in lieu of notice. Its subject is different: for any week beginning after March 31, 1980 that falls in a period during which a claimant is receiving a governmental or other pension, retirement or retired pay, annuity, or similar periodic payment based on the claimant's previous work, the statute requires the claimant's unemployment compensation benefits, extended duration benefits, and federal-state extended benefits to be reduced — though never below zero — by the amount of that pension-type payment reasonably attributable to that week. The statute goes on, in subdivisions not quoted here, to limit when this pension offset applies (among other things, to pensions maintained or contributed to by a base-period or chargeable employer, subject to further conditions) and to state that it does not apply at all if the claimant made any personal contribution to the pension or retirement plan. None of this concerns severance, dismissal, or wage-continuation pay, which are addressed in the separate clauses below.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text — Unemployment Insurance Code § 1255.3(a) — directly fetched and verified twice from the California Legislative Information website using two different User-Agent strings, with byte-identical results after whitespace normalization. This document's drafter was asked to verify, rather than assume, that § 1255.3 governs how severance, dismissal, or wage-continuation pay affects unemployment insurance eligibility. Having fetched and read the actual current statutory text directly, the honest finding is that this assumption was incorrect: § 1255.3 is, and on its face has always been since its operative 1980 date, a pension/retirement-pay offset provision, unrelated to severance or dismissal pay. This clause quotes only subdivision (a), the operative reduction rule; subdivisions (b) through (e) (the federal-conformity trigger, the two-part test limiting when the offset applies, the no-personal-contribution exception, and a retroactivity clause) are described above only in general terms and are not quoted verbatim here. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1255.3); no additional independent source was sought for it, since its only role in this document is to state accurately what it does and does not cover. The statutory provisions that do govern severance, dismissal, and wage-continuation pay are identified and cited in the other clauses of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1255.3(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: (a) Except as provided by subdivisions (c) and (d), the amount of unemployment compensation benefits, extended duration benefits, and federal-state extended benefits payable to an individual for any week which begins after March 31, 1980, and which begins in a period with respect to which that individual is receiving a governmental or other pension, retirement or retired pay, annuity, or any other similar periodic payment which is based on the previous work of the individual shall be reduced, but not below zero, by an amount equal to the amount of the pension, retirement or retired pay, annuity, or other payment, which is reasonably attributable to that week.

clauses.title: Payments Under an Employer-Wide or Group Plan Are Not Treated as 'Wages'
clauses.body: A separate statute carves out a category of post-employment payments that are not treated as "wages" or "compensation for personal services" for unemployment insurance purposes at all, regardless of the general § 1252 wages test described above: payments to an individual under a plan or system that an employer has established for its employees generally, or for a class or group of its employees, for the purpose of supplementing unemployment compensation benefits. Benefits are not to be denied or reduced because a claimant received payments under such an arrangement or plan. On its own text, this statute is written in terms of employer-established "plans" or "systems" that supplement unemployment benefits for a class or group of employees; it does not use the words "severance" or "dismissal." How this provision has actually been read to reach group severance and dismissal pay specifically is addressed in the following clause.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text — Unemployment Insurance Code § 1265 — directly fetched and verified twice from the California Legislative Information website using two different User-Agent strings, with byte-identical results after whitespace normalization. This clause cites a single statutory section; no additional independent statutory source was sought for it. The limitation disclosed in the body is a genuine one: because the statutory text itself does not mention severance or dismissal pay by name, this document does not treat § 1265's plain text alone as establishing that severance or dismissal pay is covered by it — that construction is addressed, with its own separate sourcing and its own disclosed limitations, in the next clause. This document does not address every plan or arrangement that might qualify as a § 1265 'plan or system' (for example, formal SUB-pay trust arrangements bargained into a union contract), only the specific severance/dismissal-pay application at issue here.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1265 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provisions of this division, payments to an individual under a plan or system established by an employer which makes provisions for his employees generally, or for a class or group of his employees, for the purpose of supplementing unemployment compensation benefits shall not be construed to be wages or compensation for personal services under this division and benefits payable under this division shall not be denied or reduced because of the receipt of payments under such arrangements or plans.

clauses.title: Group Severance or Dismissal Pay Under a Plan or Bargaining Agreement
clauses.body: The California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board, in a published precedent decision, has construed § 1265 (described in the clause above) as reaching severance and dismissal pay in a specific circumstance: where the payment results from a plan or system, or from a collective bargaining agreement, and is available to a class or group of employees, the Board treats it as falling within § 1265 and therefore not as "wages" that would defeat unemployment eligibility. The Board's decision traces this construction to the California Supreme Court's 1965 decision in Powell v. California Department of Employment, which held that the Legislature's declared intent in enacting § 1265 was broad enough to reach dismissal and severance payments, and rejected an argument that whether a payment counted as "wages" should turn on the label an employer's plan documents gave it rather than on the plan's actual character.
clauses.gap: The primary source directly fetched and verified for this clause (twice, byte-identical across two User-Agent strings) is California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4 (Feb. 15, 1968), a public administrative precedent decision published as a PDF on the Board's own website. Both citations below come from that same document and are not independent corroborating sources. One of the two citations reproduces language the Board itself attributes to, and quotes from, the California Supreme Court's opinion in Powell v. California Dept. of Employment (1965) 63 A.C. 99. This document's drafter attempted to independently locate and read that Powell opinion directly from a primary case-law source — Justia, FindLaw, and CourtListener were each tried — but every attempt was blocked by network access restrictions before the opinion's text could be read, and CourtListener's own search tool separately returned a daily rate-limit error. Rather than cite the Powell opinion as though it had been independently read and verified, this document sources the quoted Powell language only as it is itself quoted, verified, and reproduced within the P-B-4 precedent decision that was actually fetched and read — a genuine limitation disclosed here rather than concealed. This clause does not address how a plan's severance/dismissal-pay coverage of only some, rather than a genuine class or group, of an employer's employees would be treated, and it does not itself determine that any specific employer's severance arrangement does or does not meet this plan-or-agreement, class-or-group standard. An administrative precedent decision, as construed here, is not itself a California appellate court opinion, though the Board is bound by it and it is designated as precedential by the Board's own statutory authority.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd., Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4, In re Claim of Arthur Harman (Feb. 15, 1968)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4
citations.quote: As we interpret the Powell case, the courts have equated severance pay or dismissal pay with the type of payments covered by section 1265 of the code. If such payments result from a plan or system or from the provisions of a collective bargaining agreement and are available to a class or group of employees, then the payments do not constitute wages.

citations.case: Powell v. California Dept. of Employment (1965) 63 A.C. 99, as quoted in Cal. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd., Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4 (Feb. 15, 1968)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4
citations.quote: In essence, respondents would draw a material distinction between the supplemental unemployment benefit plans and severance or dismissal pay on the basis of the label by which the additional benefits are described in the documents which provide for the benefits. But there would appear to be no reason why collective bargaining agreements which now provide for severance or dismissal pay could not be modified to give such payments a different label and concededly qualify the discharged employee for his full unemployment insurance benefits without doing violence to the integrity of the Unemployment Insurance Fund or any party involved. To resolve the issue according to the label attached, as respondents urge, would accord greater weight to form than to substance and such a resolution is not in keeping with the obvious legislative intent expressed in section 1265 to broaden the coverage of unemployment insurance benefits.

clauses.title: Individually Continued Wages and Pay 'In Lieu of Notice': A Different Result
clauses.body: The same Board precedent decision addressed a payment that did not fit the group-plan category above and reached the opposite result. There, an individual employee's employer kept him on the payroll at full salary for a period after he was told his job responsibilities had ended, paying him on the same dates and in the same amounts he would have received had he kept working, rather than as a single lump sum. The Board held these were not § 1265 severance or dismissal payments and did not fit the pattern of a normal lump-sum severance payment; instead, because each payment was tied to the specific pay period for which a normal wage payment would otherwise have been due, the Board held the payments were "wages" payable "with respect to" those specific weeks under § 1252, defeating the individual's eligibility for those weeks. Separately, the Board addressed the employer's argument that part of the payment was owed "in lieu of notice" of dismissal, and held that a payment is not meaningfully "in lieu of notice" unless the employee actually had a right to advance notice — whether by contract or by an employer custom or practice substantial enough to create an enforceable expectation of it; absent such a right, calling a payment "notice pay" does not by itself take it outside the § 1252 wages analysis either.
clauses.gap: The source directly fetched and verified for this clause (twice, byte-identical across two User-Agent strings) is the same California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4 (Feb. 15, 1968) cited in the clause above; all citations below come from that one document and are not independent corroborating sources of one another, though they corroborate the § 1251/§ 1252 statutory text quoted in an earlier clause of this document. This decision is now more than five decades old; this document's drafter independently re-verified, by directly fetching current statutory text, that §§ 1251, 1252, and 1265 as construed in this decision remain in force in materially the same operative terms today (see the earlier clauses of this document), but did not attempt to verify whether any more recent published decision has refined, limited, or distinguished this particular precedent's 'wage continuation' label or its in-lieu-of-notice holding, and none is cited here. This document does not determine that any specific payment any specific claimant received was, or was not, paid 'with respect to' any specific week, was or was not part of a genuine class-or-group plan, or was or was not owed under any actual notice obligation — those are fact-specific determinations the EDD, a referee, or the Board would make case by case.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd., Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4, In re Claim of Arthur Harman (Feb. 15, 1968)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4
citations.quote: The issues in this case are whether the payments made to the claimant upon termination of the employment relationship constitute "wages," and if so, to what period should the payments be allocated.

citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4
citations.quote: The payments in the present case were not made in a lump sum, usable immediately in their entirety like normal severance payments. They were paid in installments at the regular wage-payment times, as though the claimant's services had been continuing.

citations.quote: More important than the label, it is clear that each payment was made for the period in which services would have been furnished to earn a normal wage payment due at the time when the wage continuation payments were made.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the California statutory will created by California Probate Code Section 6200 et seq. -- a will form that the California Legislature drafted and set out verbatim in the statute itself -- for {{testatorName}}, a resident of {{testatorCounty}} County, California, who may be considering whether to use it. It states facts about this specific form under California law generally. It does not determine whether this form fits {{testatorName}}'s particular estate, and it does not advise on whether to adopt it.

clauses.title: What a California Statutory Will Is
clauses.body: California law recognizes one specific, codified will form: the California statutory will. Its content is fixed by the Probate Code itself, in Section 6240, rather than being freely drafted the way a custom will is. The statute defines a "testator," for purposes of this specific instrument, as a person choosing to adopt a California statutory will. There is only one California statutory will, and it consists of the text of the Section 6240 form (apart from that section's introductory questions and answers), together -- by reference -- with the statute's own definitions and rules of construction, whichever property disposition clauses the testator selects on the form, and a fixed set of mandatory clauses set out elsewhere in the statute. If {{testatorName}} were to adopt this form, {{testatorName}} would be adopting this same fixed instrument, not a custom-drafted one.
clauses.gap: Three separate statutory sections are cited here (Section 6200, Section 6201, and Section 6223), not subdivisions of a single section; Section 6223 itself has its own subdivisions (a) and (b)(1), quoted together below because they directly define what the statutory will is and what it includes. This clause does not reproduce the operative fill-in-the-blank text of the Section 6240 form itself: the version of Section 6240 published by the Legislature's own online law database (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) does not carry that text. In its place, the fetched page states, verbatim: "NOTICE OF INCOMPLETE TEXT: The California Statutory Will appears in the hard-copy publication of the chaptered bill. See Sec. 88, Chapter 50 (pp. 77-82), Statutes of 2016." So the actual paragraph-and-blank text of the form is not available from this source and is not quoted or reproduced anywhere in this corpus; a separate drafting clause in this document describes the form's structure from the introductory material that is published, without presenting that description as the form's own text.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6200 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, definitions and rules of construction govern this chapter
citations.quote: Unless the provision or context clearly requires otherwise, these definitions and rules of construction govern the construction of this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6201 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, definition of "testator" for the statutory will
citations.quote: “Testator” means a person choosing to adopt a California statutory will.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6223(a)-(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, there is only one California statutory will and what it includes
citations.quote: (a) There is only one California statutory will.  (b) The California statutory will includes all of the following:  (1) The contents of the California statutory will form set out in Section 6240, excluding the questions and answers at the beginning of the California statutory will.

clauses.title: How a Statutory Will Must Be Executed
clauses.body: The statutory will is not executed under the same statute that governs a custom-drafted will; the Probate Code sets a separate, self-contained execution rule for it. Any individual of sound mind and over the age of 18 -- which would include {{testatorName}}, if that description applies -- may execute a California statutory will. To execute it, the testator completes the form's blanks and signs the will, and each witness must observe the testator's signing and sign the witness's own name in the testator's presence. A completed attestation clause signed by two or more witnesses satisfies the separate Probate Code requirement for proving a witnessed will at probate.
clauses.gap: Three separate sections are cited (Section 6220, Section 6221, and Section 6222), not subdivisions of one section. Section 6221's text, as quoted, requires each witness to observe the testator's signing and sign in the testator's presence, but -- unlike the general will-execution statute already cited elsewhere in this corpus (Cal. Prob. Code Section 6110(c)(1), which expressly requires the witnesses to be present at the same time as each other) -- Section 6221's text does not itself state whether the two witnesses must be present at the same time as one another; this clause does not resolve that difference and does not assume Section 6110's simultaneous-presence requirement carries over. Section 6222 cross-references Section 8220 of the Probate Code (a proof-of-will-at-probate provision) rather than restating its text; Section 8220 was not independently fetched or verified for this clause, and only the fact of the cross-reference is stated. A separate clause in this document covers Section 6226(c), which provides an additional, "notwithstanding Section 6110," path to validating a defectively executed statutory will.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6220 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, who may execute a California statutory will
citations.quote: Any individual of sound mind and over the age of 18 may execute a California statutory will under the provisions of this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6221 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, execution requirements specific to the statutory will
citations.quote: A California statutory will shall be executed only as follows: (a) The testator shall complete the appropriate blanks and shall sign the will. (b) Each witness shall observe the testator’s signing and each witness shall sign his or her name in the presence of the testator.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6222 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, attestation clause satisfies the proof-at-probate requirement
citations.quote: The execution of the attestation clause provided in the California statutory will by two or more witnesses satisfies Section 8220.

clauses.title: What the Statutory Will Form States It Is Not Designed For
clauses.body: The statutory will form's own text places real limits on what it is designed to do. It states that it is a simple will, not designed to reduce death taxes or other taxes, and that a person should talk to a lawyer about tax planning instead, especially if the person's assets will be worth more than $600,000 (or the amount currently excluded from federal estate tax at death), the person owns business-related assets, wants to create a trust fund for children's education or other purposes, owns assets in another state, wants to disinherit a spouse, domestic partner, or descendants, or has valuable pension or profit-sharing plan interests. The same text states that a person completing the form may only fill in its blanks -- adding or crossing out any other words risks making the will invalid or having the added or crossed-out words disregarded by a court -- and, separately, states that trusts generally are "too complicated to be used in this Statutory Will."
clauses.gap: All three quotes below come from the same statutory section, Section 6240 -- specifically from the numbered questions-and-answers text (questions 8, 9, and 20) that the statute places before the form itself. Section 6223(b)(1), quoted in another clause in this document, expressly excludes that questions-and-answers text from the definition of "the California statutory will" -- meaning this limitations text is explanatory material the Legislature placed in the statute, not itself an operative clause of the will. The $600,000 figure is the fixed number written into the statute; the statute's own text ties the actual test to whichever figure is "the current amount excluded from estate tax under federal law" at the testator's death, which is a materially larger, adjusting figure today, so the $600,000 number by itself is not a current test. This clause does not cover every scenario the questions-and-answers text flags as a reason not to use the form (for example, its separate caution about stepchildren and foster children who have not been adopted).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6240 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, statutory will form's own caution against tax planning, business assets, trusts, out-of-state assets, disinheriting a spouse or partner or descendants, and pension interests
citations.quote:
8. Are there any reasons why I should NOT use this Statutory Will?  Yes. This is a simple Will. It is not designed to reduce death taxes or other taxes. Talk to a lawyer to do tax planning, especially if (i) your assets will be worth more than $600,000 or the current amount excluded from estate tax under federal law at your death, (ii) you own business-related assets, (iii) you want to create a trust fund for your children’s education or other purposes, (iv) you own assets in some other state, (v) you want to disinherit your spouse, domestic partner, or descendants, or (vi) you have valuable interests in pension or profit-sharing plans. You should talk to a lawyer who
				knows about estate planning if this Will does not meet your needs.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6240 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, statutory will form's own instruction that only the blanks may be filled in
citations.quote: 9. May I add or cross out any words on this Will?  No. If you do, the Will may be invalid or the court may ignore the crossed out or added words. You may only fill in the blanks. You may amend this Will by a separate document (called a codicil). Talk to a lawyer if you want to do something with your assets which is not allowed in this form.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6240 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, statutory will form's own statement that trusts are too complicated for this form
citations.quote:
20. What is a trust?  There are many kinds of trusts, including trusts created by Wills (called “testamentary trusts”) and trusts created during your lifetime (called “revocable living trusts”). Both kinds of trusts are long-term arrangements
				in which a manager (called a “trustee”) invests and manages assets for someone (called a “beneficiary”) on the terms you specify. Trusts are too complicated to be used in this Statutory Will. You should see a lawyer if you want to create a trust.

clauses.title: Effect of an Incompletely or Improperly Completed Statutory Will
clauses.body: The statute directly addresses what happens when the form's property disposition clauses are selected incorrectly or the form is altered outside its instructions. If more than one of certain alternative disposition clauses is selected where the form calls for a single choice, no gift is made under that clause; and if the form's residuary-estate clause has more than one option selected, or none, the residuary estate instead passes to the testator's heirs at law, determined as though the testator had not made a will. Separately, any addition to or deletion from the statutory will form, made other than by following the form's own instructions, is given effect only if clear and convincing evidence shows it would carry out the testator's clear intent; absent such a showing, a court may either disregard the addition or deletion or find that all or part of the will is invalid, whichever better matches the testator's intent. Notwithstanding the general will-execution statute that otherwise governs, a document executed on the statutory will form can still be held valid as a will despite a defect if clear and convincing evidence establishes that the testator signed the form, that the testator knew of and approved its contents and intended it to have testamentary effect, and that the testamentary intent reflected in the document is clear.
clauses.gap: Section 6224 and Section 6226 are two separate sections; Section 6226(b) and Section 6226(c), both quoted below, are two subdivisions of that same section. Section 6226(c)'s cross-reference to "Section 6110" is to the general will-execution statute already cited elsewhere in this corpus, in the Last Will and Testament document's execution-requirements clause; this clause states only that Section 6226(c) operates notwithstanding Section 6110, and does not restate Section 6110's text here. This clause does not cover Section 6226(a) (the general statement that a statutory will may be revoked or amended by codicil like other wills).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6224 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, effect of selecting more than one, or no, disposition clause
citations.quote: If more than one property disposition clause appearing in paragraphs 2 or 3 of a California statutory will is selected, no gift is made. If more than one property disposition clause in paragraph 5 of a California statutory will form is selected, or if none is selected, the residuary estate of a testator who signs a California statutory will shall be distributed to the testator’s heirs as if the testator did not make a will.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6226(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, effect of additions to or deletions from the statutory will form
citations.quote: Any additions to or deletions from the California statutory will on the face of the California statutory will form, other than in accordance with the instructions, shall be given effect only where clear and convincing evidence shows that they would effectuate the clear intent of the testator.  In the absence of such a showing, the court either may determine that the addition or deletion is ineffective and shall be disregarded, or may determine that all or a portion of the California statutory will is invalid, whichever is more likely to be consistent with the intent of the testator.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6226(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, validating a defectively executed statutory will notwithstanding Section 6110
citations.quote: Notwithstanding Section 6110, a document executed on a California statutory will form is valid as a will if all of the following requirements are shown to be satisfied by clear and convincing evidence:  (1) The form is signed by the testator.  (2) The court is satisfied that the testator knew and approved of the contents of the will and intended it to have testamentary effect.  (3) The testamentary intent of the maker as reflected in the document is clear.

clauses.title: Effect of a Later Divorce or Dissolution on a Statutory Will
clauses.body: As with wills generally, a later dissolution or annulment of the testator's marriage, or termination of the testator's registered domestic partnership, has an automatic effect on a previously executed California statutory will: it revokes any disposition of property the will made to the former spouse or partner, and any nomination of the former spouse or partner as executor, trustee, guardian, or custodian. If the testator later remarries that same former spouse, or re-enters a registered domestic partnership with that same former partner, the revoked disposition or nomination is revived.
clauses.gap: This is Cal. Prob. Code Section 6227(a) -- a provision written specifically for the statutory will, in the same chapter of the Probate Code as the rest of this document's citations. It runs in parallel to, but is a textually separate statute from, Cal. Prob. Code Section 6122, the general will's divorce-revocation rule already cited elsewhere in this corpus (the Last Will and Testament document's will_revocation_by_divorce clause); this clause does not independently verify Section 6122's text or confirm the two provisions are worded identically. This clause covers only subdivision (a); it does not cover subdivisions (b) through (d), which address how the revoked property passes, define "dissolution or annulment" for this purpose, and carve out dissolutions or annulments finalized before January 1, 1985.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6227(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, revocation of dispositions and nominations to a former spouse or partner
citations.quote: If after executing a California statutory will the testator’s marriage is dissolved or annulled, or the testator’s registered domestic partnership is terminated, the dissolution, annulment, or termination revokes any disposition of property made by the will to the former spouse and any nomination of the former spouse as executor, trustee, guardian, or custodian made by the will. If any disposition or nomination is revoked solely by this section, it is revived by the testator’s remarriage to, or entry into a subsequent registered domestic partnership with, the former spouse.

clauses.title: Structure of the Statutory Will Form (Informational Only)
clauses.body: This is a description of the California statutory will form's structure, drawn from the introductory questions-and-answers and instructions the Legislature placed in Probate Code Section 6240 -- it is not the form itself, and completing it is not the same as completing a California statutory will. As that introductory material describes it: the form must be dated and signed by the testator, and signed by two witnesses who follow the notice to witnesses printed on the form; the testator fills in blanks to name an executor (and may name an alternate) and to say whether the executor must post a bond; the testator fills in blanks to select property disposition clauses for specific gifts and for the residuary estate, choosing among the alternatives the form provides; and, if the testator has children under 18, the testator may fill in blanks to nominate a guardian (and an alternate) and, separately, to name a custodian to manage a minor's or young adult's assets under the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act. The form's introductory material states that a person should not add words to the form or cross words out, beyond filling in the blanks it provides.

clauses.title: Certification of Understanding
About This CalSavers Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's CalSavers Retirement Savings Program, established under Government Code § 100000 et seq. (Title 21 of the Government Code, "The CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust Act," originally enacted as the California Secure Choice Retirement Savings Trust Act), as it relates to {{companyName}}, which reports approximately {{employeeCount}} employees in California, and to {{employeeName}}. It states facts drawn from the statute's own text about what the CalSavers program is, which employers the statute requires to register and by when, the statutory exemption for employers that already sponsor a qualifying retirement plan, the automatic-enrollment and opt-out mechanism available to an eligible employee such as {{employeeName}}, and the penalty a noncompliant employer may face.

This information sheet does not determine whether {{companyName}} is or is not an "eligible employer" under the statute, whether any plan {{companyName}} offers qualifies for the statutory exemption, whether {{companyName}}'s own registration deadline has already passed, whether {{employeeName}} is or is not an "eligible employee," or what {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} should do about any of the facts it describes.

clauses.title: What the CalSavers Program Is
clauses.body: The CalSavers Retirement Savings Trust is a trust "administered by the [CalSavers Retirement Savings] board for the purpose of promoting greater retirement savings for California private employees in a convenient, voluntary, low-cost, and portable manner." The CalSavers Retirement Savings Program itself is statutorily defined to "include, as determined by the board, one or more payroll deduction IRA arrangements." A "payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement" is defined as an arrangement by which an employer allows employees to remit payroll-deduction contributions to a retirement savings program, which may include an IRA, and in the case of a payroll deduction IRA arrangement, to remit specifically to an IRA. The statute defines "IRA" to mean an individual retirement account or individual retirement annuity under 26 U.S.C. § 408(a), 408(b), or 408A — the last of which is the Internal Revenue Code section governing Roth IRAs.
clauses.gap: The four citations below are all subdivisions or sections of the same statutory title (Government Code, Title 21) rather than independent outside sources: § 100004(a) (trust purpose), § 100008 (program definition), § 100000(h) (payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement definition), and § 100000(e) (IRA definition). The statutory text fetched for this document does not itself state that a Roth IRA (26 U.S.C. § 408A) is the default account type for a CalSavers participant who does not choose otherwise — that default is understood to be set by the CalSavers Retirement Savings Board's implementing regulations (Title 10, California Code of Regulations, Chapter 15, commencing at § 10000), which this document was not able to independently fetch and verify from a primary regulatory source with the same two-fetch discipline used for the Government Code text below. This clause therefore states only that the statute's own "IRA" definition includes the Internal Revenue Code section governing Roth IRAs, and does not itself assert that Roth is the default. This clause also does not cover the program's governance structure (the nine-member CalSavers Retirement Savings Board, § 100002), the trust's fund segregation and investment powers (§ 100004(b)-(f), § 100010), or the separate Retirement Investments Clearinghouse and vendor-registration system (§§ 100016-100030), none of which this document addresses.

clauses.title: Which Employers Must Register, and By When
clauses.body:
The statute phases in the registration requirement by reference to the size of an "eligible employer," measured in "eligible employees," and to the date the CalSavers board opened the program for enrollment. Within 12 months after that date, eligible employers with more than 100 eligible employees, and that do not offer a retirement savings program under subdivision (h), were required to have a payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement in place. Within 24 months, the threshold dropped to eligible employers with more than 50 eligible employees. Within 36 months, the threshold dropped to eligible employers with five or more employees. And "by December 31, 2025," the requirement extended to eligible employers with one or more eligible employees. The board "may extend the time limits" set by these four deadlines "in its discretion."

A statutory "eligible employer" is a business, industry, profession, trade, or other enterprise operating in California — for profit or not for profit — that has at least one eligible employee and satisfies the requirements to establish or participate in a payroll deposit retirement savings arrangement; the definition excludes sole proprietorships, self-employed individuals, and other business entities that employ no one but the business's own owners, as well as the federal government, the state, any county, any municipal corporation, and the state's own units or instrumentalities. An "eligible employee" is a person employed by an eligible employer, but the definition excludes an employee covered under the federal Railway Labor Act (or otherwise engaged in interstate commerce beyond the state's legislative power) and an employee for whom an employer makes contributions to a Taft-Hartley pension trust fund — so the count that triggers each deadline is a count of statutorily "eligible" employees, not necessarily an employer's total headcount.

Separately, an employer that already "provides an employer-sponsored retirement plan, such as a defined benefit plan or a 401(k), Simplified Employee Pension (SEP) plan, or Savings Incentive Match Plan for Employees (SIMPLE) plan, or that offers an automatic enrollment payroll deduction IRA," is exempt from the CalSavers registration requirement altogether, provided the plan or IRA "qualifies for favorable federal income tax treatment under the federal Internal Revenue Code," and an employer "retain[s] the option at all times" to set up such a qualifying plan instead of registering for CalSavers.
clauses.gap:
Government Code § 100032(b), (c), (d), (e), (f), and (h) are all subdivisions of a single statutory section, not independent sources; § 100000(d)(1) and (d)(3), and § 100000(c), are subdivisions of a separate section (the definitions section) cited here because the deadlines in § 100032 turn on those defined terms. This document independently confirmed a cross-reference discrepancy in the currently codified text: § 100000(d)(3) says an "eligible employer" does not include an employer that provides a qualifying retirement savings program "as described in subdivision (g) of Section 100032," but the actual exemption for an employer-sponsored plan is codified in § 100032, subdivision (h), not subdivision (g) — subdivision (g) of the current text instead governs the automatic-enrollment and opt-out mechanism. This document quotes both provisions exactly as codified and does not resolve or correct the apparent uncorrected cross-reference; it flags the discrepancy rather than assuming which subdivision letter is the "right" one. 

Because today's date is after December 31, 2025, the final phase-in deadline in subdivision (e) has, by its terms, already passed for an eligible employer that was not otherwise exempt — but this document did not independently research whether the CalSavers Retirement Savings Board has since exercised its discretion under subdivision (f) to extend that or any other deadline, and takes no position on whether any particular employer's specific deadline has or has not passed. This clause also does not cover: the date the board actually "opened the program for enrollment" (a factual/historical question this document did not research, since the statute itself does not state that date); the special in-home-supportive-services employer-of-record provisions of § 100046; or § 100043's separate conditions under which the board may operate the program at all (keeping it from being classified as an ERISA plan).

clauses.title: CalSavers Is Not an Employer-Sponsored Plan
clauses.body:
The statute states directly that employers registered for CalSavers are not the plan's sponsor: "Employers shall not be a fiduciary, or considered to be a fiduciary, over the trust or the program. The program is a state-administered program, not an employer-sponsored program. ... An employer shall not bear responsibility for the administration, investment, or investment performance of the program. An employer shall not be liable with regard to investment returns, program design, and benefits paid to program participants." The statute separately provides that "[e]mployers shall not have any liability for an employee's decision to participate in, or opt out of, the program, or for the investment decisions of employees whose assets are deposited in the program." The board is required to disclose the same facts to employees directly: the employee information packet the board designs must state that "[t]his retirement program is not sponsored by the employer, and therefore the employer is not responsible for the plan or liable as a plan sponsor," and that employees seeking financial advice should contact financial advisors rather than their employer, "that employers do not provide financial advice," and "that employees are not to contact their employers for financial advice."

Nothing in the statute requires a registered employer to make any financial contribution to a participating employee's account. A participating employer instead "allow[s]" employee payroll deductions to be remitted to the program; the board's own powers separately include the power to "[a]llow participating employers to make their own contributions to their employees' IRAs," but only if permitted under the Internal Revenue Code and only if doing so would not cause the program to be treated as an employee benefit plan under the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) — describing an option, not a requirement.
clauses.gap: § 100034(a) and § 100034(b) are subdivisions of the same statutory section; § 100014(c) is a different section (governing the content the board must include in the mandatory employee disclosure form) and § 100012(j) is a different section still (a board power provision), so all four citations below draw from three genuinely distinct sections of the same title, not one source repeated. This clause does not cover § 100034(c) or (d), which address a voluntary employer contribution's effect on the rest of this liability framework and an employer's civil liability for acting under board regulations defining employer roles, or § 100043, which separately conditions the program's operation on the board avoiding ERISA classification in the first place. This document takes no position on whether CalSavers, or an employer's participation in it, is in fact preempted by ERISA or any other federal law — it reports only what the California statute itself says about an employer's liability and fiduciary status.

The program is a state-administered program, not an employer-sponsored program. If the program is subsequently found to be preempted by any federal law or regulation, employers shall not be liable as plan sponsors. An employer shall not bear responsibility for the administration, investment, or investment performance of the program. An employer shall not be liable with regard to investment returns, program design, and benefits paid to program participants.

clauses.title: Automatic Enrollment, Default Contribution, and the Opt-Out Mechanism
clauses.body:
The statute automatically enrolls an eligible employee of a participating employer: "Each eligible employee shall be enrolled in the program unless the employee elects not to participate in the program. An eligible employee may elect to opt out of the program by making a notation on the opt-out form or by contacting the program by telephone." At least once every two years after the program's initial implementation, the board may designate an open enrollment period in which an employee who previously opted out is again given the disclosure and opt-out forms and may choose to enroll or opt out again. An employee "may also terminate their participation in the program at any time" by the same opt-out mechanisms.

Absent a different election by the employee, "a participating employee shall contribute 3 percent of the employee's annual salary or wages to the program." The board may adjust that default by regulation, but only to somewhere between 2 and 5 percent. The board may also implement annual automatic escalation of a participant's contribution rate, subject to statutory limits: escalated contributions may not exceed 8 percent of salary, and escalation may raise a participant's contribution rate by no more than one percentage point of salary per calendar year; a participant may separately opt out of automatic escalation and set their own contribution percentage.
clauses.gap: § 100032(g)(1), (g)(2), (i), (j), (k), and (l) are all subdivisions of the single statutory section already discussed in this document's coverage-and-deadlines clause, not independent sources — they are treated here as one clause because they together describe a single mechanism (automatic enrollment and its opt-out and contribution-rate features) rather than the separate question of which employers must register. This clause does not cover the content or format the board must give the required disclosure and opt-out forms themselves (§ 100014), the process by which an individual or an employee of a nonparticipating employer may separately enroll and contribute (§ 100012(k)), or any Internal Revenue Code contribution limit that independently caps how much may be contributed to an IRA in a given year regardless of the percentage elected — this document did not research current IRA contribution limits under federal tax law.

clauses.title: Penalty for Employer Noncompliance
clauses.body: The CalSavers Retirement Savings Board has "the power and duties necessary to administer the enforcement of employer compliance with this title." Where an employer fails to allow its eligible employees to participate in the program, the board must first issue "a notice of penalty application." A penalty attaches only after a further step: "[e]ach eligible employer that, without good cause, fails to allow its eligible employees to participate in the CalSavers Retirement Savings Program pursuant to Sections 100014 and 100032, after the CalSavers Retirement Savings Board serves a final notice of penalty application, shall be subject to a penalty of two hundred fifty dollars ($250) per eligible employee and an additional penalty of five hundred dollars ($500) per eligible employee if noncompliance continues," as further described in Revenue and Taxation Code § 19287. The Franchise Tax Board, not the CalSavers board itself, issues the actual first notice of penalty imposition once the CalSavers board informs it of an employer's noncompliance, and an eligible employer may appeal any penalty imposed under this section in writing to the Franchise Tax Board under Revenue and Taxation Code § 19288.
clauses.gap: § 100033(a), (b)(1), (b)(2), (c), and (d) are subdivisions of a single statutory section. This clause quotes the Government Code's own cross-references to Revenue and Taxation Code §§ 19287 and 19288 (the statutes actually governing the Franchise Tax Board's notice and appeal procedure and any further mechanics of penalty calculation) but did not independently fetch and verify the text of either Revenue and Taxation Code section with the same two-fetch discipline used for the Government Code text above — a real limitation in this document's research, disclosed rather than papered over. This clause also does not state what "good cause" means (the phrase is used but not defined anywhere in the Title 21 text this document reviewed), does not address whether the $250/$500 per-employee penalty figures have been adjusted since last amended, and does not cover any other consequence of noncompliance that might exist outside this statute.

clauses.title: Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes selected requirements of California's Immigrant Worker Protection Act (Stats. 2017, Ch. 492 (AB 450)), codified at Labor Code § 90.2 and Government Code §§ 7285.1–7285.3, in connection with {{companyName}}'s employment of {{employeeName}}. It covers the notice an employer must give current employees after a federal immigration agency gives notice that it will inspect Form I-9 or other employment records, and it covers California's restrictions on an employer voluntarily granting a federal immigration enforcement agent access to nonpublic work areas or to employee records during such an enforcement action. It does not address the separate, hiring-stage Form I-9 verification process, the E-Verify program, the federal anti-discrimination provisions of 8 U.S.C. § 1324b, or Labor Code § 1019.2's separate restriction on reverifying an existing employee's work authorization — each addressed, where covered in this library, in a different information sheet.

clauses.title: Notice to Employees of an I-9 or Employment-Records Inspection
clauses.body: California law requires an employer, except as otherwise required by federal law, to notify each current employee within 72 hours of receiving a federal immigration agency's notice that it will inspect Form I-9 or other employment records. The employer must give this notice by posting it in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information to employees, and must separately give written notice within 72 hours to the employee's authorized representative, if any. The posted notice must identify the inspecting agency, the date the employer received the inspection notice, the nature of the inspection to the extent known, and must include a copy of the Notice of Inspection itself. Upon an affected employee's reasonable request, the employer must also provide that employee a copy of the Notice of Inspection.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of the specific pre-inspection notice duty Labor Code § 90.2(a) creates — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any particular employer has received, or will receive, a Notice of Inspection. All three citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 90.2(a): the first quotes paragraph (a)(1)'s core 72-hour notice duty and its posting-language and authorized-representative requirements; the second quotes paragraph (a)(1)'s list of required notice contents, subparagraphs (A) through (D); the third quotes paragraph (a)(3)'s separate duty to furnish an affected employee a copy of the Notice of Inspection on request. This clause does not cover paragraph (a)(2), a duty running to the Labor Commissioner (not the employer) to develop a model posting by July 1, 2018 — a now-historical administrative deadline this clause's drafter judged not to state an ongoing employer obligation worth quoting. This clause also does not cover the separate post-inspection notice duty in § 90.2(b), addressed in a different clause of this information sheet, or the civil penalty for failing to comply with either notice duty, addressed in a separate clause.

citations.quote: an employer shall provide a notice to each current employee, by posting in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information to the employee, of any inspections of I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification forms or other employment records conducted by an immigration agency within 72 hours of receiving notice of the inspection. Written notice shall also be given within 72 hours to the employee’s authorized representative, if any.
