clauses.title: Notice to Affected Employees of Inspection Results
clauses.body: Separately from the pre-inspection notice, California law requires an employer, except as otherwise required by federal law, to provide each current affected employee — and that employee's authorized representative, if any — a copy of the written immigration agency notice reporting the inspection's results, within 72 hours of the employer's receipt of that notice. Within the same 72 hours, the employer must also give each affected employee, and the employee's authorized representative, written notice of the obligations the inspection results create for the employer and for that employee. This notice must relate to the affected employee only, must be hand-delivered at the workplace if possible, and otherwise sent by mail and, if the employee's email address is known, by email. The notice must describe any deficiencies identified as to that employee, the time period for correcting them, the time and date of any meeting scheduled to correct them, and the employee's right to representation at that meeting. An "affected employee" is defined as an employee the immigration agency's inspection results identify as potentially lacking work authorization, or whose work-authorization documents the inspection identified as deficient.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of the post-inspection notice duty Labor Code § 90.2(b) creates once an employer receives the immigration agency's written results of an I-9 or other employment-records inspection — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any particular employee is or will become an "affected employee" as the statute defines that term. All four citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section: the first three quote paragraph (b)(1) (the results-notice duty, the separate obligations-notice duty, and the required contents of that notice, respectively); the fourth quotes paragraph (b)(2)'s definition of "affected employee." This clause does not independently evaluate whether any particular immigration-agency communication would qualify as the "written immigration agency notice" the statute describes, and does not cover the pre-inspection notice duty of § 90.2(a), addressed in a different clause of this information sheet.

citations.quote: Within 72 hours of its receipt of this notice, the employer shall also provide to each affected employee, and to the affected employee’s authorized representative, if any, written notice of the obligations of the employer and the affected employee arising from the results of the inspection of I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification forms or other employment records.

citations.quote: The notice shall contain the following information: (A) A description of any and all deficiencies or other items identified in the written immigration inspection results notice related to the affected employee. (B) The time period for correcting any potential deficiencies identified by the immigration agency. (C) The time and date of any meeting with the employer to correct any identified deficiencies. (D) Notice that the employee has the right to representation during any meeting scheduled with the employer.

clauses.title: Civil Penalty for Failure to Provide the Required Notices
clauses.body: An employer that fails to provide either of the notices described above is subject to a civil penalty of $2,000 up to $5,000 for a first violation, and $5,000 up to $10,000 for each subsequent violation, recoverable by the Labor Commissioner. No penalty applies, however, where the employer's failure to notify an employee occurs at the express and specific direction or request of the federal government. For purposes of this section, an employee's "authorized representative" means an exclusive collective bargaining representative, and the section applies to both public and private employers. Nothing in the chapter containing this section restricts or limits an employer's compliance with a memorandum of understanding governing the employer's use of the federal E-Verify system.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of the civil-penalty amounts, the federal-direction exception, and two definitional/scope provisions Labor Code § 90.2 attaches to the notice duties described in the two preceding clauses — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about any specific employer's actual liability. The four citations below are all subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 90.2: (c) the penalty and federal-direction exception, (d) the "authorized representative" definition, (e) the public/private scope statement, and (f) the E-Verify savings clause. This clause does not identify who besides the Labor Commissioner, if anyone, may enforce the penalty, and does not address whether a private right of action exists — the statutory text quoted here names only the Labor Commissioner as recovering the penalty. This clause does not cover the separate, differently structured civil penalties Government Code §§ 7285.1 and 7285.2 attach to the nonpublic-area and employee-records access restrictions, addressed in separate clauses of this information sheet.

citations.quote: An employer who fails to provide the notices required by this section shall be subject to a civil penalty of two thousand dollars ($2,000) up to five thousand dollars ($5,000) for a first violation and five thousand dollars ($5,000) up to ten thousand dollars ($10,000) for each subsequent violation. This section does not require a penalty to be imposed upon an employer or person who fails to provide notice to an employee at the express and specific direction or request of the federal government. The penalty shall be recoverable by the Labor Commissioner.

clauses.title: Restriction on Voluntary Access to Nonpublic Work Areas
clauses.body: Separately from the notice duties above, California law makes it unlawful — except as otherwise required by federal law — for an employer, or a person acting on the employer's behalf, to provide voluntary consent to a federal immigration enforcement agent to enter a nonpublic area of a place of labor. This restriction does not apply if the immigration enforcement agent provides a judicial warrant. It also does not prevent an employer, or someone acting on the employer's behalf, from taking the agent to a nonpublic area where employees are not present solely to verify whether the agent has a judicial warrant, provided the employer gives no consent to search a nonpublic area in the process. An employer who violates this restriction is subject to a civil penalty of $2,000 up to $5,000 for a first violation and $5,000 up to $10,000 for each subsequent violation, except that no penalty applies if a court finds the agent was permitted to enter without the consent of the employer or other person in control of the place of labor. The restriction applies to both public and private employers, and only the Labor Commissioner or the Attorney General may enforce it, through a civil action, with any penalty recovered deposited into the Labor Enforcement and Compliance Fund.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of the specific consent-to-enter restriction Government Code § 7285.1 creates and of the penalty and enforcement mechanism attached to it — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether voluntary consent was or was not given in any particular encounter with a federal agent. The five citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 7285.1: (a) the consent bar and its judicial-warrant exception, (b) the penalty amounts and the no-penalty-if-a-court-finds-permission-was-given proviso, (c) the warrant-verification carve-out, (d) the exclusive-enforcement-authority and penalty-deposit provisions, and (e) the public/private scope statement. This clause does not cover Government Code § 7285.2's separate restriction on access to employee records, addressed in a different clause of this information sheet, or Government Code § 7285.3's E-Verify savings clause, whose substance duplicates Labor Code § 90.2(f) quoted in a separate clause of this information sheet. This clause also takes no position on what counts as a "public" versus "nonpublic" area of a particular workplace — a fact-specific determination the statutory text quoted here does not itself define.

If a court finds that an immigration enforcement agent was permitted to enter a nonpublic area of a place of labor without the consent of the employer or other person in control of the place of labor, the civil penalty shall not apply.

clauses.title: Restriction on Voluntary Access to Employee Records
clauses.body: California law also makes it unlawful — except as otherwise required by federal law — for an employer, or a person acting on the employer's behalf, to provide voluntary consent to a federal immigration enforcement agent to access, review, or obtain the employer's employee records without a subpoena or a judicial warrant. This restriction does not prohibit an employer, or someone acting on the employer's behalf, from challenging the validity of a subpoena or judicial warrant in federal district court. The restriction does not apply, however, to Form I-9 or other documents for which the employer has received a Notice of Inspection. An employer who violates this restriction is subject to a civil penalty of $2,000 up to $5,000 for a first violation and $5,000 up to $10,000 for each subsequent violation. The restriction applies to both public and private employers, and only the Labor Commissioner or the Attorney General may enforce it, through a civil action, with any penalty recovered deposited into the Labor Enforcement and Compliance Fund.
clauses.gap: This is California law, used as evidence of the specific consent-to-access-records restriction Government Code § 7285.2 creates, its Notice-of-Inspection exception, and the penalty and enforcement mechanism attached to it — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether voluntary consent was or was not given as to any particular record. The five citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 7285.2: (a)(1) the consent bar and the right to challenge a subpoena or warrant in federal court, (a)(2) the Notice-of-Inspection exception, (b) the penalty amounts, (c) the exclusive-enforcement-authority and penalty-deposit provisions, and (d) the public/private scope statement. This clause does not independently define "employee record" beyond the Form I-9 example the statute itself carves out from the restriction, and unlike the parallel penalty provision in Government Code § 7285.1(b), the text of § 7285.2(b) quoted here does not itself state a court-finding-based exception to the penalty — this clause draws no further conclusion from that difference in wording between the two sections. This clause does not cover Government Code § 7285.1's separate restriction on entering nonpublic work areas, addressed in a different clause of this information sheet.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the housing-discrimination provisions of California's Fair Employment and Housing Act (Government Code section 12955 et seq.) as they may apply to the property at {{propertyAddress}}. It states what California law provides regarding discrimination in the sale, rental, lease, and financing of housing accommodations in this state -- the statute's own definitions of "housing accommodation" and "owner," the characteristics it protects, examples of what the statute treats as discrimination, and a separate, specifically cross-referenced anti-discrimination statute (the Unruh Civil Rights Act). It does not authorize, direct, or prohibit any particular transaction or practice at {{propertyAddress}} or elsewhere, and it does not tell any reader what to do about a specific property, application, or dispute.

clauses.title: Scope: "Housing Accommodation," "Owner," and Real Estate-Related Transactions
clauses.body: The statute defines "housing accommodation" broadly: any building, structure, or portion of one that is occupied, or intended for occupancy, as a residence by one or more families, and any vacant land offered for sale or lease for the construction of such a building or structure -- a definition that separately extends to a dwelling occupied, or intended to be occupied, through a transaction facilitated by a short-term-rental hosting platform. The statute's definition of "owner" is likewise broad: it includes not only a title holder but a lessee, sublessee, assignee, managing agent, real estate broker or salesperson, or any other person holding a legal or equitable right of ownership or possession or the right to rent or lease a housing accommodation, as well as the state and its political subdivisions and agencies. A separate definition reaches the financing side of housing: "real estate-related transactions" include the making or purchasing of loans or providing other financial assistance for purchasing, constructing, improving, repairing, or maintaining a dwelling, or secured by residential real estate.
clauses.gap: These three definitions -- "housing accommodation," "owner," and "real estate-related transactions" -- are subdivisions (d), (e), and (h) of the same statutory section, Government Code section 12927, not independent sources of each other; each is quoted below from that one section. Section 12927 states that its definitions apply "as used in this part in connection with housing accommodations," and the prohibited-practices section quoted elsewhere in this document, Government Code section 12955, sits within that same part (Part 2.8 of Division 3 of Title 2) -- this document treats section 12927's definitions as governing section 12955's terms on that textual basis, but did not separately verify every intervening section of the part. The "real estate-related transactions" definition has two further categories this clause does not quote: the selling, brokering, or appraising of residential real property, and certain territorial-underwriting requirements tied to earthquake insurance -- summarized here but not independently verified against the statute's exact wording. Section 12927(c)(2) also states that "discrimination" does not include an owner's refusal to rent or lease a portion of an owner-occupied single-family house to a roomer or boarder living within the household, under stated conditions -- an exception to the general scope this document does not quote or further verify.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12927(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Government Code, definition of "housing accommodation"
citations.quote: “Housing accommodation” means any building, structure, or portion thereof that is occupied as, or intended for occupancy as, a residence by one or more families and any vacant land that is offered for sale or lease for the construction thereon of any building, structure, or portion thereof intended to be so occupied.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12927(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Government Code, definition of "owner"
citations.quote: “Owner” includes the lessee, sublessee, assignee, managing agent, real estate broker or salesperson, or any person having any legal or equitable right of ownership or possession or the right to rent or lease housing accommodations, and includes the state and any of its political subdivisions and any agency thereof.

citations.quote: “Real estate-related transactions” include any of the following: (1) The making or purchasing of loans or providing other financial assistance that is for the purpose of purchasing, constructing, improving, repairing, or maintaining a dwelling, or that is secured by residential real estate.

clauses.title: Protected Characteristics Under FEHA's Housing-Discrimination Article
clauses.body: Government Code section 12955(a) makes it unlawful for the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of that person's race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information. A separate subdivision of the same section states that this list of characteristics, wherever it is used in the section, includes a perception that a person has any of those characteristics, or that the person is associated with someone who has, or is perceived to have, any of those characteristics.
clauses.gap: Government Code section 12955(a) and section 12955(m) are two subdivisions of the same statutory section, not independent sources of each other. This document verifies the housing-discrimination protected-characteristics list stated in section 12955 itself; it does not independently verify Government Code section 12940, FEHA's separate employment-discrimination section, or confirm point-by-point how that list compares to this one -- 12940 was not fetched as part of this research, so this document does not assert any specific similarity or difference between the two lists beyond what each states on its own. Several of the listed terms ("disability," "familial status," "source of income," "genetic information") are themselves given further statutory definitions elsewhere in this part (for example, section 12955.3 defines "disability" and section 12927 defines "source of income") that are not restated in this clause; "source of income" is addressed in a separate clause of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12955(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Government Code, housing-discrimination protected characteristics
citations.quote: (a) For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of that person.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12955(m) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Government Code, perceived or associational discrimination
citations.quote: (m) As used in this section, “race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information,” includes a perception that the person has any of those characteristics or that the person is associated with a person who has, or is perceived to have, any of those characteristics.

clauses.title: Examples of Prohibited Practices: Refusal, Terms, and Advertising
clauses.body: The statute's definitional section states that "discrimination," for purposes of the housing-discrimination provisions, includes a list of specific practices: refusal to sell, rent, or lease housing accommodations; refusal to negotiate for their sale, rental, or lease; representing that a housing accommodation is not available for inspection, sale, or rental when it is in fact available; any other denial or withholding of housing accommodations; providing inferior terms, conditions, privileges, facilities, or services in connection with housing accommodations; harassment in connection with housing accommodations; cancellation or termination of a sale or rental agreement; and providing segregated or separated housing accommodations. Separately, the prohibited-practices section itself makes it unlawful for any person to make, print, or publish, or cause to be made, printed, or published, any notice, statement, or advertisement regarding the sale or rental of a housing accommodation that indicates a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on the characteristics that section protects, or an intention to make such a preference, limitation, or discrimination.
clauses.gap: The discrimination-definition quote is drawn from Government Code section 12927(c)(1); the advertising prohibition is drawn from a separate section, Government Code section 12955(c) -- these are independent statutory sections, not subdivisions of the same one, though section 12927 states its definitions govern terms as used in the same part that contains section 12955. Section 12927(c)(1) contains further listed practices this clause does not quote, including refusal to permit a disabled person to make reasonable modifications to premises at the disabled person's expense (subject to a landlord's right, in a rental, to condition permission on restoring the interior afterward) and refusal to make reasonable accommodations in rules, policies, practices, or services necessary for a disabled person's equal use and enjoyment of a dwelling; this document does not restate those disability-specific provisions in full. Section 12955 itself lists further prohibited practices beyond advertising that this clause does not cover, including retaliation against a person who has opposed a practice the section makes unlawful (subdivision (f)), aiding, abetting, inciting, compelling, or coercing any of the acts the section declares unlawful (subdivision (g)), blockbusting -- inducing a sale or rental through representations about the entry of persons of a particular protected characteristic into the neighborhood (subdivision (h)) -- discrimination in real estate-related transactions and appraisals (subdivision (i)), denial of access to a multiple listing service or similar real estate service (subdivision (j)), and discrimination through public or private land use practices, decisions, and authorizations, including restrictive covenants and certain zoning and permit denials (subdivision (l)).

citations.cite: Government Code, definition of "discrimination" for housing-accommodation purposes
citations.quote: (c) (1) “Discrimination” includes refusal to sell, rent, or lease housing accommodations; includes refusal to negotiate for the sale, rental, or lease of housing accommodations; includes representation that a housing accommodation is not available for inspection, sale, or rental when that housing accommodation is in fact so available; includes any other denial or withholding of housing accommodations; includes provision of inferior terms, conditions, privileges, facilities, or services in connection with those housing accommodations; includes harassment in connection with those housing accommodations; includes the cancellation or termination of a sale or rental agreement; includes the provision of segregated or separated housing accommodations

citations.quote: (c) For any person to make, print, or publish, or cause to be made, printed, or published any notice, statement, or advertisement, with respect to the sale or rental of a housing accommodation that indicates any preference, limitation, or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information or an intention to make

clauses.title: "Source of Income" as a Protected Characteristic
clauses.body: "Source of income" is one of the characteristics section 12955(a) protects. The statute defines it, for purposes of that section, as lawful, verifiable income paid directly to a tenant, to a representative of a tenant, or to a housing owner or landlord on behalf of a tenant -- including federal, state, or local public assistance and federal, state, or local housing subsidies, such as (but not limited to) federal housing assistance vouchers issued under Section 8 of the United States Housing Act of 1937. The definition separately states that "source of income" includes a federal Department of Housing and Urban Development Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing voucher, and that for purposes of this definition a housing owner or landlord is not treated as a tenant's "representative" unless the source of income is that specific type of voucher.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Government Code section 12955(p)(1); a materially identical definition of "source of income" also appears in the separate definitional section, Government Code section 12927(i) -- this document treats the two as duplicative restatements within the same part rather than independent corroboration, and did not attempt to verify whether their wording is word-for-word identical. A separate subdivision, section 12955(p)(2) (not quoted here), states that it does not constitute source-of-income discrimination to make a written or oral inquiry about the level or source of a person's income. This clause does not cover the additional source-of-income protections in section 12955(o), which govern income-standard and credit-history practices specifically where a government rent subsidy is involved.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12955(p)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Government Code, definition of "source of income"
citations.quote: (p) (1) For the purposes of this section, “source of income” means lawful, verifiable income paid directly to a tenant, or to a representative of a tenant, or paid to a housing owner or landlord on behalf of a tenant, including federal, state, or local public assistance, and federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including, but not limited to, federal housing assistance vouchers issued under Section 8 of the United States Housing Act of 1937 (42 U.S.C. Sec. 1437f). “Source of income” includes a federal Department of Housing and Urban Development Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing voucher. For the purposes of this section, a housing owner or landlord is not considered a representative of a tenant unless the source of income is a federal Department of Housing and Urban Development Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing voucher.

clauses.title: Relationship to the Unruh Civil Rights Act (Civil Code § 51)
clauses.body: FEHA's housing-discrimination section itself cross-references a separate California civil rights statute: it makes it unlawful for any person subject to Civil Code section 51 -- as that section applies to housing accommodations -- to discriminate against any person on the basis of a list of characteristics substantially overlapping the one section 12955(a) protects, or on any other basis Civil Code section 51 prohibits. Civil Code section 51, cited by that cross-reference, is the Unruh Civil Rights Act. Unruh states that all persons within California's jurisdiction, regardless of sex, race, color, religion, ancestry, national origin, disability, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sexual orientation, citizenship, primary language, or immigration status, are entitled to full and equal accommodations, advantages, facilities, privileges, or services in all business establishments of every kind whatsoever.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two independently enacted statutes: Government Code section 12955(d), which is the FEHA housing-discrimination provision's own cross-reference to Civil Code section 51, and Civil Code section 51 itself (the Unruh Civil Rights Act), fetched and verified separately. Section 12955(d)'s cross-reference is the verified basis for stating that Unruh applies to housing accommodations in some respect -- the words "as that section applies to housing accommodations" appear in the FEHA text itself, quoted below. Unruh's own text, by contrast, speaks generally of "business establishments of every kind whatsoever" and does not itself use the word "housing" in the portion quoted here; this document does not independently verify, from statutory text alone, every respect in which -- or every type of housing transaction to which -- Unruh has been held to apply, since that is developed through case law this research did not review. The two statutes' protected-characteristic lists are not identical: Unruh's list quoted here includes citizenship, primary language, immigration status, and medical condition, none of which appear in the FEHA housing list quoted in this document's protected-characteristics clause, while the FEHA housing list includes source of income, familial status, and veteran or military status, none of which appear in the portion of Unruh quoted here. This document does not resolve which statute, if either, would govern a specific situation, or whether both could apply to the same facts.

citations.quote: (d) For any person subject to the provisions of Section 51 of the Civil Code, as that section applies to housing accommodations, to discriminate against any person on the basis of sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, color, race, religion, ancestry, national origin, familial status, marital status, disability, genetic information, source of income, veteran or military status, or on any other basis prohibited by that section.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Which Corporations the Minimum Franchise Tax Reaches
clauses.body: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(b) defines the corporations the minimum franchise tax reaches, unless expressly exempted elsewhere in the Corporation Tax Law or by the California Constitution: a corporation incorporated under California law, a corporation qualified to transact intrastate business in California under the Corporations Code, or a corporation doing business in California. Section 23153(c) then carves two entity types out of the tax entirely: credit unions, and a narrow category of agricultural nonprofit cooperative associations organized under the Food and Agricultural Code and holding a specified board-of-supervisors certificate, which are exempt for five consecutive taxable years starting with the year the certificate issued -- and only if the cooperative organized on or after January 1, 1994. Limited liability companies are not reached by this section directly; a separate statute, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17941, imposes an annual LLC tax and cross-references subdivision (d) of this section only to set that tax's dollar amount.
clauses.gap: Subdivisions (b) and (c) quoted here are further subsections of the same statutory section already partly quoted elsewhere in this project -- Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(a), (d)(1), and (f)(1)-(2) appear in the Articles of Incorporation document's annual-franchise-tax clause, and § 23153(d)(1) is separately cross-referenced in the LLC Articles of Organization document and the LLC Annual Fee document -- all one statutory source, not independent ones. This clause does not cover every subdivision of § 23153: it omits the reduced $25 rate for a narrow category of inactive pre-1950s gold-mining or pre-1971 quicksilver-mining corporations formed under California law (subdivision (d)(2)-(3)), an expired 1999-2000 reduced second-year rate for certain small newly incorporated corporations (subdivision (e)), an anti-abuse rule for reorganizations undertaken solely to avoid the tax (subdivision (f)(3)), a narrow dissolution-linked exemption tied to a since-amended Corporations Code filing procedure that is distinct from the currently operative dissolution relief mechanism this project verifies elsewhere as Rev. & Tax. Code § 23332(c) (subdivision (g)), and a small-business exemption for a corporation solely owned by a deployed member of the U.S. Armed Forces, operative for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2020 and becoming inoperative for taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2030 (subdivision (i)) -- all left unaddressed here as narrow, historical, or niche provisions outside this clause's scope. This clause also does not address whether, or under what circumstances, an LLC that elects corporate tax treatment is itself treated as a "corporation" reached directly by § 23153(b) rather than by § 17941; the statutory text of § 23153 itself does not resolve that question, and no further source was fetched to verify it.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(b)
citations.cite: The Corporation Franchise Tax, which corporations the minimum tax applies to
citations.quote: Unless expressly exempted by this part or the California Constitution, subdivision (a) shall apply to each of the following: (1) Every corporation that is incorporated under the laws of this state. (2) Every corporation that is qualified to transact intrastate business in this state pursuant to Chapter 21 (commencing with Section 2100) of Division 1 of Title 1 of the Corporations Code. (3) Every corporation that is doing business in this state.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(c)
citations.cite: The Corporation Franchise Tax, express exemptions for credit unions and certain agricultural cooperatives
citations.quote: The following entities are not subject to the minimum franchise tax specified in this section: (1) Credit unions. (2) Nonprofit cooperative associations organized pursuant to Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 54001) of Division 20 of the Food and Agricultural Code that have been issued the certificate of the board of supervisors prepared pursuant to Section 54042 of the Food and Agricultural Code. The association shall be exempt from the minimum franchise tax for five consecutive taxable years, commencing with the first taxable year for which the certificate is issued pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 54042 of the Food and Agricultural Code. This paragraph only applies to nonprofit cooperative associations organized on or after January 1, 1994.

clauses.title: Statutory Limit on Raising the $800 Figure
clauses.body: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153(h) caps how quickly the Legislature may raise the $800 minimum franchise tax figure set in subdivision (d)(1): the Legislature may not increase it by more than 10 percent during any calendar year. The $800 figure itself is therefore not fixed permanently by this section's text -- it is a ceiling on the rate of legislative increase, not a promise that the amount will stay at $800 indefinitely.
clauses.gap: This is a single subdivision of the same statutory section quoted elsewhere in this project, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23153 -- one source, not an independent one. This clause states only the existence and terms of the statutory cap; it does not report whether the Legislature has exercised, or is currently proposing to exercise, this authority, and it does not track the tax's historical dollar amount before it reached $800.

citations.cite: The Corporation Franchise Tax, 10% annual cap on legislative increases to the minimum tax
citations.quote: The minimum franchise tax imposed by paragraph (1) of subdivision (d) shall not be increased by the Legislature by more than 10 percent during any calendar year.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Criminal Trade Secret Theft Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California Penal Code section 499c, the state's criminal trade secret theft statute -- what conduct it defines as a crime, how it defines "trade secret" for that purpose, and the penalties it specifies. It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning a situation involving {{companyName}} and, where relevant, {{adversePartyName}}. The trade secret information at issue is described as follows: {{tradeSecretDescription}}. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference describing what section 499c says. Section 499c is a criminal statute: violations are prosecuted by public prosecutors (a district attorney or the Attorney General), not through a private lawsuit, and this document does not initiate, threaten, or request any criminal prosecution or investigation. It does not state that any specific conduct described above does or does not violate section 499c, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is also distinct from, and does not replace, this project's existing Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter and Trade Secret Preemption Doctrine Information Sheet documents, both of which concern California's separate civil Uniform Trade Secrets Act (CUTSA) framework.

clauses.title: Penal Code Section 499c's Definition of "Trade Secret"
clauses.body: Penal Code section 499c defines "trade secret," for purposes of this criminal statute, as information -- including a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, or process -- that derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to the public or to other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclosure or use, and that is the subject of efforts reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy. This definition is a separate statutory definition, stated within section 499c itself for criminal-law purposes, from the civil definition of "trade secret" in California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act (CUTSA), Civil Code section 3426.1, subdivision (d). As fetched and compared side by side, the operative wording of the two definitions is the same, differing only in that section 499c labels its two conditions (A) and (B) where CUTSA labels the same two conditions (1) and (2).
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Cal. Penal Code § 499c(a)(9), one subdivision (subparagraph (9) of subdivision (a)) of a single statutory section; it does not restate the other eight definitions in subdivision (a) ("access," "article," "benefit," "computer system," "computer network," "computer program," "copy," and "representing"), which are not otherwise addressed in this document. The observation that this definition's wording matches Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1(d)'s CUTSA definition is this researcher's own side-by-side textual comparison of the two statutes as fetched from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, not a holding from any case that has compared them, and no case law testing that comparison is included here. That the wording matches does not mean the two statutes necessarily apply identically in every case: section 499c is a criminal statute construed by criminal courts and, where applicable, the standard of proof and rules of construction applicable to penal statutes, while Civil Code section 3426.1 is a civil statute; this document does not address whether or how those differences could affect how the same wording is applied in a criminal case versus a civil case. Both Cal. Penal Code § 499c and Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1 were each retrieved twice directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as separate HTTP requests using two different User-Agent headers; the statutory-text portion of each pair of retrievals was byte-identical (the only differences between the two retrievals of the same page were session-specific timestamp/ID strings embedded in unrelated page JavaScript, not the statutory text itself).

citations.quote: (9) “Trade secret” means information, including a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, or process, that: (A) Derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to the public or to other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclosure or use; and (B) Is the subject of efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy.

citations.quote: (d) “Trade secret” means information, including a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, or process, that: (1) Derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to the public or to other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclosure or use; and (2) Is the subject of efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy.

clauses.title: Prohibited Acts: Theft of a Trade Secret Under Subdivision (b)
clauses.body: Penal Code section 499c, subdivision (b), states that a person is guilty of theft if, with intent to deprive or withhold control of a trade secret from its owner, or intent to appropriate a trade secret to their own use or another's use, that person does any of four things: (1) steals, takes, carries away, or uses a trade secret without authorization; (2) fraudulently appropriates any article representing a trade secret entrusted to them; (3) having unlawfully obtained access to the article, without authority makes or causes to be made a copy of any article representing a trade secret; or (4) having obtained access to the article through a relationship of trust and confidence, without authority and in breach of the obligations created by that relationship, makes or causes to be made a copy of the article directly from and in its presence. Subdivision (b) itself states that a person who does any of these things "is guilty of theft"; it does not, within subdivision (b), separately state a felony/misdemeanor classification or a specific term of imprisonment or fine amount for this theft, unlike subdivision (c), addressed in a companion clause of this document, which does state its own specific penalty.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the full text of Cal. Penal Code § 499c(b), including its four numbered paragraphs (b)(1) through (b)(4); it does not quote subdivision (a) (the section's definitions, addressed in a companion clause), subdivision (c) (the bribery/inducement offense, addressed in a separate companion clause), or subdivision (d) (also addressed separately). This clause does not state what penalty applies to a violation of subdivision (b): because subdivision (b) states only that the described conduct "is guilty of theft" without itself specifying a punishment, this document does not independently trace or verify how California's general theft-classification statutes (which distinguish, among other things, grand theft from petty theft, generally based on the value involved) apply to a subdivision (b) violation, since those statutes were not fetched or verified as part of this research; a reader wanting that information would need to separately research those statutes. This clause does not state that any specific conduct does or does not fall within one of these four paragraphs.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 499c(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California's criminal trade secret theft statute, prohibited theft acts
citations.quote: (b) Every person is guilty of theft who, with intent to deprive or withhold the control of a trade secret from its owner, or with an intent to appropriate a trade secret to his or her own use or to the use of another, does any of the following: (1) Steals, takes, carries away, or uses without authorization, a trade secret. (2) Fraudulently appropriates any article representing a trade secret entrusted to him or her. (3) Having unlawfully obtained access to the article, without authority makes or causes to be made a copy of any article representing a trade secret. (4) Having obtained access to the article through a relationship of trust and confidence, without authority and in breach of the obligations created by that relationship, makes or causes to be made, directly from and in the presence of the article, a copy of any article representing a trade secret.

clauses.title: Prohibited Acts and Penalty: Bribery or Inducement to Obtain a Trade Secret Under Subdivision (c)
clauses.body: Penal Code section 499c, subdivision (c), separately makes it a crime to promise, offer, give, or conspire to promise or offer to give a present or former agent, employee, or servant of another a benefit as an inducement, bribe, or reward for conveying, delivering, or otherwise making available an article representing a trade secret to a person not authorized by the owner to receive or acquire it. The same subdivision equally makes it a crime for a present or former agent, employee, or servant to solicit, accept, receive, or take such a benefit for doing the same thing. Unlike subdivision (b), subdivision (c) states its own specific penalty: imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or imprisonment under Penal Code section 1170, subdivision (h), or a fine not exceeding five thousand dollars, or both that fine and imprisonment.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the full text of Cal. Penal Code § 499c(c), including its stated penalty; it does not separately quote or explain Penal Code section 1170, subdivision (h) -- the realignment-era provision referenced within this penalty for the imprisonment option other than county jail -- which was not independently fetched or verified for this document. This clause does not restate subdivision (b) (the separate theft-type prohibited acts, addressed in a companion clause of this document) or subdivision (d) (also addressed separately). This clause does not state that any specific conduct does or does not fall within subdivision (c), and does not state that any specific penalty would or would not be imposed for any conduct.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 499c(c) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California's criminal trade secret theft statute, bribery/inducement offense and penalty
citations.quote: (c) Every person who promises, offers or gives, or conspires to promise or offer to give, to any present or former agent, employee or servant of another, a benefit as an inducement, bribe or reward for conveying, delivering or otherwise making available an article representing a trade secret owned by his or her present or former principal, employer or master, to any person not authorized by the owner to receive or acquire the trade secret and every present or former agent, employee, or servant, who solicits, accepts, receives or takes a benefit as an inducement, bribe or reward for conveying, delivering or otherwise making available an article representing a trade secret owned by his or her present or former principal, employer or master, to any person not authorized by the owner to receive or acquire the trade secret, shall be punished by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or by imprisonment pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1170, or by a fine not exceeding five thousand dollars ($5,000), or by both that fine and imprisonment.

clauses.title: Returning the Article Is Not a Defense Under Subdivision (d)
clauses.body: Penal Code section 499c, subdivision (d), states that in a prosecution for a violation of the section, it is no defense that the person returned, or intended to return, the article. By its own terms, this rule applies to a prosecution "for a violation of this section" generally -- it is not stated as limited to only subdivision (b) or only subdivision (c).
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the entirety of Cal. Penal Code § 499c(d), a single one-sentence subdivision. It does not address any other defense that may or may not be available in a prosecution under this section, and no case law construing this subdivision was researched or is cited here.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 499c(d) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California's criminal trade secret theft statute, return of article not a defense
citations.quote: (d) In a prosecution for a violation of this section, it shall be no defense that the person returned or intended to return the article.

clauses.title: Relationship of This Criminal Statute to California's Civil CUTSA Framework
clauses.body: Penal Code section 499c is a criminal statute, enforced by public prosecutors, separate from California's civil Uniform Trade Secrets Act (CUTSA), Civil Code section 3426 et seq., which is enforced through private civil lawsuits. CUTSA's own non-supersession provision, Civil Code section 3426.7, states in subdivision (a) that CUTSA "does not supersede any statute relating to misappropriation of a trade secret, or any statute otherwise regulating trade secrets," and states in subdivision (b) that CUTSA "does not affect ... criminal remedies, whether or not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret." As fetched, section 3426.7 does not name Penal Code section 499c, or any other specific criminal statute, by section number; it preserves "criminal remedies" and other trade-secret-related statutes only as a general category. This document does not go further than the statutory text to determine whether, or how, the two statutes' shared conduct requirements have been construed by courts.
clauses.gap: This clause cites Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.7, subdivisions (a) and (b) -- two subdivisions of one statutory section -- for the general proposition that CUTSA does not displace criminal remedies; it does not cite subdivision (c) of that same section (a public-records-specific carve-out addressed in a companion clause of this project's existing Trade Secret Preemption Doctrine Information Sheet document, not repeated here). The statement that section 3426.7 "does not name Penal Code section 499c ... by section number" is this researcher's own direct text search of the fetched statutory text of section 3426.7 for the string "499c," which did not appear; it is not a holding of any case. This clause does not identify or discuss any other statute that might also fall within CUTSA's general "any statute relating to misappropriation of a trade secret" language, and does not address whether a single set of underlying facts that supports a section 499c prosecution could also support a CUTSA civil claim, or how a criminal prosecution and a civil CUTSA claim arising from the same facts might interact procedurally (for example, as to timing, discovery, or use of one proceeding's evidence in the other) -- none of which is addressed by the statutory text quoted here or elsewhere researched for this document. Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.7 was retrieved twice directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as two separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical statutory text.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.7(a)-(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, effect on other statutes and other remedies, including criminal remedies
citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise expressly provided, this title does not supersede any statute relating to misappropriation of a trade secret, or any statute otherwise regulating trade secrets. (b) This title does not affect (1) contractual remedies, whether or not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret, (2) other civil remedies that are not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret, or (3) criminal remedies, whether or not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment Block -- Criminal Trade Secret Theft Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{preparerName}}: ☐ _________________________
