It is not a court filing, a police report, a request for prosecution, or legal advice about whether any specific conduct described above violates section 499c or any other statute, and completing or signing it does not itself determine that outcome. A decision about whether to report suspected criminal conduct to law enforcement or a prosecuting authority is a separate decision this document does not make and does not recommend.]

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet states California's statutory exceptions to the general rule voiding noncompete restraints, as those exceptions apply to (1) a sale of the goodwill or ownership interests of {{businessName}}, and (2) a partner's or member's departure from {{businessName}} by dissolution or dissociation. It states the statute's own conditions for each exception — who qualifies, and what limits apply to the resulting restriction. It is not advice about whether any specific proposed noncompete restriction actually satisfies those conditions for {{businessName}}.

clauses.title: These Are Exceptions to a General Ban
clauses.body: California's default rule voids, to that extent, every contract restraining anyone from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business. The sale-of-goodwill exception and the partnership/LLC dissolution-or-dissociation exceptions described in this information sheet are exceptions to that general rule, not a separate freestanding source of authority to restrain competition — a restriction that doesn't satisfy one of the statute's own exceptions remains void under the general rule.
clauses.gap: This clause cites the general voiding rule only for framing — it is a single subdivision of Business and Professions Code Section 16600 and does not itself state the sale-of-business or partnership/LLC dissolution exceptions, which are separate sections addressed in the other clauses of this information sheet. Section 16600 also has a subdivision (b) (an employment-context reading rule) and a subdivision (c) (extending the rule to restraints on non-parties) that are not addressed here because they concern the general employment-noncompete rule covered by this project's separate Non-Compete Agreement document, not the sale-of-business or dissolution exceptions that are this document's subject.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, general rule voiding restraints on lawful business
citations.quote: Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void.

clauses.title: The Sale-of-Goodwill Exception
clauses.body: California law permits a noncompete agreement in three specific sale-of-business situations: (1) a person sells the goodwill of a business; (2) an owner of a business entity sells or otherwise disposes of all of that owner's ownership interest in the entity; or (3) an owner of a business entity sells all or substantially all of the entity's operating assets together with its goodwill (or the operating assets of a division or subsidiary together with that division's or subsidiary's goodwill, or all of a subsidiary's ownership interest). In any of those situations, the seller may agree with the buyer not to carry on a similar business within a specified geographic area in which the business, division, or subsidiary being sold has been carried on — but only for so long as the buyer, or anyone who derives title to the goodwill or ownership interest from the buyer, itself carries on a like business there.
clauses.gap: This is a single, continuous statutory sentence — the (a)/(b)/(c) markers quoted below are the statute's own internal list of the asset-sale scenarios within that one sentence, not separate numbered subdivisions of Section 16601 (Section 16601 has no lettered subdivisions at its top level; a companion clause quotes its separately paragraphed definitions). The restriction's validity is conditioned on the buyer's continued operation: the statute ties the seller's restraint to the buyer (or a successor in title to the goodwill or ownership interest) actually carrying on a like business in the specified area, not to a fixed time period — this document does not address what happens if the buyer stops operating the business, which the statute's text does not itself resolve. "Specified geographic area" is not defined further by this section, and the statute does not itself require the area to match the area the business previously served, only that it be an area in which the business, division, or subsidiary sold has been carried on.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16601 (first paragraph)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, sale-of-goodwill/ownership-interest/asset-sale exception
citations.quote: Any person who sells the goodwill of a business, or any owner of a business entity selling or otherwise disposing of all of his or her ownership interest in the business entity, or any owner of a business entity that sells (a) all or substantially all of its operating assets together with the goodwill of the business entity, (b) all or substantially all of the operating assets of a division or a subsidiary of the business entity together with the goodwill of that division or subsidiary, or (c) all of the ownership interest of any subsidiary, may agree with the buyer to refrain from carrying on a similar business within a specified geographic area in which the business so sold, or that of the business entity, division, or subsidiary has been carried on, so long as the buyer, or any person deriving title to the goodwill or ownership interest from the buyer, carries on a like business therein.

clauses.title: Who Counts as a Covered Seller
clauses.body: Section 16601 defines its own key terms, and those definitions control who can use the sale-of-goodwill exception. A “business entity” means a partnership (including a limited partnership or limited liability partnership), a limited liability company (including a series LLC), or a corporation. An “owner of a business entity” means a partner (for a partnership), a member (for an LLC), or a stockholder (for a corporation). An “ownership interest” means, correspondingly, a partnership interest, a membership interest, or (the statute's own, non-parallel wording) “a capital stockholder” in the case of a corporation. A “subsidiary” means a business entity over which the selling business entity has voting control, a right to receive a majority share of liquidating distributions, or both.
clauses.gap: All four citations below are separate definitional paragraphs within the same statutory section (§ 16601), not independent sections — no additional independent source was sought or needed for these definitions beyond the statute's own text. One definition is worth flagging as an apparent drafting inconsistency in the statute's own text, not a transcription choice made here: the “ownership interest” definition defines the corporate-context term as “a capital stockholder,” which describes a person, not an interest — inconsistent with the parallel “partnership interest” / “membership interest” phrasing in the same sentence for the other two entity types. That inconsistency is quoted here exactly as it appears in the current codified text, and this document does not attempt to resolve or correct it.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16601 (“business entity” definition)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, sale-of-goodwill exception, definition of “business entity”
citations.quote: For the purposes of this section, “business entity” means any partnership (including a limited partnership or a limited liability partnership), limited liability company (including a series of a limited liability company formed under the laws of a jurisdiction that recognizes such a series), or corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16601 (“owner of a business entity” definition)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, sale-of-goodwill exception, definition of “owner of a business entity”
citations.quote: For the purposes of this section, “owner of a business entity” means any partner, in the case of a business entity that is a partnership (including a limited partnership or a limited liability partnership), or any member, in the case of a business entity that is a limited liability company (including a series of a limited liability company formed under the laws of a jurisdiction that recognizes such a series), or any owner of capital stock, in the case of a business entity that is a corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16601 (“ownership interest” definition)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, sale-of-goodwill exception, definition of “ownership interest”
citations.quote: For the purposes of this section, “ownership interest” means a partnership interest, in the case of a business entity that is a partnership (including a limited partnership a limited liability partnership), a membership interest, in the case of a business entity that is a limited liability company (including a series of a limited liability company formed under the laws of a jurisdiction that recognizes such a series), or a capital stockholder, in the case of a business entity that is a corporation.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16601 (“subsidiary” definition)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, sale-of-goodwill exception, definition of “subsidiary”
citations.quote: For the purposes of this section, “subsidiary” means any business entity over which the selling business entity has voting control or from which the selling business entity has a right to receive a majority share of distributions upon dissolution or other liquidation of the business entity (or has both voting control and a right to receive these distributions.)

clauses.title: The Partnership Dissolution/Dissociation Exception
clauses.body: A separate statute permits a noncompete agreement between partners of {{businessName}}, tied to the partnership's dissolution or to one partner's dissociation from it. A partner may agree, upon or in anticipation of either a dissolution of the partnership or that partner's own dissociation from it, not to carry on a similar business within a specified geographic area where the partnership business has been transacted — but, as with the sale-of-goodwill exception, only for so long as another partner (or someone who derives title to the business or its goodwill from that other partner) itself carries on a like business there.
clauses.gap: The two citations below are subdivisions (a) and (b) of a single statutory section (§ 16602); no additional independent source was needed for this specific exception beyond the statute's own text. This exception is distinct from, and does not depend on, the sale-of-goodwill exception in § 16601 — a partner can invoke it on dissociation or dissolution without any sale of the business occurring at all. This document does not address the separate statutory definitions of “dissolution” and “dissociation” of a partnership themselves (found elsewhere in the Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, not in this section), only the noncompete exception that Section 16602 ties to those two events.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16602(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, partner noncompete on dissolution or dissociation
citations.quote: (a) Any partner may, upon or in anticipation of any of the circumstances described in subdivision (b), agree that he or she will not carry on a similar business within a specified geographic area where the partnership business has been transacted, so long as any other member of the partnership, or any person deriving title to the business or its goodwill from any such other member of the partnership, carries on a like business therein.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16602(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, the two circumstances subdivision (a) covers
citations.quote: (b) Subdivision (a) applies to either of the following circumstances: (1) A dissolution of the partnership. (2) Dissociation of the partner from the partnership.

clauses.title: The LLC Dissolution/Termination-of-Interest Exception
clauses.body: A parallel statute extends the same kind of exception to members of {{businessName}}, if {{businessName}} is a limited liability company (including a series of an LLC formed under the laws of a jurisdiction that recognizes series LLCs). A member may agree, upon or in anticipation of a dissolution of the LLC or the termination of that member's own interest in it, not to carry on a similar business within a specified geographic area where the LLC's business has been transacted — again, only for so long as another member (or someone who derives title to the business or its goodwill from that other member) itself carries on a like business there.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory sentence with no internal lettered or numbered subdivisions, so only one citation is given below; it is nonetheless one full, independent statutory section (§ 16602.5), not a subdivision of § 16601 or § 16602, though its structure closely parallels § 16602's partnership exception. Unlike § 16602(b), this section does not separately enumerate “termination of interest” the way § 16602 enumerates “dissociation” and “dissolution” as two distinct listed circumstances — it instead names “a dissolution of, or the termination of his or her interest in,” the LLC as a single compound trigger phrase. This document does not address the LLC statute's own separate definitions of dissociation or dissolution (found in the Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, not in this section) beyond what Section 16602.5 itself says.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16602.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, LLC member noncompete on dissolution or termination of interest
citations.quote: Any member may, upon or in anticipation of a dissolution of, or the termination of his or her interest in, a limited liability company (including a series of a limited liability company formed under the laws of a jurisdiction recognizing such a series), agree that he or she or it will not carry on a similar business within a specified geographic area where the limited liability company business has been transacted, so long as any other member of the limited liability company, or any person deriving title to the business or its goodwill from any such other member of the limited liability company, carries on a like business therein.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose and Scope — Director and Officer Indemnification Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a California corporation, and describes California Corporations Code section 317 in full: the statute governing when {{companyName}} may, or must, indemnify a director, officer, employee, or other agent for costs and liability arising out of that role, the statute's own procedure for deciding whether indemnification is proper in a specific case, and the statute's separate authorization for {{companyName}} to purchase director and officer liability insurance.

This project's existing Corporate Bylaws document already includes three clauses drawn from this same statute — the general permissive indemnification power, the mandatory rule for an agent successful on the merits, and the expense-advancement mechanism. This information sheet is meant to accompany, not replace, that treatment: it restates those same statutory subdivisions for a reader who wants this single topic addressed on its own, and it adds three subdivisions the Corporate Bylaws document's clauses do not reach — the statute's own definitions, the full standard specific to a derivative action (a suit by or in the right of the corporation), the statutory approval procedure naming who may authorize indemnification in a specific case, the statute's limits on when indemnification is barred outright, and the corporation's separate power to purchase and maintain director and officer liability insurance.

This information sheet is educational only. It states what the statute provides; it does not determine whether {{directorName}} is, or was, entitled to indemnification or insurance coverage for any specific proceeding, and it is not a substitute for {{companyName}}'s own bylaws, articles, or any separate indemnification agreement, which may set different or additional terms within what the statute allows.

clauses.title: Who and What the Statute Covers — Statutory Definitions
clauses.body: Section 317 defines three terms that control how far it reaches. "Agent" is defined broadly: it covers a person who is or was a director, officer, employee, or other agent of the corporation, and it extends to a person serving at the corporation's request as a director, officer, employee, or agent of another corporation, partnership, joint venture, trust, or other enterprise, and to a person who held one of those roles with a predecessor corporation or enterprise at that predecessor's request. "Proceeding" is defined to include a threatened, pending, or completed action or proceeding of any kind — civil, criminal, administrative, or investigative — not just a completed lawsuit. "Expenses" is defined to include, without limitation, attorneys' fees, plus the expenses of establishing a right to indemnification under the statute's mandatory-indemnification rule or under a court application for indemnification. This information sheet uses these three terms as the statute defines them wherever they appear below, in connection with {{directorName}}'s role at {{companyName}}.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subdivision, Corporations Code section 317, subdivision (a); it is not an independent source and should not be read as corroborating the other clauses in this information sheet, which quote other subdivisions of this same section. This clause states the statute's definitions themselves; it does not determine whether a particular director, officer, employee, or other agent in fact falls within the statutory definition of "agent" for any specific proceeding, nor does it address how a court has applied these definitions to a disputed set of facts — no case law is cited or verified anywhere in this document. The definition of "expenses" cross-references two other subdivisions of this same section (the mandatory-indemnification rule and the court-application approval method) rather than standing alone; both are addressed in this information sheet's other clauses.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, statutory definitions of "agent," "proceeding," and "expenses"
citations.quote: For the purposes of this section, “agent” means any person who is or was a director, officer, employee or other agent of the corporation, or is or was serving at the request of the corporation as a director, officer, employee or agent of another foreign or domestic corporation, partnership, joint venture, trust or other enterprise, or was a director, officer, employee or agent of a foreign or domestic corporation which was a predecessor corporation of the corporation or of another enterprise at the request of the predecessor corporation; “proceeding” means any threatened, pending or completed action or proceeding, whether civil, criminal, administrative or investigative; and “expenses” includes without limitation attorneys’ fees and any expenses of establishing a right to indemnification under subdivision (d) or paragraph (4) of subdivision (e).

clauses.title: A Different Standard for a Derivative Action — a Suit by or in the Right of the Corporation
clauses.body: Section 317 sets two different permissive standards depending on who the proceeding is against whom. For a third-party proceeding — one not brought by or in the right of the corporation itself — this project's existing Corporate Bylaws document already describes the statute's good-faith standard, under which {{companyName}} may indemnify {{directorName}} against expenses, judgments, fines, and settlements. A derivative action is different: where the proceeding is brought by or in the right of {{companyName}} itself to procure a judgment in {{companyName}}'s favor, the statute allows {{companyName}} to indemnify {{directorName}} only for expenses actually and reasonably incurred defending or settling that action — not for judgments, fines, or settlement amounts owed to the corporation — and only if {{directorName}} acted in good faith, in a manner {{directorName}} believed to be in the best interests of {{companyName}} and its shareholders. Unlike the third-party standard, this derivative-action standard has no separate "no reasonable cause to believe the conduct was unlawful" prong tied to a criminal proceeding, because a derivative action is a civil suit by the corporation's own shareholders on the corporation's behalf, not a criminal prosecution.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the introductory standard of Corporations Code section 317, subdivision (c) — a different subdivision from the ones already quoted in this project's Corporate Bylaws document, which quotes subdivision (b) in full and only the first limitation, paragraph (1), of subdivision (c), not this introductory standard sentence. Both are subdivisions of the same statutory section rather than independent sources. This clause states the derivative-action standard itself; it does not restate the separate, further limitations on derivative-action indemnification found later in subdivision (c) — including the bar on indemnifying a person adjudged liable to the corporation absent a specific court determination, already quoted in this project's Corporate Bylaws document, and two additional bars (on amounts paid settling a pending action without court approval, and on expenses of defending a pending action settled without court approval) that no clause in this corpus currently quotes. This clause does not determine whether any specific proceeding against a given director or officer is, or was, a derivative action within the meaning of this subdivision.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, permissive indemnification standard for a derivative action
citations.quote: A corporation shall have power to indemnify any person who was or is a party or is threatened to be made a party to any threatened, pending, or completed action by or in the right of the corporation to procure a judgment in its favor by reason of the fact that the person is or was an agent of the corporation, against expenses actually and reasonably incurred by that person in connection with the defense or settlement of the action if the person acted in good faith, in a manner the person believed to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders.

clauses.title: Who Decides — the Statutory Approval Procedure for a Specific Case
clauses.body: Outside the mandatory rule for an agent successful on the merits, section 317 does not let indemnification happen automatically just because the good-faith standard could be met — the statute requires that indemnification be authorized in the specific case, upon a determination that {{directorName}} met the applicable standard, and it names four specific ways that determination can be made: (1) a majority vote of a quorum of {{companyName}}'s directors who are not themselves parties to the proceeding; (2) if such a quorum cannot be obtained, a written opinion from independent legal counsel; (3) approval by {{companyName}}'s shareholders, with any shares owned by {{directorName}} not entitled to vote on the question; or (4) the court in which the proceeding is or was pending, on application by {{companyName}}, {{directorName}}, or the attorney or other person who rendered the defense services, whether or not {{companyName}} opposes that application.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subdivision, Corporations Code section 317, subdivision (e); it cross-references, but is not itself, the good-faith standards of subdivisions (b) and (c) described elsewhere in this information sheet and in this project's Corporate Bylaws document. No clause currently in this corpus quotes this approval-procedure subdivision, so this is new coverage rather than a restatement. This clause states the four statutory approval methods themselves; it does not determine which method, if any, a given corporation has in fact used or would use for a specific proceeding involving a specific director or officer, and it does not address how a corporation's own bylaws might elaborate on this procedure (for example, by specifying which officer calls a vote) beyond what the statute itself requires.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, statutory approval procedure for indemnification in a specific case
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (d), any indemnification under this section shall be made by the corporation only if authorized in the specific case, upon a determination that indemnification of the agent is proper in the circumstances because the agent has met the applicable standard of conduct set forth in subdivision (b) or (c), by any of the following: (1) A majority vote of a quorum consisting of directors who are not parties to such proceeding. (2) If such a quorum of directors is not obtainable, by independent legal counsel in a written opinion. (3) Approval of the shareholders (Section 153), with the shares owned by the person to be indemnified not being entitled to vote thereon. (4) The court in which the proceeding is or was pending upon application made by the corporation or the agent or the attorney or other person rendering services in connection with the defense, whether or not the application by the agent, attorney or other person is opposed by the corporation.

clauses.title: When Indemnification Is Barred Outright
clauses.body: Section 317's permissive indemnification power and its approval procedure both give way to two specific bars. Except for the mandatory-indemnification rule and a court's own application-based approval, {{companyName}} may not indemnify or advance expenses to {{directorName}} where doing so would be inconsistent with a provision of {{companyName}}'s own articles, bylaws, a shareholder resolution, or an agreement that was in effect at the time the underlying claim accrued and that prohibits or otherwise limits indemnification, or where it would be inconsistent with a condition a court expressly imposed in approving a settlement.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subdivision, Corporations Code section 317, subdivision (h); no clause currently in this corpus quotes it. This clause states the two statutory bars themselves; it does not determine whether a given corporation's own articles, bylaws, or any agreement in fact contain a provision that limits or prohibits indemnification, and it does not address subdivision (g) of this same section, which separately allows a corporation's articles to authorize indemnification rights broader than this statute's own default permissive power — a distinct, additional mechanism this clause does not describe.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(h) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, statutory bars on indemnification or advancement
citations.quote: No indemnification or advance shall be made under this section, except as provided in subdivision (d) or paragraph (4) of subdivision (e), in any circumstance where it appears: (1) That it would be inconsistent with a provision of the articles, bylaws, a resolution of the shareholders, or an agreement in effect at the time of the accrual of the alleged cause of action asserted in the proceeding in which the expenses were incurred or other amounts were paid, which prohibits or otherwise limits indemnification. (2) That it would be inconsistent with any condition expressly imposed by a court in approving a settlement.

clauses.title: Separate Statutory Authorization to Purchase Director and Officer Liability Insurance
clauses.body: Apart from indemnification itself, section 317 separately authorizes {{companyName}} to purchase and maintain liability insurance on behalf of {{directorName}} against liability asserted against, or incurred by, {{directorName}} in that role or arising out of that status — and this insurance-purchasing power exists whether or not {{companyName}} would actually have the power to indemnify {{directorName}} against that same liability under the rest of this statute. In other words, D&O insurance can reach some liability that the indemnification provisions above would not permit {{companyName}} to cover directly out of its own funds.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the core authorizing sentence of Corporations Code section 317, subdivision (i); it is a single statutory subdivision, not an independent source corroborating the other clauses in this information sheet. This clause does not quote or address the remainder of subdivision (i), which imposes conditions on a corporation's power to purchase insurance from a company the corporation itself wholly or partly owns (an affiliated or "captive" insurer) — conditions this clause does not describe and that a corporation considering that kind of arrangement would need to review separately. clauses.title: Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Temporary (Pendente Lite) Spousal Support Information Sheet concerns {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, who were married on {{marriageDate}} and separated on {{separationDate}}, in connection with a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, legal separation, or nullity filed or to be filed in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes California's statutory authority for a court to order spousal support while such a proceeding is pending, before any final judgment, and how that authority and its governing standard differ from the post-judgment spousal-support standard addressed elsewhere in this corpus's Marital Settlement Agreement document. It is not itself a request for order, notice of motion, declaration, or court order, and completing it does not create, modify, or terminate any temporary spousal support obligation between {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. Only a court order, applying the statutes described here to the facts of an actual pending proceeding, can do that.

clauses.title: Court's Authority to Order Support While a Proceeding Is Pending
clauses.body: California's Family Code authorizes a court to order support during the pendency of a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, during the pendency of a proceeding under the state's child-custody provisions, or in any proceeding where the support of a minor child (or a child for whom support is otherwise authorized) is at issue. On that authority, the court may order either spouse to pay any amount necessary for the support of the other spouse, subject to a statutory cross-reference addressed separately in this document, and may separately order either or both parents to pay any amount necessary for the support of a child. This authority for a support order during the pendency of the case is distinct from, and does not depend on, a final judgment of dissolution, legal separation, or nullity; it is commonly referred to as "temporary" or "pendente lite" support because it operates only while the underlying proceeding remains pending.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 3600); no additional independent source was found for this. The same section also authorizes support orders for a minor child (the clause of the quoted text beginning "or (b)"); that child-support authority is not the subject of this document, which addresses only the spousal-support half of the section. Section 3600 sits in Family Code Division 9, Part 1, Chapter 4 ("Spousal and Child Support During Pendency of Proceeding," §§ 3600-3604) — a correction from an initial assumption that the chapter ran only through § 3603; it in fact runs through § 3604, and an adjoining section in that same chapter, § 3601, was reviewed but not used here because it addresses only when a child-support order (not a spousal-support order) terminates by operation of law. This document does not address every type of proceeding referenced in § 3600 (for example, a standalone custody proceeding under Division 8, or a proceeding concerning a child for whom support is authorized under Sections 3901 or 3910); it focuses on support pending a dissolution, legal-separation, or nullity proceeding between spouses.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3600 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's authority to order spousal and child support during the pendency of a proceeding
citations.quote: During the pendency of any proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties or under Division 8 (commencing with Section 3000) (custody of children) or in any proceeding where there is at issue the support of a minor child or a child for whom support is authorized under Section 3901 or 3910, the court may order (a) either spouse to pay any amount that is necessary for the support of the other spouse, consistent with the requirements of subdivisions (i) and (m) of Section 4320 and Section 4325, or (b) either or both parents to pay any amount necessary for the support of the child, as the case may be.

clauses.title: How the Temporary-Support Standard Differs From the Post-Judgment Standard
clauses.body: When a court orders temporary spousal support under this pendency authority, the statute does not require the court to weigh the full, multi-factor list of circumstances that governs a post-judgment spousal-support order. Instead, the statute requires only that a temporary spousal-support order be consistent with two specific subdivisions of that post-judgment factor list — the history-of-domestic-violence factor and the abusive-spouse-conviction factor — together with a separate statute addressing a domestic-violence-related misdemeanor conviction. The domestic-violence-history factor directs consideration of all documented evidence of any history of domestic violence between the parties, including matters such as a plea of nolo contendere, emotional distress from domestic violence, a prior protective order, or a court's finding of domestic violence during the pendency of certain proceedings. The abusive-spouse-conviction factor separately provides that the criminal conviction of an abusive spouse must be considered toward a reduction or elimination of a spousal support award. The cross-referenced separate statute establishes a rebuttable presumption that, where one spouse has certain domestic-violence-related misdemeanor convictions against the other spouse, an award of spousal support to the convicted spouse from the injured spouse is prohibited. Outside of these specific cross-references, the statutory text examined for this document does not itself list the broader set of factors — such as the marital standard of living, each party's earning capacity, or the duration of the marriage — that governs a final, post-judgment spousal-support order under a separate part of the Family Code.
clauses.gap: Family Code § 4320(i) and § 4320(m) are two non-contiguous subdivisions of the same statutory section; they are quoted below as two separate citation entries rather than stitched together with an ellipsis. Family Code § 3600 and § 4325 are each independent statutory sections, not subdivisions of § 4320. This document does not reproduce or address the remaining lettered subdivisions of § 4320 (for example, marketable skills, standard of living, or duration of the marriage) that govern a post-judgment support order — those are addressed in this corpus's Marital Settlement Agreement document. This document also does not independently fetch or verify Family Code § 4324.5, which § 4320(m) cross-references alongside § 4325. Separately, on the question of any local-court guideline-formula practice for temporary spousal support: the statutory sections fetched for this document (§§ 3600, 4320(i), 4320(m), 4325) contain no reference to a computerized or numeric guideline formula for temporary spousal support. That is a real difference from child support, where a separate statute (Family Code § 4055, cited and quoted in this corpus's Child Support Agreement document) codifies a guideline formula in the statute itself. Because no comparable formula language appears in the temporary-spousal-support provisions verified here, this document does not describe or endorse any specific county's local-rule guideline-formula practice (sometimes used by California courts to compute a proposed temporary spousal support figure) — that practice, if any, rests on local court rule rather than on the statutory sections this document verifies, and this document takes no position on which counties use it or how any such formula is calculated.

clauses.title: Automatic Unenforceability During a Period of Reconciliation
clauses.body: Unless the support order itself specifies otherwise, an order for spousal or child support made under this pendency authority is not enforceable during any period in which the parties have reconciled and are living together. This reconciliation-based unenforceability operates by statute rather than by separate court order; it applies unless the order's own terms provide differently.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 3602); no additional independent source was found for this. The statute does not itself define "reconciled" or specify what evidence establishes that the parties are "living together" for this purpose, and it does not state whether or how a party must raise this unenforceability in order to rely on it. This document does not address how a court or the parties determine, in a particular case, whether either condition is met.

citations.cite: the reconciliation-based unenforceability of a temporary support order
citations.quote: Unless the order specifies otherwise, an order made pursuant to this chapter is not enforceable during any period in which the parties have reconciled and are living together.

clauses.title: Modification, Termination, and the Limit on Retroactivity
clauses.body: An order for spousal or child support made under this pendency authority may be modified or terminated at any time while the underlying proceeding remains pending, except as to any amount that already accrued before the date the modifying or terminating party filed the notice of motion or order to show cause. Separately, an order made under this pendency authority does not prejudice either party's rights, or a child's rights, with respect to any subsequent order the court may make in the same proceeding — for example, a final, post-judgment support order entered later in the case.
clauses.gap: § 3603 and § 3604 are independent statutory sections within the same chapter (Chapter 4, §§ 3600-3604), not subdivisions of a single section. Neither section specifies what showing, if any, a party must make to obtain a modification or termination of a temporary support order, or otherwise states the standard a court applies in deciding whether to grant one; this document does not address that standard. This document also does not address how or whether a temporary support order automatically terminates upon entry of a final judgment of dissolution or legal separation, beyond the non-prejudice principle stated in § 3604 — that question was not independently researched for this document.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California Penal Code section 487m -- the state's criminal statute allowing intentional theft of wages to be punished as grand theft -- along with Labor Code section 1197.1's separate, pre-existing civil penalty scheme for underpayment of the minimum wage. It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning a situation described here as: {{wageClaimBasis}}, involving {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}, in an amount currently identified as approximately {{unpaidWagesAmount}}.

Penal Code section 487m is a criminal statute. A violation of it is prosecuted, if at all, by a public prosecutor -- a district attorney or the Attorney General -- not through a private lawsuit. This information sheet does not initiate, threaten, or request any criminal investigation or prosecution, and it does not state that any specific conduct described above does or does not violate section 487m; that is a case-specific determination this document does not make.

This document is also distinct from, and does not replace, this project's existing Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter and Wage Claim with the California Labor Commissioner (Berman Hearing) -- Information Sheet documents, both of which describe civil remedies for unpaid wages rather than this separate criminal statute.

clauses.title: The Dollar Thresholds That Make Intentional Wage Theft Punishable as Grand Theft
clauses.body: Penal Code section 487m, added to California law in 2021 by Assembly Bill 1003 and effective January 1, 2022, states that the intentional theft of wages may be punished as grand theft once it crosses one of two dollar thresholds measured over any consecutive 12-month period: an amount greater than $950 taken from any one employee, or an amount totaling $2,350 or more in the aggregate taken from two or more employees. The statute's own text uses the word "may," not "shall" or "must" -- classification as grand theft under this section is something a prosecution may pursue once a threshold is crossed, not an automatic legal consequence that attaches the moment a threshold is crossed. The statute's threshold is expressly stated to apply "notwithstanding" two other Labor Code sections, 215 and 216, meaning it operates independently of whatever those two sections separately provide.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Penal Code § 487m(a)), used as real evidence of the dollar thresholds and their permissive "may be punished" phrasing -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific situation, and not a claim that any specific amount of unpaid compensation has or has not crossed either threshold. This clause quotes a single subdivision, § 487m(a); the statute's remaining subdivisions -- its definition of "theft of wages," its expanded definitions of "employee" and "employer," its restitution and civil-action-preservation provisions, and its relationship to the general grand theft statute -- are addressed in this document's companion clauses, not repeated here. Labor Code sections 215 and 216, which this subdivision references by name as sections it operates "notwithstanding," were not independently fetched or verified for this document; this clause reports only that § 487m(a) itself references them, not what they themselves say. This document does not independently verify, through Penal Code section 487 itself or through case law, what dollar threshold applies to grand theft generally outside this specific wage-theft context, or how a sentencing court would actually apply this section's "may be punished" language in a specific case; a CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions interpreting § 487m, attempted for this document, returned a daily rate-limit error before any results could be reviewed, so that gap is disclosed here rather than filled with an unverified assertion. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific employer's conduct did or did not cross either threshold, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 487m(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California's criminal wage-theft grand-theft statute, dollar thresholds
citations.quote: (a) Notwithstanding Sections 215 and 216 of the Labor Code, the intentional theft of wages in an amount greater than nine hundred fifty dollars ($950) from any one employee, or two thousand three hundred fifty dollars ($2,350) in the aggregate from two or more employees, by an employer in any consecutive 12-month period may be punished as grand theft.

clauses.title: What Counts as "Theft of Wages": The Definition and Its Intent Element
clauses.body: Penal Code section 487m defines "theft of wages," for purposes of this statute, as the intentional deprivation of wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation, by unlawful means, done with the knowledge that the wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation is due to the employee under the law. The statute borrows its definitions of two of these four categories from elsewhere in the Labor Code rather than defining them itself: "wages" takes the definition already stated in Labor Code section 200, and "gratuities" takes the definition already stated in Labor Code section 350. Labor Code section 200 defines "wages" broadly, as all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whatever method -- time, task, piece, commission, or otherwise -- is used to fix or ascertain the amount. Labor Code section 350 defines "gratuity" to include any tip, gratuity, money, or part of one that a patron of a business has paid, given, or left for an employee over and above the amount actually due the business for the services, goods, food, drink, or articles the patron received. Section 487m's own text does not separately define "benefits" or "other compensation" beyond these words' ordinary meaning; the statute leaves both categories otherwise undefined.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text -- one subdivision of Cal. Penal Code § 487m (subdivision (b)) together with two Labor Code sections it incorporates by cross-reference, Cal. Lab. Code § 200(a) and § 350(e) -- used as real evidence of what "theft of wages" means for this statute's purposes, not a claim about which state's law governs any specific situation, and not a claim that any specific conduct did or did not meet this definition. The two Labor Code citations are cross-referenced definitions section 487m itself borrows by name, not independent corroborating sources for the same proposition; they are quoted here because section 487m's own text does not restate them. Labor Code § 200 contains a second subdivision, (b), defining "labor" -- not quoted here because section 487m does not cross-reference it. Labor Code § 350 contains five other subdivisions, (a) through (d) and (f), defining "employer," "employee," "employing," "agent," and "business" for its own article -- not quoted here for the same reason; only its gratuity definition, subdivision (e), is what section 487m actually cross-references. This clause does not address what case law, if any, has said about the meaning of "intentional," "unlawful means," or the knowledge requirement in subdivision (b), or about the undefined terms "benefits" and "other compensation"; a CourtListener case-law search attempted for this document returned a daily rate-limit error before any results could be reviewed, and given that this statute took effect January 1, 2022, this document does not independently know whether published case law interpreting it yet exists. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific deprivation of wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation was intentional, was accomplished by unlawful means, or was done with the knowledge this statute requires.

Any amounts paid directly by a patron to a dancer employed by an employer subject to Industrial Welfare Commission Order No. 5 or 10 shall be deemed a gratuity.

clauses.title: Section 487m's Expanded Definitions of "Employee" and "Employer"
clauses.body: For purposes of Penal Code section 487m specifically, the statute expands who counts as an "employee" and an "employer" beyond the conventional employment relationship: "employee" includes an independent contractor, and "employer" includes the hiring entity of an independent contractor. This means a hiring entity's intentional, unlawful-means deprivation of compensation due to an independent contractor -- not only a common-law or statutory employee -- can fall within this statute's reach, once the statute's other elements (the dollar thresholds and the intent element, addressed in this document's companion clauses) are also met.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, a single subdivision of the same section addressed throughout this document -- Cal. Penal Code § 487m(c) -- used as real evidence of who this specific statute treats as an "employee" and "employer," not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific person is or is not an independent contractor under California law generally. Section 487m's own text does not itself define "independent contractor" or "hiring entity"; this document does not independently trace those terms to California's separate statutory and case-law tests for distinguishing an independent contractor from an employee (for example, the ABC test codified elsewhere in the Labor Code), and does not determine that any specific working relationship is or is not an independent-contractor relationship. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific person is a covered "employee" or "employer" under this section, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

clauses.title: Restitution, the Preserved Civil Action, and the Relationship to the General Grand Theft Statute
clauses.body: Penal Code section 487m addresses what happens to the underlying compensation once a prosecution under this section occurs, and how this criminal statute relates to two other legal avenues. First, wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation that are the subject of a section 487m prosecution may be recovered as restitution, through the general criminal restitution procedures set out in Penal Code sections 1202.4 and 1203.1. Second, the statute expressly states that it does not prohibit the employee, or the Labor Commissioner, from separately commencing a civil action to seek the remedies the Labor Code otherwise provides for the same underlying acts -- meaning a criminal prosecution under section 487m and a civil wage claim or lawsuit over the same conduct are not mutually exclusive under this statute's own terms. Third, section 487m states that it does not itself change, expand, or limit the scope of conduct already prohibited by California's general grand theft statute, Penal Code section 487; section 487m adds a specific, wage-focused path to a grand theft charge without altering what section 487 itself separately prohibits.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, two subdivisions of the same section addressed throughout this document -- Cal. Penal Code § 487m(d) and (e) -- used as real evidence of the restitution mechanism, the preserved civil action, and the no-change-to-section-487 language, not a claim about which state's law governs any specific matter, and not a claim that restitution would be ordered, or that a civil action would succeed, in any specific case. This document does not independently fetch or verify the text of Penal Code sections 1202.4 or 1203.1 (the general criminal restitution provisions cross-referenced here), or the text of Penal Code section 487 itself (the general grand theft statute this section says it does not change); each is treated here as a named cross-reference within § 487m's own verified text, not as independently researched authority. This corpus's existing Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter and Wage Claim with the California Labor Commissioner (Berman Hearing) -- Information Sheet documents describe what those separate civil remedies actually involve; this clause states only that section 487m itself preserves access to remedies of that kind, not what a specific civil claim arising from the same facts would recover. This clause is informational only: it does not itself seek restitution, does not commence or describe the mechanics of any specific civil action, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

This section does not prohibit the employee or the Labor Commissioner from commencing a civil action to seek remedies provided for under the Labor Code for acts prosecuted under this section.

clauses.title: A Separate, Pre-Existing Civil Track: Labor Code Section 1197.1's Minimum-Wage Civil Penalty
clauses.body: Separately from Penal Code section 487m's criminal grand-theft classification, California law has long provided its own, distinct civil penalty scheme for a related but narrower problem: paying an employee less than the applicable minimum wage. Labor Code section 1197.1 states that an employer or other person who pays or causes to be paid to an employee a wage less than the minimum fixed by an applicable state or local law, or by a wage order, is subject to a civil penalty, restitution of wages, liquidated damages payable to the employee, and any applicable waiting-time penalties -- enforced administratively by the Labor Commissioner through the citation, hearing, and appeal procedures that section and related sections set out, not through a criminal prosecution. Section 1197.1 was last amended effective January 1, 2021, before Assembly Bill 1003 added Penal Code section 487m in 2022; nothing in section 1197.1's own current text refers to section 487m, to grand theft, or to either of section 487m's dollar thresholds, and section 487m's text does not refer to section 1197.1 either. The two statutes address overlapping subject matter -- an employer's failure to pay compensation actually owed -- through separate legal tracks with separate triggers, separate enforcing bodies, and separate consequences: section 1197.1's civil penalty applies specifically to minimum-wage underpayment, without the dollar thresholds section 487m requires, while section 487m's criminal classification applies to the broader category of intentionally, unlawfully withheld wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation, but only once one of its own dollar thresholds is crossed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1197.1(a)), used as real evidence of what California's civil minimum-wage penalty scheme says and how it differs in structure from Penal Code section 487m -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that any specific employer's conduct would trigger one statute, the other, both, or neither. This clause quotes the same subdivision, § 1197.1(a), that this corpus's existing Wage Theft Prevention Act Notice to Employee -- Information Sheet document also quotes, in a different clause, for a different purpose (there, to show that § 1197.1 does not itself reference the separate hiring-notice statute, Labor Code § 2810.5); this document independently re-fetched and re-verified that same subdivision's text, twice, with two different User-Agent headers, rather than assuming the earlier quote remained current, and confirms it is unchanged. Section 1197.1 contains eleven further subdivisions, (b) through (l), addressing citation procedure, hearing and appeal rights, and other administrative mechanics; those are not restated here, since this corpus's existing DLSE Wage Claim and Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter documents already describe the administrative wage-claim process (Labor Code §§ 98 through 98.2) that operates alongside section 1197.1's citation authority in practice, and duplicating that description here was judged unnecessary. This document does not independently verify, through case law, how often conduct severe enough to cross section 487m's dollar thresholds also happens to involve minimum-wage underpayment within the meaning of section 1197.1, or vice versa; the two statutes' overlap or non-overlap in any specific case is a fact-specific question this clause does not resolve. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific employer's conduct is or is not a minimum-wage violation under section 1197.1, is or is not conduct described by section 487m, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

clauses.title: Post-Foreclosure Tenant Notice to Quit: Introduction and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, a California statutory tenant protection that applies after a residential property has been sold at a foreclosure sale: California Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b, which requires the purchaser or other successor in interest to give certain residential tenants a longer written notice to quit than the notice period that would otherwise apply, before an unlawful detainer action to remove them may proceed. It concerns a rental housing unit commonly known as {{propertyAddress}}, reportedly sold at a foreclosure sale on or about {{foreclosureSaleDate}}, previously occupied by {{tenantName}} as tenant, with {{buyerName}} identified as the purchaser or successor in interest following that sale. Section 1161b does not itself use the phrase "bona fide tenant" as a defined statutory term; this sheet uses that commonly-used shorthand only to describe a tenant whose lease is not disqualified from the statute's protections under the specific conditions Section 1161b itself lists, which are described in the clauses below. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself serve, calculate the deadline for, or determine the adequacy of any notice to quit; it does not determine whether any specific tenancy is a month-to-month or periodic tenancy, is under a fixed-term lease, or falls within any exception this statute states; and it does not initiate, advance, or complete any unlawful detainer action concerning this or any other property.

clauses.title: The 90-Day Notice to Quit for a Periodic Tenancy After a Foreclosure Sale
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b(a) requires that a tenant or subtenant in possession of a rental housing unit under a month-to-month lease or other periodic tenancy at the time the property is sold in foreclosure — such as the unit at {{propertyAddress}}, if {{tenantName}}'s tenancy was on that basis — be given at least 90 days' written notice to quit, served under Code of Civil Procedure § 1162, before the tenant or subtenant may be removed from the property under this chapter's summary eviction procedure. The statute expressly states that this 90-day requirement applies "notwithstanding Section 1161a" — meaning it displaces, for this specific situation, the shorter notice period that Section 1161a would otherwise set for a tenant whose unit is sold in various other circumstances (execution sale, judicial foreclosure, private sale, and others), which is described in a companion clause of this sheet. Section 1161b(a) does not itself distinguish among 90-day-notice recipients based on the arm's-length, non-relative, or fair-market-rent conditions that Section 1161b(b) lists — those conditions instead govern a separate, additional protection available specifically to a fixed-term lease tenant, described elsewhere in this sheet.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b, subdivision (a) only, which is the sole citation for this clause. It does not address how the 90-day period is counted (calendar days versus court days, or whether weekends and holidays are excluded), which Section 1161b's text does not itself state and which this clause does not resolve. It does not address the separately-numbered statute governing how a written notice to quit under Section 1162 must be served (personal delivery, substituted service, or posting and mailing) — Section 1162's service mechanics are outside this clause's scope. It does not determine whether any specific tenancy is, in fact, a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy, or whether a specific sale is, in fact, a foreclosure sale within the meaning of this statute.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161b(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 1161b(a)
citations.quote: (a) Notwithstanding Section 1161a, a tenant or subtenant in possession of a rental housing unit under a month-to-month lease or periodic tenancy at the time the property is sold in foreclosure shall be given 90 days’ written notice to quit pursuant to Section 1162 before the tenant or subtenant may be removed from the property as prescribed in this chapter.

clauses.title: The General Post-Sale Notice Period This Statute Displaces
clauses.body: Section 1161b's 90-day notice requirement operates against the backdrop of a separate, more general statute, California Code of Civil Procedure § 1161a, which governs removal of a person holding over after several kinds of post-sale transfers of real property — including, under Section 1161a(b)(3), property "sold in accordance with Section 2924 of the Civil Code, under a power of sale contained in a deed of trust," which is the nonjudicial trustee's-sale foreclosure process most California residential mortgage foreclosures use. Absent Section 1161b's specific 90-day carve-out, Section 1161a(c) would instead require only that a tenant or subtenant be given written notice to quit "at least as long as the term of hiring itself but not exceeding 30 days" before removal. Section 1161b's own text signals this relationship expressly, stating that its 90-day requirement applies "notwithstanding Section 1161a."
clauses.gap: This clause cites two subdivisions of the same statutory section, Code of Civil Procedure § 1161a — subdivision (b)(3) (identifying a trustee's sale under Civil Code § 2924 as one of the causes Section 1161a covers) and subdivision (c) (the general notice-period rule, capped at 30 days, that would apply in the absence of Section 1161b) — grouped together because they together describe the general rule Section 1161b's 90-day requirement overrides for a foreclosure-sale tenant, not because they independently corroborate each other. This clause does not address Section 1161a's other enumerated causes (execution sale, judicial foreclosure, private sale, or a conditional sale contract default under Health and Safety Code § 18037.5), which involve property dispositions other than a nonjudicial foreclosure sale and so are outside the scope of a sheet about Section 1161b. It does not resolve whether Section 1161a's 30-day-or-term-of-hiring notice period, rather than Section 1161b's 90-day period, applies to any specific tenancy — that depends on whether the underlying sale was a foreclosure sale within Section 1161b's meaning, which this clause does not determine.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161a(b)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 1161a(b)(3)
citations.quote: (3) Where the property has been sold in accordance with Section 2924 of the Civil Code, under a power of sale contained in a deed of trust executed by such person, or a person under whom such person claims, and the title under the sale has been duly perfected.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161a(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 1161a(c)
citations.quote: (c) Notwithstanding the provisions of subdivision (b), a tenant or subtenant in possession of a rental housing unit which has been sold by reason of any of the causes enumerated in subdivision (b), who rents or leases the rental housing unit either on a periodic basis from week to week, month to month, or other interval, or for a fixed period of time, shall be given written notice to quit pursuant to Section 1162, at least as long as the term of hiring itself but not exceeding 30 days, before the tenant or subtenant may be removed therefrom as prescribed in this chapter.

clauses.title: Fixed-Term Lease Survival and Its Four Statutory Exceptions
clauses.body: Beyond the 90-day notice requirement for a periodic tenancy, Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b(b) grants a distinct, additional protection to a tenant or subtenant holding possession under a fixed-term residential lease entered into before transfer of title at the foreclosure sale: such a lease-holding tenant "shall have the right to possession until the end of the lease term, and all rights and obligations under the lease shall survive foreclosure." That survival right is not absolute. The statute allows the tenancy to be terminated on 90 days' written notice to quit under subdivision (a) — the same 90-day period described elsewhere in this sheet, not a separate, shorter period — if any one of four listed conditions applies: the purchaser or successor in interest (such as {{buyerName}}) will occupy the unit as a primary residence; the lessee is the mortgagor or the mortgagor's child, spouse, or parent; the lease was not the result of an arm's-length transaction; or the lease requires rent substantially less than fair market rent for the property (unless that reduced or subsidized rent results from a federal, state, or local subsidy or law). Whether a fixed-term lease affecting {{propertyAddress}} is entitled to this survival protection, or instead falls within one of these four conditions, is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b, subdivision (b) in its entirety, including its four numbered conditions — all part of a single statutory subdivision, not independent sources. The statute itself does not use the term "bona fide tenant" anywhere in this subdivision or elsewhere in Section 1161b; this sheet's introductory clause discloses that this sheet's use of that shorthand is not a quotation of statutory language. This clause does not address who bears the burden of proving whether one of the four disqualifying conditions applies (that burden-of-proof rule is addressed in a separate clause of this sheet, sourced to Section 1161b(c)), and it does not determine, for any specific lease, whether it was entered into before transfer of title at the foreclosure sale, whether any occupant is the mortgagor's relative, whether a given transaction was at arm's length, or what fair market rent for a specific unit is — all of which are factual questions this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161b(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 1161b(b)
citations.quote: (b) In addition to the rights set forth in subdivision (a), tenants or subtenants holding possession of a rental housing unit under a fixed-term residential lease entered into before transfer of title at the foreclosure sale shall have the right to possession until the end of the lease term, and all rights and obligations under the lease shall survive foreclosure, except that the tenancy may be terminated upon 90 days’ written notice to quit pursuant to subdivision (a) if any of the following conditions apply: (1) The purchaser or successor in interest will occupy the housing unit as a primary residence. (2) The lessee is the mortgagor or the child, spouse, or parent of the mortgagor. (3) The lease was not the result of an arms’ length transaction. (4) The lease requires the receipt of rent that is substantially less than fair market rent for the property, except when rent is reduced or subsidized due to a federal, state, or local subsidy or law.

clauses.title: Burden of Proof on the Purchaser or Successor in Interest
clauses.body: California Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b(c) places the burden of proof on the party seeking to remove a fixed-term lease tenant early: "The purchaser or successor in interest shall bear the burden of proof in establishing that a fixed-term residential lease is not entitled to protection under subdivision (b)." In other words, if {{buyerName}}, as purchaser or successor in interest for {{propertyAddress}}, contends that {{tenantName}}'s fixed-term lease falls within one of the four disqualifying conditions described in subdivision (b) — owner-occupancy intent, a mortgagor-relative lessee, a non-arm's-length lease, or below-market rent not attributable to a subsidy — the statute assigns that party, not the tenant, the burden of proving it.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b, subdivision (c) only, a single subdivision distinct from, though textually dependent on, subdivision (b)'s four conditions quoted in a separate clause of this sheet. It does not address in which proceeding or forum this burden is applied (for example, as an issue litigated within an unlawful detainer action), what quantum of proof the statute requires, or how a specific dispute over whether a lease is entitled to subdivision (b) protection would be resolved — those procedural questions are not addressed by the statutory text this clause quotes.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161b(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 1161b(c)
citations.quote: (c) The purchaser or successor in interest shall bear the burden of proof in establishing that a fixed-term residential lease is not entitled to protection under subdivision (b).

clauses.title: Two Further Statutory Limits: A Party to the Note, and Local Just-Cause Ordinances
clauses.body: Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b states two further limits on its own application. First, subdivision (d) provides that the entire section "shall not apply if any party to the note remains in the property as a tenant, subtenant, or occupant" — so an occupant who is, or remains, a party to the promissory note the foreclosed deed of trust secured is not within Section 1161b's protection, regardless of whether that occupancy is on a periodic or fixed-term basis. Second, subdivision (e) is an express savings clause: "Nothing in this section is intended to affect any local just cause eviction ordinance," and the section "does not, and shall not be construed to, affect the authority of a public entity that otherwise exists to regulate or monitor the basis for eviction." A city or county ordinance imposing its own just-cause-for-eviction requirements is therefore not preempted or altered by Section 1161b.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b, subdivisions (d) and (e) together, as one contiguous passage of the same statutory section — they are grouped here because both operate as limits on Section 1161b's own application, not because they address the same subject matter as each other. Subdivision (d)'s reference to 'a party to the note' is not itself defined further within this section; this clause does not resolve who counts as a party to the note for a specific loan, or how that status is established. Subdivision (e) does not identify any specific local just-cause ordinance, and this sheet does not research or describe the just-cause or eviction-control ordinance, if any, of the city or county where the affected property is located — a reader would need to consult that jurisdiction's own ordinance separately. This clause also does not address the separate, statewide just-cause eviction and rent-cap statute (Civil Code § 1946.2, under AB 1482), which is the subject of a different information sheet elsewhere in this corpus and operates independently of Section 1161b.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161b(d)-(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. C. § 1161b(d), (e)
citations.quote: (d) This section shall not apply if any party to the note remains in the property as a tenant, subtenant, or occupant. (e) Nothing in this section is intended to affect any local just cause eviction ordinance. This section does not, and shall not be construed to, affect the authority of a public entity that otherwise exists to regulate or monitor the basis for eviction.

clauses.body:
I have reviewed this information sheet describing California's statutory 90-day notice-to-quit requirement and fixed-term lease survival protection under Code of Civil Procedure § 1161b, as they may relate to the rental housing unit at {{propertyAddress}}. I understand that this document is informational only: it does not itself serve any notice to quit, does not determine whether any tenancy is periodic or fixed-term, does not determine whether any of Section 1161b's stated conditions or exceptions applies to {{tenantName}}'s tenancy or {{buyerName}}'s status as purchaser or successor in interest, and does not initiate, advance, or complete any unlawful detainer action.
