clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This is an informational sheet about California Labor Code §§ 221-224 — the statutes that limit an employer's ability to collect back, or withhold, wages already paid to an employee — prepared in connection with a payment made or promised by {{companyName}} to {{employeeName}}: {{repaymentTriggerDescription}}. Amount at issue: {{repaymentAmount}}.

This document explains, using the statutes' own text, what California law says (and does not say) about an employer collecting back wages already paid, the statutes' own narrow exception for certain deductions, and the separate question of whether California law specifically addresses recouping a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training cost after early departure. It is informational only. It does not determine whether {{repaymentAmount}}, or any part of it, is lawfully owed, collectible, or deductible in this or any other specific case, does not determine which state's law applies, and is not a substitute for advice from a qualified attorney.

clauses.title: The Core Rule: An Employer Cannot Collect Back Wages Already Paid
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 221 makes it unlawful for an employer to collect or receive back any part of wages it has already paid to an employee. The statute is a single, general sentence — it does not single out signing bonuses, relocation payments, training costs, or any other specific category of payment, and the words "repayment," "clawback," "chargeback," and "training repayment agreement" appear nowhere in its text. Whatever a specific payment to {{employeeName}} is called by {{companyName}}, § 221's prohibition applies to it once, and only once, that payment has actually become wages already paid to {{employeeName}} — a threshold question this section's own text does not answer for any particular payment.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, quoted from its own current text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific payment, and not a claim that § 221 applies (or does not apply) to any specific signing bonus, relocation payment, or training-cost arrangement. This is a single, self-contained statutory section with no lettered subdivisions; no additional independent source was needed to confirm its internal structure. The statute's own text does not define which payments count as "wages theretofore paid" for its purposes, and in particular does not say whether a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training cost is, by its nature, a wage rather than something else (such as a loan or an advance) — that distinction has instead been addressed by California courts and, separately, by Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (DLSE) opinion letters, addressed honestly and separately in this document's companion clauses rather than folded into this one.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 221 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the prohibition on collecting back wages already paid
citations.quote: It shall be unlawful for any employer to collect or receive from an employee any part of wages theretofore paid by said employer to said employee.

clauses.title: Two Related, but Narrower, Prohibitions — §§ 222 and 223
clauses.body: In the same chapter as § 221, two other Labor Code sections prohibit related but distinct conduct. Section 222 makes it unlawful, specifically "in case of any wage agreement arrived at through collective bargaining," to withhold any part of the agreed wage willfully, unlawfully, or with intent to defraud an employee, a competitor, or any other person. Section 223 makes it unlawful, where a statute or contract requires an employer to maintain a designated wage scale, to secretly pay a lower wage while purporting to pay the designated one. Neither section, on its own text, is written around a departing employee's signing bonus, relocation payment, or training cost: § 222 requires a collective-bargaining wage agreement and a showing of willfulness, unlawfulness, or intent to defraud, and § 223 requires a statute or contract that designates a wage scale and a secret underpayment against it — facts that are not present in most bonus, relocation, or training-repayment arrangements, though whether they are present in {{employeeName}}'s specific arrangement with {{companyName}} is not something this clause determines.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, quoted from its own current text for two independently numbered sections (§ 222 and § 223) within the same chapter as § 221 — they are genuinely separate statutory provisions, not subdivisions of one section or of § 221 itself, though this clause treats them together because both are narrower, fact-specific prohibitions rather than the general rule stated in § 221. Each is a single, self-contained section with no lettered subdivisions. This clause does not determine whether any collective-bargaining wage agreement or any statute or contract designating a wage scale exists in a specific reader's situation, and does not claim that § 222 or § 223 is either satisfied or foreclosed by any particular signing-bonus, relocation, or training-repayment provision.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 222 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the collective-bargaining wage-withholding prohibition
citations.quote: It shall be unlawful, in case of any wage agreement arrived at through collective bargaining, either wilfully or unlawfully or with intent to defraud an employee, a competitor, or any other person, to withhold from said employee any part of the wage agreed upon.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 223 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the secret-underpayment-against-a-designated-wage-scale prohibition
citations.quote: Where any statute or contract requires an employer to maintain the designated wage scale, it shall be unlawful to secretly pay a lower wage while purporting to pay the wage designated by statute or by contract.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own Exception — § 224
clauses.body: Sections 221, 222, and 223 are not absolute: Labor Code § 224 states that none of them makes it unlawful for an employer to withhold or divert part of an employee's wages in three specific circumstances stated on the statute's own face — (1) when the employer is required or empowered to do so by state or federal law; (2) when a deduction is expressly authorized in writing by the employee to cover insurance premiums, hospital or medical dues, or other deductions not amounting to a rebate or deduction from the standard wage arrived at by collective bargaining or pursuant to a wage agreement or statute; or (3) when a deduction to cover health and welfare or pension plan contributions is expressly authorized by a collective bargaining or wage agreement. Section 224 separately makes clear that nothing in it authorizes an employer to withhold or divert wages to pay any tax, fee, or charge prohibited by Government Code § 50026, regardless of whether the employee has authorized it. Section 224's own text does not list a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training cost as a fourth qualifying category, and does not say that a separately signed repayment agreement automatically satisfies category (2)'s "expressly authorized in writing" language for a deduction of that kind.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, quoted in full from its own current text — a single statutory section with no lettered subdivisions of its own (the numbering (1)-(3) above is this drafter's organization of the section's one long sentence, not the Legislature's own subdivision lettering), so the full text is quoted as one contiguous passage below rather than split into separately cited subdivisions. This clause does not independently fetch or verify the text of Government Code § 50026, which § 224 cross-references only to disclaim authorizing withholding to pay a prohibited tax, fee, or charge; only the fact and wording of that cross-reference is stated here. Section 224's text does not resolve, and this clause does not determine, whether a specific signed repayment agreement for a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training cost would qualify as a category-(2) deduction "expressly authorized in writing by the employee" and "not amounting to a rebate" — that is a fact-specific application of the statute's general language that no independently verified case law or DLSE guidance in this clause set resolves directly.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 224 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the exception for legally required, individually authorized, and collectively bargained deductions
citations.quote: The provisions of Sections 221, 222 and 223 shall in no way make it unlawful for an employer to withhold or divert any portion of an employee’s wages when the employer is required or empowered so to do by state or federal law or when a deduction is expressly authorized in writing by the employee to cover insurance premiums, hospital or medical dues, or other deductions not amounting to a rebate or deduction from the standard wage arrived at by collective bargaining or pursuant to wage agreement or statute, or when a deduction to cover health and welfare or pension plan contributions is expressly authorized by a collective bargaining or wage agreement. Nothing in this section or any other provision of law shall be construed as authorizing an employer to withhold or divert any portion of an employee’s wages to pay any tax, fee or charge prohibited by Section 50026 of the Government Code, whether or not the employee authorizes such withholding or diversion.

clauses.title: How Courts Have Read "Wages Already Paid"
clauses.body: California courts applying § 221 have read its prohibition on collecting back "wages" as reaching only wages that have actually been earned by the employee's performance of whatever the payment's own terms required — not a payment that was, by its own terms, merely a conditional advance against something not yet earned. This is the same statutory language and the same judicial gloss already addressed, in the different setting of a commission chargeback, by this corpus's separate Commission Payout Upon Termination document; it is restated here because it bears directly on a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training-cost repayment as well. Whether § 221 protects a specific payment to {{employeeName}} from being collected back therefore depends on whether that payment was, by its own terms, already earned when {{companyName}} paid it — a question this judicial gloss identifies but does not answer for any particular signing bonus, relocation payment, or training-repayment arrangement.
clauses.gap: This is one state's case law, used as real evidence of how a California Court of Appeal has read § 221's "wages already paid" language — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific payment, and not a claim that any particular signing bonus, relocation payment, or training-repayment provision was or was not already earned. This exact quotation was independently verified against the opinion's primary text by an earlier session of this project (for this corpus's Commission Payout Upon Termination document, clause id commpayout_forfeiture_unlawful) and is reused verbatim here rather than re-fetched this session: this session's CourtListener MCP tool returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125 requests/day, quota not resetting until after this session ends), a direct curl fetch of the opinion's page on courtlistener.com returned an AWS WAF "challenge" response (HTTP 202 with an empty body, not the opinion text), and the WebFetch tool reported that the courtlistener.com domain itself is blocked by this environment's network egress proxy (error type EGRESS_BLOCKED) — all three access paths were tried and all three failed, so this citation is disclosed as reused-and-previously-verified rather than independently re-verified this session. Separately, and more importantly for this clause set's specific topic: Steinhebel was a commission-chargeback case, not a case about a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training-repayment agreement; no case squarely addressing the recoupment of a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training cost was independently verified against a primary source this session (see this document's companion clause on DLSE opinion letters for what non-statutory agency guidance, as distinct from independently verified case law, says about a closely related bonus-repayment scenario).

citations.case: Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC
citations.quote: In referring to “wages” paid, section 221 prohibits an employer only from collecting or receiving wages that have already been earned by performance of agreed-upon requirements.

clauses.title: Agency Guidance, Not the Statute: DLSE Opinion Letters
clauses.body: Separately from the statute's own text, the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (DLSE) — the state agency that enforces the Labor Code's wage provisions — has addressed an employer's bonus-repayment provision directly in at least one opinion letter, and has described the legal weight of its own opinion letters in another. Responding in 1987 to an employer's proposed policy of requiring an already-paid bonus to be repaid if the employee did not remain employed for a full year, DLSE's Chief Counsel identified two problems with the proposal: first, that structuring an annual bonus as quarterly payments subject to repayment raises the question of whether the bonus was actually earned quarterly rather than annually; and second, that two California court decisions, described in the letter only by short name and not independently verified in this clause set, "can be interpreted to prevent an employer from deducting the amount of the bonus from any wages due" — meaning an employer wanting the bonus back would have to pursue the employee through the civil courts rather than simply withholding it from wages. Separately, in a 1993 letter on a different bonus question, DLSE described the weight its own opinion letters carry: an "official opinion" by the Division "would be entitled to little or no weight in the courts," because interpreting bonus contracts is not an area the Legislature has given DLSE authority to set binding standards. Neither letter is the statute itself, and neither is a court decision; both are the agency's own non-binding interpretive guidance about bonus repayment specifically, offered here because {{employeeName}} or {{companyName}} may encounter this kind of guidance cited elsewhere as though it settled the question.
clauses.gap: These are two DLSE opinion letters, fetched directly from dir.ca.gov/dlse/opinions and independently verified this session — each PDF was fetched twice, using two distinct User-Agent strings, and the two fetches were byte-identical for both letters. Both are non-binding agency guidance, not statutes and not court decisions; the 1993 letter's own text says so explicitly, in the language quoted above, about DLSE opinion letters generally. The 1987 letter's reference to two court decisions (given in the letter only as "Kerr's Catering and Barnhill," without a full citation) is reported here only as the letter's own characterization of those cases; this clause does not independently verify either case's citation or holding, for the same CourtListener rate-limiting and blocked-network-access reasons disclosed in this document's companion clause on the § 221 judicial gloss. The 1987 letter concerns a quarterly-versus-annual bonus repayment scenario specifically, not a signing bonus, relocation payment, or training-repayment agreement by name; no DLSE opinion letter specifically addressing a signing bonus, relocation cost, or training-repayment agreement by that name was found in DLSE's own opinion-letter index (searched by subject at dir.ca.gov/dlse/OpinionLetters-bySubject.htm) during this session's research, and this clause does not assume one exists. A separate, related 1993 DLSE letter in the same index addresses a different question — whether a bonus not yet paid must be paid at all when an employee voluntarily leaves before a vesting date — rather than clawing back a bonus already paid, and is not addressed in this clause set.

citations.case: Cal. Dep't of Indus. Relations, Div. of Labor Standards Enforcement, Opinion Letter 1987.07.01 (bonus repayment upon early termination)
citations.cite: DLSE Opinion Letter 1987.07.01
citations.quote: Paying a yearly bonus on a quarterly basis would not be violative of any of the State’s wage payment laws; however, requiring the quarterly bonus to be repaid if the employee does not remain for one year presents several problems.

citations.case: Cal. Dep't of Indus. Relations, Div. of Labor Standards Enforcement, Opinion Letter 1987.07.01 (bonus repayment upon early termination)
citations.cite: DLSE Opinion Letter 1987.07.01
citations.quote: The second problem with your concept is the application of two court decisions, Kerr's Catering and Barnhill, which can be interpreted to prevent an employer from deducting the amount of the bonus from any wages due.

citations.cite: DLSE Opinion Letter 1993.01.19
citations.quote: Any "official opinion" by this Division would be entitled to little or no weight in the courts.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Receipt
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement under Government Code § 12950.1, as it relates to {{companyName}}, which reports approximately {{employeeCount}} employees, and to {{employeeName}}. It states facts drawn from the statute's own text about which employers the statute covers, how many hours of training the statute requires and for which category of employee, how often the statute requires that training to repeat, the timing the statute sets for a new hire's or new supervisor's first training, the content categories the statute specifies, and the statute's own limits on what compliance with it does and does not establish in a harassment case.

This information sheet does not determine whether {{companyName}} is an employer the statute covers, whether {{employeeName}} holds a "supervisory" or "nonsupervisory" position for purposes of the statute, whether {{companyName}}'s training as actually delivered satisfies every requirement described here, or what {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} should do about any of the facts it describes.

clauses.title: Which Employers Must Comply
clauses.body: California law requires an employer having five or more employees to provide the sexual harassment prevention training described in this information sheet. For purposes of this particular statute, an "employer" is defined to include any person who regularly employs five or more persons, or who regularly receives the services of five or more persons providing services under a contract — meaning the count that triggers this training requirement is not limited to an employer's own common-law employees — as well as any person acting as an employer's agent, the state, its political or civil subdivisions, and cities.
clauses.gap: Both quotes below are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Government Code § 12950.1 — the first from subdivision (a)(1) and the second from subdivision (h)(1), which defines "employer" only "for purposes of this section." This clause does not cover the separate, more general definition of "employer" used elsewhere in the Fair Employment and Housing Act (Government Code § 12926), which differs from this section's own definition and governs other FEHA protections, including the harassment prohibition itself, which under a separate FEHA provision (Government Code § 12940(j)) is not limited to employers of any particular size — this clause does not independently verify that separate provision's current text. This clause also does not independently verify how "regularly receiving the services of five or more persons providing services pursuant to a contract" has been construed in practice — that is a factual/interpretive question the statute's text alone does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the employer coverage threshold
citations.quote: By January 1, 2021, an employer having five or more employees shall provide at least two hours of classroom or other effective interactive training and education regarding sexual harassment to all supervisory employees and at least one hour of classroom or other effective interactive training and education regarding sexual harassment to all nonsupervisory employees in California.

citations.quote: For purposes of this section only, “employer” means any person regularly employing five or more persons or regularly receiving the services of five or more persons providing services pursuant to a contract, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state, or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities.

clauses.title: Two Hours for Supervisory Employees, One Hour for Nonsupervisory Employees
clauses.body: The statute sets a different minimum number of training hours depending on the employee's role. It requires at least two hours of classroom or other effective interactive training and education regarding sexual harassment for supervisory employees, and at least one hour of the same kind of training for nonsupervisory employees. The same two-hour/one-hour division carries over to the state-developed online training courses the statute separately directs the state to make available: the online course for nonsupervisory employees is one hour long, and the online course for supervisory employees is two hours long.
clauses.gap: Both quotes are subdivisions of Government Code § 12950.1 — (a)(1) and (j). The statute permits the required hours to be completed individually or in a group, and in shorter segments, "as long as the applicable hourly total requirement is met" (also subdivision (a)(1), a phrase this clause does not separately quote). This clause does not define "supervisory employee"; that term is defined elsewhere in the Fair Employment and Housing Act (Government Code § 12926), which this clause does not independently fetch, quote, or verify.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the two-hour/one-hour split
citations.quote: By January 1, 2021, an employer having five or more employees shall provide at least two hours of classroom or other effective interactive training and education regarding sexual harassment to all supervisory employees and at least one hour of classroom or other effective interactive training and education regarding sexual harassment to all nonsupervisory employees in California.

citations.cite: California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the length of the state's own online training courses
citations.quote: The course for nonsupervisory employees shall be one hour in length and the course for supervisory employees shall be two hours in length.

clauses.title: Two-Year Retraining Cycle and New-Hire/New-Supervisor Timing
clauses.body: Once an employer has provided the initial round of training, the statute requires the employer to provide sexual harassment training and education to each covered employee again once every two years. The statute sets separate deadlines for employees who join, or are newly promoted into, a covered role between two-year cycles: a new nonsupervisory employee must be trained within six months of hire, and a new supervisory employee must be trained within six months of assuming the supervisory position.
clauses.gap: Both quotes are from subdivision (a)(1) of Government Code § 12950.1. This clause does not cover the statute's separate, narrower timing rule for seasonal, temporary, or other employees hired to work less than six months, which — per subdivision (f), not quoted here — instead requires training within 30 calendar days of the hire date or within 100 hours worked, whichever occurs first. It also does not cover subdivision (m)'s portability rule for an employee already trained in compliance with this section by a current, prior, alternate, or joint employer within the preceding two years, nor the multiemployer-collective-bargaining-agreement construction-industry alternative in subdivision (l). The statute's own text separately notes a now-historical rule, not quoted here, that an employer who provided this training to an employee in 2019 was not required to provide refresher training to that employee again until two years thereafter.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the recurring two-year training cycle
citations.quote: Thereafter, each employer covered by this section shall provide sexual harassment training and education to each employee in California once every two years.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the six-month deadline for new nonsupervisory and new supervisory employees
citations.quote: New nonsupervisory employees shall be provided training within six months of hire. New supervisory employees shall be provided training within six months of the assumption of a supervisory position.

clauses.title: What the Training Must Cover
clauses.body: The statute specifies particular content categories the training must include, beyond the hours themselves. The training must include information and practical guidance regarding the federal and state statutory provisions concerning the prohibition against, and the prevention and correction of, sexual harassment, and the remedies available to victims of sexual harassment in employment, along with practical examples aimed at instructing supervisors in the prevention of harassment, discrimination, and retaliation, presented by trainers or educators with knowledge and expertise in the prevention of harassment, discrimination, and retaliation. Separately, the statute requires that the training include prevention of "abusive conduct" as a component, and that it include training inclusive of harassment based on gender identity, gender expression, and sexual orientation as a component.
clauses.gap: All three quotes are subdivisions of Government Code § 12950.1: the first from (a)(1), the second from (a)(2), and the third from (a)(3). The statute separately defines "abusive conduct" in subdivision (h)(2), a definition this clause does not quote. This clause also does not cover subdivision (i)'s option for an employer to develop its own training module or to direct employees to the state's online course instead, nor the further detail the statute gives (in subdivision (l)(5)(B)) about what a "qualified trainer" must be able to teach when relied on under the separate multiemployer-collective-bargaining-agreement alternative in subdivision (l) — that detail is specific to that alternative and does not itself define what every employer's general training content must cover.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, mandatory sexual harassment prevention training requirement, the required general content
citations.quote: The training and education required by this section shall include information and practical guidance regarding the federal and state statutory provisions concerning the prohibition against and the prevention and correction of sexual harassment and the remedies available to victims of sexual harassment in employment. The training and education shall also include practical examples aimed at instructing supervisors in the prevention of harassment, discrimination, and retaliation, and shall be presented by trainers or educators with knowledge and expertise in the prevention of harassment, discrimination, and retaliation.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12950.1(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)

citations.quote: An employer shall also include prevention of abusive conduct as a component of the training and education specified in paragraph (1).

clauses.title: Compliance Is Not a Shield, and Non-Compliance Is Not Automatic Liability
clauses.body: The statute draws an explicit two-way line around what compliance with it proves in a harassment case. On one side, a claim that the required training did not actually reach a particular individual does not, by itself, make an employer liable to that individual in a lawsuit alleging sexual harassment. On the other side, an employer's compliance with the training requirement does not insulate the employer from liability for sexual harassment of any current or former employee or applicant. Separately, the statute gives a state agency — not the individual employee — the mechanism for enforcing the training requirement itself: if an employer violates this section, the department may seek an order requiring the employer to comply with these requirements.
clauses.gap: Both quotes are subdivisions of Government Code § 12950.1 — (c) and (d). Subdivision (c) also cross-references Government Code § 12940, subdivisions (j) and (k) (the general FEHA harassment-liability and reasonable-steps provisions), which this clause does not independently fetch, quote, or verify. "The department" in subdivision (d) is not separately defined within the quoted text; the chapter heading on the fetched source page identifies the enclosing part of the Government Code as governing the "Civil Rights Department," the name given by a 2022 renaming to the same agency this chapter has long treated as its enforcing department, but this clause does not independently trace that renaming's legislative history beyond what the fetched source's own heading shows.

citations.quote: a claim that the training and education required by this section did not reach a particular individual or individuals shall not in and of itself result in the liability of any employer to any present or former employee or applicant in any action alleging sexual harassment. Conversely, an employer’s compliance with this section does not insulate the employer from liability for sexual harassment of any current or former employee or applicant.

clauses.title: Training Record and Acknowledgment
How the Federal Estate Tax Credit Mechanism Works
clauses.body: Federal estate tax law does not exempt a decedent's estate from tax outright below a stated dollar line. Instead, it works through a credit: every estate is allowed a credit against the estate tax otherwise imposed under 26 U.S.C. § 2001, and that credit is defined as the amount of tax that would apply, under the same tax-rate schedule used to compute the estate tax itself, to a dollar amount called the "applicable exclusion amount." The practical effect is that no federal estate tax is owed unless and until the value being taxed exceeds the applicable exclusion amount — but the statute frames this as a credit computation, not a flat exemption line written as a single number.
clauses.gap: 26 U.S.C. § 2010(a) and § 2010(c)(1) are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 2010), not independent sources. This clause explains the credit mechanism only; it does not restate the tax-rate schedule in § 2001(c) that the credit computation depends on, which was not independently fetched or cited here. It does not compute a specific credit or tax amount for any actual estate. § 2010(b)'s separate, narrower rule (a reduction to the credit for certain pre-1977 gifts) is not addressed by this clause.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2010(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, general rule allowing a unified credit against estate tax
citations.quote: A credit of the applicable credit amount shall be allowed to the estate of every decedent against the tax imposed by section 2001.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, definition of the applicable credit amount
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, the applicable credit amount is the amount of the tentative tax which would be determined under section 2001(c) if the amount with respect to which such tentative tax is to be computed were equal to the applicable exclusion amount.

clauses.title: The Basic Exclusion Amount and Its Inflation-Adjustment Mechanism
clauses.body: The "applicable exclusion amount" used to compute the credit described elsewhere in this document is defined by statute as the sum of two components: a "basic exclusion amount," and, for a surviving spouse, a "deceased spousal unused exclusion amount" carried over from a deceased spouse (addressed in a separate clause below). As of the statute's current text, the basic exclusion amount is set at a specific figure: $15,000,000. The statute's text further provides that, for a decedent dying in a calendar year after 2026, this $15,000,000 figure is increased for inflation using a cost-of-living formula tied to the Internal Revenue Code's general inflation-adjustment provision (26 U.S.C. § 1(f)(3)), rounded to the nearest $10,000. Because the statute sets 2026 as the base year for this inflation adjustment — the adjustment applies only to a decedent dying "after 2026" — the $15,000,000 figure stated directly in the statute's text is, by its own terms, the operative basic exclusion amount for a decedent dying in calendar year 2026 itself, without any further adjustment. For a decedent dying in a later calendar year, the statute establishes only the method for adjusting that figure; it does not state what the resulting adjusted dollar amount will be. That later-year figure is published annually by the IRS (typically in a Revenue Procedure) and is not part of the statute's own text.
clauses.gap: 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(2), § 2010(c)(3)(A), and § 2010(c)(3)(B) are all subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 2010(c) — not independent sources of authority, though they define a single connected mechanism. Research finding disclosed for accuracy: the current $15,000,000 basic exclusion amount and the 'after 2026' inflation-adjustment trigger were both written into § 2010(c)(3) by Pub. L. 119-21, § 70106(a) (signed July 4, 2025); that same 2025 law repealed a prior provision, former § 2010(c)(3)(C) (added by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act), which would otherwise have reverted the basic exclusion amount to a lower, $5,000,000-indexed figure for estates of decedents dying after December 31, 2025. That repealed sunset provision is no longer part of the current statute and is described here only as historical context, not cited as current law. This clause does not state any inflation-adjusted dollar figure for a decedent dying after calendar year 2026; determining that figure requires independently fetching and citing the applicable IRS Revenue Procedure for that later year, which this research did not do since no such figure is currently needed to state the law accurately for a 2026 death. This clause also does not address the separate generation-skipping transfer tax exemption (26 U.S.C. § 2631), a related but distinct provision not researched here, or any state-level estate or inheritance tax (California currently imposes none, but this clause makes no representation about any other state).

citations.quote: the applicable exclusion amount is the sum of— (A) the basic exclusion amount, and (B) in the case of a surviving spouse, the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, current basic exclusion amount as stated in the statute's text ($15,000,000)
citations.quote: For purposes of this subsection, the basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000.

citations.quote: In the case of any decedent dying in a calendar year after 2026, the dollar amount in subparagraph (A) shall be increased by an amount equal to— (i) such dollar amount, multiplied by (ii) the cost-of-living adjustment determined under section 1(f)(3) for such calendar year by substituting “calendar year 2025” for “calendar year 2016” in subparagraph (A)(ii) thereof. If any amount as adjusted under the preceding sentence is not a multiple of $10,000, such amount shall be rounded to the nearest multiple of $10,000.

clauses.title: Portability: A Surviving Spouse's Use of a Deceased Spouse's Unused Exclusion Amount
clauses.body: Federal estate tax law allows a surviving spouse's own applicable exclusion amount to include not just that spouse's own basic exclusion amount, but also any unused exclusion amount left over from a deceased spouse — a mechanism commonly called "portability." The statute defines this carried-over amount, the "deceased spousal unused exclusion amount," as the lesser of (1) the basic exclusion amount, or (2) the excess of the deceased spouse's own applicable exclusion amount over the amount actually used in computing the tentative tax on that deceased spouse's estate — in short, whatever exclusion the deceased spouse had available but did not use. This carried-over amount is not automatic. The statute requires an affirmative election: it may not be taken into account by the surviving spouse unless the executor of the deceased spouse's estate files an estate tax return that computes the amount and elects that it may be used, and that return must be filed by the deadline the law otherwise prescribes for that return (including any extensions). Once made, the statute states that this election is irrevocable, and no election may be made at all if the return is filed after that deadline has passed.
clauses.gap: 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(2)(B), § 2010(c)(4), and § 2010(c)(5)(A) are all subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 2010(c) — not independent sources, though together they state the complete portability mechanism and its election requirement. This clause covers only the estate-tax applicable exclusion amount; it does not address whether the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount is likewise usable for generation-skipping transfer tax purposes — a separate question this research did not investigate, and one where the general understanding in secondary sources is that GST exemption is not portable, though that was not independently verified against statutory text here. This clause does not detail the separate examination rule in § 2010(c)(5)(B) (allowing the IRS to examine a deceased spouse's return after the normal limitations period has run, solely to verify the unused exclusion amount) beyond noting its existence, and it does not address the mechanics or requirements of a 'portability-only' estate tax return filed by an estate that would not otherwise be required to file one — that procedural detail is governed by separate Treasury regulations and IRS guidance not fetched or cited here.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(2)(B) (Cornell LII text)

citations.quote: the applicable exclusion amount is the sum of— (A) the basic exclusion amount, and (B) in the case of a surviving spouse, the deceased spousal unused exclusion amount

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(4) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, definition of "deceased spousal unused exclusion amount"
citations.quote: the term “deceased spousal unused exclusion amount” means the lesser of— (A) the basic exclusion amount, or (B) the excess of— (i) the applicable exclusion amount of the last such deceased spouse of such surviving spouse, over (ii) the amount with respect to which the tentative tax is determined under section 2001(b)(1) on the estate of such deceased spouse.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2010(c)(5)(A) (Cornell LII text)

Such election, once made, shall be irrevocable. No election may be made under this subparagraph if such return is filed after the time prescribed by law (including extensions) for filing such return.

clauses.title: The Marital Deduction Under Section 2056
clauses.body: In computing the federal taxable estate, the statute allows a deduction from the gross estate for the value of any property interest that passes, or has passed, from the decedent to the decedent's surviving spouse, to the extent that interest is included in the gross estate in the first place. The statute's own text states no dollar ceiling on this deduction — it is limited only by the restrictions the statute separately places on the type of interest that qualifies (described in the gap note below), not by any cap on value. Because the statute states no maximum amount, this deduction is commonly referred to as the "unlimited marital deduction": property passing outright to a qualifying surviving spouse can, as a matter of the deduction's own terms, be deducted from the gross estate in full, regardless of its value.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes and describes § 2056(a) only, the general allowance rule. It does not detail § 2056(b), a substantial and separately numbered limitation within the same section that denies the deduction for many kinds of "terminable interests" (property interests that will end or fail on a future event, such as most ordinary life estates), subject to several statutory exceptions (including a qualified terminable interest property, or "QTIP," election under § 2056(b)(7)) that were not researched or cited here. That limitation is real and frequently determinative in practice; this clause does not resolve whether it applies to any specific bequest. Separately, § 2056(d) (not researched or cited here) imposes a materially different rule where the surviving spouse is not a United States citizen, generally requiring the property to pass through a Qualified Domestic Trust for the deduction to apply — that distinct rule is not addressed by this clause and is flagged here as a real gap rather than assumed away. This clause addresses the federal estate tax marital deduction only, not the separate, parallel gift tax marital deduction under 26 U.S.C. § 2523, which was not researched here.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2056(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, general rule allowing an estate tax deduction for property passing to a surviving spouse
citations.quote: For purposes of the tax imposed by section 2001, the value of the taxable estate shall, except as limited by subsection (b), be determined by deducting from the value of the gross estate an amount equal to the value of any interest in property which passes or has passed from the decedent to his surviving spouse, but only to the extent that such interest is included in determining the value of the gross estate.

clauses.title: The Annual Per-Donee Gift Tax Exclusion Under Section 2503(b)
clauses.body: In computing a donor's total taxable gifts for a calendar year, federal gift tax law excludes a set amount of present-interest gifts (as opposed to gifts of a future interest, which do not qualify) made to any one recipient during that year. The statute's own text states a base figure for this per-recipient exclusion of $10,000, and separately directs that this base figure be increased for inflation for gifts made in a calendar year after 1998, using the same type of cost-of-living formula used elsewhere in the estate and gift tax statute, rounded down to the nearest $1,000. As with the estate tax basic exclusion amount addressed elsewhere in this document, the statute's own text establishes only the $10,000 base figure and the method for adjusting it — it does not state the resulting inflation-adjusted dollar amount that applies to a gift made in any specific current or future calendar year. That current figure is published annually by the IRS, typically in a Revenue Procedure, and is not contained in the statute's text itself.
clauses.gap: 26 U.S.C. § 2503(b)(1) and § 2503(b)(2) are subdivisions of the same statutory subsection, § 2503(b) — not independent sources, though together they state one connected mechanism (a base amount plus an adjustment formula). This clause deliberately does not state any specific current per-donee exclusion dollar figure, because that figure is not part of the statute's own text and this research did not independently fetch and cite a current IRS Revenue Procedure to establish it — stating an unverified or potentially stale figure as "the current annual exclusion" was avoided rather than risk presenting outdated information as settled law. § 2503(b)(1)'s text also states that only gifts of a "present interest" (not a "future interest") qualify for this exclusion at all; this clause states that distinction as the statute frames it but does not detail the case law or regulatory tests for what makes a given gift a present versus future interest, which were not researched here. Related provisions not addressed by this clause include § 2503(c) (a special present-interest rule for certain gifts to a minor, sometimes implemented through a Uniform Transfers to Minors Act custodial account, addressed elsewhere in this corpus), § 2503(e) (a separate, unlimited exclusion for qualifying tuition and medical-expense payments made directly to the provider), and § 2513 (the gift-splitting election allowing a married couple to treat gifts as made half by each spouse) — none of which were fetched or cited here.

citations.quote: In the case of gifts (other than gifts of future interests in property) made to any person by the donor during the calendar year, the first $10,000 of such gifts to such person shall not, for purposes of subsection (a), be included in the total amount of gifts made during such year.

If any amount as adjusted under the preceding sentence is not a multiple of $1,000, such amount shall be rounded to the next lowest multiple of $1,000.

clauses.title: Federal Estate Tax Informational Disclosure
clauses.body: This informational note addresses federal estate tax law generally, under 26 U.S.C. §§ 2010 and 2056, and does not calculate or determine any federal estate tax liability for the estate of {{decedentName}}, who died on {{dateOfDeath}}, or for any other estate. The federal basic exclusion amount, the marital deduction, and the portability election described elsewhere in this document are rules of law that apply the same way to every qualifying estate; whether {{decedentName}}'s estate is large enough for federal estate tax to become relevant, whether a deceased spousal unused exclusion amount is or will be available for use by {{survivingSpouseName}}, and whether a portability election has been or should be filed on {{decedentName}}'s estate tax return, are factual and legal determinations specific to this estate that this document does not make. An estimated total estate value of {{estimatedEstateValue}} is recorded here for reference only and is not a valuation for federal estate tax purposes.

clauses.title: Federal Gift Tax Informational Disclosure
clauses.body: This informational note addresses the federal annual per-donee gift tax exclusion under 26 U.S.C. § 2503(b) generally. It does not state the specific dollar amount of that exclusion currently in effect for any calendar year, because the statute's own text sets only a base figure and an inflation-adjustment formula, not a fixed current number; the operative amount changes periodically based on separately published IRS guidance. Nothing in this document determines whether any transfer made by {{giftDonorName}} qualifies for the exclusion, whether the value of a particular gift exceeds the exclusion amount in effect for the calendar year in which it was made, or whether a federal gift tax return is required to be filed as a result.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Inheritance Disqualification for Elder or Dependent Adult Abuse Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California Probate Code § 259 — part of Probate Code Part 7, “Effect of Homicide or Abuse of an Elder or Dependent Adult” (Prob. Code §§ 250–259) — a statute that can disqualify a person from inheriting from, or serving as a fiduciary for, {{decedentName}}, an elder or dependent adult decedent, based on specific findings or a criminal conviction concerning that person's abuse of {{decedentName}} during {{decedentName}}'s lifetime. It states general facts about how § 259 works: the conditions that can trigger disqualification, the “deemed to have predeceased” mechanism the statute uses to describe the consequence, and the definitions § 259 cross-references. It is not a finding, determination, accusation, or admission that any specific person abused {{decedentName}}, and it does not identify, name, or make any claim about any individual. This Information Sheet is distinct from two other, related documents in this corpus. It is not the corpus's Slayer Statute — Disqualification from Inheriting Information Sheet, which describes Prob. Code §§ 250–254, the separate statutory scheme disqualifying a person who feloniously and intentionally kills the decedent; § 259 instead addresses abuse of a decedent who was an elder or dependent adult during that person's lifetime, applies its own distinct evidentiary requirements, and does not require that the abuse caused the decedent's death. It is also not the corpus's Elder and Dependent Adult Financial Abuse Information Sheet, which describes the civil damages remedies that Welfare and Institutions Code §§ 15657.5 and 15657.7 make available to, or on behalf of, an elder or dependent adult during that person's life; § 259 instead operates after the elder or dependent adult's death, as part of distributing that person's own estate, and its consequence is disqualification from inheriting or serving as a fiduciary rather than a money-damages award. This Information Sheet is prepared by {{preparerName}} in connection with the estate of {{decedentName}}.

clauses.title: The Civil Path: Four Findings Required to Disqualify Under §259(a)
clauses.body: Probate Code § 259(a) allows a person to be deemed to have predeceased the decedent — with the consequence described in § 259(c) — only where all four of the following are found. First, it must be proven by clear and convincing evidence, a higher standard than the ordinary civil preponderance-of-the-evidence standard, that the person is liable for physical abuse, neglect, or financial abuse of the decedent, who was an elder or dependent adult. Second, the person must be found to have acted in bad faith. Third, the person must be found to have been reckless, oppressive, fraudulent, or malicious in committing the abuse. Fourth, the decedent must be found to have been substantially unable to manage their financial resources or to resist fraud or undue influence at the time the abuse occurred and thereafter until the decedent's death. All four findings are required for this civil path; § 259(a) does not disqualify a person based on a liability finding alone, and its list of conduct that can support the liability finding — physical abuse, neglect, or financial abuse — does not include false imprisonment, which enters § 259 only through the separate criminal-conviction path in § 259(b). Whether {{decedentName}} met the statutory definition of an elder or dependent adult, and whether these four findings have been made concerning {{decedentName}}'s estate, are facts this Information Sheet does not determine.
clauses.gap: This citation covers all of Prob. Code § 259(a), including its four numbered requirements, (a)(1)-(4), as a single subdivision of one statutory section; it has not been checked against any other code section. This clause does not cover the criminal-conviction path in § 259(b), the disqualification's effect and its regained-capacity limit in § 259(c), or the cross-referenced definitions in § 259(d) (each addressed by a separate clause in this document). It also does not address the procedure by which a court makes these findings — in what proceeding, on whose petition, at what point in estate administration — because § 259 itself does not specify that procedure and this research did not independently investigate it.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 259(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, elder/dependent-adult-abuse disqualification — the four findings required for the civil path
citations.quote: (a) Any person shall be deemed to have predeceased a decedent to the extent provided in subdivision (c) where all of the following apply: (1) It has been proven by clear and convincing evidence that the person is liable for physical abuse, neglect, or financial abuse of the decedent, who was an elder or dependent adult. (2) The person is found to have acted in bad faith. (3) The person has been found to have been reckless, oppressive, fraudulent, or malicious in the commission of any of these acts upon the decedent. (4) The decedent, at the time those acts occurred and thereafter until the time of his or her death, has been found to have been substantially unable to manage his or her financial resources or to resist fraud or undue influence.

clauses.title: The Criminal-Conviction Path: §259(b) and the Penal Code Offenses It Cross-References
clauses.body: Probate Code § 259(b) provides a second, independent path to being deemed to have predeceased the decedent: a person convicted of a violation of Penal Code § 236 — California's general false imprisonment offense, defined as “the unlawful violation of the personal liberty of another” — or of any offense described in Penal Code § 368 is deemed to have predeceased the decedent, without the separate clear-and-convincing findings that § 259(a)'s civil path requires. Penal Code § 368, part of the Penal Code chapter titled “Crimes Against Elders, Dependent Adults, and Persons with Disabilities,” describes a range of offenses against a person the defendant knows or reasonably should know is an elder or dependent adult, including, under § 368(b)(1), willfully causing or permitting an elder or dependent adult to suffer unjustifiable physical pain or mental suffering, or to be injured or endangered, under circumstances likely to produce great bodily harm or death; under § 368(d), theft, embezzlement, forgery, fraud, or identity theft against an elder's or dependent adult's property or personal identifying information by a person who is not the victim's caretaker; and, under § 368(f), false imprisonment of an elder or dependent adult specifically by the use of violence, menace, fraud, or deceit — the § 368 provision that corresponds to § 259(d)(3)'s cross-referenced definition of “false imprisonment,” as the definitions clause of this Information Sheet describes. Whether {{decedentName}}'s estate involves a conviction of this kind, and if so under which subdivision of § 236 or § 368, is a fact this Information Sheet does not determine.
clauses.gap: Prob. Code § 259(b), Penal Code § 236, and Penal Code § 368 are independent statutory sections in different codes, not subdivisions of one section; § 259(b) is the Probate Code provision that cross-references the other two. Penal Code § 368 has additional subdivisions this clause does not quote or independently verify beyond (b)(1), (d), and (f): among them § 368(a) (a legislative-findings preamble), § 368(c) (a misdemeanor version of the § 368(b)(1) conduct), § 368(e) (the caretaker-specific version of the § 368(d) theft offense), § 368(g)-(i) (definitions of ‘elder,’ ‘dependent adult,’ and ‘caretaker’ for purposes of § 368 itself, which are not necessarily identical to the Welfare and Institutions Code definitions the rest of this document and the corpus's existing Elder and Dependent Adult Financial Abuse Information Sheet use), and § 368(j)-(l) (sentencing and other procedural provisions). This clause does not address how ‘any offense described in Section 368’ applies to a conviction resting on a subdivision not summarized here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 259(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, elder/dependent-adult-abuse disqualification — the criminal-conviction path
citations.quote: (b) Any person shall be deemed to have predeceased a decedent to the extent provided in subdivision (c) if that person has been convicted of a violation of Section 236 of the Penal Code or any offense described in Section 368 of the Penal Code.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 236
citations.cite: California Penal Code, general false imprisonment offense
citations.quote: False imprisonment is the unlawful violation of the personal liberty of another.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 368(b)(1)
citations.cite: California Penal Code, elder/dependent adult abuse — physical pain, suffering, injury, or endangerment offense
citations.quote: (b) (1) A person who knows or reasonably should know that a person is an elder or dependent adult and who, under circumstances or conditions likely to produce great bodily harm or death, willfully causes or permits any elder or dependent adult to suffer, or inflicts thereon unjustifiable physical pain or mental suffering, or having the care or custody of any elder or dependent adult, willfully causes or permits the person or health of the elder or dependent adult to be injured, or willfully causes or permits the elder or dependent adult to be placed in a situation in which their person or health is endangered, is punishable by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or by a fine not to exceed six thousand dollars ($6,000), or by both that fine and imprisonment, or by imprisonment in the state prison for two, three, or four years.

citations.quote: (d) A person who is not a caretaker who violates any provision of law proscribing theft, embezzlement, forgery, or fraud, or who violates Section 530.5 proscribing identity theft, with respect to the property or personal identifying information of an elder or a dependent adult, and who knows or reasonably should know that the victim is an elder or a dependent adult, is punishable as follows:

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 368(f)
citations.cite: California Penal Code, elder/dependent adult abuse — false imprisonment by violence, menace, fraud, or deceit
citations.quote: (f) A person who commits the false imprisonment of an elder or a dependent adult by the use of violence, menace, fraud, or deceit is punishable by imprisonment pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1170 for two, three, or four years.

clauses.title: The Predecease Mechanism: What Disqualification Bars, and the Regained-Capacity Limit
clauses.body: Probate Code § 259(c) states the consequence for a person found liable under § 259(a) or convicted under § 259(b). That person shall not receive any property, damages, or costs awarded to the decedent's estate in the action establishing the abuse — whether the person's entitlement would otherwise arise under a will, a trust, or the laws of intestacy — and shall not serve as a fiduciary, as Prob. Code § 39 defines that term, if the instrument nominating or appointing the person was executed while the decedent was substantially unable to manage their financial resources or resist fraud or undue influence. Unlike the general slayer statute's predecease mechanism in Prob. Code § 250(b), § 259(c) does not itself say the disqualified person is treated “as if” they had predeceased the decedent; instead, § 259(a) and § 259(b) each independently state that the disqualified person “shall be deemed to have predeceased” the decedent “to the extent provided in subdivision (c),” and § 259(c) is where that extent is defined — the bar on receiving estate property, damages, or costs, and the bar on serving as a nominated fiduciary, described above. Section 259(c) also states a limit: the section does not apply to a decedent who, at any time after the abusive act or acts, was substantially able to manage their financial resources and resist fraud or undue influence, within the meaning of Prob. Code § 1801(b) and Civil Code § 39(b) — meaning a decedent's later, sufficiently established regained capacity can take the decedent's estate outside § 259's disqualification rule entirely, even where the § 259(a) findings or a § 259(b) conviction would otherwise apply. Whether that limit applies to {{decedentName}}'s estate is a fact this Information Sheet does not determine.
clauses.gap: This citation covers all of Prob. Code § 259(c) as a single subdivision. Section 259(c)'s own text cross-references Prob. Code § 39 (defining ‘fiduciary’), Prob. Code § 1801(b), and Civil Code § 39(b) (both bearing on the capacity standard used for the regained-capacity limit); this research fetched and verified Prob. Code § 259 itself but did not independently fetch or verify the text of Prob. Code § 39, Prob. Code § 1801(b), or Civil Code § 39(b), so this clause's description of those three cross-referenced provisions is limited to how § 259(c) itself characterizes them, not to their full, independently verified text. This clause does not restate the § 259(a) findings or the § 259(b) conviction path themselves (covered by earlier clauses).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 259(c)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, elder/dependent-adult-abuse disqualification — the predecease consequence and the regained-capacity limit
citations.quote: (c) Any person found liable under subdivision (a) or convicted under subdivision (b) shall not (1) receive any property, damages, or costs that are awarded to the decedent’s estate in an action described in subdivision (a) or (b), whether that person’s entitlement is under a will, a trust, or the laws of intestacy; or (2) serve as a fiduciary as defined in Section 39, if the instrument nominating or appointing that person was executed during the period when the decedent was substantially unable to manage his or her financial resources or resist fraud or undue influence. This section shall not apply to a decedent who, at any time following the act or acts described in paragraph (1) of subdivision (a), or the act or acts described in subdivision (b), was substantially able to manage his or her financial resources and to resist fraud or undue influence within the meaning of subdivision (b) of Section 1801 of the Probate Code and subdivision (b) of Section 39 of the Civil Code.

clauses.title: Cross-Referenced Definitions Under §259(d)
clauses.body: Probate Code § 259(d) does not define its four key terms itself; it cross-references other code sections. “Physical abuse” is defined in Welfare and Institutions Code § 15610.63, which lists categories including assault, battery, assault with a deadly weapon or force likely to produce great bodily injury, unreasonable physical constraint, and prolonged or continual deprivation of food or water, as well as (in subdivisions this clause does not separately quote) several forms of sexual assault and use of a physical or chemical restraint or psychotropic medication for punishment, beyond a physician's ordered period, or for an unauthorized purpose. “Neglect” is defined in Welfare and Institutions Code § 15610.57(a) as, in relevant part, the negligent failure of a person having care or custody of an elder or dependent adult — or of an elder or dependent adult personally — to exercise the degree of care a reasonable person in a like position would exercise; § 15610.57(b), not separately quoted here, lists non-exclusive examples including failure to assist with personal hygiene, food, clothing, or shelter, failure to provide needed medical care, failure to protect from health and safety hazards, failure to prevent malnutrition or dehydration, and substantial inability or failure to manage one's own finances. “False imprisonment” is defined by cross-reference to Penal Code § 368 rather than to the Penal Code's general false imprisonment offense in § 236, because — as the criminal-conviction-path clause of this Information Sheet describes — § 368(f) contains an elder- and dependent-adult-specific false imprisonment offense, and it is that specific offense to which § 259(d)(3) points. “Financial abuse” is defined in Welfare and Institutions Code § 15610.30, the same definition described in the corpus's existing Elder and Dependent Adult Financial Abuse Information Sheet, which this Information Sheet does not separately restate.
clauses.gap: The Prob. Code § 259(d) citation covers all four numbered definitions, (d)(1)-(4), as a single subdivision. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.63 and § 15610.57 are independent sections, not subdivisions of § 259 or of each other. The § 15610.63 citation quotes only its chapeau and subdivisions (a)-(d) (assault, battery, assault with a deadly weapon, and unreasonable restraint or food/water deprivation); it does not quote § 15610.63(e) (a list of eight sexual-assault offenses defined by further cross-reference to the Penal Code) or § 15610.63(f) (the restraint-or-psychotropic-medication list), though the body above summarizes both without quoting them verbatim. The § 15610.57 citation quotes only its subdivision (a) (the two-prong negligent-failure definition); it does not quote § 15610.57(b) (the seven-item non-exclusive illustrative list) or § 15610.57(c) (treating homelessness as neglect under specified conditions), though the body summarizes several (b) items without quoting them verbatim. This clause does not independently fetch or quote Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.30 (financial abuse), because that section is already fetched, verified, and quoted in this corpus's existing Elder and Dependent Adult Financial Abuse Information Sheet (clause elderabuse_financial_abuse_definition); this clause points to that existing coverage rather than duplicating it.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, elder/dependent-adult-abuse disqualification — cross-referenced definitions
citations.quote: (d) For purposes of this section, the following definitions shall apply: (1) “Physical abuse” as defined in Section 15610.63 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. (2) “Neglect” as defined in Section 15610.57 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. (3) “False imprisonment” as defined in Section 368 of the Penal Code. (4) “Financial abuse” as defined in Section 15610.30 of the Welfare and Institutions Code.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 15610.63(a)-(d)
citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.63, “physical abuse” (chapeau and subdivisions (a)-(d))
citations.quote: “Physical abuse” means any of the following: (a) Assault, as defined in Section 240 of the Penal Code. (b) Battery, as defined in Section 242 of the Penal Code. (c) Assault with a deadly weapon or force likely to produce great bodily injury, as defined in Section 245 of the Penal Code. (d) Unreasonable physical constraint, or prolonged or continual deprivation of food or water.

citations.cite: Welf. & Inst. C. § 15610.57(a), “neglect”
citations.quote: (a) “Neglect” means either of the following: (1) The negligent failure of any person having the care or custody of an elder or a dependent adult to exercise that degree of care that a reasonable person in a like position would exercise. (2) The negligent failure of an elder or dependent adult to exercise that degree of self care that a reasonable person in a like position would exercise.

clauses.title: Severance to a Separate Civil Action
clauses.body: Probate Code § 259(e) states that nothing in § 259 is to be construed to prohibit the severance and transfer of an action or proceeding to a separate civil action under Prob. Code § 801. Section 801 is a general probate-jurisdiction provision, not specific to § 259: it allows the court, on its own motion or a party's motion, to order that an action or proceeding not specifically provided for in the Probate Code be determined in a separate civil action, and, once the appropriate filing fees are paid, to order the severed action or proceeding transferred to that separate civil action. Section 259(e) thus confirms that a § 259 disqualification dispute is not required to be resolved entirely within the probate proceeding itself; § 801's general severance-and-transfer mechanism remains available for it.
clauses.gap: Prob. Code § 259(e) and Prob. Code § 801 are independent sections, though § 259(e) is the specific provision confirming § 801 applies to a § 259 dispute. Section 801 is a general Probate Code jurisdiction provision (Division 2, Part 16) that applies well beyond § 259; this clause describes only its severance-and-transfer mechanism as § 259(e) invokes it, not the whole of Part 16's jurisdictional scheme, and does not address what other Probate Code provisions besides § 259 rely on § 801.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 259(e)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, elder/dependent-adult-abuse disqualification — severance to a separate civil action
citations.quote: (e) Nothing in this section shall be construed to prohibit the severance and transfer of an action or proceeding to a separate civil action pursuant to Section 801.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 801
citations.cite: California Probate Code, general severance and transfer to a separate civil action
citations.quote: The court, on its own motion or on the motion of any interested party, may order that an action or proceeding not specifically provided in this code be determined in a separate civil action. Upon the payment of the appropriate filing fees, the court may order transfer of the severed action or proceeding to the separate civil action.
