clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's computer software employee overtime exemption, codified at Labor Code § 515.5, in connection with the position of {{jobTitle}} held or to be held by {{employeeName}} at {{companyName}}.

Labor Code § 515.5 is a separate and independent statutory exemption from the general executive, administrative, and professional exemptions addressed elsewhere in this corpus's Exempt / Non-Exempt Classification Notice document. Those general exemptions are established by the Industrial Welfare Commission under Labor Code § 515(a) and depend on a duties test plus a salary set as a multiple of the state minimum wage. Section 515.5 instead sets its own specific duties criteria and its own specific, dollar-denominated rate-of-pay floor, adjusted annually by the Department of Industrial Relations, that is not tied to the minimum wage. A position can potentially qualify for the Section 515.5 exemption without qualifying for the general exemptions, and vice versa — meeting one test does not by itself show that the other is met.

This information sheet does not itself determine that {{employeeName}}'s position at {{companyName}} does or does not qualify for the Section 515.5 exemption, does not apply this test to any specific facts, does not investigate or make any finding about any specific position, and does not file anything with any agency or court.

clauses.title: California's Overtime Default and How the Computer Software Exemption Differs From the General Exemptions
clauses.body:
California law generally requires overtime compensation for work beyond eight hours in a workday or 40 hours in a workweek, and for the first eight hours worked on a seventh consecutive day of work in a workweek, at not less than one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay under Labor Code § 510. Labor Code § 515.5(a) provides that, except as stated in its own subdivision (b), an employee in the computer software field is exempt from this Section 510 overtime requirement if the criteria described below are all met.

This is a structurally different path to exemption than the one Labor Code § 515(a) provides for executive, administrative, and professional employees. Section 515(a) authorizes the Industrial Welfare Commission to establish those exemptions where the employee is primarily engaged in duties meeting an IWC-adopted duties test and earns a monthly salary equivalent to at least two times the state minimum wage. Section 515.5, by contrast, is a self-contained statutory exemption: its duties criteria are written into the statute itself rather than adopted by IWC regulation, and its rate-of-pay requirement is a specific dollar figure adjusted annually by the Department of Industrial Relations based on a consumer price index, independent of the state minimum wage.
clauses.gap: Labor Code §§ 515.5(a) and 515(a) are independent statutory sections (515.5 is not a subdivision of 515); § 510 is likewise an independent section that both 515 and 515.5 reference as the overtime requirement they provide exemptions from. This clause does not address Labor Code § 511 (alternative workweek schedules), § 514 (exemptions under a qualifying collective bargaining agreement), the outside salesperson exemption, or the separate federal FLSA computer employee exemption (29 U.S.C. § 213(a)(17)) — none of those are covered by this document. It also does not address the remainder of § 515 (subdivisions (b) through (f), covering matters such as the treatment of nonexempt salaried employees' regular rate and special rules for registered nurses), which are not relevant to the Section 515.5 computer software exemption described here.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 510(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Any work in excess of eight hours in one workday and any work in excess of 40 hours in any one workweek and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in any one workweek shall be compensated at the rate of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay for an employee.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 515.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), an employee in the computer software field shall be exempt from the requirement that an overtime rate of compensation be paid pursuant to Section 510 if all of the following apply:

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 515(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (a) The Industrial Welfare Commission may establish exemptions from the requirement that an overtime rate of compensation be paid pursuant to Sections 510 and 511 for executive, administrative, and professional employees, if the employee is primarily engaged in the duties that meet the test of the exemption, customarily and regularly exercises discretion and independent judgment in performing those duties, and earns a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment.

clauses.title: The Computer Software Employee Duties and Skill Test
clauses.body: Labor Code § 515.5(a) lists four conditions that must all apply for the exemption to be available; the first three describe the nature of the work and the employee's skill level. The employee must be primarily engaged in work that is intellectual or creative and that requires the exercise of discretion and independent judgment. The employee must also be primarily engaged in duties consisting of one or more of: applying systems analysis techniques and procedures (including consulting with users) to determine hardware, software, or system functional specifications; the design, development, documentation, analysis, creation, testing, or modification of computer systems or programs, including prototypes, based on and related to user or system design specifications; or the documentation, testing, creation, or modification of computer programs related to the design of software or hardware for computer operating systems. Finally, the employee must be highly skilled and proficient in the theoretical and practical application of highly specialized information to computer systems analysis, programming, or software engineering. The statute itself states that a job title is not determinative of whether this exemption applies.
clauses.gap: This clause covers Labor Code § 515.5(a)(1) through (a)(3) — three of the four paragraphs within subdivision (a) of the same statutory section as the rate-of-pay requirement covered in a separate clause of this document (§ 515.5(a)(4)). All four paragraphs of subdivision (a) must be satisfied together for the exemption to apply; meeting the duties and skill criteria in (1) through (3) without also meeting the rate-of-pay requirement in (4) does not qualify a position for this exemption, and vice versa. This clause also does not cover subdivision (b)'s exclusions, which are addressed in a separate clause, and it does not determine whether any specific employee's actual duties meet this test.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 515.5(a)(1)-(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (1) The employee is primarily engaged in work that is intellectual or creative and that requires the exercise of discretion and independent judgment. (2) The employee is primarily engaged in duties that consist of one or more of the following: (A) The application of systems analysis techniques and procedures, including consulting with users, to determine hardware, software, or system functional specifications. (B) The design, development, documentation, analysis, creation, testing, or modification of computer systems or programs, including prototypes, based on and related to user or system design specifications. (C) The documentation, testing, creation, or modification of computer programs related to the design of software or hardware for computer operating systems. (3) The employee is highly skilled and is proficient in the theoretical and practical application of highly specialized information to computer systems analysis, programming, or software engineering. A job title shall not be determinative of the applicability of this exemption.

clauses.title: The Minimum Rate-of-Pay Requirement and Its Statutory Adjustment Mechanism
clauses.body: As the fourth condition of the Labor Code § 515.5(a) test, the employee's hourly rate of pay must not be less than a specific statutory dollar figure, or, if the employee is paid on a salaried basis, the employee must earn an annual salary of not less than a specific statutory figure for full-time employment, paid at least once a month in a monthly amount of not less than a further specific statutory figure. The statute's own codified text — last amended in 2012 — prints these figures as $36.00 per hour, $75,000 per year, and $6,250 per month. But the statute does not leave those figures fixed: by its own terms, the Department of Industrial Relations is directed to adjust both the hourly rate and the salary levels every October 1, effective the following January 1, by the percentage increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. Because that adjustment is made administratively by the department rather than by amending the statute's printed text, the dollar figures appearing in the codified version of Section 515.5 are the figures as last set by the Legislature (2012) and do not, by themselves, reflect the current operative amount for any given year.
clauses.gap: This clause covers Labor Code § 515.5(a)(4) only — the fourth paragraph of the same subdivision (a) whose first three paragraphs (the duties and skill test) are covered in a separate clause of this document. The $36.00/hour, $75,000/year, and $6,250/month figures quoted here are the statute's own printed baseline as of its last legislative amendment (2012); they are not represented as the current operative figures for any particular year. The actual dollar figure the Department of Industrial Relations has most recently published under this adjustment mechanism, as independently verified from the department's own publication, is stated in a separate clause of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 515.5(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (4) The employee’s hourly rate of pay is not less than thirty-six dollars ($36.00) or, if the employee is paid on a salaried basis, the employee earns an annual salary of not less than seventy-five thousand dollars ($75,000) for full-time employment, which is paid at least once a month and in a monthly amount of not less than six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($6,250). The department shall adjust both the hourly pay rate and the salary level described in this paragraph on October 1 of each year to be effective on January 1 of the following year by an amount equal to the percentage increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers.

clauses.title: The Department of Industrial Relations' Most Recently Published Adjusted Rate
clauses.body: The Department of Industrial Relations publishes the dollar figures that result from the annual Labor Code § 515.5(a)(4) adjustment described above. As of the date this clause was verified, the department's own published notice states that, in accordance with Section 515.5(a)(4), it adjusted the computer software employee's minimum hourly rate of pay exemption from $56.97 to $58.85, the minimum monthly salary exemption from $9,888.13 to $10,214.44, and the minimum annual salary exemption from $118,657.43 to $122,573.13, effective January 1, 2026, reflecting a 3.3% increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers measured from August 2024 to August 2025.
clauses.gap: This clause reports the figures published by the Department of Industrial Relations as of the checkedDate above, drawn directly from the department's own webpage rather than from the codified statutory text (which prints only the 2012 baseline figures, covered in a separate clause of this document). The department's notice states these figures took effect January 1, 2026 and were calculated from the department's own August 2024-to-August 2025 index comparison. By the statute's own adjustment mechanism, the department recalculates and republishes new figures each October for the following January 1 — meaning a later adjustment (for January 1, 2027 and beyond) will supersede the figures quoted here, and this document's text does not update itself as new figures are published. This clause does not address the parallel computer software employee exemption language found in the applicable IWC wage order, which restates a version of this same dollar threshold.

citations.case: California Department of Industrial Relations, Overtime Exemption for Computer Software Employees (Office of the Director – Research, effective January 1, 2026)
citations.cite: California Department of Industrial Relations
citations.quote: In accordance with Labor Code Section 515.5(a)(4), the department has adjusted the computer software employee’s minimum hourly rate of pay exemption from $56.97 to $58.85, the minimum monthly salary exemption from $9,888.13 to $10,214.44, and the minimum annual salary exemption from $118,657.43 to $122,573.13 effective January 1, 2026, reflecting the 3.3% increase in the California Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers.

clauses.title: Statutory Exclusions From the Exemption
clauses.body: Labor Code § 515.5(b) states that the exemption described in subdivision (a) does not apply to an employee if any of six listed circumstances apply. Those circumstances are: the employee is a trainee or entry-level employee still learning to become proficient in the theoretical and practical application of highly specialized information to computer systems analysis, programming, and software engineering; the employee is in a computer-related occupation but has not attained the level of skill and expertise necessary to work independently and without close supervision; the employee is engaged in the operation of computers or in the manufacture, repair, or maintenance of computer hardware and related equipment; the employee is an engineer, drafter, machinist, or other professional whose work is highly dependent upon or facilitated by computers and computer software (including someone skilled in computer-aided design software such as CAD/CAM) but who is not engaged in computer systems analysis, programming, or another similarly skilled computer-related occupation; the employee is a writer of material such as box labels, product descriptions, documentation, promotional material, or setup and installation instructions, whether for print or onscreen media, or who provides content intended to be read by customers, subscribers, or visitors to computer-related media such as the web or CD-ROMs; or the employee is engaged in the subdivision (a) duties for the purpose of creating imagery for effects used in the motion picture, television, or theatrical industry.
clauses.gap: This clause covers Labor Code § 515.5(b), an independent subdivision of the same statutory section as subdivision (a) covered in this document's other authority clauses. The statute does not itself define terms such as 'trainee,' 'entry-level position,' or 'close supervision' used within this list, and this clause does not supply definitions for those terms or determine whether any specific employee's circumstances fall within any of the six listed exclusions.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 515.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (b) The exemption provided in subdivision (a) does not apply to an employee if any of the following apply: (1) The employee is a trainee or employee in an entry-level position who is learning to become proficient in the theoretical and practical application of highly specialized information to computer systems analysis, programming, and software engineering. (2) The employee is in a computer-related occupation but has not attained the level of skill and expertise necessary to work independently and without close supervision. (3) The employee is engaged in the operation of computers or in the manufacture, repair, or maintenance of computer hardware and related equipment. (4) The employee is an engineer, drafter, machinist, or other professional whose work is highly dependent upon or facilitated by the use of computers and computer software programs and who is skilled in computer-aided design software, including CAD/CAM, but who is not engaged in computer systems analysis, programming, or any other similarly skilled computer-related occupation. (5) The employee is a writer engaged in writing material, including box labels, product descriptions, documentation, promotional material, setup and installation instructions, and other similar written information, either for print or for onscreen media or who writes or provides content material intended to be read by customers, subscribers, or visitors to computer-related media such as the World Wide Web or CD-ROMs. (6) The employee is engaged in any of the activities set forth in subdivision (a) for the purpose of creating imagery for effects used in the motion picture, television, or theatrical industry.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes the federal Economic Espionage Act, 18 U.S.C. §§ 1831–1839 -- specifically its two criminal offenses, 18 U.S.C. § 1831 (economic espionage benefiting a foreign government, instrumentality, or agent) and 18 U.S.C. § 1832 (theft of trade secrets generally, without any foreign-benefit element) -- what conduct each defines as a federal crime, the statutory definition of "trade secret" that applies to both offenses, and the penalties each statute specifies. It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning a situation involving {{companyName}} and, where relevant, {{adversePartyName}}. The trade secret information at issue is described as follows: {{tradeSecretDescription}}. Both 18 U.S.C. § 1831 and § 1832 are federal criminal statutes: violations are investigated and prosecuted by federal law enforcement and the U.S. Department of Justice, not through a private lawsuit, and this document does not initiate, threaten, or request any criminal investigation or prosecution. It does not state that any specific conduct described above does or does not violate either statute, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is also distinct from, and does not replace, this project's existing Criminal Trade Secret Theft Information Sheet (California Penal Code section 499c, a separate state criminal statute) or this project's existing trade secret misappropriation documents describing the federal civil Defend Trade Secrets Act cause of action, 18 U.S.C. § 1836 -- a separate, non-criminal federal statute discussed further in a companion clause below.

clauses.title: The Foreign-Benefit Offense: 18 U.S.C. § 1831 (Economic Espionage)
clauses.body: 18 U.S.C. § 1831 makes it a federal crime to steal, or without authorization appropriate, take, or obtain by fraud a trade secret; to copy, transmit, or otherwise convey a trade secret without authorization; to knowingly receive, buy, or possess a trade secret known to have been stolen; or to attempt or conspire to do any of those things -- but only where the person acts "intending or knowing that the offense will benefit any foreign government, foreign instrumentality, or foreign agent." This foreign-government-benefit element is what distinguishes section 1831 from section 1832, addressed in a companion clause, and it does not require that the foreign government itself direct or know of the conduct -- only that the person committing the offense intend or know that a foreign government, instrumentality, or agent will benefit. Except for organizations (addressed in a companion clause on organizational penalties), a violation of section 1831 is punishable by a fine of not more than $5,000,000, imprisonment of not more than 15 years, or both.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the full text of 18 U.S.C. § 1831(a), a single subsection consisting of an introductory clause, five numbered paragraphs describing the prohibited acts, and a closing penalty clause; it does not quote subsection (b) (the separate organizational penalty, addressed in a companion clause of this document) or the statutory definitions in section 1839 that give meaning to "trade secret," "foreign instrumentality," and "foreign agent" as used here (addressed in a companion clause). The $5,000,000 individual fine figure quoted above reflects a 2013 amendment (Pub. L. 112-269) that raised it from a prior $500,000 cap, per this section's own Cornell LII editorial notes, which this document did not independently verify against the amending Public Law's own text -- only against Cornell LII's summary of the amendment as fetched. This clause does not state that any specific conduct does or does not fall within section 1831, does not state that any specific defendant would or would not be found to have intended or known of a foreign-government benefit, and no case law construing section 1831 was researched or is cited here.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1831(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Economic Espionage Act, foreign-benefit offense and individual penalty
citations.quote: (a) In General.—Whoever, intending or knowing that the offense will benefit any foreign government, foreign instrumentality, or foreign agent, knowingly— (1) steals, or without authorization appropriates, takes, carries away, or conceals, or by fraud, artifice, or deception obtains a trade secret; (2) without authorization copies, duplicates, sketches, draws, photographs, downloads, uploads, alters, destroys, photocopies, replicates, transmits, delivers, sends, mails, communicates, or conveys a trade secret; (3) receives, buys, or possesses a trade secret, knowing the same to have been stolen or appropriated, obtained, or converted without authorization; (4) attempts to commit any offense described in any of paragraphs (1) through (3); or (5) conspires with one or more other persons to commit any offense described in any of paragraphs (1) through (3), and one or more of such persons do any act to effect the object of the conspiracy, shall, except as provided in subsection (b), be fined not more than $5,000,000 or imprisoned not more than 15 years, or both.

clauses.title: The General Offense: 18 U.S.C. § 1832 (Theft of Trade Secrets)
clauses.body: 18 U.S.C. § 1832 separately makes it a federal crime to commit the same kind of acts described in section 1831 -- stealing, copying, receiving, attempting, or conspiring to obtain a trade secret without authorization -- but section 1832 does not require any intent or knowledge that a foreign government, instrumentality, or agent will benefit. Instead, section 1832 requires: intent to convert the trade secret to the economic benefit of someone other than its owner; that the trade secret be related to a product or service used in, or intended for use in, interstate or foreign commerce; and intent or knowledge that the offense will injure the trade secret's owner. Except for organizations (addressed in a companion clause), a violation of section 1832 is punishable by imprisonment of not more than 10 years -- five years less than the maximum for section 1831 -- and by a fine "under this title," rather than the specific $5,000,000 individual cap that section 1831 states by its own terms.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the full text of 18 U.S.C. § 1832(a), a single subsection with the same five-paragraph structure as section 1831(a); it does not quote subsection (b) (the organizational penalty, addressed in a companion clause). The phrase "fined under this title" is quoted directly from the statute as fetched; this document does not independently trace or quote the general federal fine statute that phrase cross-references (18 U.S.C. § 3571, which sets default fine ceilings for federal offenses generally, including alternative fines tied to gain or loss in some cases), because section 3571 was not fetched or verified as part of this research -- a reader wanting the actual individual dollar exposure for a section 1832 violation would need to separately research section 3571. This document's initial working assumption, before this statutory text was fetched, was that section 1831 and section 1832 stated the same specific individual fine figure; that assumption is corrected here: only section 1831 states a specific individual dollar cap in its own text, and section 1832 does not. This clause does not state that any specific conduct does or does not fall within section 1832, and no case law construing section 1832 was researched or is cited here.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1832(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Economic Espionage Act, general trade secret theft offense and individual penalty
citations.quote: (a) Whoever, with intent to convert a trade secret, that is related to a product or service used in or intended for use in interstate or foreign commerce, to the economic benefit of anyone other than the owner thereof, and intending or knowing that the offense will, injure any owner of that trade secret, knowingly— (1) steals, or without authorization appropriates, takes, carries away, or conceals, or by fraud, artifice, or deception obtains such information; (2) without authorization copies, duplicates, sketches, draws, photographs, downloads, uploads, alters, destroys, photocopies, replicates, transmits, delivers, sends, mails, communicates, or conveys such information; (3) receives, buys, or possesses such information, knowing the same to have been stolen or appropriated, obtained, or converted without authorization; (4) attempts to commit any offense described in paragraphs (1) through (3); or (5) conspires with one or more other persons to commit any offense described in paragraphs (1) through (3), and one or more of such persons do any act to effect the object of the conspiracy, shall, except as provided in subsection (b), be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than 10 years, or both.

clauses.title: Organizational Penalties Differ Between the Two Offenses
clauses.body: Both 18 U.S.C. § 1831 and § 1832 state a separate, higher-ceiling penalty for an organization (rather than an individual) that commits the offense. Under section 1831(b), an organization that commits the foreign-benefit offense is subject to a fine of not more than the greater of $10,000,000 or three times the value of the stolen trade secret to the organization, including research-and-design and other reproduction costs the organization avoided by the theft. Under section 1832(b), an organization that commits the general offense is subject to a fine of not more than the greater of $5,000,000 or that same three-times-value measure. The $10,000,000 organizational floor for section 1831 is twice the $5,000,000 organizational floor for section 1832, mirroring the two offenses' different individual-penalty severity.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two different statutory sections' organizational-penalty subsections -- 18 U.S.C. § 1831(b) and § 1832(b) -- which are independent provisions of independent sections, not subdivisions of one section, grouped here only because both describe the same kind of organizational fine. Per each section's own Cornell LII editorial notes (not independently verified against the amending Public Laws' own text), the "greater of [amount] or 3 times the value" formulation was added to section 1831(b) by a 2013 amendment (replacing a flat $10,000,000 cap) and to section 1832(b) by a 2016 amendment (replacing a flat $5,000,000 cap); this document does not further trace either amendment's legislative history. This clause does not address how "the value of the stolen trade secret to the organization" is calculated or proven in any specific case, and no case law construing either organizational-penalty subsection was researched or is cited here.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1831(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Economic Espionage Act, organizational penalty for the foreign-benefit offense
citations.quote: (b) Organizations.— Any organization that commits any offense described in subsection (a) shall be fined not more than the greater of $10,000,000 or 3 times the value of the stolen trade secret to the organization, including expenses for research and design and other costs of reproducing the trade secret that the organization has thereby avoided.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1832(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Economic Espionage Act, organizational penalty for the general offense
citations.quote: (b) Any organization that commits any offense described in subsection (a) shall be fined not more than the greater of $5,000,000 or 3 times the value of the stolen trade secret to the organization, including expenses for research and design and other costs of reproducing the trade secret that the organization has thereby avoided.

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of "Trade Secret" Governing Both Offenses
clauses.body: 18 U.S.C. § 1839(3) defines "trade secret," for purposes of this entire chapter of the federal criminal code (Chapter 90 of Title 18, which contains sections 1831 through 1839), as all forms and types of financial, business, scientific, technical, economic, or engineering information -- regardless of how it is stored or memorialized -- if its owner has taken reasonable measures to keep it secret and it derives independent economic value from not being generally known to, or readily ascertainable by, others who could profit from disclosing or using it. Because section 1839 defines this term for the chapter as a whole rather than separately within section 1831 or section 1832, the identical statutory text governs the "trade secret" element of both federal criminal offenses described in this document. That same section 1839 definition also governs the federal civil cause of action for trade secret misappropriation under 18 U.S.C. § 1836, discussed in a companion clause and elsewhere in this project's confidentiality-agreement documents -- so the criminal and civil definitions are not merely similar, as California's separate criminal (Penal Code section 499c) and civil (CUTSA) trade secret definitions are; they are the same statutory text, because Congress placed sections 1831 (criminal), 1832 (criminal), 1836 (civil), and 1839 (definitions) in the same chapter and had section 1839 apply chapter-wide.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 18 U.S.C. § 1839(3), one paragraph of a single statutory section that also separately defines "foreign instrumentality," "foreign agent," "owner," "misappropriation," "improper means," and "Trademark Act of 1946" in its other paragraphs, none of which are requoted here. The observation that section 1839's definition governs section 1836 as well as sections 1831 and 1832 is based on this section's own introductory phrase, "As used in this chapter," and this researcher's confirmation that sections 1831, 1832, 1836, and 1839 are all part of the same chapter (Chapter 90 of Title 18) as fetched from Cornell LII's own breadcrumb navigation on each page; it is not a holding from any case construing that structural point, and no case law is cited here. This document does not independently verify that this exact text is the version currently in force by any means other than the Cornell LII page fetched on the date below; Cornell LII states this paragraph was last amended in 2016.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1839(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Economic Espionage Act, definition of "trade secret" applicable chapter-wide
citations.quote: (3) the term “trade secret” means all forms and types of financial, business, scientific, technical, economic, or engineering information, including patterns, plans, compilations, program devices, formulas, designs, prototypes, methods, techniques, processes, procedures, programs, or codes, whether tangible or intangible, and whether or how stored, compiled, or memorialized physically, electronically, graphically, photographically, or in writing if— (A) the owner thereof has taken reasonable measures to keep such information secret; and (B) the information derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to, and not being readily ascertainable through proper means by, another person who can obtain economic value from the disclosure or use of the information;

clauses.title: How This Federal Criminal Statute Relates to State Criminal Law and Federal Civil Law
clauses.body: 18 U.S.C. §§ 1831 and 1832 are federal crimes, investigated and prosecuted by federal authorities. They are legally distinct from two other trade-secret-related mechanisms addressed elsewhere in this project: (1) California Penal Code section 499c, a separate state criminal statute prosecuted by California district attorneys or the California Attorney General, addressed in this project's own Criminal Trade Secret Theft Information Sheet; and (2) the federal civil cause of action for trade secret misappropriation under 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b), which a private trade secret owner -- not a prosecutor -- may bring in federal court, addressed in this project's trade secret misappropriation and NDA documents. Section 1836 is not solely private, either: section 1836(a) separately authorizes the U.S. Attorney General to bring a civil action for injunctive relief against a violation of this chapter, a third, non-criminal, non-private federal mechanism distinct from both a private section 1836(b) lawsuit and a section 1831/1832 criminal prosecution. The Economic Espionage Act's own construction provision, 18 U.S.C. § 1838, states that -- apart from one whistleblower-notice-related exception -- the chapter is not to be construed to preempt or displace other civil or criminal remedies provided by federal, state, or territorial law for trade secret misappropriation, meaning this federal criminal statute, a state Penal Code section 499c prosecution, and a federal or state civil suit over the same underlying conduct are not mutually exclusive as a matter of the statute's own text.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two separate statutory sections -- 18 U.S.C. § 1838 (a single section) and 18 U.S.C. § 1836(a) (one subsection of a different section already partly addressed, as to its private-suit subsection (b), by other clauses in this project's separate trade secret misappropriation documents) -- grouped together here only because both illustrate that sections 1831/1832 do not occupy the field. This clause does not address whether, or how, a single set of underlying facts that supports a federal section 1831 or 1832 prosecution could also support a Penal Code section 499c prosecution, a private section 1836(b) civil suit, or an Attorney General section 1836(a) civil action, or how such proceedings might interact procedurally (for example, as to timing, double jeopardy, parallel discovery, or use of evidence from one proceeding in another) -- none of which is addressed by the statutory text quoted here or elsewhere researched for this document. The reference above to a "whistleblower-notice-related exception" describes section 1838's own cross-reference to section 1833(b) exactly as fetched; section 1833(b) itself is not requoted in this document (it is quoted elsewhere in this project's trade secret misappropriation documents). No case law construing section 1838 or section 1836(a) was researched or is cited here.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1838 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Economic Espionage Act, construction with other civil and criminal remedies
citations.quote: Except as provided in section 1833(b), this chapter shall not be construed to preempt or displace any other remedies, whether civil or criminal, provided by United States Federal, State, commonwealth, possession, or territory law for the misappropriation of a trade secret, or to affect the otherwise lawful disclosure of information by any Government employee under section 552 of title 5 (commonly known as the Freedom of Information Act).

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Economic Espionage Act, Attorney General civil action for injunctive relief
citations.quote: The Attorney General may, in a civil action, obtain appropriate injunctive relief against any violation of this chapter.

clauses.title: Closing Notice
Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California statutory law on the Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement, Civil Code section 1102 et seq. (Article 1.5 of Chapter 2 of Title 4 of Part 4 of Division 2 of the Civil Code, sections 1102 through 1102.19), as it may relate to the transfer of the real property at {{propertyAddress}}, where {{sellerName}} is named as seller and {{buyerName}} is named as buyer. It states what California law provides about which transfers this disclosure article covers, the statute's own list of exempt transfers, the statutory disclosure form and the underlying duty to disclose material facts, when the completed disclosure statement must be delivered, the buyer's statutory right to terminate an offer after a late or amended disclosure, and the stated consequence of noncompliance. It is separate from, and in addition to, any Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement, Mello-Roos special tax notice, smoke alarm/carbon monoxide compliance statement, HOA/CC&R disclosure, lead-based paint disclosure, or Megan's Law database notice provided in connection with this transaction, each of which is a distinct disclosure obligation under separate statutory provisions. This information sheet is not itself the statutory Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement that Civil Code section 1102.6 requires, and it does not tell {{sellerName}}, {{buyerName}}, or any real estate agent involved whether this specific transaction is covered, which exemption (if any) applies, or how to proceed.

clauses.title: Which Transfers This Disclosure Law Covers
clauses.body: California's transfer disclosure statute applies to any transfer of single-family residential property by sale, exchange, real property sales contract, lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements, except as separately provided by the statute's own list of exemptions. The statute borrows certain definitions used elsewhere in real estate licensing law for purposes of this article. Any waiver of the article's requirements is void as against public policy — a seller and buyer cannot agree around this disclosure requirement by contract.
clauses.gap: The statute's own scope term is "single-family residential property" — this article does not itself define that term by a numeric unit count (e.g., "one to four dwelling units"), and this clause does not equate it with the differently-worded "one to four dwelling units" scope language that a separate California disclosure statute (the Megan's Law database notice, cited elsewhere in this corpus) uses; a specific property's classification under either phrase is not resolved here. Subdivision (b)'s cross-reference is to the definitions chapter of the Business and Professions Code real estate license law (commencing at Section 10000), which is a body of licensing definitions, not a further definition of "single-family residential property" itself. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines the scope of its residential transfer-disclosure law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer; disclosure scope and terminology vary by state. All three citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1102); none is an independent source for another.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope of the transfer disclosure statement requirement
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 1102.2, this article applies to any transfer by sale, exchange, real property sales contract as defined in Section 2985, lease with an option to purchase, any other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements of any single-family residential property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, cross-reference to real estate licensing definitions
citations.quote: For purposes of this article, the definitions contained in Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 10000) of Part 1 of Division 4 of the Business and Professions Code shall apply.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102(c)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, waiver of the disclosure requirement is void
citations.quote: Any waiver of the requirements of this article is void as against public policy.

clauses.title: Statutory Exemptions From the Disclosure Requirement
clauses.body: The statute lists specific categories of transfers to which this disclosure article does not apply. These include: sales or transfers preceded by a subdivision public report, or made under the exception to that public-report requirement; sales or transfers made pursuant to court order, including probate-court sales, writ-of-execution sales, foreclosure sales, bankruptcy-trustee transfers, eminent-domain sales, and decree-of-specific-performance sales; a separately stated category of sales or transfers to a mortgagee, deed-of-trust beneficiary, or their successor arising out of a default and a foreclosure-type sale (including sales of a manufactured home or mobilehome by reason of default or foreclosure of a security interest); sales or transfers by a fiduciary administering a trust, guardianship, conservatorship, or decedent's estate, subject to its own exception where the trustee is a natural person who is also a former owner or recent occupant of the property; transfers from one co-owner to one or more other co-owners; transfers to a spouse or to a person in the transferor's line of consanguinity; transfers between spouses resulting from a dissolution or legal-separation judgment or an incidental property settlement agreement; sales or transfers by the Controller administering unclaimed property under the Code of Civil Procedure; sales or transfers under specified Revenue and Taxation Code tax-sale provisions; sales, transfers, or exchanges to or from a governmental entity; transfers of a portion of a property that does not itself constitute single-family residential property; and the sale, creation, or transfer of a lease of any duration, other than a lease with an option to purchase or a ground lease coupled with improvements.
clauses.gap: This is a longer and more specific exemption list than commonly assumed — twelve separate lettered categories in the statute as currently in force, not only the handful most often cited (court order, fiduciary, co-owner, spouse, divorce-related, and governmental-entity transfers). This corpus's Residential Purchase Agreement document already cites six of these same lettered exemptions (subdivisions (b), (d), (e), (f), (g), and (j)) in an embedded clause covering the transfer disclosure statement generally; this clause independently verifies those six and adds citations to six further exemption categories from the same statutory section — subdivisions (a), (c), (h), (i), (k), and (l) — that are not otherwise cited elsewhere in this corpus. All twelve citations below are subdivisions of one statutory section (Civil Code § 1102.2); none is an independent source for another. A thirteenth subdivision of the same section, not quoted here, states an interpretive rule about the meaning of "sale" and "transfer" and a savings clause for a 2018 amendment — it is not itself an exemption category. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines its exemptions from a residential transfer-disclosure law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer, and it does not determine whether any specific transfer actually falls within any of these categories.

clauses.title: The Statutory Disclosure Form and the Underlying Duty to Disclose
clauses.body: The disclosures this article requires must be made on a copy of a specific statutory disclosure form. Separately, the Legislature has stated that this article does not affect the existing obligation of the parties to a real estate contract, or their agents, to disclose any fact materially affecting the value and desirability of the property — including the property's physical conditions and previously received reports of physical inspections — and that this article does not change a real estate broker's or salesperson's separate statutory duty of disclosure. The Legislature has also stated its intent that delivery of a real estate transfer disclosure statement may not be waived in an "as is" sale, citing a 1993 California Court of Appeal decision on that point.
clauses.gap: The exact, current checkbox-by-checkbox wording of the statutory disclosure form itself (Civil Code § 1102.6) could not be confirmed from a fetchable primary source, re-verified independently on 2026-09-05: leginfo's own page for § 1102.6 displays a literal "NOTICE OF INCOMPLETE TEXT" placeholder rather than the form's actual content, stating that the Real Estate Transfer Disclosure Statement instead appears in the published bill (Sec. 25, Chapter 370, Statutes of 2020, pages 34-38) rather than on the statute page itself. Because of that, this clause does not quote the form's specific line items (named systems, appliances, or specific defect/environmental/legal categories) as statutory language — doing so would have meant asserting text that could not be independently verified from the fetched leginfo source. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a residential transfer-disclosure obligation — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer. The two quotes below credited to § 1102.1(a) are from a single statutory subdivision, itself independent from § 1102.6(a); no additional independent source was located for either § 1102.1(a) point.

citations.quote: It is also the intent of the Legislature that the delivery of a real estate transfer disclosure statement may not be waived in an “as is” sale, as held in Loughrin v. Superior Court (1993) 15 Cal. App. 4th 1188.

clauses.title: When the Disclosure Statement Must Be Delivered
clauses.body: The statute sets separate delivery deadlines depending on the type of transfer. In the case of a sale, the seller must deliver the completed disclosure statement to the prospective buyer as soon as practicable before transfer of title. In the case of a sale by a real property sales contract, a lease together with an option to purchase, or a ground lease coupled with improvements, the seller must instead deliver it as soon as practicable before execution of the contract — with "execution" meaning, for this purpose, the making or acceptance of an offer.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's disclosure-timing rule — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer; timing rules vary by state. The two citations below are separate lettered subdivisions ((a) and (b)) of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1102.3); the buyer's right to terminate after a late-delivered disclosure is addressed in a separate clause, drawn from a third subdivision ((c)) of this same section.

citations.quote: In the case of a sale, as soon as practicable before transfer of title.

clauses.title: Buyer's Right to Terminate After a Late or Amended Disclosure
clauses.body: If any disclosure, or any material amendment of a disclosure, required by this article is delivered after the buyer's offer to purchase has already been executed, the statute gives the prospective buyer a fixed period to terminate that offer by delivering written notice of termination to the seller or the seller's agent: three days after delivery in person, five days after delivery by deposit in the mail, or five days after delivery of an electronic record where the parties have agreed to conduct the transaction electronically under the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act. Separately, the statute specifies when this notice-and-termination period begins to run for the disclosure statement as a whole: it commences when Sections I and II of the statutory form — and, if the seller is represented by an agent in the transaction, Section III as well — are completed and delivered to the buyer or the buyer's agent.
clauses.gap: This termination right is triggered specifically by a disclosure or material amendment delivered after the buyer's offer to purchase was already executed; the statute's own text does not, by its terms, create a freestanding right to cancel at some later time based solely on having received a disclosure that was delivered before the offer was signed. The statute's own term for this right is to "terminate the offer" by written notice — not "rescind" the contract — though this right is sometimes informally described using rescission-type language; that informal shorthand is not the statute's own wording. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's late-disclosure cure mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer; termination windows and triggering events vary by state. Both citations below are the same lettered subdivision ((c)) of Civil Code § 1102.3; the separate, independent consequence of a seller's or agent's noncompliance with this article generally (as opposed to this specific termination right) is addressed in another clause, citing Civil Code § 1102.13.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the 3/5/5-day termination right for a late-delivered disclosure
citations.quote: If any disclosure, or any material amendment of any disclosure, required to be made by this article, is delivered after the execution of an offer to purchase, the prospective buyer shall have three days after delivery in person, five days after delivery by deposit in the mail, or five days after delivery of an electronic record in transactions where the parties have agreed to conduct the transaction by electronic means, pursuant to provisions of the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (Title 2.5 (commencing with Section 1633.1) of Part 2 of Division 3), to terminate the offer by delivery of a written notice of termination to the seller or the seller’s agent.

clauses.title: Effect of Noncompliance
clauses.body: The statute specifies a particular consequence for noncompliance with this disclosure article. No transfer subject to the article is invalidated solely because of a failure to comply with any of its provisions. However, any person who willfully or negligently violates or fails to perform any duty this article prescribes is liable to a transferee for the transferee's actual damages.
clauses.gap: This is a single, independent statutory section (Civil Code § 1102.13), not a subdivision of a section quoted elsewhere in this document. The statute's own text does not define "willfully," "negligently," or "actual damages" for this purpose, and this clause does not resolve whether any specific act or omission meets that standard, or what a transferee's actual damages would be in any given case. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of one jurisdiction's remedy for noncompliance with its residential transfer-disclosure law — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential transfer; remedies for disclosure noncompliance vary by state.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1102.13
citations.cite: California Civil Code, noncompliance does not invalidate the transfer, but creates liability for actual damages
citations.quote: No transfer subject to this article shall be invalidated solely because of the failure of any person to comply with any provision of this article. However, any person who willfully or negligently violates or fails to perform any duty prescribed by any provision of this article shall be liable in the amount of actual damages suffered by a transferee.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Receipt and Review
Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}}, states what California law provides about the limited offering exemption from securities qualification found at California Corporations Code § 25102(f) — a state-law exemption sometimes relied on for a narrowly offered sale of securities, such as to friends, family, or other insiders, by {{companyName}}. Section 25102(f) exempts a qualifying offer or sale from the qualification (registration) requirement of Corporations Code § 25110; it is a distinct exemption, available independently of whether the same offering also relies on a federal Regulation D exemption. Where a specific business name is named below, that is {{companyName}}; this sheet can also be read on its own, without it filled in, as a general reference to what this statute and its implementing regulation say. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any particular offer or sale by {{companyName}} meets the conditions of this exemption, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: The 35-Purchaser Limit and the Relationship/Sophistication Requirement
clauses.body: California Corporations Code § 25102(f) exempts a qualifying offer or sale of a security from the qualification requirement of Section 25110 if the transaction meets each of several statutory criteria. Two of those criteria govern who may purchase. First, the security may not be sold to more than 35 persons in the transaction, counting persons both inside and outside California. Second, every purchaser must either have a preexisting personal or business relationship with the offeror (or with any of the offeror's partners, officers, directors, or controlling persons — or, if the offeror is a limited liability company, its managers) or, by reason of the purchaser's own business or financial experience (or that of the purchaser's unaffiliated, uncompensated professional adviser), be one who could reasonably be assumed capable of protecting the purchaser's own interests in the transaction. The statute itself excludes certain persons from the 35-purchaser count — including officers, directors, and affiliates of the issuer, and purchasers who qualify under a separate institutional-investor exemption in the same section (subdivision (i)) — and provides that spouses are counted as a single person, as is an organization not formed specifically for the purpose of making the purchase.
clauses.gap: Corporations Code § 25102(f)(1) and (f)(2) are two paragraphs of a single statutory subdivision — Section 25102(f) — not independent sources of authority; this clause and the two authority clauses that follow it in this document all draw on different paragraphs of that same subdivision. The quoted citation below covers the subdivision's opening clause and paragraphs (1) and (2); it does not itself quote the statute's separate purchaser-counting exclusions (for officers, directors, affiliates, spouses, and certain entities not formed to make the purchase), which are summarized, but not quoted verbatim, in the body above. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular purchaser has a qualifying preexisting relationship or the requisite business or financial sophistication, and it does not address the many other, separately conditioned limited-offering and private-transaction exemptions found elsewhere in Section 25102 (including subdivisions (h), (i), (n), (p), (q), and (r)), each of which has its own distinct requirements not covered by this document.

citations.cite: California Corporations Code, limited offering exemption — 35-purchaser limit and preexisting relationship/sophistication test
citations.quote: (f) Any offer or sale of any security in a transaction (other than an offer or sale to a pension or profit-sharing trust of the issuer) that meets each of the following criteria: (1) Sales of the security are not made to more than 35 persons, including persons not in this state. (2) All purchasers either have a preexisting personal or business relationship with the offeror or any of its partners, officers, directors or controlling persons, or managers (as appointed or elected by the members) if the offeror is a limited liability company, or by reason of their business or financial experience or the business or financial experience of their professional advisers who are unaffiliated with and who are not compensated by the issuer or any affiliate or selling agent of the issuer, directly or indirectly, could be reasonably assumed to have the capacity to protect their own interests in connection with the transaction.

clauses.title: Investment Representation and the No-Advertisement Condition
clauses.body: Two further conditions of the Section 25102(f) exemption govern how the offer and sale must be conducted. Each purchaser must represent that the purchaser is buying for the purchaser's own account (or, if the purchaser is a trustee, for a trust account) and not with a view toward reselling or otherwise distributing the security. And the offer and sale, taken as a whole, must not be accomplished by the publication of any advertisement — a condition addressed independently in this California statute from the prohibition on general solicitation found in the federal Regulation D exemption discussed elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Corporations Code § 25102(f)(3) and (f)(4) — two paragraphs of the same statutory subdivision, Section 25102(f), quoted in the preceding clause of this document; they are not independent sources. The statute does not define "advertisement" for purposes of paragraph (4), and this clause does not attempt to define it. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular purchaser's investment representation is accurate, whether any particular communication would constitute a prohibited advertisement, or whether use of a written offering or disclosure document, by itself, would violate paragraph (4).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(f)(3)-(4)
citations.cite: California Corporations Code, limited offering exemption — investment-intent representation and prohibition on advertisement
citations.quote: (3) Each purchaser represents that the purchaser is purchasing for the purchaser’s own account (or a trust account if the purchaser is a trustee) and not with a view to or for sale in connection with any distribution of the security. (4) The offer and sale of the security is not accomplished by the publication of any advertisement.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own Notice-Filing Directive and Cure Provision
clauses.body: Section 25102(f) itself directs the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation to require, by rule, that an issuer file a notice of a transaction conducted under this exemption; the statute does not itself state the filing deadline, leaving that to the Commissioner's implementing regulation (addressed in the next clause). The statute is explicit, however, that failing to file the notice, or filing it late, does not by itself forfeit the exemption. Instead, an issuer that fails to file the required notice must, within 15 business days after discovering the failure or after the Commissioner demands the notice — whichever happens first — file the notice and pay the Commissioner a fee equal to what would have been payable had the transaction instead been qualified (registered) under Section 25110.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the unlettered paragraph of Corporations Code § 25102(f) that follows paragraph (f)(4) — the same statutory subdivision quoted in the two preceding clauses of this document, not an independent source. That paragraph is not itself separately lettered or numbered in the current, 2022-amended (effective January 1, 2023) text of Section 25102 fetched for this document. A separately verified regulation, 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.102.14 (in Item 2 of the instructions to its notice form), cross-references this cure provision as "Corporations Code section 25102(f)(4)" — a citation that does not match the current statutory paragraph lettering, since current paragraph (4) is the no-advertisement condition quoted in the preceding clause of this document, not the notice/cure paragraph. This appears to be an unrevised cross-reference carried forward in the regulation rather than an error in the statute's current text; this document does not further resolve that discrepancy, and a person relying on this document should not assume the regulation's internal cross-references to statutory paragraph numbers are current. This clause does not itself state what the filing deadline is — that is addressed, from the implementing regulation, in the next clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(f) (unlettered notice-filing and cure paragraph)
citations.cite: California Corporations Code, limited offering exemption — statutory directive to require notice by rule, and cure/fee provision for a late or missed notice
citations.quote: The commissioner shall by rule require the issuer to file a notice of transactions under this subdivision. The failure to file the notice or the failure to file the notice within the time specified by the rule of the commissioner shall not affect the availability of the exemption. Any issuer that fails to file the notice as provided by rule of the commissioner shall, within 15 business days after discovery of the failure to file the notice or after demand by the commissioner, whichever occurs first, file the notice and pay to the commissioner a fee equal to the fee payable had the transaction been qualified under Section 25110.

clauses.title: The 15-Calendar-Day Deadline and Form 25102(f) Under the Implementing Regulation
clauses.body: The Commissioner's regulation implementing the notice-filing requirement described in the preceding clause is 10 California Code of Regulations § 260.102.14. It sets the deadline the statute itself leaves open: a notice under Section 25102(f) must be filed with the Commissioner no later than 15 calendar days after the first sale of a security in the transaction in California, and no notice at all is required if none of the securities in the transaction are purchased in California. The regulation also gives an issuer that is separately relying on the federal Regulation D exemption an optional shortcut: if the issuer is filing a notice with the SEC under Regulation D (or under former Securities Act § 4(6)), the California notice may simply be a copy of that federal filing, accompanied by the statutory fee and — for an issuer that is not a California corporation — a consent to service of process. The Commissioner's form for this notice is titled "Notice of Transaction Pursuant to Corporations Code Section 25102(f)," commonly referred to for short as "Form 25102(f)."
clauses.gap: 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.102.14 is a regulation adopted under, and separate from, Corporations Code § 25102(f) — an independent source from the statutory citations in the preceding clauses of this document, not a subdivision of the same statutory section. This regulation's text was verified through two independently fetched copies of the Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute's mirror of the California Code of Regulations (using two different User-Agent strings), which were byte-for-byte identical to each other after whitespace normalization; the official state platform for the current Code of Regulations (govt.westlaw.com, used under contract with the Office of Administrative Law) could not be retrieved as a scripted fetch during this research — attempts returned a "Document not found" page and, for a search query, an unresolved redirect — so this citation was not independently cross-checked against that primary state-hosted source, unlike the Corporations Code citations in this document, which were verified directly against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov. The Cornell mirror's text still refers to the "Department of Business Oversight" and a "www.dbo.ca.gov" filing address — the predecessor name and web address of the agency now called the Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI) — which suggests the mirrored codification may not reflect the regulation's most recent administrative (name/URL) updates, even though the substantive 15-calendar-day deadline and the Regulation D dual-filing option match DFPI's own current public-facing guidance found during research; that guidance was not itself verified to the same two-fetch standard applied to the sources quoted directly in this document. This clause does not restate the regulation's electronic-filing default and its consequences, its narrow hardship exception for paper filing, or its filing-fee schedule.

The fee required by section 25608(c) of the Code must accompany the filing. Each issuer (other than a California corporation) must also file a consent to service of process (Form 260.165), unless it already has a consent to service on file with the Commissioner. The filing should be accompanied with a cover letter indicating that the filing is pursuant to section 25102(f), and if a consent to service is not included, a statement that the issuer already has a consent to service on file with the Commissioner. If the issuer claims the exception under subsection (f), the notice shall be in the form and contain the information specified by subsection (c) and in accordance with the instructions in subsection (d).

clauses.title: How the Purchaser-Based Conditions Differ From Regulation D
clauses.body: Section 25102(f) is a state-law-only exemption from qualification under Corporations Code § 25110; nothing in its text conditions its availability on the same offering also qualifying for a federal Regulation D exemption, and the exemption's own conditions are not defined by reference to the federal "accredited investor" concept that Regulation D uses. Concretely, the two frameworks' purchaser-based conditions differ: Section 25102(f) permits no more than 35 purchasers total, counting both California and out-of-state purchasers (subject to the statute's own exclusions for certain insiders and institutional purchasers), and requires every purchaser — regardless of wealth or income — to either have a preexisting relationship with the issuer or its principals or be sophisticated; Regulation D's Rule 506(b), by contrast, permits an unlimited number of accredited investors plus up to 35 non-accredited purchasers within any 90-calendar-day period, and tests only the non-accredited purchasers for sophistication. The one point at which the two frameworks are administratively linked, rather than substantively unified, is the dual-filing accommodation in the implementing regulation described in the preceding clause: an issuer relying on both exemptions for the same transaction may satisfy California's own notice-filing requirement by submitting a copy of its federal Regulation D filing.
clauses.gap: This clause compares only the purchaser-count and purchaser-qualification conditions of the two exemptions; it does not compare, and does not purport to compare, every other difference between them — including Regulation D Rule 506(c)'s accredited-investor verification obligations, the general-solicitation rules under Rule 506(b) versus 506(c), or the federal preemption of state qualification (as distinct from notice-filing) authority that this corpus addresses elsewhere for offerings that rely on Rule 506 as a federally covered security; Section 25102(f) is not itself a federally covered exemption and is not addressed by that preemption. The federal citation below, 17 C.F.R. § 230.506(b)(2)(i), is an independent regulatory source with no textual cross-reference to Corporations Code § 25102(f); the comparison this clause draws between the two is this document's own analysis of both verified texts, not a comparison stated in either source. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular offering would qualify under either framework, and it does not address the several other California exemptions in Section 25102 (noted in the first authority clause of this document) that have their own, differently structured purchaser conditions.

(2) All purchasers either have a preexisting personal or business relationship with the offeror or any of its partners, officers, directors or controlling persons, or managers (as appointed or elected by the members) if the offeror is a limited liability company, or by reason of their business or financial experience or the business or financial experience of their professional advisers who are unaffiliated with and who are not compensated by the issuer or any affiliate or selling agent of the issuer, directly or indirectly, could be reasonably assumed to have the capacity to protect their own interests in connection with the transaction.
