clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's "compelled self-publication" doctrine in defamation law -- a body of case law addressing when the originator of a false, defamatory statement about why {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}} ended can be held liable for defamation based on {{employeeName}}'s own later repetition of that statement to a prospective employer. It is a companion resource to, and distinct from, this project's Employer Reference Immunity information sheet (which addresses California Civil Code section 47(c) immunity for a reference communication the employer itself makes) and its Blacklisting a Former Employee information sheet (which addresses Labor Code sections 1050-1054). This document states California case law as background information. It does not determine whether any particular statement made about {{employeeName}}'s termination was, or was not, defamatory, whether any repetition of it was legally compelled, or what {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} should say or do about any actual dispute.

clauses.title: The General Rule and the Foreseeability Exception
clauses.body: Under the general rule of California defamation law, a person cannot create their own defamation claim by repeating a statement to others; the publication element of the claim must be supplied by the defendant, not manufactured by the plaintiff's own disclosure. California case law recognizes a narrow, foreseeability-based exception to that general rule: where it was foreseeable that the defendant's act would result in the plaintiff's own publication of the statement to a third person, the plaintiff may still maintain a defamation action despite having done the actual repeating. This exception is often called the "compelled self-publication" or "self-compelled defamation" doctrine.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general rule and the existence of the exception as established by published California appellate authority; it does not resolve, for any particular statement, whether the foreseeability exception would apply. The quotes below are drawn from a 1991 Court of Appeal decision that itself restates rules developed earlier (including in the case addressed in this document's next clause); it is not an independent, unrelated source confirming the rule from scratch. Research for this document was limited to a small number of published California appellate decisions actually read and quote-verified against their retrieved text (Live Oak Publishing Co. v. Cohagan, McKinney v. County of Santa Clara, and Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co.); it does not survey every California or out-of-state case discussing this doctrine.

citations.case: Live Oak Publishing Co. v. Cohagan
citations.quote: A plaintiff cannot manufacture a defamation cause of action by publishing the statements to third persons; the publication must be done by the defendant.

citations.case: Live Oak Publishing Co. v. Cohagan
citations.quote: There is an exception to this rule. When it was foreseeable that a defendant’s act would result in publication to a third person, the plaintiff may maintain a libel action.

clauses.title: The Doctrine's Origin in the Termination Context -- McKinney v. County of Santa Clara
clauses.body: California first recognized the compelled self-publication doctrine in the employment-termination context in a 1980 Court of Appeal decision. The plaintiff, a former probationary deputy sheriff, alleged his former employer gave him a false, defamatory reason for his dismissal, and that he was placed in a position of having to repeat that reason to police agencies at which he later sought employment. The court held that where the originator of a defamatory statement has reason to believe the person it defames will be under a strong compulsion to disclose the statement's contents to a third person after receiving it, the originator can be held liable for the foreseeable repetition -- because the causal link between the originator's conduct and the resulting reputational harm remains strong even though the plaintiff, rather than the originator, is the one who physically repeats the statement.
clauses.gap: This clause describes a single published Court of Appeal decision from 1980; it is not a survey of how every California court has since applied or distinguished it, and it predates -- and has since been substantially engaged with by -- the more recent appellate decision addressed in this document's later clauses. The case was decided on a motion to dismiss, so the court's holding was that the plaintiff's allegations were sufficient to create a triable issue, not a final determination that the employer was in fact liable.

citations.case: McKinney v. County of Santa Clara
citations.quote: The second context where this exception has been applied is where the originator of the defamatory statement has reason to believe that the person defamed will be under a strong compulsion to disclose the contents of the defamatory statement to a third person after he has read it or been informed of its contents.

citations.case: McKinney v. County of Santa Clara
citations.quote: The rationale for making the originator of a defamatory statement liable for its foreseeable republication is the strong causal link between the actions of the originator and the damage caused by the republication. This causal link is no less strong where the foreseeable republication is made by the person defamed operating under a strong compulsion to republish the defamatory statement and the circumstances which create the strong compulsion are known to the originator of the defamatory statement at the time he communicates it to the person defamed.

clauses.title: What a Plaintiff Must Show -- Current Elements
clauses.body: A 2020 Court of Appeal decision -- addressed in full in this document's later clauses -- restated the doctrine's elements while applying it to affirm a jury verdict, and its restatement reflects California law as currently applied. To succeed on a compelled self-publication defamation theory, a plaintiff must show: (1) the defendant made a false, defamatory statement about the plaintiff; (2) the plaintiff was under a strong compulsion to disclose the statement's contents to a third person, arising from some necessity -- most commonly, a need to explain the reason for a job loss to a prospective employer who will otherwise learn of or ask about it; (3) the circumstances creating that compulsion were known to, or reasonably anticipated by, the defendant at the time the defendant communicated the statement to the plaintiff; and (4) the plaintiff in fact disclosed the statement to a third party. Because the plaintiff must actually have been compelled to repeat the statement in order to counter or explain it, a plaintiff cannot manufacture a claim by voluntarily repeating a statement with no such compulsion.
clauses.gap: This clause synthesizes the elements as restated in one 2020 published decision, which in turn cites several earlier California appellate decisions (Beroiz v. Wahl and Davis v. Consolidated Freightways among them) that were not independently retrieved or quote-verified for this document; only their restatement within the quoted source was verified. This clause does not state a damages standard (e.g., whether general or special damages must be pleaded) or a statute of limitations, neither of which was researched for this document.

citations.case: Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co. (citing Beroiz v. Wahl (2000) 84 Cal.App.4th 485, 497; Davis v. Consolidated Freightways (1994) 29 Cal.App.4th 354, 373; Live Oak Publishing Co. v. Cohagan, 234 Cal.App.3d at p. 1285; McKinney v. County of Santa Clara, 110 Cal.App.3d at p. 796)
citations.quote: For the exception to apply, the defamed party must operate under a strong compulsion to republish the defamatory statement, and the circumstances creating the compulsion must be known to the originator of the statement at the time he or she makes it to the defamed individual.

citations.case: Live Oak Publishing Co. v. Cohagan
citations.quote: This exception has been limited to a narrow class of cases, usually where a plaintiff is compelled to republish the statements in aid of disproving them.

clauses.title: Current Law -- Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co. Applied, Did Not Abolish, the Doctrine
clauses.body: In 2020, the California Court of Appeal for the Fourth Appellate District, in Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co., squarely addressed the compelled self-publication doctrine on appeal from a jury verdict -- the jury had found a former employer liable for defamation and awarded damages after the employer disclosed the stated reason for the employee's termination on a form the employer was required to file with a securities-industry regulator, a disclosure that was accessible to any firm considering hiring the employee. The employer argued on appeal that the doctrine should not support a defamation-per-se theory, that its statement was privileged and substantially true, and that punitive damages should not be available for a self-published statement. The Court of Appeal rejected the employer's arguments and affirmed that the doctrine remains valid California law, reasoning that the additional requirements of proving strong compulsion, necessity, and foreseeability already guard against a plaintiff manufacturing a claim, and that the doctrine does not, by itself, restrict an employer's underlying right to terminate at-will employment. Tilkey did not limit or narrow the doctrine; if anything, it extended it, holding for the first time in a published California decision that punitive damages can be available in a compelled self-publication defamation case -- while nonetheless ordering the punitive damages award in that case reduced to comply with the due-process limits that generally cap the ratio of punitive to compensatory damages. The defamation liability finding itself, and the underlying punitive-damages availability, were affirmed; only the dollar amount of the punitive award was reduced on remand.
clauses.gap: This clause covers only the portions of Tilkey addressing compelled self-publication defamation and punitive damages; the same decision separately addressed the employer's use of an out-of-state domestic-violence diversion program under Labor Code section 432.7 (a wrongful-termination claim the court reversed on grounds unrelated to defamation) and an after-acquired-evidence defense, neither of which is addressed in this document. This clause also does not address a narrower, industry-specific privilege question the same opinion resolved -- whether the particular regulatory filing at issue was absolutely privileged under Civil Code section 47(b) as a communication in anticipation of an official proceeding (the court held it was not, on the facts of that filing) -- because that analysis turned on rules specific to securities-industry regulatory filings rather than on the compelled self-publication doctrine generally.

citations.case: Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co.
citations.quote: Nothing about compelled self-published defamation limits an employer’s right or ability to terminate employment unfairly or capriciously.

citations.case: Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co.
citations.quote: Allstate provided a written explanation for Tilkey’s termination of employment on the Form U5 to FINRA, which was available to every prospective employer of similarly-licensed employees.

citations.case: Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co.
citations.quote: The slander here was self-published, but that does not change access to punitive damages.

citations.case: Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co.
citations.quote: We affirm the portions of the judgment finding Allstate liable for defamation and punitive damages.

clauses.title: Interaction With the Civil Code Section 47(c) Reference Privilege
clauses.body: The compelled self-publication doctrine does not displace the qualified common-interest privilege available under California Civil Code section 47(c) -- the same privilege addressed in this project's Employer Reference Immunity information sheet for communications an employer makes directly to a reference-checker. Published California case law confirms that this qualified privilege, which protects a communication about an employee's job performance made without malice to an interested party, is available to an employer as a defense even where the claim against the employer is framed as compelled self-publication rather than as a direct communication to a prospective employer -- because the compelled self-publication doctrine changes who physically repeats the statement, not whether a privilege defense to the underlying statement exists. As with any other application of section 47(c)'s privilege, it can be defeated by a showing of malice, and it does not protect a statement found not to be substantially true.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only the qualified privilege under Civil Code section 47(c); it does not address the separate absolute privilege under Civil Code section 47(b) for communications made in or in anticipation of an official proceeding, which the same source decision analyzed in a securities-industry-specific context not generalized here. This clause states that the qualified privilege remains available as a defense; it does not predict whether that defense would succeed on any particular set of facts, which depends on whether malice or a lack of substantial truth is shown.

citations.case: Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co. (citing Cal. Civ. Code, § 47, subd. (c); Noel v. River Hills Wilsons, Inc. (2003) 113 Cal.App.4th 1363; Neal v. Gatlin (1973) 35 Cal.App.3d 871, 877)
citations.quote: Additionally, the qualified privilege that attaches to communications about an employee’s job performance when made without malice or abuse to a third party likewise protects an employer against compelled self-published defamation.

citations.case: Tilkey v. Allstate Ins. Co. (citing Noel v. River Hills Wilsons, Inc. (2003) 113 Cal.App.4th 1363, 1373-1374)
citations.quote: This conditional privilege helps protect the free flow of reference information.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Client Employer / Labor Contractor Liability Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California Labor Code Section 2810.3, which addresses civil legal responsibility between a "client employer" that obtains workers through a "labor contractor" (such as a staffing agency or temporary services provider) and that labor contractor. {{companyName}} has described its use of labor contractors as follows: {{laborContractorUseDescription}}. This document states the content of the statute; it does not determine whether Section 2810.3 applies to any particular arrangement, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: Definitions: "Client Employer" and "Labor Contractor"
clauses.body: California Labor Code Section 2810.3 defines a "client employer" as a business entity, regardless of its form, that obtains or is provided workers to perform labor within its usual course of business from a labor contractor. A "labor contractor" is defined as an individual or entity that supplies, with or without a contract, a client employer with workers to perform labor within the client employer's usual course of business. "Usual course of business" means the regular and customary work of a business, performed within or upon the premises or worksite of the client employer.
clauses.gap: The statute's definitions of "labor," "wages," and "worker" incorporate other Labor Code sections (Section 200 and the Industrial Welfare Commission's overtime-exemption wage orders under Section 515) by reference rather than restating them, so a full determination of who counts as a covered "worker" can require consulting those other provisions.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "client employer"
citations.quote: “Client employer” means a business entity, regardless of its form, that obtains or is provided workers to perform labor within its usual course of business from a labor contractor.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "labor contractor"
citations.quote: “Labor contractor” means an individual or entity that supplies, either with or without a contract, a client employer with workers to perform labor within the client employer’s usual course of business.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(6) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "usual course of business"
citations.quote: “Usual course of business” means the regular and customary work of a business, performed within or upon the premises or worksite of the client employer.

clauses.title: Size Thresholds and Definitional Exclusions
clauses.body: Section 2810.3 excludes certain entities from its definitions entirely, which removes them from the statute's liability-sharing scheme. A business entity is not a "client employer" if its total workforce (including workers hired directly and those obtained from any labor contractor) numbers fewer than 25, or if it has five or fewer workers supplied by a labor contractor or labor contractors at any given time. The state and any political subdivision of the state, including a city, county, city and county, or special district, are also excluded from the "client employer" definition. Separately, the term "labor contractor" does not include a bona fide nonprofit community-based organization that provides services to workers; a bona fide labor organization, apprenticeship program, or hiring hall operated under a collective bargaining agreement; a motion picture payroll services company as defined by reference to the Unemployment Insurance Code; or a third party to a qualifying employee leasing arrangement (as defined by a specified 1995 workers' compensation experience rating plan rule, as that rule read on January 1, 2014) where the arrangement contractually obligates the client employer to assume all civil legal responsibility and liability under the statute.
clauses.gap: These are two distinct exclusion lists: one narrows who counts as a "client employer" (the workforce-size and public-entity exclusions), and the other narrows who counts as a "labor contractor" (the nonprofit, labor-organization, motion-picture-payroll, and employee-leasing exclusions). The statute does not contain a separately labeled exclusion for "small businesses" as such, for motor carriers as a category, or for unionized construction generally beyond the labor-organization/hiring-hall and collective-bargaining language quoted above; whether a given arrangement fits one of the statute's specific exclusions is a fact-specific determination this sheet does not make.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(1)(B)(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, workforce-size exclusion
citations.quote: A business entity with a workforce of fewer than 25 workers, including those hired directly by the client employer and those obtained from, or provided by, any labor contractor.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(1)(B)(ii) (California Legislative Information text)

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(1)(B)(iii) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, state/political-subdivision exclusion
citations.quote: The state or any political subdivision of the state, including any city, county, city and county, or special district.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, nonprofit community-based organization exclusion
citations.quote: A bona fide nonprofit, community-based organization that provides services to workers.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(3)(B) (California Legislative Information text)

citations.quote: A bona fide labor organization or apprenticeship program or hiring hall operated pursuant to a collective bargaining agreement.

clauses.title: Scope of Shared Civil Liability
clauses.body: Where Section 2810.3 applies, a client employer shares with its labor contractor all civil legal responsibility and civil liability, as to workers supplied by that labor contractor, for the payment of wages and for any failure to secure valid workers' compensation coverage as required by Labor Code Section 3700. This shared liability applies even where the client employer is not otherwise the workers' direct employer for purposes of separate wage-payment statutes. Section 2810.3 separately provides that a client employer may not shift to its labor contractor any legal duties or liabilities arising under Division 5 of the Labor Code (the occupational safety and health provisions commencing with Section 6300) with respect to workers the labor contractor supplies -- meaning the client employer retains those duties itself rather than sharing or delegating them. The statute states that this liability-sharing and non-delegation scheme is in addition to, and supplemental of, any other theories of liability or requirement established by other statutes or the common law.
clauses.gap: Section 2810.3 itself addresses wage payment, workers' compensation coverage, and occupational safety and health duties; it does not, by its own text, create shared liability for other types of claims (such as anti-discrimination or retaliation claims brought under different statutes), and this sheet does not address whether or how other statutes might separately extend liability to a client employer for those other claim types.

citations.quote:
Thus, even if the business entity is not the wage claimant’s employer, and therefore owes
no duty to pay wages under section 1194, the entity is nonetheless liable because section
2810.3 imposes joint liability.

clauses.title: Additional Liability Carve-Outs for Specific Business Categories
clauses.body: Beyond the definitional exclusions, Section 2810.3 states that it does not impose individual liability on a homeowner for labor or services received at the home, or on the owner of a home-based business for labor or services received at the home. It also does not impose liability on a client employer for its use of an independent contractor other than a labor contractor, and does not change the definition of independent contractor. The statute further states that it does not impose liability on several specific categories of arrangements, including a client employer that is not a motor carrier of property, based solely on its use of a third-party motor carrier with interstate or intrastate operating authority to ship or receive freight; a motor carrier of property subcontracting with another motor carrier using the other carrier's own employees and vehicles; a client employer that is not a household mover, based solely on its use of a permitted third-party household mover; a permitted household mover subcontracting with another permitted mover using the other mover's own employees and vehicles; a cable operator, direct-to-home satellite service provider, or telephone corporation contracting with a company to build, install, maintain, or repair using that company's own employees and vehicles where the contractor's name is visible on uniforms and vehicles; and a motor club contracting with a third party to provide motor club services using that third party's own employees and vehicles where the contractor's name is visible on its vehicles.
clauses.gap: This clause paraphrases the motor-carrier, household-mover, cable/satellite/telephone, and motor-club categories in subdivision (p); only the introductory language and the motor-carrier and cable/telephone-corporation examples are reproduced as exact quotations below. Each of these carve-outs has its own specific conditions (for example, the contractor's name being visible on uniforms or vehicles) that determine whether it applies to a given arrangement.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, homeowner and home-based business exclusion
citations.quote: This section does not impose individual liability on a homeowner for labor or services received at the home or the owner of a home-based business for labor or services received at the home.

citations.quote: This section does not impose liability on the following:

clauses.title: Notice, Enforcement, and Anti-Retaliation
clauses.body: Before filing a civil action against a client employer for violations covered by Section 2810.3, a worker or the worker's representative must, at least 30 days beforehand, notify the client employer of the violations described in subdivision (b) (the wage-payment and workers' compensation coverage provisions). Neither the client employer nor the labor contractor may take adverse action against a worker for providing that notification or for filing a claim or civil action. Separately, upon request by a state enforcement agency or department, a client employer or labor contractor must provide the agency or department with information within its possession, custody, or control that is required to verify compliance with applicable state laws, and must make records available promptly for inspection and copying. The statute authorizes the Labor Commissioner, the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, and the Employment Development Department each to adopt regulations and rules of practice and procedure to administer and enforce the provisions within their respective jurisdictions.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, 30-day pre-filing notice requirement
citations.quote: At least 30 days prior to filing a civil action against a client employer for violations covered by this section, a worker or the worker’s representative shall notify the client employer of violations under subdivision (b).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, anti-retaliation provision
citations.quote: Neither the client employer nor the labor contractor may take any adverse action against any worker for providing notification of violations or filing a claim or civil action.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, information requests by state enforcement agencies
citations.quote: Upon request by a state enforcement agency or department, a client employer or a labor contractor shall provide to the agency or department any information within its possession, custody, or control required to verify compliance with applicable state laws.

clauses.gap: These citations are to different subdivisions of the same statute (Section 2810.3) rather than independent sources. This clause does not describe any implementing regulations the Labor Commissioner, the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, or the Employment Development Department may have adopted under their respective enforcement authority, and does not address the required contents or method of the 30-day pre-filing notice.

clauses.title: Contractual Remedies Between the Parties and Anti-Waiver Rule
clauses.body: Section 2810.3 does not prohibit a client employer from establishing, exercising, or enforcing by contract any otherwise lawful remedies against a labor contractor for liability created by the labor contractor's acts, and it does not prohibit a labor contractor from doing the same against a client employer for liability created by the client employer's acts. This preserves the parties' ability to allocate responsibility between themselves by contract (for example, through indemnification provisions), separate from the liability-sharing the statute itself imposes toward workers. The statute also provides that a waiver of Section 2810.3 is contrary to public policy and is void and unenforceable.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, client employer's contractual remedies against labor contractor preserved
citations.quote: This section does not prohibit a client employer from establishing, exercising, or enforcing by contract any otherwise lawful remedies against a labor contractor for liability created by acts of a labor contractor.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(h) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, labor contractor's contractual remedies against client employer preserved
citations.quote: This section does not prohibit a labor contractor from establishing, exercising, or enforcing by contract any otherwise lawful remedies against a client employer for liability created by acts of a client employer.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, anti-waiver provision
citations.quote: A waiver of this section is contrary to public policy, and is void and unenforceable.

clauses.gap: These citations are to different subdivisions of the same statute (Section 2810.3) rather than independent sources. This clause states that the statute preserves the parties' ability to allocate responsibility between themselves by contract; it does not describe how any particular indemnification provision should be drafted or would be interpreted, and does not address whether a specific contractual term between a given client employer and labor contractor is enforceable.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's default statutory rules for when a married person's community property, earnings, or separate property can be used to satisfy a debt that the other spouse incurred, before or during the marriage. These are the rules that apply automatically, under Family Code sections 910 through 916, in the absence of a premarital agreement, postnuptial agreement, or other written agreement that changes them. It concerns {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}.

This document is limited to the statutory default liability scheme as between a debtor spouse, the other spouse, and an outside creditor. It is not this project's Premarital Agreement document, which addresses how spouses may contractually reallocate responsibility for debts between themselves -- a valid agreement under the Uniform Premarital Agreement Act can change what this document describes. It is also not this project's Family Code section 2640/2641 reimbursement documents, which address tracing and reimbursing a spouse's separate-property contributions toward the acquisition of community assets at the time of division, a different question from whether an outside creditor can reach property to satisfy a debt in the first place. This document states what the statutes provide; it does not determine whether any particular debt, account, or item of property of {{party1Name}} or {{party2Name}} is or is not reachable by a creditor, which depends on the specific facts and, where disputed, is decided by a court.

clauses.title: Community Estate's Default Liability for Either Spouse's Debt
clauses.body: Under Family Code section 910, except as otherwise expressly provided by statute, the community estate is liable for a debt incurred by either spouse before or during the marriage. This liability applies regardless of which spouse has management and control of the property, and regardless of whether one or both spouses are parties to the debt or to a judgment on the debt. For this purpose, the statute defines "during marriage" to exclude the period after the date of separation and before a judgment of dissolution of marriage or legal separation. A separate section of the same statutory chapter, Family Code section 912, extends this same liability rule to quasi-community property, providing that quasi-community property is liable to the same extent, and treated the same in all other respects, as community property.
clauses.gap: Family Code sections 910(a) and 910(b) are subdivisions of the same enacted section, and section 912 is a companion provision within the same statutory chapter (General Rules of Liability, sections 910-916); the citations below are not independent sources of one another. Section 910(a) begins "Except as otherwise expressly provided by statute" -- this document does not catalog every statutory exception to the general community-liability rule (for example, the earnings-protection and necessaries-of-life provisions addressed in this document's other clauses are themselves such exceptions), and a reader should not assume the general rule stated here applies without checking for an applicable exception.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 910(a)-(b)
citations.cite: community estate's liability for a debt incurred by either spouse before or during marriage, and the definition of "during marriage"
citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise expressly provided by statute, the community estate is liable for a debt incurred by either spouse before or during marriage, regardless of which spouse has the management and control of the property and regardless of whether one or both spouses are parties to the debt or to a judgment for the debt. (b) “During marriage” for purposes of this section does not include the period after the date of separation, as defined in Section 70, and before a judgment of dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 912
citations.cite: quasi-community property is liable to the same extent, and treated the same in all other respects, as community property
citations.quote: quasi-community property is liable to the same extent, and shall be treated the same in all other respects, as community property.

clauses.title: Default Rule: Separate Property Liable Only for Its Owner's Own Debts
clauses.body: Family Code section 913 states the default rule for a married person's own separate property: it is liable for a debt that person incurred before or during the marriage. Except as otherwise provided by statute, section 913 also states the converse default rule protecting the other spouse: a married person's separate property is not liable for a debt incurred by that person's spouse before or during the marriage. The statute further provides that a person's joinder in, or consent to, an encumbrance of community estate property to secure a debt the person's spouse incurred does not, by itself, subject that person's separate property to liability for the debt, unless the joining or consenting person also incurred the debt.
clauses.gap: Family Code section 913(a) and section 913(b) (including its two numbered clauses) are subdivisions of the same enacted section; the citations below are not independent sources of one another. Section 913(b) begins "Except as otherwise provided by statute" -- section 914, addressed in this document's companion clause on necessaries of life, is itself one such statutory exception to the protection described here, and this document does not catalog any other exception to section 913's default rules.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 913(a)
citations.cite: a married person's own separate property is liable for a debt that person incurred before or during marriage
citations.quote: (a) The separate property of a married person is liable for a debt incurred by the person before or during marriage.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 913(b)
citations.cite: a married person's separate property is not liable for the other spouse's debt, and joinder in an encumbrance alone does not create such liability
citations.quote: (b) Except as otherwise provided by statute: (1) The separate property of a married person is not liable for a debt incurred by the person’s spouse before or during marriage. (2) The joinder or consent of a married person to an encumbrance of community estate property to secure payment of a debt incurred by the person’s spouse does not subject the person’s separate property to liability for the debt unless the person also incurred the debt.

clauses.title: Protection of a Spouse's Earnings From the Other Spouse's Premarital Debt
clauses.body: Family Code section 911 provides a specific protection for a married person's own earnings against a debt the person's spouse incurred before marriage. Under this section, the earnings of a married person during marriage are not liable for a debt incurred by the person's spouse before marriage. That protection continues after the earnings are paid to the person, for as long as the earnings are held in a deposit account over which the spouse has no right of withdrawal and are not commingled with other community estate property, other than an insignificant amount. The statute separately defines "earnings" as compensation for personal services performed, whether as an employee or otherwise, and defines "deposit account" by reference to the Commercial Code.
clauses.gap: This clause draws only on Family Code section 911. It is included as a distinct exception to the general community-liability rule of section 910 (addressed in this document's companion clause), which would otherwise make the community estate -- including a spouse's earnings once they become community property -- liable for a premarital debt of either spouse. Section 911 protects only earnings meeting its own conditions (held in a segregated, no-withdrawal-right deposit account); it does not protect earnings once commingled beyond an insignificant amount, and it does not apply to a debt a spouse incurs during the marriage, which is governed by section 910's general rule instead.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 911(a)
citations.cite: a married person's earnings during marriage are not liable for a debt the spouse incurred before marriage, subject to conditions on how the earnings are held
citations.quote: (a) The earnings of a married person during marriage are not liable for a debt incurred by the person’s spouse before marriage. After the earnings of the married person are paid, they remain not liable so long as they are held in a deposit account in which the person’s spouse has no right of withdrawal and are uncommingled with other property in the community estate, except property insignificant in amount.

clauses.title: Exception: Personal Liability for a Spouse's Debt for Necessaries of Life
clauses.body: Family Code section 914 creates an exception to section 913's default protection of a nondebtor spouse's separate property. Notwithstanding section 913, a married person is personally liable for two categories of debt incurred by the person's spouse during the marriage: a debt incurred for necessaries of life of the spouse before the date of separation, and, except as provided in Family Code section 4302, a debt incurred for common necessaries of life of the spouse after the date of separation. Where a person's separate property is applied to satisfy a debt for which the person is personally liable under this section, the statute grants a right of reimbursement to the extent that nonexempt community estate property or the spouse's own separate property was available at the time but was not applied to the debt instead.
clauses.gap: Family Code section 914(a) and section 914(b) are subdivisions of the same enacted section; the citations below are not independent sources of one another. Section 914 does not itself define "necessaries of life" or "common necessaries of life"; this document does not supply a definition of that statutory term, and whether a particular debt qualifies is a fact-specific determination the statute's text does not resolve. Section 914(a)(2) is itself made subject to a further statutory exception, Family Code section 4302, which this document does not separately address. Section 914(c)-(d) (not quoted here) set a special statute-of-limitations rule for this liability if the debtor spouse dies, which this document does not otherwise cover.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 914(a)
citations.cite: personal liability for a spouse's debt for necessaries of life, before and after separation
citations.quote: (a) Notwithstanding Section 913, a married person is personally liable for the following debts incurred by the person’s spouse during marriage: (1) A debt incurred for necessaries of life of the person’s spouse before the date of separation of the spouses. (2) Except as provided in Section 4302, a debt incurred for common necessaries of life of the person’s spouse after the date of separation of the spouses.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 914(b)
citations.cite: the reimbursement right when separate property is applied to a necessaries debt while other available property was not
citations.quote: (b) The separate property of a married person may be applied to the satisfaction of a debt for which the person is personally liable pursuant to this section. If separate property is so applied at a time when nonexempt property in the community estate or separate property of the person’s spouse is available but is not applied to the satisfaction of the debt, the married person is entitled to reimbursement to the extent such property was available.

clauses.title: Liability of Property After Division of the Community Estate
clauses.body: Family Code section 916 addresses what happens to this liability scheme once the community and quasi-community estate has been divided in a dissolution or legal separation proceeding. Notwithstanding any other provision of this statutory chapter, after that division: the separate property a married person owned at the time of division, and the property the person received in the division, remains liable for a debt that person incurred before or during the marriage, and the person remains personally liable for it, whether or not the debt was assigned for payment by the person's spouse in the division. Conversely, that same property is not liable for a debt incurred by the person's spouse before or during the marriage, and the person is not personally liable for it, unless the debt was assigned for payment by the person in the division -- though the statute notes this does not affect the liability of property for satisfying a lien already on it. Where a debt was assigned to the person in the division and the person's property is later applied to satisfy a money judgment on that debt, the statute gives the person a right of reimbursement from the spouse to whom the debt was assigned, with interest at the legal rate, plus reasonable attorney's fees incurred in enforcing that reimbursement right.
clauses.gap: Family Code section 916(a) (including its three numbered paragraphs) and section 916(b) are subdivisions of the same enacted section; the citations below are not independent sources of one another. Paragraph (a)(3)'s judgment-enforcement mechanics are paraphrased in this clause's body rather than reproduced as a separate quoted citation. This section applies only after an actual division of the community and quasi-community estate under Division 7 (commencing with Family Code section 2500); it does not describe the liability rules that apply before such a division, which are addressed in this document's other clauses.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 916(a)
citations.cite: post-division liability of a person's separate property and awarded property for the person's own debts versus the spouse's debts

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet explains California Family Code section 271, a fee-shifting sanctions provision that a family court may apply in the proceeding between {{petitionerName}} and {{respondentName}}, case number {{courtCaseNumber}}, filed in {{countyOfFiling}}. It states the text of the statute and how published California Court of Appeal decisions have described and applied it. It does not tell either party whether a section 271 sanction should be requested, opposed, or is likely to be granted in this or any other case, and it is not a substitute for advice from a licensed attorney about the facts of a specific matter.

clauses.title: The Section 271 Standard: Conduct That Furthers or Frustrates Settlement Policy
clauses.body: Family Code section 271(a) states that, notwithstanding any other provision of the Family Code, a court may base an award of attorney's fees and costs on the extent to which the conduct of each party or attorney furthers or frustrates the policy of the law to promote settlement of litigation and, where possible, to reduce the cost of litigation by encouraging cooperation between the parties and attorneys. The statute states that an award under this section is in the nature of a sanction. The statute further states that in making an award under this section, the court must take into consideration all evidence concerning the parties' incomes, assets, and liabilities, and that the court may not impose a sanction under this section that imposes an unreasonable financial burden on the party against whom the sanction is imposed.
clauses.gap: This clause covers Family Code section 271(a) except its final sentence, which states that the requesting party need not show financial need and is addressed in a separate clause. It does not cover subdivision (b) (notice and an opportunity to be heard) or subdivision (c) (the source from which the award is payable), each addressed in a separate clause. The statute does not define 'unreasonable financial burden' numerically or otherwise, and does not state how a court is to weigh a party's income, assets, and liabilities against a proposed sanction amount on any particular record.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 271(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the standard for a section 271 sanction, its nature as a sanction, and the income/assets/liabilities and unreasonable-financial-burden limits on it
citations.quote: (a) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, the court may base an award of attorney’s fees and costs on the extent to which any conduct of each party or attorney furthers or frustrates the policy of the law to promote settlement of litigation and, where possible, to reduce the cost of litigation by encouraging cooperation between the parties and attorneys. An award of attorney’s fees and costs pursuant to this section is in the nature of a sanction. In making an award pursuant to this section, the court shall take into consideration all evidence concerning the parties’ incomes, assets, and liabilities. The court shall not impose a sanction pursuant to this section that imposes an unreasonable financial burden on the party against whom the sanction is imposed.

clauses.title: No Showing of Financial Need Required
clauses.body: Family Code section 271(a) states that, in order to obtain an award under this section, the party requesting an award of attorney's fees and costs is not required to demonstrate any financial need for the award. Published California Court of Appeal decisions have described section 271 in the same terms: one decision stated that section 271 authorizes sanctions to advance the policy of promoting settlement of litigation and encouraging cooperation of the litigants, and does not require any actual injury, and that a party seeking a section 271 sanction is not required to establish any particular harm as a prerequisite to the award. That same decision stated that because section 271 is not a need-based statute and does not require a correlation between the sanctioned conduct and specific attorney's fees, the requesting party need not demonstrate her own current financial situation, and that a section 271 sanction need not be limited to the cost the sanctioned conduct actually imposed on the other side.
clauses.gap: The 'does not require any actual injury' language quoted here comes from In re Marriage of Corona, which was itself quoting and applying In re Marriage of Feldman; this clause does not independently trace or re-verify every authority that Corona or Feldman in turn rely on for these propositions. This clause states how these two published decisions described section 271's no-need, no-actual-injury character; it does not survey the full body of section 271 case law for contrary or qualifying statements, and it does not address Family Code section 2030's separate need-based standard, which is covered in a different document in this corpus.

citations.quote: In order to obtain an award under this section, the party requesting an award of attorney’s fees and costs is not required to demonstrate any financial need for the award.

clauses.title: Notice and an Opportunity to Be Heard; Source of Payment
clauses.body: Family Code section 271(b) states that an award of attorney's fees and costs as a sanction under this section may be imposed only after notice by the requesting party or the court to the party against whom the sanction is proposed, and an opportunity for that party to be heard. Family Code section 271(c) states that such an award is payable only from the property or income of the party against whom the sanction is imposed, except that the award may be made against the sanctioned party's share of the community property.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (b) and (c) of Family Code section 271 in full; it does not address what specific form of notice (for example, a noticed motion or order to show cause versus another mechanism) satisfies subdivision (b) on particular facts, or how a court identifies a party's 'share of the community property' under subdivision (c) before a final division of community property has occurred. Those questions are not resolved by the statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 271(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the notice-and-opportunity-to-be-heard requirement before a section 271 sanction may be imposed
citations.quote: (b) An award of attorney’s fees and costs as a sanction pursuant to this section shall be imposed only after notice by the requesting party or the court to the party against whom the sanction is proposed and opportunity for that party to be heard is provided by the court.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 271(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the source from which a section 271 award is payable
citations.quote: (c) An award of attorney’s fees and costs as a sanction pursuant to this section is payable only from the property or income of the party against whom the sanction is imposed, except that the award may be against the sanctioned party’s share of the community property.

clauses.title: Case Law: Standard of Review and Application Without an Independent Bad-Faith Finding
clauses.body: A section 271 sanctions order is reviewed on appeal for abuse of discretion. Applying that standard, California courts have stated that the trial court's order will be overturned only if, considering all the evidence viewed most favorably in support of the order, no judge could reasonably make the order. In one published decision applying this standard, the Court of Appeal affirmed a section 271 sanctions award as an alternative basis for a sanction the family court had also described using the language of Code of Civil Procedure sanctions provisions, including a finding that a party's conduct was in "bad faith"; the appellate court's section 271 analysis did not treat a separate bad-faith finding as a required element, instead relying on the statute's furthers-or-frustrates-settlement-policy standard and on the absence of any requirement that the requesting party show particular harm.
clauses.gap: This clause describes how one published Court of Appeal decision (In re Marriage of Corona) applied section 271 to conduct that the family court had also labeled 'bad faith' under a different, non-family-law sanctions statute; it does not establish that a 'bad faith' finding is legally irrelevant to every section 271 case, and it is not a survey of the full body of section 271 case law on that question — only the decisions actually reviewed for this document are described here. It also does not describe the underlying facts of the cited decision (a dispute over housing-cost arrearages) as establishing what conduct will or will not qualify for a sanction in a different case.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Feldman (2007) 153 Cal.App.4th 1470, 1478 [64 Cal.Rptr.3d 29], quoting In re Marriage of Burgard (1999) 72 Cal.App.4th 74, 82
citations.cite: abuse-of-discretion standard of review for a section 271 sanctions order
citations.quote: “A sanction order under . . . section 271 is reviewed under the abuse of discretion standard. ‘ “[T]he trial court’s order will be overturned only if, considering all the evidence viewed most favorably in support of its order, no judge could reasonably make the order.” ’ ”

citations.case: In re Marriage of Corona (2009) 172 Cal.App.4th 1205, 1226 [92 Cal.Rptr.3d 17], citing In re Marriage of Feldman (2007) 153 Cal.App.4th 1470, 1479-1480
citations.cite: no particular harm need be established as a prerequisite to a section 271 award, applied where the family court had also invoked bad-faith language under a different statute
citations.quote: Claire was not required to establish any particular harm as a prerequisite to a sanctions award under section 271.

clauses.title: How Section 271 Differs From Section 2030 and the Disclosure Sanctions Statutes
clauses.body: Family Code section 271 is codified in Part 5 (Attorney's Fees and Costs) of Division 2 (General Provisions) of the Family Code, and by its own terms applies notwithstanding any other provision of the code. California case law has described a section 271 analysis as one that does not consider the relative circumstances of the respective parties, but instead focuses on the behavior of an individual party or attorney — in contrast with a need-based fee award under Family Code section 2030, which turns on the parties' relative circumstances. Unlike cost shifting under section 2030, a section 271 award is described in the statute itself as in the nature of a sanction, subject to the statute's own limits that it may not impose an unreasonable financial burden on the sanctioned party and is payable only from that party's property or income (or the party's share of community property). Family Code sections 2100-2113, covered in a separate document in this corpus, authorize a different, mandatory sanctions and judgment-set-aside remedy limited to a party's noncompliance with the disclosure chapter's specific financial-disclosure requirements; section 271 is not limited to disclosure violations and, by its statutory standard, may be based on any conduct of a party or attorney that furthers or frustrates the policy of promoting settlement and reducing litigation costs through cooperation.
clauses.gap: The case-law portion of this clause quotes a single Court of Appeal footnote comparing section 271 to section 2030 specifically; that footnote did not address the disclosure sanctions statutes, Family Code sections 2100-2113. The statement that section 271 is not limited to disclosure violations reflects this document's own reading of section 271's general, code-wide 'notwithstanding any other provision of this code' text and its placement in a different part of the code from the disclosure chapter, rather than a case holding addressing that specific three-way comparison. This clause does not resolve whether particular conduct could support relief under more than one of these three provisions at once, or how a court would sequence or combine such requests.

citations.case: In re Marriage of Smith (2015) 242 Cal.App.4th 529, 536, fn. 6 [195 Cal.Rptr.3d 162]
citations.cite: section 271 focuses on individual conduct rather than relative circumstances, and is described as a sanction
citations.quote: The section 271 analysis does not consider the relative circumstances of the respective parties, but focuses on the behavior of an individual party and his or her counsel. Section 271 allows the trial court to reward or punish conduct by a party or attorney that “furthers or frustrates the policy of the law to promote settlement of litigation and, where possible, to reduce the cost of litigation by encouraging cooperation between the parties and attorneys.” (§ 271, subd. (a).) Unlike cost shifting under section 2030, a section 271 award is “in the nature of a sanction.” (§ 271, subd. (a).)

citations.case: In re Marriage of Smith (2015) 242 Cal.App.4th 529, 536, fn. 6 [195 Cal.Rptr.3d 162]
citations.cite: the unreasonable-financial-burden limit and community-property source of payment restated
citations.quote: Nevertheless, the trial court may not impose a sanction under section 271 that “imposes an unreasonable financial burden on the party against whom the sanction is imposed.” (Id., subd. (a).) Section 271 provides that an award under that section “is payable only from the property or income of the party against whom the sanction is imposed, except that the award may be against the sanctioned party’s share of the community property.” (Id., subd. (c).)

clauses.title: Restriction
clauses.body: This is a restraint between two businesses -- {{companyName}} and {{secondCompanyName}} -- rather than a promise by an individual worker. During the term of the parties' business relationship and for {{restrictionPeriod}} after it ends, neither {{companyName}} nor {{secondCompanyName}} will solicit, recruit, or hire any person who is, or was during the preceding twelve months, an employee or independent contractor of the other party, without that party's prior written consent. This is a separate question from a departing individual employee's own promise not to recruit former co-workers, which is addressed in a different document in this set.

clauses.title: California's General Rule Against Restraints of Trade
clauses.body: California law voids, as a restraint of trade, contracts that restrain anyone from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business -- a rule not limited to noncompete clauses in individual employment contracts. On its face, the statute reaches "every contract" fitting that description, of any kind, unless a specific statutory exception applies.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text does not confine this general voidness rule to the employment relationship; a separate subdivision (quoted in the next clause) confirms that reach. A different part of this same statutory chapter carries narrow exceptions not addressed here (for example, restraints tied to the sale of a business's goodwill or the dissolution of a partnership or LLC) -- this document does not evaluate whether any such exception could apply to a particular no-hire arrangement. This is California law only; other states treat business-to-business no-hire and no-poach agreements differently, including some that permit them if reasonable in scope.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600(a) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code section 16600, subdivision (a) (as amended by Stats. 2023, ch. 828, § 1 (AB 1076), eff. Jan. 1, 2024)
citations.quote: Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void.

clauses.title: This Rule Is Not Limited to Contracts the Restrained Worker Signed
clauses.body: This restraint-of-trade rule is not limited to contracts to which the restrained person is a party. A contract between two businesses -- neither of which is the worker whose hiring or job mobility the contract restricts -- can still fall within this rule; the statute says so directly, in a subdivision added specifically to address that scenario.
clauses.gap: This subdivision was added to the statute effective January 1, 2024 (by AB 1076); it states that it 'does not constitute a change in, but is declaratory of, existing law' as to the broad-reading directive in the surrounding subdivision, but the third-party-reach language itself is a more recent textual addition. Separately, federal antitrust law offers an independent framework that can also apply to a business-to-business no-hire agreement, evaluated under different tests than this state statute -- litigation between two competing healthcare staffing companies over a non-solicitation-of-employees provision in their business collaboration agreement has been reported as applying federal Sherman Act rule-of-reason analysis (treating such a provision as not automatically unlawful, unlike this statute's near-automatic voidness rule) rather than California Business and Professions Code section 16600. This document does not cite a specific opinion for that antitrust analysis: this research session located secondary reporting describing that Ninth Circuit litigation but could not locate and independently verify a quotable opinion text for it through the primary-source channels available, so no case citation is given for it. Where both frameworks could apply to the same agreement, they are separate bodies of law with separate tests and can reach different results.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16600(c) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code section 16600, subdivision (c) (as amended by Stats. 2023, ch. 828, § 1 (AB 1076), eff. Jan. 1, 2024)
citations.quote: This section shall not be limited to contracts where the person being restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business is a party to the contract.

clauses.title: State Enforcement Interest in Business-to-Business No-Poach Provisions
clauses.body: Business-to-business no-hire and no-poach provisions -- including those between a franchisor and its franchisees, or among a franchisor's franchisees -- have also drawn attention from state enforcement authorities as a competition and worker-mobility concern, separate from private contract litigation between the businesses themselves. In March 2019, California's Attorney General announced settlements with several national franchise companies requiring them to stop including no-poach provisions of this kind in their franchise agreements.
clauses.gap: This reflects a settlement of enforcement claims, not a court ruling interpreting Business and Professions Code section 16600 or any other statute -- it establishes no binding legal test, and its terms bind only the companies that signed it. Other states' attorneys general participated in the same multistate settlement, and separate, later settlements covering other franchise companies were announced afterward; this document cites only the March 2019 announcement covering four named companies as one verifiable example, not a complete account of all such state enforcement activity.

citations.case: California Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General, press release
citations.cite: Attorney General Becerra Announces Multistate Settlements Targeting "No-Poach" Policies that Harm Workers (Cal. DOJ, published Mar. 12, 2019)
citations.quote: Many of these anticompetitive no-poach provisions required franchise operators to contractually agree to not hire or solicit the employees of another franchise operator.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the federal beneficial ownership information ("BOI") reporting regime created by the Corporate Transparency Act (CTA), codified at 31 U.S.C. § 5336, and implemented by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) at 31 C.F.R. § 1010.380. It reflects the scope of that regime as revised by FinCEN rulemaking effective March 26, 2025 and made permanent by a final rule effective August 14, 2026. This is a federal reporting obligation separate from any California filing. This document states the regulatory text as fetched and independently verified on the date checked above; it does not determine whether {{companyName}} currently has a reporting obligation, which depends on facts about its jurisdiction of formation and the citizenship or residency of its owners.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Reporting Company"
clauses.body: The Corporate Transparency Act, as codified at 31 U.S.C. § 5336(a)(11), defines a "reporting company" as a corporation, limited liability company, or other similar entity that either (i) is created by filing a document with a secretary of state or similar office under the law of a State or Indian Tribe, or (ii) is formed under the law of a foreign country and registered to do business in the United States by such a filing. This statutory definition has not been amended since enactment; the current, narrower scope of who must actually report is instead the product of implementing regulations described in a separate authority clause below.
clauses.gap: This clause states the statute's own definition, which by its terms would include domestic (U.S.-formed) entities. It does not by itself describe the current, narrower regulatory scope -- the implementing regulation, addressed in this document's next clause, currently excludes all domestic entities from reporting-company status. Reading this clause alone, without the next one, would give an inaccurate picture of who currently must report.

citations.case: 31 U.S.C. § 5336(a)(11)(A) — Corporate Transparency Act, beneficial ownership information reporting requirements
citations.quote: (11) Reporting company .-The term "reporting company"- (A) means a corporation, limited liability company, or other similar entity that is- (i) created by the filing of a document with a secretary of state or a similar office under the law of a State or Indian Tribe; or (ii) formed under the law of a foreign country and registered to do business in the United States by the filing of a document with a secretary of state or a similar office under the laws of a State or Indian Tribe

clauses.title: 2025-2026 Narrowing: Domestic Entities and U.S. Persons Excluded by Regulation
clauses.body: FinCEN's implementing regulation, 31 C.F.R. § 1010.380, was revised effective March 26, 2025 (an interim final rule) and that revision was made permanent by a further final rule effective August 14, 2026. As currently in effect, the regulatory definition of "reporting company" at 31 C.F.R. § 1010.380(c)(1) no longer includes any category of domestic (U.S.-formed) entity — the paragraph that formerly defined domestic reporting companies is marked "[Reserved]" — and instead defines a reporting company only as an entity formed under the law of a foreign country that is registered to do business in a State or tribal jurisdiction by such a filing. The regulation separately states that reporting companies are exempt from reporting the beneficial ownership information of any United States persons who are beneficial owners or company applicants, and that United States persons are themselves exempt from any obligation to provide beneficial ownership information with respect to a reporting company for which they are beneficial owners or company applicants. As a result, under the rule currently in effect, entities formed in the United States (including California-formed entities) are not reporting companies regardless of size, and no U.S. person is required to be reported as, or to supply information as, a beneficial owner or company applicant of any entity, including a foreign-formed reporting company.
clauses.gap: The Federal Register documents for the March 26, 2025 interim final rule (90 FR 13697) and the August 14, 2026 final rule (91 FR 52528) could not be fetched directly this session — federalregister.gov, fincen.gov, and home.treasury.gov were all blocked by this environment's network egress controls, as was every law-firm secondary-source page attempted (Sidley, Morrison Foerster, BDO). The dates and Federal Register citations above are drawn from the amendment history embedded in the current eCFR text itself (an official primary source, independently confirmed twice), corroborated only in general terms by search-engine result snippets describing an August 2026 FinCEN final rule that adopted the 2025 interim rule 'without substantive changes.' No portion of the FinCEN or Federal Register rule preambles is quoted here because that text could not be independently verified against a fetched primary copy this session.

citations.case: 31 C.F.R. § 1010.380(c)(1)-(2) — Definition of reporting company (eCFR, current as of Sept. 3, 2026)
citations.quote: (i) [Reserved] (ii) Any entity that is: (A) A corporation, limited liability company, or other entity; (B) Formed under the law of a foreign country; and (C) Registered to do business in any State or tribal jurisdiction by the filing of a document with a secretary of state or any similar office under the law of that State or Indian tribe.

citations.quote: (5) Special exemptions. (i) Reporting companies are exempt from any requirement under 31 U.S.C. 5336 and this section to report the beneficial ownership information of any United States persons who are beneficial owners or company applicants. (ii) United States persons are exempt from any requirement under 31 U.S.C. 5336 and this section to provide beneficial ownership information with respect to any reporting company for which they are beneficial owners or company applicants.

citations.cite: 31 C.F.R. § 1010.380, Source Credit

clauses.title: "Beneficial Owner" and "Company Applicant" Defined
clauses.body: 31 U.S.C. § 5336(a)(3) defines a "beneficial owner," with respect to an entity, as an individual who, directly or indirectly, exercises substantial control over the entity or owns or controls not less than 25 percent of its ownership interests, subject to statutory exclusions for minor children (where a parent's or guardian's information is reported instead), nominees acting on behalf of another, employees whose control derives solely from employment status, individuals with a mere inheritance expectancy, and certain creditors. Under the current implementing regulation, however, this definition is only operative for a foreign-formed reporting company, and only as to individuals who are not United States persons, because United States persons are exempt from beneficial-owner and company-applicant reporting under 31 C.F.R. § 1010.380(c)(5).
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the statute's core substantial-control/25-percent-ownership test; it does not restate the statutory text of each of the five listed exclusions (minor children, nominees, employees, inheritance expectancy, creditors) in full. The statutory "company applicant" definition, a related but separate term, is not separately quoted here.

citations.case: 31 U.S.C. § 5336(a)(3) — definition of "beneficial owner"
citations.quote: (3) Beneficial owner .-The term "beneficial owner"- (A) means, with respect to an entity, an individual who, directly or indirectly, through any contract, arrangement, understanding, relationship, or otherwise- (i) exercises substantial control over the entity; or (ii) owns or controls not less than 25 percent of the ownership interests of the entity

clauses.title: Reporting Obligation and Timing Under Federal Law
clauses.body: 31 U.S.C. § 5336(b)(1)(A) directs that, in accordance with regulations prescribed by the Secretary of the Treasury, each reporting company shall submit to FinCEN a report containing the beneficial ownership information described in the statute. FinCEN's implementing regulation sets specific deadlines keyed to the current, narrowed definition of reporting company: an entity that becomes a reporting company on or after March 26, 2025 must file an initial report within 30 calendar days of the earlier of actual or public notice of its registration to do business, and an entity that became a reporting company before that date was required to file no later than April 25, 2025. A reporting company must also file an updated report within 30 calendar days of any change to previously reported information, and a corrected report within 30 calendar days of discovering that a filed report was and remains inaccurate. This document does not address the mechanics of FinCEN's electronic filing system, which is described only on FinCEN's own website and could not be independently verified from a primary source in this session.
clauses.gap: FinCEN's BOI E-Filing System interface and step-by-step filing instructions are published only on fincen.gov, which was unreachable from this research environment; the filing deadlines above come from the regulatory text itself (31 C.F.R. § 1010.380(a)), not from fincen.gov guidance.

citations.quote: (A) In general .-In accordance with regulations prescribed by the Secretary of the Treasury, each reporting company shall submit to FinCEN a report that contains the information described in paragraph (2).

clauses.title: HOA Member Discipline and Fines — Introduction and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, the procedural due-process requirements that the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act imposes on a California common interest development association before its board may impose a monetary penalty (fine), impose a monetary charge to reimburse the association for common-area damage, or otherwise discipline a member for an alleged violation of the governing documents, in connection with {{hoaName}}. The relevant statutory provisions are Civil Code §§ 5850, 5855, and 5865, part of Article 1 ("Discipline and Cost Reimbursement") of Chapter 10 ("Dispute Resolution and Enforcement") of the Act, together with the related internal dispute resolution provisions of Civil Code § 5910 in Article 2 of that same chapter. This topic — the pre-fine notice-and-hearing procedure and the board's internal disciplinary process — is distinct from a seller's document-disclosure obligations to a buyer under the Act's disclosure article (addressed in this corpus's HOA/CC&R Disclosure document), from an association's lien and nonjudicial foreclosure remedy for delinquent assessments (addressed in this corpus's HOA Assessment Lien and Foreclosure — Information Sheet), from the secret-ballot procedures that govern certain membership votes (addressed in this corpus's HOA Board Election Procedures — Information Sheet), and from the open-meeting notice and agenda requirements for board meetings generally (addressed in this corpus's Common Interest Development Open Meeting Act — Information Sheet). This sheet is informational only. It does not itself notice, conduct, or decide any disciplinary hearing; it does not impose, waive, reduce, or collect any fine or monetary charge; it does not invoke or conduct any internal dispute resolution procedure; and it does not determine whether any actual notice, hearing, decision, or fine relating to {{hoaName}} has complied — or failed to comply — with the statutory requirements it describes.

clauses.title: Monetary Penalty Schedule and Statutory Cap
clauses.body: Before an association may impose a monetary penalty on a member for a violation of the governing documents, California law requires the board to have adopted and distributed a schedule of the penalties that may be assessed. Civil Code § 5850(a) provides that if an association adopts a policy imposing a monetary penalty for a violation of the governing documents, "the board shall adopt and distribute to each member, in the annual policy statement prepared pursuant to Section 5310, a schedule of the monetary penalties that may be assessed for those violations, which shall be in accordance with authorization for member discipline contained in the governing documents. Monetary penalties shall be reasonable." A new or revised penalty may instead be distributed in an individual supplement under Section 4040. Section 5850(c) caps most penalties: "A monetary penalty for a violation of the governing documents shall not exceed the lesser of the following: (1) The monetary penalty stated in the schedule of monetary penalties or supplement that is in effect at the time of the violation. (2) One hundred dollars ($100) per violation." Section 5850(d) allows a higher penalty only for a violation with adverse health or safety consequences, and only after a specific written finding: "Notwithstanding subdivision (c), the board may impose a penalty stated in the schedule of monetary penalties or supplement that is in effect at the time of the violation that is greater than one hundred dollars ($100) per violation, if the violation may result in an adverse health or safety impact on the common area or another association member’s property. (2) Before imposing a penalty on a violation pursuant to this subdivision, the board shall make a written finding specifying the adverse health or safety impact in a board meeting open to the members." Section 5850(e) provides: "A late charge or interest shall not be charged to a member for a monetary penalty." Section 5850(f) provides: "An association shall provide a copy of the most recently distributed schedule of monetary penalties, along with any applicable supplements to that schedule, to any member upon request." These requirements concern {{hoaName}} in general terms; this clause does not state what {{hoaName}}'s own schedule of monetary penalties provides or whether any specific penalty amount complies with it.

This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's HOA discipline framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific association; other states impose different or no comparable fine-schedule and fine-cap requirements.
