clauses.title: Required Notice and Hearing Before Discipline
clauses.body: Before a board may consider or impose discipline on a member — or impose a monetary charge to reimburse the association for repairing damage to the common area or facilities caused by a member or the member's guest or tenant — California law requires advance written notice of the meeting at which the matter will be considered. Civil Code § 5855(a) provides that "the board shall notify the member in writing, by either personal delivery or individual delivery pursuant to Section 4040, at least 10 days prior to the meeting." Section 5855(b) specifies the minimum content of that notice and the member's rights at the meeting: "The notification shall contain, at a minimum, the date, time, and place of the meeting, the nature of the alleged violation for which a member may be disciplined or the nature of the damage to the common area and facilities for which a monetary charge may be imposed, and a statement that the member has a right to attend and may address the board at the meeting. The board shall meet in executive session if requested by the member." Section 5855(c) requires that the member be given a chance to cure the violation before discipline may be imposed: "A member shall have the opportunity to cure the violation prior to the meeting. The board shall not impose discipline in either of the following circumstances: (1) The member cures the violation prior to the meeting. (2) If curing the violation would take longer than the time between the notice provided pursuant to subdivision (a) and the meeting, the member provides financial commitment to cure the violation." These notice, attendance, executive-session, and cure-opportunity requirements apply to {{hoaName}} in general terms; this clause does not describe the content of any specific notice issued by, or any specific hearing held by, {{hoaName}}.

The statute uses the term "meeting," not "hearing," for the proceeding at which discipline is considered; this clause follows the statute's own terminology. clauses.title: Outcome of the Meeting and Written Decision
clauses.body: California law specifies what must happen after the board's disciplinary meeting concludes, depending on whether the board and the member reach agreement, and requires written notice of any decision to discipline. Civil Code § 5855(d) addresses disagreement: "If the board and the member are not in agreement after the meeting, a member shall have the opportunity to request internal dispute resolution pursuant to Section 5910." Section 5855(e) addresses agreement: "If the board and the member are in agreement after the meeting, the board shall draft a written resolution. The written resolution, signed by the board and the member of the dispute pursuant to procedures not in conflict with the law or governing documents, binds the association and is judicially enforceable." Section 5855(f) requires written notice of an adverse decision within a fixed period: "If the board imposes discipline on a member or imposes a monetary charge on the member for damage to the common area and facilities, the board shall provide the member with a written notification of the decision, by either personal delivery or individual delivery pursuant to Section 4040, within 14 days following the action." Section 5855(g) ties the validity of the discipline to compliance with all of these requirements: "A disciplinary action or the imposition of a monetary charge for damage to the common area shall not be effective against a member unless the board fulfills the requirements of this section." Separately, Civil Code § 5865 clarifies that none of this is meant to expand or narrow the board's underlying disciplinary authority: "Nothing in Section 5850 or 5855 shall be construed to create, expand, or reduce the authority of the board to impose monetary penalties on a member for a violation of the governing documents." These provisions concern {{hoaName}} in general terms; this clause does not state whether the board of {{hoaName}} reached agreement with any specific member, issued any specific written resolution or written notification, or met the 14-day deadline in any specific instance.

clauses.title: Internal Dispute Resolution — A Related but Separate Procedure
clauses.body: The Davis-Stirling Act contains a separate procedure, distinct from the disciplinary notice-and-meeting process itself, called internal dispute resolution (IDR). Civil Code § 5855(d) allows a member who disagrees with the board's disciplinary decision to "request internal dispute resolution pursuant to Section 5910," and Civil Code § 5910, in Article 2 of the same chapter, sets the minimum requirements any such association procedure must meet: "A fair, reasonable, and expeditious dispute resolution procedure shall, at a minimum, satisfy all of the following requirements:". Among those requirements, Section 5910(c) and (d) address who must participate: "If the procedure is invoked by a member, the association shall participate in the procedure," while "If the procedure is invoked by the association, the member may elect not to participate in the procedure. If the member participates but the dispute is resolved other than by agreement of the member, the member shall have a right of appeal to the board." Section 5910(f) addresses the parties' ability to explain their positions: "The procedure shall provide a means by which the member and the association may explain their positions. The member and association may be assisted by an attorney or another person in explaining their positions at their own cost." Section 5910(g) provides: "A member of the association shall not be charged a fee to participate in the process." IDR under § 5910 is a post-decision, member-invocable dispute procedure that operates alongside the discipline-specific notice-and-meeting requirements of § 5855; it is not itself the pre-fine hearing described elsewhere in this document. This provision concerns {{hoaName}} in general terms; this clause does not state what IDR procedure {{hoaName}} has adopted or whether any specific IDR request has been made.

clauses.title: About This Overtime Pay-Rate Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet states California's general daily and weekly overtime and double-time pay-rate rules under Labor Code sections 510 and 511, and explains how the "regular rate of pay" used to compute overtime is determined. It is provided by {{companyName}} to {{employeeName}} for informational purposes. It states the baseline rule that applies to most nonexempt California employees; it does not itself classify any employee as exempt or nonexempt, does not address the separate statutory overtime formulas that apply to agricultural occupations or to personal attendants under the Domestic Worker Bill of Rights, does not describe the exemption for certain computer software employees, and does not walk through the election procedure by which an employer and its employees may adopt an alternative workweek schedule — each of those topics is addressed in a separate document.

clauses.title: Daily Overtime and Double-Time Triggers
clauses.body: Labor Code section 510(a) states that eight hours of labor constitutes a day's work. Under the statute's general rule, work in excess of eight hours in one workday is compensated at no less than one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay, up through 12 hours in that workday. Work in excess of 12 hours in one workday is compensated at no less than twice the employee's regular rate of pay. These daily thresholds apply independently of, and in addition to, the weekly overtime threshold and the seventh-consecutive-day premium the same subdivision also states.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, section 510(a); it is not corroborated by an independent second source. Section 510(a) itself states that its daily-overtime requirements do not apply to an employee working under an alternative workweek schedule adopted under section 511, under a collective-bargaining alternative workweek schedule under section 514, or under section 554; this document addresses that alternative-workweek cross-reference in a separate clause below rather than repeating it here. This document does not address the separate, different daily/weekly overtime thresholds that other statutes set for agricultural occupations, personal attendants, or other categories carved out elsewhere in this corpus.

citations.quote: Any work in excess of eight hours in one workday and any work in excess of 40 hours in any one workweek and the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in any one workweek shall be compensated at the rate of no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay for an employee.

citations.quote: Any work in excess of 12 hours in one day shall be compensated at the rate of no less than twice the regular rate of pay for an employee.

clauses.title: Weekly Overtime Trigger (Over 40 Hours)
clauses.body: Separately from the daily overtime threshold, Labor Code section 510(a) also requires that any work in excess of 40 hours in a single workweek be compensated at no less than one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay. This weekly threshold operates on its own: an employee who works no more than eight hours on any single day, but more than 40 hours across the workweek, is entitled to overtime pay for the hours over 40 even though no individual workday exceeded the daily threshold. Section 510 does not itself define "workweek"; a workweek is a fixed and regularly recurring period of seven consecutive days that an employer establishes.
clauses.gap: The core statutory quote for the weekly threshold is drawn from the same sentence of section 510(a) already quoted in this document's daily-triggers clause; it is not an independent source. This document does not independently trace the definition of "workweek" to a specific statutory or wage-order provision beyond the general concept stated above; that concept is treated here as background context rather than as a citation-verified rule with its own quoted source.

clauses.title: Seventh-Consecutive-Day Premium
clauses.body: Labor Code section 510(a) sets a separate premium for the seventh consecutive day of work in a workweek. The first eight hours worked on the seventh consecutive day of work in a workweek are compensated at no less than one and one-half times the employee's regular rate of pay. Any work beyond eight hours on that seventh consecutive day is compensated at no less than twice the employee's regular rate of pay. This premium is tied to the seventh consecutive day of work within a single workweek, not to the seventh calendar day of any period, and applies in addition to the separate daily and weekly overtime thresholds the same subdivision states.

This document does not address the separate day-of-rest statute (Labor Code section 551 and related provisions) governing an employee's entitlement to one day of rest in seven, which is a distinct legal question from the overtime premium described in this clause and is addressed, where covered, in a separate document.

clauses.title: No Stacking of Overtime Rates, and the Alternative Workweek Cross-Reference
clauses.body: Labor Code section 510(a) states that nothing in the section requires an employer to combine more than one rate of overtime compensation to calculate the amount owed for a single hour of overtime work — that is, the same hour of work is not stacked with more than one premium multiplier. Section 510(a) also states that its daily/weekly overtime requirements do not apply to an employee working under an alternative workweek schedule adopted under Labor Code section 511, under a collective-bargaining alternative workweek schedule adopted under section 514, or under a schedule to which the general overtime chapter is inapplicable under section 554. Section 511, in turn, allows the employees of an employer to adopt a regularly scheduled alternative workweek authorizing up to 10 hours of work per day within a 40-hour workweek without a daily overtime premium for those scheduled hours, but only through a specific statutory procedure: a proposal is deemed adopted only if it is approved by a secret-ballot election in which at least two-thirds of the affected employees in a readily identifiable work unit vote in favor.
clauses.gap: This document describes the existence of the section 511 alternative-workweek-schedule mechanism and its two-thirds secret-ballot election requirement only as background for understanding section 510(a)'s cross-reference; it does not independently walk through the full election procedure (the pre-election disclosure requirement, the reporting requirement, repeal mechanics, or anti-coercion protections), which is addressed in a separate document in this corpus. The quoted no-stacking sentence and the quoted alternative-workweek cross-reference both come from section 510(a); the two section 511(a) quotes both come from section 511(a); within each pair the sources are not independent of one another.

clauses.title: What Counts as the "Regular Rate of Pay"
clauses.body: Overtime and double-time premiums under Labor Code section 510 are calculated as multiples of an employee's "regular rate of pay," a term the statute uses but does not itself define. The state agency responsible for enforcing California's wage and hour laws describes the regular rate of pay as the compensation an employee normally earns for the work performed, which can include hourly earnings, salary, piecework earnings, commissions, and certain bonuses — not only a stated hourly wage. When a nondiscretionary bonus is paid as compensation for hours worked, production, proficiency, or as an incentive to remain employed, it is included in determining the regular rate of pay used to compute overtime. When an employee is paid two or more different hourly rates by the same employer during a single workweek, the regular rate of pay for that workweek is a weighted average, calculated by dividing total earnings for the workweek (including earnings during overtime hours) by the total hours worked during the workweek (including the overtime hours).
clauses.gap: This clause relies on published guidance from the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (DLSE), a state enforcement agency, rather than on statutory text or a wage order provision defining "regular rate of pay" directly — this document did not locate a Labor Code section or IWC Wage Order section that itself defines the term for general nonexempt employees; the concept has instead developed through agency guidance and California case law (see the following clause on flat-sum bonuses). DLSE guidance documents such as this one are not themselves regulations adopted through the formal rulemaking procedure of the Administrative Procedure Act, and a California appellate case has held that at least one prior DLSE enforcement policy on a related overtime-calculation question was void for that reason; this document treats the quoted DLSE guidance as the agency's current published interpretation, not as binding law with the force of a statute or a properly promulgated regulation. This clause's two citations are drawn from different questions within the same DLSE FAQ page rather than from two independent publications.

clauses.title: Flat-Sum Bonuses: The Divisor Used to Compute the Regular Rate
clauses.body: The California Supreme Court has addressed how to convert a flat sum bonus earned during a single pay period into a per-hour value for purposes of calculating overtime pay. In Alvarado v. Dart Container Corp. of California (2018) 4 Cal.5th 542, the court considered three candidate divisors for that per-hour value: the number of hours the employee actually worked during the pay period (including overtime hours); the number of nonovertime hours the employee worked during the pay period; or the number of nonovertime hours that exist in the pay period regardless of hours actually worked. The court held that the correct divisor is the number of nonovertime hours the employee actually worked during the pay period — not the larger total that would include overtime hours. Dividing by a smaller, nonovertime-hours-only denominator produces a higher per-hour value for the bonus, and therefore a higher overtime premium, than dividing by total hours worked would produce.
clauses.gap: This clause is based on one appellate decision (a published California Supreme Court opinion), corroborated only by state agency guidance describing a similar divisor rule for flat-sum bonuses (quoted in the preceding clause's gap discussion, not repeated here as a separate citation), not by a second independent judicial decision. The Alvarado opinion itself notes that the agency guidance it discusses was, at the time, a DLSE enforcement-policy-manual position that had not been adopted through formal rulemaking, and the court reached its holding through its own interpretation of the governing statutes and wage order rather than by deferring to that manual. This document did not research whether later legislation or case law has modified Alvarado's specific holding. Alvarado addressed a flat sum bonus paid during a single pay period to an hourly employee; it does not by itself resolve every possible bonus, commission, or piece-rate regular-rate scenario, and this document does not attempt to catalog those other scenarios beyond the general description in the preceding clause.

citations.case: Alvarado v. Dart Container Corp. of California
citations.quote: we decide how an employee’s overtime pay rate should be calculated when the employee has earned a flat sum bonus during a single pay period. Specifically, we consider whether the divisor for purposes of calculating the per-hour value of the bonus should be (1) the number of hours the employee actually worked during the pay period, including overtime hours; (2) the number of nonovertime hours the employee worked during the pay period; or (3) the number of nonovertime hours that exist in the pay period, regardless of the number of hours the employee actually worked. We conclude that the divisor should be the second of these options.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Anti-SLAPP Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's anti-SLAPP statute, Code of Civil Procedure section 425.16, and summarizes how published California case law has addressed its application to confidentiality, trade secret, and other intellectual-property-related claims. It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning a matter involving {{companyName}} and {{adversePartyName}}. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing what the statute says and how courts have construed it; it does not determine whether any specific claim described in that matter does or does not arise from activity protected under the statute, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination.

clauses.title: The Anti-SLAPP Statute: Purpose and the Special Motion to Strike
clauses.body: Code of Civil Procedure section 425.16 is California's anti-SLAPP statute (SLAPP stands for Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation). Subdivision (a) states the Legislature's finding that there has been a disturbing increase in lawsuits brought primarily to chill the valid exercise of the constitutional rights of freedom of speech and petition, and directs that the section be construed broadly to encourage continued participation in matters of public significance. The statute creates a "special motion to strike" that a defendant may bring against a cause of action arising from the defendant's protected petitioning or free-speech activity. The motion must generally be filed within 60 days of service of the complaint, though the court has discretion to permit a later filing on terms it deems proper, and the clerk must schedule a hearing not more than 30 days after the motion is served unless docket conditions require a later date. Filing the motion automatically stays all discovery in the action until the court rules on the motion, subject to the court's authority to order specified discovery to proceed on a noticed motion and for good cause shown. An order granting or denying a special motion to strike is itself immediately appealable.

clauses.title: The Two-Step Analysis Courts Apply to a Special Motion to Strike
clauses.body: Subdivision (b)(1) of section 425.16 states the statute's core operative rule: a cause of action arising from a person's act in furtherance of that person's right of petition or free speech in connection with a public issue is subject to a special motion to strike, unless the court determines the plaintiff has established a probability of prevailing on the claim. Published California case law construing this subdivision describes it as a two-step (or two-prong) analysis. At the first step, the defendant bringing the motion has the burden of showing that the challenged cause of action arises from protected activity, as defined in subdivision (e). If the defendant makes that showing, the analysis moves to the second step, at which the burden shifts to the plaintiff to demonstrate a probability of prevailing on the claim; subdivision (b)(2) directs the court to consider the pleadings and supporting and opposing affidavits stating the facts on which liability or a defense is based in making that determination. If the plaintiff does not carry that burden, the claim is stricken. Subdivision (b)(3) further provides that a finding the plaintiff has established a probability of prevailing is not itself admissible at a later stage of the case or in a subsequent action, and does not affect any burden or degree of proof otherwise applicable later in the case.

The description of the mechanism as a "two-step" or "two-prong" analysis is standard terminology used throughout California case law construing this subdivision (including in the case discussed in the case-law clause below, which describes a "first prong" and burden-shifting to the plaintiff); it is not itself statutory text and is not separately cited to a specific opinion in this clause.

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of Protected Petitioning and Free Speech Activity
clauses.body: Subdivision (e) of section 425.16 defines the phrase "act in furtherance of a person's right of petition or free speech under the United States or California Constitution in connection with a public issue" to include four categories of conduct: (1) any written or oral statement or writing made before a legislative, executive, or judicial proceeding, or any other official proceeding authorized by law; (2) any written or oral statement or writing made in connection with an issue under consideration or review by a legislative, executive, or judicial body, or any other official proceeding authorized by law; (3) any written or oral statement or writing made in a place open to the public or a public forum in connection with an issue of public interest; and (4) any other conduct in furtherance of the exercise of the constitutional right of petition or the constitutional right of free speech in connection with a public issue or an issue of public interest. Confidentiality- and trade-secret-related disputes that involve anti-SLAPP motions most often implicate the third and fourth categories, since a defendant in that context typically argues that the conduct the plaintiff sues over (a public statement, a business communication, or similar conduct) touched on a public issue or an issue of public interest, rather than arguing the conduct occurred before, or in connection with, an official proceeding.

clauses.title: Fee-Shifting Consequences of a Special Motion to Strike
clauses.body: Section 425.16 attaches significant fee-shifting consequences to the special motion to strike. Under subdivision (c)(1), except as provided in subdivision (c)(2), a defendant who prevails on a special motion to strike is entitled to recover that defendant's attorney's fees and costs. The same subdivision also runs in the opposite direction: if the court finds that a special motion to strike is frivolous or is solely intended to cause unnecessary delay, the court must award costs and reasonable attorney's fees to a plaintiff who prevails on the motion, pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 128.5. Subdivision (c)(2) carves out certain government-related causes of action (those brought under Government Code sections 11130, 11130.3, 54960, or 54960.1, or under the California Public Records Act provisions commencing with Government Code section 7923.100) from the prevailing defendant's automatic fee entitlement, while preserving other, more specific fee-recovery provisions that may apply to those same causes of action.

clauses.title: Case Law: Anti-SLAPP Motions Against Trade Secret and Confidentiality-Related Claims
clauses.body: Whether a trade secret misappropriation, breach-of-confidentiality, or related claim qualifies for anti-SLAPP treatment is a fact-intensive question that published California case law resolves by looking to the specific conduct the claim is based on, not the general subject matter of the dispute. In World Financial Group, Inc. v. HBW Insurance & Financial Services, Inc., a company sued a competitor and several of its own former sales associates for, among other claims, misappropriation of trade secrets and breach of contract, based on allegations that the defendants used the company's confidential associate and customer lists and other trade secrets to solicit its associates and customers to switch to the competing company. The defendants brought a special motion to strike, arguing that their solicitation activity was protected free speech in connection with a public issue because it involved "the pursuit of lawful employment" and "workforce mobility and free competition." The Court of Appeal rejected that argument and affirmed denial of the motion, holding that the complaint did not arise from protected activity: although employee mobility and competition can be issues of public interest "considered in the abstract," the defendants' actual communications were commercial solicitations of a competitor's employees and customers made for the sole purpose of furthering a business interest, not statements about, or intended to inform the public on, those broader topics. The court explained that the relevant test looks to "the principal thrust or gravamen" of the cause of action, so that allegations of protected activity that are merely incidental to a claim based essentially on nonprotected activity do not bring the claim within the statute, and warned that treating ordinary noncompetition or trade-secret claims as categorically subject to anti-SLAPP motions merely because they touch on employee mobility would improperly extend the statute to swallow the underlying substantive law. This same fact-specific, gravamen-focused approach is the framework California courts have applied more generally to determine whether a trade-secret or confidentiality-related claim is or is not based on protected petitioning or speech activity; the outcome in any given case turns on the specific conduct alleged, not on the mere presence of a business or competitive relationship between the parties.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the basic legal structure of a charitable remainder trust (CRT) under federal tax law, including the two statutory forms — the charitable remainder annuity trust (CRAT) and the charitable remainder unitrust (CRUT) — and the qualification requirements set out in 26 U.S.C. § 664. A charitable remainder trust of this type would typically be established by {{settlorName}}, with {{trusteeName}} acting as trustee, {{beneficiaryName}} named as the individual (non-charitable) income beneficiary, and {{charityBeneficiaryName}} named as the qualified charitable remainder beneficiary. This sheet states general federal tax rules; it is not a trust instrument and does not itself create, qualify, or fund any trust.

clauses.title: Basic Structure: Split-Interest Trust
clauses.body: A charitable remainder trust is a split-interest trust: it pays an income interest to one or more named beneficiaries for a term (a fixed number of years not exceeding 20, or the life or lives of one or more individuals), after which the remaining trust property (the "remainder") passes to or is retained for one or more organizations described in Internal Revenue Code § 170(c) — i.e., organizations eligible to receive tax-deductible charitable contributions. At least one of the income beneficiaries must not itself be a § 170(c) organization, and if any income beneficiary is an individual, that individual must be living at the time the trust is created. Under 26 U.S.C. § 664(a), a trust qualifying under this section is treated, by regulation, as either a charitable remainder annuity trust or a charitable remainder unitrust.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the general split-interest structure common to both statutory CRT forms under 26 U.S.C. § 664(d)(1) and (d)(2). It does not address non-statutory variations (e.g., net-income unitrusts with make-up provisions, flip unitrusts, or charitable remainder trusts holding qualified employer securities transferred to an ESOP), state-law trust administration requirements, or state charitable-trust registration and reporting duties, which are covered separately in this corpus's Registry of Charitable Trusts information sheet.

citations.quote: the provisions of this section shall, in accordance with regulations prescribed by the Secretary, apply in the case of a charitable remainder annuity trust and a charitable remainder unitrust.

citations.quote: for a term of years (not in excess of 20 years) or for the life or lives of such individual or individuals

clauses.title: Charitable Remainder Annuity Trust (CRAT)
clauses.body: A charitable remainder annuity trust (CRAT) is defined in 26 U.S.C. § 664(d)(1) as a trust that pays a "sum certain" — a fixed dollar amount set when the trust is created — not less often than annually, to the named income beneficiaries. That fixed payment must equal at least 5 percent and not more than 50 percent of the initial net fair market value of the property placed in the trust, and it does not change even if the trust's investment performance later causes its value to rise or fall. No additional contributions may be made to a CRAT after it is initially funded.
clauses.gap: This clause paraphrases the CRAT payout-percentage rule from § 664(d)(1)(A). It does not address how the sum certain is calculated when the trust's term begins on a date other than the first day of the taxable year, or IRS-prescribed adjustments for a short first year; those computational details are set out in Treasury regulations under § 664, which were not independently fetched and verified for this clause.

citations.case: Definition of charitable remainder annuity trust
citations.quote: a charitable remainder annuity trust is a trust- (A) from which a sum certain (which is not less than 5 percent nor more than 50 percent of the initial net fair market value of all property placed in trust) is to be paid, not less often than annually, to one or more persons

clauses.title: Charitable Remainder Unitrust (CRUT)
clauses.body: A charitable remainder unitrust (CRUT) is defined in 26 U.S.C. § 664(d)(2) as a trust that pays a fixed percentage — again, not less than 5 percent and not more than 50 percent — of the net fair market value of the trust's assets, revalued annually, not less often than annually, to the named income beneficiaries. Because the trust's assets are revalued each year, the dollar amount of a unitrust payment rises and falls with the trust's investment performance, unlike a CRAT's fixed sum certain. Unlike a CRAT, a CRUT may generally accept additional contributions after it is first funded. Federal law also permits a limited exception, described in § 664(d)(3), under which a unitrust may pay the lesser of trust income or the stated unitrust percentage, with a right to make up prior shortfalls in later years to the extent trust income allows (commonly called a net-income or net-income-with-makeup unitrust).
clauses.gap: This clause covers only the statutory fixed-percentage unitrust payout described in § 664(d)(2)(A) and the existence of the net-income/make-up exception in § 664(d)(3); it does not walk through the make-up computation itself, the separate "flip" unitrust rules found in Treasury regulations, or the severance-of-additional-contributions mechanics of § 664(d)(4), none of which were independently verified against primary source text for this clause.

citations.case: Definition of charitable remainder unitrust
citations.quote: a charitable remainder unitrust is a trust- (A) from which a fixed percentage (which is not less than 5 percent nor more than 50 percent) of the net fair market value of its assets, valued annually, is to be paid, not less often than annually, to one or more persons

clauses.title: The 5%/50% Payout Limits and the 10% Minimum Remainder Value
clauses.body: Both statutory CRT forms are subject to two numeric qualification tests found directly in 26 U.S.C. § 664(d): (1) the annual payout — the CRAT's sum certain or the CRUT's fixed percentage — must be at least 5 percent and not more than 50 percent of the relevant trust value; and (2) the present value of the charitable remainder interest, computed under 26 U.S.C. § 7520, must be at least 10 percent of the initial net fair market value of the property placed in the trust (for a CRAT) or, for a CRUT, at least 10 percent of the value of each contributed property as of its contribution date. A trust that fails either test at the time it is created (or, for a CRUT, at the time of a later contribution) does not qualify as a charitable remainder annuity trust or charitable remainder unitrust under § 664.
clauses.gap: Both numeric tests were located and verified directly within § 664(d) itself (subparagraphs (d)(1)(A)/(D) for the CRAT and (d)(2)(A)/(D) for the CRUT) rather than in a separate section — the statute states both the payout-percentage range and the 10%-remainder-value test in the same subsection. This clause does not walk through the § 7520 present-value computation itself (the applicable federal discount rate and IRS actuarial tables), which is a separate mechanical topic governed by § 7520 and its regulations and was not independently fetched for this clause.

citations.case: CRAT minimum remainder value requirement
citations.quote: the value (determined under section 7520) of such remainder interest is at least 10 percent of the initial net fair market value of all property placed in the trust.

citations.case: CRUT minimum remainder value requirement
citations.quote: the value (determined under section 7520) of such remainder interest in such property is at least 10 percent of the net fair market value of such property as of the date such property is contributed to the trust.

clauses.title: Trust-Level Tax Exemption and the Charitable Income Tax Deduction
clauses.body: A qualifying charitable remainder annuity trust or unitrust is, for any taxable year, not subject to the federal income tax otherwise imposed on trusts under 26 U.S.C. § 664(c)(1), although the trust may owe an excise tax equal to any unrelated business taxable income it earns. Amounts later distributed to the non-charitable income beneficiary retain the trust's underlying tax character under a four-tier ordering rule in § 664(b) (ordinary income first, then capital gain, then other income, then a tax-free return of corpus). Separately, under 26 U.S.C. § 170(f)(2)(A), a donor who transfers property into a trust may not claim a federal charitable income tax deduction for the value of a remainder interest in that trust unless the trust is a charitable remainder annuity trust or charitable remainder unitrust described in § 664 (or a pooled income fund described in § 642(c)(5)). Because the trust itself generally pays no income tax on its earnings and the CRAT/CRUT structure is one of the few trust forms for which a remainder-interest charitable deduction is available at all, it is the combination of these two rules — trust-level tax exemption plus deductibility of the present value of the remainder interest — that gives the CRAT/CRUT structure its tax significance.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general income-tax-exemption and deduction-eligibility rules found directly in §§ 664(c)(1), 664(b), and 170(f)(2)(A). It does not address the separate rules governing the deduction's dollar-amount limits based on adjusted gross income, the reduction of a donor's deduction for contributions of ordinary-income or short-term-capital-gain property, gift or estate tax charitable deductions for remainder interests, or the excise tax consequences for unrelated business taxable income in § 664(c)(2) beyond the general statement above — those are distinct, more detailed topics not independently verified for this clause.

citations.case: Charitable remainder trusts — income tax exemption
citations.quote: A charitable remainder annuity trust and a charitable remainder unitrust shall, for any taxable year, not be subject to any tax imposed by this subtitle.

citations.case: Charitable contribution deduction for a remainder interest transferred in trust
citations.quote: no deduction shall be allowed under this section for the value of a contribution of a remainder interest unless the trust is a charitable remainder annuity trust or a charitable remainder unitrust (described in section 664 ), or a pooled income fund (described in section 642(c)(5)).

clauses.title: How This Differs From Charitable Trust Registration and Reporting
clauses.body: This information sheet addresses the federal tax-law structure that makes a trust a qualifying charitable remainder annuity trust or unitrust in the first place — the income/remainder split, the 5%/50% payout limits, and the 10% minimum remainder-value test under 26 U.S.C. § 664. It is distinct from this corpus's separate Registry of Charitable Trusts information sheet, which addresses an unrelated, later-stage California state-law duty: the ongoing obligation of charitable trustees and organizations to register and file annual reports with the California Attorney General under the Supervision of Trustees and Fundraisers for Charitable Purposes Act. A trust can be validly formed and can fully satisfy the federal § 664 qualification rules described here while its trustee separately remains subject to (or exempt from) the state registration and reporting duties described in that other sheet; the two sets of rules serve different purposes and arise under different bodies of law.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet summarizes California's Medi-Cal Estate Recovery Program under Welfare and Institutions Code Section 14009.5, as it applies to the estate of {{decedentName}} (date of death: {{dateOfDeath}}; estimated estate value: {{estimatedEstateValue}}). It states what the law provides in general; it does not calculate whether the California Department of Health Care Services (DHCS) has asserted, or will assert, a claim against this specific estate, and it is not a substitute for DHCS's own accounting of amounts it may claim.

clauses.title: What Can Trigger a Recovery Claim
clauses.body: Under Welfare and Institutions Code Section 14009.5, DHCS may claim against the estate of a deceased Medi-Cal member, or against a recipient of that decedent's property by distribution, for an amount equal to the Medi-Cal payments made for that person's health care services or the value of the property received, whichever is less. That claim is authorized only in two circumstances: against the real property of a Medi-Cal member of any age who was an inpatient in a nursing facility and met specified federal Medicaid eligibility criteria, or where the decedent was 55 years of age or older when the individual received the health care services being recovered.
clauses.gap: The statute limits recovery to these two triggers, but whether a specific person's Medi-Cal benefits meet the federal 'health care services' definition subject to recovery, or whether a person met the nursing-facility criteria the statute cross-references in federal law, are determinations this document does not make for a particular estate.

clauses.title: Recovery Is Limited to the Probate Estate
clauses.body: For an individual who dies on or after January 1, 2017, Section 14009.5 defines 'estate' for Medi-Cal recovery purposes as only the real and personal property and other assets in the decedent's probate estate that federal law requires be subject to a claim for recovery. Before that date, California's Medi-Cal estate recovery statute defined 'estate' more broadly, and DHCS could reach some property that passed outside of probate, such as property held in joint tenancy, assets held in a revocable living trust, or assets passing by a beneficiary designation. This narrowing took effect through a 2016 amendment (SB 833, Stats. 2016, ch. 30), whose own statement of legislative intent describes limiting Medi-Cal estate recovery to only what federal law requires and limiting the definition of 'estate' accordingly.
clauses.gap: This document's description of the pre-2017 rule (that it reached certain non-probate transfers such as joint tenancy property, living trust assets, and beneficiary designations) reflects the current statute's own statement of what the 2016 amendment was intended to change, and is consistent with how this amendment is widely described in secondary legal sources; this session did not independently fetch and diff the pre-amendment text of Section 14009.5 against the current text, so the exact wording and full scope of the prior, broader 'estate' definition is not verified word-for-word against primary-source text from that era.

citations.quote: (2) Limit the definition of “estate” to include only the real and personal property and other assets required to be collected under federal law.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: effective date of the narrower definition
citations.quote: The amendments made to this section by the act that added this subdivision shall apply only to individuals who die on or after January 1, 2017.

clauses.title: Exemption for a Surviving Spouse or Minor/Disabled Child
clauses.body: Under the age-55-or-older recovery trigger, Section 14009.5 bars DHCS from claiming against the estate when the decedent is survived by a spouse or registered domestic partner, by a child who is under 21 years of age, or by a child who is blind or disabled within the meaning of the federal Supplemental Security Income disability standard. The statute separately states that prohibiting recovery from the estate of a deceased Medi-Cal member survived by a spouse or registered domestic partner was itself one of the stated purposes of the amendment that added this framework.
clauses.gap: This bar applies by its own terms to the age-55-or-older trigger in subdivision (b)(2); the statute's separate nursing-facility-inpatient trigger in subdivision (b)(1) is not made subject to this same list of surviving-spouse-or-child exceptions by its own text. This document does not resolve how DHCS treats an estate where both triggers could otherwise apply.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(b)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: surviving spouse, domestic partner, and child exceptions to the age-55 trigger
citations.quote: (B) The department shall not claim under this paragraph when there is any of the following: (i) A surviving spouse or surviving registered domestic partner. (ii) A surviving child who is under 21 years of age. (iii) A surviving child who is blind or disabled, within the meaning of Section 1614 of the federal Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. Sec. 1382c).

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: stated legislative intent to prohibit recovery when survived by a spouse or domestic partner
citations.quote: (4) Prohibit recovery from the estate of a deceased Medi-Cal member who is survived by a spouse or registered domestic partner.

clauses.title: Hardship Waiver and the Modest-Value Homestead
clauses.body: Apart from the surviving-spouse-or-child limitation, Section 14009.5 separately requires DHCS to waive its claim, in whole or in part, if enforcing it would cause substantial hardship to other dependents, heirs, or survivors of the person whose estate is subject to the claim. In deciding whether that substantial hardship exists, DHCS must, subject to federal approval, waive its claim when the estate being recovered from is a 'homestead of modest value' — a home whose fair market value is 50 percent or less of the average price of homes in the county where it is located, valued as of the decedent's date of death. The statute directs DHCS to notify individuals of this waiver provision and of the opportunity for a hearing to establish that a waiver should be granted.
clauses.gap: The statute states the substantial-hardship standard and the homestead-of-modest-value definition, and directs DHCS to give notice of the waiver opportunity, but it does not itself set out the application procedure, required forms, or evidentiary showing DHCS uses to decide a hardship-waiver request — those mechanics are left to DHCS regulations and administrative guidance. This session attempted to reach dhcs.ca.gov directly for that procedural detail; the requests returned only an automated bot-detection challenge page (an Incapsula interstitial) rather than substantive content, so no DHCS regulatory or procedural detail beyond this statute's own text could be independently verified this session.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: mandatory substantial-hardship waiver
citations.quote: (1) The department shall waive its claim, in whole or in part, if it determines that enforcement of the claim would result in substantial hardship to other dependents, heirs, or survivors of the individual against whose estate the claim exists.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: mandatory waiver for a homestead of modest value
citations.quote: (2) In determining the existence of substantial hardship, in addition to other factors considered by the department consistent with federal law and guidance, the department shall, subject to federal approval, waive its claim when the estate subject to recovery is a homestead of modest value.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(f)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definition of 'homestead of modest value'
citations.quote: “Homestead of modest value” means a home whose fair market value is 50 percent or less of the average price of homes in the county where the homestead is located, as of the date of the decedent’s death.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: notice of the waiver provision and hearing opportunity
citations.quote: (3) The department shall notify individuals of the waiver provision and the opportunity for a hearing to establish that a waiver should be granted.

clauses.title: Right to Request an Accounting While the Member Is Living
clauses.body: Section 14009.5 gives a current or former Medi-Cal member, or that member's authorized representative, the right to request from DHCS a statement of the Medi-Cal expenses that may be recoverable under this section through the date of the request. DHCS may respond within 90 days of a complete request and may charge a fee of up to five dollars, once per calendar year, for a member who was 55 or older when receiving the services, or who is a permanently institutionalized inpatient in a nursing facility, intermediate care facility for the intellectually disabled, or other medical institution.
clauses.gap: This request right, as the statute states it, belongs to the living member or their authorized representative. The statute does not describe a parallel mechanism by which an estate's personal representative can request this same accounting after the member has died, and this document does not assume one exists.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(e)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: member's right to request an accounting of recoverable expenses
citations.quote: The department shall provide a current or former member, or his or her authorized representative designated under Section 14014.5, upon request, a copy of the amount of Medi-Cal expenses that may be recoverable under this section through the date of the request.

citations.case: Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(e)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: 90-day response deadline
citations.quote: (4) Upon receiving a request for the information described in paragraph (1) and all necessary supporting documentation, the department shall provide the information requested within 90 days after receipt of the request.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Document
clauses.body: This document explains how a California general partnership like {{partnershipName}} actually dissolves and winds up under Article 8 of the California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, "Winding Up Partnership Business" (Corp. Code §§ 16801–16807), and how that process differs from a single partner's dissociation. It is written as a statement of California law, not as advice about whether or how {{partner1Name}} and {{partner2Name}} should end their own partnership. Where the parties have identified an actual or anticipated dissolution, this document records it: {{partnershipName}} is treated as dissolved effective {{dissolutionDate}}, based on {{dissolutionReason}}.

clauses.title: Dissociation of a Partner Is Not the Same Event as Dissolution of the Partnership
clauses.body: California's partnership statute treats a partner's "dissociation" — that partner's individual exit from partner status — as a legally distinct event from the partnership's "dissolution." Dissociation of one partner does not by itself end the partnership's existence or trigger winding up; the statute instead identifies a specific list of events that actually dissolve a partnership (addressed in a companion clause of this document), and only actual dissolution starts the winding-up process. Once a partnership is in fact dissolved, California law states that the partnership continues in existence after that point only for the limited purpose of winding up its business, and is terminated once that winding up is complete. A California Court of Appeal decision illustrates why this distinction matters in a two-partner partnership specifically: because a partnership by definition requires at least two persons, one partner's withdrawal from a two-person partnership does not merely dissociate that partner while the partnership continues — it dissolves the partnership outright, because no single remaining person can carry on the business "as partners."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and one published California appellate decision, used as real evidence of how California's modern (RUPA-based) partnership law treats the dissociation/dissolution distinction — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular general partnership, or about how any other state's partnership statute draws this line. This document does not say whether any specific partner's departure would itself dissolve a given partnership; that depends on which statutory event actually occurred and on the partnership's own agreement, addressed in the companion clauses below and in this corpus's separate General Partnership Agreement document. The cited case addressed a two-partner partnership; its reasoning about a single remaining partner does not by its own terms resolve how the dissociation/dissolution line applies in a partnership with three or more partners.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16802(a)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, a partnership continues after dissolution only to wind up
citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivision (b), a partnership continues after dissolution only for the purpose of winding up its business. The partnership is terminated when the winding up of its business is completed.

citations.case: Corrales v. Corrales
citations.quote: When Richard withdrew from RCE, the partnership dissolved by operation of law; by definition, a partnership must consist of at least two persons.

clauses.title: The Full Statutory List of Events That Actually Dissolve a Partnership
clauses.body: California's partnership statute dissolves a partnership, and requires its business to be wound up, only on the occurrence of specific listed events. Beyond the at-will and term-partnership dissociation-related triggers, the statute's list also includes: an event the partnership agreement itself designates as causing winding up; an event making it unlawful to continue substantially all of the partnership's business (subject to a 90-day cure that applies retroactively); and three distinct judicial-dissolution grounds available on a partner's own application — that the partnership's economic purpose is likely to be unreasonably frustrated, that another partner's conduct makes it not reasonably practicable to carry on the business with that partner, or that it is otherwise not reasonably practicable to carry on the business in conformity with the partnership agreement. A further, narrower judicial-dissolution ground is available specifically to a transferee of a partner's transferable interest (such as a judgment creditor holding a charging order), letting that transferee ask a court to wind up a term or particular-undertaking partnership as equitable once its term or undertaking has expired.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the complete statutory dissolution-event list — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular general partnership, or a prediction that any court would actually grant judicial dissolution on these or similar facts; the judicial grounds quoted below require an actual court application and a judicial determination, not merely a partner's own belief that one applies. This document does not requote the statute's at-will-partnership and definite-term/particular-undertaking dissolution triggers in full here, since this corpus's separate General Partnership Agreement document already addresses those two triggers (Corp. Code § 16801(1)–(2)) in detail; this clause instead completes the picture with the remaining statutory grounds — agreed events, illegality, and judicial dissolution — that a single passing reference to § 16801 does not itemize. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 16801).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16801
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissolution occurs only on a listed event
citations.quote: A partnership is dissolved, and its business shall be wound up, only upon the occurrence of any of the following events:

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16801(3)-(4)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, dissolution by agreed event or illegality
citations.quote: (3) An event agreed to in the partnership agreement resulting in the winding up of the partnership business. (4) An event that makes it unlawful for all or substantially all of the business of the partnership to be continued, but a cure of illegality within 90 days after notice to the partnership of the event is effective retroactively to the date of the event for purposes of this section.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16801(5)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, judicial dissolution grounds on a partner's application
citations.quote: (5) On application by a partner, a judicial determination that any of the following apply: (A) The economic purpose of the partnership is likely to be unreasonably frustrated. (B) Another partner has engaged in conduct relating to the partnership business that makes it not reasonably practicable to carry on the business in partnership with that partner. (C) It is not otherwise reasonably practicable to carry on the partnership business in conformity with the partnership agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16801(6)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, judicial dissolution on a transferee's application
citations.quote: (6) On application by a transferee of a partner’s transferable interest, a judicial determination that it is equitable to wind up the partnership business after the expiration of the term or completion of the undertaking, if the partnership was for a definite term or particular undertaking at the time of the transfer or entry of the charging order that gave rise to the transfer.

clauses.title: Winding Up Can Be Waived — Dissolution Is Not Always the End
clauses.body: Even after a partnership has actually dissolved, California law lets the partners undo that outcome before winding up is complete. At any time after dissolution and before the winding up of the business is completed, all of the partners — including a dissociating partner other than one who wrongfully dissociated — may waive the right to have the business wound up and the partnership terminated. If they do, the partnership resumes carrying on its business as if the dissolution had never happened, and liability incurred between the dissolution and the waiver is determined the same way. That waiver, however, cannot retroactively harm a third party's rights that already accrued in reliance on the dissolution before that third party knew or was notified of the waiver.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's dissolution/winding-up framework is not automatically a one-way street — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular general partnership, or a statement that any particular partnership's own agreement permits or forecloses this waiver. The statute requires waiver by all of the partners (with the stated exception for a wrongfully dissociating partner); this document does not say whether the partners named in this document have in fact agreed to any such waiver. All quoted text below is a single subdivision of one statutory section (§ 16802(b)).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16802(b)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, waiver of winding up after dissolution
citations.quote: (b) At any time after the dissolution of a partnership and before the winding up of its business is completed, all of the partners, including any dissociating partner other than a wrongfully dissociating partner, may waive the right to have the partnership’s business wound up and the partnership terminated. In that event both of the following apply: (1) The partnership resumes carrying on its business as if dissolution had never occurred, and any liability incurred by the partnership or a partner after the dissolution and before the waiver is determined as if dissolution had never occurred. (2) The rights of a third party accruing under paragraph (1) of Section 16804 or arising out of conduct in reliance on the dissolution before the third party knew or received a notification of the waiver may not be adversely affected.

clauses.title: Who May Wind Up the Partnership, and What That Authority Covers
clauses.body: By default, California law lets any partner who has not dissociated participate in winding up the partnership's business after dissolution, though a court may order judicial supervision of the winding up on application of any partner, a partner's legal representative, or a transferee, for good cause shown. If the partnership has only one surviving partner left, the legal representative of that last surviving partner may wind up the business. A person conducting the winding up has broad statutory authority to act for the partnership in doing so: preserving the business or property as a going concern for a reasonable time, prosecuting and defending civil, criminal, or administrative actions, settling and closing the business, transferring partnership property, discharging partnership liabilities, distributing partnership assets under the statute's own priority rule, settling disputes by mediation or arbitration, and performing other acts necessary to the winding up.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who may conduct a California general partnership's winding up and what that role covers by default — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular general partnership, or about who is actually conducting any specific partnership's winding up in fact. A partnership's own written agreement can supply different or additional terms governing who winds up its affairs; this document does not say whether a given partnership's own agreement does that. This document also does not address the separate statement-of-dissolution recording mechanism (Corp. Code § 16805), by which a partner may file a public statement giving third parties constructive notice of the dissolution and limiting the dissociated or dissolved partnership's apparent authority — that recording option is outside the scope of this clause. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 16803).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16803(a)-(b)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, default authority to wind up and judicial supervision
citations.quote: (a) After dissolution, a partner who has not dissociated may participate in winding up the partnership’s business, but on application of any partner, partner’s legal representative, or transferee, the court, for good cause shown, may order judicial supervision of the winding up. (b) The legal representative of the last surviving partner may wind up a partnership’s business.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16803(c)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, scope of a winding-up person's authority
citations.quote: (c) A person winding up a partnership’s business may preserve the partnership business or property as a going concern for a reasonable time, prosecute and defend actions and proceedings, whether civil, criminal, or administrative, settle and close the partnership’s business, dispose of and transfer the partnership’s property, discharge the partnership’s liabilities, distribute the assets of the partnership pursuant to Section 16807, settle disputes by mediation or arbitration, and perform other necessary acts.

clauses.title: The Partnership's and Partners' Exposure for Acts Taken After Dissolution
clauses.body: Dissolution does not immediately strip a partner's power to bind the partnership. California law binds the partnership to a partner's post-dissolution act if that act is either appropriate for winding up the partnership's business, or is an act that would have bound the partnership before dissolution and the other party to the transaction did not have notice of the dissolution. Because that second category can bind the partnership to obligations the other partners never wanted, the statute separately makes an acting partner personally answerable within the partnership for it: after dissolution, a partner is generally liable to the other partners for that partner's share of any such partnership liability, and a partner who, knowing of the dissolution, incurs a liability of that kind by an act that was not appropriate for winding up is liable to the partnership itself for the resulting damage.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California law allocates exposure for acts taken after a partnership has dissolved but before winding up is complete — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular general partnership, or about whether any specific partner's act falls into either statutory category. Both of these rules expressly except registered and foreign limited liability partnerships, which this document does not address; it also does not address the separate statement-of-dissolution filing (Corp. Code § 16805) that affects when a person outside the partnership is deemed to have notice of the dissolution for these purposes. The two citations below are to two different statutory sections (§ 16804 and § 16806), not subsections of a single section.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16804
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, when the partnership is bound by a post-dissolution act
citations.quote: Subject to Section 16805, a partnership is bound by a partner’s act after dissolution that is either of the following: (1) Appropriate for winding up the partnership business. (2) Would have bound the partnership under Section 16301 before dissolution, if the other party to the transaction did not have notice of the dissolution.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16806
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, a partner's liability for incurring a post-dissolution obligation
citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (b) and except for registered limited liability partnerships and foreign limited liability partnerships, after dissolution a partner is liable to the other partners for the partner’s share of any partnership liability incurred under Section 16804. (b) Except for registered limited liability partnerships and foreign limited liability partnerships, a partner who, with knowledge of the dissolution, incurs a partnership liability under paragraph (2) of Section 16804 by an act that is not appropriate for winding up the partnership business is liable to the partnership for any damage caused to the partnership arising from the liability.

clauses.title: The Priority Order for Applying Partnership Assets in Winding Up
clauses.body: California's partnership statute fixes a specific order for applying a partnership's assets during winding up. Creditors come first: the partnership's assets, including any contributions the statute requires from the partners, must be applied to discharge the partnership's obligations to creditors — which, to the extent the law permits, includes partners who are themselves creditors of the partnership. Only after creditors are paid does any surplus go to the partners, and even then it is distributed according to a settlement of accounts: profits and losses from liquidating the partnership's assets are credited and charged to each partner's own account, a partner with a net credit balance receives a cash distribution equal to that excess, and (apart from a registered or foreign limited liability partnership) a partner with a net charge balance must instead contribute that excess to the partnership. If a partner fails to contribute the full amount that partner owes, the other partners must make up the shortfall in proportion to how they share partnership losses, though a partner who contributes more than that partner's own share of the personally-liable obligations may recover the excess from the other partners. A California Court of Appeal decision applying this same statute underscores why the sequence matters: a partner who is merely dissociating (not dissolving the partnership) is bought out of their own interest first, while a partner exiting through an actual dissolution has no such priority — creditors are paid ahead of any partner.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute and one published California appellate decision, used as real evidence of California's own default winding-up priority rule — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular general partnership, or about the specific dollar amounts, if any, that would result from winding up any given partnership's own accounts. This document does not address the further statutory contribution obligations that can arise after the initial settlement of accounts, for partnership obligations not known at the time of settlement, or a deceased partner's estate's own contribution liability — those exist in the same statutory section but are not detailed here. This is also a default rule; it does not say whether a given partnership's own written partnership agreement modifies it, since a partnership agreement can generally vary many of these default rules among the partners themselves. All statutory citations below are subsections of a single section (§ 16807).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16807(a)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, creditors are paid before any surplus reaches partners
citations.quote: (a) In winding up a partnership’s business, the assets of the partnership, including the contributions of the partners required by this section, shall be applied to discharge its obligations to creditors, including, to the extent permitted by law, partners who are creditors. Any surplus shall be applied to pay in cash the net amount distributable to partners in accordance with their right to distributions under subdivision (b).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16807(b)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, settlement of partner accounts on winding up
citations.quote: (b) Each partner is entitled to a settlement of all partnership accounts upon winding up the partnership business. In settling accounts among the partners, the profits and losses that result from the liquidation of the partnership assets shall be credited and charged to the partners’ accounts. The partnership shall make a distribution to a partner in an amount equal to any excess of the credits over the charges in the partner’s account.

citations.case: Corrales v. Corrales
citations.quote: This rule is necessary to protect the partnership’s creditors. In a dissociation, the partnership assets are used to buy out the withdrawing partner. (§ 16701.) In a dissolution, the assets go first to pay the creditors. (§ 16807, subd. (a).) A partner cannot get first dibs on partnership assets by dissociating when in fact the withdrawal effects a dissolution.
