clauses.title: Unincorporated Nonprofit Association — Introduction and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, how California law treats an unincorporated nonprofit association under Title 3 of the Corporations Code (Corp. Code §§ 18000–24001.5), which governs unincorporated associations generally, and Part 2 of that title (Corp. Code §§ 18605–21401), which contains provisions specific to nonprofit associations. It concerns {{associationName}}, an unincorporated group formed for the common purpose described as {{nonprofitPurpose}}. This sheet addresses the statutory definition of an unincorporated association and a nonprofit association, the statutory rule on personal liability of members, directors, officers, and agents for the association's own debts and obligations, and the association's statutory capacity to hold property and to sue or be sued in its own name. It does not address incorporation as a nonprofit corporation under a different part of the Corporations Code, tax-exempt status under state or federal law, or the Attorney General's charitable-trust registration requirements for an association that holds property for charitable purposes, each of which — where covered at all — is addressed in a separate document in this library. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself form, dissolve, or alter the governance of any association, and it does not determine whether {{associationName}} or any other group meets the statutory definition of an unincorporated association or a nonprofit association on its particular facts.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of Unincorporated Association and Nonprofit Association
clauses.body: California's Corporations Code defines the terms used throughout Title 3's provisions on unincorporated associations. By statute, "‘Unincorporated association’ means an unincorporated group of two or more persons joined by mutual consent for a common lawful purpose, whether organized for profit or not." The same section states that certain arrangements do not, by themselves, create an unincorporated association: joint tenancy, tenancy in common, community property, or other property co-ownership does not establish an unincorporated association merely because the co-owners share a common purpose, and neither does marriage or a registered domestic partnership. Within that broader category, the statute defines a narrower one: "‘Nonprofit association’ means an unincorporated association with a primary common purpose other than to operate a business for profit," and the statute clarifies that such an association may still carry on a business for profit and apply the resulting profit to any activity in which it may lawfully engage. The statute also fixes the meaning of "member": where an association's own governing principles define its membership, that definition controls; where they do not, a person is a member if, under the association's governing principles, that person "has a right to participate in the selection of persons authorized to manage the affairs of the unincorporated association or in the development of policy of the unincorporated association, but does not include a person who participates solely as director, officer, or agent of the association."
clauses.gap: These definitions govern Title 3's general provisions on unincorporated associations, which by their own terms do not apply to a corporation, a government or governmental subdivision or agency, a partnership or joint venture, a limited liability company, or a labor organization governed by a constitution or bylaws (Corp. Code § 18055); this clause does not quote § 18055's exclusion list itself. It also does not address the separate definitions used for a specific kind of unincorporated group elsewhere in California law — for example, a homeowners association under the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act (Civ. Code § 4000 et seq.) or a cooperative corporation — both of which appear only incidentally, and for unrelated purposes, in other documents already in this corpus. Whether a particular group's arrangement satisfies the "mutual consent for a common lawful purpose" standard, or whether its own governing principles define "member" differently from the statutory default, are fact-specific questions this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 18035(a)
citations.cite: Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, statutory definition of "unincorporated association"
citations.quote: “Unincorporated association” means an unincorporated group of two or more persons joined by mutual consent for a common lawful purpose, whether organized for profit or not.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 18020(a)
citations.cite: Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, statutory definition of "nonprofit association"
citations.quote: “Nonprofit association” means an unincorporated association with a primary common purpose other than to operate a business for profit.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 18015(b)
citations.cite: Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, default statutory definition of "member"
citations.quote: “member” means a person who, pursuant to the governing principles of the unincorporated association, has a right to participate in the selection of persons authorized to manage the affairs of the unincorporated association or in the development of policy of the unincorporated association, but does not include a person who participates solely as director, officer, or agent of the association.

clauses.title: Personal Liability of Members, Directors, and Agents for Association Debts
clauses.body: California's Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act states a general rule shielding individuals from an association's own debts: "A member, director, or agent of a nonprofit association is not liable for a debt, obligation, or liability of the association solely by reason of being a member, director, officer, or agent." This codifies a principle California courts had already recognized at common law: one Court of Appeal decision, quoting earlier authority, stated that "[a] member of an unincorporated association does not incur liability for acts of the association or acts of its members which he did not authorize or perform." The statutory shield is not unconditional. The same chapter separately makes a member, director, officer, or agent liable for injury, damage, or harm caused by an act or omission of the association, or of one of its directors, officers, or agents, where the individual expressly assumes liability for the conduct, personally engages in tortious conduct causing the harm, or is otherwise liable under some other statute; the statute describes this as "a nonexclusive list of existing grounds for liability, and does not foreclose any common law grounds for liability." The chapter also preserves common-law alter-ego exposure: "a member or person in control of a nonprofit association may be subject to liability for a debt, obligation, or liability of the association under common law principles governing alter ego liability of shareholders of a corporation, taking into account the differences between a nonprofit association and a corporation."
clauses.gap: This chapter's protection runs against liability "solely by reason of" status as a member, director, or officer; it does not immunize a person for conduct falling within § 18620(a)'s own exceptions, for alter-ego liability under § 18630, or for a contractual obligation the person personally assumes or ratifies under § 18610, which is addressed in a separate clause of this document. The Heiman decision cited here applied the underlying no-personal-liability-for-unauthorized-acts principle in the context of a homeowners association member's potential status as an "employer" for workers' compensation purposes, drawing on Corp. Code § 18250's general rule that an association is liable for its own and its agents' acts to the same extent as a natural person, rather than on § 18605 itself; it is cited here only because it states and applies the same common-law principle that § 18605 codifies for nonprofit associations specifically, not because it interprets § 18605. Whether a particular member, director, or agent's conduct falls within one of § 18620(a)'s exceptions, or satisfies the alter-ego factors referenced in § 18630, are fact-specific determinations this clause does not make.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 18605
citations.cite: Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, general rule against personal liability solely from membership or office
citations.quote: A member, director, or agent of a nonprofit association is not liable for a debt, obligation, or liability of the association solely by reason of being a member, director, officer, or agent.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 18620(a)
citations.cite: Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, statutory grounds for individual liability for injury, damage, or harm
citations.quote: A member, director, officer, or agent of a nonprofit association shall be liable for injury, damage, or harm caused by an act or omission of the association or an act or omission of a director, officer, or agent of the association, if any of the following conditions is satisfied: (1) The member, director, officer, or agent expressly assumes liability for injury, damage, or harm caused by particular conduct and that conduct causes the injury, damage, or harm. (2) The member, director, officer, or agent engages in tortious conduct that causes the injury, damage, or harm. (3) The member, director, officer, or agent is otherwise liable under any other statute.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 18630
citations.cite: Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, preservation of common-law alter-ego liability
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of this chapter, a member or person in control of a nonprofit association may be subject to liability for a debt, obligation, or liability of the association under common law principles governing alter ego liability of shareholders of a corporation, taking into account the differences between a nonprofit association and a corporation.

citations.case: Heiman v. Workers' Compensation Appeals Board, 149 Cal. App. 4th 724 (2007)
citations.quote: [a] member of an unincorporated association does not incur liability for acts of the association or acts of its members which he did not authorize or perform.

clauses.title: When a Member, Director, Officer, or Agent May Be Liable on the Association's Contracts
clauses.body: The general no-personal-liability rule for a nonprofit association's obligations has a separate, more detailed counterpart for contracts. By statute, "A member of a nonprofit association is not liable for a contractual obligation of the association unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) The member expressly assumes personal responsibility for the obligation in a signed writing that specifically identifies the obligation assumed. (b) The member expressly authorizes or ratifies the specific contract, as evidenced by a writing. This subdivision does not apply if the member authorizes or ratifies a contract solely in the member's capacity as a director, officer, or agent of the association. (c) With notice of the contract, the member receives a benefit under the contract. Liability under this subdivision is limited to the value of the benefit received. (d) The member executes the contract without disclosing that the member is acting on behalf of the association. (e) The member executes the contract without authority to execute the contract." A parallel statute states a similar rule for a director, officer, or agent, conditioned on a narrower set of three circumstances: "A director, officer, or agent of a nonprofit association is not liable for a contractual obligation of the association unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) The director, officer, or agent expressly assumes responsibility for the obligation in a signed writing that specifically identifies the obligation assumed. (b) The director, officer, or agent executes the contract without disclosing that the director, officer, or agent is acting on behalf of the association. (c) The director, officer, or agent executes the contract without authority to execute the contract." Apart from these specific rules, general agency law fills the gaps: "Except to the extent this title provides a specific rule, the general law of agency ... applies to an unincorporated association."
clauses.gap: These two statutes were enacted together in 2004 and, unlike § 18605's blanket shield, apply specifically to an association's contractual obligations. They differ from each other in one respect: only the member-liability statute (§ 18610) includes a receipt-of-benefit ground (subdivision (c)); the director/officer/agent statute (§ 18615) does not. Both statutes turn on fact-specific questions — whether a writing satisfies the "signed writing that specifically identifies the obligation assumed" standard, what counts as "ratification" of a specific contract, or whether a person disclosed that they were acting on the association's behalf — that this clause does not resolve for any particular contract. This clause quotes § 18065's cross-reference to general agency law only in part, omitting the specific Civil Code article and title citations it names; it does not itself state what that general agency law requires for a particular officer's authority to bind the association, which depends on the association's own governing documents and on the agency-law provisions § 18065 references.

citations.cite: Uniform Unincorporated Nonprofit Association Act, conditions for a member's contractual liability
citations.quote: A member of a nonprofit association is not liable for a contractual obligation of the association unless one of the following conditions is satisfied: (a) The member expressly assumes personal responsibility for the obligation in a signed writing that specifically identifies the obligation assumed. (b) The member expressly authorizes or ratifies the specific contract, as evidenced by a writing. This subdivision does not apply if the member authorizes or ratifies a contract solely in the member’s capacity as a director, officer, or agent of the association. (c) With notice of the contract, the member receives a benefit under the contract. Liability under this subdivision is limited to the value of the benefit received. (d) The member executes the contract without disclosing that the member is acting on behalf of the association. (e) The member executes the contract without authority to execute the contract.

citations.quote: Except to the extent this title provides a specific rule, the general law of agency, including Article 2 (commencing with Section 2019) of Chapter 2 of Title 6 of, and Title 9 (commencing with Section 2295) of, Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code, applies to an unincorporated association.

clauses.title: Capacity to Hold Property and to Sue or Be Sued in the Association's Own Name
clauses.body: Because an unincorporated association is not a natural person or a corporation, California law states expressly that it may nonetheless act, and be dealt with, in its own name. By statute, "An unincorporated association may, in its name, acquire, hold, manage, encumber, or transfer an interest in real or personal property." Property obtained this way belongs to the association itself, not to its members individually: "Property acquired by or for an unincorporated association is property of the unincorporated association and not of the members individually." A separate statute, in the Code of Civil Procedure, gives an unincorporated association the same kind of standing in litigation: "A partnership or other unincorporated association, whether organized for profit or not, may sue and be sued in the name it has assumed or by which it is known." Acquiring, transferring, or encumbering an interest in real property specifically must be executed in a defined way: "The acquisition, transfer, or encumbrance of an interest in real property by an unincorporated association shall be executed by its president and secretary or other comparable officers, or by a person specifically designated by a resolution adopted by the association, or by a committee or other body or person authorized to act by the governing principles of the association."
clauses.gap: Sections 18105 and 18115's property-holding rules and § 369.5's litigation capacity are general default rules; a statute governing a particular kind of association — for example, the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act's rules for a homeowners association, addressed elsewhere in this corpus, or the Cooperative Corporation Law — can supply a different rule that prevails to the extent of any inconsistency (Corp. Code § 18060). Code of Civil Procedure § 369.5 has a second subdivision, not quoted here, that separately allows a member to be joined as a party in a suit against the association and addresses how a judgment against that individual member may be obtained in that same action; this clause addresses only the association's own capacity to sue and be sued in its name, not that separate joinder mechanism. Nothing quoted in this clause itself transfers title to any specific property into an association's name, creates or dissolves the association, or determines who currently holds signing authority on the association's behalf — those depend on the association's own governing documents and, for real property, on the recorded instrument itself.

citations.quote: An unincorporated association may, in its name, acquire, hold, manage, encumber, or transfer an interest in real or personal property.

clauses.title: Limits on Enforcing a Judgment Against the Association's Members
clauses.body: California law also states how a money judgment against an unincorporated association may be enforced, and limits when a judgment based on the association's own liability can instead be enforced against an individual member, director, officer, or agent. By statute, "A money judgment against an unincorporated association, whether organized for profit or not, may be enforced only against the property of the association." A related statute extends this protection to individuals in most circumstances: "A judgment creditor of a member, director, officer, or agent of an unincorporated association may not levy execution against the assets of the member, director, officer, or agent to satisfy a judgment based on a claim against the unincorporated association unless a judgment based on the same claim has been obtained against the unincorporated association and any of the following conditions is satisfied: (1) A writ of execution on the judgment against the unincorporated association has been returned unsatisfied in whole or in part. (2) The unincorporated association is a debtor in bankruptcy. (3) The member, director, officer, or agent has agreed that the creditor need not exhaust the assets of the unincorporated association. (4) A court grants permission to the judgment creditor to levy execution against the assets of a member, director, officer, or agent based on a finding that the assets of the unincorporated association subject to execution are clearly insufficient to satisfy the judgment, that exhaustion of the assets of the unincorporated association is excessively burdensome, or that the grant of permission is an appropriate exercise of the court's equitable powers." This exhaustion requirement applies only to a claim against the individual that is itself based on a claim against the association: "Nothing in this section affects the right of a judgment creditor to levy execution against the assets of a member, director, officer, or agent of an unincorporated association if the claim against the member, director, officer, or agent is not based on a claim against the unincorporated association."
clauses.gap: These enforcement limits are procedurally separate from the substantive liability rules in Corp. Code §§ 18605–18630: a member may already be substantively liable on some independent ground — for example, under § 18610's contract-liability exceptions or § 18620's tort-liability exceptions, each addressed in a separate clause of this document — and still benefit from § 18270(a)'s requirement that a creditor first obtain, and attempt to enforce, a judgment against the association itself unless one of § 18270(a)'s four listed conditions is met. Corp. Code § 18250, not quoted in this clause, separately makes the association itself liable for its own and its agents' acts or omissions to the same extent as a natural person; this clause addresses only how a resulting judgment may then be enforced, not the association's own underlying liability. Whether a judgment creditor has satisfied one of § 18270(a)'s conditions, or whether a specific claim against an individual is "based on" a claim against the association within the meaning of § 18270(b), are fact-specific determinations this clause does not make.

citations.quote: A money judgment against an unincorporated association, whether organized for profit or not, may be enforced only against the property of the association.

clauses.title: Supplemental Job Displacement Benefit — Overview
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the Supplemental Job Displacement Benefit (SJDB) available under California workers' compensation law, Labor Code § 4658.7. It concerns {{employeeName}}'s work injury at {{companyName}} with a reported injury date of {{injuryDate}} ({{injuryDescription}}). The SJDB is a voucher for retraining or skill enhancement that may become available to a worker who has sustained permanent partial disability from a work injury and whom the employer does not offer, or who does not receive a qualifying offer of, regular, modified, or alternative work. This sheet states the general provisions of the law; it does not determine whether any particular worker qualifies for the benefit, and it is not a claim form, a voucher, or a substitute for the notices and forms that the workers' compensation claims administrator is separately required to provide.

clauses.title: Eligibility Trigger: Permanent Partial Disability and No Qualifying Return-to-Work Offer
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 4658.7, applicable to injuries occurring on or after January 1, 2013, a worker whose work injury causes permanent partial disability is entitled to a Supplemental Job Displacement Benefit unless the employer makes a qualifying offer of regular, modified, or alternative work as defined in Labor Code § 4658.1. To be qualifying, the offer must (1) be made no later than 60 days after the claims administrator receives the first report from the primary treating physician, an agreed medical evaluator, or a qualified medical evaluator finding the disability permanent and stationary and that it has caused permanent partial disability, and (2) be for regular, modified, or alternative work lasting at least 12 months. An offer that is not timely made, that does not last at least 12 months, or that the employer never makes at all does not defeat entitlement to the benefit.
clauses.gap: This statute defines the SJDB voucher trigger but incorporates by reference the separate definitions of 'regular work,' 'modified work,' and 'alternative work' in Labor Code § 4658.1, which are not reproduced here. Whether a specific job offer meets those definitions, whether an offer was actually timely under the 60-day period, and whether an employee's PD rating in a specific claim is in fact 'permanent partial' (as opposed to permanent total, or not yet permanent and stationary) are factual and medical determinations for the workers' compensation claims process, not something this sheet can resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7(a)-(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: If the injury causes permanent partial disability, the injured employee shall be entitled to a supplemental job displacement benefit as provided in this section unless the employer makes an offer of regular, modified, or alternative work, as defined in Section 4658.1, that meets both of the following criteria

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: The offer is for regular work, modified work, or alternative work lasting at least 12 months.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: This section shall apply to injuries occurring on or after January 1, 2013.

clauses.title: Timing of the Return-to-Work Offer and the Voucher Offer
clauses.body: The 60-day period for a qualifying offer of regular, modified, or alternative work runs from the claims administrator's receipt of the first physician report finding the worker's disability permanent and stationary and permanently partially disabling. If no qualifying offer is made within that 60-day period, Labor Code § 4658.7(c) requires that the Supplemental Job Displacement Benefit itself be offered to the employee within 20 days after that 60-day period expires.
clauses.gap: The statute measures the 60-day period from the claims administrator's receipt of a qualifying physician report, an event this sheet cannot independently verify or calendar; the precise date that period began, and whether the 20-day voucher-offer deadline was met, depend on claims-file records outside this document.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7(b)(1)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: The offer is made no later than 60 days after receipt by the claims administrator of the first report received from either the primary treating physician, an agreed medical evaluator, or a qualified medical evaluator, in the form created by the administrative director pursuant to subdivision (h), finding that the disability from all conditions for which compensation is claimed has become permanent and stationary and that the injury has caused permanent partial disability.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7(c)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: The supplemental job displacement benefit shall be offered to the employee within 20 days after the expiration of the time for making an offer of regular, modified, or alternative work pursuant to paragraph (1) of subdivision (b).

clauses.title: Voucher Value and Permitted Uses
clauses.body: The Supplemental Job Displacement Benefit takes the form of a voucher currently redeemable up to an aggregate of $6,000 per Labor Code § 4658.7(d). The voucher may be applied, at the injured employee's choice, to: education-related retraining or skill enhancement (including tuition, fees, books, and other required expenses) at a California public school or a provider certified on the state's Eligible Training Provider List; occupational licensing or professional certification fees, related examination fees, and examination preparation course fees; the services of licensed placement agencies, vocational or return-to-work counseling, and résumé preparation (together capped at 10 percent of the voucher amount); tools required by an enrolled training or educational program; computer equipment, up to $1,000; and up to $500 as a miscellaneous expense reimbursement or advance payable without itemized documentation. The statute expressly excludes voucher payment for transportation, travel expenses, telephone or internet access, clothing or uniforms, or other incidental expenses beyond that $500 miscellaneous allowance.
clauses.gap: The $6,000 aggregate figure and the sub-limits described here are the amounts currently codified in the text of Labor Code § 4658.7 as verified directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov on the date checked above; this figure has been changed by the Legislature before (the pre-2013 version of this benefit used a different, PD-rating-tiered schedule) and could be amended again, so the amount should be confirmed against the current statute at the time of use rather than assumed from this sheet indefinitely.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7(d)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: The supplemental job displacement benefit shall be in the form of a voucher redeemable as provided in this section up to an aggregate of six thousand dollars ($6,000).

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7(e)(1)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: Payment for education-related retraining or skill enhancement, or both, at a California public school or with a provider that is certified and on the state’s Eligible Training Provider List (EPTL), as authorized by the federal Workforce Investment Act (P.L. 105-220), including payment of tuition, fees, books, and other expenses required by the school for retraining or skill enhancement.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7(e)(3)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: Payment for the services of licensed placement agencies, vocational or return-to-work counseling, and résumé preparation, all up to a combined limit of 10 percent of the amount of the voucher.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7(e)(6)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: Up to five hundred dollars ($500) as a miscellaneous expense reimbursement or advance, payable upon request and without need for itemized documentation or accounting. The employee shall not be entitled to any other voucher payment for transportation, travel expenses, telephone or Internet access, clothing or uniforms, or incidental expenses.

clauses.title: Voucher Expiration
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 4658.7(f), the voucher expires two years after the date it is furnished to the employee, or five years after the date of injury, whichever is later. To be reimbursed, expenses must be incurred and submitted to the employer with appropriate documentation before that expiration date; the statute states there is no entitlement to payment or reimbursement of expenses not incurred and documented in time.
clauses.gap: Because the deadline runs from whichever furnishing date and injury date apply to the specific claim, and 'the date of injury' for a cumulative-trauma or multiple-incident claim can itself be a disputed determination in workers' compensation practice, this sheet cannot calculate a specific expiration date for any individual worker's voucher.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7(f)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: The voucher shall expire two years after the date the voucher is furnished to the employee, or five years after the date of injury, whichever is later.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7(f)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: The employee shall not be entitled to payment or reimbursement of any expenses that have not been incurred and submitted with appropriate documentation to the employer prior to the expiration date.

clauses.title: Restriction on Settlement of the Benefit; Employer Liability While Using the Voucher
clauses.body: Labor Code § 4658.7(g) prohibits settlement or commutation of a claim for the Supplemental Job Displacement Benefit under the Chapter 2 (compromise and release, commencing with Section 5000) or Chapter 3 (commutation, commencing with Section 5100) procedures of Part 3 of the Labor Code's workers' compensation provisions. Separately, Labor Code § 4658.7(i) provides that an employer is not liable for compensation for injuries incurred by the employee while using the voucher.
clauses.gap: This statute bars settlement of the SJDB claim specifically under the two named chapters; it does not address, and this sheet does not opine on, how a broader workers' compensation compromise and release agreement that references or lists the SJDB voucher as a settled item may be interpreted, which is a matter of case-specific contract and settlement-agreement construction.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7(g)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: Settlement or commutation of a claim for the supplemental job displacement benefit shall not be permitted under Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 5000) or Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 5100) of Part 3.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7(i)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 4658.7
citations.quote: An employer shall not be liable for compensation for injuries incurred by the employee while utilizing the voucher.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Receipt of Information
clauses.body: This information sheet regarding the Supplemental Job Displacement Benefit was provided to {{employeeName}} by {{companyName}} on {{dateSigned}} in {{cityState}}. Signing below acknowledges receipt of this information sheet only; it does not waive, establish, or resolve any entitlement to the Supplemental Job Displacement Benefit or any other workers' compensation benefit.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's bed bug disclosure and inspection statute, Civil Code §§ 1954.600-1954.605, as it may apply to the tenancy of the dwelling unit at {{propertyAddress}}, as between {{landlordName}} and {{tenantName}}. It states what California law provides on this subject. It does not itself serve as the written bed bug information notice the statute describes, and it does not determine whether a suspected or confirmed infestation exists at any specific property.

clauses.title: The Legislature's Stated Findings on Bed Bug Control
clauses.body: In enacting this chapter, the Legislature found and declared that controlling bed bugs is uniquely challenging because bed bug resistance to existing insecticidal control measures is significant, and that cooperation among landlords, tenants, and pest control operators is required for successful control; with such cooperation, most bed bug infestations can be successfully controlled. The Legislature further found that effective control is more likely when landlords and tenants are informed of best practices for bed bug control, that early detection and reporting is an important component of prevention, that tenants should not face retaliation for reporting a problem, and that lack of cooperation by landlords and tenants can undermine a pest control operator's efforts to identify and control an infestation.
clauses.gap: This is a legislative findings-and-declarations section, not itself a set of operative legal duties -- the statement that "tenants should not face retaliation for reporting a problem" appears only here, as a finding, and this chapter does not itself set out a retaliation cause of action, remedy, or enforcement mechanism; whether other, separate California statutes prohibiting landlord retaliation apply to a bed bug report is outside this chapter's text and outside this document. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction has framed bed bug control policy -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific tenancy. No California appellate decision construing this chapter was located in a CourtListener search conducted for this document; this document is accordingly based on statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.600(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, legislative finding on the difficulty of bed bug control and the need for cooperation
citations.quote: Controlling bed bugs is uniquely challenging, as bed bug resistance to existing insecticidal control measures is significant. Cooperation among landlords, tenants, and pest control operators is required for successful control. With cooperation among landlords, tenants, and pest control operators, most bed bug infestations can be successfully controlled.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.600(c)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, legislative finding on early reporting and retaliation
citations.quote: Early detection and reporting of bed bugs is an important component required for preventing bed bug infestations. Tenants should not face retaliation for reporting a problem.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.600(d)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, legislative finding on the effect of lack of cooperation
citations.quote: Lack of cooperation by landlords and tenants can undermine pest control operator efforts to identify the presence of bed bugs and control an infestation.

clauses.title: Written Bed Bug Information Notice Required Before a New Tenancy
clauses.body: On and after July 1, 2017, before creating a new tenancy for a dwelling unit, a landlord must provide a written notice to the prospective tenant, in at least 10-point type, that includes -- but is not limited to -- general information about bed bug identification, behavior, and biology, the importance of cooperation for prevention and treatment, and the importance of prompt written reporting of suspected infestations to the landlord, with that information to be in substantially the statutorily specified form, plus the procedure for reporting a suspected infestation to the landlord. As a one-time transition matter, this same written notice also had to be provided to all other (already-existing) tenants by January 1, 2018.
clauses.gap: The January 1, 2018 deadline for delivering this notice to existing tenants was a one-time historical transition requirement tied to the chapter's July 1, 2017 operative date; it does not by its own terms recur at each lease renewal, and this document takes no position on whether a landlord in fact provided this notice by that date for any specific tenancy. The statute's "include, but is not limited to" language means the specified content is a floor, not a ceiling, on what the written notice may need to contain; this document does not attempt to reproduce the full statutorily specified informational text. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a pre-tenancy bed bug notice requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific tenancy. No California case law construing this section was located.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.603
citations.cite: California Civil Code, timing, form, and minimum content of the required written bed bug notice
citations.quote: On and after July 1, 2017, prior to creating a new tenancy for a dwelling unit, a landlord shall provide a written notice to the prospective tenant as provided in this section. This notice shall be provided to all other tenants by January 1, 2018. The notice shall be in at least 10-point type and shall include, but is not limited to, the following:

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.603(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, required general bed bug information and reporting emphasis
citations.quote: General information about bed bug identification, behavior and biology, the importance of cooperation for prevention and treatment, and the importance of and for prompt written reporting of suspected infestations to the landlord. The information shall be in substantially the following form:

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.603(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, required reporting-procedure content
citations.quote: The procedure to report suspected infestations to the landlord.

clauses.title: Limit on Showing, Renting, or Leasing a Known-Infested Vacant Unit
clauses.body: A landlord may not show, rent, or lease a vacant dwelling unit to a prospective tenant if the landlord knows that unit has a current bed bug infestation. This section does not itself impose a duty on a landlord to inspect a dwelling unit or the common areas for bed bugs where the landlord has no notice of a suspected or actual infestation -- but where an infestation is evident on visual inspection, the landlord is considered to have notice for purposes of this section.
clauses.gap: This provision, by its own text, is limited to a vacant dwelling unit being shown, rented, or leased to a prospective tenant -- it does not on its face create a freestanding, ongoing duty to disclose an infestation in an occupied unit, in a different (e.g., adjacent) unit, or once a tenancy is already underway; whether some other disclosure duty applies to those situations is outside this chapter's text and outside this document. The statute's "knows" standard is defined here only in terms of what is evident on visual inspection; it does not address what other facts might or might not give a landlord notice. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction limits leasing of a known-infested vacant unit -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific tenancy. No California case law construing "current bed bug infestation" or "notice" under this section was located.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.602(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, prohibition on showing, renting, or leasing a known-infested vacant unit
citations.quote: A landlord shall not show, rent, or lease to a prospective tenant any vacant dwelling unit that the landlord knows has a current bed bug infestation.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.602(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, no freestanding inspection duty absent notice, and visual evidence as notice
citations.quote: This section does not impose a duty on a landlord to inspect a dwelling unit or the common areas of the premises for bed bugs if the landlord has no notice of a suspected or actual bed bug infestation. If a bed bug infestation is evident on visual inspection, the landlord shall be considered to have notice pursuant to this section.

clauses.title: Entry to Inspect for Bed Bugs, and the Tenant's Cooperation Duty
clauses.body: Entry to inspect a tenant's dwelling unit for bed bugs must comply with Civil Code § 1954, the general statute governing a landlord's right of entry. Entry to inspect any unit selected by the pest control operator, and to conduct followup inspections of surrounding units until bed bugs are eliminated, is itself treated as a "necessary" purpose for entry under Section 1954. For purposes of this chapter, a "pest control operator" means an individual holding a Branch 2 operator, field representative, or applicator license from the Structural Pest Control Board. Tenants must cooperate with the inspection to facilitate detection and treatment of bed bugs, including by providing information the pest control operator requests that is necessary to facilitate that detection and treatment.
clauses.gap: Section 1954's own separate requirements for entry (such as its notice provisions) are incorporated by reference here, not restated in full in this chapter or in this document. The chapter states that followup inspection of "surrounding units" is a necessary service under Section 1954 but does not itself define how far "surrounding" extends. The tenant cooperation duty is stated in this chapter without this chapter itself specifying a remedy for a tenant's non-cooperation. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction ties bed bug inspection to its general entry statute -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific tenancy. No California case law construing this section was located.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.604
citations.cite: California Civil Code, entry to inspect for bed bugs treated as a necessary purpose under the general entry statute
citations.quote: Entry to inspect a tenant’s dwelling unit shall comply with Section 1954. Entry to inspect any unit selected by the pest control operator and to conduct followup inspections of surrounding units until bed bugs are eliminated is a necessary service for the purpose of Section 1954.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.604
citations.cite: California Civil Code, tenant's duty to cooperate with a bed bug inspection
citations.quote: Tenants shall cooperate with the inspection to facilitate the detection and treatment of bed bugs, including providing requested information that is necessary to facilitate the detection and treatment of bed bugs to the pest control operator.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.601
citations.cite: California Civil Code, definition of "pest control operator" for this chapter
citations.quote: For purposes of this chapter, the term “pest control operator” means an individual holding a Branch 2 operator, field representative, or applicator license from the Structural Pest Control Board.

clauses.title: Landlord's Duty to Notify Tenants of the Pest Control Operator's Findings
clauses.body: The landlord must notify the tenants of the units the pest control operator inspected of that operator's findings. This notification must be in writing and made within two business days of the landlord's receipt of the pest control operator's findings. Where the confirmed infestation is in a common area, all tenants -- not only those whose units were inspected -- must be provided notice of the findings.
clauses.gap: By its own terms, this notification duty runs to "the tenants of those units inspected" (plus, separately, to all tenants for a confirmed common-area infestation) -- it does not extend this specific duty to tenants of units that were not inspected outside that common-area situation. The two-business-day period is measured from the landlord's receipt of the pest control operator's findings, not from the date of the inspection itself, and this document does not address what counts as "receipt." This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction structures a post-inspection notification duty -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific tenancy. No California case law construing this section was located.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.605
citations.cite: California Civil Code, written notification of inspection findings within two business days
citations.quote: The landlord shall notify the tenants of those units inspected by the pest control operator pursuant to Section 1954.604 of the pest control operator’s findings. The notification shall be in writing and made within two business days of receipt of the pest control operator’s findings.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1954.605
citations.cite: California Civil Code, all tenants notified for a confirmed common-area infestation
citations.quote: For confirmed infestations in common areas, all tenants shall be provided notice of the pest control operator’s findings.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Common Law Marriage in California — Non-Recognition Information Sheet concerns {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. It describes what California law says, in general terms, about two related subjects: (1) the requirements California itself imposes to form a marriage within the state, and why living together and presenting oneself as married does not, by itself, create a marriage here; and (2) the separate rule under which California courts will generally recognize a marriage — including one formed under another jurisdiction's common law marriage doctrine — that was validly contracted under the law of the jurisdiction where it was formed. This information sheet states general legal facts. It does not determine, and takes no position on, whether {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} are or are not married under the law of California or any other jurisdiction; that determination depends on the specific facts of their relationship and history and, if disputed, is for a court to decide.

clauses.title: California's Own Requirements for Forming a Marriage
clauses.body: California statute defines marriage as "a personal relation arising out of a civil contract between two persons, to which the consent of the parties capable of making that contract is necessary," but the statute is explicit that the parties' mutual consent to be married is not, by itself, enough. Consent must be followed by the issuance of a marriage license and solemnization of the marriage as authorized by the Family Code, subject to two named statutory exceptions: Section 425 (which concerns marriage by a party who is confined or physically incapacitated) and Part 4 of the same division, commencing with Section 500 (which concerns the state's confidential-marriage license track). Outside those two exceptions, a couple in California must obtain a license and have the marriage solemnized for a marriage to be formed; consent and cohabitation alone do not suffice.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes and summarizes Family Code section 300(a) only; it does not independently verify the text of Section 425 or of Part 4 (commencing with Section 500), the two exceptions the statute itself names, beyond quoting that they are named exceptions. It does not quote or summarize subsection (b) of Section 300, which addresses when a license becomes a marriage certificate, because that subsection is not relevant to this topic. No case law was independently verified for this clause; California case law construing and applying Section 300 was not fetched or reviewed in the course of preparing this document, so this clause rests on the current statutory text alone, fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific couple has satisfied, or failed to satisfy, these requirements.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 300(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: consent alone insufficient; license and solemnization required, subject to two named exceptions
citations.quote: Consent alone does not constitute marriage. Consent must be followed by the issuance of a license and solemnization as authorized by this division, except as provided by Section 425 and Part 4 (commencing with Section 500).

clauses.title: No Marriage Is Formed Within California by Cohabitation Alone
clauses.body: Because California's own marriage-formation statute requires a license and solemnization — and expressly states that the parties' consent by itself does not constitute a marriage — no marriage is formed within California merely because two people live together and present themselves to others as a married couple, no matter how long that arrangement continues. This is sometimes described as California not recognizing "common law marriage" formed within the state. The absence of a license and solemnization is not cured by any particular length of cohabitation, by the couple's own description of themselves as married, by filing joint tax returns, by sharing a residence or finances, or by using a shared surname.
clauses.gap: This clause is this document's own inference from the plain text of Family Code section 300(a) — the same statutory text quoted in this document's companion clause on California's formation requirements — rather than a quotation from a case holding that specific proposition. A substantial body of California case law is understood to confirm that California does not recognize common law marriage formed within the state, but no such case was independently fetched or verified in the course of preparing this document: CourtListener searches were attempted (queries for "common law marriage California recognition" and related terms, run against California courts and generally), but the CourtListener API's daily request quota was exhausted before any candidate opinion's actual text could be fetched and confirmed, so no case citation is included here. This document is informational only and does not itself determine any specific couple's marital status.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 300(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: consent alone does not constitute a marriage
citations.quote: Consent alone does not constitute marriage.

clauses.title: California's Recognition of a Marriage Validly Contracted Elsewhere
clauses.body: A separate California statute addresses marriages formed outside California: "A marriage contracted outside this state that would be valid by laws of the jurisdiction in which the marriage was contracted is valid in California." This rule is not limited to marriages formed by license and ceremony elsewhere; on its face it extends to any marriage — including one formed under another jurisdiction's common law marriage doctrine, where that jurisdiction recognizes such marriages — that was validly contracted under the law of the place where it was formed. California courts generally give this kind of recognition to an out-of-state marriage.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes and summarizes Family Code section 308 in isolation; it does not independently verify any other Family Code section that might qualify or limit this general rule (for example, statutory exceptions for marriages entered into in violation of another state's own laws, or marriages this state might refuse to recognize as against a strong California public policy). No case law was independently verified for this clause: CourtListener searches were attempted, but the API's daily request quota was exhausted before any candidate opinion applying Section 308 (or its predecessor rule) to a common law marriage could be fetched and confirmed, so this clause rests on the current statutory text alone, fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website. This document does not itself determine that any specific marriage was, or was not, validly contracted under the law of any other jurisdiction.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 308 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a marriage valid where contracted is valid in California
citations.quote: A marriage contracted outside this state that would be valid by laws of the jurisdiction in which the marriage was contracted is valid in California.

clauses.title: Recognition Depends on Actual Validity Under the Other Jurisdiction's Own Law
clauses.body: The California statute recognizing an out-of-state marriage measures validity "by laws of the jurisdiction in which the marriage was contracted" — not by California law, and not by the couple's own description of their relationship. A jurisdiction that recognizes common law marriage typically imposes its own set of requirements before treating a couple as married without a license or ceremony — requirements that commonly include matters such as the couple's capacity to marry, their mutual and present agreement to be married, cohabitation, holding themselves out as married, and, in a number of states that recognize common law marriage, that the couple be domiciled in that state at the relevant time. These requirements vary by jurisdiction and are set by each jurisdiction's own law, not by California's Family Code. Under the statute's own terms, a couple's travel through, vacation in, or temporary presence in a jurisdiction that recognizes common law marriage does not by itself establish that a marriage was contracted there.
clauses.gap: The specific common law marriage requirements of any other state (which states recognize it at all, and each one's own elements such as a domicile requirement) are not addressed by California's Family Code and were not independently researched or verified against any other state's statutes or case law in the course of preparing this document; this clause describes, in general terms, how the California statute's own "valid by laws of the jurisdiction in which the marriage was contracted" language directs the inquiry to that other jurisdiction's law, without asserting the specific content of any other state's law. No California case law applying this principle to a specific common law marriage was independently verified for this clause: CourtListener searches were attempted, but the API's daily request quota was exhausted before any candidate opinion's text could be fetched and confirmed. This document does not itself determine whether any specific couple met any other jurisdiction's common law marriage requirements, or was domiciled in any other jurisdiction at any particular time.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 308 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: validity measured by the law of the jurisdiction where the marriage was contracted
citations.quote: valid by laws of the jurisdiction in which the marriage was contracted
