clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California and federal law governing when {{companyName}} may require a job applicant for the position of {{jobTitle}}, such as {{applicantName}}, to complete a physical or agility test before or after a conditional job offer, and the legal framework that applies when such a test screens out applicants at different rates based on a protected characteristic. It states facts about what the Fair Employment and Housing Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, and their implementing regulations permit, require, and restrict in this area. It is not itself a physical or agility test, a job description, or a validation study, and it does not tell {{companyName}} or {{applicantName}} what to do about any particular hiring decision. This document is distinct from this corpus's existing Post-Offer, Pre-Employment Medical Examination and Pre-Employment and Workplace Drug Testing information sheets: a physical or agility test that measures an applicant's ability to perform actual or simulated job tasks is treated differently under federal regulatory guidance than a medical examination or medical inquiry.

clauses.title: FEHA's General Prohibition on Hiring Discrimination
clauses.body: California's Fair Employment and Housing Act makes it unlawful for an employer, because of an applicant's race, national origin, physical disability, sex, age, or several other listed characteristics, to refuse to hire the person or to discriminate against the person in the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment. A physical or agility test that {{companyName}} requires of applicants for {{jobTitle}} is a hiring practice subject to this general prohibition: if the test causes a person to be refused employment because of a listed characteristic, the statute's prohibition is implicated regardless of whether the employer intended to discriminate.
clauses.gap: Government Code section 12940, as fetched and reviewed in full for this document, states this general prohibition and separately addresses medical and psychological examinations and inquiries in subdivisions (e) and (f), but this document's research did not find language in section 12940 itself that spells out a disparate-impact/business-necessity framework in the way 42 U.S.C. section 12112(b)(6) and 42 U.S.C. section 2000e-2(k) do for federal law. This document's research did not verify whether a California regulation (such as a provision of title 2 of the California Code of Regulations) supplies a state-specific codification of that framework for employment tests generally, because the primary free-text source checked for the California Code of Regulations was not accessible during this research session; readers should not assume section 12940's silence on this point means no such state regulation exists. This document is informational only and does not determine whether any specific test or hiring decision violates this statute.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California FEHA, general prohibition on employment discrimination because of listed characteristics
citations.quote: For an employer, because of the race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, reproductive health decisionmaking, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, or veteran or military status of any person, to refuse to hire or employ the person or to refuse to select the person for a training program leading to employment, or to bar or to discharge the person from employment or from a training program leading to employment, or to discriminate against the person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment.

clauses.title: Disability-Based Disparate Impact: The Job-Related, Business-Necessity Standard
clauses.body: Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, it is a form of unlawful discrimination for a covered employer to use qualification standards, employment tests, or other selection criteria that screen out or tend to screen out an individual with a disability, or a class of individuals with disabilities, unless the employer shows that the standard, test, or criteria, as used, is job-related for the position in question and consistent with business necessity. The EEOC's implementing regulation restates this same standard for qualification standards, tests, and other selection criteria that screen out on the basis of disability.
clauses.gap: The statute and its implementing regulation are treated together here as one connected source, since the regulation restates the statutory standard rather than adding an independent one. This provision addresses disparate impact on the basis of disability specifically; it does not by itself address a physical or agility test that has a disparate effect based on sex, age, or another characteristic, which are addressed elsewhere in this document under different statutes. This document is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific physical or agility test screens out individuals with disabilities, and it does not perform or substitute for the job-relatedness or business-necessity showing the law requires an employer to make on the specific facts.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 12112(b)(6) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Americans with Disabilities Act, disparate-impact prohibition for qualification standards, tests, and selection criteria
citations.quote: using qualification standards, employment tests or other selection criteria that screen out or tend to screen out an individual with a disability or a class of individuals with disabilities unless the standard, test or other selection criteria, as used by the covered entity, is shown to be job-related for the position in question and is consistent with business necessity

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 1630.10(a) (eCFR text)
citations.cite: EEOC ADA regulation, qualification standards, tests, and other selection criteria
citations.quote: It is unlawful for a covered entity to use qualification standards, employment tests or other selection criteria that screen out or tend to screen out an individual with a disability or a class of individuals with disabilities, on the basis of disability, unless the standard, test, or other selection criteria, as used by the covered entity, is shown to be job related for the position in question and is consistent with business necessity.

clauses.title: A Physical Agility Test Is Not a Medical Examination
clauses.body: The EEOC's official interpretive guidance to its ADA regulations states that physical agility tests are not medical examinations, and so, unlike a medical examination, may be given at any point in the application or employment process. That guidance also states that such tests must be given to all similarly situated applicants or employees regardless of disability, and that if such a test screens out or tends to screen out an individual with a disability, or a class of individuals with disabilities, the employer would have to demonstrate that the test is job-related and consistent with business necessity and that performance cannot be achieved with reasonable accommodation.
clauses.gap: This quotation comes from the appendix of interpretive guidance to 29 C.F.R. Part 1630, which the EEOC itself describes as guidance rather than a binding regulatory text with independent legal force; it explains the agency's own reading of the regulation rather than adding new statutory or regulatory text. This document's research did not find a parallel statement in California's Government Code section 12940 addressing whether, or at what stage, a physical agility test is distinct from a "medical or psychological examination" for purposes of that section's separate pre-offer and post-offer provisions; whether California law treats physical agility tests the same way this federal guidance does is not resolved by the statutory text this document reviewed. This document is informational only and does not determine whether any specific test is a physical agility test or a medical examination for these purposes.

citations.case: Appendix to 29 C.F.R. Part 1630 (Interpretive Guidance on Title I of the ADA, section on § 1630.14) (eCFR text)
citations.cite: EEOC interpretive guidance, physical agility tests distinguished from medical examinations
citations.quote: Physical agility tests are not medical examinations and so may be given at any point in the application or employment process. Such tests must be given to all similarly situated applicants or employees regardless of disability. If such tests screen out or tend to screen out an individual with a disability or a class of individuals with disabilities, the employer would have to demonstrate that the test is job-related and consistent with business necessity and that performance cannot be achieved with reasonable accommodation.

clauses.title: Disparate Impact Based on Sex or Another Title VII Characteristic
clauses.body: Separately from the ADA's disability-specific framework, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 provides that an unlawful employment practice based on disparate impact is established if a complaining party demonstrates that an employer uses a particular employment practice that causes a disparate impact on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin, and the employer fails to demonstrate that the challenged practice is job-related for the position in question and consistent with business necessity. A physical or agility test with a minimum strength, speed, height, or similar performance threshold is a type of employment practice that has historically been analyzed for disparate impact under this statutory framework where it screens out a disproportionate share of applicants of one sex or another protected group.
clauses.gap: This statutory provision codifies a disparate-impact burden-of-proof framework that predates this specific statutory text; a full account of how courts have applied it to physical or agility testing (for example, in cases addressing height, weight, or strength requirements) requires case law that this document's research was not able to independently verify through primary case-law sources within this research session, and no such case is cited here. This document is informational only: it does not determine whether any specific test causes a disparate impact on the basis of sex or another characteristic, and it does not perform or substitute for the statistical showing or the job-relatedness and business-necessity showing the law requires on the specific facts.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(k)(1)(A)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, disparate-impact burden of proof
citations.quote: An unlawful employment practice based on disparate impact is established under this subchapter only if— (i) a complaining party demonstrates that a respondent uses a particular employment practice that causes a disparate impact on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin and the respondent fails to demonstrate that the challenged practice is job related for the position in question and consistent with business necessity;

clauses.title: FEHA's Pre-Offer and Post-Offer Timing Rules for Medical or Psychological Examinations
clauses.body: Separately from the disparate-impact framework described above, California's FEHA restricts when {{companyName}} may require a "medical or psychological examination" or make a "medical or psychological inquiry" of {{applicantName}} as a job applicant for {{jobTitle}}. Before a conditional offer, FEHA prohibits requiring such an examination or making such an inquiry, while permitting an inquiry into the applicant's ability to perform job-related functions. After a conditional offer has been made but before employment duties begin, FEHA permits such an examination or inquiry only if it is job-related and consistent with business necessity and all entering employees in the same job classification are subject to the same examination or inquiry.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes FEHA's pre-offer and post-offer provisions for "medical or psychological" examinations and inquiries; whether a given physical or agility test qualifies as a "medical or psychological examination or inquiry" within the meaning of this statute, as opposed to a physical agility test that federal interpretive guidance treats as a non-medical, any-stage test, is not resolved by the statutory text this document reviewed and is not addressed by this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself authorize, conduct, or determine the lawfulness of any specific examination or test, and it does not determine whether a conditional offer has been extended in any given case.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(e)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California FEHA, pre-offer prohibition on medical or psychological examination and inquiry
citations.quote: for any employer or employment agency to require any medical or psychological examination of an applicant, to make any medical or psychological inquiry of an applicant, to make any inquiry whether an applicant has a mental disability or physical disability or medical condition, or to make any inquiry regarding the nature or severity of a physical disability, mental disability, or medical condition.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(e)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California FEHA, permitted pre-offer inquiry into job-related functions
citations.quote: an employer or employment agency may inquire into the ability of an applicant to perform job-related functions and may respond to an applicant’s request for reasonable accommodation.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(e)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California FEHA, permitted post-offer examination or inquiry with job-related/business-necessity requirement
citations.quote: an employer or employment agency may require a medical or psychological examination or make a medical or psychological inquiry of a job applicant after an employment offer has been made but prior to the commencement of employment duties, provided that the examination or inquiry is job related and consistent with business necessity and that all entering employees in the same job classification are subject to the same examination or inquiry.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This is an informational sheet about California Labor Code §§ 350-356 — the statutes governing gratuities (tips) paid by patrons to employees of a business, prepared in connection with {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}.

This document explains, using the statutes' own text, what California law says about who owns a gratuity, what an employer or its agents may and may not do with a gratuity, an employer's record-keeping duty for gratuities received, and the timing rule for gratuities patrons pay by credit card. It is informational only. It does not describe {{companyName}}'s own tip-pooling or service-charge policies, does not determine how any particular payment, charge, or pooling arrangement should be classified or handled, and is not a substitute for advice from a qualified attorney.

clauses.title: What Counts as a Gratuity, and Who Owns It
clauses.body: Under California law, a "gratuity" is any tip, gratuity, money, or part of one, that a patron has paid, given, or left for an employee over and above the actual amount the patron owes the business for the services, goods, food, drink, or articles provided. Every gratuity is the sole property of the employee, or employees, to whom it was paid, given, or left.
clauses.gap: This clause covers only the statutory definition in Labor Code § 350(e) and the ownership declaration in § 351(a); it does not address how a specific charge on a specific bill should be classified. The definition's own "over and above the actual amount due the business" language is the statutory hook courts have used to distinguish a voluntary gratuity from a charge that is part of what a patron owes the business (such as certain mandatory service charges) — but this document does not independently verify any case law applying that distinction, for the reason disclosed in the pooling/service-charge clause below.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 350(e)
citations.cite: Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), definitions
citations.quote: “Gratuity” includes any tip, gratuity, money, or part thereof that has been paid or given to or left for an employee by a patron of a business over and above the actual amount due the business for services rendered or for goods, food, drink, or articles sold or served to the patron.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 351(a)
citations.cite: Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), sole property of the employee
citations.quote: Every gratuity is hereby declared to be the sole property of the employee or employees to whom it was paid, given, or left for.

clauses.title: Employer and Agent May Not Take a Gratuity
clauses.body: No employer or agent may collect, take, or receive any gratuity, or part of one, paid, given to, or left for an employee by a patron. An employer may not deduct any amount from wages due an employee on account of a gratuity, and may not require an employee to credit a gratuity, or part of one, against the wages the employer owes that employee. The Labor Commissioner may investigate and issue a citation, or file a civil action, for a gratuity taken or withheld in violation of this rule.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general prohibition in Labor Code § 351(a)-(b). It does not address the statute's separate, non-managerial mandatory tip-pooling practice, which is discussed in the pooling/service-charge clause below along with the honest limitation on this session's case-law research. "Agent" is a defined term (§ 350(d)): every person other than the employer who has authority to hire or discharge, or to supervise, direct, or control, employees — this document does not independently determine which specific job titles or roles at any particular business meet that definition.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 351(a)
citations.cite: Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), prohibition on employer/agent taking gratuities
citations.quote: No employer or agent shall collect, take, or receive any gratuity or a part thereof that is paid, given to, or left for an employee by a patron, or deduct any amount from wages due an employee on account of a gratuity, or require an employee to credit the amount, or any part thereof, of a gratuity against and as a part of the wages due the employee from the employer.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 351(b)
citations.cite: Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), Labor Commissioner enforcement
citations.quote: The Labor Commissioner may investigate and issue a citation or file a civil action for gratuities taken or withheld in violation of this section.

clauses.title: Credit-Card Gratuities: No Fee Deduction, and Payment Timing
clauses.body: When an employer permits patrons to pay gratuities by credit card, the employer must pay employees the full amount of the gratuity the patron indicated on the credit card slip, with no deduction for any credit card payment processing fee or cost the credit card company charges the employer. A gratuity a patron pays by credit card must be paid to the employee no later than the next regular payday following the date the patron authorized the credit card payment.
clauses.gap: This rule is codified in Labor Code § 351(a) (as currently amended), not in § 356 — a research task describing this timing rule as located in § 356 does not match the current statutory text; § 356 is instead the article's legislative purpose declaration, covered in the enforcement/penalties clause below. This clause does not address gratuities paid by other electronic or app-based payment methods that are not, by their terms, a "credit card," and does not independently verify whether any additional or different timing rule applies to those methods.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 351(a)
citations.cite: Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), credit-card gratuities
citations.quote: An employer that permits patrons to pay gratuities by credit card shall pay the employees the full amount of the gratuity that the patron indicated on the credit card slip, without any deductions for any credit card payment processing fees or costs that may be charged to the employer by the credit card company. Payment of gratuities made by patrons using credit cards shall be made to the employees not later than the next regular payday following the date the patron authorized the credit card payment.

clauses.title: Employer Record-Keeping for Gratuities
clauses.body: An employer must keep accurate records of all gratuities it receives, whether received directly or indirectly through a deduction from an employee's wages or otherwise. Those records must be open to inspection at all reasonable hours by the Department of Industrial Relations.
clauses.gap: Section 353's text is general — it requires accurate records of gratuities "received," without a separate itemized-statement mechanism or credit-card-specific record format; this document does not treat § 353 as imposing a credit-card-specific paperwork requirement distinct from the general recording duty, since the current statutory text does not draw that distinction. This section has not been substantively amended since its original 1937 enactment, so it predates the credit-card gratuity provisions now found in § 351(a).

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 353
citations.cite: Labor Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 3, Article 1 (Gratuities), employer record-keeping
citations.quote: Every employer shall keep accurate records of all gratuities received by him, whether received directly from the employee or indirectly by means of deductions from the wages of the employee or otherwise. Such records shall be open to inspection at all reasonable hours by the department.

clauses.title: Mandatory Tip Pooling and Service Charges: What the Statute Does and Does Not Say
clauses.body: The text of Labor Code §§ 350-356 does not itself use the phrase "tip pooling," does not itself list which categories of employee may or may not share in a pooled gratuity, and does not itself define "service charge" as a term separate from "gratuity." The statute's definition of "gratuity" is limited to an amount paid over and above the actual amount a patron owes the business for services, goods, food, drink, or articles — a boundary that bears on whether a particular charge added to a patron's bill is, or is not, a "gratuity" within the statute's own terms.
clauses.gap: This is a genuine and important gap, not a stylistic choice: California courts have developed real, substantial case law addressing which non-managerial employees may be required to share in a mandatory tip pool, and addressing when a mandatory service charge is or is not treated as a "gratuity" under this article — but this session's CourtListener access was rate-limited ("Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") on the very first lightweight search call made for this topic, before any case could be retrieved, with the daily quota not resetting for roughly 5-6 more hours. Rather than wait out the reset or state a case-law rule from memory without verifying it against the actual opinion text, this document proceeds on the statute's text alone and discloses that choice here. Anyone relying on this document should treat the case-law gloss on tip pooling and service charges as an unverified, separate body of law that this document does not state.

citations.quote: “Gratuity” includes any tip, gratuity, money, or part thereof that has been paid or given to or left for an employee by a patron of a business over and above the actual amount due the business for services rendered or for goods, food, drink, or articles sold or served to the patron.

clauses.title: Purpose, Enforcement, and Criminal Penalty
clauses.body: The Legislature has declared that this article's purpose is to prevent fraud on the public in connection with tipping, that the article is passed for a public reason, and that it cannot be overridden by a private agreement. The Department of Industrial Relations enforces the article, and any fines collected under it are paid into the state treasury's general fund. Separately, an employer who violates any provision of this article is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not more than one thousand dollars ($1,000), imprisonment of not more than 60 days, or both.
clauses.gap: Sections 354, 355, and 356 are three separate statutory sections, treated here together because each addresses enforcement or the article's binding, non-waivable character rather than a substantive tipping rule. This document does not independently verify how often, or under what circumstances, the misdemeanor penalty in § 354 has actually been charged or prosecuted, and does not address civil remedies (such as those available through the Labor Commissioner under § 351(b) or through a private civil action) beyond what those other clauses already state.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Receipt
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California Penal Code § 637.7, a criminal statute addressing the use of an electronic tracking device to determine a vehicle's location or movement, and the related civil remedy in Penal Code § 637.2. It states facts about the statutory text as currently in effect. It does not evaluate whether any particular tracking device, vehicle, or practice complies with the law, and does not recommend for or against installing, disabling, disclosing, or consenting to the use of any tracking device on any vehicle.

clauses.title: General Prohibition on Using an Electronic Tracking Device
clauses.body: California Penal Code § 637.7(a) states that no person or entity in California shall use an electronic tracking device to determine the location or movement of a person. This prohibition appears within the Invasion of Privacy chapter of the Penal Code's criminal provisions (Penal Code §§ 630-638.55).
clauses.gap: Subdivision (a)'s prohibition is worded in terms of tracking the location or movement of "a person," while the consent exception in subdivision (b) (addressed in a separate clause of this document) is worded specifically in terms of a vehicle's registered owner, lessor, or lessee. The statute's text does not itself reconcile or further explain that difference in wording, and this clause does not attempt to resolve it. Penal Code § 637.7 is a criminal statute; it does not purport to be a comprehensive statement of all California law touching electronic location tracking (for example, it does not address tracking through a cell phone application or other means not involving a device attached to a vehicle or movable thing, which is discussed in a separate clause of this document).

citations.case: California Penal Code § 637.7(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 637.7(a)
citations.quote: No person or entity in this state shall use an electronic tracking device to determine the location or movement of a person.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Electronic Tracking Device"
clauses.body: Penal Code § 637.7(d) defines "electronic tracking device," for purposes of this section, as any device attached to a vehicle or other movable thing that reveals its location or movement by the transmission of electronic signals. The definition is not limited to any particular technology (such as GPS); it turns on the device being attached to a vehicle or other movable thing and revealing location or movement through transmitted electronic signals.
clauses.gap: The statute does not define "attached," and its text does not specify whether a tracking function built into a vehicle's own factory-installed telematics or infotainment system (as opposed to an aftermarket device physically affixed to the vehicle) falls within this definition. No California appellate decision addressing that question was located or reviewed during this research session; CourtListener's case-law search tool returned a rate-limit error (125 requests/day, already exhausted earlier in this project, reported as not resetting for roughly another 5-6 hours) when queried for this topic, so this clause is based on the statutory text alone rather than on any judicial construction of "attached" or "device."

citations.case: California Penal Code § 637.7(d)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 637.7(d)
citations.quote: As used in this section, “electronic tracking device” means any device attached to a vehicle or other movable thing that reveals its location or movement by the transmission of electronic signals.

clauses.title: Consent Exception, Including Business-Owned Vehicles
clauses.body: Penal Code § 637.7(b) states that the general prohibition in subdivision (a) does not apply when the registered owner, lessor, or lessee of a vehicle has consented to the use of the electronic tracking device with respect to that vehicle. Where a vehicle is registered to, owned by, or leased by a business entity rather than an individual, the business is the registered owner, lessor, or lessee for purposes of this consent requirement, so the business's own consent to tracking a vehicle it owns or leases satisfies subdivision (b), including where an employee or agent of the business is the person who drives or uses that vehicle. Separately, Penal Code § 637.7(c) states that the section does not apply to the lawful use of an electronic tracking device by a law enforcement agency.
clauses.gap: Penal Code § 637.7 does not use the phrase "business entity" and does not contain a separately worded exception naming employer-employee or business-vehicle tracking as such. What is commonly described as a "business vehicle exception" is this clause's own characterization of applying subdivision (b)'s general consent rule (consent by the vehicle's registered owner, lessor, or lessee) to circumstances where a business is that registered owner, lessor, or lessee; the statutory text does not add any further condition to that consent, such as a requirement that the business separately notify the employee or agent who drives the vehicle, and does not distinguish for consent purposes between an owner who drives the vehicle personally and one who authorizes an employee or agent to drive it. This clause does not determine whether a particular business's relationship to a particular vehicle (for example, under a lease, a title held by a financing party, or a vehicle owned by an affiliated entity) actually makes that business the vehicle's "registered owner, lessor, or lessee" within the meaning of subdivision (b), and it does not address whether any other California law outside Penal Code § 637.7 imposes notice or other requirements on tracking a vehicle used by an employee or agent. CourtListener's case-law search was unavailable during this research session (125-request daily quota already exhausted before this topic was researched), so no California appellate decision construing subdivision (b) or applying it to an employer-owned-vehicle fact pattern was located or verified this session; this clause is based on the statutory text alone.

citations.case: California Penal Code § 637.7(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 637.7(b)
citations.quote: This section shall not apply when the registered owner, lessor, or lessee of a vehicle has consented to the use of the electronic tracking device with respect to that vehicle.

citations.case: California Penal Code § 637.7(c)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 637.7(c)
citations.quote: This section shall not apply to the lawful use of an electronic tracking device by a law enforcement agency.

clauses.title: Criminal Penalty and Professional License Consequences
clauses.body: Penal Code § 637.7(e) states that a violation of the section is a misdemeanor. Penal Code § 637.7(f) further states that a violation by a person, business, firm, company, association, partnership, or corporation licensed under Division 3 (commencing with Section 5000) of the Business and Professions Code constitutes grounds for revocation of that license, under the license-revocation provisions of Division 3.
clauses.gap: Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code covers numerous distinct licensed occupations and businesses. This clause does not determine which, if any, specific license category a particular person or business holds, or whether a licensing board would in fact pursue revocation for a given violation; the statute states only that a violation constitutes grounds for revocation, and the revocation process itself is governed by Division 3's own separate procedures, which are not restated in this clause.

citations.case: California Penal Code § 637.7(e)-(f)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 637.7(e), (f)
citations.quote: A violation of this section is a misdemeanor.

clauses.title: Civil Remedy for a Violation of the Invasion of Privacy Chapter
clauses.body: Penal Code § 637.2, part of the same Invasion of Privacy chapter as § 637.7, states that a person injured by a violation of that chapter may bring a civil action against the person who committed the violation, for the greater of $5,000 per violation or three times the plaintiff's actual damages, if any. Section 637.2(b) states that a person may also bring an action, under Code of Civil Procedure Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 525) of Title 7 of Part 2, to enjoin and restrain a violation of the chapter, and may seek the same damages in that same action. Section 637.2(c) states that it is not a necessary prerequisite to such an action that the plaintiff has suffered, or be threatened with, actual damages.
clauses.gap: Section 637.2 applies to a violation of the entire Invasion of Privacy chapter (Penal Code §§ 630-638.55), not solely to § 637.7, and this clause does not determine whether any particular use of a tracking device would in fact be found to violate § 637.7 in the first place — the civil remedy described here becomes available only once a violation of the chapter has been established. Section 637.2(d) also states that the section does not affect a separate body of law (Civil Code Title 4, commencing with § 3425.1, addressing trade secrets); that interaction is noted but not analyzed further here.

citations.case: California Penal Code § 637.2(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(a)
citations.quote: Any person who has been injured by a violation of this chapter may bring an action against the person who committed the violation for the greater of the following amounts: (1) Five thousand dollars ($5,000) per violation. (2) Three times the amount of actual damages, if any, sustained by the plaintiff.

citations.case: California Penal Code § 637.2(c)
citations.cite: Cal. Penal Code § 637.2(c)
citations.quote: It is not a necessary prerequisite to an action pursuant to this section that the plaintiff has suffered, or be threatened with, actual damages.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: {{companyName}} maintains this On-Call and Standby Time information sheet to describe how California wage law approaches time that {{employeeName}} or another employee spends on call or on standby — that is, time before the employee has been called in or has otherwise reported for work. California's wage orders define "hours worked" using a control-based test, and courts have applied that test to determine whether on-call or standby time itself counts as compensable hours worked. This document addresses that question and is separate from this corpus's Reporting Time Pay information sheet, which addresses the narrower situation of an employee who has already reported to work and is then not put to work, or is furnished less than half the usual scheduled day.

clauses.title: The General "Hours Worked" Definition: Subject to Employer Control
clauses.body: Under the applicable California IWC Wage Order, "hours worked" means the time during which an employee is subject to the control of an employer, and includes all the time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so. This control-based definition is not limited to time an employee spends actively performing tasks; it turns on the degree to which the employer controls how {{employeeName}} may use the time in question, including time before {{employeeName}} has been called in to perform any specific task.
clauses.gap: This is a single regulatory subdivision within IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 ("Professional, Technical, Clerical, Mechanical and Similar Occupations"), the same catch-all wage order this corpus's Reporting Time Pay information sheet and other during-employment documents already verify. It was fetched directly from the Department of Industrial Relations at https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf, which was reachable in this session and was fetched twice with two distinct User-Agent strings, producing byte-identical files (confirmed by checksum). The "subject to control" language is a long-standing, frequently-quoted definition, but this session did not independently confirm whether its wording has changed since Wage Order 4-2001's original adoption — the fetched PDF reflects the wage order's currently operative text, which includes minimum wage figures effective through January 1, 2026, well after 2001. Other numbered wage orders (for example, Wage Order 5 for public housekeeping or Wage Order 7 for mercantile employees) contain an hours-worked definition in the same numbered subdivision with materially the same "subject to control" formula, but those other orders were not independently fetched or checked in this session — this clause verifies Wage Order 4-2001 only. This is one state's regulatory text, offered as documented evidence of what California provides — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law, or which industry's wage order, governs a specific employment relationship.

citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(L)
citations.quote: “Hours worked” means the time during which an employee is subject to the control of an employer, and includes all the time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so.

clauses.title: A Different "Hours Worked" Standard for the Health Care Industry
clauses.body: The same wage order provision states a separate definition of "hours worked" for employees in the health care industry: for those employees, "hours worked" means the time during which the employee is suffered or permitted to work for the employer, whether or not required to do so, as interpreted in accordance with the provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act — a formulation that does not repeat the general definition's "subject to the control of an employer" language.
clauses.gap: This is the same regulatory subdivision as the general hours-worked definition cited elsewhere in this document (§ 2(L)) — not an independent source, but a second sentence within it describing a narrower, industry-specific standard. In the source PDF, a footnote about minimum-wage rate adjustments is inserted mid-sentence at a page break, which is why this clause's citations are split into two separately-quoted fragments rather than one continuous quote; nothing was omitted between them beyond that footnote's own text, and each fragment quoted below is independently an exact, contiguous substring of the fetched text. The wage order incorporates federal Fair Labor Standards Act interpretive standards by reference for health-care-industry employees but does not itself state what those federal interpretive standards say about on-call time, and this document does not independently research or summarize federal FLSA on-call case law. "Employees in the health care industry" is itself a separately defined term in this same wage order (§ 2(H)); this document does not independently verify which employees fall within that definition. This is one state's regulatory text; not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employment relationship.

citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(L)
citations.quote: Within the health care industry, the term “hours worked” means the time during which an employee is suffered or permitted to work for the employer, whether or not

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 2(L)

citations.quote: required to do so, as interpreted in accordance with the provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act.

clauses.title: Judicially Developed Factors for Applying the Control Test to On-Call and Standby Time
clauses.body: California courts have applied the wage order's control-based "hours worked" definition to on-call and standby arrangements in decisions addressing a range of industries and on-call structures. In doing so, this body of case law has generally examined a set of practical factors bearing on how much control an employer retains over an employee's own time during an on-call or standby period, including: the extent of any geographic restriction on where the employee may go while on call; how much advance notice or response time the employee is given before being required to report or begin working if called; whether the on-call arrangement leaves the employee free to engage in personal activities during the on-call period; and how frequently the employee is actually called in to work during on-call periods. Courts applying these factors have generally treated the inquiry as one of degree, weighing the factors together against the wage order's control-based definition rather than treating any single factor as automatically dispositive.
clauses.gap: This clause describes considerations that recur in this area of California case law only in general terms; it does not cite, quote, or rely on any specific court decision for the factor list itself, and that description should be read as a general, unverified summary of the doctrine rather than a confirmed holding of any case. This corpus's verification discipline calls for independently confirming case law through CourtListener before citing it. Before drafting this document, a single lightweight CourtListener search call was made to check whether the daily request quota was available; it returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response reporting that CourtListener's daily request cap (125 requests/day) had already been exhausted by earlier research in this same session, with the next availability approximately 5.7 hours out (server-reported: 20,464 seconds) at the time of the attempt. Rather than waiting out that rate limit or presenting an unverified case citation as verified, this document proceeds on a statute/regulation-only basis for this point: it does not cite Mendiola v. CPS Security Solutions, Inc. (2015) 60 Cal.4th 833 — a California Supreme Court decision commonly associated with on-call/standby compensability, addressing on-call sleep time for security guards — or any other specific case, because this session did not independently verify that or any other case's actual holding against its opinion text. The only source cited for this clause is the wage order's own control-based definition, quoted elsewhere in this document and reused here as the anchor text this body of case law interprets; the factor list is offered as a general description of a well-developed area of law, not as a verified quotation from, or holding of, any specific opinion.

citations.quote: “Hours worked” means the time during which an employee is subject to the control of an employer, and includes all the time the employee is suffered or permitted to work, whether or not required to do so.

clauses.title: "Hours Worked" Classification Governs Minimum Wage and Overtime Calculations
clauses.body: Time that qualifies as "hours worked" under the definition described above is counted for purposes of California's minimum wage and overtime requirements in the same way as any other work time. The wage order requires that every employer pay each employee not less than the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked in the payroll period, regardless of whether wages are measured by time, piece, commission, or another method, and separately requires overtime compensation once hours worked in a workday or workweek exceed specified thresholds. This document does not determine, for any particular on-call or standby arrangement involving {{employeeName}}, whether that time in fact meets the "hours worked" definition.
clauses.gap: Section 4(B) (minimum wage) and Section 3(A)(1) (daily/weekly overtime) are separate, independently numbered subdivisions of the same wage order already cited elsewhere in this document for the hours-worked definition, and, in this corpus's existing Reporting Time Pay information sheet, for reporting time pay — they are cited here for the narrower point that both the minimum-wage and overtime provisions operate on whatever time counts as "hours worked," not as independent corroboration of each other. This clause states a structural relationship between provisions; it does not calculate, and does not purport to calculate, wages owed for any actual on-call or standby period, and it does not resolve whether any particular period is "hours worked" in the first place — that threshold determination is the subject of the definition and factors described elsewhere in this document. The overtime quotation below reflects a minor internal spacing irregularity ("one and one- half ( 1½)") present in the source PDF's own text extraction; it is quoted exactly as extracted. This is one state's regulatory text; not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employment relationship.

citations.quote: Every employer shall pay to each employee, on the established payday for the period involved, not less than the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked in the payroll period, whether the remuneration is measured by time, piece, commission, or otherwise.

citations.quote: Such employees shall not be employed more than eight (8) hours in any workday or more than 40 hours in any workweek unless the employee receives one and one- half ( 1½) times such employee’s regular rate of pay for all hours worked over 40 hours in the workweek.

clauses.title: How This Document Differs From Reporting Time Pay
clauses.body: The same wage order's reporting-time-pay provisions include a separate, narrower carve-out: they do not apply to an employee on paid standby status who is called to perform assigned work at a time other than the employee's scheduled reporting time. That carve-out concerns whether the reporting-time-pay formula — which is triggered when an employee is required to report for work and does report — applies to a standby employee's later call-in. It does not address, and does not answer, the separate and broader question addressed in this document: whether time spent on call or on standby, before any call-in occurs, itself counts as compensable "hours worked" under the control-based definition described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This clause cites the same wage order subdivision (§ 5(D)) already quoted in this corpus's Reporting Time Pay information sheet (clause reportingtime_exceptions); it is independently re-verified here from a separate fetch of the same source PDF made in this session, for this document's distinct interpretive point about scope, not as a new or different source. This document does not restate the Reporting Time Pay information sheet's core rule, second-reporting rule, or its other exceptions; readers are directed to that existing document for the requirements it covers. This is one state's regulatory text; not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employment relationship.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This DMCA Anti-Circumvention Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes 17 U.S.C. § 1201, the Digital Millennium Copyright Act's anti-circumvention provisions, which prohibit circumventing a technological measure that effectively controls access to a copyrighted work and prohibit trafficking in tools designed to do so, along with the statutory exemptions most relevant to reverse engineering for interoperability (§ 1201(f)) and encryption research (§ 1201(g)). It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning {{companyName}}'s {{softwareDescription}}. Section 1201 is a distinct part of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act from 17 U.S.C. § 512, the notice-and-takedown safe harbor addressed by this project's existing DMCA Takedown Notice and DMCA Counter-Notification documents: § 512 concerns a service provider's liability for hosting allegedly infringing material and the process for its removal or restoration, while § 1201 concerns circumventing technological access or copy controls, an entirely separate legal question that does not depend on whether any infringement notice has been sent. This Information Sheet is also distinct from, and does not restate, this project's existing trade secret documents: those describe when reverse engineering is or is not "improper means" under state trade secret law, a different body of law from the federal copyright statute described here. This document is a general informational reference describing what the statute says; it is not a court filing, a compliance certification, or legal advice about whether any specific technological measure, product, or activity involving {{softwareDescription}} complies with or falls within an exemption to § 1201.

clauses.title: The General Prohibition on Circumventing an Access Control
clauses.body: 17 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(1)(A) states the statute's core prohibition: no person shall circumvent a technological measure that effectively controls access to a work protected under Title 17 (copyright). This is an access-control prohibition — it applies to bypassing a measure that controls access to a work, and is analytically separate from § 1201(b), which instead addresses trafficking in technology designed to circumvent a measure that protects a copyright owner's specific exclusive rights (such as the right to copy) rather than access itself; § 1201(b) does not contain its own use-based prohibition parallel to (a)(1)(A). Section 1201(a)(2) separately prohibits manufacturing, importing, offering to the public, providing, or otherwise trafficking in technology, products, services, devices, or components that are primarily designed to circumvent an access control, that have only limited other commercially significant purpose, or that are marketed for circumvention use. A person injured by a violation of § 1201 may bring a civil action for that violation under 17 U.S.C. § 1203.
clauses.gap: This describes only the general prohibition in (a)(1)(A) and the related trafficking prohibitions in (a)(2) and (b); it does not restate the statute's own periodic rulemaking exception described in (a)(1)(B) through (E) (under which the Librarian of Congress designates specific classes of works exempt from the (a)(1)(A) prohibition for renewable three-year periods), nor the further statutory exemptions in subsections (d) through (k) (for nonprofit libraries and archives, law enforcement, reverse engineering, encryption research, protection of minors, personally identifying information, and security testing), some of which are described in other clauses of this document. This clause also does not describe 17 U.S.C. § 1204's separate criminal penalties, which apply only to willful violations committed for purposes of commercial advantage or private financial gain and are not addressed by this civil-remedies-oriented document. Whether any specific measure "effectively controls access" to a specific work, or whether specific conduct "circumvents" it, are fact-specific applications of the statutory definitions addressed in a separate clause of this document.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, general prohibition on circumventing a technological access-control measure
citations.quote: No person shall circumvent a technological measure that effectively controls access to a work protected under this title.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 1203(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, civil action for a violation of section 1201
citations.quote: Any person injured by a violation of section 1201 or 1202 may bring a civil action in an appropriate United States district court for such violation.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own Definitions of "Circumvent" and "Effectively Controls Access"
clauses.body: Section 1201(a)(3) supplies the statutory definitions that determine the scope of the access-control prohibition in (a)(1)(A). "To circumvent a technological measure" is defined as descrambling a scrambled work, decrypting an encrypted work, or otherwise avoiding, bypassing, removing, deactivating, or impairing a technological measure, without the authority of the copyright owner. A technological measure "effectively controls access to a work" if, in the ordinary course of its operation, it requires the application of information, or a process or a treatment, with the authority of the copyright owner, to gain access to the work. Subsection (b)(2) defines the parallel terms used for the separate rights-protection trafficking prohibition in (b)(1) in similar, but not identical, terms — "to circumvent protection afforded by a technological measure" there means avoiding, bypassing, removing, deactivating, or otherwise impairing a technological measure, without the "without the authority of the copyright owner" clause that appears in the (a)(3)(A) definition.
clauses.gap: These are the statute's own codified definitions; this clause quotes them but does not summarize how courts have applied terms such as "effectively controls access" or "without the authority of the copyright owner" to particular technologies, because case-law research for this document was not completed (see the interoperability-exemption clause of this document for the specific reason). This clause also does not address whether a particular measure a reader may have in mind is, or is not, a "technological measure" that "effectively controls access" within the statutory definition — that is a technical, fact-specific question the statute's general definitions do not themselves resolve.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of "circumvent a technological measure"
citations.quote: to “circumvent a technological measure” means to descramble a scrambled work, to decrypt an encrypted work, or otherwise to avoid, bypass, remove, deactivate, or impair a technological measure, without the authority of the copyright owner

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(3)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of a measure that "effectively controls access to a work"
citations.quote: a technological measure “effectively controls access to a work” if the measure, in the ordinary course of its operation, requires the application of information, or a process or a treatment, with the authority of the copyright owner, to gain access to the work.

clauses.title: The Reverse-Engineering / Interoperability Exemption Is Conditional, Not Automatic
clauses.body: 17 U.S.C. § 1201(f) creates a reverse-engineering exemption, but it is narrowly conditioned rather than a blanket permission to reverse engineer software. Under § 1201(f)(1), a person may circumvent an access-control measure protecting a computer program only where: (1) the person has lawfully obtained the right to use a copy of that program; (2) the circumvention is for the sole purpose of identifying and analyzing elements of the program necessary to achieve interoperability of an independently created computer program with other programs; (3) those elements have not previously been readily available to the person engaging in the circumvention; and (4) the acts of identification and analysis, to the extent performed, do not themselves constitute copyright infringement. Section 1201(f)(2) separately permits developing and employing the technological means to circumvent — notwithstanding the trafficking prohibitions in (a)(2) and (b) — where necessary to enable that identification and analysis or to enable the resulting interoperability, again only to the extent doing so does not constitute infringement. Section 1201(f)(3) permits making the information or means acquired under (f)(1) or (f)(2) available to others, but only where done solely to enable interoperability of an independently created program, and only to the extent doing so does not infringe copyright or violate other applicable law. Section 1201(f)(4) defines "interoperability" to mean the ability of computer programs to exchange information, and of such programs mutually to use the information that has been exchanged.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes and summarizes the statutory conditions themselves; it does not resolve whether any specific act of reverse engineering satisfies them — questions such as whether a person's purpose was truly "sole," whether particular program elements were "previously readily available," whether a right to use a copy was "lawfully obtained," or whether resulting conduct "constitutes infringement" are fact-specific determinations that published case law addresses (courts have applied § 1201(f) and the related access-control prohibition in disputes involving, for example, video game console and emulator software and printer or garage-door-opener authentication chips). This document does not summarize that case law: CourtListener's case-law search tool was unavailable during this research session (its daily request quota, shared with earlier research in this project, had already been exhausted, returning a rate-limit error on the first attempted query), so no case-law citations were added rather than relying on unverified recollection of specific holdings. This is a statute-only treatment of § 1201(f) as a result.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 1201(f)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, reverse engineering exemption — permitted act of circumvention
citations.quote: a person who has lawfully obtained the right to use a copy of a computer program may circumvent a technological measure that effectively controls access to a particular portion of that program for the sole purpose of identifying and analyzing those elements of the program that are necessary to achieve interoperability of an independently created computer program with other programs, and that have not previously been readily available to the person engaging in the circumvention, to the extent any such acts of identification and analysis do not constitute infringement under this title.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 1201(f)(4) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, definition of "interoperability" for the reverse-engineering exemption
citations.quote: the term “interoperability” means the ability of computer programs to exchange information, and of such programs mutually to use the information which has been exchanged.

clauses.title: The Encryption Research Exemption's Conditions
clauses.body: 17 U.S.C. § 1201(g) creates a separate, similarly conditioned exemption for encryption research, defined in (g)(1)(A) as activities necessary to identify and analyze flaws and vulnerabilities of encryption technologies applied to copyrighted works, conducted to advance the state of knowledge in the field of encryption technology or to assist in developing encryption products. Under § 1201(g)(2), circumventing an access-control measure applied to a published work is not a violation of (a)(1)(A) in the course of good faith encryption research only if: the person lawfully obtained the encrypted copy, phonorecord, performance, or display; the act is necessary to conduct the research; the person made a good faith effort to obtain authorization before the circumvention; and the act does not constitute infringement or violate other applicable law, including the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act provisions in Title 18. Section 1201(g)(3) lists factors relevant to whether a person qualifies for this exemption, including how any resulting information was disseminated, whether the person is engaged in a legitimate course of study or is otherwise appropriately trained or experienced in encryption technology, and whether the person gave the copyright owner notice of the research findings. Section 1201(g)(4) separately permits developing and employing, or sharing with a collaborator, the technological means needed to perform or verify that good faith encryption research.
clauses.gap: This describes only the encryption-research exemption; § 1201 contains several other, separately conditioned exemptions this document does not detail — including for law enforcement and government activity (§ 1201(e)), nonprofit library and archive access for acquisition decisions (§ 1201(d)), protection of personally identifying information (§ 1201(i)), and security testing (§ 1201(j)) — each with its own specific conditions. Whether a particular research activity was conducted in "good faith," was "necessary," or involved a sufficient "good faith effort to obtain authorization" are fact-specific determinations this clause does not resolve for any particular activity.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 1201(g)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, permissible acts of encryption research
citations.quote: it is not a violation of that subsection for a person to circumvent a technological measure as applied to a copy, phonorecord, performance, or display of a published work in the course of an act of good faith encryption research

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 1201(g)(2)(C) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, encryption research condition — good faith effort to obtain authorization
citations.quote: the person made a good faith effort to obtain authorization before the circumvention

clauses.title: Two Different Bodies of Law: DMCA Circumvention Versus Trade Secret Reverse Engineering
clauses.body: 17 U.S.C. § 1201 and California trade secret law address reverse engineering from different legal angles and can reach different results for the same underlying conduct. California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act, Civil Code § 3426.1(a), defines "improper means" for purposes of trade secret misappropriation to include theft, bribery, misrepresentation, breach or inducement of a breach of a duty to maintain secrecy, and espionage, but expressly states that reverse engineering or independent derivation alone is not considered improper means — meaning reverse engineering a product to learn how it works is not, by itself, trade secret misappropriation under California law. Section 1201, by contrast, is a federal copyright statute concerned with a different act: circumventing a technological measure that controls access to a copyrighted work. It does not ask whether the underlying information is a trade secret, and it is not excused merely because the reverse engineering is directed at learning non-secret or independently discoverable information. As a result, an act of reverse engineering that trade secret law would not treat as improper may still involve circumventing a technological access control within the meaning of § 1201(a)(1)(A) — and would require satisfying § 1201(f)'s own, separate conditions (described in another clause of this document) to fall within that statute's reverse-engineering exemption, rather than relying on the trade secret law's more permissive treatment of reverse engineering.
clauses.gap: This clause states an analytical distinction between two separately sourced bodies of law — federal copyright law under § 1201 and California's state trade secret statute — based on each statute's own text; it does not resolve whether any specific act of reverse engineering would, in fact, violate § 1201, satisfy the § 1201(f) exemption, or constitute or avoid trade secret misappropriation, which depends on the specific technology, conduct, and agreements involved. This project's existing Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter document addresses the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act's parallel "improper means" definition (18 U.S.C. § 1839(6)), which is worded similarly to California's statute but is a distinct federal statute not quoted again here to avoid duplication.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, definition of "improper means"
citations.quote: “Improper means” includes theft, bribery, misrepresentation, breach or inducement of a breach of a duty to maintain secrecy, or espionage through electronic or other means. Reverse engineering or independent derivation alone shall not be considered improper means.

citations.case: 17 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, general prohibition on circumventing a technological access-control measure
citations.quote: No person shall circumvent a technological measure that effectively controls access to a work protected under this title.
