clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet explains California's Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit, a statutory tool under Family Code §§ 6550 and 6552 that a caregiver signs on their own, without going to court, to gain authority to enroll {{minorChildName}} in school and consent to school-related medical care. It is fundamentally different from a Nomination of Guardian: a guardian nomination is a written request that a specific person be appointed by a court as {{minorChildName}}'s legal guardian, and it only takes effect once a probate court grants a guardianship. The Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit is not a step toward that court proceeding — it is self-executing the moment {{caregiverName}} signs it, requires no judge, no guardianship case, and no court order, and it never gives {{caregiverName}} legal custody of {{minorChildName}}.

clauses.title: Caregiver and Minor Information
clauses.body: I, {{caregiverName}}, declare that {{minorChildName}} currently lives in my home, that I am 18 years of age or older, and that my relationship to {{minorChildName}} is: {{relationshipToChild}}. I intend to complete and sign California's statutory Caregiver's Authorization Affidavit under Family Code § 6552 so that I may enroll {{minorChildName}} in school and consent to school-related medical care on {{minorChildName}}'s behalf. I understand that {{parentName}}, as {{minorChildName}}'s parent, retains full legal rights regarding {{minorChildName}}'s care, custody, and control, and that this declaration is a preparatory record for my own files rather than the statutory affidavit form itself.

clauses.title: Who May Sign the Affidavit, and What It Authorizes
clauses.body: Any caregiver 18 or older who completes items 1 through 4 of the statutory affidavit form and signs it is authorized to enroll {{minorChildName}} in school and consent to school-related medical care on {{minorChildName}}'s behalf — relative status is not required for this baseline authority. A broader authority, covering the same medical and dental care a court-appointed guardian could authorize under Probate Code § 2353, is available only to a caregiver who additionally qualifies as a statutory "relative" and completes items 5 through 8.
clauses.gap: This describes what the statute itself authorizes; it does not address how a particular school, doctor, or health plan will in practice treat an affidavit, which can vary. A CourtListener case-law search for this topic returned a 429 daily-quota error before any search results could be reviewed, so this clause and the others in this document rely on the statutory text alone, with no case law confirming how courts or agencies apply it in disputed situations.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6550(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A caregiver’s authorization affidavit that meets the requirements of this part authorizes a caregiver 18 years of age or older who completes items 1 to 4, inclusive, of the affidavit provided in Section 6552 and signs the affidavit to enroll a minor in school and consent to school-related medical care on behalf of the minor.

clauses.title: Which Relatives Qualify for the Fuller Medical Authority
clauses.body: Whether {{caregiverName}} can obtain the fuller, guardian-level medical and dental authority under items 5 through 8 of the affidavit turns on the statutory definition of "relative." California Family Code § 6550(h)(2) defines a qualifying relative as an adult related to the child by blood, adoption, or affinity within the fifth degree of kinship, expressly including stepparents, stepsiblings, "great," "great-great," or "grand" relatives, and the spouse of any such relative, even after that marriage has ended by death or dissolution.
clauses.gap: This definition governs only who may use items 5 through 8 of this specific affidavit; it is not necessarily the same definition of "relative" used elsewhere in California law (for example, in relative-placement or probate-guardianship contexts), and this clause does not compare those other definitions.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6550(h)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Relative” means an adult who is related to the child by blood, adoption, or affinity within the fifth degree of kinship, including all stepparents, stepsiblings, and all relatives whose status is preceded by the words “great,” “great-great,” or “grand,” or the spouse of any of the persons specified in this definition, even after the marriage has been terminated by death or dissolution.

clauses.title: What "School-Related Medical Care" Covers
clauses.body: "School-related medical care" — the category of care that any caregiver (relative or not) can consent to using only items 1 through 4 of the affidavit — is statutorily defined to include immunizations, along with physical and medical examinations conducted in schools, when required by state or local governmental authority as a condition of school enrollment or of participating in local-educational-agency extracurricular activities.
clauses.gap: This definition was itself amended effective January 1, 2026 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 664, Sec. 4 (AB 495)), so older descriptions of this statute may not reflect that immunizations are now expressly listed. Naming immunizations in this definition establishes that they fall within the affidavit's baseline authority; it does not by itself override the parent-supersession rule described elsewhere in this statute, which can still control the outcome for a specific immunization decision.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6550(h)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “School-related medical care” means medical care, including immunizations, physical examinations, and medical examinations conducted in schools for pupils, that is required by state or local governmental authority as a condition for school enrollment or participation in local educational agency-related extracurricular activities.

clauses.title: A Parent's Contrary Decision Controls
clauses.body: A caregiver's decision to consent to or refuse medical or dental care for {{minorChildName}} is superseded by any contrary decision of {{parentName}} or another person with legal custody, unless that contrary decision would jeopardize {{minorChildName}}'s life, health, or safety. Separately, before a relative caregiver can rely on the fuller items 5–8 medical/dental authority, the affidavit requires the caregiver to state that they have advised the parent or other legal custodian of their intent to authorize medical care and received no objection, or that they were unable to contact that parent or custodian.
clauses.gap: The statute's supersession rule applies generally to a caregiver's medical and dental decisions; the text does not carve out immunizations as a separate category with its own objection rule, so a general description that the affidavit categorically cannot authorize immunizations over parental objection overstates a rule that is actually broader and applies to medical/dental care generally. Neither this clause nor the underlying statute defines how "jeopardize the life, health, or safety of the minor" is applied in a specific dispute, and the CourtListener search that could have surfaced case law construing that phrase returned a quota-exceeded error rather than results.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6550(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The decision of a caregiver to consent to or to refuse medical or dental care for a minor shall be superseded by any contravening decision of the parent or other person having legal custody of the minor, provided the decision of the parent or other person having legal custody of the minor does not jeopardize the life, health, or safety of the minor.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6552 (statutory affidavit form text, California Legislative Information)
citations.cite: Fam. C. § 6552, item 6
citations.quote: I have advised the parent(s) or other person(s) having legal custody of the minor of my intent to authorize medical care, and have received no objection.

clauses.title: This Affidavit Does Not Create a Guardianship or Legal Custody
clauses.body: The statutory affidavit form itself states that signing it does not affect the legal rights of {{minorChildName}}'s parents or legal guardian over {{minorChildName}}'s care, custody, and control, and does not give {{caregiverName}} legal custody. Consistent with that, the form requires no court seal or judicial signature and does not need to be notarized.
clauses.gap: This describes what the affidavit itself does not do; it says nothing about how a specific existing court order (such as a custody order or a prior guardianship) would interact with a caregiver's use of this affidavit in a given family's situation, which these sections do not address.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6552 (statutory affidavit form text, California Legislative Information)
citations.cite: Fam. C. § 6552, Notice 1
citations.quote: This declaration does not affect the rights of the minor’s parents or legal guardian regarding the care, custody, and control of the minor, and does not mean that the caregiver has legal custody of the minor.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6552 (statutory affidavit form text, California Legislative Information)
citations.cite: Fam. C. § 6552, Warning to Local Educational Agencies and Health Care Service Providers
citations.quote: Warning to Local Educational Agencies and Health Care Service Providers: A seal or signature from a court is not required. This form is not required to be notarized.

clauses.title: When the Affidavit Stops Being Valid, and Who Can Rely On It
clauses.body: If {{minorChildName}} stops living with {{caregiverName}}, {{caregiverName}} is required to notify any school, health care provider, or health care service plan that was given the affidavit, and the affidavit becomes invalid once that notice is received. A separate provision protects anyone who acts in good-faith reliance on the affidavit to provide medical or dental care, without actual knowledge of facts contrary to what the affidavit states: that person is not subject to criminal liability, civil liability to any person, or professional disciplinary action for that reliance, so long as the applicable parts of the affidavit were completed.
clauses.gap: Invalidity under this statute is tied to the school, provider, or plan actually receiving notice that the child no longer lives with the caregiver, not automatically to the date the living arrangement changes, so an affidavit can remain outwardly valid to a recipient who has not yet been notified. The reliance protection runs to the person relying on the affidavit (such as the school or provider), not to the caregiver's own underlying decision to consent to or refuse care.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6550(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If the minor stops living with the caregiver, the caregiver shall notify any school, health care provider, or health care service plan that has been given the affidavit. The affidavit is invalid after the school, health care provider, or health care service plan receives notice that the minor is no longer living with the caregiver.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6550(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A person who acts in good faith reliance on a caregiver’s authorization affidavit to provide medical or dental care, without actual knowledge of facts contrary to those stated on the affidavit, is not subject to criminal liability or to civil liability to any person, and is not subject to professional disciplinary action, for that reliance if the applicable portions of the affidavit are completed.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Escrow Law, Financial Code sections 17000 through 17703, which regulates escrow agents — the licensed corporations that hold funds, documents, and instructions for property transactions on behalf of others. It is prepared in connection with a transaction involving the property at {{propertyAddress}}, between {{sellerName}} and {{buyerName}}. This sheet states what the statute says about who must be licensed as an escrow agent, who is exempt, what escrow instructions generally must contain, and how escrowed funds must be handled. It does not recommend which escrow provider to use, does not evaluate any particular escrow agent's compliance, and is not a substitute for the escrow instructions governing this specific transaction.

clauses.title: What "Escrow" and "Escrow Agent" Mean Under the Statute
clauses.body: The Escrow Law defines "escrow" as a transaction in which one person delivers a written instrument, money, evidence of title, or other thing of value to a third person, to be held until a specified event happens or a condition is performed and then delivered to the party entitled to it. An "escrow agent" is any person engaged in the business of receiving escrows for deposit or delivery, and a "licensee" is any person holding a valid, unrevoked license as an escrow agent. These definitions describe the function performed, not any particular job title — a person who receives and holds funds or documents this way for a property transaction is acting as an escrow agent under the statute regardless of what they call themselves.
clauses.gap: The statutory definition of "escrow" in Section 17003(a) is written broadly around real or personal property transactions generally; Section 17003(b) separately extends the term to certain Internet-based transactions in personal property or services, a variant this clause does not detail because it falls outside a real-property escrow context. Also, meeting this functional definition does not by itself determine whether a license is required — that depends on whether one of the statutory exemptions applies, which is addressed in a separate clause.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17003(a) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17003(a)
citations.quote: “Escrow” means any transaction in which one person, for the purpose of effecting the sale, transfer, encumbering, or leasing of real or personal property to another person, delivers any written instrument, money, evidence of title to real or personal property, or other thing of value to a third person to be held by that third person until the happening of a specified event or the performance of a prescribed condition, when it is then to be delivered by that third person to a grantee, grantor, promisee, promisor, obligee, obligor, bailee, bailor, or any agent or employee of any of the latter.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17004 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17004
citations.quote: “Escrow agent” means any person engaged in the business of receiving escrows for deposit or delivery.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17005 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17005
citations.quote: “Licensee” means any person holding a valid, unrevoked license as an escrow agent.

clauses.title: Licensing Requirement for Escrow Agents
clauses.body: California law makes it unlawful for a person to engage in business as an escrow agent within the state except through a corporation organized for that purpose and licensed by the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation. A licensed escrow agent corporation must also deposit and maintain a bond — at least $25,000, and more depending on the size of its trust fund obligations — as a condition of holding the license.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general licensing rule; it does not cover the statute's separate exemption list, which removes certain categories of persons from the licensing requirement entirely for escrow work performed within their own exempt capacity — that is addressed in a separate clause. It also does not describe the corporation's other ongoing licensing conditions (minimum tangible net worth, qualified-personnel staffing, and periodic examination by the Commissioner), which this sheet does not exhaustively catalog.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17200 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17200
citations.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to engage in business as an escrow agent within this state except by means of a corporation duly organized for that purpose licensed by the commissioner as an escrow agent.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17202(a) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17202(a)
citations.quote: At the time of filing an application for an escrow agent’s license, the applicant shall deposit with the commissioner a bond satisfactory to the commissioner in the amount of at least twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000).

clauses.title: Persons Exempt From the Escrow Agent License Requirement
clauses.body: The Escrow Law does not apply to certain categories of persons handling property transactions in their own separate capacity: banks, trust companies, building and loan or savings and loan associations, credit unions, and insurance companies; an attorney licensed to practice law in California who has a bona fide client relationship with a principal in the transaction and who is not actively engaged in the business of an escrow agent; a person whose principal business is preparing abstracts or title searches used as the basis for a title insurance policy; and a real estate broker performing acts in the course of, or incidental to, a real estate transaction in which the broker is an agent or party and is performing an act for which a real estate license is required. None of these exempt categories needs a separate escrow license to handle funds or documents within that described role. The person invoking an exemption carries the burden of proving it applies.
clauses.gap: The attorney and real estate broker exemptions are narrower than a blanket profession-based exemption: the statute itself labels them "personal to the persons listed," meaning that person cannot delegate the exempt escrow work to others (beyond staff under their own direct supervision), and neither exemption is available at all for an arrangement entered into for the purpose of performing escrows for more than one business. The title-company exemption likewise applies only to the specific business of preparing abstracts or title searches underlying a title policy, not to title companies generally. This sheet cannot determine whether a given attorney, broker, or title company's actual conduct in a particular transaction stays within its exempt role or crosses into operating an unlicensed escrow business — that is a case-by-case factual question the statute leaves to be proven.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17006(a) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17006(a)
citations.quote: (a) This division does not apply to: (1) Any person doing business under any law of this state or the United States relating to banks, trust companies, building and loan or savings and loan associations, credit unions, or insurance companies. (2) Any person licensed to practice law in California who has a bona fide client relationship with a principal in a real estate or personal property transaction and who is not actively engaged in the business of an escrow agent. (3) Any person whose principal business is that of preparing abstracts or making searches of title that are used as a basis for the issuance of a policy of title insurance by a company doing business under any law of this state relating to insurance companies. (4) Any broker licensed by the Real Estate Commissioner while performing acts in the course of or incidental to a real estate transaction in which the broker is an agent or a party to the transaction and in which the broker is performing an act for which a real estate license is required.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17006(b) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17006(b)
citations.quote: (b) The exemptions provided for in paragraphs (2) and (4) of subdivision (a) are personal to the persons listed, and those persons shall not delegate any duties other than duties performed under the direct supervision of those persons. Notwithstanding the provisions of this subdivision, the exemptions provided for in paragraphs (2) and (4) of subdivision (a) are not available for any arrangement entered into for the purpose of performing escrows for more than one business.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17006.5 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17006.5
citations.quote: In any proceeding under this law, the burden of proving an exemption or an exception from a definition is upon the person claiming it.

clauses.title: How Escrow Instructions Function Under the Statute
clauses.body: The statute regulates the mechanics of escrow instructions themselves, not just who may act as an escrow agent. An escrow agent may not solicit or accept an escrow instruction containing a blank to be filled in after it is signed or initialed, and no addition, deletion, or alteration may be made afterward unless it is signed or initialed by everyone who signed or initialed the original. A copy of each executed escrow instruction, and of any amendment or supplement, must be delivered to everyone who executed it. And every written escrow instruction executed by a buyer or seller — whether prepared by a licensed escrow agent or by a person exempt under Section 17006, such as an attorney or real estate broker — must contain a statement, in not less than 10-point type, identifying the license name and the department issuing the license or authority under which the preparer is operating.
clauses.gap: The 10-point-type disclosure requirement in Section 17403.4 does not apply to supplemental escrow instructions or modifications to escrow instructions, so a later amendment to instructions for a particular property transaction is not independently required to repeat that disclosure. This clause describes the instructions' required form and delivery; it does not address their substantive content requirements (such as what escrow instructions must specify about the terms of closing), which the statute leaves largely to what the commissioner's regulations and the parties' own agreement require rather than prescribing in the text reviewed here.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17403.2(a) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17403.2(a)
citations.quote: No person subject to this division shall solicit or accept an escrow instruction or amended or supplemental escrow instruction containing any blank to be filled in after signing or initialing of the escrow instruction or amended or supplemental escrow instruction, nor permit any person to make any addition to, deletion from, or alteration of an escrow instruction or amended or supplemental escrow instruction, unless the addition, deletion or alteration is signed or initialed by all persons who had signed or initialed the escrow instruction or amended or supplemental escrow instruction prior to the addition, deletion or alteration.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17403.3(a) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17403.3(a)
citations.quote: At the time of execution a copy of each escrow instruction or amended or supplemental escrow instruction shall be delivered to all persons executing the same.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17403.4 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17403.4
citations.quote: All written escrow instructions and all escrow instructions transmitted electronically over the Internet executed by a buyer or seller, whether prepared by a person subject to this division or by a person exempt from this division under Section 17006, shall contain a statement in not less than 10-point type which shall include the license name and the name of the department issuing the license or authority under which the person is operating.

clauses.title: Trust-Fund Handling Requirements
clauses.body: Money deposited in escrow to be delivered at closing or on another contingency must be deposited and maintained in a noninterest-bearing demand or checking account (or a qualifying noninterest-bearing account subject to immediate withdrawal) at a bank, state or federal savings institution, or an approved industrial loan company. Funds may later be moved to an interest-bearing account only if kept separate, distinct, and apart from the escrow agent's own funds. Deposited funds must be designated as "trust funds," "escrow accounts," or some other appropriate name showing they do not belong to the escrow agent. The statute reinforces that separation by making escrow or trust funds unreachable by a money judgment against the escrow agent and by providing that such funds are never to be treated as an asset of the escrow agent, and separately by making it unlawful to knowingly keep funds under a "trust funds" or "escrow accounts" label unless they are actual escrow or trust funds.
clauses.gap: These trust-fund handling rules govern licensed escrow agents and persons otherwise subject to the division; the statute defines "trust funds" and "escrow accounts," for purposes of these sections, to include all funds an escrow agent is required to hold under any federal or state law or governmental-agency requirement, which is broader than only funds received directly in a transaction's escrow. This clause does not address the separate, more detailed requirements for maintaining distinct trust accounts by licensed location and by escrow type (Sections 17409(b) and 17409.1), which go beyond the general deposit and labeling rules described here.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17409(a) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17409(a)
citations.quote: All moneys deposited in escrow to be delivered upon the close of the escrow or upon any other contingency shall be deposited and maintained in a noninterest-bearing demand or checking account in a bank, a state or federal savings bank, or a state or federal savings association or in a noninterest-bearing account subject to immediate withdrawal in an industrial loan company insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and approved to receive those moneys by the commissioner.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17410(a) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17410(a)
citations.quote: Escrow or trust funds are not subject to enforcement of a money judgment arising out of any claim against the licensee or person acting as escrow agent, and in no instance shall such escrow or trust funds be considered or treated as an asset of the licensee or person performing the functions of an escrow agent.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17411 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17411
citations.quote: No person shall knowingly keep or cause to be kept any funds or money in any bank or state or federal savings and loan association under the heading of “trust funds” or “escrow accounts” or any other name designating such funds or money as belonging to the clients of any escrow agency, except actual escrow or trust funds deposited with such agency.

clauses.title: Consequences for Misappropriating Escrow Funds or Operating Without a License
clauses.body: The Escrow Law backs its trust-fund and licensing rules with penalties. A director, officer, stockholder, trustee, employee, or agent of an escrow agent who abstracts or willfully misappropriates money, funds, trust obligations, or property deposited with an escrow agent is guilty of a felony. More generally, a person who willfully violates any provision of the Escrow Law, or any rule or order issued under it, is subject on conviction to a fine of up to $10,000, imprisonment in county jail for up to one year (or, in some cases, imprisonment under Penal Code section 1170(h)), or both. The statute also authorizes a separate civil penalty of up to $2,500 per violation, recoverable by the Commissioner in a civil action, and states that these remedies are not exclusive of one another.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the penalty provisions found in the text reviewed; it does not describe every enforcement tool available to the Commissioner (for example, license suspension or revocation proceedings, or the Commissioner's separate authority to order a person to desist from unlicensed escrow activity), which operate independently of these criminal and civil penalty sections. A CourtListener case-law search to confirm how these penalty provisions have actually been applied or interpreted by California courts could not be completed for this sheet: CourtListener's daily search quota (125 requests/day) was already exhausted when checked, so no case law is cited here — this clause relies on the statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17414(b) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17414(b)
citations.quote: Any director, officer, stockholder, trustee, employee, or agent of an escrow agent, who abstracts or willfully misappropriates money, funds, trust obligations or property deposited with an escrow agent, is guilty of a felony.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17700 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17700
citations.quote: Any person who willfully violates any provision of this division, or who willfully violates any rule or order under this division, shall, upon conviction, be fined not more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000), imprisoned in a county jail for not more than one year, imprisoned pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1170 of the Penal Code, or be punished by both that fine and imprisonment, but no person may be imprisoned for the violation of any rule or order unless he or she had knowledge of the rule or order.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 17701(a) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Financial Code § 17701(a)
citations.quote: Any person who violates any provision of this division, or who violates any rule or order under this division, shall be liable for a civil penalty not to exceed two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500) for each violation, which shall be assessed and recovered in a civil action brought in the name of the people of the State of California by the commissioner in any court of competent jurisdiction.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
clauses.body: This information sheet was prepared for reference in connection with the transaction involving {{propertyAddress}} and does not itself constitute escrow instructions, a legal opinion, or advice about which escrow arrangement to use. Prepared and reviewed as of {{dateSigned}}, at {{cityState}}.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: California's Commercial Financing Disclosure Law, Financial Code sections 22800 through 22807, requires many non-bank providers of commercial financing — including factoring companies, asset-based lenders, and merchant cash advance and other online lenders — to give a written disclosure to the recipient of the financing before the transaction is consummated. The law was originally enacted as SB 1235 (2018) and has since been amended, including changes effective January 1, 2024 (SB 33) and January 1, 2026 (SB 362). This information sheet describes the law's general framework as it could apply to financing between {{companyName}} and {{recipientName}}; it states facts about what the statute requires and does not determine whether the law applies to any specific offer of financing involving {{companyName}} or {{recipientName}}, or complete the disclosure itself.

clauses.title: What Counts as "Commercial Financing"
clauses.body: The disclosure law applies to "commercial financing," a defined term covering an accounts receivable purchase transaction (including factoring), an asset-based lending transaction, a commercial loan, a commercial open-end credit plan, or a lease financing transaction — but only when the financing is intended by the recipient for use primarily for something other than personal, family, or household purposes. If financing from {{companyName}} to {{recipientName}} fits one of these categories and is for a business purpose, it falls within this defined term, subject to the exemptions and dollar threshold described elsewhere in this law.
clauses.gap: The statute lets a provider rely on the recipient's own signed, written statement of intended use to determine whether financing is "commercial" rather than personal, family, or household in nature, and does not require the provider to verify that the proceeds were actually used that way. This document doesn't determine what use the recipient intends for any particular financing, or whether a signed purpose statement exists for it — both are facts specific to the transaction.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22800(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: “Commercial financing” means an accounts receivable purchase transaction, including factoring, asset-based lending transaction, commercial loan, commercial open-end credit plan, or lease financing transaction intended by the recipient for use primarily for other than personal, family, or household purposes.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22800(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: The provider shall not be required to ascertain that the proceeds of the commercial financing are used in accordance with the statement of intended purposes.

clauses.title: Dollar Threshold for a Covered "Recipient"
clauses.body: The disclosure law only reaches offers presented to a "recipient" as the statute defines that term: a person presented a specific commercial financing offer that is equal to or less than $500,000. An offer above that amount is outside the disclosure law's coverage, regardless of what kind of commercial financing is involved.
clauses.gap: This $500,000 ceiling on the "recipient" definition is a separate figure from the $5,000 floor that appears in the statute's definition of a "commercial loan" specifically; that $5,000 figure only sets the minimum principal amount for a loan to count as a "commercial loan" and does not set a floor on disclosure coverage generally — financing structured as an accounts receivable purchase, lease financing, or open-end credit plan is not subject to that $5,000 minimum. This document doesn't calculate the dollar amount of any specific offer to the recipient or confirm it falls at or under the $500,000 ceiling.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22800(n) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: “Recipient” means a person who is presented a specific commercial financing offer by a provider that is equal to or less than five hundred thousand dollars ($500,000).

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22800(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: “Commercial loan” means a loan of a principal amount of five thousand dollars ($5,000) or more, or any loan under an open-end credit plan, the proceeds of which are intended by the recipient for use primarily for other than personal, family, or household purposes.

clauses.title: Transactions and Providers Exempted From the Disclosure Law
clauses.body: The disclosure law does not apply to a provider that is itself a depository institution (a bank, savings association, or credit union) or a federal Farm Credit Act lender, to a commercial financing transaction secured by real property, to certain vehicle-dealer financing of at least $50,000, or to a provider that makes only one commercial financing transaction in California in a 12-month period, or that makes five or fewer such transactions in that period where they are incidental to that provider's business.
clauses.gap: The depository-institution exemption applies to the entity that is itself a bank, savings association, or credit union — it does not automatically exempt a separate, nondepository company that arranges financing on a bank's behalf. The statute's definition of "provider" expressly reaches a nondepository institution that enters a written agreement with a depository institution to arrange for the depository institution's extension of commercial financing through an online lending platform the nondepository institution administers. Whether a particular provider is itself a depository institution, arranges financing for one under such an agreement, or fits one of the other listed exemptions is a fact this document doesn't determine.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22801(a),(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: Any person who makes no more than one commercial financing transaction in California in a 12-month period or any person who makes five or fewer commercial financing transactions in California in a 12-month period that are incidental to the business of the person relying upon the exemption.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22800(m) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: “Provider” also includes a nondepository institution, which enters into a written agreement with a depository institution to arrange for the extension of commercial financing by the depository institution to a recipient via an online lending platform administered by the nondepository institution.

clauses.title: Required Disclosure Content and Timing
clauses.body: A provider subject to the law must disclose the total amount of funds provided, the total dollar cost of the financing, the term or estimated term, the method, frequency, and amount of payments, a description of prepayment policies, and the total cost of the financing expressed as an annualized rate. The disclosure must be given at the time the provider extends a specific commercial financing offer, and the provider must obtain the recipient's signature on the disclosure before consummating the transaction — meaning {{companyName}}, if it is a covered provider, cannot close a covered transaction with {{recipientName}} until {{recipientName}} has signed the disclosure.
clauses.gap: The statute names these six disclosure items but does not itself define how each is calculated or formatted — that detail is delegated to regulations the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation must adopt, described in a separate clause of this document. This document verifies only the Financial Code statutory text; it does not independently verify the commissioner's current implementing regulations, which supply the operative definitions, calculation methods, and formatting requirements for each disclosure item.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22802(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: A provider subject to this division shall disclose all of the information in subdivision (b) or in Section 22803, if applicable, to a recipient at the time of extending a specific commercial financing offer to that recipient, and shall obtain the recipient’s signature on the disclosure before consummating the commercial financing transaction.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22802(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: (1) The total amount of funds provided. (2) The total dollar cost of the financing. (3) The term or estimated term. (4) The method, frequency, and amount of payments. (5) A description of prepayment policies. (6) The total cost of the financing expressed as an annualized rate.

clauses.title: Alternative Disclosure for Factoring and Asset-Based Lending
clauses.body: A provider offering factoring or asset-based lending under a general agreement — one that describes the general terms and conditions of the financing that will occur under it, rather than a single specific transaction — may give an alternative, example-based disclosure instead of the standard six-item disclosure. That alternative illustrates, for a given amount of accounts receivable, what an amount financed, total dollar cost, term, payment method and amount, prepayment policy, and annualized rate would look like for a transaction under the general agreement.
clauses.gap: This alternative is optional ("may provide") and is available only to a factoring or asset-based lending provider using a general agreement of this kind; it is not available to other kinds of commercial financing, and a factoring or asset-based lending provider that doesn't use a qualifying general agreement must still use the standard disclosure. This document doesn't determine which disclosure approach a particular provider used or is required to use for any specific transaction.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22803 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: As an alternative to the disclosures required in subdivision (b) of Section 22802, a provider who offers commercial financing that is factoring or asset-based lending and that offers the recipient an agreement that describes the general terms and conditions of the commercial financing transaction that will occur under the agreement, may provide the following disclosures as an example of a transaction that could occur under the general agreement for a given amount of accounts receivables

clauses.title: Disclosure Requirements Depend on Commissioner Regulations
clauses.body: The statute directs the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation to adopt regulations defining and setting calculation and format requirements for each disclosure item, including the annualized rate disclosure. By the statute's own terms, a provider is not required to comply with the disclosure requirements at all until the commissioner's final regulations are adopted and become effective.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn solely from the Financial Code text fetched from the California Legislative Information website; it does not independently verify the commissioner's actual regulations (which would appear in the California Code of Regulations, not the Financial Code) or confirm their current effective status. Separately, a lightweight CourtListener case-law search performed for this document returned a 429 quota-exceeded response (125 requests/day limit) before any case law could be checked, so this entire document is statute-only — no judicial interpretation of any provision of this law was reviewed, and the gaps identified here rest only on the statutory text itself.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22804(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: The commissioner shall adopt regulations governing the disclosures described in paragraphs (1) to (5), inclusive, of subdivision (b) of Section 22802 and subdivisions (a) to (e), inclusive, of Section 22803.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22804(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: A provider shall not be required to comply with the disclosure requirements of this division until the final regulations are adopted by the commissioner pursuant to this section and become effective on the applicable date described in Section 11343.4 of the Government Code.

clauses.title: APR Terminology, Safe Harbor, and Enforcement
clauses.body: The law also addresses how providers may describe financing cost outside the required disclosure itself, and how the disclosure law is enforced. A provider is barred from using the term "interest" or "rate" in a way that could reasonably mislead a recipient, and once a provider states a charge, pricing metric, or financing amount for a specific offer during an application process, it must also state the annual percentage rate using the term "annual percentage rate" or the acronym "APR." No provision of the law imposes liability on a provider solely because the actual APR later charged differs from an estimated APR that was disclosed consistent with the commissioner's regulations, orders, or written interpretive opinions. A violation by a provider licensed under the California Financing Law is treated as a California Financing Law violation, and a violation by a provider not subject to that law is treated as an unfair, deceptive, or abusive act or practice under the California Consumer Financial Protection Law.
clauses.gap: The anti-deception, APR-terminology, and enforcement provisions cited here (Financial Code sections 22806 and 22807, and the current section 22805) were added or renumbered by SB 362, effective January 1, 2026 — they go well beyond the disclosure mechanics of the original 2018 SB 1235 enactment that the research brief for this document was framed around, and are recent enough that this document did not find (and did not attempt to search for, given the CourtListener quota limit noted elsewhere in this document) any court decisions interpreting them. Section 22805 itself was renumbered from former Section 22806 by that same 2025 legislation, so a reader consulting an older source that cites "Financial Code section 22806" for the APR safe-harbor rule is looking at a since-superseded section number for that particular rule.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22806(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: A provider shall not use the term “interest” or “rate” in a deceptive way that could reasonably result in the recipient being misled.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22805 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: No provision of this division imposes any liability on a provider as a result of the actual Annual Percentage Rate (APR) charged by a provider differing from the Estimated APR disclosed in conformity with any regulation, order, or written interpretive opinion of the commissioner or any such opinion of the Attorney General

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22807(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Financial Code
citations.quote: A violation of this division by a person licensed under the California Financing Law (Division 9 (commencing with Section 22000)) shall be deemed a violation of the California Financing Law if the violation relates to a commercial financing transaction that is subject to the California Financing Law.

clauses.title: What This Document Covers and How It Differs from a Restraining Order
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Address Confidentiality Program, known as "Safe at Home," which the Secretary of State administers under Government Code sections 6205 through 6210.7 (Chapter 3.1, covering victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, child abduction, and elder or dependent adult abuse) and sections 6215 through 6216.6 (Chapter 3.2, covering reproductive and gender-affirming health care providers, employees, volunteers, and patients, and other individuals who face threats or violence because of work for a public entity, such as election workers). Safe at Home is an administrative program run by the Secretary of State's office, not a court proceeding: a program participant applies to have mail routed through a substitute address that state and local agencies may accept in place of {{applicantName}}'s actual residential address on public records. It is a separate mechanism from this project's Domestic Violence Restraining Order (DVRO) document: a DVRO is a court order directing a named respondent's conduct toward a petitioner and requires a judge's finding of abuse under Family Code section 6200 et seq., while Safe at Home issues no order against anyone, names no respondent, and does not depend on obtaining or having obtained a restraining order. The two can be used together or separately, and Safe at Home's eligibility categories are broader than domestic violence alone. This document is informational; it does not itself enroll {{applicantName}} in the program, and only the Secretary of State can approve an application.

clauses.title: Eligibility Under the Core Safe at Home Chapter (Chapter 3.1)
clauses.body: Government Code section 6205(a) states the Legislature's finding that persons escaping actual or threatened domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, child abduction, or elder or dependent adult abuse frequently change names or addresses to avoid their assailants, and that Chapter 3.1 exists to let state and local agencies respond to public records requests without disclosing a program participant's changed name or location. Section 6206(a)(1)(A) requires the applicant's sworn statement that {{applicantName}}, or the minor or incapacitated person on whose behalf the application is made, is a victim of one of those same six categories -- domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, child abduction, or elder or dependent adult abuse -- or is a household member of such a victim, unless the applicant is the perpetrator. {{eligibilityCategory}} states which of these categories the application would be based on.
clauses.gap: Section 6205(a) and section 6206(a)(1)(A) are two different subdivisions within the same statutory section family but not the same section -- 6205 is a legislative-findings section and 6206 is the separate application-and-certification section -- so this is not a single-section citation, though both are within Chapter 3.1. This is California's own statute, used as evidence of what that state's program covers -- not a claim that every state with an address confidentiality program uses the same six categories, or that any other state recognizes these same terms. Child abduction and elder or dependent adult abuse are included as independent eligibility categories under this chapter alongside the more commonly cited domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, and human trafficking; a household member of a qualifying victim may also independently qualify. This clause does not resolve whether a specific applicant's facts satisfy any category -- that determination is made by the Secretary of State on the application, not by this document.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 6205(a)
citations.cite: legislative findings and purpose of Chapter 3.1
citations.quote: The Legislature finds that persons attempting to escape from actual or threatened domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, child abduction, or elder or dependent adult abuse frequently establish new names or addresses to prevent their assailants or probable assailants from finding them.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 6206(a)(1)(A)
citations.cite: the six qualifying victim categories for the sworn application statement
citations.quote: is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, child abduction, or elder or dependent adult abuse, or is a household member of a victim who is making or has made an application pursuant to this section, unless the applicant is the perpetrator of the crime that provided the basis for that victim’s application.

clauses.title: Eligibility Under the Reproductive Health Care and Public Entity Worker Chapter (Chapter 3.2)
clauses.body: A second, separately enacted Safe at Home chapter -- Government Code sections 6215 through 6216.6 -- covers different applicant categories than Chapter 3.1. Section 6215(b) states the Legislature's finding that, since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, individuals who work with the public face increasing harassment, threats, and violence because of that work, giving as examples public health officers and workers, election workers, school board members, and code enforcement officers. Section 6215.1(c) defines a "designated health care services provider, employee, volunteer, or patient" as a gender-affirming health care or gender-affirming mental health care provider, employee, volunteer, or patient, or a reproductive health care services provider, employee, volunteer, or patient. Chapter 3.2 also allows an application on the separate basis that {{applicantName}} is employed by, or performs work under a contract with, a public entity and faces threats, violence, or harassment from the public because of that work.
clauses.gap: Section 6215(b) is a legislative-findings subdivision and section 6215.1(c) is a separate definitions section, so this is not a single-section citation. Election workers are named in section 6215(b) only as an illustrative example within the Legislature's findings, not as a standalone defined eligibility category with its own subsection; the operative eligibility basis in section 6215.2(b) is the broader category of a person who works for, or under contract with, a public entity and faces threats or violence because of that work, which sweeps in election workers along with the other named examples and others not named. This chapter also covers gender-affirming health care providers, employees, volunteers, and patients as of a 2025 amendment (Stats. 2025, Ch. 679), which is broader than "reproductive health care" alone; a research brief describing this program only as covering reproductive health care and election workers would understate both the health-care-services definition and the general public-entity-worker basis. This is California's own statute and does not describe any other state's program.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 6215(b)
citations.cite: legislative findings on public entity workers facing threats and violence
citations.quote: Other individuals are also subject to harassment, threats, and acts of violence from the public because of their work with the public, which have become more frequent and serious since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. They include, but are not limited to, public health officers and public health workers, election workers, school board members, and code enforcement officers.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 6215.1(c)
citations.cite: definition of a designated health care services provider, employee, volunteer, or patient
citations.quote: “Designated health care services provider, employee, volunteer, or patient” means a gender-affirming health care or a gender-affirming mental health care provider, employee, volunteer, or patient, or a reproductive health care services provider, employee, volunteer, or patient.

clauses.title: How an Application Is Filed and Certified
clauses.body: Under Government Code section 6206(a), an applicant to the core Chapter 3.1 program must complete the application in person at a community-based victims' assistance program, or a community-based program serving victims of elder or dependent adult abuse, and the application process must include meeting with a victims' assistance counselor and receiving orientation information about the program. Section 6206(d) provides that once the Secretary of State receives a properly completed application, the Secretary of State certifies the applicant as a program participant, and applicants are certified for four years from the filing date unless certification is withdrawn or invalidated earlier. {{applicantName}} would file the application with the Secretary of State's office, not with a court.
clauses.gap: Section 6206(a) and section 6206(d) are two subdivisions of the same statutory section, so this is a single-section citation for that pairing. Chapter 3.2 (the reproductive health care and public entity worker chapter) has its own, separately worded application and in-person counseling requirement in section 6215.2(a)-(b) that this clause does not quote; the four-year certification period stated here from section 6206(d) applies to the Chapter 3.1 program, and Chapter 3.2 applies a similar four-year period with a shorter six-month period for designated health care services facility volunteers, per section 6215.2(f). This clause does not describe the specific documentary evidence requirements (police records, sworn statements, and similar supporting materials) in either chapter's application in full detail. This is California's own statute; it does not describe any other state's application procedure.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 6206(a)
citations.cite: in-person application requirement and counselor orientation
citations.quote: An application shall be completed in person at a community-based victims’ assistance program or a community-based assistance program that serves victims of elder or dependent adult abuse pursuant to the Elder Abuse and Dependent Adult Civil Protection Act (Chapter 11 (commencing with Section 15600) of Part 3 of Division 9 of the Welfare and Institutions Code). The application process shall include a requirement that the applicant meet with a victims’ assistance counselor and receive orientation information about the program.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 6206(d)
citations.cite: certification upon a properly completed application and the four-year certification period
citations.quote: Upon filing a properly completed application, the Secretary of State shall certify the applicant as a program participant. Applicants shall be certified for four years following the date of filing, unless the certification is withdrawn or invalidated before that date.

clauses.title: Use of the Substitute Address with State and Local Agencies
clauses.body: Government Code section 6207(a) provides that when a state or local agency creates a public record, the agency must accept the Secretary of State's designated substitute address as a program participant's address, unless the Secretary of State has determined that the agency has a bona fide statutory or administrative requirement for the actual address and will use that address only for that purpose without public dissemination. Section 6207(b) applies the same substitute-address requirement when an agency modifies or maintains a public record, but expressly excludes birth, fetal death, death, and marriage records registered under the Health and Safety Code. Section 6207(c) additionally allows a program participant to use the designated address as a work address, and section 6207(d) requires the Secretary of State's office to forward first-class mail and government mail to program participants.
clauses.gap: Section 6207(a) and section 6207(b) are subdivisions of the same statutory section, so this is a single-section citation for that pairing. This clause quotes the general public-record acceptance rule and its vital-records carve-out; it does not restate the separate Vehicle Code provisions on DMV record suppression referenced in section 6207(e), or the parallel but independently worded agency-acceptance rule for the Chapter 3.2 program in section 6215.5. "Public record" and "bona fide statutory or administrative requirement" are not further defined within this section, and this clause does not resolve how a specific agency would apply that standard to a specific applicant's situation. This is California's own statute and describes only California agencies' obligations.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 6207(a)
citations.cite: acceptance of the substitute address when creating a public record
citations.quote: When creating a public record, state and local agencies shall accept the address designated by the Secretary of State as a program participant’s substitute address, unless the Secretary of State has determined both of the following: (1) The agency has a bona fide statutory or administrative requirement for the use of the address which would otherwise be confidential under this chapter. (2) This address will be used only for those statutory and administrative purposes and shall not be publicly disseminated.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 6207(b)
citations.cite: the same rule when modifying or maintaining a public record, excluding vital records
citations.quote: When modifying or maintaining a public record, excluding the record of any birth, fetal death, death, or marriage registered under Division 102 (commencing with Section 102100) of the Health and Safety Code, state and local agencies shall accept the address designated by the Secretary of State as a program participant’s substitute address, unless the Secretary of State has determined both of the following:

clauses.title: Confidentiality of a Participant's Actual Address and Effect on Discovery
clauses.body: Government Code section 6208 provides that the Secretary of State may not make a program participant's actual address, or a participant's name change, available for inspection or copying, except if requested by a law enforcement agency, directed by a court order to a person named in the order, or after certification has been terminated for use of false information to qualify for the program. Separately, section 6209.7(b)(1) provides that a participant's registration in the program creates a rebuttable presumption that disclosing information about the participant's location and activities -- including current and past residential, work, or school addresses -- would lead to discovery of the participant's actual address, would endanger the participant's safety, and is not authorized; this presumption governs discovery requests generally, including under the Civil Discovery Act.
clauses.gap: Section 6208 and section 6209.7(b)(1) are two different statutory sections, so no single-section disclosure applies to that pairing. Section 6209.7 also states that the presumption is rebuttable by clear and convincing evidence and is not overcome merely by another party's desire to know the address, and that a court finding the presumption rebutted must state its reasons on the record; this clause does not restate that full rebuttal standard or the separate custody/visitation provisions in section 6209.7(a) and (c). No CourtListener case law search was performed for this clause: this session's one permitted lightweight quota check returned a 429 rate-limit response (125/day exhausted, reset roughly 5.4 hours out), so per this project's practice the clause proceeds on the statutory text alone rather than waiting, and no judicial interpretation of section 6208 or section 6209.7 is represented here. This is California's own statute and does not describe any other state's confidentiality rule.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 6208
citations.cite: limits on disclosing a participant's actual address
citations.quote: The Secretary of State may not make a program participant’s address, other than the address designated by the Secretary of State, or a program participant’s name change available for inspection or copying, except under any of the following circumstances:

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 6209.7(b)(1)
citations.cite: rebuttable presumption against disclosure of a participant's location information
citations.quote: The fact that a participant is registered with the program shall create a rebuttable presumption that disclosure of information about the participant’s location and activities during the period of the registration, including, but not limited to, the participant’s current and past residential, work, or school addresses and other location information, would lead to the discovery of the participant’s actual residential address or physical location, would endanger the safety of the participant, and is not authorized.

clauses.title: Fees and Certification Length Differ Between the Two Chapters
clauses.body: The two Safe at Home chapters do not use identical fee or duration rules. Chapter 3.1's application section (6206) does not state any application or annual fee for its domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, child abduction, or elder/dependent adult abuse applicants. By contrast, Government Code section 6215.2(d), in Chapter 3.2, requires submitted applications to be accompanied by a fee set by the Secretary of State not exceeding the actual enrollment cost, permits annual fees to defray the program's maintenance costs, and expressly exempts any applicant who is a patient of a designated health care services facility from both the application fee and the annual fee. On certification length, section 6215.2(f) certifies most Chapter 3.2 applicants for four years, the same period as Chapter 3.1, but certifies a designated health care services facility volunteer only until six months after the volunteer's last date of volunteering with the facility.
clauses.gap: Section 6215.2(d) and section 6215.2(f) are subdivisions of the same statutory section, so this is a single-section citation for that pairing; the statement that Chapter 3.1 charges no fee is an inference from the absence of fee language in section 6206 rather than an affirmative statutory statement that Chapter 3.1 is free, and this clause does not cite a separate provision expressly saying so. This clause does not state the actual dollar amount of any Chapter 3.2 fee, which section 6215.2(d) leaves to the Secretary of State to set administratively rather than fixing in the statute itself; a current fee amount would need to be confirmed with the Secretary of State's office or its published forms, not this statutory text. This is California's own statute and does not describe any other state's fee structure.

In addition, annual fees may also be assessed by the Secretary of State to defray the actual costs of maintaining this program. Annual fees assessed by the Secretary of State shall also be used to reimburse the General Fund for any amounts expended from that fund for the purposes of this chapter.
