clauses.title: Acknowledgment and Signature
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet explains California Civil Code Section 1542, the statute that limits what a general release actually covers. It is a companion to {{companyName}}'s Severance Agreement and its general release clause, not a replacement for it. The Severance Agreement's release clause releases {{employeeName}}'s known claims against {{companyName}} in broad terms, but it does not quote or reference Civil Code Section 1542 or its rule about unknown claims. This sheet fills that gap by stating what Section 1542 itself says and what is and is not known about waiving its protection, so that {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}} can read the Severance Agreement's release alongside the actual statutory text it operates against.

clauses.title: Text of Civil Code Section 1542
clauses.body: California Civil Code Section 1542 currently reads: 'A general release does not extend to claims that the creditor or releasing party does not know or suspect to exist in his or her favor at the time of executing the release and that, if known by him or her, would have materially affected his or her settlement with the debtor or released party.' This is a default rule of California law that applies to general releases unless the parties provide otherwise.
clauses.gap: This is the current, in-force text as codified on the California Legislature's official site; it does not capture the statute's amendment history or how courts have applied it to particular fact patterns, and a settlement's own release language can change how this default rule applies to that specific agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1542 (current text, official California Legislative Information site)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Code § 1542
citations.quote: A general release does not extend to claims that the creditor or releasing party does not know or suspect to exist in his or her favor at the time of executing the release and that, if known by him or her, would have materially affected his or her settlement with the debtor or released party.

clauses.title: What the Statute's Rule Actually Requires
clauses.body: Section 1542's rule has two parts, both of which must be true for a claim to fall outside a general release under this default rule: first, the releasing party must not have known or suspected the claim existed at the time of signing, and second, had the releasing party known of it, the claim would have materially affected the settlement reached. A claim the releasing party already knew about, or one that would not have changed the settlement even if known, is not the kind of claim this statute protects.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text does not define 'suspect to exist' or 'materially affected' any further, and whether a particular claim meets either part of this test is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This corpus was unable to check current case law applying these two elements to specific fact patterns because the case-law research tool's daily query quota was exhausted at the time of this research (see the companion clause on that gap).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1542 (current text, official California Legislative Information site)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Code § 1542
citations.quote: does not know or suspect to exist in his or her favor at the time of executing the release and that, if known by him or her, would have materially affected his or her settlement with the debtor or released party

clauses.title: The Statute's Text Does Not Itself Describe How to Waive It
clauses.body: Section 1542's own text, quoted above, states only the default rule about what a general release does not cover. It contains no language describing a waiver of that protection, no list of drafting requirements, and no 'knowing and voluntary' standard anywhere in its text. Any requirements for how a releasing party validly gives up Section 1542's protection come from sources outside the statute's own wording, such as case law interpreting it and general contract principles about waiver, not from the text of Section 1542 itself.
clauses.gap: This is a correction of a common assumption: the research brief for this document expected the statute's own text to state what a valid waiver requires, but the current statutory text has no such language at all. This corpus was unable to identify squarely-on-point case law describing what makes an express Section 1542 waiver enforceable, because the case-law research tool used for this project (CourtListener) returned a daily-quota-exceeded error on the single lightweight check made for this document, and this corpus's practice is not to wait out that quota. As a result, this clause and this document describe only what the statute's text does and does not say, and do not state a judicially-derived waiver standard.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1542 (current text, official California Legislative Information site)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Code § 1542
citations.quote: A general release does not extend to claims that the creditor or releasing party does not know or suspect to exist in his or her favor at the time of executing the release

clauses.title: Common Practice: Express Section 1542 Waiver Language
clauses.body: Because Section 1542 states a default rule, settlement and severance agreements in California commonly include a separate paragraph in which the releasing party expressly acknowledges Section 1542, states its text or effect, and states that the releasing party is waiving its protection so that the release also covers claims not known or suspected at signing. This practice exists precisely because a general release that does not mention Section 1542 or unknown claims is understood, under the statute's default rule, to leave unknown and unsuspected claims outside its scope.

clauses.title: How This Relates to the Severance Agreement's Release Clause
clauses.body: {{companyName}}'s Severance Agreement contains a general release clause releasing {{companyName}} from claims {{employeeName}} 'has or may have' arising from employment or its ending. That clause does not mention Civil Code Section 1542, unknown claims, or suspected claims anywhere in its text. Under Section 1542's default rule described above, a general release that is silent on unknown and unsuspected claims does not, by that silence alone, extend to claims {{employeeName}} did not know or suspect existed at the time of signing. This information sheet does not add waiver language to that release clause; it only describes the statutory backdrop against which that release clause operates.

clauses.title: Research Note: Case Law Not Accessed
clauses.body: This information sheet is limited to the current text of Civil Code Section 1542 itself. A single check of this corpus's case-law research tool (CourtListener) returned a daily-quota-exceeded response before any case search could run, and this corpus's practice is to disclose that honestly rather than wait for the quota to reset or substitute weaker, off-point authority. As a result, this sheet does not cite or summarize any judicial decision interpreting Section 1542 or describing what makes an express waiver of it effective, including on questions such as whether particular language must name the statute, and readers should not assume the absence of case law here means no such case law exists.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California State Disability Insurance (SDI) — the wage-replacement benefit payable under the Unemployment Insurance Code when a worker cannot perform their own regular or customary work because of their own non-occupational illness, injury, or other qualifying condition. SDI is not the same program as Paid Family Leave (PFL), which is a separate, related benefit under the same statutory part that instead compensates a worker for time away to care for a seriously ill family member or to bond with a new child — a different qualifying reason covered by this corpus's separate Paid Family Leave (PFL) — Information Sheet. SDI is also not the same program as regular Unemployment Insurance (UI), which compensates a worker who is unemployed and able and available for work; this corpus's separate Unemployment Insurance documents address that program's claim, appeal, and overpayment rules. This sheet is limited to the statutory rules governing whether {{employeeName}}, as a claimant, meets SDI's own disability, wage-earning, and waiting-period eligibility requirements, including how those requirements interact with a period of unemployment from {{companyName}} or eligibility for regular UI benefits for the same period.

clauses.title: Statutory Purpose Distinguishes SDI From Paid Family Leave
clauses.body: The Unemployment Insurance Code states the purpose of the disability compensation part in a single sentence that names two distinct wage-loss situations: an individual's own sickness or injury, and separately, the sickness or injury of a family member or the birth, adoption, or foster care placement of a new child. Both situations are compensated from the same statutory part and the same disability fund, but California administers them as two distinct benefit programs built on that shared statutory foundation: State Disability Insurance for a claimant's own condition, and Paid Family Leave for the family-care and bonding situations. This document addresses only the first — SDI eligibility for a claimant's own disability.
clauses.gap: Section 2601 is a declaration of legislative purpose, not itself an eligibility or benefits rule; it states that the part is to be construed liberally toward that purpose but does not by itself define who qualifies, which is instead governed by the eligibility provisions cited elsewhere in this document. This document does not independently trace how or when the Legislature split the single statutory purpose in Section 2601 into the two administratively separate SDI and PFL programs described elsewhere in this part (Sections 3300 et seq. for PFL) beyond what Section 2601's own text shows.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2601 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2601
citations.quote: The purpose of this part is to compensate in part for the wage loss sustained by any individual who is unable to work due to the employee’s own sickness or injury, the sickness or injury of a family member, or the birth, adoption, or foster care placement of a new child, and to reduce to a minimum the suffering caused by unemployment resulting therefrom.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Disability"
clauses.body: The Unemployment Insurance Code defines when an individual is "disabled" for SDI purposes: an individual is deemed disabled on any day on which, because of their physical or mental condition, they are unable to perform their regular or customary work. The statute specifies that this definition includes illness or injury (physical or mental, including one resulting from pregnancy, childbirth, or a related medical condition), inability to work under a health officer's quarantine-type order for a communicable disease, and, to a more limited extent, medically treated acute alcoholism or drug-induced illness.
clauses.gap: The statute does not itself define what counts as an individual's "regular or customary work" when the individual has no current employer at the onset of the disability — for example, someone who became unemployed before becoming disabled. That question is addressed, if at all, by EDD regulations rather than by the statutory text examined here, and this document does not independently verify or state the regulatory answer. This document also does not detail the additional conditions attached to the alcoholism and drug-treatment categories in Sections 2626.1 and 2626.2, which were not independently fetched.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2626(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2626(a)
citations.quote: (a) An individual shall be deemed disabled on any day in which, because of his or her physical or mental condition, he or she is unable to perform his or her regular or customary work.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2626(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2626(b)
citations.quote: (b) For purposes of this section, “disability” or “disabled” includes: (1) Illness or injury, whether physical or mental, including any illness or injury resulting from pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical condition. (2) Inability to work because of a written order from a state or local health officer to an individual infected with, or suspected of being infected with, a communicable disease. (3) Acute alcoholism being medically treated or, to the extent specified in Section 2626.1, resident status in an alcoholic recovery home. (4) Acute drug-induced illness being medically treated or, to the extent specified in Section 2626.2, resident status in a drug-free residential facility.

clauses.title: Current Employment Is Not Itself an SDI Eligibility Requirement
clauses.body: The statutory definition of a "valid claim" for SDI does not require that the claimant be currently employed at the time the disability begins. It requires that the individual be unemployed and disabled and have been paid qualifying wages during a defined disability base period. Consistent with this, the statute's definition of the disability base period expressly addresses individuals who do not have an unexpired benefit year for unemployment compensation benefits — that is, individuals with no open UI claim — showing that the statute contemplates SDI claims filed by people who are not currently working and are not currently drawing UI. Under this statutory framework, a person who has recently lost a job and has sufficient wages in the applicable base period may still be able to establish a valid SDI claim if they later become disabled, whether or not they are working, or looking for work, at that time.
clauses.gap: This document does not verify the outer time limit within which a former employee's past wages remain usable toward a disability base period after employment ends, nor does it address whether or how a gap in employment before the disability onset affects the base-period calculation beyond what Sections 2609 and 2610 state on their face. It also does not address EDD's non-statutory claim-filing deadlines or procedural requirements for filing after employment has ended.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2609 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2609
citations.quote: “Valid claim” means any claim for unemployment compensation disability benefits made in accordance with the provisions of this code and rules and regulations adopted thereunder if the individual is unemployed and disabled and has been paid wages in employment for employers necessary to qualify for benefits under Section 2652.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2610 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2610
citations.quote: “Disability base period,” with respect to an individual who does not have an unexpired benefit year for unemployment compensation benefits, means for disability benefit periods beginning in October, November, or December, the four calendar quarters ended in the next preceding month of June; the disability base period for disability benefit periods beginning in January, February, or March, shall be the four calendar quarters ended in the next preceding month of September; the disability base period for disability benefit periods beginning in April, May, or June, shall be the four calendar quarters ended in the next preceding month of December; the disability base period for disability benefit periods beginning in July, August, or September shall be the four calendar quarters ended with the next preceding month of March.

clauses.title: Wage-Earning Requirement and the Disability Base Period
clauses.body: An individual cannot establish a valid SDI claim unless they were paid at least $300 in wages for employment by employers during their disability base period. Which quarters make up that base period depends on the claimant's circumstances: if the individual also has an unexpired benefit year for regular unemployment compensation benefits, the base period is the same one used for the disability base period generally if qualifying earnings there are sufficient, or otherwise the same base period used to establish the individual's unemployment compensation benefit year.
clauses.gap: The $300 wage-earning threshold in Section 2652 was last amended in 1957 and, as codified, has not been adjusted for inflation by that section's own text; this document does not verify whether any other statute, since superseded or amended, has raised the operative qualifying amount in practice. This document also does not state the formula used to calculate the dollar amount of weekly disability benefits (addressed elsewhere in this part, including Section 3301 as covered in this corpus's Paid Family Leave document, which shares the same benefit-computation provisions) — only the base-period and minimum-earnings gate to establishing a claim at all.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2652 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2652
citations.quote: An individual cannot establish a valid claim unless he has during his disability base period been paid wages for employment by employers of not less than three hundred dollars ($300).

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2611 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2611
citations.quote: “Disability base period,” with respect to an individual who has an unexpired benefit year for unemployment compensation benefits, shall be: (a) The same as the disability base period in Section 2610 if the individual has sufficient qualifying earnings in that disability base period. (b) The same as the base period used to establish the benefit year for unemployment compensation benefits if the individual does not have sufficient qualifying earnings in the disability base period in Section 2610.

clauses.title: Seven-Day Unpaid Waiting Period
clauses.body: Among the conditions the statute sets for disability-benefit eligibility, an individual must have been unemployed and disabled for a waiting period of seven consecutive days during each disability benefit period, and no disability benefits are payable for that waiting period. The statute exempts a person from re-serving the waiting period on a later, related claim: if the person already satisfied the waiting period on an initial claim and files a subsequent claim for the same or a related cause or condition within 60 days after the original disability benefit period, the waiting period requirement does not apply again.
clauses.gap: This document addresses only the waiting-period condition in subdivision (b) of Section 2627; it does not independently detail the other conditions listed in the same section (the claim-filing requirement, the examination requirement, and the certification-filing requirement), which govern eligibility in addition to the waiting period. It also does not address any temporary executive or emergency waiver of the waiting period that may have applied during a declared emergency; it states only the standing codified rule as currently in effect.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2627(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2627(b)
citations.quote: (b) (1) He or she has been unemployed and disabled for a waiting period of seven consecutive days during each disability benefit period with respect to which waiting period no disability benefits are payable. (2) The waiting period requirement shall not apply to a person who has met the waiting period requirements on the initial claim for disability benefits when that person files a subsequent claim for disability benefits for the same or a related cause or condition within 60 days after the original disability benefit period.

clauses.title: No Concurrent SDI and Unemployment Insurance Benefits for the Same Period
clauses.body: The statute directly addresses the interaction between SDI and regular Unemployment Insurance: an individual is not eligible for disability benefits for any period for which the director finds the individual has received, or is entitled to receive, unemployment compensation benefits under Part 1 of the Unemployment Insurance Code (California's regular UI program) or under an unemployment compensation act of another state or the federal government. Separately, regular UI eligibility itself requires that the claimant be able to work and available for work for the week claimed — a requirement that a person who is fully disabled from their regular or customary work will typically not satisfy for the same period. Together, these two provisions mean a claimant generally cannot draw SDI and UI benefits for the identical period, though they operate through two separate statutory tests rather than a single unified "either/or" rule.
clauses.gap: Section 2628, on its face, bars disability-benefit eligibility when UI benefits were received or the claimant was entitled to receive them for the same period; this document did not locate, within the sections reviewed, a mirror-image provision in Part 1 that independently disqualifies a claimant from UI merely because they received SDI benefits — the practical bar on the UI side in this document rests on the separate "able to work and available for work" requirement in Section 1253(c), not on a UI-side statute naming SDI receipt directly. This document also does not address partial-disability or light-duty situations where a claimant might satisfy Section 1253(c) for a portion of a week while also being found disabled for another portion. Case law interpreting these provisions was not reviewed for this document: a CourtListener case-law search was attempted before drafting, but returned a 429 daily-quota-exceeded error, so this document relies on statutory text only and does not represent that no relevant case law exists.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2628 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 2628
citations.quote: An individual is not eligible for disability benefits with respect to any period for which the director finds that he has received or is entitled to receive unemployment compensation benefits under Part 1 of this division or under an unemployment compensation act of any other state or of the Federal Government.

citations.case: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 1253(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Unemp. Ins. Code § 1253(c)
citations.quote: (c) He or she was able to work and available for work for that week.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This is an informational sheet about California law on wage advances and "draw against commission" arrangements offered at hire, prepared in connection with an arrangement between {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}, hired as {{jobTitle}} effective {{startDate}}. Draw arrangement: {{drawAmount}}, applied against the following commission structure: {{commissionStructure}}. It states facts drawn from California Labor Code §§ 221 and 224, and from a California Industrial Welfare Commission wage order, about (1) why an employer paying a draw before any commission is earned is generally extending an advance rather than paying a wage that the no-clawback rule already protects, (2) the written-authorization mechanism California law uses for deductions taken from wages to recover such a draw, and (3) a wage-floor rule that applies to commission-based pay regardless of how a draw is later reconciled. It does not determine whether {{drawAmount}}, or any part of it, is lawfully structured as an advance rather than a wage, whether any specific written authorization {{employeeName}} may sign satisfies Labor Code § 224, or whether any specific pay period's total pay to {{employeeName}} satisfies the wage-floor rule described here.

clauses.title: Why a Repayable Draw Extended at Hire Is Not Automatically a § 221 Problem
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 221 makes it unlawful for an employer to collect or receive back any part of wages it has already paid to an employee. On its own text, § 221 says nothing about draws, advances, or commissions specifically; it turns entirely on whether a payment was already a "wage" at the moment the employer seeks to take part of it back. California courts have read the word "wage" in this setting to mean a payment that has actually been earned by completion of whatever the payment's own terms required — and have held that a payment made before that condition is satisfied, where the employer cannot yet tell whether the underlying commission will ever be earned, is by its own nature an advance rather than a wage. A guaranteed draw offered to {{employeeName}} at hire, paid before any commission tied to {{commissionStructure}} has been earned, fits this description: because it is paid in advance of the condition that would make it a commission wage, § 221's no-clawback rule does not, by itself, make the draw's later recoupment unlawful. Whether {{drawAmount}} in {{employeeName}}'s specific arrangement is actually structured this way, or instead functions as an already-earned wage under a different label, is not something this clause determines.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, fetched and independently verified twice this session against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov's own current text, together with one state's case law on how courts have read that statute — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific draw arrangement, and not a claim that any particular draw, however labeled, is actually an advance rather than a wage. The case-law quotation below (Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC) was not independently re-verified against the opinion's primary text this session: this session's CourtListener MCP search tool returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125 requests/day, quota exhausted, not resetting for roughly 5 more hours), a direct curl fetch of the opinion's page on courtlistener.com returned an HTTP 202 response with an empty body (an access-control challenge page, not the opinion text), and the WebFetch tool reported that courtlistener.com is blocked by this environment's network egress proxy (error type EGRESS_BLOCKED) — all three paths were tried and failed. This exact quotation was independently verified against the opinion's primary text by an earlier session of this project (for this corpus's Commission Payout Upon Termination document, clause id commpayout_earned_vs_contingent) and is reused verbatim here rather than re-fetched, disclosed as reused-and-previously-verified rather than independently re-verified this session. Separately, Steinhebel itself addressed a chargeback of commissions already advanced against sales that were later cancelled or modified, not a guaranteed draw paid to a newly hired salesperson before any sale occurs at all; this clause applies the same advance-versus-wage reasoning to the hiring-stage draw scenario, but no case squarely addressing a guaranteed draw extended at hire (as opposed to a per-sale commission advance) was independently verified against a primary source this session.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 221 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the prohibition on collecting back wages already paid
citations.quote: It shall be unlawful for any employer to collect or receive from an employee any part of wages theretofore paid by said employer to said employee.

citations.case: Steinhebel v. Los Angeles Times Communications, LLC
citations.quote: The essence of an advance is that at the time of payment the employer cannot determine whether the commission will eventually be earned because a condition to the employee’s right to the commission has yet to occur or its occurrence as yet is otherwise unascertainable. An advance, therefore, by definition is not a wage because all conditions for performance have not been satisfied.

clauses.title: Recovering a Draw Through a Payroll Deduction: § 224's Written-Authorization Mechanism
clauses.body: Labor Code § 224 states that §§ 221, 222, and 223 do not make it unlawful for an employer to withhold or divert part of an employee's wages in certain listed circumstances, including "when a deduction is expressly authorized in writing by the employee to cover insurance premiums, hospital or medical dues, or other deductions not amounting to a rebate or deduction from the standard wage arrived at by collective bargaining or pursuant to wage agreement or statute." Read together with § 221, this is the statutory mechanism California law provides for an employer to take a payroll deduction from {{employeeName}}'s later, actually-earned commission wages to recover an outstanding draw balance under {{drawAmount}}, rather than relying on the advance-versus-wage distinction alone: the deduction must be expressly authorized in writing by {{employeeName}}, and § 224's own listed examples (insurance premiums, hospital or medical dues) illustrate the kind of individually-authorized, non-rebate deduction the exception was written around.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, fetched and independently verified twice this session against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov's own current text — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific draw arrangement, and not a claim that any specific written authorization an employee may sign for draw recoupment actually satisfies § 224's "expressly authorized in writing" language or its "not amounting to a rebate" limitation. Section 224's own text does not use the words "draw," "advance," or "commission" anywhere, and does not say that a signed draw-recoupment authorization is, by its nature, the same kind of deduction as the insurance-premium and medical-dues examples it does list; that is an application of the statute's general language this clause does not resolve. Separately, and contrary to one common assumption about this statute: § 224's own text, read in full, contains no minimum-wage floor, no reference to "net wages," and no limitation tied to hours worked — a wage-floor limitation on commission-based pay does exist in California law, but it comes from a different, independently sourced provision described in this document's companion clause on the IWC wage order minimum-wage requirement, not from § 224 itself. This clause does not independently fetch or verify Government Code § 50026, which § 224 separately cross-references only to disclaim authorizing withholding to pay a prohibited tax, fee, or charge.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 224 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the written-authorization exception for wage deductions
citations.quote: a deduction is expressly authorized in writing by the employee to cover insurance premiums, hospital or medical dues, or other deductions not amounting to a rebate or deduction from the standard wage arrived at by collective bargaining or pursuant to wage agreement or statute

clauses.title: The Actual Source of a Minimum-Wage Floor on Commission Pay: An IWC Wage Order, Not § 224
clauses.body: Separately from Labor Code §§ 221 and 224, California's Industrial Welfare Commission Wage Order No. 4-2001 (covering professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations) requires that "every employer shall pay to each employee, on the established payday for the period involved, not less than the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked in the payroll period, whether the remuneration is measured by time, piece, commission, or otherwise." This is the source of the rule that a commission-based employee's total pay for a given pay period — including a period in which {{companyName}} has deducted part of {{employeeName}}'s pay to recover an outstanding draw balance under {{drawAmount}} — must still reach at least the applicable minimum wage, expressed as {{applicableMinimumWage}}, for every hour {{employeeName}} actually worked in that pay period; the statute does not permit averaging a shortfall in one period against a surplus in another to satisfy this floor.
clauses.gap: This is one California administrative wage order, fetched and independently verified twice this session (byte-for-byte identical downloads, confirmed by matching file checksums) directly from dir.ca.gov — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific draw arrangement, and not a claim that Wage Order No. 4-2001 is the wage order that actually covers a specific employee's occupation. California has 17 industry- and occupation-specific wage orders, several of which contain their own, separately numbered version of this same minimum-wage-for-all-hours-worked provision; only Wage Order No. 4-2001 was independently fetched and checked this session, and this clause does not verify that every other wage order's minimum-wage provision is worded identically, nor does it determine which wage order applies to any particular employee's job classification. This clause's statement that shortfalls cannot be averaged across pay periods reflects this provision's own "for all hours worked in the payroll period" language on its face; a California Supreme Court decision (commonly cited on this exact point) was not independently verified against its primary opinion text this session for the same CourtListener rate-limiting and network-egress-blocking reasons disclosed in this document's companion clause on § 221, so no case citation is offered here beyond the wage order's own text.

citations.quote: Every employer shall pay to each employee, on the established payday for the period involved, not less than the applicable minimum wage for all hours worked in the payroll period, whether the remuneration is measured by time, piece, commission, or otherwise.

clauses.title: Written Authorization for Draw-Recovery Deductions and Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's statutory requirement that an employer give a new employee, at the time of hire or by the end of the first pay period, written notice of information about workers' compensation benefits — including how to obtain treatment and how the claims process works — as set out in California Labor Code § 3551 and, by incorporation, § 3550. It is prepared in connection with {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}, hired effective {{startDate}}.

This time-of-hire written notice is a different document from two other pamphlets and notices this corpus separately addresses. It is not the workplace-posted notice that Labor Code § 3550 also requires an employer to keep conspicuously posted (a companion, but separately-timed and separately-displayed, obligation described in this information sheet only to the extent § 3551 incorporates its content). It is also not the Employment Development Department's unemployment-insurance pamphlet ("For Your Benefit: California's Programs for the Unemployed," EDD form DE 2320) that a different California statute requires an employer to give a departing employee at separation — that is a distinct pamphlet, required by a different statute (Unemployment Insurance Code § 1089), addressing different benefits (unemployment insurance, not workers' compensation), given at a different time (termination, not hire), and is covered by this corpus's separate "Notice to Employee as to Change in Relationship" document. This information sheet does not determine whether {{companyName}} has in fact provided this notice to {{employeeName}}, does not determine whether any specific workplace injury is compensable, and is not a substitute for the actual text of the statutes and regulations it describes.

clauses.title: The Time-of-Hire Written Notice Duty
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 3551(a) requires every employer subject to the compensation provisions of the Labor Code, with one statutory exception, to give every new employee — either at the time the employee is hired or by the end of the first pay period — written notice of the information contained in Labor Code § 3550. The statutory exception is for employers of employees defined in Labor Code § 3351(d). The content of this notice is prescribed by the Administrative Director (within the Department of Industrial Relations) after consultation with the Commission on Health and Safety and Workers' Compensation, not by the text of § 3551 itself.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, stating a fact about what California law requires of a covered employer generally at the time a new employee is hired — not a claim about whether any specific employer has in fact provided this notice to any specific employee, or about whether that employee falls within the § 3351(d) exception, which this document does not independently research. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions construing this notice duty could not be completed this session because CourtListener's daily search quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked (the API returned an HTTP 429 quota-exceeded response); rather than wait for the quota to reset, this document proceeds on the statutory and regulatory text alone and discloses that no case-law search was performed.

citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3551(a)
citations.quote: Every employer subject to the compensation provisions of this code, except employers of employees defined in subdivision (d) of Section 3351, shall give every new employee, either at the time the employee is hired or by the end of the first pay period, written notice of the information contained in Section 3550.

clauses.title: Additional Required Content and the Bilingual Requirement
clauses.body: Labor Code § 3551(b) requires the time-of-hire notice to be easily understandable and available in both English and Spanish, and requires it to include — beyond the information already contained in § 3550 — three further items: (1) generally, how to obtain appropriate medical care for a job injury; (2) the role and function of the primary treating physician; and (3) a form the employee may use as an optional method of notifying the employer of the name of the employee's "personal physician" (as defined by Labor Code § 4600) or "personal chiropractor" (as defined by Labor Code § 4601). Section 3551(c) further requires that the content of this notice be made available to employers and insurers by the administrative director, and requires insurers to provide the notice to each of their policyholders along with advice about the requirements of the section and the penalties for a failure to provide it to all employees.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, stating a fact about what content California law requires this notice to contain — not a claim about the content of any specific notice a specific employer has actually used, and not a restatement of the § 3550 content this section incorporates by reference, which is addressed in a separate clause of this information sheet. The statute's text does not itself spell out what "penalties" it refers to in subdivision (c); this document does not locate a separate penalty provision specific to a § 3551 violation and discloses that gap rather than assuming one.

clauses.title: The Incorporated § 3550 Content
clauses.body: Because Labor Code § 3551 requires the time-of-hire notice to contain "the information contained in Section 3550," the substantive list set out in § 3550(d) is, by that cross-reference, also part of what the time-of-hire notice must cover. That list includes: how to get emergency medical treatment if needed; the kinds of events, injuries, and illnesses covered by workers' compensation; the injured employee's right to receive medical care; that the injured employee may consult a licensed attorney, with attorney's fees in most instances paid from the employee's recovery; the employee's rights to select and change the treating physician under Labor Code § 4600; the employee's rights to receive temporary disability, permanent disability, supplemental job displacement, and death benefits as appropriate; to whom injuries should be reported; the existence of time limits for notifying the employer of an occupational injury; the anti-discrimination protections of Labor Code § 132a; and the internet website address and contact information (including the nearest information and assistance officer) employees may use to learn more about the claims process and their rights and obligations.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, stating a fact about the content California law requires this incorporated list to cover — not a claim about the content of any specific notice a specific employer has actually used. Section 3550 (and therefore this incorporated list) was last amended effective January 1, 2025 (Stats. 2024, Ch. 87 (AB 1870)); this document reflects the version in effect as of the checked date above and does not attempt to reconstruct what the list read before that amendment. Section 3550's own posted-notice duty, and the separate misdemeanor and treat-with-personal-physician consequences that attach to a failure to keep that specific posted notice displayed, are addressed in a separate clause of this information sheet and are not restated here.

clauses.title: The Separate, Workplace-Posted Notice Under § 3550
clauses.body: Independent of the time-of-hire written notice, Labor Code § 3550(a) separately requires every employer subject to the compensation provisions to post and keep posted, in a conspicuous location frequented by employees where it may be easily read during the hours of the workday, a notice stating the name of the employer's current compensation insurance carrier (or that the employer is self-insured) and who is responsible for claims adjustment. Section 3550(b) makes a failure to keep this posted notice conspicuously displayed a misdemeanor and prima facie evidence of noninsurance, and § 3550(e) provides that an employer's failure to provide the notice required by that section automatically permits the employee to be treated by their own personal physician for an injury occurring during the failure.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, stating a fact about a workplace-posting duty that exists alongside, but is legally and operationally distinct from, the time-of-hire written notice this information sheet centers on — not a claim about whether any specific employer has in fact posted this notice or which insurance carrier or self-insurance status any such posting states. The misdemeanor penalty and personal-physician consequence in subdivisions (b) and (e) attach to the posted-notice duty in § 3550 itself; § 3551 does not, by its own text, say that the same misdemeanor penalty or personal-physician consequence also attaches to a failure to give the separate time-of-hire notice, and this document does not assume that it does.

citations.cite: Lab. Code § 3550(a)
citations.quote: Every employer subject to the compensation provisions of this division shall post and keep posted in a conspicuous location frequented by employees, and where the notice may be easily read by employees during the hours of the workday, a notice that states the name of the current compensation insurance carrier of the employer, or when appropriate, that the employer is self-insured, and who is responsible for claims adjustment.

citations.quote: Failure of an employer to provide the notice required by this section shall automatically permit the employee to be treated by their personal physician with respect to an injury occurring during that failure.

clauses.title: The Implementing Regulation's Written-Notice Content List
clauses.body: The Administrative Director's implementing regulation for the time-of-hire notice, Title 8, California Code of Regulations § 9880, restates the § 3551 duty and lists the notice's required content in non-technical terms — including, among other items, the name of the employer's current compensation insurance carrier or self-insured status and claims-adjustment contact, how to get emergency medical treatment, the kinds of events and injuries covered, the employee's right to receive medical care, the role and function of the primary treating physician, the employee's rights to select and change the treating physician and to predesignate a personal physician or medical group, an optional personal-physician or personal-chiropractor notification form, disability and death benefit rights, reporting and time-limit information, the § 132a anti-discrimination protections, information-and-assistance officer contact information, and a description of medical provider networks (MPNs).
clauses.gap: This regulation's text could not be independently fetched from a primary California source this session: California regulations are not on eCFR, this project's usual leginfo-style approach does not host full current CCR text, and the Office of Administrative Law's own published-text search and Westlaw's govt.westlaw.com/calregs (the government's designated official publisher of the CCR) were not reachable from this environment; www.dir.ca.gov's own title-8 regulation pages (e.g., dir.ca.gov/title8/9880.html) returned HTTP 404 when fetched directly. The text quoted here instead comes from the Legal Information Institute (Cornell Law School)'s secondary compilation of Title 8 CCR § 9880, fetched twice with distinct User-Agent strings and confirmed byte-identical between the two fetches; LII is a well-established secondary legal-research compiler, not the primary California state publisher, and this document was not able to independently cross-check its text against an official OAL or Westlaw source this session. LII's own regulatory-history notes for this section show it was last substantively amended effective October 8, 2010 (Register 2010, No. 33); this document reflects that version and does not claim to have checked for any more recent amendment beyond what LII's own "updated quarterly" comparison shows (which found no more recent version).

clauses.title: Employer- or Insurer-Published Versions of the Notice
clauses.body: Title 8, California Code of Regulations § 9883 allows insurers, employers, or private enterprises to prepare and publish their own version of the Written Notice to New Employees (and of the separate Notice to Employees poster) for their own use or for sale, but only upon prior approval of the form and content by the Administrative Director, and any such published Written Notice to New Employees must be available in English and Spanish and include the information specified in § 9880. A logotype may be added to a previously approved notice without requiring additional approval, and material published after the regulation's effective date must indicate that it has been approved by the Administrative Director.
clauses.gap: As with the preceding clause, this regulation's text comes from the Legal Information Institute's secondary compilation, not from a primary California source independently verified this session, for the reasons disclosed there. This is one state's regulation, stating a fact about what California law permits an employer or insurer to do when publishing its own version of this notice — not a claim about whether any specific version a specific employer has used has, in fact, received the Administrative Director's prior approval, which this document does not investigate.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature Block — Time-of-Hire Workers' Compensation Rights Notice Information Sheet
Reproductive Loss Leave Entitlement
clauses.body: Under California law, it is an unlawful employment practice for a covered employer to refuse a covered employee's request to take up to five days of reproductive loss leave following a reproductive loss event. The days taken need not be consecutive. If an employee experiences more than one reproductive loss event within a 12-month period, the employer is not obligated to grant more than a combined total of 20 days of reproductive loss leave within that 12-month period.
clauses.gap: The statute caps combined reproductive loss leave at 20 days within a 12-month period when an employee has more than one qualifying event, but it does not itself state whether that 12-month period is measured as a rolling 12 months from a given event or a fixed 12-month period (such as a calendar or employer-designated leave year); this document does not resolve that ambiguity.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.6 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.6(b)(1), core entitlement and 20-day cap
citations.quote: It shall be an unlawful employment practice for an employer to refuse to grant a request by any employee to take up to five days of reproductive loss leave following a reproductive loss event. If an employee experiences more than one reproductive loss event within a 12-month period, an employer shall not be obligated to grant a total amount of reproductive loss leave time in excess of 20 days within a 12-month period.

citations.quote: The employer shall allow the days an employee takes for reproductive loss leave to be nonconsecutive.

clauses.title: Definition of a Reproductive Loss Event
clauses.body: A "reproductive loss event" is the day of, or for a multiple-day event the final day of, a failed adoption, a failed surrogacy, a miscarriage, a stillbirth, or an unsuccessful assisted reproduction. "Assisted reproduction" means a method of achieving a pregnancy through an artificial insemination or an embryo transfer, and includes gamete and embryo donation, but does not include any pregnancy achieved through sexual intercourse; "unsuccessful assisted reproduction" means an unsuccessful round of intrauterine insemination or of an assisted reproductive technology procedure. Each of these terms extends to an event experienced by the employee, by the employee's current spouse or domestic partner, or by another individual, where the employee would have been a parent of the child involved.
clauses.gap: This is a research correction to a common shorthand: the statute does not use the phrase "IVF" or limit "unsuccessful assisted reproduction" to in vitro fertilization — the statutory term is broader, covering any unsuccessful round of intrauterine insemination or of an assisted reproductive technology procedure, without itself defining what qualifies as an "assisted reproductive technology procedure." This document does not independently verify that term against any separate statute or regulation that might define it.

clauses.title: Employee Eligibility and Employer Coverage
clauses.body: For purposes of this leave, an "employee" is a person who has been employed by the employer for at least 30 days before the leave begins. This requirement applies to an "employer," defined as a person who employs five or more persons to perform services for a wage or salary, as well as to the state and any of its political or civil subdivisions, including cities and counties.
clauses.gap: These employee and employer definitions are worded identically to the ones used in California's bereavement leave statute (Gov. Code § 12945.7), but they are separately defined within this section; this document does not assume that a determination made under one leave statute automatically controls the other, only that the operative text is the same.

citations.quote: “Employee” means a person employed by the employer for at least 30 days prior to the commencement of the leave.

citations.quote: “Employer” means either of the following: (A) A person who employs five or more persons to perform services for a wage or salary. (B) The state and any political or civil subdivision of the state, including, but not limited to, cities and counties.

clauses.title: Timing of Leave and Interaction With Other Leave
clauses.body: Reproductive loss leave generally must be completed within three months of the reproductive loss event. If, before or immediately after the event, the employee is on or chooses to go on leave under Government Code § 12945 (relating to pregnancy disability), § 12945.2 (the California Family Rights Act), or any other state or federal leave entitlement, the three-month window instead runs from the end date of that other leave.
clauses.gap: This clause states that the three-month window can be extended by an overlapping leave under § 12945, § 12945.2, or another leave entitlement, but it does not independently restate or verify the eligibility rules, duration, or scope of those other leave laws; they are addressed, where covered, in this corpus's separate documents on pregnancy disability leave and the California Family Rights Act.

citations.quote: Except as provided in subparagraph (B), reproductive loss leave shall be completed within three months of the event entitling the employee to that leave under paragraph (1).

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.6 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 12945.6(b)(3)(B), extension when combined with other leave
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subparagraph (A), if, prior to or immediately following a reproductive loss event, an employee is on or chooses to go on leave from work pursuant to Section 12945, 12945.2, or any other leave entitlement under state or federal law, the employee shall complete their reproductive loss leave within three months of the end date of the other leave.

clauses.title: Paid or Unpaid Status of the Leave
clauses.body: Reproductive loss leave is taken under the employer's own existing applicable leave policy, if it has one. If the employer has no existing applicable leave policy, the leave may be unpaid, except that the employee may use vacation, personal leave, accrued and available sick leave, or compensatory time off that is otherwise available.
clauses.gap: The statute does not create a freestanding state-paid reproductive loss leave benefit; payment, where it exists, comes from the employer's own policy or the employee's own accrued paid leave. This document does not address whether a separate wage-replacement program, such as State Disability Insurance, may apply to the underlying medical event itself, since that is a different program not created or modified by this leave statute.

clauses.title: Confidentiality, Anti-Retaliation, and Independence From Other Rights
clauses.body: The employer must maintain the confidentiality of any employee requesting leave under this statute, and any information provided to the employer under this section must be kept confidential and disclosed only to internal personnel or counsel as necessary, or as otherwise required by law. It is a separate unlawful employment practice for an employer to retaliate against an individual — including by refusing to hire, discharging, demoting, fining, suspending, expelling, or discriminating against them — because the individual exercised the right to reproductive loss leave or gave information or testimony about their own or someone else's reproductive loss leave in a related inquiry or proceeding, and it is likewise unlawful for an employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of any right this section provides. An employee's right to reproductive loss leave is a separate and distinct right from any other right under this part of the Government Code.
clauses.gap: Unlike California's bereavement leave statute (Gov. Code § 12945.7(f)), this reproductive loss leave statute does not include a provision expressly authorizing the employer to request supporting documentation of the event within a set number of days. This document does not conclude from that silence that an employer has, or lacks, any documentation right under this section; it states only that the statute itself does not spell one out the way the bereavement leave statute does.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
What This Document Covers: The Statutory NIL Regime Against Schools and Athletic Associations, Not a Private Consent-to-Use Release
clauses.body: California Education Code section 67456 is part of the Student Athlete Bill of Rights (Education Code Part 40.3) and provides that a postsecondary educational institution shall not uphold any rule, requirement, standard, or other limitation that prevents a student participating in intercollegiate athletics at that institution from earning compensation as a result of the use of the student's name, image, likeness, or athletic reputation, and that the same student's scholarship eligibility is not affected by earning that compensation. This statute regulates a different relationship than this corpus's separate Model/Publicity Release information sheet, which addresses the right-of-publicity consent a person gives a private party (such as an advertiser) to use that person's own identity under Civil Code section 3344. Section 67456 instead addresses whether a student athlete's own postsecondary institution, or an athletic association, conference, or other group or organization with authority over intercollegiate athletics, may itself restrict that student's ability to earn compensation from third parties for use of the student's name, image, likeness, or athletic reputation. Section 67456's text does not itself supply, or substitute for, whatever separate consent a student athlete may still need to give any specific third party under the general right-of-publicity framework before that third party could use the athlete's identity.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California's own Student Athlete Bill of Rights framework restricts (institution and athletic-association conduct toward a student athlete) as distinct from what a general right-of-publicity consent statute like Civil Code section 3344 addresses (a private party's use of a person's identity with that person's consent) — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that Section 67456 itself creates, defines, or limits the separate consent that a right-of-publicity statute would otherwise require for a specific third-party use. This document's connection to CourtListener's case-search tool returned a daily-quota-exhausted (HTTP 429) response before any search could be run, so no case law interpreting Section 67456 or the scope of a student athlete's NIL rights is cited anywhere in this document; every authority clause here rests on the statute's own text only. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific institutional rule, athletic-association policy, team contract, or NIL contract complies with, or is prohibited by, Section 67456 or any other law, and completing this information sheet does not itself resolve any of those questions or constitute legal advice about any reader's specific situation.

clauses.title: Athletic Associations and Conferences — Including the NCAA by Name — Are Also Barred From Preventing NIL Compensation, and From Penalizing the Institution
clauses.body: Section 67456's prohibition on restricting a student athlete's NIL compensation is not limited to the student's own institution. The statute separately states that an athletic association, conference, or other group or organization with authority over intercollegiate athletics — naming the National Collegiate Athletic Association as one example, without limiting the prohibition to that organization — shall not prevent a student of a postsecondary educational institution from earning compensation as a result of the use of the student's name, image, likeness, or athletic reputation. The statute goes further still: the same kind of athletic association, conference, or other group or organization also shall not prevent the postsecondary educational institution itself from participating in intercollegiate athletics as a result of a student athlete's NIL compensation — that is, the statute bars retaliation against the school, not only against the individual athlete.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what it says about athletic associations, conferences, and similar organizations generally — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about how any specific athletic association's current bylaws, rules, or NIL policies compare to what this statute requires, which this document does not research. The statute's own phrase "including, but not limited to, the National Collegiate Athletic Association" means the prohibition is not confined to the NCAA by name; this document does not identify every organization the phrase might reach. This document's connection to CourtListener's case-search tool had already returned a daily-quota-exhausted (HTTP 429) response before any search could be run, so no case law applying this subdivision to any specific association's rule is cited here. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific institutional rule, athletic-association policy, team contract, or NIL contract complies with, or is prohibited by, Section 67456 or any other law.

clauses.title: A Separate, Opposite-Direction Rule: Institutions and Associations May Not Pay a Prospective Student Athlete NIL-Related Compensation
clauses.body: Section 67456 contains two rules that point in different directions and should not be collapsed into one another. Subdivision (a) bars a postsecondary institution or athletic association from stopping a current student athlete from earning outside NIL compensation from third parties. Subdivision (b) instead separately bars the postsecondary educational institution, athletic association, conference, or other group or organization with authority over intercollegiate athletics from itself providing compensation to a prospective student athlete in relation to that athlete's name, image, likeness, or athletic reputation. Read together, the statute's own text protects a student athlete's ability to earn NIL compensation from others; it does not, by its own terms, permit the institution or association itself to pay a not-yet-enrolled prospective athlete in connection with NIL as a recruiting inducement.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a textual distinction between what subdivision (a) permits (a student athlete earning outside compensation) and what subdivision (b) restricts (the institution or association itself paying a prospective athlete) — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation. The statute's list of restricted payors is "a postsecondary educational institution, athletic association, conference, or other group or organization with authority over intercollegiate athletics"; this document does not resolve, and the statute's text does not on its face address, whether a separate, non-institutional third-party organization (for example, an independent collective not itself an athletic association, conference, or other group with authority over intercollegiate athletics) falls inside or outside that list. This document's connection to CourtListener's case-search tool had already returned a daily-quota-exhausted (HTTP 429) response before any search could be run, so no case law construing subdivision (b) or the phrase "prospective student athlete" is cited here. This document is informational only and does not itself determine whether any specific payment to any specific prospective or current student athlete is permitted or prohibited under this section.

clauses.title: Right to Obtain Licensed Professional Representation for NIL Contracts and Legal Matters
clauses.body: Section 67456 states that a postsecondary educational institution, athletic association, conference, or other group or organization with authority over intercollegiate athletics shall not prevent a California student participating in intercollegiate athletics from obtaining professional representation in relation to contracts or legal matters, including representation provided by athlete agents or legal representation provided by attorneys. The statute's own text further specifies that this representation must come from persons licensed by the state: athlete-agent representation must be provided by persons licensed under Chapter 2.5 of Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code (commencing with Section 18895), and legal representation must be provided by attorneys licensed under Article 1 of Chapter 4 of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code (commencing with Section 6000). Section 67456 also states that athlete agents representing student athletes must comply with the federal Sports Agent Responsibility and Trust Act, codified starting at Section 7801 of Title 15 of the United States Code, in their relationships with student athletes.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Section 67456's own text describing and cross-referencing the Business and Professions Code licensing chapters and the federal Sports Agent Responsibility and Trust Act; it does not independently fetch or quote the text of Business and Professions Code Section 18895 et seq., Section 6000 et seq., or 15 U.S.C. Section 7801 et seq. themselves, so this document does not verify what those separately cross-referenced provisions require beyond what Section 67456's own text states about them. Subdivision (c)(1)'s protected class is phrased as "a California student participating in intercollegiate athletics," which is not verbatim the same phrase ("a student of that institution participating in intercollegiate athletics") used in subdivision (a)(1) elsewhere in this same section; this document notes that textual difference without resolving whether it is meant to narrow or simply restate the same protected group. This document's connection to CourtListener's case-search tool had already returned a daily-quota-exhausted (HTTP 429) response before any search could be run, so no case law is cited here. This document is informational only and does not itself determine whether any specific person's representation of any specific student athlete satisfies this section's licensing requirements.

clauses.title: A Cost-of-Attendance Scholarship Is Not "Compensation" Under This Section, and Cannot Be Revoked for Earning NIL Money or Getting Legal Representation
clauses.body: Section 67456's own text draws a line between a student athlete's cost-of-attendance scholarship and the NIL compensation the section otherwise addresses. It states that a scholarship from the postsecondary educational institution in which a student is enrolled, providing the student with the cost of attendance at that institution, is not compensation for purposes of this section, and that a scholarship shall not be revoked as a result of a student earning compensation or obtaining legal representation pursuant to this section. This is consistent with, and reinforces, the separate statement elsewhere in the same section that earning NIL compensation does not affect a student's scholarship eligibility.
clauses.gap: This clause is limited to what Section 67456's own text says about a cost-of-attendance scholarship and this specific section's compensation and legal-representation provisions; the statute's text as quoted here does not address, and this document does not research, other financial-aid rules (for example, need-based aid recalculation under federal financial aid law), NCAA or conference scholarship rules apart from this statute, or the tax treatment of NIL income. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how it treats a cost-of-attendance scholarship for purposes of this section — not a claim about which state's law, or which other body of financial-aid or tax law, governs any reader's situation. This document's connection to CourtListener's case-search tool had already returned a daily-quota-exhausted (HTTP 429) response before any search could be run, so no case law is cited here. This document is informational only and does not itself determine whether any specific scholarship was properly awarded, maintained, or revoked.

clauses.title: Disclosure to the Institution, and the Prohibition on an NIL Contract That Conflicts With a Team Contract
clauses.body: Section 67456 imposes disclosure obligations tied to a student athlete's NIL contract. Its text states that a student athlete shall not enter into a contract providing compensation for use of the athlete's name, image, likeness, or athletic reputation if a provision of that contract is in conflict with a provision of the athlete's team contract. Separately, the statute's text requires a student athlete who does enter into such a compensation contract to disclose the contract to an official of the institution, to be designated by the institution. The statute also imposes a corresponding disclosure obligation running the other direction: an institution asserting that a conflict of the kind just described exists must disclose to the athlete, or to the athlete's legal representation, the relevant contractual provisions that are in conflict.
clauses.gap: Section 67456's own text, as quoted here, does not specify a deadline by which the athlete's disclosure to the institution must be made (for example, before or after signing), the form that disclosure must take, or any penalty for a student athlete's failure to disclose; this document does not supply those missing details or assume any particular disclosure procedure. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what its own text requires — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific NIL contract does or does not conflict with any specific team contract, which depends on the actual wording of both documents. This document's connection to CourtListener's case-search tool had already returned a daily-quota-exhausted (HTTP 429) response before any search could be run, so no case law construing this disclosure or conflict provision is cited here. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve any conflict between an NIL contract and a team contract, or determine that any specific disclosure satisfies this section.

clauses.title: A Team Contract Cannot Bar Commercial NIL Use Outside Official Team Activities — and the Statute's Text Limits This Rule to Certain Contracts
clauses.body: Section 67456's text separately restricts what a postsecondary educational institution's athletic program can put in a team contract. It states that a team contract of a postsecondary educational institution's athletic program shall not prevent a student athlete from using the athlete's name, image, likeness, or athletic reputation for a commercial purpose when the athlete is not engaged in official team activities. The same subdivision then states the Legislature's intent that this particular prohibition applies only to contracts entered into, modified, or renewed on or after the enactment of this section.
clauses.gap: This subdivision's own text limits its prohibition to contracts "entered into, modified, or renewed on or after the enactment of this section," but Section 67456 has been amended more than once since it was first added; this document, having fetched only the section's current, in-force text, does not independently trace which specific enactment or amendment date this legislative-intent statement refers to, and does not resolve that dating question for any specific team contract. The statute's text also does not define "official team activities"; this document does not supply that definition. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what its own text and stated legislative intent say — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific team-contract provision does or does not fall within this prohibition. clauses.title: NIL Contract Disclosure to Institution — Declaration and Signature
Purpose and Scope — A Different Transaction From a Foreclosure Process
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, California's Home Equity Sales Contract Act, Civil Code §§ 1695-1695.17. That statute is a completely different subject from the corpus's existing Notice of Default / Nonjudicial Foreclosure Process information sheet and its companion Homeowner Bill of Rights information sheet. Those two documents describe the process by which a lender or its trustee forecloses on a borrower under a deed of trust that already exists between the borrower and the lender. This sheet instead describes a separate, private transaction: the direct sale of a home by a distressed owner to an investor — called an "equity purchaser" under the statute — who is not the borrower's lender and is not conducting a foreclosure sale at all. It concerns a potential sale of the real property commonly known as {{propertyAddress}} between {{sellerName}} as equity seller and {{buyerName}} as equity purchaser. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself create, cancel, rescind, or otherwise affect any contract for the sale of this or any other property; it does not determine whether {{propertyAddress}} meets the statutory definition of "residence in foreclosure" or whether {{buyerName}} meets the statutory definition of "equity purchaser"; and it does not determine whether any actual contract, notice, or practice relating to a sale of this property has complied — or failed to comply — with the requirements this sheet describes.

clauses.title: Who the Act Covers — "Equity Purchaser," "Residence in Foreclosure," and "Equity Seller"
clauses.body: The Home Equity Sales Contract Act applies only to transactions that fit its defined terms. Civil Code § 1695.1(a) provides that “Equity purchaser” means any person who acquires title to any residence in foreclosure, except a person who acquires such title as follows, and then lists exclusions including a purchase for use as a personal residence, a deed in lieu of foreclosure, a trustee's deed at a foreclosure sale, a statutorily authorized sale, a court order or judgment, or a transfer from a spouse or blood relative. Section 1695.1(b) defines “residence in foreclosure” (and “residential real property in foreclosure”) narrowly: it means "residential real property consisting of one- to four-family dwelling units, one of which the owner occupies as his or her principal place of residence, and against which there is an outstanding notice of default, recorded pursuant to Article 1 (commencing with Section 2920) of Chapter 2 of Title 14 of Part 4 of Division 3." A property does not meet this statutory definition merely because the owner is behind on payments or expects a foreclosure — a notice of default must actually have been recorded against it. Section 1695.1(c) provides that “Equity seller” means any seller of a residence in foreclosure, and section 1695.1(e) provides that “Contract” means any offer or any contract, agreement, or arrangement, or any term thereof, between an equity purchaser and equity seller incident to the sale of a residence in foreclosure. If a Notice of Default affecting {{propertyAddress}} has been recorded, its recording date is stated as: {{noticeOfDefaultRecordingDate}}.
clauses.gap: This clause states the Act's own defined terms; it does not determine whether any particular property or transaction actually satisfies them — for example, whether a notice of default has in fact been recorded, whether the property is a one- to four-family dwelling occupied by its owner, or whether an exclusion (such as a purchase for use as a personal residence, or a purchase from a blood relative) applies to a particular buyer. Those are factual and legal determinations outside the scope of this information sheet. Research for this clause relied on a statute-only pass: a CourtListener case-law search returned a daily-quota error (HTTP 429, 125/day limit) before any case law could be checked, so this clause is not verified against how courts have applied these defined terms in practice.

clauses.title: Required Contract Form and Contents
clauses.body: The Act requires that a contract between an equity purchaser and an equity seller take a particular written form. Civil Code § 1695.2 requires that "Every contract shall be written in letters of a size equal to 10-point bold type, in the same language principally used by the equity purchaser and equity seller to negotiate the sale of the residence in foreclosure and shall be fully completed and signed and dated by the equity seller and equity purchaser prior to the execution of any instrument of conveyance of the residence in foreclosure." Section 1695.3 requires that "Every contract shall contain the entire agreement of the parties and shall include the following terms," including "The name, business address, and the telephone number of the equity purchaser," "The address of the residence in foreclosure," and "The total consideration to be given by the equity purchaser in connection with or incident to the sale," along with a description of payment terms, the time possession transfers, the terms of any rental agreement, a notice of cancellation, and a boldface warning statement naming the equity purchaser. A contract affecting {{propertyAddress}} between {{sellerName}} and {{buyerName}} that omits these statutorily required terms, or that is not in the required type size and language, does not comply with section 1695.2 or 1695.3 as written.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the statute's form and content requirements; it does not evaluate whether any specific contract for a particular sale in fact satisfies them (for example, its actual type size, its completeness, or the specific consideration and payment terms it states), and it does not reproduce every one of section 1695.3's eight lettered required-term subdivisions verbatim. Research for this clause relied on a statute-only pass because CourtListener's daily case-law search quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked, so no case law on what counts as adequate compliance was reviewed.
