(b) The address of the residence in foreclosure. (c) The total consideration to be given by the equity purchaser in connection with or incident to the sale.

clauses.title: The Seller's Statutory Right to Cancel
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1695.4(a) gives every equity seller a statutory cancellation right independent of any other rescission right: "In addition to any other right of rescission, the equity seller has the right to cancel any contract with an equity purchaser until midnight of the fifth business day following the day on which the equity seller signs a contract that complies with this chapter or until 8 a.m. on the day scheduled for the sale of the property pursuant to a power of sale conferred in a deed of trust, whichever occurs first." "Business day" excludes Sundays and the enumerated statutory holidays under section 1695.1(d). Section 1695.4(b) states that "Cancellation occurs when the equity seller personally delivers written notice of cancellation to the address specified in the contract or sends a telegram indicating cancellation to that address." Section 1695.4(c) adds that "A notice of cancellation given by the equity seller need not take the particular form as provided with the contract and, however expressed, is effective if it indicates the intention of the equity seller not to be bound by the contract." A contract affecting {{propertyAddress}} signed by {{sellerName}} on {{dateSigned}} would, under this section, remain cancellable through the statutory period described above, unless a scheduled trustee's sale cuts that period short.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general statutory cancellation period and its two possible end points; it does not calculate the specific date and time by which cancellation must occur for any actual contract, which depends on the signing date, the applicable business days and holidays, and whether a foreclosure sale has been scheduled and for what date. It also does not address the separate cancellation-form requirements of section 1695.5, covered in a companion clause. Research for this clause relied on a statute-only pass because CourtListener's daily case-law search quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked.

clauses.title: Required Cancellation Notice and Warning Language
clauses.body: The Act requires that the seller's cancellation right be disclosed in specific, prominent language attached to the contract. Civil Code § 1695.5(a) requires the contract to contain, near the seller's signature line, a statutory notice — in at least 12-point bold type — telling the seller that the sale may be cancelled without any penalty or obligation before a stated date and time, and directing the seller to an attached notice-of-cancellation form. Section 1695.5(b) requires that "The contract shall be accompanied by a completed form in duplicate, captioned “notice of cancellation” in a size equal to 12-point bold type, if the contract is printed or in capital letters if the contract is typed," containing statutory language allowing the seller to cancel by personally delivering a signed and dated copy of the notice, or sending a telegram, to the purchaser's stated business address before the stated deadline. Section 1695.5(c) requires that "The equity purchaser shall provide the equity seller with a copy of the contract and the attached notice of cancellation." Section 1695.5(d) provides that "Until the equity purchaser has complied with this section, the equity seller may cancel the contract" — meaning the seller's cancellation window does not close if the purchaser never gives the required notice.
clauses.gap: This clause paraphrases, rather than quotes, the exact wording of the statutory cancellation warning in section 1695.5(a) itself, because the copy of that subdivision obtained from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov contains what appears to be a stray line-break formatting artifact inside the word "without" in the official site's HTML; the surrounding subdivisions quoted directly below were unaffected. This clause also does not certify that any actual notice-of-cancellation form used for a particular sale matches the required type size, language, and content. Research for this clause relied on a statute-only pass because CourtListener's daily case-law search quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked.

clauses.title: Practices Prohibited During the Cancellation Period and Generally
clauses.body: The Act restricts what an equity purchaser may do while a seller's cancellation right is still open, and prohibits certain misrepresentations at any time. Civil Code § 1695.6(b) provides: "Until the time within which the equity seller may cancel the transaction has fully elapsed, the equity purchaser shall not do any of the following," and then lists accepting or inducing execution of any instrument of conveyance, recording any document signed by the seller, transferring or encumbering any interest in the property, and paying the seller any consideration. Section 1695.6(c) requires that "Within 10 days following receipt of a notice of cancellation given in accordance with Sections 1695.4 and 1695.5, the equity purchaser shall return without condition any original contract and any other documents signed by the equity seller." Section 1695.6(d) separately prohibits an equity purchaser, without a time limit, from making "untrue or misleading statements regarding the value of the residence in foreclosure, the amount of proceeds the equity seller will receive after a foreclosure sale, any contract term, the equity seller's rights or obligations incident to or arising out of the sale transaction, the nature of any document which the equity purchaser induces the equity seller to sign, or any other untrue or misleading statement concerning the sale of the residence in foreclosure to the equity purchaser." Separately, section 1695.13 makes it "unlawful for any person to initiate, enter into, negotiate, or consummate any transaction involving residential real property in foreclosure, as defined in Section 1695.1, if such person, by the terms of such transaction, takes unconscionable advantage of the property owner in foreclosure."
clauses.gap: This clause states the categories of conduct the statute prohibits; it does not evaluate whether any specific conduct by a particular equity purchaser toward a particular equity seller falls within them, and "unconscionable advantage" under section 1695.13 is an undefined statutory standard this sheet does not attempt to apply. Research for this clause relied on a statute-only pass because CourtListener's daily case-law search quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked, so no case law interpreting "unconscionable advantage" or the section 1695.6 prohibitions was reviewed.

clauses.title: Civil Remedies, Rescission of Completed Sales, and Criminal Penalties
clauses.body: The Act backs its requirements with layered remedies. Civil Code § 1695.7 gives an equity seller a civil action for a violation of section 1695.6 or 1695.13: "An equity seller may bring an action for the recovery of damages or other equitable relief against an equity purchaser for a violation of any subdivision of Section 1695.6 or Section 1695.13. The equity seller shall recover actual damages plus reasonable attorneys' fees and costs." The court may additionally award exemplary damages or equitable relief, and for a violation of the section 1695.6(b)(3) transfer-or-encumbrance prohibition or of section 1695.13, the court "shall award exemplary damages in an amount not less than three times the equity seller's actual damages" or, alternatively, "a civil penalty of up to two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500)" — but not both — with any such action to be "commenced within four years after the date of the alleged violation." Separately, even after a sale has closed, section 1695.14(a) makes a transaction that violates section 1695.13 voidable, and "the transaction may be rescinded by the property owner within two years of the date of the recordation of the conveyance of the residential real property in foreclosure," subject to the protections for a bona fide purchaser or encumbrancer for value described in section 1695.14(c). Beyond civil liability, section 1695.8 makes a violation of section 1695.6, or conduct "which would operate as a fraud or deceit upon an equity seller," punishable "upon conviction" by "a fine of not more than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000), by imprisonment in the county jail for not more than one year," or both.
clauses.gap: This clause states the remedies and penalties the statute makes available; it does not determine whether any violation has occurred with respect to a particular property or transaction, does not calculate any specific damages, penalty, or limitations deadline, and does not address how these civil remedies interact with the separate criminal penalty in section 1695.8 (for example, whether both can apply to the same conduct). Research for this clause relied on a statute-only pass because CourtListener's daily case-law search quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked, so no case law applying these remedy provisions was reviewed.

clauses.title: Nonprofit Tax-Exempt Status Application — Introduction and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet concerns {{companyName}} and describes, in general terms, the federal and California processes for a nonprofit corporation to obtain recognized tax-exempt status. Several other documents in this library — covering nonprofit public benefit, nonprofit mutual benefit, nonprofit religious, and unincorporated nonprofit association formation — each note that forming a nonprofit entity under California law is a separate question from obtaining tax-exempt recognition, without themselves addressing that separate question. This document is the one those documents point to as unaddressed: it covers (1) the federal organizational and operational requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3), (2) the federal notice requirement of 26 U.S.C. § 508(a) that generally must be satisfied before a new organization is treated as a § 501(c)(3) organization, (3) California's parallel state-law exemption under Revenue and Taxation Code § 23701d, and (4) the two statutory pathways to recognized California exemption set out in Revenue and Taxation Code § 23701(a)-(b). It does not address obtaining an employer identification number, unrelated business income tax, the private-foundation-versus-public-charity classification tests beyond the basic presumption described below, state or local sales and property tax exemptions, or the Attorney General's charitable-trust registration and reporting requirements, each of which is a separate matter this document does not cover. This document is informational only. It does not itself apply for, obtain, or confer tax-exempt status for {{companyName}} or any other organization under any federal or California statute, and it does not determine whether {{companyName}} or any other organization meets any statutory requirement described below on its particular facts.

clauses.title: Federal Organizational and Operational Requirements — 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3)
clauses.body: Federal tax exemption under 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) is available to a corporation, community chest, fund, or foundation only if it is organized and operated exclusively for one or more of a specific, closed list of purposes named in the statute — religious, charitable, scientific, testing for public safety, literary, or educational purposes, fostering national or international amateur sports competition (subject to a further athletic-facilities-and-equipment limitation), or the prevention of cruelty to children or animals. The same statutory sentence adds three further conditions that apply regardless of which listed purpose an organization pursues: no part of its net earnings may inure to the benefit of any private shareholder or individual; no substantial part of its activities may consist of carrying on propaganda or otherwise attempting to influence legislation, except as otherwise provided in a separate subsection of the same section; and the organization must not participate in, or intervene in, any political campaign on behalf of or in opposition to any candidate for public office. All of these conditions come from the single statutory paragraph defining the § 501(c)(3) category itself, rather than from separate provisions.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) itself, one paragraph within the longer list of exempt-organization categories in § 501(c); it does not restate the Treasury regulations implementing the "organizational test" and "operational test" (already discussed, for the organizational test, in this project's nonprofit_purpose_state_vs_federal clause), which add further detail — for example on how an organization's articles must be worded — beyond what the statutory text itself says. No case law is cited in this clause: before relying on any court decision, this document's preparation included one lightweight CourtListener case-law search to confirm quota availability, and that search returned a 429 rate-limit response indicating the daily quota was already exhausted; rather than wait for the quota to reset, this document proceeds on statutory text alone and discloses that choice here. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any organization's purposes or activities satisfy this statute, which is a determination made by the IRS, not by this document.

clauses.title: Federal Notice Requirement for Recognition and the Private-Foundation Presumption — 26 U.S.C. § 508
clauses.body: A separate section of the Internal Revenue Code, 26 U.S.C. § 508, governs whether and when an organization otherwise meeting § 501(c)(3)'s substantive requirements is actually treated as a § 501(c)(3) organization. Under subsection (a), an organization organized after October 9, 1969 is not treated as described in § 501(c)(3) unless it has given notice to the Secretary, in the manner the Secretary prescribes by regulation, that it is applying for recognition of that status — and if notice is given late, the organization is not treated as a § 501(c)(3) organization for any period before the notice was given. Separately, under subsection (b), any organization described in § 501(c)(3) that does not notify the Secretary that it is not a private foundation is presumed to be a private foundation. Subsection (c) exempts two categories from both of these rules without any notice at all: churches, their integrated auxiliaries, and conventions or associations of churches; and any organization that is not a private foundation and whose gross receipts in each taxable year are normally not more than $5,000.
clauses.gap: The statutory text of § 508(a) says only that notice must be given "in such manner as the Secretary may by regulations prescribe" and "within the time prescribed by the Secretary by regulations" — it does not itself name a specific application form or a specific number of months, and this clause does not restate the separate Treasury regulations that fill in those details, which this document did not independently verify against a fetched regulatory source. No case law is cited in this clause for the same quota-exhaustion reason disclosed in this document's federal-organizational-test clause. This document is informational only: it does not itself give notice to the IRS on behalf of any organization and does not determine whether any organization has satisfied this section's notice requirement or fits within either exception in subsection (c).

clauses.title: California's Parallel Organizational and Operational Test — Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701d
clauses.body: California's own state-law exemption for the kind of organization that would qualify federally under § 501(c)(3) is codified as a separate numbered statute, Revenue and Taxation Code § 23701d — note that, in California's own numbering convention, the letter is appended directly to the section number with no parenthesis or period between them, rather than being written as a lettered subdivision of a single "§ 23701." Section 23701d(a) tracks the federal purposes list closely: a corporation, community chest, or trust organized and operated exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, testing-for-public-safety, literary, or educational purposes (with the same amateur-sports and cruelty-prevention categories and the same no-inurement, limited-lobbying, and no-political-campaign conditions found in the federal statute). California's statute goes further than the bare text of the federal one, however: § 23701d(a) itself spells out an "irrevocable dedication of assets" requirement, stating in the statutory text that an organization is not organized exclusively for exempt purposes unless its assets are irrevocably dedicated to those purposes, meaning that on dissolution or on the impossibility of carrying out its specific purposes, the assets must continue to be devoted to exempt purposes.
clauses.gap: This corrects an assumption worth stating plainly: the requirement that an organization's assets be irrevocably dedicated to exempt purposes on dissolution is written directly into the text of California's own statute, Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701d(a); the equivalent federal requirement is not found in the text of 26 U.S.C. § 501(c)(3) itself, but rather in the Treasury regulations implementing it. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of that one state's own parallel exemption category and its added dedication-of-assets language, not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. No case law is cited here for the same CourtListener quota-exhaustion reason disclosed elsewhere in this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any organization's articles or activities satisfy this section, which is a determination made by the Franchise Tax Board, not by this document.

Dedication of assets requires that in the event of dissolution of an organization or the impossibility of performing the specific organizational purposes the assets would continue to be devoted to exempt purposes.

clauses.title: California's Two Statutory Pathways to Recognized State Exemption — Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701(a)-(b)
clauses.body: Revenue and Taxation Code § 23701 — the general section governing all of the lettered exemption categories that follow it, including § 23701d — sets out two different statutory routes to recognized state exemption. Under subdivision (a), an organization is exempt only if an application for exemption is submitted in the form prescribed by the Franchise Tax Board and the Franchise Tax Board issues a determination exempting the organization from tax. Under subdivision (b), however, an organization organized and operated for nonprofit purposes under any of several listed sections — including § 23701d — is exempt upon its submission to the Franchise Tax Board of either a copy of the determination letter or ruling issued by the Internal Revenue Service recognizing the organization's federal tax exemption under specified Internal Revenue Code categories, or a copy of a group exemption letter covering the organization as a subordinate. Upon receipt of either document, the statute requires the Franchise Tax Board to issue an acknowledgment that the organization is exempt, rather than a full determination — a materially different, IRS-determination-dependent process from the general application-and-determination route in subdivision (a).
clauses.gap: This section's text does not itself name any specific form number, such as the numbers commonly used to refer to the Franchise Tax Board's general exemption application and its shorter counterpart for organizations that already hold IRS documentation; this document did not independently verify current form numbers, form-revision dates, or filing fees against the Franchise Tax Board's own website, which returned an access-denied response (HTTP 403) when checked while preparing this document, so no specific current fee or form-revision date is stated anywhere in this document. This is one state's statute, describing that one state's own application framework, not a claim about which state's procedures govern a specific corporation. No case law is cited here for the same CourtListener quota-exhaustion reason disclosed elsewhere in this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself submit any application or determination-letter copy to the Franchise Tax Board and does not determine which of the two pathways is available to any particular organization.

clauses.title: Procedural Details This Document Does Not State
clauses.body: Neither the federal statutes nor the California statutes described in this document name specific application form numbers, specific dollar filing-fee amounts, or specific form-revision dates; those details are set administratively by the IRS and by the Franchise Tax Board, and this document does not restate them because they change from time to time and could not be verified, at the time this document was prepared, against a current, independently-fetched Franchise Tax Board web page (which returned an access-denied response) and were only partially checkable against the IRS's own published guidance rather than against statutory or regulatory text itself. What the statutes described above do establish is the structure of the choice involved: a new organization seeking § 501(c)(3) recognition must satisfy 26 U.S.C. § 508(a)'s notice requirement in whatever manner and timeframe the Secretary's regulations prescribe, and an organization that has already obtained an IRS determination letter or ruling recognizing its federal exemption may submit a copy of that document to the Franchise Tax Board under Rev. & Tax. Code § 23701(b)(1)(A), rather than proceeding through the separate general application-and-determination process in § 23701(a), to obtain California's parallel state exemption. Current form numbers, current fee schedules, and current filing procedures for either the federal or the state process are not stated anywhere in this document.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This document describes the federal income-tax basis rule of 26 U.S.C. § 1014, commonly called "stepped-up basis at death." This is a different federal tax concept from this corpus's separate Federal Estate and Gift Tax Basics — Information Sheet document, which addresses the federal estate tax exemption, portability, the marital deduction, and the gift tax annual exclusion under 26 U.S.C. §§ 2010, 2056, and 2503 — those are transfer-tax provisions governing whether tax is owed on a transfer itself. Section 1014, by contrast, is an income-tax provision: it governs how much capital gain, if any, {{decedentName}}'s heirs or beneficiaries would recognize for income-tax purposes if they later sell property they acquired from {{decedentName}}, by fixing that property's income-tax "basis" (the reference figure against which gain or loss is measured) as of the date of death rather than at whatever {{decedentName}} originally paid for it. A decedent's estate can be entirely exempt from federal estate tax and still involve property whose income-tax basis is governed by this section.

clauses.title: General Rule: Basis Set to Fair Market Value at Death
clauses.body: Under 26 U.S.C. § 1014(a)(1), the default federal income-tax basis of property in the hands of a person who acquires it from a decedent, or to whom it passes from a decedent, is the property's fair market value at the date of the decedent's death — not the decedent's own original cost basis. This applies to property such as {{propertyAddress}} that {{executorName}} distributes from {{decedentName}}'s estate, so long as the property is not sold, exchanged, or otherwise disposed of by the acquiring person before the decedent's death. This rule is the mechanism behind what is commonly called a "stepped-up basis": built-in appreciation that accrued during the decedent's lifetime is generally not carried forward as taxable gain to the person who inherits the property.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the default rule of paragraph (a)(1). Paragraph (a) itself begins "[e]xcept as otherwise provided in this section," and the statute lists several exceptions and modifications addressed in separate clauses of this document (an alternate valuation date election, a special-use valuation election, an anti-abuse rule for appreciated property gifted to the decedent shortly before death, and a basis-consistency rule tied to the estate tax return) as well as one this document does not independently address: paragraph (a)(4)'s basis rule for property to which the exclusion described in section 2031(c) (a qualified conservation easement) applies. It also does not address subsection (d)'s separate rule for DISC stock. No CourtListener case-law search was performed for this document: a preliminary quota-availability check this session received an HTTP 429 ("Rate limit exceeded: 125/day"), so this document was deliberately limited to primary statutory text rather than case law, consistent with this corpus's practice of disclosing that choice rather than waiting out or working around the quota.

citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this section, the basis of property in the hands of a person acquiring the property from a decedent or to whom the property passed from a decedent shall, if not sold, exchanged, or otherwise disposed of before the decedent’s death by such person, be— (1) the fair market value of the property at the date of the decedent’s death,

clauses.title: Alternate Valuation Date and Special Use Valuation Elections
clauses.body: Section 1014(a) does not always fix basis at the date-of-death value. If the estate makes an election under 26 U.S.C. § 2032 (the alternate valuation date, generally six months after death), the property's basis under section 1014 is instead its value at that later, statutorily prescribed valuation date. Separately, if the estate makes a special-use valuation election for qualified real property under 26 U.S.C. § 2032A (a lower valuation available for certain farm or closely held business real property), the section 1014 basis is the value determined under that section rather than ordinary fair market value. Whether {{executorName}} makes either election for {{decedentName}}'s estate is a separate determination under section 2032 or section 2032A itself.
clauses.gap: This clause identifies that these two elections exist and that each changes the section 1014 basis figure when made; it does not restate the eligibility requirements, election deadlines, or valuation mechanics of section 2032 or section 2032A themselves, neither of which was independently fetched or verified for this document. No CourtListener case-law search was performed for this document: a preliminary quota-availability check this session received an HTTP 429 ("Rate limit exceeded: 125/day"), so this document was deliberately limited to primary statutory text rather than case law, consistent with this corpus's practice of disclosing that choice rather than waiting out or working around the quota.

citations.quote: in the case of an election under section 2032, its value at the applicable valuation date prescribed by such section, (3) in the case of an election under section 2032A, its value determined under such section, or

clauses.title: Community Property: Both Halves May Receive a Stepped-Up Basis
clauses.body: 26 U.S.C. § 1014(b)(6) treats the surviving spouse's own one-half share of community property as property "acquired from" or "passed from" the decedent for purposes of section 1014(a), when the decedent died after December 31, 1947 and at least one-half of the whole community interest in the property was includible in the decedent's gross estate for federal estate tax purposes. Because California is a community property state, this means that when one spouse of {{decedentName}} and {{survivingSpouseName}} dies owning community property such as {{propertyAddress}}, both halves of that community property — not only the half the decedent owned — can receive a new, stepped-up income-tax basis equal to fair market value at the date of death under section 1014(a). This is commonly referred to as a "double step-up" and is a materially different result from the general rule applicable to separate property or to property held in forms such as joint tenancy with a non-spouse, where ordinarily only the decedent's own fractional interest receives a new basis and the survivor's pre-existing interest keeps its original, unstepped basis.
clauses.gap: This is a federal statute construing the effect of state community-property law generally, not a claim that any specific asset held by a decedent and a surviving spouse is, or was, community property under California law; whether a particular asset is community property, separate property, or some other form of co-ownership is a state-law characterization question this clause does not resolve. Section 1014(b)(6) also requires that at least one-half of the whole community interest actually was includible in the decedent's gross estate under chapter 11 (the federal estate tax) or the corresponding 1939 Code provision; this document does not independently verify that inclusion requirement was met for any specific property. The statute's cross-reference to "the community property laws of any State" means this same double-step-up mechanism applies in other community-property states as well, not only California, and this clause does not survey other states' community property statutes. No CourtListener case-law search was performed for this document: a preliminary quota-availability check this session received an HTTP 429 ("Rate limit exceeded: 125/day"), so this document was deliberately limited to primary statutory text rather than case law, consistent with this corpus's practice of disclosing that choice rather than waiting out or working around the quota.

clauses.title: Why the Property's Character Matters
clauses.body: The size of the basis adjustment available under 26 U.S.C. § 1014 can depend on how property was characterized and held before the decedent's death. For community property includible in the decedent's gross estate, section 1014(b)(6) adjusts the basis of both the decedent's one-half interest and the surviving spouse's one-half interest. For property that is separate property of the decedent, or that is held in a form such as joint tenancy between spouses or between non-spouses, the general basis rules instead typically adjust only the fractional interest attributable to the decedent, leaving the survivor's own pre-existing fractional interest with its original, unstepped basis. This document does not determine how {{propertyAddress}} or any other specific asset of {{decedentName}} was characterized or held immediately before death; that characterization is a separate factual and legal question.

clauses.title: Limit on Step-Up for Property Gifted to the Decedent Shortly Before Death
clauses.body: 26 U.S.C. § 1014(e) limits the stepped-up basis rule for appreciated property that was given to a decedent within the one-year period ending on the date of the decedent's death, if that property is then acquired from the decedent by (or passes to) the original donor or the donor's spouse. In that situation, the basis in the hands of the donor or the donor's spouse is not stepped up to fair market value; it is instead the same adjusted basis the property had in the decedent's hands immediately before death — the same basis it would have had if the decedent had never held it. "Appreciated property" for this purpose means property whose fair market value on the date it was transferred to the decedent by gift exceeded its adjusted basis at that time.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general rule of paragraph (e)(1) and the "appreciated property" definition in paragraph (e)(2)(A); it does not separately restate paragraph (e)(2)(B)'s extension of the same rule to appreciated property sold by the decedent's estate or by a grantor trust of the decedent, which this document does not address further. This clause does not determine whether any specific gift to a decedent falls within this one-year rule. No CourtListener case-law search was performed for this document: a preliminary quota-availability check this session received an HTTP 429 ("Rate limit exceeded: 125/day"), so this document was deliberately limited to primary statutory text rather than case law, consistent with this corpus's practice of disclosing that choice rather than waiting out or working around the quota.

citations.quote: appreciated property was acquired by the decedent by gift during the 1-year period ending on the date of the decedent’s death, and (B) such property is acquired from the decedent by (or passes from the decedent to) the donor of such property (or the spouse of such donor), the basis of such property in the hands of such donor (or spouse) shall be the adjusted basis of such property in the hands of the decedent immediately before the death of the decedent.

clauses.title: Basis Must Be Consistent With the Estate Tax Return
clauses.body: 26 U.S.C. § 1014(f), added effective for property with respect to which an estate tax return is filed after July 31, 2015, caps the basis of property under section 1014(a) so that it cannot exceed the value finally determined for federal estate tax purposes, or, where no final value has yet been determined, the value most recently reported to the beneficiary and the IRS under the separate reporting requirement of 26 U.S.C. § 6035(a). This consistency requirement applies only to property whose inclusion in the decedent's gross estate increased the estate's federal estate tax liability (after allowable credits); it does not apply to property that had no effect on the estate's tax liability, such as property in an estate with no federal estate tax due.
clauses.gap: This clause does not restate the further mechanics of paragraph (f)(3) (how a value counts as "determined" for this purpose) beyond identifying the general concept, and does not address paragraph (f)(4)'s grant of regulatory authority to the Secretary to create exceptions. It also does not restate the separate section 6035 reporting statute in full; only its role as a value-reporting trigger under section 1014(f)(1)(B) is described here. No CourtListener case-law search was performed for this document: a preliminary quota-availability check this session received an HTTP 429 ("Rate limit exceeded: 125/day"), so this document was deliberately limited to primary statutory text rather than case law, consistent with this corpus's practice of disclosing that choice rather than waiting out or working around the quota.

citations.quote: The basis of any property to which subsection (a) applies shall not exceed— (A) in the case of property the final value of which has been determined for purposes of the tax imposed by chapter 11 on the estate of such decedent, such value, and (B) in the case of property not described in subparagraph (A) and with respect to which a statement has been furnished under section 6035(a) identifying the value of such property, such value. (2) Exception Paragraph (1) shall only apply to any property whose inclusion in the decedent’s estate increased the liability for the tax imposed by chapter 11 (reduced by credits allowable against such tax) on such estate.

clauses.title: Exception: Income in Respect of a Decedent
clauses.body: 26 U.S.C. § 1014(c) states that section 1014 does not apply to property that constitutes a right to receive an item of income in respect of a decedent, as that term is used in 26 U.S.C. § 691. Income in respect of a decedent generally refers to amounts a decedent was entitled to receive as income but had not yet received or reported before death — for example, uncollected wages, or a traditional IRA or retirement account balance. Property of that kind does not receive a stepped-up basis under section 1014, regardless of the property's fair market value at the date of death.
clauses.gap: This clause identifies the existence and general subject matter of the income-in-respect-of-a-decedent exception by cross-reference to 26 U.S.C. § 691, but § 691 itself was not independently fetched or verified for this document, so this clause does not restate § 691's own operative text or its detailed rules for what counts as income in respect of a decedent or how it is taxed. It does not determine whether any specific asset of a decedent's estate is income in respect of a decedent. No CourtListener case-law search was performed for this document: a preliminary quota-availability check this session received an HTTP 429 ("Rate limit exceeded: 125/day"), so this document was deliberately limited to primary statutory text rather than case law, consistent with this corpus's practice of disclosing that choice rather than waiting out or working around the quota.

clauses.title: When a Court May Appoint Minor's Counsel, and How the Appointment Continues
clauses.body: Under California Family Code § 3150(a), if the court determines that it would be in {{childName}}'s best interest, the court may appoint private counsel to represent {{childName}}'s interests in a custody or visitation proceeding, provided that the court and counsel comply with the requirements set forth in Rules 5.240, 5.241, and 5.242 of the California Rules of Court. The statute states this appointment in discretionary terms — the court "may appoint" counsel — tied to the court's own determination of {{childName}}'s best interest, rather than a right either parent can invoke or a showing that triggers a mandatory appointment. Once counsel has entered an appearance for {{childName}} under this chapter, Family Code § 3150(b) provides that counsel continues to represent {{childName}} unless relieved by the court upon the substitution of other counsel or for cause.
clauses.gap: Family Code § 3150 states only a discretionary standard — this document found no provision in §§ 3150-3153 making appointment of minor's counsel mandatory in any circumstance; the research brief for this document assumed the statute might state both permissive and mandatory grounds, and that assumption does not match the actual current text. Section 3150(a) also does not define "best interest" for this purpose, and it cross-references California Rules of Court 5.240, 5.241, and 5.242 for procedural requirements that this document does not independently verify or summarize. Section 3150(b) does not define "cause" for relieving counsel, leaving that determination to the court.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3150(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 3150(a)
citations.quote: If the court determines that it would be in the best interest of the minor child, the court may appoint private counsel to represent the interests of the child in a custody or visitation proceeding, provided that the court and counsel comply with the requirements set forth in Rules 5.240, 5.241, and 5.242 of the California Rules of Court.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3150(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 3150(b)
citations.quote: Upon entering an appearance on behalf of a child pursuant to this chapter, counsel shall continue to represent that child unless relieved by the court upon the substitution of other counsel by the court or for cause.

clauses.title: How Minor's Counsel Differs From a Guardian Ad Litem
clauses.body: California law recognizes two distinct court appointments concerning a child or minor in litigation, and this document covers only one of them. A guardian ad litem, appointed under Code of Civil Procedure § 372 (covered in this corpus's separate Guardian Ad Litem Appointment document), exists because a minor or a person who lacks legal capacity generally cannot appear as a party in a civil action or proceeding at all without one; that appointee's litigation authority is tied to court approval of specific case decisions such as compromising the action. Minor's counsel, appointed under Family Code § 3150 specifically in a custody or visitation proceeding, is a separate appointment that does not depend on {{childName}} being otherwise unable to appear as a party — {{childName}} is ordinarily not a party to the custody proceeding at all. Family Code § 3151(a) charges minor's counsel with "the representation of the child's best interests" and directs that, if {{childName}} so desires, counsel must present {{childName}}'s wishes to the court — combining independent best-interest advocacy with a duty to report the child's own stated preferences, which is a different function from a guardian ad litem's role of enabling a minor to appear in litigation at all.
clauses.gap: This clause's description of the guardian ad litem role rests on Code of Civil Procedure § 372 text already verified elsewhere in this corpus's separate guardian ad litem document; that statute was not independently refetched or re-quoted in this session, so this clause cites only Family Code § 3151(a) directly. Family Code §§ 3150-3153 do not themselves state whether the same child could simultaneously have both a guardian ad litem and minor's counsel in overlapping or related proceedings, and this document does not resolve that question.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 3151(a)
citations.quote: The child’s counsel appointed under this chapter is charged with the representation of the child’s best interests.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 3151(a)
citations.quote: If the child so desires, the child’s counsel shall present the child’s wishes to the court.

clauses.title: Scope of Minor's Counsel's Duties Toward the Child
clauses.body: Family Code § 3151(a) describes minor's counsel's role as gathering evidence bearing on {{childName}}'s best interests and presenting that admissible evidence to the court in any manner appropriate for counsel of a party. Unless it is inappropriate under the circumstances to exercise a given duty, § 3151(a) lists counsel's duties as including interviewing {{childName}}, reviewing the court files and all accessible relevant records available to both parties, and making any further investigations counsel considers necessary to ascertain evidence relevant to the custody or visitation hearings.
clauses.gap: Family Code § 3151(a) does not define what circumstances make exercising a listed duty "inappropriate," leaving that judgment to counsel and the court. The statute requires counsel to present the child's wishes if the child so desires, but does not state how counsel is to reconcile a best-interest recommendation that differs from the child's stated wishes; this document does not resolve that question beyond quoting what § 3151(a) itself says.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 3151(a)
citations.quote: The role of the child’s counsel is to gather evidence that bears on the best interests of the child, and present that admissible evidence to the court in any manner appropriate for the counsel of a party.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 3151(a)
citations.quote: The counsel’s duties, unless under the circumstances it is inappropriate to exercise the duty, include interviewing the child, reviewing the court files and all accessible relevant records available to both parties, and making any further investigations as the counsel considers necessary to ascertain evidence relevant to the custody or visitation hearings.

clauses.title: Minor's Counsel's Procedural Powers and Access to the Child and Records
clauses.body: Family Code § 3151(b) requires counsel to serve notices and pleadings on all parties consistent with the requirements for parties, and provides that counsel shall not be called as a witness in the proceeding; counsel may introduce and examine counsel's own witnesses, present arguments to the court concerning {{childName}}'s welfare, and participate further in the proceeding to the degree necessary to represent {{childName}} adequately. Family Code § 3151(c) lists eight specific rights held by minor's counsel, including reasonable access to {{childName}}, standing to seek affirmative relief on {{childName}}'s behalf, and notice of any proceeding or phase of a proceeding affecting {{childName}}. Among those listed rights, § 3151(c)(5) gives counsel access to {{childName}}'s medical, dental, mental health, and other health care records and educational records, and the right to interview school personnel, caretakers, health care providers, and mental health professionals who have assessed or cared for {{childName}} — release of that information to counsel does not itself waive the confidentiality of those records.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes § 3151(b) and a representative subset of the eight enumerated rights in § 3151(c) — reasonable access, standing, notice, and records access — rather than every numbered right; § 3151(c) also separately addresses counsel's right to take any action available to a party, to receive advance notice of and refuse a non-court-ordered examination, to assert or waive privilege on the child's behalf, and to seek an independent evaluation with court approval, which this document does not quote in full here. Section 3151(c)(5) also cross-references Family Code §§ 3177 and 3182 governing counsel's interviews of mediators; those cross-referenced sections were not independently fetched or verified in this session.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 3151(b)
citations.quote: Counsel shall serve notices and pleadings on all parties, consistent with requirements for parties. Counsel shall not be called as a witness in the proceeding. Counsel may introduce and examine counsel’s own witnesses, present arguments to the court concerning the child’s welfare, and participate further in the proceeding to the degree necessary to represent the child adequately.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3151(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 3151(c)
citations.quote: The child’s counsel shall have the following rights: (1) Reasonable access to the child. (2) Standing to seek affirmative relief on behalf of the child. (3) Notice of any proceeding, and all phases of that proceeding, including a request for examination affecting the child.

citations.quote: Access to the child’s medical, dental, mental health, and other health care records, school and educational records, and the right to interview school personnel, caretakers, health care providers, mental health professionals, and others who have assessed the child or provided care to the child. The release of this information to counsel shall not constitute a waiver of the confidentiality of the reports, files, and any disclosed communications.

clauses.title: Minor's Counsel's Access to Child Protective Services Records
clauses.body: Family Code § 3152(a) lets minor's counsel, upon noticed motion to all parties and the local child protective services agency, request the court to authorize release of relevant reports or files concerning {{childName}} held by the relevant local child protective services agency. Under § 3152(b), the court reviews those reports or files in camera to determine whether they are relevant to the pending action and whether, and to what extent, they should be released to counsel. Section 3152(c) provides that neither the court's in camera review nor release to counsel waives the confidentiality of the reports or files, and that counsel may not disclose their contents or existence to anyone unless otherwise permitted by law.
clauses.gap: Family Code § 3152 does not define "relevant" for purposes of the court's in camera determination, does not set a deadline for the noticed motion, and does not state what "otherwise permitted by law" means for purposes of counsel's nondisclosure duty in § 3152(c); this document does not resolve those undefined terms.

citations.cite: Fam. Code § 3152(a)
citations.quote: The child’s counsel may, upon noticed motion to all parties and the local child protective services agency, request the court to authorize release of relevant reports or files, concerning the child represented by the counsel, of the relevant local child protective services agency.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3152(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 3152(b)
citations.quote: The court shall review the reports or files in camera in order to determine whether they are relevant to the pending action and whether and to what extent they should be released to the child’s counsel.

clauses.title: Compensation for Minor's Counsel and Allocation of the Cost
clauses.body: Family Code § 3153(a) provides that, if the court appoints counsel under this chapter to represent {{childName}}, counsel receives a reasonable sum for compensation and expenses in an amount the court determines, and — except as provided in subdivision (b) — that amount is paid by the parties in the proportions the court deems just. Section 3153(b) adds a county-pay fallback: on its own motion or a party's motion, the court determines whether {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} together are financially unable to pay all or part of the cost of appointed counsel, and whatever portion the court finds the parties unable to pay is paid by the county; the Judicial Council adopts guidelines to assist in determining financial eligibility for that county payment.
clauses.gap: The research brief's framing of this section as allocating cost only "between the parties" does not match the actual text — § 3153(b) makes a county-pay fallback part of the statutory scheme whenever the court finds the parties financially unable to pay all or part of the cost, not merely a discretionary option. Section 3153 does not itself state how a "reasonable sum" for compensation is calculated (for example, by hourly rate or flat fee) or what the Judicial Council's financial-eligibility guidelines require; this document does not independently source or summarize those guidelines.

citations.cite: Fam. Code § 3153(a)
citations.quote: If the court appoints counsel under this chapter to represent the child, counsel shall receive a reasonable sum for compensation and expenses, the amount of which shall be determined by the court. Except as provided in subdivision (b), this amount shall be paid by the parties in the proportions the court deems just.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3153(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 3153(b)

The Judicial Council shall adopt guidelines to assist in determining financial eligibility for county payment of counsel appointed by the court pursuant to this chapter.

[If counsel has been appointed for {{childName}} in this proceeding, the appointed counsel's name may be recorded here: {{minorsCounselName}}.] This document states facts about California's statutory scheme for appointment of minor's counsel. It is not itself an application, motion, or order, and it does not appoint counsel for {{childName}} or determine who pays for that counsel — only a court order can do that.

clauses.title: This Information Sheet Addresses Which State's Courts Have Authority, and Transfer of an Existing Conservatorship — Not the Initial California Petition
clauses.body: This information sheet describes a different subject from this corpus's companion document, "Conservatorship of an Adult — Petition Information Sheet." That document describes the process for establishing a brand-new California conservatorship over an adult who has no existing conservatorship anywhere. This document instead describes California's enactment of a modified version of the Uniform Adult Guardianship and Protective Proceedings Jurisdiction Act, cited under California law as the "California Conservatorship Jurisdiction Act" — the law that addresses which state's courts have authority to appoint or supervise a conservator for {{conserveeName}} when {{conserveeName}} has connections to more than one state, and the statutory process for transferring an existing conservatorship for {{conserveeName}} into California from another state, or out of California to another state, without starting an entirely new proceeding from scratch. This document does not itself establish, transfer, or terminate any conservatorship, does not itself register any out-of-state order, and does not determine which state's courts actually have jurisdiction over {{conserveeName}}'s case; only a court order does that.

clauses.title: California's Modified Enactment of the Uniform Act, and What It Does Not Cover
clauses.body: By enacting Probate Code Division 4, Part 3, Chapter 8 (Probate Code §§ 1980-2033), the California Legislature stated its intent "to enact a modified version of the Uniform Adult Guardianship and Protective Proceedings Jurisdiction Act," and the chapter "may be cited as the 'California Conservatorship Jurisdiction Act.'" The chapter governs conservatorships of an adult; it does not apply to a minor, "regardless of whether the minor is or was married," and it does not apply to a guardianship proceeding for a minor. It also does not apply to a proceeding for involuntary commitment to a mental health facility or other involuntary mental health care, including proceedings under the Lanterman-Petris-Short Act and several enumerated Penal Code and Welfare and Institutions Code commitment schemes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own enactment of a modified version of the Uniform Adult Guardianship and Protective Proceedings Jurisdiction Act and of that enactment's basic scope — not a claim about which state's law governs any specific proposed conservatee's case. Because California's version is expressly a "modified" version of the uniform act, this clause does not attempt to identify every respect in which California's text departs from the uniform act as originally drafted or as enacted in other states; a conservatorship with connections to another state may be governed differently there. This clause quotes only the minor and involuntary-commitment exclusions from § 1981(a)-(b); it does not quote the further exclusion in § 1981(c) for certain developmental-disability proceedings, addressed in this document's companion clause on registration. No case law search was performed for this clause: CourtListener's daily search quota (125 requests/day) was already exhausted at the time of this research (confirmed by a 429 rate-limit response before any substantive query was run), so this document is statute-only and discloses that choice rather than waiting out the quota.

clauses.title: "Home State" and "Significant-Connection State" — The Two Threshold Terms the Jurisdiction Test Turns On
clauses.body: The jurisdictional test described in this document's companion clause depends on two defined terms. A proposed conservatee's "home state" means the state in which the proposed conservatee was physically present, including any period of temporary absence, for at least six consecutive months immediately before the filing of a petition for a conservatorship order — or, if none, the state where the proposed conservatee was so present for at least six consecutive months ending within the six months before the petition was filed. A "significant-connection state" means a state, other than the home state, with which the proposed conservatee has a significant connection other than mere physical presence, and in which substantial evidence concerning the proposed conservatee is available.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California's version of the uniform act defines these two threshold terms — not a claim about which state actually qualifies as any particular proposed conservatee's home state or a significant-connection state in any specific case; that depends on facts about that individual's own history of presence and ties to each state. This clause quotes only the two defined terms from § 1991(a)(2)-(3); it does not quote § 1991(a)(1)'s definition of "emergency" or the four-factor list in § 1991(b) that a court consults to decide whether a significant connection exists (family location, duration of presence, location of property, and ties such as voting registration, tax filings, vehicle registration, and driver's license). It also does not address § 1982's separate, broader set of chapter-wide definitions (for example, of "conservator," "conservatee," and "state," the last of which is defined to include a federally recognized Indian tribe, Puerto Rico, the District of Columbia, and other listed jurisdictions in addition to the fifty states). No case law search was performed for this clause because CourtListener's daily quota was already exhausted at the time of this research.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 1991(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)

clauses.title: Which State's Courts May Appoint a Conservator — the Exclusive Statutory Priority Order
clauses.body: For a conservatorship proceeding governed by this article, the statute "provides the exclusive basis for determining whether the courts of this state, as opposed to the courts of another state, have jurisdiction to appoint a conservator of the person, a conservator of the estate, or a conservator of the person and estate." Under that exclusive basis, a California court has jurisdiction to appoint a conservator for a proposed conservatee if California is the proposed conservatee's home state. If California is not the home state, a California court has jurisdiction if, on the date the petition is filed, California is a significant-connection state and the proposed conservatee does not have a home state at all. The statute goes on to provide further, lower-priority bases for California jurisdiction — including where the home state has expressly declined jurisdiction in California's favor, where no petition is pending elsewhere and no timely objection or competing petition is filed, and a residual "appropriate forum" basis where no other state has jurisdiction — as well as a separate, narrower category of special jurisdiction (for example, for a true emergency) addressed in a different section.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's exclusive statutory jurisdiction test for appointing a conservator — not a claim about which state's courts actually have jurisdiction over any specific proposed conservatee. This clause quotes § 1992's exclusivity rule and § 1993(a)-(b), the two highest-priority jurisdictional bases (home state; significant-connection state with no home state); it does not quote the full text of § 1993(c)-(f), which set out three further, lower-priority bases and cross-reference the forum-appropriateness factors in § 1996 and the special jurisdiction described in § 1994. It also does not address § 1995 (a California court's exclusive and continuing jurisdiction once it has appointed a conservator), § 1996 (a California court's discretion to decline jurisdiction in favor of a more appropriate forum), § 1997 (the effect of unjustifiable conduct in acquiring jurisdiction), or the notice and simultaneous-petition rules of §§ 1998-1999. No case law search was performed for this clause because CourtListener's daily quota was already exhausted at the time of this research.

clauses.title: Transferring an Existing California Conservatorship to Another State
clauses.body: A conservator appointed in California, such as {{conservatorName}}, "may petition the court to transfer the conservatorship to another state" — such as {{otherState}} — rather than requiring the other state to start an entirely new conservatorship proceeding for {{conserveeName}} from scratch. After notice and a hearing, a California court will issue only a provisional order granting the transfer, and only if the court is satisfied the conservatorship will be accepted by the other state's court and finds, among other things, that {{conserveeName}} "is physically present in or is reasonably expected to move permanently to the other state," and that either no objection to the transfer has been made or, if one has, "the court determines that the transfer would not be contrary to the interests of the conservatee." A final order confirming the transfer and terminating the California conservatorship issues only after the receiving state's court has issued its own provisional order accepting the case, and the required termination documents (including any required accounting) have been filed in California.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual outbound-transfer petition process available to an existing California conservator — not advice that transfer to any particular state is appropriate for any particular conservatee, and not a guarantee that another state's courts will accept the transfer. This clause quotes only § 2001(a) and one physical-presence finding and one objection finding drawn from § 2001(d) (the findings required for transferring a conservatorship of the person); it does not quote the parallel but not identical findings required for a conservatorship of the estate under § 2001(e) (which also allows a significant-connection basis, not only physical presence or an expected permanent move), the combined-findings rule of § 2001(f) for a conservatorship of the person and estate, or the exact final-order mechanics of § 2001(g). It also does not address § 1981(c)'s exclusion of certain developmental-disability proceedings from this transfer article, or § 2003's special rule for transfers to or from a California tribe's court. No case law search was performed for this clause because CourtListener's daily quota was already exhausted at the time of this research.

citations.quote: An objection to the transfer has not been made or, if an objection has been made, the court determines that the transfer would not be contrary to the interests of the conservatee.

clauses.title: Accepting an Existing Out-of-State Conservatorship Transferred Into California
clauses.body: The mirror-image process applies when a conservatorship for {{conserveeName}} was established in another state, such as {{issuingState}}, and that state's court has already issued a provisional order transferring the case out. "To confirm transfer of a conservatorship transferred to this state under provisions similar to Section 2001, the conservator shall petition the court in this state to accept the conservatorship," and "[t]he petition shall include a certified copy of the other state's provisional order of transfer." The California court must appoint an investigator to conduct a preliminary investigation, hold a hearing, and will grant only a provisional order accepting the case unless it finds the transfer would be contrary to {{conserveeName}}'s interests, that {{conservatorName}} is ineligible to serve as conservator under either the transferring state's law or California law without an identified eligible replacement, or that the chapter does not apply. A final order accepting the proceeding and appointing the conservator in California issues only after a further conformity determination and review confirming the conservatorship complies with California law.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual inbound-transfer acceptance process available once another state's court has provisionally granted an outbound transfer — not advice that transfer into California is appropriate for any particular conservatee, and not a claim that a California court will necessarily accept any particular transfer. This clause quotes only § 2002(a)(1)-(2); it does not quote the notice requirements of § 2002(b), the full list of grounds on which a person may object under § 2002(c), the investigator and hearing requirements of § 2002(d)-(e), the full list of grounds on which the court must deny provisional acceptance under § 2002(f), the post-provisional 60-day conformity-determination and review process of § 2002(h), or the final-order and effective-date rules of § 2002(i) (including the specific pre-effectiveness steps: the conservator's oath, any required bond, delivery of the information required by § 1835, and issuance of letters of conservatorship). No case law search was performed for this clause because CourtListener's daily quota was already exhausted at the time of this research.

clauses.title: Registering an Out-of-State Conservatorship Order in California Is a Narrower, Different Tool Than Transferring the Case
clauses.body: Separately from the transfer process described in this document's other clauses, California law gives an out-of-state conservator a narrower option: registering the existing out-of-state order in a California superior court without moving the underlying conservatorship proceeding itself. Where a conservator of the person has been appointed for {{conserveeName}} in another state, such as {{issuingState}}, and no California petition for a conservator of the person is pending, that conservator, after providing the required notice, "may register the conservatorship order in this state by filing certified copies of the order and letters of office, and proof of notice as required herein, together with a cover sheet approved by the Judicial Council, in the superior court of any appropriate county of this state." Registration lets {{conservatorName}} exercise the out-of-state order's powers in California — for example, over property {{conserveeName}} owns here — while {{conserveeName}} continues to reside in the other state; the underlying conservatorship remains supervised by {{issuingState}}'s court, which the California case ({{issuingCaseNumber}}) is not replacing. That registered authority is expressly conditional on where {{conserveeName}} actually resides: it "applies only when the conservatee resides out of this state," and "[w]hen the conservatee resides in this state, a conservator may not exercise any powers pursuant to a registration under this article."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that registration under Article 4 of this chapter is a distinct, narrower mechanism from the full transfer process described in this document's other clauses — not advice about which mechanism is appropriate for any particular conservatee's situation. This clause quotes only § 2011 (registration for a conservator of the person) and § 2016(c); it does not quote the parallel registration provisions for a conservator of the estate (§ 2012) or of the person and estate (§ 2013), the advance-notice requirements of § 2014, the written-information and fee provisions of § 2015, the rest of § 2016 (including the requirement to seek California court approval before taking an action that would require it under California law, and the specific California statutes listed there that impose special requirements on a registered conservator), the good-faith third-party reliance protection of § 2017, the recordation option of § 2018, or the special rules for a California tribe's order under § 2019. No case law search was performed for this clause because CourtListener's daily quota was already exhausted at the time of this research.

clauses.title: Declaration of Purpose — Adult Adoption Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Adult Adoption — Information Sheet describes California's statutory process, set out in Family Code Division 13, Part 3, Chapter 2 (Procedure for Adult Adoption, §§ 9320-9328), for {{petitionerName}} to adopt {{adopteeName}}, an adult. It is prepared for use alongside an actual adult-adoption petition contemplated for filing in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}.

Adult adoption is a legally separate track from every minor-adoption process this corpus otherwise documents. This corpus's Stepparent Adoption — Information Sheet (Family Code Chapter 5, §§ 9000-9007) and Independent Adoption — Information Sheet (Family Code Chapter 3, §§ 8800-8823) both govern the adoption of a child under 18, built around a birth parent's or existing legal parent's consent, and this corpus's Guardianship of the Person (Petition Information Sheet) governs custody of a minor without creating any new parent-child relationship at all. Adult adoption instead begins from a written agreement between two adults — the prospective adoptive parent and the person proposed to be adopted, who must already be 18 or older — that both of them sign, and it does not involve a birth parent's consent to the adoption at all. This document's companion clauses describe who may enter that agreement, what a petition for its approval must contain, the hearing and appearance requirements, when an investigation is and is not required, a narrower notice requirement specific to adoptions of adults with developmental disabilities, the court's approval standard, and the adoption's effect on inheritance from the adoptee's birth family.

This information sheet is not itself a court filing. Completing it does not adopt {{adopteeName}}, does not affect any person's inheritance rights, and does not determine that any specific adoption should or will be granted. Only a final court order of adoption, entered after the statutory petition, hearing, and approval process described in this document's companion clauses, can actually do that.

clauses.title: Who May Adopt Whom, and the Written Adoption Agreement
clauses.body: Family Code § 9320(a) provides that "An adult may adopt another adult who is younger, except the spouse of the prospective adoptive parent, by an adoption agreement approved by the court, as provided in this chapter." Two eligibility limits appear in that single sentence: the proposed adoptee must be younger than {{petitionerName}}, and {{petitionerName}} may not adopt a current spouse. Unlike the minor-adoption processes this corpus separately documents, in which a birth parent or existing legal parent consents to the child's adoption by someone else, an adult adoption under this chapter rests on the adoptee's own act, not a third party's consent on the adoptee's behalf. Family Code § 9320(b) states this directly: "The adoption agreement shall be in writing, executed by the prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee, and shall state that the parties agree to assume toward each other the legal relationship of parent and child and to have all of the rights and be subject to all of the duties and responsibilities of that relationship." That jointly executed written agreement — not a separate one-sided consent form signed only by {{adopteeName}} — is the mechanism by which {{adopteeName}}'s agreement to the adoption is expressed under this chapter.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own eligibility rule and its own written-agreement mechanism for adult adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular adult adoption, and not a claim that any specific adoption agreement between the prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee named in this document has been, or will be, approved. § 9320(a) and § 9320(b) are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated as one source. This clause corrects one assumption sometimes made about this process: this chapter's own text does not require a separate written consent document signed only by the adoptee, and it does not require the consent of the adoptee's spouse (if any) to the adoption at all — the only spouse this chapter's eligibility rule mentions is the prospective adoptive parent's own spouse, whom the prospective adoptive parent may not adopt. This clause does not address whether a court could decline to approve a specific adoption agreement on other, case-specific grounds; that determination is addressed by this document's companion clause on the court's approval standard at the hearing.

clauses.title: The Petition for Approval of the Adoption Agreement
clauses.body: Family Code § 9321(a) provides that "The prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee may file in the county in which either person resides a petition for approval of the adoption agreement" — meaning venue for {{petitionerName}} and {{adopteeName}}'s petition may rest on either person's residence in {{countyOfFiling}}, not only {{petitionerName}}'s. Family Code § 9321(b) then lists six specific items the petition must state, including "The length and nature of the relationship between the prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee," "The degree of kinship, if any," "The reason the adoption is sought," "A statement as to why the adoption would be in the best interest of the prospective adoptive parent, the proposed adoptee, and the public," the names and addresses of the proposed adoptee's living birth parents or adult children, if any, and "[w]hether the prospective adoptive parent or the prospective adoptive parent's spouse has previously adopted any other adult and, if so, the name of the adult, together with the date and place of the adoption."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own venue rule and its own required petition content for adult adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular adult adoption, and not a claim that any specific petition by the prospective adoptive parent and proposed adoptee named in this document states or omits any of these six items. § 9321(a) and § 9321(b) are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated as one source. This clause quotes four of the six numbered items in § 9321(b) verbatim and paraphrases the remaining two (the degree-of-kinship item and the living-birth-parents/adult-children item) only to the extent needed to introduce the sixth quoted item in context; it does not restate every procedural detail a specific superior court's local rules or forms may additionally require for filing. This document does not itself state, and does not verify, the length or nature of any relationship, the degree of kinship, or the reason for the adoption described in a specific petition.

clauses.title: Setting the Hearing, Notice to Interested Persons, and Personal Appearance
clauses.body: Once {{petitionerName}} and {{adopteeName}} file their petition, Family Code § 9322 requires that "[w]hen the petition for approval of the adoption agreement is filed, the court clerk shall set the matter for hearing." Family Code § 9323 then allows the court to bring in others who may have an interest in the outcome: "The court may require notice of the time and place of the hearing to be served on any other interested person and any interested person may appear and object to the proposed adoption." At the hearing itself, Family Code § 9324 requires personal presence rather than representation by counsel alone, subject to one cross-referenced exception: "Both the prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee shall appear at the hearing in person, unless the court allows otherwise pursuant to Section 8613.5."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own hearing-setting, notice, and appearance rules for adult adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular adult adoption, and not a claim that any specific hearing has been, or will be, set for the petition described in this document. §§ 9322, 9323, and 9324 are three separate, independently numbered sections and are treated as three independent sources. This clause does not itself state the content of § 8613.5 (remote appearance), which is quoted here only by cross-reference within § 9324's own text; this clause does not independently verify § 8613.5's substantive remote-appearance criteria. This session's one lightweight CourtListener check for California appellate decisions construing "interested person" under § 9323, or the personal-appearance requirement under § 9324, returned a 429 daily-quota-exceeded error (125 requests/day) before any case could be retrieved, so this clause is statute-text-only and does not report how courts have applied either provision on specific facts. Family Code § 9324 was last amended in 2022 (effective January 1, 2023); this clause reports its current text as fetched from the state's own legislative information website on the date above, not an earlier or later version.
