clauses.title: No General Investigation Requirement, and a Narrower Notice Requirement for Adults With Developmental Disabilities
clauses.body: Family Code § 9325 states the general rule for adult adoption: "No investigation or report to the court by any public officer or agency is required, but the court may require the county probation officer or the department to investigate the circumstances of the proposed adoption and report thereon, with recommendations, to the court before the hearing." That default — no mandatory home study or investigation, with the court retaining discretion to order one — does not apply without exception. Family Code § 9326 requires {{petitionerName}} to give specific additional notice "in any case in which both of the following conditions exist: (a) The proposed adoptee is an adult with developmental disabilities. (b) The prospective adoptive parent is a provider of board and care, treatment, habilitation, or other services to persons with developmental disabilities or is a spouse or employee of a provider," including notice to "the director of the regional center for the developmentally disabled" at least 30 days before the hearing. Where {{petitionerName}} is such a provider (or that provider's spouse or employee) and seeks to adopt an unrelated adult with developmental disabilities, Family Code § 9327 requires that regional center to "file a written report with the court regarding the suitability of the proposed adoption in meeting the needs of the proposed adoptee and regarding any known previous adoption by the prospective adoptive parent."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own default investigation rule and its own narrower exception for adults with developmental disabilities adopted by their care providers — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular adult adoption, and not a claim that the proposed adoptee named in this document is or is not an adult with developmental disabilities, or that the prospective adoptive parent named in this document is or is not a provider within the meaning of these sections. §§ 9325, 9326, and 9327 are three separate, independently numbered sections and are treated as three independent sources; the § 9326(a)-(b) quotation is drawn from that one section's own subdivisions. This clause paraphrases § 9326's cross-reference to the Welfare and Institutions Code defining a regional center, and does not independently verify that cross-referenced Welfare and Institutions Code text. This clause does not restate every procedural detail of how or on whom notice under § 9326 must be served beyond the regional center director and the proposed adoptee's living birth parents or adult children, and it does not determine whether the conditions triggering §§ 9326-9327 are met in any specific case.

clauses.title: The Court's Approval Standard at the Hearing
clauses.body: Family Code § 9328(a) requires the court itself to question the parties at the hearing: "At the hearing the court shall examine the parties, or the counsel of any party not present in person." § 9328(b) then sets the standard for approval or denial: "If the court is satisfied that the adoption will be in the best interests of the persons seeking the adoption and in the public interest and that there is no reason why the petition should not be granted, the court shall approve the adoption agreement and make an order of adoption declaring that the person adopted is the child of the adoptive parent. Otherwise, the court shall withhold approval of the agreement and deny the petition." § 9328(c) relaxes the ordinary evidentiary rules for that determination: "In determining whether or not the adoption of any person pursuant to this part is in the best interests of the persons seeking the adoption or the public interest, the court may consider evidence, oral or written, whether or not it is in conformity with the Evidence Code."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own approval standard for adult adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular adult adoption, and not a claim that any specific petition described in this document will be approved or denied. § 9328(a), (b), and (c) are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated as one source. This clause does not identify what would, in a specific case, constitute a reason the petition should not be granted; § 9328(b) leaves that determination to the court on the facts and evidence before it, admissible under § 9328(c)'s relaxed standard or not. This document does not itself examine the parties, weigh evidence, or make any best-interest determination — only the court conducting the hearing described in this document's companion clause on hearing notice and appearance can do that.

clauses.title: Effect on Inheritance From the Adoptee's Birth Family
clauses.body: Family Code Chapter 2 itself does not state how a completed adult adoption affects {{adopteeName}}'s inheritance rights from {{adopteeName}}'s birth family; that question is addressed by California's separate intestate-succession statute, Probate Code § 6450 and § 6451, which apply to "an adopted person" without distinguishing an adult adoptee from a minor one. Probate Code § 6450(b) provides that "[t]he relationship of parent and child exists between an adopted person and the person's adopting parent or parents" for intestate-succession purposes. Probate Code § 6451(a) then sets the default rule for the birth-family relationship: "An adoption severs the relationship of parent and child between an adopted person and a natural parent of the adopted person unless both of the following requirements are satisfied: (1) The natural parent and the adopted person lived together at any time as parent and child, or the natural parent was married to or cohabiting with the other natural parent at the time the person was conceived and died before the person's birth. (2) The adoption was by the spouse of either of the natural parents or after the death of either of the natural parents." Because an adult adoption under Family Code §§ 9320-9328 does not require the adoptive parent to be a spouse of {{adopteeName}}'s natural parent or to be adopting after a natural parent's death, this severance default, not its narrow exception, will typically govern an adult adoption completed under this chapter for intestate-succession purposes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own default inheritance-severance rule for adopted persons generally, and of that rule's own narrow exception — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular estate, and not a claim that the proposed adoptee's specific circumstances do or do not satisfy Probate Code § 6451(a)'s exception. Probate Code § 6450 and § 6451 are separate, independently numbered sections and are treated as two independent sources; § 6450(a) (concerning natural parents generally) and § 6451(b)-(c) (concerning who inherits from or through the adopted person, and prior adoptive relationships) are not quoted or independently verified here. This clause corrects one assumption sometimes made about this topic: Probate Code §§ 6450-6451 do not contain a rule written specifically for adult adoption, or a rule that differs in its own terms from the rule that applies to the adoption of a minor; both draw on the same statutory text. This clause addresses only intestate succession — inheritance in the absence of a valid will — and does not address testate succession under a will, nonprobate transfers, or any other body of law that may treat an adopted adult differently for other purposes. This document does not itself determine the proposed adoptee's inheritance rights in any specific estate.

clauses.title: About School Activities Leave
Which Employers Are Covered
clauses.body: Labor Code § 230.8 applies only to an employer that employs 25 or more employees working at the same location. A covered employer may not discharge or in any way discriminate against an employee who is a parent of one or more children of the age to attend kindergarten or grades 1 to 12, or a licensed child care provider, for taking off up to 40 hours each year for the child-related activities the statute describes.
clauses.gap: The statute does not define "the same location," and does not say how an employer with employees spread across multiple sites, or an employee who works at more than one site, is measured against the 25-employee threshold. This 25-or-more-employees-at-the-same-location coverage threshold is a real limit on who this law protects — it is not a companywide headcount test, and an employee at a smaller location may fall outside this particular statute even if the employer is large overall.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(a)(1), employer coverage threshold and core prohibition
citations.quote: An employer who employs 25 or more employees working at the same location shall not discharge or in any way discriminate against an employee who is a parent of one or more children of the age to attend kindergarten or grades 1 to 12, inclusive, or a licensed child care provider, for taking off up to 40 hours each year, for the purpose of either of the following child-related activities:

clauses.title: What Time Off Is Covered
clauses.body: The statute covers two distinct categories of child-related activities, within an overall cap of up to 40 hours in a year. The first category is finding, enrolling, or reenrolling a child in a school or with a licensed child care provider, or participating in activities of the child's school or licensed child care provider, after the employee gives the employer reasonable notice of the planned absence in advance; time off in this first category cannot exceed eight hours in any calendar month. The second category is addressing a "child care provider or school emergency," a defined term covering situations such as the school or provider requesting the child be picked up or excluding the child under an attendance policy, behavioral or discipline problems, closure or unexpected unavailability of the school or provider, or a natural disaster, after the employee gives the employer notice.
clauses.gap: The statute's opening 40-hours-per-year cap applies to both categories of activity together, but the additional eight-hours-per-calendar-month sub-cap is written to apply only to the first category (finding, enrolling, or participating) — the statute does not say the emergency-pickup category is separately capped at eight hours a month. The statute also does not state a minimum amount of advance notice that counts as "reasonable" for the first category, and, for the emergency category, only requires that the employee "gives notice," without using the word "reasonable." No case law interpreting these terms is cited in this document; a CourtListener case-law search for this statute was not completed because the research session's daily case-law search quota was already exhausted, so this document is limited to the statutory text.

Time off pursuant to this subparagraph shall not exceed eight hours in any calendar month of the year.

clauses.title: Who Counts as a "Parent" and Priority Between Two Parents
clauses.body: For purposes of this statute, "parent" is defined broadly: a parent, guardian, stepparent, foster parent, or grandparent of a child, or a person who stands in loco parentis to a child. Where more than one parent of the same child is employed by the same employer at the same worksite, the entitlement to take a planned absence as to that child belongs, at any one time, only to whichever parent first gives the employer notice; the other parent may take a simultaneous planned absence for that same child only with the employer's approval.
clauses.gap: The current text of this statute defines eligibility by this list of family relationships and by the child being of an age to attend kindergarten through grade 12, or by the employee being a licensed child care provider — it does not use a separate "custody" test, and it does not single out grandparents as needing to have custody of the child to qualify. This document is based on the statute as currently in effect; it does not trace the legislative history of this eligible-relationship list or confirm it has not changed since this text was last amended.

clauses.title: Notice, and Whether the Time Off Is Paid
clauses.body: This leave is not automatically paid on top of an employee's other leave banks: the employee must use existing vacation, personal leave, or compensatory time off for the planned absence, unless a collective bargaining agreement entered into before January 1, 1995 and still in effect provides otherwise; an employee may also use unpaid time for this purpose to the extent the employer makes that available. If all of an employer's permanent, full-time employees are given vacation during the same period of the year, an employee may not use accrued vacation at any other time of year for this purpose.
clauses.gap: The statute does not create a separate, additional paid-leave bank for this purpose — it directs the employee to an existing vacation, personal leave, or compensatory time balance (or unpaid time, if the employer makes that available), so how much paid time off is actually available depends on the employee's own accrued balances and the employer's own unpaid-time practices, not on this statute alone. The statute also says an employee's entitlement under this section cannot be diminished by a collective bargaining agreement term agreed to on or after January 1, 1995, a detail this document does not further develop.

citations.quote: The employee shall utilize existing vacation, personal leave, or compensatory time off for purposes of the planned absence authorized by this section, unless otherwise provided by a collective bargaining agreement entered into before January 1, 1995, and in effect on that date. An employee also may utilize time off without pay for this purpose, to the extent made available by his or her employer.

citations.quote: Notwithstanding paragraph (1), in the event that all permanent, full-time employees of an employer are accorded vacation during the same period of time in the calendar year, an employee of that employer may not utilize that accrued vacation benefit at any other time for purposes of the planned absence authorized by this section.

clauses.title: Documentation the Employer May Request
clauses.body: If the employer requests it, the employee must provide documentation from the school or licensed child care provider showing that the employee engaged in the covered child-related activity on a specific date and at a particular time. The statute defines "documentation" as whatever written verification of parental participation the school or licensed child care provider itself deems appropriate and reasonable.
clauses.gap: The statute leaves the content and format of acceptable "documentation" to what the school or child care provider itself deems appropriate and reasonable — it does not specify a required form, and different schools or providers may verify participation differently. The documentation requirement is worded as proof of having "engaged in child-related activities permitted in subdivision (a)" generally; this document does not resolve whether, or how, that requirement is meant to apply to the emergency-pickup category as distinct from the finding/enrolling/participating category.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(c), documentation the employer may require
citations.quote: The employee, if requested by the employer, shall provide documentation from the school or licensed child care provider as proof that he or she engaged in child-related activities permitted in subdivision (a) on a specific date and at a particular time. For purposes of this subdivision, “documentation” means whatever written verification of parental participation the school or licensed child care provider deems appropriate and reasonable.

clauses.title: Anti-Discrimination Protection and Remedies
clauses.body: An employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment because the employee took time off for a covered child-related activity is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement of lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts. If an employer willfully refuses to rehire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee or former employee who has been determined eligible for rehiring or promotion through a grievance procedure, arbitration, or hearing authorized by law, the employer is subject to a civil penalty equal to three times the amount of the employee's lost wages and work benefits.
clauses.gap: The statute itself does not name a specific agency or set a specific filing deadline for pursuing these remedies, and no case law construing this remedy provision is cited here: a CourtListener case-law search for this statute returned a 429 daily-quota-exceeded error before any results could be reviewed, so this document relies on the statutory text alone rather than waiting out or retrying that quota.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.8(d), prohibition on retaliation and available remedies
citations.quote: Any employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or in any other manner discriminated against in terms and conditions of employment by his or her employer because the employee has taken time off to engage in child-related activities permitted in subdivision (a) shall be entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer. Any employer who willfully refuses to rehire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee or former employee who has been determined to be eligible for rehiring or promotion by a grievance procedure, arbitration, or hearing authorized by law shall be subject to a civil penalty in an amount equal to three times the amount of the employee’s lost wages and work benefits.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet summarizes federal obligations that apply when {{companyName}} sponsors {{employeeName}} for H-1B nonimmigrant work authorization for the position of {{jobTitle}}. It describes requirements under the Immigration and Nationality Act's Labor Condition Application (LCA) provisions, 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n), and the Department of Labor's implementing wage regulation, 20 C.F.R. § 655.731. It states facts about these federal requirements; it does not instruct {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} on how to respond to their particular circumstances, and it is not a substitute for the LCA and petition documents themselves.

clauses.title: LCA Wage Attestation Requirement
clauses.body: Before an H-1B nonimmigrant may be admitted or provided status in an occupational classification, the sponsoring employer must file a Labor Condition Application (LCA) attesting that it is offering and will offer wages that are at least the greater of two figures: the actual wage level the employer pays to other individuals with similar experience and qualifications for the same specific employment, or the prevailing wage level for the occupational classification in the area of employment. The employer must also attest that it will provide working conditions for the H-1B worker that will not adversely affect the working conditions of workers similarly employed.
clauses.gap: The statute states the wage floor as a comparison of two figures determined at the time the LCA is filed; it does not itself specify the methodology for calculating the prevailing wage or actual wage — that methodology, along with permissible wage sources, is set out separately in the Department of Labor's implementing regulation at 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(a), not in the statutory text quoted here.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(A)(i)(I) (Cornell LII text)
citations.quote: the actual wage level paid by the employer to all other individuals with similar experience and qualifications for the specific employment in question

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(A)(i)(II) (Cornell LII text)
citations.quote: the prevailing wage level for the occupational classification in the area of employment

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(A)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.quote: will provide working conditions for such a nonimmigrant that will not adversely affect the working conditions of workers similarly employed.

clauses.title: LCA Notice Requirement
clauses.body: At the time an LCA is filed, the employer must also attest that it has provided notice of the filing. If a bargaining representative exists for the employer's employees in the occupational classification and area for which H-1B workers are sought, notice must go to that representative. If there is no bargaining representative, the employer must instead provide notice through methods such as physical posting in conspicuous locations at the place of employment, or electronic notification to employees in that occupational classification.
clauses.gap: The statute names physical posting and electronic notification as illustrative methods ("such methods as") rather than an exclusive list, and it does not itself specify posting duration, content, or location requirements — those operational details are set by Department of Labor regulation (20 C.F.R. § 655.734) rather than by the statutory text quoted here.

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(C)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.quote: has provided notice of the filing under this paragraph to the bargaining representative (if any) of the employer’s employees in the occupational classification and area for which aliens are sought

citations.case: 8 U.S.C. § 1182(n)(1)(C)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.quote: if there is no such bargaining representative, has provided notice of filing in the occupational classification through such methods as physical posting in conspicuous locations at the place of employment or electronic notification to employees in the occupational classification for which H–1B nonimmigrants are sought.

clauses.title: Determining the Required Wage
clauses.body: Department of Labor regulations implementing the LCA wage attestation specify that the required wage is the greater of the actual wage rate or the prevailing wage, and that this required wage generally must be paid to the H-1B worker in cash, in hand, free and clear, when due. A cash wage below the required wage level is permitted only to the extent a deduction from wages qualifies as an authorized deduction under the regulation's separate deduction criteria.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general cash-in-hand rule and its stated exception for authorized deductions; it does not itself catalog which deductions qualify as authorized (for example, legally required withholding, or deductions meeting the regulation's voluntary-authorization and benefit-of-employee criteria) — those criteria appear in a separate paragraph of the same regulation, addressed in the next clause below.

citations.case: 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(a) (eCFR text)
citations.quote: that is, that the wage shall be the greater of the actual wage rate (as specified in paragraph (a)(1) of this section) or the prevailing wage (as specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section)

The required wage must be paid to the employee, cash in hand, free and clear, when due, except that deductions made in accordance with paragraph (c)(9) of this section may reduce the cash wage below the level of the required wage.

clauses.title: No Recoupment of Attorney Fees or H-1B Filing Costs
clauses.body: Department of Labor regulations governing the H-1B required wage treat attorney fees and other costs connected to performing H-1B program functions the employer is required to perform — such as preparing and filing the LCA and the H-1B petition — as the employer's own business expense. A wage deduction may not be used to recoup that business expense, whether the deduction is one that would otherwise be authorized because it is customary in the occupation or area of employment, or one that would otherwise be authorized because the employee voluntarily agreed to it in writing.
clauses.gap: This no-recoupment rule is a limit on what counts as an authorized wage deduction under two separate criteria sets in the same subsection (20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(9)(ii) and (c)(9)(iii)(C)) — it is not a single freestanding prohibition codified in one subsection, and it does not by its terms reach costs an employee pays out of pocket rather than through a wage deduction, or costs that are not connected to functions the employer itself is required to perform.

citations.quote: except that the deduction may not recoup a business expense(s) of the employer (including attorney fees and other costs connected to the performance of H-1B program functions which are required to be performed by the employer, e.g., preparation and filing of LCA and H-1B petition)

citations.case: 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(9)(iii)(C) (eCFR text)
citations.quote: Is not a recoupment of the employer's business expense (e.g., tools and equipment; transportation costs where such transportation is an incident of, and necessary to, the employment; living expenses when the employee is traveling on the employer's business; attorney fees and other costs connected to the performance of H-1B program functions which are required to be performed by the employer (e.g., preparation and filing of LCA and H-1B petition))

clauses.title: Penalties Versus Liquidated Damages for Early Departure
clauses.body: Separately from the attorney-fee recoupment rule, Department of Labor regulations prohibit an employer from requiring, directly or indirectly, that an H-1B worker pay a penalty for ceasing employment before a date agreed to by the worker and employer, and prohibit any wage deduction made to collect such a penalty. The regulation distinguishes this from bona fide liquidated damages, which an employer is permitted to receive from a departing H-1B worker, provided the deduction otherwise satisfies the regulation's separate authorized-deduction criteria.
clauses.gap: Whether a given payment obligation is a prohibited "penalty" or a permitted "liquidated damages" provision is determined under applicable state contract law, not by a federal test stated in this regulation — the regulation identifies the distinction and points to state law to draw it, so the classification of any particular provision cannot be determined from the federal text alone.

citations.quote: The employer is not permitted to require (directly or indirectly) that the nonimmigrant pay a penalty for ceasing employment with the employer prior to an agreed date. Therefore, the employer shall not make any deduction from or reduction in the payment of the required wage to collect such a penalty.
The employer is permitted to receive bona fide liquidated damages from the H-1B nonimmigrant who ceases employment with the employer prior to an agreed date.

clauses.title: No Rebate of the Employer's ACWIA Filing Fee
clauses.body: Department of Labor regulations separately prohibit an employer from receiving, and an H-1B worker from paying, any part of the additional $500 or $1,000 filing fee the employer owes under section 214(c) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, whether the payment would run directly or indirectly, voluntarily or involuntarily.
clauses.gap: This rule addresses only the employer's own statutory ACWIA/fraud-prevention filing fee under INA § 214(c); it does not address other filing fees associated with an H-1B petition (such as the base I-129 filing fee or premium processing fee), and current fee amounts should be confirmed against U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services' fee schedule in effect at the time of filing rather than assumed from this regulation's stated dollar figures.

citations.quote: The employer may not receive, and the H-1B nonimmigrant may not pay, any part of the $500 additional filing fee (for a petition filed prior to December 18, 2000) or $1,000 additional filing fee (for a petition filed on or subsequent to December 18, 2000), whether directly or indirectly, voluntarily or involuntarily.

clauses.title: Recordkeeping and Further Information
clauses.body: {{companyName}} is required to maintain documentation supporting the wage statement and wage payments described above for as long as required by federal regulation, and to make certain records available for public examination. This information sheet reflects the LCA wage, notice, and deduction provisions described above as of {{dateSigned}}; it does not address every LCA attestation or every H-1B compliance obligation, including obligations that apply specifically to H-1B-dependent employers or employers with a history of willful violations.

clauses.title: About This Document: The Federal Speak Out Act, and How It Differs From California Non-Disparagement Law
clauses.body: This information sheet describes a single federal statute: the Speak Out Act, Pub. L. 117-224 (Dec. 7, 2022), codified at 42 U.S.C. §§ 19401-19404. It is a separate body of law from this corpus's Non-Disparagement Agreement — Information Sheet, which covers California's settlement-agreement disclosure ban (Code Civ. Proc. § 1001), California's broader Silenced No More Act (Gov. Code § 12964.5), and federal labor-law limits on severance non-disparagement clauses under the National Labor Relations Act (29 U.S.C. §§ 157-158). This document does not restate any of that material. Instead, it addresses a narrower question the other document does not reach: whether a nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause signed before a sexual assault or sexual harassment dispute ever arose — for example, in a standard employment agreement, offer letter, or business contract signed when a relationship began, with no dispute yet in sight — can later be enforced in court to silence someone about that dispute once it does arise. {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}} are identified here for reference throughout this document; the document describes federal statutory text and does not itself determine whether the Speak Out Act applies to any specific clause, contract, or dispute between them.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: “Sexual Assault Dispute” and “Sexual Harassment Dispute”
clauses.body: The Speak Out Act defines two categories of dispute that trigger its rule. A “sexual assault dispute” means a dispute involving a nonconsensual sexual act or sexual contact, using terms defined in the federal criminal code at 18 U.S.C. § 2246, or a similar applicable Tribal or State law definition, and it expressly includes a dispute where the victim lacked the capacity to consent. A “sexual harassment dispute” means a dispute relating to conduct alleged to constitute sexual harassment under applicable Federal, Tribal, or State law — the statute does not define “sexual harassment” itself; it borrows whatever definition already exists under the law governing the dispute at hand.
clauses.gap: The “sexual assault dispute” definition cross-references 18 U.S.C. § 2246's definitions of “sexual act” and “sexual contact”; that cross-referenced section was not independently fetched or verified in this research — only 42 U.S.C. § 19402's own text, which names it, was fetched and confirmed. The “sexual harassment dispute” definition supplies no federal definition of “sexual harassment” of its own; it points outward to whatever Federal, Tribal, or State law already defines that term for the dispute at hand, so what counts as a covered dispute can vary by jurisdiction and cause of action. Correction to an initial research assumption: the Speak Out Act's Public Law number is Pub. L. 117-224 (Dec. 7, 2022, 136 Stat. 2290), confirmed directly in the statute's own short-title note as fetched from law.cornell.edu — not Pub. L. 117-90, an earlier assumption this document corrects. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the parties are in, but whether it applies to a specific clause or dispute still turns on facts this document doesn't resolve. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is enforceable in a specific case.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 19402(3) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, definition of “sexual assault dispute”
citations.quote: The term “ sexual assault dispute ” means a dispute involving a nonconsensual sexual act or sexual contact, as such terms are defined in section 2246 of title 18 or similar applicable Tribal or State law, including when the victim lacks capacity to consent.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 19402(4) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, definition of “sexual harassment dispute”
citations.quote: The term “ sexual harassment dispute ” means a dispute relating to conduct that is alleged to constitute sexual harassment under applicable Federal, Tribal, or State law.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: “Nondisclosure Clause” and “Nondisparagement Clause”
clauses.body: The statute separately defines the two kinds of clauses it reaches. A “nondisclosure clause” means a provision in a contract or agreement that requires the parties not to disclose or discuss conduct, the existence of a settlement involving conduct, or information covered by the contract or agreement's terms and conditions. A “nondisparagement clause” means a provision in a contract or agreement that requires one or more parties not to make a negative statement about another party relating to the contract, agreement, claim, or case. Both definitions are broad enough to reach many contract types — not only settlement agreements, but also employment agreements, offer letters, severance agreements, and ordinary business or consumer contracts.
clauses.gap: These definitions are specific to this federal chapter (42 U.S.C. §§ 19401-19404); this document's use of “nondisclosure clause” and “nondisparagement clause” tracks this statute's own wording, which does not necessarily match how similar terms are used in this corpus's separate Non-Disparagement Agreement — Information Sheet or the California statutes it covers. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the parties are in, but whether a specific contract provision meets these definitions still turns on that provision's own wording. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is enforceable in a specific case.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 19402(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, definition of “nondisclosure clause”
citations.quote: The term “ nondisclosure clause ” means a provision in a contract or agreement that requires the parties to the contract or agreement not to disclose or discuss conduct, the existence of a settlement involving conduct, or information covered by the terms and conditions of the contract or agreement.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 19402(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, definition of “nondisparagement clause”
citations.quote: The term “ nondisparagement clause ” means a provision in a contract or agreement that requires 1 or more parties to the contract or agreement not to make a negative statement about another party that relates to the contract, agreement, claim, or case.

clauses.title: What Is Voided: A Predispute Clause, Not Any Nondisclosure or Nondisparagement Clause
clauses.body: The statute's operative rule is narrow and specific about timing. With respect to a sexual assault dispute or sexual harassment dispute, no nondisclosure clause or nondisparagement clause agreed to before the dispute arises is judicially enforceable, in instances where the conduct at issue is alleged to have violated Federal, Tribal, or State law. In plain terms: a confidentiality or non-disparagement clause signed before any dispute existed — such as one included in an employment agreement, offer letter, or standard business contract signed when the relationship began — cannot be enforced in court to block someone from later speaking about a sexual assault or sexual harassment dispute that subsequently arises.
clauses.gap: The statute bars “judicial enforceability” specifically — its text does not say the clause is void, illegal, or unenforceable for every purpose; it says a court will not enforce it in this context, which is what a court considers if someone tries to invoke the clause against a person speaking out. The statute does not itself define when a dispute “arises” for timing purposes; that threshold question is not resolved in the statutory text, and no case law addressing it was checked in this research (CourtListener's case-law search was rate-limited/exhausted before this document could be checked there). The rule's effect also requires that the underlying conduct be “alleged to have violated Federal, Tribal, or State law” — a factual and legal threshold this document doesn't resolve for any specific situation. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the parties are in, but whether it makes a specific clause unenforceable in a specific case still turns on facts this document doesn't resolve. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is enforceable in a specific case.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 19403(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, limitation on judicial enforceability of a predispute nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause
citations.quote: With respect to a sexual assault dispute or sexual harassment dispute , no nondisclosure clause or nondisparagement clause agreed to before the dispute arises shall be judicially enforceable in instances in which conduct is alleged to have violated Federal, Tribal, or State law.

clauses.title: Post-Dispute Settlement Agreements Fall Outside This Federal Bar
clauses.body: The predispute limitation described above cuts both ways: by its own terms, the statute reaches only a nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause “agreed to before the dispute arises.” A nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause that is instead negotiated and signed after a sexual assault or sexual harassment dispute has already arisen — the typical case of a settlement agreement resolving that specific dispute — is not made judicially unenforceable by this federal statute. The Speak Out Act does not prohibit, restrict, or otherwise address confidentiality or non-disparagement terms in a post-dispute settlement agreement; its text is silent on that category of agreement.
clauses.gap: This clause's citation is the same statutory subsection as the previous clause (42 U.S.C. § 19403(a)) — it is not independent corroboration, only the flip side of the same predispute/post-dispute line drawn by that subsection's own wording. Separate state-law rules — including, in California, the settlement-agreement disclosure ban and Silenced No More Act covered in this corpus's separate Non-Disparagement Agreement — Information Sheet — may still restrict what a post-dispute settlement agreement can require, even where this federal statute does not; this document does not restate that material, and a reader evaluating a post-dispute settlement agreement should look to that separate document rather than this one. Whether a specific agreement was reached before or after a dispute “arose” is a factual question this document doesn't resolve, and no case law addressing that timing question was checked in this research. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific settlement agreement is enforceable in a specific case.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 19403(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, predispute-timing limit that leaves post-dispute agreements outside the bar
citations.quote: no nondisclosure clause or nondisparagement clause agreed to before the dispute arises shall be judicially enforceable

clauses.title: Carve-Outs: State Law, Pseudonym Rules, and Trade Secrets
clauses.body: The statute preserves three things outside its core rule. First, it doesn't stop a state or locality from enforcing its own, separate law governing nondisclosure or nondisparagement clauses, as long as that state or local law is at least as protective of a person's right to speak freely as this federal statute is. Second, it doesn't override any Federal, State, or Tribal law governing the use of pseudonyms when filing a claim involving a sexual assault or sexual harassment dispute. Third, it doesn't stop an employer and employee from protecting trade secrets or proprietary information.
clauses.gap: All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section as the two clauses above (42 U.S.C. § 19403(b), (c), and (d)) — they are treated as one source with those clauses, not independent corroboration of each other. The “at least as protective” standard in subsection (b) is not itself defined by any measurable criterion in the statutory text; how a specific state or local law compares is not resolved here. The trade-secret carve-out in subsection (d) does not define “trade secrets or proprietary information” — neither term is defined anywhere in this chapter. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the parties are in, but whether a specific state law is “at least as protective,” or a specific clause protects a genuine trade secret, are questions this document doesn't resolve. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is enforceable in a specific case.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 19403(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, continued applicability of more-protective state or local law
citations.quote: Nothing in this chapter shall prohibit a State or locality from enforcing a provision of State law governing nondisclosure or nondisparagement clauses that is at least as protective of the right of an individual to speak freely, as provided by this chapter.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 19403(c) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, continued applicability of pseudonym-filing law
citations.quote: the use of pseudonyms in the filing of claims involving sexual assault or sexual harassment disputes.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 19403(d) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, trade secret and proprietary information carve-out
citations.quote: Nothing in this chapter shall prohibit an employer and an employee from protecting trade secrets or proprietary information.

clauses.title: Applicability: Claims Filed On or After December 7, 2022
clauses.body: The statute applies to a claim filed under Federal, State, or Tribal law on or after December 7, 2022 — the date the Speak Out Act was signed into law. The trigger for applicability is the filing date of the claim, not the date the underlying nondisclosure or nondisparagement clause was originally signed. That means a clause signed years before December 7, 2022 — for example, in an older employment agreement — can still be reached by this statute's predispute rule if the sexual assault or sexual harassment claim to which it relates is filed on or after that date.
clauses.gap: The statute doesn't define what counts as a claim being “filed” for this purpose — whether that means a civil lawsuit, an administrative charge, an internal complaint, or something else is not resolved by the statutory text, and no case law addressing that question was checked in this research (CourtListener's case-law search returned a 429 rate-limit response, 125/day exhausted, before this document could be checked there; given how recent this 2022 statute is, case law interpreting it may also simply be scarce). This applicability provision uses a different timing concept (“filed”) from the predispute-clause rule's own timing concept (“before the dispute arises”); the two dates need not coincide, and this document doesn't resolve how they interact in every case. This is federal law, generally applicable regardless of which state the parties are in, but whether a specific claim was “filed” on or after December 7, 2022 is a factual question this document doesn't resolve. This document is informational only and does not itself resolve whether a specific clause is enforceable in a specific case.

citations.case: 42 U.S.C. § 19404 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Speak Out Act, applicability to claims filed on or after December 7, 2022
citations.quote: This chapter shall apply with respect to a claim that is filed under Federal, State, or Tribal law on or after December 7, 2022

clauses.title: Closing Note and Relationship to This Corpus's Other Non-Disparagement Document
Purpose of This Information Sheet and How TAA Differs From Unemployment Insurance and WARN
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the federal Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA) program for workers, authorized by the Trade Act of 1974 as amended, 19 U.S.C. § 2271 et seq. TAA is a separate federal program from the documents elsewhere in this corpus concerning California's state unemployment insurance (UI) system (the claimant information sheet, employer response, appeal, overpayment, and severance-and-UI documents, administered by California's Employment Development Department under the state Unemployment Insurance Code) and from the WARN Act documents (the federal and California WARN Acts, which require advance notice of certain layoffs and plant closings but do not themselves provide any wage-replacement, training, or relocation benefit). TAA instead is a federal program, administered by the U.S. Department of Labor, that can make extended income support (called Trade Readjustment Allowances, or TRA), job training, job search and relocation allowances, and a health coverage tax credit available to a group of workers whom the Department of Labor has certified as adversely affected by increased imports or a shift in production to a foreign country. {{employeeName}} was employed by {{companyName}} until {{separationDate}}. This document states facts about how TAA eligibility is established and how TAA benefits relate to state unemployment insurance; it does not determine that {{employeeName}}'s own separation qualifies for TAA, and it is not itself a TAA petition or application.

clauses.title: Current Operational Status: TAA Benefits Under This Part Are Not Currently Authorized
clauses.body: The Trade Act of 1974's worker program, 19 U.S.C. §§ 2271-2298 (the sections describing petitions, certification, Trade Readjustment Allowances, training, and job search and relocation allowances), has lapsed. An editorial note carried in the current U.S. Code text following 19 U.S.C. § 2271 (and repeated after related sections in this part), captioned "Termination Date," states that no trade adjustment assistance, vouchers, allowances, or other payments or benefits may be provided under this part after June 30, 2022, except as otherwise provided. This is not a new or unusual event for this program: the same note and the amendment history recite a series of earlier lapses and temporary revivals (for example, a lapse addressed by a temporary revival running from 2011 to January 1, 2014, and a further temporary revival running from June 29, 2015 to July 1, 2021, after which the statute reverted to an earlier version before again lapsing on June 30, 2022). The text fetched for this document does not itself show a further reauthorization enacted after that June 30, 2022 lapse.
clauses.gap: This finding corrects an assumption in this document's research brief, which described TAA as a presently operating benefits program without qualification. Having fetched and read the actual current 19 U.S.C. § 2271 text (and the parallel note on §§ 2272 and 2297) directly from Cornell's Legal Information Institute, the honest finding is that, as carried in that text, new TAA benefits under this part are not authorized after June 30, 2022, subject to whatever transition or savings provisions Congress may have separately enacted for petitions filed before that date (the "except as otherwise provided" language, and the detailed transition rules in note material accompanying Pub. L. 114-27 § 405, which this document does not attempt to restate in full). This document's drafter could not independently corroborate current program status against the Department of Labor's own TAA program pages, because the network access available for this research was blocked from reaching dol.gov; this finding rests on the Cornell-hosted U.S. Code text and its official notes alone, fetched twice with distinct User-Agent strings and confirmed byte-identical, without independent confirmation of whether Congress has since reauthorized the program in legislation not yet reflected in that text. A reader should not treat this document as confirming that any TAA benefit is currently obtainable for a new petition.

citations.case: 19 U.S.C. § 2271, Termination Date note (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.cite: 19 U.S.C. § 2271 note ("Termination Date")
citations.quote: No trade adjustment assistance, vouchers, allowances, or other payments or benefits may be provided under this part after June 30, 2022, except as otherwise provided

clauses.title: How a Group of Workers Becomes Certified: Petition and Group Eligibility
clauses.body: Under 19 U.S.C. § 2271(a)(1), an individual worker does not petition for TAA benefits alone. A petition for certification of eligibility to apply for adjustment assistance for a group of workers is instead filed simultaneously with the Secretary of Labor and with the Governor of the State where the workers' firm or subdivision is located, and may be filed by the group of workers itself, by the workers' certified or recognized union or other duly authorized representative, or by the workers' employer (acting together with one-stop operators or one-stop partners, on the workers' behalf). Once a petition is filed, 19 U.S.C. § 2272 sets out the group eligibility requirements the Secretary applies before certifying the group: the Secretary must determine that a significant number or proportion of the firm's workers have become, or are threatened to become, totally or partially separated, and that either (1) the firm's sales or production have decreased while imports of like or directly competitive articles increased and contributed importantly to the separations, or (2) the firm shifted production of such articles to a foreign country under the conditions § 2272(a)(2)(B) describes. Only after the Secretary certifies the group as eligible can members of that certified group individually apply for TAA benefits.
clauses.gap: This clause covers 19 U.S.C. §§ 2271(a) and 2272(a) as currently printed; it does not cover § 2271(b)'s hearing procedure, § 2272(b)'s separate "adversely affected secondary worker" (supplier/downstream producer) pathway, or the agricultural-firm and oil-and-gas-firm definitions in § 2272(c), all of which can matter to a particular group's eligibility. As the preceding clause discloses, new certifications and benefits under this part are not currently authorized past June 30, 2022 absent a further reauthorization this document's drafter could not independently confirm.

clauses.title: Trade Readjustment Allowances: How TRA Follows, Rather Than Replaces, State Unemployment Insurance
clauses.body: Trade Readjustment Allowances (TRA) are the extended income-support benefit available to a certified adversely affected worker. TRA does not replace state unemployment insurance and is not payable independently of it. Under 19 U.S.C. § 2291(a)(3), a worker qualifies for a TRA payment for a week of unemployment only if the worker was entitled (or would have been entitled) to unemployment insurance for a week within the applicable benefit period, has exhausted all rights to that unemployment insurance (except for state-funded additional compensation not reimbursed from federal funds), and has no unexpired waiting period remaining for it. In other words, a worker must first draw down, and exhaust, state UI eligibility before TRA becomes payable; TRA generally picks up where UI leaves off rather than running alongside it. The amount of TRA also derives directly from the worker's UI experience: under 19 U.S.C. § 2292(a), the weekly TRA amount equals the worker's most recent weekly UI benefit amount for a week of total unemployment preceding the worker's first exhaustion of UI, reduced (but not below zero) by any deductible training allowance and by income deductible from UI under the applicable state or federal disqualifying-income rules.
clauses.gap: This corrects a framing choice in this document's research brief, which described the UI-TRA relationship only as TRA 'generally supplements/follows' UI without identifying the operative statutory mechanism. Having read the current text of §§ 2291(a)(3) and 2292(a) directly, the more precise statement is that UI exhaustion is an express eligibility condition for TRA, and the weekly TRA amount is computed from the worker's own prior UI weekly benefit amount rather than set independently. This clause does not cover the separate rule in § 2291(a)(4) tying TRA to the work-search and acceptance requirements of the Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1970, nor § 2292(b) and (c)'s separate rules for workers who are undergoing training or who receive a training allowance under other federal law, both of which can further affect the TRA amount or the count of weeks remaining. As the earlier clause in this document discloses, TRA payments under this part are not currently authorized for weeks after June 30, 2022, absent transition provisions or reauthorization not independently confirmed here.

clauses.title: Training, Job Search Allowances, and Relocation Allowances
clauses.body: Beyond TRA, the statute authorizes three other categories of benefit for a certified adversely affected worker. Training: under 19 U.S.C. § 2296(a), the Secretary of Labor may approve payment of training costs when the Secretary determines, among other conditions, that no suitable employment is available for the worker, the worker would benefit from appropriate training, there is a reasonable expectation of employment following training, and approved training is reasonably available. Job search allowances: under 19 U.S.C. § 2297, a worker who has been totally separated and cannot reasonably be expected to secure suitable employment in the local commuting area may apply for reimbursement of 90 percent of necessary job search expenses, up to a maximum of $1,250. Relocation allowances: under 19 U.S.C. § 2298, a worker who has obtained (or has a bona fide offer of) suitable long-term employment in another area, and cannot reasonably be expected to find suitable local employment, may apply for reimbursement of 90 percent of the reasonable and necessary expenses of moving the worker, the worker's family, and household effects, plus a lump-sum payment equal to three times the worker's average weekly wage, up to a maximum of $1,250.
clauses.gap: This clause summarizes the qualifying conditions and dollar figures in 19 U.S.C. §§ 2296(a), 2297(a)-(b), and 2298(a)-(b) as currently printed; it does not cover the detailed application deadlines in §§ 2297(a)(2)(C) and 2298(a)(2)(E), the training-approval limitations and exceptions elsewhere in § 2296, or § 2298(c)'s further limitations on relocation allowances. It also does not independently verify whether these dollar caps have been adjusted by regulation since this text was last amended. As the program-status clause in this document discloses, none of these benefits are currently authorized for weeks or events after June 30, 2022, absent transition provisions or reauthorization not independently confirmed here.

clauses.title: The Health Coverage Tax Credit: A Related Benefit That Expired Earlier Than the Rest of TAA
clauses.body: Separately from the Trade Act benefits described above, the Internal Revenue Code has authorized a Health Coverage Tax Credit (HCTC) for certain individuals, including TAA recipients, at 26 U.S.C. § 35(a): a credit against federal income tax equal to 72.5 percent of the amount the taxpayer paid for qualified health insurance coverage for eligible coverage months. However, 26 U.S.C. § 35(b)(1)(A)(B) defines an "eligible coverage month" to include only a month that begins more than 90 days after the enactment of the Trade Act of 2002 and before January 1, 2022. On the face of this statutory text, the HCTC is therefore not available for coverage months beginning on or after January 1, 2022, regardless of the separate lapse of the other TAA benefits described above.
clauses.gap: This is a second, independent correction to this document's research brief, which listed the health coverage tax credit as one of TAA's currently available benefits without qualification. Having fetched and read the current 26 U.S.C. § 35 text directly, the honest finding is that its own "eligible coverage month" definition ended before January 1, 2022 -- roughly six months earlier than the June 30, 2022 cutoff described for the other TAA benefits in the program-status clause above. This clause covers only § 35(a) and the relevant part of § 35(b)(1); it does not cover § 35's other eligibility conditions (qualifying-individual categories, the bar on other specified coverage, the incarceration exclusion, or the advance-payment mechanism), nor whether Congress has enacted a further extension not reflected in the fetched text. This document's drafter could not independently confirm current HCTC status against an IRS source; this finding rests on the Cornell-hosted U.S. Code text alone, fetched twice with distinct User-Agent strings and confirmed byte-identical.

clauses.title: General Nature of TAA Benefits, in Plain Terms
clauses.body: Taken together, the statutory provisions described in this document authorize four broad categories of benefit for a worker in a group the Department of Labor has certified as adversely affected by trade: (1) Trade Readjustment Allowances, which are weekly cash payments computed from the worker's own prior unemployment insurance benefit amount and payable only after the worker has exhausted regular unemployment insurance; (2) approved training, intended to help the worker qualify for suitable employment; (3) a job search allowance, reimbursing costs of looking for work outside the worker's local commuting area; (4) a relocation allowance, reimbursing moving costs and providing a lump-sum payment when a worker relocates for a new job; and, historically, (5) a health coverage tax credit toward the cost of health insurance premiums. This document does not state that {{employeeName}} qualifies for any of these benefits, does not compute any amount {{employeeName}} might receive, and is not a substitute for reviewing the current, effective text of 19 U.S.C. § 2271 et seq. and 26 U.S.C. § 35, including whatever transition or reauthorization provisions may apply after the termination date disclosed elsewhere in this document.

clauses.title: Self-Dealing and Interested Director/Officer Transactions
clauses.body: This information sheet addresses a specific, narrow question under California corporations law: whether a contract or transaction between {{companyName}} and one of its own directors or officers — including {{directorName}} or {{officerName}} — or between {{companyName}} and another entity in which a director has a material financial interest, can be voided by the corporation, a shareholder, or a court solely because that director was on both sides of it. This is different from two other topics addressed elsewhere in this corpus. A director's or officer's general Duty of Care and the business judgment rule concern whether a decision-maker exercised reasonable care and informed judgment in a decision that does not necessarily involve a personal financial conflict. Indemnification concerns whether the corporation may or must reimburse a director or officer for expenses or liability incurred by reason of having served in that role, after the fact of a claim. This document instead addresses the specific statutory procedure — described in this document's companion clauses — that a corporation, its board, and an interested director can follow, at the time a self-dealing transaction is authorized, so that the transaction is not automatically void or voidable merely because of the director's or officer's personal interest in it. This document states what the statutes require; it does not tell {{companyName}} or {{directorName}} what to do about any specific transaction.

clauses.title: The General-Corporation Safe Harbor for a Director's Own Interested Transaction — Corporations Code § 310(a)
clauses.body: For a California general (for-profit) corporation such as {{companyName}}, Corporations Code § 310(a) provides that a contract or transaction between the corporation and one or more of its own directors, or between the corporation and another entity in which a director has a material financial interest, is not automatically "void or voidable" merely because the interested director was a party, or was present at the board meeting that authorized it. Instead, § 310(a) sets out three independent ways the transaction can be validated: (1) full disclosure of the material facts and the director's interest to the shareholders, followed by shareholder approval in good faith, with the interested director's own shares not entitled to vote on it; (2) full disclosure to the board or a committee, followed by board or committee approval in good faith by a vote sufficient without counting the interested director's vote, where the transaction is also just and reasonable to the corporation at the time it was authorized; or (3), if the transaction was not approved either way, the person asserting the transaction's validity carries the burden of proving it was just and reasonable to the corporation at the time it was authorized. Section 310(a) also states that "a mere common directorship does not constitute a material financial interest" for this purpose, and that a director is not "interested" merely because a board resolution fixes another director's compensation as a director, officer, or employee.
clauses.gap: This is the actual, current statutory text of Corporations Code § 310(a), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches with different User-Agent strings — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation or transaction, and not a claim that meeting one of these three pathways is the only way a court could ever uphold an interested-director transaction. A CourtListener case-law search to locate judicial decisions construing how courts actually apply § 310(a)'s "just and reasonable" standard, or how the three numbered pathways interact with each other, returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (125/day quota already exhausted) before any search could run; this clause and its companions therefore rest on the statutory text alone, with no case law verified for this document. This clause quotes only isolated phrases from a longer subdivision; the full subdivision (a) text, including its numbered paragraphs in full and its two additional interpretive sentences, is not reproduced verbatim here.

clauses.title: The Separate Safe Harbor for Interlocking-Director Transactions Between Two Corporations — Corporations Code § 310(b)
clauses.body: Corporations Code § 310(b) addresses a related but distinct scenario from subdivision (a): a contract or transaction between {{companyName}} and another corporation or association where one or more people (potentially including {{directorName}}) serve as a director of both, but without any director holding a "material financial interest" of the kind subdivision (a) addresses. For that common-directorship scenario, § 310(b) provides that the transaction is not void or voidable because the common director was present at the authorizing meeting, if either: (1) the material facts of the transaction and the common directorship are disclosed to the board or committee, which approves the transaction in good faith by a vote sufficient without counting the common director's vote, or the transaction is approved by the shareholders in good faith; or (2), if not approved either way, the transaction is just and reasonable to the corporation at the time it was authorized. Section 310(b) expressly states that it "does not apply to contracts or transactions covered by subdivision (a)" — meaning the two subdivisions are mutually exclusive safe harbors for two different fact patterns.

This corrects a simplification in the research brief that prompted this document: the safe-harbor conditions for a common-directorship transaction under subdivision (b) are not identical to the material-financial-interest safe harbor in subdivision (a) — subdivision (b) does not include a shareholder-vote-exclusion-of-interested-shares mechanism and instead uses a simpler two-path structure, and the two subdivisions are, by the statute's own terms, mutually exclusive.

clauses.title: Interested and Common Directors May Still Be Counted Toward a Quorum — Corporations Code § 310(c)
clauses.body: Corporations Code § 310(c) provides a separate, narrow rule that applies regardless of which safe harbor in subdivisions (a) or (b) a transaction relies on: "Interested or common directors may be counted in determining the presence of a quorum at a meeting of the board or a committee thereof which authorizes, approves or ratifies a contract or transaction." This means that {{directorName}}'s presence as an interested or common director does not, by itself, prevent the board or committee meeting considering the transaction from having a valid quorum — although, as described in this document's companion clauses, that same director's vote is not counted toward the separate vote-sufficiency requirement in subdivisions (a)(2) and (b)(1).

No CourtListener case-law search could be completed for this clause; the daily quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked. This clause addresses only the quorum question; it does not restate the separate vote-counting requirement described in this document's companion clauses on subdivisions (a) and (b), and a reader should not assume that being counted for quorum purposes means the interested director's vote is also counted toward approval.

clauses.title: The Parallel Safe Harbor for Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporations — Corporations Code § 7233
clauses.body: For a California nonprofit mutual benefit corporation, Corporations Code § 7233 closely tracks the general-corporation structure of § 310 described in this document's companion clauses, adapted for a membership organization. Section 7233(a) provides that a contract or transaction between the corporation and one or more of its directors, or an entity in which a director has a material financial interest, is not void or voidable solely because the director was a party or present at the authorizing meeting, if: (1) the material facts and the director's interest are disclosed to the members, and the transaction is approved by the members in good faith, with any membership owned by the interested director not entitled to vote on it; (2) the material facts and interest are disclosed to the board or committee, which approves the transaction in good faith by a vote sufficient without counting the interested director's vote, with the transaction also just and reasonable to the corporation at the time it was authorized; or (3), absent either approval, the person asserting validity bears the burden of proving the transaction was just and reasonable at the time it was authorized. Section 7233(b) provides a parallel, separate safe harbor for common-directorship transactions between the corporation and another entity, materially identical in structure to § 310(b).
clauses.gap: This is the actual, current statutory text of Corporations Code § 7233, fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches with different User-Agent strings. No CourtListener case-law search could be completed for this clause; the daily quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked. This confirms one assumption in the research brief that prompted this document: § 7233 is, in fact, a close structural parallel to § 310, adapted so that member approval (and member voting rights on the interested director's own membership) substitutes for shareholder approval. This document's companion clause on Corporations Code § 5233 discloses that the other statute named in the same research brief — the nonprofit public benefit corporation provision — is not a comparably close parallel to § 310, and should not be assumed to work the same way.

clauses.title: A Different Structure for Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporations — Corporations Code § 5233 Defines and Regulates "Self-Dealing Transactions" Rather Than Simply Validating Them
clauses.body: Corporations Code § 5233, which applies to a California nonprofit public benefit corporation, is not organized the same way as § 310 or § 7233. Rather than stating that an interested-director transaction is "not void or voidable" if certain conditions are met, § 5233(a) first defines a "self-dealing transaction" as "a transaction to which the corporation is a party and in which one or more of its directors has a material financial interest, and which does not meet the requirements of paragraph (1), (2), or (3) of subdivision (d)" — making that director an "interested director" for purposes of the section. Section 5233(c) then identifies who may bring an action in superior court over such a transaction: the Attorney General; the corporation itself, or a member suing derivatively on the corporation's behalf; a director of the corporation; an officer of the corporation; or a person granted relator status by the Attorney General.
clauses.gap: This is the actual, current statutory text of Corporations Code § 5233, fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches with different User-Agent strings. No CourtListener case-law search could be completed for this clause; the daily quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked. This corrects a framing assumption in the research brief that prompted this document: the brief described § 5233 as a likely parallel to § 310's "not void or voidable if disclosed and approved" safe-harbor formula, but § 5233's actual text is built around a different mechanism — defining a regulated category of transaction and then specifying, in the companion clause on subdivision (d), the facts that must be established before a court may grant a remedy in litigation over it — with Attorney General oversight and standing built directly into the statute in a way § 310 and § 7233 do not have. This clause does not restate § 5233(b)'s three carve-outs (director compensation-fixing, certain charitable-program transactions, and small transactions below a dollar/percentage threshold of which the interested director had no actual knowledge), which are addressed in this document's companion clause.

clauses.title: When a Court May Not Grant a Remedy for a Public Benefit Corporation's Self-Dealing Transaction — Corporations Code § 5233(d)
clauses.body: Corporations Code § 5233(d) identifies the conditions under which the remedies described in subdivision (h) — such as an accounting for profits, or return of property or its value, described in this document's companion clause on subdivision (h) — "shall not be granted" against a director of a nonprofit public benefit corporation. This includes prior Attorney General or court approval of the transaction, or a showing of several facts together: that the corporation entered into the transaction for its own benefit; that the transaction was fair and reasonable to the corporation at the time it was entered into; that, before consummating the transaction, "the board authorized or approved the transaction in good faith by a vote of a majority of the directors then in office without counting the vote of the interested director or directors, and with knowledge of the material facts concerning the transaction and the director's interest in the transaction"; and that the board determined, or the corporation in fact could not have obtained, a more advantageous arrangement with reasonable effort under the circumstances. Section 5233(d)(3) separately allows a committee or authorized person's approval, followed by board ratification at its next meeting, where board pre-approval was not reasonably practicable. Section 5233(e) further requires that an action under subdivision (c) generally be filed within two years after written notice of the transaction is filed with the Attorney General, or within three years if no such notice is filed — except the Attorney General itself, which has ten years to sue.

clauses.title: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act Information Sheet — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet relates to a transfer of property, or an obligation incurred, by {{debtorName}} that {{creditorName}} believes may be a "voidable transaction" affecting property described as {{propertyDescription}}. It describes California's Uniform Voidable Transactions Act (Civil Code section 3439 et seq.), a statute that lets a creditor ask a court to void — or obtain other relief against — certain transfers a debtor made, or obligations a debtor incurred, that hindered, delayed, or defrauded the creditor, or that left the debtor without enough assets or ability to pay its debts. The statute was enacted under that name effective January 1, 2016; before that date the same chapter was known as the Uniform Fraudulent Transfer Act, and California courts and other sources may still refer to it by that earlier name when discussing older transfers or older case law. This information sheet does not itself void, ratify, or otherwise determine the legal effect of any transfer involving {{debtorName}} or {{creditorName}}, does not determine whether any particular transfer was made with the intent or under the financial circumstances the statute describes, and does not evaluate the merits of any specific claim. Whether a particular transfer or obligation is voidable under this statute is a determination made by a court applying the statute to the facts of a specific case.

clauses.title: Key Terms: "Transfer," "Creditor," "Debtor," and "Asset"
clauses.body: The Uniform Voidable Transactions Act defines several terms broadly. A "transfer" is every mode, direct or indirect, absolute or conditional, voluntary or involuntary, of disposing of or parting with an asset or an interest in an asset — the statute expressly includes payment of money, a release, a lease, a license, and the creation of a lien or other encumbrance within that definition, so the statute reaches far more than an outright sale or gift of property. A "creditor" is a person that has a "claim" (a right to payment, whether or not that right has been reduced to judgment, is liquidated, is fixed, is contingent, or is disputed), and a "debtor" is a person liable on a claim; a creditor need not already hold a judgment, or even an undisputed claim, to be a creditor under the statute. "Asset" means property of a debtor, but the statute excludes from "asset" property already encumbered by a valid lien, property that is generally exempt from creditors under nonbankruptcy law, and certain tenancy-by-the-entireties interests not subject to a single tenant's individual creditors.
clauses.gap: This clause reproduces the current statutory definitions in Civil Code section 3439.01(c), (d), (e), (m), and (a) exactly as codified; it does not address the chapter's several other defined terms ("claim," "lien," "organization," "person," "property," "record," "sign," "electronic," and "valid lien") that are not directly at issue in the rest of this information sheet, and it does not determine whether any specific item of property held by the debtor named in this information sheet meets or falls outside this definition of "asset." "Insolvent" is a separate, substantive term defined in a different section (Civil Code section 3439.02) and is addressed in its own clause below rather than here.

citations.quote: “Transfer” means every mode, direct or indirect, absolute or conditional, voluntary or involuntary, of disposing of or parting with an asset or an interest in an asset, and includes payment of money, release, lease, license, and creation of a lien or other encumbrance.
