clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of "Insolvent"
clauses.body: The Uniform Voidable Transactions Act defines "insolvent" as a balance-sheet test: a debtor is insolvent if, at a fair valuation, the sum of the debtor's debts is greater than the sum of the debtor's assets. Separately, the statute creates a presumption of insolvency for a debtor that is generally not paying its debts as they become due, other than as a result of a bona fide dispute; once that presumption applies, it shifts the burden to the party against whom the presumption is directed to prove that it is more probable than not that the debtor was not insolvent. The statute also refines what counts as an "asset" or a "debt" for this insolvency calculation: property that has been transferred, concealed, or removed with intent to hinder, delay, or defraud creditors, or transferred in a manner making the transfer voidable under the statute, is excluded from the debtor's assets for this test, and an obligation is excluded from the debtor's debts to the extent it is secured by a valid lien on property of the debtor that is not itself counted as an asset.
clauses.gap: This clause reproduces Civil Code section 3439.02(a) and (b) verbatim and describes subdivisions (c) and (d) of the same section in its own words rather than by direct quotation; it does not perform, or supply the financial data needed to perform, an actual fair-valuation insolvency calculation for the debtor named in this information sheet, and it does not determine whether that debtor was or was not insolvent at any particular time.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.02(a)-(b)
citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, definition of insolvency and presumption
citations.quote: A debtor is insolvent if, at a fair valuation, the sum of the debtor’s debts is greater than the sum of the debtor’s assets.(b) A debtor that is generally not paying the debtor’s debts as they become due other than as a result of a bona fide dispute is presumed to be insolvent. The presumption imposes on the party against which the presumption is directed the burden of proving that the nonexistence of insolvency is more probable than its existence.

clauses.title: Actual Intent to Hinder, Delay, or Defraud
clauses.body: Under the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, a transfer made, or an obligation incurred, by a debtor is voidable as to a creditor if the debtor made the transfer or incurred the obligation with actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud any creditor of the debtor. This ground for voidability is available to a creditor regardless of whether that creditor's claim against the debtor arose before or after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred — a creditor whose claim did not yet exist at the time of the transfer can still invoke this provision. A creditor asserting this claim for relief has the burden of proving the elements of the claim by a preponderance of the evidence; the statute does not require clear and convincing evidence or any higher standard.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Civil Code section 3439.04(a) (introductory clause and paragraph (1)) and section 3439.04(c). It does not address the separate, additional constructive-fraud grounds for voidability found in the same subdivision, paragraph (2) of section 3439.04(a) (covered in a separate clause below), and it does not determine whether any specific debtor acted with the actual intent this provision describes with respect to any specific transfer.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.04(a) & (a)(1)
citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, actual-intent voidability ground
citations.quote: A transfer made or obligation incurred by a debtor is voidable as to a creditor, whether the creditor’s claim arose before or after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred, if the debtor made the transfer or incurred the obligation as follows:(1) With actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud any creditor of the debtor.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.04(c)
citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, burden of proof
citations.quote: A creditor making a claim for relief under subdivision (a) has the burden of proving the elements of the claim for relief by a preponderance of the evidence.

clauses.title: "Badges of Fraud" — Factors Bearing on Actual Intent
clauses.body: The statute lists eleven specific factors — commonly called "badges of fraud" — that may be considered, among other factors, in determining whether a debtor acted with the actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud a creditor: whether the transfer or obligation was to an insider; whether the debtor retained possession or control of the transferred property after the transfer; whether the transfer or obligation was disclosed or concealed; whether the debtor had been sued or threatened with suit before the transfer or obligation; whether the transfer was of substantially all of the debtor's assets; whether the debtor absconded; whether the debtor removed or concealed assets; whether the consideration the debtor received was reasonably equivalent to the value of the asset transferred or the amount of the obligation incurred; whether the debtor was insolvent or became insolvent shortly after the transfer or obligation; whether the transfer occurred shortly before or after the debtor incurred a substantial debt; and whether the debtor transferred the business's essential assets to a lienor that then transferred them to an insider of the debtor. The statute frames this as a non-exclusive list — a court may give consideration to "any or all" of these factors "among other factors," so no single factor is required and no fixed number of factors must be present.
clauses.gap: This clause reproduces the eleven factors listed in Civil Code section 3439.04(b) verbatim and in full; it is a complete list of the current statutory factors, not an excerpt, but the statute's own introductory language confirms courts may also consider factors beyond this list. This clause does not evaluate whether any of these factors is present with respect to any specific transfer involving any particular debtor, and satisfying one or more of these factors does not, by itself, establish actual intent to hinder, delay, or defraud under the statute.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.04(b)
citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, badges-of-fraud factors
citations.quote: In determining actual intent under paragraph (1) of subdivision (a), consideration may be given, among other factors, to any or all of the following:(1) Whether the transfer or obligation was to an insider.(2) Whether the debtor retained possession or control of the property transferred after the transfer.(3) Whether the transfer or obligation was disclosed or concealed.(4) Whether before the transfer was made or obligation was incurred, the debtor had been sued or threatened with suit.(5) Whether the transfer was of substantially all the debtor’s assets.(6) Whether the debtor absconded.(7) Whether the debtor removed or concealed assets.(8) Whether the value of the consideration received by the debtor was reasonably equivalent to the value of the asset transferred or the amount of the obligation incurred.(9) Whether the debtor was insolvent or became insolvent shortly after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred.(10) Whether the transfer occurred shortly before or shortly after a substantial debt was incurred.(11) Whether the debtor transferred the essential assets of the business to a lienor that transferred the assets to an insider of the debtor.

clauses.title: Constructive Fraud — Transfers Voidable Without Proof of Intent
clauses.body: Separate from actual intent, the statute lets a creditor void a transfer or obligation based purely on the debtor's objective financial circumstances, with no need to prove the debtor's state of mind. One provision, available to any creditor regardless of whether the creditor's claim arose before or after the transfer, makes a transfer or obligation voidable if the debtor did not receive a reasonably equivalent value in exchange, and the debtor either was engaged in or about to engage in a business or transaction for which the debtor's remaining assets were unreasonably small in relation to that business or transaction, or intended to incur, or believed or reasonably should have believed the debtor would incur, debts beyond the debtor's ability to pay them as they became due. A second, narrower provision applies only to a creditor whose claim arose before the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred: it makes the transfer or obligation voidable if the debtor did not receive a reasonably equivalent value in exchange and the debtor either was already insolvent at that time or became insolvent as a result of the transfer or obligation. In both provisions, the creditor bears the burden of proving the elements of the claim for relief by a preponderance of the evidence.
clauses.gap: This clause covers two distinct statutory provisions with different creditor eligibility: Civil Code section 3439.04(a)(2), open to any creditor regardless of when the claim arose and keyed to unreasonably small remaining assets or an intent/belief about future ability to pay debts; and Civil Code section 3439.05, limited to creditors whose claim predates the transfer and keyed to actual insolvency rather than merely a risk of it. The research brief that framed this document described these as a single combined test (no reasonably equivalent value plus insolvency, unreasonably small assets, or intent to incur debts beyond ability to pay, treated as three interchangeable alternatives); the statute as actually codified instead splits these into two separate provisions with different creditor scope, which this clause corrects and states separately rather than merging. This clause does not determine whether any specific debtor received reasonably equivalent value for, or was insolvent or undercapitalized at the time of, any specific transfer.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.04(a)(2)
citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, constructive fraud available to any creditor
citations.quote: Without receiving a reasonably equivalent value in exchange for the transfer or obligation, and the debtor either:(A) Was engaged or was about to engage in a business or a transaction for which the remaining assets of the debtor were unreasonably small in relation to the business or transaction.(B) Intended to incur, or believed or reasonably should have believed that the debtor would incur, debts beyond the debtor’s ability to pay as they became due.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.05(a)
citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, constructive fraud limited to pre-existing creditors
citations.quote: A transfer made or obligation incurred by a debtor is voidable as to a creditor whose claim arose before the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred if the debtor made the transfer or incurred the obligation without receiving a reasonably equivalent value in exchange for the transfer or obligation and the debtor was insolvent at that time or the debtor became insolvent as a result of the transfer or obligation.

clauses.title: Time Limits: Four-Year Periods and a Seven-Year Outer Limit
clauses.body: The statute extinguishes a cause of action under the Uniform Voidable Transactions Act unless the creditor brings an action, or makes a levy, within specific time limits, and those limits differ by which ground for voidability is invoked. For an actual-intent claim, the action must be brought no later than four years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred, or, if later, no later than one year after the transfer or obligation was or reasonably could have been discovered by the claimant. For either constructive-fraud claim, the action must be brought no later than four years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred, with no discovery-based extension. Separately, and regardless of which of these grounds applies or when the transfer or obligation was or could have been discovered, the statute imposes an absolute seven-year outer limit: a cause of action under the statute is extinguished if no action is brought and no levy is made within seven years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred, notwithstanding any other provision of law.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Civil Code section 3439.09(a), (b), and (c) in full; the research brief that framed this document referred generally to a single "statute of limitations/repose period," but the statute as actually codified sets three different time rules — a four-year-or-one-year-discovery period for actual-intent claims, a flat four-year period for constructive-fraud claims, and a seven-year absolute repose period that overrides both — which this clause states separately rather than as one period. This clause does not calculate any specific deadline for any particular debtor or creditor and does not address how a court would determine when a transfer or obligation "was or could reasonably have been discovered" on any particular set of facts.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.09(a)
citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, limitations period for actual-intent claims
citations.quote: Under paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 3439.04, not later than four years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred or, if later, not later than one year after the transfer or obligation was or could reasonably have been discovered by the claimant.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.09(b)
citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, limitations period for constructive-fraud claims
citations.quote: Under paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3439.04 or Section 3439.05, not later than four years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.09(c)
citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, seven-year outer repose period
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, a cause of action under this chapter with respect to a transfer or obligation is extinguished if no action is brought or levy made within seven years after the transfer was made or the obligation was incurred.

clauses.title: Remedies Available to a Creditor
clauses.body: In an action for relief against a voidable transfer or obligation, and subject to the statute's protections for good-faith transferees, the statute lets a creditor obtain: avoidance of the transfer or obligation to the extent necessary to satisfy the creditor's claim; an attachment or other provisional remedy against the transferred asset or other property of the transferee, following the attachment procedures in the Code of Civil Procedure or other applicable law; and, subject to equitable principles and applicable procedural rules, an injunction against further disposition of the transferred asset or other property of the transferee by the debtor or transferee, appointment of a receiver to take charge of the transferred asset or other such property, or any other relief the circumstances may require. In addition, if the creditor has already obtained a judgment against the debtor, the creditor may levy execution on the transferred asset or its proceeds.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Civil Code section 3439.07(a) and (c); it does not restate subdivision (b) of the same section (attachment while an action on the underlying claim is pending, before judgment) or subdivision (d) (rights of an assignee for the benefit of creditors), and it does not address the separate rules in Civil Code section 3439.08 that limit or qualify these remedies against a good-faith transferee for value, which the quoted text expressly cross-references but which this clause does not independently detail. This clause does not determine what specific remedy, if any, a court would grant to any particular creditor against any particular debtor on any particular transfer.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.07(a)
citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, remedies in an action for relief
citations.quote: In an action for relief against a transfer or obligation under this chapter, a creditor, subject to the limitations in Section 3439.08, may obtain:(1) Avoidance of the transfer or obligation to the extent necessary to satisfy the creditor’s claim.(2) An attachment or other provisional remedy against the asset transferred or other property of the transferee in accordance with the procedures described in Title 6.5 (commencing with Section 481.010) of Part 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or as may otherwise be available under applicable law.(3) Subject to applicable principles of equity and in accordance with applicable rules of civil procedure, the following:(A) An injunction against further disposition by the debtor or a transferee, or both, of the asset transferred or other property of the transferee.(B) Appointment of a receiver to take charge of the asset transferred or other property of the transferee.(C) Any other relief the circumstances may require.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3439.07(c)
citations.cite: Uniform Voidable Transactions Act, levy of execution after judgment
citations.quote: If a creditor has obtained a judgment on a claim against the debtor, the creditor may levy execution on the asset transferred or its proceeds.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Manufactured Home Ownership and Title Transfer Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's statutory system for registering a manufactured home or mobilehome and transferring ownership of it as personal property with the Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) -- HCD's certificate-of-title system, comparable in structure to vehicle titling with the Department of Motor Vehicles. It concerns the home described as {{mobilehomeDescription}}, bearing HCD serial and/or insignia identification {{serialOrDecalNumber}}, situated at {{propertyAddress}}, as between {{sellerName}} as the transferring registered owner and {{buyerName}} as the incoming registered owner. This document addresses a different subject than this corpus's separate Mobilehome Park Tenancy (Mobilehome Residency Law) Information Sheet: that document describes the landlord-tenant relationship between a mobilehome resident and the park that rents the underlying space -- the rental agreement, park rules, and statutory grounds for terminating the tenancy -- and says nothing about who owns the home itself or how that ownership changes hands. This Information Sheet, by contrast, addresses only ownership of the home and the transfer of title to it, independent of any space-rental relationship the home may also be subject to. This Information Sheet is further limited to a manufactured home or mobilehome that remains registered as personal property with HCD. A manufactured home that has instead been installed on a foundation system and converted into a fixture or improvement to the real property it sits on leaves this HCD registration and title system entirely and, from that point on, changes hands through the real property recording system instead -- a distinct process not covered by this Information Sheet. This is a general informational reference describing the statutory registration and title-transfer system; it is not itself a certificate of title, an application for registration, a bill of sale, escrow instructions, or a determination that any specific home is currently registered as personal property, has instead become part of the real estate, or has been lawfully transferred.

clauses.title: "Manufactured Home" and "Mobilehome": Two Age-Based Statutory Terms for the Same Kind of Structure
clauses.body: California's manufactured-housing title and registration statute (Health and Safety Code, Division 13, Part 2) uses two separately defined terms for what a lay reader might informally call a mobile home, distinguished by construction date rather than by function. Section 18007(a) defines "manufactured home" as a structure built on or after June 15, 1976: "'Manufactured home,' for the purposes of this part, means a structure that was constructed on or after June 15, 1976, is transportable in one or more sections, is eight body feet or more in width, or 40 body feet or more in length, in the traveling mode, or, when erected on site, is 320 or more square feet, is built on a permanent chassis and designed to be used as a single-family dwelling with or without a foundation when connected to the required utilities, and includes the plumbing, heating, air conditioning, and electrical systems contained therein." Section 18008(a) defines "mobilehome" in nearly identical terms, but for a structure built before that date: "'Mobilehome,' for the purposes of this part, means a structure that was constructed prior to June 15, 1976, is transportable in one or more sections, is eight body feet or more in width, or 40 body feet or more in length, in the traveling mode, or, when erected onsite, is 320 or more square feet, is built on a permanent chassis and designed to be used as a single-family dwelling with or without a foundation system when connected to the required utilities, and includes the plumbing, heating, air conditioning, and electrical systems contained therein." The June 15, 1976 dividing line corresponds to the effective date of the federal construction and safety standards referenced in both definitions; a manufactured home and a mobilehome are registered, titled, and transferred under the identical statutory procedures described in the remainder of this document.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the core structural sentence from each subdivision; both § 18007 and § 18008 continue with an additional inclusion for a structure that meets all listed requirements except size where the manufacturer voluntarily certifies compliance with the referenced federal standards, and each section's subdivision (b) separately addresses how the defined term should be read when other statutes use it -- neither elaboration is reproduced here. Two independently numbered sections are treated as two separate sources, not one. This is one state's statute, offered as real evidence of California's own definitions for these terms -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific structure; other states classify and title factory-built housing differently, and some do not use a 1976 construction-date dividing line at all. This document does not address a "commercial coach," "floating home," "truck camper," or "recreational vehicle," each separately defined elsewhere in this same statute and each subject to its own variations on the registration and title system described in the remainder of this document.

clauses.title: The General Registration Requirement, and Its Trigger on Sale or Transfer of Title
clauses.body: Health and Safety Code section 18075(a) makes titling and registration with the department the general rule for a manufactured home or mobilehome: "Except as provided in Section 18075.7, all manufactured homes, mobilehomes, commercial coaches, truck campers, and floating homes shall be subject to the provisions of this code for the purposes of titling and registration." Section 18075.5 makes that registration an ongoing, annual obligation rather than a one-time event: "Manufactured homes, mobilehomes, commercial coaches, and floating homes sold or used within this state shall be subject to annual registration with the department and payment of registration fees prescribed by Section 18114 except as follows:" Subdivision (a) of that same section then ties registration specifically to a sale of a home not installed on a foundation system: it is subject to registration and fee payment "at the time of original registration with the department, and upon subsequent sale, resale, or transfer of title," and the statute defines a covered "transfer of title" broadly, so that it "includes, but is not limited to, any change, addition, or deletion of one or more registered owners, legal owners, or junior lienholders."
clauses.gap: "The department" in this chapter is the Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD); this clause does not reproduce § 18075(b)'s separate account of HCD's transition into a role for this title and registration system previously held in part by the Department of Motor Vehicles. Section 18075(a)'s own cross-referenced exception (§ 18075.7) and § 18075.5's further exceptions in subdivisions (c) through (f) -- covering homes newly entering California, active-duty and recently discharged military members, and new, unoccupied dealer inventory -- are not reproduced here. This clause treats two independently numbered sections (18075 and 18075.5) as two separate sources; the two quotations drawn from § 18075.5 (its introductory sentence and subdivision (a)) are treated as one source. This is one state's statute, offered as real evidence of California's own registration requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific home; registration and titling schemes for factory-built housing vary by state.

For purposes of this section, a transfer of title includes, but is not limited to, any change, addition, or deletion of one or more registered owners, legal owners, or junior lienholders.

clauses.title: Where This HCD Title System Stops: A Home Converted to Real Property
clauses.body: The HCD registration and title system described in this Information Sheet applies only for as long as a manufactured home or mobilehome remains personal property. Health and Safety Code section 18075.5(b) exempts a home installed on a foundation system from this registration system entirely, for as long as it stays affixed: "Manufactured homes, mobilehomes, and commercial coaches installed or to be installed on foundation systems pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 18551 shall be exempt from registration so long as they remain affixed to the foundation system. In the event that the manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial coach, is removed from a foundation system for any purpose other than dismantling or reinstallation on a foundation system, it shall be immediately subject to registration with the department." Section 18551, which governs foundation systems, confirms that installation on a foundation system presents a genuine either/or choice between two different legal statuses, not a matter of degree: "A manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial modular may be installed on a foundation system as either a fixture or improvement to the real property, in accordance with subdivision (a), or a manufactured home or mobilehome may be installed on a foundation system as a chattel, in accordance with subdivision (b)." For the fixture-or-improvement path, § 18551(a)(2)(A) identifies the specific document that completes the conversion to real property and where it must be filed -- not with HCD, but with the county recorder: "Within five business days of the issuance of the certificate of occupancy for the manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial modular by the appropriate enforcement agency, the enforcement agency shall record a document naming the owner of the real property, describing the real property with certainty, and stating that a manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial modular has been affixed to that real property by installation on a foundation system pursuant to this subdivision. The document shall be recorded with the county recorder of the county where the real property, upon which the manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial modular that has been installed, is situated." Once that recorded document exists, the home has left HCD's certificate-of-title system described in the remainder of this Information Sheet and instead changes hands, like other real property, through the county recording system; a home installed as a chattel under § 18551(b) instead remains within the HCD title system this Information Sheet describes.
clauses.gap: This clause does not reproduce § 18551(a)'s own detailed prerequisites for fixture-or-improvement status before that certificate of occupancy and recorded document can issue -- including a building permit, specified written evidence that the manufactured home owner owns, holds title to, or is purchasing (or holds a qualifying long-term lease of) the real property, and written evidence that the home is free of liens and encumbrances or that any legal owner and lienholders have consented -- nor § 18551(b)'s parallel requirements for installation as a chattel. This clause also does not address what happens to a certificate of title already on file with HCD once the county-recorded document is filed, nor the reverse process for later removing the home from the foundation system and returning it to HCD registration, both of which this document does not cover. This clause draws three quotations from two independently numbered sections (18075.5 and 18551); the two quotations from § 18551 (its opening fixture/chattel sentence and subdivision (a)(2)(A)) are treated as one source. This is one state's statute, offered as real evidence of California's own personal-property/real-property dividing line for a manufactured home -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific home, and not a determination that any specific home in fact remains chattel or has in fact become real property.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 18075.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health & Saf. C. § 18075.5(b)
citations.quote: (b) Manufactured homes, mobilehomes, and commercial coaches installed or to be installed on foundation systems pursuant to subdivision (a) of Section 18551 shall be exempt from registration so long as they remain affixed to the foundation system. In the event that the manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial coach, is removed from a foundation system for any purpose other than dismantling or reinstallation on a foundation system, it shall be immediately subject to registration with the department.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 18551 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health & Saf. C. § 18551
citations.quote: A manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial modular may be installed on a foundation system as either a fixture or improvement to the real property, in accordance with subdivision (a), or a manufactured home or mobilehome may be installed on a foundation system as a chattel, in accordance with subdivision (b).

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 18551(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health & Saf. C. § 18551(a)(2)(A)
citations.quote: Within five business days of the issuance of the certificate of occupancy for the manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial modular by the appropriate enforcement agency, the enforcement agency shall record a document naming the owner of the real property, describing the real property with certainty, and stating that a manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial modular has been affixed to that real property by installation on a foundation system pursuant to this subdivision. The document shall be recorded with the county recorder of the county where the real property, upon which the manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial modular that has been installed, is situated.

clauses.title: Registered Owner, Legal Owner, and Junior Lienholder: The Three Roles on an HCD Title Record
clauses.body: HCD's title record for a manufactured home or mobilehome, like a Department of Motor Vehicles vehicle title record, can name up to three distinct roles rather than a single "owner." Section 18009.5 defines the possessory owner: "'Registered owner' means a person registered by the department as the owner of a manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, floating home, or truck camper." Section 18005.8 defines a first-position secured party: "'Legal owner' means a person holding a security interest in a manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, floating home, or truck camper perfected by filing the appropriate documents with the department pursuant to Section 18080.7 if the person is entitled to the designation, as provided in Article 3 (commencing with Section 18085) or 4 (commencing with Section 18098) of Chapter 8." Section 18005.3 defines a subordinate secured party: "'Junior lienholder' means a person, other than a legal owner, holding a security interest in a manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, floating home, or truck camper perfected by filing the appropriate documents with the department pursuant to Section 18080.7." A home with an outstanding loan against it will typically show a registered owner and a legal owner (the lender) on the same title record, and may show one or more junior lienholders behind the legal owner as well.
clauses.gap: This clause reproduces the core definitions of all three roles but does not reproduce § 18005.8's own carve-out (a lien created under a different section, § 18080.9, does not itself make its holder a "legal owner" for purposes of this definition) or the perfection mechanics of § 18080.7 that all three definitions cross-reference, none of which this document independently describes. Three independently numbered sections are treated as three separate sources. This is one state's statute, offered as real evidence of California's own three-role structure for a manufactured home title record -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific home's title, and not a claim that title records for other kinds of property (including an ordinary vehicle title, which this clause draws an analogy to only for orientation) use identical role definitions or the identical department.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 18009.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health & Saf. C. § 18009.5
citations.quote: “Registered owner” means a person registered by the department as the owner of a manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, floating home, or truck camper.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 18005.8 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health & Saf. C. § 18005.8
citations.quote: “Legal owner” means a person holding a security interest in a manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, floating home, or truck camper perfected by filing the appropriate documents with the department pursuant to Section 18080.7 if the person is entitled to the designation, as provided in Article 3 (commencing with Section 18085) or 4 (commencing with Section 18098) of Chapter 8.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 18005.3 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health & Saf. C. § 18005.3
citations.quote: “Junior lienholder” means a person, other than a legal owner, holding a security interest in a manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, floating home, or truck camper perfected by filing the appropriate documents with the department pursuant to Section 18080.7.

clauses.title: Applying for Original HCD Registration and Title: What the Application Must Contain
clauses.body: Health and Safety Code section 18085 sets the baseline procedure for putting a manufactured home or mobilehome onto HCD's title record for the first time. Subdivision (a) requires a department-approved application accompanied by the manufacturer's certificate of origin: "Application for the original registration of a manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home required to be registered under this part shall be made to the department upon the appropriate forms approved by the department, and shall be accompanied by the filing fee prescribed by the department." Subdivision (b)(4) then requires the application to identify the specific structure by its manufacturer, date of manufacture, and serial and label or insignia numbers -- the same kind of identifiers a vehicle title uses a VIN for: "A description of the manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home, including all of the following: (A) The manufacturer's name and identification number. (B) The date of manufacture. (C) The serial number or numbers. (D) The federal label number or numbers affixed pursuant to the National Manufactured Housing Construction and Safety Standards Act of 1974 (42 U.S.C. Sec. 5401 et seq.) or department insignia number or numbers affixed pursuant to Section 18026."
clauses.gap: This clause does not reproduce subdivision (a)'s remaining sentences on what happens when the original certificate of origin is not in existence (a marked duplicate from the manufacturer may be substituted), nor the rest of subdivision (b)'s list -- including the registered owner's, legal owner's, and any junior lienholder's names and addresses, the county of the owner's residence, and the situs address of the home -- which this clause omits in favor of the description requirements in paragraph (4). Subdivisions (a) and (b) of the same section are treated as one source. This is one state's statute, offered as real evidence of California's own original-registration procedure -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific home's original registration, and not a determination that any specific application would be accepted or rejected.

citations.quote: Application for the original registration of a manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home required to be registered under this part shall be made to the department upon the appropriate forms approved by the department, and shall be accompanied by the filing fee prescribed by the department.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Safety Code § 18085(b)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Health & Saf. C. § 18085(b)(4)
citations.quote: (4) A description of the manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home, including all of the following: (A) The manufacturer’s name and identification number. (B) The date of manufacture. (C) The serial number or numbers. (D) The federal label number or numbers affixed pursuant to the National Manufactured Housing Construction and Safety Standards Act of 1974 (42 U.S.C. Sec. 5401 et seq.) or department insignia number or numbers affixed pursuant to Section 18026.

clauses.title: Transferring Title on a Sale: The Certificate of Title Execution Process
clauses.body: Health and Safety Code section 18100.5(a) sets out what must happen with HCD once a manufactured home or mobilehome already on the title record changes ownership. The statute requires notice to the department within 20 days: "If the title or interest of a registered owner, legal owner, junior lienholder in a manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, or truck camper, or floating home for which an original registration under this part has been obtained is transferred to another person, or, if all outstanding secured obligations previously held by a legal owner registered on the original or a subsequent registration or by a junior lienholder are satisfied and the person no longer has any obligation to extend credit, incur obligations, or otherwise give value to be secured by the manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home, or, if a security interest is taken in a manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home after the permanent title record has been established, the department shall be notified within 20 days." Paragraph (1) then describes the specific mechanism for an ownership sale -- execution of the existing certificate of title itself by both parties, followed by HCD's issuance of a new one: "If the title or interest of a registered owner or legal owner is being transferred, the transferor and the transferee of the title or interest shall execute in the manner prescribed by the department the certificate of title for the manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home." The statute goes on to require the executed certificate of title, with supporting documents and fees, to be forwarded to HCD, which then amends the permanent title record and issues a new certificate of title and an amended registration card reflecting the change.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the introductory notice requirement and paragraph (1) (transfer of a registered owner's or legal owner's title or interest); § 18100.5 continues with paragraphs (2) through (5), covering the different mechanics for transferring a junior lienholder's interest, a creditor newly acquiring a security interest, and the release of a satisfied lien by a legal owner or junior lienholder, none of which is reproduced here. This same section also contains an unrelated set of subdivisions (d) through (h), addressing a judgment-lien-for-unpaid-rent mechanism tied to Civil Code section 798.56a, which this clause does not address and which this document treats as outside its scope. This is one state's statute, offered as real evidence of California's own title-transfer mechanism for a manufactured home -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific home's transfer, and not a determination that the described process, by itself, completes a lawful transfer of any specific home (which also depends on matters such as sales-and-escrow requirements addressed elsewhere in this same statutory scheme and not reproduced in this Information Sheet).

clauses.title: Whose Signature Transfers Title When a Home Has More Than One Registered Owner
clauses.body: Health and Safety Code section 18080 allows a manufactured home or mobilehome to be registered to more than one person, and fixes different signature rules for transferring title depending on the form of co-ownership chosen. For joint tenancy, every joint tenant's signature is required to transfer title, and a deceased joint tenant's interest passes automatically to the survivors: "A manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home may be registered in the names of two or more persons as joint tenants. Upon the death of a joint tenant, the interest of the decedent shall pass to the survivor or survivors. The signature of each joint tenant or survivor or survivors, as the case may be, shall be required to transfer or encumber the title to the manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home." For registration as community property between spouses, both spouses' signatures are required: "A manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home may be registered as community property in the names of the spouses. The signature of each spouse shall be required to transfer or encumber the title to the manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home."
clauses.gap: This clause omits § 18080's separate subdivision (b), governing registration as tenants in common, under which whether one co-owner alone can transfer full title without the others' signatures depends on whether the names on the registration are separated by "and" or by "or" -- a distinct and more conditional rule this clause does not reproduce -- and subdivision (d), a 1985 transition rule for older tenant-in-common registrations. Subdivisions (a) and (c) of the same section are treated as one source. This is one state's statute, offered as real evidence of California's own signature rules for co-owned manufactured home title -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific home's co-ownership, and not a determination of how any specific home is currently registered or whether every signature required by this statute has in fact been obtained.

Upon the death of a joint tenant, the interest of the decedent shall pass to the survivor or survivors. The signature of each joint tenant or survivor or survivors, as the case may be, shall be required to transfer or encumber the title to the manufactured home, mobilehome, commercial coach, truck camper, or floating home.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California statutory law on who must hold a real estate license to act as a real estate broker or real estate salesperson, Business and Professions Code section 10130 et seq. It is prepared with reference to {{brokerName}} as broker and, if applicable, {{salespersonName}} as salesperson. This sheet is separate from, and covers different subject matter than, a Real Estate Agency Relationship Disclosure: that document addresses the fiduciary duties an already-licensed agent owes to a buyer or seller once an agency relationship exists in a transaction, while this sheet addresses a threshold question that comes before any agency relationship — the statutory licensing requirement itself, who the statute defines as needing a broker's license, how a salesperson's license differs from a broker's license, and the statute's own stated consequences for engaging in licensed real estate activity without a license. This sheet does not determine whether {{brokerName}} or {{salespersonName}} holds a current, valid license, does not evaluate whether any particular activity requires a license, and does not tell any person what to do about their own licensing status.

clauses.title: Basic Licensing Requirement
clauses.body: California law makes it unlawful for any person to engage in the business of, act in the capacity of, advertise as, or assume to act as a real estate broker or a real estate salesperson within the state without first obtaining a real estate license from the Department of Real Estate. The same section separately makes it unlawful to engage in the business of, act in the capacity of, advertise as, or assume to act as a mortgage loan originator without having obtained a license endorsement. The statute assigns the Real Estate Commissioner a role in bringing a complaint for a violation, and it makes it the duty of the district attorney of each county to prosecute violations occurring in that county.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general licensing requirement itself; it does not state what activities count as acting as a broker or salesperson (a separate clause addresses the statutory definition), does not describe the statute's own exemptions from the requirement (also addressed separately), and does not itself determine whether any particular person's conduct falls within or outside the licensing requirement.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10130 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code § 10130
citations.quote: It is unlawful for any person to engage in the business of, act in the capacity of, advertise as, or assume to act as a real estate broker or a real estate salesperson within this state without first obtaining a real estate license from the department, or to engage in the business of, act in the capacity of, advertise as, or assume to act as a mortgage loan originator within this state without having obtained a license endorsement.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of Activities Requiring a Broker's License
clauses.body: California law defines a real estate broker, for purposes of the licensing chapter, as a person who does or negotiates to do, for another or others and for a compensation or in expectation of a compensation, one or more of a defined list of acts: selling, buying, or soliciting or obtaining listings for the sale, purchase, or exchange of real property or a business opportunity; leasing or renting real property or a business opportunity, soliciting tenants or rental listings, negotiating leases, or collecting rents; assisting in filing an application to purchase or lease, or to locate or enter upon, land owned by the state or federal government; soliciting borrowers or lenders, negotiating loans, or collecting payments or performing services for borrowers, lenders, or note owners on loans secured by real property or a business opportunity; and selling, buying, or exchanging a real property sales contract or a note secured by a lien on real property or a business opportunity, and performing services for the holders of such a contract or note. The statute contains several additional sections extending the broker definition to other specific activities, such as certain loan and mineral-, oil-, or gas-property transactions, that this clause does not separately catalog.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only Business and Professions Code section 10131; it does not quote the several adjoining sections (10131.01 through 10131.7) that extend the broker definition to additional specific activities, such as advance-fee listing arrangements, securities transactions described in the Corporations Code, and mineral, oil, or gas property, nor does it address the statutory exemptions from the licensing requirement, which are addressed in a separate clause. It also does not determine whether any specific act by any particular person falls within this definition.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10131 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code § 10131
citations.quote: A real estate broker within the meaning of this part is a person who, for a compensation or in expectation of a compensation, regardless of the form or time of payment, does or negotiates to do one or more of the following acts for another or others: (a) Sells or offers to sell, buys or offers to buy, solicits prospective sellers or buyers of, solicits or obtains listings of, or negotiates the purchase, sale, or exchange of real property or a business opportunity.

clauses.title: Broker License Versus Salesperson License
clauses.body: California law defines these as two distinct license types with a defined relationship to each other. A "real estate broker" is a person licensed as a broker. A "real estate salesperson" is a natural person licensed as a salesperson who, for a compensation or in expectation of a compensation, is retained by a real estate broker to perform one or more of the acts that require a real estate license. A salesperson's license is thus defined by statute as operating through, and by retention of, a licensed broker, rather than as an independent authorization to act on one's own.
clauses.gap: This clause states the statutory definitions of the two license types; it does not itself state every statutory consequence that follows from a salesperson's license being tied to a broker (the compensation-flow and supervision rules are addressed in a separate clause), and it does not determine whether any particular salesperson's retention by any particular broker, or any other arrangement between them, satisfies these definitions.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10015 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code § 10015
citations.quote: “Real estate broker” means a person licensed as a broker under Chapter 3 of this part.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10016 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code § 10016
citations.quote: “Real estate salesperson” means a natural person licensed as a salesperson under Chapter 3 of this part and who, for a compensation or in expectation of a compensation, is retained by a real estate broker to do one or more of the acts set forth in Sections 10131, 10131.1, 10131.2, 10131.3, 10131.4, and 10131.6.

clauses.title: Compensation Must Flow Through the Employing Broker
clauses.body: Consistent with a salesperson's license being tied to a specific broker, the statute makes it unlawful for a licensed broker to retain or compensate any person for performing licensed activity who is not a licensed broker or a salesperson licensed under that same responsible broker. It further provides that no salesperson may accept compensation for activity requiring a real estate license from anyone other than the broker under whom the salesperson is at the time licensed, and makes it unlawful for a salesperson to pay compensation for such activity to any real estate licensee except through that broker; two licensees may agree to share compensation only if it is paid through the responsible broker. Separately, the statute assigns the officer designated by a corporate broker licensee responsibility for supervision and control of the salespersons licensed to that corporation.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses the compensation-flow rule of section 10137 and the corporate-broker supervision rule of section 10159.2; it does not address every other statutory supervision duty a broker owes with respect to a salesperson's conduct, and it does not determine whether any particular broker's or salesperson's actual compensation arrangement complies with this rule.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10137 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code § 10137
citations.quote: No real estate salesperson shall accept compensation for activity requiring a real estate license from any person other than the broker under whom he or she is at the time licensed.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10159.2(a) (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code § 10159.2(a)
citations.quote: The officer designated by a corporate broker licensee pursuant to Section 10211 shall be responsible for the supervision and control of the activities conducted on behalf of the corporation by its officers and employees as necessary to secure full compliance with the provisions of this division, including the supervision of salespersons licensed to the corporation in the performance of acts for which a real estate license is required.

clauses.title: Statutory Exemptions From the License Requirement
clauses.body: The statute lists categories of persons for whom the acts described in the broker definition are not acts requiring a real estate license: a regular corporate officer or general partner acting for the corporation or partnership's own owned or leased property, if not acting for special compensation; a person holding a duly executed power of attorney from the property owner; an attorney at law rendering legal services to a client; a receiver, bankruptcy trustee, or other person acting under court order; and a trustee under a deed of trust selling under that deed of trust's authority. The statute itself states that these exemptions do not apply to a person who uses or attempts to use them to evade the licensing requirement.
clauses.gap: This clause covers only the exemption list in section 10133; the statute contains a separate, more detailed exemption scheme (section 10133.1 and related sections) for loan-related and lender-affiliated activity that this clause does not cover, and this sheet does not determine whether any exemption applies to any particular person's actual conduct.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10133 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code § 10133
citations.quote: (a) The acts described in Section 10131 are not acts for which a real estate license is required if performed by: (1) A regular officer of a corporation or a general partner of a partnership with respect to real property owned or leased by the corporation or partnership, respectively, or in connection with the proposed purchase or leasing of real property by the corporation or partnership, respectively, if the acts are not performed by the officer or partner in expectation of special compensation.

clauses.title: Bar on Suing to Collect Compensation Without a License
clauses.body: The statute bars a person engaged in the business or acting in the capacity of a real estate broker or real estate salesperson from bringing or maintaining any action in the courts of this state to collect compensation for performing any of the licensed acts, unless that person alleges and proves that they were a duly licensed real estate broker or real estate salesperson at the time the cause of action arose. Because this pleading-and-proof requirement is a precondition to maintaining the action at all, it is the statutory basis on which unlicensed status has been raised as a defense to a claim for a real estate commission.
clauses.gap: This clause is confined to what section 10136 itself provides — a bar on maintaining a court action absent alleged and proved licensure at the time the claim arose. It does not address how courts have applied this rule to particular fact patterns (for example, substantial-compliance or licensing-at-time-of-suit arguments), since that requires case law this document does not independently verify here (a CourtListener case law search for this topic returned a quota-exceeded error at the time this sheet was prepared, so no case law is cited). This clause also does not determine whether any particular broker or salesperson was licensed at any particular time.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10136 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code § 10136
citations.quote: No person engaged in the business or acting in the capacity of a real estate broker or a real estate salesperson within this state shall bring or maintain any action in the courts of this state for the collection of compensation for the performance of any of the acts mentioned in this article without alleging and proving that he or she was a duly licensed real estate broker or real estate salesperson at the time the alleged cause of action arose.

clauses.title: Criminal Penalty for Unlicensed Activity
clauses.body: Separately from the bar on collecting compensation through the courts, the statute makes it a public offense for any person to act as a real estate broker, real estate salesperson, or mortgage loan originator without a license or license endorsement, or to advertise using words indicating that they are one of these without being so licensed or endorsed. The statute sets the penalty at a fine not exceeding $20,000, imprisonment in the county jail for not more than six months, or both, or, for a corporation, a fine not exceeding $60,000.
clauses.gap: This clause states the criminal penalty provision itself; it does not address how or whether it has been enforced in any particular circumstance, and it is separate from the civil consequence described in the compensation-bar clause (section 10136), which does not require a criminal conviction.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 10139 (leginfo text)
citations.cite: Business and Professions Code § 10139
citations.quote: Any person acting as a real estate broker, real estate salesperson, or mortgage loan originator without a license or license endorsement, or who advertises using words indicating that he or she is a real estate broker, real estate salesperson, or mortgage loan originator without being so licensed or without having obtained a license endorsement, shall be guilty of a public offense punishable by a fine not exceeding twenty thousand dollars ($20,000), or by imprisonment in the county jail for a term not to exceed six months, or by both fine and imprisonment; or if a corporation, be punished by a fine not exceeding sixty thousand dollars ($60,000).

Prepared and reviewed as of {{dateSigned}}, at {{cityState}}.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes how California's Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) defines "race" for purposes of its hiring-discrimination prohibition, and how that definition -- commonly associated with the CROWN Act amendments to Government Code section 12926 -- applies to {{companyName}}'s consideration of {{employeeName}} as an applicant for {{jobTitle}}. Government Code section 12926 states that "race" is inclusive of traits associated with race, including hair texture and protective hairstyles such as braids, locs, and twists, and Government Code section 12940(a) makes it an unlawful employment practice, subject to stated exceptions, for a covered employer to refuse to hire a person because of race. This document states facts about what those two statutory provisions say and whom they cover; it does not evaluate any particular grooming policy, application, or hiring decision. This corpus separately includes a document addressing FEHA's religious dress and grooming accommodation requirement under a different part of the same definitions section, Government Code section 12926(q), which covers hair, clothing, and other practices connected to an individual's observance of a religious creed and the accommodation duty that observance can trigger. That document addresses a religious-accommodation obligation; this document addresses a definition of "race" that does not depend on, and is not limited to, religious observance. This document is not itself a job application, a job posting, a grooming or dress-code policy, an offer of employment, or a determination of whether any specific policy or decision complies with the statutes described, and it does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} what to do about any particular hiring decision, application, or workplace policy.

clauses.title: "Race" Is Defined to Include Hair Texture and Protective Hairstyles
clauses.body: FEHA's definitions section, Government Code section 12926, states that as used in the part of the Government Code containing FEHA's unlawful-practices provisions, "race" is inclusive of traits associated with race, including, but not limited to, hair texture and protective hairstyles. This definition supplies the meaning of "race" wherever that term is used in FEHA's unlawful-practices provisions, including the hiring-related prohibitions in Government Code section 12940.
clauses.gap: The statute states that race is "inclusive of traits associated with race" and names hair texture and protective hairstyles as examples, but its text does not itself list, or supply a general test for identifying, any other traits that might likewise be "associated with race" beyond the two it names.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(w) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code § 12926(w)
citations.quote: “Race” is inclusive of traits associated with race, including, but not limited to, hair texture and protective hairstyles.

clauses.title: "Protective Hairstyles" Includes Braids, Locs, and Twists
clauses.body: The same definitions section separately defines the term "protective hairstyles" used in the race definition above. It states that protective hairstyles includes, but is not limited to, such hairstyles as braids, locs, and twists.
clauses.gap: The list of example hairstyles in the statute -- braids, locs, and twists -- is expressly non-exhaustive ("includes, but is not limited to"), but the statute's text does not state a general definition of what makes a hairstyle "protective" beyond naming these three examples, so its text alone does not resolve whether a hairstyle not on this list falls within the term.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(x) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code § 12926(x)
citations.quote: “Protective hairstyles” includes, but is not limited to, such hairstyles as braids, locs, and twists.

clauses.title: FEHA's Refusal-to-Hire Prohibition Applies to Race as So Defined
clauses.body: FEHA's general unlawful-practices provision states that it is an unlawful employment practice, unless based upon a bona fide occupational qualification or an applicable security regulation established by the United States or California, for an employer, because of a person's race (among other listed characteristics), to refuse to hire or employ the person or to refuse to select the person for a training program leading to employment. Because Government Code section 12926 defines "race" to be inclusive of hair texture and protective hairstyles, this refusal-to-hire prohibition incorporates that definition wherever "race" is the basis asserted for the employer's action.
clauses.gap: Section 12940(a) states a "bona fide occupational qualification" exception and a security-regulation exception to the prohibition it states, but its own text does not define what qualifies as a bona fide occupational qualification or otherwise state how, if at all, either exception applies to a hairstyle-related job qualification; this document does not resolve that question, and the same section's text also does not itself define "refuse to hire."

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code § 12940(a), introductory clause
citations.quote: It is an unlawful employment practice, unless based upon a bona fide occupational qualification, or, except where based upon applicable security regulations established by the United States or the State of California:

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code § 12940(a), refusal-to-hire clause
citations.quote: For an employer, because of the race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, reproductive health decisionmaking, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, or veteran or military status of any person, to refuse to hire or employ the person or to refuse to select the person for a training program leading to employment, or to bar or to discharge the person from employment or from a training program leading to employment, or to discriminate against the person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment.

clauses.title: Which Employers the FEHA Definition of "Employer" Covers
clauses.body: The same definitions section that defines race states which entities are an "employer" for purposes of FEHA's unlawful-practices provisions, including the refusal-to-hire prohibition described above. It states that employer includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, and it separately excludes a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit from that definition.
clauses.gap: The statute's text does not itself state how the "five or more persons" threshold is counted -- for example, over what time period, in what location, or whether part-time or out-of-state personnel are included -- leaving that computation to sources outside this section's text.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code § 12926(d), general employer definition
citations.quote: “Employer” includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12926(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code § 12926(d), religious-association exclusion
citations.quote: “Employer” does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit.
