clauses.title: Health Care Surrogate Decision-Making — Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet explains California's statutory scheme, set out in Probate Code Chapter 3 of the Health Care Decisions Law (Prob. Code §§ 4711-4717), for who may make health care decisions for a patient who currently lacks the capacity to make them personally. It covers the informal, provider-recorded oral surrogate designation a patient with capacity may make under § 4711; the descending statutory order of priority among a § 4711 surrogate, an agent under a power of attorney for health care or advance health care directive, and a conservator or guardian under § 4712(a); the separate process by which a health care provider or facility designee may choose a surrogate under § 4712(b) when none of those decisionmakers exists; the decision-making standard a surrogate must apply under § 4714; a patient's right to disqualify a person from serving as surrogate under § 4715; domestic-partner parity under § 4716; and a hospital emergency department's contact-effort duty under § 4717. This sheet does not create, execute, or record a surrogate designation, an advance health care directive, or a power of attorney for health care — {{patientName}} is described here in the general terms the statute uses, without this sheet determining who {{patientName}}'s decisionmaker is, will be, or should be in any actual situation. It is distinct from this corpus's existing Advance Health Care Directive document (which lets a person execute a written directive naming an agent) and its existing Individual Health Care Instruction document (which lets a person record wishes directly without naming any agent or surrogate) — this sheet instead explains the fallback statutory framework that determines who may decide when no such written instrument, or no effective one, controls the moment. This sheet states facts about California law generally. It is not legal advice, and it does not determine who has authority to make a health care decision for any specific patient, in any specific hospital or facility, at any specific moment — that determination depends on facts (capacity, existing documents, family relationships, provider assessments) that only apply to one real situation at a time.

clauses.title: A Patient May Designate an Oral Surrogate Directly to a Health Care Provider
clauses.body: California law lets a patient designate an adult as a health care surrogate without any written instrument, simply by personally informing the supervising health care provider or a designee of the health care facility caring for the patient; that designation must then be promptly recorded in the patient's health care record. This is a separate, lighter-weight mechanism from executing a power of attorney for health care or advance health care directive, and it exists specifically for use within a course of treatment.
clauses.gap: This clause describes only how a § 4711 surrogate designation is made — it does not state or determine how long any particular designation lasts (covered in a separate clause on § 4711(b)'s time limit), what decisions the surrogate may make, or whether a specific health care provider's recording of a specific designation was done correctly. It also does not address a facility's own internal documentation forms or policies, which the statute does not standardize.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4711(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the oral surrogate designation mechanism
citations.quote: A patient may designate an adult as a surrogate to make health care decisions by personally informing the supervising health care provider or a designee of the health care facility caring for the patient. The designation of a surrogate shall be promptly recorded in the patient’s health care record.

clauses.title: A § 4711 Surrogate Designation Is Time-Limited and Only Temporarily Outranks an Agent
clauses.body: A surrogate designation made under § 4711 is not permanent. Unless the patient specifies a shorter period, it lasts only for the course of the treatment or illness, or the stay in the health care institution, during which it was made, or 60 days — whichever of those is shorter. During that limited period, if the patient has also designated an agent under a power of attorney for health care, the surrogate has priority over the agent notwithstanding the general rule (stated in a separate section, § 4685) that a reasonably available, willing agent otherwise has priority over any other person. But making a surrogate designation does not itself revoke the agent's designation — the agent's authority resumes once the surrogate designation expires, unless the patient separately communicates an intent to revoke the agent designation in the manner § 4695(a) requires (a signed writing or personally informing the supervising health care provider).
clauses.gap: This clause states the duration and priority rules § 4711 itself sets out — it does not determine whether a specific patient's designation has expired at a given moment, whether a specific provider correctly treated a designation as still in effect, or whether a specific patient's later statements amounted to a revocation of an agent's designation under § 4695(a). The interaction described here is between a § 4711 surrogate and an agent specifically; it does not address how a surrogate designation interacts with a conservator's or guardian's authority, which a separate clause on § 4712(a)'s priority order covers.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4711(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the time limit on a surrogate designation
citations.quote: Unless the patient specifies a shorter period, a surrogate designation under subdivision (a) is effective only during the course of treatment or illness or during the stay in the health care institution when the surrogate designation is made, or for 60 days, whichever period is shorter.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4711(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, a surrogate's temporary priority over an agent
citations.quote: Notwithstanding Section 4685, if the patient has designated an agent under a power of attorney for health care, the surrogate designated under subdivision (a) has priority over the agent for the period provided in subdivision (b), but the designation of a surrogate does not revoke the designation of an agent unless the patient communicates the intention to revoke in compliance with subdivision (a) of Section 4695.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4685 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the general rule that a reasonably available agent has priority
citations.quote: Unless the power of attorney for health care provides otherwise, the agent designated in the power of attorney who is known to the health care provider to be reasonably available and willing to make health care decisions has priority over any other person in making health care decisions for the principal.

clauses.title: The Statutory Order of Priority Among Legally Recognized Decisionmakers
clauses.body: When a patient lacks the capacity to make a health care decision, California law sets a descending order of priority among the decisionmakers it recognizes: first, a surrogate the patient selected under § 4711; second, an agent under an advance health care directive or a power of attorney for health care; and third, a conservator or guardian of the patient who has authority over health care decisions. This order determines which recognized decisionmaker's decision controls when more than one such decisionmaker exists for the same patient at the same time.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the three-tier order the statute sets among decisionmakers who already qualify under one of its three categories — it does not determine whether a specific person actually qualifies as a valid § 4711 surrogate, agent, or conservator/guardian in a given case, and it does not address what happens when none of the three exists (covered in a separate clause on § 4712(b)'s provider-selected surrogate process). A CourtListener case-law search for judicial interpretation of this priority order returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, quota exhausted) before any results could be reviewed, so this clause rests on the statutory text alone and does not reflect whether courts have construed this ordering in any reported decision.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4712(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the descending priority order of health care decisionmakers
citations.quote: If a patient lacks the capacity to make a health care decision, the following legally recognized health care decisionmakers may make health care decisions on the patient’s behalf, in the following descending order of priority:(1) The patient’s surrogate selected pursuant to Section 4711.(2) The patient’s agent pursuant to an advance health care directive or a power of attorney for health care.(3) The conservator or guardian of the patient having the authority to make health care decisions for the patient.

clauses.title: When No Recognized Decisionmaker Exists, a Provider May Choose a Surrogate From an Enumerated List
clauses.body: California law does not automatically hand health care decision-making authority to a next of kin simply because a patient lacks capacity and has no surrogate, agent, conservator, or guardian. Instead, in that situation, a health care provider or a designee of the health care facility caring for the patient may choose a surrogate, as appropriate to the situation. The person chosen must be an adult who has demonstrated special care and concern for the patient, is familiar with the patient's personal values and beliefs to the extent known, and is reasonably available and willing to serve. The statute lists categories from which that surrogate may be chosen, in the order given: a spouse or domestic partner, an adult child, a parent, an adult sibling, an adult grandchild, or an adult relative or close personal friend. This selection is subject to any disqualification the patient made under § 4715 while the patient still had capacity.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the qualifying standard and the list of eligible categories the statute sets — it does not determine that any specific person meets that standard for any specific patient, does not resolve a dispute among family members over who should be chosen, and does not address California's separate, more procedurally detailed surrogate decision-making rules for skilled nursing facility residents under Health & Safety Code § 1418.8, which this sheet was not researched to cover and does not describe.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4712(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the provider-selected surrogate process and eligible categories
citations.quote: Except as set forth in Section 4715, if a patient lacks the capacity to make a health care decision, but does not have a legally recognized health care decisionmaker pursuant to subdivision (a), a health care provider or a designee of the health care facility caring for the patient may choose a surrogate to make health care decisions on the patient’s behalf, as appropriate in the given situation. The patient’s surrogate shall be an adult who has demonstrated special care and concern for the patient, is familiar with the patient’s personal values and beliefs to the extent known, and is reasonably available and willing to serve. A surrogate may be chosen from any of the following persons:(1) The spouse or domestic partner of the patient.(2) An adult child of the patient.(3) A parent of the patient.(4) An adult sibling of the patient.(5) An adult grandchild of the patient.(6) An adult relative or close personal friend.

clauses.title: The Standard a Surrogate Must Apply in Deciding
clauses.body: A surrogate does not decide freely. California law requires a surrogate (including a person acting as a surrogate) to make a health care decision in accordance with the patient's own individual health care instructions, if any, and the patient's other wishes to the extent the surrogate knows them. Only if the patient's wishes are not known does the surrogate decide according to the surrogate's determination of the patient's best interest — and even then, the surrogate must consider the patient's personal values to the extent known.
clauses.gap: This clause states the legal standard itself — it does not determine what a specific patient's wishes or values actually were, whether a specific surrogate correctly applied this standard in a specific decision, or how a dispute over what the standard requires in a given case would be resolved. A CourtListener search for case law interpreting this substituted-judgment/best-interest standard returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted) before any case could be reviewed, so no judicial gloss on this standard is reflected here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4714 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the surrogate's decision-making standard
citations.quote: A surrogate, including a person acting as a surrogate, shall make a health care decision in accordance with the patient’s individual health care instructions, if any, and other wishes to the extent known to the surrogate. Otherwise, the surrogate shall make the decision in accordance with the surrogate’s determination of the patient’s best interest. In determining the patient’s best interest, the surrogate shall consider the patient’s personal values to the extent known to the surrogate.

clauses.title: A Patient May Disqualify a Specific Person From Ever Acting as Surrogate
clauses.body: While a patient still has capacity, California law lets that patient disqualify another person — including a member of the patient's own family — from acting as the patient's surrogate. This can be done at any time, either by a signed writing or by personally informing the supervising health care provider of the disqualification.
clauses.gap: This clause states only that the disqualification right exists and how it may be exercised — it does not determine whether a specific communication to a specific provider was sufficient to accomplish a disqualification, how a disqualification is recorded or verified afterward, or whether a disqualified person might still qualify to act under some other legal authority (such as a later-appointed conservatorship) that this statute does not reach.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4715 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, a patient's right to disqualify a person from serving as surrogate
citations.quote: A patient having capacity at any time may disqualify another person, including a member of the patient’s family, from acting as the patient’s surrogate by a signed writing or by personally informing the supervising health care provider of the disqualification.

clauses.title: A Registered Domestic Partner Has the Same Authority as a Spouse
clauses.body: California law gives a patient's domestic partner the same authority a spouse has to make a health care decision for an incapacitated partner, when the patient lacks capacity. The statute is explicit that it does not expand or restrict a spouse's own existing authority to make health care decisions for an incapacitated spouse — it equalizes the domestic partner's position with whatever the spousal rule already is, rather than creating a new or different rule.
clauses.gap: This clause states only that domestic-partner parity exists as a matter of statute — it does not itself state what a spouse's authority to make health care decisions for an incapacitated spouse consists of in any given circumstance (that depends on the other provisions of this same statutory scheme, including the priority order and decision standard covered in this sheet's other clauses), and it does not determine whether a specific relationship qualifies as a domestic partnership within the meaning the statute cross-references.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4716(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, domestic-partner parity with a spouse's health care decision-making authority
citations.quote: If a patient lacks the capacity to make a health care decision, the patient’s domestic partner shall have the same authority as a spouse has to make a health care decision for his or her incapacitated spouse. This section may not be construed to expand or restrict the ability of a spouse to make a health care decision for an incapacitated spouse.

clauses.title: A Hospital Emergency Department's 24-Hour Duty to Attempt Contact
clauses.body: California law imposes a specific, time-bound duty on a general acute care hospital: within 24 hours of the arrival in its emergency department of a patient who is unconscious or otherwise incapable of communication, the hospital must make reasonable efforts to contact the patient's agent, surrogate, or a family member or other person the hospital reasonably believes has authority to make health care decisions for the patient. The statute also describes specific steps — examining personal effects and medical records, contacting the identified person, and checking the Advance Health Care Directive Registry when there is evidence of a registry card — that, if all performed, are deemed to satisfy this duty, and requires the hospital to document its efforts in the patient's medical record. This duty is suspended while the hospital is operating under its own disaster and mass-casualty or fire and internal disaster program.
clauses.gap: This clause states the hospital's duty to attempt contact — it does not determine that any specific hospital did or did not make reasonable efforts in a specific case, does not itself grant the contacted person decision-making authority (that depends on the priority-order and provider-selection rules covered in this sheet's other clauses), and does not apply outside a general acute care hospital's emergency department (it does not, for example, describe any comparable duty for other kinds of health care facilities).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 4717(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, a hospital emergency department's duty to attempt contacting a decisionmaker
citations.quote: within 24 hours of the arrival in the emergency department of a general acute care hospital of a patient who is unconscious or otherwise incapable of communication, the hospital shall make reasonable efforts to contact the patient’s agent, surrogate, or a family member or other person the hospital reasonably believes has the authority to make health care decisions on behalf of the patient.

clauses.title: Certification of Understanding
clauses.body: I, {{patientName}}, certify that I have read this information sheet describing California's statutory scheme for who may make health care decisions on behalf of a patient who currently lacks capacity, including the oral surrogate designation process, the statutory priority order among decisionmakers, the process for a provider-selected surrogate, the decision-making standard a surrogate must apply, the disqualification right, domestic-partner parity, and a hospital emergency department's contact duty. I understand that this sheet states facts about California law generally, that it is not legal advice, and that it does not determine who is or will be authorized to make a health care decision for me, or for anyone else, in any specific situation.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California Code of Civil Procedure section 2019.210, a civil-procedure statute that applies once a lawsuit alleging trade secret misappropriation under California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act (Civil Code section 3426 et seq.) has already been filed. It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning a case involving {{companyName}} and {{adversePartyName}}, identified by court case number {{courtCaseNumber}} in {{courtName}}, and concerning the following trade secret: {{tradeSecretDescription}}. Section 2019.210 requires the party alleging misappropriation to identify the claimed trade secret with reasonable particularity before that party may begin discovery relating to the trade secret. This document explains what that statute's text says and does not say. It does not identify any trade secret with the particularity the statute requires, does not draft or file a trade secret identification statement, and does not evaluate whether any specific description of a trade secret meets the reasonable-particularity standard in a given case. This document is separate from, and does not repeat, the corpus's existing Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter (which addresses the substantive definitions of misappropriation and improper means and the remedies for a completed violation), Trade Secret Preemption Doctrine Information Sheet (which addresses which other civil claims survive alongside a misappropriation claim), Criminal Trade Secret Theft Information Sheet and Economic Espionage Act Information Sheet (which address criminal liability), and the corpus's DTSA-focused NDA and cease-and-desist documents (which address the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act rather than this state civil-discovery statute). None of those documents describe the pre-discovery identification requirement covered here.

clauses.title: Scope: Actions Alleging Misappropriation Under the Uniform Trade Secrets Act
clauses.body: By its own text, Code of Civil Procedure section 2019.210 applies specifically "in any action alleging the misappropriation of a trade secret under the Uniform Trade Secrets Act," which the statute cross-references as Title 5, commencing with Civil Code section 3426. The section appears within the Civil Discovery Act, in the chapter governing the methods and sequence of discovery, as a discovery-sequencing rule tied to that specific type of state-law civil action.
clauses.gap: The statute's text does not state whether it applies of its own force to an action alleging misappropriation only under the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act and brought only in federal court, as opposed to a California Uniform Trade Secrets Act claim; that question depends on how a federal court treats a state procedural statute, which is outside this section's text and was not researched or verified in this session. This clause also does not address whether or how California trial courts apply an identification requirement in a case combining a California Uniform Trade Secrets Act claim with other claims.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 2019.210 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 2019.210
citations.quote: In any action alleging the misappropriation of a trade secret under the Uniform Trade Secrets Act (Title 5 (commencing with Section 3426) of Part 1 of Division 4 of the Civil Code)

clauses.title: Requirement to Identify the Trade Secret Before Discovery
clauses.body: Section 2019.210 states a sequencing rule: before the party alleging misappropriation may commence discovery relating to the claimed trade secret, that party must identify the trade secret with reasonable particularity. The identification requirement is expressly made "subject to any orders that may be appropriate under Section 3426.5 of the Civil Code," the companion provision addressing court-ordered secrecy protections.
clauses.gap: The statute's text does not specify the form the identification must take (for example, a standalone written statement versus a discovery response), does not set a numerical deadline, and does not itself define which discovery methods count as "discovery relating to the trade secret." Those procedural details are not addressed in the statutory text quoted here.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 2019.210 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 2019.210
citations.quote: before commencing discovery relating to the trade secret, the party alleging the misappropriation shall identify the trade secret with reasonable particularity subject to any orders that may be appropriate under Section 3426.5 of the Civil Code.

clauses.title: The Statute's Text Does Not Define "Reasonable Particularity"
clauses.body: The phrase "reasonable particularity" is the operative standard in section 2019.210, but the statute's text supplies no definition, list of required elements, or example of what identifying a trade secret with reasonable particularity looks like in practice.
clauses.gap: How much detail satisfies "reasonable particularity" has reportedly been addressed in published California appellate decisions interpreting this section, but a case-law search on that question could not be completed in this research session: a CourtListener search for California case law discussing section 2019.210 and "reasonable particularity" returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125-request daily quota exhausted) before any result was retrieved. This document accordingly describes only the statute's own text and does not describe how courts have applied or elaborated the standard.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 2019.210 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 2019.210
citations.quote: identify the trade secret with reasonable particularity

clauses.title: The Statute's Text Does Not State a Consequence for Noncompliance
clauses.body: Section 2019.210's operative sentence imposes the identification requirement but does not itself state what happens if the party alleging misappropriation proceeds with discovery relating to the trade secret without first identifying it with reasonable particularity. No sanction, dismissal, evidence-exclusion rule, or automatic stay is written into the text of this section.
clauses.gap: Reported California decisions may describe procedural consequences courts have imposed for noncompliance (such as staying or limiting discovery), but that question could not be verified in this session because the same CourtListener rate-limit error (125-request daily quota exhausted, HTTP 429) that blocked research for the "reasonable particularity" clause also blocked any search on this point. This clause is limited to what the statute's own text does and does not say.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 2019.210 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 2019.210
citations.quote: In any action alleging the misappropriation of a trade secret under the Uniform Trade Secrets Act (Title 5 (commencing with Section 3426) of Part 1 of Division 4 of the Civil Code), before commencing discovery relating to the trade secret, the party alleging the misappropriation shall identify the trade secret with reasonable particularity subject to any orders that may be appropriate under Section 3426.5 of the Civil Code.

clauses.title: Protective Measures Available Under the Companion Secrecy-Preservation Statute
clauses.body: Civil Code section 3426.5, the provision section 2019.210 cross-references, requires a court in an action under the Uniform Trade Secrets Act to preserve the secrecy of an alleged trade secret by reasonable means. The statute's text lists several examples of such means: granting protective orders in connection with discovery proceedings, holding in-camera hearings, sealing the records of the action, and ordering any person involved in the litigation not to disclose an alleged trade secret without prior court approval.
clauses.gap: Section 3426.5's text states that a court "shall preserve the secrecy of an alleged trade secret by reasonable means" and lists examples using the word "may include," but it does not itself specify a procedure, motion, or timeline for a party to request one of these measures in connection with the section 2019.210 identification step specifically, and no case law on that interaction was verified in this session for the reasons stated in the companion clauses above.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.5 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.5
citations.quote: a court shall preserve the secrecy of an alleged trade secret by reasonable means, which may include granting protective orders in connection with discovery proceedings, holding in-camera hearings, sealing the records of the action, and ordering any person involved in the litigation not to disclose an alleged trade secret without prior court approval.

clauses.title: Relationship to Other Trade Secret Statutes in This Corpus
clauses.body: Section 2019.210 sits within the Civil Discovery Act's chapter on the methods and sequence of discovery, not within the Uniform Trade Secrets Act itself. Its text does not define "trade secret" or "misappropriation," does not state a limitations period, and does not create or limit any substantive claim or defense; it cross-references the Uniform Trade Secrets Act (Civil Code section 3426 et seq.) only to identify which actions it applies to, and cross-references Civil Code section 3426.5 only for the available secrecy-preservation orders.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the statute's placement and cross-references as they appear on the two official Leginfo pages fetched for this document; it does not describe how this discovery-sequencing rule interacts procedurally with the substantive misappropriation definitions, the preemption doctrine, or the criminal trade secret statutes covered in this corpus's other documents, beyond noting that section 2019.210's own text does not address those subjects.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 2019.210, chapter heading (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code, Pt. 4, Tit. 4, Ch. 5
citations.quote: CHAPTER 5. Methods and Sequence of Discovery [2019.010 - 2019.210]

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the requirements California law imposes before a person under 18 years of age may obtain a marriage license, under Family Code sections 300 through 306 and sections 420 and 423 (Part 1, Validity of Marriage, and Part 3, Solemnization of Marriage, of Division 3 of the Family Code). It covers the general age-18 baseline for consenting to marriage, the court-order and parental- or guardian-consent requirements that apply when one or both parties are under 18, the Family Court Services interview and reporting process the court must follow before ruling on such an order, the 30-day waiting period and its statutory exceptions, the court's discretionary authority to order premarital counseling, the information a minor must be given once an order is issued, and how licensing and solemnization proceed once an order has been granted. It is distinct from this project's Confidential Marriage document, which describes a separate license track under Family Code Part 4 (commencing with Section 500) available to adults living together as spouses, and from this project's Common Law Marriage document, which addresses California's non-recognition of marriage formed by cohabitation and consent alone rather than the minor-specific consent and court-order requirements addressed here. This document is for parties named {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. This document is informational only. It states what the statutes require; it does not determine whether any specific minor, parent, guardian, or court will grant, deny, or condition a particular request for permission to marry, and it is not a substitute for legal advice about a specific person's situation. Only a court, applying these statutes to the actual facts before it, can determine whether a particular minor may be issued a marriage license.

clauses.title: The General Rule for Persons 18 or Older — Family Code Section 301
clauses.body: Family Code section 301 states the general baseline: two unmarried persons who are 18 years of age or older, and who are not otherwise disqualified from marrying, are capable of consenting to and consummating a marriage without any court order or parental consent. The court-order and consent requirements described in the rest of this document apply only when at least one party to the intended marriage is under 18.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the age-18 baseline in section 301 itself. It does not address what "not otherwise disqualified" means -- for example, the separate statutory rules on incestuous or bigamous marriages found elsewhere in the Family Code -- because that is a distinct topic from the minor-specific consent and court-order requirements this document addresses.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 301
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 301
citations.quote: Two unmarried persons 18 years of age or older, who are not otherwise disqualified, are capable of consenting to and consummating marriage.

clauses.title: The Court-Order Requirement for a Person Under 18 — Family Code Section 302
clauses.body: Family Code section 302 provides the general rule for a minor with at least one parent or guardian able to consent: an unmarried person under 18 years of age may be issued a marriage license only upon obtaining a court order granting permission to marry, following the procedure Family Code section 304 describes. The court order itself is not the last step -- section 302(b) also requires that the court order and the written consent of at least one parent or the guardian of each underage party be filed with the clerk of the court, and that a certified copy of the order be presented to the county clerk at the time the marriage license is issued.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only the case where the minor has a parent or guardian available and able to consent. It does not address the different pathway under Family Code section 303 for a minor who has no parent, or no parent capable of consenting, which is addressed in a separate clause of this document. It also does not independently verify the county clerk's own administrative procedures for accepting the certified copy of the order, which are not stated in section 302 itself.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 302
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 302(a)
citations.quote: An unmarried person under 18 years of age may be issued a marriage license upon obtaining a court order granting permission to the underage person or persons to marry, in accordance with the requirements described in Section 304.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 302
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 302(b)
citations.quote: The court order and written consent of at least one of the parents or the guardian of each underage person shall be filed with the clerk of the court, and a certified copy of the order shall be presented to the county clerk at the time the marriage license is issued.

clauses.title: When a Minor Has No Parent Able to Consent — Family Code Section 303
clauses.body: Family Code section 303 addresses the situation where the minor has no parent, or no parent capable of giving consent. If it appears to the court's satisfaction, on the minor's own application, that the minor requires a written consent to marry and has no parent or no parent capable of consenting, the court itself may make an order consenting to the issuance of a marriage license and granting the minor permission to marry, following the same section 304 procedure that applies to an order under section 302. As under section 302, the order must be filed with the clerk of the court and a certified copy presented to the county clerk when the marriage license is issued.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes section 303 as currently written. It does not independently verify how a court determines that a parent is "not capable of consenting" in practice, or what evidence a minor's application under this section must contain beyond the statute's own general standard, because section 303 does not itself define those terms further.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 303
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 303
citations.quote: If it appears to the satisfaction of the court by application of a minor that the minor requires a written consent to marry and that the minor has no parent or has no parent capable of consenting, the court may make an order consenting to the issuance of a marriage license and granting permission to the minor to marry, in accordance with the requirements described in Section 304.

clauses.title: The Family Court Services Interview and Report — Family Code Section 304(a)
clauses.body: Before a court may issue an order granting permission to marry under section 302 or 303, Family Code section 304(a) requires it to take several specific steps. The court must require Family Court Services to separately interview the parties intending to marry and, if applicable, at least one parent or the guardian of each party who is a minor -- and if more than one parent or guardian is interviewed, they must be interviewed separately from one another. Family Court Services must then prepare and submit to the court a written report assessing any potential force, threat, persuasion, fraud, coercion, or duress by either party or their family members relating to the intended marriage, along with a recommendation on whether to grant or deny permission to marry; if Family Court Services knows or reasonably suspects either party is a victim of child abuse or neglect, it must also report that to the county child protective services agency. After receiving that report, the court must separately interview each party in camera before making its final determination, and must consider whether there is evidence of coercion or undue influence on the minor.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the statutory steps a court must take before ruling; it does not describe how a specific Family Court Services office schedules or conducts these interviews in practice, nor what its written report format looks like, because section 304(a) leaves those operational details to the court and to Family Court Services rather than specifying them in the statute itself.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 304
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 304(a)(1)
citations.quote: Require Family Court Services to separately interview the parties intending to marry and, if applicable, at least one of the parents or the guardian of each party who is a minor.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 304
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 304(a)(2)
citations.quote: Require Family Court Services to prepare and submit to the court a written report, containing any assessment of potential force, threat, persuasion, fraud, coercion, or duress by either of the parties or their family members relating to the intended marriage.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 304
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 304(a)(3)-(4)
citations.quote: Consider whether there is evidence of coercion or undue influence on the minor.

clauses.title: The 30-Day Waiting Period Before a License May Be Requested — Family Code Section 304(b)
clauses.body: Family Code section 304(b) imposes a waiting period after a court order is issued, in the specific circumstance where one or both of the parties are 17 years of age or younger: the parties become eligible to request a marriage license no earlier than 30 days from the time the court order was issued. This waiting period is separate from, and additional to, the underlying requirement to obtain the court order itself.
clauses.gap: This clause states the 30-day rule as section 304(b) itself frames it, keyed to a party being 17 or younger rather than to every case involving a minor. It does not address the statutory exceptions to this specific 30-day requirement, which are addressed in a separate clause of this document covering section 304(f).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 304
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 304(b)
citations.quote: if one or both of the parties are 17 years of age or younger, the parties shall be eligible to request a marriage license no earlier than 30 days from the time the court order was issued

clauses.title: The Court's Discretionary Authority to Order Premarital Counseling — Family Code Section 304(c)
clauses.body: As part of a court order granting permission to marry under section 302 or 303, Family Code section 304(c) gives the court discretionary authority -- not a mandatory duty -- to require the parties to a prospective minor's marriage to participate in premarital counseling concerning the social, economic, and personal responsibilities that come with marriage, if the court considers it necessary. The statute specifically provides that the parties cannot be required to confer with counselors provided by religious organizations of any denomination. In deciding whether to order counseling, the court must consider, among other factors, the parties' ability to pay for it, and the court may impose a reasonable fee to cover the cost of counseling provided by the county or the court, which must be used exclusively for that purpose.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the court's authority and the constraints the statute places on it; it does not identify which counseling providers a given county actually makes available, or what a reasonable fee amount looks like in practice, because section 304(c) leaves those specifics to the counseling provider and the court's own fee-setting rather than fixing them in the statute.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 304
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 304(c)
citations.quote: the court shall, if it considers it necessary, require the parties to the prospective marriage of a minor to participate in premarital counseling concerning social, economic, and personal responsibilities incident to marriage. The parties shall not be required to confer with counselors provided by religious organizations of any denomination.

clauses.title: What the Court Order Itself Must Document — Family Code Section 304(d)
clauses.body: Family Code section 304(d) specifies information the court order granting permission to marry must document. Only for purposes of completing the document described in Health and Safety Code section 102233, and not for purposes of deciding the underlying request, the gender of each party intending to marry, if provided, must be documented on the order. The date of birth of each party intending to marry must also be documented on the order. In addition, so the person solemnizing the marriage can meet the requirement in Family Code section 423(b) and the local registrar can meet the requirement in Health and Safety Code section 102356(a), the court must provide the parties who are granted permission to marry with a copy of the order itself.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes section 304(d)'s own text describing what must appear on the order and to whom a copy must go. It does not independently verify the text of Health and Safety Code sections 102233 or 102356, which section 304(d) cross-references but which were not fetched or reviewed in preparing this document.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 304
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 304(d)(1)-(2)
citations.quote: the gender of each party intending to marry, if provided, shall be documented on the court order granting permission to marry

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 304
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 304(d)(3)
citations.quote: the court shall provide parties who are granted permission to marry with a copy of the court order granting permission to marry

clauses.title: Information the Minor Must Be Given When an Order Issues — Family Code Section 304(e)
clauses.body: Family Code section 304(e) requires that, upon issuance of the order granting permission to marry, the minor be provided with several categories of information: the rights and responsibilities of an emancipated minor, including the effects of emancipation described in the Family Code's emancipation chapter beginning at section 7050; the circumstances under which a marriage may be judicially determined void or voidable and adjudged a nullity, and the procedure for obtaining that determination; the procedures for legal separation or dissolution of marriage; telephone numbers for the National Domestic Violence Hotline and the National Sexual Assault Hotline; and the conditions under which an unemancipated minor may leave home and remain in a shelter or otherwise live separately from a parent or guardian, whether a parent's or guardian's consent or acquiescence is required for that, the minor's rights to seek a protective or restraining order to prevent abuse, and the minor's rights to enter into contracts, including contracts for legal services and mental health counseling.
clauses.gap: This clause lists the categories of information section 304(e) requires be given to the minor; it does not itself reproduce that underlying substantive information (for example, the actual emancipation rights under Family Code section 7050 et seq., or the actual nullity grounds), which this project's own separate Emancipation of a Minor and Nullity of Marriage documents address in more depth. It also does not verify who is responsible for actually delivering this information to the minor in practice, since section 304(e) states that it "shall be provided" without naming the specific person or office who provides it.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 304
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 304(e)
citations.quote: Upon issuance of the order granting permission to marry, the minor shall be provided with the following information:

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 304
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 304(e)(3)
citations.quote: Telephone numbers for the National Domestic Violence Hotline and the National Sexual Assault Hotline.

clauses.title: Exceptions to the Interview/Report Process and the 30-Day Wait — Family Code Section 304(f)
clauses.body: Family Code section 304(f) creates two distinct, narrower exceptions. First, subdivisions (a) and (b) -- the Family Court Services interview-and-report process and the 30-day waiting period -- do not apply to a minor who is 17 years of age and who has achieved a high school diploma or a high school equivalency certificate. Second, and separately, subdivision (b) alone -- only the 30-day waiting period -- does not apply to a minor who is 16 or 17 years of age and who is pregnant, or whose prospective spouse is pregnant; that narrower pregnancy exception does not excuse the party from the Family Court Services interview-and-report process, only from the 30-day wait.
clauses.gap: This clause states the two exceptions exactly as section 304(f) draws them; note that they are not interchangeable -- the diploma/equivalency exception in paragraph (1) reaches both subdivisions (a) and (b), while the pregnancy exception in paragraph (2) reaches only subdivision (b). This clause does not address how a minor or the court verifies a high school equivalency certificate or a pregnancy for these purposes, because section 304(f) does not itself specify a verification procedure.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 304
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 304(f)(1)
citations.quote: Subdivisions (a) and (b) do not apply to a minor who is 17 years of age and who has achieved a high school diploma or a high school equivalency certificate.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 304
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 304(f)(2)
citations.quote: Subdivision (b) does not apply to a minor who is 16 or 17 years of age and who is pregnant or whose prospective spouse is pregnant.

clauses.title: Licensing, Solemnization, and Returning the License After an Order Issues — Family Code Sections 306, 420, and 423
clauses.body: Once a court order granting permission to marry has been obtained, the marriage still must go through California's general licensing and solemnization process. Family Code section 306 states that, with an exception not relevant here, a marriage must be licensed, solemnized, and authenticated, and the authenticated license returned to the county recorder of the county where it was issued; noncompliance with these requirements by a nonparty to the marriage does not itself invalidate the marriage. Family Code section 420(a) states that no particular form of ceremony is required for solemnization, but the parties must declare, in the physical presence of the person solemnizing the marriage and necessary witnesses, that they take each other as spouses. Finally, Family Code section 423(b) adds a minor-specific requirement at the return-of-license stage: the person solemnizing the marriage must include with the returned marriage license a copy of the section 304 court order granting permission to marry, if one or both of the parties were minors at the time of solemnization.
clauses.gap: This clause does not independently verify Family Code section 307 (the exception section 306 itself cross-references), section 422 (the endorsement requirement section 423(a) cross-references), or the identity of who is authorized to solemnize a marriage in California, all of which are governed by other Family Code sections not fetched for this document. It also does not address the separate confidential-marriage license track under Part 4 of this division, which this project's Confidential Marriage document covers.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 306
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 306
citations.quote: a marriage shall be licensed, solemnized, and authenticated, and the authenticated marriage license shall be returned to the county recorder of the county where the marriage license was issued, as provided in this part

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 420
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 420(a)
citations.quote: No particular form for the ceremony of marriage is required for solemnization of the marriage, but the parties shall declare, in the physical presence of the person solemnizing the marriage and necessary witnesses, that they take each other as spouses.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 423
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 423(b)
citations.quote: the person solemnizing the marriage shall include with the marriage license described in subdivision (a) a copy of the court order granting permission to marry described in Section 304, if one or both of the parties to the marriage were minors at the time of solemnization of the marriage

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
The Statute's Name and Scope
clauses.body: The chapter of the Labor Code addressed in this document is formally named the Employee Literacy Education Assistance Act. It consists of five sections, numbered 1040 through 1044, appearing within the Labor Code's general employment-regulation provisions on privileges and immunities.
clauses.gap: This naming section imposes no obligation on its own -- it only establishes the chapter's title and numbering. The threshold, duty, and protection provisions live in the sections that follow, and each of those carries its own separate limitation (a size threshold, an undue-hardship qualifier, and no stated penalty provision, among others), so the short title by itself does not indicate who is covered or what is required. No case law is cited for this section because a CourtListener case-law search for this chapter returned a 429 daily-rate-limit-exceeded error before any results could be reviewed, and this research session did not wait out or retry that quota.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1040 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1040, short title
citations.quote: This chapter shall be known and may be cited as the Employee Literacy Education Assistance Act.

clauses.title: The Accommodation-and-Assistance Duty
clauses.body: A private employer that regularly employs 25 or more employees is required to reasonably accommodate and assist an employee who reveals a problem of illiteracy and requests the employer's assistance in enrolling in an adult literacy education program. This duty is qualified: it applies only if the requested accommodation does not impose an undue hardship on the employer.
clauses.gap: The statute conditions the duty on the employer "regularly employing 25 or more employees," but its text does not define that phrase -- it states no measurement period, no method for counting part-time employees or employees across multiple locations, and no cross-reference to how the phrase is defined elsewhere in the Labor Code. The statute also does not define "undue hardship" or list any factors for weighing it, unlike some other California accommodation statutes that enumerate specific hardship factors, and it sets no deadline by which the employer must respond to a request. By its own terms the duty applies only to a "private employer"; the text does not say whether or how a public-sector employer is covered. No case law construing any of these terms is cited here because a CourtListener search for this statute returned a 429 daily-quota-exceeded error before results could be reviewed.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1041 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1041(a), accommodation-and-assistance duty and undue-hardship qualifier
citations.quote: Every private employer regularly employing 25 or more employees shall reasonably accommodate and assist any employee who reveals a problem of illiteracy and requests employer assistance in enrolling in an adult literacy education program, provided that this reasonable accommodation does not impose an undue hardship on the employer.

clauses.title: What "Employer Assistance" Means
clauses.body: The statute describes employer assistance to include, without limitation, providing the employee with the locations of local literacy education programs, or arranging for a literacy education provider to visit the jobsite.
clauses.gap: The statute's list is expressly non-exhaustive ("includes, but is not limited to"), so its outer boundary is not fixed by the text itself. The two named examples describe directing an employee to existing resources or arranging an on-site provider visit; the statute does not say whether an employer must pay any cost of the literacy program itself, does not specify any minimum duration for which assistance must continue, and does not address what other forms of assistance, if any, a court might find required beyond these two examples. No case law is cited because CourtListener's search quota was exhausted for this research session before this statute could be queried.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1041 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1041(b), definition of employer assistance
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, employer assistance includes, but is not limited to, providing the employee with the locations of local literacy education programs or arranging for a literacy education provider to visit the jobsite.

clauses.title: Duty to Safeguard Privacy
clauses.body: The statute requires the employer to make reasonable efforts to safeguard the privacy of the employee as to the fact that the employee has a problem with illiteracy.
clauses.gap: The duty is to make "reasonable efforts," not to guarantee confidentiality, and the statute does not itself state what counts as a reasonable effort or list any exceptions -- for example, disclosure required by another law, or disclosure to a supervisor who has a legitimate need to know -- the way some other California confidentiality statutes expressly do. The statute also states no remedy specific to a violation of this privacy duty; any remedy would have to come from some other source of law not addressed in this document. No case law construing this duty is cited because a CourtListener search for this statute returned a 429 daily-quota-exceeded error before any results could be reviewed.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1042 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1042, privacy-safeguarding duty
citations.quote: The employer shall make reasonable efforts to safeguard the privacy of the employee as to the fact that he or she has a problem with illiteracy.

clauses.title: No Paid Time Off Required by This Chapter
clauses.body: The statute states that nothing in this chapter is to be construed to require an employer to provide time off with pay for an employee to enroll and participate in an adult literacy education program.
clauses.gap: This section forecloses only one specific reading of the chapter -- that the chapter itself creates a right to paid time off. Its text does not say whether an employee may instead use their own accrued vacation, paid time off, or other paid leave for this purpose, and it does not address how this chapter interacts with any other, separately governed leave or accommodation entitlement an employee's particular circumstances might independently trigger. No case law is cited because CourtListener's daily search quota was already exhausted when this statute was researched.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1043 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1043, no paid-time-off requirement
citations.quote: Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to require an employer to provide time off with pay for an employee to enroll and participate in an adult literacy education program.

clauses.title: Protection Against Termination for Disclosure
clauses.body: The statute provides that an employee who reveals a problem of illiteracy, and who satisfactorily performs their work, is not subject to termination of employment because of the disclosure of illiteracy.
clauses.gap: This protection, by its own text, reaches only "termination of employment." It does not use the broader language -- discharge, demotion, suspension, or other discrimination in the terms and conditions of employment -- that some other, similarly structured California leave and accommodation statutes in this corpus use, so its plain wording does not itself state whether it also reaches those other adverse actions. The protection is also expressly conditioned on the employee "satisfactorily" performing their work, a standard the statute does not define. Separately, this chapter's own text contains no penalty, treble-damages, or other explicit enforcement provision for a violation of this section, unlike some neighboring California leave statutes that state a specific remedy. No case law construing this section is cited because a CourtListener search for this statute returned a 429 daily-rate-limit error before any case-law results could be retrieved, and this research session did not wait out or retry that quota.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1044 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1044, protection against termination for disclosure
citations.quote: An employee who reveals a problem of illiteracy and who satisfactorily performs his or her work shall not be subject to termination of employment because of the disclosure of illiteracy.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Special Enrollment Rights Information Sheet describes two federal-law rights that can let {{employeeName}} enroll in a *different* health plan after health coverage from {{companyName}} ends on {{terminationDate}}: (1) the right under the federal Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act ("HIPAA") of 1996 to a special enrollment period in another group health plan for which {{employeeName}} is otherwise eligible, such as a spouse's employer-sponsored plan; and (2) the right under the Affordable Care Act to a special enrollment period in a health insurance marketplace plan, such as one offered through Covered California.

This document is not the same as, and does not repeat, this project's COBRA and Cal-COBRA information sheets and election-notice forms. Those documents describe the right to continue enrollment in the *same* group health plan the employee already had, purchased at a group rate. This document instead describes the separate right to move onto a *new and different* plan — a spouse's plan or a marketplace plan — triggered by the same loss of job-based coverage. A person who has lost job-based coverage may have both kinds of rights available at the same time, and this document does not state which one, if either, better fits {{employeeName}}'s own circumstances.

This document also has nothing to do with the different, more commonly cited part of HIPAA — its Privacy Rule governing the confidentiality of protected health information, referenced elsewhere in this project's medical-authorization and accommodation documents. The "HIPAA" right described here comes from a separate part of the same 1996 federal statute: the portability and nondiscrimination provisions that added special enrollment periods to federal group-health-plan law, codified at 29 U.S.C. § 1181(f) (among parallel provisions in the Internal Revenue Code and the Public Health Service Act). This document states the federal statutory and regulatory text on special enrollment; it does not determine whether {{employeeName}}'s own prior plan or a specific spouse's plan is subject to these requirements, and it is not a claim, notice, or election form.

clauses.title: HIPAA's Special Enrollment Right to Join Another Group Health Plan
clauses.body: Federal law requires a group health plan, and a health insurance issuer offering group health insurance coverage in connection with a group health plan, to permit an employee who is eligible but not enrolled for coverage under the plan's terms (or an eligible-but-unenrolled dependent of that employee) to enroll for coverage if certain conditions are met. This is the right that can let {{employeeName}} enroll in a spouse's or other family member's group health plan, mid-year and outside that plan's normal open-enrollment window, once each of the statute's own conditions is satisfied.
clauses.gap: This clause states the federal statutory rule itself; it does not determine that any particular plan — a former employer's plan or a family member's plan — is a "group health plan" covered by this statute, since certain plans (including many church plans and governmental plans) are wholly or partly exempt from this part of federal law under other statutory provisions not addressed here. A targeted case-law search on how courts have applied this special-enrollment provision could not be completed for this clause because the research tool's daily query quota had already been exhausted at the time of research; this clause relies on the statutory text alone.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1181(f)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, HIPAA special enrollment periods — core rule
citations.quote: A group health plan , and a health insurance issuer offering group health insurance coverage in connection with a group health plan, shall permit an employee who is eligible, but not enrolled, for coverage under the terms of the plan (or a dependent of such an employee if the dependent is eligible, but not enrolled, for coverage under such terms) to enroll for coverage under the terms of the plan if each of the following conditions is met:

clauses.title: What Counts as a Qualifying Loss of Coverage Under HIPAA's Special Enrollment Rule
clauses.body: The statute defines the kind of coverage loss that can open a HIPAA special enrollment period. It covers two situations: prior coverage that was under a COBRA continuation provision and has since been exhausted, and prior coverage that was not under COBRA and was terminated because of a loss of eligibility — the statute's own examples of a loss of eligibility include legal separation, divorce, death, termination of employment, or a reduction in the number of hours of employment — or because employer contributions toward that coverage were terminated. A loss of job-based coverage that follows {{employeeName}}'s employment ending on {{terminationDate}} falls within the statute's own listed examples of a loss of eligibility.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the statute's own list of qualifying circumstances; it does not itself determine that a given employee's coverage loss meets every element of the statute (for example, whether the loss resulted from termination of employment as opposed to some other cause the statute does not cover, such as a voluntary drop in coverage while still eligible). Unlike COBRA's qualifying-event definition, this HIPAA provision contains no exclusion for coverage lost due to the employee's own misconduct; this clause does not resolve whether some other statute or plan term might treat a given termination differently.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1181(f)(1)(C) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, HIPAA special enrollment — qualifying loss-of-coverage events
citations.quote: (C) The employee ’s or dependent’s coverage described in subparagraph (A)— (i) was under a COBRA continuation provision and the coverage under such provision was exhausted; or (ii) was not under such a provision and either the coverage was terminated as a result of loss of eligibility for the coverage (including as a result of legal separation, divorce, death, termination of employment, or reduction in the number of hours of employment) or employer contributions toward such coverage were terminated.

clauses.title: A Precondition Most Summaries Omit: The Prior Written Statement Requirement
clauses.body: The statute's special enrollment right is not available solely because coverage was lost. It also requires that, at the earlier time the employee declined enrollment in the new plan because of other coverage, the employee stated in writing that other coverage was the reason for declining — but the statute makes this written-statement requirement apply only if the plan sponsor or issuer had itself required such a statement at that earlier time and had given the employee notice of that requirement and its consequences. Where a plan never imposed or gave notice of this written-statement requirement when {{employeeName}} originally declined enrollment, this particular precondition does not apply at all.
clauses.gap: This clause states a conditional rule from the statute's own text; it does not determine, for any particular plan, whether that plan actually required a written statement of the reason for declining enrollment or gave the required notice of that requirement at the time enrollment was originally declined — that is a fact about the specific plan's own enrollment materials and administration that this document does not investigate.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1181(f)(1)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, HIPAA special enrollment — conditional written-statement requirement
citations.quote: (B) The employee stated in writing at such time that coverage under a group health plan or health insurance coverage was the reason for declining enrollment, but only if the plan sponsor or issuer (if applicable) required such a statement at such time and provided the employee with notice of such requirement (and the consequences of such requirement) at such time.

clauses.title: The 30-Day Deadline to Request HIPAA Special Enrollment
clauses.body: The statute requires the enrollment request itself to be made within a specific window measured from the coverage-loss event: under the terms of the plan, the employee must request enrollment no later than 30 days after the date the earlier COBRA coverage was exhausted, or 30 days after the date the other coverage or employer contribution toward it was terminated. This 30-day period is the statutory floor for special enrollment in another group health plan; it is a different, and shorter, period than the separate marketplace special enrollment period described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This clause states the statutory minimum request window; it does not calculate the specific calendar deadline that applies following a given employee's own coverage loss, which depends on the exact date coverage was exhausted or terminated. A plan may allow a longer period than this 30-day statutory floor, but this clause does not identify whether any particular plan does so.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 1181(f)(1)(D) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, HIPAA special enrollment — 30-day request deadline
citations.quote: (D) Under the terms of the plan , the employee requests such enrollment not later than 30 days after the date of exhaustion of coverage described in subparagraph (C)(i) or termination of coverage or employer contribution described in subparagraph (C)(ii).

clauses.title: Loss of Job-Based Coverage as a Marketplace Special Enrollment Trigger
clauses.body: Separately from the group-health-plan right described above, federal regulations implementing the Affordable Care Act require a health insurance exchange — including a state-based exchange such as Covered California — to allow a qualified individual to enroll in or change a marketplace health plan when a "triggering event" listed in the regulation occurs. The first listed triggering event is the loss of minimum essential coverage by the qualified individual or a dependent, with the date of that loss of coverage defined as the last day the consumer would have coverage under the previous plan.
clauses.gap: This clause states the federal regulatory trigger itself; it does not determine that a given former employer-sponsored plan was "minimum essential coverage" within the meaning of the cross-referenced tax regulation (26 CFR 1.5000A-1(b)), which this research did not independently fetch or verify. It also does not address any additional or different procedural rules a specific state-based exchange, such as Covered California, may layer on top of this federal floor.

citations.case: 45 C.F.R. § 155.420(d)(1)(i) (Cornell LII / e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, ACA marketplace special enrollment — loss of coverage trigger
citations.quote: (1) The qualified individual or his or her dependent either: (i) Loses minimum essential coverage . The date of the loss of coverage is the last day the consumer would have coverage under his or her previous plan or coverage;

clauses.title: The Marketplace's General 60-Day Special Enrollment Window
clauses.body: The general rule stated in the regulation gives a qualified individual or enrollee 60 days from the date of a triggering event, such as the loss of job-based coverage, to select a marketplace health plan, unless the regulation specifically states a different rule for a particular category of triggering event.
clauses.gap: This clause states the regulation's default 60-day figure; a following clause in this document describes a materially different rule that applies specifically to loss-of-coverage events, so this general-rule clause alone should not be read as the complete special enrollment timeline for a coverage-loss situation like this one.

citations.case: 45 C.F.R. § 155.420(c)(1) (Cornell LII / e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, ACA marketplace special enrollment — general 60-day rule
citations.quote: (1) General rule. Unless specifically stated otherwise herein, a qualified individual or enrollee has 60 days from the date of a triggering event to select a QHP.

clauses.title: A Correction to the General Rule: 60 Days Before, Not Just 60 Days After, a Loss of Coverage
clauses.body: For a loss-of-coverage triggering event specifically, the regulation does not simply apply the general 60-days-after rule. It instead gives "advanced availability": a qualified individual or dependent described in the loss-of-minimum-essential-coverage provision has 60 days *before* the triggering event, and (unless the exchange exercises a specific option to shorten this) 60 days *after* the triggering event, to select a marketplace plan. This differs from an initial assumption that a marketplace special enrollment period for a coverage loss runs only forward from the loss date — the regulation's own text extends the window to include the 60 days leading up to the loss of coverage as well.
clauses.gap: This clause states the regulatory text defining the length of this particular special enrollment window; it does not address the separate exchange option (referenced in the regulation as paragraph (c)(6)) to shorten the post-event portion of this window, which this research did not fetch or verify, nor does it state which specific dates result from a given employee's own coverage loss.

citations.case: 45 C.F.R. § 155.420(c)(2) (Cornell LII / e-CFR text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, ACA marketplace special enrollment — advanced availability for loss of coverage
citations.quote: (2) Advanced availability. A qualified individual or their dependent who is described in paragraph (d)(1), (d)(6)(iii), or (d)(15) of this section has 60 days before and, unless the Exchange exercises the option in paragraph (c)(6) of this section, 60 days after the triggering event to select a QHP.

clauses.title: Two Separate Federal Deadlines Measured From the Same Coverage-Loss Date
clauses.body: The same loss of job-based coverage can start two different federal enrollment clocks that run on different schedules and lead to different destinations. The HIPAA special enrollment right runs for 30 days from the coverage-loss event and can lead to enrollment in another group health plan such as a spouse's employer plan. The Affordable Care Act marketplace special enrollment right, for this same kind of triggering event, runs for a longer window — beginning 60 days before the triggering event and continuing 60 days after it — and leads to enrollment in a marketplace plan such as one offered through Covered California. Neither statutory or regulatory provision states that a person must choose only one of these two tracks, or that using one forecloses the other.
clauses.gap: This clause synthesizes the deadlines already stated in the statute and the regulation quoted elsewhere in this document; it does not itself resolve any conflict, coordination rule, or state-specific administrative practice — for example, how Covered California's own enrollment platform treats a person who is also mid-window on a HIPAA special enrollment election — because no additional independent source addressing that specific interaction was located, and a case-law search on this topic could not be completed because the research tool's daily quota had already been exhausted at the time of research.

citations.quote: (1) General rule. Unless specifically stated otherwise herein, a qualified individual or enrollee has 60 days from the date of a triggering event to select a QHP.
