Acknowledgment and Signature
What This Information Sheet Covers
clauses.body: This Pet Animal Custody and Ownership Information Sheet concerns {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, whose marital dissolution or legal separation proceeding is pending, or may be filed, in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes what California Family Code section 2605 says about a pending-proceeding order for the interim care of a pet animal and about the court's authority, at final property division, to assign sole or joint ownership of a pet animal by considering the animal's care rather than applying the community estate's usual equal-division rule. It also describes how section 2605 defines "pet animal" and "care" for purposes of that section. This document is about {{animalDescription}}. This information sheet states what the Family Code says about pet animal ownership and interim care in general terms. It does not determine, calculate, or assert that section 2605 applies to any particular animal connected with {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}'s case, whether an animal is community property, or how a court would weigh any party's care of the animal; those are matters for the court to decide based on the specific facts, or for {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} to resolve by their own written agreement. This document is distinct from this corpus's existing Pet Trust Information Sheet, which concerns a Probate Code mechanism for naming a caretaker and funding an animal's care after a settlor's death or incapacity, not a family court's division of property between spouses or domestic partners during a dissolution or legal separation.

clauses.title: Interim Order for Care of a Pet Animal During the Proceeding
clauses.body: Family Code section 2605(a) allows the court, at a party's request in a dissolution or legal separation proceeding, to enter an order requiring a party to care for a pet animal before the court makes its final determination of who owns the animal. The statute expressly states that the existence of such an interim care order does not affect the court's later, final ownership determination -- the two are treated as separate questions decided at different points in the case.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2605(a), fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. The statute's text does not itself specify what factors a court considers in deciding whether to grant an interim care order, what the order may or must contain beyond requiring a party to provide care, or how long such an order remains in effect; this document does not address those questions further because the statute's text does not resolve them. This session's CourtListener case-law search for judicial interpretation of section 2605 returned a 429 quota-exhausted error (125/day limit) before any result could be retrieved, so this clause relies on the statutory text alone and has not been checked against any case law.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2605(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the interim pet-animal care order and its non-effect on the final ownership determination
citations.quote: The court, at the request of a party to proceedings for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, may enter an order, prior to the final determination of ownership of a pet animal, to require a party to care for the pet animal. The existence of an order providing for the care of a pet animal during the course of proceedings for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties shall not have any impact on the court’s final determination of ownership of the pet animal.

clauses.title: Final Ownership Assignment: A Care-Based Standard, Not the Equal-Division Default
clauses.body: Family Code section 2605(b) states that, notwithstanding any other law -- including, but not limited to, Family Code section 2550 -- the court, at a party's request in a dissolution or legal separation proceeding, may assign sole or joint ownership of a pet animal by taking into consideration the care of the pet animal. Family Code section 2550 separately states the general rule that, apart from the parties' own written agreement or oral stipulation in open court, the court divides the community estate equally. Section 2605(b)'s own text singles out section 2550 by name as a rule that does not control a pet animal's ownership assignment -- the statute allows the court to award one party sole ownership of a community-property pet animal, considering that party's care of the animal, rather than applying the community estate's default of an equal division.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2605(b) and, for the general rule it displaces, section 2550, both fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) across two fetches of each section made with different User-Agent strings. Section 2605(b)'s text does not itself define "taking into consideration," state how much weight a court must give the care factor relative to other considerations, or resolve what happens if more than two parties assert care of the same animal; this document does not address those questions because the statute's text does not resolve them. This session's CourtListener case-law search returned a 429 quota-exhausted error (125/day limit) before any result could be retrieved, so this clause relies on the statutory text alone and has not been checked against any judicial gloss on how courts actually apply the care factor.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2605(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's authority to assign sole or joint pet-animal ownership considering care, notwithstanding other law including section 2550
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other law, including, but not limited to, Section 2550, the court, at the request of a party to proceedings for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, may assign sole or joint ownership of a pet animal taking into consideration the care of the pet animal.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2550 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the general rule requiring equal division of the community estate absent agreement or another provision of the division
citations.quote: the court shall, either in its judgment of dissolution of the marriage, in its judgment of legal separation of the parties, or at a later time if it expressly reserves jurisdiction to make such a property division, divide the community estate of the parties equally

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of "Care"
clauses.body: Family Code section 2605(c)(1) defines "care," as that term is used in section 2605, to include -- without being limited to -- the prevention of acts of harm or cruelty described in Penal Code section 597, and the provision of food, water, veterinary care, and safe and protected shelter. Because the statute's list is stated as nonexclusive ("includes, but is not limited to"), other conduct may also count as "care" for purposes of section 2605, even though the statute does not enumerate what that other conduct might be.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2605(c)(1), fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. This document has not independently fetched or verified the text of Penal Code section 597 referenced within this definition; it reports only that section 2605(c)(1) cross-references that section for the meaning of "harm or cruelty," without stating what Penal Code section 597 itself provides. This session's CourtListener case-law search returned a 429 quota-exhausted error (125/day limit) before any result could be retrieved, so this clause relies on the statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2605(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the nonexclusive statutory definition of "care" for purposes of section 2605
citations.quote: “Care” includes, but is not limited to, the prevention of acts of harm or cruelty, as described in Section 597 of the Penal Code, and the provision of food, water, veterinary care, and safe and protected shelter.

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of "Pet Animal" -- Community Property Only
clauses.body: Family Code section 2605(c)(2) defines "pet animal," as that term is used in section 2605, to mean any animal that is community property and is kept as a household pet. Both parts of this definition are conditions on the statute's reach: an animal that is not community property (for example, an animal one party owned before the marriage or received as a separate-property gift or inheritance and did not transmute) is not a "pet animal" within section 2605's own definition, and section 2605 does not by its terms apply to it. Likewise, an animal that is community property but is not kept as a household pet -- the statute does not define that phrase further -- falls outside this definition as well.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2605(c)(2), fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. The statute's text does not define "kept as a household pet," does not state how a court determines whether a given animal is community or separate property in a contested case, and does not address an animal that is only partly community property (for example, purchased partly with separate-property funds); this document does not resolve those questions because the statute's text does not resolve them. This session's CourtListener case-law search returned a 429 quota-exhausted error (125/day limit) before any result could be retrieved, so this clause relies on the statutory text alone.

citations.cite: the statutory definition of "pet animal" as community property kept as a household pet
citations.quote: “Pet animal” means any animal that is community property and kept as a household pet.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California statutory law on the coastal development permit requirement created by the California Coastal Act of 1976, Public Resources Code section 30000 et seq., as it may relate to real property at {{propertyAddress}}, {{county}} County, California (Assessor's Parcel Number {{parcelNumber}}), owned by {{ownerName}}, in connection with the following proposed activity: {{developmentDescription}}. It states what California law provides about which activities count as "development" under the Coastal Act, the geographic "coastal zone" the Act applies within, which agency (the California Coastal Commission or a local government implementing a certified Local Coastal Program) has permitting authority over a given development at a given time, the statute's own listed exemptions from the permit requirement, and the civil penalties the statute states for a violation. It is separate from, and does not substitute for, the California Environmental Quality Act review, any Subdivision Map Act approval (final map, parcel map, or lot line adjustment), any local zoning or building permit, or any other state, regional, or local permit that may separately apply to the same activity. This information sheet is not itself a coastal development permit application, and it does not tell {{ownerName}}, {{applicantName}}, or any other person whether the described activity requires a coastal development permit, which agency currently holds permitting jurisdiction over {{propertyAddress}}, or whether any statutory exemption applies to it.

clauses.title: The Statutory "Coastal Zone"
clauses.body: The Coastal Act's permit requirement applies only within a defined geographic area the statute calls the "coastal zone." Public Resources Code section 30103(a) defines that zone as the land and water area of California from the Oregon border to the Mexican border, extending seaward to the state's outer limit of jurisdiction and including all offshore islands, and states a general inland extent of 1,000 yards from the mean high tide line of the sea. The same subdivision states that in significant coastal estuarine, habitat, and recreational areas the zone extends inland further — to the first major ridgeline paralleling the sea or five miles from the mean high tide line, whichever is less — while in developed urban areas the zone generally extends inland less than 1,000 yards. Section 30103(b) separately gives the Coastal Commission authority to prepare a detailed map of the zone and to adjust its inland or seaward boundary within stated limits to avoid bisecting a single lot or parcel.
clauses.gap: Section 30103(a)'s own text states that the coastal zone's precise boundary is fixed by maps — those identified in Section 17 of Chapter 1330 of the Statutes of 1976, and the more detailed map the Commission adopts under subdivision (b) — not solely by the general distance figures quoted above; this clause quotes those general distance rules and does not itself examine any map to determine whether a particular parcel lies within the coastal zone. The statute also excludes the separate area of jurisdiction of the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission from the coastal zone, a carve-out this clause states exists but does not independently evaluate for this property. The two quotations below are both drawn from subdivision (a) of the same section and are not independent of each other. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of how California defines its coastal zone — not a claim about which jurisdiction's coastal management law applies to a particular property.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30103(a)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, definition of "coastal zone" — general extent
citations.quote: “Coastal zone” means that land and water area of the State of California from the Oregon border to the border of the Republic of Mexico, specified on the maps identified and set forth in Section 17 of Chapter 1330 of the Statutes of 1976, extending seaward to the state’s outer limit of jurisdiction, including all offshore islands, and extending inland generally 1,000 yards from the mean high tide line of the sea.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30103(a)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, definition of "coastal zone" — extended and urban-area boundaries
citations.quote: In significant coastal estuarine, habitat, and recreational areas it extends inland to the first major ridgeline paralleling the sea or five miles from the mean high tide line of the sea, whichever is less, and in developed urban areas the zone generally extends inland less than 1,000 yards.

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of "Development"
clauses.body: The coastal development permit requirement applies to activity that falls within the Coastal Act's own, broader-than-colloquial definition of "development." Public Resources Code section 30106 defines "development" to include placing or erecting solid material or structures; discharging or disposing of dredged material or waste; grading, removing, dredging, mining, or extracting materials; a change in the density or intensity of use of land — expressly including subdivision under the Subdivision Map Act and any other division of land, including lot splits (subject to a stated exception for a land division brought about by a public agency's purchase for public recreational use); a change in the intensity of use of water or access to it; and construction, reconstruction, demolition, or alteration of the size of any structure, including a utility facility. The statute separately includes the removal or harvesting of major vegetation, subject to stated exceptions for agricultural purposes, kelp harvesting, and timber operations conducted under a Z'berg-Nejedly Forest Practice Act timber harvesting plan. Section 30106 also states that "structure" includes, without limitation, a building, road, pipe, flume, conduit, siphon, aqueduct, telephone line, and electrical power transmission and distribution line.
clauses.gap: The quotation below reproduces section 30106's definition through its structure-alteration clause; it omits the statute's separate vegetation-removal clause and the immediately following sentence defining "structure," both of which this body text paraphrases rather than quotes. This clause does not determine whether any specific described activity falls within this definition, and it does not address the Subdivision Map Act's own separate approval procedure (Government Code section 66410 et seq.) that section 30106 cross-references only to establish that a Map Act subdivision counts as Coastal Act "development." This is one state's statute, used as evidence of how California defines "development" for coastal permitting purposes — not a claim about which jurisdiction's land-use law applies to a particular activity.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30106
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, definition of "development"
citations.quote: “Development” means, on land, in or under water, the placement or erection of any solid material or structure; discharge or disposal of any dredged material or of any gaseous, liquid, solid, or thermal waste; grading, removing, dredging, mining, or extraction of any materials; change in the density or intensity of use of land, including, but not limited to, subdivision pursuant to the Subdivision Map Act (commencing with Section 66410 of the Government Code), and any other division of land, including lot splits, except where the land division is brought about in connection with the purchase of such land by a public agency for public recreational use; change in the intensity of use of water, or of access thereto; construction, reconstruction, demolition, or alteration of the size of any structure, including any facility of any private, public, or municipal utility

clauses.title: General Permit Requirement
clauses.body: Public Resources Code section 30600(a) states that, except as provided in subdivision (e) and in addition to any other permit required by law from any local government or state, regional, or local agency, any person wishing to perform or undertake development in the coastal zone must obtain a coastal development permit. Section 30600(e) separately states that the section does not apply to certain emergency work and certain emergency highway repairs, subject to a 14-day post-commencement notification requirement to the Commission. Which agency issues the coastal development permit depends on the status of the local government's Local Coastal Program: section 30600(b) and (c) describe a local government's option, before its Local Coastal Program is certified, to establish its own permit procedures for development within its jurisdiction (subject to statutory limits), with the Commission or the local government issuing the permit depending on whether that option is exercised; and section 30600(d) states that, after certification of its Local Coastal Program, a coastal development permit is obtained from the local government as provided in section 30519.
clauses.gap: This clause states section 30600's own general structure; it does not determine, for any specific parcel, whether the local government in whose jurisdiction that parcel lies has a certified Local Coastal Program, has exercised the pre-certification permitting option under subdivision (b), or otherwise currently holds permitting authority under subdivision (d) — a fact-specific determination this clause does not make. The two quotations below are subsections (a) and (d) of the same statutory section; this clause does not separately quote subsections (b) and (c), which are described only in narrative form above. Section 30600(a)'s reference to "any person, as defined in Section 21066" incorporates a Public Resources Code definition (from a different division, the California Environmental Quality Act) that this clause does not itself reproduce or verify. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions interpreting the scope of this permit requirement returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (daily quota exhausted); no case law was reviewed for this clause, which rests on the statutory text of section 30600 alone. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own coastal permitting framework — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a particular property or activity.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30600(a)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, general coastal development permit requirement
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (e), and in addition to obtaining any other permit required by law from any local government or from any state, regional, or local agency, any person, as defined in Section 21066, wishing to perform or undertake any development in the coastal zone, other than a facility subject to Section 25500, shall obtain a coastal development permit.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30600(d)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, permit issuance after Local Coastal Program certification
citations.quote: After certification of its local coastal program or pursuant to the provisions of Section 30600.5, a coastal development permit shall be obtained from the local government as provided for in Section 30519 or Section 30600.5.

clauses.title: Additional Commission Permit Requirement in Sensitive Areas
clauses.body: Before a Local Coastal Program is certified, Public Resources Code section 30601 requires a coastal development permit from the Commission itself — in addition to, not instead of, any local government permit under section 30600(b) or (d) — for development in certain geographically sensitive locations. Those locations include development between the sea and the first public road paralleling the sea, or within 300 feet of the inland extent of any beach or of the mean high tide line where there is no beach, whichever distance is greater; development on tidelands, submerged lands, or public trust lands, or within 100 feet of a wetland, estuary, or stream, or within 300 feet of the top of the seaward face of a coastal bluff, if not already covered by the first category; and any development that constitutes a major public works project or a major energy facility.
clauses.gap: This clause states section 30601 as it stood after its 1981 amendment; it does not verify whether any later amendment has changed this text, and it does not determine, for any specific property, whether that property in fact lies within any of the described distance zones from the sea, a beach, a wetland, an estuary, a stream, or a coastal bluff — a factual, often survey-dependent determination this clause does not make. The two quotations below are paragraphs (1) and (2) of the same statutory sentence, not independent sources. This clause also does not address whether or how this additional Commission jurisdiction changes once a Local Coastal Program is certified for the area, a topic addressed in the following clause. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own coastal permitting framework — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a particular property.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30601(1)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, Commission permit jurisdiction — shoreline and beach areas
citations.quote: Prior to certification of the local coastal program and, where applicable, in addition to a permit from local government pursuant to subdivision (b) or (d) of Section 30600, a coastal development permit shall be obtained from the commission for any of the following: (1) Developments between the sea and the first public road paralleling the sea or within 300 feet of the inland extent of any beach or of the mean high tide line of the sea where there is no beach, whichever is the greater distance.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30601(2)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, Commission permit jurisdiction — tidelands, wetlands, and bluffs
citations.quote: (2) Developments not included within paragraph (1) located on tidelands, submerged lands, public trust lands, within 100 feet of any wetland, estuary, stream, or within 300 feet of the top of the seaward face of any coastal bluff.

clauses.title: Delegation to Local Government After Certification
clauses.body: Public Resources Code section 30519(a) states that once a Local Coastal Program, or a portion of one, has been certified and all implementing actions in the affected area have become effective, the development review authority described in Chapter 7 of the Coastal Act (the coastal development permit chapter) is no longer exercised by the Commission over new development in that area, and is instead delegated to the local government implementing the program — subject to a stated exception for appeals to the Commission under section 30603. Section 30519(b) states that this delegation does not apply to development on tidelands, submerged lands, or public trust lands, nor to development within ports covered by a separate statutory chapter or within a state university or college in the coastal zone, with a further exception restoring delegation for a port or harbor district's or authority's development on legislatively granted lands where the certified Local Coastal Program includes that district's or authority's specific development plans.
clauses.gap: This clause does not determine, for any specific property, whether the local government with jurisdiction over that property has in fact certified a Local Coastal Program covering it, or whether all implementing actions for that program have become effective — both preconditions to this delegation under the statute's own terms. It also does not evaluate whether a particular property falls within any of section 30519(b)'s stated exceptions (tidelands, submerged or public trust lands, ports, or a state university or college). This clause quotes only subdivision (a); subdivision (b)'s exceptions and subdivision (c)'s separate provision allowing the Commission to recommend program amendments for uses of greater-than-local importance are described above only in narrative form. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of how California allocates coastal permitting authority between a state commission and local government — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a particular property.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30519(a)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, delegation of coastal permit authority to local government
citations.quote: after a local coastal program, or any portion thereof, has been certified and all implementing actions within the area affected have become effective, the development review authority provided for in Chapter 7 (commencing with Section 30600) shall no longer be exercised by the commission over any new development proposed within the area to which the certified local coastal program, or any portion thereof, applies and shall at that time be delegated to the local government that is implementing the local coastal program or any portion thereof.

clauses.title: Statutory Exemptions from the Permit Requirement
clauses.body: The Coastal Act lists categories of activity for which no coastal development permit is required. Public Resources Code section 30600(e) exempts specified emergency work — immediate emergency work to protect life or property, and certain emergency highway repairs undertaken within one year of storm, fire, flood, earthquake, or similar damage — subject to a 14-day post-commencement notification to the Commission and excluding highway-widening or -expansion projects. Separately, section 30610 lists further exemptions, including improvements to an existing single-family residence, subject to the Commission's own regulatory authority to require a permit for classes of improvement that involve a risk of adverse environmental effect; repair or maintenance activity that does not add to, enlarge, or expand the object being repaired or maintained, subject to a similar Commission regulatory carve-out for extraordinary repair methods that risk substantial adverse environmental impact; certain improvements to non-single-family structures; maintenance dredging of existing navigation channels under an Army Corps of Engineers permit; installation of certain utility connections to already-approved development; replacement, within stated size and siting limits, of a structure destroyed by disaster; and other categories the statute itself lists.
clauses.gap: Section 30610 lists more exemption categories than this clause's two quoted subsections; subdivisions (b), (c), (e), (f), (g), (h), and (i) are described only in narrative summary above and are not independently quoted. Both quoted exemptions — subdivisions (a) and (d) — are themselves qualified by the Commission's own regulatory authority to pull a class of development back into the permit requirement; this clause does not check whether the Commission has adopted such a regulation for any specific class of improvement or repair, and it does not determine whether any particular described activity in fact falls within any exemption listed here. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own coastal-permit exemption structure — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a particular activity.

citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, exemption for improvements to an existing single-family residence
citations.quote: Improvements to existing single-family residences; provided, however, that the commission shall specify, by regulation, those classes of development which involve a risk of adverse environmental effect and shall require that a coastal development permit be obtained pursuant to this chapter.

citations.quote: Repair or maintenance activities that do not result in an addition to, or enlargement or expansion of, the object of those repair or maintenance activities; provided, however, that if the commission determines that certain extraordinary methods of repair and maintenance involve a risk of substantial adverse environmental impact, it shall, by regulation, require that a permit be obtained pursuant to this chapter.

clauses.title: Civil Penalties for Violation
clauses.body: Public Resources Code section 30820 states civil liability for a Coastal Act violation. Under subdivision (a)(1), a superior court may impose civil liability, in an amount not less than $500 and not more than $30,000, on a person who performs or undertakes development that violates the Coastal Act or is inconsistent with a previously issued coastal development permit. Under subdivision (a)(2), civil liability up to $30,000 may be imposed for any other Coastal Act violation. Subdivision (b) states a separate, higher-exposure liability for a person who intentionally and knowingly performs or undertakes development in violation of the Act or inconsistent with a previously issued permit: liability of not less than $1,000 nor more than $15,000 per day for each day the violation persists. Subdivision (c) lists factors a court considers in setting the amount of civil liability, including the nature and gravity of the violation, whether it can be remedied, the sensitivity of the affected resource, the state's cost of bringing the action, and, as to the violator, any voluntary remedial measures, prior violation history, culpability, and any resulting economic profit.
clauses.gap: This clause states the civil-liability structure of section 30820 alone; the Coastal Act contains separate provisions elsewhere in the same chapter for injunctive relief, cease-and-desist orders, restoration orders, and criminal penalties, none of which this clause quotes or describes. The dollar figures quoted are those stated in the current text of section 30820 as fetched; this clause does not track any subsequent legislative amendment to those figures. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific activity in fact violates the Coastal Act or is inconsistent with any permit. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions applying this penalty provision returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (daily quota exhausted) before any search could be completed; no case law was reviewed for this clause. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own Coastal Act enforcement framework — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs particular conduct.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30820(a)(1)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, civil liability for a Coastal Act violation
citations.quote: Civil liability may be imposed by the superior court in accordance with this article on any person who performs or undertakes development that is in violation of this division or that is inconsistent with any coastal development permit previously issued by the commission, a local government that is implementing a certified local coastal program, or a port governing body that is implementing a certified port master plan, in an amount that shall not exceed thirty thousand dollars ($30,000) and shall not be less than five hundred dollars ($500).

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 30820(b)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, enhanced civil liability for an intentional and knowing violation
citations.quote: when the person intentionally and knowingly performs or undertakes the development in violation of this division or inconsistent with any previously issued coastal development permit, may, in addition to any other penalties, be civilly liable in accordance with this subdivision. Civil liability may be imposed by the superior court in accordance with this article for a violation as specified in this subdivision in an amount which shall not be less than one thousand dollars ($1,000), nor more than fifteen thousand dollars ($15,000), per day for each day in which the violation persists.

clauses.title: Social Purpose Corporation — What This Information Sheet Covers
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's Social Purpose Corporations Act, Corporations Code Division 1.5 (§§ 2500-3503) — a distinct for-profit corporate form under California's General Corporation Law, separate from an ordinary for-profit corporation and separate from this corpus's existing Benefit Corporation information sheet, which covers a different statute (Corp. Code Part 13, §§ 14600-14631) with its own purpose language, its own annual-report content, and its own enforcement mechanism. A social purpose corporation is formed by filing articles of incorporation with the California Secretary of State that state both a general business purpose and one or more enumerated "special purposes," and it is subject to recurring reporting obligations tied to those special purposes that a regular corporation does not have. {{companyName}} is considering, or has adopted, this form for its California operations.

This sheet states facts about the statute: what the articles must and may contain, how a director's statutory duty of care is defined for this specific corporate form, what the statute says about who a social purpose corporation's assets and purposes actually run to, and what recurring shareholder reports the statute requires and when. It does NOT draft a full set of articles of incorporation, bylaws, or an annual report; it does not tell {{companyName}} whether the social purpose corporation form, the benefit corporation form, or an ordinary corporation is the right choice for its specific business or fundraising plans; it does not evaluate any specific special-purpose language for legal sufficiency; and it does not address the separate question of what happens to a pre-2015 "flexible purpose corporation" that has not amended its articles, beyond stating what the statute itself says about that scenario.

clauses.title: The Social Purpose Corporations Act and Its 2011 Predecessor
clauses.body: California's statute governing this entity form states its own name: "This division shall be known and may be cited as the Social Purpose Corporations Act." That name is not the one the Legislature originally used. The division was enacted in 2011 (Stats. 2011, Ch. 740) creating the "flexible purpose corporation," and the Legislature later renamed the form via SB 1301 (Stats. 2014, Ch. 694), effective January 1, 2015, substituting "social purpose corporation" throughout. The statute did not force existing entities to convert. A pre-2015 flexible purpose corporation may elect the new name by amending its articles — the statute states a corporation "may elect to change its status from a flexible purpose corporation to a social purpose corporation by amending its articles of incorporation to change its name to replace “flexible purpose corporation” with “social purpose corporation” and to replace the term “flexible purpose corporation” with “social purpose corporation” as applicable in any statements contained in the articles." — but a corporation that has not made that amendment keeps operating under the old name and the old statutory label: "For any flexible purpose corporation formed before January 1, 2015, that has not amended its articles of incorporation to change its status to a social purpose corporation, any reference in this division to social purpose corporation shall be deemed a reference to “flexible purpose corporation.”" The division's scope provision confirms the same continuity from the other direction, stating that the division applies to social purpose corporations "including all flexible purpose corporations formed under this division prior to January 1, 2015, and now existing"
clauses.gap: This is the current text of a division that has been amended repeatedly since 2011 (most recently by 2022 and 2023 chaptering shown in the fetched sections' own history notes); it does not track every intermediate version of the statute, only the version in force as of the checked date. It also does not identify whether any specific existing entity is, in fact, an unconverted flexible purpose corporation — that is a question about that entity's own articles of incorporation, not about the statute.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2500
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, statutory short title
citations.quote: This division shall be known and may be cited as the Social Purpose Corporations Act.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2601(b)(3)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, election to rename a flexible purpose corporation and the default rule for one that has not elected
citations.quote: may elect to change its status from a flexible purpose corporation to a social purpose corporation by amending its articles of incorporation to change its name to replace “flexible purpose corporation” with “social purpose corporation” and to replace the term “flexible purpose corporation” with “social purpose corporation” as applicable in any statements contained in the articles.

citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, deemed reference to "flexible purpose corporation" absent an amendment
citations.quote: For any flexible purpose corporation formed before January 1, 2015, that has not amended its articles of incorporation to change its status to a social purpose corporation, any reference in this division to social purpose corporation shall be deemed a reference to “flexible purpose corporation.”

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2502
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, scope provision covering pre-2015 flexible purpose corporations still existing under that name
citations.quote: including all flexible purpose corporations formed under this division prior to January 1, 2015, and now existing

clauses.title: The General Corporation Law Fills In Everything the Act Does Not Say
clauses.body: A social purpose corporation is not governed only by Division 1.5. The statute makes California's general, Division 1 corporate law the default backdrop: "Except as otherwise expressly stated, the provisions of Division 1 (commencing with Section 100) shall apply to corporations organized under this division" In practice this means that matters this division does not address for a social purpose corporation — such as most shareholder meeting, voting, and inspection mechanics — are governed by the same General Corporation Law provisions that apply to an ordinary for-profit corporation, unless Division 1.5 itself states a different rule for social purpose corporations specifically.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general incorporation-by-reference rule only; it does not catalog every Division 1 section that applies, and it does not resolve a conflict between a specific Division 1.5 provision and a specific Division 1 provision for facts not addressed here — that requires reading both provisions together for the particular question at hand.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2501
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, incorporation by reference of the General Corporation Law (Division 1)
citations.quote: Except as otherwise expressly stated, the provisions of Division 1 (commencing with Section 100) shall apply to corporations organized under this division

clauses.title: Formation by Filing Articles, and the Required Name Element
clauses.body: A social purpose corporation is formed the same basic way as any other California corporation — by filing articles with the Secretary of State. The statute states: "One or more natural persons, partnerships, associations, social purpose corporations, or corporations, domestic or foreign, may form a social purpose corporation under this division by executing and filing articles of incorporation." and that "The corporate existence begins upon the filing of the articles and continues perpetually, unless otherwise expressly provided by law or in the articles." The articles must also flag the entity's form in its own name: the statute requires "The name of the social purpose corporation that shall contain the words “social purpose corporation” or an abbreviation of those words."
clauses.gap: This clause covers only the act-of-filing and naming mechanics stated in this division; it does not restate the Secretary of State's separate name-distinguishability rules that apply to corporations generally under Division 1, and it does not address the filing fee, which the statute (Corp. Code § 2502.05) sets by cross-reference to the Government Code fee schedule for corporations generally rather than stating a dollar figure itself.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2600(a)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, formation by filing articles of incorporation
citations.quote: One or more natural persons, partnerships, associations, social purpose corporations, or corporations, domestic or foreign, may form a social purpose corporation under this division by executing and filing articles of incorporation.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2600(c)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, corporate existence begins on filing and continues perpetually absent a contrary provision
citations.quote: The corporate existence begins upon the filing of the articles and continues perpetually, unless otherwise expressly provided by law or in the articles.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2602(a)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, required name element
citations.quote: The name of the social purpose corporation that shall contain the words “social purpose corporation” or an abbreviation of those words.

clauses.title: The Articles Must State Both a General Purpose and an Enumerated Special Purpose
clauses.body: What sets this entity form apart from an ordinary corporation is not the filing mechanics — it is what the articles must say about purpose. The statute requires a general-purpose statement drawn from a prescribed form; a corporation not organized to practice a licensed profession must state that "The purpose of this social purpose corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a social purpose corporation may be organized under Division 1.5 of the California Corporations Code" (with the corporation's own enumerated purposes filled in). Beyond that general statement, the articles must separately include "A statement that a purpose of the social purpose corporation, in addition to the purpose stated pursuant to paragraph (1), is to engage in one or more of the following enumerated purposes" one of the following two statutory categories: first, "One or more charitable or public purpose activities that a nonprofit public benefit corporation is authorized to carry out." or second, "The purpose of promoting positive effects of, or minimizing adverse effects of, the social purpose corporation’s activities upon any of the following, provided that the corporation consider the purpose in addition to or together with the financial interests of the shareholders and compliance with legal obligations, and take action consistent with that purpose:" — followed by a list of specific beneficiaries the statute itself supplies: the corporation's employees, suppliers, customers, and creditors; the community and society; or the environment. "Special purpose," as a defined statutory term, means exactly this articles-stated purpose: "“Special purpose” means the special purpose set forth in a social purpose corporation’s articles pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 2602."
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the two statutory purpose categories and their required lead-in language; it does not draft the specific enumerated purpose to insert into either blank, does not address the separate prescribed purpose statement for a professional social purpose corporation (Corp. Code § 2602(b)(1)(B)) or for one subject to the Banking Law or Insurance Code (Corp. Code § 2602(b)(4)-(5)), and does not evaluate whether any specific proposed purpose text would satisfy the statute — that is a drafting judgment about the specific language chosen, not a fact this sheet can state in the abstract.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2602(b)(1)(A)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, required general purpose statement for a non-professional social purpose corporation
citations.quote: The purpose of this social purpose corporation is to engage in any lawful act or activity for which a social purpose corporation may be organized under Division 1.5 of the California Corporations Code

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2602(b)(2)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, required additional special-purpose statement and its lead-in language
citations.quote: A statement that a purpose of the social purpose corporation, in addition to the purpose stated pursuant to paragraph (1), is to engage in one or more of the following enumerated purposes

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2602(b)(2)(A)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, first enumerated special-purpose category (public-benefit-type activities)
citations.quote: One or more charitable or public purpose activities that a nonprofit public benefit corporation is authorized to carry out.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2602(b)(2)(B)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, second enumerated special-purpose category (stakeholder and environmental effects)
citations.quote: The purpose of promoting positive effects of, or minimizing adverse effects of, the social purpose corporation’s activities upon any of the following, provided that the corporation consider the purpose in addition to or together with the financial interests of the shareholders and compliance with legal obligations, and take action consistent with that purpose:

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2513
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, statutory definition of "special purpose"
citations.quote: “Special purpose” means the special purpose set forth in a social purpose corporation’s articles pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 2602.

clauses.title: General Business Powers, Bounded by the Corporation's Own Stated Special Purpose
clauses.body: Once formed, a social purpose corporation has broad business powers, but the statute makes those powers expressly conditional on the purpose the corporation put in its own articles: "Subject to any limitation contained in the articles, to compliance with any other applicable laws, and to consistency with the special purpose of the social purpose corporation, any social purpose corporation other than a social purpose corporation subject to the Banking Law or a professional social purpose corporation may engage in any business activity."
clauses.gap: This clause states the general powers rule and its express purpose-consistency condition; it does not identify what counts as an activity inconsistent with a specific corporation's stated special purpose, which depends on the actual purpose language that corporation adopted, nor does it address the separate,  narrower powers rules that apply to a social purpose corporation subject to the Banking Law or organized as a professional corporation, which the same section (Corp. Code § 2604) addresses in its second sentence.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2604
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, general business powers conditioned on consistency with the corporation's special purpose
citations.quote: Subject to any limitation contained in the articles, to compliance with any other applicable laws, and to consistency with the special purpose of the social purpose corporation, any social purpose corporation other than a social purpose corporation subject to the Banking Law or a professional social purpose corporation may engage in any business activity.

clauses.title: A Director's Statutory Duty of Care, Including the Corporation's Stated Purposes as a Factor
clauses.body: This division sets its own director standard-of-care statute for a social purpose corporation, separate from the general corporate business-judgment-rule statute (Corp. Code § 309) that governs an ordinary corporation's directors. The core standard is worded the same way: "A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the social purpose corporation and its shareholders, and with that care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances." But the factors a director is told to weigh are not the same. The statute states that "In discharging his or her duties, a director shall consider those factors, and give weight to those factors, as the director deems relevant, including the overall prospects of the social purpose corporation, the best interests of the social purpose corporation and its shareholders, and the purposes of the social purpose corporation as set forth in its articles." — expressly listing the articles-stated purposes of the social purpose corporation as one of the factors a director may consider and weigh, alongside the corporation's prospects and the shareholders' best interests, in a way the general corporate business-judgment-rule statute for an ordinary corporation does not.
clauses.gap: This clause states the statutory factors a director is permitted to consider; it does not state that a director is required to act on the special purpose in any particular instance — the statute's own wording gives the director discretion to decide how much weight each factor gets — and it does not address how a court would apply this standard to any specific board decision, since no California appellate authority construing this specific director-duty section was located in this research pass (see the CourtListener search note in this document's supporting research).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2700(a)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, director's core statutory duty of care
citations.quote: A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the social purpose corporation and its shareholders, and with that care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2700(c)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, statutory factors a director may weigh, including the corporation's articles-stated purposes
citations.quote: In discharging his or her duties, a director shall consider those factors, and give weight to those factors, as the director deems relevant, including the overall prospects of the social purpose corporation, the best interests of the social purpose corporation and its shareholders, and the purposes of the social purpose corporation as set forth in its articles.

clauses.title: The Special Purpose Does Not Make the Corporation Hold Assets for, or Owe Duties to, Outsiders
clauses.body: Naming a stakeholder group or the environment in the articles' special-purpose statement does not give that group or the environment an enforceable stake in the corporation. The statute is direct about this: "Notwithstanding any of the purposes set forth in its articles, a social purpose corporation shall not be deemed to hold any of its assets for the benefit of any party other than its shareholders." — though the same subdivision preserves separately existing law by adding that "nothing in this division shall be construed as negating existing charitable trust principles or the Attorney General’s authority to enforce any charitable trust created." The following subdivision closes the loop for directors specifically: "Nothing in this section, express or implied, is intended to create or grant or shall create or grant any right in or for any person or any cause of action by or for any person, and a director shall not be responsible to any party other than the social purpose corporation and its shareholders."
clauses.gap: This clause states what the statute itself says about who may enforce a social purpose corporation's special purpose and who its assets are held for; it does not address whether a different body of law outside this division — such as a specific charitable trust already in existence, or a separate contractual promise the corporation made to a named stakeholder — could independently create an enforceable right, since the statute expressly carves out that possibility without itself resolving whether one exists in any given case.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2700(e)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, statement that the corporation does not hold assets for the benefit of any party other than its shareholders
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any of the purposes set forth in its articles, a social purpose corporation shall not be deemed to hold any of its assets for the benefit of any party other than its shareholders.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2700(e)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, preservation of existing charitable trust law and Attorney General enforcement authority
citations.quote: nothing in this division shall be construed as negating existing charitable trust principles or the Attorney General’s authority to enforce any charitable trust created.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2700(f)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, no third-party right or cause of action created; director responsible only to the corporation and its shareholders
citations.quote: Nothing in this section, express or implied, is intended to create or grant or shall create or grant any right in or for any person or any cause of action by or for any person, and a director shall not be responsible to any party other than the social purpose corporation and its shareholders.

clauses.title: The Annual Report: Financial Statements Plus a Special Purpose Management Discussion and Analysis
clauses.body: A social purpose corporation's board has a recurring, statute-driven reporting duty to its own shareholders. The statute states a deadline: "The board of a social purpose corporation shall cause an annual report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 120 days after the close of the fiscal year." Beyond ordinary financial statements, the same section requires a distinct narrative document: "The board shall cause to be provided with the annual report, a management discussion and analysis (special purpose MD&A) concerning the social purpose corporation’s stated purpose or purposes as set forth in its articles pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 2602, and, to the extent consistent with reasonable confidentiality requirements, shall cause the special purpose MD&A to be made publicly available by posting it on the social purpose corporation’s Internet Web site or providing it through similar electronic means."
clauses.gap: This clause covers the annual report and special purpose MD&A requirement running to shareholders under this division; it does not address the separate, narrower exception for a corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record (covered in this document's small-corporation clause) or the separate compliance path available to a corporation already reporting under the federal Securities Exchange Act (Corp. Code § 3502(h)), and it is not a claim that this reporting duty is the same as, or satisfies, the different annual benefit report this corpus's Benefit Corporation document describes for the separate benefit-corporation statute.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 3500(a)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, 120-day deadline for the annual report to shareholders
citations.quote: The board of a social purpose corporation shall cause an annual report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 120 days after the close of the fiscal year.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 3500(b)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, required special purpose management discussion and analysis (special purpose MD&A)
citations.quote: The board shall cause to be provided with the annual report, a management discussion and analysis (special purpose MD&A) concerning the social purpose corporation’s stated purpose or purposes as set forth in its articles pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 2602, and, to the extent consistent with reasonable confidentiality requirements, shall cause the special purpose MD&A to be made publicly available by posting it on the social purpose corporation’s Internet Web site or providing it through similar electronic means.

clauses.title: A Separate, Event-Triggered "Special Purpose Current Report" Between Annual Reports
clauses.body: Beyond the annual report, this division imposes an interim reporting duty that does not have a counterpart in this corpus's existing Benefit Corporation document. The statute requires: "The board shall cause a special purpose current report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 45 days following the occurrence of any one or more of the events specified in subdivision (b) or (c)" Among the triggering events the same section lists is a board or management decision to "Determine that the special purpose has been satisfied or should no longer be pursued, whether temporarily or permanently."
clauses.gap: This clause states only the reporting deadline and one of several statutory triggering events; it does not list every triggering event the same section defines (material expenditures and withheld planned expenditures are also covered, in Corp. Code § 3501(b) and (c)(1), and are not quoted here), and it does not address the good-faith forward-looking-statement liability exclusion the statute separately provides for these reports (Corp. Code § 3502(d)).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 3501(a)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, 45-day deadline for a special purpose current report following a triggering event
citations.quote: The board shall cause a special purpose current report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 45 days following the occurrence of any one or more of the events specified in subdivision (b) or (c)

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 3501(c)(2)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, one statutory triggering event for a special purpose current report
citations.quote: Determine that the special purpose has been satisfied or should no longer be pursued, whether temporarily or permanently.

clauses.title: A Narrower Financial-Statement Standard for a Social Purpose Corporation With Few Shareholders
clauses.body: The statute relaxes the accounting standard for the financial statements required in the annual and current reports for a small social purpose corporation: "The financial statements of any social purpose corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record of its shares, determined as provided in Section 605, required to be furnished by Sections 3500 and 3501 are not required to be prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles if they reasonably set forth the assets and liabilities and the income and expense of the social purpose corporation and disclose the accounting basis used in their preparation."
clauses.gap: This clause states the numeric shareholder-count threshold and the alternative disclosure standard the statute substitutes for GAAP; it does not address how "holders of record," cross-referenced to Corp. Code § 605, is counted in any specific ownership structure (for example, shares held in street name or through a nominee), which depends on the facts of that structure.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 3502(g)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, relaxed financial-statement standard for a corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record
citations.quote: The financial statements of any social purpose corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record of its shares, determined as provided in Section 605, required to be furnished by Sections 3500 and 3501 are not required to be prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles if they reasonably set forth the assets and liabilities and the income and expense of the social purpose corporation and disclose the accounting basis used in their preparation.

clauses.title: Personal Liability for a False Annual or Current Report
clauses.body: The statute attaches personal liability to a false statutory report. It states that "Any officers, directors, employees, or agents of a social purpose corporation who do any of the following shall be liable jointly and severally for all the damages resulting therefrom to the social purpose corporation or any person injured by those actions who relied on those actions or to both:" — and one of the listed acts triggering that liability is to "Make, issue, deliver, or publish any prospectus, report, including the reports required pursuant to Sections 3500 and 3501, circular, certificate, financial statement, balance sheet, public notice, or document respecting the social purpose corporation or its shares, assets, liabilities, capital, dividends, business, earnings, or accounts which is false in any material respect, knowing it to be false, or participate in the making, issuance, delivery, or publication thereof with knowledge that the same is false in a material respect."
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the introductory liability standard and one of the four listed acts that trigger it (Corp. Code § 3503(a)); the other three listed acts — false book or record entries, altering records with intent to deceive, and a knowing material omission from a required report — are not separately quoted here. This clause does not address how a court would apply the knowledge and materiality requirements to any specific report's contents.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 3503
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, introductory joint-and-several liability standard for a false statutory report
citations.quote: Any officers, directors, employees, or agents of a social purpose corporation who do any of the following shall be liable jointly and severally for all the damages resulting therefrom to the social purpose corporation or any person injured by those actions who relied on those actions or to both:

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 3503(a)
citations.cite: Social Purpose Corporations Act, liability for knowingly publishing a false report respecting the corporation
citations.quote: Make, issue, deliver, or publish any prospectus, report, including the reports required pursuant to Sections 3500 and 3501, circular, certificate, financial statement, balance sheet, public notice, or document respecting the social purpose corporation or its shares, assets, liabilities, capital, dividends, business, earnings, or accounts which is false in any material respect, knowing it to be false, or participate in the making, issuance, delivery, or publication thereof with knowledge that the same is false in a material respect.

clauses.title: About This Powers of Appointment Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}}, describes the general body of California law governing powers of appointment — Probate Code Division 2, Part 14 (§§ 600–695) — as that law may bear on {{appointmentInstrumentDescription}}, under which {{appointmentDonorName}} is identified as donor and {{appointmentPowerholderName}} is identified as powerholder. A power of appointment is a mechanism, most often created inside a will or trust, by which one person (the donor) authorizes another (the powerholder) to designate later who receives specified property, without the powerholder owning that property outright. This sheet covers, on a general informational basis only: the statutory definitions of donor, powerholder, appointee, and appointive property; the distinction between a general and a special (nongeneral) power; the distinction between an imperative and a discretionary power; the formal requirements for exercising a power, including the specific-reference requirement and the separate rule that an ordinary residuary clause does not exercise a power; the rules governing contracts to appoint and releases of a power; what happens when an exercise is defective, overbroad, or never made; and how the creditors of a powerholder are, and are not, exposed to appointive property. It is distinct from this project's Rule Against Perpetuities information sheet, which addresses how long a power of appointment may remain unexercised before it becomes invalid under Probate Code §§ 21200–21231 (a timing limit) rather than how a power is defined, created, exercised, or released (the subject of this sheet); from the Certification of Trust and California Uniform Directed Trust Act information sheets, which address a trustee's or trust director's fiduciary authority rather than a nonfiduciary power held by an individual powerholder; and from the Disclaimer information sheet, which addresses declining an interest or power outright rather than exercising, contracting to exercise, or releasing one. This sheet does not identify, draft, or evaluate the validity of any specific exercise, release, or contract to appoint involving {{appointmentInstrumentDescription}}; whether a particular attempted exercise satisfies the creating instrument's requirements and this statutory scheme depends on the instrument's precise terms and is a legal determination this sheet does not make.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: Donor, Powerholder, Appointee, and Appointive Property
clauses.body: Probate Code § 610 defines the vocabulary used throughout Part 14. A power of appointment is a power, held by a powerholder acting in a nonfiduciary capacity, to designate who receives an ownership interest in the appointive property or a further power over it — a category of authority the statute expressly distinguishes from a power of attorney. The person who creates or reserves the power is the donor; the writing that does so — a deed, will, trust, or other instrument — is the creating instrument; and a person in whose favor the power can be exercised is a permissible appointee, while a person in whose favor it actually is exercised is the appointee. Here, {{appointmentInstrumentDescription}} is the creating instrument, {{appointmentDonorName}} is the donor, and {{appointmentPowerholderName}} is the powerholder.

citations.quote: “Power of appointment” means a power that enables a powerholder acting in a nonfiduciary capacity to designate a recipient of an ownership interest in or another power of appointment over the appointive property. The term does not include a power of attorney.

clauses.title: General Powers Versus Special (Nongeneral) Powers
clauses.body: Probate Code § 611 classifies every power of appointment as either general or special. A power is general only to the extent it can be exercised in favor of the powerholder, the powerholder's estate, the powerholder's creditors, or the creditors of the powerholder's estate; any power that is not general is, by the statute's own terms, special. The statute carves out two situations that would otherwise look like general powers: a support-limited power to consume or invade property for someone's health, education, support, or maintenance under an ascertainable standard is not a general power, and neither is a power the powerholder can exercise only jointly with someone whose interest in the property is adverse to an exercise in the powerholder's own favor. A single power can also be general as to some appointive property and special as to the rest. This general/special classification then determines, among other things, how far a powerholder's creditors can reach the appointive property, addressed elsewhere in this sheet.

citations.quote: A power of appointment is “general” only to the extent that it is exercisable in favor of the powerholder, the powerholder’s estate, the powerholder’s creditors, or creditors of the powerholder’s estate, whether or not it is exercisable in favor of others.

clauses.title: Imperative Powers Versus Discretionary Powers
clauses.body: Separately from the general/special classification, Probate Code § 613 classifies a power of appointment as either imperative or discretionary based on the donor's intent as shown in the creating instrument. A power is imperative when the creating instrument shows the donor intended the permissible appointees to be benefited even if the powerholder never exercises the power — and a power can still be imperative even though the powerholder is free to select some permissible appointees and exclude others. Every other power is discretionary, meaning the powerholder is free to exercise it, or not, as the powerholder chooses. This classification affects what happens if {{appointmentPowerholderName}} never exercises the power created by {{appointmentInstrumentDescription}}, addressed elsewhere in this sheet.

Section 613 states the definition itself but does not, by its own terms, resolve whether any particular creating instrument's language manifests the donor's intent to make a given power imperative rather than discretionary; that is a matter of interpreting the specific instrument, which this clause does not do.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 613 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, definition of “imperative” and “discretionary” powers
citations.quote: A power of appointment is “imperative” where the creating instrument manifests an intent that the permissible appointees be benefited even if the powerholder fails to exercise the power. An imperative power can exist even though the powerholder has the privilege of selecting some and excluding others of the designated permissible appointees. All other powers of appointment are “discretionary.” The powerholder of a discretionary power is privileged to exercise, or not to exercise, the power as the powerholder chooses.

clauses.title: Complying With the Creating Instrument's Formal Requirements
clauses.body: Probate Code § 630 states the baseline rule for how a power of appointment must be exercised: if the creating instrument specifies requirements for the manner, time, or conditions of exercise, the power can be exercised only by complying with those requirements, subject to other provisions of Part 14 (such as the substantial-compliance rule of § 631, not addressed in this sheet). The statute also supplies a default rule for a gap the creating instrument often does not address: unless the creating instrument expressly prohibits it, a power stated to be exercisable by an inter vivos (lifetime) instrument can also be exercised by a written will.

This clause does not address § 631's separate substantial-compliance doctrine, under which a court may excuse a defective attempt to comply with the creating instrument's formal requirements in certain circumstances; whether that doctrine applies to any specific attempted exercise under a given creating instrument is not addressed here.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, compliance with the creating instrument's formal requirements
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this part, if the creating instrument specifies requirements as to the manner, time, and conditions of the exercise of a power of appointment, the power can be exercised only by complying with those requirements. (b) Unless expressly prohibited by the creating instrument, a power stated to be exercisable by an inter vivos instrument is also exercisable by a written will.

clauses.title: The Specific-Reference Requirement
clauses.body: Probate Code § 632 addresses a creating instrument that goes further than § 630's general manner-of-exercise rule by expressly requiring that any exercise refer specifically to the power itself or to the instrument that created it. Where the creating instrument imposes that requirement, the power can be exercised only by an instrument that actually contains the required specific reference; an instrument attempting to exercise the power without that reference does not satisfy this section.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, specific-reference requirement
citations.quote: If the creating instrument expressly directs that a power of appointment be exercised by an instrument that makes a specific reference to the power or to the instrument that created the power, the power can be exercised only by an instrument containing the required reference.

clauses.title: An Ordinary Residuary Clause Does Not Exercise a Power of Appointment
clauses.body: Probate Code § 641 states a rule distinct from — and easy to overlook alongside — the specific-reference rule of § 632: even where the creating instrument imposes no specific-reference requirement at all, a general residuary clause in a will, or a will that makes a general disposition of all the testator's property, does not by itself exercise a power of appointment the testator holds. Exercise occurs only if the will specifically references the power or otherwise shows an indication of intent to exercise it. The statute states that this rule applies where the powerholder dies on or after July 1, 1982.

clauses.title: Contracting to Appoint, and Releasing, a Power of Appointment
clauses.body: Probate Code § 660 ties a powerholder's ability to contract to make an appointment to whether the power is currently exercisable: the powerholder of a power that is presently exercisable — general or special — can contract to appoint to the same extent an actual appointment could be made, but the powerholder of a power that is not yet presently exercisable cannot contract to appoint at all (with a separate rule the statute states for the case where the donor and powerholder are the same person). Probate Code § 661 addresses the separate act of releasing a power altogether: unless the creating instrument provides otherwise, a general or special power that is discretionary may be released, with or without consideration, by a written instrument signed by the powerholder and delivered as the statute specifies — including, where the appointive property is held by a trustee, delivery to that trustee.

clauses.title: An Exercise That Goes Too Far Is Saved to the Extent Permissible
clauses.body: Probate Code § 670 addresses an exercise of a power of appointment that attempts to do more than the power actually authorizes — for example, appointing to someone who is not a permissible appointee, or attaching a restriction the power does not allow. Rather than voiding the entire attempted exercise, the statute makes it valid to the extent the exercise was within what the power actually permitted, treating only the excess as ineffective.

clauses.title: Default Rules When the Power Is Never Exercised
clauses.body: Probate Code §§ 671 and 672 supply different default outcomes depending on whether an unexercised power was imperative or discretionary, as classified under § 613. For an imperative power, § 671 provides that, unless the creating instrument or the powerholder in writing manifests a contrary intent, if the powerholder dies without exercising the power in whole or in part, the permissible appointees take the unappointed property equally among themselves. For a discretionary power, § 672 provides a different default: if the powerholder fails to appoint the property, releases the entire power, or makes an ineffective appointment, the unappointed property passes instead to whomever the donor named as taker in default, or, if the donor named no one, the property reverts to the donor.

clauses.title: Creditor Exposure Differs for General and Special Powers
clauses.body: Probate Code §§ 680–682 tie a powerholder's creditors' access to appointive property to the general/special classification under § 611, and § 680 states that a donor cannot override this creditor-rights scheme by contrary language in the creating instrument. Under § 681, property subject to a special power is, with limited statutory exceptions, not reachable by the powerholder's creditors or by the expenses of administering the powerholder's estate. Under § 682, the opposite is true for a general power that is presently exercisable during the powerholder's lifetime: to the extent the powerholder's own property is inadequate to satisfy the powerholder's creditors, the appointive property is reachable to the same extent it would be if the powerholder owned it outright, and a parallel rule reaches a general testamentary power (or a general power presently exercisable at death) after the powerholder dies, to the extent the powerholder's estate is inadequate for the estate's creditors and administration expenses.
