clauses.title: How This Part Connects to the Statutory Rule Against Perpetuities
clauses.body: Probate Code § 690 is the provision within Part 14 that connects the powers-of-appointment rules described in this sheet to the separate statutory Rule Against Perpetuities: it states that the perpetuities rule set out in Division 11, Part 2 (§§ 21200 et seq.) applies to powers of appointment governed by this Part 14. This sheet's own definitions, exercise, release, and default rules govern whether and how a power of appointment is created, exercised, or released; the separate perpetuities rule those provisions cross-reference governs, instead, how long a power may remain unexercised before it becomes invalid on timing grounds alone — the subject of this project's separate Rule Against Perpetuities information sheet.

clauses.title: What This Information Sheet Covers
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes the federal false marking statute, 35 U.S.C. § 292. That statute addresses false or deceptive statements about patent status: marking or advertising an article as patented when it is not, imitating another person's patent marking, or stating that a patent application is pending when none has been filed or none remains pending. It covers the categories of conduct the statute addresses, the criminal penalty for that conduct and who may sue to collect it, the separate private civil action available to a competitor who has suffered a competitive injury, and the statutory exception for continuing to reference a patent that covered a product but has since expired.

This document is distinct from this corpus's existing Patent Infringement Information Sheet, which separately addresses 35 U.S.C. § 287(a) — a different marking-related statute that limits how far back in time a patentee can recover infringement damages if the patentee's own product went unmarked. Section 287(a) protects an accused infringer's exposure to damages; the statute described in this document instead addresses false statements about patent status on their own terms, independent of any infringement claim, and is enforced differently — by the United States as a criminal penalty, or by an injured competitor in a private civil action, rather than by an accused infringer. This document is also distinct from this corpus's Patent Assignment Agreement, Patent License Agreement, and Provisional Patent Application Information Sheet documents, which address ownership, licensing, and the filing of a patent application rather than marking practices.

Regarding {{markingDescription}} attributed to {{adversePartyName}}, and any competitive injury {{companyName}} associates with that marking, this sheet sets out the statutory framework the law provides. It does not determine whether that marking violates the statute, whether a civil action under it would succeed, or what {{companyName}} should do in response.

clauses.title: Three Categories of Prohibited False Marking
clauses.body: The false marking statute describes three separate categories of prohibited conduct, each carrying its own required mental state. The first covers marking, affixing, or advertising something with the name (or an imitation of the name) of an actual patentee, the patent number, or words like "patent" or "patentee," done without the patentee's consent and with the intent of counterfeiting or imitating the patentee's mark, or of deceiving the public into believing the item came from or was authorized by the patentee. The second covers marking, affixing, or advertising an unpatented article with the word "patent" or any word or number suggesting it is patented, done for the purpose of deceiving the public. The third covers marking, affixing, or advertising any article with words like "patent applied for" or "patent pending," or any word suggesting a patent application has been made, when no application has actually been made — or, if one was made, when it is no longer pending, done for the purpose of deceiving the public. All three categories require a purpose or intent to deceive or to counterfeit; the statute does not, by its terms, reach an innocent or merely careless mismarking made without that purpose.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the categories of conduct the statute addresses in subsection (a); it does not resolve whether any specific marking, advertisement, or statement about a patent's status meets the statute's intent-or-purpose-to-deceive requirement, which courts have described as a factual question turning on the circumstances of the particular marking. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions construing this intent element was attempted but returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (125/day quota exhausted) before any results could be retrieved, so this clause relies on the statutory text alone and does not reflect how courts have actually applied the intent requirement in practice.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 292 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: 35 U.S.C. § 292(a) (three categories of prohibited conduct)
citations.quote: Whoever, without the consent of the patentee, marks upon, or affixes to, or uses in advertising in connection with anything made, used, offered for sale, or sold by such person within the United States, or imported by the person into the United States, the name or any imitation of the name of the patentee, the patent number, or the words “patent,” “patentee,” or the like, with the intent of counterfeiting or imitating the mark of the patentee, or of deceiving the public and inducing them to believe that the thing was made, offered for sale, sold, or imported into the United States by or with the consent of the patentee; or Whoever marks upon, or affixes to, or uses in advertising in connection with any unpatented article, the word “patent” or any word or number importing that the same is patented, for the purpose of deceiving the public; or Whoever marks upon, or affixes to, or uses in advertising in connection with any article, the words “patent applied for,” “patent pending,” or any word importing that an application for patent has been made, when no application for patent has been made, or if made, is not pending, for the purpose of deceiving the public—

clauses.title: The Fine Is Capped Per Offense, and Only the United States May Collect It
clauses.body: A violation of the false marking statute is punishable by a fine of not more than $500 for every such offense. The statute expressly reserves the right to sue for that penalty to the United States: no private person — including a competitor, a consumer, or anyone else — may bring an action to collect this particular fine. This is a change from how the statute once read; the current single-government-plaintiff rule for this penalty was added to the statute in 2011.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the current text of subsection (a) as amended in 2011; it does not address how the Department of Justice or another United States authority decides, as a matter of enforcement discretion, whether to bring an action for this penalty in any given case, nor how frequently such actions are actually filed. That is an enforcement-practice question the statutory text alone does not answer.

citations.cite: 35 U.S.C. § 292(a) (penalty and exclusive government standing)
citations.quote: Shall be fined not more than $500 for every such offense. Only the United States may sue for the penalty authorized by this subsection.

clauses.title: Before 2011, Any Person Could Sue for This Penalty
clauses.body: Before a 2011 amendment, the false marking statute worked differently: it allowed any person — not just the United States — to sue for the $500-per-offense penalty, with the recovery split so that half went to the person who sued and half went to the United States. That prior version of subsection (b) is no longer in effect. The 2011 amendment eliminated this private-suit mechanism for the government's penalty and replaced it with the competitive-injury civil action described elsewhere in this statute. The amendment applies to all cases, without exception, that were pending on or commenced on or after September 16, 2011.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the historical and current statutory text as reported in Cornell LII's editorial notes and amendment history for this section; it does not independently verify the text of the pre-2011 version of the U.S. Code against a contemporaneous 2010 or earlier source, only against the current section's own notes describing that prior text. It also does not address litigation that was already filed under the old qui tam version before September 16, 2011, and how the 2011 amendment's retroactive application to then-pending cases was resolved in specific disputes.

citations.cite: 35 U.S.C. § 292, Editorial Notes (quoting the pre-2011 text of subsection (b))
citations.quote: Any person may sue for the penalty, in which event one-half shall go to the person suing and the other to the use of the United States.

clauses.title: A Competitor's Own Civil Action Requires a Competitive Injury
clauses.body: Separate from the government-only criminal penalty, the statute gives a private civil remedy to a narrower category of plaintiff: a person who has suffered a competitive injury as a result of a violation of the statute. That person may file a civil action in a United States district court, and the recovery available is damages adequate to compensate for the injury — not the flat $500-per-offense penalty available only to the United States, and not a fixed statutory amount. This civil action is the only private remedy the statute itself provides for a false marking violation.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the text of subsection (b); it does not define what showing establishes a "competitive injury" in a particular factual scenario, nor how a district court calculates "damages adequate to compensate" for one. Those are questions the statutory text leaves to case-by-case adjudication. A CourtListener search for decisions applying this standard was attempted but returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (125/day daily quota already exhausted), so no case law interpreting the competitive-injury or damages standards was reviewed for this clause.

citations.quote: A person who has suffered a competitive injury as a result of a violation of this section may file a civil action in a district court of the United States for recovery of damages adequate to compensate for the injury.

clauses.title: Marking With an Expired Patent Is Not a Violation
clauses.body: The statute contains an express exception: marking a product, in the manner otherwise described in subsection (a), with matter relating to a patent that covered that product but has since expired is not a violation of this section. In other words, the statute's false marking prohibitions are directed at markings that were never accurate or that misrepresent whether a patent exists or is pending — not at markings that were accurate when the patent was in force and have simply not been updated after the patent's term ended.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the text of subsection (c) only. It does not address how this exception interacts with the separate intent-to-deceive requirements in subsection (a), whether continuing to use an expired-patent marking could still support liability under some other legal theory outside this statute (such as a false-advertising claim under a different law), or how a person would go about verifying whether a specific patent number referenced in a marking has, in fact, expired.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 292 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: 35 U.S.C. § 292(c) (expired-patent exception)
citations.quote: The marking of a product, in a manner described in subsection (a), with matter relating to a patent that covered that product but has expired is not a violation of this section.

clauses.title: How This Differs From the Failure-to-Mark Damages Statute
clauses.body: The statute described in this document, captioned "False marking," should not be confused with the separate marking statute addressed in this corpus's existing Patent Infringement Information Sheet document. That other statute, 35 U.S.C. § 287(a), addresses the opposite situation: a patentee who does not mark its own patented products at all limits how far back in time it can later recover infringement damages from an accused infringer. The statute described in this document instead addresses marking, advertising, or claiming a patent status that is false or no longer accurate, done with an intent or purpose to deceive. One statute constrains a patentee's own recovery for under-marking; the other penalizes false or deceptive over-marking by anyone, whether or not that person holds any patent at all.
clauses.gap: This clause is a comparative summary of two statutes' subject matter and does not itself restate the full text of 35 U.S.C. § 287(a) (which is verified separately in this corpus's Patent Infringement Information Sheet); it does not address any scenario in which both statutes might be implicated by the same set of facts, which is a legal question this sheet does not resolve.

citations.cite: 35 U.S.C. § 292, title ("False marking")
citations.quote: 35 U.S. Code § 292 - False marking

clauses.title: Signature and Certification
About This Work Opportunity Tax Credit Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes the federal Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC), a general business tax credit under 26 U.S.C. § 51 available to an employer for wages paid to an individual the employer certifies as a member of one of several statutorily defined "targeted groups," in connection with {{companyName}}'s hiring of {{employeeName}} for the position of {{jobTitle}} with a start date of {{startDate}}. It summarizes selected requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 51: how the credit amount and wage limits are calculated, the certification process built around a pre-screening notice and a 28-day submission deadline, what happens when a certification is denied or later found incorrect, categories of individuals whose wages never qualify, and the credit's current statutory expiration date.

This document is distinct from this corpus's existing New Hire Reporting — Information Sheet, which describes an unrelated legal duty — reporting a new hire to a state new-hire reporting agency under Unemployment Insurance Code § 1088.5 and 42 U.S.C. § 653a, a program aimed at locating parents who owe child support and preventing certain benefit overpayments. WOTC is a separate, voluntary federal income tax credit program with its own certification agency and deadline; a hiring event can potentially implicate both requirements independently, but satisfying one does not satisfy the other. This document is also distinct from this corpus's Apprenticeship Agreement — Information Sheet and EIN information sheet, neither of which addresses a hiring-related federal tax credit.

This information sheet does not itself request, complete, submit, or obtain a WOTC certification for {{employeeName}}, does not determine whether {{employeeName}} is or is not a member of any targeted group, does not claim any tax credit on {{companyName}}'s behalf, and does not state whether {{companyName}} has met the certification deadline described below for this particular hire.

clauses.title: How the Credit Amount and Wage Caps Are Calculated
clauses.body: Under 26 U.S.C. § 51(a), the amount of the work opportunity credit for a taxable year equals 40 percent of an employer's "qualified first-year wages" for that year — wages paid or incurred during the employer's taxable year to an individual who is a certified member of a targeted group, attributable to service during the 1-year period beginning with the day the individual begins work. Section 51(b)(3) caps how much of an individual's qualified first-year wages can be taken into account: generally $6,000 per year, but a higher cap applies for certain categories of qualified veteran — $12,000, $14,000, or $24,000 per year depending on which veteran category applies. At the general $6,000 cap, the resulting credit is $2,400 (40 percent of $6,000); at the highest $24,000 veteran cap, the resulting credit is $9,600 (40 percent of $24,000) — the maximum-credit figure California's Employment Development Department cites in its own public description of the program.
clauses.gap: This clause covers only the general 40-percent rate and the wage caps stated in § 51(a) and § 51(b)(3); it does not cover the separate, reduced 25-percent rate that applies to an individual who has performed at least 120 but fewer than 400 hours of service (addressed in this document's companion clause on ineligible individuals and minimum hours), the special summer-youth-employee wage substitution rules in § 51(d)(7)(B), or the separate "qualified second-year wages" and $10,000 cap that § 51(e) provides for long-term family assistance recipients specifically. It also does not address how the credit interacts with the general business credit limitations under 26 U.S.C. § 38, to which § 51(a) itself cross-refers. This clause does not state whether any particular employer qualifies for any specific dollar amount of credit for any particular hire.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 51(a) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: the amount of the work opportunity credit determined under this section for the taxable year shall be equal to 40 percent of the qualified first-year wages for such year.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 51(b)(3) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: The amount of the qualified first-year wages which may be taken into account with respect to any individual shall not exceed $6,000 per year ($12,000 per year in the case of any individual who is a qualified veteran by reason of subsection (d)(3)(A)(ii)(I), $14,000 per year in the case of any individual who is a qualified veteran by reason of subsection (d)(3)(A)(iv), and $24,000 per year in the case of any individual who is a qualified veteran by reason of subsection (d)(3)(A)(ii)(II)).

citations.case: California EDD, "Work Opportunity Tax Credit" program page (Employment Development Department)
citations.cite: EDD's own description of the maximum credit amount
citations.quote: Give employers a federal tax credit of up to $9,600 for hiring these individuals.

clauses.title: The Ten Statutory "Targeted Group" Categories
clauses.body: Section 51(d)(1) provides that an individual is a member of a "targeted group" — the threshold requirement for any wages paid to that individual to qualify for the credit — only if the individual falls into one of ten statutorily listed categories: a qualified IV-A recipient (certain public-assistance recipients), a qualified veteran, a qualified ex-felon, a designated community resident (an 18-to-39-year-old residing in a designated economically distressed area), a vocational rehabilitation referral, a qualified summer youth employee, a qualified supplemental nutrition assistance program (SNAP) benefits recipient, a qualified SSI recipient, a long-term family assistance recipient, or a qualified long-term unemployment recipient. Each category has its own detailed statutory definition in the rest of § 51(d), generally built around certification by a "designated local agency" that the individual meets that category's specific conditions (for example, a particular public-benefits history, a discharge date from military service, or a conviction and release date). Membership in a targeted group is not self-declared or determined by the employer alone — it depends on the certification process described in this document's companion clause.
clauses.gap: This clause states that ten targeted-group categories exist and names them, but does not restate each category's full, detailed statutory definition (for example, the specific benefit-duration and time-window requirements within each subparagraph of § 51(d)(2) through (d)(10)) — a reader would need to consult the relevant subparagraph directly to evaluate a specific individual's category membership. This clause also does not address § 51(d)(14), a now-expired category that applied only to individuals beginning work in 2009 or 2010, since it has no continuing relevance to a current hire.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 51(d)(1) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: An individual is a member of a targeted group if such individual is—

clauses.title: The Certification Mechanism: Pre-Screening Notice and the 28-Day Deadline
clauses.body: Section 51(d)(13)(A) sets out two, and only two, ways an individual's wages can be treated as paid to a member of a targeted group. The first is straightforward: the employer receives an actual certification from a "designated local agency" on or before the day the individual begins work. The second, more commonly used path involves two separate deadlines: a "pre-screening notice" — defined as a document, in a form the Secretary of the Treasury prescribes, containing information from which the employer believes the individual is a member of a targeted group — must be completed on or before the day the individual is offered employment, and then, not later than the 28th day after the individual begins work, the employer must submit that signed notice to the designated local agency as part of a written request for certification. Section 51(d)(12) defines "designated local agency" as a State employment security agency established under the federal Wagner-Peyser Act of June 6, 1933. In California, the Employment Development Department (EDD) performs this function: EDD's own WOTC program page lists an EDD unit — the "Work Opportunity Tax Credit Authorization Center" — as the mailing destination for a paper certification request, and separately describes an online submission option called eWOTC.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the statutory pre-screening-notice-and-28-day mechanism in § 51(d)(13)(A) and the general definition of "designated local agency" in § 51(d)(12); it does not independently verify, from an irs.gov source, the specific current IRS form number (commonly referenced elsewhere as Form 8850) that the Secretary has prescribed for the pre-screening notice, since this research pass was limited to Cornell LII's U.S. Code text and California EDD's own program page rather than an IRS.gov fetch. It also does not address § 51(d)(13)(D)'s separate, alternative certification pathway specific to certain unemployed veterans, or the Secretary's regulatory authority under § 51(d)(13)(D)(ii) to prescribe alternative certification methods. This clause does not state whether the 28-day deadline has been met, or could still be met, for any particular hire's start date.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 51(d)(13)(A) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: on or before the day the individual is offered employment with the employer, a pre-screening notice is completed by the employer with respect to such individual, and

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 51(d)(13)(A) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: not later than the 28th day after the individual begins work for the employer, the employer submits such notice, signed by the employer and the individual under penalties of perjury, to the designated local agency as part of a written request for such a certification from such agency.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 51(d)(12) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: The term “designated local agency” means a State employment security agency established in accordance with the Act of June 6, 1933, as amended (29 U.S.C. 49–49n).

citations.case: California EDD, "Work Opportunity Tax Credit" program page (Employment Development Department)
citations.cite: EDD's description of where a mailed WOTC certification request is sent in California
citations.quote: Employment Development Department Attn: Work Opportunity Tax Credit Authorization Center 2901 50th Street Sacramento, CA 95817

clauses.title: Denied Requests and Revocation of an Incorrect Certification
clauses.body: Certification under this program is not necessarily final or immune from later correction. Section 51(d)(13)(B) provides that if an individual has been certified as a member of a targeted group and that certification is later found incorrect because it was based on false information the individual provided, the certification is revoked, and any wages the employer pays after the employer receives notice of that revocation no longer count as qualified wages for the credit — but the statute does not disturb the wages already paid and treated as qualified before the revocation notice arrived. Separately, § 51(d)(13)(C) gives an unsuccessful applicant a specific procedural right: if a designated local agency denies a request for certification of targeted-group membership, the agency must provide the person who made the request a written explanation of the reasons for the denial.
clauses.gap: The statutory text reviewed states that a written explanation of denial must be provided, but does not itself specify a deadline for the designated local agency to provide it, or an appeal process beyond that explanation. This clause also does not address whether an employer, an individual, or both are the intended recipient of a denial explanation when a request names both, nor does it address any consequence to the individual (as opposed to the employer's lost wage-qualification) that may follow a revoked certification.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 51(d)(13)(B) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: the certification shall be revoked and wages paid by the employer after the date on which notice of revocation is received by the employer shall not be treated as qualified wages.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 51(d)(13)(C) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: If a designated local agency denies a request for certification of membership in a targeted group, such agency shall provide to the person making such request a written explanation of the reasons for such denial.

clauses.title: Related Individuals, Rehires, and the Minimum-Hours Requirement
clauses.body: Even a properly certified targeted-group member's wages do not always qualify. Section 51(i)(1) excludes wages paid to certain "related individuals" — most notably, an individual related to the employer (or, for a corporate employer, related to a more-than-50-percent owner) within the family relationships the Internal Revenue Code defines for dependency purposes, as well as certain estate or trust grantors, beneficiaries, and fiduciaries. Section 51(i)(2) separately excludes any individual the employer had already employed at any time before that individual's current hiring date — a "nonqualifying rehire" is not eligible regardless of targeted-group membership. Finally, § 51(i)(3) ties the credit to a minimum amount of actual work: no wages qualify at all for an individual who performs fewer than 120 hours of service for the employer, and for an individual who performs at least 120 but fewer than 400 hours, the credit rate drops from 40 percent to 25 percent of qualified first-year wages.
clauses.gap: This clause states the existence and general shape of the § 51(i)(1) related-individual exclusion but does not restate the full family-relationship definitions incorporated by cross-reference from 26 U.S.C. § 152(d)(2)(A) through (H) and § 267(c); a reader would need to consult those separate sections to evaluate a specific family or ownership relationship. This clause also does not address § 51(f) (the separate requirement that more than half of an individual's remuneration be for trade-or-business services), § 51(h) (special agricultural- and railway-labor wage rules), or § 51(k) (successor-employer and leased-employee rules). This clause does not state whether any particular individual falls into any excluded category or has performed any particular number of hours of service for any particular employer.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 51(i)(2) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: No wages shall be taken into account under subsection (a) with respect to any individual if, prior to the hiring date of such individual, such individual had been employed by the employer at any time.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 51(i)(3)(A) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: In the case of an individual who has performed at least 120 hours, but less than 400 hours, of service for the employer, subsection (a) shall be applied by substituting “25 percent” for “40 percent”.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 51(i)(3)(B) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: No wages shall be taken into account under subsection (a) with respect to any individual unless such individual has performed at least 120 hours of service for the employer.

clauses.title: Current Statutory Expiration: December 31, 2025
clauses.body: The credit is not currently open-ended. Section 51(c)(4) defines "wages" for purposes of this program to exclude any amount paid or incurred to an individual who begins work for the employer after December 31, 2025 — meaning that, as carried in the current U.S. Code text, no wages paid to an individual hired after that date qualify for the credit at all, regardless of targeted-group membership or certification. California's own EDD, in the WOTC program page fetched for this document (current as of this document's own drafting), confirms this same cutoff in plain terms and describes its own current practice for hires made after it: federal authorization for the program expired on December 31, 2025, EDD states that employers should continue submitting WOTC applications within the required timeframes, and EDD states that it will accept and retain applications for individuals with 2026 and later start dates pending federal reauthorization, rather than rejecting them outright.
clauses.gap: This finding corrects an assumption in this document's initial research framing, which treated WOTC as a presently operating, open-ended hiring credit without qualification. Having fetched and read the actual current 26 U.S.C. § 51(c)(4) text directly from Cornell's Legal Information Institute, and cross-checked it against California EDD's own current WOTC program page, the honest finding is that, as of both sources' text at the time of this research (September 2026), no wages paid to an individual who begins work after December 31, 2025 currently qualify for the credit, unless Congress has since enacted a reauthorization not yet reflected in either fetched source. This program's amendment history (recorded in the same U.S. Code text) shows a long pattern of Congress retroactively extending this same December 31 cutoff date after prior lapses, so a lapse of this kind is not unprecedented for this specific credit and does not necessarily mean the program has permanently ended — but this document takes no position on whether, or when, any future reauthorization will occur, and states only what the fetched text shows as of the dates given. This session's CourtListener case-law search for this topic returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, quota exhausted) rather than results, so this clause and this document rest on the statutory and EDD text alone, without a case-law check for any judicial decision addressing this or a prior WOTC lapse.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 51(c)(4) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.quote: The term “wages” shall not include any amount paid or incurred to an individual who begins work for the employer after December 31, 2025.

citations.case: California EDD, "Work Opportunity Tax Credit" program page (Employment Development Department)
citations.cite: EDD's own "WOTC Program Update" notice
citations.quote: Federal authorization for the Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC) expired on December 31, 2025. Employers should continue submitting WOTC applications within required timeframes. Applications with start dates of January 1, 2026, and after will be accepted and retained pending federal reauthorization.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California Labor Code § 1137, the "California Worker Freedom from Employer Intimidation Act," which took effect January 1, 2025. Section 1137 addresses so-called "captive audience" meetings: it restricts an employer's ability to require attendance at, or participation in, employer-sponsored meetings or communications whose purpose is to communicate the employer's opinion about religious or political matters, and it sets out the exceptions, exempt entities, and remedies the statute itself defines. This document is distinct from {{companyName}}'s existing information sheet on Labor Code §§ 1101-1106, which protects an employee's own political activities and affiliations away from work. Section 1137 instead regulates what an employer may require employees to attend or listen to at work concerning the employer's own religious or political opinions. This sheet states the text and structure of the statute. It does not describe {{companyName}}'s own meeting practices, does not determine whether any particular meeting falls within the statute's exceptions or exemptions, and does not advise {{employeeName}} on whether to raise a concern or take any action.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1137(b) defines the terms used elsewhere in the statute. "Employee" means any individual who performs services for and under the control and direction of an employer for wages or other remuneration. "Employer" is defined broadly and expressly reaches government entities. "Political matters" is defined to include not only partisan elections but also legislation, regulation, and the decision to join or support a political or labor organization. "Religious matters" is defined to include religious affiliation and practice and the decision to join or support a religious organization or association.
clauses.gap: The statute does not further define terms within these definitions, such as "control and direction" or "wages or other remuneration"; those terms carry whatever meaning they have elsewhere in the Labor Code and case law, which this sheet does not survey. The definition of "political matters" expressly includes the decision to join or support a "labor organization," meaning this section can overlap with separate labor-relations statutes not covered here.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(b)(2) (definition of "Employer")
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(b)(2)
citations.quote: “Employer” means any individual, partnership, association, corporation, or any agent, representative, designee, or person or group of persons acting directly or indirectly on behalf of or in the interest of an employer with the employer’s consent and shall include all branches of state government, or the several counties, cities and counties, and municipalities thereof, or any other political subdivision of the state, or a school district, or any special district, or any authority, commission, or board or any other agency or instrumentality thereof.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(b)(3) (definition of "Political matters")
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(b)(3)
citations.quote: “Political matters” means matters relating to elections for political office, political parties, legislation, regulation, and the decision to join or support any political party or political or labor organization.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(b)(4) (definition of "Religious matters")
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(b)(4)
citations.quote: “Religious matters” means matters relating to religious affiliation and practice and the decision to join or support any religious organization or association.

clauses.title: Short Title and Effective Date
clauses.body: The chapter containing Labor Code § 1137 is officially titled the "California Worker Freedom from Employer Intimidation Act." It was added by Statutes 2024, Chapter 670, Section 1 (Senate Bill 399), and became effective January 1, 2025.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the statute's own title and effective date. It does not address whether any conduct that occurred before January 1, 2025 is affected, and it does not describe any local ordinance or other state's law that may independently regulate similar meetings.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(a) (short title)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(a)
citations.quote: This chapter shall be known, and may be cited, as the “California Worker Freedom from Employer Intimidation Act.”

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137, historical note (effective date)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137, Historical Note
citations.quote: (Added by Stats. 2024, Ch. 670, Sec. 1. (SB 399) Effective January 1, 2025.)

clauses.title: Core Prohibition on Mandatory Religious or Political Meetings
clauses.body: Subject to the exceptions and exemptions the statute defines, Labor Code § 1137(c) prohibits an employer from subjecting or threatening to subject an employee to discharge, discrimination, retaliation, or any other adverse action because the employee declines to attend an employer-sponsored meeting, or affirmatively declines to participate in, receive, or listen to communications with the employer, where the purpose is to communicate the employer's opinion about religious or political matters. The statute separately provides that an employee who is working at the time of such a meeting and elects not to attend continues to be paid while the meeting is held.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general rule of subdivision (c) only; it does not restate the specific exceptions in subdivision (g) or the categorical exemptions in subdivision (h), both of which limit when subdivision (c) applies and are addressed in separate clauses. The statute does not define "adverse action" for purposes of this section, and no reported California appellate decision construing Section 1137 was located in this research (the statute took effect January 1, 2025).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(c) (prohibition on adverse action for declining attendance)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(c)
citations.quote: shall not subject, or threaten to subject, an employee to discharge, discrimination, retaliation, or any other adverse action because the employee declines to attend an employer-sponsored meeting or affirmatively declines to participate in, receive, or listen to any communications with the employer or its agents or representatives, the purpose of which is to communicate the employer’s opinion about religious or political matters.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(c) (continued pay while meeting held)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(c)
citations.quote: An employee who is working at the time of the meeting and elects not to attend a meeting described in this subdivision shall continue to be paid while the meeting is held.

clauses.title: Communications the Statute Does Not Prohibit
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1137(g) states that the section does not prohibit an employer from communicating information the employer is legally required to communicate (limited to the extent of that legal requirement), or from communicating information necessary for employees to perform their job duties. Subdivision (g) also states the section does not prohibit an institution of higher education from meeting with employees as part of coursework, symposia, or an academic program, and does not prohibit a public entity employer from communicating information related to a public policy or a law or regulation the public entity administers.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes two of the four items listed in subdivision (g); the higher-education and public-entity-policy items are stated in summary rather than quoted verbatim. The statute does not define how much communication falls within "the extent of that legal requirement" or what makes information "necessary" to job duties, so where a specific communication falls on either side of that line is not addressed by the statutory text itself.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(g)(1) (legally required communications)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(g)(1)
citations.quote: An employer from communicating to its employees any information that the employer is required by law to communicate, but only to the extent of that legal requirement.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(g)(2) (job-duty-necessary communications)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(g)(2)
citations.quote: An employer from communicating to its employees any information that is necessary for those employees to perform their job duties.

clauses.title: Entities and Activities the Statute Does Not Cover
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1137(h) lists six categories to which the section does not apply at all, including: certain religious corporations, entities, associations, educational institutions, or societies (with respect to speech on religious matters to employees connected with their religious activities, as described in subdivision (h)(1)); a political organization or party requiring attendance at a meeting to communicate the organization's own political tenets or purposes; an educational institution requiring attendance at lectures that are part of regular coursework; a nonprofit tax-exempt training program requiring attendance related to its mission; an employer requiring training to comply with legal obligations, including civil rights and occupational safety and health laws; and a public employer holding a statutorily defined new employee orientation, or certain other statutorily defined orientations.
clauses.gap: The religious-corporation exemption in subdivision (h)(1) cross-references Title VII of the federal Civil Rights Act and several California Government Code and Labor Code provisions defining which employers and what conduct qualify; this clause summarizes rather than quotes that cross-referenced exemption, and this research did not independently verify the current text of those cross-referenced provisions. Determining whether a specific entity or meeting fits within any of the six listed exemptions requires matching its facts against the statute's own wording, which this sheet does not do.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(h)(2) (political organization exemption)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(h)(2)
citations.quote: A political organization or party requiring its employees to attend an employer-sponsored meeting or to participate in any communications with the employer or its agents or representatives, the purpose of which is to communicate the employer’s political tenets or purposes.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(h)(5) (legal-compliance training exemption)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(h)(5)
citations.quote: An employer requiring employees to undergo training to comply with the employer’s legal obligations, including obligations under civil rights laws and occupational safety and health laws.

clauses.title: Enforcement and Remedies
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1137 provides more than one enforcement path. Under subdivision (d), an employer who violates the section is subject to a civil penalty of five hundred dollars ($500) per employee for each violation, in addition to any other remedy. Under subdivision (e), the Labor Commissioner may enforce the section, including investigating an alleged violation, ordering temporary relief, and issuing a citation, using the procedures set out in Labor Code §§ 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1. Under subdivision (f), as an alternative to Labor Commissioner enforcement, an employee who has suffered a violation of subdivision (c) may instead bring a civil action for damages, including punitive damages, and may petition the superior court for temporary or preliminary injunctive relief.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the remedies subdivision (d), (e), and (f) make available; it does not reproduce the full text of the cross-referenced enforcement procedures in Labor Code §§ 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1, which were not independently fetched and verified in this research. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions applying Section 1137 returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, quota exhausted) before any results could be reviewed, so this sheet cannot state whether courts have yet interpreted these remedies; given the statute's January 1, 2025 effective date, reported appellate decisions may not yet exist regardless.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(d) (civil penalty)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(d)
citations.quote: an employer who violates this section shall be subject to a civil penalty of five hundred dollars ($500) per employee for each violation.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(e) (Labor Commissioner enforcement)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(e)
citations.quote: The Labor Commissioner may enforce this section, including investigating an alleged violation, and ordering appropriate temporary relief to mitigate a violation or maintain the status quo pending the completion of a full investigation or hearing through the procedures set forth in Section 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1, including issuing a citation against an employer who violates this section and filing a civil action.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1137(f)(1) (private civil action)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1137(f)(1)
citations.quote: any employee who has suffered a violation of subdivision (c) may bring a civil action in a court of competent jurisdiction for damages caused by that adverse action, including punitive damages.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Receipt
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California statutory law under the Subdivision Map Act, Government Code section 66410 et seq., as it may relate to real property at {{propertyAddress}}, {{county}} County, California (Assessor's Parcel Number {{parcelNumber}}), owned by {{ownerName}}, in connection with the following described land division: {{proposedDivisionDescription}}. It states what the Act provides about the statutory definition of "subdivision," when a tentative and final map (as opposed to a parcel map) is required, the Act's own listed exemptions including the lot line adjustment exemption, the statutory prohibition on selling, leasing, or financing land before a required map is recorded, how long an approved tentative map remains valid before it expires, and the requirement that an approved subdivision be consistent with the applicable general or specific plan. This information sheet is separate from, and does not substitute for, the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act's own recording requirements for a condominium plan or declaration, the California Coastal Act's coastal development permit requirement, the common-law agreed-boundary doctrine that can fix an uncertain boundary line between adjoining owners without dividing a parcel, or any local subdivision ordinance, environmental review, or other permit that may separately apply to the same land. It does not tell {{ownerName}} or any other person whether the described land division is a "subdivision" under the Act, whether it qualifies for a statutory exemption, whether a tentative map, final map, or parcel map is required for it, or what to do next.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Subdivision"
clauses.body: The Subdivision Map Act applies to a "subdivision," a term the Act defines in its own definitions article rather than leaving to common usage. Government Code section 66424 defines "subdivision" as the division of a unit or units of land shown on the latest equalized county assessment roll, for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing, whether the sale, lease, or financing is immediate or future. Parcels are treated as contiguous, and therefore as a single unit capable of being "divided," even where they are separated by a road, street, utility easement, or railroad right-of-way. The statutory definition also expressly reaches certain forms of ownership restructuring beyond a physical division of land: a condominium project, a community apartment project, and the conversion of five or more existing dwelling units to a stock cooperative are each included within "subdivision" by the statute's own terms.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the general definition in section 66424. It does not address the Act's separate exemption provisions (Government Code section 66412 and related sections), which remove specific categories of land division or ownership change from the Act's coverage even though they might otherwise fit this definition, nor does it determine whether any specific transaction described in this document falls within or outside the definition. A CourtListener search for judicial decisions construing this definition returned a 429 rate-limit error (125/day quota exhausted) before any results could be reviewed, so no case law confirming or narrowing this statutory language is cited here.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code Section 66424
citations.cite: Cal. Gov't Code § 66424
citations.quote: “Subdivision” means the division, by any subdivider, of any unit or units of improved or unimproved land, or any portion thereof, shown on the latest equalized county assessment roll as a unit or as contiguous units, for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing, whether immediate or future.

clauses.title: When a Tentative and Final Map Is Required
clauses.body: The Act sets a numeric threshold, subject to listed exceptions, for when the more extensive tentative-and-final-map procedure applies rather than the simpler parcel map procedure. Government Code section 66426 requires a tentative and final map for a subdivision that creates five or more parcels, five or more condominiums, a community apartment project of five or more parcels, or a conversion to a stock cooperative of five or more dwelling units. The same section then lists six circumstances in which, even though a five-or-more-parcel subdivision is being created, a parcel map is required instead of the tentative-and-final-map procedure: among them, where the land before division is under five acres, each resulting parcel abuts a maintained public street, and the local legislative body requires no dedications or improvements; where each resulting parcel is 20 acres or more with approved access to a maintained public street; where the land is part of an industrial- or commercial-zoned tract with governing-body-approved street alignments; where each resulting parcel is at least 40 acres or a quarter of a quarter section; and where the division is solely to create an environmental subdivision under section 66418.2.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the section 66426 threshold and its listed exceptions as written; it does not state which procedure applies to any property or transaction described in this document, and it does not address the separate, narrower parcel-map-only threshold that applies to subdivisions of four or fewer parcels under other sections of the Act, which this clause does not cover. A CourtListener search for case law was not completed because of an exhausted 125/day quota (429 rate-limit response); no judicial authority is cited here.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code Section 66426
citations.cite: Cal. Gov't Code § 66426
citations.quote: A tentative and final map shall be required for all subdivisions creating five or more parcels, five or more condominiums as defined in Section 783 of the Civil Code, a community apartment project containing five or more parcels, or for the conversion of a dwelling to a stock cooperative containing five or more dwelling units, except where any one of the following occurs:

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code Section 66426
citations.cite: Cal. Gov't Code § 66426(a)
citations.quote: The land before division contains less than five acres, each parcel created by the division abuts upon a maintained public street or highway, and no dedications or improvements are required by the legislative body.

clauses.title: The Lot Line Adjustment Exemption
clauses.body: The Act does not apply to every rearrangement of a boundary between parcels. Government Code section 66412(d) exempts a "lot line adjustment," defined for this purpose as an adjustment between four or fewer existing adjoining parcels where land taken from one parcel is added to an adjoining parcel and no greater number of parcels than originally existed is created, provided the local agency or advisory agency approves it. The statute limits that agency's review to whether the resulting parcels conform to the local general plan, any applicable specific plan or coastal plan, and zoning and building ordinances, and bars the agency from imposing conditions beyond that conformance check (with limited exceptions for prepayment of property taxes and utility relocation). The statute further provides that no tentative map, parcel map, or final map is required for a lot line adjustment, that the adjustment is instead reflected in a recorded deed, and that a record of survey is not required unless separately required by Business and Professions Code section 8762.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the statutory lot line adjustment exemption in section 66412(d) only; it does not address the separate common-law agreed-boundary doctrine, which can also fix an uncertain boundary between adjoining owners but operates independently of this statute and does not require local agency approval. It also does not evaluate whether any specific line adjustment described in this document meets the four-or-fewer-parcels and no-net-increase conditions the statute states. CourtListener search results were not obtained (429 rate-limit error, 125/day quota exhausted), so no case law is cited on how courts have applied this exemption.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code Section 66412
citations.cite: Cal. Gov't Code § 66412(d)
citations.quote: A lot line adjustment between four or fewer existing adjoining parcels, where the land taken from one parcel is added to an adjoining parcel, and where a greater number of parcels than originally existed is not thereby created, if the lot line adjustment is approved by the local agency, or advisory agency.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code Section 66412
citations.cite: Cal. Gov't Code § 66412(d)
citations.quote: No tentative map, parcel map, or final map shall be required as a condition to the approval of a lot line adjustment.

clauses.title: Prohibition on Sale, Lease, or Financing Before a Required Map Is Recorded
clauses.body: The Act backs its map requirements with a direct prohibition on certain transactions. Government Code section 66499.30(a) provides that no person shall sell, lease, or finance a parcel, or commence construction of a building for sale, lease, or financing on it (other than a model home), or allow occupancy of it, where a final map is required, until that final map has been filed for record by the county recorder; subdivision (b) states the same rule for a parcel map. Subdivision (c) separately prohibits conveying any part of a division of real property by parcel or block number or other designation until the required final or parcel map has been recorded. The statute qualifies this prohibition in two ways relevant here: subdivision (d) states that the prohibition does not apply to a parcel offered, contracted, sold, or leased in compliance with, or exempt from, the law regulating subdivision design and improvement in effect when the subdivision was established; and subdivision (e) states that the prohibition does not bar an offer or contract to sell, lease, or finance, or to construct improvements, where that sale, lease, financing, or construction is expressly conditioned on the approval and filing of the required final or parcel map. Subdivision (g) also tolls the limitation period for an enforcement action for any period during which there was no constructive notice of the violating transaction because no deed, lease, or financing document was recorded.
clauses.gap: This clause states the transactional prohibition and its own stated conditions and qualifications as written in section 66499.30; it does not state what legal effect, if any, a violation has on the validity of a deed or other conveyance actually made in violation of the section, since that consequence (if any) is not addressed within the text of this section itself and this clause does not rely on any other section or on case law to fill that gap. A CourtListener search for judicial decisions construing this prohibition, including its effect on title, could not be completed because of an exhausted CourtListener quota (429 rate-limit response, 125/day limit); no case law is cited here.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code Section 66499.30
citations.cite: Cal. Gov't Code § 66499.30(a)
citations.quote: No person shall sell, lease, or finance any parcel or parcels of real property or commence construction of any building for sale, lease or financing thereon, except for model homes, or allow occupancy thereof, for which a final map is required by this division or local ordinance, until the final map thereof in full compliance with this division and any local ordinance has been filed for record by the recorder of the county in which any portion of the subdivision is located.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code Section 66499.30
citations.cite: Cal. Gov't Code § 66499.30(e)
citations.quote: Nothing contained in subdivisions (a) and (b) shall be deemed to prohibit an offer or contract to sell, lease, or finance real property or to construct improvements thereon where the sale, lease, or financing, or the commencement of construction, is expressly conditioned upon the approval and filing of a final subdivision map or parcel map, as required under this division.

clauses.title: How Long an Approved Tentative Map Remains Valid
clauses.body: An approved tentative map does not remain valid indefinitely. Government Code section 66452.6(a)(1) provides that an approved or conditionally approved tentative map expires 24 months after approval, or after any additional period prescribed by local ordinance not exceeding an additional 24 months, subject to a separate rule extending that period by 48 months per phased final map filing where the subdivider must spend at or above a stated, annually inflation-adjusted dollar threshold on off-site public improvements, up to a maximum of 10 years from approval. The statute separately provides, in subdivision (d), that once a tentative map expires, all proceedings on it terminate and no final map or parcel map covering any part of the land may be filed without first processing a new tentative map, although a filing made before expiration remains valid even if the local agency's subsequent processing, approval, or recording of it occurs after the expiration date. The statute also tolls the running of this period during a development moratorium (subdivision (b)), during litigation over the map's approval where the local agency grants a stay (subdivision (c)), and allows the subdivider to apply for a discretionary extension of up to six years in addition to the base period (subdivision (e)).
clauses.gap: This clause describes the expiration, tolling, and extension mechanics stated in section 66452.6 as written, including the version of the inflation-adjusted dollar threshold (currently stated as $236,790 in the fetched text) in effect on the date this text was fetched; because the statute itself directs that figure to be increased annually by a specified construction cost index, the current dollar amount at any later date will differ from the figure quoted and is not independently verified here. It does not address a vesting tentative map's separate statutory rules under a different article of the Act, which are not covered by this clause. CourtListener search results could not be obtained due to an exhausted 125/day quota (429 rate-limit error); no case law is cited on how courts have applied these expiration and tolling rules.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code Section 66452.6
citations.cite: Cal. Gov't Code § 66452.6(a)(1)
citations.quote: An approved or conditionally approved tentative map shall expire 24 months after its approval or conditional approval, or after any additional period of time as may be prescribed by local ordinance, not to exceed an additional 24 months.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code Section 66452.6
citations.cite: Cal. Gov't Code § 66452.6(d)
citations.quote: The expiration of the approved or conditionally approved tentative map shall terminate all proceedings and no final map or parcel map of all or any portion of the real property included within the tentative map shall be filed with the legislative body without first processing a new tentative map.

clauses.title: Required Consistency With the General or Specific Plan
clauses.body: Approval of a subdivision under the Act is conditioned on a required local finding. Government Code section 66473.5 provides that no local agency may approve a tentative map, or a parcel map for which no tentative map was required, unless the legislative body finds that the proposed subdivision, together with its provisions for design and improvement, is consistent with the applicable general plan or any applicable specific plan. The statute further states that a proposed subdivision is consistent with such a plan only if the local agency has officially adopted the plan and the proposed subdivision or land use is compatible with the objectives, policies, general land uses, and programs the plan specifies.
clauses.gap: This clause states the consistency-finding requirement in section 66473.5 as written; it does not describe the separate substantive standards a general plan or specific plan itself must contain, nor does it evaluate whether any particular proposed subdivision described in this document would be found consistent with any particular jurisdiction's adopted plan. CourtListener search results could not be obtained (429 rate-limit error, 125/day quota exhausted), so no case law construing this consistency requirement is cited here.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code Section 66473.5
citations.cite: Cal. Gov't Code § 66473.5
citations.quote: No local agency shall approve a tentative map, or a parcel map for which a tentative map was not required, unless the legislative body finds that the proposed subdivision, together with the provisions for its design and improvement, is consistent with the general plan required by Article 5 (commencing with Section 65300) of Chapter 3 of Division 1, or any specific plan adopted pursuant to Article 8 (commencing with Section 65450) of Chapter 3 of Division 1.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose and Scope — Preemptive Rights Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's statutory treatment of preemptive rights for {{companyName}}: the default rule that applies to a California corporation unless its articles of incorporation say otherwise, and the specific mechanism by which the articles can create such rights instead. A preemptive right, where one exists, is a shareholder's right to be offered a proportionate share of a new issuance of stock or securities before the corporation offers that issuance to others. This sheet does not draft, recommend, or evaluate specific preemptive-rights language for {{companyName}}'s articles, does not calculate any shareholder's proportionate entitlement under a preemptive-rights provision that may already exist, and does not address the separate topics covered elsewhere in this corpus: original formation of the articles of incorporation (Articles of Incorporation document), the general procedure for amending existing articles (Certificate of Amendment to Articles of Incorporation — Information Sheet), or the mechanics of issuing or replacing stock certificates once shares are issued (Stock Certificates and Uncertificated Shares — Information Sheet). It states what California's General Corporation Law itself says on this one topic and no more.

clauses.title: The Default Rule: No Preemptive Rights Unless the Articles Provide Otherwise
clauses.body: Under California's General Corporation Law, a corporation's board of directors is free, as a default matter, to issue new shares, options, or securities with conversion or option rights without first offering them to any existing shareholder. This default applies to {{companyName}} unless {{companyName}}'s own articles of incorporation state otherwise. A shareholder of {{companyName}} has no preemptive right arising automatically from status as a shareholder, from the number of shares already held, or from any class of shares held; the statute makes shareholder-level preemptive rights the exception that must be affirmatively created, not the rule.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the default rule under California's General Corporation Law (Corporations Code Chapter 4, Shares and Share Certificates). It does not address whether a particular corporation's own articles of incorporation already displace that default — that depends on the actual text of the articles, which this sheet does not review. It also does not address preemptive-rights doctrine for entities other than California stock corporations (for example, statutes or agreements governing LLC membership interests or limited partnership interests), which are outside Corporations Code Chapter 4 and are not addressed here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 406
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 406
citations.quote: Unless the articles provide otherwise, the board may issue shares, options or securities having conversion or option rights without first offering them to shareholders of any class.

clauses.title: How the Default Can Be Changed: Preemptive Rights as an Optional Articles Provision
clauses.body: California law lists preemptive rights among a specific set of optional provisions that a corporation's articles of incorporation are permitted to include. If {{companyName}}'s articles were to include such a provision, it would grant shareholders a right to subscribe to some or all future issuances of shares or securities, reversing the default rule that a shareholder has no such right. The statute frames this as a matter of drafting choice at the articles level, not something that arises from board resolution, bylaw amendment, or shareholder vote alone.
clauses.gap: This clause identifies that a preemptive-rights provision is one of the optional articles provisions California law lists (Corporations Code § 204, subdivision (a)); it does not state whether any particular corporation's articles actually contain one, and it does not supply drafting language, a proportionality formula, an exercise period, or any other implementing mechanic for such a provision — the statute itself does not prescribe those mechanics, leaving them (if the right is created at all) to the articles' own text.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 204(a)(2)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 204, subd. (a)(2)
citations.quote: Granting to shareholders preemptive rights to subscribe to any or all issues of shares or securities.

clauses.title: Silence Is Not Enough: An Articles Provision on This Point Must Be Express
clauses.body: The same statutory list that includes preemptive rights states that none of the provisions on that list — preemptive rights among them — takes effect unless the articles expressly provide for it. This means that an articles of incorporation that is merely silent on preemptive rights, or that references the topic ambiguously, does not create a preemptive right for {{companyName}}'s shareholders; under the default rule described above, the absence of an express grant leaves the board free to issue shares without first offering them to existing shareholders.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only the express-provision requirement found in the introductory clause of Corporations Code § 204, subdivision (a). It does not address how a reviewing court would characterize particular non-standard or ambiguous articles language as "express" or not, since that determination depends on the specific wording used and is not resolved by the statute's text; a case-law search for this topic could not be completed in this research because the CourtListener research API returned a daily quota-exhausted (HTTP 429) error before any query could run, so this clause relies on the statutory text alone and no judicial gloss on the express-provision requirement has been checked.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 204(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 204, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Any or all of the following provisions, which shall not be effective unless expressly provided in the articles:

clauses.title: Closing and Acknowledgment — Preemptive Rights Information Sheet
Purpose of This Trade Dispute Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet states facts about a single, specific California unemployment insurance disqualification: Unemployment Insurance Code Section 1262, which bars unemployment compensation benefits to an individual who left work because of a "trade dispute" (a labor dispute such as a strike or lockout), for as long as that dispute remains in active progress at the establishment where {{employeeName}} was employed by {{companyName}}. It does not determine whether any particular work stoppage involving {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}} is or is not a "trade dispute" within the meaning of Section 1262 — that determination is made by the Employment Development Department and, on appeal, by an administrative law judge or the courts, based on the specific facts of the dispute. This document is a separate, distinct topic from this corpus's Unemployment Insurance Benefits — Claimant Information Sheet, which states the general disqualification standard for voluntarily quitting without good cause or being discharged for misconduct under a different statute, Unemployment Insurance Code Section 1256; a trade-dispute separation is not evaluated under that misconduct/voluntary-quit standard. It is also distinct from the notice-of-change-in-relationship duty addressed elsewhere in this corpus, which identifies a work stoppage caused by a trade dispute only as one circumstance the Employment Development Department's guidance treats as not requiring that separate written notice — this document instead addresses the benefits-eligibility question itself. This document does not address rights or protections under the federal National Labor Relations Act that may apply to strikers or locked-out employees, does not address an employer's or union's bargaining obligations, does not address replacement-worker or reinstatement rights, and does not address whether severance, WARN Act, or other termination-related obligations apply to any employer action taken during a labor dispute. Nothing here instructs {{employeeName}} or {{companyName}} to take, or refrain from taking, any particular action with respect to an actual or anticipated labor dispute.

clauses.title: The Trade Dispute Disqualification: Leaving Work Because of a Labor Dispute
clauses.body: A distinct provision of the California Unemployment Insurance Code, separate from the general misconduct/voluntary-quit disqualification, makes an individual ineligible for unemployment compensation benefits if that individual left work because of a trade dispute. The statutory text does not limit this disqualification to individuals who personally called, organized, or voted for the dispute, and it does not contain any textual exception for an individual who did not participate in, finance, or have a direct interest in the dispute, or who worked in a different grade or class of work than the employees involved in it. On the face of the statute, the disqualifying question is why the individual left work — because of a trade dispute — not what role, if any, that individual played in causing it.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the first sentence of Unemployment Insurance Code Section 1262, fetched directly from California Legislative Information and confirmed byte-identical across two independently user-agented fetches; the statute itself does not define "trade dispute," and does not, on its face, distinguish a strike (a work stoppage initiated by employees) from a lockout (a work stoppage initiated by the employer) or resolve whether an employee excluded from work by an employer-initiated lockout has "left" work within the meaning of this section. California courts and the California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board have construed this term and this strike/lockout distinction in published decisions, but this document's drafter could not verify any specific case citation this session: the CourtListener research tool used for that purpose returned a rate-limit error (429, "125/day" quota exhausted, roughly 9,437 seconds remaining) before any search could be completed. Rather than rely on an unverified case citation or an assumption about how courts have resolved the strike/lockout distinction, this document discloses that limitation and does not characterize how any court has applied this statute to a lockout, a sympathy strike, or a dispute an individual did not personally join. This clause also does not determine whether any specific work stoppage is a "trade dispute," and does not address the separate false-statement penalty, the general misconduct/voluntary-quit standard, or any other unemployment insurance disqualification.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1262 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: An individual is not eligible for unemployment compensation benefits, and these benefits shall not be payable to him or her, if the individual left his or her work because of a trade dispute.

clauses.title: Duration of the Disqualification: Tied to the Dispute's Active Progress at That Establishment
clauses.body: The same statutory section that creates the trade dispute disqualification also fixes its duration and its geographic scope. The disqualification does not run for a fixed number of weeks; instead, it lasts only for as long as the individual continues out of work because the trade dispute remains in active progress in the specific establishment where that individual was employed. Read together with the disqualification itself, this means the statute ties both the trigger and the end of ineligibility to the same underlying fact — the status of the dispute at that particular establishment — rather than to a separate waiting period, a fixed number of weeks, or a requirement that the individual earn a minimum amount in new wages before requalifying, of the kind that applies to some other disqualifications under this code.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the second sentence of the same Unemployment Insurance Code Section 1262 already cited in this document's core-disqualification clause; it is drawn from the same statutory section and is not an independent corroborating source. The statute does not define "establishment," and does not state how this provision applies where an individual works for an employer with multiple locations, only one of which is affected by the dispute, or where an individual is reassigned to a different location during the dispute. This document's drafter could not verify any case law construing "establishment" or the active-progress requirement this session because the CourtListener research tool returned a rate-limit error (125/day quota exhausted) before any search could be run; no case citation is offered on this point, and this clause does not determine when, on any specific set of facts, a trade dispute has stopped being in "active progress."

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1262 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: The individual shall remain ineligible for the period during which he or she continues out of work by reason of the fact that the trade dispute is still in active progress in the establishment in which he or she was employed.

clauses.title: The EDD's Duty to Investigate a Trade Dispute Is Separate From, and Not a Substitute for, an Eligibility Determination
clauses.body: A companion statutory section requires the Employment Development Department, whenever it learns that a trade dispute is in progress, to promptly investigate and make findings about the dispute's nature, location, and the labor organizations and employers involved, and to share those findings with its field offices and, on request, with any employer, employers' association, or labor organization involved in the dispute. The same statute expressly separates that fact-finding role from the individual eligibility question: the department's investigation findings about the dispute itself are based on the information then available to the department and are not a determination of any particular claimant's eligibility for benefits under the trade dispute disqualification. An individual claimant's eligibility is decided through the department's separate claim-determination process, not by the department's general findings about the dispute.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Unemployment Insurance Code Section 1262.5, fetched directly from California Legislative Information and confirmed byte-identical across two independently user-agented fetches. The statute does not specify a deadline by which the department must complete its investigation or issue its findings, does not state whether or how a claimant may obtain or contest the department's dispute-level findings independently of that claimant's own individual benefits determination, and does not address the general claim-filing, employer-notice, or appeal procedures that apply once an individual eligibility determination is made — those general procedures are addressed elsewhere in this corpus and are not repeated here. This document's drafter located no published case law construing this section this session because the CourtListener research tool returned a rate-limit error (125/day quota exhausted) before a search could be run; no case citation is offered on this point.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1262.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code
citations.quote: The department’s investigation findings shall be based upon the information then available to it and shall not be a determination as to the eligibility of any claimant for benefits under Section 1262.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Background Information — Modifying or Terminating an Irrevocable Trust by Consent
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the statutory mechanisms California's Probate Code provides for modifying or terminating an irrevocable trust — potentially {{trustName}}, executed {{originalTrustDate}}, of which {{trusteeName}} serves, or has been asked to serve, as trustee — through the consent of the settlor, the beneficiaries, or both, rather than through a settlor's unilateral exercise of a reserved power.
