It covers two distinct statutory paths found at Probate Code §§ 15403-15404: a court-petition route available to all beneficiaries of an irrevocable trust acting together, without any need for the settlor's involvement, and a written-consent route available to a settlor and all beneficiaries acting together, without any need for court approval. It also covers two related, consent-independent statutory bases on which a court can modify or terminate a trust: unanticipated changed circumstances (§ 15409) and a trust whose value has become too low relative to administration costs (§ 15408), including a trustee's own statutory power to terminate a sufficiently small trust without going to court at all. This information sheet does not itself modify or terminate {{trustName}} or any other trust, does not constitute the written consent that §§ 15403-15404 describe, does not constitute a petition to any court, and does not determine whether any specific trust, settlor, or beneficiary satisfies the requirements described in this document. This document is distinct from this corpus's Trust Amendment document, which addresses a settlor's own power under Probate Code § 15402 to amend or revoke a trust that remains revocable by that settlor alone, and from this corpus's Trust Decanting document, which addresses a trustee's power under the Uniform Trust Decanting Act to redirect trust principal without beneficiary consent at all. The mechanisms described here instead apply once a trust is no longer one a settlor can simply amend alone, or apply regardless of revocability, and in every version described here except the settlor-and-beneficiaries written-consent route, at least one beneficiary's agreement or participation is part of the statutory requirement.

clauses.title: Two Distinct Consent-Based Routes: All Beneficiaries to Court, or Settlor and All Beneficiaries Without Court
clauses.body: Probate Code § 15403(a) provides that if all beneficiaries of an irrevocable trust consent, they may petition the court for modification or termination of the trust — a route open to the beneficiaries acting together, without the statute requiring the settlor's consent or participation. Separately, Probate Code § 15404(a) provides that a trust may be modified or terminated by the written consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries without court approval of the modification or termination — a route that dispenses with a court petition entirely, but only when the settlor, not just the beneficiaries, joins in written consent. These are two different statutory mechanisms with two different sets of required participants and two different procedural paths (court petition versus no court at all), not two descriptions of the same option.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trust-modification framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust; other states' versions of the Uniform Trust Code or their own modification statutes can differ from California's in scope and detail, and this document addresses California's enactment only. This clause cites two different statutory sections, Probate Code §§ 15403(a) and 15404(a); both come from the same single source (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov), fetched twice independently using distinct User-Agent headers on separate requests, with identical text returned both times. This document does not determine whether any specific trust is, in fact, irrevocable, whether a specific group of people constitutes all of a specific trust's beneficiaries, or whether a specific settlor is alive, competent, and willing to join a written consent — those are fact- and instrument-specific questions this document does not resolve. A CourtListener case-law search on this topic returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125/day quota exhausted) at the time this document was researched, so no California case law is cited in this document; the clauses in this document rest on statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15403(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the beneficiary-consent, court-petition route
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), if all beneficiaries of an irrevocable trust consent, they may petition the court for modification or termination of the trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15404(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the settlor-and-beneficiary written-consent route, without court approval
citations.quote: A trust may be modified or terminated by the written consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries without court approval of the modification or termination.

clauses.title: The Material-Purpose Limitation on the All-Beneficiaries Court-Petition Route
clauses.body: The beneficiary-consent court-petition route described in Probate Code § 15403(a) is not unconditional. Under § 15403(b), if the continuance of the trust is necessary to carry out a material purpose of the trust, the trust cannot be modified or terminated even with all beneficiaries' consent unless the court, in its discretion, determines that the reason for doing so under the circumstances outweighs the interest in accomplishing that material purpose. A separate, additional limitation applies where the trust contains a valid spendthrift-type restraint on transfer of a beneficiary's interest under Probate Code §§ 15300-15309: § 15403(b) provides that such a trust may not be terminated unless the court determines there is good cause to do so, independent of the material-purpose balancing test.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trust-modification framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document does not determine whether any specific trust provision constitutes a 'material purpose' within the meaning of § 15403(b), whether the balance the statute describes favors modification or termination in any particular case, whether a specific trust's spendthrift-type language is a 'valid restraint on the transfer of a beneficiary's interest' under Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 15300), or what would constitute 'good cause' for a court in a specific case — those are fact-, instrument-, and case-specific determinations this document does not make. A CourtListener case-law search on the material-purpose doctrine returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125/day quota exhausted) at the time this document was researched; no California case law construing what counts as a 'material purpose' is cited in this document, though that phrase has been the subject of substantial published California case law that this document does not reach.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15403(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the material-purpose limitation on modification or termination by beneficiary consent
citations.quote: If the continuance of the trust is necessary to carry out a material purpose of the trust, the trust cannot be modified or terminated unless the court, in its discretion, determines that the reason for doing so under the circumstances outweighs the interest in accomplishing a material purpose of the trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15403(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the separate good-cause requirement for terminating a trust with a valid spendthrift-type restraint on transfer
citations.quote: If the trust is subject to a valid restraint on the transfer of a beneficiary’s interest as provided in Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 15300), the trust may not be terminated unless the court determines there is good cause to do so.

clauses.title: The Without-Court Route Requires the Settlor's Own Consent, Not Only the Beneficiaries'
clauses.body: Probate Code § 15404(a)'s without-court-approval route describes the written consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries — both, not either. Section 15404(b) addresses what happens when unanimity is incomplete on that route: if any beneficiary does not consent to the modification or termination of the trust, the court may modify or partially terminate the trust upon petition to the court by the other beneficiaries, with the consent of the settlor, if the interests of the beneficiaries who do not consent are not substantially impaired. Even this partial-consent variant, in other words, is framed around the settlor's consent being present; § 15404 does not describe a version of its own procedure in which beneficiaries proceed under that section without the settlor. A settlor who has died, or who lacks the capacity to consent, is accordingly not a participant § 15404 contemplates being able to supply; § 15403's all-beneficiaries court-petition route, described in a separate clause of this document, does not have a settlor-consent requirement built into its own text.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trust-modification framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust, and not a claim that a deceased or incapacitated settlor forecloses every path to modification or termination described in this document; it forecloses only the specific § 15404 without-court-approval and partial-consent routes described in this clause, which by their own terms require the settlor's consent. This document does not determine whether a specific settlor is, in fact, deceased, incapacitated, or otherwise unable to consent, or whether a specific proposed modification would 'substantially impair' a non-consenting beneficiary's interests within the meaning of § 15404(b) — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make. A CourtListener case-law search on this topic returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125/day quota exhausted) at the time this document was researched, so no California case law is cited in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15404(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the written-consent, without-court route requiring both the settlor and all beneficiaries
citations.quote: A trust may be modified or terminated by the written consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries without court approval of the modification or termination.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15404(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the partial-consent variant, which also requires the settlor's consent
citations.quote: If any beneficiary does not consent to the modification or termination of the trust, the court may modify or partially terminate the trust upon petition to the court by the other beneficiaries, with the consent of the settlor, if the interests of the beneficiaries who do not consent are not substantially impaired.

clauses.title: Limiting Whose Consent Is Needed When Remainder Beneficiaries Are Described Only as 'Heirs' or 'Next of Kin'
clauses.body: Both § 15403(c) and § 15404(c) address the same recurring drafting problem in identical language: where a trust provides for the disposition of principal to a class of persons described only as 'heirs' or 'next of kin' of the settlor, or using other words describing the class of all persons who would take under the rules of intestacy, obtaining every such person's consent to a modification or termination can be impractical, since the membership of that class is not fixed until the settlor's death. To address this, both sections give the court a narrowing power: the court may limit the class of beneficiaries whose consent is necessary to modify or terminate a trust to the beneficiaries who are reasonably likely to take under the circumstances. This narrowing power applies identically whether the beneficiaries are proceeding under § 15403's court-petition route or under § 15404's settlor-and-beneficiary route.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trust-modification framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document does not determine whether a specific trust's remainder-beneficiary language in fact falls within the 'heirs' or 'next of kin' class described in §§ 15403(c) and 15404(c), or which specific persons a court would find 'reasonably likely to take under the circumstances' in a given case — those are instrument- and fact-specific determinations this document does not make, and only a court can exercise the narrowing power these sections describe. A CourtListener case-law search on this topic returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125/day quota exhausted) at the time this document was researched, so no California case law construing 'reasonably likely to take' is cited in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15403(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's power to narrow the consenting class where beneficiaries are described only as heirs or next of kin
citations.quote: the court may limit the class of beneficiaries whose consent is necessary to modify or terminate a trust to the beneficiaries who are reasonably likely to take under the circumstances.

clauses.title: A Separate, Consent-Independent Basis: Circumstances the Settlor Did Not Know About or Anticipate
clauses.body: Probate Code § 15409 provides a statutory basis for court modification or termination that does not depend on beneficiary or settlor consent at all. On petition by a trustee or beneficiary, the court may modify the administrative or dispositive provisions of the trust or terminate the trust if, owing to circumstances not known to the settlor and not anticipated by the settlor, the continuation of the trust under its terms would defeat or substantially impair the accomplishment of the purposes of the trust. If necessary to carry out the trust's purposes in that situation, § 15409(a) further allows the court to order the trustee to do acts that are not authorized or are forbidden by the trust instrument. Section 15409(b) directs the court to consider any restraint on transfer of a beneficiary's interest as one factor in its decision, without that restraint by itself precluding the court from modifying or terminating the trust. This is a materially different statutory basis from the consent-based routes described elsewhere in this document: it can be invoked by a single trustee or a single beneficiary through a petition, without needing any other beneficiary's or the settlor's agreement, but only on the specific and narrower showing that unanticipated circumstances are defeating or substantially impairing the trust's purposes.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trust-modification framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document does not determine whether any specific circumstance was, in fact, unknown to or unanticipated by a specific settlor, or whether continuation of a specific trust under its existing terms would defeat or substantially impair that trust's purposes — those are fact-specific determinations only a court can make on a full record, and this document does not attempt to apply this standard to any actual trust. A CourtListener case-law search on this topic returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125/day quota exhausted) at the time this document was researched, so no California case law applying § 15409 is cited in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15409(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: court modification or termination for circumstances not known to or anticipated by the settlor
citations.quote: On petition by a trustee or beneficiary, the court may modify the administrative or dispositive provisions of the trust or terminate the trust if, owing to circumstances not known to the settlor and not anticipated by the settlor, the continuation of the trust under its terms would defeat or substantially impair the accomplishment of the purposes of the trust.

clauses.title: Court Termination, and a Trustee's Own Power to Terminate, a Trust That Has Become Too Small to Justify Its Administration Costs
clauses.body: Probate Code § 15408(a) provides another consent-independent basis: on petition by a trustee or beneficiary, if the court determines that the fair market value of the principal of a trust has become so low in relation to the cost of administration that continuation of the trust under its existing terms will defeat or substantially impair the accomplishment of its purposes, the court may, in its discretion and in a manner that conforms as nearly as possible to the intention of the settlor, order any of the following: termination of the trust, modification of the trust, or appointment of a new trustee. Separately, § 15408(b) gives the trustee a self-executing power that does not require a court petition at all: notwithstanding subdivision (a), if the fair market value of the principal of a trust does not exceed one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) in value, the trustee has the power to terminate the trust. Section 15408(c) confirms that a spendthrift-type restraint on transfer of a beneficiary's interest does not by itself prevent application of this section.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trust-modification framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. The $100,000 self-termination threshold in § 15408(b) reflects a 2024 amendment (effective January 1, 2025); this document does not represent that this threshold has always been $100,000 or that it will remain $100,000 going forward, and this document does not determine the fair market value of the principal of any specific trust or whether that value in fact falls at or below the statutory threshold. This document also does not determine whether a specific trust's administration costs are, in fact, disproportionate to its principal for purposes of § 15408(a)'s separate, no-dollar-threshold court-petition route. A CourtListener case-law search on this topic returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125/day quota exhausted) at the time this document was researched, so no California case law applying § 15408 is cited in this document.

citations.quote: if the court determines that the fair market value of the principal of a trust has become so low in relation to the cost of administration that continuation of the trust under its existing terms will defeat or substantially impair the accomplishment of its purposes, the court may, in its discretion and in a manner that conforms as nearly as possible to the intention of the settlor, order any of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15408(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trustee's own power to terminate a trust with principal not exceeding $100,000, without a court petition
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (a), if the fair market value of the principal of a trust does not exceed one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000) in value, the trustee has the power to terminate the trust.

clauses.title: How Trust Property Is Distributed When a Trust Is Terminated by Consent of the Settlor and All Beneficiaries
clauses.body: Probate Code § 15410 addresses how trust property is disposed of once a trust terminates, and treats termination by consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries as its own distinct category, separate from termination by revocation. Under § 15410(c), in the case of a trust that is terminated by the consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries, the property is disposed of as agreed by the settlor and all beneficiaries — the statute defers to whatever distribution those parties actually agreed to as part of consenting to the termination, rather than imposing a default distribution scheme on that category the way § 15410 does for revocation (subdivisions (a) and (b)) or for other cases (subdivision (d)).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's trust-modification framework — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific trust. This document does not determine what distribution terms any specific settlor and beneficiaries actually agreed to, or whether a specific termination in fact falls within § 15410(c)'s consent-based category rather than one of § 15410's other categories (revocation under subdivisions (a) or (b), or the residual category under subdivision (d)) — those are fact-specific determinations this document does not make. A CourtListener case-law search on this topic returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit response (125/day quota exhausted) at the time this document was researched, so no California case law applying § 15410 is cited in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15410(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: disposition of trust property on termination by consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries
citations.quote: In the case of a trust that is terminated by the consent of the settlor and all beneficiaries, as agreed by the settlor and all beneficiaries.

clauses.title: How This Document Differs From This Corpus's Trust Amendment and Trust Decanting Documents
clauses.body: This corpus's Trust Amendment document addresses a settlor's own statutory power under Probate Code § 15402 to amend a trust that remains revocable by that settlor alone, exercised by the settlor without needing any beneficiary's consent. This corpus's Trust Decanting document addresses a trustee's power under California's Uniform Trust Decanting Act (Probate Code § 19501 et seq.) to distribute principal from an existing irrevocable trust into a new trust with different terms, exercised by an authorized fiduciary without needing beneficiary consent as a precondition, subject to a notice-and-objection process. This document, by contrast, addresses modification or termination of an irrevocable trust — potentially {{trustName}} — through the consent-based mechanisms of Probate Code §§ 15403-15404 (which in every version require at least one category of person's affirmative consent: all beneficiaries, or the settlor and all beneficiaries), and the related, consent-independent court mechanisms of §§ 15408-15409 (which instead require a specific statutory showing: unanticipated changed circumstances, or disproportionate administration costs). None of the mechanisms described in this document is available merely because a settlor, trustee, or beneficiary of {{trustName}} would prefer different terms; each requires either the specific consent, or the specific statutory showing, that the corresponding clause of this document describes.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet explains California Family Code section 3047, the statute that addresses child custody and visitation orders when a parent or party is activated to military duty, mobilized, or deployed. It covers what the statute says about: modification of existing orders due to a party's military absence, the temporary and reversible nature of any resulting order change, visitation rights the court may extend to a stepparent, grandparent, or other family member during a deploying party's absence, expedited-hearing and remote-participation options before a party departs, and the statute's effect on continuing court jurisdiction under the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (UCCJEA) during deployment. It does NOT calculate or propose a specific custody or visitation schedule for {{childName}}, does not tell {{parent1Name}} or {{parent2Name}} whether to file a motion or what outcome to request, and does not substitute for advice from a licensed attorney about a particular family's situation. This sheet is distinct from a move-away/relocation custody information sheet, which addresses a parent's voluntary decision to relocate with a child for reasons unrelated to military orders, and from an emergency custody order information sheet, which addresses ex parte emergency relief generally. This sheet is not a substitute for reading the full text of Family Code section 3047 or for consulting the court or a licensed attorney about a specific case.

clauses.title: Military Absence Alone Is Not Grounds for Modification
clauses.body: Under California Family Code section 3047(a), a party's absence, relocation, or failure to comply with an existing custody or visitation order does not, by itself, justify modifying that order when the reason is the party's activation to military duty or temporary duty, mobilization in support of a combat or other military operation, or military deployment out of state.
clauses.gap: The statute states this rule as a limit on using military absence alone as grounds for modification; it does not exempt a party from every possible ground for modification, and it does not define how a court weighs this factor against other best-interest considerations in a contested proceeding. No case law analysis was performed for this clause (see the CourtListener research-limitation note in the document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(a)
citations.quote: A party’s absence, relocation, or failure to comply with custody and visitation orders shall not, by itself, be sufficient to justify a modification of a custody or visitation order if the reason for the absence, relocation, or failure to comply is the party’s activation to military duty or temporary duty, mobilization in support of combat or other military operation, or military deployment out of state.

clauses.title: Modifications During Deployment Are Temporary, With a Presumption of Reversion
clauses.body: Under California Family Code section 3047(b)(1)-(2), when a party with sole or joint physical custody or visitation receives temporary duty, deployment, or mobilization orders that require moving a substantial distance or that otherwise materially affect the party's ability to exercise custody or visitation, any resulting modification of the existing custody order is deemed a temporary order made without prejudice. When that temporary order is reviewed upon the party's return, there is a presumption that the custody order will revert to what was in place before the modification, unless the court determines reversion is not in the child's best interest. The statute also provides that the court is not to order a child custody evaluation under Family Code section 3111 or Evidence Code section 730 as part of that return review, unless the party opposing reversion makes a prima facie showing that reversion is not in the child's best interest.
clauses.gap: The statute does not define 'substantial distance' or specify how a court determines whether an effect on custody or visitation ability is 'material'; those determinations are left to case-by-case application. No case law analysis was performed for this clause (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time — see document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(1)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(1)
citations.quote: If a party with sole or joint physical custody or visitation receives temporary duty, deployment, or mobilization orders from the military that require the party to move a substantial distance from the party’s residence or otherwise has a material effect on the ability of the party to exercise custody or visitation rights, any necessary modification of the existing custody order shall be deemed a temporary custody order made without prejudice, which shall be subject to review and reconsideration upon the return of the party from military deployment, mobilization, or temporary duty.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(2)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(2)
citations.quote: If the temporary order is reviewed upon return of the party from military deployment, mobilization, or temporary duty, there shall be a presumption that the custody order shall revert to the order that was in place before the modification, unless the court determines that it is not in the best interest of the child. The court shall not, as part of its review of the temporary order upon the return of the deploying party, order a child custody evaluation under Section 3111 of this code or Section 730 of the Evidence Code, unless the party opposing reversion of the order makes a prima facie showing that reversion is not in the best interest of the child.

clauses.title: Visitation for a Stepparent, Grandparent, or Other Family Member During Deployment
clauses.body: Under California Family Code section 3047(b)(3), when a court makes a temporary custody order because of a party's military duty, deployment, or mobilization, the court is to consider appropriate orders to help the relocating party maintain frequent and continuing contact with the child. On a motion by the relocating party, the court may grant reasonable visitation rights to a stepparent, grandparent, or other family member if the court finds a preexisting bonded relationship between that family member and the child such that visitation is in the child's best interest, finds the visitation will facilitate the child's contact with the relocating party, and balances the child's interest in that visitation against the parents' right to exercise parental authority. The statute states that this provision does not increase the family member's independent authority to seek visitation, and that visitation granted to a nonparent under this provision does not affect the calculation of child support.
clauses.gap: This family-member visitation right arises only on a motion by the relocating (deploying) party in this specific temporary-order context under section 3047(b)(3); the statute expressly states it does not create an independent right for a stepparent, grandparent, or other family member to seek visitation on their own. It does not describe how courts apply the three required findings in practice. No case law analysis was performed for this clause (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time — see document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(3)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(3)
citations.quote: Upon a motion by the relocating party, the court may grant reasonable visitation rights to a stepparent, grandparent, or other family member if the court does all of the following:(i) Finds that there is a preexisting relationship between the family member and the child that has engendered a bond such that visitation is in the best interest of the child.(ii) Finds that the visitation will facilitate the child’s contact with the relocating party.(iii) Balances the interest of the child in having visitation with the family member against the right of the parents to exercise parental authority.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(3)(C)-(D)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(b)(3)(C)-(D)
citations.quote: This paragraph does not increase the authority of the persons described in subparagraph (B) to seek visitation orders independently.(D) The granting of visitation rights to a nonparent pursuant to subparagraph (B) shall not impact the calculation of child support.

clauses.title: Expedited Hearings and Remote Participation Before Deployment
clauses.body: Under California Family Code section 3047(c), when a party's deployment, mobilization, or temporary duty will materially affect that party's ability, or anticipated ability, to appear in person at a regularly scheduled hearing, the court is to do either of two things on the party's motion: hold an expedited hearing to determine custody and visitation issues before the party departs, or allow the party to present testimony and evidence and participate in court-ordered child custody mediation by electronic means — including telephone, video teleconferencing, or the internet — to the extent that technology is reasonably available to the court and protects the due process rights of all parties.
clauses.gap: The statute conditions electronic participation on the technology being 'reasonably available to the court,' a standard that is not further defined and may vary by county and courtroom. No case law analysis was performed for this clause (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time — see document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(c)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(c)
citations.quote: If a party’s deployment, mobilization, or temporary duty will have a material effect on the party’s ability, or anticipated ability, to appear in person at a regularly scheduled hearing, the court shall do either of the following:(1) Upon motion of the party, hold an expedited hearing to determine custody and visitation issues prior to the departure of the party.(2) Upon motion of the party, allow the party to present testimony and evidence and participate in court-ordered child custody mediation by electronic means, including, but not limited to, telephone, video teleconferencing, or the internet, to the extent that this technology is reasonably available to the court and protects the due process rights of all parties.

clauses.title: Effect on Continuing Court Jurisdiction Under the UCCJEA
clauses.body: Family Code section 3047(d) states that a relocation by a nondeploying parent during the period of a deployed parent's absence, while a temporary modification order for a parenting plan is in effect, does not by itself terminate the court's exclusive and continuing jurisdiction. Section 3047(e) states that when a California court has issued a custody or visitation order, a child's absence from the state during a parent's deployment is considered a 'temporary absence' for purposes of the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (Family Code section 3400 et seq.), and the court retains exclusive continuing jurisdiction under Family Code section 3422. Section 3047(f) states that a parent's deployment cannot be used as a basis to assert inconvenient forum under Family Code section 3427.
clauses.gap: These provisions describe how deployment interacts with the UCCJEA's jurisdiction and inconvenient-forum rules in general terms; they do not resolve jurisdiction disputes involving courts of other states or countries, which depend on the full text of Family Code sections 3400–3465 and that jurisdiction's own law. No case law analysis was performed for this clause (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time — see document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(d)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(d)
citations.quote: A relocation by a nondeploying parent during a period of a deployed parent’s absence while a temporary modification order for a parenting plan is in effect shall not, by itself, terminate the exclusive and continuing jurisdiction of the court for purposes of later determining custody or parenting time under this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(e)-(f)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(e)-(f)
citations.quote: When a court of this state has issued a custody or visitation order, the absence of a child from this state during the deployment of a parent shall be considered a “temporary absence” for purposes of the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction and Enforcement Act (Part 3 (commencing with Section 3400)), and the court shall retain exclusive continuing jurisdiction under Section 3422.(f) The deployment of a parent shall not be used as a basis to assert inconvenience of the forum under Section 3427.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: Deployment, Mobilization, and Temporary Duty
clauses.body: Family Code section 3047(g) defines three terms used throughout the statute. 'Deployment' means the temporary transfer of a member of the Armed Forces in active-duty status in support of combat or some other military operation. 'Mobilization' means the transfer of a member of the National Guard or Military Reserve to extended active-duty status, but does not include National Guard or Military Reserve annual training. 'Temporary duty' means the transfer of a servicemember from one military base to a different location, usually another base, for a limited period of time to accomplish training or to assist in the performance of a noncombat mission.
clauses.gap: These definitions apply only 'for purposes of this section' (Family Code section 3047) and may not carry the same meaning in other statutes or in federal military law such as the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. National Guard or Military Reserve annual training is expressly excluded from 'mobilization.' No case law analysis was performed for this clause (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time — see document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(g)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(g)
citations.quote: “Deployment” means the temporary transfer of a member of the Armed Forces in active-duty status in support of combat or some other military operation.(2) “Mobilization” means the transfer of a member of the National Guard or Military Reserve to extended active-duty status, but does not include National Guard or Military Reserve annual training.(3) “Temporary duty” means the transfer of a servicemember from one military base to a different location, usually another base, for a limited period of time to accomplish training or to assist in the performance of a noncombat mission.

clauses.title: Statement of Legislative Intent
clauses.body: Family Code section 3047(h) states that it is the intent of the Legislature that section 3047 provide a fair, efficient, and expeditious process to resolve child custody and visitation issues when a party receives temporary duty, deployment, or mobilization orders, and at the time the party returns and moves to revert to the prior custody order. The statute states the Legislature's intent that family courts, to the extent feasible within existing resources and court practices, prioritize the calendaring of these cases, avoid unnecessary delay or continuances, and ensure that parties who serve in the military are not penalized for their service by delay in appropriate access to their children.
clauses.gap: A legislative-intent statement expresses purpose and expectation; it directs courts on calendaring priorities 'to the extent feasible within existing resources and court practices' but does not itself create an enforceable deadline or a specific remedy if a court does not prioritize a case. No case law analysis was performed for this clause (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time — see document-level disclosure); this clause is based on statutory text only.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(h)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3047(h)
citations.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature that this section provide a fair, efficient, and expeditious process to resolve child custody and visitation issues when a party receives temporary duty, deployment, or mobilization orders from the military, as well as at the time that the party returns from service and files a motion to revert back to the custody order in place before the deployment. The Legislature intends that family courts shall, to the extent feasible within existing resources and court practices, prioritize the calendaring of these cases, avoid unnecessary delay or continuances, and ensure that parties who serve in the military are not penalized for their service by a delay in appropriate access to their children.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes a specific, narrow rule of California law: the prohibition on requiring, as a condition of getting or keeping a job, a promise about whether {{employeeName}} will or will not join or remain a member of a labor organization or an employer organization. This rule is codified at California Labor Code §§ 920-923, sometimes referred to by the older term "yellow-dog contract" prohibition. It states facts about what that statute declares void, what conduct it makes a misdemeanor, and how a related federal statute treats the same subject. It is not itself a labor organization membership agreement, a union authorization card, a collective bargaining agreement, or a determination that any particular promise, policy, or practice at {{companyName}} does or does not violate this law. It does not tell {{employeeName}} or {{companyName}} what to do about any particular hiring decision, employment application, or workplace dispute. It is also distinct from this project's Restriction on Requiring Arbitration as a Condition of Employment information sheet, which describes a different California statute (Labor Code § 432.6) addressing a different condition an employer might try to impose at hiring — arbitration agreements, not labor organization membership.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Promise"
clauses.body: The chapter containing this prohibition opens with a definitions section. It gives the word "promise," as used throughout the chapter, a deliberately broad meaning: the term covers not only a formal promise but also an undertaking, contract, or agreement, and it applies regardless of whether that promise, undertaking, contract, or agreement was written or oral, or express or implied. This means the prohibition described in the following clauses is not limited to a signed document — an oral or implied understanding between an employer and an employee or applicant can fall within the same statutory definition.
clauses.gap: This section defines "promise" but does not define "labor organization" or "employer organization" anywhere in this chapter of the Labor Code — those terms are used throughout §§ 921-923 without a chapter-specific statutory definition, so their scope (for example, whether a given professional association or works council would qualify) is not resolved by this chapter's text alone. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 920 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, chapter definition of "promise"
citations.quote: includes promise, undertaking, contract, or agreement, whether written or oral, express or implied.

clauses.title: Core Prohibition on Union-Membership Promises
clauses.body: California law declares that a promise made after August 21, 1933, between an employee or prospective employee and an employer, prospective employer, or any other person, is contrary to public policy if either party promises any of three things: (a) to join or remain a member of a labor organization or an employer organization; (b) not to join or not to remain a member of a labor organization or an employer organization; or (c) to withdraw from an employment relation if the person joins or remains a member of a labor organization or an employer organization. The statute's own text covers both directions — a promise to join a labor organization and a promise not to join one are both listed as contrary to public policy — and it applies at the hiring stage ("prospective employee," "prospective employer") as well as during an existing employment relationship.
clauses.gap: The statute declares such a promise "contrary to public policy"; it does not, in this section's own text, create a private civil cause of action for damages against an employer who extracts such a promise — the consequence the statute's own text spells out is addressed in the next clause. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions construing Labor Code §§ 921-923 was attempted for this document and returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, quota exhausted) rather than results, so no case law confirming or narrowing this reading of the statute's plain text has been checked here.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 921 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, promises against public policy regarding labor organization membership
citations.quote: Every promise made after August 21, 1933, between any employee or prospective employee and his employer, prospective employer or any other person is contrary to public policy if either party thereto promises any of the following:(a) To join or to remain a member of a labor organization or to join or remain a member of an employer organization,(b) Not to join or not to remain a member of a labor organization or of an employer organization,(c) To withdraw from an employment relation in the event that he joins or remains a member of a labor organization or of an employer organization.

clauses.title: The Promise Provides No Basis for Court Relief
clauses.body: The same statutory section that lists the three prohibited promises also states the specific legal consequence for them: such a promise does not afford any basis for a court to grant legal or equitable relief against a person who made it, and it likewise does not afford a basis for relief against any other person who advises, urges, or induces either party to disregard the promise — so long as that advice, urging, or inducement is given without fraud or violence or a threat of fraud or violence. In effect, the statute makes the promise itself legally inert: an employer cannot go to court to enforce it, and a person who counsels an employee to break such a promise is protected from suit over that advice under the same statutory sentence.
clauses.gap: The statute's carve-out withdrawing this protection when a person's advice, urging, or inducement involves "fraud or violence or threat thereof" is not itself defined further in this chapter's text — where the line falls between protected advice and disqualifying conduct is not answered by the statute's own words. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation, and not a claim that any particular advice given to any particular reader falls on one side of that line or the other.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 921 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, unenforceability of a prohibited labor-organization-membership promise
citations.quote: Such promise shall not afford any basis for the granting of legal or equitable relief by any court against a party to such promise, or against any other persons who advise, urge, or induce, without fraud or violence or threat thereof, either party thereto to act in disregard of such promise.

clauses.title: Coercion as a Condition of Employment Is a Misdemeanor
clauses.body: A separate section of the same chapter addresses active coercion rather than a mere promise: it makes it a crime for any person, agent, or officer to coerce or compel another person to enter into a written or verbal agreement not to join or become a member of any labor organization, when that coercion is used as a condition of securing employment or of continuing in employment. The statute's own text classifies this conduct as a misdemeanor. Unlike the preceding section, which addresses the promise itself and its unenforceability in court, this section addresses the act of coercing or compelling someone to make such a promise, and attaches criminal liability to that act.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text names the conduct a misdemeanor but does not, in this section, specify a fine amount, a jail-term range, or which government office is responsible for charging it — those particulars, if any apply specifically to this section, are not stated in the text of Labor Code § 922 itself and were not independently researched for this document. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular person's conduct meets or fails to meet this section's definition of coercion or compulsion.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 922 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, misdemeanor for coercing a promise not to join a labor organization
citations.quote: Any person or agent or officer thereof who coerces or compels any person to enter into an agreement, written or verbal, not to join or become a member of any labor organization, as a condition of securing employment or continuing in the employment of any such person is guilty of a misdemeanor.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own Declaration of Public Policy
clauses.body: The same chapter closes its core prohibition with the Legislature's own explanation of the policy behind it. The statute's text states that negotiation of terms and conditions of labor should result from voluntary agreement between employer and employees, and — after describing employers' ability to organize into corporate and other forms of capital control, and the individual unorganized worker's resulting difficulty in exercising real liberty of contract — declares that it is necessary for an individual worker to have full freedom of association, self-organization, and choice of representatives to negotiate the terms and conditions of employment, free from an employer's interference, restraint, or coercion in that self-organization or in other concerted activities for collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection.
clauses.gap: This section is framed by its own text as an interpretive aid — "in the interpretation and application of this chapter, the public policy of this State is declared as follows" — rather than as a standalone operative rule with its own separate remedy; how much independent legal weight this declaration carries beyond interpreting §§ 921 and 922 is a question this document does not resolve, and a CourtListener search for judicial decisions construing this section returned a rate-limit error (quota exhausted) rather than results, so no case law on that question was checked here. This is California law only, described here as evidence of what California law provides — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 923 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, declared public policy favoring freedom of association and self-organization
citations.quote: it is necessary that the individual workman have full freedom of association, self-organization, and designation of representatives of his own choosing, to negotiate the terms and conditions of his employment, and that he shall be free from the interference, restraint, or coercion of employers of labor, or their agents, in the designation of such representatives or in self-organization or in other concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining or other mutual aid or protection.

clauses.title: Comparison to the Federal National Labor Relations Act
clauses.body: Separately from this California statute, a federal law — the National Labor Relations Act — also addresses discrimination tied to union membership in hiring and employment. It makes it an unfair labor practice for a covered employer, by discrimination in regard to hire or tenure of employment or any term or condition of employment, to encourage or discourage membership in any labor organization. Unlike the California statute described in the preceding clauses, which voids the prohibited promise and criminalizes coercion to obtain it, the federal statute is enforced through a different mechanism entirely: an unfair-labor-practice charge processed by the National Labor Relations Board, not a state civil-void doctrine or a state misdemeanor prosecution.
clauses.gap: The National Labor Relations Act's coverage has statutory exclusions — for example, for agricultural laborers, domestic-service workers, and independent contractors, defined in a different section of the same federal title (29 U.S.C. § 152) — that were not independently fetched or verified for this document, so this clause does not state whether any particular reader's work relationship falls inside or outside federal NLRA coverage. This document also does not attempt to resolve any question of whether or how federal law might preempt or coexist with the California statute described elsewhere in this document for a particular employer; a CourtListener search for judicial decisions on that preemption question returned a rate-limit error (quota exhausted) rather than results, so no case law on it was checked here. This is a federal statute, described here only as a separately confirmed comparison point — not a claim about which law, state or federal, governs any particular reader's situation.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 158(a)(3) (National Labor Relations Act) (Cornell Legal Information Institute text)
citations.cite: 29 U.S.C. § 158(a)(3), unfair labor practice to discriminate regarding hire to encourage or discourage union membership
citations.quote: by discrimination in regard to hire or tenure of employment or any term or condition of employment to encourage or discourage membership in any labor organization

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Declaration
clauses.body: This information sheet describes patent term adjustment ("PTA") under 35 U.S.C. § 154(b) — the federal statutory mechanism that extends the term of a utility or plant patent, day for day, to compensate for certain delays in the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office's own examination process. It is prepared with reference to {{patentDescription}}, held by or applied for by {{patentHolderName}}, with an application filing date of {{filingDate}}. This sheet describes the general operation of the three statutory delay guarantees in § 154(b)(1), the limitations that reduce or cap an adjustment in § 154(b)(2), and the Patent and Trademark Office's determination and appeal procedure in § 154(b)(3)-(4); it does not calculate, request, contest, or verify any specific number of adjustment days for {{patentDescription}}, which depends on prosecution-history facts (the specific dates of every Office action, response, and procedural event in that application's file) that this sheet does not contain. This document is distinct from the corpus's existing Provisional Patent Application, Patent Assignment, Patent License, Patent Infringement, and False Patent Marking documents, none of which address how long a patent's term lasts or how that term can be lengthened. It is also distinct from patent term extension under 35 U.S.C. § 156 (a separate mechanism compensating for regulatory review delay, most commonly used for pharmaceutical and other FDA-regulated products) and from the term of a design patent under 35 U.S.C. § 173, neither of which this sheet addresses. This sheet is educational only; it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed patent attorney or registered patent practitioner, and it does not itself request, calculate, or contest any patent term adjustment before the Patent and Trademark Office.

clauses.title: The Baseline 20-Year Term and What Adjustment Extends
clauses.body: For a utility or plant patent, federal law sets the baseline term at 20 years, running from the date the application was filed (or, where the application claims priority to an earlier-filed application, from the date that earliest application was filed) and continuing to the date the patent issues. Patent term adjustment under § 154(b) operates on top of this baseline: it does not change how the 20-year period is measured, but instead adds days to the end of that period — one day for each day of certain kinds of Patent and Trademark Office delay described in the guarantees below, subject to the limitations described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general filing-date-to-issuance term rule in § 154(a)(2) and does not address the priority-disregarding rule of § 154(a)(3), continuing applications, terminal disclaimers, or the pre-1995 transitional term rule in § 154(c) for patents in force when the current 20-year-from-filing measure took effect, none of which is restated here.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, contents and term of patent; provisional rights — term
citations.quote: Subject to the payment of fees under this title, such grant shall be for a term beginning on the date on which the patent issues and ending 20 years from the date on which the application for the patent was filed in the United States or, if the application contains a specific reference to an earlier filed application or applications under section 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c), from the date on which the earliest such application was filed.

clauses.title: The First Guarantee — Prompt Patent and Trademark Office Responses
clauses.body: The first of three statutory delay guarantees addresses the Patent and Trademark Office's own responsiveness at specific procedural checkpoints. It applies if the Office fails to meet deadlines that include providing an initial notification or notice of allowance within 14 months of filing, or responding to a reply or an appeal within 4 months of it being filed. Where the Office misses one of these listed deadlines, the statute extends the patent's term one day for each day between the deadline and the date the Office actually takes the missed action.
clauses.gap: This clause summarizes only two of the four listed checkpoints in § 154(b)(1)(A) — the 14-month initial-notification deadline and the 4-month reply/appeal-response deadline — and omits the two remaining checkpoints (timely action after a Patent Trial and Appeal Board or court decision, and timely issuance after the issue fee is paid), as well as the cross-reference to the overlap and applicant-delay limitations in § 154(b)(2) that can reduce or cap any extension calculated under this guarantee.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — guarantee of prompt Patent and Trademark Office responses
citations.quote: provide at least one of the notifications under section 132 or a notice of allowance under section 151 not later than 14 months after—

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)(A)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — 4-month reply/appeal response deadline
citations.quote: respond to a reply under section 132, or to an appeal taken under section 134, within 4 months after the date on which the reply was filed or the appeal was taken;

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — day-for-day extension for a missed checkpoint
citations.quote: the term of the patent shall be extended 1 day for each day after the end of the period specified in clause (i), (ii), (iii), or (iv), as the case may be, until the action described in such clause is taken.

clauses.title: The Second Guarantee — No More Than 3-Year Application Pendency
clauses.body: The second statutory guarantee addresses the total time an application spends pending before the Patent and Trademark Office, independent of any specific missed checkpoint. If the Office fails to issue a patent within 3 years of the application's actual U.S. filing date (or, for an international application, the date the national stage commenced), the term is extended one day for each day beyond that 3-year period until the patent issues. This 3-year count itself excludes certain periods, including time consumed by a request for continued examination that the applicant made, time consumed by specified interference-type proceedings, secrecy orders, or appellate review, and delay in processing that the applicant itself requested.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general 3-year guarantee and its request-for-continued-examination exclusion in § 154(b)(1)(B)(i); it does not restate the full text of the other two listed exclusions (delay from certain proceedings/orders/appellate review, and applicant-requested processing delay other than as permitted elsewhere in the statute), nor the separate applicant-delay reduction in § 154(b)(2)(C) that operates independently of these exclusions and is addressed in a separate clause of this document.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — guarantee of no more than 3-year application pendency
citations.quote: if the issue of an original patent is delayed due to the failure of the United States Patent and Trademark Office to issue a patent within 3 years after the actual filing date of the application under section 111(a) in the United States or, in the case of an international application, the date of commencement of the national stage under section 371 in the international application, not including—

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)(B)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — continued-examination exclusion from the 3-year count
citations.quote: any time consumed by continued examination of the application requested by the applicant under section 132(b);

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — day-for-day extension beyond the 3-year period
citations.quote: the term of the patent shall be extended 1 day for each day after the end of that 3-year period until the patent is issued.

clauses.title: The Third Guarantee — Derivation Proceedings, Secrecy Orders, and Successful Appeals
clauses.body: The third statutory guarantee covers delay caused by three specific kinds of proceedings outside the applicant's control: a derivation proceeding, a secrecy order imposed on the application, or an appellate review by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board or a federal court that results in a decision reversing an adverse determination of patentability. Where one of these applies, the term is extended one day for each day of the pendency of the proceeding, order, or review, without the 3-year threshold that applies to the second guarantee.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general rule without addressing how the statute defines when a derivation proceeding or secrecy order 'begins' and 'ends' for purposes of counting pendency days, or how this third guarantee interacts with the overlap-limitation rule in § 154(b)(2)(A) when the same delay period also qualifies under the first or second guarantee.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)(C) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — guarantee of adjustments for derivation proceedings, secrecy orders, and appeals
citations.quote: if the issue of an original patent is delayed due to—

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)(C)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — derivation proceeding as a qualifying delay
citations.quote: a proceeding under section 135(a);

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)(C) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — day-for-day extension for the pendency period
citations.quote: the term of the patent shall be extended 1 day for each day of the pendency of the proceeding, order, or review, as the case may be.

clauses.title: No Double-Counting for Overlapping Delay
clauses.body: The three guarantees described above can, on the same application, point to overlapping stretches of calendar time. The statute does not let those overlapping days be counted more than once: to the extent periods of delay attributable to the different guarantees overlap, the total adjustment is capped at the actual number of days the patent's issuance was in fact delayed, rather than the sum of the days computed separately under each guarantee.
clauses.gap: The statute states this overlap rule in a single general sentence and does not itself define what counts as 'overlap' between two differently-defined delay periods; how a period counted under the first guarantee (missed checkpoints) is compared against a period counted under the second guarantee (3-year pendency) for overlap purposes is a question the statutory text leaves to Patent and Trademark Office regulation and interpretation that this sheet does not address, and CourtListener case-law research on this point was not completed for this document (a search request returned a rate-limit error rather than results).

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — limitation on overlapping periods of delay
citations.quote: To the extent that periods of delay attributable to grounds specified in paragraph (1) overlap, the period of any adjustment granted under this subsection shall not exceed the actual number of days the issuance of the patent was delayed.

clauses.title: No Adjustment Beyond a Terminal Disclaimer
clauses.body: Where a patent's term has been disclaimed beyond a specified date — most commonly through a terminal disclaimer filed to overcome an obviousness-type double patenting rejection — the statute does not permit any adjustment under § 154(b) to push the term past the date named in that disclaimer, regardless of how many adjustment days the delay guarantees would otherwise produce.
clauses.gap: This clause states the disclaimer cap itself; it does not describe the separate legal requirements for filing or the effect of a terminal disclaimer, which are governed by other statutory and regulatory provisions not addressed in this document.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(2)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — disclaimed term limitation
citations.quote: No patent the term of which has been disclaimed beyond a specified date may be adjusted under this section beyond the expiration date specified in the disclaimer.

clauses.title: Reduction for the Applicant's Own Lack of Reasonable Efforts
clauses.body: Patent term adjustment is not a one-way benefit that runs regardless of the applicant's own conduct. The statute reduces any adjustment otherwise available under the three guarantees by the amount of time during which the applicant failed to engage in reasonable efforts to conclude prosecution of the application. For adjustments calculated under the second guarantee (the 3-year pendency guarantee) specifically, the statute deems the applicant to have failed to engage in reasonable efforts for any cumulative period, in excess of 3 months, that the applicant takes to respond to an Office notice raising a rejection, objection, argument, or other request — measured from the date the Office gave or mailed that notice.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general reduction rule and the specific 3-month response-time deeming rule tied to the second guarantee; it does not address the Director's separate regulatory authority to define what else constitutes a failure of reasonable efforts, or the reinstatement procedure that lets an applicant recover some of a reduced period on a showing of due care, which is addressed in a separate clause.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(2)(C)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — reduction for applicant's failure to engage in reasonable efforts
citations.quote: The period of adjustment of the term of a patent under paragraph (1) shall be reduced by a period equal to the period of time during which the applicant failed to engage in reasonable efforts to conclude prosecution of the application.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(2)(C)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — deemed failure of reasonable efforts for responses exceeding 3 months
citations.quote: With respect to adjustments to patent term made under the authority of paragraph (1)(B), an applicant shall be deemed to have failed to engage in reasonable efforts to conclude processing or examination of an application for the cumulative total of any periods of time in excess of 3 months that are taken to respond to a notice from the Office making any rejection, objection, argument, or other request, measuring such 3-month period from the date the notice was given or mailed to the applicant.

clauses.title: How the Adjustment Is Determined, Reconsidered, and Reviewed
clauses.body: The Director of the Patent and Trademark Office, not the applicant, makes the initial determination of how many days of patent term adjustment a given application has earned, and must transmit notice of that determination no later than the date the patent issues. The applicant has one opportunity to request reconsideration of that determination. If the applicant remains dissatisfied after reconsideration, the statute's exclusive remedy is a civil action against the Director in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, filed within 180 days of the Director's decision on reconsideration; a favorable final judgment requires the Director to alter the patent's term accordingly. A third party has no statutory right to appeal or challenge a patent term adjustment determination before the patent is granted.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the reconsideration and judicial-review pathway; it does not address the separate procedural regulations the Director is directed to prescribe for applying for an adjustment in the first place, nor the reinstatement mechanism in § 154(b)(3)(C) that can restore part of a reduced adjustment period on a due-care showing, both of which sit outside the scope of this sheet.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(3)(B)(i)-(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — Director's determination and applicant's reconsideration opportunity
citations.quote: provide the applicant one opportunity to request reconsideration of any patent term adjustment determination made by the Director.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(4)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — exclusive judicial remedy in the Eastern District of Virginia
citations.quote: An applicant dissatisfied with the Director’s decision on the applicant’s request for reconsideration under paragraph (3)(B)(ii) shall have exclusive remedy by a civil action against the Director filed in the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia within 180 days after the date of the Director’s decision on the applicant’s request for reconsideration.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(4)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, adjustment of patent term — no pre-grant third-party challenge
citations.quote: The determination of a patent term adjustment under this subsection shall not be subject to appeal or challenge by a third party prior to the grant of the patent.

clauses.title: What This Adjustment Mechanism Does Not Cover
clauses.body: Section 154(b)'s day-for-day adjustment mechanism is written against the backdrop of the utility/plant patent term described above — a term measured in years from the application's filing date. A design patent's term is set by an entirely separate statute using a different measure: a design patent's term runs 15 years from the date of grant, not from filing, and § 154(b)'s adjustment mechanism is not written to apply to it. This adjustment mechanism is also a distinct legal concept from patent term extension under 35 U.S.C. § 156, which compensates for regulatory review delay (most often FDA review) rather than Patent and Trademark Office examination delay, uses different eligibility criteria and a different application procedure, and is not addressed in this document.
clauses.gap: This clause draws a scope boundary using the plain text of § 154(a)-(b) and § 173; it does not independently research or cite the text of § 156 (patent term extension for regulatory review delay), so no specific representation is made here about that separate statute's requirements beyond noting that it exists and addresses a different kind of delay.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 173 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, term of design patent
citations.quote: Patents for designs shall be granted for the term of 15 years from the date of grant.
