clauses.title: About This Workers' Rights in Emergencies Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Workers' Rights in Emergencies — Information Sheet describes California Labor Code section 1139, a statute added by SB 1044 (Stats. 2022, ch. 829) that took effect January 1, 2023, as that statute relates to the working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.

Section 1139 does two specific things: first, it bars an employer from taking or threatening adverse action against an employee for refusing to report to, or leaving, a workplace or worksite within an area affected by an "emergency condition" (a defined term covering natural-disaster or criminal-act peril, or an evacuation order) where the employee has a reasonable belief the workplace or worksite is unsafe; second, it bars an employer from preventing an employee from accessing a mobile device or other communications device during an emergency condition to seek help, assess safety, or check on someone's safety. The statute lists thirteen categories of employees to whom the first protection does not apply, ties the employee's notice duty to whether advance notice is feasible, and states that it is not intended to apply once an emergency condition's imminent and ongoing risk has ceased.

This is narrower than it may sound. Section 1139's own text does not create a paid-leave entitlement, an accrual bank, a certification or medical-documentation process, a minimum-service or employer-size eligibility threshold, or a job-guarantee/reinstatement right of the kind found in leave statutes such as the California Family Rights Act or the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act paid sick leave law — both covered by this corpus's own separate information sheets. It is, on its own text, an anti-retaliation and device-access statute keyed to a specific factual trigger (an emergency condition), not a scheduled or approved absence benefit. It is also distinct from this corpus's Right to Refuse Hazardous Work information sheet, which describes a different, older statute (Labor Code §§ 6310-6312) tied to a safety-standard violation rather than to a natural-disaster, criminal-act, or evacuation-order emergency condition, and from this corpus's Workplace Violence Prevention Plan information sheet, which describes an employer's affirmative planning duty rather than an individual employee's right to leave or refuse to report.

This information sheet states facts about what section 1139's own text says. It is not legal advice, does not determine that any "emergency condition" exists or existed at any particular time or place, does not determine that any employee's belief that a workplace or worksite was unsafe was or was not reasonable, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney or the California Labor Commissioner's Office about a specific situation.

clauses.title: The Defined Term "Emergency Condition"
clauses.body: Labor Code section 1139 applies only when an "emergency condition" exists, and the statute defines that term specifically rather than leaving it to general usage. The statute's own text defines it as either of two things: conditions of disaster or extreme peril to the safety of persons or property at the workplace or worksite caused by natural forces or a criminal act, or an order to evacuate a workplace, a worksite, a worker's home, or the school of a worker's child due to natural disaster or a criminal act. The statute's own text then expressly carves out one thing the term does not include: a health pandemic. This chapter's protections accordingly do not extend, by the statute's own terms, to a pandemic-driven workplace-safety dispute, however serious.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text does not further define "extreme peril," "disaster," or how localized or widespread a natural-forces or criminal-act condition must be to qualify, and this research session did not independently verify any published California appellate decision construing those terms because a CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted) rather than results, so this clause states only what the statute's own text says. This document does not determine that any particular event was or was not an "emergency condition" within the statute's definition.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: “Emergency condition” means the existence of either of the following: (i) Conditions of disaster or extreme peril to the safety of persons or property at the workplace or worksite caused by natural forces or a criminal act. (ii) An order to evacuate a workplace, a worksite, a worker’s home, or the school of a worker’s child due to natural disaster or a criminal act.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(a)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: “Emergency condition” does not include a health pandemic.

clauses.title: The "Reasonable Belief the Workplace Is Unsafe" Standard
clauses.body: Beyond an emergency condition existing at all, section 1139's core protection also depends on whether the employee had "a reasonable belief that the workplace or worksite is unsafe." The statute's own text defines this as an objective standard measured from the vantage point of a reasonable person under the circumstances known to the employee at the time, concluding there is a real danger of death or serious injury from entering or remaining on the premises — not simply a subjective fear, and not simply any risk. The statute's own text also identifies one specific factor relevant to that objective inquiry: whether health and safety regulations specific to the emergency condition exist, whether the employer complied or failed to comply with them, and whether that information was known to the employee or the employee received legally mandated training on those regulations at the relevant time.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text describes this specific-regulation-compliance fact as "a relevant factor," not as the exclusive or a dispositive one, and does not otherwise enumerate what other facts bear on "reasonable belief" or on "real danger of death or serious injury." This research session did not independently verify any published California appellate decision applying this standard, for the reason disclosed in the companion definitions clause (a CourtListener rate-limit error). This document does not determine that any specific employee's belief was or was not reasonable in any specific circumstance.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: “A reasonable belief that the workplace or worksite is unsafe” means that a reasonable person, under the circumstances known to the employee at the time, would conclude there is a real danger of death or serious injury if that person enters or remains on the premises.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: The existence of any health and safety regulations specific to the emergency condition and an employer’s compliance or noncompliance with those regulations shall be a relevant factor if this information is known to the employee at the time of the emergency condition or the employee received training on the health and safety regulations mandated by law specific to the emergency condition.

clauses.title: The Core Right — No Adverse Action for Refusing to Report or Leaving During an Emergency Condition
clauses.body: The statute's own text states the core prohibition as follows: in the event of an emergency condition, an employer may not take or threaten adverse action against an employee for refusing to report to, or leaving, a workplace or worksite within the affected area because the employee has a reasonable belief the workplace or worksite is unsafe. Read on its own terms, this is an anti-retaliation rule tied to a specific act (refusing to report, or leaving) and a specific belief (reasonable belief of unsafety during an emergency condition) — it does not, by its own text, obligate an employer to pay the employee for time not worked as a result, and it does not itself require the employer to excuse the absence as a category of paid or unpaid leave with its own accrual or scheduling mechanics.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text does not define "the affected area," "adverse action," or "threaten," leaving the geographic and conduct scope of the protection to be worked out case by case; this research session did not independently verify any published California appellate decision construing those terms, for the reason disclosed in the companion definitions clause (a CourtListener rate-limit error). This protection is also subject to the thirteen categorical exemptions described in a companion clause, which this clause does not restate. This document does not determine that any specific refusal or departure was or was not protected in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: In the event of an emergency condition, an employer shall not do either of the following: (1) Take or threaten adverse action against any employee for refusing to report to, or leaving, a workplace or worksite within the affected area because the employee has a reasonable belief that the workplace or worksite is unsafe.

clauses.title: Thirteen Categories of Employees to Whom the Core Right Does Not Apply
clauses.body: The statute's own text states that the refuse-to-report/leave protection above does not apply to thirteen listed categories of employees, introduced by the phrase "This paragraph does not apply to the following," followed by items (A) through (M). Those items are, by the statute's own description: first responders as defined by Government Code section 8562; disaster service workers as defined by Government Code section 3101; employees required by law to render aid or remain on the premises during an emergency; employees or contractors of a health care facility who provide direct patient care, support patient care operations during an emergency, or are required by law or policy to participate in emergency response or evacuation; employees of a private entity contracting with government to provide or aid emergency services; employees working on a military base or in the defense industrial base sector; employees performing essential work on nuclear reactors or nuclear materials or waste; employees of a utility, communications, energy, or roadside-assistance company while actively engaged in or called upon to aid emergency response, including maintaining public access to services such as energy and water; employees of a licensed residential care facility; employees of a depository institution as defined by Financial Code section 1420; transportation employees participating directly in emergency evacuations during an active evacuation; employees of a privately contracted private fire prevention resource operating as a "qualified insurance resource" under specified Health and Safety Code provisions; and employees whose primary duties include assisting members of the public to evacuate during an emergency.
clauses.gap: This research session fetched and verified Labor Code section 1139's own text describing these thirteen categories, but did not independently fetch or verify the cross-referenced definitions in Government Code sections 8562 and 3101, Financial Code section 1420, or the Health and Safety Code provisions on qualified insurance resources; whether a specific employee falls within one of these categories can turn on those other statutes' own definitions, which this document does not independently confirm. This document does not determine that any specific employee is or is not within an exempt category.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(b)(1)(A)-(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: This paragraph does not apply to the following: (A) A first responder, as defined in Section 8562 of the Government Code. (B) A disaster service worker, as defined in Section 3101 of the Government Code.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(b)(1)(M) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (M) An employee whose primary duties include assisting members of the public to evacuate in case of an emergency.

clauses.title: A Separate Right — Access to a Communications Device During an Emergency Condition
clauses.body: Section 1139 states a second, textually separate prohibition from the refuse-to-report/leave right above: during an emergency condition, an employer may not prevent an employee from accessing the employee's mobile device or other communications device for seeking emergency assistance, assessing the safety of the situation, or communicating with a person to verify their safety. The statute's own text extends this device-access protection to public-sector employees as well as employees of private entities — specifically, to any employee of the state or of a city, county, or political subdivision, including a special district. The statute's own text then exempts three narrower categories from the device-access right: employees of a depository institution as defined by Financial Code section 1420, employees of any correctional facility, and employees actively operating equipment permitted under specified provisions of the Business and Professions Code (governing private investigators, private security services, and related licensed activities).
clauses.gap: The statute's own text does not define "prevent," and does not specify whether a generally applicable device-use or device-storage policy that is not aimed at emergencies would itself "prevent" access within the meaning of this provision. This research session did not independently fetch or verify the cross-referenced Business and Professions Code provisions defining the equipment-operation exemption. This document does not determine that any specific employer practice does or does not violate this provision.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(b)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: Prevent any employee from accessing the employee’s mobile device or other communications device for seeking emergency assistance, assessing the safety of the situation, or communicating with a person to verify their safety.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(b)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: In addition to employees of private entities, this paragraph applies to any employee of the state or any city, county, or political subdivision of the state, including a special district.

clauses.title: The Employee's Notice Duty
clauses.body: Section 1139 conditions the refuse-to-report/leave protection on a notice duty, but structures that duty around feasibility rather than requiring notice in every case. The statute's own text states that when feasible, an employee shall notify the employer of the emergency condition requiring the employee to leave or refuse to report to the workplace or worksite prior to leaving or refusing to report; and that when prior notice is not feasible, the employee shall instead notify the employer of the emergency condition after leaving or refusing to report, as soon as possible.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text does not specify the form the notice must take (written, verbal, or otherwise), to whom at the employer it must be directed, or what consequence follows if an employee's notice is late, incomplete, or omitted where notice was in fact feasible. This document does not determine whether any specific employee's notice, or lack of notice, satisfied this duty in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (1) When feasible, an employee shall notify the employer of the emergency condition requiring the employee to leave or refuse to report to the workplace or worksite prior to leaving or refusing to report. (2) When prior notice described by paragraph (1) is not feasible, the employee shall notify the employer of the emergency condition that required the employee to leave or refuse to report to the workplace or worksite after leaving or refusing to report as soon as possible.

clauses.title: When the Protection Stops Applying
clauses.body: The statute's own text places a temporal limit on itself: section 1139 is not intended to apply once emergency conditions that pose an imminent and ongoing risk of harm to the workplace, the worksite, the worker, or the worker's home have ceased. Read together with the notice-duty clause above, the protection is tied to the period during which the imminent and ongoing risk exists, not to a fixed number of days or to the underlying disaster event's total duration.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text does not define when an emergency condition's "imminent and ongoing risk of harm" has "ceased," including in a case where an underlying disaster (for example, a wildfire or flood) continues in the broader area but no longer poses an imminent, ongoing risk to a specific workplace or worksite. This document does not determine that any specific emergency condition had or had not ceased at any particular time.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: This section is not intended to apply when emergency conditions that pose an imminent and ongoing risk of harm to the workplace, the worksite, the worker, or the worker’s home have ceased.

clauses.title: Enforcement — PAGA and the Employer's Right to Cure
clauses.body: Section 1139's own text does not create its own standalone civil-penalty or complaint procedure; the only enforcement mechanism its text specifically addresses is a Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA) civil action. The statute's own text states that in any PAGA action a current or former employee could bring for a violation of this chapter, the employer has the right to cure the alleged violation as set forth in a separate statute, Labor Code section 2699.3. Section 2699.3's own text, independently fetched for this document, in turn sets out more than one differently structured pre-suit notice and cure procedure depending on which Labor Code provision is at issue and, for one of those procedures, the employer's number of employees; the version of that procedure applicable to a violation of a provision (such as section 1139) that is not listed in Labor Code section 2699.5 and is not part of Division 5 (the occupational safety and health division) lets an employer that employed fewer than 100 employees during the notice period submit a confidential cure proposal to the Labor and Workforce Development Agency within 33 days of the employee's notice.
clauses.gap: This research session did not independently fetch or verify Labor Code section 2699.5's own list of provisions to confirm that section 1139 is (or is not) omitted from that list, which is what determines whether the fewer-than-100-employees cure procedure quoted here, rather than a different procedure elsewhere in section 2699.3, actually governs a given chapter 11 PAGA claim; that determination is left undone here rather than assumed. This research session also did not independently verify any published court decision applying section 2699.3's cure procedure to a section 1139 claim specifically, because a CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted) during this session. This document does not determine that any specific employer's cure attempt was or was not sufficient, and does not describe any non-PAGA remedy (such as a Labor Commissioner retaliation complaint) that may or may not separately be available for a section 1139 violation.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1139(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: In any action by a current or former employee that could be brought pursuant to the Labor Code Private Attorneys General Act of 2004 (Part 13 (commencing with Section 2698)) for violations of this chapter, the employer shall have the right to cure alleged violations as set forth in Section 2699.3.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2699.3(c)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: an employer that employed fewer than 100 employees in total during the period covered by the notice may submit to the agency a confidential proposal to cure one or more of the alleged violations

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Receipt
Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}}, explains what federal tax law says happens to unused funds in a health flexible spending account (a "health FSA") -- a benefit commonly offered through an employer's cafeteria plan under Internal Revenue Code section 125 -- when a covered employee's job ends, and how that treatment differs from a health savings account (an "HSA") under Internal Revenue Code section 223. Where a specific employer and employee are named below, those names are {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}; this sheet can also be read on its own, without any specific employer or employee named, as a general reference to what the law says. It covers the federal statutory rule against a cafeteria plan providing "deferred compensation" -- the anti-deferral rule that underlies what is commonly called a health FSA's "use-it-or-lose-it" treatment of unused balances -- the contrasting nonforfeitable, portable nature of an HSA balance, and the narrow circumstance in which federal COBRA continuation coverage can still apply to an underspent health FSA after a qualifying event such as termination of employment. This sheet addresses federal tax and COBRA law; no California-specific statute or regulation addressing a health FSA's or HSA's treatment at job separation is cited here. It is distinct from this project's Cal-COBRA Election Notice document, which addresses continuation of a fully insured group health plan generally, not a health FSA's internal forfeiture or COBRA-obligation mechanics, and from this project's Deferred Compensation/Equity Vesting and 401(k) Distribution Notice documents, which address different, retirement-oriented benefits governed by different Code sections. This sheet does not state whether any particular health FSA balance has been or will be forfeited, does not calculate any COBRA premium, does not identify whether a particular employer's plan document offers a grace period or a carryover feature, and is not a substitute for consulting the applicable plan document, the plan administrator, or a person licensed to practice law or provide tax advice in the relevant jurisdiction.

clauses.title: What a Cafeteria Plan and a Health FSA Are
clauses.body: Under 26 U.S.C. section 125(d)(1), a "cafeteria plan" is a written plan under which all participants are employees and the participants may choose among two or more benefits consisting of cash and "qualified benefits." A health flexible spending account is one common way of structuring such a qualified benefit: an employee elects to reduce salary in exchange for the employer's promise to reimburse the employee's substantiated health expenses, up to the elected amount, during the plan year.
clauses.gap: Section 125(d)(1) defines "cafeteria plan" generally; the statute does not itself use the term "flexible spending account" or "health FSA" for the salary-reduction health-reimbursement structure described here -- those are terms of art from Treasury guidance and common employee-benefits usage, not from this statutory text. This clause does not address the separate excepted-benefit, minimum-value, or nondiscrimination-testing requirements that determine whether a particular employer's arrangement in fact qualifies as a cafeteria plan or a health FSA within it.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 125(d)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Cafeteria plans
citations.quote: The term “cafeteria plan” means a written plan under which—

clauses.title: The Statutory Root of Health FSA "Use-It-or-Lose-It" Treatment
clauses.body: 26 U.S.C. section 125(d)(2)(A) provides that the term "cafeteria plan" does not include any plan which provides for deferred compensation. This anti-deferral rule is the statutory root of what is commonly described as a health FSA's "use-it-or-lose-it" treatment of unused amounts: if a cafeteria plan let participants carry forward or cash out unused health FSA amounts from one plan year to the next without limit, the plan would be providing deferred compensation and would risk failing to qualify as a cafeteria plan under the statute at all, which would change the tax treatment of everything offered through it, not only the health FSA.
clauses.gap: This clause verifies only the statutory anti-deferral rule in section 125(d)(2)(A) itself. The detailed operational rules that Treasury has issued interpreting this rule for health FSAs specifically -- including the regulation commonly cited for the "use-or-lose" principle (26 C.F.R. section 1.125-5) and the separate IRS guidance permitting a limited carryover amount or an extended grace period as exceptions to strict use-or-lose treatment -- were not independently fetched or verified for this document; this sheet does not state their current dollar limits or conditions. A lightweight case-law search for this topic on CourtListener returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, daily quota exhausted) before any results could be reviewed, so this clause is not informed by any case law and none is cited.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 125(d)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Cafeteria plans -- deferred compensation plans excluded
citations.quote: The term “cafeteria plan” does not include any plan which provides for deferred compensation.

clauses.title: HSA Balances Are Nonforfeitable and Portable, Unlike a Health FSA
clauses.body: An HSA is legally structured as a trust, and 26 U.S.C. section 223(d)(1)(E) requires that the interest of an individual in the balance in the individual's HSA be nonforfeitable. A distribution from an HSA used exclusively to pay the qualified medical expenses of the account beneficiary is not includible in gross income under section 223(f)(1). Because section 125(d)(2)(D) allows a cafeteria plan to let an employee direct pre-tax salary-reduction amounts into an HSA without that arrangement being treated as prohibited deferred compensation, an employee's HSA balance -- unlike a health FSA balance -- continues to belong to the employee, and remains available to pay qualified medical expenses, after the employee's job with the contributing employer ends.
clauses.gap: This clause verifies the nonforfeitability and tax-free-qualified-distribution rules and the specific statutory carve-out that lets HSA contributions run through a cafeteria plan without triggering the deferred-compensation exclusion. It does not verify or state the separate eligibility conditions for contributing to an HSA (including the high-deductible-health-plan coverage requirement), the annual contribution limits, or the additional tax that section 223 imposes on a distribution not used for qualified medical expenses.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, Health savings accounts -- nonforfeitability
citations.quote: The interest of an individual in the balance in his account is nonforfeitable.

citations.quote: Any amount paid or distributed out of a health savings account which is used exclusively to pay qualified medical expenses of any account beneficiary shall not be includible in gross income.

clauses.title: COBRA Applies to a Health FSA, But Only to the Coverage Actually Being Received
clauses.body: The Treasury regulation implementing COBRA confirms that health care benefits do not escape being a "group health plan" merely because they are offered through a cafeteria plan, including a health FSA. However, the regulation also states that the COBRA continuation-coverage requirements apply only to the type and level of coverage a qualified beneficiary was actually receiving under the cafeteria plan or other flexible benefit arrangement on the day before the qualifying event -- for example, a termination of employment. The same regulation then sets out separate rules, described in a companion clause, that can limit or eliminate a health FSA's own COBRA obligation beyond that.
clauses.gap: This clause verifies only the general framing rule quoted below. It does not by itself determine whether COBRA continuation is or is not available for any particular health FSA in any particular circumstance -- that depends on the two-part test addressed in this sheet's companion clause on underspent health FSAs, and on facts (such as the qualified beneficiary's remaining potential benefit as of the qualifying event) that this sheet does not evaluate.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-2, Q&A-8(a)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Treasury Regulations, Definition of group health plan -- cafeteria plans and flexible benefit arrangements
citations.quote: The provision of health care benefits does not fail to be a group health plan merely because those benefits are offered under a cafeteria plan (as defined in section 125) or under any other arrangement under which an employee is offered a choice between health care benefits and other taxable or nontaxable benefits. However, the COBRA continuation coverage requirements apply only to the type and level of coverage under the cafeteria plan or other flexible benefit arrangement that a qualified beneficiary is actually receiving on the day before the qualifying event.

clauses.title: The Limited COBRA Obligation for an "Underspent" Health FSA
clauses.body: The same COBRA regulation limits a health FSA's obligation to offer continuation coverage when two conditions are both satisfied for the plan year: the health FSA's benefits qualify as "excepted benefits" within the meaning of the federal excepted-benefit statutes, and the maximum amount the health FSA can require to be paid for a year of COBRA continuation coverage equals or exceeds the maximum benefit available under the health FSA for that year. Where both conditions are met, the regulation further provides that the health FSA is not obligated to make COBRA continuation coverage available for the plan year in which the qualifying event occurs unless, as of the date of the qualifying event, the qualified beneficiary could become entitled to receive, during the remainder of the plan year, a benefit exceeding the maximum amount the health FSA could require to be paid for COBRA coverage for that remaining period -- a comparison sometimes summarized as whether the account is "underspent" as of the qualifying event.
clauses.gap: This clause verifies the two-condition test and the underspent-account comparison as the regulation itself states them. It does not verify or restate the regulation's own worked numerical example, which uses dollar figures and a 2002 plan year for illustration only and does not reflect current contribution limits or premium amounts. Whether any particular health FSA in fact meets the "excepted benefit" condition, and whether any particular qualified beneficiary's account is in fact underspent as of a given qualifying event, are fact-specific determinations this sheet does not make. This clause also does not address a dependent care FSA, which is a separate arrangement not subject to COBRA.

citations.quote:
(1) Benefits provided under the health FSA are excepted benefits within the meaning of sections 9831 and 9832; and 

(2) The maximum amount that the health FSA can require to be paid for a year of COBRA continuation coverage under Q&A-1 of § 54.4980B-8 equals or exceeds the maximum benefit available under the health FSA for the year.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes two devices that California's General Corporation Law recognizes for pooling or delegating how shares get voted: a written voting agreement among shareholders, and a voting trust in which shares are transferred to one or more trustees who vote them. It states the requirements, time limits, and filing obligations that Corporations Code §§ 705 and 706 attach to these arrangements for {{companyName}}, a {{entityType}}. It does not cover a proxy given for a single meeting or a short period (that is a different, narrower mechanism also addressed in § 705), it does not cover a close corporation's shareholder management agreement that dispenses with a board of directors under Corporations Code § 300(b) (a separate statutory device available only to a corporation that has made the statutory close-corporation election), and it does not cover the mechanics of cumulative voting for directors. This document states facts about what the statute requires and permits; it does not recommend whether {{shareholderName}} or any other shareholder should enter into a voting trust or voting agreement, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about a specific transaction.

clauses.title: Two Distinct Statutory Devices for Controlling How Shares Are Voted
clauses.body: California Corporations Code § 706, part of the General Corporation Law's chapter on "Voting of Shares" (§§ 700–711), recognizes two distinct arrangements by which shareholders can control how their shares are voted, in addition to the ordinary proxy governed by § 705. Under subdivision (a), two or more shareholders can sign a written agreement specifying how their shares will be voted, without transferring the shares to anyone. Under subdivision (b), shareholders can instead transfer their shares by written agreement to one or more trustees, who then hold the right to vote and otherwise represent the shares — a "voting trust." The statute treats these as separate mechanisms with separate formal requirements, and expressly provides that an agreement valid under one need not satisfy the formalities of the other.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the existence and basic structure of the two devices under § 706; it does not state which device, if either, suits a particular set of shareholders, and it does not address how a voting trust or voting agreement interacts with a corporation's existing bylaws, a shareholders' buy-sell agreement, or a close corporation's shareholder management agreement under § 300(b), each of which is a separate statutory or contractual arrangement not analyzed here.

citations.quote: CHAPTER 7. Voting of Shares [700 - 711]

clauses.title: The Shareholder Voting Agreement: No Transfer of Shares Required
clauses.body: A voting agreement under § 706(a) requires only that two or more shareholders sign a written agreement specifying how their shares will be voted — by a fixed rule stated in the agreement, by the shareholders' subsequent mutual agreement, or by a procedure the agreement sets up. The shareholders are not required to transfer their shares to a third party to make the agreement effective, though they may choose to do so. The statute overrides the general contract-law objection that an agreement to vote a certain way should not be specifically enforced because money damages would be an adequate remedy: it states directly that such an agreement cannot be denied specific performance on that ground, or on other grounds relating to a court of equity's jurisdiction.
clauses.gap: The statute displaces one specific defense to specific performance (adequacy of the legal remedy) and one category of equity-jurisdiction objections; it does not state that every voting agreement will be specifically enforced regardless of other defenses (for example, a defense based on fraud, unconscionability, or a defect in the agreement's formation), and those questions are for a court applying ordinary contract principles.

citations.quote: the parties may but need not transfer the shares covered by such an agreement to a third party or parties with authority to vote them in accordance with the

citations.quote: Such an agreement shall not be denied specific performance by a court on the ground that the remedy at law is adequate or on other grounds relating to the jurisdiction of a court of equity.

clauses.title: Creating a Voting Trust: A Written Transfer Capped at 10 Years
clauses.body: A voting trust is created when shares are transferred by written agreement to one or more trustees who are thereby given the right to vote and otherwise represent the shares. The period for which a voting trust may run is set by the agreement itself, but the statute caps that period at 10 years. Once created, the trust's validity during that 10-year window is not undercut by the fact that its own terms might be read to let it run longer than 10 years — the statute expressly says so — but this does not mean the trust can lawfully exceed 10 years without using the extension procedure described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: The statute caps the trust's stated term at 10 years and separately protects the trust's validity during that period; it does not itself state what happens to the trustees' voting authority after the 10 years run without a timely extension, or what remedy a beneficiary has if a trustee refuses to vote the shares as the trust agreement directs — those are questions of trust and contract law not answered by the text of § 706 alone.

citations.quote: Shares in any corporation may be transferred by written agreement to trustees in order to confer upon them the right to vote and otherwise represent the shares for such period of time, not exceeding 10 years, as may be specified in the agreement.
