citations.quote: The validity of a voting trust agreement, otherwise lawful, shall not be affected during a period of 10 years from the date when it was created or last extended as hereinafter provided by the fact that under its terms it will or may last beyond such 10-year period.

clauses.title: Extending a Voting Trust Before It Expires
clauses.body: A voting trust can be extended beyond its original (or previously extended) expiration date, but only within a specific window and only by specific parties. The extension must be agreed to within the two years immediately before the trust's then-current expiration date. It requires a written agreement by one or more of the trust's beneficiaries together with the written consent of the voting trustee or trustees. Each extension, like the original trust, is capped at an additional period of not more than 10 years, measured from the expiration date as it stood before that extension.
clauses.gap: The statute is specific about the two-year window, the need for beneficiary agreement plus trustee consent, and the 10-year cap on each extension, but it does not address what happens if some beneficiaries extend and others do not (the text says the extension operates "with respect to their shares"), and it does not specify a required form for the written consent beyond writing itself.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 706(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, procedure and time window for extending a voting trust
citations.quote: At any time within two years prior to the time of expiration of any voting trust agreement as originally fixed or as last extended as provided in this subdivision, one or more beneficiaries under the voting trust agreement may, by written agreement and with the written consent of the voting trustee or trustees, extend the duration of the voting trust agreement with respect to their shares for an additional period not exceeding 10 years from the expiration date of the trust as originally fixed or as last extended as provided in this subdivision.

clauses.title: Filing the Voting Trust Agreement and the Right to Inspect It
clauses.body: A duplicate of the voting trust agreement, and of any extension of it, must be filed with the secretary of the corporation whose shares are held in trust. Once filed, that duplicate must be open to inspection by a shareholder, a holder of a voting trust certificate, or the agent of either — on the same terms that apply to inspecting the corporation's record of shareholders. This filing-and-inspection duty applies to voting trusts formed under subdivision (b); it is a separate requirement from the specific-performance rule that applies to voting agreements under subdivision (a).
clauses.gap: The statute does not specify a deadline (measured in days) for filing the duplicate after the trust or its extension is created, and it does not state what consequence follows if the corporation's secretary fails to file or make available the duplicate, beyond whatever general remedies the corporation's record-inspection statutes otherwise provide.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 706(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, voting trust filing and inspection requirement
citations.quote: A duplicate of the voting trust agreement and any extension thereof shall be filed with the secretary of the corporation and shall be open to inspection by a shareholder, a holder of a voting trust certificate or the agent of either, upon the same terms as the record of shareholders of the corporation is open to inspection.

clauses.title: A Voting Agreement Does Not Have to Satisfy Voting-Trust or Proxy Formalities
clauses.body: The statute forecloses a specific argument that could otherwise be used to attack a § 706(a) voting agreement: that it should be treated as invalid because it looks like a voting trust that does not comply with subdivision (b)'s formalities, or like a proxy that does not comply with § 705. Subdivision (c) states that an agreement made under subdivision (a) may not be held invalid or unenforceable on either of those grounds. Separately, subdivision (d) confirms that § 706 does not invalidate any other voting or shareholder agreement, or any irrevocable proxy that complies with § 705(e), as long as that agreement or proxy is not otherwise illegal.
clauses.gap: These subdivisions remove two specific grounds for invalidating an agreement (mischaracterization as a noncompliant voting trust or a noncompliant proxy); they do not immunize an agreement from being challenged on other grounds, such as an argument that its subject matter is otherwise illegal or that it was not properly formed under ordinary contract law.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 706(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, voting agreements are not invalidated by voting-trust or proxy formalities
citations.quote: No agreement made pursuant to subdivision (a) shall be held to be invalid or unenforceable on the ground that it is a voting trust that does not comply with subdivision (b) or that it is a proxy that does not comply with Section 705.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 706(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, section does not invalidate other shareholder agreements or compliant irrevocable proxies
citations.quote: This section shall not invalidate any voting or other agreement among shareholders or any irrevocable proxy complying with subdivision (e) of Section 705, which agreement or proxy is not otherwise illegal.

clauses.title: A Related but Separate Device: The Irrevocable Proxy Tied to a § 706 Agreement
clauses.body: Corporations Code § 705 governs proxies generally, and as a default rule a proxy is revocable at will by the person who executed it. Subdivision (e) lists specific categories of proxy holders for whom a proxy can instead be made irrevocable for a stated period, including, as one of six listed categories, "a person designated by or under an agreement under Section 706" — tying an irrevocable proxy to the same voting-agreement mechanism described in this document. Consistent with that link, subdivision (e) also provides that such a proxy becomes revocable once the underlying § 706 agreement has terminated, alongside the other listed events (redemption of a pledge, termination of a purchase option, payment of a secured debt, and so on) that end the other categories of irrevocable proxy.
clauses.gap: This clause describes how one category of irrevocable proxy under § 705(e)(5) is linked to a § 706 agreement; it does not restate the full list of six categories under which a proxy can be made irrevocable, or the separate rule in § 705(f) that an irrevocable proxy can still be cut off as to a transferee who takes shares without notice of the proxy's existence unless that existence appears on the share certificate or transaction statement.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 705(e)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, irrevocable proxy held by a person designated under a § 706 agreement
citations.quote: (5) A person designated by or under an agreement under Section 706.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 705(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, an irrevocable proxy tied to a § 706 agreement becomes revocable once that agreement terminates
citations.quote: the agreement under Section 706 has terminated, or the person ceases to be a beneficiary of the trust

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Document: The Williamson Act
clauses.body:
This document concerns real property located at {{propertyAddress}}, in {{county}} County, California, identified by Assessor's Parcel Number {{parcelNumber}} and described as {{legalDescription}}, owned by {{ownerName}}.

This document describes California's Land Conservation Act of 1965, commonly known as the Williamson Act (Government Code Section 51200 et seq.): a state law under which a city or county may enter into a contract with an agricultural or open-space landowner restricting the land to agricultural or open-space use in exchange for the land being valued, for property tax purposes, based on its restricted use rather than its unrestricted fair market value. It covers how a Williamson Act contract is formed and automatically renews, the notice-of-nonrenewal procedure that lets either party let a contract run out, the separate and more difficult cancellation procedure and its cancellation fee, and the income-capitalization method used to value enforceably restricted land for property tax purposes.

This document is distinct from this corpus's Subdivision Map Act document, which concerns the different process of dividing land into parcels, and from this corpus's Property Tax Parent-Child Transfer Exclusion (Proposition 19) document, which concerns a different property tax mechanism (a reassessment exclusion on an intra-family transfer) with no connection to a Williamson Act contract. It does not itself create, renew, give notice of nonrenewal for, or cancel any Williamson Act contract, and does not determine whether any specific parcel is eligible for, or currently subject to, such a contract; this is not a substitute for consulting the contracting city or county, the county assessor, or a licensed attorney about a specific parcel.

clauses.title: The Statute's Name and Its Core Definitions
clauses.body: California's Government Code states that the chapter establishing this framework "shall be known as the California Land Conservation Act of 1965 or as the Williamson Act." The same chapter defines an "agricultural preserve" as an area devoted to agricultural use, recreational use, or open-space use, or any combination of those uses, established in accordance with the chapter's own provisions, and defines "agricultural use" as the use of land, including greenhouses, for the purpose of producing an agricultural commodity for commercial purposes. A Williamson Act contract restricts land within an agricultural preserve to one or more of these defined uses.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the chapter's own popular name and two of its statutory definitions; it does not evaluate whether any specific parcel in fact lies within an established agricultural preserve, or whether any specific use in fact qualifies as an "agricultural use," "recreational use," or "open-space use" as those terms are separately defined elsewhere in the same section — those are fact-specific determinations for the contracting city or county.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51200
citations.cite: California Government Code, the chapter's popular name
citations.quote: This chapter shall be known as the California Land Conservation Act of 1965 or as the Williamson Act.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51201(d)
citations.cite: California Government Code, definition of "agricultural preserve", treated as one source with § 51201(b) below, not an independent source
citations.quote: “Agricultural preserve” means an area devoted to either agricultural use, as defined in subdivision (b), recreational use as defined in subdivision (n), or open-space use as defined in subdivision (o), or any combination of those uses and which is established in accordance with the provisions of this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51201(b)
citations.cite: California Government Code, definition of "agricultural use", treated as one source with § 51201(d) above, not an independent source
citations.quote: “Agricultural use” means use of land, including but not limited to greenhouses, for the purpose of producing an agricultural commodity for commercial purposes.

clauses.title: A City or County's Authority to Enter Into a Williamson Act Contract
clauses.body: California's Government Code authorizes, but does not require, a city or county to contract with a landowner to limit the use of agricultural land for the purpose of preserving that land, subject to the conditions the contract itself states and the conditions this chapter states. The statute also permits a contract to include restrictions, terms, and conditions — including payments and fees — that are more restrictive than, or in addition to, what the chapter itself requires. A Williamson Act contract is accordingly a voluntary agreement between a landowner and a city or county, not a restriction the statute itself imposes on land directly.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the general contracting authority the statute grants; it does not evaluate whether any specific city or county has in fact established an agricultural preserve or elected to offer Williamson Act contracts, whether any specific parcel is eligible, or what additional restrictions, terms, or conditions a specific contract in fact contains — those are matters for the contracting city or county and the specific contract's own text.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51240
citations.cite: California Government Code, authority of a city or county to contract limiting agricultural land use
citations.quote: Any city or county may by contract limit the use of agricultural land for the purpose of preserving such land pursuant and subject to the conditions set forth in the contract and in this chapter. A contract may provide for restrictions, terms, and conditions, including payments and fees, more restrictive than or in addition to those required by this chapter.

clauses.title: Minimum Contract Term and Automatic Annual Renewal
clauses.body: California's Government Code requires that a Williamson Act contract be for an initial term of no less than 10 years. The statute then adds a self-renewing feature: each contract must provide that, on the contract's anniversary date or another annual date the contract specifies, a year is added automatically to the initial term, unless a party serves a notice of nonrenewal as the statute separately provides. As a result, a Williamson Act contract that no party ever moves to end continues to roll forward with a rolling term of approximately 10 years measured from whatever the current year happens to be, rather than expiring on a fixed date.
clauses.gap: This clause states the chapter's general 10-year minimum term and automatic-renewal rule. The same section contains additional, more detailed provisions — not quoted or summarized in this clause — governing a county's option to phase in a shortened 9-year or 18-year term under specified conditions tied to a county revenue determination, and exceptions to that phase-in for certain contract types; a landowner or county should consult the full text of Government Code Section 51244 for those details, which this document does not attempt to restate in full.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51244(a)
citations.cite: California Government Code, minimum contract term and automatic annual renewal
citations.quote: Each contract shall be for an initial term of no less than 10 years. Each contract shall provide that on the anniversary date of the contract or such other annual date as specified by the contract a year shall be added automatically to the initial term unless notice of nonrenewal is given as provided in Section 51245.

clauses.title: Ending a Contract by Notice of Nonrenewal
clauses.body: California's Government Code lets either the landowner or the contracting city or county end the automatic-renewal cycle described elsewhere in this document by serving written notice of nonrenewal on the other party in advance of the contract's annual renewal date. The statute sets different minimum notice periods for each party: a landowner must serve notice at least 90 days before the renewal date, and a city or county must serve notice at least 60 days before the renewal date; a notice served later than that is not effective to prevent that year's automatic renewal. A landowner who receives a nonrenewal notice from the city or county may make a written protest of it, and the city or county may withdraw its own notice at any time before the renewal date. Once a party serves an effective notice of nonrenewal, the contract does not end immediately: because each earlier year's automatic renewal already added a year to the term, an effective notice of nonrenewal instead stops any further automatic renewal, so the existing contract term runs out on its own schedule, winding down year by year, rather than terminating on the notice's effective date. The statute also requires the clerk of the board or council to record a copy of the notice of nonrenewal, or of any withdrawal of that notice, with the county recorder within 20 days after the city or county receives, serves, or withdraws it.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the general notice-of-nonrenewal procedure and its minimum notice periods; it does not evaluate whether a specific notice was in fact served within the statutory deadline, or state what remains of a specific contract's term at any given point, because that depends on the specific contract's own anniversary date and renewal history. The statute also permits a board or council, on the owner's request, to authorize a notice of nonrenewal covering only a portion of the land under contract — a partial-nonrenewal option this clause notes but does not further describe.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51245
citations.cite: California Government Code, notice of nonrenewal procedure and minimum notice periods
citations.quote: If either the landowner or the city or county desires in any year not to renew the contract, that party shall serve written notice of nonrenewal of the contract upon the other party in advance of the annual renewal date of the contract. Unless such written notice is served by the landowner at least 90 days prior to the renewal date or by the city or county at least 60 days prior to the renewal date, the contract shall be considered renewed as provided in Section 51244 or Section 51244.5.

clauses.title: Cancellation: A Separate, More Difficult Process Than Nonrenewal
clauses.body: Separately from letting a contract run out through nonrenewal, California's Government Code lets a landowner petition the contracting board or council to cancel a Williamson Act contract before its term ends, as to all or part of the land. The board or council may give tentative approval to cancel a contract only if it makes one of two required findings: that the cancellation is consistent with the chapter's purposes, or that the cancellation is in the public interest. For a finding that cancellation is consistent with the chapter's purposes, the statute requires the board or council to make a further set of findings, including that a notice of nonrenewal has already been served for the land, that the cancellation is not likely to cause adjacent land to leave agricultural use, that the proposed alternative use is consistent with the applicable general plan, that it will not result in discontiguous patterns of urban development, and that there is no proximate, suitable, noncontracted land available for the proposed alternative use (or that using the contracted land would create more contiguous development than using such other land). The statute separately states that the uneconomic character of an existing agricultural use is not, by itself, sufficient reason for cancellation, unless there is no other reasonable or comparable agricultural use to which the land may be put.
clauses.gap: This clause states the chapter's own required findings for cancellation; it does not evaluate whether any of those findings would in fact be made for a specific parcel, which the statute commits to the contracting board or council after notice and hearing on a specific petition and a specific proposed alternative use, not to any generalized fact stated in this document. The statute's alternative "public interest" finding, and further procedural requirements for the landowner's petition and proposed alternative use, are addressed only in part in this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51282(a)
citations.cite: California Government Code, petition for cancellation and the two required findings, treated as one source with § 51282(b) and (d) below, not an independent source
citations.quote: The landowner may petition the board or council for cancellation of any contract as to all or any part of the subject land. The board or council may grant tentative approval for cancellation of a contract only if it makes one of the following findings: (1) That the cancellation is consistent with the purposes of this chapter. (2) That cancellation is in the public interest.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51282(b)
citations.cite: California Government Code, findings required for a "consistent with purposes" cancellation, treated as one source with § 51282(a) and (d), not an independent source
citations.quote: That the cancellation is for land on which a notice of nonrenewal has been served pursuant to Section 51245. (2) That cancellation is not likely to result in the removal of adjacent lands from agricultural use. (3) That cancellation is for an alternative use which is consistent with the applicable provisions of the city or county general plan. (4) That cancellation will not result in discontiguous patterns of urban development.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51282(d)
citations.cite: California Government Code, uneconomic character of existing use is not by itself sufficient, treated as one source with § 51282(a) and (b) above, not an independent source
citations.quote: For purposes of subdivision (a), the uneconomic character of an existing agricultural use shall not by itself be sufficient reason for cancellation of the contract. The uneconomic character of the existing use may be considered only if there is no other reasonable or comparable agricultural use to which the land may be put.

clauses.title: The Cancellation Fee: Valuation and the 12.5% Rate
clauses.body: Before giving tentative approval to cancel a contract, California's Government Code requires the county assessor to determine the land's current fair market value as though it were free of the contractual restriction, and to certify that "cancellation valuation" to the board or council for the purpose of calculating the cancellation fee. The board or council must then determine and certify to the county auditor the cancellation fee the landowner is to pay the county treasurer upon cancellation, which the statute sets at an amount equal to 12.5 percent of that cancellation valuation. The statute separately states the Legislature's intent that this fee is not a tax, but a payment that, when made, confers a private benefit tending to increase the value of the property.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general valuation and fee-rate rule; it does not restate the statute's separate provisions letting a board or council waive or defer all or part of the fee, in the public interest and with the state Secretary of the Natural Resources Agency's approval, where cancellation results from an involuntary transfer or change in permitted land use and other conditions are met — a discretionary exception this clause notes but does not evaluate for any specific parcel.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51283(a)
citations.cite: California Government Code, assessor's fair-market-value determination for the cancellation fee, treated as one source with § 51283(b) and (f) below, not an independent source
citations.quote: Prior to any action by the board or council giving tentative approval to the cancellation of any contract, the county assessor of the county in which the land is located shall determine the current fair market value of the land as though it were free of the contractual restriction.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51283(b)
citations.cite: California Government Code, the 12.5% cancellation fee rate, treated as one source with § 51283(a) and (f), not an independent source
citations.quote: Prior to giving tentative approval to the cancellation of any contract, the board or council shall determine and certify to the county auditor the amount of the cancellation fee that the landowner shall pay the county treasurer upon cancellation. That fee shall be an amount equal to 12 1 / 2 percent of the cancellation valuation of the property.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51283(f)
citations.cite: California Government Code, legislative intent that the cancellation fee is not a tax, treated as one source with § 51283(a) and (b) above, not an independent source
citations.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature that fees paid to cancel a contract do not constitute taxes but are payments that, when made, provide a private benefit that tends to increase the value of the property.

clauses.title: Certificate of Tentative Cancellation and the Landowner's Conditions
clauses.body: California's Government Code describes the recorded paper trail that follows tentative approval of a cancellation petition accompanied by a specified alternative-use proposal. The clerk of the board or council must record, with the county recorder, a certificate of tentative cancellation stating the landowner's name, that a certificate of cancellation will be issued and recorded once specified conditions and contingencies are satisfied, a description of those conditions and contingencies, and a legal description of the property. Payment in full of the cancellation fee is one required condition, and the statute warns that if the fee is not paid, or a certificate of cancellation is not issued, within one year from the assessor's valuation date, the fee is subject to recomputation. The statute also requires the landowner to obtain all permits necessary to commence the proposed alternative-use project as one of the conditions to be satisfied.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general certificate-of-tentative-cancellation procedure; it does not restate the statute's separate provisions on a landowner's right to request an earlier recomputation of the valuation, or on the certificate-of-withdrawal procedure that applies if the landowner is unable to satisfy the stated conditions and contingencies (under which, the statute states, the landowner is not entitled to a refund of any cancellation fee already paid) — both addressed in the same section but not quoted in this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51283.4(a)
citations.cite: California Government Code, recorded certificate of tentative cancellation and its required content
citations.quote: Upon tentative approval of a petition accompanied by a proposal for a specified alternative use of the land, the clerk of the board or council shall record in the office of the county recorder of the county in which is located the land as to which the contract is applicable a certificate of tentative cancellation, which shall set forth the name of the landowner requesting the cancellation, the fact that a certificate of cancellation of contract will be issued and recorded at the time that specified conditions and contingencies are satisfied, a description of the conditions and contingencies which must be satisfied, and a legal description of the property.

clauses.title: Judicial Review of a Cancellation Decision
clauses.body: California's Government Code channels any challenge to a board of supervisors' or city council's decision to cancel a Williamson Act contract, on the ground of alleged noncompliance with the chapter's requirements, into a specific procedure: such an action or proceeding must be brought under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1094.5, the state's general statute for judicial review of a local agency's adjudicatory decision. The statute also sets a short limitations period: the action or proceeding must be commenced within 180 days of the date of the council's or board's order acting on the cancellation petition.
clauses.gap: This clause states the chapter's own procedural vehicle and limitations period for challenging a cancellation decision; it does not describe the substantive standard of review a court applies under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1094.5 itself, which was not separately fetched or cited in this document, and does not evaluate whether any specific challenge would in fact be timely or meritorious.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 51286
citations.cite: California Government Code, judicial review procedure and 180-day limitations period
citations.quote: Any action or proceeding which, on the grounds of alleged noncompliance with the requirements of this chapter, seeks to attack, review, set aside, void, or annul a decision of a board of supervisors or a city council to cancel a contract shall be brought pursuant to Section 1094.5 of the Code of Civil Procedure. (b) The action or proceeding shall be commenced within 180 days from the date of the council or board order acting on a petition for cancellation filed under this chapter.

clauses.title: Property Tax Valuation: Capitalized Income, Not Fair Market Value
clauses.body: California's Revenue and Taxation Code states the property tax valuation method that makes a Williamson Act contract financially significant to a landowner. Rather than the sales-comparison approach ordinarily used to value real property, when valuing enforceably restricted open-space land the county assessor is directed not to consider sales data on land (restricted or not), and instead to value the land by the capitalization-of-income method the statute describes. The statute directs that, where sufficient rental information is available, the income capitalized is the fair rent imputed to the land based on actual and typical rentals for similar land in similar use where the owner pays the property tax; where sufficient rental information is not available, the income is what the land can reasonably be expected to yield under prudent management, subject to the applicable enforceable restriction. It is this substitution of a capitalized-income valuation for a fair-market-value valuation, while a contract remains in force, that typically produces a lower assessed value and lower property tax bill than the same land would carry if unrestricted.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general capitalization-of-income valuation rule; it does not restate the statute's own listed exceptions (land used for commercial timber production, and land addressed by Revenue and Taxation Code Sections 423.7 and 423.8, neither of which was separately fetched or cited in this document), and does not calculate or estimate what assessed value or tax bill would in fact result for any specific parcel, which depends on rent and income data this document does not have.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 423
citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, capitalization-of-income valuation method for enforceably restricted open-space land
citations.quote: Except as provided in Sections 423.7 and 423.8, when valuing enforceably restricted open-space land, other than land used for the production of timber for commercial purposes, the county assessor shall not consider sales data on lands, whether or not enforceably restricted, but shall value these lands by the capitalization of income method

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Review
Purpose of This Trade Secret Injunctive Relief Standards Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes the statutory standards governing injunctions in trade secret misappropriation cases under California Civil Code section 3426.2, part of the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act (CUTSA), and under the parallel federal injunctive-relief provision of the Defend Trade Secrets Act, 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(3)(A). It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning {{companyName}}'s trade secret, described as follows: {{tradeSecretDescription}}, in a situation involving {{adversePartyName}}. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference describing what these statutes say about the injunction remedy specifically -- when a court may enjoin actual or threatened misappropriation, when such an injunction must be terminated or may be continued, when a court may substitute a reasonable royalty for an injunction, and when a court may compel affirmative acts to protect a trade secret. It does not itself determine whether an injunction would be granted, denied, modified, or terminated in any specific case, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is also distinct from, and is meant as a companion to, this project's existing Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter document: that document addresses the definition of misappropriation and the damages and attorney's-fee remedies available for it, while this one addresses a separate question -- the standards governing the injunctive relief remedy specifically.

clauses.title: California: Enjoining Actual or Threatened Misappropriation, and When an Injunction Must End
clauses.body: Under California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act, actual or threatened misappropriation of a trade secret may be enjoined -- meaning an injunction is available not only after misappropriation has occurred, but also against misappropriation that is merely threatened. The statute also sets a rule for when such an injunction must end: upon application to the court, an injunction must be terminated once the trade secret has ceased to exist. But the statute allows an exception to immediate termination -- the injunction may instead be continued for an additional period of time where doing so is needed to eliminate a commercial advantage that would otherwise still be derived from the earlier misappropriation, even after the trade secret itself no longer exists as a trade secret.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of CUTSA's own stated standard for enjoining misappropriation and for terminating or continuing that injunction -- not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that an injunction would be granted, denied, terminated, or continued on any specific set of facts. This clause quotes subdivision (a) of Cal. Civ. Code section 3426.2; companion clauses in this document quote subdivisions (b) and (c) of that same section -- all three are subdivisions of one statutory section, not independent sources of each other, and are disclosed as such throughout this document. The statute does not itself define what showing a plaintiff must make to obtain a preliminary injunction (for example, likelihood of success or irreparable harm) -- those procedural standards come from other law, including the general California statute governing preliminary injunctions and case law construing it, neither of which is addressed here. A CourtListener case-law search for this clause was attempted but returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted) before any case could be retrieved, so no case law on how California courts apply this standard -- including how courts treat a merely "threatened" misappropriation -- is included in this document; only the statutory text is quoted. The full text of section 3426.2 was retrieved twice directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov -- the official California Legislative Information website -- as two separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical text for the whole section.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.2(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, injunctive relief -- enjoining misappropriation and termination of injunctions
citations.quote: Actual or threatened misappropriation may be enjoined. Upon application to the court, an injunction shall be terminated when the trade secret has ceased to exist, but the injunction may be continued for an additional period of time in order to eliminate commercial advantage that otherwise would be derived from the misappropriation.

clauses.title: California: Reasonable Royalty in Place of an Injunction
clauses.body: California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act does not treat an injunction as the only, or an automatic, remedy once misappropriation is shown. Where a court determines that it would be unreasonable to prohibit a defendant's future use of the trade secret, the statute allows the court instead to condition that future use upon payment of a reasonable royalty, running for no longer than the period during which the use could otherwise have been prohibited by injunction. This royalty-in-lieu-of-injunction mechanism is a distinct statutory option from the reasonable-royalty damages measure available under a separate provision of the same act.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of CUTSA's own stated standard for substituting a reasonable royalty for an injunction -- not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that a court would find prohibition of future use "unreasonable," or would order any particular royalty, on any specific set of facts. This clause quotes subdivision (b) of Cal. Civ. Code section 3426.2; a companion clause in this document quotes subdivision (a) of that same section, and another quotes subdivision (c) -- all three are subdivisions of one statutory section, not independent sources of each other. The statute does not define "reasonable royalty" or specify a method for calculating one in this injunction-substitute context; this clause does not address how a court would calculate such a royalty. A CourtListener case-law search for this clause was attempted but returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted) before any case could be retrieved, so no case law illustrating when California courts have found prohibition of future use "unreasonable" is included here. The full text of section 3426.2 was retrieved twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two different User-Agent headers, and both retrievals returned byte-identical text.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.2(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, injunctive relief -- reasonable royalty in lieu of prohibiting future use
citations.quote: If the court determines that it would be unreasonable to prohibit future use, an injunction may condition future use upon payment of a reasonable royalty for no longer than the period of time the use could have been prohibited.

clauses.title: California: Court-Ordered Affirmative Acts to Protect a Trade Secret
clauses.body: Beyond prohibiting future misappropriation, California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act allows a court, in appropriate circumstances, to go further and affirmatively compel acts to protect a trade secret by court order. The statute does not itemize which specific acts a court may order; it states only that such affirmative acts may be compelled where circumstances make that appropriate, leaving the specific content of any such order to the court's judgment on the facts before it.
clauses.gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of CUTSA's own stated authorization for affirmative-act orders -- not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that any particular affirmative act would be ordered on any specific set of facts. This clause quotes subdivision (c) of Cal. Civ. Code section 3426.2; companion clauses in this document quote subdivisions (a) and (b) of that same section -- all three are subdivisions of one statutory section, not independent sources of each other. The statute's use of "appropriate circumstances" is undefined and unelaborated in the statutory text itself; no case law construing what circumstances qualify was checked in this research (a CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error, HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted, before any case could be retrieved), so this clause describes only the bare statutory authorization, not how courts have applied it. The full text of section 3426.2 was retrieved twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two different User-Agent headers, and both retrievals returned byte-identical text.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.2(c) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, injunctive relief -- compelled affirmative acts
citations.quote: In appropriate circumstances, affirmative acts to protect a trade secret may be compelled by court order.

clauses.title: Federal DTSA: Enjoining Actual or Threatened Misappropriation
clauses.body: The federal Defend Trade Secrets Act contains its own injunctive-relief provision, structured similarly to California's but written and codified separately. In a civil action under the DTSA, a court may grant an injunction to prevent any actual or threatened misappropriation, on terms the court deems reasonable. As with California's statute, the DTSA's injunction authority reaches threatened misappropriation, not only misappropriation that has already occurred -- but the DTSA's grant of injunctive authority is also expressly made subject to limits set out elsewhere in the same subparagraph, addressed in a companion clause of this document, that do not appear in the California statute's text.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the DTSA's own stated standard for enjoining misappropriation -- not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that an injunction would be granted on any specific set of facts. This clause quotes the opening portion of 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(i); a companion clause in this document quotes the two express limits that follow in the same clause (§ 1836(b)(3)(A)(i)(I)-(II)), and other companion clauses quote § 1836(b)(3)(A)(ii) and (iii) -- all from the same statutory subparagraph, not independent sources of each other. This document's existing companion clause on federal civil remedies (in the Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter document) already quotes § 1836(b)(3) as a whole but abridges the injunctive-relief detail with an ellipsis; this clause and its companions here quote that previously-abridged detail in full. A CourtListener case-law search for this clause was attempted but returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted) before any case could be retrieved, so no case law applying this standard is included here; only the statutory text is quoted. The text was retrieved twice from Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (law.cornell.edu), an unofficial but widely used republication of the U.S. Code, using two different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical files. This is not the U.S. Government Publishing Office's official U.S. Code text; Cornell LII's text was used because it is the source suggested for federal statutes, and no discrepancy between the two fetches was found.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, injunctive relief -- enjoining actual or threatened misappropriation
citations.quote: to prevent any actual or threatened misappropriation described in paragraph (1) on such terms as the court deems reasonable

clauses.title: Federal DTSA: Express Limits Protecting Employment Mobility and State Law
clauses.body: The DTSA's injunction authority to prevent actual or threatened misappropriation is expressly qualified by two limits that California's own trade secret injunction statute does not separately state in its own text. First, an injunction under the DTSA may not prevent a person from entering into an employment relationship; any conditions placed on such employment must be based on evidence of threatened misappropriation, not merely on the information the person knows. Second, a DTSA injunction may not otherwise conflict with an applicable state law prohibiting restraints on the practice of a lawful profession, trade, or business. Together, these limits mean a federal DTSA injunction cannot be used simply to bar someone from taking a new job based on the trade secrets they carry in their head, and cannot override a state's own restrictions on noncompete-style restraints.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the DTSA's own express limits on its injunction remedy -- not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that any specific injunction request would or would not run afoul of these limits. This clause quotes 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(i)(I) and (II) together, as one contiguous quotation spanning both subclauses; a companion clause in this document quotes the opening portion of the same subparagraph, (b)(3)(A)(i), and others quote (ii) and (iii) -- all from the same statutory subparagraph, not independent sources of each other. This clause does not identify which California statute(s) qualify as "applicable State law prohibiting restraints on the practice of a lawful profession, trade, or business" for purposes of the second limit (California's own restrictions on noncompete agreements are addressed in this project's separate Non-Compete Agreement and Noncompete Void Notification documents, not here); no case law construing how courts have applied either limit was checked in this research (a CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error, HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted, before any case could be retrieved). The text was retrieved twice from Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute using two different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical files.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(i)(I)-(II) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, injunctive relief -- limits protecting employment relationships and state law on restraints of trade
citations.quote: prevent a person from entering into an employment relationship, and that conditions placed on such employment shall be based on evidence of threatened misappropriation and not merely on the information the person knows; or (II) otherwise conflict with an applicable State law prohibiting restraints on the practice of a lawful profession, trade, or business

clauses.title: Federal DTSA: Court-Ordered Affirmative Actions to Protect a Trade Secret
clauses.body: Paralleling California's statute, the DTSA also allows a court, if the court determines it appropriate, to require affirmative actions be taken to protect the trade secret. As with the California provision, the DTSA text does not enumerate which specific actions qualify, leaving that determination to the court on the facts of the case.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the DTSA's own authorization for affirmative-action orders -- not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that any particular affirmative action would be ordered on any specific set of facts. This clause quotes 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(ii); companion clauses in this document quote (i), (i)(I)-(II), and (iii) of the same subparagraph -- all from the same statutory subparagraph, not independent sources of each other. No case law construing what actions courts have found "appropriate" under this provision was checked (a CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error, HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted, before any case could be retrieved). The text was retrieved twice from Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute using two different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical files.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, injunctive relief -- compelled affirmative actions
citations.quote: if determined appropriate by the court, requiring affirmative actions to be taken to protect the trade secret

clauses.title: Federal DTSA: Reasonable Royalty in Exceptional Circumstances
clauses.body: The DTSA also contains its own royalty-in-lieu-of-injunction mechanism, narrower in its stated trigger than California's parallel provision. Where exceptional circumstances render an injunction inequitable, a court may instead condition future use of the trade secret upon payment of a reasonable royalty, for no longer than the period during which that use could otherwise have been prohibited. California's parallel provision is triggered by a court's determination that prohibiting future use would be "unreasonable," while the DTSA's text instead requires "exceptional circumstances" that render an injunction "inequitable" -- the two statutes use different trigger language for a similar remedy, and this document does not resolve whether that difference in wording produces a different practical standard.
clauses.gap: This is federal law, used as real evidence of the DTSA's own stated standard for substituting a reasonable royalty for an injunction -- not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that any court would find "exceptional circumstances" or order any particular royalty on any specific set of facts. This clause quotes 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(iii); companion clauses in this document quote (i), (i)(I)-(II), and (ii) of the same subparagraph -- all from the same statutory subparagraph, not independent sources of each other. The observation that the DTSA's "exceptional circumstances"/"inequitable" trigger differs in wording from California's "unreasonable" trigger is this document's own textual comparison of the two statutes, not a holding from any court; no case law addressing whether the two standards function differently in practice was checked (a CourtListener case-law search returned a rate-limit error, HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted, before any case could be retrieved). The text was retrieved twice from Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute using two different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical files.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(A)(iii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, injunctive relief -- reasonable royalty in exceptional circumstances
citations.quote: in exceptional circumstances that render an injunction inequitable, that conditions future use of the trade secret upon payment of a reasonable royalty for no longer than the period of time for which such use could have been prohibited

clauses.body:

[This Information Sheet is a general reference describing the statutory standards for injunctive relief in trade secret misappropriation cases under California Civil Code section 3426.2 and the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act, 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(3)(A). It is not a court filing, a pleading, or legal advice about whether an injunction would be granted, denied, modified, or terminated in the situation described above, and completing or signing it does not itself determine that outcome.]

clauses.title: Declaration -- Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Family Law Facilitator Act (Family Code sections 10000 through 10015), which requires each superior court to maintain an office of the family law facilitator to assist parties in a matter between {{petitionerName}} and {{respondentName}}, case number {{courtCaseNumber}}, pending in {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes the Legislature's stated purpose in creating the office, the office's required staffing, the categories of proceedings the statute reaches, the services the statute lists, the additional duties a superior court may add by local rule (including facilitator-conducted mediation of support-related issues and a domestic-violence-specific meeting protocol), the statute's no-cost-to-the-parties and hearing-access provisions, how the statute interacts with services provided by a local child support agency, and the statute's own limits on the facilitator's role, including that the facilitator does not represent any party and that no attorney-client relationship or privilege is created. It does not itself request or grant any facilitator appointment, service, mediation, or order, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about how the Family Law Facilitator Act applies to a specific case.

clauses.title: The Legislature's Stated Findings and Purpose
clauses.body: Under California law, the Legislature that enacted the Family Law Facilitator Act found that child and spousal support are serious legal obligations whose enforcement was frequently delayed by protracted custody and visitation litigation, and that family courts were unduly burdened with heavy caseloads and insufficient personnel. The Legislature further found a compelling state interest in a speedy, conflict-reducing, cost-effective system for resolving child support, spousal support, and health insurance issues that is accessible to families who cannot afford legal representation, and stated its intent to make services piloted in the Superior Courts of Santa Clara and San Mateo Counties available statewide.
clauses.gap: Both citations below are subdivisions of the same statutory section, Family Code section 10001 -- the first is finding (a)(1) and the second is finding (a)(4) together with the adjoining statement of intent in subdivision (b) -- so they are not independent sources of each other, only two excerpts of one legislative findings section. Legislative findings describe the Legislature's own stated rationale for enacting a statute; they are not themselves an operative rule of law, and a court is not bound to reach the same policy conclusions the findings recite. This clause also does not address findings (a)(2) and (a)(3), which describe the Santa Clara and San Mateo pilot-project reports and survey results underlying the Legislature's conclusion.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10001(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Family Code section 10001, subdivision (a)(1) -- a legislative finding on support-order delay and court caseloads (a subdivision of the same Section 10001 as the next citation, not an independent source)
citations.quote: Child and spousal support are serious legal obligations. The entry of a child support order is frequently delayed while parents engage in protracted litigation concerning custody and visitation. The current system for obtaining child and spousal support orders is suffering because the family courts are unduly burdened with heavy case loads and do not have sufficient personnel to meet increased demands on the courts.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10001(a)(4)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Family Code section 10001, subdivision (a)(4) and the adjoining statement of legislative intent in subdivision (b) -- also part of Section 10001, not an independent source from the previous citation
citations.quote: There is a compelling state interest in having a speedy, conflict-reducing system for resolving issues of child support, spousal support, and health insurance that is cost-effective and accessible to families that cannot afford legal representation. (b) Therefore, it is the intent of the Legislature to make the services provided in the family law pilot projects in the Counties of Santa Clara and San Mateo available to unrepresented parties in the superior courts of all California counties.

clauses.title: Required Office, Attorney Staffing, and Appointment
clauses.body: Under California law, each superior court is required to maintain an office of the family law facilitator, and that office must be staffed by an attorney licensed to practice law in California who has mediation or litigation experience, or both, in the field of family law. The family law facilitator is appointed by the superior court.
clauses.gap: The statute states a staffing qualification and an appointment mechanism, but does not itself specify the facilitator's term of appointment, removal process, caseload or minimum staffing levels, or funding source for the office beyond what is addressed elsewhere in this division; those details are left to each superior court's own administration and local rules, which this clause does not survey.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10002 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the office, staffing qualification, and appointment requirement
citations.quote: Each superior court shall maintain an office of the family law facilitator. The office of the family law facilitator shall be staffed by an attorney licensed to practice law in this state who has mediation or litigation experience, or both, in the field of family law. The family law facilitator shall be appointed by the superior court.

clauses.title: The Categories of Proceedings This Division Reaches
clauses.body: Under California law, the Family Law Facilitator Act applies to actions or proceedings for temporary or permanent child support, spousal support, health insurance, child custody, or visitation arising in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, nullity of marriage, legal separation, or exclusive child custody, or arising under the Uniform Parentage Act or the Domestic Violence Prevention Act.
clauses.gap: This section defines the division's scope by reference to two other statutory schemes -- the Uniform Parentage Act (Family Code Part 3 of Division 12, commencing with Section 7600) and the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Family Code Division 10, commencing with Section 6200) -- without restating either scheme's own substantive rules, which this clause does not independently verify. It also does not address Section 10008's separate carve-out and re-inclusion for cases receiving local child support agency services under Section 17400, covered in a separate clause of this document, or reach family law matters outside the listed categories, such as pure property-division disputes.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10003 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory scope provision
citations.quote: This division shall apply to all actions or proceedings for temporary or permanent child support, spousal support, health insurance, child custody, or visitation in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, nullity of marriage, legal separation, or exclusive child custody, or pursuant to the Uniform Parentage Act (Part 3 (commencing with Section 7600) of Division 12) or the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200)).

clauses.title: The Non-Exhaustive List of Core Services
clauses.body: Under California law, the services a family law facilitator provides include, but are not limited to: providing educational materials to parents about the process of establishing parentage and establishing, modifying, and enforcing child support and spousal support in the courts; distributing necessary court forms and voluntary declarations of paternity; providing assistance in completing forms; preparing support schedules based on statutory guidelines; and providing referrals to the local child support agency, family court services, and other community agencies and resources serving parents and children. In counties where a family law information center exists, the facilitator must provide assistance on child support issues.
clauses.gap: The statute's own "shall include, but are not limited to" language means this list is a floor rather than an exhaustive ceiling, so the services actually offered in a given county can exceed this list (or, where staff and funding are constrained, fall short of fully delivering it), and this clause does not survey any particular county's actual practice. It also does not address whether any of these services amount to legal advice; a related, separate provision of this division addresses the facilitator's no-representation limits.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10004 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the enumerated, non-exhaustive services provision
citations.quote: Services provided by the family law facilitator shall include, but are not limited to, the following: providing educational materials to parents concerning the process of establishing parentage and establishing, modifying, and enforcing child support and spousal support in the courts; distributing necessary court forms and voluntary declarations of paternity; providing assistance in completing forms; preparing support schedules based upon statutory guidelines; and providing referrals to the local child support agency, family court services, and other community agencies and resources that provide services for parents and children.

clauses.title: Additional Duties a Court May Add by Local Rule
clauses.body: Under California law, a superior court may, by local rule, designate additional duties for the family law facilitator beyond the core services statute. These optional duties can include meeting with litigants to mediate issues of child support, spousal support, and maintenance of health insurance -- with priority given to actions in which one or both parties are unrepresented -- drafting stipulations on issues the parties agree to, reviewing paperwork and preparing support schedules to advise the judge whether a matter is ready to proceed, assisting the clerk in maintaining records, preparing formal orders consistent with the court's announced order when both parties are unrepresented, and serving as a special master and making findings to the court, unless the facilitator already served as mediator in that same case.
clauses.gap: These duties are locally optional -- the statute says a court "may" designate them by local rule -- so whether a particular county's facilitator actually performs mediation, drafts stipulations, or serves as a special master depends on that county's own local rules, which this clause does not survey. The mediation duty is also expressly made subject to a separate domestic-violence meeting protocol addressed in another clause of this document, and this clause does not restate the statute's separate, resource-conditioned list of further discretionary duties (court research assistance and bar/community outreach programs) found in the same section's subdivision (b).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10005(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the local-rule additional-duties provision, subdivision (a)
citations.quote: By local rule, the superior court may designate additional duties of the family law facilitator, which may include, but are not limited to, the following: (1) Meeting with litigants to mediate issues of child support, spousal support, and maintenance of health insurance, subject to Section 10012. Actions in which one or both of the parties are unrepresented by counsel shall have priority.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10005(a)(6) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the special-master duty and its own-mediator disqualification, a further paragraph of the same subdivision (a) as the previous citation, not an independent source from it
citations.quote: Serving as a special master in proceedings and making findings to the court unless the family law facilitator has served as a mediator in that case.

clauses.title: A Domestic-Violence Safeguard for Facilitator-Conducted Mediation
clauses.body: Under California law, where a superior court has designated facilitator-conducted mediation of support and health-insurance issues as a local-rule duty, and there has been a history of domestic violence between the parties or a protective order is in effect, the facilitator must meet with the parties separately and at separate times if the party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury, or the party protected by the order, requests it. Any intake form the facilitator's office requires before mediation begins must state that this separate-meeting option is available on request.
clauses.gap: This safeguard is tied specifically to the facilitator's own optional mediation duty under Section 10005, subdivision (a)(1); it is a separate mechanism from the mandatory custody-and-visitation mediation program under Family Code Chapter 11 (commencing with Section 3160), which has its own, independently verified domestic-violence procedures addressed elsewhere in this corpus. This clause does not address what happens if a facilitator's office lacks the staffing to hold genuinely separate sessions, which the statute does not itself resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10012(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the separate-meeting requirement, subdivision (a) (a subdivision of the same Section 10012 as the next citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.quote: In a proceeding in which mediation is required pursuant to paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 10005, where there has been a history of domestic violence between the parties or where a protective order as defined in Section 6218 is in effect, at the request of the party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury or protected by the order, the family law facilitator shall meet with the parties separately and at separate times.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10012(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the intake-form disclosure requirement, subdivision (b) of the same Section 10012 as the previous citation, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: Any intake form that the office of the family law facilitator requires the parties to complete before the commencement of mediation shall state that, if a party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury or a party protected by a protective order so requests, the mediator will meet with the parties separately and at separate times.

clauses.title: No Cost to the Parties, and Ultimate Access to a Hearing
clauses.body: Under California law, the court must provide the family law facilitator to the parties at no cost, and the court must adopt a protocol under which all litigants -- whether represented by counsel or not -- retain ultimate access to a hearing before the court.
clauses.gap: These two one-sentence requirements come from separate statutory sections (10006 and 10007) within the same division, so unlike some other clauses in this document they are independent of each other, but each is stated only at a high level: the statute does not specify what a court's hearing-access "protocol" must contain beyond guaranteeing that ultimate access, and "no cost" applies to the facilitator's own services -- it does not address court filing fees or other litigation costs, which are set by separate statutes and local court fee schedules this clause does not survey.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10006 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the hearing-access protocol requirement
citations.quote: The court shall adopt a protocol wherein all litigants, both unrepresented by counsel and represented by counsel, have ultimate access to a hearing before the court.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10007 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the no-cost requirement
citations.quote: The court shall provide the family law facilitator at no cost to the parties.

clauses.title: Interaction With Local Child Support Agency (Title IV-D) Cases
clauses.body: Under California law, this division generally does not apply to a child for whom services are provided or required to be provided by a local child support agency under Family Code Section 17400. Where local child support agency services are being provided, either parent may still use the facilitator's core services listed in Section 10004, but a custodial parent receiving local child support agency services must obtain the agency's written authorization before using the facilitator's local-rule support-related services under Section 10005. The statute states that it is not intended to limit a local child support agency's own duties to seek child support or to limit or supersede other provisions of the code respecting temporary child support.
clauses.gap: This section describes the interaction between the two programs but does not itself state the procedure or standard a local child support agency uses to grant or deny the written authorization it requires, and it does not restate Section 17400's own scope, which this clause does not independently verify. It also singles out the "custodial parent" for the written-authorization requirement without addressing a noncustodial parent's access to Section 10005 services in a Section 17400 case.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10008 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the Title IV-D interaction provision, subdivisions (a) and (b) together (both part of the same Section 10008, not independent of each other)
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b), nothing in this chapter shall be construed to apply to a child for whom services are provided or required to be provided by a local child support agency pursuant to Section 17400. (b) In cases in which the services of the local child support agency are provided pursuant to Section 17400, either parent may utilize the services of the family law facilitator that are specified in Section 10004. In order for a custodial parent who is receiving the services of the local child support agency pursuant to Section 17400 to utilize the services specified in Section 10005 relating to support, the custodial parent must obtain written authorization from the local child support agency.

clauses.title: No Representation, No Attorney-Client Relationship, No Privilege
clauses.body: Under California law, the family law facilitator does not represent any party, and no attorney-client relationship is created between a party and the facilitator as a result of any information or services the facilitator provides. The facilitator must give conspicuous notice that no attorney-client relationship exists, and that notice must include the advice that the absence of an attorney-client relationship means communications between a party and the facilitator are not privileged, and that the facilitator may provide services to the other party as well.
clauses.gap: The statute requires "conspicuous notice" of these limits but does not itself prescribe the notice's exact wording or format; a separate provision of this division (Section 10015, not independently verified in this document) directs the Judicial Council to create the forms that carry out this and related notice requirements. This clause also addresses only the attorney-client privilege; it does not address whether any other evidentiary privilege could apply to a facilitator communication.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 10013 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the no-representation, no-attorney-client-relationship, and no-privilege provision
citations.quote: The family law facilitator shall not represent any party. No attorney-client relationship is created between a party and the family law facilitator as a result of any information or services provided to the party by the family law facilitator. The family law facilitator shall give conspicuous notice that no attorney-client relationship exists between the facilitator, its staff, and the family law litigant. The notice shall include the advice that the absence of an attorney-client relationship means that communications between the party and the family law facilitator are not privileged and that the family law facilitator may provide services to the other party.
