clauses.title: Purpose of This Beneficiary's Right to a Trust Accounting Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's statutory framework governing a trust beneficiary's right to receive a formal accounting from a trustee, as background in connection with {{trustName}}, executed {{originalTrustDate}}, for which {{trusteeName}} serves or has been asked to serve as trustee. {{beneficiaryName}} is referenced for identification only. This document covers when a trustee's duty to account arises, what a compliant account must contain, the limited circumstances in which that duty does not apply or can be waived, and how a beneficiary may seek court enforcement of the duty. It does not itself constitute an accounting, does not itself satisfy any trustee's duty to account for any specific trust, and does not evaluate whether accounting has been properly given or waived for {{trustName}} or any other trust. This is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about a specific trust's accounting obligations.

clauses.title: The Baseline Duty to Keep Beneficiaries Reasonably Informed
clauses.body: Separate from any specific formal accounting, California law imposes a general duty on a trustee of {{trustName}} to keep the trust's beneficiaries reasonably informed of the trust and its administration. This general duty is the statutory backdrop for the more specific rules elsewhere in this document — the periodic formal account, its required contents, and the circumstances in which the duty to account does or does not apply.
clauses.gap: This single sentence states a general standard ("reasonably informed") without itself defining what specific disclosures satisfy it in a given situation; the more detailed rules on formal accounting content and timing appear in the separate sections addressed elsewhere in this document. No case law identifying how California courts have applied this general standard could be verified here — a CourtListener search for relevant authority returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, daily quota of 125 exhausted) rather than results, so this clause relies on the statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16060 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trustee's general duty to keep beneficiaries reasonably informed
citations.quote: The trustee has a duty to keep the beneficiaries of the trust reasonably informed of the trust and its administration.

clauses.title: When a Formal Account Is Required, and Which Beneficiaries Are Entitled to One
clauses.body: Subject to the exceptions addressed elsewhere in this document, a trustee of {{trustName}} must furnish a formal account at least annually, at the trust's termination, and upon any change of trustee. That duty runs only to each beneficiary to whom income or principal is currently required or authorized, in the trustee's discretion, to be distributed — a narrower group than every person named or contingently interested in {{trustName}}.
clauses.gap: The statute conditions the accounting duty on the beneficiary being one to whom a distribution is "currently" required or authorized; it does not itself define that term for every fact pattern (for example, a beneficiary with only a future or contingent remainder interest and no current distribution right is not, by this provision alone, entitled to an account). The statute also does not specify what counts as the trust's "annual" accounting period when a trust's fiscal year changes or is irregular.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16062(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the annual/termination/change-of-trustee triggers and which beneficiaries are entitled to an account
citations.quote: the trustee shall account at least annually, at the termination of the trust, and upon a change of trustee, to each beneficiary to whom income or principal is required or authorized in the trustee’s discretion to be currently distributed.

clauses.title: A Narrow Exception for Certain Pre-1987 Trusts
clauses.body: California's statutory accounting duty does not apply to every trust. A trustee of a living trust created by an instrument executed before July 1, 1987, is not subject to that duty, and the same is true of a trustee of a testamentary trust created by a will executed before July 1, 1987, unless that testamentary trust has since been removed from continuing court jurisdiction, in which case the accounting duty applies after all.
clauses.gap: Cal. Prob. Code § 16062(b) and § 16062(c) are both cited here as subdivisions of the same section, so they are not independent sources of each other — both come from the same 1990-enacted statute. This exception is date-limited and narrows over time: it applies only to instruments executed before a fixed 1987 cutoff, so it has no bearing on any trust created or restated on or after that date, and the statute does not address how an amendment or restatement of a pre-1987 instrument after that date affects the exception.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16062(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: exception for living trusts created by pre-July 1987 instruments — a subdivision of the same section as the § 16062(c) citation below, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: A trustee of a living trust created by an instrument executed before July 1, 1987, is not subject to the duty to account provided by subdivision (a).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16062(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: exception for testamentary trusts created by pre-July 1987 wills, and its own exception for trusts removed from continuing court jurisdiction — a subdivision of the same section as the § 16062(b) citation above, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: A trustee of a trust created by a will executed before July 1, 1987, is not subject to the duty to account provided by subdivision (a), except that if the trust is removed from continuing court jurisdiction pursuant to Article 2 (commencing with Section 17350) of Chapter 4 of Part 5, the duty to account provided by subdivision (a) applies to the trustee.

clauses.title: What a Compliant Account Must Contain
clauses.body: A formal account furnished under California's trustee-accounting statute must include financial content — receipts and disbursements of principal and income, a statement of assets and liabilities, the trustee's compensation, and the trustee's paid agents and their compensation, each for the last complete fiscal year or since the last account — as well as two specific statutory notices that alert the recipient to legal rights and deadlines: that the recipient may petition the court under Probate Code § 17200 for court review of the account and the trustee's acts, and that a claim against the trustee for breach of trust is barred if not brought within three years of receiving an account or report that discloses the facts giving rise to it.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes two separate portions of the same subdivision, § 16063(a) — the financial-content requirement in paragraph (1) and the two mandatory notices in paragraphs (5) and (6) — so the two citations below are not independent sources of each other. The statute prescribes required content but does not prescribe a required format, medium (paper versus electronic), or independent audit or CPA review, and it does not itself state what happens if an account omits one of the two mandatory notices short of the separate consequences addressed elsewhere in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16063(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the financial-content requirement — a paragraph of the same subdivision as the § 16063(a)(5)-(6) citation below, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: shall contain the following information: (1) A statement of receipts and disbursements of principal and income that have occurred during the last complete fiscal year of the trust or since the last account.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16063(a)(5)-(6) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the two mandatory statutory notices an account must contain — paragraphs of the same subdivision as the § 16063(a)(1) citation above, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: (5) A statement that the recipient of the account may petition the court pursuant to Section 17200 to obtain a court review of the account and of the acts of the trustee. (6) A statement that claims against the trustee for breach of trust may not be made after the expiration of three years from the date the beneficiary receives an account or report disclosing facts giving rise to the claim.

clauses.title: Waiving the Duty to Account, and the Limits on That Waiver
clauses.body: The duty to account can be limited in two ways: the trust instrument itself can waive it, or an individual beneficiary can waive the right to an account in writing (a waiver that beneficiary may later withdraw in writing as to future transactions). Neither form of waiver is absolute. Regardless of either kind of waiver, a court may compel the trustee to account upon a showing that it is reasonably likely a material breach of trust has occurred. And a trust instrument's waiver of accounting is void outright — without regard to any court showing — as to a sole trustee who is a disqualified person under the donative-transfer disqualification statutes, a separate protection aimed at self-dealing or undue-influence risk.
clauses.gap: The § 16064(a) and § 16064(b) citations below are both subdivisions of the same section and are not independent sources of each other; the § 16062(e) citation is from a different section and is included for the disqualified-trustee limit on waiver. The "reasonably likely" material-breach standard that lets a court override a waiver is not itself defined by this statute, and § 16062(e)'s disqualified-person trigger depends on separate statutory definitions (former § 21350.5 and current §§ 21380/21382) that are not reproduced or independently verified in this document. No case law applying either standard could be verified here — a CourtListener search returned a rate-limit error rather than results.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16064(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: trust-instrument waiver of accounting, and the court's power to compel an account despite a waiver upon a showing of likely material breach — a subdivision of the same section as the § 16064(b) citation below, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: To the extent the trust instrument waives the account, except that no waiver described in subdivision (e) of Section 16062 shall be valid or enforceable. Regardless of a waiver of accounting in the trust instrument, upon a showing that it is reasonably likely that a material breach of the trust has occurred, the court may compel the trustee to account.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16064(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: an individual beneficiary's written waiver of the right to an account, and its written revocability — a subdivision of the same section as the § 16064(a) citation above, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: As to a beneficiary who has waived in writing the right to an account. A waiver of rights under this subdivision may be withdrawn in writing at any time as to accounts for transactions occurring after the date of the written withdrawal.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16062(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a trust instrument's waiver of accounting is void as to certain disqualified sole trustees
citations.quote: Any limitation or waiver in a trust instrument of the obligation to account is against public policy and shall be void as to any sole trustee who is either of the following: (1) A disqualified person as defined in former Section 21350.5 (as repealed by Chapter 620 of the Statutes of 2010). (2) Described in subdivision (a) of Section 21380, but not described in Section 21382.

clauses.title: Further Circumstances Where No Accounting Duty Runs to a Beneficiary
clauses.body: Beyond the revocable-trust rule addressed elsewhere in this document, California law excuses a trustee of {{trustName}} from accounting to a beneficiary who is also the trustee — there being no one else to whom that duty could meaningfully run in that capacity. Separately, if a revocable trust's settlor loses the capacity needed to exercise the power to revoke and no one else holds that power, the trustee's accounting duty shifts away from the settlor to the beneficiaries the statute identifies for that situation, rather than remaining suspended.
clauses.gap: The § 16069(a)(2) and § 16069(b) citations below are both subdivisions of the same section and are not independent sources of each other. The incapacity rule in subdivision (b) depends on a cross-reference to Probate Code § 15800(b)(2) to identify exactly which beneficiaries then become entitled to an accounting — that cross-referenced provision was not independently fetched or verified for this document.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16069(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no duty to account where beneficiary and trustee are the same person — a subdivision of the same section as the § 16069(b) citation below, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: (2) If the beneficiary and the trustee are the same person.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16069(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the accounting duty shifts to specified beneficiaries if no one competent holds the power to revoke — a subdivision of the same section as the § 16069(a)(2) citation above, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (a), in the case of a revocable trust, if no person holding the power to revoke the trust, in whole or in part, is competent, the trustee’s duties to account shall be owed to those beneficiaries specified in paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 15800.

clauses.title: Court Enforcement: Petitioning to Compel an Account
clauses.body: A trustee or beneficiary of a trust may petition the court concerning the trust's internal affairs, and the statute specifically lists compelling the trustee to account, subject to the waiver provisions addressed elsewhere in this document, among the purposes such a petition can serve — available once the trustee has failed to provide a requested account within 60 days of a beneficiary's written request, and no account has otherwise been furnished within the six months preceding that request.
clauses.gap: The § 17200(a) and § 17200(b)(7)(C) citations below are both subdivisions of the same section and are not independent sources of each other. The statute makes filing such a petition available ("may petition") but does not itself guarantee any particular outcome or timeline for the court's ruling once a petition is filed, and it does not address what happens if the trustee provides a facially compliant but substantively deficient account in response to the 60-day request.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 17200(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a trustee or beneficiary may petition the court on the trust's internal affairs — a subdivision of the same section as the § 17200(b)(7)(C) citation below, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: a trustee or beneficiary of a trust may petition the court under this chapter concerning the internal affairs of the trust or to determine the existence of the trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 17200(b)(7)(C) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: compelling the trustee to account after a 60-day/six-month unanswered written request — a subdivision of the same section as the § 17200(a) citation above, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: (C) Account to the beneficiary, subject to the provisions of Section 16064, if the trustee has failed to submit a requested account within 60 days after written request of the beneficiary and no account has been made within six months preceding the request.

clauses.title: The Three-Year Deadline to Sue the Trustee for Breach After Receiving an Account
clauses.body: Once a beneficiary receives a written account or report that adequately discloses a claim against the trustee for breach of trust, California law bars that claim unless the beneficiary begins a proceeding to assert it within three years of receiving the account or report. If the account or report does not adequately disclose the claim, or if the beneficiary never received any written account or report at all, the same three-year period instead runs from when the beneficiary actually discovered, or reasonably should have discovered, the subject of the claim.
clauses.gap: This single quote spans both paragraph (1) and paragraph (2) of Probate Code § 16460(a), which are contiguous in the statutory text, so this is presented as one citation rather than two. The statute's "adequately discloses" standard is defined only in general terms ("sufficient information so that the beneficiary knows of the claim or reasonably should have inquired") and its application to any specific account's contents is a fact-specific determination the statute leaves to the courts; no case law on how that standard has been applied could be verified here — a CourtListener search returned a rate-limit error (daily quota exhausted) rather than results.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16460(a)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the three-year limitations period, running from receipt of an adequately disclosing account or, otherwise, from actual or constructive discovery
citations.quote: If a beneficiary has received an interim or final account in writing, or other written report, that adequately discloses the existence of a claim against the trustee for breach of trust, the claim is barred as to that beneficiary unless a proceeding to assert the claim is commenced within three years after receipt of the account or report. An account or report adequately discloses existence of a claim if it provides sufficient information so that the beneficiary knows of the claim or reasonably should have inquired into the existence of the claim. (2) If an interim or final account in writing or other written report does not adequately disclose the existence of a claim against the trustee for breach of trust or if a beneficiary does not receive any written account or report, the claim is barred as to that beneficiary unless a proceeding to assert the claim is commenced within three years after the beneficiary discovered, or reasonably should have discovered, the subject of the claim.

clauses.title: A Trust Instrument's Shortened Objection Period, and Its Required Boldface Notice
clauses.body: A trust instrument may go further than the general three-year rule and release the trustee from liability if a beneficiary fails to object to an item in an account within a specified period — but only if the account sets forth the item, the objection period is at least 180 days (or the trustee otherwise follows the statute's alternative procedure), and the account is accompanied by a specific written notice, printed in 12-point boldface type, in the exact form the statute prescribes, telling the beneficiary how long they have to object and what happens if they do not. Where that notice and timing are used correctly, a beneficiary who fails to object in writing within the period is barred from later asserting any claim about an item the account adequately disclosed.
clauses.gap: The § 16461(c) and § 16461(e) citations below are both subdivisions of the same section and are not independent sources of each other; § 16461 also contains subdivisions (a), (b), (d), (f), (g), (h), (i), and (j) not quoted in this clause, including the rule that a trust instrument cannot use this procedure to relieve a trustee of liability for intentional, grossly negligent, bad-faith, or recklessly indifferent breaches. This procedure operates only when a trust instrument actually adopts it with the statute's exact required elements; the statute does not address the consequence of a notice that substantially, but not exactly, matches the prescribed boldface language, and no case law on that question could be verified here — a CourtListener search returned a rate-limit error rather than results.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16461(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the conditions for a valid shortened-objection-period provision, including the 180-day minimum and required boldface notice — a subdivision of the same section as the § 16461(e) citation below, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: a provision in a trust instrument that releases the trustee from liability if a beneficiary fails to object to an item in an interim or final account or other written report within a specified time period is effective only if all of the following conditions are met

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16461(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the effect of a beneficiary's failure to timely object under a compliant shortened-objection-period provision — a subdivision of the same section as the § 16461(c) citation above, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: a beneficiary who fails to object in writing to an account or report that complies with the requirements of subdivision (c) within the specified, valid period shall be barred from asserting any claim against the trustee regarding an item that is adequately disclosed in the account or report.

clauses.body:

It does not itself constitute a trust accounting, does not itself satisfy any trustee's duty to account for {{trustName}} or any other trust, and does not itself constitute or replace a court petition under § 17200. This is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about a specific trust's accounting rights or obligations.]

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the federal civil penalty and excise tax that can apply when a COBRA election notice required by 29 U.S.C. § 1166 is not provided, or is provided late or in a defective form. It is a companion to, and distinct from, this project's COBRA Election Notice document, which contains the notice and election form itself — this document instead explains what federal law provides when that notice obligation is not met. It addresses two separate federal enforcement tracks: a civil penalty against the plan administrator under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), and an excise tax against the employer or plan under the Internal Revenue Code. It does not address California's Cal-COBRA counterpart, which is the subject of a separate document in this project. It states the law generally and does not determine whether a penalty or tax applies to any particular notice sent, or not sent, by {{companyName}} to {{employeeName}}.

clauses.title: ERISA Civil Penalty Against the Plan Administrator
clauses.body: Under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act, an administrator who fails to meet the COBRA notice requirements described in 29 U.S.C. § 1166(a)(1) or (a)(4) with respect to a participant or beneficiary may, in a court's discretion, be held personally liable to that participant or beneficiary in an amount of up to $100 a day from the date of the failure, and the court may also order such other relief as it considers proper. This is a distinct statutory track from the excise tax described elsewhere in this document, which runs against the employer or the plan rather than against the administrator personally.
clauses.gap: This clause states the maximum penalty amount set by the bare statutory text; the adjusted-amount clause elsewhere in this document explains that the amount actually assessed under current regulations is $110, not the $100 stated here, and that even more recent inflation adjustments may not be reflected in that regulation. This clause also does not resolve who qualifies as the 'administrator' of a particular plan, whether a given notice failure falls within the scope of section 1166(a)(1) or (a)(4), or whether a court would exercise its discretion to impose the maximum amount, a lesser amount, or no penalty at all — that determination is fact-specific and requires litigation.

citations.quote: Any administrator (A) who fails to meet the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4) of section 1166

citations.cite: 29 U.S.C. § 1132(c)(1) — the same paragraph as the citation above; not an independent statutory source from it
citations.quote: may in the court’s discretion be personally liable to such participant or beneficiary in the amount of up to $100 a day from the date of such failure or refusal, and the court may in its discretion order such other relief as it deems proper.

clauses.title: Each Notice Failure to Each Person Is a Separate Violation
clauses.body: The same ERISA civil-penalty provision specifies how violations are counted. A notice failure described in the paragraph covering required-notice failures is treated as a separate violation with respect to each single participant, and a failure described in the paragraph covering refusal to furnish requested information is treated as a separate violation with respect to each single participant or beneficiary. Because the statutory daily penalty described elsewhere in this document runs from the date of the failure, a single defective or missing notice affecting more than one qualified beneficiary of the same qualifying event (for example, {{employeeName}} together with a covered spouse or dependent) can be counted, and penalized, separately as to each of them.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the same paragraph of 29 U.S.C. § 1132(c)(1) as the administrator-penalty clause elsewhere in this document — it is not an independent statutory source, only a different sentence of the same paragraph. It states how violations are counted; it does not itself establish that any particular notice was in fact untimely or defective, which is a factual question outside the scope of this information sheet.

citations.cite: 29 U.S.C. § 1132(c)(1) — same paragraph as the administrator-penalty clause in this document; not an independent source
citations.quote: For purposes of this paragraph, each violation described in subparagraph (A) with respect to any single participant, and each violation described in subparagraph (B) with respect to any single participant or beneficiary, shall be treated as a separate violation.

clauses.title: The Penalty Amount as Adjusted by Regulation
clauses.body: The $100-a-day maximum set out in the ERISA statute itself has been adjusted upward by regulation. Under a Department of Labor regulation implementing a statutory inflation-adjustment requirement, the maximum civil penalty under 29 U.S.C. § 1132(c)(1) was increased from $100 a day to $110 a day, effective for violations occurring after July 29, 1997.
clauses.gap: This regulation fixes only the adjustment made effective in 1997; the underlying statutory framework requiring periodic inflation adjustment of civil penalties has since been amended (in 2015) to require more frequent republication of adjusted maximums, and this specific Code of Federal Regulations section does not itself state any dollar figure more recent than $110. The current inflation-adjusted maximum applicable to a specific violation date must be confirmed against the Department of Labor's most recent published adjustment, which is not reproduced in this citation.

citations.quote: In accordance with the requirements of the 1990 Act, as amended, the maximum amount of the civil monetary penalty established by section 502(c)(1) of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 , as amended ( ERISA ), is hereby increased from $100 a day to $110 a day. This adjusted penalty applies only to violations occurring after July 29, 1997.

clauses.title: Enforcement Requires a Civil Action
clauses.body: The ERISA penalty described elsewhere in this document is not self-executing. The statute authorizes a civil action to be brought by a participant or beneficiary for the relief provided for under the penalty provision, among other kinds of relief a participant or beneficiary may seek under the same section of ERISA.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a different subsection (the civil-enforcement subsection, § 1132(a)) of the same 29 U.S.C. § 1132 discussed throughout this document — it is not an independent statutory source from the administrator-penalty and separate-violations clauses, only a different subsection of one section. It states that a civil action is the enforcement mechanism; it does not address venue, statute of limitations, or other procedural requirements for bringing such an action, which are outside the scope of this information sheet.

citations.cite: 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(1)(A) — same section as the administrator-penalty and separate-violations clauses in this document; not an independent source
citations.quote: A civil action may be brought— (1) by a participant or beneficiary— (A) for the relief provided for in subsection (c) of this section, or (B) to recover benefits due to him under the terms of his plan , to enforce his rights under the terms of the plan , or to clarify his rights to future benefits under the terms of the plan ;

clauses.title: A Separate Federal Excise Tax on the Employer or Plan
clauses.body: Apart from the ERISA civil penalty described elsewhere in this document, the Internal Revenue Code separately imposes an excise tax on a group health plan's failure to meet COBRA's continuation-coverage requirements. The tax is imposed on the failure of a group health plan to meet those requirements with respect to any qualified beneficiary, and the amount of the tax is $100 for each day in the 'noncompliance period' with respect to that failure.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the general excise-tax rule and its base per-day amount; it does not by itself state who is liable to pay the tax (addressed in a separate clause in this document), the daily caps that can reduce the amount owed, or the correction and reasonable-cause exceptions that can eliminate the tax entirely (both addressed in other clauses in this document).

citations.quote: (a) General rule There is hereby imposed a tax on the failure of a group health plan to meet the requirements of subsection (f) with respect to any qualified beneficiary .

citations.cite: 26 U.S.C. § 4980B(b)(1) — same section as § 4980B(a) cited above; not an independent source from it
citations.quote: (1) In general The amount of the tax imposed by subsection (a) on any failure with respect to a qualified beneficiary shall be $100 for each day in the noncompliance period with respect to such failure.

clauses.title: Daily Caps on the Excise Tax
clauses.body: The Internal Revenue Code caps the excise tax described elsewhere in this document. Except in the case of more than one qualified beneficiary, the maximum tax imposed for failures on any single day with respect to one qualified beneficiary is $100; if more than one qualified beneficiary is affected by the same qualifying event, the maximum tax imposed for failures on any single day with respect to all of those qualified beneficiaries together is $200.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the same Internal Revenue Code section, § 4980B, as the base excise-tax clause elsewhere in this document — it is not an independent statutory source, only a different subsection of the same section. It states only the per-day caps; it does not state the separate overall (taxable-year) cap described in another clause in this document, which can further limit the total tax owed for unintentional failures.

citations.cite: 26 U.S.C. § 4980B(c)(3) — same section as the other Internal Revenue Code clauses in this document; not an independent source
citations.quote: (3) $100 limit on amount of tax for failures on any day with respect to a qualified beneficiary (A) In general Except as provided in subparagraph (B), the maximum amount of tax imposed by subsection (a) on failures on any day during the noncompliance period with respect to a qualified beneficiary shall be $100. (B) Special rule where more than 1 qualified beneficiary If there is more than 1 qualified beneficiary with respect to the same qualifying event, the maximum amount of tax imposed by subsection (a) on all failures on any day during the noncompliance period with respect to such qualified beneficiaries shall be $200.

clauses.title: An Overall Annual Cap and a 30-Day Correction Safe Harbor
clauses.body: Two further limits can reduce or eliminate the excise tax described elsewhere in this document. First, no tax is imposed on a failure that was due to reasonable cause and not to willful neglect if the failure is corrected during a 30-day period beginning on the date any liable person first knew, or exercising reasonable diligence would have known, that the failure existed. Second, for failures due to reasonable cause and not willful neglect that are not corrected under that safe harbor, the Internal Revenue Code separately caps the total excise tax imposed on a single-employer plan's failures during the employer's taxable year at the lesser of 10 percent of the amount the employer paid for group health plans during the preceding taxable year, or $500,000.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the same Internal Revenue Code section, § 4980B, as the other excise-tax clauses in this document — it is not an independent statutory source. It does not address the separate, higher minimum-tax rule that applies once a notice of examination of income tax liability has been sent to the employer, nor the multiemployer-plan version of the overall cap, both of which are outside the scope of this clause.

citations.quote: (2) Tax not to apply to failures corrected within 30 days No tax shall be imposed by subsection (a) on any failure if— (A) such failure was due to reasonable cause and not to willful neglect, and (B) such failure is corrected during the 30-day period beginning on the 1st date any of the persons referred to in subsection (e) knew, or exercising reasonable diligence would have known, that such failure existed.

citations.cite: 26 U.S.C. § 4980B(c)(4)(A) — same section as the other Internal Revenue Code clauses in this document; not an independent source
citations.quote: (4) Overall limitation for unintentional failures In the case of failures which are due to reasonable cause and not to willful neglect— (A) Single employer plans (i) In general In the case of failures with respect to plans other than multiemployer plans, the tax imposed by subsection (a) for failures during the taxable year of the employer shall not exceed the amount equal to the lesser of— (I) 10 percent of the aggregate amount paid or incurred by the employer (or predecessor employer) during the preceding taxable year for group health plans , or (II) $500,000.

clauses.title: Who Owes the Excise Tax, as Distinct from Who Owes the ERISA Penalty
clauses.body: The excise tax described elsewhere in this document is owed by a different party than the ERISA civil penalty described earlier in this document. Except as otherwise specifically provided, the person liable for the excise tax is, in the case of a plan other than a multiemployer plan, the employer, and in the case of a multiemployer plan, the plan itself. The ERISA civil penalty, by contrast, runs against the plan's administrator personally, not necessarily against the employer. Depending on how {{companyName}}'s group health plan is structured and administered, the employer and the plan administrator may or may not be the same party.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the general liability rule of 26 U.S.C. § 4980B(e)(1)(A) — the same section as the other excise-tax clauses in this document, not an independent source. It does not reproduce the statute's separate rule making certain third-party plan administrators or other responsible persons also liable for the excise tax in specified circumstances, which is a narrower rule not addressed here.

citations.cite: 26 U.S.C. § 4980B(e)(1)(A) — same section as the other Internal Revenue Code clauses in this document; not an independent source
citations.quote: (e) Liability for tax (1) In general Except as otherwise provided in this subsection, the following shall be liable for the tax imposed by subsection (a) on a failure: (A) (i) In the case of a plan other than a multiemployer plan, the employer. (ii) In the case of a multiemployer plan, the plan.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's health care worker minimum wage, Labor Code § 1182.14 (added by Stats. 2023, Ch. 890 (SB 525), and amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 40, Sec. 27 (SB 159), effective June 29, 2024), as it may relate to {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}}. It explains how the statute defines a “covered health care employee” and a “covered health care facility,” the tiered minimum wage schedules the statute sets for different categories of covered health care facility employers, the annual cost-of-living adjustment mechanism, the related salary-basis exemption threshold, the statute's enforcement mechanisms, its waiver program for certain clinics, and its preemption of local minimum wage ordinances for covered health care facility employees. This document does not itself determine whether {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}}'s position meets the statute's coverage definitions, and it is not a substitute for consulting the full text of Labor Code § 1182.14 or a licensed attorney.

clauses.title: Who Is a “Covered Health Care Employee”
clauses.body: California's health care worker minimum wage law defines a “covered health care employee” broadly to include an employee of a health care facility employer who provides patient care, health care services, or services supporting the provision of health care — a category the statute says includes, without limitation, nurses, physicians, caregivers, medical residents, patient care technicians, janitors, housekeeping staff, groundskeepers, guards, clerical and administrative workers, food service and gift shop workers, technical and ancillary services workers, medical coding and billing personnel, schedulers, call center and warehouse workers, and laundry workers, regardless of formal job title. The definition also extends to certain contracted or subcontracted employees, if the employee's employer contracts with the covered health care facility employer (or a contractor/subcontractor to it) to provide health care services or supporting services, and either the covered facility employer exercises the control over the employee's wages, hours, or working conditions associated with joint-employer status under the IWC wage orders, or the employee performs the contracted work primarily (more than half the employee's work time in a workweek) on the premises of a covered health care facility. The statute separately excludes certain categories from “covered health care employee” status, including employment as an outside salesperson, as well as (subject to conditions the statute itself states) certain public employees, delivery or waste-collection workers, and medical transportation workers who are not employed by the facility itself.
clauses.gap: The occupation list quoted below is illustrative (“includes, but is not limited to”), not exhaustive, so whether a specific job title falls within or outside the definition can turn on the duties actually performed rather than the title used. The three citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(b)(2)) rather than independently authored sources — not independent of one another. This clause does not restate every exclusion the statute lists (e.g., the specific conditions for excluding certain public employees, delivery/waste-collection workers, or medical transportation workers), only the outside-salesperson exclusion is quoted in full below.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(b)(2)(A)(i)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of “covered health care employee” — core occupational list
citations.quote:
An employee of a health care facility employer who provides patient care, health care services, or services supporting the provision of health care, which includes, but is not limited to, employees performing work in the occupation of a nurse, physician, caregiver, medical resident, intern or fellow, patient care technician, janitor, housekeeping staff person, groundskeeper, guard, clerical worker, nonmanagerial administrative worker, food service worker, gift shop worker, technical and ancillary services worker, medical coding and medical billing personnel,
				  scheduler, call center and warehouse worker, and laundry worker, regardless of formal job title.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(b)(2)(B)(i)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, extension to certain contracted/subcontracted employees
citations.quote: “Covered health care employee” includes a contracted or subcontracted employee, if clauses (i) and (ii) apply:(i) The employee’s employer contracts with the covered health care facility employer, or with a contractor or subcontractor to the covered health care facility employer, to provide health care services, or services supporting the provision of health care.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(b)(2)(C)(i)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, outside-salesperson exclusion
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subparagraph (A), “covered health care employee” does not include:(i) Employment as an outside salesperson.

clauses.title: Which Employers Are a “Covered Health Care Facility”
clauses.body: The statute defines “covered health care facility” through a long, specific list of licensed and certified facility types — including, among others, a facility within an integrated health care delivery system, a licensed general acute care hospital, a licensed acute psychiatric hospital, a special hospital, certain skilled nursing facilities, licensed home health agencies, clinics and dialysis clinics, psychology clinics, certain residential care facilities for the elderly, psychiatric health facilities, mental health rehabilitation centers, community and rural health clinics, urgent care clinics, certain ambulatory surgical centers, physician groups, and certain county correctional and mental health facilities. The statute then excludes two categories from that definition: a listed facility type that is owned, controlled, or operated by the state or a state agency of the executive branch (a carve-out that does not extend to a health care district or the University of California, which remain covered), and a tribal clinic exempt from licensure or an outpatient setting operated by a federally recognized tribe, tribal organization, or urban Indian organization.
clauses.gap: This clause paraphrases and partially quotes a facility list running to roughly twenty separate subclauses in the statute (§ 1182.14(b)(3)(A)(i)-(xx)); it does not reproduce every listed facility type verbatim, so a facility not mentioned above may still be covered (or a facility resembling one on this list may still fall outside it) depending on its specific licensure and ownership structure. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(b)(3)) and are not independent of one another.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(b)(3)(A)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, opening of the “covered health care facility” list
citations.quote: “Covered health care facility” means any of the following:(i) A facility or other work site that is part of an integrated health care delivery system.(ii) A licensed general acute care hospital, as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 1250 of the Health and Safety Code, including a distinct part of any such hospital.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(b)(3)(B)(i)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, state-agency-owned-facility exclusion
citations.quote: “Covered health care facility” does not include either of the following:(i) Any health care facility described in subparagraph (A) that is owned, controlled, or operated by the state or any state agency of the executive branch. As used in this subparagraph, “state agency” includes every state office, officer, department, division, bureau, board, and commission under the executive branch, including any constitutional offices or officers, California State University, or California Community College, but does not include a health care district or the University of California.

clauses.title: Minimum Wage Schedule — Large Systems, Dialysis Clinics, and High-Medicare/Medi-Cal-Mix Hospitals
clauses.body: For a covered health care facility employer with 10,000 or more full-time-equivalent employees (including as part of an integrated health care delivery system or health care system with that many), any employer that is or operates a dialysis clinic, or a covered facility owned or operated by a county with a population over 5,000,000 as of January 1, 2023, the statute sets a minimum wage of $23.00 per hour from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2025, $24.00 per hour from July 1, 2025 through June 30, 2026, and $25.00 per hour from July 1, 2026 onward (subject to the annual cost-of-living adjustment described elsewhere in this document). A separate, slower schedule applies to a hospital with a high governmental payor mix, an independent hospital with an elevated governmental payor mix, a rural independent covered health care facility, or a facility owned or operated by a county with a population under 250,000 as of January 1, 2023: $18.00 per hour from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2033, with 3.5 percent annual increases, then $25.00 per hour from July 1, 2033 onward. A county-owned, -affiliated, or -operated covered facility is not required to comply with any of these schedules before January 1, 2025.
clauses.gap: This clause covers only two of the statute's four minimum-wage tiers; the tiers for specified clinics and for “all other” covered health care facility employers are addressed in a separate clause. The statutory terms “hospital with a high governmental payor mix,” “independent hospital with an elevated governmental payor mix,” and “rural independent covered health care facility” each carry their own detailed statutory definitions (turning on Medicare/Medi-Cal payor-mix percentages and facility classification data published by the Department of Health Care Access and Information) that this clause does not reproduce. The three citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(c)) and are not independent of one another.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(c)(1)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, minimum wage schedule for large systems/dialysis clinics/large counties
citations.quote:
the minimum wage for all covered health care employees shall
				  be as follows:(A) From July 1, 2024, to June 30, 2025, inclusive, twenty-three dollars ($23) per hour.(B) From July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026, inclusive, twenty-four dollars ($24) per hour.(C) From July 1, 2026, and until adjusted pursuant to subdivision (d), twenty-five dollars ($25) per hour.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(c)(2)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, minimum wage schedule for high-governmental-payor-mix and rural hospitals
citations.quote: For any hospital that is a hospital with a high governmental payor mix, an independent hospital with an elevated governmental payor mix, a rural independent covered health care facility, or a covered health care facility that is owned, affiliated, or operated by a county with a population of less than 250,000 as of January 1, 2023, the minimum wage for all covered health care employees shall be as follows:(A) From July 1, 2024, to June 30, 2033, inclusive, eighteen dollars ($18) per hour, with 3.5 percent increases annually.(B) From July 1, 2033, and until adjusted pursuant to subdivision (d), twenty-five ($25) per hour.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(c)(5)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, delayed compliance date for county-owned facilities
citations.quote:
Notwithstanding any other provision of this subdivision, a covered health care facility that is county owned, affiliated, or operated shall not be required to comply with this subdivision before January 1, 2025. Commencing
				  January 1, 2025, a covered health care facility that is county owned, affiliated, or operated shall comply with the appropriate schedule described in this subdivision.

clauses.title: Minimum Wage Schedule — Specified Clinics and All Other Covered Facilities
clauses.body: For four specified categories of clinic — a community-clinic-type facility not operated by or affiliated with a licensed clinic, a licensed community clinic (and any associated intermittent clinic exempt from licensure), a rural health clinic that is not license-exempt, and an urgent care clinic owned by or affiliated with one of those clinics — the statute sets a minimum wage of $21.00 per hour from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2026, $22.00 per hour from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027, and $25.00 per hour from July 1, 2027 onward. For all other covered health care facility employers not otherwise addressed by one of the statute's schedules, the minimum wage is $21.00 per hour from July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2026, $23.00 per hour from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2028, and $25.00 per hour from July 1, 2028 onward. Both schedules are subject to the annual cost-of-living adjustment described elsewhere in this document once each reaches its final $25.00-per-hour step.
clauses.gap: The four clinic categories in the first schedule are cross-defined by reference to specific subdivisions of Health and Safety Code §§ 1204 and 1206 and to 42 U.S.C. § 1396d(l)(1); this clause does not reproduce those cross-referenced definitions. The clinic categories described in the first schedule are also the categories eligible for the statute's separate 12-month waiver program, addressed in a separate clause. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(c)) and are not independent of one another.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(c)(3)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, minimum wage schedule for specified clinics
citations.quote:
For any health care facility specified in clauses (i) to (iv), inclusive, the minimum wage for all covered health care employees shall be as set forth in subparagraph (B).(i) A clinic as defined in subdivision (h) of Section 1206 of the Health and Safety Code, that is not operated by or affiliated with a clinic described in subdivision (b) of Section 1206 of the Health and Safety Code.(ii) A community clinic licensed under subdivision (a) of
				  Section 1204 of the Health and Safety Code, and any associated intermittent clinic exempt from licensure under subdivision (h) of Section 1206 of the Health and Safety Code.(iii) A rural health clinic, as defined in paragraph (1) of subdivision (l) of Section 1396d of Title 42 of the United States Code, that is not license-exempt.(iv) An urgent care clinic that is owned by or affiliated with a facility defined in clause (ii) or (iii).

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(c)(4)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, minimum wage schedule for all other covered health care facility employers
citations.quote: For all other covered health care facility employers, the minimum wage for all covered health care employees shall be as follows:(A) From July 1, 2024, to June 30, 2026, inclusive, twenty-one dollars ($21) per hour.(B) From July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2028, inclusive, twenty-three dollars ($23) per hour.(C) From July 1, 2028, and until adjusted pursuant to subdivision (d), twenty-five dollars ($25) per hour.

clauses.title: Annual Cost-of-Living Adjustment After Each Schedule's Final Step
clauses.body: Once a covered health care facility employer's applicable minimum wage schedule reaches its final step (the point at which the statute's text says the wage is set at $25.00 per hour “until adjusted”), the California Director of Finance calculates an adjusted health care worker minimum wage on or before August 1 of the following year, and each August 1 after that. The adjustment increases the health care worker minimum wage by the lesser of 3.5 percent or the percentage change in the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' nonseasonally adjusted Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (U.S. CPI-W), comparing the most recent July 1-to-June 30 period to the preceding one, rounded to the nearest ten cents. Each calculated increase takes effect the following January 1. If the relevant CPI-W rate of change is negative, the statute provides that there is no increase or decrease to the health care worker minimum wage for that cycle.
clauses.gap: This mechanism only begins to operate after a given employer's tier reaches its statutory final step (2026, 2027, 2028, or 2033 depending on the tier); it does not itself set the initial step-up amounts described in the wage-schedule clauses. The statute does not describe what happens if the Director of Finance fails to publish a timely calculation. The two citations below are both subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(d)) and are not independent of one another.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(d)(1)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, the annual CPI-based adjustment calculation
citations.quote:
the Director of Finance shall calculate an adjusted minimum wage. The calculation shall increase the health care worker minimum wage by the lesser of 3.5 percent or the rate of change in the averages of the most recent July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period over the preceding July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period for the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics nonseasonally adjusted United States
				  Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (U.S. CPI-W). The result shall be rounded to the nearest ten cents ($0.10). Each adjusted health care worker minimum wage increase calculated under this subdivision shall take effect on the following January 1.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(d)(2)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, no decrease if CPI-W change is negative
citations.quote: If the rate of change in the averages of the most recent July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period over the preceding July 1 to June 30, inclusive, period for the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics nonseasonally adjusted U.S. CPI-W is negative, there shall be no increase or decrease in the health care worker minimum wage pursuant to this subdivision on the following January 1.

clauses.title: Salary-Basis Threshold to Qualify as Exempt From Minimum Wage and Overtime
clauses.body: For covered health care employment compensated on a salary basis, the statute requires the employee's monthly salary to equal no less than 150 percent of the applicable health care worker minimum wage, or 200 percent of the general California minimum wage under Labor Code § 1182.12, whichever amount is greater, for full-time employment, in order for the employee to qualify as exempt from the payment of minimum wage and overtime under California law. This threshold applies even where the employer is a political subdivision of the state, a health care district, the University of California, or a municipality.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the salary-level component of the exempt-status test; California's separate duties tests for exemption (e.g., executive, administrative, or professional duties) are not addressed by this statute or this clause, and satisfying this salary threshold alone does not establish that a given position is properly classified as exempt.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(g)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, the health-care-specific exempt salary threshold
citations.quote: For covered health care employment where the compensation of the employee is on a salary basis, the employee shall earn a monthly salary equivalent to no less than 150 percent of the health care worker minimum wage or 200 percent of the minimum wage, as described in Section 1182.12, whichever is greater, for full-time employment in order to qualify as exempt from the payment of minimum wage and overtime under the law of this state

clauses.title: Enforcement, Posting, and Employee Notice Requirements
clauses.body: The statute makes the health care worker minimum wage enforceable by the Labor Commissioner through the same procedures used for other state minimum wage violations — Labor Code §§ 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1 — or by a covered worker through a civil action, with the same means and relief available for a violation of any other state minimum wage requirement. The statute separately requires the Department of Industrial Relations to amend, supplement, and republish the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders to be consistent with this section, and requires an employer subject to the statute to post a copy of the order as amended in a conspicuous location frequented by employees during the workday, and to provide each employee, on the effective date of the earliest minimum wage increase under the applicable tier, a written notice, in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information, stating which paragraph of the wage-schedule subdivision applies to the employer and the resulting health care worker minimum wage schedule applicable to the employee. The statute also states that the health care worker minimum wage constitutes the state minimum wage for covered health care employment for all purposes under the Labor Code and the wage orders.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the enforcement pathways and the posting/notice obligations the statute lists; it does not itself constitute the posted wage order or the written notice the statute requires, and it does not describe the separate procedural requirements of each cross-referenced Labor Commissioner section (§§ 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, 1197.1) in detail. The posting/notice citation and the enforcement-mechanism citation below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(f)) and are not independent of one another.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(f)(1)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Labor Commissioner and civil-action enforcement
citations.quote: A health care worker minimum wage shall be enforceable by the Labor Commissioner through the procedures set forth in Section 98, 98.1, 98.2, 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, or 1197.1, or by a covered worker through a civil action, through the same means and with the same relief available for violation of any other state minimum wage requirement.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(f)(2)(B)(i)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, posting requirement
citations.quote: Post a copy of the order as amended, supplemented and republished by the Department of Industrial Relations under this section and keep it posted in a conspicuous location frequented by employees during the hours of the workday, as required by Section 1183.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(f)(2)(B)(ii)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, written employee notice requirement
citations.quote: Provide to each employee on the effective date of the earliest minimum wage increase pursuant to subdivision (c), a written notice, in the language the employer normally uses to communicate employment-related information to the employee, indicating the paragraph of subdivision (c) that applies to the employer and the health care worker minimum wage schedule applicable to the employee.

clauses.title: The Delayed-Compliance Waiver Program for Specified Clinics
clauses.body: For the four specified clinic categories subject to the clinic minimum wage schedule described elsewhere in this document, the statute directs the Department of Industrial Relations, in collaboration with the Department of Health Care Access and Information, to administer a waiver program allowing a qualifying clinic to apply for a 12-month delay in that schedule, on a showing of specified financial hardship criteria (including audited financial statements, forecasting from an independent CPA, and balance sheets showing limited cash on hand and a low current ratio). If a waiver is issued, the wage-schedule step dates applicable to that clinic are postponed by 12 months. A clinic may apply for and receive a waiver in consecutive years, but the statute caps this relief: no waiver is available after July 1, 2032, and every eligible clinic must pay the fully adjusted wage beginning July 1, 2033, regardless of how many waivers it previously received.
clauses.gap: This clause summarizes the waiver program's eligibility, effect, and outer time limit; it does not restate the full financial-hardship documentation the statute requires an applicant to submit, nor the separate notice-to-employees and posting obligations that apply once a waiver is issued. The three citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(i)) and are not independent of one another.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(i)(1)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, the waiver program's existence and eligible clinics
citations.quote: The Department of Industrial Relations shall, in collaboration with the Department of Health Care Access and Information, administer a waiver program for covered health care facilities described in clauses (i) to (iv), inclusive, of subparagraph (A) of paragraph (3) of subdivision (c), which will allow a covered health care facility to apply for a 12-month delay in schedule of the health care minimum wage requirements in this section.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(i)(3)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, the 12-month postponement effect of an issued waiver
citations.quote: If a covered health care facility is issued a waiver, all dates in clauses (i) to (iii), inclusive, of subparagraph (B) of paragraph (3) of subdivision (c), or any superseding dates pursuant to a previously issued waiver that are on or after the effective date of the issued waiver, are postponed by 12 months for that covered health care facility.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(i)(6)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, the July 1, 2032 cap on the waiver program
citations.quote: a waiver shall not be available after July 1, 2032, and every covered health care facility described in clauses (i) to (iv), inclusive, of subparagraph (A) of paragraph (3) of subdivision (c) shall pay the adjusted wage required by subdivision (d) beginning July 1, 2033, regardless of whether the facility received any waivers.

clauses.title: Preemption of Local Minimum Wage Ordinances for Covered Health Care Employees
clauses.body: The statute provides that a city, county, or city and county — including a charter city, charter county, or charter city and county — may not enact or enforce an ordinance, regulation, or administrative action that establishes, requires, imposes, limits, or otherwise relates to wages or compensation for covered health care facility employees, and that any such local measure enacted or taking effect after September 6, 2023 is void. This state occupation of the field does not, however, preclude any employer (including a public employer) from voluntarily establishing higher wage, salary, or compensation rates for its own employees or contracted/subcontracted employees, nor does it preclude a locality from adopting a minimum wage that applies uniformly across all industries rather than singling out covered health care facility employees. The statute also builds in future off-ramps from preemption: a locality may establish or enforce a health-care-specific minimum wage after January 1, 2034 (subject to ordinary preemption principles), and may enact an ordinance or take administrative action relating to compensation for covered health care facility employees after January 1, 2030 (also subject to ordinary preemption principles).
clauses.gap: This clause describes the preemption rule and its stated exceptions as of the statutory text fetched; it does not evaluate whether any particular local ordinance, before or after the stated dates, would in fact be preempted, which the statute itself says is to be judged under “ordinary preemption principles” rather than a rule this clause can state in advance. This entire subdivision is itself conditional — the statute says it applies only if the provisions of the section requiring health care worker minimum wages take effect. The three citations below are all subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1182.14(j)) and are not independent of one another.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, the core preemption rule and voiding of post-September 6, 2023 local measures
citations.quote: An ordinance, regulation, or administrative action applicable to a covered health care facility, as defined in this section, that establishes, requires, imposes, limits, or otherwise relates to wages or compensation for covered health care facility employees, as defined in this section, shall not be enacted or enforced in or by any city, county, city and county, including charter cities, charter counties, and charter cities and counties.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(j)(3)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, exception allowing voluntarily higher employer-set wages
citations.quote: This subdivision does not preclude any employer, including a city, county, city and county, including charter cities, charter counties, and charter cities and counties, that employs health care employees, from establishing higher wage, salary, or compensation rates for its employees or contracted or subcontracted employees.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1182.14(j)(5)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, the January 1, 2034 sunset on health-care-specific preemption
citations.quote: This subdivision does not preclude a city, county, city and county, including charter cities, charter counties, and charter cities and counties, from establishing or enforcing a minimum wage applicable to covered health care facility employees, as defined in this section, after January 1, 2034. Any such ordinance, regulation, or administrative action shall be evaluated under ordinary preemption principles.
