clauses.title: About This Farm Labor Contractor Licensing Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Farm Labor Contractor Licensing Law, Labor Code Sections 1682 through 1699, which requires a person who recruits, supplies, or hires workers for a fee on behalf of an agricultural employer -- and who furnishes board, lodging, or transportation, supervises or directs the work, or disburses wages in connection with that activity -- to hold a license issued by the Labor Commissioner before acting as a farm labor contractor. {{companyName}} has described its use of labor contractors, if any, as follows: {{laborContractorUseDescription}}. This document states the content of the statute; it does not determine whether any particular individual or arrangement meets the statutory definition of "farm labor contractor," and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice or for consulting a licensed attorney.

clauses.title: Who Is a "Farm Labor Contractor" Under Labor Code Section 1682
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1682 defines a "farm labor contractor" as any person who, for a fee, employs workers to render personal services in connection with the production of farm products to, for, or under the direction of a third person, or who recruits, solicits, supplies, or hires workers on behalf of an agricultural employer, and who -- for that fee -- also furnishes board, lodging, or transportation for the workers, supervises or otherwise directs or measures their work, or disburses wage payments to them. Section 1682.5 removes two categories of activity from the chapter's coverage entirely: services performed by a nonprofit corporation or organization for its own members, and services performed by a person only within the scope of that person's employment by the third person on whose behalf the person is acting, provided the person is not acting as an independent contractor.
clauses.gap: The statute's exemptions turn on whether a person is acting "within the scope of his employment" for the user of the labor rather than as an independent contractor, and on whether an organization is a genuine "nonprofit corporation or organization" acting "for its members"; Section 1682.5 does not itself define those terms or state how they interact with the multi-factor tests used elsewhere in California law (such as the ABC test) to distinguish employees from independent contractors, so this sheet does not resolve how the exemption applies to any particular arrangement.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1682(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, definition of "farm labor contractor"
citations.quote: “Farm labor contractor” designates any person who, for a fee, employs workers to render personal services in connection with the production of any farm products to, for, or under the direction of a third person, or who recruits, solicits, supplies, or hires workers on behalf of an employer engaged in the growing or producing of farm products, and who, for a fee, provides in connection therewith one or more of the following services: furnishes board, lodging, or transportation for those workers; supervises, times, checks, counts, weighs, or otherwise directs or measures their work; or disburses wage payments to these persons.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1682.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, nonprofit-member-services exemption
citations.quote: A nonprofit corporation or organization with respect to services specified in subdivision (b) of Section 1682, which are performed for its members.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1682.5(b) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, employee-acting-within-scope-of-employment exemption
citations.quote: Any person who performs the services specified in subdivision (b) of Section 1682 only within the scope of his employment by the third person on whose behalf he is so acting and not as an independent contractor.

clauses.title: License Requirement and Civil Penalty for Acting Without One
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1683(a) states that a person shall not act as a farm labor contractor until a license has been issued by the Labor Commissioner and the license is in full force and effect and in the person's possession. Subdivision (b) establishes a tiered civil penalty schedule for a violation of this licensing requirement: an initial citation carries a penalty of $100 per farmworker employed by the unlicensed person plus $100 per calendar day of violation, capped at $10,000; a second citation doubles those figures to $200 per farmworker and per day, capped at $20,000; and a third or subsequent citation raises the figures to $500 per farmworker and per day, capped at $50,000.
clauses.gap: Section 1683's civil penalty schedule applies to the act of operating without a license; it does not by its own text address the separate question of whether, or under what circumstances, an agricultural employer who engages an unlicensed farm labor contractor (as opposed to the contractor itself) bears civil liability, which may instead arise under other statutes such as Labor Code Section 2810.3 or general joint-employer principles that are outside this chapter and not addressed by this sheet.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1683(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, license required to act as a farm labor contractor
citations.quote: A person shall not act as a farm labor contractor until a license to do so has been issued to the person by the Labor Commissioner and the license is in full force and effect and in the person’s possession.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1683(b)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, initial-citation civil penalty tier
citations.quote: For any initial citation, one hundred dollars ($100) for each farmworker employed by the unlicensed person, plus one hundred dollars ($100) for each calendar day that a violation occurs, for a total penalty not to exceed ten thousand dollars ($10,000).

clauses.title: License Application: Sworn Statement and Commissioner Investigation
clauses.body: Under Labor Code Section 1684(a), the Labor Commissioner may not issue or renew a farm labor contractor license until several conditions are satisfied. Among them, the applicant must execute a written application, subscribed and sworn to, in a form prescribed by the Labor Commissioner, that discloses the applicant's character, competency, and responsibility, the names and addresses of anyone else financially interested in the proposed operation, a consent to service of process on the Labor Commissioner if the applicant later becomes unavailable for service, and the names of persons who performed farm-labor-contracting services on the applicant's behalf in the preceding calendar year. The Labor Commissioner must also independently investigate and become satisfied as to the applicant's character, competency, and responsibility before a license may issue.
clauses.gap: This clause describes only the sworn-application and character-investigation conditions in paragraphs (1) and (2) of subdivision (a); it does not restate the bond, fee, examination, sexual harassment training, or federal registration conditions that appear in the remaining paragraphs of the same subdivision (addressed in separate clauses of this sheet), and the statute does not itself specify the evidentiary standard or procedure the Labor Commissioner uses to become "satisfied" as to character, competency, and responsibility.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1684(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, written and sworn license application requirement
citations.quote: The person has executed a written application in a form prescribed by the Labor Commissioner, subscribed and sworn to by the person, and containing all of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1684(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Labor Commissioner investigation requirement
citations.quote: The Labor Commissioner, after investigation, is satisfied as to the character, competency, and responsibility of the person.

clauses.title: Surety Bond and License Fee Tied to Payroll Size
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1684(a)(3) requires an applicant to deposit a surety bond with the Labor Commissioner in an amount tied to the size of the applicant's annual payroll: a $25,000 bond for payrolls up to $500,000, a $50,000 bond for payrolls between $500,000 and $2,000,000, and a $75,000 bond for payrolls above $2,000,000. Subdivision (a)(4) requires payment of a license fee, stated in the current text as $500 plus a $10 filing fee (not required on a timely renewal application), with the license fee itself having increased by $100 to $600 effective January 1, 2015. A portion of each licensee's annual fee -- $150, as stated in the current text -- is deposited into the Farmworker Remedial Account, from which the Labor Commissioner disburses funds to persons determined to have been damaged by a licensed or unlicensed farm labor contractor.
clauses.gap: The dollar figures quoted for the bond tiers, license fee, and Farmworker Remedial Account allocation are the amounts stated in the version of Section 1684 in effect as of the date this sheet was checked; the statute's own text shows the license fee has already been increased once by amendment (from $500 to $600 effective January 1, 2015), so these figures could change again if the Legislature amends the section after that date, and this sheet does not track amendments made after the checked date.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1684(a)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, payroll-tiered surety bond amounts
citations.quote: The person has deposited with the Labor Commissioner a surety bond in an amount based on the size of the person’s annual payroll for all employees, as follows: (i) For payrolls up to five hundred thousand dollars ($500,000), a twenty-five-thousand-dollar ($25,000) bond. (ii) For payrolls of five hundred thousand dollars ($500,000) to two million dollars ($2,000,000), a fifty-thousand-dollar ($50,000) bond. (iii) For payrolls greater than two million dollars ($2,000,000), a seventy-five-thousand-dollar ($75,000) bond.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1684(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, license fee and filing fee
citations.quote: The person has paid to the Labor Commissioner a license fee of five hundred dollars ($500) plus a filing fee of ten dollars ($10). However, when a timely application for renewal is filed, the ten-dollar ($10) filing fee is not required. The license fee shall increase by one hundred dollars ($100), to six hundred dollars ($600), on January 1, 2015.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1684(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citations, not an independent source of them)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Farmworker Remedial Account allocation
citations.quote: The Labor Commissioner shall deposit one hundred fifty dollars ($150) of each licensee’s annual license fee into the Farmworker Remedial Account. Funds from this account shall be disbursed by the Labor Commissioner only to persons determined by the Labor Commissioner to have been damaged by any licensee or to persons determined by the Labor Commissioner to have been damaged by an unlicensed farm labor contractor.

clauses.title: Written Examination and Sexual Harassment Prevention Training as Licensing Conditions
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1684(a)(5) conditions licensure on the applicant passing a written examination -- covering wages, hours, working conditions, penalties, employee housing and transportation, collective bargaining, field sanitation, and pesticide safe-work practices, including the identification and prevention of sexual harassment -- with a passing score of at least 85 percent correct answers. Separately, subdivision (a)(8) conditions licensure on the applicant executing a written statement, provided to the Labor Commissioner, attesting that the applicant's supervisory employees have received at least two hours of sexual harassment prevention training each calendar year, that new nonsupervisory employees have been trained at the time of hire, and that nonsupervisory employees are retrained at least once every two years in identifying, preventing, and reporting sexual harassment.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the licensing-stage examination and sexual-harassment-training attestation conditions only; it does not address the further content, language-access, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements that subdivision (a)(8) attaches to that training (such as the specific topics the training must cover or the three-year recordkeeping duty), and it does not address the general, separately codified duty of California employers with five or more employees to provide sexual harassment prevention training under Government Code Section 12950.1, which is a different statute outside this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1684(a)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, written examination requirement and passing score
citations.quote: The person has taken a written examination that demonstrates an essential degree of knowledge of the current laws and administrative regulations concerning farm labor contractors as the Labor Commissioner deems necessary for the safety and protection of farmers, farmworkers, and the public, including the identification and prevention of sexual harassment in the workplace. To successfully complete the examinations, the person must correctly answer at least 85 percent of the questions posed.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1684(a)(8)(A) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, sexual harassment prevention training attestation
citations.quote: The person has executed a written statement, that has been provided to the Labor Commissioner, attesting that the person’s supervisorial employees, including any supervisor, crewleader, mayordomo, foreperson, or other employee whose duties include the supervision, direction, or control of agricultural employees, have been trained at least once for at least two hours each calendar year in the prevention of sexual harassment in the workplace, and that all new nonsupervisorial employees, including agricultural employees, have been trained at the time of hire, and that all nonsupervisorial employees, including agricultural employees, have been trained at least once every two years in identifying, preventing, and reporting sexual harassment in the workplace.

clauses.title: Grounds on Which a License Shall Not Be Granted
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1685 identifies specific circumstances in which the Labor Commissioner shall not grant a farm labor contractor license, including where the applicant sells or proposes to sell intoxicating liquors on the premises where the applicant operates or proposes to operate as a farm labor contractor, where the applicant's license was revoked within the preceding three years, and where the applicant -- within the preceding three years -- has been found by a court or administrative agency to have committed sexual harassment of an employee, or knowingly employed a supervisory employee found to have done so within the preceding three years of that employee's employment with the applicant.
clauses.gap: Section 1685 does not itself define the evidentiary standard for a determination that a person "has been found by a court or an administrative agency to have committed sexual harassment," nor does it address whether an out-of-state finding or a private employer's internal investigation (as opposed to a court or administrative agency) triggers the bar; the subdivision does provide a knowledge-presumption mechanism tied to a Labor Commissioner-issued attestation form, which this sheet does not separately detail.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1685(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, denial ground: sale of intoxicating liquors on premises
citations.quote: To any person who sells or proposes to sell intoxicating liquors in a building or on premises where he or she operates or proposes to operate as a farm labor contractor.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1685(c) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, denial ground: sexual harassment finding within preceding three years
citations.quote: To a person who, within the preceding three years, has been found by a court or an administrative agency to have committed sexual harassment of an employee, or who, within the preceding three years, employed any supervisor, crewleader, mayordomo, foreperson, or any other employee of the applicant whose duties include the supervision, direction, or control of any agricultural worker whom the applicant knew or should have known has been found by a court or an administrative agency, within the preceding three years of his or her employment with the applicant, to have committed sexual harassment of an employee.

clauses.title: Grounds on Which a License May Be Revoked, Suspended, or Not Renewed
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1690 authorizes the Labor Commissioner to revoke, suspend, or refuse to renew a farm labor contractor license on any of several grounds, including a violation of this chapter, misrepresentation in the license application, a change in the conditions under which the license was issued, a violation of state law regulating agricultural employment, wages, or workplace health and safety applicable to the licensee's farm-labor-contracting business, a violation of Vehicle Code provisions governing farm labor vehicles, a violation of the federal Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act where federal registration is required, and a finding that the licensee (or a supervisory employee the licensee knew or should have known about) committed sexual harassment of an employee within the preceding three years.
clauses.gap: Section 1690 uses permissive language -- the Labor Commissioner "may" revoke, suspend, or refuse to renew -- rather than mandatory language, so a licensee's conduct falling within one of these grounds does not automatically terminate the license; the statute does not itself state the discretionary factors the Labor Commissioner applies in deciding whether to act, or the procedural sequence (addressed in a different section of this chapter not covered by this sheet) by which that discretion is exercised.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1690 (introductory clause) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, discretionary revocation/suspension/non-renewal authority
citations.quote: The Labor Commissioner may revoke, suspend, or refuse to renew any license if it is shown that any of the following have occurred:

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1690(d) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, revocation ground: violation of agricultural employment/wage/safety law
citations.quote: The licensee, or any agent of the licensee, has violated, or has willfully aided or abetted any person in the violation of, or failed to comply with, any law of the State of California regulating the employment of employees in agriculture, the payment of wages to farm employees, or the conditions, terms, or places of employment affecting the health and safety of farm employees, which is applicable to the business, activities, or operations of the licensee in his or her capacity as a farm labor contractor.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1690(g) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citations, not an independent source of them)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, revocation ground: sexual harassment finding
citations.quote: The licensee has been found by a court or an administrative agency to have committed sexual harassment of an employee, or has employed any supervisor, crewleader, mayordomo, foreperson, or any other employee of the licensee whose duties include the supervision, direction, or control of any agricultural worker on behalf of the licensee, whom the licensee knew or should have known has been found by a court or an administrative agency, within the preceding three years, to have committed sexual harassment of an employee.

clauses.title: Ongoing Duties While Licensed: Carrying the License and Disclosing Pay Rates
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1695(a) imposes continuing duties on every licensee. The licensee must carry the license and proof of registration at all times and exhibit them to anyone the licensee intends to deal with as a farm labor contractor before dealing with that person. The licensee must also keep available for inspection by employees and by the grower a written statement, in English and Spanish, showing the rate of compensation the licensee receives from the grower and the rate the licensee pays to employees for services rendered to or under the control of the grower, provide that statement to a current or former employee or the grower within 21 calendar days of a written request, and pay a $750 civil penalty (recoverable by the employee or grower) for failing to comply. The licensee must further display prominently, at the worksite and on vehicles used to transport employees, the rate of compensation being paid to employees, printed in English and Spanish in a lettering size prescribed by the Department of Industrial Relations.
clauses.gap: This clause describes only three of the nine numbered duties listed in subdivision (a) of Section 1695; it does not restate the licensee's separate duties to file a change-of-address notice with the Labor Commissioner and county agricultural commissioner, promptly distribute entrusted funds, comply with contracts entered into as a farm labor contractor, maintain vehicle liability insurance, register annually with the county agricultural commissioner, or provide safety and sexual-harassment-related training and information to supervisory employees, all of which appear elsewhere in the same subdivision.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1695(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, duty to carry and exhibit license
citations.quote: Carry his or her license and proof of registration issued pursuant to paragraph (8) with him or her at all times and exhibit the same to all persons with whom he or she intends to deal in his or her capacity as a farm labor contractor prior to so dealing.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1695(a)(5) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, written bilingual pay-rate disclosure statement and penalty for noncompliance
citations.quote: Have available for inspection by his or her employees and by the grower with whom he or she has contracted a written statement in English and Spanish showing the rate of compensation he or she receives from the grower and the rate of compensation he or she is paying to his or her employees for services rendered to, for, or under the control of the grower. Upon written request, the statement shall be provided to a current or former employee or the grower within 21 calendar days. A licensee who fails to comply with this paragraph is subject to a civil penalty of seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) recoverable by the employee or the grower.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1695(a)(7) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citations, not an independent source of them)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, posted bilingual pay-rate notice at worksite and on vehicles
citations.quote: Have displayed prominently at the site where the work is to be performed and on all vehicles used by the licensee or his or her employees or agents for the transportation of employees the rate of compensation the licensee is paying to his or her employees for their services, printed in both English and Spanish and in lettering of a size to be prescribed by the Department of Industrial Relations.

clauses.title: Criminal Penalties and Private Civil Remedies for Violations
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1697(a) makes any violation of this chapter -- or causing or inducing another to violate it -- a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of up to $1,000, imprisonment in county jail for up to six months, or both. Subdivision (b) gives an employee aggrieved by a violation of the chapter (other than conduct also covered by the Agricultural Labor Relations Act's unfair-labor-practice provisions in Labor Code Sections 1153 through 1155) the right to bring a civil action for injunctive relief, damages, or both, with recovery of reasonable attorney's fees, costs, and expert witness fees upon prevailing, and the right to enforce the claim against the farm labor contractor's bond. Subdivision (c) imposes a heightened penalty -- a fine of not less than $10,000, imprisonment of not less than six months and not more than one year, or both -- on a farm labor contractor who continues contracting activity after the contractor's license has been suspended, revoked, or denied reissuance.
clauses.gap: Subdivision (b)'s private civil action expressly excludes conduct "also proscribed by Sections 1153, 1154, and 1155" of the Labor Code, which are unfair-labor-practice provisions of the Agricultural Labor Relations Act; this sheet does not describe what conduct those excluded sections cover or the separate procedures (before the Agricultural Labor Relations Board) that apply to claims falling within that exclusion.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1697(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, misdemeanor penalty for a chapter violation
citations.quote: Any person who violates this chapter, or who causes or induces another to violate this chapter, is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not more than one thousand dollars ($1,000), or imprisonment in the county jail for not more than six months, or both.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1697(b) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, aggrieved employee's private civil action and bond remedy
citations.quote: Any employee aggrieved by any violation of this chapter, other than acts and conduct also proscribed by Sections 1153, 1154, and 1155, may do all of the following: (1) Bring a civil action for injunctive relief or damages, or both, against a farm labor contractor or unlicensed farm labor contractor who violates this chapter and, upon prevailing, shall recover reasonable attorney’s fees and costs, including expert witness fees.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1697(c) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citations, not an independent source of them)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, heightened penalty for contracting while suspended, revoked, or denied reissuance
citations.quote: Any farm labor contractor who engages in farm labor contracting activities after his or her license has been suspended, revoked, or denied reissuance is guilty of an offense punishable by a fine of not less than ten thousand dollars ($10,000), or by imprisonment for not less than six months and not more than one year, or both.

clauses.title: Purpose of This DTSA Civil Seizure Remedy Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act's ex parte civil seizure remedy, 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2), a distinct procedural mechanism separate from the ordinary injunction, damages, and attorney's-fee remedies available under 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(3). It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning {{companyName}}'s trade secret, described as follows: {{tradeSecretDescription}}, in a situation involving {{adversePartyName}}. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference describing what the statute says about when a court may order the seizure of property to prevent a trade secret's propagation or dissemination, what an applicant must show, what protections the statute builds in for the party whose property is seized and for third parties, and what liability can follow a wrongful or excessive seizure. It does not itself determine whether a seizure order would be sought, granted, denied, dissolved, or modified in any specific case, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is also distinct from, and is meant as a companion to, this project's existing Trade Secret Injunctive Relief Standards Information Sheet (which addresses the ordinary injunction remedy under section 1836(b)(3)(A)) and its existing Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter document (whose federal-remedies clause identifies the civil seizure provision by name but does not quote or describe it) -- this Information Sheet is what fills that specific, previously-disclosed gap.

clauses.title: DTSA Civil Seizure: An Extraordinary, Ex Parte Remedy
clauses.body: The Defend Trade Secrets Act authorizes a court, based on an affidavit or verified complaint meeting the statute's requirements, to issue an order for the seizure of property necessary to prevent the propagation or dissemination of the trade secret at issue in the action. The statute frames this as an extraordinary remedy available only on ex parte application -- meaning the application may be made and the order may be sought without prior notice to the party whose property would be seized -- and the statute itself limits the remedy to "extraordinary circumstances," a threshold distinct from the showing required for an ordinary injunction under the same section.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of what 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(A)(i) authorizes on its face -- not a claim about how often courts actually grant this relief, which circumstances courts have treated as sufficiently "extraordinary," or whether any specific set of facts would qualify. Courts have applied this remedy sparingly since its 2016 enactment, and the specific findings a court must make before granting it are addressed in this document's companion clauses rather than in this one. A CourtListener case-law search for this clause returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (125/day quota already exhausted) before any case could be retrieved, so no case law on how courts have applied this ex parte, extraordinary-circumstances threshold is included here; only the statutory text is quoted.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(A)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- application
citations.quote: Based on an affidavit or verified complaint satisfying the requirements of this paragraph, the court may, upon ex parte application but only in extraordinary circumstances, issue an order providing for the seizure of property necessary to prevent the propagation or dissemination of the trade secret that is the subject of the action.

clauses.title: DTSA Civil Seizure: Required Findings on Necessity and Harm
clauses.body: Before granting a seizure application, the statute requires the court to find that it clearly appears from specific facts that an order under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65 (the ordinary preliminary-injunction rule) or another form of equitable relief would be inadequate because the party to be ordered would evade, avoid, or otherwise not comply with it; that immediate and irreparable injury will occur without the seizure; and that the harm to the applicant of denying the application outweighs the harm to the legitimate interests of the person against whom seizure would be ordered, and substantially outweighs the harm to any third parties who may be harmed by the seizure. The statute also requires findings that the person against whom seizure would be ordered would destroy, move, hide, or otherwise make the property inaccessible to the court if given notice, and that the applicant has not publicized the requested seizure.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the necessity- and harm-related findings 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(A)(ii) requires before a seizure order may issue -- not a claim about how any court would weigh these factors on particular facts. This clause paraphrases and summarizes five of the statute's eight numbered findings (subclauses (I), (II), (III), (VII), and (VIII)); the remaining three findings, concerning the merits of the trade secret and misappropriation claims and the location of the property, are quoted in a companion clause of this document rather than repeated here. A CourtListener case-law search for this clause was not separately attempted beyond the single rate-limited search already disclosed elsewhere in this document; that search returned an HTTP 429 error before any results were retrieved, so no case law interpreting these findings is included here.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(A)(ii)(I)-(III) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- requirements for issuing order (inadequacy of other relief, irreparable injury, balance of harms); subclauses of the same paragraph as the citation in the companion clause on merits findings, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: an order issued pursuant to Rule 65 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure or another form of equitable relief would be inadequate to achieve the purpose of this paragraph because the party to which the order would be issued would evade, avoid, or otherwise not comply with such an order

clauses.title: DTSA Civil Seizure: Required Findings on the Merits and Location of Property
clauses.body: In addition to the necessity and harm findings, the statute requires the court to find that the applicant is likely to succeed in showing that the information is a trade secret and that the person against whom seizure would be ordered either misappropriated the trade secret by improper means or conspired to use improper means to misappropriate it. The court must also find that the person against whom seizure would be ordered has actual possession of both the trade secret and the property to be seized, and that the application describes with reasonable particularity the matter to be seized and, to the extent reasonable, identifies the location where it is to be seized.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the merits- and location-related findings 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(A)(ii) requires -- not a claim that any particular information qualifies as a trade secret or that any particular conduct constitutes misappropriation by improper means on the facts described elsewhere in this document. This clause quotes and paraphrases three of the statute's eight numbered findings (subclauses (IV), (V), and (VI)); the other five, concerning necessity and harm, are addressed in a companion clause rather than repeated here, and both clauses draw from the same statutory subparagraph rather than independent sources. No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt already disclosed in this document's other clauses.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(A)(ii)(IV)-(VI) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- requirements for issuing order (likelihood of success, possession, particularity); subclauses of the same paragraph as the citation in the companion clause on necessity/harm findings, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: the applicant is likely to succeed in showing that— (aa) the information is a trade secret ; and (bb) the person against whom seizure would be ordered— (AA) misappropriated the trade secret of the applicant by improper means ; or (BB) conspired to use improper means to misappropriate the trade secret of the applicant

clauses.title: DTSA Civil Seizure: Narrowest Seizure and Protection of Seized Property
clauses.body: If a seizure order issues, the statute requires it to provide for the narrowest seizure of property necessary to achieve the statute's purpose, and to direct that the seizure be conducted in a manner that minimizes any interruption of third parties' business operations and, to the extent possible, does not interrupt the legitimate business operations of the person accused of misappropriation. The order must also be accompanied by a provision protecting the seized property from disclosure -- prohibiting access by the applicant or the person against whom the order is directed, and prohibiting copies of the seized property -- until the parties have an opportunity to be heard at the seizure hearing.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of what 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(B) requires an issued seizure order to contain -- not a claim about how narrowly any particular court has construed "narrowest seizure of property necessary" on specific facts. This clause quotes and paraphrases two of the six elements a seizure order must include under subparagraph (B) (clauses (ii) and (iii)(I)); the hearing-deadline and security-bond elements of the same subparagraph are addressed in a companion clause rather than repeated here. No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt disclosed elsewhere in this document.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(B)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- elements of order (narrowest seizure); part of the same subparagraph as the companion clause on the hearing deadline and security bond, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: provide for the narrowest seizure of property necessary to achieve the purpose of this paragraph and direct that the seizure be conducted in a manner that minimizes any interruption of the business operations of third parties and, to the extent possible, does not interrupt the legitimate business operations of the person accused of misappropriating the trade secret

clauses.title: DTSA Civil Seizure: Seven-Day Hearing Deadline and Security Bond
clauses.body: A seizure order must set a date for a hearing at the earliest possible time, and not later than seven days after the order issues, unless the party against whom the order is directed and others harmed by it consent to a later date; any party against whom the order issued, or any person harmed by it, may move at any time to dissolve or modify the order after giving notice to the applicant. The order must also require the person who obtained it to post security, in an amount the court determines adequate, for the payment of damages that any person may be entitled to recover from a wrongful or excessive seizure or attempted seizure.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the hearing-timing and security-bond requirements 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(B) imposes on an issued seizure order -- not a claim about what amount of security any court would set, or how quickly any specific hearing would actually be scheduled. This clause quotes and paraphrases two of the six required elements of a seizure order under subparagraph (B) (clauses (v) and (vi)); the narrowest-seizure and disclosure-protection elements of the same subparagraph are addressed in a companion clause rather than repeated here. No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt disclosed elsewhere in this document.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(B)(v) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- elements of order (hearing deadline); part of the same subparagraph as the companion clause on narrowness and disclosure protection, not an independent source of it
citations.quote: set a date for a hearing described in subparagraph (F) at the earliest possible time, and not later than 7 days after the order has issued, unless the party against whom the order is directed and others harmed by the order consent to another date for the hearing

clauses.title: DTSA Civil Seizure: Execution Only by Law Enforcement, Not the Applicant
clauses.body: The statute requires that service of the seizure order be made by a federal law enforcement officer, who then carries out the seizure. The court may allow state or local law enforcement to participate, but may not permit the applicant or any agent of the applicant to participate in the seizure itself. At the request of law enforcement, the court may allow an unaffiliated technical expert bound by a court-approved non-disclosure agreement to participate if doing so would aid an efficient, minimally burdensome execution.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of who the statute requires to execute a seizure order under 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(E) -- not a claim about how this requirement operates in practice in any particular judicial district or how any specific seizure would actually be staffed. This clause quotes and paraphrases subparagraph (E) in full; it does not address the separate custody-of-materials provisions of subparagraph (D), which are covered in a companion clause. No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt disclosed elsewhere in this document.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(E) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- service of order
citations.quote: The court shall order that service of a copy of the order under this paragraph, and the submissions of the applicant to obtain the order, shall be made by a Federal law enforcement officer who, upon making service, shall carry out the seizure under the order. The court may allow State or local law enforcement officials to participate, but may not permit the applicant or any agent of the applicant to participate in the seizure.

clauses.title: DTSA Civil Seizure: Custody of the Court and Confidentiality Protections
clauses.body: Materials seized under the statute are taken into the custody of the court, which must secure them from physical and electronic access during the seizure and while in its custody. If the seized material includes or is stored on a storage medium, the court must prohibit that medium from being connected to a network or the internet without both parties' consent, until the required seizure hearing. The court must also take appropriate measures to protect the confidentiality of seized materials unrelated to the trade secret information ordered seized, unless the person against whom the order was entered consents to disclosure, and the court may appoint a special master -- bound by a court-approved non-disclosure agreement -- to locate and isolate the misappropriated trade secret information and facilitate return of unrelated property.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the custody and confidentiality safeguards 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(D) imposes once property has been seized -- not a claim about how any specific court's clerk's office or IT security practices would actually implement these safeguards, or about whether a special master would be appointed in any particular case. This clause summarizes and quotes from subparagraph (D)'s four clauses together; it does not separately address the publicity-protection provisions of subparagraph (C), which are distinct language in the same paragraph. No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt disclosed elsewhere in this document.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(D)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- materials in custody of court
citations.quote: Any materials seized under this paragraph shall be taken into the custody of the court. The court shall secure the seized material from physical and electronic access during the seizure and while in the custody of the court.

clauses.title: DTSA Civil Seizure: Liability for a Wrongful or Excessive Seizure
clauses.body: A person who suffers damage because of a wrongful or excessive seizure has a cause of action against the applicant who obtained the seizure order, and is entitled to the same relief provided under the parallel wrongful-seizure provision of the Lanham Act, 15 U.S.C. section 1116(d)(11) (a trademark-counterfeiting seizure statute the DTSA's drafters used as a model). The statute specifies that the security the applicant was required to post does not limit third parties' recovery of damages. Separately, at any time -- including on an ex parte motion -- a party or a person claiming an interest in the seized material may move to have material stored on a storage medium encrypted.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the wrongful-seizure cause of action and encryption-motion mechanism in 18 U.S.C. section 1836(b)(2)(G) and (H) -- not a claim about the amount of damages any court has awarded, or how the incorporated Lanham Act relief standard, 15 U.S.C. section 1116(d)(11), has actually been applied in a DTSA seizure case (that provision's own text is not independently fetched or quoted in this clause; it is identified here only as a cross-reference within the DTSA text quoted). No CourtListener case-law search specific to this clause was run beyond the single rate-limited attempt disclosed elsewhere in this document, so no case applying the wrongful-seizure cause of action is included here.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(2)(G) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Defend Trade Secrets Act, civil seizure -- action for damage caused by wrongful seizure
citations.quote: A person who suffers damage by reason of a wrongful or excessive seizure under this paragraph has a cause of action against the applicant for the order under which such seizure was made, and shall be entitled to the same relief as is provided under section 34(d)(11) of the Trademark Act of 1946 ( 15 U.S.C. 1116(d)(11) ).

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's statutory process for reviving a corporation or limited liability company whose powers, rights, and privileges have been suspended (for a domestic entity) or forfeited (for a foreign entity) by the Franchise Tax Board for nonpayment of tax, penalty, or interest — the certificate-of-revivor process under Revenue and Taxation Code sections 23301 through 23305.5. It is a companion to, and distinct from, this corpus's Statement of Information document, which addresses a separate suspension mechanism: the Secretary of State's suspension of a corporation or LLC for failing to file a periodic Statement of Information, which that document explains is cured simply by filing the delinquent statement rather than through the Franchise Tax Board revivor process described here. This sheet was prepared in connection with {{companyName}}. It does not state whether {{companyName}}'s powers are currently suspended or forfeited, whether any specific application for revivor or for relief from contract voidability would be granted, or what amounts the Franchise Tax Board would require to be paid in a specific case.

clauses.title: Grounds for FTB Suspension or Forfeiture
clauses.body: Beyond the Secretary of State's own suspension mechanism for a missed Statement of Information, California law gives the Franchise Tax Board a separate statutory power to suspend a domestic corporation's or LLC's powers, rights, and privileges (or, for a foreign entity, forfeit its exercise of them in this state) for nonpayment of tax, penalty, or interest. One of the triggering conditions is a straightforward payment deadline: any tax, penalty, or interest due and payable that remains unpaid by 6 p.m. on the last day of the 12th month after the close of the taxable year. The statute carves out one narrow exception to the suspension or forfeiture itself: it does not bar the entity from filing an application for exempt status, or from amending its articles of incorporation or organization where necessary either to perfect that exemption application or to set forth a new name.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23301's general rule and its first triggering condition, subdivision (a); both quotes below come from that same section, not independent sources of each other. Section 23301 itself sets out two further triggering conditions, subdivisions (b) and (c) (a notice-and-demand nonpayment trigger, and a nonpayment trigger tied to a specific liability under Article 7 of Chapter 4 of Part 10.2), neither of which is independently detailed here. The statute also cross-references a parallel provision, Section 23301.5, and a further provision, Section 23775, at several points; neither was independently fetched or verified for this clause, so what specifically triggers suspension or forfeiture under those sections is not stated here. This clause does not state whether any specific entity's own tax, penalty, or interest obligations have gone unpaid past the relevant deadline.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23301 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Suspension of a domestic taxpayer's powers, rights, and privileges / forfeiture as to a foreign taxpayer, general rule and exempt-status carve-out (subd. introductory clause; not an independent source of the subd. (a) quote below, which comes from the same section)
citations.quote: Except for the purposes of filing an application for exempt status or amending the articles of incorporation or organization as necessary either to perfect that application or to set forth a new name, the powers, rights, and privileges of a domestic taxpayer may be suspended, and the exercise of the powers, rights, and privileges of a foreign taxpayer in this state may be forfeited, if any of the following conditions occur:

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23301(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Suspension of a domestic taxpayer's powers, rights, and privileges / forfeiture as to a foreign taxpayer, first triggering condition (subd. (a); not an independent source of the introductory-clause quote above, which comes from the same section)
citations.quote: If any tax, penalty, or interest, or any portion thereof, that is due and payable under Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 19001) of Part 10.2, or under this part, either at the time the return is required to be filed or on or before the 15th day of the 9th month following the close of the taxable year, is not paid on or before 6 p.m. on the last day of the 12th month after the close of the taxable year.

clauses.title: Suspension Takes Effect Only on Notice, and a Real-Property Disability
clauses.body: Suspension or forfeiture under the Franchise Tax Board's statute does not happen silently or automatically the moment a payment deadline is missed. It occurs and becomes effective only as the statute itself provides, in conjunction with a separate notice statute that requires notice before an entity's powers, rights, and privileges are suspended. The Franchise Tax Board transmits the names of entities that suspension or forfeiture applies to to the Secretary of State, and suspension or forfeiture becomes effective at that point; the Secretary of State's own certificate is treated as prima facie evidence that the suspension or forfeiture occurred. While suspended or forfeited, an entity is also subject to a specific, separate disability: it is not entitled to sell, transfer, or exchange real property in California during the suspension or forfeiture period.
clauses.gap: All three quotes below are drawn from subdivisions (a), (c), and (d) of the same section, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23302, and are not independent sources of one another. This clause does not independently state the content or timing requirements of Section 21020, the cross-referenced notice statute itself — only that Section 23302 requires that notice before suspension or forfeiture takes effect. It also does not address subdivision (b)'s extension of the same notice requirement to voidability under subdivision (d) of Section 23304.1, a narrower voidability trigger not detailed in this document's contract-voidability clause. This clause does not state whether notice was in fact given, or an entity's name in fact transmitted to the Secretary of State, in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23302(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Suspension/forfeiture effective only as provided, in conjunction with the Section 21020 notice requirement (subd. (a); not an independent source of the subd. (c) and (d) quotes below, from the same section)
citations.quote: Forfeiture or suspension of a taxpayer’s powers, rights, and privileges pursuant to Section 23301, 23301.5, or 23775 shall occur and become effective only as expressly provided in this section in conjunction with Section 21020, which requires notice prior to the suspension of a taxpayer’s powers, rights, and privileges.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23302(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: FTB transmittal of names to the Secretary of State and the prima facie effect of the Secretary of State's certificate (subd. (c); not an independent source of the subd. (a) and (d) quotes, from the same section)
citations.quote: The Franchise Tax Board shall transmit the names of taxpayers to the Secretary of State as to which the suspension or forfeiture provisions of Section 23301, 23301.5, or 23775 are or become applicable, and the suspension or forfeiture therein provided for shall thereupon become effective. The certificate of the Secretary of State shall be prima facie evidence of the suspension or forfeiture.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23302(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Disability from selling, transferring, or exchanging California real property during suspension or forfeiture (subd. (d); not an independent source of the subd. (a) and (c) quotes, from the same section)
citations.quote: the taxpayer shall not be entitled to sell, transfer, or exchange real property in California during the period of forfeiture or suspension.

clauses.title: Contracts Made During Suspension Are Voidable — at the Other Party's Election
clauses.body: A contract an entity makes in California while its powers, rights, and privileges are suspended or forfeited under this statute is voidable — but the statute gives that option only to the other party to the contract, not to the suspended or forfeited entity itself.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23304.1(a), the general voidability rule. The same section sets out additional, narrower voidability triggers not detailed here: subdivision (b), for a foreign entity that is neither qualified to do business nor holds a Franchise Tax Board account number and fails to file a required return, with the applicable time period defined in subdivision (c) (and a different starting date for an LLC than for other entities); and subdivision (d), a distinct 60-day-demand-triggered voidability window for an entity that holds an account number but has not qualified to do business, tied to the relief procedure in Section 23305.1 addressed elsewhere in this document. This clause also does not independently state the content of Section 23304.5, the cross-referenced statute both subdivisions (a) and (b) make this voidability 'subject to' — it was not independently fetched, and this clause does not state how, or under what conditions, a court might actually rescind a voidable contract under that section. This clause does not state whether any specific contract is in fact voidable.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23304.1(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: General voidability rule for contracts made during suspension or forfeiture
citations.quote: Every contract made in this state by a taxpayer during the time that the taxpayer’s powers, rights, and privileges are suspended or forfeited pursuant to Section 23301, 23301.5, or 23775 shall, subject to Section 23304.5, be voidable at the request of any party to the contract other than the taxpayer.

clauses.title: What the Certificate of Revivor Requires
clauses.body: An entity that has suffered suspension or forfeiture may be relieved from it, but only by satisfying every element the statute lists: a written application to the Franchise Tax Board, the filing of all tax returns required to be filed, and payment of the tax, additions to tax, penalties, interest, and any other amounts that caused the suspension or forfeiture — together with all other amounts of the same kinds due under the same statutory part, not only the ones that triggered the suspension. Once those conditions are met, the Franchise Tax Board issues a certificate of revivor. The application itself need not come from the entity's own current management: the statute lets it be made by any stockholder or creditor, by a majority of the surviving trustees or directors, by an officer, or by any other person who has an interest in the relief from suspension or forfeiture.
clauses.gap: Both quotes below are drawn from the same section, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23305, and are not independent sources of each other. The statute's text does not itself state a separate filing fee for the certificate-of-revivor application (as opposed to the underlying tax, penalty, and interest amounts it requires be paid) — fee amounts of that kind are commonly set by Franchise Tax Board form and administrative practice rather than by this statutory text, and this clause does not state what fee, if any, currently applies. This clause also does not address how 'all other taxes...due under this part' is determined when an entity has gone an extended period without filing returns — a practical question this statutory text does not itself answer. It does not state whether any specific entity currently satisfies these conditions.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23305 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Certificate-of-revivor conditions: application, filing of returns, and payment (not an independent source of the second, application-by-whom quote below, from the same section)
citations.quote: Any taxpayer which has suffered the suspension or forfeiture provided for in Section 23301 or 23301.5 may be relieved therefrom upon making application therefor in writing to the Franchise Tax Board and upon the filing of all tax returns required under this part, and the payment of the tax, additions to tax, penalties, interest, and any other amounts for nonpayment of which the suspension or forfeiture occurred, together with all other taxes, additions to tax, penalties, interest, and any other amounts due under this part, and upon the issuance by the Franchise Tax Board of a certificate of revivor.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23305 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Who may apply for the certificate on the entity's behalf (not an independent source of the first quote above, from the same section)
citations.quote: Application for the certificate on behalf of any taxpayer which has suffered suspension or forfeiture may be made by any stockholder or creditor, by a majority of the surviving trustees or directors thereof, by an officer, or by any other person who has interest in the relief from suspension or forfeiture.

clauses.title: The Name Check Before Revivor, and What Reinstatement Does and Doesn't Undo
clauses.body: Before issuing a certificate of revivor, the Franchise Tax Board must obtain an endorsement from the Secretary of State confirming that the entity's name still meets the Corporations Code's own distinguishability requirements — the same substantive standard, cross-referenced here, that governs an entity's name at formation. Once the certificate issues, the entity becomes reinstated, but reinstatement is not a clean slate: it is expressly 'without prejudice to any action, defense, or right which has accrued by reason of the original suspension or forfeiture.' The one stated exception is narrow: a contract that was voidable under the voidability statute, and that has not already been rescinded, can still have that voidability separately cured through the relief procedure described elsewhere in this document — revivor by itself does not cure it.
clauses.gap: Both quotes below are drawn from the same section, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23305a, and are not independent sources of each other. This clause does not independently verify the cross-referenced Corporations Code name-distinguishability provisions themselves (Sections 201(b) and 17701.08(b) for a domestic entity, Sections 2106(b) and 17708.05 for a qualified foreign entity) — those are the subject of this corpus's separate Name Availability and Reservation document, and their current text was not re-fetched for this clause. It also does not catalogue every kind of accrued action, defense, or right that reinstatement leaves undisturbed; the statute states the principle without an exhaustive list, and this clause does not resolve how it would apply to any specific act taken during a specific entity's suspension.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23305a (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Required Secretary of State name endorsement before a certificate of revivor issues (not an independent source of the reinstatement-effect quote below, from the same section)
citations.quote: Before the certificate of revivor is issued by the Franchise Tax Board, it shall obtain from the Secretary of State an endorsement upon the application of the fact that the name of the taxpayer then meets the requirements of subdivision (b) of Section 201 or subdivision (b) of Section 17701.08 of the Corporations Code in the case of a domestic taxpayer or of subdivision (b) of Section 2106 or Section 17708.05 of the Corporations Code in the case of a foreign taxpayer that has qualified to do business.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23305a (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Reinstatement is without prejudice to accrued rights, with a narrow voidable-contract exception (not an independent source of the name-endorsement quote above, from the same section)
citations.quote: Upon the issuance of the certificate by the Franchise Tax Board the taxpayer therein named shall become reinstated but the reinstatement shall be without prejudice to any action, defense, or right which has accrued by reason of the original suspension or forfeiture, except that contracts which were voidable pursuant to Section 23304.1, but which have not been rescinded pursuant to Section 23304.5, may have that voidability cured in accordance with Section 23305.1.

clauses.title: A Separate, Narrower Path: Relief From Contract Voidability Alone
clauses.body: Apart from full revivor, the statute lets an entity apply to the Franchise Tax Board for relief from the contract-voidability rule specifically, without necessarily reviving its full powers, rights, and privileges. Obtaining that relief carries its own cost: the Franchise Tax Board assesses a daily penalty of $100 for each day of the period for which relief is granted, capped at the amount of tax for the period requested. Once relief is granted and the statute's conditions are satisfied, contracts made during the covered period — as long as they have not already been rescinded by a final court order — become enforceable in the same manner and to the same extent, as to both the contracting parties and third parties, as if they had never been voidable in the first place.
clauses.gap: All three quotes below are drawn from the same section, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23305.1, and are not independent sources of one another. This clause does not detail every condition subdivision (a) lists for relief (it states only the opening application requirement), including the alternative path for a taxpayer under an approved voluntary disclosure agreement; it also does not state the different, higher penalty formula subdivision (b)(2) applies when relief from voidability is sought for a period already covered by an issued certificate of revivor, the special rule for an exempt organization's unrelated-business-income tax in subdivision (b)(2)(C), or the separate real-property-sale validation in subdivision (c)(1)(B). This is a substantially more detailed and conditional statute than these clauses can fully summarize, and this clause does not state whether relief would be available, or what daily penalty would apply, in any specific case.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23305.1(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Application for relief from Section 23304.1 voidability (subd. (a) introductory text; not an independent source of the subd. (b) and (c) quotes below, from the same section)
citations.quote: A taxpayer may make application to the Franchise Tax Board for relief from the voidability provisions of Section 23304.1.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23305.1(b)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: The $100-per-day penalty for relief from voidability, capped at the period's tax amount (subd. (b)(1)(B); not an independent source of the subd. (a) and (c) quotes, from the same section)
citations.quote: The Franchise Tax Board shall assess a daily penalty equal to one hundred dollars ($100) for each day of the period for which relief from voidability is granted, but not to exceed a total penalty equal to the amount of the tax for the period for which relief is requested.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23305.1(c)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Effect of granted relief: contracts enforceable as if never voidable (subd. (c)(1)(A); not an independent source of the subd. (a) and (b) quotes above, from the same section)
citations.quote: All contracts entered into during the period for which relief is granted that have not been rescinded by a final court order pursuant to Section 23304.5 may be enforced in the same manner and to the same extent, with regard to both the parties to the contract and any third parties, as if the contract had never been voidable.

clauses.title: This Scheme Reaches Both Corporations and LLCs
clauses.body: The suspension, forfeiture, and revivor statutes summarized in this document are not limited to corporations. A separate definitional statute states that, for purposes of the article containing these provisions, "taxpayer" means either a corporation subject to tax under the relevant chapter, or a business entity organized under a statute or law that describes or refers to it as a limited liability company (including one the Franchise Tax Board's own regulations identify as an LLC-equivalent formed under a foreign country's laws). For an LLC, the statute translates the corporation-oriented terms used elsewhere in the article: a reference to "articles of incorporation" includes an LLC's articles of organization, and a reference to "tax" includes the separate LLC tax and fee imposed under the California LLC tax and annual-fee statutes.
clauses.gap: Both quotes below are drawn from the same section, Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23305.5, and are not independent sources of each other. The statute defines "taxpayer" only "for purposes of this article," and this clause does not independently verify the exact statutory boundaries of that article (which sections it comprises beyond those addressed elsewhere in this document) — that boundary was not separately confirmed against the code's own division/part/chapter/article structure. This clause also does not address entity types outside this definition, such as a general or limited partnership, which is not itself subject to this entity-level suspension and revivor scheme in the same way; it does not state how or whether a partnership's own tax filings could affect its partners' separate individual tax obligations.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 23305.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Definition of “taxpayer” to include an LLC (subd. (a); not an independent source of the subd. (b) quote below, from the same section)
citations.quote: “Taxpayer” means either: (1) A corporation subject to tax under this chapter. (2) A business entity organized under a statute or law, under a state or a federally recognized Indian tribe, under another jurisdiction, if the statute or law describes or refers to the entity as a limited liability company or if regulations of the Franchise Tax Board identify a business entity organized under the laws of a foreign country as a limited liability company.
