citations.quote: With regard to a limited liability company: (1) “Articles of incorporation” shall include a limited liability company’s articles of organization. (2) “Tax” shall include the tax and fee imposed by Sections 17941 and 17942, or former Sections 23091 and 23092, respectively.

clauses.title: Closing Acknowledgment
clauses.body: This information sheet was completed by {{preparerName}} on {{dateSigned}} in {{cityState}}, in connection with {{companyName}}. It summarizes California's certificate-of-revivor and contract-voidability-relief statutes as a matter of public record. It does not state whether {{companyName}} has been suspended or forfeited, whether any specific application for revivor or for relief from contract voidability would be granted, or what amounts the Franchise Tax Board would require to be paid in a specific case, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney or tax professional.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope — Informational Only
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, California's regulation of "foreclosure consultants" under the Mortgage Foreclosure Consultants article of the Civil Code, California Civil Code §§ 2945–2945.11. It concerns the residence commonly known as {{propertyAddress}}, owned by {{ownerName}}, and a person or business identified as {{foreclosureConsultantName}}, located at {{foreclosureConsultantAddress}}, who has solicited or offered to perform, for compensation, one or more services described in this article in connection with that residence. This sheet summarizes, at a general level: who is and is not a "foreclosure consultant" as the statute defines that term; the legislative findings underlying the article; the written-contract and mandatory-notice content the statute requires; the owner's statutory right to cancel a foreclosure-consultant contract; the statute's advance-fee and loan-interest-rate limits; its bars on security interests, powers of attorney, and property-interest acquisitions by a foreclosure consultant; the private right of action and its limitations period; and the license/bonding disclosures required of certain representatives. It is distinct from — and does not duplicate — information sheets elsewhere in this corpus describing California's general nonjudicial foreclosure process under Civil Code § 2924 et seq., the Homeowner Bill of Rights servicer-conduct protections, and the Home Equity Sales Contract Act's separate regulation of "equity purchasers" who buy a residence in foreclosure outright; a foreclosure consultant, as defined here, provides services to an owner rather than purchasing the owner's property. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself form, cancel, or enforce any contract with {{foreclosureConsultantName}}, determine whether {{foreclosureConsultantName}} meets the statutory definition of a foreclosure consultant or any exemption from it, or determine whether any conduct toward {{ownerName}} concerning {{propertyAddress}} has complied — or failed to comply — with any statute described here.

clauses.title: Legislative Findings Underlying the Foreclosure Consultant Statute
clauses.body: The article regulating foreclosure consultants opens with the Legislature's own statement of the problem it addresses. California Civil Code § 2945(a) states: "The Legislature finds and declares that homeowners whose residences are in foreclosure are subject to fraud, deception, harassment, and unfair dealing by foreclosure consultants from the time a Notice of Default is recorded pursuant to Section 2924 until the time surplus funds from any foreclosure sale are distributed to the homeowner or his or her successor." The same subdivision goes on to describe how such consultants "often charge high fees, the payment of which is often secured by a deed of trust on the residence to be saved, and perform no service or essentially a worthless service," and how vulnerable homeowners are sometimes induced to assign surplus foreclosure-sale proceeds to a consultant for a fee that a homeowner could otherwise recover directly from the trustee at minimal cost. Subdivision (c) directs that the article's provisions "shall be liberally construed" to effectuate its remedial purposes. Whether any dealings between {{foreclosureConsultantName}} and {{ownerName}} involving {{propertyAddress}} match the pattern these findings describe is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: This quotation states the Legislature's own findings as background to the operative rules that follow in this sheet's later clauses — it is not itself an operative rule imposing a duty or granting a right, and a court could decline to treat it as an independent source of liability separate from the specific operative subdivisions (§§ 2945.2 through 2945.11) it introduces. This is California statutory law, presented as evidence of one state's approach to regulating foreclosure-assistance services — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular consultant's conduct.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The Legislature finds and declares that homeowners whose residences are in foreclosure are subject to fraud, deception, harassment, and unfair dealing by foreclosure consultants from the time a Notice of Default is recorded pursuant to Section 2924 until the time surplus funds from any foreclosure sale are distributed to the homeowner or his or her successor.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Foreclosure Consultant"
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2945.1(a) defines the term this article regulates: "“Foreclosure consultant” means any person who makes any solicitation, representation, or offer to any owner to perform for compensation or who, for compensation, performs any service which the person in any manner represents will in any manner do any of the following:(1) Stop or postpone the foreclosure sale." The remainder of subdivision (a) lists eight further categories of represented service — among them obtaining forbearance, assisting with reinstatement or loan extensions, obtaining a loan or advance of funds, avoiding impairment of the owner's credit, "saving" the residence from foreclosure, and assisting the owner to obtain remaining sale proceeds — any one of which brings a paid solicitor or performer within the definition. Whether {{foreclosureConsultantName}}'s solicitations or services concerning {{propertyAddress}} fall within this definition is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: The definition is broad by design and reaches solicitation alone ("makes any solicitation, representation, or offer") even absent a completed contract; this sheet quotes only the introductory clause and its first enumerated category (stopping or postponing the foreclosure sale) rather than reproducing all nine enumerated categories in subdivision (a), so the quoted text is not the definition's complete substantive reach.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.1(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: “Foreclosure consultant” means any person who makes any solicitation, representation, or offer to any owner to perform for compensation or who, for compensation, performs any service which the person in any manner represents will in any manner do any of the following:(1) Stop or postpone the foreclosure sale.

clauses.title: Persons the Definition Excludes
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2945.1(b) lists categories of persons who are not "foreclosure consultants" even if they perform services described in subdivision (a). It begins: "A foreclosure consultant does not include any of the following:(1) A person licensed to practice law in this state when the person renders service in the course of his or her practice as an attorney at law." Subdivision (b) continues through nine numbered exclusions, also covering persons licensed as prorater, real estate broker or salesperson acting under that license, licensed contractors, persons acting under express HUD or other government-agency authority, a lienholder servicing its own obligation, licensed consumer lenders, banks and similar regulated depository or title/escrow entities, and licensed residential mortgage lenders or servicers acting under that license. Subdivision (c) then narrows one of those exclusions: a person who arranges for payment of an owner's remaining foreclosure-sale surplus proceeds (the ninth category of service in subdivision (a)) is a foreclosure consultant "unless he or she is the owner's attorney," regardless of any other exemption. Whether {{foreclosureConsultantName}} qualifies for any listed exclusion is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the attorney-practicing-law exclusion, the first of nine listed in subdivision (b); the other eight exclusions (summarized but not quoted here) carry their own conditions — for example, several apply only when the person is "acting under the authority of" a specified license, so licensure alone does not automatically exempt someone performing unrelated services. Subdivisions (b) and (c) of the same section are described together in this clause; they are not independent sources of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.1(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A foreclosure consultant does not include any of the following:(1) A person licensed to practice law in this state when the person renders service in the course of his or her practice as an attorney at law.

clauses.title: Owner's Statutory Right to Cancel a Foreclosure Consultant Contract
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2945.2(a) gives an owner a statutory cancellation window independent of any other rescission right: "In addition to any other right under law to rescind a contract, an owner has the right to cancel such a contract until midnight of the fifth business day, as defined in subdivision (e) of Section 1689.5, after the day on which the owner signs a contract that complies with Section 2945.3." Under subdivisions (b) through (d), cancellation occurs when the owner gives written notice to the foreclosure consultant by mail, facsimile, or electronic mail at the address or number specified in the contract; mailed notice is effective on deposit in the mail, postage prepaid; and the notice need not use any particular form so long as it indicates the owner's intent not to be bound. Whether a contract between {{foreclosureConsultantName}} and {{ownerName}} complies with Civil Code § 2945.3 — the trigger for this cancellation window — or whether any cancellation right concerning that contract has been exercised or has expired, is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: The five-business-day period runs from the day the owner signs a contract that complies with Section 2945.3; a noncompliant contract does not necessarily start this clock in the same way, and Civil Code § 2945.3(h) (addressed separately, not quoted in this sheet) separately provides that an owner may cancel until the consultant has complied with the content requirements of Section 2945.3 at all. This sheet does not evaluate compliance with Section 2945.3 for any specific contract.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.2(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: In addition to any other right under law to rescind a contract, an owner has the right to cancel such a contract until midnight of the fifth business day, as defined in subdivision (e) of Section 1689.5, after the day on which the owner signs a contract that complies with Section 2945.3.

clauses.title: Required Written Contract Content and Statutory Warning Notice
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2945.3(a) requires that any foreclosure-consultant contract take a specific written form: "Every contract shall be in writing and shall fully disclose the exact nature of the foreclosure consultant’s services and the total amount and terms of compensation." Subdivision (b) additionally requires a specific statutory warning to appear on the contract in large boldface type: "The following notice, printed in at least 14-point boldface type and completed with the name of the foreclosure consultant, shall be printed immediately above the statement required by subdivision (d):" As set out in the statute, that notice must state, in substance, that the named consultant cannot take or ask for money until everything promised has been completely finished, and cannot ask the owner to sign any lien, deed of trust, or deed. Subdivisions (c) through (g) add further requirements: the contract must be in the language principally used to negotiate it (with a translated copy available on request in specified circumstances); it must be dated, signed, and carry a boldface right-to-cancel statement near the owner's signature; it must list the consultant's contact information and the signing date on its first page; and it must be accompanied by a duplicate, easily detachable "Notice of Cancellation" form. Whether any contract concerning {{propertyAddress}} satisfies these requirements is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: Both quoted passages are drawn from the same statutory section, Civil Code § 2945.3, subdivisions (a) and (b) — they are quoted together, rather than as independent sources, because subdivision (b)'s notice requirement is one of several form requirements subdivision (a) generally imposes. The full statutory notice text embeds contract-specific fill-in blanks (for the consultant's name) that do not render as continuous prose once extracted from the statute's HTML formatting; this sheet quotes only the clean introductory sentence describing where and how the notice must be printed, not the fill-in notice language itself, so the exact wording a compliant contract must display is not reproduced here.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.3(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Every contract shall be in writing and shall fully disclose the exact nature of the foreclosure consultant’s services and the total amount and terms of compensation.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.3(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The following notice, printed in at least 14-point boldface type and completed with the name of the foreclosure consultant, shall be printed immediately above the statement required by subdivision (d):

clauses.title: Prohibition on Advance Compensation and Cap on Loan Fees/Interest
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2945.4 opens by declaring certain conduct a violation for a foreclosure consultant, beginning with subdivision (a): a consultant may not "Claim, demand, charge, collect, or receive any compensation until after the foreclosure consultant has fully performed each and every service the foreclosure consultant contracted to perform or represented that he or she would perform." Subdivision (b) separately bars a consultant from charging excessive amounts on any loan the consultant itself makes to the owner: a consultant may not "Claim, demand, charge, collect, or receive any fee, interest, or any other compensation for any reason which exceeds 10 percent per annum of the amount of any loan which the foreclosure consultant may make to the owner." Whether any compensation sought or received by {{foreclosureConsultantName}} from {{ownerName}} in connection with {{propertyAddress}} complies with either limitation is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: Subdivisions (a) and (b) of Civil Code § 2945.4 are quoted together in this clause as related but textually distinct prohibitions within the same section — they are not independent sources of each other. Civil Code § 2945.6(a) (addressed in this sheet's remedies clause) ties a mandatory treble-damages remedy specifically to violations of subdivisions (a), (b), and (d) of this section, so the practical stakes of a subdivision (a) or (b) violation are addressed only partially by this clause standing alone.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.4(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Claim, demand, charge, collect, or receive any compensation until after the foreclosure consultant has fully performed each and every service the foreclosure consultant contracted to perform or represented that he or she would perform.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.4(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Claim, demand, charge, collect, or receive any fee, interest, or any other compensation for any reason which exceeds 10 percent per annum of the amount of any loan which the foreclosure consultant may make to the owner.

clauses.title: Bars on Security Interests, Powers of Attorney, and Acquiring an Interest in the Residence
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2945.4 further prohibits a foreclosure consultant from securing its compensation against the owner's property. Subdivision (c) bars a consultant from taking "Take any wage assignment, any lien of any type on real or personal property, or other security to secure the payment of compensation. That security shall be void and unenforceable." Subdivision (e) separately bars a consultant from acquiring an ownership interest in the residence from an owner it has contracted with: a consultant may not "Acquire any interest in a residence in foreclosure from an owner with whom the foreclosure consultant has contracted. Any interest acquired in violation of this subdivision shall be voidable, provided that nothing herein shall affect or defeat the title of a bona fide purchaser or encumbrancer for value and without notice of a violation of this article." The same subdivision states that this bar does not affect a bona fide purchaser or encumbrancer for value without notice, and that mere knowledge the property was in foreclosure does not itself constitute notice of a violation. Subdivision (f) separately bars a consultant from taking "Take any power of attorney from an owner for any purpose." Whether {{foreclosureConsultantName}} has sought or obtained any security interest, power of attorney, or ownership interest concerning {{propertyAddress}} from {{ownerName}} is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: Subdivisions (c), (e), and (f) of Civil Code § 2945.4 are quoted together in this clause as related but textually distinct prohibitions within the same section — they are not independent sources of each other. Subdivision (e)'s voidability rule and its bona-fide-purchaser carve-out are fact-intensive; this sheet does not determine whether any particular transfer or purchaser would qualify for that carve-out.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.4(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Take any wage assignment, any lien of any type on real or personal property, or other security to secure the payment of compensation. That security shall be void and unenforceable.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.4(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Acquire any interest in a residence in foreclosure from an owner with whom the foreclosure consultant has contracted. Any interest acquired in violation of this subdivision shall be voidable, provided that nothing herein shall affect or defeat the title of a bona fide purchaser or encumbrancer for value and without notice of a violation of this article.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.4(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Take any power of attorney from an owner for any purpose.

clauses.title: Private Right of Action, Damages, and the Limitations Period
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2945.6(a) gives an owner a private right of action for a violation of the article: "An owner may bring an action against a foreclosure consultant for any violation of this chapter. Judgment shall be entered for actual damages, reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs, and appropriate equitable relief." The same subdivision requires the court to award exemplary damages equal to at least three times the compensation the consultant received for violations of subdivision (a), (b), or (d) of Section 2945.4, and three times the owner's actual damages for violations of subdivision (c), (e), or (g) of that section, in addition to any other damages award; for other violations the court may, in its discretion, award exemplary damages. Subdivision (b) sets the time limit for bringing such an action: "Any action brought pursuant to this section shall be commenced within four years from the date of the alleged violation." Whether {{ownerName}} has, or has timely exercised, any claim under this section concerning {{foreclosureConsultantName}} is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: Subdivisions (a) and (b) of Civil Code § 2945.6 are quoted together in this clause — they are not independent sources of each other. Subdivision (a)'s mandatory treble-damages rule cross-references particular subdivisions of a different section (Civil Code § 2945.4, addressed in two other clauses of this sheet); this clause does not itself determine whether any specific conduct falls within those cross-referenced subdivisions, and the remedies described here are cumulative to, not a limitation of, other rights and remedies available under other law.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.6(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: An owner may bring an action against a foreclosure consultant for any violation of this chapter. Judgment shall be entered for actual damages, reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs, and appropriate equitable relief.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.6(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Any action brought pursuant to this section shall be commenced within four years from the date of the alleged violation.

clauses.title: License and Bond Disclosure Required of Certain Representatives
clauses.body: California Civil Code § 2945.11(a) imposes additional requirements on a specific category of representative acting for a foreclosure consultant (one meeting the definition cross-referenced in Civil Code § 2945.9(b)). Before any interest in the property transfers, such a representative must provide "Written proof to the owner that the representative has a valid current California Real Estate Sales License and that the representative is bonded by an admitted surety insurer in an amount equal to at least twice the fair market value of the real property that is the subject of the contract." Subdivision (a) also requires a written statement, under penalty of perjury, attesting to the same license and bond and to compliance with the written-proof requirement, delivered to all parties to the contract before any transfer of an interest in the property. Subdivision (b) provides that failure to comply renders the contract voidable at the owner's option and makes the foreclosure consultant liable for resulting damages. Whether this representative-specific requirement applies to any particular person acting for {{foreclosureConsultantName}} in connection with {{propertyAddress}} is not addressed by this sheet.
clauses.gap: This requirement, by its terms, applies only to a "representative" as defined by cross-reference to Civil Code § 2945.9(b) — a section this sheet has not independently fetched or quoted — not to every foreclosure consultant or every person who deals with an owner; this sheet does not determine who qualifies as such a representative in any given transaction.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 2945.11(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Written proof to the owner that the representative has a valid current California Real Estate Sales License and that the representative is bonded by an admitted surety insurer in an amount equal to at least twice the fair market value of the real property that is the subject of the contract.

clauses.body:

I further understand that this sheet is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about any specific contract, dispute, or transaction.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's "Freedom from Parental Custody and Control" proceeding under Family Code Part 4 (commencing with Section 7800) — the statutory action by which a court may declare a child free from the custody and control of a parent, terminating that parent's rights. It summarizes the recognized statutory grounds, the standard of proof, who may petition, notice and counsel procedures, and the effect of a resulting judgment as reflected in the current Family Code. This document concerns the interested-person action brought under Family Code Part 4; it does not summarize the separate termination process that occurs inside a juvenile dependency case, and it does not itself prepare, file, or serve a petition on behalf of {{petitionerName}} regarding {{childName}}. This is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.

clauses.title: Purpose of the Proceeding and Legal Effect of a Judgment
clauses.body: Family Code section 7802 authorizes a proceeding under Part 4 "for the purpose of having a minor child declared free from the custody and control of either or both parents." Family Code section 7803 states the consequence of a resulting declaration: it "terminates all parental rights and responsibilities with regard to the child." These are two separate sections within the same Part 4 general-provisions chapter — section 7802 states the proceeding's purpose while section 7803 states its ultimate legal effect — and neither restates or independently confirms the other's text.
clauses.gap: Section 7803 states that a declaration terminates parental rights and responsibilities, but neither section addresses what happens to the child's custody or legal status after termination (for example, whether an adoption follows), nor whether a later Probate Code guardianship or a separate adoption proceeding is required to establish a new legal parent. This document does not address the juvenile dependency system's parallel termination process under Welfare and Institutions Code section 366.26, which involves a different petitioning party (the county agency), a different procedural posture, and different governing standards than the Family Code Part 4 action described here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7802
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7802 (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: A proceeding may be brought under this part for the purpose of having a minor child declared free from the custody and control of either or both parents.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7803
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7803 (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: A declaration of freedom from parental custody and control pursuant to this part terminates all parental rights and responsibilities with regard to the child.

clauses.title: Clear and Convincing Evidence Standard
clauses.body: Family Code section 7821 states that "a finding pursuant to this chapter shall be supported by clear and convincing evidence, except as otherwise provided." This heightened standard governs the findings on the statutory grounds set out in Chapter 2 of Part 4 (the grounds described elsewhere in this document, including abandonment, neglect or dependency-based deprivation, felony conviction, and mental disability).
clauses.gap: Section 7821 by its terms applies to findings "pursuant to this chapter" — Chapter 2's grounds provisions — and its own text notes an exception ("except as otherwise provided") that this clause does not enumerate. Other procedural findings within Part 4 carry their own, separately stated clear-and-convincing requirements (for example, a finding supporting in-chambers child testimony under section 7892, addressed elsewhere in this document); this section does not itself establish the standard applicable to every finding made in the proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7821
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7821 (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: A finding pursuant to this chapter shall be supported by clear and convincing evidence, except as otherwise provided.

clauses.title: Statutory Ground: Abandonment
clauses.body: Family Code section 7822(a) permits a proceeding where, among other listed circumstances, "the child has been left without provision for the child's identification by the child's parent or parents" or has been left in another's care and custody for six months (or, under a related provision, by one parent in the other parent's care for one year) "without any provision for the child's support, or without communication from the parent or parents, with the intent on the part of the parent or parents to abandon the child." Subdivision (b) provides that "the failure to provide identification, failure to provide support, or failure to communicate is presumptive evidence of the intent to abandon," and that if the parent has made "only token efforts to support or communicate with the child, the court may declare the child abandoned."
clauses.gap: The statute does not define "token efforts" numerically or by any bright-line test; whether a given level of contact or support crosses that threshold is left to case-by-case determination that this document does not resolve. Section 7822 also contains a separate publication-notice pathway, for a child left without identification and parents of unknown whereabouts, that this clause does not summarize in full.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7822(a)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7822, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: (a) A proceeding under this part may be brought if any of the following occur: (1) The child has been left without provision for the child’s identification by the child’s parent or parents. (2) The child has been left by both parents or the sole parent in the care and custody of another person for a period of six months without any provision for the child’s support, or without communication from the parent or parents, with the intent on the part of the parent or parents to abandon the child.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7822(b)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7822, subd. (b) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivision (a) of the same section 7822; not an independent source from it
citations.quote: The failure to provide identification, failure to provide support, or failure to communicate is presumptive evidence of the intent to abandon. If the parent or parents have made only token efforts to support or communicate with the child, the court may declare the child abandoned by the parent or parents.

clauses.title: Statutory Ground: Neglect, Cruel Treatment, or Prolonged Dependency
clauses.body: Family Code section 7823(a) permits a proceeding, on satisfaction of all its listed requirements, where "the child has been neglected or cruelly treated by either or both parents" — a finding of severe sexual abuse under a cross-referenced Welfare and Institutions Code provision serves as prima facie evidence of this — or where "the child has been a dependent child of the juvenile court under any subdivision of Section 300 of the Welfare and Institutions Code and the parent or parents have been deprived of the child's custody for one year before the filing of a petition pursuant to this part."
clauses.gap: This ground incorporates the juvenile dependency system's jurisdictional finding under Welfare and Institutions Code section 300, but this document does not itself state that section's criteria for dependency jurisdiction, which are governed by a different code with its own procedures. The statute also provides that physical custody "for insubstantial periods of time" does not interrupt the one-year clock, a fact-specific determination this clause does not further quantify.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7823(a)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7823, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: (1) The child has been neglected or cruelly treated by either or both parents. A finding that a parent committed severe sexual abuse, as described in paragraph (6) of subdivision (b) of Section 361.5 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, against the child shall be prima facie evidence that the parent has neglected or cruelly treated the child within the meaning of this subdivision. (2) The child has been a dependent child of the juvenile court under any subdivision of Section 300 of the Welfare and Institutions Code and the parent or parents have been deprived of the child’s custody for one year before the filing of a petition pursuant to this part.

clauses.title: Statutory Ground: Felony Conviction Proving Unfitness, and Conception by Rape
clauses.body: Family Code section 7825(a) permits a proceeding where "the child is one whose parent or parents are convicted of a felony" and "the facts of the crime of which the parent or parents were convicted are of such a nature so as to prove the unfitness of the parent or parents to have the future custody and control of the child." A separate subdivision (b) permits a mother to bring a proceeding against a father "where the child was conceived as a result of an act in violation of Section 261 of the Penal Code, and where the father was convicted of that violation," in which circumstance "there is a conclusive presumption that the father is unfit to have custody or control of the child."
clauses.gap: The felony ground in subdivision (a) is not automatic upon any felony conviction — the statute requires the court to find that the facts of the particular crime prove unfitness for future custody, a case-by-case determination this document does not resolve. The conclusive presumption in subdivision (b) applies only to the narrow class of cases involving a Penal Code section 261 conviction resulting in the child's conception; it does not extend to convictions for other sex offenses.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7825(a)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7825, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: (1) The child is one whose parent or parents are convicted of a felony. (2) The facts of the crime of which the parent or parents were convicted are of such a nature so as to prove the unfitness of the parent or parents to have the future custody and control of the child.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7825(b)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7825, subd. (b) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivision (a) of the same section 7825; not an independent source from it
citations.quote: The mother of a child may bring a proceeding under this part against the father of the child, where the child was conceived as a result of an act in violation of Section 261 of the Penal Code, and where the father was convicted of that violation. For purposes of this subdivision, there is a conclusive presumption that the father is unfit to have custody or control of the child.

clauses.title: Statutory Ground: Parental Mental Disability, and Its Evidentiary and Counsel Requirements
clauses.body: Family Code section 7827 defines "mentally disabled," for purposes of this ground, to mean "that a parent or parents suffer a mental incapacity or disorder that renders the parent or parents unable to care for and control the child adequately," and permits a proceeding where the parent is mentally disabled and likely to remain so in the foreseeable future. Except as the statute otherwise provides for out-of-state parents, a finding under this ground requires "the evidence of any two experts, each of whom shall be a physician and surgeon, certified either by the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology or under Section 6750 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, a licensed psychologist who has a doctoral degree in psychology and at least five years of postgraduate experience in the diagnosis and treatment of emotional and mental disorders." Separately, if the parent facing termination under this section lacks an attorney, "the court shall appoint an attorney for the parent pursuant to Article 4 (commencing with Section 7860) of Chapter 3, whether or not a request for the appointment is made by the parent."
clauses.gap: The two-expert evidentiary requirement is unique to this ground among those described in this document — it does not apply to the abandonment, neglect/dependency, or felony grounds addressed elsewhere. The statute also gives the court discretion to call additional licensed therapists, counselors, or clinical social workers in specified circumstances, and bars calling one who served as the case's adoption service provider; this document does not catalog every such qualification or restriction. The mandatory-counsel provision quoted here applies specifically to this mental-disability ground and cross-references the general counsel-appointment article described in a separate clause of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7827(a)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7827, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: “Mentally disabled” as used in this section means that a parent or parents suffer a mental incapacity or disorder that renders the parent or parents unable to care for and control the child adequately.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7827(c)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7827, subd. (c) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivisions (a) and (e) of the same section 7827; not independent sources of one another
citations.quote: the evidence of any two experts, each of whom shall be a physician and surgeon, certified either by the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology or under Section 6750 of the Welfare and Institutions Code, a licensed psychologist who has a doctoral degree in psychology and at least five years of postgraduate experience in the diagnosis and treatment of emotional and mental disorders, is required to support a finding under this section.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7827(e)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7827, subd. (e) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivisions (a) and (c) of the same section 7827; not independent sources of one another
citations.quote: If the rights of a parent are sought to be terminated pursuant to this section, and the parent does not have an attorney, the court shall appoint an attorney for the parent pursuant to Article 4 (commencing with Section 7860) of Chapter 3, whether or not a request for the appointment is made by the parent.

clauses.title: Who May Bring the Proceeding
clauses.body: Family Code section 7841(a) provides that "an interested person may file a petition under this part for an order or judgment declaring a child free from the custody and control of either or both parents." Subdivision (b) states that, for this purpose, "an 'interested person' is one who has a direct interest in the action, and includes, but is not limited to, a person who has filed, or who intends to file within a period of 6 months, an adoption petition under Section 8714, 8802, or 9000, or a licensed adoption agency to whom the child has been relinquished by the other parent."
clauses.gap: The statutory definition of "interested person" is illustrative rather than exhaustive — it expressly "includes, but is not limited to" the listed examples — so the outer boundary of who qualifies as having a sufficient direct interest is left to case-by-case judicial determination that this document does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7841(a)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7841, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: An interested person may file a petition under this part for an order or judgment declaring a child free from the custody and control of either or both parents.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7841(b)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7841, subd. (b) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivision (a) of the same section 7841; not an independent source from it
citations.quote: an “interested person” is one who has a direct interest in the action, and includes, but is not limited to, a person who has filed, or who intends to file within a period of 6 months, an adoption petition under Section 8714, 8802, or 9000, or a licensed adoption agency to whom the child has been relinquished by the other parent.

clauses.title: Appointment of Counsel for the Parent and the Child
clauses.body: Family Code section 7860 states that "at the beginning of the proceeding on a petition filed pursuant to this part, counsel shall be appointed as provided in this article," that the public defender or private counsel may serve, and that "the same counsel shall not be appointed to represent both the child and the child's parent." A separate section in the same article, section 7862, provides that "if a parent appears without counsel and is unable to afford counsel, the court shall appoint counsel for the parent, unless that representation is knowingly and intelligently waived."
clauses.gap: Section 7862 does not itself define what makes a waiver of counsel "knowing and intelligent," nor does it or section 7860 specify the indigency standard the court applies in determining inability to afford counsel; both are left to the court's determination in the individual case. Section 7860's appointment mandate and section 7862's indigent-parent entitlement are separate sections within the same Article 4 of Chapter 3 and are not restatements of one another.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7860
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7860 (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: At the beginning of the proceeding on a petition filed pursuant to this part, counsel shall be appointed as provided in this article. The public defender or private counsel may be appointed as counsel pursuant to this article. The same counsel shall not be appointed to represent both the child and the child’s parent.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7862
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7862 (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: If a parent appears without counsel and is unable to afford counsel, the court shall appoint counsel for the parent, unless that representation is knowingly and intelligently waived.

clauses.title: The Child's Right to Be Heard and In-Chambers Testimony
clauses.body: Family Code section 7891(a) provides that, subject to stated exceptions, "if the child who is the subject of the petition is 10 years of age or older, the child shall be heard by the court in chambers on at least" the child's feelings about the proceeding, the child's feelings about the parent or parents, and the child's custody preference under section 3042. A related section, 7892, separately permits a child's testimony to be taken in chambers and outside a parent's presence where the parent is represented by counsel, counsel is present, and "the testimony of the child may be taken in chambers and outside the presence of the child's parent or parents ... and any of the following circumstances exist" — including that in-chambers testimony is necessary to ensure truthful testimony, that the child is likely to be intimidated by a formal courtroom setting, or that the child is afraid to testify in front of the parent.
clauses.gap: Section 7891's right to be heard applies only to children age 10 or older and does not apply if the child is confined by illness or other incapacity and therefore unable to attend; it also allows the child's counsel to waive the in-chambers hearing. Section 7892's separate in-chambers testimony mechanism applies only in the narrower circumstance where the parent is represented by counsel and that counsel is present, and any finding supporting its use must independently meet the clear-and-convincing-evidence standard stated in that same section — the two sections address related but distinct procedures and are not restatements of each other.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7891(a)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7891, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: if the child who is the subject of the petition is 10 years of age or older, the child shall be heard by the court in chambers on at least the following matters: (1) The feelings and thoughts of the child concerning the custody proceeding about to take place. (2) The feelings and thoughts of the child about the child’s parent or parents. (3) The child’s preference as to custody, according to Section 3042.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7892(a)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7892, subd. (a) (West, current through 2025 legislation)
citations.quote: The testimony of the child may be taken in chambers and outside the presence of the child’s parent or parents if the child’s parent or parents are represented by counsel, the counsel is present, and any of the following circumstances exist: (1) The court determines that testimony in chambers is necessary to ensure truthful testimony. (2) The child is likely to be intimidated by a formal courtroom setting. (3) The child is afraid to testify in front of the child’s parent or parents.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 7892(c)
citations.cite: Fam. Code § 7892, subd. (c) (West, current through 2025 legislation) — quoted alongside subdivision (a) of the same section 7892; not an independent source from it
citations.quote: A finding pursuant to this section shall be supported by clear and convincing evidence.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Federal WARN Act Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet supplements this corpus's WARN Act Layoff Notice document, which explains the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act's basic 100-employee/50-or-500-employee coverage thresholds, the 60-day notice requirement running to {{employeeName}} or a union representative, the three statutory exceptions to that 60-day period, and back-pay liability for a violation. It does not restate any of that. Instead it addresses a separate set of federal WARN Act rules that document does not state: who besides affected employees must also receive notice, how notice content differs for those additional recipients, how the law counts job losses that come in smaller separate rounds, how it defines the "single site of employment" a layoff is measured against, how a sale of {{companyName}}'s business affects who is responsible for notice, and how back-pay liability can be offset. It states general legal rules and does not determine how any of them applies to {{companyName}}'s specific circumstances, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.

clauses.title: Notice Must Also Go to a State Dislocated Worker Unit and Local Government Officials
clauses.body: Federal WARN Act notice of a covered plant closing or mass layoff is not owed only to affected employees or their union representative. The statute separately requires the employer to serve the same 60-day advance notice on the state entity designated to carry out rapid-response dislocated-worker activities and on the chief elected official of the unit of local government where the closing or layoff will occur. If more than one unit of local government could receive it, the statute picks the one to which the employer pays the highest taxes for the preceding year. A Department of Labor regulation implementing this section confirms that whoever within the employer's organization is assigned to prepare notice is responsible for delivering it to all three recipient categories, not just to employees.
clauses.gap: This clause states who must receive notice, not what happens if the state or local recipients are omitted while employees are timely notified — that consequence (a local-government civil penalty, addressed elsewhere in this document) is a separate statutory provision with its own conditions. It also does not address California's separate and more demanding Cal/WARN notice-recipient and content rules, already covered in this corpus's California WARN Act (Cal/WARN) Information Sheet, which independently apply to employers meeting Cal/WARN's own, lower coverage threshold.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2102(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, WARN Act, notice to employees, State dislocated worker units, and local governments
citations.quote: to the State or entity designated by the State to carry out rapid response activities under section 3174(a)(2)(A) of this title , and the chief elected official of the unit of local government within which such closing or layoff is to occur.

citations.case: 20 C.F.R. § 639.4(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Department of Labor WARN regulation, who must give notice and to whom
citations.quote: It is the responsibility of the employer to decide the most appropriate person within the employer 's organization to prepare and deliver the notice to affected employees or their representative (s), the State dislocated worker unit and the chief elected official of a unit of local government .

clauses.title: The Government-Unit Notice Must Contain Different Information Than the Employee Notice
clauses.body: The regulation implementing the WARN Act's notice requirement sets separate content lists for each recipient. Notice to an employee representative must include the site's name and address, a company contact, whether the action is permanent or temporary, the expected date of the first separation and the schedule for further separations, and the job titles and names of affected workers. Notice to an unrepresented affected employee must be written in understandable language and state whether the action is permanent or temporary, the expected commencement and the employee's own separation date, whether bumping rights exist, and a company contact. The notice sent separately to the state dislocated worker unit and the local government's chief elected official is different again: it must state the site's name, address, and company contact; whether the action is permanent or temporary; the expected date of the first separation and the schedule; the job titles affected and the number of employees in each classification (not their individual names); whether bumping rights exist; and the name and address of each union and its chief elected officer.
clauses.gap: The regulation also allows an employer to send the state and local government units an abbreviated alternative notice (site name/address, a company contact, the date of the first separation, and the number of affected employees) as long as the remaining required content is kept on site and produced on request — this clause states the full content list, not that shorter alternative or the on-site recordkeeping condition attached to using it.

citations.case: 20 C.F.R. § 639.7(e) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Department of Labor WARN regulation, required content of the notice to the State dislocated worker unit and local government
citations.quote: The notices separately provided to the State dislocated worker unit and to the chief elected official of the unit of local government are to contain: (1) The name and address of the employment site where the plant closing or mass layoff will occur, and the name and telephone number of a company official to contact for further information; (2) A statement as to whether the planned action is expected to be permanent or temporary and, if the entire plant is to be closed, a statement to that effect; (3) The expected date of the first separation, and the anticipated schedule for making separations; (4) The job titles of positions to be affected, and the number of affected employees in each job classification; (5) An indication as to whether or not bumping rights exist; (6) The name of each union representing affected employees , and the name and address of the chief elected officer of each union.

clauses.title: Smaller Job Losses Within 90 Days Can Be Added Together to Reach a Covered Threshold
clauses.body: The federal WARN Act's plant-closing and mass-layoff thresholds are ordinarily measured over any 30-day period. A separate statutory rule prevents an employer from avoiding coverage by staging job losses in smaller rounds: if two or more groups of job losses at the same single site of employment each fall under the 30-day minimum but together exceed it within any 90-day period, they are treated as a single covered plant closing or mass layoff. The employer can avoid that result only by demonstrating the separate rounds resulted from separate and distinct actions and causes and were not an attempt to evade the Act. The Department of Labor's implementing regulation directs an employer to look both 30 days and 90 days forward and backward from any planned action to determine whether this aggregation rule is triggered.
clauses.gap: The regulation cited alongside the statute in this clause does not add an independent legal requirement of its own; it is the Department of Labor's interpretation of the same 90-day rule Congress wrote into 29 U.S.C. § 2102(d), so the two citations are not independent sources confirming each other. Separately, this clause does not state how an employer demonstrates that separate rounds of job losses were genuinely "separate and distinct" rather than staged to evade the Act — that determination turns on facts specific to each situation this document does not resolve.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2102(d) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, WARN Act, determinations with respect to employment loss (90-day aggregation rule)
citations.quote: in determining whether a plant closing or mass layoff has occurred or will occur, employment losses for 2 or more groups at a single site of employment, each of which is less than the minimum number of employees specified in section 2101(a)(2) or (3) of this title but which in the aggregate exceed that minimum number, and which occur within any 90-day period shall be considered to be a plant closing or mass layoff unless the employer demonstrates that the employment losses are the result of separate and distinct actions and causes and are not an attempt by the employer to evade the requirements of this chapter.

citations.case: 20 C.F.R. § 639.5(a)(1)(ii) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Department of Labor WARN regulation implementing the same 90-day aggregation rule as 29 U.S.C. § 2102(d), not an independent source
citations.quote: Look ahead 90 days and behind 90 days to determine whether employment actions both taken and planned each of which separately is not of sufficient size to trigger WARN coverage will, in the aggregate for any 90-day period, reach the minimum numbers for a plant closing or a mass layoff and thus trigger the notice requirement. An employer is not, however, required under section 3(d) to give notice if the employer demonstrates that the separate employment losses are the result of separate and distinct actions and causes, and are not an attempt to evade the requirements of WARN.

clauses.title: What Counts as a "Single Site of Employment"
clauses.body: Both the 30-day and 90-day job-loss thresholds are measured against a "single site of employment," a term the federal WARN Act itself does not define but the Department of Labor's regulation does. A single site can be one location or a group of contiguous locations, such as a campus or facilities across the street from each other; a single building can contain multiple single sites if separate employers operate within it; and non-contiguous buildings can still count as one single site if they are in reasonable geographic proximity, serve the same purpose, and share staff and equipment. Conversely, contiguous buildings under common ownership are treated as separate single sites if they have separate management, different products, and separate workforces. For employees whose duties involve regular travel rather than a fixed workplace, the regulation assigns them to the single site that serves as their home base, from which their work is assigned, or to which they report.
clauses.gap: This clause states the regulatory framework, not how it resolves any particular facility arrangement — the regulation itself acknowledges "truly unusual organizational situations" it says its own listed criteria do not reasonably reach, leaving that residual category to case-by-case application. It also does not state the separate rule that foreign sites of employment are not covered under the Act at all, though U.S. workers stationed there still count toward whether the employer meets the Act's 100-employee coverage threshold.

citations.case: 20 C.F.R. § 639.3(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Department of Labor WARN regulation, definition of "single site of employment"
citations.quote: For workers whose primary duties require travel from point to point, who are outstationed, or whose primary duties involve work outside any of the employer 's regular employment sites (e.g., railroad workers, bus drivers, salespersons), the single site of employment to which they are assigned as their home base, from which their work is assigned, or to which they report will be the single site in which they are covered for WARN purposes.

clauses.title: Part-Time Employees Are Excluded From the Coverage and Threshold Counts, Under Their Own Statutory Definition
clauses.body: The federal WARN Act's employer-coverage threshold (100 or more employees) and its plant-closing and mass-layoff thresholds are all measured excluding "part-time employees," a term the statute defines on its own terms rather than by reference to how an employer classifies a job. Under the statute, a part-time employee is someone employed for an average of fewer than 20 hours a week, or someone who has been employed for fewer than 6 of the preceding 12 months — regardless of how many hours that person actually works. The Department of Labor's regulation adds that this 20-hours-a-week average is calculated over the shorter of the employee's actual tenure or the most recent 90 days, and that the category can include workers who would ordinarily be called "seasonal."
clauses.gap: Excluding an employee from the threshold count under this definition does not mean that employee is excluded from receiving notice if a plant closing or mass layoff is otherwise triggered — the sale-of-business clause elsewhere in this document states a related but distinct point about which employees on a seller's payroll count for notice purposes after a sale. This clause also does not address how the 90-day lookback interacts with a newly hired part-time employee who has not yet worked 90 days, a scenario the regulation's text does not itself resolve.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2101(a)(8) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, WARN Act, definition of "part-time employee"
citations.quote: the term “ part-time employee ” means an employee who is employed for an average of fewer than 20 hours per week or who has been employed for fewer than 6 of the 12 months preceding the date on which notice is required.

citations.case: 20 C.F.R. § 639.3 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Department of Labor WARN regulation elaborating on the same statutory "part-time employee" definition, not an independent source
citations.quote: The term “part-time” employee means an employee who is employed for an average of fewer than 20 hours per week or who has been employed for fewer than 6 of the 12 months preceding the date on which notice is required, including workers who work full-time. This term may include workers who would traditionally be understood as “seasonal” employees. The period to be used for calculating whether a worker has worked “an average of fewer than 20 hours per week” is the shorter of the actual time the worker has been employed or the most recent 90 days.

clauses.title: Sale of a Business: The Seller and the Buyer Have Separate Notice Obligations
clauses.body: When part or all of an employer's business is sold, the WARN Act splits notice responsibility at the sale's effective date rather than treating either party as excused. The seller is responsible for notice of any plant closing or mass layoff up to and including the effective date of the sale; the buyer is responsible for any plant closing or mass layoff after that date. Separately, the statute deems every person who was an employee of the seller (other than a part-time employee) as of the sale's effective date to be an employee of the buyer immediately after that date, regardless of what the sale agreement itself says about who employs them. The Department of Labor's regulation adds a practical mechanism: if the seller learns of the buyer's definite plans for a post-sale plant closing or mass layoff within 60 days of the purchase, the seller may give notice to affected employees as the buyer's agent, but the buyer remains legally responsible for notice being given even if the seller does so on its behalf.
clauses.gap: This clause states who bears the notice obligation on each side of a sale; it does not address how the 90-day aggregation rule stated elsewhere in this document applies when job losses occur on both sides of a sale date, nor does it address a stock sale that leaves the corporate employer entity unchanged (as opposed to a sale of the business's assets or operations), which the statute's own text does not separately distinguish.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2101(b)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, WARN Act, sale of a business — seller's and purchaser's notice responsibility, and continuity of employment
citations.quote: In the case of a sale of part or all of an employer ’s business, the seller shall be responsible for providing notice for any plant closing or mass layoff in accordance with section 2102 of this title , up to and including the effective date of the sale. After the effective date of the sale of part or all of an employer’ s business, the purchaser shall be responsible for providing notice for any plant closing or mass layoff in accordance with section 2102 of this title . Notwithstanding any other provision of this chapter, any person who is an employee of the seller (other than a part-time employee) as of the effective date of the sale shall be considered an employee of the purchaser immediately after the effective date of the sale.

citations.case: 20 C.F.R. § 639.4(c) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Department of Labor WARN regulation, seller-as-agent mechanism for sale-of-business notice
citations.quote: The seller is responsible for providing notice of any plant closing or mass layoff which takes place up to and including the effective date (time) of the sale, and the buyer is responsible for providing notice of any plant closing or mass layoff that takes place thereafter.

clauses.title: An Offered Transfer Can Keep a Relocation or Consolidation From Counting as a Job Loss
clauses.body: Apart from the sale-of-business rule, the WARN Act carves out a second situation where an employee affected by a relocation or consolidation of part or all of the business is not treated as having experienced an "employment loss" that could trigger notice. That happens if, before the closing or layoff, the employer offers to transfer the employee to a different site within a reasonable commuting distance with no more than a 6-month break in employment, or offers a transfer to any other site regardless of distance with no more than a 6-month break, and the employee accepts that offer within 30 days of the offer or of the closing or layoff, whichever is later.
clauses.gap: The statute does not define "reasonable commuting distance"; the Department of Labor's regulation says the term varies with local and industry conditions and depends on factors like road quality, available transportation, and usual travel time, and separately warns that an offer of reassignment is not a qualifying "transfer" at all if the new job amounts to a constructive discharge — a fact-specific determination this clause does not resolve for any particular offer.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2101(b)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, WARN Act, exclusion from "employment loss" for an offered qualifying transfer
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subsection (a)(6), an employee may not be considered to have experienced an employment loss if the closing or layoff is the result of the relocation or consolidation of part or all of the employer’ s business and, prior to the closing or layoff— (A) the employer offers to transfer the employee to a different site of employment within a reasonable commuting distance with no more than a 6-month break in employment; or (B) the employer offers to transfer the employee to any other site of employment regardless of distance with no more than a 6-month break in employment, and the employee accepts within 30 days of the offer or of the closing or layoff, whichever is later.

clauses.title: Back-Pay Liability Can Be Offset, and a Federal Court Cannot Block the Closing or Layoff Itself
clauses.body: The federal WARN Act's back-pay and benefits liability for a notice violation is not simply added on top of whatever else the employee is paid. The statute reduces the amount an employer owes by any wages actually paid to the employee for the violation period, by any voluntary and unconditional payment the employer makes that isn't otherwise legally required, and by payments the employer makes to a third party or trustee on the employee's behalf for that period, such as health-benefit premiums or defined-contribution pension contributions. Separately, the statute makes the back-pay and civil-penalty remedies it creates the exclusive remedies for a WARN Act violation, and expressly denies a federal court the authority to issue an injunction blocking a plant closing or mass layoff, even one ordered without the required notice.
clauses.gap: This clause states the statute's own offset categories and remedy structure; it does not address how a court applies the separate good-faith defense allowing it to reduce liability or a civil penalty when an employer shows it had reasonable grounds to believe its conduct wasn't a violation, which is a distinct, discretionary determination the statute leaves to the court rather than defining with a fixed standard.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2104(a)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, WARN Act, statutory offsets to back-pay and benefits liability
citations.quote: The amount for which an employer is liable under paragraph (1) shall be reduced by— (A) any wages paid by the employer to the employee for the period of the violation; (B) any voluntary and unconditional payment by the employer to the employee that is not required by any legal obligation; and (C) any payment by the employer to a third party or trustee (such as premiums for health benefits or payments to a defined contribution pension plan) on behalf of and attributable to the employee for the period of the violation.

citations.case: 29 U.S.C. § 2104(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, WARN Act, exclusivity of remedies and bar on federal injunctive relief
citations.quote: The remedies provided for in this section shall be the exclusive remedies for any violation of this chapter. Under this chapter, a Federal court shall not have authority to enjoin a plant closing or mass layoff.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature Block — Federal WARN Act Government Notice, Aggregation, and Business Transfer Information Sheet
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's law on escheat of a decedent's estate to the state — Probate Code Part 4 (commencing with Section 6800) and the related unclaimed-property provisions of Code of Civil Procedure Title 10, Part 3 — as it may bear on the estate of {{decedentName}} (date of death: {{dateOfDeath}}; character and estimated value of estate property: {{estimatedEstateValue}}). It states what this law provides in general. It does not determine whether {{decedentName}}'s estate has any heirs or devisees under California law, whether any escheat proceeding has been or will be commenced regarding this estate, or what a court would decide in a particular case, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about this estate's own facts.

clauses.title: When a Decedent's Property Escheats
clauses.body: Under Probate Code Section 6800(a), a decedent's property escheats to the State of California — automatically, at the moment of death, without anyone having to petition for it — only if two conditions are both met: no one takes the property by testate succession (that is, there is no valid will disposing of it, or the will fails to dispose of it), and no one other than a government or governmental subdivision or agency takes it by intestate succession under the law of this state or any other jurisdiction. This rule applies whether or not the decedent was domiciled in California. Section 6800(b) then subjects escheated property to the same charges and trusts it would have carried had it passed by succession, and separately makes it subject to the unclaimed-property provisions of Code of Civil Procedure Title 10 (commencing with Section 1300) governing escheated estates — the procedural framework described in the rest of this sheet.
clauses.gap: Section 6800(a) states the trigger in the abstract; it does not itself determine, for any particular decedent, whether every possible taker under California's intestate succession statutes (Probate Code Sections 6400-6455) and every other jurisdiction's law has in fact been exhausted — that determination depends on the specific family and property facts of the estate, which this sheet does not evaluate.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6800(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, general escheat trigger
citations.quote: If a decedent, whether or not the decedent was domiciled in this state, leaves no one to take the decedent’s estate or any portion thereof by testate succession, and no one other than a government or governmental subdivision or agency to take the estate or a portion thereof by intestate succession, under the laws of this state or of any other jurisdiction, the same escheats at the time of the decedent’s death in accordance with this part.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6800(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, subject to CCP Title 10 (this is subdivision (b) of the same Section 6800 quoted immediately above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: Property that escheats to the state under this part, whether held by the state or its officers, is subject to the same charges and trusts to which it would have been subject if it had passed by succession and is also subject to the provisions of Title 10 (commencing with Section 1300) of Part 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure relating to escheated estates.

clauses.title: Real Property and Tangible Personal Property
clauses.body: California's escheat statute assigns different property types to the state under different tests. Real property located in California escheats to California under Probate Code Section 6801. Tangible personal property escheats to California under Section 6802 if it was customarily kept in California before the decedent's death, regardless of where it is located at death. A related but separate rule in Section 6803(a) reaches tangible personal property that is subject to the control of a California superior court for purposes of probate administration, but Section 6803(b) carves out an exception: that property goes to another jurisdiction instead, if that jurisdiction claims it and establishes that it is entitled to the property under its own law, that the decedent customarily kept the property there, and that California would have the reciprocal right to claim tangible property being administered in that jurisdiction if the decedent had customarily kept it in California.
clauses.gap: Sections 6801-6803 do not define 'customarily kept' or resolve close cases (property that moved between states, or was kept in more than one place) — nor do they say how a competing jurisdiction's claim under Section 6803(b) is to be adjudicated procedurally; this sheet does not apply these tests to any specific item of property.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6801 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, real property escheat
citations.quote: Real property in this state escheats to this state in accordance with Section 6800.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6802 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, tangible personal property customarily kept in California
citations.quote: All tangible personal property owned by the decedent, wherever located at the decedent’s death, that was customarily kept in this state prior to the decedent’s death, escheats to this state in accordance with Section 6800.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6803(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, tangible personal property under California probate administration
citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivision (b), all tangible personal property owned by the decedent that is subject to the control of a superior court of this state for purposes of administration under this code escheats to this state in accordance with Section 6800.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6803(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, reciprocal other-jurisdiction exception (this is subdivision (b) of the same Section 6803 quoted immediately above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: (1) The other jurisdiction is entitled to the property under its law. (2) The decedent customarily kept the property in that jurisdiction prior to the decedent’s death. (3) This state has the right to escheat and take tangible personal property being administered as part of a decedent’s estate in that jurisdiction if the decedent customarily kept the property in this state prior to the decedent’s death.

clauses.title: Intangible Property
clauses.body: Intangible property (such as bank accounts, securities, or contract rights) is governed by domicile rather than by where the asset is physically kept. Under Probate Code Section 6804, intangible property owned by the decedent escheats to California only if the decedent was domiciled in California at death. Section 6805(a) separately reaches intangible property subject to the control of a California superior court for purposes of probate administration, and does so whether or not the decedent was domiciled in California — but Section 6805(b) carves out the same kind of reciprocal exception found in Section 6803(b): the property instead goes to another jurisdiction that claims it and establishes entitlement under its own law, the decedent's domicile there at death, and California's reciprocal right to intangible property administered there if the decedent had instead been domiciled in California.
clauses.gap: These sections turn on 'domicile,' a legal concept the statute does not define here and that can be genuinely contested where a decedent had connections to more than one state; this sheet does not determine any decedent's domicile.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6804 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, intangible property and domicile
citations.quote: All intangible property owned by the decedent escheats to this state in accordance with Section 6800 if the decedent was domiciled in this state at the time of the decedent’s death.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6805(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, intangible property under California probate administration
citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivision (b), all intangible property owned by the decedent that is subject to the control of a superior court of this state for purposes of administration under this code escheats to this state in accordance with Section 6800 whether or not the decedent was domiciled in this state at the time of the decedent’s death.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6805(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, reciprocal other-jurisdiction exception (this is subdivision (b) of the same Section 6805 quoted immediately above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: (1) The other jurisdiction is entitled to the property under its laws. (2) The decedent was domiciled in that jurisdiction at the time of the decedent’s death. (3) This state has the right to escheat and take intangible property being administered as part of a decedent’s estate in that jurisdiction if the decedent was domiciled in this state at the time of the decedent’s death.

clauses.title: Carve-Out for Employee Benefit Plan Trusts and Funds
clauses.body: Probate Code Section 6806 removes one category of benefit from the escheat rules described elsewhere in this sheet: a benefit of money or other property distributable from a trust established under a plan providing health and welfare, pension, vacation, severance, retirement, death, unemployment insurance, or similar benefits does not escheat to the state under this part, and instead goes back to the trust or fund it would have been paid from, subject to Code of Civil Procedure Section 1521. Section 6806 also states the reverse of this carve-out: if the plan itself has already terminated and its trust or fund has already been distributed to the plan's beneficiaries before the estate's own distribution of the unclaimed benefit occurs, then the carve-out no longer applies, and the benefit passes to, and escheats to, the state under this part after all.
clauses.gap: Section 6806 cross-references Code of Civil Procedure Section 1521 without restating its terms here; this sheet does not independently verify what Section 1521 requires or whether a given benefit plan and its trust or fund meet this carve-out's description.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6806 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, employee benefit plan carve-out
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, a benefit consisting of money or other property distributable from a trust established under a plan providing health and welfare, pension, vacation, severance, retirement benefit, death benefit, unemployment insurance or similar benefits does not pass to or escheat to the state under this part but goes to the trust or fund from which it is distributable, subject to the provisions of Section 1521 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 6806 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Probate Code, reversion of the carve-out on plan termination (this is the same Section 6806 quoted immediately above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: However, if such plan has terminated and the trust or fund has been distributed to the beneficiaries thereof prior to distribution of such benefit from the estate, such benefit passes to the state and escheats to the state under this part.

clauses.title: The Attorney General's Escheat Proceeding
clauses.body: Escheat under Probate Code Section 6800 happens automatically at death as a matter of law, but establishing it in a way that can be enforced against property requires a court proceeding.
