Code of Civil Procedure Section 1420(a) gives the Attorney General authority — not before two years have passed after the decedent's death — to commence a proceeding on the state's behalf in the Superior Court for the County of Sacramento, by filing a petition, to have the state's entitlement adjudged. Section 1420(b) requires that petition to describe the property, name the person last in possession of it, name any person claiming it, and state the facts and circumstances making it escheated property. Section 1420(c) then requires the court, on the petition's filing, to order everyone interested in the estate to appear and show cause within 60 days why the estate should not vest in the state, and requires that order to be published at least once a week for four consecutive weeks in a Sacramento County newspaper, with the last publication at least 10 days before the hearing date.
clauses.gap: Section 1420 sets the Attorney General's authority and the petition and publication requirements; it does not obligate the Attorney General to commence a proceeding on any particular estate within any deadline, and this sheet does not report whether such a proceeding has been filed regarding any specific decedent's property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, two-year wait and petition to Sacramento County Superior Court
citations.quote: At any time after two years after the death of any decedent who leaves property to which the state is entitled by reason of it having escheated to the state, the Attorney General shall commence a proceeding on behalf of the state in the Superior Court for the County of Sacramento to have it adjudged that the state is so entitled. The action shall be commenced by filing a petition, which shall be treated as the information elsewhere referred to in this title.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, required petition contents (this is subdivision (b) of the same Section 1420 quoted above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: The petition shall set forth a description of the property, the name of the person last in possession thereof, the name of the person, if any, claiming the property, or portion thereof, and the facts and circumstances by virtue of which it is claimed the property has escheated.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, order to show cause and publication (this is subdivision (c) of the same Section 1420 quoted above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: Upon the filing of the petition, the court shall make an order requiring all persons interested in the estate to appear and show cause, if any, within 60 days from the date of the order, why the estate should not vest in the state. The order must be published at least once a week for four consecutive weeks in a newspaper published in the County of Sacramento, the last publication to be at least 10 days prior to the date set for the hearing.

clauses.title: Interaction with an Existing Probate Administration
clauses.body: When a probate administration for the decedent's estate is already open, Section 1420(d) provides a path to distribution without a separate escheat lawsuit: if no one entitled to succeed to the property has appeared and claimed it before the decree of final distribution (or before the Attorney General commences a proceeding), or if the court finds that anyone who did appear is not entitled to it, the probate court itself — upon final settlement of the administration, after paying all debts and expenses — distributes the remaining money and property to the State of California. Separately, Section 1420(e) gives the Attorney General authority to direct the public administrator to commence estate administration if no administration proceeding has been commenced within six months of the decedent's death, so that an estate with no known heirs does not simply sit unadministered.
clauses.gap: Section 1420(d) describes what the probate court does once administration is under way and no claimant has appeared or prevailed; it does not itself say when a probate case must be opened for an estate with no known heirs in the first place, apart from the six-month administration-referral trigger in subdivision (e) that this clause also describes.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, distribution to the state at final settlement of a pending administration
citations.quote: If proceedings for the administration of any estate of the decedent have been instituted and none of the persons entitled to succeed thereto have appeared and made claim to the property, or any portion thereof, before the decree of final distribution therein is made, or before the commencement of a proceeding by the Attorney General, or if the court shall find that the persons as have appeared are not entitled to the property of the estate, or any portion thereof, the court shall, upon final settlement of the proceedings for the administration of the estate, after the payment of all debts and expenses of administration, distribute all moneys and other property remaining to the State of California.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1420(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, Attorney General may direct public administrator to commence administration (this is subdivision (e) of the same Section 1420 quoted above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: If proceedings for the administration of any estate have not been commenced within six months from the death of any decedent the Attorney General may direct the public administrator to commence the same forthwith.

clauses.title: A Known Heir's or Legatee's Share That Is Never Collected
clauses.body: The rules described elsewhere in this sheet address estates with no known heirs at all. A related but distinct rule addresses money or property that was distributed to a known heir, legatee, or devisee — identified and entitled — but that the person simply never collected. Under Code of Civil Procedure Section 1444, when such distributed money or property has been deposited in a county treasury to the credit of known heirs, legatees, or devisees (or remains on deposit to the credit of an estate after final distribution to them), it is not held there indefinitely: at the next county settlement following the expiration of one year from the date of that deposit, it is paid over to the State Treasurer or Controller, as provided in the statute's Chapter 2 receipt-and-deposit provisions, placing it on the same unclaimed-property track as other escheated funds.
clauses.gap: Section 1444 sets the one-year county-treasury holding period and the county settlement mechanism for transfer to the state; it does not itself restate the notice a known distributee may have received before the deposit, nor the further claim rights and permanent-escheat timeline described elsewhere in this sheet that apply once the funds reach the state.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1444 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, uncollected known-distributee shares transferred to the state after one year
citations.quote: At the time of the next county settlement following the expiration of one year from the date of its deposit in the county treasury, all money or other property distributed in the administration of an estate of a deceased person and heretofore or hereafter deposited in the county treasury to the credit of known heirs, legatees, or devisees, and any money or other property remaining on deposit to the credit of an estate after final distribution to such known heirs, legatees or devisees, shall be paid to the Treasurer or Controller as provided in Chapter 2.

clauses.title: The Five-Year Window Before Escheat Becomes Permanent
clauses.body: An initial escheat judgment does not permanently close the door to a later claim. Code of Civil Procedure Section 1430(a) provides that property covered by an escheat proceeding permanently escheats to the state only upon the expiration of five years after entry of judgment in the proceeding (or, for a notice-by-publication escheat action under Section 1415, five years after the publication is completed) — except as subdivision (b) provides. Section 1430(b) preserves a claim right during that five-year window, and even afterward in a limited sense, for infants and persons of unsound mind born before the five-year period expires, subject to a presumption (rebuttable only by the person appearing and claiming) that no such person exists, a presumption that is conclusive in favor of a good-faith purchaser from the state. Section 1430(c) separately lets a named beneficiary of the escheated property — or, if that beneficiary is dead or adjudicated dead, a blood relative of the beneficiary — claim the property at any time within the same five-year period following judgment, with entitlement to immediate payment, subject to an exception for a person whose interest was specifically restricted or barred by the donating or transferring instrument.
clauses.gap: Section 1430 measures its five-year period from entry of judgment in 'any proceeding pursuant to this chapter' or from completion of Section 1415 publication; it does not itself specify which of the several escheat-proceeding paths described elsewhere in this sheet (the Attorney General's Section 1420 petition, or distribution within a pending probate administration under Section 1420(d)) produces the 'judgment' that starts this clock for a given estate.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1430(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, five-year permanent escheat trigger
citations.quote: Upon the expiration of five years after the date of entry of judgment in any proceeding pursuant to this chapter, or upon the expiration of five years after completion of notice by publication in an escheat action taken pursuant to Section 1415, the property covered by that proceeding or action shall permanently escheat to the state, except as provided in subdivision (b).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1430(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, infant/unsound-mind claim right (this is subdivision (b) of the same Section 1430 quoted above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: Infants and persons of unsound mind shall have the right to appear and claim such property as provided in this title if born before the expiration of the five-year period; but it shall be presumed that there are no infants nor persons of unsound mind who are or will be entitled to claim this property unless and until they appear and claim the property as provided in this title.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1430(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, named-beneficiary/blood-relative claim right (this is subdivision (c) of the same Section 1430 quoted above, not an independent source)
citations.quote: a named beneficiary of property that escheats pursuant to this title or, if the beneficiary is deceased or a court renders a judgment that the beneficiary is dead, a blood relative of the named beneficiary may claim property described in subdivision (a) at any time within five years after the date of entry of judgment in any proceeding under this chapter.

clauses.title: Where Permanently Escheated Property Ultimately Goes
clauses.body: Once property permanently escheats under the five-year rule, Code of Civil Procedure Section 1431 directs its final disposition within state accounts. Money that was held in the Unclaimed Property Fund and has become permanently escheated is transferred, on the Controller's order, to the General Fund. Property other than money that was held by the Controller or Treasurer in an Unclaimed Property Fund account and has become permanently escheated is not physically transferred but is instead re-recorded: the Controller's and Treasurer's records are adjusted to show it held in the name of the General Fund.
clauses.gap: Section 1431 governs only the bookkeeping disposition of property already permanently escheated under Section 1430; it does not affect, extend, or shorten the claim rights that Section 1430 itself preserves for infants, persons of unsound mind, or named beneficiaries and their blood relatives.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 1431 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, transfer to the General Fund
citations.quote: When money in the Unclaimed Property Fund has become permanently escheated to the state, the amount thereof shall, on order of the Controller, be transferred to the General Fund. When property other than money held by the Controller or Treasurer in the name of any account in the Unclaimed Property Fund has become permanently escheated to the state, the records of the Controller and Treasurer shall be adjusted to show that such property is held in the name of the General Fund.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Declaration
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the basics of a design patent under 35 U.S.C. §§ 171-173 and 289 — the distinct category of U.S. patent protecting the ornamental appearance of an article of manufacture, as opposed to a utility patent, which protects how an article is made or used. It is prepared with reference to {{patentDescription}}, held by or applied for by {{patentHolderName}}, with an application filing date of {{filingDate}}. This sheet describes the general statutory subject-matter requirement in § 171(a), the applicability of the rest of Title 35 to design applications under § 171(b)-(c), the 15-year term measured from grant under § 173, the shortened 6-month foreign priority period under § 172, and the design-specific infringement remedy in § 289; it does not evaluate whether {{patentDescription}} qualifies for design patent protection, draft or file any application, or calculate any specific term, priority date, or damages figure. This document is distinct from the corpus's existing Provisional Patent Application, Patent Assignment, Patent License, Patent Infringement, False Patent Marking, and Patent Term Adjustment documents, all of which either focus on utility patents or, in the case of the Patent Term Adjustment sheet, mention design patent term only to distinguish it from § 154(b) adjustment without describing design patent's own statutory framework. This sheet is educational only; it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed patent attorney or registered patent practitioner, and it does not itself request, prosecute, or enforce any design patent before the Patent and Trademark Office.

clauses.title: Statutory Subject Matter — New, Original, and Ornamental
clauses.body: A design patent is available for a "new, original and ornamental design for an article of manufacture," subject to the general conditions and requirements that apply to patents under Title 35. This is a narrower subject-matter category than a utility patent: a utility patent protects a new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, while a design patent protects the way a manufactured article looks. The statute's own text supplies the three adjectives — new, original, and ornamental — but does not itself define any of them or state what makes a design "primarily ornamental" as opposed to "primarily functional."
clauses.gap: The statutory text of § 171(a) supplies only the bare words "new, original and ornamental" and does not define them; the substantial body of case law working out where the ornamental/functional line falls (for example, distinguishing a design dictated by function from one with ornamental alternatives) is not covered here because a CourtListener case-law search for this topic returned a 429 rate-limit error (125/day quota exhausted) during this research session, and no case citation is included as a result.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 171(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, patents for designs — subject-matter requirement
citations.quote: Whoever invents any new, original and ornamental design for an article of manufacture may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.

clauses.title: General Patent Provisions Apply Except as Otherwise Provided
clauses.body: Design applications are not governed by a wholly separate statutory scheme. The provisions of Title 35 that apply to utility patents — covering matters such as novelty, obviousness, specification and claim requirements, examination procedure, and ownership and assignment — apply equally to design patents, except where a specific design-patent provision (such as § 172's shortened priority period or § 173's 15-year term) displaces the general rule.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the general incorporation rule of § 171(b); it does not catalog which specific utility-patent provisions in Title 35 have been held or interpreted to apply differently, or not at all, to design applications (for example, the differing treatment of obviousness analysis for designs), which is developed through Patent and Trademark Office guidance and case law not included in this sheet.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 171(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, patents for designs — applicability of general Title 35 provisions
citations.quote: The provisions of this title relating to patents for inventions shall apply to patents for designs, except as otherwise provided.

clauses.title: Filing Date — Specification and Drawings
clauses.body: A design application's filing date is fixed by statute: it is the date on which the specification required under 35 U.S.C. § 112 and any required drawings are filed with the Patent and Trademark Office. Because a design's protected subject matter is its visual appearance, the drawings (or photographs) are typically what defines the scope of what is claimed, and the statute ties the filing date directly to their submission along with the specification.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the filing-date rule itself; it does not describe the Patent and Trademark Office's formal drawing standards (such as shading and view requirements under Patent and Trademark Office regulations rather than Title 35 itself), which this sheet does not address because they are set by regulation, not by the statute quoted here.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 171(c) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, patents for designs — filing date
citations.quote: The filing date of an application for patent for design shall be the date on which the specification as prescribed by section 112 and any required drawings are filed.

clauses.title: Term — 15 Years From Grant, Not From Filing
clauses.body: A design patent's term runs 15 years from the date the patent is granted. This differs in kind from a utility patent's term, which under a separate statute runs 20 years from the application's earliest effective U.S. filing date rather than from the date of grant. Because a design patent's term is measured from grant rather than filing, the length of time an application spends in examination does not shorten the eventual term the way it can, absent adjustment, for a utility patent measured from filing.
clauses.gap: This clause covers only the length and measurement point of the design patent term; it does not address maintenance fees (design patents, unlike utility patents, are not subject to periodic maintenance fee requirements under Title 35 to keep the patent in force for its term) or any transitional term rules for design patents that issued from applications filed before the December 18, 2013 effective date of the 15-year term (which were granted a 14-year term under the prior version of § 173), neither of which is addressed here.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 173 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, term of design patent
citations.quote: Patents for designs shall be granted for the term of 15 years from the date of grant.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, contents and term of patent — utility patent term, for contrast with § 173's design patent term
citations.quote: such grant shall be for a term beginning on the date on which the patent issues and ending 20 years from the date on which the application for the patent was filed in the United States

clauses.title: Foreign Priority — Six Months, Not Twelve
clauses.body: When an applicant claims the right of priority from an earlier-filed foreign application, the priority period for a design application is shortened to six months, rather than the twelve-month period that applies to most utility applications under the general priority statute. A separate right of priority available for certain later-filed international applications does not apply to designs at all.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the length of the design priority period and the inapplicability of the later-filed-international-application priority right; it does not describe the separate, alternative six-month priority period available to a design applicant claiming priority from an earlier international design application filed under the Hague Agreement, which is governed by a different statute (35 U.S.C. § 386) not quoted here.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 172 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, right of priority for designs — both quoted sentences are from the same section of the statute and are not independent sources of each other
citations.quote: The right of priority provided for by subsections (a) through (d) of section 119 shall be six months in the case of designs. The right of priority provided for by section 119(e) shall not apply to designs.

clauses.title: Infringement Remedy — Liable to the Extent of Total Profit
clauses.body: Design patent infringement carries its own statutory remedy, separate from the general patent damages statute. A person who, during the term of a design patent and without the owner's license, applies the patented design (or a colorable imitation of it) to an article of manufacture for sale, or who sells or offers for sale an article to which the design or a colorable imitation has been applied, is liable to the design patent owner "to the extent of his total profit" from that infringement, with a statutory floor of not less than $250, recoverable in a United States district court with jurisdiction over the parties.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the total-profit remedy and its $250 statutory minimum; it does not describe how "total profit" is calculated where an infringing article combines a patented design with other unpatented features or components (an apportionment question that has been the subject of substantial litigation), because a CourtListener search on this topic returned a 429 rate-limit error during this session and no case law is cited here as a result.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 289 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, additional remedy for infringement of design patent — first paragraph
citations.quote: Whoever during the term of a patent for a design, without license of the owner, (1) applies the patented design, or any colorable imitation thereof, to any article of manufacture for the purpose of sale, or (2) sells or exposes for sale any article of manufacture to which such design or colorable imitation has been applied shall be liable to the owner to the extent of his total profit, but not less than $250, recoverable in any United States district court having jurisdiction of the parties.

clauses.title: Cumulative With Other Remedies, but No Double Recovery
clauses.body: The § 289 total-profit remedy does not replace or foreclose other remedies a design patent owner may have under Title 35, such as the general patent damages provision. The statute states that nothing in § 289 prevents, lessens, or impeaches any other remedy an infringed patent owner has under Title 35's other provisions — but it also states expressly that the owner may not recover the infringer's profit twice for the same infringement.
clauses.gap: This is the second paragraph of the same statutory section (35 U.S.C. § 289) quoted in this sheet's infringement-remedy clause, not an independent source confirming the total-profit rule stated there; this clause does not describe how a design patent owner elects between, or combines, the § 289 profit remedy and general damages under the separate general patent damages statute (35 U.S.C. § 284) in a specific case, which depends on litigation strategy and proof this sheet does not address.

citations.case: 35 U.S.C. § 289 (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, additional remedy for infringement of design patent — second paragraph, from the same section as this sheet's infringement-remedy clause and not independent of it
citations.quote: Nothing in this section shall prevent, lessen, or impeach any other remedy which an owner of an infringed patent has under the provisions of this title, but he shall not twice recover the profit made from the infringement.

clauses.title: Signature
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California Health and Safety Code section 1278.5, a whistleblower-protection statute specific to health facilities. It covers the statute's protection for patients, employees, members of the medical staff, and other health care workers who report or participate in an investigation of suspected unsafe patient care, services, or conditions at a health facility such as {{companyName}}, along with the rebuttable presumptions, penalties, and remedies the statute creates. It is distinct from this corpus's separate information sheet on Labor Code section 1102.5, California's general whistleblower-protection statute, which is not limited to patient-care or health-facility issues and does not contain this statute's health-facility-specific presumptions, remedies, or peer-review provisions. This document explains what the statute states; it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about a specific set of facts.

clauses.title: Legislative Purpose, and What This Statute Is Not
clauses.body: California has declared it the state's public policy to encourage patients, nurses, members of the medical staff, and other health care workers to notify government entities of suspected unsafe patient care and conditions, in order to protect patients and to assist the accreditation and government entities responsible for ensuring that health care is safe. The Legislature has separately stated that this statute's whistleblower protections apply primarily to issues relating to the care, services, and conditions of a facility, and are not intended to conflict with existing state and federal law governing the employee-employer relationship generally.
clauses.gap: Both quotations in this clause are drawn from the same subdivision of the same statutory section, Health & Safety Code § 1278.5(a), not from independent sources. This clause states the Legislature's own description of the statute's purpose and intended scope; it does not resolve, for any particular report, whether that report actually concerns patient care, services, or facility conditions as opposed to a general employment matter that this statute's findings say it does not intend to reach.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(a)
citations.quote: it is the public policy of the State of California to encourage patients, nurses, members of the medical staff, and other health care workers to notify government entities of suspected unsafe patient care and conditions

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(a) (same subdivision as the preceding citation, not an independent source)
citations.quote: whistleblower protections apply primarily to issues relating to the care, services, and conditions of a facility and are not intended to conflict with existing provisions in state and federal law relating to employee and employer relations

clauses.title: What a Health Facility, or Its Owner/Operator, May Not Do
clauses.body: A health facility may not discriminate or retaliate, in any manner, against a patient, employee, member of the medical staff, or other health care worker of the facility because that person presented a grievance, complaint, or report to the facility, to an entity or agency responsible for accrediting or evaluating the facility or its medical staff, or to any other governmental entity, or because that person initiated, participated, or cooperated in an investigation or administrative proceeding related to the quality of care, services, or conditions at the facility that is carried out by such an accrediting or evaluating entity or agency, or by a governmental entity. Separately, an entity that owns or operates the health facility -- or that owns or operates any other health facility -- may not discriminate or retaliate against a person for having taken these same protected actions.
clauses.gap: The first citation in this clause spans subdivision (b)(1)'s introductory clause together with both of its listed categories of protected activity, paragraphs (A) and (B), quoted as one contiguous passage from the statute; the second citation is to a separate subdivision, (b)(2), addressing facility owners/operators rather than the facility itself. Both are from the same statutory section and are disclosed together rather than as independent sources. This clause does not itself determine whether any particular report, investigation, or proceeding falls within the statute's description of protected activity.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(b)(1), including subparagraphs (A) and (B)
citations.quote: A health facility shall not discriminate or retaliate, in any manner, against a patient, employee, member of the medical staff, or other health care worker of the health facility because that person has done either of the following:(A) Presented a grievance, complaint, or report to the facility, to an entity or agency responsible for accrediting or evaluating the facility, or the medical staff of the facility, or to any other governmental entity.(B) Has initiated, participated, or cooperated in an investigation or administrative proceeding related to the quality of care, services, or conditions at the facility that is carried out by an entity or agency responsible for accrediting or evaluating the facility or its medical staff, or governmental entity.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(b)(2)
citations.quote: An entity that owns or operates a health facility, or that owns or operates any other health facility, shall not discriminate or retaliate against a person because that person has taken any actions pursuant to this subdivision.

clauses.title: Civil Penalty for a Violation
clauses.body: A violation of this statute is subject to a civil penalty of not more than $25,000. That penalty is assessed and recovered through the same administrative process the statute establishes, at Health and Safety Code Chapter 2.4 beginning at section 1417, for long-term health care facilities.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only Health & Safety Code § 1278.5(b)(3); it does not independently fetch or verify the cross-referenced administrative process at Chapter 2.4 (commencing with Section 1417), and does not resolve how that long-term-care-facility administrative process applies procedurally to a violation involving a facility that is not itself a long-term health care facility (a separate subdivision of this same section excludes long-term health care facilities from this statute's substantive coverage; see the coverage-and-exemptions clause of this document).

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(b)(3)
citations.quote: A violation of this section shall be subject to a civil penalty of not more than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000). The civil penalty shall be assessed and recovered through the same administrative process set forth in Chapter 2.4 (commencing with Section 1417) for long-term health care facilities.

clauses.title: Rebuttable Presumption Protecting a Patient
clauses.body: If a patient -- or someone acting on a patient's behalf -- has submitted a grievance or complaint, directly or indirectly, to a governmental entity, or that grievance or complaint has been received by a health facility administrator, and any type of discriminatory treatment of that patient occurs within 180 days of the filing, a rebuttable presumption arises that the facility took the discriminatory action in retaliation for the filing.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only Health & Safety Code § 1278.5(c). A related clause of this document addresses the separate 120-day rebuttable presumption that subdivision (d) creates for employees, medical staff, and other health care workers, and the statute's own note (subdivision (e), quoted in that clause) that both presumptions affect only the burden of producing evidence under Evidence Code section 603, which this document does not independently fetch or verify. This clause does not determine, for a specific instance of treatment, whether it in fact qualifies as 'discriminatory treatment' within the 180-day window.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(c)
citations.quote: Any type of discriminatory treatment of a patient by whom, or upon whose behalf, a grievance or complaint has been submitted, directly or indirectly, to a governmental entity or received by a health facility administrator within 180 days of the filing of the grievance or complaint, shall raise a rebuttable presumption that the action was taken by the health facility in retaliation for the filing of the grievance or complaint.

clauses.title: Rebuttable Presumption Protecting an Employee, Medical Staff Member, or Health Care Worker
clauses.body: A separate rebuttable presumption arises for an employee, member of the medical staff, or other health care worker of the facility: if responsible staff at the facility (or the entity that owns or operates it) had knowledge of that person's protected report, participation, or cooperation, and discriminatory action occurs within 120 days of the filing of the grievance or complaint, a rebuttable presumption arises that the facility (or owning/operating entity) retaliated. For this purpose, the statute defines 'discriminatory treatment' to include, without limitation, discharge, demotion, suspension, or any unfavorable change in or breach of the terms or conditions of a contract, employment, or privileges -- or the threat of any of those actions. Both this presumption and the separate one protecting patients are, by the statute's own terms, presumptions that affect only the burden of producing evidence, as provided in Evidence Code section 603.
clauses.gap: This clause's three citations are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section -- § 1278.5(d)(1), (d)(2), and (e) -- disclosed here rather than presented as independent sources. This document does not independently fetch or verify the text of Evidence Code § 603, which the statute cross-references for the legal effect of a 'presumption affecting the burden of producing evidence.' This clause does not determine, for particular facts, whether the 120-day window or knowledge requirement is satisfied.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(d)(1)
citations.quote: There shall be a rebuttable presumption that discriminatory action was taken by the health facility, or by the entity that owns or operates that health facility, or that owns or operates any other health facility, in retaliation against an employee, member of the medical staff, or any other health care worker of the facility, if responsible staff at the facility or the entity that owns or operates the facility had knowledge of the actions, participation, or cooperation of the person responsible for any acts described in paragraph (1) of subdivision (b), and the discriminatory action occurs within 120 days of the filing of the grievance or complaint by the employee, member of the medical staff or any other health care worker of the facility.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(d)(2) (same section as the preceding citation, a different subdivision)
citations.quote: discriminatory treatment of an employee, member of the medical staff, or any other health care worker includes, but is not limited to, discharge, demotion, suspension, or any unfavorable changes in, or breach of, the terms or conditions of a contract, employment, or privileges of the employee, member of the medical staff, or any other health care worker of the health care facility, or the threat of any of these actions.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(e) (same section as the preceding citations, a different subdivision)
citations.quote: The presumptions in subdivisions (c) and (d) shall be presumptions affecting the burden of producing evidence as provided in Section 603 of the Evidence Code.

clauses.title: Criminal Misdemeanor for a Willful Violation
clauses.body: A person who willfully violates this statute is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not more than $75,000, in addition to the civil penalty the statute separately authorizes.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only Health & Safety Code § 1278.5(f). The statute's text does not itself further define 'willfully' for this purpose, and this clause does not determine, for particular facts, whether a violation was willful.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(f)
citations.quote: A person who willfully violates this section is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine of not more than seventy-five thousand dollars ($75,000), in addition to the civil penalty provided in paragraph (3) of subdivision (b).

clauses.title: Remedies, Which Differ by Role
clauses.body: The statute provides different remedies depending on the reporting person's relationship to the facility. An employee who has been discriminated against in employment is entitled to reinstatement, reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts, and legal costs of pursuing the case, or to any other remedy the court deems warranted under this chapter or other applicable statutory or common law. A health care worker who is not necessarily an employee (for example, an independent contractor) is entitled to reimbursement for lost income and legal costs, or to any other remedy the court deems warranted, but the statute does not list reinstatement among that person's remedies. A member of the medical staff is entitled to reinstatement, reimbursement for lost income resulting from a change in the terms or conditions of the member's privileges, and legal costs, or to any other remedy the court deems warranted. Separately, the statute states that it does not abrogate or limit any other theory of liability or remedy otherwise available at law.
clauses.gap: This clause's four citations are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section -- § 1278.5(g) (three separate sentences, each addressing a different category of person) and § 1278.5(m) -- disclosed here rather than as independent sources. This clause does not determine which of the statute's three role-based remedy categories applies to a specific reader, nor does it identify what other statutory or common-law theories of liability subdivision (m) preserves.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(g), first sentence (employee remedies)
citations.quote: An employee who has been discriminated against in employment pursuant to this section shall be entitled to reinstatement, reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer, and the legal costs associated with pursuing the case, or to any remedy deemed warranted by the court pursuant to this chapter or any other applicable provision of statutory or common law.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(g), second sentence (health care worker remedies)
citations.quote: A health care worker who has been discriminated against pursuant to this section shall be entitled to reimbursement for lost income and the legal costs associated with pursuing the case, or to any remedy deemed warranted by the court pursuant to this chapter or other applicable provision of statutory or common law.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(g), third sentence (medical staff member remedies)
citations.quote: A member of the medical staff who has been discriminated against pursuant to this section shall be entitled to reinstatement, reimbursement for lost income resulting from any change in the terms or conditions of the member’s privileges caused by the acts of the facility or the entity that owns or operates a health facility or any other health facility that is owned or operated by that entity, and the legal costs associated with pursuing the case, or to any remedy deemed warranted by the court pursuant to this chapter or any other applicable provision of statutory or common law.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(m) (same section as the preceding citations, a different subdivision)
citations.quote: This section does not abrogate or limit any other theory of liability or remedy otherwise available at law.

clauses.title: How This Statute Interacts With Medical Staff Peer Review
clauses.body: This statute does not limit the medical staff's ability to carry out its legitimate peer review activities under Business and Professions Code sections 809 to 809.5. It separately allows the medical staff to petition a court for an injunction protecting a peer review committee from evidentiary demands, in a pending peer review hearing, made by a medical staff member who has filed an action under this statute, if those evidentiary demands would impede the peer review process or endanger patient health and safety during that process; before granting an injunction, the court must conduct an in camera review of the evidence sought to determine whether a peer review hearing authorized under Business and Professions Code sections 805 and 809 through 809.5 would be impeded.
clauses.gap: This clause's two citations are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section -- § 1278.5(h) and (l) -- disclosed here rather than as independent sources. This document does not independently fetch or verify the cross-referenced Business and Professions Code sections 805 and 809 through 809.5, which govern the peer review process itself.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(h)
citations.quote: The medical staff of the health facility may petition the court for an injunction to protect a peer review committee from being required to comply with evidentiary demands on a pending peer review hearing from the member of the medical staff who has filed an action pursuant to this section, if the evidentiary demands from the complainant would impede the peer review process or endanger the health and safety of patients of the health facility during the peer review process.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(l) (same section as the preceding citation, a different subdivision)
citations.quote: This section does not limit the ability of the medical staff to carry out its legitimate peer review activities in accordance with Sections 809 to 809.5, inclusive, of the Business and Professions Code.

clauses.title: What Counts As a "Health Facility," and Who This Statute Does Not Cover
clauses.body: For purposes of this statute, a "health facility" means a facility defined under the same chapter of the Health and Safety Code, including, without limitation, the facility's administrative personnel, employees, boards and board committees, and medical staff. This statute does not apply to an inmate of a correctional facility or juvenile facility of the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, or to an inmate housed in a local detention facility such as a county jail, juvenile hall, or juvenile camp. It also does not apply to a health facility that is a long-term health care facility, as separately defined at Health and Safety Code section 1418 -- a long-term health care facility instead remains subject to Health and Safety Code section 1432.
clauses.gap: This clause's three citations are to different subdivisions of the same statutory section -- § 1278.5(i), (j), and (k) -- disclosed here rather than as independent sources. This document does not independently fetch or verify the definition of "health facility" in the chapter this subdivision cross-references (Health and Safety Code Chapter 2 of Division 2, which includes section 1250), nor the separate long-term-care-facility statutes it names, sections 1418 and 1432, so no claim is made here about their content.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(i)
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, “health facility” means a facility defined under this chapter, including, but not limited to, the facility’s administrative personnel, employees, boards, and committees of the board, and medical staff.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(j) (same section as the preceding citation, a different subdivision)
citations.quote: This section does not apply to an inmate of a correctional facility or juvenile facility of the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, or to an inmate housed in a local detention facility including a county jail or a juvenile hall, juvenile camp, or other juvenile detention facility.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(k) (same section as the preceding citations, a different subdivision)
citations.quote: This section does not apply to a health facility that is a long-term health care facility, as defined in Section 1418. A health facility that is a long-term health care facility shall remain subject to Section 1432.

clauses.title: Right to Speak Privately With a Health Facility Inspector
clauses.body: An employee, or the employee's representative, has the right to discuss possible regulatory violations or patient safety concerns with the inspector privately, during the course of an investigation or inspection carried out by the department.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only Health & Safety Code § 1278.5(n). The statute's text does not itself define which "department" conducts the referenced investigation or inspection in every context, and this document does not independently research that definition beyond the statutory text quoted here.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1278.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Health and Safety Code § 1278.5(n)
citations.quote: An employee or the employee’s representative shall have the right to discuss possible regulatory violations or patient safety concerns with the inspector privately during the course of an investigation or inspection by the department.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes the statutory standard of care that governs how a director of a California nonprofit corporation performs the duties of a director, the statutory right of a director to rely on certain other sources in performing those duties, the resulting statutory liability protection, a separate and narrower statutory immunity available to uncompensated volunteer directors and officers, and who may bring an action to enforce these duties. California's Nonprofit Corporation Law states this standard three times, once for each of the three types of nonprofit corporation it recognizes — public benefit corporations (Corporations Code section 5231), mutual benefit corporations (section 7231), and religious corporations (section 9241) — and the wording differs among them in ways this Information Sheet identifies. It is prepared with reference to {{directorName}}'s service as a director of {{companyName}}, organized as a {{entityType}}. This project's existing Director's Duty of Care and Business Judgment Rule Information Sheet covers Corporations Code section 309, which applies to general stock corporations, not nonprofit corporations; this document covers the separate nonprofit statutes instead. This project's existing Self-Dealing and Interested Director/Officer Transactions Information Sheet separately covers the regulated self-dealing-transaction and common-directorship safe-harbor rules for corporations under sections 310, 5233, and 7233; this document states the general duty-of-care standard those self-dealing statutes are carved out from, but does not restate the self-dealing rules themselves. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing what these statutes provide; it does not evaluate, and is not evidence of, whether any specific decision, vote, or other conduct by {{directorName}} as a director of {{companyName}} satisfied the standard described here, or whether any statutory liability protection or immunity described here would apply to any specific act or omission. Those are fact-specific questions this Information Sheet does not answer.

clauses.title: The Duty-of-Care Standard for Public Benefit and Mutual Benefit Corporation Directors
clauses.body: California states an almost word-for-word identical duty-of-care standard for directors of public benefit corporations and directors of mutual benefit corporations. In both cases, a director must perform the duties of a director, including as a member of a board committee, (1) in good faith, (2) in a manner the director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation, and (3) with the care, including reasonable inquiry, that an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances. This is the standard against which {{directorName}}'s performance of duties as a director of {{companyName}} is measured, if {{companyName}} is organized as a public benefit or mutual benefit corporation under California law; this clause states the standard itself and does not evaluate whether any specific decision by {{directorName}} met it.
clauses.gap: These are two separate statutes in two separate Parts of the Nonprofit Corporation Law (Part 2, public benefit corporations, and Part 3, mutual benefit corporations), not two subdivisions of one section, so they are independent enactments — but their near-identical wording (differing only in “that director believes” versus “such director believes”) reflects a common origin in the same 1978 nonprofit corporation law revision, not independent corroboration of a general common-law rule. This clause covers only subdivision (a) of each section; the reliance right, liability protection, and self-dealing carve-out in the remaining subdivisions are addressed in the following two clauses, which show that the two statutes are not actually identical once those subdivisions are reached. This clause does not address religious corporations, which use a differently worded standard covered in a later clause of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5231(a)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, director's standard of care
citations.quote: A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner that director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 7231(a)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, director's standard of care
citations.quote: A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner such director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances.

clauses.title: Public Benefit Corporation Directors: Reliance Rights, Liability Protection, and the Self-Dealing Carve-Out
clauses.body: In performing the duties described in the preceding clause, a public benefit corporation director is entitled to rely on information, opinions, reports, or statements — including financial statements and other financial data — prepared or presented by corporate officers or employees the director believes reliable and competent, by counsel, independent accountants, or other experts as to matters within their professional competence, or by a board committee the director does not serve on and believes merits confidence, so long as the director acts in good faith and without knowledge that would make the reliance unwarranted. A director who performs duties consistently with this standard and reliance right has no liability based on any alleged failure to discharge director obligations, including for actions or omissions that exceed or defeat a public or charitable purpose to which the corporation or its assets are dedicated — except as the self-dealing-transaction statute, Corporations Code section 5233, separately provides. This clause states what {{directorName}} is entitled to rely on and the resulting liability protection as a director of {{companyName}}, if organized as a public benefit corporation; it does not determine whether any specific reliance by {{directorName}} in fact falls within these categories.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (b) and (c) of the same statute quoted in the preceding clause (Corporations Code section 5231) — they are not independent sources corroborating one another, only different subdivisions of one section. This document does not independently fetch, quote, or verify Section 5233 (the self-dealing-transaction statute referenced by the “Except as provided in” language in subdivision (c)); this project's existing Self-Dealing and Interested Director/Officer Transactions Information Sheet addresses that statute's substance, and readers should consult it or Section 5233 directly rather than relying on this clause for that carve-out's content. This clause does not address the separate volunteer-director immunity statute (Section 5239), covered later in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5231(b)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, sources a director may rely on
citations.quote: In performing the duties of a director, a director shall be entitled to rely on information, opinions, reports or statements, including financial statements and other financial data, in each case prepared or presented by: (1) One or more officers or employees of the corporation whom the director believes to be reliable and competent in the matters presented; (2) Counsel, independent accountants or other persons as to matters which the director believes to be within that person’s professional or expert competence; or (3) A committee upon which the director does not serve that is composed exclusively of any or any combination of directors, persons described in paragraph (1), or persons described in paragraph (2), as to matters within the committee’s designated authority, which committee the director believes to merit confidence, so long as, in any case, the director acts in good faith, after reasonable inquiry when the need therefor is indicated by the circumstances and without knowledge that would cause that reliance to be unwarranted.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5231(c)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, liability protection subject to the self-dealing carve-out (same section as the two citations above; not an independent source)
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 5233, a person who performs the duties of a director in accordance with subdivisions (a) and (b) shall have no liability based upon any alleged failure to discharge the person’s obligations as a director, including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, any actions or omissions which exceed or defeat a public or charitable purpose to which a corporation, or assets held by it, are dedicated.

clauses.title: Mutual Benefit Corporation Directors: Reliance Rights and Liability Protection
clauses.body: A mutual benefit corporation director is entitled to rely on the same three categories of sources as a public benefit corporation director — corporate officers or employees the director believes reliable and competent, counsel or other experts as to matters within their professional competence, and a board committee the director does not serve on and believes merits confidence — subject to the same good-faith and no-unwarranted-reliance conditions. A director who performs duties consistently with this standard and reliance right has no liability based on any alleged failure to discharge director obligations, including for actions or omissions that exceed or defeat a public or charitable purpose to which the corporation's assets are dedicated. This clause states what {{directorName}} is entitled to rely on and the resulting liability protection as a director of {{companyName}}, if organized as a mutual benefit corporation; it does not determine whether any specific reliance by {{directorName}} in fact falls within these categories.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (b) and (c) of the same statute quoted two clauses above (Corporations Code section 7231) — not independent sources of one another. Unlike the parallel public benefit corporation statute's liability-protection subdivision quoted in the preceding clause, subdivision (c) of this mutual benefit corporation statute contains no “Except as provided in Section 7233” (the mutual benefit self-dealing statute) or similar cross-reference in its own text; the self-dealing carve-out for mutual benefit corporations instead appears in the separate volunteer-immunity statute, Section 7231.5, quoted later in this document, and only as to the volunteer directors and narrow category of corporations that statute covers. This clause reports that textual difference; it does not draw any conclusion about whether a compensated (non-volunteer) mutual benefit corporation director's liability protection under this section is, in substance, broader or narrower than a public benefit corporation director's when a self-dealing transaction is at issue — that would require analyzing Section 7233 and any case law construing it, neither of which this document verifies; no case law is cited anywhere in this document because a CourtListener search attempted during this research returned a daily rate-limit error before any results could be retrieved.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 7231(b)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, sources a director may rely on
citations.quote: In performing the duties of a director, a director shall be entitled to rely on information, opinions, reports or statements, including financial statements and other financial data, in each case prepared or presented by: (1) One or more officers or employees of the corporation whom the director believes to be reliable and competent in the matters presented; (2) Counsel, independent accountants or other persons as to matters which the director believes to be within such person’s professional or expert competence; or (3) A committee upon which the director does not serve that is composed exclusively of any or any combination of directors, persons described in paragraph (1), or persons described in paragraph (2), as to matters within the committee’s designated authority, which committee the director believes to merit confidence, so long as, in any case, the director acts in good faith, after reasonable inquiry when the need therefor is indicated by the circumstances and without knowledge that would cause such reliance to be unwarranted.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 7231(c)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, liability protection (same section as the citation above; not an independent source)
citations.quote: A person who performs the duties of a director in accordance with subdivisions (a) and (b) shall have no liability based upon any alleged failure to discharge the person’s obligations as a director, including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, any actions or omissions which exceed or defeat a public or charitable purpose to which assets held by a corporation are dedicated.

clauses.title: Religious Corporation Directors: A Differently Worded Standard, With an Added Reliance Category
clauses.body: A religious corporation director's duty-of-care standard shares the same good-faith and best-interests elements as the public benefit and mutual benefit corporation standards, but its care element is worded differently: instead of the care an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances, the statute requires the care that is appropriate under the circumstances, without using the phrase “ordinarily prudent person.” A religious corporation director may also rely on a fourth category of source unavailable to public benefit or mutual benefit corporation directors: religious authorities and ministers, priests, rabbis, or other persons whose position or duties in the religious organization the director believes justify reliance and confidence, on the same terms of belief in their reliability and competence as apply to the other reliance categories. This clause states what {{directorName}} is entitled to rely on as a director of {{companyName}}, if organized as a religious corporation; it does not determine whether any specific reliance by {{directorName}} in fact falls within these categories.
clauses.gap: This document does not determine, and no case law verified in this research addresses, whether the religious corporation standard's “appropriate under the circumstances” phrasing is functionally equivalent to, stricter than, or more lenient than the “ordinarily prudent person” phrasing used for public benefit and mutual benefit corporations; a CourtListener search on this topic returned a daily rate-limit error before any results were retrieved, so this document proceeds on the verified statutory text alone. This clause quotes subdivisions (a) and (b) of one statute (Corporations Code section 9241); the compensation/loan-resolution rule and the liability protection in the remaining subdivisions of the same section are addressed in the following clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 9241(a)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, director's standard of care
citations.quote: A director shall perform the duties of a director, including duties as a member of any committee of the board upon which the director may serve, in good faith, in a manner such director believes to be in the best interests of the corporation and with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as is appropriate under the circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 9241(b)(4)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, added reliance category for religious authorities (same section as the citation above; not an independent source)
citations.quote: Religious authorities and ministers, priests, rabbis, or other persons whose position or duties in the religious organization the director believes justify reliance and confidence and whom the director believes to be reliable and competent in the matters presented, so long as, in any case, the director acts in good faith, after reasonable inquiry when the need therefor is indicated by the circumstances, and without knowledge that would cause that reliance to be unwarranted.

clauses.title: Religious Corporation Directors: Compensation and Loan Resolutions, and the Section 9243 Liability Carve-Out
clauses.body: California law specifically directs that the religious corporation director statute described in the preceding clause — not the religious corporation self-dealing statute, section 9243 — governs a director's action or omission regarding director or officer compensation, or a loan of money or property to, or a guaranty of the obligation of, any director or officer; a resulting board resolution is not voidable merely because directors who benefited from it participated in adopting it. Separately, a director who performs duties consistent with the standard and reliance right described in the preceding clause has no liability based on any alleged failure to discharge director obligations, except as section 9243 separately provides. This clause states what the statute provides on these two points as applied to {{directorName}}'s service as a director of {{companyName}}, if organized as a religious corporation; it does not evaluate any specific compensation, loan, or guaranty resolution.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivisions (c) and (d) of the same statute quoted in the preceding clause (Corporations Code section 9241) — not independent sources of one another. This document does not independently fetch, quote, or verify Section 9243 (the religious corporation self-dealing statute referenced in both subdivisions); readers should consult that section directly, or this project's existing Self-Dealing and Interested Director/Officer Transactions Information Sheet, rather than relying on this clause for its substance.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 9241(c)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, compensation and loan/guaranty resolutions governed by this section
citations.quote: The provisions of this section, and not Section 9243, shall govern any action or omission of a director in regard to the compensation of directors, as directors or officers, or any loan of money or property to or guaranty of the obligation of any director or officer. No obligation, otherwise valid, shall be voidable merely because directors who benefited by a board resolution to pay such compensation or to make such loan or guaranty participated in making such board resolution.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 9241(d)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Religious Corporation Law, liability protection subject to the Section 9243 carve-out (same section as the citation above; not an independent source)
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 9243, a person who performs the duties of a director in accordance with subdivisions (a) and (b) shall have no liability based upon any alleged failure to discharge his or her obligations as a director, including, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, any actions or omissions which exceed or defeat any purpose to which the corporation, or assets held by it, may be dedicated.

clauses.title: Limited Personal-Liability Immunity for Volunteer Directors and Officers of Public Benefit Corporations
clauses.body: A separate statute limits a volunteer director's or volunteer executive officer's personal liability to a third party for monetary damages caused by a negligent act or omission in performing duties as a director or officer of a public-benefit-corporation-type nonprofit, if four conditions are all met: the act or omission was within the scope of the person's duties; it was performed in good faith; it was not reckless, wanton, intentional, or grossly negligent; and the resulting damages are covered by a liability insurance policy, or, if not covered, the corporation's board and the person made all reasonable efforts in good faith to obtain available liability insurance. This immunity does not eliminate or limit liability under the self-dealing statute (section 5233) or the statute governing certain loans and guaranties to directors and officers (section 5237), or in any action brought by the Attorney General. This clause states the conditions and carve-outs of this immunity as it could apply to {{directorName}}'s uncompensated service as a director of {{companyName}}, if {{directorName}} serves without compensation and {{companyName}} is a public benefit corporation; it does not determine whether {{directorName}} in fact qualifies as a “volunteer” under the statute's definition, whether any act or omission meets these conditions, or whether {{companyName}} carries the insurance, or made the good-faith insurance-seeking efforts, the statute describes.
clauses.gap: This statute (Corporations Code section 5239) applies only to causes of action based on acts or omissions occurring on or after January 1, 1988, by its own terms; this clause does not verify the statute's further subdivision addressing a modified insurance-inquiry standard for smaller public benefit corporations with an annual budget under $25,000 that are tax-exempt under Internal Revenue Code section 501(c)(3), which this document does not quote. This clause also does not address the differently scoped, narrower volunteer immunity statute that applies to certain mutual benefit corporations, covered in the following clause, or whether any comparable volunteer-immunity statute applies to religious corporation directors and officers — no such statute for religious corporations was located or verified in this research.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5239(a)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, volunteer director/officer immunity conditions
citations.quote: There shall be no personal liability to a third party for monetary damages on the part of a volunteer director or volunteer executive officer of a nonprofit corporation subject to this part, caused by the director’s or officer’s negligent act or omission in the performance of that person’s duties as a director or officer, if all of the following conditions are met: (1) The act or omission was within the scope of the director’s or executive officer’s duties. (2) The act or omission was performed in good faith. (3) The act or omission was not reckless, wanton, intentional, or grossly negligent. (4) Damages caused by the act or omission are covered pursuant to a liability insurance policy issued to the corporation, either in the form of a general liability policy or a director’s and officer’s liability policy, or personally to the director or executive officer.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5239(e)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, carve-outs from the volunteer immunity (same section as the citation above; not an independent source)
citations.quote: This section does not eliminate or limit the liability of a director or officer for any of the following: (1) As provided in Section 5233 or 5237. (2) In any action or proceeding brought by the Attorney General.

clauses.title: Mutual Benefit Corporation Volunteer Immunity Is Narrower in Scope Than the Public Benefit Version
clauses.body: A separate mutual benefit corporation statute grants a comparable immunity from monetary liability to a volunteer director or volunteer executive officer whose duties are performed in good faith, in a manner the person believes to be in the best interests of the corporation, and with the care an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances — except as the mutual benefit self-dealing statute (section 7233) or the statute governing certain loans to directors and officers (section 7236) separately provides. Unlike the public benefit corporation immunity described in the preceding clause, this statute by its own terms applies only to trade, professional, and labor organizations incorporated under the Mutual Benefit Corporation Law that operate exclusively for fraternal, educational, and other nonprofit purposes and under Internal Revenue Code section 501(c). This clause states this immunity's conditions and its scope limitation as they could apply to {{directorName}}'s uncompensated service as a director of {{companyName}}, if {{companyName}} is a mutual benefit corporation; it does not determine whether {{companyName}} in fact falls within the trade, professional, or labor organization category the statute requires.
clauses.gap: This is a genuine, specific scope limitation, not a boilerplate caveat: by its own subdivision (d), this statute (Corporations Code section 7231.5) does not extend to every mutual benefit corporation — a mutual benefit corporation that is not a trade, professional, or labor organization operating for the purposes and under the tax status the subdivision specifies (for example, many homeowners associations, social clubs, or membership organizations organized as mutual benefit corporations for purposes outside that description) is not shown by this statute's text to receive this immunity. This document did not locate or verify any broader volunteer-immunity statute covering other categories of mutual benefit corporations; readers should not assume this immunity applies to a mutual benefit corporation outside the described category based on this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 7231.5(a)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, volunteer director/officer immunity conditions
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 7233 or 7236, there is no monetary liability on the part of, and no cause of action for damages shall arise against, any volunteer director or volunteer executive officer of a nonprofit corporation subject to this part based upon any alleged failure to discharge the person’s duties as a director or officer if the duties are performed in a manner that meets all of the following criteria: (1) The duties are performed in good faith. (2) The duties are performed in a manner such director or officer believes to be in the best interests of the corporation. (3) The duties are performed with such care, including reasonable inquiry, as an ordinarily prudent person in a like position would use under similar circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 7231.5(d)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Mutual Benefit Corporation Law, scope limitation restricting this immunity to certain organizations (same section as the citation above; not an independent source)
citations.quote: This section shall apply only to trade, professional, and labor organizations incorporated pursuant to this part which operate exclusively for fraternal, educational, and other nonprofit purposes, and under the provisions of Section 501(c) of the United States Internal Revenue Code.

clauses.title: Who May Sue to Enforce a Public Benefit Corporation Director's Duties
clauses.body: A separate statute identifies who may bring an action to enjoin, correct, obtain damages for, or otherwise remedy a breach of charitable trust by a public benefit corporation: the corporation itself (or a member suing derivatively in the corporation's name, under a separately cross-referenced statute); an officer of the corporation; a director of the corporation; a person with a reversionary, contractual, or property interest in the assets subject to the charitable trust; and the Attorney General, or any person the Attorney General grants relator status. The Attorney General must be given notice of any action brought by the other listed persons and may intervene. This clause states who the statute identifies as able to bring such an action against, among others, a public benefit corporation director; it does not determine whether any specific person has standing under this statute in any specific dispute, or whether any specific conduct by {{directorName}} as a director of {{companyName}} would constitute a breach of charitable trust.
clauses.gap: This statute (Corporations Code section 5142) opens with “Notwithstanding Section 5141”; this document does not independently fetch, quote, or verify Section 5141, so readers should not assume this clause fully states the interaction between the two sections. This document also does not verify whether a directly parallel standing statute exists for mutual benefit or religious corporations — the charitable-trust characterization this statute relies on applies to public benefit corporation assets specifically, and this document did not locate or verify a comparable statute extending the same standing categories to mutual benefit or religious corporations. No case law addressing how courts have applied this standing statute is cited anywhere in this document; a CourtListener search attempted during this research returned a daily rate-limit error before any results could be retrieved.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 5142(a)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, standing to sue for breach of charitable trust
citations.quote: Notwithstanding Section 5141, any of the following may bring an action to enjoin, correct, obtain damages for or to otherwise remedy a breach of a charitable trust: (1) The corporation, or a member in the name of the corporation pursuant to Section 5710. (2) An officer of the corporation. (3) A director of the corporation. (4) A person with a reversionary, contractual, or property interest in the assets subject to such charitable trust. (5) The Attorney General, or any person granted relator status by the Attorney General. The Attorney General shall be given notice of any action brought by the persons specified in paragraphs (1) through (4), and may intervene.
