clauses.title: Certification
clauses.body:
I certify that the description of Corporations Code sections 5231, 7231, 9241, 5239, 7231.5, and 5142 in this Information Sheet reflects the statutory text as in effect on the date below, and that this Information Sheet is a general informational reference regarding {{directorName}}'s service as a director of {{companyName}}, not legal advice about, or a determination of, whether any specific act or omission by {{directorName}} satisfied the standard of care, qualified for the statutory reliance right, is protected from liability, is entitled to volunteer immunity, or could be the subject of an action to remedy a breach of duty under the statutes described above.

clauses.title: About This Public Works Contractor Registration Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's public-works contractor registration requirement, Labor Code Section 1725.5, and the related bid-and-award rules of Labor Code Section 1771.1, which govern who must register with the Department of Industrial Relations before bidding on, being listed as a subcontractor in a bid proposal for, or performing work on a contract for public work, as well as the parallel registration track created by Labor Code Section 1725.6 for certain non-public-works development projects that are nonetheless subject to prevailing wage and skilled-workforce requirements. {{companyName}} has described its involvement in public works contracting, if any, as follows: {{publicWorksContractingDescription}}. This document states the content of the statutes; it does not determine whether {{companyName}} or any particular project or contract falls within the statutory scope of "public work" or of the referenced Government Code development streamlining provisions, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice or for consulting a licensed attorney.

clauses.title: Registration Required to Bid, Be Listed, or Perform on Public Work
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1725.5 states that a contractor must be registered under that section to be qualified to bid on, be listed in a bid proposal for, or engage in the performance of any public work contract subject to the prevailing wage chapter, and that for this purpose "contractor" includes a subcontractor as defined in Labor Code Section 1722.1.
clauses.gap: The quoted sentence does not itself define "public work" or state the scope of "this chapter"; those definitions and scope limits appear in other sections of the same prevailing wage chapter (beginning at Labor Code Section 1720) that are outside this citation and are not reproduced here, so this sheet does not by itself establish whether a given contract is a "public work" in the first place.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1725.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, registration required to bid on, be listed in a bid proposal for, or perform public work
citations.quote: A contractor shall be registered pursuant to this section to be qualified to bid on, be listed in a bid proposal, subject to the requirements of Section 4104 of the Public Contract Code, or engage in the performance of any public work contract that is subject to the requirements of this chapter.

clauses.title: What a Contractor Must Show to Qualify for Registration
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1725.5(a) states that, in addition to registering and paying the application and renewal fees, a contractor must provide evidence, disclosures, or releases establishing several things, among them that the contractor carries workers' compensation coverage sufficient for any worker performing prevailing-wage work, that the contractor is appropriately licensed under the Business and Professions Code where applicable, that the contractor has no delinquent liability to an employee or the state for back wages or related damages under a final judgment or administrative determination (subject to an appeal-bond exception), and that the contractor is not currently debarred under Labor Code Section 1777.1 or other federal or state debarment law.
clauses.gap: The statute lists what a contractor must show but does not itself describe the registration portal, application form, or documentation format the Department of Industrial Relations requires to make that showing; those mechanics are set by department procedure rather than by the quoted statutory text, so this sheet does not describe the actual registration process.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1725.5(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, workers' compensation coverage requirement for registration
citations.quote: Workers’ compensation coverage that meets the requirements of Division 4 (commencing with Section 3200) and includes sufficient coverage for any worker whom the contractor employs to perform work that is subject to prevailing wage requirements other than a contractor who is separately registered under this section.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1725.5(a)(2)(D) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, no-current-debarment requirement for registration
citations.quote: The contractor is not currently debarred under Section 1777.1 or under any other federal or state law providing for the debarment of contractors from public works.

clauses.title: Twelve-Month Lookback for Prior Unregistered Bidding or Work, and the Registration-Fee Cure
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1725.5(a)(2)(E) states that, to qualify for registration, a contractor must not have bid on a public works contract, been listed in a bid proposal, or performed public works without being lawfully registered within the preceding 12 months (or since the requirement first applied, whichever is earlier). The same paragraph states that this disqualification is waived if the contractor has not previously been found in violation within the preceding 12 months and pays an additional nonrefundable penalty registration fee of $2,000.
clauses.gap: The statute states that disqualification applies if a contractor "is found to be in violation," but the quoted paragraph does not identify who makes that finding or what process applies to it; that determination appears to draw on the civil wage and penalty assessment procedures elsewhere in this chapter (see Labor Code Sections 1741-1742), which are not quoted or analyzed in this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1725.5(a)(2)(E) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, 12-month lookback disqualification for prior unregistered bidding or work
citations.quote: The contractor has not bid on a public works contract, been listed in a bid proposal, or engaged in the performance of a contract for public works without being lawfully registered in accordance with this section, within the preceding 12 months or since the effective date of the requirements set forth in subdivision (e), whichever is earlier

clauses.title: Consequence of an Unpaid Renewal Fee, and the Inadvertence Cure
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1725.5(c) states that a contractor who fails to pay the annual renewal fee by the expiration of the prior registration period is prohibited from bidding on or performing any public work contract until registered again, but that if the failure to pay was inadvertent, the contractor may renew retroactively by paying an additional nonrefundable penalty renewal fee equal to the amount of the renewal fee, within 90 days of the renewal fee's due date.
clauses.gap: The subdivision does not address what happens to work already in progress under a contract that was validly bid while the contractor was registered, if the registration then lapses mid-performance before the 90-day inadvertence cure is used; its interaction with the separate bid-and-contract bar in Labor Code Section 1771.1(a) for that scenario is not addressed in the quoted text.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1725.5(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, consequence of failing to pay the annual renewal fee
citations.quote: A contractor who fails to pay the renewal fee required under paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) on or before the expiration of any prior period of registration shall be prohibited from bidding on or engaging in the performance of any contract for public work until once again registered pursuant to this section.

clauses.title: Dollar-Threshold Exemption for Small Public Works Projects
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1725.5(f) states that the registration requirement does not apply to work on a public works project of $25,000 or less for construction, alteration, demolition, installation, or repair work, or to work on a public works project of $15,000 or less for maintenance work.
clauses.gap: The subdivision states flat dollar thresholds without an inflation adjustment mechanism and without specifying how the threshold is measured for a project performed under multiple change orders, phased task orders, or an indefinite-quantity contract; those measurement questions are not addressed in the quoted text.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1725.5(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, small public works project dollar-threshold exemption
citations.quote: This section does not apply to work performed on a public works project of twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000) or less when the project is for construction, alteration, demolition, installation, or repair work or to work performed on a public works project of fifteen thousand dollars ($15,000) or less when the project is for maintenance work.

clauses.title: Phase-In Dates and the Section's Current Operative Date
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1725.5(e) states that the registration requirement applies to any bid proposal submitted on or after March 1, 2015, to any public work contract executed on or after April 1, 2015, and to any work performed under a public work contract on or after January 1, 2018, regardless of when the contract was executed. The current version of the section, which restates and renumbers the requirement, states in subdivision (h) that it became operative on July 1, 2026.
clauses.gap: The version of Section 1725.5 checked here was added by Stats. 2023, Chapter 39, Section 24, and then amended by Stats. 2024, Chapter 52, Section 22, with an operative date of July 1, 2026; the quoted text does not itself explain what registration rule (if any) governed public works bidding and performance between the 2023 enactment and the July 1, 2026 operative date of this current version, so the transitional period is not covered by this sheet.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1725.5(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, original 2015/2018 phase-in dates for the registration requirement
citations.quote: The requirements of this section shall apply to any bid proposal submitted on or after March 1, 2015, to any contract for public work, as defined in this chapter, executed on or after April 1, 2015, and to any work performed under a contract for public work on or after January 1, 2018, regardless of when the contract for public work was executed.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1725.5(h) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, current operative date of the section as amended
citations.quote: This section shall become operative on July 1, 2026.

clauses.title: The Parallel Registration Track for Certain Non-Public-Works Development Projects
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1725.6 creates a second, separately numbered registration requirement for a contractor to be awarded, or to perform work on, projects or developments subject to specified Government Code streamlined-housing-approval statutes (Sections 65852.24, 65912.130, 65912.131, 65913.4, and 65913.16), or any other project where a statute or regulation requires registration under Section 1725.6, even where the project is not a "public work" governed by Section 1725.5. A contractor who has already paid the registration or renewal fee under Section 1725.6 is not required to pay a second registration or renewal fee to also register under Section 1725.5, and the reverse is likewise true.
clauses.gap: The quoted text does not explain why the Legislature created a second, structurally near-identical registration section instead of expanding Section 1725.5's own scope, and it does not state whether the Government Code housing-streamlining provisions it cross-references define "contractor" the same way as Labor Code Section 1722.1 does for purposes of Section 1725.5; that potential definitional difference is not addressed here.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1725.6 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, registration requirement for specified streamlined-housing development projects
citations.quote: A contractor shall be registered pursuant to this section to be qualified to be awarded contracts for, or engage in the performance of, any work on projects or developments subject to the requirements of Section 65852.24, 65912.130, 65912.131, 65913.4, or 65913.16 of the Government Code or any work on projects or developments where a statute or regulation requires registration pursuant to this section.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1725.5(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, registration under Section 1725.6 satisfies the Section 1725.5 fee
citations.quote: A contractor that has paid the registration or renewal fee and is registered under Section 1725.6 shall not pay the registration or renewal fee required under paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) to register as a contractor under this section.

clauses.title: The Awarding Body's Own Notice and Bid-Rejection Duties
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1771.1 places obligations on the body awarding a public works contract, not only on the contractor: notice of the registration requirement must be included in all bid invitations and public works contracts, and a bid may not be accepted, nor a contract or subcontract entered into, without proof of the contractor's or subcontractor's current registration under Section 1725.5. The Department of Industrial Relations is separately required to maintain a public list, on its internet website, of contractors currently registered to perform public work.
clauses.gap: Subdivision (a) also states that it is not a violation for an unregistered contractor to submit certain bids authorized under specified Business and Professions Code and Public Contract Code sections, provided registration occurs by contract award; those cross-referenced exceptions are named but not reproduced or analyzed here, so this clause does not describe their full scope.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1771.1(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, awarding body's notice and bid-acceptance duties
citations.quote: Notice of the requirement described in subdivision (a) shall be included in all bid invitations and public works contracts, and a bid shall not be accepted nor any contract or subcontract entered into without proof of the contractor or subcontractor’s current registration to perform public work pursuant to Section 1725.5.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1771.1(e) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, Department of Industrial Relations' public registered-contractor list
citations.quote: The department shall maintain on its internet website a list of contractors who are currently registered to perform public work pursuant to Section 1725.5.

clauses.title: Civil Penalties for Performing Public Work While Unregistered, Including Higher-Tier Contractor Exposure
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 1771.1(g) states that a contractor or subcontractor found by the Labor Commissioner to have performed public work without being registered forfeits a civil penalty of $100 for each day of work performed in violation, up to an aggregate of $8,000. Separately, subdivision (h)(1) states that a higher-tiered contractor or subcontractor found to have subcontracted with an unregistered lower-tier subcontractor to perform public work is itself subject to forfeiture of $100 per day the unregistered lower-tier subcontractor performs work, up to an aggregate of $10,000.
clauses.gap: Subdivision (h) also states, in paragraphs not quoted here, that a higher-tiered contractor is not liable under this provision if the lower-tier subcontractor's violation stems from revocation of a previously approved registration, and that a lower-tier subcontractor cannot itself be held liable for a higher-tiered contractor's penalty or be required to indemnify it; this clause states the penalty amounts but does not restate those liability-allocation carve-outs in full.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1771.1(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, civil penalty for a contractor or subcontractor performing unregistered public work
citations.quote: the contractor or subcontractor shall forfeit, as a civil penalty to the state, one hundred dollars ($100) for each day of work performed in violation of the registration requirement, not to exceed an aggregate penalty of eight thousand dollars ($8,000)

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1771.1(h)(1) (California Legislative Information text; same section as the preceding citation, not an independent source of it)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, civil penalty for a higher-tiered contractor engaging an unregistered lower-tier subcontractor
citations.quote: a higher tiered public works contractor or subcontractor who is found to have entered into a subcontract with an unregistered lower tier subcontractor to perform any public work in violation of the requirements of Section 1725.5 or this section shall be subject to forfeiture, as a civil penalty to the state, of one hundred dollars ($100) for each day the unregistered lower tier subcontractor performs work in violation of the registration requirement, not to exceed an aggregate penalty of ten thousand dollars ($10,000)

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
clauses.body: This information sheet regarding California's public-works contractor registration requirements, Labor Code Sections 1725.5, 1725.6, and 1771.1, was prepared by {{preparerName}} for {{companyName}} and reviewed in {{cityState}} on {{dateSigned}}. It reflects the statutory text as of the date checked above and does not reflect any amendments made after that date, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's vexatious litigant statute, Code of Civil Procedure sections 391 through 391.7, as it can apply in a family law proceeding between {{petitionerName}} and {{respondentName}}, case number {{courtCaseNumber}}, filed in {{countyOfFiling}}. It covers the statutory definition of a "vexatious litigant," a 2023 addition to that definition specific to a person restrained by a domestic violence restraining order, the motion procedure for requiring security or a prefiling order, and the automatic stay and dismissal consequences that can follow. It does not state whether either party in this matter is or is not a vexatious litigant, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about the facts of a specific case.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Vexatious Litigant"
clauses.body: California law defines a "vexatious litigant" to include a person who, in the immediately preceding seven-year period, has commenced, prosecuted, or maintained in propria persona at least five litigations other than in small claims court that were finally determined adversely to the person or unjustifiably left pending at least two years without trial or hearing; a person who repeatedly relitigates, in propria persona, an already-finally-determined matter against the same defendant; a person who, while acting in propria persona, repeatedly files unmeritorious motions or papers, conducts unnecessary discovery, or engages in other frivolous or delay-only tactics; or a person previously declared a vexatious litigant by any state or federal court of record in an action based on the same or substantially similar facts. "Litigation" for these purposes means any civil action or proceeding commenced, maintained, or pending in any state or federal court.
clauses.gap: This clause states the first four of five statutory definitional categories in Code of Civil Procedure section 391(b); the fifth, domestic-violence-restraining-order-based category added effective January 1, 2023, is covered in a separate clause. The statute's numeric threshold (five qualifying litigations in seven years) and its "finally determined adversely" and "unjustifiably permitted to remain pending" language are not further defined within section 391 itself, and no case law interpreting how family law motions or orders to show cause count toward that threshold could be verified for this clause because CourtListener's case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, daily quota exhausted) on the single query attempted for this research.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391(a)-(b)(1)-(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory definitions of "litigation" and "vexatious litigant," first four categories
citations.quote: “Vexatious litigant” means a person who does any of the following: (1) In the immediately preceding seven-year period has commenced, prosecuted, or maintained in propria persona at least five litigations other than in a small claims court that have been (i) finally determined adversely to the person or (ii) unjustifiably permitted to remain pending at least two years without having been brought to trial or hearing.

clauses.title: Vexatious Litigant Status Based on Violating a Domestic Violence Restraining Order
clauses.body: A fifth, family-law-specific category was added to the vexatious litigant definition effective January 1, 2023. A person qualifies as a vexatious litigant if, after being restrained by a restraining order issued at a hearing under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act (Family Code section 6300 et seq.), and while that restraining order remains in place, the person commenced, prosecuted, or maintained one or more litigations against the protected person in any court or jurisdiction, where those litigations are determined to be meritless and caused the protected person to be harassed or intimidated.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subdivision, added by a 2022 amendment (AB 2391, effective January 1, 2023), and it is the only subdivision of section 391(b) quoted for this clause; it is not an independent source from the other four categories in section 391(b), all of which appear in the same section and same amendment history. The statute does not itself define "meritless" or "harassed or intimidated" for purposes of this subdivision, and no published case applying this relatively new provision could be verified because of the CourtListener rate-limit failure disclosed elsewhere in this research.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391(b)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the domestic-violence-restraining-order-based vexatious litigant category; not an independent source from the other § 391(b) categories cited in this document's companion clause, as both come from the same statutory section
citations.quote: (5) After being restrained pursuant to a restraining order issued after a hearing pursuant to Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 6300) of Part 4 of Division 10 of the Family Code, and while the restraining order is still in place, they commenced, prosecuted, or maintained one or more litigations against a person protected by the restraining order in this or any other court or jurisdiction that are determined to be meritless and caused the person protected by the order to be harassed or intimidated.

clauses.title: Motion for Security or Dismissal; No Filing Fee for a Protected Person's Motion
clauses.body: In any pending litigation, at any time until final judgment, a defendant may move the court, on notice and hearing, for an order requiring the plaintiff to furnish security, or for an order dismissing the litigation under the merits-based dismissal provision described elsewhere in this document. A motion for security must be based on, and supported by a showing, that the plaintiff is a vexatious litigant and that there is not a reasonable probability the plaintiff will prevail against the moving defendant. Where the motion is based on the domestic-violence-restraining-order category of the vexatious litigant definition, it may be brought only by the person protected by the restraining order, and that person is not required to pay a filing fee for the motion.
clauses.gap: This clause combines subdivisions (a) and (b) of the same statutory section (section 391.1); they are not independent sources of one another. The statute does not specify a filing fee exemption for a motion brought on any basis other than the restraining-order-based category, and it does not state whether the fee waiver in subdivision (b) extends to any other papers filed in connection with the same motion.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.1(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the general motion procedure for security or dismissal
citations.quote: (a) In any litigation pending in any court of this state, at any time until final judgment is entered, a defendant may move the court, upon notice and hearing, for an order requiring the plaintiff to furnish security or for an order dismissing the litigation pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 391.3. The motion for an order requiring the plaintiff to furnish security shall be based upon the ground, and supported by a showing, that the plaintiff is a vexatious litigant and that there is not a reasonable probability that they will prevail in the litigation against the moving defendant.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.1(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the restraining-order-based motion and its filing-fee exemption; from the same statutory section as the citation above, not an independent source
citations.quote: (b) A motion pursuant to subdivision (a) on the grounds that plaintiff is a vexatious litigant pursuant to paragraph (5) of subdivision (b) of Section 391 may be brought only by a person protected by the restraining order. A person filing a motion as described in this subdivision shall not be required to pay a filing fee.

clauses.title: Hearing on the Motion Does Not Decide the Merits
clauses.body: At the hearing on a motion for security, the court considers any evidence material to the ground of the motion, written or oral, by witnesses or affidavit. Except for an order dismissing the litigation under the merits-based dismissal provision described elsewhere in this document, no determination the court makes in ruling on the motion is, or is deemed to be, a determination of any issue in the underlying litigation or of its merits.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section describing the evidentiary and non-merits-determination rules for the security motion hearing; it does not describe the evidentiary standard or procedure applicable to a hearing on a prefiling order under the separate statute covering that subject, addressed in another clause of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.2 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the hearing procedure and non-merits-determination rule
citations.quote: At the hearing upon the motion the court shall consider any evidence, written or oral, by witnesses or affidavit, as may be material to the ground of the motion. Except for an order dismissing the litigation pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 391.3, no determination made by the court in determining or ruling upon the motion shall be or be deemed to be a determination of any issue in the litigation or of the merits thereof.

clauses.title: Order Requiring Security, or Dismissal for Meritless Filings by a Represented-Turned-Self-Represented Litigant
clauses.body: If, after hearing the evidence, the court determines the plaintiff is a vexatious litigant and there is no reasonable probability the plaintiff will prevail against the moving defendant, the court orders the plaintiff to furnish security, in an amount and within a time the court fixes, for the moving defendant's benefit. A separate, narrower dismissal remedy applies only where the litigation was filed by a vexatious litigant already subject to a prefiling order, who was represented by counsel when the litigation was filed and became self-represented after that counsel withdrew: if the court determines the litigation has no merit and was filed for purposes of harassment or delay, the court orders it dismissed. A defendant may move for relief under either provision in the alternative but must combine all grounds for relief in one motion.
clauses.gap: This clause combines subdivisions (a) through (c) of the same statutory section (section 391.3); they are not independent sources of one another. The statute's "no reasonable probability" and "no merit" standards are not further defined within the statute's own text, and no case law construing how courts apply these standards could be verified because of the CourtListener rate-limit failure disclosed elsewhere in this research.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.3(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the general security order standard
citations.quote: (a) Except as provided in subdivision (b), if, after hearing the evidence upon the motion, the court determines that the plaintiff is a vexatious litigant and that there is no reasonable probability that the plaintiff will prevail in the litigation against the moving defendant, the court shall order the plaintiff to furnish, for the benefit of the moving defendant, security in such amount and within such time as the court shall fix.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.3(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the narrower merits-based dismissal remedy; from the same statutory section as the citation above, not an independent source
citations.quote: (b) If, after hearing evidence on the motion, the court determines that the litigation has no merit and has been filed for the purposes of harassment or delay, the court shall order the litigation dismissed. This subdivision shall only apply to litigation filed in a court of this state by a vexatious litigant subject to a prefiling order pursuant to Section 391.7 who was represented by counsel at the time the litigation was filed and who became in propria persona after the withdrawal of his or her attorney.

clauses.title: Dismissal for Failure to Furnish Ordered Security
clauses.body: When security that a court has ordered furnished is not furnished as ordered, the litigation is dismissed as to the defendant for whose benefit the security was ordered.
clauses.gap: This is a single, short statutory section (unchanged since its original 1963 enactment) that does not itself specify a grace period, a procedure for extending the time to furnish security, or what happens to claims against any other defendant not named as the beneficiary of the security order.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.4 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the automatic-dismissal consequence for failing to furnish ordered security
citations.quote: When security that has been ordered furnished is not furnished as ordered, the litigation shall be dismissed as to the defendant for whose benefit it was ordered furnished.

clauses.title: Automatic Stay of the Litigation While the Security Motion Is Pending
clauses.body: When a motion for security is filed before trial, the litigation is automatically stayed, and the moving defendant need not plead, until 10 days after the motion is denied, or, if granted, until 10 days after the required security has been furnished and the moving defendant given written notice of that fact. If the motion is made later than before trial, the court determines the length of the stay following denial of the motion or furnishing of the required security.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section describing the stay that follows the filing of a security motion under section 391.1; it does not by itself describe the separate automatic stay that can arise from a notice filed under the prefiling-order statute, which is addressed in another clause of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.6 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the automatic stay triggered by filing a security motion
citations.quote: Except as provided in subdivision (b) of Section 391.3, when a motion pursuant to Section 391.1 is filed prior to trial the litigation is stayed, and the moving defendant need not plead, until 10 days after the motion shall have been denied, or if granted, until 10 days after the required security has been furnished and the moving defendant given written notice thereof.

clauses.title: Prefiling Order and Its Express Reach Into Family Code Proceedings
clauses.body: A court may, on its own motion or a party's motion, enter a prefiling order prohibiting a vexatious litigant from filing any new litigation in California courts while self-represented without first obtaining leave of the presiding justice or presiding judge of the court where the filing is proposed; disobeying the order can be punished as contempt of court. The presiding justice or judge permits the filing only if it appears the litigation has merit and was not filed for harassment or delay, and may condition permission on the furnishing of security. For purposes of the prefiling-order statute specifically, "litigation" is defined to include any petition, application, or motion -- other than a discovery motion -- in a proceeding under the Family Code or Probate Code, for any order. A court clerk may not file a self-represented vexatious litigant's litigation without that leave; if filed by mistake, notice of the prefiling order automatically stays the litigation, which is then automatically dismissed unless the plaintiff obtains leave within 10 days. The clerk of the court must provide the Judicial Council a copy of each prefiling order, and the Judicial Council maintains and annually disseminates a statewide list of persons subject to a prefiling order.
clauses.gap: This clause combines several subdivisions of the same statutory section (section 391.7); they are not independent sources of one another. The prefiling-order statute's definition of "litigation" as reaching Family Code and Probate Code petitions, applications, and motions (other than discovery motions) applies only for purposes of that section, not for the broader definitional threshold in section 391(b)(1)-(4) described in a companion clause of this document -- the statute does not say whether a family law motion filed against a prefiling-order requirement also counts toward that separate five-litigation threshold. No published California case interpreting this section's application to family law filings specifically could be verified because the single CourtListener query attempted for this research returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted).

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.7(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the prefiling order authority and its contempt enforcement
citations.quote: (a) In addition to any other relief provided in this title, the court may, on its own motion or the motion of any party, enter a prefiling order which prohibits a vexatious litigant from filing any new litigation in the courts of this state in propria persona without first obtaining leave of the presiding justice or presiding judge of the court where the litigation is proposed to be filed. Disobedience of the order by a vexatious litigant may be punished as a contempt of court.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 391.7(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the definition of "litigation," for purposes of the prefiling-order statute only, as reaching Family Code and Probate Code filings; from the same statutory section as the citation above, not an independent source
citations.quote: (d) For purposes of this section, “litigation” includes any petition, application, or motion other than a discovery motion, in a proceeding under the Family Code or Probate Code, for any order.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
clauses.body: {{petitionerName}} and {{respondentName}} acknowledge having reviewed this information sheet describing California's vexatious litigant statute, Code of Civil Procedure sections 391 through 391.7, including the general definitional categories, the domestic-violence-restraining-order-based category added in 2023, the motion procedure for security and its filing-fee exemption for a protected person, the automatic stay, the dismissal consequences, and the prefiling-order procedure's express application to Family Code and Probate Code filings. Signed in {{cityState}} on {{dateSigned}}.

clauses.title: Density Bonus Application — Project Identification
Eligibility Thresholds Triggering the Density Bonus Entitlement
clauses.body: Under California's Density Bonus Law, a city, county, or city and county must grant one density bonus, in the amount specified by the statute's sliding-scale calculation, and, if requested by the applicant, incentives or concessions, waivers or reductions of development standards, and reduced parking ratios, to an applicant who seeks and agrees to construct a housing development that contains at least one of several statutorily specified thresholds. Two of the most commonly used thresholds are that at least ten percent of the total units be for rental or sale to lower income households, or that at least five percent of the total units be for rental or sale to very low income households, with the applicable income categories cross-referenced to the Health and Safety Code. Other listed thresholds address senior citizen housing developments, moderate-income for-sale developments, transitional foster youth, disabled veteran, and homeless housing, and 100-percent-affordable developments, each triggering its own density bonus percentage under a separate subdivision of the statute.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the operative grant-of-entitlement sentence and the two most commonly used percentage thresholds (lower income and very low income rental/sale units) out of at least seven alternative qualifying thresholds enumerated in the same subdivision (including senior housing, moderate-income for-sale developments, transitional foster youth or disabled veteran housing, homeless shelters, and 100-percent-affordable developments); it does not reproduce the detailed eligibility conditions attached to those other thresholds, each of which has its own cross-referenced definitions and, in some cases, its own density bonus percentage schedule addressed in other clauses of this document. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(b)(1)
citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (b)(1) (density bonus entitlement)
citations.quote: A city, county, or city and county shall grant one density bonus, the amount of which shall be as specified in subdivision (f), and, if requested by the applicant and consistent with the applicable requirements of this section, incentives or concessions, as described in subdivision (d), waivers or reductions of development standards, as described in subdivision (e), and parking ratios, as described in subdivision (p), if an applicant for a housing development seeks and agrees to construct a housing development, excluding any units permitted by the density bonus awarded pursuant to this section, that will contain at least any one of the following:

clauses.title: Two Common Qualifying Set-Asides: Lower Income and Very Low Income Units
clauses.body: Among the statutory thresholds that qualify a housing development for a density bonus, California law specifies that at least ten percent of a development's total units, including a shared housing building development, dedicated to rental or sale to lower income households (as defined by cross-reference to the Health and Safety Code) will qualify the development for the entitlement described elsewhere in the statute. Alternatively, at least five percent of the total units dedicated to rental or sale to very low income households (also cross-referenced to the Health and Safety Code) will independently qualify a development. These are minimum set-aside percentages; a development that dedicates a higher percentage of units to either income category receives a correspondingly larger density bonus under the statute's sliding-scale calculation.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only the lower income and very low income rental/sale thresholds; it does not reproduce the separate, differently worded thresholds for senior housing developments, moderate-income for-sale developments, transitional foster youth or disabled veteran housing, homeless shelters, or 100-percent-affordable developments, each of which is defined in the same subdivision but is not quoted here. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(b)(1)(A)-(B)
citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (b)(1)(A) and (B) (lower income and very low income unit thresholds)
citations.quote: (A) Ten percent of the total units of a housing development, including a shared housing building development, for rental or sale to lower income households, as defined in Section 50079.5 of the Health and Safety Code. (B) Five percent of the total units of a housing development, including a shared housing building development, for rental or sale to very low income households, as defined in Section 50105 of the Health and Safety Code.

clauses.title: How the Density Bonus Percentage Is Calculated
clauses.body: California's Density Bonus Law defines a “density bonus” as a density increase over the otherwise maximum allowable gross residential density under the local zoning ordinance in effect as of the date of the applicant's application, or, if the applicant elects, a lesser percentage of density increase, including no increase in density at all. The amount of density increase to which an applicant is entitled is not fixed; it varies according to how far the percentage of affordable housing units in the development exceeds the minimum percentage thresholds described elsewhere in the statute. The statute sets out separate sliding-scale tables tying specific affordable-unit percentages to specific density bonus percentages, with the tables differing depending on which income category (lower income, very low income, or moderate income) and which qualifying category (e.g., standard rental/sale development, 100-percent-affordable development, or land-donation development) applies.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the general definitional and variable-entitlement language that introduces the density bonus calculation; it does not reproduce the numeric sliding-scale tables themselves (which pair specific affordable-unit percentages, such as 10 percent low-income units, with specific density bonus percentages, such as 20 percent, ranging up to a 50-percent maximum bonus under the standard tables, or up to an 80-percent bonus for certain 100-percent-affordable developments), nor the additional density bonus available under a separate 2025 amendment (subdivision (v)) for developments that combine several affordability tiers. Local zoning specifics vary by jurisdiction and are not addressed here. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(f)
citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (f) (definition and variable entitlement of the density bonus)
citations.quote: For the purposes of this chapter, “density bonus” means a density increase over the otherwise maximum allowable gross residential density, as of the date of application by the applicant to the city, county, or city and county, or, if elected by the applicant, a lesser percentage of density increase, including, but not limited to, no increase in density. The amount of density increase to which the applicant is entitled shall vary according to the amount by which the percentage of affordable housing units exceeds the percentage established in subdivision (b).

clauses.title: Entitlement to Incentives or Concessions and the Narrow Grounds for Denial
clauses.body: An applicant for a density bonus may submit to the local government a proposal for specific incentives or concessions and may request a meeting to discuss it. California law requires the local government to grant the requested concession or incentive unless it makes a written finding, supported by substantial evidence, that the concession or incentive would not result in identifiable and actual cost reductions for affordable housing costs or targeted-unit rents, would have a specific adverse impact on public health or safety or on a listed historical resource without a feasible mitigation, or would be contrary to state or federal law. The number of incentives or concessions to which an applicant is entitled increases with the percentage of affordable units the development includes, on a tiered scale set out in the statute, up to five incentives or concessions for developments meeting the criteria for 100-percent-affordable projects.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the denial-standard sentence and the first two tiers of the incentive/concession count schedule (one incentive for a 10-percent lower income or 5-percent very low income set-aside; two incentives for 17-percent lower income or 10-percent very low income); it does not reproduce the third tier, the five-incentive tier for 100-percent-affordable projects, or the further, more generous tiers added by 2025 legislation for projects combining moderate-income and very low or lower income units (subdivision (b)(1)(v)). (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(d)(1)-(2)
citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (d), paragraphs (1) (denial standard) and (2)(A)-(B) (incentive/concession count) -- these two paragraphs of the same subdivision are cited together and are not independent of each other
citations.quote: The city, county, or city and county shall grant the concession or incentive requested by the applicant unless the city, county, or city and county makes a written finding, based upon substantial evidence, of any of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(d)(2)(A)-(B)
citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (d)(2)(A) and (B) (first two tiers of the incentive/concession count schedule)
citations.quote: (A) One incentive or concession for projects that include at least 10 percent of the total units for lower income households, at least 5 percent for very low income households, or at least 10 percent for persons and families of moderate income in a development in which the units are for sale. (B) Two incentives or concessions for projects that include at least 17 percent of the total units for lower income households, at least 10 percent for very low income households, or at least 20 percent for persons and families of moderate income in a development in which the units are for sale.

clauses.title: What Counts as an “Incentive or Concession”
clauses.body: California's Density Bonus Law defines “concession or incentive” to include a reduction in site development standards or a modification of zoning code or architectural design requirements that exceed minimum state building standards -- such as a reduction in setback, square footage, or parking requirements -- where the reduction results in identifiable and actual cost reductions for affordable housing costs or targeted-unit rents. The statute also lists approval of mixed-use zoning alongside the housing project, where the non-residential use will reduce the housing development's cost and is compatible with the surrounding area, and a third, catch-all category of other regulatory incentives or concessions proposed by the developer or the local government that result in identifiable, actual cost reductions.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the first enumerated category (site development standard reductions) in full and summarizes, without quoting, the mixed-use and catch-all categories that follow it in the same subdivision; the statute's full text of those remaining categories, and the separate additional incentives available for childcare facilities and 100-percent-affordable projects addressed in other subdivisions, are not reproduced here. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(k)(1)
citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (k), introductory clause and paragraph (1) (definition of concession or incentive)
citations.quote: For the purposes of this chapter, concession or incentive means any of the following: (1) A reduction in site development standards or a modification of zoning code requirements or architectural design requirements that exceed the minimum building standards approved by the California Building Standards Commission as provided in Part 2.5 (commencing with Section 18901) of Division 13 of the Health and Safety Code, including, but not limited to, a reduction in setback and square footage requirements and in the ratio of vehicular parking spaces that would otherwise be required that results in identifiable and actual cost reductions, to provide for affordable housing costs, as defined in Section 50052.5 of the Health and Safety Code, or for rents for the targeted units to be set as specified in subdivision (c).

clauses.title: Waiver or Reduction of Development Standards That Would Preclude Construction
clauses.body: Separate from the incentive-or-concession process, California law prohibits a local government from applying any development standard that would have the effect of physically precluding construction of a density-bonus-eligible development at the densities, or with the concessions or incentives, permitted by the statute. An applicant may submit a proposal for the waiver or reduction of such a development standard and may request a meeting with the local government. The statute makes this waiver process distinct from the incentive/concession count: a request for a waiver or reduction of development standards neither reduces nor increases the number of incentives or concessions to which the applicant is separately entitled. If a court finds that a local government's refusal to grant a waiver or reduction violates the statute, the statute directs the court to award the prevailing plaintiff reasonable attorney's fees and costs of suit.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses the general no-preclusion rule; it does not reproduce the statute's separate carve-outs limiting the waiver obligation where a waiver would have a specific, adverse impact on public health or safety without a feasible mitigation, would adversely affect a listed historical resource, or would be contrary to state or federal law, nor the narrower eligibility rule that applies to a development that has already received a waiver from maximum density controls under a cross-referenced clause of subdivision (f). (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(e)(1)
citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (e)(1) (no-preclusion rule for development standards)
citations.quote: In no case may a city, county, or city and county apply any development standard that will have the effect of physically precluding the construction of a development meeting the criteria of subdivision (b) at the densities or with the concessions or incentives permitted by this section.

clauses.title: Statutory Caps on Parking Ratios for Density Bonus Developments
clauses.body: Upon a developer's request, California law caps the vehicular parking ratio a local government may impose on a qualifying density bonus development, inclusive of parking for persons with a disability and guests. The default statutory caps are one onsite parking space for a unit with zero to one bedroom, one and one-half onsite spaces for a unit with two to three bedrooms, and two and one-half spaces for a unit with four or more bedrooms. The statute further reduces these caps for developments that include a higher percentage of low-income or very low income units and are located within one-half mile of a major transit stop with unobstructed access, and it sets a separate, distinct cap for single bedspaces in student housing developments.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the default parking ratio caps for zero-to-one, two-to-three, and four-or-more bedroom units; it does not reproduce the statute's additional, more restrictive 0.5-spaces-per-unit and 0.5-spaces-per-bedroom caps for developments near major transit stops, the zero-parking rule for student housing bedspaces, or the separate exceptions in paragraphs (3) and (4) of the same subdivision for special circumstances. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(p)(1)
citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (p)(1) (default parking ratio caps)
citations.quote: upon the request of the developer, a city, county, or city and county shall not require a vehicular parking ratio, inclusive of parking for persons with a disability and guests, of a development meeting the criteria of subdivisions (b) and (c), that exceeds the following ratios: (A) Zero to one bedroom: one onsite parking space. (B) Two to three bedrooms: one and one-half onsite parking spaces. (C) Four and more bedrooms: two and one-half parking spaces.

clauses.title: Additional Density Bonus for Donating Land to the Local Government
clauses.body: Separate from the affordable-unit density bonus, California law provides an additional density bonus for an applicant who, in connection with a tentative subdivision map, parcel map, or other residential development approval, donates land to the local government in accordance with the statute's conditions. A qualifying land donation entitles the applicant to a 15-percent increase above the otherwise maximum allowable residential density for the entire development, with the percentage increasing on a sliding scale as the proportion of very low income units the donated land will support increases, up to a 35-percent maximum combined density increase when the land-donation bonus is combined with the standard affordable-unit bonus.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the introductory sentence establishing the 15-percent baseline land-donation bonus and its sliding-scale structure; it does not reproduce the statute's detailed eligibility conditions for a qualifying land donation (including the required timing of the transfer, the minimum developable acreage and zoning classification of the donated land, and its required proximity to the development it serves), which are set out in subsequent, unquoted subparagraphs of the same subdivision. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(g)(1)
citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (g)(1) (land donation density bonus)
citations.quote: When an applicant for a tentative subdivision map, parcel map, or other residential development approval donates land to a city, county, or city and county in accordance with this subdivision, the applicant shall be entitled to a 15-percent increase above the otherwise maximum allowable residential density for the entire development

clauses.title: Required Duration of Continued Affordability
clauses.body: In exchange for the density bonus, California law requires an applicant to agree to, and requires the local government to ensure, the continued affordability of the very low income and low-income rental units that qualified the applicant for the density bonus for a period of 55 years, or for a longer period if a construction or mortgage financing assistance program, mortgage insurance program, or rental subsidy program applicable to the development requires it. The statute separately addresses the rent levels that must be set for those units and, in a different paragraph of the same subdivision, the conditions that apply to for-sale units that qualified the applicant for the density bonus.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only the 55-year affordability duration rule for rental units; it does not reproduce the statute's separate rent-setting formula for lower income density bonus units (including the modified rent structure that applies to 100-percent-affordable developments) or the distinct resale-price and equity-sharing conditions that apply to for-sale density bonus units under a different paragraph of the same subdivision. (Note: every citation in this document's clause set is drawn from subdivisions of the single statute Government Code Section 65915; they are not independent sources of one another and should be read together as parts of one section.)

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 65915(c)(1)(A)
citations.cite: California Government Code Section 65915, subdivision (c)(1)(A) (55-year affordability covenant)
citations.quote: An applicant shall agree to, and the city, county, or city and county shall ensure, the continued affordability of all very low and low-income rental units that qualified the applicant for the award of the density bonus for 55 years or a longer period of time if required by the construction or mortgage financing assistance program, mortgage insurance program, or rental subsidy program.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment and Signature
Right-of-Recall Notice — Identification
Which Employers and Which Workers the Statute Covers
clauses.body: Labor Code Section 2810.8 does not apply to employers generally. It reaches only an "enterprise," a term the statute defines to mean a hotel, private club, event center, airport hospitality operation, airport service provider, or the provision of building service to office, retail, or other commercial buildings, and "building service" is itself separately defined to mean janitorial, building maintenance, or security services. Within a covered enterprise, the statute's protections run only to a "laid-off employee": an employee who worked for the employer for six months or more and whose most recent separation from active employment occurred on or after March 4, 2020 for a reason related to the COVID-19 pandemic, such as a public health directive, government shutdown order, lack of business, a reduction in force, or another economic, nondisciplinary reason. The statute builds in a rebuttable presumption favoring coverage: a separation attributed to a lack of business, a reduction in force, or another economic, nondisciplinary reason is presumed to be COVID-19-related unless the employer proves otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the "building service," "enterprise," and "laid-off employee" definitions from Labor Code Section 2810.8(a). The statute defines several other terms this document does not separately quote or address in depth -- including "airport," "airport hospitality operation," "airport service provider," "event center," "hotel," and "private club" -- each of which carries its own size or scope threshold (for example, a "hotel" must have 50 or more guest rooms, counted as of the hotel's opening or December 31, 2019, whichever is greater). An enterprise's coverage cannot be confirmed from this clause alone; it requires checking the enterprise against the statute's full definitional list.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(a)(4) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, "building service" definition
citations.quote: “Building service” means janitorial, building maintenance, or security services.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(a)(7) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, "enterprise" definition
citations.quote: “Enterprise” means a hotel, private club, event center, airport hospitality operation, airport service provider, or the provision of building service to office, retail, or other commercial buildings.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(a)(10) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, "laid-off employee" definition and presumption
citations.quote: “Laid-off employee” means any employee who was employed by the employer for six months or more and whose most recent separation from active employment by the employer occurred on or after March 4, 2020, and was due to a reason related to the COVID-19 pandemic, including a public health directive, government shutdown order, lack of business, a reduction in force, or other economic, nondisciplinary reason due to the COVID-19 pandemic. There shall be a presumption that a separation due to a lack of business, reduction in force, or other economic, nondisciplinary reason is due to a reason related to the COVID-19 pandemic, unless the employer establishes otherwise by a preponderance of the evidence.

clauses.title: The Written Offer Duty and the Order of Preference
clauses.body: Once a covered employer establishes a new position, the statute gives it five business days to offer that position, in writing, to its own laid-off employees before filling it from outside that pool. The offer must be delivered either by hand or to the employee's last known physical address, and also by email and text message to the extent the employer has that contact information. A laid-off employee is "qualified" for the position -- and therefore entitled to the offer -- if the employee held the same or similar position at the enterprise at the time of that employee's most recent layoff. Where more than one laid-off employee is entitled to preference for the same position, the statute resolves the competition by length of service: the employer must offer the position to the laid-off employee with the greatest length of service, measured from that employee's date of hire, at the enterprise.
clauses.gap: The statute's own text does not define what it means to "establish" a position -- the event that starts the five-business-day offer clock -- so this clause cannot state a precise, generally applicable rule for identifying that moment; it will depend on the employer's own hiring and budgeting practices. This clause also does not address subdivision (b)(6)'s extension of these same offer-and-preference duties to certain successor, reorganized, or relocated employers, which is covered in a separate clause of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(1) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, five-business-day written offer duty and the same-or-similar-position qualification standard
citations.quote: Within five business days of establishing a position, an employer shall offer its laid-off employees in writing, either by hand or to their last known physical address, and by email and text message to the extent the employer possesses such information, all job positions that become available after the effective date of this section for which the laid-off employees are qualified. A laid-off employee is qualified for a position if the employee held the same or similar position at the enterprise at the time of the employee’s most recent layoff with the employer.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(2) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, length-of-service order of preference
citations.quote: The employer shall offer positions to laid-off employees in an order of preference subject to paragraph (1) and this paragraph. If more than one employee is entitled to preference for a position, the employer shall offer the position to the laid-off employee with the greatest length of service based on the employee’s date of hire for the enterprise.

clauses.title: The Employee's Response Window and Conditional Offers
clauses.body: A laid-off employee who receives an offer under the statute is entitled to at least five business days from the date of receipt to accept or decline it. The statute defines "business day" for this purpose as any day other than a Saturday, a Sunday, or an official state holiday. Because more than one laid-off employee can be entitled to preference for the same position before the order-of-preference rule sorts out who actually receives it, the statute allows an employer to make simultaneous, conditional offers of employment to multiple laid-off employees at once, with the final, binding offer conditioned on how the preference system described elsewhere in this document sorts out the competing claims.
clauses.gap: The statute does not itself specify what happens to a conditional offer if the employee who would receive the final offer under the preference system has already responded, or how conditional offers interact with the separate five-business-day response window for the laid-off employee ultimately awarded the position -- this clause states the statutory mechanism as written without resolving that sequencing question.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(3) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, five-business-day response window, "business day" definition, and simultaneous conditional offers
citations.quote: A laid-off employee who is offered a position pursuant to this section shall be given at least five business days, from the date of receipt, in which to accept or decline the offer. A “business day” is any day except Saturday, Sunday, or any official state holiday. An employer may make simultaneous, conditional offers of employment to laid-off employees, with a final offer of employment conditioned on application of the preference system set forth in paragraph (2).

clauses.title: Recordkeeping and the 30-Day Notice When Recall Is Declined for Lack of Qualifications
clauses.body: The statute imposes its own three-year recordkeeping duty: for each laid-off employee, the employer must retain, for at least three years measured from the date of the written layoff notice, that employee's full legal name, job classification at separation, date of hire, last known address, last known email address, and last known telephone number, along with a copy of the written layoff notice and all records of communications with the employee about offers of employment made under the statute. Separately, if an employer declines to recall a laid-off employee on the grounds that the employee lacks qualifications and instead hires someone else, the statute requires the employer to give that laid-off employee written notice within 30 days, stating both the length of service of the person hired in the laid-off employee's place and all of the employer's reasons for the decision.
clauses.gap: Unlike the written offer duty in subdivision (b)(1), which specifies delivery by hand, mail, email, and text, the statute's text for this 30-day declined-recall notice does not itself specify a required delivery method -- this clause does not assume mail, email, hand delivery, or any other channel satisfies the duty, because the statute's own words do not say so for this particular notice.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(4) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, three-year recordkeeping duty
citations.quote: An employer must retain the following records for at least three years, measured from the date of the written notice regarding the layoff, for each laid-off employee: the employee’s full legal name; the employee’s job classification at the time of separation from employment; the employee’s date of hire; the employee’s last known address of residence; the employee’s last known email address; the employee’s last known telephone number; and a copy of the written notices regarding the layoff provided to the employee and all records of communications between the employer and the employee concerning offers of employment made to the employee pursuant to this section.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(5) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, 30-day notice when declining recall for lack of qualifications
citations.quote: An employer that declines to recall a laid-off employee on the grounds of lack of qualifications and instead hires someone other than a laid-off employee shall provide the laid-off employee a written notice within 30 days including the length of service with the employer of those hired in lieu of that recall, along with all reasons for the decision.

clauses.title: Coverage Despite a Change in Ownership, Form, Assets, or Location
clauses.body: The statute anticipates that a covered enterprise might change hands or shape after a COVID-19-related layoff, and it extends coverage to four such situations rather than letting them end the employer's obligations. The statute continues to apply where the ownership of the employer changed after the layoff but the enterprise still conducts the same or similar operations as it did before the COVID-19 state of emergency; where the employer's form of organization changed after the COVID-19 state of emergency; where another entity acquired substantially all of the employer's assets and conducts the same or similar operations using substantially the same assets; and where the employer relocated the operations at which the laid-off employee worked before the COVID-19 state of emergency to a different location. The statute's definition of "employer" is written to match: it expressly includes the successor employer described in these circumstances.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (b)(6)'s four listed circumstances and the statute's own "employer" definition, but the statute does not further define "substantially all of the assets" or "same or similar operations" for purposes of this section, and this document did not locate published Division of Labor Standards Enforcement regulations interpreting those phrases under Section 2810.8 specifically (as distinct from the similarly worded but separate change-in-control test in California's grocery worker retention law, Labor Code §§ 2500-2522, covered elsewhere in this corpus).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(b)(6) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, continued coverage after a change in ownership, form, assets, or location
citations.quote: This section also applies in any of the following circumstances:(A) The ownership of the employer changed after the separation from employment of a laid-off employee but the enterprise is conducting the same or similar operations as before the COVID-19 state of emergency.(B) The form of organization of the employer changed after the COVID-19 state of emergency.(C) Substantially all of the assets of the employer were acquired by another entity that conducts the same or similar operations using substantially the same assets.(D) The employer relocates the operations at which a laid-off employee was employed before the COVID-19 state of emergency to a different location.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(a)(6) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, "employer" definition including the successor employer
citations.quote: “Employer” means any person, including a corporate officer or executive, who directly or indirectly or through an agent or any other person, including through the services of a temporary service or staffing agency or similar entity, owns or operates an enterprise and employs or exercises control over the wages, hours, or working conditions of any employee. “Employer” also means the successor employer as set forth under paragraph (6) of subdivision (b).

clauses.title: Anti-Retaliation Protection
clauses.body: The statute contains its own, separate anti-retaliation provision. An employer may not refuse to employ, terminate, reduce the compensation of, or otherwise take any adverse action against a laid-off employee for seeking to enforce rights under the statute, for participating in proceedings related to it, for opposing a practice the statute prohibits, or for otherwise asserting rights under it. That protection extends even to an employee or laid-off employee who mistakenly, but in good faith, alleges that the statute was not followed -- the protection does not depend on the underlying allegation of noncompliance turning out to be correct.
clauses.gap: The statute's text does not itself define "adverse action" for purposes of this anti-retaliation provision. This clause does not rely on case law to fill that gap: CourtListener's daily case-law search quota was exhausted when this document was researched, so no California court decision interpreting "adverse action" under this specific provision, Labor Code Section 2810.8(c), could be located or cited here.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.8(c) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, COVID-19 right of recall, anti-retaliation provision and good-faith mistaken-allegation protection
citations.quote: No employer shall refuse to employ, terminate, reduce in compensation, or otherwise take any adverse action against any laid-off employee as defined in subdivision (a) for seeking to enforce their rights under this section, for participating in proceedings related to this section, opposing any practice proscribed by this section, or otherwise asserting rights under this section. This subdivision shall also apply to any employee or laid-off employee who mistakenly, but in good faith, alleges noncompliance with this section.

clauses.title: Enforcement Through the Labor Commissioner: Remedies and Penalties
clauses.body: Unlike some other California worker-protection statutes that allow a private lawsuit, this statute channels enforcement exclusively through the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement (the Labor Commissioner's office): the statute gives that Division exclusive jurisdiction to enforce it, and states that the section may be enforced only through the procedures it sets out. A laid-off employee may file a complaint with the Division, which may award hiring and reinstatement rights; frontpay or backpay for each day a violation continues, calculated at not less than the highest of three specified rates (the employee's average regular rate over the employee's last three years in the same occupational classification, the employee's most recent regular rate with the employer, or the regular rate paid to whoever was employed in the position instead of the laid-off employee); and the value of benefits the employee would have received under the employer's benefit plan. The statute imposes no criminal penalties. A civil violation instead exposes the employer, or any agent or other person who violates or causes a violation, to a civil penalty of $100 per affected employee, plus liquidated damages of $500 per employee for each day the violation continues until cured -- both of which the Labor Commissioner recovers, deposits into the Labor and Workforce Development Fund, and pays to the employee as compensatory damages.
clauses.gap: This clause does not quote or address subdivision (d)(4) through (d)(7), which describe the Labor Commissioner's investigative and citation procedures (cross-referencing Labor Code Sections 98.3, 98.7, 98.74, and 1197.1), the court's authority to grant injunctive relief, the interest rate applied to unpaid amounts (tied to Civil Code Section 3289(b)), and the statute's cumulative-remedies clause; nor does it address subdivision (e), which gives the Division authority to issue implementing regulations, determinations, and interpretations that themselves carry the force of law. None of those cross-referenced provisions were independently fetched or verified for this document.
