clauses.title: Collective Bargaining, Local Ordinances, and the Statute's Own Sunset Date
clauses.body: This statute sits alongside, rather than displacing, several other sources of law. It does not stop a local government from enacting its own ordinance that imposes greater standards, or additional enforcement mechanisms, than the state statute provides, and it does not limit a discharged or eligible employee's separate right to bring a common-law wrongful-termination claim. It can, however, be waived by a valid collective bargaining agreement -- but only where the waiver is explicit and stated in clear and unambiguous terms; an employer's unilateral implementation of terms and conditions of employment in a collective bargaining relationship does not count as a waiver. Finally, the statute carries its own expiration date, written into its own text: as most recently amended, it remains operative only until January 1, 2027, though a violation occurring on or before December 31, 2026 remains enforceable under the statute's enforcement procedures even after that date.
clauses.gap: The January 1, 2027 sunset date reflects the statute's current text as amended by Assembly Bill 858 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 280, Sec. 1), effective January 1, 2026 and confirmed by leginfo.legislature.ca.gov's own amendment history line for this section; this document did not independently trace the statute's prior sunset dates or amendment history beyond that single history line. Because the statute is written to lapse absent further legislative action, whether it remains operative past January 1, 2027 depends on a future amendment that this document cannot anticipate; anyone relying on this document after that date should confirm the section's then-current status directly at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov before assuming it is still in force.

clauses.title: Certification
Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: {{companyName}} maintains this information sheet to describe two specific and narrower California wage-deduction rules: the IWC Wage Order restriction on deducting wages for a cash shortage, breakage, or loss of equipment, and the separate civil penalty California law imposes for certain kinds of unlawful wage withholding. This is a narrower topic than this corpus's existing Wage Repayment / Clawback information sheet, which addresses an employer collecting back a bonus, relocation payment, or similar sum already paid to {{employeeName}}, and its existing Wage Statement Itemization Policy document, which addresses how a deduction, once taken, must be disclosed on the wage statement. This document addresses only the cash-shortage/breakage/equipment-loss deduction rule and the separate civil-penalty statute.

clauses.title: Cash Shortages, Breakage, and Equipment Loss: A Deduction Requires Dishonesty, Willfulness, or Gross Negligence
clauses.body: Under the applicable California IWC Wage Order, no employer may make any deduction from wages, or require any reimbursement from an employee, for a cash shortage, breakage, or loss of equipment, unless it can be shown that the shortage, breakage, or loss was caused by a dishonest or willful act, or by the gross negligence, of the employee.
clauses.gap: This is a single regulatory subdivision (Section 8, "Cash Shortage and Breakage") within IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001 ("Professional, Technical, Clerical, Mechanical and Similar Occupations"), fetched directly from the Department of Industrial Relations at https://www.dir.ca.gov/IWC/IWCArticle04.pdf. This document did not independently fetch or confirm whether other numbered wage orders (for example, Wage Order 5 for public housekeeping or Wage Order 7 for mercantile employees) contain the identical Section 8 language -- it verifies Wage Order 4-2001 only. The source PDF's own text extraction hyphenates "breakage" across a line break ("break-" followed by "age" on the next line); the quotation below preserves that line break exactly as extracted, consistent with this corpus's established practice of quoting PDF-extracted wage-order text exactly rather than silently repairing extraction artifacts. The provision states that a deduction requires a showing of dishonesty, willfulness, or gross negligence, but does not itself specify who must make that showing, in what forum, or under what evidentiary standard. This is one state's regulatory text; not a claim about which jurisdiction's law, or which industry's wage order, governs a specific employment relationship.

citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 8
citations.quote:
No employer shall make any deduction from the wage or require any reimbursement from an employee for any cash shortage, break- 
age, or loss of equipment, unless it can be shown that the shortage, breakage, or loss is caused by a dishonest or willful act, or by the gross 
negligence of the employee.

clauses.title: Civil Penalties for Unlawfully Withholding Wages Under Sections 221, 222, or 223
clauses.body: In addition to, and independent of, any other penalty, California law subjects a person who unlawfully withholds wages due an employee in violation of Section 212, 216, 221, 222, or 223 to a civil penalty for each failure to pay each employee: one hundred dollars for an initial violation, and two hundred dollars for each subsequent violation or any willful or intentional violation, plus twenty-five percent of the amount unlawfully withheld. This penalty is recovered by the Labor Commissioner as part of a hearing to recover unpaid wages and penalties, or in an independent civil action brought in the name of the People of the State of California.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Labor Code § 225.5). Its text cross-references Labor Code sections 212 and 216 as additional grounds for the same penalty; this document does not independently fetch, quote, or verify the text of either of those sections. This document does not state whether, or under what circumstances, an unlawful cash-shortage or breakage deduction addressed elsewhere in this document would itself amount to a violation of Section 221, 222, or 223 for purposes of this penalty -- that connection is not addressed by either statute's own text and is not asserted here. This penalty is a public civil penalty recovered by the Labor Commissioner or the State, not a payment made directly to the underpaid employee, and this document does not address a private right of action or PAGA civil-penalty procedure, covered separately in this corpus's existing PAGA Pre-Suit Notice Letter document. The source text's "Amended by" line shows an effective date of January 1, 2004; this session did not independently search for any more recent amendment beyond what leginfo's own currently displayed statutory text shows as of the fetch date. This is one state's statute; not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs a specific employment relationship.

citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 225.5, subds. (a)-(b)
citations.quote: every person who unlawfully withholds wages due any employee in violation of Section 212, 216, 221, 222, or 223 shall be subject to a civil penalty as follows: (a) For any initial violation, one hundred dollars ($100) for each failure to pay each employee. (b) For each subsequent violation, or any willful or intentional violation, two hundred dollars ($200) for each failure to pay each employee, plus 25 percent of the amount unlawfully withheld.

clauses.title: Signature and Receipt
Petition to Determine Succession to Real Property — Information and Background
clauses.body: This information sheet discusses the California superior court petition procedure of Probate Code §§ 13150-13157, a court order determining succession to real property, in connection with the estate of {{decedentName}}, who died on {{dateOfDeath}}. {{petitionerName}} is a successor of {{decedentName}} with respect to real property located at {{propertyAddress}}, described as {{legalDescription}} and identified by Assessor's Parcel Number {{parcelNumber}}, with a gross value stated as {{estimatedEstateValue}}. Under this procedure, a petition may be filed in the superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}, California, requesting a court order determining that the described real property, which was {{decedentName}}'s primary residence, has passed to {{petitionerName}} as a successor of {{decedentName}}. This document is background information only. It is not the petition itself, is not filed with any court, and does not by itself request, obtain, or constitute any court order. Only a petition actually filed with the superior court, followed by the statutory notice, and a hearing resulting in a signed court order, can determine that the described real property has passed to {{petitionerName}}.

clauses.title: When This Court-Order Procedure Is Available
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 13150 limits use of the court-order-determining-succession procedure of Chapter 4 (§§ 13150-13157) to one of two situations: no proceeding for administration of the decedent's estate is being or has been conducted in California, or the decedent's personal representative has consented in writing to use of this procedure specifically to determine that real property that was the decedent's primary residence passes to the petitioners. As currently written, the chapter's own text ties this procedure to the decedent's "primary residence" specifically, and § 13150(b)(2) clarifies that for this chapter, "primary residence" is not limited to the residence the decedent occupied at the time of death.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of when this specific California court procedure is available — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific decedent's estate, or that the procedure is in fact available for any particular property. § 13150(a) and § 13150(b) are subdivisions of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as two independent ones. The current text was amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 331 (AB 2016), effective January 1, 2025, and its own "primary residence" limitation is new to that amendment; this document did not fetch or independently verify the section's pre-January 1, 2025 text, and does not describe what this chapter covered, or how it differed, before that date — only what the current, in-force text provides. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine that any specific proceeding is or is not pending for a specific decedent's estate, or that a described property was in fact a specific decedent's primary residence.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, first condition for using this procedure — no estate proceeding pending
citations.quote: 13150. The procedure provided by this chapter may be used only if one of the following requirements is satisfied: (a) No proceeding is being or has been conducted in this state for administration of the decedent’s estate.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, second condition — personal representative's written consent, and the chapter's definition of "primary residence"
citations.quote: (b) (1) The decedent’s personal representative consents in writing to use of the procedure provided by this chapter to determine that real property that was the decedent’s primary residence is property passing to the petitioners. (2) For purposes of this chapter, “primary residence” is not limited to the decedent’s residence at the time of their death.

clauses.title: Who May File, the Dollar Threshold, and the 40-Day Wait
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 13151(a) lets "the successor of the decedent to an interest in" the decedent's primary-residence real property file this petition, without first procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of the will, once two conditions are met: the real property's gross value does not exceed a statutory dollar ceiling (currently $750,000, adjusted periodically under § 890), and at least 40 days have elapsed since the decedent's death. The petition is filed "in the superior court of the county in which the estate of the decedent may be administered," and it requests a court order determining that the petitioner has succeeded to the described real property.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who may file this specific petition and under what dollar and timing conditions — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or that any specific petitioner in fact qualifies as a "successor" under this section for any specific decedent's property. The $750,000 figure quoted in § 13151(a)'s own text is the amount that currently applies only because of the specific decedent's-death date window described in a companion clause of this document (Probate Code § 13152(f)); this document did not independently fetch or verify Probate Code § 890 or the Judicial Council's own published schedule of periodically adjusted dollar amounts. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (§ 13151(a)); § 13151(b), addressing a separate notice obligation, is covered in a companion clause. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine that any specific petitioner qualifies to file, or that any specific property in fact does not exceed the applicable dollar ceiling.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13151(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, who may file, the dollar threshold, and the 40-day wait
citations.quote: (a) If a decedent dies leaving real property that was their primary residence in this state and the gross value of that real property does not exceed seven hundred fifty thousand dollars ($750,000), as adjusted periodically in accordance with Section 890, and 40 days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, the successor of the decedent to an interest in that real property, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting the probate of the will, may file a petition in the superior court of the county in which the estate of the decedent may be administered requesting a court order determining that the petitioner has succeeded to that real property.

clauses.title: The Dollar Threshold Has Changed Substantially, on a Statutory Schedule
clauses.body: The dollar ceiling that governs this procedure is not a single fixed number; California Probate Code § 13152(f) writes a four-part schedule directly into the statute's own text. For a decedent who died before April 1, 2022, the applicable amount is $166,250. For a death on or after April 1, 2022 through March 31, 2025, the applicable amount is "the adjusted dollar amount, published in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 890, in effect on the date of the decedent's death" — a figure this section does not itself restate. For a death on or after April 1, 2025 through March 31, 2028, the statute states a new flat figure directly: $750,000. For a death on or after April 1, 2028, the applicable amount reverts to whatever adjusted figure is then published under § 890. This entire schedule, including the current $750,000 figure, was written into § 13152 by Stats. 2024, Ch. 331 (AB 2016), effective January 1, 2025.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific dollar-threshold schedule California law currently applies to this procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or about which of the four listed figures applies to any decedent whose date of death this document does not itself state elsewhere. This document did not independently fetch or verify Probate Code § 890 itself or the Judicial Council's own published table of periodically adjusted dollar amounts, so the specific figure that applied between April 1, 2022 and March 31, 2025, or that will apply on or after April 1, 2028, is not stated here beyond the statute's own cross-reference. Separately, this document did not fetch or verify the pre-January 1, 2025 text of § 13152 itself, so it does not describe what dollar figure or scope applied under the prior version of this section, only that the current, in-force schedule was enacted by the cited 2024 amendment. The quoted schedule (four paragraphs of subdivision (f)) and the quoted enactment note are both drawn from the same statutory section and are treated as one source, not independent ones.

citations.quote: (f) (1) If the decedent dies prior to April 1, 2022, the dollar amount for paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) is one hundred sixty-six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($166,250). (2) If the decedent dies on or after April 1, 2022, through March 31, 2025, the dollar amount for paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) is the adjusted dollar amount, published in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 890, in effect on the date of the decedent’s death. (3) If the decedent dies on or after April 1, 2025, through March 31, 2028, the dollar amount for paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) is seven hundred fifty thousand dollars ($750,000). (4) If the decedent dies on or after April 1, 2028, the dollar amount for paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) is the adjusted dollar amount, published in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 890, in effect on the date of the decedent’s death.

clauses.title: Required Contents of the Petition, and the Probate-Referee Appraisal
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 13152(a) requires the petition to be verified by each petitioner and to state, among other things, facts establishing proper venue and that the real property's gross value (as shown by an attached inventory and appraisal) does not exceed the applicable dollar ceiling. Among the petition's other required contents, § 13152(a)(7) requires disclosure of "the name, age, address, and relation to the decedent of each heir and devisee of the decedent," the names and addresses of anyone named as an executor of the decedent's will, and, where the petitioner is trustee of a trust that is itself a devisee under the will, the names and addresses of persons interested in that trust. Separately, § 13152(b) requires an inventory and appraisal, in the form set out in Probate Code § 8802, to be attached to the petition, with the appraisal made by a probate referee the petitioner selects from those the Controller has appointed under § 400 for the county where the property is located.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what a petition under this chapter must state and attach — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or that any particular petition satisfies these requirements. This clause quotes § 13152(a)'s introductory language together with paragraphs (1) and (2), and separately quotes paragraph (7) and subdivision (b) verbatim; it does not quote paragraphs (3) through (6) or (8) verbatim (covering, among other things, the property description, the basis for the petitioner's claim, disclosure of any other-jurisdiction proceedings, and disclosure of any guardian or conservator of the decedent's estate) — those additional required items exist in the statute's text but are not independently quoted here. § 13152(a) and § 13152(b) are subdivisions of one statutory section and are treated here as one source, not independent ones. This document did not independently fetch or verify Probate Code § 8802 (the referenced inventory-and-appraisal form) or § 400 (probate referee appointment) themselves. This document is informational only; it does not itself verify, attach, or complete any petition, inventory, or appraisal.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, verification requirement and first two required contents
citations.quote: (a) The petition shall be verified by each petitioner, shall contain a request that the court make an order under this chapter determining that the property described in the petition is property passing to the petitioner, and shall state all of the following: (1) The facts necessary to determine that the petition is filed in the proper county. (2) The gross value of the real property that was the decedent’s primary residence in this state, as shown by the inventory and appraisal attached to the petition, does not exceed the dollar amount specified in subdivision (f).

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13152(a)(7)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, required disclosure of heirs, devisees, and named executors
citations.quote: (7) The name, age, address, and relation to the decedent of each heir and devisee of the decedent, the names and addresses of all persons named as executors of the will of the decedent, and, if the petitioner is the trustee of a trust that is a devisee under the will of the decedent, the names and addresses of all persons interested in the trust, as determined in cases of future interests pursuant to paragraph (1), (2), or (3) of subdivision (a) of Section 15804, so far as known to any petitioner.

The appraisal shall be made as provided in Part 3 (commencing with Section 8800) of Division 7.

clauses.title: Two Separate Notice Requirements: To Named Heirs and Devisees, and of the Hearing
clauses.body: This procedure carries two separate statutory notice obligations. First, California Probate Code § 13151(b) requires a successor who files this petition to "deliver a notice of the petition to each heir and devisee named in the petition pursuant to paragraph (7) of subdivision (a) of Section 13152" within five business days of filing. Second, and separately, Probate Code § 13153 requires that "[n]otice of the hearing shall be given as provided in Section 1220 to each of the persons named in the petition pursuant to Section 13152" — a broader notice obligation than § 13151(b)'s, since it reaches every person § 13152 requires the petition to name (heirs, devisees, named executors, trust beneficiaries where relevant, and any guardian or conservator of the decedent's estate), not only heirs and devisees.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of two distinct notice obligations this procedure imposes — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or that notice given in any specific case satisfied either requirement. § 13151(b) and § 13153 are two separately numbered, independently verified statutory sections. This document did not independently fetch or verify Probate Code § 1220, the general notice-of-hearing procedure § 13153 cross-references, so the specific mechanics of how that hearing notice must be given (method, timing before the hearing, and to whom beyond those named under § 13152) are not described here. This document is informational only; it does not itself deliver, serve, or determine the adequacy of notice to any specific heir, devisee, or other interested person.

citations.quote: (b) A successor who files a petition pursuant to subdivision (a) shall deliver a notice of the petition to each heir and devisee named in the petition pursuant to paragraph (7) of subdivision (a) of Section 13152 within five business days of filing the petition.

clauses.title: What the Court Must Determine Before Issuing the Order
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 13154(a) provides that if the court makes the determinations required under subdivision (b), the court "shall issue an order determining that the real property that was the decedent's primary residence...is property passing to the petitioners and the specific property interest of each petitioner in the described property." Subdivision (b)'s required determinations include the property's gross value, the 40-day wait, the applicable no-proceeding-or-consent condition, and that the described property is in fact property of the decedent passing to the petitioner. Section 13154(c) then supplies an evidentiary shortcut on the value determination specifically: where the petition has an inventory and appraisal attached that satisfies § 13152(b), the court makes the gross-value determination "on the basis of the verified petition and the attached inventory and appraisal," unless a person opposing the petition offers evidence that the property's gross value actually exceeds the applicable dollar ceiling.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what a court must determine, and how, before issuing an order under this chapter — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or that any specific petition would in fact satisfy these determinations. This clause quotes § 13154(a) and § 13154(c) verbatim; § 13154(b)'s four numbered determinations are described in this clause's body in paraphrase rather than quoted verbatim, and a reader should treat that paraphrase, not an independently verified quotation, as this document's account of subdivision (b)'s specific wording. § 13154(a) and § 13154(c) are subdivisions of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not independent ones. This document is informational only; it does not itself make any of these determinations or issue any order.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13154(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, the order the court must issue once it makes the required determinations
citations.quote: (a) If the court makes the determinations required under subdivision (b), the court shall issue an order determining that the real property that was the decedent’s primary residence, to be described in the order, is property passing to the petitioners and the specific property interest of each petitioner in the described property.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13154(c)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, evidentiary effect of an attached inventory and appraisal on the value determination
citations.quote: (c) If the petition has attached an inventory and appraisal that satisfies the requirements of subdivision (b) of Section 13152, the determination required by paragraph (1) of subdivision (b) of this section shall be made on the basis of the verified petition and the attached inventory and appraisal, unless evidence is offered by a person opposing the petition that the gross value of the real property that was the decedent’s primary residence in this state exceeds seven hundred fifty thousand dollars ($750,000), as adjusted periodically in accordance with Section 890.

clauses.title: The Order's Finality: Conclusive on All Persons, Whether or Not Yet in Being
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 13155 gives a final order under this chapter unusually broad, self-contained finality: "Upon becoming final, an order under this chapter determining that property is property passing to the petitioner is conclusive on all persons, whether or not they are in being." The statute's own wording extends this conclusiveness to persons not yet in existence at the time of the order — for example, a not-yet-born future heir or beneficiary — not only to the parties and persons actually given notice of the petition.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific finality effect California law gives this particular kind of order — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific order, or about when any specific order actually "becomes final" for purposes of this section. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 13155); no additional independent source was found for it, and this document did not independently fetch or verify the general California appellate-finality rules (for example, the time to appeal a probate order) that determine when an order "becomes final" in the first place — this section's text does not itself define that term. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine that any specific order concerning any specific decedent's property has become final or is conclusive on any person.

citations.cite: California Probate Code, finality and conclusiveness of the order
citations.quote: Upon becoming final, an order under this chapter determining that property is property passing to the petitioner is conclusive on all persons, whether or not they are in being.

clauses.title: The Petitioner's Personal Liability for the Decedent's Unsecured Debts
clauses.body: Receiving property under this chapter carries a liability consequence. California Probate Code § 13156(a) provides that, subject to subdivisions (b) through (d), "the petitioner who receives the decedent's property pursuant to an order under this chapter is personally liable for the unsecured debts of the decedent." Subdivision (b) caps that exposure: "[t]he personal liability of any petitioner shall not exceed the fair market value at the date of the decedent's death of the property received by that petitioner pursuant to an order under this chapter, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances on the property." Subdivisions (c) and (d), which this clause does not quote verbatim, let the petitioner assert any defense, cross-complaint, or setoff the decedent could have asserted, and bar enforcement of any claim already barred under the estate's creditor-claim statute; subdivision (e) makes Code of Civil Procedure § 366.2 applicable to an action under this section.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a specific personal-liability consequence and its statutory cap — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petitioner, or that any particular petitioner is or is not personally liable for any specific debt. This clause quotes § 13156(a) and § 13156(b) verbatim; subdivisions (c), (d), and (e) are described in paraphrase in this clause's body rather than independently quoted. § 13156(a) and § 13156(b) are subdivisions of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not independent ones. This document did not independently fetch or verify Code of Civil Procedure § 366.2 (the statute-of-limitations provision subdivision (e) cross-references) or Probate Code Part 4 (commencing with Section 9000) of Division 7 (the creditor-claim bar subdivision (d) cross-references). This document is informational only; it does not itself determine that any specific petitioner is, or is not, personally liable for any specific debt of any specific decedent.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13156(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, personal liability for the decedent's unsecured debts
citations.quote: (a) Subject to subdivisions (b), (c), and (d), the petitioner who receives the decedent’s property pursuant to an order under this chapter is personally liable for the unsecured debts of the decedent.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13156(b)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, statutory cap on that personal liability
citations.quote: (b) The personal liability of any petitioner shall not exceed the fair market value at the date of the decedent’s death of the property received by that petitioner pursuant to an order under this chapter, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances on the property.

clauses.title: Attorney's Fees, and How This Procedure Differs From the Small Estate Affidavit, the Real Property Affidavit, and Full Probate
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 13157 provides that attorney's fees for filing a petition and obtaining a court order under this chapter are "determined by private agreement between the attorney and the client and are not subject to approval by the court," with a court petition available only if the attorney and client later dispute the fee's reasonableness or the meaning of their agreement. Structurally, this procedure sits between this corpus's other small-estate mechanisms: unlike the personal-property small estate affidavit (Probate Code §§ 13100-13106) and the separate real-property small-value affidavit (§ 13200), both of which involve no court hearing, this procedure requires an actual petition, notice, and a hearing that produces a court order under § 13154. And unlike a full petition for probate, which appoints a personal representative and results in ongoing court-supervised administration of the whole estate, this procedure produces only a one-time court determination that specific real property — limited, under current law, to the decedent's primary residence — has passed to the petitioner.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own attorney's-fee rule for this specific procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific fee dispute. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 13157); no additional independent source was found for it, and this clause does not quote subdivisions of § 13157 concerning the fee-dispute or agreement-dispute petition mechanics, describing them only in paraphrase. This clause's comparison to the small estate affidavit, the real-property affidavit, and full probate draws on this corpus's separately verified Small Estate Affidavit and Petition for Probate — Information Sheet documents; it does not re-quote or independently re-verify those documents' own citations (for example, the § 13100 or § 13200 dollar ceilings) in this session, and a reader should treat that comparison as a structural summary rather than newly verified statutory text. This document is informational only; it does not itself select, complete, or file any procedure for any specific decedent's estate.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 13157
citations.cite: California Probate Code, attorney's fees for this procedure set by private agreement
citations.quote: The attorney’s fees for services performed in connection with the filing of a petition and obtaining a court order under this chapter shall be determined by private agreement between the attorney and the client and are not subject to approval by the court.

clauses.body:

clauses.title: About This Security Guard Registration Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California law requiring a person who will work as a security guard, security patrolperson, or in-house ("proprietary") security officer to register with the Bureau of Security and Investigative Services (BSIS), a bureau of the Department of Consumer Affairs, before performing those duties, and requiring the business that employs that person to itself be licensed or registered with BSIS. It states facts drawn from the Private Security Services Act and the Proprietary Security Services Act (Business and Professions Code Division 3, Chapter 11.5 and Chapter 11.4) about who must register, the background-check and training steps that precede registration, and the employer's duty to confirm that registration is current. {{companyName}} is considering {{applicantName}} for the position of {{jobTitle}}. This document does not determine whether that specific position falls within a statutory registration requirement, whether any exemption applies, or whether {{applicantName}} has in fact been registered by BSIS; it also does not address the separate general Live Scan / DOJ fingerprint background-check framework (Penal Code Section 11105.3) covered in another information sheet in this corpus, or the Farm Labor Contractor, Talent Agency, or Public Works Contractor registration schemes covered elsewhere in this corpus, none of which govern security guard or proprietary security officer registration.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Two Statutory Categories: Contract Security Guards and Proprietary (In-House) Security Officers
clauses.body: California regulates security personnel who work for a licensed private patrol operator (a contract security guard business) under the Private Security Services Act, and separately regulates unarmed security personnel who work exclusively for a single, non-security employer under the Proprietary Security Services Act. Business and Professions Code Section 7574.01 defines a "proprietary private security employer" as a person with employees who provide security services only for that employer, and defines a "proprietary private security officer" as an unarmed individual employed exclusively by one employer whose primary duty is to provide security services for that employer, whose services are not contracted to any other entity, who is required to wear a distinctive uniform identifying the individual as a security officer, and who is likely to interact with the public while performing those duties.
clauses.gap: Chapter 11.4 defines "proprietary private security officer" as an unarmed individual only; an in-house employee who carries a firearm or other deadly weapon while providing security services for a single employer falls outside that definition and is instead subject to the separate Private Patrol Operator / armed-guard and firearms-permit provisions of Chapter 11.5, which this document addresses only insofar as those provisions independently apply to contract security guards and does not analyze for an armed in-house context.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.01(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Proprietary Security Services Act, definition of "proprietary private security employer"
citations.quote: “Proprietary private security employer” means a person who has one or more employees who provide security services for the employer and only for the employer.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.01(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Proprietary Security Services Act, definition of "proprietary private security officer"
citations.quote: “Proprietary private security officer” means an unarmed individual who is employed exclusively by any one employer whose primary duty is to provide security services for their employer, whose services are not contracted to any other entity or person, and who is not exempt pursuant to Section 7582.2, and who meets both of the following criteria:(1) Is required to wear a distinctive uniform clearly identifying the individual as a security officer.(2) Is likely to interact with the public while performing their duties.

clauses.title: A Proprietary Private Security Employer Must Itself Be Registered With BSIS
clauses.body: Before an employer who is not otherwise a licensed private patrol operator uses its own unarmed, uniformed employees to provide security services solely for itself, Business and Professions Code Section 7574.12 requires that employer to register with the Department of Consumer Affairs as a proprietary private security employer, unless a specific statutory exemption applies.
clauses.gap: Section 7574.12 requires registration of the employer itself; it does not, by its own text, also state the separate requirement that each individual proprietary private security officer working for that employer be individually registered, which is addressed in a separate clause of this document. This clause also does not resolve, for a specific employer, whether that employer's use of security personnel meets the statutory definition of "proprietary private security employer" in the first place.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.12 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Proprietary Security Services Act, registration required to engage in business as a proprietary private security employer
citations.quote: No person shall engage in the business of a proprietary private security employer unless registered with the department pursuant to this chapter.

clauses.title: Application, Fingerprint-Based Background Check, and Two-Year Card for a Proprietary Security Officer
clauses.body: An individual seeking registration as a proprietary private security officer applies to the Department of Consumer Affairs and, under Business and Professions Code Section 7574.11, must submit fingerprints that the department forwards to the Department of Justice for a state and federal criminal history check, along with a statutory application fee. Upon approval, the chief of the Bureau of Security and Investigative Services issues the applicant a registration card that is valid for two years from the date of issue.
clauses.gap: This clause summarizes the application, fingerprint, and background-check requirements and the two-year card term that Section 7574.11 sets for proprietary private security officers specifically; it does not restate the separate, non-identical registration-application and fee provisions that Business and Professions Code Section 7583.9 sets for a security guard employed by a licensed private patrol operator under the different Article 4 scheme, which is addressed in a separate clause of this document, and does not report the current dollar amount of the application fee, which the statute permits to be adjusted within a stated range.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.11(b)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Proprietary Security Services Act, fingerprint submission for a Department of Justice background check
citations.quote: The department shall submit to the Department of Justice fingerprint images and related information required by the Department of Justice for all proprietary private security officer registration applicants, as defined by subdivision (f) of Section 7574.01, for the purposes of obtaining information as to the existence and content of a record of state or federal convictions and state or federal arrests

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.11(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Proprietary Security Services Act, issuance and two-year term of the registration card
citations.quote: Upon approval of an application for registration as a proprietary private security officer by the director, the chief shall cause to be issued to the applicant a registration card in a form approved by the director. A registration card shall be valid for two years from the date of issue.

clauses.title: Provisional Work Authorization for a Proprietary Officer While the Registration Card Is Pending
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code Section 7574.11(d) allows a person to begin work as a proprietary private security officer before the physical registration card arrives, provided the director has already approved the person and the person carries, while working, a hardcopy printout of the bureau's approval from the bureau's website together with either a valid California driver's license or a valid California identification card.
clauses.gap: This provisional-work provision applies by its terms to proprietary private security officers registered under Chapter 11.4. This document does not confirm whether an equivalent provision, on the same documentary terms, exists for a contract security guard employed by a private patrol operator under the separate Chapter 11.5 scheme, and does not represent that the two schemes' rules for working while an application is pending are identical.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.11(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Proprietary Security Services Act, provisional work pending receipt of the registration card
citations.quote: A person may work as a proprietary private security officer pending receipt of the registration card if he or she has been approved by the director and carries on his or her person a hardcopy printout of the bureau’s approval from the bureau’s Internet Web site and either a valid driver’s license issued pursuant to Section 12811 of the Vehicle Code or a valid identification card issued pursuant to Section 13000 of the Vehicle Code.

clauses.title: Power-to-Arrest and Skills Training as a Condition of a Contract Security Guard's Registration
clauses.body: For a security guard registration issued to work for a licensed private patrol operator, Business and Professions Code Section 7583.6(a) makes completion of a course in the power to arrest and the appropriate use of force a condition for the registration to be issued in the first place. Separately, subdivision (b) requires a registrant, after the initial registration is issued, to complete at least 32 hours of security-officer-skills training within six months, with 16 of those hours completed within the first 30 days.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subdivisions (a) and (b) of Section 7583.6, which also contains, in subdivisions (c) through (j), additional recordkeeping duties, an annual eight-hour continuing-training requirement, who may administer the trainings, and exemptions for certain peace officers and armored vehicle guards, none of which are reproduced or analyzed in this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7583.6(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Private Security Services Act, power-to-arrest/use-of-force training as a condition of registration
citations.quote: Each applicant for a security guard registration shall complete a course in the exercise of the power to arrest and the appropriate use of force as a condition for the issuance of the registration.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7583.6(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Private Security Services Act, 32-hour skills training deadline after initial registration
citations.quote: a security guard registrant shall complete not less than 32 hours of training in security officer skills within six months from the date an initial registration is issued. A security guard registrant shall complete 16 of the 32 hours within 30 days from the date the registration is issued.

clauses.title: Fingerprint-Based Background Check for a Contract Security Guard's Registration
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code Section 7583.9(a) requires an applicant for a security guard registration to submit an application, the registration fee, and fingerprints to the Bureau of Security and Investigative Services, which forwards the fingerprints to the Department of Justice, which in turn forwards a copy to the Federal Bureau of Investigation for purposes of a background check.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of Section 7583.9; the section also contains, in subdivisions (b) through (j), an allowance for the employer to advance and then withhold the application fee from the applicant's compensation, an electronic-fingerprinting alternative, and several exemptions from the fingerprint-card requirement for currently employed or reserve peace officers, none of which this clause reproduces or analyzes.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7583.9(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Private Security Services Act, application, fee, and fingerprints for a security guard registration
citations.quote: The security guard registration applicant shall submit the application, the registration fee, and their fingerprints, either in the form of classifiable fingerprint cards or in an electronic format pursuant to subdivision (c), to the bureau. The bureau shall forward the classifiable fingerprint cards to the Department of Justice. The Department of Justice shall forward one classifiable fingerprint card to the Federal Bureau of Investigation for purposes of a background check.

clauses.title: A Private Patrol Operator's Duty to Verify That Its Guards Are Currently Registered
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code Section 7583.19 places an ongoing duty on a licensed private patrol operator to ascertain that each employee subject to registration is currently registered, and bars the licensee from having a person whose registration has expired or been revoked, denied, suspended, or canceled perform security guard duties.
clauses.gap: Section 7583.19 states this verification duty and the bar on using an unregistered person for guard duties, but the statutory text of this section does not itself specify the disciplinary or civil consequences to the licensee for a violation; this document does not address the separate enforcement and license-discipline provisions elsewhere in the Private Security Services Act that may apply.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7583.19 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Private Security Services Act, licensee's duty to verify current registration of its guards
citations.quote: A licensee shall at all times be responsible for ascertaining that those of their employees who are subject to registration are currently registered as provided in this article. A licensee may not have a person whose registration has expired or been revoked, denied, suspended, or canceled perform security guard duties.

clauses.title: A Statutory Exemption Limits Who Must Register Under the Proprietary Security Services Act
clauses.body: The Proprietary Security Services Act's registration requirement is not universal. Business and Professions Code Section 7574.14 lists categories of persons to whom the chapter does not apply, including an officer or employee of the United States, this state, or a political subdivision performing official duties, which the statute states covers uniformed peace officers employed part time by a public agency under a written agreement between a chief of police or sheriff and the public agency, provided the part-time employment does not exceed 50 hours in a calendar month.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of an eight-subdivision exemption list in Section 7574.14; the remaining subdivisions (b) through (h) cover, among others, certain patrol special police officers, off-duty and retired peace officers, unarmed motion picture studio security personnel, armored contract carriers, and federally recognized tribal employers, none of which are reproduced or analyzed here. This document does not determine whether any exemption in Section 7574.14, in whole or in part, applies to a specific employer's use of a specific individual in a specific position.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7574.14(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Proprietary Security Services Act, exemption for government officers and employees performing official duties
citations.quote: An officer or employee of the United States of America, or of this state or a political subdivision thereof, while the officer or employee is engaged in the performance of their official duties, including uniformed peace officers employed part time by a public agency pursuant to a written agreement between a chief of police or sheriff and the public agency, provided the part-time employment does not exceed 50 hours in a calendar month.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Intellectual Property License Bankruptcy Protections Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes what happens, as a matter of federal Bankruptcy Code law, to a license of intellectual property when the licensor -- not the licensee -- becomes a debtor in a federal bankruptcy case and rejects the license as part of that case. It is prepared by {{preparerName}} on behalf of {{companyName}}, as licensee, concerning intellectual property licensed from {{licensorName}} and described as follows: {{licensedIpDescription}}. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference describing the general bankruptcy rule that a debtor's rejection of an executory contract operates as a breach rather than a rescission, the specific statutory protections 11 U.S.C. section 365(n) gives a licensee of certain kinds of intellectual property when its licensor's contract is rejected, which categories of intellectual property that statute's own definition does and does not reach, and how the U.S. Supreme Court has since resolved what happens to a category the statute's definition does not reach (trademark licenses). It does not itself determine what protection would apply to the intellectual property described above in any actual bankruptcy case, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is distinct from this project's existing Software License Agreement, Patent License Agreement, and Trademark License Agreement documents, none of which addresses what becomes of a licensee's rights if the licensor later files for bankruptcy protection; it is also distinct from the existing Trade Secret Preemption Doctrine and Trade Secret Injunctive Relief Standards Information Sheets, which concern trade secret litigation remedies rather than a licensor's bankruptcy.

clauses.title: The General Rule: Rejection of an Executory Contract Is a Breach, Not a Rescission
clauses.body: When a business licensor files for bankruptcy, the trustee or debtor-in-possession has authority under 11 U.S.C. section 365(a) to decide whether to assume or reject the licensor's executory contracts, which can include an intellectual property license under which royalties or performance are still owed on both sides. Section 365(g) states the legal effect of that choice when the trustee rejects: rejection of an executory contract is treated as if the debtor had simply broken the contract, not as if the contract had been undone from the start. The U.S. Supreme Court has confirmed what this means in practice: because rejection is a breach and not a rescission, it does not by itself take back the rights the contract had already conveyed to the counterparty before the bankruptcy case began -- the same result that would follow if the licensor breached the same contract outside of bankruptcy.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory and U.S. Supreme Court law of general application, used as real evidence of the rejection-as-breach rule -- not a claim about whether any specific license described on this sheet would in fact be rejected, assumed, or treated as executory in an actual bankruptcy case, which depends on case-specific facts and the bankruptcy court's own determination that this clause does not evaluate. This is federal bankruptcy law that applies uniformly in every U.S. district, including the U.S. Bankruptcy Courts for California's four federal districts; it is not a California-specific rule, though it routinely governs California businesses' IP licenses.

citations.case: 11 U.S.C. § 365(g) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Bankruptcy Code, effect of rejection of an executory contract
citations.quote: the rejection of an executory contract or unexpired lease of the debtor constitutes a breach of such contract or lease

citations.case: Mission Product Holdings, Inc. v. Tempnology, LLC
citations.cite: No. 17-1657, U.S. Supreme Court, argued February 20, 2019, decided May 20, 2019 (Cornell LII slip opinion text; commonly reported as 587 U.S. 370 (2019), not independently confirmed against the bound U.S. Reports this session)
citations.quote: We hold it does not. A rejection breaches a contract but does not rescind it.

clauses.title: What Counts as "Intellectual Property" for This Statute's Protection
clauses.body: The special licensee protection in 11 U.S.C. section 365(n), described in the following clauses, applies only to a defined list of property. The Bankruptcy Code's own definitions section, 11 U.S.C. section 101(35A), defines "intellectual property" for this purpose as a closed list of six categories: a trade secret; an invention, process, design, or plant protected under patent law (title 35); a patent application; a plant variety; a work of authorship protected under copyright law (title 17); or a semiconductor mask work protected under chapter 9 of title 17 -- each only to the extent it is actually protected under the applicable non-bankruptcy law that governs it.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the closed six-category list in 11 U.S.C. section 101(35A) -- not a claim about whether the specific intellectual property described on this sheet falls within any of these six categories or is in fact protected under the applicable non-bankruptcy law that would have to protect it (patent, copyright, trade secret, or plant variety law), which this clause does not evaluate. This definition is federal and uniform nationwide; it is not a California-specific statute, though California-based licensees and licensors routinely rely on it.

citations.case: 11 U.S.C. § 101(35A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Bankruptcy Code, definition of "intellectual property"
citations.quote: means— (A) trade secret; (B) invention, process, design, or plant protected under title 35; (C) patent application; (D) plant variety; (E) work of authorship protected under title 17; or (F) mask work protected under chapter 9 of title 17; to the extent protected by applicable nonbankruptcy law.

clauses.title: Trademarks Are Not Within This Statute's Definition
clauses.body: The six-category definition described in the preceding clause does not list a trademark, trade name, or service mark among the property it covers. The U.S. Supreme Court has confirmed the consequence of that omission directly: the licensee protection statute, 11 U.S.C. section 365(n), does not cover trademark licensing agreements at all. Because that specific statute does not reach trademark licenses, a rejected trademark license instead falls back on the general rejection-as-breach rule described in the first clause of this Information Sheet, rather than on the specific retained-rights mechanics section 365(n) provides for the six listed categories, which are described in the clauses that follow.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law and a real, verified U.S. Supreme Court statement about that statute's scope, used as real evidence that trademarks fall outside 11 U.S.C. section 365(n)'s definition -- not a claim about how any specific trademark license would be treated in an actual bankruptcy case. The Bankruptcy Code's text itself does not contain an express sentence stating that trademarks are excluded; this clause's second citation is to the Supreme Court's own description of that consequence of the statute's closed list, which this clause treats as the operative statement of the exclusion rather than independently construing the omission itself. This is federal law of general application, not California-specific.

citations.case: Mission Product Holdings, Inc. v. Tempnology, LLC
citations.cite: No. 17-1657, U.S. Supreme Court, argued February 20, 2019, decided May 20, 2019 (Cornell LII slip opinion text; commonly reported as 587 U.S. 370 (2019), not independently confirmed against the bound U.S. Reports this session)
citations.quote: that provision does not cover trademark licensing agreements, which continue to fall, along with most other contracts, within Section 365(g)’s general rule.

clauses.title: The Licensee's Choice When a Covered License Is Rejected
clauses.body: For a license within the six covered categories, section 365(n) gives the licensee -- not the trustee -- the choice of how to respond to the licensor's rejection. The licensee may elect to treat the contract as terminated by the rejection, to the same extent it could have treated the contract as terminated by a breach outside of bankruptcy, and pursue a damage claim for that breach. Alternatively, the licensee may instead elect to retain its rights under the license and any supplementary agreement to the licensed intellectual property, as those rights existed immediately before the bankruptcy case began, for the remaining duration of the contract and any extension period the licensee is entitled to exercise as of right. That retained-rights election includes the right to enforce any exclusivity provision the license contains, but the statute expressly withholds one specific remedy from it: any other right the licensee might otherwise have, under applicable non-bankruptcy law, to force specific performance of the contract.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the two-option election 11 U.S.C. section 365(n)(1) gives a licensee of covered intellectual property -- not a claim about which option would be more advantageous for any specific licensee described on this sheet, or that either election has actually been made in any pending or contemplated bankruptcy case, which are case-specific business and legal decisions this clause does not evaluate. This is federal law of general application, not California-specific.

citations.case: 11 U.S.C. § 365(n)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Bankruptcy Code, licensee's election on licensor's rejection of an intellectual property license
citations.quote: to retain its rights (including a right to enforce any exclusivity provision of such contract, but excluding any other right under applicable nonbankruptcy law to specific performance of such contract) under such contract and under any agreement supplementary to such contract, to such intellectual property (including any embodiment of such intellectual property to the extent protected by applicable nonbankruptcy law), as such rights existed immediately before the case commenced

clauses.title: What the Trustee Must Do -- and What the Licensee Must Keep Paying -- if Rights Are Retained
clauses.body: If the licensee elects to retain its rights rather than treat the license as terminated, section 365(n)(2) imposes matching obligations on both sides of the relationship. The trustee is required to let the licensee actually exercise the rights it elected to retain. On the licensee's side, retaining rights is not free: the licensee must keep making all royalty payments due under the contract for its remaining duration and for any extension period the licensee exercises, and in exchange for retaining its rights the licensee is deemed to waive any right of setoff it might otherwise have against the estate under the Bankruptcy Code or applicable non-bankruptcy law, as well as any administrative-expense claim under section 503(b) arising from the contract's performance. On written request, the trustee must also turn over any of the licensed intellectual property (or protected embodiments of it) that the trustee is holding, to the extent the contract provides for that, and must not interfere with the licensee's contractual rights to that intellectual property, including the licensee's right to obtain it from someone other than the trustee.
clauses.gap: This is federal statutory law, used as real evidence of the trustee's and the retaining licensee's respective statutory obligations under 11 U.S.C. section 365(n)(2) and (3) -- not a claim that any specific trustee, debtor, or licensee described on this sheet has performed or failed to perform these obligations in an actual case, which this clause does not evaluate. The royalty-payment quotation is drawn from paragraph (n)(2); the trustee's turn-over and non-interference obligations described in the final two sentences of this clause's body come from the separate written-request mechanism in paragraph (n)(3), which is not independently quoted here beyond the one royalty-payment sentence cited below. This is federal law of general application, not California-specific.

citations.case: 11 U.S.C. § 365(n)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Bankruptcy Code, trustee's obligation to allow the licensee to exercise retained rights
citations.quote: the trustee shall allow the licensee to exercise such rights

citations.case: 11 U.S.C. § 365(n)(2)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: U.S. Code, Bankruptcy Code, licensee's continuing royalty obligation on retaining rights
citations.quote: the licensee shall make all royalty payments due under such contract for the duration of such contract and for any period described in paragraph (1)(B) of this subsection for which the licensee extends such contract

clauses.title: The Supreme Court's Resolution for Categories the Statute Does Not Cover
clauses.body: Before 2019, federal appellate courts disagreed about what happened to a licensee's rights when a licensor rejected a license that section 365(n) did not cover, such as a trademark license -- some courts reasoned that Congress's decision to spell out retained-rights protection for the six listed categories meant Congress intended rejection to extinguish a licensee's rights in every other kind of contract. The U.S. Supreme Court rejected that reasoning in Mission Product Holdings, Inc. v. Tempnology, LLC, holding that rejection of a contract of any kind in bankruptcy operates as a breach and not as a rescission, so that a trademark licensee's rights survive rejection in the same way any other counterparty's contractual rights survive a rejection, even though no statute spells that out specifically for trademarks the way section 365(n) does for the six listed categories.
clauses.gap: This is a real, verified U.S. Supreme Court holding, used as real evidence of how rejection of an intellectual property license outside section 365(n)'s six covered categories (most notably, a trademark license) is treated -- not a claim about how any specific trademark or other uncovered license described on this sheet would be treated in an actual bankruptcy case. This session's CourtListener access returned a rate-limit error (125 requests/day, exhausted) when checked for this clause's research, so the case was not independently cross-checked against CourtListener; the opinion text was instead fetched directly from Cornell's Legal Information Institute, re-fetched with a distinct User-Agent, and confirmed byte-identical both times. The commonly reported citation, 587 U.S. 370 (2019), was not independently confirmed against the bound-volume United States Reports this session -- only the docket number (No. 17-1657), the argued and decided dates, the parties' names, and the full opinion and syllabus text were directly verified from the fetched Cornell LII source, which displayed the opinion in slip-opinion form without a U.S. Reports volume/page citation.

clauses.title: Why Section 365(n) Exists: The 1988 Response to a Fourth Circuit Patent-License Ruling
clauses.body: Section 365(n) was not part of the Bankruptcy Code as originally enacted; Congress added it in 1988 in direct response to a specific federal appellate decision. In Lubrizol Enterprises v. Richmond Metal Finishers, the Fourth Circuit had held that a debtor-licensor's rejection of an executory patent license contract worked to revoke the license it had granted, stripping the licensee of its right to keep using the patented technology. Congress responded by enacting section 365(n) specifically to reverse that ruling and ensure that licensees of patents (and the other categories later listed in the statute) keep the rights described in the preceding clauses even when their licensor's contract is rejected in bankruptcy.
clauses.gap: This account of section 365(n)'s legislative background is drawn from the U.S. Supreme Court's own recitation of that history in Mission Product Holdings, Inc. v. Tempnology, LLC, not from an independent fetch of the Fourth Circuit's 1985 Lubrizol opinion itself (756 F.2d 1043), which this session did not separately retrieve from a primary source -- this session's CourtListener access was rate-limited (125 requests/day, exhausted) when this clause's research was performed. The date this clause treats as when section 365(n) was enacted (1988) and its statutory citation come from the Supreme Court's own opinion text, which cites Pub. L. 100-506, 102 Stat. 2538 (1988), for that enactment; this clause does not independently verify the Statutes at Large volume and page against a primary Statutes at Large source. This is federal legislative and case-law history, not California-specific.
