clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment
Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}}, states what California's Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.01 et seq.) provides about the rules that govern a limited liability company's internal affairs when its members have not addressed a given matter in a written operating agreement — or have no written operating agreement at all. Where a specific business name is named below, that is {{companyName}}; this sheet can also be read on its own, without it filled in, as a general reference to what the statute says. This sheet states the law; it does not draft, adopt, or amend any operating agreement, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: What Counts as an LLC's "Operating Agreement"
clauses.body: California's LLC statute defines "operating agreement" far more broadly than the written document that phrase usually brings to mind. By statutory definition, an operating agreement is the agreement of all of a limited liability company's members concerning the matters the statute assigns to it, and that agreement can be oral, in a record (written), implied from the members' conduct, or any combination of the three — it does not need to be called an "operating agreement," and it does not need to exist as a single signed document at all. A limited liability company with only one member can have an operating agreement too: the statute specifically provides that a single-member operating agreement is not unenforceable merely because only one person is a party to it. Separately, a person does not need to sign anything to be bound: becoming a member of a limited liability company is itself, by statute, deemed assent to whatever operating agreement already governs that company.
clauses.gap: The statute does not supply an evidentiary standard or checklist for what a court accepts as proof of an oral or implied operating agreement's terms; where members disagree about what was orally agreed or implied from their conduct, that dispute is resolved case by case on the facts presented, not by any statutory formula, and this sheet cannot predict how a particular disagreement would come out.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.02(s)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.02(s)
citations.quote: “Operating agreement” means the agreement, whether or not referred to as an operating agreement and whether oral, in a record, implied, or in any combination thereof, of all the members of a limited liability company, including a sole member, concerning the matters described in subdivision (a) of Section 17701.10.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.02(s)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.02(s)
citations.quote: An operating agreement of a limited liability company having only one member shall not be unenforceable by reason of there being only one person who is a party to the operating agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.11(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.11(b)
citations.quote: A person that becomes a member of a limited liability company is deemed to assent to the operating agreement.

clauses.title: When the Operating Agreement Is Silent, the Statute Fills the Gap
clauses.body: California's LLC statute assigns four broad subjects to the operating agreement: relations among the members and between the members and the company, the rights and duties of a manager, the company's activities and the conduct of those activities, and the means and conditions for amending the operating agreement itself. Where the operating agreement — written, oral, implied, or some combination — does not address one of those subjects, the statute does not leave a void: the Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act itself governs that matter instead. This is why a limited liability company can operate lawfully with no written document at all, or with a written document that is silent on a given point: the statutory default rules described elsewhere in this sheet apply automatically to fill whatever the members have not otherwise addressed.
clauses.gap: Whether a particular matter is 'addressed' by an oral or implied agreement, as opposed to left to the statutory default, is often exactly what members disagree about after the fact; the statute does not define how much specificity is needed for an informal agreement to count as addressing a subject, so that line is drawn case by case.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(a)
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in this section, the operating agreement governs all of the following: (1) Relations among the members as members and between the members and the limited liability company. (2) The rights and duties under this title of a person in the capacity of manager. (3) The activities of the limited liability company and the conduct of those activities. (4) The means and conditions for amending the operating agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(b)
citations.quote: To the extent the operating agreement does not otherwise provide for a matter described in subdivision (a), this title governs the matter.

clauses.title: A Statutory Floor No Operating Agreement Can Waive
clauses.body: The members' freedom to override the statutory defaults by agreement is broad but not unlimited. California's LLC statute lists specific things an operating agreement — no matter how the members word it, and regardless of unanimous consent — may not do. Among them: it may not vary the company's statutory capacity to sue and be sued in its own name, and, subject to narrow, separately-listed exceptions, it may not eliminate the duty of loyalty, the duty of care, or any other fiduciary duty a member or manager owes. It likewise may not eliminate the contractual obligation of good faith and fair dealing that the statute imposes on members and managers, though the agreement may prescribe non-manifestly-unreasonable standards for measuring that obligation. These are floor-level protections that exist independent of what the members put in writing, orally agree to, or imply through their conduct.
clauses.gap: This sheet lists only a sample of the non-waivable list; Section 17701.10 enumerates well over a dozen additional items — covering matters like dissolution standing, merger approval rights, and records access — that this sheet does not individually restate, and the exceptions and cross-references attached to several of them (including the loyalty and care items) are more detailed than summarized here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(1)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(1)
citations.quote: Vary a limited liability company’s capacity under Section 17701.05 to sue and be sued in its own name.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(4)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(4)
citations.quote: eliminate the duty of loyalty, the duty of care, or any other fiduciary duty.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(5)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(c)(5)
citations.quote: eliminate the contractual obligation of good faith and fair dealing under subdivision (d) of Section 17704.09, but the operating agreement may prescribe the standards by which the performance of the obligation is to be measured, if the standards are not manifestly unreasonable as determined at the time the standards are prescribed.

clauses.title: Some Statutory Defaults Can Be Changed Only in a Written Operating Agreement
clauses.body: Not every default rule can be varied by an oral or implied operating agreement, even though oral and implied operating agreements are otherwise valid under California's LLC statute. The statute singles out certain provisions — including the liability-shield provision, the indemnification provision, and much of the meeting, notice, and voting mechanics for manager-managed companies — that may be varied only by a written operating agreement. Fiduciary duties receive an even narrower path: a member's or manager's fiduciary duties may be modified only in a written operating agreement, and only with the members' informed consent — the statute specifically states that merely becoming a member and thereby being deemed to assent to the operating agreement does not, by itself, count as the informed consent that a fiduciary-duty modification requires.
clauses.gap: The statute's list of provisions restricted to written-agreement-only variation cross-references several other code sections by number rather than describing their content in the same sentence; a member or manager relying on an oral or implied agreement to have modified one of those specific provisions cannot determine from this clause alone whether that provision is on the restricted list.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(d)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(d)
citations.quote: provided, however, that the provisions of Sections 17701.13, 17703.01, and 17704.08 and subdivisions (f) to (r), inclusive, and (u) to (w), inclusive, of Section 17704.07 shall only be varied by a written operating agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(e)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.10(e)
citations.quote: The fiduciary duties of a manager to a manager-managed limited liability company and to the members of the limited liability company and of a member to a member-managed limited liability company and to the members of such limited liability company shall only be modified in a written operating agreement with the informed consent of the members. Assenting to the operating agreement pursuant to subdivision (b) of Section 17701.11 shall not constitute informed consent.

clauses.title: The Default Management Structure and Voting Thresholds
clauses.body: Absent a contrary election, California's LLC statute makes every limited liability company member-managed by default: a company is member-managed unless its articles of organization contain the specific statement required to make it manager-managed instead. In a member-managed company, the statutory default rules are: each member has equal rights in management and conduct of the company's activities, including equal voting rights; a disagreement among members over a matter in the ordinary course of the company's activities is decided by a majority of the members; an act outside the ordinary course of the company's activities may be undertaken only with the consent of all members; and the operating agreement itself may be amended only with the consent of all members. These default thresholds — majority for ordinary matters, unanimity for extraordinary matters and for amending the operating agreement — apply automatically unless the members have provided otherwise.
clauses.gap: The statute does not define "ordinary course of the activities" versus a matter "outside the ordinary course"; that line depends on the nature of the particular company's business and is not resolved by any bright-line statutory test, so which threshold applies to a given decision can itself be disputed among the members.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(a)
citations.quote: A limited liability company is a member-managed limited liability company unless the articles of organization contain the statement required by paragraph (5) of subdivision (b) of Section 17702.01.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(2)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(2)
citations.quote: each member has equal rights in the management and conduct of the limited liability company’s activities including equal voting rights.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(3)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(3)
citations.quote: A difference arising among members as to a matter in the ordinary course of the activities of the limited liability company shall be decided by a majority of the members.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(4)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(4)
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in Article 10 (commencing with Section 17710.01), an act outside the ordinary course of the activities of the limited liability company may be undertaken only with the consent of all members.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(5)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(b)(5)
citations.quote: The operating agreement may be amended only with the consent of all members.

clauses.title: If the LLC Elects Manager-Management Instead
clauses.body: Where the articles of organization state that the company is manager-managed, a different set of default rules applies. Any matter relating to the company's activities is decided exclusively by the managers, not the members, except where the statute expressly provides otherwise. A manager is chosen by the consent of a majority of the members and remains a manager until a successor is chosen, unless the manager resigns, is removed, or dies (or, for a manager that is not an individual, terminates); the members may remove a manager at any time, without cause, by majority consent, subject to any service contract the manager has with the company. A person does not need to be a member to serve as manager, but if a member who is also a manager dissociates as a member, that dissociation removes the person as manager as well.
clauses.gap: This describes only the default management-authority and manager-selection rules; the same section separately imposes detailed meeting, notice, quorum, and written-consent mechanics for manager-managed companies (several of which, per the written-agreement clause above, can only be varied in writing) that are not restated here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(c)(1)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(c)(1)
citations.quote: any matter relating to the activities of the limited liability company is decided exclusively by the managers.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(c)(5)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(c)(5)
citations.quote: A manager may be chosen at any time by the consent of a majority of the members and remains a manager until a successor has been chosen, unless the manager at an earlier time resigns, is removed, or dies, or, in the case of a manager that is not an individual, terminates. A manager may be removed at any time by the consent of a majority of the members without cause, subject to the rights, if any, of the manager under any service contract with the limited liability company.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(c)(6)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17704.07(c)(6)
citations.quote: A person need not be a member to be a manager, but the dissociation of a member that is also a manager removes the person as a manager.

clauses.title: When a Filed Record Conflicts With the Operating Agreement
clauses.body: A limited liability company's articles of organization and other records filed with the Secretary of State are not the same thing as its operating agreement, and the two can conflict — for example, where a filed record states a management structure or authority that differs from what the members actually agreed among themselves. California's statute resolves that conflict differently depending on who is asking: as among the members, dissociated members, transferees, and managers, the operating agreement prevails. As to other persons — typically third parties dealing with the company — the filed record prevails, but only to the extent they reasonably rely on it.
clauses.gap: The statute does not define what counts as "reasonable" reliance on a filed record by a third party; that determination is fact-specific and this sheet cannot say in advance how a particular third party's reliance would be assessed.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.12(d)(1)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.12(d)(1)
citations.quote: The operating agreement prevails as to members, dissociated members, transferees, and managers.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.12(d)(2)
citations.cite: Cal. Corp. Code § 17701.12(d)(2)
citations.quote: The record prevails as to other persons to the extent they reasonably rely on the record.

clauses.title: About This Hazard Communication Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Hazard Communication Standard — Information Sheet describes California's Cal/OSHA regulation requiring employers to inform employees about hazardous chemicals present in the workplace, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194, as those requirements relate to the working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.

It summarizes selected requirements of that regulation: the section's scope and the chemicals and workplaces it covers, the written hazard communication program an employer must develop and maintain, the multi-employer-worksite notification duties that apply where employees of more than one employer share a work area, container labeling requirements, the duty to obtain and maintain safety data sheets (SDSs) and keep them accessible, employee information and training requirements, the limited circumstances in which a specific chemical identity may be withheld as a trade secret, employee and representative access to the written program and SDSs, and selected statutory exemptions from the section's labeling and coverage requirements.

{{companyName}} has identified {{programAdministratorName}} as the person responsible for {{companyName}}'s written hazard communication program.

This information sheet is not itself {{companyName}}'s written hazard communication program, does not itself satisfy 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)'s written-program requirement, and does not determine that any particular chemical, container, label, safety data sheet, or workplace practice of {{companyName}}'s is or is not compliant with California law.

clauses.title: What the Standard Requires and Which Chemicals It Covers
clauses.body: California's Hazard Communication Standard requires manufacturers and importers to classify the hazards of the chemicals they produce or import, requires all employers to provide their employees with information about hazardous chemicals to which the employees may be exposed — through a written hazard communication program, container labels and other forms of warning, safety data sheets, and employee information and training — and requires distributors to transmit the required hazard information to employers. The standard applies to any hazardous chemical that is known to be present in the workplace in a manner under which employees may be exposed under normal conditions of use or in a reasonably foreseeable emergency resulting from workplace operations; it also contains specific provisions for laboratories.
clauses.gap: This clause states the regulation's own description of its coverage; it does not itself determine whether any particular substance present at any particular workplace meets the regulatory definition of a "hazardous chemical," and it does not restate the section's laboratory-specific provisions, its Proposition 65 cross-reference provisions in subsection (b)(6), or the full list of exempted chemical categories, which are addressed in a separate clause of this information sheet. Classification of a specific chemical requires applying the hazard criteria in the section's Appendix A (health hazards) and Appendix B (physical hazards), which this clause does not reproduce.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(1) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(b)(1), scope and application — general requirement
citations.quote: This section requires manufacturers or importers to classify the hazards of chemicals which they produce or import, and all employers to provide information to their employees about the hazardous chemicals to which they may be exposed, by means of a hazard communication program, labels and other forms of warning, safety data sheets, and information and training.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(2) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(b)(2), scope and application — coverage trigger
citations.quote: This section applies to any hazardous chemical which is known to be present in the work place in such a manner that employees may be exposed under normal conditions of use or in a reasonably foreseeable emergency resulting from work place operations.

clauses.title: The Written Hazard Communication Program
clauses.body: An employer must develop, implement, and maintain at the workplace a written hazard communication program for its employees that at least describes how the standard's requirements for labels and other forms of warning, safety data sheets, and employee information and training will be met. The written program must include a list of the hazardous chemicals known to be present, using a product identifier referenced on the corresponding safety data sheet — a list that may be compiled for the workplace as a whole or for individual work areas — as well as the methods the employer will use to inform employees of the hazards of non-routine tasks, such as cleaning a reactor vessel, and of hazards associated with chemicals contained in unlabeled pipes in the employees' work areas.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the written program's required contents under 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(1); it does not itself constitute or supply that written program, does not determine whether any particular employer's existing written program is complete or current, and does not address the additional, separate content the same subsection requires for multi-employer workplaces, which is covered in a separate clause of this information sheet.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(1) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(e)(1), written hazard communication program requirement
citations.quote: Employers shall develop, implement, and maintain at the workplace a written hazard communication program for their employees which at least describes how the criteria specified in sections 5194(f), (g), and (h) for labels and other forms of warning, safety data sheets, and employee information and training will be met

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(1)(A) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(e)(1)(A), required list of hazardous chemicals
citations.quote: A list of the hazardous chemicals known to be present using a product identifier that is referenced on the appropriate safety data sheet (the list may be compiled for the workplace as a whole or for individual work areas)

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(1)(B) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(e)(1)(B), non-routine tasks and unlabeled pipes
citations.quote: The methods the employer will use to inform employees of the hazards of non-routine tasks (for example, the cleaning of reactor vessels), and the hazards associated with chemicals contained in unlabeled pipes in their work areas.

clauses.title: Additional Duties at Multi-Employer Worksites
clauses.body: Where a workplace has employees of more than one employer present, the written hazard communication program must additionally describe the methods the employer will use to inform any employer sharing the same work area of the hazardous chemicals to which that other employer's employees may be exposed while performing their work, along with any suggestions for appropriate protective measures. The standard specifies that this includes the methods used to provide the other employer access to safety data sheets (or to make them available at a central location), to inform the other employer of precautionary measures needed during normal operations and foreseeable emergencies, and to inform the other employer of the labeling system used at the workplace.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the multi-employer-worksite content requirement in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(2); it does not determine, for any particular jobsite, which employer or employers are legally responsible for a given hazard, and it does not address related but distinct multi-employer safety duties that arise under other Cal/OSHA standards outside section 5194.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(2) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(e)(2), multi-employer workplace written program content
citations.quote: In multi-employer workplaces, the written hazard communication program shall include the methods employers will use to inform any employers sharing the same work area of the hazardous chemicals to which their employees may be exposed while performing their work, and any suggestions for appropriate protective measures

clauses.title: Labeling of Containers in the Workplace
clauses.body: Except as provided by two specific alternatives in the standard, an employer must ensure that each container of hazardous chemicals in the workplace is labeled, tagged, or marked either with the full label information required for shipped containers, or with a product identifier plus words, pictures, symbols, or a combination that provides at least general hazard information, together with other information available to employees under the hazard communication program. An employer may not remove or intentionally deface an existing label on an incoming container of a hazardous chemical unless the container is immediately re-marked with the required information, and workplace labels or other forms of warning must be legible, in English (additional languages may be included), and prominently displayed on the container or otherwise readily available in the work area throughout each work shift.
clauses.gap: This clause covers workplace container labeling under 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(f)(6), (9), and (10); it does not restate the separate, more detailed labeling elements required on containers of hazardous chemicals leaving the workplace under subsection (f)(1)-(5), the stationary-process-container alternative in (f)(7), or the exemption for portable containers intended only for the immediate use of the employee who transfers the chemical, in (f)(8). It does not determine whether a specific label on a specific container currently in use satisfies these requirements.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(f)(6) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(f)(6), workplace labeling requirement
citations.quote: Workplace labeling. Except as provided in sections 5194(f)(7) and (f)(8) the employer shall ensure that each container of hazardous chemicals in the workplace is labeled, tagged, or marked with either:

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(f)(9) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(f)(9), prohibition on removing or defacing incoming labels
citations.quote: The employer shall not remove or intentionally deface existing labels on incoming containers of hazardous chemicals, unless the container is immediately marked with the required information.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(f)(10) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(f)(10), legibility, language, and display of workplace labels
citations.quote: The employer shall ensure that workplace labels or other forms of warning are legible, in English, and prominently displayed on the container, or readily available in the work area throughout each work shift.

clauses.title: Obtaining and Maintaining Safety Data Sheets
clauses.body: Manufacturers and importers must obtain or develop a safety data sheet (SDS) for each hazardous chemical they produce or import, and every employer must have an SDS for each hazardous chemical it uses. An employer must maintain copies of the required SDSs for each hazardous chemical present in the workplace and must ensure they are readily accessible to employees during each work shift when employees are in their work area(s); the standard permits electronic access and other alternatives to paper copies, so long as no barriers to immediate employee access are created.
clauses.gap: This clause covers the core SDS-availability duty in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(g)(1), (8), and (9); it does not restate the section's detailed required SDS content and format under (g)(2)-(4), the accuracy and revision-timing duties in (g)(5), the manufacturer/distributor SDS-transmission chain in (g)(6)-(7), or the specific procedure and deadlines an employer must follow when a manufacturer or importer fails to provide a required SDS, set out in (g)(12)-(13).

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(g)(1) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(g)(1), duty to obtain or develop safety data sheets
citations.quote: Manufacturers and importers shall obtain or develop a safety data sheet for each hazardous chemical they produce or import. Employers shall have a safety data sheet for each hazardous chemical which they use.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(g)(8) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(g)(8), duty to maintain and provide shift-time access to SDSs
citations.quote: The employer shall maintain copies of the required safety data sheets for each hazardous chemical in the workplace, and shall ensure that they are readily accessible during each work shift to employees when they are in their work area(s).

clauses.title: Employee Information and Training on Chemical Hazards
clauses.body: An employer must provide employees with effective information and training on hazardous chemicals in their work area at the time of initial assignment and whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced into their work area; training may address general classes of hazardous chemicals to the extent appropriate to reasonably foreseeable job exposures, but chemical-specific information must always remain available through labels and safety data sheets. The standard's required training topics include the operations in the employee's work area where hazardous chemicals are present, the location and availability of the written hazard communication program and SDSs, methods to detect a hazardous chemical's presence or release, the physical and health hazards of the workplace chemicals and the protective measures available, and the details of the employer's hazard communication program. Employers must also inform employees of specified rights, including the right to be free from discharge or other discrimination for exercising rights afforded under the Hazardous Substances Information and Training Act.
clauses.gap: This clause summarizes the initial/ongoing training trigger and the topic list in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(h)(1)-(2); it does not reproduce every training subtopic verbatim, and it does not restate the separate 30-day timing rule in (h)(3) for informing employees of newly received SDSs that reflect significantly increased risk, which is a distinct, narrower duty this clause does not cover.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(h)(1) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(h)(1), training trigger — initial assignment and new hazards
citations.quote: Employers shall provide employees with effective information and training on hazardous chemicals in their work area at the time of their initial assignment, and whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced into their work area.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(h)(2)(G)(3) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(h)(2)(G)3., anti-discrimination right employees must be informed of
citations.quote: Against discharge or other discrimination due to the employee's exercise of the rights afforded pursuant to the provisions of the Hazardous Substances Information and Training Act.

clauses.title: Trade Secret Chemical Identity and Its Limits
clauses.body: A manufacturer, importer, or employer may withhold a hazardous chemical's specific chemical identity, or the exact percentage of the substance in a mixture, from the safety data sheet as a trade secret, provided the claim can be supported, the SDS discloses the chemical's properties and effects, the SDS states that the identity or percentage is being withheld as a trade secret, and the specific identity and percentage are made available to health or safety professionals, employees, and designated representatives under the standard's disclosure procedures. Where a treating physician or nurse determines a medical emergency exists and the specific chemical identity or percentage composition is necessary for emergency or first-aid treatment, the manufacturer, importer, or employer must immediately disclose that trade-secret information to the treating physician or nurse, regardless of any written statement of need or confidentiality agreement. In non-emergency situations, the same information must be disclosed on request to a qualifying health or safety professional, employee, or designated representative who submits a written request meeting the standard's specified content and confidentiality-agreement requirements.
clauses.gap: This clause summarizes the trade-secret withholding conditions and the emergency-disclosure rule in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(i)(1)-(3); it does not restate the detailed non-emergency written-request content requirements in full, the confidentiality-agreement terms in (i)(3)(D)-(E) and (i)(4), the Director's review-and-appeal procedure in (i)(7)-(15) for a denied trade-secret disclosure request, or the outcome of any such dispute for a particular chemical, which this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(i)(1) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(i)(1), conditions for withholding a trade-secret chemical identity
citations.quote: The manufacturer, importer or employer may withhold the specific chemical identity of a hazardous chemical, or the exact percentage (concentration) of the substance in a mixture, from the safety data sheet, provided that:

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(i)(2) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(i)(2), mandatory emergency disclosure to a treating physician or nurse
citations.quote: Where a treating physician or nurse determines that a medical emergency exists and the specific chemical identity and/or specific percentage of composition of a hazardous chemical is necessary for emergency or first-aid treatment, the manufacturer, importer, or employer shall immediately disclose the specific chemical identity or percentage composition of a trade secret chemical to that treating physician or nurse, regardless of the existence of a written statement of need or a confidentiality agreement.

clauses.title: Employee and Representative Access to the Program and SDSs
clauses.body: An employer must make its written hazard communication program available, upon request, to employees, their designated representatives, the Chief of the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH). Safety data sheets must likewise be made readily available, upon request, to designated representatives and to the Chief, and NIOSH and the employee's physician must be given access to safety data sheets in the same manner. The standard separately defines a "designated representative" as any individual or organization to whom an employee gives written authorization to exercise the employee's rights under the section, with a recognized or certified collective bargaining agent automatically treated as a designated representative without a separate written authorization.
clauses.gap: This clause covers the access rights in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(3) and (g)(11), together with the "designated representative" definition in subsection (c); it does not describe the recordkeeping-retention timeline for a chemical no longer in use, which the standard cross-references to a separate Cal/OSHA regulation (8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3204) rather than specifying within section 5194 itself, and this clause does not independently verify that separate section's text.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(e)(3) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(e)(3), access to the written program
citations.quote: The employer shall make the written hazard communication program available, upon request, to employees, their designated representatives, the Chief, and NIOSH, in accordance with the requirements of section 3204(e).

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(g)(11) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(g)(11), access to safety data sheets
citations.quote: Safety data sheets shall also be made readily available, upon request, to designated representatives, and to the Chief, in accordance with the requirements of section 3204(e). NIOSH and the employee's physician shall also be given access to safety data sheets in the same manner.

clauses.title: Selected Exemptions from the Standard
clauses.body: The standard does not apply to certain categories of chemicals and operations. Among the listed exclusions are consumer products packaged for distribution to, and use by, the general public, provided that employee exposure to the product is not significantly greater than the consumer exposure occurring during the product's principal consumer use, and retail food sale establishments and other retail trade establishments, exclusive of their processing and repair work areas. The standard also addresses work operations where employees only handle hazardous chemicals in sealed containers that are not opened under normal conditions of use, such as in marine cargo handling, warehousing, or transportation — for those operations the general exemption does not fully apply, and the employer instead has narrower, specified duties concerning incoming container labels, safety data sheets, and limited employee training.
clauses.gap: This clause covers three of the several exclusions and exceptions listed in 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(4)-(5); it does not reproduce the section's other listed exclusions (pesticides, food/drug/cosmetics, distilled spirits, other consumer-product-agency-regulated items, hazardous waste, tobacco, certain wood products, articles, foods for personal consumption, and pesticide-use compliant with Department of Pesticide Regulation rules), and it does not determine whether any particular product, container, or work operation qualifies for any exclusion or exception — that is a fact-specific classification question the standard leaves to the manufacturer, importer, or employer in the first instance.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(5)(G) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(b)(5)(G), consumer product exclusion
citations.quote: Consumer products packaged for distribution to, and use by, the general public, provided that employee exposure to the product is not significantly greater than the consumer exposure occurring during the principal consumer use of the product

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(5)(F) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(b)(5)(F), retail establishment exclusion
citations.quote: Retail food sale establishments and all other retail trade establishments, exclusive of processing and repair work areas

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5194(b)(5)(I) (Hazard Communication)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5194(b)(5)(I), sealed-container work operations
citations.quote: Work operations where employees only handle chemicals in sealed containers which are not opened under normal conditions of use (such as are found in marine cargo handling, warehousing, or transportation); however, this section does apply to these operations as follows:

clauses.title: Declaration -- Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's child support license suspension and denial program under Family Code Section 17520, which allows a local child support agency to certify a support obligor as out of compliance with a support order to the Department of Child Support Services for referral to state licensing boards, in connection with a matter between {{obligorName}} and {{obligeeName}}, case number {{courtCaseNumber}}, pending in {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes the statute's definitions of "board," "license," and "compliance with a judgment or order for support," the certified-list and consolidated-list process, the temporary-license and notice provisions, the supplemental list used for suspending an existing license, the no-refund rule, the grounds on which a local child support agency must send a release, the judicial review process and its limited scope, the statute's sole-administrative-remedy provision, and the statute's specific protections for a suspended driver's license against vehicle impoundment and increased insurance costs. It does not itself certify any obligor to any board, request or grant any release, temporary license, suspension, or judicial review, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about how Family Code Section 17520 applies to a specific case.

clauses.title: Which Boards and Licenses the Statute Reaches
clauses.body: Under California law, Family Code Section 17520 defines "board" broadly to include the State Bar of California, the Department of Real Estate, the Department of Motor Vehicles, the Secretary of State, the Department of Fish and Wildlife, and any other state entity that issues a license, certificate, credential, permit, registration, or other authorization to engage in a business, occupation, or profession, or, to the extent required by federal law, for recreational purposes. "License" is defined equally broadly, reaching State Bar membership, a commercial motor vehicle authorization, a notary public commission, a Department of Motor Vehicles driver's license, a Department of Fish and Wildlife commercial fishing license, and, to the extent required by federal law, a recreational-purpose license, in addition to conventional business, occupation, and professional licenses.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the statute's own definitions of "board" and "license"; it does not identify which specific board(s) or license(s), if any, are implicated in a given case, and the statute itself notes that failing to specifically name a particular board or license type does not exclude it from these definitions, so the definitions cannot be treated as an exhaustive list.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (a)(2), definition of "Board"
citations.quote: “Board” means an entity specified in Section 101 of the Business and Professions Code, the entities referred to in Sections 1000 and 3600 of the Business and Professions Code, the State Bar of California, the Department of Real Estate, the Department of Motor Vehicles, the Secretary of State, the Department of Fish and Wildlife, and any other state commission, department, committee, examiner, or agency that issues a license, certificate, credential, permit, registration, or any other authorization to engage in a business, occupation, or profession, or to the extent required by federal law or regulations, for recreational purposes.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (a)(5), definition of "License"
citations.quote: “License” includes membership in the State Bar of California, and a certificate, credential, permit, registration, or any other authorization issued by a board that allows a person to engage in a business, occupation, or profession, or to operate a commercial motor vehicle, including appointment and commission by the Secretary of State as a notary public. “License” also includes any driver’s license issued by the Department of Motor Vehicles, any commercial fishing license issued by the Department of Fish and Wildlife, and to the extent required by federal law or regulations, any license used for recreational purposes.

clauses.title: What "Compliance With a Support Order" Means Under This Statute
clauses.body: Under California law, for purposes of Family Code Section 17520, an obligor is in "compliance with a judgment or order for support" if the obligor is no more than 30 calendar days in arrears on current support, is making periodic payments in full on a support arrearage or a public-assistance reimbursement judgment (whether court ordered or by agreement with the local child support agency), or has obtained a judicial finding that equitable estoppel precludes enforcement of the order. The statute further limits its own reach as to spousal support: a local child support agency may use Section 17520 to enforce a spousal support order only when it is also enforcing a related child support obligation owed to the same obligee by the same obligor.
clauses.gap: This clause states the statute's own 30-day/periodic-payment compliance definition and its spousal-support limitation; it does not address how "periodic payments in full" is measured against a specific payment schedule, nor does it independently verify the equitable estoppel doctrine referenced by the statute, which the statute describes only as being "provided in statute or case law" without citing a specific source.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (a)(4), definition of "Compliance with a judgment or order for support"
citations.quote: “Compliance with a judgment or order for support” means that, as set forth in a judgment or order for child or family support, the obligor is no more than 30 calendar days in arrears in making payments in full for current support, in making periodic payments in full, whether court ordered or by agreement with the local child support agency, on a support arrearage, or in making periodic payments in full, whether court ordered or by agreement with the local child support agency, on a judgment for reimbursement for public assistance, or has obtained a judicial finding that equitable estoppel as provided in statute or case law precludes enforcement of the order. The local child support agency is authorized to use this section to enforce orders for spousal support only when the local child support agency is also enforcing a related child support obligation owed to the obligee parent by the same obligor, pursuant to Sections 17400 and 17604.

clauses.title: The Certified List and Consolidated List Process
clauses.body: Under California law, a local child support agency must maintain a list of Title IV-D support obligors against whom a California support order or judgment has been rendered or registered and who are not in compliance with it, and must submit to the Department of Child Support Services a certified list containing each obligor's name, identifying number, and last known address, along with the submitting agency's name, address, and telephone number. The department then consolidates the certified lists received from all local child support agencies and, within 30 calendar days of receipt, provides a copy of the consolidated list to each board responsible for regulating the affected licenses.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the statutory certification-and-consolidation pipeline as written; it does not state how quickly a local child support agency must add or remove a given obligor's name after a change in compliance status (the statute requires only a monthly updated certified list), and it does not address the accuracy safeguards, if any, that apply before a name reaches a board.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (b), certified list submitted by the local child support agency
citations.quote: The local child support agency shall maintain a list of those persons included in a case being enforced under Title IV-D of the federal Social Security Act against whom a support order or judgment has been rendered by, or registered in, a court of this state, and who are not in compliance with that order or judgment. The local child support agency shall submit a certified list with the names, social security numbers, individual taxpayer identification numbers, or other uniform identification numbers, and last known addresses of these persons and the name, address, and telephone number of the local child support agency who certified the list to the department.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (c), department's consolidation and distribution to boards
citations.quote: The department shall consolidate the certified lists received from the local child support agencies and, within 30 calendar days of receipt, shall provide a copy of the consolidated list to each board that is responsible for the regulation of licenses, as specified in this section.

clauses.title: The 150-Day Temporary License for a New Applicant on the List
clauses.body: Under California law, before issuing or renewing a license, a board must check whether the applicant is on the department's most recent consolidated list, and if the applicant is on the list and is otherwise eligible for a license, the board must issue a temporary license valid for 150 days rather than immediately denying the application. Except for a non-commercial driver's license, that 150-day period generally cannot be extended and only one temporary license may issue per regular license term; for a non-commercial driver's license specifically, the statute allows the board to extend a 150-day temporary license by up to 150 additional days upon a request from the local child support agency or a court order on a showing of good cause.
clauses.gap: This clause covers the general 150-day temporary-license mechanism and the driver's-license-specific extension; it does not cover the separate supplemental-list suspension process that applies to an obligor who already holds a full license (addressed in a separate clause of this document), and it does not state what happens if the applicant is not otherwise eligible for a license on grounds unrelated to support compliance.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (e)(2)(A), 150-day temporary license
citations.quote: The board shall issue a temporary license valid for a period of 150 days to any applicant whose name is on the certified list if the applicant is otherwise eligible for a license.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (e)(2)(D), driver's license extension of the temporary license
citations.quote: This paragraph shall apply only in the case of a driver’s license, other than a commercial driver’s license. Upon the request of the local child support agency or by order of the court upon a showing of good cause, the board shall extend a 150-day temporary license for a period not to exceed 150 extra days.

clauses.title: The Supplemental List and Suspension of an Existing License
clauses.body: Under California law, separately from the certified-list/temporary-license process for new applicants, the department may (where economically feasible and where an obligor has been out of compliance for more than four months) provide a supplemental list of these obligors to boards with which it has an interagency agreement, and the licenses of obligors on that supplemental list become subject to suspension, provided the license would not otherwise be up for renewal within six months of the department's request. If a licensee is on a supplemental list, the board must serve notice that the license will be automatically suspended 150 days after notice is served unless compliance with Section 17520 is achieved in the meantime.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the supplemental-list suspension track only as the statute defines it, including its own "economically feasible" and "interagency agreement" preconditions on the department's use of this track; it does not state how a licensee can determine in advance whether their board participates in an interagency agreement under this paragraph, and it excludes licenses subject to annual renewal or annual fee, which the statute places outside this particular paragraph.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (e)(3)(A), supplemental list and suspension eligibility
citations.quote: The department may, when it is economically feasible for the department and the boards to do so as determined by the department, in cases where the department is aware that certain child support obligors listed on the certified lists have been out of compliance with a judgment or order for support for more than four months, provide a supplemental list of these obligors to each board with which the department has an interagency agreement to implement this paragraph. Upon request by the department, the licenses of these obligors shall be subject to suspension, provided that the licenses would not otherwise be eligible for renewal within six months from the date of the request by the department.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (e)(3)(B), 150-day suspension notice
citations.quote: If a licensee is on a supplemental list, the board shall immediately serve notice as specified in subdivision (f) on the licensee that the license will be automatically suspended 150 days after notice is served, unless compliance with this section is achieved.

clauses.title: No Refund of Fees Paid on Denial or Suspension
clauses.body: Under California law, if a license, a license application, or a license renewal is denied under Family Code Section 17520, or if a license is suspended under Section 17520, the statute states that any funds already paid by the applicant or licensee to the board are not refunded by the board.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the statute's own no-refund rule; it does not address whether a board's separate fee schedule allows any partial credit toward a future application, which the statute does not address, and it does not state whether this rule differs for a temporary license that lapses versus an application that is denied outright.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (e)(2)(C), no refund on denial
citations.quote: In the event that a license or application for a license or the renewal of a license is denied pursuant to this section, any funds paid by the applicant or licensee shall not be refunded by the board.

clauses.title: When a Local Child Support Agency Must Send a Release
clauses.body: Under California law, after an applicant makes a timely written request for review, the local child support agency must immediately send a release to the appropriate board and the applicant if the applicant is found to be in compliance, negotiates an arrearage or reimbursement payment schedule with the local child support agency, has requested review but the agency cannot complete it and notify the applicant within the statutory timeframe, has filed and timely pursued judicial review that will not be resolved within 150 days of the notice being served, or has obtained a judicial finding of compliance as the statute defines it.
clauses.gap: This clause states the four release-triggering conditions the statute lists; it does not restate the separate cross-referenced timeframe for a local child support agency to resolve a review request (Family Code Section 17800), which this clause does not independently verify, and it does not address what happens if none of the four listed conditions is met.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (h), release conditions
citations.quote: The local child support agency shall immediately send a release to the appropriate board and the applicant, if any of the following conditions are met:(1) The applicant is found to be in compliance or negotiates an agreement with the local child support agency for a payment schedule on arrearages or reimbursement.

clauses.title: Judicial Review of a Local Child Support Agency's Decision
clauses.body: Under California law, a request for judicial review of a local child support agency's decision must state the grounds for review, and judicial review is limited to those stated grounds; the court must hold an evidentiary hearing within 20 calendar days of the filing of the request. That judicial review is further limited to determining whether a support judgment, order, or payment schedule on arrearages or reimbursement exists, whether the petitioner is the obligor covered by it, and whether the obligor is or is not in compliance with it.
clauses.gap: This clause states the 20-calendar-day hearing requirement and the first three of the four review issues the statute lists (a fourth issue, the extent to which an obligor's needs warrant a conditional release, is described in subdivision (k)(4) but is not quoted in this clause's citation); it does not restate the separate seven-calendar-day service requirement on the local child support agency or the court's authority to uphold, unconditionally release, or conditionally release the license.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (k), introductory text on grounds and evidentiary hearing
citations.quote: The request for judicial review of the local child support agency’s decision shall state the grounds for which review is requested and judicial review shall be limited to those stated grounds. The court shall hold an evidentiary hearing within 20 calendar days of the filing of the request for review.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (k)(1)-(3), scope of judicial review
citations.quote: Judicial review of the local child support agency’s decision shall be limited to a determination of each of the following issues:(1) Whether there is a support judgment, order, or payment schedule on arrearages or reimbursement.(2) Whether the petitioner is the obligor covered by the support judgment or order.(3) Whether the support obligor is or is not in compliance with the judgment or order of support.

clauses.title: This Process Is the Sole Administrative Remedy, and the APA Does Not Apply
clauses.body: Under California law, the review process described in subdivision (h) of Family Code Section 17520 -- the written request for review to the local child support agency -- constitutes the sole administrative remedy for contesting the issuance of a temporary license or the denial or suspension of a license under this statute. The statute expressly states that the Administrative Procedure Act's administrative adjudication provisions do not apply to a denial, suspension, failure to issue or renew a license, or issuance of a temporary license made under Section 17520.
clauses.gap: This clause states only that the Section 17520 review process is the exclusive administrative remedy and that the Administrative Procedure Act's adjudication provisions do not apply; it does not address whether or how a party might separately pursue judicial remedies outside the review-and-judicial-review process this statute itself creates (addressed in a separate clause of this document), and it does not independently verify the scope of the referenced Administrative Procedure Act provisions.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (o), sole administrative remedy and APA inapplicability
citations.quote: The process described in subdivision (h) shall constitute the sole administrative remedy for contesting the issuance of a temporary license or the denial or suspension of a license under this section. The procedures specified in the administrative adjudication provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (Chapter 4.5 (commencing with Section 11400) and Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 11500) of Part 1 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code) shall not apply to the denial, suspension, or failure to issue or renew a license or the issuance of a temporary license pursuant to this section.

clauses.title: Specific Protections for a Suspended Driver's License
clauses.body: Under California law, when a driver's license, including a commercial driver's license, is suspended or revoked under Family Code Section 17520, the statute states that the suspension or revocation does not subject the licensee to vehicle impoundment under Vehicle Code Section 14602.6, and does not subject the licensee to increased vehicle liability insurance costs.
clauses.gap: This clause states only these two specific driver's-license protections created by subdivision (w); it does not address whether other consequences of a driver's license suspension under different statutes (for example, unrelated to Section 17520) would still apply, and it does not independently verify Vehicle Code Section 14602.6's own impoundment provisions.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: subdivision (w)(1)-(2), no impoundment and no increased insurance cost
citations.quote: The suspension or revocation of a driver’s license, including a commercial driver’s license, under this section shall not subject the licensee to vehicle impoundment pursuant to Section 14602.6 of the Vehicle Code.(2) Notwithstanding any other law, the suspension or revocation of a driver’s license, including a commercial driver’s license, under this section shall not subject the licensee to increased costs for vehicle liability insurance.
