clauses.body: This information sheet was prepared for reference in connection with the transaction involving {{propertyAddress}} between {{sellerName}} and {{buyerName}}, and does not itself constitute a withholding certificate, escrow instructions, a Franchise Tax Board form, or tax advice about whether withholding applies to this transaction or in what amount. Prepared and reviewed as of {{dateSigned}}, at {{cityState}}.

clauses.title: Information and Background — Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act at Termination
clauses.body: I, {{employeeName}}, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment as {{jobTitle}} with {{companyName}}. This information sheet describes the Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act (POBR), California Government Code sections 3300 through 3313 — a chapter of statutes that applies specifically to peace officers within the meaning of the Penal Code sections it cross-references, and that provides procedural rights connected to interrogation, punitive action (including dismissal), administrative appeal, personnel-file entries, and enforcement, separate from the wrongful-termination and general personnel-record doctrines this project addresses elsewhere. It is not an administrative appeal, a request for a Skelly-type hearing, a personnel-file correction request, or a superior court filing, and completing it does not initiate, extend, or preserve any deadline under Government Code section 3304, section 3306, section 3306.5, or any other statute or memorandum of understanding. Completing it does not establish that {{companyName}} took, or failed to take, any specific action described in this sheet, or that any statement here is true.

clauses.title: Who POBR Covers: The Statute's Own Definition of 'Public Safety Officer'
clauses.body: The Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act defines its own scope by cross-reference to the Penal Code's peace-officer classification statutes, rather than by reference to any generic notion of a 'public employee' or 'government worker.' For purposes of the chapter, the term 'public safety officer' means all peace officers specified in a listed set of Penal Code sections, with two of those cross-referenced sections carrying their own internal exceptions for a particular subdivision. The Legislature's own findings, stated in this same section, describe the chapter's rights as a matter of statewide concern grounded in the need for stable employer-employee relations in law enforcement, and direct that the chapter applies to every public safety officer as so defined wherever situated within California.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the cross-reference itself; it does not independently look up or restate what job classifications each cross-referenced Penal Code section (830.1, 830.2, 830.3, 830.31, 830.32, 830.33, 830.34, 830.35, 830.36, 830.37, 830.38, 830.4, and 830.5) actually covers, or resolve the two internal subdivision exceptions the statute itself carries (an exception within 830.33 and a different exception within 830.35). Whether a particular job title or appointment falls within one of those cross-referenced categories is a fact- and title-specific question this clause does not resolve. This chapter, and this document, do not extend to public employees generally — only to peace officers within this specific statutory definition; a different state civil-service employee, or a non-sworn public employee, is not necessarily covered by POBR even though both work for a government employer, and this clause does not determine that any specific job classification is or is not covered.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3301 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act, definition of public safety officer
citations.quote: the term public safety officer means all peace officers specified in Sections 830.1, 830.2, 830.3, 830.31, 830.32, 830.33, except subdivision (e), 830.34, 830.35, except subdivision (c), 830.36, 830.37, 830.38, 830.4, and 830.5 of the Penal Code.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own Definition of 'Punitive Action'
clauses.body: POBR's protections connected to interrogation, administrative appeal, and the other rights this document describes are keyed to the statute's own defined term, 'punitive action.' The chapter states that, for its purposes, punitive action means any action that may lead to dismissal, demotion, suspension, reduction in salary, written reprimand, or transfer for purposes of punishment. Dismissal — the termination of a public safety officer's employment — is expressly listed as one form of punitive action within this definition, which is why POBR's administrative-appeal, investigation-deadline, and enforcement provisions reach a proposed or completed termination.
clauses.gap: The definition covers a transfer only when it is 'for purposes of punishment'; it does not state how to distinguish a punitive transfer from an ordinary operational reassignment, and this clause does not resolve that line-drawing question for any specific transfer. The same is true of a 'reduction in salary' that results from a routine, non-disciplinary pay-scale change versus one imposed as discipline. This clause states the statute's own definitional text; it does not determine that any specific action taken against any particular public safety officer was, or was not, punitive action within this definition.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3303 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act, definition of punitive action
citations.quote: For the purpose of this chapter, punitive action means any action that may lead to dismissal, demotion, suspension, reduction in salary, written reprimand, or transfer for purposes of punishment.

clauses.title: Right to Representation During an Interrogation That Could Lead to Punitive Action
clauses.body: When a formal written statement of charges has been filed, or when an interrogation focuses on matters likely to result in punitive action — which, as described above, includes dismissal — against a public safety officer, that officer has the right, on request, to be represented by a representative of their own choice, who may be present throughout the interrogation. The representative cannot be a person who is also subject to the same investigation, and cannot be required to disclose, or punished for refusing to disclose, information received from the officer in a noncriminal matter. The same statutory section states that this representation right, along with the rest of section 3303's interrogation conditions, does not apply to an officer's normal-course-of-duty supervisory contact, counseling, instruction, or informal verbal admonishment, and does not apply to an investigation concerned solely and directly with alleged criminal activity.
clauses.gap: The statute conditions the representation right on the interrogation 'focus[ing] on matters that are likely to result in punitive action'; it does not itself define how imminent or certain that likelihood must be before the right attaches, and this clause does not resolve that question for any specific conversation. It also carves the right out entirely for an investigation 'concerned solely and directly with alleged criminal activities' without further defining that phrase, and does not address how a mixed administrative-and-criminal investigation is treated. CourtListener's daily search quota was exhausted when this document was researched (a 429 rate-limit response reporting 125 requests/day used), so no case law interpreting these phrases was independently verified for this document; only the statute's own text is relied on here.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3303(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, right to a representative during an interrogation likely to result in punitive action
citations.quote: Upon the filing of a formal written statement of charges, or whenever an interrogation focuses on matters that are likely to result in punitive action against any public safety officer, that officer, at his or her request, shall have the right to be represented by a representative of his or her choice who may be present at all times during the interrogation.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3303 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, carve-out for routine supervisory contact and purely criminal investigations
citations.quote: This section shall not apply to any interrogation of a public safety officer in the normal course of duty, counseling, instruction, or informal verbal admonishment by, or other routine or unplanned contact with, a supervisor or any other public safety officer, nor shall this section apply to an investigation concerned solely and directly with alleged criminal activities.

clauses.title: Prohibition on Punitive Action for Exercising POBR or Grievance Rights
clauses.body: Separately from the administrative-appeal and investigation-deadline protections described elsewhere in this document, POBR itself prohibits subjecting a public safety officer to punitive action, denying the officer a promotion, or threatening either of those, because the officer lawfully exercised a right granted by this chapter or a right under an existing administrative grievance procedure. The same section clarifies that this protection does not stop an agency head from ordering an officer to cooperate with other agencies on criminal investigations, and that an officer who fails to comply with such an order may be officially charged with insubordination.
clauses.gap: The statute's text does not itself state the causation standard a public safety officer would need to show to establish that a punitive action was taken 'because of' the exercise of a chapter right or grievance right — for example, whether the protected exercise must be the sole cause, a substantial motivating factor, or merely a contributing factor. That causation-standard question is the kind of issue ordinarily resolved by case law, and CourtListener's daily search quota was exhausted when this document was researched, so no case law on this point was independently verified; only the statute's own text is relied on here.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, prohibition on punitive action for exercising POBR or grievance rights
citations.quote: No public safety officer shall be subjected to punitive action, or denied promotion, or be threatened with any such treatment, because of the lawful exercise of the rights granted under this chapter, or the exercise of any rights under any existing administrative grievance procedure.

clauses.title: Right to an Opportunity for Administrative Appeal Before Punitive Action, Including Dismissal
clauses.body: POBR states directly that no punitive action — a category that, as described elsewhere in this document, includes dismissal — and no denial of promotion on grounds other than merit, may be undertaken by a public agency against a public safety officer who has successfully completed the applicable probationary period, without providing that officer an opportunity for administrative appeal. This is the statute's core procedural protection against termination without process: before a permanent (non-probationary) public safety officer's dismissal becomes final, the officer must be given an opportunity to appeal it administratively.
clauses.gap: This right, by its own terms, applies only to a public safety officer who 'has successfully completed the probationary period that may be required by his or her employing agency' — the statute does not itself extend the same administrative-appeal guarantee to a probationary officer, and this clause does not determine whether a particular officer's probationary period, if any, had been completed at the relevant time. The statute also does not itself prescribe the procedure, format, or forum for the 'opportunity for administrative appeal' it requires; those details are typically set by the employing agency's own rules, a memorandum of understanding, or (for a chief of police specifically) the separate procedure in subdivision (c) of this same section, which this clause does not address.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, right to an opportunity for administrative appeal before punitive action
citations.quote:
No punitive action, nor denial of promotion on grounds other than merit, shall be undertaken by any public agency
 against any public safety officer who has successfully completed the probationary period that may be required by his or her employing agency without providing the public safety officer with an opportunity for administrative appeal.

clauses.title: One-Year Deadline to Complete an Investigation and Notify the Officer of Proposed Discipline, and Its Tolling Exceptions
clauses.body: Subject to specified exceptions, POBR bars a public agency from undertaking punitive action, or denying a promotion on grounds other than merit, for any act, omission, or other allegation of misconduct if the agency's investigation of that allegation is not completed within one year of the agency's discovery of the allegation by a person authorized to initiate an investigation. This one-year period applies only to misconduct occurring on or after January 1, 1998. Where the agency determines that discipline may be taken, the statute requires it to complete its investigation and notify the officer of the proposed discipline, by a Letter of Intent or Notice of Adverse Action, within that same year — but the statute does not require the agency to have actually imposed the discipline within the year, only to have completed the investigation and given that notice. The statute also lists specific circumstances that toll (pause) the one-year clock; among them, a pending criminal investigation or prosecution of the same act, omission, or allegation tolls the period for as long as that criminal matter is pending, and an officer may separately toll the period for a specified time by waiving it in writing.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes and describes only two of the statute's listed tolling grounds — a pending criminal investigation/prosecution, and a written waiver by the officer. The same subdivision lists additional, separately enumerated tolling grounds this clause does not quote: a multijurisdictional investigation requiring a reasonable extension, an investigation involving more than one employee requiring a reasonable extension, an investigation involving an incapacitated or otherwise unavailable employee, an investigation involving a matter in civil litigation naming the officer as a party defendant, an investigation involving a matter in criminal litigation where the complainant is a criminal defendant, and an investigation involving an allegation of workers' compensation fraud by the officer. This clause also does not address the separate reopening-for-new-evidence exception found elsewhere in this same section, or the 30-day notice-of-decision requirement that applies once discipline is decided upon, both of which are outside this clause's scope.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, one-year deadline to complete investigation and notify officer of proposed discipline
citations.quote: no punitive action, nor denial of promotion on grounds other than merit, shall be undertaken for any act, omission, or other allegation of misconduct if the investigation of the allegation is not completed within one year of the public agency’s discovery by a person authorized to initiate an investigation of the allegation of an act, omission, or other misconduct. This one-year limitation period shall apply only if the act, omission, or other misconduct occurred on or after January 1, 1998.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, one-year deadline does not require discipline to be imposed within the year
citations.quote: The public agency shall not be required to impose the discipline within that one-year period.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(d)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, tolling of the one-year deadline during a pending criminal investigation or prosecution
citations.quote: If the act, omission, or other allegation of misconduct is also the subject of a criminal investigation or criminal prosecution, the time during which the criminal investigation or criminal prosecution is pending shall toll the one-year time period.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3304(d)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, tolling of the one-year deadline by the officer's written waiver
citations.quote: If the public safety officer waives the one-year time period in writing, the time period shall be tolled for the period of time specified in the written waiver.

clauses.title: Right to Read and Sign an Adverse Personnel Comment Before Entry, and to File a 30-Day Written Response
clauses.body: POBR restricts how an adverse personnel comment reaches a public safety officer's file. No comment adverse to a public safety officer's interest may be entered into that officer's personnel file, or any other file used for personnel purposes by the employer, unless the officer has first read and signed the instrument containing the comment, acknowledging awareness of it — except that the entry may still be made if the officer, after reading it, refuses to sign, in which case that refusal itself is noted on the document and signed or initialed by the officer. Separately, once an adverse comment is entered, the officer has 30 days within which to file a written response to it, and that written response must be attached to, and accompany, the adverse comment in the file going forward.
clauses.gap: The statute does not itself define what makes a comment 'adverse' to an officer's interest, beyond the ordinary meaning of that phrase, and this clause does not resolve whether any specific comment about a particular officer would qualify. The right described here is a right to read, sign or note a refusal to sign, and to attach a written response — the statute's text quoted here does not itself state that filing a response causes the adverse comment to be removed, corrected, or given reduced weight; the personnel-file correction and inspection procedure in a separate section (addressed in a different clause of this document) is the mechanism this chapter provides for seeking correction or deletion of file material believed to be mistaken or unlawful.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3305 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, right to read and sign an adverse personnel comment before entry
citations.quote: No public safety officer shall have any comment adverse to his interest entered in his personnel file, or any other file used for any personnel purposes by his employer, without the public safety officer having first read and signed the instrument containing the adverse comment indicating he is aware of such comment, except that such entry may be made if after reading such instrument the public safety officer refuses to sign it.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3306 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, 30-day right to file a written response to an adverse personnel comment
citations.quote: A public safety officer shall have 30 days within which to file a written response to any adverse comment entered in his personnel file. Such written response shall be attached to, and shall accompany, the adverse comment.

clauses.title: Right to Inspect the Personnel File Used to Decide Termination or Other Discipline
clauses.body: POBR requires an employer, at reasonable times and reasonable intervals, on a public safety officer's request, during usual business hours, and with no loss of compensation to the officer, to permit that officer to inspect personnel files used or previously used to determine the officer's qualifications for employment, promotion, additional compensation, or termination or other disciplinary action. The statute also separately requires the employer to keep each officer's personnel file, or a true and correct copy of it, and to make the file or copy available within a reasonable period of time after the officer requests it. If, after examining the file, the officer believes a portion of it was mistakenly or unlawfully placed there, the officer may request in writing that it be corrected or deleted, describing the correction sought and the reasons for it; the employer then has 30 calendar days from that request to either grant it or state in writing its reasons for refusing, and either the officer's request or the employer's refusal becomes part of the personnel file.
clauses.gap: The statute requires inspection to occur 'at reasonable times and at reasonable intervals' and requires the file to be made available 'within a reasonable period of time' after a request — neither phrase is defined by a specific number of days in this section, unlike the 30-calendar-day deadline that applies once an officer has actually requested correction or deletion of file material. This clause does not resolve what interval or delay would, or would not, be 'reasonable' in any specific case, and does not address how this personnel-file inspection right interacts with the general (non-POBR) personnel-record inspection statute this corpus addresses in a separate Personnel and Payroll Record Retention Duration document and Employee's Request to Inspect Personnel and Payroll Records document, which apply more broadly to employees generally rather than specifically to public safety officers under this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3306.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, right to inspect personnel files used to decide termination or discipline
citations.quote: Every employer shall, at reasonable times and at reasonable intervals, upon the request of a public safety officer, during usual business hours, with no loss of compensation to the officer, permit that officer to inspect personnel files that are used or have been used to determine that officer’s qualifications for employment, promotion, additional compensation, or termination or other disciplinary action.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3306.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, employer's duty to keep and make available the personnel file
citations.quote: Each employer shall keep each public safety officer’s personnel file or a true and correct copy thereof , and shall make the file or copy thereof available within a reasonable period of time after a request therefor by the officer.

clauses.title: Enforcement: Superior Court Jurisdiction, Injunctive Relief, and a Civil Penalty for Malicious Violations
clauses.body: POBR gives the superior court initial jurisdiction over any proceeding a public safety officer brings against a public safety department for an alleged violation of the chapter. Where the court finds a violation, the statute directs it to render appropriate injunctive or other extraordinary relief to remedy the violation and prevent future violations of a like or similar nature, including a temporary restraining order, preliminary injunction, or permanent injunction prohibiting the department from taking punitive action against the officer. Beyond that injunctive relief, if the court finds that the department, or its employees, agents, or assigns acting within the scope of employment, maliciously violated a chapter provision with intent to injure the officer, the statute makes the department liable, for each violation, for a civil penalty of up to $25,000 awarded to the officer whose right was denied, plus reasonable attorney's fees as the court determines, and for actual damages where the evidence establishes them.
clauses.gap: The $25,000-per-violation civil penalty and fee-shifting remedy require the heightened showing that the violation was done 'maliciously' and 'with the intent to injure the public safety officer' — the ordinary injunctive relief available under subdivision (d)(1) does not require that showing, and this clause does not resolve where the line falls between an ordinary (non-malicious) violation and a malicious one. CourtListener's daily search quota was exhausted when this document was researched, so no case law construing 'maliciously violated ... with the intent to injure' was independently verified for this document; only the statute's own text is relied on here. This clause also does not address the statute's separate sanctions provision for a bad-faith or frivolous filing under this chapter, or any residual statute of limitations that might apply to filing such a proceeding, which this section's text does not itself state.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3309.5(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, superior court's initial jurisdiction over POBR violations
citations.quote: The superior court shall have initial jurisdiction over any proceeding brought by any public safety officer against any public safety department for alleged violations of this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3309.5(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, injunctive and extraordinary relief for a POBR violation
citations.quote: the court shall render appropriate injunctive or other extraordinary relief to remedy the violation and to prevent future violations of a like or similar nature, including, but not limited to, the granting of a temporary restraining order, preliminary injunction, or permanent injunction prohibiting the public safety department from taking any punitive action against the public safety officer.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 3309.5(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code, civil penalty up to $25,000 for a malicious POBR violation
citations.quote: upon a finding by a superior court that a public safety department, its employees, agents, or assigns, with respect to acts taken within the scope of employment, maliciously violated any provision of this chapter with the intent to injure the public safety officer, the public safety department shall, for each and every violation, be liable for a civil penalty not to exceed twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000) to be awarded to the public safety officer whose right or protection was denied and for reasonable attorney’s fees as may be determined by the court.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature Block — POBR at Termination Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{employeeName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes the Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act, California Government Code sections 3301, 3303, 3304, 3305, 3306, 3306.5, and 3309.5 — the statute's own definitions of "public safety officer" and "punitive action" (including dismissal), the interrogation-representation right, the prohibition on punitive action for exercising chapter or grievance rights, the right to an opportunity for administrative appeal before punitive action against a non-probationary officer, the one-year deadline (and certain tolling grounds) to complete an investigation and notify the officer of proposed discipline, the right to read, sign, and respond in writing to an adverse personnel comment, the right to inspect and obtain the personnel file used to decide termination or discipline, and the superior court enforcement mechanism including its civil penalty for a malicious violation. It does not itself determine that {{companyName}} did, or did not, comply with any provision of this chapter with respect to {{employeeName}}, is not an administrative appeal, grievance, personnel-file correction request, or court filing, is not filed with any agency or court by completing it, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting the actual statute, the employing agency's own rules or applicable memorandum of understanding, or a licensed attorney.]

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the driver-screening requirements California law imposes specifically on transportation network companies (TNCs) — online-platform businesses such as rideshare companies — under Public Utilities Code sections 5431, 5445.2, and 5445.3, a distinct statutory scheme from the general consumer-reporting-agency background check requirements (FCRA, ICRAA) and the Fair Chance Act conviction-history rules addressed elsewhere in this corpus. It states facts about what these sections require of {{companyName}} before it contracts with, employs, or retains {{employeeName}} as a participating driver. It does not itself conduct or report a background check, does not determine whether {{employeeName}} meets or fails any statutory criterion, and does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} what to do about any particular background-check result.

clauses.title: Who These Sections Cover — “Transportation Network Company” and “Participating Driver”
clauses.body: The Public Utilities Code defines a “participating driver” or “driver” as any person who uses a vehicle in connection with a transportation network company's online-enabled application or platform to connect with passengers. It defines a “transportation network company” broadly by function rather than by corporate form — an organization of any kind, including a corporation, limited liability company, partnership, or sole proprietor, operating in California that provides prearranged transportation services for compensation using an online-enabled application or platform to connect passengers with drivers using a personal vehicle. These definitions apply “for purposes of this article,” meaning Public Utilities Code Article 7 of Chapter 8 (sections 5430–5450), the article containing the driver background-check and licensing requirements described in this document.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the “participating driver” and “transportation network company” definitions in Public Utilities Code section 5431(a) and (c). It does not address the separate definitions in the same section for “personal vehicle,” “transportation network company insurance,” or “zero-emission vehicle,” and it does not independently verify how the California Public Utilities Commission's own regulatory decisions and general orders (which implement this article) may refine or apply these statutory terms in practice. It also does not determine whether any particular company or working arrangement meets this definition.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5431(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5431(a)
citations.quote: “Participating driver” or “driver” means any person who uses a vehicle in connection with a transportation network company’s online-enabled application or platform to connect with passengers.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5431(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5431(c)
citations.quote: “Transportation network company” means an organization, including, but not limited to, a corporation, limited liability company, partnership, sole proprietor, or any other entity, operating in California that provides prearranged transportation services for compensation using an online-enabled application or platform to connect passengers with drivers using a personal vehicle.

clauses.title: The Mandatory Background Check — Public Utilities Code § 5445.2(a)(1)
clauses.body: California law requires a transportation network company to conduct, or have a third party conduct, a local and national criminal background check for each participating driver. The check must include both the use of a multistate and multijurisdiction criminal records locator or other similar commercial nationwide database with validation, and a search of the United States Department of Justice National Sex Offender Public website. This is a background-check methodology requirement layered on top of, not a substitute for, the general California and federal background-check rules (ICRAA, FCRA, and the Fair Chance Act) addressed elsewhere in this corpus.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the statutory methodology requirement in Public Utilities Code section 5445.2(a)(1). The statute does not name specific approved commercial databases or vendors, does not state how frequently a background check must be repeated for a driver who continues to use the platform over time, and does not specify a maximum lookback period for the criminal records search itself (as opposed to the conviction-based disqualifications described in separate clauses of this document, which do carry stated time limits). Any California Public Utilities Commission general order or decision implementing this requirement in more operational detail was not independently verified for this document.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(a)(1)
citations.quote: A transportation network company shall conduct, or have a third party conduct, a local and national criminal background check for each participating driver that shall include both of the following:(A) The use of a multistate and multijurisdiction criminal records locator or other similar commercial nationwide database with validation.(B) A search of the United States Department of Justice National Sex Offender Public website.

clauses.title: Permanent Disqualification — Sex Offender Registration and Specified Convictions
clauses.body: California law bars a transportation network company from contracting with, employing, or retaining a driver who is currently registered on the United States Department of Justice National Sex Offender Public website, or who has been convicted of a violent felony as defined in Penal Code section 667.5, or of a violation of Penal Code section 236.1 (human trafficking), 11413, 11418, 11418.5, or 11419 (offenses involving weapons of mass destruction or related conduct). Unlike the seven-year lookback described elsewhere in this document, this bar is not stated to expire after any period of time.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the cross-referencing text of Public Utilities Code section 5445.2(a)(2); it does not independently quote or verify the underlying definitions in Penal Code sections 667.5, 236.1, 11413, 11418, 11418.5, or 11419 that establish which specific offenses trigger this bar — those definitions were not separately fetched and verified for this document. It also does not describe how a transportation network company confirms “current” sex-offender registration status in practice, or what recourse, if any, exists to challenge a disqualification based on an inaccurate record.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(a)(2)
citations.quote: A transportation network company shall not contract with, employ, or retain a driver if the driver meets either of the following criteria:(A) Is currently registered on the United States Department of Justice National Sex Offender Public website.(B) Has been convicted of any of the following offenses:(i) A violent felony, as defined in Section 667.5 of the Penal Code.(ii) A violation of Section 236.1, 11413, 11418, 11418.5, or 11419 of the Penal Code.

clauses.title: The Seven-Year Lookback Disqualifiers
clauses.body: Separately from the permanent bar, California law prohibits a transportation network company from contracting with, employing, or retaining a driver who has been convicted, within the previous seven years, of misdemeanor assault or battery, a domestic violence offense, driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, or a felony violation of specified bribery, fraud, forgery, perjury, embezzlement, grand theft, or election-law offenses identified by statutory cross-reference to the Penal Code and Elections Code.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the cross-referencing text of Public Utilities Code section 5445.2(a)(3). It does not independently quote or verify the specific Penal Code and Elections Code sections cross-referenced (Elections Code section 18540; Penal Code sections 67, 68, 85, 86, 92, 93, 137, 138, 165, 518, 530, 484(a), and 487(a)) to confirm exactly which conduct those sections define — those definitions were not separately fetched for this document. The statutory text quoted here does not itself state whether the seven-year period runs from the date of conviction, sentencing, or some other event; that computation question is not resolved by this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(a)(3)
citations.quote: A transportation network company shall not contract with, employ, or retain a driver if the driver has been convicted of any of the following offenses within the previous seven years:(A) Misdemeanor assault or battery.(B) A domestic violence offense.(C) Driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs.(D) A felony violation of Section 18540 of the Elections Code, or of Section 67, 68, 85, 86, 92, 93, 137, 138, 165, 518, or 530 of, subdivision (a) of Section 484 of, or subdivision (a) of Section 487 of, the Penal Code.

clauses.title: Out-of-State Convictions Count, and Companies May Impose Stricter Standards
clauses.body: The permanent bar and the seven-year lookback disqualifiers described elsewhere in this document are not limited to California convictions: they apply to a conviction of any offense committed in another jurisdiction that includes all of the elements of any of the disqualifying offenses. Separately, the statute confirms it does not prevent a transportation network company from imposing additional screening standards beyond what state law requires.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Public Utilities Code section 5445.2(a)(4) and (a)(5). The statute does not itself state who performs the element-by-element comparison between an out-of-state offense and its California disqualifying-offense counterpart, or what happens when that comparison is disputed. This document does not identify what additional standards, if any, a particular transportation network company has chosen to impose — subdivision (a)(5) only confirms that companies are not barred from doing so.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(a)(4)
citations.quote: Paragraphs (2) and (3) apply with respect to a conviction of any offense committed in another jurisdiction that includes all of the elements of any of the offenses described or defined in those paragraphs.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(a)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(a)(5)
citations.quote: This section shall not be interpreted to prevent a transportation network company from imposing additional standards.

clauses.title: The Penalty for Noncompliance
clauses.body: A transportation network company that violates, or fails to comply with, Public Utilities Code section 5445.2 is subject to a penalty of not less than one thousand dollars ($1,000) nor more than five thousand dollars ($5,000) for each offense.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the penalty amount stated in Public Utilities Code section 5445.2(b). It does not identify the enforcing body, the procedure for assessing or contesting a penalty, or whether “for each offense” means each disqualified driver, each violation of the check requirement, or some other unit — the statutory text does not define that phrase further. It does not address whether an individual driver or passenger has any private right of action distinct from this penalty provision, and it does not state whether the dollar amounts have been adjusted since the statute's last amendment.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(b)
citations.quote: A transportation network company that violates, or fails to comply with, this section is subject to a penalty of not less than one thousand dollars ($1,000) nor more than five thousand dollars ($5,000) for each offense.

clauses.title: A Narrow Carve-Out From ICRAA's Consumer-Reporting Rules
clauses.body: California's Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act (ICRAA) normally restricts to whom an investigative consumer reporting agency may furnish a report. Public Utilities Code section 5445.2(c) creates a specific exception for transportation network company background checks: notwithstanding Civil Code section 1786.12, an investigative consumer reporting agency may furnish an investigative consumer report to a transportation network company about a person seeking to become a participating driver, regardless of whether that driver is to be an employee or an independent contractor of the company. The statute further states that Civil Code section 1786.18(a)(7) does not apply to a report furnished to a transportation network company under this exception.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the cross-referencing exception language in Public Utilities Code section 5445.2(c); it does not independently quote or verify the underlying text of Civil Code section 1786.12 (the general list of permissible recipients of an investigative consumer report) or section 1786.18(a)(7) (the provision this exception disapplies) — neither was separately fetched for this document. This exception is narrow: it addresses only who may receive the report and one specific ICRAA provision; this clause does not establish that ICRAA's other requirements (such as disclosure and certification obligations, addressed in this corpus's separate ICRAA information sheet) cease to apply to a transportation network company's background check.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(c)(1)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding Section 1786.12 of the Civil Code, an investigative consumer reporting agency may furnish an investigative consumer report to a transportation network company about a person seeking to become a participating driver, regardless of whether the participating driver is to be an employee or an independent contractor of the transportation network company.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.2(c)(2)
citations.quote: Paragraph (7) of subdivision (a) of Section 1786.18 of the Civil Code does not apply to an investigative consumer report furnished to a transportation network company pursuant to paragraph (1).

clauses.title: The Valid Driver's License Requirement
clauses.body: Separately from the criminal background check, California law requires a participating driver to possess a valid driver's license issued by the State of California, or, for a nonresident active-duty military member or their nonresident dependent, a valid driver's license issued by the state or territory of residence, subject to additional background-check and reporting conditions stated in the same section.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Public Utilities Code section 5445.3(a)(1), the general California-license requirement, but does not quote the full nonresident-military-member exception and its accompanying conditions in section 5445.3(a)(2), or the notice-of-Vehicle-Code-provisions requirement in section 5445.3(b). The statute does not require a commercial driver's license or any particular license class or endorsement; this clause does not address vehicle-specific licensing requirements that may exist under other law.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.3(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Pub. Util. Code § 5445.3(a)(1)
citations.quote: A participating driver is required to possess either of the following:(1) A valid driver’s license issued by the State of California.

clauses.title: Signature and Certification
Purpose of This Removal of a Trustee Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the California statutory framework governing removal of a trustee, as background in connection with {{trustName}}, executed {{originalTrustDate}}, for which {{trusteeName}} serves or has been asked to serve as trustee and {{successorTrusteeName}} is referenced as a successor for identification only. {{beneficiaryName}} and {{petitionerName}} are likewise referenced for identification only, and any reference to {{countyOfFiling}} or {{courtCaseNumber}} identifies where and under what number a removal proceeding may be or has been filed. This document covers the statutory grounds on which a court may remove a trustee, who may seek removal and by what pathways, the court's own-motion authority to remove an unlicensed professional fiduciary, the circumstances that create a vacancy in the office of trustee, and the cost-shifting and interim-protection rules that apply while a removal petition is pending. It does not itself remove any trustee, does not itself constitute a petition filed with any court, and does not evaluate whether grounds for removal exist for {{trusteeName}} or any other trustee of {{trustName}} or any other trust. This is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about a specific trustee's removal.

clauses.title: Three Pathways by Which a Trustee May Be Removed
clauses.body: California Probate Code § 15642(a) identifies three distinct pathways by which a trustee of {{trustName}} may be removed from office: in accordance with a removal mechanism the trust instrument itself provides, by the court acting on its own motion, or on a petition filed under Probate Code § 17200 by a settlor, a cotrustee, or a beneficiary. These pathways are not mutually exclusive, and the statute does not require that a trust instrument address removal at all before the other two pathways become available. Probate Code § 17200(b)(10) separately confirms that appointing or removing a trustee, and § 17200(b)(11) accepting a trustee's resignation, are among the purposes for which a petition concerning a trust's internal affairs may be brought.
clauses.gap: Section 15642(a) does not itself specify a filing fee, a required notice period, or the form of a petition brought under Section 17200; those procedural requirements come from other Probate Code sections, the Judicial Council forms, and the California Rules of Court, none of which this clause reproduces.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the three pathways by which a trustee may be removed: per the trust instrument, by the court's own motion, or on petition under Section 17200
citations.quote: A trustee may be removed in accordance with the trust instrument, by the court on its own motion, or on petition of a settlor, cotrustee, or beneficiary under Section 17200.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 17200(b)(10)-(11) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: appointing or removing a trustee, and accepting a trustee's resignation, as listed purposes of a Section 17200 petition
citations.quote: (10) Appointing or removing a trustee. (11) Accepting the resignation of a trustee.

clauses.title: General Statutory Grounds for Court-Ordered Removal
clauses.body: Probate Code § 15642(b) lists the grounds on which a court may remove a trustee. Apart from the disqualified-person ground addressed separately in this document, those grounds include a breach of trust, insolvency or other unfitness to administer the trust, hostility or lack of cooperation among cotrustees that impairs administration, a trustee's failure or decline to act, and compensation that is excessive under the circumstances. The statute also lists a trustee's substantial inability — as determined under Probate Code Division 2, Part 17 (commencing with § 810) — to manage the trust's financial resources or otherwise properly execute the duties of the office, a trustee's substantial inability to resist fraud or undue influence, and, as a catch-all, 'other good cause.' For a trustee who holds the power to revoke the trust, the statute specifies that substantial inability to manage financial resources or to resist fraud or undue influence may not be proved solely by isolated incidents of negligence or improvidence.
clauses.gap: The statute states these as grounds a court may act on; it does not itself define terms such as 'unfit to administer the trust' or 'excessive' compensation, does not guarantee that removal will be ordered whenever a listed ground is shown, and does not address how these grounds interact with a no-contest clause or an exculpatory provision that a particular trust instrument might contain.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(b)(1)-(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: breach of trust, insolvency/unfitness, cotrustee hostility, failure to act, and excessive compensation as removal grounds
citations.quote: (b) The grounds for removal of a trustee by the court include the following: (1) Where the trustee has committed a breach of the trust. (2) Where the trustee is insolvent or otherwise unfit to administer the trust. (3) Where hostility or lack of cooperation among cotrustees impairs the administration of the trust. (4) Where the trustee fails or declines to act. (5) Where the trustee’s compensation is excessive under the circumstances.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(b)(7)-(9) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: substantial inability to manage trust resources or execute duties, substantial inability to resist fraud or undue influence, and 'other good cause' as removal grounds
citations.quote: (7) If, as determined under Part 17 (commencing with Section 810) of Division 2, the trustee is substantially unable to manage the trust’s financial resources or is otherwise substantially unable to execute properly the duties of the office. When the trustee holds the power to revoke the trust, substantial inability to manage the trust’s financial resources or otherwise execute properly the duties of the office may not be proved solely by isolated incidents of negligence or improvidence. (8) If the trustee is substantially unable to resist fraud or undue influence. When the trustee holds the power to revoke the trust, substantial inability to resist fraud or undue influence may not be proved solely by isolated incidents of negligence or improvidence. (9) For other good cause.

clauses.title: Removal Ground for a Sole Trustee Who Is a Disqualified Person
clauses.body: Probate Code § 15642(b)(6) provides a distinct removal ground where the sole trustee of {{trustName}} is a person described in Probate Code § 21380(a) — the categories of persons (including an instrument's drafter, a fiduciary who transcribed it, and certain care custodians) to whom a donative transfer is separately presumed the product of fraud or undue influence — regardless of whether that person is also the transferee of a donative transfer under the instrument. This removal ground does not apply if the court finds, based on evidence of the settlor's intent and all other facts and circumstances, that it is consistent with the settlor's intent for the trustee to continue serving and that this intent was not the product of fraud or undue influence, subject to three narrower statutory exceptions concerning family or cohabitant relationships, a signed Certificate of Independent Review, or court approval under a conservatorship-transfer procedure. For purposes of this ground, 'related by blood or marriage' includes persons within the seventh degree, and any waiver by the settlor of the ground itself is against public policy and void. The paragraph does not apply to instruments that became irrevocable on or before January 1, 1994.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the operative sentence of paragraph (6) and the definitional subdivision (f); it does not reproduce the full text of the three exceptions in subparagraphs (A)-(C) of paragraph (6), including the exact wording required for a Certificate of Independent Review, nor the separate donative-transfer presumption in Probate Code § 21380 itself, which this corpus addresses in its Disqualified-Transferee Donative Transfer Presumption information sheet as a distinct question from removal from the office of trustee.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(b)(6) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the removal ground applicable to a sole trustee described in Section 21380(a), and the settlor-intent finding that displaces it absent statutory exceptions
citations.quote: (6) Where the sole trustee is a person described in subdivision (a) of Section 21380, whether or not the person is the transferee of a donative transfer by the transferor, unless, based upon any evidence of the intent of the settlor and all other facts and circumstances, which shall be made known to the court, the court finds that it is consistent with the settlor’s intent that the trustee continue to serve and that this intent was not the product of fraud or undue influence. Any waiver by the settlor of this provision is against public policy and shall be void.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the definition of 'related by blood or marriage' for purposes of the removal statute
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, the term “related by blood or marriage” shall include persons within the seventh degree.

clauses.title: Court's Own-Motion Authority to Remove an Unlicensed Professional Fiduciary Trustee
clauses.body: Probate Code § 17200(c) gives the court an own-motion basis to question a trustee's continued service that is independent of the grounds listed in § 15642(b). Under that subdivision, the court may set and give notice of an order to show cause why a trustee who is a professional fiduciary required to be licensed under Business and Professions Code § 6500 et seq. should not be removed for failing to hold a valid, unexpired, unsuspended license. This authority does not require a settlor, cotrustee, or beneficiary to file a petition.
clauses.gap: Section 17200(c) authorizes but does not require the court to act on its own motion, does not itself define 'professional fiduciary' or reproduce the licensing requirements of Business and Professions Code § 6500 et seq., and does not address removal of a professional fiduciary trustee on any ground other than an unlicensed status.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 17200(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's own-motion authority to set an order to show cause why an unlicensed professional fiduciary trustee should not be removed
citations.quote: The court may, on its own motion, set and give notice of an order to show cause why a trustee who is a professional fiduciary, and who is required to be licensed under Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 6500) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code, should not be removed for failing to hold a valid, unexpired, unsuspended license.

clauses.title: Circumstances That Create a Vacancy in the Office of Trustee
clauses.body: Probate Code § 15643 identifies eight circumstances under which a vacancy exists in the office of trustee of {{trustName}}: the person named as trustee rejects the trust; the person named as trustee cannot be identified or does not exist; the trustee resigns or is removed; the trustee dies; a conservator or guardian of the person or estate of an individual trustee is appointed; the trustee is the subject of an order for relief in bankruptcy; a trust company's charter is revoked or its powers suspended for 30 days or more; or a receiver is appointed for a trust company and the appointment is not vacated within 30 days. A trustee's removal under § 15642 is therefore only one of several statutory events that can create a vacancy that must then be filled.
clauses.gap: Section 15643 identifies when a vacancy exists but does not itself address how a vacancy is filled once it arises, does not specify any deadline by which a vacancy must be filled, and does not by itself suspend trust administration during the vacancy — how a vacancy created by any of these eight circumstances is filled is governed separately by Probate Code § 15660, which is not reproduced in this document because this corpus already addresses it, with a byte-verified quotation, in the Revocable Living Trust document's 'Filling a Vacancy in the Office of Trustee' clause.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15643 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the eight circumstances that create a vacancy in the office of trustee
citations.quote: There is a vacancy in the office of trustee in any of the following circumstances: (a) The person named as trustee rejects the trust. (b) The person named as trustee cannot be identified or does not exist. (c) The trustee resigns or is removed. (d) The trustee dies. (e) A conservator or guardian of the person or estate of an individual trustee is appointed. (f) The trustee is the subject of an order for relief in bankruptcy. (g) A trust company’s charter is revoked or powers are suspended, if the revocation or suspension is to be in effect for a period of 30 days or more. (h) A receiver is appointed for a trust company if the appointment is not vacated within a period of 30 days.

clauses.title: Cost-Shifting Rules Tied to a Removal Proceeding
clauses.body: Probate Code § 15642 ties an award of costs and attorney's fees to two specific findings made in a removal proceeding, rather than creating a general fee-shifting rule for every removal petition. Under subdivision (c), if the court finds — in connection with the disqualified-person ground in paragraph (6) of subdivision (b) — that the trustee's designation was not consistent with the settlor's intent or was the product of fraud or undue influence, the trustee being removed bears all costs of the proceeding, including reasonable attorney's fees. Under subdivision (d), if the court instead finds that a petition for removal was filed in bad faith and that removal would be contrary to the settlor's intent, the court may order that the person or persons who sought removal bear all or part of the proceeding's costs, including reasonable attorney's fees.
clauses.gap: Subdivisions (c) and (d) each shift fees only on the specific findings described; the statute does not create any general fee-shifting rule for a removal proceeding brought on the other grounds listed in subdivision (b), where each side otherwise bears its own attorney's fees under the general California rule absent some other statutory or trust-instrument basis for shifting them.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: fee-shifting against the trustee on a finding under the disqualified-person ground in paragraph (6) of subdivision (b)
citations.quote: If, pursuant to paragraph (6) of subdivision (b), the court finds that the designation of the trustee was not consistent with the intent of the settlor or was the product of fraud or undue influence, the person being removed as trustee shall bear all costs of the proceeding, including reasonable attorney’s fees.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: fee-shifting against a petitioner on a finding that a removal petition was filed in bad faith and contrary to the settlor's intent
citations.quote: If the court finds that the petition for removal of the trustee was filed in bad faith and that removal would be contrary to the settlor’s intent, the court may order that the person or persons seeking the removal of the trustee bear all or any part of the costs of the proceeding, including reasonable attorney’s fees.

clauses.title: Interim Protection of Trust Property While a Removal Petition Is Pending
clauses.body: Probate Code § 15642(e) addresses the period between the filing of a removal petition concerning {{trustName}} and the court's decision, including any appellate review. If it appears to the court that trust property or a beneficiary's interests may suffer loss or injury during that period, the court — on its own motion or on petition of a cotrustee or beneficiary — may compel the trustee whose removal is sought to surrender trust property to a cotrustee, a receiver, or a temporary trustee, and may suspend the trustee's powers to the extent the court deems necessary.
clauses.gap: Section 15642(e) authorizes this interim relief 'to the extent the court deems necessary' but does not itself specify a standard of proof, a required showing of irreparable harm, or a procedure such as an ex parte application for seeking the relief before a full hearing on removal; those procedural mechanics are not addressed in this section and are not reproduced here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 15642(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's authority to compel surrender of trust property to a cotrustee, receiver, or temporary trustee, and to suspend the trustee's powers, pending decision on a removal petition
citations.quote: If it appears to the court that trust property or the interests of a beneficiary may suffer loss or injury pending a decision on a petition for removal of a trustee and any appellate review, the court may, on its own motion or on petition of a cotrustee or beneficiary, compel the trustee whose removal is sought to surrender trust property to a cotrustee or to a receiver or temporary trustee. The court may also suspend the powers of the trustee to the extent the court deems necessary.

clauses.title: About This Occupational Noise Exposure Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Occupational Noise Exposure and Hearing Conservation Information Sheet describes California's Cal/OSHA regulation controlling workplace noise exposure, Article 105 of the General Industry Safety Orders (8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 5095–5100), as those requirements relate to the working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.

It summarizes selected requirements of that regulation: which workplaces and industries are covered and which are exempt from specific provisions, the action level and permissible exposure limits that trigger the regulation's duties, the hearing conservation program and noise monitoring requirements, the audiometric testing program, the response required when an employee experiences a standard threshold shift in hearing, the duty to provide hearing protectors, employee training and information-access requirements, and recordkeeping and records-access requirements.

{{companyName}} has identified {{programAdministratorName}} as the person responsible for {{companyName}}'s hearing conservation program, where one is required.

This information sheet is not itself {{companyName}}'s hearing conservation program, does not itself satisfy any written-program or recordkeeping requirement of Article 105, and does not determine whether any particular job, work area, or noise level at {{companyName}} triggers the regulation's requirements.

clauses.title: Which Workplaces Article 105 Covers, and the Limits of Its Industry Exemption
clauses.body: Article 105 establishes requirements for controlling occupational exposures to noise. Agriculture, construction, and oil and gas well drilling and servicing operations are exempt from the provisions of Sections 5097 through 5100 — that is, from the hearing conservation program, audiometric testing, hearing protector, and recordkeeping requirements. The regulation's text does not list Section 5096, which sets the permissible noise exposure limits, among the sections from which those industries are exempted.
clauses.gap: This clause states 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5095(a)'s own scope and exemption language; because that subsection exempts agriculture, construction, and oil and gas well drilling and servicing operations only from "the provisions of Sections 5097 through 5100," and does not name Section 5096, this document does not conclude that those industries are exempt from Section 5096's exposure-limit and control-measure duties, and it does not resolve how the exemption interacts with any industry-specific safety order that may separately govern noise in those sectors. It also does not determine whether any particular employer or work area falls within an exempt classification.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5095(a) (Occupational Noise — General)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5095(a), scope and application; industry exemption
citations.quote: (a) Scope and Application. Article 105 establishes requirements for controlling occupational exposures to noise. Agriculture, construction, and oil and gas well drilling and servicing operations are exempt from the provisions of Sections 5097 through 5100.

clauses.title: The Action Level and Criterion Sound Level That Trigger the Regulation's Duties
clauses.body: Article 105 defines the "action level" as an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 decibels measured on the A-scale, slow response, or equivalently, a dose of fifty percent. It defines the "criterion sound level" — the reference level used in calculating an employee's noise dose — as a sound level of 90 decibels. The action level of 85 dBA (TWA) is the threshold at which Article 105's hearing conservation program, monitoring, audiometric testing, and training duties are triggered for a given employee.
clauses.gap: This clause reproduces only the two defined terms most directly tied to when the regulation's duties apply. Section 5095(b) defines additional terms used elsewhere in Article 105 (including "audiogram," "audiologist," "baseline audiogram," "representative exposure," and "sound level meter") that this clause does not restate, and it does not describe the technical dose-calculation methodology in Appendix A referenced elsewhere in the regulation.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5095(b) (Occupational Noise — Definitions)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5095(b), definition of "Action Level"
citations.quote: Action Level. An 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 decibels measured on the A-scale, slow response, or equivalently, a dose of fifty percent.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5095(b) (Occupational Noise — Definitions)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5095(b), definition of "Criterion Sound Level"
citations.quote: Criterion Sound Level. A sound level of 90 decibels.

clauses.title: Permissible Noise Exposure Limits and the Required Order of Controls
clauses.body: Section 5096 requires protection against the effects of noise exposure whenever sound levels exceed those set out in the regulation's Table N-1, measured on the A-scale of a standard sound level meter at slow response. Table N-1 permits a sound level of 90 dBA for a full 8-hour workday, with the permitted exposure duration shortening as the sound level rises (for example, 95 dBA is permitted for 4 hours, and 100 dBA for 2 hours). Where sound levels exceed the table, feasible administrative or engineering controls must be used first; personal protective equipment is required only if those controls fail to bring sound levels within the table's limits. Noise with maxima recurring at intervals of one second or less is treated as continuous, and exposure to impulsive or impact noise may not exceed 140 dB peak sound pressure level.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Table N-1's anchor value (90 dBA for 8 hours) rather than reproducing the full table, which sets a permitted duration for every integer sound level from 90 through 115 dBA; it does not reproduce the table's footnoted formula for combining two or more periods of exposure at different sound levels (the sum of each period's exposure-to-permitted-duration ratio), which the regulation directs be used when noise levels vary during a shift. The quoted Table N-1 row preserves the source's own dot-leader table formatting exactly as published: "90........... 8-0...... 8.00" states that a sound level of 90 dBA is permitted for a duration of 8 hours 0 minutes (8.00 hours) -- the dots are typographic table-column leaders in the source, not part of the substantive text.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5096(a) (Exposure Limits for Noise)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5096(a), general exposure-limit trigger
citations.quote: (a) Protection against the effects of noise exposure shall be provided when the sound levels exceed those shown in Table N-1 of this section when measured on the A-scale of a standard sound level meter at slow response.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5096(b) (Exposure Limits for Noise)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5096(b), hierarchy of controls: engineering/administrative controls before PPE
citations.quote: (b) When employees are subjected to sound levels exceeding those listed in Table N-1 of this section, feasible administrative or engineering controls shall be utilized. If such controls fail to reduce sound levels within the levels of the table, personal protective equipment shall be provided and used to reduce sound levels within the levels of the table.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5096, Table N-1 (Exposure Limits for Noise)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5096, Table N-1 — permitted duration at 90 dBA (quoted exactly as the source's own dot-leader table formatting renders it: sound level 90 dBA, permitted duration 8 hours 0 minutes, i.e. 8.00 hours)

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5096(c) (Exposure Limits for Noise)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5096(c), continuous-noise treatment
citations.quote: (c) If the variations in noise level involve maxima at intervals of 1 second or less, the noise is to be considered continuous.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5096(d) (Exposure Limits for Noise)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5096(d), impulsive/impact noise peak limit
citations.quote: (d) Exposure to impulsive or impact noise should not exceed 140 dB peak sound pressure level.

clauses.title: The Hearing Conservation Program Requirement and Noise Monitoring
clauses.body: An employer must administer a continuing, effective hearing conservation program whenever employee noise exposures equal or exceed an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 decibels (the action level), or equivalently a dose of fifty percent. When information indicates that an employee's exposure may equal or exceed that level, the employer must obtain noise measurements for the employees who may be exposed at or above it, using area or personal sampling. Affected employees or their representatives must be given an opportunity to observe any noise measurements taken under this requirement, and each employee exposed at or above the action level must be notified of the monitoring results.
clauses.gap: This clause states the program's overall trigger and the core monitoring, observation, and notification duties in Section 5097(a) and (b)(1), (b)(4), and (b)(5). It does not reproduce the more technical monitoring-method requirements in (b)(2) (when area sampling versus personal sampling must be used, the 80–130 dB integration range, and instrument calibration) or the circumstances requiring re-monitoring under (b)(3).

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5097(a) (Hearing Conservation Program — General)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(a), duty to administer a hearing conservation program
citations.quote: (a) General. The employer shall administer a continuing, effective hearing conservation program, as described in this section, whenever employee noise exposures equal or exceed an 8-hour time-weighted average sound level (TWA) of 85 decibels measured on the A-scale (slow response) or, equivalently, a dose of fifty percent.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5097(b)(1) (Hearing Conservation Program — Monitoring)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(b)(1), duty to obtain exposure measurements
citations.quote: (1) When information indicates that any employee's exposure may equal or exceed an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 decibels, the employer shall obtain measurements for employees who may be exposed at or above that level.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5097(b)(4) (Hearing Conservation Program — Monitoring)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(b)(4), employee opportunity to observe monitoring
citations.quote: The employer shall provide affected employees or their representatives with an opportunity to observe any measurements of employee noise exposure which are conducted pursuant to this section.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5097(b)(5) (Hearing Conservation Program — Monitoring)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(b)(5), duty to notify employees of monitoring results
citations.quote: The employer shall notify each employee exposed at or above the action level of the results of the monitoring.

clauses.title: The Audiometric Testing Program: Baseline Audiograms and Annual Testing
clauses.body: An employer must establish and maintain an audiometric testing program, at no cost to employees, making audiometric testing available to every employee whose noise exposure equals or exceeds the action level. For each such employee, the employer must establish a valid baseline audiogram against which later audiograms are compared; testing for that baseline must be preceded by at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise (a requirement that may instead be met by wearing hearing protectors that reduce the employee's exposure to 80 dBA or below during that period). Baseline testing must generally be made available within 6 months of an employee's first exposure at or above the action level (within 1 year if a mobile test van is used), and, after the baseline, the employer must obtain a new audiogram for each covered employee at least annually.
clauses.gap: This clause covers the core testing-program obligations in Section 5097(c)(1), (2), (5), (6), (8), and (10); it does not restate the technician-qualification requirements in (c)(3), the audiogram technical standards in (c)(4) (Appendix B), the historical June 1, 1983 compliance date noted in (c)(8), or the mobile-test-van interim hearing-protector proviso in (c)(9).

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5097(c)(1) (Hearing Conservation Program — Audiometric Testing)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(c)(1), duty to make audiometric testing available
citations.quote: (1) The employer shall establish and maintain an audiometric testing program as provided in this section by making audiometric testing available to all employees whose exposures equal or exceed the action level.

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(c)(2), testing provided at no cost
citations.quote: (2) The program shall be provided at no cost to employees.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5097(c)(5) (Hearing Conservation Program — Audiometric Testing)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(c)(5), baseline audiogram requirement
citations.quote: The employer shall establish for each employee exposed at or above the action level a valid baseline audiogram against which subsequent audiograms can be compared.

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(c)(6), 14-hour quiet period before baseline testing

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5097(c)(10) (Hearing Conservation Program — Audiometric Testing)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(c)(10), annual audiogram requirement
citations.quote: At least annually after obtaining the baseline audiogram, the employer shall obtain a new audiogram for each employee exposed at or above the action level.

clauses.title: Standard Threshold Shift: Definition, Notice, and Required Follow-Up
clauses.body: A "standard threshold shift" is defined as a change in hearing threshold, relative to an employee's baseline audiogram, averaging 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000, and 4000 Hz in either ear. If a comparison of an employee's annual audiogram to the baseline audiogram shows a standard threshold shift, the employee must be informed of that fact in writing within 21 days of the determination. Unless a physician determines the shift is not work-related or aggravated by occupational noise exposure, the employer must ensure follow-up steps are taken: an employee not already using hearing protectors must be fitted with them, trained in their use and care, and required to use them, and an employee already using hearing protectors must be refitted and retrained and, if necessary, provided with protectors offering greater attenuation.
clauses.gap: This clause states the standard-threshold-shift definition in Section 5097(d)(8), the 21-day written-notice duty in (d)(4), and the general follow-up obligation in (d)(5) and (d)(5)(A). It does not reproduce every follow-up sub-step in (d)(5)(B) through (D) (referral for clinical evaluation and notice of a suspected unrelated ear pathology) in full, the audiogram re-evaluation and substitution rules in (d)(2), (d)(6), and (d)(7), or the age-correction (presbycusis) procedure in (d)(9) and Appendix F, which may affect whether a given audiogram change is treated as a standard threshold shift.
