citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(d)(8), definition of "standard threshold shift"
citations.quote: As used in this section, a standard threshold shift is a change in hearing threshold relative to the baseline audiogram of an average of 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz in either ear.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5097(d)(4) (Hearing Conservation Program — Evaluation of Audiogram)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(d)(4), 21-day written notice of a standard threshold shift
citations.quote: If a comparison of the annual audiogram to the baseline audiogram indicates a standard threshold shift as defined by Section 5097(d)(8), the employee shall be informed of this fact, in writing, within 21 days of the determination.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5097(d)(5) (Hearing Conservation Program — Evaluation of Audiogram)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(d)(5), follow-up steps required after a standard threshold shift
citations.quote: Unless a physician determines that the standard threshold shift is not work related or aggravated by occupational noise exposure, the employer shall ensure that the following steps are taken when a standard threshold shift occurs:

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5097(d)(5)(A) (Hearing Conservation Program — Evaluation of Audiogram)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5097(d)(5)(A), fitting and training an employee not yet using protectors
citations.quote: An employee not using hearing protectors shall be fitted with hearing protectors, trained in their use and care, and required to use them; and

clauses.title: Hearing Protectors: Availability, Cost, Selection, and Required Attenuation
clauses.body: An employer must make hearing protectors available, at no cost, to every employee exposed to an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 decibels or greater, and must replace them as necessary. Employees who are given a choice must be allowed to select their hearing protectors from a variety of suitable types the employer provides. Hearing protectors must attenuate an employee's exposure to at least an 8-hour time-weighted average of 90 decibels, as required for the exposure-limit control hierarchy under Section 5096(b); for an employee who has experienced a standard threshold shift, hearing protectors must instead attenuate exposure to 85 decibels or below.
clauses.gap: This clause states the core availability, cost, selection, and attenuation-level duties in Section 5098(a)(1), (a)(3), and (b)(2)-(3). It does not restate the specific circumstances under which hearing protector use becomes mandatory rather than merely available under (a)(2)(A)-(B), the employer's training and proper-fitting duties in (a)(4)-(5), or the attenuation-evaluation methodology in (b)(1) and Appendix E that this document does not reproduce.

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5098(a)(1), duty to provide hearing protectors at no cost
citations.quote: (1) Employers shall make hearing protectors available to all employees exposed to an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 decibels or greater at no cost to the employees. Hearing protectors shall be replaced as necessary.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5098(a)(3) (Hearing Protectors — General)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5098(a)(3), employee's opportunity to select from a variety of protectors
citations.quote: (3) Employees shall be given the opportunity to select their hearing protectors from a variety of suitable hearing protectors provided by the employer.

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5098(b)(2), 90 dBA required attenuation level
citations.quote: (2) Hearing protectors must attenuate employee exposure at least to an 8-hour time-weighted average of 90 decibels as required by Section 5096(b).

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5098(b)(3) (Hearing Protectors — Attenuation)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5098(b)(3), 85 dBA attenuation level after a standard threshold shift
citations.quote: (3) For employees who have experienced a standard threshold shift, hearing protectors must attenuate employee exposures to an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 decibels or below.

clauses.title: Employee Training and Access to the Regulation's Text
clauses.body: An employer must institute a training program for every employee exposed to noise at or above an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 dBA and must ensure employee participation in it. The training must be repeated annually for each employee included in the hearing conservation program. Separately, the employer must make available to affected employees or their representatives copies of Article 105 itself, and must post a copy of it in the workplace.
clauses.gap: This clause states the training-program trigger and annual-repetition duty in Section 5099(a)(1)-(2), and the duty to make Article 105's text available and post it in (b)(1). It does not restate the specific training-content topics listed in (a)(3)(A)-(C) (the effects of noise on hearing; the purpose, types, and use of hearing protectors; and the purpose of audiometric testing), and it does not address the employer's separate duties in (b)(2)-(3) to pass along federal OSHA informational materials and to make training materials available to specified government representatives upon request.

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5099(a)(1), duty to institute and ensure participation in training
citations.quote: (1) The employer shall institute a training program for all employees who are exposed to noise at or above an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 dBA, and shall ensure employee participation in such program.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5099(a)(2) (Training Program — General)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5099(a)(2), annual repetition of training
citations.quote: (2) The training program shall be repeated annually for each employee included in the hearing conservation program.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5099(b)(1) (Training Program — Access to Information)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5099(b)(1), duty to provide and post the regulation's text
citations.quote: (1) The employer shall make available to affected employees or their representatives copies of Article 105 and shall also post a copy in the workplace.

clauses.title: Recordkeeping: Retention Periods, Access, and Transfer on Change of Employer
clauses.body: An employer must keep an accurate record of every employee exposure measurement required under the monitoring provisions. Noise exposure measurement records must be retained for 2 years, while audiometric test records must be retained for the duration of the affected employee's employment. All records required under this recordkeeping section must be made available on request to employees, former employees, an individual employee's designated representative, and any authorized representative of the Chief of the Division. If the employer ceases doing business, it must transfer these records to the successor employer, who must then retain them for whatever portion of the applicable retention period remains.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general exposure-measurement recordkeeping duty in Section 5100(a), the two differing retention periods in (d)(1)-(2), the access right in (e), and the business-transfer duty in (f). It does not restate the specific audiogram record-content requirements in (b)(2)(A)-(E) (employee name and job classification, audiogram date, examiner's name, calibration date, and most recent exposure assessment), the audiometric-test-room measurement recordkeeping duty in (c), or the substance of the cross-referenced access procedures in 8 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 3204(a)-(h), which this document does not independently verify or reproduce.

clauses.title: California's Choice-of-Law Rule for Out-of-State Corporations — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet relates to {{companyName}}, a {{entityType}} originally formed under the law of {{stateOfFormation}}, with a principal office at {{principalOfficeAddress}}. It describes California Corporations Code Section 2115, sometimes called California's "pseudo-foreign corporation" or "quasi-California corporation" statute. That statute applies a specified list of California General Corporation Law provisions to a foreign (out-of-state) corporation, in place of the corporate law of its state of incorporation, when the corporation's average property, payroll, and sales factors and its shareholder base are predominantly connected to California, subject to statutory exemptions. This document is not this project's Foreign LLC/Corporation Qualification to Transact Business in California information sheet. That document addresses the separate statutory requirement, under Chapter 21 of the General Corporation Law, that a foreign corporation obtain a certificate of qualification from the Secretary of State before transacting intrastate business in California, and the consequences of transacting business without qualifying. Section 2115 is a different statute, located in Chapter 21.5 rather than Chapter 21, and it operates independently of whether a corporation has qualified, or is even required to qualify, to transact business in California; a corporation can be subject to Section 2115's governance rules regardless of its qualification status, and qualifying to transact business does not itself trigger or avoid Section 2115. This information sheet is educational only. It does not determine whether {{companyName}}, or any other specific foreign corporation, currently meets Section 2115's statutory test, and it does not calculate any corporation's property, payroll, or sales apportionment factors or the residency of its shareholders of record.

clauses.title: The Two-Part Statutory Test for Whether Section 2115 Applies to a Foreign Corporation
clauses.body: California Corporations Code Section 2115 applies its governance requirements to a foreign corporation (other than a foreign association or foreign nonprofit corporation, but including a foreign parent corporation even if the parent itself does not transact intrastate business) only if two conditions are both met with respect to the corporation's latest full income year. First, the average of its property factor, payroll factor, and sales factor — the same three-factor apportionment formula used, or that would be used, on the corporation's California franchise tax return — must be more than 50 percent. Second, more than one-half of the corporation's outstanding voting securities must be held of record by persons with California addresses appearing on the corporation's books, measured as of the record date for its latest shareholders' meeting during that income year, or, if no meeting was held, as of the last day of that income year. Both conditions must be satisfied; the statute states the test in the conjunctive ("and"). For a parent corporation, the three-factor calculation is made on a consolidated, unitary basis with subsidiaries in which the parent owns more than 50 percent of the voting shares, after eliminating intercompany transactions and adjusting for minority ownership percentages.
clauses.gap: This clause states the statutory test itself; it does not apply that test to any specific corporation. Determining whether a given foreign corporation meets the more-than-50-percent property/payroll/sales average requires that corporation's own apportionment data (or the data it would use if it filed a separate California return), and determining the voting-securities prong requires that corporation's specific shareholder-of-record list as of a specific record date. The statute's cross-reference to the property, payroll, and sales factor definitions in Revenue and Taxation Code Sections 25129, 25132, and 25134 is repeated here for identification only; those three Revenue and Taxation Code sections were not independently fetched or verified in this research pass, so this clause does not represent their substantive apportionment rules as separately verified primary-source text.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, two-part test for applying Section 2115 to a foreign corporation
citations.quote: (a) A foreign corporation (other than a foreign association or foreign nonprofit corporation but including a foreign parent corporation even though it does not itself transact intrastate business) is subject to the requirements of subdivision (b) commencing on the date specified in subdivision (d) and continuing until the date specified in subdivision (e) if: (1) The average of the property factor, the payroll factor, and the sales factor (as defined in Sections 25129, 25132, and 25134 of the Revenue and Taxation Code) with respect to it is more than 50 percent during its latest full income year and (2) more than one-half of its outstanding voting securities are held of record by persons having addresses in this state appearing on the books of the corporation on the record date for the latest meeting of shareholders held during its latest full income year or, if no meeting was held during that year, on the last day of the latest full income year.

clauses.title: How Nominee-Held Securities Are Counted for Section 2115's Voting-Securities Test
clauses.body: Section 2115 contains a specific rule for securities held in "nominee name" when measuring whether more than one-half of a foreign corporation's outstanding voting securities are held of record by persons with California addresses. Securities that, to the issuer's knowledge, are held in the names of broker-dealers, broker-dealer nominees (including clearing corporations), banks, or other entities holding as nominee for a beneficial owner are not counted as "outstanding" for this purpose — unless the foreign corporation requests all of its nominee holders to certify, for each beneficial owner, the number of shares held for beneficial owners with California addresses versus non-California addresses. If the corporation obtains that certification, the certified shares are then counted as outstanding and attributed to California or non-California addresses as certified, and the certification must be retained with the shareholder record and made available for inspection and copying in the same manner as the shareholder record itself. A current beneficial-owner list a nominee holder or its agent provides under federal Securities and Exchange Commission Rule 14b-1(b)(3) or 14b-2(b)(3) (as those rules stood on January 6, 1992) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 is stated to be an acceptable certification for this purpose.
clauses.gap: This clause describes a mechanical counting and certification rule, not a substantive right or obligation independent of the Section 2115(a) test described in a separate clause of this information sheet; it applies only to measuring the voting-securities prong of that test, not the separate property/payroll/sales prong. The federal Securities Exchange Act rules referenced (Rule 14b-1(b)(3) and Rule 14b-2(b)(3)) are cross-referenced by the California statute's own text as quoted here; this pass did not independently fetch or verify the text of those federal SEC rules from a federal primary source, so this clause does not represent their substantive content as separately verified.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(a)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, nominee-holder certification rule for counting voting securities
citations.quote: For the purpose of this subdivision, any securities held to the knowledge of the issuer in the names of broker-dealers, nominees for broker-dealers (including clearing corporations), or banks, associations, or other entities holding securities in a nominee name or otherwise on behalf of a beneficial owner (collectively “nominee holders”), shall not be considered outstanding. However, if the foreign corporation requests all nominee holders to certify, with respect to all beneficial owners for whom securities are held, the number of shares held for those beneficial owners having addresses (as shown on the records of the nominee holder) in this state and outside of this state, then all shares so certified shall be considered outstanding and held of record by persons having addresses either in this state or outside of this state as so certified, provided that the certification so provided shall be retained with the record of shareholders and made available for inspection and copying in the same manner as is provided in Section 1600 with respect to that record.

clauses.title: California Director, Distribution, and Voting Provisions Applied to a Qualifying Foreign Corporation
clauses.body: When a foreign corporation meets Section 2115(a)'s test and no exemption applies, a specified list of California General Corporation Law provisions applies to it "to the exclusion of the law of the jurisdiction in which it is incorporated." That list includes, among the director- and shareholder-governance provisions: the requirement of annual election of directors; removal of directors both without cause and by court proceeding; filling director vacancies when less than a majority of directors then in office were elected by shareholders; the directors' statutory standard of care; director liability for unlawful distributions (with two specified exclusions); indemnification of directors, officers, and others; the statutory limitations on corporate distributions in cash or property; a shareholder's liability for receiving an unlawful distribution; the requirement of an annual shareholders' meeting and the remedy if one is not timely held; shareholders' statutory right to cumulate votes in electing directors; and the supermajority-vote-requirement statute.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes and paraphrases the list of section citations Section 2115(b) itself uses to identify which provisions apply — it does not restate the full substantive text of each cross-referenced section (for example, the specific duty-of-care standard in Section 309, or the specific indemnification rules in Section 317). Several of those underlying provisions may be the subject of other, separately verified information sheets elsewhere in this corpus addressing California corporations directly; this clause's citation is limited to the distinct fact that Section 2115(b) extends the listed provisions to a qualifying foreign corporation, not to the underlying provisions' own substantive content. This clause also does not determine whether any specific foreign corporation is currently subject to this list, which depends on the Section 2115(a) test and the effective/cessation timing described elsewhere in this information sheet.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, director/distribution/voting provisions applied to a qualifying foreign corporation
citations.quote: (b) Except as provided in subdivision (c), the following chapters and sections of this division shall apply to a foreign corporation as defined in subdivision (a) (to the exclusion of the law of the jurisdiction in which it is incorporated): Chapter 1 (general provisions and definitions), to the extent applicable to the following provisions; Section 301 (annual election of directors); Section 303 (removal of directors without cause); Section 304 (removal of directors by court proceedings); Section 305, subdivision (c) (filling of director vacancies where less than a majority in office elected by shareholders); Section 309 (directors’ standard of care); Section 316 (excluding paragraph (3) of subdivision (a) and paragraph (3) of subdivision (f)) (liability of directors for unlawful distributions); Section 317 (indemnification of directors, officers, and others); Sections 500 to 505, inclusive (limitations on corporate distributions in cash or property); Section 506 (liability of shareholder who receives unlawful distribution); Section 600, subdivisions (b) and (c) (requirement for annual shareholders’ meeting and remedy if same not timely held); Section 708, subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) (shareholder’s right to cumulate votes at any election of directors); Section 710 (supermajority vote requirement);

clauses.title: California Asset-Sale, Merger, Reorganization, Dissenters'-Rights, and Records Provisions Applied to a Qualifying Foreign Corporation
clauses.body: The remainder of Section 2115(b)'s list of provisions applied to a qualifying foreign corporation, in place of its home jurisdiction's law, covers: the statutory limitation on sale of assets; the statutory limitation on mergers; the first sentence of the statute governing limitations on conversions, together with the separate statute setting the requirements of conversions; the entire chapter of the General Corporation Law governing reorganizations; the entire chapter governing dissenters' (appraisal) rights; the statutes on corporate records and reports; the statute authorizing action by the Attorney General; and the entire chapter governing shareholders' rights of inspection.
clauses.gap: As with the director/distribution/voting list, this clause quotes Section 2115(b)'s own enumeration of cross-referenced provisions; it does not restate the substantive content of those provisions (for example, the specific inspection procedures in the rights-of-inspection chapter, or the specific appraisal procedure in the dissenters'-rights chapter), several of which may be addressed by other, separately verified information sheets elsewhere in this corpus for California corporations directly. This clause does not determine whether any specific foreign corporation is currently subject to this list.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(b)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, asset-sale/merger/reorganization/dissenters'-rights/records provisions applied to a qualifying foreign corporation
citations.quote: Section 1001, subdivision (d) (limitations on sale of assets); Section 1101, subdivision (b) (limitations on mergers); Section 1151 (first sentence only) (limitations on conversions); Section 1152 (requirements of conversions); Chapter 12 (commencing with Section 1200) (reorganizations); Chapter 13 (commencing with Section 1300) (dissenters’ rights); Sections 1500 and 1501 (records and reports); Section 1508 (action by Attorney General); Chapter 16 (commencing with Section 1600) (rights of inspection).

clauses.title: Statutory Exemptions From Section 2115
clauses.body: Section 2115 does not apply to a foreign corporation that falls within either of two exemptions, even if the corporation would otherwise meet the property/payroll/sales and voting-securities test. The first exemption covers a corporation with outstanding securities listed on the New York Stock Exchange, the NYSE American, the NASDAQ Global Market, or the NASDAQ Capital Market. The second exemption covers a corporation all of whose voting shares (other than directors' qualifying shares) are owned, directly or indirectly, by a corporation or corporations that are not themselves subject to Section 2115.
clauses.gap: The specific exchange names in the first exemption (NYSE American, NASDAQ Global Market, NASDAQ Capital Market) reflect the version of Section 2115 as amended by Statutes 2022, Chapter 617 (SB 1202), effective January 1, 2023, which updated older exchange terminology (for example, the statute no longer refers to the American Stock Exchange by that name). This clause reflects the statute's current text as fetched on the date shown; it does not independently verify which securities exchanges any specific corporation's securities are actually listed on, and does not address whether a corporation exempt under the second prong might itself later become subject to Section 2115 if its parent corporation's own exempt status changes.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(c)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, exchange-listing and wholly-owned-subsidiary exemptions from Section 2115
citations.quote: (c) This section does not apply to any corporation (1) with outstanding securities listed on the New York Stock Exchange, the NYSE American, the NASDAQ Global Market, or the NASDAQ Capital Market, or (2) if all of its voting shares (other than directors’ qualifying shares) are owned directly or indirectly by a corporation or corporations not subject to this section.

clauses.title: When Section 2115(b)'s Requirements Begin to Apply
clauses.body: Section 2115 does not apply its list of California provisions the moment a foreign corporation's property/payroll/sales and voting-securities figures cross the statutory threshold. Instead, the requirements of subdivision (b) become applicable only as of the first day of the corporation's first income year that either (1) commences on or after the 135th day of the income year immediately following the latest income year with respect to which the Section 2115(a) tests were met, or (2) commences on or after entry of a final order by a court of competent jurisdiction declaring that those tests have been met.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the statutory timing rule for when subdivision (b) becomes applicable; it does not calculate the specific effective date for any particular foreign corporation, which requires knowing that corporation's income-year schedule and the specific income year in which it first met the Section 2115(a) test. It also does not address what happens if a corporation's income year changes during the relevant period, a scenario the statute's text does not itself resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(d)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, effective-date rule for when Section 2115(b) requirements begin to apply
citations.quote: (d) For purposes of subdivision (a), the requirements of subdivision (b) shall become applicable to a foreign corporation only upon the first day of the first income year of the corporation (1) commencing on or after the 135th day of the income year immediately following the latest income year with respect to which the tests referred to in subdivision (a) have been met or (2) commencing on or after the entry of a final order by a court of competent jurisdiction declaring that those tests have been met.

clauses.title: When Section 2115(b)'s Requirements Cease to Apply
clauses.body: Just as Section 2115(b)'s requirements do not begin immediately upon meeting the statutory test, they do not end immediately upon ceasing to meet it. The requirements cease to be applicable to a foreign corporation either (1) at the end of the first income year immediately following the latest income year with respect to which at least one of the Section 2115(a) tests was not met, or (2) at the end of the income year during which a final order has been entered by a court of competent jurisdiction declaring that one of those tests is not met — provided that a contrary order has not been entered before the end of that income year.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the statutory timing rule for when subdivision (b) ceases to apply; it does not calculate the specific cessation date for any particular foreign corporation, which requires that corporation's own income-year schedule and the specific income year in which it first failed to meet the Section 2115(a) test. It also does not address the effect of a court order that is later reversed on appeal after the relevant income year has already closed.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(e)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, cessation-date rule for when Section 2115(b) requirements stop applying
citations.quote: (e) For purposes of subdivision (a), the requirements of subdivision (b) shall cease to be applicable to a foreign corporation (1) at the end of the first income year of the corporation immediately following the latest income year with respect to which at least one of the tests referred to in subdivision (a) is not met or (2) at the end of the income year of the corporation during which a final order has been entered by a court of competent jurisdiction declaring that one of those tests is not met, provided that a contrary order has not been entered before the end of the income year.

clauses.title: Duty to Disclose Section 2115(b) Status on Written Request
clauses.body: A foreign corporation that is subject to Section 2115(b)'s requirements must advise, in writing and within 30 days of receiving a written request, any shareholder of record, any officer, director, employee, or other agent (within the meaning of the indemnification statute, Section 317), and any creditor of the corporation, whether or not the corporation is subject to subdivision (b) at the time the request is received. If a party obtains a final determination from a court of competent jurisdiction that the corporation either failed to provide this information or provided incorrect information of the kind required, the court has discretion to include in its judgment recovery, from the corporation, of all court costs and reasonable attorneys' fees the party incurred in the legal proceeding to the extent they relate to obtaining that final determination.
clauses.gap: This clause describes a disclosure obligation and an associated cost-and-fee-shifting judicial remedy triggered by a specific procedural sequence (a written request, a 30-day response window, and a final court determination); it does not itself create a general private right of action for damages beyond that cost-and-fee recovery, and the statute's text does not define what would make attorneys' fees "reasonable" in a given case. This clause also does not address whether, or how, a corporation must respond to an oral request, or a request from someone outside the specific categories the statute lists (shareholder of record, officer, director, employee, Section 317 agent, or creditor).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 2115(f)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, duty to disclose Section 2115(b) status on written request and cost/fee-shifting remedy
citations.quote: (f) Any foreign corporation that is subject to the requirements of subdivision (b) shall advise any shareholder of record, any officer, director, employee, or other agent (within the meaning of Section 317) and any creditor of the corporation in writing, within 30 days of receipt of written request for that information, whether or not it is subject to subdivision (b) at the time the request is received. Any party who obtains a final determination by a court of competent jurisdiction that the corporation failed to provide to the party information required to be provided by this subdivision or provided the party information of the kind required to be provided by this subdivision that was incorrect, then the court, in its discretion, shall have the power to include in its judgment recovery by the party from the corporation of all court costs and reasonable attorneys’ fees incurred in that legal proceeding to the extent they relate to obtaining that final determination.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature Block — Pseudo-Foreign Corporation (Section 2115) Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet regarding {{companyName}}'s potential status under California Corporations Code Section 2115 was prepared by {{authorizedSignerName}}.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{authorizedSignerName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California Corporations Code Section 2115: the two-part test for whether it applies to a foreign corporation, the specific California governance provisions it applies in place of the corporation's home-jurisdiction law, the statutory exemptions, the timing rules for when its requirements begin and cease to apply, and the statutory duty to disclose Section 2115(b) status on written request. It is not a determination that {{companyName}} or any other entity is or is not currently subject to Section 2115(b), does not calculate any corporation's property, payroll, sales, or voting-securities figures, and does not constitute legal advice. It also does not address the separate statutory requirement that a foreign corporation obtain a certificate of qualification before transacting intrastate business in California, which this project addresses in a separate information sheet.]

clauses.title: What This Information Sheet Covers
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes the private civil remedy in the federal Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA), 18 U.S.C. section 1030(g). Section 1030(g) lets a person who suffers damage or loss from certain violations of section 1030 bring a civil lawsuit against the violator. It covers which kinds of violations qualify for a civil suit, the $5,000 aggregate-loss factor most often relied on by businesses, the limit on damages for loss-only claims, the two-year period to bring the action, the carve-out for claims about negligently designed or manufactured computer products, and the statute's own definitions of "damage," "loss," and "exceeds authorized access."

This document is distinct from this corpus's existing California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act -- Demand Letter Information Sheet, which addresses the separate California civil cause of action in Penal Code section 502(e) -- a different statute with its own elements, remedies, and three-year limitations period. Conduct can potentially be examined under either or both statutes, but this document addresses only the federal CFAA civil remedy. This document is also distinct from this corpus's trade secret documents (including the DTSA and UTSA materials), which address trade secret misappropriation specifically; the CFAA civil remedy instead turns on unauthorized access to, or damage involving, a computer, regardless of whether a trade secret is involved.

Regarding {{computerSystemDescription}} and the conduct {{companyName}} attributes to {{adversePartyName}} -- described as {{incidentDescription}}, with loss or damage described as {{lossOrDamageDescription}} -- this sheet sets out the statutory framework the law provides. It does not determine whether that conduct violates section 1030, whether a civil action under section 1030(g) would succeed, or what {{companyName}} should do in response.

clauses.title: The Section 1030(g) Private Civil Action
clauses.body: Section 1030(g) gives a private civil remedy to any person who suffers damage or loss by reason of a violation of section 1030. That person may bring a civil action against the violator to obtain compensatory damages and injunctive relief or other equitable relief.
clauses.gap: This is the statute's own text, quoted from 18 U.S.C. section 1030(g), used as evidence of the existence and general shape of the civil remedy -- not a claim that any specific access or conduct actually violated section 1030, and not a claim that any specific person suffered damage or loss as the statute defines those terms. The statute does not itself list which subsections of section 1030(a) can support a civil action; a civil action is available only for conduct that separately satisfies section 1030's substantive prohibitions and the qualifying-factor requirement addressed in the next clause. No case law on how courts have applied this remedy in practice was researched or is cited in this clause.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(g) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, private civil action
citations.quote: Any person who suffers damage or loss by reason of a violation of this section may maintain a civil action against the violator to obtain compensatory damages and injunctive relief or other equitable relief.

clauses.title: A Civil Action Requires One of Five Statutory Factors
clauses.body: Section 1030(g) does not allow a civil action for every violation of section 1030. A civil action may be brought only if the conduct involves one of five factors set out in a separate subsection, subclauses (I) through (V) of section 1030(c)(4)(A)(i): an aggregate loss of at least $5,000 in a one-year period; modification or impairment of medical examination, diagnosis, treatment, or care; physical injury to any person; a threat to public health or safety; or damage to a computer used by or for a United States government entity in furtherance of the administration of justice, national defense, or national security. (A sixth factor in that same subsection -- damage affecting ten or more protected computers in a one-year period -- is defined elsewhere in subsection (c)(4)(A)(i) but is not separately quoted here.)
clauses.gap: This clause quotes two non-adjacent fragments of the same sentence in 18 U.S.C. section 1030(g), split around a numbered footnote reference ("5") that the Office of the Law Revision Counsel inserted into the official text between the words "subclauses" and "(I)" -- confirmed present in the same location in both the Cornell LII and the official uscode.house.gov renderings of the section, where an accompanying editorial note states "So in original. Probably should be 'subclause.'" That footnote number is an editorial annotation, not part of the substantive statutory text, so it is excluded from both quoted fragments rather than being quoted mid-sentence. This clause identifies the five (in fact six, per the parenthetical) factors listed in section 1030(c)(4)(A)(i) by cross-reference and paraphrase rather than by quoting the full text of subclauses (II) through (VI); the $5,000 aggregate-loss factor, subclause (I), is quoted in full in the next clause. No case law on how courts apply any of these factors was researched or is cited in this clause.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(g) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, qualifying-factor requirement (part 1)
citations.quote: A civil action for a violation of this section may be brought only if the conduct involves 1 of the factors set forth in subclauses

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(g) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, qualifying-factor requirement (part 2)
citations.quote: (I), (II), (III), (IV), or (V) of subsection (c)(4)(A)(i).

clauses.title: The $5,000 Aggregate-Loss Factor
clauses.body: The first of the qualifying factors under section 1030(c)(4)(A)(i) -- the one most often relied on in civil suits between businesses -- is loss to one or more persons during any one-year period aggregating at least $5,000 in value. For an investigation, prosecution, or other proceeding brought by the United States only, that aggregate loss can also include loss from a related course of conduct affecting one or more other protected computers.
clauses.gap: This is the statute's own text, quoted from 18 U.S.C. section 1030(c)(4)(A)(i)(I), used as evidence of the dollar threshold and the one-year aggregation period that subclause describes -- not a claim that any specific loss actually reaches $5,000 or that it was incurred within a single one-year period. Section 1030(e)(11) defines "loss" (quoted in a separate clause of this document); this clause does not itself restate that definition or address how a court would calculate whether a particular set of costs adds up to $5,000. The related-course-of-conduct aggregation language applies only to proceedings the United States brings, not to a private civil action; this clause does not address whether or how a private plaintiff could aggregate losses across multiple incidents or victims.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(c)(4)(A)(i)(I) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, $5,000 aggregate-loss factor
citations.quote: loss to 1 or more persons during any 1-year period (and, for purposes of an investigation, prosecution, or other proceeding brought by the United States only, loss resulting from a related course of conduct affecting 1 or more other protected computers) aggregating at least $5,000 in value;

clauses.title: Damages Limited to Economic Damages for Loss-Only Claims
clauses.body: Where the only qualifying factor for the civil action is the $5,000 aggregate-loss factor described above, section 1030(g) limits the damages available to economic damages. Damages for a violation involving only conduct described in subsection (c)(4)(A)(i)(I) are limited to economic damages.
clauses.gap: This is the statute's own text, quoted from 18 U.S.C. section 1030(g), used as evidence that this damages limitation exists and of which claims it applies to -- not a claim about what dollar amount of economic damages any specific claim could support. The statute does not define "economic damages" in section 1030 itself; this clause does not supply or verify any definition of that term from another source. This limitation applies only when the $5,000 loss factor is the sole qualifying factor; a claim that also involves one of the other factors listed in section 1030(c)(4)(A)(i) (for example, physical injury or a threat to public health or safety) is not subject to this particular limitation, though this clause does not independently verify what broader damages might be available in that situation.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(g) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, economic-damages limitation
citations.quote: Damages for a violation involving only conduct described in subsection (c)(4)(A)(i)(I) are limited to economic damages.

clauses.title: Two-Year Period to Bring a Civil Action
clauses.body: A civil action under section 1030(g) may not be brought unless it is begun within two years of the date of the act complained of, or the date of the discovery of the damage, whichever comes into play under the statute's own terms.
clauses.gap: This is the statute's own text, quoted from 18 U.S.C. section 1030(g) -- not a claim about when any specific act occurred or was discovered, and not a claim about whether any tolling doctrine might extend or suspend this two-year period in a specific case. This two-year federal period is shorter than the three-year period this corpus's existing California Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act information sheet describes for the separate state civil action under Penal Code section 502(e)(5); a claim time-barred under one statute is not necessarily time-barred under the other, since they are separate statutes with separate limitations periods.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(g) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, two-year limitations period
citations.quote: No action may be brought under this subsection unless such action is begun within 2 years of the date of the act complained of or the date of the discovery of the damage.

clauses.title: No Civil Claim for Negligent Design or Manufacture of Computer Products
clauses.body: Section 1030(g) does not allow a civil action for the negligent design or manufacture of computer hardware, computer software, or firmware. No action may be brought under this subsection for the negligent design or manufacture of computer hardware, computer software, or firmware.
clauses.gap: This is the statute's own text, quoted from 18 U.S.C. section 1030(g) -- not a claim about whether any specific product-liability or negligence theory involving computer hardware, software, or firmware would or would not be barred by this carve-out in a particular case. The statute does not define "negligent design or manufacture" for purposes of this carve-out, and this clause does not address how this provision interacts with product-liability law outside of section 1030, or with claims that combine a section 1030 violation with a separate negligent-design theory.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(g) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, negligent-design-or-manufacture carve-out
citations.quote: No action may be brought under this subsection for the negligent design or manufacture of computer hardware, computer software, or firmware.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Damage"
clauses.body: Section 1030 defines "damage" for purposes of the entire section, including the civil remedy in subsection (g). The term "damage" means any impairment to the integrity or availability of data, a program, a system, or information.
clauses.gap: This is the statute's own text, quoted from 18 U.S.C. section 1030(e)(8) -- not a claim that any specific event actually impaired the integrity or availability of any particular data, program, system, or information. This is a broad, single-sentence definition; the statute does not further define "integrity," "availability," or "impairment" within section 1030 itself, and this clause does not supply or verify any further gloss on those terms from case law.

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(e)(8) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, definition of "damage"
citations.quote: the term “damage” means any impairment to the integrity or availability of data, a program, a system, or information;

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Loss"
clauses.body: Section 1030 also defines "loss" for purposes of the entire section, including the $5,000 aggregate-loss factor described above. The term "loss" means any reasonable cost to any victim, including the cost of responding to an offense, conducting a damage assessment, and restoring the data, program, system, or information to its condition prior to the offense, and any revenue lost, cost incurred, or other consequential damages incurred because of interruption of service.
clauses.gap: This is the statute's own text, quoted from 18 U.S.C. section 1030(e)(11) -- not a claim that any specific expense or lost revenue actually qualifies as "loss" under this definition, or that any particular cost was "reasonable." The statute does not itself set out how these cost categories should be itemized or proven in a given case, and this clause does not address how courts have applied this definition to specific categories of expense (for example, employee time spent on incident response, or the cost of outside forensic investigators).

citations.case: 18 U.S.C. § 1030(e)(11) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, definition of "loss"
citations.quote: the term “loss” means any reasonable cost to any victim, including the cost of responding to an offense, conducting a damage assessment, and restoring the data, program, system, or information to its condition prior to the offense, and any revenue lost, cost incurred, or other consequential damages incurred because of interruption of service;

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Exceeds Authorized Access"
clauses.body: Several of section 1030's prohibitions, including ones commonly invoked in civil suits over employees or contractors who misuse computer access they were given, turn on whether a person "exceeds authorized access." Section 1030 defines that term: the term "exceeds authorized access" means to access a computer with authorization and to use such access to obtain or alter information in the computer that the accesser is not entitled so to obtain or alter.
clauses.gap: This is the statute's own text, quoted from 18 U.S.C. section 1030(e)(6) -- not a claim that any specific person's access to any specific computer or data did or did not exceed authorized access as this definition describes. Section 1030 does not separately define the related term "without authorization," which appears in several of the section's substantive prohibitions alongside "exceeds authorized access" but is left undefined by the statute itself. The scope of both terms -- including how far an authorized user's later use of already-accessible information can itself violate the statute -- has been the subject of federal appellate and U.S. Supreme Court case law (including a 2021 Supreme Court decision construing "exceeds authorized access"). A CourtListener case-law search for that case law was attempted for this document but returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (125/day quota exhausted) before any case could be retrieved and independently verified, so no case is cited here and this clause does not describe any court's holding on the scope of either term.

citations.cite: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, definition of "exceeds authorized access"
citations.quote: the term “exceeds authorized access” means to access a computer with authorization and to use such access to obtain or alter information in the computer that the accesser is not entitled so to obtain or alter;

clauses.title: Signature and Certification
Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Stay-or-Pay and Training Repayment Provisions at Termination — Information Sheet is prepared in connection with the employment relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}, and in particular a contract term described as: {{repaymentTriggerDescription}}. It describes what California Business and Professions Code section 16608 and Labor Code section 926 say about contract terms that require a worker to pay a debt, penalty, fee, or cost — or that trigger collection of one — because the worker's employment or work relationship with a specific employer terminates. These statutes apply only to contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2026. This information sheet is not itself a determination that any specific term in any specific contract between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}} is lawful, unlawful, void, or enforceable, and it does not resolve whether the amount at issue, stated here as {{repaymentAmount}}, is or is not collectible.

clauses.title: Core Prohibition on Termination-Triggered Debts, Fees, and Penalties
clauses.body: For a contract entered into on or after January 1, 2026, California Business and Professions Code section 16608 makes it unlawful to include in an employment contract — or to require a worker to sign, as a condition of employment or a work relationship, a separate contract that includes — a term that does any of three things: requires the worker to pay the employer, a training provider, or a debt collector for a debt because the worker's employment or work relationship with a specific employer terminates; authorizes the employer, training provider, or debt collector to resume or start collecting, or to end forbearance on, a debt for that same reason; or imposes any penalty, fee, or cost on the worker for that same reason. The statute reaches the contract term itself, regardless of which of the three mechanisms it uses, so long as termination of the work relationship with a specific employer is the trigger.
clauses.gap: This prohibition is brand new: it applies only to contracts "entered into on or after January 1, 2026," so a materially identical repayment or fee provision in a contract signed before that date is not covered by this statute at all, and this clause takes no position on what law, if any, governs an earlier contract. The statute is limited to a contract term that is triggered by termination of the work relationship "with a specific employer" — its own text does not address a term triggered by some other event (for example, a fixed calendar date unrelated to separation, or a voluntary election unconnected to termination). Six statutory exceptions in subdivision (b)(2) narrow this prohibition and are addressed in this document's companion clauses rather than folded into this one. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(1)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: (b) (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), for contracts entered into on or after January 1, 2026, it shall be unlawful to include in any employment contract, or to require a worker to execute as a condition of employment or a work relationship a contract that includes, a contract term that does any of the following:(A) Requires the worker to pay an employer, training provider, or debt collector for a debt if the worker’s employment or work relationship with a specific employer terminates.(B) Authorizes the employer, training provider, or debt collector to resume or initiate collection of or end forbearance on a debt if the worker’s employment or work relationship with a specific employer terminates.(C) Imposes any penalty, fee, or cost on a worker if the worker’s employment or work relationship with a specific employer terminates.

clauses.title: Key Definitions: “Debt,” “Penalty, Fee, or Cost,” “Worker,” and “Employer”
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code section 16608 defines several terms broadly. “Debt” covers money, personal property, or their equivalent that is due, owing, or alleged to be due or owing from a natural person to another person — expressly including employment-related costs, education-related costs, or a consumer financial product or service — without regard to whether the debt is certain, contingent, or was incurred voluntarily. “Penalty, fee, or cost” is defined non-exclusively to include a replacement hire fee, retraining fee, replacement fee, quit fee, reimbursement for immigration or visa-related costs, liquidated damages, lost goodwill, and lost profit. “Worker” means a natural person permitted to work for or on behalf of an employer or business entity, or to participate in a work relationship, job training program, or skills training program, and is not limited to a common-law employee. “Employer” is likewise defined broadly to include any parent company, subsidiary, division, affiliate, contractor, hiring party, or third-party agent of an employer.
clauses.gap: These definitions apply "for purposes of this section" — they are not stated to govern how "debt," "worker," or "employer" are used elsewhere in the Business and Professions Code or the Labor Code. The definition of "debt" is deliberately broad and non-exclusive ("including, but not limited to"), and its own text does not resolve every close question about whether a specific charge, chargeback, or offset against final wages counts as a "debt" within its meaning. The statute separately defines “debt collector” by cross-reference to Civil Code section 1788.2(c), “freelance worker” by cross-reference to Section 18101, “misconduct” by cross-reference to Unemployment Insurance Code section 1256, and “transferable credential” and “training provider” with their own definitions; this clause quotes only the four terms most central to the prohibition and its trigger, not the full definitional list. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(a)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: “Debt” means money, personal property, or their equivalent that is due or owing or alleged to be due or owing from a natural person to another person, including, but not limited to, for employment-related costs, education-related costs, or a consumer financial product or service, regardless of whether the debt is certain, contingent, or incurred voluntarily.

citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: “Penalty, fee, or cost” includes, but is not limited to, a replacement hire fee, retraining fee, replacement fee, quit fee, reimbursement for immigration or visa-related costs, liquidated damages, lost goodwill, and lost profit.

clauses.title: Voidness Under Section 16600 and the January 1, 2026 Effective Date
clauses.body: A contract term that is unlawful under Business and Professions Code section 16608(b) is treated as a contract restraining a person from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business — and is void under section 16600, California's general prohibition on non-compete agreements — but only if the contract was entered into on or after January 1, 2026. Labor Code section 926(a) states the same rule from the worker's side: a contract or contract term that violates section 16608 is void as contrary to public policy, again only if entered into on or after January 1, 2026.
clauses.gap: Both statutes tie the voidness consequence expressly to the January 1, 2026 contracting date; neither statute's own text says what result follows for an identical provision in a contract entered into before that date, and this clause does not assume an answer to that question. The voidness rule operates through section 16600, so it inherits that section's general framework for void restraints of trade rather than creating a freestanding remedy of its own — the freestanding civil remedies are instead created separately by Labor Code section 926(b) and (c), addressed in this document's companion clause. This clause cites one subdivision from each of two statutes (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(c) and Lab. Code § 926(a)); each was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: (c) A contract that is unlawful under subdivision (b) is a contract restraining a person from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business, and is void under Section 16600 only if the contract was entered into on or after January 1, 2026.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 926(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (a) A contract or contract term that violates Section 16608 of the Business and Professions Code is void as contrary to public policy only if entered into on or after January 1, 2026.

clauses.title: Exception: Tuition Repayment for a Transferable Credential
clauses.body: Section 16608(b)(2)(B) exempts a contract for repayment of tuition costs for a “transferable credential” — defined elsewhere in the statute as a degree offered by an accredited third-party institution that is not required for the worker's current job and is transferable and useful for employment beyond the current employer — but only if five conditions are all met: the repayment contract is offered separately from the employment contract; obtaining the credential is not made a condition of employment; the repayment amount is specified before the worker agrees and does not exceed the employer's actual cost of the credential; any required-employment period comes with a repayment amount that is prorated to the length of that period, without an accelerated payment schedule on separation; and the worker does not owe repayment if terminated, unless the termination was for misconduct.
clauses.gap: This exception applies only to a “transferable credential” as the statute defines it — a third-party-institution degree not required for the worker's current employment — and its own text does not extend to repayment of costs for a certification, license, or in-house training program that does not meet that specific definition; those may instead fall under the separate signing-bonus/retention-payment exception in subdivision (b)(2)(D) or under no exception at all. All five listed requirements must be met; the statute's own text does not say what happens to a contract that satisfies some but not all of them, and this clause does not resolve that question. “Misconduct” for purposes of the termination carve-out in (v) is defined by cross-reference to Unemployment Insurance Code section 1256, addressed separately in this corpus's unemployment insurance disqualification materials rather than repeated here. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(B)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: (B) A contract related to the repayment of the cost of tuition for a transferable credential that meets all of the following requirements:(i) The contract is offered separately from any contract for employment.(ii) The contract does not require obtaining the transferable credential as a condition of employment. (iii) The contract specifies the repayment amount before the worker agrees to the contract, and the repayment amount does not exceed the cost to the employer of the transferable credential received by the worker.(iv) The contract provides for a prorated repayment amount during any required employment period that is proportional to the total repayment amount and the length of the required employment period and does not require an accelerated payment schedule if the worker separates from the employment.(v) The contract does not require repayment to the employer by the worker if the worker is terminated, except if the worker is terminated for misconduct.

clauses.title: Exception: Discretionary Signing Bonus With a Retention Period
clauses.body: Section 16608(b)(2)(D) exempts a contract for a discretionary or unearned monetary payment — including a financial bonus — paid at the outset of employment and not tied to specific job performance, provided five conditions are all met: the repayment terms are in a separate agreement from the main employment contract; the worker is notified of the right to consult an attorney and given at least five business days to do so before signing; any repayment obligation for early separation carries no interest and is prorated to the remaining term of a retention period capped at two years from receipt of the payment; the worker has the option to defer receiving the payment until the retention period is fully served, with no repayment obligation in that case; and the separation that would trigger repayment must have been at the worker's own sole election, or at the employer's election for misconduct.
clauses.gap: This exception is narrower than a general “signing bonus clawback” exception: it requires the payment to be discretionary or unearned and not tied to job performance, the repayment terms to be in a document separate from the employment contract, an advance attorney-consultation notice of at least five business days, no interest on repayment, proration to the remaining retention period, a retention period capped at two years, a deferral option, and a separation trigger limited to the worker's own election or an employer election for misconduct — all eight elements together, not any one of them alone. The statute's own text does not say what result follows for a bonus-repayment arrangement that satisfies most but not all of these conditions. Whether a specific payment is “discretionary or unearned” and “not tied to specific job performance” is a fact-specific characterization this document does not resolve. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(D)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(D) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: (D) A contract for the receipt of a discretionary or unearned monetary payment, including a financial bonus, at the outset of employment that is not tied to specific job performance, provided that all of the following conditions are met:(i) The terms of any repayment obligation are set forth in a separate agreement from the primary employment contract.(ii) The employee is notified that they have the right to consult an attorney regarding the agreement and provided with a reasonable time period of not less than five business days to obtain advice of counsel prior to executing the agreement.(iii) Any repayment obligation for early separation from employment is not subject to interest accrual and is prorated based on the remaining term of any retention period, which shall not exceed two years from the receipt of payment.(iv) The worker has an option to defer receipt of the payment to the end of a fully served retention period without any repayment obligation.(v) Separation from employment prior to the retention period was at the sole election of the employee, or at the election of the employer for misconduct.

clauses.title: Three Further Exceptions: Government Loan Programs, Apprenticeships, and Residential Property Contracts
clauses.body: Section 16608(b)(2) exempts three further categories of contract from the core prohibition, in addition to the transferable-credential and discretionary-bonus exceptions addressed separately in this document. First, a contract entered into under any loan repayment assistance program or loan forgiveness program provided by a federal, state, or local governmental agency is not covered. Second, a contract related to enrollment in an apprenticeship program approved by California's Division of Apprenticeship Standards is not covered. Third, a contract related to the lease, financing, or purchase of residential property — including, but not limited to, a contract under the California Residential Mortgage Lending Act — is not covered.
clauses.gap: Each of these three exceptions is stated without the multi-factor conditions attached to the transferable-credential and discretionary-bonus exceptions — the statute's own text imposes no separate list of requirements on a loan-forgiveness-program contract, an approved-apprenticeship contract, or a residential-property contract for the exception to apply. The apprenticeship exception turns on approval by the Division of Apprenticeship Standards specifically; the statute's own text does not address an unapproved or informally structured apprenticeship arrangement. The residential-property exception is illustrated, not limited, by its cross-reference to the California Residential Mortgage Lending Act (“including, but not limited to”), and this document does not attempt to catalog every residential-property financing arrangement the exception might reach. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(b)(2)(A), (C), and (E)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: (A) A contract entered into under any loan repayment assistance program or loan forgiveness program provided by a federal, state, or local governmental agency.

citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: (C) A contract related to enrollment in an apprenticeship program approved by the Division of Apprenticeship Standards.

clauses.title: Private Civil Action, Statutory Damages, and Attorney's Fees
clauses.body: Labor Code section 926(b) authorizes a worker subjected to the conduct prohibited by section 16608(b) of the Business and Professions Code, or a worker representative, to bring a civil action on behalf of that worker, other similarly situated persons, or both, in any court of competent jurisdiction. Section 926(c) states that a person found liable is liable for the worker's or workers' actual damages, or $5,000 per worker, whichever is greater, in addition to injunctive relief and reasonable attorney's fees and costs.
clauses.gap: The statute creates a per-worker damages floor of $5,000 that applies only “or,” as an alternative to actual damages, whichever amount is greater — it does not stack the two. Section 926(b) authorizes an action “on behalf of” other similarly situated persons; the statute's own text does not specify class-certification or representative-action procedures beyond that grant, and this document does not describe how such an action would be litigated. “Worker representative” is not further defined in section 926 itself. This clause cites two subdivisions of a single statutory section (Lab. Code § 926(b) and (c)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 926(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (b) A worker who has been subjected to the conduct prohibited by subdivision (b) of Section 16608 of the Business and Professions Code or a worker representative may bring a civil action on behalf of that worker, other persons similarly situated, or both, in any court of competent jurisdiction.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 926(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (c) Any person found liable for a violation of this section shall be liable for actual damages sustained by the worker or workers on whose behalf the case is brought, or five thousand dollars ($5,000) per worker, whichever is greater, in addition to injunctive relief, and reasonable attorney’s fees and costs.

clauses.title: Cumulative With Other Rights — Expense Reimbursement, Worker Classification, and Unfair Competition Law
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code section 16608(d) states that the rights, remedies, and penalties it establishes are cumulative and do not supersede or limit rights, remedies, or penalties available under other law — naming, by way of example, an employer's business-expense reimbursement obligations under Labor Code section 2802, the worker-classification provisions beginning at Labor Code section 2775, and the Unfair Competition Law beginning at Business and Professions Code section 17200. Labor Code section 926(d) states the reciprocal rule: section 926 does not limit the remedies otherwise available to a worker or other natural person under section 16608.
clauses.gap: Subdivision (d)'s list of other laws is introduced by “including, but not limited to,” so the three named provisions illustrate rather than exhaust the other legal theories that might independently apply to the same underlying facts; this document does not attempt a complete cross-reference. Whether a specific reimbursement dispute, misclassification claim, or unfair-competition claim actually applies to any given contract term is governed by those separate bodies of law, addressed in this corpus's own dedicated materials on those subjects rather than repeated here. This clause cites one subdivision from each of two statutes (Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(d) and Lab. Code § 926(d)); each was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page before being treated as verified.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16608(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code
citations.quote: (d) The rights, remedies, and penalties established by this section are cumulative and shall not be construed to supersede or limit the rights, remedies, or penalties established under other laws, or to limit the ability of any other person or entity to pursue enforcement of rights, remedies, or penalties established under other laws, including, but not limited to:(1) Obligations of employers under Section 2802 of the Labor Code.(2) Article 1.5 (commencing with Section 2775) of Chapter 2 of Division 3 of the Labor Code.(3) The Unfair Competition Law (Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 17200)).

citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (d) This section does not limit the remedies available to a worker or other natural person specified in Section 16608 of the Business and Professions Code.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Declaration of Parents and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Determination of Income for Guideline Child Support Information Sheet concerns {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}, the parents of {{childName}} (date of birth: {{childDOB}}), in connection with a child support matter pending, or that may be filed, in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes what the statutes governing California's statewide uniform child support guideline say about how a parent's income is defined, measured, and converted into the annual gross income and net disposable income figures the guideline formula uses — including what counts as gross income, when a court considers earning capacity instead of actual income, the specific statutory exclusions from gross income and deductions from gross income, and the mechanisms for adjusting the resulting figure for inaccurate, seasonal, or fluctuating income, and for financial hardship. This information sheet does not itself calculate any support amount, does not itself constitute or replace a court-ordered income and expense declaration, and is not a substitute for the moving papers, financial disclosures, or Judicial Council forms a party actually files in a support proceeding.

clauses.title: Annual Gross Income Is Broadly Defined and Non-Exhaustive
clauses.body: California's child support guideline statute defines the annual gross income of each parent, for guideline purposes, as income from whatever source derived, except as specified in the statute's own exclusions subdivision, and states that the definition includes, but is not limited to, an enumerated list. The statute's non-exhaustive list of included income types is broad: it names commissions, salaries, royalties, wages, bonuses, rents, dividends, pensions, interest, trust income, annuities, workers' compensation benefits, unemployment insurance benefits, disability insurance benefits, social security benefits, severance pay, veterans benefits that are not based on need, military allowances for housing and food, and spousal support actually received from a person who is not a party to the child support proceeding.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 4058(a) and 4058(a)(1), fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical (after whitespace normalization) across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. The statute's own list is expressly non-exhaustive ("includes, but is not limited to"), so this document does not attempt to catalog every category of receipt a court has treated as gross income; subdivisions (a)(2) and (a)(3), addressing business income and discretionary employee/self-employment benefits, are addressed in this document's companion clause rather than here. This section became operative September 1, 2024 (Stats. 2023, Ch. 213); this document does not address or quote the version of section 4058 in effect before that operative date.

citations.cite: the statute's broad, non-exhaustive definition of annual gross income
citations.quote: The annual gross income of each parent means income from whatever source derived, except as specified in subdivision (c) and includes, but is not limited to, the following:

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4058(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the enumerated (non-exhaustive) list of included income types
citations.quote: Income such as commissions, salaries, royalties, wages, bonuses, rents, dividends, pensions, interest, trust income, annuities, workers’ compensation benefits, unemployment insurance benefits, disability insurance benefits, social security benefits, severance pay, veterans benefits that are not based on need, military allowances for housing and food, and spousal support actually received from a person not a party to the proceeding to establish a child support order pursuant to this article.

clauses.title: Business Income and Discretionary Inclusion of Employee or Self-Employment Benefits
clauses.body: Beyond the enumerated list of standard income types, California's guideline statute separately addresses two further categories of income. Income from the proprietorship of a business is defined as the business's gross receipts reduced by the expenditures required to operate the business — not gross receipts alone. Separately, the statute gives a court discretion to include employee benefits or self-employment benefits as income, and directs the court, in exercising that discretion, to take into consideration the benefit to the employee, any corresponding reduction in living expenses, and other relevant facts.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 4058(a)(2) and 4058(a)(3), fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. These are two subdivisions of the same enacted section as this document's companion clause on the general definition of gross income (subdivision (a) and (a)(1)); they are not independent of one another. The statute's text does not itself define "expenditures required for the operation of the business" or specify which employee or self-employment benefits a court has found to fall within its discretionary-inclusion authority; this document does not address that further line-drawing.

citations.cite: business proprietorship income measured as gross receipts less required operating expenditures
citations.quote: Income from the proprietorship of a business, such as gross receipts from the business reduced by expenditures required for the operation of the business.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4058(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
