citations.quote: In the discretion of the court, employee benefits or self-employment benefits, taking into consideration the benefit to the employee, any corresponding reduction in living expenses, and other relevant facts.

clauses.title: Earning Capacity: Mandatory When Income Is Unknown, Discretionary and Best-Interest-Limited When Known
clauses.body: California's guideline statute distinguishes two situations for a court's consideration of a parent's earning capacity rather than the parent's actual income. When a parent's annual gross income is unknown, the statute is mandatory: the court shall consider the parent's earning capacity. When a parent's annual gross income is known, the statute instead makes earning-capacity consideration discretionary, and conditions it: the court may, in its discretion, consider earning capacity in lieu of income only consistent with the best interests of the children, taking into consideration the children's overall welfare and developmental needs and the time that parent spends with the children. When a court determines earning capacity under this subdivision, the statute directs the court to consider the specific circumstances of the parent, to the extent known.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 4058(b)(1)(A), 4058(b)(1)(B), and the opening sentence of 4058(b)(2), fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. The statute's text at 4058(b)(2) lists specific circumstances a court considers (assets, residence, employment and earnings history, job skills, educational attainment, literacy, age, health, criminal record and other employment barriers, record of seeking work, the local job market, availability of employers, and prevailing local earnings levels) that this document does not separately quote or catalog in full; this document also does not address any case law interpreting when a court's earning-capacity finding will be upheld, which is outside the scope of a document limited to the statute's own text.

clauses.title: Incarceration or Involuntary Institutionalization Is Not Treated as Voluntary Unemployment
clauses.body: California's guideline statute contains a specific rule addressing incarcerated or involuntarily institutionalized parents in the earning-capacity context: notwithstanding any other law, a parent's incarceration or involuntary institutionalization shall not be treated as voluntary unemployment in establishing or modifying support orders, regardless of the nature of the offense. The statute cross-references a defined-terms provision, Family Code section 4007.5(e), for the meaning of "incarcerated or involuntarily institutionalized."
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 4058(b)(3)'s first sentence, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. This document has not independently fetched or verified Family Code section 4007.5(e), which the quoted sentence cross-references for the definition of "incarcerated or involuntarily institutionalized"; this document states only that the cross-reference exists, and does not state what section 4007.5(e)'s definition itself provides. The statute's rule addresses only whether incarceration/involuntary institutionalization is treated as voluntary unemployment for earning-capacity purposes; it does not itself address how a support order is otherwise established, modified, or enforced during a parent's incarceration, which this document does not address.

citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other law, the incarceration or involuntary institutionalization of a parent shall not be treated as voluntary unemployment in establishing or modifying support orders regardless of the nature of the offense.

clauses.title: Statutory Exclusions from Annual Gross Income
clauses.body: California's guideline statute excludes specific categories of receipt from annual gross income. Annual gross income does not include any income derived from child support payments actually received, or income derived from any public assistance program for which eligibility is based on a determination of need. As a related but separately stated rule, child support received by a party for children from another relationship shall not be included as part of that party's gross or net income.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 4058(c)'s first and second sentences, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. This document treats the two quoted sentences as stating two related exclusions (need-based public assistance and child support actually received on the one hand; child support received for children of another relationship on the other) because the statute states them as separate sentences, but takes no position on whether they are legally coextensive in any particular case. Section 4058(c) also contains a third sentence, an operative date provision (subdivision (d) in the statute's own lettering, stating the section is operative September 1, 2024), which this document does not separately quote here because it is addressed in this document's companion clause on the general definition of gross income.

citations.quote: Annual gross income does not include any income derived from child support payments actually received, and income derived from any public assistance program, eligibility for which is based on a determination of need.

citations.quote: Child support received by a party for children from another relationship shall not be included as part of that party’s gross or net income.

clauses.title: Annual Net Disposable Income Is Gross Income Minus an Enumerated List of Deductions
clauses.body: California's guideline statute defines annual net disposable income, the figure the guideline formula actually uses, as computed by deducting from the parent's annual gross income the actual amounts attributable to a list of enumerated items or other items permitted under the statute's own article. Among the enumerated deductions: the state and federal income tax liability resulting from the parties' taxable income; deductions attributed to the employee's or self-employed worker's contribution under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA), or an equivalent capped amount for a parent not subject to FICA, provided the deducted amount is used to secure retirement or disability benefits; and any child or spousal support actually being paid by the parent under a court order to or for the benefit of a person who is not a subject of the support order being established.

Section 4059 enumerates additional deduction categories this document does not quote here — mandatory union dues and retirement benefits required as a condition of employment (subdivision (c)), health insurance or health plan and state disability insurance premiums (subdivision (d)), court-allowed job-related expenses (subdivision (f)), and a hardship deduction under sections 4070 through 4073 (subdivision (g), addressed in this document's separate hardship-deduction clause) — because this document selects representative deductions rather than reproducing the full enumerated list. This document does not address the remainder of subdivision (a) (concerning the tax-status factors used to compute income tax liability) or the remainder of subdivision (e) (concerning deductions for support of children not the subject of the order, in the absence of a court order).

clauses.title: Converting Annual Income to a Monthly Figure, and Adjusting for Inaccurate, Seasonal, or Fluctuating Income
clauses.body: California's guideline statute converts the annual net disposable income figure into the monthly figure the guideline formula uses by dividing it by 12. The statute then gives the court an express adjustment power for two circumstances: if the resulting monthly net disposable income figure does not accurately reflect the actual or prospective earnings of the parties at the time the support determination is made, the court may adjust the amount appropriately; and, in a separately stated section, the court may adjust the child support order as appropriate to accommodate seasonal or fluctuating income of either parent.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 4060 in full and Family Code section 4064 in full, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. Both statutes vest the adjustment decision in the court's discretion ("may adjust") without specifying a particular method, formula, or averaging period for the adjustment; this document does not describe or endorse any particular adjustment method, and does not address how the two adjustment provisions interact where both an inaccuracy and seasonal/fluctuating income are present in the same case.

citations.quote: The monthly net disposable income shall be computed by dividing the annual net disposable income by 12.

citations.quote: If the monthly net disposable income figure does not accurately reflect the actual or prospective earnings of the parties at the time the determination of support is made, the court may adjust the amount appropriately.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4064 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's separate power to adjust the order to accommodate seasonal or fluctuating income
citations.quote: The court may adjust the child support order as appropriate to accommodate seasonal or fluctuating income of either parent.

clauses.title: The Extreme Financial Hardship Deduction: Enumerated Circumstances, a Cap, and Required Findings
clauses.body: California's guideline statute permits an additional deduction from a parent's income for extreme financial hardship. Where a parent is experiencing extreme financial hardship due to justifiable expenses resulting from circumstances the statute enumerates, the court may, on a party's request, allow the income deductions under the net-disposable-income statute that are necessary to accommodate those circumstances. The enumerated hardship circumstances include extraordinary health expenses for which the parent is financially responsible and uninsured catastrophic losses, and the minimum basic living expenses of the parent's other natural or adopted children, from other marriages or relationships, who reside with the parent. For that second circumstance, the maximum hardship deduction for each such child may be equal to, but shall not exceed, the support allocated to each child subject to the order. If a court allows a hardship deduction, the statute requires the court to state the reasons supporting the deduction in writing or on the record, and to document the amount of the deduction and the underlying facts and circumstances.

This document does not quote section 4071(c) (authorizing the Judicial Council to develop hardship-deduction tables) or section 4072(b) (directing the court to specify the deduction's duration whenever possible) or section 4073 (a general goals-guidance provision); those provisions exist but are not reproduced here. The statute's own text states that the hardship amount is deducted from the paying party's income, not from the child support amount itself, and section 4059(g) states a court must seek equity between competing child support orders when applying the paragraph (2) hardship under section 4071(a) — that interaction is addressed in this document's companion clause on net disposable income deductions, which quotes section 4059's cross-reference to this hardship framework, and is not repeated in full here.

clauses.title: Declaration of Subdivision, Owner/Subdivider, and Prospective Purchaser
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California's Subdivided Lands Law (Bus. & Prof. Code § 11000 et seq., within the Business and Professions Code's Real Estate division), a statutory scheme administered by the California Department of Real Estate that is separate from, and imposes different requirements than, the Subdivision Map Act's local-government map-approval process. It describes this body of law as it relates to land described as: {{propertyDescription}}, offered by {{ownerName}} as owner or subdivider, to prospective purchaser {{buyerName}}. As described in the clauses below, this law can require an owner or subdivider to obtain a public report from the Department of Real Estate before offering qualifying subdivided lands for sale or lease, and can require delivery of that report to a prospective purchaser before a binding contract is signed. This declaration states these facts about the parties and the property; it does not itself determine whether this specific offering meets the statutory definition of "subdivided lands," whether a public report has been issued or is required for it, or whether any statutory exemption applies.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Subdivided Lands": The Five-or-More-Lot Threshold
clauses.body: California's Subdivided Lands Law defines its own core trigger in Bus. & Prof. Code § 11000(a). "Subdivided lands" and "subdivision" mean improved or unimproved land, anywhere in California, that is divided or proposed to be divided, for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing (whether immediate or future), into five or more lots or parcels. The statute carves out land sold in government-survey lots or parcels of not less than 160 acres, appearing as such on the current county assessment roll — unless that land is divided or proposed to be divided for oil and gas sale purposes, in which case the 160-acre carve-out does not apply and the land is treated as "subdivided lands." The statute also carves the leasing of apartments, offices, stores, or similar space within an apartment, industrial, or commercial building, or within a mobilehome park (as defined in Health & Safety Code § 18214), out of this chapter's coverage — except that offering a mobilehome-park tenant a lease longer than five years, as a mandatory condition of tenancy, is expressly pulled back into this chapter's coverage.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only the core five-or-more-lot definition and its two express statutory carve-outs in § 11000(a); it does not address the additional categories of interest that a separate statute, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11004.5, expressly folds into the "subdivided lands" definition (addressed in the next clause), and it does not determine whether any specific parcel configuration, government-survey designation, or lease arrangement actually meets or is excluded from this definition — that depends on facts about the specific land, survey records, and lease terms that this information sheet does not supply. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California itself defines the term for purposes of this chapter — not a claim about how any other state defines a comparable term, or that every state regulates land subdivision through a five-or-more-lot threshold; some states use different numeric thresholds or different triggering criteria entirely.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11000(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, definition of "subdivided lands" and "subdivision"
citations.quote: (a) “Subdivided lands” and “subdivision” refer to improved or unimproved land or lands, wherever situated within California, divided or proposed to be divided for the purpose of sale or lease or financing, whether immediate or future, into five or more lots or parcels.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11000(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, carve-out for leasing of apartments, offices, stores, or mobilehome park space
citations.quote: This chapter also does not apply to the leasing of apartments, offices, stores, or similar space within an apartment building, industrial building, commercial building, or mobilehome park, as defined under Section 18214 of the Health and Safety Code, except that the offering of leases for a term in excess of five years to tenants within a mobilehome park as a mandatory requirement and prerequisite to tenancy within the mobilehome park shall be subject to the provisions of this chapter.

clauses.title: Statutory Expansion: Planned Developments, Condominiums, Stock Cooperatives, and Similar Interests
clauses.body: A second definitional statute, Bus. & Prof. Code § 11004.5, adds to the core § 11000 definition rather than replacing it. In addition to the provisions of § 11000, "subdivided lands" and "subdivision" also include: any planned development (as defined in § 11003) containing five or more lots; any community apartment project (as defined in § 11004) containing five or more apartments; any condominium project containing five or more condominiums (as defined in Civil Code § 783); any stock cooperative (as defined in § 11003.2) with five or more shareholders, existing or intended; and any limited-equity housing cooperative (as defined in § 11003.4). The statute separately extends coverage to accompanying memberships, rights, or privileges created in connection with those forms of development, and to interests or memberships in an owners' association (as defined in Civil Code § 4080 or § 6528) created in connection with them. The statute also states an express carve-out: time-share plans, exchange programs, incidental benefits, and short-term products regulated under the separate Vacation Ownership and Time-Share Act of 2004 (Bus. & Prof. Code § 11210 et seq.) are not "subdivisions" or "subdivided lands" under this chapter.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only which categories of development or ownership interest the statute expressly folds into the "subdivided lands" definition, and the statute's express carve-out for time-share interests; it does not itself determine whether a specific planned development, condominium project, stock cooperative, or limited-equity housing cooperative meets the five-or-more-unit threshold for any of these categories, and it does not address the separate statutory public-report and disclosure requirements this corpus documents elsewhere for time-share purchases. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California itself expands its subdivided-lands definition — not a claim about how any other state defines comparable development categories.

citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, categories of development included within "subdivided lands"
citations.quote: In addition to the provisions of Section 11000, the reference in this code to “subdivided lands” and “subdivision” shall include all of the following:(a) Any planned development, as defined in Section 11003, containing five or more lots.(b) Any community apartment project, as defined by Section 11004, containing five or more apartments.(c) Any condominium project containing five or more condominiums, as defined in Section 783 of the Civil Code.(d) Any stock cooperative as defined in Section 11003.2, including any legal or beneficial interests therein, having or intended to have five or more shareholders.(e) Any limited-equity housing cooperative, as defined in Section 11003.4.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Blanket Encumbrance"
clauses.body: Bus. & Prof. Code § 11013 defines a term used elsewhere in this statutory scheme to describe liens affecting more than one lot in a subdivision. A "blanket encumbrance" means a trust deed, mortgage, or any other lien or encumbrance (including a mechanics' lien), that secures or evidences payment of money and that affects either the land to be subdivided as a whole or more than one lot or parcel of subdivided land, or an agreement affecting more than one such lot or parcel under which the owner or subdivider holds the subdivision under an option, contract to sell, or trust agreement.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the statutory definition of "blanket encumbrance" itself; it does not address the specific statutory consequences that attach when a blanket encumbrance exists on a subdivision (for example, particular financial-arrangement showings the commissioner may require before issuing a public report), which are governed by other sections of this chapter not documented in this information sheet. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California itself defines this term — not a claim about how any other state's subdivided-land or real-estate statutes define a comparable concept.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11013 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, definition of "blanket encumbrance"
citations.quote: For the purposes of this part, a blanket encumbrance shall be considered to mean a trust deed or mortgage or any other lien or encumbrance, mechanics’ lien or otherwise, securing or evidencing the payment of money and affecting land to be subdivided or affecting more than one lot or parcel of subdivided land, or an agreement affecting more than one such lot or parcel by which the owner or subdivider holds said subdivision under an option, contract to sell, or trust agreement.

clauses.title: The Public Report Application Requirement: Notice of Intention Filed With the Department of Real Estate
clauses.body: Bus. & Prof. Code § 11010 requires a person who intends to offer subdivided lands within California for sale or lease to file an application for a public report with the Department of Real Estate before doing so, except as otherwise provided in subdivision (c) or elsewhere in the chapter. That application consists of a notice of intention and a completed questionnaire, on forms the department prepares. The notice of intention must contain specified categories of information about the subdivided lands and the proposed offering, including (among eighteen enumerated categories) the name and address of the owner, the name and address of the subdivider, the legal description and area of the land, and a true statement of the condition of title, including all encumbrances. Other enumerated categories in the same subdivision separately require, where applicable, a Mello-Roos special-tax notice under Civil Code § 1102.6c (a mechanism this corpus documents in a separate Residential Purchase Agreement clause), school-district statements, an airport-vicinity notice, a soils/geologic-report statement, and, where the property lies within one mile of designated farmland, a "Notice of Right to Farm" referencing Civil Code § 3482.5.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only the filing requirement and the first several categories of required notice-of-intention content; it does not reproduce or analyze all eighteen enumerated categories in § 11010(b) — several of which (the airport notice, the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission notice, and the right-to-farm notice) contain lengthy prescribed statutory text this information sheet does not quote in full — and it does not determine which categories actually apply to any specific offering, which depends on facts about that subdivision's location and characteristics. Subdivision (c)'s questionnaire-waiver authority is also not addressed here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own application requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific offering, or that every state requires an equivalent filing.

citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided pursuant to subdivision (c) or elsewhere in this chapter, any person who intends to offer subdivided lands within this state for sale or lease shall file with the Department of Real Estate an application for a public report consisting of a notice of intention and a completed questionnaire on a form prepared by the department.

citations.quote: (b) The notice of intention shall contain the following information about the subdivided lands and the proposed offering:(1) The name and address of the owner.(2) The name and address of the subdivider.(3) The legal description and area of lands.(4) A true statement of the condition of the title to the land, particularly including all encumbrances thereon.

clauses.title: Commissioner's Examination and the Statutory Grounds for Denying a Public Report
clauses.body: Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018 governs what happens after a notice of intention and questionnaire are filed. The Real Estate Commissioner examines the subdivision and, unless statutory grounds for denial exist, must issue the subdivider a public report authorizing sale or lease of the lots or parcels in California; the report contains the data obtained under § 11010, plus whatever else the commissioner determines is needed to implement the article's purposes, and the commissioner may publish it. The statute enumerates nine grounds on which the commissioner may deny a public report: failure to comply with this chapter or the commissioner's regulations; a sale or lease that would misrepresent, deceive, or defraud purchasers or lessees; inability to deliver the title or interest contracted for; inadequate financial arrangements for offsite improvements; inadequate financial arrangements for community, recreational, or other included facilities; failure to show the parcels can be used for their offered purpose (and, for residential subdivisions, failure to show vehicular access and a source of potable domestic water is or will be available); failure to state the offered use and any applicable covenants or conditions in the contract or other writing; noncompliant management agreements or bylaws for common facilities; and inadequate financial arrangements for any guaranty or warranty included in the offering.
clauses.gap: This clause states the examination process and the nine enumerated denial grounds themselves; it does not address the separate procedures for amending, renewing, or suspending a public report once issued, does not address the commissioner's investigative or subpoena powers, and does not determine whether any specific ground for denial applies to a particular subdivision — that depends on facts about that offering's title, financing, and contract terms that this information sheet does not supply. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual grounds California's regulator applies — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific offering, or that every state's real-estate regulator reviews subdivision offerings against the same criteria.

citations.quote: The Real Estate Commissioner shall make an examination of any subdivision, and shall, unless there are grounds for denial, issue to the subdivider a public report authorizing the sale or lease in this state of the lots or parcels within the subdivision.

(f) Failure to make a showing that the parcels can be used for the purpose for which they are offered; and in the case of a subdivision being offered for residential purposes failure to make a showing that vehicular access and a source of potable domestic water either is available or will be available.(g) Failure to provide in the contract or other writing the use or uses for which the parcels are offered, together with any covenants or conditions relative thereto.(h) Agreements or bylaws to provide for management or other services pertaining to common facilities in the offering, which fail to comply with the regulations of the commissioner.(i) Failure to demonstrate that adequate financial arrangements have been made for any guaranty or warranty included in the offering.

clauses.title: Requirement to Deliver the Public Report Before a Binding Contract, and to Make It Available to the Public
clauses.body: Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(a)-(b) imposes two distinct delivery obligations once a public report has been issued. First, the owner, subdivider, or agent must give a copy of the public report to the prospective purchaser before the purchaser executes a binding contract or agreement for the sale or lease of any lot or parcel — an obligation that extends to lots or parcels the subdivider offers after repossession — and must take a receipt from the prospective purchaser in the form the Real Estate Commissioner's regulations specify. Second, separately from that purchaser-specific delivery obligation, the owner, subdivider, or agent must give a copy of the public report to any member of the public, at any time, on oral or written request, and must post a copy of the report, with a statement that a copy is available on request, in a conspicuous place at any office where sales, leases, or offers to sell or lease lots in the subdivision are regularly made.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only the delivery, receipt, and posting mechanics in § 11018.1(a)-(b); it does not address the additional statement a subdivider must give a purchaser when the subdivision is a common interest development (addressed in the next clause), and it does not itself confirm that a public report has been delivered, that a receipt was taken, or that posting occurred for any specific offering — those are factual questions this information sheet does not resolve. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own delivery mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific offering.

clauses.title: Additional Required Statement for Common Interest Development Subdivisions
clauses.body: Bus. & Prof. Code § 11018.1(c) layers an additional requirement onto the public-report delivery obligation described in the preceding clause, specifically for subdivisions that are common interest developments as defined in Civil Code § 4100. At the same time the public report must be given under subdivision (a), the owner, subdivider, or agent must also give the prospective purchaser a copy of a statutory "Common Interest Development General Information" statement — prescribed statutory text describing, among other things, that the project is a common interest development, that ownership carries mandatory association membership and assessment obligations, and that governing documents (a Declaration of Restrictions/CC&Rs, articles of incorporation, and bylaws) control the purchaser's rights. The statute separately provides that failing to give this particular statement is not treated as a violation subject to Bus. & Prof. Code § 10185, a different statutory enforcement provision.
clauses.gap: This clause states that the statement is required and that its non-delivery is carved out from § 10185 enforcement; it does not quote the full prescribed statement text (which runs to several paragraphs), does not address what other enforcement avenue, if any, applies to a failure to give this specific statement, and does not address the separate Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development disclosure obligations this corpus documents elsewhere for HOA/CC&R disclosures generally, which arise under different statutes at different points in a CID transaction. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own additional CID-specific requirement — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific offering.

clauses.title: Criminal Penalties for Violating Enumerated Provisions of the Subdivided Lands Law
clauses.body: Bus. & Prof. Code § 11023 attaches criminal exposure to violations of a specific, enumerated list of sections within this chapter: §§ 11010, 11010.1, 11010.8, 11013.1, 11013.2, 11013.4, 11018.2, 11018.7, 11018.9, 11018.10, 11018.11, 11019, and 11022. A violation of any of those enumerated sections is a public offense punishable by a fine not exceeding $10,000, or imprisonment under Penal Code § 1170(h) or in a county jail not exceeding one year, or both the fine and imprisonment.
clauses.gap: The enumerated list in § 11023 does not include every section this information sheet describes: it lists § 11010 (the notice-of-intention filing requirement) but does not list § 11018 (the commissioner's examination and public-report issuance) or § 11018.1 (delivery of the report to a purchaser or the public) among the sections whose violation triggers this specific criminal penalty — meaning this statute's own text does not extend this particular sanction to every obligation this information sheet describes, and this clause does not address what other penalty, if any, attaches to a violation of a section not on this list. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual criminal exposure and the actual enumerated sections California's own text lists — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific violation, or that every state enforces comparable subdivided-lands requirements through criminal penalties.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11023 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, criminal penalty for violating enumerated sections of the Subdivided Lands Law
citations.quote: Any person who violates Section 11010, 11010.1, 11010.8, 11013.1, 11013.2, 11013.4, 11018.2, 11018.7, 11018.9, 11018.10, 11018.11, 11019, or 11022 is guilty of a public offense punishable by a fine not exceeding ten thousand dollars ($10,000) or by imprisonment pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1170 of the Penal Code, or in a county jail not exceeding one year, or by both that fine and imprisonment.

clauses.title: Required Contents of a Subdivision Sales Contract
clauses.body: Bus. & Prof. Code § 11200 imposes a content requirement on the sales contract itself for a subdivision within this chapter's definition. Every sales contract for the purchase of real property in such a subdivision must clearly set forth: the legal description of the property, the encumbrances outstanding as of the date of the sales contract, and the terms of the contract.
clauses.gap: This clause states only this specific content requirement for the sales contract; it does not address the separate notice-of-intention content requirements for the public-report application (documented in an earlier clause), does not specify a required format for stating the legal description, encumbrances, or terms, and does not determine whether a specific sales contract's actual content satisfies this requirement — that depends on the contract's own text, which this information sheet does not supply. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own sales-contract content requirement for subdivided lands — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific sales contract.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 11200 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Business and Professions Code, required contents of a subdivision sales contract
citations.quote: Every sales contract relating to the purchase of real property in a subdivision as defined in this chapter shall clearly set forth the legal description of the property, of the encumbrances outstanding at the date of the sales contract, and the terms of the contract.

clauses.title: Identification
clauses.body: This information sheet concerns {{limitedPartnerName}}, a limited partner of {{partnershipName}}, a California limited partnership whose general partner is {{generalPartnerName}}. It addresses the statutory rule under which a limited partner may engage in certain activities without being treated, for liability purposes, as having "participate[d] in the control of the business" of the limited partnership.

clauses.title: The Safe-Harbor Rule for Limited Partner Conduct
clauses.body: California's limited partnership statute qualifies the general "participating in control" liability test with a safe harbor: a limited partner does not participate in the control of the business, within the meaning of the general liability rule, solely by doing, attempting to do, or having the right or power to do one or more of thirteen enumerated things. The statute separately states that this enumeration does not mean that other conduct, or the possession or exercise of other powers, by a limited partner automatically counts as participating in control — the list defines what is safe, not what is unsafe.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the introductory clause of Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(b) and all of subdivision (c). It does not state the underlying “participates in the control of the business” liability rule itself (Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(a)), which this project's California Limited Partnership Formation Information Sheet addresses in a separate clause (id: lpform_lp_liability_shield) citing the same statute's subdivision (a). The thirteen specific enumerated activities referenced here are stated individually in the companion clauses of this document, not in this clause. This clause does not state what conduct, beyond the enumerated list, a court has found does or does not amount to participation in control — subdivision (c) leaves that question open, and no case law was independently researched for this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, safe-harbor introductory clause
citations.quote: A limited partner does not participate in the control of the business within the meaning of subdivision (a) solely by doing, attempting to do, or having the right or power to do, one or more of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, enumeration is not exhaustive of what constitutes control
citations.quote: (c) The enumeration in subdivision (b) does not mean that any other conduct or the possession or exercise of any other power by a limited partner constitutes participation by the limited partner in the control of the business of the limited partnership.

clauses.title: Safe Harbor: Holding a Related Role or Transacting Business
clauses.body: Among the activities the statute places inside the safe harbor is holding certain roles connected to the limited partnership or its general partner. The statute lists, as things that alone do not amount to participating in control: being an independent contractor for, an agent or employee of, or a party transacting business with, the limited partnership or a general partner; being an officer, director, or shareholder of a corporate general partner; being a member, manager, or officer of an LLC general partner; being a limited partner of a partnership that is itself a general partner; being a trustee, administrator, executor, custodian, or other fiduciary or beneficiary of an estate or trust that is a general partner; and being a trustee, officer, adviser, shareholder, or beneficiary of a business trust that is a general partner.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(b)(1)(A)-(F). It does not address whether a specific person's actual role or business dealings fall within one of these six listed categories, nor does it address what other conduct that same person might separately engage in that could fall outside the safe harbor — the safe harbor protects only the listed status or activity itself, not necessarily every other thing the same person does. Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(b)(1) was not cross-checked against the parallel Delaware or other-state limited partnership statutes on which it is modeled.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, roles connected to the limited partnership or a general partner
citations.quote: (1) Being any of the following:(A) An independent contractor for, an agent or employee of, or transacting business with, the limited partnership or a general partner of the limited partnership.(B) An officer, director, or shareholder of a corporate general partner of the limited partnership.(C) A member, manager, or officer of a limited liability company that is a general partner of the limited partnership.(D) A limited partner of a partnership that is a general partner of the limited partnership.(E) A trustee, administrator, executor, custodian, or other fiduciary or beneficiary of an estate or trust that is a general partner.(F) A trustee, officer, adviser, shareholder, or beneficiary of a business trust that is a general partner.

clauses.title: Safe Harbor: Consulting, Advising, and Extending or Receiving Credit
clauses.body: The statute also places two financial and advisory activities inside the safe harbor. First, consulting with and advising a general partner regarding the business of the limited partnership does not, by itself, amount to participating in control. Second, a list of credit-related dealings with the limited partnership or a general partner — acting as surety, guaranteeing specific debts, providing collateral, borrowing money, or lending money — likewise does not, by itself, amount to participating in control.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(b)(2) and (b)(3). It does not address how much consulting or advising, or how large or frequent a credit transaction, might combine with other conduct outside this safe harbor to support a finding of control in a specific case — the statute does not quantify a limit, and no case law applying these paragraphs was independently researched for this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, consulting with and advising a general partner
citations.quote: (2) Consulting with and advising a general partner with respect to the business of the limited partnership.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, suretyship, guaranty, collateral, and lending or borrowing
citations.quote: (3) Acting as surety for the limited partnership or for a general partner, guaranteeing one or more specific debts of the limited partnership, providing collateral for the limited partnership or general partner, borrowing money from the limited partnership or a general partner, or lending money to the limited partnership or a general partner.

clauses.title: Safe Harbor: Voting, Meetings, and Approval Committees
clauses.body: The statute places core governance participation inside the safe harbor as well. Approving or disapproving an amendment to the partnership agreement does not, by itself, amount to participating in control. Voting on, proposing, or calling a meeting of the partners does not, by itself, amount to participating in control. Serving on a committee of the limited partnership or the limited partners for the purpose of approving actions of the general partner does not, by itself, amount to participating in control. And calling, requesting, attending, or participating at any meeting of the partners or the limited partners does not, by itself, amount to participating in control.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(b)(4), (b)(5), (b)(9), and (b)(10). It does not address what a limited partner does or says at such a meeting, vote, or committee session beyond the acts of attending, voting, proposing, calling, or serving — conduct at a meeting that goes beyond these listed acts is not addressed by this clause. It also does not address any quorum, notice, or voting-threshold rules that might separately govern how partnership-agreement amendments or partner meetings are conducted, which were not independently researched for this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, approving or disapproving a partnership agreement amendment
citations.quote: (4) Approving or disapproving an amendment to the partnership agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, voting on, proposing, or calling a partner meeting
citations.quote: (5) Voting on, proposing, or calling a meeting of the partners.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, serving on a committee that approves general partner actions
citations.quote: (9) Serving on a committee of the limited partnership or the limited partners for the purpose of approving actions of the general partner.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, calling, requesting, attending, or participating at a meeting
citations.quote: (10) Calling, requesting, attending, or participating at any meeting of the partners or the limited partners.

clauses.title: Safe Harbor: Winding Up and Certain Secretary of State Filings
clauses.body: The statute places two administrative and wind-down activities inside the safe harbor. Winding up the limited partnership under the statute's own winding-up provision does not, by itself, amount to participating in control. Executing and filing a certificate under the statute's certificate-of-limited-partnership provision, a certificate of withdrawal under a specified paragraph of the statute's certificate-of-limited-partnership-amendment provision, or a certificate of cancellation under another specified paragraph of that same provision, likewise does not, by itself, amount to participating in control.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(b)(6) and (b)(7). The cross-referenced statutes it names — Cal. Corp. Code §§ 15908.03 (winding up), 15902.05 (certificate contents), and 15902.04(a)(4) and (a)(6) (withdrawal and cancellation certificates) — were not independently fetched or verified for this clause; their own text, and any conditions those statutes place on when a limited partner may wind up the partnership or execute these filings, are outside what this clause states.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, winding up the partnership
citations.quote: (6) Winding up the partnership pursuant to Section 15908.03.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, executing and filing certain certificates
citations.quote: (7) Executing and filing a certificate pursuant to Section 15902.05, a certificate of withdrawal pursuant to paragraph (4) of subdivision (a) of Section 15902.04, or a certificate of cancellation of the certificate of limited partnership pursuant to paragraph (6) of subdivision (a) of Section 15902.04.

clauses.title: Safe Harbor: Audit Oversight, Derivative Actions, Related-Entity Roles, and the Catch-All
clauses.body: The statute places four further categories inside the safe harbor. Serving on an audit committee, or a committee performing audit-committee functions, does not, by itself, amount to participating in control. Taking any action required or permitted by law to bring, pursue, settle, or terminate a derivative action on the limited partnership's behalf does not, by itself, amount to participating in control. Serving on the board or a committee of, consulting with or advising, acting as an officer, director, stockholder, partner, member, manager, agent, or employee of, or acting as a fiduciary for, any entity in which the limited partnership itself holds an interest, does not, by itself, amount to participating in control. And, as a residual catch-all, exercising any right or power the statute permits to limited partners that is not specifically listed in the enumeration does not, by itself, amount to participating in control.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03(b)(8), (b)(11), (b)(12), and (b)(13). The catch-all in paragraph (13) reaches only rights or powers the statute itself permits to limited partners — it does not extend the safe harbor to conduct that is not otherwise a right or power granted by the Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, and this clause does not attempt to enumerate what those other statutory rights or powers are. What qualifies as a derivative action, or as the requirements for bringing one, is governed by other statutory and procedural rules not addressed by this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, audit committee service
citations.quote: (8) Serving on an audit committee or committee performing the functions of an audit committee.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, derivative action conduct
citations.quote: (11) Taking any action required or permitted by law to bring, pursue, settle, or terminate a derivative action on behalf of the limited partnership.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, roles in an entity in which the limited partnership has an interest
citations.quote: (12) Serving on the board of directors or a committee of, consulting with or advising, being or acting as an officer, director, stockholder, partner, member, manager, agent, or employee of, or being or acting as a fiduciary for, any person in which the limited partnership has an interest.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, residual catch-all for unenumerated statutory rights or powers
citations.quote: (13) Exercising any right or power permitted to limited partners under this chapter and not specifically enumerated in this subdivision.

clauses.title: A Separate Protection for a Good-Faith but Mistaken Limited Partner
clauses.body: California's limited partnership statute separately protects a person who invests in a business enterprise erroneously but in good faith believing they have become a limited partner. Such a person is not liable for the enterprise's obligations by reason of making the investment, receiving distributions, or exercising rights of or appropriate to a limited partner, if, on discovering the mistake, the person either causes an appropriate certificate of limited partnership, amendment, or certificate of correction to be filed with the Secretary of State, or withdraws from future participation by filing a certificate of withdrawal on the form the Secretary of State prescribes. That protection has its own limit: the same person remains liable to the same extent as a general partner to a third party who, before the correcting or withdrawal filing is made, enters into a transaction with the enterprise in the good-faith belief that the person is a general partner.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.06(a) and (b). It does not address subdivision (c)'s separate rule permitting withdrawal, notwithstanding a contrary agreement with co-owners, for a person who diligently but unsuccessfully attempts in good faith to file a correcting certificate — that rule is addressed in a separate companion clause of this document. This clause does not state what facts are sufficient to show a person's belief that they had become a limited partner was held erroneously but in good faith, nor whether any specific investor's belief or conduct meets that standard; that is a fact-specific inquiry this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.06 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, protection for a good-faith erroneous investor who cures the mistake
citations.quote: (a) Except as otherwise provided in subdivision (b), a person that makes an investment in a business enterprise and erroneously but in good faith believes that the person has become a limited partner in the enterprise is not liable for the enterprise’s obligations by reason of making the investment, receiving distributions from the enterprise, or exercising any rights of or appropriate to a limited partner, if, on ascertaining the mistake, the person:

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.06 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, curing by a correcting Secretary of State filing
citations.quote: (1) causes an appropriate certificate of limited partnership, amendment, or certificate of correction to be signed and delivered to the Secretary of State for filing; or

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.06 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, curing by a certificate of withdrawal
citations.quote: (2) withdraws from future participation as an owner in the enterprise by signing and delivering to and on a form prescribed by the Secretary of State for filing a certificate of withdrawal containing the name of the limited partnership and the Secretary of State’s file number of the limited partnership under this section.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.06 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, liability to a third party who relied before the correcting filing
citations.quote: (b) A person that makes an investment described in subdivision (a) is liable to the same extent as a general partner to any third party that enters into a transaction with the enterprise, believing in good faith that the person is a general partner, before the Secretary of State files a certificate of withdrawal, certificate of limited partnership, amendment, or certificate of correction to show that the person is not a general partner.

clauses.title: The Right to Withdraw When a Diligent Good-Faith Correction Effort Fails
clauses.body: The statute adds a further rule for the good-faith erroneous investor described elsewhere in this document: if that person makes a diligent, good-faith effort to file the correcting certificate described in the statute but is unable to cause it to be signed and delivered to the Secretary of State for filing, the person still has the right to withdraw from the enterprise by filing a certificate of withdrawal — and the statute states that this withdrawal right exists even if the withdrawal would otherwise breach an agreement with others who are or have agreed to become co-owners of the enterprise.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.06(c). It does not define what constitutes a “diligent effort in good faith” for purposes of this subdivision, nor does it address any liability the withdrawing person might otherwise have already incurred under subdivision (b) toward a third party who relied on the person's apparent status before the withdrawal certificate was filed. Whether a specific person's effort to obtain a correcting signature was sufficiently diligent is a fact-specific question this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.06 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, diligent good-faith effort that fails to secure a correcting certificate
citations.quote: (c) If a person makes a diligent effort in good faith to comply with paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) and is unable

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15903.06 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, withdrawal permitted despite a contrary co-owner agreement
citations.quote: to cause the appropriate certificate of limited partnership, amendment, or certificate of correction to be signed and delivered to the Secretary of State for filing, the person has the right to withdraw from the enterprise pursuant to paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) even if the withdrawal would otherwise breach an agreement with others that are or have agreed to become co-owners of the enterprise.
