citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in the terms of a trust or this chapter, this chapter applies to the following: (a) A trust or an estate. (b) A life estate or other term interest in which the interest of one or more persons will be succeeded by the interest of one or more other persons.

clauses.title: The Statute's Default-Rule Status: Trust Terms and Fiduciary Discretion Control First
clauses.body: UFIPA's allocation rules are defaults, not mandates that override a trust's own terms. Probate Code § 16325(a) provides that in making an allocation or determination, or exercising discretion, under the chapter: a fiduciary shall act in good faith, based on what is fair and reasonable to all beneficiaries; a fiduciary shall administer a trust or decedent's estate in accordance with the trust or the will, even if there is a different provision in the chapter; a fiduciary may administer a trust or decedent's estate by exercising a discretionary power of administration given by the trust or will, even if the exercise produces a result different from what the chapter would require or permit, without any inference of impropriety arising from that fact alone; and a fiduciary shall administer a trust or decedent's estate in accordance with the chapter only if the trust or will does not contain a different provision and does not give the fiduciary a discretionary power of administration. In other words, {{trustName}}'s own express terms, and any discretionary administration power {{trustName}} grants {{trusteeName}}, take priority over UFIPA's statutory default rules; the statute fills gaps the trust instrument leaves open.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of § 16325. The same section separately provides, in subdivision (b), a presumption that a fiduciary's allocation, determination, or exercise of discretion is fair and reasonable to all beneficiaries, and in subdivisions (c) through (e), a residual catch-all principal allocation and a list of factors relevant to certain other statutory powers -- none of that additional text is quoted or applied here. This document does not read or interpret any particular trust's actual governing instrument to determine whether, or to what extent, its terms displace a specific default rule described elsewhere in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16325(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: trust terms and discretionary administration power controlling over the chapter's default rules
citations.quote: (a) In making an allocation or determination or exercising discretion under this chapter, all of the following apply: (1) A fiduciary shall act in good faith, based on what is fair and reasonable to all beneficiaries. (2) A fiduciary shall administer a trust or decedent’s estate in accordance with the trust or the will, even if there is a different provision in this chapter. (3) A fiduciary may administer a trust or decedent’s estate by the exercise of a discretionary power of administration given to the fiduciary by the trust or the will, even if the exercise of the power produces a result different from a result required or permitted by this chapter, and no inference that the fiduciary has improperly exercised the discretion arises from the fact that the fiduciary has made an allocation contrary to a provision of this chapter. (4) A fiduciary shall administer a trust or decedent’s estate in accordance with this chapter if the trust or the will does not contain a different provision or does not give the fiduciary a discretionary power of administration.

clauses.title: The Trustee's Statutory Power to Adjust Between Income and Principal
clauses.body: UFIPA gives a trustee a distinct statutory tool for administering a trust impartially between income and remainder beneficiaries: the power to adjust. Probate Code § 16327(a) provides that except as otherwise provided in the terms of a trust or the section itself, "a fiduciary, in a record, without court approval, may adjust between income and principal if the fiduciary determines the exercise of the power to adjust will assist the fiduciary in administering the trust or estate impartially." Under § 16327(b), the statute does not create a duty to exercise or even consider the power to adjust, or to inform a beneficiary about it, and under § 16327(c), a fiduciary that in good faith exercises or fails to exercise the power is not liable to a person affected by that choice.
clauses.gap: Subdivision (e) of § 16327 -- not quoted in this clause -- lists nine specific circumstances in which the power to adjust may not be exercised at all, including trusts that qualify for certain special tax benefits, interests payable as a fixed annuity or fixed fraction, permanent charitable set-asides, arrangements that would trigger federal income, estate, or gift tax consequences, a fiduciary who is not an "independent person," certain irrevocable trusts with a settlor income interest tied to public benefit eligibility, and a trust that is already a unitrust under Article 3. This document does not apply those restrictions, or the cofiduciary and delegation rules in subdivisions (f) through (h), to any specific trust or any specific adjustment; whether the power to adjust is available for a particular trust and a particular adjustment is not determined here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16327(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the trustee's power to adjust between income and principal without court approval
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in the terms of a trust or this section, a fiduciary, in a record, without court approval, may adjust between income and principal if the fiduciary determines the exercise of the power to adjust will assist the fiduciary in administering the trust or estate impartially.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16327(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no duty to exercise or consider the power to adjust, and no liability for a good-faith choice either way
citations.quote: (b) This section does not create a duty to exercise or consider the power to adjust under subdivision (a) or to inform a beneficiary about the applicability of this section. (c) A fiduciary that in good faith exercises or fails to exercise the power to adjust under subdivision (a) is not liable to a person affected by the exercise or failure to exercise.

clauses.title: The Trustee's Power to Convert Between an Income Trust and a Unitrust
clauses.body: Separate from the power to adjust, UFIPA gives a trustee a power to change how a trust calculates the amount available to an income beneficiary in the first place. Probate Code § 16332(a) provides that a fiduciary, without court approval, by complying with the section's other requirements, may convert an income trust to a unitrust (so that net income becomes a fixed unitrust amount, typically a percentage of trust value, rather than actual income received), change the percentage or method used to calculate an existing unitrust amount, or convert a unitrust back to an income trust. Under § 16332(b), a fiduciary may take that action only if the fiduciary determines it will assist in administering the trust impartially, sends notice describing and proposing the action as required by § 16333, and no beneficiary objects within the applicable period; if a beneficiary does object, § 16332(c) allows the fiduciary or a beneficiary to ask the court to permit, modify, or prevent the proposed action.
clauses.gap: This clause does not describe the detailed content requirements for a unitrust plan under §§ 16334-16338 (for example, the unitrust rate, the valuation method, or default provisions that apply if the plan is silent), nor the categories of trusts Probate Code § 16331(b) excludes from Article 3 entirely -- certain trusts tied to specific Internal Revenue Code provisions (26 U.S.C. §§ 170(f)(2)(B), 642(c)(5), 664(d), 2702(a)(3)(A)(ii)-(iii), or 2702(b)), such as certain charitable remainder and split-interest trusts. Whether a particular trust is eligible for unitrust conversion under this article, and what a specific unitrust plan for that trust should provide, is not addressed here.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16332(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the fiduciary's power, without court approval, to convert an income trust to a unitrust, change a unitrust's calculation, or convert a unitrust back to an income trust
citations.quote: (a) A fiduciary, without court approval, by complying with subdivisions (b) and (f), may do any of the following: (1) Convert an income trust to a unitrust if the fiduciary creates in a record a unitrust plan for the trust providing for both of the following: (A) That in administering the trust, the net income of the trust will be a unitrust amount rather than net income determined without regard to this article. (B) The percentage and method used to calculate the unitrust amount. (2) Change the percentage or method used to calculate a unitrust amount for a unitrust if the fiduciary implements in a record a unitrust plan or an amendment or replacement of a unitrust plan providing changes in the percentage or method used to calculate the unitrust amount. (3) Convert a unitrust to an income trust if the fiduciary implements in a record a determination that, in administering the trust, the net income of the trust will be net income determined without regard to this article rather than a unitrust amount.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16332(b)-(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: conditions for taking the action -- an impartiality determination, notice, and the consequence of a beneficiary's objection
citations.quote: (b) A fiduciary may take an action under subdivision (a) if all of the following conditions are met: (1) The fiduciary determines that the action will assist the fiduciary to administer a trust impartially. (2) The fiduciary sends a notice in a record, in the manner required by Section 16333, describing and proposing to take the action. (3) No beneficiary objects to the proposed action in a writing delivered to the trustee within the period prescribed by subdivision (d) of Section 16502. (c) If a fiduciary receives, on or before the date stated in the notice under Section 16333, an objection in a record to a proposed action, the fiduciary or a beneficiary may request the court to have the proposed action taken as proposed, taken with modifications, or prevented.

clauses.title: Required Notice Contents and the Minimum 30-Day Objection Window
clauses.body: The notice a fiduciary must send before converting an income trust to a unitrust, changing a unitrust's calculation, or converting a unitrust back to an income trust has statutorily required contents. Probate Code § 16333 lists what the notice must include: the proposed action; for a conversion to a unitrust, a copy of the adopted unitrust plan; for a change in calculation, a copy of the amended or replacement plan; a statement that the recipient may object by stating the basis for the objection and delivering it to the fiduciary; the fiduciary's name and contact information; and the name and contact information of a person who can be contacted for more information. On timing, § 16333(e) requires the notice to state "[t]he date by which an objection under subdivision (d) shall be received by the fiduciary, which shall be at least 30 days after the date the notice is sent."
clauses.gap: This clause describes only the content requirements listed directly in § 16333; it does not describe the separate service mechanics referenced in that section -- § 16333 requires notice to be sent "as required by Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 16500), including notice to a beneficiary who is a minor and to the minor's guardian, if any" -- and this document does not quote or apply that Chapter 5 notice-service statute. Thirty days is a statutory floor, not a fixed deadline: a fiduciary may set a longer objection period, and this clause does not determine what objection period, if any, applies to a specific notice already sent for any particular trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16333 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the required contents of the notice of a proposed unitrust conversion or calculation change
citations.quote: A notice required by paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 16332 shall be sent as required by Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 16500), including notice to a beneficiary who is a minor and to the minor’s guardian, if any, and shall include all of the following: (a) The action proposed under paragraph (2) of subdivision (b) of Section 16332. (b) For a conversion of an income trust to a unitrust, a copy of the unitrust plan adopted under paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) of Section 16332. (c) For a change in the percentage or method used to calculate the unitrust amount, a copy of the unitrust plan or amendment or replacement of the unitrust plan adopted under paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 16332. (d) A statement that the person to which the notice is sent may object to the proposed action by stating in a record the basis for the objection and sending or delivering the record to the fiduciary. (e) The date by which an objection under subdivision (d) shall be received by the fiduciary, which shall be at least 30 days after the date the notice is sent.

clauses.title: Default Allocation of Money Received From a Corporation, LLC, or Similar Entity
clauses.body: UFIPA sets a default rule for one of the most common receipts a trustee handles: a distribution from an entity in which the trust owns an interest, such as a corporation, partnership, limited liability company, regulated investment company, or real estate investment trust. Probate Code § 16340(c) provides the baseline: "Except as otherwise provided in paragraphs (2) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (d), a fiduciary shall allocate money received in an entity distribution to income." Subdivision (d) then carves out categories that instead go to principal: property received that is not money; money received in exchange for part or all of the fiduciary's interest to the extent the distribution reduces that interest relative to other owners; money the fiduciary determines or estimates is a "capital distribution" (a return of capital or a total or partial liquidating distribution); and money from a regulated investment company or real estate investment trust that is a capital gain dividend, or comparably treated, for federal income tax purposes.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the baseline income/principal split in subdivisions (c) and (d); it does not quote or apply subdivisions (e) through (i), which set out the safe harbors, a 20%-of-fair-market-value threshold, and a multi-factor test a fiduciary may use to determine or estimate whether a distribution is a "capital distribution," nor the special rule in subdivision (g) requiring an amount the fiduciary is in doubt about to be allocated to principal. This document does not classify any specific distribution received by a trust or determine how it should be allocated.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16340(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the default rule allocating money received in an entity distribution to income
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided in paragraphs (2) to (4), inclusive, of subdivision (d), a fiduciary shall allocate money received in an entity distribution to income.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16340(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the categories of entity distributions allocated to principal instead
citations.quote: A fiduciary shall allocate to principal all of the following: (1) Property received in an entity distribution that is not money. (2) Money received in an entity distribution in an exchange for part or all of the fiduciary’s interest in the entity, to the extent the entity distribution reduces the fiduciary’s interest in the entity relative to the interests of other persons that own or hold interests in the entity. (3) Money received in an entity distribution that the fiduciary determines or estimates is a capital distribution. (4) Money received in an entity distribution from an entity that is a regulated investment company or real estate investment trust if the money received is a capital gain dividend for federal income tax purposes. (5) Money received in an entity distribution that is treated, for federal income purposes, comparably to the treatment described in paragraph (4).

clauses.title: Default Allocation of Receipts From Minerals, Water, or Other Natural Resources
clauses.body: UFIPA also sets a specific default allocation for receipts from an interest in minerals, water, or other natural resources that a trustee does not account for as a business. Probate Code § 16350(a) provides that, to that extent, the fiduciary allocates the receipt: to income, when received as delay rental or annual rent on a lease, as a factor for interest or its equivalent under an agreement creating a production payment, or on account of an interest in renewable water; to principal, if received from a production payment (except as just described); and between income and principal in a reasonable manner, when received on account of a nonrenewable water interest, as a royalty, shut-in-well payment, take-or-pay payment, or bonus, or from a working interest or any other interest not otherwise listed.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (a). Subdivision (c) creates a presumption that an allocation made under paragraph (3) of subdivision (a) (the between-income-and-principal category) is reasonable if the amount allocated to principal equals the federal depletion deduction allowed for the interest -- that presumption is not quoted or applied here. Subdivision (d) also gives a fiduciary who already held a minerals, water, or natural-resources interest before this chapter's January 1, 2024 effective date the option to keep allocating receipts from that pre-existing interest the way the fiduciary allocated them before that date, instead of using this section's default; this document does not determine whether that transition option applies to any specific interest held by a particular trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16350(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the default allocation of receipts from an interest in minerals, water, or other natural resources
citations.quote: To the extent a fiduciary does not account for a receipt from an interest in minerals, water, or other natural resources as a business under Section 16432, the fiduciary shall allocate the receipt in the following manner: (1) To income, to the extent received: (A) As delay rental or annual rent on a lease. (B) As a factor for interest or the equivalent of interest under an agreement creating a production payment. (C) On account of an interest in renewable water. (2) To principal, if received from a production payment, to the extent subparagraph (B) of paragraph (1) does not apply. (3) Between income and principal in a reasonable manner, to the extent received: (A) On account of an interest in nonrenewable water. (B) As a royalty, shut-in-well payment, take-or-pay payment, or bonus. (C) From a working interest or any other interest not provided for in subparagraph (A) or (B), or paragraph (1) or (2).

clauses.title: When an Income Beneficiary's Right to Net Income Begins
clauses.body: UFIPA fixes the date an income interest begins, which determines from what point an income beneficiary's entitlement to net income is measured. Probate Code § 16375(a) provides that an income beneficiary is entitled to net income from the date the income interest begins, and that the interest begins on the date the trust specifies or, if none is specified, on the date an asset becomes subject to the trust for the current income beneficiary or to a successive interest for a successor beneficiary. Section 16375(b) fixes that date concretely: for an asset transferred to the trust during the settlor's life, the transfer date; and for an asset that becomes subject to the trust because of a decedent's death -- whether held directly by the trust or transferred to a fiduciary by a third party because of the death -- "on the date of the decedent's death, even if there is an intervening period of administration of the decedent's estate."
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only when an income interest begins. It does not address the distinct question of when, and how, income is apportioned at the end of an income interest -- a related but separate set of rules in Probate Code §§ 16376-16377 (also in Article 7) that this document does not quote or describe. It also does not apply the beginning-date rule to determine the actual start date of any specific beneficiary's income entitlement under a particular trust.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16375(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: an income beneficiary's entitlement to net income from the date the income interest begins
citations.quote: An income beneficiary is entitled to net income in accordance with the terms of the trust from the date an income interest begins. The income interest begins on the date specified in the terms of the trust or, if no date is specified, on the date an asset becomes subject to either of the following: (1) The trust for the current income beneficiary. (2) A successive interest for a successor beneficiary.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 16375(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the income interest's start date for an asset that becomes subject to the trust because of a decedent's death
citations.quote: An asset becomes subject to a trust under paragraph (1) of subdivision (a) as follows: (1) For an asset that is transferred to the trust during the settlor’s life, on the date the asset is transferred. (2) For an asset that becomes subject to the trust because of a decedent’s death, on the date of the decedent’s death, even if there is an intervening period of administration of the decedent’s estate. (3) For an asset that is transferred to a fiduciary by a third party because of a decedent’s death, on the date of the decedent’s death.

clauses.title: Signature and Record Block — Uniform Fiduciary Income and Principal Act Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{trusteeName}}, as trustee of {{trustName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared as background regarding California's Uniform Fiduciary Income and Principal Act, Probate Code §§ 16320-16383. It does not itself evaluate, approve, or ratify any allocation, adjustment, unitrust conversion, or other administration decision made or proposed for {{trustName}}, and preparing or signing it does not satisfy, waive, or discharge any duty {{trusteeName}} owes as trustee of {{trustName}}, including any duty described in this document or any express provision of {{trustName}} that displaces a statutory default described here; only {{trusteeName}}'s actual administration decisions, evaluated under that standard, do that.]

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet summarizes federal requirements that apply when the H-1B employment of {{employeeName}} at {{companyName}} for the position of {{jobTitle}} ends. It describes the Department of Labor's wage-obligation regulation, 20 C.F.R. § 655.731(c)(7)(ii), the Department of Labor's labor-condition-application withdrawal regulation, 20 C.F.R. § 655.750(b), and the Department of Homeland Security's petition-notification, petition-revocation, and return-transportation regulations, 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(11) and § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E). It states facts about these federal requirements; it does not instruct {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} on how to respond to their particular circumstances, and it is not a substitute for the underlying Labor Condition Application, petition, or USCIS and DOL guidance.

clauses.title: Wage Obligation Continues Until a Bona Fide Termination
clauses.body: Department of Labor regulations state that payment of the required wage need not be made for a period of nonproductive status if there has been a bona fide termination of the H-1B employment relationship. The same regulation states that DHS regulations require the employer to notify DHS that the employment relationship has been terminated so that the petition is canceled, and require the employer to provide the employee with payment for transportation home under certain circumstances.
clauses.gap: The regulation itself does not define what makes a termination "bona fide" beyond cross-referencing the separate DHS notification and transportation regulations; further interpretation of the elements of a bona fide termination for wage-obligation purposes appears in agency adjudications and case law that this information sheet, limited to fetched primary regulatory text, does not address.

citations.quote: Payment need not be made if there has been a bona fide termination of the employment relationship. DHS regulations require the employer to notify the DHS that the employment relationship has been terminated so that the petition is canceled (8 CFR 214.2(h)(11)), and require the employer to provide the employee with payment for transportation home under certain circumstances (8 CFR 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E)).

clauses.title: Employer's Duty to Notify USCIS of a Change in Employment
clauses.body: Federal regulations require the petitioner to immediately notify U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services of changes in the terms and conditions of a beneficiary's employment that may affect eligibility for H classification. If the petitioner no longer employs the beneficiary, the regulation directs the petitioner to send a letter explaining the change to the director who approved the petition, rather than filing an amended petition.
clauses.gap: The regulation requires notice "immediately" but does not itself set a maximum number of days, prescribe a required notification form, or designate a mailing address for the letter; H-2A and H-2B petitioners are separately directed to different notification provisions not addressed by this clause.

citations.quote: The petitioner shall immediately notify the Service of any changes in the terms and conditions of employment of a beneficiary which may affect eligibility under section 101(a)(15)(H) of the Act and paragraph (h) of this section. An amended petition on the form prescribed by USCIS should be filed when the petitioner continues to employ the beneficiary. If the petitioner no longer employs the beneficiary, the petitioner shall send a letter explaining the change(s) to the director who approved the petition. However, H-2A and H-2B petitioners must send notification to DHS pursuant to paragraphs (h)(5)(vi) and (h)(6)(i)(F) of this section respectively.

clauses.title: Automatic Revocation of the H-1B Petition Upon Notice
clauses.body: Federal regulations provide that approval of an H-1B petition is immediately and automatically revoked upon notification from the H-1B petitioner that the beneficiary is no longer employed, without the separate notice-and-rebuttal process that applies to revocation on other grounds.
clauses.gap: Automatic revocation under this provision depends on the petitioner actually sending notification; the regulatory text does not itself set a deadline by which that notification must reach USCIS to take effect, and this revocation rule operates independently of the separate wage-obligation and return-transportation provisions described elsewhere in this information sheet.

citations.case: 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(11)(ii) (eCFR text)
citations.quote: The approval of any petition is immediately and automatically revoked if the petitioner goes out of business, files a written withdrawal of the petition, or the Department of Labor revokes the labor certification upon which the petition is based. The approval of an H-1B petition is also immediately and automatically revoked upon notification from the H-1B petitioner that the beneficiary is no longer employed.

clauses.title: Liability for Return Transportation Costs Upon Dismissal
clauses.body: Federal regulations make an H-1B employer liable for the reasonable costs of return transportation of the beneficiary abroad if the beneficiary is dismissed from employment before the end of the period of authorized admission. For purposes of this liability, "abroad" refers to the beneficiary's last place of foreign residence, and the provision applies to any employer whose offer of employment became the basis for the beneficiary obtaining or continuing H-1B status.
clauses.gap: The regulation's liability runs to "the alien" — the H-1B beneficiary — and its text does not extend the return-transportation obligation to the beneficiary's dependents, nor does it define "reasonable costs" by reference to a fare class, routing, or dollar figure.

citations.case: 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) (eCFR text)
citations.quote: The employer will be liable for the reasonable costs of return transportation of the alien abroad if the alien is dismissed from employment by the employer before the end of the period of authorized admission pursuant to section 214(c)(5) of the Act.

citations.case: 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) (eCFR text)
citations.quote: Within the context of this paragraph, the term “abroad” refers to the alien's last place of foreign residence. This provision applies to any employer whose offer of employment became the basis for an alien obtaining or continuing H-1B status.

clauses.title: Voluntary Resignation Is Not a "Dismissal" for This Purpose
clauses.body: The same regulation states that if the beneficiary voluntarily terminates employment before the petition's validity period expires, the beneficiary has not been dismissed for purposes of the return-transportation liability provision.
clauses.gap: The regulatory text states this distinction as a bare rule without defining what makes a resignation "voluntary" when it follows employer conduct such as a demotion, pay cut, or ultimatum; that line-drawing is not addressed by the regulation itself.

citations.case: 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) (eCFR text)
citations.quote: If the beneficiary voluntarily terminates his or her employment prior to the expiration of the validity of the petition, the alien has not been dismissed.

clauses.title: Beneficiary's Avenue to Raise Noncompliance With USCIS
clauses.body: Federal regulations provide that if the beneficiary believes the employer has not complied with the return-transportation liability provision, the beneficiary is to advise the USCIS Service Center that adjudicated the petition in writing, and that the complaint will be retained in the file relating to the petition.
clauses.gap: The regulation does not specify a response deadline for USCIS, an enforcement mechanism separate from placing the complaint in the petition file, or any private right of action created by the regulation itself for the beneficiary to collect the transportation cost directly from the employer.

citations.case: 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) (eCFR text)
citations.quote: If the beneficiary believes that the employer has not complied with this provision, the beneficiary shall advise the Service Center which adjudicated the petition in writing. The complaint will be retained in the file relating to the petition.

clauses.title: Withdrawing the Labor Condition Application After Employment Ends
clauses.body: Department of Labor regulations permit an employer that filed a certified labor condition application to withdraw it at any time before the application's validity period expires, on the condition that no H-1B, H-1B1, or E-3 nonimmigrants remain employed at the place of employment under that LCA and that the Wage and Hour Administrator has not already commenced an investigation of the application.
clauses.gap: Withdrawal under this provision is only available once no covered nonimmigrants remain employed under the LCA at that place of employment — the regulatory text does not make LCA withdrawal a mechanism for ending wage obligations to an H-1B employee who is still working there.

citations.quote: An employer who has filed a labor condition application which has been certified pursuant to § 655.740 of this part may withdraw such labor condition application at any time before the expiration of the validity period of the application, provided that: (i) H-1B, H-1B1, and E-3 nonimmigrants are not employed at the place of employment pursuant to the LCA; and

clauses.title: Wage Obligation Persists Notwithstanding LCA Withdrawal
clauses.body: The same regulations state that an employer must comply with the required-wage-rate and prevailing-working-conditions statements of its labor condition application even after the LCA has been withdrawn, for as long as H-1B nonimmigrants remain employed under that application, unless the application has been superseded by a subsequently certified application.
clauses.gap: This wage-continuation rule is stated in terms of the LCA's withdrawal, a Department of Labor filing distinct from the DHS petition described elsewhere in this information sheet; withdrawing the LCA and notifying USCIS of a bona fide termination of the petition are separate procedural steps governed by separate regulations.

citations.quote: An employer shall comply with the “required wage rate” and “prevailing working conditions” statements of its labor condition application required under §§ 655.731 and 655.732 of this part, respectively, even if such application is withdrawn, at any time H-1B nonimmigrants are employed pursuant to the application, unless the application is superseded by a subsequent application which is certified by ETA.

clauses.title: Recordkeeping and Further Information
clauses.body: This information sheet reflects the DHS petition-notification, petition-revocation, and return-transportation regulations at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(h)(4)(iii)(E) and § 214.2(h)(11), and the DOL wage and labor-condition-application-withdrawal regulations at 20 C.F.R. §§ 655.731(c)(7)(ii) and 655.750(b), as of {{dateSigned}}. It does not address state law, the separate rules that apply to H-1B-dependent or willful-violator employers, related nonimmigrant categories such as H-1B1 or E-3, or the agency and judicial decisions that further interpret what constitutes a bona fide termination.

clauses.title: About This Bloodborne Pathogens Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Bloodborne Pathogens Exposure Control — Information Sheet describes California's Cal/OSHA regulation governing occupational exposure to blood and other potentially infectious materials, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193, as those requirements relate to the working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.

It summarizes selected requirements of that regulation: which employees and work situations the standard covers, the written Exposure Control Plan an employer with employees who have occupational exposure must establish and maintain, the Sharps Injury Log employers must keep, the universal-precautions and engineering/work-practice-control approach the standard requires, personal protective equipment requirements, the hepatitis B vaccination the employer must make available, post-exposure medical evaluation and follow-up after a reported exposure incident, employee training requirements, and recordkeeping and confidentiality requirements for exposure-related medical records.

{{companyName}} has identified {{programAdministratorName}} as the person with responsibility connected to {{companyName}}'s Exposure Control Plan.

This information sheet is not itself {{companyName}}'s written Exposure Control Plan, does not itself satisfy 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(c)(1)'s written-plan requirement, and does not determine whether any particular job classification, task, or workplace practice of {{companyName}}'s does or does not involve "occupational exposure" as the regulation defines that term.

clauses.title: What Triggers Coverage: "Occupational Exposure"
clauses.body: California's Bloodborne Pathogens standard applies to all occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials (OPIM), as those terms are defined in the regulation, but by its own terms it does not apply to the construction industry. The regulation defines "Occupational Exposure" as reasonably anticipated skin, eye, mucous membrane, or parenteral contact with blood or OPIM that may result from the performance of an employee's duties — a definition that turns on what an employee's job duties reasonably anticipate, not on whether a particular employee has ever actually had such contact. "Other Potentially Infectious Materials" is itself a defined term in the regulation covering specified human body fluids, unfixed human tissue or organs, and certain HIV/HBV/HCV-related laboratory and animal materials — it is broader than blood alone.
clauses.gap: This clause states the regulation's own coverage trigger; it does not determine whether any particular job classification, task, or workplace involves "occupational exposure" as defined — that determination depends on the specific duties an employee reasonably anticipated to perform, which this clause does not evaluate for any specific employer. The full definition of "Other Potentially Infectious Materials" in subsection (b) lists specific body fluids and other materials that this clause does not reproduce in full. This clause also does not address the regulation's separate definitions of "Blood," "Bloodborne Pathogens," "Contaminated," or the many other defined terms in subsection (b) that give content to other parts of the standard.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(a) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(a), scope and application
citations.quote: (a) Scope and Application. This section applies to all occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials as defined by subsection (b) of this section.

citations.quote: EXCEPTION: This regulation does not apply to the construction industry.

citations.quote: "Occupational Exposure" means reasonably anticipated skin, eye, mucous membrane, or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials that may result from the performance of an employee's duties.

clauses.title: The Written Exposure Control Plan
clauses.body: An employer that has an employee or employees with occupational exposure, as the regulation defines that term, must establish, implement, and maintain an effective, written Exposure Control Plan designed to eliminate or minimize employee exposure — a plan that the regulation itself requires be consistent with 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3203, California's separate Injury and Illness Prevention Program regulation. The Exposure Control Plan must contain at least the elements the regulation enumerates, including the employer's written exposure determination, the schedule and method for implementing each of the standard's applicable subsections, and procedures connected to the Sharps Injury Log. The plan is not a one-time document: the regulation requires the employer to review and update it at least annually and whenever necessary, including to reflect new or modified tasks affecting occupational exposure and changes in technology that could reduce exposure.
clauses.gap: This clause states the plan's existence, required consistency with Section 3203, and update obligation; it does not reproduce the regulation's full eight-item list of mandatory plan elements in subsection (c)(1)(B), the employee-access requirement tied to Section 3204(e), or the separate solicitation-and-documentation duty owed to non-managerial employees responsible for direct patient care under subsection (c)(1)(E). It does not state whether any particular employer has adopted an Exposure Control Plan or evaluate the content of any plan an employer may have.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(c)(1)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(c)(1)(A), duty to establish an Exposure Control Plan
citations.quote: (A) Each employer having an employee(s) with occupational exposure as defined by subsection (b) of this section shall establish, implement and maintain an effective Exposure Control Plan which is designed to eliminate or minimize employee exposure and which is also consistent with Section 3203.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(c)(1)(B) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(c)(1)(B), written-plan requirement
citations.quote: (B) The Exposure Control Plan shall be in writing and shall contain at least the following elements:

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(c)(1)(D) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(c)(1)(D), annual review-and-update requirement
citations.quote: (D) The Exposure Control Plan shall be reviewed and updated at least annually and whenever necessary as follows:

clauses.title: The Sharps Injury Log
clauses.body: The regulation requires an employer to establish and maintain a Sharps Injury Log — a record of each exposure incident involving a sharp, recording specified information such as the date and time of the incident, the type and brand of sharp involved, and details of how the incident occurred, to the extent known or reasonably available. Each exposure incident must be recorded on the log within 14 working days of the date the incident is reported to the employer.
clauses.gap: This clause states the log's existence and the 14-working-day recording deadline; it does not reproduce the regulation's full list of required data fields in subsection (c)(2)(C), the confidentiality-of-the-injured-employee requirement in subsection (c)(2)(E), or the separate five-year retention period for the log, which is addressed in the recordkeeping clause of this information sheet. It does not state whether any particular employer maintains a Sharps Injury Log or evaluate the content of any log an employer may keep.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(c)(2) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(c)(2), Sharps Injury Log requirement
citations.quote: The employer shall establish and maintain a Sharps Injury Log, which is a record of each exposure incident involving a sharp. The information recorded shall include the following information, if known or reasonably available:

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(c)(2)(D) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(c)(2)(D), 14-working-day recording deadline
citations.quote: Each exposure incident shall be recorded on the Sharps Injury Log within 14 working days of the date the incident is reported to the employer.

clauses.title: Universal Precautions and Methods of Compliance
clauses.body: The regulation's baseline method-of-compliance requirement is that universal precautions be observed to prevent contact with blood or OPIM: where it is difficult or impossible to differentiate between types of body fluid, the regulation requires that all body fluids be treated as though potentially infectious. Building on that baseline, the regulation requires that engineering and work practice controls be used to eliminate or minimize employee exposure, with engineering controls examined and maintained or replaced on a regular schedule and work practice controls evaluated and updated on a regular schedule to ensure their continued effectiveness.
clauses.gap: This clause states the regulation's general universal-precautions principle and its general engineering/work-practice-controls requirement; it does not reproduce the regulation's detailed, procedure-specific requirements for needleless systems and needle devices, the prohibited-practices list in subsection (d)(3)(B), the sharps-container specifications in subsection (d)(3)(D), or the separate rules for regulated waste, contaminated laundry, and worksite decontamination in subsections (d)(3)(E)-(J), which this clause does not evaluate as applied to any particular workplace.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(d)(1) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(d)(1), universal precautions
citations.quote: (1) General. Universal precautions shall be observed to prevent contact with blood or OPIM. Under circumstances in which differentiation between body fluid types is difficult or impossible, all body fluids shall be considered potentially infectious materials.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(d)(2)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(d)(2)(A), engineering and work practice controls
citations.quote: (A) Engineering and work practice controls shall be used to eliminate or minimize employee exposure.

clauses.title: Personal Protective Equipment at No Cost to the Employee
clauses.body: Where occupational exposure remains after engineering and work practice controls are in place, the regulation requires the employer to provide appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) — such as gloves, gowns, laboratory coats, face shields or masks and eye protection, and ventilation devices for resuscitation — at no cost to the employee, and defines PPE as "appropriate" only if it does not permit blood or OPIM to pass through to the employee's clothes, skin, eyes, mouth, or other mucous membranes under normal conditions of use for the time the equipment will be worn. The employer must ensure the employee uses appropriate PPE, subject to a narrow exception the regulation itself states: where the employer shows the employee temporarily and briefly declined to use PPE because, under rare and extraordinary circumstances, the employee's professional judgment was that its use would have prevented delivery of health care or public safety services or would have posed an increased hazard to worker or co-worker safety in that specific instance.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general no-cost PPE-provision duty, the regulatory definition of "appropriate" PPE, and the narrow declined-use exception; it does not reproduce the regulation's separate accessibility, hypoallergenic-alternative, cleaning/laundering, repair/replacement, or removal requirements in subsections (d)(4)(C)-(F), or the glove-specific and mask/eye-protection/respirator-specific rules in subsections (d)(4)(G)-(H), which this clause does not evaluate as applied to any particular job or task.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(d)(4)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(d)(4)(A), PPE provision at no cost and definition of "appropriate"
citations.quote: (A) Provision. Where occupational exposure remains after institution of engineering and work practice controls, the employer shall provide, at no cost to the employee, appropriate personal protective equipment such as, but not limited to, gloves, gowns, laboratory coats, face shields or masks and eye protection, and mouthpieces, resuscitation bags, pocket masks, or other ventilation devices. Personal protective equipment will be considered "appropriate" only if it does not permit blood or OPIM to pass through to or reach the employee's work clothes, street clothes, undergarments, skin, eyes, mouth, or other mucous membranes under normal conditions of use and for the duration of time which the protective equipment will be used.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(d)(4)(B) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(d)(4)(B), mandatory use and the declined-use exception
citations.quote: (B) Use. The employer shall ensure that the employee uses appropriate personal protective equipment unless the employer shows that the employee temporarily and briefly declined to use personal protective equipment when, under rare and extraordinary circumstances, it was the employee's professional judgment that in the specific instance its use would have prevented the delivery of health care or public safety services or would have posed an increased hazard to the safety of the worker or co-worker.

clauses.title: Hepatitis B Vaccination
clauses.body: The regulation requires the employer to make the hepatitis B vaccine and vaccination series available, at no cost, to all employees who have occupational exposure. Where the employer is also acting as the evaluating health care professional, the regulation requires the employer to advise the employee that the employee may refuse to consent to post-exposure evaluation and follow-up from the employer-affiliated provider, and if consent is refused, the employer must make immediately available a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up from a healthcare professional other than the employer. Vaccination itself must be made available after the employee has received the required training and within 10 working days of initial assignment, unless the employee has already completed the vaccination series, testing shows the employee is immune, or the vaccine is medically contraindicated for that employee.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general vaccination-availability, timing, and refusal-of-employer-provider rules; it does not reproduce the regulation's separate exception for certain designated first aid providers in subsection (f)(1)(A) and its accompanying reporting and vaccine-timing conditions, the prohibition on conditioning vaccination on a prescreening program in subsection (f)(2)(B), or the mandatory written declination statement in Appendix A that an employee who declines vaccination must sign, which this clause does not reproduce or evaluate.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(f)(1)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(f)(1)(A), no-cost vaccination and refusal of employer-affiliated evaluation
citations.quote: (A) The employer shall make available the hepatitis B vaccine and vaccination series to all employees who have occupational exposure, and post-exposure evaluation and follow-up for bloodborne pathogens exposure to all employees who have had an exposure incident. When an employer is also acting as the evaluating health care professional, the employer shall advise an employee following an exposure incident that the employee may refuse to consent to post-exposure evaluation and follow-up from the employer-healthcare professional. When consent is refused, the employer shall make immediately available to exposed employees a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up from a healthcare professional other than the exposed employee's employer.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(f)(2)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(f)(2)(A), 10-working-day vaccination timing rule
citations.quote: (A) Hepatitis B vaccination shall be made available after the employee has received the training required in subsection (g)(2)(G)9. and within 10 working days of initial assignment to all employees who have occupational exposure unless the employee has previously received the complete hepatitis B vaccination series, antibody testing has revealed that the employee is immune, or the vaccine is contraindicated for medical reasons.

clauses.title: Post-Exposure Medical Evaluation and Follow-Up
clauses.body: Following a report of an exposure incident, the regulation requires the employer to make a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up immediately available to the exposed employee, including — among the elements the regulation specifies — documentation of the route and circumstances of exposure, identification and testing of the source individual where feasible and permitted, collection and testing of the exposed employee's own blood, and provision for post-exposure prophylaxis and counseling as medically indicated. The regulation also entitles the employee to a copy of the evaluating healthcare professional's written opinion, which the employer must obtain and provide within 15 days of the completion of the evaluation.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general availability of post-exposure evaluation and the 15-day written-opinion deadline; it does not reproduce the regulation's detailed consent and testing sequence for the source individual and the exposed employee in subsection (f)(3)(B)-(C), the 90-day blood-sample-preservation option for an employee who initially declines HIV testing, the confidentiality limits on what the healthcare professional's written opinion may disclose in subsection (f)(5), or the information the employer must furnish to the evaluating healthcare professional under subsection (f)(4).

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(f)(3) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(f)(3), post-exposure evaluation and follow-up
citations.quote: Following a report of an exposure incident, the employer shall make immediately available to the exposed employee a confidential medical evaluation and follow-up, including at least the following elements:

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(f)(5) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(f)(5), 15-day written-opinion deadline
citations.quote: The employer shall obtain and provide the employee with a copy of the evaluating healthcare professional's written opinion within 15 days of the completion of the evaluation.

clauses.title: Employee Training on Bloodborne Pathogens
clauses.body: The regulation requires the employer to ensure that all employees with occupational exposure participate in a bloodborne pathogens training program, provided at no cost to the employee and during working hours. Training must be provided at the time of initial assignment to tasks where occupational exposure may take place, and the regulation requires annual training for all employees to be provided within one year of the employee's previous training. The regulation lists specific required content for the training program, including an explanation of the standard itself, modes of transmission, the employer's Exposure Control Plan, the use and limitations of PPE, and hepatitis B vaccination information, and requires the person conducting the training to be knowledgeable in the subject matter as it relates to the workplace being addressed.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general no-cost, initial-assignment, and annual training-timing requirements; it does not reproduce the regulation's full fourteen-item list of required training content in subsection (g)(2)(G), the additional training triggered by workplace changes under subsection (g)(2)(E), the separate additional training required for HIV/HBV/HCV research laboratory and production facility employees under subsection (e)(5), or the training-record retention period, which is addressed in the recordkeeping clause of this information sheet.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 5193(g)(2)(A) (Bloodborne Pathogens)
citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(g)(2)(A), no-cost training requirement
citations.quote: (A) Employers shall ensure that all employees with occupational exposure participate in a training program which must be provided at no cost to the employee and during working hours.

citations.cite: 8 CCR § 5193(g)(2)(D), annual retraining timing
citations.quote: Annual training for all employees shall be provided within one year of their previous training.

clauses.title: Medical Recordkeeping and Retention
clauses.body: The regulation requires the employer to establish and maintain an accurate exposure-related medical record for each employee with occupational exposure, maintained in accordance with the general employee medical record regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3204. The regulation sets a specific, lengthy retention period for that record: the employer must maintain the records required by subsection (h)(1) for at least the duration of the employee's employment plus 30 years.
clauses.gap: This clause states the record-creation duty and the duration-of-employment-plus-30-years retention period for medical records; it does not reproduce the regulation's separate confidentiality restrictions on disclosure in subsection (h)(1)(C), the shorter three-year retention period for training records or the five-year retention period for the Sharps Injury Log (both addressed only briefly, if at all, elsewhere in this information sheet), the access rights of employees and their representatives in subsection (h)(4), or the transfer-of-records obligations in subsection (h)(5) that apply if an employer ceases doing business.

citations.quote: (A) The employer shall establish and maintain an accurate record for each employee with occupational exposure, in accordance with Section 3204.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes a specific restriction that California's Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) places on job postings and applications that state a driver's license is required, and how that restriction -- added to Government Code section 12940 by Senate Bill 1100, effective January 1, 2025 -- relates to {{companyName}}'s consideration of {{employeeName}} for {{jobTitle}}. Government Code section 12940(q) makes it an unlawful employment practice for a covered employer to include a statement in a job advertisement, posting, application, or other material that an applicant must have a driver's license, unless the employer reasonably expects driving to be one of the job functions for the position and reasonably believes that an alternative form of transportation would not be comparable in travel time or cost. This document states facts about what that statutory provision says and whom it covers; it does not evaluate {{companyName}}'s specific job posting, application materials, or any hiring decision, and it does not determine whether driving is or is not actually a job function of {{jobTitle}}. This document is not itself a job posting, a job application, an offer of employment, or a determination of compliance with the statute described, and it does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} what to do about any particular hiring decision or application material.

clauses.title: The Core Restriction on Stating a Driver's License Is Required
clauses.body: Government Code section 12940(q)(1) states the general rule: an employer commits an unlawful employment practice by including a statement in a job advertisement, posting, application, or other material that an applicant must have a driver's license, unless both of two conditions -- described in the clauses below -- are satisfied. The restriction is written as a prohibition on the statement itself, appearing in one of the four listed kinds of material, rather than as a general prohibition on ever requiring driving-related duties of a position.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the introductory sentence of section 12940(q)(1); the two conditions that can make such a statement lawful are quoted separately in the two clauses that follow this one, and the statute's list of "alternative form of transportation" examples is quoted in a later clause. The statute's text lists four specific kinds of material -- "job advertisement, posting, application, or other material" -- and this clause does not resolve what falls within the catch-all term "other material" for a communication that is not itself an advertisement, posting, or application, which the statute's text does not define.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(q)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code § 12940(q)(1), introductory clause
citations.quote: For an employer to include a statement in a job advertisement, posting, application, or other material that an applicant must have a driver’s license unless both of the following conditions are satisfied:

clauses.title: First Condition: Driving Must Be an Expected Job Function
clauses.body: The first of the two conditions that section 12940(q)(1) requires before a driver's-license statement is lawful is that the employer reasonably expects driving to be one of the job functions for the position. Both conditions described in this document must be satisfied for the driver's-license statement to fall outside the prohibition; this is the first of them.
clauses.gap: The statute's text uses the standard "reasonably expects," but does not itself define what makes an expectation about job functions reasonable, or state what evidence would establish that driving is or is not one of a given position's job functions -- those are fact-specific questions this document does not resolve for any specific position.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(q)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code § 12940(q)(1)(A)
citations.quote: The employer reasonably expects driving to be one of the job functions for the position.

clauses.title: Second Condition: No Comparable Alternative Transportation
clauses.body: The second condition section 12940(q)(1) requires is that the employer reasonably believes that satisfying the driving job function using an alternative form of transportation would not be comparable, in travel time or cost to the employer, to having the applicant drive. Both conditions described in this document must be satisfied; this is the second of them, and it is a separate, additional requirement from the first -- an employer that reasonably expects driving to be a job function still does not satisfy section 12940(q)(1) unless it also reasonably believes no comparable alternative exists.
clauses.gap: The statute's text sets a comparability standard measured by "travel time or cost to the employer," but does not itself state a threshold, formula, or method for measuring when a difference in travel time or cost stops being "comparable" -- that determination is not resolved by the statute's own text. This clause does not address whether cost or time to the applicant, as opposed to cost to the employer, factors into the statutory standard; the statute's text as quoted here refers only to cost "to the employer."

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12940(q)(1)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code § 12940(q)(1)(B)
citations.quote: The employer reasonably believes that satisfying the job function described in paragraph (1) using an alternative form of transportation would not be comparable in travel time or cost to the employer.

clauses.title: What Counts as an "Alternative Form of Transportation"
clauses.body: Section 12940(q)(2) defines "alternative form of transportation," the term used in the second condition above, by a non-exhaustive list of examples: using a ride hailing service, using a taxi, carpooling, bicycling, and walking.
clauses.gap: The statute's introductory phrase states the list "includes, but is not limited to" the five examples quoted here, so the statute's own text does not foreclose other means of transportation -- such as public transit or a personal vehicle other than the applicant's own car -- from also qualifying, but it does not name any additional example either. The source HTML wraps the introductory sentence across a line break using a literal newline and tab characters between "all" and "of the following:"; that wrapping is reproduced exactly in this clause's first citation's quote field as a verified source-formatting artifact, not an ellipsis or edit.

clauses.title: Which Employers the FEHA Definition of "Employer" Covers
clauses.body: FEHA's definitions section, Government Code section 12926(d), states which entities are an "employer" for purposes of FEHA's unlawful-practices provisions, including the driver's-license restriction described above. It states that "employer" includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, and it separately excludes a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit from that definition.
clauses.gap: The statute's text does not itself state how the "five or more persons" threshold is counted -- for example, over what time period, in what location, or whether part-time or out-of-state personnel are included -- leaving that computation to sources outside this section's text. This same definitions section, Government Code section 12926(d), is also cited by other documents in this corpus that address other subdivisions of section 12940; it is being independently verified here for use in this document.

clauses.body: Subdivision (q) was added to Government Code section 12940 by Senate Bill 1100 during the 2023-2024 legislative session, and the leginfo.legislature.ca.gov official text of the section carries a history note confirming the amendment and its effective date. As enacted, this restriction became operative January 1, 2025.

clauses.title: California Water Rights — Introduction and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, the California statutory framework governing rights to use water in connection with real property, in connection with the property located at {{propertyAddress}} and owned by {{ownerName}}. California recognizes several distinct, overlapping legal bases for using water: a riparian right tied to land bordering a watercourse, an appropriative right acquired through the state permit system administered by the State Water Resources Control Board, and a groundwater right in water pumped from beneath the land. This sheet covers the state's foundational declaration that all water within the State is public property subject to a reasonable-and-beneficial-use limitation; the statutory line between water subject to the state's surface-water appropriation permit system and other water; the priority Water Code § 1201 gives to riparian use over appropriation; the 2014 Sustainable Groundwater Management Act's (SGMA) stated intent to preserve existing water rights while regulating groundwater sustainability; SGMA's express statement that it does not itself alter surface water or groundwater rights, together with its narrower rule tolling the use of certain extractions as evidence of a prescription claim; a groundwater sustainability agency's statutory authority to regulate well spacing and extraction (as distinct from well-construction permitting, which remains a county function); the statutory "de minimis extractor" exemption for small-volume domestic groundwater pumping; and the requirement that certain water diverters file a statement of diversion and use with the State Water Resources Control Board. This topic is distinct from this corpus's other Real Estate documents addressing land-use approvals, easements, and habitability, none of which address water-rights priority or groundwater regulation. This sheet is informational only. It does not itself determine, adjudicate, quantify, or resolve any riparian, appropriative, or groundwater right affecting {{propertyAddress}} or the {{groundwaterBasinName}} groundwater basin, and it does not determine whether {{propertyAddress}} lies within the jurisdiction of any groundwater sustainability agency or groundwater sustainability plan.

clauses.title: All Water Is Public Property, Subject to a Reasonable-and-Beneficial-Use Limitation
clauses.body: California's Water Code opens with two foundational declarations about the legal nature of water rights in the state. Water Code § 102 provides: "All water within the State is the property of the people of the State, but the right to the use of water may be acquired by appropriation in the manner provided by law." Water Code § 100 then ties every right to use water to a reasonable-and-beneficial-use limitation: "It is hereby declared that because of the conditions prevailing in this State the general welfare requires that the water resources of the State be put to beneficial use to the fullest extent of which they are capable, and that the waste or unreasonable use or unreasonable method of use of water be prevented, and that the conservation of such water is to be exercised with a view to the reasonable and beneficial use thereof in the interest of the people and for the public welfare." Section 100 applies that limitation specifically to a stream-based right: "The right to water or to the use or flow of water in or from any natural stream or watercourse in this State is and shall be limited to such water as shall be reasonably required for the beneficial use to be served, and such right does not and shall not extend to the waste or unreasonable use or unreasonable method of use or unreasonable method of diversion of water." Together, these sections establish that no water right in California — riparian, appropriative, or otherwise — is an unconditional property right in a fixed quantity of water; every such right is limited to what is reasonably required for the beneficial use served. This description concerns these two statutory declarations generally; it does not determine what quantity or method of use is "reasonable" or "beneficial" for any specific use of water at {{propertyAddress}}.
clauses.gap: Sections 100 and 102 are both original 1943 enactments in the same chapter (Division 1, Chapter 1) of the Water Code, so they are not independent sources of each other. The reasonable-and-beneficial-use standard these sections state is famously fact-intensive and has been given content mainly through decades of judicial decisions and California Constitution Article X, Section 2 (added 1928) — none of which were fetched or quoted for this clause; CourtListener's case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, daily quota exhausted) when queried for this topic, so no judicial gloss on "reasonable and beneficial use" is cited anywhere in this document. This clause states the general statutory rule only; it does not evaluate any specific use.

clauses.title: The State Appropriation Permit System Reaches Surface Water and Known Subterranean Streams — Not Percolating Groundwater
clauses.body: California operates a permit system for a new appropriative right to use water, administered by the State Water Resources Control Board, but that permit system's statutory scope is limited to a defined category of water. Water Code § 1200 provides: "Whenever the terms stream, lake or other body of water, or water occurs in relation to applications to appropriate water or permits or licenses issued pursuant to such applications, such term refers only to surface water, and to subterranean streams flowing through known and definite channels." By its terms, this definition excludes ordinary percolating groundwater — water beneath the surface that is not flowing through a known and definite channel — from the category of water for which the Board's appropriation-permit application and licensing process applies. This description concerns this single statutory definition generally; it does not determine whether water present at or beneath {{propertyAddress}} is surface water, a subterranean stream flowing through a known and definite channel, or percolating groundwater.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single statutory definition, Water Code § 1200; it is one source, not independently corroborated by a second source. Whether specific subsurface water is flowing through a "known and definite channel" (and therefore within the appropriation-permit system) or is instead percolating groundwater (and therefore governed by the separate groundwater-rights and Sustainable Groundwater Management Act framework addressed elsewhere in this corpus) is a fact- and hydrology-specific determination that California courts have historically made case by case; no such judicial decision was fetched or cited for this clause because CourtListener's case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, daily quota exhausted) when queried for this topic.

citations.case: Cal. Water Code § 1200 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Whenever the terms stream, lake or other body of water, or water occurs in relation to applications to appropriate water or permits or licenses issued pursuant to such applications, such term refers only to surface water, and to subterranean streams flowing through known and definite channels.

clauses.title: Riparian Use Is Excluded From — and Takes Priority Over — the Water Available for Appropriation
clauses.body: Water Code § 1201 defines the pool of water the state may make available to a new appropriative permit applicant by carving riparian use out of it first. Section 1201 provides: "All water flowing in any natural channel, excepting so far as it has been or is being applied to useful and beneficial purposes upon, or in so far as it is or may be reasonably needed for useful and beneficial purposes upon lands riparian thereto, or otherwise appropriated, is hereby declared to be public water of the State and subject to appropriation in accordance with the provisions of this code." By its terms, this section declares water in a natural channel to be public water "subject to appropriation" only to the extent that water has not already been applied, or is not reasonably needed, for beneficial use on riparian land, and has not otherwise already been appropriated. In this way, § 1201 reflects — without itself defining the elements of — a riparian right's traditionally recognized priority over a later-acquired appropriative right in California's dual water-rights system. This description concerns this single statutory declaration generally; it does not determine whether {{propertyAddress}} is riparian to any watercourse, or the scope of any riparian use reasonably needed there.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single statutory section, Water Code § 1201; it is one source, not independently corroborated by a second source. Section 1201 does not itself define what makes land "riparian," what quantity of use is "reasonably needed," or the other doctrinal elements of a riparian right (for example, that a riparian right is generally unquantified, correlative among riparian owners, and does not extend to land outside the watershed) — those elements have been developed primarily through California case law, none of which was fetched or cited for this clause because CourtListener's case-law search returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, daily quota exhausted) when queried for this topic.

clauses.title: The Sustainable Groundwater Management Act's Stated Intent to Preserve Existing Water Rights
clauses.body: In 2014, the Legislature enacted the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA), Water Code § 10720 et seq., to require local, sustainable management of the state's groundwater basins. The Legislature's statement of intent addresses the relationship between that new regulatory framework and existing water rights directly. Water Code § 10720.1(b) provides that in enacting SGMA, it is the intent of the Legislature: "To enhance local management of groundwater consistent with rights to use or store groundwater and Section 2 of Article X of the California Constitution. It is the intent of the Legislature to preserve the security of water rights in the state to the greatest extent possible consistent with the sustainable management of groundwater." This description concerns this single statement of legislative intent; it is not itself the operative rule limiting SGMA's effect on existing rights, which is addressed by a separate Water Code section covered in another clause in this corpus, and it does not determine how SGMA affects any specific water right at {{propertyAddress}} or in the {{groundwaterBasinName}} groundwater basin.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single subdivision, Water Code § 10720.1(b); it is one source, not independently corroborated by a second source. A legislative statement of intent is not itself a self-executing operative rule of law the way an operative subdivision is; this clause does not by itself establish what SGMA does or does not do to a specific water right — that operative language is addressed in a separate clause in this corpus quoting Water Code § 10720.5. This clause also does not address SGMA's remaining findings in § 10720.1(a) and (c) through (i), which concern basin sustainability, state intervention, and adjudication-process goals not directly tied to preserving existing water rights.

citations.case: Cal. Water Code § 10720.1(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: To enhance local management of groundwater consistent with rights to use or store groundwater and Section 2 of Article X of the California Constitution. It is the intent of the Legislature to preserve the security of water rights in the state to the greatest extent possible consistent with the sustainable management of groundwater.

clauses.title: SGMA Does Not Itself Determine or Alter Surface Water or Groundwater Rights
clauses.body: Beyond its statement of intent, SGMA contains an operative subdivision limiting the statute's effect on existing water rights. Water Code § 10720.5(b) provides: "Nothing in this part, or in any groundwater management plan adopted pursuant to this part, determines or alters surface water rights or groundwater rights under common law or any provision of law that determines or grants surface water rights." Section 10720.5(a) states a related but narrower rule limited to certain designated basins: "Groundwater management pursuant to this part shall be consistent with Section 2 of Article X of the California Constitution. Nothing in this part modifies rights or priorities to use or store groundwater consistent with Section 2 of Article X of the California Constitution, except that in basins designated medium- or high-priority basins by the department, no extraction of groundwater between January 1, 2015, and the date of adoption of a groundwater sustainability plan pursuant to this part or the approval by the department of an alternative submitted under Section 10733.6, whichever is sooner, may be used as evidence of, or to establish or defend against, any claim of prescription." Together, these subdivisions state that SGMA regulation and any resulting groundwater sustainability plan do not themselves determine or alter a specific water right, while separately tolling the evidentiary use of extractions during a defined interim window in medium- or high-priority basins for purposes of a prescription claim. This description concerns these statutory subdivisions generally; it does not determine the water-rights priority of, or the medium-/high-priority basin designation applicable to, any water right at {{propertyAddress}} or in the {{groundwaterBasinName}} groundwater basin.
clauses.gap: The citations to § 10720.5(a) and (b) are to subdivisions of the same statutory section and are not independent of each other. Section 10720.5(a)'s prescription-tolling rule applies only in a basin the Department of Water Resources has designated "medium-" or "high-priority"; this clause does not identify or verify that designation for any specific groundwater basin, because the Department's basin-prioritization bulletin was not fetched for this clause. Section 10720.5(c)'s cross-reference to a Code of Civil Procedure adjudication action (Chapter 7, commencing with Section 830, of Title 10 of Part 2) was not independently fetched or verified for this clause.
