citations.quote: Groundwater management pursuant to this part shall be consistent with Section 2 of Article X of the California Constitution. Nothing in this part modifies rights or priorities to use or store groundwater consistent with Section 2 of Article X of the California Constitution, except that in basins designated medium- or high-priority basins by the department, no extraction of groundwater between January 1, 2015, and the date of adoption of a groundwater sustainability plan pursuant to this part or the approval by the department of an alternative submitted under Section 10733.6, whichever is sooner, may be used as evidence of, or to establish or defend against, any claim of prescription.

clauses.title: A Groundwater Sustainability Agency's Statutory Authority to Regulate Extraction and Wells
clauses.body: Where a groundwater sustainability agency (GSA) has been formed and is regulating a basin under SGMA, the statute grants it specific extraction-regulation authority distinct from — and narrower than — well-construction permitting. Water Code § 10726.4(a)(1) authorizes a GSA "[t]o impose spacing requirements on new groundwater well construction to minimize well interference and impose reasonable operating regulations on existing groundwater wells to minimize well interference, including requiring extractors to operate on a rotation basis." Section 10726.4(a)(2) further authorizes a GSA "[t]o control groundwater extractions by regulating, limiting, or suspending extractions from individual groundwater wells or extractions from groundwater wells in the aggregate, construction of new groundwater wells, enlargement of existing groundwater wells, or reactivation of abandoned groundwater wells, or otherwise establishing groundwater extraction allocations." That same subdivision expressly limits the legal effect of such a limitation: "A limitation on extractions by a groundwater sustainability agency shall not be construed to be a final determination of rights to extract groundwater from the basin or any portion of the basin." The statute separately makes clear that this extraction-control authority is not a well-construction-permitting authority. Section 10726.4(b) provides: "This section does not authorize a groundwater sustainability agency to issue permits for the construction, modification, or abandonment of groundwater wells, except as authorized by a county with authority to issue those permits." This description concerns this statutory authority generally; it does not determine whether {{propertyAddress}} lies within the jurisdiction of any groundwater sustainability agency, or how any specific agency has exercised or not exercised this authority in the {{groundwaterBasinName}} groundwater basin.
clauses.gap: The citations to § 10726.4(a)(1), (a)(2), and (b) are to subdivisions of the same statutory section and are not independent of each other. This authority exists only where a GSA has been formed for the relevant basin and has adopted rules exercising it; not every California groundwater basin has a designated GSA or adopted groundwater sustainability plan, and this clause does not determine whether one exists for any specific basin. This clause also does not address § 10726.4(a)(3) and (a)(4), governing temporary and permanent transfers and carryover of groundwater extraction allocations, which were fetched but not selected for a dedicated quotation in this clause because they concern allocation trading mechanics rather than the underlying extraction-control and well-permitting authority this clause addresses.

clauses.title: The "De Minimis Extractor" Exemption for Small-Volume Domestic Groundwater Pumping
clauses.body: SGMA's definitions section sets a specific, numeric threshold distinguishing an ordinary small household well owner from the groundwater extractors its regulatory provisions primarily target. Water Code § 10721(e) defines the term used throughout the statute: "'De minimis extractor' means a person who extracts, for domestic purposes, two acre-feet or less per year." The same section defines the resource being regulated. Water Code § 10721(g) provides: "'Groundwater' means water beneath the surface of the earth within the zone below the water table in which the soil is completely saturated with water, but does not include water that flows in known and definite channels unless included pursuant to Section 10722.5." This description concerns these two statutory definitions generally; it does not calculate or determine whether extraction at {{propertyAddress}} is, or is not, at or below the two-acre-foot-per-year de minimis threshold, and it does not determine whether de minimis-extractor status by itself exempts a particular well from any other regulatory, permitting, or fee requirement.
clauses.gap: The citations to § 10721(e) and (g) are to subdivisions of the same definitions section and are not independent of each other. This clause quotes the definition of "de minimis extractor" only; it does not quote or verify the operative provisions elsewhere in SGMA (not fetched for this clause) that describe what regulatory consequences, if any, follow from having — or not having — de minimis-extractor status, such as any monitoring, reporting, or fee exemption a groundwater sustainability plan may or may not extend to a de minimis extractor. This clause also does not address Water Code § 10722.5, cross-referenced in the "groundwater" definition, which was not independently fetched or verified for this clause.

clauses.title: The Statement of Water Diversion and Use Filing Requirement
clauses.body: Separately from the state appropriation-permit system, California requires certain water diverters — including many riparian and pre-1914 appropriative right holders who do not hold a Board-issued permit or license — to file a periodic statement of diversion and use with the State Water Resources Control Board. Water Code § 5101(a) states the general filing rule and its exceptions: "Each person who, after December 31, 1965, diverts water shall file with the board a statement of their diversion and use, as provided in subdivision (b), except that a statement is not required to be filed if the diversion is any of the following:" The statute then lists several categories exempt from the filing requirement, including one aimed at small-scale use: Water Code § 5101(a)(1) exempts a diversion "[f]rom a spring that does not flow off the property on which it is located and from which the person's aggregate diversions do not exceed 25 acre-feet in any year." For a diverter who must file, the statute sets a recurring deadline tied to the water year. Water Code § 5101(b)(3) provides: "For diversions after September 30, 2021, the statement shall include diversions during the one-year period from October 1 of each year through September 30, inclusive, of the following year, and shall be filed before February 1 of the year after that one-year period." This description concerns this statutory filing requirement generally; it does not determine whether any diversion at {{propertyAddress}} is or is not subject to the filing requirement, or has been timely filed.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes § 5101(a)'s general rule, one of its seven listed exemption categories (subdivision (a)(1)), and the current filing-deadline rule in subdivision (b)(3); it does not quote the other six exemption categories in § 5101(a)(2) through (a)(7) — covering, among other things, diversions already covered by a small-use registration, permit, or license on file with the Board, diversions administered by a court- or department-appointed watermaster, and certain pre-2009 diversions — all of which were fetched but not block-quoted for this clause. It also does not quote the now-superseded filing deadlines in § 5101(b)(1) and (b)(2), which applied to diversions occurring before October 1, 2021. The definitions this section relies on, in Water Code § 5100, were fetched but are not independently quoted in this clause.

clauses.title: Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Abolished Heart-Balm Actions in California — Information Sheet concerns {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. It describes what California statute says about a group of civil lawsuits — historically called "heart-balm" actions — that a person can no longer bring in California based on the end of a courtship, engagement, or marriage: alienation of affection, criminal conversation, seduction of a person over the age of legal consent, and breach of promise of marriage. It also describes a separate, related statute that lets a person who gave a gift of money or property because a marriage was expected seek the gift's return, or the value a court or jury finds just, when the marriage does not take place. This information sheet states general legal facts about these statutes. It does not determine, and takes no position on, whether any claim by {{party1Name}} or {{party2Name}} is barred, available, or would succeed; that depends on the specific facts and, if disputed, is for a court to decide.

clauses.title: Four Named Causes of Action No Longer Exist Under California Law
clauses.body: California statute provides that no cause of action arises for four named claims: alienation of affection; criminal conversation; seduction of a person over the age of legal consent; and breach of promise of marriage. The statute bars all four by name in a single list, without conditioning the bar on which party was at fault, how long the relationship lasted, or whether a wedding date had been set.
clauses.gap: This clause states only that Civil Code section 43.5 bars a cause of action under each of these four names; the statute itself does not define any of the four terms it uses, so what conduct historically fell within "alienation of affection," "criminal conversation," "seduction," or "breach of promise of marriage" is not stated in this text. CourtListener's case-law search was attempted for this document and returned a rate-limit error (125/day exhausted) before any pre-1939 or later California decision construing these terms could be fetched and verified this session, so no case law defining these terms is cited anywhere in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 43.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no cause of action arises for four named claims
citations.quote: No cause of action arises for: (a) Alienation of affection. (b) Criminal conversation. (c) Seduction of a person over the age of legal consent. (d) Breach of promise of marriage.

clauses.title: Alienation of Affection and Criminal Conversation Are Barred
clauses.body: Among the four claims the statute bars are alienation of affection and criminal conversation. These two were historically directed at a third party rather than at a spouse or partner directly — alienation of affection at someone accused of damaging a marriage, and criminal conversation, despite its name, at someone accused of having a sexual relationship with a person's spouse. California statute states that no cause of action arises for either one.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the two-item list; it does not itself state which third party, if any, could historically have been sued, what evidence such a claim required, or how the tort of criminal conversation — a civil claim despite its name — differed from any criminal statute. No case law defining these two torts as they existed before the 1939 bar was fetched or verified this session.

clauses.title: Seduction of a Person Over the Age of Legal Consent Is Barred
clauses.body: California statute also bars a cause of action for seduction of a person over the age of legal consent. The bar is limited by its own terms to a person over that age; this section does not use the word "seduction" anywhere else, and it does not itself state what age counts as the age of legal consent.
clauses.gap: This clause states only that the statute bars a claim labeled "seduction of a person over the age of legal consent"; it does not identify which other California statute sets that age, and it does not address a claim involving a person under that age, which this section does not purport to cover one way or the other. No case law was fetched or verified for this clause this session.

clauses.title: Breach of Promise of Marriage Is Barred
clauses.body: The fourth claim the statute bars is breach of promise of marriage — historically a lawsuit for damages when one person called off an expected wedding after promising to marry the other. California statute states that no cause of action arises for breach of promise of marriage, without an exception based on how far wedding planning had progressed or which party ended the engagement.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only the cause of action for damages based on a broken promise to marry; it does not address, and this section does not by its own text speak to, a separate question covered by a different statute — the return of a specific gift given because a marriage was expected. That separate question is addressed in the companion clauses of this information sheet describing Civil Code section 1590.

clauses.title: A Separate Statute Lets a Donor Seek Return of a Gift Given Because Marriage Was Expected
clauses.body: A different Civil Code section, enacted the same year as the bar on breach-of-promise lawsuits, addresses gifts given because a marriage was expected. It states that where either party to a contemplated marriage in California makes a gift of money or property to the other on the basis or assumption that the marriage will take place, and the marriage does not happen because the donee refuses to go through with it or because it is called off by mutual consent, the donor may recover the gift.
clauses.gap: This clause states only that a recovery right exists under the statute's own terms — it does not address a marriage that is called off unilaterally by the donor rather than the donee, or called off in circumstances outside the two categories the statute names, does not address gifts made after (rather than in contemplation of) a wedding, and does not state a limitations period within which a donor must act. No California case applying this section — for example, to a specific engagement ring — was fetched or verified this session.

clauses.title: The Amount Recoverable Is Whatever a Court or Jury Finds Just, Not Automatically the Full Gift
clauses.body: The same statute does not state that a donor automatically recovers the entire gift or its full value. Instead, the statute allows recovery of "such gift or such part of its value" as a court or jury finds, under all the circumstances of the case, to be just.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the statutory standard — that the amount is left to a finding of what is "just" under the circumstances of the case — it does not itself list what circumstances a court or jury may consider, and no case law applying this discretionary standard to a specific set of facts was fetched or verified this session.

clauses.body: The statute barring alienation of affection, criminal conversation, seduction, and breach-of-promise lawsuits, and the separate statute allowing a donor to recover a gift given because a marriage was expected, were both added to the Civil Code by the same legislative act, identified in the statutory text of each section as Statutes 1939, Chapter 128.

clauses.title: The Uniform TOD Security Registration Act: Purpose and Core Definitions
clauses.body: California enacted the Uniform TOD Security Registration Act as Part 3 of Division 5 of the Probate Code (§§ 5500-5512), a nonprobate-transfer statute separate from the Multiple-Party Accounts Law that governs bank accounts and separate from the statute that governs a Transfer-on-Death Deed on real property. Its stated purpose is to let an owner register a security in a title form that transfers the security at death without probate or estate administration, and to protect the entity that implements that title form. Under the Act, a "beneficiary form" is the registration itself — a registration of a security that shows the present owner and the owner's intention about who becomes the owner at the owner's death. A "registering entity" is the person who originates or transfers title to the security by registration, which the statute's own definition says includes a broker maintaining security accounts for customers and a transfer agent or other person acting for or as an issuer of securities. This document addresses a registration of {{accountDescription}} held with {{financialInstitutionName}} in the name of {{ownerName}}.
clauses.gap: This is the Uniform TOD Security Registration Act specifically, codified at Probate Code §§ 5500-5512. It is a distinct statutory scheme from the California Multiple-Party Accounts Law (Part 2 of Division 5, commencing with § 5100, which governs P.O.D. bank accounts and Totten trust accounts) and from the Transfer-on-Death Deed statute (which governs real property); this document does not restate those other schemes. The § 5500(a)-(c) quote below is drawn from three contiguous subdivisions of one statutory section and is treated as one source, not three independent ones; § 5501(a) and § 5501(c) are two separate definitions within the same definitions section and are likewise not independent corroboration of each other. § 5501(b), defining "register" and its derivatives, is not quoted here. This clause states only what the statute's short title, stated purpose, and two of its definitions say; it does not address whether a specific security, account, or instrument actually qualifies for registration in beneficiary form, which depends on the remaining sections of the Act.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5500(a)-(c)
citations.cite: short title, construction, and stated purpose of the Act
citations.quote: (a) This part shall be known as and may be cited as the Uniform TOD Security Registration Act.(b) This part shall be liberally construed and applied to promote its underlying purposes and policy.(c) The underlying purposes and policy of this act are to (1) encourage development of a title form for use by individuals that is effective, without probate and estate administration, for transferring property at death in accordance with directions of a deceased owner of a security as included in the title form in which the security is held and (2) protect issuers offering and implementing the new title form.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5501(a)
citations.cite: definition of “beneficiary form”
citations.quote: (a) “Beneficiary form” means a registration of a security that indicates the present owner of the security and the intention of the owner regarding the person who will become the owner of the security upon the death of the owner.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5501(c)
citations.cite: definition of “registering entity”
citations.quote: (c) “Registering entity” means a person who originates or transfers a security title by registration, and includes a broker maintaining security accounts for customers and a transfer agent or other person acting for or as an issuer of securities.

clauses.title: What Counts as a “Security” and a “Security Account” — and the Statute's Own Line Against Bank Multiple-Party Accounts
clauses.body: The Act defines "security" broadly: a share, participation, or other interest in property, in a business, or in an obligation of an enterprise or other issuer, which the statute says includes a certificated security, an uncertificated security, and a security account. "Security account" is itself separately defined, and includes (among other listed categories) a reinvestment account associated with a security, a securities account with a broker, a cash balance in a brokerage account, cash, cash equivalents, and interest, earnings, or dividends earned or declared on a security in such an account — whether or not credited to the account before the owner's death. The statute draws its own express boundary against the bank-account statute covered elsewhere in this document set: § 5501 itself states that it may not be construed to govern cash equivalents in multiple-party accounts that are governed by the California Multiple-Party Accounts Law.
clauses.gap: Only subdivision (e)(1)(A) of the "security account" definition is quoted below; subdivisions (e)(1)(B) (investment management and custody accounts with a trust company or bank trust department) and (e)(1)(C) (replacement or product cash balances), and the separate (e)(2) definition of "cash equivalent," are part of the same statutory definition but are not independently quoted here. The § 5501(f) boundary against the Multiple-Party Accounts Law is narrow on its own terms — it excludes only "cash equivalents in multiple-party accounts," not every brokerage or investment account outright — so this clause does not resolve which statute governs a specific account that could plausibly be described under either scheme; that determination depends on how a specific account is actually titled and structured with the financial institution or registering entity holding it.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5501(d)
citations.cite: definition of “security”
citations.quote: (d) “Security” means a share, participation, or other interest in property, in a business, or in an obligation of an enterprise or other issuer, and includes a certificated security, an uncertificated security, and a security account.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5501(e)(1)(A)
citations.cite: one category within the definition of “security account”
citations.quote: (A) A reinvestment account associated with a security, a securities account with a broker, a cash balance in a brokerage account, cash, cash equivalents, interest, earnings, or dividends earned or declared on a security in an account, a reinvestment account, or a brokerage account, whether or not credited to the account before the owner’s death.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5501(f)
citations.cite: express carve-out for cash equivalents governed by the Multiple-Party Accounts Law
citations.quote: This section may not be construed to govern cash equivalents in multiple-party accounts that are governed by the California Multiple-Party Accounts Law, Part 2 (commencing with Section 5100).

clauses.title: Who May Register in Beneficiary Form, and Which State's Law Applies
clauses.body: Only individuals may obtain a registration in beneficiary form — sole ownership by one individual, or multiple ownership by two or more individuals holding with right of survivorship rather than as tenants in common. The statute's own text states that multiple owners of a security registered in beneficiary form hold as joint tenants with right of survivorship, as tenants by the entireties, or as owners of community property held in survivorship form, and not as tenants in common. Separately, the Act sets out which jurisdiction's law can authorize a beneficiary-form registration: California's version applies if the form is authorized by this or a similar statute of the state where the issuer or registering entity is organized, where the registering entity's principal office or transfer-agent office is located, where the registration is made, or of the state listed as {{ownerName}}'s address at the time of registration.
clauses.gap: The statutory text of § 5502 lists "tenants by the entireties" as one of the three forms in which multiple owners hold a security registered in beneficiary form. California does not generally recognize tenancy by the entirety as a form of concurrent ownership between spouses (unlike some other states) — this appears to be uniform-act language carried into the California statute without adaptation, and this document does not resolve what legal effect, if any, that listed form would have for California owners. Separately, § 5503's final sentence — that a registration is "presumed to be valid" even under the law of a jurisdiction where no similar TOD-security statute is or was in force — is a presumption, not a guarantee, and this document does not resolve how that presumption would be rebutted in a specific jurisdiction or dispute.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5502
citations.cite: eligible owners and the forms in which multiple owners hold
citations.quote: Only individuals whose registration of a security shows sole ownership by one individual or multiple ownership by two or more individuals with right of survivorship, rather than as tenants in common, may obtain registration in beneficiary form. Multiple owners of a security registered in beneficiary form hold as joint tenants with right of survivorship, as tenants by the entireties, or as owners of community property held in survivorship form, and not as tenants in common.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5503
citations.cite: which jurisdiction's law can authorize the registration
citations.quote: A security may be registered in beneficiary form if the form is authorized by this or a similar statute of the state of organization of the issuer or registering entity, the location of the registering entity’s principal office, the office of its transfer agent or its office making the registration, or by this or a similar statute of the law of the state listed as the owner’s address at the time of registration. A registration governed by the law of a jurisdiction in which this or similar legislation is not in force or was not in force when a registration in beneficiary form was made is nevertheless presumed to be valid and authorized as a matter of contract law.

clauses.title: How a Registration in Beneficiary Form Is Created, and the “TOD” / “POD” Labels
clauses.body: A security — whether evidenced by a certificate or held in an account — is registered in beneficiary form when the registration includes a designation of a beneficiary to take ownership at the death of the owner, or at the death of the last survivor of multiple owners. The statute specifies how that designation may be shown: by the words "transfer on death" or the abbreviation "TOD," or by the words "pay on death" or the abbreviation "POD," placed after the name of the registered owner and before the name of the beneficiary.
clauses.gap: These two sections state only what wording shows a beneficiary-form registration; they do not themselves address the account-opening or reregistration paperwork through which a registering entity actually implements a TOD or POD designation — that is addressed in a separate clause of this document describing a registering entity's own terms and conditions. The identical "TOD" and "POD" abbreviations are also used under California's separate Transfer-on-Death Deed statute (for real property) and its Multiple-Party Accounts Law (for bank accounts); this clause addresses only the security-registration meaning of those abbreviations under Probate Code § 5505, not their use under those other, separately governed statutes.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5504
citations.cite: when a security is registered in beneficiary form
citations.quote: A security, whether evidenced by certificate or account, is registered in beneficiary form when the registration includes a designation of a beneficiary to take the ownership at the death of the owner or the deaths of all multiple owners.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5505
citations.cite: the “TOD” and “POD” wording that shows the designation
citations.quote: Registration in beneficiary form may be shown by the words “transfer on death” or the abbreviation “TOD,” or by the words “pay on death” or the abbreviation “POD,” after the name of the registered owner and before the name of a beneficiary.

clauses.title: No Effect Until Death, and Free Revocability by the Owner
clauses.body: A TOD beneficiary designation on a registration in beneficiary form has no effect on ownership of {{accountDescription}} until {{ownerName}}'s death. Until then, the registration may be canceled or changed at any time by the sole owner, or by all then-surviving owners if there is more than one, and the statute states this can be done without the consent of {{beneficiaryName}} or any other named beneficiary.
clauses.gap: This single statutory section (§ 5506) does not itself specify the mechanical steps or paperwork by which an owner would cancel or change a registration — those mechanics are set by the registering entity's own terms and conditions under a separate section of the Act, addressed elsewhere in this document. The statute also requires that all then-surviving owners agree to a change where a security is jointly owned; it does not itself address what happens if surviving co-owners disagree, or supply a mechanism to resolve such a disagreement.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5506
citations.cite: no effect on ownership until death, and revocability without beneficiary consent
citations.quote: The designation of a TOD beneficiary on a registration in beneficiary form has no effect on ownership until the owner’s death. A registration of a security in beneficiary form may be canceled or changed at any time by the sole owner or all then surviving owners without the consent of the beneficiary.

clauses.title: Effect at the Owner's Death: Passage to Surviving Beneficiaries, Tenancy in Common Among Multiple Beneficiaries, and Lapse to the Estate
clauses.body: On the death of a sole owner, or the death of the last survivor of multiple owners, ownership of a security registered in beneficiary form passes to the beneficiary or beneficiaries who survive all the owners. On proof of the owners' deaths and compliance with the registering entity's own applicable requirements, the security may be reregistered in the surviving beneficiary's or beneficiaries' names. If more than one beneficiary survives, the statute states that — until the security is divided — those beneficiaries hold their interests as tenants in common. If no beneficiary survives the death of all owners, the statute directs that the security belongs to the estate of the deceased sole owner, or the estate of the last owner to die.
clauses.gap: This single statutory section (§ 5507) states the default outcomes at death; it does not itself define what counts as "surviving" the owner for these purposes — for example, it does not set out a required survival period comparable to the 120-hour rule found in California's Uniform Simultaneous Death Act, which is addressed elsewhere in this document set as a separate statutory scheme, not part of this Act's own text. It also does not address the registering entity's own documentation requirements for "proof of death," which the Act leaves to that entity's terms and conditions.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5507
citations.cite: passage of ownership at death, tenancy in common among survivors, and lapse to the estate
citations.quote: On death of a sole owner or the last to die of all multiple owners, ownership of securities registered in beneficiary form passes to the beneficiary or beneficiaries who survive all owners. On proof of death of all owners and compliance with any applicable requirements of the registering entity, a security registered in beneficiary form may be reregistered in the name of the beneficiary or beneficiaries who survive the death of all owners. Until division of the security after the death of all owners, multiple beneficiaries surviving the death of all owners hold their interests as tenants in common. If no beneficiary survives the death of all owners, the security belongs to the estate of the deceased sole owner or the estate of the last to die of all multiple owners.

clauses.title: The Registering Entity's Discretion to Offer TOD Registration, and Its Discharge From Claims After a Good-Faith Transfer
clauses.body: {{financialInstitutionName}} is not statutorily required to offer or accept a request for security registration in beneficiary form. If it does offer registration in beneficiary form, the statute treats the owner requesting it as assenting to the protections the Act gives to the registering entity. Once a registering entity registers a transfer under the death-transfer section described elsewhere in this document, and does so in good-faith reliance on the registration itself, on the Act, and on information such as an affidavit of the deceased owner's personal representative or information from the surviving beneficiary, the statute discharges the registering entity from all claims to the security by the deceased owner's estate, creditors, heirs, or devisees. That statutory protection does not extend to a reregistration or payment made after the registering entity has received written notice from any claimant objecting to implementation of the beneficiary-form registration.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes § 5508(a) and § 5508(c); it does not separately quote § 5508(b) (the registering entity's agreement to implement a registration it accepts) or § 5508(d), which states that the registering entity's own protection from claims does not affect the rights of beneficiaries in disputes between themselves and other claimants over the security, its value, or its proceeds — in other words, this discharge protects the registering entity as an institution, but does not itself resolve a dispute among people claiming the security or its proceeds.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5508(a)
citations.cite: no statutory requirement to offer beneficiary-form registration
citations.quote: (a) A registering entity is not required to offer or to accept requests for security registration in beneficiary form. If a registration in beneficiary form is offered by a registering entity, the owner requesting registration in beneficiary form assents to the protections given to the registering entity by this part.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5508(c)
citations.cite: discharge from claims after a good-faith transfer, and the written-notice exception
citations.quote: (c) A registering entity is discharged from all claims to a security by the estate, creditors, heirs, or devisees of a deceased owner if it registers a transfer of the security in accordance with Section 5507 and does so in good faith reliance (1) on the registration, (2) on this part, and (3) on information provided to it by affidavit of the personal representative of the deceased owner, or by the surviving beneficiary or the surviving beneficiary’s representatives, or other information available to the registering entity. The protections of this part do not extend to a reregistration or payment made after a registering entity has received written notice from any claimant to any interest in the security objecting to implementation of a registration in beneficiary form. No other notice or other information available to the registering entity shall affect its right to protection under this part.

clauses.title: Nontestamentary Character of the Transfer, and Preservation of Surviving-Spouse, Creditor, and Community-Property Rights
clauses.body: The statute characterizes a transfer on death resulting from a registration in beneficiary form as effective by reason of the contract between the owner and the registering entity and the Act itself — and states that it is "not testamentary." The Act also states, in the same section, that it does not limit the rights of a surviving spouse or of creditors of a security owner against beneficiaries and other transferees under other California law. Separately, the Act states that nothing in it alters the community character of community property or community rights in community property, and that it is subject to a separate chapter of the Probate Code (Chapter 2, commencing with § 5010, of Part 1 of Division 5).
clauses.gap: "Not testamentary" describes how the transfer takes legal effect — by contract and statute rather than as a testamentary disposition subject to the Probate Code's will-execution formalities — and this document does not otherwise restate what those will-execution formalities require. § 5509(b)'s preservation of surviving-spouse and creditor rights "under other laws of this state" does not itself identify what those other laws provide or how a specific spouse's or creditor's claim would be resolved against a specific beneficiary. § 5511's cross-reference to Chapter 2 (commencing with § 5010) of Part 1 of Division 5 is quoted here only as a cross-reference; this document does not independently fetch, quote, or verify the text of that other chapter, and does not represent what it provides beyond what § 5511 itself says.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5509
citations.cite: nontestamentary character, and preservation of surviving-spouse and creditor rights
citations.quote: (a) Any transfer on death resulting from a registration in beneficiary form is effective by reason of the contract regarding the registration between the owner and the registering entity and this part and is not testamentary.(b) This part does not limit the rights of a surviving spouse or creditors of security owners against beneficiaries and other transferees under other laws of this state.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5511
citations.cite: no alteration of community property character; cross-reference to Chapter 2 of Part 1
citations.quote: Nothing in this part alters the community character of community property or community rights in community property. This part is subject to Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 5010) of Part 1 of Division 5.

clauses.title: The Registering Entity's Own Terms and Conditions, Substituted (“LDPS”) Beneficiaries, and When This Act Applies
clauses.body: A registering entity that offers to accept registrations in beneficiary form may establish its own terms and conditions for receiving requests for registration and for implementing them, including requests to cancel a previously registered TOD designation or to reregister for a change of beneficiary. Among other things the statute permits those terms and conditions to address, the Act specifically recognizes a way to name a substitute beneficiary: appending the letters "LDPS" (for "lineal descendants per stirpes") to the name of the primary beneficiary. That designation substitutes the named beneficiary's descendants, if the beneficiary does not survive the owner, with those descendants identified and sharing according to the law of the beneficiary's domicile at the owner's death governing inheritance by descendants of an intestate. Separately, the Act states its own applicability: it applies to registrations of securities in beneficiary form made before, on, or after January 1, 1999, by decedents dying on or after January 1, 1999.
clauses.gap: § 5510(b)'s LDPS mechanism determines a substitute beneficiary's shares by reference to "the law of the beneficiary's domicile at the owner's death" — a law that could be a jurisdiction other than California depending on where the named beneficiary was domiciled, and that this document does not independently identify or apply. § 5510(a) is quoted only as to a registering entity's authority to set terms and conditions; the statute's own illustrative registration formats in § 5510(c) (for example, "John S. Brown TOD John S. Brown, Jr.") are the statute's own examples of formats a registering entity may authorize, not a representation that any specific brokerage firm or transfer agent uses that exact format. § 5512's applicability rule means that a decedent who died before January 1, 1999 is not covered by this Act regardless of when a beneficiary-form registration was made.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5510(a)
citations.cite: registering entity's authority to set its own terms and conditions
citations.quote: (a) A registering entity offering to accept registrations in beneficiary form may establish the terms and conditions under which it will receive requests for (1) registrations in beneficiary form, and (2) implementation of registrations in beneficiary form, including requests for cancellation of previously registered TOD beneficiary designations and requests for reregistration to effect a change of beneficiary.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5510(b)
citations.cite: the “LDPS” substitute-beneficiary designation
citations.quote: Substitution may be indicated by appending to the name of the primary beneficiary the letters LDPS, standing for “lineal descendants per stirpes.” This designation substitutes a deceased beneficiary’s descendants who survive the owner for a beneficiary who fails to so survive, the descendants to be identified and to share in accordance with the law of the beneficiary’s domicile at the owner’s death governing inheritance by descendants of an intestate.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 5512
citations.cite: applicability of the Act by registration and date-of-death
citations.quote: This part applies to registrations of securities in beneficiary form made before, on, or after January 1, 1999, by decedents dying on or after January 1, 1999.

clauses.title: Security Owner and TOD Beneficiary Declaration
clauses.body: {{ownerName}} is the owner of {{accountDescription}} held with {{financialInstitutionName}}. {{ownerName}} intends this security or account to be registered in beneficiary form under California's Uniform TOD Security Registration Act, naming {{beneficiaryName}} as TOD beneficiary. If {{additionalBeneficiaryName}} is also named, {{beneficiaryName}} and {{additionalBeneficiaryName}} are both named as TOD beneficiaries, to hold as tenants in common if both survive {{ownerName}} and the security has not yet been divided between them, unless {{financialInstitutionName}}'s own terms and conditions provide otherwise. If {{contingentBeneficiaryName}} is named, {{contingentBeneficiaryName}} is named as a substitute or contingent beneficiary, to take {{beneficiaryName}}'s (or {{additionalBeneficiaryName}}'s) share only if that named beneficiary does not survive {{ownerName}}. This declaration records {{ownerName}}'s intended designation for {{ownerName}}'s own planning purposes; it does not, by itself, register the security or account in beneficiary form. A registration in beneficiary form becomes legally effective only when it is reflected in the registration, account agreement, or other instrument that {{financialInstitutionName}} itself uses to register, open, or modify the security or account.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment
clauses.body:
SIGNATURE AND DATE: {{ownerName}} signs and dates this declaration below.

Signature of {{ownerName}}: _________________________ Date: _______________

Printed name: _________________________

ACKNOWLEDGMENT: {{ownerName}} understands that this declaration is a planning worksheet reflecting {{ownerName}}'s intended TOD beneficiary designation for {{accountDescription}} at {{financialInstitutionName}}, and that it does not itself register, open, or modify any security or account. {{ownerName}} understands that to make the designation legally effective, {{ownerName}} must separately complete {{financialInstitutionName}}'s own registration, beneficiary form, or account agreement naming {{beneficiaryName}} (and {{additionalBeneficiaryName}} and {{contingentBeneficiaryName}}, if applicable) as TOD or POD beneficiary, and that {{financialInstitutionName}} may require government-issued identification, an original signature, or additional paperwork of its own choosing before doing so, and is not required by statute to offer this form of registration at all. {{ownerName}} further understands that the designation can generally be canceled or changed at any time before {{ownerName}}'s death — by {{ownerName}} alone if sole owner, or by all then-surviving owners if jointly owned — without {{beneficiaryName}}'s consent, and that it has no effect on ownership until {{ownerName}}'s death.

NOTARIZATION NOTICE: California's Uniform TOD Security Registration Act does not require this declaration to be notarized or witnessed to be effective; what governs is the registration or account agreement actually on file with {{financialInstitutionName}}. This declaration is kept for {{ownerName}}'s own records, alongside a copy of the TOD or POD registration paperwork {{financialInstitutionName}} provides.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's trade secret evidentiary privilege, set out in Evidence Code sections 1060 through 1062, and the criminal-proceeding procedures that accompany it. It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning a matter involving {{companyName}} and {{adversePartyName}}, identified by case number {{courtCaseNumber}} in {{courtName}}, and concerning the following trade secret: {{tradeSecretDescription}}. Section 1060 creates a privilege letting the owner of a trade secret (or the owner's agent or employee) refuse to disclose the secret, and prevent others from disclosing it, in a judicial, administrative, or other proceeding, subject to a fraud/injustice exception. Sections 1061 and 1062 then set out a specific procedure, available in criminal proceedings, for a protective order limiting who may see the secret and for closing part of a criminal proceeding to the public to keep the secret from being disclosed. This document explains what the text of these three sections says and does not say. It is separate from, and does not repeat, the corpus's existing Trade Secret Pre-Discovery Identification Information Sheet (which addresses Code of Civil Procedure section 2019.210 and Civil Code section 3426.5, civil-discovery-sequencing and civil-protective-order provisions of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act), Criminal Trade Secret Theft Information Sheet (which addresses Penal Code section 499c's definition of the criminal offense itself, not courtroom secrecy procedure), Trade Secret Injunctive Relief Standards Information Sheet, and Trade Secret Preemption Doctrine Information Sheet. None of those documents describe the evidentiary privilege or the criminal-proceeding protective-order and closure mechanics covered here. This document does not itself assert the privilege, does not draft or file a motion for a protective order or for closure of a proceeding, and does not evaluate whether any specific information qualifies as a trade secret.

clauses.title: The Trade Secret Privilege and Its Fraud/Injustice Limit
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1060 gives the owner of a trade secret — or the owner's agent or employee, if either of them claims it — a privilege to refuse to disclose the secret and to prevent another person from disclosing it. The statute's text conditions that privilege on a single stated limit: the privilege applies only if allowing it will not tend to conceal fraud or otherwise work an injustice.
clauses.gap: Section 1060's text does not itself define "trade secret," does not state in which kinds of proceedings (civil, criminal, or administrative) the privilege may be claimed, and does not describe any procedure for claiming it or for a court to decide whether the fraud/injustice exception applies. The specific motion-and-affidavit procedure described in the companion clauses below, drawn from section 1061, applies only "during a criminal proceeding" by that section's own terms; section 1060's text supplies no comparable procedure for civil or administrative proceedings.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1060 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1060
citations.quote: If he or his agent or employee claims the privilege, the owner of a trade secret has a privilege to refuse to disclose the secret, and to prevent another from disclosing it, if the allowance of the privilege will not tend to conceal fraud or otherwise work injustice.

clauses.title: Definitions Borrowed for the Criminal-Proceeding Procedure
clauses.body: For purposes of section 1061 itself, and of sections 1062 and 1063, Evidence Code section 1061(a) defines "trade secret" by cross-reference to the definition in Civil Code section 3426.1(d) (the Uniform Trade Secrets Act's definition) or, alternatively, to the definition in Penal Code section 499c(a)(9) (the criminal trade secret theft statute's definition). Section 1061(a) separately defines "article" by cross-reference to Penal Code section 499c(a)(2).
clauses.gap: Section 1061(a) states that these definitions apply "for purposes of this section, and Sections 1062 and 1063"; its text does not say whether the same definitions govern the general privilege stated in section 1060 itself, which contains no definition of "trade secret" of its own. This document did not independently compare the Civil Code 3426.1(d) and Penal Code 499c(a)(9) definitions to determine whether they are identical in scope; section 1061(a) offers them as alternatives ("or") without stating whether they differ.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(a) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(a)
citations.quote: (a) For purposes of this section, and Sections 1062 and 1063:(1) “Trade secret” means “trade secret,” as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 3426.1 of the Civil Code, or paragraph (9) of subdivision (a) of Section 499c of the Penal Code.

clauses.title: Motion, Affidavit, and Opposition Procedure for a Criminal-Case Protective Order
clauses.body: Section 1061(b) sets out a procedure that applies whenever the owner of a trade secret wishes to assert the section 1060 privilege during a criminal proceeding. The owner must file a motion for a protective order (or the prosecution may file it on the owner's behalf and with the owner's permission), supported by an affidavit based on personal knowledge that lists the affiant's qualifications, identifies without revealing the alleged trade secret and the articles disclosing it, and presents evidence that the secret meets the statutory definition; the motion and affidavit must be served on all parties. Any party may oppose the motion by submitting affidavits based on personal knowledge; those opposing affidavits are filed under seal but must be provided to the trade secret owner and to all parties, and neither the owner nor any party may disclose them to anyone other than counsel of record without prior court approval.
clauses.gap: This procedure applies, by its own text, only "during a criminal proceeding"; the statute's text does not extend this specific motion-and-affidavit mechanism to civil or administrative proceedings, and does not state a deadline, measured from any specific event in the criminal proceeding, by which the motion must be filed.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(1) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(1)
citations.quote: The owner of the trade secret shall file a motion for a protective order, or the people may file the motion on the owner’s behalf and with the owner’s permission.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(2) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(2)
citations.quote: The affidavits shall be filed under seal, but shall be provided to the owner of the trade secret and to all parties in the proceeding.

clauses.title: Standard for Granting a Protective Order and the Optional In-Camera Hearing
clauses.body: Under section 1061(b)(3), the party moving for a protective order must show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that issuing the order is proper; the court may rule without an evidentiary hearing, but may in its discretion hold an in-camera evidentiary hearing limited to the trade secret owner, the prosecution's representative, the defendant, and defense counsel. Section 1061(b)(4) then states the standard for granting the order: if the court finds that a trade secret may otherwise be disclosed during the criminal proceeding and that issuing a protective order would not conceal a fraud or work an injustice, the court shall issue a protective order limiting the use and dissemination of the trade secret and of articles disclosing it.
clauses.gap: Section 1061(b)(3)'s text does not define "preponderance of the evidence" or list what evidence suffices to meet it, and it makes the in-camera hearing entirely discretionary with the court ("the court may choose to hold" one) rather than something a movant can compel. The statute's text also does not state what happens if the court neither holds a hearing nor grants the motion outright — for example, whether further briefing may be ordered.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(3) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(3)
citations.quote: The movant shall, by a preponderance of the evidence, show that the issuance of a protective order is proper.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(4) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(4)
citations.quote: If the court finds that a trade secret may be disclosed during any criminal proceeding unless a protective order is issued and that the issuance of a protective order would not conceal a fraud or work an injustice, the court shall issue a protective order limiting the use and dissemination of the trade secret, including, but not limited to, articles disclosing that secret.

clauses.title: Permissible (Not Mandatory) Contents of the Protective Order
clauses.body: Section 1061(b)(4) lists provisions a protective order "may, in the court's discretion, include": limiting dissemination of the trade secret to counsel and their staff and to law enforcement or clerical officials; requiring the defendant to view the secret only in the presence of counsel; requiring court approval before showing the secret to anyone not designated by the order, including a vetting procedure for any expert who would receive it; barring public filing of articles disclosing the secret without court approval and notice to the owner; and any other order the court deems necessary to protect the trade secret's integrity.
clauses.gap: Every listed provision is introduced with "may" — the statute's text makes each one an option the court can choose to include, not a required term of any protective order, and subsection (E) makes the list expressly non-exhaustive ("other orders as the court deems necessary"). The text does not rank the options, does not say which combination is presumptively appropriate, and does not state a standard for reviewing an expert the court has already approved if new information later emerges.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(4)(A) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(4)(A)
citations.quote: That the trade secret may be disseminated only to counsel for the parties, including their associate attorneys, paralegals, and investigators, and to law enforcement officials or clerical officials.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(4)(E) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(b)(4)(E)
citations.quote: Other orders as the court deems necessary to protect the integrity of the trade secret.

clauses.title: A Protective-Order Ruling Does Not Decide Trade Secret Status or Bind Civil Litigation
clauses.body: Section 1061(c) states that a ruling granting or denying a motion for a protective order under subsection (b) is not to be construed as a determination that the alleged trade secret is or is not a trade secret, and that such a ruling has no effect on any civil litigation. Section 1061(d) states that the section has prospective effect only and does not invalidate protective orders entered before it took effect.
clauses.gap: Section 1061(c)'s text addresses effect on "civil litigation" specifically; it does not state what effect, if any, the ruling has on a different criminal proceeding or on an administrative proceeding involving the same alleged trade secret. Section 1061(d)'s "prospective effect only" language is tied to a 2003 effective date for the version of the statute fetched in this research session; the statute's text does not itself restate what procedure, if any, governed protective-order motions filed before that date.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(c) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(c)
citations.quote: Such a ruling shall not have any effect on any civil litigation.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(d) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1061(d)
citations.quote: This section shall have prospective effect only and shall not operate to invalidate previously entered protective orders.

clauses.title: Closing Part of a Criminal Proceeding to the Public to Protect a Trade Secret
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1062(a) lets a court, in a criminal case, exclude the public from part of a criminal proceeding on motion of the trade secret owner (or the prosecution with the owner's consent), if the proponent of closure demonstrates a substantial probability that the trade secret would otherwise be disclosed to the public during that proceeding and a substantial probability that disclosure would cause serious harm to the owner, and if the court finds no overriding public interest in an open proceeding. The same subsection states a limit: no evidence may be excluded under this section if doing so would conceal a fraud, work an injustice, or deprive the prosecution or the defendant of a fair trial.
clauses.gap: Section 1062(a)'s closure authority applies, by its own text, "in a criminal case"; the statute's text does not address closing a civil or administrative proceeding to protect a trade secret. The text does not define "substantial probability," "serious harm," or "overriding public interest," leaving those standards' practical content to case law that was not verified in this research session (see the companion clause on this document's case-law limitation).

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(a) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(a)
citations.quote: in a criminal case, the court, upon motion of the owner of a trade secret, or upon motion by the People with the consent of the owner, may exclude the public from any portion of a criminal proceeding where the proponent of closure has demonstrated a substantial probability that the trade secret would otherwise be disclosed to the public during that proceeding and a substantial probability that the disclosure would cause serious harm to the owner of the secret, and where the court finds that there is no overriding public interest in an open proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(a) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(a)
citations.quote: No evidence, however, shall be excluded during a criminal proceeding pursuant to this section if it would conceal a fraud, work an injustice, or deprive the People or the defendant of a fair trial.

clauses.title: Scope of Closure, Appellate Review, and Later Public Access to the Transcript
clauses.body: Section 1062(b) requires that any closure motion be preceded by an in-camera hearing limited to the trade secret owner, the prosecution's representative, the defendant, and defense counsel, with a court reporter present, and that the hearing transcript and any articles presented at it be sealed. Section 1062(c) requires the court, before granting closure, to close only the portion of the proceeding necessary to prevent disclosure and to state on the record that the moving party met its burden and that closure will not deprive the prosecution or the defendant of a fair trial. Section 1062(d) allows the trade secret owner, the prosecution, or the defendant to seek relief from a closure ruling by petitioning a higher court for extraordinary relief. Section 1062(e) requires that once a portion of a proceeding is closed under this section, a transcript of the closed proceeding be made available to the public as soon as practicable, with the court redacting any trade-secret information first.
clauses.gap: Section 1062(e)'s text requires public release of the transcript "as soon as practicable" but sets no specific deadline in days or a comparable fixed measure. Section 1062(d)'s text does not state the standard of review an appellate court applies to a petition for extraordinary relief from a closure ruling, and this document does not address section 1062(f) (concerning witnesses under a related section 1061 protective order remaining in the courtroom during a closed proceeding), which was excluded from this document because the fetched official text of that subsection contains an apparent typographical error ("pursaunt" for "pursuant") that this document did not attempt to interpret or correct.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(c) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(c)
citations.quote: the court shall close only that portion of the criminal proceeding necessary to prevent disclosure of the trade secret.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(e) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1062(e)
citations.quote: a transcript of that closed proceeding shall be made available to the public as soon as practicable.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment
Corporation's Annual Report to Shareholders — What This Information Sheet Covers
clauses.body: This information sheet addresses a specific, recurring statutory duty that runs from {{companyName}}'s board of directors to its own shareholders: the duty, under California Corporations Code § 1501, to send an annual financial report. This is different from several other topics addressed elsewhere in this corpus. A shareholder's or member's statutory right to inspect and copy a corporation's books, records, and minutes (Corporations Code §§ 1600-1603) is a demand-driven right the shareholder exercises; § 1501 instead obligates the board to send a report on its own initiative, without waiting for any shareholder to ask. This is also different from the specialized annual reporting statutes this corpus describes for two particular corporate subtypes: the Benefit Corporation's annual benefit report and the Social Purpose Corporation's annual report with its special purpose management discussion and analysis are separate statutes, layered on top of (or, for the Social Purpose Corporation, expressly cross-referencing) the general rule this information sheet describes, and neither of those documents states what § 1501 itself requires of an ordinary corporation that is not organized under either of those specialized statutes. This document states what § 1501 requires; it does not tell {{companyName}} or {{preparerName}} what to do about any specific fiscal year's report.

clauses.title: The Board's Duty to Send an Annual Report Within 120 Days — Corporations Code § 1501(a)(1)
clauses.body: Corporations Code § 1501(a)(1) imposes an affirmative duty on the board itself, not merely a right a shareholder must invoke: "The board shall cause an annual report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 120 days after the close of the fiscal year, unless in the case of a corporation with less than 100 holders of record of its shares (determined as provided in Section 605) this requirement is expressly waived in the bylaws." The same paragraph fixes the report's minimum content: "This report shall contain a balance sheet as of the end of that fiscal year and an income statement and a statement of cashflows for that fiscal year, accompanied by any report thereon of independent accountants or, if there is no report, the certificate of an authorized officer of the corporation that the statements were prepared without audit from the books and records of the corporation." For {{companyName}}, whose fiscal year ends {{fiscalYearEndDate}}, this section supplies the deadline and the minimum content that any report sent under it must contain, subject to the waiver and small-corporation provisions described in this document's companion clauses.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what § 1501(a)(1) itself says about the duty, the 120-day deadline, and minimum content; it does not restate the small-corporation waiver mechanics or the separate GAAP exception (both addressed in this document's companion clauses), and it does not address what happens if a corporation with 100 or more holders of record attempts to waive the requirement by bylaw — the waiver is textually available only to a corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record. This is the current statutory text of § 1501(a)(1), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches using two distinct User-Agent strings. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions construing this subdivision returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (125/day quota already exhausted) before any search could run; this clause and its companions therefore rest on the statutory text alone, with no case law verified for this document.

citations.quote: The board shall cause an annual report to be sent to the shareholders not later than 120 days after the close of the fiscal year, unless in the case of a corporation with less than 100 holders of record of its shares (determined as provided in Section 605) this requirement is expressly waived in the bylaws.

clauses.title: The Report May Be Sent by Electronic Transmission — Corporations Code § 1501(a)(1)
clauses.body: The same subdivision that creates the annual report duty also authorizes one specific method of sending it: "Unless otherwise provided by the articles or bylaws and if approved by the board of directors, that report and any accompanying material sent pursuant to this section may be sent by electronic transmission by the corporation (Section 20)." For {{companyName}}, this means the board's approval — and the absence of a contrary provision in the articles or bylaws — are both preconditions to sending the report and any accompanying material electronically rather than by mail.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what § 1501(a)(1)'s electronic-transmission sentence itself says; it does not independently examine Section 20, the cross-referenced definition of "electronic transmission by the corporation," which was not separately fetched or quoted for this clause, so this clause does not state what that definition itself requires (for example, any recipient-consent or delivery-confirmation mechanics Section 20 may impose). This is the current statutory text of § 1501(a)(1), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches using two distinct User-Agent strings. No CourtListener case-law search could be completed for this clause; the daily quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked.

clauses.title: Timing Relative to the Annual Meeting — Corporations Code § 1501(a)(2)
clauses.body: Beyond the 120-day outer deadline, § 1501(a)(2) ties the report's timing to the corporation's next annual shareholders' meeting: "Unless so waived, the report specified in paragraph (1) shall be sent to the shareholders at least 15 (or, if sent by third-class mail, 35) days before the annual meeting of shareholders to be held during the next fiscal year, but this requirement shall not limit the requirement for holding an annual meeting as required by Section 600." This means {{companyName}}'s board must account for its method of delivery — ordinary mail, third-class mail, or another method — in calculating how far in advance of the annual meeting the report must go out, where the small-corporation waiver described elsewhere in this section does not apply.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the timing rule in § 1501(a)(2); it does not restate the small-corporation waiver mechanics (addressed in this document's companion clause on § 1501(a)(1)) or the separate annual-meeting requirement in Section 600, which the quoted text cross-references but which this clause does not independently examine or quote. This is the current statutory text of § 1501(a)(2), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches using two distinct User-Agent strings. No CourtListener case-law search could be completed for this clause; the daily quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked.

citations.quote: Unless so waived, the report specified in paragraph (1) shall be sent to the shareholders at least 15 (or, if sent by third-class mail, 35) days before the annual meeting of shareholders to be held during the next fiscal year, but this requirement shall not limit the requirement for holding an annual meeting as required by Section 600.

clauses.title: A Relaxed Accounting Standard for Corporations With Fewer Than 100 Holders — Corporations Code § 1501(a)(3)
clauses.body: Section 1501(a)(3) provides a distinct accounting-standard exception, separate from the bylaw waiver described elsewhere in this section: "Notwithstanding Section 114, the financial statements of any corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record of its shares (determined as provided in Section 605) required to be furnished by this subdivision and subdivision (c) are not required to be prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles if they reasonably set forth the assets and liabilities and the income and expense of the corporation and disclose the accounting basis used in their preparation." For a corporation such as {{companyName}} with fewer than 100 holders of record, this exception applies whether or not the corporation has also exercised the separate bylaw waiver of the report itself — the two provisions address different questions.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what § 1501(a)(3) itself says; it does not independently examine Section 114 (the general financial-statement definition this subdivision displaces) or Section 605 (the cross-referenced method for determining who counts as a "holder of record"), neither of which was separately fetched or quoted for this clause. This exception governs only the accounting standard used to prepare the statements — it does not excuse a corporation from sending the report at all; that separate question is governed by the bylaw waiver described in this document's companion clause on § 1501(a)(1). This is the current statutory text of § 1501(a)(3), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches using two distinct User-Agent strings. No CourtListener case-law search could be completed for this clause; the daily quota (125/day) was already exhausted when checked.

citations.cite: Corp. Code § 1501(a)(3)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding Section 114, the financial statements of any corporation with fewer than 100 holders of record of its shares (determined as provided in Section 605) required to be furnished by this subdivision and subdivision (c) are not required to be prepared in conformity with generally accepted accounting principles if they reasonably set forth the assets and liabilities and the income and expense of the corporation and disclose the accounting basis used in their preparation.

clauses.title: Additional Disclosure for Mid-Size Corporations: Related-Party Transactions Over $40,000 — Corporations Code § 1501(b)(1)
clauses.body: For a corporation that is neither small enough to fall under the waiver described elsewhere in this section nor already subject to federal securities reporting, § 1501(b) adds two further disclosure items to the annual report: "In addition to the financial statements required by subdivision (a), the annual report of any corporation having 100 or more holders of record of its shares (determined as provided in Section 605) either not subject to the reporting requirements of Section 13 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, or exempted from those reporting requirements by Section 12(g)(2) of that act, shall also describe briefly both of the following:" The first of these, § 1501(b)(1), requires disclosure of certain related-party transactions: "Any transaction (excluding compensation of officers and directors) during the previous fiscal year involving an amount in excess of forty thousand dollars ($40,000) (other than contracts let at competitive bid or services rendered at prices regulated by law) to which the corporation or its parent or subsidiary was a party and in which any director or officer of the corporation or of a subsidiary or (if known to the corporation or its parent or subsidiary) any holder of more than 10 percent of the outstanding voting shares of the corporation had a direct or indirect material interest, naming the person and stating the person’s relationship to the corporation, the nature of the person’s interest in the transaction and, where practicable, the amount of the interest; provided that in the case of a transaction with a partnership of which the person is a partner, only the interest of the partnership need be stated; and provided further that no report need be made in the case of any transaction approved by the shareholders (Section 153)." This disclosure duty exists independently of, and describes a different thing than, the statutory self-dealing safe-harbor procedures this corpus's separate Self-Dealing and Interested Director/Officer Transactions document addresses under Corporations Code § 310 — this § 1501(b)(1) provision is a reporting obligation, not a procedure for validating the underlying transaction.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what § 1501(b) and § 1501(b)(1) themselves say; it applies only to a corporation with 100 or more holders of record that is not already subject to, or exempted under Section 12(g)(2) from, federal Exchange Act reporting — it does not apply to a corporation that has waived the underlying annual report under the small-corporation provision described in this document's companion clause, nor to a corporation already filing under federal securities law. The $40,000 threshold and the cross-referenced Sections 13, 12(g)(2), and 153 were not independently fetched or verified as part of this clause; this clause states only what § 1501(b)(1)'s own text says about them. clauses.title: Additional Disclosure for Mid-Size Corporations: Indemnification Over $10,000 — Corporations Code § 1501(b)(2)
clauses.body: The second item § 1501(b) requires of a qualifying mid-size, non-SEC-reporting corporation's annual report concerns indemnification payments: "The amount and circumstances of any indemnification or advances aggregating more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000) paid during the fiscal year to any officer or director of the corporation pursuant to Section 317; provided that no report need be made in the case of indemnification approved by the shareholders (Section 153) under paragraph (2) of subdivision (e) of Section 317." This is a disclosure duty about indemnification payments already made — it describes a different question than the corpus's separate Director and Officer Indemnification document, which addresses the substantive Section 317 standards governing when and how a corporation may or must indemnify an agent in the first place.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what § 1501(b)(2) itself says; like the related-party transaction disclosure in this document's companion clause, it applies only to a corporation with 100 or more holders of record that is not already subject to, or exempted under Section 12(g)(2) from, federal Exchange Act reporting (the qualifying condition is stated in § 1501(b)'s introductory text, quoted in that companion clause, not repeated in this clause's own quoted text). This clause does not independently restate or verify what Section 317 itself provides about when indemnification is proper — that substantive standard is addressed in this corpus's separate Director and Officer Indemnification document. clauses.title: A Shareholder's Right to Demand Statements When No Report Was Sent — Corporations Code § 1501(c)
clauses.body: Section 1501(c) gives an individual shareholder, such as {{shareholderName}}, a fallback right to demand financial statements when the board did not send the annual report: "If no annual report for the last fiscal year has been sent to shareholders, the corporation shall, upon the written request of any shareholder made more than 120 days after the close of that fiscal year, deliver or mail to the person making the request within 30 days thereafter the financial statements required by subdivision (a) for that year." The same subdivision gives a larger holding group a separate, broader right to more current interim financial information: "A shareholder or shareholders holding at least 5 percent of the outstanding shares of any class of a corporation may make a written request to the corporation for an income statement of the corporation for the three-month, six-month, or nine-month period of the current fiscal year ended more than 30 days before the date of the request and a balance sheet of the corporation as of the end of the period and, in addition, if no annual report for the last fiscal year has been sent to shareholders, the statements referred to in subdivision (a) for the last fiscal year."
clauses.gap: This clause states only what § 1501(c)'s two quoted sentences say; it does not restate the remainder of subdivision (c), which separately requires the resulting statements to be delivered or mailed within 30 days and kept on file at the principal office for 12 months, nor subdivision (d)'s requirement that any such quarterly statements be accompanied by an accountant's report or officer's certificate. This is a written-demand right exercised by the shareholder — it does not describe a right the corporation must satisfy without a request, which is instead the board's affirmative duty addressed in this document's companion clause on § 1501(a)(1). clauses.title: Court Enforcement and Fee-Shifting for an Unjustified Failure to Report — Corporations Code § 1501(e)-(f)
clauses.body: Section 1501 backs its reporting duties with a specific court-enforcement mechanism. Subdivision (e) states: "In addition to the penalties provided for in Section 2200, the superior court of the proper county shall enforce the duty of making and mailing or delivering the information and financial statements required by this section and, for good cause shown, may extend the time therefor." Subdivision (f) then adds a discretionary fee-shifting remedy: "In any action or proceeding under this section, if the court finds the failure of the corporation to comply with the requirements of this section to have been without justification, the court may award an amount sufficient to reimburse the shareholder for the reasonable expenses incurred by the shareholder, including attorney’s fees, in connection with the action or proceeding."
clauses.gap: This clause states only what subdivisions (e) and (f) themselves say; it does not independently examine Section 2200, the separate penalty provision subdivision (e) cross-references, which was not fetched or quoted for this clause. The fee award under subdivision (f) is discretionary ("may award") and conditioned on the court finding the corporation's noncompliance to have been "without justification" — a standard this section does not itself further define, and this clause does not predict how a court would apply it to any particular set of facts. This is the current statutory text of § 1501(e) and (f), fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website and verified byte-identical across two separate fetches using two distinct User-Agent strings.
