clauses.title: Which Corporations This Section Reaches — Corporations Code § 1501(g)
clauses.body: Section 1501 is not limited to corporations formed in California. Subdivision (g) states its scope directly: "This section applies to any domestic corporation and also to a foreign corporation having its principal office in California or customarily holding meetings of its board in this state." For {{companyName}}, this means the analysis in this document's other clauses turns on where the corporation's principal office is located or where its board customarily meets, not solely on the state of incorporation named in its articles.
clauses.gap: This clause states only what § 1501(g) itself says; it does not independently examine how "customarily holding meetings of its board in this state" would be established or contested for a particular corporation, a term this subdivision does not further define. This clause also does not restate or cross-reference how this scope provision interacts with Corporations Code § 2115, the pseudo-foreign corporation statute this corpus's separate Section 2115 document addresses, which applies a different multi-factor test to determine which of California's corporate statutes reach an out-of-state corporation more generally — that document was not re-examined as part of this clause, and this clause does not claim the two statutes' scope tests are identical. clauses.title: About This Emergency Action Plan Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This Emergency Action Plan Information Sheet describes California's Cal/OSHA regulation requiring most employers to establish an emergency action plan covering fire and other workplace emergencies, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220, as that regulation relates to the working relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}.

It summarizes selected requirements of that regulation: what the plan must cover and when it must be written, the six elements the regulation itself requires the plan to include, the employee alarm system and evacuation-type requirements, when the employer must designate and train evacuation personnel, when and how employees must be advised of their responsibilities under the plan, and where the written plan must be kept, including the regulation's own exception for employers with 10 or fewer employees.

{{companyName}} has identified {{programAdministratorName}} as the person or department who can be contacted for further information or an explanation of duties under its plan.

This information sheet is not itself {{companyName}}'s emergency action plan, does not itself satisfy 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220's plan requirement, and does not determine that any particular practice of {{companyName}}'s is or is not compliant with California law.

clauses.title: Scope and the Written-Plan Requirement
clauses.body: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220(a) itself states that the section applies to all emergency action plans, that the plan shall cover those designated actions employers and employees must take to ensure employee safety from fire and other emergencies, and that the plan shall be in writing except as provided in the last sentence of subsection (e)(3) of the same section. That last sentence, addressed in a companion clause of this information sheet, is the regulation's own exception for employers with 10 or fewer employees.
clauses.gap: The regulation's own text does not itself state which employers are covered — it says the section 'applies to all emergency action plans' without separately defining which workplaces or industries must have one, or listing any industry-specific exemption from the underlying duty to have a plan at all (as distinct from the small-employer exception to the writing requirement, which is stated and is addressed separately). This document did not independently verify whether any other Title 8 provision narrows or exempts particular categories of employers from § 3220 itself; none was found in the text quoted here or elsewhere in this section. The quotation is drawn from a single subdivision of one regulation and is not corroborated by any second, independent source.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3220, subd. (a)
citations.quote: (a) Scope and Application. This section applies to all emergency action plans. The emergency action plan shall be in writing, except as provided in the last sentence of subsection (e)(3) of this section, and shall cover those designated actions employers and employees must take to ensure employee safety from fire and other emergencies.

clauses.title: The Six Elements the Plan Must Include
clauses.body: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220(b) itself states that, at a minimum, six elements shall be included in the plan: procedures for emergency evacuation, including the type of evacuation and exit route assignments; procedures to be followed by employees who remain to operate critical plant operations before they evacuate; procedures to account for all employees after emergency evacuation has been completed; procedures to be followed by employees performing rescue or medical duties; the preferred means of reporting fires and other emergencies; and the names or regular job titles of persons or departments who can be contacted for further information or explanation of duties under the plan. {{companyName}} has identified {{programAdministratorName}} as the person or department who can be contacted for that purpose.
clauses.gap: The regulation's own phrase — 'at a minimum' — means the six listed elements are a floor, not a ceiling; the text quoted here does not itself state what, if anything, beyond these six elements a particular plan must contain. All six citations below are drawn from the same regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220(b), and its numbered subparagraphs (1) through (6) — they are not independent sources of one another. This document did not independently verify the 2017 regulatory history note appearing on the source page, which states that subsections (b)(1) and (b)(4) were amended effective June 5, 2017; that amendment is not itself quoted or analyzed here, only the current text as fetched.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3220, subd. (b)
citations.quote: (b) Elements. The following elements, at a minimum, shall be included in the plan:

citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3220, subd. (b)(1)
citations.quote: (1) Procedures for emergency evacuation, including type of evacuation and exit route assignments;

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3220, subd. (b)(2)
citations.quote: (2) Procedures to be followed by employees who remain to operate critical plant operations before they evacuate;

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3220, subd. (b)(3)
citations.quote: (3) Procedures to account for all employees after emergency evacuation has been completed;

citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3220, subd. (b)(4)
citations.quote: (4) Procedures to be followed by employees performing rescue or medical duties;

clauses.title: The Employee Alarm System Requirement
clauses.body: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220(c) itself requires the employer to establish an employee alarm system that complies with Article 165 of Title 8, and, if that alarm system is used for alerting fire brigade members or for other purposes in addition to signaling an emergency evacuation, it requires a distinctive signal to be used for each separate purpose.
clauses.gap: This clause does not independently verify the content of Article 165 itself, the separate Title 8 employee-alarm-system standard that § 3220(c)(1) cross-references — that article was not fetched or quoted in this information sheet, so no claim is made here about what Article 165 itself requires of an alarm system beyond the requirement to comply with it. Both quotations in this clause are drawn from subdivisions (c)(1) and (c)(2) of the same regulation, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220, not from two independent sources.

citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3220, subd. (c)(1)
citations.quote: (1) The employer shall establish an employee alarm system which complies with Article 165.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3220, subd. (c)(2)
citations.quote: (2) If the employee alarm system is used for alerting fire brigade members, or for other purposes, a distinctive signal for each purpose shall be used.

clauses.title: Establishing the Types of Evacuation
clauses.body: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220(d) itself requires the employer to establish, within the emergency action plan, the types of evacuation to be used in emergency circumstances.
clauses.gap: The regulation's own text does not itself list or define what the available 'types of evacuation' are — it requires only that the plan establish which types apply, without naming categories (such as full-building evacuation versus a partial or phased evacuation) in the text quoted here. This is a single subdivision of one regulation, not corroborated by any second, independent source in this clause.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3220, subd. (d)
citations.quote: (d) Evacuation. The employer shall establish in the emergency action plan the types of evacuation to be used in emergency circumstances.

clauses.title: Designating and Training Evacuation Personnel
clauses.body: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220(e)(1) itself requires that, before implementing the emergency action plan, the employer designate and train a sufficient number of persons to assist in the safe and orderly emergency evacuation of employees.
clauses.gap: The regulation's own text does not itself state a numeric ratio, ratio of designated persons to total employees, or specific training curriculum — it requires only a 'sufficient number' of trained persons, a standard the text quoted here does not further define. This clause quotes a single subdivision of one regulation; the training obligations described in the companion clause of this information sheet covering subdivision (e)(2) are a separate requirement of the same subdivision (e), not an independent source.

clauses.title: When Employees Must Be Advised of Their Responsibilities
clauses.body: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220(e)(2) itself requires the employer to advise each employee of his or her responsibility under the plan at three specified times: initially when the plan is developed; whenever the employee's responsibilities or designated actions under the plan change; and whenever the plan itself is changed.
clauses.gap: The regulation's own text does not itself specify a method of notice (written memo, posted notice, verbal briefing, or otherwise) for advising employees at these three times, nor does it state a deadline measured in days after a change to the plan or to an employee's responsibilities. All three quotations in this clause — subparagraphs (A), (B), and (C) — are part of the same subdivision, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220(e)(2), and are not independent of one another or of the other clauses of this information sheet that also cite this regulation.

citations.quote: (A) Initially when the plan is developed,

citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3220, subd. (e)(2)(B)
citations.quote: (B) Whenever the employee's responsibilities or designated actions under the plan change, and

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3220, subd. (e)(2)(C)
citations.quote: (C) Whenever the plan is changed.

clauses.title: Plan Availability and the Small-Employer Exception
clauses.body: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220(e)(3) itself requires the employer to review with each employee, upon initial assignment, those parts of the plan the employee must know to protect the employee in the event of an emergency, and it requires that the written plan be kept at the workplace and made available for employee review. The same subdivision then states the exception that subdivision (a) cross-references for the writing requirement: for employers with 10 or fewer employees, the plan may be communicated orally to employees, and the employer need not maintain a written plan.
clauses.gap: The regulation's own text does not itself state whether the 10-or-fewer-employee count is measured company-wide, per worksite, or in some other way — the phrase quoted here is 'employers with 10 or fewer employees,' without further definition of how that number is calculated. This clause quotes a single subdivision, 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220(e)(3); it is the same subdivision that subdivision (a), addressed in a companion clause of this information sheet, cross-references as the source of the writing exception, so the two clauses describe the same regulatory text from two subdivisions of one section rather than from independent sources.

citations.case: 8 Cal. Code Regs. § 3220 (California Department of Industrial Relations, Title 8 text)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 3220, subd. (e)(3)
citations.quote: (3) The employer shall review with each employee upon initial assignment those parts of the plan which the employee must know to protect the employee in the event of an emergency. The written plan shall be kept at the workplace and made available for employee review. For those employers with 10 or fewer employees the plan may be communicated orally to employees and the employer need not maintain a written plan.

clauses.title: California Solar Shade Control Act — Introduction and Scope
The Statute's Name and Legislative Policy Statement
clauses.body: California's Public Resources Code states that Chapter 12 of Division 15 (Public Resources Code §§ 25980–25986) "shall be known and may be cited as the Solar Shade Control Act." The same section states it is the policy of the state to promote all feasible means of energy conservation and all feasible uses of alternative energy supply sources, and that the state, in particular, encourages the planting and maintenance of trees and shrubs to create shading, moderate outdoor temperatures, and provide various economic and aesthetic benefits. The same section also states that there are certain situations in which the need for widespread use of alternative energy devices, such as solar collectors, requires specific and limited controls on trees and shrubs. This section is the chapter's own name and policy statement; it does not itself impose the shading restriction, define "solar collector," or state the exemptions, each of which appear in other sections of the same chapter described elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: Public Resources Code § 25980 is a legislative policy and findings statement, not an operative restriction on any specific tree, shrub, or solar collector; it does not, by its own text, prohibit or require anything with respect to any particular property. Its reference to "alternative energy devices, such as solar collectors" is general language in a policy statement, not the statute's own operative definition of "solar collector," which appears only in Section 25981 and is quoted in a companion clause of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 25980
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, Solar Shade Control Act, statutory name and legislative policy statement
citations.quote: This chapter shall be known and may be cited as the Solar Shade Control Act. It is the policy of the state to promote all feasible means of energy conservation and all feasible uses of alternative energy supply sources. In particular, the state encourages the planting and maintenance of trees and shrubs to create shading, moderate outdoor temperatures, and provide various economic and aesthetic benefits. However, there are certain situations in which the need for widespread use of alternative energy devices, such as solar collectors, requires specific and limited controls on trees and shrubs.

clauses.title: Statutory Definition of "Solar Collector"
clauses.body: For purposes of the Solar Shade Control Act, California's Public Resources Code defines "solar collector" as a fixed device, structure, or part of a device or structure, on the roof of a building, that is used primarily to transform solar energy into thermal, chemical, or electrical energy; the solar collector must be used as part of a system that makes use of solar energy for any or all of three listed purposes: water heating; space heating or cooling; or power generation. Notwithstanding that roof-mounted definition, the statute separately provides that "solar collector" also includes a fixed device, structure, or part of a device or structure used primarily for that same energy transformation that is installed on the ground, where a solar collector cannot be installed on the roof of the building receiving the energy due to inappropriate roofing material, slope of the roof, structural shading, or orientation of the building. The statute also states an exclusion: "solar collector" does not include a solar collector that is designed and intended to offset more than the building's electricity demand.
clauses.gap: Public Resources Code § 25981(a), (b), and (c) are all subsections of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as independent sources corroborating one another. The three listed purposes in subdivision (a) are "water heating," "space heating or cooling," and "power generation"; the statute's own text, as fetched and reviewed in full, does not use the word "pool" or the phrase "pool heating" anywhere in Section 25981, unlike Civil Code § 714 (the separate California Solar Rights Act, addressed in this corpus's own information sheet), which does set a distinct cost-and-efficiency threshold specifically for solar pool-heating systems. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific device or structure in fact meets this definition.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 25981(a)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, roof-mounted definition of "solar collector" and its three listed purposes
citations.quote: As used in this chapter, “solar collector” means a fixed device, structure, or part of a device or structure, on the roof of a building, that is used primarily to transform solar energy into thermal, chemical, or electrical energy. The solar collector shall be used as part of a system that makes use of solar energy for any or all of the following purposes:(1) Water heating.(2) Space heating or cooling.(3) Power generation.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 25981(b)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, ground-mounted extension of the definition, treated as one source with § 25981(a) above, not an independent source
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (a), for the purpose of this chapter, “solar collector” includes a fixed device, structure, or part of a device or structure that is used primarily to transform solar energy into thermal, chemical, or electrical energy and that is installed on the ground because a solar collector cannot be installed on the roof of the building receiving the energy due to inappropriate roofing material, slope of the roof, structural shading, or orientation of the building.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 25981(c)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, exclusion for a collector designed to offset more than the building's electricity demand, treated as one source with § 25981(a)-(b) above, not an independent source
citations.quote: For the purposes of this chapter, “solar collector” does not include a solar collector that is designed and intended to offset more than the building’s electricity demand.

clauses.title: Siting Requirements a Solar Collector Itself Must Meet
clauses.body: California's Public Resources Code states that, for purposes of the Solar Shade Control Act, the location of a solar collector is required to comply with local building and setback regulations, and to be set back not less than five feet from the property line, and not less than 10 feet above the ground. The statute allows a solar collector to be less than 10 feet in height only if, in addition to the five-foot setback, the collector is set back three times the amount its height is lowered below 10 feet.
clauses.gap: Public Resources Code § 25981(d)'s own text, as fetched and reviewed in full, states these siting requirements without stating what legal consequence follows if a solar collector does not meet them — in particular, it does not itself state whether a noncompliantly sited collector remains an "affected solar collector" entitled to the shading restriction and private-nuisance provisions described elsewhere in this document, or the written-notice procedure tied to them. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific installed collector in fact meets these siting requirements.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 25981(d)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, setback and height requirements for a solar collector's location
citations.quote: For purposes of this chapter, the location of a solar collector is required to comply with the local building and setback regulations, and to be set back not less than five feet from the property line, and not less than 10 feet above the ground. A solar collector may be less than 10 feet in height only if, in addition to the five-foot setback, the solar collector is set back three times the amount lowered.

clauses.title: The Statutory 10-Percent Shading Restriction
clauses.body: California's Public Resources Code states the Solar Shade Control Act's core restriction: after the installation of a solar collector, a person owning or in control of another property shall not allow a tree or shrub to be placed or, if placed, to grow on that property so as to cast a shadow greater than 10 percent of the collector absorption area upon that solar collector surface at any one time between the hours of 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., local standard time. By its own terms, the restriction applies only after the solar collector's installation, to a tree or shrub on another person's property (not the solar collector owner's own property), and only during the specified four-hour window.
clauses.gap: Public Resources Code § 25982's own text, as fetched and reviewed in full, does not define "collector absorption area" or state a required measurement method, instrument, season, or date for determining whether a shadow exceeds 10 percent of it — the statute states a percentage and a time window, not a testing protocol. The statute's own phrase "local standard time" is not further defined in the text and, on its face, does not itself state whether or how it accounts for daylight saving time. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific tree or shrub in fact casts a shadow meeting or exceeding this statutory threshold on any specific solar collector.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 25982
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, the 10-percent shadow restriction between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m.
citations.quote: After the installation of a solar collector, a person owning or in control of another property shall not allow a tree or shrub to be placed or, if placed, to grow on that property so as to cast a shadow greater than 10 percent of the collector absorption area upon that solar collector surface at any one time between the hours of 10 a.m. and 2 p.m., local standard time.

clauses.title: Private-Nuisance Status and the Written-Notice Prerequisite
clauses.body: California's Public Resources Code states that a tree or shrub maintained in violation of the shading restriction described elsewhere in this document is a private nuisance, as defined in Civil Code § 3481, but only if the person who maintains or permits the tree or shrub to be maintained fails to remove or alter it after receiving a written notice from the owner or agent of the affected solar collector requesting compliance with the shading restriction. Private-nuisance status under this statute is therefore conditioned on two things happening in sequence: a written notice requesting compliance, and a subsequent failure to remove or alter the tree or shrub.
clauses.gap: Public Resources Code § 25983's own text, as fetched and reviewed in full, does not itself state any required content, format, delivery method (such as personal delivery or mail), or waiting period for the written notice it makes a prerequisite to private-nuisance status — unlike, for example, Civil Code § 841(b)(2) (the separate Good Neighbor Fence Act, addressed in this corpus's own information sheet), which itemizes specific required content for its own 30-day notice. Civil Code § 3481, cross-referenced by this section for the definition of "private nuisance," was not independently fetched or verified in this research session; this clause relies on Section 25983's own cross-reference to it, not on Section 3481's fetched text. This clause does not evaluate whether any specific notice sent regarding any specific tree or shrub in fact satisfies Section 25983, or whether that tree or shrub has in fact been removed or altered after any such notice.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 25983
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, private-nuisance status for a violating tree or shrub, conditioned on written notice and failure to remove or alter
citations.quote: A tree or shrub that is maintained in violation of Section 25982 is a private nuisance, as defined in Section 3481 of the Civil Code, if the person who maintains or permits the tree or shrub to be maintained fails to remove or alter the tree or shrub after receiving a written notice from the owner or agent of the affected solar collector requesting compliance with the requirements of Section 25982.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own Listed Exemptions
clauses.body: California's Public Resources Code states that the Solar Shade Control Act does not apply to any of four listed situations: a tree or shrub planted prior to the installation of a solar collector; a tree planted, grown, or harvested on timberland as defined in Public Resources Code § 4526 or on land devoted to the production of commercial agricultural crops; the replacement of a tree or shrub that had been growing prior to the installation of a solar collector and that, subsequent to the collector's installation, dies or is removed for the protection of public health, safety, or the environment; and a tree or shrub that is subject to a city or county ordinance.
clauses.gap: Public Resources Code § 25984's cross-reference to the definition of "timberland" in Section 4526 was not independently fetched or verified in this research session; this clause relies on Section 25984's own cross-reference, not on Section 4526's fetched text. The fourth exemption, for "a tree or shrub that is subject to a city or county ordinance," is stated broadly in the statute's own text — it is not, on its face, limited to an ordinance that itself regulates solar shading, tree preservation, or the same subject matter as this chapter; this clause does not evaluate whether any specific city or county ordinance in fact makes any particular tree or shrub "subject to" it within the meaning of this subdivision. This clause does not evaluate whether any of the four exemptions in fact applies to any specific tree or shrub.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 25984
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, the chapter's four listed exemptions
citations.quote: This chapter does not apply to any of the following:(a) A tree or shrub planted prior to the installation of a solar collector.(b) A tree planted, grown, or harvested on timberland as defined in Section 4526 or on land devoted to the production of commercial agricultural crops.(c) The replacement of a tree or shrub that had been growing prior to the installation of a solar collector and that, subsequent to the installation of the solar collector, dies, or is removed for the protection of public health, safety, or the environment.(d) A tree or shrub that is subject to a city or county ordinance.

clauses.title: Local Opt-Out and Superseding Local Ordinance Authority
clauses.body: California's Public Resources Code gives cities and counties two distinct forms of local authority over the Solar Shade Control Act. First, a city, or for unincorporated areas a county, may adopt, by majority vote of its governing body, an ordinance exempting its jurisdiction from the chapter's provisions altogether; the statute states that adopting that ordinance is not itself subject to the California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources Code § 21000 and following). Second, and notwithstanding the chapter's requirements, the statute states that a city or county ordinance specifying requirements for tree preservation or solar shade control shall govern within the jurisdiction of the city or county that adopted it.
clauses.gap: Public Resources Code § 25985(a) and (b) are both subsections of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not as independent sources corroborating one another. Subdivisions (a) and (b) describe what appear to be two different mechanisms — a full opt-out ordinance under (a), and a substantively different local ordinance that "shall govern" under (b) — and the statute's own text, as fetched and reviewed in full, does not state whether a governing ordinance under (b) must first be adopted as, or accompanied by, an exemption ordinance under (a), or is independent authority. The statute's own text also does not state, in subdivision (b), that the CEQA exemption stated for subdivision (a)'s ordinance extends to a subdivision (b) ordinance. This clause does not evaluate whether any particular city or county has in fact adopted an ordinance under either subdivision.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 25985(a)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, local ordinance exempting a jurisdiction from the chapter, and CEQA inapplicability to its adoption
citations.quote: A city, or for unincorporated areas, a county, may adopt, by majority vote of the governing body, an ordinance exempting their jurisdiction from the provisions of this chapter. The adoption of the ordinance shall not be subject to the California Environmental Quality Act (commencing with Section 21000).

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 25985(b)
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, a superseding local ordinance on tree preservation or solar shade control, treated as one source with § 25985(a) above, not an independent source
citations.quote: Notwithstanding the requirements of this chapter, a city or a county ordinance specifying requirements for tree preservation or solar shade control shall govern within the jurisdiction of the city or county that adopted the ordinance.

clauses.title: Equitable Relief for a Passive or Natural Solar System
clauses.body: California's Public Resources Code provides a separate exemption mechanism for a person who plans a passive or natural solar heating system, cooling system, or heating and cooling system that would impact an adjacent active solar system: that person may seek equitable relief in a court of competent jurisdiction to exempt the passive or natural system from the chapter's provisions. The statute states that the court may grant that exemption based on a finding that the passive or natural system would provide a demonstrably greater net energy savings than the active system that would be impacted.
clauses.gap: Public Resources Code § 25986's own text, as fetched and reviewed in full, does not define "passive or natural solar heating system," does not name the specific court or type of civil action in which this relief is to be sought beyond "a court of competent jurisdiction," and does not further specify how "demonstrably greater net energy savings" is to be calculated or proven. No case law construing this section could be located and verified in this research session: a CourtListener search for "Solar Shade Control Act" returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, "Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") before any result could be reviewed, so this clause is based on the statute's own text alone, not on any judicial interpretation of it.

citations.case: Cal. Pub. Res. Code § 25986
citations.cite: California Public Resources Code, equitable-relief exemption for a passive or natural solar system impacted by an active solar system
citations.quote: Any person who plans a passive or natural solar heating system or cooling system or heating and cooling system which would impact on an adjacent active solar system may seek equitable relief in a court of competent jurisdiction to exempt such system from the provisions of this chapter. The court may grant such an exemption based on a finding that the passive or natural system would provide a demonstrably greater net energy savings than the active system which would be impacted.

clauses.title: Written Notice Requesting Compliance, and Acknowledgment
Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Vocational Training Counselor Evaluations in Spousal Support Proceedings Information Sheet concerns {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, who were married on {{marriageDate}} and separated on {{separationDate}}, in connection with a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation filed or to be filed in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes a specific chapter of California's Family Code governing spousal support upon dissolution or legal separation (Family Code Chapter 3, Sections 4330 through 4339): the court's general authority to set a support amount and duration, the self-sufficiency advisement a court may give a supported party, the court's authority to order an examination by a vocational training counselor and that counselor's required qualifications, mandatory findings on the marital standard of living, retroactivity of a support order, termination of a contingent support order and the resulting refund obligation, termination of support on death or remarriage, and the order in which property is resorted to when enforcing a spousal support order. It is not itself a request for order, notice of motion, declaration, or court order, and completing it does not create, modify, terminate, or enforce any spousal support obligation between {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}. Only a court order, applying these statutes to the facts of an actual pending or completed proceeding, can do that.

clauses.title: Court's Authority to Order Spousal Support Based on the Marital Standard of Living
clauses.body: In a judgment of dissolution of marriage or legal separation, California's Family Code authorizes a court to order one party to pay the other party support in an amount, and for a period of time, that the court determines is just and reasonable. The statute directs that this determination be based on the standard of living established during the marriage, taking into consideration the circumstances set out in a separate chapter of the Family Code governing spousal support factors. This is the general, post-judgment order-making authority for spousal support; it operates once a judgment of dissolution or legal separation is entered, rather than while the case is only pending.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subsection (Family Code Section 4330(a)); no additional independent source was found for it. By its own terms, this subsection's grant of authority is tied to "a judgment of dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties" — it does not on its face extend to a judgment of nullity, unlike the temporary (pendente lite) support authority addressed elsewhere in this corpus, which by its own text does reach nullity proceedings. This clause does not restate or quote the multi-factor list in the chapter it cross-references ("Chapter 2, commencing with Section 4320"); that separate chapter's factors are addressed in this corpus's Marital Settlement Agreement document. The statute does not itself define "just and reasonable" or set any numeric cap on amount or duration.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4330(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's general authority to order post-judgment spousal support based on the marital standard of living
citations.quote: (a) In a judgment of dissolution of marriage or legal separation of the parties, the court may order a party to pay for the support of the other party an amount, for a period of time, that the court determines is just and reasonable, based on the standard of living established during the marriage, taking into consideration the circumstances as provided in Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 4320).

clauses.title: Court's Discretion to Advise a Supported Party of an Expectation of Self-Support
clauses.body: When making a spousal support order, California's Family Code permits, but does not require, a court to advise the party receiving support that the recipient should make reasonable efforts to assist in providing for their own support needs. The statute directs that any such advisement take into account the same particular circumstances the court considered under the spousal-support-factors chapter it cross-references. The statute separately allows a court to decide the advisement is inadvisable in the case of a marriage of long duration, a term the Family Code defines and addresses in a different, adjoining section of this same chapter.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory subsection (Family Code Section 4330(b)); no additional independent source was found for it. The statute uses the word "may" for the advisement itself and for a court's decision that the advisement is inadvisable in a long-duration marriage — both are discretionary, not mandatory, on the face of this text. This clause does not quote Family Code Section 4336, which the subsection cross-references for the definition and consequences of a "marriage of long duration"; that section already has a verified, quoted clause elsewhere in this corpus. The statutory text itself does not use the term "Gavron warning" — that is a term of judicial usage from case law, and no case law was independently fetched or verified for this document (see the Deliverables report for the CourtListener rate-limit that prevented case-law research in this session). The statute does not specify any required form, wording, or timing for the advisement.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4330(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's discretionary authority to advise a supported party of an expectation of self-sufficiency
citations.quote: (b) When making an order for spousal support, the court may advise the recipient of support that the recipient should make reasonable efforts to assist in providing for their support needs, taking into account the particular circumstances considered by the court pursuant to Section 4320, unless, in the case of a marriage of long duration as provided for in Section 4336, the court decides this warning is inadvisable.

clauses.title: Court's Authority to Order a Vocational Training Counselor Examination
clauses.body: In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation, California's Family Code authorizes a court to order a party to submit to an examination by a vocational training counselor. The examination must include an assessment of that party's ability to obtain employment, based on the party's age, health, education, marketable skills, employment history, and the current availability of employment opportunities, with the examination's focus on whether the party could obtain employment that would allow the party to maintain the marital standard of living. The statute limits when such an order may be made: only on motion, for good cause, and on notice to the party to be examined and to all parties, with the order itself required to specify the time, place, manner, conditions, and scope of the examination and who is to conduct it. A party who does not comply with such an order is subject to the same consequences that apply to noncompliance with an examination ordered under a specified chapter of the Code of Civil Procedure.
clauses.gap: Family Code Section 4331(a), (b), and (c) are combined into a single quotation below because they are directly contiguous in the fetched statutory text, not because they are independent sources stitched together — no ellipsis or omitted text separates them. This clause does not independently fetch or verify the cross-referenced Code of Civil Procedure provision, Chapter 15 (commencing with Section 2032.010) of Title 4 of Part 4, which defines the actual consequences for noncompliance; it states only that Section 4331(c) points to that chapter. The statute does not itself say who bears the cost of the examination — that is addressed by a separate subsection, Section 4331(f), covered in a different clause in this document, and the two are not combined here because a quote spanning (c) through (f) would also have to reproduce (d) and (e), the counselor-qualification provisions.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4331(a)-(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's authority to order a vocational training counselor examination, the procedural prerequisites for the order, and the consequence of noncompliance
citations.quote: (a) In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, the court may order a party to submit to an examination by a vocational training counselor. The examination shall include an assessment of the party’s ability to obtain employment based upon the party’s age, health, education, marketable skills, employment history, and the current availability of employment opportunities. The focus of the examination shall be on an assessment of the party’s ability to obtain employment that would allow the party to maintain their marital standard of living.(b) The order may be made only on motion, for good cause, and on notice to the party to be examined and to all parties. The order shall specify the time, place, manner, conditions, scope of the examination, and the person or persons by whom it is to be made.(c) A party who does not comply with an order under this section is subject to the same consequences provided for failure to comply with an examination ordered pursuant to Chapter 15 (commencing with Section 2032.010) of Title 4 of Part 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

clauses.title: Required Qualifications of a Vocational Training Counselor and Allocation of Cost
clauses.body: California's Family Code defines a "vocational training counselor," for purposes of an examination ordered in a dissolution or legal separation proceeding, as an individual with sufficient knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education in interviewing, administering and interpreting marketable-skills tests, formulating career goals, planning courses of training and study, and assessing the job market, so as to qualify as an expert in vocational training under a specified section of the Evidence Code. The statute lists minimum qualifications such a counselor must have: a master's degree in the behavioral sciences or another postgraduate degree the court finds sufficient; qualification to administer and interpret career-potential inventories; demonstrated ability in interviewing clients and assessing marketable skills, with an understanding of age, health, education, experience, and mobility constraints; knowledge of current employment conditions, job markets, and wages in the relevant geographic area; and knowledge of local education and training programs, with their costs and time plans. Separately, the statute authorizes a court to order the supporting spouse to pay the necessary expenses and costs of counseling, retraining, or education, in addition to spousal support.
clauses.gap: Family Code Section 4331(d), (e), and (f) are combined into a single quotation below because they are directly contiguous in the fetched statutory text; this is one statutory section, not three independent sources. This clause does not independently fetch or verify Evidence Code Section 720, which subsection (d) cross-references for the general expert-witness-qualification standard. The statute does not itself define how much postgraduate training a court must find "sufficient" under subsection (e)(1) for a non-master's-degree counselor to qualify — that determination is left to the court. The cost-allocation authority in subsection (f) is worded as "may order," so it is discretionary rather than mandatory, and it applies only to "the supporting spouse" paying costs — the statute's text examined here does not describe any mechanism for a supported spouse to be ordered to pay these costs.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4331(d)-(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the definition and minimum qualifications of a vocational training counselor, and the court's authority to allocate the cost of counseling, retraining, or education
citations.quote: (d) “Vocational training counselor” for the purpose of this section means an individual with sufficient knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education in interviewing, administering, and interpreting tests for analysis of marketable skills, formulating career goals, planning courses of training and study, and assessing the job market, to qualify as an expert in vocational training under Section 720 of the Evidence Code.(e) A vocational training counselor shall have at least the following qualifications:(1) A master’s degree in the behavioral sciences, or other postgraduate degree that the court finds provides sufficient training to perform a vocational evaluation.(2) Qualification to administer and interpret inventories for assessing career potential.(3) Demonstrated ability in interviewing clients and assessing marketable skills with an understanding of age constraints, physical and mental health, previous education and experience, and time and geographic mobility constraints.(4) Knowledge of current employment conditions, job market, and wages in the indicated geographic area.(5) Knowledge of education and training programs in the area with costs and time plans for these programs.(f) The court may order the supporting spouse to pay, in addition to spousal support, the necessary expenses and costs of the counseling, retraining, or education.

clauses.title: Mandatory Factual Findings on the Marital Standard of Living
clauses.body: In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation, California's Family Code requires the court to make specific factual findings on the standard of living established during the marriage. The statute separately requires the court, at the request of either party, to make appropriate factual determinations with respect to other circumstances. The standard-of-living finding this statute requires is what the general spousal-support order-making authority elsewhere in this same chapter directs the court to base its support amount and duration on.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (Family Code Section 4332); no additional independent source was found for it. The statute does not specify a required format, level of detail, or timing for these "specific factual findings," and it does not itself define what "other circumstances" a party may request findings on beyond the standard-of-living finding — it states only that the court "shall make appropriate factual determinations" on request.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4332 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mandatory factual findings on the marital standard of living
citations.quote: In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties, the court shall make specific factual findings with respect to the standard of living during the marriage, and, at the request of either party, the court shall make appropriate factual determinations with respect to other circumstances.

clauses.title: Retroactivity of a Spousal Support Order
clauses.body: California's Family Code permits a spousal support order made in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or legal separation to be made retroactive. The retroactivity the statute describes runs to the date of filing the notice of motion or order to show cause that requested the support order, or to any subsequent date the court chooses.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (Family Code Section 4333); no additional independent source was found for it. On its face, the statute permits retroactivity only back to the filing date of the request for the order (or a later date) — it does not authorize retroactivity to a date before that filing, such as the date of separation or the date of marriage. The statute's use of "may be made retroactive" is permissive, not mandatory, and it does not list any factors a court must weigh in deciding whether, or to what date, to make an order retroactive.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4333 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's authority to make a spousal support order retroactive to the filing of the request or a later date
citations.quote: An order for spousal support in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage or for legal separation of the parties may be made retroactive to the date of filing the notice of motion or order to show cause, or to any subsequent date.

clauses.title: Termination of Contingent Spousal Support and the Resulting Refund Obligation
clauses.body: Where a court orders spousal support for a contingent period of time, California's Family Code provides that the supporting party's obligation terminates when the contingency happens, and the court may order the supported party to notify the supporting party, or that party's attorney of record, when the contingency occurs. If the supported party fails to give that notice and continues to accept spousal support payments, the statute requires the supported party to refund the payments that accrued after the contingency happened, with any overpayment applied first to spousal support payments then in default.
clauses.gap: Family Code Section 4334(a) and (b) are combined into a single quotation below because they are directly contiguous in the fetched statutory text; this is one statutory section, not two independent sources. This statute governs only a support order for "a contingent period of time" — it is distinct from, and this document does not address, either the non-extension rule for a support order with a fixed, non-contingent end date under a separate section of this same chapter (Section 4335), or the automatic termination of support on death or remarriage addressed in a different clause in this document (Section 4337). The statute does not itself define what qualifies as a "contingency" for this purpose, and the notification requirement ("the court may, in the order, order the supported party to notify") is discretionary, contingent on the court including it in the order, rather than an automatic statutory duty.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4334(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: termination of a contingent spousal support order and the refund obligation for payments accepted after the contingency occurred
citations.quote: (a) If a court orders spousal support for a contingent period of time, the obligation of the supporting party terminates on the happening of the contingency. The court may, in the order, order the supported party to notify the supporting party, or the supporting party’s attorney of record, of the happening of the contingency.(b) If the supported party fails to notify the supporting party, or the attorney of record of the supporting party, of the happening of the contingency and continues to accept spousal support payments, the supported party shall refund payments received that accrued after the happening of the contingency, except that the overpayments shall first be applied to spousal support payments that are then in default.

clauses.title: Automatic Termination of Spousal Support on Death or Remarriage
clauses.body: California's Family Code provides that a party's obligation under a spousal support order terminates automatically upon the death of either party, or upon the remarriage of the party receiving support. This default rule applies except to the extent the parties have agreed otherwise in writing.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section (Family Code Section 4337); no additional independent source was found for it. The statute is a default rule only: it expressly yields to a written agreement of the parties providing otherwise, so it does not, by itself, determine the outcome in every case. This document does not address the separate question of a written agreement's own requirements or effect, which is addressed elsewhere in this corpus's Marital Settlement Agreement and Premarital Agreement documents. The statute uses "remarriage" without further definition, and does not address the effect of a registered domestic partnership on the termination rule.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4337 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the automatic termination of a spousal support obligation on death or remarriage, absent a contrary written agreement
citations.quote: Except as otherwise agreed by the parties in writing, the obligation of a party under an order for the support of the other party terminates upon the death of either party or the remarriage of the other party.

clauses.title: Order in Which Property Is Resorted to When Enforcing a Spousal Support Order
clauses.body: When enforcing an order for spousal support, California's Family Code directs the court to resort to specified categories of property in a set order. First is the earnings, income, or accumulations of either spouse after the date of separation that would have been community property had the spouses not separated. Next is the community property, then the quasi-community property, and finally the other separate property of the party required to make the support payments.
clauses.gap: Family Code Section 4338's introductory clause and subsections (a) through (d) are combined into a single quotation below because they are directly contiguous in the fetched statutory text; this is one statutory section. This clause does not independently fetch or quote Family Code Section 70, which subsection (a) cross-references for the definition of "date of separation" — that definition is addressed elsewhere in this corpus (the Postnuptial Agreement document). This statute governs only the order of resort to property in enforcing an already-existing spousal support order; it does not by its own text govern the initial characterization or division of community, quasi-community, or separate property in the underlying dissolution or legal separation.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 4338 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the required order of resort to a party's property when enforcing a spousal support order
citations.quote: In the enforcement of an order for spousal support, the court shall resort to the property described below in the order indicated:(a) The earnings, income, or accumulations of either spouse after the date of separation, as defined in Section 70, which would have been community property if the spouse had not been separated from the other spouse.(b) The community property.(c) The quasi-community property.(d) The other separate property of the party required to make the support payments.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment — Not a Court Filing
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{party1Name}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for background use alongside an actual request for order, notice of motion, or other pleading concerning spousal support, filed with the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that filing, and it does not create, modify, terminate, or enforce any spousal support obligation between {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}; only a court order, applying Family Code Sections 4330 through 4339 and the related sections they cross-reference to the facts of an actual proceeding, does that.]

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Exempt Employee's Pay in the Final (and First) Week of Employment — Information Sheet is prepared in connection with the employment relationship between {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}}, whose last day of work is stated here as {{terminationDate}}. {{employeeName}}'s stated weekly salary before termination is {{salary}}, and the number of days actually worked during that final week is stated here as {{finalWeekDaysWorked}}. It describes what the federal salary-basis regulation at 29 C.F.R. § 541.602 says about paying a salaried, overtime-exempt employee for a week of employment that starts or ends mid-week, the general full-week rule that provision is an exception to, how the California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual and a specific California statute (Labor Code § 515.7) each treat that federal test, and what the applicable Industrial Welfare Commission Wage Order separately does and does not adopt by reference. This information sheet does not itself determine whether {{employeeName}} was properly classified as an exempt employee, whether {{companyName}}'s payment for the week including {{terminationDate}} satisfied the salary-basis requirement, or what amount, if any, is owed for that week.

clauses.title: General Rule: Full Salary for Any Week in Which Any Work Is Performed
clauses.body: Under the federal regulation that defines what it means for an employee to be paid on a "salary basis" for purposes of the federal executive, administrative, and professional overtime exemptions, an employee is paid on a salary basis if the employee regularly receives, each pay period on a weekly or less frequent basis, a predetermined amount that is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of the work performed. Subject to specific exceptions, an exempt employee must receive the full salary for any week in which the employee performs any work, without regard to the number of days or hours worked, and an employer is not required to pay an exempt employee for a workweek in which the employee performs no work at all.
clauses.gap: This is the general, full-week rule only; by its own terms it does not address what may happen in a week where the employment relationship itself begins or ends partway through — that specific situation is addressed by a separate exception described in this document's companion clauses. This clause quotes two subdivisions of a single federal regulation, 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a) and § 541.602(a)(1); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the eCFR page (fetched with two distinct User-Agent strings), and the two fetches differed only in a per-request CSP nonce value embedded in the page's script tags, not in the regulatory text itself.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, general salary-basis definition
citations.quote: An employee will be considered to be paid on a “salary basis” within the meaning of this part if the employee regularly receives each pay period on a weekly, or less frequent basis, a predetermined amount constituting all or part of the employee's compensation, which amount is not subject to reduction because of variations in the quality or quantity of the work performed.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a)(1) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, full-salary-for-any-week-worked rule
citations.quote: Subject to the exceptions provided in paragraph (b) of this section, an exempt employee must receive the full salary for any week in which the employee performs any work without regard to the number of days or hours worked. Exempt employees need not be paid for any workweek in which they perform no work.

clauses.title: Exception for the Initial or Terminal Week of Employment
clauses.body: The salary-basis regulation carves out a specific exception to the full-week rule described above, applicable to the start or the end of an employment relationship. The regulation lists deductions that do not violate the salary-basis requirement, and one of those permitted deductions addresses this exact situation: an employer is not required to pay the full salary in the initial or terminal week of employment, and may instead pay a proportionate part of the employee's full salary for the time actually worked in the first and last week of employment, without losing the exemption for that week.
clauses.gap: The regulation's own text does not define "week" for this purpose as necessarily aligned with a calendar week that includes the actual last calendar day worked — it speaks in terms of the "initial or terminal week of employment," which is ordinarily the employer's established workweek that happens to contain the first or last day of the employment relationship. This clause quotes one sentence group of 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(6); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the eCFR page (fetched with two distinct User-Agent strings), and the two fetches differed only in a per-request CSP nonce value, not in the regulatory text itself.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, introductory clause to the list of salary-basis exceptions
citations.quote: The prohibition against deductions from pay in the salary basis requirement is subject to the following exceptions:

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(6) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, initial-or-terminal-week proration rule
citations.quote: An employer is not required to pay the full salary in the initial or terminal week of employment. Rather, an employer may pay a proportionate part of an employee's full salary for the time actually worked in the first and last week of employment. In such weeks, the payment of an hourly or daily equivalent of the employee's full salary for the time actually worked will meet the requirement.

clauses.title: Limit: Not for an Employee Who Works Only Occasional, Isolated Days
clauses.body: That exception is narrow, and the same regulation immediately qualifies it. An individual is not paid on a salary basis if the person is employed only occasionally for a few days at a time and the employer pays a proportionate part of the weekly salary whenever so employed — that pattern describes casual or occasional employment rather than salaried employment, regardless of what portion of the weekly salary is paid. The initial-or-terminal-week exception applies only at the two edges of a single, ongoing employment relationship — its first week and its last week — not to some other week in which work happens to be performed on fewer than the usual number of days.
clauses.gap: The regulation's own text does not supply a bright-line test for how many consecutive weeks of full salary must occur before a relationship stops being "occasional employment for a few days" and becomes a genuine ongoing salaried relationship with a single terminal week; that line-drawing is left to the facts of a particular employment relationship. This clause quotes the sentence of 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(6) that continues directly after the sentences quoted in this document's companion clause; the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the eCFR page (fetched with two distinct User-Agent strings), and the two fetches differed only in a per-request CSP nonce value, not in the regulatory text itself.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(6) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, occasional-employment limitation
citations.quote: However, employees are not paid on a salary basis within the meaning of these regulations if they are employed occasionally for a few days, and the employer pays them a proportionate part of the weekly salary when so employed.

clauses.title: How the Proportionate Amount May Be Calculated
clauses.body: The same regulation addresses how a permitted deduction under its list of exceptions — including the initial-or-terminal-week proration described above — may be calculated. An employer may use the hourly or daily equivalent of the employee's full weekly salary, or any other amount proportional to the time actually missed by the employee.
clauses.gap: This calculation-method provision applies to permitted salary-basis deductions generally, not solely to the initial-or-terminal-week exception; a second sentence of the same subdivision separately addresses the amount of a deduction imposed as a penalty for a major safety-rule violation under a different exception, 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(4), which is unrelated to the timing of a termination and is not addressed by this document. The regulation does not itself mandate the hourly method over the daily method, or specify how the number of scheduled workdays in a partial week is identified when an employee's schedule varies week to week. This clause quotes 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(c); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the eCFR page (fetched with two distinct User-Agent strings), and the two fetches differed only in a per-request CSP nonce value, not in the regulatory text itself.

citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(c) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text)
citations.cite: Code of Federal Regulations, method for calculating a permitted deduction
citations.quote: When calculating the amount of a deduction from pay allowed under paragraph (b) of this section, the employer may use the hourly or daily equivalent of the employee's full weekly salary or any other amount proportional to the time actually missed by the employee.

clauses.title: What the California Wage Order's Incorporation by Reference Does Not Cover
clauses.body: California's own overtime-exemption test for executive employees comes from Industrial Welfare Commission Wage Order No. 4-2001, not directly from the federal salary-basis regulation quoted elsewhere in this document. For the duties portion of the executive exemption, the wage order incorporates specific federal regulations by section number, as they existed on the date the wage order was issued. That incorporated list addresses only the duties test for the executive exemption — it does not include 29 C.F.R. § 541.602, the salary-basis regulation.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the executive-exemption duties-test incorporation clause of Wage Order No. 4-2001; the same wage order's administrative- and professional-exemption provisions separately incorporate their own, similarly limited lists of federal duties-test section numbers that this document's own review of the wage order's text likewise found do not include § 541.602, but this clause does not separately quote those parallel provisions. The wage order's silence on § 541.602 does not, by itself, mean the salary-basis rule described in this document's other clauses fails to apply in California — only that the wage order's own incorporation-by-reference clause is not its source; this document's other clauses look instead to DLSE Enforcement Manual guidance and a direct statutory cross-reference for that. This clause quotes a single subdivision of Wage Order No. 4-2001; the source PDF was independently refetched with a second, distinct User-Agent string and confirmed byte-for-byte identical (matching MD5 checksum) to the first fetch.

citations.case: Cal. Code Regs. tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 1(A)(1)(e) (Industrial Welfare Commission Wage Order No. 4-2001, official PDF text)
citations.cite: California Industrial Welfare Commission Wage Order No. 4-2001, Section 1(A)(1)(e), executive exemption
citations.quote: shall be construed in the same manner as such items are construed in the following regulations under the Fair Labor Standards Act effective as of the date of this order: 29 C.F.R. Sections 541.102, 541.104-111, and 541.115-116.

clauses.title: DLSE's Stated Policy of Following the Federal Salary-Basis Guidelines
clauses.body: The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement's own Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual states its general approach to the salary-basis test. Citing the California Supreme Court's instruction to compare the state and federal statutory schemes before giving weight to federal authority, the manual states that DLSE has concluded that the IWC intended enforcement of the salary requirement to follow the federal guidelines so far as possible, while certain federal guidelines may not be utilized in California because they conflict with California statutory law, case law, or public policy.
clauses.gap: This is DLSE's own enforcement-guidance manual, not a statute or regulation, and a court is not bound to follow it. The quoted passage states DLSE's general orientation toward the federal salary-basis guidelines as a category; it does not, by itself, specifically confirm or reject the initial-or-terminal-week proration rule addressed in this document's other clauses. This document's own attempt to locate California case law specifically addressing 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(b)(6)'s initial-or-terminal-week rule was blocked by CourtListener's free-tier daily search quota (HTTP 429, "Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") at the time of research, so no case law is cited anywhere in this document — only statutory, regulatory, and DLSE-manual sources are cited. This clause quotes a single passage of the manual; the source PDF was independently refetched with a second, distinct User-Agent string and confirmed byte-for-byte identical (matching MD5 checksum) to the first fetch.

citations.case: DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual § 51.6.4 (rev. Dec. 2022)
citations.cite: California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual
citations.quote: In making this determination for purposes of the salary basis test, DLSE has concluded that, to the extent possible, the IWC intended that the enforcement of the “salary” requirement was to follow the federal guidelines so far as possible; but that certain of the federal guidelines may not be utilized in California because they conflict with California statutory law, case law, or public policy.

clauses.title: DLSE's Manual Reproduces the Same Initial-and-Terminal-Week Rule
clauses.body: The same DLSE manual includes an appendix compiling the text of the federal salary-basis regulations that were in effect on July 1, 2000, under the section numbering the regulation used before a 2004 renumbering (former 29 C.F.R. § 541.118, now § 541.602). That reproduced text includes a subsection on initial and terminal weeks, stating that failure to pay the full salary in the initial or terminal week of employment is not considered inconsistent with the salary basis of payment, and that in such weeks, payment of a proportionate part of the employee's salary for the time actually worked will meet the requirement.
clauses.gap: This passage is a DLSE-compiled reproduction of the pre-2004 numbering of the federal salary-basis regulation (former § 541.118(c)), not an independent DLSE ruling. The manual's own introduction to this appendix states that only some of the reproduced federal text was adopted by the IWC for enforcement purposes, with inapplicable portions marked in strikeout and portions used for enforcement without further DLSE direction marked in italics; this document's PDF text-extraction process (character- and vector-level inspection of the underlying page) found no strikethrough line or italic font applied to this specific passage, but could not conclusively determine which of the manual's own marked categories, if any, the passage falls into. This clause therefore treats the quoted text only as confirmation that DLSE's own manual contains and reproduces a rule identical to the current federal one — not as an independent DLSE determination that the rule is binding on California employers beyond the current federal regulation quoted in this document's other clauses. This clause quotes one paragraph from the manual's appendix; the source PDF was independently refetched with a second, distinct User-Agent string and confirmed byte-for-byte identical (matching MD5 checksum) to the first fetch.

citations.case: DLSE Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, Federal Regulations Appendix, reproducing former 29 C.F.R. § 541.118(c) (text current through June 20, 2000; 65 Fed. Reg. 38332)
citations.cite: California Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, Enforcement Policies and Interpretations Manual, Appendix compiling federal regulations in effect July 1, 2000
citations.quote: Failure to pay the full salary in the initial or terminal week of employment is not considered inconsistent with the salary basis of payment. In such weeks the payment of a proportionate part of the employee's salary for the time actually worked will meet the requirement.

clauses.title: One Direct California Statutory Cross-Reference: Adjunct Faculty
clauses.body: At least one California statute expressly imports the federal salary-basis test by its current section number. Labor Code section 515.7, which extends the professional exemption to certain part-time faculty at independent institutions of higher education, requires — among other conditions — that the employee is paid on a salary basis as defined by 29 C.F.R. § 541.602, in addition to meeting one of the statute's own minimum compensation amounts.
clauses.gap: Labor Code section 515.7 is narrow: by its own terms it applies only to an employee employed to provide instruction for a course or laboratory at an independent institution of higher education, not to exempt employees generally. This clause cites it only as a concrete example of a California statute directly incorporating 29 C.F.R. § 541.602 by its current section number — it is not a general California codification of the initial-or-terminal-week proration rule for the executive, administrative, and professional exemptions addressed in this document's other clauses, and this document's own review found no equivalent direct cross-reference to § 541.602 in Labor Code § 515 or in Wage Order No. 4-2001's own text. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (Lab. Code § 515.7(a)(2)); the text was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies of the official California Legislative Information page — the only differences between the two fetches were dynamic per-request JSF ViewState tokens and a timestamp-seeded debug function, not the statutory text — before being treated as verified.
