citations.cite: California Labor Code
citations.quote: (2) The employee is paid on a salary basis, as defined by Section 541.602 of Title 29 of the Code of Federal Regulations, and receives one of the following minimum compensations:

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Purpose of This Probate Referee and Inventory-and-Appraisal Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet states general facts about the statutory inventory-and-appraisal procedure set out in Probate Code Part 3 (commencing with § 8800) and the probate-referee appointment provisions in Probate Code Part 12 (commencing with § 400), as those provisions apply to the pending administration of {{decedentName}}'s estate before {{courtName}} in {{countyOfFiling}}, case number {{courtCaseNumber}}, in which {{personalRepresentativeName}} has been appointed personal representative. It describes the deadline for filing an inventory and appraisal, how a probate referee is appointed, which items the personal representative appraises directly and which items go to the referee, the duty to supplement the inventory for later-discovered property, and how the referee is compensated. It does not itself file any inventory and appraisal, does not select or appoint any probate referee, and does not advise {{personalRepresentativeName}} what to do about any specific item of estate property.

clauses.title: Duty to File an Inventory and Appraisal, and the Four-Month Deadline
clauses.body: Probate Code § 8800(a) requires a personal representative to file with the court clerk an inventory of the property to be administered in {{decedentName}}'s estate, together with an appraisal of that property, combined in a single document. Under § 8800(b), the inventory and appraisal must be filed within four months after letters are first issued to a general personal representative, though the court may allow further time as is reasonable under the circumstances of the particular case. Section 8800(c) permits the personal representative to file partial inventories and appraisals where appropriate, so long as all of them are filed before the four-month period (or any court-allowed extension) expires.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only §8800(a)-(c). It does not address §8800(d), a separate requirement (added by a 1992 amendment) that the personal representative concurrently file a certification regarding whether a change-in-ownership statement under Revenue and Taxation Code § 480 has been filed with the county recorder or assessor for any California real property the decedent owned at death — that certification requirement is not independently verified or explained here. Nor does this clause address what counts as letters being 'first issued to a general personal representative' in cases involving a prior special administrator, or how the deadline interacts with an extension the court has already granted in a particular county.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8800(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8800(a)
citations.quote: The personal representative shall file with the court clerk an inventory of property to be administered in the decedent’s estate together with an appraisal of property in the inventory. An inventory and appraisal shall be combined in a single document.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8800(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8800(b)
citations.quote: The inventory and appraisal shall be filed within four months after letters are first issued to a general personal representative. The court may allow such further time for filing an inventory and appraisal as is reasonable under the circumstances of the particular case.

clauses.title: How Probate Referees Are Appointed for the County
clauses.body: Probate Code § 400(a) requires the State Controller to appoint at least one person in each county to act as probate referee for that county. Section 400(b) addresses counties where too few qualified people are available: if there are fewer than three qualified applicants to serve in a county, the Controller may designate a probate referee from another county, or make an interim appointment, to serve until the vacancy is filled by a qualified applicant.
clauses.gap: This clause does not state how many probate referees the Controller has currently appointed for any particular county, nor whether a given county presently has fewer than three qualified applicants triggering the out-of-county-designation or interim-appointment provision in § 400(b) — that is a factual, county-specific condition this document does not independently verify. It also does not address how the personal representative selects among the referees a county does have, which is governed by a separate section not quoted in this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 400(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 400(a)
citations.quote: The Controller shall appoint at least one person in each county to act as a probate referee for the county.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 400(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 400(b)
citations.quote: If there are fewer than three qualified applicants to serve in a county, the Controller may designate a probate referee from another county or make an interim appointment, to serve until the vacancy has been filled by a qualified applicant.

clauses.title: Qualification Requirements for Appointment as a Probate Referee
clauses.body: Probate Code § 401(a) provides that appointment as a probate referee is made from among persons who have passed a qualification examination, and that a person who passes the examination remains eligible for appointment for five years from the date of the examination. Section 401(b) separately requires that appointment be made on the basis of merit, without regard to sex, race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, marital status, or political affiliation.
clauses.gap: Section 401 does not itself state how often the qualification examination is offered, who administers it, or what subject matter it covers — this clause does not independently research or verify those examination details. Nor does it address what happens if a person's five-year eligibility window under § 401(a) expires without appointment.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 401(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 401(a)
citations.quote: Appointment shall be from among persons passing a qualification examination. A person who passes the examination is eligible for appointment for a period of five years from the date of the examination.

clauses.title: Required Form and Contents of the Inventory and Appraisal
clauses.body: Probate Code § 8802 requires that the inventory and appraisal separately list each item of {{decedentName}}'s estate property and state the fair market value of that item, as of the date of {{decedentName}}'s death, in monetary terms opposite the item. Section 8850(a) requires that the inventory — including any partial or supplemental inventories — include all property to be administered in {{decedentName}}'s estate. Separately, § 8850(c) requires the inventory to show, to the extent {{personalRepresentativeName}} can ascertain it, which portions of the property are community, quasi-community, and separate property of {{decedentName}}.
clauses.gap: This clause does not quote § 8850(b), which separately lists specific categories of property the inventory must particularly specify (money owed to the decedent, a decedent's partnership interest, and money and cash items as defined in § 8901) — it only notes that such a subdivision exists. It also does not address the Judicial Council's prescribed inventory-and-appraisal form (referenced in other Probate Code provisions this clause does not cite), which sets out the mechanical layout these statutory content requirements are filled into.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8802 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8802
citations.quote: The inventory and appraisal shall separately list each item and shall state the fair market value of the item at the time of the decedent’s death in monetary terms opposite the item.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8850(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8850(a)
citations.quote: The inventory, including partial and supplemental inventories, shall include all property to be administered in the decedent’s estate.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8850(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8850(c)
citations.quote: The inventory shall show, to the extent ascertainable by the personal representative, the portions of the property that are community, quasi-community, and separate property of the decedent.

clauses.title: Property the Personal Representative Appraises Directly
clauses.body: Probate Code § 8901 lists categories of property that the personal representative — rather than the probate referee — appraises, excluding any item whose fair market value is, in {{personalRepresentativeName}}'s opinion, different from its face value. The listed categories include money and other cash items (defined as a check, draft, money order, or similar instrument issued on or before {{decedentName}}'s date of death that can be immediately converted to cash), certain checks issued after death, financial-institution accounts, cash deposits and money market mutual funds, and, separately, proceeds of life and accident insurance policies and of retirement plans and annuities payable on death in lump sum amounts.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the introductory clause together with subdivision (a) (cash items) and subdivision (e) (life insurance and retirement proceeds); it does not separately quote subdivisions (b), (c), or (d), which cover post-death checks, financial-institution accounts, and cash deposits or money market mutual funds, though the body text above summarizes them. The exclusion for items whose value the personal representative believes differs from face value is a judgment call the statute leaves to the personal representative's own opinion, and § 8901 does not itself define how that opinion is to be formed or documented.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8901 intro & (a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8901(a)
citations.quote: The personal representative shall appraise the following property, excluding items whose fair market value is, in the opinion of the personal representative, an amount different from the face value of the property: (a) Money and other cash items. As used in this subdivision, a “cash item” is a check, draft, money order, or similar instrument issued on or before the date of the decedent’s death that can be immediately converted to cash.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8901(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8901(e)
citations.quote: Proceeds of life and accident insurance policies and retirement plans and annuities payable on death in lump sum amounts.

clauses.title: Delivery of the Inventory to the Referee, and the Referee's Appraisal of Remaining Property
clauses.body: Probate Code § 8902 requires the personal representative to deliver the inventory to the probate referee designated by the court, together with the supporting data the referee needs to appraise the property assigned to the referee, and requires the referee to appraise all property other than the property the personal representative appraises directly under § 8901. Section 8901(d) itself points forward to this division of labor: all mutual funds, stocks, bonds, and other securities other than cash deposits and money market mutual funds are, by that subdivision's own terms, to be appraised under §§ 8902 through 8909.
clauses.gap: Section 8902 begins with the qualifying phrase 'Except as otherwise provided by statute,' signaling that other Probate Code provisions — including a provision (not fetched or independently verified in this session) allowing an independent expert to appraise certain property under § 8904, which § 8961(a) elsewhere cross-references — can shift particular property outside this default personal-representative/referee split. This clause does not verify the text or scope of § 8904.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8902 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8902
citations.quote: Except as otherwise provided by statute: (a) The personal representative shall deliver the inventory to the probate referee designated by the court, together with necessary supporting data to enable the probate referee to make an appraisal of the property in the inventory to be appraised by the probate referee. (b) The probate referee shall appraise all property other than that appraised by the personal representative.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8901(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8901(d)
citations.quote: All other mutual funds, stocks, bonds, and other securities shall be appraised pursuant to Sections 8902 to 8909, inclusive.

clauses.title: Duty to File a Supplemental Inventory and Appraisal for Later-Discovered Property
clauses.body: Probate Code § 8801 provides that if the personal representative acquires knowledge of estate property that was not included in a prior inventory and appraisal, the personal representative must file a supplemental inventory and appraisal of that property, prepared in the manner prescribed for an original inventory and appraisal. That supplemental filing is due within four months after the personal representative acquires knowledge of the property, though the court may allow further time as is reasonable under the circumstances of the particular case.
clauses.gap: Section 8801 does not itself define what it means to 'acquire knowledge' of previously undisclosed property, or specify any particular standard a court applies in deciding whether an extension request is 'reasonable under the circumstances of the particular case' — the same reasonableness language used, and left equally undefined, in § 8800(b)'s original-filing deadline. This clause does not address how a supplemental filing interacts with an estate that has already closed.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8801 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8801
citations.quote: If the personal representative acquires knowledge of property to be administered in the decedent’s estate that is not included in a prior inventory and appraisal, the personal representative shall file a supplemental inventory and appraisal of the property in the manner prescribed for an original inventory and appraisal. The supplemental inventory and appraisal shall be filed within four months after the personal representative acquires knowledge of the property. The court may allow such further time for filing a supplemental inventory and appraisal as is reasonable under the circumstances of the particular case.

clauses.title: How the Probate Referee Is Compensated
clauses.body: Probate Code § 8960(a) provides that the commission and expenses payable to a probate referee are paid from {{decedentName}}'s estate. Under § 8960(b), the referee may not withhold the appraisal pending payment of the commission and expenses, and must instead deliver the appraisal to the personal representative promptly upon completion. Section 8960(c) classifies the referee's commission and expenses as an expense of administration, entitled to the payment priority set out in § 11420, paid in the course of administration. As for the amount, § 8961(a) sets the commission at one-tenth of one percent of the total value of the property for each estate appraised, computed excluding property the personal representative appraised under § 8901 or an independent expert appraised under § 8904.
clauses.gap: Section 8961(a) states its one-tenth-of-one-percent commission is itself 'subject to Section 8963' — a separate section, not fetched or independently verified in this session, that (based on the cross-reference alone) appears to set some further limit on the commission; this clause does not state what that limit is. This clause also does not quote § 8961(b), which separately requires the referee to file a verified account of expenses with the inventory and appraisal, beyond noting that such a requirement exists.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8960(a)-(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) The commission and expenses provided by this article as compensation for the services of the probate referee shall be paid from the estate. (b) The probate referee may not withhold the appraisal until the commission and expenses are paid, but shall deliver the appraisal to the personal representative promptly upon completion.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8960(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8960(c)
citations.quote: The commission and expenses of the probate referee are an expense of administration, entitled to the priority for payment provided by Section 11420, and shall be paid in the course of administration.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 8961(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Prob. C. § 8961(a)
citations.quote: A commission of one-tenth of one percent of the total value of the property for each estate appraised, subject to Section 8963. The commission shall be computed excluding property appraised by the personal representative pursuant to Section 8901 or by an independent expert pursuant to Section 8904.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
clauses.body: This information sheet was reviewed on {{dateSigned}}, in {{cityState}}. It states general facts about California's statutory inventory-and-appraisal procedure and probate-referee appointment provisions in the administration of {{decedentName}}'s estate before {{courtName}} in {{countyOfFiling}}, case number {{courtCaseNumber}}. It is not legal advice about any specific item of estate property, does not itself file any inventory and appraisal or select any probate referee, and does not extend, shorten, or waive any deadline this procedure imposes.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the federal Commercial Driver's License Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse — a database maintained by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) under 49 CFR Part 382, Subpart G — and the pre-employment and annual query duties that Subpart G places on an employer of a commercial motor vehicle driver, in connection with {{companyName}}'s employment or prospective employment of {{employeeName}} in the position of {{jobTitle}}. This is a federal regulatory framework, not a California statute; it applies regardless of state to an employer and driver within its coverage. It is separate from, and does not replace, this corpus's other driver-related documents — the DMV Employer Pull Notice Program (a California driving-record system) and the Transportation Network Company Driver Background Check Requirements (California's rideshare-specific screening statute) — because the Clearinghouse addresses a different subject: a driver's own record of verified drug and alcohol testing violations under the federal testing rules, not a driving record or a rideshare-specific criminal background check. This sheet does not itself query the Clearinghouse, does not determine whether {{employeeName}}'s position in fact requires a commercial driver's license or otherwise falls within Part 382's coverage, and does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} what to do about any particular query result.

clauses.title: Who Part 382 Covers
clauses.body: The Clearinghouse query duties described in this document arise under 49 CFR Part 382, and Part 382 states its own coverage in terms of a driver's licensing requirement rather than a job title: it applies to every person, and to all employers of such persons, who operate a commercial motor vehicle in commerce in any state and are subject to the commercial driver's license requirements of 49 CFR Part 383 (or the equivalent Mexican or Canadian commercial-license requirements). Part 382 also states its own exceptions — among them, employers and drivers who are subject only to a different DOT agency's testing rules (49 CFR Part 655, for certain transit operations), specified military and covered-farm-vehicle drivers a state must or may exempt from the Part 383 licensing requirement, and firefighters operating emergency vehicles under the conditions the regulation states.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 49 CFR § 382.103(a) (the general coverage rule) and paraphrases, without independently quoting, the exceptions listed in § 382.103(d) — the exact conditions attached to the military, farm-vehicle, covered-farm-vehicle, and firefighter exceptions are more detailed than this paraphrase states, and this clause does not restate them in full. It does not determine whether a specific position requires a commercial driver's license, involves a vehicle meeting Part 383's licensing thresholds, or otherwise falls within or outside Part 382's coverage — that depends on facts about the vehicle and role this sheet does not address. This is federal law, applicable regardless of state; it is not a claim about any California-specific requirement.

citations.case: 49 CFR § 382.103(a) (eCFR text, title 49, current as of Sept. 3, 2026)
citations.quote:
This part applies to service agents and to every person and to all employers of such persons who operate a commercial motor vehicle in commerce in any State and are subject to:
(1) The commercial driver's license requirements of part 383 of this subchapter;
(2) The Licencia Federal de Conductor (Mexico) requirements; or
(3) The commercial drivers license requirements of the Canadian National Safety Code.

clauses.title: The Clearinghouse and "Employer," Defined
clauses.body: Part 382's own definitions section describes the Clearinghouse as the FMCSA database that Subpart G requires employers and service agents to report information to, and to query, regarding drivers subject to the federal controlled-substance and alcohol testing regulations. The same section defines "employer," for purposes of the whole part, as a person or entity employing one or more employees (including a self-employed individual) that is subject to DOT agency regulations requiring compliance with Part 382 — the entity responsible for overall implementation of the DOT drug and alcohol program requirements — and it separately states that a service agent (a term covering entities such as a consortium/third-party administrator that helps administer a testing program) is not itself an "employer" for the part's purposes.
clauses.gap: Both quotations below come from the same statutory-note-equivalent section, 49 CFR § 382.107, treated together here as one connected source rather than as independent corroboration of each other. This clause does not restate the balance of § 382.107's lengthy definitions list (covering terms such as "driver," "safety-sensitive function," "actual knowledge," and "refuse to submit," among others), several of which matter to how the query and prohibition rules described in this document's other clauses actually apply; those terms are used in this document's other clauses without being independently defined here. It does not determine whether a specific business meets this definition of "employer" in its own circumstances.

citations.case: 49 CFR § 382.107 (eCFR text, title 49, current as of Sept. 3, 2026), defining "Commercial Driver's License Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse"
citations.quote: Commercial Driver's License Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse (Clearinghouse) means the FMCSA database that subpart G of this part requires employers and service agents to report information to and to query regarding drivers who are subject to the DOT controlled substance and alcohol testing regulations.

citations.case: 49 CFR § 382.107 (eCFR text, title 49, current as of Sept. 3, 2026), defining "Employer"
citations.quote: Employer means a person or entity employing one or more employees (including an individual who is self-employed) that is subject to DOT agency regulations requiring compliance with this part. The term, as used in this part, means the entity responsible for overall implementation of DOT drug and alcohol program requirements, including individuals employed by the entity who take personnel actions resulting from violations of this part and any applicable DOT agency regulations. Service agents are not employers for the purposes of this part.

clauses.title: The Pre-Employment Query Requirement
clauses.body: Federal regulation prohibits an employer from employing a driver, who is subject to the federal controlled-substance and alcohol testing rules, to perform a safety-sensitive function without first conducting a pre-employment query of the Clearinghouse. The query is meant to show whether that driver has a verified positive, adulterated, or substituted controlled-substance test result; an alcohol confirmation test result of 0.04 or higher; a refusal to submit to testing; or an employer's report of actual knowledge of certain alcohol or controlled-substance use. This kind of query is called a "full query" — one that releases the underlying Clearinghouse information to the employer and requires the individual driver's specific consent.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 49 CFR § 382.701(a) only. It does not cover the separate annual query requirement for continuing employees (covered in this document's next clause), the driver-consent mechanics that make a full query possible (also covered separately), or the recordkeeping and prohibition provisions found later in the same section. It does not determine whether a particular driver is subject to controlled substances and alcohol testing under this part, or whether a particular role involves a "safety-sensitive function" as Part 382 defines that term — both threshold questions this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: 49 CFR § 382.701(a) (eCFR text, title 49, current as of Sept. 3, 2026)
citations.quote:
(1) Employers must not employ a driver subject to controlled substances and alcohol testing under this part to perform a safety-sensitive function without first conducting a pre-employment query of the Clearinghouse to obtain information about whether the driver has a verified positive, adulterated, or substituted controlled substances test result; has an alcohol confirmation test with a concentration of 0.04 or higher; has refused to submit to a test in violation of § 382.211; or that an employer has reported actual knowledge, as defined at § 382.107, that the driver used alcohol on duty in violation of § 382.205, used alcohol before duty in violation of § 382.207, used alcohol following an accident in violation of § 382.209, or used a controlled substance, in violation of § 382.213.
(2) The employer must conduct a full query under this section, which releases information in the Clearinghouse to an employer and requires that the individual driver give specific consent.

clauses.title: Driver Consent to a Clearinghouse Query
clauses.body: Federal regulation requires the driver's own consent before an employer may query the Clearinghouse at all. To determine only whether any record exists for a particular driver, the employer must first obtain that driver's written or electronic consent, which the querying employer must retain for three years from the date of the last query. To actually access the substantive information in a driver's Clearinghouse record — a verified positive, adulterated, or substituted test result; a qualifying alcohol confirmation result; a testing refusal; a specified employer report of actual knowledge; or the SAP, return-to-duty, or follow-up-testing records described in the regulation — the driver must separately submit electronic consent through the Clearinghouse itself, granting the employer access to those specific records. The regulation also states the consequence of a refusal: an employer may not permit a driver to perform a safety-sensitive function if that driver refuses to grant the required consent.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 49 CFR § 382.703(a) through (c) of the same section; they are treated together here as one connected source. It does not cover subdivisions (d) and (e), which describe the mechanics of how a driver's consent is transmitted to FMCSA through the Clearinghouse itself. It does not determine whether any specific driver has given or refused consent, and it does not itself constitute a consent form.

citations.case: 49 CFR § 382.703(a) (eCFR text, title 49, current as of Sept. 3, 2026)
citations.quote: No employer may query the Clearinghouse to determine whether a record exists for any particular driver without first obtaining that driver's written or electronic consent. The employer conducting the search must retain the consent for 3 years from the date of the last query.

citations.case: 49 CFR § 382.703(c) (eCFR text, title 49, current as of Sept. 3, 2026)
citations.quote: No employer may permit a driver to perform a safety-sensitive function if the driver refuses to grant the consent required by paragraph (a) or (b) of this section.

clauses.title: The Annual Query Requirement for Continuing Drivers
clauses.body: Beyond the pre-employment query, federal regulation requires an employer to query the Clearinghouse at least once per year for every employee subject to the federal controlled-substance and alcohol testing rules, to determine whether Clearinghouse information exists about that employee. In place of a full query, an employer may instead obtain the driver's consent to a "limited query" to satisfy this annual requirement — a query that tells the employer only whether Clearinghouse information about the driver exists, without releasing that information. If a limited query shows that information does exist, the employer must then conduct a full query within 24 hours; if the employer does not do so within that window, the driver may not continue performing any safety-sensitive function until the employer completes the full query and the results confirm the driver's record contains none of the regulation's stated prohibitions.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 49 CFR § 382.701(b)(1) through (3) — subdivisions of the same section as this document's pre-employment-query clause, treated together with it as one connected source rather than independent corroboration. It does not cover § 382.701(c), the separate 30-day post-query notification duty FMCSA itself owes the employer, which is not an employer obligation and is not restated here. It does not state which specific query method any particular employer has used or will use for any particular driver.

citations.case: 49 CFR § 382.701(b) (eCFR text, title 49, current as of Sept. 3, 2026)
citations.quote:
(1) Employers must conduct a query of the Clearinghouse at least once per year for information for all employees subject to controlled substance and alcohol testing under this part to determine whether information exists in the Clearinghouse about those employees.
(2) In lieu of a full query, as described in paragraph (a)(2) of this section, an employer may obtain the individual driver's consent to conduct a limited query to satisfy the annual query requirement in paragraph (b)(1) of this section. The limited query will tell the employer whether there is information about the individual driver in the Clearinghouse, but will not release that information to the employer. The individual driver may give consent to conduct limited queries that is effective for more than one year.
(3) If the limited query shows that information exists in the Clearinghouse about the individual driver, the employer must conduct a full query, in accordance with paragraph (a)(2) of this section, within 24 hours of conducting the limited query. If the employer fails to conduct a full query within 24 hours, the employer must not allow the driver to continue to perform any safety-sensitive function until the employer conducts the full query and the results confirm that the driver's Clearinghouse record contains no prohibitions as defined in paragraph (d) of this section.

clauses.title: The Prohibition and Its Return-to-Duty Exception
clauses.body: Federal regulation states a general prohibition: no employer may allow a driver it employs or intends to hire or use to perform any safety-sensitive function if a Clearinghouse query shows a verified positive, adulterated, or substituted controlled-substance test result; a disqualifying alcohol confirmation result; a testing refusal; or a specified employer report of actual knowledge of alcohol or controlled-substance use — except where the query also shows that the driver has completed the SAP (substance abuse professional) evaluation, referral, and education or treatment process, achieved a negative return-to-duty test result, and completed the prescribed follow-up testing plan (or, for a driver still completing follow-up testing, has met the same SAP and return-to-duty conditions while the employer itself assumes responsibility for managing the remaining follow-up testing).
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 49 CFR § 382.701(d), a single subdivision of the same section as this document's other § 382.701 clauses; it does not independently corroborate them, and they do not independently corroborate it. It does not describe the SAP evaluation and return-to-duty process itself (governed by 49 CFR Part 40, Subpart O), which this clause references only as the regulation itself references it, without independently fetching or verifying Part 40's own text. It does not determine whether any specific Clearinghouse query result falls within this exception.

citations.case: 49 CFR § 382.701(d) (eCFR text, title 49, current as of Sept. 3, 2026)
citations.quote:
No employer may allow a driver the employer employs or intends to hire or use to perform any safety-sensitive function if the results of a Clearinghouse query demonstrate that the driver has a verified positive, adulterated, or substituted controlled substances test result; has an alcohol confirmation test with a concentration of 0.04 or higher; has refused to submit to a test in violation of § 382.211; or that an employer has reported actual knowledge, as defined at § 382.107, that the driver used alcohol on duty in violation of § 382.205, used alcohol before duty in violation of § 382.207, used alcohol following an accident in violation of § 382.209, or used a controlled substance in violation of § 382.213, except where a query of the Clearinghouse demonstrates:
(1) That the driver has successfully completed the SAP evaluation, referral, and education/treatment process set forth in part 40, subpart O, of this title; achieves a negative return-to-duty test result; and completes the follow-up testing plan prescribed by the SAP.

clauses.title: Query Recordkeeping
clauses.body: Federal regulation requires an employer to retain, for three years, a record of each Clearinghouse query it makes and all information it receives in response. As of January 6, 2023, the regulation treats an employer's own valid Clearinghouse registration as satisfying this recordkeeping requirement.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 49 CFR § 382.701(e) only, the same section as this document's other § 382.701 clauses, treated as one connected source with them rather than independent corroboration. It does not describe how, mechanically, a Clearinghouse registration "fulfills" the recordkeeping requirement, or what an employer's registration record actually contains — the regulation's text quoted here states the rule but not its underlying mechanics. It does not state what records, if any, any particular employer currently retains for any particular driver.

clauses.title: Penalties for Noncompliance
clauses.body: Federal regulation states that an employer or driver who violates any requirement of Part 382 — including the pre-employment and annual query duties, the consent requirements, and the recordkeeping duty described in this document — is subject to the civil and/or criminal penalty provisions of 49 U.S.C. § 521(b). The regulation states the same consequence for a violation of the related testing-procedure rules in 49 CFR Part 40.

It does not determine whether any violation has occurred or what penalty, if any, would apply in a specific case.

In addition, any employer or driver who violates the requirements of 49 CFR part 40 shall be subject to the civil and/or criminal penalty provisions of 49 U.S.C. 521(b).

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Declaration
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the federal Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984, codified at 17 U.S.C. §§ 901-914 (chapter 9 of the Copyright Act) -- a distinct, sui generis intellectual property right that protects the topography of a semiconductor chip's layered circuitry design, called a "mask work," separately from copyright, patent, or trade secret law. It is prepared with reference to {{workDescription}}, associated with {{ownerName}}. This sheet describes the statutory definitions of "mask work" and "semiconductor chip product" in § 901, the eligibility and non-originality/idea-exclusion limits on protection in § 902, ownership and transfer under § 903, the 10-year term in § 904, the exclusive rights in § 905, the reverse-engineering limitation in § 906, the 2-year registration deadline in § 908, the optional notice form in § 909, and the preemption of equivalent state-law protection in § 912; it does not evaluate whether {{workDescription}} qualifies for mask work protection, does not prepare or file any application with the Register of Copyrights, and does not calculate any specific term, registration deadline, or infringement remedy. This document is distinct from the corpus's existing Copyright Assignment, Patent Assignment, Patent License, Trademark License, Software License, and trade-secret documents -- mask work protection is a separate statutory scheme from all of them, sharing an administering office (the Register of Copyrights) with copyright but not copyright's own subject-matter or duration rules. This sheet is educational only; it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney, and it does not itself request, register, or enforce protection for any mask work.

clauses.title: What Counts as a "Mask Work" and a "Semiconductor Chip Product"
clauses.body: The statute defines two closely related terms. A "semiconductor chip product" is the final or intermediate form of any product having two or more layers of metallic, insulating, or semiconductor material placed on, or etched away from, a piece of semiconductor material in a predetermined pattern, and intended to perform electronic circuitry functions. A "mask work" is the layered design itself: a series of related images, however fixed or encoded, that represent the predetermined, three-dimensional pattern of material present or removed from the layers of a semiconductor chip product, where each image in the series corresponds to the pattern of one layer of the chip product. In short, the semiconductor chip product is the physical object; the mask work is the layout pattern embodied in it.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the bare statutory definitions in 17 U.S.C. § 901(a)(1)-(2); it does not address the statute's separate defined terms for "fixed," "owner," "innocent purchaser," or "infringing semiconductor chip product" in the same subsection, none of which are quoted here, and it does not evaluate whether the specific product or design described elsewhere in this document actually meets either definition. Both quotations below come from the same statutory subsection, § 901(a), so they are treated as one source consulted once, not as two independent sources. This is a federal statute of nationwide application, not California-specific law. clauses.title: What the Statute Does Not Protect: Non-Original and Staple Designs, and Ideas
clauses.body: Protection under the statute is not automatic for every chip layout. It is unavailable for a mask work that is not original, and separately unavailable for a mask work that consists of designs that are staple, commonplace, or familiar in the semiconductor industry -- or variations of such designs -- combined in a way that, considered as a whole, is not itself original. The statute also draws an idea/expression-style line similar to copyright's: in no case does protection extend to any idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation, concept, principle, or discovery, regardless of the form in which it is described, explained, illustrated, or embodied in the mask work.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 17 U.S.C. § 902(b) and § 902(c), two subsections of the same statutory section, so they are treated as one source consulted once, not as independent sources. Neither subsection is defined further by the statute -- the statute does not itself explain what makes a combination of staple or commonplace elements "original" as a whole, and this clause does not evaluate whether the specific mask work described in this document meets or fails either exclusion. Section 902(a)'s separate nationality/treaty eligibility requirements (protection generally requires the owner to be a U.S. national or domiciliary, a national of a treaty country, a stateless person, or for the work to be first commercially exploited in the United States) are not addressed in this clause. This is a federal statute of nationwide application. clauses.title: Ownership and Transfer of Mask Work Rights
clauses.body: The exclusive rights in a mask work subject to protection belong to the owner of the mask work. The owner may transfer all of those rights, or license all or less than all of them, by any written instrument signed by the owner or the owner's duly authorized agent; the statute also allows the rights to be transferred or licensed by operation of law, bequeathed by will, or to pass as personal property under the applicable laws of intestate succession.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 17 U.S.C. § 903(a) and § 903(b), two subsections of the same statutory section, treated as one source consulted once, not independent sources. It does not address § 903(c)'s separate optional recordation procedure with the Copyright Office (which affects priority between conflicting transfers) or § 903(d)'s rule for mask works prepared by federal government officers or employees, neither of which is quoted here. The statute's own definitions section, § 901(a)(6), separately provides that for a mask work made within the scope of a person's employment, the "owner" is the employer (or the employer's transferee) rather than the individual creator -- that employment-work-for-hire-style rule is not quoted or further developed in this clause. This is a federal statute of nationwide application. clauses.title: Duration: Ten Years From Registration or First Commercial Exploitation
clauses.body: Protection commences on the date the mask work is registered with the Register of Copyrights under § 908, or the date it is first commercially exploited anywhere in the world, whichever occurs first. Protection then lasts ten years from that commencement date, and every term of protection under the statute runs to the end of the calendar year in which it would otherwise expire. The date recorded for this document as the mask work's first commercial exploitation, if any, is {{firstUseDate}}.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 17 U.S.C. § 904(a), (b), and (c) -- three subsections of the same statutory section, treated as one source consulted once, not independent sources -- and does not itself calculate a specific term for any particular mask work, since that calculation depends on the actual registration date or first-commercial-exploitation date, neither of which this clause determines. "Commercially exploited" is itself a defined term in § 901(a)(5) (distributing a semiconductor chip product embodying the mask work to the public for commercial purposes, or, in some circumstances, a written offer to do so) that is not independently developed in this clause. This is a federal statute of nationwide application; ten years is markedly shorter than the terms available under copyright or utility-patent law, which this clause does not otherwise compare. clauses.title: The Owner's Exclusive Rights
clauses.body: The owner of a protected mask work has the exclusive rights to do, and to authorize, three things: to reproduce the mask work by optical, electronic, or any other means; to import or distribute a semiconductor chip product in which the mask work is embodied; and to induce or knowingly cause another person to do either of those acts.
clauses.gap: This clause states the full text of 17 U.S.C. § 905 as a single, undivided statutory provision; it does not address the separate limitations on these exclusive rights found in §§ 906 and 907 (reverse engineering and innocent-purchaser limitations), which are addressed in other clauses of this document, nor § 910's remedies for infringement of these rights, which is not addressed anywhere in this document. This is a federal statute of nationwide application. The statutory text was fetched directly from Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/905) on 2026-09-06, re-fetched a second time with a distinct User-Agent header, and confirmed byte-identical both times. No case law construing the scope of these exclusive rights was checked: a CourtListener case-law search for this topic returned a 429 rate-limit error (125 requests/day quota exhausted) during this research session, so no case citation is included as a result.

citations.quote: The owner of a mask work provided protection under this chapter has the exclusive rights to do and to authorize any of the following: (1) to reproduce the mask work by optical, electronic, or any other means; (2) to import or distribute a semiconductor chip product in which the mask work is embodied; and (3) to induce or knowingly to cause another person to do any of the acts described in paragraphs (1) and (2).

clauses.title: The Reverse-Engineering Limitation
clauses.body: The exclusive rights described above are subject to a built-in reverse-engineering limitation. It is not an infringement for a person to reproduce a mask work solely to teach, analyze, or evaluate the concepts or techniques embodied in the mask work, or the circuitry, logic flow, or organization of components it uses, and it is likewise not an infringement for a person who performs that analysis or evaluation to incorporate the results in an original mask work that is made to be distributed. A separate provision of the same section allows the owner of a particular lawfully made semiconductor chip product to import, distribute, or otherwise dispose of or use -- but not reproduce -- that particular chip product without the mask work owner's authority.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only 17 U.S.C. § 906(a); it does not quote § 906(b) (the first-sale-style limitation for a particular lawfully made chip product), though it is paraphrased in the clause's last sentence, so that paraphrase is not independently supported by a verified quotation. The statute does not itself define how much reproduction is "solely for the purpose of" teaching, analyzing, or evaluating, as opposed to exceeding that purpose, and this clause does not evaluate whether any specific act of reverse engineering described to the user of this document falls within or outside the limitation. This is a federal statute of nationwide application; this clause does not address how the analogous, differently worded reverse-engineering exemptions in the DMCA's anticircumvention provisions (addressed in a separate document in this corpus) compare to this one. clauses.title: The Two-Year Registration Deadline
clauses.body: Unlike copyright, which now exists automatically on fixation, mask work protection carries a hard registration deadline tied to commercial use. The mask work owner may apply to the Register of Copyrights for registration of a claim of protection, and protection under the statute terminates if that application is not made within two years after the date the mask work is first commercially exploited anywhere in the world.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the first two sentences of 17 U.S.C. § 908(a); it does not address § 908's remaining subsections governing the Register of Copyrights's administrative procedures, the application form and identifying-material deposit requirements, the certificate of registration's evidentiary effect, or the judicial-review procedure for a refused application, none of which are quoted here. This clause does not calculate any specific two-year deadline for the mask work described in this document, since that calculation depends on an actual first-commercial-exploitation date that this clause does not determine. This is a federal statute of nationwide application. clauses.title: Optional Mask Work Notice
clauses.body: The statute permits, but does not require, an owner to affix a notice to a protected mask work and to masks and semiconductor chip products embodying it. Affixing the notice is not itself a condition of protection, but it does constitute prima facie evidence of notice of protection -- a fact relevant to the statute's separate innocent-purchaser limitation on remedies. The notice consists of the words "mask work," the symbol *M*, or the symbol Ⓜ (the letter M in a circle), together with the name of the mask work's owner or an abbreviation by which that name is recognized or generally known.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 17 U.S.C. § 909(a) and § 909(b), two subsections of the same statutory section, treated as one source consulted once, not independent sources. It does not describe or quote the specific affixation methods and notice placement the Register of Copyrights has prescribed by regulation (referenced in § 909(a) itself but not independently researched here), and it does not develop the separate innocent-purchaser limitation in § 907 to which "notice of protection" is relevant beyond naming that connection. This is a federal statute of nationwide application. clauses.title: Preemption of Equivalent State-Law Protection
clauses.body: This federal scheme displaces overlapping state law. The statute preempts the laws of any state to the extent those laws provide rights or remedies with respect to a mask work that are equivalent to the rights or remedies the federal statute itself provides, though the statute limits that preemption to actions filed on or after January 1, 1986.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only 17 U.S.C. § 912(c); it does not address § 912(a)'s separate rule that nothing in this chapter affects rights or remedies available under copyright (chapters 1-8 or 10 of title 17) or patent law (title 35), § 912(b)'s cross-reference rule, or § 912(d)'s saving clause for rights concerning a mask work first commercially exploited before July 1, 1983, none of which are quoted here. This clause states only that the federal statute preempts equivalent state-law rights and remedies concerning mask works specifically -- it does not state, and should not be read to suggest, that California trade secret law (which protects the confidentiality of an unpublished chip design or manufacturing process, not a mask work already embodied in a distributed product) is preempted by this statute; trade secret protection and mask work protection address different subject matter and can both apply to different aspects of the same underlying chip design at different points in its development. This is a federal statute of nationwide application; this clause does not evaluate whether any specific California statute or common-law doctrine would in fact provide a "right or remedy" "equivalent" to this chapter's own rights and remedies. clauses.title: Signature
Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet states California law on what happens to personal property that {{tenantName}} ("the former tenant") leaves behind at {{propertyAddress}} after a tenancy there has terminated and the premises have been vacated, under California Civil Code Chapter 5 of Title 5 of the Civil Code, Civil Code §§ 1980–1991. That chapter creates an optional statutory procedure landlords may use for handling personal property a former tenant does not take when leaving; a landlord's use of this procedure is not the only way California law allows a landlord to handle such property, and this document does not determine that {{landlordName}} has used, will use, or must use this procedure for the property left at {{propertyAddress}} after {{tenantName}}'s tenancy there ended on or about {{moveOutDate}}. This chapter does not apply to manufactured homes, mobilehomes, or commercial coaches as those terms are defined in the Health and Safety Code, to property a landlord reasonably believes to be lost rather than left behind at the end of a tenancy, to certain animals, or to certain other categories of property addressed by other statutes, each described further in this document. This document states California statutory law as of the date signed below. It does not determine that any specific item of property found at {{propertyAddress}} is covered by this chapter, does not determine the value of any specific item, and does not determine that any specific notice, storage, or disposal step described in this document has been or will be carried out correctly in a specific case.

clauses.title: Definitions Under This Chapter
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1980 defines several terms "as used in this chapter" — meaning these definitions govern only Civil Code §§ 1980–1991 and are not necessarily the meanings the same words carry elsewhere in California law. "Landlord" means any operator, keeper, lessor, or sublessor of any furnished or unfurnished premises for hire, or that person's agent or successor in interest. "Owner" means any person other than the landlord who has any right, title, or interest in the personal property. "Premises" includes any common areas associated with the rented space. "Tenant" includes any paying guest, lessee, or sublessee of any premises for hire. "Reasonable belief" means the actual knowledge or belief a prudent person would have without making an investigation, including any investigation of public records, except that where the landlord has specific information indicating that such an investigation would more probably than not reveal pertinent information and the cost would be reasonable relative to the property's probable value, "reasonable belief" includes what a prudent person would have known or believed had that investigation been made.
clauses.gap: Civil Code § 1980 defines "Premises" only by stating that it "includes any common areas associated therewith" — the statute does not itself supply a general definition of the primary term. These definitions apply only within this chapter; other California statutes governing landlord-tenant relationships (for example, the unlawful detainer statutes) define "tenant" and related terms separately, and this document does not state whether or how those definitions differ.

clauses.title: An Optional Procedure, and What This Chapter Does Not Cover
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1981 states that this chapter "provides an optional procedure for the disposition of personal property that remains on the premises after a tenancy has terminated and the premises have been vacated by the tenant." The chapter does not apply whenever certain other statutes apply instead (Civil Code §§ 1862.5, 2080.8, 2080.9, or 2081 to 2081.6), and it does not apply to property that exists for the purpose of providing utility services and is owned by a public utility. It also does not apply to any manufactured home, mobilehome, or commercial coach as those terms are defined in the Health and Safety Code, including attachments to or contents of those structures, regardless of whether the structure is subject to registration — nor does it apply to the disposition of certain animals covered by other statutes. Separately, Civil Code § 1982 directs that personal property a landlord reasonably believes to have been lost (as opposed to left behind at the end of a tenancy) must instead be handled under the general lost-property statutes beginning at Civil Code § 2080; a landlord who complies with that separate statute is not liable to the property's owner on account of that property. If the local police or sheriff's department refuses to accept property offered to it as lost property under that statute, the landlord may instead dispose of the property under this chapter.
clauses.gap: Civil Code § 1981(e) states that if this chapter's requirements are not satisfied, "nothing in this chapter affects the rights and liabilities of the landlord, former tenant, or any other person" — meaning this chapter is a safe-harbor procedure a landlord may choose to follow, not the exclusive framework governing what happens to property left behind. Because manufactured homes, mobilehomes, and commercial coaches are expressly excluded from this chapter, a tenancy involving one of those structures is governed by different statutes not addressed in this document. This document also does not determine, for any specific item of property, whether a landlord's belief that the item was lost (triggering § 1982) rather than left behind at the end of a tenancy (triggering the rest of this chapter) is factually correct.

(b) If the appropriate police or sheriff’s department refuses to accept property pursuant to subdivision (a), the landlord may dispose of the property pursuant to this chapter.

clauses.title: Notice to the Former Tenant and Other Owners: Contents, Timing, and Delivery
clauses.body: Under Civil Code § 1983(a), where personal property remains on the premises after a tenancy has terminated and the premises have been vacated, the landlord must give written notice to the former tenant and to any other person the landlord reasonably believes to be the owner of the property; if the property consists of records, the former tenant is presumed to be their owner for purposes of this chapter. Under § 1983(b), the notice must describe the property in a manner reasonably adequate to permit its owner to identify it — though a locked, fastened, or tied container that deters immediate access to its contents may be described as such without describing what is inside — and must advise the recipient that reasonable storage costs may be charged before the property is returned, where it may be claimed, and the date by which it must be claimed. That date must be no less than 15 days after the notice is personally delivered, or, if mailed, no less than 18 days after the notice is deposited in the mail. Under § 1983(c), the notice must be personally delivered or sent by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to the recipient's last known address, and also to any other address known to the landlord where the recipient may reasonably be expected to receive it if there is reason to believe the first address will not reach them; a copy mailed to the former tenant must also be sent to the vacated premises; and if the former tenant provided the landlord with an email address, the landlord may also send the notice by email.
clauses.gap: Civil Code § 1983(b) ties the adequacy of the property description directly to the liability limitation available under § 1989 — that limitation does not protect a landlord for property not described in the notice, except for the locked-container exception — so whether a given description is "reasonably adequate" can affect a landlord's later liability, and this document does not evaluate the adequacy of any specific description. The statute allows email notice only as an addition ("may also send") where the former tenant provided an email address; it does not make email a substitute for personal delivery or mail, and does not address notice to an other-than-tenant owner by email at all.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1983(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, duty to give written notice
citations.quote: Where personal property remains on the premises after a tenancy has terminated and the premises have been vacated by the tenant, the landlord shall give written notice to the tenant and to any other person the landlord reasonably believes to be the owner of the property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1983(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, required notice contents and the 15/18-day deadline
citations.quote: The date specified in the notice shall be a date not less than 15 days after the notice is personally delivered or, if mailed, not less than 18 days after the notice is deposited in the mail.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1983(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, permitted methods of delivery, including optional email
citations.quote: If the former tenant provided the landlord with the tenant’s email address, the landlord may also send the notice by email.

clauses.title: The Statutory Notice Forms and the Required Disclosure Statement
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1984(a) sets out a form of notice titled "Notice of Right to Reclaim Abandoned Property" that, if given to the former tenant in substantially that form, satisfies § 1983's requirements. Under § 1984(b), that notice must also contain one of two statements, depending on how the landlord intends to proceed: a public-sale statement disclosing that unclaimed property will be sold at public sale after published notice, that the recipient has the right to bid at that sale, and that after the sale and deduction of storage, advertising, and sale costs, the remaining money is paid to the county and may be claimed within one year; or, alternatively, a statement that because the property is believed to be worth less than $700, it may be kept, sold, or destroyed without further notice if not reclaimed in time. Civil Code § 1985 sets out a separate statutory notice form for use when the person being notified is not the former tenant but someone else the landlord reasonably believes to be an owner of the property; a notice given in substantially that form likewise satisfies § 1983.
clauses.gap: Both statutory forms need only be followed "in substantially" the form set out in the statute, not verbatim — California law does not define how much deviation from the printed form remains "substantial" compliance, and this document does not resolve that question for any specific notice. The two disclosure statements in § 1984(b) are mutually exclusive alternatives tied to which disposal path under § 1988 applies to the property; this document does not determine which statement applies to any specific item of property, since that turns on the landlord's reasonable belief about the property's resale value, a factual determination this document does not make.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1984(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the statutory notice form's title and function
citations.quote: A notice given to the former tenant which is in substantially the following form satisfies the requirements of Section 1983: Notice of Right to Reclaim Abandoned Property

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1984(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the required public-sale disclosure statement
citations.quote: “If you fail to reclaim the property, it will be sold at a public sale after notice of the sale has been given by publication. You have the right to bid on the property at this sale. After the property is sold and the cost of storage, advertising, and sale is deducted, the remaining money will be paid over to the county. You may claim the remaining money at any time within one year after the county receives the money.”

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1984(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the required under-$700 disclosure statement
citations.quote: “Because this property is believed to be worth less than $700, it may be kept, sold, or destroyed without further notice if you fail to reclaim it within the time indicated above.”

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1985 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the statutory form for a non-tenant owner
citations.quote: A notice which is in substantially the following form given to a person (other than the former tenant) the landlord reasonably believes to be the owner of personal property satisfies the requirements of Section 1983

clauses.title: Storing the Property Pending Release or Disposal
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1986 requires that personal property described in the notice either be left on the vacated premises or be stored by the landlord in a place of safekeeping until the landlord either releases it under Civil Code § 1987 or disposes of it under Civil Code § 1988. The landlord must exercise reasonable care in storing the property, but is not liable to the tenant or any other owner for any loss that was not caused by the landlord's own deliberate or negligent act.
clauses.gap: Civil Code § 1986 has not been amended since its original 1974 enactment, even though several neighboring sections of this same chapter were amended as recently as 2012 — it does not define "place of safekeeping," does not set a minimum storage standard beyond "reasonable care," and does not address modern storage arrangements such as third-party self-storage facilities. Whether a particular storage location or method meets the "reasonable care" standard in a specific case is a factual question this document does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1986 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the storage duty and standard of care
citations.quote: The personal property described in the notice shall either be left on the vacated premises or be stored by the landlord in a place of safekeeping until the landlord either releases the property pursuant to Section 1987 or disposes of the property pursuant to Section 1988.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1986 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the limit on the landlord's liability for stored property
citations.quote: The landlord shall exercise reasonable care in storing the property, but he is not liable to the tenant or any other owner for any loss not caused by his deliberate or negligent act.

clauses.title: Releasing the Property: Storage Cost, the Two-Day Window, and How Cost Is Assessed
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1987(a) requires the landlord to release the described property to the former tenant or, at the landlord's option, to another person reasonably believed to be its owner, if that person pays the reasonable cost of storage and takes possession by the date specified in the notice. Under § 1987(b), if the property was not released and the notice stated it would be sold at public sale, the landlord must still release it to the former tenant if the tenant claims it before the sale and pays the reasonable costs of storage, advertising, and sale incurred up to that point. Under § 1987(c), notwithstanding subdivision (a), the landlord must release the property to the former tenant without charging for storage if the property remained in the dwelling and the former tenant or reasonably-believed owner reclaims it within two days of vacating. Civil Code § 1990 governs how storage costs are assessed: a former tenant reclaiming property may be required to pay the reasonable costs of storage for all property remaining at the end of the tenancy that are unpaid at the time of the claim, while an owner other than the former tenant may be required to pay only for storage of the property in which that owner claims an interest; the landlord may not charge more than one person for the same costs; and if the landlord stores the property on the premises, the cost of storage is the fair rental value of the space reasonably required for that storage, with no cost assessed at all if the former tenant reclaims property stored on the premises within two days of vacating.
clauses.gap: Neither § 1987 nor § 1990 sets a dollar figure or formula for "reasonable cost of storage" beyond tying on-premises storage to "the fair rental value of the space reasonably required" — this document does not calculate or estimate a specific dollar amount for any specific situation. The two-day free-reclaim rule in § 1987(c) applies where the property "remained in the dwelling"; the statute does not address whether that rule still applies if the landlord moved the property to off-site storage before the two days elapsed, and this document does not resolve that unaddressed situation.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1987(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, release of property upon payment of storage cost
citations.quote: The personal property described in the notice shall be released by the landlord to the former tenant or, at the landlord’s option, to any person reasonably believed by the landlord to be its owner if that tenant or other person pays the reasonable cost of storage and takes possession of the property not later than the date specified in the notice for taking possession.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1987(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the two-day free-reclaim window
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (a), the landlord shall release the personal property described in the notice to the former tenant and shall not require the former tenant to pay the cost of storage if the property remained in the dwelling and the former tenant or other person reasonably believed by the landlord to be its owner reclaims the property within two days of vacating the dwelling.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1990(a)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, how storage costs are assessed between a former tenant and another owner
citations.quote: Where a former tenant claims property pursuant to Section 1987, he or she may be required to pay the reasonable costs of storage for all the personal property remaining on the premises at the termination of the tenancy which are unpaid at the time the claim is made. (2) Where an owner other than the former tenant claims property pursuant to Section 1987, he or she may be required to pay the reasonable costs of storage for only the property in which he or she claims an interest.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1990(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, storage cost when the property is stored on the premises
citations.quote: If the landlord stores the personal property on the premises, the cost of storage shall be the fair rental value of the space reasonably required for that storage for the term of the storage.

clauses.title: Disposal Once the Notice Period Expires: Public Sale or Low-Value Retention
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1988(a) provides that personal property not released under § 1987 must be sold at public sale by competitive bidding — unless the landlord reasonably believes the total resale value of the unreleased property is less than $700, in which case the landlord may instead retain the property for personal use or dispose of it in any manner. The statute expressly permits the landlord or the tenant to bid on the property at the public sale. Under § 1988(b), notice of the time and place of a public sale must be published under Government Code § 6066 in a newspaper of general circulation in the county where the sale will be held, with the last publication no less than five days before the sale, and that sale notice cannot be published before the deadline date specified in the § 1983 notice; the sale notice must describe the property adequately for its owner to identify it, subject to the same locked-container exception as the § 1983 notice. Under § 1988(c), after deducting the costs of storage, advertising, and sale, any unclaimed balance of the sale proceeds must be paid into the treasury of the county where the sale took place no later than 30 days after the sale; the former tenant or other owner may claim that balance within one year of the county's receipt of it by applying to the county treasurer or other designated county official, and if the county pays the balance to a claimant, neither the county nor its officers or employees are liable to any other claimant for the amount paid.
clauses.gap: The $700 resale-value threshold in § 1988(a) is a fixed dollar figure as last amended effective January 1, 2013 — the statute does not index it for inflation or provide for automatic adjustment, so the same $700 figure has applied without change since that date. Whether the landlord's belief that a specific item's total resale value is under $700 is itself "reasonable" is a factual determination this document does not make.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1988(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, public sale requirement and the under-$700 exception
citations.quote: If the personal property described in the notice is not released pursuant to Section 1987, it shall be sold at public sale by competitive bidding. However, if the landlord reasonably believes that the total resale value of the property not released is less than seven hundred dollars ($700), the landlord may retain the property for his or her own use or dispose of it in any manner.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1988(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, publication requirements for the sale notice
citations.quote: Notice of the time and place of the public sale shall be given by publication pursuant to Section 6066 of the Government Code in a newspaper of general circulation published in the county where the sale is to be held. The last publication shall be not less than five days before the sale is to be held.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1988(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, disposition of unclaimed sale proceeds and the one-year claim period
citations.quote: After deduction of the costs of storage, advertising, and sale, any balance of the proceeds of the sale which is not claimed by the former tenant or an owner other than such tenant shall be paid into the treasury of the county in which the sale took place not later than 30 days after the date of sale. The former tenant or other owner may claim the balance within one year from the date of payment to the county by making application to the county treasurer or other official designated by the county.

clauses.title: Landlord's Limitation of Liability, and Coordination With a Notice of Belief of Abandonment
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1989 limits a landlord's liability for property handled under this chapter. Under § 1989(a), a landlord who releases property to the former tenant is not liable with respect to that property to any person. Under § 1989(b), a landlord who releases property under § 1987 to a reasonably-believed owner other than the former tenant is not liable to anyone who was given notice under § 1983, nor to anyone who was not given notice unless that person proves the landlord believed or reasonably should have believed they had an interest in the property and also knew or reasonably should have known their address. Section 1989(c) applies the identical two-part rule to property disposed of under § 1988. Separately, Civil Code § 1991 addresses how the notice required by this chapter interacts with a notice of belief of abandonment given under the different statute at Civil Code § 1951.3: where a landlord gives a tenant a notice of belief of abandonment under § 1951.3, the notice required by § 1983 of this chapter may — but need not — be given at the same time, even though the tenancy does not terminate until the period specified in the abandonment notice ends; and if both notices are given, they may, but need not, be combined into a single notice containing all the information each underlying statute requires.
clauses.gap: Every liability limitation in § 1989 protects only a landlord who has actually satisfied this chapter's requirements; under § 1981(e), noncompliance leaves the landlord's underlying rights and liabilities unaffected by this chapter, so this document does not determine whether any specific notice, storage, or disposal step was carried out correctly in a way that would trigger § 1989's protection. Civil Code § 1951.3's own notice-of-belief-of-abandonment requirements are governed by a separate statute this document does not itself state in full; § 1991's permission to combine notices is optional and does not excuse compliance with either statute's individual requirements.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1989(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, no liability after release to the former tenant
citations.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (c) of Section 1981, where the landlord releases to the former tenant property which remains on the premises after a tenancy is terminated, the landlord is not liable with respect to that property to any person.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1989(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, no liability after release to a reasonably-believed owner
citations.quote: Where the landlord releases property pursuant to Section 1987 to a person (other than the former tenant) reasonably believed by the landlord to be the owner of the property, the landlord is not liable with respect to that property to:

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1989(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the two-part proof required of an unnoticed claimant after disposal
citations.quote: Any person to whom notice was not given pursuant to Section 1983 unless such person proves that, prior to disposing of the property pursuant to Section 1988, the landlord believed or reasonably should have believed that such person had an interest in the property and also that the landlord knew or should have known upon reasonable investigation the address of such person.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1991 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, coordinating this chapter's notice with a § 1951.3 notice of belief of abandonment
citations.quote: Where a notice of belief of abandonment is given to a lessee pursuant to Section 1951.3, the notice to the former tenant given pursuant to Section 1983 may, but need not, be given at the same time as the notice of belief of abandonment even though the tenancy is not terminated until the end of the period specified in the notice of belief of abandonment.

clauses.title: Notice of Right to Reclaim Abandoned Property — Worksheet and Signature
clauses.body:
