When you vacated the premises at {{propertyAddress}} on or about {{moveOutDate}}, the following personal property remained: {{personalPropertyDescription}}.

You may claim this property at {{claimLocationAddress}}. If you fail to claim this property by {{claimDeadlineDate}}, unless you pay the landlord's reasonable cost of storage for the above-described property and take possession of the property you claim not later than that date, this property may be disposed of under Civil Code § 1988.

Landlord's own recordkeeping notes on the statement required by Civil Code § 1984(b) (select the one that applies and complete accordingly — the two statements are alternatives, not both): (1) public-sale statement, if the property will be sold at public sale after published notice; or (2) under-$700 statement, if the property's reasonably-believed total resale value is ${{estimatedResaleValue}} and is therefore stated to be less than $700. Only one of these two statements is included in the notice actually given, as Civil Code § 1984(b) requires.

It does not determine that the property described is actually covered by Civil Code §§ 1980–1991, does not determine which of the two required disclosure statements applies, and does not itself constitute the notice required by statute unless completed and delivered in the manner Civil Code § 1983 describes.

clauses.title: About This Shared Work (Work Sharing) Information Sheet
The Statutory Definitions of "Affected Unit" and "Work Sharing Plan"
clauses.body: California's Unemployment Insurance Code defines an "affected unit" as a specified plant, department, shift, or other definable unit that includes at least two workers and not less than 10 percent of the employer's regular permanent workforce involved in the unit. A "work sharing plan" is a plan an employer submits to the director of the Employment Development Department for approval, requesting payment of "work sharing compensation" to employees in an affected unit, in lieu of layoffs. The statute separately defines "usual weekly hours of work" as an employee's usual full- or part-time hours when the affected unit is operating on its regular basis, capped at 40 hours and excluding overtime hours.
clauses.gap: This is California's Shared Work (work sharing) statute, Unemployment Insurance Code section 1279.5, used as evidence of what the statute itself provides for an employer that chooses to submit a plan to the Employment Development Department — not a claim that any specific employer's workforce reduction, or any specific employee's reduced hours, actually is, or is not, covered by an approved work sharing plan. This information sheet does not itself submit, approve, disapprove, modify, or revoke any work sharing plan, and it does not determine that any employer's or employee's own circumstances satisfy this section. No case law is cited in this clause: the topic is governed almost entirely by this statutory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and a CourtListener search attempted this session for California appellate decisions construing section 1279.5 returned a 429 rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) before it could complete, so no case law is cited here rather than relied on from memory. Both quotations below are drawn from the same statutory subsection, section 1279.5(a) — they are presented together as definitions from one source, not as independently corroborating sources. The 10-percent-of-workforce and two-or-more-worker thresholds in the "affected unit" definition mean that a workforce reduction affecting only a single worker, or affecting a smaller slice of the workforce than 10 percent (in every week, or in at least one week of a two-week period), does not fit this statutory definition, regardless of how an employer or employee might otherwise describe the reduction.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program
citations.quote: “Affected unit” means a specified plant, department, shift, or other definable unit that includes two or more workers and not less than 10 percent of the employer’s regular permanent work force involved in the affected unit or units in each week, or in at least one week of a two-consecutive-week period, to which an approved work sharing plan applies.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program
citations.quote: “Work sharing plan” means a plan submitted by an employer, for approval by the director, under which the employer requests the payment of work sharing compensation to employees in an affected unit of the employer in lieu of layoffs.

clauses.title: How Work Sharing Redefines "Unemployed" So Reduced-Hour Employees Can Draw Partial Benefits
clauses.body: The statute displaces the ordinary definition of "unemployed" used elsewhere in the Unemployment Insurance Code for employees covered by an approved work sharing plan. For those employees, working fewer than their usual weekly hours because their regular employer is participating in an approved work sharing plan — reducing employment and stabilizing the workforce in lieu of a layoff — itself makes the employee "unemployed" for purposes of this section, regardless of what the general unemployment definitions elsewhere in the code would otherwise require.
clauses.gap: This is California's Shared Work (work sharing) statute, Unemployment Insurance Code section 1279.5, used as evidence of what the statute itself provides for an employer that chooses to submit a plan to the Employment Development Department — not a claim that any specific employer's workforce reduction, or any specific employee's reduced hours, actually is, or is not, covered by an approved work sharing plan. This information sheet does not itself submit, approve, disapprove, modify, or revoke any work sharing plan, and it does not determine that any employer's or employee's own circumstances satisfy this section. No case law is cited in this clause: the topic is governed almost entirely by this statutory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and a CourtListener search attempted this session for California appellate decisions construing section 1279.5 returned a 429 rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) before it could complete, so no case law is cited here rather than relied on from memory. This clause states the special "unemployed" definition created for this section; it does not restate or verify the text of Sections 1252 or 1252.2, the general provisions this section overrides "notwithstanding." A reader who wants to compare the ordinary unemployment definition against this special one would need to separately consult those sections, which this document does not quote.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program
citations.quote: Notwithstanding Section 1252 or 1252.2 or any other provision of this part, for the purposes of this section an employee is “unemployed” in any week if the employee works less than their usual weekly hours of work for the employee’s regular employer, as the result of the regular employer’s participation in a work sharing plan that meets the requirements of this section and has been approved by the director, pursuant to which the employer, in lieu of layoff, reduces employment and stabilizes the workforce.

clauses.title: What an Employer's Work Sharing Plan Application Must Contain
clauses.body: An employer wishing to participate in the work sharing program submits a signed written plan to the director for approval, using an application form the director develops. Among other required content, the application must identify the affected unit and the usual weekly hours of work for its employees, and state the specific percentage by which those hours will be reduced during all weeks the plan covers — a percentage the statute confines to a range of not less than 10 percent and not more than 60 percent. The application must also include an effective date and duration, which cannot extend beyond the end of the 12th full calendar month after the plan's effective date.
clauses.gap: This is California's Shared Work (work sharing) statute, Unemployment Insurance Code section 1279.5, used as evidence of what the statute itself provides for an employer that chooses to submit a plan to the Employment Development Department — not a claim that any specific employer's workforce reduction, or any specific employee's reduced hours, actually is, or is not, covered by an approved work sharing plan. This information sheet does not itself submit, approve, disapprove, modify, or revoke any work sharing plan, and it does not determine that any employer's or employee's own circumstances satisfy this section. No case law is cited in this clause: the topic is governed almost entirely by this statutory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and a CourtListener search attempted this session for California appellate decisions construing section 1279.5 returned a 429 rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) before it could complete, so no case law is cited here rather than relied on from memory. The quoted text is one requirement among the nine listed in subdivision (c) of section 1279.5; this clause does not quote the other eight (for example, the required certifications about continuing health and retirement benefits, and about the reduction being in lieu of layoffs), though the body text above summarizes the duration cap from a separate paragraph of the same subdivision. The 10-to-60-percent range is a hard statutory boundary: a plan proposing a reduction outside that range does not fit within what section 1279.5 authorizes the director to approve, and this clause does not address what, if anything, an employer could do about a workforce reduction outside that range.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program
citations.quote: A requirement that the employer identify, in the application, the usual weekly hours of work for employees in the affected unit and the specific percentage by which their hours will be reduced during all weeks covered by the plan. The percentage of reduction of usual weekly hours of work for which a work sharing plan may be approved shall not be less than 10 percent or more than 60 percent.

clauses.title: The Director's 10-Working-Day Decision Deadline and the Employer's 20-Day Appeal Window
clauses.body: Once a completed work sharing plan application is received, the director must approve or disapprove it in writing, and communicate that decision to the employer, no later than the close of business on the 10th working day afterward. A disapproval must clearly identify the reasons for it. An employer then has 20 days to submit a request for review of a disapproved plan to a work sharing administrator the director designates for that purpose; that administrator's decision on review is final, though the employer may submit a different plan application afterward.
clauses.gap: This is California's Shared Work (work sharing) statute, Unemployment Insurance Code section 1279.5, used as evidence of what the statute itself provides for an employer that chooses to submit a plan to the Employment Development Department — not a claim that any specific employer's workforce reduction, or any specific employee's reduced hours, actually is, or is not, covered by an approved work sharing plan. This information sheet does not itself submit, approve, disapprove, modify, or revoke any work sharing plan, and it does not determine that any employer's or employee's own circumstances satisfy this section. No case law is cited in this clause: the topic is governed almost entirely by this statutory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and a CourtListener search attempted this session for California appellate decisions construing section 1279.5 returned a 429 rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) before it could complete, so no case law is cited here rather than relied on from memory. The statute does not state what happens, or what remedy an employer has, if the director simply fails to act within the 10-working-day window — this clause does not resolve that silence. Nor does it state a standard the work sharing administrator must apply on review beyond "decision ... shall be final"; the statute does not describe the scope or grounds of that review.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program
citations.quote: The director shall approve or disapprove a work sharing plan in writing by the close of business no later than 10 working days from the date the completed plan is received and communicate the decision to the employer. A decision disapproving the plan shall clearly identify the reasons for the disapproval. Within 20 days, the employer may submit a request for review of the disapproved work sharing plan to the director’s work sharing administrator, whom the director shall designate for this purpose.

clauses.title: Plan Duration, Employer Termination, and the Director's Revocation Power
clauses.body: An approved work sharing plan expires on the date stated in its notice of approval — either the end of the 12th full calendar month after its effective date, or an earlier date the employer and director mutually agree on. Separately, an employer may terminate its own plan at any time on written notice to the director, and may apply to renew a plan within 10 days after a previously approved plan expires. The director, for the director's own part, may revoke approval of a plan for good cause at any time, by a written order specifying the reasons and effective date of the revocation.
clauses.gap: This is California's Shared Work (work sharing) statute, Unemployment Insurance Code section 1279.5, used as evidence of what the statute itself provides for an employer that chooses to submit a plan to the Employment Development Department — not a claim that any specific employer's workforce reduction, or any specific employee's reduced hours, actually is, or is not, covered by an approved work sharing plan. This information sheet does not itself submit, approve, disapprove, modify, or revoke any work sharing plan, and it does not determine that any employer's or employee's own circumstances satisfy this section. No case law is cited in this clause: the topic is governed almost entirely by this statutory text rather than by litigated interpretation, and a CourtListener search attempted this session for California appellate decisions construing section 1279.5 returned a 429 rate-limit error (125 requests/day exhausted) before it could complete, so no case law is cited here rather than relied on from memory. The two quotations below are drawn from adjacent subdivisions of the same statutory section — (e) on expiration and (f) on revocation — and are presented together as provisions from one source, not as independently corroborating sources. The statute's list of what counts as "good cause" for revocation is illustrative, not exhaustive (it "includes, but is not limited to" four listed examples), so this clause cannot state a complete or closed list of what would justify revocation.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program
citations.quote: The plan shall expire on the date specified in the notice of approval, which shall be either the date at the end of the 12th full calendar month after its effective date or an earlier date mutually agreed upon by the employer and the director.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1279.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code, Shared Work Program
citations.quote: The director may revoke approval of a work sharing plan for good cause at any time. The revocation order shall be in writing and shall specify the reasons for the revocation and the date the revocation is effective.

clauses.title: Individual Employee Eligibility and the Weekly Compensation Formula
clauses.body: An individual employee is eligible for work sharing compensation for a given week only if the employee is monetarily eligible for unemployment compensation generally, is not otherwise disqualified, is employed as a member of an affected unit under a plan approved before that week and in effect for it, and remains available for the employee's usual hours of work with the work sharing employer (which can include director-approved skills training). The amount of work sharing compensation payable for a week is set by formula: the regular weekly unemployment compensation amount for a week of total unemployment, multiplied by the percentage reduction in the employee's usual weekly hours of work under the plan.

clauses.title: The Combined-Benefits Cap and the 52-Week Limit on Work Sharing Compensation
clauses.body: Work sharing compensation is not paid on top of an employee's regular unemployment compensation entitlement without limit. Within a benefit year, an employee's combined work sharing compensation and regular unemployment compensation cannot exceed the maximum entitlement already established for regular unemployment compensation, and an employee cannot be paid work sharing benefits for more than 52 weeks under a work sharing plan. Work sharing compensation paid to an employee is deducted from that employee's maximum regular-unemployment-compensation entitlement for the benefit year.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
California State Trademark Registration Information Sheet — Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet relates to {{applicantName}}, having a business address at {{principalOfficeAddress}}, concerning the mark described as {{trademarkDescription}}, used on or in connection with {{goodsServicesDescription}}, claimed to have first been used anywhere on {{firstUseDate}} and first used in California on {{firstUseInCaliforniaDate}}. It describes California's own state-level trademark and service mark registration system — the Model State Trademark Law, codified at California Business and Professions Code Sections 14200 through 14272 and administered by the California Secretary of State — including who may apply, what an application must contain, the grounds on which the Secretary of State may refuse registration, the examination and priority procedure, what a certificate of registration shows and proves, the five-year renewable term, the grounds on which a registration may be canceled, and how this state registration system relates to a federal trademark registration and to common-law trademark rights. This document is not this project's Trademark Registration (USPTO Application) Information Sheet, Trademark Assignment Agreement Information Sheet, or Fictitious Business Name (DBA) Statement document. Those documents concern, respectively: registration of a mark with the United States Patent and Trademark Office under the federal Lanham Act; the assignment of an already-registered mark (state or federal); and a county-level filing that discloses the true owner of a business operating under a name other than its legal name, which identifies a business, not a source of goods or services. A California state trademark or service mark registration is a further and separate filing, made with the California Secretary of State rather than a county recorder or the USPTO, and it protects a word, name, symbol, or device used to identify and distinguish goods or services — not a business's legal or fictitious name as such, though the same wording can sometimes serve both functions. A business can hold a fictitious business name statement, a federal trademark registration, both, or neither, and can separately hold, or not hold, a California state trademark or service mark registration; none of these filings substitutes for any other. This information sheet is informational only. It does not itself register any mark for {{applicantName}} or any other person, does not determine whether {{trademarkDescription}} qualifies for registration under California or federal law, and does not constitute legal advice.

clauses.title: The Model State Trademark Law and What Counts as a Registrable Mark
clauses.body: California's state-level trademark statute is formally named by its own text: the chapter of the Business and Professions Code governing state registration "shall be known and may be cited as the Model State Trademark Law." That chapter defines a "trademark," for purposes of state registration, as any word, name, symbol, or device, or any combination of those, used by a person to identify and distinguish that person's goods from goods manufactured or sold by others and to indicate the source of the goods, even where that source is not otherwise known to the public. A parallel, separately worded definition in the same section covers a "service mark" on the same terms but for services rather than goods, and further provides that titles, character names, and other distinctive features of radio or television programs may themselves be registered as service marks even though they, or the programs carrying them, may advertise a sponsor's goods. The statute's own defined term "mark" is broader still: it includes any trademark or service mark entitled to registration under this chapter, whether or not it has actually been registered.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only two of California Business and Professions Code Section 14202's fifteen lettered definitions — subdivision (a) ("trademark") and, by paraphrase rather than direct quotation, subdivision (b) ("service mark") — and Section 14200's short-title sentence; both cited sections are subdivisions of, or the whole of, two independently enacted sections of the same chapter, not a single unified definitions list restated here in full. Section 14202 separately defines "mark," "trade name," "person," "applicant," "registrant," "use," "abandoned," "secretary," "dilution," "dilution by blurring," "dilution by tarnishment," "counterfeit," and "comparative commercial advertising," none of which is quoted in this clause even where a later clause in this document uses the term (for example, "abandoned" appears in the refusal-grounds and cancellation clauses below without restating this section's own definition of it). This clause does not determine whether the specific mark described in this document in fact functions as a "trademark" or "service mark" as statutorily defined, which depends on facts about actual use that this document does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14200
citations.cite: Model State Trademark Law, short title
citations.quote: This chapter shall be known and may be cited as the Model State Trademark Law.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14202(a)
citations.cite: California's statutory definition of "trademark" for state registration
citations.quote: “Trademark” means any word, name, symbol, or device, or any combination thereof, used by a person to identify and distinguish the goods of that person, including a unique product, from those manufactured or sold by others, and to indicate the source of the goods, even if that source is unknown.

clauses.title: Registration Requires an Underlying "Use" of the Mark, Statutorily Defined
clauses.body: State registration under the Model State Trademark Law is built on an underlying, statutorily defined concept of "use." The statute defines "use" to mean the bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade, and specifically excludes a use made merely to reserve a right in a mark. The same section goes on to specify, in two further subdivisions, what counts as "in use" for goods (placement on the goods, their containers, displays, or tags, or on associated documents where physical placement is impracticable, coupled with the goods being sold or transported in commerce in California) and for services (use or display in the sale or advertising of services that are themselves rendered in California). That in-state-rendering and in-state-commerce framing is why an application under this chapter calls for two separate dates — the date of first use anywhere and the date of first use specifically in California — addressed in the application-contents clause below.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the lead sentence of Section 14202(h)'s "use" definition; the same subdivision's two further, numbered sub-parts describing in-state use for goods versus services are paraphrased here, not quoted verbatim, and a reader relying on this clause for the precise statutory wording of either sub-part should consult the section directly. This clause does not determine whether any specific, described use of the mark on or in connection with the goods or services identified in this document meets this statutory definition, which is a fact-specific determination this document does not make. Separately, Section 14202(i) defines "abandoned" to include, among other things, nonuse for two consecutive years as prima facie evidence of abandonment; that definition bears directly on the durability of any use-based rights described in this clause but is not quoted here.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14202(h)
citations.cite: California's statutory definition of "use" for purposes of state trademark registration
citations.quote: “Use” means the bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade, and not made merely to reserve a right in a mark.

clauses.title: Statutory Grounds on Which the Secretary of State May Refuse to Register a Mark
clauses.body: The Model State Trademark Law lists six independent criteria, any one of which bars registration of an otherwise-distinguishing mark. As enacted, the list includes marks that consist of or comprise immoral, deceptive, or scandalous matter; marks that disparage or falsely suggest a connection with a person, institution, belief, or national symbol, or that bring any of those into contempt or disrepute; flags, coats of arms, or other governmental insignia; a living individual's name, signature, or portrait used without that individual's written consent; marks that are merely descriptive, deceptively misdescriptive, primarily geographically descriptive or misdescriptive, or primarily merely a surname (each subject to a statutory exception where the mark has become distinctive of the applicant's goods or services through five years of continuous use in California); and, as the statute's own words provide, a mark that "consists of or comprises a mark that so resembles a mark registered in this state or a mark or trade name previously used by another and not abandoned, as to be likely, when used on or in connection with the goods or services of the applicant, to cause confusion or mistake, or to deceive."
clauses.gap: This clause quotes verbatim only the sixth of Section 14205's six lettered refusal criteria, subdivision (f) (the likelihood-of-confusion ground); the other five are paraphrased, not quoted. More significantly, the first two criteria as written — barring marks that consist of or comprise "immoral, deceptive, or scandalous matter" (subdivision (a)) or matter that may "disparage" persons, institutions, or beliefs (subdivision (b)) — track language nearly identical to federal Lanham Act provisions that the United States Supreme Court held unconstitutional as viewpoint-based restrictions on speech in Matal v. Tam (2017) (the disparagement bar) and Iancu v. Brunetti (2019) (the "immoral or scandalous" bar). This document did not verify either of those decisions, or any California case addressing this state statute's own disparaging/immoral/scandalous language, against a primary source this session: CourtListener's search tool returned a rate-limit error ("429—Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") when queried for this topic, and no case-law citation is included anywhere in this document as a result. This clause should therefore not be read as confirming that Section 14205(a) or (b), as written on the books, is currently enforced by the Secretary of State as written; it reports only the statutory text found at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, not any judicial narrowing or invalidation of it.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14205(f)
citations.cite: grounds for refusing registration of a mark — likelihood of confusion with a previously registered or used mark or trade name
citations.quote: It consists of or comprises a mark that so resembles a mark registered in this state or a mark or trade name previously used by another and not abandoned, as to be likely, when used on or in connection with the goods or services of the applicant, to cause confusion or mistake, or to deceive.

clauses.title: What a State Trademark Application Must Set Forth, Including Two Separate Use Dates
clauses.body: A person who uses a mark may file an application for its registration with the Secretary of State, on a form the Secretary prescribes, setting forth specified information, including the applicant's name and business address, the goods or services and the manner in which the mark is used on or in connection with them, a statement of the applicant's ownership and belief that no other person has a superior right to use the mark, and, as the statute specifically requires, "the date on which the mark was first used anywhere and the date when it was first used in this state by the applicant or a predecessor in interest." The application must include a declaration of accuracy, and the statute attaches a specific consequence to a knowingly false declaration: a person who "willfully states as true in the declaration a material fact that he or she knows to be false" is subject to a civil penalty of up to $10,000, enforceable in an action brought by a public prosecutor, and the statute requires that the declarant be informed of this penalty in writing. The Secretary may also require a statement of any related United States Patent and Trademark Office filing, a drawing of the mark, three specimens showing the mark as actually used, the application fee, and, if the mark is in a language other than English, a certified English translation.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes two of Section 14207's several requirements — the dual first-use dates in subdivision (a)(3) and the false-declaration penalty in subdivision (d) — and paraphrases the rest; both citations are subdivisions of the same enacted section, not independent statutory sources. This clause does not itself state whether the first-use-anywhere and first-use-in-California dates given in this document would in fact satisfy the statute's dual-date requirement, and does not confirm whether the Secretary of State, as a matter of current administrative practice, still requires every item this 2008-enacted text describes (for example, the specimen and drawing requirements) exactly as written, since this document verified only the statutory text itself, not any current Secretary of State regulation, form instructions, or filing-fee schedule, none of which this document reproduces.

citations.quote: The date on which the mark was first used anywhere and the date when it was first used in this state by the applicant or a predecessor in interest.

citations.quote: If the person signing the declaration willfully states as true in the declaration a material fact that he or she knows to be false, he or she shall be subject to a civil penalty of not more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000).

clauses.title: Examination, Priority Between Concurrent Applications, and the Mandamus Remedy for a Refusal
clauses.body: After an application is filed and the fee paid, the Secretary of State may cause the application to be examined for conformity with the Model State Trademark Law, may request additional information or amendments, and, if the applicant is found not entitled to registration, must advise the applicant of the reasons and allow a specified period to reply or amend; this reply-and-reexamine cycle may repeat until the Secretary finally refuses registration or the applicant fails to respond, at which point the application is deemed abandoned. Where the Secretary is concurrently processing more than one application for the same or a confusingly similar mark covering the same or related goods or services, the statute resolves the conflict by filing date: "the secretary shall grant priority to the applications in the order of filing," with any rejected applicant then left to bring a statutory cancellation action against the prior-filed registrant. If the Secretary finally refuses registration, the statute gives the applicant a specific judicial remedy rather than an administrative appeal within the Secretary's own office: "the applicant may seek a writ of mandamus to compel registration," which "may be granted, but without costs to the secretary, on proof that all statements in the application are true and that the mark is otherwise entitled to registration."
clauses.gap: This clause's two citations are drawn from two subdivisions of the same enacted section, Section 14209(f) and (g), not independent statutory sources. The mandamus remedy described here runs against the Secretary of State's refusal to register; this clause does not describe, and this document does not separately address, any private right of action a competing mark owner might have to challenge a registration once issued, which is instead addressed by the cancellation clause below. This clause also does not state the ordinary time limit, if any, within which a mandamus petition must be filed following a final refusal, which this document did not locate in the text of this chapter.

citations.quote: In the instance of applications concurrently being processed by the secretary seeking registration of the same or confusingly similar marks for the same or related goods or services, the secretary shall grant priority to the applications in the order of filing.

A writ may be granted, but without costs to the secretary, on proof that all statements in the application are true and that the mark is otherwise entitled to registration.

clauses.title: The Certificate of Registration: What It States and What It Proves in a California Court
clauses.body: Once an applicant has complied with the chapter's requirements, the statute directs that "the secretary shall cause a certificate of registration to be issued and delivered to the applicant," under the Secretary's signature and the seal of the state, showing the registrant's name and business address, the claimed dates of first use anywhere and first use in California, the class and description of the goods or services, a reproduction of the mark, and the registration date and term. The statute then gives that certificate a specific evidentiary role in state court: "any certificate of registration issued by the secretary under the provisions of this chapter or a copy thereof duly certified by the secretary shall be admissible in evidence as competent and sufficient proof of the registration of the mark in any action or judicial proceeding in any court of this state."
clauses.gap: This clause's two citations are drawn from two subdivisions of the same enacted section, Section 14215(a) and (b), not independent statutory sources. The statutory text quoted here makes the certificate proof of the fact of registration itself; it does not, on its own quoted terms, state that the certificate is prima facie evidence of the mark's validity, of the registrant's ownership, or of an exclusive right to use the mark in commerce — evidentiary presumptions that a different statute, the federal Lanham Act, expressly attaches to a federal registration certificate under 15 U.S.C. Section 1057(b), which this project's Trademark Registration (USPTO Application) Information Sheet document addresses and which this state-law clause does not restate or extend to state registration.

clauses.title: Five-Year Renewable Term
clauses.body: A state registration is time-limited and must be affirmatively renewed to continue. The statute provides that "a registration of mark pursuant to this chapter shall be effective for a term of five years from the date of registration and, upon application filed within six months prior to the expiration of the term, in a manner complying with the requirements of the secretary, the registration may be renewed for a like term from the end of the expiring term," accompanied by a renewal fee. The statute further provides that "a registration may be renewed for successive periods of five years in like manner," so that a registration can in principle be kept in force indefinitely through repeated five-year renewals. Every renewal application, whether of a registration made under this chapter or one carried over from a prior state trademark act, must include a verified statement that the mark has been and is still in use, together with a specimen showing that actual use.
clauses.gap: This clause's two citations are drawn from two subdivisions of the same enacted section, Section 14217(a) and (b), not independent statutory sources. The quoted text states a six-month pre-expiration renewal-filing window; this document did not locate, within this chapter's text, any express grace period or reinstatement procedure for a registration that lapses because no renewal application was filed within that window, and this clause does not state what becomes of an unrenewed registration beyond the fact that Section 14230, addressed in a separate clause below, lists a registration "not renewed in accordance with the provisions of this chapter" as one ground for cancellation.

citations.quote: A registration of mark pursuant to this chapter shall be effective for a term of five years from the date of registration and, upon application filed within six months prior to the expiration of the term, in a manner complying with the requirements of the secretary, the registration may be renewed for a like term from the end of the expiring term.

clauses.title: Grounds on Which the Secretary of State Must Cancel a Registration
clauses.body: The statute lists several distinct grounds requiring the Secretary of State to cancel a registration, in whole or in part: a voluntary request from the registrant or record assignee; a court finding that the registered mark has been abandoned, that the registrant is not the mark's owner, that the registration was granted improperly or obtained fraudulently, or that the mark has become the generic name for the goods or services it covers; a court-ordered cancellation on any ground; a dishonored payment check, following notice and a further 30-day cure period; and a registration issued in error within the preceding six months in violation of the confusing-similarity refusal ground. A separate, non-discretionary ground applies simply where a registration was "not renewed in accordance with the provisions of this chapter." The statute also addresses the specific interaction between a state registration and a prior federal one covering the same mark: where a state registration is challenged as confusingly similar to a mark registered earlier with the United States Patent and Trademark Office, "should the registrant prove that the registrant is the owner of a concurrent registration of a mark in the United States Patent and Trademark Office covering an area including this state, the registration hereunder shall not be canceled for that area of the state."
clauses.gap: This clause's two citations are drawn from two subdivisions of the same enacted section, Section 14230(b) and the proviso within subdivision (c)(6), not independent statutory sources; several of the other listed cancellation grounds are paraphrased rather than quoted. The federal-registration proviso quoted here protects a registrant only for "that area of the state" covered by the registrant's own concurrent federal registration — it does not, on its quoted terms, immunize the state registration statewide, and this clause does not attempt to state how "area" is determined or proven in a cancellation proceeding, which this document did not locate addressed elsewhere in this chapter's text.

citations.quote: All registrations granted under this chapter and not renewed in accordance with the provisions of this chapter.

citations.quote: However, should the registrant prove that the registrant is the owner of a concurrent registration of a mark in the United States Patent and Trademark Office covering an area including this state, the registration hereunder shall not be canceled for that area of the state.

clauses.title: State Registration's Own Statement of Its Relationship to the Federal Trademark System
clauses.body: The Model State Trademark Law states its own intended relationship to the federal trademark system. The statute recites a legislative intent "to provide a system of state trademark registration and protection substantially consistent with the federal system of trademark registration and protection under the Trademark Act of 1946 (15 U.S.C. Sec. 1051 et seq.), as amended," and directs that federal case law construing the Lanham Act "should be examined as nonbinding authority for interpreting and construing this chapter" — meaning federal decisions inform, but do not control, how a California court or the Secretary of State applies this state statute. A California state registration remains, on this statute's own terms, a separate legal act from any federal registration or application with the United States Patent and Trademark Office; obtaining one does not itself obtain, or substitute for, the other. Separately from this state's relationship to the federal system, this chapter also expressly preserves common-law trademark rights that arise from actual use without any registration at all, a point addressed, with its own citation to this chapter, by this project's existing Trademark Infringement — Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet document and not repeated here.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the first sentence of Section 14272; the statute's directive to examine federal case law as "nonbinding authority" runs in one direction — it tells a court how to interpret this state statute by reference to federal case law — and does not itself mean that a state registration confers any federal right, or that a federal registration confers any right under this state chapter. This clause does not identify, and this document does not cite, any actual California case applying Section 14272's interpretive cross-reference, because CourtListener's case-law search returned a rate-limit error ("429—Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") when queried this session, and no case law is cited anywhere in this document as a result. This clause also does not restate or re-cite Section 14259's separate preservation of common-law trademark rights, since that specific point, quoting that same section, already appears verbatim in this project's existing Trademark Infringement — Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet document (clause id trademarkcd_ca_common_law_rights); a reader is directed there rather than to a duplicate restatement here.

citations.cite: legislative intent that this chapter be substantially consistent with, and interpreted with reference to, the federal Lanham Act
citations.quote: The intent of this chapter is to provide a system of state trademark registration and protection substantially consistent with the federal system of trademark registration and protection under the Trademark Act of 1946 (15 U.S.C. Sec. 1051 et seq.), as amended.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes two related but distinct California job protections for an employee who serves as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel: (1) the right under Labor Code § 230.3 not to be discharged or discriminated against for taking time off to perform actual emergency duty, which applies regardless of employer size but does not apply to certain public safety or emergency medical services employers; and (2) the separate right under Labor Code § 230.4, available only at employers with 50 or more employees, to take up to 14 days per calendar year of leave for fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training. It does not cover unrelated leave topics such as jury duty, witness leave, or military leave under USERRA, which are addressed in separate information sheets.

clauses.title: Who Is Covered: Volunteer Firefighter, Emergency Rescue Personnel, Health Care Provider
clauses.body: Labor Code § 230.3 protects an employee who serves as a "volunteer firefighter," a "reserve peace officer," or "emergency rescue personnel." "Volunteer firefighter" has the same meaning as "volunteer" in Government Code § 50952, which defines it as a person registered as a volunteer member of a regularly organized fire department. "Emergency rescue personnel" is defined broadly to include any officer, employee, or member of a federal, state, or local fire department or firefighting agency, a sheriff's department, a police department, a private fire department, or a state-sponsored disaster medical response entity — whether that person is a volunteer, partly paid, or fully paid — while actually engaged in providing emergency services as defined by Health & Safety Code § 1799.107. A "health care provider" is any person licensed or certified under Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code, or under the Osteopathic Initiative Act or the Chiropractic Initiative Act.
clauses.gap: The definition of "emergency rescue personnel" cross-references Health & Safety Code § 1799.107 for the meaning of "emergency services," and this document did not independently fetch and verify the text of that section — so it does not state, beyond the statutory label, exactly which activities count as "actually engaged in providing emergency services." The definition covers a person only while actually engaged in providing those emergency services, meaning off-duty volunteer-department membership without an active emergency response or training event is not, by this text alone, established as covered conduct under § 230.3(a). Both the "volunteer firefighter" and "emergency rescue personnel" definitions were verified from the same fetched-and-confirmed copy of Labor Code § 230.3(d); the Government Code § 50952 definition was independently fetched and confirmed from a separate source page.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3(d)(1)-(2), definitions of volunteer firefighter and emergency rescue personnel
citations.quote: (d) (1) For purposes of this section, “volunteer firefighter” shall have the same meaning as the term “volunteer” in Section 50952 of the Government Code.(2) For purposes of this section, “emergency rescue personnel” means any person who is an officer, employee, or member of a fire department or fire protection or firefighting agency of the federal government, the State of California, a city, county, city and county, district, or other public or municipal corporation or political subdivision of this state, or of a sheriff’s department, police department, or a private fire department, or of a disaster medical response entity sponsored or requested by this state, whether that person is a volunteer or partly paid or fully paid, while he or she is actually engaged in providing emergency services as defined by Section 1799.107 of the Health and Safety Code.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 50952 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Gov. Code § 50952(p), definition of "volunteer"
citations.quote: (p) “Volunteer” means a person registered as a volunteer member of a regularly organized fire department as defined in subdivision (k).

clauses.title: Emergency Duty Time-Off Notice
clauses.body:
{{employeeName}} provides this notice to {{companyName}} of time off taken or requested under Labor Code § 230.3 to perform emergency duty for {{respondingAgencyName}}, in the role checked below.

☐ Volunteer firefighter
☐ Reserve peace officer
☐ Emergency rescue personnel

Dates of emergency duty: {{serviceStartDate}} through {{serviceEndDate}}
Nature of the emergency duty performed (brief description): _______________________________________________
If {{employeeName}} is a health care provider, date this employee notified {{companyName}} of their designation as emergency rescue personnel: _______________
Date this notice is given to {{companyName}}: _______________

clauses.title: Protection From Discharge or Discrimination for Emergency Duty
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 230.3(a), an employer shall not discharge or in any manner discriminate against an employee for taking time off to perform emergency duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel. This protection applies regardless of the employer's size, unlike the training-leave right described elsewhere in this document, which applies only at employers with 50 or more employees.
clauses.gap: The statute's text does not itself state any cap on the number of days of emergency-duty time off that is protected, in contrast to the 14-day annual cap the same statutory scheme places on training leave under § 230.4(a); this document does not assert that emergency-duty absences are protected without any limit, only that the verified text of § 230.3(a) does not state a numerical limit. The statute is also silent on whether time off under this subdivision must be paid by the employer, and this document does not assert that it is.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3(a), anti-discrimination protection for emergency duty absence
citations.quote: 230.3. (a) An employer shall not discharge or in any manner discriminate against an employee for taking time off to perform emergency duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel.

clauses.title: Notice Duty for Employees Who Are Health Care Providers
clauses.body: An employee who is a health care provider must notify their employer at the time the employee becomes designated as emergency rescue personnel, and again when the employee is notified that they will be deployed as a result of that designation.
clauses.gap: This notice duty, verified from Labor Code § 230.3(c)(2), applies by its own terms only to an employee who meets the statute's separate definition of "health care provider" (licensed or certified under Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code, or under the Osteopathic Initiative Act or the Chiropractic Initiative Act); this document does not assert that any other volunteer firefighter, reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel has an equivalent statutory notice duty, because the verified text imposes this specific duty only on the health-care-provider subset.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3(c)(2), health care provider notice duty
citations.quote: (2) An employee who is a health care provider shall notify his or her employer at the time the employee becomes designated as emergency rescue personnel and when the employee is notified that he or she will be deployed as a result of that designation.

clauses.title: Exception for Certain Public Safety and Emergency Medical Services Employers
clauses.body: The protections in Labor Code § 230.3(a) and (b) do not apply to any public safety agency or provider of emergency medical services if, as determined by that employer, the employee's absence would hinder the availability of public safety or emergency medical services.
clauses.gap: This exception applies only when the employer itself is a public safety agency or an emergency medical services provider, and the statute leaves the hindrance determination to that employer's own judgment ("as determined by the employer") without stating any external standard, review process, or documentation requirement this document could verify; this document does not describe how, if at all, an employee could challenge that employer determination, because the verified statutory text does not itself specify one.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3(c)(1), exception for certain public safety and EMS employers
citations.quote: (c) (1) Subdivisions (a) and (b) of this section shall not apply to any public safety agency or provider of emergency medical services if, as determined by the employer, the employee’s absence would hinder the availability of public safety or emergency medical services.

clauses.title: Remedies for Violation of the Emergency Duty Protection
clauses.body: An employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment because the employee took time off to perform emergency duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts. An employer who willfully refuses to rehire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee or former employee who has been determined eligible for rehiring or promotion through a grievance procedure, arbitration, or hearing authorized by law is guilty of a misdemeanor.
clauses.gap: This clause, verified from Labor Code § 230.3(b), does not itself describe the procedural mechanism (such as a Labor Commissioner complaint) by which an employee obtains this reinstatement and reimbursement; § 230.3 does not contain an explicit cross-reference to Labor Code § 98.7 the way § 230.4(c) does for the separate training-leave right, so this document does not assert that the § 98.7 complaint procedure described elsewhere in this document applies to a § 230.3 emergency-duty violation, only that it applies to a § 230.4 training-leave violation, where the statute expressly says so.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.3(b), reinstatement, reimbursement, and misdemeanor penalty
citations.quote: (b) An employee who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or in any other manner discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment by his or her employer because the employee has taken time off to perform emergency duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel shall be entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer. Any employer who willfully refuses to rehire, promote, or otherwise restore an employee or former employee who has been determined to be eligible for rehiring or promotion by a grievance procedure, arbitration, or hearing authorized by law, is guilty of a misdemeanor.

clauses.title: Fire, Law Enforcement, or Emergency Rescue Training Leave Request
Right to Training Leave at Employers With 50 or More Employees
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 230.4(a), an employee who performs duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or emergency rescue personnel, and who works for an employer employing 50 or more employees, must be permitted to take temporary leaves of absence, not to exceed an aggregate of 14 days per calendar year, for the purpose of engaging in fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training.
clauses.gap: This training-leave right is expressly limited to employers employing 50 or more employees; the verified text does not extend it to smaller employers, and this document does not independently address how "50 or more employees" is counted (for example, whether part-time employees, employees at affiliated entities, or a rolling headcount are counted), because the verified text of § 230.4 does not itself define that counting method. The 14-day figure is an aggregate annual cap across all training leave taken under this subdivision in a calendar year, not a per-training-event allowance, and the statute does not state whether this leave must be paid.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.4 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.4(a), training leave for employers with 50 or more employees
citations.quote: 230.4. (a) An employee who performs duty as a volunteer firefighter, a reserve peace officer, or as emergency rescue personnel, as defined in Section 230.3, and who works for an employer employing 50 or more employees, shall be permitted to take temporary leaves of absence, not to exceed an aggregate of 14 days per calendar year, for the purpose of engaging in fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training.

clauses.title: Remedies for Violation of the Training Leave Right
clauses.body: An employee who works for an employer employing 50 or more employees, and who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment because the employee took time off for fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training under § 230.4(a), is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts.
clauses.gap: Unlike the parallel emergency-duty remedy in § 230.3(b), § 230.4(b) does not itself contain a misdemeanor penalty for an employer's willful refusal to reinstate; this document does not assert that a comparable criminal penalty applies to a § 230.4 training-leave violation, because the verified text of § 230.4(b) does not state one. This remedy is available only to an employee at an employer employing 50 or more employees, consistent with the size-limited scope of the underlying right.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.4 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.4(b), reinstatement and reimbursement remedy
citations.quote: (b) An employee who works for an employer employing 50 or more employees who is discharged, threatened with discharge, demoted, suspended, or in any other manner discriminated against in the terms and conditions of employment by his or her employer because the employee has taken time off to engage in fire, law enforcement, or emergency rescue training as provided in subdivision (a), is entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the acts of the employer.

clauses.title: Filing a Training-Leave Complaint With the Labor Commissioner
clauses.body: An employee seeking reinstatement and reimbursement under § 230.4 may file a complaint with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement under Labor Code § 98.7, and upon receiving that type of complaint the Labor Commissioner proceeds as provided in § 98.7. Under § 98.7(a)(1), a person who believes they were discharged or otherwise discriminated against in violation of a law under the Labor Commissioner's jurisdiction may file a complaint with the division within one year after the violation occurred, and that one-year period may be extended for good cause.
clauses.gap: Labor Code § 230.4(c) expressly cross-references the § 98.7 complaint procedure for a training-leave violation; § 230.3 does not contain the same cross-reference, so this document does not assert that the § 98.7 procedure is the exclusive or even an applicable route for an emergency-duty violation under § 230.3, only that it is the route the statute names for a training-leave violation under § 230.4. Section 98.7 itself is a general Labor Commissioner complaint procedure that applies to many Labor Code protections beyond this one, and this document does not describe those other uses; it covers only the one-year filing deadline and its good-cause extension, not the full investigation, hearing, injunctive-relief, and appeal procedures § 98.7 also establishes.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.4 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 230.4(c), cross-reference to the Section 98.7 complaint procedure
citations.quote: (c) An employee seeking reinstatement and reimbursement pursuant to this section may file a complaint with the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement in accordance with Section 98.7 and, upon receipt of this type of complaint, the Labor Commissioner shall proceed as provided in that section.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 98.7 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 98.7(a)(1), one-year filing deadline and good-cause extension
citations.quote: Any person who believes that they have been discharged or otherwise discriminated against in violation of any law under the jurisdiction of the Labor Commissioner may file a complaint with the division within one year after the occurrence of the violation. The one-year period may be extended for good cause.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Support for an Adult Child Incapacitated from Earning a Living Information Sheet concerns {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}, the parents of {{childName}}, in connection with a proceeding pending, or that may be filed, in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes what California's Family Code says about a parent's duty of support toward a child who, regardless of the child's age, is incapacitated from earning a living and without sufficient means — a distinct statutory duty from the ordinary child-support obligation that applies to a minor child or to an unmarried child who has turned 18 and is still a full-time high school student. This information sheet states what the statute says in general terms. It does not determine, calculate, or assert that {{childName}} is or is not incapacitated from earning a living within the meaning of that statute, that either parent owes or does not owe a support duty under it, or what amount of support (if any) would be appropriate; those are matters for the court to decide based on the specific facts, or for {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} to resolve by their own agreement.

clauses.title: The Statutory Duty — Support of a Child Incapacitated from Earning a Living
clauses.body: California's Family Code imposes on each parent of a child an equal responsibility, to the extent of that parent's ability, to maintain their child of whatever age who is incapacitated from earning a living and without sufficient means. This duty is not limited by the child's age; it applies regardless of whether the child has reached adulthood, so long as the child is both incapacitated from earning a living and lacks sufficient means of their own support.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own statutory support duty toward an incapacitated adult child — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific family, and not a claim that the child named in this document, or any other specific person, meets the statutory description. The statute does not itself define "incapacitated from earning a living" or "sufficient means," and this document does not supply definitions for those terms; a CourtListener case-law search for California appellate decisions construing this phrase, attempted during this research, returned a 429 rate-limit response (CourtListener's 125-request daily quota was exhausted) rather than usable results, so this clause rests on the statutory text alone and does not report on how courts have applied it in practice. The source's raw HTML places a non-breaking space (character U+00A0) between the subsection label "(a)" and the word "Each"; that non-breaking space is rendered as a regular space in the quote below, verified against the raw fetched HTML of both User-Agent fetches, which were textually identical.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3910(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: each parent's equal, ability-based duty to support a child of any age who is incapacitated from earning a living and without sufficient means
citations.quote: (a) Each parent of a child has an equal responsibility to maintain, to the extent of their ability, their child of whatever age who is incapacitated from earning a living and without sufficient means.

clauses.title: How This Duty Relates to the Ordinary Duty to Support a Minor Child
clauses.body: The statute creating this incapacitated-adult-child support duty expressly states that it does not limit the separate, ordinary duty of a parent to support a minor child, or an unmarried child who has turned 18, is a full-time high school student, and is not self-supporting, until that child completes the 12th grade or turns 19. The two duties are independent statutory provisions that can apply to the same family at different times or in different circumstances; a family's ordinary minor-child support duty ending because a child has turned 19 or is no longer in high school does not by itself end any separate duty that may exist under the incapacitated-adult-child provision.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California's own Family Code treats the incapacitated-adult-child support duty as a distinct provision layered on top of, not a substitute for, the ordinary minor/high-school-student support duty codified elsewhere in the same chapter (Family Code sections 3900 and 3901) — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case. This document does not restate or re-verify the text of sections 3900 or 3901 themselves (already addressed elsewhere in this corpus); it verifies only this section's own cross-reference to them. The source's raw HTML inserts a line-break-and-tab artifact between the words "3900" and "and 3901" (the point where the official page's underlying paragraph markup wraps); that artifact is rendered as a single regular space in the quote below, verified against the raw fetched HTML of both User-Agent fetches, which were textually identical.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3910(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the incapacitated-adult-child duty does not limit the separate minor/high-school-student support duty
citations.quote: (c) This section does not limit the duty of support under Sections 3900 and 3901.

clauses.title: Court's Option to Direct Payment to a Special Needs Trust
clauses.body: California's Family Code gives the court an option, in a proceeding under this incapacitated-adult-child support provision, to order that a support payment be paid to a special needs trust rather than directly to the adult child or the child's other parent. The statute defines "special needs trust," for this purpose, by cross-reference to specific federal Medicaid-trust provisions and a specific California regulation governing trusts that do not count against certain public-benefit resource limits.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California law gives a family court this specific option — not a claim that a court will exercise it in any particular case, and not a claim about what other states' law provides. This document quotes the statute's own cross-reference to 42 U.S.C. section 1396p(d)(4)(A) and (C) and to California Code of Regulations, title 22, section 50489.9(a)(3) and (4), but this research did not independently fetch or verify the text of either the federal statute or the state regulation; readers should not assume this document has verified what those cross-referenced provisions themselves say, only that Family Code section 3910(b) cites them by this description. This document also does not address the separate body of law (addressed elsewhere in this corpus in an estate-planning context) governing how a special needs trust must be drafted or administered to preserve a beneficiary's eligibility for means-tested public benefits; it addresses only the family court's statutory option to direct a support payment into such a trust.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3910(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the court's option to order a support payment paid to a special needs trust, and the statute's cross-referenced definition of that term
citations.quote: (b) The court may order that a support payment be paid to a special needs trust. For purposes of this section, “special needs trust” means a trust that meets the requirements described in subparagraph (A) or (C) of paragraph (4) of subsection (d) of Section 1396p of Title 42 of the United States Code and paragraph (3) or (4) of subdivision (a) of Section 50489.9 of Title 22 of the California Code of Regulations.

clauses.title: Where This Duty Sits in the Family Code, and Its Recent Amendment
clauses.body: This support duty is codified in its own article of the Family Code — Article 2, "Support of Adult Child" — which today consists of this single section, within the chapter governing a parent's duty to support a child generally. The special-needs-trust payment option described in this document's companion clause is a comparatively recent addition to this section: the version of the statute in effect as of this research was last amended effective January 1, 2025.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of where California places this duty within its own code structure and of when its current text took effect — not a claim about any other state's statutory organization. This research did not fetch or review the pre-amendment version of section 3910 (as it read before the 2024 amendment), so this document does not describe what the special-needs-trust option looked like, or whether it existed at all, before that amendment; it states only that the amendment identified in the quote below is the most recent one reflected on the official legislative information website as of the checked date. A CourtListener search was not separately attempted for this clause; the single CourtListener attempt made for this document's core-duty clause returned a 429 rate-limit response, so no case law confirming or discussing this amendment's legislative history was located or is relied on here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code, Div. 9, Pt. 2, Ch. 1, Art. 2 heading (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: this duty is codified as its own single-section article, titled "Support of Adult Child"
citations.quote: ARTICLE 2. Support of Adult Child [3910- 3910.]

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3910, amendment history note (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the current text was last amended effective January 1, 2025
citations.quote: (Amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 25, Sec. 1. (AB 2397) Effective January 1, 2025.)

clauses.title: Explanatory Note — No Stated Marital-Status Condition in This Provision
clauses.body: This document's companion clause on the core statutory duty quotes the full text of the operative subsection. Readers comparing that text to the separate minor/high-school-student support provision (which by its own terms applies only to an "unmarried" child) may notice that the incapacitated-adult-child provision quoted in this document does not itself state an unmarried-child condition. This document does not interpret what that difference in wording means or does not mean for any specific family's circumstances; it only draws the reader's attention to it as a textual point worth discussing with a court or, where appropriate, a lawyer.

clauses.title: Explanatory Note — Relationship to California's Statewide Child Support Guideline
clauses.body: California's statewide uniform guideline for calculating child support, addressed in this corpus's own guideline child-support and income-determination materials, is generally framed around the support of a minor child (or a child within the extended high-school-student period). This document does not restate that guideline formula, and it does not assert that the guideline formula does or does not apply, in whole or in part, to a support determination under the incapacitated-adult-child provision described in this document. Whether, and how, guideline principles inform a court's exercise of discretion under that separate provision is a legal question this document does not resolve.

clauses.title: Explanatory Note — Possible Interaction with Public Benefits and Conservatorship
clauses.body: An adult child who is incapacitated from earning a living may, depending on individual circumstances, also be a recipient of means-tested public benefits, or may be subject to a probate conservatorship of the person or estate, or both. This document does not describe the rules governing eligibility for any public benefit program, and it does not describe the law governing conservatorship proceedings; those are each addressed, where this corpus addresses them, in separate materials. This document notes only that a support order or a special needs trust under the provision described in this document may need to be considered alongside those other, separate legal frameworks, without stating how any such consideration should come out in a particular family's situation.

clauses.title: Information Commonly Gathered Before Raising This Duty in a Proceeding
clauses.body: Parties who wish to raise the incapacitated-adult-child support duty described in this document, whether by request to a court or by their own agreement, commonly gather information such as: {{childName}}'s current living situation and sources of income or support, if any; documentation bearing on the nature and duration of the incapacity; each parent's current ability to contribute to support, to the extent that is relevant; and, if a special needs trust is under discussion, the trust's name and any trustee already identified ({{trustName}}). Gathering this information does not itself establish that the statutory duty applies; it is simply background information commonly assembled before the question is raised with a court or discussed between the parties.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment — Not a Court Filing
clauses.body:
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{parent1Name}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet is prepared for background use alongside an actual family law proceeding pending, or to be filed, in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It does not itself assert, calculate, or resolve whether {{childName}} is incapacitated from earning a living within the meaning of Family Code section 3910, or what support (if any) is owed; only the court — or {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}'s own written agreement — can do that.]

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California Government Code section 12951, a Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA) provision that limits when {{companyName}} may adopt or enforce a workplace policy restricting which language {{employeeName}}, in the position of {{jobTitle}}, may use on the job. It states facts about what the statute requires, permits, and defines -- the two conditions a language restriction must satisfy, the statute's own definition of "business necessity," and which employers the statute covers -- and it compares the statute to a related, though not identical, federal EEOC guideline on the same subject. This document is informational: it does not evaluate whether any specific policy at {{companyName}} complies with section 12951, and it does not tell {{companyName}} or {{employeeName}} what to do about any particular language-related workplace rule.

clauses.title: Restricting Language Use Is an Unlawful Employment Practice Unless Two Conditions Are Met
clauses.body: California Government Code section 12951(a) states that it is an unlawful employment practice for an employer, as FEHA defines that term, to adopt or enforce a policy that limits or prohibits the use of any language in any workplace, unless both of two conditions the statute itself lists are satisfied. The prohibition is written broadly -- it reaches a policy that "limits or prohibits the use of any language," not only a policy that bans a specific named language -- and it applies to "any workplace," without the statute's own text distinguishing by industry, job duties, or the size of the restriction. The statute's two conditions, addressed in separate clauses of this document, are that the restriction be justified by a business necessity and that the employer have given employees a specific kind of notice about it.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what California law provides -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer or employee, and not a claim that any specific policy at any specific workplace does or does not violate this section. The statute's text does not itself define "workplace" or "any language," and this clause does not attempt to resolve, for example, whether the statute reaches a policy limited to a single work area, a single shift, or written communications as opposed to spoken ones -- no case law construing those terms was located or verified in this research session. This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, section 12951(a); the two conditions it refers to are addressed with their own citations in separate clauses below rather than repeated here.
