citations.cite: California Government Code § 12951(a)
citations.quote: (a) It is an unlawful employment practice for an employer, as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 12926, to adopt or enforce a policy that limits or prohibits the use of any language in any workplace, unless both of the following conditions exist:

clauses.title: First Condition: The Restriction Must Be Justified by a Business Necessity
clauses.body: The first of section 12951(a)'s two conditions is that the language restriction be justified by a business necessity. The statute states this as a one-sentence requirement and separately defines what "business necessity" means for purposes of the section, in the companion clause of the same statute addressed elsewhere in this document. By the statute's own structure, this condition and the notice condition addressed in the next clause are both required -- the statute's introductory sentence uses the word "both," not "either."
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory paragraph, section 12951(a)(1); it does not restate the statute's own definition of "business necessity," which appears in a separate clause below quoting subdivision (b). This clause does not determine whether any specific reason an employer might give for a language restriction meets this statutory standard -- that is a fact-specific inquiry the statute's own text leaves to be applied to particular circumstances, and no case law applying it was located or verified in this research session. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California law -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 12951(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code § 12951(a)(1)
citations.quote: (1) The language restriction is justified by a business necessity.

clauses.title: "Business Necessity" Is Defined by the Statute Itself, in Three Parts
clauses.body: Government Code section 12951(b) defines "business necessity," for purposes of the section, as an overriding legitimate business purpose such that three things are all true: the language restriction is necessary to the safe and efficient operation of the business; the language restriction effectively fulfills the business purpose it is supposed to serve; and there is no alternative practice to the language restriction that would accomplish the business purpose equally well with a lesser discriminatory impact. By its own terms, the definition combines a necessity requirement, an effectiveness requirement, and a least-discriminatory-alternative requirement -- it does not treat a restriction as justified merely because the employer can articulate some legitimate business reason for it.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, section 12951(b); no additional independent source was sought for this specific definition, and no case law applying it to particular facts was located or verified in this research session. The statute does not itself state which party bears the burden of proving or disproving business necessity in a dispute over a specific policy, and this clause does not resolve that question. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California law -- not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific business justification does or does not meet this three-part definition.

citations.quote: (b) For the purposes of this section, “business necessity” means an overriding legitimate business purpose such that the language restriction is necessary to the safe and efficient operation of the business, that the language restriction effectively fulfills the business purpose it is supposed to serve, and there is no alternative practice to the language restriction that would accomplish the business purpose equally well with a lesser discriminatory impact.

clauses.title: Second Condition: Employees Must Be Notified of the Circumstances and Consequences
clauses.body: The second of section 12951(a)'s two conditions is that the employer has notified its employees of the circumstances and the time when the language restriction is required to be observed, and of the consequences for violating it. Read together with the business necessity condition, the statute requires both a substantive justification for the restriction and a specific kind of advance communication about it -- when it applies and what happens if an employee does not comply -- before the restriction can be enforced consistent with this section.

The raw HTML of the fetched leginfo page contains a line-wrap with embedded tab characters in the middle of this paragraph -- between the words "language" and "restriction" -- which this document's citation below reproduces exactly as fetched (verified in the raw HTML on two independent fetches) rather than silently smoothing over; it renders as ordinary whitespace in a browser. clauses.title: Which Employers Section 12951 Reaches: FEHA's General "Five or More" Definition
clauses.body: Section 12951(a) applies to "an employer, as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 12926" -- FEHA's own general definitions section, rather than a definition written specifically for section 12951. That definition states that "employer" includes any person regularly employing five or more persons, or any person acting as an agent of an employer, directly or indirectly, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities, with one stated exception: "employer" does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit.
clauses.gap: This clause combines two citations that are not independent of one another: the cross-reference in section 12951(a) points directly to section 12926(d), and both are part of the same FEHA scheme within the same code. This clause states the statutory text only; it does not determine whether any specific business regularly employs five or more persons within the meaning of this definition, or whether any specific entity falls within the religious-association-or-nonprofit exception. This corpus separately relies on this same definition, section 12926(d), in other documents addressing different FEHA provisions that use the identical "employer" definition -- it is a single shared definitional source across those documents and this one, not independent corroboration for any of them.

clauses.title: Section 12951 Sits Within FEHA's Chapter on Discrimination Prohibited
clauses.body: Government Code section 12951 is codified within Part 2.8 of the Government Code (the Civil Rights Department), Chapter 6 of that part -- captioned "Discrimination Prohibited" -- and within Article 1 of that chapter, captioned "Unlawful Practices, Generally," a span of sections running from 12940 to 12954. Section 12951's own text independently confirms this placement by describing a violation as "an unlawful employment practice," the same phrase FEHA's other unlawful-practices provisions use for conduct such as discriminatory refusal to hire or discharge.

clauses.title: Federal EEOC Guidance Draws a Related, But Not Identical, Line
clauses.body: Separately from California law, a federal EEOC regulation addresses "speak-English-only" workplace rules under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. That regulation, 29 C.F.R. § 1606.7, does not track California's structure exactly: it distinguishes a rule applied "at all times," which the EEOC states it will presume violates Title VII and will closely scrutinize, from a rule applied "only at certain times," which the regulation states an employer may have where the employer can show the rule is justified by business necessity. For a certain-times rule, the regulation adds that if an employer believes it has a business necessity for the rule, the employer should inform its employees of the general circumstances when speaking only in English is required and of the consequences of violating the rule, and states that a failure to effectively notify employees, followed by an adverse action for a rule violation, will be considered by the EEOC as evidence of national-origin discrimination.
clauses.gap: This is a federal regulation, not California statutory law, and this clause does not determine how a specific workplace rule would be analyzed under either body of law, or whether compliance with one necessarily satisfies the other. Unlike California's section 12951, which imposes its business-necessity-and-notice conditions on any policy that "limits or prohibits the use of any language," the EEOC regulation's business-necessity/notice framework by its own terms applies only to a rule applied "at certain times" -- a rule applied "at all times" is instead treated under a separate, stricter presumption in subdivision (a) of the regulation, a distinction California's statute does not draw in its own text. This clause does not address whether any specific employer, position, or language restriction is covered by Title VII at all (which has its own employer-size threshold, not verified or restated here), and no case law applying this EEOC regulation was located or verified in this research session; the regulation's own text was fetched twice independently and found byte-identical, but this research did not independently confirm that the version fetched is free of any since-published amendment beyond what the fetched eCFR page itself shows as current. The eCFR page renders this regulation's text using separate inline HTML elements (a paragraph-number span and a heading span) rather than a single unbroken text node; the quotes below reflect that underlying text with the whitespace between those elements normalized to single spaces, verified against the raw fetched HTML rather than assumed.

clauses.title: Employee Acknowledgment of Receipt
Declaration of Facts Concerning an International Child Abduction Claim
clauses.body: I, {{petitionerName}}, state that {{childName}}'s country of habitual residence immediately before the removal or retention described below was {{childHabitualResidenceCountry}}. On or about {{dateOfRemovalOrRetention}}, {{respondentName}} removed {{childName}} from {{childHabitualResidenceCountry}}, or retained {{childName}} outside of {{childHabitualResidenceCountry}}, in a manner I believe breached rights of custody that I was exercising, or would have been exercising but for the removal or retention, at that time. {{childName}} is currently believed to be located in {{childCurrentCountry}}. This declaration collects the category of facts a petition under the International Child Abduction Remedies Act, 22 U.S.C. § 9003(b), and the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction would need to state; it does not itself constitute that petition, does not itself establish that a removal or retention was wrongful within the meaning of the Convention, and does not itself determine where {{childName}}'s habitual residence was at the relevant time -- only a court, applying 22 U.S.C. § 9003 and the Convention to the facts of a filed case, can make those determinations.

clauses.title: Congressional Findings Behind ICARA, and the Rule That a Return Proceeding Is Not a Custody Case
clauses.body: The International Child Abduction Remedies Act (ICARA), 22 U.S.C. §§ 9001-9011, is the federal statute implementing, within the United States, the 1980 Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. Congress found that "The Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, done at The Hague on October 25, 1980, establishes legal rights and procedures for the prompt return of children who have been wrongfully removed or retained, as well as for securing the exercise of visitation rights." A return proceeding brought under this framework, however, is not a vehicle for deciding who should ultimately have custody of {{childName}}: Congress declared that "The Convention and this chapter empower courts in the United States to determine only rights under the Convention and not the merits of any underlying child custody claims." A court hearing a Convention return petition therefore decides only whether {{childName}} should be returned to {{childHabitualResidenceCountry}} for the courts there to resolve custody -- it does not itself decide custody or visitation.
clauses.gap: This is one federal statute's stated findings and declared purpose (22 U.S.C. § 9001(a)(4) and (b)(4)), not a description of every circumstance in which a court might, in practice, touch on custody-adjacent facts (for example, when assessing a grave-risk defense) while formally deciding only the return question. It also does not address the separate, narrower California statutory framework for preventing an abduction before it happens (Family Code § 3048, covered in this corpus's Child Abduction Prevention Orders document) or the UCCJEA's jurisdictional rules for an ordinary interstate or international custody case that does not involve an alleged wrongful removal or retention (covered in this corpus's Child Custody Jurisdiction (UCCJEA) document) -- a Convention return action is a third, distinct track from both. Both quotes were fetched directly from Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (law.cornell.edu), confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and confirmed programmatically as exact (whitespace-normalized) substrings of the fetched section text.

clauses.title: Who Is a “Petitioner,” a “Respondent,” and What “Rights of Access” Means
clauses.body: ICARA's definitions section, 22 U.S.C. § 9002, fixes the vocabulary used throughout a Convention return or access proceeding. A petitioner is defined as any person who files the court petition: the statute provides that "the term “petitioner” means any person who, in accordance with this chapter, files a petition in court seeking relief under the Convention." The person on the other side is the respondent, defined so that "the term “respondent” means any person against whose interests a petition is filed in court, in accordance with this chapter, which seeks relief under the Convention." Separately, the Convention's second remedy -- distinct from return of the child -- is addressed through what the statute calls “rights of access,” and "the term “rights of access” means visitation rights." These definitions apply to {{petitionerName}} and {{respondentName}} only if and to the extent a court having jurisdiction determines that {{petitionerName}}'s filing qualifies as a petition under this chapter.
clauses.gap: This clause states only three of the nine defined terms in 22 U.S.C. § 9002 (petitioner, respondent, and rights of access); it does not state the statute's separate definitions of “applicant,” “Convention,” “Parent Locator Service,” “person,” “State,” or “United States Central Authority,” though all appear in the same fetched section text. It also does not define -- because § 9002 itself does not define -- the Convention's own substantive terms “wrongful removal or retention,” “habitual residence,” or “rights of custody”; those turn on the Convention's text and on federal case law construing it (addressed, to the extent this document reaches it, in the separate wrongful-removal clause below). clauses.title: State and Federal Courts Share Jurisdiction, and a Petition Is Filed Where the Child Is Located
clauses.body: A Convention return or access petition concerning {{childName}} is not confined to one court system: ICARA provides that "The courts of the States and the United States district courts shall have concurrent original jurisdiction of actions arising under the Convention." That means {{petitionerName}} may generally choose to file in a California superior court or in the appropriate United States district court, subject to that court's own jurisdictional and venue rules. Wherever filed, the petition is filed as an ordinary civil action: "Any person seeking to initiate judicial proceedings under the Convention for the return of a child or for arrangements for organizing or securing the effective exercise of rights of access to a child may do so by commencing a civil action by filing a petition for the relief sought in any court which has jurisdiction of such action and which is authorized to exercise its jurisdiction in the place where the child is located at the time the petition is filed." The place-of-filing rule is keyed to where {{childName}} is located when the petition is filed, not to where {{childHabitualResidenceCountry}} is or where {{respondentName}} resides.
clauses.gap: This clause states the concurrent-jurisdiction and where-to-file rules in 22 U.S.C. § 9003(a)-(b); it does not state subsection (c)'s separate notice rule (notice is given “in accordance with the applicable law governing notice in interstate child custody proceedings”) or subsection (d)'s rule that the court decide the case in accordance with the Convention, both of which were fetched and confirmed in the same section but are not quoted here. It also does not identify which specific California superior court or federal district would have jurisdiction and be an appropriate venue over any particular petitioner, respondent, or child -- that depends on facts (residence, where the child is actually located) this document does not and cannot determine. clauses.title: Two Different Burdens: Preponderance to Show Wrongful Removal, Clear and Convincing for the Narrowest Defenses
clauses.body: ICARA assigns the initial burden to {{petitionerName}}: a petitioner must establish by a preponderance of the evidence, "in the case of an action for the return of a child, that the child has been wrongfully removed or retained within the meaning of the Convention." If {{petitionerName}} makes that showing, the burden shifts to {{respondentName}} to establish a recognized exception, and the statute sets two different standards depending on which exception is invoked. For the narrowest, most serious exceptions -- the Convention's grave-risk-of-harm exception (article 13b) and its human-rights exception (article 20) -- a respondent must show the exception applies "by clear and convincing evidence that one of the exceptions set forth in article 13b or 20 of the Convention applies." For every other exception -- including the Convention's one-year/well-settled exception and its consent, acquiescence, and child's-objection exceptions (articles 12 and 13) -- a respondent need only show the exception applies "by a preponderance of the evidence that any other exception set forth in article 12 or 13 of the Convention applies." This two-tier structure means the hardest defenses to prove are exactly the ones most often invoked to resist return.
clauses.gap: This clause states the burden-allocation rules of 22 U.S.C. § 9003(e) as enacted; it does not state or quote the Convention's own article 12, 13, 13b, or 20 text describing what each exception requires substantively (habitual attachment for the one-year/well-settled exception, the nature of the grave risk, and so on) -- an attempt to fetch the Convention's original treaty text directly from the Hague Conference (hcch.net) and the U.S. State Department (state.gov, travel.state.gov) failed in this research session because the outbound network proxy configured for this environment rejected connections to those hosts (HTTP 403 on the CONNECT tunnel, logged as organization policy denials, not a fault of the underlying sites); this clause is therefore built only from ICARA's own enacted statutory text describing those articles, not from the Convention's original wording, and it does not evaluate whether any specific set of facts would meet either burden. This clause also does not state § 9003(e)(1)(B) or (e)(1) generally, which governs the separate burden for a rights-of-access petition rather than a return petition. clauses.title: A Wrongful Removal Can Predate Any Custody Order, and What Starts the Convention's One-Year Clock
clauses.body: ICARA clarifies two application questions that its enactment left open. First, a wrongful removal or retention of {{childName}} does not require that a custody order already existed at the time: "the terms “wrongful removal or retention” and “wrongfully removed or retained”, as used in the Convention, include a removal or retention of a child before the entry of a custody order regarding that child." A parent who was exercising -- or would have been exercising -- rights of custody by operation of law, without any court order yet in place, can still bring a Convention claim. Second, the Convention's article 12 gives extra significance to whether a return petition is filed within one year of the wrongful removal or retention, and ICARA fixes what starts that one-year clock for a child located in the United States: "the term “commencement of proceedings”, as used in article 12 of the Convention, means, with respect to the return of a child located in the United States, the filing of a petition in accordance with subsection (b) of this section." In other words, the clock runs until {{petitionerName}} actually files the petition described in the concurrent-jurisdiction clause above -- not until some earlier request for help, such as an application to a Central Authority.
clauses.gap: This clause states only 22 U.S.C. § 9003(f)(2) and (f)(3); it does not state § 9003(f)(1) (the separate clarification of who counts as “authorities” under article 15), and it does not state or quote article 12 of the Convention itself, which is what actually creates the one-year significance and the “well settled in its new environment” standard that applies after one year -- that treaty text could not be independently fetched in this research session for the network-proxy reasons noted in the burden-of-proof clause above, so this clause describes article 12's existence and the commencement-of-proceedings definition only as ICARA's own enacted text describes them, not as independently verified against the Convention's original wording. It also does not address what happens, or what showing is required, once the one-year period has passed. clauses.title: Interim Measures a Court May Take While a Return Petition Is Pending, and Their Limit
clauses.body: While a petition concerning {{childName}} is pending and undecided, ICARA authorizes interim protective measures: "any court exercising jurisdiction of an action brought under section 9003(b) of this title may take or cause to be taken measures under Federal or State law, as appropriate, to protect the well-being of the child involved or to prevent the child’s further removal or concealment before the final disposition of the petition." That authority is not unlimited, however. The same statute immediately restricts the most drastic interim measure -- physically removing {{childName}} from whoever currently has physical control -- unless ordinary state-law requirements for such a removal are independently satisfied: "No court exercising jurisdiction of an action brought under section 9003(b) of this title may, under subsection (a) of this section, order a child removed from a person having physical control of the child unless the applicable requirements of State law are satisfied." A court cannot use the Convention proceeding itself as a shortcut around the state-law standards that would otherwise govern removing a child from a caretaker's physical control.
clauses.gap: This clause states 22 U.S.C. § 9004(a)-(b) in full; it does not describe what “the applicable requirements of State law” actually require in California for removing a child from a person's physical control on an interim basis -- that depends on the separate body of California law governing emergency and temporary custody orders (addressed in this corpus's Emergency (Ex Parte) Custody Order document), which this clause does not itself state or attempt to reconcile with § 9004(b)'s cross-reference. It also does not address what showing a party must make to obtain such interim relief in a particular case. Fetched directly from Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute, confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and confirmed programmatically as exact substrings of the fetched section text.

citations.case: 22 U.S.C. § 9004(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: ICARA provisional remedies -- interim protective measures pending disposition
citations.quote: any court exercising jurisdiction of an action brought under section 9003(b) of this title may take or cause to be taken measures under Federal or State law, as appropriate, to protect the well-being of the child involved or to prevent the child’s further removal or concealment before the final disposition of the petition

citations.case: 22 U.S.C. § 9004(b) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: ICARA provisional remedies -- limitation requiring state-law removal standards to be met
citations.quote: No court exercising jurisdiction of an action brought under section 9003(b) of this title may, under subsection (a) of this section, order a child removed from a person having physical control of the child unless the applicable requirements of State law are satisfied.

clauses.title: No Administrative Fee for a Convention Application, and a Presumption of Fee-Shifting After a Successful Return Petition
clauses.body: Applying to a Central Authority for help under the Convention does not itself cost anything in government fees: "No department, agency, or instrumentality of the Federal Government or of any State or local government may impose on an applicant any fee in relation to the administrative processing of applications submitted under the Convention." Litigating a return petition in court is a different matter -- {{petitionerName}} ordinarily bears the initial cost of legal counsel and court costs -- but ICARA creates a presumption that shifts those costs to {{respondentName}} if the petition succeeds: "Any court ordering the return of a child pursuant to an action brought under section 9003 of this title shall order the respondent to pay necessary expenses incurred by or on behalf of the petitioner, including court costs, legal fees, foster home or other care during the course of proceedings in the action, and transportation costs related to the return of the child, unless the respondent establishes that such order would be clearly inappropriate." That presumption places the burden on {{respondentName}} to show why fee-shifting would be clearly inappropriate on the facts of a particular case; it is not automatic in every successful case, and it applies only once a court has actually ordered {{childName}}'s return.
clauses.gap: This clause states 22 U.S.C. § 9007(a) and (b)(3); it does not state § 9007(b)(1)-(2), which describe the default rule that a petitioner initially bears these costs and that they may be covered by legal-assistance programs, both fetched in the same section but not quoted here. It also does not describe what showing would make a fee-shifting order “clearly inappropriate,” does not address costs in an unsuccessful petition or in a rights-of-access proceeding rather than a return proceeding, and does not address costs at all if a case is litigated in a foreign Contracting State's courts rather than a U.S. court. Fetched directly from Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute, confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and confirmed programmatically as exact substrings of the fetched section text.

clauses.title: The U.S. Central Authority: A Coordinating Office, Not a Party's Lawyer
clauses.body: ICARA requires the designation of a single federal coordinating office: "The President shall designate a Federal agency to serve as the Central Authority for the United States under the Convention." That office has been designated by regulation: "The Office of Children's Issues in the Bureau of Consular Affairs is designated as the U.S. Central Authority to discharge the duties which are imposed by the Convention and the International Child Abduction Remedies Act upon such authorities." Its role toward {{childName}}'s case is cooperative and administrative, not representational -- by regulation, "The U.S. Central Authority shall cooperate with the Central Authorities of other countries party to the Convention and promote cooperation by appropriate U.S. state authorities to secure the prompt location and return of children wrongfully removed to or retained in any Contracting State, to ensure that rights of custody and access under the laws of one Contracting State are effectively respected in the other Contracting States, and to achieve the other objects of the Convention." It does not appear in court as {{petitionerName}}'s or {{respondentName}}'s attorney and does not decide the case; the return or access determination itself is made by a court under the separate judicial-remedies framework addressed elsewhere in this document.
clauses.gap: This clause states 22 U.S.C. § 9006(a) together with the Central Authority's designation and general cooperative function under 22 C.F.R. §§ 94.2-94.3; it does not state § 9006(b)-(f) (the Central Authority's further functions, regulatory authority, Parent Locator Service access, grant authority, and the limited liability regime for grantees), and it does not state 22 C.F.R. § 94.4's express prohibition on the Central Authority acting as a party's agent or attorney or bearing legal costs, or § 94.5's application procedure, though all were fetched in the course of this research. It does not describe how to actually apply to the Central Authority (the Office of Children's Issues) or what that application must contain. The 22 C.F.R. Part 94 quotes were fetched directly from the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations (ecfr.gov) rather than from leginfo (an appropriate substitute given this is a federal, not California, regulation), confirmed identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings after normalizing an expected per-request Content-Security-Policy script nonce that differed between the two fetches (an artifact of the page's own anti-caching behavior, not of the regulatory text), and confirmed programmatically as exact substrings of the fetched section text.

clauses.title: One Court's Return Decision Binds Others, and the Convention Does Not Replace Other Available Remedies
clauses.body: A decision on {{childName}}'s return is not confined to the court that issued it. ICARA requires that "Full faith and credit shall be accorded by the courts of the States and the courts of the United States to the judgment of any other such court ordering or denying the return of a child, pursuant to the Convention, in an action brought under this chapter." A California court and a federal court, in other words, must each respect a return-related judgment already entered by the other, rather than re-litigating the same Convention question. Separately, ICARA does not displace whatever other legal avenues {{petitionerName}} may have: "The remedies established by the Convention and this chapter shall be in addition to remedies available under other laws or international agreements." A Convention petition is an addition to, not a substitute for, remedies such as a UCCJEA custody proceeding or a state-law emergency custody order.
clauses.gap: This clause states 22 U.S.C. § 9003(g) and (h) in full; it does not address how full faith and credit interacts with a foreign Contracting State's own return decision (as opposed to a decision by another U.S. state or federal court), and it does not identify which other specific remedies -- beyond naming the UCCJEA and state emergency custody orders by way of example -- might be available on any given set of facts; that depends on the family's particular circumstances. clauses.title: Signature and Certification -- Not a Petition, Not a Return Order
clauses.body:
I, {{petitionerName}}, declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing statement concerning {{childName}} is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on {{dateSigned}}, at {{cityState}}.

It does not itself constitute that petition, does not itself constitute an application to the United States Central Authority or any foreign Central Authority, and does not order the return of, or access to, {{childName}} -- only a court can do that.]

clauses.title: Purpose of This Document
clauses.body: California law prescribes four specific statutory forms that a claimant -- a contractor, subcontractor, supplier, or other person or entity furnishing labor, service, equipment, or material to a California work of improvement -- may use to waive and release mechanics lien, stop payment notice, and payment bond rights in exchange for payment: a Conditional Waiver and Release on Progress Payment, an Unconditional Waiver and Release on Progress Payment, a Conditional Waiver and Release on Final Payment, and an Unconditional Waiver and Release on Final Payment. This document reproduces the required statutory text of each of the four forms and states the statutory rules under which each form takes effect, becomes null and void, or fails to release the owner, construction lender, or payment bond surety. It does not itself tell any specific claimant, owner, contractor, or lender which of the four forms applies to their circumstances, when to sign one, or whether to accept one in exchange for a particular payment.

clauses.title: These Statutory Waiver-and-Release Rules Apply to Works of Improvement
clauses.body: The waiver-and-release chapter of California's mechanics lien law -- the source of the four statutory forms in this document -- applies to a work of improvement governed by Part 6 (Works of Improvement) of Division 4 of the Civil Code, the same part of the Civil Code that governs preliminary notices, stop payment notices, payment bond claims, and mechanics liens on California private works.
clauses.gap: This clause states only that the waiver-and-release chapter applies to works of improvement governed by Part 6; it does not itself define "work of improvement" or identify which specific projects fall inside or outside Part 6's scope (for example, the boundary between private works covered by this part and public works, which are governed by a separate statutory scheme) -- those definitions appear in other Civil Code sections this document does not reproduce.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8120
citations.cite: California Civil Code, applicability of the waiver-and-release chapter
citations.quote: The provisions of this chapter apply to a work of improvement governed by this part.

clauses.title: A Contract Cannot Waive Another Claimant's Lien Rights in Advance
clauses.body: An owner, direct contractor, or subcontractor cannot use a contract -- or any other means -- to waive, affect, or impair a different claimant's mechanics lien, stop payment notice, or payment bond rights in advance, whether or not that other claimant has notice of the attempt. A contract term that purports to do this is void and unenforceable, unless and until the affected claimant itself signs and delivers one of the statutory waiver and release forms.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only advance, third-party waiver attempts -- a contract clause by which an owner or contractor tries to waive a different claimant's rights on that claimant's behalf. It does not address a claimant's own voluntary waiver of its own rights using one of the four statutory forms reproduced elsewhere in this document, and it does not state what remedy (if any) the affected claimant has against the party who inserted the void contract term, a question this section does not answer.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8122
citations.cite: California Civil Code, prohibition on advance third-party waiver of another claimant's rights
citations.quote: An owner, direct contractor, or subcontractor may not, by contract or otherwise, waive, affect, or impair any other claimant’s rights under this part, whether with or without notice, and any term of a contract that purports to do so is void and unenforceable unless and until the claimant executes and delivers a waiver and release under this article.

clauses.title: When a Waiver and Release Actually Protects the Owner, Lender, or Surety
clauses.body: A claimant's signed waiver and release does not, by itself, release the owner, construction lender, or payment bond surety from a lien or claim. Two conditions must both be satisfied: the waiver and release must be in substantially the statutory form and signed by the claimant, and -- if the release is a conditional release -- there must also be evidence of payment to the claimant, which California law allows to be shown either by the claimant's endorsement on a single or joint payee check that has actually been paid by the bank it was drawn on, or by the claimant's own written acknowledgment of payment.
clauses.gap: This clause states the statutory two-part test for when a release actually protects the owner, lender, or surety; it does not identify who bears the burden of proving evidence of payment in a lien-foreclosure or bond-claim dispute, and does not address what happens when a claimant signs an unconditional release without actually having been paid (that consequence, for the claimant rather than for the owner or lender, is addressed in the notice language of the unconditional forms themselves, reproduced in separate drafting clauses in this document). A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions construing Civil Code § 8124 was attempted for this document and returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (CourtListener's 125-request daily quota was exhausted) rather than search results, so this clause is based on statutory text alone and cites no case law.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8124
citations.cite: California Civil Code, conditions under which a waiver and release binds the owner, lender, or surety
citations.quote: A claimant’s waiver and release does not release the owner, construction lender, or surety on a payment bond from a lien or claim unless both of the following conditions are satisfied:(a) The waiver and release is in substantially the form provided in this article and is signed by the claimant.(b) If the release is a conditional release, there is evidence of payment to the claimant. Evidence of payment may be either of the following:(1) The claimant’s endorsement on a single or joint payee check that has been paid by the financial institution on which it was drawn.(2) Written acknowledgment of payment by the claimant.

clauses.title: When the Conditional Waiver and Release on Progress Payment Form Is Required
clauses.body: If a claimant is required to sign a waiver and release in exchange for, or to induce, a progress payment, and the claimant has not actually been paid in exchange for it (or is being given a single-payee or joint-payee check, rather than cash or a cleared payment, in exchange for it), the waiver and release is null, void, and unenforceable unless it is in substantially the Conditional Waiver and Release on Progress Payment form that California law sets out (reproduced in a companion drafting clause in this document).
clauses.gap: This clause describes only the trigger and consequence for the progress-payment conditional form under Civil Code § 8132; it does not address the separate, differently-worded rules for a final-payment waiver (covered in separate clauses below for Civil Code §§ 8136 and 8138), and it does not define what makes a waiver "substantially" in the statutory form for purposes of substantial compliance -- that phrase is used in the statute but not further defined by it.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8132
citations.cite: California Civil Code, when an unpaid conditional progress-payment waiver is void
citations.quote: If a claimant is required to execute a waiver and release in exchange for, or in order to induce payment of, a progress payment and the claimant is not, in fact, paid in exchange for the waiver and release or a single payee check or joint payee check is given in exchange for the waiver and release, the waiver and release shall be null, void, and unenforceable unless it is in substantially the following form:

clauses.title: Conditional Waiver and Release on Progress Payment — Statutory Form
When the Unconditional Waiver and Release on Progress Payment Form Is Required
clauses.body: If a claimant is required to sign a waiver and release in exchange for, or to induce, a progress payment, and the waiver itself asserts that the claimant has, in fact, already been paid the progress payment, the waiver and release is null, void, and unenforceable unless it is in substantially the Unconditional Waiver and Release on Progress Payment form that California law sets out, with the required "Notice to Claimant" warning printed in at least as large a type as the largest type otherwise used in the form.
clauses.gap: This clause covers only the unconditional progress-payment form's validity requirement and its type-size rule for the "Notice to Claimant" warning; the statute requires that warning to be printed in type at least as large as the largest type elsewhere in the form, but does not specify any particular point size, so this document cannot state a numeric minimum. It also does not address what recourse, if any, a claimant who signs this form without having actually been paid has against the party who obtained the unconditional release -- the form's own warning text (reproduced in the companion drafting clause) states only that the document remains enforceable against the claimant regardless.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 8134
citations.cite: California Civil Code, validity and type-size requirements for the unconditional progress-payment waiver
citations.quote: If the claimant is required to execute a waiver and release in exchange for, or in order to induce payment of, a progress payment and the claimant asserts in the waiver that the claimant has, in fact, been paid the progress payment, the waiver and release shall be null, void, and unenforceable unless it is in substantially the following form, with the text of the “Notice to Claimant” in at least as large a type as the largest

clauses.title: Unconditional Waiver and Release on Progress Payment — Statutory Form
When the Conditional Waiver and Release on Final Payment Form Is Required
clauses.body: If a claimant is required to sign a waiver and release in exchange for, or to induce, a final payment, and the claimant has not actually been paid in exchange for it (or is being given a single-payee or joint-payee check, rather than cash or a cleared payment, in exchange for it), the waiver and release is null, void, and unenforceable unless it is in substantially the Conditional Waiver and Release on Final Payment form that California law sets out.
clauses.gap: This clause mirrors the progress-payment conditional rule in Civil Code § 8132, but for final payment under § 8136 -- a textually separate section, not a subdivision of § 8132. Unlike the progress-payment forms, the final-payment forms reproduced in this document have no "Through Date" field and no exception for previously-waived-but-unpaid progress payments; the final-payment conditional form's Exceptions section instead covers only disputed claims for extras, a narrower carve-out this clause does not further explain.

clauses.title: Conditional Waiver and Release on Final Payment — Statutory Form
When the Unconditional Waiver and Release on Final Payment Form Is Required
clauses.body: If a claimant is required to sign a waiver and release in exchange for, or to induce, a final payment, and the waiver itself asserts that the claimant has, in fact, already been paid the final payment, the waiver and release is null, void, and unenforceable unless it is in substantially the Unconditional Waiver and Release on Final Payment form that California law sets out, with the required "Notice to Claimant" warning printed in at least as large a type as the largest type otherwise used in the form.
clauses.gap: This clause states the validity and type-size requirement for the unconditional final-payment form under Civil Code § 8138, the last section in this waiver-and-release chapter; the chapter contains no sections numbered above 8138, so this document's coverage of the chapter (Civil Code §§ 8120-8138) is complete on its face, but this document does not address related sections outside this chapter -- for example, the separate rules governing a lien claimant's rights on a public work of improvement, or the mechanics lien claim and preliminary notice requirements covered in a separate document in this collection.

clauses.title: Unconditional Waiver and Release on Final Payment — Statutory Form
clauses.body:
UNCONDITIONAL WAIVER AND RELEASE ON FINAL PAYMENT

NOTICE TO CLAIMANT: THIS DOCUMENT WAIVES AND RELEASES LIEN, STOP PAYMENT NOTICE, AND PAYMENT BOND RIGHTS UNCONDITIONALLY AND STATES THAT YOU HAVE BEEN PAID FOR GIVING UP THOSE RIGHTS. THIS DOCUMENT IS ENFORCEABLE AGAINST YOU IF YOU SIGN IT, EVEN IF YOU HAVE NOT BEEN PAID. IF YOU HAVE NOT BEEN PAID, USE A CONDITIONAL WAIVER AND RELEASE FORM.

Identifying Information

The claimant has been paid in full.
