clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes California's general mediation confidentiality statute, Evidence Code sections 1115 through 1129, together with the related witness-competency rule in Evidence Code section 703.5. It is prepared by {{preparerName}} concerning a mediation or mediation consultation involving {{clientName}}, represented by {{attorneyName}}, and (where applicable) mediated by {{mediatorName}}, concerning the following dispute: {{disputeDescription}}. Case number {{courtCaseNumber}} in {{courtName}} is referenced where applicable. This document is separate from, and does not repeat, two other confidentiality documents already in this corpus: the Mandatory Child Custody Mediation Information Sheet (which addresses Family Code mediation of child custody and visitation disputes and the official-information confidentiality rule of Evidence Code section 1040, a different statutory scheme limited to that context) and the Trade Secret Evidentiary Privilege Information Sheet (which addresses the separate trade-secret-specific privilege in Evidence Code sections 1060 through 1062, applicable in litigation generally rather than to mediation). Evidence Code sections 1115 through 1129 apply to mediations and mediation consultations of any kind of civil dispute, including confidentiality and intellectual property disputes such as trade secret, licensing, and non-disclosure-agreement matters that parties often route to mediation. This document does not itself constitute the printed disclosure required by Evidence Code section 1129 (a separate clause below reproduces that statutory disclosure and acknowledgment form for that purpose), does not evaluate whether any particular communication qualifies for confidentiality, and does not represent that mediation confidentiality applies to any specific dispute.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: Mediation, Mediator, and Mediation Consultation
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1115 defines three terms used throughout the mediation confidentiality chapter. "Mediation" means a process in which a neutral person or persons facilitate communication between the disputants to assist them in reaching a mutually acceptable agreement. "Mediator" means a neutral person who conducts a mediation, and the term also includes any person the mediator designates to assist in the mediation or to communicate with participants in preparation for one. "Mediation consultation" means a communication between a person and a mediator for the purpose of initiating, considering, or reconvening a mediation, or of retaining the mediator.
clauses.gap: Section 1115's definition of "mediation" does not require that the process be court-ordered, court-connected, or conducted by a certified or licensed mediator; its text imposes no qualification requirement on who may act as a neutral. The definition also does not distinguish facilitative from evaluative mediation, and does not state whether a settlement conference presided over by a judge or a privately retained neutral acting in an evaluative or arbitral capacity qualifies, leaving that line-drawing to case law that this document does not address (see the companion clause on this document's case-law limitation).

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1115(a) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1115(a)
citations.quote: “Mediation” means a process in which a neutral person or persons facilitate communication between the disputants to assist them in reaching a mutually acceptable agreement.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1115(c) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1115(c)
citations.quote: “Mediation consultation” means a communication between a person and a mediator for the purpose of initiating, considering, or reconvening a mediation or retaining the mediator.

clauses.title: The Core Rule: Mediation Communications Are Inadmissible, Non-Discoverable, and Confidential
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1119 states the chapter's general rule, subject to the exceptions found elsewhere in the chapter. Under subdivision (a), no evidence of anything said or any admission made for the purpose of, in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation or a mediation consultation is admissible or subject to discovery, and disclosure cannot be compelled, in any arbitration, administrative adjudication, civil action, or other noncriminal proceeding in which testimony can be compelled by law. Under subdivision (b), the same rule applies to any writing (as defined in section 250) prepared for the purpose of, in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation or mediation consultation. Under subdivision (c), all communications, negotiations, or settlement discussions between participants in the course of a mediation or mediation consultation must remain confidential.
clauses.gap: Section 1119's text opens with "[e]xcept as otherwise provided in this chapter," so its scope is defined only in combination with the exceptions in the other sections summarized in this document's companion clauses; read alone, subsection (a) does not say what counts as "for the purpose of, in the course of, or pursuant to" a mediation, and does not fix a bright-line rule for communications that occur before a mediation is formally scheduled. The rule as written applies only to noncriminal proceedings in which testimony can be compelled by law; its text does not extend the same protection to criminal proceedings.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1119(a) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1119(a)
citations.quote: No evidence of anything said or any admission made for the purpose of, in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation or a mediation consultation is admissible or subject to discovery, and disclosure of the evidence shall not be compelled, in any arbitration, administrative adjudication, civil action, or other noncriminal proceeding in which, pursuant to law, testimony can be compelled to be given.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1119(c) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1119(c)
citations.quote: All communications, negotiations, or settlement discussions by and between participants in the course of a mediation or a mediation consultation shall remain confidential.

clauses.title: What Section 1119 Does Not Reach: Otherwise-Admissible Evidence and Four Specific Carve-Outs
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1120(a) provides that evidence otherwise admissible or subject to discovery outside of a mediation does not become inadmissible or protected from disclosure solely because it was introduced or used in a mediation or mediation consultation. Section 1120(b) then lists four things the chapter does not limit: the admissibility of an agreement to mediate a dispute; the effect of an agreement not to take a default, or to extend the time to act, in a pending civil action; disclosure of the mere fact that a mediator has served, is serving, will serve, or was contacted about serving as a mediator in a dispute; and the admissibility of the family-law financial disclosure declarations required by Family Code sections 2104 and 2105, even if those declarations were prepared for a mediation or mediation consultation.
clauses.gap: Section 1120(a)'s "otherwise admissible outside of a mediation" test does not itself explain how to determine, for a specific document or statement, whether it was independently discoverable apart from the mediation or whether its only source is the mediation itself; the statute's text supplies the rule but not a method for applying it to contested evidence. The list of four carve-outs in subsection (b) is not stated to be exhaustive or non-exhaustive on its face, and this document takes no position on whether courts have read additional implied carve-outs into the statute.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1120(a) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1120(a)
citations.quote: Evidence otherwise admissible or subject to discovery outside of a mediation or a mediation consultation shall not be or become inadmissible or protected from disclosure solely by reason of its introduction or use in a mediation or a mediation consultation.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1120(b)(3) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1120(b)(3)
citations.quote: Disclosure of the mere fact that a mediator has served, is serving, will serve, or was contacted about serving as a mediator in a dispute.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1120(b)(4) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1120(b)(4)
citations.quote: The admissibility of declarations of disclosure required by Sections 2104 and 2105 of the Family Code, even if prepared for the purpose of, in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation or a mediation consultation.

clauses.title: A Mediator's Report, Evaluation, or Recommendation Generally Cannot Reach the Court
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1121 bars a mediator, or anyone else, from submitting to a court or other adjudicative body — and bars that court or body from considering — any report, assessment, evaluation, recommendation, or finding of any kind by the mediator concerning a mediation the mediator conducted. The only exceptions the section's text states are a report mandated by court rule or other law that states only whether an agreement was reached, and a report all parties to the mediation expressly agree in writing (or orally under the section 1118 procedure) to allow.
clauses.gap: Section 1121's bar runs to a "court or other adjudicative body"; its text does not address a mediator's report or recommendation shared only with the parties themselves outside any adjudicative proceeding, or communicated to a non-adjudicative body such as a licensing board, an employer, or the press. The section also does not define what makes a report "mandated by court rule or other law" for purposes of the narrow exception it allows for an agreement-reached-or-not report.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1121 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1121
citations.quote: Neither a mediator nor anyone else may submit to a court or other adjudicative body, and a court or other adjudicative body may not consider, any report, assessment, evaluation, recommendation, or finding of any kind by the mediator concerning a mediation conducted by the mediator, other than a report that is mandated by court rule or other law and that states only whether an agreement was reached, unless all parties to the mediation expressly agree otherwise in writing, or orally in accordance with Section 1118.

clauses.title: The Consent Exception: Disclosure by Agreement of the Participants
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1122(a) allows a mediation communication or writing to be disclosed, notwithstanding section 1119, in three situations. First, under paragraph (1), all persons who conduct or otherwise participate in the mediation may expressly agree in writing, or orally under the section 1118 procedure, to disclosure. Second, under paragraph (2), if a communication or writing was prepared by or on behalf of fewer than all the mediation participants, those participants may agree to its disclosure, provided the communication does not disclose anything said or done, or any admission made, in the course of the mediation. Third, under paragraph (3), a communication or writing related to an attorney's compliance with the section 1129 disclosure-and-acknowledgment duty (described in a companion clause below), and that does not disclose anything said or done in the mediation itself, may be used in an attorney disciplinary proceeding to determine whether the attorney complied with section 1129. Section 1122(b) provides that if the mediator agrees to disclosure, that agreement also binds any other person the mediator designated under section 1115(b) to assist in or communicate about the mediation.
clauses.gap: Section 1122(a)(1)'s text requires agreement of "all persons who conduct or otherwise participate in the mediation," which is not the same population as "all parties" used elsewhere in the chapter (for example in section 1121); the statute does not itself define who counts as a "participant" for this purpose (a support person, an expert, or observing counsel, for instance). The narrow attorney-discipline exception in paragraph (3) applies only to the compliance question under section 1129 and, by its own terms, still forbids using it to disclose anything said or done in the mediation itself.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1122(a)(1) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1122(a)(1)
citations.quote: All persons who conduct or otherwise participate in the mediation expressly agree in writing, or orally in accordance with Section 1118, to disclosure of the communication, document, or writing.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1122(a)(3) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1122(a)(3)
citations.quote: The communication, document, or writing is related to an attorney’s compliance with the requirements described in Section 1129 and does not disclose anything said or done or any admission made in the course of the mediation, in which case the communication, document, or writing may be used in an attorney disciplinary proceeding to determine whether the attorney has complied with Section 1129.

clauses.title: When a Written Settlement Agreement Reached in Mediation Is Not Confidential
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1123 provides that a written settlement agreement prepared in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation is not made inadmissible or protected from disclosure by the mediation confidentiality chapter if the agreement is signed by the settling parties and at least one of four conditions is satisfied: the agreement itself states that it is admissible or subject to disclosure (or words to that effect); the agreement states that it is enforceable or binding (or words to that effect); all parties to the agreement expressly agree, in writing or orally under section 1118, to its disclosure; or the agreement is used to show fraud, duress, or illegality relevant to an issue in dispute.
clauses.gap: Section 1123's exception is conditioned on the agreement being "signed by the settling parties"; its text does not address an unsigned draft settlement agreement, or one signed by fewer than all the settling parties, and does not itself supply model language for a party who wants to satisfy condition (a) or (b) — this document's drafting clause below offers such language as an illustration only, not as an assertion that any particular wording is legally sufficient in every case.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1123 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1123
citations.quote: A written settlement agreement prepared in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation, is not made inadmissible, or protected from disclosure, by provisions of this chapter if the agreement is signed by the settling parties and any of the following conditions are satisfied:

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1123(b) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1123(b)
citations.quote: The agreement provides that it is enforceable or binding or words to that effect.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1123(d) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1123(d)
citations.quote: The agreement is used to show fraud, duress, or illegality that is relevant to an issue in dispute.

clauses.title: Oral Settlement Agreements: The Section 1118 Conditions and the Section 1124 Exception
clauses.body: An oral agreement made in the course of a mediation is not automatically confidential under Evidence Code section 1124, but only if it meets one of that section's conditions, each of which incorporates the definition of an oral agreement made "in accordance with Section 1118." Section 1118 defines that phrase to mean an oral agreement that is recorded by a court reporter or reliable means of audio recording; whose terms are recited on the record in the presence of the parties and the mediator, with the parties expressing on the record that they agree to those terms; for which the parties expressly state on the record that the agreement is enforceable or binding, or words to that effect; and which is reduced to a writing signed by the parties within 72 hours after it is recorded. Section 1124(a) makes an oral agreement meeting all four section 1118 conditions non-confidential outright; section 1124(b) and (c) allow an oral agreement meeting only the first, second, and fourth section 1118 conditions (that is, omitting the on-the-record enforceable-or-binding statement) to be disclosed if either all parties expressly agree to disclosure or the agreement is used to show fraud, duress, or illegality relevant to an issue in dispute.
clauses.gap: Section 1118's 72-hour deadline for reducing the recorded oral agreement to a signed writing is a fixed, unextendable period as stated in the text — the section does not itself provide for any extension of that deadline by agreement or court order, unlike some other deadlines in this chapter. Both sections' text also does not address what happens to an oral agreement that satisfies subdivisions (a) through (c) but not (d) (the 72-hour writing requirement) — for example, whether it can qualify under the more limited section 1124(b) or (c) pathway, which requires only subdivisions (a), (b), and (d).

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1118(a) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1118(a)
citations.quote: The oral agreement is recorded by a court reporter or reliable means of audio recording.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1118(c) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1118(c)
citations.quote: The parties to the oral agreement expressly state on the record that the agreement is enforceable or binding, or words to that effect.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1124(b) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1124(b)
citations.quote: The agreement is in accordance with subdivisions (a), (b), and (d) of Section 1118, and all parties to the agreement expressly agree, in writing or orally in accordance with Section 1118, to disclosure of the agreement.

clauses.title: When a Mediation "Ends" for Confidentiality Purposes
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1125(a) states that a mediation ends, for purposes of this chapter's confidentiality rules, when any one of five things happens: the parties execute a written settlement agreement that fully resolves the dispute; an oral agreement that fully resolves the dispute is reached under section 1118; the mediator gives the participants a signed writing stating the mediation is terminated (or words to that effect); a party gives the mediator and other participants a writing stating the mediation is terminated (or words to that effect); or ten calendar days pass with no communication between the mediator and any party relating to the dispute, a period the mediator and parties may shorten or extend by agreement. Subsection (b) states a parallel rule for a mediation that only partially resolves a dispute. Subsection (c) clarifies that the section does not preclude a party from ending a mediation without an agreement, and does not otherwise affect a party's ability to terminate a mediation.
clauses.gap: Section 1125(a)'s five triggering events are not mutually exclusive on the statute's face, and the section does not state what happens if two different triggering events point to different end dates (for example, a mediator's termination letter sent during the ten-day silence period). In a mediation with more than two parties, subsection (a)(4)'s text allows the mediation to continue as to remaining parties after one party terminates, but does not specify a procedure for determining which parties remain bound once that split occurs.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1125(a) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1125(a)
citations.quote: For purposes of confidentiality under this chapter, a mediation ends when any one of the following conditions is satisfied:

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1125(a)(5) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1125(a)(5)
citations.quote: For 10 calendar days, there is no communication between the mediator and any of the parties to the mediation relating to the dispute. The mediator and the parties may shorten or extend this time by agreement.

clauses.title: Confidentiality Continues After the Mediation Ends
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1126 provides that anything said, any admission made, or any writing that was inadmissible, protected from disclosure, and confidential under this chapter before a mediation ended remains inadmissible, protected from disclosure, and confidential to the same extent after the mediation ends.
clauses.gap: Section 1126 preserves confidentiality only to "the same extent" that applied before the mediation ended — its text does not expand protection for material that was only conditionally or partially protected, and does not address whether a later, independent waiver under section 1122 after the mediation has ended can still lift confidentiality for material covered by this section (the chapter's other sections describing waiver do not specify whether they operate only during, or also after, the mediation).

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1126 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1126
citations.quote: Anything said, any admission made, or any writing that is inadmissible, protected from disclosure, and confidential under this chapter before a mediation ends, shall remain inadmissible, protected from disclosure, and confidential to the same extent after the mediation ends.

clauses.title: Mandatory Fee-Shifting Against a Person Who Improperly Subpoenas a Mediator
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1127 states that if a person subpoenas or otherwise seeks to compel a mediator to testify or produce a writing, and the court or other adjudicative body determines the testimony or writing is inadmissible or protected from disclosure under this chapter, that court or adjudicative body "shall" award reasonable attorney's fees and costs to the mediator against the person who sought the testimony or writing.
clauses.gap: Section 1127 uses the mandatory "shall," leaving the court or adjudicative body no textual discretion to decline a fee award once it makes the inadmissibility or non-disclosure determination, but the statute's text does not itself set a fee amount, a procedure for the mediator to request fees, or a standard for what makes requested fees "reasonable." It also does not address a case in which the compelled testimony or writing is found only partly protected.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1127 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1127
citations.quote: If a person subpoenas or otherwise seeks to compel a mediator to testify or produce a writing, as defined in Section 250, and the court or other adjudicative body determines that the testimony or writing is inadmissible under this chapter, or protected from disclosure under this chapter, the court or adjudicative body making the determination shall award reasonable attorney’s fees and costs to the mediator against the person seeking the testimony or writing.

clauses.title: Consequences of an Improper Reference to a Mediation in a Later Proceeding
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1128 states two consequences for referencing a mediation in a later proceeding in violation of this chapter. Any reference to a mediation during a subsequent trial is treated as an irregularity in the trial proceedings for purposes of Code of Civil Procedure section 657 (the statute governing new-trial motions). Any reference to a mediation during any other subsequent noncriminal proceeding is grounds for vacating or modifying the decision in that proceeding, in whole or in part, and for granting a new or further hearing on all or part of the issues, but only if the reference materially affected the substantial rights of the party requesting relief.
clauses.gap: Section 1128's second sentence conditions relief on the reference having "materially affected the substantial rights of the party requesting relief" — the statute's text does not define that standard or state how a party demonstrates material effect. The section addresses only "subsequent" proceedings; its text does not address a reference to the mediation made within the mediation-connected proceeding itself, and does not address criminal proceedings at all.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1128 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1128
citations.quote: Any reference to a mediation during any subsequent trial is an irregularity in the proceedings of the trial for the purposes of Section 657 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1128 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1128
citations.quote: Any reference to a mediation during any other subsequent noncriminal proceeding is grounds for vacating or modifying the decision in that proceeding, in whole or in part, and granting a new or further hearing on all or part of the issues, if the reference materially affected the substantial rights of the party requesting relief.

clauses.title: A Separate Rule: Mediators Are Not Competent to Testify About the Proceeding
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 703.5, located in the Evidence Code's general witness-competency chapter rather than the mediation chapter, states that no person presiding at a judicial or quasi-judicial proceeding, and no arbitrator or mediator, is competent to testify in a later civil proceeding about any statement, conduct, decision, or ruling occurring at or in connection with the prior proceeding. The section lists four exceptions: a statement or conduct that could give rise to civil or criminal contempt; that could constitute a crime; that could be the subject of State Bar or Commission on Judicial Performance investigation; or that could give rise to judicial disqualification proceedings under Code of Civil Procedure section 170.1(a)(1) or (a)(6). The section's text also states that it does not apply to a mediator in a mediation conducted under Family Code sections 3160 and following (child custody and visitation mediation).
clauses.gap: Section 703.5's four exceptions are stated as circumstances where the underlying statement or conduct "could" give rise to contempt, a crime, State Bar or judicial-performance investigation, or disqualification proceedings — the text does not state who decides whether that conditional possibility is met, or by what standard, before a mediator can be forced to testify about it. The section's carve-out for Family Code child custody mediation is a testimonial-competence carve-out only; it does not, by its own text, alter the separate confidentiality rules in Evidence Code sections 1115 through 1129 addressed elsewhere in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 703.5 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 703.5
citations.quote: No person presiding at any judicial or quasi-judicial proceeding, and no arbitrator or mediator, shall be competent to testify, in any subsequent civil proceeding, as to any statement, conduct, decision, or ruling, occurring at or in conjunction with the prior proceeding, except as to a statement or conduct that could (a) give rise to civil or criminal contempt, (b) constitute a crime, (c) be the subject of investigation by the State Bar or Commission on Judicial Performance, or (d) give rise to disqualification proceedings under paragraph (1) or (6) of subdivision (a) of Section 170.1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 703.5 (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 703.5
citations.quote: However, this section does not apply to a mediator with regard to any mediation under Chapter 11 (commencing with Section 3160) of Part 2 of Division 8 of the Family Code.

clauses.title: An Attorney's Duty to Disclose Confidentiality Restrictions Before Mediation
clauses.body: Evidence Code section 1129(a) requires that, except in a class or representative action, an attorney representing a client who will participate in a mediation or mediation consultation must, as soon as reasonably possible before the client agrees to participate, give the client a printed disclosure containing the confidentiality restrictions described in section 1119, and obtain a printed acknowledgment signed by the client stating that the client has read and understands those restrictions. Section 1129(b) applies the same duty, on the same "as soon as reasonably possible" timing, to an attorney retained after the client has already agreed to participate. Section 1129(c) sets format requirements for the printed disclosure: it must be in the client's preferred language, in at least 12-point font, printed on a single page not attached to any other document given to the client, and must include the names of the attorney and client and be signed and dated by both. Section 1129(e) states that an attorney's failure to comply with section 1129 is not a basis to set aside an agreement prepared in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation.
clauses.gap: Section 1129 imposes this duty only on an attorney "representing a client"; its text does not impose any comparable disclosure duty on an unrepresented party, on the mediator, or on opposing counsel toward a party they do not represent. Subsection (e)'s statement that non-compliance is "not a basis to set aside" a mediation agreement addresses only that one specific remedy; the statute's text does not state whether non-compliance has any other consequence, such as a basis for attorney discipline (addressed separately in the section 1122(a)(3) exception covered above) or malpractice exposure.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1129(a) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1129(a)
citations.quote: Except in the case of a class or representative action, an attorney representing a client participating in a mediation or a mediation consultation shall, as soon as reasonably possible before the client agrees to participate in the mediation or mediation consultation, provide that client with a printed disclosure containing the confidentiality restrictions described in Section 1119 and obtain a printed acknowledgment signed by that client stating that he or she has read and understands the confidentiality restrictions.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1129(c)(2) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1129(c)(2)
citations.quote: Be printed on a single page that is not attached to any other document provided to the client.

citations.case: Cal. Evid. Code § 1129(e) (Leginfo official text)
citations.cite: Cal. Evid. Code § 1129(e)
citations.quote: Failure of an attorney to comply with this section is not a basis to set aside an agreement prepared in the course of, or pursuant to, a mediation.

clauses.title: Statutory Safe-Harbor Text: Mediation Disclosure Notification and Acknowledgment
clauses.body:
Evidence Code section 1129(d) states that if the format requirements of section 1129(c) are met, the following disclosure is deemed to comply with the section 1129(a) disclosure-and-acknowledgment duty. It is reproduced below, near-verbatim from the statute's text, with bracketed blanks for the client's and attorney's names and signature dates. This document does not modify or supplement the statutory text; a preparer using it should independently confirm the 12-point single-page formatting requirement of section 1129(c), which cannot be verified from this document's text alone.

MEDIATION DISCLOSURE NOTIFICATION AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT

To promote communication in mediation, California law generally makes mediation a confidential process. California's mediation confidentiality laws are laid out in Sections 703.5 and 1115 to 1129, inclusive, of the Evidence Code. Those laws establish the confidentiality of mediation and limit the disclosure, admissibility, and a court's consideration of communications, writings, and conduct in connection with a mediation. In general, those laws mean the following:
• All communications, negotiations, or settlement offers in the course of a mediation must remain confidential.
• Statements made and writings prepared in connection with a mediation are not admissible or subject to discovery or compelled disclosure in noncriminal proceedings.
• A mediator's report, opinion, recommendation, or finding about what occurred in a mediation may not be submitted to or considered by a court or another adjudicative body.
• A mediator cannot testify in any subsequent civil proceeding about any communication or conduct occurring at, or in connection with, a mediation.

This means that all communications between you and your attorney made in preparation for a mediation, or during a mediation, are confidential and cannot be disclosed or used (except in extremely limited circumstances), even if you later decide to sue your attorney for malpractice because of something that happens during the mediation.

I, {{clientName}} [Name of Client], understand that, unless all participants agree otherwise, no oral or written communication made during a mediation, or in preparation for a mediation, including communications between me and my attorney, can be used as evidence in any subsequent noncriminal legal action including an action against my attorney for malpractice or an ethical violation.

NOTE: This disclosure and signed acknowledgment does not limit your attorney's potential liability to you for professional malpractice, or prevent you from (1) reporting any professional misconduct by your attorney to the State Bar of California or (2) cooperating with any disciplinary investigation or criminal prosecution of your attorney.

{{clientName}}  [Date signed: {{dateSigned}}]
{{attorneyName}}  [Date signed: {{dateSigned}}]

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California wage-and-hour law as it applies to time {{applicantName}} spends performing an actual work trial, skills demonstration, working interview, or unpaid trial shift in connection with {{companyName}}'s hiring process for the {{jobTitle}} position -- as distinct from ordinary interview conversation, watching a demonstration, completing a written test, or touring a workplace. It summarizes selected provisions of the California Labor Code and the applicable Industrial Welfare Commission wage order addressing when time is compensable "hours worked" regardless of whether the person performing it has been formally hired. It is not a determination that any specific activity {{applicantName}} performed, or will perform, for {{companyName}} during the hiring process is or is not compensable work, and it does not itself calculate any amount owed.

clauses.title: Who Counts as "Employed": The Wage Order's Definitions
clauses.body: Under the wage order that governs professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations, "employ" is defined broadly, and "employee" is defined in terms of that broad definition. Neither definition turns on whether a hiring decision has been made, whether the person has signed an offer letter, or what label -- "applicant," "candidate," "trainee," or "trial worker" -- the business uses for the person performing the activity.
clauses.gap: This is Wage Order 4-2001's own numbering (the order covering professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations); California's other numbered wage orders (for example, Wage Order 5 for the public housekeeping industry or Wage Order 7 for the mercantile industry) contain their own definitions section, and while their "employ"/"employee" language is understood to be substantially similar across the numbered wage orders, this document verified Wage Order 4-2001's text only -- it does not independently confirm the wording or numbering in the other sixteen wage orders, and which order applies to a given business depends on its industry or the occupation involved. This clause also does not by itself resolve whether a specific pre-hire activity was actually "work" within these definitions -- it establishes only that the wage order recognizes no separate, lesser category of coverage for someone who has not yet formally been offered or accepted a job.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 2(F)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(F)
citations.quote: “Employ” means to engage, suffer, or permit to work.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 2(G)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 2(G)
citations.quote: “Employee” means any person employed by an employer.

clauses.title: No Statutory Exception for Trial, Tryout, or Interview Work
clauses.body: California's minimum wage statute ties the duty to pay to whether the wage fixed by the applicable wage order or other law was paid to a covered worker -- it does not carve out an exception based on the label attached to the activity, such as a job interview, tryout, working interview, orientation, or unpaid trial period.
clauses.gap: Section 1197 sets the floor at whatever minimum wage is "fixed by the commission or by any applicable state or local law" -- it does not itself state a dollar figure, and it does not itself define who counts as an "employee" to whom it applies (that question is addressed by the wage order definitions cited elsewhere in this document, not by this section). Dozens of California cities and counties have adopted local minimum wage ordinances setting a floor higher than the statewide rate; this document does not catalog local ordinances, and the rate actually owed for a specific trial-work arrangement depends on the work location.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1197 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1197
citations.quote: The minimum wage for employees fixed by the commission or by any applicable state or local law, is the minimum wage to be paid to employees, and the payment of a lower wage than the minimum so fixed is unlawful.

clauses.title: An Agreement to Work Unpaid Does Not Override This Duty
clauses.body: California law gives a worker who was paid less than the applicable minimum wage a civil right to recover the shortfall, and it says this right exists notwithstanding any agreement to work for a lesser wage -- meaning a person's own advance agreement to perform trial work, a tryout, or a working interview without pay does not, by itself, extinguish a claim for the unpaid minimum wage if the activity performed was covered work.
clauses.gap: Section 1194 refers throughout to "employee" without itself defining that term -- whether a specific person performing trial or tryout work was legally an "employee" at all, as opposed to a genuine unpaid observer who performed no work, is a threshold, fact-specific question this document does not resolve; see the wage order definitions cited elsewhere in this document for the applicable standard. This document also does not verify whether any published California appellate decision has applied Section 1194 specifically to a pre-hire trial-work or working-interview scenario: an attempted CourtListener case-law search for on-point authority (query: unpaid trial work period "working interview" minimum wage California, California courts) returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, "Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") rather than results, and this document does not substitute case law recalled from memory for a verified search.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1194(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1194, subd. (a)
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any agreement to work for a lesser wage, any employee receiving less than the legal minimum wage or the legal overtime compensation applicable to the employee is entitled to recover in a civil action the unpaid balance of the full amount of this minimum wage or overtime compensation, including interest thereon, reasonable attorney’s fees, and costs of suit.

clauses.title: The Current Statewide Minimum Wage Rate
clauses.body: Absent a higher state or local minimum wage or another applicable exception, the statewide minimum wage under the wage order that governs professional, technical, clerical, mechanical, and similar occupations is currently {{applicableMinimumWage}} per hour for all hours worked.
clauses.gap: This is the wage order's own default statewide figure, not necessarily the rate that applies everywhere in California. Numerous California cities and counties (among them Los Angeles, San Francisco, and dozens of others) have adopted local minimum wage ordinances that set a floor higher than this statewide figure, and separate, sector-specific minimum wage schedules apply to some occupations (for example, certain fast food and health care employees) under other statutes this document does not verify or cite. This clause verified only the Wage Order 4-2001 text current as of the September 2026 fetch date and reflects the rate effective January 1, 2026; it will become outdated once the Department of Industrial Relations publishes a new adjusted rate for a later year.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 4(A)(1)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 4(A)(1)
citations.quote: Sixteen dollars and ninety cents ($16.90) per hour for all hours worked, effective January 1, 2026

clauses.title: Payroll Record Duty Once Trial Work Is Paid
clauses.body: If {{companyName}} pays {{applicantName}} for time worked during a trial or working-interview period, California law imposes the same payroll recordkeeping duty on that pay as on any other wage payment: an employer must keep payroll records showing the hours worked and the wages paid.
clauses.gap: Section 1174(d) also requires these records be kept "on file for not less than three years," a retention duration this clause's quoted text does not restate but that appears in the same subdivision. This document does not address the separate itemized wage-statement duty under Labor Code Section 226 or the waiting-time penalty for a willful failure to pay wages due at separation under Section 203, both of which are addressed by other documents already in this corpus and are not duplicated here. This clause also assumes the trial work was actually paid -- it does not itself say what recordkeeping or other obligation, if any, attaches when trial work should have been paid under the standard described elsewhere in this document but was not.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1174(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1174, subd. (d)
citations.quote: Keep, at a central location in the state or at the plants or establishments at which employees are employed, payroll records showing the hours worked daily by and the wages paid to, and the number of piece-rate units earned by and any applicable piece rate paid to, employees employed at the respective plants or establishments.

clauses.title: No Small-Employer or First-Hire Exception
clauses.body: The wage order's minimum wage duty applies to every covered employer regardless of size -- including a business making its first hire and running a trial shift before that hire is finalized. Nothing in the wage order's minimum wage section conditions the duty on the employer having a minimum number of employees.
clauses.gap: This clause's quote runs across a line break in the source PDF ("pay to" / "each employee"); the fetched PDF text was joined with a single space at that line break rather than quoted with the mid-word line-wrap left in, a normalization confirmed against the raw extracted PDF text and not a substantive change. The wage order text quoted here begins "Except as provided in Subdivision (E)," which is a separate minimum wage schedule for certain covered health care facilities that this document does not describe. This section also contains a "Learners" provision, in the same subdivision, permitting an employer to pay as little as 85 percent of the minimum wage, rounded to the nearest nickel, during an employee's first 160 hours of employment in an occupation in which the employee has no previous similar or related experience -- a provision that could apply to some trial-work arrangements and that this document does not otherwise analyze or apply.

citations.case: IWC Wage Order No. 4-2001, § 4(A)
citations.cite: Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 11040, subd. 4(A)
citations.quote: Except as provided in Subdivision (E) of this section, every employer, regardless of the number of employees, shall pay to each employee wages not less than the following:

clauses.title: Record of the Trial Work Arrangement
Signature and Acknowledgment
clauses.body:
{{applicantName}} and {{companyName}} each acknowledge that they have reviewed the record above and this information sheet's description of the California wage-and-hour standards that can apply to trial work performed during a hiring process.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{applicantName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes selected provisions of the California Labor Code and the applicable IWC wage order addressing when time spent during a hiring process is compensable "hours worked." clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the federal tax-law structure and California insurance-law mechanics of an irrevocable life insurance trust (ILIT) — a trust deliberately made irrevocable and designed to own a life insurance policy (or receive an existing one by transfer) so that the policy's death proceeds are kept out of the insured's taxable gross estate. An ILIT of this kind would typically be established by {{settlorName}} as settlor, insuring the life of {{insuredName}}, with {{trusteeName}} acting as initial trustee (and {{successorTrusteeName}} as successor trustee), {{beneficiaryName}} named as the trust's beneficiaries, and a policy issued by {{insurerName}} (policy number {{policyNumber}}) held as the trust's primary asset. This sheet states general federal tax and California insurance-law rules; it is not a trust instrument, does not itself create or fund any trust, and does not evaluate whether an ILIT is an appropriate estate-planning tool for any particular reader's circumstances.

clauses.title: Why an ILIT Exists: Section 2042 and ‘Incidents of Ownership’
clauses.body: Under federal estate tax law, a decedent's gross estate includes the proceeds of a life insurance policy on the decedent's own life that are payable to a beneficiary other than the decedent's executor, if the decedent possessed at death any ‘incidents of ownership’ in the policy — a power exercisable either alone or together with another person. An irrevocable life insurance trust is structured so that {{insuredName}}, as the insured, holds no incidents of ownership in a policy owned by the trust: {{trusteeName}} as trustee, not {{insuredName}}, holds the power to change the beneficiary, borrow against the policy, surrender it, or assign it, so that the death proceeds are not included in {{insuredName}}'s gross estate under this rule.
clauses.gap: This states one paragraph of one estate-tax inclusion provision — 26 U.S.C. § 2042(2) — and does not address § 2042(1) (proceeds receivable by the decedent's own executor, which are included regardless of incidents of ownership), nor the extensive body of IRS and Tax Court case law interpreting what specific policy powers (for example, a power to change a mode of premium payment, or a power held only in a corporate capacity) do or do not count as an ‘incident of ownership’ — none of which was independently researched or verified here. It also does not address the community-property complication that can arise if the insured's spouse contributes community funds toward premiums on a trust-owned policy, which California community-property law can treat as attributing a partial interest to the spouse even though the policy is nominally owned by the trust; that issue is not addressed by this clause.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2042(2) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: gross estate inclusion for life insurance proceeds where the decedent held any incidents of ownership
citations.quote: To the extent of the amount receivable by all other beneficiaries as insurance under policies on the life of the decedent with respect to which the decedent possessed at his death any of the incidents of ownership, exercisable either alone or in conjunction with any other person.

clauses.title: The Three-Year Rule for Transferring an Existing Policy
clauses.body: If {{insuredName}} already owns a life insurance policy on {{insuredName}}'s own life and transfers that policy — or otherwise relinquishes incidents of ownership in it — into an existing or new irrevocable life insurance trust, federal estate tax law pulls the transferred property back into {{insuredName}}'s gross estate if {{insuredName}} dies within three years of that transfer, producing the same estate-tax result as if the transfer had never happened. A policy that {{trustName}} itself applies for and owns from the outset, rather than one {{insuredName}} first owned individually and later transferred into the trust, is not a transfer of a previously retained interest for purposes of this three-year rule.
clauses.gap: 26 U.S.C. § 2035(a) applies broadly to any transfer, by trust or otherwise, of property that would have been included in the gross estate under §§ 2036, 2037, 2038, or 2042 if retained — this clause states only its application to a life-insurance transfer implicating § 2042, not its application to the other three referenced sections (retained life estates, transfers taking effect at death, and revocable transfers), which govern different kinds of property transfers not addressed here. The statute's own text does not use any phrase like ‘new policy exception’ — the conclusion that a trust-originated policy avoids § 2035(a)'s three-year look-back altogether is this research's reading of the statute's ‘transfer … of an interest in any property’ language, not language appearing in the statute itself, and it was not independently checked against any IRS ruling or Tax Court decision.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2035(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: three-year look-back pulling back transfers that would have been includible under section 2042 (among others) if retained
citations.quote: the value of such property (or an interest therein) would have been included in the decedent’s gross estate under section 2036, 2037, 2038, or 2042 if such transferred interest or relinquished power had been retained by the decedent on the date of his death, the value of the gross estate shall include the value of any property (or interest therein) which would have been so included.

clauses.title: Why Gifts to Fund an ILIT Usually Need a ‘Present Interest’
clauses.body: Federal gift tax law's annual per-donee exclusion is available only for a gift of a ‘present interest’ — an unrestricted right to the immediate use, possession, or enjoyment of property or its income — and is not available for a ‘future interest,’ an interest limited to commence in use, possession, or enjoyment at some future date or time. A federal Treasury regulation illustrates this distinction with a life-insurance-specific example: a transfer of existing life insurance policies into a trust, where income is not payable to the trust's beneficiary until after the insured's death, is treated as a gift of a future interest for which no annual exclusion is allowed. Because {{settlorName}}'s payments toward premiums on a policy held by {{trustName}} function economically as gifts to the trust for {{beneficiaryName}}'s eventual benefit, those contributions do not automatically qualify as present-interest gifts merely because they are used to pay a premium.
clauses.gap: This clause relies on 26 CFR § 25.2503-3, a Treasury regulation interpreting the ‘present interest’ requirement of 26 U.S.C. § 2503(b)(1); the base statutory text of § 2503(b) itself, including its current-year exclusion dollar amount, is addressed elsewhere in this corpus's federal estate and gift tax basics information sheet and is not restated here. This research located and verified the regulation's own text, including its Example (2) (a life-insurance-to-trust fact pattern), but a CourtListener search for Crummey v. Commissioner — the 1968 Ninth Circuit decision most commonly cited for the proposition that giving a beneficiary a right to demand withdrawal of a contribution can itself convert a future interest into a present interest — returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, 125/day quota exhausted) before this research could independently fetch and verify the case's text. No holding, quote, or citation from that case is included anywhere in this sheet as a result; only the regulation's own present-interest/future-interest text and worked example are cited here.

citations.case: 26 CFR § 25.2503-3(b) (eCFR text)
citations.cite: definition of a present interest as an unrestricted right to immediate use, possession, or enjoyment
citations.quote: An unrestricted right to the immediate use, possession, or enjoyment of property or the income from property (such as a life estate or term certain) is a present interest in property.

citations.case: 26 CFR § 25.2503-3(c), Example (2) (eCFR text)
citations.cite: regulatory example applying the future-interest rule to life insurance policies transferred into a trust
citations.quote: C transfers certain insurance policies on his own life to a trust created for the benefit of D. Upon C's death the proceeds of the policies are to be invested and the net income therefrom paid to D during his lifetime. Since the income payments to D will not begin until after C's death the transfer in trust represents a gift of a future interest in property against which no exclusion is allowable.

clauses.title: The Withdrawal-Right Technique Referred to as a ‘Crummey Power’
clauses.body: Estate planning practice commonly addresses the present-interest problem described elsewhere in this sheet by giving each beneficiary named by {{settlorName}} — such as {{beneficiaryName}} — a limited-duration right to withdraw some or all of any contribution {{settlorName}} makes to {{trustName}}, typically before {{trusteeName}} as trustee uses those funds to pay an upcoming premium. A right of this kind, commonly called a ‘Crummey power’ or ‘Crummey withdrawal right’ in estate-planning practice (a name drawn from a federal tax case this sheet does not independently cite, for the reason disclosed in the preceding clause), is a drafting and administrative technique — not itself a separate statute — aimed at satisfying the present-interest requirement described in that clause. This sheet does not draft the specific withdrawal-right, notice, or timing provisions of any trust instrument.

clauses.title: When a Withdrawal Right Lapses: the ‘Release’ Rule and the 5-and-5 Exception
clauses.body: If a beneficiary such as {{beneficiaryName}} is given a right to withdraw a contribution to {{trustName}} and does not exercise it before the right expires, federal gift tax law treats that lapse as if the beneficiary had released a power of appointment — potentially a taxable gift by the beneficiary to the trust's other beneficiaries. This lapse-as-release rule applies only to the extent that the property the beneficiary could have withdrawn in a given calendar year, counting that lapse together with any other lapsed withdrawal rights during the same year, exceeds the greater of $5,000 or 5 percent of the value of the assets the withdrawal right could reach.
clauses.gap: 26 U.S.C. § 2514(e) states this rule and its $5,000-or-5%-of-corpus threshold (sometimes called the ‘5-and-5’ limit) as a general lapse-of-power-of-appointment rule — it is not written as, and this clause does not claim it to be, a life-insurance-trust-specific statute. This clause does not address the drafting techniques, such as a withdrawal power that ‘hangs’ and carries an unlapsed balance forward into later years, that estate planning practice has developed to limit a beneficiary's exposure to this rule when annual contributions exceed the 5-and-5 threshold; those techniques are not found in the statute's own text and were not independently researched for this sheet.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2514(e) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: lapse of a power of withdrawal treated as a release, subject to the $5,000-or-5%-of-corpus exception
citations.quote: The lapse of a power of appointment created after October 21, 1942, during the life of the individual possessing the power shall be considered a release of such power. The rule of the preceding sentence shall apply with respect to the lapse of powers during any calendar year only to the extent that the property which could have been appointed by exercise of such lapsed powers exceeds in value the greater of the following amounts: (1) $5,000, or (2) 5 percent of the aggregate value of the assets out of which, or the proceeds of which, the exercise of the lapsed powers could be satisfied.

clauses.title: Automatic Allocation of GST Exemption to an ILIT That Is a ‘GST Trust’
clauses.body: If {{settlorName}}'s lifetime transfers to {{trustName}} are subject to federal gift tax and the trust could have a generation-skipping transfer with respect to {{settlorName}} — for example, because a grandchild of {{settlorName}} is among its potential future beneficiaries — then, unless {{settlorName}} elects out, federal law automatically allocates {{settlorName}}'s unused generation-skipping transfer (GST) tax exemption to the property transferred to {{trustName}}, to the extent needed to make the trust's inclusion ratio zero.
clauses.gap: 26 U.S.C. § 2632(c)(1) states this automatic-allocation rule for an ‘indirect skip’ to a ‘GST trust,’ terms defined in § 2632(c)(3) and addressed in the next clause of this sheet. This clause does not address direct skips under § 2632(b) (a related but separate automatic-allocation rule for outright transfers to skip persons), the election-out mechanics under § 2632(c)(5), or the substantive GST tax computation itself under 26 U.S.C. §§ 2601–2663 — none of which were researched for this sheet. Whether a given trust in fact has beneficiaries who are ‘skip persons’ for GST purposes depends on that trust's own beneficiary provisions, which this sheet does not draft or evaluate.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2632(c)(1) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: automatic allocation of unused GST exemption to an indirect skip made to a GST trust
citations.quote: If any individual makes an indirect skip during such individual’s lifetime, any unused portion of such individual’s GST exemption shall be allocated to the property transferred to the extent necessary to make the inclusion ratio for such property zero.

clauses.title: What Makes a Trust a ‘GST Trust’ for the Automatic-Allocation Rule
clauses.body: For purposes of the automatic GST exemption allocation described in the preceding clause, federal law defines an ‘indirect skip’ as a gift-tax-subject transfer, other than a direct skip, made to a ‘GST trust,’ and defines a ‘GST trust’ as a trust that could have a generation-skipping transfer with respect to the transferor — subject to a list of exceptions, including an exception for a trust instrument requiring more than 25 percent of the trust corpus to be distributed to, or be withdrawable by, one or more non-skip-person individuals before those individuals turn 46.
clauses.gap: This clause states the base ‘GST trust’ definition together with only the first of § 2632(c)(3)(B)'s several listed exceptions (clause (i), the 25%-before-age-46 exception) — the statute lists additional exceptions in clauses (ii) through (vi) covering other distribution and testamentary-power patterns, none of which are stated here. Whether a given trust's own beneficiary and distribution provisions would place it within any exception — and therefore outside automatic GST-exemption allocation — depends entirely on that trust instrument's specific terms, which this sheet does not draft.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2632(c)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: definition of an ‘indirect skip’
citations.quote: For purposes of this subsection, the term “indirect skip” means any transfer of property (other than a direct skip) subject to the tax imposed by chapter 12 made to a GST trust.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2632(c)(3)(B) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: definition of a ‘GST trust’ and its 25%-before-age-46 exception
citations.quote: The term “GST trust” means a trust that could have a generation-skipping transfer with respect to the transferor unless— (i) the trust instrument provides that more than 25 percent of the trust corpus must be distributed to or may be withdrawn by one or more individuals who are non-skip persons— (I) before the date that the individual attains age 46,

clauses.title: An Individual's Own Insurable Interest, and Naming Any Payee
clauses.body: Under California insurance law, {{insuredName}} has an unlimited insurable interest in {{insuredName}}'s own life and may lawfully take out a policy insuring that life with the policy made payable to whomever {{insuredName}} chooses — regardless of whether the person or entity named, such as {{trusteeName}} as trustee of {{trustName}}, independently has an insurable interest in {{insuredName}}'s life.
clauses.gap: This states only Cal. Ins. Code § 10110.1(b), the subdivision addressing an individual's own-life policies; it does not restate subdivision (a)'s general definition of ‘insurable interest’ or subdivision (c)'s separate employer-insurable-interest rule, and the next clause of this sheet addresses subdivision (d)'s distinct limits on a trust that itself originates coverage. Insurable interest under this subdivision governs who may lawfully be named payable on a policy insuring the insured's own life when the insured personally applies for it — a distinct question from whether a trustee, acting as such, may independently apply for and own a new policy directly in the trust's own name in the first instance, addressed next.

citations.case: Cal. Ins. Code § 10110.1(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: individual's unlimited insurable interest in own life and right to name any payee
citations.quote: An individual has an unlimited insurable interest in his or her own life, health, and bodily safety and may lawfully take out a policy of insurance on his or her own life, health, or bodily safety and have the policy made payable to whomsoever he or she pleases, regardless of whether the beneficiary designated has an insurable interest.

clauses.title: A Trust That Originates Its Own Coverage: the Insurable-Interest Limit
clauses.body: California insurance law separately provides that a trust used to apply for and initiate the issuance of a life insurance policy — as opposed to receiving an existing policy by transfer, or being named payee on a policy the insured personally applied for — violates California's insurable-interest laws and the prohibition against wagering on life if one or more beneficiaries of that trust do not themselves have an insurable interest in the life of the person insured.
clauses.gap: Cal. Ins. Code § 10110.1(d) is worded to reach ‘trusts and special purpose entities that are used to apply for and initiate the issuance of policies of insurance for investors’ — language that, on its face, targets stranger-originated life insurance (STOLI) arrangements rather than an ordinary family ILIT whose beneficiaries are the insured's own spouse, descendants, or other close relatives (who separately may qualify as having an insurable interest under § 10110.1(a)'s ‘love and affection’ clause, mentioned only in passing in this sheet's other insurable-interest clause and not independently researched here). This research did not locate California case law construing how subdivision (d) applies to an ordinary family ILIT specifically, and given the CourtListener rate-limit failure already disclosed elsewhere in this sheet, a separate search was not attempted for this subdivision; whether a given trust's actual beneficiaries satisfy the insurable-interest requirement as to the insured depends on their real relationship to the insured, which this sheet does not evaluate.

citations.case: Cal. Ins. Code § 10110.1(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: trusts used to originate life insurance policies violate insurable-interest laws unless trust beneficiaries have an insurable interest in the insured
citations.quote: Trusts and special purpose entities that are used to apply for and initiate the issuance of policies of insurance for investors, where one or more beneficiaries of those trusts or special purpose entities do not have an insurable interest in the life of the insured, violate the insurable interest laws and the prohibition against wagering on life.

clauses.title: How This Differs From Other Trust and Life Insurance Documents in This Corpus
clauses.body: This information sheet addresses a trust deliberately made irrevocable to own a life insurance policy and keep its proceeds outside the insured's taxable estate, together with the annual-exclusion ‘present interest’ and California insurable-interest rules that arise specifically from that structure. It is distinct from this corpus's Revocable Living Trust document, which addresses a trust the settlor can amend or revoke during life; from its Life Insurance Beneficiary Designation information sheet, which addresses naming a beneficiary directly on a policy the insured — not a trust — owns; and from its Testamentary Trust information sheet, which addresses a trust that does not exist, and holds no assets, until the testator's death. A given individual's estate plan may use any combination of these documents for different purposes; this sheet does not evaluate which combination, if any, fits a particular reader's circumstances.

This sheet is signed in {{cityState}} on {{dateSigned}}. Prepared by: {{preparerName}}.

clauses.title: About This Furlough Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Furlough (Temporary Reduction in Work or Pay) — Information Sheet is prepared with respect to {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}}, in the position of {{jobTitle}}, beginning a period of reduced or suspended work on {{furloughStartDate}}. As used in this document, "furlough" refers to an employer-initiated, ordinarily temporary, interruption of an employee's usual work and pay — a full or partial reduction in scheduled hours, or a full suspension of work for a defined or expected period — where the employer does not treat the employment relationship itself as ended and generally anticipates the employee's return. This document addresses a question the rest of this project's Ending Employment documents generally assume has already been answered — that a termination, layoff, or discharge has definitely occurred — by instead examining the narrower, specifically-defined thresholds at which a temporary reduction in work or pay starts to trigger some of the same statutory notice duties, benefit-continuation rights, and wage-and-hour consequences that apply to a full separation, even though the employer does not consider the employee separated. It describes: how California's WARN Act (Cal/WARN) and the federal WARN Act each define the kind of event that triggers their own notice duties, and how a furlough relates to each definition; how California's unemployment insurance law treats a week of reduced hours or reduced pay; how the federal salary-basis regulation for exempt employees treats a deduction from salary tied to a furlough; and how federal COBRA regulations treat a reduction in hours as a possible qualifying event for continued group health coverage. This document deliberately does not restate this corpus's existing California WARN Act, federal WARN Act, exempt employee's final-week salary, COBRA, Cal-COBRA, or unemployment insurance claimant information sheets — each of which addresses its own statute in more general depth — and instead focuses narrowly on how a temporary, employer-initiated furlough interacts with the specific triggering definitions each of those statutes and regulations uses. This document does not determine that any specific reduction in {{employeeName}}'s hours or pay at {{companyName}} is, or is not, a furlough, a layoff, or a termination for any particular legal purpose, and it does not calculate any specific notice deadline, benefit amount, or continuation-coverage election deadline.

clauses.title: "Furlough" Is Not Itself a Defined Legal Term in Any Source This Document Addresses
clauses.body: None of the statutes or regulations described in this document use the word "furlough" as a defined term of its own. California's Cal/WARN statute defines "layoff"; the federal WARN Act defines "employment loss"; California's unemployment insurance law defines when an individual is "unemployed"; the federal salary-basis regulation for exempt employees describes when a salary deduction is or is not permitted; and the federal COBRA regulations define "reduction of hours" and describe when that reduction causes a "loss of coverage." Each of these sources uses its own defined vocabulary, tied to its own statutory purpose, and this document maps the commonly used word "furlough" to each source's own terms separately rather than assuming that qualifying as one (for example, a "reduction of hours" under the COBRA regulations) automatically means qualifying as another (for example, a "layoff" under Cal/WARN, which by its own text requires a "separation from a position").

clauses.title: Cal/WARN's Own Definition of "Layoff" Requires a Separation From a Position
clauses.body: California's WARN Act (Cal/WARN) does not use the word "furlough" anywhere in its own definitions section. It instead defines "layoff" — one of the three kinds of events (along with "relocation" and "termination") that can trigger the statute's notice duty for a covered establishment — to mean "a separation from a position for lack of funds or lack of work." On the statute's own text, this definition is built around a "separation from a position," a phrase Cal/WARN's definitions section does not itself further define. A reduction in an employee's hours or a period of unpaid time off, standing alone, is not obviously the same thing as a "separation from a position" in the way that phrase is ordinarily understood, and Cal/WARN's own text does not resolve whether, or at what point, a furlough becomes a "separation" for purposes of this definition.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Labor Code § 1400.5(c)), used as real evidence of how Cal/WARN itself defines the event that (together with a covered-establishment size threshold and other conditions this clause does not restate) can trigger its notice duty — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular employer's or employee's situation, and not a determination that any specific reduction in hours or pay is or is not a "layoff" within this statute's meaning. This corpus's existing California WARN Act (Cal/WARN) — Information Sheet independently cites and quotes several other subdivisions of this same statutory section, § 1400.5 — subdivisions (a), (b), (d), (e), (f), (g), and (h) — for the covered-establishment, employer, mass-layoff, relocation, termination, and employee definitions; this clause cites subdivision (c), the "layoff" definition, which that existing document does not quote. This clause does not resolve the undefined term "separation from a position" itself, and does not determine how long a furlough must last, or how definite or indefinite its expected end date must be, before it would be treated as such a separation. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two distinct User-Agent strings (a Windows Chrome string and a macOS Safari string); the two fetches were confirmed byte-identical after normalizing expected per-request noise — a page-load debug-output timestamp and a JSF ViewState token, both of which change on every request to this site regardless of the underlying statutory text. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific reduction in the employee's hours or pay at the employer does or does not meet this definition.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 1400.5(c) (California Legislative Information, official text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code § 1400.5, subdivision (c), definition of "layoff"
citations.quote: “Layoff” means a separation from a position for lack of funds or lack of work.

clauses.title: Federal WARN Act's "Employment Loss" Definition Separately Reaches an Extended Reduction in Hours
clauses.body: The federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act defines the trigger for its own notice duty differently from Cal/WARN's "layoff" definition. Federal law defines "employment loss" to mean any of three things: an employment termination other than a discharge for cause, voluntary departure, or retirement; a layoff exceeding six months; or a reduction in hours of work of more than 50 percent during each month of any six-month period. This third category does not require that the employee's position be eliminated or that the employee be separated at all — an employee who keeps their job title and keeps working, but whose hours are cut by more than half in every month across a six-month span, has experienced an "employment loss" under this federal definition, a result that does not obviously follow from Cal/WARN's own, narrower "layoff" definition (a "separation from a position") described in a companion clause of this document.
clauses.gap: This is federal law (29 U.S.C. § 2101(a)(6)), applicable nationwide, used as real evidence of how the federal WARN Act itself defines the event that can trigger its notice duty — not a claim about whether any specific employer or specific reduction in the employee's hours meets the federal Act's separate size, duration, and covered-employer thresholds for "plant closing" or "mass layoff," which this clause does not restate. This corpus's existing federal WARN Act document independently cites and quotes this same statutory section's plant-closing and mass-layoff definitions (§ 2101(a)(2) and (a)(3)) and its 90-day aggregation rule (§ 2102(d)); this clause cites the same section's "employment loss" definition itself, § 2101(a)(6), which those existing citations do not quote. This clause's own reference to "subject to subsection (b)" points to a further statutory carve-out (for certain temporary facilities and strikes or lockouts, among other things) that this clause does not independently describe. This session attempted a CourtListener case-law search relevant to how courts have applied the reduction-in-hours prong of this "employment loss" definition to a furlough or similar temporary reduction; the search returned an HTTP 429 rate-limit error (CourtListener's 125-request/day quota, already exhausted from other research this session), so no case law is cited in this document, and this clause proceeds on the statutory text alone rather than on any recollection of case law. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from law.cornell.edu, using two distinct User-Agent strings, and confirmed byte-identical both times, with no normalization needed. This document is informational only and does not itself determine that any specific reduction in the employee's hours meets this definition.
