citations.cite: 29 U.S.C. § 2101(a)(6), definition of "employment loss"
citations.quote: subject to subsection (b), the term “employment loss” means (A) an employment termination, other than a discharge for cause, voluntary departure, or retirement, (B) a layoff exceeding 6 months, or (C) a reduction in hours of work of more than 50 percent during each month of any 6-month period;

clauses.title: A Week of Reduced Hours Can Itself Make an Employee "Unemployed" for Unemployment Insurance Purposes
clauses.body: California's Unemployment Insurance Code does not require a complete separation from employment before an individual can be treated as "unemployed" for a given week. The statute separately defines an individual as "unemployed" for any week of less-than-full-time work if the wages payable to the individual for that week, reduced by $25 or by 25 percent of those wages (whichever amount is greater), do not equal or exceed the individual's weekly benefit amount. This is a distinct basis for "unemployed" status from the more familiar case of a week in which the individual performs no work and no wages are payable at all; it is the basis that can apply to an employee who is furloughed for part of a week, or whose hours are cut but not eliminated, rather than an employee who is not working at all.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute (California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1252(a)(2)), used as real evidence of California's own reduced-hours eligibility test — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular claimant's situation, and not a determination that the employee or any other specific claimant qualifies as "unemployed" for any specific week, meets the separate eligibility conditions the Unemployment Insurance Code imposes elsewhere, or would actually receive any particular benefit amount. This corpus's existing Unemployment Insurance Benefits — Claimant Information Sheet and Severance Pay and Unemployment Insurance Eligibility Information Sheet each independently cite and quote different subdivisions of this same statutory section — § 1252(a)(1) (no work performed, no wages payable) and § 1252(c) (definition of "wages" for this section) — for a different point, about whether severance or dismissal pay counts as "wages payable" for a week; this clause cites § 1252(a)(2), the reduced-hours/reduced-wages test itself, which those existing citations do not quote, and does not restate their severance-pay analysis. This clause does not describe the statute's own weekly-benefit-amount calculation, work-search requirements, or any other eligibility condition found elsewhere in the same chapter. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two distinct User-Agent strings, and confirmed byte-identical after normalizing the same expected per-request debug-timestamp and ViewState-token noise described in a companion clause of this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself file a claim, calculate a benefit amount, or determine eligibility for any specific week.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1252(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Unemployment Insurance Code § 1252(a)(2), reduced-hours "unemployed" test
citations.quote: Any week of less than full-time work, if the wages payable to him or her with respect to the week, when reduced by twenty-five dollars ($25) or 25 percent of the wages payable, whichever is greater, do not equal or exceed his or her weekly benefit amount.

clauses.title: A Deduction Tied to Lack of Available Work Can Itself Defeat Exempt Salary-Basis Status
clauses.body: The federal regulation defining what it means to pay an employee on a "salary basis" — a requirement for most federal overtime-exemption categories — states that an employee is not paid on a salary basis if deductions from the employee's predetermined compensation are made for absences that the employer, rather than the employee, occasions, or that the operating requirements of the business occasion. The same provision states directly that if the employee is ready, willing, and able to work, deductions may not be made for time when work is simply not available. This is a different rule from the general full-week rule addressed elsewhere in this project's Exempt Employee's Pay in the Final (and First) Week of Employment document, which concerns a week in which the employment relationship itself begins or ends partway through; this rule instead concerns a week of continuing employment in which the employer furloughs an otherwise-exempt employee for part of the week because work is not available, and states that deducting pay for that kind of partial-week, employer-caused absence can itself cost the employee their exempt salary-basis status.
clauses.gap: This is federal law (29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a)(2)), applicable nationwide regardless of which state's law otherwise governs the employment relationship. This corpus's existing Exempt Employee's Pay in the Final (and First) Week of Employment document independently cites and quotes § 541.602(a) (the general salary-basis rule) and, by its own description, the full-week exception within § 541.602(a)(1); this clause cites the immediately following subdivision, § 541.602(a)(2), which addresses a legally distinct scenario — a mid-employment furlough rather than a week bookended by hiring or termination — and does not restate that existing document's first/last-week analysis. This clause does not address the regulation's separate list of specific, narrow exceptions in § 541.602(b) (for example, full-day disciplinary suspensions or full-day personal absences), which can permit a deduction in other circumstances this clause does not describe; whether any of those specific exceptions applies to a particular furlough is a fact-specific question this document does not resolve. This clause also does not determine whether the employee's position is properly classified as exempt in the first place, which is a separate, threshold question this document does not address. citations.case: 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a)(2) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text)
citations.cite: 29 C.F.R. § 541.602(a)(2), deductions for employer-occasioned absences
citations.quote: An employee is not paid on a salary basis if deductions from the employee's predetermined compensation are made for absences occasioned by the employer or by the operating requirements of the business. If the employee is ready, willing and able to work, deductions may not be made for time when work is not available.

clauses.title: Federal COBRA Regulations Treat a Temporary Layoff as a Kind of "Reduction of Hours"
clauses.body: The Treasury Department's own regulations implementing COBRA describe, in detail, what counts as a "reduction of hours" of a covered employee's employment — one of the events that can be a COBRA "qualifying event." The regulation states that a reduction of hours occurs whenever there is a decrease in the hours the covered employee is required to work or actually works, but only where the decrease is not accompanied by an immediate termination of employment, and that this is true regardless of whether the employee keeps performing services after the reduction. The regulation's own examples name a temporary layoff specifically: an absence from work due to disability, a temporary layoff, or any other reason (other than an FMLA leave) counts as a reduction of hours under this definition if it is not accompanied by an immediate termination of employment.
clauses.gap: This is federal law (26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4, Q&A-1(e), a Treasury regulation), applicable nationwide. This corpus's existing COBRA Election Notice document independently cites and quotes the statutory list of COBRA qualifying events at 29 U.S.C. § 1163, including "termination ... or reduction of hours" as one category; this clause instead cites the Treasury Department's own implementing regulation, a different source (a regulation rather than the underlying statute), for its more granular definition of what "reduction of hours" itself means — a definition the statute's own text does not spell out, and which the existing COBRA document's citation to § 1163 does not quote. This clause's example naming "a temporary layoff" is the regulation's own illustrative example, not this document's characterization; the regulation does not use the word "furlough." Naming this event as a "reduction of hours" is a separate question from whether it actually causes a "loss of coverage" sufficient to make it a COBRA qualifying event — a further condition addressed in the next clause of this document, which this clause does not resolve. The regulatory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from ecfr.gov, using two distinct User-Agent strings, and confirmed byte-identical after normalizing the same per-request CSP-nonce noise described in a companion clause of this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific reduction in the employee's hours at the employer is a COBRA qualifying event.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4, Q&A-1(e) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text)
citations.cite: 26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4, Q&A-1(e), definition of "reduction of hours"
citations.quote: A reduction of hours of a covered employee's employment occurs whenever there is a decrease in the hours that a covered employee is required to work or actually works, but only if the decrease is not accompanied by an immediate termination of employment.

clauses.title: A Reduction of Hours Is a COBRA Qualifying Event Only If It Actually Causes a Loss of Coverage Under the Plan's Own Terms
clauses.body: Naming an event as a "reduction of hours" is not, by itself, enough to make it a COBRA qualifying event. The same Treasury regulation states that an event only satisfies this part of the qualifying-event test if, under the terms of the particular group health plan, the event causes the covered employee (or the employee's spouse or dependent child) to lose coverage under that plan — and defines "lose coverage," for this purpose, to mean ceasing to be covered under the same terms and conditions that applied immediately before the event. A furlough or other reduction of hours that does not actually change the employee's coverage under the specific group health plan's own eligibility terms — for example, because the plan's own rules keep a furloughed employee enrolled for some defined period regardless of hours worked — does not meet this loss-of-coverage condition and, on this regulation's own terms, is not a COBRA qualifying event merely because hours were reduced.
clauses.gap: This is the same federal regulation (26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4) as the preceding clause, but a different subdivision — Q&A-1(c), the loss-of-coverage condition, rather than Q&A-1(e), the reduction-of-hours definition — so the two clauses are not independent sources of each other, though together they state the regulation's two-part test. This clause does not describe how any particular group health plan's own eligibility terms treat a furloughed employee, which is a plan-specific fact this document does not resolve, and does not describe the regulation's separate bankruptcy-specific loss-of-coverage rule (also part of the same Q&A-1(c)) or its statement that a loss of coverage need not occur immediately after the event, so long as it occurs before the end of the maximum coverage period — points this clause does not quote or further address. The regulatory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from ecfr.gov, using two distinct User-Agent strings, and confirmed byte-identical after normalizing the same per-request CSP-nonce noise described in a companion clause of this document. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether the employer's own group health plan treats the employee's furlough as causing a loss of coverage, and does not determine that any COBRA notice obligation has or has not been triggered.

citations.case: 26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4, Q&A-1(c) (Electronic Code of Federal Regulations text)
citations.cite: 26 C.F.R. § 54.4980B-4, Q&A-1(c), definition of "lose coverage"
citations.quote: An event satisfies this paragraph (c) if, under the terms of the group health plan, the event causes the covered employee, or the spouse or a dependent child of the covered employee, to lose coverage under the plan. For this purpose, to lose coverage means to cease to be covered under the same terms and conditions as in effect immediately before the qualifying event.

clauses.body: This Furlough Information Sheet describes selected statutory and regulatory definitions and rules that can bear on a temporary reduction in {{employeeName}}'s work or pay at {{companyName}} — from Cal/WARN, the federal WARN Act, California's unemployment insurance law, the federal salary-basis regulation for exempt employees, and the federal COBRA regulations. It does not describe every law that could apply to a furlough, including state and local paid-sick-leave, disability, or predictive-scheduling laws that this document's research did not address. It does not calculate any notice deadline, benefit amount, or continuation-coverage election deadline, and it does not determine that {{companyName}}'s furlough of {{employeeName}}, as actually carried out, does or does not comply with any of the sources described above.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}}, states what California law provides about an unincorporated joint venture — an arrangement in which two or more people or businesses carry on a specific undertaking together — including how California's general partnership statute treats such an arrangement in the absence of any separate "joint venture" entity statute, when two or more licensed contractors who jointly bid or contract must first obtain a distinct joint venture contractor's license, and how California's income tax law classifies a joint venture for state tax purposes. Where a venture name, participants, or a contractor's license number are given below, those are {{partnershipName}}, {{partner1Name}} and {{partner2Name}}, and {{contractorLicenseNumber}}; this sheet can also be read on its own, without any of them filled in, as a general reference to what the law says. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any specific arrangement is or is not a joint venture, does not evaluate whether any specific undertaking requires a contractor's joint venture license, and is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: California Has No Separate "Joint Venture" Business-Entity Statute
clauses.body: Outside the licensed-contractor context addressed later in this sheet, California has not enacted a business-entity statute that defines or separately governs a "joint venture" as such, the way it has separate statutes for a corporation, a limited liability company, or a limited partnership. When people carrying on a joint venture together share the venture's profits, California's general partnership statute — the same statute this project's General Partnership Agreement and General Partnership Dissolution and Winding-Up documents draw on for an arrangement the participants themselves call a "partnership" — supplies a default rule for identifying the relationship: a person who receives a share of a business's profits is presumed to be a partner in that business, subject to statutory exceptions for profits received as a debt payment, wages or independent-contractor compensation, rent, a retirement annuity, loan interest, or the price of purchased goodwill. Because this presumption is not limited by its terms to arrangements the participants call a "partnership," an arrangement the participants call a "joint venture" that meets this profit-sharing test is analyzed under the same statutory presumption.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the profit-sharing presumption itself, Section 16202(c)(3); it does not quote the six lettered exceptions to that presumption that the same subdivision lists (subparagraphs (A) through (F), covering debt payments, wages or independent-contractor pay, rent, retirement annuities, loan interest, and goodwill-sale proceeds), each of which can determine the outcome in a specific case. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of how California's own partnership law treats an arrangement styled as a joint venture — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific joint venture, and other states classify joint ventures differently. This sheet does not itself determine whether any specific arrangement rises to the level of a "joint venture" or a "partnership" under this or any other test. California courts have also developed their own case-law factors for identifying a joint venture apart from this statutory presumption; a CourtListener case-law search for those decisions was attempted during this research and returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, "Rate limit exceeded... 125/day") rather than results, so no case law is cited or relied on anywhere in this sheet, and that gap is not independently filled here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16202(c)(3)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, presumption that a profit-sharer is a partner
citations.quote: A person who receives a share of the profits of a business is presumed to be a partner in the business, unless the profits were received for any of the following reasons:

clauses.title: Co-Owning Property Does Not by Itself Create a Joint Venture
clauses.body: The same statutory section draws a specific line around the profit-sharing presumption described above: holding property together — as joint tenants, tenants in common, tenants by the entireties, or other joint or common property or part ownership — does not by itself establish a partnership, even when the co-owners share the profits the property produces. Because California has no separate joint-venture statute, this same carve-out is what applies to an arrangement styled as a joint venture: two or more people jointly owning an asset such as rental real estate or a piece of equipment, and splitting what it earns, are not by that fact alone in a joint venture under this statute.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the property-co-ownership carve-out at Section 16202(c)(1); it does not restate the separate, related carve-out at Section 16202(c)(2) for merely sharing gross returns from jointly held property, a different subdivision addressing a related but distinct fact pattern (gross returns rather than net profits). This clause does not evaluate whether any specific co-ownership arrangement crosses over into a joint venture — that can turn on facts, such as active joint management of the property as a business rather than passive co-ownership, that this statute's bare text does not itself resolve, and that this sheet does not independently address.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16202(c)(1)
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, co-ownership of property does not by itself establish a partnership
citations.quote: Joint tenancy, tenancy in common, tenancy by the entireties, joint property, common property, or part ownership does not by itself establish a partnership, even if the coowners share profits made by the use of the property.

clauses.title: Property the Venture Acquires Belongs to the Venture, Not to Any One Participant
clauses.body: Where a joint venture is characterized as a partnership under the rules described above, California's partnership statute states a baseline ownership rule: property the partnership acquires is the partnership's property, not the individual property of any one partner. Applied to a joint venture characterized as a partnership, this means an asset the venture acquires in carrying out its purpose — for example, materials, equipment, or a leasehold the venture obtains for a specific project — is attributed to the venture itself rather than to whichever participant happened to sign for it, which affects what becomes of that property if one participant dies, is individually sued, or the venture ends.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the general rule of Section 16203; it does not restate the separate, more detailed statutory test in Section 16204 for determining whose name property is legally acquired in (covered in this project's General Partnership Agreement document), which governs close cases this general rule alone does not resolve. This clause also does not address what becomes of venture property on dissolution or winding up, a separate question this project's General Partnership Dissolution and Winding-Up Information Sheet addresses for a general partnership generally, not specifically for a joint venture.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 16203
citations.cite: California Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, partnership property belongs to the partnership
citations.quote: Property acquired by a partnership is property of the partnership and not of the partners individually.

clauses.title: Venture and Participants Described in This Sheet
A Joint Venture of Licensed Contractors Generally Needs Its Own Contractor's License
clauses.body: Separately from the general partnership-law analysis above, California's Contractors State License Law creates a specific license category for a joint venture that will act as a contractor: a joint venture license, issued to a combination of individuals, corporations, limited liability companies, partnerships, or other joint ventures, each of which already holds a current, active contractor's license in good standing. A joint venture license can be issued in a given classification (for example, a specific trade) as long as at least one of the combined entities is licensed in that classification — not all of them. The license is also self-policing: it is automatically suspended by operation of law during any period in which any one member of the joint venture stops holding a current, active license in good standing, without a separate suspension proceeding against the joint venture license itself.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Section 7029 in full, but does not independently trace the licensing classification rules it cross-references (which classification a given trade or project requires) or the separate statutes governing suspension or revocation of an individual member's underlying contractor's license, which is what triggers the automatic joint venture license suspension described here. The Contractors State License Board's own regulations (16 Cal. Code Regs. §§ 821-822) govern the joint venture license application procedure in more operational detail than this statute alone provides; this sheet attempted no fetch of that regulatory text because the California Code of Regulations is not one of the primary-source hosts confirmed reachable in this research session, and no unverified description of it is included here.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7029
citations.cite: Contractors State License Law, definition and automatic suspension of a joint venture license
citations.quote: A joint venture license is a license issued to any combination of individuals, corporations, limited liability companies, partnerships, or other joint ventures, each of which holds a current, active license in good standing. A joint venture license may be issued in any classification in which at least one of the entities is licensed. An active joint venture license shall be automatically suspended by operation of law during any period in which any member of the entity does not hold a current, active license in good standing.

clauses.title: Acting as a Contractor Jointly Without First Securing the License
clauses.body: The statute that creates the joint venture license also makes it unlawful, except as the statute itself provides, for two or more separately licensed contractors to be awarded a contract jointly, or otherwise act as a contractor jointly, without first securing a joint venture license. The statute carves out one specific step from that prohibition: before obtaining the joint venture license, the same contractors may jointly submit a bid for covered work — bidding jointly is permitted even though contracting jointly without the license is not. That carve-out for bidding does not eliminate other legal consequences of submitting a bid: if a combination of licensees bids on work that requires a joint venture license and then fails to obtain one, the statute states that this failure does not prevent the imposition of whatever penalty already applies by law to a contractor who submits a bid and then fails to enter into the resulting contract. Separately, the statute states that violating this section is itself cause for disciplinary action.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes all three subdivisions of Section 7029.1 in full. It does not independently trace or quote the "penalty specified by law for the failure of a contractor who submits a bid to enter into a contract" that subdivision (b) cross-references only by description, or the specific disciplinary procedures the Contractors State License Board applies under subdivision (c) — both are separate statutory or regulatory provisions this sheet does not independently verify. This is one state's statute, applicable to contractors licensed under this specific chapter; it says nothing about joint bidding or contracting requirements for any occupation licensed under a different licensing scheme.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7029.1(a)
citations.cite: Contractors State License Law, prohibition on jointly contracting without a joint venture license
citations.quote: Except as provided in this section, it is unlawful for any two or more licensees, each of whom has been issued a license to act separately in the capacity of a contractor within this state, to be awarded a contract jointly or otherwise act as a contractor without first having secured a joint venture license in accordance with the provisions of this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7029.1(b)
citations.cite: Contractors State License Law, permitted joint bidding before a joint venture license is obtained
citations.quote: Prior to obtaining a joint venture license, contractors licensed in accordance with this chapter may jointly bid for the performance of work covered by this section.  If a combination of licensees submit a bid for the performance of work for which a joint venture license is required, a failure to obtain that license shall not prevent the imposition of any penalty specified by law for the failure of a contractor who submits a bid to enter into a contract pursuant to the bid.

citations.case: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7029.1(c)
citations.cite: Contractors State License Law, violation is cause for disciplinary action
citations.quote: A violation of this section constitutes a cause for disciplinary action.

clauses.title: California Tax Law Classifies an Unincorporated Joint Venture as a Partnership
clauses.body: For California personal income tax purposes, the state's Revenue and Taxation Code adopts federal partnership tax law wholesale: California's own statute states that Subchapter K of the Internal Revenue Code, the federal subchapter governing partners and partnerships, applies for state law purposes except where California law separately provides otherwise. Subchapter K's own definitional section, in turn, does not limit the term "partnership" to arrangements the participants call a partnership: it defines "partnership" to include a syndicate, group, pool, joint venture, or other unincorporated organization through or by means of which any business, financial operation, or venture is carried on, so long as the arrangement is not, for tax purposes, a corporation or a trust or estate. Read together, these two provisions are why an unincorporated joint venture carrying on a business is generally classified as a partnership for California income tax purposes, with the tax filing and reporting consequences that follow from that classification.
clauses.gap: This clause verifies California's conformity statute (Rev. & Tax. Code § 17851, in the Personal Income Tax Law) and the federal definition it incorporates (26 U.S.C. § 761(a)); it does not independently trace the separate conformity provisions of California's Corporation Tax Law, which governs the franchise or income tax treatment of a corporate participant in a joint venture rather than an individual one, and which is not the same statute quoted here. It also does not trace the election-out mechanism the same federal subsection creates — a joint venture organized only for investment, for joint production or use of property without selling the output, or by securities dealers for short-term underwriting can, on the unanimous election of its members and under Treasury regulations, be excluded from Subchapter K's partnership treatment — which this sheet does not independently restate or evaluate for any specific venture. 26 U.S.C. § 761 is a federal statute, fetched from Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute rather than a California government source, because it is the specific provision Rev. & Tax. Code § 17851 incorporates by reference.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 17851
citations.cite: Personal Income Tax Law, California's adoption of federal Subchapter K partnership tax rules
citations.quote: Subchapter K of Chapter 1 of Subtitle A of the Internal Revenue Code, relating to partners and partnerships, shall apply, except as otherwise provided.

citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, federal tax-law definition of "partnership" includes a joint venture
citations.quote: For purposes of this subtitle, the term “partnership” includes a syndicate, group, pool, joint venture, or other unincorporated organization through or by means of which any business, financial operation, or venture is carried on, and which is not, within the meaning of this title, a corporation or a trust or estate.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet, prepared by {{preparerName}}, states what California and federal law provide about the securities-law exemption a corporation or limited liability company commonly relies on when it issues stock options, restricted stock, or other equity awards to its own workforce under a written equity plan — here, {{companyName}}'s plan identified as: {{equityPlanName}}. That exemption, California Corporations Code § 25102(o), is a different provision from this project's existing California Limited Offering Exemption information sheet, which addresses Corporations Code § 25102(f) — a private-placement exemption capped at 35 purchasers and conditioned on a preexisting relationship or investor sophistication — and from this project's existing California Notice Filing for Federally Covered Rule 506 Offerings clause, which addresses Corporations Code § 25102.1's separate notice-filing regime for offerings that raise outside investment capital under federal Regulation D. Section 25102(o) instead exempts compensatory equity issued to an issuer's own employees, directors, and certain other service providers under a written plan, by incorporating a federal exemption — Rule 701 of the Securities Act of 1933 (17 C.F.R. § 230.701) — and adding California-specific conditions of its own. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any specific plan, grant, or issuance by {{companyName}} meets the conditions of this exemption, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

clauses.title: California's Compensatory Benefit Plan Exemption From Securities Qualification
clauses.body: California Corporations Code § 25102(o) exempts from the state's securities qualification requirement (Corporations Code § 25110) an offer or sale of a security issued by a corporation or limited liability company under a purchase plan or agreement, or under an option plan or agreement, provided the security is exempt from federal registration under Rule 701 at the time of issuance or grant. The statute does not create a freestanding state-law standard; it incorporates Rule 701's federal conditions by reference and then layers on three further, California-specific conditions: a purchase plan or agreement must comply with 10 California Code of Regulations §§ 260.140.42, 260.140.45, and 260.140.46; an option plan or agreement must comply with 10 California Code of Regulations §§ 260.140.41, 260.140.45, and 260.140.46; and the issuer must file a notice of transaction with the Commissioner of Financial Protection and Innovation no later than 30 days after the initial issuance of any security under the plan, accompanied by a filing fee.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(o) itself, fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical (the raw HTML places a non-breaking space, not a plain space, immediately after the “(o)” subsection label — verified in the raw HTML and normalized to a plain space in the quote below). Of the four California Code of Regulations sections this subdivision cross-references, this document independently fetched and separately quotes only two — 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.140.41 (compensatory option plans) and 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.140.46 (financial statements to security holders), both from the Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute's mirror — in later clauses of this same document; 10 Cal. Code Regs. § 260.140.42 (compensatory purchase plans) and § 260.140.45 were not independently fetched or verified this session, so this clause does not state their substantive content, only that § 25102(o) requires compliance with them. The filing fee amount under Corporations Code § 25608(y), referenced by § 25102(o) itself, was likewise not independently fetched. This clause does not determine whether any specific plan, grant, or issuance by a given company in fact meets Rule 701's conditions or these California regulatory conditions.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(o)
citations.cite: California Corporations Code, the compensatory benefit plan exemption from securities qualification, incorporating Rule 701 and layering on state regulatory and notice-filing conditions
citations.quote: (o) An offer or sale of any security issued by a corporation or limited liability company pursuant to a purchase plan or agreement, or issued pursuant to an option plan or agreement, where the security at the time of issuance or grant is exempt from registration under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended, pursuant to Rule 701 adopted pursuant to that act (17 C.F.R. 230.701), the provisions of which are hereby incorporated by reference into this section, provided that (1) the terms of any purchase plan or agreement shall comply with Sections 260.140.42, 260.140.45, and 260.140.46 of Title 10 of the California Code of Regulations, (2) the terms of any option plan or agreement shall comply with Sections 260.140.41, 260.140.45, and 260.140.46 of Title 10 of the California Code of Regulations, and (3) the issuer files a notice of transaction in accordance with rules adopted by the commissioner no later than 30 days after the initial issuance of any security under that plan, accompanied by a filing fee as prescribed by subdivision (y) of Section 25608.

clauses.title: The Notice Filing's Cure Provision and the Single-Offering Rule
clauses.body: The same subdivision that imposes the 30-day notice-filing requirement also provides two further rules. First, missing the 30-day deadline does not, by the statute's own text, cause the exemption to be lost: an issuer that fails to timely file must instead file the notice and pay an additional, larger fee — equal to what the full qualification fee under Section 25110 would have been — within 15 business days after discovering the failure or after the Commissioner demands it, whichever comes first. Second, all offers and sales made in reliance on this exemption are treated as a single, discrete offering that is not integrated with any other offering or sale by the issuer, whether that other offering is qualified under the general qualification statute, separately exempt, or not subject to qualification at all.
clauses.gap: Both quotations below come from the same statutory subdivision, Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(o), immediately following the sentence quoted in the preceding clause of this document — they are not independent sources of each other or of that clause. Fetched twice from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical. The raw HTML places the first quoted sentence and the second in separate, adjacent paragraph elements with no whitespace character between them at all (the source text reads “...qualified under Section 25110.Offers and sales...” with no space before “Offers”) — verified in the raw HTML; this clause quotes the two sentences as two separate citation entries rather than bridging that gap with an invented space. This clause does not address what “filing the notice” and “paying the fee” after a missed deadline require procedurally, and does not state the dollar amount of either fee.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(o)
citations.cite: California Corporations Code, the cure provision for a late or missed notice of transaction
citations.quote: The failure to file the notice of transaction within the time specified in this subdivision shall not affect the availability of this exemption. An issuer that fails to file the notice shall, within 15 business days after discovery of the failure to file the notice or after demand by the commissioner, whichever occurs first, file the notice and pay the commissioner a fee equal to the maximum aggregate fee payable had the transaction been qualified under Section 25110.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 25102(o)
citations.cite: California Corporations Code, the single-discrete-offering / no-integration rule for offers and sales exempt under this subdivision
citations.quote: Offers and sales exempt pursuant to this subdivision shall be deemed to be part of a single, discrete offering and are not subject to integration with any other offering or sale, whether qualified under Chapter 2 (commencing with Section 25110), or otherwise exempt, or not subject to qualification.

clauses.title: Rule 701's Federal Exemption, Its Coexistence With State Law, and Which Issuers May Use It
clauses.body: Rule 701, adopted by the Securities and Exchange Commission under the Securities Act of 1933, exempts from federal registration an offer or sale of securities made in compliance with all of the rule's conditions. The rule's own preliminary notes state that satisfying it does not excuse compliance with any other body of law: an issuer relying on Rule 701 must still comply with any applicable state securities law — which, for a California issuer or an offering reaching California persons, is where Corporations Code § 25102(o)'s own additional conditions come in. Rule 701 is also not available to every issuer: by its own terms, it is available only to an issuer that is not subject to the reporting requirements of Exchange Act § 13 or § 15(d) (that is, a company that does not already file periodic reports with the SEC) and that is not an investment company registered or required to be registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940.

clauses.title: Who May Receive Securities Under the Exemption
clauses.body: Rule 701 exempts offers and sales made under a written compensatory benefit plan or written compensation contract established by the issuer (or its parent or majority-owned subsidiaries) for the participation of a defined group: employees, directors, general partners, trustees of a business-trust issuer, officers, and consultants and advisors, together with family members who acquire the securities from one of those persons by gift or under a domestic relations order. A former member of one of these groups may still receive an exempt offer, but only if the person was employed by, or providing services to, the issuer at the time the securities were offered — an offer made after the relationship has already ended falls outside this exemption on the rule's own terms. The rule also expands "employee" to include certain exclusive insurance agents of the issuer.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(c), fetched twice this session directly from ecfr.gov using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical apart from an expected analytics-tag nonce. This clause states the general eligible-recipient group and the former-service-provider limitation; it does not address the rule's separate treatment of guarantees under paragraph (d)(2)(ii) mentioned in this same subsection's opening clause, which this clause does not independently trace or explain. This is federal law that applies the same way regardless of which state's law otherwise governs a specific plan; it does not by itself address who may receive securities under California's own, separately conditioned exemption.

citations.cite: Securities Act Rule 701, the defined group of eligible recipients and the former-service-provider condition
citations.quote: (c) Transactions exempted by this section. This section exempts offers and sales of securities (including plan interests and guarantees pursuant to paragraph (d)(2)(ii) of this section) under a written compensatory benefit plan (or written compensation contract) established by the issuer, its parents, its majority-owned subsidiaries or majority-owned subsidiaries of the issuer's parent, for the participation of their employees, directors, general partners, trustees (where the issuer is a business trust), officers, or consultants and advisors, and their family members who acquire such securities from such persons through gifts or domestic relations orders. This section exempts offers and sales to former employees, directors, general partners, trustees, officers, consultants and advisors only if such persons were employed by or providing services to the issuer at the time the securities were offered. In addition, the term “employee” includes insurance agents who are exclusive agents of the issuer, its subsidiaries or parents, or derive more than 50% of their annual income from those entities.

clauses.title: Consultants and Advisors' Special Conditions, and What Counts as a "Compensatory Benefit Plan"
clauses.body: Not every consultant or advisor to an issuer qualifies for this exemption. Rule 701 makes it available to a consultant or advisor only if the person is a natural person (not an entity), provides bona fide services to the issuer or a qualifying parent or subsidiary, and the services are not connected to a capital-raising securities offer or sale and do not promote or maintain a market for the issuer's securities — a condition aimed at keeping this exemption for genuine service providers rather than for a substitute channel to raise investment capital or create trading liquidity. Separately, the rule defines what plans this exemption reaches: a "compensatory benefit plan" is any purchase, savings, option, bonus, stock appreciation, profit sharing, thrift, incentive, deferred compensation, pension, or similar plan.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes two subparagraphs of the same rule, 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(c)(1) and (c)(2), fetched twice this session directly from ecfr.gov using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical apart from an expected analytics-tag nonce. This clause does not address subparagraph (c)(3), the rule's separate definition of "family member," which lists specific relationships and is not restated here. This clause does not determine whether any specific person's relationship to a given issuer in fact qualifies as bona fide consulting or advisory services under this condition.

citations.cite: Securities Act Rule 701, special conditions limiting the exemption for consultants and advisors
citations.quote: (1) Special requirements for consultants and advisors. This section is available to consultants and advisors only if: (i) They are natural persons; (ii) They provide bona fide services to the issuer, its parents, its majority-owned subsidiaries or majority-owned subsidiaries of the issuer's parent; and (iii) The services are not in connection with the offer or sale of securities in a capital-raising transaction, and do not directly or indirectly promote or maintain a market for the issuer's securities.

citations.cite: Securities Act Rule 701, definition of "compensatory benefit plan"
citations.quote: (2) Definition of “compensatory benefit plan.” For purposes of this section, a compensatory benefit plan is any purchase, savings, option, bonus, stock appreciation, profit sharing, thrift, incentive, deferred compensation, pension or similar plan.

clauses.title: The Rolling 12-Month Dollar and Percentage Ceiling on Sales
clauses.body: Rule 701 does not cap the amount of securities an issuer may offer, but it does cap the aggregate sales price or amount of securities actually sold in reliance on the exemption during any rolling 12-month period. That ceiling is the greatest of three alternative measures: $1,000,000; 15% of the issuer's total assets (measured at its most recent balance sheet date, if no older than its last fiscal year end); or 15% of the outstanding amount of the class of securities being offered and sold in reliance on the exemption, measured the same way. Because the statute takes the greatest of these three figures, a larger or asset-heavy issuer's usable ceiling under this exemption can substantially exceed the flat $1,000,000 figure.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(d)(2), fetched twice this session directly from ecfr.gov using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical apart from an expected analytics-tag nonce. This clause does not restate paragraph (d)(1) (the separate, uncapped rule for mere offers, as distinct from completed sales) or paragraph (d)(3)'s detailed rules for calculating "aggregate sales price" and the timing of that calculation for options and deferred-compensation plans — both addressed by the same subsection but not quoted here. This clause does not calculate, and does not state, what a specific issuer's own applicable ceiling is under any of the three alternative measures.

citations.cite: Securities Act Rule 701, the 12-month aggregate sales ceiling and its three alternative measures
citations.quote: (2) Sales. The aggregate sales price or amount of securities sold in reliance on this section during any consecutive 12-month period must not exceed the greatest of the following: (i) $1,000,000; (ii) 15% of the total assets of the issuer (or of the issuer's parent if the issuer is a wholly-owned subsidiary and the securities represent obligations that the parent fully and unconditionally guarantees), measured at the issuer's most recent balance sheet date (if no older than its last fiscal year end); or (iii) 15% of the outstanding amount of the class of securities being offered and sold in reliance on this section, measured at the issuer's most recent balance sheet date (if no older than its last fiscal year end).

clauses.title: The $10 Million Disclosure Trigger
clauses.body: Below a certain scale, Rule 701 requires only that the issuer deliver a copy of the compensatory benefit plan or contract itself. But once the aggregate sales price or amount of securities sold under the exemption during any rolling 12-month period exceeds $10 million, the rule requires the issuer to deliver additional disclosure to investors a reasonable time before the date of sale — including a summary of the plan's material terms (or, for an ERISA-covered plan, the ERISA summary plan description), risk-factor information about the securities, and specified financial statements. This $10 million figure is measured the same way, and over the same rolling 12-month window, as the aggregate sales ceiling addressed elsewhere in this document — it is a disclosure trigger layered on top of that ceiling, not a separate transaction limit.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the introductory sentence of 17 C.F.R. § 230.701(e), fetched twice this session directly from ecfr.gov using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical apart from an expected analytics-tag nonce. This clause does not restate the five enumerated disclosure items themselves (paragraphs (e)(1) through (e)(5)) in the level of specific, item-by-item detail the rule sets out — including the specific financial-statement staleness limit of 180 days before sale, and the special timing rules for options and deferred-compensation elections — nor does it address paragraph (e)(6)'s separate timing rule for stock options and deferred compensation. This clause does not determine whether any specific issuer's own sales under any specific plan have crossed, or are projected to cross, this $10 million threshold.

citations.quote: In addition, if the aggregate sales price or amount of securities sold during any consecutive 12-month period exceeds $10 million, the issuer must deliver the following disclosure to investors a reasonable period of time before the date of sale:

clauses.title: California's Required Terms for a Compensatory Option Plan
clauses.body: Where an issuer's plan grants options rather than selling shares outright, California's implementing regulation, 10 California Code of Regulations § 260.140.41, requires the option plan or agreement itself to contain specific protective terms in order for the underlying grants to qualify for this state exemption. Two of those required terms set outer limits on how the option may be structured: the option's exercise period may not exceed 120 months from the date it is granted, and — unless the option holder's employment is terminated for cause — the right to exercise an already-vested option must remain open for at least 6 months after termination caused by death or disability, or at least 30 days after a termination for any other reason, in each case until no later than the option's own expiration date.

Code Regs. § 260.140.41(b) and (e), fetched twice this session from the Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute's mirror (law.cornell.edu) using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical after whitespace normalization. As in the corpus's existing California Limited Offering Exemption document, this regulation's text was verified only against the Cornell mirror; the official state platform (govt.westlaw.com, operated under contract with the Office of Administrative Law) could not be retrieved as a scripted fetch during this research, so this citation was not independently cross-checked against that primary state-hosted source. This clause does not restate the regulation's remaining required terms — the total-number-of-securities and eligible-persons disclosure of subsection (a), the non-transferability condition of subsection (c), the anti-dilution adjustment of subsection (d), the 10-year outer limit on granting options under the plan in subsection (f), the security-holder-approval condition of subsection (g) (with its narrow foreign-private-issuer carve-out), or the cross-reference to the financial-statement regulation in subsection (h), addressed separately elsewhere in this document — none of which are quoted here. This is a California-specific regulatory condition layered on top of, not a restatement of, Rule 701's own federal conditions addressed elsewhere in this document.

(2) At least 30 days from the date of termination if termination was caused by other than death or disability.

clauses.title: The Annual Financial Statement Requirement to Security Holders
clauses.body: A separate California regulation, 10 California Code of Regulations § 260.140.46, requires that a plan or agreement under which securities are issued to employees, officers, directors, managers, advisors, or consultants — including option, purchase, and bonus plans — provide that the security holder will receive financial statements at least annually. This requirement does not mandate any particular accounting standard for those statements. It also does not apply in two situations: where issuance is limited to key persons whose role with the issuer already gives them access to equivalent information, and where the plan or agreement complies with all of Rule 701's own conditions — in which case, for purposes of judging that Rule 701 compliance, the regulation treats a registered domestic partner as a "family member" within Rule 701's own definition of that term.

Code Regs. § 260.140.46, fetched twice this session from the Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute's mirror (law.cornell.edu) using two different User-Agent headers and found byte-identical after whitespace normalization; as with the preceding clause, this regulation was not independently cross-checked against the state's own Westlaw-hosted platform, which could not be retrieved as a scripted fetch this session. clauses.title: Information and Background — State Civil Service Disciplinary Due Process at Termination
clauses.body: I, {{employeeName}}, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment as {{jobTitle}} with {{companyName}}. This information sheet describes the disciplinary-proceedings article of the State Civil Service Act, California Government Code sections 19570 through 19589 — a chapter of statutes that applies to employees of the California state civil service (agencies and departments under the jurisdiction of the State Personnel Board), and that provides procedural rights connected to a written notice before dismissal, demotion, suspension, or other disciplinary action, the right to file a written answer, the right to a hearing, and administrative and judicial review, separate from the Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act, the wrongful-termination doctrines, and the general personnel-record statutes this project addresses elsewhere. It is not an answer filed with the State Personnel Board, an administrative appeal, a petition for rehearing, a writ of mandate petition, or a superior court filing, and completing it does not initiate, extend, or preserve any deadline under Government Code section 19574, section 19575, section 19586, or any other statute, board rule, or memorandum of understanding. Completing it does not establish that {{companyName}} took, or failed to take, any specific action described in this sheet, or that any statement here is true.

clauses.title: Source and Scope: The State Civil Service Act's Disciplinary-Proceedings Article
clauses.body: The rights described in this document come from a specific statutory article — Article 1 (Disciplinary Proceedings) of Chapter 7 (Separations From Service) of Part 2 (State Civil Service) of Division 5 (Personnel) of Title 2 of the Government Code, Government Code sections 19570 through 19589 — not from a general common-law or constitutional theory of public-employee due process. The article's own authorization provision ties any adverse action to two sources: the article itself and the disciplinary rule adopted by the board (the State Personnel Board), and applies to an employee or to a person whose name appears on an employment list, for any cause for discipline the article specifies.
clauses.gap: This article is part of the State Civil Service Act and, by its own terms and placement, governs employees within the state civil service under the State Personnel Board's jurisdiction — it does not apply to a private-sector employee, to a peace officer's separate procedural rights under the Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act (addressed in a different document in this project), or, without more research this clause does not undertake, necessarily to every category of local-government civil service employee, whose procedural rights typically come instead from a city or county charter, civil-service ordinance, or memorandum of understanding rather than from this state statute. This clause also does not resolve whether a specific appointment is state civil service as opposed to an exempt, at-will, or contract position to which this article does not apply.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19571 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: authorization for adverse action under the disciplinary-proceedings article
citations.quote: In conformity with this article and the board rule, adverse action may be taken against any employee, or person whose name appears on any employment list for any cause for discipline specified in this article.

clauses.title: The Article's Own Definition of "Adverse Action," and the Managerial-Employee Exclusion
clauses.body: The article defines its own trigger term. "Adverse action" — the term used throughout the notice, answer, hearing, and appeal provisions described in this document — means dismissal, demotion, suspension, or other disciplinary action. The article carves out a separate category of state employee: it does not apply to an adverse action affecting a managerial employee subject to the separate article governing managerial employees, except to the limited extent three specific cross-referenced sections of that other article say otherwise.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the definition and the cross-reference itself; it does not independently research or restate what Government Code sections 19590.5, 19592, and 19592.2 (the exceptions to the managerial exclusion) actually provide, or what makes a given position a "managerial employee" under the separate article (commencing with Section 19590) that this section cross-references. Whether a specific classification is treated as managerial for this purpose, and so falls outside this article entirely, is a title- and classification-specific question this clause does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19570 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definition of "adverse action" and the managerial-employee exclusion
citations.quote: As used in this article “adverse action” means dismissal, demotion, suspension, or other disciplinary action. This article shall not apply to any adverse action affecting managerial employees subject to Article 2 (commencing with Section 19590), except as provided in Sections 19590.5, 19592, and 19592.2.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own List of What Constitutes "Cause for Discipline"
clauses.body: Adverse action under this article must rest on one or more of the causes for discipline the statute itself enumerates — an employer using this article is not free to discipline for any reason at all. The statute lists 24 lettered causes, opening with fraud in securing appointment, incompetency, and inefficiency, and continuing through categories such as inexcusable neglect of duty, insubordination, dishonesty, inexcusable absence without leave, conviction of a felony or a misdemeanor involving moral turpitude, discourteous treatment of the public or other employees, willful disobedience, misuse of state property, unlawful discrimination or harassment on a basis listed in the Fair Employment and Housing Act, and unlawful retaliation against an employee or member of the public who reports a suspected legal violation to the Attorney General or another appropriate authority.
clauses.gap: This clause's quoted citation reproduces only the introductory sentence and the first three lettered causes (a) through (c) verbatim; the remaining causes, (d) through (x), are described narratively above rather than quoted exactly. In the raw fetched HTML, leginfo renders each lettered subdivision abutting the next with a non-breaking space (not a regular space) immediately after each subdivision's parenthetical letter, and with no space at all between one subdivision's closing period and the next subdivision's opening parenthesis (for example, the source reads ‘appointment.(b)Incompetency.(c)Inefficiency.’ with a non-breaking space consumed after each letter but none before it) — this was verified byte-for-byte in the raw HTML from both fetches and is preserved exactly, non-breaking spaces included, in the quoted text rather than corrected. This clause does not determine whether any specific conduct meets one of these 24 statutory causes, and does not address the separate disciplinary criteria a department may adopt under Government Code section 19573.

citations.quote: Each of the following constitutes cause for discipline of an employee, or of a person whose name appears on any employment list:(a) Fraud in securing appointment.(b) Incompetency.(c) Inefficiency.

clauses.title: The Pre-Discipline Written Notice: Its Five Required Contents and 15-Day Board Filing Deadline
clauses.body: Before adverse action against a covered employee becomes valid, the appointing power (or its authorized representative) must serve the employee, personally or by mail, with a written notice, prior to the action's effective date, containing five specific elements: a statement of the nature of the adverse action; the action's effective date; a statement of the reasons for it in ordinary language; a statement advising the employee of the right to answer the notice orally or in writing; and a statement advising the employee of the time within which an appeal must be filed. The appointing power must separately file the notice with the board no later than 15 calendar days after the adverse action's effective date.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of the statute; subdivision (b), which materially narrows who this subdivision currently reaches, is addressed in a separate clause of this document and should be read together with this one before assuming this notice procedure applies to a given state employee. The statute leaves "as defined by board rule" undefined here — the precise administrative timing of when a notice must be served "prior to the effective date of the action" depends on a State Personnel Board rule this clause does not independently look up or quote. This clause also does not address what happens, or what remedy is available, if a notice omits one of the five required elements or is filed with the board late.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19574(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the five required contents of the pre-adverse-action written notice and the 15-day board-filing deadline
citations.quote: (a) The appointing power, or its authorized representative, may take adverse action against an employee for one or more of the causes for discipline specified in this article. Adverse action is valid only if a written notice is served on the employee prior to the effective date of the action, as defined by board rule. The notice shall be served upon the employee either personally or by mail and shall include: (1) a statement of the nature of the adverse action; (2) the effective date of the action; (3) a statement of the reasons therefor in ordinary language; (4) a statement advising the employee of the right to answer the notice orally or in writing; and (5) a statement advising the employee of the time within which an appeal must be filed. The notice shall be filed with the board not later than 15 calendar days after the effective date of the adverse action.

clauses.title: A Major Limitation: Subdivision (a)'s Notice Rule Is Now Confined to State Bargaining Unit 5, and a Memorandum of Understanding Can Override the Hearing Rules
clauses.body: The same section that states the five-element notice requirement also narrows it: effective January 1, 1996, subdivision (b) states that subdivision (a) shall apply only to state employees in State Bargaining Unit 5, and that the section does not apply to discipline as defined by a separate section, 19576.1. A related section elsewhere in this article makes the same point about a memorandum of understanding generally: if a memorandum of understanding reached under the State Employer-Employee Relations Act conflicts with this article's provisions on whether a hearing must be held, the memorandum of understanding controls without further legislative action, unless it would require an expenditure of funds not approved by the Legislature in the annual Budget Act.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (b) exactly as codified, but the subdivision's own wording is ambiguous on its face about whether "this subdivision" in its first sentence means subdivision (a) (the notice requirement) or subdivision (b) itself; this clause does not resolve that ambiguity and instead flags it so a reader does not assume subdivision (a)'s notice procedure applies to their own bargaining unit without checking. This clause also does not identify which state employees fall within "State Bargaining Unit 5" (historically the California Highway Patrol's bargaining unit) as opposed to the many other state bargaining units, does not reproduce the separate definition of "discipline" in Government Code section 19576.1 that this subdivision cross-references, and does not identify the specific memorandum of understanding, if any, that actually governs a given reader's adverse-action procedure in place of this article's default rules — that document, not this information sheet, controls in case of conflict.

citations.cite: subdivision (b)'s State Bargaining Unit 5 limitation on subdivision (a)'s notice rule
citations.quote: (b) Effective January 1, 1996, this subdivision shall apply only to state employees in State Bargaining Unit 5. This section shall not apply to discipline as defined by Section 19576.1.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19576 (California Legislative Information text)

citations.quote: If the provisions of this section concerning whether a hearing should be held are in conflict with the provisions of a memorandum of understanding reached pursuant to the State Employer-Employee Relations Act (SEERA), commencing with Section 3512, the memorandum of understanding shall be controlling without further legislative action, except that if those provisions of a memorandum of understanding require the expenditure of funds, the provisions shall not become effective unless approved by the Legislature in the annual Budget Act.

clauses.title: The 30-Day Deadline to File a Written Answer, and the Consequence of Missing It
clauses.body: An employee who receives a notice of adverse action has 30 calendar days after the action's effective date to file a written answer with the board. The answer is treated as denying every allegation in the notice not expressly admitted, and as a request for a hearing or investigation under this article. With the board's or its authorized representative's consent, the employee may later file an amended answer. If the employee does not answer within the 30-day period, or later withdraws the appeal after answering, the adverse action taken by the appointing power becomes final.
clauses.gap: This clause does not address whether, or under what circumstances, the 30-day period can be extended or excused (for example, for a late-discovered notice defect), and does not address how a partial or ambiguous answer is treated beyond the statute's own default rule that an unadmitted allegation is deemed denied. It also does not describe the format an answer must take or where or how it must be filed with the board beyond what this section itself states, and does not address whether a period shorter than 30 days for an employee to answer could ever be substituted by an applicable memorandum of understanding, a question this clause does not research.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19575 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the 30-calendar-day deadline to file a written answer and the finality consequence of missing it
citations.quote: The employee has 30 calendar days after the effective date of the adverse action to file with the board a written answer to the notice of adverse action. The answer shall be deemed to be a denial of all of the allegations of the notice of adverse action not expressly admitted and a request for hearing or investigation as provided in this article. With the consent of the board or its authorized representative an amended answer may subsequently be filed. If the employee fails to answer within the time specified or after answer withdraws his or her appeal the adverse action taken by the appointing power shall be final.

clauses.title: The Right to a Hearing Once an Answer Is Filed, and How It Must Be Conducted
clauses.body: Once an employee files an answer to a notice of adverse action, the board or its authorized representative must, within a reasonable time, hold a hearing (subject to the separate, narrower investigation-only procedure this article allows for certain minor discipline). The board must notify the parties of the hearing's time and place. The hearing itself must be conducted under the Government Code's general administrative-adjudication procedure section governing agency hearings, except that witness examination follows this article's own separate section on examination, and the parties may submit all proper and competent evidence for or against the stated causes.
clauses.gap: This clause does not independently look up or restate what Government Code section 11513 (the cross-referenced general hearing-procedure statute) itself requires, or what the narrower investigation-only procedure under Government Code section 19576 covers and how it differs from a full hearing — those are addressed, if at all, elsewhere in this project or not at this depth. It also does not address the employee's right (if any) to be represented by counsel or a union representative at the hearing, a topic this section's text does not itself state and that this clause does not research further.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19578 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the right to a hearing once an answer is filed and the applicable hearing procedure
citations.quote: Except as provided in Section 19576, whenever an answer is filed to an adverse action, the board or its authorized representative shall within a reasonable time hold a hearing. The board shall notify the parties of the time and place of the hearing. The hearing shall be conducted in accordance with the provisions of Section 11513 of the Government Code, except that the employee and other persons may be examined as provided in Section 19580, and the parties may submit all proper and competent evidence against or in support of the causes.

clauses.title: The Board's Decision Standard, and How Backpay and Benefits Are Calculated (and Reduced) If the Action Is Reversed
clauses.body: After the hearing or investigation, the board must render a decision within a reasonable time; the adverse action stands unless the board modifies or revokes it. If the board finds the stated cause or causes insufficient or not sustained, or that the employee's conduct was justified, it may modify or revoke the action and order the employee returned to the position, with appropriate restoration of backpay and lost benefits as of the adverse action's date or a later date the board specifies. When the board does revoke or modify an adverse action this way, it must direct payment of salary and accrued interest and reinstate all benefits that otherwise would have normally accrued. But that backpay obligation has real limits: salary is not authorized for any period the employee was not ready, able, and willing to perform the position's duties (whether or not the adverse action itself was valid), and the statute requires an offset — from any salary due, the board must deduct compensation the employee earned, or reasonably could have earned, for any period beginning more than six months after the suspension's initial date.
clauses.gap: This clause does not resolve fact-specific questions such as what counts as being "ready, able, and willing" to perform the position's duties during a disputed period, or what amount of substitute earnings a board would treat as having been "reasonably" earned for purposes of the six-month offset rule — both are case-specific determinations for the board to make on the evidence, not a formula this clause supplies. It also does not address the separate constitutional-discretion cross-reference this same section (19583) makes to Article VII, Section 3 of the California Constitution and to Government Code section 19573's disciplinary criteria, an aspect of the decision standard this clause does not quote or analyze further.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19583 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the board's decision standard and its authority to order backpay and restoration of lost benefits
citations.quote: The board shall render a decision within a reasonable time after the hearing or investigation. The adverse action taken by the appointing power shall stand unless modified or revoked by the board. If the board finds that the cause or causes for which the adverse action was imposed were insufficient or not sustained, or that the employee was justified in the course of conduct upon which the causes were based, it may modify or revoke the adverse action and it may order the employee returned to his or her position with appropriate restoration of backpay and lost benefits either as of the date of the adverse action or as of such later date as it may specify.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19584 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the board's duty to direct payment of salary, interest, and reinstated benefits when it reverses or modifies an adverse action
citations.quote: Whenever the board revokes or modifies an adverse action and orders that the employee be returned to his or her position, it shall direct the payment of salary and all interest accrued thereto, and the reinstatement of all benefits that otherwise would have normally accrued.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19584 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the limitation that salary is not payable for a period the employee was not ready, able, and willing to work
citations.quote: Salary shall not be authorized or paid for any portion of a period of adverse action that the employee was not ready, able, and willing to perform the duties of his or her position, whether the adverse action is valid or not or the causes on which it is based state facts sufficient to constitute cause for discipline.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19584 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the mitigation offset for compensation earned, or reasonably earned, more than six months after the suspension began
citations.quote: From any such salary due there shall be deducted compensation that the employee earned, or might reasonably have earned, during any period commencing more than six months after the initial date of the suspension.

clauses.title: Petitioning the Board for Rehearing, and the Separate, Preserved Right to Seek Judicial Review
clauses.body: After the board serves its decision, either party has 30 days to petition the board in writing for rehearing, stating all grounds on which rehearing should be granted. Separately, and importantly, the statute preserves an employee's right to petition a court for a writ of mandate, or to bring or maintain any action or proceeding based on or related to any civil service law of California or its administration — that right is not affected by a failure to first petition the board for rehearing.
clauses.gap: This clause does not address the statutory deadline for filing a writ of mandate petition in superior court itself (a question of the Code of Civil Procedure this project may address elsewhere, if at all, but that this clause does not research or cite here), does not describe the standard of judicial review a court applies to the board's decision, and does not address the separate 90-day deadline this article's rehearing section imposes on the board to act on a rehearing petition once filed (addressed only in the board's own procedural timeline, not the employee's filing deadline, and not fully quoted in this clause).

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19586 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the 30-day deadline to petition the board for rehearing of its decision
citations.quote: Within 30 days after the day a copy of the decision rendered by the board in a proceeding under this article is served by the board upon the parties to the decision, either party may petition the board for rehearing of the decision. The petition for rehearing shall be in writing and shall contain all of the grounds upon which a rehearing should be granted.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19588 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the preserved right to petition a court for a writ of mandate regardless of whether rehearing was sought
citations.quote: The right to petition a court for writ of mandate, or to bring or maintain any action or proceeding based on or related to any civil service law of this State or the administration thereof shall not be affected by the failure to apply for rehearing by filing written petition therefor with the board.

clauses.title: Letters of Reprimand Must Be Removed From the Personnel File and Destroyed After Three Years
clauses.body: Separately from the adverse-action notice, answer, and hearing process, this article requires that a letter of reprimand be removed from the state employee's personnel file and destroyed no later than three years from the date the letter was issued.
clauses.gap: This clause does not address whether or how an employee can request or enforce this removal if an agency fails to act after three years, does not address whether the underlying facts described in a removed reprimand letter can still be referenced from other agency records or in a later disciplinary action, and does not address the retention rules for any other type of personnel record (such as a notice of adverse action itself or investigative material) which are not covered by this specific three-year reprimand-letter rule.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 19589 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the three-year removal-and-destruction requirement for letters of reprimand
citations.quote: Letters of reprimand shall be removed from the personnel file of the state employee and destroyed not later than three years from the date the letters were issued.

clauses.title: Closing and Signature Block — State Civil Service Disciplinary Due Process Information Sheet
clauses.body:
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{employeeName}}: ☐ _________________________
