[This information sheet describes Article 1 (Disciplinary Proceedings) of Chapter 7 of Part 2 of the State Civil Service Act, California Government Code sections 19570, 19571, 19572, 19574, 19575, 19576, 19578, 19583, 19584, 19586, 19588, and 19589 — the article's definitions of "adverse action" and its enumerated causes for discipline, the five-element pre-action written notice and its current State Bargaining Unit 5 limitation, the 30-day right to answer, the right to a hearing, the board's decision standard and backpay/mitigation rules if an action is reversed or modified, the right to petition for rehearing, the separately preserved right to seek judicial review by writ of mandate, and the three-year reprimand-letter removal rule. It does not itself determine that {{companyName}} did, or did not, comply with any provision of this article with respect to {{employeeName}}, is not an answer, administrative appeal, petition for rehearing, writ of mandate petition, or court filing, is not filed with any agency or court by completing it, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting the actual statute, the employing agency's own board rules or applicable memorandum of understanding, or a licensed attorney.]

clauses.title: Declaration -- Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet addresses California's statutory scheme governing court-appointed child custody evaluators and investigators under Family Code Chapter 6 (Custody Investigation and Report, commencing with Section 3110), in a contested custody or visitation matter concerning {{childName}} between {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}} pending in {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes what a court-appointed evaluation is, who may serve as an evaluator and the training and licensing requirements that apply, how evaluation costs may be allocated between the parties, the confidentiality of the resulting report and the sanctions for its unwarranted disclosure, a domestic-violence-specific interview safeguard, the right to cross-examine the evaluator, and a separate, heightened evaluation protocol that applies when a serious allegation of child sexual abuse is at issue. This is distinct from this project's Mandatory Child Custody Mediation information sheet, which addresses Family Court Services mediation and recommending counseling under a different Family Code chapter, and from its Guardian Ad Litem and Minor's Counsel information sheets, which address representation of the child rather than the evaluator's own role.

clauses.title: "Court-Appointed Investigator" Is a Defined Term Covering Three Kinds of Personnel
clauses.body: Family Code Chapter 6 uses the term "court-appointed investigator" as an umbrella label. Section 3110 defines it to mean a probation officer, a domestic relations investigator, or a court-appointed evaluator, in each case directed by the court to conduct an investigation under this chapter. Where a reference is made in this document, or in an order concerning {{childName}}, to a "court-appointed investigator," that phrase can refer to any of these three types of personnel, not only to a licensed mental-health evaluator.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only Section 3110's definition. It does not independently verify how a specific superior court in California actually staffs custody investigations -- for example, whether a given county uses in-house probation or domestic relations investigators, contracts with private evaluators, or some combination -- which varies by county and is not addressed by the statute itself. No case law interpreting this definition was reviewed (see this document's overall CourtListener disclosure).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3110
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3110
citations.quote: As used in this chapter, “court-appointed investigator” means a probation officer, domestic relations investigator, or court-appointed evaluator directed by the court to conduct an investigation pursuant to this chapter.

clauses.title: A Court May Appoint an Evaluator in a Contested Case, and Reports Must Be Filed at Least 10 Days Before the Hearing
clauses.body: In a contested proceeding involving child custody or visitation, Family Code section 3111(a) authorizes -- but does not require -- the court to appoint a child custody evaluator to conduct an evaluation, where the court determines doing so is in the child's best interest. Any such evaluation must be conducted according to standards the Judicial Council adopts under Section 3117, and a court may consider an evaluation, investigation, or report only if it was conducted consistent with those standards (minor, nonsubstantive errors do not disqualify a report). If the court directs a written report, it must be filed with the court clerk and served on the parties or their attorneys, and on any separate counsel appointed for {{childName}} under Section 3150, at least 10 days before the custody hearing.
clauses.gap: Section 3111(a) does not itself define "best interest of the child" for purposes of deciding whether to order an evaluation, and does not list the Judicial Council standards it cross-references (those are adopted separately under Section 3117 and in California Rules of Court, which this clause does not independently fetch or quote). The statute is permissive ("may appoint"), not mandatory, and nothing in this clause should be read as stating that a court is required to order, or will order, an evaluation in any particular case. No case law addressing when a trial court's decision to grant or deny a request for an evaluation is an abuse of discretion was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time -- see this document's overall disclosure).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(a)
citations.quote: In a contested proceeding involving child custody or visitation rights, the court may appoint a child custody evaluator to conduct a child custody evaluation in cases where the court determines it is in the best interest of the child. The child custody evaluation shall be conducted in accordance with the standards adopted by the Judicial Council pursuant to Section 3117, and all other standards adopted by the Judicial Council regarding child custody evaluations. If directed by the court, the court-appointed child custody evaluator shall file a written confidential report on the evaluation. At least 10 days before a hearing regarding custody of the child, the report shall be filed with the clerk of the court in which the custody hearing will be conducted and served on the parties or their attorneys, and any other counsel appointed for the child pursuant to Section 3150.

clauses.title: Since 2005, an Evaluator Must Generally Hold One of Six Specified Licenses or Certifications
clauses.body: Family Code section 3110.5(c) limits who may serve as a child custody evaluator -- whether appointed under this chapter, under Evidence Code section 730, or under the discovery statute governing mental examinations -- to six categories of licensed or certified professionals: a physician who is a board-certified psychiatrist or has completed a psychiatric residency; a licensed psychologist; a licensed marriage and family therapist; a licensed clinical social worker; a licensed professional clinical counselor; or a court-connected evaluator certified by the court as meeting the Judicial Council's qualifications for court-connected evaluators. An evaluator proposed to assess {{childName}}'s custody or visitation situation must fit one of these six categories, subject to the narrow unavailability exception addressed in this document's companion clause on that exception.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the six-category licensing list in subdivision (c). It does not restate the separate education, experience, and training requirements the Judicial Council was directed to formulate by rule under subdivision (b) (which this document does not independently fetch), and it does not verify the current text of California Rules of Court 5.220 or 5.225, which implement these qualification standards in more operational detail. This is a single statutory subdivision; no independent second source was located for it, and no case law addressing disqualification of an evaluator for failing to meet these categories was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time -- see this document's overall disclosure).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3110.5(c)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3110.5(c)
citations.quote: a person may be a child custody evaluator under this chapter, Section 730 of the Evidence Code, or Chapter 15 (commencing with Section 2032.010) of Title 4 of Part 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure only if the person meets one of the following criteria:(1) The person is licensed as a physician under Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 2000) of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code and either is a board certified psychiatrist or has completed a residency in psychiatry.(2) The person is licensed as a psychologist under Chapter 6.6 (commencing with Section 2900) of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code.(3) The person is licensed as a marriage and family therapist under Chapter 13 (commencing with Section 4980) of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code.(4) The person is licensed as a clinical social worker under Article 4 (commencing with Section 4996) of Chapter 14 of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code.(5) The person is licensed as a professional clinical counselor under Chapter 16 (commencing with Section 4999.10) of Division 2 of the Business and Professions Code.(6) The person is a court-connected evaluator who has been certified by the court as meeting all of the qualifications for court-connected evaluators as specified by the Judicial Council pursuant to subdivision (b).

clauses.title: An Evaluator Must Complete Domestic-Violence and Child-Sexual-Abuse Training as a Precondition to Serving
clauses.body: Independent of the licensing categories in Section 3110.5(c), Section 3110.5(a) requires that a court-connected or private child custody evaluator have completed the domestic violence and child abuse training program described in Family Code section 1816 and have complied with California Rules of Court 5.220 and 5.230 before serving in that role at all. Section 3110.5(f) adds a separate, later-enacted bar specific to child sexual abuse: on and after January 1, 2005, a court-connected or private evaluator may not evaluate, investigate, or mediate a custody issue unless that person has completed the child-sexual-abuse training the section requires.
clauses.gap: This clause cites two different subsections of the same statutory section (§ 3110.5(a) and § 3110.5(f)); they are treated as one source, not independent corroboration. It does not independently fetch or quote Family Code section 1816 (the cross-referenced training-program statute) or Rules of Court 5.220/5.230, so the actual content and hour requirements of the training program are not verified here -- only the fact that completion is a statutory precondition to serving as an evaluator. No case law addressing the consequence of an evaluator's noncompliance with this training requirement (for example, whether it renders a report inadmissible or merely subjects the evaluator to licensing discipline) was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3110.5(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3110.5(a)
citations.quote: A person may be a court-connected or private child custody evaluator under this chapter only if the person has completed the domestic violence and child abuse training program described in Section 1816 and has complied with Rules 5.220 and 5.230 of the California Rules of Court.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3110.5(f)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3110.5(f)
citations.quote: On or after January 1, 2005, a court-connected or private child custody evaluator may not evaluate, investigate, or mediate an issue of child custody in a proceeding pursuant to this division unless that person has completed child sexual abuse training as required by this section.

clauses.title: The Court Inquires Into Ability to Pay Before Ordering Repayment of Evaluation Costs
clauses.body: When a court-appointed investigator is directed to conduct a custody investigation or evaluation, or to undertake related visitation work, Family Code section 3112(a) requires the court to inquire into the financial condition of the parent, guardian, or other person charged with supporting {{childName}}. If the court finds that person able to pay all or part of the expense of the investigation, report, and recommendation, it may order repayment to the court of an amount it determines proper; under subdivision (b), that repayment is made to the court itself, which keeps accounts of the expenses and repayments and deposits the collections as the Judicial Council directs.
clauses.gap: The statute does not set a fee schedule, a cap, or a formula for allocating cost between two parents -- it leaves the amount to the court's determination after the required ability-to-pay inquiry, and does not distinguish here between a court-connected evaluator's cost and a private evaluator's cost (private evaluators are frequently paid directly rather than through court repayment, a distinction this section's text does not itself address). This clause quotes both subdivisions of a single statutory section; no independent second source was located, and no case law on how courts apply the ability-to-pay inquiry in practice was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3112
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3112
citations.quote: Where a court-appointed investigator is directed by the court to conduct a custody investigation or evaluation pursuant to this chapter or to undertake visitation work, including necessary evaluation, supervision, and reporting, the court shall inquire into the financial condition of the parent, guardian, or other person charged with the support of the minor. If the court finds the parent, guardian, or other person able to pay all or part of the expense of the investigation, report, and recommendation, the court may make an order requiring the parent, guardian, or other person to repay the court the amount the court determines proper.

clauses.title: The Evaluator's Report Is Confidential, Stipulated-In as Evidence, and Its Unwarranted Disclosure Can Draw Sanctions
clauses.body: Family Code section 3111 places several controls on the report itself, separate from the confidentiality rule this project's Move-Away Custody information sheet addresses (Section 3025.5). Under subdivision (b), the report may not be made available except as subdivision (a) or Section 3025.5 provides, or as described in Welfare and Institutions Code section 204 or Probate Code section 1514.5. Under subdivision (c), the report may be received in evidence on stipulation of all interested parties and, once stipulated in, is competent evidence as to everything it contains. Under subdivision (d), if the court finds an unwarranted disclosure of the written confidential report, it may impose a monetary sanction -- sufficient to deter repetition, potentially including attorney's fees and costs -- against the disclosing party, unless the party acted with substantial justification or other circumstances make a sanction unjust, and the court may not impose a sanction that would create an unreasonable financial burden on the sanctioned party. Subdivision (f) defines "unwarranted": a disclosure is unwarranted only if it is done recklessly or maliciously and is not in {{childName}}'s best interest.
clauses.gap: This clause cites four different subsections of the same statutory section (§ 3111(b), (c), (d), and (f)); they are treated as one source, not independent corroboration. It does not restate subdivision (a) (appointment and filing, covered in this document's companion clause) or subdivision (e) (the Judicial Council's confidentiality-notice form requirement), and it does not independently fetch or quote Welfare and Institutions Code section 204, Probate Code section 1514.5, or Family Code section 3025.5 -- each is only cross-referenced here as subdivision (b) names it. No case law construing "recklessly or maliciously" for purposes of the unwarranted-disclosure sanction was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(b)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(b)
citations.quote: The report shall not be made available other than as provided in subdivision (a) or Section 3025.5, or as described in Section 204 of the Welfare and Institutions Code or Section 1514.5 of the Probate Code.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(c)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(c)
citations.quote: The report may be received in evidence on stipulation of all interested parties and is competent evidence as to all matters contained in the report.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(d)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(d)
citations.quote: If the court determines that an unwarranted disclosure of a written confidential report has been made, the court may impose a monetary sanction against the disclosing party. The sanction shall be in an amount sufficient to deter repetition of the conduct, and may include reasonable attorney’s fees, costs incurred, or both, unless the court finds that the disclosing party acted with substantial justification or that other circumstances make the imposition of the sanction unjust.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(f)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3111(f)
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, a disclosure is unwarranted if it is done either recklessly or maliciously, and is not in the best interest of the child.

clauses.title: A History of Domestic Violence Triggers a Right to Meet With the Investigator Separately
clauses.body: Family Code section 3113 provides a specific safeguard distinct from this project's other domestic-violence-related custody clauses: where there has been a history of domestic violence between {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}, or where a protective order as defined in Section 6218 is in effect, the party alleging domestic violence -- by written declaration under penalty of perjury -- or the party protected by the order can require that the parties meet with the court-appointed investigator separately and at separate times, rather than together.
clauses.gap: This is a single statutory section; no independent second source was located for it. The statute does not specify a deadline or procedural mechanism for making the request (beyond a written declaration under penalty of perjury by the alleging party), and does not address whether it extends to other participants in the evaluation process, such as collateral witnesses. No case law addressing this section was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time -- see this document's overall disclosure).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3113
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3113
citations.quote: Where there has been a history of domestic violence between the parties, or where a protective order as defined in Section 6218 is in effect, at the request of the party alleging domestic violence in a written declaration under penalty of perjury or at the request of a party who is protected by the order, the parties shall meet with the court-appointed investigator separately and at separate times.

clauses.title: A Party Does Not Lose the Right to Cross-Examine the Investigator by Something Said or Done Before Receiving the Report
clauses.body: Family Code section 3115 protects a party's ability to cross-examine the court-appointed investigator about the evaluation. A statement -- written or oral -- or a course of conduct is not treated as waiving that right unless the statement was made, or the conduct occurred, after the report was received by the party or the party's attorney. Something {{parent1Name}} or {{parent2Name}} said or did before receiving the report on {{childName}}'s evaluation therefore cannot, by itself, be used to argue that person gave up the right to cross-examine the investigator about it.
clauses.gap: The statute addresses only when a waiver is not found (before the report is received); it does not describe what statements or conduct after receipt of the report would actually constitute a waiver, and does not itself set the procedure or timeline for requesting cross-examination (that is addressed by the Judicial Council guidelines under the companion Section 3117, referenced but not independently fetched or quoted in this document). This is a single statutory section; no independent second source was located, and no case law construing this waiver rule was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3115
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3115
citations.quote: A statement, whether written or oral, or conduct shall not be held to constitute a waiver by a party of the right to cross-examine the court-appointed investigator, unless the statement is made, or the conduct occurs, after the report has been received by a party or the party’s attorney.

clauses.title: A Serious Child-Sexual-Abuse Allegation Triggers a Separate, Heightened Evaluation Protocol
clauses.body: Family Code section 3118 imposes minimum requirements on top of the general evaluation rules described elsewhere in this document, once a court determines there is a "serious allegation of child sexual abuse" in a contested custody or visitation case where an evaluator has been appointed or a case referred for evaluation. The statute defines that term specifically: a serious allegation of child sexual abuse means an allegation of child sexual abuse, as defined in Penal Code section 11165.1, that is based in whole or in part on statements the child made to law enforcement, a child welfare services agency investigator, a mandated reporter, or other court-appointed personnel, or that is supported by substantial independent corroboration under Family Code section 3011(a)(2)(B). Once triggered, Section 3118(a)(3) requires that any evaluation or investigation conducted under this section be performed by an evaluator or investigator who meets the Section 3110.5 qualifications described in this document's companion clauses, and Section 3118(b)(6) requires a confidential written report filed with the court clerk and served on the parties or their attorneys at least 10 days before the hearing.
clauses.gap: Section 3118 is a long, multi-part section; this clause quotes only the definitional sentence, the cross-reference to Section 3110.5 qualifications, and the report-timing requirement. It does not restate the section's detailed list of required investigative steps (agency consultation, review of the child welfare file, criminal-background-check information, the multidisciplinary child interview team process, a forensic medical examination or a written explanation for not seeking one), the report's required contents, the emergency-order carve-out in subdivision (a)(1), the family-court-mediation information handling in subdivision (c), the temporary-visitation-limitation consideration in subdivision (f), or the juvenile-dependency-proceeding suspension and coordination rules in subdivisions (g) and (h) -- all of which this document does not independently verify or quote. No case law applying this section was reviewed (CourtListener quota was exhausted at research time -- see this document's overall disclosure).

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3118(a)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3118(a)
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, a serious allegation of child sexual abuse means an allegation of child sexual abuse, as defined in Section 11165.1 of the Penal Code, that is based in whole or in part on statements made by the child to law enforcement, a child welfare services agency investigator, any person required by statute to report suspected child abuse, or any other court-appointed personnel, or that is supported by substantial independent corroboration as provided for in subparagraph (B) of paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 3011.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3118(a)(3)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3118(a)(3)
citations.quote: Any evaluation, investigation, or assessment conducted pursuant to this section shall be conducted by an evaluator or investigator who meets the qualifications set forth in Section 3110.5.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3118(b)(6)
citations.cite: Cal. Fam. Code § 3118(b)(6)
citations.quote: File a confidential written report with the clerk of the court in which the custody hearing will be conducted and which shall be served on the parties or their attorneys at least 10 days prior to the hearing.

clauses.title: How This Chapter Relates to Other California Custody Procedures
clauses.body: A Chapter 6 court-appointed child custody evaluation, as described in this document, is a distinct procedure from several others this project separately documents or that California law separately provides. It is not the same as Family Court Services mediation or recommending counseling under Family Code Chapter 11 (commencing with Section 3160), addressed in this project's Mandatory Child Custody Mediation information sheet -- a case can go through mediation, an evaluation, both, or neither. It is not the same as the appointment of counsel to represent {{childName}} under Section 3150, addressed in this project's Minor's Counsel information sheet, although Family Code section 3114 (not independently verified or quoted in this document) allows a court-appointed investigator to recommend that the court appoint such counsel. An evaluation under this chapter can also be ordered under, or run alongside, an evaluation under Evidence Code section 730 or the civil discovery statute governing mental examinations (Code of Civil Procedure section 2032.010 et seq.) -- Section 3110.5's evaluator-qualification rules apply across all three routes, but this document does not independently verify Evidence Code section 730 or the Code of Civil Procedure provisions themselves. Nothing in this document requests, orders, or predicts whether a court will order an evaluation in any specific case involving {{childName}}.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment -- Not a Court Order or Determination
clauses.body:
I, {{parent1Name}}, and I, {{parent2Name}}, each acknowledge that I have reviewed this information sheet describing California's statutory scheme for court-appointed child custody evaluations and investigations in connection with the matter concerning {{childName}} pending in {{countyOfFiling}}.

Executed on {{dateSigned}}.

☐ _________________________ {{parent1Name}}, signature

☐ _________________________ {{parent2Name}}, signature

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual filing or proceeding in the appropriate California superior court. It does not itself appoint an evaluator, does not order or request an evaluation, does not determine which of the six Section 3110.5(c) qualification categories a specific evaluator satisfies, and does not allocate evaluation costs between {{parent1Name}} and {{parent2Name}}. Only the court, applying Family Code Chapter 6 and the Judicial Council standards and forms it references, determines whether an evaluation is ordered in a specific matter concerning {{childName}} and how it proceeds.]

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet states, using the statutes' own text, the framework California Business and Professions Code §§ 480 through 484 and § 7.5 impose on every state licensing board named in that code when the board considers denying an occupational or professional license to {{applicantName}} based on the applicant's criminal history, in connection with {{applicantName}}'s pursuit of licensure as a {{professionType}} before the {{licensingBoardName}}. It states facts about what the statutes require, permit, and prohibit. It does not predict how {{licensingBoardName}} will apply these standards to {{applicantName}}'s particular record, and it does not instruct {{companyName}} or {{applicantName}} on what to do about any specific application, disclosure, or denial.

clauses.title: The Two Grounds on Which a Board May Deny a License for Criminal History
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 480(a) states that, notwithstanding any other provision of the code, a board may deny a license regulated by the code on the grounds that the applicant has been convicted of a crime or has been subject to formal discipline only if one of two conditions is met. The first, stated in paragraph (a)(1), is that the applicant has been convicted of a crime, within the preceding seven years from the date of application, that is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession for which the application is made — regardless of whether the applicant was incarcerated for that crime — or has been convicted of such a substantially related crime and is presently incarcerated for it or was released from incarceration for it within the preceding seven years.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the seven-year conviction ground of paragraph (a)(1); it does not state the separate formal-discipline ground of paragraph (a)(2) (a companion clause in this document does), and it does not state the statute's own exceptions removing the seven-year limitation entirely for certain offenses (also a companion clause).

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(a)
citations.quote: (a) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, a board may deny a license regulated by this code on the grounds that the applicant has been convicted of a crime or has been subject to formal discipline only if either of the following conditions are met:(1) The applicant has been convicted of a crime within the preceding seven years from the date of application that is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession for which the application is made, regardless of whether the applicant was incarcerated for that crime, or the applicant has been convicted of a crime that is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession for which the application is made and for which the applicant is presently incarcerated or for which the applicant was released from incarceration within the preceding seven years from the date of application.

clauses.title: The Separate Formal-Discipline Ground, and Its Own Carve-Back for Dismissed Convictions
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 480(a)(2) states the second ground on which a board may deny a license: that the applicant has been subjected to formal discipline by a licensing board in or outside California, within the preceding seven years, based on professional misconduct that would have been cause for discipline before the board receiving the present application and that is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of that business or profession. The statute states its own limit on this ground: prior disciplinary action within the preceding seven years is not a basis for denial if that discipline rested on a conviction that has since been dismissed under Penal Code § 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, 1203.42, or 1203.425, or a comparable dismissal or expungement. The statute separately states a narrow exception reaching further back than seven years, tied to a comparison against the standard that would apply to a physician and surgeon's sexual misconduct with a patient under Business and Professions Code §§ 726 and 729.
clauses.gap: The 'would have constituted an act of sexual abuse, misconduct, or relations with a patient' comparator is stated by cross-reference to Sections 726 and 729; this clause does not independently verify or reproduce the text of either of those sections, which a board applying this older-than-seven-years exception would need to consult.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(a)(2)
citations.quote: (2) The applicant has been subjected to formal discipline by a licensing board in or outside California within the preceding seven years from the date of application based on professional misconduct that would have been cause for discipline before the board for which the present application is made and that is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession for which the present application is made. However, prior disciplinary action by a licensing board within the preceding seven years shall not be the basis for denial of a license if the basis for that disciplinary action was a conviction that has been dismissed pursuant to Section 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, 1203.42, or 1203.425 of the Penal Code or a comparable dismissal or expungement. Formal discipline that occurred earlier than seven years preceding the date of application may be grounds for denial of a license only if the formal discipline was for conduct that, if committed in this state by a physician and surgeon licensed pursuant to Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 2000) of Division 2, would have constituted an act of sexual abuse, misconduct, or relations with a patient pursuant to Section 726 or sexual exploitation as defined in subdivision (a) of Section 729.

clauses.title: When the Seven-Year Limitation on the Conviction Ground Does Not Apply
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 480(a)(1) states two situations in which the seven-year limitation on the conviction ground for denial does not apply at all, meaning a conviction of any age may be considered. The first is a conviction of a 'serious felony' as defined in Penal Code § 1192.7, or a crime requiring registration under Penal Code § 290(d)(2) or (3). The second is a conviction of a financial crime currently classified as a felony that is directly and adversely related to the fiduciary duties of the profession, under regulations the particular board has adopted, and only for applicants seeking licensure under specifically named chapters of the code — including State Bar-adjacent fiduciary licensure categories, funeral director or cemetery manager licensure, and Division 4 licensure (real estate).
clauses.gap: This clause does not independently verify which occupations fall within each of the five named chapters and divisions listed in subparagraph (B) (i)-(v); a reader would need to consult Chapter 6 commencing with § 6500, Chapter 9 commencing with § 7000, Chapter 11.3 commencing with § 7512, Chapter 12 commencing with § 7600, and Division 4 commencing with § 10000 directly to identify the specific licensed occupations the financial-crime exception reaches.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(a)(1)(A)-(B)
citations.quote: However, the preceding seven-year limitation shall not apply in either of the following situations:(A) The applicant was convicted of a serious felony, as defined in Section 1192.7 of the Penal Code or a crime for which registration is required pursuant to paragraph (2) or (3) of subdivision (d) of Section 290 of the Penal Code.(B) The applicant was convicted of a financial crime currently classified as a felony that is directly and adversely related to the fiduciary qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession for which the application is made, pursuant to regulations adopted by the board, and for which the applicant is seeking licensure under any of the following:(i) Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 6500) of Division 3.(ii) Chapter 9 (commencing with Section 7000) of Division 3.(iii) Chapter 11.3 (commencing with Section 7512) of Division 3.(iv) Licensure as a funeral director or cemetery manager under Chapter 12 (commencing with Section 7600) of Division 3.(v) Division 4 (commencing with Section 10000).

clauses.title: The Three Statutory Criteria for 'Substantially Related'
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 481 requires every board under the code to develop criteria to determine whether a crime is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession it regulates — the standard that § 480 uses without independently defining. Subdivision (b) states that these board-level criteria must include, at minimum, three factors: the nature and gravity of the offense; the number of years elapsed since the date of the offense; and the nature and duties of the profession in which the applicant seeks licensure or in which the licensee is licensed. Subdivision (d), not reproduced here, separately requires each board to post a summary of its criteria on its own website.
clauses.gap: Section 481 requires each board to develop its own criteria consistent with these three minimum statutory factors; this clause does not state, and cannot state generically across all boards, the specific substantially-related criteria any particular licensing board has actually adopted and posted under subdivision (d) — those must be located on that board's own website.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 481 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 481(b)
citations.quote: (b) Criteria for determining whether a crime is substantially related to the qualifications, functions, or duties of the business or profession a board regulates shall include all of the following:(1) The nature and gravity of the offense.(2) The number of years elapsed since the date of the offense.(3) The nature and duties of the profession in which the applicant seeks licensure or in which the licensee is licensed.

clauses.title: Certificate of Rehabilitation, Pardon, or Board Showing of Rehabilitation Bars Denial
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 480(b) states that a person shall not be denied a license on the basis of a conviction, or the acts underlying it, if the person has obtained a certificate of rehabilitation under Penal Code §§ 4852.01 et seq., has been granted clemency or a pardon by a state or federal executive, or has made a showing of rehabilitation under § 482. Section 482, in turn, requires every board to develop criteria to evaluate rehabilitation for this purpose, and states that a board must consider a person to have made a showing of rehabilitation if either the person completed the criminal sentence at issue without a parole or probation violation, or the board — applying its own rehabilitation criteria — finds the applicant rehabilitated.
clauses.gap: This clause does not state the substantive rehabilitation criteria any particular board has adopted under § 482(a), only the statute's floor requirement that completing a sentence without a parole or probation violation must itself count as a showing of rehabilitation; a board's own published criteria may recognize additional or different pathways.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(b)
citations.quote: (b) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, a person shall not be denied a license on the basis that the person has been convicted of a crime, or on the basis of acts underlying a conviction for a crime, if that person has obtained a certificate of rehabilitation under Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 4852.01) of Title 6 of Part 3 of the Penal Code, has been granted clemency or a pardon by a state or federal executive, or has made a showing of rehabilitation pursuant to Section 482.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 482 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 482(a)-(b)
citations.quote: (a) Each board under this code shall develop criteria to evaluate the rehabilitation of a person when doing either of the following:(1) Considering the denial of a license by the board under Section 480.(2) Considering suspension or revocation of a license under Section 490.(b) Each board shall consider whether an applicant or licensee has made a showing of rehabilitation if either of the following are met:(1) The applicant or licensee has completed the criminal sentence at issue without a violation of parole or probation.(2) The board, applying its criteria for rehabilitation, finds that the applicant is rehabilitated.

clauses.title: A Dismissed or Expunged Conviction Cannot Be a Basis for Denial
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 480(c) states that a person shall not be denied a license on the basis of any conviction, or the acts underlying it, that has been dismissed under Penal Code § 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, 1203.42, or 1203.425, or a comparable dismissal or expungement. The statute places a documentation burden on the applicant: an applicant with a conviction dismissed under §§ 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, or 1203.42 must provide proof of the dismissal if it is not already reflected on the criminal history report the Department of Justice furnishes to the board.
clauses.gap: The statute's list of qualifying dismissal mechanisms in the first sentence includes § 1203.425, but the applicant's own proof-of-dismissal obligation in the second sentence is stated only for §§ 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, and 1203.42 — the statute's own text does not extend that specific proof obligation to a § 1203.425 dismissal or to an unnamed 'comparable dismissal or expungement,' and this clause does not resolve that asymmetry.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(c)
citations.quote: (c) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, a person shall not be denied a license on the basis of any conviction, or on the basis of the acts underlying the conviction, that has been dismissed pursuant to Section 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, 1203.42, or 1203.425 of the Penal Code, or a comparable dismissal or expungement. An applicant who has a conviction that has been dismissed pursuant to Section 1203.4, 1203.4a, 1203.41, or 1203.42 of the Penal Code shall provide proof of the dismissal if it is not reflected on the report furnished by the Department of Justice.

clauses.title: Arrests Without Conviction, Infractions, Citations, and Juvenile Adjudications Cannot Be a Basis for Denial
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 480(d) states that a board shall not deny a license on the basis of an arrest that resulted in a disposition other than a conviction, including an arrest that resulted in an infraction, a citation, or a juvenile adjudication.
clauses.gap: This subdivision restricts what a board may use as a basis for denying a license; it does not, by its own text, restrict what a board may ask an applicant on a license application — that separate disclosure question is governed by § 480(f), stated in a companion clause of this document.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(d)
citations.quote: (d) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, a board shall not deny a license on the basis of an arrest that resulted in a disposition other than a conviction, including an arrest that resulted in an infraction, citation, or a juvenile adjudication.

clauses.title: Most Boards May Not Require Disclosure of Criminal History on the Application at All
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 480(f) states the procedures a board must follow in requesting or acting on an applicant's criminal history information. Paragraph (f)(1) names a specific, limited list of code chapters and divisions whose boards may require applicants to disclose criminal conviction history on a license application. Paragraph (f)(2) states the default rule for every other board: except as provided in paragraph (1), a board shall not require an applicant to disclose any information or documentation regarding the applicant's criminal history at all — though a board may request mitigating information voluntarily, provided the applicant is told the disclosure is voluntary and that declining to disclose will not itself count against the application.
clauses.gap: This clause does not independently verify which occupations the seven named chapters and divisions in paragraph (f)(1) cover (Chapter 3 commencing with § 5500, Chapter 3.5 commencing with § 5615, Chapter 10 commencing with § 7301, Chapter 20 commencing with § 9800, and Chapter 20.3 commencing with § 9880 of Division 3, and Chapter 3 commencing with § 19000 and Chapter 3.1 commencing with § 19225 of Division 8); whether a given applicant's board falls inside or outside that list determines which of the two very different disclosure rules applies, and that must be checked against the named chapters directly.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(f)(1)-(2)
citations.quote: (f) A board shall follow the following procedures in requesting or acting on an applicant’s criminal history information:(1) A board issuing a license pursuant to Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 5500), Chapter 3.5 (commencing with Section 5615), Chapter 10 (commencing with Section 7301), Chapter 20 (commencing with Section 9800), or Chapter 20.3 (commencing with Section 9880), of Division 3, or Chapter 3 (commencing with Section 19000) or Chapter 3.1 (commencing with Section 19225) of Division 8 may require applicants for licensure under those chapters to disclose criminal conviction history on an application for licensure.(2) Except as provided in paragraph (1), a board shall not require an applicant for licensure to disclose any information or documentation regarding the applicant’s criminal history. However, a board may request mitigating information from an applicant regarding the applicant’s criminal history for purposes of determining substantial relation or demonstrating evidence of rehabilitation, provided that the applicant is informed that disclosure is voluntary and that the applicant’s decision not to disclose any information shall not be a factor in a board’s decision to grant or deny an application for licensure.

clauses.title: Required Written Notice When a Board Denies a License for Conviction History
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 480(f)(3) states that if a board decides to deny a license application based solely or in part on the applicant's conviction history, the board shall notify the applicant in writing of four things: the denial or disqualification of licensure; any existing board procedure to challenge the decision or request reconsideration; that the applicant has the right to appeal the board's decision; and the process for the applicant to request a copy of their complete conviction history and question its accuracy or completeness under Penal Code §§ 11122 through 11127.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the four items the written notice must contain; it does not state a deadline by which the board must send that notice, nor the substantive procedures (challenge, reconsideration, or appeal) any particular board has adopted to implement subparagraph (B) and (C) — those procedures vary by board and are outside this clause's scope.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 480 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 480(f)(3)
citations.quote: (3) If a board decides to deny an application for licensure based solely or in part on the applicant’s conviction history, the board shall notify the applicant in writing of all of the following:(A) The denial or disqualification of licensure.(B) Any existing procedure the board has for the applicant to challenge the decision or to request reconsideration.(C) That the applicant has the right to appeal the board’s decision.(D) The processes for the applicant to request a copy of the applicant’s complete conviction history and question the accuracy or completeness of the record pursuant to Sections 11122 to 11127 of the Penal Code.

clauses.title: A Single Statutory Definition of 'Conviction' Controls, With a Named Exception
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 7.5(a) defines 'conviction,' for purposes of the code, as a judgment following a plea or verdict of guilty, a plea of nolo contendere, or a finding of guilt. The statute states that an action a board is permitted to take following a conviction may be taken once the time for appeal has elapsed, once the conviction is affirmed on appeal, or once an order granting probation suspends imposition of sentence — but that a board may not deny a license to an applicant otherwise qualified under § 480(b) or (c) (the rehabilitation and dismissed-conviction protections stated in companion clauses of this document). Section 7.5(c) states that, except as provided in subdivision (b), this definition controls over and supersedes the definition of 'conviction' contained within individual practice acts elsewhere in the code. Subdivision (b)(1) states one named exception: nothing in § 7.5 applies to licensure of persons under Chapter 4 (commencing with § 6000) of Division 3 — the State Bar Act governing attorney licensure.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (b)(1)'s State Bar exception and subdivision (c)'s general controls-and-supersedes rule as two separate citations because the intervening text of subdivision (b)(2), naming the State Athletic Commission, the Bureau for Private Postsecondary Education, and the California Horse Racing Board as further exceptions, is not reproduced verbatim here; a reader needing the complete list of entities subdivision (b) exempts should consult the statute's full text directly.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 7.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7.5(a)
citations.quote: (a) A conviction within the meaning of this code means a judgment following a plea or verdict of guilty or a plea of nolo contendere or finding of guilt. Any action which a board is permitted to take following the establishment of a conviction may be taken when the time for appeal has elapsed, or the judgment of conviction has been affirmed on appeal or when an order granting probation is made suspending the imposition of sentence. However, a board may not deny a license to an applicant who is otherwise qualified pursuant to subdivision (b) or (c) of Section 480.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 7.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7.5(b)(1)
citations.quote: (b) (1) Nothing in this section shall apply to the licensure of persons pursuant to Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 6000) of Division 3.

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 7.5 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7.5(c)
citations.quote: (c) Except as provided in subdivision (b), this section controls over and supersedes the definition of conviction contained within individual practice acts under this code.

clauses.title: No Board May Require Third-Party Attestations of Good Moral Character
clauses.body: Business and Professions Code § 484 states that no person applying for licensure under the code shall be required to submit to any licensing board any attestation by other persons to their good moral character.
clauses.gap: This section, last amended in 1974, bars a board from requiring third-party character attestations as a submission requirement; its brief text does not address, and this clause does not resolve, whether a board may still ask the applicant to self-attest to their own good moral character, or may independently investigate character through other statutorily authorized channels such as the criminal-history procedures stated in § 480(f).

citations.case: Business and Professions Code § 484 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 484
citations.quote: No person applying for licensure under this code shall be required to submit to any licensing board any attestation by other persons to his good moral character.

clauses.title: Certification
Proposed Claimant — Information and Declaration Regarding a Contract Concerning a Will or Devise
clauses.body: I, {{claimantName}}, assert a claim arising from a promise or agreement made with {{decedentName}}, who died on {{dateOfDeath}}. My relationship to {{decedentName}} is: {{relationshipToDecedent}}. The promise or agreement I am relying on is dated (or was made on or about): {{agreementDate}}. The property or interest I claim {{decedentName}} promised or agreed to leave to me, or not to revoke a provision leaving to me, is described as follows: {{underlyingClaimDescription}}. This declaration relates to a proceeding that would be filed in the Superior Court of California, County of {{countyOfFiling}}, under Probate Code § 21700 and Code of Civil Procedure § 366.3. This declaration provides background information for use with an actual pleading asserting a claim to distribution based on a contract concerning a will, devise, or other instrument. It is not itself a court filing, a will, a trust, or a binding contract, and signing it does not establish that any contract existed, that {{decedentName}} made any such promise or agreement, or that {{claimantName}} is entitled to any distribution — only a court, applying Probate Code § 21700's methods of proof to the actual facts, can determine that.

clauses.title: A Contract Concerning a Will Can Be Proven Only in the Ways the Statute Lists
clauses.body: Probate Code § 21700(a) governs a contract to make a will or devise or other instrument, a contract not to revoke a will or devise or other instrument, or a contract to die intestate, when the contract was made after the statute's effective date. Such a contract regarding {{decedentName}}'s testamentary plan or intestate succession can be established only by one of five methods the statute lists in § 21700(a)(1)-(5); no other form of proof will do, however persuasive it might otherwise seem.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rule for proving a contract concerning a will — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific decedent's estate, or about whether a particular claimant's facts satisfy any of the five listed methods. The word 'only' in § 21700(a) makes this list exclusive on its face, but this clause does not resolve how a court treats evidence that falls just short of one category (for example, an unsigned draft, or a witness's uncorroborated account of a decedent's oral statement) — the statute's text does not itself define an evidentiary sufficiency threshold below the five listed methods, and this document does not supply one. This document is informational: it does not itself establish, or determine the existence of, any contract concerning a decedent's will, devise, or intestate succession — only a court can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21700(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A contract to make a will or devise or other instrument, or not to revoke a will or devise or other instrument, or to die intestate, if made after the effective date of this statute, can be established only by one of the following:

clauses.title: Three Document-Based Ways to Prove a Contract Concerning a Will
clauses.body: Of the five methods Probate Code § 21700(a) allows, the first three are document-based: (1) the material provisions of the contract are stated directly in a will or other instrument; (2) a will or other instrument expressly refers to a contract, and extrinsic evidence proves the contract's terms; or (3) a writing signed by {{decedentName}} evidences the contract, even if that writing is not itself a will or a reference within one.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rule for proving a contract concerning a will — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific estate, or about whether any specific document a claimant holds qualifies under (1), (2), or (3). § 21700(a)(2)'s 'extrinsic evidence proving the terms of the contract' and § 21700(a)(3)'s 'writing signed by the decedent evidencing the contract' are not further defined within this section — the statute does not state, for example, how complete a signed writing must be to 'evidence' a contract, or what quantum of extrinsic evidence 'proves' a contract's terms under (2). This document does not resolve those undefined terms for any specific writing. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that any writing or will provision satisfies (1), (2), or (3) — only a court can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21700(a)(1)-(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (1) Provisions of a will or other instrument stating the material provisions of the contract. (2) An expressed reference in a will or other instrument to a contract and extrinsic evidence proving the terms of the contract. (3) A writing signed by the decedent evidencing the contract.

clauses.title: Two Ways to Prove a Contract Without Any Writing, by Clear and Convincing Evidence
clauses.body: Probate Code § 21700(a)(4) and (a)(5) allow a contract concerning {{decedentName}}'s will, devise, or other instrument to be proven without any writing at all, but only by clear and convincing evidence: (4) an agreement between {{decedentName}} and {{claimantName}}, or a promise by {{decedentName}} to {{claimantName}}, that is enforceable in equity; or (5) an agreement between {{decedentName}} and a third person for {{claimantName}}'s benefit, or a promise by {{decedentName}} to a third person for {{claimantName}}'s benefit, that is enforceable in equity.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rule for proving a contract concerning a will — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific estate, or about whether any specific account of an agreement or promise meets the clear-and-convincing standard. § 21700 uses the phrase 'clear and convincing evidence' but does not itself define that evidentiary standard, define what makes a promise 'enforceable in equity,' or list the elements of an enforceable-in-equity promise (such as reliance or part performance); this document has not independently fetched or verified the text of whatever Evidence Code or case-law source defines those terms, and does not supply that definition here. This document is informational: it does not itself weigh evidence or determine that any agreement or promise meets this standard — only a court can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21700(a)(4)-(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (4) Clear and convincing evidence of an agreement between the decedent and the claimant or a promise by the decedent to the claimant that is enforceable in equity. (5) Clear and convincing evidence of an agreement between the decedent and another person for the benefit of the claimant or a promise by the decedent to another person for the benefit of the claimant that is enforceable in equity.

clauses.title: Signing a Joint or Mutual Will Does Not, By Itself, Prove a Contract Not to Revoke It
clauses.body: Probate Code § 21700(b) provides that the mere execution of a joint will, or of mutual wills, does not create a presumption of a contract not to revoke the will or wills. If two people — for example, {{decedentName}} and another testator — sign a joint will or mirror-image mutual wills, that fact alone does not shift any burden toward finding a binding contract between them; a contract not to revoke still has to be established under one of the five methods listed in § 21700(a).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's rule on joint and mutual wills — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific pair of wills, or about whether any specific joint or mutual will happens to also satisfy one of § 21700(a)'s five methods (for example, by stating the contract's material provisions within the will itself, which would independently satisfy (a)(1)). § 21700(b) does not itself define 'joint will' or 'mutual wills'; this document does not supply definitions for those terms beyond the statute's own text. This document is informational: it does not itself determine whether any specific joint or mutual will was, or was not, made under a binding contract not to revoke — only a court can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21700(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The execution of a joint will or mutual wills does not create a presumption of a contract not to revoke the will or wills.

clauses.title: Contracts Made Before January 1, 2001 Are Governed by the Prior Law, Not This Statute's List
clauses.body: Probate Code § 21700(c) carves out contracts made before the statute's effective date: a contract to make a will or devise or other instrument, not to revoke one, or to die intestate, if made before § 21700 took effect, is construed under whatever law applied to that contract before § 21700's effective date — not under the five-method list in § 21700(a). The statute's own enactment history states it was added effective January 1, 2001.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's transition rule for pre-existing contracts concerning a will — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific older contract, or about what the substantive 'law applicable to the contract' before January 1, 2001 actually required. § 21700(c) does not itself restate that prior law; determining it would require researching pre-2001 case law and any predecessor statute, which this document has not done — a CourtListener case-law search for this topic was attempted separately and is disclosed in a companion clause. This document is informational: it does not itself determine which body of law governs any specific pre-2001 contract, or resolve any dispute over one — only a court can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 21700(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: A contract to make a will or devise or other instrument, or not to revoke a will or devise or other instrument, or to die intestate, if made prior to the effective date of this section, shall be construed under the law applicable to the contract prior to the effective date of this section.

clauses.title: A Claim to Distribution Based on a Promise or Agreement Must Be Brought Within One Year of Death
clauses.body: Code of Civil Procedure § 366.3(a) sets a special filing deadline for a claim like {{claimantName}}'s: if a person has a claim that arises from a promise or agreement with a decedent — such as {{decedentName}} — to distribution from an estate or trust or under another instrument, whether that promise or agreement was oral or in writing, an action to enforce the claim to distribution may be commenced within one year after the date of death. That one-year period replaces whatever limitations period would otherwise have applied to the underlying promise or agreement (for example, the limitations period that would normally apply to a written or oral contract claim).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's filing deadline for claims based on a decedent's promise or agreement — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific claim, or about when any specific claimant's one-year period actually expires. § 366.3(a) displaces 'the limitations period that would have been applicable,' but this document has not independently identified or verified what that otherwise-applicable period would have been for any specific promise or agreement (a written contract and an oral contract carry different default limitations periods under other statutes this document does not cite). This document is informational: it does not itself calculate any deadline or determine whether any specific claim is timely — only a court, applying this statute to the actual filing date, can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 366.3(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: If a person has a claim that arises from a promise or agreement with a decedent to distribution from an estate or trust or under another instrument, whether the promise or agreement was made orally or in writing, an action to enforce the claim to distribution may be commenced within one year after the date of death, and the limitations period that would have been applicable does not apply.

clauses.title: The One-Year Deadline Is Not Tolled or Extended, Except by Two Narrow Statutory Exceptions
clauses.body: Code of Civil Procedure § 366.3(b) makes the one-year filing period in § 366.3(a) essentially rigid: it may not be tolled or extended for any reason, except as provided in Code of Civil Procedure §§ 12, 12a, and 12b, and except as provided in former Probate Code Part 3 (commencing with § 21300) of Division 11, as that former part read before its repeal by Chapter 174 of the Statutes of 2008.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's tolling rule for this one-year deadline — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific claim, or about whether either exception actually extends time in any specific case. This document has not independently fetched or verified the text of CCP §§ 12, 12a, or 12b (which govern how deadlines falling on weekends, holidays, or court-closure days are computed), or the text of former Probate Code Part 3 (commencing with § 21300) as it read before its 2008 repeal; this clause relies only on § 366.3(b)'s own cross-reference to those provisions, not on their substance. This document is informational: it does not itself toll, extend, or compute any deadline for any specific claim — only a court, applying these cross-referenced provisions, can do that.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 366.3(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: The limitations period provided in this section for commencement of an action shall not be tolled or extended for any reason except as provided in Sections 12, 12a, and 12b of this code, and former Part 3 (commencing with Section 21300) of Division 11 of the Probate Code, as that part read prior to its repeal by Chapter 174 of the Statutes of 2008.

clauses.title: The One-Year Deadline Applies Only to Deaths On or After the Statute's Effective Date
clauses.body: Code of Civil Procedure § 366.3(c) limits the one-year filing rule in § 366.3(a)-(b) to actions brought on claims concerning persons who died on or after this section's effective date. The version of § 366.3 quoted in this document's companion clauses carries a legislative history note that it was amended effective January 1, 2010.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's effective-date limitation on this filing rule — not a claim about which state's law would govern any specific decedent's estate, or about what version of § 366.3 (if any different wording) applied to deaths before January 1, 2010. § 366.3(c) refers to 'the effective date of this section' without restating a specific date within subdivision (c) itself; this clause draws the January 1, 2010 date from the statute's own history note rather than from subdivision (c)'s text, and this document has not independently fetched or verified the wording of any earlier version of § 366.3 that governed deaths before that date. This document is informational: it does not itself determine which version of this statute governs any specific decedent's estate — only a court can do that.
