clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the Civil Air Patrol Employment Protection Act, Labor Code §§ 1500-1507, which gives an eligible employee at a covered California employer the right to unpaid leave to respond to an emergency operational mission of the California Wing of the Civil Air Patrol, protects the employee's Civil Air Patrol membership and service from discrimination or discharge, and requires reinstatement to an equivalent position afterward. It does not cover the corpus's separate volunteer firefighter, reserve peace officer, and emergency rescue personnel leave document (Labor Code §§ 230.3-230.4), which is a different statute with different definitions, a different employer-size threshold, and a different enforcement route; it also does not cover jury duty, witness leave, or USERRA military leave, addressed elsewhere in this corpus.

clauses.title: Who and What Is Covered: Key Definitions
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1501 defines four terms used throughout this part. "Civil Air Patrol leave" means leave requested by an employee who is a volunteer member of the California Wing of the Civil Air Patrol (the civilian auxiliary of the United States Air Force) and who has been duly directed and authorized by the U.S. Air Force, the California Emergency Management Agency, or another political subdivision of the state with authority to authorize an emergency operational mission, to respond to that mission within or outside California. "Employee" means a person permitted, required, or directed by an employer for wages or pay to engage in any employment, who has been employed by that employer for at least a 90-day period immediately preceding the commencement of the leave. "Employee benefits" means all benefits other than salary and wages, including group life insurance, health insurance, disability insurance, and pensions. "Employer" means any person, partnership, corporation, association, or other business entity, or the State of California, a municipality, or other unit of local government, that employs more than 15 employees.
clauses.gap: The § 1501(d) "employer" definition (more than 15 employees) is defined only "in this part" (Labor Code Part 5) and this document does not assert it matches the employee-count threshold used by any other California leave or anti-discrimination statute (for example, FEHA's 5-employee threshold or the 50-employee threshold in this corpus's separate volunteer-responder training-leave document); each statute sets its own threshold independently. The statute does not define how "more than 15 employees" is counted (full-time versus part-time, a rolling headcount, or employees at affiliated entities), and this document does not resolve that gap. The § 1501(b) "employee" definition ends with the circular phrase "if otherwise eligible for leave," and the verified text does not itself state what makes an employee "otherwise eligible" beyond the 90-day tenure requirement and the leave conditions described in the other clauses of this document.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1501 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1501(a)-(d), definitions of Civil Air Patrol leave, employee, employee benefits, and employer
citations.quote: (a) “Civil Air Patrol leave” means leave requested by an employee who is a volunteer member of the California Wing of the civilian auxiliary of the United States Air Force commonly known as the Civil Air Patrol and who has been duly directed and authorized by the United States Air Force, the California Emergency Management Agency, or other political subdivision of the State of California that has the authority to authorize an emergency operational mission of the California Wing of the Civil Air Patrol, to respond to an emergency operational mission, within or outside of the state, of the California Wing of the Civil Air Patrol.(b) “Employee” means a person who may be permitted, required, or directed by an employer for wages or pay to engage in any employment and who has been employed by that employer for at least a 90-day period immediately preceding the commencement of leave, if otherwise eligible for leave.(c) “Employee benefits” means all benefits, other than salary and wages, provided or made available to an employee by an employer and includes group life insurance, health insurance, disability insurance, and pensions, regardless of whether benefits are provided by a policy or practice of an employer.(d) “Employer” means any person, partnership, corporation, association, or other business entity; or the State of California, a municipality, or other unit of local government; that employs more than 15 employees.

clauses.title: Right to Up to 10 Days of Unpaid Leave Per Calendar Year
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 1503(a)(1), a covered employer must provide not less than 10 days per calendar year of unpaid Civil Air Patrol leave to an employee responding to an emergency operational mission of the California Wing of the Civil Air Patrol. Leave for a single mission cannot exceed three days unless an extension is both granted by the governmental entity that authorized the mission and separately approved by the employer. Under § 1503(a)(2), an employer is not required to grant this leave to an employee who is required to respond to the same or another simultaneous emergency operational mission as a first responder or disaster service worker for a local, state, or federal agency.
clauses.gap: The three-day per-mission cap can only be extended if two separate approvals both occur — the authorizing governmental entity's extension of time, and the employer's own approval of that extended leave — and the statute does not state what happens if one is given without the other. The § 1503(a)(2) exception turns on whether the employee is "required to respond" to a simultaneous mission "as a first responder or disaster service worker," and the verified text does not itself define either of those two terms for purposes of this part, so this document does not state which job titles or roles qualify beyond the statute's own bare language. The raw HTML for § 1503(a)(2) contains a mid-sentence line wrap (a tab-and-newline sequence between "required to" and "grant") that both independently fetched copies of the page reproduced identically; the quoted text below preserves it exactly rather than silently normalizing it.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1503 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1503(a)(1)-(2), 10-day annual entitlement, 3-day per-mission cap, and first-responder exception
citations.quote:
(a) (1) An employer shall provide not less than 10 days per calendar year of unpaid Civil Air Patrol leave to an employee responding to an emergency operational mission of the California Wing of the Civil Air Patrol. Civil Air Patrol leave for a single emergency operational mission shall not exceed three days, unless an extension of time is granted by the governmental entity that authorized the emergency operational mission, and the extension of the leave is approved by the employer.(2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), an employer is not required to
					 grant Civil Air Patrol leave to an employee who is required to respond to either the same or other simultaneous emergency operational mission as a first responder or disaster service worker for a local, state, or federal agency.

clauses.title: Notice and Certification Requirements
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 1503(b)(1), an employee must give the employer as much notice as possible of the intended dates the Civil Air Patrol leave will begin and end. Under § 1503(b)(2), the employer may require certification from the proper Civil Air Patrol authority to verify the employee's eligibility for the leave, and the employer may deny the leave if the employee fails to provide that required certification.
clauses.gap: The statute's notice standard ("as much notice as possible") is not tied to any specific number of days or a written-notice requirement, and this document does not state a numeric deadline because the verified text does not set one. The statute does not specify what form Civil Air Patrol certification must take, which official may issue it, or how quickly the employee must produce it after a request, so this document does not describe a certification procedure beyond what § 1503(b)(2) itself says. As with the leave-entitlement clause, the raw HTML for § 1503(b)(2) contains a mid-sentence line wrap (between "deny the" and "leave") that both independently fetched copies reproduced identically; it is preserved exactly in the quoted text below.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1503 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1503(b)(1)-(2), notice and certification requirements
citations.quote:
(b) (1) An employee shall give the employer as much notice as possible of the intended dates upon which the Civil Air Patrol leave will begin and end.(2) An employer may require certification from the proper Civil Air Patrol authority to verify the eligibility of the employee for the leave requested or taken. The employer may deny the
					 leave to be taken as Civil Air Patrol leave if the employee fails to provide the required certification.

clauses.title: Leave Is Unpaid Unless the Employer Chooses Otherwise, and Other Leave Cannot Be Forced First
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1503(a)(1) itself describes the entitlement as "unpaid Civil Air Patrol leave." Under § 1503(c), an employee taking leave under this part is not required to exhaust all accrued vacation leave, personal leave, compensatory leave, sick leave, disability leave, or any other available leave in order to take Civil Air Patrol leave. Under § 1503(d), nothing in the statute prevents an employer from choosing to provide paid leave instead.
clauses.gap: Section 1503(d) permits, but does not require, an employer to pay for this leave, and the statute does not itself create any wage-replacement benefit, state disability insurance eligibility, or other income-replacement mechanism for the unpaid days; this document does not address whether or how an employee might separately qualify for a different wage-replacement program during a period of Civil Air Patrol leave, because § 1503 is silent on that question. The no-forced-exhaustion rule in § 1503(c) protects the employee from being compelled to draw down other leave balances, but it does not itself say whether an employee may voluntarily elect to use paid leave concurrently, only that the employer cannot require it.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1503 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1503(c)-(d), no forced exhaustion of other leave, and employer option to pay
citations.quote: (c) An employee taking leave under this part shall not be required to exhaust all accrued vacation leave, personal leave, compensatory leave, sick leave, disability leave, and any other leave that may be available to the employee in order to take Civil Air Patrol leave.(d) Nothing in this act prevents an employer from providing paid leave for leave taken pursuant to this part.

clauses.title: Protection Against Discrimination Based on Civil Air Patrol Membership
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 1502, an employer shall not discriminate against or discharge from employment a member of the Civil Air Patrol because of that membership, and shall not hinder or prevent a member from performing service as part of the California Wing of the Civil Air Patrol during an emergency operational mission for which the member is entitled to leave under this part.
clauses.gap: Section 1502 states the prohibition itself but does not, in its own text, specify a remedy for its violation; the remedies and enforcement mechanism this document describes elsewhere (reinstatement rights under § 1504, the anti-retaliation provision of § 1506, and the civil action authorized by § 1507) are stated in separate sections of this same part, not within § 1502 itself, so this clause does not restate them here. The protection against being hindered from "performing service" is not, by its own terms, expressly limited to the specific 10-day/3-day leave allowance described in § 1503; this document does not resolve whether § 1502's protection against hindering service extends beyond days that would otherwise qualify as Civil Air Patrol leave under § 1503, because the verified text does not itself draw that boundary.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1502 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1502, prohibition on discrimination based on Civil Air Patrol membership
citations.quote: An employer shall not discriminate against or discharge from employment a member of the Civil Air Patrol because of such membership and shall not hinder or prevent a member from performing service as part of the California Wing of the Civil Air Patrol during an emergency operational mission of the California Wing of the Civil Air Patrol for which a member is entitled to leave under this part.

clauses.title: Right to Reinstatement After Leave
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 1504(a), upon expiration of a leave authorized by this part, an employer must restore the employee to the position held when the leave began, or to a position with equivalent seniority status, employee benefits, pay, and other terms and conditions of employment. An employer may decline to restore an employee as required by this subdivision because of conditions unrelated to the employee's exercise of rights under this part. Under § 1504(b), the employer and employee may negotiate for the employer to maintain the employee's benefits, at the employer's expense, during the leave.
clauses.gap: Section 1504(a)'s exception for declining restoration “because of conditions unrelated to the exercise of rights under this part” is not defined or illustrated by any list of qualifying conditions in the verified text (for example, it does not name layoffs, reorganization, or position elimination as examples), so this document does not state which employer circumstances would qualify, only that the statute allows some unspecified category of unrelated conditions to excuse restoration. Section 1504(b) is a negotiation mechanism, not a mandate: nothing in the verified text requires an employer to agree to maintain paid benefits during the leave, only that the parties may negotiate for it.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1504 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1504(a)-(b), reinstatement duty and benefits-continuation negotiation
citations.quote: (a) An employer shall, upon expiration of a leave authorized by this part, restore an employee to the position held by him or her when the leave began or to a position with equivalent seniority status, employee benefits, pay, and other terms and conditions of employment. An employer may decline to restore an employee as required in this subdivision because of conditions unrelated to the exercise of rights under this part by the employee.(b) An employer and an employee may negotiate for the employer to maintain the benefits of the employee at the expense of the employer during the leave.

clauses.title: No Loss of Previously Accrued Benefits, and Effect on Collective Bargaining Agreements
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 1505(a), taking Civil Air Patrol leave does not result in the loss of an employee benefit accrued before the leave began. Under § 1505(b), this part does not affect an employer's obligation to comply with any collective bargaining agreement or employee benefit plan that provides greater leave rights than this part provides. Under § 1505(c), the rights provided by this part cannot be diminished by a collective bargaining agreement or employee benefit plan entered into on or after January 1, 2010. Under § 1505(d), this part does not affect or diminish the contract rights or seniority status of an employee who is not entitled to Civil Air Patrol leave.
clauses.gap: Section 1505(c)'s anti-diminishment protection is expressly limited to collective bargaining agreements or benefit plans entered into “on or after January 1, 2010”; the verified text does not state what effect, if any, this part has on an agreement or plan that predates that date, and this document does not resolve that gap. The raw HTML for § 1505(d) contains a mid-sentence line wrap (a tab-and-newline sequence between "seniority" and "status") that both independently fetched copies reproduced identically; it is preserved exactly in the quoted text below rather than silently normalized.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1505 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1505(a)-(d), no loss of accrued benefits and effect on collective bargaining agreements
citations.quote:
(a) Taking Civil Air Patrol leave under this part shall not result in the loss of an employee benefit accrued before the date on which the leave began.(b) This part does not affect the obligation of an employer to comply with any collective bargaining agreement or employee benefit plan that provides greater leave rights to employees than the rights provided under this part.(c) The rights provided under this part shall not be diminished by any collective bargaining agreement or employee benefit plan entered into on or after January 1, 2010.(d) This part does not affect or diminish the contract rights or seniority
					 status of an employee not entitled to Civil Air Patrol leave.

clauses.title: Prohibition on Interference and Retaliation
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 1506(a), an employer shall not interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise or attempted exercise of a right established by this part. Under § 1506(b), an employer shall not discharge, fine, suspend, expel, discipline, or otherwise discriminate against an employee who exercises a right provided under this part or who opposes a practice made unlawful by this part.
clauses.gap: Section 1506 states the prohibition on interference and retaliation but, unlike Labor Code § 230.4 in this corpus's separate volunteer-responder document (which expressly cross-references a Labor Commissioner complaint procedure under § 98.7 with a one-year filing deadline), this part contains no cross-reference to § 98.7 or any other administrative complaint procedure, and no statute-specific limitations period for a private civil action is stated anywhere in §§ 1500-1507. This document does not assert what limitations period applies to a § 1506 claim, because the verified text of this part does not state one.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1506 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1506(a)-(b), prohibition on interference and retaliation
citations.quote: (a) An employer shall not interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise or the attempt to exercise a right established by this part.(b) An employer shall not discharge, fine, suspend, expel, discipline, or in any other manner discriminate against an employee who does any of the following:(1) Exercises a right provided under this part.(2) Opposes a practice made unlawful by this part.

clauses.title: Enforcement: A Private Civil Action, Not an Administrative Complaint
clauses.body: Under Labor Code § 1507(a), an employee may bring a civil action in the superior court of the appropriate county to enforce this part. Under § 1507(b), the court may enjoin any act or practice that violates this part and may order any equitable relief necessary and appropriate to redress the violation or to enforce this part.
clauses.gap: Section 1507 is the only enforcement mechanism stated anywhere in Labor Code §§ 1500-1507: this part contains no administrative Labor Commissioner or Division of Labor Standards Enforcement complaint procedure (in contrast to the § 98.7 complaint route this corpus's separate volunteer-responder training-leave document describes for a Labor Code § 230.4 violation), and no misdemeanor or other criminal penalty for an employer's noncompliance (in contrast to the misdemeanor penalty Labor Code § 230.3(b) attaches to a willful refusal to reinstate). The verified text of § 1507(b) authorizes only an injunction and “equitable relief”; it does not itself mention compensatory damages, statutory penalties, or attorney's fees, and this document does not assert that any of those remedies are available under this part, because § 1507's own text does not name them. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions construing this part (queries for "Civil Air Patrol Employment Protection Act" and for "Civil Air Patrol" together with Labor Code §§ 1500-1507) returned zero results rather than a rate-limit error, so this document proceeds on the statutory text alone and does not describe how any court has applied § 1507 in practice.

What This Document Covers: A Contract-Formation Rule for Living Performers, Not the Postmortem Digital-Replica Liability Statute
clauses.body: California Labor Code section 927, added effective January 1, 2025, addresses a narrow and specific question: whether a particular provision inside a personal-or-professional-services contract — the provision that lets one side create and use a "digital replica" of a living individual's voice or likeness instead of having that individual actually perform the work in person — is enforceable. It regulates contract formation between {{individualName}} and {{companyName}}, not use of an already-existing recording or image after the fact. This is a different statute from this corpus's separate Right of Publicity Demand Letter Information Sheet, which addresses Civil Code section 3344 (a living person's right against unauthorized use of identity) and Civil Code section 3344.1 (a deceased personality's postmortem digital-replica liability, added by a different 2024 bill). Section 927 does not create a liability claim for an unauthorized digital replica the way section 3344.1 does; instead, it makes certain digital-replica contract provisions unenforceable when specific statutory conditions are met, leaving the rest of the contract, and any other legal claim {{individualName}} might have, untouched.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what Labor Code section 927 itself covers and how its subject matter (contract-provision enforceability for a living performer's own future contract) differs from Civil Code section 3344.1 (postmortem tort liability for an already-made unauthorized digital replica), both already covered independently elsewhere in this corpus — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific contract provision described using this document falls on one side or the other of that line, which depends on facts this document does not resolve. Labor Code section 927 was added by Stats. 2024, ch. 259 (AB 2602), operative January 1, 2025; it is a brand-new provision, and this document does not represent that any court has yet interpreted it. A CourtListener case-law search for this statute and for "digital replica" California performer contracts was run twice with different search terms and returned, respectively, one unrelated case (a patent/trade-dress dispute with no connection to this statute) and zero results — not a rate-limit failure, but a genuine absence of any case law located, consistent with the statute's newness. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific contract provision is unenforceable under section 927, and completing it does not resolve that question for the individual's or the other contracting party's specific contract.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 927 (California Legislative Information text, added by Stats. 2024, ch. 259 (AB 2602), operative Jan. 1, 2025)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, digital replica provisions in personal or professional services contracts
citations.quote: A provision in an agreement between an individual and any other person for the performance of personal or professional services is unenforceable only as it relates to a new performance, fixed on or after January 1, 2025, by a digital replica of the individual if the provision meets all of the following conditions:

clauses.title: The Operative Rule: Unenforceable Only As To a New Performance Fixed On or After January 1, 2025, and Only If All Conditions Are Met
clauses.body: Section 927(a)'s own text draws a narrow, conjunctive rule. First, it is limited in time: the provision is unenforceable "only as it relates to a new performance, fixed on or after January 1, 2025, by a digital replica of the individual." A digital replica of a performance already fixed before that date is not reached by this statute's unenforceability rule at all, on the statute's own terms. Second, the provision is unenforceable only "if the provision meets all of the following conditions" — meaning the statute lists a set of conditions that must all be satisfied together before the digital-replica provision becomes unenforceable, not a list of independent, alternative grounds. Those conditions — described in the following clauses of this document — cover what the provision must lack (a sufficiently specific use description) and how the individual was, or was not, represented when the contract was made.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of section 927(a)'s own temporal scope and its all-conditions structure — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about how a court would resolve a dispute over whether a particular performance was "fixed" before or after January 1, 2025, which is a factual and technical question (for example, involving partial recording sessions spanning that date) this document does not address. This clause quotes the same lead-in sentence of subdivision (a) quoted in the companion scope-and-distinction clause of this document; it is not an independent source, only the same sentence read for its temporal-scope and all-conditions structure rather than its overall subject matter. No case law construing the "fixed" requirement or the January 1, 2025 date has been located, for the CourtListener search reasons disclosed in the companion scope clause.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — temporal scope and all-conditions structure
citations.quote: is unenforceable only as it relates to a new performance, fixed on or after January 1, 2025, by a digital replica of the individual if the provision meets all of the following conditions

clauses.title: Condition One: The Provision Substitutes a Digital Replica for Work the Individual Would Otherwise Have Performed In Person
clauses.body: The first of the statute's listed conditions describes the kind of provision section 927 reaches at all: one that "allows for the creation and use of a digital replica of the individual's voice or likeness in place of work the individual would otherwise have performed in person." On its own terms, this condition targets substitution — a contract clause letting the other contracting party use a digital replica instead of having {{individualName}} actually show up and perform the work — rather than every contract clause that happens to mention a digital replica for any purpose.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the first listed condition's own wording — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific provision in a particular individual's contract with a particular other party does or does not "allow for the creation and use of a digital replica... in place of work the individual would otherwise have performed in person," which depends on the specific contract language and is not evaluated here. This clause cites a single statutory paragraph, section 927(a)(1); the remaining conditions in section 927(a)(2) and (a)(3) are addressed in separate clauses of this document and are not repeated here. No case law construing this condition's "in place of" substitution language has been located, for the reasons disclosed in this document's scope clause.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — the in-place-of-in-person-work condition
citations.quote: The provision allows for the creation and use of a digital replica of the individual’s voice or likeness in place of work the individual would otherwise have performed in person.

clauses.title: Condition Two: A Missing 'Reasonably Specific Description' of Intended Uses — Unless the Uses Match the Contract's Own Terms and Character
clauses.body: The statute's second listed condition looks at what the provision does not say. Under subparagraph (A), except as provided in subparagraph (B), a digital-replica provision satisfies this condition — moving it a step closer to unenforceability — if "the provision does not include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of the digital replica." Subparagraph (B) then supplies its own exception: a missing reasonably-specific-use description does not, by itself, make the provision unenforceable if the actual uses made of the digital replica "are consistent with the terms of the contract for the performance of personal or professional services and the fundamental character of the photography or soundtrack as recorded or performed." Read together, the statute rewards a contract that either specifically describes the digital replica's intended uses up front, or whose actual digital-replica uses stay consistent with the underlying contract's own terms and the fundamental character of what was actually recorded.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the wording of subparagraphs (A) and (B) of section 927(a)(2) — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific contract provision, or any specific actual use, does or does not satisfy either subparagraph, which depends on facts this document does not evaluate. The quoted text of subparagraph (A) is drawn from leginfo's raw HTML source, which line-wraps mid-sentence (a literal newline-and-tab sequence appears in the source between "reasonably" and "specific description") as a page-formatting artifact of leginfo's own markup, not a gap in the statutory text itself; that whitespace has been normalized to a single space here, and this was verified against leginfo's raw HTML directly rather than assumed. No case law construing either subparagraph, including what counts as "reasonably specific" or what "fundamental character... as recorded or performed" means in a specific dispute, has been located, for the reasons disclosed in this document's scope clause.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — the reasonably-specific-description condition
citations.quote: Except as provided in subparagraph (B), the provision does not include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of the digital replica.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — the consistent-uses exception
citations.quote: Failure to include a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of a digital replica does not render the provision unenforceable if the uses are consistent with the terms of the contract for the performance of personal or professional services and the fundamental character of the photography or soundtrack as recorded or performed.

clauses.title: Condition Three: Two Statutory Safe Harbors — Independent Legal Counsel, or a Union Contract That Expressly Addresses Digital Replicas
clauses.body: The statute's third listed condition asks how the individual was represented — or not — when the digital-replica provision was agreed to: "The individual was not represented in any of the following manners." Two manners of representation are listed, and either one takes a provision outside this condition (and so outside the overall unenforceability rule, since all conditions must be met). The first is representation "by legal counsel who negotiated on behalf of the individual licensing the individual's digital replica rights, and the commercial terms are stated clearly and conspicuously in a contract or other writing signed or initialed by the individual." The second is representation "by a labor union representing workers who do the proposed work, and the terms of their collective bargaining agreement expressly addresses uses of digital replicas."
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the two representation safe harbors' own wording — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific individual was or was not represented by legal counsel in the manner described, or was or was not covered by a qualifying collective bargaining agreement, when a specific contract was signed, which depends on facts this document does not evaluate. The quoted legal-counsel safe harbor is drawn from leginfo's raw HTML source, which line-wraps mid-sentence (a literal newline-and-tab sequence between "contract" and "or other writing") as a page-formatting artifact of leginfo's own markup; that whitespace has been normalized to a single space here and was verified against leginfo's raw HTML directly. This clause does not address what makes collective-bargaining-agreement language "expressly address[]" digital replica uses, nor does it identify which unions' agreements currently contain such language, neither of which was researched for this document. No case law construing either safe harbor has been located, for the reasons disclosed in this document's scope clause.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — the representation condition
citations.quote: The individual was not represented in any of the following manners:

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — the legal-counsel safe harbor
citations.quote: By legal counsel who negotiated on behalf of the individual licensing the individual’s digital replica rights, and the commercial terms are stated clearly and conspicuously in a contract or other writing signed or initialed by the individual.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 927(a)(3)(B) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — the labor-union safe harbor
citations.quote: By a labor union representing workers who do the proposed work, and the terms of their collective bargaining agreement expressly addresses uses of digital replicas.

clauses.title: What Unenforceability Does Not Reach: The Rest of the Contract, and Any Exclusivity Grants, Are Unaffected
clauses.body: Subdivision (b) narrows what a finding of unenforceability under subdivision (a) actually does. It states that "this section does not affect provisions of a contract other than a provision that falls under subdivision (a)" — so even where a specific digital-replica provision is unenforceable, the rest of {{individualName}}'s and {{companyName}}'s contract is not automatically affected by that one provision's unenforceability. The same subdivision separately preserves exclusivity grants: the statute "does not impact, abrogate, or otherwise affect any exclusivity grants contained in, or related to, a provision subject to subdivision (a)." An exclusivity grant tied to a digital-replica provision therefore is not itself unwound merely because the digital-replica provision it relates to becomes unenforceable under subdivision (a).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of subdivision (b)'s own limiting language — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about how a specific contract's severability clause, if any, would interact with subdivision (b), or about what counts as an "exclusivity grant... related to" a digital-replica provision in a specific contract, neither of which this document evaluates. This clause quotes subdivision (b) in full as one integrated sentence pair from the same statutory subsection; it is one source, not two independent ones. No case law construing subdivision (b), including how courts have treated the exclusivity-grant carve-out, has been located, for the reasons disclosed in this document's scope clause.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 927(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — limited effect of unenforceability
citations.quote: This section does not affect provisions of a contract other than a provision that falls under subdivision (a) and does not impact, abrogate, or otherwise affect any exclusivity grants contained in, or related to, a provision subject to subdivision (a).

clauses.title: The Statutory Definition of 'Digital Replica'
clauses.body: Section 927(c)(1) defines "digital replica," for purposes of this section, as "a computer-generated, highly realistic electronic representation that is readily identifiable as the voice or visual likeness of an individual that is embodied in a sound recording, image, audiovisual work, or transmission in which the actual individual either did not actually perform or appear, or the actual individual did perform or appear, but the fundamental character of the performance or appearance has been materially altered." This definition reaches two distinct situations: a representation of an individual who never actually performed or appeared in the underlying recording or work at all, and a representation of an individual who did perform or appear, but whose actual performance or appearance was materially altered such that its fundamental character changed.
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of section 927(c)(1)'s own definition — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific representation of a particular individual does or does not meet this definition, which depends on the specific representation and is not evaluated here. This clause cites a single statutory paragraph, section 927(c)(1); it does not compare this definition against the separately defined "digital replica" term used in Civil Code section 3344.1(a)(2)(B)(ii)(I) (already quoted and sourced elsewhere in this corpus's Right of Publicity Demand Letter Information Sheet) beyond noting, in this document's scope clause, that the two statutes serve different purposes; a side-by-side textual comparison of the two definitions was not performed for this document. No case law construing this definition has been located, for the reasons disclosed in this document's scope clause.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 927(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — statutory definition of "digital replica"
citations.quote: computer-generated, highly realistic electronic representation that is readily identifiable as the voice or visual likeness of an individual that is embodied in a sound recording, image, audiovisual work, or transmission in which the actual individual either did not actually perform or appear, or the actual individual did perform or appear, but the fundamental character of the performance or appearance has been materially altered.

clauses.title: What 'Digital Replica' Does Not Include: Authorized Sampling, Remixing, and Remastering
clauses.body: Section 927(c)(2) narrows the definition described in the preceding clause by excluding certain ordinary audio and audiovisual production practices, so long as they are authorized by the copyright holder: "'Digital replica' does not include the electronic reproduction, use of a sample of one sound recording or audiovisual work into another, remixing, mastering, or digital remastering of a sound recording or audiovisual work authorized by the copyrightholder." A copyright-holder-authorized sample, remix, master, or remaster of an existing sound recording or audiovisual work therefore falls outside this section's "digital replica" definition on the statute's own terms, regardless of whether it otherwise resembles the kind of computer-generated representation described in subdivision (c)(1).
clauses.gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of section 927(c)(2)'s own exclusion language — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific sample, remix, master, or remaster is or is not authorized by a copyright holder in a specific case, which is a separate factual and copyright-law question this document does not evaluate. This clause cites a single statutory paragraph, section 927(c)(2), which itself does not define "authorized" or identify who must grant that authorization when more than one copyright holder has an interest in the underlying work; this document does not research or resolve that question, and does not address federal copyright law's own separate rules on joint authorship or licensing that might bear on it. No case law construing this exclusion has been located, for the reasons disclosed in this document's scope clause.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 927(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, digital replica provisions — exclusion for authorized sampling, remixing, and remastering
citations.quote: “Digital replica” does not include the electronic reproduction, use of a sample of one sound recording or audiovisual work into another, remixing, mastering, or digital remastering of a sound recording or audiovisual work authorized by the copyrightholder.

clauses.title: Digital Replica Contract Provision — Documentation Record
Closing Statement and Signature
Purpose and Scope of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes, in general terms, California's statutory framework for Property Assessed Clean Energy ("PACE") financing: a voluntary contractual assessment that a property owner enters into with a public agency or its designated private program administrator to pay for renewable-energy, energy-efficiency, water-efficiency, or similar improvements permanently fixed to real property, primarily under Streets and Highways Code Chapter 29 (commencing with Section 5898.10) and the program-administrator provisions of Financial Code Sections 22680-22697. It concerns the property commonly known as {{propertyAddress}} in {{county}} County, California (Assessor's Parcel Number {{parcelNumber}}), owned by {{ownerName}}, and financing under discussion, if any, with {{businessName}} for improvements described as: {{workDescription}}. This document does not itself create, approve, or record any assessment or lien; it does not calculate the specific cancellation deadline, financing amount, or eligibility outcome for any actual transaction; and it does not determine whether any actual PACE contract, disclosure, or program has complied with the requirements described here. It is meaningfully different from the corpus's existing California Solar Rights Act information sheet, which addresses an HOA's ability to restrict a member's *installation* of a solar system, not how that (or any other qualifying) improvement is *financed* through a property-tax-collected assessment.

clauses.title: What a PACE Assessment Is
clauses.body: A PACE assessment is a form of voluntary contractual assessment authorized by Streets and Highways Code Chapter 29, under which a public agency finances qualifying improvements permanently fixed to real property and the property owner repays that financing as an assessment collected together with the property's regular tax bill, rather than as a conventional mortgage or home-improvement loan. The Legislature's stated intent for this chapter includes financing distributed generation renewable energy sources and energy or water efficiency improvements that are permanently affixed to the property, as well as certain other public improvements, described elsewhere in this chapter.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the chapter's legislative-intent language in Section 5898.12(b), which states the Legislature's purpose in enacting the chapter; it is not itself an operative rule establishing an individual owner's rights or obligations, and it does not address the chapter's separate public-improvement or water-efficiency-only financing purposes described in Section 5898.12(c)-(d), which this document does not cover. A CourtListener search for on-topic California case law (query: "PACE assessment Property Assessed Clean Energy California contractual assessment lien") returned results rather than a rate-limit error, including a currently pending California Supreme Court matter, Morgan v. Ygrene Energy Fund, Inc., S277628 (argued from the Fourth Appellate District, opinion filed by the Court of Appeal Nov. 1, 2022 and Nov. 21, 2022, Supreme Court docket entry Dec. 4, 2025); this document nonetheless relies only on the statutory text itself, because verifying an exact contiguous quotation from a PDF-formatted judicial opinion was outside the scope of the leginfo-webpage-based double-fetch method used to verify every citation in this document, and because that litigation's outcome was not established as final at the time this sheet was checked.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.12(b)
citations.quote: It is also the intent of the Legislature that this chapter should be used to finance the installation or prepaid service contract, or both, of distributed generation renewable energy sources or energy efficiency improvements that are permanently fixed to residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, or other real property.

clauses.title: The Assessment Is a Voluntary Contract, Not a Government Mandate
clauses.body: A PACE assessment program exists only where a public agency's legislative body has designated an area and adopted a resolution making the financing available, and within that area, participation by any individual property owner is a matter of the owner's own voluntary contractual assessment with the public agency (or its program administrator) — not an assessment the public agency imposes on the owner without the owner's agreement.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Section 5898.20(a)(2), the provision authorizing the renewable-energy/efficiency-improvement branch of the program; it does not quote the separate, older public-improvement branch in Section 5898.20(a)(1), which this document does not otherwise cover, and it does not describe the resolution-of-intention and public-hearing process (Sections 5898.20(b), 5898.22, 5898.24) by which a public agency establishes such a program in the first place, which is a public-agency-side procedural matter distinct from an individual owner's contract.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.20(a)(2)
citations.quote: The legislative body of any public agency may also determine that it would be convenient, advantageous, and in the public interest to designate an area within the public agency, which may encompass the entire public agency or a lesser portion, within which authorized public agency officials and property owners may enter into voluntary contractual assessments to finance the installation of distributed generation renewable energy sources or energy or water efficiency improvements that are permanently fixed to real property pursuant to this chapter.

clauses.title: The Assessment Becomes a Lien Collected With the Property Tax Bill
clauses.body: Once levied, a PACE assessment, together with any interest and penalties on it, becomes a lien against the property that continues until paid, and the assessment is collected in the same manner and at the same time as the general property taxes on the property, subject to the same delinquency and default remedies, unless a different collection procedure is separately authorized.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the two operative sentences of Section 5898.30; it does not itself resolve, and the statute's text alone does not state, the relative lien priority between a PACE assessment and a first mortgage or deed of trust recorded before the assessment in every circumstance — that question is addressed by cross-referenced Government Code lien-priority provisions this document does not quote, and has also been the subject of litigation (see the CourtListener disclosure in the companion 'What a PACE Assessment Is' clause above) that this document does not resolve.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.30 (first sentence)
citations.cite: Sts. & High. C. § 5898.30
citations.quote: Assessments levied pursuant to this chapter, and the interest and any penalties thereon shall constitute a lien against the lots and parcels of land on which they are made, until they are paid.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.30 (second sentence)
citations.cite: Sts. & High. C. § 5898.30
citations.quote: Division 10 (commencing with Section 8500), insofar as those provisions are not in conflict with this chapter, Article 13 (commencing with Section 53930) of, and Article 13.5 (commencing with Section 53938) of, Chapter 4 of Part 1 of Division 2 of Title 5 of the Government Code apply to the imposition and collection of assessments contracted for pursuant to this chapter, including, but not limited to, provisions related to lien priority, the collection of assessments in the same manner and at the same time as the general taxes of the city or county on real property, unless another procedure has been authorized by the legislative body or by statute, and any penalties and remedies in the event of delinquency and default.

clauses.title: The Statutory 5% Cap on Combined Annual Taxes and Assessments
clauses.body: A public agency may not allow a property owner to participate in a PACE program if doing so would make the property's total annual property taxes and assessments exceed 5 percent of the property's market value, measured at the time the owner's contractual assessment is approved. This cap does not, however, excuse the owner from the contract once entered: the statute expressly provides that the owner's contractual obligations are not voided or released even if the 5% figure is later exceeded after the contract is in place.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes both subsections (a) and (b) of Section 5898.15; it does not describe how 'market value' for purposes of this specific cap is determined (the statute does not, in this section, specify a required valuation method for the cap itself, in contrast to the separate value-representation restriction in Section 5898.17(c) addressed in a companion clause), and it does not address the parallel, differently-worded 5% test that applies specifically to the residential-four-units-or-fewer right-to-cancel program under Section 5898.16(a)(1), which this document does not separately quote.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.15(a)
citations.quote: (a) A public agency shall not permit a property owner to participate in any program established pursuant to this chapter if the owner’s participation would result in the total amount of any annual property taxes and assessments exceeding 5 percent of the property’s market value, as determined at the time of approval of the owner’s contractual assessment.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.15(b)
citations.quote: Nothing in this chapter shall be construed to void or otherwise release a property owner from the contractual obligations incurred by a contractual assessment on a property, particularly in the event that the total amount of annual property taxes and assessments exceeds 5 percent of a property’s market value after the property owner has entered into a contractual assessment pursuant to this chapter.

clauses.title: The Statutory Right to Cancel — Three Business Days, Five for Senior Citizens
clauses.body: For a PACE contractual assessment on residential property with four or fewer units, the property owner has a statutory right to cancel without cost, running through the third business day after the latest of: the date the owner signed the contractual assessment, the date the owner received the Financing Estimate and Disclosure, or the date the owner received the notice of the right to cancel. For a property owner who is a senior citizen, this deadline is extended: every reference to the third or third business day in the statutory cancellation document is changed to the fifth business day instead. A 'senior citizen' for this purpose is an individual who is 65 years of age or older.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes the statutory Right to Cancel document text set out in Section 5898.16(b)(1)(A)-(B) and the senior-citizen definition in Section 5898.16(d)(2); it does not calculate an actual cancellation deadline for any specific transaction, which depends on identifying the latest of the three triggering events for that transaction and counting business days from it. It also does not cover the separate mechanics of how a cancellation notice is deemed given (Section 5898.16(b)(2)) or the program administrator's own 20-calendar-day obligation to discharge the lien and refund money after a valid cancellation, both of which this document does not quote. Section 5898.16 is itself scheduled to be repealed and replaced by a differently-numbered successor version of the same section effective January 1, 2029; this clause reflects the version of Section 5898.16 in effect as of the date checked above, not the version that becomes operative on that later date.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.16(b)(1)(A)
citations.quote: You may cancel this transaction, without cost, on or before midnight on the third business day after whichever of the following events occurs last:

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.16(b)(1)(B)
citations.quote: References to “third” in the notice to cancel document set forth in subparagraph (A) shall be changed to “fifth” for a property owner who is a senior citizen.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.16(d)(2)
citations.quote: “Senior citizen” means an individual who is 65 years of age or older.

clauses.title: The Required Financing Estimate and Disclosure
clauses.body: Before a residential property owner (four or fewer units) may consummate a PACE contractual assessment, the statutorily prescribed Financing Estimate and Disclosure — or a substantially equivalent document displaying the same information in a substantially similar format — must be completed and delivered to the owner. That disclosure must be given as a printed paper copy in type no smaller than 12 points, unless the owner affirmatively opts out of the paper copy in writing by signing a printed paper document, in which case an electronic copy is provided instead.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the threshold delivery-and-format requirement in Section 5898.17(a); the disclosure form itself is a lengthy, multi-part document (cost breakdown, APR, prepayment terms, and the acknowledgment items quoted in the companion 'statutory penalty' and 'sale or refinance' clauses below) that this document does not reproduce in full. This requirement, by its own terms in Section 5898.17(b)(1), applies only to residential property with four or fewer units; commercial, industrial, or agricultural PACE financing is not covered by this document.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.17(a)
citations.quote: (a) The disclosure set forth below, or a substantially equivalent document that displays the same information in a substantially similar format, shall be completed and delivered to a property owner before the property owner consummates a voluntary contractual assessment described in this chapter for purposes specified in paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 5898.20 or Section 5899, 5899.3, or 5899.4, or a special tax described in Section 53328.1 of the Government Code.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.17(a) (format requirement)
citations.quote: The disclosure shall be provided to the property owner as a printed paper copy in no smaller than 12-point type, unless the property owner opts out of receiving a printed paper copy in writing by signing a printed paper document.

clauses.title: Restriction on Representations That Financed Improvements Will Increase Property Value
clauses.body: A public agency or other party to a PACE contractual assessment may not make any monetary or percentage representation to a property owner that the financed improvements will increase the property's value, unless that estimate is derived from an automated valuation model, a licensed real estate broker's price opinion, or an appraisal by a state-licensed real estate appraiser.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the opening restriction of Section 5898.17(c) and the introduction to its list of three permitted valuation-method categories; it does not reproduce the detailed sub-criteria the statute separately specifies for automated valuation models (found elsewhere in the program-administrator provisions), and it does not address representations about value that are not framed in monetary or percentage terms, which this section's plain text does not appear to reach.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.17(c)
citations.quote: A public agency or other party to a voluntary contractual assessment described in this chapter for the purposes specified in paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) of Section 5898.20 or Section 5899, 5899.3, or 5899.4, or a special tax described in Section 53328.1 of the Government Code shall not make any monetary or percentage representations of increased value to a property owner regarding the effect the financed improvements will have on the market value of the property unless that public agency or other party derives its estimates of the market value using one of the following:

clauses.title: Required Disclosure of Late-Payment Penalties
clauses.body: The statutory Financing Estimate and Disclosure form that must be delivered to a residential PACE applicant includes a required acknowledgment, initialed separately by the owner, that a late property tax payment carries a 10% penalty, late fees, and 1.5% per month interest, and that the property may become subject to foreclosure.
clauses.gap: This is the disclosure form's own summary language in Section 5898.17(b)(1); it states the general California property-tax delinquency penalty structure that applies once a PACE assessment is added to the tax bill, but this document does not separately verify or quote the underlying Revenue and Taxation Code provisions that actually set the 10% penalty and 1.5%-per-month rate, since the disclosure text itself, not those separate provisions, was this clause's chosen primary source.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.17(b)(1) (Financing Estimate and Disclosure form)
citations.quote: Statutory Penalties: If your property tax payment is late, the amount due will be subject to a 10% penalty, late fees, and 1.5% per month interest penalty as established by state law, and your property may be subject to foreclosure.

clauses.title: Required Disclosure That a Sale or Refinance May Require Payoff
clauses.body: The same statutory disclosure form also requires the owner to separately acknowledge, in writing, that a mortgage lender refinancing the home may require payoff of the remaining PACE balance, and that if the home is sold, the buyer or the buyer's mortgage lender may likewise require the balance to be paid off as a condition of the sale.
clauses.gap: This is the disclosure form's own acknowledgment language in Section 5898.17(b)(1); it describes what a lender or buyer 'may' require rather than guaranteeing that outcome in every transaction, and the underlying legal basis for any such demand (for example, a lender's due-on-encumbrance or underwriting policy) arises from the separate mortgage contract or the buyer's own financing terms, not from this statute, which this document does not address.

citations.case: Cal. Sts. & High. Code § 5898.17(b)(1) (Financing Estimate and Disclosure form)
citations.quote: I understand that I may be required to pay off the remaining balance of this obligation by the mortgage lender refinancing my home. If I sell my home, the buyer or their mortgage lender may require me to pay off the balance of this obligation as a condition of sale.

clauses.title: Program Administrator Prerequisites Before Executing a Residential Assessment Contract
clauses.body: Separately from the disclosure and cancellation requirements above, California's PACE program administrator statute bars a program administrator from executing an assessment contract — and bars commencement of the underlying home improvement work — unless a defined list of eligibility criteria is satisfied, including that all property taxes on the property are current, with the administrator required to ask the owner whether there has been more than one late property-tax payment in the previous three years or since the current owner acquired the property.
clauses.gap: Financial Code Section 22684 lists fourteen lettered eligibility criteria, subsections (a) through (n); this clause quotes only the introductory bar and the property-tax-currency criterion in subsection (a). It does not quote the other twelve criteria (no large involuntary liens, no unrescinded notice of default, bankruptcy and mortgage-payment-history lookbacks, program geographic and measure eligibility, useful-life term limits, duplicate-assessment verification, no prepayment penalty, no reverse-mortgage properties, and a general verification-method mandate), which are addressed only in this gap note, not quoted as citations.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22684 (introductory clause)
citations.quote: A program administrator shall not execute an assessment contract, and no work shall commence under a home improvement contract that is financed by that assessment contract nor shall that home improvement contract be executed unless the following criteria are satisfied:

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22684(a)
citations.quote: All property taxes for the property that will be subject to the assessment contract are current. The program administrator shall ask a property owner whether there has been no more than one late payment of property taxes on the property for the previous three years or since the current owner acquired the property, whichever period is shorter.

clauses.title: Program Administrator Limits on the Amount Financed
clauses.body: Among the same eligibility criteria, the program administrator statute also caps the size of the financing itself: the assessment must be for less than 15% of the property's value on the first $700,000 of value (inclusive of existing assessments), and less than 10% of any remaining value above $700,000, and the combined total of PACE assessments plus mortgage-related debt on the property may not exceed 97% of the property's market value as established under the statute's separate valuation-methodology section.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subsections (h) and (i) of Financial Code Section 22684 only; it does not quote or describe the separate valuation methodology required by Section 22685 (automated valuation models, broker price opinions, or appraisals, with detailed sub-criteria for each) that this 97% figure depends on, and it does not address what happens, beyond the general verification duty in subsection (k), if a property owner has an unrecorded PACE assessment the administrator was not told about.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22684(h)
citations.quote: The financing is for less than 15 percent of the value of the property, up to the first seven hundred thousand dollars ($700,000) inclusive of the existing assessments, and is for less than 10 percent of the remaining value of the property above seven hundred thousand dollars ($700,000).

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22684(i)
citations.quote: The total PACE assessments and the mortgage-related debt on the property subject to the PACE assessment will not exceed 97 percent of the market value of the property as established by the valuation required by Section 22685.

clauses.title: The Program Administrator's Ability-to-Pay Determination Requirement
clauses.body: Independent of the specific eligibility criteria above, the program administrator statute separately bars a program administrator from executing an assessment contract, or allowing the underlying home improvement work to begin, unless the administrator has made a reasonable, good-faith determination that the property owner has a reasonable ability to pay the annual payment obligations the PACE assessment will create.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only Section 22686's general 'reasonable good faith determination' standard; it does not quote the more detailed income/asset/debt-obligation factors and documentation process set out in the separate Financial Code Section 22687, which this document does not reproduce, so the specific method by which any given administrator must reach that determination is not addressed here.

citations.case: Cal. Fin. Code § 22686
citations.quote: A program administrator shall not execute an assessment contract, and no work shall commence under a home improvement contract that is financed by that assessment contract nor shall that home improvement contract be executed unless the program administrator makes a reasonable good faith determination that the property owner has a reasonable ability to pay the annual payment obligations for the PACE assessment.

clauses.title: Purpose and Scope
clauses.body: This information sheet addresses California's statutory Notice of Belief of Abandonment procedure for real property leased by {{tenantName}} from {{landlordName}} at {{propertyAddress}}. That procedure — set out in Civil Code § 1951.3 for real property other than commercial real property, and in the separate, parallel Civil Code § 1951.35 for commercial real property — lets a lessor who reasonably believes a lessee has abandoned leased real property give written notice that, if the lessee does not respond in the manner and within the time the statute specifies, causes the real property to be deemed abandoned and the lease to terminate. It is a distinct statutory mechanism from an unlawful detainer notice to pay rent or quit under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 1161–1162, and from the separate statute governing disposition of a departed tenant's personal property left behind after a tenancy has already ended — this document does not address either of those. This document states California statutory law as of the date signed below. It does not determine that any specific lessee has abandoned any specific property, does not determine that any particular belief of abandonment was reasonable, and does not determine whether {{propertyAddress}} is or is not "commercial real property" within the meaning of the statute.

clauses.title: General Effect of an Unrebutted Notice
clauses.body: Under Civil Code § 1951.3(b), real property is deemed abandoned by the lessee, within the meaning of Civil Code § 1951.2, and the lease terminates, if the lessor gives written notice of belief of abandonment as the statute provides and the lessee fails to give the lessor written notice — before the date of termination stated in the lessor's notice — both stating that the lessee does not intend to abandon the property and stating an address at which the lessee may be served by certified mail in an unlawful detainer action. This is a conditional, self-executing statutory consequence: the deemed-abandonment and lease termination follow automatically from the lessee's failure to respond in the specified way, not from any separate adjudication at the time the notice is given.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the general rule of subdivision (b). It does not state the separate conditions in subdivision (c) that make giving the notice available in the first place, the delivery rules in subdivision (d), the required form in subdivision (e), or the four statutory grounds in subdivision (f) on which a lessee can prevent the property from being deemed abandoned even after an unrebutted notice — each addressed in other clauses of this document. Subdivision (b) itself does not define "written notice" from the lessee beyond the two things that notice must state, and this document does not address what form a lessee's responsive notice must take beyond the statute's own words.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, general rule on deemed abandonment and lease termination
citations.quote: Real property shall be deemed abandoned by the lessee, within the meaning of Section 1951.2, and the lease shall terminate if the lessor gives written notice of belief of abandonment as provided in this section and the lessee fails to give the lessor written notice, prior to the date of termination specified in the lessor’s notice, stating that the lessee does not intend to abandon the real property and stating an address at which the lessee may be served by certified mail in any action for unlawful detainer of the real property.

clauses.title: Scope and Threshold Conditions (Non-Commercial Real Property)
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1951.3(a) states that this section applies to real property other than commercial real property, as defined in Civil Code § 1954.26(d). For that non-commercial real property, § 1951.3(c) permits the lessor to give a notice of belief of abandonment only where the rent on the property has been due and unpaid for at least 14 consecutive days and the lessor reasonably believes that the lessee has abandoned the property. Both conditions — the 14-consecutive-day unpaid-rent period and the lessor's reasonable belief of abandonment — must be present before this particular notice procedure is available for this category of property.
clauses.gap: This clause covers only the threshold conditions for real property that is not "commercial real property" as Civil Code § 1954.26(d) defines that term; the parallel statute for commercial real property, Civil Code § 1951.35, sets a different threshold (tied to the lease's own rent-default period, with a 3-day floor rather than a fixed 14 days) and is addressed in a separate clause of this document. Section 1951.3(c) does not itself define "reasonably believes," and this document does not determine whether any specific lessor's belief in any specific case was reasonable — subdivision (f)(2), addressed elsewhere in this document, separately provides that a lessor's mere knowledge that the lessee left personal property behind does not by itself defeat reasonableness, but that is a limited negative rule, not an affirmative definition of what makes a belief reasonable.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, scope limited to non-commercial real property
citations.quote: This section applies to real property other than commercial real property, as defined in subdivision (d) of Section 1954.26.

citations.quote: The lessor may give a notice of belief of abandonment to the lessee pursuant to this section only where the rent on the property has been due and unpaid for at least 14 consecutive days and the lessor reasonably believes that the lessee has abandoned the property.

clauses.title: What Counts as "Commercial Real Property"
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1954.26(d) defines "commercial real property" — the term that determines whether § 1951.3 or the separate § 1951.35 governs a notice of belief of abandonment — to include any part, portion, or unit of real property and any related facilities, space, or services, except four listed categories: a dwelling or dwelling unit subject to Civil Code § 1940; an accommodation in a residential hotel as defined in Health and Safety Code § 50519, or comparable accommodations specifically regulated by a public entity in structures where 20 percent or more of the accommodations are occupied as a primary residence; certain hotel units in structures meeting a similar occupancy and rent-control history threshold as of August 5, 1987; and any space or dwelling unit in a mobilehome park as defined in Health and Safety Code § 18214.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (d)'s definition of "commercial real property," the term dispositive of which of the two parallel abandonment-notice statutes applies. It does not quote or independently verify the cross-referenced definitions in Civil Code § 1940, Health and Safety Code § 50519, or Health and Safety Code § 18214, which subdivision (d) itself relies on; a determination of whether a specific property falls within one of the four excluded categories may turn on those other statutes' own text, which this document does not state.

citations.quote: “Commercial real property” includes any part, portion, or unit thereof, and any related facilities, space, or services, except the following:

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the four excluded (non-commercial) categories

clauses.title: How the Notice Must Be Delivered
clauses.body: For non-commercial real property, Civil Code § 1951.3(d) requires that the lessor's notice of belief of abandonment be personally delivered to the lessee or sent by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to the lessee's last known address, and — if there is reason to believe the notice sent to that address will not be received by the lessee — also sent to any other address known to the lessor where the lessee may reasonably be expected to receive it.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the delivery methods available for the non-commercial-property notice under § 1951.3(d). The parallel commercial-property statute, § 1951.35(d), authorizes an additional delivery method (a recognized overnight carrier) not available under § 1951.3(d), addressed in a separate clause of this document. This document does not determine, for any specific case, whether a lessor had "reason to believe" a notice would not be received at a given address, which is a factual determination the statute leaves unaddressed beyond its own words.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, delivery methods for non-commercial real property
citations.quote: The lessor’s notice of belief of abandonment shall be personally delivered to the lessee or sent by first-class mail, postage prepaid, to the lessee at the lessee’s last known address and, if there is reason to believe that the notice sent to that address will not be received by the lessee, also to any other address known to the lessor where the lessee may reasonably be expected to receive the notice.

clauses.title: Minimum Time Before the Stated Termination Date
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1951.3(c) requires that the date of termination of the lease be specified in the lessor's notice, and that this date be not less than 15 days after the notice is served personally, or, if the notice is mailed, not less than 18 days after the notice is deposited in the mail.
clauses.gap: These are minimums fixed by this one statute for non-commercial real property; the notice must state a termination date at least this far out, but nothing in this clause addresses whether a lessor may or must state a later date, and this document does not calculate any specific termination date for any specific notice. The parallel commercial-property statute uses a single 15-day minimum regardless of delivery method (addressed in a separate clause), which is a different rule from the mail-based 18-day minimum stated here.
