citations.cite: California Civil Code, minimum time before the stated termination date
citations.quote: The date of termination of the lease shall be specified in the lessor’s notice and shall be not less than 15 days after the notice is served personally or, if mailed, not less than 18 days after the notice is deposited in the mail.

clauses.title: Statutory Grounds That Defeat Deemed Abandonment
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1951.3(f) provides that the real property shall not be deemed abandoned under this section if the lessee proves any of four things: that at the time the notice was given, the rent was not in fact due and unpaid for 14 consecutive days; that at the time the notice was given, it was not reasonable for the lessor to believe the lessee had abandoned the property — and the statute adds that the lessor's mere knowledge that the lessee left personal property on the property does not, of itself, justify a finding that the lessor's belief was unreasonable; that before the date specified in the lessor's notice, the lessee gave the lessor written notice of intent not to abandon the property along with a certified-mail service address; or that during the period beginning 14 days before the notice was given and ending on the date the lease would otherwise have terminated, the lessee paid the lessor all or part of the unpaid rent.
clauses.gap: Subdivision (f) places the burden of proving each of these grounds on the lessee, and this document does not determine whether any specific lessee has proved, or could prove, any of them in any specific case. The fourth ground (partial or full rent payment during the specified window) does not by its own terms say whether it requires payment sufficient to cure the full 14-day delinquency or merely some payment during that window; this document states the statute's own "all or a portion of" language without resolving that ambiguity.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the four statutory grounds defeating deemed abandonment
citations.quote: The fact that the lessor knew that the lessee left personal property on the real property does not, of itself, justify a finding that the lessor did not reasonably believe that the lessee had abandoned the real property.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.3(f)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the rent-payment-during-the-window ground
citations.quote: During the period beginning 14 days before the time the notice of belief of abandonment was given and ending on the date the lease would have terminated pursuant to the notice, the lessee paid to the lessor all or a portion of the rent due and unpaid on the real property.

clauses.title: Relationship to Other Notices and Proceedings
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1951.3(g) states that nothing in the section precludes the lessor or the lessee from otherwise proving that the real property has been abandoned by the lessee within the meaning of § 1951.2 — that is, the statutory notice procedure is one way to establish abandonment, not the exclusive way. Section 1951.3(h) separately states that nothing in the section precludes the lessor from serving a notice requiring the lessee to pay rent or quit under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 1161 and 1162 at any time those sections permit, and that giving the notice of belief of abandonment does not satisfy the requirements of those sections.
clauses.gap: This clause establishes only that the two procedures are legally independent and that one does not substitute for the other; it does not address the separate statute at Civil Code § 1991, which permits — but does not require — combining a notice of belief of abandonment with a related notice concerning a departed tenant's personal property left on the premises, a topic addressed in this corpus's separate document on disposition of abandoned personal property, not in this document. This document does not determine which procedure, or combination of procedures, is applicable or advisable in any specific case.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, notice procedure is not the exclusive way to prove abandonment

clauses.title: The Parallel Procedure for Commercial Real Property
clauses.body: Civil Code § 1951.35, added effective January 1, 2019 by the same legislation that limited § 1951.3 to non-commercial real property, applies only to commercial real property as defined in § 1954.26(d) and sets a different threshold for when a lessor may give the notice: the rent must have been due and unpaid for at least the number of days required for the lessor to declare a rent default under the terms of the lease, but in no case less than three days, and the lessor must reasonably believe the lessee has abandoned the property. Unlike the non-commercial statute's split 15-day/18-day timing, § 1951.35(c) requires the stated termination date to be not less than 15 days after the notice is served personally, sent by an overnight courier service, or deposited in the mail — a single 15-day minimum regardless of delivery method. Section 1951.35(d) also permits delivery by a recognized overnight carrier, an option § 1951.3(d) does not include for non-commercial real property. The commercial statute's rebuttal grounds, exclusivity language, and relationship to Code of Civil Procedure §§ 1161–1162 in § 1951.35(f)–(h) otherwise track the non-commercial statute's structure, adjusted for the lease-default-based timing rather than the fixed 14-day period.
clauses.gap: This clause summarizes § 1951.35's points of difference from § 1951.3 rather than quoting the commercial statute's rebuttal-grounds subdivision (f) in full; a lessor or lessee dealing with commercial real property should consult § 1951.35's own complete text rather than this comparative summary. Published California case law construing a notice of belief of abandonment for a commercial lease — 250 L.L.C. v. Photopoint Corp. (USA), 131 Cal. App. 4th 703 (2005), and Avalon Pacific-Santa Ana, L.P. v. HD Supply Repair & Remodel, LLC, 192 Cal. App. 4th 1183 (2011) — was decided before § 1951.35 existed, when a single, undifferentiated § 1951.3 governed both commercial and non-commercial property; this document does not treat that pre-2019 case law as authority for how a court would apply the current, commercial-property-specific § 1951.35.

clauses.title: Declaration and Purpose
clauses.body:
This information sheet concerns a work titled {{workTitle}}, created by {{artistName}} (the “work”). {{sellerName}} is identified here as the person reselling the work, and {{purchasePrice}} and {{saleDate}} are identified here as the reported gross sale price and date of that resale, for reference only. This sheet summarizes provisions of California Civil Code § 986, sometimes called the California Resale Royalties Act, which as originally enacted required the seller of a work of fine art (or the seller's agent) to pay the work's artist a 5 percent royalty on specified California resales.

This sheet is an informational record only. It does not determine whether the resale identified above meets § 986's own definitions and conditions, does not determine whether any royalty is or was owed with respect to that resale, and does not itself assert, waive, calculate, or collect any royalty or other right under § 986 or any other law. As later sections of this sheet describe, federal courts have since held significant parts of § 986 unconstitutional or preempted by federal copyright law; this sheet is not legal advice and is not a substitute for reading the statute and that case law directly.

clauses.title: The Royalty Obligation, Its Waiver Rule, and Assignment
clauses.body:
California Civil Code § 986(a), as enacted, states the core rule: “Whenever a work of fine art is sold and the seller resides in California or the sale takes place in California, the seller or the seller’s agent shall pay to the artist of such work of fine art or to such artist’s agent 5 percent of the amount of such sale.”

The statute makes the artist's right to that 5 percent difficult to waive down. It states: “The right of the artist to receive an amount equal to 5 percent of the amount of such sale may be waived only by a contract in writing providing for an amount in excess of 5 percent of the amount of such sale.”

The statute separately allows the artist to assign the right to collect the royalty, while preserving the same waiver limit: “An artist may assign the right to collect the royalty payment provided by this section to another individual or entity. However, the assignment shall not have the effect of creating a waiver prohibited by this subdivision.”

As written, subdivision (a) applies to a sale whenever either the seller resides in California or the sale takes place in California. As the next section of this sheet describes, a federal appellate court has since held the “seller resides in California” branch of that rule unconstitutional as applied to sales occurring entirely outside California.

clauses.title: How the Royalty Is Withheld and Paid
clauses.body:
Subdivision (a)(1) places the withholding duty on the person who handles the sale on the seller's behalf: “When a work of fine art is sold at an auction or by a gallery, dealer, broker, museum, or other person acting as the agent for the seller the agent shall withhold 5 percent of the amount of the sale, locate the artist and pay the artist.”

Subdivision (a)(2) addresses what happens if the artist cannot be found: “If the seller or agent is unable to locate and pay the artist within 90 days, an amount equal to 5 percent of the amount of the sale shall be tranferred to the Arts Council.”

Subdivision (a)(5) then places a continuing duty on the Arts Council itself, and states what becomes of the money if the artist is never located: “The Arts Council shall attempt to locate any artist for whom money is received pursuant to this section. If the council is unable to locate the artist and the artist does not file a written claim for the money received by the council within seven years of the date of sale of the work of fine art, the right of the artist terminates and such money shall be transferred to the council for use in acquiring fine art pursuant to the Art in Public Buildings program set forth in Chapter 2.1 (commencing with Section 15813) of Part 10b of Division 3 of Title 2, of the Government Code.”

clauses.title: The Civil Action the Statute Authorizes, and Its Time Limit
clauses.body: Subdivision (a)(3) states the remedy for nonpayment and the deadline to pursue it: “If a seller or the seller’s agent fails to pay an artist the amount equal to 5 percent of the sale of a work of fine art by the artist or fails to transfer such amount to the Arts Council, the artist may bring an action for damages within three years after the date of sale or one year after the discovery of the sale, whichever is longer. The prevailing party in any action brought under this paragraph shall be entitled to reasonable attorney fees, in an amount as determined by the court.”

citations.quote: If a seller or the seller’s agent fails to pay an artist the amount equal to 5 percent of the sale of a work of fine art by the artist or fails to transfer such amount to the Arts Council, the artist may bring an action for damages within three years after the date of sale or one year after the discovery of the sale, whichever is longer. The prevailing party in any action brought under this paragraph shall be entitled to reasonable attorney fees, in an amount as determined by the court.

clauses.title: What Happens to the Right After the Artist's Death
clauses.body:
Subdivision (a)(7) extends the right beyond the artist's lifetime, but only for artists who died after a specific date: “Upon the death of an artist, the rights and duties created under this section shall inure to his or her heirs, legatees, or personal representative, until the 20th anniversary of the death of the artist. The provisions of this paragraph shall be applicable only with respect to an artist who dies after January 1, 1983.”

Subdivision (b)(3) confirms that this is the only circumstance in which a post-death resale is covered: “Except as provided in paragraph (7) of subdivision (a), to a resale after the death of such artist.”

The statute does not define “heirs, legatees, or personal representative” for purposes of this subdivision, and this clause does not determine who, as a factual or probate-law matter, would qualify as one with respect to any particular artist.

clauses.title: Sales the Statute Exempts
clauses.body:
Subdivision (b) lists sales to which the royalty obligation in subdivision (a) does not apply. Among them: “To the initial sale of a work of fine art where legal title to such work at the time of such initial sale is vested in the artist thereof.”; “To the resale of a work of fine art for a gross sales price of less than one thousand dollars ($1,000).”; “To the resale of the work of fine art for a gross sales price less than the purchase price paid by the seller.”; “To the resale of a work of fine art by an art dealer to a purchaser within 10 years of the initial sale of the work of fine art by the artist to an art dealer, provided all intervening resales are between art dealers.”; and “To a sale of a work of stained glass artistry where the work has been permanently attached to real property and is sold as part of the sale of the real property to which it is attached.”

A separate exemption for a work of fine art exchanged for other fine art or property worth less than $1,000, and the post-death exemption addressed in this sheet's preceding clause, are also part of subdivision (b) but are not separately quoted here.

clauses.title: The Statute's Definitions of “Artist,” “Fine Art,” and “Art Dealer”
clauses.body:
Subdivision (c) defines three terms the rest of the section depends on. Its own text states: “Artist” means the person who creates a work of fine art and who, at the time of resale, is a citizen of the United States, or a resident of the state who has resided in the state for a minimum of two years .

“Fine art” means an original painting, sculpture, or drawing, or an original work of art in glass.

“Art dealer” means a person who is actively and principally engaged in or conducting the business of selling works of fine art for which business such person validly holds a sales tax permit.

clauses.title: The Out-of-State Sales Clause Was Held Unconstitutional
clauses.body:
Subdivision (a) applies “whenever a work of fine art is sold and the seller resides in California or the sale takes place in California.” Sitting en banc, the Ninth Circuit held that the first branch of that rule — reaching a sale merely because the seller resides in California, even when the sale itself happens entirely elsewhere — cannot stand: “we hold that the Act’s clause regulating sales outside the state of California facially violates the “dormant” Commerce Clause but that the offending provision is severable from the remainder of the Act.”

The court did not strike the statute in its entirety. It relied on the severability clause the Legislature itself wrote into the statute, Civil Code § 986(e): “If any provision of this section or the application thereof to any person or circumstance is held invalid for any reason, such invalidity shall not affect any other provisions or applications of this section which can be effected, without the invalid provision or application, and to this end the provisions of this section are severable.” Applying that clause, the court severed the unconstitutional “seller resides in California” branch and left the “sale takes place in California” branch of subdivision (a) standing.

This is Sam Francis Foundation v. Christie's, Inc., 784 F.3d 1320 (9th Cir. 2015) (en banc). clauses.title: Post-1978 Resales Are Preempted by Federal Copyright Law
clauses.body:
In a later stage of the same litigation, the Ninth Circuit panel addressed a separate defect: whether the federal Copyright Act displaces § 986 entirely. The panel held that it does, for sales occurring on or after the effective date of the 1976 Copyright Act: “Plaintiffs’ CRRA claims covered by the 1976 Copyright Act—i.e., those concerning sales postdating the 1976 Act’s effective date of January 1, 1978—are expressly preempted by 17 U.S.C. § 301(a). We therefore affirm dismissal of those claims.”

The panel drew a narrow exception for a specific one-year window, because the earlier 1909 Copyright Act contained no comparable preemption provision: “The 1909 Copyright Act, however, has no express preemption provision. As such, plaintiffs’ CRRA claims covered only by the 1909 Act—i.e., those concerning sales that occurred between the CRRA’s effective date of January 1, 1977, and the 1976 Act’s effective date of January 1, 1978—cannot be expressly preempted.”

The panel summarized the practical effect of both rulings together: “Our decision today means that the CRRA had a short effective life. California’s statute permissibly coexisted for exactly one year alongside the 1909 Act.”

The panel's holding that pre-1978 claims (for sales between the CRRA's January 1, 1977 effective date and the 1976 Copyright Act's January 1, 1978 effective date) are not preempted only means those claims were remanded for further proceedings, not that they were ultimately proven or that any plaintiff recovered on them; the opinion expressly declines to decide a separate Takings Clause argument the defendants raised as to that narrow window, leaving it to the district court on remand. Combined with the dormant Commerce Clause holding described in this document's preceding clause, this means the royalty scheme as originally written has, per these two decisions, no live application to an in-state sale occurring after January 1, 1978 and only a contested, unresolved application to the narrow 1977–1978 window; this clause does not track whether any further appellate or trial-court decision has since addressed that remaining window, and this document does not independently verify the current docket status of the remanded case.

clauses.title: Record
Oil Drilling Industry Final-Wage Timing — Applicability Note
clauses.body: California Labor Code section 201.7 sets a distinct timing rule for the payment of final wages to an employee, or a group of employees, engaged in the business of oil drilling who is laid off — a rule that operates differently from the general immediate-on-discharge deadline in Labor Code section 201 that applies to most other laid-off employees. This concerns {{employeeName}}'s employment with {{companyName}}, recorded here as ending on {{terminationDate}}. Section 201.7's own rule, described in the information that follows, turns on whether the work {{employeeName}} performed for {{companyName}} falls within the statute's description of the business of oil drilling and whether the separation was a layoff. Naming {{employeeName}} and {{companyName}} here does not itself determine that {{employeeName}}'s work was in the business of oil drilling, and does not determine which final-wage timing rule applies to this particular employment relationship.

clauses.title: The Core Rule: Up to 24 Hours (Excluding Weekends and Holidays), With a Mailing Option
clauses.body: Labor Code section 201.7 states that an employer who lays off an employee or a group of employees engaged in the business of oil drilling is deemed to have made immediate payment within the meaning of Section 201 if the wages of those employees are paid within such reasonable time as may be necessary for computation or payment — provided that this reasonable time may not exceed 24 hours after discharge, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays. The statute further provides that this payment may be mailed, and that the date of mailing is treated as the date of payment. The statute frames this as a deeming rule tied to Section 201's own "immediate payment" requirement, rather than as a separate, freestanding due date of its own.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.7, first paragraph), used as real evidence of this section's own timing and mailing rule for a layoff of oil-drilling employees — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a determination that any particular employer, employee, or job duties fall within the statute's description of "the business of oil drilling," a term the statute itself does not further define. Section 201.7 by its own terms addresses only a layoff ("an employer who lays off"); its text does not say whether or how it applies to an oil-drilling employee's resignation, and this clause does not resolve that question — Labor Code section 202's 72-hour-on-quit rule, which this corpus's general final-wage-timing clause addresses, is not restated here. This clause also does not resolve what counts as "such reasonable time as may be necessary for computation or payment," beyond the stated 24-hour outer limit; the statute does not itself define that phrase further. The single citation below is the operative text of this paragraph of Section 201.7 as currently in force; it is not corroborated by a second, independent source.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 201.7 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, oil drilling layoff final-wage timing rule
citations.quote: An employer who lays off an employee or a group of employees engaged in the business of oil drilling shall be deemed to have made immediate payment within the meaning of Section 201 if the wages of such employees are paid within such reasonable time as may be necessary for computation or payment thereof; provided, however, that such reasonable time shall not exceed 24 hours after discharge excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays; and provided further, such payment may be mailed and the date of mailing is the date of payment.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own Stated Reason for This Rule
clauses.body: Labor Code section 201.7 recites the Legislature's own finding that special provision must be made for the payment of wages on discharge of employees engaged in oil drilling, because their employment at various locations is often far removed from the employer's principal administrative offices, which the Legislature found makes the computation and payment of wages on an immediate basis unduly burdensome.
clauses.gap: This is California statutory text (Labor Code § 201.7, second paragraph), presented as the statute's own recital of legislative purpose — not independent historical or legislative-history research into why the provision was enacted (it was added by Statutes 1980, Chapter 440, according to the same fetched page, but this clause does not independently verify any legislative committee analysis or bill history beyond that enactment note), and not a claim that this stated purpose determines the outcome of any particular reader's situation. The recital describes remoteness from "the employer's principal administrative offices" as the justification; the statute does not define how remote a location must be, and this clause does not supply such a definition because the fetched text of Section 201.7 does not state one. The single citation below is the operative text of this paragraph of Section 201.7 as currently in force; it is not corroborated by a second, independent source.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, oil drilling final-wage rule — legislative finding
citations.quote: The Legislature finds and determines that special provision must be made for the payment of wages on discharge of employees engaged in oil drilling because their employment at various locations is often far removed from the employer’s principal administrative offices, which makes the computation and payment of wages on an immediate basis unduly burdensome.

clauses.title: Section 203's Penalty List Does Not Name Section 201.7 Separately
clauses.body: Labor Code section 203 states that if an employer willfully fails to pay, without abatement or reduction, wages in accordance with Sections 201, 201.3, 201.5, 201.6, 201.8, 201.9, 202, and 205.5, to an employee who is discharged or who quits, the employee's wages continue as a penalty from the due date at the same rate until paid or until an action is commenced, capped at 30 days. That list, as currently in force, names Section 201 but does not separately name Section 201.7. Section 201.7 itself, described elsewhere in this material, frames its 24-hour-with-mailing rule as a basis for an oil-drilling employer to be deemed to have made "immediate payment within the meaning of Section 201" — language that ties Section 201.7's own timing rule to Section 201's immediate-payment requirement, which is a section Section 203's penalty list does name.

Section 201.7 ties its own deeming rule to Section 201 rather than stating an independent penalty of its own, and Section 201 is on Section 203's list; but this clause does not resolve how that textual relationship is applied in practice, since no case law construing this specific relationship was located in the CourtListener search performed for this clause. This clause also does not restate the remainder of Section 203(a) (the secretes-or-absents-themselves exception) or Section 203(b)'s statute-of-limitations provision, which this corpus's dedicated Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter document addresses generally rather than this clause duplicating them. clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California Constitution Article I, Section 31 -- the provision added by Proposition 209 (1996) that bars the state and its political subdivisions from discriminating against, or granting preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in the operation of public employment. It concerns a hiring decision by {{publicEntityName}} regarding the position of {{jobTitle}}, potentially involving the applicant {{applicantName}}. It states facts about what the constitutional text itself says -- the prohibition, which entities it covers, its stated exceptions, its remedies provision, and its effective-date and severability language. Article I, Section 31 also addresses public education and public contracting; this document focuses on the public-employment application only and does not address the education or contracting contexts. This corpus separately includes documents addressing FEHA-based hiring restrictions such as the Fair Chance Act and the California Fair Pay Act, which apply to different employers (including private employers) under different statutory schemes; this document does not restate those and addresses only the distinct constitutional rule that applies to public employers. It is not itself a job posting, an offer, or any notice, and it does not tell {{publicEntityName}} or {{applicantName}} what to do about any particular hiring decision.

clauses.title: The Core Prohibition: No Discrimination or Preferential Treatment in Public Employment
clauses.body: California Constitution Article I, Section 31, subdivision (a) states that the State shall not discriminate against, or grant preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in the operation of public employment (the same sentence also names public education and public contracting as covered activities). The provision was added to the California Constitution by Proposition 209, an initiative measure approved by voters on November 5, 1996.
clauses.gap: The constitutional text does not itself define "discriminate," "preferential treatment," or "the operation of public employment," and does not itemize which specific personnel decisions (recruitment, testing, hiring, promotion, layoff, or other decisions) fall within "the operation of" public employment. This document quotes the text of subdivision (a) as written; it does not attempt to summarize the substantial body of published California case law interpreting the scope of that language, because case-law research for this document could not be completed -- CourtListener's search tool returned a rate-limit error (HTTP 429, "Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") on every attempt made while drafting this document, and no case citations are included here as a result. A reader relying on this document should not assume the absence of case citations means no relevant case law exists.

citations.cite: California Constitution, Article I, Section 31, subdivision (a)
citations.quote: The State shall not discriminate against, or grant preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in the operation of public employment, public education, or public contracting.

clauses.title: Which Public Employers Are Covered: The Definition of "State"
clauses.body: Article I, Section 31 defines "State" broadly for purposes of the section. The definition names the State itself, along with any city, county, city and county, public university system (including the University of California), community college district, or school district, and it adds special districts and "any other political subdivision or governmental instrumentality of or within the State" as covered entities as well. The statutory phrase "but not necessarily be limited to" signals that the named list of entities is illustrative rather than a closed, exhaustive list.
clauses.gap: The California Legislative Information HTML for this subdivision contains a mid-sentence line break in the source markup between "school district," and "special district" (confirmed by inspecting the raw fetched HTML, where the text node itself contains a literal newline character at that point, not a rendering artifact introduced afterward); this document treats that as a source-formatting line wrap and quotes the sentence with the line break preserved rather than silently removing it. Separately, the subdivision does not define "governmental instrumentality," so this document cannot state with precision where the outer boundary of coverage lies for an entity that is not on the named list -- for example, a joint powers authority or a quasi-public corporation created by statute.

special district, or any other political subdivision or governmental instrumentality of or within the State.

clauses.title: Exception for Bona Fide Sex Qualifications
clauses.body: Article I, Section 31 states that nothing in the section is to be interpreted as prohibiting bona fide qualifications based on sex that are reasonably necessary to the normal operation of public employment (the same sentence also names public education and public contracting). The provision does not create a parallel exception for bona fide qualifications based on race, color, ethnicity, or national origin -- the exception as written is limited to sex.

The constitutional text does not itself define "bona fide qualifications" or "reasonably necessary," and this document does not attempt to state how those terms have been applied to any specific job classification or qualification standard, because the case-law research needed to do so could not be completed (see the gap disclosure on the core-prohibition clause in this document, describing the CourtListener rate-limit error encountered while drafting).

clauses.title: Exceptions: Pre-Existing Court Orders and Federal Program Eligibility
clauses.body: Article I, Section 31 states two further exceptions. First, nothing in the section is to be interpreted as invalidating any court order or consent decree that was already in force as of the section's effective date. Second, nothing in the section is to be interpreted as prohibiting action that must be taken to establish or maintain eligibility for a federal program, where ineligibility would result in a loss of federal funds to the State.
clauses.gap: The text does not state a mechanism for identifying which court orders or consent decrees were "in force as of the effective date" (November 5, 1996), and does not address what happens when such an order or decree is later modified, extended, or expires. It also does not name which federal programs the federal-funding exception might apply to, or specify what showing an entity would need to make to invoke it; this document does not attempt to supply that missing detail.

citations.quote: Nothing in this section shall be interpreted as prohibiting action which must be taken to establish or maintain eligibility for any federal program, where ineligibility would result in a loss of federal funds to the State.

clauses.title: Remedies Available for a Violation
clauses.body: Article I, Section 31 states that the remedies available for a violation of the section are the same, regardless of the injured party's race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin, as the remedies that are otherwise available for violations of then-existing California antidiscrimination law.
clauses.gap: The provision defines the remedy by cross-reference to "then-existing California antidiscrimination law" rather than stating a remedy directly, and it does not identify which antidiscrimination statutes or common-law causes of action that cross-reference points to, or how a court is to select among them when more than one might apply. This document does not attempt to trace that cross-reference to any specific antidiscrimination statute's remedial provisions.

citations.case: Cal. Const. art. I, § 31, subd. (g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Constitution, Article I, Section 31, subdivision (g)
citations.quote: The remedies available for violations of this section shall be the same, regardless of the injured party’s race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin, as are otherwise available for violations of then-existing California antidiscrimination law.

clauses.title: Prospective Effect, Self-Executing Nature, and Severability
clauses.body: Article I, Section 31, subdivision (b) states that the section applies only to action taken after the section's effective date. Subdivision (h) states that the section is self-executing, that if any part of the section is found to be in conflict with federal law or the United States Constitution the section is to be implemented to the maximum extent that federal law and the United States Constitution permit, and that any provision held invalid is severable from the remaining portions of the section. The California Legislative Information text carries a history note stating that Section 31 was added on November 5, 1996, by Proposition 209, an initiative measure.
clauses.gap: The text does not itself state the calendar date on which the section's "effective date" fell (as distinct from the November 5, 1996 election date on which the initiative was approved) -- for a voter initiative, the effective date and the election date are not necessarily the identical calendar day, and this document does not resolve that distinction. This document also does not summarize any published decision addressing a federal-law or federal-constitutional conflict under subdivision (h), for the case-law-access reason disclosed in the gap field of the core-prohibition clause in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Const. art. I, § 31, subd. (b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Constitution, Article I, Section 31, subdivision (b)
citations.quote: This section shall apply only to action taken after the section’s effective date.

citations.case: Cal. Const. art. I, § 31, subd. (h), history note (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Constitution, Article I, Section 31, subdivision (h), and enactment history note
citations.quote: This section shall be self-executing. If any part or parts of this section are found to be in conflict with federal law or the United States Constitution, the section shall be implemented to the maximum extent that federal law and the United States Constitution permit. Any provision held invalid shall be severable from the remaining portions of this section. (Sec. 31 added Nov. 5, 1996, by Prop. 209. Initiative measure.)

clauses.title: Acknowledgment of Receipt
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This document explains, using the statute's own text, how and when a California limited partnership such as {{partnershipName}} dissolves and winds up under Article 8, "Dissolution," of the California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008 (Corp. Code §§ 15908.01–15908.09). It covers the statutory events that dissolve a limited partnership, the judicial-dissolution standard, winding-up authority, a general partner's power to bind the limited partnership after dissolution, the procedures for barring claims against a dissolved limited partnership, and the statutory priority for distributing assets during winding up. It is distinct from this project's California Limited Partnership Formation Information Sheet (formation under the same Act), Limited Partner Control Safe Harbor Information Sheet (a limited partner's participation in winding up without losing the liability shield), and General Partnership Dissolution and Winding-Up Information Sheet (a different entity type governed by the Uniform Partnership Act of 1994, Corp. Code §§ 16801-16807).

clauses.title: The Statutory Events That Dissolve a Limited Partnership
clauses.body: California's limited partnership statute dissolves a limited partnership, and requires its activities to be wound up, only on the occurrence of specific listed events (subject to the separate judicial-dissolution ground described elsewhere in the statute). Those listed events include an event the partnership agreement itself specifies, and the consent of all general partners together with limited partners owning a majority of the rights to receive distributions as limited partners. Two further events turn on a general partner's dissociation: if the limited partnership still has a remaining general partner, dissolution follows a majority-in-interest partner consent given within 90 days of that dissociation; if it does not, dissolution follows automatically 90 days after the dissociation unless the limited partners consent to continue the business and admit a new general partner within that period. A parallel 90-day rule applies to the dissociation of the limited partnership's last limited partner.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the consent-based dissolution trigger of Corp. Code § 15908.01(b); the agreement-specified-event trigger of subdivision (a), the general-partner-dissociation timelines of subdivision (c), and the last-limited-partner-dissociation timeline of subdivision (d) are paraphrased in this clause's body from the same fetched statutory text but are not independently quoted here. This clause also does not state the judicial-dissolution ground of § 15908.02, which the statute's introductory clause carves out as a separate basis for dissolution.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15908.01 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, consent-based dissolution trigger
citations.quote: (b) the consent of all general partners and of limited partners owning a majority of the rights to receive distributions as limited partners at the time the consent is to be effective;

clauses.title: Judicial Dissolution: "Not Reasonably Practicable"
clauses.body: A partner may ask a court to order a limited partnership's judicial dissolution. California's statute sets a single substantive standard for that relief: dissolution is available on application by a partner if it is not reasonably practicable to carry on the limited partnership's activities in conformity with the partnership agreement. This is a distinct dissolution pathway from the consent- and dissociation-based events described elsewhere in the statute, and it operates through a court of competent jurisdiction rather than partner action alone.
clauses.gap: This clause states only the substantive standard of Corp. Code § 15908.02(a). The same section's subdivisions (b) through (g) — a buyout mechanism letting the other partners avoid dissolution by purchasing the moving party's partnership interest for cash at a court-determined fair market value, including an appraisal procedure and a bond requirement — were fetched but are not quoted or summarized in this clause. A CourtListener case-law search for judicial interpretation of the "not reasonably practicable" standard, attempted for this clause, returned an HTTP 429 daily rate-limit error (the tool's 125/day quota was already exhausted), so no case law was retrieved, reviewed, or relied on for this clause or any other clause in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15908.02 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, judicial dissolution standard
citations.quote: (a) On application by a partner, a court of competent jurisdiction may order dissolution of a limited partnership if it is not reasonably practicable to carry on the activities of the limited partnership in conformity with the partnership agreement.

clauses.title: Continued Existence and Winding-Up Authority
clauses.body: Once dissolved, a limited partnership does not simply cease to exist; California's statute continues it in existence for the sole purpose of winding up its activities. If a dissolved limited partnership has no general partner left to conduct that winding up, the statute lets the limited partners themselves fill the gap: a person to wind up the partnership's activities may be appointed by the consent of limited partners owning a majority of the rights to receive distributions as limited partners.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Corp. Code § 15908.03(a) and (c). Subdivision (b)'s list of specific winding-up acts (amending the certificate of limited partnership to reflect dissolution, preserving the business as a going concern, prosecuting or defending actions, transferring property, mediating or arbitrating disputes, and filing a certificate of cancellation under Corp. Code § 15902.03), subdivision (c)'s further requirement that an appointed winding-up person promptly amend the certificate of limited partnership to disclose the appointment, subdivision (d)'s court-supervised winding-up procedure, and subdivision (e)'s reasonable-compensation entitlement for limited partners who wind up the partnership are not quoted or independently verified here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15908.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, continued existence for winding up only
citations.quote: (a) A limited partnership continues after dissolution only for the purpose of winding up its activities.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15908.03 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, appointment of a person to wind up absent a general partner
citations.quote: (c) If a dissolved limited partnership does not have a general partner, a person to wind up the dissolved limited partnership’s activities may be appointed by the consent of limited partners owning a majority of the rights to receive distributions as limited partners at the time the consent is to be effective.

clauses.title: A General Partner's Power to Bind the Limited Partnership After Dissolution
clauses.body: Dissolution does not immediately strip a general partner's power to bind the limited partnership. California's statute binds the limited partnership to a general partner's post-dissolution act if that act is appropriate for winding up the partnership's activities, or if it is an act that would have bound the partnership before dissolution under the statute's ordinary agency rule and the other party to the transaction had no notice of the dissolution at the time of the transaction.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Corp. Code § 15908.04(a). Subdivision (b), which lets a person dissociated as a general partner similarly bind the limited partnership through a post-dissolution act for up to two years after the dissociation under stated notice conditions, and Corp. Code § 15908.05's rule making a general partner or dissociated general partner personally liable to the limited partnership (and to other obligated partners) for damage caused by an inappropriate post-dissolution obligation, are related provisions in the same fetched statutory article that are not quoted or summarized in this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15908.04 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, a general partner's post-dissolution act binding the limited partnership
citations.quote: (a) A limited partnership is bound by a general partner’s act after dissolution which:(1) is appropriate for winding up the limited partnership’s activities; or(2) would have bound the limited partnership under Section 15904.02 before dissolution, if, at the time the other party enters into the transaction, the other party does not have notice of the dissolution.

clauses.title: Cutting Off Known Creditors' Claims by Direct Notice
clauses.body: California's statute gives a dissolved limited partnership a direct-notice procedure for cutting off claims from creditors it already knows about. The dissolved limited partnership may notify each known claimant of the dissolution in a record that specifies what the claim must contain, gives a mailing address for it, sets a deadline of at least 120 days from the claimant's receipt of the notice, and states that a late claim will be barred.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Corp. Code § 15908.06(b), the content requirements for a known-claimant notice. Subdivision (a) (the general authorization to use this procedure), subdivision (c) (the two ways a claim is actually barred — missing the notice's deadline, or failing to sue within 90 days after the limited partnership rejects a timely claim in writing), and subdivision (d) (the carve-out for claims based on events after the dissolution's effective date, or contingent liabilities) are paraphrased in this document but not quoted or independently verified in this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15908.06 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, known-claimant notice content requirements
citations.quote: (b) A dissolved limited partnership may notify its known claimants of the dissolution in a record. The notice must:(1) specify the information required to be included in a claim;(2) provide a mailing address to which the claim is to be sent;(3) state the deadline for receipt of the claim, which may not be less than 120 days after the date the notice is received by the claimant; and(4) state that the claim will be barred if not received by the deadline.

clauses.title: Cutting Off Unknown Claims by Published Notice
clauses.body: Beyond notifying known claimants directly, a dissolved limited partnership may also publish notice of its dissolution and request persons having claims against it to present them in accordance with the notice. For a claimant who was not given direct notice, or whose claim was timely submitted but never acted on, or whose claim is contingent or based on a later event, published notice under the statute cuts off the claim unless the claimant sues to enforce it within four years after the notice's publication date.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Corp. Code § 15908.07(a) (the authorization to publish notice) and (b)(3) (the four-year enforcement deadline the published notice must state). Subdivision (b)'s other required newspaper-notice contents, subdivision (c)'s full list of which claimant categories the bar reaches, subdivision (d)'s rule on how a non-barred claim may still be enforced (against the dissolved limited partnership's undistributed assets, or against a partner or transferee up to that person's proportionate share of assets received in liquidation), and subdivision (e)'s carve-out preserving the state's own tax-collection remedies are not quoted or independently verified here.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15908.07 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, authorization to publish notice of dissolution
citations.quote: (a) A dissolved limited partnership may publish notice of its dissolution and request persons having claims against the limited partnership to present them in accordance with the notice.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15908.07 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, four-year enforcement deadline stated in published notice
citations.quote: (3) state that a claim against the limited partnership is barred unless an action to enforce the claim is commenced within four years after publication of the notice.

clauses.title: Creditor-First Priority for Distributing Assets During Winding Up
clauses.body: California's statute fixes the order in which a dissolved limited partnership's assets must be applied during winding up. Creditors come first: the partnership's assets, including any contributions the statute requires, must be applied to satisfy the limited partnership's obligations to creditors — a category that reaches partners who are themselves creditors of the partnership, to the extent otherwise permitted by law. Only after those obligations are satisfied does any surplus return to the partners, in the shares they hold in distributions generally.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Corp. Code § 15908.09(a) and (b). Subdivision (c)'s rules for what happens when the limited partnership's assets are insufficient to satisfy its obligations — requiring general partners who have not been released under Corp. Code § 15906.07 to contribute in proportion to their distribution rights, with further shortfall-sharing rules among those general partners — are not quoted or independently verified in this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15908.09 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, creditors-first application of assets during winding up
citations.quote: In winding up a limited partnership’s activities, the assets of the limited partnership, including the contributions required by this section, must be applied to satisfy the limited partnership’s obligations to creditors, including, to the extent permitted by law, partners that are creditors.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15908.09 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, surplus returned to partners after creditors are satisfied
citations.quote: Any surplus remaining after the limited partnership complies with subdivision (a) must be returned to the partners as they share in distributions.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment and Signatures
About This End of Life Option Act Information Sheet
clauses.body: This document states facts about California's End of Life Option Act, Health & Safety Code §§ 443–443.22, as it applies to {{patientName}}. The Act creates a statutory pathway under which a terminally ill adult who meets its requirements may request a prescription for a self-administered aid-in-dying drug from an attending physician — here, {{physicianName}}, if acting in that role for {{patientName}}. This document does not recommend whether {{patientName}} should make a request under the Act, does not constitute the written request form the Act itself requires (Health & Safety Code § 443.11), and is not the attending physician checklist and compliance form referenced in Health & Safety Code § 443.22. Those statutory forms, and the two-physician, two-witness process the Act requires, are completed separately and directly with a participating attending physician. This document instead states what the statute itself says about eligibility, procedure, and legal effect.

clauses.title: Statutory Definitions: Qualified Individual, Terminal Disease, and Aid-in-Dying Drug
clauses.body: The Act defines a “qualified individual” as an adult who has the capacity to make medical decisions, is a resident of California, and has satisfied the Act's requirements in order to obtain a prescription for a drug to end their life. It defines “terminal disease” as an incurable and irreversible disease that has been medically confirmed and will, within reasonable medical judgment, result in death within six months. And it defines “aid-in-dying drug” as a drug determined and prescribed by a physician for a qualified individual, which the qualified individual may choose to self-administer to bring about their death due to a terminal disease.
clauses.gap: All three quotations below are subsections of a single statutory section (Health & Safety Code § 443.1), not independently authored sources. Section 443.1 defines eighteen separate terms (subdivisions (a) through (r)); this clause reproduces only these three central ones and does not independently verify or reproduce the statute's other defined terms here (for example, “capacity to make medical decisions,” “informed decision,” or “mental health specialist assessment,” each separately defined in the same section).

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.1(p) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definition of “qualified individual”
citations.quote: “Qualified individual” means an adult who has the capacity to make medical decisions, is a resident of California, and has satisfied the requirements of this part in order to obtain a prescription for a drug to end their life.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.1(r) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definition of “terminal disease”
citations.quote: “Terminal disease” means an incurable and irreversible disease that has been medically confirmed and will, within reasonable medical judgment, result in death within six months.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.1(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definition of “aid-in-dying drug”
citations.quote: “Aid-in-dying drug” means a drug determined and prescribed by a physician for a qualified individual, which the qualified individual may choose to self-administer to bring about their death due to a terminal disease.

clauses.title: Conditions the Statute Requires Before a Request May Be Made
clauses.body: By statute, an adult with the capacity to make medical decisions and a terminal disease may request a prescription for an aid-in-dying drug only if several conditions are all satisfied, including that an attending physician has diagnosed a terminal disease, the individual has voluntarily expressed the wish to receive the prescription, the individual is a California resident (established through means such as a California driver's license, voter registration, property ownership or lease, or a recent California tax return), the individual has documented the request in the statutory manner, and the individual has the physical and mental ability to self-administer the aid-in-dying drug. The statute separately states that a person is not disqualified from being a “qualified individual” solely because of age or disability.
clauses.gap: The quotations below verify only the statute's introductory sentence and the physical/mental self-administration condition (§ 443.2(a) and (a)(5)); this clause's prose summary of the other listed conditions — diagnosis, voluntary expression of the wish, California residency and its four listed proof methods, and statutory documentation — restates but does not separately quote-verify each numbered subpart of § 443.2(a)(1)–(4) here. Section 443.2 also does not itself define “capacity to make medical decisions” (that definition is in a separate subsection of § 443.1, verified in a companion clause of this document) or specify what “physical and mental ability to self-administer” requires beyond this bare statement.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.2(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: introductory conditions for a request
citations.quote: An individual who is an adult with the capacity to make medical decisions and with a terminal disease may make a request to receive a prescription for an aid-in-dying drug if all of the following conditions are satisfied:

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.2(a)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: physical and mental ability to self-administer
citations.quote: The individual has the physical and mental ability to self-administer the aid-in-dying drug.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.2(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: age or disability alone does not disqualify
citations.quote: A person shall not be considered a “qualified individual” under the provisions of this part solely because of age or disability.

clauses.title: A Request Under the Act Cannot Be Made Through a Power of Attorney, Advance Directive, or Conservator
clauses.body: The statute states that a request for a prescription for an aid-in-dying drug must be made solely and directly by the individual diagnosed with the terminal disease, and cannot be made on that individual's behalf through a power of attorney, an advance health care directive, a conservator, a health care agent, a surrogate, or any other legally recognized health care decisionmaker.
clauses.gap: This clause rests on a single statutory subsection (§ 443.2(c)); no independent second source was located restating this exact rule. The subsection states that a request cannot be made through these substitute-decisionmaking mechanisms, but does not itself state a specific legal consequence (for example, invalidity of a request or a particular remedy) if one of these mechanisms is nonetheless used to attempt a request — this document does not assert such a consequence because it was not found stated in this section's text. This document's separate Financial Power of Attorney, Advance Health Care Directive, and adult conservatorship materials describe those instruments generally; none of them independently restates this specific carve-out, so a reader relying on any of those documents together with this one would need to look at this clause for this particular limitation.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.2(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a request cannot be made through a power of attorney, advance directive, conservator, or other decisionmaker
citations.quote: A request for a prescription for an aid-in-dying drug under this part shall be made solely and directly by the individual diagnosed with the terminal disease and shall not be made on behalf of the patient, including, but not limited to, through a power of attorney, an advance health care directive, a conservator, health care agent, surrogate, or any other legally recognized health care decisionmaker.

clauses.title: The Two Oral Requests and Written Request Procedure
clauses.body: By statute, an individual seeking a prescription must submit two oral requests, a minimum of 48 hours apart, and a written request to the attending physician. A valid written request must be signed and dated by the individual seeking the aid-in-dying drug in the presence of two witnesses.
clauses.gap: This clause verifies § 443.3(a) and the witness-signing requirement in § 443.3(b)(2); it does not separately quote-verify § 443.3(b)(1) (that the written request must be in the statutory form described in § 443.11) or § 443.3(b)(3) (the witnesses' attestations), which are addressed only in general terms here and, for witness qualifications specifically, in a companion clause of this document. The current 48-hour minimum interval reflects a 2021 amendment (Stats. 2021, Ch. 542 (SB 380), effective January 1, 2022); this document does not address the interval that applied to requests made before that effective date.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.3(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: two oral requests 48 hours apart plus a written request
citations.quote: An individual seeking to obtain a prescription for an aid-in-dying drug pursuant to this part shall submit two oral requests, a minimum of 48 hours apart, and a written request to their attending physician.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.3(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: written request must be signed and dated before two witnesses
citations.quote: The request shall be signed and dated, in the presence of two witnesses, by the individual seeking the aid-in-dying drug.

clauses.title: Limits on Who May Serve as a Witness to the Written Request
clauses.body: The statute limits who may witness the signing of the written request: of the two required witnesses, no more than one may be related to the individual by blood, marriage, registered domestic partnership, or adoption, or be entitled to a portion of the individual's estate upon death, and no more than one may own, operate, or be employed at a health care entity where the individual is receiving medical treatment or resides.
clauses.gap: This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision (§ 443.3(c)), read together with its two numbered items. It does not address the further, separately stated rule in § 443.3(d) that the attending physician, consulting physician, or mental health specialist may not serve as one of the witnesses required under § 443.3(b)(3), nor does it state what legal consequence follows if a written request is witnessed in violation of these limits — no such consequence is stated in this subdivision's text. This witness-eligibility structure is similar in kind to, but is a legally separate statute from, the interested-witness rules that apply to a will under the Probate Code; this document does not assert that the two sets of rules are identical.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.3(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: no more than one witness may be a relative or estate beneficiary
citations.quote: Only one of the two witnesses at the time the written request is signed may:

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.3(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: relationship or estate-interest limit
citations.quote: Be related to the qualified individual by blood, marriage, registered domestic partnership, or adoption or be entitled to a portion of the individual’s estate upon death.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.3(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: health care entity ownership/employment limit
citations.quote: Own, operate, or be employed at a health care entity where the individual is receiving medical treatment or resides.

clauses.title: Effect on Life, Health, and Annuity Policies
clauses.body: By statute, the sale, procurement, or issuance of a life, health, or annuity policy — or the rate charged for one — may not be conditioned upon or affected by a person making or rescinding a request for an aid-in-dying drug. Separately, the statute states that a qualified individual's act of self-administering an aid-in-dying drug shall not have an effect upon a life, health, or annuity policy other than that of a natural death from the underlying disease.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two subdivisions of a single section (§ 443.13(a)(1) and (b)); it does not separately quote-verify subdivision (a)(2) (cross-referencing § 443.18 for the statement that such a death is not suicide) or subdivision (c) (restricting what an insurance carrier may communicate to an individual about aid-in-dying drug availability). No provision addressing how a death certificate itself must record cause of death was located within Health & Safety Code §§ 443–443.22 during this research; this document does not assert a rule on that separate point.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.13(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a policy's sale, issuance, or rate cannot be conditioned on a request
citations.quote: The sale, procurement, or issuance of a life, health, or annuity policy, health care service plan contract, or health benefit plan, or the rate charged for a policy or plan contract may not be conditioned upon or affected by a person making or rescinding a request for an aid-in-dying drug.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.13(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: self-administration treated as a natural death from the underlying disease for policy purposes
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other law, a qualified individual’s act of self-administering an aid-in-dying drug shall not have an effect upon a life, health, or annuity policy other than that of a natural death from the underlying disease.

clauses.title: How the Act Characterizes a Qualifying Death, and Limits on Its Use in Conservatorship or Elder Abuse Proceedings
clauses.body: The statute provides that a request by a qualified individual to an attending physician for an aid-in-dying drug, made in good faith compliance with the Act, shall not by itself provide the sole basis for the appointment of a guardian or conservator, and that actions taken in compliance with the Act shall not constitute or provide the basis for any claim of neglect or elder abuse for any purpose of law. Separately, the statute states that nothing in the Act authorizes a physician or any other person to end an individual's life by lethal injection, mercy killing, or active euthanasia, and that actions taken in accordance with the Act do not, for any purpose, constitute suicide, assisted suicide, homicide, or elder abuse under the law.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two independently numbered statutory sections (§ 443.14, specifically its subdivision (d), and § 443.18), which are genuinely separate sections rather than subsections of one. Section 443.14 contains additional immunity provisions for persons present at self-administration and for health care providers who participate or decline to participate (subdivisions (a) through (c) and (e)), which are not reproduced in this clause. Both quoted provisions are conditioned on compliance “with the provisions of this part” or “in accordance with this part”; this document does not address what follows if the Act's other requirements were not actually met in a given case.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.14(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a request is not the sole basis for a guardian or conservator appointment
citations.quote: A request by a qualified individual to an attending physician to provide an aid-in-dying drug in good faith compliance with the provisions of this part shall not provide the sole basis for the appointment of a guardian or conservator.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.14(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: compliant actions are not a basis for a neglect or elder abuse claim
citations.quote: Actions taken in compliance with the provisions of this part shall not constitute or provide the basis for any claim of neglect or elder abuse for any purpose of law.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.18 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: not euthanasia, and not suicide, assisted suicide, homicide, or elder abuse under the law
citations.quote: Nothing in this part may be construed to authorize a physician or any other person to end an individual’s life by lethal injection, mercy killing, or active euthanasia. Actions taken in accordance with this part shall not, for any purposes, constitute suicide, assisted suicide, homicide, or elder abuse under the law.

clauses.title: A Governmental Entity's Claim Against the Estate for Costs of a Public-Place Death
clauses.body: The statute gives a governmental entity that incurs costs resulting from a qualified individual terminating their life under the Act in a “public place” a claim against that individual's estate to recover those costs and reasonable attorney's fees related to enforcing the claim. “Public place” is separately defined by statute to mean any street, alley, park, public building, place of business or assembly open to or frequented by the public, or other place open to public view or public access; a health care entity is expressly excluded from that definition.
clauses.gap: This clause draws on two sections (§ 443.21 for the claim itself, and § 443.1(o) for the cross-referenced definition of “public place”). Section 443.21's text does not itself state a limitations period for when the entity must bring this claim, nor does it specify the claim's priority relative to other creditor claims against the estate in a probate proceeding — this document's separate materials on creditor's claims against a decedent's estate describe the general claims process but were not cross-verified here against this specific claim type. The statute does not address costs incurred from a death occurring outside a “public place” as so defined.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.21 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: governmental entity's claim against the estate for public-place death costs
citations.quote: Any governmental entity that incurs costs resulting from a qualified individual terminating his or her life pursuant to the provisions of this part in a public place shall have a claim against the estate of the qualified individual to recover those costs and reasonable attorney fees related to enforcing the claim.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 443.1(o) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: definition of “public place”
citations.quote: “Public place” means any street, alley, park, public building, any place of business or assembly open to or frequented by the public, and any other place that is open to the public view, or to which the public has access. “Public place” does not include a health care entity.

clauses.title: Litigation History: The Act's Manner of Enactment Was Challenged, but Not Resolved on the Merits by This Published Decision
clauses.body: A published California Court of Appeal decision recounts that the Act was enacted in 2015 during a special legislative session the Governor called for health-care-cost and related purposes, and that a trial court later ruled the Act unconstitutional on the ground that enacting it exceeded the scope of that special session. On the parties' writ petition, the Court of Appeal held that the individual physicians and organization challenging the Act had not adequately alleged standing to do so, and on that basis directed the trial court to vacate its order and judgment — expressly stating that it did not reach the constitutional question of whether the Legislature exceeded its special-session authority in enacting the Act.
clauses.gap: This is the only case-law source in this document; a CourtListener search located this decision without difficulty, and this document's quotes were verified directly against the opinion's text, so no CourtListener quota or access issue is disclosed here. The court's holding was limited to standing — it did not decide, and this document does not assert, whether the Act was validly enacted. (One separate opinion filed in the same case did go on to conclude the Act was constitutionally enacted, but that view was not the basis of the court's disposition and is not treated here as a holding.) This document did not locate or verify any later reported appellate decision resolving the underlying constitutional question on the merits after remand; if the case continued in the trial court after this 2018 decision, that later history is not covered here.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California Family Code section 6305, which limits when a family court may issue a mutual domestic violence restraining order -- one that restrains both {{petitionerName}} and {{respondentName}} -- in the proceeding bearing case number {{courtCaseNumber}} filed in {{countyOfFiling}}. It states the text of section 6305, a related Penal Code provision it cross-references, and how one published California Court of Appeal decision has construed it. It does not state whether a mutual order should be requested, opposed, or is likely to be granted on the facts of this or any other case, and it is not a substitute for advice from a licensed attorney.

clauses.title: Scope: A Restriction on Mutual Orders, Not a General DVRO Procedure
clauses.body: Section 6305 does not create a restraining order remedy of its own. It applies only where a court is considering restraining both parties to a domestic violence proceeding against each other in the same order -- a 'mutual order.' The general procedure for requesting a Domestic Violence Restraining Order under the Domestic Violence Prevention Act, including qualifying relationships, the statutory definition of abuse, the standard of proof, and firearm relinquishment, is addressed in this project's separate Domestic Violence Restraining Order (Request for Order) Information Sheet and is not repeated here. This information sheet covers only the additional statutory conditions that apply specifically when a court is asked to, or is considering whether to, restrain both parties in a single mutual order.

clauses.title: Statutory Condition: Personal Appearance and Written Evidence From Each Party
clauses.body: Family Code section 6305 states that a court shall not issue a mutual order enjoining the parties from specific acts of abuse described in section 6320 unless both of two conditions apply. The first condition is that both parties personally appear and each party presents written evidence of abuse or domestic violence in an application for relief using a mandatory Judicial Council restraining order application form. The statute specifies that written evidence of abuse or domestic violence contained in a responsive pleading does not, by itself, satisfy a party's obligation to present written evidence of abuse or domestic violence for this purpose.
clauses.gap: This clause covers only the personal-appearance and written-evidence condition in subdivision (a)(1); the separate detailed-findings condition in subdivision (a)(2) and the dominant-aggressor cross-reference in subdivision (b) are addressed in separate clauses. It does not cover the sentence in subdivision (a)(1) directing the Judicial Council to modify forms by July 1, 2016, which is spent and administrative. The leginfo.legislature.ca.gov source HTML renders the space after each subdivision letter/number (e.g., between "(a)" and "The court") as a non-breaking space ( , Unicode U+00A0) rather than an ordinary space; this was confirmed against the raw fetched HTML and is preserved verbatim, character-for-character, in the quotes below rather than being silently converted to a regular space. This clause does not address how a court applying section 6305 has treated evidence presented at a continued or later hearing, or what counts as an 'application for relief' beyond the mandatory Judicial Council form itself -- no case law on those points was reviewed for this clause.
