citations.cite: the introductory bar on mutual orders and the first of the two conditions that must both apply -- personal appearance and written evidence on a mandatory Judicial Council form
citations.quote: (a) The court shall not issue a mutual order enjoining the parties from specific acts of abuse described in Section 6320 unless both of the following apply:

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6305(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the personal-appearance and written-evidence condition, and the statement that written evidence in a responsive pleading alone does not satisfy it
citations.quote: (1) Both parties personally appear and each party presents written evidence of abuse or domestic violence in an application for relief using a mandatory Judicial Council restraining order application form. For purposes of this paragraph, written evidence of abuse or domestic violence in a responsive pleading does not satisfy the party’s obligation to present written evidence of abuse or domestic violence.

clauses.title: Statutory Condition: Detailed Findings That Both Parties Were Primary Aggressors
clauses.body: The second condition Family Code section 6305 requires before a mutual order may issue is that the court make detailed findings of fact indicating that both parties acted as a primary aggressor and that neither party acted primarily in self-defense. Both statutory conditions -- personal appearance with written evidence, and these detailed findings -- must be satisfied; the statute states that a mutual order shall not issue 'unless both of the following apply.'
clauses.gap: This clause covers only subdivision (a)(2). It does not state what quantum or type of evidence a court has found sufficient to support 'detailed findings' in a published decision, nor does it address subdivision (b)'s cross-reference to the Penal Code's dominant-aggressor factors, which is covered in a separate clause. The source HTML again renders the space after "(2)" as a non-breaking space, preserved verbatim in the quote below.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 6305(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the detailed-findings condition -- that both parties acted as a primary aggressor and neither acted primarily in self-defense
citations.quote: (2) The court makes detailed findings of fact indicating that both parties acted as a primary aggressor and that neither party acted primarily in self-defense.

clauses.title: How 'Primary Aggressor' Is Assessed: The Penal Code's Dominant-Aggressor Factors
clauses.body: Family Code section 6305(b) directs that, in determining whether both parties acted primarily as aggressors for purposes of the detailed-findings condition, the court shall consider the provisions concerning dominant aggressors set forth in Penal Code section 836(c)(3). That Penal Code provision, enacted for a different purpose -- identifying which party a peace officer may arrest when mutual protective orders are already in place -- states that the dominant aggressor is the person determined to be the most significant, rather than the first, aggressor, and lists four factors an officer is to consider in that identification: the intent of the law to protect victims of domestic violence from continuing abuse, the threats creating fear of physical injury, the history of domestic violence between the persons involved, and whether either person involved acted in self-defense.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Family Code section 6305(b) in full and the arrest-context sentence identifying who qualifies as a 'dominant aggressor' under Penal Code section 836(c)(3); it does not quote the four lettered factors (A)-(D) that follow that sentence in the Penal Code, nor address how, if at all, a family court applying section 6305(b) has actually weighed those factors on a specific record -- no case law applying section 6305(b)'s cross-reference to a family-law fact pattern was located or reviewed for this clause. Penal Code section 836(c)(3) is written for peace officers deciding whom to arrest, not for family court judges deciding whether to issue a mutual order; section 6305(b) borrows its 'dominant aggressor' concept by cross-reference but does not restate it, so a reader comparing the two statutes should not assume every part of section 836(c)(3) transfers to the family-court context. The source HTML renders the space after "(b)" and after "(3)" as a non-breaking space (Unicode U+00A0) rather than an ordinary space, and wraps the sentence in section 6305(b) with a line break and leading whitespace between "acted" and "primarily"; both were confirmed against the raw fetched HTML and are preserved verbatim, character-for-character, in the quotes below rather than being silently converted to a regular space.

citations.cite: the direction that, in determining whether both parties acted primarily as aggressors, the court shall consider the Penal Code's dominant-aggressor provisions
citations.quote:
(b) For purposes of subdivision (a), in determining if both parties acted
 primarily as aggressors, the court shall consider the provisions concerning dominant aggressors set forth in paragraph (3) of subdivision (c) of Section 836 of the Penal Code.

citations.case: Cal. Penal Code § 836(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text)

citations.quote: (3) In situations where mutual protective orders have been issued under Division 10 (commencing with Section 6200) of the Family Code, liability for arrest under this subdivision applies only to those persons who are reasonably believed to have been the dominant aggressor.

clauses.title: Case Law: A Mutual Order Requires a Request by Both Parties
clauses.body: In a published 2015 decision, a California Court of Appeal addressed whether a trial court may issue a mutual restraining order under Family Code section 6305 when only one party has filed a written request for a restraining order and the responding party has not filed any request seeking restraints against the moving party. Construing section 6305 in the context of the Domestic Violence Prevention Act's statutory scheme, including the act's notice-of-hearing provisions, the court held that a mutual order may issue only where both parties have filed their own requests for that relief, so that each party receives the notice the statute otherwise contemplates.
clauses.gap: This clause describes the holding of a single published Court of Appeal decision, Isidora M. v. Silvino M. (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 11; it is not a survey of all published decisions applying section 6305, and it does not address unpublished trial court rulings or how often courts issue mutual orders without a cross-request in practice. The court's reasoning rested substantially on legislative history and the statutory scheme surrounding section 6305 (including Family Code section 6302's notice requirement), which this clause summarizes but does not quote in full. CourtListener's opinion search was used (not raw retrieval from courtlistener.com, which this environment's network proxy blocks) and the exact holding sentence was verified as a literal, contiguous match in the opinion's full text via the search tool's document-search function (match_count: 1); the daily CourtListener search quota was not exhausted during this research.

citations.case: Isidora M. v. Silvino M. (2015) 239 Cal.App.4th 11, 17-18 [190 Cal.Rptr.3d 502]
citations.cite: holding that a trial court may issue a mutual DVRO under section 6305 only where both parties have filed their own requests for that relief
citations.quote: We conclude that a trial court may issue a mutual domestic violence restraining order under section 6305 only if both parties have filed requests for such relief, so as to give the requisite notice to the opposing party.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes Labor Code § 1171.5, which declares that the protections, rights, and remedies available under California labor and employment law extend to workers regardless of immigration status, subject to a federal-law limit on reinstatement, and which restricts inquiry into a person's immigration status in a proceeding to enforce those laws. It does not cover the corpus's separate Immigrant Worker Protection Act document, which addresses a different subject — restrictions on an employer's cooperation with federal immigration enforcement at the worksite, such as agent access to nonpublic areas and notice around an I-9 inspection — rather than the scope of the underlying labor-law protections addressed here.

clauses.title: Protections, Rights, and Remedies Available Regardless of Immigration Status
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1171.5(a) declares that all protections, rights, and remedies available under California state law — with one exception for a reinstatement remedy that federal law prohibits — are available to every individual regardless of immigration status who has applied for employment, or who is or has been employed, in California.
clauses.gap: This subdivision states that 'all protections, rights, and remedies' are available regardless of immigration status 'except any reinstatement remedy prohibited by federal law,' but the statute itself does not say which reinstatement remedies federal law actually prohibits; that is left to case law construing the federal Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, addressed in a separate clause of this document citing Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co. This document does not resolve, for any specific employment situation, whether a federal-law reinstatement bar would apply.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1171.5(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1171.5(a), as amended by Stats. 2017, Ch. 160, Sec. 4 (AB 1690), eff. Jan. 1, 2018
citations.quote: (a) All protections, rights, and remedies available under state law, except any reinstatement remedy prohibited by federal law, are available to all individuals regardless of immigration status who have applied for employment, or who are or who have been employed, in this state.

clauses.title: Immigration Status Is Irrelevant to Liability; Restriction on Inquiry
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1171.5(b) states that, for purposes of enforcing state labor, employment, civil rights, consumer protection, and housing laws, a person's immigration status is irrelevant to the issue of liability. It further provides that, in a proceeding or discovery undertaken to enforce those state laws, no inquiry into a person's immigration status is permitted unless the party seeking to make the inquiry has shown, by clear and convincing evidence, that the inquiry is necessary to comply with federal immigration law.
clauses.gap: The raw HTML for this subdivision contains two formatting artifacts that both independently fetched copies (using two distinct User-Agent strings on 2026-09-07) reproduced identically: a non-breaking space, rather than an ordinary space, immediately after '(b)', and a mid-sentence line wrap — a newline followed by six tab characters — between 'housing' and 'laws'. Both are preserved exactly in the quote below rather than silently normalized. The statute does not itself define what showing would satisfy the 'clear and convincing evidence' standard for when an immigration-status inquiry is 'necessary...to comply with federal immigration law,' and this document does not resolve that open question for any specific proceeding.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1171.5(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1171.5(b), as amended by Stats. 2017, Ch. 160, Sec. 4 (AB 1690), eff. Jan. 1, 2018
citations.quote:
(b) For purposes of enforcing state labor, employment, civil rights, consumer protection, and housing
						laws, a person’s immigration status is irrelevant to the issue of liability, and in proceedings or discovery undertaken to enforce those state laws no inquiry shall be permitted into a person’s immigration status unless the person seeking to make this inquiry has shown by clear and convincing evidence that the inquiry is necessary in order to comply with federal immigration law.

clauses.title: Declaratory of Existing Law; Severability
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1171.5(c) states that the section is declaratory of existing law. Subdivision (d) makes the section's provisions severable: if any provision, or its application, is held invalid, that invalidity does not affect other provisions or applications that can still be given effect.
clauses.gap: The raw HTML renders subdivisions (c) and (d) as adjacent paragraph elements with no visible space between the period ending (c) and the '(d)' marker that follows it — both independently fetched copies reproduced this identically, and the quote below preserves it exactly rather than inserting a space that is not in the source. Subdivision (c)'s statement that the section is 'declaratory of existing law' is a legislative characterization; this document does not independently verify what specific pre-2002 case law or statute the Legislature understood itself to be declaratory of, beyond what is addressed in a separate clause of this document citing Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co.

citations.case: Cal. Lab. Code § 1171.5(c)-(d) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 1171.5(c)-(d), as amended by Stats. 2017, Ch. 160, Sec. 4 (AB 1690), eff. Jan. 1, 2018
citations.quote: (c) The provisions of this section are declaratory of existing law.(d) The provisions of this section are severable. If any provision of this section or its application is held invalid, that invalidity shall not affect other provisions or applications that can be given effect without the invalid provision or application.

clauses.title: Why the Statute Was Enacted: The 2002 Response to Hoffman Plastic Compounds
clauses.body: Section 1171.5 originated in Senate Bill No. 1818 (2002), a package of four nearly identical provisions added across the Civil, Government, Health and Safety, and Labor Codes. The California Supreme Court has explained that the Legislature enacted SB 1818 the same year the U.S. Supreme Court decided Hoffman Plastic Compounds, Inc. v. NLRB (2002) 535 U.S. 137 — a case holding that the National Labor Relations Board could not award backpay to an undocumented worker for a violation of federal labor law — in order to ensure that unauthorized workers in California would continue to receive the same protections and remedies as other workers under the state's own employment and labor laws, apart from reinstatement when federal law prohibits it.
clauses.gap: This clause describes Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co.'s account of why SB 1818 was enacted, not an independent legislative-history source such as a committee report; this document did not separately verify that legislative history beyond what the Salas opinion itself states. The Salas preemption analysis discussed elsewhere in this document was decided in a case about FEHA discrimination and retaliation claims specifically; the opinion does not purport to resolve preemption for every other California labor and employment statute that § 1171.5(a) says is available regardless of immigration status. This document also does not independently verify Hoffman Plastic Compounds' own holding against the U.S. Reports text; it relies on the Salas court's characterization of that holding.

citations.case: Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co.
citations.quote: to ensure that in California unauthorized alien workers would continue to have the same protections and remedies (apart from reinstatement when prohibited by federal law) afforded other workers under California’s employment and labor laws.

clauses.title: Section 1171.5 Is One of Four Nearly Identical Statutes
clauses.body: Labor Code § 1171.5 was enacted alongside three companion provisions using substantially the same operative language: Civil Code § 3339, Government Code § 7285, and Health and Safety Code § 24000. The California Supreme Court has noted a wording difference among them in how each historically defined the category of state law covered by its subdivision (b).
clauses.gap: This footnote reflects Labor Code § 1171.5(b)'s wording as it existed when Salas was decided in 2014 — the footnote states that subdivision (b) then referred only to 'state labor and employment laws.' Labor Code § 1171.5 was subsequently amended by Stats. 2017, Ch. 160, § 4 (AB 1690), effective January 1, 2018, and the current text of subdivision (b) — quoted in a separate clause of this document from a 2026 fetch of leginfo.legislature.ca.gov — now refers to 'state labor, employment, civil rights, consumer protection, and housing laws,' bringing its wording closer to Government Code § 7285's wording as Salas described it, though this document does not verify whether the two are now identical. This document does not independently fetch or verify the current text of Civil Code § 3339, Government Code § 7285, or Health and Safety Code § 24000 themselves.

citations.case: Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co.
citations.quote: The language of Civil Code section 3339 and Government Code section 7285 is the same. The language of the other two provisions — Health and Safety Code section 24000 and Labor Code section 1171.5 — differs only in the wording of subdivision (b). While Civil Code section 3339 and Government Code section 7285 refer to “state labor, employment, civil rights, and employee housing laws,” Health and Safety Code section 24000 and Labor Code section 1171.5 both refer only to “state labor and employment laws.”

clauses.title: A Federal-Law Limit Courts Have Applied to This Section's Remedies
clauses.body: Section 1171.5(a) makes 'all protections, rights, and remedies' available regardless of immigration status, 'except any reinstatement remedy prohibited by federal law.' Applying that framework to a FEHA discrimination and retaliation claim, the California Supreme Court held that federal immigration law does not preempt an award of lost pay for the period before an employer discovers a worker's ineligibility to work in the United States under federal law, but does preempt such an award for the period after that discovery — because continuing to employ a worker known to be unauthorized is itself prohibited by federal immigration law.
clauses.gap: This holding was reached in a case applying California's FEHA specifically. In the raw opinion text, this sentence is immediately followed by a footnote marker and a full footnote (numbered 3 in the opinion) before the sentence's continuation resumes on the next page; this quote reproduces only the continuation clause that appears after that footnote, not the words immediately preceding the footnote marker on the prior page, so as to avoid quoting across that intervening footnote as if it were contiguous text. That footnote itself states that the court's preemption analysis for the post-discovery period is limited to an employer who discovers a worker's unauthorized status after the worker has already been discharged or not rehired — the court left open, as a distinct situation, an employer who knowingly hired or continued to employ an unauthorized worker in the first place; this document does not quote that footnote. The quoted continuation clause also contains a mid-sentence line wrap in the raw opinion text (a literal newline between "an" and "unauthorized," verified directly against the source), normalized to a single space here rather than reproduced as a literal newline. This document does not address whether or how this same prediscovery/post-discovery distinction has been applied by any court to a California labor statute other than FEHA, and does not resolve whether a specific reinstatement or lost-pay remedy in a specific case would or would not be found preempted.

citations.case: Salas v. Sierra Chemical Co.
citations.quote: to the extent that it makes a California FEHA lost pay award available to an unauthorized alien worker for the post-discovery period.

clauses.title: Relationship to Other Documents in This Corpus
clauses.body: This document addresses only Labor Code § 1171.5's extension of state labor and employment law protections, rights, and remedies to workers regardless of immigration status. It does not cover the corpus's separate Immigrant Worker Protection Act document, which instead restricts an employer's cooperation with federal immigration enforcement at the worksite — including access by immigration enforcement agents to nonpublic areas and to employee records, and notice to employees around a federal immigration inspection of I-9 forms. It also does not cover the definition of a 'protected individual' used elsewhere in this corpus for national-origin or citizenship-status discrimination claims, which draws on a different body of law — federal immigration-related unfair employment practices — from the state-law remedies-and-liability statute addressed here.

clauses.title: What This Document Does and Does Not Do
clauses.body: This document states the text of Labor Code § 1171.5 and describes how one California appellate court has applied it in a reported decision. It does not determine, for any specific employment relationship, what protections, rights, or remedies are or are not available, whether a particular inquiry into a specific person's immigration status would or would not meet the 'clear and convincing evidence' standard the statute describes, or whether a federal-law reinstatement bar would or would not apply in a specific case.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet explains three related provisions of the California Family Code that can come into play when an allegation of child abuse is made during a custody or visitation proceeding between {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} regarding {{childName}}, case number {{courtCaseNumber}}, filed in {{countyOfFiling}}: the court's authority under Family Code section 3027 to take temporary protective steps and request an agency investigation, the monetary-sanctions remedy under Family Code section 3027.1 for an accusation later found false and knowingly so, and the reporting protections and false-report limitation under Family Code section 3027.5. It states the text of these statutes and how published California Court of Appeal decisions have described and applied them. It does not state whether any allegation made in this proceeding is true or false, whether a motion for sanctions should be filed or opposed, or what the court is likely to do, and it is not a substitute for advice from a licensed attorney about the facts of a specific matter.

clauses.title: Temporary Protective Steps While an Allegation Is Pending
clauses.body: Family Code section 3027(a) states that if allegations of child abuse, including child sexual abuse, are made during a child custody proceeding and the court has concerns regarding the child's safety, the court may take any reasonable, temporary steps it deems appropriate under the circumstances, in its discretion, to protect the child's safety until an investigation can be completed. The statute states that nothing in the section affects the separate applicability of Welfare and Institutions Code sections 16504 or 16506, which concern child welfare services investigations and case plans.
clauses.gap: The statute does not enumerate what 'reasonable, temporary steps' a court may take, and leaves that choice to the court's discretion under the circumstances of each case; this clause does not predict what steps a court would take in any particular case. It also does not cover subdivision (b) of section 3027, the agency-investigation-referral provision, which is addressed in a separate clause. The statute is triggered by allegations being made and the court having 'concerns regarding the child's safety' — it does not require that the allegation be shown true, or even plausible, before temporary steps may be taken, and it does not state what showing is needed to establish such 'concerns.'

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3027(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a court's authority to take reasonable temporary protective steps when child abuse allegations, including child sexual abuse, arise during a custody proceeding and the court has safety concerns
citations.quote: If allegations of child abuse, including child sexual abuse, are made during a child custody proceeding and the court has concerns regarding the child’s safety, the court may take any reasonable, temporary steps as the court, in its discretion, deems appropriate under the circumstances to protect the child’s safety until an investigation can be completed. Nothing in this section shall affect the applicability of Section 16504 or 16506 of the Welfare and Institutions Code.

clauses.title: The Court's Discretion to Request a Child Welfare Agency Investigation
clauses.body: Family Code section 3027(b) states that if allegations of child abuse, including child sexual abuse, are made during a child custody proceeding, the court may request that the local child welfare services agency conduct an investigation of the allegations under Welfare and Institutions Code section 328, and that upon completing the investigation the agency must report its findings to the court.
clauses.gap: The statute uses 'may request,' not 'must' or 'shall request' — a family court is not required to request an agency investigation merely because an allegation has been made, and this clause does not describe what factors, if any, guide that discretionary choice. It also does not examine Welfare and Institutions Code section 328 itself, which governs the mechanics, timing, or scope of the agency's own investigation once requested. The source statute's official published text line-wraps mid-phrase between 'conduct an investigation of the' and 'allegations pursuant to Section 328' (verified directly against the raw fetched leginfo.legislature.ca.gov HTML, where a literal line break and indentation whitespace appear at that point with no missing or added words); the quote below renders that wrap as a normal single space, consistent with ordinary sentence flow.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3027(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: a court's discretion to request a local child welfare services agency investigation of child abuse allegations made during a custody proceeding, and the agency's duty to report findings
citations.quote: If allegations of child abuse, including child sexual abuse, are made during a child custody proceeding, the court may request that the local child welfare services agency conduct an investigation of the allegations pursuant to Section 328 of the Welfare and Institutions Code. Upon completion of the investigation, the agency shall report its findings to the court.

clauses.title: Sanctions for a Knowingly False Accusation: The Statutory Elements
clauses.body: Family Code section 3027.1(a) states that if a court determines, based on the section 3027 investigation or other evidence presented to it, that an accusation of child abuse or neglect made during a child custody proceeding is false and the person making the accusation knew it to be false when it was made, the court may impose reasonable money sanctions against that person, not to exceed all costs the accused party incurred as a direct result of defending the accusation, plus reasonable attorney's fees incurred in recovering the sanctions. The statute defines 'person' for this purpose to include a witness, a party, or a party's attorney, so the sanctions remedy can reach someone other than the party who was accusing the other party.
clauses.gap: The statute makes a sanctions award discretionary ('may impose'), not automatic, even where a court has found an accusation false and knowingly so — this clause does not describe how courts exercise that discretion. It does not define 'reasonable money sanctions' numerically, and it caps the award at costs actually incurred defending the specific accusation, not general litigation costs in the broader custody case. It also does not cover the false-accusation timing deadline or the order-to-show-cause procedure required to seek these sanctions, each addressed in separate clauses.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.1(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the elements for a discretionary monetary-sanctions award against a person who made a knowingly false child abuse or neglect accusation during a custody proceeding, its cap, and its definition of 'person'
citations.quote: If a court determines, based on the investigation described in Section 3027 or other evidence presented to it, that an accusation of child abuse or neglect made during a child custody proceeding is false and the person making the accusation knew it to be false at the time the accusation was made, the court may impose reasonable money sanctions, not to exceed all costs incurred by the party accused as a direct result of defending the accusation, and reasonable attorney’s fees incurred in recovering the sanctions, against the person making the accusation. For the purposes of this section, “person” includes a witness, a party, or a party’s attorney.

clauses.title: The Order-to-Show-Cause Procedure, 15-Day Notice, and Cumulative Remedy
clauses.body: Family Code section 3027.1(b) states that on motion by any person requesting sanctions under the section, the court must issue an order to show cause why the requested sanctions should not be imposed; that order must be served on the person against whom sanctions are sought, and a hearing on it must be scheduled at least 15 days after the order is served. Section 3027.1(c) states that the remedy the section provides is in addition to any other remedy provided by law, meaning it does not by its terms replace other statutory or common-law remedies that might otherwise be available.
clauses.gap: This clause covers only the procedural mechanics stated in subdivisions (b) and (c); it does not state a deadline for when, relative to the underlying custody proceeding or the judgment resolving the abuse allegation, a section 3027.1 motion must first be filed — the statute itself is silent on that question, which published case law has since addressed and is described in a separate clause. It also does not describe what other remedies subdivision (c)'s 'in addition to any other remedy' language might reach in a given case, or how courts reconcile overlapping sanctions requests under section 3027.1 and other statutes such as section 271. The source statute's official published text line-wraps mid-phrase within subdivision (b), between 'a hearing thereon shall be' and 'scheduled by the court' (verified directly against the raw fetched leginfo.legislature.ca.gov HTML, where a literal line break and indentation whitespace appear at that point with no missing or added words); the quote below renders that wrap as a normal single space.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.1(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the order-to-show-cause procedure and 15-day minimum notice period before a hearing on a section 3027.1 sanctions motion
citations.quote: On motion by any person requesting sanctions under this section, the court shall issue its order to show cause why the requested sanctions should not be imposed. The order to show cause shall be served on the person against whom the sanctions are sought and a hearing thereon shall be scheduled by the court to be conducted at least 15 days after the order is served.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.1(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the section 3027.1 remedy is cumulative, in addition to any other remedy provided by law
citations.quote: The remedy provided by this section is in addition to any other remedy provided by law.

clauses.title: Case Law: A Presumptive Filing Deadline, and Strict Enforcement of the Notice Procedure
clauses.body: Because section 3027.1 does not itself state a deadline for filing a sanctions motion, one published Court of Appeal decision addressed the question as one of first impression. The court held that, absent further direction from the Legislature, equitable principles govern the timing of a section 3027.1 motion, and that a party moving for section 3027.1 sanctions should file the motion on or before the earliest of two dates measured from the judgment or order exonerating that party of the child abuse or neglect allegations: 60 days after that judgment or order is served, or 180 days after it is entered. The court described these deadlines as drawn by analogy from California Rules of Court provisions governing motions for attorney's fees in civil proceedings, which also apply in family law cases; a party who files after these presumptive deadlines bears the burden of showing the delay was excusable and did not unduly prejudice the person the motion is directed against. A second published decision illustrates that the statute's own procedural requirements are enforced strictly: where a party sought section 3027.1 sanctions over an opponent's alleged false abuse allegations but did so within a written closing argument, rather than by the order-to-show-cause procedure with the required 15-day advance notice of a hearing, the Court of Appeal held the trial court correctly declined to award sanctions on that defective request.
clauses.gap: The timing deadline described here comes from a single published Court of Appeal decision (Robert J. v. Catherine D.) applying equitable principles by analogy to civil-fee-motion timing rules; because it was announced as an issue of first impression, that same decision also held its own new procedural rule should not be applied retroactively to the party before it — this clause does not track whether or how later decisions have applied, narrowed, or extended this timing rule, and CourtListener's search index was not queried for every possible later citing case given this document's research budget. The second decision (Niko v. Foreman) denying sanctions for noncompliance with the order-to-show-cause and notice procedure does not establish that a properly noticed section 3027.1 motion filed in a written closing argument would always fail — the court's holding turned on the absence of both a hearing and the statutorily required notice opportunity, not on the closing-argument format standing alone. Neither decision was located through a search for case law interpreting section 3027.5 specifically, and no case law is cited in this document's clauses covering that section for that reason.

citations.case: Robert J. v. Catherine D. (2009) 171 Cal.App.4th 1500
citations.cite: elements of a section 3027.1 sanctions claim, restated by the Court of Appeal
citations.quote: Section 3027.1 gives a court discretion to impose monetary sanctions against a party, the party’s attorney or a witness if the moving party establishes that the accusation of child abuse or neglect was made in a child custody proceeding, the accusation was false and the person or persons making it knew it was false when the accusation was made.

citations.case: Robert J. v. Catherine D. (2009) 171 Cal.App.4th 1500
citations.cite: the presumptive deadline the Court of Appeal established for filing a section 3027.1 sanctions motion
citations.quote: 60 days after the judgment or order exonerating him or her from child abuse or neglect allegations is served, or 180 days from the entry of such judgment or order.

citations.case: Niko v. Foreman (2006) 144 Cal.App.4th 344
citations.cite: the party's own request for section 3027.1 sanctions over the opponent's alleged false abuse allegations
citations.quote: Niko asserts the trial court erred in not awarding sanctions pursuant to sections 3027.1 and 271 based on Foreman’s false allegations of abuse.

citations.case: Niko v. Foreman (2006) 144 Cal.App.4th 344
citations.cite: strict enforcement of section 3027.1's order-to-show-cause and 15-day notice procedure, and the resulting denial of sanctions
citations.quote: Niko was required to serve an OSC regarding section 3027.1 sanctions against Foreman at least 15 days before a scheduled hearing on the matter

clauses.title: Protection for a Parent Who Lawfully Reported or Investigated Suspected Sexual Abuse
clauses.body: Family Code section 3027.5(a) states that a parent must not be placed on supervised visitation, denied custody of or visitation with the parent's child, or have custody or visitation rights limited, solely because that parent lawfully reported suspected sexual abuse of the child; otherwise acted lawfully, based on a reasonable belief, to determine whether the child was a victim of sexual abuse; or sought treatment for the child from a licensed mental health professional for suspected sexual abuse.
clauses.gap: This protection is limited by its own terms to child sexual abuse, not child abuse or neglect generally — sections 3027 and 3027.1, by contrast, apply to 'child abuse or neglect' without that limitation. The statute's protection also applies only where one of the listed acts was the sole reason for the custody or visitation limitation ('solely because'); it does not state how a court is to determine whether a limitation imposed for stated reasons that include, but are not limited to, a listed act falls inside or outside that protection. It does not itself define 'lawfully reported' or what counts as 'a reasonable belief' for the second listed act.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.5(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the bar on placing a parent on supervised visitation or limiting custody or visitation solely because the parent lawfully reported suspected sexual abuse, lawfully investigated it, or sought treatment for the child
citations.quote: A parent shall not be placed on supervised visitation, or be denied custody of or visitation with the parent’s child, and custody or visitation rights shall not be limited, solely because the parent did any of the following: (1) Lawfully reported suspected sexual abuse of the child. (2) Otherwise acted lawfully, based on a reasonable belief, to determine if the child was the victim of sexual abuse. (3) Sought treatment for the child from a licensed mental health professional for suspected sexual abuse.

clauses.title: The Statutory Exception: A Knowingly False Sexual Abuse Report Made to Interfere With the Other Parent
clauses.body: Family Code section 3027.5(b) states the limits of the protection described in subdivision (a): a court may order supervised visitation or limit a parent's custody or visitation if it finds substantial evidence that the parent, intending to interfere with the other parent's lawful contact with the child, made a report of child sexual abuse — during the custody proceeding or at any other time — that the reporting parent knew was false when made. The statute further states that any such limitation, whether imposed under this subdivision or under a different statute addressing a false child abuse report, may be imposed only after the court has determined the limitation is necessary to protect the child's health, safety, and welfare, and only after the court has considered the state's policy, declared in Family Code section 3020(b), of ensuring children have frequent and continuing contact with both parents.
clauses.gap: The statute requires 'substantial evidence' of both the parent's knowledge that the report was false and an intent to interfere with the other parent's lawful contact — it does not define that evidentiary standard for this specific context or state how it compares to the standards used elsewhere in the Family Code, including the 'knew it to be false' standard in section 3027.1. This clause does not describe Family Code section 3020(b)'s text directly (only that section 3027.5(b) cross-references it), and no case law construing section 3027.5(b) was located within this document's CourtListener research budget — the two published decisions cited elsewhere in this document (Robert J. v. Catherine D. and Niko v. Foreman) address section 3027.1, not section 3027.5, and neither was found by a targeted search for section 3027.5 case law.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the substantial-evidence finding required before a court may limit custody or visitation for a knowingly false sexual abuse report made to interfere with the other parent's contact
citations.quote: The court may order supervised visitation or limit a parent’s custody or visitation if the court finds substantial evidence that the parent, with the intent to interfere with the other parent’s lawful contact with the child, made a report of child sexual abuse, during a child custody proceeding or at any other time, that the reporting parent knew was false at the time it was made.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 3027.5(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the required best-interest finding and consideration of the frequent-and-continuing-contact policy before any such limitation, including under a different false-report statute
citations.quote: A limitation of custody or visitation, including an order for supervised visitation, pursuant to this subdivision, or a statute regarding the making of a false child abuse report, shall be imposed only after the court has determined that the limitation is necessary to protect the health, safety, and welfare of the child, and the court has considered the state’s policy of ensuring that children have frequent and continuing contact with both parents as declared in subdivision (b) of Section 3020.

clauses.title: How These Statutes Differ From Related Family Law Topics
clauses.body: These statutes are distinct from several other family-law topics that can arise in the same custody proceeding. They are not the Family Code section 3044 rebuttable presumption against awarding custody to a parent who has perpetrated domestic violence, which turns on a judicial finding of domestic violence rather than on the truth or falsity of an abuse allegation. They are not the mandated-reporter laws under the Child Abuse and Neglect Reporting Act, which impose independent reporting duties on certain professionals regardless of any custody proceeding. They are not a domestic violence restraining order or a civil harassment restraining order, which are separate proceedings with their own statutory standards. And a section 3027.1 sanctions motion is not the same statute as a Family Code section 271 sanctions motion for litigation conduct that furthers or frustrates settlement, though the two are sometimes sought together, as illustrated by the case law discussed elsewhere in this document.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California Military and Veterans Code section 394, a state statute that prohibits discrimination against a member of the military or naval forces of California or of the United States because of that membership, and that separately prohibits an employer from discharging, hindering, or otherwise penalizing an employee for performing ordered military duty, training, or drill, or for enlisting or accepting a warrant or commission in the California National Guard, State Guard, Naval Militia, or a federal reserve component. Section 394 applies to private employers as well as to state and local government employers; a violation is a misdemeanor and also gives rise to a civil claim for actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. This document does not cover section 394's separate provisions addressing a uniformed member's access to public entertainment or places of amusement (subdivision (c)) or lending and financing discrimination (subdivision (f)), and it does not cover the temporary military leave-of-absence, salary-continuation, and reinstatement provisions found elsewhere in the same statutory chapter (Military and Veterans Code sections 395 through 395.08, 395.1, and 395.3), which by their own terms apply only to public employees and public agencies, not to private-sector employment. Federal reemployment and leave rights connected to military service for private-sector employees are instead addressed under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA), described in this corpus's separate USERRA information sheet.

clauses.title: General Prohibition on Discrimination Because of Military Membership
clauses.body: Under Military and Veterans Code section 394(a), a person may not discriminate against a member of the military or naval forces of the state or of the United States because of that membership, and a member of the military forces may not be prejudiced or injured by a person, employer, or officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm in the terms, conditions, or privileges of that member's employment, position, or status, or be denied or disqualified for employment, by virtue of membership or service in the military forces of this state or of the United States.
clauses.gap: Subdivision (a)'s own text does not define what conduct counts as "discriminate," "prejudiced," or "injured," does not list any example of a prohibited or permitted employment decision, and does not state any employer-size threshold or exemption. It also does not itself create a remedy or private right of action; the misdemeanor penalty and civil damages/attorney's-fees remedy are supplied by a different subsection, (g), described in a separate clause of this document. This document does not determine whether any specific employer decision or practice would meet subdivision (a)'s standard.

citations.case: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(a), general prohibition on discrimination because of membership in the military or naval forces
citations.quote: (a) A person shall not discriminate against a member of the military or naval forces of the state or of the United States because of that membership. A member of the military forces shall not be prejudiced or injured by a person, employer, or officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm in terms, conditions, or privileges with respect to that member’s employment, position or status or be denied or disqualified for employment by virtue of membership or service in the military forces of this state or of the United States.

clauses.title: Parallel Prohibition Specifically Naming State and Local Government Employers
clauses.body: Under Military and Veterans Code section 394(b), an officer or employee of the state, or of any county, city and county, municipal corporation, or district, may not discriminate against a member of the military or naval forces of the state or of the United States because of that membership, and a member of the military forces may not be prejudiced or injured by such an officer or employee in the terms, conditions, or privileges of that member's employment, appointment, position, or status, or be denied, disqualified, or discharged from that employment or position by virtue of membership or service in the military forces.
clauses.gap: Subdivision (b) uses different wording from subdivision (a): it names "an officer or employee of the state, or of any county, city and county, municipal corporation, or district" as the regulated actor, rather than subdivision (a)'s broader "a person, employer, or officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm." The statute's text does not state whether subdivisions (a) and (b) are meant to be mutually exclusive or overlapping as applied to a government employer, and this document does not resolve that overlap question. Subdivision (b) also does not itself state a remedy; like subdivision (a), it relies on subdivision (g) for the misdemeanor penalty and civil damages/attorney's-fees claim.

citations.case: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(b), parallel prohibition naming state and local government officers and employees
citations.quote: (b) An officer or employee of the state, or of any county, city and county, municipal corporation, or district shall not discriminate against a member of the military or naval forces of the state or of the United States because of that membership. A member of the military forces shall not be prejudiced or injured by an officer or employee of the state, or of any county, city and county, municipal corporation, or district in terms, conditions, or privileges with respect to that member’s employment, appointment, position, or status or be denied or disqualified for or discharged from that employment or position by virtue of membership or service in the military forces of this state or of the United States.

clauses.title: Protection From Discharge or Hindrance for Performing Military Duty
clauses.body: Under Military and Veterans Code section 394(d), an employer, or an officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm, or other person, may not discharge a person from employment because of the performance of ordered military duty or training, or because of membership in the military or naval forces of the state or the federal reserve components of the Armed Forces, and may not hinder or prevent a person from performing military service or from attending a military encampment, drill, or instruction the person is called upon to attend, or prejudice or harm the person in the terms, conditions, or privileges of employment for doing so. The same subdivision separately prohibits dissuading, preventing, or stopping a person from enlisting or accepting a warrant or commission in the California National Guard, State Guard, or Naval Militia, or a federal reserve component, by threatening injury to the person's employment terms, status, trade, or business.
clauses.gap: Subdivision (d)'s text does not define "ordered military duty," does not state a maximum number of protected days (contrast the separate 180-calendar-day cap that section 395(a) places on a public employee's temporary military leave of absence, described in a separate clause of this document, which section 394(d) does not reference or incorporate), and does not itself describe a complaint or reinstatement procedure. It also does not state whether the discharge or hindrance must be the sole reason for the adverse action or merely a substantial or motivating factor; this document does not resolve that question from the statutory text alone.

citations.case: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(d) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(d), protection from discharge or hindrance for performing military duty or seeking to enlist
citations.quote: (d) An employer or officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm, or other person, shall not discharge a person from employment because of the performance of any ordered military duty or training or by reason of being a member of the military or naval forces of this state or of the federal reserve components of the Armed Forces of the United States, or hinder or prevent that person from performing any military service or from attending any military encampment or place of drill or instruction the person may be called upon to perform or attend by proper authority; prejudice or harm the person in any manner in the person’s terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, position, or status by reason of performance of military service or duty or attendance at military encampments or places of drill or instruction; or dissuade, prevent, or stop any person from enlistment or accepting a warrant or commission in the California National Guard, State Guard, or Naval Militia or the federal reserve components of the Armed Forces of the United States by threat or injury to the person in respect to the person’s terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, position, status, trade, or business because of enlistment or acceptance of a warrant or commission.

clauses.title: Protection of Collateral Benefits During Temporary Incapacitation Incident to Duty
clauses.body: Under Military and Veterans Code section 394(e)(1), a private employer, or an officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm, or other person, may not restrict or terminate an employee's collateral benefit because of the employee's temporary incapacitation incident to duty in the National Guard, State Guard, Naval Militia, or a federal reserve component, where "temporary incapacitation" is defined as any period of incapacitation of 52 weeks or less. Section 394(e)(2) defines "benefit" for purposes of this subdivision to include, but not be limited to, health care (which may be continued at the employee's expense), life insurance, disability insurance, and seniority status.
clauses.gap: Subdivision (e)(1) is worded to reach a "private employer," a narrower category than the "person" language of subdivision (a) or the state/local-government language of subdivision (b); this document does not determine whether subdivision (e) also reaches state or local government employers by virtue of subdivisions (a) or (b) applying more broadly, because subdivision (e)'s own text does not say so. The 52-week definition of "temporary incapacitation" means an incapacitation lasting longer than 52 weeks falls outside this specific protection, and the statute's text does not state what protection, if any, applies beyond that point. Subdivision (e)(2)'s statement that health care "may be continued at the employee's expense" means the employer is not shown by this text to be required to pay the premium, only to permit continued coverage; the statute does not describe the continuation mechanism (for example, whether it resembles COBRA continuation) in any further detail.

citations.case: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(e)(1) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(e)(1), protection of collateral benefits during temporary incapacitation incident to duty
citations.quote: (e) (1) A private employer or officer or agent of a corporation, company, or firm, or other person, shall not restrict or terminate any collateral benefit for employees by reason of an employee’s temporary incapacitation incident to duty in the National Guard, State Guard, or Naval Militia or the federal reserve components of the Armed Forces of the United States. As used in this subdivision, “temporary incapacitation” means any period of incapacitation of 52 weeks or less.

citations.case: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(e)(2) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(e)(2), definition of "benefit" for purposes of subdivision (e)
citations.quote: (2) As used in this subdivision, “benefit” includes, but is not limited to, health care which may be continued at the employee’s expense, life insurance, disability insurance, and seniority status.

clauses.title: Misdemeanor Penalty, Civil Damages, and Non-Exclusive Remedies
clauses.body: Under Military and Veterans Code section 394(g), a person who violates section 394 is guilty of a misdemeanor, and a person who violates any provision of the section is also liable for actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees incurred by the injured party. Section 394(h) states that the remedies provided in section 394 are not intended to be exclusive, but are in addition to remedies provided in other laws, including Civil Code sections 51 and 52.
clauses.gap: Subdivision (g)'s text does not state a limitations period for the civil damages claim, does not name the court in which such a claim may be brought, does not describe a filing or notice procedure, and does not state whether "actual damages" includes noneconomic loss such as emotional distress or only economic loss. The subdivision also does not describe how a misdemeanor prosecution would be initiated, since criminal charges are ordinarily brought by a public prosecutor rather than the injured employee; section 394's text does not itself address that mechanic. Subdivision (h)'s cross-reference to Civil Code sections 51 and 52 is stated without elaborating what additional remedy those sections would add in an employment context beyond what section 394 itself provides, and this document does not independently verify Civil Code sections 51 and 52 here.

citations.case: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(g) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(g), misdemeanor penalty and civil damages/attorney's-fees remedy
citations.quote: (g) A person violating this section is guilty of a misdemeanor. In addition, a person violating any of the provisions of this section shall be liable for actual damages and reasonable attorney’s fees incurred by the injured party.

citations.case: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(h) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 394(h), remedies not exclusive, cumulative with other laws
citations.quote: (h) The remedies provided for in this section are not intended to be exclusive but are in addition to the remedies provided for in other laws, including Sections 51 and 52 of the Civil Code.

clauses.title: Only the Employer, Not Individual Supervisors, May Be Held Liable Under Section 394
clauses.body: In Haligowski v. Superior Court, 200 Cal. App. 4th 983 (2011), the California Court of Appeal held, as a matter of first impression, that although section 394(g) attaches liability to "a person" who violates the section, an employee who is subject to military duty or training that interrupts their work may hold their employer liable for discrimination or retaliation in violation of section 394, but may not hold an individual supervisor personally liable for acts arising out of the performance of normal management duties. The court reasoned that section 394's use of "person" is analogous to the California Fair Employment and Housing Act's use of "employer," which California courts have likewise construed not to impose individual liability on supervisors for ordinary personnel-management decisions.
clauses.gap: This document read only Haligowski v. Superior Court in full; a CourtListener keyword search for "Military and Veterans Code" section 394 employment discrimination in California courts returned four results, and the other three (Del Monte v. Wilson, Kopp v. Fair Political Practices Commission, and In re Cox) were not read or relied on here, so this document does not state whether or how those decisions discuss section 394. The search was a single keyword search rather than a citator or cited-by analysis, so this document cannot rule out other published California appellate decisions on section 394 that did not match the search terms used. The California Supreme Court denied review of Haligowski (noted in the opinion itself), which means Haligowski remains a published, citable Court of Appeal decision, but denial of review does not itself signify Supreme Court endorsement of the reasoning, only a decision not to review it. This document does not address whether the same employer-only, not-individual, liability rule would apply to a claim brought under section 394(a) or (b) alone rather than the discharge/hindrance claim actually before the Haligowski court.

citations.case: Haligowski v. Superior Court, 200 Cal. App. 4th 983 (2011)
citations.cite: Haligowski v. Superior Court, 200 Cal. App. 4th 983, 996 (2d Dist. 2011)
citations.quote: Plaintiffs who are subject to military duty or training that interrupts their work may hold their employers, but not individuals, liable for discrimination in violation of section 394. The plaintiff employee’s target remains the employer.

clauses.title: Scope Limit: The Chapter's Leave-of-Absence and Reinstatement Provisions Apply Only to Public Employees
clauses.body: Section 394 sits within the same statutory chapter (Military and Veterans Code, Division 2, Part 1, Chapter 7) as a separate group of sections, beginning with section 395(a), that grant a temporary military leave of absence and a right of reinstatement. Unlike section 394's antidiscrimination language, section 395(a) is worded to cover only a "public employee": it entitles a public employee who is a member of the reserve corps of the Armed Forces, the National Guard, or the Naval Militia to a temporary military leave of absence, as provided by federal law, for ordered duty not exceeding 180 calendar days including travel time.
clauses.gap: This document independently fetched and double-verified (with two different User-Agent strings) only section 394 in full and section 395(a) in full; it separately fetched the full text of the entire chapter (sections 389 through 399.5) in one additional request, used only to identify section numbers and to confirm, from each section's own opening sentence, that sections 395.01 through 395.08, 395.1, and 395.3 all likewise use "public employee," "public officer," or "public agency" language. That single-fetch chapter read was not independently double-fetched or re-verified word-for-word the way section 394 and section 395(a) were, so this document does not quote those later sections and does not assert their complete or current content beyond the opening-sentence phrasing observed. This document does not identify what "as provided by federal law" in section 395(a) refers to, and does not state whether any state-law leave-of-absence or reinstatement right, parallel to section 395, exists for a private-sector employee outside of section 394 itself; private-sector federal reemployment rights connected to military service are addressed separately under USERRA in this corpus's USERRA information sheet, which this document does not restate.

citations.case: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 395(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: Cal. Mil. & Vet. Code § 395(a), public-employee temporary military leave of absence, 180-calendar-day cap
citations.quote: (a) Any public employee who is a member of the reserve corps of the Armed Forces of the United States or of the National Guard or the Naval Militia is entitled to a temporary military leave of absence as provided by federal law while engaged in military duty ordered for purposes of active military training, inactive duty training, encampment, naval cruises, special exercises, or like activity, providing that the period of ordered duty does not exceed 180 calendar days, including time involved in going to and returning from that duty.

clauses.title: Military Status Discrimination or Retaliation — Incident Record
Acknowledgment
Purpose and Parties: Boundary Trees
clauses.body:
{{party1Name}}, the owner of the real property located at {{party1PropertyAddress}} ("Party One"), and {{party2Name}}, the owner of the adjoining real property located at {{party2PropertyAddress}} ("Party Two"), are owners of adjoining parcels of real property in {{county}}, California. This document concerns the following tree or trees: {{treeShrubDescription}}.

This document states facts about California law addressing who owns a tree growing on or near the boundary between two adjoining properties, the circumstances under which an adjoining landowner may trim back branches or roots that cross onto that landowner's own property, and the civil penalty California's Civil Code imposes for a wrongful injury to another's timber, trees, or underwood. It draws on Civil Code Sections 833, 834, and 3346, and on a published California Court of Appeal decision, Booska v. Patel (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 1786, that discusses the scope of a landowner's right to trim encroaching growth. This document states facts about that law; it does not tell Party One or Party Two what to do about the specific tree or trees described above, and it does not evaluate whether either party's conduct toward those trees is or was reasonable, authorized, or a trespass.

clauses.title: Ownership of a Tree Whose Trunk Stands Wholly on One Owner's Land
clauses.body: California's Civil Code states a rule for trees whose trunk stands entirely within the boundary of a single owner's land: that owner owns the tree exclusively, even though the tree's roots may grow into a neighboring owner's land. The statute expresses this as a rule of exclusive ownership tied to the location of the trunk specifically, not the roots or any overhanging branches. This section has not been amended since its original enactment in 1872, and its text still uses the gender-specific pronoun "him" from that original enactment rather than gender-neutral language.
clauses.gap: Civil Code Section 833 is a single, one-sentence statute; its fetched text does not itself define what counts as a tree's "trunk," does not address a trunk that grows across a boundary line rather than standing wholly on one side of it (a circumstance the companion statute quoted in this document's next clause, Section 834, separately addresses), and does not itself state any remedy for wrongful injury to a tree it identifies as belonging to one owner (a separate topic addressed by Civil Code Section 3346, quoted elsewhere in this document). This clause states only what the statute's text says about ownership; it does not evaluate whether a specific tree's trunk in fact stands wholly on one side of a specific boundary.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 833
citations.cite: California Civil Code, ownership of a tree whose trunk stands wholly on one owner's land
citations.quote: Trees whose trunks stand wholly upon the land of one owner belong exclusively to him, although their roots grow into the land of another.

clauses.title: Common Ownership of a Tree Standing on the Boundary Itself
clauses.body: A separate, adjoining Civil Code section addresses a different situation from the one described in this document's preceding clause: a tree whose trunk stands partly on the land of two or more adjoining ("coterminous") owners. For that situation, the statute states that the tree belongs to those owners in common, rather than exclusively to either one of them. A published California Court of Appeal decision, Booska v. Patel, later described this same basic distinction in its own words while resolving an unrelated dispute about root-cutting, characterizing boundary-line trees as "jointly owned by the neighbors" and contrasting that with a tree whose trunk stands solely on one owner's property.
clauses.gap: Civil Code Section 834's text states that a boundary-line tree belongs to the coterminous owners "in common" but does not itself specify the proportion of that common ownership (for example, whether it is necessarily equal between two owners, or apportioned some other way), and does not define "coterminous." The Booska v. Patel passage quoted here is the Court of Appeal's own paraphrase of a distinction it attributes to two older cases, Anderson v. Weiland (1936) 12 Cal.App.2d 730 and Scarborough v. Woodill (1907) 7 Cal.App. 39; neither of those two older cases was independently fetched or verified in this research, and Booska's own opinion text does not cite Civil Code Section 833 or Section 834 by number — this document treats the Booska passage as case-law corroboration of the same substantive distinction the statute draws, using different wording ("jointly owned" rather than the statute's "belong to them in common"), not as a citation to either statute. This clause does not evaluate whether a specific tree's trunk in fact stands on a boundary line.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 834
citations.cite: California Civil Code, common ownership of a tree whose trunk stands on the boundary between two or more owners' land
citations.quote: Trees whose trunks stand partly on the land of two or more coterminous owners, belong to them in common.

citations.case: Booska v. Patel (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 1786, 1791, fn. 4
citations.cite: California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, describing the boundary-tree/solely-owned-tree distinction
citations.quote: Patel notes a difference in the legal treatment of trees growing on a boundary line and trees entirely on the property of one owner which overhang the property of another. The only difference, however, seems to be that the boundary line trees are deemed to be jointly owned by the neighbors, while the tree with a trunk solely on the property of one belongs to that one.

clauses.title: The Right to Trim Encroaching Branches or Roots, and Its Limits
clauses.body: In Booska v. Patel, the California Court of Appeal addressed a dispute in which one landowner had hired a contractor to sever the roots of a neighbor's tree that had grown into his yard, and the trial court had granted the landowner summary judgment on the theory that landowners have an unqualified, absolute right to sever any encroaching roots from their own property. The Court of Appeal described the origin of that "absolute right" language in an earlier case, Bonde v. Bishop (1952) 112 Cal.App.2d 1, which had stated that a landowner may remove encroaching portions of a neighbor's tree whether or not they cause damage, without first needing to sue and prove the encroachment is a nuisance. But the Booska court held that this right is not unlimited: after reviewing secondary authorities and other California cases addressing a landowner's duty to manage property reasonably, the court concluded that a landowner's rights in managing tree roots or branches on the landowner's own property are tempered by a duty to act reasonably, and it reversed the summary judgment because triable issues of fact existed about whether the specific conduct at issue had been reasonable.
clauses.gap: Booska v. Patel is a published Court of Appeal (First Appellate District) decision; its own closing lines state that a petition for rehearing was denied and that the California Supreme Court denied a petition for review, meaning the decision became final without merits review by the Supreme Court. Booska reversed a summary judgment because triable issues of fact existed; it did not itself decide whether the defendant's actual conduct was or was not reasonable, and it does not state a numeric or bright-line test for what counts as reasonable management of encroaching roots or branches. The quoted "absolute right" language is Booska's own quotation of the earlier case Bonde v. Bishop (1952) 112 Cal.App.2d 1, 6; Bonde itself was not independently fetched or verified in this research, only Booska's verbatim quotation of it as it appears within Booska's own fetched opinion text. This case-law source was retrieved once via the CourtListener MCP tool (not the dual-User-Agent raw HTTP fetch method used elsewhere in this document for the leginfo.legislature.ca.gov statutory sources); CourtListener's plain_text field for this opinion was empty, so its html_with_citations field was used and searched directly for the quoted text.

citations.case: Booska v. Patel (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 1786, 1789, quoting Bonde v. Bishop (1952) 112 Cal.App.2d 1, 6
citations.cite: California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, on the scope of the right to remove encroaching tree growth
citations.quote: While it is the absolute right of a landowner to remove those portions of trees which encroach on his land whether they cause damage or not, it is rather anomalous that to obtain court help in the matter he must first prove that the encroachment constitutes a nuisance.

citations.case: Booska v. Patel (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 1786, 1791
citations.cite: California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, holding the right to manage encroaching growth is tempered by a duty of reasonableness
citations.quote: Thus, whatever rights Patel has in the management of his own land, those rights are tempered by his duty to act reasonably.

clauses.title: A Co-Owner's Limits Regarding a Jointly Owned Boundary Tree
clauses.body: Booska v. Patel's discussion of boundary-line trees, described elsewhere in this document, continues with a further point drawn from two older California cases: because a boundary-line tree is jointly owned by the adjoining owners, one of those co-owners does not have the unilateral right to destroy the tree. The Court of Appeal described this as subject to a duty on each of the joint owners to use their own part of the tree in a way that does not unreasonably injure or destroy the whole of it.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Booska v. Patel's own statement of this rule, drawn from footnote 4 of its opinion; that footnote in turn attributes the rule to two older California cases, Anderson v. Weiland (1936) 12 Cal.App.2d 730 and Scarborough v. Woodill (1907) 7 Cal.App. 39, neither of which was independently fetched or verified in this research — this clause relies only on Booska's own quotation and characterization of them. The raw HTML fetched from CourtListener for this passage contains an unusual character (an asterisk) immediately before the ellipsis in the sentence "subject to the duty of both owners to ‘ *. . .so use his part as not unreasonably to injure or destroy the whole.’ ”"; this was verified directly in the fetched html_with_citations field and appears to be a rendering or OCR artifact from the underlying source rather than a substantive part of the quoted sentence, so this clause's citation begins its quotation after that character and the ellipsis, from "so use his part," rather than reproducing the ambiguous leading character. This passage is part of the Court of Appeal's published opinion responding to an argument the appellee made in that case; it is not part of the case's core holding, which concerned triable issues of fact on summary judgment over a different, solely-owned tree's roots. This clause does not evaluate what remedy (for example, an action for partition, injunction, or damages) is available to a co-owner of a jointly owned tree, or address Civil Code Section 3346's penal-damages provision, described in a separate clause, as applied to a dispute between co-owners of the same tree.
