citations.cite: California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, on a co-owner's lack of unilateral right to destroy a jointly owned boundary tree
citations.quote: The boundary line cases state that one co-owner does not have the right to destroy the trees

citations.case: Booska v. Patel (1994) 24 Cal.App.4th 1786, 1791, fn. 4, quoting Anderson v. Weiland (1936) 12 Cal.App.2d 730 and Scarborough v. Woodill (1907) 7 Cal.App. 39
citations.cite: California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, on each co-owner's duty regarding a jointly owned boundary tree
citations.quote: so use his part as not unreasonably to injure or destroy the whole

clauses.title: Treble and Double Damages for Wrongful Injury to Trees, and the Five-Year Limitations Period
clauses.body: California's Civil Code sets a specific, elevated measure of damages for a wrongful injury to "timber, trees, or underwood" on another person's land, or the wrongful removal of it. As a default rule, the statute sets the measure of damages at three times the sum that would compensate for the actual detriment. The statute reduces that multiplier in two specified situations: to twice the actual detriment where the trespass was casual or involuntary, or where the defendant had probable cause to believe the land was the defendant's own (or the land of a person the defendant was acting for); and, in a narrower situation involving wood taken by highway officers to repair a public highway or bridge, to a sum equal to the actual detriment only, with no multiplier. The same statute separately states that an action for these damages must be commenced within five years from the date of the trespass.
clauses.gap: The raw HTML fetched from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov for this section contains a mid-phrase line wrap in two places, verified directly against the fetched HTML using two different User-Agent strings whose results matched exactly: within subdivision (a), between "the authority of" and "highway officers," and within subdivision (c), between "Any action" and "for the damages." Both are rendered here as ordinary single spaces rather than as the literal line breaks present in the source markup, consistent with this being a source formatting artifact rather than a substantive gap in the sentence. This clause quotes subdivisions (a) and (c) of Section 3346 as two citations from the same statutory section, not as independent sources. Section 3346(a) applies to "timber, trees, or underwood" generally; its own text is not limited to boundary trees specifically and does not cross-reference Civil Code Sections 833 or 834, and its own text does not define "wrongful" or address how it interacts with the encroachment-trimming right described elsewhere in this document. Section 3346(b), which reduces the damages multiplier in a specific boundary-survey situation, is addressed in a separate clause of this document. Section 3346(c)'s own text states that its five-year period runs "from the date of the trespass" but does not itself address any discovery-rule tolling or define what counts as the relevant trespass date where a tree's decline or death from a root- or branch-cutting event becomes apparent only sometime after the cutting itself. This clause does not evaluate whether a specific injury to a specific tree is "wrongful," or whether any particular claim would be timely.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3346(a)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, measure of damages for wrongful injury to timber, trees, or underwood
citations.quote: For wrongful injuries to timber, trees, or underwood upon the land of another, or removal thereof, the measure of damages is three times such sum as would compensate for the actual detriment, except that where the trespass was casual or involuntary, or that the defendant in any action brought under this section had probable cause to believe that the land on which the trespass was committed was his own or the land of the person in whose service or by whose direction the act was done, the measure of damages shall be twice the sum as would compensate for the actual detriment, and excepting further that where the wood was taken by the authority of highway officers for the purpose of repairing a public highway or bridge upon the land or adjoining it, in which case judgment shall only be given in a sum equal to the actual detriment.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3346(c)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, five-year limitations period for damages under this section
citations.quote: Any action for the damages specified by subdivisions (a) and (b) of this section must be commenced within five years from the date of the trespass.

clauses.title: Reduced Damages Where a Trespass Relied on a Licensed Boundary Survey
clauses.body: Civil Code Section 3346 states a further, separate exception from the treble- or double-damages measure described elsewhere in this document. Where a trespass onto another's land (including a trespass injuring trees) was committed in reliance on a survey of boundary lines that improperly fixed the location of a boundary, the statute limits the measure of damages to the actual detriment incurred, but only if two specific conditions both exist: the trespass must have been committed by a defendant who either personally procured the survey, or whose principal, lessor, or immediate predecessor in title procured it; and the survey itself must have been made by a person licensed under California law to practice land surveying.
clauses.gap: This exception applies only if both of Section 3346(b)'s stated conditions are met; its own text does not define "procured," does not address a survey performed by someone other than a person licensed to practice land surveying (for example, a civil engineer performing boundary-related work), and does not state what measure of damages applies if a trespass relied on an unlicensed or informal survey instead. This clause quotes the full text of subdivision (b) as fetched; it does not evaluate whether a specific survey or a specific party's reliance on it would satisfy either of the two stated conditions.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 3346(b)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, reduced damages where a trespass relied on a licensed boundary survey
citations.quote: The measure of damages to be assessed against a defendant for any trespass committed while acting in reliance upon a survey of boundary lines which improperly fixes the location of a boundary line, shall be the actual detriment incurred if both of the following conditions exist:(1) The trespass was committed by a defendant who either himself procured, or whose principal, lessor, or immediate predecessor in title procured the survey to be made; and(2) The survey was made by a person licensed under the laws of this State to practice land surveying.

clauses.title: Boundary Tree Factual Record
Purpose of This Life Estate Deed Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Information Sheet describes a deed reserving a life estate — a form of property conveyance recognized under California's Civil Code by which an owner of real property conveys a remainder interest in that property to another person now, while the transferor keeps the exclusive right to possess and use the property for the rest of the transferor's life. It is a different instrument from a revocable transfer-on-death deed and from a living trust, both of which this corpus describes in separate documents. This Information Sheet concerns a deed by {{grantorName}}, reserving a life estate, conveying a remainder interest in the real property located at {{propertyAddress}}, described as {{legalDescription}}, to {{granteeName}}. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing California statutes and reported case law about life estates; it is not a deed, a legal opinion, or advice about whether reserving a life estate is an appropriate way to convey any specific property, or about the tax, Medi-Cal, or other consequences for {{grantorName}} or {{granteeName}} of doing so.

clauses.title: Life Estates as a Recognized Category of Real Property Estate
clauses.body: California's Civil Code classifies every estate in real property, by the duration of its enjoyment, into one of four categories. A life estate — an estate lasting for the duration of someone's life — is one of those four listed categories, distinct from an estate of inheritance (a fee simple, which lasts perpetually), an estate for years (a lease), or an estate at will.
clauses.gap: The statutory text itself contains a formatting oddity that this clause preserves rather than silently corrects: the first item in the list is numbered with a lowercase letter “l.” rather than the numeral “1.” in the version currently published by the California Legislative Information website (verified directly against the raw fetched HTML, which renders the same character both times the section was fetched). This clause lists the four categories the statute names; it does not itself state what rights or duties attach to a life estate specifically (addressed in other clauses of this document), and it does not address how a life estate is created by a particular deed.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 761
citations.cite: California Civil Code, the four durational categories of estates in real property
citations.quote: Estates in real property, in respect to the duration of their enjoyment are either: l. Estates of inheritance or perpetual estates; 2. Estates for life; 3. Estates for years; or, 4. Estates at will.

clauses.title: A Life Estate's Classification as a Freehold Estate
clauses.body: California law places a life estate in the same broader classification as a fee simple estate: both are “estates of freehold,” a classification distinct from a lease (a “chattel real”) or a tenancy at will (a “chattel interest”).
clauses.gap: This clause is definitional and classificatory only. It does not itself state what rights, duties, or remedies attach to a freehold estate beyond this durational classification — those are addressed, for a life estate specifically, in other clauses of this document — and it does not address recording, tax, or Medi-Cal consequences of holding or creating a freehold estate.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 765
citations.cite: California Civil Code, freehold classification of estates of inheritance and for life
citations.quote: Estates of inheritance and for life are called estates of freehold; estates for years are chattels real; and estates at will are chattel interests, but are not subject to enforcement of a money judgment.

clauses.title: Why a Deed Must Expressly Reserve a Life Estate
clauses.body: A deed's default legal effect in California is to convey the fee simple — full ownership — of the property it describes. California law presumes that a fee simple title is intended to pass by any grant of real property, unless the grant itself shows that a lesser estate, such as a life estate, was intended. A deed meant to reserve a life estate to the grantor while conveying only a remainder interest to the grantee must therefore say so on its face.
clauses.gap: This presumption in § 1105 applies to any grant of real property, not only to one attempting to reserve a life estate; this clause does not evaluate whether the wording of any particular deed — including the deed described in this document — achieves an effective reservation of a life estate, and it does not address other formalities a deed also requires, such as execution, acknowledgment, or recording, which this corpus addresses in its Grant Deed document.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1105
citations.cite: California Civil Code, fee-simple title presumed from a grant
citations.quote: A fee simple title is presumed to be intended to pass by a grant of real property, unless it appears from the grant that a lesser estate was intended.

clauses.title: The Life Tenant's Statutory Duty to Maintain the Property and Pay Taxes
clauses.body: While a life estate is in effect, California law places two ongoing statutory obligations on the life tenant: to keep the buildings and fences on the property in repair from ordinary wear (which the statute calls “ordinary waste”), and to pay the property taxes and other annual charges, along with a just proportion of any extraordinary assessment that benefits the whole inheritance.
clauses.gap: This clause describes only the two obligations stated in this particular section. Section 840 does not itself specify who, as between the life tenant and the remainderman, bears the cost of extraordinary repairs, capital improvements, or insurance, and it does not itself state what remedy is available to a remainderman if a life tenant fails to meet these duties; this document does not address those separate questions.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 840
citations.cite: California Civil Code, life tenant's duty to repair and pay taxes
citations.quote: The owner of a life estate must keep the buildings and fences in repair from ordinary waste, and must pay the taxes and other annual charges, and a just proportion of extraordinary assessments benefiting the whole inheritance.

clauses.title: The Life Tenant's Use of the Property, and the Limit Against Injuring the Inheritance
clauses.body: California law gives a life tenant broad freedom to use the property in the same manner an owner of a fee simple could, subject to one express statutory limit: the life tenant must do no act to the injury of “the inheritance” — the remainder interest that will pass to the remainderman when the life estate ends. Applying this section, a California Court of Appeal has held that whether a particular act amounts to such an injury turns on whether it results in a substantial depreciation of the property's market value, and that the burden of proving that depreciation rests on the remainderman bringing the claim.
clauses.gap: Sallee v. Daneri is a single intermediate appellate decision (Third Appellate District, decided January 1942); the California Supreme Court denied a petition for hearing, which leaves this Court of Appeal decision, not a Supreme Court opinion, as the controlling authority quoted here. The case itself involved a dispute over cutting timber and deteriorated farm buildings on agricultural land; this clause does not claim the same market-value-depreciation test would be applied identically to every other kind of act on every kind of property, and § 818 itself does not define “inheritance” or “injury.” This clause does not evaluate whether any specific act by any specific life tenant would constitute an injury to the inheritance.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 818
citations.cite: California Civil Code, life tenant's use of the property and the limit against injury to the inheritance
citations.quote: The owner of a life estate may use the land in the same manner as the owner of a fee simple, except that he must do no act to the injury of the inheritance.

citations.case: Sallee v. Daneri
citations.quote: The burden of proving depreciation in market value of the land, as a result of the alleged wrongful acts of waste rests upon the remainderman, who must establish that fact by satisfactory evidence, even though a life tenant may not use what might appear to be the best of care in the cultivation and care of the property.

clauses.title: How a Deed Reserving a Life Estate Differs From a Revocable Transfer-on-Death Deed
clauses.body: This corpus describes California's revocable transfer-on-death deed in a separate document. A deed reserving a life estate is a different kind of instrument: once it is executed and delivered, it is a present conveyance that immediately vests a remainder interest in the named remainderman — here, {{granteeName}} — rather than a transfer that takes effect only at the transferor's death and that the transferor may revoke unilaterally at any time before then, as a revocable transfer-on-death deed does. Changing or undoing a deed reserving a life estate after it has been delivered and accepted generally calls for a new conveyance signed by whoever then holds the remainder interest, rather than a unilateral act by the life tenant alone.

clauses.title: Property Tax Change-in-Ownership Treatment of Creating and Ending a Life Estate
clauses.body: For purposes of California's property tax reassessment rules, creating a life estate is treated differently from ending one. A transfer made by an instrument whose terms reserve to the transferor an estate for life is, by that reservation alone, excluded from the definition of a “change in ownership” that would otherwise trigger reassessment. California law separately provides that when that life estate later terminates, the termination itself does constitute a change in ownership, subject to certain other statutory exceptions.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (e) of Revenue and Taxation Code § 62, a section with many other subdivisions addressing other kinds of transfers not described here. Subdivision (e) itself cross-references subdivision (d) and Section 63 as containing further exceptions to the termination-is-a-change-in-ownership rule; this clause does not quote or describe the content of subdivision (d) or Section 63, and it does not determine the reassessed value or resulting tax consequence for any specific property.

citations.case: Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 62(e)
citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, change-in-ownership treatment of an instrument reserving an estate for life
citations.quote: (e) Any transfer by an instrument whose terms reserve to the transferor an estate for years or an estate for life. However, the termination of such an estate for years or estate for life shall constitute a change in ownership, except as provided in subdivision (d) and in Section 63.

clauses.title: Recording an Affidavit of Death to Reflect the End of a Life Estate
clauses.body: When a life tenant dies, the remainder interest that a deed reserving a life estate already vested in the remainderman does not pass through probate. California law provides a mechanism to place the fact of that death on the public record for the property: any person may record, in the county where the property is located, an affidavit of death — executed by a person with knowledge of the facts, including a particular description of the real property and an attested or certified copy of the death record — establishing that title to the property was affected by a death.
clauses.gap: Probate Code § 210 applies broadly to any situation in which title to real property is affected by a death — it is the same statutory mechanism used, for example, to record an affidavit of death of a joint tenant — and is not written specifically for a life estate; no separate Probate Code section addresses life estates alone. This clause quotes only subdivision (a) of § 210; subdivision (b), not quoted here, separately allows recording a certified copy of a court order determining the fact of death under Probate Code Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 200) or another statute. Recording an affidavit of death under this section does not itself resolve any dispute about the validity of the original deed reserving the life estate or about who holds the remainder interest.

citations.case: Cal. Prob. Code § 210(a)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, recording an affidavit of death to establish that title to real property was affected by a death
citations.quote: If title to real property is affected by the death of a person, any person may record in the county in which the property is located any of the following documents establishing the fact of the death: (a) An affidavit of death executed by a person having knowledge of the facts.

clauses.title: Signature and Acknowledgment — Life Estate Deed Information Sheet
Purpose
clauses.body: This document describes what California Labor Code §§ 232 and 232.5 say about an employer's ability to restrict an employee's disclosure of wage amounts and of information about working conditions, and about the express carve-out those statutes leave in place for an employer's proprietary information, trade secrets, and privileged information. It is provided for information about {{employeeName}}'s and {{companyName}}'s rights and obligations under those statutes; it does not itself instruct either party on what to do in any specific situation.

clauses.title: Wage-Amount Disclosure: What an Employer May Not Do
clauses.body: California Labor Code § 232 prohibits an employer from doing any of three things regarding an employee's disclosure of the amount of the employee's own wages: requiring, as a condition of employment, that the employee refrain from disclosing that amount; requiring the employee to sign a waiver or other document purporting to deny the employee the right to disclose that amount; and discharging, formally disciplining, or otherwise discriminating against an employee who discloses that amount. The statute's prohibition runs specifically to an employee's own wage amount — it does not, on its face, address an employee disclosing a co-worker's wage information obtained from the employer in confidence, a distinct scenario this clause does not resolve.
clauses.gap: All three quoted prohibitions come from a single statutory section, Labor Code § 232, subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) — they are treated here as one source, not three independent ones. The statute's own text does not define what counts as a "waiver" sufficient to trigger subdivision (b), nor does it specify a private civil remedy, penalty, or enforcement mechanism for a violation; this clause does not address how a violation of § 232 is enforced (for example, through a Labor Commissioner complaint, a private lawsuit, or another avenue), because the statute's own text is silent on that question and no separate enforcement statute was researched for this document. The section text was retrieved directly from California's official Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) on 2026-09-08, and re-fetched a second time with a distinct User-Agent header; both retrievals were byte-identical.

citations.case: California Labor Code § 232
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 232
citations.quote: No employer may do any of the following: (a) Require, as a condition of employment, that an employee refrain from disclosing the amount of his or her wages. (b) Require an employee to sign a waiver or other document that purports to deny the employee the right to disclose the amount of his or her wages. (c) Discharge, formally discipline, or otherwise discriminate against an employee who discloses the amount of his or her wages.

clauses.title: Working-Conditions Disclosure: What an Employer May Not Do
clauses.body: A separate statute, California Labor Code § 232.5, extends a parallel set of three prohibitions to an employee's disclosure of information about the employer's working conditions generally, rather than only wage amounts. An employer may not require, as a condition of employment, that an employee refrain from disclosing information about the employer's working conditions; may not require an employee to sign a waiver or other document purporting to deny the employee that right; and may not discharge, formally discipline, or otherwise discriminate against an employee who discloses such information. The statute does not itself define "working conditions," and this clause does not address where that term's boundaries lie.
clauses.gap: All three quoted prohibitions come from a single statutory section, Labor Code § 232.5, subdivisions (a), (b), and (c) — they are treated here as one source, not three independent ones. As with § 232, the statute's own text does not specify a private civil remedy or enforcement mechanism for a violation of these three subdivisions, and this clause does not address enforcement. A CourtListener search for case law construing § 232.5's working-conditions prohibition specifically (as opposed to § 232's wage-disclosure prohibition) returned only tangential results — cases citing the section in passing among a longer list of claims, without construing its terms — so no case law is included in this clause. The section text was retrieved directly from California's official Legislative Information website on 2026-09-08, and re-fetched a second time with a distinct User-Agent header; both retrievals were byte-identical.

citations.case: California Labor Code § 232.5
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 232.5(a)-(c)
citations.quote: No employer may do any of the following: (a) Require, as a condition of employment, that an employee refrain from disclosing information about the employer’s working conditions. (b) Require an employee to sign a waiver or other document that purports to deny the employee the right to disclose information about the employer’s working conditions. (c) Discharge, formally discipline, or otherwise discriminate against an employee who discloses information about the employer’s working conditions.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own Carve-Out for Trade Secrets, Proprietary Information, and Privilege
clauses.body: Labor Code § 232.5 contains its own express limit on the working-conditions disclosure right it creates: the same section states that it is not intended to permit an employee to disclose the employer's proprietary information, trade secret information, or information that is otherwise subject to a legal privilege, without the employer's consent. This carve-out sits within the same statutory section as the working-conditions disclosure protection described in a companion clause of this document — the protection and the carve-out are two subdivisions of one section, not separately enacted provisions. Labor Code § 232, the parallel wage-disclosure statute described in another companion clause, contains no equivalent carve-out in its own text.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes a single subdivision, Labor Code § 232.5(d); it is the same statutory section as the wageconf_workingconditions_disclosure_prohibition clause's subdivisions (a)-(c), so the two clauses are not independent sources of each other. The statute's own text does not define "proprietary information" or state how this subdivision interacts with California's separate Uniform Trade Secrets Act definition of "trade secret" (Civil Code § 3426.1(d)), and this clause does not resolve that interaction — it states only that § 232.5 itself uses the broader, undefined phrase "proprietary information" in addition to "trade secret information." No case law construing this specific subdivision was located: a CourtListener search returned only cases mentioning § 232.5 in passing without construing subdivision (d), so none is cited here. The section text was retrieved directly from California's official Legislative Information website on 2026-09-08, and re-fetched a second time with a distinct User-Agent header; both retrievals were byte-identical.

citations.case: California Labor Code § 232.5(d)
citations.cite: Cal. Lab. Code § 232.5(d)
citations.quote: This section is not intended to permit an employee to disclose proprietary information, trade secret information, or information that is otherwise subject to a legal privilege without the consent of his or her employer.

clauses.title: A California Court's Recognition of a Public-Policy Wrongful Termination Claim
clauses.body: In Grant-Burton v. Covenant Care, Inc., a California Court of Appeal addressed a marketing director who alleged she was discharged after discussing bonus amounts with coworkers. The court held that the employee had a right, rooted in public policy and grounded in Labor Code § 232, to join in a discussion with other employees about whether they were being equitably compensated, and reversed summary judgment against her wrongful-termination-in-violation-of-public-policy claim. The court's holding treats § 232 as more than an internal wage-disclosure rule: it treats the statute as capable of supplying the public-policy basis for a separate common-law tort claim for wrongful termination, distinct from any claim under the statute itself.
clauses.gap: This is a single published California Court of Appeal decision from one district (Second Appellate District, Division One), decided in 2002; this clause does not address whether other California appellate districts, or the California Supreme Court, have independently addressed the same public-policy question, and no further case-law search beyond this decision and its own citations was performed. The decision itself quotes a version of Labor Code § 232(c) that included additional language ("for job advancement") not present in the current, currently-operative statutory text quoted elsewhere in this document — consistent with the statute having been amended by Stats. 2002, Ch. 934, effective January 1, 2003, shortly after this opinion issued; this clause quotes only the court's own reasoning about the public-policy right, not the court's quotation of the now-superseded statutory language, to avoid misstating the current text of § 232. This clause does not address whether the same public-policy reasoning would extend to § 232.5's working-conditions disclosure right, which the court did not consider. The opinion was retrieved via the CourtListener API (opinion id 2285001) on 2026-09-08 and the quoted text was confirmed as an exact contiguous substring of the retrieved html_with_citations field, stripped of markup.

citations.case: Grant-Burton v. Covenant Care, Inc.
citations.quote: We conclude that the employee had a fundamental right rooted in public policy to join in a discussion with other employees about whether they were being equitably compensated. Labor Code section 232 prohibits the discharge of employees for discussing the amount of their wages.

clauses.title: "Wages" Under § 232 Reaches Beyond Base Pay
clauses.body: The same Grant-Burton decision addressed what "wages" means for purposes of § 232's protection, in a case where the disclosed information was a discretionary bonus rather than base salary. The court held that § 232 protects an employee who discloses "wages" as that term is broadly defined elsewhere in the Labor Code to include all amounts for labor performed, and on that basis concluded that the bonuses at issue — tied to increases in patient count or facility growth — came within the statute's protection.
clauses.gap: This clause describes one Court of Appeal decision's application of the term "wages" to one specific category of compensation (facility-growth-linked bonuses); it does not address how the same reasoning would apply to other forms of compensation such as equity, commissions, or benefits, which the court did not consider. The quoted passage itself cross-references Labor Code § 200, subdivision (a)'s definition of "wages" rather than restating it in full; that separate statutory definition was not independently fetched or verified for this document, so this clause relies on the Court of Appeal's own characterization of it rather than on independently confirmed statutory text. This clause is a companion to wageconf_public_policy_tort_recognition, drawn from the same single opinion; it is not an independent corroborating source for that clause's public-policy holding. The opinion was retrieved via the CourtListener API (opinion id 2285001) on 2026-09-08 and the quoted text was confirmed as an exact contiguous substring of the retrieved html_with_citations field, stripped of markup.

citations.case: Grant-Burton v. Covenant Care, Inc.
citations.quote: Section 232 protects an employee who discloses his or her “wages,” which is broadly defined to include “all amounts for labor performed.”

clauses.title: What This Document Does Not Cover
clauses.body: This document addresses only Labor Code §§ 232 and 232.5 and the single Court of Appeal decision described above. It does not address other, separate California statutes that also touch employee pay disclosure and transparency — including Labor Code § 1197.5 (equal-pay and pay-history provisions), Labor Code § 432.3 (pay scale disclosure in job postings), or the federal National Labor Relations Act's separate protection for concerted activity among employees discussing wages — none of which is described here. It also does not address the corpus's separate documents on trade secret misappropriation, the Uniform Trade Secrets Act, or the Silenced No More Act (Government Code § 12964.5) and the settlement-confidentiality statute (Code of Civil Procedure § 1001), each of which concerns different statutory confidentiality restrictions from the ones described here.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
About This Home Care Aide Registry Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California law governing the Home Care Aide Registry, established under the Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act (Health and Safety Code Sections 1796.10 through 1796.70) and administered by the State Department of Social Services. It states facts about who must be listed on the registry before providing home care services, the licensing requirement for a business that arranges those services, the background-check and training steps involved, and a licensed home care organization's own duties toward its affiliated home care aides. {{companyName}} is considering {{applicantName}} for the position of {{jobTitle}}. This document does not determine whether that specific position, or {{companyName}}'s own business, falls within this chapter's definitions, whether any statutory exclusion applies, or whether {{applicantName}} has in fact been listed on the registry; it also does not address the separate general Live Scan / DOJ fingerprint background-check framework (Penal Code Section 11105.3) or the In-Home Supportive Services program, both covered elsewhere in this corpus or excluded from this chapter by its own terms.

clauses.title: An Affiliated Home Care Aide Must Be Listed on the Registry Before Providing Services
clauses.body: Health and Safety Code Section 1796.14(b) requires an individual who is employed by a home care organization to provide home care services to a client — an "affiliated home care aide" — to be listed on the department-maintained Home Care Aide Registry before providing those services to a client.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (b) of Section 1796.14. Subdivisions (c) and (d) of the same section list categories of individuals this chapter's "home care aide" definition does not reach at all — including people providing services through a licensed home health agency, hospice, or health facility, an In-Home Supportive Services provider, certain community care, residential care, or child day care licensees, a clinic, a home medical device retail facility, certain regional-center-vendored providers, an alcoholism or drug recovery facility, specified Indian Child Welfare Act placements, and a nonrelative extended family member as defined elsewhere in state law — none of which this clause restates or applies to a particular arrangement.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1796.14(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act, registry listing required before an affiliated home care aide provides services
citations.quote: An affiliated home care aide shall be listed on the home care aide registry prior to providing home care services to a client.

clauses.title: Arranging Home Care Services Requires a Home Care Organization License
clauses.body: Health and Safety Code Section 1796.35(a) states that, subject to statutory exceptions, an individual, partnership, corporation, limited liability company, joint venture, association, or other entity may not arrange for the provision of home care services by a registered home care aide to a client in California before obtaining a home care organization license under this chapter, and that doing so without a license is deemed "unlicensed home care services."
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subdivision (a). Subdivisions (b) through (d) of the same section describe the department's enforcement response to a violation — a written notice of noncompliance, a civil penalty of $900 per day per violation, referral to the Attorney General or a district attorney or city attorney, and the availability of a cease-and-desist order or an unfair-competition-law action — none of which this clause restates. The quoted text also cross-references exceptions set out in Section 1796.17, which this document does not separately address, and this clause does not determine whether any particular arrangement meets the statutory definition of "arrang[ing] for the provision of home care services."

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1796.35(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act, license required to arrange home care services
citations.quote: an individual, partnership, corporation, limited liability company, joint venture, association, or other entity shall not arrange for the provision of home care services by a registered home care aide to a client in this state before obtaining a license pursuant to this chapter. This shall be deemed “unlicensed home care services.”

clauses.title: Criminal-History Review as Part of a Home Care Aide Registration Application
clauses.body: In deciding whether to approve a home care aide's registration application, Health and Safety Code Section 1796.19(a)(2) directs the department to consider evidence that the applicant is of reputable and responsible character, including a review of the applicant's criminal offender record information conducted under Health and Safety Code Section 1522 or 1522.7.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only paragraph (2) of a four-paragraph, non-exclusive list of factors the department "shall consider" under Section 1796.19(a); paragraphs (1), (3), and (4) address the applicant's general ability to comply with the chapter, prior revocations or pending disciplinary action related to the care of individuals, and other unspecified information the department may consider, none of which this clause restates. This clause also does not restate the separate substantive standards Sections 1522 and 1522.7 themselves set for what criminal history disqualifies an applicant, and does not determine the outcome of any particular applicant's background review.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1796.19(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act, criminal-history review as a registration-approval factor
citations.quote: Evidence satisfactory to the department that the home care aide applicant is of reputable and responsible character. The evidence shall include, but is not limited to, a review of the independent home care aide applicant’s criminal offender record information pursuant to Section 1522 or 1522.7.

clauses.title: A Home Care Organization's Duty to Confirm Registry Clearance Before Client Contact
clauses.body: Health and Safety Code Section 1796.43(a) states that a home care organization that employs affiliated home care aides must ensure those aides are cleared on the Home Care Aide Registry before placing them in direct contact with clients.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the opening sentence of subdivision (a). The same subdivision goes on, in paragraph (1), to extend a parallel pre-contact clearance requirement (referencing Sections 1796.23 through 1796.28) to "any staff person, volunteer, or employee of a home care organization" with client contact or access to confidential client information, and in paragraph (2) requires a tuberculosis-free demonstration under a separate section; neither is restated here. Subdivision (b), which allows a licensee to require a criminal-record clearance for an individual exempt from this section who nonetheless has client contact, is also not addressed.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1796.43(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act, home care organization's duty to clear affiliated aides before client contact
citations.quote: Home care organizations that employ affiliated home care aides shall ensure the affiliated home care aides are cleared on the home care aide registry before placing the individual in direct contact with clients.

clauses.title: Minimum Entry-Level Training Before an Affiliated Home Care Aide Is Present With a Client
clauses.body: Health and Safety Code Section 1796.44(b), as currently in effect, requires an affiliated home care aide to complete a minimum of five hours of entry-level training before being present with a client: two hours of orientation training on the aide's role and the applicable terms of employment, and three hours of safety training covering basic safety precautions, emergency procedures, and infection control. Subdivision (a) places the responsibility for ensuring this occurs on the licensee.
clauses.gap: Section 1796.44 currently exists in two chaptered versions. The version quoted here is the one operative now: it states, by its own terms, that it "shall remain in effect only until January 1, 2027," per amendments made by Stats. 2025, Ch. 414, Sec. 1. A second, already-enacted version of the same section becomes operative January 1, 2027 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 414, Sec. 2); the five-hour entry-level breakdown quoted here is identical in both versions, but the later version adds "the special care needs of clients with dementia" as an additional required topic within the section's separate five-hour annual-training requirement (subdivision (c)), which this clause does not quote or analyze. Because this section has more than one enacted version, its individual leginfo.legislature.ca.gov citation page redirects to a version-selection page rather than displaying text directly; the citation url below instead points to the full chapter-13, article-8 text display, from which the quoted subdivision (b) language was independently confirmed against two separately fetched copies.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1796.44(b) (California Legislative Information text, currently operative version)
citations.cite: Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act, entry-level training required before presence with a client
citations.quote: An affiliated home care aide shall complete a minimum of five hours of entry-level training prior to presence with a client, as follows: (1) Two hours of orientation training regarding their role as home care aide and the applicable terms of employment. (2) Three hours of safety training, including basic safety precautions, emergency procedures, and infection control.

clauses.title: Tuberculosis Examination as a Condition of Employment as an Affiliated Home Care Aide
clauses.body: Health and Safety Code Section 1796.45(a) requires an affiliated home care aide hired on or after January 1, 2016, to submit to an examination for active tuberculosis disease either 90 days before employment begins or within seven days after it begins. Subdivision (e) states that this examination is a condition of both initial and continuing employment with the home care organization.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only subdivisions (a) and (e). Subdivision (b) defines "examination" (a CDC-recommended, FDA-licensed infection test, followed by a chest X-ray if positive) and states an aide may not work unless the licensee obtains documentation of no risk of spreading the disease; subdivision (c) requires retesting at least every two years unless a positive test has already been followed by an X-ray; subdivision (d) requires the aide to submit, and the organization to keep on file, an examining practitioner's certificate; and subdivision (f) allows an aide transferring between home care organizations to satisfy the requirement by producing or having verified a certificate from within the past two years. None of those subdivisions is restated here.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1796.45(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act, tuberculosis examination timing for a newly hired affiliated home care aide
citations.quote: Affiliated home care aides hired on or after January 1, 2016, shall submit to an examination 90 days prior to employment, or within seven days after employment, to determine that the individual is free of active tuberculosis disease.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1796.45(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act, tuberculosis examination as a condition of employment
citations.quote: The examination is a condition of initial and continuing employment with the home care organization.

clauses.title: A Home Care Aide's Registration Must Be Renewed Every Two Years
clauses.body: Health and Safety Code Section 1796.31(a)(1) requires a registered home care aide to renew registration every two years to remain on the Home Care Aide Registry, with the registration expiring on the anniversary of the initial registration date if not timely renewed.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the opening sentence of paragraph (1) of subdivision (a). The remainder of paragraph (1), and paragraph (2), describe the mechanics of requesting renewal (submitting a renewal application form and paying a nonrefundable fee before the expiration date) and the consequence of a late renewal (forfeiture under Section 1796.26(b)); subdivision (b)'s multi-part list of conditions on which renewal itself is conditioned was not reviewed for this clause. This clause does not state what those renewal conditions are or resolve any particular aide's renewal status.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1796.31(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act, biennial renewal of home care aide registration
citations.quote: To remain on the home care aide registry, a registered home care aide shall renew his or her registration every two years.

clauses.title: A Home Care Organization Must Notify the Department When an Affiliated Aide's Employment Ends
clauses.body: Health and Safety Code Section 1796.43(a)(3) requires a home care organization to immediately notify the department when it no longer employs an individual as an affiliated home care aide.
clauses.gap: This is one of three duties enumerated in Section 1796.43(a); the other two (pre-contact clearance under paragraph (1) and tuberculosis-status confirmation under paragraph (2)) are addressed in a separate clause of this document. The statutory text quoted here does not define "immediately" in days or hours, does not specify a required notification method or form, and does not state a penalty for a late or missed notification; this document does not address the department's enforcement provisions found elsewhere in this chapter.

citations.case: Cal. Health & Saf. Code § 1796.43(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Home Care Services Consumer Protection Act, notice to the department when affiliated-aide employment ends
citations.quote: Immediately notify the department when the home care organization no longer employs an individual as an affiliated home care aide.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Identification
clauses.body: This information sheet concerns {{generalPartnerName}}, general partner of {{partnershipName}}, a California limited partnership, and {{limitedPartnerName}}, a limited partner of that limited partnership. It addresses the fiduciary duties that California's Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008 assigns to a general partner, and the extent to which the limited partnership's own partnership agreement may narrow those duties.

clauses.title: The Two Statutory Fiduciary Duties
clauses.body: California's limited partnership statute states that a general partner's fiduciary duties to the limited partnership and to the other partners consist of exactly two duties — a duty of loyalty and a duty of care — and that each of those duties is defined and limited by a separate subdivision of the statute.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08(a), the introductory sentence identifying the two duties. It does not state the content of either duty, which the companion clauses of this document address separately by quoting subdivisions (b) and (c). It does not address whether a general partner that is itself an entity (for example, a corporation or LLC serving as general partner) owes these duties through its own directors, managers, or officers, a question the statute does not answer in this subdivision. No case law was independently researched for this clause; a CourtListener search for California opinions citing this section by name returned no results, so this document does not represent that any court has construed subdivision (a).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, the two fiduciary duties a general partner owes
citations.quote: The fiduciary duties that a general partner owes to the limited partnership and the other partners are the duties of loyalty and care under subdivisions (b) and (c).

clauses.title: Duty of Loyalty: Accounting for Property, Profit, and Limited Partnership Opportunities
clauses.body: The first component of a general partner's statutory duty of loyalty is an accounting duty: the general partner must account to the limited partnership, and hold as trustee for it, any property, profit, or benefit the general partner derives in the conduct or winding up of the limited partnership's activities, or derives from using limited partnership property — and the statute specifically includes within this duty the appropriation of a limited partnership opportunity.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08(b)(1). It does not define what makes an opportunity a "limited partnership opportunity" for purposes of the appropriation rule, a line-drawing question the statute leaves to case-by-case application. It does not address the partnership agreement's power to narrow this duty by identifying categories of activity that do not violate it or by authorizing specific transactions in advance, which a separate clause of this document addresses (id: lpgpduty_agreement_cannot_eliminate_loyalty, citing Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10(b)(5)). No case law was independently researched for this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, accounting for property, profit, or benefit including appropriation of a limited partnership opportunity
citations.quote: to account to the limited partnership and hold as trustee for it any property, profit, or benefit derived by the general partner in the conduct and winding up of the limited partnership’s activities or derived from a use by the general partner of limited partnership property, including the appropriation of a limited partnership opportunity

clauses.title: Duty of Loyalty: Refraining From Adverse-Interest Dealing
clauses.body: The second component of the statutory duty of loyalty requires a general partner to refrain from dealing with the limited partnership, in the conduct or winding up of its activities, as or on behalf of a party whose interest is adverse to the limited partnership's own interest.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08(b)(2). It does not define what makes an interest "adverse," nor does it address whether or how the partnership agreement's ratification mechanism (a separate clause of this document, id: lpgpduty_agreement_cannot_eliminate_loyalty, citing § 15901.10(b)(5)(B)) can authorize a specific adverse-interest transaction after full disclosure. It does not address remedies for a violation of this component. No case law was independently researched for this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, refraining from adverse-interest dealing
citations.quote: to refrain from dealing with the limited partnership in the conduct or winding up of the limited partnership’s activities as or on behalf of a party having an interest adverse to the limited partnership

clauses.title: Duty of Loyalty: Refraining From Competing With the Limited Partnership
clauses.body: The third component of the statutory duty of loyalty requires a general partner to refrain from competing with the limited partnership in the conduct or winding up of its activities.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08(b)(3). It does not define what constitutes "competing" with the limited partnership, does not address whether the partnership agreement can carve out specific competitive activities in advance (a separate clause of this document, id: lpgpduty_agreement_cannot_eliminate_loyalty, addresses that general mechanism), and does not address any duty that might continue, or end, after the general partner dissociates. No case law was independently researched for this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, refraining from competing with the limited partnership
citations.quote: to refrain from competing with the limited partnership in the conduct or winding up of the limited partnership’s activities

clauses.title: Duty of Care: A Gross-Negligence Standard
clauses.body: The statutory duty of care owed by a general partner to the limited partnership and the other partners, in the conduct and winding up of the limited partnership's activities, is limited to refraining from grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law. Ordinary negligence, standing alone, is not stated as a basis for a duty-of-care violation under this subdivision.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08(c). It does not define "grossly negligent," "reckless," or "knowing violation of law" beyond the statute's own words, and it does not address the partnership agreement's power to reduce this standard further, which is limited by a separate provision (a companion clause of this document, id: lpgpduty_agreement_care_and_good_faith_limits, citing Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10(b)(6), which permits reducing but not "unreasonably" reducing this duty). No case law construing this specific subdivision was independently researched for this clause; a CourtListener search for California opinions applying this gross-negligence standard to a limited partnership general partner returned no on-point results within the scope of this research.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, the duty-of-care standard for a general partner
citations.quote: A general partner’s duty of care to the limited partnership and the other partners in the conduct and winding up of the limited partnership’s activities is limited to refraining from engaging in grossly negligent or reckless conduct, intentional misconduct, or a knowing violation of law.

clauses.title: The Obligation of Good Faith and Fair Dealing, and the Self-Interest Carve-Out
clauses.body: Beyond the two named fiduciary duties, the statute separately requires a general partner to discharge its duties to the partnership and other partners, and to exercise any of its rights, consistently with an obligation of good faith and fair dealing. The statute then adds a limiting principle: a general partner does not violate a duty or obligation merely because its conduct furthers the general partner's own interest.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08(d) and (e). It does not define "good faith and fair dealing" beyond the statute's own words, and it does not resolve how the self-interest carve-out in subdivision (e) interacts with the specific duty-of-loyalty prohibitions in subdivision (b) — for example, whether conduct that both furthers the general partner's own interest and independently breaches subdivision (b)(2)'s adverse-interest rule is excused by subdivision (e) or still prohibited by subdivision (b). The statute's text does not itself resolve that interaction, and no case law was independently researched for this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, the good faith and fair dealing obligation
citations.quote: A general partner shall discharge the duties to the partnership and the other partners under this chapter or under the partnership agreement and exercise any rights consistently with the obligation of good faith and fair dealing.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15904.08 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, self-interested conduct alone is not a violation
citations.quote: A general partner does not violate a duty or obligation under this chapter or under the partnership agreement merely because the general partner’s conduct furthers the general partner’s own interest.

clauses.title: What the Partnership Agreement May Not Do: Eliminate the Duty of Loyalty
clauses.body: California's limited partnership statute lists specific things a partnership agreement is not permitted to do, and one of them is eliminating the general partner's duty of loyalty defined in the duty-source statute discussed elsewhere in this document. The statute does, however, permit the partnership agreement to do two narrower things instead: identify specific categories of activity that do not violate the duty of loyalty, so long as doing so is not manifestly unreasonable, and specify what number or percentage of partners may authorize or ratify — after full disclosure of all material facts — a specific act or transaction that would otherwise violate the duty of loyalty.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10(b)(5), including its two lettered sub-provisions. It does not define "manifestly unreasonable," a standard the statute leaves undefined, and it does not address the other thirteen restrictions the same subdivision (b) places on what a partnership agreement may vary, several of which are unrelated to fiduciary duty (for example, the power to sue and be sued, or the requirements for a certificate of limited partnership); this document addresses only the fiduciary-duty-related restrictions in paragraphs (5) through (7). No case law was independently researched for this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, the partnership agreement may not eliminate the duty of loyalty
citations.quote: Eliminate the duty of loyalty under Section 15904.08, but the partnership agreement may do either or both of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, identifying non-violating categories of activity
citations.quote: Identify specific types or categories of activities that do not violate the duty of loyalty, if not manifestly unreasonable.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, authorization or ratification after full disclosure
citations.quote: Specify the number or percentage of partners which may authorize or ratify, after full disclosure to all partners of all material facts, a specific act or transaction that otherwise would violate the duty of loyalty.

clauses.title: What the Partnership Agreement May Not Do: Unreasonably Reduce Care, or Eliminate Good Faith
clauses.body: The same statutory list of restrictions on a partnership agreement also addresses the duty of care and the good-faith-and-fair-dealing obligation. A partnership agreement may not unreasonably reduce the duty of care described elsewhere in this document. It also may not eliminate the good-faith-and-fair-dealing obligation, though the statute permits the partnership agreement to prescribe the standards by which performance of that obligation is measured, so long as the standards are not manifestly unreasonable.
clauses.gap: This clause states only Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10(b)(6) and (b)(7). Unlike the loyalty restriction in paragraph (5), paragraph (6) permits some reduction of the duty of care — only an "unreasonable" reduction is barred — and the statute does not itself define the line between a reasonable and an unreasonable reduction. It does not address the other paragraphs of subdivision (b) beyond (5), (6), and (7). No case law was independently researched for this clause; a CourtListener search located no California opinion applying paragraph (6) or (7) to a specific partnership agreement provision.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, no unreasonable reduction of the duty of care
citations.quote: Unreasonably reduce the duty of care under subdivision (c) of Section 15904.08.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 15901.10 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Uniform Limited Partnership Act of 2008, no elimination of the good faith and fair dealing obligation
citations.quote: Eliminate the obligation of good faith and fair dealing under subdivision (b) of Section 15903.05 and subdivision (d) of Section 15904.08, but the partnership agreement may prescribe the standards by which the performance of the obligation is to be measured, if the standards are not manifestly unreasonable.
