clauses.title: Recitals — Merger of a Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation
clauses.body: {{constituentCorporationNames}} (each a constituent corporation) are considering a merger under California's Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, Chapter 10 (Mergers), Cal. Corp. Code §§ 6010-6022. Upon the merger becoming effective, {{survivingCorporationName}} will be the surviving corporation, and the separate existence of each other constituent corporation will cease. This information sheet describes the statutory merger procedure that applies specifically to a public benefit corporation — a separate, independently codified scheme from the General Corporation Law merger procedure (Cal. Corp. Code §§ 1100-1113) that governs a merger between for-profit business corporations, and from the statutory conversion procedure that changes an entity's type rather than combining two or more entities. It records the statutory requirements and the approvals obtained for a proposed merger; it does not itself effect the merger of {{constituentCorporationNames}} or any other entity.

clauses.title: Who a Public Benefit Corporation May Merge With Freely, and Who Requires the Attorney General's Consent
clauses.body: California's public benefit corporation merger statute starts from a broad textual allowance — a public benefit corporation may merge with any domestic corporation, any foreign corporation, or any other business entity — but then narrows that allowance sharply. Without the Attorney General's prior written consent, a public benefit corporation may only actually merge with a limited, enumerated set of entities: another public benefit corporation, a religious corporation, a foreign nonprofit corporation, or an unincorporated association whose own governing documents irrevocably dedicate its assets to charitable, religious, or public purposes. A merger with any other kind of entity — including an ordinary for-profit business corporation — falls outside that free list and requires the Attorney General's prior written consent before it may proceed.
clauses.gap: This clause states the general rule and the enumerated exempt-merger-partner list; it does not reproduce the separate statutory definitions the section cross-references (Cal. Corp. Code § 171's definition of "foreign corporation" and § 5063.5's definition of "other business entity"), and it does not address the section's own further, narrower exemption for a public benefit corporation that is itself exempt from Attorney General supervision as a campaign-finance "committee" under Government Code §§ 12581, 12583, and 82013 merging with another similarly exempt public benefit corporation. The text quoted here is drawn from a single subdivision, § 6010(a); the two quotes below are two separate sentences from that same subdivision, not stitched from non-adjacent parts of the statute. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides for a public benefit corporation specifically — the parallel, separately numbered merger-partner rules for a mutual benefit corporation (Chapter 15, commencing with § 8010) and a religious corporation (which largely borrows this chapter by cross-reference, subject to its own carve-outs) are not addressed here. This document is informational only and does not determine whether the Attorney General's consent is or is not required for any specific proposed merger.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6010(a)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, general merger-partner allowance
citations.quote: A public benefit corporation may merge with any domestic corporation, foreign corporation (Section 171), or other business entity (Section 5063.5).

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6010(a)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the enumerated merger partners a public benefit corporation may merge with without the Attorney General's consent
citations.quote: However, without the prior written consent of the Attorney General, a public benefit corporation may only merge with another public benefit corporation or a religious corporation or a foreign nonprofit corporation or an unincorporated association the governing documents of which provide that its assets are irrevocably dedicated to charitable, religious, or public purposes.

clauses.title: Advance Notice to the Attorney General, and the Limit on What a Member May Receive
clauses.body: Separate from the consent requirement for merging outside the enumerated partner list, California law imposes a notice duty that applies to every merger the statute allows: at least 20 days before the merger is consummated, the Attorney General must be given a copy of the proposed agreement of merger. The same section also limits what a member of a constituent corporation may receive when a merger of this kind occurs: without the Attorney General's prior written consent, a member may only receive or keep a membership in the surviving corporation, and only for or as a result of that member's membership in the constituent corporation — not some other form of payment or property.
clauses.gap: The 20-day advance-notice requirement is quoted here with internal whitespace normalized: the raw fetched HTML places a line-wrap (a literal newline and tab characters) between the words "proposed" and "agreement of merger," confirmed identical across two independent fetches using different User-Agent headers on 2026-09-08; the quote below collapses that whitespace to a single space without altering any word or punctuation. This section does not itself state what happens if the Attorney General objects during the 20-day window, or specify a required form or delivery method for the notice — the statute imposes a timing duty, not an approval or waiting-period mechanism, and this document does not address the Attorney General's own administrative practices (such as Registry of Charitable Trusts filing conventions) for handling that notice, which are not codified in this section. The membership-limit provision in subdivision (c) applies "when a merger occurs pursuant to subdivision (a)" — i.e., it is tied to the same merger-partner framework as the preceding clause in this document, not a freestanding rule.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6010(b)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, 20-day advance notice to the Attorney General
citations.quote: At least 20 days prior to consummation of any merger allowed by subdivision (a), the Attorney General must be provided with a copy of the proposed agreement of merger.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6010(c)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, limit on what a member may receive absent Attorney General consent
citations.quote: Without the prior written consent of the Attorney General, when a merger occurs pursuant to subdivision (a), each member of a constituent corporation may only receive or keep a membership in the surviving corporation for or as a result of the member’s membership in the constituent corporation.

clauses.title: Board Approval and Required Contents of the Agreement of Merger
clauses.body: The board of each corporation that wants to merge must approve an agreement of merger. The constituent corporations are parties to that agreement, and other persons may be made parties to it as well. The statute specifies what the agreement must state: the terms and conditions of the merger; any amendments to the surviving corporation's articles that the merger will effect, including naming conventions if the surviving corporation takes a new name; any amendments to the surviving corporation's bylaws the merger will effect; the name and place of incorporation of each constituent corporation and which one is the surviving corporation; the manner, if any, of converting memberships of the constituent corporations into memberships of the surviving corporation; and any other details or provisions the parties want to include.
clauses.gap: This clause covers board approval and the required contents of the agreement itself; it does not address the separate member-approval requirement for the agreement's principal terms, which a companion clause in this document covers. It also does not reproduce the two cross-referenced statutes this section incorporates by reference — Cal. Corp. Code §§ 5810 and 5816, which govern what a public benefit corporation's articles may and may not provide, and constrain what article amendments a merger agreement may make, and § 5122(b), which conditions a surviving corporation's use of a disappearing corporation's name. Item (f) ("such other details or provisions as are desired") is an open-ended catch-all in the statute itself, not a specific requirement this document can enumerate further.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6011
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, board approval of the agreement of merger
citations.quote: The board of each corporation which desires to merge shall approve an agreement of merger. The constituent corporations shall be parties to the agreement of merger and other persons may be parties to the agreement of merger.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6011
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, required contents of the agreement of merger
citations.quote: The agreement shall state:(a) The terms and conditions of the merger;(b) The amendments, subject to Sections 5810 and 5816, to the articles of the surviving corporation to be effected by the merger, if any; if any amendment changes the name of the surviving corporation, the new name may be the same as or similar to the name of a disappearing corporation, subject to subdivision (b) of Section 5122;(c) The amendments to the bylaws of the surviving corporation to be effected by the merger, if any;(d) The name and place of incorporation of each constituent corporation and which of the constituent corporations is the surviving corporation;(e) The manner, if any, of converting memberships of the constituent corporations into memberships of the surviving corporation; and(f) Such other details or provisions as are desired, if any.

clauses.title: Member Approval of the Principal Terms of the Merger
clauses.body: Beyond board approval, the principal terms of the merger must separately be approved by the members of each constituent corporation, and by any other person or persons whose approval of an articles amendment is required under that corporation's own articles. This member (or other-person) approval can be given either before or after the board's own approval — the statute does not fix a required sequence between the two.
clauses.gap: This section defines "members" by cross-reference to Cal. Corp. Code § 5034, which this document does not reproduce; it also does not address how this approval requirement applies to a public benefit corporation that has no members at all, a structure California law separately permits for this corporation type. This document does not state what counts as the "principal terms" of a merger for purposes of triggering this approval requirement — that term is used but not separately defined in this section.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6012
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, member approval of the merger's principal terms
citations.quote: The principal terms of the merger shall be approved by the members (Section 5034) of each constituent corporation and by each other person or persons whose approval of an amendment of articles is required by the articles; and the approval by the members (Section 5034) or such other person or persons required by this section may be given before or after the approval by the board.

clauses.title: The Officers' Certificate, Filing, and When the Merger Becomes Effective
clauses.body: After the board and any required member approval, the surviving corporation must file a copy of the agreement of merger, together with an officers' certificate from each constituent corporation, with the California Secretary of State. That certificate must state the total number of memberships of each class entitled to vote on the merger, identify any other person or persons whose approval was required, and state that the principal terms of the agreement were duly approved by the required vote of the members and, if applicable, by those other persons. The merger, and any amendment to the surviving corporation's articles contained in the agreement, becomes effective upon that filing.
clauses.gap: The effective-date rule quoted here is itself made subject to two other cross-referenced provisions this document does not detail: Cal. Corp. Code § 5008(c) and § 6018 (the latter addresses mergers involving a foreign corporation and can shift which jurisdiction's law governs the merger's mechanics and effective date when the surviving entity is foreign). This document also does not address the general instrument-filed-with-the-Secretary-of-State rule elsewhere in California corporate law that allows a delayed effective date of up to 90 days after filing — whether that general rule applies to a merger filed under this specific section was not independently verified for this document.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6014
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, the officers' certificate and filing requirement
citations.quote: After approval of a merger by the board and any approval by the members (Section 5034) or other person or persons required by Section 6012, the surviving corporation shall file a copy of the agreement of merger with an officers’ certificate of each constituent corporation attached stating the total number of memberships of each class entitled to vote on the merger, identifying any other person or persons whose approval is required, and stating that the principal terms of the agreement in the form attached were duly approved by the required vote of the members and (if applicable) such other person or persons.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6014
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, when the merger becomes effective
citations.quote: The merger and any amendment of the articles of the surviving corporation contained in the merger agreement shall thereupon be effective (subject to subdivision (c) of Section 5008 and subject to the provisions of Section 6018) and the several parties thereto shall be one surviving corporation.

clauses.title: Merging With a Business Corporation: Which Statutes Apply to Which Party
clauses.body: California law separately addresses a merger between a nonprofit corporation and a business corporation by specifying, for each type of constituent corporation, which statutory sections govern that constituent's side of the transaction. For a constituent public benefit corporation, Sections 6011, 6012, 6014, and 6015 apply; for a constituent mutual benefit corporation, Sections 8011, 8011.5, 8012, 8014, and 8015 apply; for a constituent religious corporation, Sections 6014 and 6015 and subdivisions (c) and (d) of Section 9640 apply; and for a constituent business corporation, Sections 1101, 1101.1, 1103, and 1104 (the General Corporation Law merger provisions) apply.
clauses.gap: This cross-reference list is notable for what it does not include: it does not list Section 6010 — the section that otherwise requires the Attorney General's prior written consent for a public benefit corporation to merge with an entity outside the enumerated exempt list, and that requires 20 days' advance notice to the Attorney General — among the sections it says apply to a constituent public benefit corporation in this specific hybrid scenario. Because a business corporation is not one of the entity types Section 6010(a) exempts from the consent requirement, whether Section 6010's consent and notice duties nonetheless continue to apply to a public benefit corporation merging with a business corporation (as part of the same chapter's general framework) or whether this section's silence about 6010 has some narrower significance is a real textual question this document does not resolve; it was not able to locate secondary authority (case law or Attorney General guidance) addressing this specific cross-reference gap within the scope of this document's research. This document also does not address the Corporate Transparency Act, federal or California tax consequences, or securities-law implications of converting a nonprofit corporation's assets into a business corporation structure through this kind of merger.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6019
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, applicable statutes for a merger between a nonprofit corporation and a business corporation
citations.quote: If an agreement of merger is entered into between a nonprofit corporation and a business corporation: (i) Sections 6011, 6012, 6014, and 6015 shall apply to any constituent public benefit corporation; (ii) Sections 8011, 8011.5, 8012, 8014, and 8015 shall apply to any constituent mutual benefit corporation; (iii) Sections 6014 and 6015 and subdivisions (c) and (d) of Section 9640 shall apply to any constituent religious corporation; and (iv) Sections 1101, 1101.1, 1103, and 1104 shall apply to any constituent business corporation.

clauses.title: Effect of the Merger: Successor Liability and Preserved Creditor Rights
clauses.body: Once a merger under this chapter is effective, the separate existence of each disappearing party ceases, and the surviving party succeeds — without any separate transfer being needed — to all of the rights and property of each disappearing party. At the same time, the surviving party becomes subject to all of the debts and liabilities of each disappearing party, and to any trust obligations resting on a disappearing party's property, in the same manner as if the surviving party had incurred those obligations itself. The statute separately preserves all rights of creditors and all liens and trusts on or arising from a constituent corporation's property, though a lien or trust obligation on a disappearing party's property remains limited to the property it affected immediately before the merger's effective date.
clauses.gap: This section does not itself define what makes property subject to a "trust obligation" for these purposes — that determination (for example, whether a donor-restricted or dedicated-purpose asset is impressed with such an obligation) depends on separate California charitable-trust and cy pres doctrine that this document does not address. This document also does not quote subdivision (c) of this section, which addresses pending litigation continuing against the surviving party; the raw fetched HTML contains a stray double space at one point in that subdivision ("the surviving  party"), confirmed identical across two independent fetches on 2026-09-08, and this document omits a direct quotation of that subdivision rather than reproduce the anomaly.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6020(a)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, succession to rights, property, debts, and liabilities on merger
citations.quote: Upon merger pursuant to this chapter the separate existences of the disappearing parties to the merger cease and the surviving party to the merger shall succeed, without other transfer, to all the rights and property of each of the disappearing parties to the merger and shall be subject to all the debts and liabilities of each and trust obligations upon the property of a disappearing party in the same manner as if incurred by the surviving party to the merger.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 6020(b)
citations.cite: California Nonprofit Public Benefit Corporation Law, preservation of creditors' rights, liens, and trusts
citations.quote: All rights of creditors and all liens and trusts upon or arising from the property of each of the constituent corporations and other parties to the merger shall be preserved unimpaired, provided that the liens and trust obligations upon property of a disappearing party shall be limited to the property affected thereby immediately prior to the time the merger is effective.

clauses.title: Record of Approvals Obtained
CalPERS 'Golden Handshake' Early Retirement Incentive — Introduction
clauses.body: I, {{employeeName}}, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment as {{jobTitle}} with {{companyName}}, a local public agency that contracts with the California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS). This information sheet describes California Government Code section 20903 — a statute in the Public Employees' Retirement Law that lets a CalPERS contracting agency's governing body offer eligible local members up to two years of additional retirement service credit (a program commonly called a "golden handshake") when the agency determines that an impending curtailment of, or change in the manner of performing, its services makes doing so in the agency's best interests, and specific statutory conditions are met. If {{companyName}} has adopted a contract amendment or resolution under this section, its stated effective date is: {{effectiveDate}}. It is not a notice that {{companyName}} has adopted, or intends to adopt, this program, is not a certification, resolution, or contract amendment under this section, and does not itself grant, calculate, or guarantee any amount of additional service credit for {{employeeName}} or any other employee. Completing it does not establish that any of the statutory conditions described below currently exist at {{companyName}}, or that {{companyName}} is even a CalPERS contracting agency that has elected to be subject to this section.

clauses.title: The Statutory Trigger: Impending Curtailment or Change in Service, and the Agency's Own "Best Interests" Determination
clauses.body: Government Code section 20903 opens by identifying who may use it and why: the section applies when the governing body of a CalPERS contracting agency itself determines that an impending curtailment of, or change in the manner of performing, its services makes offering additional retirement service credit to eligible local members in the agency's own best interests. The statute frames this as a threshold determination the agency's own governing body makes — not a right an individual employee can independently trigger — and, by its own terms, that determination only opens the door to eligibility: a local member becomes eligible for the additional service credit only if a further set of lettered conditions also exist, several of which are addressed in other clauses of this document.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the section's opening sentence, which states the trigger and cross-references the lettered conditions that follow; it does not itself determine whether a particular agency's own governing-body determination of "impending curtailment" or "change in the manner of performing service" would be upheld if challenged. No reported California appellate decision interpreting this specific statutory phrase was located: a CourtListener case-law search for the exact phrase "impending curtailment" together with "retirement service credit" returned zero results in this session. This clause also does not address whether a court would review such a determination at all, or under what standard, if an employee or taxpayer challenged it — a threshold and standard-of-review question this clause does not research.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 20903 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the section's opening sentence stating the impending-curtailment/change-in-service trigger and the agency's best-interests determination
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provisions of this part, when the governing body of a contracting agency determines that because of an impending curtailment of, or change in the manner of performing service, the best interests of the agency would be served, a local member shall be eligible to receive additional service credit if the following conditions exist:

clauses.title: Condition (a): The Retirement Window the Agency Designates Must Run Between 90 and 180 Days
clauses.body: One of the section's lettered conditions ties eligibility to timing the agency itself sets. A member is eligible only if the member is employed in a job classification, department, or other organizational unit the agency's governing body has designated, and retires within a window the agency designates — either in the contract amendment that first adopts this section, or in a later resolution the governing body adopts for a subsequent round. The statute bounds how long that window may run: not less than 90 days, and not more than 180 days.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (a) exactly; it does not itself state what window, if any, a specific contracting agency has designated, or when a window opens or closes for a specific employee — those facts depend on the agency's own contract amendment or subsequently adopted resolution, not on the statute's text alone. It also does not address how "job classification, department, or other organizational unit" is defined for a specific agency, a designation the statute leaves entirely to the agency's own governing body, and does not address what happens if an agency designates a window shorter than 90 days or longer than 180 days by mistake.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the designated job classification/unit and the 90-to-180-day retirement window condition
citations.quote: The member is employed in a job classification, department, or other organizational unit designated by the governing body of the contracting agency and retires within any period designated in and subsequent to the effective date of the contract amendment, or any additional period or periods designated in any subsequently adopted resolution of the governing body of the contracting agency, provided the period is not less than 90 days nor more than 180 days.

clauses.title: Condition (c): A 1 Percent Layoff Certification Measured Against the Agency's Own Designated Unit
clauses.body: The governing body may not simply decide, without more, that offering the credit serves the agency's best interests. It must also certify that it is electing to use this section because of impending mandatory transfers, demotions, and layoffs that meet a specific numeric threshold: at least 1 percent of the job classification, department, or organizational unit the governing board itself has designated, resulting from the curtailment of, or change in the manner of performing, the agency's services.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (c) exactly. The statute measures "at least 1 percent" against "the job classification, department, or organizational unit as designated by the governing board" — a base the agency's own governing body defines for this purpose, not a fixed, agency-wide, or independently verifiable headcount. This clause does not calculate whether any specific number of transfers, demotions, or layoffs meets that 1 percent threshold at a particular agency, and does not address how, or whether, a governing body's designation of the relevant unit could itself be reviewed or challenged by an employee or member of the public.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the governing body's certification of impending transfers, demotions, and layoffs meeting a 1 percent threshold
citations.quote: The governing body shall certify that it is electing to exercise the provisions of this section, because of impending mandatory transfers, demotions, and layoffs that constitute at least 1 percent of the job classification, department, or organizational unit as designated by the governing board, resulting from the curtailment of, or change in the manner of performing, its services.

clauses.title: Condition (d): A Certified Intent to Leave at Least One Resulting Vacancy Permanently Unfilled
clauses.body: The section also requires the governing body to certify its own intent, made at the time the section is made operative, that the program will actually shrink the workforce rather than simply rotate who fills existing positions. Specifically, the governing body must certify that if any early retirements are granted after a member receives service credit under this section, any vacancies thus created — or at least one vacancy in any position in any department or other organizational unit — will remain permanently unfilled, resulting in an overall reduction in the workforce of the department or organizational unit.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (d) exactly. The statute requires only a governing-body certification of intent, made "at the time that this section is made operative," that a resulting vacancy — in any department or organizational unit, not necessarily the same one a particular retiring member left — will remain permanently unfilled; it does not require, and this clause does not address, any ongoing monitoring or enforcement mechanism confirming that an agency's later staffing decisions actually matched that certified intent, nor does it address what remedy, if any, would exist if an agency later filled a position it had certified would remain vacant.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the certified intent that a resulting vacancy remain permanently unfilled
citations.quote: The governing body shall certify that it is its intention at the time that this section is made operative that if any early retirements are granted after receipt of service credit pursuant to this section, that any vacancies thus created or at least one vacancy in any position in any department or other organizational unit shall remain permanently unfilled thereby resulting in an overall reduction in the workforce of the department or organizational unit.

clauses.title: Condition (e): A Flat Two Years of Additional Service Credit, Regardless of a Member's Actual Years Served
clauses.body: The headline benefit itself is a fixed, non-proportional amount: the statute sets the amount of additional service credit at two years, regardless of how much service credit the member already has. A member with only a few years of actual credited service and a member with decades of service both receive the same flat two-year addition under this subdivision, if the section's other conditions are met.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (e) exactly; it states only the amount of service credit added (two years, regardless of credited service), not the dollar value that credit produces under a particular member's own retirement formula, final compensation, and age at retirement — a calculation this clause does not perform. A separate subdivision of the same section, subdivision (h) (not independently quoted in this document), narrows this benefit further for a member who is not currently employed by the contracting agency during the subdivision (a) window and who has less than five years of service credit; this clause does not analyze that additional condition in depth, and a reader should not assume the flat two-year credit applies without also checking subdivision (h) and the other lettered conditions addressed elsewhere in this document.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the flat two-years-of-additional-service-credit rule
citations.quote: The amount of additional service credit shall be two years regardless of credited service.

clauses.title: Condition (f): Disqualification for Receiving Unemployment Insurance Payments During the Window
clauses.body: The section builds in a specific disqualifying event tied to a different benefit system entirely. A member who would otherwise be eligible for the additional service credit is disqualified from this section if the member receives any unemployment insurance payments during the specified period — that is, during the retirement window the agency has designated under subdivision (a).
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (f) exactly. The statute disqualifies a member who "receives any unemployment insurance payments during the specified period" — it does not itself redefine "the specified period" here (that phrase refers back to the window period a governing body designates under subdivision (a), addressed in a separate clause of this document), does not address whether disqualification would also result from unemployment insurance payments received before the window opens or after it closes, and does not address how this rule interacts with the general California Unemployment Insurance Code eligibility and disqualification rules this project addresses in separate documents outside this one. This is a narrow, agency-side eligibility condition for the additional service credit, not a restatement of general unemployment insurance law.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(f) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: disqualification for receiving unemployment insurance payments during the specified period
citations.quote: This section is not applicable to any member otherwise eligible if the member receives any unemployment insurance payments during the specified period.

clauses.title: Condition (g): Forfeiting the Added Credit Upon Subsequent Reentry Into the System
clauses.body: The credit is not necessarily permanent once granted. The statute provides that any member who qualifies for the additional service credit under this section, upon subsequent reentry into the retirement system, forfeits the service credit that had been acquired under this section.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes subdivision (g) exactly. The statute does not itself define what counts as "subsequent reentry to this system" — for example, whether reemployment in any position covered by the Public Employees' Retirement Law with any contracting agency counts as reentry, or only reemployment with the same agency that granted the credit — and does not state any time limit after which reentry would no longer trigger forfeiture. This clause does not research CalPERS' own regulations or administrative guidance interpreting "reentry" for this purpose, and does not address whether forfeiture affects only the two years of added credit or any other, separately earned service credit.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(g) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: forfeiture of the added service credit upon subsequent reentry to the retirement system
citations.quote: Any member who qualifies under this section, upon subsequent reentry to this system shall forfeit the service credit acquired under this section.

clauses.title: Condition (i): The Agency Must Affirmatively Elect Into This Section Through a Public, Non-Consent-Calendar Process
clauses.body: A CalPERS contracting agency is not automatically subject to this section merely because it contracts with CalPERS. The statute states that the section does not apply to any contracting agency unless and until the agency elects to be subject to it — by amending its CalPERS contract in the manner prescribed for approval of contracts (without needing a vote among the employees), or, for contracts made after January 1, 2000, by express provision in the contract itself. Before a governing body may adopt this provision at all, the statute layers on a specific public process: with timely public notice, the governing body must place consideration of this section on the agenda of a public meeting, disclose the additional employer contributions and the funding for them, and give the public an opportunity to be heard — and the matter may not be placed on the agenda as a consent item. Only after that public meeting may the governing body adopt the section.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes two consecutive parts of subdivision (i) exactly. It does not itself state whether any specific contracting agency has, in fact, elected to be subject to this section — that depends on the agency's own contract and contract amendments, which this clause does not look up for any specific reader. It also cross-references, but does not independently quote or analyze, Government Code section 7507 (a separate statute on actuarial cost disclosures the governing body must also comply with before adopting this section) and subdivision (j)'s savings clause for contracting agencies that had already adopted a now-repealed, earlier version of this same Section 20903 before its January 1, 1999 repeal — both are outside the scope of this clause.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the agency's own election requirement to become subject to this section
citations.quote: This section does not apply to any contracting agency unless and until the agency elects to be subject to the provision of this section by amendment to its contract made in the manner prescribed for approval of contracts, except an election among the employees is not required, or, in the case of contracts made after January 1, 2000, by express provision in the contract making the contracting agency subject to the provisions of this section.

citations.case: Cal. Gov. Code § 20903(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the public-meeting, non-consent-calendar prerequisite before adoption
citations.quote: Before adopting this provision, the governing body of a contracting agency shall, with timely public notice, place the consideration of this section on the agenda of a public meeting of the governing body, at which time disclosure shall be made of the additional employer contributions, and the funding therefor, and members of the public shall be given the opportunity to be heard. The matter may not be placed on the agenda as a consent item. Only after the public meeting may the governing body adopt this section.

clauses.title: The Term "Golden Handshake" in California Practice: A Cautionary Comparison
clauses.body: The phrase "golden handshake" is not defined anywhere in the text of Government Code section 20903 itself; it is a colloquial label used in California public-sector practice for a temporary, agency-initiated early-retirement service-credit incentive of this general kind. In at least one reported California appellate decision, an employee's own contemporaneous letter — quoted by the Court of Appeal in reciting the case's undisputed facts — used the phrase "golden handshake" to describe a different institution's own, separate one-time early-retirement incentive program.
clauses.gap: This citation is offered only to document that California practice uses the term "golden handshake" for early-retirement service-credit incentives generally; it is not authority interpreting Government Code section 20903 itself. The quoted sentence is an employee's own letter, quoted by the Court of Appeal solely in its recitation of undisputed facts — not a statement of law, a holding, or the court's own characterization of the program. The "golden handshake" program actually at issue in this case was the University of California's own separate retirement plan (the University of California Retirement Plan and its "Plus 5" early-retirement addendum), which is not CalPERS, is not governed by the Public Employees' Retirement Law, and is not subject to Government Code section 20903; the case's actual holding — about contract interpretation and administrative-mandate review of the University's own denial of a different, unrelated retirement-incentive application — does not address, and this clause does not extend it to, any question about a CalPERS contracting agency's obligations under Section 20903. No reported California decision interpreting Government Code section 20903 by name, or squarely addressing a CalPERS local member's eligibility dispute under it, was located in this session's CourtListener searches (a search for "Section 20903" together with "PERS" and "additional service credit" returned zero results, and this session's CourtListener query quota limits how exhaustive that search could be).

citations.case: Bunnett v. Regents of University of California
citations.quote: the special meeting will deal mainly with the ‘golden handshake’ early retirement scheme that the President contemplates to present to the Regents at their September meeting.

clauses.title: Signature
clauses.body:
I declare that the information above is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on {{dateSigned}} at {{cityState}}.

Signature of {{employeeName}}: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California Government Code section 20903 — the Public Employees' Retirement Law's statutory basis for a CalPERS contracting agency's "golden handshake" program of up to two years of additional retirement service credit, including the section's impending-curtailment/change-in-service trigger, the 90-to-180-day retirement window condition, the 1 percent layoff-certification condition, the permanent-vacancy workforce-reduction condition, the flat two-years-of-credit rule, the unemployment-insurance disqualification rule, the reentry-forfeiture rule, and the agency's own election and public-meeting prerequisites to adopting the section — and a reported California decision's use of the colloquial term "golden handshake" in a different, non-CalPERS context. It does not itself determine that {{companyName}} has elected to be subject to Section 20903, that any of the section's lettered conditions currently exist at {{companyName}}, or that {{employeeName}} is, or will be, eligible for any amount of additional retirement service credit. It is not a certification, resolution, contract amendment, CalPERS filing, or court filing, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting the actual statute, CalPERS' own published guidance, the contracting agency's specific contract with CalPERS, or a licensed attorney.]

clauses.title: Information and Background — Certificated Teacher Dismissal for Cause
clauses.body: I, {{employeeName}}, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment as {{jobTitle}} with {{companyName}}. This information sheet describes the statutory scheme that governs the dismissal of a permanent certificated employee of a California K-12 school district for cause — California Education Code sections 44929.21 and 44932 through 44944, within Article 3 (Resignations, Dismissals, and Leaves of Absence) of Chapter 4 of the Education Code — together with Morrison v. State Board of Education (1969) 1 Cal.3d 214, the California Supreme Court decision that narrowed several of that statute's conduct-based dismissal grounds to require a showing that the conduct indicates the employee's unfitness to teach. It is separate from this project's State Civil Service Disciplinary Due Process and Public Safety Officers Procedural Bill of Rights Act documents, neither of which addresses this Education Code chapter, and from a private-sector at-will or wrongful-termination analysis, which does not apply to a permanent certificated public school employee dismissed under this statutory scheme. It is not a written answer, a request for a hearing before a Commission on Professional Competence, an administrative appeal, a writ of mandate petition, or a superior court filing, and completing it does not initiate, extend, or preserve any deadline under Education Code section 44934, section 44944, or any other statute or collective bargaining agreement. Completing it does not establish that {{companyName}} took, or failed to take, any specific action described in this sheet, or that any statement here is true.

clauses.title: Permanent (Tenured) Status: How It Is Acquired Under Education Code Section 44929.21
clauses.body: This document addresses the dismissal of a "permanent employee" as that status is defined by the Education Code — not a probationary or temporary certificated employee, whose own, more limited procedural rights come from different Education Code provisions this document does not address. In a school district with an average daily attendance of 250 or more, an employee in a position requiring certification qualifications who is employed for two complete consecutive school years and reelected for a third becomes a permanent employee of the district at the start of that third year, and the governing board must notify the employee by March 15 of the second year if it does not intend to reelect the employee, or the employee is deemed reelected.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only the two-consecutive-year path to permanent status that applies to a probationary period commencing in the 1983-84 fiscal year or later (Education Code section 44929.21(b)); an earlier three-consecutive-year path in subdivision (a) applies only to a probationary period that commenced before that date and is not analyzed here. This document does not address a school district with an average daily attendance under 250 pupils, whose permanent-status and dismissal procedures differ in ways this document does not research; it does not address community college faculty, whose parallel tenure and dismissal provisions appear in a different part of the Education Code (beginning around section 87600) that this document does not cover; and it does not determine whether a specific employee has, in fact, satisfied this section's reelection and notice requirements. The raw fetched HTML also renders a non-breaking space (not a regular space) immediately after the subdivision letter, and a doubled space between "requiring" and "certification" in the same sentence — both confirmed identical in two independently fetched copies of this section using distinct User-Agent strings — and both are preserved exactly, rather than corrected, in the quoted citation below.

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 44929.21 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: two-year path to permanent (tenured) status for a certificated employee
citations.quote: (b) Every employee of a school district of any type or class having an average daily attendance of 250 or more who, after having been employed by the district for two complete consecutive school years in a position or positions requiring  certification qualifications, is reelected for the next succeeding school year to a position requiring certification qualifications shall, at the commencement of the succeeding school year be classified as and become a permanent employee of the district.

clauses.title: The Statute's Own List of Causes for Dismissing a Permanent Certificated Employee
clauses.body: Education Code section 44932(a) provides that a permanent certificated employee shall not be dismissed except for one or more of eleven causes the statute itself enumerates. They include immoral conduct (a category the statute further defines to include, but not be limited to, a narrower category the statute calls "egregious misconduct"), unprofessional conduct, advocating or committing acts of criminal syndicalism, dishonesty, unsatisfactory performance, evident unfitness for service, a disqualifying physical or mental condition, persistent violation of or refusal to obey school laws or reasonable board regulations, conviction of a felony or of a crime involving moral turpitude, violation of a specified statute or Government Code provision, and alcoholism or other drug abuse that makes the employee unfit to instruct or associate with children.
clauses.gap: This clause's citations quote the introductory sentence and four of the eleven lettered causes verbatim (immoral conduct, unprofessional conduct, evident unfitness for service, and conviction of a felony or crime involving moral turpitude); the remaining seven causes are described narratively above rather than quoted exactly. In the raw fetched HTML, leginfo renders a non-breaking space (not a regular space) immediately after each subdivision's numbering, for example "(1) Immoral conduct" — confirmed identical in two independently fetched copies of this section using distinct User-Agent strings — and that non-breaking space is preserved exactly, rather than corrected, in each quoted citation below. This clause does not determine whether any specific conduct falls within one of these eleven statutory causes, and does not address subdivision (b)'s separate suspension-without-pay procedure for unprofessional conduct.

citations.quote: (a) A permanent employee shall not be dismissed except for one or more of the following causes:

citations.quote: (1) Immoral conduct, including, but not limited to, egregious misconduct.

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 44932(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: unprofessional conduct as a cause for dismissal
citations.quote: (2) Unprofessional conduct.

citations.quote: (6) Evident unfitness for service.

citations.quote: (9) Conviction of a felony or of any crime involving moral turpitude.

clauses.title: Morrison v. State Board of Education: Conduct-Based Grounds Require a Nexus to Fitness to Teach
clauses.body: In Morrison v. State Board of Education, the California Supreme Court considered a state board's revocation of a teacher's life diplomas for "immoral and unprofessional conduct" and "acts involving moral turpitude" under a predecessor Education Code provision using language closely resembling several of section 44932's current causes. The court held that these general, conduct-based terms cannot be applied in the abstract; conduct falls within them only if it indicates that the individual is unfit to teach. California courts applying section 44932's own immoral-conduct, unprofessional-conduct, and moral-turpitude causes to a permanent certificated employee's dismissal have since drawn on this same fitness-to-teach nexus requirement, reasoning that the statutory language Morrison construed is substantially the same language section 44932 now uses.
clauses.gap: Morrison itself did not arise under Education Code section 44932 — it reviewed the State Board of Education's revocation of a teaching credential under a former Education Code section 13202, a different statute directed at credentialing rather than a governing board's dismissal of its own certificated employee, decided in 1969 and since renumbered and amended. This document has not independently researched and does not cite a specific California Court of Appeal decision expressly extending Morrison's nexus holding to a section 44932 dismissal proceeding, nor confirmed that every one of Morrison's specific holdings remains undisturbed by later statutory amendment (section 44932 was itself last amended in 2015, well after Morrison was decided, including the addition of the "egregious misconduct" sub-definition Morrison's 1969 opinion could not have addressed) or by later case law. A reader considering this nexus doctrine in connection with a section 44932 proceeding, rather than a credential-revocation proceeding, is relying on an analogy between two related but textually distinct statutes, not on a holding that construed section 44932 itself.

citations.case: Morrison v. State Board of Education
citations.quote: In the instant case the terms denote immoral or unprofessional conduct or moral turpitude of the teacher which indicates unfitness to teach.

clauses.title: Morrison's Non-Exhaustive List of Factors Bearing on Fitness to Teach
clauses.body: Morrison identified a set of factors a board may consider in determining whether particular conduct indicates unfitness to teach, including the likelihood that the conduct adversely affected students or fellow teachers, the degree of that anticipated adversity, and the proximity or remoteness in time of the conduct. The opinion's footnoted list continues with several additional considerations described only narratively here rather than quoted exactly: the type of teaching certificate held, any extenuating or aggravating circumstances surrounding the conduct, and the praiseworthiness or blameworthiness of the underlying motive. The opinion closes the list with the likelihood that the conduct will recur, and the extent to which disciplinary action might inflict an adverse impact or chilling effect on the constitutional rights of the teacher involved or of other teachers. The court framed all of these factors as relevant only to the extent they help determine whether the teacher's future classroom performance and overall impact on students are likely to meet the board's standards.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes two separate, non-adjacent spans of Morrison's factor list rather than the entire passage verbatim, because the source opinion interrupts the list with footnote markers between several of the factors (for example, immediately after "the proximity or remoteness in time of the conduct," and again after several of the factors that follow). The three factors in between — type of certificate held, extenuating or aggravating circumstances, and praiseworthiness or blameworthiness of motive — are described narratively above rather than quoted, to avoid presenting footnote-interrupted text as a single contiguous quotation. This clause does not indicate how a court or a Commission on Professional Competence would weigh these factors against each other in any specific case, and Morrison's own list is expressly non-exhaustive ("the board may consider such matters as"), meaning a decisionmaker is not limited to only these factors.

citations.case: Morrison v. State Board of Education
citations.quote: In determining whether the teacher’s conduct thus indicates unfitness to teach the board may consider such matters as the likelihood that the conduct may have adversely affected students or fellow teachers, the degree of such adversity anticipated, the proximity or remoteness in time of the conduct,

citations.case: Morrison v. State Board of Education
citations.quote: the likelihood of the recurrence of the questioned conduct, and the extent to which disciplinary action may inflict an adverse impact or chilling effect upon the constitutional rights of the teacher involved or other teachers.

clauses.title: Written Notice and Statement of Charges Before Dismissal (Education Code Section 44934)
clauses.body: Before dismissing a permanent employee for a cause specified in section 44932, the governing board must act on written charges — either filed by another person and duly signed and verified, or formulated by the board itself — and, by majority vote, give the employee notice of its intention to dismiss at the expiration of 30 days from the date the notice is served, unless the employee demands a hearing within that period. The statute requires that any written statement of charges be specific enough that the employee can prepare a defense: it must specify instances of behavior and the acts or omissions constituting the charge, state, where applicable, the statutes and rules the employee is alleged to have violated, and set forth the facts relevant to each charge.
clauses.gap: This clause addresses only the general notice-and-charges procedure in section 44934; it does not address section 44934.1, a separate procedure the statute specifies applies instead when a dismissal or suspension is based solely on egregious-misconduct charges, nor the rule in section 44934(d) permitting charges to be amended less than 90 days before a hearing only on a showing of good cause. It does not address whether a specific school district's charges in a specific case meet this specificity requirement, and does not address the separate procedures many school districts follow instead under a collective bargaining agreement adopted pursuant to Government Code section 3543.2(b), which section 44934(b) itself states can displace the suspension procedure this section otherwise authorizes.

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 44934(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: written charges and 30-day dismissal notice
citations.quote: the governing board of the school district may, upon majority vote, except as provided in this article if it deems the action necessary, give notice to the permanent employee of its intention to dismiss or suspend him or her at the expiration of 30 days from the date of service of the notice, unless the employee demands a hearing as provided in this article.

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 44934(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: specificity requirement for a written statement of charges
citations.quote: Any written statement of charges shall specify instances of behavior and the acts or omissions constituting the charge so that the employee will be able to prepare his or her defense.

clauses.title: The Right to a Hearing Before a Commission on Professional Competence
clauses.body: An employee who demands a hearing after receiving notice under section 44934 is entitled to a hearing conducted under the Administrative Procedure Act's formal hearing chapter. Unless both parties waive it in writing and stipulate to a single administrative law judge instead, that hearing is conducted by a three-member Commission on Professional Competence: one member selected by the employee, one selected by the governing board, and one who is an administrative law judge of the Office of Administrative Hearings, who serves as chairperson, is a voting member, and is responsible for assuring that the legal rights of the parties are protected at the hearing.
clauses.gap: This clause does not address the detailed hearing-timeline rules in section 44944(b) — including the six-month deadline to commence a hearing and seven-month deadline to close the record after a demand for hearing, the extraordinary-circumstances and good-cause continuance exceptions to those deadlines, or a separate rule limiting evidence of conduct occurring more than four years before the notice was filed — nor the eligibility and selection-timing rules for commission members, nor the compensation rules for a commission member who is a current or retired school district employee. It does not address whether a specific district has adopted a collective bargaining agreement that displaces the suspension authority referenced elsewhere in this statutory scheme.

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 44944(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: composition of the Commission on Professional Competence
citations.quote: one member of the commission shall be selected by the employee, one member shall be selected by the governing board of the school district, and one member shall be an administrative law judge of the Office of Administrative Hearings who shall be chairperson and a voting member of the commission and shall be responsible for assuring that the legal rights of the parties are protected at the hearing.

clauses.title: The Commission's Decision, Its Three Possible Dispositions, and Its Binding Effect
clauses.body: The Commission on Professional Competence decides by majority vote and must prepare a written decision containing findings of fact and determinations of issues, resolving into exactly one of three dispositions: that the employee should be dismissed, that the employee should be suspended for a specific period without pay, or that the employee should not be dismissed or suspended. The statute states that the commission's decision is deemed to be the final decision of the governing board of the school district itself — the board does not separately vote to adopt or reject it.
clauses.gap: This clause does not address section 44944(d)(2)'s limitation on a not-dismissed-or-suspended decision resting on nonsubstantive procedural errors (only a prejudicial procedural error may support that disposition), nor section 44944(d)(3)'s separate limitation on the commission's power to dispose of a dismissal charge by imposing probation or another alternative sanction instead. It does not address how a governing board or an employee may seek judicial review of the commission's decision — that avenue exists under a separate body of administrative-mandate law (Code of Civil Procedure section 1094.5 and related case law) that this document has not researched. It also does not address the suspension-without-pay disposition's own separate statutory limits, which apply only where suspension proceedings were properly authorized under section 44932(b) or section 44933 in the first place.

citations.cite: majority-vote decision and its three possible dispositions
citations.quote: The decision of the Commission on Professional Competence shall be made by a majority vote, and the commission shall prepare a written decision containing findings of fact, determinations of issues, and a disposition that shall be, solely, one of the following:

citations.case: Cal. Educ. Code § 44944(d)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the decision is deemed the governing board's final decision
citations.quote: The decision of the Commission on Professional Competence shall be deemed to be the final decision of the governing board of the school district.

clauses.title: About This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes the legal structure of a "QTIP trust" — a trust holding "qualified terminable interest property" within the meaning of 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7) — as that structure is defined by federal estate-tax law and by the California Probate Code's construction rules for marital deduction gifts (Probate Code §§ 21520-21526). A QTIP trust of this type would typically be created by {{settlorName}} for the benefit of {{survivingSpouseName}} as the income beneficiary, with {{trusteeName}} acting as trustee and {{beneficiaryName}} named to receive whatever remains in the trust after {{survivingSpouseName}}'s death. This sheet states general federal and California statutory rules; it is not a trust instrument, will, or tax election, and it does not itself create, qualify, or fund any trust or make any election on anyone's behalf.

clauses.title: Federal Effect of a QTIP Election: Property Treated as Passing to the Surviving Spouse
clauses.body: Under federal estate tax law, when an executor makes a valid election with respect to qualified terminable interest property, that property is treated, for purposes of the marital deduction, as passing to the surviving spouse, and no part of it is treated as passing to any other person for purposes of the rule that would otherwise deny the deduction for a terminable interest. This is what allows property held in a QTIP trust — where the surviving spouse receives only an income interest, not outright ownership, and does not control who receives the principal after their death — to qualify for the federal estate tax marital deduction despite the general rule against deducting terminable interests.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(A)(i), the operative "treated as passing" rule. It does not address the mechanics of making the election itself — under § 2056(b)(7)(B)(v) (not quoted here), the election is made by the executor on the federal estate tax return and, once made, is irrevocable. It does not address what happens if no valid election is made (the property then does not qualify for the marital deduction under this provision), the gift-tax analog for lifetime QTIP trusts under 26 U.S.C. § 2523(f), or the separate rule for certain survivor annuities under § 2056(b)(7)(C). It also does not address how California community property or separate property characterization of the transferred property interacts with this federal rule, which was not researched here.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(A)(i) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, election with respect to life estate for surviving spouse — general rule
citations.quote: for purposes of subsection (a), such property shall be treated as passing to the surviving spouse, and

clauses.title: Federal Definition: The Surviving Spouse's "Qualifying Income Interest for Life"
clauses.body: For property to qualify as "qualified terminable interest property" eligible for a QTIP election, the surviving spouse must have a "qualifying income interest for life" in it. Under federal estate tax law, this requires that the surviving spouse be entitled to all the income from the property, payable at least annually (or have an equivalent usufruct interest for life in the property), and that no one hold a power to appoint any part of the property to anyone other than the surviving spouse during the spouse's lifetime. This is the federal-law counterpart to the mandatory-income and sole-beneficiary features that California's construction statute separately imposes on a marital deduction trust.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(B)(ii)(I), the core income-entitlement requirement. It does not address subclause (II) of the same provision (the related no-power-to-appoint-elsewhere requirement, apart from powers exercisable only after the spouse's death), the annuity-treated-as-income rule, the "specific portion" severability rule of § 2056(b)(7)(B)(iv), or any IRS regulations or case law interpreting how strictly or literally the annual-income requirement must be satisfied in a trust's actual administration, none of which were researched here.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7)(B)(ii)(I) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, definition of "qualifying income interest for life"
citations.quote: the surviving spouse is entitled to all the income from the property, payable annually or at more frequent intervals, or has a usufruct interest for life in the property, and

clauses.title: Federal Rule: QTIP Property Is Included in the Surviving Spouse's Later Gross Estate
clauses.body: Property for which a QTIP election was made and the marital deduction was allowed at the first spouse's death is not permanently removed from the transfer-tax system. Federal law includes the value of that property in the surviving spouse's own gross estate when the surviving spouse later dies, because the surviving spouse is treated as having had a "qualifying income interest for life" in it. This is the tradeoff at the center of a QTIP election: the marital deduction defers estate tax at the first spouse's death, but the property (or property later traceable to it) is generally taxed again as part of the surviving spouse's own estate, under the surviving spouse's own estate tax exemption and rates, rather than escaping estate taxation altogether.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the general rule of 26 U.S.C. § 2044(a). It does not address § 2044(b), which limits which property this section applies to (property for which a marital deduction was allowed under § 2056(b)(7) or § 2523(f), and only where § 2519 did not already apply to a lifetime disposition of the interest), nor § 2044(c), which treats the included property as "passing from the decedent" for other transfer-tax purposes. It also does not address the surviving spouse's statutory right of reimbursement from the QTIP property for the estate tax attributable to it under 26 U.S.C. § 2207A, or the gift-tax acceleration rule under § 2519 for a lifetime disposition of the income interest, none of which were researched here.

citations.case: 26 U.S.C. § 2044(a) (Cornell LII text)
citations.cite: Internal Revenue Code, inclusion of certain property on which marital deduction was previously allowed — general rule
citations.quote: The value of the gross estate shall include the value of any property to which this section applies in which the decedent had a qualifying income interest for life.

clauses.title: California Construction Rule: Instruments and Fiduciaries Must Be Read to Preserve the Marital Deduction
clauses.body: California has its own statutory construction rules for an instrument (such as a will or trust) that makes a "marital deduction gift" — defined by statute as a transfer of property intended to qualify for the federal estate or gift tax marital deduction, which includes a gift structured as a QTIP trust. Where such an instrument is governed by California law, its provisions — including any power, duty, or discretionary authority given to a fiduciary such as a trustee — are, by default, construed to comply with the marital deduction provisions of the Internal Revenue Code, and a fiduciary is barred from taking any action or holding any power that would impair the deduction as applied to that gift.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Probate Code § 21522(a) and (b) only; it does not quote subdivision (c), which separately provides that a marital deduction gift may be satisfied only with property that qualifies for the marital deduction. These are default, gap-filling construction rules: under Probate Code § 21502(a) (not quoted here), this entire statutory part does not apply to an instrument whose own terms, expressly or by necessary implication, make the part inapplicable, so an instrument's actual language can displace what this clause describes. This clause also does not address § 21521, which exempts a trust qualifying as an "estate trust" under 26 C.F.R. § 20.2056(e)-2(b) from two of the related sections in this chapter (§§ 21524 and 21526), or § 21523's separate transitional rule for instruments executed before September 12, 1981, neither of which was researched in detail here.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21522(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, construction of instruments containing a marital deduction gift
citations.quote: The provisions of the instrument, including any power, duty, or discretionary authority given to a fiduciary, shall be construed to comply with the marital deduction provisions of the Internal Revenue Code.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21522(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, fiduciary bar on impairing the marital deduction
citations.quote: The fiduciary shall not take any action or have any power that impairs the deduction as applied to the marital deduction gift.

clauses.title: California Rule: The Spouse Must Be the Sole Income Beneficiary, Paid at Least Annually
clauses.body: For a marital deduction gift made in trust — the structure a QTIP trust uses — California's construction statute imposes two additional default requirements that track the federal "qualifying income interest" rule described elsewhere in this sheet: the transferor's spouse must be the only beneficiary of income or principal of the marital deduction property for as long as the spouse is alive, and the spouse must be entitled to all of the trust's income from that property, paid no less often than annually, for as long as the spouse is alive.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Probate Code § 21524(a) and (b) only. It does not quote the balance of § 21524(b), which separately defines how "income" is construed for this purpose (consistent with 26 U.S.C. §§ 2056(b) and 2523(f)) and allows a unitrust payment or other reasonable total-return apportionment to count as income if it meets the requirements of 26 U.S.C. § 643 and its regulations — a distinct and technical accounting question not analyzed here. It also does not address § 21524(a)'s savings clause for a trust that separately qualifies as a "general power of appointment" marital deduction trust, a different (non-QTIP) statutory route to the marital deduction that this sheet does not otherwise cover.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21524(a) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, spouse as sole income/principal beneficiary of a marital deduction trust
citations.quote: The transferor’s spouse is the only beneficiary of income or principal of the marital deduction property as long as the spouse is alive.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21524(b) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, spouse's entitlement to all income at least annually
citations.quote: The transferor’s spouse is entitled to all of the income of the marital deduction property not less frequently than annually, as long as the spouse is alive.

clauses.title: California Rule: The Spouse May Require Unproductive Trust Property to Be Made Productive
clauses.body: California's construction statute also gives the transferor's spouse a specific enforcement right connected to the mandatory-income requirement: as long as the spouse is alive, the spouse has the right to require that the trustee of a marital deduction trust make unproductive marital deduction property productive, or convert it into productive property, within a reasonable time. This addresses the practical problem of a trust funded with an asset (such as raw land or non-dividend-paying stock) that generates little or no income, which could otherwise defeat the spouse's statutory entitlement to the trust's income.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Probate Code § 21524(c). The source text wraps mid-phrase ("within a" / "reasonable time") purely as an HTML line-wrap in the leginfo.legislature.ca.gov rendering; that wrap was confirmed identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings, and the quote here normalizes it to a single space with no other change to wording, capitalization, or punctuation. This clause does not define "reasonable time" or "unproductive," does not address what remedy applies if a trustee declines to comply, and does not address how this state-law right interacts with a trustee's duties under the Uniform Prudent Investor Act (covered elsewhere in this corpus) or with the federal "usufruct interest" alternative described in the federal qualifying-income-interest clause of this sheet, none of which were researched here.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21524(c) (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, spouse's right to require unproductive marital deduction property be made productive
citations.quote: The transferor’s spouse has the right to require that the trustee of the trust make unproductive marital deduction property productive or to convert it into productive property within a reasonable time.

clauses.title: California Rule: Fiduciary Protection for a Good-Faith Election Decision
clauses.body: Because the QTIP election is made by an estate's executor (or, for lifetime gifts, by the donor for gift-tax purposes) and is irrevocable once made, California law separately addresses the fiduciary's exposure for that decision: a fiduciary is not liable for a good faith decision to make, or not to make, an election referred to in 26 U.S.C. § 2056(b)(7) or § 2523(f).
clauses.gap: This clause quotes Probate Code § 21526 in full but does not define "good faith" for this purpose, does not address what standard of proof or process a fiduciary must satisfy to establish good faith if the decision is later challenged, and does not address a fiduciary's separate potential liability under general trust or probate fiduciary-duty law (such as the duty of impartiality between the income beneficiary and remainder beneficiaries) apart from the election decision itself, none of which was researched here.

citations.case: Cal. Probate Code § 21526 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
citations.cite: California Probate Code, fiduciary immunity for a good-faith QTIP or gift-tax marital-deduction election decision
citations.quote: A fiduciary is not liable for a good faith decision to make any election, or not to make any election, referred to in Section 2056(b)(7) or Section 2523(f) of the Internal Revenue Code.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body:
This information sheet describes California's statutory requirement, under Unemployment Insurance Code § 2613, that the Director of Employment Development maintain a program of education about State Disability Insurance rights and benefits, and that every employer give each new employee a written notice of those rights and benefits at the time of hire. It is prepared in connection with {{companyName}} and {{employeeName}}, hired effective {{startDate}}.

This document addresses only the hiring-triggered branch of § 2613's notice duty. The same statute separately requires the notice to be given again when an employee leaves work for a qualifying reason; that separation-triggered duty is not covered here.

clauses.title: The Director's Program-of-Education Duty
clauses.gap: This subsection creates an administrative duty resting on the Director of Employment Development to develop and maintain a program of education; it does not, by its own text, specify what that program must contain, how it must be kept current, or what recourse (if any) exists if the Director does not do so, and this document does not attempt to fill in those specifics. A CourtListener case-law search this session -- run both as a targeted phrase query for "Section 2613" together with "Unemployment Insurance Code," and as a broader keyword query on the subject matter -- returned no opinions construing this subsection.
clauses.body: California Unemployment Insurance Code § 2613(a) directs the Director of Employment Development to develop and maintain a program of education concerning disability insurance rights and benefits. This duty rests on the Director, not directly on any individual employer; the employer-facing notice duties described in the following clauses derive from subsections (b) and (c) of the same section.
