citations.cite: Unemp. Ins. Code § 2613(a)
citations.quote: The Director of Employment Development shall develop and maintain a program of education concerning disability insurance rights and benefits.

clauses.title: The Original At-Hire Notice Duty (1988)
clauses.gap: Subsection (b)'s notice duty was substantively broadened by the 2004 amendment addressed in a separate clause of this document; because both the 1988-dated and 2004-dated notice-content descriptions remain in the statute's current text as separate subsections, this document does not resolve whether the 1988-dated notice content in subdivision (b) still operates independently for any employee, or has in practice been fully superseded by subdivision (c)'s later, broader notice for every employee hired on or after January 1, 2004. Nothing in the statutory text of § 2613 itself specifies the notice's required delivery format (paper, electronic, a specific EDD form number, or otherwise), and no penalty provision for an employer's failure to give this particular notice appears within § 2613. A CourtListener case-law search this session returned no opinions construing this subsection.
clauses.body: Unemployment Insurance Code § 2613(b) requires the Director to provide each employer with a notice informing workers of their disability insurance rights and benefits due to sickness, injury, or pregnancy, and requires every employer to give that notice to each new employee -- a duty that, by its own terms, has applied to every employee hired on or after June 1, 1988. The same subsection separately requires the notice to be given to an employee leaving work for a qualifying reason, on or after July 1, 1989 -- a distinct, separation-triggered duty this document does not address.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 2613, subd. (b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Unemp. Ins. Code § 2613(b)
citations.quote: The director shall provide to each employer of employees subject to this part a notice informing workers of their disability insurance rights and benefits due to sickness, injury, or pregnancy.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 2613, subd. (b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Unemp. Ins. Code § 2613(b)
citations.quote: The notice shall be given by every employer to each new employee hired on or after June 1, 1988, and to each employee leaving work due to pregnancy or nonoccupational sickness or injury on or after July 1, 1989.

clauses.title: The 2004 Expansion: Family Care and Bonding Leave Content
clauses.gap: This document addresses only this subsection's hiring-triggered notice duty. The same sentence imposes a separate, separation-triggered duty -- for "each employee leaving work on or after July 1, 2004" for the listed reasons -- that this document does not cover. The statutory text does not itself name a specific EDD form (such as the DE 2515 pamphlet commonly associated with this duty) as the required notice, does not require bilingual delivery (contrast the separate time-of-hire notice for workers' compensation rights under Labor Code § 3551(b), which does expressly require English and Spanish), and does not define what happens if an individual is rehired after a prior separation for purposes of the "hired on or after" trigger. No case law construing this subsection was located in a CourtListener case-law search this session.
clauses.body: Effective January 1, 2004, Unemployment Insurance Code § 2613(c) expanded the notice's required content beyond an employee's own sickness, injury, or pregnancy to also cover the employee's need to provide care for a sick or injured family member, and the employee's need to bond with a minor child within the first year of the child's birth or placement in connection with foster care or adoption -- rights associated with California's Paid Family Leave program. The subsection also requires the notice to instruct the employee to provide notification of the reason for taking leave in a manner consistent with company policy, and requires every employer to give this expanded notice to each new employee hired on or after January 1, 2004.

citations.cite: Unemp. Ins. Code § 2613(c)
citations.quote: Commencing January 1, 2004, the director shall provide to each employer of employees subject to this part a notice informing workers of their disability insurance rights and benefits due to the employee’s own sickness, injury, or pregnancy, or the employee’s need to provide care for any sick or injured family member, or the employee’s need to bond with a minor child within the first year of the child’s birth or placement in connection with foster care or adoption.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 2613, subd. (c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Unemp. Ins. Code § 2613(c)
citations.quote: The notice shall also instruct the employee to provide notification of the reason for taking leave in a manner consistent with company policy.

citations.case: Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 2613, subd. (c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Unemp. Ins. Code § 2613(c)
citations.quote: The notice shall be given by every employer to each new employee hired on or after January 1, 2004, and to each employee leaving work on or after July 1, 2004, due to pregnancy, nonoccupational sickness or injury, or the need to provide care for any sick or injured family member, or the need to bond with a minor child within the first year of the child’s birth or placement in connection with foster care or adoption.

clauses.title: How This Notice Differs From Other Hiring- and Separation-Related Notices
clauses.body: The disability-insurance and paid-family-leave notice described in this information sheet, required by Unemployment Insurance Code § 2613, is a distinct legal requirement from other notices a new employee may separately be entitled to receive around the time of hire or separation -- including a time-of-hire notice about workers' compensation rights (required by a different statute, Labor Code § 3551), a Wage Theft Prevention Act notice about pay rate and related terms (Labor Code § 2810.5), and a notice concerning unemployment compensation benefits that a different statute requires an employer to supply when an individual becomes unemployed (Unemployment Insurance Code § 1089). Each of these operates under its own statutory text, its own trigger, and its own required content. This document addresses only the hiring-triggered disability-insurance and paid-family-leave notice duty under Unemployment Insurance Code § 2613.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
Declaration of Parties and Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This Family Code Section 2556 Omitted or Unadjudicated Community Property Information Sheet concerns {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}}, whose marital dissolution, nullity of marriage, or legal separation proceeding is pending, has concluded by judgment, or may be filed, in the California superior court for {{countyOfFiling}}. It describes what California law says about a community estate asset or liability that was not addressed, or not fully addressed, by a judgment in such a proceeding — sometimes called an "omitted asset." It states, in general terms, the court's continuing jurisdiction over such items under Family Code section 2556, the procedural mechanism the statute provides, the equal-division standard the statute applies, how published California decisions have described what counts as "omitted or not adjudicated," and the historical background of this area of law. This information sheet does not determine, calculate, or assert that any particular asset or liability connected to {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} was, or was not, adjudicated by any judgment in their case, whether any statutory ground supports an unequal division of such an item, or whether an express written agreement between them addresses the point; those are matters for the court to decide based on the specific facts and the language of the specific judgment, or for {{party1Name}} and {{party2Name}} to resolve by their own written agreement.

clauses.title: What “Community Estate” Means for Purposes of This Statute — Family Code Section 63
clauses.body: Family Code section 2556, addressed in this document's companion clauses, uses the term “community estate” to describe the assets and liabilities over which it grants the court continuing jurisdiction. Family Code section 63 defines that term for purposes of the Family Code generally: “community estate” includes both community property and quasi-community property. This means that, by this separate definitional section, section 2556's continuing jurisdiction is not limited to community property in the narrower sense; it extends to quasi-community property as well, because quasi-community property falls within the defined term “community estate” that section 2556 itself uses.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 63, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. Section 2556's own text does not use the phrase “quasi-community property” anywhere within it; the conclusion that section 2556 reaches quasi-community property rests on this separate general definition in section 63 (added by the same 1993 enactment that amended section 2556) rather than on any language internal to section 2556 itself. This document does not restate the separate definition of “quasi-community property” found in Family Code section 125, nor does it address how a party establishes, as an evidentiary matter, that a particular asset acquired outside California would have been community property had the acquiring spouse been domiciled in California — the substantive test section 125 states for quasi-community property. This clause also does not address the narrower statutory definition of “community property” itself, which appears elsewhere in the Family Code and is not restated here.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 63 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the statutory definition of “community estate”
citations.quote: “Community estate” includes both community property and quasi-community property.

clauses.title: Continuing Jurisdiction Over Community Estate Assets and Liabilities Not Previously Adjudicated — Family Code Section 2556
clauses.body: Family Code section 2556 states that, in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, for nullity of marriage, or for legal separation of the parties, the court has continuing jurisdiction to award community estate assets or community estate liabilities to the parties that have not been previously adjudicated by a judgment in the proceeding. By its own terms, this continuing jurisdiction attaches specifically to the three listed proceeding types and specifically to community estate assets or liabilities — as opposed to, for example, separate property, or matters such as child or spousal support that are governed by their own separate statutory frameworks.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2556's first sentence, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. The statute's own text does not itself define “previously adjudicated,” and California Court of Appeal decisions interpreting that phrase are addressed in this document's separate companion clause on what counts as omitted or not adjudicated — that companion clause states a judicial interpretation, not the statute's own text, and this clause does not restate it. This clause also does not address whether, or how, section 2556's continuing jurisdiction interacts with a party's separate property claims, with support orders, with a summary dissolution proceeding, or with a nonmarital relationship such as a Marvin action, all of which are addressed, if at all, by separate authorities outside this document. Section 2556 is part of Family Code Division 7 (Division of Property), Part 2 (General Provisions), sections 2550 through 2556; this clause does not restate or analyze section 2550's general equal-division rule for the community estate as a whole, which is addressed separately in this document's companion clause on the equal-division standard only insofar as it distinguishes that rule from section 2556's own good-cause standard for omitted items.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2556 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the continuing-jurisdiction grant over previously unadjudicated community estate assets and liabilities
citations.quote: In a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, for nullity of marriage, or for legal separation of the parties, the court has continuing jurisdiction to award community estate assets or community estate liabilities to the parties that have not been previously adjudicated by a judgment in the proceeding.

clauses.title: How Adjudication Is Obtained: Postjudgment Motion or Order to Show Cause in the Same Proceeding — Family Code Section 2556
clauses.body: Family Code section 2556 states that a party may file a postjudgment motion or order to show cause in the proceeding in order to obtain adjudication of any community estate asset or liability omitted or not adjudicated by the judgment. By its own terms, this provision identifies the procedural vehicle — a postjudgment motion or order to show cause filed in the same family law proceeding, rather than a separate lawsuit — available for that adjudication.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2556's second sentence, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. This citation is to the same statutory section, 2556, cited by this document's other authority clauses; they are not independent of one another. The statute's own text does not itself state a filing deadline or statute of limitations for this postjudgment motion or order to show cause, does not itself state what showing a moving party must make to establish that a particular asset or liability was in fact omitted or not adjudicated (a question this document's separate companion clause addresses only insofar as published decisions have described a general standard, not as it would apply to any specific asset), and does not address what happens procedurally if the original case file is no longer available under the applicable court records retention schedule. This clause also does not address whether a different procedural vehicle, such as a separate civil action, remains available or necessary in any particular circumstance; this document's companion clause on historical background addresses only how the law in this area has changed over time in general terms.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2556 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the postjudgment motion or order to show cause mechanism
citations.quote: A party may file a postjudgment motion or order to show cause in the proceeding in order to obtain adjudication of any community estate asset or liability omitted or not adjudicated by the judgment.

clauses.title: The Equal-Division Default and the Good-Cause Exception — Family Code Section 2556
clauses.body: Family Code section 2556 states that in these cases — that is, cases in which a party has filed a postjudgment motion or order to show cause to obtain adjudication of an omitted or unadjudicated community estate asset or liability — the court shall equally divide the omitted or unadjudicated community estate asset or liability, unless the court finds upon good cause shown that the interests of justice require an unequal division of the asset or liability. By its own terms, the statute states equal division as the default outcome and permits an unequal division only upon a good-cause finding tied to the interests of justice.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Family Code section 2556's third sentence, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed byte-identical across two fetches made with different User-Agent strings. This citation is to the same statutory section, 2556, cited by this document's other authority clauses; they are not independent of one another. The statute's own text does not itself define “good cause” or list factors relevant to “the interests of justice” for this purpose; that determination is a matter for the court based on the specific facts. This standard is textually distinct from Family Code section 2550's general rule for dividing the community estate as a whole, which permits an unequal division whenever the parties themselves agree to it in writing or by oral stipulation in open court, without requiring any court finding of good cause; section 2556, by contrast, requires an affirmative good-cause finding by the court for an unequal division of an omitted or unadjudicated item even where the statute's own text does not on its face condition that standard on the absence of a party agreement. This document does not analyze how those two distinct provisions apply together, or address whether a party agreement concerning an omitted asset would be treated under section 2556's good-cause standard, section 2550's agreement-based exception, or some other authority; that is a matter for the court.

citations.case: Cal. Fam. Code § 2556 (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: the equal-division default and the good-cause exception for an unequal division
citations.quote: In these cases, the court shall equally divide the omitted or unadjudicated community estate asset or liability, unless the court finds upon good cause shown that the interests of justice require an unequal division of the asset or liability.

clauses.title: What Counts as “Omitted or Not Adjudicated”: The Actually-Litigated-and-Divided Standard
clauses.body: California's Sixth District Court of Appeal has addressed how to determine whether a particular community estate item was, or was not, previously adjudicated for purposes of Family Code section 2556. In Thorne v. Raccina, the court explained that the mere mention of an asset in the judgment is not controlling, and that, quoting an earlier appellate decision, the crucial question is whether the benefits were actually litigated and divided in the previous proceeding. Applying that standard, the court held that a pension the original judgment expressly and unambiguously divided by a fixed formula — even where a party later asserted the formula understated her community interest — was not an omitted asset within the meaning of section 2556, distinguishing it from a separate case in which only a portion of a pension had actually been divided by the original judgment.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Thorne v. Raccina (2012) 203 Cal.App.4th 492, 501, fetched directly from CourtListener (opinion_id 5666330, a lead opinion whose id differs from the cluster id 5810875) and confirmed as an exact substring of the fetched html_with_citations after stripping HTML tags. This is a Court of Appeal decision applying section 2556, not the statute's own text; it is binding only within its own reasoning and does not itself resolve whether any particular asset was actually litigated and divided in any other case. The “crucial question” phrase quoted here is itself drawn by the Thorne court from an earlier decision, Miller v. Miller (1981) 117 Cal.App.3d 366, 371, which this document cites as it appears quoted with approval in Thorne's own opinion; this document does not independently fetch or verify Miller's original opinion text. Whether a specific asset was “actually litigated and divided” by a specific judgment is inherently a fact-specific inquiry turning on the wording of that particular judgment or marital settlement agreement, as Thorne itself illustrates by contrasting the judgment before it with the judgments in Melton and Simundza, two other cases the opinion discusses; this document does not assess that question for any specific judgment.

citations.quote: The mere mention of an asset in the judgment is not controlling.

citations.case: Thorne v. Raccina
citations.cite: 203 Cal.App.4th 492, 501, quoting Miller v. Miller (1981) 117 Cal.App.3d 366, 371
citations.quote: crucial question is whether the benefits were actually litigated and divided in the previous proceeding.

clauses.title: Historical Background: Tenancy in Common Pending Adjudication, Before Continuing Jurisdiction Existed by Statute
clauses.body: Before Family Code section 2556 was enacted, the California Supreme Court addressed the same underlying problem — a community property asset a divorce decree did not adjudicate — in Henn v. Henn. The court there described the settled principle that property which is not mentioned in the pleadings as community property is left unadjudicated by decree of divorce, and is subject to future litigation, the parties being tenants in common meanwhile. At that time, however, the court in Henn also observed that the Legislature had not provided courts of dissolution with continuing jurisdiction to modify a judgment dividing community property after it has become final, which is why the case before it proceeded as a separate civil action rather than as a motion in the original family law case.
clauses.gap: This is the actual text of Henn v. Henn (1980) 26 Cal.3d 323, fetched directly from CourtListener (a combined opinion whose opinion_id and cluster_id both equal 1356599) and confirmed as an exact substring of the fetched html_with_citations after stripping HTML tags. The first quoted passage is itself a nested quotation: Henn quotes In re Marriage of Brown (1976) 15 Cal.3d 838, 850-851, which in turn quotes In re Marriage of Elkins (1972) 28 Cal.App.3d 899, 903; this document cites the passage as it appears quoted in Henn's own opinion and does not independently fetch or verify the Brown or Elkins opinions. Henn's procedural holding — that the family court itself lacked continuing jurisdiction to modify a final property judgment, so that a separate civil action was the only available remedy — predates and has been legislatively superseded by Family Code section 2556, enacted roughly thirteen years later, which now allows the same adjudication to proceed by postjudgment motion or order to show cause within the original family law proceeding, as this document's companion clause on the procedural mechanism describes; this clause cites Henn only for its substantive tenancy-in-common principle, not for its now-superseded procedural holding. A California Court of Appeal decision, Thorne v. Raccina, has itself made this same point, describing Henn as reflecting the pre-section-2556 rule that a separate partition action was required; this document's companion clause on what counts as omitted addresses Thorne for a different point and does not restate that observation. This document does not address how, if at all, the tenancy-in-common characterization described in Henn affects rights or remedies as between the parties themselves prior to any court adjudication under section 2556.

clauses.title: Purpose of This Information Sheet
clauses.body: This information sheet describes California law on "reproductive health decisionmaking" as a protected characteristic under the California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA). It is provided to {{employeeName}} by {{companyName}}. It states facts about what the relevant statutes say and about what one California Court of Appeal decision has said about this characteristic's scope and history. It does not evaluate, and takes no position on, any specific employment decision, request, or dispute involving {{employeeName}} or any other person.

clauses.title: What "Reproductive Health Decisionmaking" Means Under FEHA
clauses.body: California Government Code § 12926(y) defines "reproductive health decisionmaking" for purposes of the FEHA. The definition is expressly non-exhaustive: it "includes, but is not limited to," a decision to use or access a particular drug, device, product, or medical service for reproductive health. The same subdivision also clarifies that listing "reproductive health decisionmaking" as its own characteristic does not mean the FEHA's separate definition of "sex" — which independently includes pregnancy and pregnancy-related medical conditions — excludes reproductive health decisionmaking; the two categories can overlap.
clauses.gap: This definition is expressly non-exhaustive ("includes, but is not limited to"), and no published California appellate decision located in this research construes where its outer boundary lies — for example, whether a decision about a medical service that is not itself contraception, fertility treatment, abortion, or a similarly reproductive-health-specific service would still qualify. This clause quotes the current text of § 12926(y), which was itself most recently amended effective January 1, 2026; this document does not track or compare any earlier version of the subdivision's wording, and does not address whether that 2026 amendment changed the definition's substance or only its surrounding subdivisions.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 12926(y) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: “Reproductive health decisionmaking” includes, but is not limited to, a decision to use or access a particular drug, device, product, or medical service for reproductive health. This subdivision and other provisions in this part relating to “reproductive health decisionmaking” shall not be construed to mean that subdivision (r) of this section and other provisions in this part related to “sex” do not include reproductive health decisionmaking.

clauses.title: The Prohibition: Reproductive Health Decisionmaking as a Listed Protected Characteristic
clauses.body: California Government Code § 12940(a) makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer to refuse to hire or employ a person, to refuse to select a person for a training program leading to employment, to bar or discharge a person from employment or from such a training program, or to discriminate against a person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment, because of that person's reproductive health decisionmaking. The same sentence lists reproductive health decisionmaking alongside race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, and veteran or military status.
clauses.gap: This clause quotes only the opening sentence of subdivision (a); it does not address FEHA's separate harassment prohibition (§ 12940(j)) or retaliation prohibition (§ 12940(h)), each of which uses different statutory language that was not independently fetched or verified for this document. It also does not address § 12940's own introductory qualifiers — a bona fide-occupational-qualification exception and an exception for conduct based on applicable federal or California security regulations, both stated in the statute's chapeau rather than in subdivision (a) itself — so this document does not resolve whether either exception could apply to any particular reproductive-health-decisionmaking-based employment action.

citations.case: Cal. Gov't Code § 12940(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Government Code
citations.quote: For an employer, because of the race, religious creed, color, national origin, ancestry, physical disability, mental disability, reproductive health decisionmaking, medical condition, genetic information, marital status, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, age, sexual orientation, or veteran or military status of any person, to refuse to hire or employ the person or to refuse to select the person for a training program leading to employment, or to bar or to discharge the person from employment or from a training program leading to employment, or to discriminate against the person in compensation or in terms, conditions, or privileges of employment.

clauses.title: Which Employers This Prohibition Reaches
clauses.body: For purposes of this prohibition, California Government Code § 12926(d) defines "employer" to include any person regularly employing five or more persons, as well as any person acting as an agent of an employer, the state or any political or civil subdivision of the state, and cities. The statute then carves out a specific exception to that definition: it does not include a religious association or corporation not organized for private profit.
clauses.gap: This document does not evaluate whether any specific religious or nonprofit entity qualifies for the statutory exception. It also does not verify whether FEHA provisions outside this general Article 1 employer definition — for instance, provisions elsewhere in § 12940 that by their own terms may apply without regard to employee count — use a different threshold; only this general employer definition was fetched and confirmed for this document. Independent-contractor status, joint-employer questions, and staffing-agency or franchise arrangements are also not addressed.

clauses.title: When and How This Protection Was Added
clauses.body: A California Court of Appeal decision states that reproductive health decisionmaking protection was added to the FEHA through Senate Bill No. 523 (2021-2022 Regular Session), effective January 1, 2023. A separate, later Court of Appeal decision — issued in a different, non-employment context — independently describes the same statutory definition as having been added by "the Contraceptive Equity Act of 2022," and identifies the specific chaptered-law citation for that enactment.
clauses.gap: The second citation below comes from a Court of Appeal opinion analyzing the Unruh Civil Rights Act's incorporation of FEHA definitions in a public-accommodations dispute, not an employment case; it is quoted here only for its description of this definition's legislative history, not for any employment-law holding, and this document does not otherwise rely on or summarize that case's substantive ruling. Neither citation below is to the enacted bill text, the Legislative Counsel's Digest, or the Secretary of State's chaptered-statute record itself — this document did not independently fetch or verify those primary sources, and instead relies on these two appellate descriptions of them, which corroborate each other on the year of enactment (2022 session) but describe the underlying act by two different names ("Senate Bill No. 523" and "the Contraceptive Equity Act of 2022").

clauses.title: What One Court Did Not Decide: Retroactivity and the Pre-Amendment Framework
clauses.body: In the same decision cited above, the employee raised the reproductive-health-decisionmaking amendment on appeal after her employment had already ended and after the trial court had already ruled against her. The Court of Appeal did not decide whether the amendment applies to conduct that occurred before its effective date; it found that the employee had forfeited any argument about retroactive application by not raising it in her opening brief. Applying the pre-amendment framework instead, the same court held that the employee — who had undergone an elective egg-retrieval and freezing procedure without an underlying medical condition related to pregnancy — did not have a protected characteristic under the FEHA as it existed before the amendment.
clauses.gap: Both quotations in this clause are to the same appellate decision as the enactment-history clause above, not to independent corroborating sources. Because the retroactivity question was resolved on forfeiture rather than on the merits, no appellate authority located in this research decides whether reproductive-health-decisionmaking protection reaches conduct that predates January 1, 2023. Separately, because the amendment did not apply to the case, the court's holding that an elective procedure without an underlying medical condition was unprotected was reached under the pre-amendment "sex"/pregnancy framework only — this document does not determine, and no case found in this research resolves, whether the same or similar facts would come out differently today under the current, amended definition of reproductive health decisionmaking.

As we have indicated, the issue of retroactivity was not addressed in her opening brief, and we thus find it forfeited.

She was undergoing an elective medical procedure but, without an underlying medical condition related to pregnancy, appellant does not have a protected characteristic under the FEHA.

clauses.title: Acknowledgment
